"Qiè" (怯) means "timid," "inferior," or "cowardly. The *Cangjie pian* states that it means "timidity, fear, and inferiority"; the *Jixun* says it means "fear"; and the *Yunquan* says it means "weakness. According to the *Shuowen jiezi*, it is written with the radical "dog" (*quán*) as 㹤; because dogs are often timid, it takes the "dog" radical. It is a compound character formed by combining a semantic and a phonetic element. It is pronounced in the departing tone (*qùshēng*).

*Samāhita* (the *hi* sound is a transliteration of the Sanskrit; here it is translated as "cessation," meaning the mind comes to rest). It is also called "concentration" (*samādhi*), which has many synonyms such as "equipoise" (*samāpatti*) and "even-induction" (*samādhāna*); this refers to the same thing.

*Tāotiè* (饕餮): The first character is pronounced *gāo* (high tone) with the radical *du* (杜); the *Zuǒzhuan* commentary states that one who is greedy for wealth is called *tāo*. It is also written as *dāo*, which is a vulgar form. The second character is pronounced *tié* (天結, high tone). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that one who is greedy for food is called *tiè*. The *Boyá* dictionary writes it as *yìng* (飻). Both characters above have the lower part as their phonetic and the upper part as their tone.

Regarding "xuánzá" (喧雜): the upper character is pronounced *xiōng* (兄) with the *yuán* (圓) rhyme; its meaning has already been fully explained in the first fascicle of the preceding scripture. Regarding the lower character: it is pronounced *cái* (才) with the *lìng* (令) rhyme; its meaning has already been fully explained in the one hundred eighty-first fascicle of the preceding scripture.

"Fen" (紛) in "fenrǎo" (紛擾) is pronounced *fú* (as in *fúwén*) and is explained in the first preface of the preceding scripture; "rǎo" (擾) is pronounced *zhǎo* (as in *zhǎo*) and is explained in the third fascicle of the preceding scripture.

*Dàn* (pronounced *tán*, with the second tone): Zheng’s commentary on the Mao version of the *Shijing* states that *dàn* means "difficulty"; the *Han Shi* says it means "fear. The *Ji Xun* glosses it as "words"; the *Cang Jie Pian* defines it as "startlement"; and the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "haste," stating it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xin*) and the phonetic "dān."

Regarding *jù* (據): following the *Mao Shī Zhuàn*, "jù" means to rely upon; according to the phonology, it means to lean against. Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒ Zhuan* states it means "peaceful security. The *Shuowén* says it means "to support," composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "qū" (*qū*, with the lower part pronounced *gù*). It is also written as *jù* (倨) or *qū* (豦). Regarding *ào* (傲): the *Kǒng Zhù* on the *Shàngshū* says it means "arrogance. The *Guǎngyá* says it means "recklessness. The *Shuowén* says it means "haughtiness," composed of the radical "mind" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "áo" (*áo*). Alternatively, it is written with the "person" radical (*rén*) as *ào* (傲). According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of "to go out" (*chū*) and "to let loose" (*fàng*); the current scriptural text uses the "earth" radical (*tǔ*) for *ào*, which is a gradual corruption and abbreviation.

Regarding the character *jī* (譏) in the phrase "at the censure" (*yú jī shàng*): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is composed of *yǎn* (偃) with the phonetic *ji* (幾). This is incorrect; the scripture version uses the radical for the hand (*shǒu*). The lower part, *jū yī* (居依), is the phonetic. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to admonish"; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "to slander," composed of the radical for speech (*yán*) with *ji* as its phonetic.

Volumes 367–368: Volumes 367 and 368 of this scripture contain no characters that require phonetic transcription. Volume 369: Regarding the character 響 (xiǎng) in Volume 369—“xiǎng” is pronounced with the two initials *gǔ* and *xiāng*. The *Kǎoshēng* (Investigation of Sounds) states that “xiǎng” refers to the resonance of sound. The commentary on the *Shàngshū* by Kǒng [Yǎng] says, “It is like an echo responding to a voice. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical for “sound” (*yīn*) and the phonetic element *xiāng*. It is sometimes written as 響 or with the radical for “speech” (*yán*) as 嚮; however, in this scripture, it is written as 嚮 using the radical for “direction” (*xiàng*), which is incorrect.

370–375: From the three hundred and seventieth fascicle to the three hundred and seventy-fifth fascicle, these six fascicles from 370 through 375 inclusive all lack phonetic glosses (*yinxun*). 376: The Three Hundred and Seventy-Sixth Fascicle. Regarding "chariot" (*chéng*) in the title: the upper character *chē* (車) has the pronunciation *chāngzhē fǎn*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, this character is a pictograph; when written horizontally, it is the archaic form of *chē*. The lower character *shèng* (乘) has the pronunciation *shízhèng fǎn*. Confucius’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states: "To *chéng* means to ride upon victory. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states: "*Chéng* means to ascend. Zheng Zhong’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "Four horses make one *chéng*. According to the *Shuowen*, *chéng* means "to cover"; it is composed of *rù* (入) and *jié* (桀). *Jié* is pronounced *jié*; it refers to the clever and shrewd. Military law refers to a *chéng*. In clerical script (*lìshū*), it is written as *chéng*, which is a modified form of the character.

*Miǎo* (marrow): The upper radical is *ruí* (pronounced with the *shuǐ* tone). The *Shuowen* states it is the fat within the bones; it is composed of the "bone" radical and the abbreviated form of "follow" (*suí*) as the phonetic. The lower part is pronounced *nángǎo*. The *Wenzi jílüè* states it is the solid substance within the head. This character has many corruptions: some versions have three "stop" (*zhǐ*) radicals, some have the "moon" (*yuè*) radical, some have the "mouth" (*kǒu*) radical, some have "suddenly" (*hū*) or "mountain" (*shān*)—none of these are correct. The correct form according to the *Shuowen* consists of the "spoon" (*bǐ*) radical and the "fontanelle" (*xìng*, pronounced *xìn*) radical. "Fontanelle" (*xìng*) refers to the head. It is composed of the "three rivers" (*kuān*) radical—which represents hair—and the "spoon" (*bǐ*) radical, which signifies being joined together. The phonetic element is *nángǎo*; this is an ancient character.

377–380: Volumes Three Hundred Seventy-seven through Three Hundred Eighty. From volume 377 down to 380, totaling four volumes, there are no characters with difficult pronunciations; thus, they are not provided with phonetic glosses. 381: Volume Three Hundred Eighty-one. Regarding the character *lián* (奩): it is pronounced *lì yán* (力鹽反). In the *Cāngjié piān* (蒼頡篇), it is a name for a type of vessel. According to the *Shuōwén jiězì* (說文解字), it refers to a mirror case (*jìng lián*). Examining the character *lián*, it is synonymous with the *xiāng lián* (perfume case) and the *qí lián* (go-board case), among others. It appears to have a flat bottom while having ridges or corners on top. The scripture uses the character *dà* (大) and *pǐn* (品); the character *lián* does not form a standard word [in this context]. When the scripture speaks of the "bottom of the *lián*" (*lián dǐ*), it takes the flatness of the bottom as a metaphor. The character *lián* consists of the radical *fāng* (匚) and the phonetic component *qiān* (僉); *qiān* also serves as the phonetic. The pronunciation of *fāng* is *fāng* (方).

"Dǎo" (所蹈): Pronounced *dào* (徒到反). Liu Zhao’s commentary on the *Guliang Zhuan* states that "dǎo" means "to tread upon. The *Guoyaya* states that "dǎo" means "to walk. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines "dǎo" as "to step upon," composed of the radical "foot" (*zú*) and the phonetic "yǎo" (舀); the pronunciation of "yǎo" is *yángxiǎo* (羊小反).

*Tán* (pronounced *tǎn* with the departing tone): The *Cāngjié piān* states that "tàn" means "to manifest. The *Guǎngyá* says "tàn" means "level. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "peaceful," composed of the radical "earth" (*tǔ*) and the phonetic "dàn. The character "dàn" consists of the "sun" (*rì*) above and "one" (*yī*) below.

The character 𨊾 (gǔ) is pronounced *máng* (with the *fǎn* [rhyme] *fǎi*). The *Kǎo Shēng* states it refers to the hub of a carriage (*chē gǔ*). The character 𨎶 is pronounced *qú*. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* says that the circumference and length of the carriage hub (*chē gǔ*) were two zhang and seven chi; this is what is called the "hub" (*gǔ*) of the present day. Its diameter was nine chi, all according to ancient standards. The hubs of carriages today are eighteen chi in circumference and six chi in diameter; this is the "carriage foot" (*chē jiǎo*). The reading for the lower part is *gōng wū fǎn*. The *Shuowén* defines it as the point where the spokes (*fú*) converge. The *Lǎozǐ* says: "Thirty spokes converge upon a single hub. It is composed of the radical 車 (carriage) and the abbreviated form of 穀 (grain) as the phonetic element.

Tūla-maya is a Sanskrit term; it refers to fine cotton from the Western Regions. The ancient translation was "dōluómián" (兜羅綿). This has already been fully explained in the three hundred and tenth fascicle of the previous sutra.

The character for *mó* (鞔) is pronounced with the initial *mo* and the final *pán*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "It is the leather covering of a grass carriage. The *Guoyaya* says it means "to patch. The character for *wǎng* (䋄) is pronounced with the initial *wǎng* and the final *fǎng*. This refers to the web-like membrane between the ten fingers of the Tathāgata. The *Yijing* says: "The Lord of Pao and Yi knotted cords to make *shuǐ* (䋄). The *Shuowen Jiezi* uses the character *shuǐ* (󲍽), which is an archaic form; it is also written simply as *gāng* (冈), a pictographic character.

"Qi-hua" (綺畫) [the first character pronounced as *qǐ* with the ancient reading *jì*; the second character is *huà*]. Fanzi’s *Jirán* states: "Qi comes from Qí-jùn; today it is produced in Wú-yuè. "Xià-huá" (下華) [the first character pronounced as *xià* with the ancient reading *mà*]. The *Erya* says: "To paint is to create forms and images. Guo Pu says: "Painting is that by which one produces forms and images. In the original lexicons, this specific character does not exist; the character "hua" (畫) is used here as a phonetic loan.

*Xiān* (纖): The rhyme is *xián*. The *Guǎngyá* states it means "minute"; the *Fānyán* states it means "small"; the *Shuōwén* states it means "fine. It is composed of the radical *xì* (糸) and the phonetic *xiān* (韯). Furthermore, regarding the character *xiān* (韯), the *Shuōwén* notes that its lower part is *fēi* (非) with the phonetic *jiàn* (箋). *Jiàn* is pronounced *jié yán*. [The character consists of] two people (*ér rén*) following [the radical]; *cóng* (從) has the pronunciation *cóng* (from *gōng jīng*). [In some versions] it is written with *tǔ* (土) and *fēi* (非), forming the character *zào* (󲑘), which is not a valid character. The lower part [of the phonetic] is *zhàng liáng* (丈良). Zheng’s commentary on the *Shī* says it means "long and distant. The *Guǎngyá* says it means "constant"; the *Shuōwén* says it means "long-lasting. It is composed of *wù* (兀)—which conveys the sense of being high and remote—and *bǐ* (匕), which has the pronunciation *huà* (化). When something lasts long, it undergoes transformation. The upper part is *máng* (𰀄) with the phonetic *wáng* (亾). The character *wáng* is written inverted; in seal script (*zhuànshū*), the archaic form is *zào* (󲗡), while in modern clerical script (*lìshū*), it is written as *cháng* (長). The common saying today is that this is the character. Since *wù* and *huà* appear at the bottom, they are all variant forms that cannot be distinguished.

*Eṇeya* is the Sanskrit term for the "antelope king" (referring to the *eṇi* antelope). This king of deer possesses a coat of various colors that is glossy, radiant, and brilliant; because his calves and knees are long, slender, and well-proportioned, he is cited as a metaphor. The character *zhuǎn* (腨) is pronounced *chuán* with the second tone (*rǎn*).

The character 傭 (yōng) is a variant of 癡 (chī). "Lóng" (龍) is a reversed reading of the sound. "Shàngxià jūn yì dà yě" (上下均也大也) means that it is even above and below, and great. It rhymes with 英 (yīng) and 庸 (yōng), meaning straight. The scriptural text contains the form 𦟛 (from 肉), which is a vulgar character. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Jūn" (均) means straight; it takes the radical 人 and the phonetic 庸."

*Kǎn* (紺): The first character is pronounced *gān* (with the level tone), and the second is pronounced *qì* (with the rising tone). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Silk dyed blue with a reddish luster. It is also written as *chuan* (絟) or *xian* (𦇝); their pronunciations are the same as above. These are all archaic characters used by [the scholars] Ma Rong and Zheng Xuan. Regarding the character *qīng* (靑) below: according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of *shēng* (生, "to grow") and *dān* (丹, "vermilion"); in modern clerical script (*lìshū*), it has become corrupted and abbreviated.

Regarding "moistening" (rùn): as in the *Shūjìng* (Book of Documents), it says, "Water flows downward and moistens; moistening downward produces salt. The pronunciation of "salt" (xián) is the same as "together" (xián). According to the *Guǎyá*, it means "moisture" (shī). The character for "downward" (xià) is pronounced with the initial *huán* and the final *guā*. The *Shuōwén* states that "smoothness" (huá) means "lubricity" (lì). The character for "scratch" (guā) is pronounced with the initial *kāi* and the final *huá*. Both are compound characters consisting of a semantic radical (*shuǐ*) and a phonetic component.

Huǎngyào (晃燿): The first character is read as huáng (上黃廣反). The *Guǎngyá* defines it as "radiance" (*huī*). The *Kǎoshēng* states it is the light of the sun; it is also written as huàn (晄), which the *Shuōwén* explains as "brightness. It is composed of the radical for "sunlight" and the phonetic element yáo (姚照反). The *Guǎngyá* defines it as "shining radiance. The *Yùnyīng* says it means "brilliance. It may also be written as yào (曜), which is likewise acceptable. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical for "fire" (作燿); the version with the radical for "light" (作耀) is a vulgar form and not the correct one.
"Bō" (upper tone) and "yì" (lower tone) for *skandha*—these two characters have both already been fully explained in the first fascicle of the preceding scripture.

*Nagrodha* (pronounced with the respective tones)—this is the name of a tree in the Sanskrit language; some call it *nyagrodha*. This tree is upright, straight, perfectly round, and lovely; it does not exist in this country. To say it is a willow is incorrect.

*Hèyì* (頷臆): The first character is pronounced *gǎn* (感) with the retroflex *fǎn* (反); the second is pronounced *xià* (下) with the *lì* (力) *fǎn* (反). Both have already been explained in the first fascicle of the preceding scripture.

*Yú kě xuě* (逾珂雪): The first character is pronounced *yǔ* (庾) with the *jù* (俱) *fǎn* (反). The *Yùnquán* (韻詮) states that it means "to surpass" (*yuèyú*, 逾越), or it may be written as *yú* (踰). The second character is pronounced *kě* (可) with the *hé* (何) *fǎn* (反). The *Yùnquán* states that it refers to white jade pendants; their color is like white snow.

*Fēng* (鋒): Pronounced *fāng kōng fǎn*. The *Kǎośēng* says it means "the tip of a blade" (*dāomò*). It is also written as *cāng*. The *Shuowén* states it refers to the edge of a weapon; it is composed of the radical *jīn* (metal) and the phonetic *fēng* (abbreviated).

*Yǒng* (擁): Pronounced *yōng qū yōng gǒng fǎn*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Yílǐ* says it means "to embrace. The *Kǎoshēng* says it means "to hold" or "to protect. Lexicons say it means "to block. The *Shuowén* states it is composed of the radical *shǒu* (hand) and the phonetic *yōng*. Its original standard form is *bǐng*, which is an archaic character (*gǔzì*).

"Yuanyue" (婉約): "Yuan" (惌) is pronounced *yuǎn* (according to the Duan [Zheng] commentary on the *Zuozhuan*, it means "elegant and ornate speech"; the *Yunquan* says it means "graceful and charming"; the *Shuowen Jiezi* says it means "docile and compliant"). It is composed of the radical "woman" (女) and the phonetic "wan" (宛); both are examples of compound characters formed from both shape and sound.

*Kalaviṅka* is a term from the Sanskrit language; it is the name of a bird in the Western regions. To be fully expressed, it should be called *kalaviṅka*; while still within its eggshell, this bird is able to produce a beautiful sound that causes people to delight in hearing it.

"Eye" (yǎn) is a phonetic loan character; this character originally did not exist. According to the *Jīng* (Essence), it refers to the eyeball. The *Cuànyùn* states that it is the black pupil of the eye. The ancients called it the *móuzi* (pupil); in common parlance it is called the *mùtóngzǐ* (eyeball) or the *mùtóngrén* (eyeball-person). The *Lùnwén* (Treatise on Literature) defines it as the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), having pure matter produced by the four great elements as its substance.

*Uṣṇīṣa* is a Sanskrit term, a designation for the mark of the Tathāgata’s crown. The *Buddhāvataṃsaka-samādhi-sāgara-sūtra* states: "On the crown of the Tathāgata’s head, the *uṣṇīṣa* is perfectly round, rising up in the center, lofty, prominent, and majestic, resembling a celestial canopy. Another translation calls it the "Invisible Crown Mark" (*anavalokitamūrdhatā*); each carries its own profound significance.

Regarding "xiá" (陿), it is pronounced with the *xián* and *jiǎ* finals; this was already explained in the three hundred and fourth fascicle of the preceding scripture as being incorrect for the character derived from "quàn" (犬).

Regarding "jīn-mài" (筋脈): the upper part is pronounced with the *jū* and *yín* finals, composed of "zhú" (竹), "ròu" (肉), and "lì" (力); the lower part is pronounced with the *má* and *bǎi* finals, composed of "xuè" (血) and "lí" (𠂢), or alternatively "ròu" (肉). The scriptural text uses "yuè" (月) and "yǒng" (永) to form "mài" (脉), which is a vulgar character. These two characters were already fully explained in the fifty-third fascicle of the preceding scripture.
"Dun" (惇): The upper radical is "shang" (上), the lower is "kun" (昆).

Jia [Yan]’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states it means "to strike" (撲) or "great" (大). According to the *Fangyan*, it means "trustworthy" (信); according to the *Erya* and the *Shuowen*, it means "thick" (厚). It is composed of the radical "heart" (心) with "chun" (純) as the phonetic. The character "chun" (純) has the sound "chun" (純) and is composed of "fu" (畗)—where "fu" (畗) has the sound "xiang" (享) and its lower part is "yang" (羊)—followed by "wen" (文) in the current script, forming "dun" (敦), which also carries the sense of "pressing" (迫).
It is not that the meaning of the scripture follows what one makes of it according to one's own mind;
"sù" (肅) is pronounced with the *yù* rhyme-group.
Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states: "Sù means reverence (*jìng*) and solemnity (*yán*)."

The *Erya* states: "Susu" means "majestic. The *Shifa* (Canon of Posthumous Titles) says: "To possess strong virtue and overcome righteousness is called Susu; to maintain the mind and resolve with determination is called Susu.

The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as "to hold affairs with careful reverence. It is composed of the radical *yue* (pronounced *nie*) and the phonetic *yan* (pronounced *yuan*). *Yue* is situated above *yan*; it signifies being "trembling and cautious," a state of solemn awe and reverent gravity.
This is a *huiyi* (pictographic-ideographic) character. The same explanation is given later in the four hundred and seventieth fascicle.

Regarding "怯" (*qie*): the *Yingyun* states it means "timid fear"; according to the *Kaosheng*, it means "weakness. Gu Yewang says it means "timidity and inferiority. The *Shuowen* writes it as 㹤 with the radical 犬 (*quan*), meaning "one who is much afraid. Because dogs are often fearful, it takes the radical 犬; it is pronounced in the departing tone (*qu*). Alternatively, it is written as 怯 with the radical 心, both forms being interchangeable. Regarding "穰" (*rang*, with the phonetic *zhuo*): Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* says it means "feeble and inferior. According to the *Kaosheng*, it means "lacking strength. The *Shuowen* defines "弱" (*ruo*) as "to bend and yield. The upper part symbolizes bending and curving; "弱" itself is "yielding. Since things that are weak must combine their strength, it uses two bows (弓). Furthermore, the three strokes (彡) represent fine, thin hair, signifying weakness.

"Choumi (稠密): Long-flowing; the *Fan Cangjie pian* says 'chou' means 'multitude'; the *Guangya* says 'dense'; the *Shuowen* says 'many,' following the radical for grain (*禾*) and the phonetic *zhou* (周), with the final rhyme being *minbi* (岷筆).

Liyi (離翳): Upper character pronounced *li* (利), lower character pronounced *yinjì* (尹計); the *Yunying* says 'yi' means 'to ruin'; the *Guangya* says 'obstruction'; the *Shuowen* says 'a flowered canopy.'"

*Bù wā* (烏爪反; *wǔ zhuǎ fǎn*): The *Yùnquán* states it refers to low-lying, damp ground. Alternatively, it is written as *wā* or *wá*. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is a pictographic character (*xiàngxíng*) formed with the radical "cave" (*xué*) and the phonetic "melon" (*guā*).

*Bù diè* (田涅反; *tián niè fǎn*): The *Yùnquán* states it means a high mound. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is a pictographic character. It is also written as *diè*, referring to the mounds of earth built by ants.

"Jièxiǎn" (scabies/eczema): The upper character is pronounced *ài* (as in *āì*). In the *Rites of Zhou*, during the summer season, there was the practice of "nurturing those with scabies. The *Jixùn* states it is a "wind-sore" (*chuāngfēng*). The *Wenzí jílüè* writes it as *jiè* (from the radical for insects). The *Shuowén* defines it as "scratching" (*sāo*), composed of the radical for illness (*zhà*) and the phonetic *jiè*; the lower character is pronounced *xiānjiǎn*. The *Jixùn* states it means "to move" (*xī*). It refers to shifting, drifting, and migrating. The *Shuowén* defines it as "a dry sore" (*qiányáng*), composed of the radical for illness and the phonetic *xiān*. The pronunciation of *sāo* is *sǎodāo*, and the pronunciation of *ài* is *yīngjiè*.

"Yǎn" (黶): Pronounced *yǎn* (as in *ī-yǎn*). The *Kǎo Shēng* says it means "a black mole. The *Shuōwén* says it is a black spot within the flesh, formed from the radical "black" (*hēi*) with the phonetic "yàn" (*yàn*). Below, "dīng-yǎn": Pronounced *yǎn*. The *Kǎo Shēng* says it means "to extinguish. Wang’s commentary on the *Chǔcí* says it means "to defile. The *Shuōwén* says it is a small black spot, formed from the radical "black" (*hēi*) with the phonetic "zhàn" (*zhàn*).

Regarding "wou-zhui" (疣贅): it is pronounced *you* (憂) with a reversed tone. The *Cangjie pian* states that it refers to the disease of warts or tumors; alternatively, it is written as "yiu" (肬) with the radical for flesh. In ancient forms, it was written as "zhu" (𤿺). The character below is pronounced *zhui-rui* (隹苪). According to the *Bowuya*, "zhui" (贅) is also a wart. A dictionary of characters states it is a disease caused by the congealing of wind. The *Shuowen jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radicals "ao" (敖) and "bei" (貝).

"Zhi" (緻) is pronounced "chi-li" (池利) according to the *Kao Sheng* (考聲); it means that silk and fabrics are dense and fine. The *Ji Xun* (集訓) explains it as the seams of a patched garment; the *Guang Ya* (廣雅) defines it as a patch. It also means "to reach. It is composed of the radical "silk thread" (糸) with the phonetic "zhi" (致).
The character for *lǚtuǒ* (輪埵) is pronounced *dàngguǒ* (當果) in the vernacular; it is also written as *duò* (垛) in the *Tōngsùwén* (通俗文), which is likewise acceptable.

The character for *é* (頟) is pronounced *gé* (格) according to the *Guǎngyá* (廣雅). It is derived from *kè* (客) and used as *é* (額); it is a vulgar form. The *Fāngyán* (方言) states that *é* and *sànɡ* (顙) are synonymous. The *Shìmíng* (釋名) says that people of Youzhou call the forehead *è* (鄂). Nowadays, those outside the Yangtze River region pronounce *é* as *yà* (訝) in the Wu dialect; these are all corruptions of regional dialects. According to the *Shuōwén* (說文), it is composed of *xié* (頁) and the abbreviated form of *gé* (格) as its phonetic component.

"Di" (褫) is pronounced with the initial *shang* (上) and the final *chi* (池) reversed; the commentary states that "di" also means to fall off. "Shu" (󲍃) has the phonetic value of *tu* (土) and *lue* (捋) reversed; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means to strip away clothes. The text of the scripture uses the character "zhi" (󲖘), which does not form a valid character.

Regarding the various apertures, [the text] says "light calls" (*qīng jiào*). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "There are seven yang apertures and two yin apertures. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* identifies them as "apertures" (*qiào kǒng*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "hollow" (*kōng*), composed of the radical "cave" (*xué*) and the phonetic element "jiào" (abbreviated) with the pronunciation *jiào*. *Note: The term "jiào" (叫) here refers to the phonetic component used in the character for "aperture" (*qiào*).*

The character 𤡜 (yàn) is pronounced with the *i* and *yán* finals. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it consists of the components "sweet" (甘), "meat" (肉), and "dog" (犬), because a dog craves meat and lacks the foot-component [of the character 厭]. In the Buddhist scriptures, it is frequently written as 猒 using the "sun and moon" (日、月) components, or as 厭 using the "rock" (厂, pronounced hǎn) component; both of these are incorrect.

*Weiyi* (逶迆): the first character is pronounced *wèi* (with the radical *wei*) and the second is pronounced *yǐ* (with the radical *yi*). Xiao Gai’s *Commentary on the Phonetics of the Hanshu* states that it describes the appearance of water flowing in curves. The *Zhengzi* (Correct Characters) of the ancient and modern schools states that *tòuyǐ* (透迆) means to travel in a slanting or winding manner. Both characters follow the radical *chuò* (辵) and take *wěi* (委) as their phonetic component.

Volumes 382–383: Volumes three hundred eighty-two and three hundred eighty-three do not contain phonetic glosses. Volume 384: Volume three hundred eighty-four. The character 析 (xī): The rhyme is *chí* (亦反, yìfǎn). The *Yùnyīng* states it means "to divide. The *Shuowén* defines it as "to split wood. It is sometimes written with 斥 (chì) as 柝; the *Shijing* uses 斤 (jīn) as 析, a character formed through both shape and sound.

"Bīpò" (逼迫): "bī" is pronounced as *fǎn* (反) and "pò" is pronounced as *èr* (爾). According to the *Erya*, "bī" also means "pressing. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states it means "approaching closely. In the *Cangjie pian*, "pò" also means "near. The *Guangya* states it means "narrow" and "urgent."

"Ren-chi" (任持) means "to sustain" or "to maintain. In the *Liji* (Book of Rites), Zheng Xuan’s commentary reads it as "ren" (任), with the phonetic "ru" (入) and the secondary tone "shen" (甚). It signifies "to employ. The *Kaosheng* (考聲) states that "ren" means "to be capable of. The *Guoyaya* (廣雅) defines it as "to employ" or "to commission. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文解字) defines it as "to protect," deriving it from the radical "person" (人) with the phonetic "ren" (壬).

Volume Three Hundred Eighty-Five. Volume Three Hundred Eighty-Five: No characters require phonetic glosses. Volume Three Hundred Eighty-Six. Regarding "Piaoyou" (俳優): The upper character is read as *bài* (敗) with the *mái* (埋) rhyme; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "jesting. It is composed of the radical "person" (人) and the phonetic element "pái" (排), with the latter being abbreviated. The lower character is read as *yì* (憶) with the *jiū* (鳩) rhyme. The *Cangjie pian* states that a "piaoyou" is a performer (*leiren*). Gu Yewang says: "That which performers do is jesting for their own amusement. According to the *Shuowen*, "pai" (俳) means "jesting" and "you" (優) means "a singer/entertainer"; both are form-and-sound characters composed of "person" (人). In the canonical text, those written with the radical "hand" (手) or the radical "walking" (彳)—such as *páihuí* (徘𢖒)—are both incorrect.

Volumes 387–391: From Volume Three Hundred and Eighty-Seven to Volume Three Hundred and Ninety-One, these five volumes in total contain no characters requiring phonetic glosses or explanations. Volume 392: Volume Three Hundred and Ninety-Two. *Vaiḍūrya* (吠瑠璃): The first character is pronounced "liú" (upper tone) and the second is pronounced "lí" (lower tone). This is the name of a precious gem of blue-violet color from India. A detailed explanation has already been provided in the second fascicle of the *Qiányì* (前音義), within the thirty-ninth scroll of the sutra.

*Phoṭika* is a name for a precious gem in Sanskrit; its correct Sanskrit pronunciation is *sphāṭika*. The ancient translation "crystal" (*shuijing*) is incorrect. Although it resembles crystal, it possesses four distinct colors—purple, white, red, and green—and is exceptionally brilliant, translucent, and the most superior among gems. The red and green varieties are the rarest, while the purple and white follow. To claim that it is made from the transformation of pure, flawless "thousand-year ice" is a false statement. It is like fine lustrous sand, clear and without blemish.

"Luo" (蠃) is pronounced with the "lu" (盧) and "he" (和) finals; according to the *Erya*, it is a "sea mollusk. Guo Pu states that it belongs to the class of snails (*guawu*). It is large and white; the character used in the scripture is "luo" (螺), which is a vernacular form. This has already been explained in detail in the one hundred and eighty-first fascicle of the preceding scripture.

"Yī" (醫) refers to a physician who treats illness; it is composed of the radical "jiǔ" (酉) with the phonetic "yī" (殹). It is pronounced at-yì (於計反). In some versions of the scripture, it is written as "yī" (毉) with the character "wū" (巫), which is a vulgar form. This was already fully explained in the second section of the preceding *Pinyin Yì* (前音義).

The character 㸦 (pronounced hú gù) is defined in the *Zìshū* as "a net. The *Shuowén* writes it with the radical 竹 (bamboo) as 󲘙, meaning "that which can be used to gather ropes. In clerical script (*lìshū*), the bamboo radical was omitted to form 󲒠. The version appearing in the canonical text as 󲒠 is an erroneous vulgar form; it is incorrect to conflate it with the character 󲒠.

*Kui* (匱): The character is read as *qí* (逵) in the opposite sense; in dictionaries, it means "exhaustion" (*qióng*) or "deprivation. According to the *Shuowen*, the character *kui* is composed of the radical *fang* (匚, pronounced *fāng*) and the phonetic *guì*.

*Fèn* (憤): The upper part is read as *fēnwěn* (紛吻). It refers to the sound of indignation; it denotes the swelling of the spirit and the arousal of the vital breath. Zheng Xuan says it is when the energy of anger is full and substantial. The *Cangjie pian* calls it *fènmǎn* (憤懣); according to the *Shuowen*, it means "resentment. It is a compound character formed by shape and sound. *Mǎn* (懣) is pronounced *mùběn* (沒本).

"Xún" (尋) is pronounced with an initial *xiáng* (祥) and a final *yín* (淫). The *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲) states it means "to investigate" (*xúndù*) or "to pursue" (*zhú*). The *Shuōwén* writes it as 尋, meaning "to trace out" (*xúnyì*) or "principle" (*lǐ*). It is composed of 口 (mouth), 彡 (three strokes, *shān*), and 工 (work, *gōng*). The "mouth" represents disorder; above is 又 (hand) and below is 寸 (inch, representing measure). In modern clerical script (*lìshū*), the 彡 is omitted. The character 尋 is a semantic compound (*huìyì zì*). In ancient script, it was written as 𡬰, derived from 肘 (elbow).

"Pān" (攀): In the modern standard orthography, it means "to pull" or "to draw. In ancient script, it was written with the radical for "hand" (手) and the phonetic "fǎn" (反), forming the character 攀. "Róu" (柔): The upper part is read as "ér" (而) and "zhōu" (周);

the *Shuowen* states that when wood bends and straightens, it is called "róu," taking the radical "mu" (木) and the phonetic "máo" (矛). The lower part is read as "yuǎn" (兖); the *Shuowen* states that "ruǎn" (耎) means weak or pliant, taking the radical "dà" (大) and the phonetic "yǎn" (兖). The version in the sutra uses "ruǎn" (軟), which is incorrect.

393. Fascicle Three Hundred and Ninety-Three. [No explanatory gloss available. 394. Fascicle Three Hundred and Ninety-Four. *Dāsa* (the second character is pronounced *nu* with the *ya* tone; it is a Sanskrit term) refers to a class of low-born people, base and wicked individuals, who are of the same category as the *mleccha* mentioned in the following text.

*Mleccha* (the upper sound is pronounced *mian* with the *bie* tone; ancient translations sometimes rendered it as *Mili-che*, both of which are corruptions). The correct Sanskrit pronunciation is *Vṛṣala*, which means "one of a defiled and turbid lineage. They delight in performing evil deeds, belong to a base and lowly class, are from the remote frontiers, do not believe in the True Dharma, and are filthy people.
The term "wings" (*chì*) refers to the two feathers of a bird that lacks wings; some texts write it as *zhǎn* or *yí*, both of which are archaic characters. Volumes 395–397:

Volumes three hundred and ninety-five, three hundred and ninety-six, and three hundred and ninety-seven—these three volumes contain no phonetic glosses or explanations. Volume 398: Regarding the character for "to wail" (*tí*) in Volume 398, the *Shēngjíxùn* (Collection of Sounds and Explanations) states that crying without regular intervals is called "wailing. The *Shuōwén* says: "Wailing (*tí*) means to cry out; it is composed of the radical 'mouth' with 'xī' as the phonetic component. The sound of *xī* is the same as above. The *Shuōwén* entry for the character *xī* states: "It is composed of the radical 'tiger' with 'yàn' as the phonetic component. The sound of *yàn* is *yè*. In the scripture, it is written as *tí*, meaning "sorrowful."
*Sūn* (欻): Huī Lǜ’s *Fǎjì Xùnwén* states that it means "sudden" (*hù*). The *Shuowén Jiězì* states it means "to blow up. It is a compound character based on associative meaning (*huìyì*).

*Píjuàn* (疲倦): The upper character *pí* has the phonetic *piǎo* (皮賈). The commentary to the *Guōyǔ* states it means "exhaustion" (*píláo*). According to the *Guǎngyá*, *pí* also means "weariness" (*juàn*) and "extreme" (*jí*). The lower character *juàn* has the phonetic *yuàn* (逵願). According to the *Guǎngyá*, *juàn* means "extreme weariness. Kǒng’s commentary to the *Shàngshū* states it means "lassitude" (*juànxiè*). The *Yùpiān* states it means "to stop" (*juànzhǐ*). It may also follow the radical for the mind (*xīn*). It is written as *juàn*; alternatively, following the radical for the hand (*lì*), it is written as *quàn*.

*Zàn* (upper radical *zàng*, *dàn*; dialectal meaning "to praise") refers to praising and extolling. Guo Pu states: "To sing praises of one's virtue. The *Shiming* says: "The purpose of *zàn* is to explain the principles of things. *Lì* (lower radical *lì*, *zhì*) means "to encourage" according to the *Guiyuan Zhucóng*. In the *Zuozhuan*, it means "to exhort. It is a word formed by the combination of semantic and phonetic components.

*Zhì* (植) is pronounced *chéng* with the radical *fǎn* (反). The commentary on the *Shūjīng* by Kǒng [Yǔ] states: "Zhì means 'to grow' (*shēng*). Dù [Yǔ]'s commentary on the *Zuǒchuán* states: "Zhì means 'to grow long' (*zhǎng*). It may also be written with the radical *dài* (歹) as *zhí* (殖). *Chuī* (槌) is pronounced *zhuì* with the radical *zhuī* (追);

it is a vulgar character. The correct form is *chuí* (椎), with the radical *mù* (木). The character *xù* (勗) is pronounced *gōng* (恭). According to the *Zìshū*, one who is a *chuī* (槌) is someone who, harboring grief and resentment in their heart, destroys their own body.

*Xiàhuì* (黠慧): The upper character is read as *jiàn* (閑) with the *jiá* (戛) rhyme; according to the *Fāngyán* (方言), in the region east of Guān (the Guān Pass)—specifically between Zhào and Wèi—the term for wisdom (*huì*) is called *xià*. The lower character is pronounced *huì* (惠). Jiǎ Duī interpreted it as "to examine" (*chá*); Guō Pǔ interpreted it as "refined intention" (*yì jīng*). This was already explained in the third fascicle of the *Qiánjīng Yìnyì* (前經音義), specifically in fascicle three hundred and three.

"Yuan" (垣) [is pronounced with the departing tone of] *yuan* (元). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* says: "The *yuan* is also a *qiang* (wall). [In the character below,] "jiang" (匠) [is pronounced with the departing tone of] *yang* (羊). The *Shenglei* says: "The *qiang* is also the *yuan*. This is as stated in the *Shangshu*: "None dare to overstep the *yuan* or the *qiang*. According to the *Shuowen*, "yuan" means a dilapidated wall; it is composed of the radical "se" (嗇) and the phonetic "zhuang" (爿). The character "se" (嗇) is composed of "lai" (來) and "lin" (㐭); in the classics, it is sometimes written as "qiang" (墻), "qiang" (廧), or "qiang" (牆)—all of which are vulgar variants.

The term *lánshǔn* (欄楯) refers to a railing or balustrade; the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as such. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states: "That which runs lengthwise is called a *lán*, and that which runs crosswise is called a *shǔn*; the small bars between the *shǔn* are called *língzǐ*."

*Bǎo qiàn* (寶塹): "Qiàn" is pronounced as *yàn* (艷) in the reversed reading. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "qiàn" refers to a moat; it is composed of the radical "earth" (土) with the phonetic "zhǎn" (斬). The *Kaosheng* states it is a long pit, while the *Yunying* defines it as a small pit. The *Yupian* states that the moats surrounding a city wall are called *qiàn*, though it is also written as *jiàn* (漸).

"Jièxiàng" (街巷): "Jiè" (街) refers to the great thoroughfares within a capital city; "xiàng" (巷), according to the *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry), refers to the paths between residential wards. In the *Yùnyīng* (韻英), it is defined as a small street. It is also written as "xiàng" (衖), both being archaic characters; nowadays, it is simplified to "xiàng" (巷).

"Shì-chán" (市廛): *cháng-lián* (長連) [is the reading]. Zheng Zhong’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "Chán means dwelling. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "Chán refers to market stalls and shop-houses. The *Yupian* states: "Within a city, a half-mu of vacant land is called chán. The text reads "lǐ" (厘), which is a vulgar character for "lüè" (略).

*Jìng* (pronounced *kě dēng fǎn*) means "to pervade" (*yīng*) and "to penetrate" (*tōng*). Examining its phonetic component, it signifies "reaching far beyond. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states it means "universal" (*biàn*). According to the *Fāng Yán*, it means "to finish" (*jìng*). It is also written as *jiǎng* (古字).
"Bǎofǎng" (寶舫): "Fǎng" is pronounced with the *fù* (福) and *wàng* (望) finals; according to the *Erya*, "fǎng" refers to a boat. Guo Pu states that two boats joined together are called a "fǎng.

"Quèdì" (卻敵): "Dì" is pronounced with the *tí* (提) final. The *Kaosheng* says "dì" means "to oppose. According to this, "dì" also means "match" or "rival. "Quèdì" refers to a place where hidden troops on a city wall defend against the enemy.

Regarding the term *chì* (雉) in *chìdié* (雉堞): the *Cílǚ* (池履) states that the character *chì* means "to array" (*chén*). The *Gōngyáng Zhuan* says: "Five *bǎn* (boards) make one *dǔ*; five *dǔ* make one *chì*; one hundred *chì* make a city wall. Hé Xiū comments: "This is twenty thousand *zhī* (feet). Examining the phonology, a city wall three *zhàng* long and one *zhàng* high is called a *chì*. According to the *Lǐjì*, the city walls of a Son of Heaven are one thousand *chì*, likely because he receives one thousand cities of one hundred *chì* each. Dukes, Marquises, Earls, Viscounts, and Barons have city walls of one hundred, seventy, fifty, and fifty *chì* respectively. However, the city walls of all feudal lords have their southern faces recessed; this is to allow for the passage of those passing through. They merely dwell there and do not maintain a firm defense. [The character *tuó* (堞) is pronounced with the initial *dú* (徒) and the final *jiá* (頰). Dù Yǔ’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states: "The *dié* are the city walls; they are walls installed atop [the battlements]. The *Shuowén* defines it as a "female enclosure wall" (*nǚyuán*), composed of the radical *tǔ* (earth) and the phonetic element *yè* (葉) abbreviated.

"Ying" (pronounced *ying* with the second tone, or *yīng* with the first tone; the rhyme dictionary *Yùnquán* states it means "to grind pearls and jade"; the rhyme dictionary *Yùnyīng* states "to polish a mirror so that it is bright"; it is synonymous with "mò" [to grind] and "yíng" [to polish], though sometimes written as "yíng").

It is joined together (zhuì). Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that "zhuì" means to connect; Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states it means to join; the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as to bind and attach. It is also written as zhuì (畷); both are ancient characters.

Regarding "precious bells" (*bǎoduó*): Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that a *duó* is a large bell; Kong’s commentary on the *Lunyu* states that a wooden *duó* has a bronze exterior and a wooden tongue, used to proclaim civil instruction. As for the "precious bells" mentioned in the sutra, they proclaim the sound of the Dharma, as was already explained in the first fascicle of the preceding scripture.

"Cold" (lěng): the first character is pronounced with the *lǔ* and *gěng* rhymes (as in *lǔ*). According to the *Guǎngcāng*, it means "chilly"; according to the *Zìshū*, it means "slight cold. The *Shuōwén* states that it is composed of the radical *bīng* (ice) and the phonetic *líng*. "Warm" (nuǎn): the second character is pronounced with the *nú* and *guǎn* rhymes. The *Qúnshū Zìyào* states that "nuǎn" means "warmth. It is composed of the radical *huǒ* (fire) and the phonetic *ruǎn*. Variants such as *nuǎn* and *nuàn* are all vulgar usages.

The character *fàn* (上) is pronounced with the *fang* and *fan* rhymes; in character dictionaries, it means "to float. The version in the scripture uses *fàn* (汎), which is a vulgar form meaning "universal," and this does not accord with the meaning of the scripture. The lower character is pronounced with the *yang* and *liang* rhymes; it is sometimes written as *yǎng* (瀁), but these all have distinct meanings. The correct orthography should be combined as *yáng* (颺). As for *fànyàng* (汎漾), it carries the sense of floating and drifting freely; *yàng* (漾) refers to ripples on water. Although the meanings seem similar, they deviate from the original intent of the scripture; it should therefore be corrected to *yáng* (颺).

Regarding the four types of lotuses—*utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka*—the explanations for the first three have already been fully provided within the previous three hundred and eighteen fascicles.

"Xian-yu" (鮮郁): The first character is pronounced with the "xian" (延) rhyme. According to the *Guangya*, it means "exquisite"; according to the *Shenglei*, it means "new. Examining the term, "xian" signifies brightness. The second character, "yu" (於), has the "liu" (六) rhyme. Examining "xian-yu," it refers to the exquisite brilliance of wonderful flowers and the intense, pervasive abundance of their fragrant scent. As the *Analects* says: "How magnificent is its culture! (郁郁乎文哉).

Zhou Huan’s commentary on the *Guiliang Zhuan* states: "Within the *huán*" (the realm). Liu Zhao says: "*Huán* refers to the boundaries. The *Guiyuan Zhucóng* states: "The *qí* (boundary) refers to the thousand-li domain of the Son of Heaven."

Regarding "length and breadth" (*zhòngguǎng*): the *Fanzìshū* (Dictionary of Inverted Characters) states that vertical is length and horizontal is breadth; it further states that south-north is length and east-west is breadth—this is correct.

The meaning of *krośa* is translated as "the distance reached by the roar of a great bull. According to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, when measured by the standard of *hasta* (cubit), *dhanus* (bow), and *krośa*, one *krośa* equals two *li*; this is based on level ground. However, in elevated or remote locations, it can be heard within five *li*.

*Yìngbì* (映蔽): The first character, *yìng*, is pronounced *yú jìng* (於敬反); the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) glosses it as "radiance" (*huī*) or "concealment" (*yǐn*). The *Yùnyīng* (韻英) glosses it as "shining alongside. It may also be written as *yìng* (映), and the archaic form is likewise acceptable. The second character, *bì*, is pronounced *bēi mèi* (卑袂反); the *Yùnyīng* glosses it as "to cover," while the *Kǎoshēng* glosses it as "obscuration" (*bì zhàng*). Both characters were explained together in the first fascicle of the preceding scripture.

The *Peacock* (孔雀) [is pronounced as] *Yào* (藥). The *Chunqiu Yuanming Bao* (春秋元命包) states that "Fire-Li (離) becomes the peacock," and further says that the kingdom of Jibin has many peacocks; it is not necessarily because they mate, but rather that their sounds and shadows meet, or perhaps upon hearing the sound of thunder, they are moved to conceive and become pregnant.

The character for "parrot" (鸚鵡) has the phonetic component *wū* (烏) with the initial sound *gēng* (耕) and the final rhyme *wǔ* (武); it is sometimes written as 䳇, both forms being identical. The *Shanhai jing* (Classic of Mountains and Seas) states: "On Mount Huang there is a bird with green feathers and a red beak; it has a human tongue and can speak the language of humans, and is called the parrot (*yīngwǔ*). The *Qu lǐ* (Book of Rites) says: "The parrot can speak, yet it does not depart from the flight of birds. This refers to that very creature.

*Fú* (鳧): "Shū" (舒) and "fú" (鳬) are homophonous; *yù* (鶩) has the sound *mù* (木). Guo Pu’s commentary states it is the duck (*ā*). Examining the phonology, it is the smaller wild duck. In character dictionaries, it is composed of the radical "bird" (鳥) and the phonetic "ér" (儿), where "jǐ" (几) has the sound *shū* (殊); "jǐ" refers to the short wings of a bird that flutter as it flies. This is a character formed with the upper part as the semantic indicator and the lower part as the phonetic. *Xī* (鷖): "Xiē" (𤯞) has the sound *xī* (兮). Examining the phonology, it is said to be a type of phoenix. It is a black-colored water bird. The *Mao Shi* states, "The *fú* and *yī* are types of phoenixes. In the classics and commentaries, it is said that *yī* belongs to the category of ducks. The *Shuowen Jiezi* agrees; it is composed of the radical "bird" (鳥) and the phonetic "yī" (殹). This is a character formed with the lower part as the semantic indicator and the upper part as the phonetic.
"The wild goose (hóng) ascends; the Duke of Hú returns. Regarding the rhyme:
*yīng* (英) refers to a water bird.

Examining the phonology, *hóng* (鴻) means "succession" (*dài*). Guo Pu said, "The wild goose knows the cycles of the ages. It is also written as *hán* (𨾊) or *huí* (䲨), both of which are archaic characters.

The character 下 (xià) is used for "to admonish" (jiàn) and "to rebel" (fǎn). It is also written as 鴈 (yàn), which is the same as in the *Mao Shi Zhuan* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Book of Odes), which states:
"The large ones are called hóng (wild geese); the small ones are called yàn (wild geese)."
According to the *Hongyan* (Wild Geese),
these are birds that follow the sun.
The *Monthly Ordinances* (*Yueling*) of the *Book of Rites* states:
In the month of the last autumn, the wild geese arrive as guests.
These geese travel south with their young at the beginning of autumn to avoid the frost and snow,
and travel north again at the beginning of spring to avoid the scorching heat.
The *Shuowen* states that "ge" (wild goose) belongs to the class of swans.
It is also called "jia. According to the *Fangyan*, those east of the Guanzhong region call the wild goose "jia," while those outside the region of Nan Chu call it "cang-jia."
Nowadays, the people of Jiangdong call the wild goose *jā* (鵝).
It is sometimes written as *gē*, which is an archaic character;
it is also written as *jià*. This is as stated in the "Xiazi Xu" (Sublime Wandering) chapter of the *Fengsu Shenyan*: "The white cranes are joined by the *jā-é*."

The *huángjū* (pronounced with the second tone on *jū*, or alternatively written as *jū*) is the same bird as the *jūjiū*. The *Mao Shi* states: "Guan guan, the *jūjiū*. It is also called the *wángjū*. The *Erya* states: "The *jūjiū* is the *wángjū*. In the region east of the Pass, it is called the *è*. It frequents sandbars and islands.

*Cāngqīng* (鶬鶊): the first character is pronounced *cāng* (上音倉) and the second is pronounced *gēng* (下音庚). The *Erya* states: "The *cāngméi* (倉糜) is the *guākū* (鴰鴰). *Guākū*: the second character is pronounced *gǔhuó* (古活反). Guo Pu says: "Today this bird is called *cāngguākū* (鶬鴰). It is also called *cāngqīng*. Zhang Heng’s *Gui Tian Fu* (賦歸田) says: "The *wángjū* (王鴡) beats its wings and the *cāngqīng* laments; they join their necks. *Jiǎojū* (鴶鳩): the second character is pronounced *húlàng* (胡浪反); it is the same as *guānguān* (關關) and *jiāojiāo* (鵁鶄).
"Baihe" (白鶴) is a corruption;
the scriptural text should read "baigu" (白鵠).
"Gu" (鵠) is pronounced with the phonetic *hú* and the radical *mù*.
It is greenish-yellow in color with a short beak and is found everywhere.
The *Shuowen Jiezi* identifies it as a *honggu* (crane); the *Yupian* states that the *huanggu* (yellow crane) is shaped like a *he* (crane).
Since its color is greenish-yellow, we know it is not actually a *he*.
The crane is white in color with a long beak;
those that reach a full thousand years of age have vermilion-colored crests on their heads. According to written records, the crane resembles a *haku* (gull) but has a long bill;
it is a bird of the immortals (*shinsen*).
To see them is to behold an auspicious omen.
The *Baopuzi* states: "The crane cries out from the Nine Mounds, its voice heard by Heaven.
The *Huainanzi* states: "The rooster knows the coming dawn; the crane knows the midnight hour. This is what is meant.
The *Shuowen* explains that [the character for] "hawk" (隺) is composed of "bird" (鳥) and "he" (隺), with the phonetic component pronounced as *he gè fǎn*.
The *Shuowen* further explains that the character "he" (隺) itself is composed of "enclosure" (冂).
[The character] guǐ (癸) is pronounced yíng (營).
It is composed of the radical zhuī (隹), which refers to a bird.
"A bird flies high" refers to the desire to emerge from the opening of a cave. Regarding the "spring *ying*": it is pronounced *gēng* (耕) with a reversed radical.

The *Mao Shi* says, "The *sānghù* (桑鳸) flutters about; its wings are *ying*. The commentary states that the *ying* is a variegated bird. Examining the phonology, "the *ying* bird has a spotted pattern on its feathers. The text’s reading as *mó* (鷪) is an error. The *Beicang* states that the *qī* (鶈) is the *mó*; *qī* is pronounced *qī* (妻) and is a bird of the Eastern Yi tribes. The *Guangya* states that the *mó* belongs to the class of strange birds and is not the spring *ying*.

The character for *tū* (鶖) has the upper radical *qiū* (秋) and the lower radical *lù* (路); it is also written as *jù* (𪀖) or *zhì* (𪇸), all of which are archaic forms. Gu Yewang stated that it is a large bird whose plumage is brilliant white and can be used to make fine wool (*cuì*). The *Mao Shī* says, "There is a *tū-tū* on the bridge," and its commentary identifies it as the bald cormorant (*tū-tū*). It also says, "The *zhèn-lù* fly about. The *Erya* calls the *lù* the *chōng-chú*. Guo Pu stated that this is the white heron; it has long, bristly feathers on its head and back. People in Jiangdong today take these feathers to make eye-extensions, calling them *bái-lù-xiāng*; *xiāng* is pronounced *sū-wēi*. Thus, the bald cormorant and the white heron are each distinct birds.

The character for *yuān* (mandarin duck) is pronounced with the initial *y* and the final *-uán* (as in *yuán*), while the character for *yāng* is pronounced with the initial *y* and the final *-jiāng* (as in *jiāng*). The *Mao Shī* says, "The mandarin ducks fly," and its commentary states, "The mandarin duck is a bird that forms pairs; it means that when they rest they form a pair, and when they fly they fly as a pair."

*Jiāojīng* (鵁鶄): The first character is pronounced *jiāo* (upper tone) and the second is pronounced *jīng*. The *Shān-hǎi jīng* states that on Mount Mánlián there is a bird named *jiāojīng*, which resembles a duck and flies in flocks.

*Fěisuì* (翡翠): The first character is pronounced *fēi* (with the *wèi* rhyme). The *Nánzhōu zhì* says: "The *fěi* is larger than a swallow and smaller than a crow, being red in color; the people of the island catch it for food and do not know to value its plumage. Regarding the phonology: the male with red plumage is called *fěi*; the *Shuōwén* defines it as a red-plumaged sparrow, formed from the radical *yǔ* (feather) and the phonetic *fēi*. The second character is pronounced *suì* (with the *shuì* rhyme). The *Nánzhōu jì* says: "The *cuì* serves as the primary wing feathers (*liùhè*); its feathers are over an inch long and are greenish-blue in color, originating from the Yùlín Mountains. Regarding the phonology: the female with dark-green plumage is called *cuì*; the *Shuōwén* defines it as a sparrow, formed from the radical *yǔ* and the phonetic *zú*.

Regarding Jingwei, the *Shanhai jing* states: "The daughter of Yan Di was named Nüwa (the *Fangyan* glosses *wa* as 'a beautiful woman'). Nüwa was playing in the Eastern Sea when she drowned and did not return; she transformed into a bird called Jingwei. She takes wood and stones from the Western Mountain to fill the Eastern Sea, seeking to avenge her drowning. Another account says that when she cries out, she calls herself "Jingwei."

Regarding the character for *kūn* (鵾) with the upper radical *kun* (昆): Gu Yewang states that the *kūn* resembles a crane (*hè*) but is larger; in the "large-character" script it is sometimes written as *kūn* (鶤), which is the same as what is said in the *Chuci*: "The *kūn* and the *jī* (*cháo-jiǎo*) cry out in sorrowful song. The lower radical is sometimes written as *jī* (雞), which is also acceptable.

The character for *zhū* (𪈺) is pronounced as *zhī* (之) in the first instance and *nüè* (虐) in the second; the *Shanhaijing* (Classic of Mountains and Seas) states that in the midst of the Great Wilderness there is a bird with a yellow head, red feet, and six heads, named *zhūyù*. The *Erya* calls it the *shānwū* (mountain crow); Guo Pu says it resembles a crow but is small, with a red beak and six teats, and originates from the west. Guo Pu further states that the *zhūyù* resembles a duck but is large, with long *yù* (tail feathers), red eyes, and a beak that is entirely dark purple (*gàn*).

The *yuánjū* (pronounced yuán for the first syllable and jū for the second) is a sea bird mentioned in the *Guoyu*. During the reign of Emperor Yuan of the Han dynasty, there was a large bird resembling a horse colt in Langya; people of the time called it a *yuánjū*. The *Erya* states, "The *yuánjū* is the *záxián*," and the *Zhuangzi* records that the sea bird *yuánjū* alighted in the suburbs of Lu.
Regarding the term "kūn-fèng" (鵾鳳):
the *Mao Shi Yishu* (Commentary on the Meaning of the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry) states that the male is called fèng (鳳) and the female is called huáng (凰).
It does not perch on anything but the *wútóng* tree;
it eats nothing but the seeds of bamboo.
The *Shānhǎi jīng* says:
On Mount Danxue there is a bird shaped like a crane, possessing five colors and variegated markings; it is named the Fenghuang.
The *Guangya* states:
The phoenix has the head of a rooster, the jaw of a swallow, the neck of a snake, the body of a wild goose, and the tail of a fish; its five parts have markings.
The marking on its head says "Virtue" (德);
the marking on its wings says "Obedience" (順).
The markings on its back are called "Righteousness" (Yì);
the markings on its belly are called "Faith" (Xìn).
The markings on its breast are called "Heroic," its male call is "Jiéjié," and its female call is "Zúzú."
Crowing at dusk is naturally associated with the moon;
crowing at dawn is called "Illuminating";
crowing during the day is called "Sustaining Longevity."
Its call when rising is called "Ascending soars";
its call when settling is called "Returning prosperity.
When it is seen, the world is at peace.
The *Shuowen* states that it is a divine bird originating from the Land of the Eastern Gentlemen, derived from the radical "bird" (鳥) and the phonetic "fan" (凡).

Its name is Miaochi (妙翅)—the character "shi" (尸) pronounced as *zhì*—which is the same as the Golden-Winged Bird (*garuḍa*). It is also called *kāluola* or *jielucha*, both of which are corruptions of the Sanskrit; the correct Sanskrit pronunciation is *nirṇaya*. The sutras explain that "Miaochi" is a name based on its physical appearance and is not a literal translation of its meaning.

The *túji* (鵜鶘): the first character is pronounced *tú* (with the fanqie *tú-jī*) and the second is pronounced *hú* (or sometimes written as *tì* or *hú*). The *Erya* states: "Now the *tìhú* is fond of flying in flocks into the water to eat fish; therefore it is called the 'Wu-ze' (Muddy Marsh) bird. In common parlance, it is also called the "Tao-he" (River-Dredging) bird. The *Maoshi* says, "The *yí* is upon the weir," and the *Guliang Zhuan* says, "It is the Wu-ze bird."

*Kalaviṅka* is a name for a bird in the Sanskrit language; it is also called *kalaviṅga*, which translates as "exquisite voice. It emerges from within the shell of an egg in the Great Snowy Mountains and is immediately able to sing; its tone is harmonious and elegant, a sound that those who hear it delight to listen to.

The jīvañjīvaka bird has a Brahma-like voice; "jīvañjīvaka" is translated here as "life-giver. Based on this, its name is established according to its sound, for when it calls, it naturally utters "jīva, jīva."
*Fayong* (法涌) [the character *yǒng* is pronounced with the second tone in the *Shuowen Jiezi*, meaning "knee" or alternatively written as *yǒng* with the same meaning].
*Kajidubao* (羯鷄都寶) is a Sanskrit name for a jewel; it is an alternate name for crystal. This jewel is white in color and small, about the size of a goose egg.
*Deng* (pronounced with the *deng* and *deng* [with the *deng* reversed] tones): According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to tread. It refers to treading upon steps or a path. *Pū qǐpà*:

*Pū* (pronounced with the *pǔ* and *hú* tones): According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to display" or "to spread. The *Yùnquán* states it means "to set out bedding. Regarding the phonetics, *biàn* (all-pervasive). *Qǐ* (pronounced with the *qū* and *yǐ* tones): This is woven with two-colored silk threads into patterns and flowers; it originates from the Wu and Yue regions and is inferior to *jǐn* (brocade). *Pà* (pronounced with the *pǔ* and *bà* tones): According to the *Kǎoshēng*, *pà* is a large cloth (*fù*). Alternatively, it is written as *fù* with the radical for "clothing" (*yī*).
*Pāṭala* (pronounced *tu jié fǎn*) is the name of a plant from the Western Regions; its flower clusters can be processed into cloth. *Cīnapaṭṭa* (pronounced *zhēn rěn fǎn*) refers to a pillow.

According to the customs of the land of India, wooden or stone pillows are not used; instead, they are made with red leather or red-colored cloth. A bag is fashioned to hold *tūlā* cotton, wool, or similar materials to serve as a pillow. These may be used as head-pillows or leaning pillows; those that are vermilion, crimson, or red in color are what is employed.

The character *wéi* (幃) is pronounced as *wēi* (威). Lexicons state that it belongs to the category of curtains and canopies; that which is at the side of a canopy is called a *wéi*, though it may also be written with the radical for cloth (*jīn*).

According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it takes the radical for cloth and has *wéi* (韋) as its phonetic component. The characters *yuǎn* (綩) and *yán* (綖) are pronounced as *yuānyuǎn* (鴛遠) and *yúzhān* (餘㫋) respectively. When the classics speak of *yuǎnyán*, they refer to such things as exquisite and wonderful brocades, embroidered mats, dance platforms, and floor coverings.

*Qimàn* (綺幔): The first character is pronounced *qū* (upper radical *qù*, lower radical *móu*) and the second is pronounced *màn*. It refers to a class of objects such as curtains and canopies. Its correct form follows the "cloth" radical (*jīn*) with the "hand" radical (*yòu*) below; the form following the "mind" radical (*xīn*) in the scriptures is written as *màn*. The common vulgar form is incorrect.

Regarding "zhōng" (中) in *zhòngdú* (中毒): it is pronounced as *zhāng* (張) according to the *Kaoshēng* (考聲); it means "to hit the mark" (*zhōngdāng*) and "to attach" (*zhù*). Regarding "fèn" (奮) in *fènxùn* (奮迅):

it is pronounced as *fǔwèn* (府問) according to Zǐng’s commentary on the *Lìjì* (禮記), where he says it means "to move vigorously" (*fèndòng*); the *Yùnyīng* (韻英) says it means "to shake one's wings" (*zhèn yǔ*); the *Guǎngyá* (廣雅) says it means "to shake" (*zhèn*). Regarding "xià" (下) in *xún* (詢): it is pronounced as *xùn* (詢) with the *jùn* (俊) rhyme; this has already been fully explained in the second volume of the *Qiánjīng Yìnyì* (前經音義), section thirty-six.

The character for *bǐn* (所稟) is pronounced *pǐn* (錦反); according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical *lǐn* (㐭) with *huó* (禾) as its phonetic. Its occurrence in the sutra as *bǐn* (稟) is an error.
The character for *cè* (取) is pronounced *liàng* (量) and *jiāng* (強反), with both the level (*ping*) and departing (*qù*) tones being interchangeable.

"Chōng-chàng" (惆悵): The upper character *chōng* is pronounced with the *fǎn* rhyme of *zhōu*, and the lower character *chàng* is pronounced with the *fǎn* rhyme of *liàng*. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "grief and pain"; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means "longing and looking out. In the *Chǔcí*, it refers to "sorrowful lamentation. The *Cāngjiépiān* states that it means "losing one's will. Guō Pǔ says that "chōng-chàng" is synonymous with "regret and vexation. Both characters are composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic element "zhī" (*zhī*).

*Shunhuan* (巡環): The first character is pronounced *zūn* (遵) with a retroflex final; it means to tour or traverse. In the *Zuozhuan*, it means to go everywhere. Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states it refers to that which is guarded. Li Si used the character *yí* (䡅) for "following the carriage," with the second character pronounced *huán* (還); the *Gongyangzhuan* says it means to encircle.

The character *zhì* (贄) is pronounced as the opposite of *kǎo* (考) when used in the sense of selling goods; it signifies that the transaction is complete. Gu Yewang stated that when one sells goods and receives payment such that the buyer takes them away, this is called *zhì*. The scriptural text [of the *Shuowen*] writes it with the radical *sī* (私), which is incorrect. The correct orthography for all periods consists of the radicals *zhuī* (隹) and *kǒu* (口).

*Zhùlì* (佇立): "Zhù" (佇) is pronounced with the *lǚ* rhyme group; according to the *Erya*, it means "to stand for a long time. The *Kao Sheng* states that "zhù" means "to maintain" (*chí*). It is composed of the radical "person" (*rén*) and "níng" (宁); "níng" has the same pronunciation as above. It is also written as *zhù* (竚), both being identical in meaning.

"Rén suǐ" (人髓): "suǐ" is pronounced with the *rui* rhyme (觜反). According to the *Zītǒng* (字統), it is the fat within the bones. In the *Shuowen*, the character for "marrow" (*suǐ*) is composed of "bone" (骨) as the semantic component and "sui" (隨) abbreviated (省) as the phonetic;

it is a phono-semantic compound. "Yòu bì" (右髀): "bì" is pronounced with the *bu mi* rhyme (步米反). According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to the outer part of the thigh. It is composed of "bone" (骨) as the semantic component and "bei" (卑) abbreviated (省) as the phonetic. In antiquity it was written as 䠋 or 䯗; it also appears as 䯗 in the Classics, though this is a vulgar form.

*Pǒu* (pronounced with the initial *pǔ* and final *-kǎo*) means to split or break open; the *Yùnyuán* states it means to analyze or judge. It is composed of the radical "knife" (*dāo*) and the phonetic "tā kǒu. 399. Volume Three Hundred Ninety-Nine.

Regarding the character *qiān* (pronounced with the initial *jiē* and final *-yān*), the *Kǎoshēng* says it means error or loss; the *Shuōwén* says it means transgression. It is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "yǎn. Variants such as *qiān* are all identical in meaning. In the scriptures, the form with two "heavens" (*tiān*) above is frequently used; this is a vulgar character. Variants such as *qí* and *qín* are both archaic characters.

*Niǎn* (上挐簡反): according to the *Fānyán*, it means shame or embarrassment. In the *Xiǎoyǎ*, it is said that a face flushed with shame is called *niǎn*. Examining its phonetic component, it denotes the blushing of the face due to shame and humiliation. In the *Zìshū*, the character for *niǎn* is written with 赤 (*chì*) and 㞋 (*jiēn*), where 㞋 also serves as the phonetic. The character 𠬩 (pronounced *ní zhǎn* 反) is formed with 皮 (*pí*); this is a vulgar variant of the character.

*Youì* (愧) gives rise to *cán* (慚). [The former] moves upward toward the standard; [the latter] moves downward toward the inner self. According to the *Shuowen*, *youì* is also *cán*. The *Liji* says: "The gentleman does not distress others with what he himself is capable of, nor does he cause shame to others for what they are incapable of. The *Guangya* states it means shame. The *Erya* also says *youì* is *cán*. The *Shuowen* writes it as *youì* or as *huì* (謉); both *huì* and *yǐn* (聭) are archaic characters.

"Chāng hén (瘡痕): 'chē' rhymes with 'fǎn' (反) and 'yīng' (英). It refers to wounds or scars; it is also written as chuàng (創), which is interchangeable, or as chuàng (剏), which is likewise the same. The lower character, 'hén' (痕), has the phonetic value 'hú gēn' (胡根反). According to the *Shuowen*, a scar from an injury is called a 'hén'. The *Shuowen* states: 'Hén' is a swelling or scar from a wound. It is composed of the radical 'nà' (疒) and the phonetic 'gèn' (艮). The sound of 'nà' is 'nǚ è' (女厄反)."* *Note: The provided text contains a mix of commentary and lexicographical definitions regarding the characters for "wound" (chuang/chang) and "scar" (hen).*

Jīng-hài (驚駭): The upper radical *jū* (居) with the phonetic *yīng* (英) reversed. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to startle up"; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means "a startled horse. The lower character is pronounced *xié-ài* (諧騃). According to the *Cāngjiépiān*, it means "to be startled"; according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to rise"; according to the *Shuōwén*, it takes the radical *mǎ* (馬) and the phonetic *hài* (亥).

"Han" (函) refers to a casket; it is used for containing books or objects. It is what people today call "han-shu" (函書) or "biaohan" (表函). "Renran" (荏苒): the first character is read as "er" (而) or "zhen" (枕);

the *Kaoseng* (考聲) states that "grass renran" (草荏苒) refers to things gradually following one another over the passage of days and time, which is called "renran. The character "jing" (經) is written as "ran" (苒), which is a vulgar form.

400. The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Volume Four Hundred. Regarding the term *konghou* (箜篌): "Kong" (空) is pronounced as in "empty" (*kōng*), and "Hou" (侯) is pronounced as in "marquis" (*hóu*). It is the name of a musical instrument. The *Shiming* (釋名) states that it was created by Shi Yan as the "Mimi" music; later it emerged from the empty space between the Sangjian and Xuzhi regions, likely preserved by the customs of the state of Kong. Therefore, it is named *konghou*. Shi Juan played it for Duke Ping of Jin; when Zheng and Wei divided its territory, they inherited it, and it subsequently became known as the "Music of Zheng and Wei," which is termed licentious music.
"Zāo" (槽): The upper character is pronounced *zào* (勞反), and the lower character is pronounced *jǐng* (經井反). This refers to the hollow body (*zāo*) and the neck (*jǐng*) of a *kōng hóu* (lute).

"Shéng bì" (繩柲): The upper character is pronounced *cháng* (常仍反). It belongs to the category of sounds associated with "rope" (*suo*). Originally, it was made by Chui [the Minister of Works under Shun]. Song Zhong says: "Chui was a minister of Shun; the rope is used to obtain straightness. The *Guǎng yá* states: "The rope is straightness. The *Shuō wén* states: "Rope is a cord. It follows the radical 'silk' (*miè*) and takes the abbreviated form of 'fly' (*yíng*) as its phonetic. The lower character is pronounced *pián jié* (駢結反). It belongs to the category of sounds associated with "bend" (*āo*, pronounced *è* or *jiǎo*). Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒ zhuan* says: "A handle for grasping objects. The text in the *Jīng* (Classics) is written as *bì* (𢱧), which is also acceptable. Zheng’s commentary on the *Shàngshū dà zhuàn* says: "*Tí* (󲔈) means to push. The pronunciation of *tuī* is *tā léi*. The *Guǎng yá* says: "*Lì* (㡙) means to bend or to turn. Alternatively, it may be written as *bì* (𢱧) with the radical 'cloth,' which is also acceptable. The *Shuō wén* says it follows the radical 'hand' and uses 'bi' as its phonetic.

"Fengshu" (奉屬): "Feng" (奉) means to receive or uphold; it is composed of the radical "feng" (𢌬, pronounced gǒng) and the phonetic "feng" (丰, pronounced fēng). "Feng" (丰) is pronounced fēng. "Shu" (屬) means to entrust, according to Du Yu's commentary on the *Zuozhuan*; it means to bind or connect, according to Zheng Xuan's commentary on the *Liji*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "shu" (屬) means to link; it is composed of the radical "wei" (尾) and the phonetic "chu" (蜀). The version appearing in the scripture as "shu" (屬) is a vulgar character and erroneous.

*Yin* (隱): Upper radical *yin* (殷), read as *jin*. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to conceal" (*yì*). The *Shìfǎ* states: "To harbor feelings that are not fully expressed is called *yin*. Bāo Xián’s commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* says it means "to hide" (*nì*). Examining its phonetic, it means "to store away" (*cáng*). The *Shuōwén* states: "*Yin* also means 'to screen' (*bì*); it takes *yìn* as its radical and *é* as its phonetic. *Bì* (蔽) means "to cover" (*yǎn*). The *Guǎngyá* states: "*Bì* is *yìn*. The *Ěryá* states: "To flee in hiding" (*cuàn*). Guō Pǔ’s commentary on *bì* says it refers to "escaping and concealing oneself. The *Shuōwén* states: "*Bì* has the appearance of small grass; it takes *cǎo* as its radical and *bì* as its phonetic. *Chǎng* (敞): Read as *pímiè*.

*Luí* (羸劣): The first character is pronounced with the initial *lì* (力) and the final *zhuī* (追). It denotes extreme emaciation; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "paralysis" (*wēi*). It is composed of the radical "sheep" (*yáng*) and the phonetic element *ní* (𣎆), where *ní* is pronounced with the initial *lì* and the final *wò* (臥). The second character, *liè* (劣), means "weakness. It is a compound character formed by combining "few" (*shǎo*) and "strength" (*lì*). This was already explained in the third volume, entry number 181, of the *Qianjing Yinyi*.

*Śài* (pronounced *shā jiǎ* according to the *Dìzǐ*, and *suǒ mǎi* according to the *Yùpiān*; Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states it is like water sprinkled upon the ground; the *Shuowen Jiezi* gives the pronunciation *shān qǐ*, meaning to sprinkle, composed of the radical for water and the phonetic *lì*).

"Bèn" (pronounced with the rhyme of *pén* and *mèn*)—Yingyun states that "bèn" means dust or defilement; examining its phonetic, it means the arrival of vulgar or coarse things. The *Shuowen Jiezi* records it as "bèn," meaning dust, composed of the radical "earth" (*tǔ*) and the phonetic "fēn. The character "wǒ" (I) below it—the *Shuowen* explains that it refers to oneself in relation to one's body, composed of the radicals "hand" (*shǒu*) and "spear" (*gē*). There are instances in the classics where it is written with "grain" (*huó*) instead, which is incorrect.

"Pure" (chún): In the upper character, "lún" is reversed; the *Jīng* uses the character for "vulgar" (*sú*). Regarding its phonetic analysis, it means "to settle and soak. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Yílǐ* says it means "to pour"; the *Guǎngyá* says it means "to soak. It is pronounced "zī sì fǎn. The *Shuowén* states that "lù" (𥂖) is written with the radical "water" and the phonetic "chún" (󲒡), and "chún" (󲒡) is pronounced "chún."

*Gui* (軌): Upper radical *gui* (龜), reversed; the phonetic component is *che* (車). It means the tracks of a vehicle. According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to the ruts of a chariot, composed of the radical *che* with the phonetic *gui* (省) as the sound component; *gui* is pronounced *gui* (鬼). Lower character: *fan* (凡), reversed; *an* (黯) is the phonetic. *Yierya* states: "A model (*fan*); a constant. It is also a phonetic for "mold" (*mo*) or "standard" (*ze*). According to the *Shuowen*, it means a mold (*mo*). Pronounced *pan* (盤). Composed of the radical *che* with the phonetic *fan* (省) as the sound component. It is also written as *fan* (笵), which is interchangeable. This was already explained in the fourth volume of the *Jingyinyi* (經音義).

Volume Four Hundred and One. Volume Four Hundred and One. Regarding "Vulture Peak" (Jiǔfēngshān): [the character] 鷲 is read as *zhì* (with the radical *xiù* reversed) and *fán* (with the prefix *qián*); the preceding "Preface to the Holy Teachings" has already been fully explained. Regarding "heavy burden" (*chóngdàn*): the upper character is read as *zhí* (with the radical *yǒng* reversed) and also as *chúyòng*;

both pronunciations are valid. The lower character is read as *tānlàn*. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to carry. Examining its phonetic origin, the *Shuōwén* states that a wooden object for carrying loads is called a *dàn*, and that it is formed with the radical *shǒu* (hand) and the phonetic *zhān*.
