*Fān* (旛) and *duò* (鐸). [The character for] *fān* is pronounced with the initial *xīng* (嬔, *xián*) and the rhyme *yīng* (䊟, *wúfán*). The *Yùnyīng* (韻英) states it is a general term for banners and flags; dictionaries define it as a *fān* or *zhào* (funeral banner). Nowadays, these are made by interweaving five colors or painting flowers, fruits, birds, and beasts, which are then suspended. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *fān* means "a large bell" (*hú*); it is composed of the radical *yú* (於) and the phonetic *fān* (番), with the pronunciation *xián* (嬔, *fānwàn*). The character *wúfán* (䊟) has the pronunciation *wúfán*. The following character, *duò* (鐸), is pronounced *tángluò*. According to ancient military law, the two *sīmǎ* (commanders) held the *duò*. For civil affairs, they brandished the wooden *duò*—a bronze bell with an iron tongue. For military affairs, they brandished the metal *duò*—a bronze bell with an iron tongue. According to the *Shuowen*, it is a "large bell"; it is composed of the radical *jīn* (金) and the phonetic *yáo* (睪).

*Fù* (upper radical 手, pinyin fú, wǔ fanqie). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states that it means "to rely upon" (*fùshì*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as "a person holding a shell (*bèi*)," meaning there is something to rely upon; it further notes that because one receives loans without partiality, it is a compound character formed by the "person" radical below and the "shell" radical. The vulgar forms with the "strength" (*lì*) or "knife" (*dāo*) radicals are both contrary to the original meaning of the character. The lower part is read as *zé* (jiè fanqie). The *Yunying* states that it means "to owe money."

*Néng huàn* (能煥): The commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* states that "huàn" means "bright. It is composed of the radical "fire" (火) and the phonetic "huàn" (奐). The pronunciation of "huàn" is as stated above. *Zhǒng pào* (腫皰):

The upper character is pronounced *zhōng yǒng* (鍾勇); the lower character is pronounced *páo mào* (炮貌). The *Kǎoshēng* states it refers to fine sores on the face. The *Shuōwén* says it is "vitality arising on the face," with the phonetic "bāo" (包). In the scriptures, it is written as "pào" (疱) with the radical "illness" (疒), or sometimes as "bião" (靤) with the radical "face" (面); both are vulgar characters. The pronunciation of "nè" (疒) is *nǚ è* (女厄).

Regarding the characters "眩瞖" (xuànyì), "枯涸" (kūhè), "箱篋" (xiāngqiè), and "莖幹" (jīnggàn) and those above them, their pronunciations and meanings have already been explained in the third fascicle of the *Qian yinyi* (Commentary on Pronunciations and Meanings) within the one hundred twenty-eighth fascicle of the sutra; please consult the preceding text.
Yìn (蔭): Upper radical *yǐn*, reversed; lower radical *yīng* (with the phonetic *jǐng*).
Lì (粒): Reversed with *lín* and *yì*. This refers to a number of grains of millet. 504. Fascicle 504. Mí (迷): Reversed with *miù*.

Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states it means "error. The *Fāngyán* says it means "fraud. The *Guǎngyá* says it means "deception. The *Shìfǎ* says: "When name and reality diverge, it is called *miù*. The *Shuowén* says: "The delusory speech of a madman. It is composed of the radical *yán* (speech) and the character *liáo*; *liáo* also serves as the phonetic. *Liáo* is pronounced *lì yòu*. The [text] following *ěr* in the canon is incorrect.

Volume Five Hundred and Five. *Tuṣita* (the Sanskrit term; *shàng sāng ān fǎn* is the phonetic transcription). This is the name of a heaven located above within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). Its ancient names were *Dōushuìtuó* or *Dōushù*, both of which are corruptions or abbreviations. In the Tang language, it means "Contentment" (*zhīzú*). Because the lower heavens are characterized by excessive indulgence and the higher heavens by excessive dullness, and because beings therein enjoy pleasure without making progress toward enlightenment, it is called "Contentment. Bodhisattvas in their final birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*) who are in their last body before Buddhahood mostly serve as the kings of this heaven. Maitreya, who will appear in the future, is currently residing there as its king.

Volume Five Hundred Six, Part Five Hundred Six: Records of the Torments of Hell. The *Fan Jijuzhang* states that Gao Yao was the first to create prisons; he was a minister of Yao by name. The *Yupian* says that a place for imprisoning and binding is called a "prison" (*yù*) because of this. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "Disputes over wealth are called *sòng*; disputes over crimes are called *yù*. The *Fengsutong* states: "The Three Kings established prisons: under the Xia it was called Xiatái; under the Yin it was called Youli; under the Zhou it was called Lingyu. From the Qin and Han dynasties onwards, they were collectively termed 'prisons' (*yù*). The *Shuowen* states: "Prison (*yù*) means firmness (*què*). The character for *què* is pronounced *kǔjiǎo*. The character for prison is composed of two dogs [犾, *yújīn*] biting each other, representing the speech of those at the center. It is a compound character; two dogs are used for guarding. The sutra speaks of "hells" (*dìyù*), which are places of dark confinement under the jurisdiction of the underworld. Because they lie beneath the world, they are called "earth-hells. As the verse in the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* says:
Below this, at a distance of twenty thousand [yojanas],
lies the Avīci Hell, equal in depth, breadth, and circumference;
above it are the seven Narakas, and all eight [types of] *utsada* (supplementary hells), each numbering sixteen.

These are the so-called Pond (táng), Embers (wēi), Corpse-Heap (shī), Blades (jì), Razor-Forest (fēng-rèn), River of Fire (liè-hé), and the Increasing Torture (zēng); each resides at one of the four cardinal directions. The remaining eight are the Cold Hells. All of these are names for the great hells.

Regarding the characters for "broad" (*guǎng*) and "narrow" (*xiá*): the *Liji* (Book of Rites) states, "If it is broad, it harbors villainy; if it is narrow, one thinks of desire. The *Kaoseng* (Investigation of Sounds) says that *xiá* means "constricted" (*āì*). The *Yupian* says it means "cramped and not vast. The scriptural text uses the character with the "dog" radical (*quán*) to write *xiá*, which is an error; it should instead be the character for "to practice" (*xí*). This is because dogs and horses are "practiced" (*xiá-xí*) [in training], hence the inclusion of the "dog" radical. Furthermore, the reading *qīng-shāng* (light injury) is a grave deviation from the meaning of the scripture. Some versions use the character with the "mountain" radical (*è*) and the phonetic *fù* to write *xiǎn* (陜), which is also incorrect. This character is also pronounced *shì-rǎn* and refers to the place-name Xiǎn Prefecture. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *xiá* (陿), with the "mountain" radical (*è*), the phonetic *fù* (負), and the phonetic component *jiā* (夾).

Regarding "pāo" (胞胎): it is already reversed [in common usage], though the original ancient text reads "bāo" (包). This is a pictographic character. The Stone Classics (Shijing) write it as "pāo" (胞), which is traditionally pronounced with the fanqie *pǔ bāo*; this is incorrect. The *Shuowen jiezi* states: "The garment worn by a child while in the womb of a woman. It is composed of "bāo" (勹) and "yǐ" (已). "Bāo" (勹) is pronounced as "bāo," and "yǐ" (已) is pronounced as "sì"; together they form a character representing a child not yet fully formed within the "bāo. Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shangshu* says: "To wrap and enclose. The latter part is pronounced *tāi*. The *Shuowen* further states: "A woman carrying a fetus before birth. It is composed of "ròu" (肉) and the phonetic "tái" (台).

*Kui* (匱): The distant position [of the phonetic] is reversed; the *Shengyun* says it means "to exhaust" (*yiqiong*). This was already explained in the three hundred and ninety-first fascicle of the preceding scripture.

*Po* (迫): The upper radical is *qu* (曲) and the phonetic is *gong* (拱). The *Erya* says it means "fear. The scriptural text uses *kong* (恐), which is a vulgar character. According to the *Shuowen*, the correct form consists of the radicals for "work" (*gong*), "hand" (*shou*), "mountain" (*ya*), and "heart" (*xin*), written as *po*. Now, in the clerical script (*lingshu*), due to cursive writing, it became *kong*, and was further erroneously changed to *kong*; thus, the correct form has gradually been lost through corruption. The archaic form is *wan* (𢖶), with the lower radical being *ban* (班) and the phonetic being *mo* (陌). The *Cangjie pian* says it means "near"; the *Guangya* says it means "narrow"; the *Shengyun* says it means "to press" (*pobi*) and "constricted" (*ai*).

"Bèi" (備): On the upper character, Píng Mèi reversed it; Yuè Wáng says it means "to guard against. Zhèng Xuán says it means "to rescue. Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* says it means "to provide. The *Shuowen* says it means "caution"; it is composed of 人 (person), 用 (use), and the phonetic element 荀 (xún) in abbreviated form. It is also written as 僃; the text here uses 備, which is a vulgar form. The lower character, *zǔ láo* (祖勞) in sound, means "to encounter. The *Shuowen* says it means "to meet by chance"; it is composed of 辵 (chuò, to walk) and the phonetic element 曹 (cáo). It is also written as 傮, which is the same. It is also written as 𣩒, 𣩒, or 𣧩.

Regarding the character *xún* (循): Xuǎnyīng says it means “to inspect” (*àn xíng*). Kǎoshēng says it means “to follow” (*shùn*) or “to comply with” (*cóng*). The *Shuowén* says it means “to move along” (*xúnxíng*), composed of *chì* (彳, read as *chǒu chǐ*) and *dùn* (盾, read as *shùn*). The scriptural text [of the *Shuowén*] includes a vertical stroke from *qiān* (千) to form *xián* (𩅢), which is incorrect. The lower radical is read as *huá guān*. Zhèng Zhòng’s commentary on the *Zhoulǐ* says it means “to revolve” (*huán xuán*). Zhèng Xuān says it means “to encircle” (*huán wéi*). Hé Xiū’s commentary on the *Gōngyáng Zhuàn* says it means “to surround” (*huán rào*). The *Shuowén* says it is composed of *yù* (玉) and *huán* (睘) as its phonetic.

*Bo-lüe* (薄劣): The upper character is pronounced *bàng* (旁) with a retroflex final; dictionaries state it means "not thick. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) and the phonetic component *pǔ* (溥, with a *mò* final). The lower character is pronounced *lì-chuè* (力惙); the *Guangya* states it means "inferior" or "meager," while the *Shuowen* says it means "weak. It may also be written as *liè* (𭝂), using the "heart" radical (*xīn*), which is an archaic form.

*Jī* (飢): The upper radical is *jǐ* (几), which according to the *Kǎośēng* means "the belly is empty. The *Yùnyīng* says it means "lacking food. The *Cāngjiépiān* says it means "hunger and emaciation. The *Shuōwén* says it means "hunger and starvation," composed of the radical *shí* (食) and the phonetic *jǐ* (几). It is also written as *jì* (𩚮), an archaic character; the lower part is pronounced *lì* (力) with the tone *zhuī* (追). The *Kǎośēng* says *léi* (羸) means "extreme emaciation. The *Shuōwén* says it is composed of the radicals *yáng* (羊) and *ní* (𣎆) as its phonetic. Regarding the character *léi* (羸), it is composed of *wáng* (亡), *kǒu* (口), *ròu* (肉), and *yáng* (羊); *jì* (丮) is pronounced *yǐn* (隱). [The character] *léi* (羸) is pronounced *lì* (力) with the tone *zhuī* (追).

The *Qingshang* (Explanations of Forms) reverses [the order] and states that "craftsman" (*jiàng*) refers to a woodworker. The *Kaosheng* (Investigation of Sounds) says it is a person of skill. It is composed of the radical *jīn* (axe), which is an axe; and the phonetic component *fāng*, pronounced as *fāng*. *Fāng* denotes the making of vessels. The text of the scripture uses "craftsman" (*jiàng*), which is not incorrect.

*Weizá* (猥雜): The first character is pronounced *wǔhuì* (烏賄) with the second tone for *huì* and the fourth tone for *měi*; the second character is pronounced *cái hé* (才合). This was already explained in the previous scripture, fascicle 435.

*Mángxiè* (盲瞎): The first character is pronounced *mògēng* (莫耕). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To have no pupils in the eyes is called *máng*. The second character is pronounced *hūbā* (呼八). Dictionaries state: "The eyes do not see objects. It is also said: "One eye lacks its lens. It is sometimes written as *máng* (𣎅), which is an archaic form of the character.

*Li-tan* (黧黮): The upper character *li* is pronounced with the initial *l* and the final *chi* (力遲反). The *Tongsu Wen* states that mottled black is called *li*. The *Kaosheng* says it refers to a dark complexion (*mian-zhi*, 面𩓀, pronounced *qi-xun*); it also means a color that is black yet tinged with yellow. This was already explained in the previous volume 435. The lower character *tan* is pronounced with the final *gan* (他感反). The *Chuci* states that *yan* (黤, pronounced *wu-gan*) and *tan* mean not bright or clean. The *Shuowen* says it is the black color of mulberry fruit (*sang-shen*). The *Shenglai* says it is like the color of lacquer. This was already explained in the previous volume 435.
"Qiongzhui" (窮顇) means "to be reduced to extreme poverty and distress"; this has already been explained in the one hundred and eighty-first fascicle of the preceding scripture.

"Wanyin" (頑嚚) [the first character pronounced with the *wang* and *guan* rhymes] means "obstinate and dull-witted" according to the *Guangya*; its explanation is likewise concluded in the one hundred and eighty-first fascicle of the preceding scripture.

"Qingqiao" (輕誚) means to reprimand and to mock; the *Cangjie pian* says it means to scold (*he*), and the *Shuowen jiezi* says it means to harass (*rao*). It is sometimes written as "zhao" (譙), following the radical for speech and the phonetic "xiao" (肖).

"Jù" (拒): In the *Yǔyùn*, it is read as "fàn" (反). The *Yīngyún* states it means "to block. The *Guǎngyá* records the pronunciation of "hàn" (捍) for "jù. The *Shuōwén* states it means "to resist" (*kǔlàng* fǎn). The *Yùnquán* states it means "to oppose."

The *guāluó* (蝸蠃) is a small snail; "shànggǔ" (上古) is pronounced *huá fǎn* (華反), and "lùhé" (魯和) is pronounced *lú hé fǎn* (盧和反). In the classics it is written as *luó* (螺), which is a vulgar character and not the correct form. The *Erya* says: "The *fùluó* (附蠃) is pronounced *yí* (夷) and is the *yú* (蝓). Guo Pu states that it is the same as the snail (*guāniú*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* also says that the *luó* (蠃) belongs to the class of snails but is larger in shape and originates from the sea; its various forms are not uniform.

The character *lan* (爛) is pronounced with an initial *luo* and a final *dan* (羅旦反). The *Fāngyán* states that what is cooked by fire is called *lán*. The lower part is pronounced with an initial *fú* and a final *wèn* (夫問反). The *Yùnyīng* states it means excrement (*fèn*). It is also written as *qiè* (󲐑); the text here uses *fèn* (糞), which is a vulgar form.

The character *guàn* (慣) is discussed here as being the opposite of what was already explained in the four hundred thirty-eighth fascicle. According to the *Erya*, it means "to habituate. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is written as *jiàn* (遦), derived from the radical *chuò* (辵) with the phonetic *chǔ lüè* (丑略反). Although the scriptural text sometimes uses *cuàn* (串), this is a vulgar form and not the correct orthography.
*Taṃzhè* (耽著) [pronounced *dānzhé*]: This was already explained in the previous scripture, fascicle 331. *Qīngmiè* (輕懱): The *Shuowén* states that *miè* means to slight or despise;

it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "miè. The scriptural text uses the simplified form "miè" alone as an abbreviation. This refers to physical exhaustion and lack of vigor leading to a desire for sleep; it is not the intended meaning of the scripture.
Volume Five Hundred and Seven, Part Two. *Xiāngzhù* (相著): pronounced with a light retroflex *chí* (持). Regarding the character for "sugarcane" (*gānzhè* [甘蔗]):

the commentary on its phonetic interpretation states that sugarcane is the name of a beautiful grass; its juice can be boiled down to produce granulated sugar. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is a type of yam (*shú*). It is composed of the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) and the phonetic element "abbreviated *zhē*" (*zhē shěng*).

*Qú láo* (劬勞): The pronunciation of *qú* is like that of *fǎn kǎo* (反考); it means diligent effort. *Qú* is also labor. The lower character, *lè dāo fǎn* (勒刀反), is explained by Jia Kui as "exhausted labor. The *Erya* says it means "diligent effort. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "severe toil," derived from the radical for strength (*lì*); one who exerts physical force experiences toil.

508. Fascicle Five Hundred and Eight. Regarding the character *she* (涉): Shi Ye (時葉) says it means to traverse (*sheli*). The *Kaosheng* (考聲) says it means to cross water. It was written as *she* (󲒟) in antiquity. The *Shuowen* says it means to wade through water on foot; it is composed of the radical for "foot" (*bu*) and "water" (*xia*, with the phonetic *ku huang*). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (毛詩傳) says *kuang* (壙) means empty. The *Guoya* (廣雅) says it means great. The *Kaosheng* says *kuang* (埌, pronounced *lang*) describes the vast appearance of distant plains and fields. The text of the sutra uses *ri* (日) instead of *kuang* (曠), which is an error. Alternatively, it is written with the radical for "heart" (*xin*) as *kang* (懭) or *kuang* (懬); these mean "distant. *Kang* (懭) also carries the sense of losing one's composure, which seems to be a common usage.
Regarding "xiàn dào shàng xiāng" (險道上香), it was already fully explained in the preceding volume five hundred and six of the *Guoyu* (國語).

As for "mù" (牧) [in "xià mù bù" (下莫卜反)], Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Fangyan* states: "Mù means to raise oxen and horses. Gu Yewang says: "Mù is a general term for raising livestock; it does not refer solely to the raising of oxen and horses. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "One who raises oxen and horses. It is composed of 'pu' (普卜反) and 'niu' (牛). The character 'pu' is now written as 'pūn' (攵)."
"Pregnant" (huái) is pronounced with the upper radical *hu* (乖) and the lower radical *zhèng* (反). This was already explained in the previous scripture, fascicle 438.
"To harass" (rǎo) is pronounced with the initial *níng* (寧) and the final *niǎo* (鳥); the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means a woman deluding a man; in ancient script, it is written as *niǎn* (嬲).
Volume Five Hundred and Nine. "Nengzu" (能阻) means to obstruct; "zhuang" (莊) is a variant for "nan" (難), meaning difficulty. "Zanli" (讚勵) means to encourage and exhort;
"li" (勵) is a variant for "mian" (勉), meaning to strive.
"Bian" (辯) is pronounced *jiǔ* (久) with the rhyme *piǎn* (皮免反); "bian" here means wisdom (*huì*).

"Zu" (卒) is pronounced *cāng* (倉) with the rhyme *nè* (訥) and *shēng* (聲); the *Zhou Lǐ* says it means violent and urgent, while the *Kǎo Shēng* says it means *cāngmáng* (倉忙). "Jù" (遽) is pronounced *qú* (渠). Its standard form is written as *cù* (猝), or alternatively as *zù* (踤), both of which are identical; the text uses "zu" (卒) as a simplification for brevity. Because this character is often confused with "bīng zuò" (兵卒, soldiers), it is mentioned here.

The character 欠 (pronounced *qū*, with the phonetic component 據) was previously explained in entry 440; the *Pīcāng* states that it means "to open the mouth and breathe out. It is an error for the scriptural text to use the character 呿 (*kē*) instead, which is derived from the radical 口.

*Zào’è* (躁󲈕): the first character is pronounced *zāi gào* (反), the second is pronounced *rǎng shǎo* (反). This was already fully explained in the previous section 440. *Qiāoyì* (憍逸): the first character is pronounced *jū yí* (反).

According to the *Guǎngyá*, "qióng" means to exalt oneself; according to the *Yùpiān*, it refers to arrogance. Furthermore, the script in the sutra text uses the character 󲔹 on the right; this is a vulgar form and not the correct orthography.

*Pú* (僕): The upper radical is *pú* (蒲木反). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states: "A servant (*pú*) is one who attaches himself [to another]. The *Kaosheng* says: "A servant is an attendant; a servant is a child. Gu Yewang says: "One who drives a carriage. The *Shuowen* says: "One who performs services for others; composed of the radicals 'man' (人) and 'bushel' (菐), with 'bushel' also serving as the phonetic component. The sound of 'bushel' is *bǔ*. In ancient script it is written as *qū* (䑑); the lower part is pronounced *lì* (力計反). *Kaosheng* says: 'Slaves (*lì*)' are those of the base class; they are servants. Now, a slave is a lowly subject. The *Shuowen* says: "'To attach' (*fùzhù*). The standard form is *lì* (隸); composed of 'to follow' (隶, pronounced *dì*) and the phonetic 'nai' (柰). The scriptural text uses 'rice' (米) instead of 'bushel' (菐), forming *mí* (𧒣), which is erroneous; it is a vulgar character."
*Jiē* (黠): *xiá* (上遐軋反) and *yā* (軋烏八反). This has already been fully explained in the previous fascicle 440. *Guī* (規): *mó* (上鷄維反). Gu Yewáng says:

"The compass (*guī*) makes circles and the square (*jǔ*) makes squares. It is as Mencius said: "Without the compass and square, one cannot achieve squareness and roundness. Zhèng Xuán says: "The compass is the instrument for making perfect circles. *Kǎoshēng* says: "Guī means to make a circle perfectly; it also means to measure. *Dù* (度): *tú* (徒各反). The *Shuowén* says: "Guī means 'to possess. It is composed of the radical 'husband' (*fū*) and the phonetic 'jiàn' (*jiàn*). *Qí* (其): *hú* (下其胡反). This has already been fully explained in the previous fascicle 430.
*Kacamaṇi* is a Sanskrit name for a jewel. This jewel is not of the category of extraordinary stones or jade; it is simply another name for a pearl. Regarding the character *shen* (深):

according to the *Shuowen*, it is pronounced with the initial *shang* (傷) and the final *ren* (任), meaning "profound and unfathomable. The *Shuowen* states that it is composed of the radical *shui* (水) and the phonetic *mi* (𥥍). Regarding the character *ao* (奧): according to the *Erya*, the southwestern corner is called *ao*. The *Shuowen* states that *ao* also means "profound"; it is composed of the radical *bian* (釆) with the phonetic *bai* (白) and the final *man* (慢), and is formed by adding the character *da* (大) to become *ao*.
Yàn (pronounced with the "i" and "yán" finals reversed) means contentment; dùn (pronounced with the "xù" and "liù" finals reversed) means to possess;
qiān lìn (the first character pronounced with the "shàng" and "kǒu" finals reversed, the second with the "lí" and "zhèn" finals reversed) means stinginess and parsimony.
"Without leisure" (wú xiá): the character *xiá* is pronounced *hú jià fǎn*. The dictionary states that *xiá* means "leisurely" (*xián*).

"Resentment" (*qiàn hèn*): the upper radical is pronounced *xíng jiān fǎn*. The *Yùnyīng* states it means "to harbor resentment. This has already been explained in detail in the four hundred and forty-first fascicle of the preceding scripture.

Volume 510, Part 510: Medical Treatment (Líáo). The upper character is pronounced *jī* (with a level tone), and the lower character is pronounced *lìzhào* (with an entering tone); it is a variant form used for the time being. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the standard form is written as 𤻲 (*yuè*), and its gloss is identical to that which follows. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "To stop illness is called *líáo*. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "*Líáo* means to treat. This is the standard orthography for the ancient and modern terms for treating illness. It is composed of the radical 疒 (*nǚ'ài*) and the phonetic component 尞 (*lìzhào*).

*Yù* (悆): The *Yùn* (韻) states it means "harmonious joy"; the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it means "peaceful security"; the *Yùnjí* (韻集) states that when a Son of Heaven is ill, it is called *bùyù*. The *Shàngshū* says, "He had an illness and was not *yù*. Kǒng [An-guó] says it means "not joyful and at ease. The *Shuōwén* says *yù* means "joyful ease," composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "yú. In the scriptural texts, there is sometimes *yù* (愈) with the pronunciation *zhǔ*; this is also acceptable. The *Jíhuì* (集訓) says *yù* means "the illness has abated," "recovered," or "improved. Kǒng Ān-guó’s commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* says *yù* means "superiority. The *Yùpiān* says that the abating of an illness is called *yù*. In the *Shuōwén*, the character *yù* is composed of "boat" (*zhōu*) and "blade" (*kuǐ*), with the ancient pronunciation *wài*; it is a compound character (*huìyì*).

"Móng" (蚊蝱): the character for "móng" is read as *wù fēn* (勿芬反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as 蟁; it is an archaic variant character composed of 昏 (*hūn*). It was changed from 民 (*mín*) to 昏 (*hūn*) to avoid the imperial taboo name of Emperor Taizong.
In the sutras, "mó" (蚊) is a vulgar character. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Níjié (齧霓結), the reverse of the phonetic; it is a flying insect that bites.

The *Erya* says: "Lóng (鷏), pronounced tián; Gùopǔ says it resembles a wūzhòu (烏𪇰), pronounced bèi, but is larger, with a variegated pattern of yellow and white, and its call is like that of a pigeon."
Nowadays in Jiangdong, this bird is called the "Mosquito Mother" (*mónmǔ*). According to popular lore, this bird constantly disgorges mosquitoes and gnats, hence its name.
The *Yiyuan* states that aquatic insects transform into mosquitoes.
The reading for "xià" (下) is *gēng* (耕).
The *Shēnglèi* (聲類) states that this insect bites humans; it resembles a fly and is larger than a *zēng* (繒).
According to the evidence, the *méngchóng* (蝱虫) actually resembles a bee in shape, though its size is like that of a fly.
The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is a biting flying insect.
It is born within the flowers of grasses in mountains, marshes, rivers, and valleys, or it is transformed from within the brains of roe deer (*zhāng*) or deer;
it then sprays out from the nostrils of the deer.
[The character is pronounced] with the *pu* and *men* finals reversed. Those large in form are called *méng* (mosquitoes).
One name for them is *mùméng* (wood-mosquitoes).

The first is named *fēi* (飛); it is not the shape of a gadfly (*méng*). That which has small spotted markings is called *zhàn* (暫). *Zhàn* resembles a fly. Regarding "snake" (*shé*): when [the character for] *chài* (蠆) appears above, it is pronounced *zhē* (遮). The *Mao Shi* says, "Only the *huǐ* (虺) and only the snake.

The *Yī Jīng* says, "The hibernation of dragons and snakes" (*zhí*, 蟄, pronounced *chí lì*). The ancient script is pictographic; the *Xiǎozhuàn* writes it as *xiāo*; the *Shuōwén* writes it as *tā*; and the clerical script (*lìshū*) writes it as *yě*. These have gradually changed due to mutual influence. Cáo Yōng’s Stone Classics add the radical "insect" (*chóng*) to make the character *shé*. The *Zìshū* says, "Snakes and *huǐ* are venomous insects. The canonical text uses *shé*, which is a transformed vulgar form of the character. Below, *chì* is pronounced *jiè* (芥). The *Kǎoshēng* says it is the *chài* (蠆) or *xié* (蝎), pronounced *xiē* (歇). It is also written as *yù* (𧓵). The *Shuōwén* says, "The *chài* is a venomous insect; it follows the 'insect' radical and takes *miáo* (苗) as its form," which is a pictograph. The seal script writes it as *zhú* (󲚰), imitating the shape of a scorpion.
"Non-narrow" (*fei-xia*)—the "hu" and "jia" rhymes are reversed; this has already been fully explained in the preceding sutra.

511. Volume Five Hundred Eleven. "Fluttering and turning" (*piao-zhuan*): the upper character "piao" is pronounced *pi-yao*. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "Piao is a whirlwind. The *Mao Shi* commentary states: "Piao-feng is a wind that suddenly arises."

Regarding the character *fàn* (氾): in ancient and modern standard orthography, it is said to mean "floating" (*fú*) or "universal" (*pǔ*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* likewise states that it is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic component "fàn" (*fàn*) with its radical omitted. It is also written as *fàn* (泛) or *fàn* (氾); these are largely identical with minor differences, all describing the appearance of water flowing and drifting.

Regarding "air-bladder" (*fú náng*): the *Yùnyīng* states that "floating" (*fú*) means to drift; the *Guǎngyá* says it means to float and drift. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* says, "That which is above is called floating. Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guóyuè* says, "Floating means lightness. The *Shuowén* defines "floating" as drifting, composed of the radical "water" and the phonetic "fú" (pronounced *nuò*). The *Yùnyīng* explains "bladder" (*náng*) as a bag or pouch, with the pronunciation *tuō*. The *Jíxùn* states: "That which has a bottom is called a *náng*; that which has no bottom is called a *tuō*. It further notes that the large is called a *náng* and the small a *tuō*, both being vessels for holding things. In the Small Seal script, "bladder" is written with the character for "pouch" (*tuō*), but here the sound is confused and simplified to the character for "female" (*nǚ*) with the phonetic "gēng" (pronounced *nǚ*). According to the scriptures, the "air-bladder" refers to a pneumatic bag; when wishing to cross the great ocean, one relies upon the power of this pneumatic bag to float lightly.

Regarding the term *huài píng* (坏瓶): the former [entry] at volume 444 has already been explained. Here, the *Jìxùn* (集訓) states it is a vessel for drawing water and holding thin gruel (*jiāng*). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it resembles a *yīng* (罃), with the pronunciation *wūgēng* (乌耕), but with a small opening.

Volume Five Hundred Twelve, Part One. Regarding the term *jiangshuai* (將帥): the *Jiangjun* (將君) states that "jiang" means a leader (*jun*). The *Zishu* (字書) states it means the commander of an army or a military leader. The *Liu junjing* (六軍鏡) says: "Now, one who acts as a general must possess the six conducts, five talents, four duties, three disciplines, and one constancy; when these are fully practiced, he is called an excellent general. The *Shuowen* (說文) states: "Jiang means to lead (*shuai*). It is composed of 'cun' (寸) and the abbreviated form of 'yi' (醫) as a phonetic component. The lower character, *xiang* (襄), has the reading *lei* (類). The *Yunying* (韻英) states: "Jiang means to lead (*shuai*). The *Kaosheng* (考聲) states: "It means to command and lead. The *Jixun* (集訓) states: "It means a military general. It is also written as *jiang* (𧗵). Furthermore, the *Shuowen* gives the pronunciation *shanlü* (山律); *jiang* (𧗿) is also a term for a general.

Regarding "egg-shell" (luǎn-kuò): the upper character *luǎn* is pronounced with the *guǎn* rhyme. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Generally, those things that do not have milk are born from eggs; this is a pictographic representation. The ancient script (*gǔwén*) is written as 𤓸, the small seal script (*xiǎozhuàn*) as 𤓹, and the clerical script (*lìshū*) as 卵. Regarding the lower character *kuò*, it is pronounced with the *jiǎo* rhyme. The *Jixùn* states: "The skin of a bird's egg is called a *kuò*. The *Kǎoshēng* states: "'Egg' (*luǎn*) means empty. It is composed of the radical 'egg' (*luǎn*) and the phonetic component 'tooth' (*kǔ-jǎo*). *Note: The characters provided in the source text for the ancient and small seal scripts appear to be typographical errors or archaic variants not standard in modern editions. The standard forms are 𤓸 (古) and 𤓹 (籀).*

The character *chúnshú* (淳熟): the first radical, *shí*, is pronounced as *lún* (倫) with an inverted tone; it has already been fully explained in the preceding volume 146 of this scripture. The second radical, *shí*, is pronounced as *lù* (陸) with an inverted tone. According to the *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲), it means "to ripen into completion" or "to soften. The *Fāng Yán Wén Zì Jí Lè* (方言文字集略) states it means "to combine for eating. The character form is written as *zháo* (󲚭); according to the *Shuō Wén* (說文), it follows the radical *huǒ* (灬) with the phonetic *biāo* (熛) and the determinative *shú* (孰).
Regarding the character *wèi* (爲), it is pronounced *mò* (莫) and *bào* (豹). This has already been fully explained in the previous volume 446 of this canon.

Regarding *qiān* (牽): the *Qiānshēng* (考聲) states it means "to connect" (*qiānlían*); the *Guǎngyǎ* states it means "to pull" (*qiānwǎn*); the *Shuōwén* states it means "to lead forward. It is composed of the radical "ox" (牛) and the phonetic "mián" (宀, read as *mián*), with the phonetic "xuán" (玄). It is also written as *qiān* or *qiàn* (掔), which are archaic forms. The lower character [of the second term], *yǐn* (引), is pronounced *yǔ* (余) and *rěn* (忍). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states it means "to guide"; Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guóyǔ* states it means "to extend"; the *Ěryǎ* states it means "to arrange"; and the *Shuōwén* states it means "to draw a bow. It is composed of the radical "bow" (弓) and the phonetic "yè" (厂, read as *yè*). In the ancient script, it is composed of the radical "hand" (扌, read as *shǒu*) and the radical "bow" (弓), forming the character *gù* (㧈).

Volume 513, Part 513: *Bǐ* (比). The *Jíxùn* (集訓) states that *bǐ* means "to categorize" (*lèi*). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that *bǐ* means "to align" (*biàndìng*). The *Shuōwén* (說文) states: "To compare and arrange with one another. It is composed of the radical *fǎn* (反) and the phonetic *cóng* (從). Because two people form the ancient character *gǔ* (古), and the character *cóng* reversed forms *bǐ*, it is said to be "reversed and following" (*fǎncóng*). Below, it is read as *tángluò* (唐落). The *Kǎoshēng* states it means "measurement" (*dùliàng*). The *Jíxùn* states it means "to estimate" (*kuíduó*). It is also written as *bǐ* (𢜬), which is identical. The *Shuōwén* states: "A legal standard. It is composed of the radical *yòu* (又) and the phonetic *shěng* (省) of *zhāo* (𠮧). It is also written as *kǔ* (㡯) or *zhāo* (𢜬); these three forms are all archaic characters.

The character *chì* (翄) is pronounced *shì* (施) with a retroflex final; the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it refers to the wings of a bird. Variants such as *chì* (翨) are both archaic forms. The form *chì* (翅) found in modern scriptures is a vernacular character, yet it is also acceptable. Regarding *yóu yù* (猶豫):

the first character is pronounced *yóu* (由), and the second is *yù* (余) with a *dù* (度) final. The *Liji* states: "Divination by stalks and milfoil is used to resolve doubts and suspicions and to settle hesitations (*yóu yù*). Lexicons define *yóu yù* as a term for indecision. A detailed explanation of the characters is provided in the three hundred twenty-fifth fascicle cited previously.

514. Volume Five Hundred Fourteen. *Śaṇḍha* and *pandaka* are Sanskrit terms; this is translated as "eunuch" (*huángmén*). *Shān* (搋) is pronounced *chìjiā* (with the second tone on *jiā*), and *cuìzé* (擇) is pronounced *zhái*; *jiā* (迦) is pronounced *jūqiē* (with the second tone on *qiē*). As for eunuchs, they are those who lack the male organ, or even if it is present, they are unable to procreate. There are five such types, which have already been fully enumerated in the third volume of the *Yīnyì* (Explanations of Pronunciations); they shall not be described here at length.

*Dian* (癲): The first character is pronounced *ding* with the *jian* rhyme. The *Guangya* states it means "madness. The commentary on the *Mao Shi* says it is "epilepsy" (*dianbing*). The *Shenglei* says it is "the disease of wind-epilepsy" (*duanfengbing*). It is also written as *dian* (瘨) or *dian* (蹎). The second character is pronounced *xian*. The *Jixun* says it is "epileptic illness in children. The *Shuowen* says it is "a disease of wind," composed of the radical *nua* (疒) with the phonetic *nüe* (厄) and the determinative *jian* (間). It is also written as *zhan* (𤺛), which is likewise correct.

Regarding "jīshì" (lice): the upper character is pronounced *jǐ* (with the radical *ni*) and the *Shuowen* states it means "the offspring of lice. The *Yunying* states it means "the eggs of lice," which is pronounced *duàn*. The lower character is pronounced *suǒ* (with the radical *yǐ*). The *Ziyao* states it is an insect that bites people within clothing. The *Shuowen* indicates the character for "lice" (*shí*) is composed of the phonetic *xùn* (pronounced *xìn*) and the radical *gùn* (pronounced *kūn*). The current textual tradition that writes it with the radical *fēng* (wind) as *shī* is incorrect.

Regarding "bù xún" (不侚巡), the *Jìxùn* (集訓) states: "To follow after things with one's person is called 'xún' (侚). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states: "'Xún' means distant. The *Wén* (文) states: "'Xún' means rapid. It is composed of the radical "person" (人) and the phonetic "xún" (旬). It is also written as "mí" (󲘍), which is an archaic character.

*Shìhù* (恃怙): The first character, *shì*, is pronounced with the initial *shí* and the final *zhǐ*. The *Shēngyùn* states that it means "to rely upon" (*yī*). The *Jíxùn* states it means "to depend upon" (*fù*). It refers to riding upon, carrying, leaning against, or relying on. The *Shuōwén* states it means "to depend on" (*là*). It is composed of the radical *xīn* (heart) and the phonetic *sì*. The second character, *hù*, is pronounced with the initial *hú* and the final *gǔ*. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "reliance" (*shì*). It is composed of the radical *xīn* (the same as the heart radical, here noted as *lì*) and the phonetic *hù* (pronounced *húgǔ*). It is a compound of the phonetic and the determinative.

Volume 515, Part 515. *Hejian* (呵諫). [The character *he* is pronounced as *jia* with the *yan* rhyme. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "To admonish means to rectify; it is to correct others through the Way. The *Shangshu* says: "When a sovereign follows admonition, he becomes sage. The *Baihutong* states: "Admonition (*jian*) means 'to separate' (*jian*) and 'to change' (*gai*). It is to separate right from wrong and to reform the conduct of people. Because humans cherish the Five Constant Virtues, there are five kinds of admonition, namely: indirect admonition (*fengjian*), compliant admonition (*congjian*), formal admonition (*guijian*), direct admonition (*zhijian*), and artful admonition (*juexian*). The *Shuowen* also says: "Admonition means to rectify. It is composed of the radical 'speech' (*yan*) and the phonetic element 'jian' (*jian*)."
The preceding section, the four hundred and forty-ninth fascicle, has already provided a detailed explanation of the term *kṣaṇa* (pronounced *nai-fan* when preceded by *dai-xia*).

*Kṣaṇa* (upper tone: *cha*) is a Sanskrit term meaning "time. The verse in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "One hundred and twenty *kṣaṇas* Constitute the measure of one *tatkṣaṇa*. Sixty of these [tatkṣaṇas] make one *lava*; Thirty of these [lavas] make one *muhūrta*, Which together form one day and night. According to this verse, one day and night consists of thirty *muhūrtas*.
Each muhūrta is calculated to consist of thirty lava-s.
Furthermore, within one lava there are sixty tatkṣaṇas.
Moreover, within one tatkṣaṇa there are divided into one hundred and twenty kṣaṇas.
Time passes swiftly, not exceeding a single *kṣaṇa*.

According to the calendrical system of this country, one full day and night consists of twelve periods (*yāma*) divided into a total of one hundred *kē* (ke). Each period receives slightly more than eight *kē*. Calculating approximately by these major units, from the hour of Yín to the hour of Yǎo, within the span of one period, there are five hundred and forty thousand *kṣaṇas*.
By this calculation, a full day and night totals six million four hundred and eighty thousand kṣaṇas.
If divided by each *kṣaṇa* per *kalā*, there are approximately seventy thousand *kṣaṇas* within one *kalā*; it is said to be extremely rapid, more fleeting than a moment.

*Chóuliáng* (籌量): The first character, *chóu*, is pronounced with the *zhǎng* and *liú* tones (as in *liǎn*). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Yílǐ* states: "Chóu means calculation. The *Shuowén* says: "Chóu refers to the arrows used in the game of *hú*; it is composed of the radical 'bamboo' (*zhú*) and the phonetic 'shòu' (*shòu*). *Chèdù* (測度):

The first character, *cè*, is pronounced with the *chǔ* and *lì* tones (as in *lì*). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhōulǐ* states: "Cè is equivalent to measuring (*dù*); when one does not know the width or depth, it is called cè. The *Shuowén* says: "It is composed of the radical 'water' (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic 'zé' (*zé*). The second character, *dù*, is pronounced with the *tú* and *luò* tones (as in *luò*).
*Jiāozhù* (焦炷): The first character is pronounced *yáo* (姚) and the second is pronounced *zhù* (注). This has already been fully explained in the previous scripture, fascicle 450. *Jiàocuì* (顦顇):
The first character is pronounced *qíngyáo* (情遙) and the second is pronounced *qíngsuì* (情遂). This has already been fully explained in the previous scripture, fascicle 451.
The characters for *mò* (矛) and *làn* (䂎) are pronounced with the initial *mò* (莫候反) and the final *làn* (倉亂反); their explanation was already completed in detail in the previous volume 451.

As for *lán* (懶) and *dài* (憜), the former is pronounced *lēi-tǎn* (勒坦反) and the latter *tú-wò* (徒臥反). They signify a lack of diligence in one's studies. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that they mean "to be disrespectful," composed of the radical "heart" (心) and the phonetic "suí" (隋).

*Bo* (撥): [The character is pronounced with the initial *bō* and the final *mǔ* reversed (*bǔ-mǔ*). According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means "to remove. Zheng Xuan says it means "to brush away. The *Shuowen* states that it is composed of the radical *shou* (hand) and the phonetic *fa*.

517. Volume Five Hundred Seventeen. *Dui* (堆): [The first tone is *dūn* and the final is *léi*. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* says it means "high. The *Kaosheng* says it is the appearance of high ground. It is also said to mean "a heap" or "accumulation. The *Jixun* says it is the high form of a mound or hill. The *Shuowen* writes it as *duī* (陮), stating that *duī* (*wěi*) means "a capital city"; it is composed of the radical *fu* (hill) and the phonetic *zhui* (隹) in abbreviated form. The text here uses *tuī* (塠), which is a vulgar character. *Xia fu* (下阜): [The sound of the radical *fu* is *fù*. The *Erya* says, "High and level land is called *lu*; a large *lu* is called *fu*. The *Guangya* says, "A mound without stones is called *fu*. The *Shuowen* says, "A mountain without stones is called *fu*. The ancient script is written as *di* (𨸏) or *ji* (󲒧), representing its shape.

"Gou" (溝) is pronounced *gǔ* (anciently *kǒu*). The *Zhouli* states that a waterway for conveying water is called a *gōu*. The *Guīyuán Zhūcóng* says it is a drainage channel within a town for conveying water. The *Shuowén* says it is a depression in the water; four feet wide and four feet deep, it takes the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic "gòu" (pronounced *hòu*). The lower part is pronounced *kǔ* (anciently *gēng*). The *Erya* says it is a pit or a ruin. The *Kǎoshēng* says it is a hollow or ditch. The *Jīngǔn Zhèngzì* says it is a moat or trench, pronounced *qīngyàn* (anciently *chán*), or written as "kàng" (阬), taking the radical "earth" (*tǔ*) and the phonetic "kàng" (*kàng*).

*Zhū*: The initial sound is *yóu*; the *Kǎośēng* states that what remains after a tree has been cut down is called a *zhū*. The *Shuowén* says it refers to the roots of a tree, composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "zhū. The final rhyme is *wǔgǔ*; the *Yùnyīng* states that a tree without branches is called a *wù*, though it may also be written as *wù*.

*Tǎn* (pronounced *tān* with the initial *dàn*): According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means level and even; it is also said to mean clear and open. Wang Bi’s commentary on the *Zhouyī* states: "Tǎntǎn" means there are no dangers or obstructions (*wūjiè*). The *Cāngjiépiān* states: "Tǎn" means manifest. The *Shuowén* states: "Tǎn" means peace and security; it is composed of the radical "earth" (*tǔ*) and the phonetic "dàn."

Regarding the character *chí* (池): Kong Anguo’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that "stagnant water is called a *chí*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "a pond (*bī*)," formed with the radical for water and the phonetic element of *chí* (abbreviated) with the pronunciation *zhī* (下之繞反). The *Zuozhuan* states that "a *zhǎo* (沼) is also a *chí*. Lexicons state that "an embankment-pond is called a *zhǎo*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines *zhǎo* as "a pond," formed with the radical for water and the phonetic element of *zhào* (召) with the pronunciation *zhǎo*. The character *zhào* itself is composed of the radicals for "knife" (刀) and "mouth" (口); its appearance as *ǎo* (𠮦) in the scriptures is an error.

Regarding "tiles and rubble" (*wàlì*): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "tile" (*wà*) refers to an earthen vessel; it is a pictograph used for covering roofs. "Female" (*pìn*, pinyin: bìn) is called *zhēn* (pinyin: bǎn); "male" (*mù*, pinyin: mǔ) is called *zhèng* (pinyin: tóng). The *Shuowen Jiezi* further states that "rubble" (*lì*, pinyin: lì) refers to small stones or broken fragments of stone. "Sand" (*shā*) is written as *jiǎo*. The "tiles and rubble" mentioned in the present sutra are metaphors for broken tiles, crushed stones, and discarded debris.

The character *tǒng* (統): The commentary on the phonetics states it means "to lead" (*tǒnglǐng*) or "to continue" (*xù*). The standard orthography of antiquity and the present day states it means "to record" (*jì*). It is composed of the radical *mì* (糸), which means fine silk, and the phonetic *chōng*. The lower part, *shīyè*, according to the commentary on the phonetics, means "to govern universally" (*jiāntǒng*) or "to gather" (*liǎn*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "to pull and hold. It is composed of the radical *tǎo* (扌), which has the sound of "hand," and the phonetic *nié* (聶), pronounced *nìshè*.

*Re* (熱): The *Kao* commentary states that it means "heat" or "summer. The *Shiming* says it is pronounced *ruo* (悅) with the radical fire, meaning "to burn," like the burning of fire. The *Shuowen* says it means "warmth," composed of the radical fire and the phonetic *she* (埶), with the sound *ruo*. The lower character, *tang* (唐) with the tone *lan* (藍), the *Kao* commentary states it refers to a disease of water in the chest and diaphragm; the *Jixun* also says it is a disease of water in the chest. The *Gujin Zhengzi* says it is composed of the radical *na* (疒) with the phonetic *nüe* (女厄), and the simplified form of *tan* (談) as its phonetic.

"Qian" (潛) [pronounced with the initial *j* and final *-ien* according to the *Yǐnyùn*]: In the *Erya*, "qian" means "to sink"; in the *Guangya*, it means "to submerge"; in the *Shuowen*, it means "to wade through water. It is composed of the radical "water" (*shui*) and the phonetic "can" (*qigan*). It is incorrect for the scripture to write it as "qian" with two "heavens" (*tian*). The character below, "feng" (馮), [is pronounced with the initial *fu* and final *-en*]. The *Jixun* states that it means "to lie hidden. The *Guangya* says it means "to store away. The *Shuowen* says it means "to lie in wait. Because it refers to lying in wait for a person, it is a compound character formed from "person" (*ren*) and "dog" (*quan*). It is a word formed by combining these meanings.

*Xiáng-áo* (翔翱): "Xiáng" is pronounced with the upper tone *gāo* (高) and the lower tone *xiú-yáng* (徐羊). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Mao Shī* states: "Xiáng-áo is like *xiāoyáo* (逍遙, carefree wandering). The *Hán Shī* states: "Xiáng-áo means to roam. The *Erya* states: "Xiáng-áo is the flight of birds. The *Jixùn* says: "Xiáng-áo is high-flying. The *Kǎoshēng* says: "It is the appearance of birds flying back and forth slowly. In ancient usage it was written as *xiáng* (翔). The *Shuowén* says: "Xiáng-áo is circling flight. Both characters are composed of the radical for "feathers" (*yǔ*) and the phonetic components *gāo* (臯, pronounced *gāo*) and *yáng* (羊), which provide the sounds.

Regarding the term *jiānhuò* (箭筈): the commentary on the *Shēng* (考聲) states it is the name for a type of bamboo, similar to *xiǎo* (篠) but smaller; its large leaves can be used for arrows. It was originally called *shǐ* (矢), hence the name for an arrow is now *jiàn* (箭). The *Shuowén* says: "An arrow (*jiàn*) is a shaft (*shǐ*); it takes the radical 'bamboo' (*zhú*) and uses 'qián' (前) as the phonetic. The *Shēng* commentary further states: "The *kù* (枯) in *jiànkù* (箭口) is pronounced *huó* (活). According to this, the *jiànkù* is the mouth that receives the bowstring. The scriptural text uses the character *guǎ* (栝) with the radical 'wood' (*mù*), which is also acceptable; however, the correct form has the radical 'bamboo' (*zhú*) and uses 'guǎ' (栝) as a simplified phonetic. The pronunciation of *guǎ* is *kuò* (闊), as in *tángguǎ* (糖栝).

Volume 518, Part 1. The character *xiàng* (巷) is pronounced as *jiàng* (降). The *Mao Shī* states that it refers to a path between neighborhoods (*lǐ*). The *Shījì* states that the "Eternal Lane" (*Yǒngxiàng*) was a minor path within the palace. The *Shuōwén* states it is a road within a town or village (*yìlǐ*). Because it is said to be located within a town, it is composed of two *yì* characters to form a semantic compound (*huìyì zì*). In seal script (*zhuànwén*), it is written as 巷; in the *Ěryá*, it is written as 衖; in archaic script (*gǔwén*), it is written as 𨜕.

*Tángjuān* (徒即反): The *Zìshū* states that "táng" means "void. The *Yùpiān* states that "táng" means "idle. The *Kǎoshēng* states it refers to speech that is inappropriate. According to this, "stubborn" (*wán*) refers to a dullness and turbidity of consciousness. The *Yùnyīng* says: "It refers to weapons that are not sharp. The *Shuōwén* says: "Dùn means blunt. It is composed of the radical *jīn* (金) and the phonetic *tún* (屯), with the sound *tún*. "Blunt" (*wàndùn*) refers to being dull and unrefined. It is composed of the radical *jīn* (金) and the phonetic *tún* (屯). The sound is *tún*.

"Staying among burial mounds" (*zhǎngjiān*)—the first character is pronounced *lǒng* (with the tone reversed) and the second is pronounced *qián*; this has already been explained in the four hundred and fifty-third fascicle of the preceding scripture.

Regarding auspicious signs (*śrī-lakṣaṇa*), the *Zhouli* (Rites of Zhou), in the section on the *Dian Rui* (Director of Ritual Tokens), states that the *Yu Rui* (Jade Tokens) are what Zheng Xuan calls "auspicious tokens of trust. When virtue moves the mountains, rivers, hills, and mounds, then miraculous fungi (*zhicao*) grow; when rites and music are established, then auspicious winds arrive—all such things are auspicious omens. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as: "Auspicious token-jade; it takes the radical 'jade' (*yu*) and the phonetic 'duan' (abbreviated) to form the character."
The previous section, volume four hundred fifteen, has already fully explained how they manifest deceptive appearances and dwell above.

*Rākṣasa* is a Sanskrit name for a class of spirits; the word is pronounced with a retroflex long vowel (ra-ksha-sa), though in ancient translations it was simply called "Luoche" (羅剎). This type of ghost-spirit possesses the power of karma and supernatural abilities, flying through the air with ease and devouring the flesh and blood of sentient beings; they are the most ferocious and evil. As for the *rākṣasīs*, they have their own separate lands dwelling on islands in the great ocean; by means of their spiritual powers, they can transform themselves into beautiful and lovely forms to seduce and entice people, luring them in before devouring them, all as described in the *Buddhacarita Sūtra*.

The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "The character *bàn* (貌) [meaning 'appearance'] is composed of the radical 人 and the phonetic 半; the character 半 is composed of 八 and 牛. The *Guoyan* states that *lǚ* and *bàn* are synonymous, though it is sometimes written as *lǚ*. *Bò* (勃) with the first tone: *pú* (蒲) and *mò* (沒) as reversed; this was already fully explained in the previous volume 429. *Lǐjiàn* (履踐):

the first character *lǐ* (履) has the initial *lí* (梨) and the final *zhǐ* (旨) as reversed; the second character *jiàn* (踐) has the initial *qián* (錢) and the final *yǎn* (演) as reversed; both were already explained in the previous volume 455.

Regarding the character *tiāo* (挑): the *Tǐyáo Fǎn* (體遙反) and the *Yùnquán* (韻詮) state it means "to incite or provoke. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it means "to pick out or pry open" (*yīngyuè fǎn*). *Jǔbí* (㓷鼻): The first character, *jǔ*, is pronounced with the *yú* and *qì* rhymes. This has already been explained in the previous scripture, Volume 455. *Jùjiě* (鋸解): The first character, *jù*, is pronounced with the *jū* and *yù* rhymes.

The *Guóyǔ* states: "Among the middle punishments, knives and saws are used. The *Kǎoshēng* says: "To *qiāng-táng* is to use a saw. The *Fāngyán* says: these are variant names for a saw. *Dǐnjiè* (釘解): The second character, *dǐn*, is pronounced with the *mǎi* rhyme. The character *shè* (涉) is commonly used in the sense of "to traverse" or "to cross. According to the *Cangjie pian*, it means "to walk within water. The *Shuowen jiezi* states that to walk across water is called *shè*; it is composed of the radical *bù* (foot) and the phonetic *zhuǐ* (water), with the pronunciation *shè* (the *ruǐ* rhyme). In antiquity, it was written as *zhēn*.

Yanma Wang (琰魔王) is the name for the King of the Netherworld in the Sanskrit language; the old translation "Yanluo Wang" (閻羅王), with the characters pronounced *yán shī rǎn* and *mó*, is an erroneous and abbreviated form. The correct Sanskrit pronunciation is *Yama* (*yán yǎn*); ancient translators rendered it as "Equality."

*Líhēi* (黧黑): The upper character *lí* is pronounced with the initial *lì* and the final *zhī* (力知反). The *Tōngsùwén* states that "mottled black is called *lí*. The *Zuǒzhìchuán* says: "To bring guilt upon another is called *wù* (誤). The *Shuōwén* defines *wù* (誤) as "error"; it follows the radical *yán* (言) and takes *wú* (吳) as its phonetic.

*Zhān* (pronounced *lián* in the *Hánshī*; the *Kǎoshēng* says it means "to be soaked"; the *Shīzhí* says it means "slightly moist"). *Lǐjì*, Confucius said: "When rain *zhān*s the clothes, one loses their proper appearance. "Bù xiào" (不齅) [pinyin: bù xiū jiù fǎn]. This was already fully explained in the previous volume 456. 522. Volume 522. There are no characters in this volume that require phonetic or semantic glosses.

523. Volume 523. "Xián hài" (嫌害) [upper character: xíng yán fǎn; lower character: hé lài fǎn]. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it means "an evil mind" (烏固 fǎn).
