The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, from Volume 566 to the end of Volume 600, totaling thirty-five fascicles.
Volume 566: The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 566. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang.
Ānanda (translated into Chinese as Qìngxǐ, "Joyful Celebration";

formerly transcribed as Ānán, which is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit) and Kauṇḍinya (formerly transcribed as Jiāochénrú; he was one of the five bhikṣus whom the Buddha first delivered when he had recently attained enlightenment).
Gupta-pāda (笈防鉢底) is an abbreviation of the old translation *Kauṇḍinya*.
Haridraka (褐麗筏多) is an abbreviation of the old translation *Revata*. Mahā-maudgalyāyana (大採菽氏) retains the original Sanskrit;

he is also called Mahāmaudgalyāyana (大目乾連), or Kulidatta (俱律陁), or Kulita (拘隷多), or Kulika (俱利迦)—all of which are corruptions or abbreviations. His true Sanskrit name is *Mahā-maudgalyāyana* (摩訶冒[引]螚孽[二合]羅[引上聲]). His distant ancestor was a seer who subsisted on eating green beans (*mudga*), and thus it became his clan name. The character "螚" (nǎo) is pronounced with the second tone, as in "néngdé" (能得).
Mahākātyāyana (the "kang" and "qia" are pronounced as such; "dian" is pronounced as such).
"Najiu" [i.e., Mahākātyāyana] was formerly called Jiāzhānyán; this is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit term.
Pilindavatsa (畢藺陀筏蹉): *Vatsa* is pronounced with the *cangke* (倉柯) reversed; the old translation was Pilengqieposuo (畢陵伽婆蹉). Upāli (隖波離):
the old translation was Changpoli (償波離); the difference lies in the lightness or heaviness of the initial consonant.
Rāhula is his former name, which was Rāhula.

Regarding the explanation of "shàolóng" (紹隆), the first character is pronounced with the *cháng* (常) and *dǎo* (遶) finals reversed, and the second character has the *lì* (力) and *chōng* (沖) finals reversed; this has already been seen in the previous fascicle.

Tuṣita is the Sanskrit name for one of the six heavens within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*); in the language of Táng, it means the Heaven of Contentment (*Tuṣita*). A Bodhisattva in his final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*) appears as the king of this heaven.

"Lièshí" (礫石) is pronounced with the "fǎn" (反) of "jī" (鷄). According to the *Erya*, it refers to water flowing into a stream; the *Shuowen* states that a mountain cavity where there is no passage is also written as "xī" (谿) with the radical "water," or as "xī" (磎) with the radical "stone. This character "bōxī" (磻磎) appears in the *Zuanyun* (纂韻), but it does not carry this meaning. The second character, "gǔ" (谷), is pronounced with the "fǎn" of "gōng" (公). The *Shuowen* defines it as: "A spring emerging and flowing through is called a 'gǔ' (valley); it is a compound character formed from 'water' and 'half-visible' [the character for mouth], signifying its meaning."

The character *qiān* (愆) has three variants: the first is pronounced with the initial *kǎo* (考) and the final *yù* (遇); the second is explained as meaning "crime" (*zuì*) according to the *Yùnquán*; the *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radical "heart" (心) and the phonetic *jiān* (幵), where *jiān* is pronounced *qǐ jiān* (啟堅). It is an error for the classics to use *shēn* (𠍴) instead; the archaic script (*gǔwén*) writes it as *píng* (平), the *Zhòuwén* as *qiān* (諐), the *Shuōwén* as *qiān* (愆), and it is also written as *xī* (㥶)—all of which are ancient characters.

Regarding "慚恥" (cán chǐ): the upper character is pronounced with the *zhàng* (藏) and *nán* (南) finals; it is the "virtue of shame" (*cándé*) mentioned in the *Shàngshū*. The *Shuowén* defines it as "shame"; it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "zhǎn" (*zhǎn shēng*). The lower character is pronounced with the *chī* (癡) and *lǐ* (里) finals; according to the *Kǎoshēng*, it means "humiliation. Lexicons define it as "shame. Wèi Hóng wrote it as "誀" (*shàn*), which is an archaic form. The pronunciation of "癡" is *chǒuzhī* (丑之).

*Zhuā* (as in *zhù guā*)—the phonetic for *zhù* is *zhú kuà*. The *Shēnglèi* writes it as *lí*; it means to strike or beat. According to the *Kǎoshēng*, *zhuā* means to strike; it is also a horse-whip. It is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "guò. The lower character is pronounced *dé gěng*. The *Guǎngyá* states that *dǎ* also means to strike. The *Pīcāng* says it is a *bàng* (staff); the phonetic for *bàng* is *páng xiàng*. The *Shuōwén* says it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "dīng. Lu Fayan reads it as *dū zhì*; this Wu pronunciation is not accepted here.

The character for *mángyì* (blindness/cataract): the upper radical is pronounced *mò-péng* (反); the *Yùpiān* states it means "blind and dark. The *Shuowén* says: "Blindness (*máng*) refers to having no pupil in the eye. It is analyzed by sound as consisting of the radical "eye" (*mù*) and the phonetic "wáng" (*wángshēng*). The lower part is pronounced *yú-jì* (反); the *Kǎoshēng* says it refers to a film (*yì*) in the eye. Lexicons define it as an obstruction or film over the eye, analyzed by sound as consisting of the radical "eye" (*mù*) and the phonetic "ēi" (*ēishēng*). The pronunciation of *ēi* is the same as above. In the present scripture, the character is written with "one" (*yī*) and "eye" (*mù*), forming *yí* (𪾼), which is incorrect.

*Yíng* (鎣): The upper radical is *jīn* (金); the phonetic component is a simplified form of *yíng* (螢). It refers to the luster emitted by polished objects. The character *jīng* (經) is written with *yù* (玉) as the radical, forming *yíng* (瑩); this vulgar form is also in common use. The lower part is pronounced *shēng* (升) with the initial *lì* (力). The commentary states it means "to polish," "to carve," or "to refine. The *Jíxùn* (集訓) defines it as "to wear" (*fùzhuó*), "to cleanse," or "to purify. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means "to scrub"; it is composed of the radicals *shí* (食), *rén* (人), and *jīn* (巾).

*Shao* (如矟): Pronounced *shao* (山卓反). According to the *Guangya*, it means "spear. According to the *Beicang*, it is a spear eighteen feet long; it is formed with the radical *mao* (矛) and the phonetic *xiao* (肖). *Ru* (如): Pronounced *ru* (𧘂昌恭反).

According to the *Guangya*, it means "to face" or "to encounter," and also "to strike. In the *Zhouyi*, it refers to "walking. Regarding the sound, it means "to strike. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "a crossroads where four paths diverge"; it is formed with the radical *xing* (行) and the phonetic *tong* (童).

*Jun* (pronounced *jun*, with the second tone) means to pursue fame; it is also written as *fen* (with the third tone). It refers to the filling of the voice and the arousal of the spirit and breath. Zheng Xuan says it is the fullness of angry qi. The *Cangjie pian* identifies it as *fennan* (pronounced *men*). The *Shuowen jiezi* defines it as anger and resentment; it is also written as *lin* (𢤬), which is an archaic character.

*Xiàn-hèn* (叶鹽反): *Yùn-quán* explains it as resentment and doubt; it is a phonetic derivative of *kǎo*. It means malice of heart; *wū-gù* (烏固反). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means an unevenness of mind; it is composed of the radical "woman" (*nǚ*) with the phonetic element "jiān" (*jiān*). In the scriptures, it is written with the radical "heart" (*xīn*) as *qiàn*; this is also interchangeable. *Hé-gèn* (何艮反): According to the *Cangjie Pian*, it means resentment and grievance; it is composed of the radical "heart" with the phonetic element "gèn" (*gèn*).

The character 罩 (zhào) is pronounced with the upper radical *fāng* (wù fǎn) and the phonetic *xiùn*. Its explanation has already been seen in the preceding text. The lower part, 卓 (zhuó), is pronounced with the phonetic *jiào*. The *Mao Shī Chuán* states: "Zhào is the same as zhuò. The pronunciation of 篧 is *kuò*. Guō Pǔ’s commentary on the *Eryā* says: "Zhào is a net for catching fish. The *Shuowén Jiězì* states: "It is a bamboo vessel for catching fish, composed of the radical 岡 (gāng) and the phonetic 卓 (zhuó). It is also written as 䍜, 羄, 䈇, or 箌; all of these are archaic characters.

"Shu-hu" (儵忽) [the characters are pronounced zhù fǎn]. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that "shu-hu" denotes a state of extreme rapidity; it also says that "shu-hu" is like a flash of lightning. The *Guoyá* explains that "shu-hu" refers to light, with the phonetic component "you" (攸). The sound of "you" is *yóu*. Alternatively, it may be written as "shū" (倐) with the radical for fire, or as "shū" (跾) with the radical for feet; these are all archaic forms of the same character.
567. *Páng* (胮脹): the first character is pronounced as *pǔ* with the *jiāng* rhyme;

the second character is pronounced as *zhāng* with the *liàng* rhyme. Volume 567. *Kēngkàn* (坑坎): the first character is pronounced as *kè* with the *gēng* rhyme; the second character is pronounced as *kāng* with the *gǎn* rhyme.
*Yù* (爩熱): The first character is pronounced *wěi* (上委律反) and the second is *shè* (下然設反).
*Piàoyáng* (飄颺): The first character is pronounced *pǐ yáo* (上匹遙反) and the second is *yáng liàng* (下羊亮反).

*Ní* (淤泥): The first character is pronounced *yú jù* (於據反); according to the *Zishu*, it refers to green mud in water; according to the *Shuowen*, it means sediment (*yū zǎi*). According to the *Yupian*, the mud and grass in water is called *yū*, and foul-smelling mud is also *yū*. The second character is pronounced *nú jī* (奴雞反); according to the *Yupian*, soil that becomes soft when wet is called *ní*.
"Water-drop" (shuǐdī): the character *dī* is pronounced as *ding* with the *lì* tone; the *jīng* (scripture) version uses *tì*, which is a vulgar form.

"Fēnfù": the upper character *fēn* is pronounced as *fāngwén*; it refers to the fragrance of incense. The ancient script is written as *yūn* (𡵳), derived from *chǔè* (屮, pronounced *chǔliè*), meaning the distribution of fragrance from the initial growth of grasses; according to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of *chǔè* and the phonetic *fēn*. In modern clerical script (*lìshū*), it is written as *fēn* with the radical for grass (*cǎo*). "Fēn" means harmony. The *jīng* version uses *xiāng* (香) instead of *fèn* (馚), which is incorrect. The lower character *fù* is pronounced as *féngmù*; according to the *Hànshī*, "fēnfù" describes the appearance of fragrant scent.
*Pínyú* (嚬𡄱): The first character is pronounced *pí* (毗寅反); the second is pronounced *yù* (酒育反).

It means feigned conduct (*wèixíng*), deceit and falsehood (*zhàwàng*), and unreality (*bùshí*). According to the *Kǎoshēng*, it refers to hypocrisy (*jiǎozhà*) and deception (*qī*). Alternatively, it may be written as *wéi* (譌) with the radical for speech.

The term "guǐ" (詭) is used here as the opposite of "jūwěi" (居委). According to the *Zìshū* (字書), it means "deceitful. The *Guǎngyá* (廣雅) states that "guǐsuí" (詭隨) means "vile. The *Shuōwén* (說文) defines it as "to demand falsely," or alternatively, when written with the radical for "heart" (心), it becomes "huì" (恑), meaning "strange or extraordinary."

"Āi-hàn (懷憾). "Ū-huī (上戶)" is pronounced *guāi-fǎn* (乖反). The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (毛詩傳) states: "Āi means to think longingly. Kǒng [Yǎng] says: "Āi means to be at ease. The *Shì Fǎ* (諡法) states: "To be compassionate and benevolent yet die young is called Āi. "Zhí yì yáng shàn yì āi" (執義揚善曰懷): according to the *Shuō Wén*, "niàn sī" (念思, to think with longing) is written with the radical for the heart (*xīn*) and the phonetic *huái*. *Huái* is pronounced *hù guāi fǎn*. In archaic script it is written as 㜳, or alternatively as 褢. In the classics, there is a variant written as 褱, which is used in the sense of "to store" (*xié cáng*), but that is not the meaning here. The lower character, *xiàng* (向), is pronounced *dàn fǎn* (噉反). Kǒng's commentary on the *Lùn Yǔ* states: "Hàn means resentment. It is written with the radical for the heart and the phonetic *gǎn*.

*Sihe* (嘶喝). The first character, *si*, is pronounced with the initial *xian* (先) and the final *ji* (賫) reversed [i.e., *xi*]. Examining its phonetic value, it refers to a mournful sound. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "mournfulness" (*bei*) is a sound; it is composed of the radical "speech" (*yan*) and the phonetic element "this" (*si*). In the scriptures, it is written as "mouth" (*kou*) followed by "this" (*si*), which is a vulgar form. The *Picang* states that "sī" (*si*) means the sound is dispersed. The second character, *he*, is pronounced with the initial *jie* (芥) reversed [i.e., *ha*]. Examining its phonetic value, it says the sound is choked. The *Guangya* states that "sīhe" (*sihe*) refers to a sound that is deep and subtle. In character dictionaries, it is sometimes written as *yōng* (𡀽) or *yuan* (𣣶), both of which are archaic forms.

The character *zhuō* (拙) is pronounced with the initial *zhuan* (專) and the final *rè* (熱); it refers to a voice that is not skillful or refined. The character *sè* (澀) is pronounced with the initial *shuāng* (霜) and the final *jí* (戢); it refers to a voice that is not smooth. In the scriptures, the three stops follow [the rule for] *sè*, as the vulgar character is not valid.

*Jiangshu* (降澍): The first character, *jiang*, is pronounced with the *gang* rhyme group (as in *jiangxiang*). According to the *Erya*, "to descend" (*jiang*) means to fall down; the *Jixun* glosses it as "to drop. The *Cangjie pian* writes it as *yin*. The *Shuowen jiezi* provides a gloss identical to that of the *Erya*, stating it is composed of the radical *fu* (阜) and the phonetic *xiong* (夅). The second character, *shu*, is pronounced with the *zhu* rhyme group (as in *xiazhushu*). The *Huainanzi* states: "The irrigation and drenching of spring rains cause nothing on earth not to grow. The *Shuowen* also says: "Timely rain drenches and gives life to the myriad things. It is composed of the radical *shui* (水) and the phonetic *shu* (尌).

*Zhānrú* (霑濡): The upper character is pronounced *lián* (輒廉反). In the *Mao Shih*, it means "to moisten" (*zhān*). Regarding the phonetic component *shēng* (聲), it refers to slight dampness. The *Liji* states: "Confucius said: 'When rain moistens one's clothes, one loses their proper appearance. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: *Zhān* (霑) is pronounced *rǎn* (𩃵音染); the *Zishu* says *zhān* (霑) means "slight dampness. It is composed of the radical *yù* (雨) with the phonetic *zhān* (沾). The lower character is pronounced *shú* (而殊反). The *Jixùn* says it means "soaking" (*zhānzì*). The *Zitong* says *niǎo* (𣽈) means "slight dampness," and further notes that *niǎo* is also synonymous with *zhān*. It is composed of the radical *shuǐ* (水) with the phonetic *fú* (𦓔), which is pronounced *xū* (音須).

*He yi* (赫奕): The first character is pronounced *gé* (格) in the *Shàngxiǎng*. In the *Ěryǎ*, it says: "Hèhè" (赫赫) means "swift. Guo Pu states: "It is the appearance of being flourishing and rapid; according to the *Fāngyán*, it means 'to issue forth. The *Guǎngyǎ* says: "Hèhè" means "bright. The *Shuōwén* says: "It is the appearance of a deep red, composed of two characters for 'red' (*chì*), with the phonetic *yáng yì* (羊益). Alternatively, it is written as *chǐ* (󲃝) with the radical 'fire' (*huǒ*). The *Màoshī Zhuàn* says: "*Chǐ chǐ* (󲃝󲃝) is the appearance of fire. The *Shuōwén* agrees with this, stating it is composed of the radical 'fire' and the phonetic 'red' (*chì*).

568. Volume Five Hundred and Sixty-Eight. **Xīngsào (腥臊)**: The upper character is pronounced *xìng* (as in *xìngjīng*, "essence of victory"), though it is sometimes written as *shèng*. The commentary on the *Shūjìng* by Kǒng [Yáng] states that *shèng* means "stench. Dú Zǐchūn says it is the stench of pig fat. The *Shuōwén* says it is the stench of dog fat; it is composed of the radical for "flesh" (*ròu*) with the phonetic element *xīng*. The *Shuōwén* also records it as *yǎo* (鮏), meaning "fish stench. The *Lǐjì* states: "Among meats, those that are thin and raw are called *huì* (鱠). The lower character is pronounced *zāo* (as in *sūzāo*). The *Zhōuwǔlǐ* states: "In summer, one should use *gāosào* (膏臊). Zhèng Zhòng says it is the stench of pig fat. Dú Zǐchūn says it is the stench of great fat. The *Shuōwén* also says it is the stench of pig fat; it is composed of the radical for "flesh" with the phonetic element *sào*. *Sào* is pronounced *sāngdào*. It is sometimes written as *tāo* (鱢). In the *Zhōuwǔlǐ* passage regarding the "seasonal fats" (*shàngāohuì*), the text reads *zhǎo* (󲘷), which is a vulgar variant.

*Chòu* (臭): The upper character is pronounced *chāng* (昌) with the *shòu* (獸) radical; it appears in the "Wang" (王) section. "Stench" (*chòu*) is a general term for the vapors of all things. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "a dog knows the tracks of birds and beasts by their stench," thus it is composed of the "dog" radical and the "self" (*zì*) radical. The "self" here is the archaic form of the character for "nose. It is incorrect for the classics to write this as *zhòu* (臰). The lower character is pronounced *yì* (喙). Gu Yewang states that "filth" (*yè*) means not being clean. The *Yunying* states that "filth" means evil. Examining its phonetic, it means "wasteland. It is also written as *huì* (薉). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the "grain" (*huó*) radical and the phonetic *suì* (歲).

*Guàn-xǐ* (盥洗): "Guàn" is pronounced with the ancient initial *dǎn* (反). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means to wash the hands; it is composed of the radical *jiù* (臼) and the element *shuǐ* (水), with *míng* (皿) signifying a vessel. *Jiù* is pronounced *jū* (掬); *míng* is pronounced *měi* (美) with the final *fǎn* (反). The *Chunqiu Zhuan* says: "He presented the water and performed the *guàn-xǐ*. There is also a reading with the departing tone (*qù-shēng*), pronounced *gǔ-wán* (古翫), which is also acceptable. *Xià* (下) is pronounced *xiān-lǐ* (先禮). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means to wash the feet.
*Yán*: Upper radical *yǎ* (咸反), with the phonetic *kǎo*; it means a precipice or a mountain cliff. Lower radical *xuán* (玄決反); according to the *Zìshū*, it refers to the hollows of Confucius.

*Hǎn*: Radical *hē* (呵), with the phonetic *dàn*. The *Máo Shī Zhuàn* states that *hǎn* means "rare. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is the *gāng* (岡) radical, with *gān* (干) as its phonetic. It denotes a mountain ridge.
*Yà* (upper character pronounced *yì*, lower character pronounced *wù gù*): To loathe or detest.

*Gōu* (pronounced *gǒu* or *hòu*): To examine; to hook and take; to draw out. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to a curved piece of iron, composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic element "hook" (*gōu*).

*Pèi* (upper radical *bi*, pī; lower radical *dé*, dé): The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is the horse's bridle. It is composed of *zhuān* (pinyin: zhuān) and the semantic element *sī*. Gu Yewang says: "The bridle is that by which one controls the horses within the carriage. *Lè* (lower radical *dé*, dé): The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is the head-strap, bit, and mouthpiece of the horse. It is composed of the semantic element *gé* and the phonetic element *lì*.

Regarding "jí" (jealousy/envy): the upper radical is qíng (情) with the reversed form, and the lower is dāng (當) with the reversed form. King Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states: "To harm the worthy is called jí; to harm beauty is called dù. Zheng’s commentary on the Preface to the *Mao Shi* states: "To [harm] because of beauty is called dù; to [harm] because of conduct is called jì. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical for woman (女) and the phonetic element hù (戶).

*Yòu* (誘): To transform through enticement. In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is written as *yǒu*. It means to guide, to instruct, to lead, and to advance; it implies mutual exhortation and movement. It is composed of the radical "speech" (言) and the phonetic element "xiù" (秀).

*Tì* (鬀): Pronounced with the initial *tiān* and final *dì*. It refers to shaving the hair. The character used in the sutra is *tì* (剃), which is a vernacular form. It denotes the sound of a razor and the act of shaving.

"Xūfà" (鬚髮): The upper character, "xū" (鬚), is pronounced *yú* (逾) [in some contexts], though the *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as "xū" (須) and defines it as "moustache" (*zī*). The lower character, "fàn" (藩), is pronounced *fēn* (󰣿); according to the *Kaosheng*, it refers to the hair on the crown of the head. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "fà" (髮) means "the root of the hair," composed of the radical "biāo" (髟) with the phonetic "bó" (犮). "Biāo" is pronounced *shānrèn* (衫刃), and "bó" is pronounced *pómò* (蒱末). It is also written as "jù" (󲎪), both of which are archaic characters.

Regarding "zǎoyù" (to bathe): the *Guǎngyá* states that it means "to cleanse"; the *Cāngxiépiān* says it means "to wash the hands. Gu Yěwáng notes that "zǎo" is synonymous with "xǐ" (to wash), meaning to make something clean. The second character, "yù," according to the *Shuōwén*, means "to wash the body"; it is composed of the radical "water" (氵) and the phonetic element "gǔ" (谷) in abbreviated form.

Volume Five Hundred and Sixty-nine. [The character] *yìng* (瑩) is pronounced with the rhyme *yīng* (縈, 󲙨). It means to polish or wipe; it may also be written with the radical for metal (*jīn*) as *yìng* (鎣), which is identical. The following character, *chú* (除), is pronounced with the initial *lí* (離). [The character] *kǎo* (考) refers to investigating sounds and governing principles; it means to cultivate what is old. [The character] *xiū* (修) is formed from the water radical (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic *tái* (台). It means to cultivate or repair.

"Jiǎo-jué" (皎潔): "Jiǎo" (皎) is pronounced with the *xiǎo* rhyme-group in the upper character; the *Shuōwén* states it is composed of "bái" (white). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* says: "Jiǎo means radiance. The *Fāngyán* says: "It means clarity. In the lower character, "jiān" (堅) is the phonetic component and "niè" (嚙) is the radical; it signifies purity and stillness. It is composed of "shuǐ" (water) and "jié" (絜) as the phonetic.

*Kuài* (康膾反): A clod of earth; according to the *Zìshū*, it refers to a lump of soil. In the *Yílǐ*, it says: "While lying on a mat of straw, one rests his head upon a clod. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "a lump of earth" (*tǔpó*). The character is composed of the radical *tǔ* and the phonetic *kuǎi* (abbreviated) with the pronunciation *pǐjué* (匹角反). *Kuǎi* has the pronunciation *wǔzuì* (五罪反). It is also written as *kuì*, which is an ancient character representing its shape. Below, *chéng* (呈) has the pronunciation *shí* (石反). The *Guǎngyá* states that *zhì* (擲) means to toss or shake. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "to seize. Its correct form is *zhì* (擿); the version used in the scriptures following [the commentary of] Zhèng is a vulgar character.

*Chǎn* (磣): This character for "wounds" and "sores" is pronounced with the *bǐng* (稟) radical and the *kǎo* (考) phonetic; it refers to the dust of sand and earth. It may also be written as *chěn* (墋) with the *tǔ* (土) radical, which is identical in meaning. The lower radical is *dú* (斛), and Kǒng [Yǎng] annotated the *Shàngshū* that it means "poisonous harm. The phonetic *kǎo* (考) signifies "evil" and "pain. According to the text, "poisonous harm" (*chǎndú*) refers to jealousy and malice, or a person who is cruel. The *Shuowén* states: "A plant that harms people. From the *chuò* (屮) radical and the *dú* (毒) phonetic. *Chuò* is pronounced *chǔliè* (丑列); *dú* is pronounced *ài* (愛). In the *Zhengjian* commentary on the *Mao Shi*, "not fearing" (*budan*) is explained as follows: *Dan* means difficulty; it also means fear. *Qú láo* (劬勞): Jia Ji says it means "exhaustion"; the *Erya* says "diligence"; the *Shuowen* says "intensity. It is composed of the radical *lì* (力). Those who exert their strength undergo much toil. *Xín xiá* (親狎): Pinyin *xiá* (霞甲反). In the *Lunyu*, it says:

"The petty person is familiar with the great man. Kong Yingda says: "Familiarity (*xiá*) means proximity. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan* says: "Familiarity (*xiá*) means practice. It is also written as *xiá* (狹), which is the same character; it is composed of the radicals *quǎn* (犬) and *jiǎ* (甲) [with *jiǎ*] abbreviated for its phonetic component.

*Gēnzhū* (Root and Stump): The first character, *gēn* (root), is pronounced with the initial *gāng* (as in *gāng-ēn*) and the final *fú* (as in *fú-wù*). In his commentary on the *Laozi*, Wang Bi states: "The root is the beginning. Regarding its phonetic analysis, it is the fundamental basis.

The second character, *zhū* (stump), is pronounced with the initial *zhì* (as in *zhī-shū*). According to the *Kǎo Shēng*, the remains of a felled tree are called a stump. The *Shuowén Jìzì* explains that the character for "wood" (*mù*) consists of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic component "zhū" (*zhū-shēng*). 570. Volume Five Hundred and Seventy. The *Kǎo Shēng* states that the remainder of a tree after being cut down is called a stump. The *Shuowén* states that the character for "root" (*gēn*) takes "wood" (*mù*) as the radical and "zhū" as the phonetic.

*Yi* (抑): Pronounced *shàng* (上) with the tone *lì* (力). Jia Dui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states it means "to restrain" (*yìzhǐ* 抑止). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states it means "to diminish" (*yīsǔn* 抑損). Ru Chun’s commentary on the *Shiji* states it means "to suppress or bend" (*yūqu* 抑屈); this is as in the *Chuci*: "To bend the heart and suppress the will" (*qūxīn ér yìzhì* 屈心而抑志). The *Shuowen* writes it as *fǎnyìn* (反印), where *fǎn* (反) is pronounced *yīlì* (一力) and *yìn* (印) is pronounced *yīrèn* (一刃). In the Stone Classics, the character is written with the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) added from the character "seal" (*yìn*), forming *yì* (抑); it is a variant form. Below, *zǔ* (祖) is pronounced *guò* (過). Jia Dui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* says that "breaking the edge" is called *cuò* (挫). The *Shuowen* defines *cuò* as "to destroy" (*cuī* 摧); it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic component "zuò" (*zuòshēng* 坐聲).

"First, *zhé* (pronounced *shàn* or *yán*): the *Shuowen* says it means 'to advance,' derived from the ancient character *zǐ* (古㞢), composed of the radical *rén* (人) and the phonetic *zhāng-rè* (章熱). It also means 'to break' or 'to bend. The standard form in the *Shuowen* is composed of two *chǔo* (屮, pronounced *chǔ-liè*) and the radical *jīn* (斤), which forms the component *zhé*. The commentary explains that the two *chǔo* represent grass; to cut grass with an axe is called *zhé*. The Small Seal script subsequently joined the two *chǔo* together, erroneously resulting in the ancient form *qí* (󲑑), which was then adopted as *zhé* with the radical *shǒu* (手). The pronunciation *chū* (出) refers to the hand."

"稟性" (bǐng xìng) [means] "nature as received. Kong's commentary on the *Shūjìng* states that "稟" means "to receive. The *Shuowén Jiězì* says it means "bestowed grain," written with the radical 禾 and the phonetic 㐭; 㐭 is pronounced lǐ jǐn. It is an error for the classics to write it with the radical 示.

The character *yī* (衣) is pronounced with the *wǔ* and *fáng* finals; it refers to the sound of the grass *kǎo* (考). It is the end of a word for a type of grass. However, there is another kind of grass leaf that resembles a sword blade; if one touches it, it injures the person. The non-Buddhist practitioners of the Vātsīputrīya school (Líxì wàidào, 離繫外道) take this as clothing, inflicting injury upon their own skin and flesh as a form of asceticism (*duḥkha-caryā*).

*Máo* (茅) is pronounced *mǎo* (with the *bāo* rhyme). In the *Zhouyi*, it says "using white *máo* grass for a mat. According to the *Shuowen*, *máo* refers to the *jiān* grass; it is composed of the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) with the phonetic element "spear" (*máo*). *Jiān* is pronounced *gǔwán*. *Máo* is pronounced *mòhòu*. Regarding *bài* (稗), its pronunciation is *bài*. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that it is a grass resembling *lǎn* (a type of grain). Jiao Rong said that fine rice is called *bài*; it is also written as *bài* (粺), which is likewise acceptable.

The character *yù* (芋) [is pronounced with the initial *yú* and the rhyme *yīng*; it refers to the plant *dūchī*. Sū Jìng’s *Běncao* states that "yù" is also called *cígū* and has approximately six varieties, namely: green yù, purple yù, true yù, white yù, liánchán yù, and wild yù (*yěyù*). All of these are poisonous, and among them, the wild yù is the most severe; eating it kills people, though it may be consumed after being boiled with ash-water. The *Shījì* says, "Under Mount Mǐn, those who obtain the *dūchī* will not suffer hunger until they grow old," which refers to this. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is called "yù" because its large leaves and tuberous roots are startling; it is written with the radical for grass and the phonetic *yú*.]

"Ou" (五苟反, *wǔ gǒu fǎn*) refers to the sound of "kǎo"; it is the root of the lotus (*lián*). According to the *Erya*, "the lotus, the *hé*, the *fúqú*—its root is called *ǒu*. The *Yupian* writes it as 𦸲. The *Bencao* states that its other names are Shuizhidan (Water-Gem Cinnabar) and Liangan (Lotus-Sweet), and it may be eaten. The *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of the radical for water (*shui*) and written as 蕅; it is the root of the *fúqú*. It is composed of the radical for grass (*cao*), the radical for fruit (*guo*), and the phonetic element *shui*.

*Mù* (牧): Pronounced *mò* (with the final *-b* reversed). The Du Anshu commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "To raise cattle is called *mù*. The *Erya* says: "That which is outside the suburbs is called *mù*. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Fangyan* states: "*Mù* means to inspect. The *Shuowen Jiezi* also says it means to raise oxen and horses; it is composed of the radical "ox" (*niú*) with the phonetic element "zhi" (*zhī*). The sound of "zhi" is *pǔ-bǔ*.

The character *gòu* (搆) is used erroneously as a borrowed form (*jiǎjiè zì*) contrary to established custom; its correct orthography is *gǒu* (󲖛). Regarding its phonetic analysis: it takes "cow and sheep milk" (*niúyáng rǔ*) as its semantic component and "shǒu" (hand) as its phonetic component. Alternatively, it may be written as *gǒu* (󲖛) with "yáng" (sheep) as the semantic component. When this appears in the scripture as *jìng* (搆), it is the character for "framing timber" (*jiàncái cāomù*), which does not accord with the intended meaning of the scripture.
*Guṇḍa*: The first character is read as *jǐn* (軍) with the tone of *dí* (敵); the second character is read as *jiǔ* (窘) with the tone of *yún* (雲), reversed;

the third character is read as *fǎn* (反) with the tone of *tíng* (亭), reversed. *Kali*: The first character is read as *jiāng* (薑) with the tone of *qiē* (佉), reversed. This sound is borrowed to represent the Indic pronunciation; all instances of the character *kā* (*jiā*) in the Indic language that follow are pronounced in this same way.

"Jīchí" (賷持) is a vulgar character for "jìxī" (濟西). Examining its phonetic component, "chí" (持) means "to bestow wealth upon others. The *Shuowen Jiezi* records it as "jī" (齎), meaning "to carry and leave behind," formed with the radical "bèi" (貝) and the phonetic "qí" (齊). The version in the sutra is written as "jī" (賷), which resulted from a scribal error due to the similarity of the cursive forms.
*Yìngbì*: the first character is pronounced *yīng* (with the *qìng* tone), the second is *bēi* (with the *mèi* tone).
*Bōpóluò* (*bāpóluò*) is a tree name in the Sanskrit language; it is also called *Pípóluò*, belonging to the class of *Bodhi* trees, though one tradition identifies it as the *Bodhi* tree itself.

"Chóngdié" (repeatedly layered) is pronounced with the initial *zhǎng* and the final *tíng* (叶). Cāngjié says it means "to layer. The *Guǎngyá* says it means "thickness. Sòng Zhōng’s commentary on the *Tàixuānjīng* says it means "accumulation. Gù Yěwáng says it means "clarity. The *Shuōwén* states that in ancient times, the prison officials who adjudicated crimes would issue a verdict only after three deliberations (*sān yì*) were deemed appropriate; thus, it is composed of three "yì" (deliberation) characters. By adding "yí" (propriety), it becomes "dié. Wáng Mǎng changed the three "yì" characters—considering them too exuberant—to three "tián" (field) characters to form "dié. The text uses "dié," which is a variant form of the character.

"Xiāo" (銷) is pronounced with the initial *yáo* (小姚反); it is also written as "xiāo" (消).

"Cái" (纔) is pronounced with the initial *zàng* (藏灾反). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that it means "merely" (*càn*). The *Jíxùn* (集訓) explains it as "only able to" (*jǐn néng*). The *Shuōwén* (說文) defines it as "shallow" (*qiǎn*). It is composed of the radicals "silk" (糸) and "chūlè" (󱴹, pronounced *chǒulüè* 丑略反). The character "miǎn" (免) follows; it is formed from two "miǎn" (免) characters. This is "cái" (纔).

*Campaka* is the name for a flower and tree in the Sanskrit language; the older transcription "Zhanfu" (瞻匐) is a corruption and abbreviation thereof. This flower is fragrant, its scent being perceptible for several *li*, and it is as large as a *qiū* (楸) flower, brilliantly golden in color. It is also the name of a perfume.

The character for *men* (gate) is pronounced with the radical *tuǎn* (甜叶反). The *Zhuàn* (左傳) states: "They surrounded the city and attached [them] to the *men*. Du Yu’s commentary says: "It refers to the *nǚqiáng* (女牆, female wall) atop the city walls. The *Jīngǔ zhèngzì* (古今正字) states: "It is the *nǚyuán* (女垣, female enclosure) atop the city walls; it takes the radical *tǔ* (土) and the phonetic *yè* (叶). It is an error for modern people to universally pronounce this as *jì* (际).

"Fú-yàn" (wild duck and wild goose) is read as *shàng-fǔ* with no retroflex; Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states that "fú" means "quack-duck" (*ā*). Examining the phonology, it refers to the smallest variety of wild duck; in character dictionaries, it is composed of the radical "bird" and the phonetic "jǐ," where "jǐ" has the sound *shū*. This is a combination of form and sound, referring to the short wings of the bird that flutter (*jǐ-jǐ*) as it flies. The second character, "yàn," is read as *yán-xiàn*; it is sometimes written as "gàn" and is identical [in meaning]. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the "yàn" belongs to the class of geese (*é*). It is a bird that follows the sun, migrating south in winter and north in summer. The *Mao Shi* states: "The large are called *hóng* (swans), the small are called *yàn*. The *Shuowen* further defines "yàn" as belonging to the genus of geese.

*Baí tán* (the "tán" being pronounced *dānglán* [反]) is the name of a fragrant wood; it is fragrant both white and red, with the red variety being superior. In Sanskrit it is called *candana*, which was translated in ancient times as "Candanaxiang" (栴檀香). It originates from foreign overseas islands.

*Śirīṣa* is a term from the Sanskrit language; translated here, it means "Auspicious" (*śrī*), referring to the *saṃjñā* tree (the *kovidāra*). In common parlance, it is called the night-blooming tree (*yèhé shù*). Regarding the *śuka* (parrot):

the first character is pronounced as *wū* (with the *gēng* tone) and the second as *wú* (with the *fǔ* tone), though it is sometimes written as *shé*. The *Shān-hǎi-jīng* states that on Mount Huang there is a bird with green feathers and a red beak, possessing a human tongue and the ability to speak; it is named the parrot. The *Qūlǐ* says: "The parrot can speak, yet it does not depart from the flight of birds. This refers to it.

"Udumbara flower" is a corrupted and abbreviated transliteration of the Sanskrit term. In its original Sanskrit form, it is *udumbara*, which means "auspicious cloud-like celestial flower. This flower does not exist in the world; however, when a Tathāgata descends to birth or a Golden Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) appears in the world, this flower manifests due to the power of their great merit and virtue.
*Candana* (the first character pronounced *shān*, the second *táng-hán*) refers to the aforementioned red and white sandalwood incense.

*Vaiḍūrya* is a Sanskrit name for a jewel; it has no direct Chinese equivalent and belongs to the category of crystal. Its radiance is brilliant and transparent, pure and free from blemish; it may be slightly bluish-white, or distinguished by shades of red and purple. It is also a divine and spiritual treasure.

572. Fascicle Five Hundred and Seventy-two. *Yan'e* (掩遏): The first character, *yan*, is pronounced with the initial *yü* (at the end of the rhyme-group *jian*). It means to conceal or hide. The second character, *e*, is pronounced with the initial *an* (at the end of the rhyme-group *ge*). It means to obstruct or block.

*Gù* (辜) [pronounced *kū* in the ancient dialect]. According to the *Zhouli*, it refers to the office of "execution for treachery" (*gùlù*). Regarding the passage "All who kill the relatives of the King are executed (*gù*)," Zheng Xuan states: "The word *gù* means 'withered' (*kū*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "crime," composed of the radical *xīn* (辛) with the phonetic *gǔ* (古). The text here uses the hand radical to form *yíng* (𢪿), which is an error. *Fù* (負) [pronounced *fú* in the ancient dialect]. Gu Yewang says: "To turn one's back on kindness and forget virtue is called *fù*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to rely upon. It is composed of the upper part *rén* (人) and the lower part *bèi* (貝); it signifies that a person guards precious objects and thus has something to rely upon. Another interpretation is that it refers to receiving a loan and failing to repay it; therefore, "person" (*rén*) below "treasure" (*bèi*) forms *fù*. There is also a variant written with the hand radical as *fàn* (偩), which is a vulgar character.

Qièruò (怯弱): The first character is pronounced *qiāng* with the *yè* rhyme; the second is pronounced *ér* with the *zhé* rhyme. Píjuàn (疲倦): The first character is pronounced *píng* with the *méi* rhyme; the second is pronounced *kuáng* with the *yuàn* rhyme. Záo (鑿): The first character is pronounced *zào*.

According to the *Shēnglèi*, it refers to a chisel (*càn*; *càn* is pronounced *zǐxiàn*). The *Shuōwén* states that it means "to bore through wood. It is composed of the radical *jīn* (metal) and the phonetic *zuó* (abbreviated from *zuó*). *Zuó* is pronounced *zuò*. All characters such as *zuó*, *záo*, and *yè* share the component *zhù* (pronounced *xué* with the *fán* rhyme), which represents bamboo or wood growing in a thicket. The second character, *jǐng* (井), is a pictograph representing a well. A single dot in the center represents water; however, it is currently transmitted that this dot has been removed, leaving the form for *jǐng*.

*Geng* (stem/trunk): Pronounced *shàng xìng gēng fǎn*. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "the primary branch. According to the *Buya*, it refers to the stem of herbaceous plants. Pronounced *xià gāng yì fǎn*. According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to a tree branch; it is composed of the radical *mu* (wood) and the phonetic element *gàn* (pronounced *àn fǎn*).
*Di* (荻): Pronounced *tu* (with the *li* [歴] tone). Xu Shuchong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states: "Di means *huo* (young shoots). *Lú* (蘆):

Pronounced *láng dū* (upper tone) and *yú guǐ* (lower tone). The *Erya* states: "Jia and wei. Guo Pu says: "This is what is called *lu* today. It further states: "Jia-lu is the same as *wei*. According to this, these two plants are similar in species; the large is called *lu*, and the small is called *wei*. The *Yupian* states: "*Wei* is a large *jia*. In the *Shuowen*, the character for *lu* is composed of *peng* (廾), *ming* (皿), and the phonetic *lu* (𧆨); *lu* (𧆨) is pronounced *lǔ dū*. It is also written as *lǔ* (𧆓), which is the same. The text here uses *lu*, which is the common form.
*Kāṇḍa* (甘󰈕) means "night" and is the opposite of *kāśa* (美草).
*Dhātu* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "dharma-dhātu" (法界), where *dhātu* refers to the essence (*tattva*).

From this point downward—beginning from "the ground trodden by [the Buddha]" (*padbhyām ākrānta*) and continuing up to "the graceful chest" (*vinyasta-vakṣas*)—all [descriptions] explain the thirty-two marks of a Buddha. These were already fully explained in the fifth fascicle of the *Yinyi* (釋音義), specifically within the three hundred eighty-first fascicle of the sutra. Here, we provide only the phonetic transcriptions and do not seek their meanings.
*Lán* (in the character *lán-dǐ*) is pronounced with the *lì* and *yán* finals; the editions that write it as *xián* are incorrect.
*Suǒ-dǎo* (in the character *suǒ-dǎo*) is pronounced with the *táng* and *hào* finals, meaning "to tread. *Tǎn-rán* (in the character *tǎn-rán*) is pronounced with the *tā* and *dài* finals.
The character for *fú* (輻) in "spoke" has the initial sound of *fú* (福).
The characters for *wǎng* (輞) and *gù* (轂) in "rim" and "hub" have the initials *gāng* (岡) and *gù* (穀) respectively.
The term "soft" (*róu*)—with the rhyme *ruǎn* (兖) reversed—is written as *ruǎn* (軟) in the printed edition, which is incorrect.
Fāncháng (纖長): the character 長 is pronounced cháng with the yán (閻) rhyme. Mǎnwǎng (鞔網): the character 鞔 is pronounced mō with the mò (莫) rhyme.
Jiāoluò (交絡): the pronunciation of 絡 is luò.
Qi-hua (綺畫): the first character is pronounced as xū (墟) and the second as guà (卦).
Zú-gēn (足跟): the pronunciation is gēn (根).
Yǔ-fū (與趺): the pronunciation is fū (夫).
The two calves (shān) [are so called because] the upper part is pronounced with the *gǎng* rhyme and the lower part with the *ruǎn* rhyme;
they are *yīní* (pronounced *yíngxī*) and *zhōngyuán* (pronounced *chìlóng*).
Gànqīng (紺青): The first character is pronounced gāo (高) with the dark tone (去聲) and the second is qīng (青); the "qīng" character is derived from shēng (生) and dān (丹). Rùnhuálì (潤滑):
The first character is pronounced ér (而) with the level tone (平聲) and the second is huán (還) with the departing tone (去聲). Huàngyào (晃曜):
The first character is pronounced hú (胡) with the broad tone (廣韻) and the second is yáng (羊) with the level tone (要韻).

The neck (jǐng): the first character is pronounced as jīng (with the second tone), the second as yǐng (with the third tone). The shoulders and nape (jiānxiàng): the first character is pronounced as jiān (with the first tone), the second as hé (with the fourth tone, rhyming with gǎng).
The shoulder blades and armpits (bòyì): the first character is pronounced as bǔ (with the fourth tone), the second as gè (with the second tone); it is also read as yì (with the fourth tone).

Nāgrodha (the first character *nà* is pronounced with the *nà* and *què* tones; the second character *qiáng* is pronounced with the *yú* tone): formerly translated as *nikuluóduō*. *Han* (the first character *hàn* is pronounced with the *gǎn* tone;
the second character *yù* is pronounced with the *yú* tone). *ŭ* (the first character *yù* is pronounced with the *gǎn* tone; the second character *lì* is pronounced with the *lì* tone).
Yū-ke (the first character pronounced with the initial *yáng* and final *-zhū*, the second with *kū* and *hé*): sharp and keen (*fēng-lì*;
the first character pronounced with the initial *fāng* and final *-lì*). Wǎn-yuē (the first character pronounced with the initial *yú* and final *-yuǎn*).
The eyelashes (*akṣipakṣman*)—the character *pakṣma* is pronounced *piàn* (fǎn). The white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā*)—the character *hú* is pronounced *háo* (fǎn).
*Uṣṇīṣa* is a Sanskrit term; here it means "the mark on the crown" (*dingxiàng*), referring to the Buddha’s cranial protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*).
The sinews and veins (jīn-mò): the first character is pronounced shēng (反) and the second mò-bó (反).
The two ankles (liǎng-huǒ): pronounced hú-wǎ (反).
The kneecaps (xī-lún): pronounced yì (反).

Dūn-sù (the first character pronounced with the *shàng* tone as *qiāng-yè*; the second character pronounced with the *shàng* tone as *yì*). Qiè-ruò (the first character pronounced with the *shàng* tone as *qiāng-yè*).
Lí-yì (the first character pronounced with the *yù-jì* rhyme).
The navel is deep; it is not concave (wōuā) and not convex (tiánxié).
The skin has not yet healed. "Scabies" (jièxiǎn):
the first character is pronounced jiè; the second is pronounced xiānjiǎn.
"Moles and spots" (yǎndiǎn): the first character is pronounced īyǎn; the second is pronounced dīngyǎn.
Wen-zhui (疣贅): the first character is read as *qiú* (求) and the second as *tuǒ* (稅). Qīng-chè (清澈):
the second character is read as *lián* (纒). Chóu-mì (稠密):
the second character is read as *cháng* (長).
*Qimí* (綺靡): the first character is pronounced *qǐ*, the second is pronounced *měi*. *Lúnduǒ* (輪埵):
the second character is pronounced *duǒ* with the *dōu* and *guǒ* finals. *Yánmào* (顏貌): the second character is pronounced *máo* with the *tiáo* and *zhào* finals.
"Chou-hui" (臭穢): the first character is pronounced *chāng* with the *zhòu* tone; the second is pronounced *yāng* with the *wèi* tone.
"Dá-nà" (達那) is a Sanskrit term for the *uṣṇīṣa* (the fleshly protuberance on the crown of the Tathāgata’s head).
"Wēi-yí" (逶迤): the first character is pronounced *wěi*; the second is pronounced *yí*.
"Hung-yi" (匈臆): the first character is pronounced as *xǔ* (許) with the *gōng* (恭) rhyme group;

the second character is pronounced as *yú* (於) with the *lì* (力) rhyme group. "Yǒng-yuè" (踊躍): the first character is pronounced as *yáng* (羊) with the *zhǒng* (腫) rhyme group. Du Yu states that it means "to leap. The second character is pronounced as *yì* (弋) with the *zhuó* (灼) rhyme group. According to the *Guǎngyá*, these characters are mutually glossed as "to jump" (*tiào*) and "to advance" (*jìn*).
"Chou" (之儔) is pronounced *chí liú* (池流); it means "companion" (*pǐ*). "Qiè" (愜) is pronounced *qián jiá* (謙頰);
according to the *Kǎo Shēng*, it means "to accord with one's intent" (*dāng yì*). It is composed of the radical "small" (小) and the phonetic "kuài" (匧).
"Yīng" (縈) is pronounced *èi yíng* (恚營); according to the *Kǎo Shēng*, it means "to entangle" (*chán*) or "to wind around" (*rào*).
*He* (荷) [pronounced *dān* with the second tone] means to carry on the back or to assist; it is also written as *yán*.
*Zhòngdàn* (重擔) [the second character pronounced *dāng* with the second tone] refers to a heavy load; according to the phonetic analysis, it is a wooden device for carrying goods.
*Chíjì* (持髻) [the second character pronounced *jì*] is the name of the Brahmā-deva king.

573 (Volume 573 is missing) 574 Volume Five Hundred and Seventy-Four The "Good Yoke" (*śubha-yuga*) from the Mañjuśrī Section. The *yuga* is the transverse wooden bar at the front of a carriage. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is the yoke of a carriage, formed with the radical for "carriage" and the phonetic "e" (pronounced *ai*). In the dictionary, the character *e* is written with the radicals for "door" and "yi. The scripture uses the character *ye* (軶), which is a vulgar form. "Not abandoning the good yoke" is the name of a Bodhisattva. "Good yoke" is a metaphor for Great Compassion.

*Kātyāyana* is the Sanskrit name for a Great Arhat; the older transcription *Kātyāyán* is a corruption. *Kā* is pronounced as *jiāngqiē* (薑佉); *yán* is pronounced as *yǎn*. Volume 575, Part 575. Regarding the character "shè" (射) in *Mañjuśrī*:

it is pronounced as *chángyè* (常夜). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "The bow or crossbow is discharged from the body and hits a distant target; it is composed of 'body' (身) and 'arrow' (矢). In the Xiaozhuan script, it is written with 'cun' (寸). *Cun* refers to measurement. It is also said that *cun* is also the hand. Both forms are correct."

"Cū" (麁) is pronounced *cānggū* (反). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states that "chū" (󱍮) means "sparse" (*shū*). The *Guǎngyá* states that "chū" (󱍮) means "large. Its standard form is written as "chū" (󱍮), which according to the *Shuowén* consists of three deer characters; it is now abbreviated as "chū" (󱍮). Gu Yewang says that "chū" (󱍮) means "not good. The character below is pronounced *dīnglì*. The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* states that "dí" (的) refers to the target for archery. It may also be written as "diǎn" (㢩) with the radical "gōng" (弓). According to the *Shuowén*, "dí" (的) means "bright"; it consists of the "bái" (白) radical and the phonetic "shuó" (勺).

*Dàn* (pronounced *dōu guàn fǎn*): The *Cāngjié piān* states that it means "a hammer. *Zhí luó fǎn*: Zhèng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states that it means "to strike with a hammer. The *Shuōwén* states that it means "to refine or work [metal] slightly."
"Shāoliàn (燒鍊): 'lì' (歷) is pronounced *diàn* (殿). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means to refine metal; it is also written as *liàn* (煉), which is likewise acceptable.

In the classics, writing it with the radical 'silk' (*xi*) as *liàn* (練) is incorrect. *Jinpǔ* (金璞): 'pǔ' (普) is pronounced *bō* (剝). In Wang Bi’s commentary on the *Laozi*, 'pǔ' (璞) refers to the 'true' (*zhēn*). The *Yin Wenzixi* states that people of Zheng called unrefined jade 'pǔ'."

To "weigh" (chēngliàng) means to determine its lightness or heaviness through examination and calculation. The *Guǎngyá* states it means "measurement. The *Zìshū* states it means "to level. The *Yùnyīng* states it means "standard. The *Shuowén* states it means "a scale" (*quán*). It is composed of the radical "grain" (*huó*) and the phonetic "chèn" (pronounced *chǐ zhēng*). The archaic form is written as 爯; the form used in the classics is 秤, which is a vulgar character.

The "pao" (胞) at its initial stage is pronounced *páo* (with the radical for "tree" and the phonetic *huā*). It refers to the fetal membrane (*tao-li* heaven’s *pō-zhì-duō* tree flower). When the flowers of the *pō-zhì-duō* tree on the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven are about to open, the "pao" first appears. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is the membrane with which a woman's fetus is clothed at birth. In standard orthography, it is written as "pāo" (包); however, some write it as "pào" (皰), with the pronunciation *pú pǎo*. This meaning is also applicable.

Fényūn (上扶聞反，下迃雲反): The *Wenzi Jilüe* states that "fényūn" describes the appearance of flourishing vapors. The *Zītǒng* states that "yīnyūn" refers to the harmonious qi of yin and yang; it is a word formed with the preceding character as the semantic component (*xíng*) and the following character as the phonetic component (*shēng*).

*Chàngjiàn* (剏見): "Chàng" is pronounced *chuāng* (楚壯反) and rhymes with "yīng" (英). "Chàng" means "beginning. Examining its phonology, it signifies "the commencement. The *Jīng* (經) writes it as "chuāng" (創), which is a vulgar character. *Fēnqí* (分齊):
The first character is pronounced *fángwèn* (防問反) and the second is pronounced *jìlì* (寂麗反); it is also written as "jì" (劑).
*Zhì* (治): Pronounced *chú lí* (除離); the sound indicates "to govern," "to manage," or "to cultivate.
*Móyìng* (磨瑩): Pronounced *mò shì* (磨拭); alternatively written as *yǐng* (鎣). *Yìngchè* (映徹):
Pronounced *yīng jìng* (英敬) for the first character and *chí zhé* (持折) for the second; it means "penetrating" or "translucent. The scripture text writes this as *chè* (徹).

*Huì* (卉): Pronounced *guì* (with a level tone). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is the general name for grasses. In the Small Seal script, it is written as *hǔi* (芔), composed of three *chǒng* (屮) radicals; *chǒng* is pronounced *chǒu liè* (with a departing tone).

*Cónglín* (叢林): Pronounced *cú hóng* (with a level tone). It refers to grasses and trees growing in clusters. It is formed from the radical *zhuó* (丵) with the phonetic component *qǔ*. *Zhuó* is pronounced *chuáng xué* (with a departing tone). The version in the Classics uses *cóng* (藂), which is a vulgar character.
*Néi* (能逮): "néi" (逮) means to reach or to attain. *Rú* (如): "huàn" (幻) or "huán" (還);
the ancient forms are *yāo* (幺) and *yǔ* (予), both of which are archaic characters. 576. Fascicle Five Hundred and Seventy-Six. [The character for] *jiǎn* (羂):

the radical is *wǎng* (网) with the phonetic *jué* (决) and the classifier *quǎn* (犬). Its standard form is written as *jiǎn* (羂), though it is also written as *guàn* (罥). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that it refers to catching with a rope. The *Yùnyīng* (韻英) says it means to bind and capture. Examining *jiǎn*, it is a snare or net. *Gù Yěwáng* (顧野王) says: "Wǎng" (網) is the general name for nets and snares. The *Yì* (易) says: 'In ancient times, the Lord Páocháo tied ropes to make nets for hunting and fishing to nourish the myriad people. The *Shìběn* (世本) says: 'Língzhū created the *luó* (羅). Zhōngzhōng says: 'It was the Lord Fúcháo. It is also written as *luówǎng* (羅罔) or *wǎng* (网); these are all archaic pictographic characters."
*Nirukti* is a Sanskrit term; in the Tang language, it means "pure white consciousness" (*śukla-vijñāna*).

*Dīrgha* (pronounced *di-yi*, with the final syllable reversed) refers to a large wooden stake. The character for *qùe* (pronounced *kuáng-yuè*) is used here. According to the *Erya*: "A *zhí* is called a *yì*. Guo Jingchun states: "A *yì* is a wedge. It is also said that when it is fixed in the ground, it is called an *niè* (pronounced *yú-liè*).
"Practicing with something to be attained" (*yǒu suǒ dé xíng*); "Mèng" is pronounced *fǎn* (as in the following text).

"Awakening" (*wù*) is pronounced *kù* (according to the *Kǎo shēng*). It means that what was seen during sleep is believed upon waking; "mèi" is pronounced *mí bì*, and "jué" is pronounced *jiào*. The *Cāngjié piān* also states: "To speak while awakening from sleep is called *wù*. The *Shuōwén* agrees. It is composed of the radical *mián* (pronounced *mián*), the component *qiáng* (pronounced *qiáng*), the abbreviated form of *mèng* (pronounced *mèng*), and the phonetic *wú*. The *Zìshū* states: "*Mèng* is to awaken from sleep."

*Dǒngyè* (踊躍): The first character, *dǒng*, is pronounced with the *yōng* rhyme-group and the *shǒng* final. The *Gōngyáng Zhuan* states: "It means to ascend. The *Yùpiān* says: "To ascend. Dú Yǔ says: "To leap. It is composed of the radical *zú* (foot) and the phonetic *yǒng*. The second character, *yè*, is pronounced with the *zhé* rhyme-group. The *Ěryǎ* says: "It means rapidity. The *Guǎngyǎ* says: "It means to leap; it also means to advance. It is composed of the radical *zú* and the phonetic *dí*. *Dí* is pronounced with the *tú* and *lì* rhymes.

*Hù* (戶): The phonetic component is *jiǒu* (糺). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to piercing a wall and making a lattice window with wood; it is composed of the radical *piàn* (片) and the phonetic *fǔ* (甫). The *Guangya* states that it means "a passage" (*dào*). Dictionaries define it as "brightness. *Nyǒu* (牖): It means "a passage" according to the *Guangya*. In character dictionaries, it means "illumination."

*Qīngyáo* (傾搖): *qǐng* (頃) with the reversed *yīn* (縈) tone; it means to lean or tilt. The *Shuowen* writes this as *qǐng* (𣻳), with *xià*yángqiáo (下羊翹) as the phonetic. The *Jixun* states it means to shake or move; it takes the radical *shǒu* (扌) with *yáo* (䍃) as the phonetic. *Rǎng* (壤): *fèn* (分) with the reversed *wèn* (問) tone; it is a sound based on *kǎo* (考). *Sǎo* (󲐝) means to sweep or clear away;

*sǎo* is pronounced *sūzǎo* (蘇早). It is sometimes written as *rǎng* (𡏰), which is the same. The scripture uses *fèn* (糞), which is a vulgar character. The *Shuowen* states that *sǎo* (󲐝) means to sweep or clear away, taking the radical *tǔ* (土) with *biàn* (弁) as the phonetic; the lower part is read as *érzhǎng* (而掌). Kǒng (孔) says: "That which has no clods is called *rǎng*. Zhèng (鄭) says: "*Rǎng* is soil"; it is merely a variation of the term. The *Guǎngyá* says: "Destruction and dust; rich and supple. The *Shuowen* defines it as soft soil, taking the radical *tǔ* (土) with *xiāng* (襄) as the phonetic.

*Yan* (pronounced yān in the fanqie *yánjiǔ*) means "long duration. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states it means "long duration," and also "lingering. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Shanhaijing* states it means "stagnation" or "prolonged delay. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "water" (*shui*) and the phonetic element "yan" (*yān*).

Volume Five Hundred and Seventy-Seven. Section on the Vajracchedikā (The Diamond Cutter). *Paryaṅka* (cross-legged posture): the first character is pronounced "jiā" (upper tone), the second is pronounced "fú" (lower tone).
These are all vernacular characters;
the correct orthography is *jiāfū*.
Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Yili* states that *fū* refers to the upper part of the foot.
Gu Yewang stated that it refers to the surface of the feet.
According to the *Vajraśekhara*, the *Vairocanābhisambodhi*, and other sūtras, the methods for sitting are not uniform.
Herein, I shall briefly cite two or three examples.
It is explained that all four modes of deportment possess profound significance.
Regarding the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), there are briefly two types:
first, the "Auspicious" (Śrī), and second, the "Subduing Māra."

In all seated postures, one first presses the right toe against the left thigh, and then presses the left toe against the right thigh; this is the "right-over" position, and when the right hand likewise rests above the left, it is called the *māravijaya-āsana* (the Demon-Conquering Posture).
Most Chan schools transmit this sitting posture.

However, according to the yoga methods of the Vidyādhara-piṭaka teachings, the *śrīvatsa* (auspicious) posture is transmitted as superior for subduing māras. At times, one employs this *śrīvatsa* posture: first, press the left big toe against the right thigh; then, press the right big toe against the left thigh, so that the two palms face upward upon the two thighs. The hands likewise press the right over the left and are placed upward upon the crossed legs; this is called the *śrīvatsa* posture.
In the past, when the Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree,
his body was seated in the auspicious posture,
and his hands formed the mudrā for subduing Māra.
Therefore, the Tathāgata always remains seated upon this throne and turns the sublime wheel of Dharma.
If one relies on the secret yoga, then every movement and deportment of the activities of body, speech, and mind is none other than the secret mudrā.
The distinctions regarding the methods of sitting must all be transmitted by a teacher.

Some call it *ardhaparyaṅka* (half-lotus), some name it *bhadrapīṭha* (noble seat), some *gajarājaparyaṅka* (elephant-wheel-king seat), and some *vinītakasthāna* (the posture of the disciplined). When one accords with this dharma, one is then granted this sitting posture.

All of these are teachings revealed by the Buddha’s intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*). "Māṇava" is a term from the Sanskrit language; the Chief Translator of the Great Tang Tripiṭaka translates it as "Ju-tong" (儒童). According to the Tripitaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha’s translation of the *Mahāvairocana-sūtra* and his commentary on its meanings produced together with the śramaṇa Yi-xing, "Māṇava" should correctly be translated as "Victorious Abode" (*jaya-sthāna*). In their own tradition, non-Buddhist outsiders claim there is a self (*ātman*) within the body and mind that is the most supreme and wondrous. They constantly contemplate this self within their own bodies and minds as being perhaps one inch in size. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* also states: "They calculate that there is a self, either like a mustard seed or like a bean or wheat grain, which must be of pure color. If it were translated as "Ju-tong," the Sanskrit would have to be "Maṇu-va"; since the two translations differ, it is unknown which is correct. Please consult the Sanskrit original.

The character *bō* (橃) is pronounced with the initial *fán* (煩) and the final *yù* (󲗙). It refers to binding bamboo or wood and floating it upon water, which is called a *bō*. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "fa" (*fā*). The *Guangya* writes it as *qí* (𦪑) with the radical "boat" (*zhōu*), both of which are correct. When the scriptures use *fá* (筏) or sometimes *fá* (栰), these are both vulgar characters and are incorrect. Below [the character for "float"], *yú* (踰) is pronounced with the initial *zhù* (注). The *Guangya* states that *yù* means "to admonish. Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* explains it as "to inform and enlighten. The *Cangjie pian* defines it as "to illustrate through analogy. The *Lunyu* says: "The gentleman is enlightened by righteousness; the small man is enlightened by profit. The *Shuowen* defines *yù* as "to announce," composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic "yú" (*yú*). The character *yú* (俞) is composed of "ji" (*jīng*, 精立反) and "kē" (*kē*, 刂, 音公外反). When the scriptures write it as *yù* (喻) with the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*), this is a vulgar character.

*Mǐn'ǎng* (俛仰) is a character that reverses the conventional order. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that *mǐn* means "to bow" (*fǔ*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "lowering the head," its correct form being composed of *xié* (頁) and *zhào* (兆), written as *tiǎo* (頫). *Xié* is pronounced *jié* (頡); *yǎng* (仰) is pronounced *yúqiǎng* (魚襁反). The *Yi Jing* says, "Looking upward, one contemplates the patterns of the heavens. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines [the latter] as "raising the head," composed of *rén* (人) and *yǎng* (卬) as a phonetic component; *yǎng* is pronounced *yúliǎng* (魚兩反).

*Mén* (捫): The upper radical is *mò* (莫) with the phonetic *pén* (盆). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (毛詩傳) states: "To *mén* means to grasp. The *Yunquan* (韻詮) states: "*Mén* means to feel or to grope; *gōng* (搎) has the pronunciation *sūn* (孫), and *sò* (𢱢) has the pronunciation *suǒ* (索). The *Shuowen* (說文) states: "*Mén* means to grope; it is composed of the hand radical and the phonetic *mén* (門). The lower radical is *liáng* (良) with the phonetic *zhuì* (墜). The *Yunquan* states: "*Tì* (涕) refers to weeping tears. The *Shuowen* writes it as *tì* (涕) and states: "It is composed of the wood radical and the phonetic *lì* (戾)."

In a former life, he was King Kali (the Sanskrit term *kali* means "strife" and also refers to an unrighteous and evil king; the ancient translation as "King Kali" is a corruption). He was the king of Vārāṇasī in antiquity. (Note: *Kali* is here rendered as "Zangnengfan" [藏能反] and "Ciyongweifan" [次榮偽反] based on phonetic transcriptions.)

"Xi" (希) signifies longing or aspiration; it is derived from the rhyme for "rare. The *Fayan* (法言) states that it means "to hope. The version in the sutras uses "xi" (悕), which is a vulgar character. In ancient script, it is written as "xi" (希). "Ji" (冀) has the phonetic value of "ji" (寄); the *Yunquan* (韻詮) states that it means "to expect. The version in the sutras uses "ji" (冀), which is a vulgar character. According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to a commandery in the north, composed of "bei" (北) with "yi" (異) as its phonetic component.

The upper character 荷 (hé) is pronounced with the rhyme *háng* (as in *gěng*) according to the *Zìshū*; it means "to carry on the back. The lower character 擔 (dān) is pronounced with the rhyme *tán*; alternatively, it may be written as 儋 (dān), which is the same. According to the *Guǎngyá*, "dàn" is an auxiliary; phonetically it relates to "dān," meaning "to carry on the back. The *Zìshū* states that "dàn" means "to carry on the shoulder"; it takes the radical 手 (hand) and the phonetic 詹 (zhān). If the character is written as 檐 (yán) with the radical 木 (wood) in the scriptures, it is incorrect. "Yán" (pronounced yán) refers to the eaves of a house and does not have this meaning here.

It means to linger or delay; its upper radical is pronounced *jìngxī*. It refers to being obstructed or held back. In ancient texts it was written as 乩, and also as 卟. Its original form was 禾, and it is also written as 𮂱. According to the *Shuowen*, "稽" means to linger and stop; it is composed of 旨 (the semantic element) and 𮂱 (the phonetic). The character 禾 (grain) originally had a curved top when first sprouting from the wood, unable yet to rise upward. It is also pronounced *ài*, with the same meaning as the definition below. The character 留 (*liú*) is pronounced *lìchóu*. It is composed of 考 (the phonetic) and means to remain or stay. According to the *Shuowen*, "留" means to stop in a field; it is composed of 田 (field) and 󲄴 (the phonetic). The sound of 卯 is like that of 柳 (*liǔ*). In some versions it is written as 㽞, or as 𤲢, or as 㽜; these are all corruptions.

It is used for ascending and climbing (*dēng-xù*, pronounced *qù* with the fourth tone). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is a wooden staircase (*mùjié*), composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic element "abbreviated *dì*" (*diěi*).

"Shūhù" (儵忽) refers to the "coming and going in a flash" mentioned in the *Chuci* (*Wangyuan*), where Wang Yi’s commentary states it describes a state of extreme rapidity. It is also said that "shūhù" is like lightning; it may be written as "shū" (倏), with the character "wén" (文) added to the left, or as "shū" (𨁀)—all are identical in meaning.

Regarding the character *zhì* (質) in the *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (*The Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry*), it says: "It is the target for archery. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is written with the radical *xī* (夕); that which is written with the radical *bái* (白) is a vulgar form and is incorrect.
