*Feng* (峯): "The mountain peak; it is high and pointed. It is pronounced *fēng*. *Yìngshān* (韻英) refers to the summit of a mountain. It is sometimes written as *fēng* (峯), which combines the radical *shan* (山) with the phonetic *fēng* (夆). The lower character is pronounced *wúxián* (吾咸). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "yán" (巖) means "precipice"; the *Mao Shi Zhuan* says "yányán" (巖巖) refers to "accumulated rocks"; and the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "a cliffside. It is also sometimes written as *yán* (巖) with the radical *shí* (石), which is an archaic form.

Volume 588, Part 1 of 2. Regarding the character 莖 (*gēng*): *Guǎngyá* states that for herbaceous plants, it is called "stems" (*gēng*). According to the *Shuowén*, it means "the primary branch," written with the radical 艸 (grass) and the phonetic 巠 (*jīng*). Regarding the character 幹 (*gàn*): According to the *Shuowén*, it means "tree branches," written with the radical 木 (wood) and the phonetic 倝 (*gān*) or 岡 (*gāng*). It is a wooden pillar. It may also be pronounced in the departing tone (*gàn*), but this is not the intended meaning here and is therefore not adopted. Within the scriptures, there are instances where 幹 is written as 干 or 𦼮 (with the radical 艸), but these are all incorrect.

*Chai* (採): Pronounced *zǎi* (宰) in the upper tone, with the phonetic *kǎo* (考). It means to gather. It is also said that it means to pluck (*luō*, 捋, pronounced *kuò* [闊]). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means to gather; it is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic *cai* (采). *Xia* (下): Pronounced *zhāng* (張) in the upper tone, with the phonetic *kǎo* (考). It means to pick up or take from above. The *Tangyun* states it means to take by hand. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means to pick the fruit of a tree; it is composed of the radicals "hand" (手) and "shǎng" (啇) in abbreviated form as the phonetic.

Volume Five Hundred Eighty-nine, Chapter Five Hundred Eighty-nine: The Section on Patience (Kṣānti-varga). *Hua*: In the dialects of the Song and Wei regions, a plowshare is called *hua*. The *Shuowen* states that it has two blades; the character is composed of "metal" (*jin*) and the abbreviated form of "flower" (*hua*) as its phonetic component, with the reading *cha jia* (pronounced *chājiǎ*). It is also written as *du*. The lower part is read *tian nie* (pronounced *tiānniè*). The *Shanhaijing* says it is also written as *tie*. It is composed of "metal" (*jin*) and "ce" (*jie*) as its phonetic component. Today, iron is produced from the mountains of Taiyuan, where iron is abundant.

*Fèi* (虛費): The consort has not yet returned; it refers to the depletion of excellence and the dissipation of wealth. According to the *Guǎngyá*, *fèi* means "to diminish. The *Shuōwén* states that *fèi* means "to disperse wealth" or "to expend," composed of the radical 貝 (biàn) with the phonetic 弗 (fú).

590. Volume Five Hundred Ninety. Section on Diligence (*Jīngjìn Fēn*). *Yínggòu* (營搆): Pronounced *gǔ hòu*. According to the *Yùpiān*, it means "to join" or "to complete. It refers to the construction of structures, the assembly of materials, and roofing. The *Shuōwén* says it means "the accumulation of wealth," depicting the form of intersecting lines, composed of the radical 木 (mù) with the phonetic 芉 (miǎn). It may also be written simply as 芉, which is likewise correct.

Regarding "qiè" (怯): Qiang and Jie are reversed [in the rhyme]. Wang Yewang says that "qiè" means inferiority or timidity. In the *Fāngyán* (Dialectal Dictionary), it is said that "qiè" means to depart. The *Shuowén* writes it as 㹤; Du Lin states that the character for "qiè" is composed of the radical "heart" (心) and the phonetic "qiè," and it is also written as 祛 (qū). Below, "qú" (劬) has the rhyme yù. Regarding "kù" (懼): it means anxiety and fear. The *Shuowén* defines "kù" as terror, composed of the radical "heart" (心) and the phonetic "qú"; the archaic form is written as 愳.

*Wei* (萎): Upper radical *shang* (上), pinyin *yán* (炎) with the retroflex *huī* (麾) as the final; according to the *Kǎośēng* (考聲), it means resentment (*yuàn*). In lexicographical works, it refers to the disease of jaundice (*wěihuáng*) and weakness (*ruò*). Lower radical *xiān* (軒) with the final *yè* (謁); according to the *Kǎośēng*, it means panting (*chuǎnxì*) and coming to a halt (*tíngzhǐ*).

Volume 591, Part 591. *Gengmi* (秔米): "Geng" is pronounced *geng* (with the radical *keng*). *Jixun* states that *xian* (秈) is pronounced *xian*; it refers to rice. The character for *dao* (稻) is pronounced *dao*. According to the *Shenglü*, it is not the same as *li*. The *Shuowen* states that it belongs to the category of rice and is also written as *jing* (稉), following the radical *he* (禾) with the phonetic *gang* (亢, pronounced *gang*). The form used in the sutra, *ging* (粳), is a vulgar character.

*Dān* (with the initial *gān* reversed): an onomatopoeic word meaning to indulge in or to dally with. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "body" (*shēn*) and the phonetic element "yín" in abbreviated form. *Rǎn* (pronounced *ér yǎn* reversed): an onomatopoeic word meaning to defile or to adhere to.

592. Fascicle Five Hundred and Ninety-Two. *Pei* (皮, with the initial *mi* reversed): According to the *Guǎyá*, it means "to add. The *Hànshū* says it means "complete. Duan [Yuan] says it is a *páo* (robe). The *Shuōwén* says it is a garment for sleeping; it is one body-length plus half, composed of the radical *yī* (clothing) and the phonetic *pí*. *Xiàdé* (下德): *nài* (奈) reversed. *Kǎo* (考): the sound of the binding. Lexicons say it means "to tie. The *Shuōwén* says it is the *shēn* (sash). Men wear leather; women wear silk. It takes the form of tying and fastening a pendant, yet possesses a cloth (*jīn*), therefore the character for *dài* (belt/sash) includes the radical *jīn*. The *Jīng* (Canon) writes it as *dài* (戴, to wear on the head), which does not accord with the meaning of the Canon.

*Qi* (齊): Pronounced *hé* (何) with a retroflex final; this is a borrowed character (*jiǎjièzì*). Dictionaries divide it as *zhī* (之) and *jì* (劑), though the latter may also be written as *jì*; the following cases are analogous. *Guàn* (慣): Pronounced *guānhuàn* (關患);

according to the *Erya*, it means "habituation. It refers to being long practiced in a matter, called *guàn*. It is composed of the radical *xīn* (心) and the phonetic *guàn* (貫). The *Zhuozhuan* writes it as *guàn* (貫), and the *Shuowen* writes it with the radical *chuò* (辵) as *jiūn* (遦); the text here uses *cuàn* (串), which is a vulgar character.

The character *rěn* (荏) is pronounced with the initial *shàng* (上) and the rhyme *zhěn* (枕); it describes the appearance of grass being weak and supple. The character *rǎn* (苒) is pronounced with the initial *xià* (下) and the rhyme *yǎn* (琰); the *Qúnshū zìyào* (群書字要) states that it describes the appearance of grass flourishing. According to these sources, *rěnrǎn* (荏苒) refers to the gradual succession of events over the passage of time; this is what is called *rěnrǎn*. The version in the *Jīng* (經) uses the character *chán* (󱷴), which is a vulgar form.

"Xuán (欻)" means to move suddenly; it is the opposite of "yù" (鬱). According to the *Cāngjiépiān*, "xuán" means to startle or spring up suddenly. Xuē Cōng says it means "abruptly. The *Shuowén* states that it refers to something being blown up, composed of the radical "qian" (欠) and the phonetic element "yán" (炎).
Volume Five Hundred and Ninety-Three. Volume Five Hundred and Ninety-Three. Regarding the "white egret" (*báilù*):
The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states it is a "white bird. The *Erya* calls it the "chōngchú.
The *Fangyan* says that in the regions of Qi and Lu it is called *chōngchú*, while in the land of Wu and the region of Yangzhou it is called the "white egret. [This concludes] Lu Ji’s *Mao Shi Niao*.

The *Shouchongyushu* (Abridged Account of Beasts, Insects, and Fish) states: "The white heron (*bailu*) is as large as a rooster; its legs are green and measure one chi and seven or eight cun in length.
Its tail resembles that of a hawk, and its beak is over three cun long. On its crown and back, there are long feathers approximately one chi in length, which stand up in a bristling manner.
Guo Pu remarked: "People in Jiangdong today take these feathers to make false eyelashes; they call them 'the white heron’s mourning dress' (*bailu shuai*). They brush [them] away."
It was named for the abundance of these birds in the pond where the sūtra was preached by the side of the Śarabhaṅga Pond;
this pond is located within the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove to the north of Rājagṛha.

*Mān* (魔羂; *jué xuán fǎn*; also written as 󱺍 or 𦌾) refers to a snare used for capturing birds and beasts, according to the *Kǎo Shēng*. The *Yùn Yīng* states it means "to bind and seize. According to the *Jīn Gǔ Zhèng Zì*, *mān* (羂) is a "snare-rope" (*jué xuán*) meaning "to bind and seize. It is composed of the radical *gāng* (岡) and the phonetic *yuán* (肙), pronounced *jué xuán fǎn*, with *huàn* (詃) as its phonetic component.

*Zhì* (pronounced *zhèn*, with the radical for "stone" and the phonetic *máo*; the *Mao Shi* commentary states it means "to tether," while Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan* says it means "to restrain") is composed of the radical for "silk" (*miè*) and the phonetic *zhí*.
*Qímìu* (upper character pronounced *qīyǐ*, with the phonetic *míngjiù*)—the upper character is pronounced *qīyǐ*.
The character *jī* (激) is pronounced with the *fǎn* (反) *shēng* (聲) [radical] and means "water rushing and spraying.

The character *zhé* (折) is pronounced with the *chén* (臣) *rè* (熱) *fǎn* (反); according to the *Zuǒshì zhuàn* (左氏傳), it means "to damage" (*zhěsǔn*). It takes the *shǒu* (手) radical and the *jīn* (斤) *shēng* (聲) [radical], meaning "to break" (*cuīzhé*). The character *hóng* (紅) is pronounced with the *yuè* (岳) *fǎn* (反) and refers to the "tusk" (*shòudá*) of a beast. It is the correct form when composed of the *dāo* (刀) radical and *ròu* (肉) [radical]; its appearance as *jiǎo* (角) in the *Jīng* (經) [the *Lùóhàn jīng*] is an error.

Dà yán (dàn gàn fǎn). 594. Volume Five Hundred and Ninety-Four. CĀI YÍ (upper character: cāi, cǎi zāi fǎn; lower character: yī, yú qī fǎn). Dǔ’s commentary on the *Zuò zhuan* states: "Cāi means suspicion. The *Fāng yán* states: "Cāi means resentment. The *Shuō wén* states: "Cāi means a malicious person; it is composed of the radical 犬 (dog) and the phonetic 青 (qīng). [The second character,] YÍ (lower character: yí, yú qī fǎn): Kǎo’s commentary states: "It means to stop. It means duplicity. It means not yet determined. In antiquity it was written as 𠤗, and also as 󲀤; now it follows the Wú pronunciation with the phonetic 疏 (shū) and 󱾥 (sēng).

*Xián-lǔ* (鹹鹵): *xiá*, pronounced as in *yán* (巖); the *Shāngshū Hóngfàn* states, "Moistening downward produces saltiness. The *Erya* says, "Saltiness is bitter. The *Shuowén* says it is the flavor of the north; it is composed of *lǔ* (鹵, sound *lǔ*) with *xián* (咸) as the phonetic. The text [of some versions] uses *jiū* (酉) to form *qián* (醎), which is incorrect. *Xián-jǐn* (鹹𪉦): meaning "salty land"; *xià*, pronounced as in *lú* (盧) or *gǔ* (古). Duan’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* says it refers to land that is saline, barren, and thin. The *Shuowén* says it is the salty land of the west; it is composed of a simplified form of *xū* (𠧸) with *shēng* (省) as the phonetic. *Xū* (𠧸) is an ancient form of the character *xī* (西).

*Xiàn* (賣): [The character] *xiàn* is pronounced with the upper radical *xuan* (狷) and the phonetic *ying* (英). It means to sell or to boast of oneself; it is also written as *huán* (𧗳) or *sòng* (䝮), all sharing the same meaning of self-promotion. According to the *Shuowen*, it means to walk while selling. It is composed of the radical *xing* (行) and the phonetic *xuan* (玄). The lower part is pronounced with the initial *mo* and final *xie* (莫廨反). The *Jixun* defines it as "bringing forth goods for exchange. Its original form was written with the radical *chu* (出) as *chui* (󲏠); the current form *mai* (賣) is a simplified version.

Volume Five Hundred and Ninety-Five. Volume Five Hundred and Ninety-Five. No phonetic glosses available. 596. Volume Five Hundred and Ninety-Six. *Hóng* (虹): Pronounced *húng* (with the rhyme of *tóng*). According to the *Erya*, the *dìcǒng* is the *hóng*. In the *Monthly Ordinances* (*Yueling*), it is said that the rainbow first appears in the final month of spring and first hides in the first month of winter. The *Hanshu* writes it as *chóng* (虫). It is also pronounced *jiàng* (絳). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it resembles an insect, hence it follows the radical for insects; its pronunciation is *huǐ* (毀) with the initial *gōng* (工). The archaic form is *gòng* (羾), and the *Zhouwen* form is *qí* (󲒎). It follows the radical for lightning (*diàn*), which means "lightning. The lower part is pronounced *wǔjí* (五嵆). Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* identifies it as the female rainbow (*cīní*). This appears in the *Li Sao*. Sometimes it is written as *ní* (霓). The *Erya* says the *dìcǒng* is called *yú* (雩, pronounced *yú*). It further states: "The *ní* is called *qiè'èr*. Guo Pu says *qiè'èr* is another name [for the rainbow], appearing in the *Shizi*.
Hùcáng (昨郎反, zuóláng fǎn). 597. Fascicle Five Hundred and Ninety-Seven. Tídéng (梯蹬, tiān téng fǎn; note:

"tiān" is pronounced with the *tian* rhyme and "téng" with the *teng* rhyme). Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that it means "staircase. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is a wooden staircase, formed from the radical "wood" (*mu*) and the phonetic "di" (*di*). Xiàdāng (下當, xià dāng fǎn). Kǎoshēng (考聲, kǎo shēng). Dènglǚ (蹬履, dèng lǚ). *Yunying*: "To tread upon. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is written as *Dèng* (隥) with the radical "earth" (*fu*), meaning a steep slope (*qióng*). It is formed from the radical "foot" (*zu*) and the phonetic "dēng" (*dēng*).

598. Volume Five Hundred and Ninety-Eight. *Cuōmó* (撮磨). The upper character (*cuō*) is pronounced with the *cuàn* and *luǒ* finals and the *láng* and *kuò* initials; it is a derivative of the sound *kǎo* (to examine), meaning to grasp or pinch with the hand. It is a borrowed character. The lower character (*mó*) is pronounced with the *bō* final and the *kǎo* initial; it means to sharpen or polish, specifically to grind. In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is written as *shè*.
*Kōn* (空拳): Pronounced *kō* with the *kai* and *yuan* finals reversed;

the *Shēngyùn* states it means "a clenched hand. Volume 599, Part 599. *Huī* (灰): Upper radical *hū* with the *wēi* final reversed; the *Shuōwén* states it means "extinguished fire," composed of the radical *huǒ* (fire) and the phonetic *yòu*. Lower character *xí* with the *yìn* final; this is a vulgar form. The correct orthography is *㷄*. Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states it is "the remaining wood from a fire. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "the remains of fire," composed of the radical *huǒ* and the phonetic *yù*.

*Yān* (煙): *yàn* (宴) and *xián* (賢) are the rhymes; *guǎngpǐ* (廣疋) states it means "stench. Regarding the phonetic analysis: *huǒyān* (火煙) is the term; the *Shuowen* says it is "the vapor of fire," composed of the radical *huǒ* (火) with the phonetic *yīn* (垔). It is also written as *zhú* (燭); its ancient script is *zǔ* (󲕹) and its *Zhòuwén* (籀文) is *zǔ* (󲘔). *Xià* (下): *yìniàn* (翼念) is the rhyme. The *Shuowen* says it is "fire moving subtly. The standard form is *xián* (爓), now written in its abbreviated form. It is also written as *yàn* (𦦨), meaning "firelight"; the *Hanshu* uses *yán* (炎) as a borrowed character (*jiǎjiè*).

*Suo-lǚ* (the "lǚ" is pronounced like *sang* or *luo*; the sound is like *suo*, meaning a rope; it is composed of the radicals *shi* and *xi*, and its phonetic component is *mi*). To write it as *suo* is incorrect. *Liang-zhi* (the "zhi" is pronounced like *liang*): in the Nan-Chu region, when clothing is worn out, tattered, and poor, it is called *lan-lǚ*. According to the *Shuowen*, *lǚ* means thread; it is composed of the radical *mi* and the abbreviated phonetic *lou*.
*Āḷāra Kālāma*: This is the name of a non-Buddhist *ṛṣi* (sage) in the Sanskrit language; it has no direct equivalent in Chinese. 600. Volume Six Hundred, Part Six. *Yuán* (原): Pronounced *xí* (習).

According to the *Erya*, a high, level plain is called *yuán*, while a low, damp area is called *xí*. The *Shangshu Dazhuan* states: "The word *xí* means 'damp' (*shī*). It is also written as *yí* (隰). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to a slope below a ridge; it is composed of the radical *fù* (阜, meaning mountain/earth) with the phonetic *xiàn* (㬎).

*Xiōngbó* (凶勃): The upper character is pronounced *xǔ gōng* (許恭反) and belongs to the rhyme *xiào* (韻). It refers to a person; its phonetic component is *kǎo* (考). It means fierce or evil, and it also implies fear. Furthermore, in the third tone (*shàngshēng*), the *Shuowén* states it means "to disturb or terrify. It is composed of the radical "person" (*rén*) with *xiōng* (兇) below; the *Chunqiu Zhuan* (Spring and Autumn Annals) says, "The descendants of the people were terrified (*xiōngjù*)," which is an example of this usage. The lower character is pronounced *púmò* (蒲沒反). In the *Liji*, it means perverse or rebellious; the *Shuowén* defines it as "chaotic disorder. It is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) with the phonetic *bèi* (孛). In the scriptures, it is written as *bō* (作力), meaning vigorous, robust, and also synonymous with strength.
*Huì* (喙): Pronounced *yù* (衛) with a retroflex final; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "the mouth.
*Yǎnjiǎn* (偃蹇): The first character is pronounced *yǎn* (於蹇反) and the second is pronounced *jiàn* (囐反). According to the commentary, *yǎn* refers to arrogance and haughtiness.
*Jūqì* (拘縶): The first character is pronounced *jù*; the second is pronounced *zhīlì*. It refers to the imprisonment of a person. *Jiāngjiè* (壃界):

The first character is pronounced *jūqiáng*. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* says it means "boundaries. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *jiāng* (畺), stating: "A boundary; it is composed of two fields (*tián*), with their interior representing the three lines that mark its boundaries. It is also written as *jiāng* (疆) or *jiāng* (壃); all are interchangeable.

"Elāpattra Dragon King" is a corruption of the Sanskrit term. In its original Sanskrit pronunciation, it is correctly *Elāpattra* (with the "pa" pronounced with a retroflex [ṭ] sound and the "ttra" pronounced nasally). This is the name of a great dragon king and has no direct Chinese translation.

The Phonetic Explanations of All Scriptures, Scroll Nine.
Compiled by the Scripture-Translating Śramaṇa Huilin.
The *Damingdu Banruo Jing* (Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra) in thirty fascicles;

the *Mohe Banruo Jing* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra) in forty fascicles; the *Guangzan Banruo Jing* (Aṣṭādaśasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra) in fifteen fascicles; the *Banruo Chao* (Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra) in five fascicles; the *Daoxing Banruo Jing* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra) in ten fascicles; and the *Xiaopin Banruo Jing* (Svalpākṣara-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra) in ten fascicles—these six sūtras comprise one hundred and ten fascicles in total.
The phonetic transcriptions in this fascicle were all compiled by Xuanying.

*Fàngguāng Bōrě Jīng* (The Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra of the Emitted Light), Fascicle One. Compiled by Xuanying. *Lóuyuè* (羅閱): Pronounced with the "zhé" (拙) rhyme. According to the *Aśōrāja-sūtra* (The Sūtra of King Ajātaśatru), it is called *Lóuyuèqí* (羅閱祇); in the Jin language, this means "City of the King's Abandonment" (*Rájiyèchéng*, 王舍城). This is a corruption; the correct pronunciation is *Lóuyuèjiēlí* (羅閱揭梨). The meaning of *Lóuyuè* is "to sever and judge. Replacing "sever and judge" with "king" refers to one who is able to adjudicate the affairs of the people. *Jiēlí* (揭梨) is translated as "abode" (*shèzhōng*, 舍中). The general name for this is the City of the King’s Abandonment (*Wángshèchéng*, 王舍城). It is located within the kingdom of Magadha; this is the name of the city.

The *Nāśūtra* (那術經) also renders it as "shu" (述), with the phonetic transcription "tóng shí yù fǎn" (同食聿反). Alternatively, it is called *nayuta* (那由他); the correct term is *nayuta* (那庾多), which in the Central Kingdom (China) corresponds to one hundred thousand. The *Prabhāsa-sūtra* (*Guāngzàn jīng*) states "hundred million *nayuta* kalpas," which refers to this. According to the *Buddhacarita-sūtra* (*Fó běnxíng jīng*), one hundred thousand is called a *koṭi* (俱致), which here corresponds to ten million. One hundred *koṭis* is called an *ayuta* (阿由多), which here corresponds to ten billion. One hundred *ayutas* is called a *nayuta* (那由他), which here corresponds to one hundred billion; this should be calculated according to the preceding system.

"Po" (叵) is pronounced "wu" (我) with a reversed tone; it means to lean, tilt, sway, or move unsteadily. The scriptural text uses two forms, "po" (𧿽) and "zhe" (𨁟), or alternatively "e" (𡶅) and "e" (峨); however, the origins of these characters have not been seen [in standard lexicons].

"Dàn" (澹然) is read as *tú* or *lán*; according to the *Guǎngyá*, "dàn" means "peaceful. The scriptural text sometimes uses the two characters "dài" (憺) and "dàn" (淡), both of which share the same pronunciation and definition.

"Sāhē" (娑訶) is also called "Sāhélóutuō" (娑訶樓陀) or "Sāpó" (娑婆); these are all corruptions. The correct term is "Suǒhē" (索訶), which is translated as "Able to Endure" (*kṣānti*) or "Capable of Endurance. One term for it is the "World of Miscellaneous Assemblies."

"Xí" (習) is pronounced with the *xú* and *lǚ* rhymes; according to the *Erya*, it means "remnants" (*yù*) or "karmic undertakings" (*yè*). The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states that this refers to "severing the remnants of habitual tendencies" (*xiqì*).
"Jiāluóyuè" (迦羅越) refers to a lay devotee (*gṛhapati*) as found in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
"Fu dang fuwu fan": "fu" means the beginning; "dang" means the end. This signifies that from the initial arousal of the mind, one ultimately perfects the single kind of wisdom (*ekajñāna*).

"Wo ren" (我𪅆) is also written as "wo ren" (我𪅆), with the same pronunciation as *zilaofan*. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that "ren" (𪅆) means a group; Ru Chun’s commentary on the *Shiji* states it means a cohort.

Asura is also rendered as *asuro* or *asūra*, both of which are corruptions. The correct term is *asura*. *Sura* means "wine"; thus, it is translated here as "non-wine" (*a-* meaning "without"). It is also called "not a deva" (*a-* meaning "not"), or "heavenly being without wine. In the sūtras, they are also called "beings without virtue" (*asura*).

*Abhisambuddha* is a corruption; its correct form is *abhisambuddha*. *Abhi* means "manifest" (*xian*), *sam* means "equal" (*deng*), and *buddha* means "awakened" (*jue*). Thus, it is named "Manifest Equal Awakening. The *Chang'an-pin jing* (Sutra on the Chapter of Attaining Buddhahood) says "attaining the state of a Buddha," and the *Dapin jing* (Large Sutra) says "all dharmas in all their aspects"; these have the same meaning.

The sixth is called *kanda* (in the phonetic transcription *zāi*, with the tone *zuò* and *cái*). In the scriptures, it is also termed *sparśa* (contact). One should consider that *sparśa* can nourish mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), while a *kanda* can nourish branches, leaves, flowers, and twigs; as their functions are similar, it is so named.

"Sevenfold pain" (qī tòng) is also pronounced as "tòng-yǎng" (with the second character read with the *yí* and *zhǎng* rhymes). In the scriptures, this is termed "feeling" (*shòu*). It is called "feeling" because it is capable of receiving and experiencing suffering and pleasure.

Regarding the character *yǐ* (倚), it is pronounced as *yì-fǎn* (with the second character read with the *fǎn* rhyme); its meaning is "to abide. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "to lean" (*yǐ*) means "to rely upon. In the *Guǎngyǐ*, "to lean" (*yǐ*) means "to depend on. The scriptural text that uses the character *yī* (猗)—which is composed of the radical for "dog"—is not the correct form.
*Sarvajñā* is also called *sarvārtha*, or sometimes *sarvajña*; these are all corruptions. The correct term is *yojana*, which is translated here as "all-knowledge" (*sarvajña*).

*Yojana* (pronounced with the second syllable as *yu-zhu*) is also written as *you-xun*, *you-yan*, or *yu-sha-na*; these are all corruptions. The correct term is *yojana*, which is translated as "conjunction," "correspondence," or "calculation. It refers to a measure of distance equivalent to one *krośa* of this region (China), which is thirty *li*. According to calculation, five hundred *dhanus* make one *krośa*, and eight *krośas* make one *yojana*. This is what was formerly called the number of *li* traveled by a sage-king in a single day.

*Zhuji* (珠璣): "Ji" is pronounced as in *yīfǎn*. According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to pearls that are not perfectly round; other dictionaries state it means small pearls. *Chuāngxiàng* (窓向): "Xiàng" is pronounced as in *xǔliàngfǎn*.

The *Shijing* says, "Block the *xiàng* and seal the doors," and the commentary states that the *xiàng* is a north-facing window. The *Guǎngyǐ* says, "The *chuāng* is the *xiàng*. The *Cāngjié Jiěgǔ* says, "The *chuāng* is the main *yǒu*; the *yǒu* is the side window. It is so called because it assists in providing light."

2. Second Fascicle. [No characters can be phonetically transcribed or glossed. 3. Third Fascicle. "不惋" (bù wǎn): "wǎn" is pronounced with the "wū" and "huàn" rhymes; abbreviated as "惋," it means to sigh in lamentation, astonishment, or wonder.
Volume Four. Explanation of the Name *Tathāgata*: It means "to restrain" (*jiǎn*), for it is that by which one restrains and controls [the mind].

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, it is rendered as *tadāgata* (多他阿伽度), *arhat* (阿羅訶), and *samyaksambuddha* (三藐三佛陀); these are identical names. These are three of the ten epithets [of a Buddha]. They differ only in the lightness or heaviness of the Sanskrit pronunciation: *tathāgata* is translated here as "Thus-Come One" (*rúlái*); *arhat* as "Worthy of Offerings" (*yìnggòng*); and *samyaksambuddha* as "Perfectly and Fully Enlightened One" (*zhèngbiànzhī*).

*Pretas* (薜茘): The first character is pronounced *bì* (蒲計反) and the second is *lì* (力計反). Some say *Bide li*, some say *Bide liye*, some say *Biliduo*, and some write it as *Bilidu*; these are all corruptions. The correct term is *Pretas*. This is translated as "ancestral ghosts" (*zǔfù guǐ*). The old translation was "hungry ghosts" (*èguǐ*), which refers to the most inferior among the hungry ghosts. The pronunciation of *pí* (薜) is *bǔ miè* (補蔑反). In the *Rājā Śikhī Sūtra* (*Kǒngquèwáng jīng*), it is written as *Bilidu*; this is what the Liang dynasty called "hungry ghosts. The pronunciation of *bì* (俾) is *bī mèi* (卑寐反).

Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra (Bīnòu Wénduónízǐ; Bīnbìpín fǎn; also written as Fēnnòu or Bīnnòu Wénduófú; this should be translated as "the daughter Pūrṇamaṇḍitā," meaning "a woman fully adorned"; the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* calls her "the son of Pūrṇadarśana").

*Saṃnāha-saṃnaddha* should be translated as *mahāsaṃnāha-saṃnaddha*. The old translations render it as *mahā*, which means "great"; *saṃnāha*, which means "armor" (*kavaca*); and *saṃnaddha*, which means "donned" or "adorned. Thus, it is called "donning the great armor. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* refers to this as "the adornment of the great vow. Another interpretation states that *saṃnāha* means "great vow" and *saṃnaddha* means "self-vowed. Both of these are erroneous. The correct term is *phraṇāha*, which is translated as "armor" (*kaṅkaṭa*). *Naddha* is also said to mean "donned" or "clothed"; thus, it signifies being "donned in armor" or "clothed in armor. The character for "clothed" (*yī*) is pronounced with the initial *yǐ* (at the end of the rhyme).

"Buzhe" (不㧗) and "zimei" (側賣)—the latter being pronounced with two tones—mean to seize or take hold of. The *Tongsu wén* states that "che-wan" (掣挽) is called "buzhe"; the *Shuōwén* says "buzhe" means to drag by the hair, meaning to seize and pull. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dapin jing) uses "buqu" (不取), which is correct.

5. Fifth Fascicle. Regarding *yakṣa* (pronounced "yecha" with a retroflex *ch*, or sometimes "yecha"—both are corruptions): the correct term is *yakṣa*. This is translated as "one who can devour humans" (*néng dàn rén guǐ*), or alternatively as "the harmer" (*shāng zhě*), meaning one capable of inflicting injury upon people.

Cakravartin is correctly pronounced *cakravarti-arāja*; this is translated as "Wheel-Turning King" (*zhuanlunwang*). *Shi* (適) is pronounced with the *du* and *di* finals, and *mo* (莫) with the *mu* and *ge* finals;

it signifies that there is no one [who can equal him] and no [corresponding] characteristics. *Shi* is equivalent to "to oppose," meaning an opposing match; *mo* is equivalent to "to desire," meaning to yearn for.
The name of the samādhi is *Aniketasthita* (無態他伏).

Regarding "nest" (*ko*), it is also written as "cave" (*kuo*)—the same character with the radical for "mouth" and the phonetic *ku* (讀如苦和反). According to the *Xiao E'ya*, what chickens and pheasants hatch from is called a "nest" (*ke*), while what rabbits dwell in is called a "cave" (*ku*). This refers to resting when not living in burrows. The *Zhan Guo Ce* states, "A cunning rabbit has three caves," and this is also written as "cave" (*e*). It is the name of a samādhi.
*Gāi* (古來反, gǔ láifǎn): To encompass; it means "all" in the *Fāngyán*. Guo Pu says: "Gāi, xián, bèi, and jiē all mean 'to encompass' (*jiàn*);
it is also a term for *samādhi*. *Zhòng jì* (古文作𥟄, 同子力反, tóng zǐ lì fǎn): Millet; the foremost of the five grains. *Note: The character 𥟄 is an archaic form of 稷 (jì).*

The upper character 澆 is also written as 𣻏, both pronounced with the same phonetic *gǎo* (古堯反). The *Shuowen jiezi* defines it as "to pour water over; to irrigate. The lower character is also written in two forms, 濺 and 𠵖, both pronounced with the same phonetic *zàn* (子旦反). The *Shuowen jiezi* defines 灒 as "to splash so as to soil or sprinkle. In the *Shiji*, it says: "Within five paces, [he] splashed blood onto the Great King’s robes," using the character 濺. *Yangquan Wuli Lun* states: "Fearing that [the person] does not know the flavor, one spits 𠵖. This pronunciation is practiced in Jiangnan, while in Shandong it is pronounced *jiān* (子見反).
6. Volume Six. "Fan" (繁) and "bo" (薄) are rhymes; they are surnames of people.
"Cuo" (蹉) is pronounced with the *zhao* (󱍮) rhyme.
"E" (峨) is pronounced with the *wu-ge* (五歌) rhyme.
*Tuo* (咃) is pronounced as *shì hé* (士何). *Cuó* (嵯) is pronounced as *zuò gē* (作歌). *Lǔhù* (虜扈):

*lǔ* is pronounced as *lì gǔ* (力古) and *hù* as *hú gǔ* (胡古). According to the commentary on the *Hànshū*, *lǔhù* means "arrogant" (*zì dà*), referring to acting with unrestrained license. The *Yìnyì* (phonetic commentary) states that *hùbàhù* (跋扈) means to be self-indulgent and wanton. The scriptural text here uses *hùshì* (怙恃), but "relying upon" (*hù*) does not carry this meaning; what the sūtra refers to as arrogance (*jiāomàn*) is what is meant by "boasting and loftiness" (*gònggāo*).
*Kiṃnara* (the "giant" [pronounced *yān*] reversed) is translated here as "Incense-Seeking Spirit" (*Gandharva*).

*Xié* (pronounced *hú* reversed) means "to harmonize"; according to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it signifies harmony and union. The scripture text uses the character *ǒu* (偶) with the radical for "grass" (*cǎo*), which is incorrect. The *Shàngshū* (Book of Documents), in the passage "He was able to harmonize through music," has the commentary: "Harmony means to couple."

7. Fascicle Seven. "Wuǒ" (無耦) [the character for "wuǒ"] is pronounced with the *kǒu* rhyme group. "Wǒ" (耦) means a pair or match; it refers to being paired or matched. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, it is written as "děng bù děng" (等不等), which is correct. The text here written as "jǐ" (𧪓) is incorrect.

*Su-yāma* is sometimes rendered as *Suyāma*, which is translated here as "Heaven of Wondrous Goodness" (*Miaoshantian*). Furthermore, *yāma* means "time" (*shifen*), so *Su-yāma* signifies "Good Time"; this refers to the Lord of that heaven.
"Kuyi" (拘翼) is a corrupted abbreviation; his surname is Kauśika, which is identical to Śakra-devānām-indra, the Heavenly Lord Śakra, as they share the same title.

"Daojian" (道撿)—the character "jian" being pronounced with the rhyme *yan*—refers to restraining the mind through the Way; thus it is said, "Daojian. The *Dapin jing* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra) states: "If one enters the correct position (*samyaktva-niyāma*) of the śrāvaka," and so forth. According to the *Cangjie pian*, "jian" also means legal standard or regulation, and by extension, it implies restraint or inclusion.
"Four crossroads" (*sìjiào*, *gǔ* rhymes with *diào*) refers to the lanes at the four gates; this is precisely what is meant by the "four crossroads" in the *Lì*.

"To block" (*è*, *hé* rhymes with *jié*): according to the *Erya*, "block" means to stop. Now, "to block" is used in the sense of stopping one another in opposition; the *Cāngxiépiān* states that "block" means to intercept.
8 (The eighth fascicle is missing) 9. The Ninth Fascicle. Tishyagupta, or Tishyarakṣita, is translated as "Lamp-Light" (Dīpaṃkara); he is also called Buddha Dīpaṃkara.
The Nirmāṇarati Heaven—also called the Fanmiduotian (Brahmadeva) Heaven—is translated as the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations, or the Heaven of Joyful Emanations.
The Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven—also called the Poshebatitian (Vaśavartin) Heaven—is translated as the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations.

Ābhāsvara-deva (translated here as "Light-Sound Heaven" or "Heaven of Utmost Pure Radiance") is the third heaven of the second dhyāna. Although the scriptural text contains the character *huài* (譮), this is an error; the correct pronunciation is *huàì* (快).

Śubhakṛtsna is translated here as the Heaven of Universal Purity; it is the second of the three heavens within the third dhyāna. It is called "Universal Purity" because its bliss and purity are all-pervasive.

Regarding "Pola" (頗羅), this refers to the Heaven of Vast Results (Bṛhatphala), which is the third heaven. Among the fruits of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), this is the most excellent; therefore, it is named "Vast Result.

"Heng" (很)—pronounced with the *hu* rhyme—is used to mean a person who is stubborn and difficult to turn back, hence the name. As stated in the *Ugraparipṛcchā-sūtra*: "stubborn people," and in the *Amitābha-vyūha-sūtra*: "stubborn and deluded. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, it appears as "zēngshàngmàn" (增上慢); the text has "yuán" (元), which is pronounced with the *wǎn* rhyme (*wǎn* meaning dull and obtuse). "Wán" (頑) is not the original character.
"Baluo" (拔擢) is the opposite of "chongzhuo" (憧卓); according to the *Cangjie pian*, "zhuo" (擢) means to pull out or draw forth.

"Moqi" (摩祇) appears as "Moshe" (摩蛇) in the *Chang'an pin* and as "Mohui" (摩醯) in the *Xiaopin jing*; these are all corruptions of the Sanskrit term. In the *Mingdu jing*, it is rendered as "shendan" (神丹), which is a translation of its meaning.

10. The tenth fascicle. The ancient characters for *máo* (spear), *jiàn* (arrow), and *fēn* (pronged weapon) are three forms sharing the same pronunciation, *mò hóu*. According to the *Fāngyán*, in the state of Chǔ, the *jǐ* (halberd) was called a *máo*. The *Shuōwén* states that a *máo* is twenty *zhàng* long and is mounted upon a war chariot.
The "eight contemplations" (aṣṭa-vimokṣa) are the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vaimukhya*).

In the *Piṇḍola Sūtra*, the name is erroneously transcribed as Píngshā; its correct pronunciation is Bimbisāra. It is also called Pínpí, which translates as "firm form" (*ākṛti-dṛḍha*); alternatively, it is called Pínpí, meaning "complexion," and bālā, meaning "handsome. Or it is said that his physical appearance was exceptionally sublime.

The term *Yali* (耶利) is sometimes called *Duoshi* (墮舍利), sometimes *Duoshizhong* (墮舍種), or *Lichang* (栗唱), or *Lichang* (離昌), or *Liche* (離車), or *Liche* (𤝽車), or *Lichang* (梨昌); these are all corruptions of the Sanskrit original. The correct pronunciation is *Licchavi*, which means "Kṣatriya clan" or "royal lineage. The character *tiē* (呫) is pronounced as *chāng-yè* (昌葉反). In the sūtras and śāstras, it is sometimes written as *Liche* (離車) or *Lüche* (律車), both of which refer to the same thing.

The character for this [is pronounced] *chāo* (jiao) in reverse. "Miaozhào" (兆) is like a trigger; it refers to seeing things beforehand, and it also takes the form of the character for "traces" (*xiàng*). In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, it is written as "zuòfǎmòzhě" (作法沒者).

*Gandharva* is also called *gānduóluó* (揵陀羅), or written as *qiàndá pó* (乾沓婆), or *qiándá pó* (乾達婆), or *qiāntuó pó* (乾闥婆); these are ancient names. The current standard term is *jiàndáwǒ* (犍達嚩), which are merely differences in national pronunciations. This means "one who smells fragrance," also called "the deity of music. One version says "one who eats fragrance"; the old name "deity of fragrance" is also close to the meaning. In the sūtras, it is also rendered as "fragrance-sound deity. A semantic translation is "incense-seeking deity" (*xúnxīngshén*), which is the correct translation.

The term *kiṃnara* is erroneously rendered as *zhēnduóluó* (甄陀羅), *zhēnduóluó* (真陀羅), or *jǐnnàluó* (緊那羅). Its correct pronunciation is *jǐnnàluò* (緊捺洛), which is translated as "a human and yet not a human."
Mahoraga is also written as Mahosara or Mahoraga; these are all corruptions. The correct pronunciation is Mūhalaka, which is translated as "Great-Walking Dragon" (Dàyǒuxíng Lóng).
*Jinyue* (真越) is sometimes written as *Zhenvue* (震越); this should refer to bedding (*śayanāsana*). Volume 11:

Regarding the characters *gěng* (梗) and *sè* (歰): *gěng* is pronounced with the rhyme of *gēng* (庚) and *xìng* (杏). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states: “*Gěng* means strong; it also means harmful and diseased. *Sè* is also written as *sè* (濇), with the same pronunciation as *suòlì* (所立). This refers to being unsmooth. As for the character, its four strokes stop and block one another; this is the meaning of the character.

*Fei-lǐn* (痱癗) is also written as *fēi-lǐn* (𤷂), with the same pronunciation (*púzuì* for the first character and *lìzuì* for the second). *Fei-lǐn* refers to small swellings; here, we take its meaning in a figurative sense.

"Shù" (署) is pronounced *qù* (去) or *shì* (時); it means to assign a position or station. It refers to the act of assigning or placing something with reverence. In the *Guoyu*, it says: "Position is the establishment of governance; 'shù' refers to the assignment of positions. It also means to mark or indicate, signifying a visible sign or marker.

Volume 16, No. 16: This volume contains no characters for which phonetic glosses can be provided. Volume 17, No. 17: The character *zhǎng* (牆) is also written as *qiáng*. It is pronounced with the initial *zì* and the rhyme *yáng* (*zì yǎng fǎn*). According to the *Zílín*, it means "sail. In the region south of the Yangtze River, this pronunciation is used; however, in Guānzhōng, it is mostly called *gān*.

*Niǎo* (盧刀反): firm and solid. The character below is also written as *niǎo* (㲂) or *tíng* (楟); these two forms are identical. *Zhàngbìng* (丈鞕) and *zhàngjīng* (丈莖) [are its phonetic components]. According to the *Sāncāng*, *niǎo* means "to strike. The *Tōngsùwén* states that what comes out when struck is called *tīng*. What is currently done with wood or iron to strike objects out from within a hole and replace them is called *niǎo*. The text here uses *táng* (棠), which is not the correct form for *niǎo*.

*Zhuāng* (莊) is pronounced *suan* (算) with a level tone; the *Shēnglèi* (聲類) states it means "to adorn" (*zhuāngyán*). The character below is the same as the archaic form of *suàn* (祘), pronounced *sāngluàn* (桑亂); according to the *Erya*, it means "calculation. It is six inches long and used for counting. The character is composed of the radical for bamboo (*zhú*) and the element *nòng* (弄); this signifies that one constantly handles it so as not to err.
18. Volume Eighteen. "Jiǎoxì" (狡戲): In the *Fānyǔ* (方言), when small children are full of deception and cunning, it is called "jiǎoluó" (狡猾).
19. Volume Nineteen. The yakṣa Hārītī-vaṃśa is none other than the Vajrapāṇi deity; he is so named because he holds a vajra in his hand, and thus derives his name therefrom. This is what is meant.

20. Volume Twenty: This volume contains no characters for which phonetic glosses can be provided. 21. Volume Twenty-one: "Jiūròu" (雜糅) is an archaic transcription. The two characters are homophonous, with the pronunciation *nǚ jiù* (女救). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "jiǎo" (糅) refers to mixed rice; today, it is said that when objects of different colors are gathered together, they are called "jiǔ" (糅).

Caṇḍāla (sometimes written as Caṇḍāra) is translated here as "Fierce and Blazing"; it is the name for the class of people who are butchers. One account says they are the jailers who oversee the execution of criminals. According to the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions), if such a person travels, they must ring a bell to identify themselves, or carry a bamboo pole with a broken head; otherwise, the King would inflict punishment upon them.

*Pǒjiǎn* (跛蹇) is also written as *pǒ* (󲈧), with the same pronunciation as *bǔ* (補) for the first character and *juǎn* (免) for the second. According to the *Zìlín* (字林), "limping" (*pǒjiǎn*) means walking improperly.
*Chù* (撞) is pronounced *zhuó* (濁); according to the *Guǎngyá* (廣雅), it means to prick or poke. *Chù* (揰) is synonymous with striking.

Volume Twenty-Two. This [text] is the *A-vi-yen da-pan king* (The Great Chapter on the Sovereign), which refers to the "One-Life-to-Buddhahood" (*ekajātipratibaddha*) stage; it is also what the *Ten Stages Sutra* (*Daśabhūmika-sūtra*) calls the "Dharma-abiding of the Tenth A-vi-yen Bodhisattva."

"Oaths have no limit. In the *Liji* (Book of Rites), it is said that when feudal lords attend to the sacrificial victim, it is called an "oath" (*meng*). According to the *Zhouli* (Rites of Zhou), the *Siming* (Officer of Oaths) has the method for war. Zheng Xuan comments: "The terms are written upon a tablet; the victim is slaughtered and its blood taken for the participants to sip (*qian*). The document is then placed upon the victim and buried, thereby manifesting their sincerity. Major matters are called 'oaths' (*meng*), while minor matters are called 'sworn declarations' (*shi*)."

23. Volume Twenty-three. Regarding the character for "easy" (qìngyì): it was formerly written as 㑥 or 敭; now it is written as 易 (yì, with the phonetic component 豉). In the *Cāngjié piān*, 㑥 means arrogance; in the *Shuōwén*, 㑥 also means lightness. The text of the scripture uses 劦 (hújié), which according to the *Shuōwén* means "to exert strength together" or "urgency. However, 劦 does not carry this meaning here.

"Wild horses" refers to a mirage. According to the *Zhuangzi*, it is what is called "dust and grime. Regarding the phrase "living things blowing upon one another with their breath," the commentary states that what the Peng bird relies upon to fly is merely wandering vapors. This is as described in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: when one is extremely exhausted by hunger and thirst, one perceives hot vapors and mistakes them for water.

Regarding the "five weapons," the *Zhouli* (Rites of Zhou), in the section on the *Sibing* (Director of Weapons), states that he "presides over the five weapons. Zheng Zhong says: "The five weapons are the ge, the shu, the mo, the ji, and the wuyi. As for the five weapons of the infantry, they exclude the wuyi and instead include the bow and arrow."

24–25: Fascicle Twenty-four to Fascicle Twenty-five. Fascicles twenty-four and twenty-five contain no characters to be transcribed. 26: Fascicle Twenty-six. [The Buddha] Sūyāna (or Sūśanta), whose name in the Jin language means "Exceedingly Pure."

*Dòng* (洞): Pronounced *dú gòng*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "rapid flow," and it also describes the appearance of being deep and profound. In the scriptural text, it is written as *Dòng* (烔), pronounced *dú dōng*, meaning "heat" and also "drought."

Volume Twenty-seven; Volume Twenty-seven contains no characters that require explanation. Volume Twenty-eight: The character *qiàn* (勸) is followed by *yǎng* (󰮔). In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *yǎng* means "to entice. In the *Guoya*, it is written as *xiǎo* (謏), with the phonetic reading *xiānjiǔ* (先九反). The text of the scripture uses *xù* (恤) or *xī* (䘏), both with the phonetic reading *sīlǜ* (思律反). *Xù* means "to favor" or "to relieve"; *xī* is not used in current usage.

29. Fascicle Twenty-Nine. Furthermore, *Pōlún* is also written as *Pōlún*; this is translated as "Constantly Illuminating" (*Chángmíng*). The *Dùjīng* (Sutra on Crossing Over) says "Universal Kindness" (*Pǔcí*); these are both of one meaning.

The characters *bì ní* are also written as *bì yì* and *yí dì*. In the *Zīlín*, "bì" is pronounced *pǔmǐ* (the second tone) and "ní" is pronounced *wǔlǐ* (the third tone). The *Guǎngyá* states: "Bì ní refers to the *dié* or the female wall (*nǚqiáng*). The *Shìmíng* says: "Bì ní refers to the small parapets on top of a city wall; it means that through the openings therein, one observes unusual events."
*Padma* is also called *pamo*, or *pātumama*, or *pāṭumama*; its correct pronunciation is *paṭṭhama*, which translates as "red lotus.
*Kumuda* is also written as *kubuda*, or *kumudu*, or *kubudu*; this translates as "earth-joy," meaning a flower that brings joy.
*Utpala* (pronounced *you-bo-zhao*, with *zhao* reversed; also written as *ou-po-luo*) is translated into Chinese as "indigo flower.

*Xiāoqīng* (pronounced *jiao-jing*) is the name of a bird; it is also called *xiāolú*. This bird comes from Mount Mànlián and flies in flocks like hens; it resembles a duck but has long legs. It is kept in the Jianghuai region and can be used to ward off fire.

30. Fascicle Thirty. "Qianke" (謙恪)—the ancient form is "ke" (愙), pronounced with the *kǔ* and *gè* finals. According to the *Zilin*, "ke" means reverent and respectful; it also means veneration. "Qian" (謙) means being humble, empty, and yielding in respect.

*Kùdú* (酷毒) is also written as *Kù* (嚳) or *Hù* (俈); both share the same pronunciation, being the reverse of *kǒu-hú*. According to the *Shuowen*, *kù* means "urgent" (*jí*) or "extreme" (*shèn*), and it also means "cruel and tyrannical" (*bàoxuè*).

*Bǎoyīng* (寶罌): *yú-gēng-yú-chéng* (於耕於成). According to the *Fānyán*, *pǒu-lǚ-è-yīng* (瓿甊㼚罌) refers to a type of jar. East of the Guān region, specifically between Zhào and Wèi, it is sometimes called *yīng*; this is also a common term. *Pǒu* is pronounced *bù*; *lǚ* is pronounced *lè-kǒu*; *è* is pronounced *gāng*.

The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Volume One, Part One, compiled by Xuanying. *Bhagavat*: Formerly translated as "One of Great Merit and Supreme Holiness. Below, it is called *Bhagavān*. *Bhaga* is translated as "merit" (*guṇa*), and *vān* signifies the meaning of "accomplishment. Because he is named *Bhagavān* for having fully perfected all virtues—and because no other [name] does so—this title is placed at the beginning of all sūtras.
*Nāga* is translated here as "dragon" (*long*) or "elephant" (*xiang*); it is used as a metaphor because of its great strength.

*Samādhi* (pronounced with the final syllable as *gai* in the *mo-gai* rhyme) is also called *samāpatti* or *samāditi*, all of which are corruptions. The correct term is *samādhi*, which is translated as "equanimous concentration" (*dengchi*). "Equanimous" (*deng*) means "correct" (*zheng*), referring to correctly holding the mind; that is, maintaining all meritorious qualities. It is also called "right concentration" (*zhengding*), meaning that by relying on a single object, one remains free from all distraction and confusion.

The *Shuowen* states that "xī" (晞) is pronounced with the same initial as "xūyī" (虛依); it means "to look forward with hope. In the region between the sea and Mount Dai, it is said to mean "to gaze. The *Guangya* states that "xī" means "to look. It is pronounced with the final of "xiàwúfāng" (下無方). The *Shuowen* further states it refers to one who has gone away and is abroad looking for their return; the character is composed of "wàng" (望) abbreviated and "shēng" (聲). If pronounced with the final of "wúfàng" (無放), the *Shuowen* states it refers to the full moon facing the sun; this character is composed of "yuè" (月). However, because many people do not distinguish between the pronunciation and form of these characters, the character is written with "yuè. These two explanations are not distinguished [in common usage].

"Mind-conduct" (*xíngxíng*)—the second character being pronounced *xià* (with the *gēng* rhyme)—refers to "wandering and treading. The *Prabhāsa-sūtra* says, "that which the mind inclines toward"; the *Dapin-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* says, "that which is inclined toward and that which is practiced. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "How does one fully know the mind-conduct of sentient beings? It answers: "The Bodhisattva knows the various practices of sentient beings within their manifold phenomena. This is identical in meaning to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, which says: "Skillfully knowing the coming and going and the inclinations of sentient beings, as well as the conduct of their minds. The current reading of it with the *xià* (with the *mèng* rhyme) is an error.
*Guài* (罣礙) is also written as *huà* (罫), with the phonetic component *hú guà* (胡卦). According to dictionaries, it means a net-like obstruction;

it signifies hindrance or stopping, and reaching a limit is called an obstruction (*ài*). *Lánàluójié* (剌那盧割反) is the transliteration of the name of the Bodhisattva Ratnākara; this is translated as "Treasure Accumulation" (*Bǎojī*). The old *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* translates it as "Treasure Affairs" (*Bǎoshì*), while the *Fàngguāng jīng* (Prabhāsa-sūtra) translates it as "Treasure Arrival" (*Bǎolái*). According to the Sanskrit original, it is *Hastaka Ātapa*, which is translated as "Jewel Terrace" (*Bǎotái*) or "Jewel Treasury" (*Bǎozàng*); these all share the same meaning. There are instances in the sūtra text where it is written as *jì* (罽, with the phonetic component *jū lì* [居例]), but this is incorrect.

Regarding "Manziyu" (滿子餘) and the two sounds [of the name], the *Sancang Jiegu* (三蒼解詁) states that this is also a transliteration of the Sanskrit word for "Mañju. In the sutras, it is sometimes written as "Manru" (滿濡), sometimes as "Wenshushili" (文殊師利), or as "Manzhushili" (曼殊尸利). Translated, it means "Wonderful Virtue" (妙德) or "Venerable Head" (敬首). The old *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* calls him "Rushou" (濡首) in Chinese, while the *Prabhāsa Sūtra* writes it as "Aiyajia" (哀雅); both are corruptions. The correct term is "Mañjuśrī," which means "Wonderful Auspiciousness" (妙吉祥). In some sutras, it is written as "Pushou" (溥首). Since "Pu" (溥) is an archaic form of "Pu" (普), it is likely an error; it should instead be written as "Er" (󲚂), pronounced "er-zhu" (而朱反). However, because the characters are easily confused, many people have been misled.

"Xiàn niàn" (繫念) consists of two forms: "xiàn" (繫) and "jì" (繼). Today they are written as "xì" (係), with the same pronunciation as the ancient character for "Emperor" (帝, *dì*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "xì" means to tie up or bind; it also means to connect in an unbroken succession.

"Liang zhuan" (兩腨) is also written as "liang shan" (󰈷), with the pronunciation "tóng shí ruǎn" (同時耎). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, this refers to the calf muscles (*jìng zhuan cháng*). The *Sancang* states it refers to the calf (*fēi cháng*). The text of the sutra writes it as "chuàn" (踹, *dīng guǎn*), meaning to tread or step with the feet; however, "chuàn" is not used in this sense here.

The ancient script for "two thighs" (liǎng bì) is written as 䠋, with the same pronunciation as 蒲米 (pú mǐ). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to the outer part of the thigh. Northerners pronounce it as this [pú], while those in Jiangnan pronounce it as 方爾 (fāng ěr). The text here uses the character 䏶, which is a vulgar form derived from the radical for flesh (肉).

"Uṣṇīṣa" (肉髻) is a transliteration of the Sanskrit term *uṣṇīṣa*, which means "crown protuberance. This refers to what the *Anuttarāśrayasūtra* (無上依經) describes as the cranial bone (*uṣṇīṣa-śīrṣaka*) swelling upward to form a natural topknot. The reading of the scriptural text with the character for "knot" (結) derived from the radical for "silk" (糸) is incorrect. The pronunciation of *uṣṇīṣa* is *wǔ mò* (烏沒).

*Xi-yi* (熙怡): The first character is pronounced as *zhuan* (䖒) with a reversed final, and the second as *zhi* (之) with a reversed final. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "xi-yi" means harmonious joy. According to the *Fangyan*, "yi" means to rejoice; in the region between Xiangtan, it is called "fen-yi. Some say that the "xi" in "xi-yi" is the same as "xi" (嬉), which according to the *Shuowen* means pleasure, and according to the *Cangjie Pian*, means laughter. This "xi" is not the same as the modern usage of "xi" (戲).

"Yù" (愈) means to recover; it is the same as "yǔ" (瘉), pronounced with the initial *yóu* and the final *rǔ*. According to the *Fānyán* (Dialects), it means "to improve" or "the interval between differences.

The *Shuōwén* states that "yù" refers to the recovery from illness. "Tiánrán" (恬然) is pronounced with the initial *tú* and the final *jiān*; according to the *Fānyán*, it means "serene," and also "peaceful" or "tranquil. The *Dàlùn* (Great Treatise) writes it as "dàn rán" (淡然), pronounced with the initial *tú* and the final *làn*. Examining this, "dàn" (淡) also means "peaceful," and its explanatory meaning is identical. The text of the Sūtra writes it as "yí" (怡), pronounced with the initial *zhī* and the final *yǔ*, which is an error.

The character *niǎo* (嬈) is pronounced *nǎo* (乃了反). In the *Sāncāng*, it means "to toy with"; according to the *Shuowén*, it means "harshness" (*kē*), which refers to vexation and disturbance, or playful teasing. *Niǎo* is also synonymous with "affliction" (*nǎo*). The pronunciation of *kē* (苛) is *hé kě* (何可反).
*Bīnbīn* (the first character pronounced *pǐ*, the second *fúyún*): according to the *Guǎngyá*, "bīnbīn" means a state of abundance. *Ābí*:
according to the *Zìshū*, it is pronounced *bìxí*; this is translated as "Non-retrogression" (*Avivartika*), which the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* refers to as the seventh stage (*bhūmi*).

*Kumāra* is correctly transliterated as *Kumārābhūta*. *Kumāra* is a general term for those aged eight years and above who have not yet married; its traditional name is "Child" (*Dōji*). *Ābhūta*, translated traditionally as "True Word" (*Shingon*), means "identical with reality" (*shinjichi*) or "actual" (*jitsu*); these are synonymous meanings. Now, it should be understood as "characteristic," meaning "the characteristic of a child. To conform with worldly convention, the name "Child" designates Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward. Alternatively, it is called "Prince of the Dharma" (*Dharmaputra*), which is a specific title.
"Counting" (shù) means to calculate; to examine its numbers is called "counting.
"Burning" (shāo) means to incinerate; it refers both to natural combustion and to burning by means of human agency.

2. Second Fascicle. "Táo" (稻) and "máo" (茅): *táo* refers to awned grains; in the script of the sutra, it is sometimes written as "gānzhè" (竿蔗). *Gān* is pronounced *gǔ* (古) and *hán* (寒); *zhè* is pronounced *zhū* (諸) and *yè* (夜). According to the *Tōngsùwén* (通俗文), *gānzhè* is produced in Jingzhou; it is also sometimes written as "gānzhà" (甘柘), which is the same object.
"Because one hates the crow, one reverses propriety. In the *Book of Rites*, "How can I bear to use [it]?"—here "bear to" (*wù*) is synonymous with "hate" (*è*).

As the *Classic of Poetry* says, "How can I tolerate the lack of propriety? both cases are identical. Volume Three, Part Three. "Mó-mén" (摩捫) is pronounced *mò-bèn*. The *Shēnglèi* states that "mén" means to touch or stroke. The *Zílín* states that "mén" means to caress or hold. According to these sources, "mó-chí" (捫持) refers to grasping or holding an object with the hand; thus, when various sutras use "Mó-tí" (摩提), it refers to the sun and moon. This is correct.

Volumes Four through Six—Volumes Four, Five, and Six above contain no phonetic glosses or character explanations. Volume Seven: Regarding the character *mèng* (蒙) [written here as 󲇑], it shares the same pronunciation as *mò gōng* (莫公反); the second character is pronounced *mò duì* (莫對反). The *Yījīng* (易經) states: "Mèng means *méng* (󲇎). This refers to being covered and lacking clarity. The *Guǎngyá* (廣雅) states: "Mèi (昧) means darkness. This refers to being obscured and lacking knowledge. The *Yījīng* further states: "Mèngmèi (蒙昧) refers to the young," meaning they do not seek out the Way.

8. Fascicle Eight. "Following the Body" (*xúnshēn*). In ancient texts, it is written as *zūn* (𢓈), which is a variant; it is pronounced as *zūn* (similar to *zūn*). According to the *Erya*, "following" (*xún*) means "to follow along. Guo Pu states that it also means "to traverse" (*xúnxíng*) and "to pervade" (*biàn*). It refers to moving through or inspecting thoroughly.

*Shi-zhan* (視占) is a reversal of the *Fān-yán* (方言, Dialectal Dictionary), where *zhan* (占) means "to look" (*shì*). *Zhan* also means "to observe" (*hòu*). When things observe one another, it is called *zhan*;

it is also synonymous with *zhān* (瞻). *Zhuàn-shī* (鏇師) is pronounced *sì juàn* (似絹); according to the *Shuōwén*, *zhuàn* (鏇) refers to a circular lathe (*yuán lú*). The character *huàn* (擐) used for King Cheng of Zhou is a variant; it refers to one who uses ropes to rotate an axle and carves wood into vessels. The form *xuán* (旋) found in the canonical text is not the standard form.

"Stomach-bladder" (胃脬): "pǔ" is pronounced with the *jiāo* rhyme; according to Cāngjié Jiěgǔ, the bladder is that which holds urine. The Shuowén says it is written with the radical "flesh" (*𭴄*) on the side. The text here uses "pào" (補交反), which means "to wrap. This "pào" is not used in this sense.

"Lèi" (tears) is an archaic form identical to "jì" (𪖦), pronounced according to the *Chī jì* rhyme category; the *Sān cāng* states it is nasal mucus. In the *Zhou yī*, the phrase "zī zī tì tì" (lamenting with tears and mucus) uses "tì" for what comes from the eyes and "tì" for what comes from the nose. The scriptural text that writes "tì" (from the character for "younger brother") with the pronunciation "tā lǐ" refers to tears; this is not the meaning adopted here.

*Dàn yǐn* (淡飲): "Dàn" is read as *tú* (徒) and "yǐn" as *gān fǎn xià yú jìn fǎn* (甘反下於禁反); it refers to the liquid above the chest. In the canonical text, it is sometimes written as *yīn* (陰). *Fáng zhì* (肪𦚻):

"Fáng" is read as *fǔ* (府) and "zhì" as *xiān ān fǎn* (先安反). According to the *Guǎng yǎ*, "fáng zhì" means fat (*zhī*). The *Tōng sú wén* states: "That which is at the waist is called *fáng*; that which is in the stomach is called *zhì*."

*Píng* (pronounced *pǔ jiāng fǎn*): According to the *Běicāng*, this refers to being bloated; it means the abdomen is full and swollen. The character below may also be written as *xī* (same pronunciation), which is read as *zhū liàng fǎn*.

*Qīng yù* (pronounced *yú yù fǎn*): According to the *Shuōwén*, this refers to accumulated blood. The scriptural text also writes it as *yū*; it also refers to mud in water, or the dregs and sediment of something.

The *Shishu* states that all those who serve as "shenlang" (jackals and wolves) are rebellious; the *Erya* says that the jackal has feet like a dog's; and the *Cangjie Xungu* explains that the jackal resembles a dog, is white in color, and possesses swift claws and fangs, being skilled at pouncing and biting.

The character "爴裂" (suò liè) should be written as "攫" (jué), which is homophonous with "九縛" (jiǔ bó) and "居碧" (jū bì). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "攫" means to seize with the claws; it also means to snatch. The *Cangjie Pian* states that "攫" means to pounce. The *Huainanzi* says, "When birds are cornered, they pounce; when beasts are cornered, they claw"—this refers to this very meaning.

*Rìbó* (肋骨): "The ribs. According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to the bones of the flanks (*xié*). The character is composed of "flesh" (*ròu*) as its phonetic; however, in the scriptural text, it is written as *lè* (勒), which refers to the head-stall and bit used for horses.

*Rìbào* (日暴): "In the sun; to expose to the sun. In the *Xiaerya*, *bào* means to dry in the sun. It is composed of "sun" (*rì*) and "to emerge" (*chū*) as its semantic components, with "númǐ" (奴米) as its phonetic. [Note: The variant reading] "nù" (奴) is pronounced *jūsǒng* (居竦); it signifies holding something with both hands together.
"Kambū" (pronounced *kǎnbù*, with the initial *bǔ* reversed; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to a marine crustacean, specifically a conch shell;
"jiè" means carapace or shell).
"Luo" (pronounced *lìhà*). "Qia" (pronounced *qiūzhù*).
The character *duō* (哆) is explained in the *Shuowen* as being pronounced *dài* (殆), while in the *Zilin* it is pronounced *chǒujiā* (丑加) or *chǒuyà* (丑亞).
The character *zāo* (醝) is pronounced *cái hé* (才何).
Regarding "obstruction" (*ài*), it is read as *yǐ shì* (以豉); "obstruction" (*yì*) is a term used for that which is not difficult.

9–11 (Volumes Nine, Ten, and Eleven are missing) 12. Volume Twelve: Tuṣita (the "tu" is pronounced with a *xian* [shǎn] tone; this refers to the Lord of Heaven). This is translated as "Perfect Joy" (*zhèngxǐ*), or alternatively "Perfect Contentment. Tuṣita is translated as "Sublime Fulfillment" (*miàozú*).

*Wúyāng* (無央)—the "yāng" is pronounced *liáng* (良) in the opposite tone; in the Sanskrit language it is *asaṃkhyeya*, which means "innumerable. *Yāng* (央) means "exhaustion. The scriptural text writes it as *āng* (鞅)—the "āng" is pronounced *yú liǎng* (於兩); according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to the ligament of the neck. However, *āng* does not carry this meaning here. The pronunciation of *zhì* (鞮) is *zhī liè* (之列).
13. The Thirteenth Fascicle. *Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna*. This is translated as "One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct."

*Ka-pai* (迦憊) is also written with the two characters *𤸶* and *𢞎*, both pronounced with the same reverse of *pú* (蒲戒反). The *Aśokarāja-sūtra* states that this means "Knower of the World" (*loka-vid*).

*Shì* (適) has two forms in the ancient texts of the *Sāncāng*: *適* and *這*, both pronounced with the reverse of *shī-chǐ* (施尺反). According to the *Guǎngyá*, it is synonymous with *zhǐ* (祇); it signifies "approaching," "beginning," or "starting."

*Qi gài* (the *gài* is pronounced like *gu lai*): According to the *Cangjie pian*, "to *gai*" means to go about begging and requesting. The *Tongshu wen* states that to express a wish is called *gai*; the character's form consists of "person" (*ren*) and "loss" (*wang*), signifying that when a person stops [their current state] and loses it, they go forth to beg and request.

14. Volume Fourteen, Chapter Fourteen. *Gù* (蠱): The sound is *gōng hù fǎn*; according to the *Shēnglèi* (聲類), it is *yì zhě fǎn*. The *Shuowén* (說文) states that *gù* refers to the worms within the abdomen; it denotes the practice of administering poisonous insects.

"Reproaching" (*qiàn*) refers to the act of scolding; according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to be angry. In the scriptural text, it is sometimes written as "reprimanding" (*qìzé*), which according to the *Guǎngyá* means "to interrogate.

"Blind" (*mánggǔ*) is pronounced *gōnghù*; one who has no eyes is called "blind" (*gǔ*). The *Shìmíng* states: "The blind have eyes that are 'miánmián'; their eyes are closed flat like the skin of a drum."**

15. The fifteenth fascicle. Regarding the character for *dúchì* (毒螫): according to the *Shìzīlín* (字林), it refers to insects that move about while emitting poison. In the region west of the Pass (*Guānxī*), this pronunciation is used; it is also pronounced *hégǔ* (各反). In the region east of the Mountains (*Shāndōng*), this pronunciation is used; it is pronounced *jūzhīliè* (蛆知列反), which is a common term throughout the north and south. The pronunciation *jū* (蛆) is an error.

"Hong-piao" (red-piao) is a term used for "tian-piao" (heaven-piao); it is like silk, a bluish-white color. There is bi-piao (azure-piao), tian-piao (heaven-piao), and qing-piao (blue-piao), each named according to the specific color it represents.

16–18: Fascicles Sixteen through Eighteen. Fascicle Sixteen, Fascicle Seventeen, and Fascicle Eighteen: these three fascicles above contain no phonetic glosses for characters. 19: Fascicle Nineteen. Regarding the character *wú* (汙) in "not *wú*" (不汙): it is read as *wù* (烏) or *cuò* (莝), with two alternative pronunciations. According to the *Zílín*, it means "filth" (*wūnhuì*). According to the *Zishū*, it means "to smear" (*wūtú*). The *Shìmíng* states: "It is *wū*; it is like muddy water."

The character for *shuāi* (衰) and *mào* (耄) is written as 𤸬, with the phonetic reading *sǒu guī* (所龜反). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, 𤸬 means "to diminish. In the *Liji*, it says that at age fifty one begins to "decline" (*shuāi*), which refers to physical decay and laxity; the lower part is an ancient form of the character for "hair" (*háo*) and is now written as *hào* (耗), with the phonetic reading *mò bào* (莫報反). The *Liji* states that at eighty one is called "senile" (*mào*). The commentary notes: "Senility (*mào*) refers to mental confusion and forgetfulness, as well as disorientation."

20. Fascicle Twenty. *Mu* (pronounced *mò*, with the second tone; according to the *Sāncāng*, it means "to raise"; according to the *Fānyán*, it means "to pasture"). Guo Pu says: "It refers to raising oxen and horses. However, in the *Hànshū*, Gongsun Hong is described as having "pastured pigs" (*mù zhǐ*). Thus, "pasturing" (*mù*) is a general term for animal husbandry, not limited solely to oxen and horses.

The character *jǔ* (沮) signifies "to gradually decline" and "to be ruined. As the *Shijing* says, "When will it be that this declines? (*hé rì sī jǔ*), the commentary states that *jǔ* means "ruined. The versions found in the Classics and Histories written as *zǔ* (俎)—with the phonetic *cè lǚ*—are incorrect; [that character] refers to a meat-stand or a vessel for storing pickled fish sauce. *Zǔ* does not carry the meaning [of "decline"].

*Yǎnjiǎn* (偃蹇) means *juémiǎnjì* (居免紀). *Yǎn* (偃) is pronounced with three variations (*jù*, *yǎn*, and *sān*). In the *Zuozhuan*, it refers to arrogance and pride. In the *Guoyaya*, it refers to being haughty and overbearing; that is, an appearance of self-exaltation. The *Shiming* states: "To lie down in repose (*yǎnxī*) without attending to one's duties. *Jiǎn* (蹇) means limping; it refers to being ill and unable to perform tasks, and here it is used metaphorically to resemble this state. *Jiǎo* (撟) is pronounced with two variations (*jǐ* and *xiǎo*). The character in the received text, written as *rén* (人) with *wèi* (𠐻), is an error.

"Arrogance" (ào): The fifth [character] is written as 傲; it is also called "disrespect. According to the *Guǎngyá*, "ào" means "to treat with contempt" (*è*)—that is, to slight or despise others. The character is composed of the radical "person" (人). "Taste" (zī):

The ancient forms are both written as 孖 and 稵, pronounced *zīyí*. It means "to increase" or "to nourish. In the canonical text, it is written as 嗞 from the radical "mouth" (口). According to the *Shuōwén*, "zí" means "sighing" (*jiē*).
"Measuring" (揆): according to the *Shijing*, "measured by the sun"; the commentary states that "measuring" means to gauge, referring to the measurement of standards and laws.
Volume 21, Part 21. "But" (但): in the *Shenglei*, it is read as *dàn* (徒亶反); it means "only" (*cóng*) or "merely" (*kōng*).

The ancient forms for "yu" (aid/blessing) are written as either "yòu" or "yù," both pronounced with the same rhyme as "yóu" (jiù). The *Zhouyi* says, "Heaven aids him from above. Confucius said, "Aid means assistance; he is one whom Heaven assists."

22–23: Fascicle Twenty-two and Fascicle Twenty-three. Both Fascicle Twenty-two and Fascicle Twenty-three lack character readings and glosses. 24: Fascicle Twenty-four. Fascicle Twenty-four contains the archaic forms for "wing" (翅), written as both 翅 and 翄; they share the same pronunciation, *shì*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "翅" refers to the wings (*yì*) of a bird.
"Beifu" (被服): "bei" (被) means to wear as a sash; "fu" (服) means to employ or apply.
25. Fascicle Twenty-Five. "Tang" (唐): "tu" (徒) is the pronunciation; "tu" (徒) means empty or void.

*Líng* (凌): Pronounced *lì zēng* (with the second character reversed). According to the *Sāncāng*, "líng" means to invade or encroach; the character is composed of "ice" (*bīng*) with "or" (*huò*) below it, though it is now written as *yì* (易), pronounced *yǐ shì*. According to the *Shuōwén*, "líng" means lightness; according to the *Cāngjiépiān*, "líng" means arrogance.

"Lü" (虜) is written as "Lǔ" (鹵) in ancient texts; both are pronounced with the initial *lú* and the final *-gǔ* (盧古反), while the second character [of the compound] is pronounced *lì* and *zhù* (力著反). It means to capture or to subdue. Regarding the term "captured" (*fú*, 俘), Jìn Zhuó states in the *Hànshū*: "To capture alive is called 'lǔ'; to decapitate is called 'huò'. "Lüè" (掠) means to seize by force; it refers to taking things away through compulsion. "Fú" (俘) is pronounced *fāng yú* (芳于反); it refers to what is captured by the army.
