The *Xici* says: "In ancient times, people dwelt in caves and lived in the wilds. Later sages replaced these with houses and palaces. The character for *suì* (燧) is pronounced as *cuì* (萃). The *Baopuzi* states: In antiquity, when people were simple and plain, they ate fur and drank blood, consuming insects, fish, and various fruits raw. Consequently, many suffered from ailments of the abdomen. For this reason, the sages drilled wood to seek fire, transforming the raw into the cooked; thus they were named the Lord of Suiren (Sui Ren Shi).

*Ōng-sui* (the first character pronounced *gǒng* with a retroflex *-r* [i.e., *ǝuǝŋ*]; the *Cāngjié piān* states it means "to hold," and the *Shuowén* defines it as "to embrace," composed of the radical for "hand" and the phonetic *yōng*; alternatively written as *bǐng*, which is an archaic form in the Small Seal script). The second character is *suí* (*ruì*); the *Yùpiān* states it is a "sweeping broom. The *Fānyán* states that west of the Guān pass, it is called *sǎo-sui* (*suì*) or *sǎo-zhòu* (*zhòu*). It may also be written with the "grass" radical as *huì*.

In the term *zhèngshuò* (正朔), the first character is pronounced *zhāng* (盈反) and the second *shuāngchì* (雙捉反); the canonical text writes it as *zhì* (𦙚), which is a vulgar form. Its correct orthography follows the radical *nì* (屰) with the phonetic *shuò* (逆作朔). The commentary states that *shuò* means "beginning" (*shǐ*) or "reviving" (*sū*), referring to the first day of the month.
The "Pántáo" (Coiled Peach) is pronounced *fǎn*.
The *Shānhǎijīng* states: "In the Eastern Sea there is Mount Táodū.
Upon this mountain stands a great peach tree named Táodū."
Its roots extend and intertwine for over five hundred li,
while its branches are separated by three thousand li.
Upon the tree dwell golden celestial cocks.
When the sun first rises, its light shines upon this tree and the celestial cocks immediately crow;
all the other cocks in the world then follow suit and crow.
The *Shanhai jing* (*Classic of Mountains and Seas*) also states that there is a great peach tree whose roots spread and entwine for over five hundred li.
The branches were three thousand *li* apart.
Both the *Baosoushenji* (Record of Searching for Spirits) and the *Fengsuyongyi* (Meaning of Local Customs) cite the *Book of the Yellow Emperor*,
stating that in ancient times there were two divine beings.
The first is named Tu and the second is named Yulei; they are also called Yulidu.
On Mount Shuo there is a great peach tree, and these two men dwell by the tree.
To the northeast of the tree, there is a great cavern.
All the ghosts enter and exit through this cavern.
Cha and Yulei preside over and command the selection and sorting of the myriad ghosts.
When ghosts brought false calamities upon people, they were bound with reed ropes and seized to be fed to tigers.
Thereupon, the Yellow Emperor established ritual prohibitions against them; he set up peachwood figures at the doors and gates and painted Tu and Yü-lei along with tigers to represent them.

Nowadays, according to secular custom, at the conclusion of the *lā* festival and on New Year’s Eve, peach-wood figures are adorned and reed ropes are hung; tigers are painted on both sides of the door, and two lamps are placed there to represent the tiger’s eyes, all to dispel inauspiciousness.

"Mixing the tracks and the writings": *hun* (混) is pronounced as *shang-hun-wan-fan*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "feng" (*豐*) means "to flow. According to this, "feng-liu" (豊流) signifies "hun-hun" (混混), meaning flowing together without distinction. "Che" (車) is pronounced as *jiang-yu-fan*. "Che" refers to the ruts of a carriage; "shu" (書) refers to written characters and seals. To speak of "mixing the tracks and the writings" means that the ruts of the world are common and the written characters have no difference; under a single royal transformation, the four seas become one's home.

Regarding "Fine Willow" (*Sīliù*): The *Shānhǎijīng* states that there is a small island named Fine Willow located in the Western Sea, near the place where the sun and moon set. There is Mount Chángyáng, where the sun and moon enter; this is precisely that island. It is also called Fine Willow and is further known as Yángliǔ Island.

*Kāśyapa* is a contraction of the Sanskrit term; in its original phonetic form, it is *Kāśyapa*. This is a prominent clan (*mahā-śākya*) in the land of India. Regarding the character *yú* (pronounced with the initial *zhū*): the *Guǎngyǎ* states that it means "to pass beyond" (*dù*).

The commentary on the *Máo Shī* says it means "to transgress" (*yuè*). The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical for "foot" (*zú*) and the phonetic element *yú*. It is sometimes written as *yú*, which is a vulgar variant; it may also be written with the radical for "movement" (*chuò*) as *yú*.

"Yi" (pronounced with the initial *yì* and final *-rù*): The *Cāngjié piān* states that "yi" means to diminish; the commentary on the *Máoshī* says it means to ladle out; its phonetic value is *zhēn*. The *Shuōwén* defines "yi" as to hold, formed from the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic component "city" (*yì*).
The Yongchun era was the reign title of Emperor Taishangdi of the Tang; it was the year of Guiwei.

*Ning* (pronounced with the *zhí lǚ* rhyme) refers to the space between the gate and the screen; the *Erya* states that the area between the gate and the screen is called the *ning*. The *Guiyuan Zhucóng* states that it is the place where the sovereign stands at the side gate to preside over the court audience.

*Chun* (循): Pronounced *zun* (遵) with a retroflex *r* suffix; according to the *Erya*, it means "to follow. Guo Pu states that "it is like 'from' (*cong*). The *Kaosheng* says it means "to accord with. The *Shuowen* says it means "to move along. Pronounced *chou* (丑) with an *i* suffix. *Dun* (盾): Pronounced *shen* (脣) with a *huai* suffix; it is a pictograph. Pronounced *ji* (幾) with an *xi* suffix. Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* says it refers to the trigger of a crossbow; it is that which controls movement. The *Shuowen* says: "That which initiates [action] is called a *ji* (trigger/mechanism)."

Regarding the character *shū* (樞), the *Jíxùn* states that it refers to the point from which movement is initiated. The *Kǎoshēng* says that *shūjī* refers to speech. The *Shuowén* defines it as the pivot of a door, composed of the radical for wood (*mù*) and the phonetic element *qū*.

The *Kui* (虧) section traces back to the sounds of *kao* (考) and *sheng* (聲), stating that it means "to wither" (*kuiluo*) or "to injure. Zheng’s commentary on the *Mao Shi* states: "Kui is equivalent to ruin and destruction. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states: "Kui means deficiency. The *Guangya* states: "Kui means few. The *Shuowen* states: "Kui refers to the impairment of vital energy (*qi*). It is composed of *hu* (雐, pronounced *hu*) and the phonetic *yu* (於, which is the character *yu* [于]). Alternatively, it is written with *ci* (𠔃). The radical below is *zhi-jin* (陟矜). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "Zheng means verification. The *Shuowen* further states: "Zheng means appearance or sign. It is composed of *ren* (壬) and the phonetic *tian-ding* (天頂). It is formed by the abbreviated form of *wei* (微).
Mián (綿): The first character is pronounced as mí (彌然反) and the second as qiāng (羌于反). Pìgòu (丕構): The first character is pronounced pī (音披);

the *Shuowen* states that "pì" means "great," composed of "one" (一) and the phonetic "bù" (不), though the scriptural text uses "shí" (十) to form "pī" (㔻), which is a vulgar variant and incorrect. The second character is pronounced gǒu (苟候反); Gu Yewáng says "gòu" means "to join together. The *Mao Shi* commentary states "gòu" means "to complete"; the *Shuowen* states "gòu" means "a cover," composed of "wood" (木) and the phonetic "gǒu" (冓, gǔ hòu反).

"Xun" (尋): Pronounced *ying* (益) with a retroflex initial; the *Fangyan* states it means "to unravel" (*yili*) or "to extend. The *Guangya* defines it as "to carry out a matter" or "to conclude. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to draw out" (*chou*). It is composed of the radical "silk thread" (*mi*) and the phonetic "mi" (*yin-mi*), with the auxiliary sound "li" (*sheng*).
*Bì* (懈革賣反) means indolence. It is written as *pí* (忘疲武坊反;

in the *Guoyu*, "the exhausted soldier has no rank; the exhausted woman has no home"). Jia Dui says it means illness. The *Guangya* says it means weariness. The *Shuowen* says it means fatigue (*píláo*). It is composed of the radical *nà* (疒) and the phonetic *nǚ* (女厄反), with the sound of *pí*.
*Buò* (pronounced *chén lǐ fǎn*): The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that this refers to a book wrapper (*shūyī*). It is composed of the radical "cloth" (*jīn*) with the phonetic element "shī.

It may also be written as *zhí* or *zì*. *Zài wò* (pronounced *yā jiǎo fǎn*): According to the *Erya*, this means a case or container (*jù*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* gives the pronunciation *è* for *wò*, stating it means to hold (*chí*). It is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) with the phonetic element "wū."

Regarding the character *zuò* (祚), the fanqie is *hù* (戶). Jia Dui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states: "Zuo means weeping; it means emolument. The *Gujin Zhengzi* states: "Zuo means blessing (*fú*). It follows the radical *shì* (示) and is pronounced *zhī* (祇); *zà* (乍) is its phonetic component, with its radical omitted."

"Méng" (甿) means "to till. The *Shiji* states that "méng" refers to the common people (*bìng*). The *Guǎngyá* says that "méng" is synonymous with "máng" (the common folk) and also implies "foolishness. The *Cāngjiépiān* says it refers to those who live in the fields. The *Shuowén* says it refers to the people of the fields; it is composed of the radical "field" (田) and the phonetic "wáng" (亾).

"Heng-yi" (恒佚) is pronounced as yǐn-fǎn; the *Kǎoshēng* states it means "the mind is joyful and satisfied," or "pleasure. Kǒng Ānguó’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* says it means "leisurely ease. The *Cāngjiépiān* says it means "unfettered flow"; it is composed of the radical "person" (人) with the phonetic "shi" (失).

"寧謐" (níng mì) means "to be tranquil. In the *Erya*, it is glossed as "stillness" (*jìng*) and "caution" (*shèn*; pronounced *shèn*). The *Kǎoshēng* states that it signifies "the absence of sound. The *Jìxùn* explains that "謐" (*mì*) means "peaceful," composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic "𥁑" (*mì*).
*Jiāo* (澆): Upper radical *yáo* (堯). The phonetic analysis states it means "thin" (*jiāobó*) or "dilute" (*wò*). Examining the characters for *jiāo* and *wò*, their flavor is indeed thin.

*Chún* (淳): Upper radical *chánglún* (常倫). The vulgar form is written as *chún*; the correct orthography is *㶒* (󲘕). The phonetic analysis states it means "pure and clear. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Yīlǐ* says, "Pure and dilute" (*chúnwò*). The *Guǎngyá* says, "To soak" (*chúnzì*, pronounced *cī sì fǎn*). The *Shuōwén* defines *chún* as "to soak" (*chúnqì*, pronounced *lù*). It follows the water radical and the phonetic *lù*. The character *lù* has the same sound as *shàngxià wēiyuán* (pronounced *tóng shàng xià wēiyuán*). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* says it refers to the "source" (*yuánběn*). Gu Yewang says, "The source of water is called *yuán*."
"Zàn" (暫) is pronounced with the *qián* and *làn* finals; the *Fǎnkǎo* (反考) states that it means "not long. It is also written as "zàn" (蹔).
"Liáo" (聊) is pronounced with the *lì* and *diāo* finals; the *Jíxùn* (集訓) states that it means "merely" or "just. "Xiāngzhì" (緗帙):

the upper character "xiāng" (緗) is pronounced with the *xī* and *yáng* finals; according to the *Zìshū* (字書), it refers to "silk. The lower character "zhì" (帙) is pronounced with the *chén* and *lì* finals; the *Jíxùn* states it is a "book cover. It is composed of the "cloth" radical (*jīn*) and the phonetic "shī" (失) in abbreviated form. It may also be written with the "clothing" radical (*yī*) as "zhì" (袠); these are one and the same.

1. Volume One. *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Volume One. Compiled by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang. First Assembly: The Threefold Discipline (*Trisaṃvara*). [The character] *gāo* (high) is a colloquial variant of *sǔn* (with the radical for "bamboo" and the phonetic *jùn*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states its correct form is *lín* (with the radical for "mountain" and the phonetic *shù*). It is explained as "a high mountain. Kong Anguo’s commentary on the *Shangshu* says it means "lofty and great. The *Shuowen* defines it as "high," composed of the radical for "mountain" and the phonetic *jùn*. The pronunciation of *jùn* is the same.

*Huì* (卉) and *mù* (木): The first character, *huì*, is pronounced with the upper radical *guī* (貴) as the phonetic. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is the general name for grasses. It is composed of the radical *chǔ* (丑列反) and the radical *cǎo* (艸, sound *cǎo*). In modern clerical script (*lìshū*), the character is abbreviated from thirty strokes to *huì*. It is also pronounced with the phonetic *guǐ* (鬼) as *huǐ* (暉), which is likewise acceptable.
The upper character of "qílín" (麒麟) is pronounced "qí," and the lower character is pronounced "lín.
The *Cāngjié piān* states: "The male is called qí."
The female is called the *qí*.
The *Mao Shi* commentary, "Explanations of Birds, Beasts, Insects, and Fish," states: "The *qí* and *lí* are auspicious beasts.
When a king possesses supreme benevolence, they appear; they have the body of a deer (*jūn*, pronounced *jūn*)."

It has the tail of an ox and the hooves of a horse; its hooves are rounded, it is yellow in color, and it has a single horn at the tip of which there is flesh, so that it does not harm things. Its voice accords with the *zhong* and *lü* musical scales, and its gait conforms to the compass and square.
When traveling, it always chooses its ground, dwelling only after careful deliberation.
One does not step on living insects;
one does not break living grass;
one does not dwell in a crowd.
They do not travel in company;
they do not enter pits or traps;
they do not become entangled in nets.
The *Shuowen* also states that "ren" (benevolence) means "shou" (to hunt).

"Mi" (deer) is pronounced like "mei"; it has a cow's tail and a single horn, and is derived from "lu" (deer) with the phonetic "qi. "Qi" refers to the female of the qilin; it is derived from "lu" (deer) with the phonetic "du. In the scriptural texts, there are instances where it is written as "qilin" with the radical for horse (馬), but this is not the same [as the character for the mythical beast].

Regarding *xiong* (bear) and *pí* (brown bear): *shàngshū* (to present a memorial) is pronounced *qióng* (窮); *fǎnxià* (turning back below) is pronounced *bǐméi* (彼眉). The *Mao Shī* says, "Only bears, only brown bears. The *Shuowén* says, "A name for a wild beast; it resembles a pig but is large and black. It dwells in the mountains and hibernates in winter (*chí*, pronounced *zhì*). Its paws resemble those of humans. It follows the radical *néng* (能) and the phonetic *biāo* (必遙). The *Erya* says, "The *pí* is like a bear, yellowish-white in color. Guō Pǔ says, "The *pí* resembles a bear but is larger; it is a species of bear. Its head is long and high, and it is fierce and powerful, capable of uprooting trees. In the region west of the Pass, it is called *jiā* (猳, pronounced *jiā*). It follows the radical *pí* (罷, pronounced *pú*) and the phonetic *biāo* (灬)."
The character for "parrot" (鸚) has the upper radical *shang* with the phonetic *yan* (焉) reversed;
the lower part is *wu* (無) with the phonetic *fu* (甫) reversed.
It is also written as *yong* (䳇).
Both [the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*] agree on this point. The *Shanhai jing* states:
"On Mount Huang there is a bird whose appearance is like that of an owl (*xiāo*). It has green feathers and a red beak; it can mimic human speech with a voice like a person's tongue."
It is called the *śuka* (parrot).
Guo Pu states: "The tongue of the present-day *mingyu* resembles that of a small child; there are two [toes] each at the front and back of its feet. Those of five colors originate from beyond Funan."
There are also those that are purely white and as large as hawks. The *Jingli* (Book of Rites) states: "The parrot can speak, yet it does not depart from the category of flying birds.
The *Shuowen Jiezi* indicates that both characters for "parrot" (*yingwu*) are written with the "bird" radical.
"Ying" (嬰) and "wu" (武) are both sounds.
The *Shuowen Jiezi* further states that "ying" is pronounced as "yi-yin" (益盈反);
the character is composed of "nü" (女) and "ying" (賏).
"Yì" (益) is the reversed sound [of "yīng"].
It is composed of two "bèi" (貝, cowries).
The current version of the scripture, which takes two "mù" (目, eyes) below and adds "ān" (安) to form "yīng" (嬰), is incorrect.
The character for *wǔ* (martial) is composed of *zhǐ* (to stop) and *gē* (spear).

*Kūlúnluó* (俱𩿦羅) is the name for a bird in the language of India; it is also called *Jùshīluó* (俱翅羅) or *Jùqílúó* (俱耆羅), which are variations in the weight of the Sanskrit pronunciation. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "This bird has a beautiful voice, and its name is established according to that sound. By nature it loves splendor and does not perch upon withered trees."

"Fú-yàn" (wild duck and wild goose) is read as *wú-fǎn* (without the retroflex). The *Erya* states: "Shū-fú" (the wild duck) is pronounced *mù* (according to the *Yinmo*). Guo Pu’s commentary says it belongs to the class of ducks (*yā*). *Kao shēng* says it is the smaller variety of the wild duck. The *Wenzi Shiyao* says it is composed of the radical "bird" (*niǎo*), the phonetic "jǐ" (pronounced *shū*), and that "jǐ" refers to the short feathers of the bird; when flying, they appear "jǐ-jǐ" (fluttering), thus representing the upper part of the form and the lower part of the sound. The lower character is read as *yàn*. It is sometimes written as "yàn" (wild goose), both forms being identical in their fur-like down. Xu Zhan’s commentary says it is the larger kind called *hóng* (swan) and the smaller kind called *yàn*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it belongs to the class of geese (*é*). It is composed of the radical "bird," the component "rén" (person), and the phonetic "chǎn. Now, the *hóng* and *yàn* are birds that follow the yang. The *Liji*, "Monthly Ordinances," states: "In the month of the late autumn, the *hóng* and *yàn* arrive as guests."

Regarding the character *rú* (茹): according to the *Shǔfǎn Kǎo* (暑反考), it means "to chew" or "to eat. The radical character below it is *shí* (食), with the phonetic component *jīng* (精) and the entry number *rù* (入); its correct form is from *zào* (皂) with the entry number *lì* (立). The current scriptural text uses the character formed from *rén* (人) and *liáng* (良) as *shí*; this is a vulgar usage and not the correct form.

*Ōng-yù* (蓊欝): The upper character, *wū*, has the phonetic *kǒng*. The *Gǔjīn zhèngzì* (古今正字) states that *ōng* means "great," "excellent," or "abundant. The *Guìyuàn zhūcóng* (桂苑珠藂) states it describes the appearance of flourishing grass, taking *cǎo* as the radical and *wēng* as the phonetic. The lower character, *yù*, has the phonetic *lǜ*; it is a vulgar usage. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states *yù* means "to contain" (*yùn*). The *Wēiyùn* (威𣩵) has the phonetic *fǎn*. The *Erya* (爾雅) states *yù* means "the emergence of vapors. The *Guìyuàn zhūcóng* states *yùrán* describes the appearance of vapors emerging. The *Guǎngyá* (廣雅) states *yù* means "deep and secluded," referring to the appearance of trees being dense and remote. The *Shuowén* (說文) states it refers to trees growing in a thicket. According to the *Shuowén*, the correct form of the character *yù* consists of the radical *lín* (林), the phonetic *fǔgǒu* (甫狗), the element *bāo* (音包), the element *chàng* (丑亮), and the element *shān* (音衫). The form written as *yù* (鬱) with four *lín* radicals, the *guì* radical, and the *cùn* radical is of uncertain origin; it is now recorded here alongside the other forms.

*Āmra* is the Sanskrit name for a fruit-bearing tree. This country has no ancient translation for it; some call it *āmba-ra* or *āmra*, all of which refer to the same tree. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "It is like the *āmra* tree, which undergoes three transformations in one year: at times it produces flowers, their radiance and color flourishing; at times it produces leaves, lush and verdant; and at times they wither and fall, appearing like a dead tree. It further states: "It is like the *āmra* tree, which has many flowers but few fruits."

*Jiǎnshūjiā* (甄叔迦) [the first character pronounced *yán* and the second *jiāngqiē*] is a name for a flowering tree in the Western Regions; it is a transliteration of a Sanskrit term whose literal meaning is not sought. This tree does not exist in this land [of China]. The *Great Tang Records on the Western Regions* states that the *jianshujia* tree is common in India, its flowers being red in color and shaped like human hands. One tradition claims it is also called *Aśoka* or the "Sorrowless Tree" (*Wúyōu shù*), and its flowers are likewise red; this latter account is correct.

The character "jiā" (迦) is a phonetic loan for the Sanskrit sound *kha*. Because many readers pronounce it as if it were the original character *jiā* (伽), they mistakenly take it to mean *ga*. This error extends even to the Master Śākyamuni himself, who is called "Shijia" (釋迦); how deeply deluded this is! In this very text, there is first the *vārṣika* flower and later the *karavīra* flower; both share this same pronunciation.
"Universally soaking" (*pù qià*) means to moisten and to soften.
"Tender grasses" (*ruǎn cǎo*); the reading *ruǎn* (as in *ruǎn*) is incorrect. "Fluttering and drooping" (*huò mǐ*):

the first character is read as *suī* or *yí*, and the second as *wèi*; the rhyme dictionary *Shuān* states that "fluttering and drooping" describes the spreading of grasses. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* says it means being spread open by the wind.
"Huīyìng" (輝映): The first character is pronounced with the *huǐ* rhyme (as in *huǐ*), and the second with the *yīng* rhyme (as in *jìng*).

It refers to the mutual radiance of blue-green luster. For example, it is like the neck (*yān*) of a peacock; the *Kǎo Shēng* states that "yān" means the throat or the nape of the neck. In the scriptural text, it is written as "yàn" (from the mouth radical), which is a misused character with the departing tone; its correct form is from the flesh radical.
*Tūla* (the first character pronounced with the *shàngdù* tone; in Sanskrit it refers to fine, soft cotton) refers to the downy fluff of willow trees, grasses, and the like.

Regarding the character *zhǐ* (pronounced with the *ěrlǚ* tone), Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuǒ Zhuan* states that "foot" (*zú*) is the meaning; the *Erya* agrees with this. The subsequent character *bù* (walking) is explained in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as "walking," composed of the radical *zhǐ* (to stop) and the phonetic *tā* (with the *tuōmèi* tone). When written with two characters back-to-back, it forms the character *bù*. In current vernacular usage, the bottom part of the character has been corrupted and abbreviated by adding the element *shǎo*.

"Běi" (陂) [the character pronounced as "bēi" according to Zǐmí's recension; Zhèng Xuán’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states that "pǔ" (蓄水) means to impound water, while "chí" (池) means to dig into the ground to store water].

"Qīnglíng" (清泠) [the second character is pronounced as "lìng" according to Lì Dīng's recension; both characters in "qīnglíng" are radicalized with "shuǐ" (water); "qīnglíng" refers to crystal-clear purity; it is a compound of form and sound].

*Yojana* (the "yu" in *yúshànzhā* is pronounced with the retroflex *r*, and the "shàn" in *shànyīnshàn* is pronounced as *shàn*): this is a Sanskrit term referring to the distance a royal army could travel in one day according to the ancient sages. In various sutras and śāstras, translations for its length vary; some say forty *li*, while the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* says sixteen *li*. The *Great Tang Records on the Western Regions* states that, according to Indian custom, one *yojana* is thirty *li*; this explanation is the most authentic, and we shall follow it here.

Its stem (*jìng*, pronounced *xìng* and *gēng* respectively) is defined in the *Cāngjié piān* as "that which is called a stem for plants and grasses," while the *Shuōwén* explains it as "the primary branch; composed of the radical 'grass' and the phonetic 'jìng' (pronounced *jī*) with the classifier 'strike'. *Vaiḍūrya* is a name for a jewel in the Sanskrit language;

its orthography is not fixed, being sometimes written as *liúlí*. The upper tone is *liú* and the lower tone is *lí*. It is a divine treasure produced by heaven, blue-green in color, translucent, and brilliantly luminous; it is not the kind of *liúlí* made from smelting stones and using fire and smoke found in the human world.

Regarding the character 寶 (bǎo) on the precious bell: its correct orthography consists of 宀 (mián), 王 (wáng), 缶 (fǒu, with the phonetic *gǒu*), and 貝 (bèi). The current scriptural text uses 珍 (zhēn) to form 寶; this is a vulgar usage and not the correct orthography. The lower radical is pronounced táng luò. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that it is a large bell. Kong Anguo says: "It is made of gold and copper with a wooden tongue, used to proclaim the civil edification of the teachings."

"Jambūnada-suvarṇa" (the gold of Jambūdvīpa) is a term for the most excellent and supreme precious gold; it is a divine treasure born of heaven, not gold produced by smelting ore or refining stone in the human world.

Its "beard" (xū) [pronounced yú] is the beard of a lotus flower. According to the *Shuowen*, the correct form is written with the radical 頁 (*xián*, meaning "head") and the component 彡 (*shān*), forming the character 須, which is a pictographic representation. In modern clerical script (*lìshū*), the radical 髟 (*biāo*) is added to form 鬚, which is also used interchangeably.

The character *xiá* (pronounced *jiàn* in the *Kǎośēng*) means "to hold in the mouth and chew. The *Shuōwén* states it refers to the bit in a horse's mouth; it is a compound character formed by combining the radicals for "metal" (*jīn*) and "walking" (*xíng*).

Regarding the character *chì* (廁): at the beginning, it is pronounced as *shǎn* (使反) or *kǎo* (考聲). The *Cāngjié piān* states that *chì* means "intermingled" (*zá*). The *Guǎngyá* states that *chì* means "interval" (*jiàn*). At the bottom, it is pronounced as *tíng* (亭) or *yán* (延) with the *rǎn* (反) tone. Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guóyǔ* states that *tián* (填) means "to add" (*jiā*). The *Guǎngyá* states that *tián* means "to fill up" (*sè*). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states that *tián* means "to fill full" (*mǎn*). It is also written as *tián* (闐), which is likewise acceptable.
*Aśvajit* is a term from the Sanskrit language; in the Tang language, it means "Horse-Winner" (*Ma-sheng*). Regarding *li-yì*:

the upper character *li* is pronounced as *lì*, and the lower character *yì* is pronounced as *yì* (with the phonetic component *yī* reversed). According to local dialects, *yì* refers to *lí* (a screen or curtain). The *Yunying* states that *yì* means "to obstruct. The *Guangya* states that *yì* means "an obstruction. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *yì* refers to a ceremonial canopy (*huagai*), composed of the radical *yu* (feathers) with the phonetic component *yī* (abbreviated) providing the sound.

Regarding "chóulín" (dense forest) and "chángliú" (long current): the *Fǎncāngjiépiān* states that "chóu" means "multitude"; the *Guǎngyá* states that "chóu" means "dense grain," with the phonetic reading *jì*; the *Shuōwén* states that "chóu" means "much," composed of the radical "grain" (*禾*) and the phonetic "zhōu" in abbreviated form.

*Chí* (馳) and *chěng* (騁): *shàng* (upper) [radical] is *zhì* (雉), with the phonetic *lí* (離). This is the standard character; it is also commonly written as *tuó* (駞). Although this is the correct form, it has two pronunciations, one being *tuó* (陀). For now, we follow the common usage and write it as *chí* (馳). Gu Yewang says: "To gallop. The *Guǎngyǎ* says: "To run. *Xià* (lower) [radical] is *chì* (敕), with the phonetic *yǐng* (郢). Dú Yù’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* says: "To gallop; to run. The *Guǎngyǎ* says: "To gallop; to run. The *Shuowén* says: "To drive straight ahead. It is composed of *mǎ* (馬) and the phonetic *zhēn* (𦥚)."

*Liúzhù* (流澍): The upper character *liú* has the meaning of "to pour down," serving as a metaphor for rain. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Timely rain that nourishes all things; it belongs to the water radical and is pronounced with the phonetic *shù*.
*Dǎn* (減): The upper character *dǎn* is pronounced *jué* (悅).
The phonetic category of "shēng" (聲) derives from "chuí" (垂) to form "xiū" (𡙇).
According to the *Shuowen*, "xiū" refers to a ceramic vessel with a small mouth; it is pronounced "ègēng" (厄耕反).
The correct radical form of the character "xiū" (𡙇) in the *Shuowen* is "fǒu" (缶), pronounced "fǔgǒu" (甫苟反), and is written as "quē" (缺).
Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "A *fan* is a basin.
The *Cangjie pian* states: "'Que' means a flaw; it is pronounced *quē* (with the *zhui* rhyme).
Gu Yewang says: "'Que' refers to a blemish."

The *Shuowen* states: "Qiè (器) means 'to break. It is composed of the radical 缶 (fàn) and the phonetic component 夬 (guài) in its abbreviated form. [Regarding the character 減 (jiǎn): the lower part has two pronunciations, both being in the rising tone (shǎngshēng). [Regarding the character 鹹 (xián): it is composed of 水 (shuǐ) and 咸 (xián); the calligraphic structure is identical, yet the phonetic values and the meanings employed for each are distinct. Its original pronunciation is gēngzhǎn (耕斬).
The *Kǎośēng* states: "To diminish it so that it becomes less is called 'reduction' (*jiǎn*).

The *Shuōwén* states: "'Jiǎn' means to diminish. It also has the pronunciation *xián'àn* (咸黯) or *yājiǎn* (鵶減). The *Zìdiǎn* states: "To decrease from below on one's own is called 'reduction' (*jiǎn*)."
The *Jìxùn* says it means "to diminish and waste.
Dictionaries say it means "deficient and sunken.
Here, we take the latter pronunciation.

Regarding "tiánliè" (hunting): the upper character "tián" has the phonetic value of *tián*; the *Shuowen* states it means "level fields. The *Kaosheng* states that "tián" is also "liè" (to hunt), or it is written as "yún" with the radical "quǎn" (dog). The lower character "lì" has the phonetic value of *jiè*. The *Kaosheng* states that it refers to a dog pursuing game. Today, "tiánshòu" (field-hunting) is commonly referred to as "liè. In the *Shuowen*, [the character for] "dàshǔ" (large rat) has the phonetic value of *jiè*.

*Quái kuài*: The first character, *quái*, has the phonetic reading *kǔ* (with the *rén* radical). Kǒng Àngguó’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* states that *quái* means "general. The *Guǎngyá* states that *quái* means "leader. Zhèng Xuán’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states that *quái* means "head. Wáng Yì’s commentary on the *Chǔcáo* states that *quái* means "large. The second character, *kuài*, has the phonetic reading *wài*. The *Guǎngyá* states that *kuài* means "to mince. Those who perform the slaughter and mincing are called *quái kuài*.

The character for *māo* (貓) [pronounced *mào* in the Jiang region; the Wu dialect uses it for the word for "seedling"] is not accepted here. The *Zītǒng* states it is a name for hunting. Gu Yewang says it resembles a tiger but is small, and is raised by people to catch rats. Its correct form follows the radical *xián* (𮙥), with the phonetic *zhì-máo*. In the classics, the dog radical is omitted. The *Shuowen* omits this character [but provides another]. The reading is *xià-tǔ-gù*. Gu Yewang says the fur of the rabbit can be used for brushes. The *Shuowen* identifies it as a name for hunting. It depicts the crouching posture; the dots represent its tail. Because the head of the rabbit resembles the head of the elephant, the character for *tù* (兔) is formed by omitting the radical of *xiàng* (象).
Īṣāduḥkha (The Suffering of Evil) [Sanskrit: Īṣāduḥkha; Chinese phonetic transcription:
伊焰烏固反]. Volume Two. The Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra, Volume Two. Acikitsya (Incurable) [Chinese phonetic transcription:
雉离反]. Saṃkhyā (Number) [Chinese phonetic transcription: 數以霜捉反].
The first character of "wǔfāng" (武坊) is pronounced as fǎn (反).
In "fènscào yīshàngfēn" (糞掃衣上分), the first character is pronounced as fǎn (反) and the last character is pronounced as dào (到).
The "rag-robe wearer" (*pāṃśukūlika*) is a learned bhikṣu of superior practice who habitually wears such garments.
This bhikṣu, through his lofty conduct, restrains greed and does not accept gifts or profits; he discards light, fine, and high-quality clothing.
He constantly gathered discarded rags from among the refuse discarded by people in the world;
he washed them clean in rivers and streams,
then patched and sewed them together to make robes.
It is called the "rag from a dust heap" (pāṃśukūla);
today it is also generally termed the "patchwork robe" (nāṃgyī).
In the Vinaya texts, it is called the "robe of fearlessness" (abhaya-cīvara).
It cannot be seized by wicked people or bandits;
it is also called the "robe of merit" in the sutras,
and is praised by all Tathāgatas.
Those who wear these robes are constantly visited by the devas, who pay them homage and make offerings.
For this reason, the Tathāgata praised Mahākāśyapa, commanding him to sit together with him, exchange robes, and put these on.

Therefore, it is called the "Robe of Merit" (*guṇavastra*). Regarding the character *kǐ* (谿): in the *Guǎngyá*, it refers to a valley; in the *Shuowén*, it means water flowing into a stream, formed with the radical for water and the phonetic *xī*. It is also written as *xī*. Regarding the character *jiàn* (澗): in the *Máo Shī Zhuàn*, it says that where water flows through a mountain gorge, it is called a *jiàn*; the *Shàngshū* states, "The Yí, Luó, Chán, and Jiàn rivers have all entered the Hé. Kǒng Àngguó notes that the Jiàn River originates from the northern mountains of Shènchí. In the regions where these mountains are narrow, waters are all named *jiàn*. The *Shuowén* also says it refers to mountain water, formed with the radical for water and the phonetic *jiān*.

*Chuídǎng* (捶打): *jiā* (佳) and *rě* (蘂) as initials; *fǎn* (反) and *xù* (許) as finals. Zhusongzhòng’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states: "To hammer and forge. *Dū* (都) and *luàn* (亂) as finals. Examining the phonology, it is synonymous with *chì* (樀). *Cháo* (嘲) and *è* (厄) as initials. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as: "To strike with a staff. It takes the radical *shǒu* (hand) and the phonetic *chuí* (垂). Alternatively, it is written with the radical *mù* (wood) as *chuí* (棰), meaning a club or mallet. *Lěng* (冷) as the final for the latter character. The *Guǎngyá* defines it as "to strike. The *Pīcāng* states: "A club used for striking. It takes the radical *shǒu* (hand) and the phonetic *dīng* (丁). Currently, in the Wu region outside the Yangtze River, it is pronounced *dǐng* (頂); this pronunciation is not accepted here.

Regarding the character for *jué* (net): it is written as 絹 (jiàn) or 犬 (quǎn), and its standard form is 󲖡; it is also written as 𦍃. According to the *Kǎoshēng* (Investigation of Pronunciation), it means to capture birds and beasts with a rope. The *Yùnyīng* (Rhymes and Flowers) states that it means to bind and seize. Examining the term *jué*, it refers to a lasso (*jué-suǒ*). Gù Yěwáng says that "net" (*wǎng*) is the general name for various types of nets such as *luó* and *shān*. The *Yì* (Book of Changes) says: "In ancient times, the clan of Páo Qí tied ropes to make nets for hunting and fishing, thereby nourishing the myriad people. The *Shìběn* (Origin of Things) states that Máng created the net; Sòng Zhōng says he was a minister of Fúxī. It is also written as 󲐁 or 󲏿, both of which are archaic characters.

*Jǔ* (藏舉): The first character is pronounced with the upper radical *zhǎo* (昨) and the phonetic *láng* (郎); the second character is pronounced with the upper radical *jiāng* (薑) and the phonetic *yǔ* (圄). Some editions of the scripture write it as *jǔ* (弆), which is also pronounced *xū* (墟) and *yǔ* (圄), and its sound is likewise *jǔ*. *Cūguǎng* (麁獷): The first character, *cū* (麁), has the upper radical *cāng* (倉) and the phonetic *hú* (胡);

it is a simplified form of the character for "neglect" (*fǎnglüè*). It has been used in transmission for a long time; its correct form according to the *Shuowen Jiezi* is written with three *lù* (鹿) characters. The *Shuowen* states that "objects are not refined. The *Guangya* says *shǎo* (󱍮) means "large. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* says *shǎo* (󱍮) means "sparse. The second character, *guǎng* (獷), has the upper radical *hào* (號) and the phonetic *wǔ* (塢) with the tone *měng* (猛). The *Jixun* says: "A dog that is wild and evil cannot be approached. There are some versions of the scripture that write this with the stone radical as *kuàng* (礦), which is an error; that refers to copper, iron, or stone ore, and is not the original character.

Regarding the term *xièmá* (蝦蟇): the first character is pronounced *jì* (計) with the secondary tone, and the second is *xiá* (遐) with the final tone; according to the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲), it is the name of an aquatic insect. The *Erya* states: *qū* (鼁, pronounced *qù*), *qiú* (𪓰, pronounced *qiū*), *chán* (蟾, pronounced *zhān*), and *chú* (蜍, pronounced *yú*). Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* says it resembles a *xièmá* and lives on land; the *Huainanzi* calls it *qùxiū* (去𪓰). The *Erya* further states that when it is in the water, it is called *měng* (黽, pronounced *měng*). Guo Pu’s commentary notes: *gěng* (耿) is pronounced *gēng* (耕) with the third tone; it resembles a frog but has a large belly. The *Bencao* (本草) states: *xièmá* is also called *chánchú* (蟾蜍), *qūqiú* (鼁𪓰), *qùxiū* (去𪓰), *tiānfù* (田父), *hùmèng* (胡孟), *qīngwā* (青蛙), *gěngměng* (耿猛), and *chánggǔ* (長股); these are all regional variations for the names of the *xièmá*.

"Míhóu" (獼猴): the first character is pronounced "yīn-mí" (音彌) and the second is pronounced "hóu" (音侯). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "a monkey. (Note: The character is also written as 獶, which the *Shuowen* defines as a type of ape.)
It is pronounced "nú dāo fǎn" (奴刀反).
Some call it the "mother-monkey";
the *Hanshu* refers to it as the "mùhóu" (沐猴).
Nowadays they call it the "monkey-son king" (hóusūn wáng).
Yánshòu composed a rhapsody referring to it as the "prince" (wáigsūn).
Currently, in common parlance, it is called the "wild-son" (húsūn).
Examining these species of *śūra* (wild boars), they are exceedingly numerous;
to speak briefly, there are approximately ten types.
For now, I shall list their names in brief.
It would be impossible to describe each one in detail.

There are the *míhóu* (macaque), the *báiyuán* (white ape), the *yīn yuán* (the "Yuan" ape), the *qīng jiǎo* (blue monkey)—*jiǎo* pronounced as *jué*—the *qīng ní* (green monkey), the *jū* (ape)—*jū* pronounced as *jù*—the *yòu* (long-tailed monkey)—*yòu* pronounced as *jiù*—the *yuì* (gibbon)—*yuì* pronounced with the departing tone as *yí*, or again as *yúshuǐ*—and furthermore, there is the *guǒrán* (rhinopithecus); all of these are species of macaque.
The distinctions among their forms and appearances are each unique; I shall now briefly describe them.
According to the *Nanzhou Yiwuzhi* (Record of Strange Things from the Southern Region), it states:
"In the mountain forests and thickets of Jiunshanfu in Jiaozhou, as well as in Gupuchuan of Jiuqin, these beasts are found everywhere."
Its name is indeed true to its nature.

Belonging to the class of monkeys and apes, it calls out its own name when it cries; its body is like that of a monkey, its face is like that of a dog, and it is either blue in color or entirely white.
There are black spots on its flanks;
its body does not exceed three chi in length, while its tail is over four chi long.

When turned back, the tail extends beyond the head; looking at its nose, one sees two nostrils facing upward toward the sky. Its fur is long, soft, and fine. Occasionally such a beast is found among humans, and its skin is used for rugs and mats.

Regarding "xuánzá" (喧雜): The upper character is written as 暉 (huī) in the Yuan family's standard form, though it is sometimes written as 讙 (huān). It belongs to the class of sounds meaning clamor; Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* defines it as "the sound of noisy clamor" (pronounced xuānxiāo, with the second tone for the first character and the third tone for the second). The lower character is written as 財 (cái) in the common form, but its standard form is 襍 (zá). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "That which is made of five-colored silks is called zá; it follows the radical 'clothing' (衣) and takes 'jí' (集) as its phonetic. The current form "zá" is a transformed variant and a vulgar character. It is an error resulting from the cursive script (cǎoshū), where the "clothing" radical was mistakenly changed into the "standing man" (立) radical.

In the *Zhang Yong* commentary on the *Shuowen*, it is stated that "mu" (墓) means a grave; the character "zhong" (冡) is composed of "baou" (勹, pronounced bao) and "shi" (豕, pronounced chulü). It is incorrect [to claim] that in the Classics the character is composed of "mian" (冂, pronounced mi) and "shi" (豕, pronounced shi).

Regarding "qū" (趨): Yu Baoxian’s commentary on the *Lunyu* states that "qū" means rapid walking. The *Erya* says that the area outside the gate is called "qū. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "running," with its correct form consisting of the radical "walk" (走) and the phonetic "cuō" (芻, pinyin: chū). The character in the current scripture, written with "duō" (多), is a vulgar variant.

*Chí* (馳): Pronounced *shàng-cháng-lí-fǎn*. The *Shuowen* writes it as *tuó* (駝). The *Guoyá* states it means "to gallop. Gu Yewang says it means "to run. The *Shuowen* defines it as "a large horse," written with the radical *mǎ* (馬) and the phonetic *tā* (它), pronounced *tā*. The character in the current scripture is written as *chí* (馳), which is a vulgar usage. *Xia* (下): Pronounced *chì-lǐng-fǎn*. The *Guoyá* states it means "to race. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* says it means "to run. The *Shuowen* defines it as "to drive straight ahead," written with the radical *mǎ* (馬) and the phonetic *pǐ-xià-fǎn* (󲒢匹下反). The *Shuowen* further explains that the character *biàn* (󲒢) is composed of *yóu* (由) and *kǎo* (丂), pronounced *kǎo*. The version in the current scripture uses *biàn* (󲗠), which is incorrect.

"Qiang-lin" (Forest of Spears) refers to the *Cangjie pian*’s definition of a wooden object with two ends sharpened. According to current usage, a "qiang" is a weapon; when a pole of water-length or more has iron blades attached to both ends, it is called a "qiang. The *Shuowen jiezi* defines it as "a pronged weapon (*ju*), composed of the radical for wood and the phonetic 'cang'."
Xian (險): Kuang (壙), Xu (虛), Yan (儼), Fan (反).
According to the *Guangya*, it means "obstacles" (*jianzu*).
According to the *Fangyan*, it means "high" (*gao*).
Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that "xian" means perilous;
Wang Bi’s commentary on the *Zhouyi* states that "xian" means difficulty;
and the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "xian" means obstructive difficulty.

The character for "precipice" (險) in the scripture is written with the radical "mountain" (山) and the phonetic "yan" (儼); this is incorrect. It should instead be written with the phonetic "fu-qian-chi-jian-fan" (負僉七尖反).
"Xian" (險) means slightly uneven or rugged; it refers to a gully or pit.
Thus, both the meaning and the pronunciation of the current character are erroneous.
The meaning of the scripture suggests that "xiàn" (險) should be revised to follow the radical "fù" (阜).
The lower character is pronounced with the *kǔ* and *bàng* finals. According to the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲), it means "kuànglàng" (壙埌), which describes the vast appearance of distant wildernesses.
The *Cangjie pian* states that "kuàng" means sparse.
The *Guoyu* states that "kuàng" means great.
The *Shuowen jiezi* defines it as a moat; pronounced "qiyàn," it is a hole formed from the radical "earth" (土) with the phonetic component "guǎng" (廣).
In the scripture, writing "kuàng" (曠) for "rì" (日) is an error.
"Kuàng" means vastness or light, which is by no means the intended meaning of the scripture.
It should correctly be written with the "earth" radical (土).

*Zī* (貲): The upper radical is *zǐ* (紫). According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means "wealth" (*zhìhuò*). Gu Yewáng states that it refers specifically to the assets within one's household; the character written as *zī* (資) does not carry this meaning. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means to redeem oneself from a minor punishment with wealth; it is composed of the "shell-and-currency" radical (*bèi*) and the phonetic *cǐ* (此).

The character *sè* (貳) can be read as *fǎn* (反). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that it refers to borrowing capital from subordinate officials (*jìběn*). The *Jixùn* explains it as "borrowing from others. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "seeking goods from others. It is composed of the radical *rén* (人) and the phonetic *yì* (弋), which has the sound *yì*. In the scriptural text, it is sometimes written as *dài* (貸), pronounced *tài*, which is an error; the character *rén* (人) should be removed. *Tái* (台) is pronounced *zǎi* (載). Such erroneous usages should be eliminated.

"Xiāo (銷) means to extinguish; it is pronounced with the *qiao* rhyme of *xi* (息). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states that it means 'to disperse. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means 'to melt metal,' with the radical *jin* (金) and the phonetic *xiao* (肖), pronounced with the *shang* (商) rhyme. The second character, *mie* (滅), is pronounced with the *mi* (彌) rhyme. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means 'to completely annihilate. It is composed of the radicals *shui* (水), *xu* (戌), and *huo* (火). *Xu* is the foundation of fire, and water extinguishes fire; this is a compound character based on the convergence of these meanings."

*Di* (遞): Pronounced *ting* with a retroflex final (禮反), though *di* (递) is also acceptable. The *Kǎo Shēng* states that *di* means "to alternate. Guō Pǔ’s commentary on the *Eryā* says it means "to exchange. The *Chǔcí* says, "The four seasons alternate (*dì*) in coming and thus complete the year," where Wáng Yì explains it as "mutually replacing one another. Lexicons state that *di* means "to intersect" (*jiāo*). It is written with the radical *chuò* (辵) and the phonetic *chǐu lüè* (丑略反). *Tí* (虒) has the sound *tī*. The text reads *shēn* (󲚬), which is a vulgar character. Below, *hú gù* (胡固反). The *Yùnquán* says *hù* means "to differ. It represents the image of a hanging crossbar (*hu*) with a *bēn* (󲖂) in the center to distinguish it. The text reads *yǎn* (㸦), which is an erroneous vulgar character; it is not the standard form.

*Yú-chǎn* (諛諂): The character *yú* (諛) is pronounced with the initial *rāng* and final *zhū*. The *Cāngjié piān* states that "flattery (*chǎn*) follows [the will of others]. The *Zhuāngzǐ* says, "To speak without distinguishing between right and wrong is called flattery (*yú*). The *Shuōwén* defines it as "flattery (*yú*)," formed from the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic component "yú" (臾), pronounced with the initials *rāng* and *zhū*. The character *chǎn* (諂) is pronounced with the initial *chǔ* and final *rǎn*. The *Yìjīng* says, "The superior man does not flatter when interacting with those above, nor does he behave with sycophancy when interacting with those below. Hé Xiū’s commentary on the *Gōngyáng zhuan* states, "Flattery (*chǎn*) is like being fawning (*xiá*). The *Zhuāngzǐ* says, "To speak with a devious intent regarding the Way is called flattery (*chǎn*). The *Shuōwén* defines it as "flattery (*chǎn*)," formed from the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic component "xiàn" (臽), pronounced with the initials *xián* and *jiǎn*.

*Yǒngyuè* (勇躍). "Yǒng" (勇) is pronounced with the radical *yáng* (羊). The *Shìfǎ* (諡法) states: "To cast one's life for benevolence is called 'courage' (*yǒng*); to know death and not avoid it is called 'courage'. The *Shuōwén* says: "Courage (*qì*) is [the character] *yǒng*. It is composed of the radical *lì* (力) and the phonetic *yǒng* (甬, pronounced *yáng*). Alternatively, it is written with the radical *gē* (戈, pronounced *gǔhuó*). When used as *zào* (造), it forms *zào* (𠿑, an archaic form). Alternatively, it is written with the radical *zú* (足), forming *yǒng* (踴). The *Guǎngyá* states: "To leap; to ascend; to advance. The *Shuōwén* further states: "It is the appearance of walking. It is composed of the radical *zú* (足) and the phonetic *zhé* (翟). *Yuè* (躍). Pronounced with the radical *yáng* (羊) and *zhuó* (灼). The *Guǎngyá* states: "To leap; to jump; to ascend; to advance. The *Shuōwén* states: "The appearance of movement. It is composed of the radical *zú* (足) and the phonetic *zhé* (翟)."

*Yìngbì* (映蔽): The upper character *yīng* (英) is pronounced *jìng* (敬) with a retroflex rhyme; *yīng* is glossed as "shining alongside. Lexicons state it means "mutually obscuring. Its correct form follows *yīng*. The *Jīngwén* (經文) version following *yāng* (央), pronounced *yújiāng* (於薑), is incorrect. When written as *yìng* (映), it is pronounced *wūlǎng* (烏朗). The *Yùpiān* (玉篇) states that *yìng* and *zhēn* (𦿔) mean "lack of clarity," but this is not the meaning in the context of the scripture. The lower character is pronounced *bēi* (卑) with a retroflex rhyme, or *míbì* (彌弊). Dú Yù’s commentary on the *Zuòchuán* (左傳) glosses it as "obstructing. The *Guǎngyá* (廣雅) glosses it as "concealing. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) glosses it as "covering. It follows the radical for grass (*cǎo*) and the phonetic *bì* (敝), pronounced *píyì* (毘曳).
Cǎnlì (慘厲): The upper character is read as *qīgǎn* (七感反).
The *Jíxùn* (集訓) states it means "to be vexed and resentful.
The *Yùnyīng* (韻英) states it means "sorrow and grief."
Furthermore, the pronunciation of "yōu" (又) is *chū-jǐn* (初錦反).
The *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲) states that it means "extreme bitterness.

The *Shuōwén* defines it as "poison," composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) with the phonetic component "cān" (*cān-shēng*). The character "cān" (*cān-zì*) is composed of "lěi" (*lěi-yīn*, pronounced *léi*) and the phonetic component "zhī-rěn" (*zhī-rěn-fǎn*).
Nowadays, it is commonly written as "cān" (參) in its variant form.
Alternatively, it is written with the radical for speech (言) as "yín" (𦙍), implying that one uses words to mock others covertly.
The lower radical is pronounced lì (力) with the tone zhì (滯).
Yunying says: "The *Shiming* commentary on the *Mao Shi* states that 'li' means 'evil.
Zheng Xuan’s annotation to the *Liji* states that 'li' means 'severity.
The *Kaosheng* states it refers to the disharmony of the vital breath (*qi*)."
Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "Lì (厲) means fierce and violent.
It is composed of the radical 厂 (pronounced hǎn) and the phonetic 萬;
it is incorrect for the text to use 力 as the phonetic to form 勵 (lì).
"Exerting effort" means to encourage or urge. This is not the intended meaning of the scripture.
Alternatively, it may be written with the radical "sickness" (疒) and the phonetic "nü è" (女厄), forming the character "lì" (癘), which refers to a contagious disease.

This is certainly not the intended meaning of the sūtra. Regarding the term *pín* (嚬): according to the *Kǎo Shēng*, it means *pín mǎn* (嚬懣), pronounced with the tone of *mèn*. Dictionaries state that *pín yí* (嚬𡂔) refers to knitting the eyebrows. Xu Shen’s *Shuōwén Jiězì* states: "Those who wade through water knit their brows (*pín yí*). Gu Yewáng says: "According to the texts, *pín yí* is the appearance of one who is sorrowful, anxious, and unhappy. The standard form in the *Shuōwén* is composed of the radicals *bēi* (卑) and *bīn* (瀕). In modern clerical script (*lìshū*), it is abbreviated by replacing *shè* (涉) with *bù* (步) and omitting *bēi* for *kǒu* (口), thus forming *pín*; this is a reduction. The lower character, pronounced *jiǔ yù* (酒育), is identified as *yí* (𡂔) in the *Kǎo Shēng*. The *Shujing* records: "He sighed deeply (*zhāi*) and felt bashful (*niùní*)," sometimes written with *kǒu* (口) as *ōu* (㗤), which is the same character, or with *mù* (目) as *chù* (𥉷), which is an archaic form. The text of the sūtra uses *cù* (蹙) with the radical *zú* (足); this is not the original character.

The character for *fanyi* (trade) is read as *fānwàn* (上發萬反) in the rhyme; the *Yīngyùn* states it means "to buy cheap and sell dear. It is composed of the radical *bèi* (貝, meaning "shell money") and the phonetic *fǎn* (反). The lower part is read as *yángyì* (羊益反); the *Kǎoshēng* states it means "to change," "to exchange," or "to transform. It is a pictographic character.

*Kiè* (篋): The upper character, *qián* (謙), with the phonetic *jiá* (頰); the *Kǎo Shēng* states it is a type of chest. The *Shuōwén* says *kiè* means a small box; it is composed of the radical *fāng* (匚, pronounced *fāng*) and the phonetic *jiá* (夾, pronounced *jiǎ*). The lower character is pronounced *sì* (四); the *Kǎo Shēng* states that *sì* (笥) is also a small box, composed of the radical *zhú* (竹) and the phonetic *sī* (司).

The gallbladder dares to act against all; the *Baixhutong* states that the gallbladder is the palace (*fu*) of the liver. The liver presides over benevolence (*ren*), and since benevolence is characterized by an inability to bear [cruelty], it uses the gallbladder to exercise decisive judgment. Therefore, one who possesses benevolence must necessarily possess courage. The *Maijing* of Wang Shuhe states that the gallbladder presides over the spirit (*shen*); when the gallbladder is diseased, the spirit cannot maintain its stability, and thus this is known.

*Qiè* (怯): The upper radical is *qiāng* (羌) with the phonetic *kǎo* (考); it is the sound of the character. It means timidity (*qiè luò*). The *Yùpiān* states that *qiè* means much fear. The *Yùnyīng* says *qiè* means dread and apprehension. It is composed of the "heart" radical (*xīn*) with the fourth tone. The lower part is *lì chuō* (力惙); it means having little strength. This is a compound character formed by combining its semantic components.

*Zhu* (upper character pronounced *zhāng lǚ* [with the second tone], according to Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan*, it means "to store up"; *chì* [pronounced *cì* with the fourth tone] means "to conceal"). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to accumulate wealth," composed of the radical *jù* (*zhí lǜ* [with the fourth tone]) and the phonetic *níng*. The lower character is pronounced *qíng yù* [with the fourth tone], or alternatively *cí yú* [with the third tone]; the latter is also acceptable in rhyme. The *Yingyun* states it means "to assemble. The *Kaosheng* states it means "to gather together. He Xiu’s commentary on the *Gongyangzhuan* states it means "to collect. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to assemble," composed of the radical *qín* (pronounced *yín*, meaning "standing in a crowd") and the phonetic *qǔ* (abbreviated form). The archaic script is written as *zuì*.

The term *tongbo* (銅鈸)—the character *bo* being pronounced *mo-fan*—refers to a musical instrument. It is cast in two pieces, shaped like the lids of small jars, with a handle (*bi*) on each; one holds them in hand and strikes the two openings against each other to produce sound for harmonizing music. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "metal" (*jin*) and the phonetic component "ba" (*ba*). Although some versions of the scripture use the character "ba" (跋) with the "foot" (*zu*) radical, this is not the original character; it is merely a variant of the word "bashi" (跋涉), meaning "to traverse."

*Kuì* (上): Pronounced *gōng* (上) or alternatively *huí* (迴) or *wài* (外); it is also interchangeable. The *Jixùn* (集訓) states: "The mind is vexed and disordered. The *Shuowén* (說文) states: "It means confusion. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical *xīn* (心) and the phonetic *huì* (潰), with the sound abbreviated as *huì*. *Niào* (下): Pronounced *niǎo* (效). The *Jixùn* states: "Many people causing disturbance and turmoil. The *Yùnyīng* (韻英) states: "To be confused and mixed. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radicals *shì* (市) and *rén* (人), forming a compound character (*huìyì zì*). The character used in the scripture is *nào* (閙), which is a vulgar form. Some write it as *bǐng* (丙), which is an error made by scribes that does not form a valid character.
*Chenbi* (瞋蔽): The first character is pronounced *chāng rén* (昌人反); the second is pronounced *bīmèi* (卑袂反), with the phonetic *mí bì* (彌閉反).

*Zǐ* (滓) means turbid; according to the *Kǎoshēng*, it means filth. The *Shuowén* states that *zǐ* (滓) means dregs, composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic "zhǎi" (*zǎi*) abbreviated; alternatively, it is written as *cǎn* (䔂) with the radical "grass" (*cǎo*), meaning vegetables used in soup.

Regarding the character for "conch" (螺貝): the upper part is pronounced *luo* (with the retroflex *he* [huǎn] tone). This is a vernacular usage; its standard form is written as 蠃. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "Luo is the same as the snail (*guāniú*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* also says it belongs to the class of snails, though its shape is large and it originates from the sea. Its appearance varies in several ways and is not uniform.

Regarding "jue-wù" (覺寤): the upper character is pronounced *jiào* and the lower *wù*. The *Kǎo Shēng* states it means "awakening from sleep. The *Jí Xùn* states it means "waking from sleep. The *Shuō Wén* defines it as "awakening from sleep. The scriptural form [with the radical for "cave"] containing "zhōng" (中) and "xīn" (心), and with "gào" (告) as the phonetic component, forming "jì" (𥧦), is erroneous. Upon examining all dictionaries and the *Jiàozì Yùn*, this character does not exist; it is mostly a product of scribes' dictation or copyists' arbitrary fabrications and is incorrect. "Wù" (寤) means "to awaken" (*wù*). The *Cāng Jié Piān* states: "To wake from sleep and speak is called *wù*. The *Kǎo Shēng* states: "That which one sees while asleep and, upon waking, believes to be true. The *Shuō Wén* [defines it] with the abbreviated form of "mèng" (㝱) and "wú" (吾) as the phonetic component.

The character *sàn* (葢): The *Sāng Yù Piān* states that *sàn* is simply a canopy (*gài*). The *Tōng sú wén* says: "To use silk to avoid rain is called *sàn*; it follows the radical for 'silk' (*mì*) and takes the phonetic *yì*. Furthermore, the original form of the character *yì* was *lín* (㪔), following the radicals for 'forest' (*lín*) and 'to bow' (*bài*, pronounced *píng*). This refers to the forest being divided by *yì*. Today, in clerical script (*lìshū*), it has been transmitted as *sàn*, which is an erroneous abbreviation. In the scriptures, it is sometimes written as *sǎn*, which is a vulgar character. The lower part is read as *ài*. A canopy (*gài*) is also a type of *sǎn*. According to the *Shuōwén*, the canopy (*gài*) consists of the radicals for 'grass' (*cǎo*) and 'to cover' (*hé*, pronounced *hé*). The form in the scripture using the 'sheep' radical (*yáng*) to make *gài* is due to errors resulting from cursive script (*cǎoshū*).

*Chòu* (臭): The upper radical is *chāng* (昌) with the tone *shòu* (狩). The *Yùpiān* states that "odor" (*chòu*) is the general term for the vapors of things. The *Shuowén* says: "A dog knows the tracks of a fleeing bird by its scent; therefore, the character for 'odor' is composed of 'dog' (*quán*) and 'nose' (*zì*). 'Nose' (*zì*) is the ancient script for 'nose' (*bí*). It is incorrect for the text of the scriptures to use *sì* (𣦸) as the lower radical to form *wǎ* (󲗏). The lower radical is *yú* (於) with the tone *qī* (𠿒). Gù Yěwáng says: "It means defilement. The *Yùnyīng* says: "It means foulness. The *Kǎoshēng* says: "It means wilderness. It is also written as *huì* (薉); according to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of 'grain' (*huó*) and the phonetic 'year' (*suì*).
"Enveloped" (chánwǒ): the first character is pronounced with the *shàng* tone and the *zhī* rhyme; the second character is pronounced with the *lián* rhyme and the *gē* rhyme.
"Small insects" (xiǎochóng): the *chóng* is pronounced with the *cháng* rhyme; the text reads it as "worms" (cóng), which is incorrect. "To infer" (tuīduó):
the *tuī* is pronounced with the *táng* and *luò* rhymes; it means to measure.

*Xiàn-tuò* (涎唾): The upper character is pronounced *qiú-yán* (囚延) and is a vernacular form; according to the *Shuowen*, the correct orthography is *sì* (㳄). It means "saliva," composed of the radical *shui* (水) and the semantic element *qian* (欠), with *kao* (考) as the phonetic. It is said to mean "the moisture of the mouth. *Shu Xi* wrote it as *tián* (唌), *Shi Zhou* wrote it as *fu* (󲀦), and *Jia Kui* wrote it as *yàng* (漾) or *lü* (𣵿); these are archaic forms. The various variant forms for the upper character all state that it means "saliva. The lower character is pronounced *tǔ-kè* (吐課); the *Shuowen* states it means "saliva," composed of the radical *kou* (口) and the abbreviated semantic element *chui* (垂), with *sheng* (省) as the phonetic. It may also be written with the radical *shui* (水) as *tuò* (涶), which is also acceptable.

"Flowing over" (yì) is derived from "one turn" (yī fǎn); its standard form is written as yì, though it is also written as sì, both of which are archaic and correct characters. According to the *Erya*, yì means "fullness"; according to the *Guangya*, it means "overflowing"; and according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "the vessel being full. It is composed of the radical for water (水) with the phonetic element yì (益).

*Shìniè* (噬齧): The upper character is pronounced with the *shí* rhyme (the *yè* rhyme in the *Kǎośēng*). The *Kǎośēng* states that *shìniè* is also *shì*. The lower character is pronounced with the *jiàn* rhyme. According to the *Shuōwén*, *niè* is also *shì*; it is composed of the radical "teeth" (*chǐ*) and the phonetic element "zhòu" (pronounced *bā*), which signifies "skillful. *Zhòu* means "dexterity."

*Zhé* (讁) [pronounced *zhāng* and *gé* in the upper register; this is a vulgar usage of the character]. The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* states: "To *zhé* is to reprimand. Du Yù’s commentary on the *Zuǒ Zhuan* says: "*Zhé* means to censure. The *Fān Yán* states: "*Zhé* means anger. Guō Pǔ says: "This refers to mutual reprimanding and angering. The *Shuō Wén* defines *zhé* as punishment. Its correct form is written as *zhí* (𧬍), composed of the radical for speech (*yán*), the character *dì* (帝), and the character for mouth (*kǒu*). The current text uses *zhé* (讁), which is a vulgar form derived from *shì* (適). *Xí* (罰) [pronounced *fán* and *wà* in the lower register]. The *Shàngshū* says: "Punishing those who commit crimes. The *Shuō Wén* says: "A minor offense; one who merely holds a blade and reviles should be punished. It is composed of the radical for cursing (*lì*) and the character for blade (*dāo*). Cáo Yōng’s Stone Classics changed the *gāng* (岡) to four strokes and changed the *dāo* (刀) to one inch (*cùn*).

*Guān* (關): Upper radical *gào*, reversed *huán*. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states it is the gate at the boundary. *Shènglèi* says it is a *guānghóng* (a door-bolt). *Guǐ* is reversed *yíng*. The *Shuowén* says it is to hold the door with water; it is composed of the radical *mén* and the phonetic *guǎn* (reversed *huán*). The character *guǎn* is composed of the radical *yōu* (sound *yōu*) and the phonetic *guàn* (reversed *guàn*). Lower radical *lè* (reversed *è*). The *Kǎoshēng* says *luò* means to block. The *Jixùn* says: "Wandering troops and scouts who block and patrol."

3. Fascicle Three. *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Fascicle Three. Regarding the character "yù" (瘀): according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means accumulated blood; it is composed of the radical "nà" (疒) [the phonetic component is pronounced "nüè"]. People of the time called this radical "bìngjiǎo" (病脚), but this is a colloquialism and not the standard terminology. The text of the sūtra uses the character "yù" (淤) with the water radical, which is incorrect; "yù" refers to greenish mud.

*Diao* (掉): The initial rhyme is *kao* (考). It means to sway or move. *Ji* (譏): Following the commentary of Zheng Xuan on the *Liji*, it means to reproach or censure. The final rhyme is *xi* (奚). *Fen* (紛): The rhyme is *wen* (文). According to the *Guoya*, it means disorder;

according to the *Shuowen*, it takes *mi* (糸) as its radical and *fen* (分) as its phonetic component. The final rhyme is *zhao* (沼). *Kao* (攪): This refers to the act of agitating one thing by means of another. It describes the appearance of indulging in desires. According to the *Shuowen*, *jiao* (攪) means "to vex" (*fan*). It takes *tou* (扌)—meaning "hand"—as its radical and *nu* (奴) with the final rhyme *dao* (刀) as its phonetic component.

*Jiǎoluàn* (矯亂): "Jiǎo" (矯) is pronounced *jiān* (姜夭反). The *Jixùn* (集訓) states it means "deceitful. Gu Yewang says: "To falsely assume a title is called *jiǎo*. The *Shuowén* explains *jiǎo* as "to usurp," written with the radical for "arrow" (*shì*) and the phonetic *qiáo*. Furthermore, the *Shuowén* explains the character *qiáo* as being composed of "arrow" and "sound"; the current vulgar usage of the character with the radical for "right" (*yòu*) is erroneous. "Luàn" (亂) is pronounced *lùduàn* (盧段反). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it means "confusion and disorder. It is sometimes written as "luàn" (亂); according to the ancient characters, the *Shuowén* writes it with the radical for "insect" (*yǐ*) and the phonetic *lù* (𤔔), which is the sound of "luàn."
"Canran" (慘然) is a transliteration; according to the *Mao Shih Zhuan*, "can" (慘) means "sorrowful," and the *Erya* states that "can" (慘) means "grief.
"Aṭavī" is a Sanskrit term referring to the palace where Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King of Abundant Hearing, resides; it is also called "Anawanduo" (阿拏挽多) City.

"Hao-tao" (號咷): "Hao" is pronounced with the *hu* and *gao* finals reversed; Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states it means "wailing," while the *Erya* defines it as "calling out. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as "the sound of pain. The second character, "Tao," is pronounced with the *tang* and *lao* finals reversed. In sum, "hao-tao" refers to loud, bitter weeping, as in the *Yijing*: "First there is hao-tao, and afterwards there is laughter."

*Tou* (投): *cuan* (竄) is the phonetic component; *tu* (徒) and *hou* (侯) are the radicals. Xu’s commentary on the *Shijing* states it means "to throw down. Examining the sound, it also means "to rush toward. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *chao* (𣪌), meaning "to strike from afar" (the lower radical is pronounced *cang-luan*). Gu Yewang says it means "to flee. Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* says it means "to hide. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* says it means "to conceal. The *Gujin Zhengzi* says *cuan* means "to store away," derived from a rat inside its hole. *Cuan* (竄): It means "to escape. In the *Guoyu*, Jia’s commentary says it means "to hide. In Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan*, it means "to conceal. The *Gujin Zhengzi* says *cuan* means "to store away," following the form of a rat within its burrow.

*Yao* (殀): Pronounced *jiǎo fǎn* (the "fǎn" indicating the tone). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that being "shortened and broken" is called *yao*; it refers to dying young. *Xia* (下): Pronounced *qǔ sù fǎn*. The *Guǎngyá* says it means "near"; the *Shuowén* says it means "to press. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* says it means "swift."

"Locusts" (huángchóng): "huáng" is pronounced as *hú* with the *guāng* rhyme; "chóng" is pronounced as *róng* with the *zhú* rhyme. According to the *Erya*: "That which eats the heart of the seedling is called *míng*; that which eats the leaves is called *yù* (pronounced *tú* with the *dé* rhyme); that which eats the roots is called *móu* (pronounced *máo*); that which eats the joints is called *zé*. These four types are all locusts; they are alternative names for various insect calamities."

Regarding "not mute" (bù yǎ): the ancient pronunciation was *yā* (as indicated by the rhyme), and the commentary states that it means one cannot speak. The standard character for this in both ancient and modern usage is *yǎn* (瘖), which consists of the radical *nà* (疒) with the phonetic *è* (厄) and the semantic element *yà* (亞). It is incorrect for the scriptures to write it as *yǎ* (啞) with the radical *kǒu* (口).

The character *bǐ* (斤乙反) is also written as *jí* (󲘅), both being acceptable according to the *Kǎoshēng*. The *Yùnquán* states it means "redundant," while the *Shuōwén* states it means "difficult. It is composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) with the phonetic "qǐ" (*qí*).

Regarding *fù* (負): the phonetic transcription is *cū yú* (蒭虞反). The *Jìxùn* (集訓) states that "cū" (*蒭*) is the general name for grass; however, the forms written as *gǔ* (󲕄) or *gǔ* (󲐉) are incorrect. Regarding *dān fù* (擔負): the phonetic transcription is *dōu nán* (都南反). The *Jìxùn* states that "dān" (*擔*) is also "fù" (*負*), meaning to carry or bear objects; it is composed of the radical *shǒu* (扌, meaning hand) and the phonetic *zhān* (詹, meaning zhān). The *Wénzì Shìyào* (文字釋要) states that the character *zhān* (詹) is composed of *wěi* (厃, pinyin wěi, meaning "to bend over") and the components *bā* (八) and *yán* (言); the form in the scripture using the wood radical (*mù*, 木) to form *yán* (檐) is incorrect. *Yán* (檐) has the phonetic transcription *yè zhān* (葉占反) and refers to the eaves of a roof; it does not accord with the meaning of the scripture. Regarding *fù* (負): the phonetic transcription is *fú wǒ* (浮缶反). Gu Yewang says: "To turn one's back on kindness and loathe virtue is called *fù*. The *Yùnyuán Xuān* (韻銓) says: "To receive a loan and fail to repay it is called *fù*. The *Shuowén* (說文) says: "*Fù* means to rely upon. It is composed of the ancient person radical (*gǔ rén*, 古人) above and the "treasure" radical (*bèi*, 貝) below, signifying that a person guards treasure because they have something to rely upon. The form in the scripture using the knife radical (*dāo*, 刀) to form *fù* is incorrect.

*Duó* (毒蛇): "Constantly obstructing. The *Jíxùn* says: "The character *zhì* [𮙥] has the phonetic value of *chì*; it belongs to the class of venomous insects. The *Yì* says: 'The hibernation of dragons and snakes' refers to this.

*Zèngyí* (贈遺): "To bestow as a gift. The *Jíxùn* says: "'Zèng' means to oppose; it refers to sending objects to the deceased. The *Yùnyīng* says: "To mutually present objects as gifts. The lower radical, *wéi*, has the phonetic value of *jì*. The *Yùnyīng* says: "'Yí' means to give; to give objects to others. 'Yí' is also synonymous with 'zèng'."

"Blind" (*máng*): "blind" is pronounced with the *mài* rhyme and the *bǎi* rhyme; one whose eyes lack pupils is called blind. [The character] below is pronounced *yǔ*. The *Jíxùn* states it means "not extending. The *Guǎngyá* states that "hunchbacked" (*yǒu*) means "crooked"; a curved back is a hunchback (*yǒulǚ*).

The *fúbiān* (bat); "bǔ" means "to supplement sleep," while "xiàfēng" is a variant reading. According to the *Erya*, the *fúyì* is the bat; Guo Pu states that people of Qi call it *shémò* (pronounced zhīmò) and also name it the "Immortal Mouse. Its head resembles that of a mouse, and it has membranous wings. The *Fangyan* says that from the Guanzhong region westward, between Qin and Long, it is called a *fúbiān*. It hibernates in winter and flies in summer; it remains hidden by day and emerges at night.

The character 梨 (lí) in the upper part is pronounced with the *lì* rhyme (with the initial *lì* reversed), used here as a borrowed character. Its correct radical form is 黧 (lí), which the *Yùnchuán* (Rhyme Commentary) defines as "a color that is blackish-yellow. The lower part is read with the *jiǎn* rhyme; Wang Sù states that it signifies a dark-black appearance, a bluish-black color.
*Fàn-mài* (upper character pronounced *wàn-fǎn*, lower character pronounced *máng-bài-fǎn*).

Regarding *méi-gòu*: *měi-lái-fǎn*. Zheng Xuan says: "The word 'méi' means 'to plan'; it refers to bringing together those of different surnames so that they may reach harmony and completion. The lower character is *gōu-hòu-fǎn*. In the *Guoyu* (Discourses of the States), it says: "Now one will act as a matchmaker (*méi-gòu*. Jia Kui says: "A repeated marriage is called a *méi*."*

"Mengli" (猛厲) means "blindly fierce"; according to the *Kaozheng* (考證), it signifies being both extremely evil and robust. The second character, "Li" (力), is pronounced with the *zhi* (滯) rhyme; according to the *Kaozheng*, it means to transgress against what is correct and commit evil—it is perilous and stern. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is composed of "Han" (厂, *han*) and "Chai" (蠆, *chai*), with "Xing" (省, *xing*) as the phonetic component. The current scriptural text uses "Li" (力) instead, which is incorrect. "Li" (勵) means to exert effort, which does not accord with the meaning of this scripture; it should simply be written as "Li" (厲).
*Chǔ* (pronounced *zhāng lǚ*): In the *Zuozhuan*, it means to store or accumulate (*xù*). The *Shuowen* defines it as "to accumulate," written with the radical 貝 (bèi) and the phonetic 宁 (níng).

*Tuó* (pronounced *tāng luò*; second character pronounced *nuò láng*): The *Kaosheng* states it is a bottomless bag. According to the text, the *tuónáng* is the same as the *tuóyuè*. Laozi said: "The space between heaven and earth is like a bellows. It is commonly called a *péi* (pronounced *bài*) bag; it is used to fan fire by blowing air into it.

The character *dāo* (刀) with the phonetic *zhēn* (之壬反): according to the *Guǎngyá*, *zhēn* means "to prick"; according to the *Shuōwén*, it is the awl used for sewing clothes. Lexicons state that it is an iron tool for drawing out thread. The form appearing in the scripture as *zhēn* (鍼) is also acceptable; its correct form follows the radical "metal" (金) and uses *zhēn* (之壬反) as its phonetic. Variants written as *zhēn* (針) are vulgar forms.

Regarding the "long hammer" (chángzhui) used for removing and correcting characters, some say it is a square-headed iron hammer weighing eight *jin* with a handle three or four feet long, used for forging iron. The character 椎 (*chuí*) consists of the radical 木 (*mù*) and the phonetic 隹 (*zhuī*). It is incorrect to write it as 推 (*tuī*), which belongs to the radical 手 (*shǒu*).
*Dǐn* (pronounced *zhī lín fǎn*) refers to the sound of a *dǐn*; it denotes the base of a block, specifically a square iron block. The character used in the Canon (*zhēn*) is a vulgar form.

*Duàn* (pronounced *dōu luàn fǎn*) means a hammer; the *Cāngjié piān* states that *duàn* is a mallet. Zheng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* says it is a hammer. The *Shuowén* defines it as "minor treatment," composed of the radical for metal with *duàn* as the phonetic.

The character *jiān* (鉆) is pronounced with the *jiǎn* and *yán* finals. The *Zìshū* (Dictionary of Characters) states it is an iron clamp; the *Shuowén* (Explanations of Simple and Compound Characters) states it is an iron collar (*jiè*), pronounced with the *nǚ* and *chè* finals. The *Cāngjiépiān* (Cangjie’s Dictionary) states it is an iron clamp used for holding. The scriptural text uses the character *qián* (鉗), which follows the radical *gān* (甘); this refers to an iron collar wrapped around the neck, and does not accord with the meaning of the scripture. The following character, *zhí* (直), is pronounced with the *zhuī* final, as previously explained. It belongs to the wood radical and takes *zhuī* (隹) as its phonetic component.

"Lan duo" (懶惰): "Lang dan" (郎旦) is pronounced with a reversed *kao* (考) tone; it means not diligent. According to the *Shuowen*, it means indolence (*xie dai*). It is composed of the radical "heart" (*xin*) and the phonetic "lai" (*lai*). Alternatively, it may be written with the radical "woman" (*nü*) as "lan" (󱁅), which is identical. The following character, "tu wo" (徒臥), has the tone *fan*. The *Guoyaya* states that "duo" (惰) is "lan" (󱁅). The *Yunying* states it means laxity and indolence. According to the *Shuowen*, it means lack of reverence. It is composed of the radical "heart" and the phonetic "sui" (*sui*). The form used in the scriptures is "duo" (墮), which is a vulgar character.
"Disgust" (厭) is pronounced *yàn* (with the initial *i* reversed and the final *wū* and *gù* reversed); it means the mind does not rejoice.

"Greed" (𤡜) is pronounced *zú* (with the initial *yán* reversed). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is like a dog that craves meat; because one is greedy and never satisfied, it is composed of the radicals for "sweetness" (甘), "meat" (肉), and "dog" (犬), forming a word through the combination of these meanings.

Volume Four of the *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra*, the Second Assembly on Boundless Adornment, Volume Four. Regarding the term "eggshell" (*aṇḍakośa*) in the scripture: according to the dictionary, it refers to the membrane surrounding a bird's egg; phonetically, it denotes the outer skin of an egg. The scripture uses the metaphor of the "eggshell of ignorance" (*avidyā-kośa*) to illustrate how fundamental ignorance and craving encompass immeasurable fetters and afflictions, forging the life-karma of sentient beings so that they revolve within the cycle of birth and death, unable to escape. Just as a bird dwells within its eggshell, the "cave-dwelling" of ignorance is thus cited as a metaphor.

*Jù* (pronounced *jiāng xiàng fǎn*). In the *Erya*, "descend" (*xiáng*) is explained as "to fall down. The *Jixùn* says it means "to descend and fall. The *Cangjie pian* writes it as *𡲣*. The *Shuowen jiezi* agrees with the *Erya*, stating that it is composed of the radical *阜* (mountain/earth) and the phonetic *夅*. *Xià* (down) is pronounced *zhǔ shù fǎn*. The *Huainanzi* states: "The spring rains irrigate such that there is no place where they do not *jù* (drench). The *Shuowen* also says: "Timely rain *jù* (nourishes) the growth of the myriad things," composed of the radical *水* (water) and the abbreviated phonetic *樹* (tree). *Jù* (pronounced *shù*). The *Shuowen* also says: "Timely rain *jù* (nourishes) the myriad things," composed of the radical *水* (water) and the abbreviated phonetic *樹* (tree). (Note: The final sentence regarding the second definition of *jù* appears to be a repetition of the previous entry in the source text.)

The letter *A* is the first; it is the Sanskrit letter *A* pronounced with the rising tone (*shǎngshēng*). The *Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi Sūtra* states: "The letter-gate *A* signifies that all phenomena are fundamentally unborn, yet it can give rise to all worldly letters. A verse says: "The letter *A* is the foremost phrase; the luminous Dharma universally pervades, surrounded by a wheel of letters. Because that Honored One is without marks, for this reason [the letter *A*] occupies the first place among all letters.
