Regarding the term *Bhagavat*—the title of the Tathāgata used by the Buddha in the Sanskrit language, a designation for his manifold virtues—the verse in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Sovereignty (*vaśitā*), brilliance (*tejas*), majesty (*yaśas*), renown (*śrī*), auspiciousness (*bhaga*), and nobility (*ādhipatya*): one should know that these six distinct meanings are collectively expressed by the term *Bhagavat*. Because this term contains many meanings, the translators of the scriptures retained the Sanskrit word, fearing they could not fully convey its subtle nuances through translation."

Śrāvastī is the Sanskrit name for the country in the Western Regions; its ancient translations as "Shewei" (舍衛) or "Shepoti" (舍婆提) are all phonetic corruptions. In the language of Tang, it means "Country of the Famous" (聞物國), signifying that this land produces many people of great learning who are like precious treasures. The *Sudarsana-vinaya* also calls it "Country of the Many" (多有國), meaning that it abounds in wise and intelligent people, and that all the rare and wonderful things of various nations converge here. Because it is rich in products and resources, the sense of "having much" is one and the same. In ancient times, there were inhabitants of Śrāvastī who resided in this place, and thus it was named Śrāvastī; it is located within the borders of Central India.

The name of the Māra King is transcribed as *Mohe* (莫何), though this character does not exist in the original script; the translator altered *ma* (摩) to create it. In Sanskrit, he is called *Māra*; ancient translations state that he is so named because he "can obstruct" those engaged in the practice of world-transcending deeds, or because he "can kill" and sever the life-force of wisdom. The *Sūtra on the Arising of the World* states that above the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*) and below the First Dhyāna Heaven lies the palace of the Māra King Pāpīyān. His bodily radiance and lifespan surpass those of the lower heavens, and his sovereign power is equal to that of the Heavenly King of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations. He constantly vies in strength with all Buddhas. He belongs to the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations. In Sanskrit, his name is *Pāpīyān* (波畢𢮑, pronounced *pi-yi-an*), which in the Tang language means "evil desire," as he possesses excessive lust and craving.
Asura— formerly called *ā-xū-lún* (阿須倫) or *ā-xiū-luó* (阿脩羅)—
are all phonetic corruptions of the Sanskrit term.
The correct pronunciation is *asura* (with the initial *a* in the rising tone), with the retroflex *r*.
This is translated as "Non-Gods" (*fei-tian*). Alternatively, it is said that among the various ghosts and spirits, they possess the greatest merit and fortune.
According to Indian custom, all those possessing supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) are generally designated as "Gods" (*deva*).
Because this class constantly vies for supremacy with the various devas, they are distinguished from them by the term "Asura" (Non-deva).
The *Qishi yinben jing* states that their followers consist of four classes,
and their lands and palaces are situated beneath the great ocean.
On each of the four sides of Mount Sumeru there is a country:
on the eastern side is Vimalacitra;
on the southern side is Utsada.
To the west, there is illusory transformation.
To the north is Rāhu. Above the waters of the ocean, ten thousand *yojana*s away, four wind-circles arise that hold the water so it remains stationary:
the first is called Abiding, the second Firm Abiding, the third Non-falling, and the fourth Solidity.
Various other attendants, whether dwelling among mountain people, in human settlements, or on islands in the sea, have occasionally heard of an asura cave;
this is precisely the place where the Bodhisattva Vimalakīrti entered, as described in the biographical records.
*Yakṣa* (formerly transliterated as *yuecha*, *yecha*, or *yecha*; all are erroneous phonetic shifts) refers to the host of beings governed by the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa.

*Magadha* (pronounced with the final syllable as *jing* [jìng] and *ye* [yè]; also called *Mojieduō* or *Mojieti*; all refer to the same place) is described in the *Xiyuji* as being within the borders of Central India; it was formerly known as the city of Pāṭaliputra. Its soil is low-lying and damp, producing fine non-glutinous rice, and it was the capital ruled by King Aśoka, containing the greatest number of sacred sites.

"Gṛdhrakūṭa" (Vulture Peak) is sometimes called "Spiritual Vulture," "Vulture Head," or "Vulture Terrace"; these are all merely colloquial expressions. Because vultures dwell there and it resembles a high terrace, it is named "Vulture Terrace. Since vultures perch upon its peaks, it is called "Vulture Peak. *Saṃghāṭī*: The ancient pronunciation was *saṃghārī*, which translates as "double-layered robe"; this refers to the great outer robe (*mahākāṣāya*) worn by monks today. Ranging from nine strips at the minimum to twenty-five strips at the maximum, it must consist of an odd number of strips. The nine varieties of its distinctions are fully explained in the Vinaya texts. The Buddha ordained that this robe should be worn when entering a royal palace, when entering a village, when subduing non-Buddhists, and when encountering fierce beasts.
