*Wúniáo* (無橈): "Nú" (奴) and "jiào" (教)—the latter being read with two tones—are both attested in the *Guǎngyá* as meaning "disorder. Examining the phonetics, it is "quǎo" (曲). It is composed of the radical "mù" (木) and the phonetic "yáo" (堯). *Ruǎn* (耎): "Rénì" (膩)—read with the upper tone as *rǎn* (兖)—is defined in the *Shuōwén* as "weakness.

It is composed of the radical "chén" (從) and "huǒ" (火). The text of the classics uses "chē" (車) instead of "ruǎn" (軟), which is incorrect; this character did not originally exist [in that form]. The lower part is read as *nízhì* (尼致). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states it means "smooth. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "fat upon the flesh," composed of the radical "ròu" (肉) and the phonetic "èr" (貳), pronounced as *èr* (二).
*Anjana* is the Sanskrit name for an eye medicine; this medicine is of the mineral class, deep blue in color with a touch of purple-garnet hue, and resembles *kāñcanaprabhāsa*.
*Indranīla* is the name of a jewel; only the Lord of Devas possesses this blue gem, and thus it is called "Indra-blue" (*indranīla*).

The "Celestial Bow" (tiāngōng), also known as the "Emperor’s Bow" (dìgōng), refers to the rainbow; in common parlance, the character for "rainbow" (hóng) is pronounced with the *jiàng* tone. The *Shijing* states that the "chídōng" and [the celestial bow] are one and the same. Regarding the term *xiá* (瑕): it is pronounced with the *hú jiā* rhyme.

The *Yùpiān* states it means a flaw in jade; in character dictionaries, it signifies impurity or turbidity. The character for *yù* (於) is pronounced with the *wèi* rhyme. It means not being clear and pure, or being turbid.

To cast gold into seals and set them up so as to look back is what Wang Yewang called *zhù* (casting). The *Shuowen* explains it as "melting copper to make vessels"; it is composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic element "abbreviated *shòu*" (*shǒu*). *Śamatha* is a Sanskrit term;
in the Tang language, it means "concentration" (*dìng*), or alternatively, it is said to mean "tranquility" (*jìjìng*). These two meanings are one and the same.
"Yàn-xíng" (雁行) is pronounced yán jiàn fǎn; it is also written as "yàn" (雁). The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (Mao Commentary on the Classic of Poetry) states:

"The larger are called hóng (鴻), the smaller are called yàn (雁). "Jiāodá mó" (喬答摩) is a Sanskrit term; its meaning is translated as "Bull-Dung Lineage," also known as "Sugarcane Lineage" or "Clay Lineage. The ancient form "Qiú tán" (瞿曇) is a corruption of the Sanskrit term.

"Suǎn-í" (the first character pronounced *suǎn* with the rhyme *wán*, the second character pronounced *ní* with the rhyme *hú-làn*): according to the *Erya*, the *suǎn-í* resembles a wildcat and eats tigers and leopards; Guo Pu states that it is the lion, which originates from Western countries and was presented by the King of Shule during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Han dynasty. "Hàn" refers to the jaw.

*Xián*: (homophone of *xiàn*) means "fine" or "delicate. (The second character is pronounced *cái hé*). It is composed of the radical for "clothing" (*yī*) and the character for "to gather" (*jí*); a garment gathered with five colors is called *zá* ("variegated").
*Jiān bó*: (the first character is pronounced *jiān*, the second *bó*). These were already explained previously.

*Bi* (髀): The *Shuowen* states this refers to the outer part of the thigh; the inner part is called *gu* (股), while the outer part is called *bi*. It is composed of the radical "bone" (*gu*) and the phonetic element "bei" (*bi*). *Xia* (下): Pronounced *shiruan* (時耎). Also written as *zhuo* (󰈷). The *Shuowen* states this refers to the calves (*zhuan*) of the feet. It is composed of the radical "inner" (*nei*) and the phonetic element "duan" (*dun*), with the latter abbreviated. *Zhuan* (䠊) is pronounced *fei* (肥); *chang* (膓) is pronounced *zhang* (長).

*Jāla-hasta-pāda* (網鞔): The first character is pronounced *wǎng* (罔) and the second is *mò ān fǎn* (莫安反). According to the *Guǎngyá*, *màn* (鞔) means "to patch. The Tathāgata has a web-like membrane between his ten fingers, resembling the feet of a goose.
*Shuāng zhǐ* (雙跖): The second character is also read as *zhì* (蹠); the *Shuōwén* states it refers to the sole of the foot.

*Gulapu* (瞿拉坡): The first character is pronounced as *yu* (愚) with a reversed tone, and the second as *lang-da* (郎答) with a reversed tone; the third is pronounced as *pu-po* (普波). This is a Sanskrit term referring to the flesh of the two buttocks (*tun*; 臋). *Dao-kong* (蹈空): The first character is pronounced as *dao* (到) with a reversed tone.

Liu Zhao’s commentary on the *Gongyang Zhuan* states that "to tread" (*dao*) means to walk or practice. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to step upon," composed of the radical "foot" (*zu*; 足) and the phonetic element "yao" (*yang-xiao*; 舀).

I privately harbor a thousand knots of resentment; examining the phonetic analysis, it says "private shame" and "to look down upon. According to the *Shuowen*, "thief" (*qiè*) emerges from a hole, composed of the radical "hole" and the character "grain" (*mǐ*). The phonetic component is "yún" (pronounced *zhì*), and "ér" (pronounced *jí*) is also a phonetic element. Now, "ér" has been omitted, making it "slight" (*lüè*). The lower radical is pronounced with the *huī* rhyme.

*Nayuta* (the "羊" [yang] and "主" [zhu] are reversed; it is a transliteration of a Sanskrit term for a numerical value in the Western [Indic] tradition). What was formerly called *nayuta* in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, "Chapter on the Incalculable" (*Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta*), states: "A *koṭi* [of koṭis] makes one *nayuta*; a *nayuta* [of nayutas] makes one *mahā-nayuta*. Among these three grades of numerical systems, this refers to the system of large numbers.

*Koṭi* is also a numerical term for that region; the *Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta* chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "One hundred thousand is one *lakṣa*; one hundred *lakṣas* is one *koṭi*. This is the intermediate number.

The character 駛 (shì) is derived from the *Cangjie pian*, where it means "swift. The *Guiyuan zhucóng* states that it signifies rapid movement, taking "ma" (horse) as its radical and "shi" (史) as its phonetic. The scriptural text that uses 駃 (jié), with the radical "guai" (夬) and the phonetic "jue" (𪫦), is an error; there is no instance where this character is pronounced "jue. Furthermore, the character for "downward flow" (下流) consists of the radicals "water" (水) and "lù" (㐬, read as tǔgǔ). The version lacking the dot on the right side of the "lù" radical is a vulgar character.

"Piao" (匹遙反): The *Shuowen* says it means to float; the *Guangya* says it means to drift (*piao-jie*). "Mie" (篇篾反) is the second character, with the phonetic "men-bei" (門悖反). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states it means to sink; the *Shenglei* states it means to drown. According to the *Shuowen*, it means to submerge (*zhan*). It is composed of the radical "water" and the element "yin" (𠬛)—which is the archaic form of the character "yin"—forming a compound ideogram (*huiyi zi*).

*Marma* (the Sanskrit term, pronounced "mo po fan" in Chinese) is here translated as "vital point of death. This refers to the joints and vital parts of the human body; if these are struck or damaged, the person dies prematurely, and is therefore called a "vital point of death."

Regarding "poisonous flame" (*dúyàn*) and "salt trench": according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to the subtle, flickering movement of fire, appearing as *yànyàn*. It is sometimes written as *xián*; the *Yunying* states it means "firelight. Alternatively, the character is simplified by omitting the "gate" radical to become *yàn*, which is a vulgar form.

"Dull and blind" (*chigǔ*): the upper character *chí* (pronounced with the initial *zhǐ*) is explained in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as "lack of wisdom. The lower character *gǔ* (pronounced with the initials *gōng wǔ*) is glossed by Zheng Zhong in his commentary on the *Zhouli* as "one who has no eyes," meaning "staring blankly like the skin of a drum."
This has already been explained in detail within the *Yanmo qian dabanruo yinyi* (Phonology and Meaning of the Great Prajñāpāramitā Before Yama).

Regarding the character *huífù* (洄澓): the upper character is pronounced *huí* (the phonetic value of the character for "to return"); its meaning is "a great body of water flowing in a circle. The lower character is pronounced *fú*; according to the *Kǎoshēng* (Investigation of Sounds), it means "water swirling in a current," or it may also be written as *fú* (洑).

"Wave and surge" (bōtāo). [The character] "tāo" is pronounced as in the rhyme of "táng-láo. Xu Shuchong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states: "When the tidal waters surge and shift, it is called a tāo. The *Cangjie pian* states: "A great wave is called a tāo."

"Dānzhù (耽著): The upper character, dān (耽), is pronounced with the rhyme *nan* (南反) and the tone *yīng* (英); it means "to indulge in" (*tānhào*, 耽好). The lower character, zhù (著), is pronounced with the sound *hūbào* (呼報反) and *kǎoshēng* (考聲); it means "to play with" (*wán*, 翫) or "to attach to" (*zhuó*, 著). It is composed of the radical for the body (*shēn*, 身) and the phonetic *yín* (冘省). The lower part is read as *chílüè* (馳略反). The *Guìyuàn Zhūcóng* (桂苑珠叢) states it means "to adhere to" (*fù*, 附). The *Hànshū* (漢書) states it means "to reach" (*zhì*, 至). It is composed of the radical for grass (*cǎo*, 艹) and the character *zhě* (者). The scriptural text uses the form *zhuó* (著), which is a vernacular character used in running script."

The character for "lǐ" (羸) has the phonetic component "lì" (力) as its radical and "wéi" (為) as the phonetic; the commentary states it means "exhausted and worn out. In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is defined as "emaciated"; it is the correct form for "emaciation," composed of "yáng" (羊) as the semantic component and "lì" (力) as the phonetic. The character for "lüè" (劣) has the phonetic component "chuò" (輟) as its radical; according to the *Zishu*, it means "weak. It is a compound character formed by combining "shǎo" (少) and "lì" (力) to convey its meaning.

The six bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are called *āyatanāni* in Sanskrit; this is translated as "place by place" (*chù chù*), meaning the locations where [the sense-faculties] arise. The older translation, "six entrances" (*liù rù*), is erroneous. In the Sanskrit original, *praveśa* means "entrance."

"Hun-mao" (惛耄): The first character, "hun" (惛), is pronounced with the initial *hū* and the final rhyme *kūn* (呼昆反). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "forgetfulness"; according to the *Guangya*, it means "delusion. The second character, "mao" (耄), is pronounced with the final rhyme *bao* (報反). According to the *Zishu*, it means "confusion"; it is composed of the radical "old" (老) with the phonetic component "mao" (毛).

"Pi-huǎn" (皮緩): according to the *Erya*, "huǎn" means relaxed; Gu Yewang says it means spacious. Examining this, "pi-huǎn" means lax and negligent. It is composed of the radical "silk" (糸) with the phonetic "mì" (覓), and the sound component "yuán" (爰).
"Face-creased" (*miàn zhòu*);

*zhòu* is pronounced with the *jiù* rhyme. "Māṇava" is a term from the Sanskrit language; it is also called *mānava*, *naramāṇava*, *māṇavaka*, or *naramāṇa*, or simply "māṇava"—all of which are phonetic corruptions and shifts of the same word, sharing a single meaning. This is translated as "Youth" (*rútóng*).
The character *cuō* (撮) is pronounced with the *cāng* (倉) and *huó* (活) rhymes; the *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲) states it means "to grasp with the hand," and the *Guǎng Yǎ* (廣雅) states it means "to hold.

Regarding *pṛthagjana* (異生), some say "foolish ordinary beings" (*yú pìshēng* 愚異生); this refers to being foolish and darkened, as they do not give rise to untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas. The old translations call them "small children" (*xiǎ'ér* 小兒) or "separately born" (*biéshēng* 別生), because their delusion is like that of a small child. Some also call them "infant ordinary beings" (*xiǎ'ér fánfū* 小兒凡夫), or "infant-foolish ordinary beings" (*yīngyú fánfū* 嬰愚凡夫), or "hair-path ordinary beings" (*máodào fánfū* 毛道凡夫), or "hair-tip ordinary beings" (*máotóu fánfū* 毛頭凡夫). Although the meaning is the same, these [other] renderings have gone far astray; the initial explanation is correct.

Caṇḍāla is a Sanskrit term; it refers to those who are butchers, executioners, jailers, or those who carry away excrement and filth, and so forth. (The character "上" [shàng] is pronounced with the second tone, while "反" [fǎn] is pronounced with the fourth tone.)

The character *kǎo* (考) is pronounced with a retroflex initial (*qù* [向反]), meaning "to take birds or beasts using a bow-bone. The dictionary states that it refers to placing bones on a road; its form resembles a bow, and it is composed of the radical "bow" (*gōng*) with the phonetic element "jīng" (*亰*).

*Mòjuàn* (魔罥) [the radical *juàn* is pronounced *xuán* with the reversed tone; it is also written as *juàn* or *jiān*; the *Kǎoshēng* says it means "to catch with a rope" or "to entangle"]; *wānbǎn* (彎板) reversed tone; the *Yùnyīng* says it means "to bind and seize"; the phonetic component is *guān* (岡) with *yuán* (肙) reversed tone. The Sūtra states that the *mòjuàn* (魔羂) refers to the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*); the Māra King uses this to bind sentient beings.
"Bùjué" (不覺) means not being aware; it is a variant of "sù" (睡), meaning to sleep. Furthermore, its original pronunciation is "jiǎo" (角), which is also acceptable.
"Tīng" (聽) is pronounced "tǐng" (丁) in this context; the character dictionary states that "tīng" means to permit or to allow, and it takes the phonetic element "rén" (壬).

Volume Thirty-Six, *The Great Treasure Accumulation Sūtra*, Volume Thirty-Six, Chapter on the Prophecy of the Deva Kumbhīra, concluding the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-parivarta*. *Kaṃdarva* is a Sanskrit term meaning "captive" (*lu-zhi*). In the Tang language, it is translated as "eater of fragrance" (*shi-xiang*), because they sustain themselves by means of fragrance; hence they are also called "deities of fragrant conduct" (*xiang-xing-shen*). Alternatively, they are called "smellers of fragrance" (*xiu-xiang*), or "seekers of fragrance" (*xun-xiang-shen*). Some say they are called "residents of Fragrance Mountain" (*ju-xiang-shan*), while others say their bodies possess a unique fragrance. The term "deities of music" (*yin-yue-shen*) is a semantic translation. The old translations *gandharva* and *gandhavaha* are merely variations in the phonetic weight of different regional dialects.

*Garuda* is also a Sanskrit term that is not perfectly rendered [in Chinese]. It is correctly transliterated as *jīlu zhuan shen na*. In older translations it was called *kalola*, or "Golden-Winged Bird" (*jīnshì niǎo*), as has already been explained previously.

The *Kinnara* (the first character pronounced with the *jīng* rhyme and the second with the *nú gē* rhyme) refers to a deity with a human body and a horse's head; females are like humans in appearance, upright and capable of song. They frequently serve as wives and members of the retinue for the *Gandharva* devas.

*Mahoraga* (sometimes written as *muhuluo* or *muhuluo*, which are erroneous and abbreviated forms) translates here as "Great-Bellied Walker"; he is a great serpent deity who, through the power of karma and supernormal faculties, can transform himself into human form.

*Utpala* (the "wēn-gǔ" [pronounced with a retroflex -g] in the original text) is a transliteration of the Sanskrit term; in the Tang language it means "blue lotus. This flower is blue in color, with narrow and long petals, and its fragrance is perceived from afar—a rarity among human beings. It is also sometimes called *utpala*.
*Padma*, sometimes called *paduma* or *pam̐dma*; in its correct Sanskrit form it is *paṅkaja*. This refers to the red lotus flower, though some say it is reddish-yellow.
*Kumuda* is sometimes called *kumo* or *kumudu*; in its original Sanskrit it is *kumuda*, which refers to a deep crimson lotus flower, or alternatively, one that is the color of fire.

*Puṇḍarīka*, also called *Puṇḍarī*—in the correct Sanskrit it is *puṇḍarīka* (pronounced with the *nu* and *ya* reversed)—is translated in Chinese as "White Lotus. Its flowers are like snow in color and are rare among humans. These four kinds of lotuses mostly grow in the Great Dragon Pond of Anavatapta, also known as Lake Anavatapta.
"Āśraya" (依怙)—the "hu" in "hu-gu" is pronounced with a reversed tone; according to the *Erya*, it means to rely upon or depend on. "Tuṣita" is a Sanskrit term;
it is the name for a class of gods dwelling in the air within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Formerly it was called Tuṣita;
alternatively, it was called Doushu or Doushiduo.
These are all corruptions, omissions, and inaccuracies of the Sanskrit.
In Chinese, it is translated as "Contentment" (Zhizu) or "Exquisite Contentment" (Miaozu).
The *Fan sheng jie di zhang* states that because the lower heavens are characterized by much negligence and the higher heavens by much dullness, it is called "Contentment."
Bodhisattvas in their final birth before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha) often serve as this celestial king.
Although they have perfected all ten perfections through the simultaneous cultivation of myriad practices, they specifically emphasize the perfection of diligence.
According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, the ground of that heaven consists of precious clouds.
It is located thirty-two hundred thousand *yojana*s below the great ocean.
Four hundred years among humans constitute one day and night for that heaven;
their lifespan is four thousand years.
The physical stature of these beings is two *li* tall.

Regarding the "Four Continents" (*caturdvīpa*), the *Erya* states: "Any land within the water that can be inhabited is called a continent (*dvīpa*). As for the four continents—namely, Pūrvavideha in the east, Jambudvīpa in the south, Aparagoyānī in the west, and Uttarakuru in the north—the differences in physical stature and lifespan within each continent are not uniform, as explained in detail in such works as the *Lokaprajñapti-śāstra* and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.

"Ganges-sand" (gaṅgā-vāluka) is the name of a river in the Western regions according to the Sanskrit language. This river originates from its upper source at Lake Anavatapta; its sands are so fine, like motes of dust, that their number cannot be known, and thus it is cited as a metaphor.
*Zhuān* (brick) is pronounced *yuán* (in the first tone); the second character is pronounced *guǎ* (in the fourth tone).

*Lì* (gravel) has the initial sound *lì*; the *Kǎoshēng* states it means "broken stone. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical *shí* (stone) and the phonetic component *yuè* (abbreviated) with the final sound *lè*.

The character *zhū* (株) has the radical *shàng* (上) with the phonetic *yú* (瑜) reversed; the *Shuowen* states it means "the root of a tree. The lower part, *wǔ* (五) with the phonetic *gǔ* (骨), is explained in the *Zishu* as "the remains of a felled tree are called *zhū* (株). The *Shuowen* writes this character as *wǎ* (瓦).
*Dūci* (毒刺): This is a variant of *zì*. In the *Rituals of Zhou* (*Zhōu Lǐ*), it means "to stab to death. It is composed of the radical "knife" (刀) and the phonetic "zì" (此恣反).

The text reads *lì* (刾), which is a vulgar character. *Bhūtana* (布單那) is a name for a ghost in Sanskrit; it is also called *Pūtana* (富單那) or *Bhudhana* (富陀那), all of which are corrupt, abbreviated, and incorrect forms. This term means "stench and filth"; although their physical bodies are foul-smelling and filthy, they are the most fortunate among the hungry ghosts (*preta*).

Maudgalyāyana is a corruption and abbreviation of the Sanskrit term; its correct Sanskrit pronunciation is Mūrdhagatāgra, with the retroflex *ṭ* (a "turned tongue" sound). In the language of Tang, it means "the Clan of the Bean Gatherer. This great Arhat was the progenitor of his lineage; he was of the clan of the bean-gathering mung-bean (*mudga*) sages, and thus took that as his family name.
*Uttarāsaṅga* is the Sanskrit term for the seven-strip *kāṣāya*, the regular robe worn by monks; it is also called the *khaṇḍa-sīva-cīvara* (cut-and-sewn robe).
*Zìrǔ* (恣汝) is a four-syllable rhyme meaning "to let loose" or "to indulge," as stated in the *Yùnyīng* (韻英).

*Niǎo* (嬈): The character is pronounced with the "nu" and "niao" finals reversed; in ancient texts it was written as *niǎn* (嬲). The *Jixun* (集訓) states that it means "to mock, jest, and disturb one another. The *Sancang* (三蒼) states it means "to toy with. The pronunciation of *xiè* (謔) is *xiāngyuē*.

The character 爲 (wei) has two readings: one is *yǒng* (with the rhyme *yìng*), meaning "to assist," derived from the radical 爪 (claw) and the component 作 (to act); in the scriptural text, it is used in the sense of "to act.
Another reading is *pǔ* (with the rhyme *qiú*), as the *Kǎo Shēng* states that 爲 means "to act. The more than ten characters below follow this same pronunciation.

*Tí* (梯): The upper radical is *tǐ* (隥), pronounced *dì* (反) according to the *Yùnyīng*, which states it means a wooden staircase (*mùjiē*). It is composed of the radical *mù* (木) with the phonetic *dì* (弟). The lower character is *dēng* (登), pronounced *guàn* (亘) according to the *Yùnyīng*. Guō’s commentary on the *Mùtiānzǐzhuàn* says it means a slope or embankment (*bǎn*). The *Yùnyīng* also states that *dèng* (隥) is also a staircase. According to the *Zìshū*, *dèng* (隥) refers to a ditch or pit (*kǎn*), composed of the radical *fù* (阜).

Regarding the character *qiáo* (橋): the phonetic component is *yāo* (妖). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "a bridge" (*qiáoliáng*). The dictionary defines it as "a beam for crossing water," formed from the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "qí yāo. In the canonical text, there are instances where it is written as *qiào* (槗), which is incorrect.

*Láo* (pronounced with the initial *lú* and final *dāo* as a reversed rhyme). According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "firm. It is composed of the radical "ox" (*niú*) and a simplified form of "boat" (*zhōu*). The *Shuowén* states that "boat" takes the sense of being surrounded on all four sides. Gu Yewáng says that *láo* also means "solid. The *Shuowén* further defines it as "an enclosure for breeding oxen and sheep," pronounced with the initial *kuáng* and final *yuàn*. There are versions written with the "cave" (*xué*) radical, which are incorrect.

*Jué* (蹶): The first character is pronounced *jūe* (with the radical *jué*). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states: "Jué means to move. Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* says: "Jué means to run. Gu Yewang says: "Jué is like being startled; it conveys a sense of urgency and haste. The *Guangya* defines it as leaping or kicking. It is sometimes written as *qù* (趣) or *jué* (蹶), which are identical. Regarding the following character *shī* (失), the *Shuowen* defines it as "to let loose" (*zòng*). It is composed of the hand radical and the phonetic *yǐ*. It is also written as *chì* (𢪛).

"Chuān" (穿) is read as *chuān* (專反) and *chūan* (出專反). Yingyun (*Yingyun*) states it means "to pierce. The *Shuowen* says it means "to penetrate," written with the radical 穴 (*xué*) and the component 牙 (*yá*, read as *wǔjiā fǎn*). The following character is 纏 (*chán*, read as *liè fǎn*). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* says "chè" (徹) means "to reach through. The *Shuowen* says it means "to pass through," written with the radical 彳 (*chì*, read as *chǒuchī fǎn*) and the component 支 (*zhī*, read as *pǔbǔ fǎn*), with 育 (*yù*) as the phonetic. The character 育 is read as *yù* (土骨反) and is written with the radical 肉 (*ròu*).

*Jìnglù* (静虑), formerly called *chándìng* (禅定): according to the *Shuowén*, "jing" (静) means "tranquil and careful examination," while "shēng" (声) [in the context of the character's phonetic] means "peaceful" or "resting. The *Jíxùn* (集訓) explains that "lù" (虑) means "recollection" or "thought"; it is composed of the radical "heart" (心) with the phonetic "lú" (𧆨), which has the pronunciation *lú*.

*Kui* (逵, alternative reading: *wei*, fanqie: *máo*). The *Commentary on the Mao Shijing* states: "Kui means 'exhausted'. The *Kao Sheng* says: "Kui means 'to reach the limit'. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as a chest (*xia*), written with the radical *fang* (匚) and the phonetic *gui* (貴). It is also written as *gui* (櫃). The character below [in the variant] is *fan* (凡, fanqie: *fa*). The *Great Commentary on the Shangshu* states: "To travel without provisions is called *fa* (乏); *fa* means 'few'. In the *Zuo Zhuan*, the character *zheng* (正) is inverted to form *fa*; in ancient scripts, it was written as *zhu* (󲓍).
*Samādhi* is a Sanskrit term; in the Tang language, it is called "concentration" (*ding*), or alternatively "equipoise" (*dengchi*), or "equilibrium-attainment" (*dengzhi*);

all these are definitions of concentration. *Prajñā*: the first syllable is pronounced *bo*, which is a corruption of the Sanskrit; the correct Sanskrit pronunciation is *prajñā*. In the Tang language, it means "wisdom. Ancient translations rendered it as "wisdom," the meaning of which is such that nothing remains unclarified.

*Sattva* (薩埵) is a term from the Sanskrit language; in the Tang language it means "sentient being" (有情). The ancient translation "sentient beings" (眾生) does not capture the full meaning. *Lèdǔ* (樂覩): the first character is pronounced with the final *fǎn* (反);

the second is pronounced *zào* (躁) with the final *dòng* (動) and the initial *zǎo* (早) and *gào* (告). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lunyu* states that it means "not being at peace. Jia Kui says it means "restless agitation. The *Shifa* (諡法) states: "One who delights in change and movement is called *zào* (躁). The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文解字) defines it as "a quick-tempered nature," composed of the radical for "feet" (*zú*) and the phonetic *sào* (喿), pronounced *xiāndào* (先到).
*Dāna* is a corruption of the Sanskrit term; its correct form is *dāna*. In the language of Tang, it means "giving" (*shi*).

Regarding the character *li* (in the rhyme *zhi*), the *Mao Shih Zhuan* states: "Violence (*li*) is evil. Zheng Xuan says: "To transgress the administration and act wickedly is called *li*. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan* states: "*Li* means fierce. The *Shi Fa* (Canon of Posthumous Titles) says: "To be violent and arrogant toward one's kin is called *li*; to slaughter without restraint is called *li*. The text [of the *Shuowen*] uses the radical for "force" (*li*) to form *li*, which is an erroneous usage. According to the *Shuowen*, it uses the radical for "cliff" (*han*) with the pronunciation *hu dan* and the sound of "ten thousand" (*wan*).
The Phonetic Explanations of All Scriptures, Volume Twelve;
The Phonetic Explanations of All Scriptures, Volume Thirteen.
Compiled by the Tang Dynasty *fanjing* śramaṇa Huilin.
The Phonetic Explanations for the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Volume Three.

Volumes thirty-seven through fifty-five, totaling nineteen volumes. 37. The Thirty-seventh Volume of the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*. Regarding "Śīla" (尸羅): in the language of India, it means "Precept" (戒), or "Discipline" (律), or is generally referred to as the "Vinaya Piṭaka" (戒律藏).

Regarding "not timid" (*bù qiè*): Wang Yě says that "timid" (*qiè*) means "fearful and inferior. Examining the phonetics, it is said that "timid" (*qiè*) means "cowardly" (*nuǎn*), with the phonetic *nú luàn*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as 㹤, which follows the radical for dog (*quǎn*); it is a word formed by associative meaning (*huìyì zì*), as dogs are generally fearful.

Regarding *tì* (洟): on the *Tījì* (梯計), it is written as *fǎnzhèng* (反正). It is derived from *bí* (鼻) or *dì* (弟), and is written as *yǒu* (䶏) or *tí* (啼); see the *Yùnyīng* (韻英). It refers to nasal mucus. In the scriptures, it is written as *tì*; its original pronunciation was *yí*. The *Shuowén* (說文) is also erroneous here; this error arose because the character for *yí* (夷) was confused with the character for *dì* (弟) in the *Shūyí* (󲚑書) script, leading to this mistake that was subsequently emulated by others. Now, several dictionaries such as the *Yùpiān*, *Kǎoshēng*, and *Yùnyīng* all give the pronunciation *zhī* (脂). The *Zhouyì* (周易), in the *Cuìguǎ* (萃卦), states: "Qián zī tì tì" (齋咨涕洟), which serves as clear evidence. *Tì* is also the liquid from the mouth and nose. Below [the entry for *tuò*], it is pronounced *wò* (臥). The *Shuowén* defines it as "liquid from the mouth. It is sometimes written as *tuò* (涶); the *Kǎoshēng* says it is "saliva and froth in the mouth."

The character 犛 (máo) is pronounced *pāo* with the alternative reading *máo*. The *Shanhai jing* states: "On Mount Panhou there is a beast shaped like an ox, with long hair growing on its four limbs; it is called the *liáoniu*. Guo Pu’s commentary notes: "On its back, knees, thighs, and tail, there are all long hairs. The *Shuowen jiezi* states: "It is the long-haired ox of the southwestern tribes, pronounced *máo*; it is composed of the radical 'ox' (*niú*) and the phonetic element '𠩺' (*mǎo*) in abbreviated form."

*Upāsaka* is a term from the Sanskrit language; ancient translations rendered it as *youbopojia* (優波婆迦) or *youbosai* (優婆塞), both of which are corruptions and abbreviations. In the Tang period, it was translated as "near-virtuous man" (*jin shan nan*). According to the Vinaya of the Mūlasarvāstivāda school, it is also called "near-attendant man" (*jinsi nan*) or "near-dwelling man" (*jinsu nan*), meaning one who dwells near and serves the Three Jewels. Alternatively, the terms "pure-faith gentleman" (*qingxin shi*) or "virtuous-dwelling man" (*shansu nan*) are interpretive translations.

*Upāsikā*—translated into Chinese as "near-to-the-virtuous woman" (*jìnshàn nǚ*) or "laywoman" (*jìnsì nǚ*)—has the same meaning as explained previously. The addition of the feminine suffix *kā* is noted here; the ancient translations *upāsikā* or *upāsī* are all corruptions.
*Bùbìng* (不鞕): The rhyme is *gèng* (更). Yingyun states it means "hard. The vulgar form is written as *yìng* (硬) or *jù* (䩕), which are identical in meaning.

*Bùshè* (不歰): The rhyme is *lì* (立). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that "shè" (澀) means "difficult. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Fangyan* states that "shè" (歰) is synonymous with "hù" (𠫤). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "not smooth. It is a compound character formed by four "zhǐ" (止) radicals—two written inverted and two written upright. The text above erroneously uses two "rèn" (刃) radicals. There are also versions with two "zhǐ" and a "shuǐ" (水) radical, forming "shè" (澁); these are vulgar characters and not the standard orthography.
"Yìjiě" (易解): "yí" (夷) is pronounced *dì* (地) with a retroflex; "xià" (下) is pronounced *mài* (賣) with a retroflex.
Those who read it with a dental [retroflex] are incorrect.
"Yìshí" (易識): "yáng" (羊) is pronounced *yì* (益); it means "to change. "Jiéluófēnggā" (羯羅頻伽), also called "jiālíngfēnggā" (迦陵頻伽), is translated as "the bird of beautiful voice."

*Liúyǒng* (Flowing and surging). *Zhoufǎn Shuōwén*: "The movement of water; composed of the radical 水 (water) and the phonetic 㐬 (pronounced tāgù). 㐬 means 'sudden'. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of two waters (two 水) following 㐬, written as 󲄲; the current vulgar form 流 is an error. The lower character is pronounced yǒng. Gù Yěwáng says: "The billowing and surging of waves. It is also written as 湧. The *Shuōwén* states: "To surge; pronounced túnéng. It is composed of the radical 水 and the phonetic 甬.*

"Stem" (莖): "Geng" (耕) with the *shang* (上) tone; according to the *Bóyá*, it refers to the stalks of herbaceous plants. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "zhī" (枝) is the primary meaning, written with the radical "hand" (廾, sound *cǎo*) and the phonetic "xing" (巠, sound *xíng*). "Xing" (巠) has the sound *xíng*; below it is "gāng" (岡), pronounced *gāng*. The *Shuowen* further states that "zhī" (枝) refers to tree branches, written with the radical "wood" (木) and the phonetic "gan" (干, sound *àn*). This character [枝] may also be written with "wood" (木) and "gan" (干); both forms are interchangeable. Both [the second and third characters] have the *qu* (去) tone, but here we take the *shang* (上) tone.
"Analyze" (fēnxī): the character is sometimes written as "fan" (fǎn) or as the vernacular "xī" (xī) formed from the fragment "piàn" (piàn).

"Unknowable" (pōzhī): sometimes written as "pō" (pō); the fanqie is "pǔ-wo-fǎn" (pǔ-wo-fǎn). Gu Yewang states that "pō" means "not possible" (bù kě), a particle. The *Shuowen Jiezi* lacks an explanation for this term.
"Dī" (one drop) is pronounced *ding* with the tone *liǎn* (reversed); some write it as *shì* (from *shì*) or *dì* (from *dì*), but these are incorrect.
"Huífù" (eddying): the upper character is pronounced *huí* and the lower is pronounced *fú*. The dictionary states that "huífù" describes the appearance of swirling water currents.

*Yíng huǒ* (firefly) is the name for a type of insect that emerges from dark holes; the *Erya* writes it as *yíng huǒ*. Guo Pu states: "They fly at night, and beneath their bellies there is a firelight. *Zhào* is simply the character *zhào* (to illuminate). The *Liji*, "Monthly Ordinances" (*Yueling*), says: "On the day of Great Heat (*Dashu*), decaying grass transforms into fireflies. The *Yunying* writes this as *fú*.

*Tíngliáo* (court torches) appears twice in the *Lìdiào* (Rites of Mourning). The commentary on the *Zhou Lǐ* states: "Those set up outside the gate are called *dàzhù* (great candles), and those inside the gate are called *tíngliáo* (court torches); both are used to illuminate the multitude for the sake of clarity. Zheng Xuan says: "It is a 'ground candle' (*dìzhù*). It is composed of the radical 'fire' and the phonetic 'liáo'; *liáo* is the archaic form of the character *liáo*."

*Jambūnada-suvarṇa* (贍部捺陀金) is a term from the Sanskrit language. The upper character, *shí* (時), is pronounced with the *yàn* (焰) tone; it is derived from the phonetic *jiān* (占) and the sound *zhān* (詹). The lower character, *nú* (奴), is pronounced with the *gē* (割) tone; it is derived from the radical for "hand" and the sound *nài* (奈). This is the Sanskrit name for the finest gold. Formerly referred to as *Yamunā-gold* (閻浮檀金), the *Lokotpatti-sūtra* (*Qishi yinben jing*) states: "In this Jambudvīpa, beneath the waters along the great seashore, there is this gold. On the land above the shore stands the Jambu tree. When a Cakravartin King appears in the world, he employs spirits and deities to extract this gold. For this reason, this gold occasionally appears in the human world; it is the most supreme and excellent, surpassing all other gold."

The character for "collar" (yīn-jīn) is pronounced yǐn-fǎn. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* states it refers to the crossed collar (*jiaoling*). It is also called "sleeve" (*yī-mèi*), pronounced mí-yè-fǎn; the *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as 䘳 (*jiāorèn*), meaning "crossed lapel," composed of the radical "clothing" with the phonetic "forbid" (*jìn*). The character for "lapel" (*rèn*) is pronounced rěn.

*Sugata* (the "jue" and "ye" in the original transcription are reversed; it is a transliteration of the Sanskrit term, which is one of the titles of the Tathāgata). This is translated as "Well-Gone" (*shanshi*). The old translations "Xiujiadu," "Xiujia-duo," or "Xiujia-tuo" are all corruptions. This term has three meanings: first, praising his virtues; second, not turning back; third, perfection. These all share a single underlying meaning.

*Mukhaliṇḍa* is a name for a mountain in the Sanskrit language; it has two distinctions, the large and the small. The ancient *Mujinlinda* was a transcription of the non-Sanskrit (barbarian) pronunciation. In correct Sanskrit, it is pronounced *Muñjina* with a rising tone (*śruti*) on the final syllable; this means "reed. There is a dragon on this mountain that bears the same name.
For the duration of a single kṣaṇa, a single muhūrta, or a single lava (the character *lao* is pronounced with the *quǎn* tone;
the *Kǎoshēng* says it means "a brief moment";
the *Jìxùn* says it means "near" or "a short interval").
*Kṣaṇa*, *lava*, and *muhūrta* are all names for divisions of time in the Sanskrit language of that region.
There are two distinct types of *kṣaṇa*.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that one hundred and twenty *kṣaṇas* constitute the measure of a *tatkṣaṇa*; in reality, this is identical to a *lava*.
*Muhūrta* is also called *muhurta*. The treatise states:
the *Sūryagatiśāstra* says that *muhūrtas* and *muhurs* are one and the same name.

This meaning is fully clarified in the fourth and tenth fascicles of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā* (Kusha-p'o-sha), where the calculations of their respective quantities have already been performed and the definitions fully explained.

*Xiǎnchǎng* (顯敞): The phonetic component is *zhàng* (掌) with the reversed radical *kǎo* (考); the meaning is "to open," "to clarify," or "to expose. It is formed from *pǔ* (攴, pronounced *pǔ*) with the phonetic *shàng* (尚). *Qīngcuì* (青翠): The phonetic component is *zuì* (醉) with the reversed radical *qī* (七);
the phonetic gloss says it is the clarity of the color green. It is formed from *yǔ* (羽) with the phonetic *zú* (卒).
*Kācalindika* is a Sanskrit term; in the language of Tang (Chinese), it means "the finest, softest, lightest, and most exquisite upper garment.

*Kūṣa* (氍毹)—with the first syllable pronounced as *qú* and the second as *shuāng chū*—is said by those who examine sounds to mean "weaving hair into patterns"; it is originally a foreign word. It has no direct equivalent in Chinese, so it is colloquially called "hair-patterned brocade" (*máo jǐn*), which is the same as *wén jì* (文罽). [The character for] *jù* (居) is pronounced with the *yòu* (又) rhyme, or it may be written as *kū* (𣮔) or *lín* (󱮣).

*Mianru* (綿褥): The first character is pronounced *biān* (彌編反) and the second has the phonetic value *rù* (下音辱). "Cotton for a mattress" (*mián wéi rù*) is correctly written with the radical *yī* (衣); it refers to a padded mat. *Zhīpèi* (之帔):
The first character is pronounced *pī* (丕被反) and the second has the phonetic value *pí* (皮聲).

It takes the radical *jīn* (巾). It refers to a large pillow used as a headrest; one fills a bag with soft materials and leans against it. *Yǐzhěn* (倚枕): The first character is pronounced *qǐ* (上綺反) and the second is pronounced *zhī-rèn* (下之荏反). This is a large pillow. One places soft objects inside a pouch and leans against it.
The *utpala* flower is the blue lotus (formerly called *youboluo*).
The *padma* flower is the red lotus, or as some say, the yellow lotus.
The *kumuda* flower is the crimson lotus, a deep red color, or as some say, a color like fire.
The *pundarīka* flower is a white lotus, white as the color of snow; the old transcription "fendali" is erroneous.
Its blossoms radiate brilliance (the character for "blossom" is pronounced *ying* with the second tone, whereas the version in the *jing* [classics] using the character *ying* is incorrect).

*Atimuktaka* (the first character pronounced with the *ding* and *yi* tones, the second with the *jiang* and *qie* tones; the same applies below; formerly called *atimukta*, correctly *adimudika*; in reality, it is but a single flower, yet this country lacks it).

Campa (formerly transcribed as *zhānbōjiā*, *zhānpǒjiā*, *zhānpō*, or *zhānbù*; also transcribed as *zhànbo*): these are all merely variations in the phonetic renderings of the words used in the regions of the East and the West. This [term] means "golden flower. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that it is a yellow-flowered tree with a tall and large trunk; its fragrance is also extremely potent, following the wind for a great distance.

Sumana-mabàn (formerly called sumo-na); its flowers are yellowish-white or red and very fragrant; it is only three or four feet high, with petals drooping downward in a shape resembling a covered bowl.
Vāsikā (formerly transcribed as *pó shī jiā*, which is an error).
Aśokapāṭalakaṇṭhī. Raktotpala-nīlotpala. (The character for *ni* is pronounced with the *qù* and *yú* tones.)
All the flowers mentioned above, such as the *tāraṇī*, exist in that land; these are merely brief mentions of fragrant flowers, and none of them exist in this country.

"Wěi-cuì" (萎悴)—the first character pronounced with the *wěi* rhyme and the second with the *cuì* rhyme—refers to the state of being withered and exhausted; the sound of the word *qíng-suì* (情遂) is said to mean "sorrow."
*Koṭi* is a Sanskrit term for a numerical unit; the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that one hundred *lakṣas* equal one *koṭi*.

*Saṃkhyā*, *kalā*, *gaṇanā*, *upamā*, and *upaniṣad*—these five terms above are Sanskrit names for numerical units. They increase and expand progressively until they reach the limit of immeasurable numbers. These are used as metaphors for the immeasurable supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) of the śrāvakas, the lesser sages, yet even when compared to a single fraction of the Tathāgata’s divine power, they do not approach it.

"Sā rán" (颯然): The commentary on the ancient phonetics and meanings explains this as "the appearance of rapidity. According to the *Guǎngyá*, "sā sā" refers to the wind; it is the sound of leaves falling when blown by the wind. "Vēlán-sēngqié-lǔ" (吠嵐僧伽魯):
This is the name for the great, violent winds at the time of the kalpa-ending disaster (*kalpasaṃvarta*). These winds are so fierce and violent that they can destroy the world system.

Volume Thirty-Eight. *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Volume Thirty-Eight. Regarding the term "biaozhi" (幖幟): in the *Tōngsúwén* (通俗文), it is stated that a "huíhào" (徽號, insignia or title) is called a "biao. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "biaozhi" (幖幟). The *Guìyuànzhúcóng* (桂苑珠叢) notes that "zhì" (幟) refers to the same category as banners and flags; it is formed from the radical "jīn" (巾, cloth) with the phonetic component "piáo" (票). The text of the sūtra uses "biāo" (熛) with the radical "huǒ" (火, fire), which is an error. "Huǒfēi" (火飛) means "fire flying. The lower character is pronounced "chì" (叱, chì). The *Guǎngyǎ* (廣雅) states: "Zhì" (幟) is a banner. The *Shījì* (史記) says: "A person holds a red zhì," meaning a banner. Regarding the phonetics, "zhì" (幟) has the head radical "jì" (記, record). The *Tōngsúwén* states: "Private records are called 'zhì'. The *Shuōwén* agrees. The *Guǎngyǎ* says it is formed from "jīn" (巾) with the phonetic "zhī" (戠). Alternatively, it may be written as "zhì" (󲐜) with the radical "zhì" (志), which is the same. The text of the sūtra uses "chì" (熾) with the radical "huǒ" (火); this means "fire blazing," which is not the intended meaning of the sūtra. "Piáo" (票) is pronounced "pǐ yáo" (疋遙). "Zhī" (戠) is pronounced "zhī yì" (之翼).

"Xiá" (陿): *jiǎ* (咸甲反). Yě Wáng says: "To be cramped and narrow; not broad and great. The text of the scripture uses the character with the radical 犬 (dog) and the phonetic 夾 (jiā), forming 狹; this is incorrect. It is actually 狹, meaning to train dogs and horses, which does not accord with the intent of the scripture. The correct form according to the *Shuowen Jiezi* has the radical 𠂤 (duī) and the container 匚 (fāng), with the phonetic 夾 (jiā); the lower part is read as *liàn* (掇反), and the commentary on the sounds states it means "weak" or "small. It is a compound character (*huìyì zì*). Sometimes it is written as 寽 or 埒, which are archaic forms.

"Circular" (*xúnhuán*): following and obeying. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* states that "xún" means to follow; it is derived from the phonetic "shùn," meaning compliant and good. Guo Pu further states that "xún" means to patrol. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to move along. It is composed of the radical "chì" (phonetic value: *chǔ chǐ*) and the phonetic "dùn. Furthermore, the character "dùn" is composed of "yè" (the character for "to drag") and "shí" and "mù. The current text frequently errs by using "rén" and a vertical stroke to form "xún," which is incorrect. "Dùn" has the pronunciation "shùn"; below it is "huá wán. Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that "huán" means to revolve; Zheng Xuan says it means to surround and to encircle.

*Dùn* (dull faculty). Pronounced *dùn* (with the tone of *tóng* [inverted]). The *Cāngjié piān* states that "dùn" means stubborn. Rú Chūn’s commentary on the *Shìjì* says that "stubborn and dull" (*wán dùn*) is like having no corners or edges. The *Shēnglèi* says it means "unfavorable. It is a phono-semantic compound character.

*Samāpatti* is a Sanskrit term; in the Tang language, it is translated as "concentration" (*ding*) or "equilibrium-attainment" (*dengzhi*). It refers to the initial entry into meditative absorption. Regarding the character *luan* (亂):

the upper radical *hun* (魂) is pronounced with the *wang* (反) tone, while the lower radical *kao* (考) is pronounced with the *shui* (水) tone, meaning the appearance of flowing water. The lower radical *luan* (鸞) is pronounced with the *duan* (段) tone. The *Zuo Zhuan* states: "When people turn virtue into disorder (*luan*), calamities arise. The *Kaosheng* (考聲) commentary explains that *luan* means "confusion" or "error," and it denotes "rebellion. It is sometimes written as *luan* (乱), which is an archaic form. In the *Yishan Stele Inscription*, Li Si used the character with the *cun* (寸) radical, written as *nao* (𡝩). The *Shuowen Jiezi* uses the character with the *you* (又) radical, written as *luan* (亂). *Luan* (亂) signifies "to govern" or "to regulate"; it derives from *yi* (乙), signifying the act of governing. The sound of *luan* is also represented by the character *luo* (𤔔).
"Yìngduó" (映奪) is a reversal of "jìng" (敬); it is incorrect to write it as "yìng" (央). The pronunciation is "wūlǎng" (烏朗); it does not accord with the meaning of the scripture. "Pòzé" (迫迮):
the upper character is pronounced "bǎi" (百), and the lower is pronounced "zhēnggé" (爭革).
The character for "poisonous thorn" (dú cì) is written with the correct radical; the reading "xiǎn" is an error. Regarding the character for "ashes" (huī jìn):

according to the *Fāngyán*, in the regions west of Guān, specifically between Qín and Jìn, that which remains when firewood has not been fully consumed is called "jìn. The *Shuowén* states that "jìn" refers to the remaining wood of a fire. It is composed of the radicals "brush" (yù) and "fire" (huǒ); it is an error to write it as "cì" today.

39. Volume Thirty-nine of the Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra. "Yishì" (怡適): The first character, "yī" (怡), is read with the upper radical "wood" (木) and the phonetic "zhī" (之); its sound is that of *xǐyuè* (喜悅). It means harmony. The second character, "shì" (適), is read with the lower radical "shū" (舒); it is also pronounced as *lè* (樂) or *shàn* (善). It means joy and goodness.
*Āo* (pronounced *gào* with a retroflex *k* sound) means arrogance, haughtiness, or dissipation; it is sometimes written as *niǎo*.

*Táo* (pronounced *tú láo*) means to flee or escape, according to Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji*; Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* says it means to hide away; the *Shuowen Jiezi* says it means to perish; the *Yupian* says it means to disperse and run; it is also sometimes written as *pén*.
The various editions of the *Jing* (Classic) have the character "ding" (定), which is sometimes written as "jing" (逕).

The character "huang" (隍) is pronounced with the initial *hú* and the final rhyme *guāng*. The *Cangjie pian* states that it refers to the moat beneath a city wall; the *Shuowen jiezi* states it refers to a city moat (*chengchi*). That which has water is called a "chi" (池); that which lacks water is called a "huang" (隍). It is derived from the radical "e" (阝, pronounced *fù*) and the phonetic component "huang" (皇).

"Ōng-bì (擁閉): In the *Cāngjié piān*, 'yōng' (擁) means to hold; it is a word formed by both shape and sound. As for 'bì' (閉), it follows the radical 'shǎo' (扌); those versions where it follows 'xià' (下) are incorrect. 'Shě-gēng' (䋞縆):

The upper character is pronounced 'gāng' (岡), and the lower is 'gǔ-héng' (古恒). According to the *Kǎoshēng*, 'gēng' (縆) refers to a great rope. The text uses 'guàn' (亘) to form 'héng' (絙), which is an error and a simplification. The *Yùpiān* gives the pronunciation 'hú-guān' (胡官) meaning 'slack,' and claims it is an archaic form of the character 'guàn' (亘), but this is not the intended meaning in the scripture."
*Chán* (纏): The upper radical is *chí* (持, with the *lián* [連] tone);

the lower phonetic is *guǒ* (果). 40. The Fortieth Fascicle. *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Fascicle XL. *Bìn* (擯): The upper radical is *sī* (司); the lower phonetic is *mǎo* (卯). Sima Biao’s commentary on the *Zhuangzi* states: "To banish and discard. The *Shiji* states: "To exclude and repel. Examining its sound, it means "to fall. It is a compound character formed from both semantic and phonetic elements.

"Píjuàn" (疲倦): the upper character is pronounced *pí* (as in *piǎo*). Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states it means "toiling with fatigue. The *Kaosheng* says it means "exhaustion" or "weariness. The lower character is pronounced *yuàn* (as in *quān*). Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shangshu* says it means "lassitude and laxity. Gu Yewang says it means "to cease."

*Jiǎn-chí* (謇吃): The first character is pronounced with the *jiàn* (建偃) radical. The *Yìjīng* (易經) states that *jiǎn* means "difficulty. According to the *Fānyán* (方言), *jiǎn* also refers to stammering. It may be written with the *hǔ* (虎) radical as *huò* (諕), or with the *liǎo* (了) radical as *láo* (󲌚), or with the *gān* (干) radical as *gàn* (󱿡), or as *hài* (𧮈); these variants all share the same meaning. The second character is pronounced *yǐ* (乙). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) says it means "difficulty in speech" or "speaking with labored breath. The *Tōngsúwén* (通俗文) states that speech which is not fluent is called *jiǎn-chí*. It may also be written with the *qiàn* (欠) radical as *qian* (󲘅), which is an archaic form.

The upper phoneme of *tóngjí* (詷疾) is pronounced *dòng*. The *Zuǎnwén* states that *chóngtóng* (𧩟詷) means "hasty. The *Tōngsùwén* says that to speak excessively is called *chóngtóng*. The *Kǎoshēng* says it refers to playful or hasty speech; it describes the manner in which the breath and voice are both hurried. The character *jīng* (經) is written as *zhōu* (周) in the *Zhōu* [edition], but this is an error in the *Shū* (Book). The phoneme of *chóng* (𧩟) is *chuāngnòng* (忩弄) in rhyme.

"Dùn" (塵黷): In the *Cāngjié piān*, it is read as *tú wù* (徒屋反); in the *Guǎngyá*, it means "dirt" (*gòu*) or "to obscure" (*méng*). It may also be written as "Nü" (女) to form "Nù" (嬻) or "Yì" (䢱), with the same meaning; these are archaic characters.
*Śāi* (穢): The first character is pronounced *zū* with a retroflex final (反), and the second is *wēi* with a *guì* final (反).

*Qièdàn* (怯憚): The first character is pronounced *qiàn* with a *yè* final (反), or alternatively written as *qī* (㹤). Zheng’s commentary on the *Shijing* states that *qī* means "difficulty" (*nán*). The *Han Shih* states it means "evil" (*è*). Pronounced *wù* with a *gù* final (反). The *Guǎngyá* states it means "startled. The *Shuowén* states it means "much *jìn*" (𭔉). It is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and has a departing tone (*qùshēng*).

The *Huánglí* (Yellow Oriole) is known by its phonetic transcription as *huánglí cāngqīng*. To the west of Guān, it is called the *huánglí*; in common parlance, it is called the *huángyīng*, or the *chǔquè*. The *Guǎngzhì* calls it the *huánglíliú*, though it may also be written as *huánglíliú* or *huánglíliú*, which are archaic characters.

The character *duì* (對) is pronounced with the initial *qíng* and the final *yè*, meaning "to respond" or "to face. Regarding the character *duì* (對), it is composed of *chóu* (愁) and *xué* (學) as its phonetic components; the reading *shì* (仕) is incorrect when derived from *tǔ* (土). It is also composed of *cùn* (寸) and *zhì* (至), which is not [the correct derivation].

41. Fascicle Forty-one. The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Fascicle Forty-one. The character *xuān* (諠) is pronounced with the initial *huī* and *yuán*. It is also written as *guàn* (灌); the vernacular form is *xuān* (喧), and the ancient form was *hún* (吅). According to the *Guǎngyá*, *xuān* means "clamorous sound. The *Shēnglèi* states that *yì* (誼) is also *huá* (譁). The *Yùpiān* defines it as "ambition" (*zhì*). The lower radical is pronounced *huā* (花). According to the *Kǎoshēng*, *huá* (譁) is also *xuān* (諠); they are mutually defined by one another.

*Yú* (pronounced with the initial *zhū* and final *chǒu/rǎn*) has already been explained previously. The ancients said: "To speak without discerning right from wrong is called *yú*; to flatter by seeking out another's intentions and repeating their words is called *chǎn*."

"Qiáo" (橋) [pronounced *jiao* with the final consonant *dǎo* reversed; a vulgar character]. It is correctly written with the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "qió" (喬), forming "jiǎo" (撟). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "It means deceitful and false. "Xià" (下) [pronounced *shī* with the final consonant *lì* reversed] is the phonetic for "kǎo" (考). It means to rectify and to be careful and correct.

"Jin-fa" (矜伐): The upper radical is *ju* (居) with the reversed component *yi* (疑). Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "Jin means to exalt oneself. The *Shifa* (諡法) says: "To consider oneself virtuous is called jin. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *mo* (矛) and the phonetic *jin* (今); the text here, which uses *ling* (令) instead, is an error.

The character *juān* (捐): The *Yuánxū* (悅玄) reverses this by citing the *Kǎośēng* (考聲), stating it means "to discard. The *Shuōwén* says it is composed of the radical *shǒu* (hand) and the phonetic *yuān* (緣, with the *yīn* [radical] omitted). The character *bó* (搏): Pronounced *bǔ gè*. The *Guǎngyá* states it means "to strike.

The *Yùnquán* says it means "to strike with the hand. The *Cāngjiépian* says it means "to reach. The *Shēnglèi* says it means "to capture. The *Shuōwén* says it means "to search and seize," composed of the radical *shǒu* and the phonetic *bó* (with the *yīn* [radical] omitted). The character *zhuān* (專) is written with the *fǔ* (甫) radical and the *cùn* (寸) radical; it is not correct to follow the *jīng* (經) [tradition] which uses *zhuān* (專). The character *zhú* (逐): Pronounced *chóng liù*. Gù Yěwáng says it means "to pursue" or "to drive. The *Shuōwén* says it means "to run after," composed of the radical *chuò* (辵, pronounced *chǐ lüè*) and the phonetic *zhū* (豖, pronounced *chǐ lù*). Furthermore, the character *zhū* (豖) means "a tethered pig"; one adds a stroke to the character *shǐ* (豕) to form it. The *jīng* (經) [tradition] uses *zhū* (豕) to form *zhú* (逐); this is a vulgar character.

*Táo* (to flee/escape): The rhyme dictionary (*Yùnchuān*) states it means to disperse and run away. It is composed of the radical *chuò* (辵) with *bìng* (并) as the phonetic; it may also be written as *péng* (跰). *Háo* (to howl/cry out):

The upper character is read as *hú gāo* (胡高); the *Zuǒzhuan* says "jackals and wolves howl. It is composed of the phonetic *kǎo* (考) and refers to the roaring of beasts. The *Shuōwén* defines it as *hēng páo* (噑咆). It is composed of the radical *kǒu* (口) with *gāo* (臯) as the phonetic. The lower character is read as *jiāo yào* (驍曜); the *Yùnyīng* states it means to shout loudly. It is composed of the radical *kǒu* (口) with *jīng yóu* (經由) as the phonetic. Those who use *diāo* (刁) as the phonetic are in error.

"Hun" (圂): "zhū" (豬) is pronounced with the initial *h* and the final *mèn* (魂悶反). According to the *Cāngjiépiān*, it refers to the place where pigs dwell; according to the *Shuowén*, it is a compound character meaning "privy. "Zǔ" (貯): pronounced with the initial *zhù* and the final *lǚ* (貯驢反). According to the *Shuowén*, a pig in which three hairs grow together in a tuft is called a "zhū"; this is a phono-semantic compound formed from the radical "pig" (*shǐ*) and its phonetic. The form of "zhū" used in the canonical text, written with the radical "dog" (*quán*), is a vulgar character.

*Mò* (膜): "Without wisdom. The *Shuowen* says it refers to the membrane between the flesh; it is formed from the radical for "flesh" (*肉*) with the phonetic *mò*. *Qí* (祗): Pronounced *zhǐyǎng* (上旨夷反). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* says "qí means reverence.

It is formed from the radical for "altar/tablet" (*示*) with the phonetic *dī*. The lower part is pronounced *yúyǔ* (下魚雨反). The *Shuowen* says it means "to look up. It is composed of the radicals for "seven" (*匕*) and "seal" (*卩*, sound *jié*). *Yǎng* was the ancient form; today it is written as *yǎng* (仰) with the radical for "person" (*人*).

Regarding *jiàn* (key/lock): The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "to hold the door with wood. It is composed of the radical *mén* (door) and the phonetic *gǔhuán*. The *Yupian* states it is what is now called the *mén-yán* (the lintel or door-ledge). In the scripture, it is sometimes written as *biàn* (弁), which is incorrect; its pronunciation is *biàn*. Below, it is read as *qúyàn*. Zheng Zhong’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states it refers to the *guǎnyuè* (tubes and keys). The *Shuowen* defines *jiàn* (as in *jiànxuán*) as having the sound *xuán*, composed of the radical *jīn* (metal) and the phonetic *jiàn*. It is also written as *tá* (闥) or with the radical *mù* (wood) as *jiàn* (楗). The *Fangyan* states: "East of the Guanzhong pass, it is called *jiàn*; west of the Guanzhong pass, it is called *yuè*. The *yuè* is the male [bolt]."

*Ni* (pronounced with the *li* rhyme) means "near" according to the *Erya*; *ni* also means "near. Du’s commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan* states that *ni* means "intimate. According to the *Erya*, *ni* also means "frequent" (pronounced with the *qi* rhyme); the *Kao Sheng* says it means "numerous" and "respectful. The text also uses the character *bi* (written as 󱿷), which also means "pervasive."

*Quèkuài*: The first character is pronounced *kǔ* (with the *huí* rhyme) and the second is pronounced *gǔ* (with the *wài* rhyme). "Què" means a leader or chief; "kuài" means to mince or slice. Both are phonetic-semantic compounds (*xíngshēng*). *Língyǔ*:
The first character is pronounced *líng* (with the *zhèn* rhyme) and the second is pronounced *yǔ*. This was the name of a prison during the Zhou dynasty.

Regarding *zhì* (桎) and *gù* (梏): the former is pronounced *zhēn* (真) with the initial *rì* (日) and the latter *gǔ* (古) with the final *wò* (沃). Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "That which is on the feet is called *zhì*; that which is on the hands is called *gù*. The *Erya* says: "*Gù* means straight. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "*Zhì* is a fetter for the feet; it is used to bind one to the earth. *Gù* is a fetter for the hands; it is used to appeal to Heaven. Both are characters formed with the left side as the semantic component and the right side as the phonetic. Zheng Xuan says: "To 'add the *minggù*' (明梏) means to write one's name, surname, and crime upon the *gù* and affix it there."

The character *qiú* (毬)—in the *Zi shu*, it refers to a leather ball—is a game played either on foot or on horseback by striking it with a stick to compete for possession; it is a compound character formed from a semantic and a phonetic component. The scriptural text uses *jù* (匊) as its radical, which is a vulgar form of the character.

The character for *kāipò* (開闢) is composed of *jiān* (幵, pronounced qiān) with *pí* (毘, also pronounced pí) as its phonetic. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to open up"; it is a compound character formed from both the semantic and the phonetic components. The character for *jiāogāo* (憍高) is pronounced jiāoyāo;

it is composed of the radical *xīn* (心) and the element *qiáo* (喬). To write it as *jiāo* (憍) is correct. To write it as *jiǎo* (憍) with the right side being either *yòu* (右) or *yǒu* (有), or as *jiǎo* (憍) with the right side being *zhào* (召) or *zhào* (兆), are all incorrect and are merely vulgar characters.

*Qiè* (下羌業反): The *Yùpiān* states that *qiè* means "timid," "fearful," or "inferior. Alternatively, it is written as *qī* (㹤) with the radical for dog (*quǎn*). Dū Lín says that because dogs are often timid, the character includes the dog radical.

*Tāo* (眼體姚反): According to the *Shēnglèi*, *tāo* is pronounced *yuānyuè* (淵悅反). The *Yùnyīng* defines it as "to remove" or "to clear away. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical for hand (*shǒu*) and the phonetic element *zhào* (省) in abbreviated form.

*Yuezu* (刖足)—the first character pronounced *jue* (厥) and the second *fu* (反)—is the name of an ancient penal law. The explanations in the Classics (*jing*) and Histories (*shi*) differ: some call it the *fei-xing* (腓刑), pronounced *ren* (󲎓); others call it the *pi-yin-xing* (𩪯刑), pronounced *yin* (毘胤). As for the punishment itself, it is one and the same: when a person crosses passes or bridges, or climbs over city walls and moats to commit robbery or plunder, the punishment is *yue*. According to the *Kao-sheng* (考聲), this means "severing the feet. It is also written as *ren* (󲌪); the *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "knife" (*dao*) with "moon" (*yue*) as the phonetic.

*Pinzhu* (頻蹙): The first character is pronounced *bīyín* (反) [in the old notation], which is now abbreviated as *jīngyù* (反). It is sometimes written as *cù* (蹙) or *zhǎo* (蹵); the meanings are identical. This was already explained in the second fascicle of the beginning of this scripture. *Ācārya* is a Sanskrit term;
in the Tang language it means "Master of Discipline" (*guǐfàn shī*) or "Teacher of Receiving Instruction" (*shòujiào shī*). The older transliteration *āshālì* (阿闍梨) is an error.

The character 欝 (yù) is pronounced with the upper radical 女 (nǚ) and the phonetic component 千 (qiān), with the auxiliary sound 考 (kǎo). It means "to wind" or "to curve"; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to bend. It is a compound character formed from shape and sound. The lower part is pronounced yùn (律 lǜ). The commentary on the *Shangshu* by Confucius states that 欝 means "grieving thoughts. The *Guoya* says it means "profound. The auxiliary sound 考 (kǎo) indicates "longing thoughts" or "obstruction. It is composed of the radicals 林 (lín), 󳹇 (míng), and 一 (yī), with the decorative strokes 彡 (shān).

"貶退" (biǎn tuì) means to degrade or dismiss; Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that "貶" (biǎn) means to diminish, while He Xiu’s commentary on the *Gongyang zhuan* says it means to reduce, and the *Mao shi zhuan* says it means to fall. It is also sometimes written as "卑" (bēi).
*Dāna* (pronounced *tuo na* with the first syllable reversed; in the language of India, it is translated as "giving" [Skt. *dāna*]; formerly called *tana*).
*Kṣānti* (the first syllable pronounced *cha xian*, the second *ding yi*; in the language of India, it is translated as "patience" or "tolerance").
*Vīrya* is translated into Chinese as "diligence" (*jingjin*) or "heroic progress" (*yongjin*).
*Prajñā* is a corrupted abbreviation of the Sanskrit; its correct Sanskrit pronunciation is *prajñā*, which is translated into Chinese as "wisdom" (*hui*) or "transcendent wisdom" (*zhixue*).

*Kyō* (肴): The rhyme is *kō*. Guo Yu’s commentary states that *kyō* refers to meat on a sacrificial stand (*zǔ*). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* says it refers to the contents of a *dòu* vessel. The *Shi Jian* says it refers to pickled vegetables (*zhū*). The *Kao Sheng* says it refers to dried meats, delicacies, cakes, fruits, and the like. The *Shuowen* defines it as "to eat," written with the radical for meat and the phonetic *xiào*. It is commonly written as *yáo*. The lower character is pronounced *shàn*. Zheng Xuan says: "Dish" (*shàn*) means excellent; what we now call fine food is called *shàn*. The *Shuowen* [defines it] as having the radical for meat.
The character for "vehicle" (chē) is pronounced as *zhèng* (反) when used in the sense of "time.

The character for "road" (lù) is pronounced as *jǔ* (魚反). The *Shìmíng* (Explanations of Names) states: "In antiquity, the pronunciation of 'vehicle' (chē) was like that of 'dwell' (*jū*). It is that by which people dwell. 'Road' (*lù*) is also a vehicle; it is that by which one travels upon a road. It is also written as *luò* (輅), with the same meaning.

"Yǎo" (邀) is explained as "to intercept" (*yāo*) according to the commentary of Du Yu on the *Zuozhuan*. Jia Gongyan’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states it means "to seek. The *Yinyi* (Phonetic Explanations) of the *Hanshu* states it means "to block. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical *chuò* (辵) and the phonetic element *jiǎo* (敫) in its abbreviated form.

*Yònglì* (勇勵): The first character, *yǒng*, is pronounced with the *shǒng* rhyme of the "Yang" (羊) series. The *Tàixuānjīng* by Yang Xiong states: "To resolve and decide is courage (*yǒng*). The *Shìfǎ* says: "To manifest a profound mandate through benevolence is called courage; to know death yet not avoid it is called courage. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "the spirit of courage," composed of the radical "force" (*lì*) and the phonetic "yǒng. The second character, *lì*, is pronounced with the *zhì* rhyme of the "Lì" (滯) series. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* explains it as "mutually encouraging and stimulating. The *Gōngjīn Zhèngzì* states that *lì* means "to exert oneself," composed of the radical "force" (*lì*) and the phonetic "lì."

*Sarvajña* (the *r* and *e* reversed) is an incorrect abbreviation of the Sanskrit; the correct Sanskrit pronunciation is *sarvajña*, which in the Tang language means "all-knowledge" (formerly translated as *sabbaññu*).

Regarding "marrow" (suǐ): although the character above is pronounced shì (𭪿), the *Shuowen* states it is the fat within the bones, a compound character based on both form and sound. Regarding "brain" (nǎo): the *Shuowen* states it is the marrow within the head, a pictographic-sound compound character; it is composed of "flesh" (ròu) and the phonetic element "zhì" (ㄙ). In the *Shuowen*, it is written with "bǐ" (匕) as 󱹗, while Wei Hong wrote it simply as 󲓸.

The character for *tíhú* (醍醐) has the upper radical *shí* (食) and the phonetic *dǐ* (氐, with the pronunciation *dīng lǐ*); it is a common error to use *hù* (互) instead. The lower part has the pronunciation *hú*. *Tíhú* refers to the refined essence of clarified butter (*sūzhōng jīngchún*). Regardless of winter or summer, it remains clear and does not congeal; it can penetrate the muscles and skin of humans. Alternatively, it may be written with the radical *yǒu* (酉), as in *tíhú*; this usage is also acceptable in common parlance.

"Hào" (皓) in "皓齒" (white teeth): according to the *Erya*, it means white; it is formed from the radical "mouth" (自) with the phonetic "gào" (告). In the scriptures, it is written as "jīng" (經), which is a colloquial variant used interchangeably. "Xiàng" (象) below [in "xiàngyǐng"] is pronounced "chāngzhǐ" (昌止); it is a pictographic character.

Regarding the character *fǎng* (紡): the upper radical is *fāng* (芳) with the phonetic *gāng* (岡). The commentary states that it refers to twisting and winding [fibers] to make them tight; this is called *fǎng*. The lower part is *jīng* (精) with the phonetic *yì* (亦). According to the *Erya*, *jì* (績) means "to tie" (*jié*) and "to continue" (*xù*). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to continue" and "silk. It is a compound character formed from both shape and sound.

"Spinning thread" (fǎng xiàn): "xiàn" is read as qián; it is the term used by Zheng Xuan in his commentary on the *Liji* (Book of Rites), where he states that "thread" (*xiàn*) means "fibers. It is an archaic character for "line.
"A single fiber" (*yī lǚ*): "lǚ" is read as lǐ yǔ; "fiber" (*lǚ*) is also "thread" (*xiàn*).

The character for "jealousy" (dù) is pronounced as gù-fǎn. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Mao Shi* states: "To be jealous on account of one's beauty is called dù. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as: "A woman who is jealous of her husband; it is formed with the radical 'woman' and the phonetic 'hù'. The version in the [present] scripture that uses the stone radical (石) to form "dù" is an error.

Volume Forty-two. The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Forty-two. Upādhyāya (Sanskrit; translated into Chinese as *qīnjiàoshī*, "Preceptor"; formerly translated as *héshàng*, "Upādhyāya"). This is originally a Hu-language term that has been corrupted and abbreviated; it is here rendered as "Doctor," which is not a literal translation.

"Chǔ" (貯) is pronounced with the *lǚ* rhyme (知呂反). In the commentary on the *Zuozhuan*, Du Yu states that it means "to preside over" (*zhǔ*) and refers to storing away. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "accumulation," formed from the radical "貝" (*bèi*) with the phonetic component "宁" (*níng*). The pronunciation of "宁" is with the *chú* rhyme (除呂反).

*Diankuang* (癲狂): The first character, *dian*, has the phonetic *ding* with the *jian* rhyme; the *Yunying* states it refers to the disease of epilepsy (*diānbìng*). The *Wenzí jílüè* states that *zhēng* (𨈟) is a wind entering the internal organs (*zàngbìng*), though *diān* is also acceptable.

*Tōujié* (㿈癤): The first character is pronounced *yōng* and the second *jié*. The *Wenzí jílüè* states it is an internal ulceration (*huànxuě*). It is not read as *tōu*; furthermore, it is said that *jié* refers to a small *tōu*. According to the *Kǎoshēng*, *zuòjié* (痤癤) is the term used.

Regarding "ju" (疽) and "xian" (癬): the former is pronounced with the initial *q* and final *-yu* (七余反); the *Ji-lüe* (集略) states that a chronic ulcer is called "ju" (疽). The latter, "xian" (癬), is pronounced with the initial *x* and final *-yan* (仙演反); the *Shuowen* (說文) defines it as a dry sore, with the phonetic *yi* (易). Yan Xie (顏氏) notes that today there are two types of "xian": the dry and the moist.

Regarding the character *è* (惡): the force of the term implies stagnation. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "It refers to pestilential vapors that are disharmonious and thus cause disease. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Shanhaijing* states: "It refers to malignant sores. It is also pronounced with the rhyme *lùdàfǎn*. Lexicons define it as a disease caused by a great wind; the vulgar form *là* (癩) is incorrect. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as a malignant ailment (*èbìng*), written with the radical *nà* (疒), pronounced *nǚ'ài*, and the phonetic component *wàn* (萬) in abbreviated form. There is also a variant written with *hǎn* (𠂆) as the phonetic, forming *lì* (厲), which is trained to mean "to employ" (*yòng*)—this is likewise not the meaning here.

*Zhuàn* (洗濯): The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry) says it means "to wash and cleanse. The *Shuowén* (Explaining Characters and Analyzing Words) states it means "to wash"; it is composed of the radical *shuǐ* (water) and the phonetic *zhái* (pronounced *zhái*).

*Táo* (陶): Pronounced *táng láo*. The *Jíxùn* (Collected Explanations) says it means "kiln," pronounced *yáo*. A kiln is an earthen chamber for firing ceramic vessels; the correct character is 窰 (*yáo*), composed of the phonetic *fǔ gǒu* (pronounced *fǔ*) and the enclosure *bāo* (pronounced *bāo*). In current scriptures, the character is written with the radical *fù* (earth/mound), as in *Táochū* (陶丘). This traditional usage is also acceptable.

*Shian* (挻): *shang* and *yan* rhyme; Song Zhong’s commentary on the *Taixuan jing* states that *shian* means "to harmonize. Ru Chun’s commentary on the *Hanshu* says it means "to strike," but the version following the phonetic *yan* with the radical *earth* (*tu*) is incorrect. *Chi* (埴): *shi* and *li* rhyme. Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that "sticky soil is called *chi*. The *Shiming* says that soil which is yellow, fine, and dense is called *chi*; *chi* means "glossy. The Imperial Commentary on the *Laozi* also says it means "harmonized. *Chi* is soil; a potter blends soil to make vessels such as tiles and jars. It follows the radical *earth* and has the phonetic *zhi*.

*Níng* (凝) [the character is pronounced *jìng* with the *qǐng* rhyme]. Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states that it means "to form. Zheng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states that it means "firm. The *Yīzhōu* says: "Treading on hoarfrost, one sees the formation of hard ice; this is when the Yin begins to congeal. The *Shuowén* states: "Water that has become solid. It is composed of *bīng* (ice) as the phonetic component and *yí* as the semantic indicator. The character *yí* is composed of *bǐ* and *shǐ* with *shāo* as the phonetic component. *Shāo* is pronounced *suǒ yú*. The lower part is *dīng lì*. The *Shuowén* further says: "Water dripping and freezing. It is composed of *shuǐ* and *shāng* as the phonetic component. To claim it is composed of *dì* is incorrect.
"Phā" (pào-mo) is the transliteration of *phena*, meaning water-foam.

"Chu" (chù) is pronounced with the initial *g* (宅庚反), though it is sometimes written as "dàng" (㲂), "cáng" (掁), or "zhèng" (掁); these four characters share the same pronunciation and belong to the category of sounds meaning "to strike. In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, this character is missing; it follows the radical for "hand" (*shǒu*) and is pronounced with the phonetic *tíng* (亭). It is also read as "cáng" (刾), meaning to prick or poke.

"Trade" (mào): Mo (莫) and Hou (侯) are the phonetic components; Yu Ye Wang (顧野王) says it means "exchanging. The *Erya* says it is "market" (shì) or "selling" (mài). The text here uses "mǎn" (𧴵), which is a scribal error for "mào. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "It is the exchange of goods. It is composed of '貝' (bèi, shell/wealth) and '酉' (yǒu); the pronunciation is that of '卯' (mǎo)."

*Huài* (坏): meaning "unfired earthenware vessel"; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical *tu* (earth) and the phonetic *pǐ* (abbreviated from *pǐ*). *Fēi* (非): meaning "to negate" or "to reject";
according to the *Pǐ* (彼) and *bō* (撥) radicals, it means to remove or eliminate.

The upper radical is *láng* (郎) and the phonetic is *gē* (各), with the tone *tāng* (湯) and *luò* (洛), second tone; both forms are attested in the *Zìshū* (字書). The scriptural text writes it as *luò* (馲), which is incorrect. The lower part is read as *dá* (達) or *hé* (河); it is sometimes written as *dí* (𫾠) and commonly as *tuó* (駞). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that it is the name for a beast of burden of the northern Hu peoples. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Shānhǎijīng* (*Classic of Mountains and Seas*) says: "The *luòtuó* has a fleshy hump on its back, capable of carrying a thousand *jīn* and traveling three hundred *lǐ* in a day; it can know the location of springs and water sources. Both [the upper and lower parts] are *xíngshēng* (形聲) characters.

*He* (呵): pronounced as *hu* (阿反) or sometimes written as *he* (訶). The *Zhouli* states: "Those who are disrespectful shall be rebuked (*he*) and punished. In ancient texts, it is written with the radical for "stop" (*zhǐ*) as *qì* (㱒); the reading *hè* (遏反) is incorrect. The current text uses *hè* (喝), which is pronounced *wùjiè* (烏介反). The *Guǎngcāng* says that *qì* (𠿒) is also *he* (訶). The *Guǎngyá* says it means anger. The *Shuowén* says it is a loud sound of anger; it is composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic "xiē" (*xiē*).

One *huò* (a cauldron). Huang Guo’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states it is a vessel for boiling meat. The *Guangya* calls it a *ding* (tripod). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as *huò*; its pronunciation is *xié*, composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic element "shuō" (*shuō*) with the abbreviated form of "huó" (*huó*). "Huó" is pronounced *hóngguó*.

*Cuòkuài* (剉膾): The first character, *cuò*, is pronounced as *cānghuà* (倉貨反); according to the *Yùpiān*, it means "to chop. The second character, *kuài*, is pronounced as *gōngwài* (公外反); according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to mince," and according to the *Zìtǒng*, it refers to finely minced raw meat. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means "finely minced meat"; it is composed of the radical "flesh" (*ròu*) with the phonetic component "huì" (*huì*).

"Jù" (saw) is pronounced *jū* (with the *yù* rhyme). The *Cāngjiépiān* states that it is a saw used for cutting objects. The character 笮 (zé): the upper radical is 于 (yú) with the phonetic component 甲 (jiǎ); it denotes the sound of "examining" (kǎo) and signifies "to press down" (zhèn), following the phonetic 厭 (yàn). The lower part is read as zhuāng or gé; alternatively written as 迮 (zé), which the *Shuowen Jiezi* explains as "to constrain" (pò), following the phonetic 乍 (zhà). The ancient commentary on pronunciation and meaning states that it refers to pressing out juice using a trough (*cáo*).

*Bian* (鞭): *Bumianfan* (補綿反) states that it refers to using leather to strike those who have committed offenses. *Kao* (考) means to strike; according to the *Shuowen*, it means to drive or urge. It is composed of the radical "leather" (*革*) and the phonetic "bian" (*便*). The *Guangya* states that *bian* means "hard. It is composed of the abbreviated form of *meng* (夢) and the phonetic *nie* (臬). *Nie* is pronounced *e* (蘖); *meng* (臬) is synonymous with *meng* (夢). *Nie* (臬): Pronounced *e* (蘖). *Meng* (夢) refers to dreaming.

*Yúzhòu* (愚戇): The first character is pronounced *zhuó* (卓) with the *jiàng* (降) rhyme, or alternatively *zhuó* (濁) with the *xiàng* (巷) rhyme. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "ignorant," following the radical for the mind (*xīn*) and taking *gù* (𥫔) as the phonetic component. *Gù* (𥫔) is pronounced *gòng* (貢) or *gàn* (紺); it is composed of *zhāng* (章) and *xiàng* (夅), the latter being pronounced *jiāng* (江). It is a variant of *bèi* (貝).
"Fènluàn" (憤亂): "fèn" is pronounced as in "fū" (枎) and "wèn" (問);

the *Fānyán* states it means "píchī" (疲癡, exhausted delusion). *Qū* (pronounced *qiú*, with the rhyme of *yú*): The *Cāngjié piān* states that to follow behind is called *qū*; the *Guǎngyá* says it means to run. In ancient script it was written as *qū*, meaning to drive or pursue.
*Xié* (pronounced *pǐ*, with the rhyme of *yì*): The *Kǎoshēng* states it means "oblique," "to avoid," or "erroneous. It is composed of the radical "man" (人) and the phonetic element "bì" (辟).

43. Fascicle Forty-Three of the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*. **Lǚ (逆旅)**: This character means "to welcome" (*yíng*).
