From the fifty-sixth to the ninety-first fascicle of the *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra*, there are thirty-six fascicles in total. Fascicle 56:

The fifty-sixth fascicle of the *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra*, the fourteenth assembly, the *Garbha* (Womb) Assembly, in two fascicles. Regarding the following term, "Kapilavastu," it is the name of a city in the language of Brahmā. Formerly it was called "Jiawei" (迦維), or "Jiapi" (迦毘羅), or "Jiapirowei" (迦毘羅衛); these are all corruptions, omissions, or inaccuracies. In its full form, it should be pronounced "Kapilavastu," which is the city ruled by King Śuddhodana.

*Hàn* (䍑): Pronounced with the initial *hē* (呵) and the final *ㄜ* (󱁅). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "net" (*wǎng*), formed from the radical "net" (*wǎng*) and the phonetic "gān" (*gān*). In character dictionaries, it also means "rare" or "few. The version in the sutras written with the "cave" radical (*xué*) as *hǎn* is incorrect.

*Nuò* (腕): Pronounced *wū guàn* (烏灌). It refers to the joint behind the wrist of the palm. It is formed from the radical "flesh" (*ròu*) and the phonetic "yuǎn" (*yuǎn*). This is a vernacular character.

*Guǒ* (upper tone): According to the *Shuowen*, this character is composed of "clothing" (*yī*) and "fruit" (*guǒ*). *Shǒu*: Pronounced with the second tone (*liú*). It is composed of "hand" (*yòu*) and "jiū" (pronounced *jíyóu*).

In the Classics, it is written with the "hand" radical (*tǎn*), which is incorrect. *Fàng*: Pronounced *zhāngliù*. A broom for sweeping away filth. In the *Shuowen*, it is written as *zhǒu*, composed of "hand" (*yòu*) holding a "cloth" (*jīn*) to sweep within the enclosure (*mìng*; pronounced *guǐyíng*).
"Even if the thief has sufficient means" is a phrase used for a counter-argument.
*Viśākhā* (毘舍佉)—the "shè" being pronounced as *qié*—is a proper name in the Sanskrit language.

Regarding the term "glancing" (顧眄): the lower character is pronounced *miàn*; the *Yìnyīng* (韻英) states it means to look askance. It is composed of the radical "eye" (目) and the phonetic "gài" (丐), where the pronunciation of "gài" is the same as the preceding [character]. The version of the scripture that uses "nǎn" (䀎) is incorrect.

"Blind monkey" (*xiá míhóu*): "xiá" is pronounced with the *yà* (戞) rhyme and the *kǎo* (考) tone; it means that the eyes cannot see objects. It is also written as *xiá* (𦅂), which has been explained previously. "Yà" (呀) is pronounced with the *hè* (嚇) rhyme and the *jiā* (加) tone; "jiá" (戞) is pronounced with the *jiā* (加) rhyme and the *bā* (八) tone.

*Chuáng*: "Wéi" (with the phonetic component *wěi*) is the sound for "curtain" (*wéimàn*). According to the *Shuowen*, that which is on the sides is called a *wéi*; it follows the radical *jīn* (cloth) with the phonetic *zhuī*. There is a version following the radical *xīn* (heart), which is incorrect.

*Bù*: The upper character is pronounced *fēng*. According to the *Shuowen*, it means to stitch clothes with a needle; it follows the radical *xì* (silk thread) with the phonetic *mì* and the sound *fēng*. The character *bù* itself follows the radical *yī* (clothing).

*Naraka* (the first character pronounced with the *nu* and *ge* tones, the second with the *ju* and *qie* tones) is the Sanskrit name for hell. It has many names; here, I shall briefly cite one or two: in the Tang language, it is called "That Which Is Unpleasant," or "That Which Cannot Be Saved," or "That Without Rest," or "The Uninterrupted."

"Fènshǐ" (filth/urine) is a vernacular character pronounced with the upper radical *mèn* (to be distressed); the *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as 󲚠, meaning to discard or sweep away refuse. The *Yunying* states it means "impurity. The *Kaosheng* writes it as 𡑝 or 𡓴; the lower phonetic is *shǐ* (to begin).

*Jianba* (鉆拔): The upper character is pronounced *qiáng-lián* (強廉) with a *kǎo* (考) sound; it refers to an iron clamp (*xié*). The lower character is pronounced *nǚ-zhé* (女輒). It denotes using an iron clamp to grasp an object. The scriptural text uses *jiān* (鉗) with the radical for "sweetness" (*gān*), which is an erroneous usage; it actually refers to the neck-clamp or iron collar (*xiàngjiān*). The lower character is pronounced *biàn-bā* (辨八) with a *kǎo* (考) sound. *Bá* (拔) means to pull out. Gu Yewang says it means to draw out. The *Guǎngyǎ* says it means "to bring forth. The *Shuōwén* says it means "to extract. It takes the radical for "hand" and the phonetic *bà* (犮). *Bà* is pronounced *pán-mò* (盤末). The *Shuōwén* states that *bà* is the sound of a dog running.

*Liè* (捩): The rhyme *liè* is pronounced as *niè* (拈). Yingyun states it means "to twist" (*ǎoliè*). It is formed from the radical 手 (hand) and the phonetic 戾 (lì). *Niè* is pronounced as *nián* (年) with the final *tiě* (䥫). *ǎo* (拗) is pronounced as *ài* (厄) with the final *jiǎo* (絞).

*Tāo* (𢮓): The rhyme *yuān* (淵) is pronounced as *jué* (決). Kaosheng states that *tāo* means "to pick" or "to pluck. It is formed from the radical 手 (hand) and the phonetic 𢮓 (táo). *Tāo* is pronounced as *tǐ* (體) with the final *yáo* (遙).
The character for *jù* (saw) was previously explained. The character for *lī* (to split) is the opposite of *lǐ* (to arrange).

Regarding its phonetic component, it is *kǎo*. *Lī* means to cut or to incise; the *Zílín* dictionary writes it as *lì*, while the scriptural text writes it as *gēng*, which is incorrect. Upon examining all dictionaries, this character does not exist; only the meaning in the scripture fits the character *lī*, which is composed of the radical *dāo* (knife) and the phonetic component *zǐ* (abbreviated from *zǐ*) with the sound *kǎo*.

The character 鑱 (chàn) has the upper radical 倉 (cāng) with the reversed sound 亂 (luàn). The *Pīcāng* states it is a short spear; the lower part is pronounced as 仕 (shì) and 咸 (xián), meaning a sharp appearance. The *Guǎngyá* says "chàn" means a dagger (bǐ); the *Cāngjiépiān* says it is a chisel (càn). The *Shuōwén* defines it as "a sharp chisel," composed of the radical 金 (metal) and the phonetic 毚 (chán) in abbreviated form. It is also written as 劖 or 欃; these three forms are identical. The sound of 鈹 (bǐ) is like 披 (pī); the sound of 鏨 (càn) is like 慙 (cán), which is the same as 鑱. Alternatively, the upper tone may be read as an ascending tone (qùshēng).

*Shao* (矟): The upper character is pronounced *shuang* (雙) with the *cao* (反) tone; it refers to a long spear. The lower character is pronounced *qing* (清) with the *ji* (積) tone; it is composed of the radicals "knife" (刀) and "thorny" (朿, sound *ci*).

The *Jing* (經) text writes it as *li* (刾), which is a vulgar form. *Bang* (棒): Pronounced *bai* (白) with the *xiang* (項) tone; this is a vulgar form. According to character dictionaries, it means "to strike. It may also be written as *bang* (棓); it refers to a large staff used for flogging. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文解字) defines it as "to strike," composed of the radical "wood" (木).

*Tièchuí* (鐵鎚): Pronounced *zhí duī* (直追) or alternatively *chuí* (槌). The *Jìxùn* (集訓) states it means "to strike. It is also written as *chuí* (椎), which is examined as meaning "to strike"; it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic element "jūi" (*zhuī*). The text of the sutra uses *tièchuí*, which is an erroneous usage for *chēngchuí* (稱鎚).
*Yóngtóng* (熔銅): "Molten copper surging upward"; it follows the character *fǎn* (反) and is cast from [the phonetic].

*Kè* (鑯): [Pronounced *huáng* with the *guō* rhyme]; the *Shēngyùn* says it refers to a cauldron (*dǐng*) that has no feet; it follows the radical *jīn* (金) and takes *shuò* (蒦) in abbreviated form as its phonetic.
*Ākǒu* (鵶口): [Pronounced *èjiā*].

"Ōu" (upper character, pronounced *wū* with the *guā* rhyme; alternatively, *yā* with the *jiāo* rhyme) and "tié" (lower character, pronounced *xié*) are both ancient characters representing their forms. They may also be written as *wā* and *diè*.
"Lí" (pronounced *lǐ* with the *zhī* rhyme) refers to a thorn hedge or a brushwood fence.
*Kalala* is the Sanskrit term, also transliterated as *garala*.

The character for "bottle" (*píng*) is pronounced with the upper radical *pú* (míng fǎn) and the lower radical *zuǎn* (luán fǎn). It means "solidified butter. In the script of the sutra, it is written with the hand radical as *cuán*, which is incorrect; it should be corrected to the metal radical as *jīn* (zhèng yě).
*Khi* (榍): The phonetic transcription is *sian* (先) and *jue* (節). The commentary states it means a wooden wedge; it is composed of the "wood" radical (*mu*). *Guo* (鍋):
The phonetic transcription is *gu* (古) and *he* (禾). It refers to a cooking vessel. Lexicons state it is a small cauldron (*pao*).
*Arbuda*: This has already been fully explained in the preceding commentary; it is like "doubtful ghee. *Kṣuradhāra* (knife-sheath):
The character for *xiào* is pronounced with the *yào* rhyme; according to dictionaries, it refers to a sheath for knives.
*Lohajaṅgha* (iron-legged): Pronounced as *zhí lù*; the *Kǎo Shēng* states that it refers to a ladle or spoon.

The first character of "earthworm" (*qiūyǐn*) is pronounced *qiū* and the second *yǐn*. According to the *Zhōu Gōng Shíxùn*, five days after the commencement of summer, the earthworms emerge; on the day of the winter solstice, the earthworms coil up. The *Ěryá* also calls them *chǐnyǐn*; they are called "Singing Maidens" (*gēnǚ*) in Jiangdong, which is likely a local dialect term.
*jiàn*: (the initial *qú* is pronounced as *yàn*;
the upper character of *xiéjiàn* is pronounced as *xiá* and the lower as *xuān*). The *Jixùn* states: "The shape and style of a boot is called *jiàn*.
*Tí* (in *tícǎo*) is pronounced *yí*; it refers to weeds.

The character *qù* (聚) is formed from the radical *qíng* (情) with the phonetic *fǎn* (反); *xià* (下) is pronounced *yín* (吟) and is formed from *zhòng* (衆) with the phonetic *lì* (立). *Mò* (沫) is pronounced *bō* (鉢) and is formed from the radical *shuǐ* (水) with the phonetic *mò* (末). The *Shuowen Jiezi* further states that the character *mò* (末) is formed by adding a single stroke above the character *mù* (木) to make *mò* (末).
*Suìtái* (水苔): "suì" is pronounced *dàilǎn*; it refers to green moss in water.
*Chuīzhàng* (吹脹): "chuī" is pronounced *zhāngliàng*; it means bloated or swollen. *Duànshī* (鍛師): "duàn" is pronounced *dùluàn*.
*Tuo* (橐) is pronounced *shang tang* (上湯) with the *lo* (洛) rhyme; it refers to a bellows (*wei*) used as a tool for blowing fire. *Wei* (韛) is pronounced *bai* (敗).
It is composed of the radical *qi* (䐡), which is pronounced *zi* (齊), meaning "flesh" according to the *Shuowen*; it is the same as *biqian* (毘䐡).
"Jíyǐqíng" (藉以情) is a variant of "jiànyè" (薦夜).
"Xiàn" (線) in "xiàn kǒu" (線口) is originally "jiàn" (薦); it is also written as "xiàn" (綫).

"Qiānjīn" (千筋) has the pronunciation qīn; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radicals for "bamboo," "flesh," and "strength," whereas its appearance in the *Jing* (Classics) with the radical for "grass" is incorrect.
The character *qìng* (隙) is a graph for "contradiction" (*yìfǎn*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of *fù* (阜) and *bái* (白), with the upper and lower parts being small.

To write it as *cháo* (巢) following the *Jīng* (經) is incorrect. *Chǔn* (舛) has the phonetic *cèjiā* (策迦). It is a regular form (*zhèngtǐ*) character meaning "duality" (*èr*) according to the *Shuowen*. It means "to differ" or "to be inconsistent," such that they do not correspond. Its regular form is composed of *chuí* (垂) and *zuǒ* (左), written as *chǔn* (󲙛). Cáo Yōng’s Stone Classics follow common usage and write it as *chā* (差). The lower part is pronounced *chuānrǎn* (川耎反). The *Guǎngyá* states that "chǔn" means "to turn one's back. Gù Yěwáng says "chāchǔn" means "uneven. The *Shuowen* defines it as "mutually facing away. It is composed of *xī* (夕) and is pronounced *zhèjǐ* (陟紀反); it is composed of *kǒuguǎ* (󱸰) and is pronounced *kǒuguǎ* (口寡反).

*Shuǎng* (爽): [The character] is pronounced *shuāng* with the *chuāng* (愴) rhyme. The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (Mao Commentary on the Book of Poetry) states: "Shuǎng means 'to deviate' (*chāi*). Guo's commentary on the *Ěr Yǎ* says: "It refers to the mind being errant and lacking single-mindedness. Jia’s commentary on the *Guó Yuǎn* states: "Shuǎng means 'duplicity' (*èr*). Guo's commentary on the *Fān Yǔ* says: "It means 'to exceed' (*guò*). According to the *Shuō Wén*, it is composed of 㸚 (pronounced *lì'ěr*) and 大; the *Jīng* (經) version erroneously uses four people (四). The lower character 失 is composed of 手 and 乙, with 乙 also serving as the phonetic component. The *Guǎng Yǎ* states: "Shī means 'error' (*wù*). The *Yù Piān* states: "Shī means 'to miss' (*chí*)."

The *Qingsiang Fanyun* explains that "artisan" (*jiang*) refers to one who is skillful in a craft. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "artisan" (*jiang*) refers to a woodworker; it is composed of the radical "work" (*gong*), the phonetic "fang," and the enclosure "fang" (*fang*), which represents the vessel being fashioned—a word formed through associative meaning.

"Dust" (chén): the upper radical is "long" (láng) with the reversed "lin" (lín); the *Shuowen* states it means "dust and grime" (*chēn'ái*). It is composed of "deer" (lù) and "earth" (tǔ). The lower part is "yù" with the phonetic "jì"; Guo's commentary on the *Fangyan* says it means "to screen," and the *Guoyá* says it means "to obstruct. Examining its sound, it also means "to cover. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of "feather" (yǔ) and the phonetic "yī"; the sound of "yī" is "yù" with the reversed "jì. The sound of "yì" is "yù" with the reversed "jì."

The first tone of *kai-shi* (揩拭) is pronounced with the initial *ke* (客) and the final *gui* (皆) reversed. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means to rub or polish. The *Shuōwén* states that it is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "guī" (皆). The character *guī* (皆) is composed of "white" (白) below and "shāng-yì" (傷翼) as its phonetic. Zheng’s commentary on the *Yílǐ* says: "It means to wipe clean. In the *Lǐjì*, it means to purify. The *Shuōwén* further states that it is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "shì" (式).

*Kua* (𦝫): pronounced *hua* with an initial *q* and also in the third tone; it is also interchangeable with *kao*. The *Kaoseng* states that it refers to the bone above the hip (*bi*). It is also written as *kuo* (𡱼), which is an archaic character. The *Yunying* states that it refers to the bone below [the hip]. It is also written as *kuà* (胯), following the radical for flesh (*肉*) with the phonetic *yù* (𡗢); the pronunciation of *yù* is the same as the former. The version in the scriptures as *kuà* is a vulgar character and is erroneous.

*Qiān* (慳): The radical *shuǐ* (water) and the phonetic *sì zhǐ* (four stops)—a compound character formed by combining these meanings. In the sutras, it is written with three stops (*sān zhǐ*), which is incorrect; it should be *shè* (澁). *Chā* (插): The pronunciation is *chǔ xià*. It means to pierce or prick.

According to the *Shuowen*, it takes the radical *shǒu* (hand) and the phonetic *zhā* (臿); the sound of *zhā* is the same as above. The character *zào* (𠚏) has the same pronunciation as the former. The character *chā* (𠚏) is said to have the ancient pronunciation *jiù*; in the old sutra texts, it is written with *qiān* (千) and *jiù* (臼), which is incorrect. The lower part, *zài* (在): according to the *Shuowen*, it means "to exist. It takes the radical *tǔ* (earth) and the phonetic *hàn* (扌), where *hàn* also serves as the phonetic component.

The upper part of the character *biao* (幖) is a semantic component meaning "to meet" (pronounced yán-fàn); the lower part is a phonetic component pronounced bì-yáo. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "a banner" (*chì*); according to other character dictionaries, it refers to the top of a pole. Its correct form consists of the radical *jīn* (巾) with *piào* (票) as the phonetic. The two characters *biāo* (灬) and *piào* (票) share the same pronunciation; in the scriptural texts, the forms with the radical *mù* (木) or the hand radical (*shǒu*) are erroneous variants of *biāo* (標).

"Dry" (gān): pronounced *dào fǎn kǎo shēng*; it means parched and dry. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "fire" (*huǒ*) and the phonetic "sào" (*shēng*). "Sào" has the same pronunciation as "shàng" (up). "Lí" (blackish-brown): pronounced *lǚ fǎn kǎo shēng*.

The commentary states it is black with a yellowish tint. The *Shuowen* entry for this character is missing; the *Gujin Zhengzi* states it means black. It is composed of "black" (*hēi*) and a simplified form of "lǜ" (*lì*). The character "lí" (as in "lí huáng") is composed of "grain" (*huò*), "yè" (*yè*), and "ěr" (*ěr*). "Huò" has the pronunciation of "jī"; it refers to the curved top of a tree.
*Wǎn* (煗): The *Yùnyuán* states that "wǎn" means warm; it is also written as *niǎn* (㬉), though *nuǎn* (暖) and *nuàn* (煖) are vulgar variants.
*Yúpí* (榆皮): A name for a river. *Yú* (榆) is pronounced *yǔ* (庾) or *zhū* (朱).

Fēng (鋒): Pronounced *fū* with the *róng* rhyme; it refers to the tip of a blade or weapon. It is sometimes written as *cāo*. In the canon, it is erroneously written with the radical *fēng* (夆). Xià (下): Pronounced *fāng*; the *Zìshū* states it means the edge of a blade or the tip of a grass leaf. It is composed of the radicals *cǎo* (草) and *wáng* (亾). The character *wáng* consists of *rén* (人) and *jiàn* (𠃊), where *jiàn* is pronounced *yùjìn*. In the canon, it is written as *máng* (芒), which is a vulgar and erroneous form.

Fù (腐): The upper part is pronounced *fú* (扶甫反) and the lower part is *shēng* (聲). It means the rotting and decay of flesh; it is composed of the radical "meat" (*ròu*) with the phonetic "fǔ" (*fǔ*). The lower part is pronounced *láng-dàn* (郎旦反), which has already been explained previously.

Tuī (推): Pronounced *tā-léi* (他雷反) according to the *Yùnyīng*. It means to push or to displace; it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) with the abbreviated form of "duī" (*duī*) as the phonetic. *Duī* is pronounced *dū-huí* (都回反).

*Luàn* (臠): Pronounced *shàng-liè-zhuǎn-fǎn-kǎo-shēng*. It refers to a piece of meat. It is composed of the radical "flesh" (*ròu*) and the abbreviated phonetic "liàn" (*liàn*). The lower character is pronounced *qián-là-fǎn*. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to cut. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of "hài" (害) and "dāo" (刀). The character "hài" is composed of "kǒu" (口) and "bàn" (半); the pronunciation of "bàn" is the same as the upper [radical], while the pronunciation of "là" (辢) is *jí-gē-fǎn*.

Volume Fifty-seven. The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Fifty-seven. *Yáo* (搖): The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "to move. It is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "yóu" (󲓢). The sound of 󲓢 is *yóu*. The character 󲓢 is composed of the radicals "flesh" (肉) and "fǔgǒu" (󳹇). The sound of 󳹇 is *fǔgǒu*.

*Biǎngbǎo* (襁褓): "Biǎng" is pronounced *jiāng* (two tones). According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to a garment for carrying a child on the back, formed with the radical "clothing" (*yī*) and the phonetic "qiáng" (*qiángshēng*). The lower character is pronounced *bǎo*. The *Cangjie pian* states that *bǎo* means "blessing. The *Shenglei* says it is the wrap worn by an infant; it is also written as *biàodào* (緥䙗), with the pronunciation *tì*.
*Xiù* (朽) means aged and decrepit; *mài* (邁) means distant. *Gěnggài* (梗槩): *gěng* (梗) is pronounced with the initial *kè* and final *xìng*;

King Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that *gěng* means "forceful," while the *Erya* states it means "straight. The *Guangya* states it means "brief" (*lüè*). It is composed of the radical *mu* (木) and the phonetic *hài* (該). *Gài* (槩) has the pronunciation *jié* (節); Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states it means "to measure. Xue Cong says that *gěnggài* does not mean "fine or detailed. It is composed of the radical *mu* (木) and the phonetic *jì* (既).

*Diao* (掉): "Xi" (戲) is pronounced with the initial *ting* and the final *yao*. According to the *Guoyu*, "diao" means to shake; according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "zhuo" (卓) in abbreviated form. "Xi" (下): pronounced with the initial *xi* and the final *yi*. The *Mao Shi* states that "xi" means leisure and indulgence (*yi-yu*). The *Erya* states that "xi" means jesting (*xu-e*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "spear" (戈) and the phonetic "qian" (䖒). "Qian" is pronounced *xi*; it is composed of "hu" (虍) and "dou" (豆). The received text uses "xu" (虛) and "go" (戈) to form "xi" (戱), which is incorrect. "Hu" (虍) is pronounced *hu*. *Note:* This passage provides a philological analysis of the characters for "diao-xi" (flapping/playful movement) and "xi" (jesting/leisure), citing various lexicographical sources to establish their etymologies and correct forms. It specifically critiques the variant character "xi" (戱) found in the canonical texts.

*Kài* (upper character pronounced *kǎi*, lower character pronounced *sòu*): according to the *Shuowen*, this is a vulgar form of the character meaning "reversal of qi" (*qì nì*). The correct form is *xiào* (𠿒), which is defined as the sound of qi surging up into the throat. Lexicons define it as a disease of phlegm in the chest; it is also written as *xiào* (𠿔) with the same meaning.
*Tan-yin* (痰癊): The first character is pronounced *tán*; the second is pronounced with the *yù* and *jìn* rhymes (*āng*). It refers to diseases of the chest and diaphragm.
*Kǎo-chǔ* (栲楚): The first character is pronounced *kǎo*. It means to beat or strike. *Jù-zhuó* (咀嚼):

The first character is pronounced *qíng* and *yǔ* rhymes. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means *zǔ* (to chew). The *Cāngjiépiān* says it means *jiào* (to gnaw), with the pronunciation *jiāo*. The *Shuōwén* says it means "to savor flavor," written with the mouth radical and the phonetic *qiě*. Another version uses the teeth radical to form *zhǔ* (齟). The second character is pronounced *qiáng* and *yào* rhymes. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means *rú* (to eat). Lexicons define it as *zǔ*. According to the commentary, *jué* (嚼) also means *niè* (to bite); it is written with the mouth radical and the phonetic *jué*.

The character *shī* (溼) is pronounced with the initial *xǐ* (尸) and the final *rù* (入) [as in *shīrù*]. It means "moist" (*shīrùn*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "dark dampness" (*yōushī*). It is composed of the radicals for water (*shuǐ*), old age (*sàn*), and earth (*tǔ*). The character is a semantic compound (*huìyì*) meaning that there is water beneath a covering of earth. The version in the *Jīngwén* (Classic Text) which uses the radicals for sun (*rì*) and silk (*sī*) to form *shī* (濕) is incorrect. The original sound of *shī* is *táhé* (他合); it is the name of a river located in Wuyang, Dongjun.

"Saliva" (xián) is a vulgar character; according to the *Shuowen*, it refers to the liquid of the mouth. Its correct form is written with the radical for water (氵) and the element for "to want" (欠), forming 㳄 (sì). The latter, "tǔhuò," refers to the moisture within the mouth.
*Ōu* (嘔逆): The character *ǒu* is pronounced with the *wū* and *kǒu* rhymes; the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to vomit. Its correct form is *ōu*.
It is a compound character (*huìyì*) composed of *huǒ* (fire) and *rén* (flesh), signifying flesh [rising] upon fire.

*Sù* (拳縮): Pronounced with the *shuāng* and *yún* rhymes. Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that it means "to retreat" or "to exhaust. Song Zhong’s commentary on the *Taixuanjing* says it means "to stop. The *Han Shi* says it means "to contract. It is a character formed from both semantic and phonetic components (*xíngshēng*).

*Fēng* (蜂) is a name for a type of insect; it forms a hive in trees or a nest in the earth and has many varieties. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that a flying insect that stings is written with the radical *fún* and the phonetic *féng*. It is also written as *fēng* (𧒒), while the scripture uses *fēng* (蜂), which is a vulgar form. *Tiánjié* (甜頰) is the pronunciation. Sima Biao’s commentary on the *Zhuangzi* identifies it as a *jiébó* (蛺蝶). The scripture uses *jiébó* (󲖪), which is a vulgar form.

"蚤蝨" (yǎo shī): The upper character is pronounced "lǎo fǎn" (the retroflex -r). The *Shuowen* defines it as "a jumping insect that bites humans," written with the radical "䖵" and the phonetic "叉" (chā; sound of zhuǎo). In the scriptures, it is written with "欠" (qiàn) as "𧈸" or "𧈸," which are abbreviated forms and do not constitute valid characters. The lower character is pronounced "suǒ yǐ fǎn. The *Shuowen* states it is "an insect that bites within clothing," written with the radicals "䖵" and "卂" (xìn; sound of xìn). In the scriptural texts, it is incorrectly written with "半" and "風" as "虱" (shī). This is erroneous.

The character for "maggot" (蛆) is read as *jū* (upper radical 7, remainder 余; alternatively formed from 肉 [flesh] with 䏣 as the phonetic). It is said to refer to maggots in putrid meat or in fermented sauces. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to insects that are the larvae of flies within meat, formed from 肉 with 且 as the phonetic. In the scriptures, it is written as 蛆 with the radical 虫; this is a vulgar form. The lower part is read as *zhúróng* (逐融); it is formed from three 虫 radicals. The *Erya* states: "Those with feet are called 'insects' (蟲)."

The character for "tortoise" (鼈) has "fish" (魚) as its radical; according to the *Shuowen*, it is formed from "knife" (刀) to represent its shape. Its tail resembles that of a swallow, which happens to resemble the character for "fire" (火), but it does not derive from "fire. The lower part is pronounced *bian* (鞭滅反); the *Kaoseng* says it is an aquatic creature. The *Shuowen* states it is an amphibious insect (*shui-jie-chong*) formed from "mǒng" (黽, pronounced *měng*) and "biè" (敝) as the phonetic. In the scriptures, the fish radical is used to form "tortoise" (鱉), but this is a vulgar character and incorrect. The pronunciation of "biè" is the same as above.

The character for *yuán* (黿) has the upper radical *yuán* (元); according to the *Shuowen*, it means "a large turtle" and is formed from *mǐn* (黽) with *yuán* as its phonetic. The lower part, *tuó* (鼉), has the reading *tú hé* (徒何反); according to the *Shuowen*, it is an aquatic insect resembling a lizard but larger, formed from *mǐn* (黽) with *hān* (𠹈) as its phonetic—the sound of *hān* being *nà* (那). According to the *Shuowen*, the character *hān* (𠹈) is composed of *kòu* (叩) and *lǐ* (里); the character in the scripture is written with *yī* (𠫹), which is incorrect. It is close to the sound of *měng* (黽). The common usage of the two characters *yuán* and *tuó* both employing the radical *mǐn* (黽) is erroneous.

*Zhì* (pronounced *zhàn* in the *Shān-hǎi-jīng*): The *Shān-hǎi-jīng* states that this is the *huá-yú* (slippery fish), shaped like an earthworm. Guō Jǐngchún’s commentary on the *Ěryǎ* states that the *shān-yú* resembles a snake and has spots; the *Shuowén* says it is a fish whose skin can be used to make drums. This is a phono-semantic compound character, the lower radical being *zhēn* with the tone *rì*. The *Ěryǎ* identifies it as the *zhì* (leech); Guō’s commentary notes that it is an aquatic leech-like insect that enters human flesh and drinks its blood.

Regarding the character *hé* (蛤): the first radical is pronounced *péng* (彭) with the *xiàng* (項) tone, and the second is pronounced *gān* (甘) with the *là* (臘) tone. The *Lüshi Chunqiu* states: "The clam (*bèng*) and the *hégǔ* (𧊧) are yin creatures. When the moon is at its fullness, the clams and *hégǔ* are full; when the moon is at its end, the clams and *hégǔ* are empty. This is a mutual resonance. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *hégǔ* (𧊧), and there are three types, all of which are born from the sea: the *lìhégǔ* (厲蛤) is transformed from a thousand-year-old sparrow; the Qin people call it the *mùlì* (牡厲); the *hǎihégǔ* (海蛤) is transformed from a hundred-year-old swallow; and the *kuíhégǔ* (魁蛤)—also known as the *fùluó* (復螺)—is transformed from an old *fùyì* (復翼). It follows the radical for insects and uses *hé* (合) as the phonetic component. The text here writes it as *hé* (蛤), which is the same.
*Xiā-má* (蝦蟇): The first character is pronounced *xiá*, the second *má*. *Hú-yě-gān* (狐野干): A type of wild jackal; according to the *Shuowen*, it is a "demon beast" ridden by ghosts.

The second character, *hégé* (何各), is explained in the *Shuowen* as being like a fox but smaller and fond of sleep. In the sutras, it is written as *mò* (狢) with the radical for "large. The *Shuowen*, the *Gujin Zhengzi Dian* (Dictionary of Ancient and Modern Correct Characters), and others all erroneously write it with the radical for "boat" (*zhōu*) as *hé* (貈) or *hè* (貈). The correct form uses the radical for "neck" (*kàng*), pronounced *gè dāng fǎn* (各當反); the *Kaosheng* (Examination of Sounds) also writes it as *hè* (貈), which serves as sufficient evidence. Sometimes it is also written as *mò* (貉), which is likewise acceptable.
"Diao-jiu" (雕鷲): the first character is pronounced "diao" (上音) and the second "jiu" (下音).

"Qie-lang" (𧏙蜋): the first character is pronounced with the "que" and "jiang" finals (却薑反) and the second "liang" (音良). According to the *Erya*, it is the "geng-qie" (蛣𧏙); Guo Pu says it is that which devours excrement. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "qie" (䖼) is a word formed from the shape and sound of the "lang" (蜋).

*Ròu* (flesh) is pronounced *péng-mào-fǎn*. *Hàn* (chin/jaw) is pronounced *chē-hé-làn-fǎn*; it refers to the jaw (*hàn*). The character used in the sutra is a vulgar form; the lower part is pronounced *chāng-chē-fǎn*. *Tǐ* (thigh) is pronounced *zú-tuì-nǎi-fǎn*; this is a vulgar form and not the correct one.

The correct orthography is written with the radical *gǔ* (bone) and the phonetic *shěng* (to examine), forming *tǐng* (thigh). It refers to the thigh or the hip. Lexicons identify it as the hip. The correct ancient and modern forms take the radical *gǔ* (bone) and the phonetic *tuǒ* (to settle); the pronunciation of *tuǒ* is the same as *tǐng*. The pronunciation of *nǎi* is *nú-huì-fǎn*. The *Shuōwén* omits this entry.

*Zhuì* (in *Gōu-zhuì*, pronounced *zhāng wèi fǎn*): Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states it means "to attach. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to join and adhere," following the radical *mì* (silk thread) with the phonetic *chùe*. The pronunciation of *mì* is *mì*, and the pronunciation of *chùe* is *zhū luò fǎn*.

The character 󲂬 (pronounced *chui*, with the variant *sui*) means "delicate" according to the *Guǎngyǎ*. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "small, soft, and easily broken. It is composed of the radical 肉 (flesh) and the phonetic component 絕 (abbreviated). Furthermore, the character 絕 itself is a semantic compound consisting of 糸 (silk), 刀 (knife), and 卩 (seal), with the pronunciation of 卩 being *jie*.

*Shāo* (無梢): [The character] *shāo* is pronounced with the *jiāo* (交) rhyme; it is derived from the radical "wood" (*mù*) or "hand" (*shǒu*), with *xiào* as the phonetic. It is the same as the character *yǔ* (與) on top of *chuán* (篅).

According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of *yú* (余) in the middle and *shíluán* (時攣) at the bottom; this is the vulgar form. The correct orthography is *chuí* (圌). Xu Shuchong’s commentary on the *Zhuangzi* states: "A *chuí* is a grain container. The *Jixun* (集訓) says: "It is a granary. The *Shuowen* explains: "A *chuí* is made by splitting bamboo into a circle to store grain."

Regarding "𪖦" (tòu): the upper character is *tì* (nasal mucus), though the scripture erroneously writes it as *tí*. Its original phonetic is *yí*, and it is not the character *tì*. The lower character is pronounced *tǔ huò* (referring to saliva); both have already been fully explained in the preceding fascicle.

*Qiáng* (強): The upper radical is *qú* (渠, with the *liáng* [良] tone). It is traditionally transmitted as being used interchangeably, though it is not the original character; the correct form is *qiàn* (弜), composed of two bows. Furthermore, the pronunciation is *qú* (渠, with the *liàng* [亮] tone), which is also consistent with the meaning. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "Strong means firm and exhortative transformation. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "Diligent. The *Cangjie pian* states: "Vigorous. The *Shifa* (Canon of Posthumous Titles) states: "To be broad and gentle yet respectful is called strong; not to retaliate against the unprincipled is called strong; to be harmonious without being swept away is called strong. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "A bow that possesses power. It is composed of 'insect' (*chóng*) and 'vast' (*hóng*); the lower part is pronounced *pán* (盤, with the *wèi* [未] tone). The *Zishu* states: "It refers to twisting with the hand; it also means to pull out. In the context of this scripture, it means to assist and to rescue and deliver. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of 'hand' (*shǒu*) and the phonetic element *bà* (犮, pronounced *pán* [盤], with the *wèi* [未] tone)."

"Sòng (森竦)": The upper character is pronounced *sè* (簪). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "the appearance of many trees growing tall," composed of the radical 木 and the element 林, with 林 also serving as the phonetic. It is sometimes written as 槮. The lower character is pronounced *yǒng* (粟勇). The *Kaosheng* states it means "to rise. In the *Zhuangzi*, it is used in the sense of "towering high. The *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of 立 and 束; it is a compound character (*huìyì zì*) meaning "to bind oneself from head to toe."

Regarding the character *jiè* (屆) with the upper radical *shàng* (上): it appears in the *Shàngshū* (Book of Documents) as "to arrive at. Zheng’s commentary on the *Máo Shī* (Mao Commentary on the Book of Poetry) states that *jiè* means "to halt" (*shè*). The *Shuōwén Jiězì* (Explaining Simple and Analyzing Compound Characters) says it means "inconvenience in walking" or "the extreme"; it is composed of the radical *hù* (戶) and the phonetic *yóu* (由).
*Stūpa* (the syllable *du* pronounced as *dǔ*; a Sanskrit term) refers to a reliquary brick stupa; it was formerly called "Futu," which is an abbreviated transliteration.
*Vārāṇasī* (the syllable *ni* pronounced as *nǎn xiá*; a Sanskrit name for a city) was formerly called "Bolanai," which is a corrupted and abbreviated form.

Volume Fifty-Eight. The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Fifty-Eight. Chapter Fifteen: The Prediction for Mañjuśrī. Part Three of the Three-Volume Edition. *Bibin* (from the radical for "silk" and "shell," with the phonetic *bin*; the sound is *bin*; followed by *fuwen* [the sound is *fu*], meaning the appearance of celestial flowers falling in profusion).

*Tián* (恬): Pronounced *kū* (reversed) according to the commentary on the *Shūjìng* by Kǒng [Yáng], it means "tranquil and at ease. According to the *Fānyǔ*, it means "serene. The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic element "tián" (abbreviated). The character below is pronounced *pú-bái*. According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, *pà* (怕) means "quiet"; the *Shuōwén* defines it as "non-action" (*wúwéi*), composed of the radical "heart" and the phonetic element "bái. *Niān* (拈) is pronounced *niàn-tián*.

Each person carried [the offerings]. (Jī: *jing* with the *xi* rhyme; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "to carry" or "to leave behind," composed of the radical 貝 [bao] and the phonetic 齊 [qi]. The text here uses 賫, which is a vulgar character resulting from corruption; it arose because the ancient form 齎 was altered into 賫.)

"Kun" (坤) and "wen" (穩) are reversed [in the following gloss]. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "The *kun* is the threshold of the gate. The *Shuowen Jiezi* contains the characters *que* (闕) and *kun* (閫), as well as *nie* (闑) and *xie* (榍). Although the object is one and the same, it has many names: *menyu* (門閾), *menyu* (門閾), *menxie* (門榍), and *menqi* (門砌) all refer to the threshold. It is colloquially called *menqi*; because stones were used to construct it, *qi* (砌) was adopted as the phonetic component, with the pronunciation *qie* (切). *Yu* (韋) is pronounced *bi* (逼); *nie* (闑) is pronounced *yu lie* (魚烈); *xie* (㨝) is pronounced *xian jie* (先結); and *wen* (穩) is pronounced *wen ben* (溫本).”

"Nuò" (倮) is a borrowed phonetic character; its original pronunciation is *lúguǒ*. Gu Yewáng states that it means "to strip off clothes and expose the shoulders. It is composed of the radical "person" (人) and the phonetic "guǒ" (果). The scriptural text writes it as 󱸝, or as 裸, or with the radical "body" (身) as 躶; all these refer to being naked.

*Gǔ* (pronounced with the initial *mōng* and final *-gēng*): The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that this refers to having no pupils in the eyes; it is composed of the radical "eye" (*mù*) and the abbreviated phonetic "wáng. The lower character is pronounced *gǔ*. The *Shuowen* further explains that when the eyes have only a slight glint (*zhì màn*) like the skin of a drum, one is called *gǔ*; it is composed of the radical "eye" and the phonetic "gǔ."

*Nǒngkuì* (聾聵): The first character is pronounced *lù* with the *dōng* rhyme; it means the ears have no hearing. It appears in the *Guìyuàn* (桂苑). The second character, *kuài*, is pronounced with the *wǎ* rhyme; it refers to an extreme deafness resulting from the impairment of sound. It is composed of the radical "ear" (*ěr*) and the phonetic element "abbreviated *guì*" (*guì*). The version of the text that uses the "eye" radical (*mù*) to form *kuì* (瞶) is incorrect.

"Pínjù" (貧窶): the first character is pronounced *jù* (with the initial being an aspirated palatal), as explained in the *Shuowen Jiezi*: "To be poor and lack the wealth to prepare for ritual ceremonies is called *jù*; it is written with a simplified form of *lǚ*. "Cuīguì" (摧過咎):

the second character is pronounced *qiú yǒu* (with the final being a rounded labial). The *Kaosheng* states: "Guì means sin, anger, or illness. This is an archaic form of the character *jiù* (咎); it is composed of *bǔ* (a divination board) and *kǒu* (mouth), with *jiǔ* (久) serving as the phonetic.

*Chéngsuì* (澄粹): Although the character *chéng* (澄) is read as *zuò* (酢) [in some contexts], the *Guǎngyá* states that *suì* (粹) means "pure. The *Zhouyī* says, "Pure and refined essence" (*chúnpǐ jīng*). Lexicons define it as "subtle and minute. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical *mǐ* (米) with the phonetic *zú* (卒). *Lán sì* (廛肆): The upper character *lán* (廛) is read as *chánglián* (長連).

The *Yùpiān* states it refers to empty space within a marketplace. The lower character *sì* (肆) has the sound *sì* (四). The commentary on the *Shàngshū* by Kǒng [Yǔ] says, "Sì means to display. Dǔ [Yǔ]’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* says, "Sì means to arrange. It refers to displaying goods in the market. Lexicons also state it can mean a dwelling or house. It is composed of the radical *cháng* (長) with the abbreviated form of *yù* (聿) as the phonetic.

Regarding "zhēnzuó" (斟酌): Jia Ji’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that "zhēn" means to take up and "zuó" means to carry out. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines "zuó" as a ladle (*sháo*), written with the radical "dǒu" and the phonetic "shèn. Regarding "jù" (據): It is pronounced *jū yù*. The *Kaosheng* states that "jù" means to rest secure and that which one relies upon.

The *Yunyi* says it means to press down; it is written with the radical "shǒu" and the phonetic "qū," pronounced *qú*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* further explains it is written with "hū" (pronounced *hū*) and "shǐ" (pronounced *jīng*). The current text uses "jù," which is a vulgar error. Furthermore, regarding the character for "bēi" (卑), it is composed of "jiǎ" and "zuǒ. The *Zitong* says that to call something "bēi" is to say it is "at the left," for the left side signifies inferiority. The character for "chuáng" (床) is composed of "mù" (wood) and "qiāng" (pronounced *qiáng*).

*Jiàn* (鑒): The upper radical is *gè* (革), pronounced *xiàn* (陷); the *Yùpiān* (玉篇) states it means "mirror," while the *Guǎngyá* (廣雅) states it means "to reflect. It is also written as *jiàn* (鑑). The lower radical is *chán* (廛), pronounced *liè* (列). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it means "to penetrate" (*tōng*). The *Shuōwén* (說文) explains it as being composed of *chì* (彳, pronounced *chǔ* or *chī*) and *yù* (育) with *zhī* (支) below; it is incorrect to include *qù* (去) or *yuè* (曰) in the composition.

*Kǐngkài* (謦欬): The first character is pronounced *qīngyǐng* (輕郢) and the second is *kāng'ài* (康愛). The second character (*kài*) refers to the passage of breath through the throat; it is the sound of coughing. *Jìhū* (暨乎): The first character is pronounced *jù yì* (渠義).
The *Yùnyīng* (韻英) states that *jì* means "to reach" (*zhì*) and also "to scold" (*hē*). It is composed of the radical *qiě* (且) with the phonetic *jì* (既).
"Xiǎn-bì" (險詖): The *Cāngjié piān* states it means "flattery"; the *Guǎngyá* states it means "cleverness"; the *Shuōwén* defines it as "discursive persuasion. "Xī-wàng" (悕望):

The upper character is "xī" (希), which the *Shuōwén* writes as "shē" (𭤔). The lower part is "gāng-fāng" (岡方) with the phonetic "fāng" (方). It is composed of "yuè" (月)—the pronunciation of which is "yuè"—and "rén-máng" (壬亾) as the phonetic component.

The character *kǒng* (恐) is composed of the radical "heart" (心) and the phonetic "gǒng" (𢀜). The character *gǒng* (𢀜) is composed of the radicals "jié" (丮) and "gōng" (工), with the pronunciation *jì* (戟). Its appearance in the *Jīng* (經) as *kǒng* (恐) is an error; the lower part should be read as *xiāng* (香) and *yè* (葉) combined. The *Shàngshū* (尚書) states that [the character] is formed from "gang" (冈). According to the *Guǎngyá* (廣雅), *kǒng* means "timidity. Gù Yěwáng (顧野王) says it means to intimidate by means of power and majesty. It correctly consists of three "forces" (力); its appearance in the *Jīng* as three "swords" (刀) is erroneous.

Volume Fifty-nine. *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Volume Fifty-nine. *Xiàn* (羨): In the *Hanshi* (韓詩), it means "to wish for. According to phonetic analysis, it signifies "love" or "longing. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "greed and desire," composed of the radical *měi* (美) with the phonetic *mí* (眉) and the suffix *sì* (㳄). *Sì* is pronounced *xī yán*. It refers to "saliva," composed of the radicals *shuǐ* (水) and *qiàn* (欠). The current vulgar usage, which employs the characters *yáng* (羊) and *cì* (次) to form *xiàn*, is incorrect.

The character 稸 (xù) is pronounced with the initial *chǒu* and the final *liù*. The *Kǎo Shēng* states that it means "to accumulate"; it is composed of the radical 禾 (grain) and the phonetic 畜 (chù). In the scriptures, there are instances where it is written simply as 畜 (pronounced xù, with the initial *xǔ* and final *liù*), which is also consistent with the meaning.

*Zhòngyán* (重檐): The rhyme is *dàn* (擔) reversed; the correct character for its meaning is "to lift. The *Shuowen* defines it as "to carry on the back," composed of the radical 手 (hand) and the phonetic 詹 (abbreviated).

It is also written as 󲒓. *Rúxī* (如犀): The pronunciation is *xī* (西); it is the name of a beast. The *Erya* states: "The rhinoceros resembles a pig. Guo Pu’s commentary says: "Its shape is like that of a water buffalo; it has the head of a pig, a large belly, short legs, and three hooves on each foot. It is black in color and has three horns—one on the crown of its head and one on its nose. The one on the nose is called the 'eating horn' (*shíjiǎo*), as it is fond of eating thorns. There are also those with only a single horn. The sutra uses this as a metaphor for the "single horn" (*yījiǎo*). The *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of the radical 牛 (ox) and the abbreviated form of 尾 (tail).

Regarding the character *língmèi* (淩懱): the upper radical *líng* (凌) is used here by extension; it originally denotes a river name and should properly be written with the radical for "force" (*li*) as *lì* (𠿒). The lower part is pronounced *miánjié* (眠結); its phonetic component is *qiāo* (考), and its sound is light and weak. It is formed from the heart radical (*xīn*) with the phonetic *miè* (蔑). It is incorrect for the canonical text to write this simply as *miè*. Furthermore, the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that the character *miè* (蔑) is composed of the radical *shù* (戍) with the phonetic *xiǎn* (𦭝); the pronunciation of *xiǎn* is also *miánjié*, identical to the above.

The character for "narrow" (陜) is composed of the radical 阜 (mountain/slope) and the phonetic 匧; the scriptural text uses 狹 (composed of 犬), which is not the original character. The preceding text has already fully explained that the pronunciation of 匧 is qián-yè.

60. Volume Sixty of the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Volume Sixty: "The One Beyond Sound and Definition. 61. Volume Sixty-one of the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Chapter Sixteen: "The Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Seeing Reality. Regarding the name Kālodāyin: according to the correct Sanskrit pronunciation it is *Kālodayin* (the old transcription being *Kālyodāyi*), which is the name of an Arhat.
"Qiānzǎi (千載): The character is *cái* (才), meaning 'to carry' (*zài* [載]). It has been altered in common usage to the character *zài* (在). Gàiguàn (溉灌):
The upper radical is pronounced *jī* (飢) and the lower is pronounced *huàn* (喚). Jìcì (棘刺): The upper radical is pronounced *jīnyì* (矜嶷).

According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of two *cì* (朿, sound *cì*) side by side. In the scriptures, it is erroneously written with two *shù* (束). The lower part is pronounced *cì*; according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *dāo* (刀) and *cì* (朿). In the scriptures, it is incorrectly written with *jiá* (夾). Zǎo (棗): Pronounced *zǎo*. It consists of two *cì* (朿). The vulgar form using two *cì* is incorrect."

*Ying* (膺): Pronounced *ping* (平) and *ni* (凝). The *Cangjie pian* states it is the bone above the two breasts. Wei Zhao of the *Hanshu* says that the area where the four sides of the chest rise up while the center is low is called *ying*. The *Shuowen jiezi* defines *ying* as the chest; it is composed of the radical "flesh" (*rou*) with the phonetic "geese" (*yan*), or alternatively written as *yin* (𩪠) using the radical "bone" (*gu*), which is an archaic form.

The character *xiān* (纖) is pronounced with the initial *chōu* (丑) and the final rhyme *lóng* (龍), with the tone being level (*shàng-shì-yǔ-xià-jūn*). It means "straight" (*zhí*). According to the *Shuowen*, "it means even and straight (*jūn-zhí*); it is composed of the radical 'person' (*rén*) and the phonetic 'yōng' (*yōng-shēng*). The character *jīng* (經) is written as *zhēng* (𦟛) using the radical 'moon' (*yuè*); this is a vulgar form. The lower part is pronounced with the initial *xián* (相) and the final rhyme *yán* (閻). The *Guǎngyá* states that *xiān* means "minute" (*wēi*); according to the *Shuowen*, it means "fine" (*xì*); it is composed of the radical 'silk thread' (*mì*) and the phonetic *xiān* (韱). Alternatively, it is written as *xiān* (孅) using the radical 'woman' (*nǚ*). The phonetic *xiān* (韱) has the pronunciation *jiān* (尖). The character *jīng* (經) [in the *Shuowen*] uses *jié* (截) [as its phonetic], which is incorrect.
"Lu" (鹿) is pronounced with the "ruan" (󰈷) radical and the final consonant "chang" (常); "piao" (漂) is pronounced with the final consonant "yao" (匹遙).

Regarding "jian" (劍) and "shao" (矟), the *Kaosheng* (考聲) states that a long spear is called a "shao. (Note: "Jian" means sword; here it likely refers to a specific type of weapon or is used in conjunction with "shao" to denote a particular armament.)
*Bì* (蔽): "Various low-lying plants. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means the appearance of small grasses; it is formed from the radical "grass" (艸) and the phonetic "bì" (敝).

*Yuán* (原): *xún* (尋) and *lì* (立) combined as a reversed reading. According to the *Erya*, "low and damp ground is called *xí* (隰)," referring to its marshy nature. It is also written as *zé* (漝), which is a vulgar character. The pronunciation of *jū* (󲇀) is *jù* (居).

*Ōng-yü* (蓊欝): The first character is pronounced *wǔ* (屋孔反) and the second is *yùn* (蘊律反); it is a vulgar form. The *Kǎo Shēng* states that "蓊欝" describes the lush appearance of flourishing vegetation.

*Bǎo* (寶): Pronounced *guā-měng* (瓜猛反). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhou Lǐ* says it refers to gold and jade not yet fashioned into vessels. The *Kǎo Shēng* also states it refers to the unworked ore of copper, iron, and so forth; it may also be written as *kuàng* (礦) or *huáng* (磺). According to the *Shuō Wén*, it is composed of the radical for "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic *xìng* (廾), where *xìng* has the same pronunciation as *shàng* (上).

The character *chóu* (綢) is pronounced with the final *-liú* (留) reversed; according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to entwine" (*chán*) or "to enclose" (*tāo*). Examining its phonetic component, *zhōu* (周), it signifies "to bind and constrain. It may also be written as the character for "rare" or "thick" (*chóu* 稠); this meaning is likewise applicable.
*Jing* (旌): "Above, it accumulates and fills" (*jīng*, with the phonetic *yíng* reversed); alternatively written as *jīn*. The commentary on the *Erya* states:

"That which has a *máo* [ox-tail] at its tip is called a *jing*. Guo Pu says: "One places a *máo* at the top of the pole. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* says: "The *jing* is a symbol of distinction.

Jia Gongyan’s commentary on the *Guoyu* says: "The *jing* is a mark of honor. Gu Yewang says: "In general, a *máo* is the tail of a *máo* ox; it is applied to the tip of a banner or flag, as is done today."
*Fei yemáo*: The character *máo* (旄) is pronounced as *máo*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to a banner carried on a traveling chariot (*youche*) used to inspire the soldiers to advance.
It is composed of the radical *yǒng* (從) and the phonetic *shēng* (生). *Xià yīn gǔ*: The character *gǔ* (鼓) is pronounced as *gǔ*. It is the instrument used to alert the multitude.
According to the *Zhouli* (Rites of Zhou), there are six types of drums: the *léi*, the *líng*, the *lù*, the *fén* (扶文), the *gāo* (公刀), and the *zhòu* (𨑲刃).
The *I Ching* states: "To drum is to stir; it is the sound of *Zhen*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Yili* says: "It means to strike. The *Baihutong* states: "The drum is the qi of *Kan*.
According to the *Shuowen*, "drum" (*gu*) means an enclosure; it is composed of the radical *zhu* (bamboo hook) and the phonetic *zhi*.
The scriptural text uses the character *gu* with the radical *pi* (skin), which is a vulgar form and incorrect.

The character *yì* (悒) in *yìqì* (悒慼) has the phonetic *lì* as its initial. The *Cāngjié piān* states that it describes the appearance of being "oppressed and unable to relax. The *Shuowén* defines it as "insecurity"; it is a compound character formed from a semantic and a phonetic element. The character *qǐng* (請) serves as its phonetic, or it may be written as *qì* (慽). Hé Xiū’s commentary on the *Gōngyáng zhuan* says it means "pain"; Zhèng’s commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* says it means "much anxiety and fear. The *Shuowén* further explains that *qì* (慽) is a synonym for anxiety and fear. Furthermore, regarding the character *qī* (戚), it is derived from *wù* (戊) with the phonetic *qiū* (尗); *qiū* is pronounced *qiān yuè*. *Qiū* (尗) is pronounced *qiān*. (Note: The character *qiū* [豆] is rendered here as 󱮫 to match the source's transcription.)

In the original texts of the *Svayaṃ-snāna-paras-snāna-sūtra*, the term is mostly written as "yùchí" (浴池, bathing pool), which is incorrect; it is a scribal error. The character "tā" (他, other) is the correct reading.

Regarding "xiàn jīn" (綫金): the former is pronounced jiān (先箭反); sometimes it is written as "xiàn" (線). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, this means "thread" (縷), composed of the radical "silk" (糸) with the phonetic "zan" (戔); the vulgar form "yán" (綖) is incorrect.

62. Fascicle Sixty-two of the *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra*. "Tián (Sweet)": The character "tián" is pronounced with the initial *dian* (亭閻反) and the final rhyme *kao* (考), signifying "sweet. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "beautiful. It is a compound character formed by combining "tongue" (舌) and "sweetness" (甘). It is also written as "tián" (甜), which is the same character. The lower part, "méi" (眉), is pronounced with the initial *bi* (鄙) and the final rhyme *pi* (鄙). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it signifies "the taste of sweetness. It is composed of "sheep" (羊) and "great" (大). Within the phonetic system, "sheep" (羊) refers to the great sweetness provided for the kitchen and meals; therefore, it is a compound character formed by combining "sheep" (羊) and "great" (大). Thus, it is merely a compound character formed by combining these two meanings.

Regarding the character for *ān* (鞍) in the word *ān-zhàn* (鞍韉): it is also written as *án* (鞌). The lower part is formed by reversing the character *jiǎn* (剪). The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *fēn* (𦆉). *Ān* (鞍) refers to a saddle-cloth (*tiān*). Regarding *qiū* (鞦) and *pèi* (轡): *qī* (七) and *yóu* (遊) are the phonetic components; it refers to the horse's bit or traces.

It is also written as *zhuì* (䋺) or *jiū* (鞧), all of which refer to the same thing. The lower part of *pèi* (轡) is *bēimèi* (悲媚); it refers to the horse's bridle. It is composed of the radical "silk" (糸) and the character *zhuān* (叀), where *zhuān* is pronounced *huì*. In the scriptures, it is sometimes written with the "chariot" (車) radical and the "mouth" (口) radical as *pèi* (轡), which is a vulgar form.

*Xié* (鞾) [homophone of *huī jiā*]: *Yùnquán* states it is a boot with a collar; dictionaries state it is a *hújiè*. *Jiè* is pronounced *qiāng jiāo*. Examining the phonology, its correct form is *xié* (㞜); the form in the scriptures is *lèi* (𩋖). Both *xié* (靴) and *xiē* (靴) are vulgar characters. Below, *máo* (毛) is pronounced *bào*; alternatively written as *mò* (󲴤). Examining the phonology, it is a head-garment. The *Shuowén* states it is a head-garment for infants and barbarians. Its original form is *mào* (冒); in modern clerical script (*lìshū*), it takes *jīn* (巾) as the radical and *mào* as the phonetic.

The "Divine Tortoise" (Shenguī) is ashamed of its reversal in the waters; "jiè" (介) refers to a shell. In the *Rites of Zhou* there are six types of tortoises, and in the *Erya* there are ten; this is the first of them, the Divine Tortoise. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it has an outer shell and inner flesh, and the character is formed from the pictograph of a "tuó" (鼉, a crocodile-like creature). The characters for "táo" (黿, a large turtle), "bié" (鼈, a soft-shelled turtle), and "měng" (黽, a toad) all derive from "tuó."

"Jiù" (舊) is pronounced "bié" (卑滅反), the name of an aquatic creature. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "mǐng" (黽) with the phonetic "bì" (敝). In the scriptures, it is often written with the "yú" (魚) radical or the "mǐng" (黽) radical as "bié" or "biè"; both of these are incorrect.

*Jìzōng* (髻鬉): The upper character is pronounced *jì* (計) or *jié* (結). Zheng Xuan says it means "bound hair. In the current scriptural text, it refers to the tied-up mane and tail of a horse. The lower character is pronounced *zōng* (宗). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it refers to the horse's *lì* (巤); it is also written as *lì* (巤) or *dà* (𩭤), with the pronunciation *liè* (獵).

Regarding "liūsū" (旒蘇): the upper character "liú" (旒) is pronounced according to the *Kǎośēng* as "liú," meaning the streamers at the corners of a banner; it is now used for the hanging pearl-strings and ribbons that imitate the "liú" (pendants) of a ceremonial cap. In ancient script, it was written as "lǚ" (㐬), a pictographic character.

*Caichu* (硨磲): the first character is pronounced *che* (upper tone) and the second is pronounced *qu* (lower tone). According to the *Guangya*, *caichu* is a stone treasure that ranks just below jade.

*Shengfa-zhi-dai* (盛髮之帒): the character *dai* (帒) is pronounced *daokao* (大考); it means a bag for holding hair, derived from the radical "cloth" (*jin*) and written as *dai* (袋), which is a vulgar form of the character.

*Menkǔn* (門閫): *Kǔn* is pronounced as *běn fǎn* (本反). Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states that *kǔn* refers to the threshold of a door. In the *Shuowen*, it is written with the radical for wood (*mù*) and the phonetic *yíng* (𠪱), forming a compound character based on shape and sound.

*Ménchū* (門樞): *Chū* is pronounced as *zhū fǎn* (朱反). The *Kaosheng* states it is the place where the door leaf rotates. It is now colloquially called the "door elbow" (*ménzhǒu*) or the "rotating elbow" (*zhuǎnzhǒu*). The old glosses claim it refers to the "door socket" (*ménjiù*), but this is likely incorrect. The *Guangya* states that *chū* is the base [of the door]. In the *Han Shi*, it says: "The pivot (*chū*) and mechanism (*jī*) are the masters that control motion. It is formed with the radical for wood and the phonetic *qū* (區).

*Luǒgǒng* (櫨栱): The character *luǒ* (櫨) is pronounced with the *dū* rhyme (as in *lǔdū*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to the *bóluǒ* (薄櫨), the wooden block atop a column; the *Cangjie Pian* states it is the wood placed upon a column. The character *gǒng* (栱) is pronounced with the *yōng* rhyme (as in *gōngyōng*); it refers to the curved wood on top of a column that supports the *dǒu* (斗). It is so named because its shape resembles a person’s arm (*gǒng*). In common parlance, it is sometimes pronounced with the departing tone.

Regarding the phrase "the yellow-handled weapon was ordered to return to Zheng," the *Zhouli* commentary states: "The handle (*bìng*) is that by which one grasps. Jia Gui says: "Handle means power (*quán*). The *Shuowen* says: "Handle is the branch. The *Cangjie pian* says: "Handle is *niào*. The *Guangya* says: "Handle is a pillar. It is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "bǐng"; *niào* is pronounced *chìlì*. *Note: The term *niào* (尿) appears to be a scribal error or archaic variant for *bìng* (柄) in this context; it is likely intended as a gloss or a specific regional reading.*

*Dòu-tīng* (奪聽): The first character is pronounced *tú-huó* (徒活) and the second is *tǐ-tíng* (體廷). It means to examine sounds and hear with the ears; according to the *Shuowen*, it means to listen (*líng*). It is composed of the radical "virtue" (*dé*) and the phonetic "obtain" (*dé*), with "rén" (*rén*) as the phonetic component. The pronunciation of "rén" is *tiān-yǐng* (天郢).

*Dāng* (the upper tone) means "ear-ornament" (*dāngkě*). The *Shìmíng* states: "To pierce the ear and apply a bead is called a *dāng*. *Qū* (the lower tone) means "ear-ornament. The *Kǎoshēng* states: "A *qū* is like a wheel. According to this, the ear-ornament resembles a wheel; the kings and nobles of the Western Regions all fashion ear-ornaments from gold, silver, and exquisite jewels to wear in their pierced ears, resembling precious wheels with various gems set between them for adornment. The scriptural text uses *qū*, which is a borrowed character.

*Bāzhī* (跋墀): The first character is pronounced *pú* (with the tone reversed) and the second is pronounced *chí*. Formerly it was transcribed as *Pózhì* (婆雉), which is all a corruption and abbreviation of the Sanskrit term that does not approximate the original sound. This is the name of an Asura king. The correct Sanskrit pronunciation is *Vālin* (*vā* is pronounced with a non-cut [unaspirated] *a*; *li* is pronounced *ní-lǐ*). Since there is no direct equivalent in Chinese, the Sanskrit term is retained. The old translation calls him "Bound" (*Bó*, 縛). He constantly dwells at the head of the Asura armies; because he was defeated in battle and bound by Śakra, yet escaped through his vow, he was given this name.

*Chí-chú* (踟蹰): The first character is pronounced *zhǐ* (上) with the *zhì* (雉) rhyme; the second is pronounced *chú* (下) with the *zhū* (誅) rhyme. The *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲) states that *chí-chú* is synonymous with *páihuái* (俳佪). It is also written as *chóu-chú* (躊躇); the first character has the sound *chóu* (音籌) and the second has the sound *chú* (音除). The *Guǎng Yǎ* (廣雅) states that *chóu-chú* means hesitation (*yòu-yù*). The *Kǎo Shēng* states that *chóu-chú* refers to not proceeding immediately. The *Máo Shī Zhuàn* (毛詩傳) states that *chóu-chú* is synonymous with *zhí-zhù* (躑䠱). Although *chí-chú* and *chóu-chú* differ in their tonal weight according to the *Fān Yǔ* (方言), their meaning—having a mind that is doubtful and undecided—is one and the same. Both characters are formed from the radical "foot" (*zú*) and are phonetic-semantic compounds.

Volume Sixty-Three. The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Sixty-Three. *Samāpatti* is a Sanskrit term; in Chinese it is translated as "Excellent Concentration" (*shàn dìng*) or "Sublime Concentration" (*miào dìng*). It is also transcribed as *samāpatti* or *samāpata*, both of which are corruptions of the Sanskrit term.

The character for *suì* (睡) is composed of the radical *mián* (宀) and the phonetic *lèi* (累). The *Cāngjié piān* states it means "desiring to lie down"; the *Shuōwén* defines it as "sitting while asleep. It is a compound character formed from a semantic and a phonetic element; *lèi* is pronounced like *lèi* (類). The character for *wù* (寤) is pronounced like *wù* (悟). The *Máoshī zhuan* states that *wù* means "to awaken" (*jue*). In the *Shuōwén*, it is defined as "when one awakens from sleep and speaks, it is called *wù*"; it is formed with the radical *mèng* (㝱) and the phonetic *wǔ* (吾) in abbreviated form. It may also be written as *hài* (害), which is a simplification. The scriptural variant with the radicals *xué* (穴) and *xīn* (心) forming *qín* (寑) is incorrect. The correct orthography consists of the radical *mián* (宀) and the element *qiáng* (爿).
*Yàn* (pronounced *yī yán fǎn*, sometimes written as *yàn*);
*gōu lán* (upper character pronounced *gǔ hóu fǎn*, lower character pronounced *lán*; also called *lán shǔn*, with *shǔn* pronounced *shùn*).

Regarding *xún liáng* (upper character pronounced *xiáng yín fǎn*, already fully explained in the preceding text; lower character pronounced *lì qiáng fǎn*): "cross-beam" (*xún liáng*) refers to the cross-bars of a railing (*gōu lán*) today. The upper character for "cross-beam" (*xún*) is the wooden staff. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the character *liáng* (beam) consists of the radicals for water (*shui*), field (*tian*), and wood (*mu*); its ancient form consisted of water, root (*ben*), and wood. The version in the sutra with the radical for ice (*bing*) is incorrect.

"Curved lattice" (*qūlíng*) refers to the balustrades of a pavilion. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "shǔn" (balustrade) refers to the railing itself, while "líng" (lattice) refers to the cross-bars between the balusters; in common parlance, these are collectively called "gōulán" (hooked railings). "Agate" (*mǎnǎo*):

the first character is pronounced as "mǎ" (horse), and the second as "nǎo" (distress); it is the most exquisite of stone treasures, second only to jade. It may have variegated patterns and belongs to the same category as jade. This is a word formed by combining its shape and sound.

*Caṅkha* (pronounced *chē* for the first character and *qú* for the second) is a precious stone of a brilliant white color, second only to white jade; it is a word formed from its appearance and sound. *Airāvaṇa* (the first character is pronounced *yīngxī* as a reversed reading;

the classics erroneously write it as *shěn*): this is the name of the king of white elephants in the Sanskrit language. He is constantly ridden by Śakra, the Lord of Devas; he is fully endowed with divine knowledge, understands the capacities of beings, and is skilled at manifesting transformations in accordance with the will of the Heavenly Lord.

*Jiāng* (pronounced *jiān* with the *liáng* rhyme) is defined in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as "the tether for a horse," written with the radical *mì* (silk thread) and the phonetic *jiāng*. It may also be written with the radical *gé* (metal/leather) as *jiāng*, which is likewise correct. The character *xiè* (tether) has the pronunciation *sīliè* (with the second tone on the final syllable), while the following character [in the compound] has the pronunciation *kǔgòng*. The *Pīcāng* states it is "the bridle of a horse."

The character 鶬 (cāng) is pronounced gāng (with the initial reversed). Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "It is the *chuànggài* (pronounced guà); the *Shēnglèi* writes it as 𩀞. The lower radical is pronounced hónggǔ. It is also called the *huánggù* (yellow crane), with joined wings that can travel a thousand li in a single flight. Some say it is the *hónggù* (red crane), commonly known as the *hóng hè*. These are all characters formed from both shape and sound.

Volume Sixty-Four. The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Sixty-Four. *Chuán* (椽): A roof rafter; according to the *Shuowen*, it refers to a *chuí* (榱). In the state of Qin it was called *chuán*; in the states of Zhou it was called *chuí*; in the states of Qi and Lu it was called *jué* (桷). It is composed of the radical "wood" and the phonetic "lǐ" (𮕱). It is also written as *quán* (槫). *Lǐ* (𮕱) is pronounced *chí-liàn* (池戀); *chuí* (榱) is pronounced *chuí* (𮕱); *jué* (桷) is pronounced *jué* (角).

*Pañcūṣṇīṣa* is the name of a precious stone found among the Trāyastriṃśa gods. This stone is soft, lustrous, exquisite, and majestic; it is a supreme jewel of the celestial palaces. The pronunciation of *jiān* (緘) is *jiān* with the second tone (咸反).

"㓷" (ěr) is pronounced as "yì" (冀) according to the *Shūjì* (尚書記). The commentary on the *Shūjì* by Kǒng [Yǎng] states that "㓷" means "to cut. The commentary on the *Zhōuwǔlǐ* by Zhèng [Xù] states that it means "to sever the nose. It is also written as "劓" (yì), which has the same meaning. It is composed of the radical "knife" (刀) and the phonetic "niè" (臬); "niè" is pronounced as "yú liè" (魚列). Regarding the character 𢤱 (pronounced lù, with the initial *l* and rhyme *dǒng*; it does not appear in any standard dictionaries as being composed of the radical "person" [亻]), it was likely created by the translator according to his own judgment and has been passed down as a phonetic transcription.
