Both versions [of the dictionary] take it as being composed of the radical "mind," whereas its appearance in this sūtra as being composed of the radical "person" is incorrect.

*Kuìzhōn* (憒𠆴): The upper character is *hù* (戶) with the variant *gǔ* (古); the lower character is *wài* (外) with the variant *guǎi* (古外), second tone; the phonetic is *ná* (拏), second tone. It is composed of the radicals for "market" (*shì*) and "person" (*rén*). The *Jīng* (經) [scripture] version writes it as *zhuì* (𡗚), which does not form a valid character.

*Xūfà* (鬚髮): The upper character is pronounced *xū* (須). This is a vulgar character; the original character is simply written as *xū* (須). According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of *yè* (頁)—meaning "head"—and *shān* (衫); *shān* is the phonetic, meaning "a mass of hair. In common usage, the character *xū* (須) is used, but this is incorrect. *Xū* (湏) is actually the archaic form of the character *huǐ* (󲏥), pronounced *huǐ* (悔). Gu Yǎowáng says it means "hair on the head. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means "the root of the hair," composed of *biāo* (髟) and the phonetic *bá* (犮). The archaic form is written as *pōyè* (頗頁). *Yè* (頁) is pronounced *jié* (頡); *bá* (犮) is pronounced *pómò* (蒲末); *biāo* (髟) is pronounced *bìyáo* (必遙).
*Jiè*: the first character is pronounced *jì* (with the initial *qí*) and the second is pronounced *fèi* (with the initial *wēi*).

*Tíqì*: the first character is pronounced *dì* (with the initial *ní*); it is a vulgar form; the correct form is *tí*. The *Yùpiān* states: "To weep without regular intervals. It is also written as *huò zuò huò* (or written as *huò*). The *Shuōwén* says: "To cry out (*hào*); it is composed of the radical 口 (mouth) and the phonetic 虒; the sound of 虒 is *tī*."

Volume Seventy-nine. *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Volume Seventy-nine. Regarding "Merchant" (Jià): the upper tone is *gǔ*. The commentary on the *Zuòzhuàn* states that "jià" means to sell. Zhèng Xuán says it means to reside in selling. The *Zìshū* states that sitting to trade is called *jǐ*; those who pronounce it as *jiǎ* are incorrect.

*Āi* (pronounced *yīng jiè fǎn*). According to the *Guǎng yá*, it means narrow and constricted, as well as urgent. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states it means "mean" (*lòu*). It is composed of the radical *fù* (mountain) with the phonetic *yì*. It is also written as *ài*. Dú Yù says it refers to terrain that is rugged and uneven. It is composed of the radical *é* (cliff) with the phonetic *è*. The pronunciation of *è* is *é*.

The term *chán* (纏) means to wrap around; the phonetic transcription of its sound is *cháo* (繞), meaning to encircle or to bind. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means to contract; it is composed of the radical *mì* (糸, silk thread) with the phonetic *zhān* (廛). The lower part is pronounced *guǒ*. Gu Yewang states that *guǒ* (裹) is synonymous with *bāo* (苞, to envelop). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means to wind around; it is composed of the character *yī* (衣, clothing) above and below, with *guǒ* (果) in the middle as the phonetic.

The upper character [of 瘡] is pronounced *chǔ* (with the *shuāng* rhyme); the *Kǎo Shēng* states it means "to form a sore. The *Shuōwén* records it as written with the character 刃 (*rèn*), which is an archaic form; it is also written as 創 (*chuàng*). The lower character [of 痕] is pronounced *bá* (with the *qiū* rhyme); the *Kǎo Shēng* states it means "a scar. It is composed of the radical 疒 (*nà*, pronounced *nǚ è*) and the phonetic 槃 (*pán*, pronounced *mò ān*). The sound of 瞞 is *mò ān*.

*Jiànshǎo* (箭矟): "shǎo" is pronounced with the *chuǎn* (反) tone. *Kiàntuó-dáduō* (蹇陁達多) is the Sanskrit name for Devadatta; it is the name of the five hundred bhikṣus who were his followers. Volume 80, The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra (*Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra*), Volume 80, The Eighteenth Assembly:

The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Rāṣṭrapāla. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuánzàng. *Yōng* (傭): Pronounced with the *chǒu* (丑) tone. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that it means "even from top to bottom. The *Yùnyīng* (韻英) states it means "straight. It is composed of the radical "person" (*rén*) and the phonetic "yōng" (*yōng*). The version of the sutra using the "moon" radical (*yuè*) is incorrect. *Xījiān* (息尖): Pronounced with the *xiān* (尖) tone. It means "subtle and fine."
*Henli* (佷戾): The first character is pronounced *hen* (恨);

the second is pronounced *li* (禮) with the phonetic *ji* (計). *Binchu* (擯出): Pronounced *bi yin* (必胤). Zhuang Zhou stated that it means "to cast aside," "to discard," or "to expel. It is formed with the radical "hand" (*shou*) and the phonetic "bin" (*bin*). It is incorrect for the scripture to use the character "ren" (*ren*, person) instead; the meaning and the explanation do not correspond, and it is a mistaken usage.

"Jùkǔ (劇苦): The character *qú* (渠) has the phonetic inversion *fǎn* (反). It is not pronounced *cāng* (倉) or *dān* (單); the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) says it means "to chew" (*chàn* [噉]), and the *Shuōwén* (說文) says it means "to swallow. It is composed of the radical 食 with the phonetic *zǎo* (𣦼), or sometimes written with the water radical as *cān* (湌). The version in the *Jīng* (經) uses the ice radical [冫], which is incorrect. The pronunciation of *zǎo* (𣦼) is *cán* (殘)."*

*Fénliào* (焚燎): "Liao" is pronounced *yào* (曜). The *Yùnyīng* states it means "to illuminate the world. The *Shuowén* says it means "to set fire to," composed of the radical "fire" (*huǒ*) and the phonetic "láo" (*lǎo*).

*Wàngmù* (王募): "Mù" is pronounced *mó* (模). The *Yùnyīng* states it means "to summon. The *Kǎoshēng* says it means "to seek extensively," composed of the radical "force" (*lì*) and the phonetic "mò" (*mò*).

"Chījiāo" (黐膠) is pronounced with the initial *chí* and the final *zhǐ* (知反); the commentary states it means "sticky. It is made by pounding the bark of trees and can be used to catch birds and beasts; it takes the phonetic element *lí* (离) from *shǔlí* (黍离). The character *lí* has the pronunciation *chī*; its appearance in the Classics as *lí* is an error.

Gāo (High): The radical is "mountain" (山) and the phonetic is "ya" (牙). The commentary states it refers to steep and dangerous cliffs on the edge of mountain torrents. The pronunciation of "yá" (崖) is the same as above. 81. Volume Eighty-One, *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Chapter Eighty-One:

The Assembly of the Bodhisattva Rāṣṭrapāla. Wújiǎo (No-horn): The character is composed of "gān" (甘), "ròu" (肉), and "quán" (犬). It is a compound character formed by combining these semantic elements; it means a dog eating sweet meat. The initial "ī" (伊) is pronounced with the retroflex "yan" (鹽) rhyme. The character is formed with "gān" (甘) and "ròu" (肉) as the semantic components and "quán" (犬) as the determinative.

"Xi-bi" (繫閉): Ji (鷄) is pronounced as yi (詣). Wang Yewang states it means "to bind and restrain" or "to detain. Zheng Xuan says it means "to connect and tie. It is composed of the radical "silk" (糸) with "cai" (𣪠) abbreviated as the phonetic component. In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the character "bi" (閉) is written with the "hand" radical (扌); the form in the current text with the "bottom" radical (下) is a vulgar variant.

The upper character *láo* (牢) is pronounced as in "labor. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "A pen for confining and raising oxen and sheep; it is composed of the radical 'ox' (牛) and a simplified form of 'boat' (舟), where the boat signifies being enclosed on all four sides. Its vulgar usage with the radical 'cave' (穴) is incorrect. The lower character is read as *yù* (獄). Gu Yewang says: "It refers to mutual contention and litigation; because it is the place where those are imprisoned and bound, it is named 'jù' (獄). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "Contention over wealth is called *sòng* (訟); contention over guilt is called *yù* (獄). The *Shuowen* [further] explains it as composed of the character *lín* (犾, pronounced yín), which consists of two dogs, signifying those that bark to guard [the enclosure]. It is a compound character formed through associative meaning (*huìyì*).

"Dùjí" (妬嫉): the first character is pronounced with the *dù* (都) and *gù* (固) finals; the second is pronounced with the *qín* (秦) and *lì* (栗) finals. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states: "To harm the worthy is called *jí* (嫉); to harm [another's] beauty is called *dù* (妒). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *dù* (妒) means "a wife being jealous of her husband"; it is composed of the radical *nǚ* (女) and the phonetic *hù* (戶). Those who commonly write it with *hòu* (后) or *shí* (石) are incorrect. *Jí* (嫉) is likewise a compound character formed by semantic and phonetic elements.
*Běi* (cup/vessel): *pèi* (to pair) with the reversed radical; the phonetic gloss says it is an unbaked earthenware vessel, though some write it as *zhēn*.

*Xīxì* (play/pleasure): The first character, *xī*, has the phonetic *xū jǐ*; the *Cāngjié piān* states it means "jesting. The second character, *xì*, has the phonetic *xǐ yì*; the *Máoshī chuán* says "play" means "leisurely ease. The *Erya* calls it "jesting" (*xuè*). Guō Pǔ says it is "chirping. The *Shuowén* states it is composed of the radical *gē* (spear) and the phonetic *qiàn*; the character *qiàn* is written with the radical *dòu* (bean) and pronounced *xū*, with the phonetic *yí*. The classics use the form with the radical *xū* and the phonetic *yì* (written as *xì*), which is incorrect.

The character for *chuáng* (bed) is pronounced with the initial *zhuāng* (㽵) and the final *fū* (夫). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of "wood" (木) and "tablet" (爿); in the sutras it is written as *chuáng* (床), which does not form a valid character. The character for *fù* (to spread) is pronounced with the initial *fāng* (芳) and the final *fū* (夫). It means to spread or to lay out. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of "hand" (攴, pronounced *pǔbǔ*) and "broad" (尃, pronounced *fǔ*). The character *fǔ* (尃) itself is composed of "beginning" (甫) and "inch" (寸). When the sutras write it with "beginning" (甫) and the sound *zhuān* (專), or with "ten thousand" (万) below, these are all vulgar forms and not the correct orthography.

Regarding "zhān" (felt mat): the first character is pronounced *rán* (with the tone reversed) and the second is pronounced *rù*. The *Kǎośēng* states that felt (*zhān*) is made by pounding animal hair; when it is covered with silk and colored cloth, it is called a "mattress" (*rù*).

Regarding "liǎn" (palanquin/litter): the first character is pronounced *lián* (with the tone reversed). The *Kǎośēng* states that a vehicle carried by men is called a "liǎn," which is a palanquin. The *Shuōwén* states that a "liǎn" is a carriage pulled by men, following the "chē" radical with the "bàn" radical (pronounced *bàn*) before the carriage, meaning it is drawn in front of the carriage. The second character is pronounced *shǔ* (with the tone reversed), or alternatively *yú*. According to the *Shuōwén*, a "yù" is a vehicle carried by people while walking, following the "chē" radical with the abbreviated "yǔ" as its phonetic component. It has both level and departing tones and is used interchangeably.

The character 𩓣 (xū) is used in the sense of "to wait. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical 立 (standing) and the phonetic 彡 (pronounced shān), with the head radical 頁 (yè). In current editions of the scriptures, this is frequently written as 須 (xū) with the radical 水 (water); however, this is incorrect. That [character 須] is a name for a river and is not the character 𩓣.

The character 鸚 (yīng) is composed of the upper radical 鳥 (niǎo), pronounced gēng (as in "to plow"), and the lower phonetic 武 (wǔ). It refers to a green bird. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Shanhai jing* states that outside of Funan there are five-colored *yīngwǔ* birds, as well as those that are pure white; they are as large as hawks and have four toes, two on each foot, and are able to mimic human speech. The *Qu lǐ* says, "The *yīngwǔ* can speak, yet it does not depart from the category of flying birds. This is a form-and-sound character (*xíngshēng zì*). The phonetic component 武 (wǔ) provides the sound, while 嬰 (yīng) is formed from two 貝 (bèi) characters.

The *qúyù* (鸜鵒) is composed of the upper radical *jù* (具, with the phonetic *jù*)—which may also be written as *qù* (鴝)—and the lower character *yù* (欲). This bird resembles the *bǎishé* (百舌, starling) in shape, but is black in color; only its two wings have white spots, and there is a tuft of hair-like filaments above its silver-colored beak, which distinguishes it. The *Yìyuàn* (異苑) states: "If one cuts the tongue of a *qúyù* on the fifth day of the fifth month, it can then learn to speak like a human. The *Huáinánzǐ* says: "The *qúyù* is also called *hánbí* (寒鼻). Both are *xiángxīng* (形聲, phono-semantic) characters according to the *Shuōwén*. It is further said that the *qúyù* does not cross the Jǐ River.

"Hóng hè" (Hóng and hè): the upper tone for "hóng" is "hóng," referring to the *suíyáng* bird. The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* states that the larger are called *hóng* and the smaller are called *yàn*; both are waterfowl belonging to the genus of geese. The lower character, "hé," is pronounced "gè. The white crane (*bái hè*) is an auspicious bird ridden by immortals; its lifespan reaches a thousand years. There is also the red crane (*hóng hè*), which is an ordinary bird found everywhere. The *cānghóng* crane—also known as the *hóng hú*—is shaped like a crane but smaller; it is also a waterfowl.
*Ku-lie-lo* (formerly transcribed as *Ku-ji-lo*): This is the name of a bird in the Western regions according to the Sanskrit language;

it does not exist in this country. *Chao-chui* (the first character pronounced with the initial *qíng* and final *yáo*; the second character with the initial *qíng* and final *suì*): Also written as *chao-zui*, it means emaciated and wretched.

*Chàng* (悵): The *Cāngjié piān* states that it means "to be despondent and lose one's will. The *Shuowén* states that *chàng* is synonymous with *chàngwàng* (to look longingly toward something). *Xià* (下): *yāngliàng* (殃亮) rhyme. *Qiáng* (悏): The *Guǎngyá* states it means "strong"; the *Shuowén* states it means "discontented. Both are phono-semantic compounds (*xíngshēng zì*).
The leather bag is called *nǎoláng* (囊郎); the phonetic transcription says it is a "sack. Regarding the sinews and bones:

the upper character is *jīn* (筋), composed of the radical for bamboo, the radical for flesh, and the radical for strength. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it refers to the strength of the flesh. There is also a variant composed of the radical for grass and the radical for moon, which is incorrect.

*Jùn* (浚): Pronounced *xún* (反). The *Kǎoshēng* states it means a rapid current of water. It is also written as *yún* (𤀹); the lower character for "current" (*liú*) is composed of *shuǐ* (water), *yún* (cloud), and *mí* (󲆮).

*Niào* (㵱) and *lù* (𣴬): The upper character is pronounced *pǐ yáo* (匹遙). The *Shuōwén* defines it as floating. It is also written as *piāo* (漂); the lower character "submerge" (*mò*) is defined in the *Shuōwén* as being phonetically determined by *mín* (旻). The pronunciation of *mín* is *mò*.
"Zhàn-lì" (戰栗) means trembling. "Bì" (臂) is pronounced *chǒu* (with the *lóng* rhyme) and means straight. Regarding "yòu-xi" (右脇), it is composed of "xiāng" (香);
the reading with the "yè" (業) rhyme is incorrect. As for "ròu" (肉), it is composed of "sān-lì" (三力) and "sān-dāo" (三刀); [the other readings] are not correct.

Volume Eighty-Two. *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Volume Eighty-Two. The *Ugra-paripṛcchā*, the Nineteenth Assembly. One scroll. Translated during the Wei dynasty by Kang Senghui. [The text begins with] "Listen" (聽) in the departing tone (*qùshēng*), starting from the ninth [note].
*Ugra* (郁伽) is a transliteration of the Sanskrit word for "heroic" (*vīra*). *Bodhisattva* (億) is the name for a bodhisattva.
*Hedān* (荷擔)—the first character is pronounced with the initial *hé* (何) and the final rhyme *dūgān* (都甘); it means to carry on one's back. *Qiáo* (橋) refers to a bridge over water;

the radical is *mù* (木), and the phonetic is *qiáo* (喬). The character *qiáo* is composed of *yāo* (夭) [a bird in flight] as its phonetic; the character *chuán* (船) is derived from a simplified form of *yuán* (沿) [to follow the bank].

*Chāohuā* (謿譁): The first character is read as *chāo* (䝖交反) or written as *cháo* (嘲); it means to mock or jest. The second character is pronounced *tà* (吒狡反), composed of the radicals *mǎn* (𭶮) and *zhuǎo* (爪). The lower part is pronounced *huā*. The *Huāguìyuàn* (華桂苑) states that it means clamor and noise.

The character *qiān* (牽) is pronounced as *jiān* (上啟堅反). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to pull" (*qiānyǐn*). It is composed of the radical *xuán* (玄) below and the character *niú* (牛) below, which is pronounced as *chāngshì* (昌世反). Gu Yewang states that *dòu* (𤸪) is synonymous with "pulling. The *Shuowen* further explains it as "to lead and release" (*yǐn ér zòng yě*). It is sometimes written as *chè* (掣), which is a vulgar form; the version in the current sutra as *yè* (抴) is an error.
*Cuǐhuì* (灰退): "Huì" means wealth (*cuǐ*). It is also written as *huì*. *Dízhú* (躑躅):
Pronounced *zhèngjù* (鄭劇) for the first character and *chóngjú* (重局) for the second. *Dízhú* means to loiter or hesitate; it refers to not advancing, or leaping about.

"Māo" (貓) [the character is pronounced "máo" in its original sense; it is the name of a beast]. The *Kǎoshēng* states: "The short-haired variety of the great tiger is called a *zánmāo*. Its shape and size are exactly like the cat kept by common households today for catching mice. The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radicals 𭶮 and 苗. The current scriptural text uses 猫 with the dog radical; this is a vulgar character. The pronunciation of 𭶮 is zhì.

*Zhé* (讁): Pronounced *gé* (革) with a retroflex final. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that "zhé" means "to reprimand. Guo's commentary on the *Fangyan* says it means "mutual reprimand and anger" or "guilt and transgression. It is composed of the radical "speech" (言) and the phonetic "shí" (適). An alternative form is written as *zhé* (謫), where the lower part is pronounced *fá* (伐) and consists of the radicals "net" (罒) and "punish" (討).

*Tí* (staircase): the upper character is read as *xì* (奚) with the phonetic component *kǎo* (考); it means that which can be ascended. *Dèng* (step/platform): the lower character is read as *guàn* (亘) with the phonetic component *kǎo* (考); it means a footpath or a level surface. *Ā-lián-ér* (āraṇya): a Sanskrit term;
in the *Lǔzhì* (Lüshi) dialect it does not sound refined, and was formerly translated as *Ālánruò* (Āraṇya). In the Tang language, it means a "place of tranquility."

Volume Eighty-three. The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Eighty-three, the Twentieth Assembly: The Inexhaustible Treasury. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci. *Kěn* (懇): Upper radical *kǎng*, lower phonetic *hèn*. According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means sincerity or faith. It is composed of the radical *xīn* (heart) with the phonetic *mǔn*. The pronunciation of *mǔn* is the same as above; the initial radical is *chū*, the side radical is *cè*. According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means compassion; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means deep sorrow. It is composed of the radical *xīn* (heart) with the phonetic *zé*.

The silk cocoon (jiǎn) contains [the silkworm] within; according to the *Zhōu Lǐ* (Rites of Zhou), in the second month of spring, the Queen and the teachers of the inner and outer ranks of titled ladies begin the silkworm-rearing at the northern suburb. The *Kǎo Shēng* states that it is the name for a thread-spinning insect. The *Shuō Wén* defines it as "a silkworm that conceives [silk]," formed with the radical *guān* (insects) and the phonetic *tì*. The lower character is pronounced jiān-xiǎn. In the *Lǐjì*, it says: "When the *shìfù* (ladies of the court) have finished the silkworm-rearing, they present the cocoons to the ruler. Once the silkworm work has been completed, they present the cocoons and weigh the silk. The *Shuō Wén* further states: "A cocoon (*jiǎn*) is the garment of the silkworm," formed with the radicals *miè* (silk) and *chóng* (insect). Those who write it with *jiǎn* may also use the ancient character *jì*.

"Zōng" (綜) means to interweave; it is derived from the "sōng" (宗) phonetic with the "mì" (糸) radical, meaning that which holds the threads crossing over on a loom. It is said to mean "to weave together strands of silk. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "The term for the device on a loom that holds the crosswise threads is called 'zōng'; it follows the 'mì' radical and takes 'sōng' as its phonetic."
As soon as one sees it, the sound is reversed and examined, and it is said to mean "temporary.

84. Volume Eighty-four, *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Volume Eighty-four. "Jian" (姦): [The character] Yan (顏) is reversed; the *Cangjie pian* says it means "deceitful," and the *Shuowen jiezi* says it means "private. It is also written as "Jian" (奸), with the same meaning.

*Che* (pronounced *rè* with a retroflex initial, or alternatively *chāng zhì*). Now, taking the first pronunciation, the *Shuowen* says it means "to pull and release. It is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "zhì. It is also written as *zhuó* or *zhì*. The character below, *cháng*, is pronounced *réng*; it means "rope."

Volume Eighty-Five. The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Eighty-Five, the Twenty-First Assembly: The Assembly of the Illusionist Bhadra. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci. Regarding the term *jiào* (較): The *Jiǎoshì* (較試) states that its initial tone is *jiǎo* (角). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) says it means "to abridge" (*jiǎolüè*). Zheng Xuan says it means "to see" (*jiàn*). The *Erya* says it means "proper" (*yí*). The *Guǎngyá* says it means "clear" (*míng*). It is also written as *jiào* (挍); these are archaic and vernacular forms.

"Biànzhù" (遍澍) is a homophone for "fǎokǎo" (反考). It means "timely rain falls everywhere"; it is composed of the abbreviated form of "shù" (tree) and the phonetic "shēng" (sound). The reading in the canonical text as "yù zhù" (雨霔) is incorrect; it is merely a scribal error or a fabrication made by copyists acting on their own whims, for this character does not exist at all.

Volume Eighty-Six. The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Eighty-Six, the Twenty-Second Assembly on Great Spiritual Manifestations. Translated by Tripitaka Master Yi Jing. Regarding "niedin" (躡金屣): "Nie" (躡) is a term from the *Fangyan* (Dialectal Dictionary); it means to step upon or tread. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means to tread. The lower character is pronounced "shi" (史) with the phonetic "kao" (考). It refers to footwear that does not cover the heel. It is also written as 𦁡, 䩥, or 𩌦. According to this sutra, it is the leather sandal used in the Western Regions.

[Regarding the character] "quǎn" (醆): This is an error for the correct form "zhǎn" (琖), which follows the "jade" radical (*yù*). The *Liji* (Book of Rites) states: "For the *jué* vessel, the Xia used the *zhǎn*, the Yin used the *jiǎ*, and the Zhou used the *jué*. It is sometimes written as "zhǎn" (盞). The *Fānyán* (Dialectal Dictionary) says: "Zhǎn means a small cup. Guo Pu also says it is the smallest of cups. The script in the sūtra text uses the "wine" radical (*yǒu*), which is not the original character. The *Jíxùn* (Compendium of Explanations) states: "Zhǎn refers to *àngqí* (盎齊), a turbid wine that is slightly clear. This is certainly not the meaning intended in the sūtra.

The *Qunshu ziyao* (Essentials of Characters from Various Books) states that [the character] is composed of 奞 (*xuī*) and 又 (*yòu*, meaning "hand"). 奞 is pronounced *suī*; it refers to a large bird with feet. When one holds a large bird in the hand and loses it, it is called 奞. Furthermore, the Stone Classics of Cai Yong use 寸 (*cùn*) instead of [the radical], forming 奪 (*duó*). The current scriptural text uses 六 (*liù*) below [the radical] to form 𡙸, which is a grave error. Moreover, there is also a version using 犬 (*quǎn*) to form 奪; this is also incorrect, as it does not constitute a valid character.
*Ji* (撾打) is pronounced with the *zhuo* and *gua* finals reversed.

Regarding *zai* (齎持), the *Kao Sheng* states it means "to take wealth to give to others. The *Shuowen* defines it as "to leave behind," taking *bei* (貝) as the semantic component and *qi* (齊) as the phonetic. The current scriptural text uses *ji* (賫), which is a vulgar character and a grave error.

The characters for *jiē* (嘊喍) and *háo* (嘷吠) are as follows: the first character, *jiē*, has the phonetic value of *é* (額) with the secondary readings *chái* (柴) and *háo* (毫); the second character, *háo*, has the phonetic value of *féi huì* (肥惠). These are all vernacular forms; their correct orthography is composed of the radical "teeth" (齒) and the abbreviated form of "chái" (柴), written as 𪗶. The *Shuowen Jiezi* records it as 齜 (*chī*). The *Jixun* states: "Teeth gnashing against one another. It also says: "Opening the mouth to reveal the teeth. The *Yupian* states: "Teeth biting each other. The *Shenglei* writes it as 𪘬. The *Kaosheng* states: "𪘬 and 齜 describe the appearance of dogs fighting; they also describe the appearance of uneven teeth. The character 𪘬 likewise consists of the radicals "teeth" (齒) and "precipice" (厓). Regarding the character *fèi* (吠) below: the *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "The barking of a dog. It is composed of 'mouth' (口) and 'dog' (犬) as its phonetic."

Regarding "jealousy" (jí dù): the first character is pronounced jí (with the initial *j* and final *-i*), and the second is pronounced dù (with the initial *d* and final *-u*, formed from the radicals for "woman" and "door"). This was already explained in the preceding text; all subsequent instances in the scripture [reading it differently] are incorrect. As for "encounter" (gòu), it is pronounced gǔ hòu (with the initials *g* and *h* and finals *-ou*); this is the character for the hexagram Gòu in the *Yī Jīng*, which deviates from the intended meaning of the scripture.

The character *diān* (顛) is pronounced with the initial *d-*, the radical *zhēng* (聲), and is composed of "person" (*rén*) and a simplified form of "fill" (*tián*). It also means "upside down" or "inverted. The current version of the scripture uses the character *diān* (巔) with the "mountain" (*shān*) radical, which is an error; that character refers to a mountain peak and does not accord with the meaning of the scripture.

The character 顏貌 (yánmào) [is pronounced] xià, with the radical 茅 (máo) and the phonetic 豹 (bào); the *Kǎośēng* states it means "demeanor" or "appearance," and is sometimes written as 󲆸. The current version of the scripture uses the character 狠 (hěn), which is incorrect. The *Yùpiān* gives its pronunciation as wǔjiān; the *Shuōwén* states that 狠狠 refers to the sound of dogs fighting. This is a grave error that completely distorts the meaning of the scripture.

Volume Eighty-nine. In the eighty-ninth volume of the *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra*, regarding the character "tiè" (䥫鐷) at the end of the word, its phonetic value is "yè. This was already explained in the previous seventy-six volumes; the text's reading as "jiǎ" (鍱) is incorrect.

The character *yáng* (洋) is pronounced with the initial *zhāng* (章) and the final *fèi* (沸). The *Jìxùn* (*集訓*) states that it describes the appearance of flowing water. The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (*毛詩傳*) says that *yángyáng* (洋洋) describes the appearance of being grand and magnificent. The character *xuàn* (衒) is pronounced with the initial *xuán* (玄) and the final *jiàn* (絹). The *Shuōwén* (*說文*) states that it means to walk while selling;

it is composed of the radical *xíng* (行) and the phonetic *xuán* (玄), or alternatively, it is composed of *xuán* (玄) and *xíng* (行), with *xuàn* (衒) also serving as the phonetic. The character *mài* (買) is pronounced with the initial *hà* (下) and the final *bài* (敗). The *Shuōwén* states that it means to take goods out [for sale]; it is composed of the radical *chū* (出) and the phonetic *mǎi* (買). In the present scripture, it is written with the radical *tǔ* (土) and the element *sì* (四), which is a vulgar corruption and abbreviation. According to the *Shuōwén*, the character *mǎi* (買) is composed of the radical *gāng* (岡).

The character for *bái-dié* (白㲲) is explained by its phonetic as "woolen cloth" (*máo bù*) or "cloth made of grass and flowers. It is composed of the radical for "hair" (*máo*) and the phonetic *dié*. In the canonical texts, it is sometimes written simply as *dié*, which is not the original character; it refers to a type of vessel or utensil.

The character *zhān* (瞻) is pronounced with the initial *zhāng* and final *lián*. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that it means "to look. The character *miàn* (眄) is pronounced with the initial *piàn*. The *Kǎoshēng* says it means "to look askance"; *xié* (衺) is pronounced with the initial *xī* and final *zhèng*, and is the radical form of the character.
*Ti* (涕) and *xuei* (唾) are both secretions of the mouth; *xuei* is pronounced with the initial *dian* (天) and the final *di* (帝), reversed as *xia* (下) and *tu* (吐).

It is not *xiu* (齅)—pronounced with the initial *xiu* (休) and the final *jiu* (救)—which the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines as "to smell by means of the nose" (*yi bi jiu chou*). The *Yunying* states that it means "the nose taking in air," composed of the radical for "nose" and the phonetic *chou* (臭). The reading in the scripture using the mouth radical (*kou*) to form *xiu* (嗅) is incorrect; it does not constitute a valid character.

*Maitreya* is the Sanskrit term; what was formerly called *Mile* (彌勒) is a corruption and an abbreviation that is not correct. The authentic Sanskrit pronunciation is *Maitrī*, which in the language of Tang means "The Compassionate One" (*Cishi*). This is the name of the Bodhisattva.

The upper character 誼 (yì) is pronounced with the initial *huī* and the final *yuán* (alternatively written as 灌; in ancient script as 叩). The lower character 集 (jí) is composed of the radical 衣 (clothing) and the phonetic 集. The character 䛡 (shuō) is pronounced *hù kuài*.

Zào (*zào*)—pronounced *zǐ-dào* (反)—Gù Yěwáng says it means "restless movement"; Kǎo Shēng says it means "a quick temperament"; Zhèng Xuān says it means "lack of tranquility"; the *Shuōwén* says it means "haste," written with the radical *chuò* (辵) and the phonetic *zào* (趮). The *Yùpiān* says it is composed of the radical *zú* (足) and the phonetic *sào* (喿), where *sào* is pronounced *sāng-dào* (反). The current scriptural text uses *yōu*, which is incorrect. The character *yán* (夒) in the *Shuōwén* is composed of the radicals *xié* (頁), *zhǐ* (止), *yǐ* (已), and *zhǒu* (夂); its pronunciation is *suī*. The upper character *fán* (樊) has the phonetic value of *fán* (煩); the *Kǎo Shēng* states it refers to a birdcage. It is also pronounced *pān* (攀), or written as *bàn* (󲍝), all having the same meaning.

*Bin* (擯): Upper radical *bin* (賓), reversed. Sima Biao’s commentary on the *Zhuangzi* states: “*Bin* means to cast away (*qì*). The *Shiji* states: “They mutually *pai-bin* [pushed out and excluded] one another. The *Shuowen* writes it with the radical *ren* (人) as *bìn* (儐); the lower character is pronounced *chǐ*. Liu Zhao’s commentary on the *Gongyang Zhuan* states: “*Ai* (㡿) refers to pointing out; *Guoyaya* says it means to push (*tuī*). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states: “To expel and chase away (*chìzhú*). Xu Shuzhong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states: “*Ai* (㡿) means to expand (*tà*). The *Shuowen* states: “*Ke* (却) is a type of building; it takes *yǎn* (广) as the radical and *nì* (屰) as the phonetic. *Yǎn* is pronounced *yǎn*; *nì* is pronounced *nì*. The current scriptural text reads *chǐ* (𠕋); this is a vulgar corruption due to the transformation of the cursive script (*cǎoshū*) style.

*Jiǎn-sè*: The upper character *jiǎn* (謇) is pronounced with the initial *jiāng* and the final *yǎn*. In the *Book of Changes* (*Zhouyī*), it means "obstruction" or "difficulty. In the *Fānyán*, it means "stammering. It is also written as *jūn* (𧮈), or as *jiǎn* (寋) and *zàn* (󲌚); all are identical. The lower character *sè* (澀) is pronounced with the initial *cān* and the final *lì*. Its explanation is as before; the scripture uses the character *sè*.

Regarding the character for *chuáng* (bed): it is pronounced *zhuāng* (莊). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is "an implement for resting the body. The version in the sutra written as *chuáng* (床) is incorrect.

In current Buddhist scriptures, it is written as "lian" (鍊), derived from "melting and refining gold or iron," which is not the original character but is nonetheless acceptable.

The character *biàn* (變): The ancient sound is *tài* (他代). The commentary on the sounds states that its meaning is "changeability without constancy. The *Jíxùn* (集訓) states it means "appearance or countenance. It is composed of the radical *xīn* (心) and the phonetic *néng* (能);

the pronunciation of *néng* is *nài* (耐). The character *huì* (賄): The ancient sound is *huái* (灰外). The commentary on the sounds states it means "wealth or goods. It is sometimes written as *yǒu* (𧶅), composed of the radical *yǒu* (有) and the phonetic *bèi* (貝).

*Ziman*: The first character, *zi*, is pronounced with the *ci* rhyme (as in *cí*). Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjìng* states that *zī* means "to increase. Regarding the sound of *duō* (in *kǎoshēng duō*), it is pronounced with the *wàn* rhyme;

its explanation has already appeared in the preceding text. *Héngguà*: Both pronunciations, *guài* and *guà*, are acceptable. *Kǎoshēng* states that *guà* means "to hang" or "to suspend," and also "to stop. It may also be written as *huì*, which follows the radical for "hand" (*shǒu*) and takes *guī* as its phonetic component.
The character 篋 (xiān) has the first radical *xi* (羊反) and the second radical *qiān* (謙反).

The character 踏 (tà) is a vulgar variant; its original pronunciation is *tán* (貪反), though it is used here as *tà* (談合反). It means to tread upon the ground. Its correct form is 蹹 (tà). The *Kǎo Shēng* states that "tà" means to trample; it is composed of the radical 足 and the phonetic component 塌 (tā).

Volume Ninety-Six. The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Ninety-Six, the Twenty-Eighth Assembly: The Chapter on the Householder *Dānapati* (Qinshou). Translated by Zhu Fahu. Regarding the term "youyan" (遊讌): the *Yanyun* states it refers to the sound of joyfully drinking wine; the *Yunying* states it is a term for a drinking party. It is sometimes written as "yàn" (宴), where the radical is "speech" (言) and the phonetic is "yàn" (燕).

"Unfired clay" (huài): "huài" is pronounced as in "pǔbēi. An earthenware vessel that has not yet been fired is called "unfired. See the *Wenzi Jilüe* (Abridged Collection of Characters). Generally, when an unfired vessel encounters rain, it breaks; here, the scripture takes the sense of "brittleness."

Regarding "qīng" (圊): on the stone inscription it is pronounced *jì* (磧, yíng fǎn); in character dictionaries, *qīng* and *hùn* (圂) are synonymous. *Hùn* is pronounced *hù mén* (胡悶 fǎn). According to the *Kǎoshēng*, *qīng* is also a term for a latrine (*cè*). It is composed of the radical "mouth" (口) and the phonetic "qīng" (青). The definition of the character *cè* (廁) is also identical to the above.

*Kuài* (魁膾): The first character is pronounced with the initial *kǔ* (苦) and the final *guī* (瓌); the second character is pronounced with the initial *gǔ* (古) and the final *wài* (外). It is formed from the semantic element "flesh" (*ròu*) and the phonetic element "assembly" (*huì*).

It is like *xī* (析), which is pronounced with the initial *xīng* (星) and the final *yì* (亦); it means to split or divide. Water flows from the character *piàn* (片), which is half of the character for "wood" (*mù*). This is the correct form; alternatively, it may be written as *bō* (㭊), though the ancient script used *piàn* (片).

The character for *shǐ* (駛) is used here as a rhyming term for "swift" (*jísù*). It is composed of the radical "horse" (*mǎ*) and the phonetic "shǐ. It is also written as *jué*. The current version of the sutra uses *kuài* (夬), which is an error made by the scribe of the *Shūjīng*. The pronunciation of *kuài* is *jiānxuè* (涓血). *Kuàití* (駃騠) is the name of a type of horse and does not accord with the meaning of the sutra.

The character *tuan* (摶) is sometimes written as *tuán* (團); Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that it means "round. Examining its phonetic component, *bo* (搏) means "to grasp," while the *Mao Shi Zhuan* explains it as "to gather. It is composed of the radical "hand" (*shou*) and the phonetic "zhuan" (*zhuan*). The character *tuan* (󱻙) is correctly written with the phonetic "ling" (*ling*, pronounced *jing* with an entering tone) and the radical "zao" (*zao*, pronounced *bi* with an initial *l-*, hence *li*). According to this, "bolting food" (*tuan shi*) refers to eating where various flavors are blended together.
*Tan-yin* (痰癊): the first character is pronounced *tán*, the second is pronounced *yú-jìn*. "Biān" (編) means to connect or link together;

Liu Zhao’s commentary on the *Gōngyáng Zhuàn* states that "biān" means to arrange in sequence. The *Cāngjié Piān* says it means to weave. Gu Yewang says it means to arrange in rows. The *Shuowén Jiězì* defines it as ordering the leaves of a manuscript. The *Shēnglèi* says it means to string objects together in order with a cord. The second character below is pronounced *láng-gè-jí*.

The seven apertures (qiào): "xiāo" is the phonetic inversion of "jiào. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states that "qiào" means "pores" (kǒng). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that there are seven yang apertures and two yin apertures. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines "qiào" as "hollow" (kōng); it is composed of the radical "cave" (xué) and the phonetic "jiǎo," with the pronunciation "jiào."
The character 裹 (guǒ) is pronounced as "guǒ.
The character 殨 (huì)—with the phonetic component 潰 (huì) and the radical 歹 (dài, pronounced cán)—is explained by Yùnyīng as "the rotting of flesh.
It is also read as jiè or jīng.
The character for "nasal mucus" (zhōng-tí) has the lower radical pronounced as yí; the *Yùnyīng* says it refers to nasal fluid. It is also written as 咦 or 𪖦.

The character for "eye discharge" (yǎn-chī) has the phonetic component zhī; the *Yùnjuān* says it refers to the film on the eyes. The *Shuowén* says it is eye fluid, composed of the radical 目 with the abbreviated form of 侈 as the phonetic.
*Mó* (磨) and *yìng* (鎣): "Mó" means to polish pearls and jade; "yìng" means to polish a mirror so that it becomes bright. It is composed of the radical 金 (metal) with 熒 (yíng) as the phonetic.

*Wèi* (餧) for "foxes and wolves": the upper character is pronounced *wēi* (威) or *wèi* (位); the *Yùnyīng* (韻英) states it means to feed oxen. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it means to give food. It is composed of the radical 食 (food) with 委 (wěi) as the phonetic, or it may be written as 萎 (wěi).

The character *huàn* (𧧳) is pronounced with the initial *kǔ* and the final *guān*. The Master Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shūjìng* states: "To be arrogant and unrestrained beyond measure is to *huàn* oneself—that is, to be great [in self-importance]. The *Shìfǎ* says: "To speak flowery words without substance is called *huàn*; it follows the radical 'speech' (*yán*) and takes 'great' (*guān*) as its phonetic. The current scriptural text uses the character composed of 'sky' (*yóu*) and 'sky' (*yóu*) as *kuā*, which is an erroneous vulgar usage. Below, it is pronounced with the initial *xuán* and the final *juàn*. Regarding the character *xuán* (玄), the *Yīngyùn* states that its tone is level; it says: "To sell one's goods is called *xiàn*. The collective glosses state: "*Xiàn* means to boast of one's own arts; it follows the radical 'walking' (*xíng*) and takes 'great' (*xuán*) as its phonetic."

Volume Ninety-Seven, *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Volume Ninety-Seven, the Twenty-ninth Assembly, the *Udayana-rāja-parivarta*. Translated by Zhu Fahu. *Kuśāmbī* (the first character pronounced as *jù*, the second as *shāng* with the level tone): this term is a transcription of a Sanskrit word meaning "not seeking. It is the name of a country in Central India. During the time of the Buddha, there was a king in this country named Udayana (Táng yán: "one who gives rise to love"). In ancient translations, he was sometimes called Udayana or King Udayana (*Utian*), both of which are corruptions or abbreviations.

Regarding "jǐng" (neck) and "xiàng" (nape): the former is pronounced as *jìng* (with the initial *j-*) and the latter as *xiāng* (with the initial *x-*). The *Cāngjié piān* states that the neck is in front and the nape is behind. The *Shuowén* defines them as "the stalk of the head," both following the radical *yè* (head), which is pronounced *jié*. It is composed of the component *jīng* (axis/line) and the phonetic *jiāng* (abbreviated for *jiāng*).

"Being yoked" (*bei ye*): "ye" means the collar-bar of a carriage; it also means an obstruction. The scripture reads *e* (轭), which is a vulgar character; the correct orthography is from the radicals "door" (*hu*) and "hook" (*yi*), forming *e* (戹).

"Nursing" (*ru bu*): pronounced *pu-mu*. Xu Shuchong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states: "It refers to chewing food in the mouth and giving it to [the infant]. The *Kaoseng* says: "It refers to food in the mouth being chewed and sucked. It is like a bird feeding its young. It is composed of the radical "mouth" (*kou*) and a simplified form of "to catch" (*bu*). The text of the scripture reads *bu* (餔), which is an error. The original pronunciation of the character *bu* is *bù-hú*; it is not the primary character here.

The character 𧶻 (jiāo) is pronounced with the *mo* and *hòu* finals. According to the *Erya*, it means "market. Gu Yewang says it refers to "bartering. The *Zitong* states that it is composed of the radical 貝 (*bei*) and the phonetic 戼 (*shǔn*). The character 戼 is an archaic form of 夘 (*mǎo*). In modern clerical script (*lìshū*), it has been corrupted from the character 死 (*sǐ*). The lower component, 易 (*yì*), is pronounced with the *yì* final.

The character 叫 (jiào) means to cry out. The *Zuozhuan* states it is the howl of jackals and wolves; the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "howling" (*páo*), composed of the radical 口 (mouth) with the phonetic 皋 (gāo). The pronunciation of 皋 is gāo, composed of 白 (bái) and 本 (běn); the pronunciation of 本 is tāo (also read xiāoyào). The *Guangya* defines it as "crying out"; lexicographical works define it as "calling. According to the *Shuowen*, it also means "roaring," composed of 口 (mouth) and 𠿒 (jīng, pronounced yīng). The *Yupian* writes it as 噭 or 嘌; 嘂 and 討 are all archaic forms of the character 叫. [The claim that it is] composed of 刀 (knife) is incorrect.
*Itvaka* is a Sanskrit name for a type of insect, such as a dung beetle, that feeds on excrement. Regarding the term *zhùbó* (澍雹):

the upper character is pronounced *zhù*; the scriptural text writes it with the character *zhù* (霔) followed by the radical for rain, which is incorrect, as this character does not exist in any dictionary. The lower character is pronounced *páng* (with the phonetic *pújiāng*).
The kiln-master’s surname is Yao (姚),
with the phonetic component *yan* (猒, pronounced *yàn* or *ī*) and the radical *wu* (烏).
He detested burning and incinerating (*liao*, pronounced *liáo*).

"Saliva and mucus" (xiàn tì): the first character is pronounced with the *shī* rhyme (夕延反) and the second with the *tǐ* rhyme (體計反); they refer to the fluids of the mouth. In the scriptural text, it is written as *yí* (夷), which is an error for *tì* (涕). Although the dictionaries list the pronunciation *tì*, its original form is the character *yí*. The *Yì Jì Cù Guā* (易萃卦) states, "Carrying about saliva and mucus" (齎恣涕洟), which serves as proof of this.

"Cānglǐn" (倉廩) is pronounced as "cānglín" (倉臨); it is a character used according to its temporal [phonetic] value. The *Shuowen* writes it as "lǐn" (㐭), which means "granary" and is a pictographic character (*xiàngxíng*) representing the shape of a building; it follows the radical "rén" (人) and the "huí" (回) to represent the doors and windows within the structure. In modern clerical script (*lìshū*), the "hé" (禾) radical is added to form "bǐn" (稟). The *Zílín* (字林) writes it as "lǐn" (廩), both of which are interchangeable.

*Kǎn* (古猛反, gǔ měng fǎn). The *Cāngjiépiān* states that it refers to grain that has husks. The *Shuowén* says: "Hú (*hú*) is grain; it follows the radical for 'grain' (禾) and takes the phonetic *guǎng*. Below, *yíng* (即反, jí fǎn): the *Kǎoshēng* says it refers to the chaff of wheat; it follows the radical for 'wheat' (麥) and takes the phonetic *yì*. It is also written as *yí*.

*Dian* (顛) and *fu* (仆): "Dian" means to fall headlong; it is composed of "zhen" (眞) and "ye" (頁), or alternatively written as "dian" (傎) with "ren" (人). It denotes overturning or falling. The scriptural version uses two instances of "zhen" (㒓), which is an erroneous vulgar form. "Fu" (仆): pronounced with the initial *fú* (孚) and final *-fu* (付), it is homophonous with the character "fu" (赴). The *Kaoseng* (考聲) states that it means to lie prostrate or supine, or a prostrate corpse; it is composed of "ren" (人) and "fu" (赴) with "sheng" (省) as the phonetic.

The character for *yǒng* (swimming) is pronounced with the initial *yóu* and the final *kǎo*; it describes the manner of following the flow of water. It is composed of the radical *shuǐ* (water) and the phonetic *yóu* (abbreviated) as its sound component. The second character, *róng*, has the reading *mìng* (as in *mìngfǎn*). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states: "To move secretly. The *Erya* says: "*Yǒng* means swimming. Guo Pu explains: "It refers to moving secretly beneath the surface of the water. It is composed of the radical *shuǐ* (water) and the phonetic *yǒng* (eternal/permanent).
*Tiao* (the first character) is pronounced *ting-yao*; it means to leap. *Dai* (the second character) is pronounced *cheng-ju*; *dai* also means to leap.
Regarding the cauldron of boiling water (*huo-tang*), its pronunciation is *hu-guo*; its explanation and interpretation are as stated at the beginning of this fascicle.
Regarding "tiě cáo" (iron trough): the *Zìshū* states it refers to a horse stall. "Tiě zuǐ" (iron beak):

the rhyme dictionary *Yùnyīng* says it is the beak of a bird; it is also written as 𭪿 or 𠲿, and the *Yùnquán* likewise says it is the mouth of a bird. It is also sometimes written as 𠻘 or 喍; all of these are variants of the character "zuǐ" (beak). "Huì" (pronounced xū wèi) is the phonetic for "huì" (beak).
*Tànzuò* (探啄): the first character is pronounced *tāhán* (他含反) and the second is pronounced *zhuó* (音卓). *Dángwēi* (煻煨):

the first character is pronounced *táng* (音唐) and the second is pronounced *ūguī* (烏瓌反); it is composed of the radical *huǒ* (火) and the phonetic component *wěi* (隈) in abbreviated form; it refers to hot ashes and embers.
*Xiānlì* (銛利): The upper character is pronounced *xiān*; it means sharp and pointed. *Yángtóng* (洋銅):

The character is pronounced *yáng*. Volume Ninety-Eight: The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Ninety-Eight. This volume contains two assemblies: the Thirtieth, the Assembly of the Youth Prajñākūṭa; and the Thirty-First, the Assembly on the Banks of the Ganges. Both were translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha. *Jùhuài* (沮壞): The character is pronounced *qíng yù fǎn* (情預反) or alternatively *jí yǔ fǎn* (疾與反). According to dictionaries, it means dampness or soaking.
*Yuchan* (諛諂): The first character is pronounced *yu* (with the initial *zhù*) and the second is pronounced *chǎn* (with the initial *chǔ*).
According to the *Kǎoshēng* (Examination of Sounds), *qià* (洽) means "harmonious. *Zhuāngjiào* (裝校):
The first character is pronounced *zhuāng* (with the initial *zhuāng*) and the second is pronounced *jiào* (with the initial *jiāo*), meaning "to adorn."

The upper character, *chuān* (pronounced as in *chuānshàng*), the *Shuowén* explains as "to pierce through. It is a compound character (*huìyì*) composed of the radical *yá* (tooth) within the enclosure *xué* (cave). The lower character, *zào* (pronounced *cáng hè* as a *kǎoshēng* [entering tone] reading), the *Kǎoshēng* explains as "a wooden tool. The *Shuowén* explains it as "to bore wood," composed of the radicals *jīn* (metal) and *zhù* (clustered grass), with *jiù* (mortar) below and *shū* (pestle) at the bottom. In the Jin edition of the canon, it is written as *záo*, which is an error. *Zhù* is pronounced *chú xué* (as in *chúxué*), *jiù* is pronounced *jiù*, and *shū* is pronounced *shū*. In ancient script, it is written as *zǎo*.

Volume Ninety-nine. *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Volume Ninety-nine, "The Assembly of the Bodhisattva Abhayamati," Part Three, translated by Buddhayaśas. Regarding the character 屩 (*jiǎo*): it refers to a straw sandal or slipper. It is composed of the radical 履 (lǚ) and the phonetic element 伎 (jì) in abbreviated form. The text erroneously uses the character 跛 (*bǒ*) [meaning "lame"] instead of this.

"Xiá" (陿)—pronounced with the "xian" and "jian" finals—means narrow and confined; it is composed of the radical "fù" (阜) and the character "qiè" (匧). The text's use of "quan" (犬) to form "xiá" (狹) is an error; that is actually the character for "narrow" used in the context of training dogs and horses, and it does not accord with the meaning of the scripture.

The character *bèi* (萞) is pronounced with the *bi* rhyme and the *mí* final; the *Kǎo Shēng* states it is the name of a plant. Its seeds resemble the *niúchī* insect, hence the name. It is composed of the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) and the phonetic element *yǎn*. The current scriptural text writes it as *bì* (𦳈) or *pí* (蜱), but these are not the original characters.
The term *chichzhu* (躑躅) has already been explained with its phonetics and definitions in the eighty-second fascicle above.

Regarding *xiaofa* (小橃), the character for *fa* (橃) is pronounced *fu*; the dictionaries state that binding bamboo or wood so it floats upon the water is called *fa*. The text reads *fu* (筏), which is a vulgar character and not the correct orthography.
"Daibo" (大舶) refers to a large ship in the ocean; "bo" (舶) is pronounced "bo.
"Yidie" (一滴滴)—the second character is read as "dingli" (丁歷) with the retroflex *r*—is incorrect when written as "di" (滴).
"Nude" (女得) is pronounced "ru" (汝); the three segments in the following text all use the character for "you" (汝), as in the phrase "You now abide here" (汝今為住). Thus it is correct.

Regarding "if one licks and eats" (若舐食): the *Ershuowen* states that it means to take up an object with the tongue. It is also written as 舓 or 𦧇; both are acceptable and are archaic forms of the character 䑛. The version in the sutra uses 䑛, which is incorrect. It is unclear from what source this [variant] originated.

If one "xiū" (with the rhyme *jiù*)—meaning to bring the nose toward a smell—it is called "xiù"; this is a vulgar character, while the canonical text uses "xiù. If one "zé" (with the rhyme *hé*)—it refers to the feeding of birds. 100. *Yǎn xuàn* (眼眴): "Xuàn" refers to the appearance of winking the eyes; the reading "yǒu yīn shùn" (有音舜) is incorrect. *Chóng bì* (傭䏶):
The first character is pronounced *chì yōng* (勅庸反) and the second is pronounced *bì* (音陛).

*Chuǎn cháng* (󰈷腸): The first character is pronounced *cháng yuǎn* (常兖反). According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to the calf muscle of the leg (*zú fēicháng*). It is composed of the radical "foot" (*zú*) with "zhuān" (*zhuān*) as the phonetic. Furthermore, according to the *Shuowen*, the character "zhuān" itself is composed of "shuān" (*shuān*) and "cùn" (*cùn*); the form "chuǎn" is a vulgar variant. The second character, "cháng" (腸), is pronounced *zhǎng* (音長); it is composed of the radical "flesh" (*ròu*) with a simplified form of "yì" (*yì*) as the phonetic.

The character *qí* (麒麟) is pronounced "qí" above and "lín" below. The *qílín* is an auspicious beast with a single horn on its head; its physical appearance and the interpretation of its name have already been explained in detail previously in the first, thirtieth, and sixty-sixth fascicles.

101. *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Scroll 111. Chapter 34: The Assembly of the Bodhisattva Guṇaratnakusuma; also Chapter 35: The Assembly of Subhasthita-mati. Same scroll. "Sheshu" (射術): [The character] "she" (射) is pronounced with the initial *sh* and the final *e* reversed. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "A bow or crossbow is discharged from the body and hits a distant mark. It is composed of 'body' (身) and 'cun' (寸). 'Cun' refers to measurement. Alternatively, it is written as 'she' (䠶) with 'arrow' (矢), which is the same. [The character] "shu" (術) is pronounced with the initial *sh* and the final *l* reversed. The *Han Shi* states: "Method and principle. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "The Way; the arts. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "The roads within a city. It is composed of 'walking' (行) and the phonetic element 'shu' (术). The sound of 'shu' is pronounced with the initial *zhong* and the final *lü* reversed, and it takes the abbreviated form of 'chuang' (𧿡) as its phonetic element."

*Uttarāsaṅga* is a Sanskrit term for a monastic robe; it refers to the seven-strip *kāṣāya*, which is the everyday garment among the three robes (*tricīvara*). It is also called the "upper garment" (*shangyi*); see the *Nanhai Jiguishi* (Record of the Inner Law Sent Home from the Southern Seas).

Regarding the term *lánshǔn* (欄楯): the first character is pronounced *dān* (勒單反) and the second is pronounced *shùn* (下音順). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it refers to a "railing" (*lánhàn*). A vertical bar is called a *lán*, while a horizontal bar is called a *shǔn*. The spaces between the bars are called *língzǐ* (櫺子), which in common parlance are referred to as "hooked railings. The character for *shǔn* (楯) is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "shield" (*dùn*); the character *dùn* (盾) is pronounced *shùn* and is formed from the "ten eyes" radical (*shí mù*).

Regarding "qigai" (乞匃): the rhyme dictionary *Yingyun* states that "gai" (匃) also means to beg. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the upper radical is "ren" (人) and the lower is "wang" (亾); when a person lacks wealth and goods, they "qigai. The scriptural text writes it as "ke" (可), which is not the sound "gai" (pronounced mian-dian-fan), and thus deviates from the intended meaning of the scripture.

102. Volume One Hundred and Two, *The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra*, Volume One Hundred and Two, *The Assembly of the Devaputra Susthitamati*, Three Volumes. Regarding the term "wǎn" (剜): it is defined in the *Guānpàn* as "to gouge out. The phonetic is "huìyuán" (恚緣). The *Cāngjié piān* states that "gōu" (剈) means "to take out. The *Guǎngyǎ* explains that "gōu" and "wǎn" are used interchangeably.

*Gè* (割): Upper radical *gān* (乾), reversed; Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* says it means "to cut. The *Eryá* says it means "to tear apart. The *Guǎngyá* says it means "to sever," "to tailor," or "to slice. It is a compound character formed by shape and sound. The lower part has the phonetic value *gǔ*; Zheng’s sub-commentary on the *Máoshī* says the base of the shin is called the *gǔ*. The *Shuowén* says *gǔ* refers to the thigh (*bǐ*). It is composed of the radical *ròu* (flesh) with the phonetic *shū* (殳); alternatively, it may be written as *tòu* (骰) with the radical *gǔ* (骨). The sound of *shū* is *shū*.

"Pāngliú" (滂流): "Pāng" is pronounced as *pǔ* with the *gǎng* rhyme. In his commentary on the *Chuci*, Wang Yi states that "pāng" means a broad flow. The *Guangya* says "pāng" refers to a lateral flow. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "pàihè" (霈). It is a word formed by combining a semantic component and a phonetic component; "pài" is pronounced as *pèi*.

Regarding the character *jī* (羈) [the first character of *jīluo* (羈羅), pronounced with the initial *ji* and the final *yi*]: Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that it refers to a leather harness for the horse's head; the *Zishu* says it means "to tie"; the *Kaosheng* says it is a horse bridle; and the *Shuowen* writes it as *jī* (羈), stating: "A horse's head-harness. It is composed of the radicals *yan* (𠕀), *ge* (革), and *zhi* (𮩸); *zhi* (𮩸) is pronounced *zhilì* (知立). *Zhi* (𮩸) is a horse's tether; it is composed of the radical *wei* (囗); *wei* (囗) is pronounced *wéi* (韋), meaning 'horse's hoof. This is a compound character. The pronunciation of *zhi* (𮩸) is *zhilì* (知立). The text reads *jī* (羈), which is an erroneous usage. The character *lǚ* (旅) is the character *lù* (󰊋); it deviates from the intended meaning of the scripture. Both characters *lù* (󰊋) and *luó* (羅) are composed of the radical *yan* (𠕀).

103. Volume 130 of the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Volume 130. "Lianxuan" (輦軒): [The character] *lì* (力) is pronounced with the final *zhǎn* (展) reversed; in the *Zhou Li*, it is said that the Empress rides the five types of chariots (*wù lù*). Zheng Xuan says: "It is a light-wheeled carriage, its body covered for travel. [The character] *xiàn* (憲) is pronounced with the final *yán* (言) reversed; regarding the sound of *kǎo* (考), *xuān* (軒) refers to a comfortable carriage (*ān chē*). Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒ Zhuan* states: "The carriage of a Great Officer. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *quchē* (曲輈) means a carriage with a curved pole, and *fanchē* (藩車) is a carriage with the phonetic component *gān* (干). It is a type of following carriage.
"迫迮" (pòzé): the first character is pronounced "bǎi" (百) and the second is pronounced "zhuānggé" (莊革).

"昬耄" (hūnmào): the first character is pronounced "máo bào" (毛抱); according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "耄" means old age. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan* states it means confusion. The *Qu Li* says, "At eighty-nine or ten years of age, one is called 'mào'"; this is a transitive character (zhuanzhu).

*Luójí* (羸瘠): The first character, *lì*, is pronounced with the *zhui* rhyme; dictionaries define it as "inferior" or "weak. The second character, *qíng*, is pronounced with the *yì* rhyme. He Xiu’s commentary on the *Gongyang zhuan* states: "It means 'emaciated' or 'ill,' a term used by the people of Qi. Examining its phonology, it is *ji*. It may be written with the radical for flesh (*shòu*) as *lí* (膌) or as *yún* (𤹠); both are archaic characters.

"Li du (the *du* is pronounced as in *dou-gu*) jing" (*guò* is written as *gòu*, which is incorrect; the phonetic value is *gòu*). "Xuān wěi": the upper character is pronounced *xiāngyuán* (or written as *guàn*), both being correct.

Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states that it means "clamorous noise. The *Guǎngyá* says it means "to cry out. The text of the scripture writes it as *xuān*, a vulgar character; in ancient script it is written as *kòu*, a compound character formed by combining the meanings [of its components]. The lower character is pronounced *wūměi*. The *Guǎngyá* says *wěi* means "multitude"; the *Cāngjiépiān* says it means "sudden. The *Shuowén* explains that *fèi* (to bark) takes *quǎn* (dog) as its radical and *wèi* (to fear) abbreviated as its phonetic.

The character for "right shoulder" (yòu bō) is read as *bǔ* (with the *mò* rhyme). The *Wenzi Jílüè* states that "bō" refers to the armor on the shoulders; the *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radical "bone" (*gǔ*) and the phonetic component "abbreviated *bó*" (*bō*). The reading in the sutra text using the character "zhé" (from the "moon" radical) is incorrect. Its pronunciation is *pǔ bó*; however, the meaning of "zhé" as dried meat (dried jerky) does not accord with the meaning of the sutra.

104. Volume 104 of the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Volume 104: "The Superior Mark of the Hair and Beard" (*śmaśru*). The phonetic gloss states that "hair and beard" refers to the hair on the face. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "the facial hair"; it is composed of the radical "head" (頁, meaning head) and the element "three strokes" (彡), which represents hair; the lower part is pronounced *fan* (韈反), referring to the long hair upon the head. The *Shuowen Jiezi* further notes that it is written as 󲙖, which is an archaic character.
The shaving of the head has already been fully explained in the preceding one hundred fascicles.

*Āraṇya* (pronounced *nù jiā* in the original transcription) is a phonetic corruption of the Sanskrit term; in the language of Tang, it means a "place of tranquility," located five *li* outside of a village.
To sweep away fragrant things; according to the *Kǎoshēng* (Examination of Sounds), "fú" means to sweep, to remove, or to wipe.

105. Volume 105 of the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Volume 105. "Bǎbèng" (handle/staff): the lower character "páng" is pronounced with the *jiǎngshēng* (level tone); according to the *Kǎoshēng*, it refers to a large staff. It is sometimes written as "㭋" (from the "wood" radical) or, in common usage, as "bàng."

*Zhuokuī*: "Kuī" is pronounced *wài*; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "clod of earth. It is colloquially called a "clod of earth," though it may also be written as *yùn*, which is an archaic character.
*Fàngjuān*: "Juān" is pronounced *yuán*; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "to discard. The version in the sutra uses "juān," which is a vulgar character.

"Jù (遽)" means "to inform suddenly. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states it means "to be fearful"; Gu Yewang says it means "urgent"; the *Cangjie pian* says it means "swift"; Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* says it means "rapid"; and Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* says it means "to conclude. It takes the phonetic element "jù" (豦). In the received text, it is written as "chù" (處), which is incorrect. According to the *Shuowen jiezi*, it consists of the radicals "hú" (虍), "zhǐ" (豕), and "chuò" (辵).

In the past, Xié (pronounced jié yǎn fǎn) stated that the character 考 (kǎo) signifies "error" (*guò*); it is composed of the radical 彳 (chì) and the semantic element 心 (xīn), with 幵 (jiān) as its phonetic. The pronunciation of 幵 is qiān. It is sometimes written as 㩉 (jiān). The character 寒 (hán) is an ancient form; its appearance in the *Jīng* (Scripture) with the redundant 衍 (yǎn) is incorrect.

Regarding the character *wéi* (爲) [in "wéi jiě"], reading it as the homophone *jiǎ* (賈) is incorrect; the others follow this pronunciation. Regarding *fēnfù* (芬馥): the upper character is read as *fāngwén* (芳文).

The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "the fragrance of grass when first growing spreading about"; it is composed of the radical *cǎo* (草) and the phonetic *fēn* (分). The scriptural text uses *qì* (气) instead, reading it as *fúwén* (扶文), which is incorrect; it is actually the character for "auspicious and harmonious" (*xiángrè fēnhūn*). It does not accord with the meaning of the scripture. The lower character is pronounced *fù* (復). The *Han Shi* says that *fēnfù* describes the appearance of fragrance; it is composed of the radical *xiāng* (香) and the abbreviated phonetic *fù* (復).

Volume 106, The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume 106, The Assembly of Prince Ajātaśatru, Chapter 37; The Mahayana Skillful Means Assembly, Chapter 38. These three volumes of sutras are capable of [eradicating] ignorance (*avidyā*). [The character for "ignorance" is formed from the radical *yan* (阝) with the phonetic component *xuan* (肙) in abbreviated form.]
*Tīng-xǔ* (permission to listen): *tīng* is pronounced with the level tone (*píngshēng*) and means "to permit"; the subsequent occurrences of this phrase in the text follow this same pronunciation.

*Dì-tīng* (listen attentively): both characters are pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*) and mean "to listen respectfully. The following instances follow this same pronunciation and will not be repeated here.

First, regarding *bōshí* (搏食): the character *bō* is pronounced *túluánfǎn* (徒欒反). What was previously explained applies here by analogy. Regarding *bìdì* (躃地): the character *bì* is pronounced *píbìfǎn* (毘壁反).

The *Jìxùn* (集訓) states: "It means to fall prostrate (*bì*); it is formed with the radical for 'foot' and the phonetic *pì*. The scriptural text uses the character *pì* (僻) with the radical for 'person,' which is incorrect; it is actually the character *biànpì* (便僻). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) says: 'Neither tall nor short; one's bearing is frivolous and easygoing. It is not the character for falling over (*bìdǎo*). Furthermore, when pronounced *pǐyìfǎn* (匹亦反), it is the character for 'oblique' (*pìzé*). This greatly deviates from the intent of the scripture."

*Dònduì* (頓抴): The upper character is *dūn* (敦, with the phonetic component *tuán* [頁]) and means to drag, pull, or haul. The lower character is *yì* (藝, with the phonetic component *shì* [手]). It is also written as *yuè* (拽), which likewise carries the pronunciation *xié*. The character *tuán* (屯) has the pronunciation *tóng* (䐁), and *chè* (掣) has the pronunciation *chǎnrè* (闡熱). *Tái* (擡) has the pronunciation *tái* (臺). *Yíngyì* (盈藝): The rhyme dictionary *Yùnquán* states that this means to pull something while lying down. It is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic component "world" (*shì*). It may also be written as *yuè* (拽), and it is also interchangeable with the sound *xié* (纈). The character *tuán* (屯) is pronounced *tóng* (䐁), and *chè* (掣) is pronounced *chǎnrè* (闡熱). *Tái* (擡) is pronounced *tái* (臺).

Gopī (the "gǒu" in Gopī is pronounced with an initial *jù* and a final *-fǎn*; it is a transliteration of a Sanskrit word meaning "not seeking") is the name of Rāhula’s mother. It is also called Yaśodharā; the current term "Gopī" is a corruption and abbreviation of the ancient translation.

*Ku* (窟): The phonetic meaning is "a cave" (*kùn wù fǎn*). It is a character formed from the radical *穴* (cave) as the semantic component and [the phonetic] as the phonetic component; alternatively, it is written with the radical *土* (earth) as *堀*. *Kuì* (匱): The reading is *kuí wèi fǎn*. The *Jíxùn* states: "Kui means a casket (*pú dú*) or a box.

It is formed from the radical *匚* (box), pronounced *fāng*, with *guì* as the phonetic component. The version in the sutra as *匱* is an error. Examining the sounds, *cu* (蹙) means to contract or gather; it refers to a small facial expression. It is also written as *qī* (嘁) or *chōu* (𠯗), all four forms being identical. The *Cangjie pian* states: "*Ē* (頞) is the protrusion on the upper part of the nose. The *Shuowen jiezi* states: "*Ē* (頞) is a wrinkle on the bridge of the nose (*bí jīng*). It is composed of the radical *xié* (頁) with the phonetic *ān* (安). It is also written as *xiù* (齅).

*Xiānchángshàngxiāng* (纖長上相): *Xiān* (纖) is read as *yán* (閻) in the *Erya*, where it means "minute. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "fine" (*xì*) and is composed of the radical *mì* (糸, silk thread) with the phonetic *qiān* (籤).

It may also be written as *nián* (孅) with the radical *nǚ* (女). *Wēi* (韱) has the pronunciation *jiān* (尖). *Huǎnwànshàng* (踝腕上): *Huǎn* (踝) is read as *huáwǎ* (華瓦). The *Cangjie pian* states that the ankle is on the side of the foot. The *Shenglei* says it is the bone attached to the outside of the foot. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *zú* (足, foot) with the abbreviated *kě* (稞) as the phonetic. *Wàn* (腕) is read as *wūguàn* (烏灌); it is a vulgar character. The *Wenzi jilüe* writes it with the radical *ròu* (肉, flesh). The *Shuowen* writes it as *wàn* (𢫪), composed of the radical *shǒu* (手, hand) with the phonetic *yí* (𪱙), which is pronounced *yīhuó* (一活). The archaic form is *zhè* (󲀅). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Yili* identifies it as the knuckles of the palm. Yang Xiong says it is the wrist used for grasping. The text here uses *wǎn* (捥), which is also a vulgar character.

*Yě* (𡝩冶): The first character is pronounced *yāojiāo* (夭嬌). The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (Commentary on the Mao Odes) states: “*Yě* means young. The *Chūcí* (Elegies of Chǔ) says: “The graceful bearing and elegant beauty (*tiáotài yělì* 調態𡝩麗). The *Guǎngyǎ* (Extended Lexicon) states: “*Yě yě* (𡝩𡝩) refers to appearance. The *Mao Shī* (Odes of Mao) describes: “The blossoming beauty of the peach tree (*táo zhī yě yě*)” as the dignified appearance of a woman. The *Shuōwén* (Explaining Characters and Analyzing Words) defines it as “skillful,” composed of the radical *nǚ* (woman) and the phonetic *āo* (芺); *āo* has the same pronunciation as above. The script in the current sutra text is written as *lè* (󱷱), which is a vulgar form derived from the abbreviated *nǚ*. In the *Yùpiān* (Jade Lexicon), the current sutra text reads *púgě* (蒲葛), which is not this meaning. The second character, *yě* (冶), is pronounced *yúzhě* (餘者). The *Kǎoshēng* (Investigating Sounds) states: “It refers to the transformative expressions of a woman. The *Zòuyī Shàngxi Jì* (Appended Statements of the Upper Part of the Book of Changes) says: “A seductive appearance leads to regret and lewdness. Lǐu (劉) comments: “*Yě* is also synonymous with *yāo* (妖, seductive/spiritual). The *Shuōwén* defines it as composed of the radical *bīng* (ice/snow) and the phonetic *tái* (台); *bīng* has the pronunciation *bīng* (氷).
*Gùmiàn* (顧眄): The first character is pronounced *gù* (same as 固); the second is pronounced *mián* (with the *biàn* radical). The *Kǎoshēng* states that it means "to look askance.

This is fully explained in the preceding commentary. *Wēiyí* (逶迤): The first character is pronounced *wèi* (as in 畏) with the *wéi* radical; the second is pronounced *yī*. The *Màoshī Zhuàn* says: "To be *wēiyí* means one's path can be winding and its traces meandering. The *Hànshū* says it describes the appearance of water flowing in curves. *Yí* is also pronounced *tuóhé*. The *Hànshī* says: "*Wēiwēi yíyí* is like mountains and like rivers—the appearance of the excellence of virtue. It means that the form resembles the winding curves of mountains and rivers. The *Kǎoshēng* says it means walking slowly and leisurely. Both the *Shuōwén* and other sources treat these as characters formed from the *chuò* (辵) radical, which is a combination of shape and sound. *Chuò* is pronounced *chǔlüè*. In common parlance, this refers to "walking around" or "circling. (Note: The term *chuò* [辵] is used here as a technical term for the radical representing movement.)

"Or 'to lean against' (píng): the character 憑 is pronounced with the departing tone; it means a leaning board or armrest. It is sometimes written as 凭; the form 憑 in the classics is a phonetic loan and not the original character.
'Match' (pǐ): the rhyme is bīn."
Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states that it means "a match" (*pǐǒu*).
The *Guǎngyá* states it means "a class" (*bèi*).
The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* states it means "to pair with" (*pèi*).
The *Erya* states that "he" (*he*) means to join together.
The *Huainanzi* says that five feet is the standard measurement for an average person.
Multiplying five by eight yields forty, which constitutes one *pi* (a pair).
The *Shuowen* states that "four *zhang*" [make one *pi*]. It is composed of "eight" (八) and "box" (匚); the "box" signifies eight sheets of paper joined together to form a *pi*.

The common usage of the character "pǐ" (疋) is incorrect. This common character "pǐ" (疋) contains the number four; it is among the archaic and variant characters (*gǔwén qízì*) and is a standard (*yǎ*) character. Its pronunciation may be *shū*, *shū*, or *xū*.
The lower phonetic component, *ǒu*, has the pronunciation *gǒu* (inverted).
According to the *Guǎngyá*, "ǒu" means "to harmonize" and "pair. It is the number of Yin.
Zheng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states that it means "a pair."
Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that [the character] means "to respond.
The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "Tongren (桐人): composed of the radical 'person' (人) and the phonetic 'Yu' (禺).

Regarding "zhidi" (嫡婦), "di" (嫡) is pronounced *dingli* (丁歷); the *Kaosheng* says it means "the primary and eldest," or "the ruler. The *Zishu* says it means "to uphold correctly. The *Shuowen* says: "Nü (孎): composed of the radical 'woman' (女) and the phonetic 'Shang' (啇). The character "Shang" (啇) is composed of "Di" (帝) and "Kou" (口), forming "Chi" (啻). "Nü" (孎) is pronounced *dingjue* (丁角); it means "cautious and diligent" (*jingnü*).”

*Kuān* (寬): The upper radical is *huán* (桓); according to the *Shuowen*, it means "a large house," composed of the phonetic *mián* (綿) and the phonetic *xiàn* (莧). *Kuàng* (壙): The lower radical is *kuǎng* (晃); the *Mao Shi Zhuan* says it means "empty space," while the *Shuowen* says it means "vast," composed of the phonetic *guǎng* (廣). The character in the received text [of the *Lunyu*] erroneously uses *rì* (日) as the lower radical.

Regarding *gēng* (羹), the upper radical is *gèng* (更) and the lower is *héng* (衡). The *Erya* states that salt and plum are called *gēng*. Gu Yewang says that the harmonizing of the five flavors is called *gēng*. The *Shuowen* writes it with the radical *zhì* (󲌋) as *gēng* (󲏎), and it is also written as *hào* (𩱋) or *hào* (󲚣); these are all archaic characters. The lower part is pronounced *hè* (訶各反). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states: "That which has vegetables is called *gēng*; that which has no vegetables is called *hào*. The *Shuowen* writes it with the radical *ròu* (肉) and the phonetic *jiǎo* (寉); since *jiǎo* is pronounced *hè* (涸), its appearance as *zhāo* (臛) in the scriptures is erroneous.

*Kang-liang* (秔糧): The upper character *kang* (秔) has the phonetic value of *heng* (衡) with the tone of *shenglei* (聲類); it refers to non-sticky rice (*bu-nian-dao*). According to the *Shuowen*, it belongs to the category of *dao* (rice), being composed of the radical *he* (禾) and the phonetic *kang* (亢). In the scriptures, it is written as *jing* (粳) using *geng* (更), which is a vulgar form. The lower character, pronounced *liang* (良), is annotated by Kong [Yingda] in his commentary on the *Shangshu* as "stored food" (*chu-shi*). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "grain" (*gu*), being composed of the radical *mi* (米) and the phonetic *liang* (量). The forms *liang* (糧) and *liang* (粮) are both vulgar characters.

*Dun* (dust): The *Chánglín* (Long-lín) commentary on the *Zhuāngzǐ* states it means "dust. The *Shuōwén* states it means "soil blown up while traveling," composed of the radicals *lù* (deer) and *tǔ* (earth). Its original form was *cū* (麤), an ancient character; in modern clerical script (*lìshū*), the two *lù* radicals have been omitted. The lower character *ài* (埃) is pronounced *āi*. Wáng Yì’s commentary on the *Chūsī* states that *ài* is also dust. The *Cāngjiépiān* states that *gòu* (filth) refers to wind-blown dust. The *Shuōwén* also defines it as dust, composed of the radical *tǔ* with the phonetic *yǐ*.

Regarding "lóu-lǔ" (樓櫓): the first character is pronounced *hòu* with a retroflex initial (*lè-hòu*). The *Erya* states: "A structure that is square and high is called a *tái* (platform); one that is narrow, long, and curved is called a *lóu* (tower). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as a "double-roofed building. The lower character, *lǔ*, is pronounced *lù*. The commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan* by Du Yu states: "A *lǔ* is a large shield used to resist enemies in battle. It is also written as *lù* (樐), which is an archaic form; it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "lù" (*lú*).

Regarding the characters *tián* (窴) and *yē* (噎): the upper part of *tián* is pronounced *tián* (田), and the lower part is pronounced *yān-jie* (煙結) according to the standard reading. In the received text, it is sometimes written as *tián* (填) with the "earth" radical (*tǔ*) and sometimes as *yē* (咽) with the "cause" radical (*yīn*). Neither of these two characters is correct; both are erroneous usages. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines *tián* as "to block," stating it is composed of the "cave" radical (*xué*) and the phonetic component *zhēn* (真). Regarding *yē*, the *Shuowen* says it means "the obstruction of food," with the pronunciation *zhēn-lì* (珍栗). The *Kaoseng Sheng* states that it refers to "qi obstructing the chest and throat," composed of the "mouth" radical (*kǒu*) and the phonetic component *yī* (壹); it is also the same when written with the "food" radical (*shí*) as *yì* (饐).

Regarding the character for "humble" (bēi) in the term *bēixùn*: the *Shuowen* states it is composed of "armor" (jiǎ) and "left" (zuǒ). The *Zītǒng* explains that one who stands on the left wearing armor is humble; it is a compound character based on associative meaning (*huìyì*). The lower part, read as *sūn* (cùn), is defined in the *Shuowen* as "to yield" (*shùn*); it is formed with the radical "heart" (xīn) and the phonetic element "sūn."

The character *wán* (完) [in the sense of "complete"] is explained in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as being composed of the radical *mián* (宀, pronounced *mián*) and the phonetic *yuán* (元). There is also a variant form *mào* (皃), which is incorrect. Regarding the characters for "shoes" (*xié*) and "socks" (*wè*), the *hé* (核) radical is used; these are vulgar forms and not the original characters. Their correct forms are written with the radical *xī* (奚), resulting in *xié* (韤) and *wè* (韈). The *Jiuzi Zhengyun* defines them as "sandals" (*jiè*); they have leather soles and are bound with hemp cord. Yan Shigu’s *Zhengsuyin* states that in the present day, the interior regions use only hemp, while the various non-Han peoples of the southern lands use a mixture of leather, *gǔ* (𮈔), grass, and other materials. The *Kaosheng* identifies them as "grass sandals" (*cǎodī*) and gives the pronunciation *tí* (提). The lower part is pronounced *wǎnfā* (晚發). The *Shuowen* defines them as "footwear" (*zúyī*) and states they are composed of the radical *wéi* (韋) with the phonetic *miè* (蔑). Sometimes they are written with the radical *gé* (革) as *wè* (韈). As for the vulgar forms written with the radicals *yī* (衣), *jīn* (巾), or *pí* (皮)—namely *wò* (襪), *zhū* (袾), and *qù* (󲀼)—the *Yunquan* states that these were all fabricated by commoners of the time and none may be relied upon.

The *xié* (shoes) worn atop boots also belong to the category of footwear; the *Guǎngyá* calls them *jiǎshā*, while others call them *jì* or *wàn*, which are merely different dialectal terms of the Yi people. The *Jixùn* glosses them as *xié*, meaning shoes; they are missing from the *Shuōwén*, so it is unknown which [reading] is correct. Regarding the term *lǚ* (boots), its pronunciation is *lǐ*; it has already been explained previously that King Wu Ling of Zhao favored Hu-style clothing, which has been inherited down to the present day and is now used as court attire.

"Shēn-sù" (申縮) has six reversed forms; in the *Mao Commentary on the Classic of Poetry*, "sù" (縮) means to gather in. Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states it means to withdraw. The *Tainyan Jing* says it means to stop. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as to contract; it is composed of the radical "silk thread" (糸) with "xiù" (宿) as its phonetic component. The pronunciation of "silk thread" (糸) is "mi" (覓).
