*Zǒutiàotíng*: The first character is read as *yáo* (遙) and the second as *fǎn* (反). *Lǎnzhōng*: The first character is read as *luǎn* (卵) and the second as *kōng* (坑) with the tone of *jiǎo* (角). *Dìngpí* (額顱): This is called *dìng*. It is derived from the radical *dìng* (額) with the phonetic *chù* (𡖉). *Bìbó* (臂膊):

The first character is read as *bēi* (卑) with the tone of *yì* (義), derived from the radical *ròu* (肉) with the phonetic *pì* (辟). The second character is read as *bǔ* (補) with the tone of *mò* (莫); this is a vulgar form. The correct orthography consists of the radical *gǔ* (骨) with the abbreviated phonetic *bó* (博). The version of the scripture that uses *yuè* (月) instead is incorrect.

The character for "waist" (yāo) consists of "flesh" (ròu) above and "kǔ guà" (the phonetic component) below; it is written as "kuà" in the Classics, which is a vulgar form. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as "kuò," defining it as "the thigh. It is also written as "yōng," while the *Yunying* writes it as "yāo."
Regarding "mi" (with the *bi* [反] rhyme), the *Shuowen* states it means fine silk.

Regarding "jian" (with the *jian/xian* [反] rhyme), the *Shuowen* states it means the cocoon of a silkworm; it is composed of the radical "silk" (糸) and the character "insect" (虫), with "ni" (薾)—pronounced *zhili*—abbreviated. To write it as "er" (爾) in the *Manjing* is incorrect; it does not form a valid character, nor does the character "silk" (糸) itself form a valid character in that context.

The "small jujube" (*xiǎozǎo*) is the name for a fruit that grows on an old tree; the *Jīng* (Scripture) calls it the "sheep jujube" (*yángzǎo*). The *Shuōwén* states that two *cì* (thorny branches) joined together form "jujube" (*zǎo*), yet the common vulgar form uses two "two" (*èr*) characters to write it as *zǎo*, which is an error.

Regarding "Soma-buddhi" (the lower tone for *buddhi* indicates it is a Sanskrit term), the sutra itself provides its own commentary, stating: "In the language of Sui, it means 'True Moon' (*zhēnyuè*).
[The characters] 󲅡 (pí) and 󲅽 (fù)—with the phonetic value of *sū* and *ān* respectively—both mean 'belly' and both follow the radical for 'flesh' (*ròu*)."
"Marrow and blood" (髓血): although the character for "marrow" (髓) is pronounced *sui* (with the initial *sui* reversed), according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to the fat within the bones;

this has already been explained in detail above. "Beard and whiskers" (髭鬢): the upper character is pronounced *zi* and the lower character is pronounced *bin*; both are written with the radical *biao* (必姚反).

The character 牢 (láo): the upper part is pronounced láo; it is composed of 牛 (ox) and 宀 (roof). The lower part is read as wǔgēng. Lexicons state that it means "firm" or "solid. It is formed with 革 (leather) and the phonetic element 更 (gēng). In the *Jīng* (the *Yìjīng*), it is written as 硬 (yìng), which is a vulgar character.

"Xi-ruǎn": the upper character is pronounced *xī*; the lower character is a phonetic transcription of *rǎn*. The text of the scripture writes it as "ruǎn," which is incorrect. "Zhī-nì": the character is transcribed as *ní* (with the phonetic *zhì*).
According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "fat"; it is composed of the radical "flesh" (*ròu*) with "èr" (*èi*) as its phonetic.
"Sweet" (tián): [The character is composed of] "sweetness" (gān) with the phonetic "zhǎn" (yán fǎn).
It means sweet and delicious. "Lush" (wěng yù): [The first character is] "wǔ" (yù kǒng fǎn) and the second "yùn" (hūn lù).

This describes the flourishing appearance of groves and forests. "Reins" (kòng bì): [The character is] "kòng" (shàng kōng gòng fǎn). The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* says that to stop a horse is called "kòng," and it also says it means "to lead. It takes "shǒu" as the radical and "kōng" as the phonetic. The second character, "bì" (bǐ mèi fǎn), according to the *Shuōwén*, refers to horse reins. It takes "sī" as the radical and "shuì" (shuì yì, shuì zhě shuōwén yún chē zhóu tóu qiè yě; xiàng xíng) as the phonetic. In the scripture, it is written as "máng" (wáng zuò bì), which is incorrect.

The character 騗 (qiàng) is pronounced with the upper part as *piàn* (反) and the phonetic component as *kǎo* (考). The gloss states: "To leap up onto a horse; it takes the radical 'horse' (馬) and the phonetic 'piàn' (扁).

110. Volume 110 of the Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra. Volume 110 of the Bhadrapāla-gṛhapati-parivarta. The character 圊 (qīng) is pronounced with the lower part as *píng* (屏) and *qǐng* (請). The gloss states: "A latrine; a toilet."
*Bēngdǎo* (崩倒): The upper character *bēng* (崩) is pronounced *péng* with the *fǎn* (反) tone; it means to collapse. The lower character *dǎo* (倒) is pronounced *dāo* with the *lǎo* (老) tone;

it means to fall prostrate. *Jiànzù* (箭鏃): The upper character *jiàn* (箭) is pronounced *jiān-xiàn* (煎綫); according to the *Shuowen*, it means "the tip of an arrow. Originally a name for a type of bamboo, because arrows were made from this bamboo, the arrow itself came to be called *jiàn*. The lower character *zù* (鏃) is pronounced *zōng-lù* (宗祿); according to the *Guangya*, it means "the arrowhead" (*cì*). According to the *Shuowen*, *cì* (鏑) is the sharp point of an arrow; *zù* (鏃) means "sharp," formed with the radical *jīn* (金) and the phonetic *zú* (族). The *Yupian* gives the pronunciation *chǔjué* (楚角), which is not yet fully explained.

Regarding "dú" (毒): the phonetic transcription is *ding* (丁) with the tone *li* (歷). Examining "dú," it refers to poisonous medicinal juice. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "di" (滴) means a drop of water falling; the *Shuowen* states it is composed of the radical "water" (水) and the phonetic "ji" (ㄙ, 𠿒). The reading in the scripture as "di" (帝) is incorrect. It is also written as "di" (滴), which has the same meaning.

*Chuan* (pronounced *chuǎn*, with the rhymes *chuān* and *yǎn*): according to the *Àn*, *chuan* refers to inhalation and exhalation. The *Guǎngyá* states that *chuan* is like "turning" (*zhuǎn*). The *Shuōwén* defines it as "rapid breathing," composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic component "duān" (*duān*).
*Bōcā* (pronounced *cāng hé*): this is a Sanskrit term, explained within the sutra itself.

*Ēr-dāng* (ear-ornament): The *Pīcāng* states it is the "filler of the ear. The *Shìmíng* states that a pearl inserted through the ear is called a *dāng*; it is a precious ornament for the ear. *Bì-chuàn* (armlet): Pronounced *chuàn* (with the second tone).

Examining the term *chuàn*, it refers to rings made of gold or silver used to adorn the hands and feet. Lexicons state that what is worn on the foot is called a *zào* (pronounced *zhù* with the second tone), while what is worn on the arm is called a *chuàn*. *Zào* is pronounced *chúxué* (with the second tone).

"Quā lì" (喎戾): The upper character is pronounced *kǔ huái* (苦懷). The *Kǎo shēng* states it means the mouth is crooked or distorted. The *Shuōwén* gives the standard form as "Guā" (咼), meaning the mouth is distorted; it is composed of "mouth" (口) with "guā" (咼) as the phonetic. The lower character is pronounced *lián jié* (憐結). The *Shuōwén* states it means "curved. Because when a dog exits through a door, its lower body must bend and curve, it is thus associated with "big" (大). The text here uses "lì" (綟) with the "silk" radical (糸); this is incorrect. "Lì" (綟) means to tie, to knot, or yellow-colored dye; it does not accord with the meaning of the scripture.

The character *jù* (掬) appears six times [in this context]. Its common vulgar usage is not the original character; the correct form is *jǔ* (匊). The *Shuowen* states that *jǔ* means "to hold in the hands," and its form is that of two hands facing each other, representing the shape of the hands. The *Kaosheng* writes it as *jǔ* (𡷓), which is also written as *jǔ* (󲚟); these are all ancient characters meaning "to grasp with both hands. These are all archaic forms. Today, the character *jū* (鞠) is used interchangeably with them, but this is an error resulting from a misquotation. The lower part of the character *mǎn* (滿) is the radical *shuǐ* (水) with the phonetic *lán* (䓣). The pronunciation of *lán* is the same as the former. The *Shuowen* says: "*Lán* means level. It is composed of *fán* (凡) and the five elements (*wǔ xíng*). *Fán* is divided into one *chén* (辰). Since *fán* represents the two [halves of a cycle], it is therefore composed of two [strokes].

*Tà* (搨): [The character for] *tà* (a low seat) is pronounced with the initial *t* and the final *hé* (合). The *Shìmíng* (釋名) states: "A bed that is narrow and long is called a *tà*; it follows the radical for wood (*木*) and takes *㚘* as its phonetic. Regarding the character for *zuò* (坐) below: the *Shuowén* (說文) defines it as "to stop" (*zhǐ*). It is composed of the abbreviated form of *止* (*zhǐ*) and *土* (*tǔ*), forming *yīn* (垔); in ancient script, it is written as *zuò* (坐) using two persons (*二人*).
The character *mó* (摩) means "to rub" (*xiāo*) or "to grind" (*kǎo*);

it is pronounced with a retroflex initial and has the phonetic component *shǒu* (hand). *Jì* (驥) refers to a swift horse; Gao You’s commentary on the *Mu Tianzi Zhuan* states it is a designation for an excellent horse, and it is also said to mean "rapid. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as the "fine talent" of a horse. It is a compound character formed from both semantic and phonetic components.

"Holding both a knife and a spear" (刀槊) is a vulgar character; the correct form is "spear" (矟), which refers to a long pike. According to the *Bóyá*, "knife and spear" are weapons. The form used in the sutras is "zhé" (𣓞), which is also a vulgar character. These were fabricated by people in recent times; they did not exist originally.

"Bān" (斑) is pronounced *shàng* with the supplement *bǔ jiàn* (補間); the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "mottled markings. The *Shenglèi* states that it is derived from "bān" (班) with the radical "wén" (文). The *Yupian* states it refers to variegated colors; that which has a mixture of black and white markings is called "bó" (駮), with the supplement *jiǎo* (角) pronounced *fǎn* (反).
"Melted copper" (*róngtóng*): the first character is pronounced *róng*. To smelt metal is called "melting"; it means to liquefy. "Brass" (*tōushí*):

the second character is pronounced *tǒuhóu*. According to the commentary, brass is a type of metal similar to gold; it is more refined than copper and ranks next to gold. The superior quality is nearly indistinguishable from gold and originates from foreign lands.

*Bìliè* (擘裂): The first character, *bì*, is pronounced with the *mò* rhyme (bì-mò-fǎn). According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means "to divide. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states it means "to split open. Gù Yěwáng explains that the character is formed from the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic element "open" (*pì*). It refers to tearing apart with the hands.

*Lìfǔ* (利斧): In the *Fū* (夫) rhyme group. Lexicons identify this as a *yuèfǔ* (鉞斧), a battle-axe; the *Shuōwén* defines it as "an axe for hacking objects," formed with the radical *jīn* (斤) and the phonetic *fù* (父). The current scriptural text writes it as *fū* (鈇); this character has both level (*píng*) and rising (*shàng*) tones. The *Shuōwén* defines [the variant] as "to chop grass"; the *Zītǒng* says it means "a chopping blade"; the *Cāngjiépiān* says "a *fū* is like a block for pounding. None of these meanings apply here. Following the scripture, it should properly be written as *fǔ* (斧).

"Qiānwàn" (牽挽) is read as "shàngqiǎn jiān fǎn" (上遣堅反). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of "mìng" (冖) and "niú" (牛), with "xuán" (玄) as the phonetic component; "mìng" is pronounced "mì" (覓). The lower part, "wàn" (萬), is read as "fǎn" (返) and has "kǎo" (考) as its phonetic. It means "to pull and lead. [The character] is composed of "niú" (牛) and "miǎn" (免) as its phonetic. It is incorrect for the scripture to use the hand radical instead.
"Bean-ankle" (wǎn guān fǎn jīng): this does not form a valid character and is unfit for reliance.
111. Volume 111 of the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Chapter 111: "Flattery" (yú chǎn yáng zhū fǎn chǒu rǎn fǎn): see the previous explanation.

*Luíshòu* (羸瘦): The first character is pronounced with the *lì* rhyme (追反) and the radical *rǎng* (從羊); the second character is pronounced with the *jiù* rhyme (色救反). It is a vulgar form (*súzì*). Both characters appear in the previous explanations.
*Qígài* (乞匃): Pronounced *gài*. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radicals *rén* (人) and *wáng* (亾), which have already been explained previously.

"Miāo" (犛牛) is pronounced *mǎo* (with the rhyme category *bão*) and also has the pronunciation *máo*; it is also interchangeable with the previous term, as has already been fully explained. In the current text, it is written as *māo* (貓) following the radical for dogs, which is incorrect. This refers to the cat that catches mice; it is not the ox.
*Pái* (pronounced *tiáo tiào yáo fǎn*) is derived from the radical "hand" (*shǒu*).
*Dùliàng* (pronounced *táng luò fǎn*) means to measure.
*Bèn* (pronounced *pén mèn fǎn*) is defined in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as dust; it is also written as *bèn*, meaning dust or defilement.

"Hedàn" (荷擔): The upper character is pronounced "hé" (何) and also means "to carry. The lower character is read as "dūgān" (都甘反). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to shoulder a burden," composed of the radical "hand" (手).

112. Volume 112 of the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*. "A-vyavartita" (阿惟越致): An ancient translation from the Sanskrit; the text is archaic and plain. It is also called "Abhibhūti" (阿毘跋致), which in the Tang language means "Non-retrogression" (不退轉).
The meaning of "subverting" (*juhuài*) has already been fully explained above. Regarding the *Lokāyata Sūtra*:

in Sanskrit this is called *kudṛṣṭi*; in its correct Sanskrit pronunciation it is *lokāyatika*. This refers to the doctrines of the Lokāyata heretics, which accord with worldly common sentiments and consist of speculative views such as [the belief that] phenomena are eternal or existent.
*Zhuā*: pronounced *zhuó guā* (as in "to strike"). It refers to a horse-whip and is written with the "wood" radical (*mu*). Its preceding explanation has already been provided. *Yì*:

pronounced *yí dì* (as in "to change" or "to shift"). The lower part is pronounced *yǔ*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the character is composed of the "hand" radical (*shou*) and the phonetic component *yu*; the sound of *yu* is *yú*.
The character 𤡜 (yàn) is composed of 足 (foot) and 一 (one), with the phonetic 閻 (yán); the same applies to the "no satiety" (無厭) mentioned below.

The character 擾 (rǎo), meaning "to disturb" or "to agitate," is formed from 手 (hand) and the phonetic 夒 (náo). The sound of 夒 is nú dāo; 夒 is the name of a beast, which is the original intent of the form's construction. In seal script (篆書), the form was taken for its aesthetic momentum, with the lower portion divided into two sections where two dots hang down on both sides, left and right. From the character 止 (zhǐ) downward, it was written as 夒 using 夂 (zhuì). Consequently, it became visually similar to the character 憂 (yōu). Later, due to the cursive style (草書) prioritizing brevity, those of little learning who did not understand the original character began to imitate the form of 憂. Thus arose this error; this mistake has persisted for a long time. Alas! It is truly difficult to correct. The sound of 頁 is xié; the sound of 夂 is suī.

The character for *bi* (悲) is pronounced with the *hu* and *ao* rhymes (hào). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to howl" (*hao pao*). However, "howling" is also used for loud wailing; it is composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic "guilt" (*zuì*). Its original form is written with "white" (*bái*) and "root" (*běn*), where *běn* is pronounced *tān*. The version in the current scripture, which uses "self" (*zì*) and "pungent" (*xīn*) to form "guilt," is incorrect; this is actually the archaic form of the character for "guilt" (*zuì*).
*Zhui* (槌): The upper radical is *zhang* (長) with the *zhui* (追) phonetic; the lower part is *xiōng* (凶). It means to strike with the fist upon the chest. *Shào* (紹):

The upper radical is *shao* (遶) with the *shi* (爾) phonetic. According to the *Erya*, *shao* means "to succeed. The *Shifa* (謚法) states that one who "remotely succeeds to a former position" is called *shao*. The lower part is the phonetic *zhao* (召), which itself consists of the radical *kou* (口) and the character *dao* (刀).

Regarding the character for "fly" (*cāngyíng*): the text of the *Cāngzì jīng* (Scripture on the Character Cāng) writes it as *táng*, which is incorrect; such a character does not exist. The lower radical is pronounced *zēng*. The *Fānyán* (Dialectal Dictionary) states that west of the Guān region, they call them *yíng*. The *Shuōwén* (Explanations of Characters and Words) states that insects with large abdomens are written with the radical *chóng* (insect) and the phonetic *mǐng*; the pronunciation of *mǐng* is *měng*.

The character 栲 (kǎo) has the upper radical *kǎo* (the sound of striking), meaning to beat or to strike; in the scriptural text it is written simply with this *kǎo* sound. The lower part is *lüè*, which also has the pronunciation *liàng*. The *Zhèngzìbiàn* states that some say it means "to flog" or "to canister. The character 拷 (*kǎo*) means to strike or to interrogate by force; it is composed of the radical 手 (hand) and the element 京. It is also written as 剠.

"Chí-chěng" (to gallop) is explained by the *Zhuo* commentary on the *Zuozhuan* as "to gallop" (*chí*) and "to run" (*zǒu*). The *Guǎngyá* says it means "to rush" (*bēn*). The *Shuowén* defines it as "to drive straight ahead," composed of the radical for "horse" and the phonetic *pǐ-dīng* (the character *pǐ* with the tone *dīng*). It is composed of *yóu* and *kǎo*. The version of the text that uses the character *zhāo* (composed of *biàn*) is incorrect; *kǎo* has the pronunciation *kǎo*. *Note: The term *pǐ-dīng* refers to the character *pǐ* (匹) with the level tone *dīng* (丁), which serves as the phonetic component for the character *chí* (馳).*

Regarding "zhúkuài" (逐塊): it is explained word by word according to the *Shuowen*. It follows the radical "zhū" (豖), which is pronounced "chǔlù" (丑錄反). In the classics, it is written with the radical "shǐ" (豕), which is incorrect. "Shǐ" is pronounced "shǐ" (始); the second character is "kǒuwài" (苦外反), or alternatively written as "yùn" (𠙽).

*Shǔn* (胡外反, *hù wài fǎn*; also 古外反, *gǔ wài fǎn*; both readings are correct) and *ná* (拏効反, *ná xiào fǎn*). The former has already been explained as consisting of the radical "market" (*shì*) and the radical "person" (*rén*); the scripture uses "bǐng" (*bǐng*), which does not form a valid character. *Qiū lì* (𢤱戾):
the upper character is read as *lù dǒng fǎn* (*lù dǒng fǎn*) and the lower character is pronounced *lì*. It means perverse or stubborn.

"Thye-sai" (噎塞): the "yan" (燕) is pronounced with the "xie" (頡) radical; the *Jing* (經) reads "yan" (咽), which is incorrect. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of "kou" (口) and the phonetic "yi" (壹).
"Zeng-e" (憎惡): pronounced "wu gu" (烏固). "Yong-chuang" (癰瘡):
the upper character is pronounced "yong" (邕) and the lower is "ce shuang" (測霜); it is also written as "chuang" (創).
*Chú* (除) and *dài* (鬀)—the latter pronounced *tiān* (天) and *dì* (帝) in the opposite sense—refer to the secular act of shaving the hair.

*Xūfà* (鬚髮): "hair and beard. The character for *xū* (鬚) is formed through associative meaning (*huìyì*) according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, with the phonetic component *shù* (踰, pronounced *yú*). Both characters share the radical *biāo* (髟), which is pronounced *bìyáo*. Both are examples of *zhuǎnzhù* (transferred-notation) characters.
The term "chēng" (稱) here means "to verify" (證), as in the subsequent instances.
"Piāomò" (漂沒): "piāo" (漂) is pronounced with the *pí* and *yáo* rhymes; it means to be carried away by water. "Yàonáng" (藥囊):
"nǎi" (乃) is pronounced with the *dāng* rhyme; it refers to a bag (*dài*). A bag that has a bottom is called a "náng" (囊).
*Huài* (坏): "Unfired earthenware. It is written with the radical *tǔ* (earth) and the abbreviated form of *bēi* (cup). 113.

Volume 113 of the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Chapter 113, "The Assembly on the Jewel Peak" (*Ràoliáng huì*). *Gōngkè* (恭恪): "Respectful and reverent. It is written with the radical *xīn* (heart) and the phonetic *gòng*. The lower character is pronounced *kānggè*. The commentary on the *Shūjīng* by Kǒng states: "Kè means reverence. The *Shuowén* writes it as *kè* (愙), with the radical *xīn* and the phonetic *kè*.
In "聽著" (tīng zhù), "著" is pronounced with the *qian* tone, following the precedent of "反尊許卑" (fǎn zūn xǔ bēi) and "下文聽服我聽" (xià wén tīng fú wǒ tīng).

In "矬陋" (cuó lòu), "矬" is pronounced *cái gē* (as defined in the *Guǎngyá*: "cuó means short"); "陋" is pronounced *lóu dòu*. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that "lòu" means small; Gu Yewang says it means an ugly appearance; the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "narrow and constricted," formed from the radical "阜" (mountain/earth) and the phonetic "󱾈," or written simply as "󱾈."

The character 笑 (xiào) is composed of the radical for "teeth" (齒) with the phonetic "反" (fǎn). The *Guǎngyá* states that "蚩" (chī) means "to slight" or "to be disordered. The *Mānsìshī* says it refers to an expression where the will and mind are harmonious and joyful. [The character] follows the radical "insect" (虫) and the phonetic "㞢" (yí); the received text’s 咲 is incorrect. The *Shuōwén* writes it as 𣢑 (xiào), defining it as an expression of playful laughter. The lower part is pronounced "xiào-yào-fǎn. The *Jīngǔjīnzhèng* says "笑" means "joy. The *Shuōwén* omits this character. The *Shìyào* says it follows the radical "bamboo" (竹) and the phonetic "夭" (yāo); the vulgar form following "犮" (bó) is an error. Village elders and foolish men speak recklessly according to their own whims; such accounts are utterly unreliable.

*Tì* (tears/saliva): pronounced *shàng tiān* (upward to heaven) and *jì xià tǔ* (downward to the earth). It is composed of the radical *kǒu* (mouth) and the abbreviated form of *tuǒ* (a mound) as the phonetic.

*Lí* (separation): pronounced *yīng gé* (parrot/obstruction). The *Kǎo Shēng* says it means limitation and obstruction. It is composed of the radical *fù* (high ground) and *è* (to squeeze/block), which itself is composed of *hù* (door) and *yǐ* (one). Nowadays, the common practice of using *hàn* (rock shelter) and *yǐ* (already) to form *è* is an error; this mistake has persisted for a long time. In many scriptures, the character is written with the radical *mù* (wood) or with the hand radical (*shǒu*) as *è* (to press/clench), which refers to grasping the head and does not carry this meaning.

*Mén* (捫): The upper radical is *mò* (沒), pronounced with the *bēn* (奔) rhyme; the glosses state it means to stroke or to grasp, and also to feel with the hand. According to the analysis, *mén* (捫) also means to wipe; it is composed of the radical *shǒu* (手) and the phonetic *mén* (門). The lower character is *lì* (力), pronounced with the *xiào* (󲘽) rhyme. The *Guǎngyá* states that *tìqì* (涕泣) refers to tears; it is composed of the radical *shuǐ* (水) and the phonetic *lì* (戾).

"Bo" (搏) is pronounced as "táng luán fǎn" (唐欒反). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states that "bo" means "firmness" (*gù*). Regarding the phonetics, it means "grasping. The *Guǎngyá* states it means "to manifest" (*zhù*). According to the *Shènglèi*, it is formed with "shuǎn" (專) as the phonetic component following "shǒu" (手). The character "shuǎn" (專) is formed with "cùn" (寸) as the semantic component and "yuān" (叀) as the phonetic component; the pronunciation of "yuān" is "zhuān" (專).

The character for *zāo* (糟) is pronounced as early as *láo* (勞). Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "In the case of *yí* (醴), *yì* (酏), and *bù jǐ* (不泲)—where *yì* is pronounced *yǐ* (以)—those that are *jǐ* (泲) are called *qīng* (清), while those that are not *jǐ* are called *zāo* (糟). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "the dregs of wine," written with the radical *mi* (米) and the phonetic *cáo* (曹). The character below, *zī* (淄), is pronounced *shǐ* (史). The *Shuowen* further defines it as "filth"; it is written with the radical *shui* (水) and the phonetic *zǎi* (宰). It may also be written as *tàn* (䔂), which is the same; *diàn* (澱) is pronounced *diàn* (殿).

*Ménqiè* (門篋): The character *mén* is pronounced with the *qiān* and *yè* rhymes; it refers to a box for storing scriptures and books. It is formed from the radical "bamboo" (*zhú*) and the phonetic "qiè" (*qì*). The character *qì* has the same pronunciation as above; it is formed from the radical "box" (*fāng*) and the phonetic "jiá" (*jiá*). The character *jiá* is pronounced like *jiǎ*.

*Kuranda* is the name of a flower in the Western lands according to the Sanskrit language. Its flowers are red and their appearance is brilliant; their substance is as hard and rigid as wood or stone, and their odor is so foul and putrid that it is like rotten excrement, making it unbearable to approach.
*Chǔ* (麁) means coarse; *kuàng* (獷) means wicked.

*Shēng* (生) refers to the name of a weed, *piè* (稗), which resembles grain but is not grain. *Suì* (穟) is a term for the ears of grain (*hé*); it is also written as *suì* (穗). *Yǐng* (穎) means the tip or ear of grain. *Note:

The phonetic glosses provided in the original text are transcribed here as they appear.* *Chǔ*: (麁) cuī (瓜猛反) *Kuàng*: (獷) kù (獷惡也) *Piè*: (稗) pì (蒲賣反) *Suì*: (穟) suì (生音遂) *Yǐng*: (穎) yíng (頂反) *Zhì*: (󲏗) zhì (或作穗) *Suì*: (穗) suì (遂) *Yǐng*: (穎) yíng (頂反)

*Būshēng* (逋生): In *Bǔmóu* (補謀), Yuè Wáng says it means "late-born" or "born later. It is composed of the radical *chuò* (辵) with the phonetic *fǔ* (甫). Alternatively, it is written as *bǔ* (𨗗), where *chuò* has the pronunciation *chǐluè* (丑略反). *Jīféi* (肌肥): The upper character *jī* (肌) is read as *jìyí* (上記冝反).

The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it means "skin and flesh," composed of the radical *ròu* (肉) with the phonetic *jǐ* (几). The lower character *féi* (肥) is read as *fèiwēi* (下費微反). According to the *Zìshū* (字書), it means "abundant flesh," composed of the radical *ròu* (肉) and the abbreviated phonetic *fēi* (妃).

"Chuángwò" (創疣): The lower character is pronounced *yóu*. The *Kǎo Shēng* states it refers to wind-nodules on the skin or fleshy excrescences; sometimes written as "yōu" with the radical for flesh. In common parlance, these are called "lónghóuzi" (隆侯子) and so forth.
"Qìngtā" (倩他): The initial is pronounced *qīngxìng* (清性). The *Yùnyīng* states that borrowing the strength of another is termed "jièqiàn" (借倩).
*Xiūzhì* (修治) and *xiūlǐ* (修理) are also written as *xiūlǐ*; the reason for this is the same.

*Biān* (鞭) is pronounced as *biàn* (with the tone of *mián*). The *Guìyuàn Zhūcóng* (桂苑珠叢) states that to punish a criminal with leather is called "whipping" (*biān*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文解字) defines it as "driving or galloping"; it is composed of the radical "leather" (*pi*) and the phonetic component "bian" (*biàn*).

Regarding the character *zhé* (謫): the upper radical is *zhāng* (張) with the reversed *gē* (革), and the phonetic component is said to be *shēng* (聲). It means both "to reprimand" (*zhé*) and "to punish" (*fá*). It is composed of the radical for speech (*yán*) and the phonetic *shāng* (啇). The common variant form is incorrect; as for the lower character *fá* (罰), the upper part is *wǎng* (网) and the speech radical is *dāo* (刀); the version with four [strokes] is an error.

Regarding "nail-piercing" (ding-zhe), according to the sūtras it should correctly be the character *zhe* (磔). Although the current sūtras write the character *zho* (挓), this character does not exist in any of the various dictionaries; its pronunciation is therefore unknown. Furthermore, [the original] writes the character *zhe*.

The character 丸 (wán) is used interchangeably with 反 (fǎn) or 𡐢 (fèn); however, its use in the classics as 糞 (fèn) is incorrect. The archaic form is 𡊅, and the *Shuowen Jiezi* uses 󲚒; both of these ancient characters are correct, yet they are rarely used by people of the present day. The *Yupian* states that "糞" means to discard or filth, which has already been explained above.

Volume One Hundred Fourteen. *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Volume One Hundred Fourteen, Part Two of the *Ratnarāśi* (Jewel Pile). "Qi" (齊) [pronounced as in "jiè" (祭), meaning a limit; the lower character is pronounced as "jì"]. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of "yōu" (𢆶, pronounced yōu) and "chéng" (成). "Yōu" (𢆶) is pronounced as yōu.
Regarding "zhānglù" (麞鹿): the upper character is pronounced zhāng; those with antlers are called lù (deer), while those without antlers are called zhāng, which refers to a small deer.
Regarding "yúchǎn" (諛諂): the scriptural text often writes this as "yù," which is incorrect; its pronunciation is yù (fourth tone), as the character "yù" is not etymologically appropriate here.

*Xiùshǒu* (漱首): "jiù" (救) is also pronounced as *sāng* (桑) with the *zòu* (奏) rhyme; both are in common usage. Yingyun says: it means to rinse the mouth with water. It is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic "sù" (*sù*, pronounced *sū hóu*).
"Jìngdí" (淨滌) means to cleanse; "yǐ" (犾) is a variant.

"Fènsào" (糞掃) has the lower radical "sāng" (桑) with the tone reversed; it is a vulgar character. "Nàiyī" (納衣) is its name. It takes the abbreviated form of "shuò" (󰆠) as its phonetic. In the sutra text, "sǎo" (掃) is used as a borrowed character for this purpose. It is written with the hand radical.

The character 鄣 (zhāng) means "to block wind"; it is a barrier against the wind on the ground, formed from 阜 (fù). The character 暴 (bào) means "scorched by the sun"; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "to dry" (*xī*). It is composed of 日 (sun), 廾 (pronounced gǒng;

"gǒng" represents the image of two hands grasping an object), and below that, 米 (grain)—it is a compound character (*huìyì*) formed by combining these meanings. Since the meaning of "scorching" is already complete with this, the form in the scripture with 田 (field) and 恭 (reverence), further adding 日 (sun) to become 曝 (pò), is incorrect. This character originally had the radical 曰 (yuē), which has now been changed to 田 (tián); furthermore, the lower part was altered to 恭 (gōng). This is not the meaning of "scorching. To forcibly add a "sun" is a great delusion, and such errors have long been widespread.
*Mosquito* (wénzhǒng): the first character is pronounced *wén* and the second is pronounced *mògēng*; these are flying insects that bite humans.
*Mázi*: the pronunciation is *mò*; these are minute flying insects found in excrement, similar to mosquitoes.
*Xiǎn* (浣濯) means to wash; its pronunciation is *zhuó*.

*Shàn* (善) means to sew; it is read as *duī* (追芮反). Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that it means "to connect"; the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to join and attach," derived from the radical *mì* (糸) with the phonetic *chuò* (叕).

*Shàn féng* (善縫): "Féng" is read as *mēng fǎn* (蒙反). According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to join seams. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "sewing clothes with a needle," composed of the radical *mì* (糸) and the phonetic *fēng* (逢).

*Tàn huài* (綻壞): "Tàn" is read as *zhái xiàn fǎn* (宅限反). The *Kǎoshēng* states it means "the opening of a seam. Alternatively, it is written as *zè* (䘺) with the radical *yī* (衣). The *Shuōwén* writes it as *tàn* (袒), composed of the radical *yī* (衣) and the phonetic *dàn* (旦).
*Jinlü* (金縷): *lǜ* is pronounced *liǔ* (力禹反). In the *Shuowen*, it states: "Thread; composed of the radical *mì* (糸) and the phonetic *lóu* (婁) in abbreviated form.

*Qīngzào* (輕躁): Pronounced *zǎo* (早到反). Jia [Yan]’s commentary on the *Guoyu* says: "Agitation and disturbance. Gu Yewang says: "Movement. Zheng’s commentary on the *Lunyu* says: "Lack of tranquility. In the *Shuowen*, it is written as *zào* (趮), composed of the radical *qī* (𡗱) and the phonetic *zào* (喿).
*Kṣānti-dā* (懈怠): The first character is pronounced *jiè* (戒) and the second is pronounced *dà* (大).

115. Volume 115 of the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Chapter 115: The Assembly of Bodhisattva Akṣayamati. *Bhadrapāla*: A name for a bodhisattva within the *Bhadrakalpa* (賢劫); in the language of Tang, it means "Worthy Protector" (賢護).

*Pārijātaka-kubera*: In the Sanskrit language, this is called *pārijātaka*; in the Tang language, it is translated as "Round-Born" (*yuánshēng*). According to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, to the northeast outside the city walls of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven palace, there is the Pārijātaka tree, one hundred *yojana* in height. This is the supreme place where the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens enjoy sensual pleasures. When the flowers of this tree bloom, their fragrance spreads a hundred *yojana* with the wind, and even against the wind, it can still perfume an area of fifty *yojana*, because its branches extend everywhere.

Regarding "thicket" (*choulin*): it is the opposite of "sparse. According to the *Guangya*, it means "dense"; the *Cangjie pian* says it means "multitude"; and the *Shuowen jiezi* says it means "many," composed of the radical for grain (*he*) with the phonetic *zhou*. As for "thick" (*ji*), its pronunciation is *ji* (as in "succession"). There are various names for flowers [in this list], but none of them exist in this country in abundance, so they have not been translated. These terms have already been fully explained at the beginning of the sutra. Regarding "thicket" (*zhi*), it is as previously noted.

Volume One Hundred Sixteen. The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume One Hundred Sixteen, from the Mañjuśrī-parivarta. "Jin-huang" (金磺)—the character *guang* (磺) is pronounced *ku-meng* (古猛). It refers to metal ore; it is sometimes written as *kuang* (礦) or *gui* (𨥥). The text of the sutra uses the character *guan* (丱), which is an archaic form.
The *chui* (hammer) is an iron mallet used for striking and chasing metal; it weighs eight *jin*.
The character for *zhi* (to strike/treat) is pronounced with the upper tone *chi*.

The character for *pao* (blister) is pronounced *pu miao* (蒲皃反); according to the *Shuowen*, it means "the arising of qi on the face. According to the sutra, a *pao* is when the skin rises up, about to produce a flower [a pustule]; the sutra uses the character *bao* (胞), which is a phonetic error.

Regarding "yìng chè" (映澈), the *Chánlièfǎn* (纏列反) gloss states that it means "water is clear and transparent. It is composed of the radical for water (氵), the character "yù" (育), and the character "zhī" (支). To write it with the radical for walking (彳) and the character "qù" (去) as "chè" (徹) is an error.

Volume One Hundred Seventeen of the Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra, Chapter One Hundred Seventeen: The Assembly of Ratnaśikhin Bodhisattva. Translated by Dharmarakṣa. [The characters] "chúnshú" (淳淑) are read as *shǔn* (上, first tone) and *shù* (下, fourth tone). This has already been fully explained above.

"Dai" (逮) means "to reach" or "to attain"; the reading "dai" (柰反) is correct, while the version of the scripture using "lu" (逯) is incorrect. "Lu" (逯) is pronounced "lu" (祿); "lulü" (逯逯) means "moving with haste," which greatly deviates from the meaning of the scripture.
"Na-shu" (那術) is a transliteration of the Sanskrit term; in its original form it is "nayuta," a numerical unit for vast numbers.

*Chōu-yǔ* (瘳愈): The first character, *chōu*, has the phonetic *chōu-liú*; the Master Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states that *chōu* means "to recover. The second character, *yǔ*, has the phonetic *zhǔ*; it is also written as *yù*. The *Kǎoshēng* states that when an illness recovers, it is called *yù*.
*Gōu-suǒ* (鉤瑣): The phonetic is *sāng-guǒ*; it is the name of a Bodhisattva.
"Prabhūtaratna" (溥首) is a name for a Bodhisattva; "Pu" (溥) is derived from the sound of "water" (水), and "Shou" (首) is derived from the characters "Fu" (甫) and "Cun" (寸).

"Ru" (耎) is pronounced as "mei-er-yuan-fan" (美而兖反); according to the *Kao Sheng* (考聲), it means "weak" (耎弱), and the common vulgar form "Ruan" (軟) is incorrect. The text of the sutra uses "Ru" (濡), which is read as "ben-er-zhu-fan" (本而朱反), but this does not accord with the meaning of the scripture.
Gandharvas are also called *taghada*;
asuras are called *āśūlu*; and garuḍas are called *jialuoluo*.
*Mātara* is *kiṃnara*; *mahoraga* is *mahoraga*.
Among the translations of the various heavenly names from India into Chinese since the Dharma flowed eastward, those of the Western Jin period are the most clumsy.
"Wúyāng" (無央) is pronounced "liáng" (良); the version in the Canon as "wù'āng" (無鞅) is incorrect.
"Bǎojì" (寶髻) is pronounced "jì" (計); Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Yīlǐ* states it means "a tied topknot"; the current canonical text as "jié" (結) is incorrect.

"Xiāo-míng" (消冥): "míng" is pronounced as *mò* (莫) with a *píng* (瓶) rhyme. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radicals *mìng* (冖), *yuè* (曰), and *liù* (六). The aforementioned scripture uses the character "míng" (冥), which is incorrect.
"Xián-xià" (閑暇): the pronunciation is *xià* (夏). In character dictionaries, "xiá" (暇) is synonymous with "xián" (閑); it is composed of the radical *rì* (日) and the phonetic *duàn* (叚).

*Qījuàn* (棄捐): The first character is pronounced *qì*; the second is pronounced with the initial *y* and the final *-uán* (恱玄反). The rhyme explains that *juàn* also means "to abandon. It is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "yuān" (*huān*).

*Yìkǎo* (𡕆瑕): The first character is pronounced with the initial *y* and the final *-i* (意). The commentary states that *yì* is a sound of sorrowful lamentation. It is composed of "one" (*yī*), "deficiency" (*qiàn*), and "mouth" (*kǒu*). There is also a variant written as *zì* (恣), which is a vulgar form. *Zhù* (壴): The pronunciation is *zhù* with the final *-gǒu* (竹句反).

"Dàn-pà" (恬怕): the upper character is read as *gǎn* (敢) and the lower as *pǔ-bái* (普白). It is a phonetic compound; "dàn" (恬) means tranquility, and "pà" (怕) means peace or sufficiency. Both derive from the radical "heart" (心). To write it with the radical "water" (水) as "dàn-bó" (澹泊) is not the meaning of the scripture.
The character *zú* (族) [is pronounced] *cóng hú fǎn* (叢斛反). In the Classics, it is written with the "hand" radical (*shǒu*) and the "ya" radical (*yǐ*);

writing it as *ái* (挨) is incorrect and does not form a valid character. *Xúnxún* (恂恂) [is pronounced] *sī xún fǎn* (思巡反). Wang Su’s commentary on the *Lunyu* states that *xún* refers to an appearance of being warm and respectful; the *Yunquan* dictionary explains it as "compliance. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* states that it means "constant repentance and trepidation."

The character *jiǎo* (佼) has the phonetic *xiào* (爻) and *kǎo* (考) as its components; the gloss states it means "to learn" (*xué*) or "to emulate" (*xiàng*). It is sometimes written as *xiào* (效), *xiào* (斅), or in the vulgar form *xiào* (傚). The reading found in the canonical text as *jiào* (校) is an error. *Jiàowèi* (校尉) is the name of a military official; furthermore, the pronunciation *jiào* (教) is not semantically appropriate here.

To read "jie" (節) with the phonetic value of "jie" (解) and the rhyme of "gu" (革)—that is, as "jia" (賈)—is incorrect. To write "yi" (猗) where the rhyme is "ji" (譏) is an instance of ancient scholars' biased views leading to the erroneous use of characters.

Based on the preceding and following passages of the scripture, it should correctly be the character "yi" (依). The scripture states: "body and mind have no reliance," "there is nothing to rely upon or cling to," "not relying on this present life," and "not relying on words and phrases. Yet, in all these instances, the character "yi" (猗) is used instead; this is a grave error. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines "yi" (猗) as "a castrated dog," which is certainly not the intended meaning here. This is likely because those who transcribed the teachings by hand had little learning in the classical texts and, to avoid their own private taboos, borrowed this character. It should be rectified to the correct character "yi" (依).
The character 駛 (shǐ) means "swift. The *Yìnyùn* states it signifies rapidity; it is composed of 馬 (mǎ) as the semantic component and 史 (shǐ) as the phonetic component.

The character 泛 (fàn) means "to float" or "to drift"; it is composed of 水 (shuǐ) and 乏 (fá), or alternatively written as 汎. The character 流 (liú) means "downward flow"; it is composed of 水 (shuǐ) and 云 (yún). The character 川 (chuān) forms the word for "river," while 略 (lüè) forms the word for "briefly" or "summarily. As for 經 (jīng), it forms the word for "scripture" or "classic."

The character *yāngxìn* (殃釁) is read as *xīn* (忻覲反). The *Yùnyīng* states that *xìn* means "crime. Examining its phonetic component (*shēng*), it means "gap" (*xì*). The *Shuōwén* defines it as "sacrifice," composed of the abbreviated form of *cuàn* (爨) and the phonetic *yǒu* (酉), with *fēn* (分) as the phonetic. Due to the transformation in cursive script (*lìshū*), it was altered to *biāo* (󱿘), which is an error. Furthermore, it was changed from *yǒu-fēn* to *biāo*, resulting in the form *xì* (舋); this has been perpetuated, but it is incorrect and far removed from the original meaning. *Cuàn* is pronounced *cāngluàn* (倉亂反), and *biāo* is pronounced *biāo* (標也).
The character *chuàng* (創) is pronounced *chǔ* or *shuāng*; it is sometimes written as *chuāng*, which is a vulgar form. This [character] *zhèng* (這) is pronounced *jiàn* (上言件反);

according to dictionaries, this character is also used in the sense of "to meet" (*yíng*). However, one might simply say "to meet and arise" (*yíngqǐ*), or use "to meet" (*yíng*) alone, or use "to rise" (*qǐ*) alone; what harm is there in the meaning? Yet, you insist on seeking out this obscure text and forcibly writing this character *zhèng*, merely boasting of your vast knowledge and erudition. You mislead later students, and among those who read and examine your work, there are none who do not blink in astonishment. Furthermore, for a petty person to boast of his own clumsiness by acting as a scribe is not the vision of a gentleman.

"Xian" (尠) is pronounced *xiǎn* (with the radical *páng* and the phonetic *bó* reversed); according to the *Shuowen*, it is formed with the radical *cǎo* and the phonetic *xiānjiǎn*. In the *Yunying*, "xian" means "few.

Regarding "short-lived" (*duàn mìng*), the current text of the sutra uses the character *dòu* (梪), which is incorrect. *Dòu* is pronounced *dòu*; according to the *Shuowen*, "dòu" refers to a sacrificial vessel. In several preceding passages, the meaning of the sutra requires this to be the character "short" (*duàn*), yet the text instead writes "vessel" (*dòu*), which is utterly inconsistent. Observe that there are many such errors and discrepancies in the preceding text. For instance, the character "rely" (*yī*) is written with the radical *shǒu* and the phonetic *yǐ*; "dàn" and "pà" both use the radical *shuǐ*, yet they are written as "yú" and "chǎn," with the former pronounced *yù* and the latter *chǎn*. There are numerous other instances of "bì" and "pì. I cannot describe them all in detail. All of these stem from the fact that the scribes who transcribed the text had meager learning; thus, the text of the sutra is plain and simple, and its usage of characters contains errors that cannot be left unaddressed.
"Crawling" (qí xíng) is pronounced qì.
"Panting" (chuǎi xī) has the second character pronounced chuān yuǎn.
"Kneeling and bowing" (guì bài) has the second character pronounced kuī wéi.

*Tāotiè* (饕餮): the first character is pronounced *tāo* and the second *tiè* (as in *tiě*). The commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states: "To covet wealth is called *tāo*; to covet food is called *tiè*. It is also written as *yìng* (飻). *Pì* (癖):
pronounced *bēi* (亦) with the tone *fǎn*. *Cāngjié* says it means "unable to walk."

118. Volume 118 of the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*. "Yojana" (俞旬) [the character 旬 is pronounced with the initial *y* and final *-u*; it is a corrupted and abbreviated transcription of the Sanskrit term]. It was formerly called "youyan" (由延), or "youxun" (由旬), or "yushena" (喻闍那); none of these are correct. The Sanskrit sound is *yojana*. The *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that it is the distance a king’s army can travel in one day, approximately thirty *li* (里).

*Xuán huí yíng yǐng fǎn ěr yǎ*: "Huì" means distant; it is composed of the radical "辵" (chuò) with "冋" as its phonetic component. The pronunciation of "冋" is the same as that above. The text [of the *Shuowen*] uses "向" instead, which is incorrect.

*Qū suì shàng zhuāng suǒ fǎn kǎo shēng yún shān shí bù píng yě yì zuò zǔ zǔ xiǎn yě xià suī zuì fǎn yùn yīng yún shēn yuǎn yě cóng xué suì shēng yě.* "Qū suì": The upper character is pronounced "zhuāng suǒ. According to *Kǎoshēng*, it means that mountain rocks are uneven. It is also written as "阻," meaning "obstructed" or "precipitous. The lower character is pronounced "suī zuì. According to *Yùnyīng*, it means "deep and far-reaching. It is composed of the radical "穴" (xuè) with "遂" as its phonetic component.
"Chao-lüe" (抄掠) means to plunder; "chao" (抄) is defined in the *Zi-shu* as "to seize," with the lower radical pronounced *li-yue*.

It means to take by force or to rob. "Shi-dan" (食啖) is pronounced *tang-lan*; the *Kao-sheng* states it means to feed a person with food and drink. The *Shuo-wen* defines "dan" (噉) as "eating," written with the mouth radical and the phonetic "xian" (臽), where "xian" is pronounced *xian*. In the scriptures, it is sometimes written as "gan" (敢) to form "dan" (噉), which is a vulgar usage and not the correct character. The upper character "shi" (食) is defined in the *Shuo-wen* as being composed of "ji" (亼) with the phonetic "jing" (精) pronounced *ru*, and "zao" (皂) pronounced *bi-li*; if it is written with "liang" (良) to form "shi" (食), that is a vulgar character.

*Menkun* (門閫): The root meaning is "opposite. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states it means "the threshold of a door. The scriptural text uses the character *kun* (梱) with the radical for wood; the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "a wedge at the door.
This contradicts the intended meaning of the scripture. *Echuo* (惡𤡜): *wu guo* (烏固) and *wang yan* (往焰).
*Chuāngyǒu* (Window): The phonetic component is *jiǔ* (酒). The commentary on the sounds states that it refers to piercing a wall with wood to form a lattice-like structure;

it takes the radical *piàn* (片). *Yīn* (Mats/Bedding): The initial sound is *yīn* (因). Zheng’s commentary on the *Lìjì* says, "The *yīn* is also a *rù* (bedding). The *Yùpiān* says it is a bedding made of tiger skin. The *Shuōwén* says it refers to a double mat on a carriage; it takes the radical *cǎo* (草) and the phonetic *yīn* (因). Alternatively, it is written as *ān* (鞇) with the radical *gé* (革), the final sound being *rú* (辱). Guò Pǔ says, "The *rù* is tiger skin. According to the *Shēnglèi*, it refers to a bedding mat (*rù jiàn*).

Regarding the term *wǎnyán* (綩綖): the upper character is pronounced *wǎn* and the lower *yán*. The scripture states that *wǎnyán* refers to items such as flowered carpets, brocade cushions, and dance mats. However, according to the *Lìchuán* (Ritual Tradition) and lexicographical works, *wǎnyán* actually refers to the ornamental silk decorations on a head-dress. This greatly deviates from the meaning of the scripture; it would be more appropriate to emend it to the two characters *wǎnyán* (婉筵) to accord with the scriptural sense.
"Cū" (粗) is pronounced *zǎi gǔ* (在古反). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "Cū means coarse (*cāo*) and sparse. Gu Yewang says: "Cū means rough and brief.
"Cuō" (撮) is pronounced *chuàn cuò* (竄𢲻反). The *Kaosheng* states: "To grasp with the hand; it takes the radical 'hand' (*shou*)."
*Bèn* (pén mèn fǎn; alternatively written as *bèn*; the *Zìshū* says it means dust or defilement). *Qiébiàn* (qián yè fǎn;

the *Kǎoshēng* says it means wisdom, swiftness, speed, or vigor; it is composed of the radical "hand" [手] with the phonetic "jíe" [疌], or sometimes written with the grass radical [艹] as *jiàn* [󲘞]; its meaning is the same).

The character *chóu* (儔) is pronounced *zhǎngliú* (長流). It means "companion" (*pǐ*) and is formed from the radical "man" (人) with the phonetic "life" (壽). In the received text, it is written as *chóu* (疇) with the radical "field" (田), which is incorrect. Furthermore, the character *pǐ* (匹) is sometimes written with the lower part as "man" (人), forming *pǐ* (疋); both of these forms are erroneous.

Volume 119, *The Great Treasure Accumulation Sūtra*, Volume 119, *The Assembly of Queen Śrīmālā*, translated by Liu Qi of the Tang dynasty. Regarding the kingdom of Kośala, the Sanskrit term is not sought for its literal meaning; the self-explanation states that the "City Free from Strife" (*Ayodhyā*) is the Central Heavenly Realm (*Madhyadeśa*).

To "seek and trace" (*xúnyì*) means to investigate; *yì* also means extensive or elegant. According to the *Shuowen*, *yì* means to draw out. In the *Fangyan*, *yì* means to unravel a thread or to roll up and unroll.
"Bì" (蔽) is pronounced *bēi* (卑) with the rhyme *mèi* (袂); it means to cover or obscure.
"Yú" (逾) is pronounced *yǒu* (庾) with the rhyme *zhū* (朱); according to dictionaries, it means to surpass or leap over. It is also written as *yú* (踰), and its usage and meaning are identical.

Volume One Hundred and Twentieth of the Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra; Volume One Hundred and Twentieth: The Assembly of the Vast Sage (Vaiśvānara-rṣi-parivarta). Translated by Liu Qi of the Tang Dynasty. The term *kukkuṭa* (拘抧羅) has already been explained as "cock."

*Kaliṅga* (迦陵伽) and *śuka* (上薑佉)—the latter being pronounced with the *qiang* and *ke* finals—are both Sanskrit names for national birds; these have already been fully explained at the beginning of this sutra.

Regarding the characters *lin* (林) and *sou* (藪)—the latter being pronounced with the *zou* final—dictionaries state that they refer to grassy marshes. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "A marsh (*ze*) that has no water is called a *sou*."
*Narada* (那剌陀): This is a transliteration of a Sanskrit name for a *ṛṣi*. *Pāṅgu* (蓬):
"Páng" (蒲蒙反) means hair is disheveled like a tuft of *páng* grass.

*Qūlì* (卻粒): "Què" (上) is pronounced *qiānglüè fǎn*; the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is composed of the radical *jié* (音節) with the phonetic *gǔ* (谷聲). "Qiánglüè" (強略反) refers to the character in the classics; the common usage is "qù". Below, "lì" (力邑) and the *Shuowen* state that grain is called *lì*.

The character 蹲 (cún): the first syllable is pronounced cún; the second is the compound of 昌 (chāng) and 與 (yǔ), with the radical 虍 (hū, pronounced hū); it is composed of 夂 (suī, pronounced suī) and 几 (jǐ). The *Jīng* (scripture) uses 處 (chù) as a vulgar variant.
The character 悚 (sǒng): the pronunciation is sù yǒng fǎn; it means to tremble in fear or dread.
"White rope" (*báiséng*) refers to a white cord; "dried mulberry" (*kàozào sāngdào*) refers to being parched and dry. The "three-pronged wood" (*sānjù mù*;

*jù* pronounced as *jù*) is also called the "three-forked staff," approximately two feet in length, with one end like a stake and the other end having three prongs, each about two or three inches long. It is a personal implement used to support a water flask. In the Western Regions, pure practitioners and Brahmins all revere it; they always carry the flask to wash themselves and cleanse away physical impurities. They plant this three-pronged wood in the ground and place the water flask across the fork so that the water flows down steadily to be used for washing the hands. Scholars from those lands who travel abroad to seek the Way also carry this three-pronged wood along with their flasks and bowls.

Śakra (the upper tone "she" being a corruption of the Sanskrit; the correct Sanskrit pronunciation is Śakrā) is an alternative name for Śakra-devendra. This [sect] takes its name from its founder, following the practice of naming after the leader.

"Face wrinkled" (*miàn zhòu*; *zhòu* is pronounced with the *zōu* rhyme). "Raising the eyebrows" (*tái méi*; *tái* is pronounced as in *tāi*): because the Venerable One’s eyebrows were long enough to cover his eyes, he raised them with his right hand.

"Carrying" (*xié chí*; *xié* is pronounced with the *huì* rhyme): this is a vernacular character; its correct form is written as *xié*, composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "guī" (*shuǐ*). Its pronunciation is the same as above. It was altered from the cursive script (*cǎoshū*) by adding the "radical" *nǎi* (the "woman" radical), which is incorrect.
"Xiā mó (蝦蟆)"—the first character is pronounced xiá and the second má; it refers to an aquatic insect, a type of frog.

"Chī niǎo (䲭鳥)"—the first character is pronounced zhì (with the initial *ch* and final *-i*); it refers to a kite or hawk, sometimes written as chī, chī, or yíng. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "zhuī" (隹) also denotes a bird; these designations are mutually interchangeable. The text's reading of "zhì" (蛭) is incorrect; "zhì" is pronounced zhì and does not accord with the meaning of the scripture.

*Ganzhe* (sugarcane): the first character is pronounced as *gān* (the sound of "sweet"), and the second is pronounced as *zhè* (the opposite of "night"). It is also written as *hán* or *hān*. The juice extracted by boiling it forms sugar, such as granulated sugar, honey, and refined sugar.
*Púpú* (creeping): the second character is pronounced as *péngběi*. It refers to crawling on one's elbows and knees, prostrating oneself as the ultimate expression of reverence.

*Niṃguda* is the Sanskrit name for this tree, which is so called in the Western Regions. Its trunk is straight, without knots, perfectly round, and lovely; it is over three *zhang* above the ground before branches and leaves appear. Its seeds are minute, like the flowers of the willow. This tree does not exist in the land of Tang; those who say it is a willow tree are mistaken.
"Yun hanhan" (雲涵含): "Han" is pronounced with the *gan* (紺) rhyme; it means vast clouds are spread out. "Haoqian" (壕塹):

"Hao" is pronounced with the *gao* (晧) rhyme, following the sound of "kao" (考); "qian" (塹) refers to the deep moats surrounding a city wall. "Chengxiayia" (城下也): "Xia" (下) is pronounced with the *qian* (僉) rhyme; it refers to the long ditches beneath the city walls.

"Grain reserve" (liángzhù): the upper radical is *lì* (read as *jiǎng* in the Shuowen); the Shuowen defines it as "storing food. Du’s commentary on the Zhuan states: "To store (*zhù*) means to accumulate (*xù*) and hoard. The Shuowen further explains that *zhù* means "to accumulate," composed of the radical *bèi* (貝) with the phonetic component *níng* (宁).
The first character, *dī* (隄), has the initial *dǐng* (丁) with the final rhyme *xi* (奚);
the second character, *fáng* (防), has the phonetic *fáng* (房). *Fēngtāo* (風濤) refers to great waves;

*tāo* (濤) has the initial *táng* (唐) with the final rhyme *láo* (勞). An *yuán* (黿) is a large turtle; it is written with the radical *mǎn* (黽) [phonetic *měng* (猛)] and the phonetic *yuán* (元). A *táo* (鼉) is described in the *Shānhǎijīng* (山海經) as being common in the Yangtze River; Guō Pǔ states that it resembles a lizard but is long and large, possessing scales, and its skin can be used to make drums—this is what is referred to in the *Máoshī* (毛詩) as "the *táo* drum. It is written with the radical *mǎn* (黽) and the phonetic *nà* (𠹈), where *nà* has the phonetic *nà* (那).

The character for *jīngní* (鯨鯢) is pronounced with the initial *qú* and the final *yíng* (上渠迎反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is a large fish in the ocean. The *Huainanzi* says, "When the *jīngyú* dies, a comet appears. The *Zuozhuan* refers to it as a "great fish. Xu Shuzhong remarked that it is the king of fish; it is also written as *qīng* (䲔). The lower character is pronounced *ní* (音霓). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* identifies it as a *zhēng* (𪋤) or *jīng* (鯨); the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as a "piercing fish" (*cìyú*). Both are phono-semantic compounds (*xíngshēng zì*).

*Jiǎn* (作繭): Pronounced *jiǎn* (堅顯反). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "the cocoon of a silkworm. It is composed of the radicals for "silk" (*mì*) and "insect" (*chóng*), with a simplified form of "to cover" (*fù*). The scriptural text writes it as *jiǎn* (蠒), which is a vulgar usage that does not constitute a standard character.

*Cái* (纔): Pronounced *cái* (藏來反). The *Yunchuan* states that *cái* means "merely" or "just. It is composed of the radicals for "silk" (*mì*), "to gather" (*chùlüè*), and "rabbit" (*tù*). The phonetic for "silk" is *mò* (覔); the phonetic for "gather" is *chūlüè* (丑略反); and the phonetic for "rabbit" is *tǔ* (吐也).

*Gǎn-zǒng* (皯䵴): The first character is pronounced *gāng* (剛) with the *qie* (ㄑ) radical; the second is pronounced *zàng-dìng* (藏鄧). The *Tōngsùwén* (通俗文) writes it as *zhēn* (𤿧). A dark, tawny complexion on the face is called *zǒng* (䵴), according to the phonetic analysis (*kǎoshēng*). It refers to black moles on the face. Yán Shì’s *Zhèngyīn* (顏氏證音) states that what is currently called *zhēn* (𤿧) in the inner regions is pronounced *zèng* (贈); it is also written as *mó* (䵟) or *lǐ* (󲁎), which are vulgar characters.

*Yā* (壓): On the ground, its sound is like *yà* (鴨) or *kǎo* (考); it means to suppress or to weigh down. It is also pronounced with the rhyme of *yǎn* (黶) and *yè* (葉), meaning to fill and press down.

*Tián* (填) is pronounced *zhēn* (珍). *Shū* (姝): The upper radical is *chǐ* (齒) and the phonetic is *zhū* (朱). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (毛詩傳) says that *shū* refers to beautiful countenance. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文解字) says *shū* means "excellent. The *Fangyan* (方言) says that in the regions of Zhao, Wei, Yan, and Dai, people call what is good "shū. It is composed of the radical for woman (*nǚ*) and the phonetic *zhū*.

The upper character 輻 (fú) is pronounced as *fú* (the sound of *kǎo*); the *Shuōwén* states it is the spokes of a wheel, with the pronunciation *liáo*. Gu Yewáng says it refers to that which converges at the hub and extends to the rim. The lower character 轄 (xià) has the pronunciation *xiá*; Gu Yewáng says it is the iron linchpin at both ends of the axle. The *Shuōwén* says it is the sound of the wheel; one also calls it *hé*, or *huá* is likewise the same.

The upper character *yuán* (轅) is pronounced as *yuán*; it refers to the two shafts at the front of a carriage. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "the *yuán* is the *zhōu* (pole). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Kaogong Ji* states, "The *zhōu* is the *yuán*. The *Fangyan* says that in the regions of Chu and Wei, the *yuán* is called the *zhōu* (pronounced *zhǒuliú*). The lower character, *è* (厄), is written as *è* (軛) in the scripture, which is a vulgar form. Zheng’s commentary on the *Kaogong Ji* identifies it as the wooden block at the end of the shaft that presses against the ox’s neck; it is a corruption of what is colloquially called the "carriage-grid" (*chēgé*). It is composed of the radical "carriage" (*chē*) and the phonetic "oppression" (*è*), the latter being the character *è* with the radical "door" (*hù*) and the phonetic "yǐ" (*yǐ*). To write it as *ài* (厄) is incorrect.
*Luò* (絡) [upper tone *luò*]: a cord or network. *Dúlóu* (髑髏):
[upper tone *dú*, lower tone *lóu*]; the skull of a human head. *Chángfèi* (腸肺): [upper tone *cháng*];

the large and small intestines and the lungs. The *Báihùtōng* states: "The large and small intestines are the repositories of the heart. The *Cāngjiépian* states: "The intestines are the channels. [The character for *cháng*] follows the radical for flesh (*ròu*) with the phonetic *yì*; [the lower part of the character for *fèi*] is pronounced *huì*. The *Báihùtōng* states: "They are the essence of metal and the treasury of metal."
The character *xīn* (心) is the spleen (*bì*, pronounced with the *mí* rhyme); it is the organ of the soil. The *Báihùtōng* states: "It is the essence of earth; its color is yellow;

it follows the radical for flesh. The character *gān* (肝) is the liver; the first tone is *gān* (木藏), and the second is *wèi* (下為偽反). This is a vulgar form; the correct form is simply *wèi* (胃). The *Báihùtōng* states: "The stomach is the palace of the spleen. It follows the radical for flesh and is also a pictographic character.
*Tuán* (搏) [pronounced *tú luán*]: composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "zhuān" (專);

it has already been explained previously. *Chīwěn* (鴟吻): the upper character is read as *shí* (時) and the lower as *wǔfěn* (武粉). It refers to the ceramic animal ornament on the roof-ridge. *Wěn* (吻) means "mouth"; it is shaped like the beak of an owl (*chī*). A dictionary states that it is used for the "great beak" (*yā tiān dà quì*) [of the roof-ornament], with the sound *xū wèi* (吁衛).

*Zǎo* (藻): To adorn. It is pronounced with the *lǎo* rhyme and the *kǎo* phonetic. It means "color" or "literary composition. It is composed of the radical *cǎo* (grass) and the phonetic *sào*. The latter is pronounced with the *shèng* (yì) rhyme and the *kǎo* phonetic. *Shì* (飾): To decorate, to embellish, to refine. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to manifest"; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means "to polish. It is composed of the radical *jīn* (cloth) and the phonetic *sì*.

*Tiao* (眺) is explained as "gazing from afar" (*yuǎnshì*). Ying Shao’s commentary on the *Hanshu* states that *tiao* also means "to look toward" (*wàng*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "the eyes not being straight"; it is composed of the radical "eye" (*mù*) with "zhào" as its phonetic.

"Xuánjiàn (軒檻)": *xiāng* is pronounced *fǎn* (as in *xiānfǎn*); *wéizhào*’s commentary on the *Hànshū* states that "xuánjiàn" refers to the floorboards of a pavilion. "Diāo cuì (凋顇)": *diāo* is pronounced *dīngyáo* (as in *dīngyáo*);

Dú’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* says it means "withered and injured," while Jiǎ’s commentary on the *Guóyuè* says it means "decayed and ruined. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "half-injured," composed of the radical *bīng* (ice/snow) with *qíng* and *suì* below and *kǎo* as the phonetic component; it describes a countenance that is emaciated and haggard.
*Pò* (㽄): The initial sound is *xī* (奚) or sometimes written as *sī* (廝) or *sī* (嘶). The *Kǎo Shēng* states it is a "broken" sound. *Kān* (龕): The rhyme is *hán* (含).

The *Kǎo Shēng* states that carving into a mountain wall to form a niche is called a *kān*. The *Shuowén* defines it as the appearance of a dragon, composed of the radicals *jīn* (今) and *lóng* (龍); the common version with *hé* (合) is an error.
*Kṣa-zhù* (刹柱) refers to the flagpole of a banner.

*Yín-xiào* (吟嘯)—the second character being pronounced with the *xiào* rhyme—is explained in the Commentary on the *Shijing* by Zheng Xuan as "contracting the tongue to blow forth sound. According to the *Han Shih*, when songs have no fixed lyrics or melodies, they are called *xiào*; it is also written as *xìào*.
*Yàn* (pronounced *yān* with a retroflex initial; the sound is like that of *kǎo*) means a joyful banquet; it is also written as *yàn*. *Yǐn* (drinking) refers to a gathering for feasting.
*Hào* (to like/delight in) is pronounced *hào* (with an *āo* initial and a *xī* final).
*Liú xián* (drooling saliva): the character for *liú* (flow) is correct when there is a dot above it; *xián* (below) refers to the liquid from the mouth (*xiáng yán*).

*Mouai* (摩捼): According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to crush. It is also said that it is formed by the two hands rubbing together. It is composed of the radical "hand" (手), the element "woman" (女), and the phonetic "grain" (禾).

*Sǒngrán* (聳然): Guo’s commentary states that "sǒng" means "to stand upright. In the dictionaries, it refers to hair standing on end. It is composed of the radical "ear" (耳) and the phonetic "sound" (聲).
The *Chōng-cháng* (傭長) commands that the character for "window" (*yǒu*) in the Classics is incorrectly formed from the radical "piece" (*piàn*).

[In fact,] *chuí-zhòu* (垂皺) is pronounced with the rhyme *zōu* (鄒, with the tone *shòu*); the *Yùn-quán* (韻詮) states it means "the skin does not expand. The *Shuowén* (說文) states it means "the gathering of skin," formed from the radical "skin" (*pí*) with the phonetic component *chū* (芻).

*Li-gǎn* (黧皯): The first character is pronounced *lí*; the second is pronounced with the rhyme of *rǎo* (󲉡󲒍). According to the *Kǎoshēng*, it refers to a complexion that is blackish-yellow; the pronunciation *lí* is a corruption. *Éimáo* (耏毛): Pronounced *ér*.
According to the *Kǎoshēng*, it refers to the hair on the sides of the cheeks. It is sometimes written as *jiǎo* (髷), composed of the radical *sān* (彡) with the phonetic *ér* (而).

*Huángtǎn* (Yellow Carpet): Its name is derived from a foreign sound; some transcribe it as *tǎnkǎo*. The phonetic gloss states it is made of fine hairs and originates from Tibet. *Qīnglíng* (Clear and Cool): The character *líng* is pronounced with the *dīng* rhyme.

*Héhūn* (Conjoined at Dusk): This is the name of a tree. By evening its leaves naturally fold together two by two, and only open again the following morning. Because it opens during the day and closes at night, it is called "Conjoined at Dusk" (*héhūn*).

*Jiànròu* (雜糅): *ni* with the rhyme *zhòu* (反); *qián* (詮) means "to explain. *Ròu* (糅) also means "mixed. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "grain" (*mǐ*) and the phonetic "soft" (*róu*).

*Mílóu Shān* (彌樓山) is the same as *Xūmílú Shān* (須彌盧山); both are corruptions of the Sanskrit term. In Chinese, it is translated as "Wondrous High Mountain" (*Miàogāoshān*) or "Wondrous Radiant Mountain" (*Miàoguāngshān*).

"Pressing down" (tiānyā): the character above is read as jīn (斤) with the *fǎn* (反) tone; "as a stabilizing weight" (zuòzhèn): the character below is read as qù (去) with the *shēng* (聲) tone, which is an error. "Below" (xià): read as àn (黯) with the *jiǎ* (甲) *fǎn*;

alternatively written as yā (押). "Inhaling" (hūxī): read as yì (𩐗) with the *yì* (邑) *fǎn*. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it refers to internal breath or drinking. It may also be written as xī (吸) or xī (歙); all are interchangeable.
*Agate* (*mǎnàoshí*) is the name of a precious gem; the first character is pronounced as *mǎ*, the second as *nǎo*.

*Vīṇā* (here transcribed as *bìmáoluó gǔ*): the first character is pronounced as *bí mí* (with the *mí* having a retroflex *ṛ*-like sound), the second as *niáo* (pronounced *ná* with a retroflex *ṇ*), and the third as *luó* (in the *Cílúhé jīng* it is written as *lí*; this common usage is not the correct orthography).
Regarding "canopy" (xiǎn): the *Shìmíng* states that a vehicle canopy is used to ward off the heat; the *Shēnglèi* calls it a "carriage covering" (chēmàn). Regarding "square and even" (fāngzhěng):
the character "zhěng" is pronounced *zhēng* (with the radical for "mountain") and means "to align" or "to level."

Regarding "tái xiè" (terraces and pavilions): Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states that a "tái" (terrace) is a building erected upon a platform; it further states that a structure without an enclosed chamber is called a "xiè" (pavilion).

Regarding the character for "flower" (huā) in "huā duǒ" (flower-cluster): its occurrence as "huá" in the Classics is incorrect. Regarding "duǒ" (cluster): the *Kao* (Examination) notes that when fruit hangs down from the front or sides, it is sometimes written as "duǒ."

The *liú* (旒) is a net-like fringe that hangs from the front and back with beads; the script for this character in the Canon is written as *liú*, which is an abbreviation. It is composed of the radical "jade" (*yù*) and the phonetic "flow" (*liú*).
To tread upon it: the first character is pronounced *qián* (前) and the second is pronounced *tàn* (談) or *nà* (納).
*Luǒgǒng*: The first character is pronounced *lú*; the second is pronounced *huì* (with the phonetic components "人" and "會").

It means to paint. The Master Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states: "To join together the five colors in painting is called *huì*. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* states: "It means painting," or it is also written as *huì*.
*Indra* is a term from the Sanskrit language; it is another name for Śakra.

"Dù" (肚) is not [the correct character]; above it is *tú* (徒) with the *hù* (戶) radical, and below it is *niǎo* (鳥) with the *jià* (嫁) radical. The [standard] classic text uses the character "𢇁," which is a cursive script (*cāosū*) form that does not constitute a valid character.

*Airāvaṇa* is the Sanskrit term. This name of the elephant king is that which Śakra, Lord of the Devas, constantly rides; he possesses great supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). *Huīyàn* (輝艶) is a vernacular character;
its correct orthography is written with the radical *hé* (盇). The character *hé* (盇) is composed of *dà* (大) and *xiě* (血), and its pronunciation is *hé*.
The character 脃 (cuì) is pronounced with the *shuān* and *suì* finals; it is composed of 肉 (flesh) and a simplified 絕 (severance). It is not the case that the scripture uses 危 (perilous).
The character 旒 (liú) is pronounced with the *sāng* and *guǒ* finals.

The character 嚬 (pín), meaning to knit the brows, is pronounced with the *bī* and *mín* finals. The character 妒 (dù), meaning jealousy, has the phonetic value *dū* and *gù*; Zhong Xuan stated that "to harm one's appearance is called jealousy" (*dù*). It is composed of 女 (woman) and 戶 (door). It is not the case that the scripture uses 石 (stone) or 后 (empress).
*Jiāojù* (驕倨): Pronounced *jūyù* (居御反); it means arrogant and haughty.
*Huángjù* (惶遽): Pronounced *qùyù* (渠御反); the *Yùnquán* (韻詮) states it means rapid or urgent.
*Sàbiàn* (颯便): Pronounced *sānzhuǎn* (三匝反); it refers to a swift wind, though it is sometimes written as *sà* (颯).
*Wěi cuì*: the first character is pronounced *wěi* (with the "wei" rhyme) and the second is pronounced *suì* (with the "sui" rhyme).

*Xián zhuó*: the pronunciation is *zhuó*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the character is composed of "mouth" (*kǒu*) and "pig" (*zhū*; pronounced *chǔ lù*), and it is incorrect for the *Jing* (classical texts) to include "pig" as a component.

In the word *diǎojù* (掉舉), the upper character is pronounced *tiáo* (亭曜反) and the lower is *jǔ* (舉); it is incorrect for the scripture to write it as *táo* (桃). As for the lower part of the character *jǔ*, it follows the radical for "hand" (手);

the scripture also writes it with the radical "hand" (才亦手字也). In *xūxī* (歔欷), the upper tone is *xū* (虛) and the lower is *xī* (希). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that it refers to the appearance of weeping; He Xiu’s commentary on the *Gongyang Zhuan* states that it means sorrow. Both are words formed by combining shape and sound (*xíngshēng*).
