The twenty-three scriptures totaling thirty-four fascicles listed above by Huilin share the same phonetic commentary as this fascicle. *Mahāvaipulya-triśikṣā-sūtra*, Fascicle 1, Upper Part. Compiled by Huilin. Regarding "various grains" (*zá gǔ*): the former character, *gǔ*, is pronounced with the *cái* rhyme (合).

This was already fully explained in the eighth volume of the *Qián yìnyì* (前音義). The *Zìtǒng* (字統) states that "grain" (*gǔ*) means continuity. There are hundreds of names for grain, all of which are subsumed under five categories: namely, *jì* (millet), *shǔ* (panicled millet), *dòu* (beans), *mài* (wheat/barley), and *má* (hempseed). Those belonging to the *jì* category are called "spike-grains"; those belonging to the *shǔ* category are called "scattered-grains"; those belonging to the *dòu* category are called "pod-grains"; those belonging to the *mài* category are called "awn-grains"; and those belonging to the *má* category are called "tree-grains. Therefore, they are called the "five grains. The *Shuowén* (說文) defines "grain" (*gǔ*) as the general name for the hundred grains; it is composed of the radical "grain" (*huó*) and the phonetic "shell" (*ké*).

"Bó-biào" (貘豹): the first character is pronounced *mò*. The *Shān-hǎi jīng* states that the Southern Mountains abound with *bó-biào*. Guō Pǔ says: "The *bó* resembles a *pí* (bear) but is smaller; it is yellowish-black in color, its fur has a luster, and it is able to eat copper and iron; it originates from Shǔ. The *Ēr'á* calls it the "white leopard" (*bái-biào*). The *Shuōwén* [explains] it as belonging to the *zhì* radical. This character *bó* is often omitted in the received text, but since it exists in the Sanskrit manuscript, I have added it here. According to the textual context, it should follow [the previous entry]. The second character, "biào" (豹), is pronounced *páo*. The *Shuōwén* defines it as a beast resembling a tiger, marked with circular patterns of black flowers and smaller than a tiger; it also belongs to the *zhì* radical. The sound of *zhì* is *chì*. Both "biào" and "bó" are examples of characters formed by combining semantic and phonetic components.

The character for *xi* (rhinoceros) is pronounced *xiáng* (祥) with the radical *yǎng* (養). The *Shān-hǎi-jīng* (Classic of Mountains and Seas) states that Mount Dàoguò is abundant in rhinoceroses (*xi*). Guō Pǔ says they are the largest among beasts; their color is either blue or white, they have long snouts resembling those of pigs, and the tusks of the large ones are one *zhàng* long, while those of the small ones are still five feet long. This beast is by nature jealous. The *Shuōwén* says it gives birth once every three years and that the character is a pictograph.

The character for *yuán* (羱) is read as *yú*, *yuán*, or *wǔguān* (five tones), both of which are attested in the *Erya*. It refers to the wild sheep; Guo Pu states it resembles the domestic sheep of Wu but has larger horns. The reading in the received text as *xīng* (𦍘) is incorrect. The lower radical is pronounced *dīng-xī*. The *Commentary on the Mao Shih* states that *dǐ yáng* (羝羊) means a male sheep. According to the *Guoyá*, it is also called *xióng* (雄). A three-year-old male sheep of the Wu region is called *yuán* (𦍞); these are all characters formed from both semantic and phonetic components.

The *qúyù* (鸜鵒): the upper character is read as *jù* (具) with the phonetic *yú* (愚), or alternatively written as *qū* (鴝); the lower character is read as *yù* (欲). According to the *Sànmǔ* (󲎍鵒), it resembles a *shìjié* (似舌) bird; its beak has hair-like bristles, and its two wings are distinguished by mottled white markings. It is also known as the *hángāo* (寒皐).

*Kūṭara* (the first character pronounced *jù*, the second *jīngyǐfǎn*): This is a name for a bird in the Western regions according to the Sanskrit language. This bird is able to produce beautiful sounds that people delight in hearing; it is commonly called the "Beautiful-Sounding Bird" (*hàoshēng niǎo*).

The *heji* (the first syllable pronounced *hé*): The *Shanhai jing* states that Mount Huizhu is abundant with *heji*. Guo Pu says they resemble pheasants but are larger, blue in color, and have feathered horns on their heads; they stop fighting only when one has died. They are wild pheasants. This is a word formed from both its shape and its sound.
"Diao-jiu" (鵰鷲): the first character is pronounced "diao" and the second "jiu. Its meaning has been fully explained in the second fascicle of the *Da banruo* (Great Prajñāpāramitā).
"Chasha" (遮沙) is a Western Indian name for a bird; this bird does not exist in this country.

*Ru* (茹): pronounced as *zhu* (翥) in reverse; according to the *Liji* (Book of Rites), eating the flesh of birds and beasts is called *ru*. It refers to consuming their blood and their fur and flesh. *Jinjūka* (緊祝迦): a Sanskrit name for a jewel;
the first character is pronounced as *yin* (引) in reverse, and the second as *zhongrou* (終宍); in ancient translations it was sometimes written as *Jiānshùjiā* (堅叔迦).
*Vibhītaka* (pronounced *xīng* in the rhyme; the name of a fruit tree in the western regions, which is now called *vīraka*).

*Yùzhāng* (the second character pronounced *zhāng*): *yùzhāng* is a great timber tree. The *Nánzhōng Yìwù Zhì* states that it takes seven years for it to reach maturity; if used to build a boat, it will inevitably engage in combat with dragons.

*Niú jì* (牛棘) is pronounced *jǐn lì* (力反); it is the name of a flower pavilion in the West. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of two *cì* (朿) radicals; the version in the [classical] scriptures with two *lái* (來) radicals is incorrect.

*Gòu niú* (搆牛) is pronounced *gǔ hòu* (古候反); it means to use one's hands to milk a cow. *Niú* (𪭺) is pronounced *luán kuò* (鸞括反). The *Shijing* says: "Thinly milking the cow" (*bó qí jiāng niú*). Both characters for *gòu niú* (搆𪭺) are written with the hand radical.

"Flower garland" (huāmán) is a borrowed character; its original pronunciation was mírán. It is now borrowed to mean "flower garland. A flower garland is an article for adorning the body in the Western regions. It consists of flowers from trees and shrubs strung together with thread and dyed in five colors. Regardless of whether one is male or female, it is placed upon the head or body as an ornament, much like a sash or ribbon.
"Róu" (柔) is read as *yuǎn* (兗); the edition of the Sūtra uses "rǎo" (𣽈), which is incorrect; subsequent instances in the text follow this same principle.

"Qīnglíng" (清泠): the lower character is read as *lìng* (丁反). "Qīnglíng" describes water that is clear and pure; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "water" (*shui*) and the phonetic "líng" (*ling*). The version of the Sūtra using "bīng" (氷) is incorrect. If it is pronounced with the tone *lè* (勒打反), it does not accord with the intent of the Sūtra.
The character for "beard" (xū) is composed of the radical *yán* (a reversed lotus stamen) and the phonetic *shān* (written as *huǎn*).

It is written with *shān* (彡); it is incorrect to use *guǒ* (果). The character for "nest" (*chù*) is composed of the radical *chái* (a reversed *zhì*) and the phonetic *yíng*. According to the *Shuowen*, it is a pictograph representing a bird in a tree; it is incorrect to use *guǒ* (果) in the sutras. The character for "cavern" (*kū*) is composed of the radical *kuì* (a reversed *gǔ*). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that a cavern is an earthen chamber; according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *xué* and the phonetic *qū*. It is incorrect to use *mián* (宀) instead.
*Jia* (家) is pronounced *jìng* (上音情亦反), an archaic character; the *Shuowen* writes it as *yǔ* (𡧯). *Chíchěng* (馳騁): *chí* is pronounced *chǐ yǐng* (恥郢反).

Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "chěng" means to gallop (*bēn*). The *Shuowen* defines it as "driving straight ahead. It is composed of the radical "horse" (*mǎ*) and the phonetic "pí" (𦥤); the pronunciation of *pí* is *pǐ jī* (匹笄).

The character *xì* (戲) is read as *shàng xū jì fǎn* (upper tone, reversed from *xū* and *jì*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical *gē* (戈) and the phonetic *qian* (䖒); *qian* is pronounced *xǔ yí fǎn*. The *Jīng* (經) follows *xū* [as the phonetic], which is incorrect. The lower part is read as *lù tòng fǎn* (lower tone, reversed from *lù* and *tòng*). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to dally" (*wán*) or "to play" (*xì*). It is composed of the radicals *gǒng* (廾) and *yù* (玉); *gǒng* is pronounced *gǒng*.

Volume Two, Middle Section of the Mahāvaipulya Trisamaya Sūtra. Regarding the character *zhā* (撾): it means to strike or beat; it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mu*) with the phonetic "guō" (*dé lěng fǎn*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means to strike or to pound; it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shou*) with the phonetic "dīng."

Regarding the character *jiā* (枷): the upper part is pronounced *jiā*, and the lower part is pronounced *sāngguǒ* (桑果). The *Yùpiān* states it means "to connect" (*liánhuán*). The *Shuōwén* says: "The character *suǒ* (鎖) means 'to lock' (*sìgù*). It is composed of the radical *jīn* (金) and the phonetic *yí* (𧴪). The pronunciation of *yí* is the same as above. In the text of this scripture, the two characters *jiā* and *suǒ* are both written incorrectly.

The character for *shēng* (生) [in the term] *cì dìyù* (刺地獄) is pronounced *cí* (雌) with the rhyme *zì* (漬); the *Yùnyīng* (韻英) states it means "wooden thorns," though this is a vulgar form. Its correct orthography is written as *shù* (束). According to the *Guǎngyá* (廣雅), it means "to prick" (*cī*) or "to admonish" (*zhēn*). The forms *cì* (刺) and *cī* (茦) are both correct; however, the forms *cī* (𮏯) and *cī* (茦) are not the correct orthographies, as they derive from the radical "knife" (*dāo*) and the phonetic "cī" (*cī shēng*).

*Máo* (pronounced *bào* in reverse rhyme): Yingyun states that *máo* means "old age. The *Liji* says, "At eighty or ninety, one is called *máo*," with a pronunciation identical to the above. Zheng’s commentary states that *máo* refers to being demented and forgetful. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical for "old" (*lǎo*) and the phonetic *máo*.

*Teicai* (貣財): The upper character is pronounced *tāng-lè* (湯勒) with a reversed tone. The *Jixùn* states that to borrow from others is called *teicai*. The *Shuowén* says it means to seek goods from others; it is composed of the radical "person" (人), the element "treasure" (貝), and the phonetic "yi" (弋), where *yi* is pronounced *yì*.

Regarding the term *pin-cù* (嚬蹙): the first character is pronounced *pí yín* (毘寅反) and the second is *jiǔ yù* (酒育反). The *Jixùn* states: "Furrowing the brows and knitting the nose; it denotes an expression of anger. Examining the phonology: "Knitting the brows, knitting the nose, and glaring with angry eyes. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the character *cù* (蹙) is composed of the radical *qī* (戚) with the phonetic *qīng* (青) and the tone *yīn* (亦反); the character *zòu* (皺) has the pronunciation *zé jiù* (則救反); and the character *è* (頞) has the pronunciation *ān gé* (安葛反).

*Fàn* (販): The character is pronounced with the first tone, *fā wàn* (發萬). The *Zītǒng* (字統) states: "To buy at a low price and sell at a high price; to buy in the morning and sell by evening. *Jì dù* (嫉妒):

The first character is pronounced *jí* (疾), the second *dù* (都固反). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* (*Būcí*) states: "To harm the worthy is called *jí*; to harm [the beauty of] others is called *dù*. The *Shuowén* says: 'A wife who is jealous of her husband. Both characters are composed of the radical *nǚ* (女) and the phonetic *jí* (疾) with the suffix *hù* (戶). It is incorrect for the scripture to write this as *gòu* (姤) using the character for "empress" (*hòu*).

*Chu* (貯): Pronounced *zhū* (with the initial *lǚ* reversed). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states it means "to store" (*zhù*) or "to accumulate and preserve. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it means "to rely upon" (*jí*), taking *bèi* as the radical and *níng* as the phonetic component; the lower part is pronounced *yù*. Hé’s commentary on the *Gongyangzhuan* states it means "to gather and collect" (*jùmǎn*). Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states it means "to assemble. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it means "to meet," taking *qún* as the phonetic component; *qún* is pronounced *yín* and consists of three people.

*Xiāng* (箱): *qián* (謙) and *yè* (葉) are the phonetic components; according to Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji*, a *xiāng* is a *qié* (篋). *Qié* (㨔) has the pronunciation *xián* (咸); the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is a type of chest. A *qié* is also a *sì* (笥). In archaic script it is written as *qì* (匧), composed of *fāngjiá* (方夾) with the phonetic component *fāng* (方). *Qié* (篋): Also pronounced *xián* (咸). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is a class of chest. A *qié* is also a *sì* (笥). In archaic script it is written as *qì* (匧), composed of *fāngjiá* (方夾) with the phonetic component *fāng* (方).

The character *máo* (矛) is pronounced *shàng mǔ hóu fǎn*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to the *qiú máo* (酋矛), a spear two *zhàng* long. Based on this explanation, it uses the ancient foot-measure, which is equivalent to sixteen feet by modern standards. The character *máo* is a pictograph representing the form of what are now called *qiāng* (槍) and *shuò* (槊). It is also called *hóng* (𥎞), pronounced *xià zì fǎn*; this was already explained previously.

*Āraṇya* (阿練兒) is an ancient translation from the Sanskrit; it was rendered as *lùzhì* (虜質), which is not excellent. It is also called *āraṇya* (阿蘭若), which in the Tang language means "a place of tranquility" (*jìjìng-chù*).

*Zǐhuì* (滓穢): The upper character, *zī* (緇), is pronounced with the *shǐ* (史) rhyme. The *Pīcāng* (埤蒼) dictionary writes it as *tǎn* (䔂). The *Shuowen* (說文) defines it as "sediment. The lower character, *huì* (穢), is pronounced with the *yù* (衛) rhyme. The *Bóyá* (博雅) defines it as "waste and weeds. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical for grain (*huò*, 禾). [The *Shuowen* also notes that it may be composed of the radical for grass (*cǎo*, 草).]
*Huì* (in the second character of *cáihuì*) is pronounced with the lower radical *huī* (灰) and the phonetic *wěi* (猥). According to the *Erya*, "huì" means wealth (*cái*). *Màlì* (罵詈):

the first character is pronounced with the upper radical *má* (麻) and the phonetic *jià* (嫁), and the second character is pronounced with the upper radical *lǐ* (理) and the phonetic *zhì* (稚). According to the *Shuowen*, these two characters are mutually explained; both contain the radical *wéng* (𠕀), which signifies "crime" (*zuì*).
*Zhuī* (鍾長追反): The *Shuowen* defines this as "to strike. It is composed of the radical 木 (wood) and the phonetic 隹. *Tán* (唌唾上祥延反):

This is a vulgar character used interchangeably with the standard form, which consists of the radicals 水 (water) and 欠 (to breathe). The *Shuowen* defines it as "saliva from the mouth. It may also be written with the radical 水 as 涎, which is likewise a vulgar character. *Xia* (下土臥反): The commentary follows the above; it consists of the radical 水 (water) and the phonetic 垂.
The character 睞 (lài) is read as *dài* (downward gaze); I suspect this character is a scribal error, for according to the meaning of the scripture, it should be pronounced *shùn* (shuǐrùn).

The character 濃 (nóng) is read as *lóng* (thick/dense). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "abundant dew. Alternatively, it may be written with the radical 酉 (yǒu), forming the character 醲 (nióng); the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "rich wine. It is a compound character formed from both shape and sound.

*Zhé* (upper character *zhé*, lower character *gé*): According to the *Mao Shi Zhuan*, it means mutual reprimand; according to Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan*, it means reproach; according to the *Fang Yan*, it means anger; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means punishment. It is composed of the radical "speech" (*yan*) and the phonetic element "shāng" (abbreviated). *Fán* (lower character *fàn*, lower character *wà*): According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means minor criminal punishment. It refers to cases where the offense is slight and does not involve killing with a blade, but rather involves holding a knife and using abusive language; such a person should be punished. It is a compound character formed by the semantic elements "knife" (*dao*) and "abuse" (*li*).

*Guān* (關): Upper radical *gǔ*, lower radical *wán* (反). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "A *guān* is a gate at the border. The *Shuowen* defines it as a wooden crossbar used to hold a door shut. The *Guangya* identifies it as a barrier (*guānsài*). It is composed of the radical *mén* (門) with the phonetic element *zuò* (作); the pronunciation of *zuò* is the same as the upper radical. The version of the scripture using *biàn* (弁) to form *guān* (閞) is incorrect. *Luó* (邏): Lower radical *dá* (馱) (反). Lexicons define it as "to screen" or "to block. The *Yunlüe* states: "It refers to patrolling troops stationed at dangerous paths and military garrisons to prepare for bandits."

Volume 3, Part 2. *Mahāvaipulya-triśaraṇa-sūtra*, Volume 2. *Ācārya* (the character *qi* in *āgiri* is pronounced as *ji*; in Sanskrit it is *ācārya*, which in the language of the Lu-zhi [Lokapāla] means "not excellent," or alternatively, in the Tang language, it is translated as "Teacher of Instruction").

The character *páo* (胞) is pronounced *qián* (詮) with the tone of *suì* (歲); according to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means "tender" (*cuìruò*). The *Shuōwén* states that it refers to flesh that is soft and easily broken; it is composed of the radical *ròu* (肉) and a simplified form of *jué* (絕). It is incorrect to write this character as *cuì* (脆) using the radical *wēi* (危).

*Menmo* (捫摸): The upper character is pronounced *mén* and the lower is pronounced *mòshī*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "to *menmo*" means to stroke or hold with the hand. Both characters are *xing-ying* (phonetic-semantic) compounds formed from the radical "hand" (*shou*). *Wonian* (我弄):

The upper character "I" (*wo*) is a compound character formed by combining the radicals "hand" (*shou*) and "spear" (*ge*), conveying the meaning of the self. That which follows the grain radical (*he*) is incorrect. The lower character is pronounced *lóng* (with the tone of *tòng*). This was already explained in the previous fascicle; it is not correct to derive it from the "hand" radical as a form of *jue* (a type of wrestling).

"Huángchóng" (locust): "shàng" (upper) is pronounced as "húguāngfǎn. According to the *Erya*, that which eats the heart of the sprout is called *míng*; that which eats the leaves is called *téng*; that which eats the roots is called *móu*; and that which eats the joints is called *zé*. The *Shuowen* states that although these four types differ in name, they are all varieties of the locust (*huángchóng*). The *Guangya* states that *zhōng* is the locust; their forms resemble those of the *fùzhōng* insect, yet their actual species are distinct, differing in color and size. Thus, there are the various names: *huáng*, *míng*, *móu*, and *zé*. "Wàn": pronounced as "yǐnjiǎnfǎn," or with the sound "yǎn," or with the sound "shì. "Móu": pronounced as "mòhóufǎn. "Zhōng": pronounced as "zhōng. "Míng": pronounced as "míng. "Zé": pronounced as "zé. "Hè": pronounced as "guófǎn"; it refers to the *lóuguài* (cricket).
Regarding the pronunciation of "xiè" (懈) as "jiè" (戒): none of the various character dictionaries provide the pronunciation "jià" (嫁).

As for "lóngyǎ" (聾瘂)—the first character is pronounced *lùdōng* (祿東) and the second is *wūjià* (烏賈)—this was already fully explained in the previous *Prajñāpāramitā* phonetic commentary and need not be recounted here again. It is incorrect to write the character for "mouth" (*kǒu*) as "ǎ" (*yà*).

It should be read as *dàn* (with the initial *gān* and final *fǎn*). According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to lift"; according to the *Zìshū*, it means "to carry on the back. It may also be written with the radical for "person" (*rén*), both forms being correct. The phonetic component is *zhān* (pronounced *zhān*); that which uses the radical for "wood" (*mù*) is incorrect.

"Li" (離) is pronounced *bō* (with the *gǔ* tone reversed); "bō" (搏) is pronounced *yā*; "bō" means to bind. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Kaogongji* states that "bō" means to strike or beat. The *Yupian* says it means to pat. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as to grasp or hold, composed of the radical "hand" (*shou*) and the phonetic "zhuan" (專) with its "sheng" (聲) omitted. It is incorrect to claim that the character "zhuan" (專) is composed of "fu" (甫), "cun" (寸), and "zhuan" (專).

*Jū* (pronounced *qīyú*, with the "qī" being the opposite of "yú")—Sima Biao’s commentary on the *Zhuangzi* states: "Floating heat forms *jū*; when it does not penetrate, it becomes an *yōng*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical *nà* (sickness) and the phonetic *qiě*, which is pronounced *zǐyú*. It is also written as *rì* with *xià* below it.

Regarding the characters for *liǎolì* (繚綟): the first character is pronounced with the initial *l* and the final *wū* (力烏反); the second character is pronounced with the initial *l* and the final *jié* (蓮結反). In the canonical text, *jiǎoliǎolì* (脚繚綟) refers to feet that are curved and not straight; it is also said to mean "not upright. Both characters are *shēngxíngzì* (phonetic-semantic compounds) derived from the radical *mì* (糸). The pronunciation of *mì* is *mì* (覓).

*Nǎo* (聾): [The character] *ái* (騃) is pronounced with the rhyme *jié* (解) according to the *Cāngjié piān*; *ái* means "foolish. The *Jíxùn* states it means "stupidity. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "horse" (*mǎ*) and the phonetic component "abbreviated *yǐ*" (*yǐ* simplified).

*Mù* (勿): Pronounced *chōng* (衝) with the rhyme *zhú* (燭), according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to strike" or "to collide. In the scripture, it is written as *niú* (牛) followed by *gǔi* (𧢻); this is a vulgar character.

*Qīngzào* (輕躁): Below, it encounters *luò*; the phonetic gloss states it means "acute temperament," "movement," "agitation," or "running swiftly. It is sometimes written as *jiào* (趮), which is the same, with the radical *zú* (足) and the phonetic *sǎo* (喿).

*Mòbàn* (沫拌): Above, *màn* (漫); below, *pán* (盤). The phonetic gloss states it means "to pause" or "to linger. To mix this with that by stirring together is called *bàn*. It takes the radical *shǒu* (手) and the phonetic *bàn* (半).

*Paináng* (㰆囊): The first character is pronounced *bài*; the second is the phonetic *nuó lǎng*. According to the *Cāngjié* and *Yùpiān*, it refers to a bellows (*huǐnáng*) used for blowing a fire; sometimes written with the "metal" radical (*qì*) as *huǐ* or with the "leather" radical (*wéi*) as *pí*, both of which are correct. It is not the same as the character *pái* (排) used in the classics.

Regarding "dàn" (鍜): Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states it means "to hammer. The *Cangjie pian* says it is a "hammer," and the *Shuowen jiezi* defines it as "a small smithy. It is written with the radical for metal (金) and the phonetic "duàn" (叚). The character "duàn" (叚) is composed of the radical for mallet (殳) and the abbreviated phonetic "lì" (鴗). The pronunciation of "dàn" (掫) is *dingzhuǎn* (丁𠮧反).

The character for *chui* (hammer) is pronounced with the initial *zhí* and the final *zhuǎn* (as in *zhī-zhuǎn*). Examining its sound, it refers to an iron hammer used for striking; it is also written as *chuí* or *chuí*, both of which are acceptable. The following character, *jiǎn*, has the initial *yán*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *jiǎn* means "an iron clamp for seizing objects," composed of the radical *jīn* (metal) and the phonetic *zhàn* (abbreviated). In the scripture, it is written with the radical *gān* (sweetness) as *qián*; this refers to an iron collar or cangue and is not the usage intended here.

*Shu* (pronounced *chāng zhū*): The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that "shu" means "beautiful. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "woman" (*nǚ*) and the phonetic "zhū. *Té* (pronounced *téng dé*): Wén Yǐng’s commentary on the *Hanshu* states that "tè" means "a solitary candle. According to the *Shuowen*, "tè" refers to a "bull" (*niú fù*), composed of the radical "ox" (*niú*) and the phonetic "sì" (abbreviated).

Regarding the character "sì" (飼) in the phrase "Niu sì yīn sì" (牛飼音寺): the *Guīyuàn Zhūcóng* states that "sì" means to feed or to provide fodder. *Chuan* (蠉) and *shang* (上) [in the context of "flying up"]—the former is pronounced with the *xue* (血) and *yuan* (緣) finals, and it is also written as *yuan* (蝝); both are correct radical forms. *The Sutra of Immeasurable Life*, Volume One, Part One. Compiled by Xuanying. "Mílán" (微瀾): *Erya* states that a great wave is called a *lán* (瀾) and a small wave is called a *lún* (淪). According to the *Shuowen*, it is derived from the radical for water.

The *Shuōwén* defines it as the appearance of a small insect moving, composed of the radical "insect" (*chóng*) and the phonetic "ruì"; the text's reading as "qù" is an error. The *Cāngjié Piān* reads it as "zhǒng."

The character 央 (yāng) is pronounced with the *yuè* tone; it is incorrect for the received text to write it as 鞅 (yǎng), which is in the *shǎng* tone. *Bàng* (bàng) is pronounced with the *làng* tone.

Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that it means "to defame"; it also means "to curse. Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* says it means "to slander" (*fěibàng*); it also refers to speaking of someone's evil deeds to others. The lower radical is 仕 (shì), according to the *Mao Shih Zhuan*, which says: "Chán (讒) is to destroy a person with words. The *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of the radical 言 (speech) and the phonetic 毚 (chán). Chán is pronounced with the *shì xián* tone.

The character "ge" (膈) in the *Shuowen Jiezi* is composed of the radical "flesh" (肉) with the phonetic "li" (鬲), where "li" is pronounced as "ge" (革). The text of the sutra uses "fu" (阜) instead to form "ge" (隔); however, this latter "ge" does not carry the same meaning as the former. (Note: The character "ge" [膈] refers to the diaphragm or the internal cavity of the chest; the character "ge" [隔] used in the sutra text means separation or partition.)

On the right, regarding the character for *xiè* (脇) in "fragrant karma": it refers to the armpit. It is composed of the radical for "flesh" (肉) and the phonetic *xié* (劦). The pronunciation of *xié* is *xié* (同協).

It is also written as *yù* (䝱), which is composed of three "strengths" (力). Regarding *yú* (諛) and *chǎn* (讇): *yú* is pronounced with the *zhū* rhyme (庾珠反). The *Zhuangzi* states: "To speak without distinguishing between right and wrong is called *yú*. Kong's commentary on the *Shangshu* notes that *yú* is also *chǎn*. The text of the scripture writes this as *yù* (諭), which is incorrect. *Chǎn* (讇) is pronounced with the *rǎn* rhyme (恥冉反). He’s commentary on the *Gongyang Zhuan* states: "*Chǎn* is *yú*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "*Yú* is from the speech radical (言) and the phonetic *yán* (閻). The pronunciation of *yán* is *yí zhàn* (以占反). The text of the scripture writes this as *chǎn* (諂); *chǎn* is a vulgar usage derived by abbreviation.
*Wǎo* (往嬈): According to the *Shuowen*, it means to mock or toy with; it is also written as *niǎo*. *Pílièduō* (薜荔多):
The first character is read as *pú bì* and the second as *lǐ dì*; this is the Sanskrit name for a hungry ghost (*preta*).
*Lì* (礫石): The phonetic component is *lǚ*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "lì" refers to small pebbles; it is also written as *qí* (𥕴) in other character dictionaries. *Wǎn yán* (綩綖):

The first character is pronounced *yuǎn* and the second is pronounced *yán*. This is a scribal error in the canonical text; the correct orthography uses the radical for grass (*cǎo*), forming *yuàn zhèn* (苑莚), as seen in terms such as *wǔ yuàn* (舞莚) and *dì yī* (地衣).

"Ji" (珠璣) is pronounced as *qí* (沂反). In the Commentary on the Book of Documents (*Shūjìng*), Master Kǒng states that "ji" is a type of pearl; according to dictionaries, it refers to a small pearl. The *Shuowén Jìzì* defines it as a pearl that is not perfectly round, composed of the radical "jade" (*yù*) and the phonetic element "ji" (*jī*).
*Tài* (pronounced *tāidài*)—Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states it means "posture" (*zī*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "constantly maintaining one's intent without change.

It is also written as *yí*. *Tí* (pronounced *tǐdì*)—The *Pīcāng* states it is a "flight of stairs. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "a wooden staircase," formed with the radical for wood and the phonetic *dì*, pronounced *pílǐ*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* identifies it as a "wooden barrier for the procession" (*xíngmǎ*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* also writes it as *bì*.

"Pí" (疲) [is pronounced with the "bei" and "po" finals]. Jia [Yan]’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states it means "fatigue. The *Cangjie pian* states it means "laziness. The text of the scripture uses "bà" (罷), which is a borrowed character; this is because the ancients were simple and unadorned.

Volume 2, Lower Scroll, *The Sūtra of the Land of Akṣobhya Buddha*. "Xià" (下) is read as "zhè" (這) and "yánjiàn" (言件) according to the *Cāngjié piān* (蒼頡篇); it means "to welcome. According to the *Shuōwén* (說文), it is composed of "chuò" (辵) and "yán" (言) as phonetic components; "chuò" is pronounced "chǔlüè" (丑略). Volume 2, Lower Scroll.
*Dirimila* (the "di" and "mi" are pronounced as in *xi* and *fan* respectively) is a name for a tree in the Sanskrit language.

Regarding the *Mahāyāna-daśadharma-sūtra* (The Mahayana Sutra of the Ten Dharmas), compiled by Hui-lin: concerning "frivolous speech" (*sambhinnapralāpa*), the character "qi" (綺) is pronounced as in *che* and *ji* (欺, 紀) respectively; frivolous speech refers to the embellishment of literary expressions that exaggerates beyond their actual merit.

*Li-lou* (犁耬)—the character *li* is pronounced with the *li-xi* rhyme, and it is an implement for plowing fields. The character *lou* (耬) is pronounced with the *lu-hou* rhyme; the *Pīcāng* glosses it as "stretching. In antiquity, people pulled it by hand to stretch it out and sow the seeds. Today, oxen are used to pull it. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical *lei* (耒) and the phonetic *lou* (婁). *Lei* is pronounced with the *li-dui* rhyme, and *wan* (輓) is pronounced with the *wan* rhyme.

*Chu* (貯): Pronounced *dǔ* (呂反). According to the *Shuowen*, "to store" (*chu*) also means to accumulate; it is composed of the radical "shell" (*bei*) with the phonetic element *ning*. *Tang* (榻): Pronounced *zhuāng* (㽵反).

According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radicals "tablet" (*chuāng*) and "wood" (*mu*). *Chuāng* is pronounced *jiàng* (匠) or *yáng* (羊); the lower part is pronounced *tān* (貪) or *dá* (答). The *Shiming* states that a bed that is narrow and long is called a *tang*. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mu*) with the phonetic element *zhù* (󱫕).

*Jiā* (枷): Pronounced with the rhyme of *yā* (鴉) reversed; in the *Zìshū* it means to suppress or oppress sentient beings. The *Shuowén* also writes this as the character *yàn* (厭). *Jué* (撾): Pronounced with the rhyme of *zhǐ guā* (陟瓜);

it refers to striking the buttocks or shaking them. The *Kǎoshēng* says it means to strike. The standard form of the character from ancient times to the present consists of the radical for wood (*mù*) and the phonetic *guò* (過); the *Shuowén* writes it as *nǔ* (𥬸).

*Pudgala*: In the Sanskrit language, this is translated as "one who repeatedly takes up existence" (*shuququ*), meaning one who repeatedly wanders through the three realms. It is also called *pudgalaka*. Regarding the term for "mosquito" (*meng*):
the character is composed of the radical *gūn* (虫) and the phonetic *máng*; the text of the sutra uses the character *méng*, which is incorrect. The sound of *gūn* is *kūn*.

Regarding "māng" (蟒): the *Erya* states "Māng is the king of snakes," and Guo's commentary notes that among snakes, the largest are called *māngshé*. The version in the *Jing* (經) as "yǒngshé" (𠕀蛇) is incorrect. Regarding the *Pumenpin Jing* (*Buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*, "Universal Gate Chapter"):

Xuanying says the first tone for "Pǔ" (溥) is "pǔ. The character "pǔ" (溥) is composed of "fǔ" (甫), "shuǐ" (水), and "cùn" (寸). "Pǔshǒu" (溥首)—a term from ancient translations that is plain and not refined—is the name of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.
"Yi-hai" (億垓)—the "hai" is pronounced as in "gai-fan"—is a numerical term. Regarding the character "beng" (鞕): in the *Zishu* (Dictionary of Characters), it means "firm" or "tight";

it is derived from the phonetic "kao" and signifies hardness. There is also the vulgar character "ying" (硬). In the *Wenzi Jilüe* (Compendium of Written Characters), it is written with "mao" (卯) above and "yu" (䩕) below; however, according to the meaning of the sutra, the lower part should be the character "gang" (岡). The old commentary reads "hu-lang" (胡浪), but this is likely incorrect, as it does not form a valid character. None of the various dictionaries contain this character, and its origin remains unclear; thus, the original text is preserved here for future scholars.

The character for "full" (mǎn) at the top consists of the radical *mián* (from which the phonetic *mǎn* is derived) and the two characters *liǎng*. It is also pronounced *mǎn*. When used with the water radical, it is a functional character. The lower part is pronounced *pǔ bāo*. This refers to the bladder (*pí pāo*) within the abdomen that holds light and water; it is what we now call a balloon. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is the bladder (*pí pāo*), consisting of the radical *ròu* and the phonetic *fú* in abbreviated form.

*Pao Jing* (The Sutra on the Embryo). Spoken by the Buddha. Compiled by Hui Lin. The upper tone for *pao* is *bāo*. Sima Biao’s commentary on the *Zhuangzi* states: "The *pao-yu* is the inner garment of the infant. The *Hanshu* states: "Among those of the same *pao*," and Ru Chun says: "*Pao* refers to close brothers. The *Shuowen* says: "The clothing that wraps an infant; it follows the radical for flesh (*rou*) and takes *bao* as its phonetic component; the lower part is read as *tāi*. The *Erya* says: "The *tai* is the beginning [of gestation]. The *Guangya* says: "A woman’s pregnancy of three months is called a *tai*. The *Cangjie Pian* says: "An infant not yet born is called a *tai*. The *Shuowen* further defines it: "The state of a woman’s pregnancy at three months; it follows the radical for flesh and takes *tai* as its phonetic component."
*Yi-sha* (pronounced with the first character as *yī* and the second as *ji*, reversed) has no direct equivalent in Sanskrit.

Regarding the pupil of the eye (*tóng-zǐ*): the *Pīcāng* states that "pupil" refers to the eyeball; the *Guǎngyǎ* states that the eyeball is called the *móuzǐ*; in common parlance it is called the "pupil of the eye" (*mù-tóng-rén*); and the *Shuōwén* lacks a definition for it.
The character 肧 (péi) [is defined as] "a woman’s fetus at one month. It is composed of 肉 (flesh) and the phonetic 不 (bù).

The character 燥 (zào) [is defined in the *Shuowen* as] "fire approaching what is dry" (*Zhouyi*). The *Shuowen* states: "Dryness; composed of 火 (fire) and the phonetic 喿 (sào). The sound of 喿 is the same as above. The lower part is written as 分 (fèn), which is a vulgar form. The correct form is written with 艸 (grass/vegetation) as 𭫮. The *Shuowen* writes it as 𡊅. To discard and sweep away is called 𭫮. According to the *Yunying*, "excrement is also filth," or it may be written as 󲐓 or 󲒉. In the scriptures, it is written with 土 (earth) as 𡐢, which does not constitute a valid character.

The character *bǐn* (臏) is pronounced with the rhyme *pín*. The *Yùnqián* states it refers to the kneecap and shinbone; the *Shuowén* identifies it as the knee bone. It is correctly written with the radical for "bone" (*gǔ*) and is a phono-semantic compound.

The character *gāi* (荄) is pronounced with the rhyme *guī*. The *Erya* states that *gāi* means "root. Guo Pu notes that in common parlance, the root of chives is called *gāi*. The *Fāngyán* records that in the eastern state of Qí, the root was called *gāi*. The *Shuowén* defines it as the root of grass, formed with the radical for "grass" (*cǎo*) and the phonetic element *hài*.
*Shù* (觚杸): The ancient pronunciation is *hú* (古胡反). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radicals for "horn" (*jiǎo*) and "melon" (*guā*), with the phonetic *guǎ* (寡華反).

*Zào* (躁): The pronunciation is *zǎodào* (早到反). Zheng’s commentary on the *Lunyu* states it means "not being at peace. The *Shifa* (Mourning Titles) says: "One who likes to agitate the people is called *zào*. The *Yupian* defines it as "restless movement. The *Shuowen* writes this character as *zào* (趮).

*Duan* (pronounced *luàn* with the final *-n* reversed) refers to a smith. Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that it means "to forge and temper halberds and spears. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states it means "to hammer. The *Cangjie pian* states it means "to push and strike. The *Shuowen jiezi* defines it as "a minor smith," taking the radical 金 (*jin*) and the phonetic 叚 (*duàn*).

*Bēináng* (鞴囊): "Bēi" is pronounced *bài* (反). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is a tool for blowing fire; alternatively, it is written as *wéi* (韋) to form *bèi* (韛), or as *pó* (㰆); both have the same pronunciation as above. It is also called *tuó* (橐). The *Zishu* states that it is a bottomless bag; it is a transitive character (*zhuanzhu*). *Tuó* is pronounced *tuò*; the second character, *nuò* (諾), has the phonetic *láng* (郎) as its final.
*Piǎo*: (pǐ miǎo) According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to silk of a bluish-white color; it is formed with the radical "silk" (*mié*) and the phonetic "piao. *Yáo*:
(yáo) According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to a kiln for firing tiles; it is formed with the radicals "cave" (*xué*) and "lamb" (*gāo*), or it may be written as *táo*.

The character *guā* (刮) used here for "scraping" is a vulgar variant; it has been in use for a long time in transmitted texts. Its correct form in seal script (*zhuànshū*) is written with the radical *qí* (𠯑), as in *guǎ* (𠜜). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lìjì* states: "Scraping and rubbing. The *Guǎngyá* says: "To scrape is to reduce. According to the *Shuowén*, it means "to scrape away the flesh of a bad wound"; it is composed of the radical *dāo* (刀) and the phonetic *qí* (𠯑), which is pronounced *huán guā* (還刮). Its pronunciation is identical to that of *huá* (滑). The term *zhì* (治) below is pronounced *chí zhì* (池跱). The *Kǎoshēng* explains it as "governing and managing" and "repairing what is old. The *Shuowén* defines it as being composed of the radical *shuǐ* (水) and the phonetic *tái* (台).
*Kāi-mo* (揩摩): The phonetic reading is *kè-kài*. The commentary states it means "to rub and wipe.

It is composed of the radical 手 (hand). *Wāng-jiǎo* (尫󲒲): The upper character is read as *wǎng-wáng*. The *Shuowen* states it means "a lame person with crooked legs. It is composed of the radical 象 (elephant) to represent the form of being particularly bent and curved; the archaic form is written as 尵. The modern form 瘸 is written with the radical 省 (abbreviated). *Xǐ* (洗): The phonetic reading is *xì-zài*. The *Shuowen* states it means "minute. It is composed of the radical 糸 (silk thread) and the phonetic 㝮. The sound of 糸 is *mì*; the sound of 㝮 is *xìn*.

*Bòjiǎn* (跛蹇): The first character, *bō*, is pronounced with the *wǒ* rhyme (波我反). The *Guoyu Zhu* (Commentary on the Guoyu) states that it refers to walking unsteadily. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical 足 (*zu*) and the phonetic 皮省 (*pí*). The second character, *jiǎn*, is pronounced with the *yǎn* rhyme (偃反). The *Shuowen* states that *jiǎn* also means being lame; it is composed of the radical 足 (*zu*) and the phonetic 謇省 (*jiǎn*).
*Tù lǒu* (秃瘻): The pronunciation is *lòu*. Examining the character for *chuāng* (瘡), it is said that a long-standing sore is called *lǒu*;

it is formed with the radical *nà* (疒) and the phonetic *lóu* (婁). *Shè* (舌): Pronounced *shàn rè* (上善熱反). The *Shuowen* says: "The tongue is that which is used for speaking within the mouth; it is composed of the radicals *qiān* (千) and *kǒu* (口); *qiān* also serves as the phonetic. *Xia* (下): Pronounced *ěr* (爾反). This is a vulgar character. The *Shuowen* says: "To lick (*shì*) means to take up things with the tongue; it is composed of the radical *shé* (舌) and the phonetic *shì* (氏). The correct form is *shí* (舓). The form *mín* (𭇇) used in the scriptures with the radical *kǒu* (口) is incorrect. *Kao* (考): The sound may also be written as *tán* (狧), *chī* (𦧇), or *huài* (咶). These five characters are all ancient forms found in various historical records.

*Kài* (欬): In the *Bòyǎ*, "kài" refers to the movement of qi. It is composed of the radical *qiàn* (欠) and the phonetic *hài* (亥). In the classics, it is written with the mouth radical as *ké* (咳), which is a vulgar character. *Chī* (癡): Pronounced *chí chí* (恥持). This is a vulgar character;

the correct form is composed of the heart radical (*xīn*) and the phonetic *zhào* (𢣕), meaning "foolish. Wèi Hóng [proposed] a character composed of the person radical (*rén*) and *fá* (乏), writing it as *mín* (𠇖), which is a compound character (*huìyì*) meaning "a child is foolish. The lower part is pronounced *chuáng* (踔, *xiàng* rhyme) with the phonetic *kǎo* (考); it means a small child is foolish. Some write it with the *jiàn* (見) radical as *jiàn* (𧢆), or as *zhuó* (󲃴); the vulgar pronunciation *zhuó* (卓) and *jiàng* (降) are likely incorrect.

*Yǒulóng* (疣癃): The upper character is pronounced *yóu*, the lower *lóng*. Gu Yewang states it is a disease caused by the congealing of wind; it is also the character for *yǒu* (贅) in the sense of a wart or tumor. *Lóng* means to rise or swell. *Lǚzhàng* (𦝩脹): The upper character is pronounced *lǚzhū*.

The *Kǎoshēng* states it means skin, great, or to narrate—to report upward from below. The *Shìmíng* states that the front of the abdomen is called *lǚ*. The *Shuowén* indicates it is composed of the radical "flesh" (*ròu*) with the phonetic "lú. The lower character is pronounced *zhāngliàng*. The *Zuǒzhuan* states it means to fill again. It is a character formed from the semantic radical "flesh" and the phonetic component.

*Bǎng* (搒) is pronounced *báimáng* (白盲); *Guǐ Yěwáng* (顧野王) states it means "to strike. Lexicons define it as "to beat. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "páng" (*páng*). *Chīchí* (恥持) is its pronunciation. According to the *Shuowen*, *tái* (笞) means "to strike"; it is composed of the radical "bamboo" (*zhú*) and the phonetic *tái* (*tái*).

Examining the character dictionaries, *kǎo* (拷) means "to strike with a cudgel"; it is formed from the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic element "capital city" (*jīng*) in its abbreviated form.

According to the *Fāngyán* (Dialectal Dictionary), the pronunciation *lüè* (略) is also acceptable. From the *Wénshūshīlì Fótǔ Yánjìng Jīng* (The Sutra on the Adorned Purity of Mañjuśrī’s Buddha-land), Volume One, Part One, compiled by Xuanying: *Kègōng* (恪恭): The ancient form is *kè* (愙). It is pronounced *kǔgè* (苦各反). In the *Shàngshū* (Book of Documents), it says: "Be reverently cautious regarding the mandate of Heaven. Kǒng Āngguó (Kong An-guo) states: "Kè means reverence. The *Zílín* (Forest of Characters) states: "Kè means reverent respect."

The character *xiàng* (相) borrows the pronunciation of *wén* (文), with the initial *gēng* (庚). The character should properly be written as *táng* (摚/𢾊/棖/𢿦); these four forms are identical and pronounced *wén* (文) with the initial *héng* (衡), meaning "to touch" or "to strike. *Tán* (恬) and *dàn* (惔): *tú* (徒) and *jiān* (兼) rhyme; in the *Fāngyán* (方言), *tián* (恬) means "tranquil.

The following character should be *dàn* (淡), with *tú* (徒) and *làn* (濫) rhyming; in the Han dynasty, it was called "peaceful and quiet. The scriptural text uses the character *dàn* (惔) with the radical for "heart" (*xīn* [心]), with *tú* (徒) and *gān* (甘) rhyming, meaning "anxiety like a burning fire" (*yōu rú dān yōu* [憂心如惔憂]). This *dàn* (惔) is not used in this context.
The character 著 is also written as 昞, 炳, or 昺; these three forms share the same pronunciation, *bìng* (as in *bǐng*).

According to the *Guǎngyá*, "昺" means "bright. The characters for "one hundred million" (*yì-hài*) are written in ancient texts as 畡 or 奒; the modern form is 姟, all sharing the pronunciation *gǔcái*. It is a name for a large number. The *Fēngsùtōng* states: "Ten hundred million (*yì*) is called a *zhào*; ten *zhào* is called a *jīng*; ten *jīng* is called a *hài*. Thus, it is a designation for a vast number.
*Bai* (拜): pronounced *xie* (歇) in the *Erya*; it means to request, to inform, or to announce.

*Zhouzhang* (侜張): also written as *zhoutong* (譸同); pronounced *zheliu* (陟留) for the first character and *zhiliang* (知良) for the second. According to the *Erya*, "zhouzhang" means to deceive. Guo Pu says: "Zhouzhang refers to deluding and confusing others, cheating and deceiving people. The scriptural text reads *zhuru* (侏儒), pronounced *zhizhu* (之儒); this refers to a short person.
*Kaishi* is the Sanskrit term for *bodhisattva*. It refers to a person who opens the way through the Dharma; thus, they are called a *kaishi*.

*Tanran* (the second character pronounced *tan*, with the tone of *tu dan fan*) means a deep abyss; the people of Chu called a deep pool *tan*. The character should properly be written as *dan* (pronounced *tu lan fan*), meaning tranquil and still.
*Dùn'ái* (Dust): "Wū lái fǎn cāng jié. *Āifēng yángchén yě* (The wind of dust rises). 2.

In the lower fascicle of the *Mañjuśrī-buddhakṣetra-vyūha-sūtra*, the term *jiāojué* (crossed ankles) is also written as *pófú*. They are the same. According to the *Sāncāng*, *fú* means the top of the foot; it refers to sitting with the feet crossed. In the sutras, it is often written as *jiājū*. In the lands east of the mountains, it is called *jiājū*. The scriptural text that writes it as *jiāo* (from the foot) is incorrect.
*Zhi* (至) is pronounced *cou* (且豆反); according to the *Guǎngyá*, "to converge" (*zòu*) means "to be supreme" (*zuì*), and "to converge and compete" (*zòujìng*) means "to advance.

*Jǐng* (景) is pronounced *jī* (羇影反); the *Shījīng* says, "Grant you great fortune" (*jiè ěr jǐng fú*), and the commentary states that "great" (*jǐng*) means "vast" (*dà*). It also means "model" (*fǎ*).

The Sūtra on the Merits of the Buddha-field of the Great Sage Mañjuśrī, Volume One (of two), compiled by Huìlín. *Gǔnmén*: "Gǔn" is pronounced *kūnwěn* (the second character being read as *wěn*). In his commentary on the *Lǐjì*, Zhèng states that *gǔn* refers to the threshold of a door; it is a word formed through both semantic and phonetic elements.

Regarding "jealousy" (jí dù): Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that to harm the virtuous is called *jí* (envy), and to harm those of beauty is called *dù* (jealousy). The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains both characters as being composed of the radical "woman" (女) with the phonetic "jì" (疾) and "hù" (戶) respectively. There are instances where they are written with the character "hòu" (后) instead, which is incorrect.

"Nǔ" (pronounced huá wǎ in reverse; used here as a borrowed sound) has its radical pronunciation as lǔ guǒ. Gu Yewáng states that it means "to strip off clothes and expose the shoulders. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "clothing" (衣) with the phonetic "guǒ"; alternatively, it may be written as "luò" (倮) with the radical "person" (人), or as "nuǒ" (躶) with the radical "body" (身)—all of which have the same meaning.

*Chéngsuì* (澄睟): In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is glossed as *chénzhàn* (澄湛). Although the rhyme is given as *cuì* (翠) below, the *Kaosheng* states it means "the appearance of looking upright. The *Yupian* says it means "a glossy and moist appearance. The *Gujin Zhengzi* states that the character is composed of the radical *mu* (目) and the phonetic *zú* (卒) in its abbreviated form; *zú* is further composed of *yī* (衣) and *jiǎo* (󱫛), where *yī* is written as *yī* and *jiǎo* has the pronunciation *piānmè* (篇篾).
"Zhēnzuó" (斟酌): read as *zhí rèn* (執任) in the following chapter;

read as *ruò* (弱). "Pīhuàn" (披擐): read as *huàn* (還慢). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "to *huàn*" means to put on armor by passing it through [the arms]; according to the *Shuowen*, it is formed with the radical "hand" and the phonetic "huǒng" (*huàn*).

The character *chè* (徹) is formed from *tōu* (透), *chè* (徹), *hòu* (候), *fǎn* (反), *kǎo* (考), with the phonetic component *zǒu* (走). It is pronounced *chǐ liè* (耻列). Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that it means "clearly penetrating. The *Shuowen* explains it as "to penetrate through," formed from *chì* (彳) with the phonetic *chū lì* (丑歷); the component *shàng* (上) has the same pronunciation as *tǔ* (土).

*Kǐng* (with the light *yǐng* rhyme): According to the *Shuowen*, *kǐng* is also the sound of *kài*. It is composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic "kìng" (*kǔ jué*). The second character is *kǎi* (*kǔ ài*). The *Bóyá* states that *kài* is a disease of the upward-moving qi.

"Biàn" (捫) is pronounced with the *bo* and *jian* finals; it means "to encompass" (*bianzai*). The lower character is pronounced with the *mo* and *ben* finals. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states: "To *mou* is to grasp. The *Shenglèi* states: "*Mou* is to feel with the hands. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shou*) and the phonetic element "gate" (*men*).

*Xiǎn* (險): pǐ (彼) and jì (寄) rhyme; the *Cāngjié piān* defines it as "devious and sycophantic. The *Shuōwén* explains it as "discriminating flattery. 2. Middle Scroll, *Buddhakṣetra Sūtra*. *Zhānlìn* (占吝):

*zhàn* (上) is pronounced zhì (之) and yàn (燄); *lìn* (下) is pronounced lín (隣) and zhèn (振). Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* states that "lìn" means to be stingy and parsimonious. The *Fāngyán* says that in the regions of Jīng, Xiāng, Rǔ, and Yǐng, to be greedy and not give is called *dù* (𠫤). Guō’s commentary notes that this refers to being miserly and having much attachment to possessions. The *Shuōwén* [explains it] as consisting of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic "wén" (*wén*). In the scripture, it is written with the radical "heart" (*xīn*) as *lìn* (悋), which is also acceptable. The ancient script uses "wén" (*wén*) as the character for *lìn* (吝).

*Zhunsheng* (準繩): Upper radical *jia* (佳), phonetic *yin* (尹). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states: “*Zhun* means level (*ping*); the *Guoyu* says it means even (*jun*); the *Shuowen* says it means level. It is composed of the radical *bing* (氷) and the phonetic *sun* (隼); the vulgar form using *zhui* (隹) as the phonetic is incorrect. Lower radical *shi* (食), phonetic *ying* (蠅). The *Shiben* states: “Chui invented the compass, square, level, and line. Song Zhong says he was a minister of Shun. The *Shangshu* says: “The line corrects the crooked; it restrains and rectifies that which is contrary to the heart. It also says: “Wood follows the line and becomes straight; a ruler follows admonition and becomes sagely. Examining the term *sheng* (繩), one takes its meaning of being level and straight. The *Erya* says: “*Shengsheng* means cautious and reverent. The *Shuowen* says it means a rope, composed of the radical *mi* (糸) and the phonetic *min* (黽, abbreviated).

*Kuì* (愧): The upper radical is *gui* (軌) and the position is reversed; the Du Anzhu commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that *kuì* means "shame" (*cán*). In the *Erya*, *kuì* is also "shame. The *Shuowen* agrees with the *Zuozhuan*. It follows the radical *nü* (女) and uses *guǐ* (鬼) as the phonetic; it is also written with the heart radical (*xīn*) as *kuì*, which is likewise acceptable. *Chǐ* (耻): The lower part is read as *chīlǐ* (癡里). According to the *Zishu*, it means "to feel shame" (*xiū*). It is derived from the sound *kǎo* (考). The *Shuowen* states it means "dishonor" (*rù*). It follows the heart radical (*xīn*) and uses *ěr* (耳) as the phonetic. There is also a variant written with the stop radical (*zhǐ*), but this is vulgar usage and not the correct form.

*Chuí* (隹󲆄, pinyin: chuì): The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "to strike with a staff" is the meaning; it is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "chuí" (垂). *Lǐngmèi* (眠結, pinyin: miánjié):

The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that "lǐngmèi" also means to treat lightly. Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* says it means to abandon, and also to extinguish. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to treat lightly"; it is composed of the radical "heart" (心) and the phonetic "miè" (蔑).

*Stūpa* (the *suǒdǔpō* [窣覩波] is a transliteration from Sanskrit; in the Tang language it means "a high and prominent place," also called a "square mound," which is the site where śarīra relics are enshrined). It is also called *tāpó*, *tōupó*, or *sūtōupó*; these are all corrupted or abbreviated forms.
*Pudgala* is a Sanskrit term; in the Tang language, it is translated as "one who repeatedly takes up existence" (*shuququ*).

Regarding *jù* (in the rhyme *qú yù*): Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that *jù* means "rapid" and also "distressed. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *chuò* (to walk) with the phonetic *qù*; *qù* is pronounced *qú*, and *jǔn* is pronounced *jūn yǐn*.

In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "yi" (易) is read as *qi-xian-fan* (七仙反). The commentary on the *Mao Shi* states that it means "to move" (*xi*) and also "to change" (*bian*); its correct form is written as [the character for "yi"]. In the *Kongzhu Shangshu*, "yi" is glossed as "to alter. 3.

In the lower fascicle of the *Focha Jing* (Buddhakṣetra Sūtra), "cai" (纔) is read as *zai-lai-fan* (在來反). The *Kaosheng* states that "cai" means "momentary" (*zan*). In the lower part, "fan" (蕃) is read as *bo-fan-fan* (𦮽反). The *Guangya* states that "fa" (發) means "to depart" (*qu*).
*Phalguna* is a Sanskrit term for a type of jewel.
*Utkara* (with the "yu" and "lie" finals reversed) is a Sanskrit term for a number;
the old translation was *bimbara*, which is also a number. *Mṛṇmaya* (the initial "mi" pronounced as "min," and the final "wei" pronounced as "mo ba").
