*Jiumou*. Regarding the *Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva’s Sūtra on the Dharma for Fulfilling All Aspirations and Retaining What One Has Heard*: compiled by Hui-lin. As for *gān-xǐ* (盥洗): *gān* (盥) is pronounced with the upper radical *shàng* (上) and the phonetic *kǔ* (苦) with the *jiá* (夾) tone, and the lower radical *sù* (粟) with the *yú* (俞) tone. *Gù Yě-wáng* states that all items used for washing are called *gān*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "washing the hands"; it is composed of the *jiù* (臼) radical, the *shuǐ* (水) radical, and the *míng* (皿) radical.

In the *Guan xukongzang pusa jing* (Sūtra on the Visualization of the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja), Huilin’s commentary states: "The term *bìn* (擯) is read as *bì jìn* (必進). Sima Biao’s commentary on the *Zhuangzi* explains it as 'to discard' (*bìqì*). In the standard characters of past and present, it is written with the radical 手 (hand) and the phonetic 賓 (bin); the character in this sūtra is written with the radical 人 (person), which is a variant form used interchangeably."

Regarding "qīng" (圊) and "cè" (廁): the upper character is pronounced as *jīng* (七精反), and the lower character is pronounced as *cì* (測事反). According to the *Shìmíng* (釋名), "cè" is also called "hùn" (圂). The *Shuōwén* states that "hùn" is also "cè," and "cè" is also "qīng. "Qīng" is composed of the radical "guǐ" (囗) with "qīng" (青) as its phonetic; "cè" is composed of the radical "yǎn" (广) with "zé" (則) as its phonetic. "Guǐ" is pronounced *wéi* (韋); "hùn" is pronounced *hún wěn* (魂穩反); "yǎn" is pronounced *yǎn* (儼).

*The Scripture on the Dhāraṇī Mantra Spoken by the Seven Buddhas as Requested by Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva*, compiled by Hui-lin. Regarding the term "cord" (*xiàn*) [in the phrase] "tying with cords" (*xián jié*): according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to thread; sometimes written as "thread" (*xiàn*), but the version in this scripture uses "cord" (*yán*), which is incorrect.

The character for *chí* (匙) is pronounced *zhī-fǎn*. According to the *Fāngyán*, what is called a *bǐ* (匕) is termed *chí*; the *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radical *bǐ* with *shì* as its phonetic. The scriptural version uses the radical *mù* (木) to form *zhòu* (𣏚), which takes *kǎo* as its phonetic and refers to the horizontal beam atop a millstone; this does not accord with the meaning of the scripture. Below, *jué* (厥) is pronounced *yuàn-fǎn*. The *Guǎngyá* states that *jùn* (㪻) means to ladle (*shū*). The *Cāngjiépiān* states that *shū* means to take up. The *Shuōwén* states that [the character for] *shū* is composed of the radical *dǒu* (斗) with *luán* as its phonetic. The scriptural version uses the radical *shǒu* (手) to form *quǎn* (捲), pronounced *quán*; this does not accord with the meaning of the scripture. *Luán* is pronounced *lì-zhuān-fǎn*.

*Kie* (桔): The pronunciation is *jian* (肩) with the retroflex *-ch* (嚙) final. According to the *Shuowen*, it is the name of a medicinal herb; it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mu*) and the phonetic element "ji" (*ji*).

*Geng* (梗): The pronunciation is *gu* (古) with the *-ing* (杏) final. *Xie* (諧): The upper character is pronounced *hu* (戶) with the *-ai* (皆) final. In the commentary on the *Shangshu*, Kong [Yuan] states that *xie* means "to harmonize. In the commentary on the *Zhouli*, Zheng [Xuan] says it means "to adjust. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to unite"; it is composed of the radical "speech" (*yan*) and the phonetic element "jie" (*jie*). The lower character is pronounced *wu* (五) with the *-kou* (口) final. In the *Boya*, it is also stated that *ou* (耦) means "to harmonize. Gu Yewang says that *ou* is synonymous with "match" (*pi*). In the commentary on the *Guoyu*, Jia [Gong] says it means "to correspond. *Dui* (對): According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "plow" (*lei*) and the phonetic element "wu" (*wu*). *Lei* (耒): The pronunciation is *lei* (雷) with the *-ai* (反) final.

*Tóngzhēn* (copper needle): the character *xià* (下) is pronounced as *shēn* (深). The *Guǎyá* states it means "to prick with a needle. Gù Yěwáng says it is that by which things are joined; the *Shuōwén* says it is for sewing. It is composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic "xián" (*xián shēng*). It is also written as *zhēn* or *zhēn*; the pronunciation of "prick" (*cì*) is *qī*.

The Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha, Spoken by the Buddha. Volume One. Compiled by Xuanying. *Śrāvaka* is a name for a disciple; it is a term from the Sanskrit language. (The first character, *là*, is pronounced with the initial *lú* and the final *hé*; the second character, *ài*, is pronounced with the initial *zhé* and the final *jiā*.)

"Zhou-yin" (胄胤): "Zhou" is pronounced *shang chou* (上儔) with a reversed final; Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "zhou" means "heir" (*hou*). Jia Gui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states it means "lineage" (*yin*). The *Shuowen* also defines it as "yin. It is composed of the radical "flesh" (*rou*) and the phonetic "you" (*you*), the latter being pronounced *yin zhen* (寅振). Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that "yin" means "succession" (*si*). The *Erya* states that "yin" means "to continue. The *Shuowen* further explains: "Yin refers to the continuous succession of sons and grandsons. It is composed of 'flesh' and 'ba' (*ba*); 'ba' represents their lengthening, and 'yao' (*yao*) also represents the layering and accumulation of that length."

2. Fascicle Two. "Yīxūn" (氤氳): The first character is pronounced as yī (上) with the level tone, and the second as wén (下) with the departing tone. It refers to the primal qi; it denotes the primordial breath at the beginning when heaven and earth had not yet been differentiated.
*TING* (pronounced *di* with a reversed *jing*): According to the *Pīcāng*, water that has ceased to flow is called *ting*.
*BÀI* (pronounced *bié* with a reversed *pu*): According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to the oblique flow of water; according to the *Guangya*, it means water branching out from itself as a current.
3. Third Fascicle. Regarding the term *piṇḍapāta* (分衛): this is a corruption; the correct pronunciation is *biṇḍaya*, which is translated as "food-ball" (*shítuán*), meaning to go on alms-round.

In the capital region, it is sometimes written as *qí* (同), with the phonetic *qúyī* (渠衣反). According to the *Zhouli* (Rites of Zhou), an area of one thousand li square is called a *guójí* (國畿); *jī* (畿) means a boundary or limit.
*Jié* (慴): Pronounced *dú jiá fǎn*. According to the *Erya*, it means "to be fearful. Guo Pu says: "It is the same as being terrified (*kǒng shè*).

*Chén* (廁窴): The rhyme is *tu jiān*. The *Cāngjié piān* states that *chén* means "to block" (*sè*). The meaning in the *Shuōwén* is the same. It is composed of the radical 穴 (*xuē*) and the phonetic 眞 (*zhēn*).

*Kuǐ wěi* (傀偉): Also written as *bāo* (褒). The rhyme is *gǔ huí*. Sīmǎ Biāo’s commentary on the *Zhuāngzǐ* says: "Kuǐ means 'beautiful' (*měi*) and 'in full bloom' (*fāng shèng*). The following character, *wěi* (韋), has the rhyme *guǐ*. The *Bīcāng* says: "Wěi means 'great' (*dà*). In the *Shuōwén*, both characters are composed of the radical 人 (*rén*) and the phonetics 鬼 (*guǐ*) and 韋 (*wéi*), respectively. The canonical text uses 王 (*wáng*) instead, forming 瑰 (*guī*) and 瑋 (*wěi*), which are also used interchangeably.

2. Second Fascicle. Regarding "ting" (亭) and "zhuan" (傳): "ting" is pronounced *tu* with the second tone (dīng), while the following "zhuan" is pronounced *zhì* with the fourth tone (liàn). In the Han dynasty, following the Qin system, there was a *ting* (post station) every ten *li*; a *ting* is a place where travelers stay. *Zhuan* means to translate or transmit.

*Jian* (熸): The upper character is pronounced *jie yan* (接鹽反). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that in the regions between Wu and Chu, the extinguishing of fire is called *jian*. *Si jin* (似進反) for the lower character: Zheng’s sub-commentary on the *Mao Shi* says "the remains of fire are called *jin*"; Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* refers to the remaining wood after a fire. Both the *Shuowen Jiezi* and others derive this from the radicals "fire" and "can" (*zhan*), with "yue" as the phonetic. The original text uses "wei" (*xian*) to form *wei* (𤒯), which is incorrect; it should be *jin* (燼) formed from "jin. This is a common vulgar character.

3. Third Fascicle. [The character] "xian" (先) was not pronounced with the initial *y-*. 4. Fourth Fascicle. "Wu jian" (無謇). [The character] *jian* (謇): according to the *Fangyan*, it means stammering (*ji*). The *Chuci* says that when speech is not fluent, it is called stammering (*ji*). In the standard orthography of ancient and modern times, it is written with the radical "speech" (言) and the phonetic "jian" (蹇) abbreviated; it is also written as *jue* (𧮈).

5. Fifth Fascicle, Part Five. *Sī* (also written as *sī*, same as above; pronounced with the initial *x* of *xiān-xī* according to the *Cāngjié piān*). The *Cāngjié piān* states that *sī* means "illness" and signifies "subtlety. In the region of the East and Qi, the sound of a sob is called *sī*. According to the *Shēnglèi*, it refers to aching pain. This character did not exist in antiquity; the current standard form is composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic "sī. It is also written as *sì* (𧬊), with the same meaning.

6. The sixth fascicle. Regarding the *mén-è* (門閫): it is also written as *niè* (臬), with the same pronunciation as *yú-liè* (魚列). The *Erya* states: "The *què* (橛) is called the *è* (閫)," which refers to the threshold of a door. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "door" (*mén*) and the phonetic component "è" (*niè*). The pronunciation of *è* is the same as above.

The character for *sīyì* (厮伇) is pronounced with the new rhyme *xī* (移反). In dictionaries, it refers to "slaves and servants," meaning lowly attendants. The *Jīngǔ zhèngzì* (古今正字) states that *sīyì* means "attendants and nourishers" (*hù yǎng*) and those who are employed; it is composed of the radical *guǎn* (广) and the phonetic *sī* (斯).

Volume Seven, Part One (The character "xiān" [先] is not pronounced). Volume Eight, Part One. *Fǎtáo* (法鞉): "Táo" is pronounced as *dú dāo* (徒刀反). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Yílǐ* states: "The *táo* is like a drum but smaller; one holds its handle and shakes it. The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radical "metal" (*qié*) and the phonetic "zhào" (*zhào shēng*). It is correctly written as 鞀, and also as 䩞, 𪔛, or 𪔓; the meanings are identical. *Kan* (pronounced with the *mo* and *pan* finals) is the name for the Heavenly Lake of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven according to the scriptural text; it is a transliteration of a Sanskrit term, where one merely reproduces the sound without seeking the literal meaning of the characters. If one were to rely on the characters themselves, the word *ni-kan* would deviate from the intended meaning of the scripture.

9. Ninth Fascicle. *Qiè* (口戒反; kǒu jiè fǎn). The *Guǎyá* states that *qiè* means "blazing. The meanings of the characters in the ancient and modern *Zhèngzìyì* are identical. It is composed of the radical "fire" (*huǒ*) and the phonetic "hài" (*hài*).

10. Volume Ten. "Nian-wu" (黏污) is also written as "nian" (粘), with the same pronunciation as "nü-zhan" (女沾). The *Zishu* (字書) states that "nian" means "to stick. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文解字) defines it as "mutual adhesion," composed of the radical for "millet" (黍) and the phonetic "zhan" (占); the pronunciation of "nian" is "hu" (胡).

The character for *cānglǐn* (granary) is correctly written as 㐭 (pronounced lì, with the radical 力). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "㐭 is where grain is stored and brought in. For the sacrificial offerings (*jīchéng*) of the ancestral temple, which are golden-yellow, I take them from my 㐭; therefore it is called 㐭. It is composed of 入 (entering) and 回 (returning), representing the shape of a house with doors and windows inside. 㐭 may also be written as 廩 with the radical 广 and the character 禾, which is identical to the version in the Classics.

"Yinxi" (印璽)—the character "xi" is pronounced as *sì* (思紫反). It refers to the jade seal of the Son of Heaven. "Xi" means trust (*xìn*). It is also a sacred vessel (*shénqì*). According to the *Shuowen*, it was originally written with the radical for earth (*tǔ*) as 𤫐; now it is written with the radical for jade (*yù*) as 𤫆.

*Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra*, Scroll One, Part One. Newly supplemented by Huilin: *kě* (pronounced with the *mò* and *hòu* finals). The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* states it means "to trade. The *Yùn Yīng* states it means "to barter goods. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "the exchange of wealth," written with the radical for "treasure" (*bèi*) and the phonetic *yǎo*; *yǎo* is an archaic form of the character *mǎo*. The version in this sūtra is written as *gù*, which is incorrect.

Regarding the character *huá* (譁): the upper radical is the phonetic *huā* (花). The commentary on the *Shūjìng* states that *huá* means clamor (*xuān*). The *Kǎoshēng* says it refers to noisy chatter (*yìzào*). The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic "flower" (*huā*); the version using "mouth" (*kǒu*) is incorrect.

*Yúchǎn* (諛諂): The upper radical is *yǒu* (庾), reversed to *zhū* (朱). The *Zhuāngzǐ* says: "To speak without distinguishing between right and wrong is called *yú*. The *Cāngjiépiān* says: "*Chǎn* follows the will of others. Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* states: "*Yú* is also *chǎn*. It is pronounced with the phonetic *yù*. The text here uses *yù* (諭), which is incorrect. The lower radical is *chǔ* (丑), reversed to *rǎn* (染). The *Yìjīng* says: "The superior man does not flatter when interacting with those above, nor does he behave with sycophancy when interacting with those below. Hé Xiū says: "*Chǎn* means to bend one's body [in servility]. Zhèng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* says: "*Chǎn* refers to inclining the body to show subservience. The *Zhuāngzǐ* defines it as "speaking by conforming to the will of others is called *chǎn*. At this time, the clerical script (*lìshū*) was used for brevity; the correct form in the seal script (*zhuànwén*) is written with *yán* (閻) as *chèn* (讇). Now, it is abbreviated.

Regarding "four corners" (sì yú): Yuèqūn’s *Qián* states that it means "roof corner. *Kǎo shēng* says that the four corners are called *yú*. The *Shuowén* defines it as "a mountain ridge," formed from the radical "阜" (mountain) with "禺" as the phonetic. In the scriptures, it is written as "嵎" (*yú*), referring to the name of the mountain where the sun rises; this is what is meant in the *Shàngshū*: "At Yúyí, there is the Valley of the Rising Sun" (*Yánggǔ*).

Volume 2, Middle Volume of the Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra. "Qingyi" (輕㑥): also written as "yang" (敭) or "yi" (易), with the same pronunciation as "shi" (豉). The *Cangjie pian* states that "yi" means arrogance; it refers to being complacent and indifferent.

The *he* duck (pronounced with the initial *hu* and *ge*) resembles a pheasant; it fights to death before ceasing, which is why warriors wear a cap modeled after it. The *Shanhai jing* states that Mount Huizhu is abundant in *heji* (pheasant-fighting cocks), which pierce their heads with their tails. It also originates from Shangdang Commandery. The final syllable, "xia," refers to an aquatic bird.

Regarding "bùshàn" (slanderous calumny): it is the opposite of "jiān" (deceit). The *Cāngjiépiān* states that "shàn" means "fèi" (to revile). The *Lúnyǔ* says, "One who dwells in a low position and slanders those above. "Shàn" and "bù" both mean to defame; both are composed of the radical for speech.

The term *jālong* (蛟龍) is rendered in Sanskrit as *kumbhīra*. Those with scales are called *jālong*. The *Baopuzi* states: "The mother dragon is called a *jālong*; the male offspring is called a *qiulóng*. Its form resembles a fish, its body is like that of a crocodile (*táo*), and there are pearls within its tail-skin. Guo’s commentary on the *Shanhaijing* says: "The *jiāo* resembles a snake but has four legs; it has a small head and a slender neck, with white rings around its neck. The large ones measure several dozen spans in circumference; they lay eggs that produce young the size of one or two *hú* measures of grain. They are capable of swallowing people and possess supernatural powers."

*Jue* (㹢攫): The first character is also written as *jia* (猳, with the phonetic *gu xia*); the second is *ju bo*. It refers to a large female monkey that is skilled at seizing people and is fond of looking back.

3. *Ban zhou san mei jing*, Scroll Lower. Newly supplemented by Hui Lin: *Yuan fei* (蜎飛). The first character is pronounced *hui yuan*. The *Mao Shi* states: "The appearance of the *yuan yun* (蜎蜎) is that of a small insect; it belongs to the class of *fu you* (蜉蝣)."

*Shǎn* (蝡): On the upper part, it is pronounced *rùn* (潤). The *Zītǒng* (字統) says: "The repeated character *shǎn* (蝡蝡) describes the movement of insects; those with feet are called *chóng* (蟲), while those without feet are called *shǎn*. The *Guǎngyá* (廣雅) writes it as *zhàn* (𧔀) or *hán* (󲈃). The *Shuōwén* (說文) defines it as "movement," composed of the radical *chóng* (虫) with the phonetic *ruǎn* (耎).
The characters 𩟱 (kuì) and 餽 (kuì)—the former with the phonetic component 逵 (qí), the latter with 鬼 (guǐ)—are both form-phonetic compounds meaning "to provide provisions" (*kuìxiáng*).
*Yùnyīng* states that they may also be written as 餽. *Jūlì* is a Sanskrit term, which various sutras transcribe as *jùzhī*; it is a numerical designation for one million.
*Nayuta* is a Sanskrit term, also transliterated as *nāyuta* or *nayuta*, which corresponds here to one hundred thousand million (*koṭi*).

*Yojana* is also a Sanskrit term, transliterated as *youxun*, *youyan*, or *yushena*; its correct Sanskrit pronunciation is *yojana*. It was the distance a holy king’s army could travel in one day; calculated according to the Dharma, it is equivalent to thirty *li*.
"Muscle" (jīshòu): "jī" is pronounced as *jū* (with the *yí* rhyme); it refers to the skin and flesh of the body.

The *Mahāsannipāta-Bhadrapāla-bodhisattva-sūtra*, Volume One, Part One, compiled by Huìlín. Regarding the name Bhadrapāla found in various sūtras: he was the lay bodhisattva Elder Bhadrapāla in the city of Rājagṛha during the Buddha’s lifetime. He is one of the thousand future Buddhas of this present Bhadrakalpa. He requested the Buddha to preach this sūtra.

*Tuán* (一摶): The *Bóyǎ* states that it means to hold something in the hand so that the parts adhere together. In the *Kǎogōngjì*, it is sometimes written as *tuán*, meaning "round. *Zào* (躁): Upper radical *zāo* (遭燥反). The *Lúnyǔ* says it means "restless and not tranquil.

Jia’s commentary on the *Guóyuè* says it means "agitated. The *Yùnquān* says it means "hasty. The *Jixùn* says it means "movement. It is formed from the radical *zú* (foot) with the phonetic *sào* (喿, sound *sāngdào*). The lower character is also pronounced *qīngyì*. The *Guǎngyǎ* says *qìqì* (慼慼) means "sorrowful. It is sometimes written as *qì* (慽). The *Gōngjīn zhèngzì* says it is formed from the radical *xīn* (heart) with the phonetic *qī* (戚). The *Shuōwén* further explains the character *qì* (慼) as being formed from *yuè* (戉, sound *yuè*) and the abbreviated form of *lù* (𡧯) as the phonetic.

The character 𢓼 (piè) is pronounced with the initial *hen* (kěn fǎn) and the final *shēng* (tone). The *Kǎo shēng* states it means "stubborn" (*hèn*) or "resentful. The *Yùn quán* states it means "obstinate and perverse" (*hèn lì*). Regarding the correct orthography of ancient and modern times, it follows the radical 彳 (chì) and the phonetic 艮 (gèn). In the *Shuōwén*, the character 艮 consists of 目 (eye) and 匕 (spoon); its current form in clerical script (*lìshū*) is due to cursive abbreviation. The radical 彳 is pronounced *chǔ chǐ fǎn*. The phonetic 艮 is pronounced *kǔ běn fǎn*. The *Kǎo shēng* states that the lower part, 毘袂 (pí mèi), means "ruined" (*piè huài*) or "evil" (*è*). It takes the form of ruined and tattered clothing.

The character 蠆 (chài) is pronounced with the initial *chì* (zhī fǎn) and the final *è* (shēng yě); it is composed of the radical 虫 (insect). The character 螫 (shè) has the ancient form 㞢 (gǔ zhī zì); the version composed of 竹, 夭, and 口 is a vulgar character.

The *Qǔ* (區) is pronounced with a reversed *qū* rhyme. The *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲) states that it means "limit" (*xiànyù*). The *Erya* says, "Fifty is called a *qū*," and Guo Pu’s commentary notes: "Two fives make the number; five numbers make a *qū*. Ma Rong’s commentary on the *Lunyu* says: "It is like the distinction between different species of plants and trees. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as composed of *pǐn* (品) and *xì* (匸). *Pǐn* refers to classifying by category; *xì* refers to concealment. The upper character [of *pǐn*] has the phonetic value of *xī* (兮) with the *dì* (弟) rhyme.

3. Third Fascicle. Third [Section]. *Lúfēi* (鑪㰆) is also written as *wěipái* (韛排); both forms share the pronunciation *báixiè* (白薤). This refers to the bellows used by blacksmiths to blow the fire so that it blazes.

"Zī (consultation) and xún (inquiry) are opposites. In the *Zuǒzhuan*, it says: "To consult with those who are virtuous is called zī; to consult with one's kin is called xún. Zī refers to inquiring about the way of goodness; Du’s commentary states that xún refers to inquiring into the deliberations of one's relatives.
*Jita* is the name of this son of a householder; according to its phonetic transcription, it is pronounced as *yu* and *ji* (with the latter reversed).

*Kai* (篋) is pronounced with the initial *qian* and the final *xi* (reversed); *si* (笥) has the initial *si* and the final *li*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that a *si* is a container for clothing. The *Liji* uses *dan* (簞) and *si* interchangeably; furthermore, Zheng Xuan says they are both containers for food, where the round one is called *dan* (pronounced *dan*) and the square one is called *si*.

[pronounced *zàn* with the initial *zǐ* and final *dàn* reversed] means to assist; it also means to guide.

*Kēngqiāng* (铿锵) is also written as *xuān* (銵) with the phonetic *kǔgēng* (苦耕) for the second character, or as *qiāng* (鎗) and *cān* (傖), both having the same form and the phonetic *qīyáng* (七羊). According to the *Guǎngyá* (廣雅), *kēng* and *qiāng* together denote the sound of gold and jade; they are words formed by combining a semantic component (*shēng*) and a phonetic component (*xíng*).

"Kaijia" (鎧甲) [the first character is pronounced with the *kai* and *gai* finals]. The *Wenzi Jilüe* states that covering the body with golden armor is called *kai*. *Kang* (坑) is pronounced *keng* (耕) when referring to a guest; Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states it means a pit or trench (*keng-qian*). The *Cangjie pian* states it means a ravine (*he*) or a hollow (*han*). The lower character, *kan* (坎), is pronounced *ku-gan*. The *Zhouyi* states that *kan* also means a depression (*qiao*). "Quē" (缺) [the "quān" and "yuè" rhymes]: The *Kuájíepiān* states that "quē" means "deficient. The following "yǎ" rhyme is read as "jiē. Regarding the phonetic analysis: "quē" is composed of the radical "fǒu" (a jar) with "guài" as its phonetic; "yá" (崖) is composed of the radical "è" (a stone) with "guī" as its phonetic. *Jí* (棘): Upper radical *yǐng* (矝) with the phonetic *yì* (憶). According to the *Fānyán* (方言), in the region between the Yangtze and Huai rivers, the thorns of all grasses and trees are called *jí*. The *Màoshī Zhuàn* (Mao Commentary on the Classic of Poetry) states: "The *jí* is the sour jujube (*suǎnzǎo*). The *Shuowén* (Explanations of Words and Texts) says: "Small jujubes growing in clusters; [the character] follows the radical *bì* (朿). The original text follows *bèi* (束), which is an error. Lower radical *cí* (雌) with the phonetic *sì* (賜). Gu Yewáng says it refers to a tree whose bark has sharp thorns. The *Shuowén* says: "The thorn of a tree; a pictograph. *Shu* (pronounced *zhù*, with the radical *yu* and the phonetic *shù*). The *Huainanzi* states: "The spring rain irrigates the myriad things; there is no ground where it does not pour down, and no thing that does not grow. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "It is the timely rain by which the myriad things are nourished and brought to life. It is composed of the radical *shui* (water) and the phonetic *shù*; the sound of *shù* is *zhù*."

*Jin* (筋): On the upper part of the character, read as *jin* with the refined tone (*xin*) according to the *Shuowen*. It refers to the strength of muscle and sinew. It is composed of the radical *rou* (肉), the character *zhu* (竹)—as bamboo is among things that have many sinews—and the radical *li* (力). The *li* radical symbolizes the sinew itself. The form written with the radical *cao* (艹) and the character *jiao* (角) to form *jiu* (𮏴) is incorrect. *Xia* (下): Read as *sui* with the refined tone (*xi*). The *Shuowen* writes this as *ji* (𩪦), stating it is the fat within the bone. It is composed of the radical *gu* (骨) and the phonetic component *sui* (隨) in abbreviated form. Its correct orthography is written with the radical *sui* (隓) to form *gui* (󲖀). The pronunciation of *gui* is *xu gui* (許規反).

The character for *māo* (犛) is also written as *lí* (氂). Its radical is "hair" (毛), which is pronounced either *máo* or *lí*. The *Shanhai jing* states: "On Mount Panhou there is a beast shaped like an ox, with hair growing from its four limbs; it is called the *māoniu*. Guo Pu’s commentary notes: "Its back and tail are both covered in long hair. The *Shuowen jiezi* defines it as: "The long-haired ox of the southwestern tribes. It is composed of 'ox' (牛) and the phonetic element 'zhi' (𠩺). The pronunciation of *zhi* is *lì* (力之反). It is also written as *máo* (𠩺).

*Tiao* (in *tiaoyan*, "to pick out the eyes"): the distant sound is *chao*; it belongs to the category of sounds like *tiao*. It means to pluck or extract. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shou*) and the phonetic "zhao.

*Jue* (in *jueyue*, "to extract") has the pronunciation *juanxue*. *Mò* (in *mobó*, "foam"): the upper character is pronounced *nuo*. Gu Yewang states that *mò* refers to the floating foam upon water. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "water" (*shui*) and the phonetic "wei. The lower character is pronounced *tuán*. This was already explained previously in the fourth fascicle of the *Sūtra on the Questions of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha to the Buddha*.
Regarding the character for *pào* (bubble): it is formed with *bāo* as its phonetic component. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is derived from the sound of *bāo*.

In the *Dai'ai jing* (Sutra of Great Compassion), Volume 1, Huilin explains that *kai* (to open) is pronounced with the *pi* rhyme. The *Guoyu* says, "He opened the gate (*kai men*) and spoke with him," and Jia Kui notes that *kai* means to open (*pi*). Whether ancient or modern, the correct orthography uses the radical *men* (gate) as the phonetic component.

The character *tián* (淟) [is pronounced] *tiān* (典) with the *diǎn* rhyme; the *Jíxùn* states it means "to be weary" (*tiǎnniǎn*), and further says "niǎn" means "filth and turbidity. The pronunciation of *niǎn* is *nián* (年) with the *diǎn* rhyme. Regarding *tíngliáo* (庭燎), the *lì* (曆) rhyme is *diào* (弔). The *Lǐjì* states:

"For the great affairs of the state, one provides *sī* (燌) candles and *tíngliáo*. Zheng Zhong says: "A *liáo* is a fire candle made of hemp. The scriptural text uses the character for "metal" (*jīn*) to form *dìng* (錠), which is incorrect. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "A *dìng* is a type of hoe (*chú*). The *Guǎngyá* says: "A *dìng* is called a *nòu* (耨)," which refers to a farming tool. This greatly deviates from the meaning of the scripture.

2. Second Fascicle, Part Two. **Wù (寤):** The upper character is pronounced *wù*. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states: "Wù means to awaken. The *Cangjie Pian* says: "To speak while waking from sleep is called wù. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of 㝱 (mèng) with 省 (shěng) below; the lower character is pronounced *mí bì* (as in *mì*). Gu Yewang states: "It refers to sleeping deeply or reclining at rest. The *Shuowen* defines it as "lying down," composed of 󰡏 (yǎn) with 省 (shěng) above and 未 (wèi) providing the phonetic. **Xī (息):** The *Shuowen* defines it as "lying down," composed of 󰡏 (yǎn) with 未 (wèi) providing the phonetic. (Note: This entry appears to be a continuation or variant gloss for the preceding term regarding rest.)

It differs from the *Huishang* (回反) and the *Beicang* (埤蒼), which state that it means "extraordinary and precious" (*guǐwěi dàqí*). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) says it is the appearance of being beautiful and grand. The *Shuowén* (說文) states it takes the radical "clothing" (衣) with "guǐ" (瑰) as its phonetic; the version of the scripture that uses "huì" (潰) instead of "guǐ" (瑰) is incorrect.

"Yuduan" (愚戇): The second character, "zhuo" (卓), is pronounced with the *xiang* rhyme (降反). The *Huìxùn* (訓纂) states that it means "yùnduàn" (㤶戇), describing an appearance where the spirit is not lucid. The *Huáinán Zǐ* says: "If one views Bóyí through the eyes of Guǎn Zhòng, one will consider oneself yùnduàn. The *Shuōwén* defines "dùn" (戇) as "foolishness"; it is composed of "heart" (心) and "treasure" (貝). The pronunciation of "yùnduàn" (㤶) is "yīng xiáng fǎn" (瑛降反), and the pronunciation of "yùnduàn" (㤶) is "māng xiàng fǎn" (尨巷反).

"Dàn-pà" (憺怕): the first character is pronounced *dàn* (upper tone), and the second is pronounced *pǔ-bó* (反). The scripture says "dàn-lǜ" (澹慮); "pà" means tranquil stillness (*tián-jìng*). It is incorrect for the scripture to use the radical for water (*shuǐ*). "Xiá-cī" (瑕玼):
the first character is pronounced *xiá*, and the second is pronounced *cí*.

The upper character [of 嗹] is pronounced qiāng (two tones) and the lower is kǔ-gǎi (two tones). *Ōu* is the sound of weeping and crying; *kài* is the sound of sighing. It is correctly written as *ōu-kài*; its appearance in the sutras as *lǎn-kài* is a scribal error that does not form a valid character.

**Dì (躓礙):** The first character is pronounced *zhì* (with the radical *zhé* and the phonetic *lì*). Gu Yewang states that *dì* means "to stumble" (*dùn*). The *Guǎngyá* says it means "to tread upon," and it also refers to "falling and stumbling.

It is formed with the radical *zú* (foot) and the phonetic *zhì*. **3. Third Fascicle.** **Jí (彶彶):** The pronunciation is *jí*. The *Lǐjì* states: "To hurry as if pursuing something but not catching up. Gu Yewang says *jísè* (彶彶) means "extremely urgent. The *Shuowén* says it is the appearance of walking hurriedly; it is formed with the radical *chì* (walking) and the phonetic *jí*. Alternatively, it is written with the radical *rén* (person), pronounced *jì*, and the phonetic *jí*; the commentary says it means "tied to the heart" and "striving toward a task. The text here uses the character *jí* (汲) with the radical *shuǐ* (water), which is an error in the manuscript.
*Tan-tie* (貪餮): The second character is pronounced *tian* (天) with the *jie* (結) tone; the *Kao* (考) commentary states that "to greedily consume food" is called *tie*.

*Huang-hu* (恍惚): The first character is pronounced *huang* (荒) with the *guang* (廣) tone, and the second is pronounced *hu* (忽). In the scriptural text, it is written as *huang* (慌), which is incorrect.
Bòliè (擘裂): The first character is pronounced bǎi, and also piéng-mì-fǎn; both are written with the radical "hand" (手). Volume Four, Part Four. Nàlüè (愞劣):

The first character is pronounced nù-luàn-fǎn. The *Kǎoshēng* states that "nà" means timid or weak; it is composed of the "heart" (心) radical and the phonetic "ruǎn. Alternatively, it may be written as "wēn" (偄) with the "person" (人) radical, which has the same meaning.

The character *guàn* (亘) [is pronounced with the initial *gāng* and the final *dèng*]. The *Jíxùn* (集訓) states that *guàn* means "to extend far beyond. The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (毛詩傳) says that *guàn* means "pervasive. The *Shuōwén* (說文) writes it as *jìn* (𣕲), meaning "to reach the end. The form currently in use is the ancient version of the character *guàn*. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of a sun radical (*曰*) with a horizontal line above and below, signifying the sense of spanning from top to bottom.

Volume Five, Part Five. The two characters *hào* (晧) and *chòu* (臭) share the same pronunciation, which is *háo-lǎo-fǎn*. According to the *Erya*, *hào* means "radiance. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it denotes the appearance of the sun when first rising; it is composed of the radical "sun" (*ri*) and the phonetic "gào" (*gào*), or alternatively written with "bái" (*bái*). Regarding the character *chòu* (臭) below: it is said that the primordial qi is "white-fragrant" (*chù-bái*), which is Heaven. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *dà-hào* (大皡) refers to the Great Sun; it is composed of "dà" (大) and the ancient form of "gào" (*gào*). The current usage, composed of "rì" (曰) and "tiān" (天), is a vulgar variant.

*Qǒnglì* (𢤱戾): The upper character is pronounced *lóng* (聾) with the *dǒng* (董) rhyme; the lower character is pronounced *lì* (麗). According to the analysis, *kǒnglì* refers to being stubborn and difficult to transform. *Gōngkè* (恭恪):

The upper character, *gōng* (恭), is composed of the "heart" radical (*xīn*) and the phonetic *gòng* (共). The lower character, *kè* (恪), is pronounced *kānggè* (康各). Kong’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* states that *kè* means "reverence. In archaic texts, it is written as *kè* (愙) from the character *kè* (客); this is both a phono-semantic compound and a semantic compound.

The character for "ant" (蟲蟻) is pronounced *yi* (with the initial *yǐ*) or is written as 螘; the *Erya* states that "ant" (*yì*) refers to the *bífú*. This character has no fixed form, and former scholars have each created it according to their own preference: some include the radical 䖵 to form 𧕶, while others write it as 󱲴 or even as 蛾.

Regarding "liánshāng" (憐傷), the *Jiànxùn* (集訓) states that "lián" means "to love," while the phonetic component indicates "sorrow. It is vulgarly written as "lián" (怜); however, the scriptural text uses "miǎn" (𥼭) with the "rice" radical (米), which is incorrect. This is a scribal error that does not form a valid character.

6. Volume Six. Section Six. *Fànliú* (泛流). [The character] *fú* (孚) is pronounced with the *fàn* (梵) rhyme; it is a phonetic transcription of the sound. *Fàn* (泛) means to float. It is also written as *fàn* (氾). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *fàn* (氾) means "overflowing" (*làn*) and is composed of the radical "water" (*shui*) with the phonetic element "fá" (*fá*).

"Blowing the *sheng* at the Azure Capital": *sheng* is the name of a musical instrument. The *Shiben* (Book of Origins) states that Suí invented the *sheng*, modeling it after the body of a phoenix; its sound represents the beginning of spring. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (Explaining Graphs and Analyzing Characters) states that because things (*wu*) are born from it, and because it resembles things piercing through the earth to grow, it is called *sheng*. The version in the Classics written as *chui* (𣢡) is incorrect.
"Ēn" (pronounced with the *wēn* and *mèn* tones): according to the *Shuowen*, "to smear" (*ēn*); it is composed of the radical "hand" and the phonetic element "mò" (abbreviated).
"Zhān" (pronounced with the *tángshàng* tone as *zhān*): the name of a fragrant tree; in Guangzhou, its leaves are used to produce [incense].

7. The seventh fascicle. The term *yú'ài* (愚騃) [is pronounced with the second tone on the first character and the third tone on the second] has already been fully explained in the second fascicle above.
*Shāo zhà* (燒灹) [is pronounced with the fourth tone on the first character and the fourth tone on the second]; it refers to the sound of a fire explosion.

Regarding the character *chū* (勅猪反), its phonetic gloss states that it means "to unfold" (*shū*) or "to extend" (*zhāng*). The *Yùnquán* (韻詮) states it means "to disperse. It is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "lù" (*lù*).
Regarding *dài* (逮得臺柰反), the *Jíxùn* (集訓) states it means "to reach" (*jí*) or "to arrive at" (*jí*). The version in the scripture as *dài* is incorrect.

Volume Eight, Part Eight. Regarding the character "péng" (棚) [pronounced with the initial *b* and final *-eng*]: the *Kǎośēng* states it means a wooden platform or loft (*pén-zhàn*). The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "péng. In the sutra, it is written as "píng" (枰), which is incorrect.

The character *qiáng* (强) [is pronounced] *bā-mà-fǎn*. The *Shuowen* states: "It refers to the first appearance of the lunar phase (*bò*) when the moon begins to wax. The *Jixun* states: "It means a sovereign king. The *Zitong* states: "It means long; it is composed of the radical 'moon' (*yue*) and the phonetic 'lèi' (*lèi*). In archaic script, it is written as *shěn*.
The Akṣayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra, Scroll One. Compiled by Huilin. *Akṣayamati* is the Sanskrit term; this is translated as "Inexhaustible Intention" (*Wújìn yì*), which is the name of this bodhisattva.

"Hao hao, hao hao! This sutra, along with the previously mentioned *Mahākaruṇā* and other sutras, were all translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin; their phrasing and principles are somewhat crude and unrefined, lacking in subtle elegance. The repeated writing of 'Hao Hao' signifies that which is immeasurable, boundless, unfathomable, and vast."
"Kuai-liè-hōng-hào" (掴裂轟號) has the final rhyme "lie" (列); this is also a colloquial expression meaning "to destroy.
"Shèng-zhē" (聖喆) has the final rhyme "lie" (列), or is written as "zhé" (哲); "zhé" (哲) means wisdom and is also an archaic character.
*Shi-mo*: "shi" and "mo" rhyme with *ding-li*. *Bao-guo*: "bao" means to wrap; "guo" is pronounced as in *guǒ*, with the radical *yī* (clothing) and the phonetic *guǒ*.

2. Second Fascicle. Second Fascicle. *Di-tu*: "di" rhymes with *ding-li*, or written with the radical *niú* (ox), forming *dǐ*; "tu" rhymes with *du-nu*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, this is a compound character formed from the radicals *xué* (cave) and *quǎn* (dog).

Regarding "xiáo zhuàn" (餚饌): the first character is pronounced *jiāo* (效) with an initial *jiao* (交) and a final *fǎn* (反); the second character is pronounced *zhuàn* (撰). This has already been fully explained in the preceding text. Regarding "bù cún qù" (不存懅):
the second character is pronounced *jù* (巨) with an initial *yú* (魚) and a final *fǎn* (反), meaning "haste" or "urgency.

Volume Three, Part Three. Regarding "tián pò" (恬怕): the first character is pronounced *tíng* (亭) with an initial *jiān* (間) and a final *fǎn* (反); the second character is pronounced *pǔ* (普) with a final *bǎi* (百).

"Coarse" (cū) is a vulgar character for "to cite" (dǔ), with the phonetic component being *cāng* and the radical *hú* (read as *fǎn*). The correct form consists of three "deer" (*lù*) radicals. "To cite" means to state in brief or summary fashion. "Bó" (pronounced *bāngjiǎo fǎn*) means "clear" according to the *Guǎngyá*. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Kǎogōngjì* states: "Bó means 'to see'. This is confirmed by the *Hànshū*, which says: "It was bó-rán (distinctly clear) and easy to understand. Thus it is so.

4. Fourth Fascicle. Regarding "ma-ma" (the first "ma" pronounced with the *mo* and *ke* reversed): the *Sancang* states that "ma" means minute (*wei*) and also refers to something very small; it refers to tiny, minute insects. Although some versions of the sutra text write this as "can-can," that is incorrect.
The ancient script for *xiōngshù* (凶豎) is written with the character 豎 (*zhù*, pronounced *shūzhǔ* in the rhyme), meaning "a small child," referring here to a wicked and perverse person.

*Zhūchāng* (侏倀) should correctly be written as *zhūzhāng* (譸張), with the pronunciation *zhāngliú*. The *Mao Shi* states: "To *zhūzhāng* means to deceive," which refers to mutual delusion. In the scripture, it is written as *zhū* (侏, pronounced *zhū*), meaning "dwarf," and below it is written as *chāng* (倀, pronounced *chìliáng*), meaning "mad. These do not accord with the meaning of the scripture.

5. Fifth Fascicle. *Tàn* (pronounced *tǎn*, with the second tone). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *tàn* means "peaceful" (*ān*). According to the *Guangya*, *tàn* means "level" (*píng*). The reading in the sutra text as *㝵* (*yì*) is incorrect.
"Juàn-liàn" (眷戀): "juàn" is pronounced as *jiān* (下力眷反) and "liàn" as *liàn* (力眷反). It means to look back with longing; the text's reading as "quán" (惓) is incorrect.

"Fēn-pō" (芬葩): "fēn" is pronounced as *pǔ* (普花反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as fragrance (*fēnfāng*). "Pō" refers to blossoms (*huā*). The *Shenglei* takes it to mean the appearance of profusion.

*Dàyóu* (大猷): The remainder of the rhyme is *zhōu*. The *Fāngyán* states that in the eastern state of Qí, they call *yóu* *qiú*; it also means "plan" (*tú*) and "if" (*ruò*), as well as "to follow" (*shùn*).

Volume Six, Part Six. *Rǔbù* (乳哺): *pú* and *mù* are the rhymes. That which is called chewing food in the mouth and spitting it out for a small child is called *bù*. It is derived from the mouth with the phonetic element *fǔ*.
"Tong-yang" (痛癢) means "itching"; it is sometimes written with the radical for insects as "zhāng" (蛘), and its appearance in the scripture as "yáng" (痒) is incorrect.

Section Seven, Volume Seven: "Yòu-xù" (誘󰮔). The first character is pronounced *yóu* (由首反) and the second *xún* (詢律反). "Yòu-xù" means to gradually instruct, to lead, and to mutually exhort. Its appearance in the scriptural text as "yōu-xù" (憂恤, meaning "to grieve for") is not the intended meaning of the scripture.

"Village" (cùnluò) is colloquially written as "luò" (with the phonetic components "li" and "ge"). According to the *Guǎngyá*, "luò" means "to dwell. A place where a multitude of people reside is called a "village" (cūn).

In the *Ratnāvalī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* (translated by Huìlín), the term "hóuliáng" (provisions) has the pronunciation "húgōu. According to the *Kǎoshēng*, "hóu" refers to dry rice. The scriptural text uses the character "mì" (rice) with "hóu" to form "hòu," which is not a valid character and is incorrect.
2. Middle Scroll: *Zhōngjuǎn*. *Tángzàng* (湯藏): "Táng" is pronounced *tāng* with a retroflex *-ang* rhyme; the commentary states it refers to a treasury of gold and silk.

3. Lower Scroll: *Xiàjuǎn*. *Jūmǐn* (鞠閔): "Jū" (鞠) is pronounced *gǒu* with a labial *-ou* rhyme; it means to nourish, to love, or to instruct. "Mǐn" (閔) is pronounced *měi yǔn* with a labial *-un* rhyme; it means to grieve or to feel pain.

*Shēnshēn* (the first character pronounced *shēn*, the second *luán*): According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *shēnshēn* describes the appearance of a multitude coming together; it also describes an appearance of being orderly and well-arranged.

*Xiánshǎn* (the first character pronounced *huán*, the second *jiàn*): According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *xián* means elegant; it refers to being settled and tranquil. Today, both are written with the character *xián*.

The Akṣayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra, Volume One. Compiled by Huilin. [Note: "Not blinking" (bù shùn) means to move the eyes; the text uses the character *shùn* with the "eye" radical (*mù*), which is incorrect. It should be written with the "mouth" radical (*xún*).
"Liánmián" (縺綿): the first character is pronounced "lián"; it means continuous and uninterrupted. Volume Two, Part Two. "Bèimiàn" (䫌面):
the second character is pronounced "pǔmǐ". It refers to turning or tilting the head. In the scriptural text, it is written with the radical for "person" (亻) as "bǐ" (俾), which is incorrect.
"Liáo-zhì" (撩擲) is pronounced "liáo-diào" (遼調) in the retroflex tone;
it means to throw from afar. "Bù-yī" (不猗)—the ancient usage of the character is eccentric; according to the correct meaning of the sutra, it should properly be written as "yī" (依).
Volume Three. Third Volume. "Hǎi-tāo" (海濤)—"tāo" (濤) is pronounced "dào-láo" (道勞) in the retroflex tone. "Hǎi" (海) means the sea; "tāo" (濤) refers to large waves.
"Xiù (齅)" [pronounced xiāng jiù fǎn]: The *Shuowen* states, "To bring the nose to an odor is called xiù. The scripture uses the character "xiù" (from the mouth), which is incorrect.

"Shī (溼)" [pronounced shèn rù fǎn]: The *Shuowen* states, "It means deep dampness (*yōushī*). It is composed of 'water' and 'one' covering it; because there is water covering the earth, it is moist. The scriptural text uses the character "shī," which is incorrect.

4. Fascicle Four. Fascicle Four: *Dū* (督), meaning "to correct" (*zhèng*). It is correctly pronounced as *dōng lù* (東祿) with the second tone. According to the *Erya*, *dū* means "to correct," referring to the act of governing and correcting. According to the *Fangyan*, *dū* means "to manage" (*lǐ*) and "to examine" (*chá*).

The character 虧 (kuī) is composed of 跪 (guì) on top and 為 (wéi) below; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it signifies the depletion of vital energy (*qi*). The phonetic component 考 (kǎo) indicates falling or injury. The lower part, 孥 (nú), is pronounced with the *jian* rhyme; the *Kaoseng* states that 赧 (nǎn) means shame—a reddening of the face, a sense of bashfulness and embarrassment. It is also written as 𧹞, a compound character formed through associative meaning (*huìyì*).

Volume Five, Part One; Volume Six (the two preceding volumes are easy to read and require no phonetic gloss). *The Scripture of the Bodhisattva Sovereign King* (Zìzài Wáng Púsà Jīng), Scroll One, Upper Part. Compiled by Xuān Yìng. *Guàn* (貫): Ancient pronunciation *gǔ luàn*. The *Cāngjié Piān* states that it means "to pierce through. The *Shuōwén* [explains it] as being composed of the radical *wú* (毋) with the phonetic *guān* (官); the lower character has the pronunciation *jiǎ* (甲). In the *Fānyán*, it refers to a small, long arrow with two holes bored through the middle. *Jiǎ* (鉀): A type of armor (*lù*). Guō’s commentary states: "It is the arrow-armor (*jiǎ*) of today, with two sides bored out. The standard character for both ancient and modern usage consists of the radical *jīn* (金) with the phonetic *jiǎ* (甲).

One *jǔ* (one handful). "Gōng" is read as *fǎn*. According to the *Shuowen*, *jǔ* means to gather; it also refers to holding an object with the fingers curved. In ancient forms, it was written as 󲂌, or as 󲃽, or as 匊, or as 臼; all are used interchangeably.

*Xiù* (pronounced *xǔ jiù*): The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to bring the nose to an odor, called *xiù*"; it is composed of the radical for "nose" (*bi*) and the phonetic element "odor" (*chòu*). The archaic form is written as 齅; the version in the Buddhist scriptures written with the mouth radical (*kǒu*) as 嗅 is a vulgar character.

Volume 2, Part 2 (No characters require phonetic glosses). *The Sūtra of the Questions of the Bodhisattva Veṣṭhila-rāja*. Volume 1, Part 1. Compiled by Xuanying. Regarding "bù xià" (怖嚇): "bù" is pronounced hù jià (反); it is a term from Zheng’s commentary on the *Shijing* (Classic of Poetry), which states that to ward off people with one's elbow is called "xià. The *Pīcāng* (Supplement to the Cangjie Dictionary) describes it as the appearance of a great rage. The *Fānyǔ* (Dialectal Dictionary) records it as "kōng xì" (恐䦧). The standard character for ancient and modern times follows the radical "jié" (卩) and the phonetic "hè" (赫); "xì" (䦧) is pronounced hū jī (反).
The correct character for *bi* (feces) is composed of the radical *shi* (corpse) and the phonetic *zhi*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *wei* (urine) is composed of the radicals *wei* and *shui*;
the vulgar form is *niao*. [End of] Volume 19 of the *Yiqiejing Yinyi*. Volume 20. No characters with phonetic glosses in this volume.
[End of] Volume 20 of the *Yiqiejing Yinyi*.

Compiled by the Tang Dynasty Śramaṇa Huilin, *The Phonetic Commentary on the Ratnaketudhāraṇī Sūtra*, ten fascicles; *The Phonetic Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, sixty fascicles. Regarding the "Yi" (譯) in the title of the *Ratnaketudhāraṇī Sūtra* translated by Xuan Ying:

the preface to the *Ratnaketudhāraṇī Sūtra* states that Huilin provides the phonetics. Regarding the term "Di Yi" (狄譯): in the *Liji* (Book of Rites), it says, "The people of the five regions do not understand one another’s speech and their desires differ. To convey their will and facilitate their needs, [the office] is called Di Yi (Western Interpreters). Zheng’s commentary notes: "These are all names for people of the world, used according to the nature of their affairs. 'Di' means 'to know. According to the *Guangya*, 'Di Yi' means 'translation. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as being composed of the radical 'metal' (革) with the phonetic component 'shi' (是)."

"乃" (nǎi) is the reading of the "Shangsheng" (Imperial Pronunciations). In the *Han Shi*, it means "great. According to the *Shenglei*, it means "to arrive. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that the archaic form of the character "乃" is composed of "彡" (sān) and the phonetic "西" (xī); "西" is itself an archaic form of the character "乃."

*Yǎndùn* (掩頓): The upper character *yǎn* (掩) is pronounced as in *yǎn* (奄). The *Shàngshū* states: "To encompass (*yǎn*) the four seas is to be the ruler of the world. Kǒng Àngguó says: "Encompassing (*yǎn*) is synonymous with 'to cover' (*tóng*). The *Fānyán* says: "It means to store away (*cáng*) or to take (*qǔ*). East of the Guān region, they call taking something *yǎn*. Dù’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* says it means to hide (*nì*). Alternatively, it is written as *yǎn* (掩), and its meaning is the same. The *Shuōwén* says: "It means to cover (*fù*). It follows the radical for 'hand' (*shǒu*) and takes *yǎn* (弇) as its phonetic component; *yǎn* is pronounced as above. The lower character *dùn* (頓) is pronounced *kùn* (困) in reverse. Gù Yěwáng says: "*Dùn* refers to the halting of an army. The *Shuōwén* says: "Bowing the head down is called *dùnshǒu*. It follows the radical for 'taste' (*zhǐ*) and takes *tún* (屯) as its phonetic component; *tún* is pronounced as in *tū* (突) followed by *lùn* (論)."

Regarding "bānhóng" (八紘), Xu Shu Zhong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states that "hóng" means "dimensional cord" (*wéi*). Gu Yewang says that "bānhóng" refers to the "eight extremities" (*bājì*). In the standard characters of past and present, it is written with the radical "silk" (*mì*) and the phonetic component "gōng" (厷); the pronunciation of "gōng" is as stated above.

The "Hanshai" (瀚海) is pronounced *han-gan*. According to the *Guozhi* (括地志), it is the name of a small sea located several hundred li northwest of Tuo Luo and Tu Qu, to the northwest of the Flowing Sands and Great Desert. It lies five thousand three hundred li south of Chang'an. The Great Wall built by the Qin dynasty passed through this sea. The sea extends east and west across the territory of the Xiongnu, with several rivers flowing into it, including the Duluo River, the Xiling River, and the Jin River. The North Court (Beiting) established the Hanshai Garrison, taking this name as its designation.

Regarding "dīfēng" (embankment and fief): it is as Zhu Chūn’s commentary on the *Hànshū* states, that the term "dī" refers to the embankments on the sides and "fēng" refers to the title [of the land]. Wéi Zhāo says it means "to pile up earth to form a boundary. The *Shuowén* defines "dī" as "a raised bank," written with the radical "阜" (*fù*) and the phonetic "是" (*shì*) abbreviated. As for the character "fēng" below, the *Shuowén* states it refers to the territory of the feudal lords. For the Duke, Marquis, Earl, Count, and Viscount, the square was one hundred *lǐ*; for the Baron, seventy *lǐ*; and for the Son of Heaven and the King, fifty *lǐ*. It is written with the radical "土" (*tǔ*) and the ancient form "𡉚" (*fēng*), which is the archaic character for "fēng. Today, it is written with two "土" radicals and the "寸" (*cùn*) radical, forming a compound character based on its meaning. The *Zhòuwén* writes it with "土" and "𡵄" (*diāo*), where "𡵄" is pronounced "fēng."
The *Xuanzhong ji* (Records of the Mysterious Center) states that in the Northern Ocean there is a land of the Candle Dragon named Longting (Dragon Court).

The *Fengxue xuanzhong ji* (Records of the Phoenix’s Nest in the Mysterious Center) states that in the Southern Ocean there is Mount Zhuxue, where the phoenixes dwell; it is an island in the Sea of Milk.

*Zhǒng* (治踵): The first character is pronounced *lǐ*; the second is the phonetic *zhī yǒng fǎn*. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that "zhǒng" means succession (*jì*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "zhǒng" means to pursue (*zhuī*). One source says it refers to the appearance of coming and going; it is formed with "foot" (*zú*) as the radical and "chóng" (*chóng shēng*) as the phonetic. It may also be written with "zhǐ" (*zhǐ*) as the radical, forming *zhǒng*, and these forms are used interchangeably.

Xuānhù (pronounced hǔ gǔ) is the name of an ancient state that shared the same surname as the Xia Hou; it was located in present-day Hù County, Jīngzhào, in Youfúfēng. The *Hànshū* states: "Xia Qì fought against Yǒuhù at the wilds of Gān. This is where the present-day Hùgǔ and Gāntíng are located, marking the site where Qì destroyed the state. Regarding the character 澧 (*lǐ*), its origin is explained in the *Shuōwén* as being identical in meaning: it is formed from the radical 邑 (*yì*) with the phonetic component 戶 (*hù*). It may also be written with the radical 鄠 (*hù*), which is likewise correct.

The character *fǎn* (弘) is read as *fǔ* (無反). The *Kǎośēng* states it means "to specialize" (*zhuānbù*) or "to open. It is the standard form; according to the *Shuōwén*, it also means "to spread. It is composed of the radical *cùn* (寸) and the phonetic *fǔ* (甫). The character below, *húgēng* (胡肱), is read as *húgēng*. According to the *Shuōwén*, *hóng* (弘) means "vast" or "great. It is composed of the radical *gōng* (弓) and the phonetic *sī* (厶); *sī* is pronounced *gēng* (肱).
"Dàn" (達翰反) is glossed by Ying as "to fear. The *Shuowen* states it means "to envy," composed of the radical "heart" (心) and the phonetic "dān" (單).

"Jì" (暨) is glossed above as "qí jì" (其冀反). The *Kaosheng* states that "jì" means "to reach" (及) or "the extreme" (極). The *Shuowen* states it means "to give" (與), composed of the radical "qiè" (且) and the phonetic "jì" (既); the scriptural text uses "jì" (洎) with the water radical, meaning "meat broth," which is not the intended meaning of the scripture.

"Yuan" (爰): Pronounced as *yuǎn* (with the initial *y* and final *-uǎn*). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states: "Yuan means 'at' or 'thereby'. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to lead," following the radical *ji* (𠬪) with the phonetic *yu*. *Ji* is pronounced *bēi yuán* (with the final *-uán*), and the subsequent character is pronounced *mù*. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "Mao means 'exertion' or 'diligence'. The *Shuowen* defines "Mao" as "flourishing," following the radical *xin* (心) with the phonetic *mao*. *Mao* is pronounced as above; alternatively, it may be written as "Mao" (茂) with the radical *cao* (艹), and its meaning of "use" or "application" is the same.
The character 㥠 (yáng), with the initial "shuāng" and final "liú" according to the *Duànzhù* commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan*, means "to hide.
The *Lúnyǔ* states: "What can a person hide? (人焉㥠哉).
Kong’s commentary states: "To hide. In the *Fāngyán*, it means "to seek"; to seek something within a room is called *sòu* (the character for this is *sòu*).

In the *Zìshū*, it means "to search. The *Shuōwén* says: "The general intention [of the word]. It is composed of the radical 'hand' (*shǒu*) and the phonetic 'lǎo' (*lǎo*); it is also written as *sōu*. 'Lǎo' is pronounced *sānggǒu*."
Nowadays, the common usage mostly follows the form with "臼" (jiù).
This is a variant form resulting from clerical script (lìshū); it is not the standard orthography.
The final radical is pronounced yǎngzhāngfǎn.
Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that it means "to raise up.
Zheng’s sub-commentary on the *Shijing* states that it means "to stir up.
Wang’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that it means "to uncover."

The *Shuowen* states: "To fly upward. It is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "yi" (易). The character "yi" consists of "qie" (且) and "wu" (勿); its pronunciation is as above. In the aforementioned scripture, it is written with "zhi" (支) as "yang" (敭), which is the ancient form of "yang" (揚). "Pou" (攴) has the pronunciation *pǔbǔ*; today it is abbreviated to "pou" (攵).

1. Volume One of the Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī Sūtra. "Yi-yue" (怡悅): The former character is the reverse of 以 (yǐ). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Book of Poetry) states it means "joyful satisfaction. The *Erya* states it means "delight. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical 心 (heart) with the phonetic 台 (tái). The latter character is read as yán-jue (緣決).

"Liè (厲)" means forceful and obstructed. The commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "liè" means fierce; Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that "liè" means intense. In the *Erya*, "liè" is glossed as "to act"; in the *Guoyu*, it is glossed as "high. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as composed of the radical "han" (厂, pronounced hǎn) and the phonetic "wàn. It is incorrect for the received text to write it with the radical "yǎn" (广).

*Jùn* (峻): Upper radical *xún* (荀), reversed; lower radical *xiǎn* (儼). Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjìng* states that *jùn* means "the appearance of being lofty and great. Guo’s commentary on the *Eryā* states that *jùn* means "long. The *Shuowén* writes it as *shùin* (󲖮), stating it is "the appearance of being high and precipitous," with the phonetic component *shùn* (陖). Lexicons also write it as *yǐn* (𡺲) or *shùn* (陖); the current editions of the Classics use *jùn*. The *Zhèngzì* (正字) of the Ancient and Modern period states that *yǐn* (𡺲) may be abbreviated. The pronunciation of *jùn* is *qī xún* (七荀反). *Xiǎn* (險): Lower radical *xiǎn* (儼), reversed. The *Zhouyì* states: "The perils of the earth consist of mountains, rivers, hills, and mounds. Gu Yewang states: "Perilous" (*xiǎn*) is synonymous with "obstructed" (*zhǔ*). The *Shuowén* states: "Perilous" (*xiǎn*) means "difficulty"; it is composed of the radical *qián* (𨸏) and the phonetic component *qiǎn* (僉). The versions of the Classics that use the mountain radical to form *xiǎn* (嶮) are incorrect.

*Chuanque* (穿缺): *quē* (犬悅反). The *Cangjie pian* states that *quē* means "deficiency" (*kuī*) or "gap" (*xì*). The *Shuowen jiezi* states that *quē* refers to a broken vessel; it is composed of the radical for "jar" (*fǒu*) with the phonetic *guài*. It is also written as *qūn*.
Regarding *cōngyuì* (聰叡), the meaning has already been fully explained in the sixth fascicle of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-uttamarāja-sūtra*.

Regarding the term *xùnwèn* (問訊) for greeting a junior: the *Fǎn Máo Shī Zhuàn* (反毛詩傳) states that *xùn* means "to inquire. The *Zhèng Jiān* (鄭箋) on the *Shī* says: "*Xūn* means to obtain life; one inquires with words. Lìu Xiǎoqíng says: "A sincere inquiry is called *xùn*. The *Shuōwén* says: "*Xùn* means 'to ask. It is composed of the radical 'speech' (*yán*) and the phonetic 'xùn'."

*Āmán* (傲慢): *nài* (耐) is pronounced with the *shàng* (上) tone; *gào* (告) is reversed [to *gǎo*]. Kǒng (孔) in his commentary on the *Shūjìng* (*Shāngshū*) says: "Arrogance means not being friendly. Dù (杜) in his commentary on the *Zuǒzhuàn* says: "Arrogance means lack of reverence. The *Guǎngyá* says: "Arrogance means haughtiness. The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radical 人 and the phonetic 敖. The original text uses 慠 (from the radical 心), which is an error. *Zhōngmánbiàn* (中蠻辨) says: "Arrogance means treating others lightly and insulting them. The *Shuōwén* says: "Arrogance means a state of mind that does not fear [others]; it is composed of the radical 心 and the phonetic 曼. The pronunciation of 曼 is *wàn*; the lower character is *nàidài* (乃袋). Gù Yěwáng says: "Nài (耐) means 'to be able'. The *Shuōwén* records it as 耐, an ancient character. It is composed of 彡 and 又, and it is also said that it may be written as 耐 from 寸, signifying "various laws and measures"; therefore, it takes 寸.

Mòrán (默然): Máng Běifǎn (忙北反) says it means "to remain silent and not speak. Yìng Shǎo (應劭) says "hēhē" (嘿嘿) refers to being dissatisfied with oneself. Regarding the correct character for ancient and modern times, it follows the radical "mouth" (口) and uses "black" (黑) as its phonetic; it is also written as mò (默). Examining the phonetic, it is also written as hēi (嘿), meaning "hēhē," indicating that one's ambitions have not been fulfilled. It is sometimes also written as mò (默).

"Ji" (妓) [pronounced *qí yǐ*]: The *Cangjie pian* states that "ji" refers to a beautiful woman; the *Kaoseng* states she is a woman who performs music. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "woman" (*nǚ*) with "zhi" (*zhī*) as its phonetic component. The same applies to subsequent instances such as "jile" (妓樂).

"Xi" (戲) is pronounced with the initial *xī* and the final *fǎn*. The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* states: "Xi means leisure and ease. The *Guǎng Yǎ* states: "Xi means to discharge or to bestow. The *Shuō Wén* states: "It is formed from the radical 'go' (戈) and the phonetic 'qian' (䖒)"; the pronunciation of "qian" is *xī*, and the final of "láng" is *gè*.

"Dan" (as in *dānzhòngdàn*)—according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to lift"; according to the *Zìshū*, it means "to carry on the shoulder"; and according to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) with the phonetic "zhān" (*shēng*). The character for "xiàdān" (lowering the load) is in the departing tone (*qùshēng*), and it likewise consists of the radical "hand" with the phonetic "zhān," pronounced *zhān*.

The character *shù* (術) is pronounced with the initial *shang* (上) and the final *man* (慢) reversed [i.e., *shǎn*], and the lower part is *chún* (脣) with the final *lǜ* (律) reversed [i.e., *lún*]. The *Zhuāngzǐ* states: "The mind's *shù* manifests in the form. Zhèng Xuán says: "*Shù* is like 'skill' (*yì*). The *Hàn Shī* says: "*Shù* means 'method' (*fǎ*). The *Shuōwén* says: "It is a road within a city; it is composed of the radical for 'walking' (*xíng*) and the phonetic *shù* (which is pronounced *chéng* with the final *lǜ* reversed)."

*Shuìyìng* (Auspicious Response): The upper character is pronounced *chuí* (with the tone of *lèi*). Yě Wáng says: "When a ruler's magnificent virtue moves Heaven and Earth, they respond with sincerity. The *Cāngjié piān* says it means "auspicious response. The *Shuōwén* says: "An auspicious token (*shuì*) takes jade as its sign; it is composed of the radical 'jade' (*yù*) and the phonetic 'duān' (*duān*). (The sound of *duān* is like that of *duān*.)
*Vilana* (the *lan* and *han* rhymes; in Sanskrit, it means "great violent wind"). *Pǔyù* (the *pú* and *mào* rhymes):

The *Mao Shi* says, "The perpetual wind and the torrential rain. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says, "A swift rain; it is composed of the radical for water with the phonetic *bào*. The text of the sutra uses the character *bào*, which is the character for "to dry in the sun" (*xàibào*).

The character for *zhā* (撾) is pronounced with the "zhú" and "guā" finals. Lexicons state that it means "to strike. The *Shēnglèi* says it means "to collide. In the *Wèizhì*, it is said that [someone] "struck and broke his leg. The *Shuōwén* writes it as 𥬲 (*zhā*) from the radical "bamboo," defining it as a "whip," with the phonetic component *shì* and the final *xián*. The *Huáinánzǐ* states: "Carving the flesh and skin, piercing the leather; wounds flow with blood. The *Bīcāng* says: "The tip of a hoe or awl. The *Shuōwén* says: "It is sharp and pointed," composed of the "metal" radical and the phonetic *chán*, where *chán* has the same pronunciation as above.

Regarding the character *yuè* (月) in *yuèshàn* (月釤): the "Correct Characters of Antiquity and Today" (*Gǔjīn zhèngzì*) states that *shàn* (釤) means a large sickle; it is composed of the radical "metal" (金) and the phonetic "san" (彡), which is pronounced *shān*.

The character *qiū* (曲) in *qūliáo* (曲撩) is read as *liǎo* (了) with the tone *xiāo* (蕭); the *Guǎngyá* states that *liáo* (撩) means to take or to arrange. However, according to the meaning of the scripture, *qūliáo* (曲撩) must be a type of weapon of war and does not carry the sense of taking or arranging. Checking various dictionaries, all [definitions] contradict the intent of the scripture. I believe this should instead refer to a *gōují* (鉤戟)—a halberd with a curved blade like a hook—similar to the *gōuqiāng* (鉤槍) used today.

"Short spear" (*duǎnshào*): holding two [ends] in reverse. The *Guǎngyá* states that a *shào* is a halberd (*máo*). The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radical "halberd" (*máo*) and the phonetic "xiào. The canonical text uses the character "shuò," which is the name of a type of wood and not a weapon; this is consistent with the use of "knife" (*dāo*) and "spear" (*shào*) together later in the fourth fascicle.

*Ī* (翳): The upper character is read as *ī-jì* (翳). The *Guǎngyǎ* states: "To obstruct; to screen. The *Shuōwén* explains it as composed of the radical *yǔ* (羽) and the phonetic *ē* (殹), where *ē* has the same pronunciation as *shàng* (上).

2. Second Fascicle of the *Ratnaketu-parivarta Sūtra*. *Kāna* (𩋆): The lower character is read as *jié-xián* (劼閑). The *Běicāng* states: "To be stingy. The meanings of the ancient and modern characters are identical; it also means to cherish wealth or to be difficult. It is composed of the radical *gé* (革) with the phonetic *xiān* (臤). In the version of the sūtra, it is written with the radical *xīn* (心) as *qiān* (慳), which is a vulgar character. *Xiān* (臤) has the same pronunciation as *lìn* (遴); *lìn* (吝) has the pronunciation *lìn* (吝).

Regarding the character *fēn* (分) in the phrase "dividing the portions" (*fēnjiè*): Wáng Yǎnwáng states that *fēn* means "boundary. The *Shuōwén* says it means "to distinguish," composed of the radicals *bā* (eight) and *dāo* (knife), with the phonetic *qí* (齊). Dictionaries state that *jì* (劑) means "to divide into sections. In the standard characters of antiquity and today, this is written with *dāo* and *qí*. In the original text of the *Jīng*, it is written as *qí* (齊), which refers to the sense of "harmonizing."

"Qíngjìng" (Quiet Tranquility): The upper character, "qíng," is pronounced *líng* with the *fǎn* (rhyme) *fǎn*. The *Fāngyán* (Dialectal Dictionary) states that "qíng" means peaceful and settled. The *Shuōwén* (Explanations of Characters) states that "qíng" refers to the sound of a place where no people are present; it is composed of the radical "mián" (roof/covering, pronounced *mián*) and the phonetic "shū" (pronounced *shū*). In the scriptures, the term is written as "jì" (寂), though the common vernacular form is "jì" (寂).

The characters for "bīnbīn" (繽紛)—the first reading being *pǐ* and the second *fúwén*—along with their meanings and radical components, have all already been explained in the seventh fascicle of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*.

Regarding the character *xiǎn* (璽): it is pronounced as in *sī* (斯) and *cǐ* (此). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that *xiǎn* means a seal (*yìn*). Ying Shao’s commentary on the *Hanshu* states that *xiǎn* means a token of trust (*xìn*). Cui Yong’s *Duduan* states that the Son of Heaven’s seal is made of jade; in ancient times it was used by both the noble and the humble, but since the Qin dynasty, only the Son of Heaven has been entitled to call it so. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is the seal of a king, composed of the radical *tǔ* (土) with the phonetic *ěr* (爾). Today, it is conventionally written with the radical *yù* (玉) as *xiǎn*. The lower part is pronounced as in *yīn* (因) and *jìn* (晉). The *Cangjie pian* states it is a seal (*yìngchān*). The *Hanshu* states that the princes and kings possess seals of gold. The *Shuowen* further defines *yìn* as that which is held by those in office as a token of trust; it is composed of the radicals *zhuǎo* (爪) and *jié* (卩), where *jié* is pronounced as in *jié* (節).

*Dòuzhèng* (strife/contestation). "Dòu" is pronounced as in *dòudòu* (the *fǎn* being that of *dòu*). The *Cāngjiépiān* states it means "to contend. It refers to taking up arms to engage in mutual conflict and warfare. The *Lúnyǔ* says, "When the blood and qi are at their peak, one must be on guard against strife. The *Shuowén* states: "Dòu" means 'encountering. It is composed of the radical *dòu* (鬥) and the phonetic *zhuó* (斵); it also includes the components *mén* (門) and *mí* (𭔰). Those who write it as *dòu* (鬥) alone are incorrect. The pronunciation of *dòu* is the same as above; the pronunciation of *zhuó* is *zhuó*.

Regarding "thumb" (thǔ): the *Cāngjié piān* states that "mǔ" refers to the forefinger; Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guóyǔ* states that "mǔ" is the thumb (the large toe/finger); and the *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radical "hand" with the phonetic "mǔ. The version of the scripture that uses "mǔ" with the radical "wood" is incorrect.

*Tào cuàn* (to flee and hide). *Hóng* is pronounced *lún* (with the second tone). Wang Yewang states that *cuàn* means "to flee. The *Guǎngyá* states that *cuàn* means "to throw oneself [into hiding]. The *Ěryá* states that *cuàn* means "to conceal. The *Shuowén* states that *cuàn* means "to hide," derived from the character for "rat" (*shǔ*) inside a "hole" (*xué*). *Hóng* is pronounced *líán* (with the second tone).

"Blind" (máng): The upper character, *mài* (with the *gēng* rhyme), the *Shuowen* states means "the eyes lack pupils," composed of "eye" (*mù*) and "perish" (*wáng*), with *wáng* also serving as the phonetic. The lower character, *mì* (with the *píng* rhyme), Guo's commentary on the *Erya* states it means "obscure"; the *Shuowen* states "Ming means dark and profound," composed of "roof" (*mián*), "sun" (*rì*), and "six" (*liù*), with *mìng* (pronounced *huǐng*) as the phonetic.

3. *Ratnaketu-parivarta Sūtra*, Scroll Three. Regarding "yihen" (鬱恨): Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that "yuyi" (鬱悒) refers to facial distress. The *Cangjie pian* states that "yi" (悒) is the appearance of being unable to relax. The *Shuowen jiezi* states that "yi" (悒) means unease; it is composed of the radical "heart" (心) and the phonetic "yu" (邑), with the reading "hen-gen" (痕艮). The *Cangjie pian* states that "hen" (恨) means resentment. Gu Yewang states that when one's intentions are not fulfilled or satisfied, it is called "hen"; it is composed of the radical "heart" (心) and the phonetic "gen" (艮).
"Ām-bì (闇蔽)" is a vulgar corruption; it should be read as "bì" (蔽) when referring to the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, for the original text uses "bì" and not "bì.
"Saṃdṛmika" (珊儞弭迦)—the "ni" is pronounced with the "ni" rhyme, and the "mi" is pronounced with the "mi" rhyme—is a name for a celestial Māra in the Sanskrit language.

*Pínqī* (顰嘁): The upper character is read as *pǐn* (賓). Yuè Yěwáng states that it describes the appearance of one who is sorrowful and unhappy. The *Shuowén* states it is composed of the radical *bēi* (卑) with the phonetic *pín* (頻). It is incorrect for the canonical text to use *pín* (嚬), which is composed of the radical *jié* (卩). The lower character is read as *yù* (育). The *Fāngyán* states that *qī* (嘁) and *zī* (咨) denote *niùní* (忸怩). The *Bóyá* states that *qīzī* (嘁咨) means shame (*cán*). In the standard characters of antiquity and today, this is composed of the radical *kǒu* (口) with the phonetic *qì* (戚); it is also written as *qí* (㗤) or *qí* (𠯗). *Zhēshà* (pronounced *zhè*) for sugarcane: Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* identifies it as "cane-yam. It is what is referred to as "sugarcane" (*zhēshèng zhū*) in the *Shǔdū fù*. The *Shuowén* defines it as "written with the radical 艹 and the phonetic 𢉙."

10. The Tenth Fascicle of the Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī Sūtra. The latter character is pronounced *huài* (as in *zhōuwǔ*, the *Zhouli*, which states: "in the summer season there are the diseases of itch and scabies"). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Itch (*jiè*) is a rash; it is composed of the radical *nà* and the phonetic *jiè*. The pronunciation of *jiè* is identical to that of *jiè* (scabies).

*Kài* (coughing): the first character is pronounced *kǎi* (as in *kāi*). The *Monthly Ordinances* (*Yueling*) states: "When there is much wind in the state, people suffer from coughs. The second character is pronounced *zòu* (as in *sōuzhì*). The *Zhouli* states that in winter there is the disease of *suqì* (rapid upward qi). Examining the sound, it refers to qi surging up and striking the throat. The standard characters for both ancient and modern usage use the radical *kou* (口) with the phonetic *shòu* (欶); the pronunciation of *shòu* is the same.
