The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s Great Vaipulya. Volume One. First Fascicle. Translated previously in sixty fascicles. Pronunciations compiled by Xuanying. Magadha (摩竭提): Also called Magadha (摩竭陀), or Makedha (默偈陀); it is also written as Magadha (摩伽陀). These are all corruptions of the Sanskrit sound. The correct term is *Majjadhā* (摩揭陀), which translates as "the Land of Good Victory" (善勝國) or "the Land Without Harm" (無惱害國). One tradition states that *Maga* is the name of a constellation, meaning "not evil," and refers to the twelfth lunar day; *Dha* means "place. Thus, it is named the "Land of the Place of No Evil" (不惡處國) or the "Land of the Constellation Place" (星處國). The character 揭 (jie) is pronounced *qie* (with the second tone).

"Flower garland" (*mālā*): *mālā* is the Sanskrit term; this is translated as "garland" (*man*). According to the phonology of the Western Regions, garland-makers there mostly string together *sumana* flowers in rows to form strands. Regardless of whether they are male or female, noble or humble, all use these for adornment, either on the head or the body. Thus, the "flower garlands," "celestial garlands," and "jewel garlands" mentioned in various sutras are of the same nature. The character is written with the radical for hair (*髟*, pronounced *suo-xian*); the final component is pronounced *mi-ruan*. The version in the sutra text using the character for "hair" (*𩬞*) is not the correct form.

The character *yu* (踰) is written as *yú* (逾), with the same pronunciation as *yǒu* (庾) and *jù* (俱). According to the *Zílín*, it means "to transcend"; according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to cross over. The term *mó nǐ* (摩尼) is a corruption; its correct pronunciation is *mò nǐ* (末尼), which is the general name for pearls and gems.

The character 罣 (guà) is abbreviated as 罫 (huà), both pronounced with the *hú guà* rhyme. It means "to obstruct" (*kùn ài*). The lower part is an archaic form of 硋 (*wèi*), pronounced with the *wǎi* rhyme. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to stop. It is also written as 閡; Guo Pu considered this an archaic form of the character 礙. The *Shuowen* states that 閡 means "to close off from the outside. The text here uses 㝵, pronounced *dū lè*. According to Wei Hong’s *Zhao Ding Guzhenzi Shu*, the characters 礙 and 得 are of the same radical. In the *Shuowen*, 得 means "to obtain. This refers to the passage in the *Shangshu* concerning Gaozong’s dream of obtaining the "True" (*shì*) and the "False" (*fēi*).

Vairocana is also called Vajraṇa or Vajra; this is translated as "Illumination," meaning "Universal Illumination. This is because the pure form of the Reward Buddha (vipākaphala-buddha) pervades the entire Dharma-realm. Furthermore, the light of the sun, moon, and lamps that pervades a single location is also termed Vairocana; the meaning is the same.

"Returning again" (*huí fù*) is also written as "huí fú"; both forms are pronounced with the second syllable as *hú* or *fú*. According to the *Cāngjié piān*, "huí" means swirling water, and "fú" means deep.

"Chī gǔ" (愚瞽) has the second character pronounced as *gǔ*; according to the *Sāncāng*, one without eyes is called *gǔ*. The *Shìmíng* states that those with blind eyes have eyes that are "mián mián," meaning they are closed flat like the skin of a drum.

*Kṣetra* (忉剎) is also written as *cā* (擦), both having the same pronunciation as *chā* (察). In Sanskrit it is called *kṣetra*, which is translated here as "land" (*tǔtián*). In the sūtras, it is sometimes referred to as "country" (*guó*) and sometimes as "land" (*tǔ*); these have the same meaning. Alternatively, it is written as *chàtǔ* (剎土), which preserves both pronunciations. This is also the same as the name *Kṣatriya* (刹帝利), meaning "protector of the fields. According to the *Kṣa* (剎) dictionary, this character does not exist; it is an abbreviation of the character *lì* (𠿒). The pronunciation of *lì* is *chū yī fǎn*. The name "Buddha-field" (*fútú míng chà*) is a corruption; one should say *laśtī* (剌瑟胝). The pronunciation of *la* is *lì gè fǎn*. This is translated as "pole" (*gān*). People substitute "pillar" (*zhù*) for it and call it a "kṣetra-pillar" (*chàzhù*). It is named "kṣetra" because its purpose of enshrining the Buddha’s relics is the same as that of a field. This is because in those Western countries, śarīra are placed at the top of the stupa pole.

*Jù huài* (沮壞): "Cái" (才) is a phonetic component; it is the opposite of *Sān cāng* (三蒼). *Jù* (沮) means gradual decline; *huài* (壞) means ruin. The scriptural text reads *zǔ* (爼), with the phonetic *zé lǚ* (側呂); it refers to a vessel for holding minced meat (*hǎi*). Alternatively, it refers to a stand for placing meat. *Zǔ* (爼) is not used here in that sense.

2. Fascicle Two of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra. Second fascicle. *Ānzhì* (安跱): The ancient form was *zì* (字), and the archaic form was *zhì* (峙); the modern form is *zhì* (跱), which is the same [in meaning]. According to the *Guǎngyá*, *zhì* means "to stop" (*zhǐ*). It refers to standing tall and solitary, as if alone.

3. Third Fascicle of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Fascicle Three. *Langshu* (欄楯): Also written as *lan* (闌). [The character] *lan* is pronounced with the initial *l* and the final *han* (寒); the radical is *shi* (食). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means a railing (*kan*). The *Tongsu Wen* states that a railing is called a *shun* (楯). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* says: "A vertical one is called a *kan*; a horizontal white rail between them is called a *ling* (櫺). A *ling* is a decorative element installed upon a railing at the edge of a palace hall, also intended to prevent people from falling. What is currently called a *goulan* (鈎蘭) refers to this.

"Qunmeng" (multitude of sprouts) is the same as "mèng" (mèng, pinyin; gēng, pinyin); it refers to sprouts. According to the *Guǎngyá*, "méng" means "beginning. Examining the character, "méng" has the appearance of being obscure and dim; it describes how the common masses lack knowledge.

Volume Four of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Volume Four: The character *huàn* (煥) is also written as *huàn* (煥), both pronounced with the *huàn* rhyme (corresponding to the modern pinyin *huàn*). *Huàn* also means "bright," referring to radiance or light.

Regarding the banners and streamers (*dhvaja-patākā*), the *Shiming* (Explanations of Names) states: "The bear and tiger constitute the banner; it is that by which the military commander makes his presence known. It symbolizes his ferocity like a tiger and serves as a place to assemble the multitude beneath it."
*Xiéyǎ* (諧雅): *xié* is pronounced as *hú* (the opposite tone). It means "harmonious" (*xiéhé*), referring to a refined and elegant bearing and the harmony of one's voice.

*Liáoguān* (寮觀): *liáo* is pronounced as *lìáo* (the second tone). *Liáo* refers to a window; according to the *Cāngjiépiān*, *liáo* means a small opening. Although the scriptural text contains two forms—either with the radical for "hand" (*liáo*) or with the radical for "wood" (*lǎo*)—neither is used today.

According to the *Fānyán*, it means "overflowing" (*yíng*). This refers to the overflowing fullness of the breath of indignation; "emotion" (*qíng*) likewise implies being moved.

*E* (in its archaic form *ai*) is pronounced as *an he fan*; according to the *Cangjie pian*, *e* means "to block" or "to stop."

The *Yìmù yùnjí* (Rhyme Collection for Eye-Opacities) treats "yì" as being pronounced the same as "jì," meaning an eye disease; the *Shuowén* states that it is the formation of a film over the eye due to illness. Although some versions of the scripture write it as "yì" (曀), which refers to cloudy weather when wind arises, this is not the intended meaning here. It is written as "yì" (𦠉). It is not this [latter] meaning.

The ancient forms for "gu" (孤), "qiong" (煢), and "xing" (惸) are all written with the same phonetic component, *qíng* (蕖營). One who has no father is called *gū* (孤); one who has no son is called *dú* (獨); one who has no brothers is called *qióng* (煢). *Qióng* means solitary; *qióngqióng* means having nothing to rely upon. The character is composed of the radical *xùn* (卂) and the phonetic *yíng* (熒) in abbreviated form. The pronunciation of *xùn* is *suīrùn* (雖閏).

Regarding "yuán pǔ" (園圃): it has two pronunciations, *bǔ* and *bù*. The *Cāngjié jiègǔ* (蒼頡解詁) states that planting trees is called a *yuán* (園), while planting vegetables is called a *pǔ* (圃).

The character for *shuài* (decline) and *mào* (senility) is written as 𤸬, with the phonetic reading *suǒ guī* (same as 所龜). In the *Liji*, it is said that at the age of fifty one begins to *shuài* (become lax); the lower part is an ancient form of 𠅸. The two forms for *mào* (senility) are now written as 秏, with the phonetic reading *mò bào*. One who is eighty years old is called *mào*; *mào* refers to being muddled and forgetful, and also to being confused.

*Kai* (甲) and *jue* (胄) are homophonous; *jue* is pronounced with the initial *ch* and the final *-iu* (除救反). According to the *Guangya*, *jue* refers to a *doumou* (兜鍪, a helmet). In the Central Kingdoms, this pronunciation is used, and it is also called *dimou* (鞮鍪); in Jiangnan, this pronunciation is used, where *di* (鞮) is pronounced *di* (低) and *mou* (鍪) is pronounced *mo-hou* (莫侯反).

Regarding the character *guàn* (亘): it is pronounced with the rhyme of *shēng* (生) and *gē* (歌) with the retroflex *deng* (鄧) final; it means "pervasive" (*biàn*). In the sūtra text, it is sometimes written as *héng* (絙) with the pronunciation *huán* (桓) and *shòu* (綬); it is also written as *gēng* (縆) with the pronunciation *gōng* (公) and *céng* (曾), meaning "a large rope. Neither of these is the correct phonetic reading for the sūtra.

*The Phonetic Explanations for the Newly Translated Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*, Compiled by the Śramaṇa Huìyuǎn of the Great Táng. Volume One, Part One. Preface: The primary ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is indeed the Dharma-nature that transcends all words;

its natural outflow, the True Teaching, is truly a ferryboat across the ocean [of suffering]. Therefore, names, phrases, and syllables serve as the fundamental substance of distinct characteristics, while form, scent, taste, and touch constitute the self-substance of their abiding support. Alas! The principle that transcends speech and thought is fully realized within the realm of hearing and seeing.
Is it not because they all rely on the power of the Dharma King’s vast creation of expedient means?
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* may truly be called a scripture that comprehensively penetrates the entire Dharma-realm.
This is the teaching that exhausts the ultimate bounds of the Buddha-realm.

If, however, the words and phrases are erroneous and the correct meaning is difficult to manifest, true insight will not arise; one will lose the way while seeking its source. Therefore, by taking the near as a shortcut to the far and proceeding from the shallow to the deep, who among the Honored Ones of the past, future, and present has not followed this Great Way? Furthermore, the utility of phonology and semantics is like a clear mirror for discerning the turbid and the pure; it explains the essential purpose of words and teachings, serves as a model for correcting errors and omissions, and acts as a bell and key for opening the tube of doubt.
For instance, "páihuí" (徘徊) was erroneously written as "chíhuí" (遲廻);
consequently, "pánghuáng" (彷徨) became "jīfǎn" (稽返),
and "bìnì" (俾倪) replaced "dìyì" (隦堄).

Sì subsequently constructed a parapet wall for the bridge and wrote out the calligraphy, correcting distortions and slants, reversing the order of characters, preserving the structural integrity while refining the forms;

the trees were arranged in varying heights, and although such elements might seem to confuse the phonology and semantics, they do not introduce discordance—what need is there for further guidance? Huìyuǎn’s talent was boundless, yet being of humble capacity, I have long enjoyed playing with this scripture. For nineteen years, I have sought its hidden meanings under the tutelage of a master.
Although the meaning and intent of this work are profound and difficult to follow, I have provided these annotations for the sake of phonology and Sanskrit terminology.

It is my hope that by reading the text, one may comprehend the meaning without needing to consult others, and by deciphering the characters, one may understand the sounds without the labor of carrying heavy volumes. Furthermore, while the capacity of ants is limited to their own burrows, how could the power of thunder and lightning fail to awaken hibernating creatures both near and far? May the wise and accomplished gentlemen not reproach me for this.

**Phonetic Glossary for the Preface to the Sūtra** *Tiānzhé* (天冊): *cè*, with the *qì* (革) radical; the *Shuowén* states: "A *cè* is a mandate (*fúmìng*). It refers to the sacred symbols and instructions bestowed by the Supreme Sage to confer the imperial throne. The character may also be written with the bamboo radical, or in ancient forms as *zǎi* (󲗾), which is a pictograph.

"Zhao Hua Quan Yu": "Zao" means creation; "hua" means transformation. The *Erya* states that "quan yu" means the beginning. This refers to the commencement of the creation of heaven and earth and the transformation of the myriad things.

The Way of Heaven consists of the sun, moon, stars, and constellations, as well as the transformations of yin and yang; this is what is called the Way of Heaven. The *Yi* says, "The Way of Qian undergoes change and transformation," which refers to this.

"Gui-long-xi-xiang" (Tortoise-Dragon Attached Symbols) [the character for xi being pronounced hu ji fan]: Yao had a divine tortoise that emerged bearing a map, and Shun was moved by a yellow dragon that appeared bearing a map. "Xi" (Attached) refers to the *Xici* (Appended Statements), which is one of the two parts of the Ten Wings (*Shiyi*) as expounded by Confucius on the *Yi*.

The *Yi* says: "Observe the celestial patterns to discern the changes of the seasons; observe the human patterns to transform and perfect the world. What are called "human patterns" are the relationships between male and female, ruler and minister, father and son, and the distinctions of honor and lowliness, high and low.

Regarding the eighteen thousand years, the *Dijwang Jiazi Ji* (Record of the Heavenly Stems and Earthly Branches of the Emperors) states: "The Heavenly Sovereign (Tianhuang) ruled for eighteen thousand years; the Earthly Sovereign (Dihuang) ruled for nine thousand years; and the Human Sovereign (Renhuang) ruled for four thousand five hundred years. There is another version which says that all three sovereigns ruled for eighteen thousand years each.

"Simultaneously facing the bounded realm": the *Mao Shih* commentary states that "you-ce" means "orderly and uniform. This refers to the people of the four seas submitting and serving in a state of being "ce-er" (uniform) and orderly. "Qu" (realm) refers to a territorial region.

Seventy-two rulers are mentioned together in Sima Xiangru’s "Book on the Feng and Shan Sacrifices," which states: "Those who succeeded the [dynasties of] Shao and Xia, whose titles and posthumous names can be briefly recounted, number seventy-two. Guanzi says: "In the past, there were seventy-two houses that performed the Feng sacrifice on Mount Tai and the Shan sacrifice at Mount Liangfu. Liangfu is a small mountain beneath Mount Tai. The pronunciation of "Shan" (禪) is shàn, and the pronunciation of "Fu" (父) is fǔ.

"Human delusion regarding the four patiences. "Human delusion" refers to the delusion of human beings. Regarding the "four patiences," the *Sīsapā-sūtra* (*Siyi jing*) states: first, the patience of non-arising, because all phenomena have no coming; second, the patience of non-ceasing, because all phenomena have no going; third, the patience of causes and conditions, because all phenomena arise from causes and conditions; and fourth, the patience of non-abiding, because there is no distinct mind in the continuity [of consciousness].

"Household entanglements and the five hindrances. Household entanglements refers to the entanglements of the various households. The five hindrances are: the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt. These are the hindrances.

"Vulture Peak stands to the west": Vulture Peak refers to Gṛdhrakūṭa-parvata. Regarding "standing to the west," the *Guangya* states that "zhi" means to stand upright; this signifies that the Vulture Peak rises loftily upward, situated in the Western Regions.

Transcending the four greats and looking down from on high: Laozi said, "Within the realm there are four greats," referring to heaven, earth, the Way of Kings, and the self. Now it is said that the Buddha’s emergence surpasses even this realm; therefore, he is said to transcend the four greats.

"Mingun" (混): "Tàikōng" (太空中). [The character "hú" (胡) is read as "běn" (本) in reverse. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "mìngùn" (混) refers to the state of "chùnhùn" (混沌), where yin and yang have not yet differentiated and exist together as a single breath. Here, it means that the measure of the Huayan Dharma-gate is equal to the great void. The character is also written as "hún" (渾).

"Daocheng" (叨承) [the first "chóng" is pronounced as "táo"; the rhyme is "pǔ"; "dāotiǎn" means to receive an undeserved honor]. This is a self-deprecating statement regarding having been humbly honored by receiving the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).

"Yuyi" (玉扆) [the second character is pronounced as "yī"]. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "Yi refers to a screen (*pingfeng*). When a screen is adorned with jade, it is called a 'jade screen' (*yuyi*). Regarding the "cluster of pearls," it says: "The Son of Heaven employs the *yi* at the door and window to serve as a screen."

"Hai yanyan" (The sea is tranquil). *Yan* is pronounced as in *jianfan*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Yan means peace. This refers to the fact that both near and far are clear and settled; hence the expression "the Yellow River is clear and the sea is tranquil.
"Shu zhen" (Extraordinary auspiciousness). *Zhen* is pronounced as in *zhengyingfan*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Zhen means auspiciousness. The *Cangjie Pian* states: "Zhen means good."

"Bai-die" (貝牒): "Bai" (貝) is pronounced as *bei* with the *bei* and *bei* rhymes; "die" (牒) is pronounced as *tu-jie*. "Bai" refers to the leaves of the *bīḍāla* tree, intending here to signify a Sanskrit manuscript. "Die" refers to a slip of bamboo or wood, which is the general term for written scriptures.

"Shí zhēn suì qiá": "zhēn" is pronounced as zīng-shēn (side rhyme), and "qiá" as hóu-jiá (level rhyme). "Shí" refers to the four seasons; "suì" refers to one year. The *Yùnpǔ* states that "zhēn" means "to arrive at"; the *Shuowén* says that "qiá" means "dew reaching [all things]."

"Crossing the desert" (*yuè mò*) means that various foreign nations from afar have come across the desert sands to offer their tribute. "Tribute" (*xiàn*)—the character is pronounced *chì lín*—the *Yùpiān* states:
"Jiēn" (pronounced *bǎo*) means treasure; the character may also be written with the "jade" radical."

"To span the perilous and navigate the deep—how firm! Here, "spanning" (jià) refers to placing objects upon high-suspended structures; the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that a "boat" (*háng*) is a double-hulled vessel. This means that those coming from distant lands all must ascend and cross over these perilous heights.
*Qìng* (pronounced *qiān* with the *dìng* tone): The commentary on the *Mao Shī* states that *qìng* means "exhausted.

*Yì* (pronounced *yīn* with the *rù* tone): The *Zhū Cóng* states that whenever one pours from a vessel into water, it is called *yì*; today, when one uses the mind to fathom the Dharma, this is also called *yì*.
"Hard to fathom" (*han ce*) means "rare" (*han xi*); "fathom" (*ce*) refers to measuring or estimating.

"To spy upon" (*kuí yú*)—the first character is pronounced *qiān guī* (reversed) and the second *yú jù* (reversed)—according to Fu Qian’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan*, "to spy" means to look by lifting one's feet [to peer over something]. The *Zhūcóng* states that "to spy upon" means to harbor expectations. Here, it is said that the two vehicles (*er shèng*) have severed all hope regarding this Dharma.
Lung (隆) refers to abundance; Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states that it means "much.
Ai (隘) is pronounced with the *jie* rhyme and means "narrow.
Zhao (肇) is pronounced with the *rao* rhyme and means "beginning."
Regarding this, the *Mao Shih Zhuan* states: "Yuan" means "to do. Whatever is done in an action is termed "yuan.
As for "mian," it is pronounced as miǎn-yǎn; Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states: "Mian" is an expression of reflection.
The term "yue" (粵)—pronounced "yue" with the fanqie "yue" (月)—marks the beginning of an expository statement.

Regarding the editing of the *Book of Han* (*Hanshu*) concerning the biographies of Wei Qing and Huo Guang, it is said: "To 'xiao' (削) is to delete; to 'bi' (筆) is to add. The *Yinyi* (Explanations of Pronunciation and Meaning) states that "xiao" refers to excising and "bi" refers to augmenting. Others say that "editing the book" involves collating the text, deleting errors, and annotating them—this is what is meant by "bi-xiao" (editing).
Regarding *qin*, the *Erya* says it means "to extend"; Guo Pu says it refers to spreading out and reaching branches.
Regarding *shi*, the commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that *shi* means "to employ.
Regarding *shan*, the pronunciation is *zhàn*; the *Shuowen* says it means "to repair," while the *Zhucóng* says that all instances of restoring the old or creating the new are termed *shàn*.

"Expansive" (*kuò*) refers to the boundaries of the *dharmadhātu*. To say "expansive" means to stretch what is small and make it great. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "Boundaries" (*jiāng*) are like limits (*jiè*). The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* states: "The border (*jìng*) is the boundary (*jiāng*); the domain (*yù*) is the enclosure (*guǎn-yù*). The *Shuowén Jiězì* defines "domain" (*yù*) as an enclosed area.

The "secret pearl within the pearl casket" refers to the *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling jewel), which is a metaphor for *prajñā* (wisdom). The "casket" refers to a chest, which is a metaphor for the Buddha-body; it means that *prajñā* resides within the Buddha-body just as the wish-fulfilling jewel resides within the casket. "Secret" (*bi*) refers to the profound mystery, which is precisely *prajñā*. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 64, states: "*Prajñā* is the wish-fulfilling jewel, and the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) are the casket. Although there is no *prajñā* within the *śarīra*, because they have been permeated by *prajñā*, they are worthy of veneration. Regarding the character for "secret" (*bi*), there is a variant written with the "grain" radical (*禾*), pronounced *manjie* (mǎn jié); this, however, refers to a fragrant herb.
The *Jizhu* (Collected Annotations) on the *Shiwen* states that "mi" means "to fill.

Regarding "fu," Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Mao Shijing* says that "fu" refers to "repetition" or "turning over. The *Zhucóng* states that "fu" means "to examine repeatedly"; the character is also written as "fù."
Scroll One, Part One: The Chapter on the Sublime Adornment of the World-Ruling Lord (Lokeshvararaja-vyuha). Regarding Magadha: it is also called Magadha.
It refers to the kingdom of Magadha.
Some call it Magadha, while others say Makeda;
these various names arise from the differences in pronunciation according to the eight grammatical case endings (*vibhakti*).
However, their general meaning is not substantially different.
Some commentators explain that *ma* means "not" and *keti* means "to arrive."
It is said that his country will devise military strategies such that brave enemies cannot invade it.
Furthermore, it is said that *mā* means "pervasive" (*vyāpti*) and *keti* means "intelligent" (*prajñā*).
It is said that wise people are found throughout his kingdom.
Furthermore, there is one called Mahāketi;
"Mahā" means great, and "Keti" means body.
This means that among the five regions of India, this country is the largest and governs all other nations; therefore, it is called Mahāśarīra (Great Body).
Another interpretation states: *ma* means "no," and *kṣati* means "harm.
Thus, it signifies that no harm is inflicted [upon its people].

It is said that the law of this country does not employ corporal punishment; those who commit crimes punishable by death are merely sent to the Śītavana (Cold Forest). If the dharma of an araṇya is thus, then that which is the opposite of an araṇya is called *araṇa*.

In its correct form, it is *āraṇya*, which is translated as "the place of no contention" (*wu zheng sheng*). There are three types: First is the *dharma-araṇya*, which is what is being characterized here. This refers to the meaning that all dharmas are fundamentally tranquil and quiescent, and are without activity; because of this, the location is named a *dharma-araṇya*. The "location" (*chu*) herein refers specifically to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Second is the *mātanga-araṇya*, which refers to a cemetery. It must be at least one *krośa* from a village, a distance beyond the reach of the bellowing of a great bull. Third is the *tandaka-araṇya*, which refers to a sandy desert. The pronunciation of "qi" (in *qianli*) is reversed [to *qian*].

Regarding "Bodhimaṇḍa," *bodhi* is translated here as "awakening" (*jue*). As for *maṇḍa*, the *Yinyi* (Phonetic and Semantic Commentary) of the *Hanshu* states: "To pile up earth so that it is high is called a *tan* (altar); to clear the ground so that it is level is called a *chang* (field/site). These are both places where deities dwell and rest. There are instances where the character for *chang* is written as *chang* (to cultivate), which is erroneous.

According to various dictionaries, the character for *jué* (awakened/enlightened) is derived from *xué* (to learn); *xué* is derived from *jiào* (to teach); and *jiào* is derived from *xiào* (filial piety) and *xiáo* (the hexagram component). These characters arise through mutual transformation based on their phonetic and semantic associations.

*Mānī* is correctly called *maṇi*. *Ma* refers to *mala*, which here means "dirt"; *ni* means "to leave" or "to be free from. This signifies that the light of this jewel is pure and is not defiled by impurities. It is also said that *mānī* means "increase," implying that wherever this jewel is present, its majestic virtue necessarily increases. The older translations such as "As One Wishes" (*rúyì*) or "According to One's Intent" (*suíyì*) are literal renderings based on its specific meanings.
"Rain of inexhaustible jewels" (yù wú jìn bǎo):

"mào" (茂) is pronounced as in *mo* (搆). The *Erya* states: "A tree like the pine or cypress is called 'mào'. Guo Pu’s commentary says: "This refers to the luxuriance of its branches and leaves. The *Yinyi* (Phonetic Explanations) of the *Hanshu* states: "Mào means beautiful and flourishing."

The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "all" (*yi-qie*) means "universal," which carries the sense of being everywhere present and fully endowed. Therefore, the character for "all" (*qie*) should be derived from "ten" (*shi*). The *Shuowen* says that "ten" refers to the end of numbers; there are also versions with "seven" (*qi*), which are merely vulgar characters.

"Vaidūrya" (琉璃) is the transliteration; in Sanskrit it is fully called *vaidūrya*, which means "not far from a mountain. This refers to a mountain in the Western Regions not far from the city of Vārāṇasī, from which this gem originates, hence its name. Regarding the character for "trunk" (*gàn*), dictionaries state that a trunk is a branch—that is, the main stem. The character should follow the radical "yú" (于); those versions of the scripture where it follows the "wood" (*mù*) radical are erroneous. According to Kǒng Āngguó’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* (Book of Documents), Dù Yǔ’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan*, and a collation with the *Yùpiān*, all maintain that the character with the "gan" (干) radical denotes a tree trunk or branch, whereas the character with the "wood" radical denotes wooden planks used for building walls—specifically, those at the two ends are called *zhēn* (楨), and those forming the two sides are called *gàn* (幹).

"Jade leaves are lush and spreading. Regarding "fúshū" (扶疏), the *Yìyì* (音義) of the *Hànshū* states that it means "distributed and spreading. The *Shuowén* states that "fúshū" means "spreading in the four directions. As for the character "pū" (枎), the *Yùpiān* places it in the "Wood" (木) radical; its appearance as "tǒng" (扌) [the "hand" radical] in the current version of the scripture is an error.
Regarding "Yanli" (嚴麗), Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states: "Yan" means solemn; the *Xiaoya* says: "Li" means manifest.
Regarding "Cui" (萃), the reading is *ji* (疾) with the reversed tone; in the *Yi*, "Cui" means to gather. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* says: "Cui" means to assemble.

In the *Jingluo jing* (Sutra of Necklaces), the original text uses the two characters "yíngluò" (瓔珞); both are erroneous. "Yíng" (瓔) refers to a stone resembling jade; its pronunciation is the same as that of "yīng" (櫻, cherry), but it is not used here.

*Tángxiè* (堂榭): "Táng" is pronounced with the *xù* and *yè* finals. The *Erya* states: "A *shé* is called a *tái* (terrace); when there is timber upon it, it is called a *shù* (pavilion). Guo Pu’s commentary says this refers to a building erected atop a terrace. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "A *xiè* is a house with a projecting roof (*xiēqián*) atop an earthen terrace, and it contains trees. *Shé* is pronounced *dū*. The character *xiè* (榭) is composed of the radicals for "wood" (木) and "shoot" (射).

Regarding "steps" (*jieti*) and "windows" (*huyou*): *Jie* (pronounced *qianji fan*) refers to the path for ascending to the hall, which is the flight of stairs. The *Guangya* states that "steps" (*qie*) are the same as "ledges" (*shi*), referring to the flat stone treads on both sides of the stairway. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains that what is at the roof is called a *yue*, and what is in the wall is called a *you*. The character *shi* is pronounced *shi*.
Regarding the term *lì* (𬾨), Liu Zhao’s commentary on the *Yili* states: "Lì means 'to exhaust' (*bìjìn*). It signifies exhausting the body in its solemnity.

Regarding *yíng* (瑩) and *zhú* (燭): *Ying* is pronounced *wùdìng*; according to the *Guǎngyá*, "yíng means to polish. This refers to rubbing and wiping pearls and jade so that they emit a brilliant light. According to the *Cāngjiépiān*, "zhú means to illuminate. This refers to illuminating one another by emitting light.
"His wondrous voice resonates afar, reaching everywhere. *Er'ya* states that "xía" means "distant"; *Guǎngyá* states that "chàng" means "to reach through" and "jí" means "to arrive at.

"His majestic radiance is brilliant": "hè" (pronounced xǔgé fǎn) and "yì" (pronounced yíyì fǎn). *Guǎngyá* states that "hèhè" means "bright," and "yìyì" means "abundant. As for the character "yì," some editions of the scripture have "kǒng" (廾), which is the character for "bó" (博弈, chess).
"There is nothing that is not seen; no land where it does not return. "Mi" (靡) means "none" (無); "du" (覩) means "to see" (視).
"Acintya-kalpa": *kalpa* is a Sanskrit term; its full and correct form is *kalpāra*, which is translated as "long duration" (長時).

Regarding "Vajra-nābhi" (金剛臍), the character used here is *xiàn* (奚) with the phonetic *fàn* (反). In the Sanskrit manuscript, this "nābhi" refers to the navel (*nābhi*), which should be written with the radical for flesh (*肉*). The character *qí* (齊) used in the scripture is the "equal" (*qí*) of "equality," and is not the term intended here.

Regarding "Vairocana," according to the Sanskrit manuscript, the character *vi* should be pronounced as "wu fei" (無廢反), which means "various" (*vicitra*). "Lokiteśvara" (here rendered as *loka-nātha*) means "illuminating light. This signifies that the Buddha, through his body and wisdom, illuminates sentient beings with various radiances. Alternatively, it is said that *vi* means "pervasive" (*vyāpin*) and *lokiteśvara* means "illuminating light"; this refers to the Buddha’s unimpeded light of body and wisdom pervasively illuminating the dharma-realm where phenomena and principle are non-obstructive.

"Venerable" (*zūn*) refers to being worthy of honor; Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states that "majestic" (*yán*) means being awe-inspiring, while the *Mao Shih Zhuan* states that it denotes majesty and authority.
*Nārāyaṇa* is translated here as "firm and solid."
*Sumeru* (須彌): The full Sanskrit term is *Sumeru*, which is translated as "Wondrously High" (*Miaogao*). *Brahman* (梵): The full Sanskrit term is *Brahma*, which is translated as "Pure" (*Qingjing*).

*Candana* (栴檀): This means "Bestowing Bliss. White sandalwood can cure fevers, while red sandalwood can eliminate wind-swelling; as both are medicines for removing ailments and bringing peace to the body, they are thus called "Bestowing Bliss."
Shangshu Caiyun said: "The five colors are displayed upon the five primary hues. Gu Yewang stated: "Cai" means "color"; because these are clouds of color, they are called "caiyun" (colored clouds).

"Nuó gàn" (擢幹): "nuó" is pronounced as *chú* with the *jue* (覺) rhyme; Xu Shuchong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states that "nuó" means "to draw forth. The *Zilizan* says "gàn" means "branch. "Huǐng yào" (逈曜):
"huǐng" is pronounced as *hù* with the *ding* (𤈍) rhyme; the *Erya* states that "huǐng" means "distant."

"Beneficent assistance" (*yòu*)—the word "assistance" (*yòu*) is pronounced with the reversed final *jiǎn*. In the *Book of Changes* (*Yījīng*), Confucius says: "Assistance means aid. Examining the term "things" (*wù*), it refers to sentient beings and their lives. This means that one is able to use matters of benefit and joy to rescue and enlighten those who possess consciousness. "Assistance" (*yòu*) is also written as *yòu* or *yòu*, meaning to aid.

The "Lord of the Crops" (*zhujia shén*): *Jià* is pronounced as *jiá* (in the rhyme of *jiā*). The *Guǎngyǎ* states that it means "to guard. Mǎ Róng’s commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* says: "To plant the five grains is called 'jia' (cultivation); this refers to the planting of the sprouts and crops of the five grains in this field, which this deity guards so that they suffer no damage."
"Huanji" (環髻): "Huan" is pronounced as "hu" (with the tone of "guan" reversed).
"Xuánfú" (旋澓): "Fú" is pronounced as "fú" (with the tone of "fu"). The *Sāncāng* states that "fú" means "deep"; it refers to the places where the waters swirl and eddy within the rivers and seas.
*Miǎo* (pronounced *miǎo*, with the initial *mí* reversed): the *Fāngyán* says that *miǎo* refers to the fine twigs of a tree;
Guō Pǔ says that *miǎo* means *shāo*. *Āsūró* is also called *Āsùluó* or *Ā*.

This is translated as "Non-existent" (Asura). "Su" (無) means "extreme" or "sublime"; "Miao" (妙) means "wondrous"; and "Luo" (羅) means "play. This signifies that although these beings resemble devas in form, they lack the wondrous play of the devas.
According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, they are translated as "Non-devas" (Asura).
Although these beings are included within the celestial realms (*devagati*), they are mostly deceitful and fraudulent and lack the true virtues of devas;
therefore, they are called "non-devas" (*asura*).
This is like how a person who commits evil deeds is called a "non-human" (*amanuṣya*).
The old translation of this term as "non-liquor" (*bùjiǔ*) is a mistake made by the translators.

They claimed that in the Sanskrit language, *surā* means "liquor," and because it is phonetically close to *asu-ra*, they interpreted the syllable *a-* as meaning "not," thus rendering it "non-liquor. This is a grave error.
According to the Sanskrit original, "asura" is pronounced with a high tone,
while "asura" (or *asu-ra*) is pronounced with a low tone;
nevertheless, they both refer to the same designation.

*Rāhu* (the first *hū* is pronounced as in "hù-gòu"): *rā* means "to grasp" (*śe*) and *hū* means "affliction. Asura Rāhu is able to conceal and grasp the radiance of the sun and moon, causing suffering and affliction to the gods who dwell therein. Alternatively, it is called *Rahuna*, which means "famous everywhere. This refers to how the sun and moon universally illuminate and preside over the heavens; since he now obscures them, his name is heard throughout the world.

Vemacitra: *Vema* means "thread" (*sūtra*), and *citra* means "various. This refers to the asura who is skilled in illusory arts, being able to manifest various things from a single thread. It is also said that *vema* means "pervading the void" and *citra* means "various ornaments and regalia," signifying that when this asura battles Śakra, he arrays various military accoutrements and regalia throughout the sky. The old translations "Resounding Height" (*Xiānggāo*) or "Cave-Dweller" (*Xuéjū*) are incorrect; they are not literal translations of the opposing term.

The *garuḍa*—also called *kālūta*, which means "the sound of bitter suffering from what has been regurgitated"—is so named because whenever this bird seizes a dragon, it first swallows it into its gullet and then spits it out; at that time, while the dragon is still alive, it emits cries of bitter suffering due to the excruciating pain. Alternatively, it is called the "large-gullet-necked bird" (*mahākaṇṭha-śiro-maya*), meaning that this bird constantly stores dragons within its gullet to nourish its neck and crest. The older translations "Golden-Winged" (*jīnshì*) or "Wondrous-Winged" (*miàoshì*) are merely names based on its physical appearance and are not literal translations of the term's etymological meaning. Furthermore, its wings possess various colors of jewels and are not made of gold alone.

*Kinnara*: *Kinn* means "doubt" (*śaṅkā*) and *nara* means "man. This refers to a deity whose appearance resembles that of a human, yet there is a horn upon its head; those who see it give rise to doubt, wondering whether it is a man or not. Alternatively, it is said that *nara* means "hero" (*puruṣa*) and *kinn* means "like a cow" (*go-sadṛśa*). It is so named because its physical form is like a human's while its mouth resembles that of an ox, causing those who see it to feel uncertainty. The older translation as "Singing and Music Deity" is derived from the perspective of its artistic skills.

*Mahoraga*: *Mahu* means "great" (*mahat*), and *raga* means "belly-crawling. This refers to those included among the various classes of nāgas; the old translation as "serpent deity" (*mang shen*) is a partial rendering of the name rather than a precise correspondence.
*Yakṣa* is translated here as "one who lives in suffering" (*kǔhuó*), or alternatively as "sacrificial offering" (*cíjì*), or as "swift" (*jiéjí*);

for now, we adopt the first interpretation. *Vaiśravaṇa*, fully transcribed as *Vviśramanaṅga*, is translated as "Much-Hearing" (*duōwén*). This means that this king possesses great merit and hears and knows much. Alternatively, *vi* is "pervasive" and *śramaṇa* is "hearing," meaning he hears everywhere; the meaning is the same as the previous explanation. Another explanation states that *vi* is "E" (*ī*); this king’s original name was *Kuṭhila*. Later, on one occasion when the Buddha was preaching the Dharma for the assembly, the king came into the gathering wearing a *kāṣāya* robe. The multitude were all astonished and said to one another, "He is a *śramaṇa*! He is a *śramaṇa*! From this, he was given the title *Vaiśravaṇa*.
Regarding the term *daṇḍa* (器仗): according to the *Fengsu ji* (Record of Customs), *daṇḍa* is the general name for knives, halberds, and other weapons.

*Vaiśravaṇa* is fully transcribed as *Pīlùbōhēqīchā*. *Pī* means "various"; *lùbō* means "color"; and *hēqīchā* means "roots" (*indriya*). This refers to his various mixed colors adorning his sense organs. It is also said that *pī* means "various," *lù* means "color," and *bōhēqīchā* means "eyes. This signifies that his eyes are adorned with various colors. The old translation "ugly eyes" (*chǒumù*) is erroneous.
Sāgara means "ocean" here. Takṣaka means "the one capable of harming that which is to be harmed";

*takṣa* is the sound for "that which is to be harmed," and *ka* is the sound for "the one capable of harming. This refers to how when this dragon becomes enraged, its hissing and glare cause both humans and animals to meet their end. The old translation calls him "Many-Tongued Dragon" (*Duōshé Lóng*); this is because he speaks much and is thus named "Many-Tongued," not because there are many tongues in his mouth.

*Kumbhāṇḍa* is translated here as "scrotum" (*yīnnáng*) and is also called "egg-shaped form" (*xíngluǎn*). This class of beings has scrotums shaped like winter melons (*dōngguā*); when walking, they carry them upon their shoulders, and when sitting, they rest directly upon them. Because this debased appearance is so distinct from other classes of beings, they are named after it. The older term "Winter Melon Spirit" (*dōngguā shén*) arose because the matter was treated with such vulgar brevity that it led people to misunderstand it.

Gandharva is here translated as "Fragrance-Eater" (食香) or "Incense-Seeker" (尋香). This refers to a class of beings who seek out and pursue the fragrance of food, going to various places to enjoy themselves in order to obtain sustenance. The older translation, "Music Deity" (樂神), is not a literal rendering.

Regarding "Śākyendra": *Śākya* is correctly transcribed as *Śakara*, which means "conqueror" (*jina*); *Indra* means "lord. To have interpreted this from antiquity as being of the same lineage as the Buddha is a profound error.

*Suyāma* means *suyāma-kāla*, which signifies that the radiance of those devas is so brilliant that day and night cannot be distinguished; one discerns the time only by observing the opening and closing of flowers. Since their time is not defined by light and darkness, they are called the *Suyāma* (Good Time) devas.

Tuṣita, in full, is called *Santuṣita*; this means "Gathering of Joy. According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, it receives this name for three reasons: first, joyful matters; second, congregating; and third, sporting and enjoying. The old translations as "Contentment" (*Xi-zu*) or "Knowing Contentment" (*Zhi-zu*) are not literal translations.

The character *huā* (flower) is pronounced as *tuǒ* (according to the *Yùpiān*, it means "the black ink at the tip of a flower's stamen"). This character is composed of three *xīn* (heart/mind); those who write it with three *zhǐ* (stop/cease) are incorrect.
*Śikhin* is fully transcribed as *Śikhina*; this is translated as "having a topknot" (*yǒu jì*) or "crown topknot" (*dǐng jì*).
Volume Two, Sūtra Two. Volume Two: The Second Part of the "Exquisite Adornment" Chapter. Regarding the phrase "to initiate" (*qi*) in the explanatory text, "initiate" means to open up.
*Dhāraṇī* is translated here as "total retention" (*zongchi*).
"Not in vain" (*bù tángyuán*): "táng" means empty; "yuán" means to discard (the character *yuán* is the opposite of *zhuān*).
"Without peer" (*wú lúnpǐ*): the *Yùpiān* states that "lún" means category and "pǐ" means to compare.
"Awaken to this Way" (*wù sī dào*): the *Ěryǎ* states that "sī" means "this."
"Ten powers" (*daśabala*) means to crush and eliminate; according to the *Erya*, "to eliminate" (*tian*) means to destroy.
"In former ages" (*nangshe*)—*nang* pronounced as *na-lang*—according to the *Erya*, "former" (*nang*) means long ago; that is to say, for a vast duration.

The mind rushes and roams; "rushes" (chí) is pronounced zhí, and "roams" (tàng) is pronounced táng-lǎng. The *Guǎngyá* states that "chí" means to gallop; the *Shuōwén* states that "tàng" means to be unrestrained. The character "tàng" should properly be written as "tè" (愓); however, in the extant scriptures, these characters are commonly used interchangeably with their archaic forms, which are also written as "xiāng" (婸) or "qióng" (𢠽).
"Not following Māra" (不隨魔)—the term "Māra" (魔) is also called "Brahmā" (梵); in full, it is *Māra*, which means "obstacle to the good" (障礙善), or alternatively, "destruction of the good" (破壞善).

Regarding "inducing and instructing" (誘誨): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "inducing" (*you*) means "to teach," while Liu Huan’s commentary on the *Yi Jing* states that "instruction" (*hui*) means "to demonstrate."
"Causing there to be no delusion or confusion. Kong Anguo’s commentary on the *Shu* states: "Bi means 'to cause' or 'to employ.

'Increasing its essence and spirit'—Liu Huan’s commentary on the *Yi* says 'essence' refers to the spiritual intelligence; the *Shuowen* says 'shuang' means clarity. This means to augment the mind and spirit so that they become clear and sharp."
Scroll Three, Part Three of the Third Scripture; Chapter on Wondrous Adornment (Miaoyan-pin), Part Three. *Yin* (蔭): Pronounced *jin* (with the level tone).

It means to provide shade and protection. *Zi-rong* (滋榮) refers to flourishing growth; according to the *Shiming* (釋名), "rong" (榮) describes the appearance of shimmering illumination, signifying its radiant luster.
*Dí* (pronounced *tián lì*): The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "to wash. *Wèi* (pronounced *ān wèi yú*):
The commentary by Ying Shao in the *Hanshu* states: "To stroke those below from above is called 'consolation' (*wèi*); for those below to receive consolation from above is called 'peace' (*ān*)."

A "kṣaṇa" within a single kṣaṇa refers to the most minute unit of time. The *Ratnaketuparivarta Sūtra* (Renwang jing) states: "Within one thought-moment (cittakṣaṇa), there are ninety kṣaṇas; in one kṣaṇa, there are nine hundred births and cessations. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "One hundred and twenty kṣaṇas constitute one tatkṣaṇa; sixty tatkṣaṇas constitute one lava; thirty lavas constitute one muhūrta; thirty muhūrtas constitute one day and night; thirty days and nights constitute one month; and twelve months constitute one year."

"Delusion and obscuration (*moha-āvaraṇa*) constantly veil and confuse; 'obscuration' (*yì*, pronounced *ài* in the local dialect) means to cover. The *Zhu Cóng* states that 'āi' means to screen or conceal. The *Wénzì Jílüè* states that 'yì' means an obstruction before the eyes. The *Gōngyáng Zhuàn* states that when the eyes have pupils but there is no vision, it is called 'veiled' (*méng*). This means that delusion acts as a barrier to the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*), preventing one from seeing the True Dharma, and thus one constantly gives rise to doubt and confusion. The character for 'obscuration' should properly be written as 'yì-ài,' with the pronunciation *ài*."
"Drifting and sinking" (*piao lun*): *Lun* is pronounced with the *li* and *yun* finals; the *Yupian* states that it means "to sink.
"The perilous path" (*wei tu*): *Tu* means a road. This refers to the three evil realms, which are so terrifying that they are called the "perilous path."

Regarding "fame" (*mingwen*): *wen* is pronounced with the tone of *yunfan*; the *Zuǒshǐ zhuan* commentary states that "to hear" (*wen*) means the place where sound reaches. "Sound" (*sheng*) refers to reputation; this subsequent explanation follows that interpretation.
As for "the sound reaching" (*ji*): *ji* is pronounced with the tone of *quji*; Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states that "to reach" (*ji*) means "to arrive at" (*ji*).
"Without limit" (*wúyāngshù*): *yāng* is pronounced as *yáng* (with the *liáng* rhyme). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that *yāng* means "exhaustion.

Regarding the character for "determination" (*juédìng*): it consists of two dots and does not derive from the radical for water; if it were derived from water, its pronunciation would be that of the character for "a sudden surge of water" (*jué*).
"Unfathomable" (*pō*): the character *pō* (pronounced *bǔ* with a retroflex initial) is explained in the *Zìshū* as "that which cannot be.
"Universally delivered" (*dù*): the character *dù* (pronounced *luò* with a retroflex final) means "to cross over.
"Without exception" (*wǎng*): according to the *Ěryá*, *wǎng* means "none."

Regarding the phrase "the path of omniscience is nowhere not proclaimed" (*mi bu xuan*): *mi* means "not" (*wu*). The *Xiaoya* says that *xuan* means "to manifest" (*shi*). "To manifest" means to display; it is also said to mean "to clarify" (*ming*). "To clarify" means to make distinct; it is also said to mean "to penetrate everywhere" and "to put into practice."
*Bāzhi* (婆稚) is correctly transliterated as *Māli*, which means "possessing power.
*Shemoluo* (苫末羅) is the name of a tree found near the seacoast in the Western Regions; it is translated here as "yellow variegated," and when the *garuḍa* arrives, he dwells atop it.
"Vast kalpas and vast suffering. According to the *Guangya*, "vast" (*kuàng*) means long; it refers to being remote and distant. "Sinking into the eternal night.

According to the *Guangya*, "sinking" (*lún*) means to submerge; according to the *Erya*, "eternal" (*yǒng*) means long, and "night" (*xī*) means the evening. This means that within the realm of birth and death, one is constantly in deluded darkness; therefore, it is called the "long night."
The deity Śrī is here translated as "Universal Manifestation of Auspiciousness" (Puxian Jixiang).

Regarding the term *dharmolkā*—where *ulka* is pronounced with the reversed tone according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*—it means a bundle of firewood set ablaze, referring to a great torch. The *Zhucóng* states that *ju* refers to a bundle of grass (*guju*) ignited to provide illumination; thus, *ju* is the ancient form of the character for *jù*, with *jǔ* pronounced as *jūlǚ*.
*Ké* (克) means "to exhaust" or "to destroy"; *jiǎn* (殄) means "to annihilate. According to the *Erya*, *ké* (克) means "to be able.
Fascicle Four, Part Four; the fourth fascicle of the sutra. From the "Chapter on Wondrous Adornments," Part Four. *Muni* is translated here as "Silent Sage" (*jìmò*).

"Buddhakṣetra" (佛剎) means "possessing the correct [field]"; *kṣetra* (刹) here refers to "land" or "soil" (土田). The pronunciation of *kṣa* (刹) is like that of *chūjiè* (初芥). *Atṛpta* (無厭足) means "without satiety";
*tṛpta* (厭) is pronounced with the initial *yàn* (鹽) and means "satiated."
Langran explains the character *wen* (文), saying: "Lang" means clarity (*ming*).

The character for *qia* (𦊱) has the phonetic component *hu gua* (胡卦); its abbreviated form is *qia*, meaning "to entangle and obstruct. The character is also written as *qia*. *Samādhi*—when complete—is correctly called *samāpatti*;

this is translated as "equanimous concentration" (*dengchi*). This means being free from both dullness (*līna*) and agitation (*auddhatya*), which is termed "equanimity" (*sama*); because it causes the mind to focus on a single object and abide therein, it is called "concentration" (*āpatti*).
*Quàn* (泉): Pronounced *jiàn* (古, with the second tone). *Pàizé* (霈澤): *Pài* (霈) is pronounced *pǔgài* (普蓋).

The *Wenzí jílüè* (Textual Compendium) states that *pài* refers to heavy rain. Liu Xi’s commentary on the *Mèngzi* says: "The appearance of pouring down rain. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* says: "Inflaming drought; its heat scorches people. The *Shuowén* says: "Heat. *Qīngyánshǔ* (清炎暑): "Clearing the scorching heat. *Yán* (炎): The heat of a drought that sears and burns people. *Shǔ* (暑): Heat. The *Shuowén* says: "The heat [of summer]."
Regarding the explanation of "xuán" (宣) in the *Xiǎoyǎ*: "xuán" means to proclaim or manifest.

Regarding "tiányí" (恬怡), it refers to the most supreme Way. "Tián" is read as *tuánxián* (徒嫌) and "yí" is read as *zhīyí* (之夷). Kǒng Àngguó’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* states: "tián" means tranquility or peace; the *Ěryǎ* states: "yí" means joy.
*Jian* (蠲) [pronounced *xuanfan*]: The *Xiaoya* states that *jian* means "purity. "Purity" refers to being clean and pure.

All [characters] follow the interpretation of Zheng [Yuzuo] in his commentary on the *Shi*, which says that *cong* (從) means "to follow. The *Zhucun* states: "When instruction is perfected above and customs are transformed below, it is called 'transformation' (*hua*)."

"Xianbei" (險詖) means not cultivating virtue; "bei" (詖) is the opposite of righteousness. The Preface to the Mao Shijing says: "To have within one the will to advance the worthy, yet lack a mind of xianbei. The Cangjie Pian says: "Bei refers to being sycophantic and fawning."
"Without weariness" (*wú yàndài*): "yàn" (厭) is pronounced *yàn* (燄) in reverse; it means to grow weary or fatigued. "Transcending Mount Sumeru":
the *Zílín* (Dictionary of Characters) states that "yú" (踰) means to leap over or transcend.
"Like one born blind in this world who suddenly has no sight": "zú" (卒) is pronounced *jiāng* (將) and *yù* (聿) in reverse; it signifies the end or conclusion.

Regarding "máng-gǔ" (blind): the *Wǔfǎnsāncāng* states that one who has no eyes is called gǔ. The *Shìmíng* states that gǔ refers to the eyes being closed as flat as the skin of a drum; it says the character is derived from "skin," which is incorrect.

*Mili* (彌綸): *Lun* (綸) is pronounced as *li* (力) with the *chan* (脣) rhyme group. The *Hanshu Shiyi* (漢書拾遺) states: "Mili" means to wrap around; it refers simply to encompassing and surrounding on all sides. *Yuyü* (名譽):
*Yü* (譽) is pronounced as *yu* (余) with the *ru* (茹) rhyme group. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (毛詩傳) states: "Yü" refers to the beautiful praise and laudation bestowed upon a person.
Regarding "mingzhu" (明矚), one wishes to reverse the rhyme; the *Yunlüe* (韻略) states that "zhu" means "to gaze. Fascicle Five, Part Five of the Sutra.

Section Five, "The Chapter on Sublime Adornment" (*Miaoyan-pin*). "Like rivers rushing" (*ruanchuanwu* 如川騖): the character "wu" (騖) has the phonetic value of "yu" (羽). The *Hanyu Shuyi* (漢書音義) states that "wu" means "to gallop in disorder. This refers to how, through cultivation, one encounters the boundless ocean of Buddhas; now, as the Bodhisattvas compete to offer their service at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), they are like the convergence of a hundred rivers into the sea.
"Vajra-nābhi": the character *nābhi* (䐡) is derived from "flesh.
It means "without omission" (*wúyí*)—that is, "hidden" (*yǐng*).

"Jìlì" (綺麗): in the commentary on the *Língguāng Diànfù* (賦), it refers to "brocade patterns" (*qǐwén*). The *Xiǎoyǎ* says, "lì means 'manifest' (*zhù*)," meaning that the windows possess manifest, brilliant patterns.
Tè Míngyán’s commentary on the *Hànshū* states: “Tè” means “unique” (*dú*).

Regarding the word “tián” (in the phrase “adorned with exquisite flowers”), the character “tián” should properly be pronounced as “tián” (with the tone of Tángjiàn fǎn). Another reading is “zhǐlín” (second tone). The *Hànshū Xùnzhuàn* states: “Tián refers to pearls and jade used as ornaments to press down a seat; the *Zhōulǐ* mentions ‘tián-guī’ (adornment-jade), one chi and one cun in length, which is an ornamental inlay of jade. However, in current editions of the sutra, the character is written with the radical for earth (土), and is pronounced “tián” (with the tone of Tángxián fǎn); this is actually the character meaning “to fill” or “to pack” (*tián-sē*).

"Yí-tǎn": "yí" is pronounced with the rhyme of *zhī*, and "tǎn" with the rhyme of *tān*. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states: "Yí means 'easy' (*yì*)," referring to the Way of simplicity; it signifies that which requires little effort and is easy to practice. The *Guang Ya* states: "Tǎn means 'level' (*píng*)."

Regarding the character *yìng* (瑩), Zheng’s commentary on the *Shijing* states it means "glory" (*guāngróng*). The *Yùnyùn* (Rhyme Dictionary) defines it as "ornamentation. This refers to adorning the Buddha’s seat with famous flowers and exquisite jewels. Furthermore, consulting the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *yìng* is also written as *yíng* (鎣), and its gloss is identical to that of *yìng*. However, there is another reading, *yǔ qīng* (余傾反), which carries the meaning of "radiant adornment. In recent times, the lineage of great scholars has been severed, leading to a confusion of phonetics and meanings; the gloss associated with the sound *yíng* (營) has been indiscriminately applied to the phonetic category of *yìng* (瑩).

The World-Honored One gazes with a serene and composed countenance (*níng suì*). An alternative reading states: "The gentleman thereby rectifies his position and concentrates his mandate. Wang Bi’s commentary says: "To 'concentrate' (*níng*) means an appearance of solemnity and order; it refers to a gaze that is grave and reverent. Furthermore, Mencius says: "A serene countenance is one whose complexion is moist and lustrous. The *Yùpiān* dictionary states: "'Níng suì' is the appearance of being moist and lustrous."
*Bǐng rán* (brightly): *bǐng* is pronounced with the *píng* rhyme; it means "permanently. The *Cāngjié piān* states:
"Bǐng means bright and manifest. *Mén tã* (gate/turret): *tã* is pronounced with the *dá* rhyme. The *Hànshū jízhù* states: "Tǎ refers to a small gate."
*Dòngqǐ* (洞啟): *Dòng* is pronounced with the *dù* and *nòng* rhymes. The *Yùpiān* states that it means "to penetrate" (*dòngdá*).

*Dòngyǔ* (棟宇): *Dòng* is pronounced with the *dōu* and *nòng* rhymes. Guō Pǔ’s commentary on the *Ěryǎ* states: "The *dòng* is the ridge-pole of a house. *Yǐn* (檼) is pronounced with the *yú* and *jìn* rhymes; *yǐn* is the same as the roof-ridge (*jì*).

"Exquisite fragrance billows and swirls. (The characters are written as 氳, with the phonetic *yún* [反] and *wēn* [於云反]. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states: "Billows and swirls means abundant; it refers to the abundance of fragrant scent. It is also written as 葐蒀.)

"Shù qíqí" (樹歧歧) means [the branches] spread between the two thighs; the character is written as 𢺷 in dictionaries, meaning tree branches spreading across the head. That current editions of the sutra use the character 岐 from the "Mountain" radical, and that the *Qieyun* pronounces it as "qí," are both errors.

"Zhēng sǒng zhuó": *sǒng* is pronounced with the initial *yǒng* (as in *yǒng*), and *zhuó* is pronounced with the initials *zhí* and *jué*. The *Qièyùn* states that "sǒng" means "lofty. The *Cāngjiépiān* says "zhuó" means "to pull out," referring to pulling up the branches and twigs of trees so they grow high.
"Like heavy clouds" (*chóngyún*): "heavy" (*chóng*) is pronounced *zhí yòng fǎn*; it means dense and dark. "Pervasively covering" (*mífù*):

"pervasive" (*mí*) is pronounced *fāng fù fǎn*. The *Yìnyì* (Phonetic and Semantic Commentary) on the *Hànshū* states that "pervasive" (*mí*) means full; it refers to a pervasive covering and shading.

"Mutually sheltering and reflecting" (xiāng bì yìng): the "bì" (庇) is pronounced as *pǐ* (下卑至反). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states that "bì" means "to cover. The *Erya* states that "bì" means "shade. The *Zishu* states that "yìng" (映) means "shining alongside" or "intermingling of colors. This refers to how they mutually shelter and reflect one another, like the interlacing of five-colored silks. The ancient correct form of the character "yìng" (映) is written as 𩣺; it is formed with the sun at its center to signify "reflection," though some instances exist. To write it with the radical "sun" (日) followed by "yīng" (英) is erroneous.

Volume Six, Sūtra Six. Chapter on the Tathāgata Manifesting Signs. *Jambūnada-suvarṇa* (閻浮檀金). It is correctly transliterated as *Rañjūnanda* (染部捺陀). This is the name of a river in the Western Regions; the river flows near the *Jambūnada* tree, and the gold originates from within that river. Thus, the river is named after the tree, and the gold is named after the river. Alternatively, it is said that the juice of the *Jambū* fruit, when dropped upon objects, turns them into gold; as it flows into the river, it dyes the stones, thereby producing this *Jambūnada-suvarṇa*. Its color is reddish-yellow, suffused with a violet luster.

The *utpala* flower is correctly called *nīlotpala*; *nīla* means "blue" and *utpala* is the name for the flower. Its leaves are narrow and long, slightly rounded at the base and tapering toward the tip; the Buddha’s eyes resemble them, and it is frequently used as a metaphor in the sutras. The flower’s stem resembles the end of a lotus root and is covered with thorns.
"Phali" (頗梨) is correctly transliterated as *sphāṭika*; its form is somewhat like that of crystal (*śuijing*) in this region, though it exists in both red and white varieties.

Regarding the character "zhen" (振) in "Puzhen" (普振), it should properly be written as "zhen" (震), carrying the meaning of "to shake" or "to tremble. The "zhen" (振) used in the original scripture is actually the character meaning "to lift up" or "to rouse."

The term *pratyekabuddha* (辟支佛) is rendered in Sanskrit as *pratyekabuddhatva*; this is translated as "individually wandering Buddha. *Buddha* means "awakened. The older translation, "Solitary Awakened One" (*Dújué*), correctly captures its meaning. Alternatively, it is translated as "Conditionally Awakened One" (*Yuánjué*), which is an error of the translators; for in Sanskrit, *pratyaya* is translated as "condition" (*yuán*). Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 18, subsumes both of these categories under the term *pratyaya*.

"Qián rán zuò": "Qián" (all) is read with the rhyme of *qián* and *yán*. The *Erya* says, "Qián means 'all'"; the *Xiaoya* says, "Qián means 'together'. It is like saying "there are none who do not all do so.
"Kè zhèng": "Kè" (to be able) means "to be capable of. The *Erya* says, "Kè means 'able'."
Because the Dharma-realm circulates everywhere without not being all-pervasive and is widely diffused, it is called "circulating.
It abides either as a covering or as a lateral [orientation]. "Covering" (fù) is pronounced fáng (with the second tone); "lateral" (biàng) is pronounced bó (with the fourth tone).

"Zhou" means "to hear throughout the ten directions"; "wen" (聞) refers to the reach of sound. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states that "zhou" means "comprehensive. The *Zhucóng* says that "wen" refers to where sound arrives.
Volume Seven, Fascicle Seven. *Puxian Sanmei Pin* (Chapter on Samādhi of Samantabhadra). "Bao" (包) is also written as "bao" (苞); both are used interchangeably.

Parinirvāṇa is explained as *pari-nir-vāṇa*. *Pari* means "universal" or "ultimate"; *nir* means "to emerge from" or "liberation"; and *vāṇa* refers to the "bonds of affliction. Thus, it signifies the universal, ultimate emergence from and liberation from all bonds of affliction.
I [interpret] *zhèn* according to the commentary by Chun on the *Hanshu*, which states: "To belong to a class.

Regarding the "Vastness of Aspiration" (*zhìyù guǎngdà*) in the "Chapter on the Accomplishment of the World," the commentary on the *Lunyu* states: "Aspiration means to admire; 'admire' refers to longing for and delighting in [something]."

"Afflictions (kleśa) disturb and cloud [the mind]. "Disturb" (rǎo) is pronounced with the *shào* rhyme (as noted by Kǒng Āngguó in his commentary on the Book of Documents, where he states it means "to confuse and disorder"). The character should properly follow the radical *náo* (pronounced *miào* or *dāo*). In the extant scriptures, those that follow the radical *yōu* are erroneous.

"Or 'long' (xiū) or 'short': the *Guǎyá* states that 'xiū' means long. The original text uses the character 脩 (xiū), which refers to dried meat; it is not used in this sense. 'Xuánfù' (懸覆) and 'zhùfù' (住覆):
'fú' (孚) is the reverse of 'fú' (福); it describes a state of hanging down."

"Xián (互) xún (循) fù (復) xún (循): xián is pronounced as xiáng (祥) and lún (倫); fù is pronounced as fú (符) and fú (福). Guo Pu says: 'xún' means to patrol and travel about. Zheng's commentary on the *Shijing* says: 'fù' means to go back and forth, referring to the process of passing through and coming and going."
"Without a moment's rest" (*wú zàn yǐ*): according to the *Guǎngyá*, "yǐ" means "to stop.
"The three dimensions and the eight corners" (*sān wéi jí bā yú*): according to the *Guǎngyá*, "wéi" means "corner"; Zeng Xuan’s commentary on the *Kǎogōngjì* states that "yú" means "corner."
The shared radical for the character 美 (mei) is 廿 (niàn), not 廾 (kǒng). The horizontal strokes must be connected. The character 美 is composed of 大 (dà); it must never be written with 火 (huǒ).
Each of these is clearly distinguished. Ma Rong’s commentary on the *Lunyu* states that "distinction" (qūbié) means differentiation.
“*Pò-ài* (迫隘): *Pò* means to press or constrain; *ài* means narrow. Scroll Eight, Part One: “The Chapter on the Flower Treasury World.

“Precious grasses grow in profusion, all fragrant” (*zhēn cǎo luó shēng xī fēnfù*). *Fēn*: pinyin *fú yún fǎn*. *Fù*: pinyin *fú fú fǎn*. According to the *Erya*, “*zhēn*” means beautiful or exquisite. Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states: “*Zhēn* refers to treasures; it means taking precious things as if they were grasses. The *Chuci* says: “They grow in rows upon the hall. Wang Yi’s commentary states: “*Luó* means to grow in a row or array.”**
"Indestructible" (*bu kě jǔ huài*): "Jǔ" means to ruin; according to the *Yìnyì* (Explanations of Pronunciation) of the *Hànshū*, "jǔ" means to destroy.
"Dìyùn qí xià" (*dì yù qí xià*): "yùn" is pronounced *yú jìn*. The *Ěryá* states: "Dì is called yùn. Guō Pǔ’s commentary says: "Dì refers to dregs; in the Jiangdong region, they are called yùn."

Regarding "lanshun" (欄楯): "lan" (欄) is pronounced with the *dan* (丹) rhyme, and "shun" (楯) is pronounced with the *shu-yin* (述尹) rhyme. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means a railing (*lanhan*). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* says: "The vertical bars are called *han* (檻), and the horizontal bars are called *shun* (楯); the crossbars between the *shun* are called *ling* (櫺)."
*Puṇḍarīka* is translated here as "white lotus" and is also called the "hundred-petaled flower.
Regarding *śīla-dhvaja*, according to the Sanskrit, *śīla* means "cooling"; however, if it is read as *cīra*, it is translated as "jade," meaning a banner made of jade is called a *śīla-dhvaja*.
Regarding the phrase "Competitively perform the *Xiǎoyǎ*": "perform" (*zòu*) means to advance or to execute.

As for "the fragrant water is clear and still" (*chéngtíng*): according to the *Pīcāng*, "when water is still, it is called *tíng*; *tíng* is like *zhàn* [deeply settled]. The versions of the scripture that write this with the radical "person" (*rén*) as "tíng" are erroneous.

"Encircled by walls" (*huán qiáng liáo rào*): *huán* is pronounced as *yuán* (in the *Yuan* rhyme), and *liáo* is pronounced as *líng niǎo* (in the *Niǎo* rhyme). The *Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry* states: "Walls and enclosures. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To entwine. This means to surround and encircle on all sides. The character for "rampart" (*qiáng*) is written as *qiáng* in the *Zhouwen* script; in the *Lishuwen* it is also written as *qiáng*, though nowadays the radical "earth" (*tǔ*) is sometimes added.

"Huífù" (洄澓) means swirling; "fù" (澓) means deep, referring to the places of deep abysses within rivers and seas where the water whirls. Regarding "tánshàn" (壇墠): "tán" (壇) is pronounced *chángyǎn* (常演) as a rhyme;

the *Shàngshū* says, "He established three altars on the same level ground (*tánshàn*)," and the *Kǒngzhù* (Commentary of Kǒng) explains: "One builds up earth to form an altar (*tán*), while one clears the ground to form a leveled site (*shàn*). The *Mānshīchuán* (Tradition of the Mān Shī) states: "Shàn" is synonymous with "tán," meaning a level plain.
*Khaḷaka* means a granary; *Indra* means the Net of Indra;
*Sahā* means Endurance.
Regarding the shape of the *svastika* (卐), an examination of the Sanskrit manuscript reveals that this symbol is actually the mark of a virtuous person and is not a letter at all.
Nevertheless, throughout the scripture, according to the Chinese version, these seventeen characters—counting both the preceding and following instances—are uniformly pronounced as "wan" (萬).
According to the Sanskrit text, there are twenty-eight marks;
that is, four of the eight types of marks. Namely, *śrīvatsa*.
Nandika-vatā, Saṃvartikā, and Bhaṅgaka;
furthermore, there are the three signs of Padmākṣa, Kīla, and Vajra.
Although these are present in the "Flower Treasury" (*Gandavyūha*) and "Dedication" (*Pariṇāmanā*) chapters,
they are not included in this enumeration because they can be recognized without error.
Furthermore, the mark of the *aṅkuśa* (goad) is entirely absent from this sutra and is therefore also not listed among the seventeen marks.
It is neither the form of ten thousand characters nor the appearance of a single color.
Now, to clarify the differences and similarities: the eighth fascicle contains one śrīkhaṇḍa mark, while the ninth fascicle contains three marks.
First was Nandika-vatsa; next was Śrīgupta;
and finally, yet another Śrīgupta.
The twenty-second has one mark, namely, Sefūsittika.
The twenty-seventh has five marks;
the first is Śrīkṣa.
Next is sevāsiddhi; next is nandikā-vṛtta; next is śrīkhaṇḍa.
Later, in the forty-eighth [chapter], Nandika-vastu, there are three signs:
first, the sign of sāpattika; second, the sign of āpatti;
third, the sign of vyutthāna. First, the sign of sāpattika.
Second, śrī-vaśa; third, śrī-vaśa.
Within the fifty-seventh, fifty-eighth, sixty-third, sixty-fifth, and so forth, each contains one instance of the śrī-vaśa mark.
If one carefully follows the Sanskrit manuscript, there are twenty-eight characteristics in total, fully manifesting as explained in the *Viniścaya-ṭīkā*.
The Sanskrit text consists of ten thousand words.
Śrīghoṣa—this is translated here as "Auspicious Ocean Cloud."
Nandika-varta means "right-turning" (in Chinese).
Śaṃkhinī means "possessing bliss" (in Chinese). Pūrṇa-ghaṭa means "full jar.
Alternatively, among the eight auspicious signs, this jar may be absent and replaced by a conch shell.
Padma (padmam) means "red lotus" (*raktapadma*);
cakrā means "wheel"; and vajra means "thunderbolt."
Aṅkuśa, here translated as "curved hook.
Fascicle Nine, Sūtra Volume Nine, Chapter on the Flower Treasury World, Part Two. The world is named Śiri-Śiri; this means "Excellence" and is also called "Auspiciousness."

The *Chengguo fengsu tong* states: "The term 'city' (*cheng*) signifies 'flourishing' (*sheng*), and 'outer wall' (*guo*) signifies 'expansive' (*kuo*), meaning that which is wide and expansive and capable of receiving what flourishes.

Their shape is like that of the four continents. The *Erya* states: "Land within the water where one may dwell is called a continent (*zhou*). Since the four worlds under heaven are all situated within the four great oceans, they are all termed continents. Regarding their shapes being like those of the four continents: the eastern continent is circular like the sun; the western continent is shaped like a half-moon; the southern continent is broad in the north and narrow in the south; and the northern continent is square in shape.

Regarding "lion-stretching" (*siṃha-vijṛmbhita*), the *Mao Shi Zhuan* states: "Fen" means urgency; "shen" means extension. This refers to one who is fatigued using their hands, feet, chest, back, left, right, above, or below—either by tensing or by extending—to relieve that fatigue. Alternatively, this may be entirely a Sanskrit term, as explained in the *Kanding ji*.

The world [of this sutra] is named Tālā; its origin is unknown. Regarding "dragon-pool" (*yuan*): *yuan* is pronounced with the second tone for the initial *wu* and the fourth tone for the final *kong*. Kong An’s commentary on the *Analects* states: "A pool is a deep abyss. Regarding "habitual practice" (*guanxi*):

*guan* is pronounced with the third tone for the initial *gu* and the fourth tone for the final *huan*. Zheng’s notes on the *Odes* state: "It means habitual practice. The character should properly include the "hand" radical (*shou*). There are those who write it as "string" (*chuan*), which is actually the character for "to thread" (*guànchuàn*). In current editions of the scriptures, the version with the "mind" radical (*xin*) is used as common usage.
*Devapurī-ratna-kūṭa*. *Kūṭa* (堞) is pronounced as *tu-jié* (徒頰). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states:

"Kūṭa refers to a *nǚqiáng* (女牆, or battlement). Fascicle 10, Part 10, Sutra Scroll 10: *Puṣpakaraṇḍa-lokadhātu-parivarta* (The Chapter on the Flower-Treasury World), Part 3. *Guǐdù* (軌度). *Dù* (度) is pronounced as *tu-gù* (徒故). Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states: "Guǐ means law (*fǎ*). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: 'Dù refers to the measurements of cubits and fathoms. Because the rules and regulations have fixed measures, they are called *guǐdù*."
The Buddha’s name is Śālarāja; *śāla* here is translated as "firm" (*jiangu*) and also as "supreme" (*zuisheng*).
Regarding "peerless" (*juelun*), Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Yili* states:

"Lun means comparison. Regarding "auspicious canopy" (*jixiang wo*), the *Shangshu Zhuan* says: "Ji means good. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "Xiang refers to the premonitions of good or ill fortune. Jia Yi’s commentary on the *Guoyu* says: "Xiang is like a likeness. He Chengtian’s *Zuanyao* states: "That which is above is called a *zhang* (curtain); that which is on the sides is called a *wei* (curtain). When these four sides enclose one another like a palace, it is called a *wo* (canopy)."

To adorn and heighten the *bǐní* (俾倪). *Bǐ* (俾) is pronounced as *pǐ* (普米反); *ní* (倪) is pronounced as *yán* (研禮反). Zheng’s commentary on the *Kǎogōngjì* states: "It means lofty. The *Guǎngyá* says: "*Bǐní* refers to a *nǚqiáng* (女牆, 'women's wall' or battlement). The *Cāngjiépiān* says: "*Bǐ* is a small wall atop a city rampart. According to Jia’s commentary on the *Guóyǔ*, the character for *bǐ* is written as *bǐ* (俾); Duan’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* writes it as *pí* (陴); the *Guǎngyá* writes it as *bǐ* (隦); and the *Zhòuwén* writes it as *xī* (𩫝), which is also pronounced as *bìzhī* (避支反). As for the current edition of the scripture using the characters *bǐní* (俾倪), according to the *Shēnglèi*, these are actually the rings on the middle of a carriage seat used to hold the shaft of the canopy (*gāng*). Furthermore, there are the characters *pěi* (䫌), *pǐ* (󲃯), and *niè* (䑀睨), all of which convey the sense of tilting to the left or right or looking askance; some say they refer to looking outward from within a carriage. *Gāng* (杠) is pronounced as *jiāng* (江), referring to the pole of the canopy.
"Xiu-chu" (秀出): "Xiu" is pronounced with the private radical *jiou* (究). The *Guoyu* states: "When one stands out from the multitude, there will be good fortune. Gu Yewang says: "Xiu means beautiful.
Regarding "hui" (繢), it is pronounced with the private radical *huai* (對). Zheng’s commentary on the *Lunyu* states: "Hui refers to painted patterns."
*Kalpa-saṃvarta* (劫燒): "burning" (*shāo*) with a reversed *shū*;
"hard" (*jiānyìng*) with a reversed *yán*. *Yamaloka* (閻羅界):
*Yama-raja* (琰摩邏闍) is the complete transliteration, which means "obstructing" (*zhēzhǐ*). This refers to obstructing transgressors so that they do not create [further] karma.
*Vajra*: "Jǔchǎngyǔfǎn" (pronounced *jǔ-chǎng-yǔ-fǎn*). *Hǎibàng*: "Hǎibàngpúxiàngfǎn" (pronounced *hǎi-bàng-pú-xiàng-fǎn*).

It refers to a clam; the character is also written as *gē*. *Sānchǔ*: "Sānsūguānfǎn" (pronounced *sān-sū-guān-fǎn*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Sān means sour vinegar (*suò*); chǔ is like the gums (*yìn*). This means that the body undergoes intense suffering and pain such that it cannot be touched or approached—just as when teeth are souring at the gums, one cannot bring objects near them. Some say: "Sān" is like the word *yūsuan* (aching), referring to a painful ache; "chǔ" is a thorny staff (*jīngzhàng*), meaning being struck by a staff and feeling the pain. Others say: "Sān" refers to injury to the bones, while "chǔ" is like the teeth and gums; this means undergoing heavy suffering that pierces to the bone, with such pain that it cannot be touched or approached.

Volume 11, Fascicle 11. Regarding the "Vairocana" chapter: the phrase *nǎiwǎng* (乃往) is an archaic particle used as a temporal adverb; according to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means "long ago. When repeated, its explanatory meaning is equivalent to "pure" (*viśuddha*).

"Cannot be recorded to its limit": "ji" (紀) is pronounced as *jū* and *lǐ*; the *Guǎngyá* states that "ji" means "to record. Zheng’s commentary on the *Lìjì* explains that "jí" (極) means "exhaustion"; thus, it refers to the fact that recording them cannot be brought to an end.

According to this system of the Yellow Emperor’s numerical method, there are three grades: if based on the lower grade, it corresponds to "zhao" (兆); the middle grade is "qi" (𥞑); and the upper grade is "gou" (溝). These are explained in detail in the section on *asaṃkhyeya* as found in the *A-saṃ-khi-ye Pin* (Chapter on Incalculables).

"From *guǎng* (廣) [pronounced *guǎng* with the *zǐ* (紫) tone]. Mèng Kāng’s commentary on the *Shìjì* states: 'North and south are called *cóng* (縱); east and west are called *héng* (橫). *Héng* is the same as *guǎng*. The correct orthography is written with the radical for wood (*mù*); those written with the radical for silk (*mì*) are all vulgar forms used interchangeably.'"

The watchtowers (*lǔ*) and defensive bulwarks (*quèdì*) were all magnificent and ornate. "Lǔ" (pronounced *lánggǔ* in reverse) refers to the structures for defense atop city walls as designated in the *Qièyùn*. Around the city, separate elevated platforms were constructed at intervals and raised high; these were called *quèdì* (defensive bulwarks). Because they were both lofty and adorned, they are described as "magnificent and ornate."
*Qian* (pronounced *qiàn*, with the initial *q* reversed as *ch*) means "moat"; the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that a moat is a ditch.
The version of the sutra that includes the water radical (*shui*) is erroneous. *Pātumapuṣpa* (波頭摩花) is correctly transliterated as *padma*; this refers to the red lotus. Its stem possesses thorns.

The *kumuda* flower has stems with thorns and is either red or white; because its petals are somewhat short and it appears shriveled when it has not yet fully blossomed, it is also sometimes called the "small white flower."
Regarding "converging and stopping" (*cuì zhǐ*), the *Mao Shī Chuán* states that *cuì* means "to gather.

Regarding "the governor of a city or district" (*yì duō zǎi guān*), the *Zuǒ Zhuan* states: "A city or a capital; one that possesses the ancestral temple of a former ruler is called a 'du' (capital), while one that does not is called a 'yì' (city). Kong Āngguó’s commentary on the *Lùn Yǔ* states: "The 'zǎi' refers to a household minister. The *Yùn Pǔ* defines *zǎi* as "master," meaning the high official within a city or district who acts as its master.
