Observing this, it is sufficient to know that the translations are not clear;
having been transmitted through successive generations, they are so erroneous as to be unreliable.

Only when scholars with knowledge of Sanskrit literature examine the Sanskrit manuscripts and consult monks who have studied Sanskrit can one realize that every point of the aforementioned argument is indeed true.
The system of phonemes expounded by Brahmā is clearly defined.
For now, I shall briefly explain the sequence of their mutual generation.

Taking the first twelve characters as the foundational sounds, each subsequent phoneme is translated one by one; from each single character, eleven further characters are produced, which together with the original form twelve. When this process is repeated throughout all thirty-four characters, it is called one cycle.
Furthermore, take the syllable *ya* and append it universally beneath each of the thirty-four syllables; as before, translate each one individually, and this constitutes another cycle.

Remove the syllable *ya* and take the syllable *ra*, appending it universally beneath the thirty-four syllables; following the previous method, use the twelve phonetic powers to translate them, whereby one syllable gives rise to twelve syllables. Having translated the thirty-four syllables in this way, they become four hundred and eight syllables, which constitutes yet another cycle.
Next, by substituting and transforming the twelve syllables—la, va, sa, ha, ya, ña, ṇa, na, ma, and so forth—one completes twelve rounds.
For practical application, this is sufficient.
However, one must receive instruction from a teacher to understand the sequence of the phrases and meanings; these textual expressions are fully contained within twelve sections.

While they may be expanded and combined indefinitely, such that their principles overlap and their sounds and characters become obscure and rarely used in the human world, [the core remains complete].
Using only the first twelve syllables, he further applied them in conjunction with the eightfold grammatical analysis (*aṣṭavibhakti*),
thereby exhausting all worldly phonetic rhythms and various distinctions of terminology, discerning sounds according to their characters.
Based on sounds, meanings are established; as characters are combined and mutually augmented, the sounds and meanings diverge in myriad ways, yet remain distinct and orderly.
Though elaborate, they are not confused;
though extensive, they are easy to understand.
This was transmitted by the holy wisdom of Brahmādeva.
Five-hundred masters of the five supernatural powers, eminent sages, and skilled practitioners— both those who provide extensive expositions and those who provide concise summaries—

each exerted their intellectual power to extensively compose treatises on phonology (*śabda-śāstra*), etymology (*nirukta-śāstra*), and numerology (*saṃkhyā-śāstra*), yet in the end they could not fully describe its wondrous subtlety.

Therefore, the appearance of all Buddhas in the world throughout past and future kalpas, and their turning of the wondrous Wheel of Dharma, are all expounded based upon these Brahma-syllables, thereby exhausting the full extent of their excellence.

For this reason, within the *Mahāvairocana Sūtra*, there is the "Chapter on the Maṇḍala of the Syllable-Wheel" (*Akṣaracakra-maṇḍala-paṭala*); the merit of reciting these fifty-odd syllables is immeasurable and boundless.
It can cause the three karmas of sentient beings to become pure, ensuring they will certainly attain unsurpassed bodhi.
9. The ninth fascicle. The ninth fascicle. The *kalaviṅka* bird; in Sanskrit, this is translated as "Truly Lovely Bird."

The mandarin duck (*mandarin-duck*) is a water bird that resembles the *jue-huang* (a type of pheasant) and is reddish-yellow in color. This bird has a mate; it will not fly unless it is paired with its mate. Therefore, this bird is used [in the ritual] to symbolize moving together as a pair.

*Kīn* (pronounced *kǒng* in the ancient *mǎng* dialect): According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to the raw ore of copper and iron; it is composed of the radical "stone" (*shí*) and the phonetic element "yellow" (*huáng*). Zheng Xuan states that it is "raw stone," meaning when gold and jade remain within the stone and have not yet been smelted or refined, it is called *kuàng*. It is also written as *yán* or *kuàng*, with the same meaning.
In midsummer, the waters rise (the character is pronounced zhāng with two tones, or alternatively written as xiàng with the same pronunciation).
They wane and swell (the first character, qū, is pronounced qiū wēi; it means to diminish. There are those who write this as the character "huī," but that is not the correct form).

Regarding the term for a lunar eclipse, the *Yì* (Book of Changes) states: "When the sun is at its zenith, it wanes; when the moon is full, it eclipses. Liu Xi’s *Shìmíng* (Explanations of Names) says: "The waning of the sun and moon is called a solar eclipse; it gradually diminishes and is depleted like insects eating the leaves of trees and plants."

The *Erya* states that a comet is called *chanqiang*; the *Shiming* says its light gradually resembles a broom, hence it is called a "broom-star" (*saoxing*) by people in the world. It moves with a sharp point and reverses its direction.

*Sī* (思移反): According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to command" or "to dispatch. According to the *Zìshū*, it refers to a servant (*yì*). It is also written as *sī* or *wēi*, and all refer to a lowly servant. *Bùjù* (怖遽 渠庶反):
According to the *Guǎngyá*, *bù* means "fear" or "dread," and *jù* means "haste" or "urgency. In the canonical text, it is sometimes written as *qì* (懅), which is also acceptable.
*Duī* (上: dū; 下: fù) is also written as *dù* (上: dū; 下: wù); both refer to hills and mounds.
*Póluóchì* (婆羅翅) tree is translated here as "white heron.
*Níkālā* (尼迦羅) tree is translated here as "not black," and also as "untimely."
*Khadira* refers to the *khadira* tree; it is that whose wood is hard and solid.
"Mì" (密) means dense and compact (*zhì*, pronounced *zhì* with the second tone). It is also written as *mí* (𣗥), used interchangeably.

The thirty-two marks are clearly explained in detail in the third fascicle of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the nineteenth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Jinwang-hui* (Assembly of the Victorious King) section of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Ratnadattā-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, and this present sutra; however, as the text is extensive, it is not recorded here in full.

The eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) are fully elucidated in these texts: the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 7; the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 48; the *Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-samādhi-sūtra* (or *Jinwang-hui*); and the *Anuttara-tantra-nirdeśa-sūtra*, chapter 2.
*Qīngdǎo* (輕蹈): *Dǎo* (蹈) is pronounced *túdào*. The *Yùpiān* states it means "to tread upon. *Bùní* (不匿): *Nì* (匿) is pronounced *nílì*.
The *Yùpiān* states it means "to hide. *Yùzhēng* (鬱烝): The upper character *yù* (鬱) is pronounced *yúwù*;
Lǐ Xún’s commentary on the *Erya* states that *yù* refers to "abundant qi. The lower character *zhēng* (烝) is pronounced *zhīréng*; the *Shuōwén* states it refers to "the rising of fire-qi."

The explanation of the eight kinds of medicine: first, for treating the body; second, for treating the eyes; third, for treating sores; fourth, for treating children; fifth, for treating malevolent spirits; sixth, for treating poisons; seventh, for treating diseases of the fetus; eighth, for divining by the stars, as explained by Jīvaka.

"Rǔbù" (乳哺) [the second character pronounced bù with the phonetic bùfú] refers to "containing food," meaning chewing food within the mouth. In some scriptures, it is written as "pū" (晡) [pronounced bǔ with the phonetic bǔgū], which refers to the meal taken during the hour of the Monkey (the third watch).

"Chuāngpào" (創皰): The upper character "chuāng" (創) is pronounced chūliáng; it is also written as "chàng" (戧) or "chuàng" (剏), both of which are archaic forms. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains that "chuàng" means a fresh wound. In some scriptures, it is written as "chuāng" (瘡), which is a vulgar form and not the correct standard. The lower character "pào" (皰) is pronounced púxié; it is also written as "páo" (𤴯), which is identical. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains that it refers to a blister or sore arising on the face. In the scriptural texts, it is sometimes written as "pào" (疱), which is not the correct radical form.

*Bi* (㿃) is pronounced *dāng-lài-fǎn* and is also written as *pǔ* (䐭); according to the *Zīlín*, it refers to the two ailments of "red and white discharge" (*chìbái*) in women. In the Guānzhōng dialect, it is often pronounced *dài*. According to the *Sāncāng*, it refers to a disease involving leakage from below. The *Shìmíng* states that when diarrhea is severe and characterized by red and white discharge, it is called *bi*; this signifies a violent (*lì*) and chronic (*pǔ*) condition that is difficult to cure. The scriptural text uses the character *zhé* (蜇), which is identical to *qū* (蛆) and pronounced *zhī-liè-fǎn*, meaning "insect stinging. It is also written as *zhé* (哲), meaning "wisdom. Neither of these two characters accords with the intended meaning of the scripture.

"Chao" (to pick up) refers to picking up the front chopsticks with the back chopsticks; "zhong" (loyal) and "shu" (commoner) are homophones for "fan" (to turn/reverse), referring to the place where one speaks, or also said to mean "standing.

The *āmra* fruit has no direct Chinese equivalent; its shape resembles that of a papaya, its flavor is fragrant and sweet, and it is a fruit for which it is difficult to distinguish between raw and ripe even when handled according to the scriptures.

Regarding *saindhava*, the Tripitaka Master Jing said it is rock salt; because it originates from the banks of the Indus River, it is named after that river. The present sutra states that "one name has four realities," which serves as a metaphor for an intelligent minister who employs his skills according to the timing of the situation.
The *palaśa* tree is here translated as the "Red Flower Tree.
As for the *karnikāra* tree, its full name is *nikāgalanikā*; *nikā* means "moon," and *gala* means "to make."
*Asoka* (阿叔迦) means "Free from Sorrow" (*an-śoka*) in this language.
*Pāṭala* (波吒羅)—the second character being pronounced with the *zhù* and *jià* finals reversed—translates as the "Double-Leafed Tree.

10. Volume Ten. *Sìsì* (祠祀)—the first character pronounced with the *xú* and *lǐ* finals reversed—is defined in the *Erya* as "sacrificing. According to the *Liji*, the Son of Heaven establishes ten sacrifices for the common people: the feudal lords have five sacrifices; the Great Officers have three; the scholars have two; and the commoners have one. Or, it refers to minor deities such as the hearth-god who issue warnings and admonitions.

The character *qīngzào* (輕躁) is also written as *jiào* (趮), which the *Yì* (易) explains as "being restless. In the context of the hexagram Zhèn (震), it is said that "Zhèn represents restlessness"; "restlessness" (*zào*) implies movement. The *Lúnyǔ* states: "To speak before one's words are required is called restlessness (*zào*). Zhèng Xuán comments: "Restlessness means a lack of tranquility."
*Kou-chi* (口𠁊): pronounced *sō* (two tones), meaning "defeat. The people of Chu called a magnificent defeat *shuǎng*.
*Xiáo-zhuàn* (肴饌): pronounced *shì-quàn* (also written as 󳇺), explained as "prepared food" or "an array of dishes for a meal."
*Chàngyǎng* (悵怏): According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "yǎng" means to be dissatisfied or resentful; the *Cangjie Pian* states that it refers to resentment and indignation. *Tángjuān* (唐捐):
"táng" is pronounced with the initial *l* (徒郎反), meaning "vainly" or "in vain"; "juān" is pronounced *yizuān* (以專反), meaning "to discard" according to the *Yupian*.

The name of the country Magadha, translated from the Sanskrit, is explained as follows: *ma* means "non-" (*na*) and *gadha* means "killing" (*vadha*), signifying that the laws of this country do not employ corporal punishment; those who commit crimes punishable by death are sent to the *śītavana* (Cold Forest) cemetery, where they are left to their fate. Furthermore, another interpretation states that *ma* means "great" (*mahat*) and *gadha* means "body" (*tattva*); thus, it is called the "Great Body" because among the five regions of India, this country is the largest and governs all other lands.

A full eight *hu* (bushels) of this [measure] is used among the central regions of the kingdom of Magadha according to the celestial laws for regulating measures and weights; in other regions it is not fixed, but all take this as their standard. According to the *Sunzi Suanjing* (Master Sun’s Arithmetic Classic), the origin of measurement begins with millet: six grains of millet make one *gui*; sixty grains make one *cuo*; six hundred grains make one *miao*; six thousand grains make one *shao*; sixty thousand grains make one *he*; six hundred thousand grains make one *sheng*; six million grains make one *dou*; and sixty million grains make one *hu*. These were all consistent with the standards of the Zhou dynasty during the Buddha’s lifetime. As for the small *dou* of three *sheng*, this is equivalent to one current *dou*.

Regarding the "horned owl" (*kulinga*): this bird has feathers on its head that stand upright like horns; it belongs to the same class as the *xiu*, *jiao*, and wild chickens. This bird preys upon other birds and certainly lacks the principle of cohabitation; therefore, the Buddha cited it as a metaphor.
The *saptaparṇa* flower has seven leaflets shaped like a human hand, and its fragrance is foul.
The *vārṣika* fragrance is fragrant; this is called "creeper flower" (*mādhavī*).
"Jin huai" (浸壞) means that the water has submerged and ruined the person; "huai" (壞) is pronounced as *guài* (恠).

Regarding the explanation of the thirteen verses, there are six general headings, with six individual verses for each vow, which together constitute the thirteen verses. This begins from the verse on the horned owl and concludes with the verse beginning "For this reason."
*Yíyuè* (怡悅): The first character is pronounced with the *shàng* tone, the opposite of *ěr*. The *Erya* states: "Yí means joy; it means delight. It is also identical to *xī* (熈). *Zhū* (姝):

The first character is pronounced with the *chǐzhū* rhyme. The *Shuowen* says: "It means beautiful; it means a lovely complexion. The *Shiming* states: "In the regions of Zhao, Wei, Yan, and Dai, they call the beautiful *zhū*."
*Guǐ* (瑰): "Anciently pronounced *huí* (𢌞), also written as *kuǐ* (傀). It means excellent, flourishing, or—as defined in the *Shuowen Jiezi*—magnificent and extraordinary.
*Bì* (弊): "Pronounced *pímì* (毘謎) in the upper character. It means a wicked nature, malady, or a quick-tempered disposition."
"Spitting the pit on the ground": "pit" (hé) is pronounced *gé* (in the sense of the kernel within a fruit).
"Island" (*zhǔ*) refers to Aparagoyānī (the Western Continent of Goatherds).

"To examine" (*zhěn*)—according to the *Shuowen*, it means to look at; according to the *Sancang*, it means to observe; the *Shenglèi* says it means to verify. At times, the character *yàn* (to verify) is used interchangeably with this.
The ninety-five types of non-Buddhist paths all lead to the evil realms.

Regarding these ninety-five types of non-Buddhists, Hui-lin explains that their heterodox views are so profuse and confused as to be beyond detailed description; the practices they follow and the tenets they uphold each differ from one another.
For now, I shall briefly cite several examples to clarify their distinctions, namely: the Vaiśeṣika and Sāṃkhya schools, which cling to the notion of a self (*ātman*).

They calculate permanence through such practices as scorching the body with five fires, lying on wooden spikes, smearing oneself with ashes, eating from cupped hands, standing on one foot, remaining naked, fasting, throwing oneself into rivers, observing the precepts of chickens and dogs, wearing wooden boards, bark, or grass, leaping into fire, hurling oneself from cliffs, and practicing various perversions with skulls;
these are deluded and confused efforts that yield no benefit and do not lead to liberation. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "All these lead to the evil realms" (*yoga*).

The *Ṣaṭprakaraṇa* and the *Saptadaśaprakaraṇa* clarify [the paths], while the *Navadharmaprakaraṇa* and the *Viṃśatikā-prakaraṇa* extensively distinguish the routes of the fundamental tenets (*mūla-mārga*) as found in those two treatises.

Regarding the attachments to precepts and observances (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*), they are categorized according to their characteristics; when subsumed in general, they do not exceed sixteen types. As stated in a verse within the treatise:
They cling to the view that the effect exists within the cause,
that [the self] is manifest, that there is going and coming, that the self is eternal, and that past actions are the cause.
They falsely claim that the limits of real dharmas such as the Sovereign (Īśvara) are finite or infinite; they resort to equivocation,
asserting causelessness, nihilism, emptiness,
supremacy, purity, and auspiciousness.
These are known as the sixteen heterodox doctrines: (1) the thesis that the effect exists within the cause;
(2) the thesis that [the effect] is manifested through conditions;
(3) the thesis that the past and future truly exist.
1. The school that maintains the self truly exists; 2.
The school that maintains all things are eternal; 3.
The school that maintains the theory of past deeds as the cause.
1. The school of the seven masteries (*vaśitā*), etc.; 2.
The school of the eight substantial [elements] as the true Dharma; 3.
The school of the discourse on the finite and the infinite.
10. The school of equivocation regarding non-death; 11. The school of the doctrine of causelessness; 12.
The school of the doctrine of the seven types of annihilationism;
13. The school of the doctrine that both cause and effect are empty; 14. The school of the doctrine of false attachment to supremacy.
15. The school of false conceptualization regarding purity; 16.

The school of false conceptualization regarding auspiciousness. "Shu" (恕)—as defined in the *Cangjie pian*, it means "to accord with" (*ru*). In the *Dai Li* (Great Rites), it says, "Shu is benevolence" (*ren*). According to the *Shenglei*, "a person is one who extends the heart's forbearance toward things."

"Zongxi" (綜習)—the "zi" and "song" rhymes are reversed; the *Sancang* states that "zong" means to manage or organize. This refers to the mechanism's thread holding the warp and weft, regulating the threads so they may be opened and joined to form patterns and images. Learning is also like this: when effort is manifest and skill is perfected, it is called "zongxi."

It is not the case that all sentient beings subsist solely by means of food and drink. According to the *Kongzi Jiayu* (The Family Sayings of Confucius): "Those that drink but do not eat are cicadas; those that eat but do not drink are silkworms; those that neither eat nor drink are mayflies and midges; and those that both eat and drink are the humans and animals of the world. Thus, we know that the previous verse was spoken provisionally for the sake of sentient beings; it is not a universal statement and carries the sense of being incomplete.

*Leiji* (羸瘠): The first character is pronounced *lì* (力佳反) and the second is *qíng* (情亦反), though it is also written as *tuǐ* (𤶬) or *jí* (膌); all three forms are used interchangeably. The *Shuowen* states that *jí* means "emaciated.

*Cìcì* (刺刺): The first character is pronounced *cí* (雌自反). When thorns of plants and trees prick a person, they are called *cì*; when knives, swords, spears, or lances wound a person, they are called *cì*. The ancient script uses the character *cì* (朿). The *Shuowen* defines it as "the bud of a tree. The second character is pronounced *qīng* (清亦反). The *Guangya* defines it as "the blade or point."
The character for "máo" (spear) is pronounced *mò* (with the *mo* rhyme) in the first instance and *shuò* (with the *shuò* rhyme) in the second;
this has already been explained previously in the first fascicle.
*Yiqiejing yinyi*, Fascicle 25 and Fascicle 26.
Compiled by Shi Yungong; further revised and supplemented by the Da Tang Śramaṇa Huilin.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, from fascicle eleven to the end of fascicle forty, comprising two volumes on the section of cremation;

the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* in six volumes; the *Vaipulya-parinirvāṇa Sūtra* in two volumes; and the Southern Edition of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* in thirty-six volumes—all employ these same phonetic transcriptions. The total count above is seventy-six volumes, all sharing the phonetic system of this volume.

Volume 2, Part 2, Section 11. The eleventh fascicle of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra. Regarding the character in the text of the eleventh fascicle that appears as 㿇 (with the radical 疒 and the phonetic 女 with the reversed *gǎn* [reading as *gǎn*]), none of the various scriptural editions contains this character 㿇. It was added by people of recent times using the radical 疒.
*Ei* (pronounced *yue* with a retroflex *e*) means "to gasp" according to the *Tongsu Wen*; the *Shuowen* says it means "shortness of breath. *Lin-li* (the first character pronounced *li-jin*):

according to the *Shenglei*, this refers to frequent urination; the scriptural text writes it as *lin*. The *Shuowen* defines *lin* as "water overflowing," and the *Guangya* as "soaking," but these are not the meanings intended here.

*Chuìhèn* (懟恨): The first character is pronounced *zhì* (古音 *lèi*) and is written as *zì* (譵) in archaic texts. According to the *Erya*, it means resentment coupled with indignation. *Āgāta-yào* (阿伽陀藥):
This is translated as "freedom from illness" or "the medicine of immortality. It is also rendered as "universally removing," meaning that all ailments are completely eliminated.
*Samāpatti* is translated here as "equilibrium" (*děngzhì*); it refers to a mindless meditative absorption (*nièxīn dìng*).
*Staimitya* (𧄼瞢) [the first character pronounced *tú dēng* and the second *mò dēng*] means dullness or mental obscurity.

*Nārāyaṇa* is translated as "Wielder of Might" (*lìshì*); alternatively, it is called the "Wielder of Might among the Gods," the "Wielder of Might among Men," the "Vajra-Wielder," or the "Firm-and-Solid Wielder."
*Pāṭaliputra* is here translated as "leaping and bounding. The *malla* (wrestlers) therein were exceedingly brave, robust, agile, and swift.
*Khaṭ* (pronounced with the *xū* and *shù* finals; according to the *Tōngsú Wén*, it means the mouth passing air; some write it as *khā*, but that is not the intended meaning).

"Coiled dragon" (*pán-lóng*): during light frosts, the dialects conversely refer to a dragon that has not yet ascended to heaven as a "coiled dragon. According to the *Guǎngyá*, "pán" means to coil or bend. The character used in the scriptures is "pán," which refers to vessels and objects; it is not used in this sense here.
Regarding "㓟剝" (gāo bō), the upper character is pronounced *pī*; it is a provisional borrowing used in the scriptural text, as this character does not exist in the dictionaries.
Regarding "結加趺坐" (jié jiā fū zuò), the character "趺" (fū) is pronounced with the second tone (fu wú fǎn).
The *Sāncāng* states that it refers to the "foot-arch" (*zú fū*).
The Zheng commentary on the *Yili* states that it refers to the upper part of the foot.
According to this, the place where one grasps and holds the footwear is called the *zifu* (the instep).

Huilin says that regarding "sitting in the full lotus posture" (*jiejiafu zuo*), the character "jia" (to add) should simply be read as "jia" (to place upon); one binds the two feet together and further places the *zifu* of the left and right feet upon the two calves—this is called sitting in the full lotus posture (*jiejiafu zuo*).
The specific designations for the various methods of sitting are numerous and cannot be described in detail here;
for now, I shall briefly describe two types of sitting postures.
First, place the right foot crossed over the left calf.
Furthermore, placing the left foot upon the right thigh and causing the soles of both feet to face upward above the two thighs—
this is called the *māravijaya* posture (the posture for subduing Māra).
The second method is to turn both palms upward, extend the five fingers, and place the left hand over the right, resting them within the lap.

Most Chan masters transmit this as their sitting posture; it is the second [best] method. If one follows the teachings of the Vidyādhara-piṭaka as transmitted by the consecrated Ācārya, then the auspicious sitting (bhadrapīṭha) is considered superior.
Subduing Māra is the next [stage].
As for the Auspicious Posture (bhadrapīṭha):
first, place the left foot’s instep upon the right calf.
Furthermore, place the instep of the right foot upon the top of the left calf,
and likewise cause the palms of both feet to face upward upon the two calves.
As before, extend the fingers of both hands with the palms facing upward.
Placing the right hand over the left is called the *bhadrapīṭha* (auspicious posture).
Among all methods of sitting, this is the most supreme.
When the Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment, his body was settled in the auspicious posture.
With the left hand pointing to the ground, one forms the mudrā for subduing Māra.
If a practitioner can constantly practice this posture, they will be endowed with the marks of the hundredfold adornments of merit;
being able to accord with all samādhis, it is called the most supreme.
*Pichlie* (劈裂; *pī dì fǎn*) means "to split," according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to the flesh cracking due to freezing cold; according to the *Guangya*, it means "to divide in two.

*A-luo-lo* (阿羅羅) and *A-po-po* (阿波波) refer to the sounds of suffering from the cold in hell. These four hells are named after these sounds. Their causes and conditions are explained in detail in the fifth fascicle of the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-samādhi-sāgara-sūtra*.
The Padma Hell: these four hells are named after flowers; those destined to fall into them will certainly have flowers come to welcome their *vijñāna*.
"To split open" (*bòlì*)—the *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as "to pull apart"; it refers to the hand splitting [something]. Zheng Xuan says it means "to tear asunder."
*Khandha* is fully transcribed as *Sīkhandha*, which means "shelter" (*yin*). Master Lang says it refers to a ghost with a cleft lip.
*Ummāda*—the second character is pronounced with the *mo* rhyme and the *ke* tone reversal—means "demoniac madness," and is also said to refer to a "drunken deity."
*Apamāra* is translated here as "flowerless garland" (*muhua-man*) or "madness" (*diankuang*).
*Santāna* flowers are also called *xiantuona*, which is translated as "flowing flowers."
*Lu-zhi-na* (盧脂那) flower is also called *lu-che-na* (盧遮那), which translates as "eye-flower. Regarding the *zheng* (箏):

the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is a musical instrument played with a plectrum, similar to the *zhu* (筑). Because the people of Qin lacked righteousness, two sons contended over their father's lute (*se*), dividing it between them; thus it was called the "bamboo-sprout" (*sun*). Now, the character for "bamboo" (*zhu*) is added to form the character for "bamboo-sprout" (*sun*).

The *Shuowen* states that the *di* is a flute with seven holes; colloquially it is called the *Qiang-di*, which has three holes. The *Fengsu tong* says: "As for the *di*, 'di' means 'to cleanse' (*di*); it cleanses away depravity and filth while admitting what is elegant and correct."

Regarding the *xiāo*, the *Erya* states that the *dàxiāo* (large *xiāo*) is called the *zhèn*; Guo Pu says it consists of thirty-three pipes joined together and is fourteen inches long, while the smaller one is called the *jiàn*, consisting of sixteen pipes.
The *Shuoyuan* states: "A large se is called a *sai*. Guo’s commentary notes: "It is eight feet one inch long and one foot eight inches wide, with twenty-seven strings.

Regarding the *konghou*, the *Shiming* says: "This was the music of the 'Mimi' style created by Shi Yan; later it emerged from the lands of Sangjian and Puxiang. It was likely preserved by a marquis of the state of Kong. Shi Yan played it for Duke Ping of Jin. Later, when Zheng and Wei divided its territory, the state consequently perished; therefore, it is called the music of Zheng and Wei and is termed licentious music."
*Guchui* (鼓吹) means to rouse or incite; it also refers to striking. That which is made from leather is called a *gǔ* (drum); this is a vernacular character.
The *Duoqielouxiang Shilun* (多伽婁香釋論) states that it is a wood fragrance, which here is translated as "not perishing" (*bùmò*).

The "Qilin" (麒麟) is the opposite force of the "Qu" (渠). Regarding its true etymological explanation: it is a benevolent beast with a single horn on its head; at the tip of the horn there is flesh, and it has the body of a musk deer and the tail of an ox. The scriptural text uses the character "Qilin" (騏驎), which the *Shuowen Jiezi* explains as a horse whose markings are like those of a "qi" (a patterned cloth). The entry for "Lin" (驎) in the *Shuowen* reads "Li-zhen-fan" (力振反); the *Erya* states that a white horse with black lips is called a "Lin. Neither of these [definitions] corresponds to the meaning of the scripture.
The *kukkuḷa* bird is also called *gokhuḷa*; *go* means "ox," and it is also named *dikhila*, which means "nail.

*Khuṣṭu* (pronounced *jū-jù-shān-qian-er-fan*) is commonly known as a woven woolen rug; the text uses *lǚ* (pronounced *lì-yǔ-fan*), which refers to coarse woolen cloth (*lǚ-hé*), but this is not the intended meaning here.

Regarding *tadeng* (毾㲪): "Tad" is pronounced with the initial *th* and the final *he* (他盇反). The *Shiming* (釋名) explains that it is so named because it is spread upon the small couch (*ta*) in front of the large bed to facilitate ascending to the large bed; "deng" (㲪) is pronounced with the final *de* and *heng* (得恒反).
The *kaucapa* is shaped like a blanket with long black hair on one side; according to the Vinaya, the group of six bhikṣus wore it inverted at night to terrify people, saying it resembled a ghost.

The character *rǒng* (䩸) has three forms: *cāng* (蒼), *róng* (而容反), and *rǒng* (茸). The *Shuowen* states that it refers to a saddle (*ān*) decorated with coarse wool; it is also written as *fán* (𦶇, *róng* [而容反]) or *rì* (毦, *rén zhì rǎn*). According to the *Guoyá*, it means *jì* (罽), which is woven hair. The character *rǒng* (䩸) thus encompasses these three forms, and its usage is not lost to its meaning. Although the scripture sometimes uses *róng* (茸, *róng* [而容反]), the *Shuowen* defines this as "grass," which does not accord with the meaning of the scripture.
"Root-seeds" (gen-zi) refer to species such as ginger and taro; they are so called because they lack seeds for planting and instead propagate by splitting the root.

"Stem-seeds" (geng-zi)—the character *geng* being pronounced *hu-geng*—refer to species such as the stone pine (*shíshù*) and willow; they are so called because they grow from stems rather than roots.
*Jiezi* (節子) refers to plants such as orchid, celery, smartweed, *ti* (稊), and *ju* (秬) grasses; it is so named because they propagate from nodes.

*Jiezizi* (接子) [pronounced *jie* with the second tone] refers to species such as pear and persimmon that propagate by joining similar types. The character *jing* (經) is sometimes written as *jue* (󲖴) or *ji* (󲘝), but these are entirely incorrect forms. Furthermore, the character *ji* (󲘝) is pronounced *cai* with the second tone and means "sudden" or "swift"; it is not the form intended here.
"Zi zi" (子子) refers to various types of seed-cotton.

According to the "Dan-zhen" (丹枕), in India these are commonly made from silk, cotton cloth, fine fabrics, *rambu*, or *tūla* cotton, used either as pillows or for reclining. "Dan" (丹) signifies the color red.
The "anhuang" wooden pillow refers to a pillow with springs installed inside; when shaken, it produces a sound as if there were water within.
Regarding the "six *jiān*," the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is a board game consisting of six pieces and twelve chessmen.

*Pai ju* (the first character pronounced with the *ju* rhyme and the sixth tone; in ancient texts written as 𥷥, now written as 鞠). Guo Pu said: "It refers to things such as hair-balls or air-filled balls, used for kicking and playing. It is also a military formation. The *Xinshu* (New Book) consists of twenty-five chapters; tradition says it was composed by the Emperor.

Regarding "throwing stones," the *Hanshu* (Book of Han) mentions Gan Yanshou’s skill in "throwing stones and pulling the pole" (*toushi babu*). Zhang Yan’s commentary states: "The flying stone weighed twelve *jin*; it was set in motion by a mechanical device and could travel three hundred paces. Gan Yanshou possessed such strength that he could launch it with his bare hands. As for the "throwing of bricks" practiced today, the character for "brick" (*zhuān*) is pronounced *tuóhé* (with the second tone).

Regarding the practice of divination by *bu* (tortoise-shell) and *shi* (milfoil stalks), the *Liji* states: "The tortoise shell is used for *bu*; the milfoil stalks are used for *shi*. Both are intended to resolve doubts and determine hesitation; thus, the characters are composed of the radical for "bamboo" (*zhu*) and the character for "shaman" (*wu*). This is because one counts the milfoil stalks to derive hexagrams and breaks bamboo to form the lines (*yao*); hence the characters include the bamboo radical. *Shie* (the act of counting): pronounced *shan* (in the sense of *shen*) and *lie* (in the sense of *yu-lie*, with the second tone). *Shi* (milfoil stalks): pronounced *shi*.
In the *Vaiśāradya-sūtra* (the *Piān'ěr jīng*), the phrase "making the body fearful" (*zuò shēn kǒng*) is likely a scribal error.

In the twelfth fascicle, regarding the phrase "the various vessels of the brain and the *gài*": *gài* is pronounced *gǔ lái* (古來). The *Yùpiān* states that it refers to the big toe of the foot. This means that among the segmented body, the highest point is the brain and the lowest point is the *gài*; wherever blood and flesh reach, there are vessels. Since there are no vessels outside the brain—which is hair—or outside the *gài*—which is the nail—it is for this reason that they are excluded. The old pronunciation, reading it as *hú mài* (胡賣) and calling it "bone," is entirely contrary to the intent of the sūtra.
*Zhuǎn* (腨): The character is pronounced *chún* (時兖反). According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to the calf muscle (*fēicháng*). The character *fēi* (扶非反) is used for the calf;

it may also be written as *zǔ* (󰈷), which has the same meaning. It is used to support the *bǐ* (髀). *Bǐ* (蒲米反) is the pronunciation used by people of the North, while *bì'ěr* (必爾反) is the pronunciation current in Jiangnan. The *Shiming* explains that *bǐ* means "low" (*bēi*), as it is situated below. The archaic form is also written as *pǐ* (䠋). The forms appearing in the scriptures as *zhǐ* (𮛚) and *bǐ* (䏶) are both vulgar characters and not the correct ones.
*Huán* (髖): Pronounced *kǒu wán* (口丸) with a reversed tone; the *Pīcāng* states that *huán* refers to the buttocks (*sǎo*).

It is also written as *wǎn* (臗), with the same meaning. *Nàn* (頷): Pronounced *hòu gǎn* (侯感). Guō Pǔ says that *nàn* refers to the jawbone (*hànchē*). The *Shìmíng* calls it *fǔchē*. In the regions of Nánchǔ it is called *nàn*, while in Qín and Jìn it is called *yí*. It is so named because it supports and sustains the mouth.

The character *zì* (姿) is used here with the opposite meaning of its usual sense; it refers to being able to gauge the expressions of others' emotions. In ancient texts it was written as *shèn* (㑷), and they are used interchangeably.

*Shì shùn* (視瞚)—*shùn* is pronounced *shǐ* and *rùn*—the *Yùpiān* states that it means "the movement of the eyes. The *Lièzǐ* uses the character *shùn*, while the *Tōngsúwén* uses *xiàn* (眴); both have the same pronunciation, *xuán*.
*Di* (pronounced *qí xún fǎn*): A fine crack or split in the skin.

According to the *Shuowen*, it means "bright. The commentary states it refers to a target (*zhì*) for archery, meaning that which is clearly visible. It refers to the deer-shaped mark in the center of an archery range today; in ancient script it was written as *zhì*, and these characters are used interchangeably.
"Zhong" (仲) in "zhōngjiàn" (中箭) is pronounced with the *zhòng* (知仲) radical; the *Liji* states that one who hits the mark in archery may become a feudal lord, while one who misses it cannot.

"Chu" (楚) is pronounced with the *tà* (他達) radical; it means to strike. According to the *Guangya*, "tà" means to strike. "Chu" is another name for "Jing" (荊); "tà" is written as "shēn" (󲗤) in ancient texts, and they are used interchangeably.

*Kai* (the character for "coughing" with the phonetic *niè* [枯戴反] and the radical for "breath"; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "upward-moving qi," and according to the *Zilin*, it means "a type of asthma"). In the canonical texts, it is often written as *hai* (with the phonetic *hóulái* [侯來反]), which refers to an infant; however, "infant" is not the intended meaning here.
*Ai* (pronounced *bái*, with the initial *wǔ* and final *gài*): according to the *Erya*, it means "water terrace" (*shuǐtái*), so called because its color resembles that of mugwort (*ài*).

*Nǎn* (pronounced *ná*, with the initial *nǎ* and final *zhǎn*): this refers to being abashed or ashamed. The *Xiaoya* states that "to have a blush on one's face is called *nǎn*"; the *Shuowen* defines it as facial shame.

*Zhàngān*: "Gān" (公旦) is a phonetic transcription for "stem" (*gēng*). The character is composed of "gān" (干); the version in the received text that uses "mù" (木) to form "gàn" (幹) does not carry this meaning.
*Tié* (󱯾跌): "Tújié" (徒結) is the phonetic transcription; it means to lose one's footing.

"Back-curve" (*pèi lǚ*) refers to a crooked back; according to the *Guǎyá*, it means a curved back. The *Tōngsùwén* states that a curved spine is called "hunchback" (*yǒu lǚ*). Although the scriptural text sometimes uses the character "lèng" (瘻), with the pronunciation *lú gòu*, this refers to the disease of hemorrhoids and does not carry this meaning here.
*Ē* (惡): The radical is *shàng* (上) with the phonetic *wū gù fǎn* (烏故反). It means to loathe and despise; it is also written as the character *kě* (僫), having the same meaning.

*Léi* (螺): The phonetic is *yù lè hé fǎn* (玉勒和反). It refers to a bivalve mollusk (*bèng*). In ancient texts, it is identical to *zhèng* (正) and *léi* (羸). In the canonical scriptures, there are instances where it is written as *lì dǐ fǎn* (𧋠力底反); this is a borrowed pronunciation and is incorrect. The character for *bèng* (蚌) is pronounced *pú jiǎng fǎn* (蒲講反); the vulgar form *bǎng* (蜯) is not its original body.
*Fa* (發): to withdraw, to remove, to destroy; it is pronounced *chán* (with the second tone) and *liè* (with the fourth tone).

*Fū* (敷): to spread; to place upon the body; to touch; in the *Xiaoya* (Minor Odes), it means to pervade or to distribute; in ancient texts it is written as *zhuān* (專), while its standard form is written with the radical *fǔ* (甫).
*Śvadaṃśa* (pronounced *shòu pào*, with *pào* having the *bù* rhyme) refers to a fleshy knot upon the skin.

*Tūlaka* (cotton) is here called "wood-cotton" (*mùmián*). It is extremely fine and soft, resembling the flowers of the willow tree; because tears do not flow when this cotton touches the eyes, one knows it is soft.
The "seven limbs" refers to the four feet, tail, and trunk of the white elephant, which together constitute the seven limbs.
Their color is a deep, lustrous blue—like vaidūrya (lapis lazuli)—with an intermingled radiance of light.
*Kaibō* (開剖): "Bō" is pronounced with the third tone (*pǔ hòu fǎn*). It means to break open; according to the *Cāngjié piān*, it means to divide, to split, or to partition.

*Máo* (髦): "Máo" is pronounced *mò gāo fǎn*. According to the *Shuōwén*, *máo* refers to hair; specifically, it denotes the long hair among the fur. In the scriptural text, it is sometimes written as *zōng* (騣), pronounced *zī gōng fǎn*, which is also semantically appropriate.

*Cōng* (聰): *yí* (夷) and *suì* (歲) are the phonetic components; the *Shuowen* says it means "clear. The *Yupian* says it means "penetrating" or "wisdom. In ancient script it is written as *ruì* (睿), and in *Zhòuwén* as *róng* (壡); the usage is also interchangeable. *Nǎo* (撓):
*hū* (呼) and *gāo* (高) are the phonetic components; the *Shuowen* says it means "to disturb. The text reads *lǎo* (㧌), which is a vulgar character.

13. Fascicle Thirteen. *Dān* (pronounced with the *mian* and *tan* finals; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "joy"; according to the *Guoyu*, it means "craving"). In archaic script, it appears as two forms: *tai* and *tan*. Various character dictionaries list it as two forms: *dīn* and *dān*. *Miǎn* is pronounced *mian* (with the *shàn* final); according to the *Shuowen*, it means "to delight in wine. In archaic script, it is written as *shui*; according to the *Shuowen*, this also means "to take pleasure in wine."
*Molūka* (摩婁伽) is here translated as "wandering vine.

*Nyagrodha* (尼拘陀)—its ancient pronunciation being "Wujie" (無節)—is described in the *Huayan Yin Yi* (華嚴音義) as having leaves like those of the persimmon and fruit resembling the loquat; it possesses a prominent navel-like base (*nābhi*) and is the tallest and largest among trees that endure great age.

Regarding "chong" (虫): the *Tongsu Wen* (通俗文) states that it refers to worms within the flesh; the *Sancang* (三蒼) says they are maggots produced from flies within the flesh. The scriptural text reads "ju" (蛆), with the phonetic "zi-yu" (子余). The *Zhuangzi* says, "The dung-beetle and the maggot delight in filth," referring to its public nature. It is also written as "ju" (疽), meaning a chronic abscess. These latter two [readings] are neither in accord with the meaning of the scripture, and so forth.

*Ki* (瘜): The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "extraordinary flesh" (*qirou*) or "malignant flesh" (*erou*). It is also written as *ji* (𦞜), with the same meaning. *Cangyi* (創痍): *Cang* (創) is pronounced like *yang* (羊).
The *Sancang* states that *yi* (痍) refers to a wound. The *Tongsu* says: "A wound on the body is called *yi*; a wound on the head is called *shang* (傷)."
*Dravya* (pronounced *bi-miao* in Chinese) means "sovereign" (*adhipati*).
*Guṇa* means "basis" (*āśraya*).
*Āmalaka-vāri* means "stainless water" (*vimala-udaka*).
*Nepāla-udaka* is here translated as "unsurpassed decoction" (*musheng tang*) and is also called *harītakī-rasa*.
*Pāyasa* is also named *udañcana*; this is translated as "decoction of boiled tree leaves," similar to the tea and tangerine [confections] of the present day.
Some say that *paya* means "water" (*cǐ yún shuǐ yě*), which is the name used by the people of Kaśmīra for water.

Others say that *udaka* is the name used by the people of Eastern India for water; the pronunciation of *te* is *tú dé* (with the second tone on the final syllable), and it is incorrect to write it as *chí*.
Vārī (pronounced with the "sha" and "jia" finals) is the Sanskrit term for what people in Central India call water.
Alternatively, it is said to be *vāri*, which here means "mixed medicinal herbs and water."
Some say *paya* is also called "milk," which is a term for water in the *Śabda-śāstra*.

Volume 14, Chapter 14. *Cuo* (pronounced with the *cai* and *ge* finals): according to the *Guangya*, *cuo* means short; the *Tongshu* says a dwarf is called *cuo*. The scriptural texts often use the character *zuo*, but the *Shuowen* defines it as a small swelling, which is not the meaning here.
Āgama is here translated as "teaching" (jiao) and also as "Dharma-treasury" (fǎzàng), for it is where all virtues converge.
Viṣṇu is also written as Vainyu; this is translated as "Pervasive Equality" (biàntóng) and also as "Pervasive Victory" (biànsèng) Deva.
*Nu-po* (蒲布反) refers to nursing; it means drinking the milk given to an infant. There is also the character *pù* (餔), which has the same pronunciation.
*Kalala* (歌羅羅) is the stage at the seventh day after conception, when the impurities have combined.
The stage of *ābhudha* is also called *abuda*, which refers to the period of the second week; it is like a cocoon or a membrane.
The stage of *gahana* is also called *ghanapuruṣa*, which refers to the period of the third week; its appearance is like congealed curd.
When the hands are closed, it is also called *piśi* (閉尸).
"Crawling" (*púfú*)—the first character is pronounced *pú*, the second is pronounced with the *bó* rhyme (*púběi fǎn*)—refers to moving by prostrating oneself.

"Saliva" (*shēng xián*)—the character *xián* is pronounced *xiángyán*; according to the *Zílín*, it means the mouth extending [toward] desire; various dictionaries write this as *sì*, *shuān*, or *liú*, and these three forms are not distinct. The *Sāncāng* states: "Saliva (*xián*) is the liquid in an infant's mouth; it is spittle."

The character for "flint" (*suì*) is derived from the word for "intoxication" (*zuì*), as it is the opposite of the "fire-mother" (*huǒmǔ*). The *Lúnyǔ* states, "Drill for flint and change the firewood. Kǒng’s commentary notes that within a single year, the wood used for drilling the flint varies. The *Shìběn* records that the name of the inventor of fire was Suìrén (the Flint Man).
*Yīn zuǎn zǐ wán*: The second character is read with the *fǎn* (rhyme) *rǎn*. The *Shuōwén* states it is that which is used for piercing objects.
*Yīn fú nǔ fǎn*: This refers to the drumstick (*gǔ zhuí*). It is correct to use *bāo* as *fū*; they share the same meaning.
"Worǎng" (沃壤): the first character is pronounced as wūgǔ (烏穀) in reverse, and the second as rúzhǎng (如掌) in reverse; it refers to fertile, moist soil. "Dàojiǎn" (道撿):
the second character is pronounced as jūxiǎn (居險) in reverse; the *Yùpiān* states it means "norms and measures," and it also carries the sense of "restraining."

*Gùmiàn* (顧眄) means to look askance; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to a sidelong glance. According to the *Fangyan*, in the region west of the Guanzhong area, specifically among the Qin and Jin people, this is called *yǎn*.
*Fǎng* (舫) is pronounced with the lower radical as *fǔwàng* (甫妄反); the *Tongshu Zhang* states that "linked boats" are called *fǎng*, meaning two boats joined together.
*Yán* (炎): read as *yú lián* (于廉反); it means "blazing heat. According to the *Erya*, "intense heat" (*yányán*) refers to a scorching vapor that burns people.
*Bó* (薄): read as *yóu jiù* (尤救反); according to the *Erya*, *yòu* (祐) means "blessing."
15. Fifteenth Fascicle. 1. Sūtra: This is translated as "Agreement Scripture" (Qijing) and is also called "Dharma Source" (Faben).
2. Geya Sūtra: This is translated as "Repetitive Verse" (Chongshoujie).
The *Vyākaraṇa-sūtra* is called *vyākaraṇa* in Sanskrit.
The *Geya-sūtra* is translated here as "verse" (*gāthā*).
*Fengsong* (諷誦) [is pronounced with the first character having the *feng* rhyme and the third tone].
5. Udāna-sūtra, here translated as "Unprompted Self-Explanations";
6. Nidāna-sūtra, here translated as "Sūtras on Causes and Conditions";
7. Avadāna-sūtra, here translated as "Parables."
8. Itivṛttaka Sūtra, here translated as *Ben-shi jing* (Sūtra of Past Events);
9. Jātaka Sūtra, here translated as *Ben-sheng jing* (Sūtra of Birth Stories);
10. Vaipulya Sūtra, here translated as *Fangguang jing* (Sūtra of Extensive Teachings).
Eleventh, *Adbhutadharma*, which is translated here as "Unprecedented";
twelfth, *Upadeśa*, which is translated here as "Discourse on Exposition.
*Saṃkha*—the Sanskrit word *saṃkha* is pronounced with the retroflex *ṅ* (as in "huai-yang" reversed)—is translated here as "Complete" (*jù*) and is also known by the alternative name "Conch" (*kē*).

Krikin Buddha is also named Kuru, or Karakucunda, or Krakucchanda; these are all corruptions and abbreviations of the Sanskrit, not the precise Sanskrit pronunciation. *Kakutsunda* means "one who has extinguished the burdens [of affliction]" (*kṣīṇa-kleśa*).
Kanakamuni: *kanaka* means "tree" and *muni* means "sage. Kāśyapa Buddha: this is translated as "tortoise," which is his clan name;
it is correctly transliterated as *Kāśyapa*, and one tradition says he was of the lineage of the *ṛṣis* (seers) who subsist on food.
*Chù* (橖𢾊): This means to grasp or touch; the text of the Sūtra writes it as *táng*, which is incorrect. *Shuǐdì* (水渧): Pronounced *dīnglì*.
The *Tōngsúwén* states that what is called *língdī* is termed *yídì*. According to our current analysis, when it is in the air it is *dì*; when it reaches the ground it is *dī* (pronounced *dīnglì*).
*Qūzǒu* (pronounced *qūzǒu*, with *qū* having the phonetic *yú* as its reverse): The *Yùpiān* states that it means "to walk quickly.
*Xìnglì* (pronounced *xìnglì*, with *lì* having the phonetic *lì* as its reverse): The *Zílín* states it means "a contrary disposition"; the *Yùpiān* states it means "crookedness and perversity."
"Dun-yù" (敦喻) means "sudden warmth," which is the opposite of the *Erya*; it refers to mutual exhortation.
"Wàn-dòu" (豌豆) is read as "wǎn-wán" (碗丸); according to the *Guangya*, it is the "liú-dòu" (瑠豆). The text reads "wǎn-dēng" (宛登), which is a vulgar character and not the radical for grain (*hé*).

Regarding the character *zǔ* (pronounced *mù* with a retroflex final), the *Zílín* states it refers to the arrowhead (*jiàndì*). In the Jiangnan region, it is called the "arrow-gold" (*jiàngjīn*); in Shandong, it is called the "arrow-foot" (*jiànzú*). The *Shìmíng* explains that the base of the arrow is called the "foot," and that in antiquity the arrow-foot was termed *zhù*. The *Éryá* states: "Gold-tipped, feather-trimmed."

"Jiào-wù" (awakening) is the opposite of "shuì-jué" (sleeping). "Jiào" is also "wù. The character below, "wú," is a vulgar form; the correct character is "wù," composed of "mián" (roof), "qiáng" (board), and the phonetic "wú. The *Cāngjié piān* states: "To awaken from sleep and have words is called 'wù,' meaning to speak of a matter from within a dream."

16. Volume Sixteen. Regarding the name "Tianzhu" (India): it is also called "Shendu" (Body-Poison) or "Xiandou" (Worthy-Bean), both of which are corruptions. The correct term is "Yindu" (Indu), which here means "Moon. The moon has a thousand names, and this is one such appellation. This is because in that land, sages and saints have succeeded one another in awakening the multitude of living beings, illuminating them like the moon. Furthermore, "Xiandou" is its original name for "Devendra" (Lord of Devas); it is likely so named because it is protected by Devendra, and thus the world has come to accept this title.
*Chí-chěng* (馳騁): *zhī zhǐ fǎn xià chǒu lǐng fǎn* (直知反下丑領反). The *Guǎngyá* states: "To *chí* is to gallop; to *chéng* is to run. *Pó-sī-tuó* (婆私吒): *zhú jiā fǎn* (竹家反);
in ancient script it is written as *zhuó* (喥). This means "Most Victorious" (*jìshèng*), taking his clan name as his personal name.

"‘Míng zā’ (鳴𠯗): ‘zā’ is pronounced with the *zi* rhyme-group and the *hé* final (i.e., *za*). Because it appears in the *Nan jing* (Southern Scripture), it is said to follow the method for transcribing foreign sounds; this phrasing is ornamental and its meaning is also manifold. Many instances in the scriptural text erroneously use the character ‘shà’ (唼), which is pronounced with the *suǒ* rhyme-group and the *yā* final; this is incorrect."
"Siqu" (四衢) [the "qu" rhymes with "yu" (虞)]; according to the *Erya*, that which has four thoroughfares is called a "qu. Guo Pu states that it refers to a road branching out in four directions.
"Mahāsena" is translated here as "Great General."
He cut his thigh; the character for "five" (*gōng*) is read with the phonetic *wǔ* (alternatively, it is also read as *pú-mǐ*).
It is also interpreted as *huò* (to stew). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states: "That which contains vegetables is called *gēng* (soup); that which contains no vegetables is called *hè*."
Kosala is also called Kusa-la, which means "the Land of Artisans.
King Prasenajit is translated as "Victorious Army" (Shengjun) or "Harmonious Joy" (Heyue); according to the *Renwang jing*, he is also known as King Candraprabha ("Moonlight").
*Rì'ěr* (to cut off the ears) and *yìbí* (to cut off the nose): *rì* means to sever the ears; *yì* (read *yùqì*) means to sever the nose.
*Duànjié shǒuzú* (to amputate hands and feet): *duàn* is read as *túguǎn*; those who pronounce it as *duǎn* are incorrect.
"Shi-qu (拾取)"—the character *qu* is pronounced *kuǎn* (苦𭹹反) and also *kùnèi* (苦內反); following current custom, the former pronunciation is adopted here.
"Kǒng wéi qí huàn" (恐為其患)—the character *kǒng* is pronounced *qiūgǒng* (丘拱反); it means to fear.
*Jñā* (pronounced *guàn*) means a snare or cord.
*Nakha-bheda* (*shàng zhuāng jiào fǎn*, *xià guāi mài fǎn*) means to tear with the claws.
*Khadira* charcoal—this is translated as "tree from a pit"—is wood that is hard and solid; the ash from this charcoal is caustic, and if used to wash the body, it will surely cause it to rot away.

"Mou" (蚋) is pronounced *zǐ* (子) with the *lèi* (累) rhyme, and is also written as *wěi* (𠲿) or *zuǐ* (觜). The *Guǎngyá* states it means "mouth. Lexicons state it refers to the "crow's beak" (*wūhuì*). In the scriptural text, there is a variant reading *wěn* (𭉨), pronounced *quán* (泉) with the *ruǎn* (耎) rhyme, which is synonymous with *shuǎn* (吮); however, this is not the intended meaning of the scripture.
Regarding "constitution" (xiànzhì): the *Xuān jiàn yù piān* states that it means "law" (*fǎ*) and "prohibition" (*zhì*), referring to legal statutes.

Regarding "bear" (*xióngpí*): the *Yù piān* states it is a beast resembling a pig that dwells in the mountains and hibernates in winter; it licks its own paws, which resemble those of humans. It is also called *bī* (the character for *bī* is pronounced *píyí*). It has a large head and a mane like a horse; it is fierce, dull-witted, and possesses great strength, capable of uprooting trees. In the region west of the Pass, it is called a *jiápí*. (The character for *hǎn* [dull-witted] is pronounced *kělán*; the character for *jiā* [boar] is pronounced *jiā*).
Kumbhāṇḍa is translated here as "Winter Melon Face Ghost.
Kārūṭapāna is translated here as "Extremely Ugly Ghost. Saccako Nigaṇṭhaputta:
*Saccaka* is translated here as "Real," and *Nigaṇṭha* is translated here as "Without Continuity" (or "Bondless").

"Biān" (編) is pronounced *bēi* (卑) and *mián* (綿); the *Yùpiān* (玉篇) identifies it as such, and the *Shēnglèi* (聲類) states that to arrange objects in sequence with cords is called "biān. This refers to taking thorns and brambles to weave around the rafters and lie upon them; this is the ascetic practice of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
*Ōu*: (The character is pronounced with the *li* and *yu* finals; *han* and *ge* finals for *hu*). The *Yùpiān* states it is a woolen cloth from Jibin.
*Wéiyǎng*: (The *yú* and *liǎng* finals). The *Yùnjí* states it means "to hold. This refers to relying on others for resources, which is also called "expecting" (*wàng*).
"Rú" (茹) means to eat; according to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means "to consume. [Note: The character is pronounced with the initial *zhù* (翥) as an alternative reading.

"Shěngsī" (省思)—the first character is read with the *xǐng* (省) radical and the *sī* (思) phonetic—is defined in the *Shuōwén* as "to look at," and also "to examine. Volume Seventeen, Part One. Volume Seventeen. "Wúsuǒwèi" (無所畏)—the first character is read with the *shěng* (省) radical and the *sī* (思) phonetic—is defined in the *Shuōwén* as "to look at," and also "to examine."
Mahākauṣṭhila—this is translated as "Great Thigh.
*Jù* (pronounced with the initial *qú* and final *jù*) according to the *Yùpiān* dictionary means "how" or "what," a term used to express uncertainty.

Both jars were broken; one was joyful because he had already obtained the price for the curd from the jar that was about to be broken. The other was sorrowful because he had broken the jar of curd before obtaining its value.

*Uddhacca* (restlessness) [pronounced *diào xì*, with *xì* read as *tú diào fǎn*] is the agitation of the mind; *āghāta* (agitation/impetuosity) [pronounced *qīng zào*, with *zào* read as *zǔ gào fǎn*] is the agitation of the mind.

The eight worldly conditions (*aṣṭau lokadharmāḥ*) are: first, gain; second, loss; third, disparagement; fourth, praise; fifth, renown; sixth, insignificance; seventh, suffering; and eighth, pleasure.
The three foundations of mindfulness refer to the three dharmas of sorrow, joy, and equanimity, because these three states of mind are equal.

Volume 18, Number 18. "Liangyou" (良祐): the character "liang" (良) is pronounced with a *jiao* (反) reversal; it is an archaic form. It consists of two components: "you" (佑) meaning assistance, as in "that which Heaven assists."
*Niǎo* (撓): The first character is pronounced *qiǎo* (巧) and also *jiào* (挍). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to disturb" or "to confuse.

When applied to water, it means "to agitate," as in the rhyme *píyáo* (匹遙). In the scriptures, there are instances where it is written as *nì* (溺), which shares a common meaning; however, there are also instances where it is written as *rú* (濡), which does not carry this specific meaning.
"Kai-xuan" (繫懸) refers to Mount Sumeru; "xi-yin-mi" (糸音覓) refers to the silk from the mouth of a silkworm. This means that the fibers of the lotus stalk are as fine as [ordinary] thread.
"Gu-jiu" (酤酒): the character "gu" is pronounced as "gu" (故), meaning to sell wine to others; if pronounced as "gu" (姑), it likewise means to sell wine to others.
*Lośa* is translated here as "dyer" (*rañjaka*). This refers to grasses that harbor many insects which injure and destroy living beings; therefore, it is prohibited.
*Kauśāmbī* is translated as "not tranquil" (*aśānta*) and also as "possessing a storehouse."

Its nature is *piē* (pronounced with the final rhyme of *biàn*); it means impetuous and abrupt. There is also the variant *biē*, which has the same meaning. 19. Volume Nineteen. Vedehī— here translated as "Lady of Supreme and Wondrous Body"—
is described by the *Liú-cè* (initially pronounced *lì*) and the *Yù-piān* as "sorrowful pain," meaning she was filled with a sense of poignant grief.
Pūraṇa is translated here as "Full. Kāśyapa is his clan name, translated here as "Turtle-lineage. This refers to the non-Buddhist school that posits the absence of causes (*ahetuvāda*).
Kākola insects are translated here as "black insects"; they are born destined to harm their mothers.
Makkhali is his clan name; Kosalī is his mother’s name. This proponent of the view that suffering and pleasure arise neither from causes nor by nature is a non-Buddhist (tīrthika).

Sañjaya means "Equal Victory" (*Sañjayin*); Vairaṭī is his mother’s name. This is a non-Buddhist who claims there is no need for cultivation, asserting that one exhausts birth and death naturally after eighty thousand kalpas, like a ball of thread unwinding.
*Isika* grass—here translated as "wildcat" (*jueyi*)—the Dharma Master He Xi says that this grass is soft on the outside but hard within.
It is like the autumnal "shaving of trees," where "shaving" (kūn) means to cut off the tops of trees.
Ajita (translated here as "Unconquerable Wing") wears hair-cloth (*keśa-kaṃbala*), which is a garment made from human hair; he practices the austerity of being scorched by five fires.

Kālāma is his name, translated as "Black Collar," and Kātyāyana is his clan name. This non-Buddhist teacher responds according to the situation: if people ask whether [the self] exists, he answers that it exists; if they ask whether it does not exist, he answers that it does not exist.

*Nirgrantha* is translated here as "without succession" (*wu ji*); it is the general name for non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*). *Nyātiputra* means "friend" and is the name of his mother. This school maintains that suffering has no fixed cause, yet it must necessarily be experienced; they hold that only the non-path (*amārga*) can sever it.
King Rāma is here translated as "Void" (xū);
King Baddhi is here translated as "Worthy" (xián);
and King Vīlujina is here translated as "Delight" (àilè).
Nahuṣa means "one who does not serve" (in Chinese, *bùshìzhuàng*).
Kārtika-rāja means "the barbarian" (*yí*).
King Viśākha was named after a lunar mansion.
Vaiḍūrya-rāja (translated here as "Increase") refers to the practice of digging deep pits to capture game.

Jīvaka (translated here as "Able to Revive") was the elder brother of King Bimbisāra and the son of the daughter of King Nai; when he first appeared, the king held a medicinal seal in his hand, and upon reaching adulthood, he became a master physician.
*Run* (滋) [pronounced *zī*]: to moisten; it refers to water soaking and saturating things. *Nǔn* (讎) [pronounced *chóu*]:
according to the *Yùpiān*, it means "to face" or "a match"; it also means "to loathe. *Cài* (在): pronounced *qiáng* [qú xiàng].
Lexicons state that a *qiáng* is a snare set along a path; its shape is like a bow. There is also a vulgar character written as *jiǎn*.
*Kāmalā* disease is here translated as "great wind disease" (*mahāvātavyādhi*).

The city of *Kapilavastu* is here translated as "Yellow City. In ancient times, there was a sage with yellow hair who practiced his studies here and attained the path of immortality; therefore, it was named after him.
Pañcaśikha is translated here as "Five Topknots.
Tuṃburu is translated as "Celestial Musician" and also as "Lute-player.
Subhadra is translated as "Virtuous and Noble."
Vemacitra is translated here as "Pure Mind.
Śacī is a specific name for the Moon; she was the daughter of the Asura King and the consort of Śakra. She is also known as "Pure Measure" (Jingliang), as stated in ancient texts.

Regarding "to murder" (shī): according to the *Zuozhuan*, when a minister commits violence against his sovereign, it is called "shī"; the *Shiming* states that for one of lower rank to kill one of higher rank is termed "shī.
*Sūvīra* is translated here as "treacherous valor."
Udumbara Forest—this is translated as "Arising from Emptiness" and also as "Auspicious Response.
Śrāvastī Country—this is translated as "Abode of the Rishis.
Caṇḍāla—this is translated as "Dog-handler" and is also called "Jail-guard."

Upāli is here translated as Jìn-hù (Near Protector).
Anāthapiṇḍada is here translated as Gū-jǐ (Almsgiver to the Orphaned).
Cūḷapanthaka is also called Zhōu-lì-pán-tuó-gā; "Wèn-lì" means "Small," while "Pán-tuó" means "Path."
Uruvilvā means "wood-apple" (mucuḷinda) in this language; it is so named because he realized the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) within a wood-apple grove.
Śodāyī means "arisen together"; it is also called Sotāyī.
The character 𦀟 (pàn) is a personal name.

It is judged to be pronounced with the "pǔ" and "dàn" finals reversed; it is also written in two forms as 胖 and 牉. Zheng Xuan stated: "Pàn means 'half' (*pàn*). To obtain a mate and unite is called *pàn*. The version in the Classics written as 泮 refers to ice melting; it does not carry this meaning.
Ugra, the Elder, is here translated as "Merit" (Gongde) or also as "Majesty" (Weide).
Revata is the name of a lunar mansion.
Śrīgupta is here translated as "Auspicious Protector" (Jihu) or also as "Virtue Protector" (Dehu).

"Bī" (鄙) means sorrowful; "dào" (悼) means grief; "bēi" (悲) is the opposite of shame and denotes meanness; "lòu" (陋) means lowly; "fù" (復) is pronounced with the "dào" (到) rhyme and means repetition; "āi" (哀) means lamentation.
"Avīci" is translated here as "Without Interval" (無間), also called "Without Respite" (無釋). This has three meanings: first, suffering; second, the body; and third, the location.
Bimbisāra is also called King Piṃśa; this means "handsome" or "of fair complexion.

*Jièzhòu* (armour) [the first character pronounced with the final *-chù* reversed] refers to a helmet according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the character being composed of the radical for "moon" (*yue*) and the phonetic element *you*.
*Jiàn*: Upper radical *jū*, *xiàn* (reflexive); the *Yùpiān* states it means "separation," "alternation," or "disorder. Lower radical *gǔ*, *xián* (reflexive); it means "dwelling" or "the middle.
It is like a fish on a *yǎo* (pinyin: wǔ dào; some editions have the character *ào*, which is identical).
20. The twentieth fascicle. Ajātaśatru—this is translated as "Unborn Enemy" (Wei-sheng-yuan), and also as "Dharma-Reverse" (Fa-ni). This child was born with the nature of committing parricide.

Regarding the doubt that this refers to the end of a kalpa: the "three months of simultaneous illumination" refers to the arising of the calamity of water; the King’s thought implies that the "seven days of simultaneous burning" refers to the arising of the calamity of fire.

As for the parable of the seven sons, the *Samantaprabhā-sūtra* states: Long ago there was an old woman who had seven sons. Six had realized the state of sainthood (*ārya*), while one remained an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Suddenly, they were all accused of a crime against the king and were to be executed. The mother thought of her youngest son, who was still an ordinary person; fearing he might lose his mindfulness at the end, she loved him with particular intensity.
The *kukkuṭa* bird is also called *kukkila*; it is named after its sound.
"Resting on a pillow" (*chên*) means leaning against a pillow (the character *chên* is pronounced as *zhēn* with a prohibitive tone).
"With disheveled hair" (*pī*) means having one's hair scattered loose (the character *pī* is pronounced as *pí*).

Regarding "donkey-cart" (*lǚchē*): in the Western Regions, it is taboo to ride donkeys; according to the *Wufen lü* (Five-Part Vinaya), those who violate the royal law were executed while riding donkeys.

Regarding "Quīxīng" (*奎星*): the character *xīng* is pronounced *kǎi* (with the mouth closed). According to the *Erya*, it belongs to the *Jianglou* (*降婁*) lunar station. Li Xun stated: "Jianglou is the *Baihu* (*白虎*) lunar station. Although the scriptural text sometimes writes this as "Gold Star" (*Jinxing*), which refers to Venus (*Taibai xing*), it is appropriate to read it as "Quī" (*奎*).
Piluka incense is also called *piluka*, which means "touch-incense.
Tagara incense means "root-incense.
Tamālapatra incense means "cinnamon-leaf incense."
The *kapasa* flower is like willow catkins and can be used to make cotton; when I inquired of a Brahman monk, he said it is the same as white felt (*pāṇḍuka*).

Regarding the term for a latrine: according to the *Guangya*, "qīng" (圊), "hùn" (溷), "péng" (庰), and "cè" (廁) are all alternative names for a toilet. "Hùn" (溷) is pronounced with the second tone of the rhyme-group *huán* (魂); it means turbid.
Kokālika is also called Kokāli and Kokāli; this is translated as "Cow-keeper.
Sunakṣatra: *su* means "good" and *nakṣatra* means "star."

By means of eight kinds of sounds, also known as the eight tones: first, the most excellent sound; second, the soft and supple sound; third, the harmonious and appropriate sound; fourth, the majestic and wise sound; fifth, the non-feminine sound; sixth, the non-feeble sound; seventh, the profound and far-reaching sound; eighth, the inexhaustible sound.

"Stopping and contemplation" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*): "stopping" is concentration (*samādhi*), and "contemplation" is wisdom (*prajñā*). There is a variant reading of "correct contemplation," which is incorrect.
"The ten kinds of form" refers to the five external sense objects (*viṣaya*) and the five internal faculties (*indriya*).

Regarding "guilt and transgression" (*zuìlì*): the commentary on the *Book of Documents* by Kong [Yuan] states that it means "faults. The *Canon of Posthumous Titles* says: "One who does not repent for prior faults is called *lì* (transgressive)."
Regarding the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*), the *Analects* records that when Zi Lu asked about the ferry crossing, Zheng Xuan commented: "A 'ferry' (*jin*) is a place for crossing over.
*Vipaśyin* Buddha is here translated as "Various Observations" (*zhǒngzhǒng guān*) and also as "Superior Observation" (*shèngguān*).

21. Fascicle Twenty-one. Regarding the *Caturveda-śāstra* (Four Vedas), it is correctly called the *Catur-veda*; here it is translated as the *Catur-vidyā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Four Illuminations). It consists of one hundred thousand verses and is highly esteemed in the West. It elucidates four types of knowledge: first, longevity (*āyus*); second, sacrifice (*yajña*); third, grammar (*nirukta*); and fourth, ritual arts (*kalpa*).
The *Vyākaraṇa-śāstra* (grammar) was called "without neck and without tail" in ancient pronunciation.
The *Vaiśeṣika-śāstra* is here called "the non-conquerable treatise of the external path.
The *Kāpila-śāstra* was called "the treatise of the Yellow-headed Rishi" in ancient pronunciation.
"Chenji" (讖記) initially prohibits the reversed reading of "wen" (文). "Chen" (讖) means "verification" (驗).
That which cuts off doubt is pronounced *dūnuǎn* (都暖反). Next, "having doubt" is called "yì" (疑); the two mental states [of doubt and its object] are identical, both pronounced *dūnuǎn* (都暖反).
Then one attains the permanent severance of *tūṣṇībhāva* (徒暖反;
here meaning "idle warmth" or "vain heat"). There is the severance of views (*dṛṣṭi-prahāṇa*;
有見斷見斷徒暖反). Maṇibhadra—*maṇi* is translated here as "full" or "wish-fulfilling," and *bhadra* is translated as "virtuous."
Asita: the ancient pronunciation was *Pu-bai*; Xuanzang says it means "Peerless Sage" (*Abhijña*) and is also called "Dignified.
Udraka: the ancient pronunciation was *Sheng*; it is also called "Prosperous."
The seer Dharāra (whose ancient pronunciation is *Ārāḍa*, meaning "the Seer Without Medicine") [attained realization].
The flower *atimuktaka* (whose ancient pronunciation is *yueluò*, with "luò" pronounced as *yǎo-xiào*) [is used here].
The *campaka* flower is also called *jambū*; this is translated as "colored flower" (*se-hua*). It is extremely fragrant and pure.
The *pāṭala* flower—its ancient pronunciation being "chóng-yè-huā"—is translated as "double-layered flower" (*chóng-yīn* being pronounced *zhí-lóng-fǎn*).
The vārṣika flower is also called vārṣika; this means "summer-blooming flower.
The mallikā flower, according to its ancient pronunciation, is named "sequential flower."
The *sumanā* flower—formerly called the *ruci-dian* (following-sequence) flower—is also named *sūmanā*; Xuanzang translated it as "well-pleasing.
The *yūthikā* flower—its ancient pronunciation was *xinghua* (the character for "sequence" being read with the *hu* tone)—is so named.
*Tānǎnlìjiā* (檀㝹利迦) flower: its ancient pronunciation is *zuò* (作).

*Zhāotí* (招提), meaning a monastic dwelling (*sēngfáng*), according to ancient pronunciation refers to a place for providing for guest monks; this is because it carries the sense of "inviting" (*zhāo*) and "assisting" (*tí*). I personally once asked Tripitaka Master Jìng, who said that *zhāotí* is a Sanskrit term, which here means "monasteries of the four quarters" (*sìfāng sēngfáng*).
Ānāpāna is translated here as "contemplation of counting the breaths. *Ānā* means inhalation; *apāna* means exhalation.
It refers to the destruction of the six great elements—namely, earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness—which are also called the six kinds.

22. Fascicle Twenty-two. [The character] *shì* (恃) [is pronounced with the initials] *chě* and *hé* (古反). In the *Erya*, it means "to rely upon" (*hùshì*). The *Han Shi* states: "Without a father, what does one rely upon? Relying means depending. Without a mother, what does one depend on? Depending means being supported."
*Chūnshēn* (儭身): the first character is pronounced *xìn* (信) with a retroflex final, and the second is pronounced *zhàngjìn* (丈覲). It means "to approach" or "to draw near. *Hèn lì* (佷戾):
the upper character is pronounced *hòugèn* (侯艮), and the lower is pronounced *lǐdì* (禮帝). It refers to being difficult to tame or subdue.

"Huífú" (洄澓): the first character is pronounced *huí* (as in 迴) and the second is pronounced *fù* (as in 復). The *Sāncāng* states that it means "the turning of water. The *Annals of Emperor Xuán* state that "huífú" refers to deep whirlpools in the water.
Regarding "wéi sūn" (為蘇󰉓): as for the ancient pronunciation of "tú" (塗), it should correctly be written as the character "dǔ" (堵).
To sprinkle with medicine (bèn; bèn, pú, mèn [referring to the *Tōngsùwén*]: to scatter earth is called *bèn*; the *Shuōwén* says *bèn* means dust).
23. Fascicle Twenty-three. "Fascicle" (liánzhuì; liánzhuì, zhuī, wèi [referring to the *Yùpiān*]: to continue, to connect, to join together).
"I am far removed from the Three Vehicles" (*yuan* [yuan-fan], meaning "to be distant" or "to leave afar").
"Difficult to hope for" (*nan-ji* [ju-zhi-fan]; the *Yupian* states it means "hope," while the *Shuowen* states *ji* means "to wish for good fortune").

*Ēi* (餧) [pronounced *cí zì fǎn*]: The stone canon now reads *shí* (食). The *Yùpiān* states it means "to feed" (*bù*). There are instances where the scriptural text uses *sì* (飼), which is a vulgar character.
*Hóng* (瓨) [pronounced *xué jiāng fǎn*]: According to the *Shuōwén*, it resembles a *yīng* (甖) jar with a long neck, with a capacity of ten *shēng*.

"Boat raft" (fú): the character *fú* is pronounced with the *fu* and *yue* rhymes; some editions write it as "raft" (*bá*) or "float" (*fēi*), both of which are vulgar characters. "Holding with the hands and treading with the feet":

the *Shuowen Jiezi* correctly writes this as "raft" (*fú*), though it is also written as "embrace" (*bào*), both pronounced with the *bao* and *jiao* rhymes. The *Yupian* states that it means "to draw in. "Treading" (*tà*) is pronounced with the *tu* and *he* rhymes, meaning "to step upon and discard. This is a metaphor for crossing the river of afflictions: diligently cultivating the two kinds of goodness is the sense of "drawing in," while diligently severing the two kinds of evil is the sense of "stepping upon and discarding. In the Southern edition, Lord Xie changed this to "moving hands and stirring feet"; although these words are skillful, they lack precision in their meaning.

Contemplate the body as a casket of the four great elements: the fire element is likened to the poison of vision, the earth element to the poison of touch, the wind element to the poison of breath, and the water element to the poison of the bite.

Caṇḍāla is also called Caṇḍāra; this is translated as "Adorned with Emblems," meaning that they adorn themselves with evil karma and carry out their practices using these as insignia. When such a person walks, they must necessarily shake a bell to mark themselves; if they do not, they will surely incur a grave offense. People of the time called them "sons of slaughterers" (human-flesh cooks), "butchers," "hunters," "burden-carriers," or "dung-carriers."

*Kǎi* (駃): In the *Cāngjié piān*, it is said that *kǎi* means "swift. The character is composed of the radical *shǐ*. In the received text, it is written as *kǎi* (古穴反), referring to the *kaití* (*駃騠*), a breed of swift horse.
Regarding *Mathurā*: the *Huáyán yīn* states it is the city of Peacocks; the ancient pronunciation states it is the city of Beautiful Honey.
*Kakara* (pronounced with the *ju* and *qia* finals; here translated as "crow") is named after its sound.
*Kukkuḷa* (the second syllable pronounced with the *jiu* and *qiu* finals) refers to the sound of a rooster. *Kukkuṭa* is translated here as "rooster."
*Tattara* (the sound *da* is pronounced like *da* in *duō*, and *zhi* is the sound of a bird). The three birds mentioned above are all named after their calls.
24. Volume Twenty-four. *Yiyì* (怡懌): The lower character is pronounced *yì*. The *Yǐ'ěr yá* states: "Yiyì means joy. Guo Pu says: "Yi is the joy of the mind; yì is the joy of the mind's release."

Regarding the "court torches" (*tingliao*) used for summoning [the ruler] back [to court], the *Zhouli* (Rites of Zhou) provides for the supply of "tumulus torches" (*fenchu*) and "court torches. Zheng Xuan states: "Tumulus" means large; those set up outside the gate are called 'large torches,' while those located inside the gate are called 'court torches.'"
*Āmalaka* fruit—here translated as "stainless"—refers to the cultivation of the hundred blessings through the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*).

Initially, there are five grades of mind: first, the inferior grade of mind; second, the middling grade of mind; third, the superior grade of mind; fourth, the superior-middling grade of mind; and fifth, the superior-superior grade of mind. Each of these is endowed with the ten wholesome paths, totaling fifty, which constitutes the initial arousal of the bodhicitta. As for the subsequent minds, when they are fully perfected and definitive, another fifty are formed, thus completing the hundred blessings.
Brahmottara-deva is here translated as "the Heaven of Reduplicated Speech.
Rudra-deva is here translated as "the Terrible.
Indriya-deva is Śakra-devānām-indra.
Kumāradeva is here translated as "Youthful Deity" (Tongzi Tian).
Aṣṭabhuja-deva is here translated as "Eight-Armed Deity" (Nalayan Tian).
Maheśvara-deva is here translated as "Great Sovereign Deity" (Dazizai Tian).
The *Pañcāla* devas— here translated as "Dragon Devas"—
and the *Brahmāhmapati* devas (in Sanskrit, *Brahmāhmapati*), who created the *Siddham* script consisting of the twelve vowels and consonants, are as explained previously in the eighth fascicle.
Vāsudeva: In ancient pronunciation, this name is also rendered as "Reality" (Shi) and is also called "Earth" (Di) or "Entity" (Wu).
Gandhamādana Mountain: This is translated as "Holding the Pair" (Chishuang).
Volume 25. Number 25. The name of a medicinal herb is Saha; this is translated as "Swift Flow" (Shiliu).

Regarding "the hundred grains" (*bǎi gù*): according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "grain" (*gù*) means "to weave together. The *Huayan Yinyi* states: "According to Yang Quan’s *Wuli Lun*, 'liang' is the general name for millet and broomcorn millet; 'dào' is the general name for non-glutinous and glutinous rice; 'shū' is the general name for various beans. These three types of grain each comprise twenty varieties, totaling sixty. To these are added twenty varieties of fruits and vegetables, which assist the grains to constitute the 'hundred grains. Thus the *Shijing* says, 'Sow forth the hundred grains,' and the *Zhouyi* says, 'The hundred grains, grasses, and trees depend upon the earth.'"

Regarding *jiū* (斪) and *zhú* (斸): for the upper character *jiū*, the reading is *gǒu* (苟侯反); the *Shuowen* states that *jiū* means "to hack" (*zhá*) and is composed of the radical *jīn* (斤) with the phonetic *gù* (句). The received text uses *jīn* (金) as the phonetic, forming *gōu* (鉤), which is not its intended usage here. For the lower character *zhú*, the reading is *lù* (竹錄反); the *Kaosheng* says *zhú* means "to hack" (*zhú*) and "to be clumsy" (*zhuó*).
