The *Shuowen* states it means "to hack" (*zhá*) and is composed of the radical *jīn* (斤) with the phonetic *shǔ* (屬). The received text uses *dēng* (登) as the phonetic, forming *dēng* (𣃆), which is not a valid character and is incorrect.
Yaśa-pūrṇa: "Yaśa" in the ancient script means "Renown," and "Pūrṇa" means "Full. Vimalarāja:
"Vimala" means "Stainless," and "Rāja" means "King."
Gavāmpati is translated here as "Ox King," also called "Lord of Oxen," and also called "Ruminator.
Subhūti is translated as "Good Existence.
Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa is translated as "Owl Ascetic"; the character for *xiū* (鵂) is pronounced *xiū*, and the character for *liú* (鶹) is pronounced *liú*.
*Kāpila* is translated here as the "Yellow-Headed Rishi.

(26) Volume Twenty-Six. *Vṛkṣa-niryāsa*: *vṛkṣa* (upper character) is pronounced *chū* with the *zhī* rhyme; it refers to tree resin. *Niryāsa* (lower character) is pronounced *nián* with the *zhān* rhyme; it means to adhere or stick. This refers to the act of catching birds and wild animals.

"Wēn gù" (温故): The first character is pronounced as "wū kūn fǎn" (乌昆反). The *Lúnyǔ* says, "By warming what is old, one knows the new. Hé Yàn said: "Wēn means to seek out and also to practice. The text in the Classics reads "mèn" (慍), which is pronounced "wēi yùn fǎn" (威运反); it means anger or resentment, which is not the intended meaning in this context.

*Ān-jué* (安橛): "To fix a peg in the air. *Jué* (橛) is a wooden wedge or stake; there is also the vulgar character *shuān* (栓), which has been used indiscriminately by later generations but is not the correct form.
*Zhú-kuài* (逐塊): "To chase clods of earth. *Kuài* (塊) means a lump of soil; in ancient script, it was written with the same character as *yóu* (由).

The five obscurations (pañca-paṭala): first, smoke; second, clouds; third, dust; fourth, mist; fifth, Rāhu. "Rāhu" refers to a specific class of asuras; in this language, it means "obstruction. Once every six months, he uses his hand to obstruct the moon, which is called a lunar eclipse.
*Jiāngnài bùtǔ* (Strongly enduring without vomiting): *qiàng* is pronounced as *qú liàng* (with the *liàng* rhyme), and *nài* is pronounced as *nú dài*;
it means to endure or tolerate. *Udayana* Mountain: this is translated here as "the place where the sun rises. *Nyagrodha*:

this is translated as "the knotless tree," also known as the "long-and-wide" tree; according to the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, its leaves are like those of the persimmon and its fruit is like the loquat. Among trees that endure for long ages, it is the tallest and largest.
*Guochā*: the first character is pronounced *wò* (as in *wòshì*) and the second is pronounced *chūjiā*.
*Pōfùqiéluó*: the ancient pronunciation of this name was "the person who has perished" (*wáng rén*).
*Póxī zhǎngzhě*: the ancient pronunciation of this name was "an elder outside the city walls"; *xī* is pronounced *yī*.

The *qi-xū* (氣噓) Caṇḍāla—*Caṇḍāla* being translated here as "one who seizes and kills the wicked"—is so named because he kills people merely by exhaling his breath upon them. When a person in the kingdom commits a crime warranting death, they are handed over to him.
Śuklodāyī (瘦瞿曇彌): This is translated as "Good Lineage" (*Kulika*); she was of the ancient lineage of seers (*ṛṣi*). Jāti-bhikṣu (闍提比丘): This is translated as "One who Acts According to Will.

Śramaṇa (沙門): A term from the Sanskrit language; it is translated as "Diligent Laborer" (*qínláo*). It is the general name for both internal (Buddhist) and external (non-Buddhist) paths, all referring specifically to those who have left the household life. In ancient scriptures, it was rendered as *sāngmén* or *suómén*. Master Kumārajīva considered these terms unsuitable and thus translated it as *shāmén*.
"O Brahmin, this is a worldly person who is called one of pure conduct, noble, who has abandoned evil dharmas, and who is learned and of wide knowledge.
"I have just wished to ask"—the word "just" (shì) also has the pronunciation shī; according to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means "near" or "beginning."
*Maṅ*: The upper character is pronounced *fāng* (with the *gōng* tone) and means "weapon"; the lower character is pronounced *wǎng* (with the *fāng* tone) and means "tip of grass. *Xiào-hǒu*:
The upper character is pronounced *hū jiāo* (with the *jiāo* tone) and the lower character is pronounced *hū gǒu* (with the *gǒu* tone). The *Yùpiān* states that it means "a loud cry."

Regarding the "Ten Abodes" within this context, these ten abodes are identical to the ten stages (*bhūmi*): first, the Stage of Extreme Joy; second, the Stage of Freedom from Defilement; third, the Radiant Stage; fourth, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom; fifth, the Difficult-to-Conquer Stage; sixth, the Manifest Stage; seventh, the Far-Reaching Stage; eighth, the Immovable Stage; ninth, the Stage of Excellent Wisdom; and tenth, the Cloud of Dharma Stage. In other sutras, the ten abodes are explained as referring to the stages prior to the [ten] stages.

Regarding the bliss of the third dhyāna: the bliss of the three lower stages resides in the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), whereas the bliss of the third dhyāna exists only in the mental stage (*manobhūmi*);

therefore, its bliss is supreme. *Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*: *Anu* (the sound of *nu* is pronounced as *du* in the vernacular) and *miao* (according to the Sanskrit pronunciation, it should be *mi-lüe*)—*a* means "non-"; *anuttara* means "supreme"; *samya* means "correct"; *saṃ* means "equal," and again, "three" or "correct"; *bodhi* means "awakening. Taken together, this is called "Unsurpassed Perfectly Correct Complete Awakening. The character *nou* (耨) is frequently used for this term in the sūtras; its sound is *nu-gou*, and its radical meaning is the same as the Sanskrit *pu*. However, since the monastic community generally uses the entering tone character, it should be written as *nou* (耨), pronounced *nu-wu*. It is also named the "Determined Practice of the Valiant" (*kṣānti-caryā*). The sūtra itself explains it as: "The ultimate firmness and stability of all phenomena."
*Chuiyi*: the character *chui* (毳) is pronounced *chang* with the *rui* (芮) tone; the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it refers to the fine hair of birds and beasts.
28. Volume Twenty-eight. *Purna-bhadra*: translated as "Full Virtue" (*Manxian*); he is the same divine general mentioned previously.

Its marks are brilliant and prominent—"brilliant" (bǐng) pronounced as bǐng, and "prominent" (zhù) pronounced as zhù lù—meaning they are clearly and manifestly displayed, distinct from the marks of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*).
The city of Campā is named after the campaka flower; the flower is yellow, uniquely fragrant and pure, and because this city has many of them, it derives its name from the flower.
Vārāṇasī is here translated as "Surrounding the City" (Qiàochéng).
The *āmra* fruit is shaped like a pear and its flavor is extremely sweet and delicious.

To "stand, prop, and lift the jar" (*lì jù jǔ píng*)—the character *jù* is pronounced *gù* with the *lǚ* rhyme; older pronunciations state that non-Buddhists used jars as round as gourds, which lacked feet and were lifted off the ground by crossing three staffs over them. In various sūtras, this is sometimes called a "strange object" (*qí*) or a "triple-pronged stand" (*sānchā lì gù*); both refer to the same thing.

"Jiào" (酵) [with the ancient pronunciation *kǎo*] refers to the leavening agent used for making dough or wine. In the scriptures, it is frequently written as "lào" (醪) [with the pronunciation *luògāo*]; the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines this as "turbid wine," but this does not accord with the intended meaning in the scriptures.

"Beyond the clouds" (*yúnbiǎo*): *biǎo* is pronounced as in *piāotiān* (the sound of "piāo" and "tiān"). The *Sāncāng* states that *biǎo* means "outside. This refers to the stars being situated outside the clouds.

"Smelting furnace" (*lúyě*): the second character, *yě*, is pronounced as in *yǐzhě*. The *Shuowen* defines it as "to liquefy. The *Sāncāng* says it means "to melt away. It flows when encountering heat and solidifies when meeting cold; its meaning is identical to that of "water" (*shuǐ*), and thus the character includes the radical for "ice" (*bīng*).

29. Fascicle Twenty-nine. "Coarse" (cū): This refers to being sufficient for one's own needs. According to the *Cai* (才), it is the opposite [of fine]; the *Yùpiān* (玉篇) states it means "rough" (lù), and it also means "coarse" (cū).

The term *fu* (賦) is pronounced *fangwu* (方務). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to collect" or "to levy taxes. In the *Fangyan*, it is said that *fu* refers to "varieties" (*zhong*). Guo Pu states: "The purpose of *fu* is for the purpose of leveling and measuring.

Each of the thirty-two marks (*lakṣaṇa*) is produced by one hundred merits (*puṇya*). This means that by practicing the ten wholesome paths (*daśakuśala-karmapatha*) with the fivefold mental conduct, fifty merits are synthesized; this constitutes the initial stage of mind. Proceeding to the subsequent stages of mind, another fifty are likewise possessed, totaling one hundred which together complete a single mark. Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "A mark adorned by one hundred merits. This was already explained in the preceding text of the first twenty-four fascicles.

The term "lián-dǐ" (奩底)—the first character pronounced with the *lì* and *zhàn* finals (*lián* being a vessel for cosmetics and *dǐ* meaning the base—refers to the bottom of such a container. This refers to the flat, square, and level base of a fragrant casket, whose width and proportions serve as a metaphor for the Buddha’s feet. A sutra states that this mark was attained through the power of maintaining the precepts and speaking truthful words. The "zàng" (𧙍) character used today does not accord with the meaning of the scripture.

The mark of the thousand-spoked wheel—Sanskrit: *cakrāṅka*; Chinese: *lún* (wheel)—is located on the soles of the Tathāgata’s feet. The Sūtra states that he obtained this mark because he bestowed the wealth of the Dharma upon sentient beings.

"Jālāvanaddhahasta-pāda" (webbed fingers and toes) means that the flesh between the Buddha’s fingers and toes is like fine silk patterns, resembling the feet of geese or swans. This mark was obtained because he gathered sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). The character "màn" (網) is derived from the radical "革" (leather) with the phonetic "miǎn" (免); the reading in the sutras as "màn" (縵) with the phonetic "mò yàn" (莫晏反) is incorrect.

The ankles are well-rounded and full; "rounded" (jǔng) is pronounced *chǒng* with the rhyme *lóng* (according to the *Erya*, it means even and uniform). The Sūtra states that because one maintains the precepts and practices giving, one attains this mark.

As for the *Nyagrodha* tree—its ancient pronunciation being "Wujie Shu" (No-Knot Tree)—the Sūtra refers to the *Nyagrodha* as a tree of fivefold substance. Since the tree is straight, rounded, and full, it is used as a metaphor for the Buddha’s body. The Sūtra states that by constantly delighting in giving, visiting the sick, and providing medicine, one attains this physical mark.

There are three kinds of nutriment for the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). First, the nutriment of volition (*manahsaṃcetanāhāra*) refers to the "non-dying" power of karma. Second, the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*) means that life is sustained by depending upon the touch of warmth and moisture. Third, the nutriment of mind (*mana-āhāra*), which is the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*), is like the case of those born from eggs; because their minds constantly think of their mother, their bodies do not decay.

Regarding the three causes and conditions for affliction: first, the father; second, the mother; and third, impurity. Through these three factors, one undergoes birth. Furthermore, another explanation states that the "three afflictions" refer to: first, giving rise to aversion toward the father; second, giving rise to desire for the mother; and third, conceiving attachment to the body. Through these three conditions, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) attains birth.

The character for *shēng* (生) is pronounced with the *zī suí* (茲隨) rhyme; it represents the beak of a bird (*niǎo wěn*). The graphic form should be written as *qí* (喍), which consists of two identical parts. *Kāi pǒu* (開剖) is pronounced with the *pǔ mù* (普目) rhyme; it means to analyze or dissect.

To "attain the *dhāraṇī*" (得陀羅尼)—which is here translated as "total retention" (*zǒng chí*)—refers to various types found in the various sūtras: there is the *vartanī-dhāraṇī*, which is meditative concentration (*samādhi*); there is the *śrutadhara-dhāraṇī*, which pertains to the Dharma; and there is the *mantra-dhāraṇī*, which refers to secret incantations. In this particular sūtra, however, it specifically refers to meditative concentration.

"Qièjià" (憩駕)—the "qiè" is pronounced *lì* (去厲反); according to the *Erya*, it means "to stop. The commentary states that it means "to stop and rest from fatigue. The *Shuowen Jiezi* uses the character *kè* (愒), while the *Cangjie Pian* uses the character *qí* (𡳅). These archaic forms are not used today.
The name of the medicine is *Laṅkā*. In ancient pronunciation, this name is said to mean "ground.
If one can [attain it], according to the *Guǎngyǎ*, *gǒu* means "sincerity" or "dawn"; the *Hánshī* says *gǒu* means "to obtain."

"Marriage" (hun) is now explained as "darkness. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to the wife's family; because the *Liji* states that one takes a wife at the time of darkness when entering [the home], it is called "hun. In the *Erya*, the father of a wife is called "hun-yin. In ancient texts, this was written as "yin. According to the *Shuowen*, "yin" refers to the husband's family; because it is what the woman relies upon, it is called "yin. In the *Erya*, the father of the husband is called "yin. The character for "yin" (𦕓) is pronounced "xi."
Śrāvastī City should be called Śīlavatī; it is also called Śrāvastī, which means "Abode of the Rishis" (仙人住處) and also "Country of Renowned Things" (聞物國).
Vārāṇasī City is also called Vārāṃsī, which means "City of the Banner of Speech" (語幢城).
The city of Vaiśālī is also called Vijayā, which in this language means "City of Vast Splendor.
The river Airāvatī is also called Bhadrā, which in this language means "Worthy" or "Virtuous."
The river *Īṣmatāyī*; *Īṣma* here means "sweet," and *tāyī* here means "intoxicating.
The river *Vipaśyanā*; this is translated as the "Inexhaustible River."
The city of Kuśāvatī—its ancient pronunciation being *shuǐ* (water)—was at that time named Kapilavastu.

The *Śūramgama-sūtra* states: "Kapilavastu is the center of three thousand suns and moons and twelve thousand heavens and earths. The Bodhisattva Siṃha raised a doubt: "If Kuśinagara is a borderland, how can it be said that this city was formerly named Kapilavastu? He asked why it could be called a borderland.

Sudatta, this Elder Anāthapiṇḍada, purchased a garden to build a monastery by covering it with gold; he was one who delighted in practicing *dāna* (charity), regarding wealth lightly and valuing merit.

Regarding *saddhāna-sa*, it should be called *saddhāri-saṇa*. *Saddhā* means "correct" (*samyak*), *dāri* means "giving" (*dāna*), and *saṇa* means "seeing" (*darśana*); thus, it refers to practicing *dāna* with right view.
*Kālāma* (迦蘭陀): In ancient pronunciation, it was *Kālānda*. This name means "fine bird"; it is the name of a bird, also the name of a mountain mouse, and also the name of a country.

*Jetavana* (祇陀): In ancient pronunciation, it was *Sheng* (Victory). Previously, Sudatta purchased the grove, and this [prince] Jeta donated the trees; the Sūtra refers to it as "Jeta’s Grove" (*Jetavana*).
30. Fascicle Thirty. Āmrapālī (also called Āmra-dārikā). According to tradition, she was born from within the flower of an *āmra* tree.
The river Pārā is also called the Bālā River; in ancient pronunciation, this means "victorious" (*śreṣṭha*).

*Jùn* (駿) is pronounced with the rhyme *xùn* (迅); the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *jùn* refers to a horse of excellent talent. There is also a reading with the rhyme *sì* (思) and *rùn* (閏), but this is incorrect.

"Encoffining" (*bin*) refers to the placing of the coffin and its lid; "enveloping" (*lian*, pronounced *liàn* according to the *Yùnyì Shìyùn*) means, as the *Xuānyì Shìyùn* explains, "clothing the corpse. The *Shìmíng* states: "Lian means 'to gather' (*liàn*); it is to conceal [the body] so that it is no longer visible. The minor encoffining takes place inside the door, while the major encoffining takes place on the eastern steps.
"Huá yè" (和液)—the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines this as "moisture and lubrication," referring to the warm harmony and nourishing moisture of the second month, the middle spring.

Regarding the "hundred beasts": according to the *Kongzi Jiayu*, there are four auspicious creatures among the domesticated animals (*chù*). Among the hairy insects (*máo chóng*), there are three hundred and sixty species, with the Qílí (Qilin) as the chief; among the winged insects (*yǔ chóng*), there are three hundred and sixty species, with the Fèng (Phoenix) as the chief; among the scaly insects (*lín chóng*), there are three hundred and sixty species, with the Lóng (Dragon) as the chief; and among the armored insects (*jiǎ chóng*), there are three hundred and sixty species, with the Guī (Tortoise) as the chief.

The character *fú* (孚) is pronounced as *fǔ* (撫) with the *qùshēng* (去聲) tone. The *Tōngsùwén* (通俗文) states that "that which hatches from an egg is called *fú*. Furthermore, the character *fú* consists of the radicals *zhuǎo* (爪, "claw") and *zǐ* (子, "child"), making it a *huìyì* (會意, "composite meaning") character. The lower part is pronounced as *zhǔ* (主) with the *qùshēng* tone. Moreover, among those born from eggs, it is called *fú*, while those born from a womb are called *rǔ* (乳). Thus, the *Shuōwén* (說文) [explains *fú*] as consisting of *fú* and *yǐ* (乙); *yǐ* represents the image of milk flowing out. The pronunciation of *yǐ* is *yīn qì* (殷訖).

"Depressed and steaming" (yùzhēng): the first character is pronounced *dàn* with the *lǜ* rhyme, and the second is pronounced *zhēng* with the *zhāng* rhyme; it refers to a feverish illness. Since the moon is cool and refreshing, it is able to dispel it.

Aniruddha is also named Anuruddha and is further called Anilou-dou; these variations arise from differences in the weight of the Sanskrit pronunciation, and this is translated as "Non-extinction. Among the Buddha’s disciples, he was the foremost of those who attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). This person was the very best.

Śāriputra’s name is composed of *śāri* and *putra*. *Śāri* means "śārikā bird" (a kind of partridge), and *putra* means "son. Because the eyes of this Venerable One’s mother were clearly defined with distinct black and white parts and moved with such agility that they resembled the eyes of a śārikā bird, he was named Śāri. Thus, the Venerable One received his name from his mother and is called "Son of the Śārikā. The old translation of "Son of the Body" (*Shenzi*) is erroneous; since the Sanskrit term for "body" is *śarīra*, it is evident that these two terms are entirely distinct.

Śamatha is also called samādhi and also called samāpatti; this [latter] is translated as "concentration" (ding) or "cessation" (zhi). Concentration has many names, and this is its general designation. It is also sometimes called samāpatti.
Vipaśyanā is also called jñāna or jñāna; this is translated as "wisdom" (hui), "contemplation" (guan), or "insight" (jian). Upekṣā is translated as "equanimity" (she).
The meanings of these three—calm abiding (śamatha), contemplation (vipaśyanā), and equanimity (upekṣā)—are as described above.

31. Scroll Thirty-One. Regarding the character *zhōng* (得衷): in the *Zuǒzhuan*, it says "The state of Chu deviates from our *zhōng*" (*chū bì wǒ zhōng*). Du Yu states that *zhōng* means "correct" (*zhèng*) and "to hit the mark" (*zhōngdāng*). In the *Cāngjiépiān*, it is distinguished as a term for the interior and exterior; the text of the scripture uses the character *zhōng* (中), meaning "central" or "level. Both characters are interchangeable.
"Yìjìn (遺燼): Qín Jìn [states] it is the remaining wood of fire; its correct radical form should be 㷠 (zhēngtǐ yí zuò zhēng). Jiān (菅): Gǔ yán fǎn;

according to the *Erya*, jiān belongs to the genus of *máo* grass. The scriptural text writes it as 葌, which is synonymous with jiǎn; the *Shuowen* states that 葌 is the name of a fragrant herb. 葌 does not carry this meaning."

*Gān-gǔ* (甘𩰫) is pronounced with the initial *gǔ* (古和反) for the character *gǔ*. According to the *Fāngyán*, it is the Qin term for an earthen cauldron (*tǔfǔ*). The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radical *lì* (鬲) and the phonetic *yǎo* (󱿙); *yǎo* is pronounced *kǒuwǎ* (口瓦反), and *lì* is pronounced *lìjīng* (歷經). The character is also written as *guō* (鍋). This is not for use in a leaden carriage.

*Niǎojiǎo* (撓攪): The first character is pronounced with the *hūgāo* rhyme-group (反) and the second with the *jiāoyǎo* rhyme-group (反). According to the *Shuowen*, "niǎojiǎo" means to disturb or agitate (*jiǎoluàn*). This is as stated in the *Shijing*: "It only disturbs my heart. *Róngxiāo* (融銷): The second character is pronounced with the *xiǎodiāo* rhyme-group (反).

According to the *Shuowen*, it means to melt or smelt (*shuó*). It is composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic "xiào. In the scriptures, it is written with the "water" radical as "xiāo" (消); this is the "xiāo" of "dissipation" (*xiāosī*), not this usage.

The *Yùpiān* (Jade Lexicon) states: "Vigilance (*jue*) means to alert or to examine; observation (*guan*) means to see or to look. The *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* states: "Applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) exist in the first dhyāna. A sutra states: "Internally there is applied and sustained thought, externally one experiences the calamity of fire. The Tripitaka Master translated these as "investigation (*sought*) and analysis (*examined*")."

"Cháo-diào" (嘲調) is pronounced with the "shàng" (上) tone, followed by "zhú" (竹) and "jiāo" (交), or it is written as "zhōu" (啁) with the same meaning. The *Cāngjiépiān* states that "zhōu" is also "diào" (調), meaning to engage in mutual jesting. In the canonical text, the character "yá" (讛) is sometimes used; its traditional pronunciation is "yì" (藝), though its origin remains uncertain. Alternatively, it is written as "yèi" (譺), pronounced with the "wǔ" (五) and "jiè" (戒) tones; the *Zílín* defines this as "deceitful jesting," and also notes that a grand jest is called "yèi."

"Jiake" (賈客). "Ke" (客) is pronounced as *gong* (公) with the *hu* (戶) tone, and also as *gu* (古) with the *ya* (雅) tone. Zheng Xuan says: "One who travels is called a *shang* (商, merchant); one who stays at home is called a *jia* (賈, trader). The *Baihutong* (白虎通) states: "The meaning of 'jia' is 'solidity' (*gu*), meaning that one stabilizes their goods and awaits the arrival of the people to seek profit therefrom."

Aṅgulimāla—translated here as "Finger-Garland"—was a non-Buddhist practitioner who killed people to take their fingers and fashion them into flower garlands. Being short of one finger, he encountered the Buddha on the road and drew his sword to pursue him, shouting, "Stop, stop, Great Śramaṇa! I am Aṅgulimāla, the son of King Śuddhodana; I must pay the tax of one finger! The World-Honored One walked slowly and led him to the monastery, where he heard the Dharma and left the household life. He was then immediately ordained. This account is found in the *Aṅgulimāla Sūtra*.

Regarding "not manifesting in the present life but manifesting later": "manifesting in the present" (*pratyutpanna-vedanīya*) refers to receiving retribution immediately upon performing an action in this very body; "manifesting in the next life" (*upapadya-vedanīya*) refers to receiving retribution only when taking birth in a future life; and "manifesting later" (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*) refers to receiving retribution from the third lifetime onward.
The king’s name was Kātya (in the ancient pronunciation, this is the correct form).
He was blind; the *Shiming* (Explanations of Names) states that "blind" (*gu*) refers to eyes that are closed and motionless, meaning the eyes are shut flat like the surface of a drum skin.
"Ji" (劓) means to cut off the nose; "ji" (刖) means to amputate the hands or feet;
"fu" (副) means to store or prepare for future use. (Note:
"ji" is pronounced with the *qú* rhyme, and "fu" is pronounced with the *fáng* or *fù* rhyme.)

32. Fascicle Thirty-two. "Dǐ" (打) means to strike. "Zhì" (擲) means to throw. "Dù" (垤), with the radical "tuí" (都回反), means to fall or to drop; its standard form is written as "duī" (磓). "Yā" (押), with the radical "yā" (烏狎反), means to press down or to suppress; its ancient form is written as "yā" (古押反). "Lí" (籬) means a fence; it does not have this meaning here.

The seed, semen, and blood are ultimately impure. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are five kinds of impurity regarding the body of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*): first, impurity of the seed, which refers to the semen and blood; second, impurity of the dwelling place, which is above the receptacle for digested food (*pakvāśaya*); third, impurity of its own characteristics, which refers to the fluids of blood and flesh and their filth; fourth, impurity of its own nature, as the nine orifices constantly flow [with secretions]; and fifth, ultimate impurity, as it ultimately returns to excrement and soil.

Mount Malaya is also called Malayan; "mala" means "defilement" and "ya" means "to remove. The mountain is located within the borders of Southern India and is named after the country. Because this mountain abounds in white sandalwood incense, which is fragrant and pure for those who enter it, it is said to "remove defilements."

It is like a camel eating honey—the word "camel" (tuó) is pronounced with the initial *d* reversed [as *t*]; "honey" refers to the nectar of the *cīcī* grass. Its flavor is as sweet as honey; once the camel has obtained it to eat, it pays no heed to the fodder grass.
*Tūla* (the character is pronounced with the *ren* and *zhi* finals; the *Tōngsùwén* says it means "hair ornament"). The hair hanging from the top of a spear is called *tūla*;

it is also written as *rì*, used interchangeably. *Śṛṅbha* (the first character is pronounced with the *nǚ* and *lín* finals) is a Sanskrit word. *Śṛṅbha* is the name of a tree whose bitter leaves can be boiled to make a drink that cures headaches, much like the *kudrīṇa* tree here [in China]. The insects feed on its sweet sap, and thus they take their name from it. *Kudrīṇa* is pronounced with the *lián* final.

Regarding the fire-insect that delights in fire, the *Chuan* says: "In the region of Nanzhong there is a fire-mouse; its fur is made into cloth for clothing, and because it can be burned by fire, it is called 'fire-washed cloth' (*huǎnbù*). As for the word *xiácī*:
the first character is pronounced *hùjiā* (with the initial *hù*) and the second is *zìyí* (with the initial *zì*)."

*Guan* (古亂反, gǔ luàn fǎn): A vessel for drawing water; the text uses the character *guàn*, which refers to irrigation and is not this drawing vessel. *Gěng* (古杏反, gǔ xìng fǎn): According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is the rope used for drawing from a well; according to the *Fangyan*, it is called *gěng* in the region between Han and Wei.
"Kauśika" is the clan name of Śakra from his former stage as a bodhisattva.
As for "magnet stone," some texts write it as "compassion" (cí), but that is not the correct character form.

"Guaihuo" (葵藿)—the second character being pronounced with the *guō* rhyme—refers to bean leaves. These two things, guai and huo, are commonly seen by ordinary people to incline their bodies and turn to follow the sun; this is said to be a matter of causal conditions meeting one another, rather than the existence of a separate, intentional mind of reverence.
The *aśoka* tree—here translated as "Sorrowless Tree"—is a radish (the first character is pronounced *luó*, the second *pú* with the *bèi* tone;
it resembles the root of *sōng* [Chinese cabbage] and has a pungent flavor, with purple flowers). It is written identically to the character for *lúbo* (radish).

Regarding the chariots, cavalry, elephants, and infantry—according to the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions), there are generally four types of military forces: infantry, cavalry, chariots, and elephants. As for the elephants, they are clad in sturdy armor and their tusks are fitted with sharp spikes; one general rides securely upon them while commanding the maneuvers, and two soldiers on the left and right serve as their drivers. As for the chariots, they are drawn by four horses; the military commander sits within, surrounded by ranks of soldiers who guard him, supporting the wheels and grasping the axle-poles. The cavalry is deployed to provide dispersed defense, pursuing the defeated and charging forward. The infantry consists of light, resilient, and courageous men selected for service; they carry large shields and wield long halberds, or hold swords and blades, leading the vanguard in formation. When these four forces are combined, it is termed an "army" (*senā*).

33. Volume Thirty-three. Regarding the character *sù* (粟), when pronounced with the *měi* (美) and *bēi* (悲) finals, its standard forms are written as either *mí* (靡) or *mí* (糜); it refers to the grain *jiè* (穄). The *Fāngyán* (方言) states that in the region west of the Pass it is called *mí*, while in Jizhou it is called *jiè* (pronounced *jì*).

It is like cutting a raw gourd (the character for "gourd" is pronounced *hù*; the character for "cutting" is pronounced *jié*, meaning to slice or sever). Regarding "double-threaded bricks" (*chóngxiàn zhuān*:

the character for "thread" is pronounced *sì jiàn* [actually *shī jiàn*], and the character *yán* is incorrect; the character for "brick" is pronounced *zhǐ yuán*): this refers to those who weave bamboo blinds. They chop many broken bricks into shapes like small drums and wrap threads around them to serve as the warp for the blind. When weaving the blind according to its dimensions, each row rests upon the rafters, piling up so that they resemble a backbone. This is used as a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s emaciated body after six years of ascetic practice, where his backbone appeared prominently connected like double-stranded threads or bricks. The word "double" (*chóng*) is read with the fourth tone.
"Excavating the body" (*wān*—meaning to gouge out; *gōu* pronounced as *huìyuán*) means to hold one's breath so that there is no gasping.

The *Kǎoshēng* (Investigation of Sounds) states it means to conceal or to cause to disappear. This refers to a Bodhisattva giving away his body while manifesting the appearance of death, thereby ensuring that there is no sin of killing.

The *kapiñjala* bird—its ancient pronunciation being that of *duō* (鵽)—is identified in the *Śāstra-vyākhyā* as resembling a female osprey (*chī*). Because it is known to be a close friend of the elephant and the monkey, we know this is the one referred to. The character for *duō* is pronounced *zhuó guā* (卓刮反), and the character for *guā* is pronounced *guān bā* (關八反).

Regarding the ancient pronunciation of *Gautama* (瞿陀), it is said that this name refers to the porpoise (*liṅyú*; "liṅ" is pronounced as in "lìchéng"). The *Yùpiān* states: "The porpoise is a type of carp with four legs; it originates from the south. This signifies that the Bodhisattva, concealing his form to benefit sentient beings, manifests the body of a fish of unusual color, which is the actual appearance of one in meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

He constantly bestows favors and initiates them; according to the *Fanyu pian*, "shi" (施) means "to provide. This refers to how this Bodhisattva benefits others without partiality, bestowing favor upon all things.
Tuṣita Heaven—translated here as "Contentment"—is the fourth heaven within the Desire Realm.
The bhikṣu Śivara was so named because he was born near Mount Śivara;
Upaśivara—*upa* meaning "small," which is to say "younger brother"—was his younger sibling.
The mother of the elder Mṛgāra was named Mṛgāra; "Mṛgāra" is translated here as "Golden Girdle," so called because her body was adorned with gold and jewels.
The mother of the elder Kroḍa is not clearly known.
The mother of the householder Vaṃśa (translated as "Cage" or "Prison") and others like her were all born from eggs. As for Āmrapālī: the Tripitaka Master Jing said that "Āmra" is the name of a fruit;

its shape resembles that of a crabapple (*nài*) and its taste is like a pear. The *Śīlananda-sūtra* states that the "Crabapple Woman" is this very person; because she conceived by means of the essence of a flower, she is called "moisture-born. She was the noble consort of King Bimbisāra and the mother of the eminent physician Jīvaka.
*Kāñcana* (迦不多) is the name for a tree known as the "stinking tree" (*pūtimukta*), upon which [this being] was born.
*Pramāda* (放逸) is pronounced with a level tone (*ping sheng*).
*Tṛṇa* (稾草) is pronounced with the old-style retroflex *lao* (*gu lao fan*); it refers to the stalks of grain.
"Having strong teeth" means that for humans one counts years, for oxen one counts ages, and for horses one counts the number of teeth; hence it is said "having strong teeth.
"Curved spine" (juǎnjì): *juǎn* is pronounced *jùyuán* (巨員); it means to be bent or crooked.

The character for *cún* (存) in "squatting on the ground" (*qundì*) should be read as *jǔ* (舉). When referring to "raising the corpse," the character *jǔ* (舉) should be used in place of *chú* (除), as they correspond to one another.
Regarding "lowly persons" (*sīxià zhī rén*): *sī* (厮) is pronounced *xī* (息) with the *zhī* (支) tone; the *Yùpiān* states it means a horse stable, as such places were where lowly people resided.
"Qīngcè" (privy/toilet) should properly be written as "qīng hùn" (privy latrine).
"Jìbié" (to record and distinguish)—the character "bié" is pronounced *pī* (with the initial *b-*) and means to divide or select; the text's reading of "bié" is incorrect.

"Luǎn ké" (eggshell)—the character "ké" is pronounced *kǎo* (with the initial *k-*) in the regions of Wu and Kuaiji, though its pronunciation is *kǔ* (with the initial *k-*) in the *kǒu-mù* rhyme; now it is clear that the skin of all things is indeed a "ké."
"Yin-yi" (婬佚) is now written as "yi" (妷), with the same pronunciation as one fan. According to the *Cangjie pian*, "yin-yi" means "dissolute" (*dàng*;
pronounced *tú làng fǎn*). 34. Volume Thirty-four. "Pó-cā-pó" (婆蹉婆) is translated here as "Vajrapāṇi" (執金剛); it is also called "Adornment" (嚴飾).
Purandara: in its ancient pronunciation, *púlán* means "city" (*pura*) and *tuóluó* means "to destroy" (*dāra*).
Indrā: this is translated as "Lord of the Gods" (*devendra*).
Queen Śacī: *śacī* means "pure measure"; she was the daughter of an Asura king and was highly esteemed by the Heavenly Emperor.
Upamāna, here translated as "Parable," was a foster son of the Buddha.
Subhadra, here translated as "Virtuous and Wise," refers to the city of Rājagṛha, the City of Royal Abode.
*Chou-hui* (愁憒)—the *hui* (憒) character is pronounced with the ancient reading *gui* (古對反);

it means a confused and disordered mind. *Boluoliuzhi* (婆羅留支)—the ancient pronunciation of this name is "Victorious Joy" (*shengle* [勝樂]), with the *le* (樂) character pronounced as *wu-xiao-fan* (五孝反); it is also called "Broken Finger" (*zheshi* [折指]).
*Bhagavān* is translated here as "World-Honored One" (*Shizun*).
*Arhat* is translated as "Worthy of Offerings" (*Yinggong*), which is also similar in meaning to "Arhan.
*Samyaksaṃbuddha* is translated as "Perfectly Enlightened One" (*Zhengbianzhi*).

"Rough, coarse, and *lǜ* (麤澀𣯫褐). [Note: *lǜ* is pronounced *sè* when following the four stops and two nasals; it is written as *sè* in the three stops, which is incorrect. *Lǜ* (𣯫) is pronounced *lì zhǔ*; it refers to weaving wool into cloth."
Gautamī Bhikṣuṇī (瞿低比丘): This is translated as "Cow-keeper.
Volume Thirty-five. Prasenajit Rāja (波斯匿王): This is translated as "Moonlight King," also as "Victorious Army King," and also as "Harmonious Joy."

"Even though there is a *garbha* (womb/fetus)—the character *shí* (尸) being a variant for *huái* (懷) [meaning 'to carry a fetus']—the scripture reads *shēn* (身, body). This is like a canopy (*kāpaṭa*); while it is one, its tongues are many. It should be that the character *zhě* (赭) is actually *gài* (葢), meaning a canopy with multicolored streamers hanging from its four sides. This is a metaphor for *nirvāṇa*: although it is one, its modes of liberation are many."

The *Tathāgata-daśabala-yoga-śāstra*, fascicle fifty, states: First, the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and impossible; second, the power of knowledge regarding the individual karma of beings; third, the power of knowledge regarding meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and attainments; fourth, the power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties of beings; fifth, the power of knowledge regarding the various inclinations of beings; sixth, the power of knowledge regarding the various elements of beings; seventh, the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading everywhere; eighth, the power of knowledge regarding the recollection of past abodes; ninth, the power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth; tenth, the power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of outflows.

The four fearlessnesses are: first, fearlessness regarding perfect enlightenment; second, fearlessness regarding the obstacles to the path; third, fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows; and fourth, fearlessness regarding the path leading out of suffering.
*Śūraṅgama-samādhi* means "the samādhi of heroic vigor. This sutra itself explains it as follows: "Śūraṅgama" means that which is ultimately firm and solid regarding all matters."
36. Fascicle Thirty-Six. Regarding the *śirīṣa* fruit: in ancient translations, *śirī* means "head" and *ṣa* means "resembling"; thus, it is called the "Head-Resembling Fruit."
Pāṭali is the name of a city in the Sanskrit language; this refers to the elder (śreṣṭhin) of that city.
Kokālika means "Cow-keeper" in Chinese.
Tiṣya Bhikṣu means "Light" or alternatively "Great."
The *pāṭala* flower is here called the "double-petaled flower.

*Timira* (the first syllable pronounced with a high tone) refers to the "large-bodied fish"; there are four species of this kind, and this is the smallest among them. In the *Dharmapradīpa-sūtra*, *timirīla* is the third fish; all [these] successively devour one another.

Regarding the *chē* (䱜) fish, the *Yìwùzhì* states: "The *yōuchē* fish has a horizontal bone above its nose that is as sharp as a knife or axe. In Jiangdong, a broad-bladed axe is called a *fán*, therefore it is termed the *fán-chē*. There are twenty species of this class of fish, each with its own distinct name; their teeth are as sharp as a file and their nasal bones are like axes. Currently, all such names are written with the radical for "fish" (*yú*), as in *yōuchē*. The pronunciation of *yōu* is *fán*.

The non-Buddhists (tīrthika) contemplate only six modes of practice, namely: three consisting of rejoicing in the higher realms and three consisting of revulsion toward the lower realms. These involve revulsion toward the suffering, coarseness, and obstacles of the lower realms, and the aspiration for the purity, subtlety, and excellence of the higher realms. Taking suffering, coarseness, and obstacles as one set of three, and purity, subtlety, and excellence as another set of three, they constitute the six modes of practice; however, these are practices of false views and not correct contemplation.
My disciples possess the sixteen aspects, meaning that for each of the Four Truths there are sixteen correct practices.
*Wanshou* (腕手) bhikṣu—*wan* being pronounced as in *wu guan* (烏灌), or alternatively written as *wan* (椀).
The surname of the elder Diāo (刁) is pronounced "diāo" (upper tone); it is a clan name.

He was an Anāgāmin (*anāgāmin*, pronounced *xìng* with the *gēng* rhyme); this person possessed sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*) and, without depending on diligent practice, was able to attain cessation by himself—this refers to the one mentioned in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (*Satyasiddhi-śāstra*) as the "person who attains cessation without practicing."

Aśvajit and Pūrṇa—these two were among the group of six bhikṣus. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that these six were: first, Nanda; second, Upananda; third, Kokālika; fourth, Khandadravya; fifth, Aśvajit; and sixth, Pūrṇa.

The youth Kāśyapa is the same person as Kokālika mentioned in the Vinaya of the Sarvāstivādins, who was a native of the village of Tora in Śrāvastī; he is the master of debate who confronted [the Buddha] in this assembly, and the aforementioned text states that he was "in his early years"—this refers to him.
The bhikṣu Yaśas—alternatively called Yashi, which means "bright" (ming) in Chinese—is a term for a śramaṇa, a word from the Sanskrit language.

This meaning is translated as "one who has exhausted the path. The title "śramaṇa" signifies one who has exhausted [defilements] and follows the path; when monks refer to themselves as "poor man of the path" (bindao), it is an expression of humility and self-abasement, though it also carries many other meanings.

37. Fascicle Thirty-Seven. The corner of a rabbit’s head has never had space, and thus it does not have it now either; because space is eternal, it existed originally and exists now. The Buddha-nature is not like this: it existed originally but is absent now, or was absent originally but exists now. Therefore, that which both exists and does not exist is the meaning of the Middle Way. A sutra says: "When all afflictions (*kleśa*) and fetters, whether wholesome or indeterminate, are exhausted, they are called Buddha-nature. That which "existed originally but is absent now" refers to the afflictions; that which "was absent originally but exists now" refers to Bodhi. If one were to say that afflictions are as non-existent throughout the three periods of time as space, or that Bodhi is as non-existent throughout the three periods of time as the horn of a rabbit, this would be called slandering the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. Thus it is said: "To claim that there is no dharma existing throughout the three periods of time—such a thing is impossible."

"Qu" (去) means "to leave the tree," "to leave the house. Regarding the character "qu" (去), the *Yùpiān* states it means "to remove" or "to set aside. It is also pronounced with the initial "qiu" (丘) and the final "lü" (慮); in this latter sense, it means "to go toward" or "to depart," which is not the meaning intended here.

*Zhān* (霑): The phonetic component is *lián* (廉). The *Yùpiān* states it means "to moisten. The *Sāncāng* states it means "to soak. *Mǎo* (𧈿): The phonetic components are *wǎng* (亡) and *lìzhǎng* (力掌).

The *Shuōwén* records this as *mǎo* (𧈿), which is the same as *liǎng* (蜽). The *Tōngsùwén* states that these are spiritual monsters of wood and stone. According to the *Huáinán*, their appearance is like that of a three-year-old child, red-black in color, with red eyes, red claws, long ears, and beautiful hair; they are ghosts of those who died from drowning.

There are one hundred and thirty-six hells in total. First, there are eight hot hells: first, Saṃjīva (Reviving); second, Kālasūtra (Black String); third, Saṃghāta (Crushing); fourth, Raurava (Crying Out); fifth, Mahāraurava (Great Crying Out); sixth, Tapana (Burning); seventh, Pratāpana (Intense Burning); and eighth, Avīci Mahānaraka (the Great Hell of No Respite). Each of these hells has four gates, and outside each gate there are four additional hells: first, Kukūla (Hot Embers); second, Kuṇapa (Putrid Excrement); third, Kṣuramārga (Razor Blades); and fourth, Vaitaraṇī (Fierce River). These eight hells are the primary ones, each having sixteen as its retinue, totaling one hundred and thirty-six.

38. Fascicle Thirty-Eight. Regarding *añjana* medicine: its ancient pronunciation was also *anta*, which here is translated as "root medicine. A sutra states that it can cure eye pain; it should be *Coptis teeta* (huanglian).
*Yì* (暐) is pronounced *shàng yú guǐ fǎn*, *xià yán liè fǎn*. According to the *Fāngyán*, it denotes the appearance of abundance; according to the *Sāncāng*, it refers to radiant splendor.
*Hǔxī* (虎兕): *xū lǐ fǎn*. Guo Pu says: "The *xī* resembles an ox, is blue-black in color, has a single horn, and weighs a thousand *jīn*."

*Tuán* (搏): The "tuán" is pronounced as *tuán* (官反). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "round"; according to the *Sancang*, it means "a mouthful of food. The version in the sutra uses "chuǎi" (揣), which is a vulgar character and incorrect.
*Fǎlì* (法厲): The "lì" is pronounced as *lì* (力制反). It refers to a whetstone. In ancient texts, it was written as "lì" (礪), which is the same character.

"Coarse and wild" (麤獷): "wild" (獷) is pronounced *gu* with the *mǎng* rhyme; it means "stubborn. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "evil and unfit to associate with. The text of the sutra uses the characters 穬 or 󲎷, but these do not carry this meaning. "Laughing" (󱳸):

pronounced *xiào* with the *chì* rhyme, it means "to treat lightly or insult" according to the *Cangjie pian*. Another reading is *xiào* with the *sī miào* rhyme; according to the *Zilin*, it means "joy. The character is composed of the radical for bamboo (*zhú*) and the phonetic *quǎn*; bamboo is a musical instrument, and the noble person laughs only after having found joy.

Regarding the phrase "embracing Mount Sumeru" (*bào xūmí shàng*): the reading *bù jiāo fǎn* (step with the reversed *jiāo*) is incorrect; furthermore, the character for "file" (*pǎo*)—formed by adding the radical for metal—is also wrong. Upon examining the character *pǎo*, it does not exist within the canon of characters; it should instead be read as *póu*, which consists of two distinct forms.

*Cháiniè* (齚齧) is also written as *zhà* (齰) or *zé* (咋); *zhà* is pronounced with the same phonetic as *chái* (柴) and *zé* (責). According to the *Tōngsùwén* (通俗文), "to bite and devour" is called *cháiniè*. The lower character, *jiān* (研), is pronounced *jié* (結).

Udraka Rāmaputra—translated here as Tàxìzǐ (獺戲子)—attained the non-conceptual concentration (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and acquired the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). He flew into the royal palace, but subsequently lost his supernormal powers and concentration, returning to the mountains on foot.
Ārāḍa—here translated as "Laxity"—was also one who had attained supernormal powers and meditative concentration.
Rājā Nahuṣa—here translated as "One Who Does Not Serve Fire.
King Yayāti—according to ancient pronunciation, translated as "King of Numerous Deeds" (or "King of Many Practices").
King Śibi—his ancient pronunciation was also *Śivi*, which means "Peaceful Security" (*an-yǐn*).
The king of the *śakunta* birds—his ancient pronunciation was translated as "Sweet-Grain Mouse.
Mount Mālaya is also called Mālaya-dhara.
The Rishi Kaniṣka is also called Kaniṣkanu (the "nu" being pronounced with the *hou* tone); this is translated as "Victorious Rishi.
The Rishi Vasu was translated according to its ancient pronunciation as "Jeweled Rishi."
The city of Kālapura is translated here as "Foul Ground.

[Volume] Thirty-nine, Part Three. Jātiśrona is translated as "Vow-Courage" (Yuan-yong). The Dharma Master Yuan says that this refers to a non-Buddhist heretic of wrong views who clings to the notion that *nirvāṇa* is impermanent.
Vāsiṣṭha—here translated as "Most Excellent" (zuìshèng) or "Supreme" (zuìshàng)—is also of the same school of false views as Jaṭila.
Śreṇika and Kāśyapa are both said to be non-Buddhist practitioners of the view of self (ātman-dṛṣṭi).
Pūrṇa and Śuddhika are non-Buddhist outsiders who hold extreme views (antagrāhadṛṣṭi).
The Brahmin Vatsīputra is a non-Buddhist outsider characterized by doubt, meaning he doubts whether the Path exists or not, as well as doubting those who have attained it.

The *Nāṭaputta* (Nigaṇṭha) ascetics are naturalistic non-Buddhists (*svabhāvavādin*) who assert that all phenomena exist by way of their own nature; they are also subsumed under the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

As for Āḷāra Kālāma and Uddaka Rāmaputra, they are non-Buddhists characterized by adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*): Āḷāra Kālāma clung to alms-gathering as the path, while Uddaka Rāmaputra clung to ascetic practices as the path.

Regarding the surname *Gautama* (written as 瞿曇): the "nu" (奴) is pronounced with the "li" (禮) tone; this refers to calling the Buddha by his surname, which is an error in the transcription of the character's form, so I request that you repent. Furthermore, the character written as "ni" (你), where "nu" (奴) is pronounced with the "li" (履) tone, meaning "you" or "your," is likewise identical to this.
*Sumana* flowers—also called *sūmāna*, which in this language means "flowers of good intention.
The *chīchī* tree (the first character is pronounced with a rising tone, the second with an entering tone).

The *dànzǐ* (pomegranate): *dàn* is pronounced as in *rǔchuī*. The *Yùpiān* states: it is a fruit-bearing tree of the *ruí* genus; it grows in small clusters and has thorny seeds that are also edible.
Kāśyapa; here it is translated as the family name *Guī* (Turtle).
Pūrṇa; here it is translated as "Full. *Zhēn*:
with the earth-tone *tǐng* and the level tone *jīn*; the *Guǎngyá* states that when trees grow in clusters they are called *zhēn*, and when grasses grow in clusters they are called *bó*.

40. Fascicle Forty. "Cheryu" (車輿): The second character is pronounced *yù* (with the level tone) and is also interchangeable. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to a carriage. Ying Yin states that a carriage without wheels is called a *yù*.
The standard form for "hook and bait" (gou-er) should be written as 𧊗 (pinyin: yì, with the tone mark 去聲); Fu Qian states that "to hook a fish is called 'bait'.

"Sucking at the breast" (sou-nu) is also written as 嗽, both having the same pronunciation (suǒjiǎo). The *Sancang* states it means "to urge one to suck. The *Tongshu wén* says that "inhaling by suction is called 'sucking' (sou). The character used in the sutra text is 𡂡, which is a vulgar form.

The character 𨷲 is an archaic form used interchangeably with 鑰 (yào). According to the *Fāngyán* (Dialects), those from the region east of the pass call it *jiàn* (key), while those from the region west of the pass call it *𨷲*. The received text uses the character 籥 (*yuè*), which the *Zīlín* explains as "a bamboo tally for a scribe. The *Cuǎnwén* states that in the region west of the pass, written scrolls are called *shūyù* (book-tally), but this does not refer to the meaning of the door-key *𨷲*. The pronunciation of 笘 is *chìzhàn* (zhàn being pronounced *zhàn*).

The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Chapter on Kauṇḍinya, Section on Cremation. Volume One, Part One. Compiled by Huilin. *Hàn* (上頷): pronounced with the "gǎn" (感) rhyme; according to the *Fāngyán*, it refers to the jaw. The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radical "fù" (負) and the phonetic "hé" (合), or it is written as *hàn* (頷); the version in the sutra uses *hàn* (頷), which is a vulgar character.

"Turbid" (hùnzhuó): the first character is pronounced *hùn* (with the *wěn* rhyme). Gu Yewang states that "hùn" also means "filthy and turbid. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "water" and the phonetic "kūn"; it is also written as "hùn.
Regarding "turbulent waves" (*tāobō*), see the *Fajing jing yinji*.

2. Lower Scroll, Part Two. *Yīnyè* (喑咽): The first character, *yīn*, is pronounced with the initial *yì* (邑) and the final rhyme *ín* (吟). The *Fāngyán* (方言) states that "to weep without sound is called *yīn*. The *Jíxùn* (集訓) explains it as "muttering" (*yīn-ǎ*). In the standard orthography of both ancient and modern times, this character follows the radical for the mouth (*kǒu*) and uses the phonetic component *yīn* (音).

Fēnfù (芬馥): "Fú" is pronounced as *fén* (with the *mù* rhyme). In the *Han Shi* (韓詩), "fù" is also explained as "fēn. According to the *Mao Shi Zhuan* (毛詩傳), "fù" means "the fragrance is white. In the *Jīngǔ Zhèngzì* (古今正字), it is written with the radical "xiāng" (香) and the phonetic "xià" (夏). The pronunciation of "xià" is the same as "shàng" (上).
*Kiṅkāng* (金剛): "Kāng" is pronounced with a retroflex *lǎn* (郎) final. It denotes a sound like that of striking steel; "kāng" means firm and hard.

In the *Wenzi Jilüe* (文字集略), it is said that gold is the essence of metal. *Shù'ěr* (儵爾): "Shù" is pronounced with a retroflex *shòu* (宍) final. Wang [Yī]’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that "shùhū" describes the appearance of lightning; the *Shuowen Jiezi* says "shùhū" also denotes swiftness, formed from the radical "black" (*hēi*) and the phonetic "yōu" (*yōu*).

Regarding "máo-shào" (spear/lance): the "Mò" in "Mò-hòu" is pronounced as in "mò" (the opposite of "hòu"). In the *Lǔshì Chūnqiū*, it is said that Chīyóu invented the spear (*máo*). Examining the phonetics, it belongs to the class of "shǒu," "máo," and "gē. The *Shuōwén* states that a spear is twenty *zhàng* long and is mounted on a war chariot; it is a pictographic character. The version in the [Confucian] Classics uses "kǒu," which is a vulgar character. The lower radical is "shuāng" (pronounced as in "shuāng-zhuó"). According to the *Bóyá*, "shào" is also a spear. The *Jīngǔ Zhèngzì* says that a "shào" is eighteen *zhàng* long. The *Wénzì Diǎnshuō* says that the current "jǐ-shào" (halberd-lance) follows the "máo" radical with "xiào" as its phonetic; the Classics use "zhuì," which means a platform or shelf, and does not accord with the meaning of the Classics.

Regarding *pāśa* (羂索): the upper character is pronounced *jiān* (涓, 兗). The *Guìyuàn Zhūcóng* states that to encircle and bind an object with a rope is called a *pāśa*. The *Shuowén* defines it as "a loop" (*gāng*), formed from the radical *gāng* with the phonetic *juàn*. It is also written as *guàn* (罥), where the lower character is pronounced *sāng* (桑, 各). The *Jixùn* explains it as "rope. The *Wenzidian* states that it is formed from the radical *mí* (糸) with the phonetic *shì* (市); its appearance in the scriptures as *jù* (䌇) is an error.

Regarding "jintán" (金罎): the *Tukǎo* (徒考) states that "tán" is a type of earthenware vessel. The *Jixùn* (集訓) also says it belongs to the category of *wǔ* (甒); "wǔ" is pronounced *wǔfǔ*. The character used in the classics is *dǐng* (壜), which is a vulgar form.

"Mao-dào" (旄纛) [the character *máo* is pronounced *pú*]. The *Jixùn* states: "Its shape is like a pole, adorned with feathers; it serves as a standard in the army. Cāi Yōng’s *Dúduàn* states: "'Dào' refers to a banner made from the tail of a wild ox (*bìniú*), as large as a peck (*dǒu*), which is placed atop the head of the leftmost side-horse (*fēi*). In ancient and modern times, the correct orthography follows the radical 'silk' (*mián*) and the phonetic 'dú'. The character 'dú' consists of 'chě' (草) above and 'xuán' (縣) below; the vulgar form uses 'chě' (屮), which is pronounced *chǒuliè*."

*Kaidào* (慨悼): "Kāi" is pronounced as *kǎi* (with the initial *k-*) and the final *-ai*. The *Huáinán* [Commentary] states that it means "to be indignant when one's ambitions are not realized. The *Kǎoshēng* [Dictionary] states it means "to lament with sorrow. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical *xīn* (heart) and the phonetic *jì*.

*Dàpānníhuán jīng* (大般泥洹經), Scroll One: Compiled by Xuanying. *Āitòng* (哀慟): "Tòng" is pronounced as *tòng* (with the initial *g-*) and the final *-ong*. The *Lúnyǔ* states: "When Yán Huí died, Zǐ [Kǎng] wept for him until he was *tòng*. Mǎ Róng’s commentary states: "*Tòng* refers to grief that exceeds the ordinary."

*Zǎoshòu* (澡漱): The upper character is pronounced *zāo* (with the tone of *lǎo*) and the lower character is pronounced *shòu* (with the tone of *suì*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "zǎo" means to wash the hands, and "shòu" means to rinse the mouth.

The text’s reading as *sòu* is an error. *Liaokōng* (寮孔): The character is pronounced *liáo* (with the tone of *liǎo*). According to the *Cangjie Pian*, it refers to a small opening. The text’s reading as the distant *liáo* (遼) is not consistent with the meaning of the scripture.
The character 豪 (háo) is written as 𦬆 in ancient texts, with the same pronunciation as 無方 (wúfāng), meaning "fine and sharp like the awn of grain.

The form 󲑀 found in the current edition of the scripture is incorrect. Volume Two. Second Fascicle. The term 羅寇 (luó kòu) has the pronunciation *kòu-hòu*. In the *Shàngshū* (Book of Documents), it appears in the phrase "bandits, thieves, and treacherous rebels" (*kòuzé jiānɡǒu*). Fàn Níng’s *Jíshēng* states: "A *kòu* refers to those who move in groups to commit robbery and plunder. The *Shuowén Jiězì* defines 󲉀 as "violence. The *Guǎngyá* defines 󲉀 as "to snatch. The term 剽 (*piāo*) has the pronunciation *pǐ miào*.

"Ancestor" (zǔ) and "send off" (sòng): according to the *Erya*, "ancestor" means "beginning. The *Shijing* says, "Zhongshan set out from his ancestor's place" (*zhōng shān zì chū zǔ*). This refers to the sacrifice performed at the *bà* altar when about to depart. *Bà* is pronounced *pú dá*.
*Chángjué* (long farewell): "Jué" means to sever. The *Tōngsùwén* states that to take leave of the deceased is called *jué*. The *Yùnlèi* states that *jué* also means separation.

Volume Three, Part Three: *Yòu* (a type of rodent). Pronounced *yǒu* (rhyme with *xiù*). It resembles a macaque but is larger, dark gray or black in color, and capable of catching mice; it is a creature noted for its agility and strength.
*Chen*: (pronounced *chǔ jǐn*); according to the *Tōngsùwén*, "when sand or soil enters food, it is called *chen*.
4. Fourth Fascicle. *Gūshīluó* (pronounced *jú jù*); this is a Sanskrit term. According to the *Zhōngběnqǐjīng*, *Gūshīluó* translates as "Beautiful Sound" (*Měiyīn*).

"Raising the arms so that the sleeves turn back" (*rǎng bì ér yáng fǎn mào*). The *Commentary on the Odes* (*Shīchuán*) states: "To 'remove' (*rǎngchú*) means to pull back the sleeves to expose the arms. "Ār" (arm) is pronounced *bì mèi*; "mèi" (sleeve) is pronounced *mí shì*.

The character for "banquet" (yàn) in the Stone Classics is an archaic form of the character for "banquet" (yàn), pronounced with the same *jian* rhyme. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "yàn" means "peaceful rest," referring to an appearance of tranquility. The text in the Stone Classics instead uses the character for "pain" (xī), pronounced with the *xu* and *ji* rhymes; this character for "pain" is not used here.

5. Fascicle Five. *Jiānkuì* (堅凷)—now written as *kuài* (塊) with the phonetic *kǔduì*—the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "hard soil. The *Sancang* defines it as "a lump of earth. *Lái* (犛)—also written as *láo* (犛) or *láo* (犛)—has two forms and shares the same pronunciation;
according to Xu Zishan, it is pronounced *sì* (似). The *Erya* states: "*Lái* resembles an ox, has a single horn, is blue in color, and weighs one thousand *qīn*."
*Śé* (pronounced *xiāo*) means "to roast.
*Páo* (pronounced *āo*) [means the same].
"Lì" (pronounced *liè*, with the radical *lì* and the phonetic *zhé*)—the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "lì" means fierce fire; the *Guangya* states that "lì" means intense heat.

Regarding the *mǎcǎo* (Ephedra): it has no specific therapeutic application; it is simply called "poisonous grass" (*mǎocǎo*). It originates from Youzhou, and people there often grind it and mix it with food or place it in water. If fish eat it, they all die and float to the surface; one may then take these fish to eat without harm.

*The Vaipulya Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Volume One, Part One. (In the *Xuanying Yinzhi*, the character 臏 is also written as 𩪯; both are pronounced with the *bì* rhyme, following the *Bìrèn* [必刃] rhyme. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that the knee bone is called 髕; the *Sancang* states it is the kneecap.)

"Face-creased" (*miàn-zhòu*): according to the *Yùnlèi zhuǎn*, "wrinkling" means the skin of the face gathers together; it refers to not smoothing out the wrinkles. The text of the sutra uses the character "zhòu," which is a borrowed character.
"Measuring traces" (*liàng-jì*) is also written as "jì"; these two forms are identical and pronounced *zǐ yì*. This refers to footprints. The text of the sutra uses "jì," which is incorrect.
CHĀN (潺) and HUÁNG (橫): "Shàn" (仕) and "huán" (環), both pronounced with the second tone; according to dictionaries, *chānruán* (潺湲) describes the appearance of flowing water.

FŔ (輔) and PĪ (弼): "Fǔ" (扶) and "yù" (禹), both pronounced with the second tone; the *Māoshī* (韓詩) states it means "to assist. Below, there are also three forms: 󲖾, 㢸, and 󲇧, all pronounced with the second tone, *pí* (皮) and *bì* (筆); *bì* (弼) means "to correct."

2. End of Volume Lower. Regarding the character *bī* (卑): it should be written as *sī* (廝), with the phonetic *xīyí*. According to the dictionary, *sī* refers to a lowly servant. He (He Yan) notes that the *Gongyang zhuan* calls such people "lowly servants. *Sī* also means "subtle" or "lowly. It is sometimes written as *wēn* (㒋). The text reads *sī* (󲖊), pronounced *sī*, meaning "blessing. The character *lǐ* (㒋) does not carry this meaning.
*Śoṅ-ṅu*: "Sī" is pronounced *lóng-fǎn*; the character below is written as *ṅǎ*, which is the same. "Bì-shī-fǎn" is the name of a country. "Ā-ṅǔ":
"chū-jǐa-fǎn" is the name of a Buddha; in the scriptural text, it is written with the "grain" radical (*禾*) as *ṅǔ*, which must be an error.

Regarding the *he-ya* (鶡鴨): according to various scriptures, it is written as *he-ya*; the first character is pronounced *hu-gē* (胡割反), and the second is also written as *yǒu* (鵪), with the same pronunciation *yú-jia* (於甲反). The *he* resembles a pheasant but is larger and blue-green in color; it has bristly horns (*mao-jue*) that fall off only after it dies in combat. Therefore, warriors wear the *he-guan* (鶡冠) helmet to emulate this bird. Thus, the scriptural text uses the character *jie* (羯), pronounced *ju-yùe* (居謁反), which refers to a sheep and does not accord with the meaning of the scripture. Based on my own observation, there should subsequently be four sections concerning the Bodhisattvas Mahākāruṇika and Mahāvyūha, which have been moved forward to be appended at the end of the twenty-fourth fascicle before the section on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. Those who conduct inspections should take note of this.
The Phonetic Explanations of All Scriptures, Volume Twenty-six;
The Phonetic Explanations of All Scriptures, Volume Twenty-seven.
The phonetic readings for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (in eight fascicles) are as follows; the *Addenda to the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* uses the same [readings].

Preface to the Phonetic Readings of the Lotus Sutra, composed by the Scripture-Translating Śramaṇa Dajing, and further verified by the Scripture-Translating Śramaṇa Huilin. Regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
This is to strike upon the subtle words of the profound caverns and awaken to the deep principles of the vast mechanism;
it is to exalt the True Vehicle to propagate Emptiness.
It eclipses the brilliance of the sun’s chariot upon the celestial highway;
it unfolds the waters of awakening to provide a hidden ford;
it nurtures the vast marshes that connect the terrestrial axis.
Is this not truly the seal of the Dharma King’s virtue, the means by which living beings tread the path of practice?
Thus, the eminent monks of the Golden Land, hearing his widespread renown, universally returned to the truth and delved into its profound mysteries.
The eminent scholars of Mount Yao all draw upon the Way to seek its ultimate source;
those who savor its flavor are truly numerous,
and those who deliberate upon and chew its essence are not few.
As for the *Gong* and *Yu* [notes], they have never had even a faint trace of consistency and frequently exhibit discrepancies.
Since you, Master, have merely circulated the text as mere chapters and sentences,
I, your younger brother, have likewise only heard it by hearsay along the road.
The remaining [texts] were not omitted; they further clarified the path for those who were deluded.
Kuiji went there to consult them and translated them, thereby performing subtle merit on both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna levels.
Although the phrasing has not been refined into a masterful composition,
it has undergone considerable instruction from teachers; yet,
upon examining various compilations, I find no single source from which I can properly follow.
Thereupon, he roused his indignation to emulate the former masters and took pity upon later scholars;
he composed the *Xuanzan* (Profound Praise) in ten fascicles and the *Yinxun* (Phonetics and Exegesis) in one fascicle.
In composing this commentary, I have first consulted the original treatises,
supplementing them with insights from other classics;
in transcribing the phonetics, I have taken the *Shuowen Jiezi* as my standard.
The subtle instructions are gleaned from other sources;
their purport is indeed refined and profound.
I have roughly examined them to exhaustively trace their origins and lineages.
Though my literary elegance and refined compositions are meager, I have nonetheless gathered together the fundamental origins.
Although I have not yet established a definitive guide,
I truly consider this to be a profound pursuit of the defeated.
May those of wise discernment take this to heart; thus, may the transformation from the turbid waters of Li to the ford of Sang be realized,
and may its radiance soar like a brilliant flower without ceasing.
Mists drift over the slopes of the Yu Ridge as the transmission of its fragrance remains imperishable;
reflecting upon this without end,
I shall now describe its profound and subtle charm.
1. The Introduction: The Lotus Sutra, Chapter One, the Introduction. In the Sanskrit language, it is called *Saddharmapuṇḍarīkasūtra*.
*Sat* means "wondrous" (*miao*) and also "correct" (*zheng*).
*Dharma* means "Dharma.
In the Western Regions, the white lotus flower is called *puṇḍarīka*.
*Sūtra* means "scripture."
It should be called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Emitting white light from the ūrṇā-kośa and riding upon a white ox—
white being the source of all colors.
Because the One Vehicle serves as the foundation for the Two Vehicles, the Wondrous Dharma is likened to the white lotus flower.

Since the Sanskrit original lacks a distinct word for "white," it is simply referred to as "lotus flower. This term encompasses the meanings of upholding and gathering manifold auspiciousness; thus, the *Miaoyu pian* (Exquisite Jade Lexicon) defines it as "wondrous essence" (*miao-jing*), while others define it as "the appearance of being wondrous and excellent."
In ancient texts, "from the profound" (*xuan*) constitutes the "wondrous Dharma" (*miaofa*), which serves as a standard and model;
it is also that which is upheld.

The character "hua" (flower) signifies flourishing and blooming, encompassing all forms of beauty to manifest the lotus. The *Yupian* states: "The character 'lian' (lotus) refers to the fruit of the *fúqú* (water lily)."

The character "huā" (flower) was translated in ancient times as "huá" (silk); however, since the character "huá" does not possess the phonetic value of "huā," it is not adopted here. "Jīng" (sutra/axis) means to thread together or to encompass. The *Yùpiān* states that it means long-lasting or constant; it also refers to managing, seeking out, the measurement of distances, law, principle, and measure. Generally, east-west lines are called "wèi" (woof) and north-south lines are called "jīng" (warp); this is a metaphor for weaving.

The character *xù* (序) is pronounced with the initial *xú* and the final *lǚ*. It signifies "to lead to" (*yóu zhì*), as in "the school buildings" (*xiáng xù*) or "to explain" (*quán xù*). The *Yùpiān* states that the east and west halls are called *xù*, and it is a place for arranging the ranks of honor. *Xù* also means "leisurely learning" (*shū xué*) or "instruction according to order," where elders and juniors are distinguished. It is composed of the radical *guǎng* (广) and the phonetic *yǔ* (予).
"Pin-pin" (品品) means to gather together in groups and to classify by category. Furthermore, the *Yupian* states that it means "beneficial progress," "law," "category," or "model.
"Di" (第) is pronounced with the *ji* rhyme; it means "to dwell. The *Yupian* also states it means "sequence" and refers to a "disciple."
"Each and every one" (*ekaika*) means "foremost. The *Yùpiān* states that it signifies "sameness," the beginning of numbers, the ultimate of things, the initial, and the few.

In Sanskrit, "Buddha" is called *buddha*, which here is translated as "the Awakened One. This term omits the character *tuó* (陀) and simply says "Fó" (佛). Because he possesses all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), he is able to awaken himself and also able to awaken all sentient beings—like awakening from a dream or like the blooming of a lotus flower—and for this reason he is named "Buddha. While it contains many meanings, I have spoken briefly here.

Gṛdhrakūṭa: On the mountain, the sound "Gṛdhrakūṭa" is transcribed as *Gijjhakuṭa* in Sanskrit; this is translated as "Vulture Peak" (*Jiùfēng*) or "Vulture Terrace" (*Jiùtái*). This is because vultures frequently dwell upon its peaks, and its shape resembles a high terrace. All other phonetic transcriptions are erroneous, and all other explanations are incorrect; fearing prolixity, they are not described here. Only the correct terms are cited, and all subsequent instances should be understood according to this principle.

"Bhikṣu" is in Sanskrit called *bhikṣu*; this term possesses five meanings: first, terrifying Māra; second, mendicant; third, pure livelihood; fourth, pure precepts; and fifth, destroying evil. "Wú" (無) means "not having" or "non-existence.

Alternatively, it is written as "wú," which the *Shuowen Jiezi* states is an archaic and rare character for "non-existence. That which penetrates "wú" is the Way of Emptiness and Non-being. "Fù" (復), with the Wu dialect pronunciation *fújiù* and the Qin dialect pronunciation *féngmù*, according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, means "coming and going"; it refers to the repetition of coming and going.

The character 逮 (dài) [with the phonetic 台 (tái) and radical 辶] means "to reach" or "to arrive at. According to the *Yǎ'ěr* (Elegant and Correct), it signifies "reaching. The *Fāngyán* (Regional Vocabulary) states that from the region east and west of Guān, they call "arriving" or "reaching" *dài*. There is a variant reading 逯 (lù), pronounced *lì gù*, but this is incorrect. The *Guǎngyǎ* (Extended Elegant) defines 逯 as "a multitude," and the *Shuōwén Jiězì* (Explaining Simple and Analyzing Compound Characters) gives it another pronunciation, *lì zú*, meaning "to walk cautiously"; it also notes that it is a personal surname. None of these meanings correspond to "reaching" or "arriving."

Ājñātakauṇḍinya—its Sanskrit name is Ājñātakaundinya; *ājñāta* means "understood," so called because he was the first to understand the Dharma. *Kauṇḍinya* is a Brahmin clan name; *kaundinya* is a masculine form indicating descent from his father's lineage. In newly translated scriptures, he is rendered as "Ajñā Kauṇḍinya."

Mahākāśyapa (pronounced shé in Chinese; in Sanskrit, Mahākāśyapa, meaning "Great Drinker of Light") was of the Brahmin clan. The title "Great" (Mahā) manifests his exalted virtue, distinguishing him from the common masses.

Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, Nadī-Kāśyapa, and Gayā-Kāśyapa—the latter being so named because there was a dragon in a pond called Uruvilvā (meaning "large gourd") that had a mark on its chest resembling a gourd. Thus it was named accordingly.
Gayākāśyapa: Gayā is the name of a mountain.
Nadīkāśyapa: Nadī is the name of the river Nairañjanā.
Śāriputra: Śāri-putra; this is translated as "Son of the Śāri."

Mahāmaudgalyāyana (the "Dà Mùqiéluán" in Chinese; in Sanskrit, *Mahā-maudgalyāyana*, which means "Clansman of the Maudgalya" or "Descendant of the Green-Bean Mother") belongs to the lineage of the sage who gathered green beans (*mudga*). His father’s original name was Kṛtika (also written as Jūlìduō or Jūlùtuó, both of which are corruptions).
Mahākātyāyana (the *kā* is pronounced *chán*, though some write it as *zhān*;
*mahākātyāyana* translates as "Great One of the Kātya Clan"; *kātya* is the name of a Brahmin lineage, derived from the term for those who practice hair-cutting).
*Ānanda*: "Ānu" (with the *nu* and *gou* reversed as the phonetic transcription) means "rabbit," or it is also written as *tǔ*.
*Lodha* (with the *tang* and *zuo* reversed) is *Aniruddha*, which here means "Unextinguished."
Kapphiṇa (translated in Chinese as *Fángxiù*, "Lunar Mansion Star"); Gavāmpati Guhyapatti (this means "Ox-Aspect");

Revata Khadiravata (this means "Chamber Star," a star of the north; because one worshipped it and obtained a son, he was named after it; some versions read Revata, but *Li-bō-duō* [Revata] should be corrected to *Li-bō-duō* [Revata] as correct).
Piliṅgavatsa (畢陵伽婆蹉)— *piliṅga* being pronounced with a retroflex *ṛ* and *vatsa* meaning "remaining habit" (*vāsanā*)— and Bakula (薄拘羅)—
*bakula* being translated in the Tang language as "Good Appearance" (*śubhavarṇa*).
Mahākauṣṭhila (the *chi* and *zhi* rhymes differently);
Mahākauṣṭhila means "Great Thigh" in Chinese;
Nanda means "Joy" in the Tang language.
Sundarananda (孫陀羅難陀), here translated as "Delightful Joy.

Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra (富樓那彌多羅尼子), *pūrṇa* meaning "full" (*man*), *maitrāyaṇī* being the feminine form of "Maitrāyaṇi" used to call out "Maitrī" (Compassion), and *putra* meaning "son. Maitrī is the mother's name and Pūrṇa is his own name; thus this Venerable One is the son of the woman named Maitrī, or alternatively, both Pūrṇa and Maitrī are names for the mother, hence he is called the "Son of Pūrṇa-Maitrī. Other explanations exist, but they are all incorrect.
Subhūti; *sūbhūti* means "Well-Appeared" (*shanxian*). Ānanda;
*ānandā* means "Joyful Celebration" (*qingxi*). Rāhula; *rāhula* means "Grasper of the Sun.

Originally, he was named "Grasper of the Sun" because he was the vanguard of the Asuras, who are called "Non-Gods" (*feitian*). He grasped the sun with his hand to obstruct its intense light; thus, he is named after this metaphor.
Mahāprajāpatī Mahāprajāpatī means "Great Sovereign of Beings.
Yaśodharā Yaśodharā means "Bearer of Renown."

The term *bhikṣuṇī* (nun) and the feminine vocalization of *bhikṣu* possess five meanings as previously explained. [The character] *bá* (颰蒲撥反; also written as *bá*) is also acceptable. *Bodhisattva-mahāsattva*: *Bodhi* means awakening or wisdom; *sattva* means sentient being, courage, skillful means (*upāya*), or that which is sought.

Because one relies on the words of great vows—seeking the fruit of awakening through wisdom and delivering sentient beings through compassion—one is called a *bodhisattva*. Alternatively, it refers to those sentient beings who seek the fruit of awakening or those who possess courage. Or, because they benefit and bring joy to others through wondrous grace and excellent skillful means in every way, they are called *bodhisattva*. Regarding *mahāsattva* (great sentient being): this distinguishes them from those who seek minor awakening or those in inferior, ordinary states; thus, they are named *mahāsattva*.
*Anu*: (The "nu" is pronounced with a retroflex *vo* [反] in modern times, but in ancient pronunciation it was *nu-dou* [反]; it means to weed or cultivate, used here as a phonetic loan.

*Tāra-samyak-mi*: (The "mi" is pronounced with a retroflex *yao* [反]. Its original sound was *zi* [紫], as in the plant *zi-cao*; according to the *Yupian*, it is pronounced *mo-jiao* [反] or *mi-shao* [反], but now it is used with the borrowed sound *mi-yao* [反].)
*Tri-sambodhi-anuttara* (三菩提阿耨) and below should be rendered collectively as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (無上正等正覺). *Mārga* (末伽) means "path" (*mārga*), and *bodhi* (菩提) means "awakening" (*bodhi*).
*Dhāraṇī* (陀羅尼) means "total retention" (*dhāraṇī*), which briefly contains much within a small [term].

"Shí (殖) [top radical: zhòng (眾); [phonetic: shì (時), lì (力) reversed; in the *Cāngjié piān*, it means 'to plant'; in the *Guǎngyá*, it means 'to accumulate' or 'to establish'. For the bottom radical, both the level tone and the departing tones are acceptable.

"Chángwéi (常爲) [phonetic: róng (榮), wěi (偽) reversed; in the *Yùpiān*, it means 'to cause' or 'to be subjected to'. "Mǔhóu (母猴): this creature loves its claws for holding onto people. Mǔhóu (母猴) takes the character xiàng (象) as its image; the character xiàng (象) is used for its form."
Mañjuśrī, also known as Mañjuśiri, is translated here as Miaojixiang (Wondrous Auspiciousness).

Bhadrapāla—*bhadra* being a transliteration where *ba* is pronounced with the *pan-mo* (pa-ma) rhyme according to the Cangyun, and it is also written as *ba*; some say that *Bhadrapāla* is the Sanskrit pronunciation, which is translated as Xianhu (Worthy Protector); the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra calls him Shanshou (Good Guardian).
*Maitreya-maitriye*—this is translated as "Maitreya" (慈氏). "Maitreya" is his ancestral surname, or it may be taken as his clan name derived from his mental activity (*citta-vṛtti*).

*Śakra-devānām-indra*: *Śakra* is the Śākya clan; *deva* means "heavenly being" (*deva*); *indra* means "lord" (*indra*), specifically the Lord of the Gods in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. *Śākya-kṣatriya*: *Kṣatriya* is translated as "capable" (*neng*). *Devānām-indra* is the Sovereign of the Gods. That is, the Heavenly Lord among the Śākyas.

*Sahā* (娑婆) is translated in the Tang language as *Kāṃsaha* (堪忍), meaning "endurance. Because the Noble Ones (*ārya*) are able to endure weariness and toil while carrying out their work of conversion within this world, it is named "Endurance" (*Kāṃsaha*).
Brahmā (梵天) and Brahmā (梵摩): here translated as "tranquil" (寂靜), or "pure and clean" (清淨潔); Ge Hong’s *Ziyuan* explains *brahman* as "clean.
Bhadanta (跋難陀): "Worthy and Joyful" (賢喜).
Sāgara is also known by the name Sāgaro, meaning the "Salt Sea. Vāsuki means "Nine-Headed.
Takṣaka means "Many-Tongued."
Anavatapta (Anava-ta-da), translated in Chinese as "Pool Without Heat or Torment" (Wu re nao chi).
Mānasa (Mo-na-si), translated here as "Compassionate Mind" (Ci xin).
Utpala (Ou-po-luo), translated as "Red Lotus"; although some versions write it as "You-po," it should correctly be derived from *utpala*.
*Kinnara* (緊那羅) and *Kiṃnara* (緊捺落) are translated as "Singing Deity" (*gēshén*).

They cause others to delight in the five [sensual pleasures]; in Sanskrit they are called *manuṣya*, which here is *mānuṣa*, translated as "To the Likening" (*kěyì*) or also "As One Wishes" (*rúyì*).
