The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (Zhèngfǎhuā jīng) states: "The first is named Róuruán (Softness), the second is named Héyīn (Harmonious Sound) Devaputra. This refers to them.

*Gandharva* (the *da* in *gandharva* is pronounced with a retroflex *ṛ*, hence *dǎn fǎn*); this is translated as "Fragrance-Seeker" (*xúnxīng*) and refers to the gods who create music. They also exist within the ocean and are subordinate to the devas.
*Asura* (*ā-sù-luó*; in the Tang language, "Non-God").

*Bāzhi* (婆稚) and *Bāzhìjiā* (跋稚迦) mean "cloud"; *Zhèngfǎhuā* (正法華) states that one name for it is *zuìshèng* (最勝), which means "most excellent. *Bàtuó* (跋陀) signifies "bound" (*bǐfù*, 被縛); *zhì* (稚) may also be written as *yè* (𧙤) or *zhì* (穉), all of which have the same pronunciation, namely *zhì* (直利反).
*Kharaskandha* (pronounced *khar-kan-da*) means "Broad Shoulders.
*Vemacitra* (pronounced *ve-ma-cit-ta-ra*) means "Variegated Painting" or "Jeweled Ornament."
Rāhula (羅睺羅) means "Grasper" (of the moon). Garuḍa (迦樓羅) means "Wondrous-Winged Bird. Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī (韋提希子), [is called] Vai-dehi-jaya;

*vai* signifies "supreme" (*paramārtha*), and *dehi* means "body," which is the name for the Eastern Continent (Pūrvavideha). *Videha-nandana*—this is the name of a mountain deity; because he was obtained through a request from that deity, it became the mother's title. Aduṭṭha-setṭhu (阿杜多設咄路) means "Unborn Enemy" (*Ajātaśatru*); it is also known by the alternative name King Śakrāditya (折指王).

*Jiāzuǒ* (cross-legged sitting): according to the *Erya*, this means "to add weight" (*jiāzhòng*). It refers to sitting with the legs crossed. The *Chuzai* and *Hengjing* commentaries state that it is "binding the crossed feet in sitting. There is also the term *juzuò* (sitting on the heels), which is a vulgar character of uncertain origin. In the region south of the Yangtze River, sitting with the knees spread apart is called *pànkuà zuò* (spread-knee crossing-sitting); in Shandong, it is called *jiǎjuzuò* (shell-crossed sitting). *Pàn* is pronounced *báhuàn*; *kuà* is pronounced *kǒuhuà*.
*Amalārtha* (Infinite Meanings): the character *yù* is pronounced with a departing tone (*qùshēng*).
*Samādhi*: the character *mò* is pronounced *pèi* [as in *pèi*]; *samādhi* is translated here as "equipoise" (*děngchí*), meaning to hold the mind in equanimity while abiding in the object.
*Devavarṣa* (Heavenly Rain): the character *yú* is pronounced *jǔ* [as in *jǔ*] and also has the sound *yù*.

The character for "man" (曼) is pronounced as above; the character for "wan" (萬) has a variant form with the radical "from ten thousand" (從萬), which is a vernacular character. Here it is borrowed and pronounced "mòbān" (莫般反) to accord with the Sanskrit sound.
"Dhāra" (陀羅) refers to the "flower that satisfies the mind" (適意花).
The pronunciation of "man" (曼) is as in the upper tone.
"Shusha" (殊沙) refers to the *mṛdvīkā* flower, a soft and supple flower.
Regarding the six kinds of "earthquakes" (*ṣaḍvikāra-prakampa*), the *Yùpiān* states that "zhèn" (震) means to shake, to move, or to arise.

*Yakṣa* (藥叉) is here translated as "valiant and strong" (*yongjian*); they are those who fly through the air, though this term also encompasses those who travel on the ground. *Rākṣasa* (羅剎娑) is here translated as "violent and evil" (*baoye*), and is also called "terrifying."

*Mahoraga* (摩睺羅伽), also called *Maholaga*, translates as "Great-Bellied" (*Dabei*). They are of the class of great pythons, frogs, and the like. Regarding the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā*) between his eyebrows:

the *Zhuangzi Sushu* states that the finest of hairs are called "hairs" (*máo*); the *Yupian* states that "hair" (*máo*) refers to long body hair. According to the *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhisūtra*, when he was a prince, it extended five feet; under the Bodhi tree, it was one zhang, four chi, and five cun; and after he attained Buddhahood, it was one zhang and five chi. When released, it curls into a circle like the full autumn moon—distinct, bright, and pure, with a color like white jade or snow.
"Mí" (靡) and "mì" (密) are reversed; in the *Erya*, "mí" means "none.
"Abi" (阿鼻)—from here on it is called "Avīci," meaning "Without Interval.

Hell is called *naraka* in Sanskrit, which means "vessel of suffering," also "that which is not to be enjoyed," or "the place of non-action and unrighteous action. While some are located among mountains, in wildernesses, or in the air, what is here termed "hell" refers specifically to that which lies beneath the great earth.

Akaniṣṭha (the "A" is pronounced with a retroflex *ṇ* as in *zhà*; the ancient text reads *dù*, which has the same meaning; "ka" means obstruction or resistance; "niṣ" signifies the ultimate; "ṭha" is pronounced *chā*, with the initial sound like *chì*).
"Practicing" (xiūxíng) is the name for the act of bestowing [benefits]; it refers to the actual performance of cultivation.
"Appearance" (xiàngmào) is pronounced mòjiào; there are versions of the text that read "appearance" (mào), "blade" (rèn), or "stubbornness" (hěn), but none of these are correct.
*Pán* (般) is pronounced with the *fǎn* (反) of *guān* (官); for now, it is borrowed with the *fǎn* of *mò* (末).

*Niè* (涅) is pronounced with the *fǎn* of *niánjié* (年結). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "black earth in water," composed of the radicals for "water" (水) and "earth" (土), with the phonetic element *rì* (日). There are those who write it as *niè* (涅) with the radical for "work" (工), but this is incorrect.
*Parinirvāṇa* (translated in Chinese as *yuánjì*, "perfect quiescence"): *ni* is pronounced with the second tone (*nú jí*) and *bó* is called with the departing tone; *nǎn* is pronounced *nú xián*.
*Śarīra-śarīra* is translated here as "body" (*tǐ*).

*Tā* (塔) is, in Sanskrit, *stūpa*, which here means "high and manifest"; *caitya*, which means "sacred shrine. The Vinaya refers to it as *tapa* (塔婆); when there are no relics, it is called a *cetiya* (支提). The term "tā" used today is a corruption of *stūpa*. The character for "tā" does not exist in ancient texts; however, according to Ge Hong’s *Ziyuan* and the *Qieyun*, "tā" refers to a Buddha-hall or a Buddhist shrine.
Regarding "shuì" (瑞), the *Yuèpiān* states it means "a token of integrity"; "fúyìng" (符應) shares the same pronunciation as "shuì" (睡).
A *gāthā*—Sanskrit for which this is the Chinese translation "eulogistic verse"—refers to a song of praise. A *śloka* consists of thirty-two characters arranged in four lines, constituting one verse.

The character *róu* (柔) is pronounced with the rhyme *yǎn*. According to the *Guǎngyá*, "róu" means weak or pliant (*ruò*). In the *Tōngsùwénwù*, it is stated that what is pliant is called *ruǎn*. In the *Hànshū*, it says "pliant and unable to bear the burden. It is incorrect to write this as the common character *ruǎn*. The character *ruǎn* (耎) is interchangeable with *ruǎn* (軟); there is also a variant written as *rǎo* (𣽈), which is incorrect.
"Encountering suffering" (*zāokǔ*) means being weary of it; according to the *Yànpiān* (Rhyme Dictionary), "weary" (*yàn*) implies being satiated and having no further desire to engage in it.

"Ganges" (*héngshā*) is the name of a river deity; the river is named after its deity. This river possesses five meanings and is frequently employed as a metaphor in various sutras. The pronunciation of "Geng" (*qíngāng*) is *qín* (with the second tone) or alternatively with the third tone.

The *Shuowen* states that "Jin" (gold) refers to the yellow among the five colors of metal; it remains durable when buried for a long time, does not become light even after a hundred refinements, and does not resist being transformed according to the will of the smith. It is associated with the element of the West and thus takes the radical "earth" (土). The dots on the left and right represent the form of metal situated above the center. The current pronunciation is "yin"; it should have been written with the character "jin" (金).
Silver is white gold.
Coral is a red-colored gemstone.
Maṇi and *maṇiratna* are wish-fulfilling jewels.
*Śaṅkha-musāragalva-keśara*: this is translated as "conch-shell" (*śaṅkha*), which has slight intermingling of blue and white colors. *Aśmagarbha-keśara*:

this is translated as "vajra-treasury" (*aśma* meaning "vajra" and *garbha* meaning "treasury," or alternatively, "womb," referring to its solid core). It is called "agate" (*aśmagarbha*) because its color resembles that of a horse's brain; in various texts it is written with the character 瑪瑙 (mǎnǎo), as it belongs to the category of jade, or with the character 碼碯 (mǎnǎo), as it belongs to the category of stone.

*Nu* (奴) is pronounced with the *hu* tone reversal; in antiquity, there were those who committed crimes and were confiscated by the government to become slaves. According to the *Shuowen*, the archaic form is the character *jin* (仅).
*Bi* (婢) is pronounced with the *bi* tone reversal, where *bi* is pronounced as *bei*; according to the *Shuowen*, "slave" (*bi*) is a term for the lowly among women.

*Che* (pronounced *chāng yé* according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*) is the general term for the carriage body and wheels. It was created by Xi Zhong during the reign of the Xia dynasty. Its ancient pronunciation was *jū*. In antiquity, "carriage" (*che*) was pronounced like "dwell" (*jū*); it is that by which one dwells. Today’s "residence" (*jushè*) is derived from this. As for "dwelling" (*yánxíng suǒchǔ*), it refers to where one stays, just as a residence is a place of dwelling; it is a pictographic character representing the form of a house.
*Sheng* (乘) means "to ride" according to the *Guangya*, referring to that which may be mounted. In the *Zhouli*, four horses constitute a *sheng*; it refers to a vehicle for riding.

*Lian* (輦) [pronounced *liǎn*] is explained in the *Shuowen* as a carriage pulled by men; those in front lead it. In ancient times, high officials (*qingdafu*) also rode in *lian*. Since the Han dynasty, the Son of Heaven has used it; the *Yupian* states that the carriage used by the Son of Heaven and the Empress is called a *lian*.

*Yu*: "Yu" (余) and "ju" (與) [read as *yu* with two tones]. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as a carriage (*che-yu*). One interpretation says that a box-like structure without wheels is called a *yu*. Nowadays, the forms of carriages and carts have diverged from antiquity. The *Yupian* states it means "multitude," "to carry," "to lift," or "much. There are those who write it as *yu* (轝), but this is incorrect.

*Sì* (pronounced *xī*, with the tone reversed): According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, four horses harnessed together to one carriage are called *sì*. The *Yupian* states it means "to pursue"; the four stars of the *Fáng* mansion are called the *Tiānsì* (Celestial Chariot).

*Lán* (pronounced *luò*, with the tone reversed): A railing; sometimes written as *lán*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it is a barrier at a gate. Some original texts have *lán* meaning fragrant herb, but that is not the intended sense here. Both *lán* and *lán* are acceptable.

The character *shǔn* (楯) is pronounced with the *yǐn* (尹) rhyme-group. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "a railing or balustrade. Furthermore, Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* says, "The vertical bars are called *hàn* (檻) and the horizontal bars are called *shǔn* (楯). In the *Yupian*, under the "Wood" radical, it is pronounced with the *yǔn* (允) rhyme-group.

*Huagai* (華蓋): The character *huā* is pronounced as *hù* (with the rhyme *huān*). The *Gujin zhu* states: "When the Yellow Emperor fought with Chiyou in the wilds of Zhuolu, there were constantly five-colored clouds and vapors with golden branches and jade leaves that rested above the Emperor, appearing in the form of a flower-canopy (*huagai*). Therefore, he fashioned the flower-canopy based upon this. The character *huā* is also pronounced as *hūguā*. In the hot regions of the Western Regions, many people carry canopies adorned with flowers; these are the *dhvaja*, *patākā*, and *chattra* (banners, streamers, and canopies). *Zhuóluo* (𣵠鹿) is pronounced *zhuó*; *huǐ* (𧅅) is pronounced *huǐ*.

*Xiàn* (軒): Adorned above; "xū" (虛) and "yán" (言) are its phonetic components. The *Shēnglèi* states it is a "peaceful carriage" (*ānchē*). The *Shuōwén* says it is a carriage with curved shafts and side-panels (*fān*). It is also written as *xiǎn* (幰), with "xū" (虛) and "yǎn" (偃) as its phonetics. The *Yùpiān* states it is a cloth spread over the top of a carriage to ward off heat. It is adorned with precious objects to decorate the carriage. *Fān* (轓) is pronounced *fǔfán*. The character for "adornment" (*shì*) is composed of "food" (*sì*) and "center" (*zhōng*).

*Qī* (妻): Pronounced *qīng xī fǎn*. According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to a wife who is equal to oneself; it is composed of the radicals for "to hold" (*chí*) and "woman" (*nǚ*). She holds the duties of a wife's office.

Regarding *pí* (被): pronounced *pí yì fǎn*. It means "to wear" or "to don. There is also an original text reading *pī* (披), pronounced *fū jī fǎn*; according to the *Fāngyán*, this means "to spread," while today it means "to fasten on. It should [in this context] follow the reading *pī*.

*Māra* means "the Destroyer" (from the Chinese *pòhuài*). It is also called *Mārabhīja*, which means "the Evil One. The term *Pāpīyan* is a corruption; it refers to one who accomplishes evil dharmas and harbors an evil intent. Thus, both the name and the title of the Evil Māra, Pāpīyan, are explained.

*Yàn* (pronounced *yān*) means "to rest" (*ān-xī*). There is also a variant reading as *yàn* (pronounced *wū jiàn*), which also means "silent. In archaic script it is written as *yàn*, which likewise means "to rest.
*Cháng* (pronounced *shàng yáng*) means "to try"; the *Xiǎo Ěryǎ* states that it refers to doing something for a brief moment.

"Chui-tang" (捶打) means to strike; "shang" (上) is a counter-strike. The lower character "wǔ" (吳) is pronounced as *dǐng* (頂) with the tone of Wu, or alternatively as *dǐng* (都挺反) according to the Qin pronunciation, which is *dé-gěng* (得耿反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means to strike with a staff; the *Guangya* states that "chui" (捶) means to strike or beat.

Regarding the term *yàoshàn* (肴膳): "yào" (肴) is pronounced with the initial *hú* and rhyme *jiāo*. The *Guóyuè* states: "When drinking, there are *yáo* (肴). Jia Dui says: "*Yáo* refers to the sacrificial platter (*zǔ*). The *Yùpiān* says it refers to the contents of the bamboo basket (*dòu*). Generally, anything that is eaten which is not grain is called *yáo* (肴), meaning food or a meal consisting of vegetables and meat. The *Shuōwén* defines *shàn* (膳) as "prepared food. In the *Zhou Lǐ*, regarding the *Shànfū* (Master of the Kitchen), Zheng Xuan comments: "*Shàn* means 'excellent' (*shàn*). In modern times, fine things are also called "precious meals" (*zhēnshàn*). The *Guǎngyá* states: "*Yàoshàn* refers to meat. Both characters are formed with the radical for "meat" and the phonetic element "shàn. Furthermore, there are those who write it as *yáo shàn* (餚饍); however, these have no source and are merely vulgar characters produced in recent times.

"Candana" refers to *gośīrṣa-candana* (ox-head sandalwood) and the like; "red" refers to varieties such as *citraka* (rosewood), and "white" refers to the class of white sandalwood. The ancient transcription was "zhandan," while the *Qieyun* dictionary records it as "zhen" (𠿒), which is incorrect.

"Jiào-zhào" (敎詔) in the ancient texts is a compound of "jiào-xùn" (教訓, instruction) and "zhào-gào" (詔告, proclamation). According to the *Zìlín* (字林), "zhào" means to inform; according to the *Ěryǎ* (爾雅), it means to guide. Guō Pǔ states that it refers to instructing and leading. The *Shìmíng* (釋名) says: "Zhào" means to illuminate (*zhào*). When people are ignorant regarding established matters and commit transgressions, this is shown to them so that they may clearly (*zhàorán*) understand the source of their actions. There is a fundamental teaching (*běnjiào*) and an inviting teaching (*zhāojiào*); "zhāo" has no level tone (*píngyīn*), meaning to entice and advance [others].

Regarding the meaning of the measurement of *yojana* and *krośa*, other sūtras state that forty *li* constitute one *yojana*. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that from the *paramāṇu* (extremely minute particle), *aṇu*, *loharaja* (metal-dust), *ab-raja* (water-dust), *śaśaraja* (hare-dust), *aviraja* (sheep-dust), *goraja* (ox-dust), *chidraraja* (dust in a crevice), *likṣā* (nit), *yūkā* (louse), *yava* (barley-corn), and *aṅguli-parvan* (finger-joint), each subsequent unit increases sevenfold. Twenty-four finger-joints make one *hasta* (cubit); four *hasta* make one *dhanus* (bow-length); five hundred *dhanus* make one *krośa*; and eight *krośa* make one *yojana*, which is sixteen *li* and a half. Other [traditions] differ slightly.

"Zòng" (縱) is used interchangeably with "róng" (容). A poem says, "The fields run lengthwise and crosswise" (*cóng héng qí mǔ*). The *Màoshī Zhuàn* states that south-to-north is called "cóng" (lengthwise) and east-to-west is called "héng" (crosswise). In the *Zhou Lǐ*, regarding the dimensions of the territories of the Nine Provinces, Zhèng Xuán explains that "lún" (輪) means "cóng" (lengthwise) and "guǎng" (廣) means "héng" (crosswise). The *Guǎngyá* uses "cóng" (從), while the *Yùnshū* only uses the three characters "zōng" (蹤), "zòng" (縱), and "zìng" (䡮); as for using "cóng" (從), its origin is unknown.

"Jiāolù màn" (珠交露幔)—*màn* is pronounced as in *mòbàn* (莫半). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "a curtain (*mù*); it takes the radical 'cloth' (*jīn*) and the phonetic 'màn'. That which is on the sides is called a *wéi* (curtain), and that which is above is called a *mù* (canopy); *mù* means to cover, to cover what is exposed. In various sutras, terms such as "bead-interlaced canopy" (*zhūjiāolù gài*) and "bead-interlaced carriage" (*zhūjiāolù chē*) refer to the same thing. There is also the variant "màn" (*zhūjiāolù màn*), which the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines as "plain silk without pattern. This is not the correct form for "curtain" (*màn*). See the "Precious Stupa Chapter" (*Bǎotǎ pǐn*) for a further detailed explanation.

"Hemíng" (harmonious resonance): "Hé" is pronounced with the *gē* radical reversed [as *hú*]. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to music that is harmoniously tuned; it is as the *Shijing* says: "The bells ring out in harmony (*hé líng yāngyāng*).
As for the character "shì" (時) used here, it should be determined as being "shì" (是).
"Vei" (惟) in the *Yùpiān* means to think, to reflect, and to deliberate.
"Cǔn" (忖), with the radical *cāng* and the tone *běn*, means to measure.
"Yù" (雨) refers to the great rain of the Dharma; both characters are pronounced either as *chū* or *yú*.
"Blowing out" (*chuìchū*) refers to the *fǎn* (reversal) scale; it is now taken from the initial breath-sound. "Luóluò" (螺落) is a vulgar character for "over-reversal";
it refers to a water-insect. The correct form is "luówō" (蠃). "Asaṃkhyeya" (*āsaṃkhyeya*) is translated here as "innumerable" (*wúyāngshù*).

Regarding the limit of numbers, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that there are originally sixty fundamental numbers, but eight have been lost in transmission. "Innumerable" (*wúyāngshù*) is the fifty-second [number]. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that among one hundred and twenty numbers, "countless" (*wúshù*) is the one hundred and twentieth number.
*Kalpa* (劫) is translated here as "time-period" (*la-p'o*), which is the name for a division of time.
*Pratyekabuddha* (辟支佛) is translated as *pratyeka* (辟支迦), meaning "solitary," and *buddha* (佛陀), meaning "awakened. Regarding the term *yōng* (應):

the commentary states it means "should"; when combined with the root *chēng* (稱), it forms *chēng-yìng* (稱應), meaning "to accord with" or "to correspond to"; furthermore, when combined with *zhèng* (證), it generally means "to be in accord with" or "to harmonize with" (*qì-yìng*).

The *Shuowen* explains that "xing" (surname) refers to what is produced by a person. In ancient times, the divine beings and sages were born when their mothers were moved by celestial rain; thus they were called "Sons of Heaven. Because the surname was established based on birth, the character for "xing" is composed of "woman" (女) and "birth" (生); "sheng" also serves as the phonetic component.
*Pó* (pronounced with the *bàng* and *hé* finals):
the surname of the Brahmin *Láduō*.
*Xiè*: according to the *Yùpiān*, it means weariness, exhaustion, or indolence.

*Juàn* (pronounced *qù* with the *juàn* tone) means fatigue; according to the *Yùpiān*, it also means indolence, brilliance, exhaustion, and cessation. It is also written as *quàn* or *nuǎn*, though the origins of these variants are unknown.

The meaning of "śramaṇa" (沙門) is "one who has attained the Dharma," for by attaining the Dharma, one temporarily brings all evils to rest. Therefore, it is sometimes called *śramana* or *śramanaka*, which is translated as "merit" (*gōngláo*), meaning that there is merit in the cultivation of the Path.
Among the four classes of those who practice the pure conduct of a *brāhmaṇa*, he is so called because he has practiced that pure conduct.
*Tathāgata* means "Thus-Come One" (*tathā-āgata*).
*Arhat* means "Worthy One" (*arhan*), which is translated here as "One Who Should Be Honored."
*Samyak-saṃbuddha* is translated here as "Perfectly Awakened One" (*Zhèngděngjué*).
Regarding *lìyǎng*, the other two instances [of the character] have a different pronunciation, being the clear sound *liàng*. Regarding *xièdài*:

the first character is pronounced *gǔ* (upper tone) and *ài* (upper tone), while the second is *tú* (upper tone) and *hǎi* (upper tone). According to the *Ěryǎ*, "xiè" is equivalent to "dài. The *Jízhù* states that "xiè" means "extreme exhaustion. "Dài" refers to lassitude. The *Shìmíng* explains "xiè" as "unraveling," meaning the joints and bones become loose and slack. The *Qièyùn* defines it as "fatigue. To act with "dài" or "xiè" is to be arrogant, indolent, negligent, dissolute, or to let the body go lax and fall into decline. It signifies lassitude and exhaustion.
*Vaidūrya* (琉璃) or *vaiḍūrya* (吠瑠璃), or simply *vaidūrya*, refers to lapis lazuli. *Sphaṭika* (頗梨)—the character "li" being pronounced with the *lì-sī* (力私) tone—is *sphaṭika*;

this is translated as "crystal" (*shuǐjīng*) or "water-jade" (*shuǐyù*), and sometimes as "white pearl. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is said that this jewel comes from within mountain rocks; one account claims it is formed when ice has existed for a thousand years. This latter claim lacks evidence. Since the lands of the West are hot and have no ice, yet abound in this jewel, what could possibly transform into it? It is merely a type of stone found everywhere.
"Shì" (適) is pronounced with the initial *chì* (赤) and the final *-ǎn* (反). In the *Sāncāng*, the archaic form is written as "shì" (適), meaning "near" or "beginning.

"Zúxìng" (族姓): "zú" (族) is pronounced with the initial *cú* (徂) and the final *-lù* (鹿). The commentary on the *Shàngshū* regarding the passage "fāng mìng pǐ zú" (方命圮族) states that "zú" means "kindred" (*lèi*). In the *Zhōu Lǐ*, it is said that four *lǚ* (閭) constitute a *zú*; Zhèng Xuán notes that this refers to one hundred households. "Zú" also implies a gathering or a lineage (*xìng*).

2. Chapter on Expedient Means (Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta). The character "更" (gēng) is pronounced with the departing tone (qùshēng); the *Zītǒng* states that when a person performs unwholesome deeds, changing them leads to peace. Thus, the *Lúnyǔ* says, "In changing, all people look up to him. Therefore, it is composed of "人" (rén, person) and "更" (gēng, change). The character "更" is further composed of "丙" (bǐng) and "攴" (pū; pǔbǔ fǎn).

*Xiáng* (pronounced similar to *yáng*) means "to examine" (*shěn*). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to deliberate. The *Guoyá* states that *xiáng* is equivalent to *shì* (to verify). Its archaic form is written as 𦍹.

*Wú ài* (pronounced similar to *wǔ dài*) is the same as the archaic form of *wèi*. According to the *Shuowen*, *ài* means "to stop. The *Guoyá* states that *ài* is identical to *hài*. There is also the character *hài*, which is likewise an archaic form of *ài*. In the *Xiao Er'ya*, *ài* is defined as "limitation" (*xiàn*). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to close off from the outside. There is a variant character 㝵, but this is incorrect. *Ài* is pronounced *dé*; according to the *Shuowen*, *dé* means "to take. This refers to the passage in the *Book of Documents* (*Shangshū*) concerning Gaozong’s dream of obtaining the Way (*mèng dé shuō*). Wei Hong’s *Zhào Dìng Gǔwén Guānshū* states that the two characters *ài* and *dé* share the same radical; however, *ài* is not used in this sense [of "obtaining"].

*Jìn* (with the initial *jǐn* and final *-yin*) means "to entrust" (*rèn*) or "to exhaust" (*qióng*); alternatively, it has the initial *qín* and final *-yin*, referring to the "exhaustion" in the sense of "original exhaustion. *Sī* (with the initial *xī* and final *-zì*) refers to the ten directions. *Chà* (with the initial *chū* and final *-huá*; the *Qieyun* reads *chà*)—in the Sanskrit it is *kṣetra*, meaning "field" or "land," though some say it carries the meaning of "kingdom"; this is merely a translation. Examining the character *chà*, it does not appear in the *Shuowen*. "Dao" (稻) is pronounced with the initial *hào* and shares the same sound as "dao" (道).
"Suǒqù" (所趣) is pronounced with the finals *qū* (七句反) or *jū* (七俱反); here we follow the first reading, which signifies the sense of returning to the fundamental source.
Regarding "shènshēn miàoyǒu" (甚深妙有) and "zuò wēimiào" (作微妙), both are without error.
"Yòu-hù" (hesitation) is like a net; it is difficult for living beings to escape from it. Regarding "yòu" (上):

the first character is pronounced *yì* (with the *zhōu* rhyme), and the second is pronounced *yì* (with the *shù* rhyme). According to the *Shuowen*, in Longxi they call a puppy "yòu. The nature of the yòu is full of doubt and hesitation; because it stays before people, anything that is indecisive is called "yòu-hù," which is synonymous with "hú-yí" (fox-doubt). The *Erya* states: "The yòu is like a *jǐ*; it is skilled at climbing trees. Gù Pǔ [notes]: "It is adept at climbing up trees. *Jǐ* is pronounced *jū-lǚ*.

This term "bèi" (輩) refers to a group or cohort. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is a military term where one hundred chariots constitute one "bèi"; it is composed of the radical "che" (車) and the phonetic "běi" (北), meaning a disorderly array. The *Cangjie pian* states that "bèi" means "comparison" or "grouping. The *Guangya* says that "děngpèi" (等輩) and "bèi" are also synonyms for "category" (*lèi*). In the *Yupian*, "bèi" is defined as "classifying by category. (The character is pronounced *bùpán* [補槃]).

*Zēngshàngmàn* (增上慢): "Màn" is pronounced with the *yàn* rhyme-cut. It means to deceive (*qī*) or to treat lightly (*màn*). According to the *Yùpiān*, it signifies negligence (*mànyì*), contempt (*qīngwǔ*), tardiness (*chí*), indolence (*duò*), lack of awe (*bùwèi*), and laxity (*huǎn*). It is also synonymous with haughtiness (*jù*), or is written as the character *màn* (嫚).
*Mò* (pronounced with the initial *m-*, not *mǒ*) means "stillness. The common vulgar form *mèi* is incorrect.
*Zhì* (pronounced with the initial *zh-* and ending in *-i*, neither *zhǐ* nor *zhì*) means "to restrain" or "to prohibit.

*Jiā* (pronounced *jiā* in ancient times, according to the *Shuowen Jiezi* it means "good"; according to the *Guangya* it means "excellent"; the character *hài* has the phonetic *hù jiā*) means "to praise" or "to commend. *Hài* (with the phonetic *hù jiā*) means "to laud" or "to extol."

"Only (wéi). "Shàngyì" (唯然) is a variant reading; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "yes" (*nuò*). According to the *Guoyaya*, it means "to respond. In the *Liji*: "When the father calls, one does not say 'yes' (*nuò*); when a teacher calls, one does not say 'yes,' but says 'only' (*wéi*) and rises. Zheng Xuan commented: "'Only' is a respectful term for responding; 'only' is more reverent than 'yes. It is also borrowed for the pronunciation 'yì' (弋), with the water radical reversed, and is likewise a particle of speech. 'Rán' (然) means 'to accord with' or 'to be acceptable.'"
The *udumbara* flower is the auspiciously manifested flower of the *utpala*.
It exists fundamentally through all Buddhas, and its existence through the Buddha is likewise without fault.
As for "but" (*dan*), the phonetic classification of the upper tone indicates it is synonymous with "only" (*tu*); "only" (*tu*) means "empty" (*kong*).
*Tuo* (濁): Pronounced *zhù* with a retroflex final; it means dregs and filth. *Gòu* (垢):
Pronounced *gǔ* with a *hou*-final; it means defilement and impurity, or being stained by what is unclean. *Kān* (慳): Pronounced *kǔ* with an *jian*-final;
it refers to stinginess regarding that which has already been obtained.

*Gan* (貪): with the phonetic *han* (含). To covet what one has not yet obtained. *Ji* (嫉): upper radical *qin* (秦) with the final *xi* (悉); *qin* is an entering tone. In the *Yùpiān*, it is read as *cīlì* (辭栗). The archaic forms are *jī* (𧪠), *yǒng* (㵾), and *jiàn* (愱)—these three characters are identical. Lower radical: *dāng* (當) with the final *gù* (故). The *Chǔcí* says: "Thus the heart gives rise to jealousy" (*hùxīn érijù*). Wáng Yì’s commentary on the *Chǔcí* states: "To harm the worthy is called *jí* (嫉); to harm beauty is called *dù* (妒). The *Shuōwén* states: "A wife who is jealous of her husband. It is composed of the radical 'woman' and the phonetic 'hù' (戶)."

*Xiá* (pronounced *jí yí*) is an archaic form identical to *xiān*. It means "fault" or "transgression. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as a "blemish. The *Yuyuan* states: "A blemish within the jade is called *xiá*; a blemish on the exterior of the jade is called *cí*. The character now written as *cí* refers to a person who harbors internal afflictions, like the *xiá* within jade; it does not refer to a flaw on the exterior of the jade.
"Zāo" (pronounced as in "zāo") refers to dregs; it is the residue of wine.
"Kāng" (pronounced as in "kǔgāng") refers to husks; it is the chaff of rice.
"Sī" (pronounced as in "xīqiǎn") means few; there are also instances where it is written as "xiǎn," for in the *Yùpiān*, "xiǎn" also means few.
*Sūtra* (*suttanta*) is called "Discourse" (*kīṅ*);
*gāthā* is called "Verses";
*geyya* is called "Verses to be Chanted."

*Upadeśa* (優波提舍): *Upatiśuo* (鄔波提鑠) says it means "discourse" (*lun-yi*). There is a variant reading as *upoying* (優婆應), which should be corrected to *upo* (優波). *Jing-gao* (矜高): The first character, *jing* (矜), is pronounced with the upper radical *ju* (居) and the level tone (*ling* 陵).

The *Shangshu* (Book of Documents) states: "If you alone do not boast (*bu-jing*), none in the world will compete with you for their abilities. Kong Anguo (孔安國) explains that to consider oneself virtuous is called *jing*. In the *Liji* (Book of Rites), regarding the passage "Confucius was not *jing* yet was dignified," Zheng Xuan (鄭玄) explains that *jing* refers to self-exaltation and arrogance.

*Chǎnqū* (諂曲): "Chǎn" is pronounced *chǒu-rǎn* (丑冉反). It means "to flatter. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *xiàn* (讇), which is the same character. Zhuang Zhou said: "To seek out another's intentions and speak their words is called *chǎn*. The *Yupian* states that *chǎn* means "sycophancy" (*yú*). To incline the body as if there were something below [one] is also written as *xiàn* (讇), which is the same.

Regarding "meigui" (玫瑰), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that the first character is pronounced with the final *-hui* (莫回反) and the second with *-huikui* (胡魁反). It refers to a fire-crystal (*huqizhu*). Alternatively, it says that the beautiful stones among rocks are called *mei*, while those that are perfectly round are called *gui*. Guo Pu [in his commentary] identifies *meigui* as stone-beads. Zhang Yi [in the *Hanshu Yiwenzhi*] states that *meigui* and *langgan* beads originate from Mount Kunlun and the Kaibaimingyue Mountain.

*Shìmào* (石廟): "Máo" is pronounced *zhào* in the archaic script; it is written as *miào* in the *Báihùtōng*, *Yùpiān*, and *Miàomào*. It refers to the place where the honored ancestors reside, hence it is called a "temple" (*miào*).

*Mùxì* (木櫁): "Xì" is pronounced *mín* with one tone change; it is a fragrant wood. According to the *Qièyùn*, it is the name of a tree. The *Yùpiān* states that *xì* is a fragrant wood. Some write it as *yù*, which is incorrect. This tree resembles the *huái* tree but is extremely fragrant. Once felled, it must be used only after five years. If one wishes to extract its fragrance, the wood must be cut in advance, and the scent will only emerge after a long period.

*Qián-xī* (Lead and Tin): The first character is pronounced *zhuān*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi* and *Yupian*, it refers to "green metal. The *Book of Documents* states that the region of Qingzhou contributed lead and tin; thus, tin lies between silver and lead. *Zuò-lè* (To Make Music): The second character is pronounced *jué*.

The *Shiben* states that during the era of the Yellow Emperor, Linglun created music. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says that the five tones and eight musical instruments are collectively called *lè*. In the *Book of Rites*, it says, "To harmonize these sounds and delight in them with the *qì*, feathers, and banners is called *lè*. Zheng Xuan also notes that the term *lè* can be pronounced *lú-gè*.
"Ji" (擊) is pronounced *gū* with the *hù* rhyme; the *Yùpiān* states it means "to move. Generally, the sounding of tones is called "drumming," "striking," or "resounding.
"Chuijiao" (吹角) refers to a curved shape resembling a horn, which is the *dàjiǎo* (great horn).
*Pai* (貝) refers to a conch shell.

*Xiao* (簫), with the phonetic *su* (蘇) and the tone *diao* (彫), refers to a pipe; according to the *Yupian*, it is a set of small pipes played together, also written as *shao* (箾) with the pronunciation *shan* (山) and *zhuo* (卓), meaning musical music.

*Di* (笛), with the phonetic *tu* (徒) and *li* (歷), refers to a seven-holed flute; its vulgar name is *di*. According to the *Yupian*, there are five-holed bamboo flutes, while the *Qiang* flute has three holes.

Regarding the *qín*: the *Shuowen* states that "qín" means "to restrain"; it was created by Shennong. The *Yupian* says that a gentleman maintains correctness to restrain himself. Regarding the *kōng hóu* and *pípá*:

[the latter] is pronounced *niáo* (with the *jiao* rhyme); it is like a bell but larger. The *Guangya* lists *gong*, *luán*, *niáo*, *duó*, and *líng*. The *Shuowen* and *Yupian* state that the *niáo* is a small gong. According to military law, the commander of ten men holds the *niáo*, while five men form a *wǔ* unit; five *wǔ*s form a *liǎng* unit, and the *liǎng*-commander (*sī mǎ*) holds the *duó*.
*Tongba* (pronounced *pú bō*, also written as *bá*) refers to cymbals; nowadays, those in the region east of the Pass mostly use two plates that strike against each other to produce sound.

As for those made of bronze (*bāo*), there is no source for their origin. *Gébài* (pronounced *pú jiè*) is called *vādī* in Sanskrit, which means "praise. The initial character *pó* (pronounced *pú hè*) was formerly written as *baini*; this is an error. This is the three-fold musical cadence of the Western Regions, such as that performed by Śarvananda. The *Xuanyan ji* records that when Cao Zhi, the Prince of Chen-si, ascended Mount Yu, he suddenly heard the sound of reciting sutras from the mountain crags—pure, elegant, forceful, and resonant, with its echoes flowing through the distant valleys. He then modeled his compositions upon that sound to create Buddhist hymns (*fàn bèi*), which have been transmitted to this day. *Bèi* is also a modern term whose etymological origin is unknown.

The character *máo* (犛) is pronounced with the *jiāo* (交) rhyme. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to the long-haired ox of the southwestern tribes; today this ox exists in Longxi. The *Qieyun* records it as *máo*; its hair is called *máomáoxiū* (犛犛牛). There are those who write it as *māo* (貓), but that is the domestic animal kept by humans for catching mice; it does not carry the meaning of this ox.
"Bì" (蔽) is the opposite of "yǎn" (掩); it means to conceal the mind through greed. "Bì" (弊) is pronounced with the *pi* rhyme; it means to be exhausted by greed.
Śākyamuni: "Śākya" is his clan name.
At the beginning of the kalpa, there was no sovereign or leader.

The multitude, having deliberated, chose one who possessed the Way to serve as the custodian of the covenant and established him as their sole king, titled Mahāsammata (Greatly Agreed Upon). This refers to the fact that the great assembly, being equal in their intention, established him as king. He was the high ancestor of the Buddha; from father to son in the direct line, they never fell away from this succession, and all together praised his ability to serve as the Emperor of Men.
Because of this, his clan name became Śākya.
Muni means "the silent one" (or "the sage"),
which is an epithet of the Buddha.
This means that he is able to bring about the cessation of the evil dharmas of birth and death,
and is also able to realize the principle of the tranquility of nirvāṇa;
because both his lineage and his name are mentioned together, he is called Śākyamuni.
Now, in brief, he is called Śākyamuni.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that Śākyamuni is the same as Muni; it is a case of omitting the character "ni" (尼), thus being called Śākyamuni.

*Namo* (南無) is translated as "Right Speech" (*samyag-vāc*), though it is also rendered as *namo* (納慕) or *namo* (納莫), which here means "reverent salutation. If one says *jiàntán* (件談) or *bàntí* (伴題), these mean "prostration. The term *huónán* (和南) is likewise a corruption. There are editions that read "Namo to all Buddhas," but it is correct to follow the reading "Namo Buddha."

*Piyupin* (譬喻品): "Pi" (譬) is pronounced with the initial *p* and final *-i*, reversed from the *Yupian* (玉篇); it means "to compare" (*bili*) in order to provide mutual illustration (*xiangxiaoyu*). It is pronounced with the final *-an* (*yang-an*). Alternatively, it is written as "Yu" (諭), which also means "analogy" (*pi*). According to the *Yupian*, it means "to enlighten" (*xiao*) or "to admonish by analogy" (*pipian*).
*Yǒng* (with the phonetic *lǒng*) means to leap.
*Yuè* (with the phonetic *zhé*) means to jump.

*Bù yù* (with the phonetic *jù*) means to enter or to be settled; the *Qièyùn* records it as *yù*, and its archaic form is the same as *yǔ*. The *Erya* states that *dài* (to reach) and *yǔ* (to give) are synonymous. The *Zuozhuan* says, "The Duke must participate in it," which also implies preparing in advance, being ready, or early.
I have previously stated that "once" (*cēng*) means "to have done so at one time," while "always" (*cháng*) means "to do so constantly.

The term *měi* (with the phonetic readings *mò zǎi fǎn* in the *Zílín* and *mò gǎi fǎn* in the *Sāncāng*) is not a word of fixed meaning; "every" (*měi*) is synonymous with "frequently" (*shù*) or "repeatedly" (*lǜ*).

*Dòu* (等咎): In the *Guǎngyǎ*, "dòu" means fault (*guò*). The radical is "person" (*rén*), and "gè" (各) means each; when individuals act in opposition to one another, they form faults and transgressions.
*Duàn* (斷): Pronounced *túguǎn*. It means to cut or to sever. Also pronounced *dōuluàn*. In the *Yùpiān*, it means to decide or to settle. Here, it follows its original meaning.
"Yanchang" (演暢): "Chang" is pronounced with the retroflex *l* (liǎng fǎn). According to the *Guǎngyá*, "chang" means to be thorough, to penetrate, or to be clear.
"Huazú ānxíng" (華足安行): "Xíng" is pronounced with the labio-dental *m* (hu mèng fǎn). It refers to practicing the "peaceful and joyful conduct. "Lúnpǐ" (倫匹):

"Lún" is pronounced with the retroflex *l* (shàng lì jūn fǎn). According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means equal, comparable, or a peer; it also means categories or classes, as well as a match or mate. The character "pǐ" (匹) is composed of "xi" (匸) and "ba" (八); "ba" represents one "pǐ" (a pair), and "ba" also serves as its phonetic component.

"Profundity" (*ào*) is the opposite of "retribution. In the *Erya*, the southwest corner of a room is called the *ào*; Guo Pu identifies this as the hidden and secluded part of a chamber. The *Shiming* states that it is called "mysterious and profound" (*mì ào*) because one cannot see the light from the door. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines *ào* as "thorough investigation" (*jiù*) and "concealment" (*cáng*).

"Dào pǒ" (道叵): "Pǒ" is pronounced as in "wǒ fǎn" (我反). The *Sāncāng* states that "pǒ" means "not possible. "Fǎn" (反) is read as "fá" when the radical is reversed, and as "bǐ" when it follows [the character].

"Kě" (可) becomes "pǒ" (叵); all derive from their semantic components. However, "Shèlìfú ràn" (舍利弗然): "Ràn" is pronounced as in "rú yán fǎn" (如延反). The *Yùpiān* states that "bù rán" (不然) means "not permitting. "Ràn" (然) also means "certainly" or "likewise. The *Shuōwén* explains "rán" (然) as composed of the radicals for "flesh" (肉) and "dog" (犬); nowadays it is written as "rán" (然).
*Jùluò* (聚落): "Gǎngyǎ" (廣雅) states that *jùluò* means "to dwell" (*jū*) or "to gather" (*jù*). It refers to a place where people reside together; this is as in the *Hànshū*:

"There were no scorched villages" (*wú fán jùluò*). *Shuāimài* (衰邁): Pinyin *mò jiè fǎn*. According to the *Shuōwén*, *mài* means "to travel far. *Gǎngyǎ* states it means "to go toward" or "to return."

The *Tóng* (童) entry in the *Yùpiān* (玉篇) states that the phonetic gloss is *túdōng* (徒東), meaning "alone. The *Shuowén* (說文) defines it as: "A man who has committed a crime and becomes a slave is called a *tóng*. The *Guǎyá* (廣雅) states: "*Tóngpú* (僮僕) refers to servants and laborers. Today, all [texts] write it as *tóng* (僮).

"Pú" (蒲木反) is written as "pǔ" (蹼) in ancient texts; according to the *Guǎngyá*, "pú" also refers to one who is attached to others. The *Yùpiān* states that one who serves in a household is called a "pú," meaning a servant or laborer.

*Tuí* (隤): According to the *Shuowen*, it is pronounced with the rhyme *dàihuí* (大迴) and means "to fall downward. It is composed of the radical *huì* (𨸏) and the phonetic *zhuì* (䝿). The *Guangya* states it means "to ruin. The archaic forms are *tuí* (頹) and *diàn* (墤); these two characters share the same phonetic. Regarding its usage in the *Qieyun*: if written as *tuí* (頹), it refers to a violent wind; if written as *tuí* (禿), it means "bald"; if written as *tuó* (𤗯) or *jié* (󲆪), it refers to a dilapidated house. The *Yupian* records *tuí* (隤) as referring to Mount Tai, saying "its slopes crumble," meaning to fall down and collapse.

"Fu" (腐) means rotten; it shares the same pronunciation as "father" (父). Below it is the character "bài" (敗), which should be pronounced "fǔ" or "fǔ," just as one would not enter a village named Shèngmǔ (勝母) because of its name. Zengzi did not enter such a place.

Regarding "liáng-dòng" (梁棟): the *Erya* states that the *máng-lùn* (杗廇) is called *liáng* (梁). Guo Pu says it refers to the main beam of a house; it is merely a colloquial term. The pronunciation of *dòng* (棟) is *dōng-lòng* (東弄反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines *dòng* as "the ridgepole of a roof. The *Shiming* says it is the "center," for it resides in the middle of the house. The pronunciation of *máng* (杗) is *máng* (亡), and the pronunciation of *lùn* (廇) is *lìjiù* (力救反).

*Hū* (pronounced *shǔ* with the *wù* rhyme): According to the *Cāngjié piān*, it means "sudden onset. In the *Xījīng fù*, it appears as "suddenly visible from behind" (*hū cóng bèi jiàn*); Xuè Zōng glosses it as "sudden. In the *Qièyùn*, it denotes the appearance of a sudden or violent rising; the *Yùpiān* also states it means "sudden."

*Fénshāo* (焚燒): To burn; according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means to burn fields. The character is composed of "fire" and "to burn a forest. In ancient texts, it appears as two forms: *cè* (炃) and *sǒn* (燌), which are identical in meaning.

*Xīxì* (嬉戲): The *Shuōwén* defines this as joy (*xi*). In the *Cāngjiépiān*, under the "Woman" radical, it is written as *xī* (嬉); both are pronounced *xǐ* (喜). The second character, *xì* (戲), is pronounced *xī* (希). It means to laugh, to be beautiful, or to play. It is composed of "spear" (*gē*) and "to have" (*yǒu*). There is also a variant *xǐ* (憙) pronounced *xǔjì* (許記), but that is not the original meaning of this term.

*Qièyǐ guǎngyǎ*: "Qiè" is pronounced like *guǎng* and *yǎ*. It also means "near," "urgent," "to cut," or "to divide. The character is composed of the radical "knife" (刀) with the phonetic "qi" (七). *Yīdì* (衣裓): According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to the "Jiè-yī" (戒衣) played during ancestral temple rites.

It is composed of the radical "clothing" (衣) with the phonetic "jiè" (戒). The *Yupian*, in its section on clothing, reads it as *gǔlái* (古來). It is traditionally said to mean "lapel" (襟), with the phonetic "jiè" (戒) and the reading *gūdé* (孤得). This refers to the front pocket (*dì*) of women's clothing today. *Tiānyī* (天衣, celestial robes) are similar in form, though the origin of the character remains undetermined.
I shall now explain the character 玩 (wàn). In the *Yongwei* (玉篇), it is glossed as "to bestow" (*fūshī*) or "to assist" (*yīngwèi*).

The character is composed of the radical 爪 (claw) and the phonetic 元 (yuán). In the *Zhēnwán* (珍玩), it is read as *huàn* (喚); the *Zílín* (字林) defines it as "to dally with," while the *Guǎngyá* (廣雅) defines it as "to enjoy as a plaything. The *Yùpiān* (玉篇) further defines it as "to toy with. In the *Shàngshū* (Book of Documents), it states: "To toy with people ruins one's virtue; to toy with objects ruins one's will. Kǒng Ānguó (Kǒng Anguo) explained that to treat people as playthings leads to the loss of virtue, and to treat objects as playthings leads to the loss of will. Some editions have the character 翫 (wàn), meaning "to practice" or "to cultivate," but these are all incorrect.
*Wán* (玩): Pronounced *hù* (呼) or *fǎn* (反) with the tone of *yù* (玉) according to the *Yùpiān* (玉篇); it means "to love. Also pronounced *lǎo* (老) with the tone of *yù* (玉) according to the *Yùpiān*;

it means "appropriate," "good," or "beautiful. *Shì* (適): Pronounced *qí* (其) or *shī* (尸) with the tone of *chì* (赤) according to the *Sāncāng* (三蒼); it means "pleasure" (*yuè*). That is to say, it refers to being "fitting" (*chēng shì*). According to the *Guǎngyá* (廣雅), *shì* means "good"; that is to say, when things and affairs are excellent and pleasing, they accord with the human heart.
*Yòngruì* (羊稅反): According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means sharp and keen; according to the *Shuōwén*, it refers to the plant *ruìfū*. *Tuí* (推):

The first character is read as *chǐzhuī* (尺隹反) and the second as *wútǔ* (無土反), followed by *bùjiē* (步皆反). According to the *Cāngjiépiān*, it means to push or to advance. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means to push, to displace, or to sweep away. *Rù* (軵) is pronounced as *ér yǒng* (而勇反).

Regarding "four crossroads" (sìqú): according to the *Erya*, a road with four directions is called a *qú*; Guo Pu explains it as a road where four paths intersect. The *Shiming* states that a road with four directions is called a *qú*. In the regions of Qi and Lu, four teeth on a handle constitute a *qú*; since the ground of a *qú* has four points, this road resembles it and is thus named after it.
"Hanging various flowers" refers to the "flower-sound" (hua-yin) of the verses. Regarding the term *wànyán* (綩綖):

in the *Shang Zilin*, the upper character is read as *yuan* (一遠反), though some write it with the two forms *wǎn* (蜿) and *rú* (蠕), which are incorrect. In the lower character, the *Sancang* reads it as *zhan* (以旃反). Examining various texts, *wànyán* refers to a *hóngguān* (紘冠) or a *yànguān* (纓冠); the *Guān* (冠) is what covers the top. According to the *Yupian*, that which hangs down from the front and back of a crown cannot be the same as the layered crowns used on carriages. Here, the principle dictates it should be written with the *wǎn* (婉) of "graceful beauty. It is a type of elegant mat, such as a *xí* (蓐) or *yù* (蓐), or a patterned rug (*huāzhān*), a luxurious seat.

Regarding the statement that "a vermilion pillow contains elixirs of immortality which can prolong life," this is not so. According to the records, in India there are no wooden pillows; instead, they are made by folding red animal hides or layered cloth to form a pillow, stuffed with *tūla* cotton, wool, or similar materials. Because it is both a pillow and a cushion, and is of a vermilion-red color, it is identical to the "vermilion-colored pillows" mentioned in various scriptures. Both head pillows and leaning pillows are entirely red like cinnabar (*dan*).

*Shūhǎo* (姝好): The first character, *shū*, is pronounced with the initial *cháng* and the final *fǎn* (as per the *Zílín*). It denotes a beautiful appearance. According to the *Fāngyán*, in the regions of Zhào, Wèi, Yān, and Dài, the word for "beautiful" is *shū*. The *Shījīng* says, "The quiet maiden is *shū*," and the commentary as well as the *Yùpiān* state that a beautiful countenance is called *shū*. There is also a variant reading *zhū* (侏), pronounced with the initial *zhuāng* and the final *lǎo*; it signifies beauty, goodness, and suitability.

The character *tú* (徒) in *yòutú* (幼童) is pronounced *fǎng* (反). In antiquity it was called *gǔtóng* (古童), meaning a servant; today it is called *tóngzi* (童子), meaning a youth. In antiquity it was called *gǔtóng* (古僮), meaning a young boy; today it is called *pólì* (僕隷), meaning a slave. According to the *Yùpiān*, "tóngzi" (童子) is a designation for a young child who has not yet reached marriageable age or undergone the capping ceremony. A hornless ox is called a *zhuàngniú* (撞牛); today this should be written as *tóngtóng* (童僮), which is merely an archaic form of the same word.

*Puì* (不匱) is pronounced with the *qù* (渠) and *kuì* (愧) finals, being identical to *guì* (櫃). In the *Lǐjì*, regarding "wealth is not *puì*," Zheng Xuan explains *puì* as "lack. The *Shījīng* says, "Filial piety is not *puì*," and the commentary states that *puì* means "exhaustion."

To obtain exemption (miǎn). [The character] is pronounced biàn in the contrary sense; there are also readings as fǔ or fǔ. The *Yùpiān* states: "Miǎn is pronounced miǎn in the contrary sense; it means to pardon, to release, to liberate, to depart, and to cease of one's own accord."
*Fāngbiàn* (方便): To strive and exert oneself; some editions read *miǎn* (勉) or *miǎn* (免). *Bǎorèn* (保任):

The first character, *bǔdào* (補道), means "to be fit for"; the second character, *rúlin* (如林), means "to preserve. It signifies that something can be relied upon and trusted, or it refers to providing security, assurance, and faithful maintenance.
*Cui* (pronounced *cuō*, with the initial *huī* as a variant) means to break and to overturn.

*Pǐ*: according to the *Zílín*, it is pronounced *fǔměi*; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means to destroy. In the *Yūshū* (Book of Yu), "commanding the mandate and destroying clans," according to the *Ěryǎ*, it means to overturn. According to the *Jiǎn Yùnyùn*, it is pronounced *fúbǐ*; the initial sound is *fǔ*, meaning to ruin.

The character 𡍩 (chí): in the *Zìlín*, it is pronounced with the rhyme *gé*; in the *Shuōwén*, it means "to split. In the *Guǎngyá* and *Yùpiān*, it means "to divide. The character 塗 (dù): pronounced with the rhyme *dū*, it means "to overturn" or "to drag. The character 阤 (tí): in the *Shuōwén*, it is pronounced with the rhyme *wén-ěr*;

it means "the collapse of a mountain," following the radical 阜 (mountain) and the phonetic 也 (yé). In the *Fāngyán*, it means "to crumble"; in the *Yùpiān*, it means "to destroy" or "to fall. There is also the variant 褫; in the *Shuōwén* and *Qièyùn*, it means "to snatch away clothes," following the radical 衣 (clothes) and the phonetic 虒 (xī). In the *Qièyùn*, the character 虒 refers to a water-dwelling creature; its pronunciation is *sī*. In the *Guǎngyá*, 阤 and 󲑩 are given the pronunciation *duó*, though the correct form is 陊. In the *Qièyùn*, it means "the collapse of a mountain. There is also the variant 拕; in the *Yùpiān*, it is pronounced with the rhyme *zhí-zhǐ*, meaning "to break firewood along the grain of the wood. There is also the variant 󱪈, which is not a valid character.

*Fushiān* (覆苫): In the *Zilin*, it is read as *shūyán* (舒鹽); it refers to a thatched roof of reeds. The *Erya* states, "The *báigài* (white canopy) is called *shān*. Li Xun says, "Weaving the *báigài* together to cover a house is called *shān*."

The term *lǚ* (椽梠) is pronounced with the second tone for the initial syllable; according to the *Fānyán*, the eaves of a house are called *yán* (檐), which Guo Pu identifies as the *yuánwén* (屋檐). It is also called *liánquàn* (連縓) and named *pí* (󲔈). The *Shuowén* states that *lǚ* and *jué* (桷) are synonymous terms. *Pí* is pronounced according to the *Yùnmǔ* as *bī*; it refers to the corner-end of a rafter, which is the same as the *quèlǚ* (雀梠).

*Chātuō* (差脫): The first character is pronounced *chǔjiě*, *chǔyí*, or *chǔjiā*. Now, it follows the latter two readings. The second character is pronounced *túhuó* or *tùhuó*. *Zhàng* (障): Pronounced *zhōngliàng*. The *Shuowen* defines it as "to block or obstruct.

It is composed of the radical *tǔ* (earth) with *yǒu* (have). Some write it as *zhàng* (玉篇). The *Yupian* gives the pronunciations *zhīshàng* or *zhīyáng*. The *Shuowen* defines it as "to separate. The *Tongsuowen* states that "to fence off and separate" is called a *zhàng*. The character *fán* (蕃) is pronounced *fǔfán*.

The *chī* (owl) and *xiāo* (owlet). "Chī" is pronounced *shī* (as in *shīfǎn*). In Sanskrit it is called *kṛkaṇa*, which here means "hawk. The ancient text uses both characters *chī* and *zhī*. According to the *Erya*, the "mad *máo-chī*" (*kuáng máo chī*)—Sharen says that "mad" is another name for *chī*, and it has large eyes and delights in eating rats—is the *gù-chī* (screech owl). Guo Pu calls it the *guài-chī* (monstrous owl). The character *gù* is pronounced *xiàng* (as in *xiàngfǎn*).

*Diao* (鵰): The initial radical is *ding* (丁) with the rhyme *yao* (堯); it is written as *diao* (雕) in the *Zhouwen* (籀文) script. The *Mu Tianzi Zhuan* (穆天子傳) states: "There were white owls and blue *diao* there; they seized dogs and sheep and ate pigs and deer. Guo Pu notes that the *diao* of today can also eat *zhang* (獐) and deer. *Jiu* (鷲): The pronunciation is *jiu* (就). In Sanskrit, it is called *kṛtāra* or *kriśa*. According to the *Shanhaijing* (山海經), Mount Jing (景山) abounds in *jiu* birds. The *Shuowen* (說文) states that the *jiu* bird is black in color and has many offspring. Shi Kuang says that in the south there is a bird named *chajiu* (差鷲), which has a yellow head, a red throat, and is complete in its five colors. The *Xiyuji* (西域記) describes its color as a pale yellow and its eyes as red.
The character *yuán* (蚖) is pronounced with the "five organs" (*wǔguān*) rhyme-cut; the *Yùnyùn* also gives it the "ignorant Yuan" (*yúyuán*) rhyme-cut.

In archaic script it is written as *chúnyuán* (螈). According to the *Yùpiān*, it is the "snake-healer" (*shéyī*). The *Yíngyuán*, *xīchì*, *yàntiǎn*, and *shǒugōng* are four distinct names for it. Cui Bao’s *Gǔjīnjù* states: "The *yíngyuán* is also called the 'snake-healer'; the larger variety reaches three feet in length."
Its color is dark purple, and it is exceptionally seductive to people; it is also called the "dark *xuán*.
The *Hanshu* refers to it as a *yuán*.
Wei Zhao states that it is a black *yuán*, a type of lizard.
In the house, it is called the *shǒugōng* (alligator lizard); when its blood is smeared on a woman's arm, if she commits a transgression, the mark washes away, hence it is named *shǒugōng*.
When it dwells among grasses and stones, it is called the *yìxī* (lizard).
In the *Dazé* (Great Marsh), it is called the *yàn dìng*;
its general name is *yíng yuán*.

According to this, there is a scribal error in the *Yìjiào jīng* (Śālistamba-sūtra) which states: "For example, a black *yuán* is sleeping in your room. It should have said "black *yùán*," as the correct character is *yuán*. However, because the characters for *yuán* and *yuán* are similar in form, they were erroneously transcribed.

Some say that there are two kinds of *luán* (vipers): the first is the *shǒugōng* (gecko), and the second is the short black snake. Because the *Yìjiào jīng* (The Scripture of the Bequeathed Teaching) is unerring, it further states:
"Once the sleeping serpent has been expelled, one may sleep in peace."

The *gong* (𧈭) is a black, short snake distinct from other snakes; it is not a *shou-gong* (gecko). Otherwise, this sutra first distinguishes the *shou-gong* below and then further mentions the *luan* (viper) above—why such redundancy? Therefore, the explanations in secular texts differ from the meaning of the sutra.

I once heard a monk from the south say that when a *vān* (a type of viper) bites a person, only the *yao-wang-cao* (Medicine King Grass) can cure it; if this is not available, the victim will surely die. Regarding the *fù* (viper):

according to the *Erya*, the *fù* and *hui* are three inches wide with a head as large as a thumb. Sun Yan noted that those south of the Jianghuai region call the *hui* a *fù*. Its fangs are most venomous. The *Yinyi* states: "The *fù* snake has a needle-like protrusion on its nose; it is also called the 'Inverted-Nose Snake' (*fanbi she*). The *Sancang* says: 'The *fù* snake is colored like brocade, with scales between the patterns; the largest reach seven or eight feet. [The character] *bo* (補麥反) refers to an insect according to the *Yupian*. When the *fù* bites a hand, one must immediately amputate the hand."

The centipede is pronounced *wúgōng*; according to the *Zìlín*, it is a type of *lángqū*. It is highly capable of subduing snakes; those over a foot long and with red legs are effective, while those with yellow legs are not fit for use. Many people roast them until they turn red, but this is not the true species. *Láng* is pronounced as *jí* (also read *zǐjié*), and *qū* is pronounced as *zǐyú*.
*Yóuyán* (spelled with the phonetic values *yóu* and *yán*): in Jiangnan, the large variety is called the centipede (*wǔgōng*). The *shǒugōng* (lizard):

those found in houses are called *yuǎntín* in Jiangnan, though they are the same creature; in Shandong they are called *qìqiè*, and west of Shaanxi they are called *bìgōng*. Dongfang Shuo stated that what is not a *shǒugōng* is a *xīxí* (chameleon). *Yuǎntín*: *yǎn* is pronounced *tiǎn*; *tín* is pronounced *tiǎn*. *Qì*: this is also [pronounced] *qì*; *qiè* is pronounced *mì*.

The character for *yòu* (狖) is pronounced *yóu* (余繡反) in the *Zìlín*, which is the name used in Jiangdong; it is also pronounced *yú* (余季反), the name used in Jiāngpíng. According to the *Shānhǎijīng*, Mount Gélì is rich in *yòu* monkeys.
Guō Pǔ states that they resemble macaques but are larger.

It is dark blue-black in color with a long tail four or five feet in length, resembling the tail of a otter. It has two horns on its head; when it rains, it hangs upside down from a tree, using its tail to plug its nostrils.

In Jiangdong, people raise it to catch rats. As a creature, it is agile and robust, elegant and refined. The *Yǒu* has a prominent nose and a long tail; according to the *Qièyùn*, it is a species of insect that resembles a rat. The *Shòu* is a beast that resembles a monkey; according to the *Wèi*, it is a beast that resembles a *shòu*.
The character *yòu* (狖) is an archaic form; some write it as *yù* (㹨), but its origin is unknown. Following this, it should be understood as the *yòu* (鼬) or *yù* (貁).
This is because it is not of a malicious nature.
According to the *Yùpiān*, the *yù* resembles a wildcat (*lí*) and catches mice; according to the *Biéyùn*, the *yòu* resembles a stone-skunk (*shí*) and devours mice.

The "stone-eating rat" is also called a *shèng* (weasel); its nature and sound are the same as those of the *shǔ* (rat). This is the explanation in the *Shūlín*. As for *lí*, it is pronounced like *lǐ*;

the *Shuōwén* defines it as a crouching beast resembling a *chū*, derived from the radical *zhì* with the phonetic *lǐ*. There are also instances where it is written as *lí*, for which there is no [standard] source.

*Xiǔshǔ* (鼷鼠): according to the *Shuowen*, it is a small mouse; the *Erya* and Guo Pu’s *Yupian* state that it has a venomous sting and feeds on humans, birds, and beasts, yet even when they are completely consumed, they do not feel the pain; it is what is now called the "sweet-mouthed mouse."

"Chou-chu" (臭處): The first character, "chou," is pronounced *chiu* (with the initial *chiu* reversed) and means foul breath; the second character, "chu," is pronounced *chang-yü* (with the final *yu* reversed) and denotes a state of loathsome or base appearance. According to the *Yùpiān*, it also means "to rest" (*xi*) or "to dwell" (*ju*), referring to the halting or abiding of foul breath. Furthermore, with the second character read as *chu-shu* (with the final *shu* reversed), it refers to a place of filth and impurity.

The *fox*, *wolf*, and *yaoguan* (野干)—the latter being a term from the *Hudou* and *Yupian* lexicons for a demonic beast ridden by ghosts—possess three virtues: their color is neutral and harmonious; they walk with their hindquarters forward and their forequarters back; and when dying, they invariably face their original den. In Sanskrit, this is called *śṛgāla*, which translates as "wild jackal. Its color is bluish-yellow like that of a dog; it travels in packs and howls at night with a voice like that of a wolf cub. Regarding the *shedian* (射干) mentioned in the *Xushang Linfu* (虛上林賦), both Sima Biao and Guo Pu comment that the *shedian* can shoot at trees from afar (*she* being pronounced *ye*). The *Guozhi* states that it nests in precarious cliffs and tall trees. The *Dhyāna Sūtra* mentions seeing both a wild fox and a wild jackal, thus we know these two are distinct.

*Jù* (咀嚼): The character is pronounced *shàng cí lǚ qíng lǚ* (two rhymes). The *Zílín* writes it as *zhǔ*. The *Cāngjiépiān* states it means "to chew. The *Zílín* defines chewing (*jǔ*) as biting (*jiè*). The *Qièyùn* defines it as "to bite" (*shì*). The *Yùpiān* defines it as "to chew," "to swallow," or "to hold and gnaw. It refers to the act of chewing.

Regarding the character *jiè* (䶩齧): tradition transmits that it is pronounced *yì* (詣) in the upper radical; it refers to gnawing until the teeth are worn away (*mòchǐ*). In the *Qièyùn*, it states that when reaching the teeth, one should write *jiè* (䶩). Furthermore, *jiè* (䶩) also has the pronunciation *jié* (截); it means to bite through tendons and bones. It is unknown from where the character *jiè* (䶩) originated; some texts have *jù* (𪘨), and others have *jiè* (䶩), both with the phonetic *zhú* (竹) and the same pronunciation *jiē* (皆). The *Tōngsùwén* states that "to gnaw and pull" is called *jiè* (䶩), though I fear this may be an error for *jiè* (齧) with the lower part having the pronunciation *jié* (結). To bite slightly is *jiè* (齧); to gnaw until the teeth are worn away is *jù* (𪘨); furthermore, to wound skin and flesh is *jiè* (齧); to bite slightly is *jiè* (䶩). Only the reading *zhí* (陟) and *jiē* (皆) is correct; all others are incorrect.

*Bo* (upper character, *bǔ* with retroflex *-g*; lower character, *cuō* with retroflex *-l*): According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means to strike or attack; according to the *Yùpiān*, it means to clap or to pat. The *Zílín* and *Qièyùn* state that it means to take with the hand. The *Guǎngyá* also says it means to hold. The *Shìmíng* states that *cuō* means "sudden" (*zú*); it refers to taking something up suddenly and briefly. The *Yùpiān* further notes that four *guī* (a unit of measurement) is called a *cuō*, and that three fingers pinching together is also a *cuō*. There are instances where it is written as *zǐ kuò*, but this pronunciation does not accord with the meaning here. The *Qièyùn* records that when the hand grasps something, it is written as *zuàn* (*zǐ huó*).
*Chā* (樝): The character is pronounced with the *shàng* (上) tone, following the *Zìlín* (字林); according to the *Shìmíng* (釋名), it means "to interlace" (*chā*).
This refers to reaching out with all five fingers to grasp by interlacing them.
The *Yùpiān* (玉篇) states it means to pinch with the five fingers, to strike, or to embrace.

In the *Qieyun*, "zhā" (樝) is described as resembling a pear but being sour; it should be written as "zhā" (𭽷), which is formed by pressing with the fingers. There are also the two forms "zhā" (柤) and "zhào" (皻), both of which have the same meaning. Furthermore, there is the form "chēng" (󲏁) or "chéng" (䶥);
however, according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, this refers to misaligned teeth, which is not the meaning intended here.
Alternatively, it is pronounced as *chā* (with the tone of *chē*, meaning "to tear" or "to break apart").
The lower character is pronounced as *chōng* (with the tone of *shì*); according to the *Zílín*, it means "to drag."
The character *zì* (字) means "to pull.
According to the *Shìmíng* (Explanations of Names), it means "to restrain and control," suddenly making [the object] conform to one's will.

The *Yùpiān* (Jade Lexicon) states that it means "to draw out and extend," or it is written as *mó* (摩) with the same meaning. Furthermore, the phonetic transcription is *chǐzhé* (尺折) or *yèyánjié* (曳延結); this refers to interlacing the five fingers to drag [an object], or pressing down with the fingers to pull it along, or again, tearing and pulling it out and extending it.

*Jiēchí* (嘊喍): The first character is pronounced *wǔjiā* (五佳反) and the second is pronounced *xī* (音柴). It refers to dogs snarling at one another. The *Yùpiān* states that it means "dogs snarling at each other"; the *Pīcāng* says it means "dogs snarling in opposition. The *Shuōwén* and *Yùpiān* write it as *zhī* (齜), defining it as opening the mouth to show the teeth, called *zhī*. The *Qièyùn* defines *chí bù zhèng* (齒不正) as *zhī* (𪗶𪘲); some versions of *zhī* are written as *zhī* (𪗶), with some saying it describes the appearance of baring the lips and showing the teeth by snarling. Others write it as *chí* (喍), but it is unclear which is correct.

*Háo* (upper radical: *hú*, *dāo*; ancient form: *xiū*)—according to the *Shuowen*, *Yupian*, and *Qieyun*, it refers to the barking of a dog; according to the *Qieyun*, it is the sound of bears, *pí*, and tigers. *Lí* (upper radical: *chì*, *zhī*)—the *Shuowen* writes this as *yǎo*;

the *Sancang* and various other character books write it as *chī*; the *Yupian* and *Qieyun* write it as *lí*. *Mèi* (lower radical: *mò*, *bì*)—the *Shuowen*, *Yupian*, and *Tongsu* state that the spirits of aged objects are called *lí-mèi*; the *Zhengfahua-jing* uses the archaic forms *mèi*, *zhuì*, or *mí*, which are now written as *mèi*.

*Mānglǎng* (魍魎): the first character is read as *wáng* (亾, with the fanqie *wáng fǎn*) and the second as *lǎng* (力, with the fanqie *lì zhǎng fǎn*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to a creature that is the essence of mountains and rivers. The *Tongsu Wen* states that monsters made of wood or stone are called *mānglǎng*. The *Yupian* identifies them as water deities; in ancient texts, they were written as *wāngliǎng* (蝄蜽).

*Fú* (孚) means to nourish; in the *Tōngsùwén* it is explained as "transforming through incubation. In the *Fāngmíngzìlín*, it is read with the rhyme *fǎn* (反) as *fǎng* (芳); in the *Guǎngyǎ* and *Yùpiān*, *fú* (孚) means "to give birth. According to the *Fāngyán*, *jīfú* (雞伏) refers to a hen incubating eggs; this is what is meant by *fú*. In the *Yùpiān*, *mǔfú* (姥伏) means "to incubate" (*fú*) or "to give birth" (*fú*). In the *Qièyùn*, it is pronounced with the rhymes *rú* (濡) and *zhǔ* (主). In the *Cāngjiépiān*, *rǔ* (乳) means "to suckle"; the *Yùpiān* also states it means "to give birth. Birds nourishing their young is called *fú*; beasts nourishing their young is called *rǔ*.

The character "shēng" (生) possesses both departing tones (*qùyīn*) and should be read with the level tone (*píngshēng*). According to the *Yùpiān*, it means "to produce," "to advance," and "to create. To bring about transformation through things is called "production" (*shēngchǎn*); it also simply means "to give birth."
*Kumbhāṇḍa* (鳩槃荼): *kumbha* means "pot" and *aṇḍa* means "egg"; it is also translated as "the Terrifying. To *cúnjù* (蹲踞) is read as *cu zūn* (上) and *jū yù* (下);

it refers to sitting with the knees raised like a squat, or leaning back. According to the *Zílín* (字林), it means to sit with the feet hanging down. The old scriptures refer to this as "sitting on a winnowing basket" (*jīzuò*).

Regarding the character *tuǒ* (埵): according to the *Zilin*, it is pronounced with the rhymes *dīng* and *guǒ*. In the *Qièyùn*, it refers to a small mound of earth at a corner; this is a vulgar usage and not the *tuǒ* found in the *Yùpiān*, which is pronounced *dīng* and *guō*. *Kuò* (堁) refers to small clods of earth piled vertically; in the *Qièyùn*, the entry for *dīng* and *guō* uses the character *tún* (𨹃) to denote a small heap.

The *Pǔlìng* (樸令) reads "páng" (龐) with the reversed phonetic; the *Tōngsùwén* (通俗文) states that "zhēngdǎo" (爭倒) is called "pū" (撲), and there is also the reading "pǔ" (朴) with the phonetic "pǔbǔ" (普卜), meaning to strike. The *Yùpiān* (玉篇) defines it as "to strike," whereas the sense of "hand-to-hand combat" (*shǒubó*) is not this meaning.
*Nuò* (pronounced *hú* with a reversed *wǎ*) means "naked"; it should be written as *luò*.

*Kuī* (upper character *qiū* with a reversed *guī*) means "to look at furtively. According to the *Fāngyán*, when people steal glances of one another, the people of Chu call this *kuī*; it is also written as *kuī* (same characters), with the lower character pronounced *kǔ hán* or also *kǔ dàn*, meaning "to look."
"Belonging to" (屬) is the opposite of "to entrust" (付). It is also pronounced *shú* (時燭反) and means "to encompass" (攝) or "to penetrate" (貫); it should be written with the character 屬.

"Crackling" (爆) is pronounced *bào* (博教反) and refers to fire that is deep and fierce; it is also pronounced *pǔ* (普剝反). According to the *Shuowen*, "bào" means "to blaze intensely" (*zháo*). This refers to the skin rising and scattering. In the *Yupian*, under the "Fire" radical, it is pronounced *bù* (補角反), *pú* (蒲角反), or *pō* (頗角反), meaning "to scorch" (*zháo*), "heat," or "to rise up in agitation. The ancient form is also written as 𣀛.
*Zhouzhuang* (諸良反): "Fear"; it describes a state of being universally startled and unsettled; some versions read the character *zhāng*, meaning "to circulate," which refers to the beginning.
*Huángbù* (惶怖): the upper character (*húguāng*) means "startled," and the lower character (*pǔgù*) means "timid."
*Zàng* (pronounced *cuàn* with the second tone) means to flee; according to the *Yùpiān*, it means to hide.
*Piśāca* and *Piśāca* are explained in the commentaries as ghosts resembling winter melons.
*Shí* (pronounced *dàn* with the fourth tone) means to eat, or it is interchangeable with *chàn*.

"Péng" (蒲公反): The qi rises like the chaotic scattering of *páng* (蓬). Some write it as "fòng" (熢), which refers to the "fòng" in "fèng-huǒ" (㷭火); this fire is also like [the scattering of] *páng*. It is not correct if the pronunciation is not that of *páng*. "Mò" (蒲沒反): "bó" (勃) means flourishing. "Péng-bó" (蓬勃) is the appearance of profuse flourishing, like dust rising. Some write it as "tóng" (𡋯); for incense, some write it as "bó" (馞). What is now called "chòu-qì" (臭氣, foul odor) is written as "bóbó" (馞馞), which is also acceptable; or it may be like the chaotic profusion of *páng*, though some write it as "yě" (㶿), which has no source.

"Zhouzhang (周章) in the *Chuci* [means] 'to soar about' (*liaoxiaoxiang*). Zhouzhang—Wang Yi says it means 'to circulate' (*zhoulou*), referring to circulating back and forth; alternatively, it may mean 'panic-stricken' (*zhuanghuang*) or 'fearful. The former [reading as 'circulating'] is correct."
Zhòngnánshàngzhí-lóngzhī (衆難上職隆之): "Zhōng" (仲) has two pronunciations. "Zhāi" (宅) means "lord";

according to the *Yùpiān* (玉篇), it means "to preside over" or "to oversee. Because when the Son of Heaven marries his daughters to princes of the same surname, the prince acts as the lord, they are called "Gōngzhǔ" (公主). It also means "to guard."
"Xiān" (先) means "first"; the former "sū" (蘇) is pronounced as "jiàn" (見), while the latter "sū" (蘇) is pronounced as "qián" (前); here it follows its original meaning of "first.
"Zhì" (稚) is pronounced as "zhílì" (直利) and means "young and weak. "Gào yù" (告喻) is pronounced as "yú" (榆);

in the *Lunyu*, it says, "The gentleman is guided by righteousness (*yì*), while the small man is guided by profit (*lì*). Kǒng Ānguó explains that "yù" (喻) means "to enlighten. In the *Cāngjiépiān*, "yù" (喻) is defined as "analogy and admonition. The *Shuowén* writes this character as "yù" (諭).
Regarding "disaster" (zāi): it is pronounced *cái* when reversed. In the *Zuǒzhuan*, fire caused by humans is called "fire" (*huǒ*), while fire from Heaven is called "disaster" (*zāi*).

In the *Zhòushū*, it is written as 災. Regarding "spreading" (*màn yán*): the *Xījīng fù* says, "its form spreads and extends" (*qí xíng màn yán*). In the *Hóngfàn*, the first tone is *wàn* and the second is *yú zhàn*. The *Guǎngyá* states that "màn" means long and "yán" means pervasive. When Wang Yanshou speaks of "the balustrades spreading and extending" (*xuán hǎn màn yán*), he means they are long and uninterrupted. Some take it as "spreading fire-disaster" (*màn yán huǒ zāi*), meaning a continuous conflagration like creeping vines; others take it as *rán* (to burn), meaning a fire-disaster that spreads like mats and is long and uninterrupted.

This "place of hardship" (kǔnàn-chù) [is pronounced kǔnà-chù; the rhyme is chāngyǔ]. The *Shijing* says, "Do not let me have a place to dwell," and its commentary states that "dwelling" (chù) means "residing. The *Liji* asks, "How can I find a place to dwell? where Zheng Xuan explains that "dwelling" (chù) means "peaceful settlement. This implies a place where it is difficult to settle in peace; alternatively, both instances may be read with the departing tone (*qù*), meaning a location of suffering and hardship.

*Zhanmian* (妉湎): The first character, *zhan*, is pronounced as *dīng-hán*. It means to love and delight in [something]. There are also versions written as *tānshì* (躭嗜) or *zhù* (著). The archaic form is *dài* (媅); the *Shuowen Jiezi* also states it means "delight. The second character, *mian*, is pronounced as *shàn-mián*. The *Shuowen* defines *zhan* as "cutting for wine" (*yú jiǔ*). The *Yunjing* also defines it as "addiction and attachment. The archaic form is *huì* (䤄), and there is also a version written as *miàn* (媔); one does not know which to follow.

*Zhāngshī* (張施): *zhāng* is pronounced with the *shì* rhyme-group (*fǎn*) and *fēi*; *shī* is pronounced with the *zhì* rhyme-group (*fǎn*). *Yíngluò* (瓔珞): *yíng* is pronounced with the *yíng* rhyme-group (*fǎn*). It refers to precious necklaces; the "neck-ribbons" (*yīng*) of a crown are also called *yīng*. *Zēngguàng* (繒纊): *zēng* is pronounced with the *jíléng* rhyme-group (*fǎn*), and *guàng* with the *kǔbàng* rhyme-group (*fǎn*).

According to the *Shuōwén* and *Qièyùn*, *zēng* refers to silk fabric and *guàng* to cotton batting. The *Xiǎo Ěryǎ* states that woven silk is called *zēng*. All five colors are collectively termed *zēng*. The *Sāncāng* says it is various silks used to provide for guests when seeing them off. Because it is like the *shīnòu* flower rug, it is called an *yīnrù*. Some write it as *ān* (鞇), which is what is sat upon in a carriage; it is made of tiger skin and possesses patterns. Because it is attached to the lower part [of the seat], the *Qièyùn* defines *ān* as tiger skin. Using *ān* as a mat, some write it as *yīn* (裀); the *Qièyùn* says this means "to cover the body. Regarding these three meanings here, the *Sāncāng* says it is a bedding mat (*rùnjiàn*). The *Qièyùn* says it is a grass mat. Some write it as *rù* (褥), meaning a felt mat.

The character *dié* (㲲) is pronounced with the *tu* and *xié* rhymes; it refers to fine woolen cloth. Nowadays, however, this is not so; there is a separate "cotton-flower" (*diéhuā*) pattern woven to make cloth, whereas the various coarse woollens (*hè*) and felted rugs (*jì*) are made from [ordinary] wool.

"Phin (儐) and Cong (從) mean 'to follow' (shang bi ren fan xiang ye). According to the *Yupian*, it means 'to comply with. One who goes out to receive guests and enters to assist in the rites is called a 'xiang' (相). Furthermore, 'bin' (儐) refers to the act of advancing them forward; it may also be written as 'chui' (󲗇), with the same pronunciation. One who leads in front is a 'bin,' while one who follows behind is a 'cong.'"
*Chì* (熾) is pronounced with the *zhì* (志) tone; it means "to flourish" (*shèng*).
*Rǔ* (汝) is pronounced with the *lèi* (累) tone; it means "to accumulate" (*jī*).

*Abhibhūti* (阿鞞跋致)—*abhibhūti* is read as *bìxí* (陛兮); this is the correct form, though many passages below write it as *āwéiyuèchì* (阿惟越致), which is an error and should follow this [correct] reading. The text also writes it as *āpíbùchì* (阿毘󰍑致), which is likewise an error.

"Shàng" (尚) at the beginning is pronounced *cháng* (常) and *liǎng* (兩) according to the *Yùpiān* (玉篇); it means "perhaps" (*shùjǐ*) or "at dawn" (*dàn*). "Pín" (頻) is pronounced *pǐnlín* (牝鄰); it means to press down repeatedly (*shùshù*) and to tread upon together.

Regarding "bó" (迫), some write it as "pín" (顰); "pín" (顰) and "pín" (𩯭) refer to the contraction of the face. "Bó" (迫) is pronounced *yúlù* (予六). It means to constrain. Some write it as "pín" (顰); "pín" (顰) and "pín" (𩯭) refer to the wrinkling of the face. This is correct.

"Chuxing" (畜生) [is pronounced] with the first character having two readings: *chǒu* (sixth tone) and *hù* (fourth tone). It refers to the six domestic animals (*liùchù*). Furthermore, it has the reading *xù* (fourth tone), meaning "to accumulate. The readings *xù* (fourth tone), *yù* (fourth tone), and *chǒu* (sixth tone) all mean "to gather," which is not the intended meaning here.

The character 𩑔 (tù): In the *Shuowen*, it is read as "mouth-mò" (kǒu-mò). In the *Sancang*, it means a bald head with no hair; it is formed from the radical 頁 (head) and the phonetic 乞 (qǐ). The *Tongsuowen* and *Qieyun* state that a white bald head is called 𩑔. The *Guoyaya* states that 𩑔 and 𩮝 both mean "bald. Some say it describes a state where the skin and flesh are parched and withered, having the appearance of a shriveled skull. It is sometimes read as "mouth-hé" (kǒu-hé), but this is an error for 𩮝 and is not correct.

*Li-tan* (梨黮): The first character is pronounced with the initial *lì* and the final rhyme *zhǐ*. According to the *Fāngyán*, it refers to a facial complexion resembling that of a frozen pear. In the *Qièyùn*, it refers to a mottled or variegated color; some versions use the character *lí* (黧).
