In the *Zìlín*, it is pronounced with the initial *lì* and the final rhyme *xī*, meaning blackish-yellow. The *Tōngsùwén* states that a variegated black is called *lí*. The *Yùpiān* notes that it can also mean old age; some versions use the character *jì* (𪏭). In the *Shuōwén*, it is pronounced with the initial *dù* and the final rhyme *gǎn*, identical to *tán* (潭). In the *Qièyùn*, it refers to a dark, leaden color; it is also pronounced with the initial *tuō* and the final rhyme *gǎn*, referring to the color of the mulberry fruit (*shèn*; pronounced *shí-zhèn*). Some versions use the character *yú* (於) with the final rhyme *zhǎn*, meaning a bluish-black color; this is merely a phonetic loan, as the original character used there is *àn* (黤).

"Touching and harassing" (*chùrǎo*)—the *Shuowen* explains it as the reverse of *liǎo*, meaning "to disturb and play. The *Sāncāng* says it is "harassment" (*rǎo*). Guo Pu says it is "to toy with. The *Guǎngyá* states that "liáo-tiǎo" means "to provoke and harass. "Liáo" is pronounced *liáo*; "tiǎo" is the phonetic transcription of *túliǎo*. The *Qièyùn* defines it as "to disturb one another in play," forming the character *niǎn*. To denote "disturbance and chaos," it forms the character *jiūná* (pronounced *jiūná*). The *Yùpiān* states that "rǎo" is also "disturbance," meaning "to toy with and mock."

In the sense of "to despise" (惡賤), it is pronounced *wù* (with the first tone); for example, in the *Book of Rites*: "How can I bear to let my feelings run wild? (*吾惡用襄吾情*). In the sense of "to loathe" (*惡*, meaning to hate), it is used as in the *Analects*: "I loathe purple for usurping the place of vermilion" (*惡紫奪朱*), and in the *Odes*: "I loathe the lack of ritual propriety" (*惡無禮*).

*Luòtuó* (駱駝): The first character is pronounced *lú* (with the initial *lu*) and the second *gè* (with the initial *ge*). The *Shānhǎijīng* (Classic of Mountains and Seas) states: "The pronunciation is *tuō*. Guo Pu says: "It travels three hundred *li* per day and carries three thousand *jin*. It knows the location of springs; it distinguishes the nature of water veins, and when it digs into the earth with its hoof, a spring gushes forth. *Póu* (掊) is pronounced *pújiāo* (蒲交); in character dictionaries it is written as *𩧐* or as *luò* (駱). Regarding the color of a horse that is white with black manes, it is called *luò*; this is not the meaning here. The second character is pronounced *túhé* (徒何); in the *Bùshì* (Book of Rites) it is written as *tuó* (駞), which has the same pronunciation.
"Mǎng" (pronounced with a retroflex *l*): according to the *Erya*, it refers to the "king of snakes. Guo Pu [notes] that this is the largest among snakes, hence it is called the "king.
"Lóng'ài" (pronounced with a retroflex *h*): according to the *Cangjie pian*, it means "ignorant"; according to the *Fangyan*, it means "foolish."

"Wan-zhuan" (婉轉): the first character is pronounced as *wei-yuan* (威遠) and the second as *zhui-yuan* (追遠). This refers to a snake, which, though footless, is able to move by winding and turning as it progresses; thus the scripture itself says, "winding and turning, crawling on its belly. "Za-za" (唼唼): the second character is pronounced as *zi-da* (子荅).

According to the *Zilin* (字林), "za" means to drink blood; when insects feed, it is called "za. The *Tongsu Wen* (通俗文) and *Qieyun* (切韻) record it as "yi" (𠯗), meaning to take into the mouth; the archaic form is "zi" (㗱). The *Yupian* (玉篇) states that "za" is pronounced as *suo-jia* (所甲); when ducks and geese eat with their beaks, it is called "bai-za" (白唼).

*Cuòlòu* (矬陋): The first character, *cuò*, has the phonetic *cúgē* as its radical and is pronounced according to the *Guǎngyǎ* and *Qièyùn* as meaning "short. The *Tōngsùwén* states that a dwarf is called *cuò*; some texts write it as *zuó*, which refers to a carbuncle (*zuójié*), while the *Shuowén* defines it as a small swelling—neither of these meanings applies here. *Lòu* means "ugly."

*Luán* (𤼣): The first character is pronounced with the *lǚ* rhyme and the *yuán* final; it refers to a disease where the hands are cramped. There is also a reading as *luán* (攣), which in the *Qieyun* is classified under the *liàn* (戀) and *zhuì* (綴) rhymes; it means to be cramped or contracted. The second character is pronounced with the *zhì* rhyme and the *wèi* final; it means to be cramped or constrained. *Bì* (必): The second character is pronounced with the *yì* rhyme; it refers to being lame in the feet.

*Wǔ* (back-bending): In the *Zìlín*, it is pronounced as one *fù*. In the *Tōngsúwén*, a curved spine is called *wǔlǚ*. In the *Qièyùn*, *wǔ* means the back is bent and cannot be extended. The *Dīngmíng* of the *Chūnqiū* states: "At the first appointment one becomes *lǚ*; at the second appointment one becomes *wǔ*; at the third appointment one becomes *fǔ*. Du Yù explains that *fǔ* is more respectful than *wǔ*, and *wǔ* is more respectful than *lǚ*; as the body bends further, the reverence increases. There is also the character *yún* (in the *Zìlín*, pronounced as one *hóu*), meaning dark and obscure. There is also the character *dǐng*, the origin of which is unknown.
*Suǒshǐ suǒlǐ suǒlì* (the second character *lì* is pronounced as in the first instance;

here it follows the initial reading). *Xiāo* (痟): the upper radical is *xiāngjiāo*; the ancient text and the *Ěrpǐ* and *Shuōwén* write it as *xiāojìn*. It means "to exhaust" (*xiāojìn*). It is also the name for the disease of thirst; according to the *Qièyùn*, it refers to the disease of thirst.

*Yī* (依怙; *yī hù gǔ fǎn*; "to rely upon"): According to the *Ěryā*, it means to rely upon (*shì*). The *Guǎngyá* states that it means to depend on, rely on, look up to, or trust (*ài yī yǎng fù shì*). *Qīnfù* (親附; *qīn fù yù fǎn*; "to attach oneself to"): It means to draw near (*jìn*). *Yī* (醫; *yī yú qí fǎn*; "physician"):

The *Shuōwén* defines it as a specialist in treating illness. The nature of a physician is such that they employ medicine by means of wine; thus, the character for *yī* is composed of the radical for "wine" (*yǒu*) and the phonetic *ē* (*yī*). *Ē* is also the sound of a patient. Wine is used to treat illness because medicine does not disperse without wine. The sound of *ē* is *yú xī fǎn*. Some versions write it as *ē* (殹); in antiquity, Wu Pēng first practiced medicine (*yī*), which was written with the radical for "sorcerer" (*wū*); this is a vulgar form of the character.
*Liao* (pronounced zhào) means to treat or cure illness; it is written as *lì* in the *Sāncāng* and *shuōwén*, and is identical [in meaning].
*Miǎo* (initially pronounced jiào, now pronounced yìng) is written as *chāo* or *cāo*; according to the *Yùpiān*, it means to plunder—that is, to take things by force. This is it.
"Privately" (qiè) means to steal; it is a private act.
"To plunder" (héng luó) means to come upon [something] in an unrighteous manner.
"Gardens and pavilions" (yuán guàn) refers to towers and observation halls; if they are residences, they are called "guest-houses" (guàn).

*Ān* (瘖): The upper radical is *yì* (邑) with the phonetic *jīn* (金); it means being unable to speak, which is also *ǎ* (瘂). The lower radical is *è* (厄) with the phonetic *jiǎ* (賈). The *Běicāng* states that *ǎ* is also *ān*. Some write it as *yīn* (喑), which is *yīnyīn* (喑喑). *Yīn* has the phonetic *zǐyè* (子夜). Some write it as *yà* (啞), which has the phonetic *yībái* (乙白) in the *Zílín*; it refers to the sound of laughter. The *Yì* says, "laughing and speaking *yàyà*," but this does not carry that meaning here.
"Jū" (pronounced with a *q* initial, following the rhyme of *yú*) is also a type of carbuncle (*tān*).
"Qīngjié" (the *jié* pronounced with a *xiàn* initial; the *xiè* pronounced as *xiānjié*) is also "pure.
In the "Śraddhāparivarta" (信解品), "jiě" (pronounced with a *xié* initial, also *jiāmǎi*; *jiāmài*; now following the first reading) [is used].
Zhengzhǐng (整征): "Zhǐng" is pronounced with the initial *hù* and final *-dào* (呼到反); it means "to rejoice. "Hào" (好) is pronounced with the initial *wǔ* and final *-xiào* (五孝反);

it means "desire. Qìngxìng (慶幸): "Qìng" is pronounced with the initial *hú* and final *-gèng* (胡耿反). The *Xiǎo Ěryǎ* states: "To obtain what is not one's due is called 'xìng' (fortune/happiness). It refers to encountering good fortune, or also to hoping for it; in all cases, these are things obtained that do not rightfully belong to one.

*Táo* (to flee/escape): In the *Shìshì* (Classical Explanations), it is glossed as *fǎn* (to return); in the *Ěryǎ*, it is glossed as *shì* (to go). In the *Guǎngyǎ*, *shì* is glossed as "to move" (*xíng*) or "to depart" (*qù*).

*Chí* (to gallop) and *chěng* (to race): *Chí* is pronounced with the initial *zhí* and the final *zhī* (upper tone); *chěng* is pronounced with the initial *chǒu* and the final *lǐng* (lower tone). In the *Guǎngyǎ*, *chí* is glossed as "to run" (*bēn*) and *chěng* as "to hasten" (*zǒu*).

"Hu-po" (pronounced *pǔ* in the *Guǎngyǎ*, a name for a pearl) is also written as "po. According to the *Bówùzhì*, there is amber (*hùpò*) in the country of Jibin in the Han period. It is said that pine resin enters the earth and, after a thousand years, transforms into *fúlíng*; after another thousand years, *fúlíng* transforms into amber. It is also called "red pearl. According to the *Guǎngzhì*, amber is found within the earth; no plants or trees grow above or beside it. It reaches a depth of eight or nine feet and is as large as a *hú*. When its outer skin is pared away, the amber is formed within. It has a resinous juice that is initially like peach gum, which hardens and solidifies to become amber. The people of the West use it to make *lù* (a type of vessel), pronounced *wǔguǎn*.
"Ministers, assistants, officials, and the people": "min" (民) refers to the common populace. "Gù" (估):
the first character is pronounced as *shǐyáng* (始羊). "Gù" means to sell on the road;
according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means to travel while selling.
The *Yùpiān* states that "lǚ" (𧶜) refers to rare and exotic goods from the four quarters; it is not used in the sense of "shāng" (to deliberate or bargain).
The pronunciation of "gù" (估) is gōnghù (公戶).

This character does not appear in standard dictionaries; it appears only in the *Ěryá*, specifically in Guō Pǔ’s *Yìnyì* commentary on the "Shìyán" section, where "jiǎ" (賈, merchant) is written with this character.
*Qièyùn*: "Gù" means market tax. *Shuōwén*: "Jiǎ" (pronounced with the *jiā-yǎ* rhyme) means sitting to sell. The *Zhou Lǐ*, in the "Nine Occupations," states:

"The sixth is the Superintendent of the Market (*sīshì*), who manages the weighing and pricing of goods. Zheng Xuan and the *Yùpiān* explain that "weighing" (*gù*) refers to assessing the value of objects, while "sitting to sell" (*jiǎ*) refers to the act of selling. The *Báihūtōng* states: "'Gù' signifies 'shāng' (commerce). One assesses [the value] from afar and near, circulating goods from the four quarters to gather them together."
"Jia" (賈) means "to purchase"; it refers to acquiring goods to await the arrival of the people in order to seek profit.

"Jia" is also a common term; for instance, in the *Zuozhuan*, when Xun Ying was in Chu, a merchant from Zheng was about to place him inside a sack to carry him out, and in the *Shiji*, there is mention of merchants from Yangzhai who traveled back and forth buying low and selling high. This is such usage.
*Tán* (with the *dàn* rhyme): The *Shuowen* explains it as "peaceful. The *Guoya* and *Qieyun* explain it as "level. *Yōng* (upper character with the *yǒng* and *gōng* rhymes):

Cáo Yōng’s *Commentary on the "Encouragement to Learning"* states that "to hire out one's labor is called *yōng*. In the *Zhuangzi*, "one who hires out their labor to others" and "the Mèng family hired out their labor" refer to this. To receive wages is called *yōng*; the *Qieyun* also equates it with "renting. The *Shuowen* states that "renting is also *yōng*."

*Sa* (pronounced *suǎi*, with the "mǎi" rhyme of *sōu*): In the *Tōngsùwén*, it means to cover dust with water; in the *Yùpiān*, it means to sprinkle (*xùn*); in the *Sījiàn* [rhyme dictionary], it means to scatter (*sàn*); in the *Qièyùn*, it means to sweep or to shed.

*Chūnèi* (出內): The first character, *chū*, is pronounced as *shàng chāng suì fǎn* (上昌遂反), meaning "to go out. It is as stated in the *Shijing*: "The words spoken have a pattern" (*chū yán yǒu zhāng*).

In the *Qièyùn*, it is also pronounced as *chì lǜ fǎn* (赤律反). *Sìlì* (肆力): The first character, *sì*, is pronounced as *xiāng lì fǎn* (相利反). According to the *Guǎngyá*, *sì* means "to extend" (*shēn*) and "to set forth" (*chén*). This refers to extending and setting forth one's labor and strength.
*Qiáng* (pronounced *shàng jù liáng fǎn*): to suppress; to be firm; according to the *Cāngjié piān*, it means robust. Also read as *qí liǎng* or *qí liàng* (two pronunciations).
*Jīng è* (pronounced *wǔ gè fǎn*): to be startled and alarmed; also means to be surprised.

"Yu" (俞) is pronounced with the initial *j* and the final *-e* (as in *jue*). In the *Xiao Erya*, it means "to strengthen further. There is also the variant "yu" (愈), which in the *Erya* means "difference. There is also the variant "yu" (逾), which in the *Qieyun* means "to exceed. It also means "to agree" (*yuran*).

“Pí” (擗): This means to strike the ground and beat one’s chest; some editions read it as “bèi” (躃), meaning to fall prostrate, while others read it as “pì” (僻), meaning perverse or crooked—neither of which conveys this meaning. “Xǐngwù” (醒悟):
The first character, “xǐng” (醒), is pronounced sī (思) with the zhì (ㄓ) radical; according to the *Zílín* (字林), it means to remove intoxication.

"Hao" (豪) [in "haowei" 豪貴] is pronounced with the first tone, *hú* (as in *hú-dāo*). In the *Huainanzi*, one whose wisdom exceeds that of a hundred people is called a "hao. In ancient texts it was written as 𠢕; the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines 𠢕 as "vigorous.
"Suonan" (所難) is pronounced with the fourth tone, *nàn*. It means "calamity" (*huàn*) and "sickness" (*ā*).

*Qiáozuì* (憔悴): The first character is pronounced *jiāo* (昨焦反) and the second is pronounced *jì* (疾醉反). According to both the *Sāncāng* and the *Qièyùn*, it is written as *jiàocuì* (顦顇); the *Guǎngyá* and the *Yùpiān* write it as *qiáozuì* (憔悴), meaning "sorrowful distress. The *Erya* states that *cuì* (悴) means "illness."
Guài (上古壞反): This means "strange" or "extraordinary"; it refers to being startled or amazed. Generally, anything marvelous, extraordinary, or unusual is called guài;
the character is composed of 左 (zuǒ). Chuāng (䆫牖餘帚反): According to the *Yùpiān*, this means "pathway" or "direction."
"羸力" (lí lì) means "weakness" (*fǎn* = *ruò*).
"塵坌" (*chén pèn*; *pèn* read with the *pú dùn* rhyme; according to the *Tōngsùwén*, "to scatter earth" is called *pèn*; according to the *Qièyùn*, it means "dust and filth"): "汚穢" (*wū huì*):
the first character, "汚," is read as *wū gù* in the *Zílín*; it means "to smear. According to the *Shìmíng*, "汚" means "to become muddy" (*wū*).

*Duō* (with the phonetic components *dīng* and *wù*, reversed): According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to address one another. Lexicons state it means "to scold"; nowadays it means "to call out" or "to rebuke.
Here, we take the sense of "calling out. *Yíng* (with the phonetic component *yì* and *zhì* reversed): Means "full. It is also written as *yì*.
"Without hope" (*wú xī*) means that when one's opportunities are contrary to expectations, one must instead cultivate aspiration.
"Self-disparagement" (*zì bǐ*)—the character *bǐ* is pronounced *pǔ* (反) and *měi* (反)—is defined in the *Guǎngyǎ* as shame, humiliation, and disgrace.

Regarding "at [name]": the character *mò* (某) is pronounced *pǔ* (反) and also *mò* (厚) (反). In the *Shàngshū*, the *Ěryuán* states, "Your great-grandson [Name]. Kǒng Àngguó notes that "Name" refers to a personal name; because a subject avoids mentioning the ruler's name, it is called "Name. Generally, when a name is unknown, one says "[Name]" (*mò*).

*Língpíng* (the first character pronounced *dīng* with the level tone, the second *pǐng* with the level tone). The *Sāncāng* states that *língpíng* means "flitting about" (*liánpiān*) and also describes a state of being solitary. According to the *Qièyùn*, walking in an irregular manner is called *língpíng*. The first character *líng* is also pronounced *lángdīng*, and the second *píng* is also pronounced *pǔdīng*. Furthermore, it is said that *pìng* may also be written as *bìng*. Walking in an irregular manner is also written as *qíngtíng* (the first character *qíng* pronounced *lǚzhēn*, the second *tíng* pronounced *chìzhēn*). According to the *Qièyùn*, *tíng* refers to walking in an irregular manner. Some write it as *qíngpéng*; in the *Zìlín*, the first character *qíng* is pronounced *lìshēng* and the second *péng* is pronounced *bǔzhèng*, which is the same as *bèng* (to scatter). However, *qíng* meaning "irregular" and *bèng* meaning "to disperse" are not the meanings intended here.

*Jiānchú* (蠲除): "Jiān" is pronounced *xuán* in the ancient dialect; in the southern region of Chǔ, those who have recovered from illness are called *jiān*. Guō Pǔ says it means "to eliminate. *Lìnxī* (吝惜):
"Lìn" is pronounced *lì* in the *Lìjìn* rhyme dictionary; it means "miserliness. "Xī" (惜) is also synonymous with "lìn" (吝).

To "huǐzī" (毀呰) means to revile; the character *zī* (呰) signifies reproach. The *Book of Rites* states: "As for those who revile (*zī*), no one knows the rites. Regarding the term "shēng" (所生), Zheng Xuan’s commentary says: "To verbally revile is called *zī*. In the *Qieyun*, "huǐ" (毀) is written as "zhì" (訿); in archaic texts, "zī" (訾) and "kè" (㰣) are identical.
"Self-entertainment" (zìyú) means joy; it is pronounced with the initial *jù* and the final *fǎn*.
"To seek" (qiúsuǒ) means to beg or to request; it is pronounced with the initial *suǒ* and also with the final *gè*.
"Morning and night" (*sūyè*)—in the *Erya*, "morning" (*sū*) refers to dawn or early morning; it is pronounced with the initial *sī* and the final *liù*.

The term *zhù* (註) refers to the analogy of "upward-facing bamboo" (*shàngzhú*), which is the opposite of the broad commentary on the *Guǎyá*. It means to recognize or identify. The *Zílín* explains it as an annotation; the *Tōngsùwén* states that to record things is called *zhù*. In the *Qièyùn*, it is written as *zhù*, with the phonetic value being *zhǐ zhù zhī shù èr fǎn*.
*Qū* (驅) may also be written as *qù* (作驅); they are interchangeable. *Shā* (殺) may also be written as *shài* (作煞); they are interchangeable. Regarding *miǎo* (眇):

the upper character is pronounced *míliǎo* (彌了反). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "one eye is small. The *Shiming* states: "When the eye sockets are sunken, it is called *miǎo*. The *Fangyan* says: "*Miǎo* means small. The *Qieyun* defines it as "vision that is not correct."

The *jiàn* (薦) mat is made of boiled hemp fibers and is the reverse of the grass mat (*cǎojiàn*). It is used as a cushion for the bed, placed beneath the sitting mat (*xí*) to provide warmth. The character is pronounced with the final *-xiáng* (祥) and the initial *kǎo* (考). It is explained as meaning "to rest upon" (*jí*) or "a rug" (*yīn*). Alternatively, it is written as *xí* (蓆), which, according to the *Shuōwén*, indicates that in ritual practice the mats of the Son of Heaven and the feudal lords were adorned with *fǔ* and *fú* patterns and bordered with brocade; the character is composed of the radical *zhōng* (巾) and the phonetic *yì* (𢉙) in abbreviated form.

"Cān" (pronounced *ǎn*): According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means "a hut" (*túsū*). Examining its phonetic component, it is *lú*. It is so called because it is covered; that is, it is surrounded and covered with grass. There are those who take it to be "ān," a name for medicinal herbs, such as the *ānqié* fruit. The *Gōngjīn zhèngzì* states: "When *lú* has a ridge-pole, it is a *hùn*; *hùn* is the same as *ān*. It follows the radical *guǎng* (roof) and takes *ǎn* as its phonetic."
*He*: What can be borne? Also read as *fǎn* (in the *Húgē* rhyme-cut). In the *Yùnyīng*, it means to carry a load; it is said to mean to lift up, as well as to bear. 3.

*Yàocǎoyùpǐn* (The Chapter on the Simile of the Medicinal Herbs). *Chéng*: As noted above, its pronunciation is *shēng*. In the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means respect. In the *Shuōwén*, it means sincerity and truthfulness; it is composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) with "chéng" as the phonetic. It signifies that which is true and real. It follows the sound of "chéng."

*Xi* (溪): Upper radical *qi*, lower *xi*, with the phonetic *fan*. According to the *Erya*, "a stream flowing into a river is called a *xi*. Lower radical *gong*, lower *mu*, with the phonetic *fan*. *Hui* (卉):

Upper radical *hui*, lower *wei*, with the phonetic *fan*. According to the *Erya*, "*hui* refers to grasses. Guo Pu says: "It is the general name for the hundred plants. The *Fangyan* states: "*Hui* means 'many' [plants]; in the regions between Dongyue, Wu, and Yang, grasses are called *hui*. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of three *chuo* (屮), where *chuo* is pronounced *chu lie*.

Regarding "congr-lin" (叢林): the upper radical is pronounced *hong* (反) and *kao* (考). It is said that when trees grow in a cluster, it is called "cong" (叢); the common vulgar form is written as "cong" (藂). In the *Han Shu*, Dongfang Shuo zhuan, it is written as "chong" (樷), which is neither correct nor standard. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "a gathering. It is composed of the radical *zhuang* (󱵝, pronounced *chuang* [牀]) and the phonetic *qu* (取). It is a pictographic character.

"Deng-zhu" (等澍)—the "zhu" is pronounced as in "zhu-shu" (戍). The *Sancang* (三蒼) states it refers to seasonal rain; it means that the hundred plants are thoroughly moistened. The *Shuowen* (說文) states: "In ancient times, 'deng-zhu' was the means by which all things were brought to life."

*Pù* (pronounced *xián jiá fǎn*): According to the *Cāngjié piān*, it means "to disperse. According to the *Shuōwén*, *qiá* means "to moisten"; its archaic form is written as *hè*. *Āidài*: The upper character is *ài* and the lower is *dài*.

According to the *Bīcāng*, the *Qièyùn* is the same; according to the *Guǎngyǎ*, *ài dài* means "dense and lush. *Yì wèi* (pronounced *wū wài fǎn*) refers to the appearance of clouds rising in great abundance. The *Tōngsúwén* states that when clouds cover the sun, it is called *ài dài*.
*Chénglǎn* (承攬): To receive and take up; it is also written as *lǎn*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to grasp and hold.
*Yōusùì* (幽邃): Pronounced *sīzuì* (私醉). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "profound and distant. The archaic form is written as *èi* (㥞).

"Bai gu" (hundred grains) is pronounced "gu ku" (古木) according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*; "gu" means continuity. "Hundred grains" is a collective name for all grains. Yang Quan’s *Wuli Lun* states: "Liang" is the collective name for *shu* and *ji*; "dao" is the collective name for *rang* and *nuo*; "shu" is the collective name for various beans. Each of these three categories of grain comprises twenty types, totaling sixty. The fruits of vegetables and plants that assist the grains also comprise twenty types, making a total of one hundred varieties. Thus, the *Shijing* says, "He sows his hundred grains," and the *Zhouyi* says, "The hundred grains, grasses, and trees depend upon the earth. This refers to this very point.

Regarding "seedlings" (*miao*): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that seedlings are grasses growing in a field; the *Cangjie Pian* says they are the stage before the grain has emerged its ears. The *Lunyu* says, "The seedling grows but does not produce ears," which refers to the grain. The *Shuowen Jiezi* further explains that when the grain has produced ears and fruit it is called "grain" (*jia*), while the stalk itself is called "grain" (*he*). Another interpretation holds that what is grown in the wild is called "grain" (*jia*).
Regarding "gānzhe" (sugarcane), various texts state it is also called "yuzhe," "jizhe," or "zhe"; these all refer to the same object.

Regarding "pútáo" (grape), the *Bowuzhi* states that Zhang Qian, upon returning from his mission to the Western Regions, obtained the pomegranate, the walnut, and the grape. According to the *Guangya*, there are three kinds of *putao*: white, black, and purple. [The characters] "táo" and "tao" are both acceptable.
*Ku-gǎo* (枯槁): "Zi-lin" (字林) reads *kǔ*; "Yùn" (韻) reads *gǔ*. It means withered or parched. In ancient script it is written as 𣩅;

the *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文解字) writes it as 槀. *Yī-dī* (一滴滴): "Tong-sú-wén" (通俗文) states that a drop of spirit is called *tí*; "Yùn" (韻) writes it as 𤁷. Some write it as 渧 (*dīng-jì*); this refers to water falling, which is not the meaning here.

**Chapter on Bestowing Prophecy (Vyākaraṇa-parivarta)** *Shou* (授): To bestow; to entrust. *Ji* (讎): [Pronounced with the right-toned rhyme] *chóu*. *Wa* (瓦): [Pronounced with the forceful-toned rhyme] *lì*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi* and *Yupian*, it refers to small stones; according to the *Qieyun*, it means sand. *Lì* (礫): [Pronounced with the forceful-toned rhyme] *lì*. According to the *Shuowen*, it means small stones; according to the *Yupian*, it means sand. *Keng* (坑): [Pronounced with the level-toned rhyme] *kēng*. Alternatively written as *xíng* (硎). According to the *Yupian*, it means a void or a moat; the lower character is pronounced *kǎn* (坎). According to the *Shuowen*, it means a pitfall; according to the *Yupian*, it means a small *léi* jar. *Kǎn* (坎): [Pronounced with the level-toned rhyme] *kǎn*. According to the *Shuowen*, it means a depression or a pit; according to the *Yupian*, it means a small *léi* vessel. *Léi* (罍): [Pronounced with the level-toned rhyme] *léi*. According to the *Shuowen*, it means a large wine vessel; according to the *Yupian*, it means a small *léi* jar. *Kǎo* (考): [Pronounced with the level-toned rhyme] *kǎo*. According to the *Shuowen*, it means to investigate or examine; according to the *Yupian*, it means to verify or to pass away. *Jiè* (戒): [Pronounced with the entering-toned rhyme] *jiè*. According to the *Shuowen*, it means to warn or admonish; according to the *Yupian*, it means to restrain or to prohibit. *Jù* (具): [Pronounced with the level-toned rhyme] *jù*. According to the *Shuowen*, it means to provide or to prepare; according to the *Yupian*, it means to possess or to be complete. *Jiān* (漸): [Pronounced with the entering-toned rhyme] *jiàn*. According to the *Shuowen*, it means to gradually advance; according to the *Yupian*, it means to step forward. *Chóng* (重): [Pronounced with the level-toned rhyme] *chóng*. According to the *Shuowen*, it means to repeat or to double; according to the *Yupian*, it means to value highly or to be layered. *Chóng* (崇): [Pronounced with the level-toned rhyme] *chóng*. According to the *Shuowen*, it means to honor or to revere; according to the *Yupian*, it means to exalt or to be lofty. *Chóng* (寵): [Pronounced with the level-toned rhyme] *chǒng*. *Dui* (pronounced *dūléi*) means a mound formed by the accumulation of earth; the *Yùpiān* defines it as a small clod. The character below is pronounced *fángwǔ*; it means a hill. The *Yùpiān* states that level heights are called *líng*, while great heights are called *fù*. It signifies greatness, thickness, and length; it refers to a mountain that is broad and large despite being low in elevation.

Regarding "Qiu" (Hill/Mound): The *Shuowen* states that a hill is a height of earth not created by human hands; one definition says it is that which is high on all four sides with the center low, called a "qiu. The *Yupian* states that high ground is called a "qiu," and a large tomb is also called a "qiu. In ancient script, "qiu" is written as "tu" (earth).
"Shu" (數) is pronounced with the third tone, a retroflex *l* rhyme (*shān lǚ*). It means "to calculate"; to examine its numbers is called "counting" (*shù*).
"Li" (慄) is pronounced with the fourth tone, a *zhì* rhyme (*lì lì zhì*). It means "to tremble in battle. According to the *Yùpiān*, it also means "reverence," "fear," and "solicitude."

The character 粖 (pronounced *mo*, with the initial *ge* as a variant) is used when the hand rubs or strokes [the body]; it is written as 抹 (*mo*) when referring to anointing or adorning. Since there is now a separate term for "unguent" (*vilepana*), it should be written as 抹. According to the *Yùpiān*, 粖 has two pronunciations: *mángdá* and *mángjié*, both meaning "gruel" or "porridge. It refers to finely crushed incense like cotton wool; thus, it is written as 粖. If it were like fine dust, it should be written as 󱆙.

The name "Jambūdvīpa" (Jambudvīpa) derives from the Jambū tree; it is located on the shore of Lake Anavatapta on this continent. There is a sutra concerning this, which states that because a purple-gold light near the tree and water on the northern shore of this continent eclipses the sun and moon, it is named after them.
The Buddha Tamālapatracandanagandhābhijña-Bhadra-candana-gandha. Regarding the "long *stūpa*-pole" (*dīrgha-yaṣṭi*): in Sanskrit it is called *śamasaṇa*, which means "tomb.

When those in the Western Regions die, they may leave their remains to birds and beasts or collect their bones and burn them; some bury them underground and erect a pole upon them, piling up bricks, stones, and so forth. These resemble small *stūpas* (caityas), but their form is low and small. What is referred to here as a "long pole" is actually a golden finial (*kīla*), not that aforementioned pole. In Sanskrit it is called *cchattra-dhara*. In that land, there is no separate flagpole; rather, the banner is suspended from the top of the pillar of the inverted bowl (*kapāla*) of the *stūpa*. Although the term currently used, "finial" (*kīla*), is a corruption of the sound, because it is made of gold and stands tall as a marker, it is called a "golden finial."

Chapter Four: The Parable of the City of Illusion. "Mò" (磨) is pronounced as "mò" (莫可反), meaning to grind; if pronounced as "mō" (莫波反), it means to polish. "Zhuó" (灼) is written as "zhào" (󲉉). "Guǐ" (鬼) is written as "mó" (魔). "Piān" (偏) has the level tone (píng) [as in] "wú" (無). The level tone is [as in] "wú" (無).
"Mǒ" (pronounced with the initial *mo* and the final *fǎn*) means to rub or stroke with the hand; it is called "mǒ.

"Tiānjì" (pronounced with the initial *qí* and the final *fǎn*) refers to artistic skills; "nǚyuè" refers to female musicians performing as entertainers. Some versions read "yìlì" (standing leaning), but this is not the meaning of the scriptures.

*Tìqì* (weeping): "Tì" is pronounced with the *thā-lǐ* (thâ-li) rhyme. The *Mao Shī* commentary on the passage "tears and mucus flow profusely" states: "Tears that emerge from the eyes are called *tì*. The *Shuōwén* defines *qì* as "tears emerging without sound.

*Dàn* (serene): "Dàn" is pronounced with the *tú-làn* (tu-lân) rhyme. The *Shuōwén* defines *dàn* as "peaceful" and "tranquil," meaning to be *dàn-rán* (serenely) at ease. The *Yùpiān* gives *dàn* the pronunciation *tú-gǎn* (tu-gân), meaning "calm and still" (*tián-jìng*) and also "at ease. There are also variants: *tián* for "calm" and *jìng* for "still"; or *tán* (as in the *Shuōwén*, *tú-gān* [tu-gân]) meaning "sorrow," which is not the sense intended here. Lexicons also write it as *tán* (pronounced *tú-làn*). *Bà* (composed): "Bà" is pronounced with the *pǐ-bái* (pî-pâi) rhyme. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "non-action" (*wúwéi*). The *Guǎngyá* states: "*Dàn-bà* means tranquil and still. This is as expressed in the *Zǐxū Fù*: "Composed (*bà*) and free from desire, serene (*dàn*) and self-sustained."

"Blind and dark" (*mángmíng*) means the opposite of light; according to the *Yùpiān*, it is pronounced with the rhyme *dìng* (as in *mòdìng*), meaning night or obscurity. "Darkness" (*míng*) refers to that which obscures the eyes so that nothing can be seen, and also to being immature.
Regarding the "Dharma of peace and security free from outflows" (*anǐnyǒulèfǎ*), one should follow the Dharma through practice on the Path; it is not the case that one follows only the Path itself.

To escape from the prison of the three realms is not far off. (The *Fǎnyùn* [Rhyme Dictionary] cites this; it shares the same meaning as "to pull" (*wǎn*). There is also the variant "to exert" (*miǎn*, with the phonetic *mí biàn*). The *Guóyǔ* says, "The father exhorts his son; the elder brother exhorts his younger brother," which refers to strong encouragement—that is, urging and instructing them. In the *Xiǎo Èryǎ*, it says "exertion in affairs and strength. In ancient texts, it is identical to *lì* [to strive]).

"Qunmeng" (羣萌) means that the myriad beings have not yet sprouted; it refers to the beginning. "Meng" (萌) has the sense of being obscure and indistinct. Alternatively, it is written as "meng" (氓) with the radical for "people" (民), signifying a multitude of ignorant ones. In the *Hanshu*, "meng" refers to the common people. In ancient texts, it is written as "meng" (氓).

"Reciting" (*fèngsòng*): "Fèng" is pronounced as *fēng* (the same as *fēng* in *fēnghuáng*). Reciting from memory is called "fèng," while reciting against the text is called "sòng. According to the *Zhouli*, in teaching the sons of the nobility, it says: "There is no [method] other than fèng and sòng. Zheng Xuan explains: "Reciting against the text is called 'fèng'; modulating it with the voice is called 'sòng'."
"Akṣobhya" is a transliteration from the Sanskrit; in the Tang language, it means "Immovable.
"Amitābha" is a transliteration from the Sanskrit; "Amitāyus" (A-mi-duo-na-jing-sa) means "Infinite Life" in this language.
*Kuángjué* (曠絕): The upper character is pronounced *kǔ bàng fǎn*. Furthermore, the *Yùpiān* states it means empty, sparse, vast, long, or distant.

*Yìhài* (億姟): In the *Zílín*, this is pronounced *gǔ lái fǎn*; it is a name for a numerical unit. According to the *Fēngsùtōng*, ten thousand is called *wàn* (萬), one hundred thousand is called *yì* (億), one billion is called *zhào* (兆), ten billion is called *jīng* (京), and one hundred billion is called *hài* (姟); these are all large numbers. In archaic script, it appears as two forms: *shǎn* (󲌖) and *huán* (奒).
*Yíng* (營): Pronounced *yú* (余) and *qióng* (瓊). According to the *Cāngjié piān*, it means "to guard" (*yìngwèi*) and also refers to "military units" (*bùwǔ*).

In archaic script, it is written as *sì* (覮). *Chéngguò* (城郭): According to the *Shìběn*, Gùn (鯀) built the city walls and moats. The *Gōngyáng zhuan* asks: "What is a *guò* (郭)? It is 'vast and expansive' (*huīkuò*). There are some who write it as *diàn* (墎) with the "earth" radical, but this is incorrect. *Gùn* is pronounced *gǔběn* (古本).

Chapter Five: The Chapter on the Prophecy for the Five Hundred Disciples, Volume Four. *Shou* (受): Pronounced *zhí yǒu* (植酉). According to the *Yùpiān*, it means to receive, to contain, to obtain, and to succeed. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means to entrust one another; it is composed of the radical *jī* (𠬪) and the abbreviated form of *zhōu* (舟). *Ráoyì* (饒益): The first character is pronounced *rú zhāo* (如招). According to the *Yùpiān*, it means much, abundant, thick, beneficial, and surplus.
*Kǐjiàn* (溪澗): The first character, *kǐ*, has the phonetic *qīng-xí* (reverse); the second, *jiàn*, has the phonetic *gǔ-yàn*. According to the *Yùpiān*, it is the name of a river. *Gōuhè* (溝壑):

According to the *Shuōwén*, a *gōu* is a water channel; one four feet wide and deep is called a *gōu*. The second character, *hè*, has the phonetic *hū-gè*. According to the *Ěryá*, when a flowing stream becomes deep, it forms a *hè*; a *hè* is also a ditch or pond. According to the *Yùpiān*, a *hè* is a valley, a depth, a void, a cave, or a chamber.

Regarding "tái guàn" (terraces and towers): according to the *Érya*, that which is high on all four sides is called a *tái* (terrace); furthermore, what is called a *guàn* (tower) is termed a *què* (gate-tower). Sun Yan stated: "They are twin towers at the palace gates. The *Shiming* says: "A *guàn* is so called because one observes and looks out from atop it."
Kālodāyin, Udāyin, and Uttarin—these names mean "born at the time when the sun first appears.
Cūḍapanthaka, Svāgata, and Śabala—these names mean "Welcome."

"Qīnyǒu" (intimate friend) is the reverse of "yǒu" (friend). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, those who share the same aspirations are called "yǒu. The *Guangya* states that "yǒu" means "qīn" (intimate). The *Liji* (Book of Rites) notes: "In referring to 'liáoyǒu' (colleague), one speaks of their *dì* (fraternal respect); in referring to 'zhíyǒu' (close friend), one speaks of their *rén* (benevolence). Zheng Xuan commented: "Liáoyǒu are those who hold office together; zhíyǒu are those who share the same aspirations."

*Jiān* (pronounced *guán* in the ancient dialect) is written as *jiàn* in the Zhòuwén script. The *Shuōwén* explains it as "earth that is difficult to cultivate. The *Shìmíng* states: "It is the 'root' (*gēn*) of difficulty; like the root and sprout of a thing, it means that which people dread (*dàn*). It is called thus because it is what people avoid and fear."

*Yì* (𧶻): Upper radical *mò* (莫) with tone *hòu* (候). According to the *Sāncāng*, it means to exchange or trade goods. The character *yì* (𧶝) is composed of *bèi* (貝, "shell money") and *yǒu* (丣); *yǒu* is an archaic form of the character *yǒu* (酉). There is also a variant *yì* (𧴵), but it does not carry this meaning. In the *Yùpiān*, it is read as *jiǎ* (雅) with tone *fǎn* (反), referring to a personal surname.

Chapter Six: Bestowing Predictions upon Those in Training and Those Beyond Training. *Dao* (to tread): According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means to walk upon or to practice. According to the *Shiming*, it means to tread upon the Way, as if walking along a path with one's feet.

7. Chapter on the Dharma Master. "Shi" (仕) [with the phonetic *juan* (眷)] means to serve; it refers to the utensils for food and drink. It also means to eat or to present food. In the *Yupian*, it is also used for eating; it may also be written as *zuan* (󳇺), which is identical to *zhuan* (撰).

*Chuàn* (to bore): *zài* and *fǎn*. The *Yùpiān* states that it means to bore wood; it is also written as *zuò*, with the same meaning. *Càn*: *shì xián* rhyme. *Càn* is like a chisel. "The Tathāgata’s chamber":

according to the *Shuōwén*, a "chamber" (*shì*) is the interior space. That which is outside the door is the hall (*táng*), and that which is inside the door is the chamber. This is as stated in the *Lúnyǔ*: "Byu ascended to the hall, but had not yet entered the chamber."

The character *dòu* (句逗) is pronounced as *tú* (徒󲑁反); according to the *Zìshū* (字書), it means "to linger" (*dòuliú*). The *Shuōwén* (說文) states it means "to stop" (*dòuzhǐ*), while the *Fāngyán* (方言) states it means "to stay" (*dòuzhù*). It is also written as *dòu* (竇), meaning "to connect" (*yì*); a "phrase" (*jù*) is able to connect and explicate various principles and meanings.
"Dry" (*gān*)—the *Shuowen* also defines it as "moistureless. The *Yijing* says, "Fire seeks the dry. Regarding *qīngmó* (寂莫)—the upper character is pronounced *qíng* and the lower is *mó* (博).

The *Kaosheng* states that *qīngmò* means "to be silent and without sound. The *Yijing* says, "I opened its door, but it was desolate and empty; no one was there," referring to stillness and silence where no human voice is heard. The character *jì* (寂) is derived from *shū* (叔), a vulgar form. The character *mò* (漠) is derived from *shuǐ* (水), which refers to the "desert" (*shāmò*); neither of these is the original, correct form.
*Guài* (罣礙): *hú guà* (反). In character dictionaries, it means a net or an obstruction. According to the *Shuowen*, it means to stop or block. In ancient forms, it was written as *huà* (罫). 8.

*Jiàn Bǎotǎ Pǐn* (見寶塔品), "Chapter on Seeing the Jewel Stupa. Regarding *kǎnshì* (龕室): *kǎn* (龕) is pronounced *kǔ hán* (反). According to the *Guǎngyá*, *kǎn* means to contain or to take. In the *Shàngshū Dàzhuàn*, it means to overcome or subdue. Examining the term *kǎnshì*, it refers to something like a modern *tánkǎn* (檀龕, sandalwood shrine). Small shrines (*kǎn*) were installed on the four sides of the great stupa like rooms; therefore, they are called *kǎnshì*. Within these small rooms, there are various forms and images, such as those in a *tánkǎn*. According to the *Shuowen*, the character is composed of the radical *lóng* (龍) and the phonetic *hán* (含) with the *shěng* (省) radical.

The term "wǎng màn" (net-canopy)—the first character pronounced as mò (with the fanqie *mo* and *bàn*)—refers to what is on the sides, called a *wéi* (curtain), and what is above, called a *màn*. If the second character is read as yuàn (with the fanqie *wǔ* and *ān*), it is written as *màn*. A net is placed upon this canopy and adorned with jewels; its magnificent decoration is like that of a carriage awning (*xiǎn*), and thus it is named the "Jewel Net Canopy."

The "jeweled interlaced canopy" (ratnajāla-avataṃsaka) refers to a canopy that supports dew; it is decorated with interlaced jewels. Furthermore, whether the canopy is exposed or covered, both are decorated with interlaced jewels. Moreover, the canopy may have various parts covered and exposed, all adorned with interlaced jewels. Or, it may be a fixed canopy clearly exposed, decorated with interlaced jewels—all such cases are termed "jeweled interlaced canopies."
"Lin" (林) refers to a grove; when trees are gathered together, it is called a grove. "Sou" (藪) refers to a marsh; a body of water within a marsh that lacks flowing water is called a sou.

"Ji" (齎) means to carry wealth to give to others; the character is composed of "bei" (貝, meaning shell-currency/wealth) and takes "qi" (齊) as its phonetic. In archaic script, it is written as "ji" (齎).

*Mǎnjū* (滿掬): "Gōng" (弓) is read as *fǎn* (反). It means to grasp with both hands; when an object is held in the hands, it is sometimes written as *jū* (匊). *Guān* (關) is read as *yú* (余) and *zhuó* (灼).

According to the *Fānyán* (方言), those east of the Guān pass call it *jiàn* (鍵), while those west of the Guān pass call it *guān* (關). The archaic form is *yuè* (鑰), which is the same. There is also a version written with the "bamboo" radical as *yuè* (籥), but this refers to a musical instrument and is not the meaning intended in the scripture.

*Wúyāng* (無央)—the *yāng* is pronounced with the *liáng* (良) tone; in Sanskrit it is called *asaṃkhyeya*, meaning "innumerable" (*wúyāngshù*). *Yāng* means "to exhaust. There is also a reading as *āng* (鞅), where the *āng* is pronounced with the *yúliǎng* (於兩) tone; however, according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, this refers to the nape of the neck and does not carry the meaning intended here. The pronunciation of *zhì* (犆) is *zhīliè* (之列).
"Wherever one goes, wherever one stays, and in whatever place one arrives—whether it be a dwelling or not—it is because of abiding there. 'Yuan' (遠) means to cast far;
'zhi' (擲) means to throw back or discard; in ancient texts it was written as 'ze' (擿)."

"Holds with the hand" (shǒu bǎ): the character "bà" is pronounced *pá* (with the *bǎ* rhyme) or is written as "pá. It means to scratch or to scrape; here it follows the sense of "scraping" (*póu*), which is pronounced *pújiāo*. Both characters are radical 64 (hand). Devadatta-pin;
in the Tang dynasty, this was translated as Tiānshòu (Heaven-Bestowed).

*Juan* (捐): Upper radical *shang* with the phonetic *zhuan* (專). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "to discard. The *Erya* says it means "to abandon. Guo Pu comments: "To set aside and place down. Regarding *wei zheng* (委政) in the *Guoyu*, it says "abandoning government is failing one's responsibility.

Jia’s commentary states: "Government (*zheng*) is equivalent to office (*zhi*). In the *Zuo Zhuan*, regarding "governing affairs" (*weizheng shi yongli*), Du Yu says: "In the case of a ruler, it is 'government' (*zheng*); in the case of a minister, it is 'affairs' (*shi*). In the *Lunyu*, regarding "guiding them with government," Kong Anguo states: "Government refers to laws and instruction."

*Zhui zhōng* (椎鍾): "Zhui" (椎) is pronounced *zhí* (直) with the *zhuī* (追) rhyme; the *Shuowen* states it means "to strike. There is also a character written as *chuí* (槌) following the *zhuī* (追) radical, which is a vulgar usage and not the correct form. It is also pronounced *zhí lèi* (直淚); in the region east of the Passes, it is called a *cán chuí* (蠶槌).
Asita (阿私仙): Asita (阿私多) is translated in the Tang language as "Incomparable" (無比), and also as "Handsome" (端正). Regarding *guǒluò* (果蓏):

the character for *guǒ* (果) is pronounced with the *láng* (郎) rhyme-group and has a variant reading as *guā* (瓜, melon). To avoid vulgar usage, the *Yùpiān* (玉篇) states: "Fruit" (*guǒ*) refers to species such as peaches and plums; "gourd" (*luò*) refers to species such as melons and cucumbers. Furthermore, that which has a pit is called "fruit" (*guǒ*), while that which lacks a pit is called "gourd" (*luò*). Again, the fruit of trees is called "fruit" (*guǒ*), while the fruit of herbs is called "gourd" (*luò*). Moreover, that which grows upon trees is called "fruit" (*guǒ*), while that which grows upon the ground is called "gourd" (*luò*). [The character for] *tuó* (󲁇) is pronounced with the *dú* (徒) rhyme-group and the *jié* (結) final.

"Ren" (仁) is pronounced as *shàng* (上) or *líng* (鄰). In the *Zhouli* (周禮), among the six virtues, the first is called "ren. Zheng’s commentary states: "Loving people and things is called ren; mutual affection between superiors and subordinates is called ren; bestowing honor upon the worthy and being kind to one's kin is called ren; sacrificing one's life to complete another is called ren. The *Shiming* (釋名) says: "Ren means 'to endure' (*rěn*). To favor life and loathe killing, and to be capable of enduring both good and evil, is called ren. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文解字) derives it from two persons with the phonetic *shēng* (聲), stating that "conduct without duality is called ren."
*Kai-chan* (開闡): According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, *kai* means to open and *chan* means to clarify. *Pō* (頗): Pronounced *pǔ duō* (普多) with a borrowed sound *pǔ wǒ* (普我);

it is a discourse particle found in various texts. *Ná* (那): An extremely small measure of time. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that one hundred and twenty *kṣaṇas* constitute the measure of one *tatkṣaṇa*; sixty of these make one *lava*; thirty of these make one *muhūrta*; and thirty of these make one day and night. Thirty days and nights make a month; within a year, the nights are reduced by half, which can be calculated based on the *muhūrta*. The *Yùpiān* defines *muhūrta* as a brief interval. Although some versions of the sutra read "a thousand *kṣaṇas*" (*qiān chà nà qǐng*), the original Sanskrit manuscript lacks the character for "thousand" (*qiān*); this was likely added erroneously by later scribes.

Chapter 9: Encouraging Retention. "Bie" (弊) means wicked and oppressive; it is also read as "piel" (篇列), where the first character has the same meaning of being frivolous and easily angered. "Pieshen" (嫳妜) refers to a quick-tempered nature; "yue" (妜) is pronounced *yùe*.
*Kautamī* is correctly pronounced *Gautamī*.
In ancient times it was called *Kautamī*,
and it is also called *Gautama*.
These are all corruptions and abbreviations; the correct name is Gautama,
with Śākya as his clan name.
Gautama is a mere pretender.
The Śākya kingship has been inherited through successive generations;
yet this rebel has risen in opposition to usurp the throne of the nation.
Fearing that his sovereignty over the state would be usurped,
the King of Thieves then executed the Śākya clan and exterminated his close relatives so that no lineage remained.
At that time, there was a seer who surveyed the noble families everywhere.
Seeing a woman who was pregnant, he realized that she would surely give birth to a son; he then made a formal request in hopes that the lineage might be continued.
His mother granted his plea.
Later, a son was indeed born, and when he reached the age of childhood, the immortal returned from the stars and appeared once more.
The bandit king was terrified;
he sought out the hermit’s dwelling and learned that he resided in the mountains.
While waiting for the immortal to be away, he secretly ordered his men to capture him.
He threaded it onto a long pole and announced it to the people of the country, commanding them to cease their heterodox views.
When the rishi returned to his chamber, he did not see his son;
pursuing him in haste, he beheld him in such a state.
He then manifested supernatural powers to save him.
Knowing that the man's life could not be sustained, he sent down a fine rain to cause him to regain a slight consciousness and manifested as a woman to urge him to engage in sexual union,
saying, "If you do not comply, the Xu lineage will surely come to an end."
The boy followed his father’s instructions and together they buried the body; as it decomposed, it became stained by the soil.
A seer gathered the remains, placed them within cow dung, and set them in a sugarcane grove. As the sun’s warmth shone upon them, ten months passed, and a male child was born.
His deportment and crown were beyond compare, and his spirit was extraordinary.
After the immortal returned him to nourishment, he was once more able to become king;
from this point on, Śākya regained the succession to the throne.
Therefore, "Gautama" is translated here as "of the Ikṣvāku (Sugarcane) lineage," or "of the Sun-burnt lineage.
Among the Śākya clan, there are extremely many lineages.
The Gautama Śākyas are the most noble of lineages, their succession of heirs perpetually maintaining a position of supreme dignity.
If one disparages them by saying they are of "cow-dung seed" or "mud-born," it is for this reason that the Gautama clan is so called.
"Ma" is a masculine sound; it is the clan name of the Buddha, which is transliterated as Gautama.
"Mi" is a feminine sound;
because she was called the Buddha's maternal aunt, she is referred to as Gautamī.

Regarding the characters for *mà* (to revile) and *lì* (to curse): in the *Cāngjié piān*, it is stated that *lì* is also *mà*. Now, to address evil words directed at someone, one says *mà*; to slander, calumniate, or cast curses, one says *lì*. Both are *wǎng-xíng-shēng* (phonetic-semantic) characters.

*Āraṇya* (阿練若) means a secluded and quiet place, located more than one *krośa*—that is, over four *li*—from a village. *Pāruṣya* (誹謗): the first character is pronounced with the "fei" rhyme and also means "to slander";

according to the *Yùpiān*, it is pronounced with the "fù" rhyme, while the second character is pronounced with the "bù" and "làng" rhymes, meaning "to revile and curse. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "evil. In the *Guóyǔ*, the Left Scribe slandered [the King], and Jia Kui explained: "To speak of someone's evil to others."

*Kai* (鎧) is pronounced with the *ku* and *ai* finals; it means armor (*kavaca*). *Jian* (見) is pronounced with the *bin* and *bi* finals; it means to see. Chapter 10: The Chapter on Peaceful Conduct (*Anle-xing-pin*).

The character for "sudden" (*cu-bao*) has the radical *cun-mu* (村沒) above; it is alternatively written as *cu-zu* (猝). As for the character *zu* (卒), it is pronounced with the *mu* and *zi-chu* (沒子出) finals. In ancient works such as the *Yupian*, *cang-cu* (倉猝) is also written as *cu*. Below [the character], the *pu-bao* (蒲報) radical is used; in archaic texts, *hu-wu* (虎武) is also used.
The Nirgrantha Jñātiputra— here translated as "Son of the Nigaṇṭhas"— is skilled in both *wen* (literature),
referring to works such as poetry and songs, and *bi* (calligraphy/composition), referring to genres such as inscriptions and fu-style prose.

Among the Six Arts of the *Zhouli* as recorded in the scriptures, the fifth is the "Six Scripts" (*liushu*), namely: pictographic (*xiangxing*), associative (*huiyi*), phonetic-semantic (*zhuanzhu*), ideographic (*zhishi*), phonetic (*xingsheng*), and borrowed (*jiajie*). "Shu" (writing) means to record. To represent forms according to their categories is called "wen" (graphemes); subsequently, when forms and sounds supplement one another, they are called "zi" (characters). "Zi" means to multiply and gradually increase. When these are inscribed upon bamboo or silk, they are called "shu. "Shu" means "to resemble," for it serves to clarify all things, record the past, and know the future. Furthermore, what is written on ritual tablets, silk, or paper is called "zi"; thus, "shu" is also synonymous with "ji" (records).

*Lokāyata* was previously translated as "the one who gives evil answers"; *pratilokāyata* was previously translated as "the one who poses evil questions. The original Sanskrit for the former is *lokāyatika*.

These are non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*) who adhere to doctrines that conform to what is spoken in the world; thus they are called "World-Conformist Non-Buddhists" (*Lokāyatika*). The original Sanskrit for the latter is *vāmamārgāyatika*. These are non-Buddhist practitioners who adhere to doctrines that do not conform to what is spoken in the world, being contrary to the aforementioned adherence; thus they are named "Left-Way World-Conformist Non-Buddhists" (*Vāmamārgāyatika*).

"Xiōng" (兇) in "xiǒng xì" (兇戲) [the first character is pronounced with the *qùshēng* xǔ and the *yìpíng* róng; it means "evil"]. In the *Yùpiān*, it is read as gǎn gǒng (盰鞏), meaning "fear"; here it follows the initial radical "chū" (初). It represents the signs of gain and loss, danger, calamity, and evil; it signifies misfortune.

"Xiāngchā" (相扠) [is pronounced] jiā fǎn; it refers to placing one's fist upon another person, and the character should indeed be written as 㨝 (qūn). According to the *Qièyùn*, "fist placed upon a person" is also pronounced pī, with the side-shǐ fǎn.
"Xiāngpū" (相撲) [is pronounced] pú jué fǎn.
Those who paint their bodies with the *nara* script perform transformations and worldly illusions as a form of play.

The *caṇḍālas*—also called *caṇḍālas*—are those who maintain fierce and evil karma as their own banner; when they travel, they signal themselves by shaking a bell or carrying a bamboo staff with a broken head. Otherwise, the king punishes them. Some say that "killing" is a general term for the various classes of butchers and slaughterers.

*Liè* (pronounced *xián* in the Xian dialect) means to capture birds and beasts. According to the *Baitong* (White Tiger General Theory), it is called "field-hunting" (*tiánliè*) because one clears away pests from the fields;

hence the term "field-hunting. *Nǔ* (pronounced *jū* in the Ju dialect) also means to capture. In the *Yupian*, *nǔ* (pronounced *qù*) also refers to catching fish. The *Shuowen* likewise defines it as catching fish. In ancient script it was written as *pó*; according to the *Yingyun*, it corresponds to the ancient form *pó*.

The *śrāmaṇera* is called a "diligent restrainer" (*qínsè*). Regarding the butcher (*túér*): the first character is pronounced with the initial *hú* (reversed) according to the *Shuowén*; it means to "carve and divide the flesh of sacrificial animals. Regarding the executioner (*kuìhuì*):

the first character is pronounced with the initial *kǔ huí* (reversed) according to the *Qiyùn*; it means a master or a leader. The second character, *gài*, has the initial *gǔ wài* (reversed); it means to cut or to mince meat. To mince meat finely is called *huì*. It is not yet clear why these names were established; some suggest there is a phonetic similarity to the word for a marketplace (*huì*), but this does not accord with the meaning here.

Regarding "xiàn" (to sell): the *Shuowen* states it is written with the radical "xuán" (mysterious) and means "to walk about selling" or "to entice. In the *Qieyun*, it is glossed as "self-promotion. Regarding "píng" (screen/curtain): read as *bǐng* (俾領).

In the *Liji*, regarding "standing in attendance with screens on the left and right," Zheng Xuan glosses it as "hidden. The *Shijing* says, "the screen of the myriad states. In the *Qieyun*, if it refers to being hidden or secluded, it is written as "bìng" (偋), read as *bī zhèng*. In the *Erya*, "píng" is borrowed for "pú dìng" (蒲定), which is also acceptable.

Regarding "entering the *li*": according to the *Zhouli*, five households constitute a *lin* (neighborhood), and five *lin* constitute a *li*. It is the place where twenty-five households reside. According to the *Shiming*, five *lin* make a *li*, meaning they dwell together within a square area of one *li*.
*Qiè* (pronounced with the initial *qù* and rhyme *jié*, according to the *Yùpiān*) means "fear. It refers to being inferior; it is to have much fear. *Yuànxián*:

The upper character *yuàn* (with the initial *yú* and rhyme *yuàn*) means "to bend" or "to wrong"; it forms the word *yuǎnquēng* (wrongs). The character *yuǎn* (formed with the radical for grass) means "to cover oneself"; it forms the word *yuān* (resentment). This character *yuàn* has no reading as *yúyuán*. The lower character *huàn* (with the initial *hù* and rhyme *jiān*) means that the mind is not equanimous.
Regarding "bathing" (*zǎoyù*): the first character, *zǎo*, is pronounced *lǎo* (with the departing tone); according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to sprinkle water over the body.

It refers to being newly purified; some editions read "newly dyed," but the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that one's clothing should be clean and pure. Since the sutra further says later that one must be "pure both internally and externally," it should follow the reading "newly purified."

*Xiéwěi* (邪偽): *wēiguì* (危貴) with the departing tone; *fǎn* (反). *Qīngmiè* (輕蔑): *mòjié* (莫結) with the departing tone. According to the *Shuowen*, it means to treat others with contempt; according to the *Qieyun*, it means there is none [to equal]. The *jing* (經) uses two forms: *mèi* (懱) and [the other], which are identical. *Tǎofá* (討伐):

*tāo* (滔) with the level tone, *lǎo* (老) with the departing tone. According to the *Hanyu Shuyinyi*, it means to eliminate. In the *Liji*, regarding "the ruler punishes the rebel," Zheng Xuan states that "punishment" (*tǎo*) means execution. *Fángyuè* (房越) with the entering tone. According to the *Qieyun*, it means to campaign against. In the *Zuozhuan*, it says: "When bells and drums are used, it is called a 'fa' (伐). According to the *Baitong*, what is meant by "fa"? It means to defeat and destroy; one desires to defeat and remove them. Some write it as *fá* (罰). According to the *Shuowen*, minor offenses are called *fá*. According to the *Guangya*, "fa" means to suppress and subdue. According to the *Qieyun*, "fa" means to condemn. This is its meaning.
*Wéijì*: (The character *wéi* is pronounced *gǔ* with the *yì* rhyme;

the character *jì* is pronounced *yǒng* with the *lǒng* rhyme. According to the *Yùpiān*, "surging" (*yǒng*) means to rise upward like water surging upon the surface. It should be written as "surge" (*yǒng*); there are those who write it as "leap" (*yǒng*), meaning to jump, but that is not the intended sense here.

Question: Regarding the character *xùn* (訊), according to the *Jìn fǎn yù piān*, it means "to inquire" (*wèn*) and "words of address" (*cí yán*). To hold an inquiry or to communicate through questioning is called *xùn*.

Regarding the character *jù* (巨): *Shēngshēn* reads it as *qí lǚ*; the *Zìlín* states it means "great" (*jù dà*); the *Fāngyán* notes that in the regions of Qī and Sòng, "great" is called *jù*; and the *Shuōwén* defines it as "large" (*dà*). It is also written as *jù* (鉅).
Ajita-Aśvaghoṣa; "Aśvaghoṣa" means "Incapable of Being Conquered. Maitreya is his name.

"Bei" (the character used here) is pronounced *jìng-jìn* (diligence); it means "to wear" or "to gird on" (there are also versions written as "mó-zhāng" or "pī"). In local dialects, "pī" may mean "scattered," but that is not the meaning here.

The upper character 奮 (fèn) is pronounced *fǔ* or *wèn*; it means to raise up. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it also means to shake (*zhèn*). The lower character 迅 (xùn) is pronounced *sī* or *rùn*; it means rapid. The *Qièyùn* also gives the pronunciation *xī* or *jìn*, which is identical in meaning to "rapid. When a bird "fur-xun" (exerts itself), its feathers bristle and its body expands; therefore, the character is composed of 奞 (*suī*) atop 田. 奞 is the name for a type of bird.

Regarding *dhūta*, the term *duō* (多) is a phonetic transcription; it means "to cleanse" (*tāotài*), referring to a great sweeping away. Alternatively, it is said to mean "to discard and abandon," or "to rectify and rebuke," signifying merely the removal of dust and impurities. To interpret it as "shaking off" (*dǒushòu*) is one particular meaning, but it is not the principle intended here.

*Kuì* (上) is pronounced *gōng duì* (公對); it means "disorder" (*luàn*) according to the *Shuowen*, and "disturbance" (*fán*). *Nào* (下) is pronounced *nǚ xiào* (女孝); it means "lack of tranquility. According to the *Yunjí*, it means "a crowded multitude. The character is composed of the radicals for "market" (*shì*) and "person" (*rén*); the variant form *nào* is a vulgar character.
The City of Gayā (Gaya-nagara).

[The character for] "face" (mian) is pronounced with the side radical *zhuō* (side) and the phonetic *jiù* (reverse); [the character for] "wrinkle" (*zhòu*) is pronounced with the side radical *cì* (side) and the phonetic *jiù* (reverse). The "Chapter on the Life Span of the Tathāgata" (*Rúlái shòuliàng pǐn*). [The character for] "life span" (*shòuliàng*) is pronounced with the side radical *shòu* (plant) and the phonetic *zhí* (reverse), and the phonetic *liàng* (measure) is pronounced with the side radicals *lǚ*, *zhāng*, *lì*, and *ràng* (two).

In various sūtras of the Śākya clan, it is said that his family name is Gautama. Now, the distinction between a "name" (shì) and a "clan" (xìng) is such that the clan serves to unify and maintain the lineage for a hundred generations so that they do not become divided. One acquires a name through spiritual inspiration; a "name" (shì) is used to distinguish the origin of one's descendants—whether derived from a place or from an official rank. Thus, the *Shi ben* (Genealogies of the World) states: "When speaking of the 'clan' (xìng), it refers to what is above; when speaking of the 'name' (shì), it refers to what is below."
A *nayuta-nayuta* (那由他那庾多) is the twelfth number among the fifty-two decimal places when ten is multiplied by itself five times;
"ji" (紀) is pronounced with the initial *jū* and final *ni*, and twelve years constitute one *ji*. A *ji* is a record or a cycle.
*Bai-gui* (拜跪): The character *gui* (跪) is pronounced with the *qiu-wei* rhyme; it means to kneel and bow. It is also pronounced with the *qu-wei* rhyme, as in the *Zuozhuan*:

"He knelt and placed [the child] upon him. *Dǎo-shī* (擣簁): The characters *ji-lei* (集類) are pronounced with the *suo-jia* (所佳) and *suo-ji* (所飢) rhymes. According to the *Shuowen*, it is a bamboo vessel used for removing husks to take the fine grain. In the *Yunjing*, it is pronounced with the *suo-qi* (所綺) rhyme, meaning a sieve (*luo*). It is also pronounced with the *suo-yi* (所宜) rhyme. The lower character is written as *si* (籭) or *dao* (簛) in archaic forms; these two characters are identical in meaning.

*Chūyù* (除愈): In the *Fāngyán*, it means "to recover" (*chāi*) or "the interval between recoveries. The *Qièyùn* states it means "recovery" (*chāi*). It is also written as *hùyì*. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "the healing of illness. The *Yùpiān* states it means "increasingly superior. [The character] *ài* (㤤) denotes mental anxiety; *hùyì* (癒) denotes the recovery from illness.

In the *Yìzǎi* (The Ten Million Years), it is recorded that the Yellow Emperor established the system of calculation with ten equal orders of magnitude: *yì*, *zhào*, *jīng*, *hài*, *rǎng*, *zǐ*, *gōu*, *jiàn*, *zhèng*, and *zǎi*. Regarding their practical application, there are three types of calculation: the lower, the middle, and the upper. In the lower calculation, one hundred thousand is called a *yì*; in the middle calculation, one million is called a *yì*; and in the upper calculation, ten million is called a *yì*.
"Yóu-lè (遊樂)" means to roam at will for pleasure; alternatively, it is pronounced "yóu-jì (遊恣)," meaning to enjoy oneself freely in superior places and give rise to joy.

"Fēn-bié (分別)"—the first character is pronounced "fǔ-wén (府文)" and the second "bié-biàn (別變)"—alternatively written as "biè (莂)" or "biè (𧧸)"; the first character may also be pronounced "fú-wèn (扶問)" and the second "píng-liè (憑列). It refers to the distinct classification and differentiation of segments.

*Liàng xuán sì quán*: "fǎn" (反) and "huán" (還) are the phonetic components; *qièyùn* (切韻) states it is like water swirling, written as 𣳟 (*cí xuǎn fǎn*, 辭選反), or as *quán* (泉) with the same *fǎn* (反).

*Bīnfēn* (繽紛): upper character, *pǐ rén fǎn* (匹仁反); *Yùpiān* (玉篇) says it describes the appearance of coming and going, or abundance, meaning "many. Lower character, *fú yún fǎn* (孚云反); *Yùpiān* says it means disorderly, the appearance of abundance, or many. *Guǎngyá* (廣雅) says *bīnfēn* means "many"; *fēnfēn* (紛紛) means "disorderly," referring to a great multitude. *Zìlín* (字林) says *bīnfēn* is the appearance of abundance. *Qièyùn* (切韻) says it means "to fly."
*Dāna* (檀) is translated as "giving" (*dāna*).
*Śīla* (尸羅) is translated as "cooling"; following ancient usage, it is named "pure precepts.
*Kṣānti* (羼提)—the first character pronounced with the initial *ch'u* and the final *yan* reversed—is translated as "patience" (*kṣānti*).
Vīrya is translated as "diligence" (jìngjìn).
Dhyāna is translated as "meditative concentration" (jìnglù).
Prajñā is called *nairya* when it is on the causal stage, which here means "wisdom"; when it is the fruit, it is called *sarvajña*, meaning "omniscience," or alternatively, "supreme wisdom."

The term for "stūpa and monastery" is *vihāra* in Sanskrit, meaning a place for wandering; it refers to the place where the community wanders and practices, and is also called a "monastic garden. Today, we use the character "si" (寺) as its equivalent. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "si" means "a place of restraint"; according to the *Guangya*, "si" means "governance"; and the *Shiming* states that "si" means "succession," for those who manage affairs succeed one another within it. The character is composed of "cun" (寸) and "tu" (土), with "sheng" (聲) as the phonetic component.
The term *sengfang* (monastery) is derived from the character *fang*, meaning a separate building according to the *Fanzilin* (Dictionary of Transcribed Words).

The *tālā* tree does not exist in this region; according to ancient tradition, it is seven *ren* tall, with one *ren* being seven feet. In reality, its shape is like that of a *zōnglǐ* palm, reaching an extreme height and length of seventy or eighty feet. Its flowers resemble yellow millet, and its fruit is as large as a bowl; many people eat it.
The flowers of sumana, kumuda, mālatī, and saumanasa are fragrant and pleasing to the mind.

The campaka—pronounced "zhānbójiā" (zhānbójiā being a transcription of *campaka*, here translated as the "yellow-flowered tree")—has small but fragrant blossoms; forests of this tree are common in the Western Regions.
The *Atimuktaka* and other [flowers] not explicitly mentioned are mostly absent in this region, and thus have not been translated. Regarding "perfumed oil" (*xūnyóu*):

"xūn" is pronounced as the reverse of "hǔ" (i.e., *xūn*); it refers to fragrant herbs. By blending various fragrant herbs with *bījāpūra* seeds and allowing them to soak until moistened, one then presses them to extract the oil; this is called "perfumed oil. *Bījāpūra* refers to large sesame seeds.
Chapter Eleven: On the Merit of Rejoicing (Anumodanā-puṇya-parivarta). *Mo*: Pronounced as *mo* with a retroflex *b* (陌莫百反); according to the *Yùpiān*, it means "street" (*mò*) or "road.

*Qiān*: Pronounced as *qiān* with an upper tone *qian* (褰縮上去乾反); it means "to lift" or "to raise. The lower character is pronounced as *suo* or *lu* (所六反); it means "short," though sometimes written as *qiàn*.
"Rough and coarse" (*cū-sè*) combined to form the character for "astringent" (*sè*). "Sores and rashes" (*chuāng-zhěn*):

*zhěn* is pronounced with the second tone in both *jū-rěn* and *zhāng-rěn*, meaning an itch on the upper lip. The *Sāncāng* says it means wind or swelling; the *Zhòuwén* (Seal Script) form is written as 疹, and the *Shuōwén* agrees. There is also the form 緊, which has the meaning of "tightly woven," but this is not the meaning of "sores and rashes."

*Kuā* (the upper radical is "mouth" with the phonetic *xié*): according to the *Shuowen*, it means a distorted mouth; the *Tongsuowen* states that a crooked or distorted [mouth] is called *kuā*. It is composed of the radical "mouth" and the phonetic *guǎ*. *Kuā* is pronounced as in *gǔwǎ*; *wā* is pronounced as in *yuānguā*.
The character for "li" (黧) may also be written as "li" (黧).

The term "piè-xī" (匾㔸)—according to the *Jiyùn* and *Chuyùn*, the first character is pronounced *biān* (󱒓) and the second *xī* (體)—is explained in the *Cuǎnwén* as meaning "thin. Nowadays, the common vernacular calls what is broad and thin "piè-xī. In the Guanzhong region, it is called "bì-dì," where "bì" is pronounced *bǔ-mí*. There are also characters such as "tuō-tuó" (䐔䏲), which are merely recent variants.

The character *qu* (曲) is pronounced with the *lì* rhyme (*lìjì fǎn*) in the *Zílín*; it also means "crooked. In the *Qièyùn*, it means "discordant"; it is composed of the radicals for "dog" (*quán*) and "door" (*hù*).

In the Guanzhong region it is called *shǎndiàn* (睒電), while people in the Wu region today call it *xīnniàn* (䃱鐔); "xīnniàn" is pronounced *shàng xī niàn fǎn* (上息念反) and *xià dà niàn fǎn* (下大念反).

According to the *Fāngyán*, it also means to prepare for or guard against. In archaic texts, it is written as "jiè" (誡).

*Ka* (pronounced *kē* with a retroflex *r* sound) refers to a genus of conch shells found in the ocean that are as pure white as snow. Within the *dhāraṇī* of the Samantabhadra Chapter, it says: *tathāgata-saṃgha-tulya*. Regarding the sound of *tathā*: it is pronounced with a retroflex *r* (from the Chinese transcription *duò*, which corresponds to the Sanskrit *tathā*). Regarding *saṃgha*: it means "assembly" (*saṃgha*). Regarding *tulya*: the pronunciation of *tulya* is *lìshé* (the retroflex *ṭ* is reversed). It refers to being of the same kind. Some write it as *āḍhya*, and the tradition claims its pronunciation is *yúliù* (sixth tone). Since that is not the case, nor is there such a character, it must be *āṭava*. Now it is corrupted to *āḍhya*. This was an error in transcription where *duò* was changed to *āḍhya*; this is a most egregious mistake.

*Liao-li* (繚戾): The first character is pronounced with the *liǎo* rhyme (forceful small tone); according to the *Shuowen*, it is pronounced with the *liǎo* rhyme (forceful bird tone). It means "to wind around" (*liǎorào*) and "to entwine" (*liǎochán*). This refers to the act of wrapping and encircling. In the *Yunjing* (Rhyme Mirror), apart from the four characters *liǎodá* (了達), *liàocài* (蓼菜), *mùjīng* (目睛), and *míngliǎo* (明瞭), there are no other characters with the *liǎo* sound. The character *liao* (繚) has two readings: *liǎoxiǎo* (力小) and *liǎozhào* (力召). The first meaning is "to wind around" (*liǎorào*); the second is "to roast" (*liǎozhì*). *Liaozhi* (繚炙) is sometimes written as *liaoli* (繚戾), which is pronounced *lùdì* (魯帝).
*Jiǎolài* (pronounced *luòdài*): The *Shuowén* and *Yùpiān* state that it refers to the pupils not being aligned.

According to the *Erya*, the *guāng* resembles an ox; Guo Pu states that it has a single horn, is azure-colored, and weighs one thousand *qīn*.
*He*: *ní* (with the tone of *shí*); clay that is sticky is called *ní*. According to the *Shìmíng*, *ní* means *zhì*; it refers to the quality of being *zhì*. *Cái*: *yè*;

the ancient forms are *㮆*, *不*, and *㩵*, all three having the same pronunciation as *wùgē*. According to the *Ěryǎ*, *yè* means "to carry" (*zài*) or "to remain" (*yú*). This refers to when water has a residual remainder; the name for such a remainder is *nà*.
*Fàn* (氾) is the same as the ancient character *fàn* (泛); it is pronounced *fújiàn* (孚劒反). It describes the appearance of drifting or floating.
Volume Seven. *Tūn* (屯) is pronounced *zhílún* (陟倫反). According to the *Shuowen*, it means difficulty or distress. *Jiǎn* (蹇) means obstruction or entanglement.
In ancient texts, "Lin" (林) was written as either "Yi" (㟗) or "Bin" (豳); today it is written as "Bin" (邠), pronounced with the same phonetic as "Fu-pin" (府貧).

It is the name of a tree. Regarding "Li-xiang" (禮貺), the character "xiang" (貺) is pronounced "Hu-kuang" (許誑). According to the *Erya*, "xiang" means "bestowal"; Guo Pu states that it refers to the act of granting or giving.

8 (The eighth fascicle is missing) *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Fascicle One. Compiled by the Śramaṇa Xuanying. *Lutidu* (盧揥徒): [The character] *di* is pronounced as *ti* with a fine (*xi*) second tone; alternatively, it is written as *sajulu* (薩俱盧). This is a personal name, translated here as "Noble Lineage."

The character *yàn* (焰) is glossed as "flame. In ancient script it was written as *yàn* (燄), and nowadays it is written as *xián* (爓). The *Sāncāng* (三蒼) records it as *yàn*, with the same pronunciation as *yúzhān* (餘瞻). The *Shuowén* (說文) states that fire moves in a shimmering, flickering manner (*huī yànyàn rán*). The scripture text uses the character *lǎn* (㷿), pronounced *hǔfán*. The *Běicāng* (埤蒼) states that *lǎn* means "pungent flavor. The *Zìyuàn* (字苑) states that *lǎn* means "to burn" (*yǎo*). However, *lǎn* does not carry this meaning here; *yǎo* is pronounced *lìgē* (力割).
Regarding "zhèng mín" (蒸民): "zhèng" means "multitude. This is as in the passage, "Heaven gives birth to the multitude of the people. Regarding "huī kuò" (恢闊):
it is also written as "kūi" (󲐵) with the same pronunciation as "kǔ huí" (苦迴). The *Zílín* states that "huī" means "great" and "kuò" means "distant."

According to the *Shenglèi* (Classification of Sounds), the archaic form is written as 泉 (*quán*, with the phonetic component *qí* and radical *qǐ*). The *Zílín* (Forest of Characters) states that 暨 means "to reach" (*jí*) and also "to arrive.
*Huòrán* (*huō*, with the phonetic component *guō*) refers to the appearance of suddenness, fleetingness, and rapidity; the version of the scripture using 㸌 is not the correct form.

*Zuǎnxiū* (纂修): *zǐ* (子) and *luǎn* (卵) are reversed; alternatively, it is written as *zuàn* (纘). In the *Erya*, *zuàn* means "to succeed" (*jì*), referring to the continuation of one's scholarly work.
*Yùyuè* (煜爚): also written as *yù* (焴), both with the same pronunciation as *yúzhù* (餘祝); it describes the appearance of brilliant light. The textual reading *yùshuò* (昱鑠) is not the correct form.

*Bānlán* (斒斕) is also written as *Línfēn* (霖玢); both characters share the same pronunciation, with the first reading as *bǔjiān* (補間) and the second as *bānlìjiān* (般力間). The *Tōngsùwén* (通俗文) states that "patterns" are called *bānlán*; the version in the sutra texts as *bānlán* (斑蘭) is not the correct form.
*Pǔ*: pronounced *pǐ gǔ* (反), this is the archaic form of the character *pǔ*. The *Shīchuán* (Explanations of the Odes) states: "Pǔ means great; it also means pervasive.
Comparing the archaic forms, *jiào* is the same as *huò*, pronounced *gǔ xué* (反); *jiào* means coarse and brief. According to the *Guǎngyá*, *jiào* means clear.

"Ming" (明) and "zhe" (哲) are synonymous; "zhe" is pronounced with the "lie" (列) and "fan" (反) finals. According to the *Erya*, "zhe" means wisdom (*zhì*); this is a term from the period between the Song and Qi dynasties.

As for "shan" (繕), it is pronounced with the "shi" (市) and "zhan" (戰) finals. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "shan" means to mend or patch; the *Sancang* states that "shan" means to repair. The word "shan" signifies excellence (*shàn*).
*Chao* (pronounced *zhú jiāo*, with the second character also written as *huì* or *huǐ*, both pronounced *hù kuài*) refers to corrupted speech; according to the *Shēnglèi*, it is a form of slang.
*Ào* (pronounced *wū gè*) refers to plastering; the *Ěryá* states that a wall is called *ào*, and Guō Pǔ explains that it is the decoration of a wall with white earth.

*Niao* (鐃) is pronounced *jiao* (奴交反) with the final rhyme sound *jing* (竟); its origin is not clearly known. According to the *Zhouli* (周禮), "The metal *chun* (錞) is used to harmonize the drums; the metal *niao* (鐃) is used to stop the drums"—this must be what is meant here. *Chun* (錞) is pronounced *chui lun* (垂綸反).
*Fǔbiàn* (拊抃): *Fǔ* means to clap; the second character is also written as *pèn* (拚), with the same pronunciation (*pi biàn*).

According to the *Shuowen*, "clapping the hands is called *biàn*. *Dìèr juǎn* (第二卷): Second fascicle. *Lětí* (㣿惕): Pronounced *ruò* for the first character and *tí* for the second. *Lětí* refers to anxiety and fear; it also denotes pain and illness.
"Unhearing" (*wèi líng*): the *Cāngjié piān* states that "líng" means to listen; it is what the ear hears.
"Porch-window" (*xuān chuāng*): the *Chǔcí* says that a "xuān" is a structure on a tower that screens off wind and sunlight.
*Shuo* (pronounced *shū*, with the rhyme *zhāo*) means "flashing"; it refers to a sudden, brief illumination.
*Fu* (also written as *chù*, both pronounced *fáng wù*) means "to hasten. According to the *Guǎngyá*, *chù* means "one who walks quickly."
*Yùn* (pronounced *jiān-fǎn*) means resentment; according to the *Shuowen*, it means anger, and also wrath. *Táng-zàng* (pronounced *tāng-lǎng-fǎn*):
this is a difficult character from the *Zhou Cheng*; its pronunciation is *dàng*. According to the *Shuowen*, *táng* refers to the treasury where gold and coins are stored.

The term *chuī* (榱) [is pronounced with the first character as *guī* and the second as *dōng*]; according to the *Erya*, what is called *jué* (捔) is *chuī*, which is the same as *zhuó* (椓). *Dòng* (棟) refers to the ridgepole of a roof; in the region east of the mountains, the ridgepole is called *jìn* (󲀓), pronounced *yǔ jìn*.
*Xián* (軒) and *tá* (闥)—the latter being pronounced with the *hé* (曷) rhyme—according to the *Guǎngyǎ*, means "gate"; specifically, it refers to a side door.

*Huǐ* (虺) and *shé* (蛇)—in ancient texts written as *chóng* (虫) and *huì* (螝), both forms now appearing as *huǐ*—are pronounced with the *hū guǐ* (呼鬼) rhyme; they are venomous insects. The *Hánfēi zǐ* states: "There is an insect called *huǐ* that has one body and two mouths; competing for food, they bite and kill each other. *Xiè* (齕) means to gnaw or nibble.
*Fù* (pronounced *liù fǎn* for the first character and *hū gè fǎn* for the second): the *fù* has fangs and is the most venomous; it is this creature with needles on its head.

The text’s reading as *fú* or *bì* is an error. Regarding *pù cuàn*: the text sometimes reads *pò*; this should be the character *bū* (pronounced *bǔ hú fǎn*), meaning to flee. According to the *Guǎngyá*, "to *bū cuàn*" means to run away.
