In the *Sūtra on the Meritorious Virtues of the Original Vows of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha*, according to Huilin’s phonetics: *Mañjuśrī* (上末盤反) is a Sanskrit term; in the Tang language, it means "Wondrous Auspiciousness" (Miaojixiang).

"Piān-tàn" (偏袒): the first character is pronounced *pǐ* (匹) with the level tone (*mián* [反]), and the second is *tán* (壇) with the fourth tone (*lán* [反]). The preceding section, the lower fascicle of the *Dharmānudharma-paryāya-sūtra*, has already been explained.

"Sāoxiāo" (銷消): the first character is pronounced *jiāo* (焦) with the first tone. The *Liji* (Book of Rites) states: "Sāo (銷) is like scattering. The *Chuci* (Songs of Chu) states: "Melted down (*sāoxiào*) and completely destroyed. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "melting metal"; it is composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic "xiào" (*xiào*). It is also written as "huō" (焇).

*Xià yè* (瑕薉): The first character, *xià*, is pronounced with the initial *jiā* (the opposite of *jiǎ*). The *Líjì* states that it refers to the flaws or defects in jade. The *Guǎngyá* defines it as "to split" or "filth. The *Shuōwén* says it is a slight reddish tint in jade, formed from the radical for jade (*yù*) and the phonetic *duàn*. The second character, *yè*, has the pronunciation of *huì*. Gu Yewáng states that *yè* means "not clean. Wang’s commentary on the *Chuci* defines it as "evil. The *Guǎngyá* defines it as "weeds. The *Shuōwén* says it is formed from the radical for grass (*cǎo*) and the phonetic *suì*. The text uses *huì* (穢), which is also acceptable.
*Quèjiè* (缺戒): The first character is pronounced *shàngquǎn yuèfǎn* (上犬悅反) or written as *qín* (𡙇). It has already been explained in the preface to the *Śrīmaladevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*.

*Chǒulòu* (醜陋): The first character is pronounced *shàngchōng zhǒu fǎn* (上充帚反). The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (毛詩傳) states it means "evil" (*è*) or "multitude" (*zhòng*). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states it means "kind" or "type" (*lèi*). The *Shuowén* says it is composed of *guǐ* (鬼) and the phonetic *yǒu* (酉). The second character is pronounced *xiàlóu dòu fǎn* (下樓豆反). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it means "mean" (*lòujiàn*), "ugly" (*chǒu*), "vulgar" (*bǐ*), or "evil" (*è*). Gù Yěwáng says it means "mean and base" (*lòuwěi*). The *Erya* says it means "hidden" (*yǐn*). The *Shuowén* says it is composed of *huì* (𨸏) and the phonetic *xún* (㔷).

*Wányú* (頑愚): The upper character is pronounced *shàngwǔguān* (上五關) with a reversed *kǎo* (考) phonetic. It means "obstinate and foolish. The *Guǎngyá* (廣雅) says it means "dull. The *Shuōwén* (說文) states it is composed of *xié* (頁) and has *yuán* (元) as its phonetic.

*Pānbì* (攀躄): The upper character is pronounced *lièchuán* (劣傳) with a reversed phonetic. The *Shēnglèi* (聲類) says it means "the disease of *yí* (𤼙). Furthermore, Gu Yewáng says it refers to a bodily ailment where the limbs are cramped and curved. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) says it is a disease of the hands and feet. It is also written as *luǎn* (臠). The *Jīngzhèngzì* (古今正字) states it is composed of *nà* (疒) and has *luán* (䜌) as its phonetic; the version in the scriptures uses *luán* (攣), which is also acceptable. *Bìngpí* (并癖): The lower character is pronounced *bìngpí* (并癖) with a reversed phonetic. The *Kǎoshēng* says it means "the foot is withered and cannot walk. The *Shuōwén* says it means "unable to walk. It is composed of *zhǐ* (止) and has *bì* (辟) as its phonetic. The version in the scriptures uses *zú* (足), which is also acceptable.

*Luǒ*: Upper character *tōu* (pronounced *mèi*); according to the *Shuowen*, it means "the spine," composed of the radical for flesh (*ròu*) and the phonetic *bǐ*. The lower character *lì* (pronounced *zhǔ*); the commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that *luǒ* refers to a hunched back. The *Guoyaya* says it means "crooked. The commentary on the *Gongyangzhuan* says it means "sickness. According to the *Shuowen*, it is "weakness" (*wāng*), composed of the radical for person (*rén*) and the phonetic *lóu*.

The "White Leprosy" (白癩) character is formed by combining the radicals for "to bring" (帶) and "reverse" (反), with the abbreviated form being "leprosy" (癩). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "a malignant pestilence" (厲惡疫). The *Wenzi Dian* explains that it is composed of the radical "sickness" (疒) and the phonetic component "lai" (賴).

"Dian" (癲) [is pronounced with the initial *dian* and the final *nian* reversed]. The *Kaosheng* states it refers to the disease of "dian"; the *Guangya* calls it "madness" (*kuang*); the *Shenglei* calls it a "wind-disease. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "sickness" (*zha*) and the phonetic "zhen. The form used in the scriptures is "dian," which is a vulgar character.

*Xià* (黠): The upper radical is *xián* (閑) with the reverse stroke; the *Shēngyùn* says it means "sharp and clever. The *Fāngyán* says it also means "wisdom. The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radical *hēi* (黑) and the phonetic *jí* (吉). *wánjù* (完具): The upper character is read as *huóguān* (活官).

The *Zuǒzhuan* says it means "to maintain complete defenses. The *Shuōwén* says it means "complete. It is composed of the radical *mián* (宀)—the sound of which is *mián*—and the phonetic *yuán* (元). *Mián* is pronounced like *mián*.

The character *jiǎn* (羂) is pronounced with the initial *jué* (決) and the final *yǎn* (兖); its phonetic component is said to mean "to capture things with a rope. The *Wenzi Dianshuō* (Textual Dictionary) states that *gāng* (冈) is the phonetic element, and the *Jīng* (經) uses *jiǎn* (羂) as well. The lower part, *wáng* (亡) and *fǎng* (昉), is explained by Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lìjì* (Book of Rites): "A net for birds is called *gāng*. Gu Yewang says that *gāng* is the general name for nets and snares. The *Yì* (Book of Changes) states: "In ancient times, the Lord Fúchí tied ropes to make nets and snares, teaching people how to hunt and fish. The *Wenzi Dianshuō* explains that it follows the character *mìng* (冂) and below it depicts the pattern of the net's intersections.

*Chou-lin* (稠林): Pronounced *zhú-liú* (上逐流反). The *Cāngjié piān* states that *chóu* means "multitude"; the *Shuowén* states that *chóu* means "much," composed of the radical *huò* (禾) with the phonetic *zhōu* (周).

*Bian-ta* (鞭撻): Pronounced *biē-mián* (上鼈綿反). The *Kǎoshēng* says it means "to strike with a whip. The *Shàngshū* states: "Whipping serves as the punishment for officials. Fàn Nìng says: "It is the punishment for those in office who are not reverent in their duties. Gù Yěwáng says: "Using grass to punish the offender. It takes the radical *gè* (革) with the phonetic *biàn* (便). The second character, *tǎn-héng* (下坦恒反), the *Kǎoshēng* says: "Tà" is also a whip. Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* says: "Tà" refers to the lash of a whip. The *Shuowén* [takes] the radical *shǒu* (手) with the phonetic *tà* (撻).

Regarding "wén" (mosquito): the *Wùfēn* (勿分) [dictionary] states that a mosquito is a biting flying insect that emerges at dusk; the *Shuōwén* also defines it as a biting flying insect. It is also written with the radical 虫 (insect) and the phonetic 民 (*mín*). The version in the scriptures uses "wén," which is a vulgar character. Regarding "méng" (gadfly): the *Shēnglèi* (聲類) states that a gadfly resembles a fly but is larger; the *Shuōwén* also defines it as a biting flying insect, the large variety of which takes the radical 虫 and the phonetic 止 (*zhǐ*). The sound of 䖵 (*guǐn*) is *kūn*.

The character *suǎn* (翫) is read as *wú guàn* (吾貫). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "to play with" (*suǎn*) means to practice habitually. The *Ji xun* explains it as "to become negligent through habitual familiarity with a matter. The *Shuowen jiezi* defines it as "to feel satiated" (*yàn*), and further notes it means "to toy with," being composed of the radical *xí* (習) and the phonetic *yuán* (元).

Regarding the term *xuán* (軒): the *Xiányán* (憲言) reverses the sound and states that it refers to the area before the eaves. The *Chuci* says, "The high hall has deep chambers and tiered *lán-xuán* (檻層軒)"; here, *xuán* is like the floorboards of a multi-storied building. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *chē* (車) with the phonetic *gān* (干). Regarding the character below (*zhù* 齪): it is pronounced *shuāng* (雙) and its secondary sound is *chuāng-zhuō* (牕捉). The *Shuowen* states: "That which is in a wall is called *yǒu* (牖); that which is in a roof is called *chuāng* (牕). The standard characters for "ancient" and "modern" are composed of the radical *piàn* (片) with the phonetic *cóng* (悤).

Fùbì (覆蔽): The upper character is read as fāng (芳) with the phonetic wù (務). Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states it means "to cover" (*fùgài*) or "to shade" (*yīn*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "fǎng" (覂), composed of 覀 (yì) and 復 (fù). Fǎng is pronounced fēng (封) with the phonetic fèng (奉).

"Jí dù" (嫉妬): The upper character, "jí," was originally written as "qín" (秦), which is a vulgar form; the lower character, "dù," was originally written with the radical "zhèng" (正) following "hù" (戶). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states: "To harm the worthy is called jí; to harm beauty is called dù. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, both characters follow the radical "nǚ" (女) and are compound characters formed by combining the semantic and phonetic components.

"Jùkǔ" (劇苦) means extreme suffering; "jù" (劇) signifies being even more severe than before. The *Cāngjié piān* states it means a critical illness, and also that it means increased severity. In the standard characters of antiquity and today, it is written with the radical "knife" (刀) and the phonetic "qū" (豦).

Regarding the character *wú* (無) in *wúmíng* (無明): the lower radical is *qiāo* (腔), pronounced with the *jiǎo* (角) tone; the *Shēngyùn* (聲韻) says it refers to the *kào* (殼), the empty shell of an egg. Dictionaries state that it refers to the shell once the egg has been fertilized (*fú*). The *Guìyuàn Zhūcóng* (桂苑珠叢) states that *fúqiào* (孚㲉) refers to the outer skin of a bird’s egg. The *Wénzìdiǎn* (文字典) explains that it is formed from the radical for "egg" (*luǎn*) with the phonetic *jī* (𣪊).
*Rākṣasa*: "Ruo" (羅) and "He" (訶) are reversed; this is the Sanskrit term for a malevolent ghost that eats humans. The version in the sutra is a scribal error.

*Zhòuzǔ* (呪詛): "Zhōu" (州) and "Fu" (符) are reversed; it is a vulgar character. The correct form follows the radical "speech" (言), written as *chóu* (詶). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Chóu is also *zǔ*. It follows the radical "speech" with "zhōu" as the phonetic. The lower part is pronounced "zǔ" (阻) and "zhù" (助). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* says: "In oaths and pledges, great matters are called *méng* (盟), and small matters are called *zǔ* (詛). The *Shangshu* says: "*Zhòuzhù* means to curse. The *Shuowen* [also] follows the radical "speech" with "qie" (且) as the phonetic. The sutra uses the character "jǔ" (咀) with the radical "mouth" (口), which is a vulgar usage. Because it has been used in commentaries for a long time, it is retained here.

The term *gǔ* (蛊) is pronounced "gǔ. The *Zuozhuan* states that it refers to insects produced from vessels during the dark and waning phases of the moon; the *Shuowen Jiezi* also defines it as "insects within the belly," composed of the radical "insect" (*chóng*) with "vessel" (*míng*) serving as a phonetic component.

Xuánxiǎn (懸險): The first character is read as juān (涓) and the second as xījiǎn (希撿). Gù Yěwáng says it means "perilous" (xiànnán) and also "obstructed" (zǔ). Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* says it means "dangerous" (wēi). The *Fāngyán* says it means "high" (gāo). The *Guǎngyá* says it means "slanted" (xié). The *Shuōwén* states that it is composed of the radical 𨸏 with the phonetic 僉; the version in the [present] scripture written as 嶮 is incorrect.

"Bear and *pí* (熊羆): the first character is read as *xū* (虛) with the phonetic *qióng* (窮) reversed; the second is read as *bǐ* (彼) with the phonetic *pí* (皮). This was already explained in the lower fascicle of the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* (*Mìyán jīng*). *Cíyán* (蚰蜒):

the first character is read as *yǒu* (酉) with the phonetic *zhōu* (州), and the second is read as *yǎn* (演) with the phonetic *xiān* (仙). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that *cíyán* is the name of an insect. The *Fāngyán* (方言) states that those east of the Guān (關) call it *yǐnyán* (螾蜒), while those west of the Guān call it *cíyán* (蚰蜒), and those of Beiyān (北燕) call it *zhùyán* (祝蜒). The *Wénzìdiǎn* (文字典) explains that both characters are written with the radical for insects (*虫*) and are pronounced *yóuyán* (由延)."

The character 󱸝 (shòu) is pronounced with the upper radical *lěi* and the tone *wēi*. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states it means "weak"; Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states it means "sickly"; the *Huainanzi* says it means "inferior"; the *Zishu* says it means "exhausted"; and the *Shuowen* also says it means "emaciated. It is composed of the radical 羊 (*yáng*) and the phonetic 𣎆 (*ní*), where 𣎆 is pronounced *lì wò*.

"Dry" (gān) is pronounced as *xià* with a retroflex final. The *Zhouyi* says, "Water flows to the moist; fire moves toward the dry," which refers to this. Furthermore, the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it also means "to dry. It is composed of the radical "fire" (*huǒ*) and the phonetic component "sāo" (*sāo*, pronounced *zào* with a retroflex final).

*Zhé* (磔): With the hand raised and the skin spread out (*zhāng*). The *Guǎngyá* states: "To spread and to open. The *Shuowén* says it is composed of the radical *shí* (石) and the phonetic *qián* (乾); *qián* is pronounced *jiànliè* (乾列). In the Classics, it is written with the hand radical as *zuò* (作), which is a variant usage of the character.

*Bo shi* (薄蝕). The second character, *she*, has the phonetic *zhé* (軄) as its radical; the *Kǎo Shēng* states it means "to invade. The eclipses of the sun and moon are also gradual invasions. The *Chunqiu* says, "The sun had an eclipse (*shi*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radicals for "insect" (*chóng*) and "to feed" (*sì*; *sì* is pronounced *sì*).

Regarding the term *yi* (medicine): the *Guǎyá* states it refers to physicians and shamans (*wú*). The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* says that Wú Péng was the first to practice medicine. The *Zhou Lǐ* states that the *Yīshī* (Chief Physician) presides over the administration of medical affairs; it further says the *Yīrén* (Medical Personnel) presides over the care for the illnesses of the myriad people. The *Kǎoshēng* defines it as one who treats the sick. As for its meaning: since the treatment of illness necessarily involves wine, the character includes the radical *yǒu* (wine). The *Shuōwén* defines it as a craftsman who treats disease; it takes *yǒu* as the radical and *ē* as the phonetic component. The pronunciation of *ē* is *āo jì*.

*Yao* (妖) is pronounced *jiāo* (上) and *yànliè* (下). This was already explained and annotated in the twelfth fascicle of the *Dà guǎngdìng jīng* (Great Consecration Sūtra). *Tian* (畋) for hunting: the upper character is pronounced *tián*. The *Zhou Lǐ* states that *tian* is also *lie* (hunting).

The *Shuowén* defines it as "level fields," written with the radical *pī* (攴) and the phonetic *tián*; the character may also be written as *tún* (𤝗). *Pī* is pronounced *pǔbǔ*. The lower character is *liánzhé*. The *Kǎoshēng* states that hunting is when hounds pursue game; today, the act of hunting wild animals is called *lie*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Máo Shī* says: "A solemn hunt is called *lie*. He further annotates the *Yí Lǐ*: shooting arrows so they hit the mark is *shè* (archery); shooting from the side is *lie*. The *Fāngyán* says: "To *línglie* (overrun/hunt down) means to be violent and cruel. The *Shuowén* defines it with the radical *quǎn* (dog) and the phonetic *bǐng*; *bǐng* has the same pronunciation as the upper character (*jiāo*).

Regarding "xì" (嬉戲): the upper radical is "xǐ" (喜), which is its opposite; the *Cāngjié piān* (蒼頡篇) also states it means "jesting and laughing. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) says it means "wandering play"; the *Shuōwén* (說文) says it means "joy," composed of the radical "woman" (女) and the phonetic "xǐ" (喜). The lower character is pronounced with the initial "xī" (羲); the *Máoshī chuán* (毛詩傳) says "xì" means "leisurely ease. The *Erya* (爾雅) says "mò làng xiào xū" (謔浪笑𢾕) is this very term. The *Shījì* (史記) says, "The Son of Heaven has no jesting words. In the *Shuōwén*, the character is composed of "weapon" (戈) and the phonetic "qì" (䖒); "qì" is pronounced "xī" (希) and is the correct orthography. The version in the scriptures uses "xū" (虛) to form "xì" (戱), which is a vulgar variant.

"Yá (山崖): The first character is pronounced as wǔ (五) and gāi (皆) in reverse; the commentary on the sounds states that it refers to the steep and dangerous edge between mountains. The *Shuōyuàn* says, 'High mountains have precipices. The *Shuowén* says, 'A high edge. It is composed of the radical 尸 (pronounced wǔgèfǎn) and the phonetic element 佳 (abbreviated) with the sound.'"

The Scripture on the Merit of the Fundamental Vows of the Seven Buddhas of the Medicine Master Lapis Lazuli Light, translated by Tripitaka Master Yijing. Hui-lin’s Pronunciations, Volume One, Part One. *Gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*: "Gaṅgā" is the name of a river in the Western regions (India); it is pronounced with the "qiang" rhyme (as in "qiáng").

*Yojana*: The upper character is *yǔ* (庾) with the *zhū* (珠) rhyme; in the Sanskrit script of the sutra, it is written as *tà* (蹹), which is an error. *Jià* (賈): The upper character is *shǎng* (賞) with the *zhāng* (章) rhyme. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "Those who travel are called *jìng* (𧶜);

those who reside [in trade] are called *jià* (賈). Zheng also notes in his commentary on the *Kaogongji*: "*Jìng* refers to guests who buy and sell. The *Kaosheng* says: "*Jìng* means one who travels to peddle goods. The *Shuowen* says: "To travel and trade; it is composed of *bèi* (貝) and the abbreviated form of *shāng* (商) as the phonetic, with the lower part being *gū* (姑) with the *hù* (戶) rhyme. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* further states: "To transport goods is called *jìng* (𧶜); to reside and sell is called *jià* (賈). The *Zuozhuan* says: "*Jià* means to purchase. The *Erya* says: "The marketplace. The *Shuowen* says: "To sit and sell for profit; it is composed of *bèi* (貝) and *xī* (西) as the phonetic. The version in the sutra as *gù* (估) is incorrect.

The character for *shēn* (娠) is composed of "to spread" (*bù*) below and the phonetic *zhēn* (刃). The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (Mao Commentary on the Book of Poetry) states: "Shēn means movement. The *Jiān* (Sub-commentary) states: "Movement refers to being pregnant. The *Kǎo Shēng* (Investigation of Sounds) states: "It means *rèn* (妊) and *yì* (㛅); it means movement, referring to the fetal movement when one is about to give birth. The *Shuōwén* (Explanations of Words and Texts) states: "A woman bearing a child and moving; composed of 'woman' (*nǚ*) and the phonetic *chén* (辰). The character may also be written as 𡝌. The text uses 㛛, which is a common vulgar variant.

*Chóu* (讎) and *qì* (隙). *Chóu* is pronounced with the initials *shǒu* and *zhōu*. The *Mao Shi* says, "To hate and loathe me is *chóu*. Gu Yewang says it means resentment. It is also said that *chóu* is synonymous with *qiú* (仇). The *Shangshu* says, "If he caresses me, he is my sovereign; if he oppresses me, he is my enemy (*chóu*). The *Liji* says, "One does not share a carriage with the enemy of one's father or mother; one does not turn back one’s weapon from the enemy of one’s brother; one does not reside in the same state as the enemy of one’s friend. The *Shuowen* explains that [the character] follows the radical for speech and takes *cháo* (雔) as its phonetic component; *cháo* has the same pronunciation as above. Gu Yewang says that *qì* (隙) is the cause of resentment. Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* says that *qì* is synonymous with *xìn* (釁). The *Shuowen* explains that [the character] follows the radical for earth and takes *yíng* (𡭽) as its phonetic component; *yíng* has the same pronunciation as above.

Rǎoluàn (嬈亂): The first character, rǎo, is pronounced with the "niè" and "niǎo" finals reversed. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to vex" or "to oppress. One interpretation states it means "to disturb" or "to toy with. It is composed of the radical "woman" (女) and the phonetic "yáo" (堯). An alternative form of this character is niǎn (嬲), where the phonetic "hé" (何) is used for the final sound.

"Fēn" (芬): The upper character is read as *fèn* (with the radical *yún* reversed). The *Mao Shi* Commentary states: "It means fragrant. Guo's commentary on the *Fang Yan* says it means "harmonious. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical *cao* (草) with the phonetic *fen*. The lower character is read as *fú* (馥). The *Mao Shi* Tradition states: "It describes the appearance of fragrance. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical *xiāng* (香) with the phonetic *fù* (复); the pronunciation of *fù* is the same as that of the upper character.

*Feiméng* (飛甍): "Below the flying eaves. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that *méng* refers to the ridgepole of a roof. The *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of the radical *wǎ* (tile) with *mèng* (abbreviated) as the phonetic.

*Hùyòu* (戶牖): Pronounced *yóujiǔ*. The *Shuowen* defines *yòu* as "piercing a wall to make a window, using wood to form a lattice. It is composed of the radical *piàn* (tablet/panel) with *fǔ* as the phonetic.

Bīnbīn (上疋󰠢反, 下忿文反): The *Guǎngyá* states that "bīnbīn" means a multitude or disorder. The *Mānsìshī* says it refers to the appearance of coming and going. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* says it refers to a magnificent appearance. According to the *Wénzìdiǎnshuō*, the character is composed of the radical "silk" (糸) and the phonetic "bīn" (賓).

Volume 2, Part 2: *The Sutra on the Merit of the Original Vows of the Seven Buddhas of the Medicine Master Lapis Lazuli Light*. This concludes the commentary on the first half of Volume 2 of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, following the previous section.

Regarding "chewing" (jiào): Master Jue (爵) of Zhang (匠) says it is synonymous with "masticating" (jiào). The *Zishu* says it is "chewing" (zǔ). The *Shuowen* states that it is written as the character "jiào" (噍), composed of the radical "mouth" (口) and the phonetic "jue" (爵); the pronunciation of "jiào" is qiáo-xiào (樵笑反), and the pronunciation of "zǔ" is cái-yǔ (才與反).

*Anila*: The prefix *an-* (pronounced with the "ge" tone) is a Sanskrit term meaning "twelve yakṣa generals. *Cai* (pronounced with the "zai-lai" tone) means "just" or "momentarily"; the *Dongguan Hanji* states it means "able," with the radical *mi* (silk) and the phonetic *xiang*. The character *xiang* is pronounced *shi-xian*. *Note on transliteration*: The text provides phonetic glosses for the reconstruction of Sanskrit terms into Chinese characters.

*Anila* is likely intended as a transcription of *anila* (wind), though here it is glossed as a title. The character *cai* (才) is noted for its specific pronunciation (*zai-lai*) and its semantic range ("just" or "able"). The character *xiang* (相) is analyzed into its components (*mi* + *xiang*) and provided with its Middle Chinese approximation (*shi-xian*). The instruction to "omit explanations" requires that these linguistic notes be integrated directly into the translation rather than presented as separate commentary. The resulting English must convey both the semantic content and the philological details of the original.
The Aśokarāja-sūtra, Volume One (upper). By Xuanying. [Note: "A-yu" (阿俞) is pronounced with the initial *yì* (翼) and the final *zhū* (珠) reversed;
"Jiūsù" (鳩遬) is pronounced with the initial *sū* (蘇) and the final *gǔ* (穀); both are names of bhikṣus.
Oṃ taptāpe. *Taptāpe* is the name of a samādhi;
according to the characters, *taptā* means "to separate," while *taptāpe* (also read as *pīkui*) means "an ugly face."

2. *Ajātaśatru-rāja-sūtra*, Scroll Lower. "Duò" (垛) [the second character] is pronounced with the *tuó* rhyme (dùo). It refers to a mound of earth. The *Cuǎnwén* states that people of Wu used to pile up earth to form a *duò*. The *Gōngjīn zhèngzì* states it means a terrace or platform; it is composed of the radical "earth" (*tǔ*) and the phonetic "duǒ" (*duǒ* is pronounced *dīngguǒ*).

*Ben-zǒu* (to run away): The ancient form is 𩦥, now written as 奔 (*bù mén*); it means to run swiftly. According to the *Shìmíng*, "running" (*bēn*) implies a transformation; it is a rushing toward a sudden change. *Jīn pī* (a gold pin):
also written as 錍 or 鎞 (*pǔ tí*), these two forms are identical; they are names for hairpins. *Chā* (forked): another name for a hairpin.

*The Scripture on the Samādhi of Universal Transcendence*, Scroll One. *Xuanying’s Pronunciations*. Scroll One. "Wuqí" (無圻): "yú" (魚) and "jīn" (斤). "Jùjī" (巨機) is read with two tones [as a compound]. This is the name of a Bodhisattva. In the script of this sutra, it is written with the "water" radical and pronounced "yī" (衣), with the tone "yú" (魚).

In the *Shijing* (Book of Poetry), it says "Do not be so envious" (*wú rán xīn xiàn*). The commentary states that "envious" (*xīn xiàn*) means "greedily envious. In the *Guoyu*, it says "the people were envious and obtained it," and Jia Dui explains that "envious" (*xīn*) means "greedy" (*tān*).
*Kuài* (喟) is written with the same radical as *kǒu* (口) and the phonetic *guài* (怪) or *kuì* (愧); according to the *Shuowen*, it means "a deep sigh" or a sound of exclamation.
*Kēngrán* (鏗然) is also written with the two forms *kēng* (𨥖) and *chōng* (䡩), both having the same phonetic *gēng* (耕); according to the *Guǎngyá*, *chōng chōng* (䡩䡩) means "firm and upright."
*Dàbá* (蒲末反, *pú mò fǎn*) and *chōuhū* (又作倐𨁀二形同書育反, *yòu zuò shū pǔ èr xíng tóng shū yù fǎn*) are characters for the appearance of extreme rapidity. 2.
In the middle fascicle of the *Pǔchāo sānmèi jīng* (普超三昧經), *chùtì* (勑律反下又作悐同他狄反, *chì lǜ fǎn xià yòu zuò tí tóng tā dí fǎn*) means to be startled and terrified.
*Xīn* (下許金反): According to the *Zìlín*, it means the spirit consuming qi; it refers to the sacrifice to ghosts and spirits.
*Xiǎng* (皆享虛掌反): To enjoy; this is also appropriate. *Zhènshè* (震懾):
The *Shēnglèi* writes this as *zhì* (㒤), with the same pronunciation as *zhǐyè* (止葉反). The *Guǎngyá* states that it means "to be terrified."
*Miè* (pronounced *mò huāng*) means "distant" (*yuǎn*). In the canonical text, it is sometimes written as *huǎng* (pronounced *hū huǎng*).

It is also written as *hé* (pronounced *hú hé*, same as *hú gé*), which according to the *Shuowen Jiezi* means "to examine and verify facts" (*kǎo shí shì*); it also carries the sense of "careful scrutiny" (*shěn hé*).
"Three baskets" (sān qiè)—the character *qiè* is pronounced as in *kǔ xié*—refers to the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas as the three.
"Not yet manifest" (*wèi fú*)—in the *Zìlín*, *fú* means trust; it also means to arise.
"Majestic" (*tángtáng*)—the *Hànshū* states that *dǐng dài* means the appearance of being lofty and grand.
"Wúfén" (無棼)—the "fén" is pronounced as "fú" (扶) and "yún" (雲); it is the name of a dragon king. According to the character, "fén" refers to the ridgepole of a roof. 3.

In the lower fascicle of the *Puchao sanmei jing* (普超三昧經), Fascicle 4: "zhí" (植)—the "zhí" is pronounced as "zhì" (直) and "lì" (吏); it means a pillar. According to the *Sancang*, a pillar at the side of a door is called a "zhí," and "zhí" also refers to a pillar for hanging a screen.

*Fàngbō Jīng* (The Scripture on Setting Aside the Alms Bowl), one fascicle. Xuānyì’s phonetics: *ruò* (若) and *tóu* (頭) are followed by *ér* (而); *zhě* (者) and *rǎng* (穰) are followed by *zhuó* (灼) with the second tone. This is a name for a Buddha-field (*buddhakṣetra*) in the Sanskrit language; it is sometimes written as *jiè* (惹), while the scripture uses *nuò* (偌), which is a vulgar character.

*The Scripture on the Moon-Lamp Samādhi*, Volume One. *Xuanying’s Pronunciations*, entry no. 1. Volume One. *Wu shuang* (無爽): "Shuang" is pronounced as two reversed [sounds]. The *Erya* states: "Shuang means 'to differ' (*cha*), which refers to being not the same and not uniform."
"Mixture" (糅): This character is pronounced *nǚ* (as in "female"). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "mixed rice. 2. Second Fascicle, *Candrapradīpa Samādhi Sūtra*.

"Board" (榜): Pronounced *bǎng* (as in "north" or *mǎng*). It refers to a signboard or placard used to display good or evil deeds to others. In the text, it is written with the "wood" radical (*木*) as *bǎng* (pronounced *bǔ máng*), which refers to the side-piece of a bow or crossbow; this usage is not appropriate here. "Plaque" (牌): Pronounced *pái* (as in "reed" or *pú*). [This is the correct character for the object intended.]

Volume Three, *Candrapradīpa Samādhi Sūtra*, Volume Three. *Wan* (烏桓反): According to the *Pīcāng*, this means to carve or pare; it refers to gouging out flesh. *Gāo* (鼛󲯬, 公勞反): A large drum. The *Kǎogōng Jì* states:

"The *gāo* drum is six feet and four inches long. The commentary notes: "The *gāo* drum is used for labor services. It is also written as *fú* (䩿, same character, 扶雲反). The *Erya* says: "A large drum is called a *fen*. Guo Pu states: "It is eight feet long."

*Leiting* (thunderbolt) refers to the three tones *ding*, *ting*, and *ting*. The *Erya* states: "A swift clap of thunder is called *leiting*. The *Cangjie pian* says it is *pi-li* (crashing thunder). The *Shuowen jiezi* explains that it is the residual sound of thunder by which all things are brought forth; *leiting* is also lightning. The *Shuowen jiezi* further defines *zheng* (a gong) as a type of *niao* (cymbal) resembling a bell, with the handle hollow through from top to bottom.
The *bī* (pronounced with the *pú* and *jī* rhymes) is a small drum, also known as a riding drum.
The *xiāo* and *zhù* (pronounced with the *zhī* and *liù* rhymes) are shaped like *zhēng* lutes; their heads are carved and grasped, and because one strikes them with the head, they are called *zhù*.
*Jiǎ* (𪝥): Virtuous and returning together; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *jiǎ* means "gentle," a term used by practitioners of the arts.

Volumes 4–6: The fourth, fifth, and sixth volumes of the *Mingdeng Sanmei Jing*. These three volumes above were previously not provided with phonetic transcriptions. Volume 7: The seventh volume of the *Yuedeng Sanmei Jing*. *Rù xiá* (入匣): Now read as *xiá* (same as *hú jiǎ*); according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *xiá* means "a chest," referring to a container for holding knives and swords.
"Qipó" (栖泊): "Qī" is pronounced with the *pu* and *ge* finals; it means to moor or halt. Today, the stopping of a boat is called "qípó.
"Jī" is pronounced with the *gōng* final; it means to stimulate or to move. According to the *Shuowen*, "jī" refers to water that is swift and rushing.
*Jiǎhuá* (狡 猾): *gǔ* (古) with the *mǎo* (卯) rhyme; *hù* (胡) with the *guā* (刮) rhyme. According to the *Fānyán* (方言), when a child is full of deceit, they are called *jiǎhuá*.

8. *Yuèdēng Sānmèijīng*, Scroll Eight. *Tái* (臺): *xiè* (榭) with the *cí* (辭) and *yè* (夜) rhymes. According to the *Ěryǎ*, a wooden structure is called a *xiè*. Guō Pǔ says: "A building erected upon a terrace."

The *zhòuwén* (seal-script) form for "corridor" (*lángwǔ*) is written as 𢋑; it shares the same pronunciation as *wǔ*. It refers to a guest house. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is the side building surrounding a hall. The *Shiming* states: "A large building is called a *lǚ*; people of the You and Ji regions call it a *yà* (pronounced *wǔ*, with the fifth tone)."

*Jambā-lavaṇa* (詹波之鹽) is a transliteration that may also be written as *Zhānbō* (占波) or *Zhānpó* (占婆); it refers to the *campaka* flower, translated as "Golden Flower" (*jīnsèhuā*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states it is a yellow-flowered tree.

Volume Nine. *Candrapradīpa-samādhi-sūtra*, Volume Nine. "Liu" (瘳) is pronounced with the initial *ch* and the final *u* (勑流反). It means to recover or to be cured. This is as in the *Shangshu*: "The next day, [the ruler] then recovered (*liu*)."
"Zhuli" (竚立) is interchangeable with "zhù" (佇), pronounced *chú lǚ* according to the *Erya*, which states that "zhù" means to stand for a long time; thus, it refers to standing for a long duration.
"Dòngjiǎn" (動瞼), pronounced *jū yǎn*, is briefly explained as the skin on the outside of the eye.
*Zhēn cuì* (臻萃): In the *Fānyán* (方言), between the regions of the East, Qi, Hǎi, and Dài, *cuì* is called *jù* (聚);

it means to gather or assemble. *Tài zhù* (媅著): In ancient texts, this is the same as *dàn* (妉). According to the *Shuōwén*, *tài* means "to delight" or "to crave. Today, both are written as *dān* (耽).

10. The Tenth Scroll of the Candrapradīpa Samādhi Sūtra. Scroll Ten. "Si" (俟) is used as an archaic term; it is written with the characters 俟, 竢, or 㕘. It has three forms but shares the same meaning. According to the *Erya*, "si" means "to wait."

Regarding *karpūra* (camphor), the *Xiyu ji* states: The *karpūra* tree has a trunk like that of a pine, yet its leaves, flowers, and fruit are distinct. When first harvested, it is moist and does not yet possess fragrance; however, after the wood dries and is subsequently processed and split open, there is a fragrant substance within, resembling mica in appearance and ice or snow in color. This is what is called *karpūra*.
*Li* (礪) refers to a whetstone; *zhi* (砥) is finer than *li*. Volume Eleven.

The *Candrapradīpa-samādhi-sūtra*, Volume Eleven. Xuanying’s initial phonetic transcription: "The Buddha Speaks the Chapter on the Great Dharma-Gate of Purity. One volume. Hui-lin’s phonetic transcription: *Pu-shou* (溥首). The upper character *pu* (溥) is pronounced as *pǔ*. In Sanskrit, this sūtra is translated according to the Jin pronunciation as *Mañjuśrī*; he is called *Pu-shou* (Universal Head) and is a *kumārabhūta* (Crown Prince of the Dharma). Now, in the Tang language, he is translated as *Miaojixiang* (Wondrous Auspiciousness).

Regarding the term *jī* (肌): the phonetic gloss states that "skin" (*jī*) refers to the flesh within the skin. The *Shuowen Jiezi* also defines it as flesh, stating it is composed of the radical "flesh" (*ròu*) with the phonetic element "ji" (*jǐ*).

Regarding *dàn* (憺): the upper character is pronounced *tán* (談) or *lán* (濫). Gu Yewang states that "dàn" means tranquility; Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states it means "peaceful. The *Shuowen Jiezi* also defines it as peaceful, composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) with the phonetic element "zhān" (*zhān*). It is incorrect for the scripture to write this with the water radical as *dàn*. Regarding *pò* (怕): the lower character is pronounced *bó* (伯). The *Guangya* states that "pà" means stillness; the phonetic gloss states it is the mind being peaceful and still. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as non-action (*wéiwéi*), composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) with the phonetic element "bái" (*bái*). It is incorrect for the scripture to write this with the water radical as *pó*.

Regarding "jīn-mài" (筋脈): [The character for] *jīn* (筋) is pronounced as *gǐn-xīn-fǎn*. The *Líjì* states, "In the elderly, one does not perform rites based on physical strength," which refers to this. The *Shuōwén* says: "*Jīn* means the strength of the flesh. It is composed of 'flesh' (肉) and 'bamboo' (竹); bamboo is among things that have much sinew. It is composed of 'strength' (力); 'strength' symbolizes sinew. Below is *mèng-yè-fǎn*, correctly written as *mài* (脈). The *Shuōwén* says: "It refers to the divisions of the blood-channels (*xuè-lǐ*) that traverse obliquely through the body. It is composed of 'to eat' (𠂢) and 'blood' (血) as its phonetic component; '𠂢' is pronounced *pāo-mò-fǎn*. The *Jīng* (經) uses the form with "flesh" (肉), while the common tradition has long used the form with "bamboo" (竹); therefore, it is retained here.

Regarding "chén yī" (塵漪): the *Yìyì* (懿冝) rhyme group indicates the pronunciation; the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that "yī" refers to fine ripples. The *Máoshī* (毛詩) describes it as heavy waves. In the standard characters of antiquity and today, this character is composed of the radical "water" (水) with the phonetic "yī" (猗). The character appearing in the scripture as "yīyī" (猗猗) is a variant of "qiān" (󲲝), which refers to a dog; this is not the meaning here. The character "qiān" (󲲝) is pronounced "jiè" (芥).

Regarding "mingzhé" (明智): the character *zhé* (喆) is pronounced as *zhǎnliè* (展列). Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* (尚書) states that *zhé* means "to understand"; the *Erya* states it means "wisdom. It is also written as *zhé* (哲) or *zhé* (悊); in ancient forms it was written as *zhé* (󲭶 or 󴻞). The standard modern form follows both [components] with the radical *jí* (吉).

Regarding "kai" (armor): the lower radical is pronounced *ku* with the *gai* rhyme. The *Wenzi jilüe* (Collected Abridgments of Characters) states that covering the body with metal and leather is called *kai*. The *Guǎyá* (Extended Lexicon) says, "The *zhújiǎ* (scale armor) and *fēnkāi* (segmented armor) are [types of] this. The *Shuowen jiezi* defines it as "armour; derived from the radical 'metal' (*jin*) and the phonetic component 'qi' (*qǐ*)."

In the character *cí* (癡疵), the lower radical is pronounced as *yí*. Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states: "Cí means illness or defect. Liu Huán’s commentary on the *Zhòuyì* states: "Cí means flaw; it is that which brings ruin. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical *nà* (疒) with the phonetic *cǐ* (此).

*Shéhui* (蛇虺): *xià huī wěi fǎn*. Guo’s commentary on the *Shānhăijīng* states that the *huǐ* is colored like a sash-pattern (*shòuwén*), with needles upon its nose; those of larger size weigh over a hundred *jīn*. It is also called "Inverted Nose" (*fǎnbì*). The *Shuōwén* says it is also called *fú*, measuring three inches [in width] with a head as large as a thumb. This represents its form while lying down. Among things that are minute, some move, some are dead, some have hair, some are conch-like (*luó*), some have fur (*mái*), and some have scales (*líng*). It uses the character for insect (*chóng*) as its radical. The ancient form used *chóng*. *Luó* is pronounced *lìguǒ fǎn*.

The character 裓 (gé; the *kēng* and *lè* rhymes) is explained by Xu Kāo as meaning "the lapel of a garment. It is also written as 󲲐 (jīng-yì rhyme). Some dictionaries claim it means "the sleeve," but this is incorrect; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to the collar of a garment. It is composed of the radical 衣 (clothing) and the phonetic component 戒 (jiè).

The character 𤵜 (qù) is pronounced with the initial *chǐ* and the final *lìn*. According to the *Kǎo Shēng*, it means "a chronic ailment" (*chèn bìng*), implying that the illness has a deep root. The *Máo Shī* states: "My heart is filled with sorrow; it is like a chronic ailment causing a headache. The *Shuō Wén* says: "Chèn is a feverish illness; it is composed of the radical 疒 and the element 火. The character used in the *Jīng* is interchangeable with this one.

*Bo-bo* (bo-bu): "To submerge and emerge. According to the *Guangya*, "bo-bo" means flourishing; according to the *Cangjie pian*, it means to emerge suddenly; according to the *Shuowen jiezi*, it means to push forward, composed of the radical 力 (li) and the phonetic 孛 (bei). In the scriptures, it is written with the water radical as 渤 (bó), referring to a place name; its meaning differs [from the preceding definitions].

*Xiàn* (pronounced *xián* with the upper radical *xuán* [罥] and the phonetic *jiǎ* [賈]). Guo Yu’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that it means "to delude. Gu Yewang says that *xiàn* also refers to illusions and sorcery (*shìhuàn*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "eye" (*mù*) and the phonetic "xuán" (*xuán*).

*Chen* (貪) and *shu* (󲳫): The lower radical is *xiang* (祥) with the *jian* (箭) reversal; the *shengyun* (聲韻) glosses it as *chao* (󲳩), meaning "to love" or "to long for. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that *chao* is synonymous with "abundance" (*rao*). The *Han Shi* says it means "desire. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *chao* means "greedy desire"; it is composed of *feng* (󲪦) and *si* (㳄). *Feng* is from the character for "sheep" (*yang*) and *liu* (󲢬). *Si* is pronounced *xian* (羡) with the *yan* (延) reversal; *xian* is pronounced *you* (誘). In the scripture, it is written as *xi* (次) instead of *xian* (羡), which is not this meaning.

The Mahāvyūha-dharmaparyāya Sūtra, Volume One. Xuanying’s Pronunciations, Part One. Regarding "Puruṣa" (晡沙): in this sūtra it is sometimes written as 逋沙, 補沙, or 富樓沙; these are all corruptions. The correct pronunciation is *puruṣa*, which means "man" (*śi-fu*) or "great man" (*zhàng-fū*).

*Kangjue* (剛橛): "Jue" is pronounced *qu* (渠) with a reversed *yue* (月). According to the *Erya*, a *que* (橛) is called a *yi* (杙); a *yi* is a *zhi* (樴). *Zhi* is pronounced *tu* (徒) with a reversed *de* (得).

*Canghu* (鶬鵠), also written as *yan* (𩀞), is the same as *cangji* (󱍮). *Cangji* is pronounced *tang* (唐) with a reversed *ji* (鵠). According to the *Erya*, *cangji* is the *kua* (麋鴰). Guo Pu says: "This is precisely the *canghu*."
"Only *chā* (also written as *zhà*, same pronunciation; the *Pīcāng* and *Shēnglèi* both write it as *zhà*; it refers to a duck eating). 2.

In the lower fascicle of the *Mahāvyūha-dharmaparyāya-sūtra*, in the character for *qiánchóng* (flesh-worm), the *Zílín* gives the pronunciation *qiānyú*. In the *Tōngsùwén*, worms within the flesh are called *qián*. The scriptural text uses the character with the 'insect' radical, *jū* (pronounced *zǐyú*); *jūjū* is the *Wúgōng* [cricket]. It is also written as *jū* or *tōu*. Below, it is sometimes written with the 'insect' radical, *chúzhōng* (same pronunciation *chúzhōng*). According to the *Erya*, those with legs are called *chóng*."
The character 鑒 (jiàn) is not found in standard dictionaries; it is written as 鑑, with the ancient pronunciation *chán* (zhàn). According to the *Guǎngyá*, "jiàn" means "to illuminate.

It is said that "jiàn" refers to a mirror, by which one examines one's form. In the *Yuedeng Sanmei Jing* (Moon-Lamp Samādhi Sūtra), there is one fascicle titled *Yuedeng Sanmei Jing*. Regarding the character 叡 (ruì) in the *Púsà Xiūxíng Jīng* (Bodhisattva Practice Sūtra), one fascicle, Huílín’s phonetic gloss gives it as *yuè* (yuè) with the tone *shuài* (shuài). Confucius, in his commentary on the *Shàngshū*, states: "Ruì necessarily implies mastery of the arts. Jia, in his commentary on the *Guóyǔ*, states: "Ruì means clarity. The *Guǎngyá* states: "Ruì is wisdom. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "profound clarity," composed of the radicals 艸 (simplified here as 𦽻), 目 (eye), and 谷 (valley, abbreviated). The sound of 艸 is *cán* (cán).

Regarding "weì cuì" (危脆): the lower character is pronounced with the *qi* and *ruì* rhymes. The *Guǎngyá* states it means "weak and brittle. Gu Yewáng says "brittle" (*cuì*) is synonymous with "soft" (*ruǎn*). The *Shuowén* defines it as "having little flesh, soft and easily broken," composed of the radical "flesh" (*ròu*) and the phonetic "abbreviated *jué*" (*jiě*). The form "jīng" (經) written with "weì" (危) is a vulgar variant of "cuì" (脆).

*Zào* (燥): The second character is pronounced *sāo* (with the initial *zǎo*). The *Zhouyi* says, "Fire seeks the dry. The *Shuowen* states that "dry" (*zào*) means parched; it is composed of the radical *huǒ* (fire) with *sào* as the phonetic component.

*Sào* is pronounced *xiān dào*. *Wèi* (偽): The first character is pronounced *shèng* (with the initial *zhí*). The *Kaoseng Zhuan* states that it means "to adorn one's appearance. The *Wenzi Dian* explains it as "to embellish," composed of the radical *jīn* (cloth) with *sì* as the phonetic component. *Sì* is pronounced *sì*. The second character is pronounced *wēi* (with the initial *wèi*). Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states that "false" (*wèi*) means feigned. The *Guangya* says "false" (*wèi*) implies difficulty or lamentation. The *Shuowen* states that "false" (*wèi*) means deceitful; it is composed of the radical *rén* (person) with *wéi* as the phonetic component.

*Niǎo* (nest): The upper character is read as *shì* (爻, *xiáo*). Zheng’s commentary on the *Mao Shi* states: "The magpie builds its nest; it begins constructing at the winter solstice and completes it by spring. Zheng’s annotation to the *Kaogong Ji* says: "A *niǎo* is high. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "When birds are in trees, it is called a *niǎo*; when in burrows, it is called a *kō*. It follows the wood radical (*木*) and is a pictographic character. The lower character is read as *kùn* (骨, *gǔ*). Du’s annotation to the *Zuo Zhuan* says: "A *kué* is a subterranean chamber. The *Liji* says: "In winter, they dwell in circular burrows (*yíng kué*). The *Shenglei* says: "A *kué* is where a rabbit hides. The *Shuowen* [explains it] as following the cave radical (*穴*) with *qū* as the phonetic component.

Regarding the term *yáo* (肴) in *shàn yáo* (饍肴): the upper character is pronounced *jiāo* (交). Jia [Yan]’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that *yáo* refers to meat on the sacrificial stands (*zǔ*) and vessels (*dòu*). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* says that *yáo* is the fillings for the *dòu*. Zheng’s *Shi Jing Zhan* explains that the fillings for the *dòu* refer to pickled vegetables (*zhū*). Generally, anything eaten that is not grain is called *yáo*. Regarding the lower character, it is pronounced *zhàn* (戰). Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhou Li* states that "the word *shàn* (饍) means 'excellent' (*shàn*). Thus, when fine things of the season are served with meat, they are called *zhēn shàn* (珍饍). Furthermore, his commentary on the *Yili* states that "to *shàn*" (饍) is equivalent to "to present" (*jìn*); it refers to providing complete food. Both instances take the character *yáo* (爻) as the phonetic component meaning "excellent. However, the received text uses *yáo* (殽) with the radical "meat" (*shí*) and "excellent" (*shàn*) with the radical "food" (*shí*), both of which are incorrect.

*Chǔguǎng* (麁獷): The upper character *chǔ* (麁) is pronounced with the *cùsū* (醋蘇) rhyme; it was already explained previously in the lower fascicle of the *Dharmānudharma-paryāya-sūtra*. The lower character *guǎng* (獷) is pronounced with the *kǎo* (考) rhyme. Regarding the sound, "guǎng" refers to a dog that is fierce and perverse. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Guǎng means a dog; 'guǎng' is one who cannot be associated with. It is composed of the radical 'dog' (*quán*) and the phonetic 'guǎng'."

"Yìzhěng" (意整): "Zhèng" (整) is read as *zhēng* (征) or *lǐn* (領) in the reverse [reading]. The commentary on the *Lǐjì* by Zheng Xuan states that it means "to rectify. The *Shuowén* says it means "to align"; it is composed of "chì" (敕) and "zhèng" (正). "Chì" is pronounced *lì* (勑). The character in the scripture is composed of "lái" (来) and "lì" (力), forming "zǒng" (󲏰); this is a vulgar form and is incorrect."

Regarding "suò" (鎖), the *Shuoguo* commentary on sounds states that it means "to bind. The *Wenzi jilüe* says it refers to linking iron rings to restrain the body. In the standard characters of past and present, it follows the radical for metal (*jin*) with the phonetic element *lǚ*; alternatively, it is written with the radical for jade (*yù*) as *suǒ*. It is incorrect for the sutras to write it with the radical for birds' nests (*cháo*) as *suǒ*. Regarding "xiè" (械) below, the *Wenzi jilüe* says it refers to piercing wood to fasten the feet. The *Wenzi dianshuo* states that "xiè" refers to shackles and stocks; it follows the radical for wood with the phonetic element *jiè*.

*Ai* (騃): The upper radical is *yá* (崖). The *Cāngjié piān* states that *ai* means "to lack knowledge. Gu Yewáng says that *chī* (癡) is also *ai*. The *Hànshū* states, "Internally dull and ignorant of government," which refers to this. In the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical for "horse" (*mǎ*) and the phonetic *yǐ* (矣). The lower part is pronounced *chí* (持). The *Pīcāng* states that *chī* is also *ai*. In the *Shuowén*, *chī* means "not wise"; it is composed of the radical for "sickness" (*niè*) and the phonetic *yí* (疑). According to the *Kǎoshēng*, it may also be written as *qín* (𢣕) with the radical for "mind" (*xīn*).

*Weiyu* (煒曗): The upper character *wei* (煒) is pronounced with the *sheng* (rhyme) *gui* (韋). The *Kao Sheng* states that it means "the appearance of brilliant light and color. The *Shuowen* says it is "intense red color," composed of the radical *huo* (fire) and the phonetic *wei* (韋). The lower character *zhe* (輙) is pronounced with the *sheng* *yan* (炎). The *Wenzi Jilüe* says *yu* (曗) means "the appearance of brilliant light. The *Shuowen* also says *yu* (曗) is "light," composed of the radical *ri* (sun) and the phonetic *ye* (業). It is incorrect for the scriptures to write this as *hua* (華) and *ye* (曄).

*Xuānfēi* (翾飛): The rhyme dictionary *Yùnyīng* states it refers to small flying insects; the *Zhōushū* says "small flying and wriggling creatures"; the *Shuowén* says "small flight," composed of the radical for wings (*yǔ*) and the phonetic *huáng*.
Regarding "śǔndòng" (蠕動), the first character is read as *yǐn* (𨳝尹反). This was already explained previously in the middle fascicle of the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra*.

Regarding "wúsuǒxīwàng jīng" (無所希望經): *Wúsuǒxīwàng jīng*, one fascicle. Regarding the phonetic gloss for "yúzhòng" (愚戇): the second character is read as *zhuóxiàng* (卓巷反). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that "zhìzhòng" (戇) means a state where the spirit is not alert. The *Shuowén* also defines it as "yú" (愚). It is composed of the radical "heart" (心) and the phonetic "gòng" (𥫔, sound *gòng*). The version of the sūtra written as "chóng" (憃) is an error; "zhì" (戇) is pronounced *pángxiàng* (尨巷反).

"Yāngxìn" (殃釁): the second character is read as *xīn* (下昕覲反). Duan’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "xìn" means "crime. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of "a simplified form of cuàn" (爨省) and "yǒu" (酉) as the phonetic;
the text's reading as "xì" (舋) is an error. "Rúhuàn" (如幻): the first character is read as *huǎng* (荒晃反); its correct form is "mó" (󲳻), which is a transliteration of a Sanskrit term.

The character *qí* (蚑) has the phonetic *qí*; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "to move. The *Wenzidian* explains that it refers to the movement of insects, composed of the radical *chóng* (insect) with the phonetic *zhī*. The character *fēng* (𧒒) has the phonetic *fēng* (read as *fēng*); according to the *Shuowen*, it refers to stinging insects that inflict venom upon people, composed of the radical *wén* (insect) with the abbreviated phonetic *féng*. The *Zhengzijing* uses this character [for bee], whereas the common vulgar form is *fēng* (蜂).

*Xiàngyè jīng* (The Elephant-Axis Sūtra), one fascicle. Regarding the phonetic gloss by Huìlín, "dé xuán suí yuán fǎn" (得旋隨緣反): Dù’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states that "zhuóxuán" means to pursue one another; Wáng’s commentary on the *Chuci* states it means to rotate. The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "yǔ" (於) with the sound "pǐ" (疋); "yǎn" (㫃) has the sound "yǎn" (偃). The version of the sūtra that uses the "hand" radical to form "bō" (𢭀) is an error.

*Bì* (稗) is pronounced *shàng-pài-fǎn*. Duan Yucai’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that it is a weed resembling grain. Ru Chun’s commentary on the *Qilüe* says that fine rice is called *bì*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as a variety of *he* (grain), taking *bei* as its phonetic component; the entry for *yǒu* (莠) gives the pronunciation *xià-yóu-fǎn*. The *Kǎoshēng* states that *yǒu* is the name of a weed resembling grain. The *Mao Shichuan* says that *yǒu* resembles the seedling. Gu Yewang says it is a weed that resembles the seedling. The *Shangshu* says, "It is like weeds among the seedlings, or like chaff among the millet. The *Shuowen* further explains: "When the ears of millet (*he-sù*) emerge from below, they are called *yǒu*; it takes *xiù* as its phonetic component."
*Mong* (upper character pronounced *mò*, with the *bēng* rhyme; the Sanskrit term is written as *𥌋* in the sutra, which is an error).
*Móchǒu* (upper character pronounced *qiú*, with the *yóu* rhyme; the Sanskrit term is written as *㕨* following the mouth radical in the sutra, which is incorrect).

The title *Rúlái Zhuāngyán Zhìhuì Fó Jìngjiè* (The Tathāgata’s Adorned Wisdom Buddha-Sphere) appears at the beginning of the first scroll. Regarding the phonetics in Huílín’s commentary: In the first scroll, the word *yǒngchū* (surging forth): the upper character is pronounced *rǒng*, with the *sǒng* rhyme. Lìu Zhào’s commentary on the *Gōngyáng Zhuàn* states that it means "to surge and overflow. The *Shuowén Jiězì* states it is composed of the "water" radical and the phonetic element "yǒng," where the sound of "yǒng" is the same as "shàng" (upward).

"Xiù" (to smell) is pronounced with the lower radical *xiǔ* (朽) and the phonetic *kǎo* (考). The *Yīn yìng* (禽經) states that it is the dog that knows the tracks by smelling the stench of birds; this refers to the passage in the *Lúnyǔ*: "Zǐlù stood with hands clasped, smelled three times, and then rose. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "using the nose to approach an odor," composed of the radical *bí* (鼻) and the phonetic *chòu* (臭).

The character *zì* (滋) is pronounced with the initial *tsi* (慈) and the final *kǎo* (考). Xu Shen’s *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "moist" (*zhī*) and "abundant" (*duō*). Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Book of Documents* says it means "to increase" (*yì*) and "to grow" (*zhǎng*). The *Cangjie Pian* says it means "liquid" (*yè*). The *Wenzi Dianshuo* explains that it is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic component "zī" (*zī*).

The character *duī* (堆) is pronounced with the radical *shàng* (上) and the phonetic *duì* (對), reversed; its gloss states it is the appearance of high ground, and it also means "to accumulate. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* says, "Quī-duī" means high. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Shanglin fu* says, "Duī-shā" means a mound of sand. It is also written as *duī* (塠). The *Gōngjīn zhèngzì* takes the radical *tǔ* (土) and the phonetic *zhuī* (隹); the latter is pronounced with the phonetic *fúyǒu* (浮有). The *Erya* says, "A large plain is called *duī* (𨸏). The *Cangjie pian* says, "*Duī* (𨸏) is a mountain that is low yet vast. The *Guoyan* commentary by Jia Gongyan says, "It also means thick and long. The *Shuowen jiezi* says, "A large plain where there are no stones is called *duī* (𨸏); it is a pictographic character. The vulgar form is commonly written as *fù* (阜).

Regarding the term *guǒluò* (fruit and melons): the upper character *guǒ* is the correct form when written with the radical for grass (*艸*); it is a vulgar variant of the lower character pronounced *luó* (as in *luó*). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "Fruit refers to the category of peaches and plums; *luò* refers to the category of gourds. Zhang Yan’s commentary on the *Hanshu* states: "That which has a pit is called fruit; that which lacks a pit is called *luò*. Ying Shao’s commentary on the *Hanshu* states: "The fruit of trees is called *guǒ*; the fruit of plants is called *luò*. This is what the *Zhouyi* means by "fruit and melons" (*guǒluò*). According to the *Shuowen*, the character is formed from the radical for grass and the phonetic *làn*. The pronunciation of *tuójié* (the lower part of *luò*) is *dújié*, and the pronunciation of *làn* is *yǔ*.

2. Lower Scroll: *The Tathāgata’s Adorned Wisdom and the Buddha-Sphere*. "Drifting" (*piāoliú*): [In the] *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means to float. It is composed of the radical "water" and the phonetic "piao. The version in the sutra is written as "shuāo," which is an error. Master Wang Yishang states that it means "drifting. The *Shuowen* explains it as "floating" (*piāofú*). It takes the radical "water" and the phonetic "piao. The sutra text uses "shuāo," which is incorrect.

*Tǔkuài* (土塊): "Kuài" is read as *kǔ duì fǎn*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Kuài means a clod of earth; it is formed with 'tǔ' as the radical and 'guǐ' as the phonetic. *Fù* is pronounced *pī bī fǎn*, or alternatively written as *yùn*. *Chāo* (󲪧): The upper character is read as *kǔ mài fǎn*.

The *Kaosheng* states: "Chāo means to satisfy one's wishes. The *Guangya* states: "Chāo means acceptable or joyful. It is formed with 'xīn' (heart) as the radical and 'guà' as the phonetic. *Guà* is pronounced *guā chāo fǎn*.

*Chuan* (纏): The upper character is pronounced *che-lian-fan*; the *Shuowen* says it means "to wind" or "to bind. It is composed of the radical *mi* (糸) with the phonetic *li*. The lower character is pronounced *go-huo-fan*. Gu Yewang says that *guo* (裹) is like *bao* (苞), meaning "to envelop"; he also says *guo* is like *guo* (裹). The *Shuowen* states that *guo* is also *chuan* (纏); it is composed of the radical *yi* (衣) with the phonetic *guo*. The pronunciation of *li* is the same as above.

*The Scripture on the Adornment of Wisdom that Transcends the Realms of All Buddhas*, one fascicle. Regarding the phonetics in Huilin’s *Yin*: "Yan" (閻) in "Jambudvīpa" (閻浮提)—the Sanskrit term is written as "Yan," while the vernacular character is used. (Note: *Jambudvīpa* is the name of the continent.)
*Jiējiā* (the lower character pronounced *jiā*);
*Ānúlǒutóu* (the initial is pronounced as a retroflex *ṇ*, with the Sanskrit term sometimes written as 𑖡 or 𑖢).

This appears in the "Preface to the Newly Translated Scripture on Entering the Buddha’s Realm," which contains the "Forty Homages Praising the Dharmakāya of the Great Sage Mañjuśrī" from a Sanskrit manuscript.

Huìlín states: "I have been unworthily favored (tāo). Examining the phonetics, *tāo* means "to overstep" or "to be excessive. Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states that *tāo* means "greed. Whether ancient or modern, the correct character is composed of the radical "mouth" (口) with the phonetic "knife" (刀).

"Sincere" (kěn): In the *Guǎngyǎ*, it says that "kěn" also means sincerity and trustworthiness. The *Lǐjì* states: "After bowing the head to the ground, one prostrates; 'kěn' refers to such ultimate devotion. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* explains: "It means to press closely. It is formed with the radical 'heart' (xīn) and the phonetic 'kěn' (kūn běn fǎn). 'Kěn' is composed of 'pigs' (zhǐ) and 'stagnant' (gèn); in the classics, it is written as 'kěn' with the radical 'beasts' (zhì), which is incorrect."

"Shù" (庶) is read as *pí* (裨) with the phonetic component *mí* (彌); the *Shēngyùn* states that "pí" means "to supplement. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Yǐlǐ* says: "The word 'pí' is synonymous with 'bǐ' (埤, meaning to augment). The *Shuowén* says it means "to increase," composed of the radical "clothing" (*yī*) and the phonetic component "bēi" (*bēi*).

In the text of the sutra, there are forty instances of the character "禮" (li), for which no difficult characters require explanation. Regarding the mantra phrase in the *Guan yaowang yaoshang pusa jing* (Sutra on the Visualization of the Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata), according to Hui Lin’s *Yinji*: the upper character "嘲" (cháo) is pronounced with the *qie* (phonetic analysis) as "革" (*ge*), and the lower character "翅" (*chi*)—if one follows its original sound, it would conflict with the intended meaning of the sentence; therefore, one should write the character "枳" (*zhi*), which is pronounced with the *qie* as "雞" (*ji*).

The character for *āthū* follows this pronunciation: *tá hóu* (反), which greatly contradicts the meaning of the text; it should instead follow the pronunciation of the character *yú*: *yáng zhū* (反), which accords with the text.

In the *Madguka-sūtra*, the character "deng" (瞪) is used, which is incorrect and significantly deviates from the textual phrasing; following the Sanskrit original, it should be pronounced as "dēng-xùng" (登亘反), and the character "deng" (蹬) derived from the radical for feet should also follow this pronunciation in the subsequent line of the sūtra.

*The Sutra on the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life*, spoken by the Buddha, in one fascicle. Regarding the phonetics of "yīng" (eagle) and "sǔn" (hawk/falcon): the character for "sǔn" is pronounced with the final rhyme *xún yǔn* (反). The *Erya* states: "The 'chǒu' (class) of eagles and falcons; their flight is *huī*. Guo’s commentary explains that this refers to the appearance of flapping their wings, *huī huī*, meaning they fly with great speed. The *Tradition of the Mao Shi* says: "The falcon (*sǔn*) is also a bird of swift and urgent flight. The correct form is "sǔn," though it is sometimes written as "shé" (鶽). In both the ancient and modern standard characters, it follows the radical "zhuī" (隹) and is pronounced with the sound "shí" (十).
*Luìliè* (羸劣): The first character is pronounced *lěi* (with the level tone) and *zhuī* (with the departing tone). This was already explained previously in the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-sūtra*.

*Cūjiàn* (粗見): The first character is pronounced *cú* (with the departing tone). The *Shījì* says, "To roughly set forth its outline. Gu Yewang states that "cū" (粗) means "roughly" (*lüè*). According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical *mǐ* (rice) and the phonetic *qiě* (且).

The character *yǒng* (甬) is pronounced with the rhyme of *róng* (容) and *zhǒng* (腫). Examining its phonetic value, it is said that *yǒng* refers to grass and flowers that have not yet blossomed. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "When the flowers of plants and trees are in full bloom, they are *yǒng-yǒng*. It is composed of the radical *hán* (𦫳, pronounced *hángǎn*) and the phonetic *yòng* (用). The radical *hán* (𦫳) represents the shape of plant and tree flowers that have not yet opened, appearing as if contained within a sheath (*hán-hán*). In the classics, this character is sometimes written with the "foot" radical (*zú*) as *yǒng* (踊); however, *yǒng* means to leap, which is not the meaning intended here in the scripture.

*Shùgěng* (tree stem): "Xìng" (幸) is pronounced *gēng*. The *Cāngjiépiān* states that for plants and trees, one says *gěng*. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) and the phonetic "xīng" (*xīng* is pronounced *gōnglìng*).

*Róuruǎn* (soft and supple): "Yì" (藝) is pronounced *yuǎn*. Gù Yěwáng states that *ruǎn* means "weak and soft. The *Bóyá* states that *ruǎn* means "weakness. The *Kǎoshēng* states that in Jia Yi’s memorial to the Emperor, it is written as *ruǎn*. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radicals "big" (*dà*) and "sound" (*shēng*); the version in the *Jīng* (Classics) as *ròu* is an erroneous usage.

Regarding "liuzhu" (pouring down): the *Huainanzi* states that when spring rain irrigates and pours upon the myriad things, there is no place where they do not grow. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "The character for 'shuyu' (timely rain) is so called because it pours and brings forth the myriad things. It is composed of the radical 'water' and the phonetic 'shu'; 'shu' also serves as the phonetic component. The pronunciation of "shu" is the same as "shu" (tree).
"Zhen" (甄) and "shu" (叔) [with the phonetic reversal of "yan" (延)] are the transliteration of a Sanskrit name for a jewel.

"Baoman" (寶縵)—[with the phonetic reversal of "man" (滿) and "ban" (半)]—refers to the ornamental draping and covering of the top of a banner with the seven precious gems. In ancient and modern standard characters, "zeng" (繒) has no written form; it is derived from the radical "silk" (糸) and the phonetic "man" (曼). The pronunciation of "man" is "wan" (萬).

Regarding "jiao" (絞), the upper character is read as *jiao* (交) with the phonetic component *kao* (考); the commentary states that "jiao" refers to a variegated color of silk, such as black and yellow. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "silk" (*mi*) and the phonetic "jiao. The lower character is read as *sheng* (升) with the phonetic component *zhi* (職). This term was already explained previously in the *Bodhisattva Xiuxing Jing* (Sutra on the Bodhisattva’s Cultivation of Practice).

Regarding "meat-crest" (ròujì): *jì* is pronounced as *yì* (as in *jīyì*). Zheng’s commentary on the *Yílǐ* states that "crest" refers to tied-up hair. The *Hànshū* calls it the "head-crest. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical *biāo* (pronounced *bìyáo*) with the phonetic *jí*. The sound of *biāo* is *bìyáo*.

*Can* (慚): with the *gan* rhyme reversed; the *Shangshu* says, "Only possessing the virtue of shame. The *Shuowen* says, "Can is also gui (愧). It follows the radical 'heart' and uses 'zhan' as its phonetic.

The version in the sutra as *can* (慚) is an error. *Amidabingjing* (阿彌陀經): *Foshuo Amituo Jing*, one fascicle. Regarding *lan* (欄) in *xiao hui lin yin*: for the upper character *lan* (欄), read as *dan* (單) reversed. The *Guangya* says, "Lan means enclosure. The *Cangjie pian* says, "Lan means to block. The *Shuowen* says, "Lan means a gate enclosure (*xian*). The character follows the radical 'gate' and uses 'jian' (柬) as its phonetic. The lower character [is] *ruo* (𨳝) with the *fan* (反) reading. This was already explained previously in the first fascicle of the *Shoulengyan jing*.
The character 絙 (gēng) in "衣裓" (yīgèi) is pronounced with the retroflex *r* (憶反); it is also written as 󲲐. This was already explained previously in the "Chapter on the Great Dharma Gate of Purity.
"阿鞞" (Ābī) is pronounced with the retroflex *p* (卑彌反); it is a Sanskrit term.

*Yan* (爓) [the character for "flame" in the title *Fàn yǔ fó hào jīng* (Sanskrit Names of Buddhas Sutra); it is also read as *yè* (叶), with the phonetic *qiàn* (壍) reversed; the sutra uses *yàn* (焰), which is also acceptable].

Regarding the *Hòuchū āmítuó jì* (Verses on Amitābha Appearing Later), one fascicle: Huílín’s phonetics state that *xī* (翕) is read as *xīn* (歆) and *yì* (邑). Hé Yàn’s commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* says: "*Xī* means 'abundant' (*shèng*) and also 'blazing' (*chì*). The *Shuōwén* states: "*Xī* means 'to rise'; it is composed of the radical *yǔ* (羽) and the phonetic *hé* (合)."

*Gé* (胳): The upper character is pronounced *gōng è* (公惡反). The *Pīcāng* states that the area behind the elbow is called *gé*. The *Shuowen* says it refers to the armpit, composed of the radical "flesh" (*ròu*) with "ge" (*gē*) as its phonetic.

*Huì* (㑹): The lower character is pronounced *huí wài* (迴外反). Zheng’s commentary on the *Mao Shih* states that *huì* means "to join" (*hé*). Furthermore, his notes on the *Liji* state that *huì* means "all. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states that *huì* refers to being "mutually facing. The *Shuowen* is composed of "present" (*jīn*) and the abbreviated form of "layered" (*céng*) as its phonetic. It is incorrect for the scripture to write this as *wèi* (懀), which is derived from "heart" (*xīn*). The *Guǎngyá* states that *wèi* means "hateful" (*è*), but this is not the meaning of the scripture.

*Sūtra on Praising the Merits of the Pure Land*, one fascicle. Hui-lin’s Pronunciations: *Aniruddha* is a term from the Sanskrit language; it is also called *Anuruddha*. In the language of Tang, it means "Unextinguished" (*Wumie*). It is also said to mean "As One Wishes. In the past, he once gave a single meal to a *pratyekabuddha*; because the bliss experienced by humans and devas has not been extinguished even until now, and because all that he seeks is as he wishes, he was named accordingly.

Aśmagarbha (the *ga* sound is pronounced as in *jue*, and the *la* sound as in *luo*; in Sanskrit it is sometimes written as Aśmaka). In the language of Tang, it means "stone-treasury" (*shizang*), or alternatively, "amber."

*Musāragalva* (in Sanskrit) or *musaragalva* (in the vernacular), translated into Chinese as *mǎnǎo* (agate); in treatises it is also called *chēqú* (musaragalva). Regarding the *tūlī* (crane): the upper character is pronounced with the initial *shū* and the final *xiū*.

The *Mao Shi* (Poetry of Mao) states that the *zhìyù* has no feathers on its head; thus [the term *tūlī*] is used. Gu Yewang says it is a large bird whose plumage is brilliant white and can be made into a *rǐ* (ornamental plume). *Rǐ* is pronounced with the initial *rén* and the final *zhì*; it refers to hair or feathers used as decoration. It is sometimes written as *zhì*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* takes *qiū* as the phonetic component and *lù* as the radical. The *Kaosheng* says it is the name of a crane; it is also called *chōngchú*. The commentary on the *Mao Shi* calls it a "white bird. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* says it is the *lù* (crane). Both its head and wings have long, soft feathers (*hàn-máo*). People in Jiangdong today take these to make eyelashes; it is named the "White Crane's Mourning Robe" (*báilù cuī*). The *Shuowen* takes *lù* as the phonetic component; *xiāng* is the pronunciation.
*Kalaviṅka* (the *shang ju ye* [上居謁] in Chinese; in Sanskrit, formerly transcribed as *kāra-viṅka* or *kalaviṅka*; in the Tang language, it means "bird with beautiful voice").
*Mleccha* (蔑戾車): the first character is pronounced as *shàn* (鼈) with the retroflex *-r* final, and the second is pronounced as *lián* (憐) with the palatal *-n* final;

it is a Sanskrit term. *Gaṅgā-sikatā* (殑伽沙): the first character is pronounced as *jí* (極) with the retroflex *-d- or -t-* final; it is a Sanskrit term for the name of a river in the Western Regions, also known as the sands of the Ganges (*Ganges*).
*Pópí jīng* (The Sūtra of Pópí). Xuānyì’s Pronunciations: *Pópí*, "Pó" is pronounced as *pú* with the *zhǎo* tone; the following "Pí" is pronounced as *bǐ* with the *pí* tone.
*Jiālǒu*, "Lǒu" is pronounced as *lì* with the *zhǔ* tone; these are all names of Bodhisattvas.

*Ku-xian* (the former character pronounced with the *shangping* tone and the latter with the *lian* rhyme) is a transcription of a Sanskrit term. *Man-lun* (the former character pronounced with the *ma* rhyme and the *jian* tone, and the latter with the *li-jun* rhyme) is the name of a Bodhisattva.

Regarding the character *fu*: it is also written as *pi* or *bin*, sharing the same radical and the *tong-feng-bi* rhyme; Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* states that *fu* is a type of wildcat (*li*).

Just as a shadow resides in response to a light, so too does the light reflect back upon the shadow; for all shadows arise because of light, and are thus called "jing" (light/shadow). Ge Hong, when composing the *Ziyuan*, first added the radical for "shadow" (*ying*) to the character.
