The *Fóshuō Lǎonǚrén Jīng* (Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Old Woman) states that the *Kǎoshēng* (Examination of Sounds) says "yǎng" refers to the subtlety of pain. The *Lǐjì* (Book of Rites) says, "One does not dare to scratch [the itch]. Zheng’s commentary on the *Xiàojīng* (Classic of Filial Piety) says this refers to suppressing and scratching itching and pain. The *Shuowén* (Explaining Characters) says "yǎng" means to scratch, composed of the radical "insect" and the phonetic "yáng. The *Wenzí Jílüè* (Abridged Collection of Characters) sometimes writes it as "yǎng" (癢), and the *Yùnlüè* (Abridged Rhymes) writes it as "yǎng" (痒).

*Xiāngkuài* (相揩): *Kuài* is pronounced *kè* (反) according to the *Guǎngyǎ*, which states that it means "to rub. The *Shuōwén* indicates it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) with the phonetic element *jiē*.

*Gǔkuāng* (𣞙乘): *Chéng* is pronounced *lǎng* (朗). The *Kǎoshēng* states it refers to the frame of a drum. Lexicons identify it as the wood used for drums. The *Shuōwén* indicates it is composed of the radical "drum" (*zhù*, sound *hú*) with the phonetic element *sāng*. The sound of *zhù* is *hú*.

Regarding *bǔ* (枹): Wang Yúwáng states that it is the mallet for a drum; the *Shuowén* says it is the handle for striking a drum, composed of the radical 木 (*muò*) with the phonetic component 包 (*bāo*). In the scriptures, it is written as 桴 using the character 孚 (*fú*), which has the same pronunciation *fú*. The *Lúnyǔ* states: "The large ones are called *fá*, the small ones are called *fú*. This is not the meaning intended in the scriptures. Below, *gū* (孤) is pronounced with the fifth tone (*wǔ fǎn*). Regarding *gǔ* (鼓), the correct orthography is 鼓; the *Shuowén* explains it as composed of 豈 (*qǐ*) and 攵 (*pǔ*) [a variant of 支], representing the hand of a banner-bearer striking it. In the scriptures, it is written as 皷 using the character 皮 (*pí*); this is a vulgar form and incorrect. *Qǐ* (豈) is pronounced *zhū lǚ fǎn*; *pǔ* (攵) is pronounced *pǔ bǔ*.
The previous discussion on the *Paramārtha-dharmavijaya-sūtra* regarding the frailty and perils of old age has already been explained.

Regarding the *Buddhabhāṣita-vṛddhamātṛ-sūtra*, Huilin’s *Yinxiang*: "Drill" (zuàn) is pronounced with the initial *zǔ* and the final *luán*. Gu Yewang states that "drill" refers to carving or engraving. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it is the means for boring through, composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic "zan" (*zàn*).
*Chuí* (捶): Pronounced *guǐ* (隹, with the *fǎn* [classifier] reversed). The *Shuowen* states: "To strike with a staff. It is composed of the radical *shǒu* (hand) and the phonetic *chuí*.

*Qín* (禽): Pronounced *jīn* (今, with the *fǎn* reversed). The *Baitong* says: "Qín is the general term for birds and beasts. The *Erya* says: "Those with two feet and strong claws are called qín. The *Shuowen* states: "The head is depicted in its original form; it is composed of the radical *nóu* (禸) and the phonetic *jīn* (今). The heads of birds (*qín*) and leopards (*lí*) resemble each other. The script in the current sutra text uses *mǎo* (𤢌), which is incorrect. *Nóu* is pronounced *róu zhǒu* (柔帚, with the *fǎn* reversed).

The Buddha Spoke the Sūtra of the Old Woman and Her Six Daughters. (The Pronunciation of "Hui-lin" [Hé-lín]: *qióng*, with the rhyme of *kuí* and *yíng*). Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states that *qióng* means solitary; it refers to one who has no brothers as being *qióng*. To have no son is called "solitary. The dictionary *Zìshū* says: "*Qióngqióng* means having nothing to rely upon. This is correct. Some write it with the radical for "ear" (*ér*) as *quán*; the *Wénzìdiǎn* explains that the character *qióng* is written with the radicals for "mouth" (*kě*) and "child" (*zǐ*), and that writing it with the radical for "ear" is an error.

Regarding the character *suì* (燧): Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "a *suì* is that by which fire is taken. Xu Shuzhong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states: "A *suì* is the refined essence of five-stone copper; it is circular and faces upward, and when aligned with the sun, one obtains fire. The *Kaosheng* says: "A *suì* is what we call the fire-mirror today; it is circular with a diameter of about two inches, and all have a patterned surface that is concave. When reflecting the sun and placing tinder beneath it, one immediately obtains fire. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* states that [the radical] is *huǒ* (fire) and the phonetic is *suì*. The *Shuowen* sometimes writes it as *fēng* (鐆), where the phonetic is *kǎo*; or as *yù* (䡵), where the phonetic is also *kǎo*. The character *wā* (窊) is pronounced *ūguā* (烏蝸反).

Regarding the character *zhua* (槌): the *Shenglèi* states that it means "to strike"; the *Kǎoshēng* says it means "to beat. The *Wenzìdiǎnshuō* explains it as being composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "guò" (*guò*). The *Shuowén* writes it as *chui* (𥬸), composed of the radical "bamboo" (*zhú*) and the phonetic "guò."

*The Sūtra of the Elder Guṇaprabha*, Volume One. *Xuanying’s Pronunciations*, Volume One. "Lòu" (leakage) is pronounced with the *si* rhyme (思列反). According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to overflow. "Xiè" (to leak) is also "lòu" (to leak); it is also "to emit."
2. Lower Fascicle, Part Two. *Kǔn* (also written as *kùn*, same pronunciation as in *kǔběn*) refers to the threshold of a door; according to the *Sāncāng*, it is the door-sill.

*Wǔ* (corridor) is written in the *Zhuowén* as *mèi* (same pronunciation as in *wǎngyǔ*). According to the *Shuōwén*, it is the covered walkway surrounding a hall; *láng* (corridor) is also a type of building.
*Hita* (the "hi" is pronounced with a retroflex *ṛ*, and the "da" with a labio-velar *v*) and *Vijiti* (the "zhi" is pronounced with a retroflex *ṣṭ*) are both names of deities.
*Cīna* is the name of the country of Tang; it is sometimes called *Zhendan* or *Zhendān*, which is the general name for the continent of *Śīna*.

In the *Candraprabha-kumāra-sūtra*, regarding the phonetics of "Suo" (索) as given by Xuanying: it is pronounced with the initial *s* and the final *ge* (反). According to the *Cangjie Jiegu*, "Suo" means "to exhaust"; it also means "to seek."
*Yì* (pronounced *yú jì fǎn*): According to the *Guǎng yǎ*, *yì* means "to conceal. According to the *Fān yǔ*, *yì* also means "to conceal.

*Tāo tiān* (pronounced *tǎo gāo fǎn*): The *Shàngshū* says, "Vast and surging, it floods to heaven. Kong’s commentary states that *tāo* means "overflowing," meaning the water is so great it seems to reach the heavens.

"Ji" (鷙) means a fierce bird; according to the *Guǎngyá*, "ji" means to seize, referring to the ability to capture and subdue various birds. Among birds, those that are courageous and sharp are called "ji," such as hawks and falcons. In the scriptural text, it is written with the character "zhí" (蟄)—pronounced "chú lì"—which refers to insects and beasts hibernating; this character is not used here [in the sense of a bird].
*Jié* (慴) [ancient pronunciation *gujié*; in the *Erlǚ* it means "to fear"]. Guo’s commentary states that this is synonymous with "to be terrified.
*Dùn* (遁) or *zàng* (藏) [also written as *dùn* (遯) or *suì* (遂); same pronunciation *túdùn*] means "to flee" according to the *Guǎngyá*. It means to avoid or to hide.

*Mie* (蠛): pronounced *jié* (結) with a reversed tone; according to the *Erya*, it refers to the *mèng* (蠛蠓). Guo’s commentary states: "A small insect resembling a gadfly that appears during wind and spring rain. *Bīní* (俾倪): sometimes written as *pí'ér* (䫌兒);

these two characters are also written as *yì* (㪏) and *nì* (堄), both forms being identical in the *Zilin*. Pronounced *pǔmǐ* (普米) for the first character and *wǔlǐ* (五禮) for the second. *Bīní* means leaning or tilting, not being upright.

"Po" (叵) is pronounced as "pu" (普) with a reversed tone; it means to shake or move restlessly. The scriptural text uses the character 𧿽 (from the foot radical) or 𨁟, or sometimes 𡶅 (from the mountain radical), but these are not correct.
"Xiang" (相) and "da" (𢾛)—the ancient forms being 󲍅, 𢾊, and 楟—now appear as 打; they share the same pronunciation, "zhai heng" (宅衡反), meaning to strike or touch.
*Ti-màn*: According to the *Shuowen*, this refers to a silk cloth of reddish-yellow color; "red *ti*" is the color *quan*. *Chì-dǔ*: now written as *zhui* (same pronunciation as *zui-sui*).
According to the *Guangya*, *dǔ* means "mouth"; according to the *Zishu*, it is the "beak of a bird," or alternatively written as *zuǐ*; in ancient forms, it was written as *zǒu*.
"Huò" (pronounced with the *guǒ* rhyme) means sudden; it describes a state of urgency or rapidity. The text reads "gù," which is an error.
"Tàn" (pronounced with the *tán* rhyme) means to take hold of; according to the *Erya*, it means to seize, and the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that taking from afar is called "tàn."

*Shenrijiejing* (The Scripture of Shenri). Shenri is here called Shují Xuányìng. Yīn means "boundless"; it is also written as *yín*, with the same pronunciation as *wǔjīn*. *Yín* means "limit" (*è*); according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to the edge or bank of the earth.
*Kukī* (拘耆) is sometimes called *kucīra* (居枳羅), which in this context means "bird with a fine voice"; the text’s transcription as *jǐ* (󲦭) is an error.
*Hèyā* (鶡鴨)—the first character is pronounced *hú gé* (胡葛)—is also written as *fū* (鵪), both being pronounced *zhú jiǎ* (竹甲). The *hè* (鶡) resembles a pheasant but is larger and blue-green in color.
"Hóng" (洪) borrows its pronunciation to supplement "zhèng" (贍); the correct character is written as "yàn" (焰), and it is also written as "yànguān" (焰光), meaning flame.
"Guònrán" (亘然): "gē" (鄧) is the phonetic inversion; "guòn" (亘) is equivalent to "héng" (恒, constant) and "guòn" (亘) also means "tōng" (通, pervasive).

The Scripture on the Elder’s Son Zhi, Spoken by the Buddha. One fascicle. Regarding the phonetic transcription of "Huilin" (慧琳): for the character *gài* (匃) in the word *gàishí* (匃食), it is pronounced as *gé* (葛) and *ài* (艾). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *gài* means "to beg. When a person loses their wealth and property, they beg; the character is composed of "person" (人) and "loss" (亡). The scripture uses the character *gài* (丐), which is a vulgar form.

"High and dry" (gāozào): the second character is pronounced as *sāo* (with the final radical reversed). The *Zhouyi* says, "Water flows to the damp; fire goes to the dry. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "dry" (*zào*) means parched; it is composed of the radical "fire" and the phonetic "sāo," where "sāo" is pronounced as *sāodào* (with the final radical reversed).
"Ráo" (嬈)—in the *Shuowen*, it means "to disturb or toy with," written with the radical for "woman" (女) and the phonetic "yáo" (堯).

"Ruǎn" (蝡)—the upper character is pronounced "rùn yǐn" (閏尹); according to the *Kaosheng*, that which has no feet is called "ruǎn," while that which has feet is called "chóng" (蟲). The *Huainanzi* states, "Insects and ruǎn-moving creatures," which refers to this. The *Shuowen* also defines "ruǎn" as "movement," written with the radical for "insect" (虫) and the phonetic "ruǎn" (耎), where "ruǎn" is pronounced "ér yuǎn" (而兖). The reading "ruǎn" (蝡) in the current text is incorrect."

*Kè-lòu* (carving and engraving): the first character is pronounced *kěn-lè* (with the initial *lè* reversed) and the second is *lóu-dòu* (with the final *dòu* reversed). The *Erya* states: "That which is done to metal is called *lòu*; that which is done to wood is called *kè*. Guo Pu’s commentary notes: "Both refer to the names for working raw materials (*pǔ*). Examining their sounds, *lòu* means *cuò* (to rub/polish); it refers to the processing of gold and silver. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan* states: "*Kè* is also *lòu*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "Hard iron can be used for carving and engraving. *Kè* is composed of the radical *dāo* (knife) with *hài* as its phonetic; *lòu* is composed of the radical *jīn* (metal) with *lóu* as its phonetic. The form appearing in the scripture is *lòu*, which is a vulgar character.

The *Buddhabhāṣita-bodhisattva-cyuti-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Passing of the Bodhisattva Spoken by the Buddha), one fascicle. Regarding the phonetics of "yáo" in "Huilin yáo": In the passage concerning the elder’s son Zhi at the beginning of the sūtra, the term "yuánfēi" (蜎蜚) has already been explained.

In the *Mao Shī*, it says: "Yuányuán refers to the *shǔ* (caterpillar). The commentary states: "The *shǔ* is a red insect. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "insect" (虫) with the phonetic "yuan" (肙). In the *Zuozhuan*, Du Yu’s commentary identifies it as the "fěifēng" (fly). Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "Fěi is the same as fùpán, the stinking insect. In the *Shuowen*, both characters are examples of phono-semantic compounds.

*The Scripture on the Departure of the Youth (Śiṣya-kumāra-sūtra)*, spoken by the Buddha; one fascicle. Regarding the phonetics of "pèi" (袈裟): Huìlín states the initial sound is *pī*. Gu Yěwáng says that "pèi" refers to what is draped over the back. Wáng’s commentary on the *Chuci* states: "That which is on the back is called pèi. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as being composed of the radical "cloth" (*巾*) with the phonetic component "leather" (*皮*). In this scripture, it is written as "bèi" (被) using the "clothing" radical (*衣*), which is also a permissible phonetic loan.

The Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-bodhicitta-sūtra (The Sūtra of Mañjuśrī’s Inquiry into Bodhicitta), one fascicle. Regarding the phonetics of Huìlín: "zhòngdàn" (重擔)—the first character is pronounced with the initial *chù* (隳, reversed from 隴) and the final *dān* (躓, reversed from 耽濫). This concludes the explanation of the preceding *Paramārtha-dharmavijaya-sūtra*.
The section on "Sharp and Dull" (利鈍)—pronounced *tūn* and *kùn*—reversing the previous [entry]—has already been explained in the *Mahāyāna-sūtra on the Merit of Image-Making*.

Regarding the *Mahāyāna-gayāśīrṣa-sūtra*: the *Mahāyāna-gayāśīrṣa-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by Bodhiruci. Regarding the character 牆 (*qiáng*): In the *Yuelin yinyi* (慧琳音義), it is noted that the *Lunyu* states, "The wall of the Master was several *ren* high. Kong Qiu’s commentary states that seven feet is called a *ren*. The *Gonggong ji* states that a wall is three feet thick. The *Shangshu* states, "None dare to overstep the enclosure walls. Gu Yewang states that "wall" (*qiáng*) is also "enclosure" (*huán*). The *Shuowen jiezi* defines it as being composed of the radical 嗇 (*sè*) and the phonetic 爿 (*jiàng*), where *jiàng* is pronounced like *chuáng*. *Sè* is pronounced like *sè*. It is sometimes written as 墻, 廧, or 牆; although these are used interchangeably, none are accepted here.

At that time, the sound of the gradual reversal of the flames was like the subtle movement of fire. Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states: "It is like fire burning; though the flames are still faint, what they reach is vividly distinct and orderly, such that it cannot be severed. The *Shuowen Jiezi* also defines it as "the subtle flickering of fire," taking *yan* (炎) as the radical and *xian* (臽) as the phonetic component; *xian* is pronounced *xiàn*, and *chuō* (焯) is pronounced *zhāorùo*.

The character for "analyzing" (xī) is also written as "fān. Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shūjìng* states it means "to analyze. The *Shēnglèi* says it means "to split. The *Shuowén* defines it as "breaking wood," composed of the radical "wood" (木) and the phonetic "qīn" (斤). The form used in the scripture, with the "hand" (手) radical and the "tablet" (片) radical, is a vulgar variant.

"Looking back" (顧, *gù*): Zheng’s commentary on the Mao version of the *Shijing* states that "to look back" means to turn one's head; it further explains that "looking back" is synonymous with "beholding. The *Guangya* defines it as "longing regard. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical 頁 (*xié*, pronounced *xiánjié*) and the phonetic component 雇 (*gù*, pronounced as above). The form used in the scripture is the colloquial variant.

*The Sūtra on the Elephant Head Monastery Spoken by the Buddha*, one fascicle. Translated by [Bodhiruci] during the Later Wei dynasty. Regarding the phonetic gloss for "sā" (sand/gravel) provided by Huilin: it is pronounced like *ling* (the reverse of *ling*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "sā" (sā-lì) refers to small stones, written with the radical "stone" and the phonetic "lè. In this sūtra, it is also written as "shā" (sand), which is likewise acceptable.

"Xiè" (係) is pronounced as "xì" (奚詣反). "Kǎo" (考) is pronounced as "kǎo" (考聲). "Xiè" (係) means that thought resides in the heart without being scattered. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "person" (人) and the phonetic "xiè" (系); "xiè" is pronounced as "xì" (奚計反). "Jīng" (莖) is pronounced as "gān" (稈上幸耕反). The *Cangjie pian* states: "The stalks of grass are called 'jīng'.

According to the *Shuowen*, "kǎo" (考) refers to bamboo [stalks] called "gè" (箇) and wood [stems] called "méi" (枚); it is composed of the radical "grass" (草) and the phonetic "jīng" (巠); "jīng" is pronounced as "gōnglěng" (工冷反). The character below is pronounced as "qián" (乾󱁅反). Du’s commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan* states: "Gǎn" (稈) and "gǎo" (槀) are synonymous. According to the *Shuowen*, "gǎn" (稈) is the stalk of grain; it is composed of the radical "grain" (禾) and the phonetic "hàn" (旱). It is sometimes written as "hú" (䄨), but this is not accepted here. The scriptural text uses "cǎo" (草) to form "jiān" (𦼮); according to the *Shuowen*, "jiān" (𦼮) is the name of a plant, *Gynandropsis gynandra*. This contradicts the meaning of the scripture and is incorrect.

The Mahāyāna Gayāśīrṣa Sūtra, one fascicle. Translated by Dharmaruci of the Northern Wei dynasty. Regarding the phonetic glosses by Huilin: "Biàn fà" (braided hair). "Biàn" is defined in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as "to interweave," composed of the radical "silk" (糸) and the phonetic "piàn" (辡), with the pronunciation of "piàn" being *bié miǎn*. The character for "sūtra" (經) is sometimes erroneously written as "biān" (扁); the correct pronunciation of "biān" is *pú mián*, and that of "piàn" (in the context of the gloss) is *mián diǎn*.

Regarding "懈" (xiè): the first character is pronounced *jiā* with the *mài* rhyme, and the second is *tái* with the *nǎi* rhyme. This concludes the explanation of the first fascicle of the *Shùnquánfāngbiàn jīng* (Sūtra on Following Expedient Means).

Regarding "疲" (pí): the first character is pronounced *bèi* with the *bēi* rhyme. The commentary by Jia [Yuan] to the *Guoyu* states it means "exhaustion. The *Guǎngyá* states that "pí" is synonymous with "juàn" (weariness). According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical *nà* (sickness) and the phonetic *pí*; the sound of *nà* is *nǚ è*. "Juàn" may also be written with the radical *rén* (person).

Regarding "fèn xùn" (奮迅): the *Guǎyá* states that it means to shake (*zhèn*) or to unfold (*shū*). Zheng’s commentary on the *Lìjì* says it means to move vigorously (*fèndòng*). The *Shuōwén* explains that "fèn" (*huī*) is like flying; it is composed of "xuīn" (奞) above "tián" (田). The pronunciation of "xuīn" is suī.

The Buddha Spoke the *Vatsa Sūtra*. Regarding the phonetic gloss for "犢" (*dú*) by Huìlín: it is pronounced with the upper radical *鈎* (gōu) and the phonetic *候* (hòu). As for the sound of "考" (*kǎo*), it refers to milking the milk of oxen and sheep. Its correct form is "犇" (*bēn*). According to the *Shuowen*, it may also be written as "犗" (*jiè*) with the radical "子" (*zǐ*). In this sūtra, it is written with the radical "手" (*shǒu*) as "搆" (*gòu*). This "搆" refers to the act of milking; [to use it here] indicates a failure to clarify the principle of consciousness, which deviates from the meaning of the sūtra. The pronunciation of "擩" (*ruí*) is *núguān*.

*Pie* (pronounced with the *kao* rhyme) means *piēfú* (pronounced *piēchōu*), which refers to being prone to anger. According to the *Fāngyán* (Dialects), *pie* also means "vile. Guo's commentary states that *piefú* refers to those who are quick-tempered. Regarding the standard characters of past and present: the character is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "biè" (*bì*). The pronunciation of *biè* is *pímèi*, and the pronunciation of *fú* is *fū*.

"Rǔdòng" (乳湩)—the rhyme is *zhǒng* (塚隴反). Guo's commentary on the *Mu Tianzi Zhuan* states: "Dòng means breast milk. Even today in Jiangnan, breast milk is called *dòng*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "breast milk; it takes the radical 'water' and the phonetic 'chóng' (*zhòng*). The pronunciation of *lǒng* (隴) is *lóngyòng* (音龍用反).

In the *Kṣīraprabhāsa-buddha-sūtra*, regarding the characters for "treading" (牴蹋): the upper character 牴 (dǐ) is pronounced with the initial *d-*, the final *-i*, and the departing tone (*rì*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to butt," composed of the radical "ox" (牛) and the phonetic "氐" (dǐ), which also serves as the phonetic. The lower character 蹋 (tà) is pronounced with the initial *t-* and the final *-e* (in the *tán-hé* rhyme). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to tread upon," composed of the radical "foot" (足) and the phonetic "𠬿" (tà), which has the sound of *tà*.

The character *qiàn* (倩) has the phonetic component *qīng* (清) and the radical *xìng* (性) reversed; it means "to borrow" (*qiè*). Guo’s commentary on the *Fāngyán* states that it means "that which may be borrowed. Gu Yewang says that *qiàn* also means "borrowed. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical *rén* (人) and the phonetic *qīng* (青).

The character 謾 (màn) is read as mǎn when used in the sense of "to deceive" or "to cheat. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical 言 (speech) with the phonetic 曼 (màn, pronounced wàn). The character 抵 (dǐ) is read as dī when used in the sense of "to resist," "to ward off," or "to oppose. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical 手 (hand) with the phonetic 氐 (dǐ, which also serves as the phonetic). In the scriptures, it is sometimes written as 牴 (with the radical 牛), but this is an error; 牴 means "to gore. *Note: The original text contains a discussion on the etymologies and variant forms of the characters 謾, 抵, and 牴, clarifying their correct readings and meanings within a Buddhist or classical context.*
The *Pūrva-bodhisattva-cyuti-sūtra* (蜎飛上) has already been explained above. Regarding the *Vimaladatta-bhāryā-sūtra* (無垢賢女經):

according to Xuanying’s phonetics, "Bilou" (椑樓) is pronounced with the second tone for "bi" (臂) and the first tone for "mi" (彌); it is the name of the wife of an elder in the Western Regions. The *Garbha-kośa-sūtra* (胎藏經) writes it as "gan" (桿), which is likely a scribal error.

The Woman in the Womb Listening to the Sutra. Regarding the character "huì" (慧) in "Huìlín" (慧琳): it is pronounced *luǒ* (倮), with the phonetic component *guǒ* (果). Gù Yěwáng states that "luǒ" means to remove clothes and expose the body. The *Shuōwén* says that "luǒ" also means to strip off clothes and expose the body; it is formed from the radical "person" (*rén*) and the phonetic "guǒ. It is also written as "luò" (裸), "nù" (躶), or "luǒ" (臝); these forms are somewhat numerous, but for now we follow the *Shuōwén* and use "luǒ" (倮) with the "person" radical, while the others are not used.

The character for *chī* (鵄) is pronounced *chì* (叱) in the upper radical and *xiū* (休) in the lower. Examining its phonology and the explanations in dictionaries of characters, it is said that the *xiū-chī* (鵂鵄) is a strange bird. Observing this bird, it rests during the day and flies at night. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *xiū* is identical to *chī*; and since *chī* belongs to the category of *yuán* (鳶), both characters from ancient times to the present have the "bird" radical (*niǎo*) on the left and the phonetic element *xiū* (休) on the right. Although some versions write it with the phonetic *dǐ* (氐) as *chī* (䲻), that is not accepted here.

*The Scripture of Unprecedented Events*, spoken by the Buddha, *The Scripture of Unprecedented Events*, one fascicle. [Regarding the phonetics of "Hù" (戶) in "Hùyòu" (戶牖): Huílín’s Pronunciation Guide states it is pronounced as *yóu* (由). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "piercing a wall with wood to form a lattice window. It is composed of the radical "piàn" (片) and the radical "hù" (戶), with "fǔ" (甫) as the phonetic component; it is through this that the sun is seen.

The *Śākyamuni-buddha-avataraṇa-maitreya-bodhisattva-sūtra* (The Sutra on Maitreya’s Descent and Attainment of Buddhahood) has been fully explained above; the second fascicle of the *Xiaosheng zaoxiang gongde jing* (The Sutra on the Merit of Making Images) has also been fully explained below.

Regarding the character for *sàn* (umbrella/parasol): Yě Wáng’s *Guǐyán* states that *sàn* is simply a *gài* (cover). The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* explains it as being composed of the radical *mì* (silk) and the phonetic *sàn*. To claim it is composed of the radical *shǒu* (hand) and the phonetic *bàn* is incorrect; the sound of *mì* is *mò*.

Regarding "kǔ-mài" (穬麥): the upper character is pronounced with the rhyme *guò* and *měng*. The *Zītǒng* states that it is a name for grain; there are one hundred types, all of which ultimately reduce to five categories. Those belonging to the *jì* (millet) family are called "spike-grains" (*suì-gǔ*); those belonging to the beans family are called "pod-grains" (*jiǎo-gǔ*); those belonging to the wheat family are called "awned-grains" (*máng-gǔ*); and those belonging to the hemp family are called "tree-grains" (*shù-gǔ*). Now, "kǔ-mài" is precisely the awned-grain. The *Kǎoshēng* says that "kǔ" refers to grain that has awns. The *Shuowén* explains it as derived from "huó" (禾) and the phonetic "guǎng" (廣), correctly written as "kǔ. The scriptural text uses the character "mài" (麥) to form "dà-mài" (󰎣), which is great-barley. The *Kǎoshēng* also says this is great-barley. None of the various books contain this specific character [for "kǔ"].

Regarding "loulu" (watchtowers and parapets): "shang lou" (leaking from above) refers to the hooks [of the battlements]. The *Erya* states: "That which is narrow and long and curved is called a lou. The *Wenzi jilüe* says: "Lou is a house for defense atop a city wall. In the *Gujin zhengzi*, it is written with the radical "wood" (木) and the phonetic "lou" (婁), with the final rhyme being "lu" (盧) in the "gu" (古) tone. The *Wenzi jilüe* further states: "Lu (parapet) is that which guards the city wall and is exposed without a roof. The *Shuowen jiezi* writes it with the radical "wood" and the phonetic "lu" (魯); the sound of "lou" is the same as that of "shang" (above).

The *Suhṛlekhā-sūtra* (The Very Rare Sutra). "Very rare" (*suhṛd-*) is the title. Regarding "stūpa": the character *sōng* (孫) has the phonetic value *gǔ* (骨) as a reversed reading; it is a transliteration of the Sanskrit word for a reliquary monument (*stūpa*).
Regarding "koṭi" (俱胝): the lower character has the phonetic value *zhī* (知); it is a transliteration of a Sanskrit term.

*Zhong* (殖): pronounced *chéngzhí* (承職反). The commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "to plant" (*zhí*) means "to grow. The *Cangjie pian* states that "planting" (*zhí*) means "breathing" (*xī*). It also means "much" (*duō*). The *Guangya* states it means "to establish" (*lì*) and "to accumulate" (*jī*). The *Shuowen jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical *è* (歺) with the phonetic *zhí* (直); *è* is pronounced *wùgē* (五割反).
The *Sūtra on the Transformation of the Female Body*, also known as the *Sūtra on the Girl in the Womb*. According to Huilin’s phonetics, "Aniruddha" is a Sanskrit term; it is a name for an Arhat.

The character 盲 (máng) [is pronounced with the first tone, *mò* reversed; it was already explained previously in the *Mahāyāna-zào-xiàng-jīng*. The character 冥 (míng) [is pronounced with the fourth tone, *mò* reversed. The *Kǎo-shēng* states that it means "darkness. The *Shuōwén* says: "Míng means 'obscure. It is composed of 日 (sun) and 十 (ten), and below 六 (six). On the sixteenth day of the month, the moon begins to wane and gradually becomes dark. It is a compound character formed from 冖 (mìng, pronounced *mì*). The text of the sūtra uses 宀 (mián) and 具 (jù) to form 𡨋, which is incorrect."

"Right side" (yòu xiè): "xiè" is pronounced qiè (in the sense of a dangerous calamity). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "xiè" refers to both sides of the abdomen, composed of the radical "flesh" (肉) with the phonetic "hé" (劦), where "hé" is pronounced yè (from three "force" [力]). It is incorrect to write it as "xiè" using three "swords" (刀).

Regarding "xu" (pronounced with the *yù* rhyme): it refers to the stamens and buds on the four sides of the lotus pedestal within a lotus flower. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the character is composed of "xié" (pronounced *xián jié*) and "shān" (pronounced *shān*). The text of the sutra uses "biāo" (pronounced *pǔ diāo*), which is incorrect. Regarding "àn": it means to examine or investigate. It is composed of "xié" (pronounced *xián jié*) and "shān" (pronounced *shān*). The text of the sutra uses "biāo" (pronounced *pǔ diāo*), which is incorrect. "Biāo" is pronounced *pǔ diāo*.

"Bù wàng" (不望). "Gāng" (冈) is pronounced as "fǎn" (反). The *Zuǒzhuan* states: "It is not that which I dare to hope for. Gu Yewáng says: "Wàng" (望) is synonymous with "jì" (覬, meaning to aspire to). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of "wáng" (亾), "xī" (夕), and "wáng" (王). As for "wàng," it refers to what the mind hopes for. "Jì" (覬) is pronounced "jì" (记).

The *Jianguo kai* (Opening of the Firm Armor) [in two fascicles], previously explained in the first volume of the *Shunquan fangbian jing* (Sutra on Following Skillful Means), has already been fully expounded. Regarding *qièruò* (timid and weak): - The *Kaosheng* (Investigation of Sounds) states that it means "timid and cowardly" (*jièqiènuǎn*).

- Gu Yewang says it means "timid, fearful, and inferior. - In the standard characters of past and present, *qiè* (timid) often implies fear; it is composed of the "heart" radical with the phonetic *qù* (fourth tone). - *Nuǎn* (cowardly) is pronounced *nuǎn* (first tone) and *luàn* (fourth tone); the lower part is *rǎng* (second tone) and *zhuó* (second tone). - Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* says it means "weak, frail, and inferior. - The *Kaosheng* says "weakness implies a lack of strength. - The *Shuowen* defines it as "to bend" (*náo*). - The upper part resembles the bending of a curve, while the three strokes (*sān*) represent the fine hairs of a weak or bent object; because they are both weak and bent, they are each doubled. - *Náo* is pronounced *nú* (second tone) and *guì* (fourth tone); *guì* is pronounced *cháo* (second tone) and *zhào* (fourth tone).

"Yan-hui" (厭悔) is the opposite of "yan" (艷); it means weariness and suffering. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "shan" (厂, pronounced *han*) and the phonetic "yan" (猒). "Wu-yan" (無厭) is pronounced *yi-yán*.

The *Shuowen* states that because a dog never tires of meat, it is composed of the radicals for "meat" (肉), "sweetness/delight" (甘), and "dog" (犬). The versions of the sutras that write it with the radicals for "eye" (目) and "moon" (月) as "yan" (厭), or with the radical "shan" (厂) as "yan" (厭), are all errors.

Regarding "xiá-liè" (陿劣): "Xiá" is pronounced with the first tone as *xián* (咸甲反). Gu Yewang states that it means "narrow and constricted, not vast. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains that "ài" (隘) is composed of "guǒ" (𨸏) and "jiā" (夾); although "xiǎn" (陜) is the correct orthography, it is not adopted here because it would be confused with the character for Xianzhou (陜州). Furthermore, following the scriptural text, it is written with "qiè" (匧), which is pronounced *qián xié* (謙叶反). As for the scriptural text using "xiá" (狹) with "quǎn" (犬), this refers to "training dogs and horses" and is not used in this context. The pronunciation of "qiè" (匧) is *qián xié* (謙叶反).

"Kān (慳)"—the "xi" (閑) in "kū-xi" is a reversed reading. The *Guǎngpǐ* states that "qín" (𩋆) means "firm"; the *Běicāng* states that "qín" (𩋆) means "cautious. "Qín" (𩋆) is the correct orthographic form. In the standard characters of antiquity and today, it is composed of the radical "metal" (革) and the phonetic "jiān" (臤), with "jiān" pronounced as "jiān" (堅). In the scriptures, it is written with the "mind" radical (心) as "kān" (慳); this is a vulgar character.

*Chòu* (臭): Upper radical *chǒu*, reversed *zhòu*. The *Shuowen* says: "A dog is that which follows the scent of a fleeing bird and knows its tracks; it is composed of the radical for 'dog' and the character for 'zi' (自), which is the ancient form of 'bi' (鼻, nose); it is a pictograph. The current vulgar usage of *si* (死) instead [to form] *xiè* (臊) is incorrect. Lower radical *wēi* (威), reversed *wèi* (衛). The *Zishu* says: "Filth means not being clean; it means evil. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical for 'grain' (*huó*) and the phonetic *suì* (歲).

Regarding the character *chú* (除), the *Guǎngyǐ* states that *chú* means "to discard" or "to remove. The *Shuōwén* explains that *qì* (弃) means "to sweep away filth," composed of the radical "earth" (*tǔ*) and the phonetic "pí" (*pí*). In the sutra, it is written as *yì* (異) or *bài* (𡐢), which are vulgar characters and incorrect. The pronunciation of *pí* (𭆚) is *pí biàn fǎn*.

*Ti* (洟): The upper radical is *yi* (逸) with the reversed stroke. The *Zhou Yi* says, "Sighing and weeping, with tears and mucus. The *Shuowen* states: "Mucus (*ti*) is nasal fluid. It is composed of the radical *shui* (water) and the phonetic *yi*. Alternatively, it is pronounced *zan*. The scriptural text uses *ti* (涕), which the *Shuowen* defines as 'weeping' (*qì*). This is not the meaning of mucus. *Tuo* (唾): The lower radical is *tu* (土) with the reversed stroke. The *Zuo Zhuan* says, "Xian Zhin of Jin did not look back and spat. The *Shuowen* states: "Saliva. It is composed of the radical *kou* (mouth) and the phonetic *chui*."

*Juǎn* (as in *juàn yuán*): The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* states that "juǎn" means strength; the *Shuōwén* states that "juǎn" refers to the gathering of momentum and energy, composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "quǎn" (*juàn*).

*Dǎo* (as in *dǎoyào*): The *Guǎngyǐ* states that "dǎo" means to pound; the *Shuōwén* states that "dǎo" means to strike or ram down, composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "shòu. It is also written as *dǎo* or *tù*, which are archaic forms of the character.

*Chōngmǐ* (舂米): *cì zhōng* (朿鍾) in reverse; Yu Wang says that "chōng" means to pound grain to produce rice. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as processing millet (*sù*). It is a compound character (*huìyì zì*) composed of "two hands" (*kǒng*, pronounced *gǒng*) holding a pestle (*chǔ*) positioned above a mortar (*jiù*). The *Shiben* states that Yongfu was the first to use the pestle for pounding. Song Zhong says that Yongfu was a minister of the Yellow Emperor. *Kǒng* is pronounced like *gǒng*.

Regarding the character *ǎo* (鄭注禮記云: "Stewing is also frying"; 方言: "Stewing is drying over fire"), it refers generally to the process of drying grains and the like using fire. From the region east of the mountains, including Qi and Chu, it is called *ǎo*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to dry by frying," composed of the radical for fire (*huǒ*) and the phonetic component *áo*.
"Pulling out the *chui* (pronounced *chui-rui* in fanqie notation) to spin *zhai* [cotton].
*Chui* refers to the fine, downy hair of birds and beasts.
Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "The *chui* are the fine, dense fibers of the fur."
The Commentary on the Book of Documents by Kong [Anguo] states that *ruǎn* refers to fine, soft hair.
The *Shuowen Jiezi* also defines it as the fine hair of a beast.

According to this, those who wear *chui-yi* (hair-cloth garments) collect the fine, soft five-colored hairs of birds and beasts, spinning and weaving them into patterned *ji* (woolen cloth) to serve as their upper garments.
This refers to the garments worn by a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*).
Regarding the character *fǎng* (紡), its pronunciation is *fāng gāng fǎn*.
Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "To spin and weave is to produce *lú* (silk thread)."
In the standard characters of antiquity and today, [the character for] *xié* (㲲) is composed of the radical "silk" (糸) and the phonetic "fang" (方).
The lower part is pronounced *dié*.
As for *xié* (cotton), it is the flower of the cotton plant in Western countries, which resembles willow fluff.
In the customs of that country, they all twist and spin [fibers] to form yarn, which is then woven into cloth called *karpāsa* (㲲;
the character for "twist" is pronounced *nián*, with the second tone). Regarding the word *jī* (機), the *Guìyuàn Zhūcóng* states:

"A *jī* refers to the pivot (*guān*) that controls movement and rotation. Gù Yěwáng says: "A *jī* is an object characterized by its mechanical elegance. According to the *Shuōwén*, that which primarily initiates motion is called a *jī*; this refers to things such as crossbows. It is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic element "ji" (*jī*).

"Jin" (牽) is pronounced as "shang ju yin fan" (上居銀反). In the *Yongwang jing* (勇王經), it has already been explained. Below, it is read as "qian yan fan" (遣研反). The *Guypu* (廣疋) states that it means "to pull" (*qianwan*) and "to connect" (*lianyan*). Gu Yewang says that "qian" also means "to lead" (*yin*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of "niu" (牛, ox) and "mi" (冖, canopy) with "xuan" (玄) as the phonetic; it depicts the pulling of an ox. The character "gui" (癸) is pronounced "guǎn fan" (管反). It is incorrect for the vulgar [script] to use "shou" (手, hand) instead of "mi" (冖) to form "qian" (牽).

"Vū" (虛) [is pronounced with the initial *xǔ* and the final *-yú*]; it means "empty space" (*ākāśa*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "hill" (*qī*) and the phonetic "tiger" (*hū*), where *hū* is pronounced with the initial *hǔ* and the final *-gū*. The second character, "wèi" (偽), is pronounced with the initial *wēi* and the final *-wěi*. The *Guangya* states that "pseudo" (*wèi*) means "deception. Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* says that "pseudo" (*wèi*) means "to feign. The *Shuowen* states that "pseudo" (*wèi*) means "fraud," being composed of the radical "man" (*rén*) and the phonetic "human" (*rén*).

"Bèi" (倍) is pronounced with the initial *p* and final *-ai* (陪妹反). Gu Yewang says that "bèi" means one thing producing two. The *Kǎoshēng* says it means "many" (*duō*) and is equivalent to its radical. The *Shuowén* states it is composed of "person" (*rén*) and the phonetic "pòu" (*pòu*, pronounced *tǔkǒu fǎn*). The lower part is pronounced *fújiù fǎn*. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* says "fù" means "repeated. Gu Yewang says "fù" is synonymous with "again" (*yòu*). He further says "fù" is synonymous with "to repeat" or "to do again. The *Shuowén* states it is composed of "walking" (*chì*, pronounced *chūchǐ fǎn*) and the phonetic "fù" (*fù*, pronounced *fú*). The version in the scripture written with the "water" radical (*cì*) is incorrect.

The character 患 (huàn) is pronounced with the forceful reversal of 力 (lì). The *Zuozhuan* states: "Acting according to the timing [of the moment] so as not to involve others later. Liu Zhao’s commentary on the *Guliangzhuan* says: "‘Involving’ (*léi*) means being implicated or drawn into. In the standard orthography of ancient and modern times, this character is composed of the radical 糸 (mí) and the phonetic component 厽 (lí). The pronunciation of 糸 is mí; the pronunciation of 厽 is the same as shàng (the second tone).

*The Scripture on the Supreme Reliance*, Volume One, Phonetic Glossary by Huìlín. **Volume One: Defilement-Shell (煩惱㲉)** [The character] "kè" (㲉) is pronounced with the initial *kǔ* (苦) and the final *rén* (󲓇). The *Zìshū* (Dictionary of Characters) states that it refers to the shell of a bird's egg. Gù Yěwáng says that the skin of any object is called "shell" (*kè*). The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* (Explanations of the Dictionary of Characters) states that it refers to an egg that has already begun to hatch; it is derived from "egg" and "shell," where "shell" is pronounced *kōngyuè* (空岳). In the scriptural text, the pronunciation of "defilement-shell" (*fánǎo kè*) is used because ignorance (*avidyā*) is able to contain all unwholesome karmas; thus, this name is established.

"Cōngxiá (聰黠): The second character is pronounced with the "xián" rhyme group (eight-fold division). According to the *Fāngyán* (Dialects), in the region east of Guān, specifically between Zhào and Wèi, they call *xiá* "huì" (wisdom). Guō’s commentary states that "huì" means "to understand clearly. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* (Dictionary of Characters and Explanations) states it is composed of the radical "black" (*hēi*) and the phonetic "jí" (*jí*)."

Regarding "máo" (hair), according to the phonetic reading [pǎo fǎn], it accords with the meaning of the scriptures to write it simply as "máo. That the current scripture text uses the character "máo" from the "biāo" radical, which carries the meaning of "a talented youth," deviates from the intent of the scripture and is incorrect.

2. *Xiàjuǎn* (Lower Scroll). Regarding "kēng" (坑): the upper character is pronounced *gēng* (耕) as in "upper guest. According to the *Erya*, "kēng" means "ruins" (*xū*). Guo’s commentary states it refers to moats or ditches (*qian chi*) and ruins. The *Jīngǔ zhèngzì* says "kēng" means "an embankment pit" (*xiàn*). It is written with the radical "earth" and the phonetic "kàng" (亢); the variant form with "shuāo" (𨸏) as "kēng" (阬) is also acceptable. The lower character is pronounced *gǎn* (感). The *Zhouyi* says "kǎn" means "to sink" (*xiàn*). The *Pīcāng* says "kǎn" is also a pit. The *Shuowén* agrees. The *Zhouyi* uses "earth" and the phonetic "qiàn" (欠); the scriptural text uses "táo" (臽) as the phonetic, forming "kàn" (埳). This "kàn" has the meaning of a "pit" (*kē*), which is not the intended meaning of the scripture; it is therefore not accepted here.

*Kù* (轂): Pronounced *gǔ* (上公屋反; shàng gōng wū fǎn). According to the *Shuowen*, it is the point where the spokes converge. It is composed of the radical "chariot" (*chē*) and the phonetic component "shell" (*kè*) abbreviated. The lower character is pronounced *wǎng* (下武昉反; xià wǔ fǎng). The *Gōngjīn zhèngzì* states that *qú* (󲐾𨎶) is pronounced *qú*. It is composed of the radical "chariot" and the phonetic component "peak" (*gāng*).

"Zhōng" (傭) means upright; "shàng" (上) refers to the dragon’s reversed fur. The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* states that "zhōng" means even. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* defines it as equality. The *Shuowén Jiězì* also defines it as even and upright, composed of the radical "person" (人) and the phonetic "yōng" (庸). The character used in the classics with the "moon" (月) radical, written as 𦟛, is a vulgar variant.

*Jùgēn* (足跟): The character *gēn* is pronounced as *ēn* (艮恩反). The *Shìmíng* (釋名) states: "The rear of the foot is called the *gēn*. The *Shuōwén* (說文) says it means "heel" (*zhòng*), composed of the radical "foot" (*zú*) with the phonetic element *gèn*.

*Yīyí* (衣飴): The character *yī* is pronounced as *yǐjī* (倚機反). The *Shìběn* (世本) states that Húcáo (胡曹) invented clothing. Sòngzhōng (宋忠) says he was a minister of the Yellow Emperor. The *Báihūtōng* (白虎通) states: "Clothing (*yī*) means concealment; it conceals the form of the body. The *Shuōwén* says: "Clothing (*yī*) means reliance; what is above is called 'clothing' (*yī*) and what is below is called 'skirt' (*sháng*). It takes the radical 'enter' (*rù*) to represent the shape of two people covering themselves. The character written as *yī* (󰖊) is a corrupted and abbreviated form. *Xīyī* (下以): The character *yǐ* is pronounced as *yī* (以反). The *Máoshī* (毛詩) says: "Jǐn" (堇) has the sound *jǐn*; "chú" (荼) has the sound *tú*, which is like *yí* (飴). The *jiān* (箋) commentary says: "Sweet as *yí*. The *Shuōwén* says: "It is a decoction of rice and malt (*bò*); it takes the radical 'food' (*shí*) with the phonetic element *tái*."

"Ruan" (耎) means "supple and beautiful" (the upper radical is 而, reversed; the lower radical is 兗). The *Kaogong ji* states: "One desires it to be supple and smooth; one tests it by dipping it in fat," which refers to being supple. The *Picao* states that "ruan" means "weak. The *Shuowen jiezi* explains it as derived from the radical 大 with the phonetic 聲; however, the scripture uses the character 濡 (pronounced *ru*), meaning "moist," which does not accord with the meaning of the scripture.

Regarding "yǎn" (eye-lid): the *Jielü* (Collection of Abridged Characters) states that it refers to the outer skin of the eye. Dictionaries explain that it is derived from the character "mù" (eye) with the phonetic element "qiān.

Regarding "wúhài" (chinless): the *Guǎngyá* states that "hài" means "ugly" or "an evil appearance. The *Shuowén* explains it as being derived from "yè" (head) with the phonetic element "hài. The version of the scripture using "yuè" (moon) to form "gǎi" (big toe) is not the intended meaning of the scripture.

*Wei-tuo* (委佗): The second character is read as *hé* (何) in reverse. In the *Mao Shi Zhuan* (毛詩傳), *tuó tuó* (佗佗) is glossed as "easy and level. In the *Han Shi* (韓詩), it is described as the appearance of the excellence of virtue. The *Mao Shi Jian* (毛詩箋) states that it is also the appearance of being relaxed and self-possessed. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "man" (人) with the phonetic "ta" (它); the version in the Classics written as "tuo" (陀) is incorrect.

*Jiéqí* (捷疾): The first character is read as *qiánjié* (潛接) in reverse order. The *Zuǒshìzhuàn* states that it means "swiftness. Wang’s commentary on the *Chuci* defines it as "speed. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) with the phonetic element *zhì* (疌), which is read as *zǐqí* (子󰪑).

Regarding "zhòngdàn" (heavy burden): the character for "dàn" is pronounced with the *dān* and *làn* finals; the *Kǎośēng* says it refers to carrying loads with wood. The "Zhèngzì" of ancient and modern times states that "dàn" means to carry, taking the radical "shǒu" (hand) and the phonetic "zhān. Regarding "juédìng zǒngchí jīng" (Sūtra of the Decisive Dhāraṇī), the Buddha-spoken "Juédìng Zǒngchí Jīng," one fascicle:

In the *Huílín Yīn*, "jiāochí" (flaws/defects): the upper character "jiāo" is pronounced with the *xià* and *jiā* finals. The *Máoshī Zhuàn* says: "Xiá" is equivalent to "guò" (fault). The *Guǎngyǎ* also says "xiá" is "huì" (impurity). The *Shuōwén* takes the radical "yù" (jade) and the phonetic "duàn. The lower character "cī" is pronounced with the *zī* final. Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* says it means "bìng" (sickness/infirmity). Lú Huán reads it with the *jiǎn* final; his commentary on the *Zhōuyī* says it is "jiāochí. The *Shuōwén* also defines it as "bìng"; it takes the radical "nà" (sickness) and the phonetic "nǚ" with the *gé* final.

*Yíng* (螢): Upper radical *huǒ* (火), lower radical *jìng* (坰) with the reversed form; Guō’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "The firefly flies at night, with a light beneath its belly. The *Liji* says: "Decayed grass transforms into fireflies. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *chóng* (虫) and the phonetic element *yíng* (熒) in abbreviated form.

Regarding "virtue-armour" (德鎧): the character *kǎi* (鎧) is pronounced with the lower radical *kāi* (開) and the modified radical *gǎi* (改). The *Wénzì jílüè* (Collection of Simplified Characters) states that what shields the body with metal and leather is called *kǎi*. The *Shuōwén* says: "*Kǎi* (鎧) means armour (*jiǎ*); it is composed of the radical *jīn* (金, metal) and the phonetic *kǎi* (愷) in abbreviated form."

"Qì (棄)" [is pronounced with the upper radical *qīng* and the phonetic *yì*. The Commentary on the Book of Documents by Kǒng [Yǎng] states: "Qì means to abolish. The *Erya* states: "Qì is abandonment (*dùn*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Qì means to abandon; it is composed of the radical *gǒng* (pronounced *gǒng*) and the phonetic *bān* (pronounced *bō*, with the earth radical *tǔ* and *gǔ*). It refers to an unworthy child, hence it is abandoned—a word formed through associative meaning (*huìyì*). [The second character,] *yuè* (悅), [is pronounced *yuān*. The *Zhuangzi* says: "Leaving the state and abandoning worldly customs. The *Chuci* says: "Duan (捐) also means to abandon. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is composed of the hand radical and the phonetic *yuān*; *yuān* is pronounced *huìyuán*. [Note: This passage provides a philological analysis of the characters *qì* (abandon), *duàn* (discard), and *yuè* (joy/pleasure), citing various classical sources to define their meanings, pronunciations, and etymologies.]

The characters *chí* (馳) and *chěng* (騁)—the former pronounced with the initial *zhǐ* (知) and the latter with the final *líng* (頳)—are explained in the *Guǎngyá* as "to gallop" (*chí*) and "to rush" (*bēn*). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states that *chěng* also means "to run. The *Shuowén* defines *chěng* as "a great drive" (*dàqū*) and also as "to gallop straight ahead" (*zhíchí*). Both characters *chí* and *chěng* share the radical of "horse" (*mǎ*). The phonetic component for both is *pīng* (甹), which is pronounced *pǐdīng* (匹丁).

*Qiānxùn* (謙愻): The character *xùn* is pronounced with the second tone and the rhyme *sūn*. Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that *xùn* means "compliance" (*shùn*). He Yan’s collected commentary on the *Lunyu* states that *xùn* means "reverence" (*gōng*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic element "sūn."

The character for *shé* (snake) is pronounced with the initial *chā* and the final *kǎo*; it is said to be a venomous insect. According to the *Shuowen*, "the character for *shé* is also *tā*. *Tā* is pronounced *tā*. Because people of antiquity called a snake *tā*, those who lived in nests out of fear of snakes would ask one another, "Have you had no *tā* [snake] tonight? This refers precisely to the snake, composed of the radical *chóng* (insect) and the phonetic *yá*. The lower part is pronounced *wán*. The *Xuánzhōngjì* states: "The *yuánshé* (viper-snake) is three or four feet long and has four legs; its shape is like that of a *shǒugōng* (gecko). Its tail is coiled and possesses needles as sharp as knives; it is extremely poisonous and evil. If it bites a person, they will die in less than half a day. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *chóng* and the phonetic *yuán*.
*Dúshè* (毒螫): The second character, *shè*, is pronounced with the initial *shū* and the final *yì*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "a venomous insect that spreads its poison.

It is composed of the radical *chóng* (insect) and the phonetic *shè*. *Bàngfójīng* (謗佛經): Regarding the term *cǎi* (綵), Huílín’s phonetics give it as *nǎi* (猜) and *zǎi* (宰). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Kaogongji* states that in the art of painting and embroidery, the full range of five colors is called *cǎi*. The *Gujīn Zhèngzì* (Orthodox Characters of Antiquity and Today) explains that the five colors (*wǔcǎi*) are displayed as the five hues (*wǔsè*), referring to the colors of silk; thus, it takes the radical *mì* (silk thread) and the phonetic *cǎi*. The text here uses the character *nǚ* (woman) to form *cǎi* (婇), which is incorrect.
*Ācāpṭi* is a Sanskrit term; *dǐng* (丁) and *lǐ* (禮) are the reversed sounds.
*Pāramitā* is a Sanskrit term; the lower character is pronounced *jìng* (徑) with the *dìng* (定) rhyme.

In the *Ratnakūṭa-samādhi-sūtra*, the Buddha spoke the *Ratnakūṭa-samādhi-sūtra*. Regarding *pièlì* (薜荔): the upper character is pronounced *bēi* (鼙) and *bì* (閇), and the lower character is pronounced *lí* (𥠖) and *dì* (帝). This is a corruption of a Sanskrit term correctly rendered as *preta*; in the Tang language, it means "hungry ghost" (*gěguǐ*).

The character *bù* (不) means "not. The character *lí* (羸) means "weak" or "inferior"; it is formed from the radical for sheep (*yáng*) with the phonetic *lín* (𣎆), which is pronounced *luó* (騾) with the final *fǎn* (反) of *wò* (臥).

*Héngbiānshā* (恒邊沙) is a transliteration of the Sanskrit term; it is an ancient translation from the Jin dynasty. When the sutras speak of "sand on the banks of the Ganges," this refers to what various scriptures call "Ganges-sand. It is also called *Gengqie* (殑伽), the name of a river in the Western Regions; *gēng* (殑) is pronounced *yì* (嶷) with the final *fǎn* (反) of *jìng* (競).
Guài (upper character pronounced hù wǎ; lower character pronounced wǔ gài).

*Fajie Tixing Jing* (Sutra on Entering the Essence of the Dharma Realm). Compiled and polished by Hui Lin. The character *ying* (縈) is pronounced with the *ding* rhyme. The *Guoyu* states that *ying* means to polish; it refers to rubbing and wiping pearls and jade to cause them to emit radiance. The *Jixun* states that it means to adorn. It is sometimes written as *yìng* (鎣); according to the *Shuowen*, it refers to the color of jade, composed of the radical "jade" (*yù*) and the phonetic element "flame" (*yíng*) abbreviated.

*The Tathāgata-siṃhanāda Sūtra*. Compiled by Huìlín. **Guǎng (廣):** The ancient pronunciation is *huǎng* (上, 古晃反). Zhèng Xù’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states: "Guǎng means 'broad' (*hóng*). Kǒng Anghuǐ’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* states: "Vast and great. [The character] follows the radical *guǎng* (广). **Yán (嚴):** The sound is *jiǎn* (撿) with the phonetic *huáng* (黃). The sub-commentary (*jiàn*) on the *Máoshī* states: "Long and distant. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* states: "It means 'evening' and 'distant. It is composed of 倒 (dào), 亾 (wáng), and 兀 (wù). It refers to the ancient character for 'transformation' (*huà*), meaning to suddenly transform. The text of the sūtra uses the grass radical (*cǎo*) to form *cháng* (萇), which is not the intended meaning of the scripture. *The Tathāgata-siṃhanāda Sūtra* (Tathāgata-siṃhanāda-sūtra). Compiled by Huìlín. The term *guǎng* (廣) is glossed as "broad" (*hóng*) by Zhèng Xù in his *Lǐjì zhù*; Kǒng Anghuǐ in his *Shàngshū zhù* glosses it as "vast and great. The character follows the radical *guǎng* (广). The term *yán* (嚴) has the phonetic *huáng* (黃) with the reading *jiǎn* (撿). The sub-commentary on the *Máoshī* explains it as "long and distant. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* defines it as "evening" and "distant," composed of 倒, 亾, and 兀, referring to the archaic character for "sudden transformation" (*huà*). The version of the sūtra that uses the grass radical to form *cháng* (萇) is incorrect according to the scriptural meaning.

*Zhǐ-ǎn* (指㡿): The *Yìshì Cíhuì* (釋名) states that this refers to what the mind points toward; it also means using one’s fingers to point at things to show them to others. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it means "fingers," composed of the radical "hand" (手) with "zhǐ" (旨) as the phonetic component, read as *chǐ* (齒) with the same final rhyme. Liu Zhao’s commentary on the *Guliang Zhuan* states that "pointing" (*zhǐ*) is also "to reject" (*ǎn*). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* says "ǎn" means "to pursue. The *Hanyu Shūyì* (漢書音義) says "ǎn" means "not to employ. The *Shuowen* further notes that the character is composed of "yán" (广) with the phonetic "yǎn" (儼), and "nì" (屰) has the sound "nì" (逆). The text here uses the character *zhǐ* (㡿), which is a vulgar variant; the correct form is *zhǐ* (㡿) with the pronunciation *hàn* (旱).

*Mahāvaipulya Siṃhanāda Sūtra*. Compiled by Hui-lin. "Diàn-mán" (電鬘): the second character is pronounced *má* (with the tone of *bān*). This refers to flower garlands used in Western countries; in this land [of China], it refers to ornaments for the body such as pearl necklaces. The original pronunciation is *mí* (with the tone of *rán*), but that sound is not adopted here, as it is a borrowed character.

Regarding "yà-mò" (瘂默): the upper character is pronounced with the *wū* and *jiǎ* rhymes. The *Jìxùn* states that "yà" means one who cannot speak. Examining the term, a "yà" has sound but lacks words. In both ancient and modern standard orthography, it is written with the radical *nà* (疒) and the phonetic *yà* (亞). The radical *nà* is pronounced *nǚ è* (女厄).

*Fenpò* (分剖): The second character is pronounced with the *pǔ* rhyme (as in *pǔ*). The *Zuǒzhuan* states, "I shall divide and share it with you. The *Cāngjiépiān* defines it as "analysis" (*pōxī*). The *Shuowén* defines it as "to judge by dividing," composed of the radical *dāo* (knife) and the phonetic component *pù*, which is pronounced with the *tǔkǒu* rhyme. *Pù*.

Regarding the *Mahāvaipulya-sūtra-rāja*, the *Parivarta-sūtra*, and the *Mahāyāna-śatapuṇya-lakṣaṇa-sūtra*: these scriptures contain no phonetic transcriptions for their characters. Regarding the *Mahāyāna-śatapuṇya-lakṣaṇa-sūtra* compiled by Huilin: the term *kṛkara* is a Sanskrit sound; it refers to the name of a green bird of the West, a bird that does not exist in this land.

Regarding the character for *máo* (spear): the upper part is read as *mò* (莫侯反) and the lower part is pronounced *qiú* (酋就荖). It is a type of spear or halberd. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that the *máo* is twenty *zhàng* long and is depicted in its pictographic form when mounted on a war chariot. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* claims that the term *qiúmáo* (酋矛) appears in the Classics as *róumáo* (柔矛), but this is incorrect; we do not adopt it here. Regarding the character for *shuò* (halberd): the upper part is read as *shuāng* (雙卓反) and the lower part is *zhuó*. The *Guangya* states that a *shuò* is a spear. According to the *Gujin Zhengzi*, a *shuò* is one *zhàng* eight *chi* long; it is formed with the radical for *máo* and the phonetic *xiào* (肖).

The character for *pāśa* (羂索) is pronounced with the upper radical *jiǎn* (涓, 兗) and the phonetic *yǎn* (𠚫). Regarding its meaning, the *Shēnglèi* (聲類) states it means "to capture. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) says: "To capture with a rope. It is also written as *juàn* (絹). Dictionaries also record this form. The correct ancient and modern character is formed from the radical *wǎng* (网) and the phonetic *yuān* (肙); the pronunciation of *yuān* is *niǎoxuán* (鳥玄反), and that of the lower part is *shèngluò* (乘洛反).

*Xián* (眼𥈤): The character below "eye" is pronounced with the *jiá* and *yè* finals. According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to the eyelashes; it is composed of the radical "eye" (*mù*) and the phonetic element *zhì*. It is also written as *yǎo* (䀹). *Hǎi* (稀穊):

In the *Mahāyāna-bai-fú-zhuāng-yán-xiāng-jīng* (Sūtra on the Marks Adorned by a Hundred Blessings), compiled by Huìlín, the upper character is pronounced with the *xǐ* and *yī* finals. In the commentary on the *Lunyu* by Kong [Qiu], it means "sparse. In the *Erya*, it means "rare. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "loose"; it is composed of the radical "grain" (*huò*) and the phonetic element *xī*. The lower character is pronounced with the *jī* and *qì* finals. The *Hanshu* states: "Deep plowing and dense sowing. According to the *Shuowen*, *hài* (穊) means "dense"; it is composed of the radical "grain" (*huò*) and the phonetic element *jì*.

*Chīhuì* (疵穢): The upper character is pronounced *cí*; the lower is pronounced with the initial *wēi* and final *wèi*. Dictionaries of characters and words state that both mean "evil. In the standard orthography of ancient and modern times, it is composed of the radical *huó* (grain) and the phonetic *suì*.

*Xiānruì* (纖銳): The upper character is pronounced with the initial *qī* and final *yán*. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* states that it means "fine" or "minute," and also "small. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical *mì* (silk) and the phonetic *xiàn*. The lower character is pronounced with the initial *yuè* and final *huì*. According to the *Bóyá*, it means "sharp"; according to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical *jīn* (metal) and the phonetic *duì*.

*Mìzhì* (密緻): The second character is pronounced *zhí* with the *lì* rhyme. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states that "zhì" means "dense. The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radical *mì* (silk thread) and the phonetic *zhì*.
*Báihuì* (白𢂀): Pronounced *fēn* with the *wù* rhyme. The *Pīcāng* states it refers to hair bound up. In the *Gōngjīn zhèngzì*, it is composed of the radical *jīn* (cloth) and the phonetic *fú*.
"Gonghu" (弓弧) is the name of a type of image; "hu" (弧) is pronounced with the initial *gu* reversed [as *hu*].

"Shu" (䡴) refers to the blade on top; "zhuo" (濯) is pronounced with the initial *jiang* reversed [as *zhuo*]. Du’s commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan* identifies it as a war chariot, while the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as a chariot for penetrating enemy ranks, formed from the radical "chariot" (*che*) with the phonetic component "tong" (*tong*).

*Jīn-jù* (金鉅): *qǔ* (渠) is pronounced with the *fǎn* (反) of *jǔ* (舉). Xú Guǎng’s commentary on the *Shìjì* states: "Dàjiān" (大堅) refers to *tiějù* (鐵鉅). The *Shuōwén* says: "It means large steel; it is composed of the radical 'metal' (*jīn*) and the phonetic 'qū' (*jù*). *Mó-mài* (麰麥): The upper character *mó* (麰) is pronounced with the *fǎn* of *mò-hòu* (莫候).

Lǚ Xī’s commentary on the *Mèngzǐ* says: "The *mò-mài* (󲯫麥) has two points. Guō’s commentary on the *Fāngyán* says: "It is the large wheat (*dàmài*). Furthermore, Wáng Xiāo says: "In present-day Héběi, there is a variety sown in spring and ripening in summer. The *Shuōwén* says: "*Lái-mài* (來麥) is the *mò-mài* (󲯫麥); it is also the auspicious wheat (*ruìmài*). It is composed of the radical 'grain' (*mài*) and the phonetic 'móu'."

The "Great Āo" (大鼇)—the character for "āo" being pronounced as *gāo* with a fifth-tone shift—is described in the *Shenxian zhuan* (Biographies of Divine Transcendents) as a "Turtle of Arrayed Spirits" (*lie-líng zhī guī*) that carries Mount Penglai upon its back while sporting in the midst of the vast blue sea. Wang’s commentary on the *Chuci* states: "Āo refers to the Great Āo. In the 'Correct Characters' (*Zhengzi*) of antiquity and today, it is written with the radical 'mǐng' (黾) and the phonetic 'áo' (敖). The pronunciation of 'mǐng' is *měng*."

*Bi* (in *liǎng bì*, "two thighs"): pronounced *pí* (with the *mǐ* rhyme). The *Shuowen* states: "The outer part of the thigh; it is formed from the radical *gǔ* (bone) with *bēi* as the phonetic. It is also written as *yǒu*.

In the *Mahāyāna-caturdharma-sūtra*, according to Huilin’s phonetics, *yì* (in *suǒ yì*, "that which obscures") is pronounced *yān jì*. The *Fangyan* states: "Yì means *ài* (to obscure). *Ài* also means "to screen. The *Jixun* states: "It is a dark obscuration. The *Wenzidian* states: "Yì means 'hidden' (*yǐn*). *Ài* is pronounced *āi gǎi*. It is formed from the radical *yǔ* (feather) with *èi* (same pronunciation as above) as the phonetic.

"Coiled and winding" (pánquǎ): according to Yuè Yěwáng, it means "meandering and turning. The *Guǎngyá* says it means "coiling" (pán). In his commentary on the *Lǐjì*, Zhèng [Xuàn] explains it as "coiled and winding. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "insect" (虫) and the phonetic "fān" (番). "Pán" (蟠) also means "curved" (qū). The pronunciation of "fān" (番) is pān. The correct form is this "pán" (蟠); when the scripture uses "pán" (磐), it does not carry this meaning.

*Chóulín* (稠林): "Chóu" (稠) is pronounced *zhí liú fǎn*. The *Bóyǎ* states it means "dense and thick"; the *Máoshī Zhuàn* states it means "dense and compact"; the *Shuōwén* states it means "many," composed of the radical "grain" (*huò*) with the phonetic "zhōu.

*Mòguàn* (䋄鞔): "Mò" (莫) is pronounced *mò ān fǎn*. The *Chūnqiū* states it means "to patch"; the *Kǎoshēng* states it means "a cover. The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radical "metal" (*jié*) with the phonetic "miǎn."

*The Scripture on the Bodhisattva’s Cultivation of the Four Dharmas*, one fascicle. Compiled by Huilin. Regarding the character 憒 (guì): the radical below is 尢 (you) with the phonetic 奴 (nú) and 草 (cǎo). The *Zishu* states that it refers to the clamor and confusion of the marketplace; the *Kaosheng* states it means the noise and bustle of many people. The vulgar form is written as 鬧 (nào). In the correct orthography of past and present, it follows the radical for "market" (市) and uses "not quiet" (不靜) as the phonetic component.

How rare, how rare is this *Sūtra on the Comparative Measurement of Merit*! How rare, how rare is this *Sūtra on the Comparative Measurement of Merit*! Regarding the character "xiāng" (箱) [in the title]: - In the *Mao Shī Zhuan* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry), it says: "Xiāng refers to the carriage-box; it is the box for the carriage's load. - In the *Cāngjié Piān* (Cangjie’s Lexicon), it says: "It is the side-fender of a carriage. - In the *Shuōwén Jiězì* (Explaining Graphs and Analyzing Characters), it says: "A large carriage with a strong load; it is composed of the radical 'bamboo' (竹) and the phonetic 'xiāng' (相). [The character is pronounced] chē xiāng (車箱); the second character is pronounced xiāo yáng fǎn (削陽反). The *Mao Shī Zhuan* states that "xiāng" refers to the carriage-box, meaning the box used for the carriage's cargo. The *Cāngjié Piān* states it is the "fēn" (藩) of a carriage. The *Shuōwén* states it is the "strong load" of a large carriage, consisting of the "bamboo" radical and the phonetic "xiāng."

"Pure and clear" (*chúnjìng*): the first character, *chún*, is pronounced with the *shuāi* rhyme (lún fǎn). The *Shuowén* states: "It means clarity; it takes the radical water and the phonetic *xiǎng*. "Hundredfold" (*bǎibèi*):

the second character, *bèi*, is pronounced with the *měi* rhyme (pú měi fǎn). Wang Fǔsì’s commentary on the *Zhouyī* states that this refers to "one giving birth to two. The *Shuowén* takes the radical person and the phonetic *pò*; the pronunciation of *pò* is *tǔkǒu fǎn*.

*Jiāoliàng* (校量): "Jiāo" (交) is pronounced with the *qiǎo* (巧) rhyme-group; Jia Dui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states it means "to examine" (*xiàokǎo*). The *Shuowen* says it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "jiāo" (*jiāo shēng*).

*Zuìwúbǐ jīng* (最無比經): compiled by Huìlín. *Yánlì* (嚴麗): "Lì" (麗) is pronounced with the *lángjì* (郎計) rhyme-group; "lì" means "beautiful. Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shūshǐ* says "lì" means "bestowal" (*shī*). Gù Yěwáng says "lì" refers to "splendid beauty" (*huāmǐ*). The *Shuowen* says it is composed of the radical "deer" (*lù*) and the phonetic "lì" (*lì shēng*). The pronunciation of "lì" is *lì* (戾).

Regarding the character *kuàng* (麁獷) in the title *The Sutra on the Three Turnings of the Previous Life* (*Qianshi Sanzhuan Jing*) as compiled by Xuanying: the lower radical is *guó* (虢) with the *mǎng* (猛) radical. The *Jixùn* states that *kuàng* means "wicked. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *kuàng* means "one who cannot be associated with"; it is composed of the "dog" (*quán*) radical and the phonetic *guǎng* (廣).

"Dǎo-cí" (禱祠): the first character is pronounced as dǎo (with the "lǎo" rhyme) and the second as sì (with the "cí" rhyme). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "To seek blessings, one should employ words of petition; obtaining blessings is called cí. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains that both characters include the radical "示" (pronounced zhī), with "shòu" and "sī" serving as their phonetic components.

"Without scar" (*wú bān*): "Below," "thin," and "cold" are reversed; according to the *Cangjie pian*, it means a trace. According to the *Shuowen*, it means a wound or a scar. The text reads "pan" (*pán*), which should follow the radical "sickness" (*nà*) with the phonetic "nü è" (*nü è*). It is pronounced like "ban" (*bān*).

"Rèn" (pregnancy): the upper radical is *zhèn* (pronounced with the fanqie "zhèn-fǎn") and the lower is *lín* (pronounced with the fanqie "shū-lín-fǎn"). The *Guǎngyǐ* states: "Rèn" is also "shēn"; "shēn" is pronounced "shēn. The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* says: "Shēn" means being pregnant. The meaning in the *Shuōwén* is the same; both characters are composed of the radical *nǚ* (woman) and the phonetic *rén* (the Heavenly Stem *chén*), with *chén* serving as the phonetic component.

Regarding "feeding" (*èi*): Wang Yanshou of the Northern Wei dynasty, in his *Fanggu* (Retrospective Survey), states that it means to scatter objects as food for birds. The *Guǎngyá* (Broad Lexicon) notes that "feeding" (*èi*) is also "nourishing" (*sì*), with the pronunciation *sì*. The *Shuowén* (Explanations of Words and Texts) explains it as being composed of the radical "food" (*shí*) and the phonetic component "wěi" (*wěi*).

*Hu* (mouth-sustenance): the first character is pronounced *shàng hù* (上戶反). The *Erya* states: "Hu means *qi* (rice gruel); the pronunciation is *rán* (音之然反). The *Zuozhuan* says: "He sustained his mouth (*hu qí kǒu*) in the four quarters. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "eating by depending on others," composed of the radical for food (*shí*) and the phonetic *hú*.

*The Scripture of the Silver-Colored Woman Spoken by the Buddha*. Compiled by Hui Lin. *Bóruò* (搏若): "Bó" (搏) is pronounced with the *shàng* (上) tone and the *duó* (奪) rhyme. It means "to grasp" (*bóyǎ*). Gu Yewang also states it means "to grasp. In the *Liji*, there is no mention of "lump-food" (*bófàn*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as being composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "zhuān" (*zhuānshēng*).

*Tì* (to shave the beard). [The character is pronounced] *shàng* (上) and *tí* (梯) with the *di* (帝) rhyme; *xǔ* (許) annotates that the *Huáinán zǐ* states *tì* means to cut the hair. The *Shuōwén* [explains it] as following the radical *biāo* (髟) with the phonetic *piāo* (摽) and *dì* (弟) as the determinative. The *Kǎoshēng* says it means to shave the hair and is written with the radical *dāo* (刀), which is a vulgar form. [The second character is] *xià* (下) with the *xiāng* (相) and *yú* (逾) rhymes. Zhèng’s annotation to the *Zhōu lǐ* says it refers to the beard and hair. It also refers to the beard below the chin. The *Shuōwén* also says it is facial hair, following the radical *shān* (彡) and *xié* (頁), a pictographic character.

*Wàn* (挽): To pull upward; there is no sound of returning. The *Shènglèi* says it means "to draw. It is written with the radical 車 (wheels) as *wǎn*. The *Shuōwén* says it is written with the radical 手 (hand) and takes *miǎn* as its phonetic. *Āshèshìwángshòujuéjīng* (阿闍世王受決經): *Fóshuō Āshèshìwángshòujuéjīng*. Compiled by Huílín. *Gěnyè* (哽噎):

Upper character, *yīng* (甖) and *gěng* (綆) rhyme. The *Kǎoshēng* says it means "the breath is choked and obstructed. The *Shènglèi* says it refers to being stuck in the throat (*àihóu*). It is also the sensation of eating. The *Shuōwén* says it is written with the radical 口 (mouth) and takes *gēng* (更) as its phonetic. The lower character, *yān* (煙) and *jié* (結) rhyme. The *Máoshīchuán* (Commentary on the Mao Odes) says it is "being choked so that one cannot breathe. Guō’s commentary on the *Fāngyán* says it is "a singular pain. The *Shuōwén* says it is food remaining in the throat, written with the radical 口 and taking *yī* (壹) as its phonetic.

*The Scripture on the King Utpalavaktra Receiving the Prediction from the Buddha and Being Named Wondrous Flower*, compiled by Huilin. Regarding the character "cai" (採): the *Kao sheng* states it means "to gather. The *Shuowen jiezi* defines it as being composed of the radicals for "claw" (爪) and "wood" (木), though in this scripture it is written with the radical for "hand" (手) and is used interchangeably.

*Ērán*: The upper radical is *ǔ wǔ gè fǎn*. Dictionaries state that *ǎi* means "startled. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic *ǎi*; its pronunciation is identical to the former. *Dié zú*:

In the *Zhènggōngjìng jīng* (Sūtra on Right Reverence), the Buddha speaks the *Zhènggōngjìng jīng*. Xuānyì compiled [this entry]. The upper character is *tú yè fǎn*. The *Guǎngyá* says: "To tread upon with the feet. The *Shēnglèi* says: "To tread and step. This is the correct orthography for ancient and modern times. *Dié* means "to tread"; it is composed of the radical "foot" (*zú*) and the phonetic *yè*. The pronunciation of *yè* is *yè*.
*Chào zú* (趠足): "Chào" is pronounced with the *chǒu* rhyme (the second tone) and the *jiāo* final. In the *Shànglín fù*, it means to leap across;

according to the *Shuōwén*, it means "far," composed of the radical "to run" (*zǒu*) and the phonetic "tuó" (*zhuó*). *Sànjìng jīng* (善敬經): Compiled by Huílín. *Zhǎozhǎo* (指抓): The lower character is pronounced with the *cè* rhyme and the *jiǎo* final. The *Zuǒzhuan* states it refers to the fingernail. The *Běicāng* says it means to pinch or claw. It is also written as *zhǎo*. According to the *Shuōwén*, *zhǎo* means to scrape, composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "zhǎo."

Below "bō" (莫反), the *Jìxùn* states: "Bō refers to the chest; it is also written as 'bó'. The *Shuowén* says: 'It is the shoulder blade; it is composed of the radical 'bone' (骨) with 'fú' (尃) as the phonetic component. The pronunciation of 'fú' is 'pǔ'."

Regarding "zhui" (椎) [in the phrase *shuipō*]: it is read as *zhì* (直) when used in the sense of "to pursue," and as *tài* (太) in the *Tàigōng Liùtǎo* (*The Six Strategies of Duke Gōng*). Gu Yěwáng states that a "zhui" is an instrument for turning objects over. The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "zhuī" (*zhuī*). The text here uses the character *chuí* (槌), which is a vulgar form. Regarding "pō" (撲): it is read as *pángmiǎo* (龐邈). Dictionaries state that it refers to wrestling or hand-to-hand combat. The *Shuowén* defines it as "striking" (*pūjī*) and is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "pú" (*pú*). The character *bó* (搏) has the pronunciation *bó*. The text here uses the character with the phonetic "pú"; this is an error resulting from the character "pú" (pronounced *bǔ*) being altered into "pú" (pronounced *bó*) and subsequently into "pú" (pronounced *bǔ*), which was further corrupted into "pú" (pronounced *bó*) by adding the radical "person" (*rén*) to become "pú" (*pú*). (Note: The passage provides philological commentary on the characters *zhui*, *chuí*, *pō*, and *bó*, clarifying their readings, origins, and common errors.)

The radical below "gou" (鈎) is pronounced *zi* (with the *mei* [髓] rhyme) or alternatively written as "qi" (𠲿). According to the *Kao Sheng* (考聲), it refers to the mouth of a bird; it is derived from the character "ci" (朿) with the pronunciation *li* (刾). In dictionaries, it is sometimes written differently, but the correct form in both ancient and modern times is derived from this [character]. In the sutras, it is written as "zui" (𭉨), which is a vulgar character.

In the character 荷 (hé) of 荷擔 (hédān), the lower radical is 尞 (láo), pronounced with the *dān* and *lán* finals reversed; the *Kǎo Shēng* and the *Jīngǔ Zhèngzì* state that it means to carry a wooden load, taking "hand" (手) as its semantic component and "zhān" (詹) as its phonetic.

In the *Chēngzàn Dàshé Gōngdé Jīng*, compiled by Huìlín, the term 謗讟 (bàngdú)—where the latter character has the *shù* final—is explained in the *Zuǒ Zhuan* commentary by Dù as "to slander" (*fěi*). According to the *Fāngyán*, it means "pain"; according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "malicious speech. The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of 誩 (jíng) and takes "mài" (賣) as its phonetic; 誩 is pronounced *qiánjìng*.
*Chuídǎng*: "Chuí" is pronounced as *zhui* (with the radical *wei* reversed); according to the *Shuowen*, it means to strike with a staff, composed of the hand-radical and the phonetic *chui*.

*Biànwěi*: "Biàn" is pronounced as *bian* (with *gai* below and *tu* and *xi* reversed); the *Kaosheng* states that both "biàn" and "wěi" mean thin or flat. The version in the sutra uses "tūn" and "shuō," which are vulgar characters. "Gai" is pronounced as *mian*.

*Cuòlòu* (矬陋): *Cuò* is pronounced as in *shā* (莎) in the *Guǎngyǎ*, meaning "short. The *Gōngjīn zhèngzì* states that the character *cuò* is composed of the radical *zhǐ* (矢) and the phonetic *zuò* (坐). *Dùlòu* (澍陋): *Dù* is pronounced as in *zhūshù* (朱戍). The *Huáinánzǐ* says, "It rains *dù* yet does not rain *dù*. Regarding the spring rain that irrigates all things, the *Shuowén* states: "*Dù* is the seasonal rain by which all things are nourished and brought to life; it has no [specific] ground. It is composed of the radical *shuǐ* (水) and the phonetic *shù* (尌), where *shù* is pronounced as *zhù* (駐). The *Zhèngfǎzì* says it means "constant. The *Gù Yěwáng* says it means "without ground" or "without the rules of the precepts. Furthermore, it means "to emulate a model. The *Erya* says it means "unique. The *Guǎngyǎ* says it means "to harmonize. The *Shuowén* states: "*Fǎ* (灋) is level like water; it is that by which the *luò* (廌) removes what is not straight. It is a compound character. *Luò* is pronounced as in *zhài* (宅薤). The *Zhèngfǎzì* says it means "constant. The *Gù Yěwáng* says it means "without ground," referring to the absence of the rules of the precepts. Furthermore, it means "to emulate a model. The *Erya* says it means "unique. The *Guǎngyǎ* says it means "to harmonize. The *Shuowén* states: "*Fǎ* (灋) is level like water; it is that by which the *luò* (廌) removes what is not straight. It is a compound character. *Luò* is pronounced as in *zhài* (宅薤).

The term *zōng* (綜) [pronounced *tsung* with the initial *ts-*, as in "subsumption"] refers to the weaving shuttle used in the *Liezhuan* (Biographies of Exemplary Women). It may be used as a metaphor for governing. That which pushes the thread forward and pulls it back is called the *zōng*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is "the intersection of threads on a loom," composed of the radical *mì* (silk/thread) and the phonetic component *zōng*.

*Ku-gǎo* (枯槁): The upper character *kū* (枯) is pronounced with the initial *k-ǔ* (苦胡反) and the final consonant *k-ǎo* (考). It means that wood has become parched and dead; it is also written as *ku-āo* (㱠). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to wither and decay," composed of the radical *muò* (木) and the phonetic *gǔ* (古). The lower character *gǎo* (槁) is pronounced with the initial *k-ǔ* (苦浩反). According to the *Shuowen*, *gǎo* also means "withered"; it is composed of the radical *muò* (木) and the phonetic *gāo* (高), meaning "also dried up."

The *Sūtra on the Decisive Karmic Obstructions of the Sublime Dharma* (also known as the *Sūtra Admonishing the King* or the *Buddha-spoken Sūtra on the Decisive Karmic Obstructions of the Sublime Dharma*). There are no characters for which phonetic glosses can be provided. Regarding the term "fǔ" (黼) in the title of the *Sūtra Admonishing the King*, Xuanying’s commentary states: "In the *Kōnggōng Jì* (Record of the Craftsman), it is said that the white and black used in painting are called 'fǔ'; black and blue are called 'fú' (黻).
