In the standard characters of antiquity and today, it is written with the radical 穴 (cave) and the phonetic 洼; the pronunciation of *kuā* is the same as above.

**Yèyǔ (寱語):** The first character, 寱, is pronounced with the initial *ní* and final *jì* (according to the Shuowen). The Shuowen defines it as "words spoken while asleep," formed from a simplified version of 㝱 (*mèng*) and the phonetic component 臬 (*niè*, pronounced *yánliè*; read like *yì*). **Jiào (呌):** The first character, 呌, is pronounced with the initial *hú* and final *gāo*.

According to the Gujin Zhengzi, it is composed of 虒 (*xī*, pronounced *sī*) and the phonetic component 号 (*hào*). The Kangxi Dictionary states that 号 means "to wail loudly" or "the sound of pain. It may also be written with 皐 or 口 as 噑. The second character, 叫, is pronounced with the initial *jiāo* and final *yào*. It is a vulgar form; the Shuowen’s correct form is 噭 (*jiào*). It means "to roar" or "to call out," formed from 口 and the phonetic component 敫 (*jiǎo*, pronounced *kǒudiāo*). This is an ancient script form.
There is no deficiency; it is a great joy that reverses the scriptural text. Regarding "from the gate" (*mén*), it is written as "conclusion" (*què*);

this is not [correct]. In the third section, the single character for "lower volume" in the *Qīqìfóding jīng* (Sūtra of the Extraordinary Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa), lower volume, "bīnshēn" (頻伸) is pronounced "shēn. According to the *Kǎoshēng* (Investigation of Sounds), it means "to stretch out the four limbs."

The term "qianjie" (欠㰦) is pronounced *qu*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to the sensation of qi awakening; in common parlance, it means opening the mouth to exhale. The version in the sutra uses "aihui" (嗌噦), which deviates from the scriptural meaning; it is now corrected to "qianjie."

*Kǎi* (穬麥): Pronounced *guōměng* (反). According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to the grain *yīn* (𦬆), which is the modern-day *dàmài* (大麥, great barley). It is a word formed by combining a semantic and a phonetic component.

*Kài*sù (欬遬): The upper character is pronounced *kāi* (開愛反). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "reversed breath" (*qì nì*). It is composed of the radical *qiàn* (欠) and the phonetic *hài* (亥). In the scripture, it is written with the radical *kǒu* (口) as *kài* (咳), pronounced *hái* (孩), meaning "the laughter of a small child"; this is not the intended meaning here. The lower character is pronounced *sòu* (叟奏反). The *Kaosheng* states that it refers to "breath surging through the throat. In the scripture, it is also written with the radical *kǒu* (口) as *sòu* (嗽); this is a vulgar usage and not the correct form.

The *Ekākṣara-uṣṇīṣa-cakravartin-tantra-sādhana-vidhi*, the *Uṣṇīṣavijaya-sādhana-vidhi*, the *Ekākṣara-uṣṇīṣa-cakravartin-tantra-sādhana-vidhi*, and the *Anakṣara-śabdārtha-uṣṇīṣavijaya-sādhana-vidhi*. Regarding the character "絣" (pīng): the *Shangbo Meng* (上伯萠) states that it means to stretch black lines; the *Jixun* (集訓) says it means to measure or mark out. Alternatively, it may be written with the hand radical as "拼" (pīng); the *Gujin Zihao* (古今字誥) records it as "䍬" or "䍬," both of which are archaic and modern variants of the same character. The pronunciation of "撣" (tán) is the same as "彈" (tán).

The character *chāng* (倀) is pronounced with the initial *gēng* (更) and final *fǎn* (反); it is used by extension because this character originally did not exist. It refers to stretching out a painted image (*zhāng zhǎn huà xiàng*). Some include the radical "wood" (*mù*), writing it as *zhēn* (楨) or *zhàng* (椗), but these are all vulgar characters and are not correct.

"Shēngbēi" (盃): "shēng" is pronounced as in "luóhè" (魯和). According to the *Erya*, it refers to a marine crustacean, and it is also a large snail. "Xià" (下) is pronounced as in "běiméi" (北梅). This refers to using a conch shell (*śaṅkha*) as a vessel for perfumed water; its Sanskrit name is *argha*.

The character 𠩶 (with the phonetic "pí" from the word "mèi")—Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that "𠩶" means "short"; Gu Yewang states that "𠩶" means "lowly. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* explains that it is composed of "厂" (phonetic value: hē qiǎn fǎn) and the phonetic "卑" (bēi).

"㧙" (left upper character) is pronounced *pián* (with the initial *mìè*) and has the sound of "kǎo. It means to twist or bend. "拗" (pronounced *yāojiǎo*) refers to twisting or bending; using the fingers to form a seal (*mudrā*) serves to manifest bodily action (*kāyakarman*). [The character] "從" (cóng) has the sound of "bì."

The character *shè* (鞘) [is pronounced with the initial *x* and final *-ao*] and the phonetic element *kǎo*; it means "the sheath for a sword. It is composed of the radical *yù* (聿) and the phonetic element *xiao* (肖). Alternatively, it may also be written as *shè* (鞘) using the radical *gé* (革), which is also acceptable; this latter form is currently in use.

*Júwù* (掬物): Pronounced *gǔ* (sixth tone). The *Jíxùn* (集訓) states that it means to grasp an object with both hands. The ancient script is a pictograph representing a mortar (*jiù*), with two claws facing each other in the posture of grasping an object.

*Pán* (蟠): Pronounced *bàn màn* (fourth tone). The *Guǎngyá* (廣雅) states that it means "coiled. The *Fāngyán* (方言) says that when a dragon has not yet ascended to heaven and remains coiled within its den, it is called a "coiled dragon" (*pánlóng*). This "coiling" refers to the manner in which the prayer beads are held here.

Regarding *qiāzhū* (掐珠): the *Shàngkǒujiǎfǎn Bēicāng* states that *zhuāqiā* means to grasp or pinch; thus, it refers to grasping and pinching prayer beads (*niànzhū*). According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "xuàn" (臽).

Regarding the *Jiājù Fódǐng Zūnrú Niànsòng Fǎ* (加句佛頂尊𠢧念誦法), two fascicles, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha. Regarding the *Wúzì Dǐnglúnwáng Jīng* (無字可音訓一字頂輪王經), Fascicle One. Regarding the *yuèfǔ* (鉞斧): the character *yuè* is pronounced as *yuán* (袁) with the *yue* (月) radical. It has already been explained previously.

*Ṭakkinī* (the *ji* with the *yi* tone is a transliteration of the Sanskrit term for a female ghost in general who can bewitch people and engage in sexual intercourse with them). Regarding the character *yan* (齗): in the *Wenzi Dadian* (Dictionary of Characters), it is explained as "the root of the teeth"; in the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is explained as "the flesh of the teeth," formed from the radical "teeth" (*chi*) with the phonetic component "jin" (*jin*). As for the character *ya* (腭) below: this character does not exist in the *Yupian*, the *Shuowen*, or other such character dictionaries; it is a vulgar usage pronounced *wo* (我) or *ge* (各). Although various scholars of recent times have included it in their rhyme books following popular usage—sometimes even taking "rou" (肉) and "ya" (腭) as its phonetic components—it is likewise a vulgar character. It has already been in circulation in the world for a long time. Examining the character *ya* (腭), it refers to the upper palate within the mouth. The *Shuowen* states: "The hollow above the mouth. It is formed from the radical "mouth" (*kou*) with the phonetic component "gu" (*gu*), pronounced *qianglüe*. It is a pictographic character representing the shape of the upper part of the mouth; the double stroke at the top of the "mouth" represents the eightfold pattern of the lines of the upper palate, and it is also a character that conveys meaning through its constituent parts.

Regarding "yá" (牙): the *Yǎjià* (雅加) gloss states that the *Shuowén* defines it as "large teeth," depicting the form of upper and lower [teeth] interlocking. Its original seal-script (*zhuànwén*) form was 󲔁; the current clerical script (*língshū*) form is 牙. Regarding "hàn" (頷): the *Shuowén* defines it as "the jaw. The ancient script originally used the character 函 (pronounced *hán*); the form with the radical 頁 (making it 顄) or the variant 顄 are both archaic characters. For now, we shall follow the common usage.

The character for "heart" (心) above [the term *hṛdaya*] is a pictograph. The character below, pronounced *qí*, is defined in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as "the diaphragm" (*píqí*), formed with the radical "flesh" (肉) and the phonetic "qí. The version in the sutra text using the character "navel" (臍), which uses the radical "moon" (月), is incorrect.

*Pí* (髀): Upper radical is *bīng* (甁) with the phonetic *mǐ* (米). The *Shuowen* says it refers to the outer part of the thigh; it is composed of the radical *gǔ* (骨) and the phonetic *bēi* (卑) with the final *xīn* (辛) and the tone *qī* (七). *Xī* (膝): Lower radical is *jié* (節) with the phonetic *qī* (桼) and the tone *qī* (七). The *Shuowen* says it refers to the joint at the top of the shinbone; it is composed of *jié* (卩, pronounced *jié*) and the phonetic *qī* (桼). In the classics, this is written as *xī* (膝) with the radical *yuè* (月) and the phonetic *qī* (桼); this is a vulgar character. This character belongs to the *zhǒu* (夂) category.
*Shao-yin* (spear seal): "Shao" is pronounced with the final *fan* (retroflex) sound; the *Shuowen* states it is a *mo* (spear), formed from *mo* as the radical and *xiao* as the phonetic.

In the sutras, it is written as *shuo* with the radical *mu* (wood); this is a vulgar character. *Yu-xi* (joyful delight): "Yu" is pronounced with the final *fan* sound. Zheng’s commentary on the *Lunyu* says: "The expression 'yu-yu' refers to a harmonious countenance. The *Erya* says it means "joy," and the *Guangya* says it means "delight. It is formed from *xin* (heart) as the radical and *yu* as the phonetic. Regarding the character *yu*: the *Shuowen* states it is composed of *ji* (assembly), *zhou* (boat), and *kai* (watercourse). *Kai* is pronounced *gu-wai*; *ji* is pronounced *jing-ru*. The current vulgar usage, which employs *yue* (moon) and *dao* (knife), is an error.
*Uṣṇīṣa* is a term from the Sanskrit language; in the Tang [Chinese] it is translated as "Buddha’s Crown" (*foding*) and also as "Invisible Crown Mark" (*wujian dingxiang*).

*Chū* (樗) is the name of a tree; its radical is "wood" (*mù*), and its phonetic is *huá* (卦). It is sometimes written with the radical "grain" (*huò*) as *huó* (檴), or used colloquially as *huà* (樺); however, when the scriptural text uses the character *huà* (𣛛), it is a vulgar form and not correct.

Regarding the term *xuānlán* (旋嵐): the lower character *lán* (嵐) refers to the "Great Fierce Wind" (*mahāvāta*). During the Xiaochang era of Emperor Xiaochang of the Northern Wei, this character was commonly used in vernacular writing; it is also a word from the northern tribes, the Turks. Because the mountains and rivers of the north are subject to much wind, it originated from Lánzhōu and Kělánzhèn; later, during the Northern Zhou, it was changed to Lánzhōu. Due to this, the character *kělán* (岢嵐) came into circulation among the people—the pronunciation of *kě* being *kě*. None of the existing character dictionaries originally contained these two characters. While perusing historical records, I found their meaning within the *Book of Northern Wei*, which is how I came to know them. Thus, I have annotated and shown their origin. This is what is currently in circulation today.

Regarding the character *kuī* (窺), the *Guǐyáng* (歸陽) and others examine its phonetics and state that it means "to peek" (*kuīchù*). Alternatively, it is written with the radical for "cave" (*xué*) as *kuī*. The *Yùnchuán* (韻詮) states it means "to see surreptitiously. It is pronounced in the level tone (*píngshēng*). The character *kuí* (奎) has the phonetic *quǎn* (犬) with the *chuí* (垂) rhyme; the character *chù* (覻) has the phonetic *qū* (七) with the *yù* (豫) rhyme.

*Gǔ*, *suò*, *bàng*, *chā*. (The character for *gǔ* is pronounced as *chāngyǔ* [with the second tone]; the character for *suò* is pronounced as *chéngluò*; the character for *bàng* is pronounced as *báixiàng*; alternatively written as *pán*; the character for *chā* is pronounced as *chǔjiā*).
"Gòngdù" is pronounced as *tángluò*; in the canonical text it is written with the radical "heart" (*xin*) as *bēi*, which is incorrect.

The character *hù* (戶) is pronounced as *jiǔ* (由酒反). According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, *yòu* (牖) means "window. The *Yùnquán* states: "It is said that the center is called *chuāng* (䆫) and the sides are called *yòu* (牖). The *Shuowén* says: "To pierce a wall with wood arranged in a crisscross pattern is called *chuāng*; it is a pictographic character, or it is written with the radical *piàn* (片). The character *yòu* (牖) is composed of *hù* (戶), *fǔ* (甫), and also *piàn* (片)."

The character *pò* (打撲) has the phonetic value *pǔmù* (普木反). The *Kǎośēng* (考聲) states that *pò* also means to strike; the *Guǎngyá* (廣雅) says it means to hit; the *Cāngjiépiān* (蒼頡篇) says it means a light blow; and the *Shuōwén* (說文) says it is *chì* (抶), where *chì* also means to strike. The character for *dǎ* (打) is composed of the radical "hand" (手) with the phonetic element "ding" (丁). The pronunciation of *chì* (抶) is *tiānyìfǎn* (天逸反).

*Xīngsào* (腥臊): The upper character is pronounced *xīng*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that it refers to the stench of pig fat and dog fat. It also says that when there are grains within the meat, it resembles stars; alternatively, it is written as *shèng* or *yǎo*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Stars appear when eating pigs. This is a phono-semantic compound character. The lower part is read as *sāngdāo* (桑刀). Its explanation is identical to that of *xīng*. It is composed of the radical "flesh" (*ròu*) with "sào" (*sāo*) as the phonetic component; the pronunciation of *sāo* is as stated above. This is the character used today.
The character *yì* (𧾰) has the pronunciation *yì*. The *Lunyu* says, "He advances with the grace of wings" (*qū jìn yì rú yě*), meaning the manner of advancing.

It is composed of the radical "to run" (*zǒu*) and the phonetic element *yì*. Regarding *chōngxiān* (傭纖): the first character, *chōng*, is pronounced *zhèng lóng fǎn*. The *Zhengjian* commentary on the *Mao Shi* states that *chōng* means "even" (*jūn*). The *Shuowen* defines it as "straightness" (*jūn zhí*), composed of the radical "man" (*rén*) and the phonetic element *yōng*. The second character, *xiān* (纖), is pronounced *xié yán fǎn*. The *Kongzhù* commentary on the *Shangshu* states that *xiān* means "fine" (*máo*). The *Guǎngyá* states it means "minute" (*wēi*). The *Zhengzhù* commentary on the *Zhouli* states it means "small" (*xiǎo*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radicals "silk thread" (*mì*) and *xiān* (韱, pronounced as above). The reading *jié* (截) in this scripture is incorrect.

The character 𧹞 (lǎi) is composed of the radical 刀 (knife) and the element 月 (moon) with the phonetic 來 (lái). It is pronounced *dài*. The *Cangjie pian* states that it means "looking inward. The *Shuowen jiezi* states that it refers to the pupils of the eyes not being straight, composed of the radical 目 (eye) and the phonetic 來 (lái).

*Xià yì* (瑕翳): The upper character *xià* is pronounced *xiá*. The commentary on the *Liji* by Zheng Xuan states that "xià" means "disease. The *Shuowen Jiezi* takes *wáng* as the radical and *duàn* as the phonetic component; the lower character *yì* is pronounced *ī* (with the *kǎo* rhyme). The *Kaoseng Zhuan* states it is a disease of the eye. Guo Pu says it refers to a cataract or obstruction, meaning something that suddenly covers [the vision]. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as a "flower-canopy" (*huágài*), taking *mù* as the radical and *ē* as the phonetic component; *ē* has the same pronunciation as *shànggǔ* (the name of a remote antiquity).

The character above is pronounced *piǎn* (with the radical *zhǒu*) and the body is pronounced *jī* (with the radical *yī*). The *Zītǒng* states that *piǎn* means "not round. Examining its phonetic, it signifies a thin and broad appearance. The *Gōngjīn Zhèngzì* states that *piǎn* means "thin, broad, neither round nor square. It is a character formed from the upper part as the semantic component and the lower part as the phonetic; alternatively, it may be written with the "flesh" (*ròu*) radical as *píng* or *píng*. These are vulgar forms.

The character 窊 (wā) is pronounced with the first tone, the radical being 穴 (xué) and the phonetic being 瓜 (guā). The *Shuowen jiezi* states it means "to be low or sunken. The character 𤲍 (jiá) is pronounced with the third tone; the *Kaoseng zhuan shengyun* states it means "water channels joined together," with the radical 水 (shuǐ) and the phonetic 甲 (jiǎ). The character 夾 (jiá) is the phonetic. The version in the [Miaofa lianhua jing] uses 翈 (hè), which refers to the small feathers on a bird's wing (*huò*); this is not the intended meaning in the scripture.

"Wan" (頑) and "yin" (嚚): Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that when the mind does not fathom the principles of virtue and righteousness, one is called "wan. The reading for the character "yan" (下) is yú-jīn. Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that when the mouth does not utter words of loyalty and good faith, one is called "yin. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical 󲚯 and the phonetic 臣; the sound of 󲚯 is zhuāng-lì, and it consists of four mouths.

"Bùdài" (不迨): the rhyme is *tái* (台) reversed; the *Mao Shi Zhuan* says it means "to pursue and catch up. In ancient and modern standard characters, it is composed of the radical *chuò* (辵, meaning "to move") and the phonetic *tái* (台).

"Bǎoyá" (寶芽): the rhyme is *jiā* (加); according to the *Boyá*, the initial growth of plants and trees is called a "sprout" (*yá*). This is a word formed by combining a semantic component with a phonetic one.
**Guà (挂):** "To hang. According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means "to suspend. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "guī" (圭).

It is incorrect [to claim] that the character used in the classics is composed of the radical "wood" (木). **2. Second Fascicle.** **Sè (㵶):** "To sprinkle. Upper radical: 㵶; lower radical: 灑. Pronunciation: upper, jiān-xuē; lower, shā-gǔ. The *Kǎoshēng* states that it means "to splash" (濺). It is also written as 瀄, which is likewise acceptable. Regarding "sǎ" (灑): it refers to using an object to moisten water and scatter it. This is a borrowed pronunciation; its original pronunciation is suǒ-mǎi, which is not used here.

The *qūmù* tree—its name is certainly derived from its sound; it is a species of wood that possesses an intense fragrance. Its grain resembles white sandalwood (*śvetacandana*), yet it is not actually white sandalwood. To make it fragrant, one must cut it down and wait many years before the scent emerges. This tree belongs to the same genus as white sandalwood; the red variety is superior, though in former times most people did not recognize it and called it "white sandalwood incense."

*Xián* (in the phrase *tóu xián*, pronounced with the final *xī* reversed as *lián*): In the *Shiji*, it means "sharp"; according to the *Shuowen*, it belongs to the category of *shàoyú* (a type of weapon), composed of the radical *jīn* (metal) and the phonetic *shé*.

*Shùn mù* (pronounced *shuǐ rùn*): According to the *Shuowen*, it is written as *zhùn* (from the character *yín*), defined as "the frequent opening and closing of the eyes" or "the twinkling of the eyes. In Buddhist scriptures, the character *shùn* (from *shùn*) is also used interchangeably.

The character 縱 (zòng) has two readings: the upper radical is 忄 (xīn), read as fǎn; the lower part is ㄙ (yáng), read as táng lǎng fǎn. The Master Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjìng* states it means "to be unrestrained" (fàng yù) or "to dally" (you xì). Guō Pǐng’s commentary on the *Ěryá* says it means "deviant" (xié pì). The *Guǎngyá* says 縱 means "licentious" (yín). The *Shuōwén* says it means "to let loose" (fàng) and is composed of 心 (xīn) with 易 (yì) as the phonetic. The scriptural text uses 婸 (chóng), composed of 女 (nǚ) and 易 (yì), which is also interchangeable; here, the pronunciation of 易 is indeed yáng.
*Vijaruṇa-aja-ru-kha*. This one phrase in Sanskrit is translated into Chinese as "subduing" (*tiáofú*) or "overpowering" (*jiàngfú*).

*Tuoluo* (𩧐駝): The upper character is pronounced *tuò* or *luò*; the lower character is pronounced with the rhyme *táng-hé*. It is a beast of burden from the Hu lands of the north, as previously explained.
*Tānyè* (貪劮): The lower character is pronounced *yì*. According to the *Kǎoshēng*, it means "leisure" (*yìyù*) or "to dally."

The character for "jest" (xiè) is pronounced with the initial *xī* and the final *yì*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is a compound of the semantic element "spear" (gē) and the phonetic element "qián. The character for "mirth" (xiào) below is pronounced with the initial *xiāng* and the final *nüè*. The *Erya* states that "mirth" (*xiào*) is also "jesting" (*xiè*). The *Commentary on the Book of Poetry* says it means "joyful amusement. Both are examples of form-phonetic characters.

*Mumgheḍa* (姥󲨇馱): The first character is pronounced as *mǔ*; the second is pronounced as *lùn* with a retroflex *n* (訥) following it. This is a Sanskrit term for the name of a powerful obstacle-creating *yakṣa* king.
*Utpala* (𮨄鉢羅): The first character is pronounced as *wēn* with a velar *k* (骨) following it. This is a Sanskrit name for a flower; in ancient translations, it was called the *utpala* flower.
*Yuti* (諭底迦): The upper tone is *yu*; it was formerly written as *yu*, which is also a transliteration of the Sanskrit term.

*Xiangbo* (香馞): *Bo* is pronounced with the *pen* and *mo* finals; according to the *Guangya*, *bo* describes the appearance of fragrance being intense. In modern standard orthography, the character is composed of the radical "fragrance" (*xiang*) and the phonetic element "bo"; this is its ancient form.

*Tán* (pronounced *tān* with the second tone): The *Erya* states that it refers to sand emerging from within water. Guo Pu says: "In the Jiangnan region today, the sandy banks within the water are called *tán*. It is a character formed by combining semantic and phonetic components, meaning 'a place within water. It is sometimes written as *tān*, which is a vulgar variant."

"Cāi (猜): the upper radical is 釆 (bǎn), and the phonetic is 青 (qīng). It means to harbor suspicion or resentment; according to the *Guǎngyá*, it also means to fear. Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states it means "suspicion. In the standard characters of antiquity and today, this character is composed of the radical 犬 (dog) and the phonetic 青."

*Niān xiāng* (holding incense): *Niān* is glossed as "to grasp" in the *Guǎngyǎ*. The *Shìmíng* states it means "to pick up with two fingers. The character is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "zhàn" (*shēng*). It refers to the act of picking up or grasping with the fingers. According to the *Shuōwén*, *niān* is identical to *ní* (to pinch), pronounced *ní zhé fǎn*.

*Kǐng* (pronounced *qīng* with the *dǐng* rhyme): The *Cāngjié piān* states it means "sound. The *Shuōwén* says it means "coughing" (*kài*), composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic element *kìng* (pronounced *kè* or *lìng*). The *Kǎoshēng* says it refers to the saliva in the mouth; the *Shuōwén* calls it "oral fluid" (*kǒuyè*), a compound character formed from both shape and sound.

The characters for *xié* (shoes) and *jiè* (sandals) have the phonetic component "crab" (*xiè*) above; in the classics they are written as *xié*, which is a vulgar character. The *Shēnglèi* states: "A sole made of leather with hemp or silk. The *Shìmíng* says: "*Xié* means 'to loosen' (*jiě*); when putting them on, one contracts the upper part like a boot, and when taking them off, one loosens the upper part so it expands. The correct ancient and modern forms follow the radical "leather" (*gē*) with the phonetic "xi" (*xī*). The lower part is read as *qǐ yāo*. Alternatively, they are written as *qiào* or *jiǎo*, also pronounced *jiāng nuò*. The explanations and definitions are identical. According to the *Cāngjiépiān*, *jiè* is the same as *jī*. Xú Guǎng’s commentary on the *Shījì* states it is a grass sandal (*cǎofēi*). It is also read as *xī jì*. *Jī* is pronounced *qíng nì*; *fēi* is pronounced *féi wèi*. The *Shuōwén* defines it as a "shoe" (*lǚ*), using a simplified form of "shoe" (*lǚ*) with "qiáo" as the phonetic.

*Wèi* (socks), etc.; pronounced *wàn fā* (with the final tone reversed) or written as *㞕*, also as *襪*, or with the initial *𥿉*. It is also an archaic form of *mì*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Clothing for the feet; it is composed of the radical *wéi* (leather) and the phonetic *miè*. The pronunciation of *miè* is *mián biè*.

The character *cháo* (嘲) is a compound of semantic and phonetic elements: it takes the radical 言 (speech) as its semantic component and 朝 (zhāo) as its phonetic. It means to mock or to jest; it is a vulgar form of the character 誂 (*tiǎo*). The character *tiǎo* (誂) is pronounced with the final rhyme *xiàotiao* (下條). According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to provoke" or "to test. The *Kǎośēng* states that to first test someone with one's words is called *tiǎo*. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "mutual calling out," taking the radical 言 (speech) as its semantic component and 兆 (zhào) as its phonetic. The sound of *xiǎo* (謏) is *xiūyǒu* (修酉) or alternatively *xiǎo* (小).
Lè-xī (樂歖): The upper character is pronounced *luò* and the lower character is pronounced *xǐ*.
Volume Three, Part Three. Zhā-kāi (磔開): The upper character is read as *zhānggé* (張革). According to the *Guǎngyá*, "zhā" means to stretch and also means to open.
Regarding "xìxī" (戲嬉): the first character is pronounced with the initial *xī* and the final *xǐ*; the scripture reads it as "xīxǐ" (熙喜), which is incorrect. Regarding "yǔhè yě" (俁呬野):
the first character is pronounced *yú* (with the rhyme *gǔ*) and the second is pronounced *xīn* (with the rhyme *yǐ*). "Yǔhè yě" is a Sanskrit name for various devas.

The character *yǎn* (𩜁) is pronounced with the initial *l-*, reversed as *zhèng* (證); it is used here by borrowing [the phonetic] without taking its literal meaning, referring to the body leaning forward. It is also said that leaning the body forward is the meaning already present in the scriptural text, and its pronunciation is simply used for the sake of the rhyme.

*Tái* (擡): Pronounced *shàng dà lái fǎn* (上大來反). The *Yùchuán* (韻詮) states it means "to lift up. It is composed of the radical *shǒu* (手) and the phonetic *tái* (臺). 4. Fourth Fascicle. Fascicle Four. *Jué* (掘): Pronounced *qún qū fǎn* (群屈反).

The *Jíxùn* (集訓) states it means "to dig" or "to excavate. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it means "to sever. The meaning of the scripture intends to "hew away" (*zhù*) the foul earth within that ground, as well as ashes, charcoal, tiles, rubble, rotten bones, decayed wood, and all other filthy and evil things. The *Shuowén* (說文) states it is composed of the radical *shǒu* (手) and the phonetic *qū* (屈). In the scriptural text, it is written with the radicals *jiǎo* (角) and *jué* (厥), forming the character *jué* (𧤼); its pronunciation is *quán yuè fǎn* (權月反). This is not the common vernacular usage.

Regarding the character *tà* (拓): the glossary of sounds states that *tà* means "to open. It is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the element "stone" (石). In the Classics, it is written with the element "divide" (扸, pronounced *chìgé*). This [latter form] is incorrect; it does not constitute a valid character.

The character for "ruler" (如來) is written with the "two-handled" radical (槊), which is a variant used in secular texts; its correct form follows the "spear" radical (矛) as "shao" (矟), meaning a short spear.
The pronunciation of "mu" (姥) is "mu.
The character for "lun" (論) is pronounced "gu" (骨) and is used here as a phonetic loan.

*Ta-tien-chih-ja-kang-chieh* (the five characters above constitute one phrase of Sanskrit). The translators have provided the phonetic transcriptions as noted above; these are all borrowed sounds used to resonate with the Sanskrit name for Vajra. They do not seek to convey the literal meaning of the characters.

To make the gesture of *zhuǎn* (pronounced *kuàngmò* in the rhyme dictionary; the "Correct Characters of Past and Present" states it means "to strike," referring to striking the cheeks). Even in modern vernacular, the word *zhuǎn* is still used. This character is composed of the radical *pī* (a variant of *zhī*, meaning "to strike") and the phonetic *gè*.

The character 擲 (zhì) is pronounced with the initial *pǔ* and final *bāo* (as in "stone"). The commentary states it means "to throw an object with the hand. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to throw," composed of the radical 手 (hand) and the phonetic 尥 (*liào*). It also has the pronunciation *liáo*. The character 即 (jí) is formed from 力 (strength) and 作 (to do), meaning "to cast" (*pāo*), which is incorrect. The correct form is composed of 手 (hand), 九 (nine), and 勺 (ladle), forming a compound character based on their combined meaning.

*Zhu*: the head radical is "chu" (six strokes), or written with the "li" radical as *zhui*; according to the *Guangya*, it means "to align" or "to level. It may also be written with the "shi" radical as *zhu*, both forms being interchangeable; it takes the "yu" radical and the phonetic "zu. *Xie*: the head radical is "man" (eight strokes);

the *Kaosheng* says it means "to bind," while the *Jixun* says it means "to tie crosswise. The correct character for ancient and modern usage takes the "yi" radical and the phonetic "mo"; the character "mo" consists of the "mu" radical with a single stroke added above it.

The right hand grasps and gathers [the hair]—the character is written with the "zhuǎn" radical (括) reversed, or sometimes with "zuì" (最) as "cuō" (撮). According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to gathering with three fingers; both forms are valid. Regarding "shātàn" (沙潬):

the upper character is "shā" (沙), or sometimes written with the "shí" (石) radical as "shā" (砂); the lower character is "tǎn" (坦), pronounced "dān" (丹). The *Kǎoshēng* states that when sand emerges from within water, it is called "tànr" (潬); this is a compound character formed by both shape and sound.
*Mitrāditā* (the "da" sound is pronounced with the *ke* and *fan* [retroflex] tones): this is the Sanskrit term for the corpse of a recently deceased person.
5. Fifth Fascicle. *Cā* (the "cha" is pronounced with the *chang* and *ye* [palatal] tones): this is a Sanskrit syllable.
*Ni* (禰) and *ni* (泥) have the same pronunciation as above.
*Xun* (䞘) has the phonetic value *hen* (痕) and *mo* (沒).

*Ci* (瓷) and *zhi* (𤮲): the former is pronounced *ci*; in the sutras, it is written with the character for "stone" (*shi*) to form *cishi* (磁石), which refers to a medicinal name and is not used here. *Ci* refers to ceramic vessels.

The character *yìng* (迎) means to welcome; *yì* (翼) means to respond; *kǎo* (考) means sound. *Yì* (翼) signifies respect, assistance, escorting, aid, and harmony. *Kǎo* (考) signifies caution or diligence. Alternatively, it may be written with the radical for "running" (*zǒu*) as *xù* (𧾰), which denotes the manner of hurrying or running. In the scriptures, it is sometimes written with the radical for "roof" (*guǎng*) as *lí* (㢞); this was an error made by the translators.

*Hén* (to parch rice grains; *chǔ* [qiao] is the phonetic, or it is also written as *chǎo* or *chāo*; all are interchangeable). A local dialect gloss states that *hén* means "to dry with fire. In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, the radical is "fire" (*huǒ*) and "qǔ" serves as the phonetic.
The character 󲲰 (shǒu) is pronounced *àn* (with a reversed tone). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to cover" (*fù*).

It is composed of the abbreviated form of 暗 (*àn*) as the phonetic element. The character 聯 (*lián*) is pronounced *lì chán* (with the second tone). The *Kaosheng* states that it means "to connect. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to connect. Since the ear is connected to the cheek, it takes the radical 耳 (*ěr*). As for the inclusion of the radical 絲 (*sī*), it signifies "uninterrupted continuity"; thus, it is a compound character formed through associative meaning (*huìyì zì*).
Regarding "xiāngmù" (榓木), its pronunciation is "yìmì"; it has already been explained that it may also be written as "mì," which is likewise acceptable.
Regarding "qīngkē" (青稞), its pronunciation is "kē"; it refers to a class of barley that lacks a husk, though there is a separate pronunciation for it which is not adopted here.

The *Ekākṣara-uṣṇīṣa-cakravartin-sūtra* Spoken at the Place of Enlightenment, Volume One. First: Maudgalyāyana. The character "jian" (鍵) is a corruption of the Sanskrit; the correct Sanskrit pronunciation is *Mahā-maudgalyāyana*. In the language of Tang, it means "the descendant of the Mung-bean Sage" (*mudga*). Alternatively, he is called Mahāmaudgalyāyana. Among the Śrāvaka disciples of the Tathāgata, he was foremost in supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
*Kucīra*—the "chi" sound is as in *chī*; this is the name of an arhat.

*Kharoṭa* is likewise a phonetic corruption of a Sanskrit term; in ancient translations it was sometimes called the King of the Kāla-rūpas, which refers to the host of the Golden-Winged Bird Kings (*garuḍa*).

The character *nā* (拏) in *nārī* (拏枳你) is derived from the sound *nu*; there are those who derive it from *ru*, but that is incorrect. *Ki* (枳) is pronounced *jingyi* (經以), and *ni* (你) is pronounced *ningding* (寧頂); this is the general name for female spirits (*nārī*).

Regarding the name *Vaiśravaṇa*: the character for *niù* (in *Vai-niù*) is pronounced as *ní* with the *zhǒu* rhyme, or it may be written with the radical for "silk" (*miè*). Both forms are correct. The version with the "metal" radical (*jīn*) and the phonetic *chǒu* is an error; it should instead be from the "field" radical (*tián*). Some say he is the god *Viṣṇu*, formerly called *Piliútiān* (Vaiśravaṇa), who is the god of the *Abhidharma-kośa-śāstra* and belongs to the lineage of Nārāyaṇa. This is correct.

The character for *yuè* (axe) is pronounced with the upper radical *yuán* and the final *yuè*; its original correct form is written as *wù*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "a great axe" (*dàfǔ*). It is composed of the semantic element *gē* (weapon) and the phonetic element *jué*. In transcribing this character, people often err by confusing it with the characters for *wù* (the fifth Earthly Branch) and *jǐ* (the sixth Earthly Branch). Therefore, the former sages added the metal radical (*jīn*) to form *yuè* to distinguish it from them. Gu Yewang stated that the "axe" (*yuèfǔ*) is a military instrument and weapon. According to the *Sīmǎ Fǎ*, those of the Xia dynasty held the dark-colored axe (*xuán yuè*), while the *Shàngshū* states that the King held the yellow axe (*huáng yuè*) on his left. Thus, the axe is a great axe; the King bestowed it upon the Grand Marshal (*Dàsī mǎ*) to execute officers who held insignia of rank. It is a character formed through both shape and sound.

Maṇibhadra (the *bā* sound is pronounced like *pan-mo*; the *na* sound is pronounced like *nu-ge*; this is a Sanskrit term for a Yakṣa general; in the language of Tang [Chinese], it means "Full Virtue").
Oṣṭhānaka (the *da* sound in *ka-da* is the departing tone; the *ka* sound is pronounced like *jiang-que*; this is a Sanskrit term for a malevolent ghost, or as some say, a "suffocating ghost").

The character 凌 (líng) is pronounced with the radical 冫 (ice/snow), the phonetic 力 (lì), and the classifier 考 (kǎo); it means to encroach upon or insult. In the scriptures, it is written with the radical 水 (water), which is a name for a river. The correct orthography from ancient times to the present uses the radical 力 (strength/force) and the phonetic 夌 (líng). The pronunciation of 夌 is the same as that in the following line; 欺 (qī, to deceive), 陵 (líng, to overstep), and 辱 (rú, to disgrace) are all treated similarly.

*Pó* (from the shoulder): This refers to the shoulder blade (*jiānbó*). It is composed of the radical "bone" (*gǔ*) and the abbreviated phonetic "bó. The character *jīng* (in the context of "flesh") is a vulgar variant.
*Jiǎng* (pronounced *xíngdìng*): This refers to the shin bone of the leg.
The two ankle bones (Sanskrit: *śakti*, here transcribed as *shuoli* with the second character pronounced *shang-zhuo*) are the internal and external bones above the ankles and feet;
this is the name of a mudrā, which in the language of Tang means "spear-mudrā" (*śakti-mudrā*).

*Jù* (沮) means "to ruin" or "to destroy. The *Mao Commentary on the Classic of Poetry* states: "Jù also means to ruin," and it is pronounced with the rhyme *jīng-yù*. The *Classic of Poetry* says: "Fén jǔ rú" (汾沮洳); the commentary states: "Its *jiān-rú* (漸洳). Zheng’s commentary on the *Record of Rites* says it means "tears," while the *Erya* says it means "moist. It is composed of the radical *shui* (water) and the phonetic *qù* (且). The text here uses *zǔ* (爼), which according to the *Shuowen Jiezi* is composed of "half-flesh" and does not carry this meaning. Below, *huái* (懷) is pronounced *guài* (怪). The *Zitong* states that "to break from within" is called *huài* (壞); the *Shuowen* defines it as "to fail from within," composed of the radical *tu* (earth) and the phonetic *huái* (褱). The pronunciation of *huái* is *hū-guāi* (胡乖).

The character for *niè* (溺) is the opposite of *níng* (寧). In the *Lǐjì*, Confucius said: "The gentleman perishes at the mouth; the petty man perishes in water. This means being submerged and unable to save oneself. It is also said: "There are three occasions when one dies and is not to be condoled with: [dying from] fear, being crushed, and drowning. The *Shuowén Jiězì* states: "*Mò* (沒) means to sink in water; it is composed of the radical 'person' and 'water,' and is also written as *niè*. This is the ancient form."

"Snake" (shé): the upper radical is *du* (zhē) with the fanqie *zhā*; it is a vulgar character; the correct form follows the character *tuó*, or it is written as *shé*. The *Shuowen* states that it is a venomous insect. The *Mao Shi* says, "Only the *huǐ* and the *shé*. The *Shuowen* further notes that in ancient times people lived among the grasses and feared snakes, hence they would ask one another, "Is there nothing [to fear]? (*wú tuó hū*). The *Cangjie pian* says, "Snakes are not of one kind; their species are so numerous that they cannot be fully described. The pronunciation of *tuó* is *tā* (with the lower radical *yán* and *jié*). The *Liji* says, "Do not bite bones. The *Shuowen* defines *niè* as "to bite" (*shì*); it is composed of the radical "teeth" (*chǐ*) and the phonetic "nuǎi," and is the character representing its original form.

"Bhūrja" (樺皮)—the "hua" being pronounced with a "ma" reversal—is the name of a tree whose bark can be used for candles. That which possesses fine, smooth areas capable of writing upon is the bhūrja bark. In the Five Indic Regions, there is no paper; therefore, they cut the bhūrja bark, or the leaves of the *pāṭala* tree, or the leaves of the *tāla* tree, to fashion them into *pustaka* (Sanskrit volumes), much like the ancient people of China used bamboo slips. In this manner, the written words of the sūtras and śāstras, as well as both internal and external classics, were transmitted to this land.
*Naraka* is the Sanskrit term for hell. *Muhūrta* is also a Sanskrit term meaning "time.

According to the calendrical systems of the Western regions (India), one day and night is divided into thirty *muhūrtas*. Generally, regardless of whether it is winter or summer, this duration is fixed at thirty; however, during the equinoxes, day and night each obtain fifteen *muhūrtas*. At the times of the shortest and longest days—namely the winter solstice and the summer solstice—day and night mutually encroach upon each other by six [units], resulting in twenty-four and twenty-eight [respectively]. This is the meaning of the character now written as "form" (*xing*).

The character for "umbrella" (sàn) above is written with the radical "silk" (糸), which is a vulgar form; the correct form uses "silk" (繖). Below, the phonetic component is "canopy" (蓋); this is the standard orthography. It is composed of "grass" (艹) and "lid" (盇), where "lid" (盇) is pronounced "hé. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the character "lid" (盇) is composed of "great" (大) and "blood" (血). The scriptural text writes it as "canopy" (蓋), using "sheep" (羊) and "blood" (血), which is an error of the clerical script (隸). This has been the character for "grass" (艹) throughout antiquity and the present.
"Baoyan" (寶燄) is the correct orthography for "yàn" (焰).

"Cuò" (挫) is pronounced with the initial *zǔ* and the final rhyme *huò*; in the *Yùnchuán* (韻詮), it is explained as "frustration" (*zhécuò*). Jia’s commentary on the *Guóyuè* states that to "break its verbal acumen" is called "cuò. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "to crush," written with the radical "hand" and the phonetic "zuò."

Regarding the term *qi-dǎo* (旌纛): the upper character is pronounced *qí* and the lower *dú*. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that a *dǎo* is a feathered plume (*yùbǎo*) attached to a banner. Cāoyōng’s *Dúduàn* states: "The 'yellow canopy with the left-hand *dǎo*'; the *dǎo* is made from the tail of a *máoniú* (bos grunniens) ox and is placed atop a spear or halberd; this is what is called a *dǎo*. This is correct.

The character *lánxiāng* (蘭香) is composed of the radical "wood" (*jiǎo*) and the phonetic "zhèng" (正), with the pronunciation *shāo* (梢). This is precisely the parable spoken by the Tathāgata: whenever the *lánxiāng* flower blooms, its flower-head divides into seven parts. When the virtuous deities shatter the heads of the sinners, they break them into seven pieces, just like those flower-heads of the *lánxiāng*. The claim in ancient translations that these are "branches of the *ālī* tree" is erroneous; there is no such thing as an *ālī* tree.
The characters for "jì" (mark) and "fǎn" (reverse) in "jìfǎn" (marking on the skin) both follow the radical for flesh (月). The character for "lú" (盧) is a simplified form of "lú" (盧).

"Tuánluán" (團欒) is a colloquial term meaning "tuányuán" (團圓, round); the upper part is pronounced wán (完) according to ancient and modern standard characters, while the lower part is pronounced wán (完) with lú (盧) as the phonetic component; both are compound characters formed by semantic and phonetic elements.

2. Second Fascicle. "Twist" (cuǒ): the first character is read as *cǐ hé* (this what); the second is read as *lì zhǔ* (forceful master). The preceding phonetic meanings were already explained at the beginning of this fascicle.
"Weave cotton cloth" (*zhī dié*): the second character is read as *tián yè*. This was also already glossed and explained at the beginning of the fascicle.
The characters for "yanku" (巖窟) and "kugu" (苦骨) are actually vulgar forms; they should correctly be written as "dì" (地) and "jué" (堀).

The character for "zhì" (置) is corrected from "chí" (𠯗); "zé" (讁) is further corrected to its regular form. In the sutra, the character for "zhēn" (貞) is written as "zhēn" (楨), which is incorrect. Furthermore, in the previous section on the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-dhāraṇī*, the character for "zhuāng" (倀) was written with the "person" radical (亻), which is the character "zhāng" (張); this too is not the original character, but a borrowed character.
Regarding "white *miao* whisk" (*baimao fu*), the character for *miao* is the same as the word for "cat" (*mao'er*), referring to that animal and not the yak (*miao niu*).

Regarding the character for "net" (*luo*)—pronounced "luo guo"—Guo's commentary on the *Shanhai jing* explains it as "to encompass. The standard form of this character from ancient times to the present consists of the radical "silk" (*mi*) and the phonetic element "net" (*luo*) with its lower portion abbreviated.

*Yāotiáo* (pronounced *jiāo*): The commentary on the sounds states that it refers to weaving silk into cords to bind around the waist. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *mì* (silk) and the abbreviated form of *tiáo*. *Qìng* (pronounced *qīng*):

This is borrowed for use in the departing tone (*qùshēng*), though its original pronunciation is the entering tone (*shàngshēng*). It is not adopted here. The collected glosses state that *qìng* means "black. The correct character for this meaning from ancient times to the present is composed of the phonetic *qīng* and the semantic element *sè* (color); the character *yǐng* (disease) is composed of *shēng* (life) and *dān* (cinnabar).
"Like casting a vermilion tree, it is reversed.
*Nizhi* (泥滓): the *zhishǐ* (緇史) rhyme; the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) says it means "filth"; the *Shuōwén* (說文) says it means "sediment," composed of the radical "water" (*shui*) and the phonetic "zǎi" (*zǎi*).

"Wheel hub" (*lúndāng* 輪樘): the lower character is read as *zháhéng* (宅衡); the *Shuōwén* says "hub" (*táng* 樘) refers to a pillar for a *chà* (刹), composed of the radical "wood" (*mu*) and the phonetic "táng" (*táng*). It is used in this sense.

Suan (酸): "su" with the radical *su* (蘇) and the phonetic *duan* (端). In the *Shuowen*, it is defined as "sour vinegar" (*suan cuo*). It is also said that "cuo" (酢) means "vinegar," and "zuo" (䣻) means "vinegar broth. Both are phono-semantic compounds (xing-sheng zi) featuring the radical for "wine" (*you*) [酉].

*Shuiji* (水蛭): The character *zhen* (真) is pronounced with the final *-ri* reversed [as *-di*], and its sound is the same as *zhi* (質). The *Cangjie pian* states that a *ji* (蛭) is an aquatic insect; it is composed of the radical "insect" (*chong*) and the phonetic component "to arrive" (*zhi*).

3. Third Fascicle. *Shebo* (攝嚩): The lower part of the character is pronounced with the final *-he* reversed [as *-wo*]. This is a Sanskrit term meaning "neither at peace nor seeking. In Sanskrit it is called *śava*; in the language of Tang, it means a recently deceased person whose body has not yet decayed.
*Maṃsa* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "flesh.
*Māṃsa* (the first character is pronounced with the *mòhòu* rhyme):
according to the *Erya*, *māṃsa* means "market" or "meat."
Yunying states that *yǎn* means "to sell.
The *Shuowen* says it means "to exchange goods.
It is composed of the radical "貝" (bèi, meaning "shell-currency") and the phonetic "戼" (*shǔn*). The character *shǔn* is an archaic form of the character "酉" (*yǒu*).
It is incorrect for the sutra to derive [the term] from "mǎo" (卯) and form it as "mǎn" (𧵍).
To say "mǎng-sā" (莽娑) refers to the selling of human flesh after death;
this is a matter belonging to the rites for driving and employing ghosts and spirits.

Take the flesh of a recently deceased person that has not yet decayed, prepare it according to the methods of a kitchen, and season it with ginger, pepper, and the five flavors to make it savory; then roast and broil it until fragrant and delicious, using it as an offering for the powerful spirits and deities in the śmaśāna forest.
Once the sacrificial feast has been completed,
one employs the power of the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa mantra to coerce and compel [the deity] to act as a servant for the sake of eliminating calamities and harm from the state.
Because this food is exchanged for that power, it is called *bali-māṃsa*.
*Zhì* (炙) is pronounced *zhī* (亦反); it is derived from the character for meat (*ròu*) with the phonetic *huàn* (㷅, pronounced *chǎo*).
It is vulgarly written as *chǎo*.
*Mítáluó* (迷怛羅) is also a Sanskrit term; in the Tang language, it means "corpse-raising ghost" (*qǐshī guǐ*).

The upper character of *bō* (󰜤) has the phonetic value *bó*, and the lower character of *jīn* (津) has the reversed reading *rù*. The *Kǎo Shēng* states that *bōjīn* (󰜥㗱) means to crave food and drink; alternatively, it refers to making sounds with the mouth while imagining something as delicious. The text’s use of the character *shà* (唼) is incorrect. The phonetic value of *shà* (唼) is *suǒ xià*.

"Hammered copper" (*chuitong*) is a phonetic loan for *chui* (to hammer). Originally, there was no character for "dead" (*si*); it was first cast and then subsequently heated and forged until it was completed, hence it is called "hammered copper," following common parlance.

Regarding *zhēng* (蒸): the upper radical is *zhāng* (章) with the phonetic *róng* (仍). The commentary on the sounds states that it means "to steam to maturity," where the fire forces the vapor of the water upward. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "the movement of fire-gas. The lower character is read as *zhǔ* (諸) or *rǔ* (汝). Gu Yewang says it means "to boil" or "to cook. In archaic script, it is written as *yù* (鬻), composed of the radical *zhě* (者) and the phonetic *yù* (鬻).

*Píjiāo* (皮膠). The character *jiǎo* (爻) is pronounced as *jiǎo* (爻, with the second tone). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Kǎogōngjì* states: "Glue is made by heating animal hide. Gu Yewang says: "Glue is that which connects and joins objects so that they adhere to one another. According to the *Shīchuán* (Explanations of the Odes), it means "solidity. It is composed of the radical for "flesh" (*ròu*) and the phonetic element *liáo* (*翏*).

"㧙" (the second character): with the index fingers joined (*pián*, rhyme *miè*). The *Yùnquán* states that it means to twist or wrench with the hands; there are those who write it as "𢱧," which is an erroneous usage.

It is formed from the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "bi" (*bì*). "相柱" (*xiāngzhù*): the lower character is read as *zhū lǚ*. In ancient texts, a single dot of ink was used for this; this is the original character. In the scriptural text, it is written as "跓" (*zhù*) or "柱" (*zhù*), both of which are borrowed characters.
*Kǎomài* (穬麥): the "kǎo" is pronounced as *guōměng* (虢猛);

it refers to large-barley. Volume Four, Part Four: *Xiāoyǒng* (驍勇). The upper character *xiāo* (驍) is pronounced as *jiǎoyáo* (皎堯); according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "vigorous. The lower character *yǒng* (勇) is formed with the radical "force" (*lì*) and the phonetic element *yǒng* (*yǒngshēng*).
The character for "bó" (shoulder) in the *Yinbo jing* is pronounced with the initial *pú* and the final rhyme *bó*; it is the same as the character for "dried meat" (*zhé*).

The character for "guāng" (light) is pronounced with the initial *yán* and the final rhyme *jiàn*, and is also written as "yàn. The character for "hàn" (to shake) has the initial *hán* and the final rhyme *gàn*; it is currently borrowed for this usage.

The character *huǎn* (踝) is pronounced with the initial *wǎ* (瓦). Regarding the character *guàn* (關), the upper radical is pronounced with the initial *guǎ* (寡) and *wán* (頑). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "It refers to a wooden crossbar used to hold a door; it is composed of the radical 'gate' (*mén*) and the phonetic element *bì* (𢇂). The pronunciation of *bì* is the same as above. The character *guǎn* (閞) is composed of the radical *cǎo* (艸) and the phonetic element *guàn* (慣); the pronunciation of *cǎo* is *guàn*. The character *yōu* (𢇁) has the pronunciation *yōu* (幽). It is incorrect to use the character *biàn* (弁) [as a substitute] for *guàn*; the pronunciation of *biàn* is *biàn* (汴). This is a case of erroneous usage.

The character 󲒯 (hé) is explained in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as "the husk of grain. It is composed of 禾 (grain), 庚 (geng), and 米 (grain); it is not the same as 經 (jīng), which is composed of 糸 (silk) and 巠 (xīng).

The character 煙 (yān) is pronounced with the lower radical 𡼡 (huī) and the phonetic 雲 (yún). The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as "smoke rising from fire. It is a compound ideograph composed of 屮 (grass/sprout) and 黑 (black).

*Chù* (pronounced *chǔ*, with the second tone) means "chopsticks" according to the *Guǎngyá*. In the *Wénzì jílüè*, it is sometimes written as *zhé* or *jīn*. It refers to eating utensils; the *Hànzi* states that Zhou made chopsticks out of ivory. According to the *Shuowén*, it means "to tilt food [into the mouth]"; the character for *cài* is pronounced *gǔ xié* (first tone), while the following *jiāo* is pronounced *jiāo* (second tone).
*Jinli* (金粖): "Li" is pronounced with the *bo* (鉢) and *fan* (反) finals; it refers to crushed rice. *Helian* (合鍊):

"Lian" is pronounced with the *dian* (殿) final, though some write it as *lian* (煉). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, this character for "smelting" (*lian*) follows the radical for metal (*jin*) and the phonetic *jian* (柬), with *jian* having the same pronunciation as above. It is incorrect for the text of this scripture to use the character for "refining silk" (*lian*) [which follows the radical for silk (*mi*)].

Volume Five, Part Five. No characters can be phonetically transcribed. *Mahā-dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Single-Syllable Heart-Mantra for the Age of Dharma*. Regarding the term "xié" (鑞): the *Kǎo Shēng* states it belongs to the class of lead and tin; the *Yùn Yīng* says it is lead; the *Shuō Wén* says it is "blue metal" (*qīng jīn*) and is a word formed by a combination of semantic and phonetic components.
*Tie-ting* (iron ingot): According to the *Shuowen*, this refers to raw copper or iron. *Wu-ban* (scarless): Pronounced as *pan*;
it means to select one that is free of spots or blemishes and has no scars. This refers to using a fine, new blade that has been empowered through the ritual application of the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-mantra*.

*San-lei* (the *lei* pronounced as in *le-deng*): According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, *lei* means "to grasp" (*gǎn*). The *Jixùn* states that when wood is on four sides, it has *lei*. The *Shuowén* defines *lei* as "corners and edges," written with the radical for wood (*mu*) and the phonetic *lèng*; alternatively, it may be written with the radical for grain (*huó*) as *léng*. The pronunciation of *gǎn* is *gū*.

*The Sutra on the Essential Method for the Recitation of the Universal Buddha-Uṣṇīṣas*, one fascicle. *The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the One-Syllable Cakravartin Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Dhāraṇī*. Regarding the character "yǎn" (險) [in the title]: The *Kǎoshēng* (Investigation of Sounds) states it refers to the precipitous cliffs along mountain torrents. The *Shuowén* (Explanation of Words) defines it as the high edge of a mountain, composed of the radical "yè" (屵) and the phonetic "guī" (圭); "yè" is pronounced *wǔgè* (五割), and the following [radical] is pronounced *xǔjiǎn* (許撿). Jia’s commentary on the *Guóyuè* (Discourses of the States) says it means "perilous. The *Yùpiān* (Jade Lexicon) says it means "obstructed and difficult. According to the *Gōngjīn Zhèngzì* (Orthodox Characters of Antiquity and Today), it is composed of the radical "fù" (阜) and the phonetic "qiān" (僉). This is the Great Practice.

The character for *xiàn* (釧) is pronounced with the *liàn* rhyme; this has already been explained previously in the "Phonetic Meanings" (*Yinyì*) section of this fascicle. The text of the sutra uses the character *guàn* (串), which is incorrect;

it is not the character *xiàn*. The character for *huītūi* (花堆) is pronounced with the *huí* rhyme; according to the *Kǎoshēng*, it means "lofty. The sutra uses the characters *bù* (埠) or *dǔn* (垖), neither of which is correct.

*Nǔxī* (乳𪌘): The character *xī* is pronounced *kǒu fǎn* (口反). It refers to a cake made by mixing cow’s milk with flour and cooking it in ghee and oil. In the sutras, it is sometimes written as *shí zuò dòu* (食作餖) or *zuò tǔn* (作飩), but these are both vulgar characters and incorrect.
*Zhǐbù* (指㧙): The character *bù* is pronounced *biàn miè fǎn* (便蔑反); its meaning has already been fully explained in the preceding text.

Susiddhikara Sūtra, Volume One, Part One. Regarding the characters in the mantra *poṇaye*: the first character is pronounced with the initial *po* reversed (as *bā*) and the final *e* as *yi*. The second character is pronounced with the initial *na* reversed (as *ngeng*) and the final *e* as *yi*.
The sounds of the two syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* are of one kind; they are the sound of a bull’s roar from the throat, which is likewise difficult to articulate.
The tone *zhì zhēng* (制徵) corresponds to the Sanskrit name for the Vajragarbha Messenger (*Vajragarbhadūta*).
In the mantra *HŪṂ*, the character *he* (訶) is pronounced with the retroflex *ṛ* sound (各反).
"Axils" (*yè*)—pronounced with the *ying* (盈) and *yi* (益) finals—refers to the two armpits.

Regarding the navel (*qí*), it may also be written as *zhī* (齊); since each mantra possesses its own original phonetic value, these are not transcribed phonetically here, but are instead rendered according to the standard reading of the scripture.

*Bēi* (upper tone) for *bēi*. According to the *Erya*, the *bēi* resembles a bear (*xiónghú*) but is yellowish-white in color. Guo Pu says it resembles a bear with a long head and tall legs; it is fierce and powerful, capable of uprooting trees, and is called a *jiāxiónghú* (boar-bear) in the region west of the Passes. *Xióng* (lower tone) for *xióng*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that this beast resembles a pig, dwells in the mountains, and hibernates during winter. During hibernation, it licks its own paws, which resemble human hands; these are called *fán*. It is the most delicious among meats, though difficult to cook until done. *Hàn* is pronounced *hé ān* (rhyme). *Zhì* is pronounced *chén lì*. *Fán* is pronounced *fán*. *Jiā* is pronounced *jiā*.

*Tiào* (pronounced *xiào* in the rhyme section of the *Yīnyùn*; the *Yīngyùn* states it means "to leap over" or "to traverse"). It is sometimes written as *chào*. In the canonical text, it is written with the radical for "foot" (*zú*) and pronounced *tiáo*, which does not accord with the meaning of the scripture.

*Nǔoxíng* (pronounced *huáwǎ* [actually *luǒ*]; borrowed for its sound to avoid vulgar taboos; its original pronunciation is *luóguǒ*). It means "naked," "bare-bodied," or "exposed. It is sometimes written with the radical for "body" (*shēn*) as *nuǒ* or with the radical for "clothing" (*yī*) as *luǒ*; both mean to have the body exposed without clothing. This is a word formed by combining semantic and phonetic components (*xíngshēng zì*).
The character for *cóng* (onion) and *suàn* (garlic)—the latter pronounced *suàn* with the final tone—is composed of the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) and the element "to calculate" (*suàn*).
The character for *luó* (celery) and *pú*—the latter pronounced with the *péng* and *běi* finals—is a root vegetable.
The character for *zào* (bronze)—pronounced *chuī* with the departing tone (*qùshēng*)—has already been explained previously.
*Cháng*: (The character for "bed" is pronounced with the *tān* and *dá* rhymes; it refers to a bed from Shǔ with curved legs. A bed that is narrow and long is called a *tà*. *Ròu kǒu*:

(The character for "mouth" is pronounced with the *sōu* and *zhòu* rhymes. The *Yùnyīng* states it means to wash and cleanse the mouth. The character for *zhòu* is pronounced *zè jiù*; the character for *dí* is pronounced *dí*.)
The index finger holds the *nirbhaṅga* (the "reversed-leaf" seed).

Regarding the *ulūka-lakṣaṇa* (the "owl-characterized") seed from the western region: its seeds are arranged like the pits of fruit, with sizes ranging from those like cherry pits to small pellets; some are purple in color. These are called *vajra-bīja* (Vajra-seeds) and are suitable for making rosaries. Those who recite mantras belonging to the Vajra Family should use these beads, as they are extremely hard and durable.

The character for *huán* (ring) is composed of "metal" (*jīn*) on the left and "ring" (*huán*) on the right; it is not used in this [specific] sense. The character for "correct" (*zhèng*) is composed of "jade" (*yù*).

The character for *shū* (comb), meaning to comb the hair, is pronounced *shū*. *Jùn* (to gather) is pronounced with the first tone as *jūn* (君殞反). This is a transliteration of a Sanskrit term whose literal meaning is not sought.
The word for *pāṭala* flower (the first character pronounced as *wēn* with the *gǔ* tone reversal) has already been explained in the Sanskrit.
The word for *utpala* flower (the second character pronounced as *jié* with the *yán* tone reversal) is also a Sanskrit term;

the characters *tān* (first character pronounced as *tǎn* with the *nán* tone reversal) and *dùn* (second character pronounced as *dōng* with the *hún* tone reversal) are Sanskrit phonetics that do not convey a literal meaning.
Regarding "dāmalā" (耽忙羅): the scriptural text writes it as "tan" (耽) derived from "flesh" (肉), which is incorrect and does not form a valid character.

It refers to the coconut fruit (椰子果), pronounced "yeché" (野遮); it is a type of tree fruit that is abundant in Guangzhou. Its leaves are suitable for making mats and are very soft; its rind is fit for making ropes and lashings for ships, as it resists rotting. The fruit itself is exceptionally delicious and contains a juice as sweet as honey. The fruit has a hard shell that can be used for a wine ladle. The scriptural text writes it as "can" (𦳃) derived from "grass" (草), which is incorrect.
*Zhìzǐ* (柹子): The pronunciation is *shì*. It is the name of a fruit; it is as large as a fist and is red. *Dòuhòu* (豆䜸): The pronunciation of *hòu* is *hòu* (with the *gòu* rhyme).

It is the name of a medicinal herb. *Suxidi Jing*, Scroll 2, Scroll Lower: *Hùlù* (鶻𩪉): The upper character is pronounced *gǔ* and the lower character is pronounced *lù*. It is a bird that follows the sun; another name for it is *lǎocāng*. It belongs to the class of wild geese (*hángàn*), and its shape is like a crane, being blue-green in color.
"Huì" (暈) [upper tone yùn]: a halo around the sun or moon; [lower tone hóng]: a rainbow. "Kùn" (困): fine rain; the shadow of the sun. "Ēr zhǐ" (二指): [pronounced chǐ gé fǎn];
the span measured by the opening of the hands from the tips of the index fingers to the middle fingers.

Xiān (銛): Pronounced with the upper radical *xián* (閻) and the phonetic *lì* (利); it means sharp. It is composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic "tongue" (*shé*). Its appearance in the *Jīng* (經) as *qiān* (籤) is incorrect. Chà (剗): Pronounced with the lower radical *chǎn* (察盞). According to the *Yùnyīng* (韻英), it means to shave or pare away. It is composed of the radical "knife" (*dāo*) and the phonetic *zēn* (戔). The sound of *zēn* is that of *zé* (賾), meaning limit or boundary.

*Śòu* (鑠) is a transliteration of the Sanskrit term; in the Tang [translation] it means "spear. *Zhìbǎo* (置棓) is a transcription of the Sanskrit term; in the Tang [translation] it means "fire-stick" (*danda*). *Juānsū* (㪻酥) refers to the ladle used for scooping clarified butter (*ghṛta*); *yǎo* (舀) is pronounced *yáo* (with the minor tone) and is a compound character formed from shape and sound.

*Chángzhé* (常斫) is the second character [of the following term]. *Śòu* (鑠): Radical 169, phonetic *shè*. *Zhì* (置): Radical 117, phonetic *zhì*. *Bǎo* (棓): Radical 75, phonetic *páng*. *Juān* (㪻): Radical 120, phonetic *juàn*. *Sū* (酥): Radical 130, phonetic *sū*. *Yǎo* (舀): Radical 120, phonetic *yáo*. *Cháng* (常): Radical 40, phonetic *cháng*. *Zhé* (斫): Radical 65, phonetic *zhé*. *Xíngshēngzì* (形聲字): A compound character formed from semantic and phonetic components.
*Krī* (pronounced with a retroflex *ṛ*, as indicated by the character 唎; the following character 唎 is also pronounced with a retroflex).
*Dhīra* (the first character is pronounced with a level tone on *dān*; it is derived from "flesh" and "to pass through," not from "eye").
*Ni* (劓): Regarding the phonetic analysis, *ni* means to cut off the nose; thus, it refers to the punishment of nose-cutting. *Chāng* (倀):

[The character] is pronounced *zhēng* (更) or *zhǎn* (展); it refers to painting images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. This scripture uses the character with the "wood" radical and the "zhēn" (貞) component as *zhēn* (楨), which is incorrect; this has been the usage throughout antiquity and the present.
“Ruan” (耎) [the character is pronounced with the initial *chū* and the final *-yǎn*; it means “weak. In the sutra, it is written as “ruan” (軟), which is incorrect].
3. Scroll Lower: *Susiddhikara Sūtra*, Middle Scroll. “Yun” (熅) and “nuan” (煖) [the former is pronounced *wēn* and the latter *nǔ duǎn*; both are phono-semantic compounds].

*Āvehi*: the first character is pronounced as *yì* (翳) with the initial *yī* (伊) and the final *xīng* (馨); the second character is pronounced as *jì* (計) with the final *xīng* (馨) and *yí* (移). This phrase is a Sanskrit term; in the Tang language it is called the "phrase of summoning," meaning "come. *Xiào* (斆):
the first character is pronounced as *zhào* (之) and *hū* (乎), and the second character is pronounced as *jiào* (教) and *shēng* (聲). *Xiào* is synonymous with "learning" (*xué*).
*Mura* (the "nu" and "ge" in the rhyme reflect the Sanskrit pronunciation; this term is a transliteration from Sanskrit; in the Tang period it was translated as *mudrā*, meaning "seal-gesture").
*Kṣipati* (the "qiao" and "jia" reflect the rhyme; it means to pinch with the fingernails).
*Kṣveḍita* (the first syllable "kǐng" rhymes with *qīngyǐng*; the second syllable "kài" rhymes with *kāi'ài*; it refers to the passage of breath through the throat, i.e., clearing the throat).
*Quanjù* (蹲踞): the first character is pronounced *cún*;
the second is pronounced *jū* with the *yù* rhyme. *Sūwěn* (蘇搵): both ends are submerged (*mòrù*) [in water].

*Bītiě* (鑌鐵): the first character is pronounced *bīn*. This refers to "Bin-iron" produced from foreign lands such as Kāpiśī, made by combining various types of iron or consisting of the most refined and sharp iron—the very best among metals.
The character *shā* (樧) is used in the sense of "rafters" (*shìjiè*) and is pronounced with the final *-fǎn* (反).

The character *jiàn* (𨊾), with the upper part pronounced *gāng* (岡) or alternatively written as *jiàn* (㭎), and the lower part pronounced *yuán-xiàn* (緣縣) as a compound, refers to the outer rafters of a wheel-axle.

Regarding the character *bǐ* (𭪷): it is explained as "bird feathers" (*niǎo líng*), and the *Yùnyīng* states it means "bird plumage. It is sometimes written as *bǐ* (󲩰), but this is incorrect according to the *Jīngcóng*. As for the upper character *bǐ* (𭪷), it is suspected of being an error; the reason it is not phonetically glossed remains unclear, as it is uncertain which bird it represents.

*Pān-jì* (瘢跡): The upper character is pronounced *pán*. It refers to scars from sores, burns, branding, and the like. Both characters are read as *xià* (with the tone of *xiè*, *xī*, or *yè*) and mean "to sink" or "to settle. The lower character is pronounced *diàn* (with the tone of *diàn*). *Susiddhikara Sūtra*: Regarding the term *qiāng-shào* (槍矟), the upper character is pronounced *qī* (with the tone of *yáng*).

Alternatively, it may be written with the character for *máo* (spear). The *Kǎo Shēng* (Examination of Sounds) states that *qiāng* refers to a long spear. The *Cāng Jié Piān* (Cangjie’s Lexicon) states it is a weapon with sharp points at both ends, having a blade on top and a handle below. The lower character is pronounced *shuāng* (with the tone of *zhuō*). According to the *Guǎng Yǎ* (Guangya), *shào* is also a spear. It is not correct to write this with the character for *fú* (*fú*). *Note on the text*: The passage provided contains phonetic glosses and philological notes regarding the characters for "scars" (*pānji*), the title of the *Susiddhikara Sūtra*, and the term for a "spear" (*qiāngshào*). The translation reflects these technical details as they appear in the source.
Regarding "diào shǒu" (掉手)—the *Jīng* (經) reads "tiāo shǒu" (挑手), which is incorrect. "Cì mù" (刺木): the initial radical is pronounced as "zì" (恣).

The *Fānyán* (方言) states that when grasses or trees have thorns that injure people, they are called "cì. The *Shuōwén* (說文) defines it as "the point of wood. Thorns (*jì*) exist on sour jujubes (*suānzǎo*) and soap pods (*zàojiè*); this wood is used for such purposes. It is composed of the radical "knife" (刀) and the phonetic "shù" (束).

In the Susiddhikara Sūtra, the character for "ascending" (騗) in the phrase "ascending on horseback" (騗上馬) is pronounced with the initial *mian* (面) and the final *kao* (考), meaning to leap onto a horse from one's body. The standard orthography of ancient and modern times uses the "horse" radical with the phonetic *pian* (扁); the pronunciation of *pian* is that of *bian* (辮).
*Juǎn* (㕮咀): The first character is pronounced *fǔ* (上音甫); the second is pronounced *jiāng yǔ* (下將與反). *Xié lè* (斜勒):

The first character is pronounced *xié yé* (夕耶反). This is a vulgar character; its correct form is written with the radical *yī* (衣) and the phonetic *yá* (牙), forming *xié* (󲥌). The gloss states it means "irregular clothing" or "a shoulder strap. It is also written as *xié* (邪).

The two "ge" (哥) are written as one character, "ge" (箇), in the Classics. The *Kao sheng* states it is a particle. Since bamboo is measured by "ge" and wood by "mei," it is derived from the radical for bamboo. "Two ge" refers to the two Heavenly Kings.

The character 㮀 (pronounced with the *qián* rhyme) is glossed in the *Kǎośēng* as "a wooden box" (*mùjiè*); it is also written as 椷, both being the standard forms in the canonical texts. When written alone as 函, it refers to the name of the Guanyu Pass; this [usage] does not accord with the meaning of the scripture.

The character for "umbrella" (sàn) is pronounced *sǎn* and is a vernacular variant; it is correctly written as 繖蓋 (*sàng gài*). An explanation of this was already provided in the first fascicle of the *Uṣṇīṣavijaya-dhāraṇī Sūtra*.

Regarding the character for "to sell" (*shòu*), the *Shuōwén Jiězì* states its sound is *shòu kǎo*. It means to complete the sale of goods. In the dictionary, "sell" (*shòu*) is synonymous with "buy. It refers to a person buying and selling, or taking away what has been sold. This is a compound character formed by the semantic union of the radicals 隹 (*zhuī*) and 口 (*kǒu*).

"Lǒu" (捋) is pronounced with the upper radical *lù* and the suffix *guā* (反). It is also written as "shǎo" (󲮣), meaning to take the breast milk by stroking it with the hand. "Shǎo" is pronounced *gōu*, meaning to wait for.

"Tiějué" (鐵橛) is pronounced with the upper radical *tiě* and the suffix *quán* (權) and *yuè* (月); the *Jíxùn* (集訓) states that "jué" (橛) refers to a wooden stake. The version in the sutra using "shuān" (栓) is incorrect.

"Qinshou" (禽獸) is a collective term for birds, with "qin" (禽) pronounced as Lin (林) in the *Yunjí* (韻集), and "shou" (獸) pronounced as Shòu (守呪) in the *Guìyuàn Zhūhuì* (桂苑珠藪), which states it is a collective term for wild animals. According to this, those with two feet, feathers, and the ability to fly are called "qin" (birds); those with four feet, fur, and the habit of running wild are called "shou" (beasts). The reading "mǎoshòu" (𤢌狩) in the original scripture is incorrect.

The Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī Sūtra. Translated by Du Xingyi at the beginning of the Tang dynasty. Regarding the character for "pig" (豬): it is pronounced with the "zhu" rhyme (the second tone), while the common vulgar form is written as "zhu" (豬). This is the correct orthography from ancient times to the present. As for the character used for "sūtra" (經) here, which is written as "jiong" (𧳯) with the radical "zhai" (豸), this is incorrect; it is a compound character formed from a semantic and a phonetic element.
"癲" (diān) refers to the symptoms of epilepsy and other such ailments;
"幢" (chuáng) and "繖" (sǎn)—the latter pronounced with the initial *zhù* and final *jiāng*, and the radical *jīn* with the phonetic *sāng* and *dàn*—refer to ceremonial canopies.
"䖵" (guǒn), with the upper part pronounced *kūn* and the lower part *zhú* and *róng*, is a vulgar character for "insects" (*kūnchóng*), which appears as such in the scriptures.

The *Buddhoṣṇīṣavijaya-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, translated by Buddhapālita, together with the preface. In the preface: "Jing" (驚) [pronounced with the initial *g* and the rhymes *e* and *que*] means "to startle"; it is also written as "e" (愕). It is derived from the radical for "heart" (*xin*). It signifies being taken aback or startled.

The term *mǎngshé* (蟒蛇) is read with the pinyin *máng* and *bǎng* as its fanqie; the *Erya* states, "Mǎng is the king of snakes (*wángshé*). Guo Pu’s commentary notes that because it is the largest among snakes, it is called the "king" (*wáng*). According to the *Kuodi zhi*, the *huánglóu* snake has the character "king" (*wáng*) on its throat and the character "king" (*wáng*) on its head; these are all of the *mǎngshé* lineage. The *bāshé* (巴蛇) is precisely this [same species].

Preface to the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-sitātapatrā-anantarya-parivarta-dhāraṇī Sūtra* Translated again by Yancong and Rizi The *zhēnquè* (鸇雀) [is pronounced zhàn rán]. The *Erya* states: "Chénfēng is the *zhēn*. Guo Pu says it belongs to the category of hawks (*yào*). The *Mencius* says: "The *zhēn* drives away the sparrows; Jie and Zhou drove away Tang and Wu. It is a bird that eats sparrows, belonging to the class of hawks and falcons.

"Jǐn" (僅) is merely a phonetic approximation. The commentary by He on the *Gōngyáng Zhuàn* states that "jǐn" means inferior; according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means little. The standard character for both ancient and modern usage consists of the radical "person" (亻) and the phonetic "jǐn" (堇), which is pronounced "jǐn. It is also sometimes written as "yǒu" (㝻).

The character *chóu* (儔): at the top, *zhǎngliú* (長流); according to the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲), it means "companion. The *Yùnquán* (韻詮) says it means "who" or "equal," formed from the radical *rén* (人) with *shòu* (壽) as the phonetic. The lower part has the pronunciation *jié*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Lìjì* says it means "pure," formed from the radical *shuǐ* (水) with *jié* (絜) as the phonetic.

*Dì* (丁計反) is a phonetic category meaning "fruit-stalk" (*guǒbí*). *Yùnyīng* states that for plants and trees, the fruit is attached at the *dì*. The *Shuōwén* says it is the "peduncle" (*dāng*) of the melon. The *Cāngpiān* says it is the "stalk-base" (*zhuàn*). There is also a reading as *dài*, which is a vulgar usage and not the correct character for "earth" (*dì*).

The character *jù* (齬): the upper radical is pronounced "zhù" and the lower part is "yǔ. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as "teeth not aligning with one another"; it also refers to high and low places where waters are uneven, or to jagged cliffs. Both characters follow the form of the teeth as the semantic component and the shape as the phonetic component.

Regarding the character *qí* (祺) pronounced as *qí*: Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states that *qí* refers to auspicious omens (*zhēngxiáng*). The *Mao Shi* commentary on "longevity" (*shòukǎo*) says *qí* means "auspicious" (*jí*). The *Wenzi Dianshuō* states it means "auspiciousness" (*xiáng*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the character for longevity like *qí* is composed of the radical "altar" (*shì*) and the phonetic component "its" (*qí*), forming a character based on its shape and sound.
The character *nǜ* (恧) means "shame" (*xiāng*) for a woman; it is a dialectal term for shame. To feel ashamed of oneself is called *nǜ*; this is a compound character (*huìyì zì*). *Rèn-rǎn* (荏苒):

the first character is pronounced *ěr zhěn* (耳枕) and the second has the sound *rǎn*. According to the commentary, *rèn-rǎn* signifies following along indolently without realizing that time is filling up; this is a character formed by phonetic-semantic transference (*zhuǎnzhù zì*).

*Xiàn wǎn* (歎惋): The phonetic transcription is *wǎn* (剜), with the tone of a sigh of lamentation. Dictionaries of characters state it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "wǎn" (*shēng*).

In the *Suíshèng fódǐng tuóluóní jìngchú yèzhàng jīng* (The Sūtra of the Most Victorious Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Dhāraṇī for Purifying Karmic Obstructions), translated twice in the Eastern Capital by Divākara: *Cuò lòu* (矬陋): The upper character is pronounced *zuò* (和) with a broad tone; it means short or stunted, composed of the radical "arrow" (*shǐ*) and the phonetic "zuò" (*shēng*). The lower character is pronounced *dòu* (豆). Gù Yěwáng states that *lòu* means ugly. In his commentary on the *Chuci*, Wang explains it as "small. It is also written as *zhuō* (󱾈), with the same meaning.
"Zuo" (笮) [pronounced *zhēng gé*]: according to the *Yùpiān*, it means to press; according to the *Zìshū*, it means to constrain, written with the "bamboo" radical (*zhú*).
"Laṅkā" [pronounced *lèng qiá*]: a Sanskrit term meaning "to bind."

Regarding the character *kuāi* (乖反), the *Kǎośēng* (考聲) states that *kuāi* refers to the mouth being crooked or distorted. Although the scriptural text uses the character with the "mouth" radical (*quāi*), the common vulgar form (*kuāi*) is more appropriate;

it should properly be written simply as *kuāi*. *Fóding zūnshèng tuólóní jīng jì* (Record of the Translation Date of the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*): The *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing. [This includes] the *Wúzì gè yīnxùn jì* (Record of the Sounds and Explanations of Each Character). *Fóding zūnshèng tuólóní jīng fānyì niándài xiānhòu* (Chronology of the Translation of the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*), compiled by Huilin. At the very beginning, in the fourth year of the *Bǎodìng* era of Emperor Wǔ of the Northern Zhou dynasty, the year of Jiashen (564 CE), the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānayaśas...

At the Si Tianwang Temple in the Old City of Chang’an, he translated the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī* together with the *Method for Recitation and Its Efficacy*, in one fascicle and five sheets; the scholar Bǎo Yǒng served as the scribe.
According to the *Kaihuang Sanbao Lu*, this is said to be the first translation.

Later, in the first year of the Yifeng era of the Great Tang Emperor Tianhuang, the Brahman monk Buddhapāli arrived at Mount Wutai to pay homage to the Great Sage. Upon seeing a manifestation of Mañjuśrī, he was instructed to return to the Western Regions to retrieve the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Buddhapiṭaka-uṣṇīṣavijaya-dhāraṇī-sūtra*.

In the fourth year of the Yifeng era, the year of Yi-mao (659 CE), after returning from the Western Regions with the scriptures he had obtained, he presented a detailed report upon reaching Chang’an. By imperial decree, Tripitaka Master Sūryavarman was invited to translate the Sanskrit manuscripts within the palace; Du Xingyi, the Director of the Guest Reception Office, served as the scribe. This version consists of seven fascicles and is the second translation.

Characters bearing the temple names or the imperial name were avoided and not written. An imperial edict permitted the inclusion of Sanskrit manuscripts within [the palace] without their being removed. On this account, a copy was transcribed and bestowed upon a foreign monk; thirty bolts of silk were granted, but Pali refused the silk and instead requested the Sanskrit manuscript, which the edict then ordered to be returned to him.

Buddhapāli obtained the sūtra and traveled west to Xizhou Monastery, where he sought out the Chinese monk Shunzhen, who was proficient in Sanskrit, to translate it together. This is also a version translated in the fourth year of the Yifeng era; it consists of eight pages and is described in the preface to the sūtra as the third translation.
