Buddhapāli took the Sanskrit manuscript into Mount Wutai and has not emerged from there until the present day. Furthermore, in the first year of the Yongchun era, the year Renwu (682 CE), the Tripiṭaka Master Rizi translated this sūtra once again. The śramaṇa Yancong acted as the scribe for the oral transmission. This is the version translated by Du Xingyi, in which words that were intentionally omitted or concealed in the original text have been written out; thus it consists of eight pages and is the fourth translation. Moreover, at the beginning of the sūtra, Yancong’s preface states:

Furthermore, in the first year of the Chuigong era, the year of Yiyou (685 CE), the Tripitaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha accompanied the imperial entourage to the Eastern Capital (Luoyang) and again translated the *Buddhoṣṇīṣavijaya-nāma-karmāvaraṇaviśodhani-sūtra* in fourteen folios. This work fully explains the causes and conditions by which the Devaputra Sunirmita experienced the fruition of his past verbal karma, as well as the rules for its recitation and upholding; it is the fifth translation.

Later, in the fourth year of the Jinglong era of Emperor Zhongzong, the year of Gengxu (710 CE), Tripitaka Master Yijing translated it once more at Jianfu Temple in Chang’an; this is the sixth translation, consisting of six sheets.

Later, in the tenth year of the Kaiyuan era of Emperor Xuanzong, the year of Renxu (742 CE), the Tripitaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha translated the *Buddhoṣṇīṣavijayā-yoga-japa-vidhi* in two fascicles; this was the seventh translation.

Furthermore, in the second year of the Guangde era (the Jiachen year) of Emperor Daizong Wenwu, the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra (Bukong Daguangzhi) translated at the Great Xingshan Temple in Chang’an one fascicle of the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-vijayā-dhāraṇī-vidhi for Recitation and Offerings*, consisting of twenty sheets; the śramaṇa Feixi served as the scribe. This is the eighth translation.

Approximately two hundred years have passed since this sūtra was first brought forth, during which time it has been translated eight times. Regarding the *Mantra Recitation Method*, there are three distinct versions; however, only that translated by Śubhakarasiṃha includes the additional phrases. Within the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī*, eleven phrases and sixty-six characters have been added according to the ritual rules of the *Yogatantra*, which differ significantly from previous translations and exceed those found in other editions. As for the seven other translations, the number of characters in their dhāraṇīs is similar. When Huilin was compiling the phonetic glossaries (*yinyi*), he examined the chronological order of these translations and recorded them here to resolve the doubts of those scholars who find the matter overly complex. Recorded in the eighteenth year of the Zhenyuan era, the Renzi year (792 CE).

*Pēn-tì* (the first character pronounced *pǔ* with the tone *mèn*, the second pronounced *dì*). The *Kǎo Shēng* states that "sneezing" (*pēn-tì*) refers to the breath rushing through the nose and causing a sneeze. The *Yùn Jí* says it is "to snuff the nose and then sneeze. The *Shuō Wén* defines it as "a gust of breath"; it is a compound character formed from both semantic and phonetic components.

Regarding the character *wàn* (腕): the *Jíxùn* states it means "the hand is firm"; the *Shuōwén* defines it as "the joint at the back of the palm. The scriptural text uses the radical for meat (*ròu*), which is a vulgar form; the correct forms are those with the radical for moon (*yùè*), the character *chā*, or the radical for hand (*shǒu*).

*The Tattvasaṃgraha Sūtra*, Volume One. Regarding "Tattva" (底哩): the upper character *di* (丁) is pronounced with the *yi* (以) tone, while the lower character *li* (里) is a retroflex sound in Sanskrit. In the Tang language, it means "three," referring to the three types of *samaya*—namely, the Buddha Family, the Lotus Family, and the Vajra Family; thus it is called *tattvasamaya*.

The character *zhā* (磔) is read as *shè* (上陟革反). This has already been fully explained in the second fascicle of the *Vairocana Recitation Method*. It is composed of the radicals for "stone" (石) and "railing" (桀). The character *jìn* (近) is read as *yuán* (緣絹反) with the departing tone;

the *Zìjí xùn* (字集訓) states that it refers to the four edges of clothing. The character *chuán* (椽) in the scripture’s text—composed of the radical for "wood" (木)—is a phonetic loan and does not accord with the meaning of the scripture.
The term *jiǎn* (㪻), with the pronunciation *jué yuàn fǎn*, has already been fully explained above in the first fascicle of the *Susiddhikara-prcchā-sūtra*.

Regarding the insertion of the character *chā* (插) with the pronunciation *chǔ jiǎ fǎn*, the *Shēnglèi* (Classified Phonology) states: "To insert means to prick and enter. The correct orthography for this character from ancient times to the present consists of the radical *shǒu* (hand) and the phonetic component *zhà* (臿), where *zhà* has the same pronunciation as above. It is composed of the elements *qiān* (千) and *jiù* (臼), where *jiù* has the pronunciation *jiù*.

*Shu* (pronounced *sōu*, with the second tone; glossed as "to contract" in the *Guoyu*). The commentary to the *Guoyu* states that *shu* means "exhaustion" or "retreat. Song Zhong’s commentary to the *Taixuanjing* states that *shu* means "to stop. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines *shu* as "to contract," formed from the radical for "silk thread" (*mi*) and the phonetic component *xiù*.
The character above is *jǐ* (with the phonetic component *tōu* and the radical *kǒu*) and was already explained in the *Pūrvamastaka-cakra-sūtra*.

Regarding the character *lù*: - The upper part is pronounced *jīng* (with the phonetic *jìn*) and *gù* Yewáng states it means "gradual" (*jiàn*) or "to sink" (*chén*). - The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *zēng* (from *yòu* and *xué*), but in current vernacular usage it is simplified. - The correct ancient and modern form is from *shuǐ* (water) and *lù* (the lower part). *Gù* Yewáng states that *lù* means "to drain" (*lì*) or "to remove water. - According to the *Erya*, it means "exhausted" (*jié*); according to the *Fangyan*, it means "dried up" (*hé*) or "extreme" (*jí*); and according to the *Guangya*, it means "complete" (*jìn*). These are all characters formed through both semantic and phonetic components.

Volume 2, Part 2. There are no characters in this section requiring phonetic glosses. Regarding the *Dhāraṇī-vinaya-sūtra*, also known as the *Mantra-vinaya*: the term "silk" (*zēng*) refers generally to woven cloth; it is composed of the radical "silk thread" (*mì*) with the phonetic component "tsêng" (*zēng*). The lower character is pronounced "luò" (*luò*). Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Shanhai jing* states that "lò" means to wind or encircle; it is a transitive character.

Regarding the bow and the *shao* (lance): the character for *shao* is formed with "wood" (*mu*) as the radical and "jing" (*jing*) reversed; this is the vernacular form. This has already been explained in detail in the *Xiǎndì jīng* (Siddhi-sādhana Sūtra). As for "hawk" (*yīng*) and "falcon" (*yào*):

the former is pronounced with the initial *ji* reversed (i.e., *jīng*), while the latter is pronounced with the initial *yu* reversed (i.e., *zhào*). The *Zuǒchuán* states that the Lord of *Shuǎngjiū* (the Hawk-bird) served as the Minister of Justice. The *Guǎngyá* says they are birds of prey capable of seizing foxes and hares. Regarding the character for the latter, it is pronounced *zhào*. Gu Yěwáng states that the falcon resembles a hawk but is smaller. The *Guǎngyá* further identifies it as the *tí*, *yù*, or *zǐlóngtuō*; it is a type of falcon. In fact, falcons belong to the same category as hawks and *zhēn* (kestrels), having many different names. The pronunciation of *tí* is *tí*, and the pronunciation of *yù* is *yù*.

*Kǐng* (上): read as *qīng yǐng* (輕郢). The *Cāngjié piān* states that *kǐng* is a sound. In the *Zhuāngzi*, it says "he coughed and cleared his throat by its side. The *Shuōwén* states that *kǐng* is also *kài* (咳); it is composed of the radical *yán* (言) and the phonetic *shěng* (省). *Kài* (下): read as *kāi ài* (開愛). The *Kǎoshēng* states that *kài* means to cough (*sòu*). The *Shuōwén* [further] states it is composed of the radical *qiàn* (欠) and the phonetic *hài* (亥).

The first character, *chóu* (躊), is pronounced with the initial *zhù* (直) and the final *liú* (留), though it may also be pronounced *chí* (池); the second character, *chú* (躇), has the phonetic value of *chú* (除) and also *chú* (厨). According to the *Mao Shi Zhuan* (毛詩傳): "Loving him yet not seeing him, I toss my head and hesitate (*chóuchú*). Now, *chóuchú* refers to being hesitant and indecisive. The *Guangyi* (廣疋) likewise states that *chóuchú* means hesitation and indecision; it further states that it is synonymous with *zhíshǒu* (蹢䠱), *duòzhū* (跢跦), and so forth.

The Subāhuparipṛcchā-sūtra (The Scripture on the Questions of the Youth Subāhu), Volume One. *Gài* (溉): The upper radical is *jī* (機, pronounced as in "machine") and the lower radical is *guàn* (官, pronounced as in "official"). According to the *Kǎo Shēng* (Examination of Sounds), it means to pour or to soak. Gu Yěwáng states that *gài* is synonymous with pouring down (*zhù*). It is also said to mean to irrigate (*wò*). The *Shuō Wén* (Explaining Simple and Analyzing Compound Characters) takes both radicals as *shuǐ* (water).
The character for *hé* (river) is pronounced with the initial *yì* and final *-fǎn*. The *Yùpiān* states it means "the edge of water"; it is a phono-semantic compound.

The character for *mìzhì* (dense/compact) is pronounced with the initial *chí* and final *-lì*. In Zheng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì*, *zhì* is synonymous with *mì*. The *Guǎnyá* states it means "to reach. Regarding the correct orthography of ancient and modern times: *zhì* refers to being refined and subtle; it denotes density and compactness, as well as fineness. It is formed with the radical *mì* (silk/thread) and the phonetic *zhì*.

*Méngmèn* (瞢悶): "Mèng" is pronounced with the *shàng* tone as *mòu bēng*. The *Jíxùn* states that it means "confusion" (*luàn*) and also "depression" (*mèn*). The *Shuōwén* says it refers to unclear vision. It is composed of the radicals *mù* (苜) and *xuán* (䀏). *Mù* is pronounced *wǔ fú*; *xuán* is pronounced *xiàn*. It also contains the radical *mì* (冖), which is pronounced *bāo*.

*Kǎo* (pronounced *gāo lǎo fǎn*, with the tone of *kǎo*) is defined as the stalks of grain such as millet and sorghum. Gu Yewang states that *kǎo* refers to the stalks of grain, which are grasses. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is a word formed by a semantic radical and a phonetic component. The second character, *gān* (pronounced *gān yì fǎn*), is glossed in the *Zhuozhuan* commentary as being synonymous with *kǎo*. It is the correct orthography for the stalk of grain; it takes the "grain" radical (*禾*) and the phonetic component "drought" (*旱*). It also refers to the straw of rice.

The term "péntì" (噴嚏) is pronounced *pǔ* (upper radical) with the reverse sound *mèn*, and *dīng* (lower radical) with the reverse sound *jì*. This has already been fully explained in the preceding *Siddhi Sūtra*.

Regarding "huíhú" (𪈧鶘), the upper character is pronounced *huì* with the reverse sound *yùn*, and the lower character is pronounced *hú*. The *Kǎo Shēng* states that it refers to a strange bird; both the modern and ancient standard characters are compounds formed from both semantic and phonetic elements.

2. Middle Volume of the *Subahu-sutra*, Middle Volume. The character *bao* (󰚏) [is pronounced with the initial *yì* and the final *yán*; it is a sound of *kǎo*]. *Bao* means to ward off evil; according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means to suppress and subdue. The *Jixùn* states that it also means to fix or pin down. Examining this, *bao* is also synonymous with *dǎo* (prayer). When one prays to spirits, demons, ghosts, or deities to cause them to act as malevolent influences (*suì*) toward humans—whether by creating talismanic scripts and calling out the person's name, or by fashioning an image of that person and burying it in a shrine, beneath a hearth, or at a crossroads—this is termed *baodǎo* (warding-off prayer).

*Chī-tì* (眵涕): The first character, *chī* (叱), is pronounced as in "chì" (叱). The *Yùnquán* (韻詮) states it refers to the discharge (*chī*) in the eyes. The *Jixùn* (集訓) states it is the congealed secretion of the eyes. The *Shuowen* (說文) defines it as *méngdōu* (瞢兜); it refers to an injury to the corners of the eyes (*mèi*). It is composed of the radical "eye" (目) and the phonetic element "chǐ" (侈) in abbreviated form. The pronunciation of *chǐ* is *chǐ* (齒); *mèi* (眥) is pronounced *jié* (接); *dōu* (兜) is pronounced *dǒu-sì* (斗俟).

The character *yūn* (熅) is pronounced with the initial *wěi* and the final *yún* according to the *Guǎngyǐ*. The *Guǎngyǐ* states that it means "radiant" (*huàn*). The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* says it means "a warm heat. The *Shuōwén Jiězì* defines it as "smoky vapor" (*yù yān*), formed from the radical *huǒ* (fire) and the phonetic *wūn*; *wūn* is pronounced *wēn*. It is incorrect to claim that the character is composed of *qiú*, *mǐng*, and *rì*.

Alternatively, regarding the character *shèng* (勝): the *Kǎo Shēng* states it means "to exceed" (*yú*). The *Guǎng Yá* states it means "to present as a gift" (*zèng*) or "to escort" (*sòng*). The *Shuō Wén* states it means "the mutual increase of things" or "a counterpart. It is composed of the radical *bèi* (貝) and the phonetic component of *shèng* (勝) with its lower portion omitted. This is the character.

3. *Subahu-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, Scroll Lower. Regarding the character 扠 (chā): the phonetic gloss states that "扠" means to strike a person with the fist; it is classified under the radical 木 (*mù*). Alternatively, it is written as 搋 from the character 虒, with the same pronunciation and meaning as above. The correct orthography for modern usage is 扠, with the radical 手 (*shǒu*) and the phonetic 叉 (*chā*). The character 搰 has the pronunciation *huó* (phonetic gloss: *hún-gǔ*).

Regarding the character *pò* (𢷏): the *Kǎośēng* (Examination of Sounds) states that "pò" means to strike with the hands and throw [something] to the ground. The *Wénzì Shìyào* (Essentials of Textual Explanations) states it means to fall from a height. It is written as *pò* in the sutra, but this is incorrect; the pronunciation *pǔbǔ* (普卜反) does not accord with the meaning of the sutra.

Regarding the term *mi* (謎): the upper radical is *mi* (迷), pronounced *piàn* (弊) in reverse; the phonetic component is *kǎo* (考). It refers to obscure speech used to delude others. The *Yùnlüè* (韻略) also calls it "obscure language" (*yìnyǔ* 隱語). The *Shēnglèi* (聲類) states that it is "obscure language that confuses people."

To "moisten" (mò): the rhyme dictionary *Wēnkùn* explains it as placing an object inside water; the *Kǎoshēng* says it means a pillar or being submerged in shallow water. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "submerging," following the radical for the hand with the phonetic element *wēn*; the pronunciation of *wēn* is like that of the character for "warm."

SHAN (𤓊): The upper radical is *páo* (皃); the *Kǎoshēng* states it is the sound of burning firewood or bamboo. The *Wénzì jílüè* says it is "fire blazing. The *Jìxùn* says it is "fire fierce. It may also be written as 󲛖, with the radical *huǒ* (火) and the phonetic *shàn* (󲛙). The lower part is read *zhàn* (戰). The *Pīcāng* says it means "blazing. The *Kǎoshēng* says it means "fire is intense. It may also be written with the radical *rén* (人) as 傓; the *Gōngjīn zhèngzì* uses the radical *huǒ* (火) with the phonetic *shàn* (扇).

The character for *bìlù* (篳篥) has the upper radical *bi* (必) and the lower radical *lín* (隣), with a phonetic value of one tone. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that *bìlù* is a musical instrument; the *Guǎngyá* (廣雅) writes it as *bī* (篐) or *bì* (篳), both of which are archaic and modern variants of the same character. It refers to a horn blown by the Qiang people to startle horses. The current text of the sutra uses the vulgar character *jìlì* (𧤅栗).

"Jin-zhu" (謹孎): the "d-ing-jiao-fan" (丁角反) indicates the phonetic reading. The *Cangjie pian* states that "jin-zhu" means a virtuous appearance; the *Shuowen jiezi* states it means a compliant appearance. It is composed of the radical "woman" (女) and the phonetic "shu" (屬). There is also a reading "zhong-lü-fan" (冡綠反), with the explanation being roughly the same, so it is not recorded again here.

*Piāo* (飈): The upper character is read as *biāo* (摽). The *Erya* states: "The *fúyáo* wind is called *piāo*. Guo Pu’s commentary notes: "*Piāo* refers to a violent wind blowing from above downward; it is also called *pǎo* (考), meaning a swift wind. Regarding *zìxiàérshàng* (自下而上): the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines *yíyáo* (𩖬颻) as wind, composed of the radical for wind with *yàn* (焱) as the phonetic component; *yàn* has the same pronunciation as above. *Yí* (𩖬) has the phonetic *fú* (符), and the lower character *kài* (揩) is pronounced *kè* (客). All are reversed [in their respective definitions].

The character for "to sell" (賣) is composed of "to walk" (行) and "mysterious" (玄) as its phonetic; it is pronounced *mai* (with the final *-ai* reversed). Alternatively, it is written with "speech" (言) as the phonetic, becoming *𧗳*. The character for "to bury" (*埋*) is pronounced *bai* (with the final *-ai* reversed); according to the *Shuowen*, it means "to take things out," being composed of "to go out" (出) and "price" (賈) as its phonetic. In current vernacular usage, it is written with "earth" (土), which is a corrupted variant form. Furthermore, the character for "to buy" (*買*) is a compound character formed by "four" (四) and "treasure" (貝); in current vernacular usage, it is erroneously written with "vessel" (皿), which is a mistaken corruption.

"Or *zhǎn* (輦) [is used as a vulgar character for the same sound]. In ancient script, it is correctly written with the radical 㠭 and the radical 衣 as 󲠾㠭; the phonetic component is the same as above. The *Kǎo Shēng* states that 󲞛 means 'to extend,' 'straight,' or 'to unfold. The text's version with the radical 手 as 搌 is incorrect."

*Juánjú* (踡跼): The first character is pronounced *juàn* (倦) and the second is pronounced *qióngyù* (卭獄). The *Bīcāng* states that it describes an appearance of being cramped and unable to stretch; it refers to walking with a hunched back. *Yìxī* (蜴蜥): The first character is pronounced *yì* (易) and the second is pronounced *xī* (昔).

The *Shuōwén* states that when it is on a house wall it is called *shǒugōng* (守宮, "guardian of the palace"), and when it is in the grasses and marshes it is called *yìxī*. Its cry is its own name, and it produces offspring by laying eggs from its mouth; both are examples of "form-and-sound" characters (*xíngshēng zì*).

Regarding "xián" (涎) [saliva]: the upper character is pronounced with the *xiáng* (祥) and *yán* (延) rhymes. The *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲) states it refers to the moisture in the mouth; the *Shuōwén* (說文) states it is the liquid of the mouth, composed of the radical "water" (水) and the phonetic component "qiàn" (欠). The version in the sutra uses "xián" (涎), which is a vulgar character. Regarding "wò" (臥) [lying down]: the lower character is pronounced with the *tǔ* (土) rhyme. Its explanation is identical to the upper character; both are phono-semantic compounds.

*Niè* (in *niè-dú*): The upper character is read as *jiān* with the *jié* rhyme; the canonical text uses the character for "mouth" (*kǒu*) to form it, which is a vulgar form. It is composed of "teeth" (*chí*) and a simplified form of "crush" (*kuài*) as its phonetic.

*Hè* (in *hè-yào*): The upper character is pronounced *hè* and the lower is pronounced *yào*; both characters in the canonical text are formed with "fire" (*huǒ*) and read as *hè-yào*. These are vulgar forms and not the standard orthography.

*Jùxīyē Dǎntuōló Jīng* (The *Kūṣmāṇḍa-hṛdaya-sūtra*). Regarding the character "kō" (窠) in the title: the upper part is pronounced with the *zhú* and *róng* finals; the *Jīng* (經) text writes it as "chóng" (虫), which is an error based on popular tradition. The lower part is pronounced with the *kǔ* and *huó* finals. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "kō" means an empty space; that which is in a burrow is called a "kō," while that which is in a tree is called a "cháo" (nest). It is composed of the radical "cave" (穴) and the phonetic "guǒ" (果).

“Xián” (鹹): The upper radical is 匣 (jiá, reversed). In the *Shàngshū*, “moistening downward produces saltiness” (*rùn xià zuò xián*). The *Shuōwén* states: “The flavor of the north. It is composed of 鹵 (lǔ) as the semantic component and 咸 (xián) as the phonetic component. The *Bīcāng* says: “It is alkaline soil. The *Kǎoshēng* says: “It is salty earth. This is a word formed by the combination of shape and sound. “Xià” (下): The lower radical is 甲 (jiǎ) with the final consonant 斬 (zhǎn). The *Pīcāng* says: “Alkaline and saline. The *Kǎoshēng* says: “Salty soil. This is a word formed by the combination of shape and sound.

The character *yú* (餘) is pronounced with the *zhèng* and *yíng* finals; it means "to overflow" (*chū*) and refers to having an excess of earth. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "貝" (*bèi*) and the phonetic "𧷽" (*shēng*), where the pronunciation of "𧷽" is the same as above. It is incorrect for this scripture to write it as "𧷽" using two "貝" radicals.

In the "Tàn" section, he sighs that it is difficult to return. In the *Erlü*, it says: "When sand emerges from water, it is called a 'tà' (潬); this is a word formed by combining semantic and phonetic components. The lower character is pronounced "tán. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states: "'Tán' means 'xián' (閑). In the Nan-Chu region, deep water is called 'tán'; 'tán' means 'xián' (to be secluded) and 'deep. This is also a word formed by combining semantic and phonetic components. To write it as "tān" (灘) is not the form found in ancient texts.

Regarding "Xiān cí" (Temple of Xiān): the upper character is pronounced jiān (as in jiān-fǎn), though this character does not exist [in standard dictionaries]. The Hu people call the divine spirit *tiān* (Heaven); through phonetic shift, they call it *xiān*. Previous scholars transcribed this according to the sound, writing it with the radical for "deity" (*shì*) and the character "heaven" (*tiān*) to distinguish it from other uses. Regarding the lower character "cí": it is pronounced sì (as in zī-fǎn). According to the *Erya*, "cí" means "to sacrifice. In the *Baihūtong*, it says: "Cí means succession; the temples of all the hundred spirits are called *cí*. He (the commentator) notes that in the *Gōngyáng zhuan*, "cí" means "to eat" (referring to sacrificial feasts). It takes the radical for "deity" (*shì*), and the pronunciation of *shì* is *qí*.

The term *hūṃ* is the Sanskrit name for Trailokyavijaya-vajra. Regarding the character *sūn*: when pronounced with the correct Sanskrit sound as *su*, it involves the mouth being slightly open and the sound resonating within the throat and palate. As for the character *pó*, it is to be pronounced with the departing tone (*qu-shēng*). This is it.
*Mahe* (with the second character pronounced *xīng* [jī] in reverse) is also a term from the Sanskrit language, being the name of a celestial king (*devendra*) in the upper realms.
*Běngshéng* (with the first character pronounced *bó* [máng] in reverse) refers to the white cords used to mark out the boundaries of the ritual paths.
Regarding "jué" (橛): the *Jīng* reads it as "suān" (拴), which is an incorrect vulgarism.
Regarding "yún" (𣗩): the first character is pronounced *cānghé* (蒼何); the second is *yùnjūn* (聿均); the third is *lǎodāo* (老刀). The fourth character is "shàng" (上).
*Mākṣika* (pronounced *guōměng* in the Fangyun) is the name of a medicinal substance.
*Daṇḍa* (pronounced *dānnú*; in Sanskrit, it means "staff" or "club," and in the Tang language, it is also called a *zhàng*) is held by the deity Yama; its final character is pronounced *báixiǎng*.

*Śakti*: the first character is pronounced *shāng* (with the *qiǎn* tone) and the second is *dīngyǐ* (with the *fǎn* tone); this phrase is also a Sanskrit term, which in the Tang language means "short spear. *Maṅkuṣī*:

the first character is pronounced *mòbǎng* (with the *fǎn* tone) and the second is *jīngyǐ* (with the *fǎn* tone); it is the name of the Mother of the Vajra Family in Sanskrit. In the scriptural text it is written as 𑖨𑖿𑖦𑖽𑖯𑖿𑖩𑖿 (maṅkuṣī), though it may also be written as 䥈 due to a scribal error.

The wrathful deity Vajraśodhaka—formerly translated as *Aśuci-vajra* (Impure Vajra) or *Vajra-kṣepa* (Traces of Impurity)—is both a clumsy and incorrect translation; it is actually a derogatory term that does not reflect the true meaning. Alternatively, he is called *Vahni-mukha-vajra* (Fire-Head Vajra), which is also not a correct translation. In Sanskrit, he is called Ucchuṣma, which translates to "one who burns away impurities. This holy being, through his profound and pure great compassion, does not avoid contact with filth as he rescues and protects sentient beings. Because he uses his great majestic light, like a fierce fire, to burn away afflictions and the mental states of dualistic grasping regarding purity and impurity or arising and ceasing, he is named "Remover of Impurities" (*Śodhaka*). Furthermore, his Sanskrit name is Mahāmāla, which in Chinese is rendered as "Great Power" (*Dali*). Because he uses the power of great compassion, like a blazing fire, to burn away the impurities of the karma of birth and death, he is named "Great Power."
In the narrow passages, the character *shēng* (爭) is a variant of *zé* (迮); where the correct orthography should be used, the character now written as *chù* (處) is a vulgar form.

The text of the *Wǔyào jīng* (Sūtra of the Five Medicines) is unclear and incomplete here; we shall follow the *Jīngāngdǐng yújiā shuō wǔyào* (The Five Medicines Spoken in the Vajraśekhara Yoga). The Sanskrit names for the five medicines are: 1. Sahasrā, 2. Sahadevā, 3. Kṛtakaṇṭakā, 4. Gṛdhra-nakhī, 5. Mṛtasañjīvanī. These are all medicines from foreign lands and do not exist in this country; therefore, substitute them with the efficacious medicines produced locally: 1. Polyporus (fúlíng), 2. Cinnabar (zhūshā), 3. Realgar (xiónghuáng), 4. Ginseng (rénshēn), 5. Aconitum (chìjiàn). Take a small amount of each and place them together in a single bottle, which is then to be buried.
The five treasures and seven treasures are as follows: first, gold; second, silver; third, pearls; fourth, crystal; fifth, jade; sixth, adding lapis lazuli to the seven treasures;

and seventh, amber. Regarding the eight banners of the directions: the banner of the east is white; the banner of the southeast is fire-colored, being reddish-yellow; the banner of the south is black; the banner of the southwest is smoke-colored, being pale black; the banner of the west is red; the banner of the northwest is green, the color of water; the banner of the north is yellow; and the banner of the northeast is whitish-red. These banners are made solely according to their colors; no images or figures are painted upon them.

The *yuānquè* (鵷鵲) [the first character pronounced with the *yǎn* rhyme-group] is a species of *yuānchú* (鵷鶵), which belongs to the category of phoenixes; the second character [pronounced with the *qiāng-yào* rhyme-group] refers to the *jiànquè* (𠃵鵲). These two are both numinous birds, possessing both auspicious form and sound.
They are born from sprouts [the character pronounced with the *jié* rhyme-group], such as when seeds are sown on the fifteenth day of the seventh month and sprout.

Regarding the characters for "cow with calf" (*gò niú bìng dú*): the upper character is "mother cow" (*mǔ niú*), and the lower character is "its offspring" (*qí zǐ niú*). It is required that their coat colors be similar; this is considered superior. Although the sutras mention dozens of varieties of flowers, incense, mixed fruits, foods, and drinks, and although there are difficult characters among them, none should be phonetically transcribed. This is because the flowers, incense, fruits, and foods mentioned do not exist in this country at all. Whether the Sanskrit terms are correct or incorrect, even if one were to provide a phonetic transcription, these objects do not exist here; therefore, they are not transcribed.
This contains the *Dhāraṇīsaṃgraha* in four fascicles; this [work] contains the *Dhāraṇīsaṃgraha* in four fascicles, the collection being incomplete.
The *Mahāvairocanasūtra*, Fascicle One, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Vajrabodhi. Fascicle One:
The Bodhisattva’s Body as the Lion Throne; the Lion Throne is that which turns the Wheel of Dharma.

The seat upon which the Wheel-turning King sits is popularly known as the "high seat" (*kōza*). The scriptural text contains a hidden teaching regarding the Tathāgata’s past causal stage when he practiced the bodhisattva path:

it describes his successive cultivation of the *bhūmi-pāramitās*, from the first ground and the second ground up to the tenth ground, the Ground of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi-bhūmi*), and the Ground of Wondrous Enlightenment (*myōkaku-bhūmi*), whereby he attained perfect awakening. One should know that all of these were preceded by...
Taking the practices of the stages (*bhūmi*) as the foundation, one accumulates the merits of the preceding eleven stages to achieve wondrous enlightenment and sits upon them;
because one turns the sublime wheel of Dharma in each stage and dwells securely in that position, it is said that "the body of a bodhisattva serves as the lion throne."

*Śatavāṇa* is a name for a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) in the Sanskrit language; this is largely identical in doctrine to the "Knower" (*Vijñānavādin*) school of non-Buddhists, differing only in terminology.

Regarding the *ulūka*: the first character is pronounced *xiū* (as in *xiū* [rest]) and the second *liú* (as in *liú* [stay]). The *ulūka* is a strange bird that flies at night, such as the *xìn hóu*. It is also called *huì hóu* or *huì hú*. It is named after the sound it utters. It mostly dwells in earthen caves and burrows, remaining hidden by day and emerging at night to prey on mice, small birds such as the *bián qiáo*, and the like. Its plumage is mottled grayish-blue, its size is like that of a hawk, its eyes are round with red pupils, and its beak and talons resemble those of a hawk or a horned owl (*yǎo chī*). It belongs to the same species as the *huāng jī* and the *tǔ xiāo*, though it is slightly larger.
"Shackle" (*xiè*) refers to the wooden cangue and shackles; "foolish adherence that does not shift" is like being bound by such restraints.
"Razor" (*tìdāo*—the character for *tì* is pronounced *tǐ* with the tone-marker *fǎn* [level tone] when referring to the razor used for shaving hair; the version in the sutra as *tī* is incorrect).
*Yān* (pronounced *yán*) means to linger or remain stagnant. *Zhūwù*:
the upper character (*zhū*, pronounced *zhū*) refers to the stumps of a tree; the lower character (*wù*, pronounced *wǔgǔ*) refers to a tree stump that has no top.
*Jìfù* (pronounced *jì*): the scripture reads *xì* (to bind), which is incorrect.
*Sāizhuó* (洒濯): the first character is pronounced *xīlǐ* (西禮) in the upper tone; the second character is pronounced *zhuó* (濁). *Huǒjìn* (火燼):

the second character is pronounced *xīyìn* (夕胤); the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it refers to the remaining wood after being burned by fire. In the scripture, the character *jìn* (盡) is used instead of *jìn* (燼).
*Niu-lan* (牛欄) means "fence" (*lán*).
*He-tàn* (河潬) [the second character pronounced *tǎn*, with the radical *dān*] refers to sand emerging from within the water.

*Jiān-zōng* (兼綜) [the second character pronounced *zōng*, with the radical *sòng*] means that one who acts as a teacher must be comprehensive in both internal and external classics and must clearly understand all worldly arts; only then may one serve as a teacher.
The character for "insect" (蟲) is pronounced *rǒng* in the upper radical and *jǐ* in the lower; it is sometimes written as "ant" (螘) or "termite" (蚍蜉), being a phono-semantic compound.
*Gomaya* is a Sanskrit term meaning "cow dung," used for smearing the ground.

*Gomutra* is a Sanskrit term; in the Tang language, it means "ox urine. This sutra contains several hundred mantras and Sanskrit terms, some of which contain difficult characters that are all "echo-Sanskrit" (phonetic approximations) and do not precisely correspond to the original sounds. Furthermore, regarding the explanations of the *akṣara-cakra*, the dharma-meanings of incense and flowers, and the names of devas and humans, Lin [Yi] has already retranslated them based on the Sanskrit manuscripts within the *dhāraṇīs*. They will not be explained again here; had I forcibly provided phonetic transcriptions, they would not have been close to the Sanskrit pronunciation.
Xiǎnchǎng (顯敞): "Chǎng" is pronounced *zhǎng* with a high tone; it means lofty, prominent, and visible from afar.
Shūlì (姝麗): "Shū" is pronounced *chōng* with a level tone; according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means beautiful, and in the *Xiǎoyǎ*, it means lovely. It may also be written as 𡚾.
*Gǎo* (pronounced gāo with an upper tone): *xuán* and *quán* rhyme with it; *gǎo* means white. The *Xiǎo Ěr Yǎ* states that the finest quality of silk is called *gǎo*.
*Yǎn* (pronounced yī and yǎn with an upper tone): a black mole; it is the name of a Great Wrathful Honored One (*mahākrodha*).

*Zǎohuì* (藻繢): The upper character is pronounced *zāo* (with the tone of *lǎo*), and the *Kǎoshēng* states it means "patterns" or "colored designs. The lower character is pronounced *huí* (with the tone of *zuì*). The *Yùnyīng* states it means "painting" or "the clarity of colored designs. The upper tone character is also used with the departing tone (*qùshēng*).

2. Fascicle Two. *Mahāvairocana Sūtra*, Fascicle Two. "Kuan" (權) means provisional; "zhi" (智) means wisdom. "Juan" (倦) is pronounced with the *fan* (輔音) *quán*; "kao" (考) means to examine; "sheng" (聲) means sound. "Chang" (常) means constant; "he" (合) means to accord with;

"dao" (道) means the Way. "Kui" (揆) means to measure; "du" (度) means to gauge. It follows the radical for wood (*mu*). "Phaṭ" (癹磔迦): the upper character is pronounced with the *fan* (輔音) *pǔ mò*, and the lower character is pronounced with the *fan* (輔音) *jiāng qiē*. In mantras, this is the syllable for destruction.

*Hreḥ*: The character *hrie* above is purely a transliteration of the Sanskrit sound; it is pronounced like *hen-mo*. It may also be written as *hrī*. The character below is pronounced with a departing tone like *pi-mei*.

*Gṛhṇa*: The first syllable *gri* has the *yin-qi* (second) tone; the *li* is a retroflex (*jihvāmūlīya*), and the second syllable *na* has the *ning-jia* (fourth) tone. This is a phrase of wrathful majesty from the mantra; in the sutras it is written as *gṛhṇa*, which is also interchangeable with *gr̥hṇa*.
"Jiānchā" (pronounced jiān-chà) means to thrust or pierce.
"Qiánfù" (the first character pronounced qián, the second fù) refers to fine silk.
"Dūnjù" (the first character pronounced cún, the second jù) refers to squatting.
*Vāyu*: In the Sanskrit language this means "wind," which refers to the northwest direction. *Śarāva*:

This is a compound of the Sanskrit word *śara* (with an aspirated initial sound) and *āva*, where the latter is pronounced like the sound of a door-bolt (*ha*). [Note: The version in the sutra uses *gai*, which is incorrect. In the Chinese language, this term means "a clay bowl. At the northwest corner, in the position of the Wind Deity King, one performs the ritual to stop wind and rain by using a clay bowl to cover [the vessel].

3. Third Fascicle. *Mahāvairocana-sūtra*, Fascicle Three. [The character] "shì" (幟): the upper radical is "bi" (必) with the reversed "yáo" (遙); it is pronounced like "kǎo" (考). It means a banner or sign. It may be written with the "jīn" (巾) radical or the "mù" (木) radical as "biāo" (標). The lower part is "chāng" (昌) with the reversed "zhì" (志). The dictionary states that "shì" refers to a banner atop a signpost; it may also be written with the "jīn" radical and the phonetic "zhī" (戠).

*Xiāng* (䰅𧄜): The upper character is pronounced *xiàng* (臾反); it refers to the fine hairs and filaments (*rěi*) within a flower. The lower character is pronounced *chuí* (󲳺捶反); "filament" (*rěi*) is also synonymous with "necessity" (*xū*). *Jìdǒu* (計都): This is a Sanskrit term;
in the Tang language, it means "banner" (*chuáng*) or "joint" (*jié*), referring to what is held in the hand.
*Khaḍga* (the first character pronounced *qiān* with the *yè* tone) is also a Sanskrit term; in the Tang language it means "sword," referring thus to the Sword-Holding Immortal (*khadgadhara-ṛṣi*).
*Chhattra* (the first character pronounced *sàn* with the third tone) is a vulgar character; its correct form is *sǎn*, which is simply a "parasol" or "canopy."

*Liǎo* (𡳐): The first character is pronounced *lǐ*; the second is pronounced *suǒ qǐ*. The *Yùnyīng* states that this refers to a type of footwear (*lǚ*) whose heel is not secured; it is also written as *liǎn* (𩌦). *Ānshàn'ā* (安膳那): Pronounced *shàn*.
The Tang dynasty translation says "eye medicine. It resembles a mineral stone, blue-black in color, and is also like a *jīnjīng* (金精) stone medicine.

*Lu-chen-na* (嚧遮那) is the Sanskrit term; in the Tang language, it means "cow bezoar" (*gohuang*). These various medicinal substances are all items empowered through the corresponding *vidyādhara* (Holding-Light) sages.
*Feiwu* (霏霧) [the first character pronounced with the initial *wei* and the final *fu*; the second character pronounced as *wu*]: light mist.

Regarding "Avīci retribution": "Avīci" means that there is no selection between noble and base; whoever commits a great transgression enters it immediately, and it is named the Hell of No Interval (Avīci).
"Tóngchì" (彤赤): the first character is pronounced as in "tóng" (same as 彤); it also means crimson.
*Nalaca* (the *lan* and *ge* are pronounced as in the Sanskrit; it is the Sanskrit name for the vajra-mallet) refers to a mallet with an iron handle.
*Mukhara* (the *lan* and *dan* are pronounced as in the Sanskrit) is also a Sanskrit term, referring to a class of implements including hooks, clubs, pestles, swords, spears, and nooses.
*Kiangu* (絹縠): "Gu" is pronounced *hong* (洪) with the rhyme *wu* (屋). *Yingyun* (韻英) states it refers to *luagu* (羅縠), the thin variety of silk.

4. Fascicle Four, *Mahāvairocana Sūtra*, Fascicle Four. *Kieqie* (憩伽): Upper character pronounced *xian* (騫) and *ji* (罽). A Sanskrit term; in the Tang language, it means "sword," or alternatively, "Great Wisdom Sword."
The phonetic value of 䐡 (qiè) is the same as that of 齊 (qí).

The character 腰 (yāo)—with the phonetic value "yī yáo" (伊遙反), also written as 𦝫—is defined in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as "the center of the human body," depicted in the form of a person's waist. In the *Shuowen*, it is written as 󲛘, composed of 曰 (yuē) and a simplified 交 (jiāo) as the phonetic. In the *Zhouwen* script, it is written as 要, composed of 女 (nǚ) and a simplified 󲭫 (yào) as the phonetic. Today, the *Zhouwen* form is modified and used.

Regarding the character for *mài* (wheat/barley): the upper radical is *guó* (mǎng) and the lower is *bó* (fǎn). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of *jiá* and *jiǔ*. Although the current vernacular character uses *lái* and *zhòu* as its components, this is incorrect; *zhòu* does not have the pronunciation of *mài*. Why is this so?
*Héyéjīlíwà* is the Sanskrit term, which in the Tang language is translated as "Mañjuśrī Hayagrīva" (the Horse-Headed Vidyārāja).
*Dāosòu* (刀韒): "Sòu" is pronounced *xiāoyào* (逍曜); the *Yùnyīng* (韻英) states it means a sheath for a blade. It is a compound character formed from a semantic and a phonetic element.
*Duòyìn* (鐸印): "Yìn" is pronounced *tángluò* (唐洛); it refers to a large bell. *Chuī* (鎚):
"Chuí" is pronounced *zhíchuí* (直追); this is a vulgar form. The correct character is written with the radical "wood" (*muó*) and the component "bird" (*zhuī*). It is *chuí* (椎).

*Ji* (芰): On the upper part of the character, read *qi* (奇) with the *jia* (賈) rhyme-group. Guo Yu’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that it is *ling* (䔖). The people of Chu called *ling* *cai* (苃); Du Lin sometimes wrote it as *de* (茤).

5. Fascicle Five. *Dàrì jīng*, Fascicle Five. *Yuánzhěng* (圓整): On the lower part of *zhěng* (整), read *zhēngyǐng* (征郢). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) says it means "even" (*qí*) and "principle" (*lǐ*). The standard orthography of ancient and modern times has *zhěng* (整) meaning "to rectify. It is composed of *shù* (束) and *zhī* (支) as the radical and phonetic, respectively. It is pronounced with the sound of *zhèng* (正).

*Zhūmǐn* (朱黰): The first character is read as *zhū*; the second is read as *mǐn* (with the phonetic component *zhēn*). This is the correct orthography for ancient and modern times, meaning beautiful hair; it is formed from the radical "black" (*hēi*) with "true" (*zhēn*) as its phonetic.
*Biāozhì* (摽誌): The first character is read as *biāo* (with the phonetic component *yáo*); the second is pronounced *zhì*. The *Yùnyīng* states that recording an event is called a *zhì*.

*Kiṅkara* (羌揭梨): This is a Sanskrit term; in the language of Tang it means "small knife. It resembles a *bhaṭṭārikā-mudrā* (seal of authority). *Haṃsa* (鵝鵠): This is a water bird; its color is white as snow.

Households sometimes raise them, colloquially called "red geese" (*hóng hè*). They are also water birds resembling geese, though slightly reddish and with heads that have a hint of blue. Their nests are in tall trees; they have long necks, tall legs, and long beaks.
Mián (綿): the first character is read as mí (彌) and the second as kuàng (晃).

Cǎi (綵): the second character is read as xuán (玄). Zeng’s commentary on the *Yí Lǐ* states: "When various colors (*cǎi*) form a pattern, it is called *xuàn*. *Xuàn* refers to the appearance of flourishing and profuse adornment. It is formed with the radical for silk (糸) and the phonetic element xún (旬); the pronunciation of xún is the same as above. Both are examples of phono-semantic compounds (*xíngshēng zì*).

The character for *xiáo* (餚饍) is pronounced *jiāo* (上効交反); it is a vulgar form, its correct orthography being simply *yáo* (肴). The *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲) states that it refers to dried meat (*fǔ xiū*). The *Jí Xùn* (集訓) states that it belongs to the category of tree fruits. The lower radical is pronounced *shàn* (善). Zheng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* says: "Shàn means to present. Thus, all fine foods today are called *zhēn shàn* (珍膳). The character is formed with the radical *shí* (食) and the phonetic *shàn* (善); the vulgar form [with the radical *ròu*] is incorrect. The *Erya* says: "That which is especially added is [called *xiáo*]."

"Jìng" (淨) is the original character meaning "to follow the proper order and rectify what is inverted. The version in the *Jīng* (經) as "Chún" (醇), or with the radical for water (水) as "Chún" (淳), are both variant forms and vulgar characters.

"Yì" (翊), in the sense of "attendant," has the phonetic "jí" (即) and the gloss states it means "to assist. According to the *Shuowen*, it is a compound character formed from "feather" (羽) and "standing" (立).

Volume Six. This is the sixth volume of the *Mahāvairocana Sūtra*. Although there are few difficult characters in the text of this volume, it explains thirty-four Sanskrit syllables (*akṣara*) through repeated and layered expositions; the interpretation of these characters is entirely profound and esoteric. Furthermore, it sets forth the *homa* rites, first explaining forty-four types of mundane fire rituals and the names of the fire deities, followed by the twelve inconceivable supramundane fires and the characteristics and appearances of their respective fire deities. These have already been fully explained and annotated within the *Mantra Collection* (*Mantra-saṃgraha*). In this sūtra, however, because the transliterated Sanskrit characters do not precisely correspond to the original sounds, they have not been provided with phonetic transcriptions.
*Miàn pò* (面䩉): The character *pò* is pronounced with the third tone (*fú wǔ fǎn*). The *Yùnyīng* states it refers to the cheekbone; it is also written as *jì*. 7.

Fascicle Seven, *Mahāvairocana Sūtra*, Fascicle Seven. *Kūn* (𪚕): Pronounced *kǎn gān fǎn*. The *Guǎngpǐ* states that *kūn* and *qì* have the sound *chéng*. The *Kǎoshēng* says it refers to excavating a pit in a mountain wall. The *Shuōwén* defines it as the appearance of a dragon, formed from the "present" radical and the "dragon" radical. It is incorrect to combine [the radicals] to form *kàn* (龕). Below, it is pronounced *kǔ gǔ fǎn*. Alternatively, it may be written with the "earth" radical as *jué* (堀). Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* says it is an underground chamber. In the standard characters of the present day, it is written with the "cave" radical and the phonetic *qū* (屈).

*Bīnbīn* (繽紛): The first character is pronounced *pǐ* (匹) with the *rèn* (刃) tone; the second is pronounced *fú* (拂) with the *wén* (文) tone. The dictionaries state that it refers to flowers falling in disarray.

*Xiāohú* (綃縠): The first character is pronounced *xiāo* (消). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states that "xiāo" is a name for silk (*zēng*) used in antiquity and modern times. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* says "xiāo" is a type of *jiān* (fine silk), and further notes it belongs to the category of *qǐ* (brocade). The second character is pronounced *hóng* (紅) with the *mù* (木) tone. The *Shiming* says it is "shāhú" (silk gauze); both characters are formed by combining semantic and phonetic components.
*Bingxian* (炳現) means to shine forth clearly, like the reflection of light upon a vessel.
*Nai* (乃) is the ancient form of the character *nai* (乃).

*Samāhita*—the "xi" (呬) sound is pronounced as *xin* (馨) with a retroflex *i*—is a Sanskrit term translated into Chinese as *dengyin* (等引). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explains that because this sublime ground is free from dullness and agitation, it can equally induce all virtuous qualities; thus, it is called *samādhi*, another name for "equipoise."

*Dàn* (憺怕): The upper character is pronounced *tán* (濫) with a reversed tone; the lower character is pronounced *pò* (魄). It refers to a state where the mind and will are tranquil and the spirit is settled. The *Jīng* (經) [text] writes it as *dàn bó* (澹泊) using the water radical, which is incorrect. *Gāo* (膏): The upper character is pronounced *gào* (告).

The *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲) states that applying oil to the axle of a carriage is called "smearing the carriage" (*gāo chē*). The lower character is pronounced *xián* (閑) with a *jiá* (戛) rhyme, or it may be written as *huà* (鎋), both of which are acceptable. This refers to the iron at the end of a carriage axle.

Regarding "Śanwuwei" (善無畏): the former translation uses the character *dūn* (敦), which is pronounced with the initial *kǒng* (昆) and the final *shēng* (聲). It means "to respect" or "to honor. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is correctly written as *shù* (恕); the version in the sutra uses *dūn* (敦), which is a vulgar character.
*Li* (勵): The character for "exertion" (*li xíng*). It means to strive with effort. It is composed of the radical *lì* (force) and the phonetic *lì*. The pronunciation of *lì* is as stated above.

*Kěn* (懇): The character for "sincerity" (*chéng kěn*). It means utmost sincerity and faithfulness. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical *xīn* (heart) and the phonetic *kěn*. The pronunciation of *kěn* is as stated above.
"Jiè" (捩) means to twist; it is written with the radical for "hand" (手), as in the phrase "to twist and contort.
"Bù dàn qú láo" (不憚劬勞) means not shrinking from toil and hardship.

"Tán" (壇) is pronounced *lán* (上壇爛反); "jù" (具) is pronounced *yú* (下具愚反). "Luó bēi" (蠃盃): "luó" (蠃) is pronounced *lù hé* (魯禾反); it is a large sea snail resembling a snail. The *Erya* says: "Hǎn luó" (蚶蠃) is the same as "yí yú" (螔蝓). It is opened to serve as a water cup."
"Biting the lower lip" (chì xià chún): "jié" is pronounced as *jiàn* (in the rhyme category *mò*); it means to bite.
"To serve as a sheath" (*qiào*)—the character *xiāo* is pronounced as *yào*; the *Yùnchuán* states this refers to the scabbard of a sword. This has already been explained.
"Brandishing toward the void" (*shàng huī xūkōng*)—the character *huī* is pronounced as *huǐ* (in the rhyme category *wéi*); it means to wave one's hand toward the scabbard.
"Pungent and aromatic" (*xīnhūn*; pronounced *xūn*) refers to the category of scallions, garlic, leeks, and shallots.
"Radish" (*luófú*; the second character is pronounced *péngbǐ*) is a large-rooted vegetable with purple flowers; it was originally presented by the Fanróng people.
*Chūn* (椿) [pronounced *chún*]: A name for a type of tree. *Vairocana-tathāgata-uddhṛta-laghu-paṭha-vidhi*, translated by Vajra Tripiṭaka, Volume One.

*Shù-dǎo* (渚島): The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that this refers to a small island (*xiǎozhōu*). It is also written as *zhǔ*. The *Shuowén* (說文) says: "An island (*dǎo*) is a mountain within the sea upon which one can rely for shelter; it is composed of the radical 'mountain' (*shān*) and the phonetic 'niǎo'. It is also written as *zhǐ* or *dǐ*. *Zhū* (諸): [Pronounced *zhǔ*]. The *Kǎoshēng* says it means "small islands. It is also written as *zhǔ*. The *Shuowén* says: "In the midst of the sea, there are mountains upon which one may rely; these are called islands (*dǎo*). They take the radical 'mountain' (*shān*) and the phonetic 'niǎo'. It is also written as *zhǐ* or *dǐ*.

*Zhé* (磔豎): The upper radical is *zhāng* (張革反), meaning "to open," composed of *shí* (石) and *jié* (桀). The lower part is *shū* (殊) with the radical *zhèng* (正). It is composed of *dòu* (豆) and *lì* (立).

The common form [is incorrect]. *Ān* (安): *É* (頟) is pronounced *yá* (牙革反); according to the *Shuowen*, it means "the forehead" (*yán sǎng*). It is composed of *xié* (頁) and *gǎo* (各), with *shēng* (省) as the phonetic. In the scriptures, it is written as *kè* (客); this is the common form for *é* (額), but it is an incorrect vulgar character from ancient times to the present.

The character 腕 (wàn) is formed by adding the radical 肉 (flesh/meat) below 交 (jiāo). It is a vulgar form; the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it refers to the joint behind the palm. It is correctly written with the radical 手 (hand) and the component 叉 (chā). In archaic script, this is the character 爪 (zhǎo), which is a semantic compound consisting of the two eyes (目).
*Guàn* (pronounced *guān* with the *fǎn* [rhyme] of *huàn*): The *Shuowen* states that this means "habituation"; it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "guàn.
*Xūruí* (pronounced *xūruí* with the *fǎn* of *chuí*): This refers to the filaments within a lotus flower.

"Being armored" (被鎧): the first character is pronounced with the *kai* rhyme group (開) and the *fan* (反) tone; it is explained as "armor" (鎧甲). It is also pronounced with the *gang* rhyme group (康) and the *gai* (改) tone.

Volume 2, Lower Scroll: *Vairocana Recitation Method* (毘盧遮那念誦法), Lower Scroll. "Bell" (鈴鐸): the first character is pronounced with the *li* (歷) rhyme group and the *ding* (丁) tone; the second character is pronounced with the *tang* (唐) rhyme group and the *luo* (洛) tone.

The character *vāṃ* (鑁) is pronounced with the second tone for the initial and the third tone for the final. Regarding *cúnjù* (蹲踞): the first character is pronounced *cún* (存) and the second *jù* (據).

Regarding *tuóbiǎo* (摶󱻙): the first character is pronounced *duànluán* (段鸞); according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to place" (*zhù*); the *Lǐjì* states there is no such thing as "clumping rice into balls" (*tuófàn*); according to the *Shuōwén*, it means "round," composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic element "zhuān" (*zhuān*).

"Guǎn-sǎ": "Guǎn" (upper tone) means "to wash the hands," according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*; it is a compound character formed from the radicals for "mortar" (臼), "water" (水), and "vessel" (皿). "Xià" (pronounced xī-lǐ) is an alternative form; according to the *Shuowen*, "sǎ" means "to rinse and cleanse," and it is a character formed by combining a semantic and a phonetic component.

The *Vajraśekhara-sūtra-laghu-yoga*, Volume One. Translated by Vajrabodhi. Volume One: Akṣobhya (the Sanskrit *akṣobhya* is pronounced *ā-chù-wei* in Chinese; in the Tang language it means "Immovable Buddha").
The characters *lán* (嚂) and *lǎn* (覽) are pronounced with the tongue rolled back; these are the Sanskrit sounds.
*Cù* (蹙) is pronounced *jiǔ yù* (酒育) with a reversed final;

*xù* (漱) is pronounced *sōu zhòu* (搜皺) with a reversed final, its sound being identical to *shòu* (瘦), and it is derived from the radical for water (*shui*). Zheng Gu Yewang stated that it means to rinse the mouth with water. In the sutra, the character is written with the radical for mouth (*kou*), which is a vulgar form.

*Ukkuṭika* (the term for sitting on the heels; the note states that the buttocks do not touch the ground; the character *tun* [臀] is pronounced with the second tone *dùn* and the fourth tone *hún*, derived from the sound of *diàn* [殿]).
*Cikṣepa* (the upper character is pronounced *chēn* [瞋] and the lower character *hē* [呵], together forming the sound *kè* [磕]).

The characters for "chou" (抽) and "zhi" (擲)—the former pronounced with the *shang* tone as *chou* (with the *liu* rhyme), the latter pronounced with the *cheng* tone as *ji* (with the *ge* rhyme)—are both phono-semantic compounds (*xing-sheng*).

2. In the second fascicle of the *Vajraśekhara Sūtra*, the character for "xiang" (𦠍) [appears]. It is a phonetic derivative from "rou" (肉, flesh). The canonical text uses "chi" (齒, teeth) instead, forming the character "yu" (󲲹); this is a vulgar form. The *Shuowen Jiezi* records it as "gu" (谷), with the pronunciation *qiang* (強) and the *ge* rhyme, meaning "the upper part of the mouth. It represents the patterns of its lines and textures. Originally, this character did not exist in ancient texts; it was produced by former sages who followed common parlance in their writing. Whether it is written with "rou" or "chi," neither is the correct form. It is traditionally shared and pronounced *wu* (五) and *ge* (各). Ancient sources state that it is so.
"Refining wax" (liàn 鍊): the first tone; "diàn" is pronounced with the initial *lian* and the final *dian*. It refers to refining honey and wax, or making tin and lead supple.
"Jade pillow" (yù zhěn 玉枕): the second tone; "zhěn" is pronounced with the initial *ren* and the final *zhen*;

it refers to the area behind the brain. Volume Three. The third volume of the *Vajraśekhara Sūtra* (Jīngāngdǐng jīng 金剛頂經). "Chū tiào" (出眺): the first tone; "tiào" is pronounced with the initial *chao* and the final *diao*. It means to look out from afar. It is composed of the radical "eye" (目) and the phonetic "zhào" (兆). The version of the sūtra that uses the character "yuè" (月) is incorrect.

Regarding the character "yuan" (緣) in "si bianyuan" (四邊緣)—the "yue" (悅) being pronounced with a departing tone according to Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji*, which states that "yuan" means to adorn the edges—it is a character formed from the radical "silk" (*mi*) used with a borrowed pronunciation. In the scriptures, the character "chuan" (椽) is written with the radical "hand" (*shou*); this [character under discussion] is not used in that sense.

*Kuò* (闊): The upper radical is *kuān* (寬) with the phonetic *huó* (活). According to the *Erya*, it means "distant" or "broad. It is a standard character from ancient times meaning "sparse"; it is formed from the radical *mén* (門) with the phonetic *huó*.
*Bò* (擘): The pronunciation is *bā-mài* (巴麥); it means "to open."

*Qimò* (pronounced *mò*, with the phonetic component *kǎo*): To leap over or traverse. The *Shuowen jiezi* states that it is sometimes written as *𧻙*, which is an archaic character; it is composed of the radical "horse" (*mǎ*) and the phonetic component "mò" (*mò*).

*Yuèyùn* (pronounced *yùn*, with the phonetic component *kǎo*): The halo around the sun or moon. It refers to the atmospheric vapors surrounding the sun and moon; they may be blue or red, encircling the sun or moon like a chariot wheel.
*Bo*: The upper character is pronounced *bō*; it is derived from the hand. To snap the fingers:
simply clench the fist, bend the index finger, and press it with the thumb to produce a snapping sound. *Qiánzhui*: The upper character is pronounced *qián* (with the *yin* tone);
the lower character is *zhuī* (with the *fu* tone), derived from the wood radical and the phonetic *zhuī*. The version using *zhuī* in the sutras is a vulgar character and is incorrect.
"披拽" (pīyè) [the "yè" is pronounced with a retroflex *j*] means to drag from the hand; it is incorrect to write this as "絏" (xié) using the radical for silk.

"Chou-lin" (稠林): "Chou" (稠) means "multitude" according to the *Cangjie pian*; the *Guangya* states it means "dense. "Lu-lu" (濾漉):
the first character is pronounced with the initial *lǚ* and the final *zhù*; the second is pronounced *lù*. "Yan-mei" (掩󰻣):
the first character is pronounced with the initial *mán* and the final *bā*; the second character, according to the *Kaosheng*, means "to bind."
*Chè* (pronounced *chāng qiè* with the radical for "hand") means to pull apart.
*Niǎn* (pronounced *nián diǎn*) refers to rubbing.
An *yì* (pronounced *yīng jì*) is a white film that covers the pupil.

"Jūntú (鑿君荼)"—the first character is pronounced with the *cáng* and *luò* finals; according to the *Yùchuán* (韻詮), it means "to pierce. According to the *Shuowén*, it is a compound ideograph composed of the radicals 丵 (zhé), 臼 (jiù), 殳 (shū), and 金 (jīn). "Jūntú" is a Sanskrit term translated in the Tang as "earth-fire brazier," which is the *humā* brazier.
When newly drilling for fire, the officiant should take fresh, clean, and unsullied iron to strike the flint; it is also permissible to use bamboo or wood.
"Phan" (pronounced *pán*) means to accompany, causing them to be in harmony with one another.

Regarding the term "yáo jī" (搖激) [in the title]: Wang Yè states that it means "to clarify" (*jīng qīng*). Wang’s commentary on the *Chuci* says it means "to move emotionally" (*gǎn dòng*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "water being obstructed," meaning a rapid wave. It is composed of the radical "water" and the phonetic "jiào" (*jiào shēng*).
*Ābhoga* is a Sanskrit term; in the language of Tang (Chinese), it means "subtle vajra-contemplation," also referred to as "arising from the True to manifest function.

In a single *kṣaṇa*—the Sanskrit term for which has no direct equivalent in Chinese according to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*—one hundred and twenty *kṣaṇas* accumulate to form one *tatkṣaṇa*; sixty *tatkṣaṇas* accumulate to form one *lava*; thirty *lavas* accumulate to form one *muhūrta*; and thirty *muhūrtas* accumulate to form one day and night. Calculating a single day and night, there are thirty *muhūrtas*, nine hundred *lavas*, fifty-four thousand *tatkṣaṇas*, and six million four hundred and eighty thousand *kṣaṇas*. Among these durations, the most brief cannot exceed a *kṣaṇa*. When divided into the twelve periods of the day and night, such as Zi, Chou, and so forth, within each period from Mao to Chen, there are five hundred and forty thousand *kṣaṇas*.
*Uddāna* is a term from the Sanskrit language; translated according to its meaning, it is like a footprint. The ancient translations rendered it as *gāthā*.
[The character] 揮 (huī) is pronounced with the first tone as 暉 (huī), and the second character 斫 (zhé) is pronounced with the fourth tone as 章藥反 (zhāng yào fǎn).

2. Middle Volume of the *Vajraśekhara Sūtra*, Middle Volume, Recitation (fēngyìng): "Feng" (風) [pronounced fèng]. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "To double the text is called 'fēng' (reciting with intonation); to regulate it with sound is called 'sòng' (chanting). The preface to the *Mao Shijing* states: "Feng means 'to influence. The superior influences and transforms the subordinates; the subordinates influence and criticize the superior. Regarding the characters for form and sound, the preface to the *Mao Shijing* further states: "When speech is insufficient, one sighs and exclaims; when sighing and exclaiming are insufficient, one chants and sings; when chanting and singing are insufficient, one does not know but moves the hands in dance."

*Tóng* (僮): The upper character is pronounced *tóng*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "Tóng refers to the designation for those who have not yet undergone the capping ceremony. The lower character is pronounced *péng* (木反). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* explains it as "to attach. The *Liji* states that one who serves in a household is called a *pú*. Gu Yewang says he is the driver of a carriage. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines him as a messenger. *Bù* (僕): The lower character is pronounced *fù*. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* explains it as "to attach. The *Liji* states that one who serves in a household is called a *pú*. Gu Yewang says he is the driver of a carriage. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines him as a servant.

*Jù* (上): Pronounced *jū* (with the initial *jū* reversed to *yù*). According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "arrogance. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means "lack of deference," composed of the radical *rén* (人) and the phonetic *jù* (居). *Wù* (下): Pronounced *wù* (with the initial *wù* reversed to *gào*). According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "haughty pride. Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* defines it as "disrespect. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is also "arrogance," composed of the radical *rén* (人) and the phonetic *áo* (敖).
*Diànshì* (upper character pronounced *tián*, with the phonetic loan *jiè*; lower character pronounced *shēng*, with the phonetic loan *zī*): to decorate by inlaying precious gems.

*Chōu* (upper character pronounced *chòu*, with the phonetic loan *sōu*; according to the *Kǎoshēng*: to hook and grasp an object with the fingers): to take hold of a vajra with the hand and brandish it.

"Huàn" (擐) is a borrowed phonetic character; in the *Zhuo* commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan*, it means "to put on" or "to wear. Its radical pronunciation is "huàn. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the character for "armor" (*yijia*) is composed of the radical "hand" (*shou*) and the phonetic element "huán" (睘) in abbreviated form.

The General Method for the Yoga Recitation of All Deities. *Ying* (瑩): According to the *Commentary on the Tai Xuán Jīng* (Zhuò Tàxuánjīng), it means "to polish and clarify the profound Way (*xuándào*). The *Guǎngpǐ* states that *yíng* means "to rub. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical for "jade" (*yù*) and the phonetic component of *yíng* with its stroke reduced. The *Yùnquán* defines it as "to penetrate and pierce. *Chè* (徹): [From the *Yùnquán*, meaning] to pass through and pierce.

"Suddenly ascending," [the character] "fǎn" (反) means to look back; Yěwáng (野王) says it refers to coming and going with great rapidity. According to the *Shuowen*, it is the appearance of a dog running; it is composed of the radical "fire" (火) and the phonetic "yōu" (攸), where "yōu" is pronounced "yóu.

"Cù" (蹙) has the form of "bǎo" (寶); "jiǔyù" (酒育) is its pronunciation. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) says it means "swift" and "urgent. In the *Gōngjīn Zhèngzì* (古今正字), "qióng" (窮) and "pò" (迫) are derived from "qī" (戚) and the phonetic "zú" (足). It means "exhausted" and "constrained."
*Guà* (upper tone): Examining the sounds, *guà* means "to hang. It is homophonous with *guài*, which is defined as "to use.

*Jiàn* (lower tone, pronounced *suō*): The *Hánshī* says it means "to contract and gather. Jia’s commentary on the *Guóyǔ* says it means "to retreat. The *Shuowén* says it means "lengthwise" or "disorderly"; it is composed of the radical *mì* (silk thread) and the phonetic *xiù*.

Regarding the character for *ge* (革) in *ge-xie* (𠦶屣): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it refers to treating animal hide by removing the fur and processing it. In ancient times, the character for *ge* was written with thirty strokes; since thirty years constitute a generation (*yishì*), the Way undergoes transformation and renewal (*gēng-gè*). The current form is a simplified version of this. As for *xie* (屣), pronounced *sī-zǎi*, it refers to sandals made from leather, hence the name *ge-xie*. These are the leather shoes of the five regions of India (*pañcāla*); they have no heels and no laces, and belong to the category of *jue* (屩).

Regarding "nail" (*kīla*): according to the *Guangya*, a "nail" (*jue*) refers to a wooden peg. Examining the term "nail," it may be made of iron, bamboo, or wood, used as a slender spike driven into the ground or walls. In ancient and modern times, the correct character was written with the "wood" radical and the phonetic "jue. The scripture uses the character "shuan" (a wooden wedge), explaining that wood inserted into the earth is a "nail" (*jue*). During the Tianhou era, someone forged this [text] and presented it [to the court], but it was subsequently suppressed and discarded, being unfit for practice. This explains the Vajra-Nail Seal (*vajrakīlamudrā*).

Regarding the method of cultivating the yoga contemplation of the Prajñāpāramitā, there are no phonetic transcriptions available. As for the "Method of the Yoga of Avalokiteśvara’s Wish-Fulfilling Wheel," *Pūrṇa-īśvara-rāja* is the Sanskrit term; in the Tang language, it means "King of Sovereign Prostration," which refers to Amitāyus Buddha.

"Pengfà (蓬髮): disheveled hair. Nù (躶): naked; the character is pronounced with the initial *lú* (盧) and the final *guǒ* (果) [as a borrowed sound], used to avoid vulgar taboos; the pronunciation is *huá* (華) and *wǎ* (瓦). It means to strip off clothes and expose the body. It is sometimes written as *luò* (倮), which has the same meaning. Fēnfù (芬馥):
the upper character is pronounced *fèn* (忿) and *wén* (文), and the lower character is *fēng* (馮) and *mù* (目). *Fēnfù* refers to the appearance of fragrant scents."

Regarding the character for "impetuous" (jí): the upper part is explained in the *Shuowen* as being derived from "to reach" (jí) with "ye" as its phonetic component; the lower part is "dào" with the reversed order, having "kǎo" as its phonetic component, meaning a temperament that is hasty. Gu Yewang says it means "restless agitation" or "lack of composure. It is composed of the radical "foot" (zú) with "sào" as its phonetic component; "sào" is pronounced "sǎo" with the reversed order.

The Method for Recitation of Vajrasattva of Great Bliss according to the Yoga of the Vajraśekhara. Regarding the term *pe* (佩) in the title of the earlier translation: the *Shuowen* states that *pe* is composed of the radicals "man" (人) and "fan" (凡). It must necessarily have a cloth (*jin* 巾); the cloth serves as its ornament, and therefore it is written with the radical "cloth" (巾).

"Zuǒkǎ (左髁): The phonetic component is *huà* (化) and the radical is *kǎo* (考); it refers to the bone above the hip, or it means to sit back. The scriptural text uses the character with the *yuè* (月) radical, which is incorrect.

Qīngxié (傾斜): The upper part is pronounced *quǎn yíng* (犬營) and the lower part is *xī zhē* (夕嗟); this is a vulgar form. According to the *Shuowen*, the correct form consists of the *yī* (衣) radical with the abbreviated *xié* (邪); this is the standard orthography."
*Zhì* (𢫦): The glossary *Shuowen* states that *zhì* means "to strike" (*fǔ*), composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic element "hundred" (*bǎi*).
*Tǐng*: The glossary *Yierya* states that *tǐng* means "to arrive" (*zhì*). The *Shuowen* states it is composed of the radical "to arrive" (*zhì*) and the phonetic element "Qin" (*qín*).
The character 鋜 (zhù) is pronounced with the *chú* and *jiǎo* finals; it is said to be the ancient and elegant form of the seal character for "vajra-pin" (金剛銷印).

The character 擲 (zhì) is written above with the radical 呈 and the phonetic 戟, though it is a vulgar form; it is derived from 適 and written as 擿. Nowadays, it is used interchangeably with the character 張 (zhāng), which is why it is not employed. The character 旦 (dàn) is derived from 鄭, and 下散 (xià sàn) is the correct orthographic form.

*Chong* (寵) meets with the Imperial Edict; *yong* (勇) reverses the examination of sounds, for it signifies nobility (*gui*). *Yun* (韻) is love (*ai*); according to Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu*, it means glory (*rong*). The *Shuowen* says it means rank (*wei*); it is composed of the radical *mian* (roof) and the phonetic *long*.
*Bu shun* (不瞬) is pronounced *shui run* (水潤); it means to move the eyes, or is also written as *zhun* (瞚).

also written as *lì* or with the hand radical as *liè*. The *Jíxùn* states: "To twist and contort. Although the scriptural text uses the silk-radical character *lì*, this refers to the word for twisting silk; since that is not the usage here, it is not accepted.

"Bending the bow" (wān gōng): the upper radical is "cord" (qiǎn) and the phonetic component is "luán. The *Cangjie pian* states it means "to draw a bow. It is the standard character for "drawing the bow and releasing the arrow," composed of the radical "bow" (gōng) and the phonetic "luán" (pronounced like *luán*).

The two *bì* (pronounced with the *pí* rhyme; sometimes written as 䯗). The phonetic gloss states that *bì* refers to the thighs. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means the outer part of the thigh, composed of the radical for "bone" (*gǔ*) and the phonetic *bēi*. In the scriptural text, it is written with the radical for "flesh" (*yuè*), forming the character *pī*; this is not the correct character.

*Khaṭaka* is a term from the Sanskrit language; translated according to its meaning, it refers to bringing the left and right wrists close together with the palms soft and the ten fingers spread, performing three rotations of the dance before the heart while the mind dwells in joyful contemplation.

The first character, *zhān* (瞻), has the phonetic *zhān* (占) as its upper radical and *shǔ* (屬) as its lower component; the *Kǎo Shēng* states that "to gaze" (*zhānzhù*) means to look or to examine closely. The *Jí Huì* explains it as that which is the focus of many eyes; it is a compound character formed from both semantic and phonetic elements.
*Spandan* (pronounced *rui chun fan*): *Yunying* says it means the movement of the eyes; *Kaosheng* says that when the eyes move spontaneously without cause, it is called *spandan*.

It is a phono-semantic character (*xing-sheng zi*). Regarding the *Trailokyavijaya-Avalokiteśvara-hṛdaya-dhāraṇī-vidhi*, translated by Amoghavajra: *yun dan* (upper tone for *yun*): to apply colors with a soft, radiant wash over the painting.
*Zéngbó* (繒帛) refers to silken fabrics with reversed colors.
*Fùpò* (縛撲), with the second character pronounced *páng* (邈) and *fǎn* (反), means to strike with the hand and throw [the object] to the ground.
*Jiàn* (󱯾), the character for "treading upon" with the foot; the lower radical is *tà* (踏) and the phonetic is pronounced *tán* (談) and *hé* (合). According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means to tread upon.
*Tiao* (with the *yao* rhyme) means to wave with the hand. Regarding the *Samantabhadra-Vajrasattva-Yoga-Japa-Dharmā*:

translated by Amoghavajra Tripiṭaka Master. *San-chie* (pronounced *chāi*, with the *xiang-re* rhyme): the sound of slapping the chest; it means to pull or drag suddenly. It is derived from the character for "hand" (*shou*) with the phonetic element *zhi*. Next, *pu* (pronounced *bo*, with the *kao* rhyme): the sound of clapping; it means to strike or beat. It is derived from the character for "hand" (*shou*) with the phonetic element *bai*.

*Yángyàn* (陽燄): "Yán" is pronounced with the *yán* rhyme of *jiàn* (閻) or alternatively written as *tán* (談) or *yàn* (燄). As for *yángyàn*, it refers to the state where yang energy predominates, appearing like a mass of fire with rising smoke and flames.

Regarding *sǎdì* (洒滌): the first character is pronounced *xīlǐ* (西禮) and the second is pronounced *dí* (狄). Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states it means "to cleanse and remove"; He Xiu’s commentary on the *Gongyang Zhuan* says it means "to purify and clean. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "water" (*shui*) and the phonetic component "tiáo" (*tiáo*).
