*Lí* (羸): The upper radical is *lèi* (累), which according to the commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* by Du Yu means "weak. Jia Gui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states it means "sick" or "inferior. The *Guǎngyá* defines it as "extreme" or "exhausted. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "emaciated," composed of the radicals *yáng* (羊) and *ní* (𣎆).

The character *jié* (結) is pronounced *juān* (㳙) with the tone *yuè* (悅); the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it means "to decide" (*juédùan*) and is also written as *jiè* (鈌), meaning "to cut. This refers to causing all calamities and afflictions to be severed. The current edition of the scripture uses the character *jié* (駃) from the "Horse" radical; this is the character for *jiétí* (駃騠), a type of horse. To use this instead of the "severance" meaning is a profound error in the scriptural sense.
"Nèn" (腝): The first character is read as *zì* (自) and the second as *cháo* (巢). It refers to the root of the lotus (*lián-gēn*). Regarding "cè" (瓷), the *Kǎo Shēng* states it is a type of pottery;

it is polished with medicinal minerals so that its surface is lustrous. Both ancient and modern standard characters follow the "tile" radical (*wǎ*) and the phonetic "cì" (次), and are also written as "cí" (𦈱). The current scriptural reading "cí" (礠) is actually the name of a mineral stone suitable for medicinal use, not the aforementioned ceramic ware.

*Fuyun* (福蘊): The first character is pronounced *jūn* (with the initial *jǔ* reversed). The *Kǎo Shēng* states that it means "urgent" (*jǐnjí*). It is also written as *tiǎn* (殄), with the second character pronounced *qiányè*.

*Miàn gǎn* (面皯): Pronounced *gǎn* (with the initial *gān* reversed). The *Shuōwén* says: "A dark complexion on the face; derived from *pí* (skin) and *gān* (sound). It is also written as *yín* (𩈅). The current versions of the sutra use *méi* (䵟) with the radical for "black," which is a vulgar form and incorrect.
*Míngyíng* (明鎣): *yíng* is pronounced with the *huánghuí* (縈迴) tone; this has already been fully explained in the seventh fascicle above.
*Jié* (󲦵節): the upper character is pronounced *zhī*; this has already been fully annotated in the sixth fascicle above.

*Jiāyòu* (加祐): *yòu* is pronounced with the *yóujiù* (尤救) tone. Confucius said, "Yòu means assistance. That which Heaven assists is that which is compliant. The *Yì* says, "Assisted by Heaven, there will be good fortune and nothing that is not beneficial. In the *Shuowén*, it is written with the radical *shì* (示) and the phonetic *yòu* (右); the pronunciation of *shì* is *qí* (祇).
The fabrication and embellishment [of this passage] has already been explained in the first fascicle above.
For "xián-pì" (痃癖): the upper character is pronounced *xián* and the lower is pronounced *pǐyì*.

For "xūn-fù" (𡼡複): the upper character is glossed as *yún*; the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "xūn" refers to the vapors of fire, written with the radicals for "black" (*hēi*) and "grass" (*cǎo*). The scripture uses the character "xūn" (熏), which is a vulgar form that has been in circulation for a long time and cannot be altered; the lower character is pronounced *fēngfú*.

In "móhuà" (摹畫), the first character is pronounced *wú hú* (毋胡) [as in *mǔ*]; the *Jīng* (經) version reads *mō* (摸), which is the phonetic for the character meaning "to touch. Is this not the intended meaning of the scripture?
In "mǎnǎo" (碼瑙), the upper sound is *mǎ* (馬) and the lower sound is *nǎo* (惱).
In "sàbō" (馺嚩), the upper sound is *sān jué* (三迊) [as in *sà*] and the lower is *wú kě* (無可) [as in *bō*].

"Xi-yú" (喜愉)—the "yú" is pronounced *zhū*—means joy. This was already explained in detail in the ninth fascicle above; the text's reading as "ài-yōu" (㤤憂) is a significant error regarding the meaning of the scripture.

"Jǐng-jué" (警覺)—the "jǐng" is pronounced *jīng*yǐng*—Zheng Xuan says it means "to arouse. The *Guǎngyá* says it means "restlessness. In both ancient and modern standard characters, this is written with the radical "speech" (言) and the phonetic "jìng" (敬).

The character *yìzhǐ* (意恉) is pronounced *shǐ* (史). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Yizhi means intention; it is composed of the radical 'heart' (*xin*) and the phonetic 'zhi' (*zhǐ*)," and it is also written as *zhǐ*.

The character *zhànchù* (占𥬰) is pronounced *cè* (策); it is the archaic form of the character *chù* (𥬕) in the *Shuowen*, while its appearance in the scripture is incorrect. It is also pronounced *zhōu* (舟), meaning "the weak state of bamboo," which does not accord with the meaning of the scripture.

*Dì* (邸): Upper radical *dī* (低), with the phonetic *lǐ* (禮). The *Cāngjié piān* states that a *dì* is a lodging within a city. The *Shuōwén* states it is the residence for those from subordinate states (*shǔguó*).

It is composed of the radical *yì* (邑) with the phonetic *dǐ* (氐). 13. Volume Thirteen. *Pǔ* (溥): Upper tone, pronounced *pǔ*. The scripture reads *pǔ*; it is the name of a river and does not carry this meaning here.

*Pòu*: Pronounced *tōu* (with the retroflex *lòu* reversed). The *Guǎngyǎ* states that *pòu* means "to harass. In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, this character is composed of the radical *chuò* (辵) and the phonetic *xiù* (秀).

*Qiàn*: Pronounced *qiǎn* (with the retroflex *zhào*). The *Shuōwén* states that *qiàn* means "to reprimand or question. It is composed of the radical *yán* (言) and the phonetic *qiǎn* (遣). *Zhé* (謫) is pronounced *zhé* (with the retroflex *zhú*). *Zhé*: Pronounced *zhé* (with the retroflex *gē*). [Note: This entry appears to be a variant or related gloss for the preceding term.]
The pronunciation of *chōng chuǎng* (充娧) is *yuè*; this has already been fully explained in the first fascicle above.
*zhóu dì shàng* (㧻地上) is pronounced *dīng jiǎo fǎn*, meaning "to dig.

*zhù* (𮂎) is pronounced *shàng jì fǎn*; this character does not exist in any of the various dictionaries, and was created by the translator of the sutra according to his own whim. Below it, *zhū* (下誅) is pronounced *lǚ fǎn*.

14. Chapter Fourteen: *Zhàng* (障). [The character] is pronounced with the initial *r* and the final *k*. It means to obstruct, to partition, or to screen. Some write it as *zhàng* (嶂) with the radical for "mountain" (*shan*). According to the *Shuowen*, it takes the radical for "earth/mound" (*fu*) and the phonetic *zhāng*. The character *zhàng* also has a level tone (*ping sheng*), and its meaning is identical to the departing tone (*qu sheng*). The version in the sutras that uses the hand radical (*shou*) to form *yǎn* (𭢓) is incorrect; it does not constitute a valid character.

*Zuàn* (上歸迫反, 下纂活反): The *Guǎngyá* states that it means "to grasp. The *Shuōwén* correctly writes this as *cuō* (撮), with the radical 手 and the phonetic 最. It means to pinch or gather. *Guǎn* (關患反): The *Kǎoshēng* states that it means "to pierce" or "to put on clothes.

The *Shuōwén* writes this as *huàn* (擐), meaning "to don armor and take up weapons," with the radical 手 and the phonetic 睘. The text here uses the character 慣 (from the radical 心), which carries the meaning of "habituation"; this is not the intended meaning in the scripture.

*Li* (儷): Upper radical *li* (犂), pinyin *diǎn* (反); lower radical *di* (帝), pinyin *fǎn* (反). According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to pair" (*hào*) or "to beautify" (*měi*). This has already been fully explained in the seventh fascicle.

*Yùyuè* (煜爚): Upper character *róng* (融), pinyin *sù* (反); lower character *yáng* (羊), pinyin *zhuó* (反). The *Guǎngyá* states that *yùyuè* refers to the blazing intensity of fire. The *Pīcāng* states it is an appearance of abundance. In the *Shuōwén*, both characters are composed of the radical *huǒ* (fire) with *yù* (昱) and *yuè* (龠) as their phonetic components.
*Gēn* (根): the radical *wù* (杌) with the phonetic *xià* (下) and *gǔ* (骨) as the reversed component;
it refers to the root. *Yá* (芽): the radical *shàng* (上) with *yǎ* (雅) and *jiā* (加) as the phonetic; it refers to the initial sprouting of grasses and trees. *Zhì* (馹):
the radical *shàng* (上) with *rén* (人) and *zhì* (質) as the phonetic; it refers to sound and resonance, a transliteration of a Sanskrit term.
15. Volume Fifteen. Regarding the character 賸 (shèng), the *Shēngyùn* states it means "remainder.
Regarding the term 𣌑誐 (lèi-é), the first character is pronounced pǎo-mào; it is a Sanskrit word.
Regarding "bǎo" (棓) in the title, it is pronounced *páng* (講反); its meaning was already explained in the fourth fascicle.
Regarding "shuò" (槊), it is pronounced *shuāng* (霜) and *zhuō* (捉); the correct form is "shuò" (矟).

Regarding "Xīduōhé" (枲多河), the first character is pronounced *sī* (思) and *zǐ* (子) [as a rhyme], and the second has the sound *duō* (多); in Sanskrit this means "Yellow River" (Huanghe) in the language of Tang.

*Shēng* (to ascend): The character is pronounced *shí qǔ* (反). The *Cāngjié piān* states it means "to ascend. The *Guǎngyá* states it means "to advance. The standard orthography of the present day consists of the radical *fù* (阜) with the phonetic *tǔ* (土) and the sound *shēng* (升).

*Tángchù* (to strike/bump into): The character is pronounced *dàng láng* (反). The *Guǎngyá* states it means "to jostle" (*tángpù*). The standard orthography of the present day consists of the radical *shǒu* (手) with the phonetic *táng* (唐). The pronunciation of *tù* (揬) is *tū* (突).
*Ni* (mud): read as *nián* (with the second tone reversed).

Regarding the character *yuán* (border/edge) in the phrase "walled outside" (*yuán wài*), it is pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*). Zheng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states that "bordering" (*yuán*) means "adorned edges. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical *mì* (silk) and the phonetic *huàn*. The text reads *chuán* (rafters), which is the name for an official office and does not carry this meaning here. *Huàn* is pronounced *tuān* (with the second tone reversed).
"Locusts" (luángchóng): the first character is pronounced huáng;
the second is the phonetic zhú with the radical róng. "Treads upon" (tàzhě): the first character is pronounced tán with the radical là;
the character "zhě" consists of the radical "white" (bái) below it. Volume 16, Number 16. "Rinsing" (yǐnshòu): the phonetic is sōu with the radical zhòu; it means to splash and rinse with water.
"Three handfuls" (sānjù) is pronounced *jiū* (sixth tone).

"Dish-shaped topknot" (*pánjì*)—the lower character is pronounced *jì*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Yīlǐ* states that it refers to the hair tied in a topknot; whether ancient or modern, the correct orthography uses the radical for "hair" (*biāo*) with the phonetic component *jí*.
"Tapered upper body" (*shēngshàng*)—the upper character is pronounced *jié*; this was already explained in the seventh fascicle.

"Chunbai" (pure white) refers to hanging cords; the ancient pronunciation is "chunmei" (pure beauty), meaning the color is unmixed. In the *Fangyan*, it means "excellent. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "silk" (糸) and the phonetic "zhun" (屯); the form using "you" (酉) as the phonetic for "chun" (醇) is incorrect.

*Dì* (the first character in *dìliàng*, "measurement") is pronounced as *dié* (upper tone). Volume Seventeen, Part One. Regarding *duò* (the first character in *duòliàng*, "measurement"): it is pronounced with the initial *táng* and the final *luò*. Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that *duò* means "to measure" (*duī*). Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that *duò* means "to gauge and measure" (*kuíduò jiàoliàng*). The *Zuozhuan* states: "When the mind can regulate what is right, it is called *duò*. The *Shuowen* defines it as "law and regulation," written with the radical 又 and the phonetic 庶 (abbreviated). The text here uses 𢜬, which is incorrect. The standard form for the second character, *liàng* ("measure"), is pronounced *lìzhāng*.

The character 倣 (fǎng) is pronounced with the final sound of 罔 (wǎng), meaning "to imitate" or "to model oneself after. According to the *Yùnlüè*, it is also written as 學 (xué), with the lower radical 爻 (xiáo) and the phonetic 教 (jiào). The *Kǒngzhù* on the *Shūjīng* states: "Fǎng means to teach. In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, this character follows the radical 支 (zhī) and takes 學 (xué) as its phonetic.

The characters 倱 (pinyin: hún; ancient pronunciation: huǒn) and 伅 (pinyin: dùn; ancient pronunciation: wěn) are explained in the *Zuozhuan* commentary as "those who are ignorant and dark-minded, lacking understanding. Regarding the standard orthography of these characters from antiquity to the present: those following the radical for "person" (亻) have "kūn" and "tún" as their phonetic components. Those in the classics following the radical for "water" (氵) are written as 渾 (hún) and 沌 (dùn); both are names of rivers.

*Yíngnǚ* (娙女): The first character, *yíng*, is pronounced with the initial *qì* (鶂) and also with *yǎ* (雅) or *xún* (𥝷). The *Cāngjié piān* states that it refers to the name for a noblewoman; it was also the personal name of the consort of Emperor Wu of the Han. The *Shuowén* defines it as having the appearance of being tall and beautiful, composed of the radical "woman" (*nǚ*) and the phonetic "jīng" (*jīng*). The reading *yóu* (媱) found in the *Jīng* [edition] is incorrect.

The character for *xù* (䰅) is pronounced with the upper radical *xiāng* (相, yú fǎn) and the lower radical *shuǐ* (𮒂, bì fǎn). The *Bóyá* states that it refers to the "heart of a flower" (*huāxīn*). The *Shuowén* defines it as "a cluster" (*róng*) and explains it as being composed of the radical *gòng* (廾) and the phonetic *ruǐ* (繠). It is incorrect for the scripture to write this as *rěi* (蘂) with the radical *mù* (木); the pronunciation of *ruǐ* (橤) is the same as above.

18. Volume Eighteen, Chapter Eighteen. Regarding "jiǎo" (撟): [The character] is pronounced with the initial *qiāo* (嬌夭). Gu Yewang states that to falsely claim something is "jiǎo," which is also synonymous with "wú" (誣, to slander). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "tán" (檀) and says it is formed from the hand radical and the phonetic *qiáo* (喬); however, the version used in the scriptures writes it as "jiǎo" (矯), which denotes a martial appearance and does not carry this meaning. Regarding "kuàng" (誑): [The character] is pronounced with the final *kuáng* (狂). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Chunqiu* states it means "to deceive. Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states it means "to delude. According to the standard characters of antiquity and today, it belongs to the "yan" (言, speech) radical and has the phonetic *kuáng* (狂).
*Kubhāra* (the first syllable pronounced with an upper tone): this is the Sanskrit term for a human skull. *Taṇḍula-kṣāra*: the character *kṣāra* is incorrectly written as *zhǎo*;

it should correctly be written as *xiāo*. Regarding "the pulp of a lotus seed" (*lián-zǐ-ráng*): dictionaries state that *rǎng* refers to the internal fruit of a melon; the correct character for ancient and modern usage is *guā* (melon) with *xiāng* as its phonetic component. The version in the sutra using *rǎng* is incorrect.

The character for "point" (點) is pronounced *xìn* (with the initial *x-*, as opposed to the common reading); it is also correctly written as 囟 (*xìn*), which is a pictograph. Regarding "cleansing" (潔滌):

the first character is pronounced *jié* (as in *jié*) and the second is pronounced *dìng* (with the final *-ng*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "滌" means to wash; it is composed of the radical "water" (*shui*) and the phonetic component "tiáo" (*tiao*).

*Yǎn* (臥): Upper radical *niān* (㦥) with the phonetic *jiǎ*. The *Guoyu* commentary states it means "to rest. The *Guoyi* says it means "to look up" or "to stop. The standard character of ancient and modern times follows the radical *ren* (人) and the phonetic *yàn* (匽). The version in the scriptures written as *yàn* (堰) is incorrect. Lower radical: *wǔ* with the tone *guò*. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* says it means "to rest. It follows the radical *ren* (人) and *chén* (臣), taking the latter for its meaning of "prostrate."

19. Nineteenth Fascicle. Nineteenth Fascicle. *Zhè shǒu* (磔手): *zhè* (磔) means to spread apart; it refers to spreading the hands and taking the distance from the thumb to the middle finger as the measure.
The character 搵 (pronounced *wèn*, with the *kùn* rhyme) is explained in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as "to dip shallowly into water," composed of the radical 手 (hand) and the phonetic 昷.

The character 摶 (pronounced *bó*, with the *mò* rhyme) is explained in the *Zhangshuo Kaosheng* as "to attach or adhere. It is incorrect for the sutras to use the hand radical to form 搏 instead [of 摶].

The character for "bud" (dǒu) on the upper part of the platform [in the character 朶] is pronounced cháng (with the level tone) and lüè (with the departing tone). Regarding the character for "bud" (dǒu) on the upper part of the stem, it is pronounced xìng (with the rising tone) and gēng (with the level tone). Dictionaries state that it refers to grasses and water plants drooping. The lower part is pronounced dōu (with the third tone). The *Wenzi Dianshuo* explains: "A 'bud' (dǒu) refers to the clusters of flowers hanging from trees; it follows the radical 'wood' (木) and is a pictograph. The current version of the scripture uses the character 朶 with the radical 巳, which is a grave error and incorrect.
*Shùshēn* (豎伸): The first character is pronounced *shū* (殊) with the *rǔ* (乳) rhyme;

the second is pronounced *shēn* (申). *Shūsǎn* (梳綰): The first character is pronounced *sū* (䟽); the second is pronounced *wān* (彎) with the *bǎn* (版) rhyme. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that it means "to tie in a knot. The *Shuowén* (說文) explains it as being composed of the radical *mì* (糸, silk thread) and the phonetic *guān* (官).
The character 𤁢 (guàn) has the upper radical *shān* (官) with the reversed form and the lower phonetic *jié* (節).

The character 夗 (yuǎn) has the upper radical *wǎn* (宛阮) reversed; the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "夗轉" means to lie down. It is composed of the radical 夕 (evening) and the character 臥 (to lie down), with the phonetic *yǐ* (已). The version in the sutra uses 踠, which is incorrect. The phonetic for *yǐ* is *jié*.

20. The twentieth fascicle. Regarding the "tangerine" (*chengzi*): the pronunciation of the character *zhì* (枝) is *zhí* (直), with the phonetic component *gēng* (耕). The *Kǎośēng* (考聲) states that it resembles the mandarin orange (*jú*) but is larger. According to the *Shuowén* (說文), it belongs to the category of mandarin oranges and is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) with the phonetic component "climb" (*dēng*). It is incorrect for the scriptures to write this as *táng* (棠) or *tóng* (橖).

*Mújiàn* (無間): "Jiàn" is pronounced as *xiàn* (莧). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that it means "intervals" (*jiàngé*) or "intermingled" (*zá*). This is as in the *Zuǒzhuan*: "Interweaving the institutions of the former kings. *Chóuyè* (稠酪): The upper character "chóu" (稠) is pronounced as *zhòuliú* (紂流). The *Guǎngyá* (廣雅) states it means "dense" (*chóujì*).

It is derived from the radical "grain" (*huó*) with the phonetic "zhōu" (周). The lower character "lào" (酪) is pronounced as *lánggè* (郎各). The *Shìmíng* (釋名) states it is "that which is made from milk. The *Guǎngyá* states it is "fermented drink" (*jiāng*). According to the standard characters of antiquity and today, it is derived from the radical "wine" (*yǒu*) with the phonetic "gè" (各).

"Lián" (䏈) is pronounced with the upper radical "mián" (綿) having the phonetic value of *shàng* (上) and the lower radical "biān" (鞭) having the phonetic value of *xià* (下). The *Shēnglèi* (聲類) states that "lián" means "uninterrupted continuity. The *Shuowén* (說文) says "lián" means "to connect," composed of the "ear" (耳) radical joined to the "cheek" (頰); it further includes the "silk" (絲) radical, taking "silk" to signify mutual connection and non-interruption. The character "lì" (縷) is composed of the "thread" (糸) radical and the phonetic component "bó" (帛).

The upper character 幖 (biǎo) is pronounced as 必遙反 (bì yáo fǎn), and the lower character 幟 (chì) is pronounced as 嗤志反 (chī zhì fǎn). The *Guǎngyá* states: "Both 幖 and 幟 are banners (*fān*). The *Jīngǔjīnzhèngzì* states: "Holding one red banner (*chìfān*) is [the meaning]. Both characters are composed with the radical 巾; 票 and 戠 are their phonetic components. The text’s use of 摽 is incorrect. 幟 is also written as 󲋪, with the same meaning.
21. Fascicle Twenty-one. Regarding "yú" (虞) in "xíng yú" (形㑨): according to the *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (毛詩傳), it means "a large appearance. Regarding "zhàng" (障) and "ài" (閡):
the former is pronounced zhāng (章讓反) and the latter is pronounced yù (俣愛反); these were already explained previously in Fascicle Two.

"Luo" (絡) in "luobō" (絡髆) is pronounced *luò* (with the initial *l-*) and the rhyme *gē* (各). Guo’s commentary on the *Shanhai jing* states that "luo" means to encircle. The *Fangyan* states that from the region east of the Guanzhong pass, including Zhou, Luo, Han, and Wei, they call "encircling" (*rào*) "luo. In the *Shuowen*, it is written with the radical for silk (*miè*) and the phonetic *gē*; the version in the [present] scripture as "zhuó" (𩊚) is incorrect. The next character, "bō" (膊), is pronounced *bó*. The version in the scripture as "pō" (膊) is incorrect. The final character is pronounced *sāng* (桑) and *gē* (各).
In the phrase "pútáo duō," the *Yīnyì* (Phonetic Meaning) commentary on the *Hànshū* states that "duō" is pronounced with the second tone, the *dōu* rhyme, and the *guǒ* final.

[The character] "xiān" (銛) is pronounced with the upper part *biàn* (爕) and the lower part *yán* (閻). In the *Hànshū Yīnyì*, it says "xiān" means "sharp. The *Shuowén* states it is composed of the radical "metal" (金) and the phonetic "tongue" (舌). The lower part is pronounced with the *bān* (般) and *mò* (末) rhymes. The *Màoshī Zhuàn* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry) says "bō" (撥) means "to manage" or "to treat. The *Shuowén* states it is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "fā" (發). The text's reading of "bō" as "bǐ" (𭯆) is incorrect.

The character *jù* (倨) has the first radical *jū* (居) with the phonetic *yù* (御) as its initial, and the second radical *áo* (敖) with the phonetic *gào* (誥). Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "To be *jù* is to lack reverence. The *Guǎngyá* states: "It means arrogant and disdainful. The *Shuowén* states: "*Jù* means to be insolent. Both characters are composed of the radical "person" (*rén*) and "dwell" (*jū*), with *áo* and *gào* serving as their respective phonetics.
The character 㜝 (hài) is pronounced with the upper radical 昂 (áng) and the phonetic 感 (gǎn). It was already explained in the ninth fascicle above.

Regarding the character 緻 (zhì), Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states that "緻" means "dense" (*mì*). The *Guǎngyá* states that "緻" means "to patch" (*bǔ*). In the standard characters of antiquity and today, it follows the radical 糸 (silk thread) and takes 致 (zhì) as its phonetic.

"Shen" (瞫) is pronounced with the upper radical "shēn" (深) and the phonetic "rěn" (稔). The *Cāngjié piān* states that "shen" means to look down or to see secretly. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "eye" (目) and the phonetic "tán" (覃). Examining this, "shènzhī" (瞫知) should be read as "shènshèn" (審審), meaning to examine closely, to determine, or to discern with precision.

22. Fascicle Twenty-two. "Sǒngshù" (聳豎): The upper character is pronounced *sù* (with the phonetic component *yǒng* [勇] as a variant); its meaning should be taken as "to raise up" (*sǒng*). The lower character is pronounced *shū* (with *rǔ* [乳] as a variant); it is correctly written as *shù* (竪).

*Śvetā* (濕廢多): "Wet" (*śe*) and "abandoned" (*fei*), with the first character pronounced as *shēn* (深) and the second as *rù* (入); in the middle, it is pronounced *lǐ* (禮). In the Sanskrit language, this is translated into Chinese as "white color. *Karṇapūra* (耳璫):

"Ear" (*ěr*) and "ornament" (*dāng*), with the second character pronounced as *láng* (郎). *Avamanyate* (懱他): "To despise" (*miè*) and "others" (*tā*), with the first character pronounced as *miánjié* (眠結). It means to treat others with contempt; the character for "contempt" (*yí*) is pronounced as *yí* (移) and *dì* (地).

*Yīshì* (猗適): The upper character is pronounced *yī*. According to the *Erya*, "yī" means "beautiful. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is composed of the radical for "dog" (*quán*) with the phonetic component "qí" (*qí shēng*). *Zǎoguàn* (澡罐): The upper character is pronounced *zǎo*;
the lower character is pronounced *guàn* (with the pinyin *huàn* as an alternative).

"Jù (妒)" and "bì (詖)": the former was already explained in the fifth scroll above; the latter is pronounced *pí* (陂, *mèi*). The *Cāngjié piān* states that "bì" means flattery (*chǎn*). According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) with "pí" as its phonetic.

*Pinzhu* (頻蹙): The first character is read as *pin* (賓反) and the second as *zhu* (子六反). Gu Yewang states that it is the appearance of one who is distressed, sorrowful, and unhappy. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *pin* (顰), with the same definition and explanation.

*Zi* (upper character *zi*, read as *sīfǎn*; lower character *wěi*, read as *wěiyǐfǎn*): According to the *Shuowen*, it means "posture" (*zītài*). *Wěi* means "extraordinary. It is composed of the radical *rén* (person) with the phonetic component *wěi*.

*Xūrán* (upper character *xūn*, read as *yùfǎn*): *Yùcóng* states that *xū* means "sudden" or "hasty. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "something suddenly blowing up. It is composed of the radical *qiàn* (to pant/breath) with the phonetic component *yán*.
*Jībó* (縶縛): The first character is pronounced *zhēn* (砧) with the level tone (*lìfǎn*).
*Rúnjīng* (瞤精): The first character is pronounced *rùn* (閏) with the level tone (*lúnlǎnfǎn*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Rúnmù" (瞤目) means the eyes move;

it is composed of the radical "eye" (*mù*) and the phonetic "rùn. 23. Volume Twenty-three. [The character] *gǎi* (改) is pronounced *sūhóngfǎn*. Volume Twenty-three. [The character] *sù* (󲲟) is pronounced *sūhóngfǎn*.
*Jue* (拳) is pronounced *quan*.
*Vasini* (婆枲抳)—the first character is read as *si* (思) and the second as *ni* (尼)—is a Sanskrit term.
*Kīlikīla* (計利枳攞)—the first character is pronounced *ji* (吉) and the second *la* (羅)—is also a Sanskrit term; it is the name of a great messenger within the Vajra family.
Huàng-yuè (晃爚): the pronunciation is yào.

Regarding "xì-lùn" (戲論), the first character is pronounced with the initial *xī* and the final *qí* reversed [i.e., *xián*]; it is incorrect to derive it from the sense of "empty" (*xū*) as meaning "playful" (*xì*).
Bàng-dú (謗讟): the pronunciation is dú.
24. The twenty-fourth fascicle. [The term] "非𢜬" (fēi luó) has already been explained in the seventeenth fascicle above. Regarding "絛襻" (tiāo pàn):
the first character is pronounced *tǎo* (as in *dāo*), and the second is pronounced *pān* (as in *màn*).
In "chāi dāng shàng chǔ," all [characters] are reversed.

"Yǎnrán" (儼然): "yǎn" is pronounced as "yán" (嚴) with a reversed final; the *Mao Shi Zhuan* says it means a dignified and solemn appearance, that which the people look up to. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it means a beautiful appearance, composed of the radical "ren" (人) and the phonetic "yán" (嚴); the text here reads "qiàn" (嬐), which has the same pronunciation but does not carry the meaning of "yǎnrán."
"Ām-ǎ" (瘖瘂): the upper character is pronounced *yīn* (音), and the lower character is pronounced *yǎ* (雅) with the *niǎo-yǎ* (鳥雅) rhyme; the Classics write this as "ǎ" (啞), which is incorrect.
"Bō-bì" (跛躄): the upper character is pronounced *bō-mò* (波麼) and the lower character is pronounced *bì-yì* (必亦).
"Gè" (各): the pronunciation is *shēng* (升).
Āi-dài (the first character is pronounced *ài*; the second is pronounced *dài*).
Róu-ruǎn (the second character is the variant *ruǎn*, which is a vulgar form of the classical character).

Volume 25. Second Part of Volume 25. Còu-huì (the first character is pronounced *cāng hòu*; in Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci*, it means "to gather"; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to where waters meet, composed of the radical "water" with the phonetic element "zòu").

*Jìn* (身): Pronounced *cí* (辭) with the final consonant *fǎn* (反). Zheng’s commentary on the *Mao Shi* states: "The remains of fire are called *jìn*. The *Shuowen* says it is composed of the radical *huǒ* (火) and the phonetic *yù* (聿), and is interchangeable with *jìn* (燼).

The text’s reading as *jìn* (賮) is an error. *Nào* (秏): Pronounced *shāo* (蒿) with the final consonant *dào* (到). Zheng’s commentary on the *Shi* states: "To decay and perish. The *Cangjie pian* says it means "to dissolve" (*xiāo*). The *Shuowen* says it is composed of the radical *huò* (禾) and the phonetic *máo* (毛).

The character for *yuán* (黿) is pronounced with the upper tone as *yuán*; the *Shuowen* states it is a turtle. The character for *táo* (鼉) is pronounced with the *quī* and *hé* finals; the *Shuowen* states it is an aquatic creature shaped like a lizard, five or six feet long. Both characters for *yuán* and *táo* include the radical *mǐn* (黽); *yuán* has *yuán* as its phonetic component, while *táo* has *ná* (𠹈) as its phonetic component. Those who claim the phonetic component of *táo* is *dān* (單) are incorrect.

The characters for *guī* (tortoise) and *biè* (turtle) are explained as follows: Regarding *guī*: The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "guī" means "ancient. It is a creature with its shell on the outside and flesh on the inside; it takes the character *tuó* (it). The head of the tortoise resembles the head of the *tuó*. According to the nature of Heaven and Earth, among the species of turtles and turtles, there is no male; they take the female (*tuó*) as their mate. This [character] depicts the form of the four legs, head, and tail. The lower part is read as *bǐmiè* (卑滅); the *Shuowen* states it is an aquatic shelled insect. It is formed from *mǐn* (黽) and the phonetic *bì* (敝). In the scriptures, the character *biè* (鱉) is used with the radical of fish; this is a vulgar form.

*Jīngáo* (鯨鼇): The upper character, *jīng*, is pronounced as *jù* (劇) with the *jiǎng* (京) radical; it refers to a large fish in the ocean. The lower character, *áo* (鼇), has the phonetic value *áo*. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* identifies it as a "great tortoise. The *Liezhuan* states that there was a giant spirit-tortoise (*jùlíng zhī guī*) which bore Mount Penglai on its back and sported amidst the blue seas. In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, this character is formed from the radical *mǐn* (黾) with the phonetic value *áo*.

*Níyú* (鯢魚): "Ní" is pronounced as *jì* (藝) with a retroflex final; Dú Yù’s commentary on the *Chūnqiū* states that the *ní* is a large fish. Guō Pǐng’s commentary on the *Ěryá* says: "The *níyú* resembles a catfish (*huán*), has four fins, and its sound is like that of a small child; those over eight or nine feet long are now called *yì* in Jiangdōng and *lì* in Jīngzhōu. In the standard characters of the present day, it is written with the radical for "fish" and the phonetic *ér* (兒); the pronunciation of *lì* (鰨) is *tānglà* (湯蠟).
The characters for *pán* (盤) and *xià* (檄) have the phonetic values *jiào* (晈) and *shuài* (率) respectively; I composed them according to my own whim, though they do not form standard characters.
The characters for *chēn* (瞋) and *xī* (謑) have the phonetic values *zhì* (叱眞反) and *xǔ xiè* (許懈反) respectively.

Regarding *ǎi* (㜝) and *qí* (懠), the translators of the scriptures provided their own phonetic transcriptions at the end of the scrolls as *hàn* (頷) and *jì* (劑). These were created by chance (*lǜ'ěr*) based on the colloquial speech of an old villager (*cūn sǒu*). I am uncertain what kind of words or phrases *ǎi* and *qí* actually represent.
The *huángmǐ* (yellow honey) is pronounced *mì*.

Regarding *bìmá* (the character for "hemp" with the phonetic *zǐ* and the radical *bi*), the *Kǎoshēng* states that it is the name of a plant; the *Wénzìdiǎn* explains that it is correctly written as *bī*, following the radical for grass (*cǎo*).
*Ma-cha-pi-cha*: "Ma-cha" is pronounced with the *pi* sound reversed (as in *chi*). This is a Sanskrit term. *Tsi-tu*:
The first character is pronounced as in *zi*, and the same applies below;

the second character is pronounced as in *lu*. *Yi-mo*: The first character is pronounced as in *jin-ji*; it refers to a cataract in the eye. The second character is pronounced as in *mo*; it is derived from the character for "flesh" (*rou*) and the phonetic element *mo*.

Volume Twenty-Six, Part Two. *Du-yi* (妬裔): The first character is pronounced with the "shang" tone (上聲) and follows the *hu* rhyme; it is not the same as the character for "stone" (石). The second character is pronounced with the "yi" rhyme (祭韻).
"Jìngshūyīnshú" (敬淑音熟):

"Sǒngbiàn" (竦變) — the upper character is pronounced *sù* with the *yǒng* rhyme, while the lower character is composed of the radical "branch" (*zhī*) and the phonetic "luán" (*luán* meaning "to long for").
"Dùfù" (妒󲶐) — the latter character is pronounced *kū* with the *jié* rhyme.

The hairs on the body stand erect (sǒngshù; *sǒng* pronounced as *sù*, with the "yǒng" rhyme). Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Fāngyán* states that "sǒng" means to be startled and terrified. This is the correct character from ancient times to the present, composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "sǒng.
Īnyūn: the upper tone is *yīn*; the lower is *wēiyún*.
*Shùn-mù* (瞬目): The upper character is pronounced *shùn* (with the phonetic component *xún*); it is a vulgar form, its correct form being *zhèn* (瞚). Regarding *xī-dàn* (吸噉):

the upper character is pronounced *xīn* (及) with a reversed tone; the *Guǎngyá* states that "xī" means "to drink. The *Shuowén* explains it as consisting of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic "jí" (*jí*). The lower character is pronounced *tán* (敢) with a reversed tone; the *Guǎngyá* states that "dàn" means "to eat. The standard characters for both ancient and modern usage consist of the radical "mouth" and the phonetic "gǎn" (*gǎn*). The *Shēnglèi* sometimes writes this as *tàn* (啗).

"Jingce" (儆策) means "to warn" according to Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shangshu*. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* explains it as "to admonish. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is composed of the radical "person" (人) and the phonetic "jing" (敬). The final character, "chu" (初), has the pronunciation "ge" (革).
"瘻病" (liù bìng): the first character is pronounced as *lóu* (with the initial *h* reversed). "癥塊" (zhēng kuài): the first character is pronounced as *zhēng* (with the initial *ch* as *zh*;

the second character is pronounced as *kuài* [with *huī* and *wài* as its phonetic components]). 27. Fascicle Twenty-Seven. "蔓菁" (màn jīng): the first character is pronounced as *mán* (with *pán* as its phonetic component); the second character is pronounced as *jīng* (with *jǐng* as its phonetic component). The *Fān yǔ* states: "In the regions of Dongchu it is called *sōng*; in the regions east and west of the Pass it is called *wú jīng*; today in common parlance it is also called *wú jīng*. The *Lǚshì chūnqiū* says: "Among the finest vegetables, there is the *jīng* of Jūqū. The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radical for grass (*艹*) and the phonetic *qīng*.

*Niú* (牛) [the character is pronounced *níng yào* in the vernacular; it is a vulgar form]. The *Shuowen* states that *huí* (浘) means human urine; it is composed of the radicals *wěi* (尾) and *shuǐ* (水), and is also written as *yáo* (󲣨).
*Jiào* (窖) [is pronounced *jiāo xiào*].

Xuàndòng (眩動): The first character, xuàn, is pronounced with the *xuán* rhyme (玄絹反). Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that it means "to delude" (*huànhé*). Gu Yewang says it means "illusion" (*huàn*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "eye" (目) and the phonetic "xuán" (玄).
Luóhú (羅縠): The second character, hú, is pronounced with the *wū* rhyme (江屋反).

*Quǔ* (曲): [The radical] is *gōng* (弓). The standard character for ancient and modern usage is *qiūqiū* (匑匑), meaning a state of being cautious and reverent as if fearing something. It is composed of *bāo* (勹) and the phonetic *kōng* (躳); *bāo* is pronounced *bāo*. *Jué* (掘): [The radical] is *qún* (群) with *wèi* (蔚) as the phonetic;

it is pronounced *qù* (去). It means to pierce through or to cut. *Zhù* (斸) refers to hacking away at the bad soil. In the scriptures, it is written as *xiào* (𧤼) with *jiǎo* (角) as the radical; this was an erroneous character used by the translators of the sutras.

28. Fascicle Twenty-Eight. "Kāi-pǒu" (開剖): "Pǒu" is pronounced *pǒu* with a retroflex initial (普厚反). The commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states that it means "to divide in the middle. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to split," written with the radical 刀 (knife) and the phonetic 咅; the pronunciation of 咅 is *tā kǒu* (他口反).

*Yì-zhàng* (obscuration/veil): The upper character is read as *yī-lì* (繄麗) in the *Fāng-yán*. The *Fāng-yán* states: "Yì means 'to cover' (*yǎn*). Guo's commentary says: "It refers to covering over; it is a curtain or screen. According to the *Shuō-wén*, it is composed of the radical for "feather" (*yǔ*) with the phonetic *ē* (殹). The sound of *ē* is the same as in the following chapters, read as *ràng-fǎn* (讓反). This has already been explained in detail above.
*Xiǎn*: "Scarce fortune" (*xiǎnfú*). The upper character is *xiān* (pronounced *zhèng*, *fǎn*) and is also written as *xiān* today.

It means "to manifest" or "to dazzle. The *Pīcāng* states that it refers to the appearance of radiance; the *Shuowén* says it means "to shine," composed of the radical *huǒ* (fire) and the phonetic *xuán*.

"Zhàn" (to dip) is used in the phrase "dipping [it] on top. The *Wenzi Dadian* explains: "Zhàn means to place an object into water; it is composed of the 'grass' radical and the phonetic 'zhàn. Regarding 'miàn nián' (glutenous paste):

the upper character is read as 'mián' (with the pinyin piàn), and the lower is pronounced 'hú zhāng jiǎn,' according to the *Kaosheng*. It says that boiling glutinous millet and flour produces 'yù' (porridge), which can be used to glue objects. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: 'Nián' means to be sticky; it is composed of the 'glutinous millet' radical and the phonetic 'gǔ. An ancient form is written as '𩚩,' and the *Shenglei* writes it as 'zhān' or 'nián. The character for 'yù' in the sutras is written with the 'wheat' radical as '󲵻,' which is a vulgar form."
29. Fascicle Twenty-Nine. *Xiāoshuò* (銷鑠): The first character is pronounced *xiǎo* (small) with the initial *yáo* (遙); the second character is pronounced *shāng* (商) with the final *ruò* (若).

*Cāilǜ* (猜慮): The first character is pronounced *cǎi* (寀) with the initial *cái* (才). Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states it means "suspicion"; the *Fānyán* states it means "resentment. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "dog" (*quán*) and the phonetic "qīng" (*qīng*).

Regarding "zhua" (槌): the upper radical is "zhe" (陟) with the phonetic "gua" (瓜). The *Kao* states that it refers to the joints of plants and trees, and also to a horse's hoof. In the *Gujin Zhengzi*, it is written with the "mu" (木) radical and the phonetic "guo" (過); the reading given as "guō" (鍋) with the tone "huò" (禍) is incorrect. Regarding "xia" (下): the lower part is "zhui" (追).
*Mitara* (in the original, pronounced *miǎi dǐ luó duō*; in the vernacular, it corresponds to the Sanskrit term for "corpse"). Volume Thirty. [Section] Thirty. *Hǐxì* (嬉戲):

the upper character *hǐ* (嬉) is pronounced with the initial *xǐ* and final *yí*. The *Gǔjīn zhèngzì* (古今正字) states that it means "joyful play" (*xǐlè*) or "laughter" (*xìxiào*). It is composed of the radical *nǚ* (woman/wife) and the phonetic *xǐ* (喜). The lower character *xì* (戲) is pronounced with the initial *xī* and final *jì*.

Preface to the Amoghapāśa Dhāraṇī Sūtra, translated by Huìlín and Lǐ Wúchǎn. The character 該 (gāi) [is pronounced with the second tone, the rhyme coming from 來 (lái), and the glossary *Guóyǔ* states it means "comprehensive"; the *Fāngyán* says it means "all-inclusive"; according to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical 言 with the phonetic 亥].
*Shèng hé*: "hé" is pronounced as *héng* with the *gē* (革) radical. The *Ěryá* states: "The base of a feather is called *hè*. The *Shuowén* says: "The stem of a feather;

it is composed of the radical 'feather' (*yǔ*) and the phonetic 'lì' (*lì*). *Lian rěi*: "rěi" is pronounced as *chuí*. The *Shuowén* says: "To hang down; it is composed of the radicals 'grass' (*cǎo*) and 'silk thread' (*mì*), and the phonetic 'suǐ' (*suǐ*). The text's reading as *rěi* is an error. *Suǐ* is pronounced as *cái wò* (才𰴐).
*De* (德) is pronounced *fu* (孚) with the *wang* (務) final.

*Qiong* (瓊) is pronounced *ang* (昂) with the *ge* (各) final; it refers to the calyx (*hua-die*) of a flower. The *Guiyuan Zhucun* (桂苑珠叢) states that beneath the flowers of plants and trees there are all "supporting calyxes" (*fu-die*) that receive the name of the flower. Regarding the character *die* (𰱹): according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of *xuan* (吅), *ni* (屰), and *cao* (草). The scripture uses *e* (萼), which is a vulgar form of this character. *Xuan* (吅) is pronounced *xuan* (暄); *ni* (屰) is pronounced *ni* (逆).

The Amoghapāśa Dhāraṇī Sūtra, one fascicle. *Vaitaraṇī* (the first character pronounced with the upper tone *bi*; in Sanskrit it is not a compound; in Chinese it means "hungry ghosts" as a general name). In the sūtra, the character is written as *zǎo* (from the mouth) rather than *zhuǎn* (to turn the tongue).

*Kang-mi* (秔米): The character *kang* is pronounced with the initial *geng* (衡反). The *Shenglèi* states it means "not glutinous. The *Shuowén* says it belongs to the category of grain, formed from the radical *huò* (禾) and the phonetic *kàng* (亢);

the vulgar form is *jing* (粳). *Bai-hu* (白縠): The character *hu* is pronounced with the initial *hong* (屋反). The *Shìmíng* states that *hu* refers to fine gauze (*sha-hu*). The *Shuowén* defines it as "fine silk," formed from the radical *mi* (糸) and the phonetic *gu* (穀, in abbreviated form); the character *zhùo* (縳) has the pronunciation *zhí-zhuǎn* (直轉反).

Regarding the character *piàn* (匾): the upper radical is pronounced *shǎn* (󱒓) and the lower body is pronounced *lí* (𥠖). The *Kǎo Shēng* states that *piàn* means "thin. It is incorrect for the sutras to write this as *pō* (䐔) or *rù* (䏲).

Regarding *shì* (舓): the upper part is pronounced *shí* (時尒). Gù Yěwáng says it means "to take food with the tongue. The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radical "tongue" (*shé*) and the phonetic "yì" (易); it is also written as *zhì* (𦧇). The current sutra version uses *shì* (舐), which is a vulgar form; the lower part is pronounced *shūlún* (殊倫).

"Zēngxiān" (憎嫌): The character "zēng" (憎) is read as *shèng* (僧) with the fanqie *fǎnjīng* (反經); the character "jīng" (經) is an error for "zēng" (增). The character "xiān" (嫌) is read as *jiān* (兼) with the fanqie *fǎnjīng* (反經); the original text of the canon has "qiàn" (慊), which is an alternative character.

"Yùjīn" (鬱金): The character "yù" (鬱) is read as *wù* (惲) with the fanqie *fǎnwù* (反勿). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that "yùjīn" is the name of a fragrant grass; it is also written as "yù" (欝), which is a vulgar character.

*Śoṭi*: "Shang" (商) is pronounced with the *zhǎo* (斫) tone; the text reads it as *shuò* (爍), which is incorrect. The subsequent text uses *dīng* (丁) for the middle tone and *fúyuán* (孚袁) for the final tone; these are Sanskrit terms. It is like the edge of a spear, with a small banner attached below.

Regarding "jiū" (灸) with the phonetic *shàng* (上) as *jiǔ* (鳩友反): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "to cauterize" (*zhì* [炙]) by fire, composed of the radical "fire" (*huǒ*) and the phonetic "jiǔ" (*jiǔ*). Regarding "bàn" (瘢) with the phonetic *xià* (下) as *pàn* (伴鏝反): the *Cangjie Pian* states it means "scar" (*hénbān* [瘢痕]); the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "wound" (*bānyī* [痍]), composed of the radical "sickness" (*nà*) and the phonetic "bān" (*bān*). The character used in the scripture is "bǎn" (𤻷), which is a vulgar form.

*Jiào* (pronounced *jiāo*, with the radical for "wine" and the phonetic *jiāo*; also written as *qiáo*) means "to sacrifice," according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*. *Hégǔo* (pronounced *guǒ*, with the radical for "mouth" and the phonetic *guǒ*) refers to kneading flour;
it is read as *sōuyǒu* (with the radical for "hand" and the phonetic *yǒu*) meaning to mix. It is correctly written as *zhāo*.
In the *Niujing* (牛𡊅), it is read as *fenwenfan*; the character *zhai* (󲕪) used in the secular texts is incorrect.
For "dark hair" (*ganfa*), the upper radical is read as *ganlanfan*.
For "tending" (*liaoli*), the upper radical is read as *xiangfan*; the correct character is *li* (󲲙).

*You-lǚ* (the character for *lǚ* is pronounced with the *dòu* rhyme): Guo’s commentary on the *Shānhǎijīng* states that it means "a swelling"; the *Shuōwén* says it is a swelling of the neck, formed from the radical *nà* and the phonetic *lóu*.
*Lài* (upper tone) and *xiàn* (lower tone, pronounced as *xián*): both are wind-related illnesses.

The character *chāo* (抄) is pronounced with the initial *chiao* (交) and the final *fan* (反). The *Guǎngyá* states it means "to plunder. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "to seize with malice," composed of the radical "metal" (金) and the phonetic "shǎo" (少).
The character *zuàn* (攅) is pronounced with the final *fan* *juàn* (倦) or *yuán* (圓); it is also written as *quán* (拳).
The two characters *wàn* (腕) and *jiǎo* (𠛠) are interchanged; they are correctly written as *qián* (掔) and *jiǎo* (𠛠), with the pronunciation *wǎn* (椀) and *guān* (官) respectively.

In the first fascicle of the *Amoghapāśa-dhāraṇī-īśvara-mantra-sūtra*, the character *píng* (瓶) is transcribed as *jíxiáng* (吉祥). According to the *Fānyǔ* (方言), a small vessel for water is called a *píng*. Gu Yewang states it is a vessel used for drawing water. The *Shuowén* writes this character as *bīng* (缾), derived from the radical *wǎn* (缶) with the phonetic component *bìng* (并).

Regarding "white thread" (*báixiàn*): the *Zhèngzhòng zhù* on the *Zhōulǐ* states that "thread" (*xiàn*) is another term for "cord" (*fēn*). Whether ancient or modern, the correct character is written with the radical *mì* (糸) and the phonetic *jiān* (戔), and it is also written as *xiàn*. It is incorrect to write it as *yán* (*cí yán fēi yě*); *yán* has the pronunciation *yán*.

*Eṇeya* (the first character pronounced *yì*, the second *ní*; this is a transliteration from the Sanskrit language) refers to a golden-colored deer; the version of the sutra that reads *yī* is an error.
*Pāṇḍu* (the first character pronounced *mǎn*, the second *bàn*)—the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "unpatterned silk," composed of the radical for "silk" (*mì*) and the phonetic *màn*.

The character "𭣝" (zhēn) above is a scribal error for "楨" (zhēn); "楨" is pronounced *kè-gēng* and refers to the sound of the *qín* and *sè* lutes. If one were to take it as the character "楨" (meaning a pillar), it would deviate from its meaning and be erroneous. Now, using the character "𭣝" alongside "𭣜," it is somewhat closer to reason; following common usage, it is pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*).

2. In the middle fascicle, regarding the character *páng* (棓): following the *Kǎo Shēng* (Examination of Sounds), it is said to mean a large staff; it is also written as *pán* (柈) or *yì* (𣘙). According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radicals for "wood" (*mù*) and "sound" (*pǒu*). It is an error to follow the *Jīng* (Classics) and write it with the radical for "hand" (*shǒu*) as *póu* (掊).

Regarding the character *hóng* (䂎), it is pronounced with the "luan" rhyme group (qī luàn fǎn). The *Yùnlüè* states that it is a small spear; examining its phonetic component (*shēng*), it is a short halberd, shaped like a *qiāng* but with a broad blade. The *Guǎngyá* says that *hóng* is called a *chán*. In ancient and modern standard characters, it follows the "máo" radical with the phonetic "zàn. In character dictionaries, it is written as *chán* (𥎝), with the same pronunciation as above. The version in the *sūtra* written as *cuì* (鑹) is incorrect. The pronunciation of *chán* is *yán*.

Regarding "ce-li" (策勵), the *Fanzheng* (反切) indicates it is pronounced as *zhì*. Wang Yewang states that "li" (勵) is synonymous with "mian" (勉, to exert). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Spring and Autumn Annals* explains it as "mutually encouraging and exerting. In both ancient and modern times, the correct character is written with the radical for "force" (力) and the phonetic "li" (厲).
3. Lower Fascicle. *Mama-kī* (the first character pronounced as *ma-mo-ji*, the second as *ji-li*; in Sanskrit, this is the name for the Mother of the Vajra Family).
*Er-dang*: the sound is *dang*.
Regarding "huì" (繪): it is read as huí-duì-fǎn-kǎo. The *Shuōwén* states that "huì" also means "to paint," and it is composed of the radical "silk" (糸) with the phonetic "guì" (貴).
Regarding "niè" (躡): it is read as nián-zhé-fǎn. The *Shuōwén* states that "niè" means "to tread upon" or "to step on," and it is composed of the radical "foot" (足) with the phonetic "niè" (聶).

*Kiè-sì* (篋笥): *qián* (頰) is the phonetic component for the upper character; the *Shuowen* states it means "a lid" (*jiān*) and is composed of the radical "bamboo" (*zhú*) with the phonetic *qiè*. It is also written as *qiè* (匧). *Sī* (思) is the phonetic component for the lower character; *zì* (漬) is its pronunciation. Gu Yewang states that a *sì* is a container for clothing; according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "bamboo" with the phonetic *sī*.

*Ji-yì* (𧶝易): Pronounced *móu-hòu*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to trade goods"; it is composed of the radical 貝 (*bèi*) and the phonetic 丣 (*yǒu*). 丣 is an archaic form of the character 夘 (*mǎo*). The version appearing in the scriptures as 𧴵 is a vulgar character.
*Gēng-shí* (耕殖): Pronounced *chéng-zhí*. It means "to sow. The version appearing in the scriptures as 植 (*zhí*) is also acceptable.

"Yāoqī" (邀期): "Yāo" means "to intercept. According to the Du Anshu commentary on the *Zuozhuan*, it is a character from ancient and modern standard orthography, formed with the radical "chuò" (辵) and the phonetic "jiǎo" (敫).

"Yàn mèi" (魘魅): "Yàn" is read as "yàn-yán" (懕琰); this is a vulgar character not found in any of the various character dictionaries, and one should follow the reading of the scripture text. "Mèi" (魅) is read as "méi-bì" (眉祕). The *Shanhaijing* states that the creature known as a "mèi" has a human body and black hair, originating from the eyes. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as having the phonetic "kǎo" (考). It is the essence of a thing; the character is formed with the radical "guǐ" (鬼) and the element for hair (*máo*) with three strokes (*sān*). The correct form is "mí" (鬽).

"Anus" (zhǐ): The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it refers to a disease of the posterior passage; it is composed of the radical "sickness" (疒) and the phonetic "si" (寺), with the lower character pronounced as "lòu.
*Bukong juansuo shenzhou xin jing* (*The Heart Sutra of the Divine Incantation of the Amoghapāśa*), translated by Xuanzang. "Soft grass" (ruǎn cǎo): The upper character is read as "rǎn" (而兖反).

*Yin* (齗): The upper character is read as *jīn* (斤) according to the *Cāngjié piān*, which states that *yǐn* (齗) refers to the gums, the roots of the teeth; the *Shuowén* states it is the flesh of the teeth, formed with the radical "tooth" (*chǐ*) and the phonetic "jīn. The lower character, *áng* (昂), is read as *gè* (各); the *Kǎoshēng* states that *áng* (昂) is synonymous with *yǐn* (齗).

Yīn (陰): The character *guǎn* is the phonetic component. The *Pīcāng* states that *guǎn* refers to the buttocks (*kāo*). The *Shuowen* writes it as *guǎn*, defining it as being above the thighs (*bǐ*). The *guǎn* found in the canonical text is merely a vulgar variant.

Regarding "yān" (胭) in the neck: the *Shēnglèi* states that "yān" refers to the throat. In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, it is composed of the radical "flesh" (肉) with the phonetic "yīn" (因), the latter being pronounced "xuéjiǎng" (學講). The *Shuowén* states that "xiàng" (項) refers to the back of the neck; it is composed of the radical "head" (頁) with the phonetic "gōng" (工).

*Kū-pi* (癵癖): The first character, *kū*, is pronounced with the level tone (*yuanfan*); Wang Yewang states it means "sickness," referring to the body being afflicted by stiffness and curvature. The second character, *pi*, is pronounced with the departing tone (*pīyifan*); the *Shenglèi* states it refers to indigestion where food remains in the stomach. This is the correct orthography according to both ancient and modern standards.

Regarding the character for "pustule" (皰): it is pronounced *pào* (with the radical *máo* reversed). Xu Shuchong stated that "pustule" refers to facial gas; examining its phonetic component (*shēng*), it refers to fine sores on the face. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "skin" (*pí*) with the phonetic "bao. It is also written as "pào" (疱), with the pronunciation *báimáo*.

*Shu* (舒) and *juan* (捲): the former is pronounced as *shu* (暑), the latter as *juan* (倦) with the *fan* (反) tone. These have already been fully explained and annotated previously. Regarding *huī* (撝):
Gu Yewang states that it refers to the direction indicated by the hand. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shou*) and the phonetic element "wei" (*wei*).

Regarding the character *biàn* (遍) in *gǔ* (罟): the ancient commentary on the *Zhouli* states that it means "a net. In antiquity, the official *Paoqinshi* (疱𦏁氏) created nets by tying knots in ropes. Whether ancient or modern, the correct orthography follows the radical *gāng* (冈) with the phonetic *gǔ* (古). The version in the Classics that uses *jí* (吉) to form *jiǎn* (罫) is incorrect.

*Jiǎo* (剿): Repeatedly submitted; the small radical is *jiāo* (焦) with the phonetic *fǎn* (反). The commentary on the sounds says it means "to exterminate" or "to cut. The standard character for all times past and present takes *dāo* (刀) as the radical and *cháo* (巢) as the phonetic;

the latter is pronounced *lù wèi fǎn*. *Jiān* (殲): Former character *jiē lián fǎn* (接廉反). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* says it means "to exhaust" or "to finish. The *Shuowen Jiezi* takes *è* (歺) as the radical and *xiān* (韱) as the phonetic; *xiān* is pronounced *xī lián fǎn*.
*Mo*: Pronounced *bó* (in the *Mao Shi Zhuan*, "mo" means illness). In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, it is composed of the radical *nà* (疒) and the phonetic *mò*.

*Hún yáo*: The upper character is pronounced *hún* (also *wěn*) and is correctly written as *hùn*; the lower character is pronounced *xiào jiāo* and is correctly written as *yáo*. Together they mean turbid confusion and disorder.
*Mò zhì* (莫晣): The first character is pronounced with the *zhēn* rhyme (*tián*). The *Shuowen* states: "Zhāozhì" means bright; it is composed of the radical "sun" (*rì*) and the phonetic "zhé.

It is also written as *zhé*. *Jiàn* (鑑): Pronounced *tú shàng jiàn* (*dàn*). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "Jiàn" means to illuminate and examine. The *Shuowen* writes it as *jiàn*, stating: "A large basin. One interpretation says it is used for overseeing [the ritual]. It can also be used to take the 'bright water' from the moon. It is composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic "jiàn."

*Amoghapāśakalparāja Sūtra*, one fascicle, compiled by Huilin. Regarding "purple *jiāng* wood" (the character for *jiāng* is pronounced *yǎng*): the *Shān-hǎi jīng* states that Mount Yīng abounds in purple *jiāng*. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is a type of wood; it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic component "jiāng" (*jiāng* is pronounced *fāng*). The pronunciation of *fāng* is [as noted above].

*Xián* (鹹): pronounced *xiàn* (with the rhyme of *jiān*). The *Erya* states: "Salt is bitter. Guo Pu’s commentary notes: "Bitter refers to extreme saltiness. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "It is the flavor of the north; it is composed of the radical *lǔ* (鹵) with the phonetic *xián* (咸)."

The *Sūtra on the Merit of the Virtuous Rosary*, the *Sūtra on the Merit of Comparing Rosaries*, and the *Sūtra on the Merit of Comparing Rosaries*—these five sūtras, totaling fifty-two works in fifty-five fascicles, share the same phonetic glosses as this volume.

In the *Sūtra on the Secret Treasury of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva’s Divine Incantations for Eradicating All Evil Karma*: regarding the term "pú" (仆) in the title, Hui-lin’s gloss states it is pronounced with the initial *péng* (朋) and the final *běi* (北). The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "Pú means to fall prostrate; it is composed of the radical 'person' (人) and the phonetic 'bǔ' (卜)."

*Tan-yin* (痰癊): The upper character, *tan* (談), according to the *Wenzi jilüe* (文字集略), refers to the fluids within the chest; the lower character is pronounced *jìn* (禁). *Kuō-yáng* (𤺍痒): The upper character is pronounced *guǒ-hé* (果和); the *Cāngjié piān* (蒼頡篇) states it means a sore or ulcer, or baldness.

The correct orthography of ancient and modern times follows the radical *nà* (疒) with the phonetic *guā* (瓜). The scriptural text uses *kuò* (瘑), which is a vulgar character. The lower character is pronounced *yáng-chiǎng* (羊蔣); the *Ēryá* (爾雅) states it means the disease of itching. According to the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲), it means an ulcer, a slight form of pain. The *Shuowén* (說文) records it as *yáng* (蛘), meaning a sore (*yáng* [瘍]); it takes the radical *yóu* (由) with the phonetic *yáng* (羊).

The character for *zhīzhū* (spider): the upper radical is pronounced "zhī" and the lower is pronounced "zhū. Examining its phonetic, it is the name for a *wǎnggǔ* (web-spinning insect). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "The *zhīzhū* is a *máo* [insect]; it takes *miǎn* as its radical and *shǔ* as its phonetic. It also takes *miǎn* as its radical and *zhū* as its phonetic, and is also written as *zhì* or *hǔ*. The version in the scriptures as *zhīpá* is incorrect. The pronunciation of *shǔ* is "zhì."
*The Sutra of the Cintāmaṇicakra Dhāraṇī*. Compiled by Huilin. Regarding the character *bì* (雞喇斯中闌葛反): according to the *Yùnlüè*, it means "to fall prostrate on the ground" (*bìdì*).
The *Shuowén* records it as 𣦢, stating that it refers to a person who cannot walk; it is composed of the radical "stop" (止) with the phonetic "bi" (辟).

Regarding "to rescue" (拯濟): the upper character is taken as the third tone (zhǒng). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that it means "to assist. The *Fangyan* states that to pull someone out of drowning is called "rescue" (拯). The *Shuowen Jiezi* records the correct form as "chēng" (抍), meaning "to lift upward," composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "qí" (𠿞). The text here uses "zhì" (䒱), pronounced *zhí róng fǎn*, which is incorrect and is not adopted here.

The character for *pín* (嬪) is composed of the radical *mǐn* (民) with the phonetic *fāng* (方) and *lì* (隸). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that *pín* refers to "wives" (*fù*). Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* says it is a designation for women who possess ritual propriety and standards. The character for *fēi* (妃) refers to the ladies-in-waiting (*yùnǚ*) and also to the *shìfù* (ladies of the court). In both ancient and modern standard characters, these are written with the radical *nǚ* (女), and *bīn* (賓) and *jǐ* (己) serve as their phonetics.
The character 𭠒 (pān-bō) is a transliteration of a Sanskrit mantra syllable; it is sometimes written as 𠎆. The character 笄 (jī-sòu-sōu-yòu) means "to rinse";
according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to rinsing and washing the mouth, composed of the radical for water with the phonetic element 欶.
*Jiānsǎ*: the first character is pronounced *jié*; the second character is pronounced with the radical *sā* and the phonetic *jiǎ*.

Guān Yù (as cited by Zhèng in his commentary on the *Lǐjì*) states that it refers to a lock or key. The *Shuōwén* explains it as consisting of the radical "gate" (*mén*) and the phonetic "flute" (*yù*). The text uses the character *yào*, which is a vulgar form; the pronunciation of *yù* is the same as above.

*Fu* (各訃): *fu*, with the phonetic *fu* (孚) reversed; Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states that "to announce" (*fu*) means "to arrive. This is the correct character for both ancient and modern usage, composed of the radical "speech" (*yan*) and the phonetic "bu" (*bo*). It is also written as *zhu* (䟔). *Zhuang* (相柱):
*zhu*, with the phonetic *zhu* (縷).

"Cán niǎn" (to pinch/gather): "cú" (徂) is the phonetic component; the *Gōngjīn zhèngzì* (Correct Characters of the Ancients and Present) states that "cán" means "thicket" (*cóng*). This refers to gathering the five fingers together like a thicket to pinch the bead. The character is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "zàn" (*zàn*). In the scriptures, it is written with the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) as "zǎn," which is incorrect. The lower part is pronounced "níng dié."
"Stirring so as to cause [the upper] to intersect is skillful.
At the time of erosion, 'upper' (shàng) is pronounced zhí (職) in reverse;
'digging into the ground' (chōu dì) is pronounced quán (權) in reverse."
"Tiánzhù" (填築): the upper character is pronounced tián (a common usage; the correct form is tián [窴]); the lower character is pronounced zhú. "Píngmáo" (平𭻁):
pronounced tiánliàn (田鍊) with the level tone.
"Wǒpō" (鄔波): the upper character is pronounced wūgǔ (烏古); the classics write it as wǒ (隖), which is a vulgar character.
Sù (pronounced with the *wu* and *fa* finals reversed).

*Chǎo* (the first character is pronounced with the *dao* and *lao* finals reversed; the *Jīng* [Canon] uses the vulgar character 㨶; the second character is pronounced with the *shī* and *zǐ* finals reversed).
*Jiǎn* (the first character is pronounced with the *jū* and *yǎn* finals reversed; the *Wénzì Jílüè* states: "The eyelid is the outer skin of the eye; it follows the radical for 'eye'").
Xià-yì (瑕翳): the first character is pronounced with the *xià* rhyme and the second with the *yī* rhyme.
Chéng-hài (棖害): the first character is pronounced *zhái-gēng* and the second *liáng-zhàng*.

Bái-yùn (白暈): the *yun* is pronounced *yún-jùn*; the *Shiji* states it refers to the halos surrounding the sun and moon. According to the "Correct Characters" of ancient and modern times, this character is composed of the radical 日 (sun) and the phonetic 軍 (jūn).

*Chī* (眵) is the opposite of *chǐ* (齒). The *Kǎo Shēng* states it refers to the discharge (*chī*) in the eyes. The *Shuōwén* says: "The character *chīmèng* (眵瞢) means blurred vision; it is composed of the radical 'eye' and the phonetic 'duō'. As for *chìmó* (赤膜), *mó* is pronounced *bó*.
In the scriptures, it is written as *mò* (瞙) with the 'eye' radical, which does not accord with the meaning of the scripture.

"Find medicine" (wèn yào): "wèn" is pronounced with the *shàng* tone and the radical *kùn*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "to sink," following the phonetic *mò*. In the sutra, it is written as *qiè* (from the wood radical), which is incorrect.

"Do not leak lightly" (*qīng xiè*): "xiè" is pronounced with the *liè* tone. The *Guangya* states it means "to leak. According to this, "do not treat people with slight leakage" should be the character *xiè* (媟). *Xiè* means "insolence"; it means one must not obtain full knowledge [of others] and then treat them with slight insolence.
Regarding "efficacy" (xiào): the character is written as 效 in the scripture, which is a homophone for "instruction" (jiào); it is not the intended meaning of the scripture.

In the *Avalokiteśvara-bodhisattva-yathā-manas-citta-dhāraṇī-mantra-sūtra*, the term "boil" (*yōng*)—the first character pronounced with the initial *yǒng* and the final *gōng*, and the second pronounced with the initial *yīng* and the final *jǐng*—is defined in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as a "goiter on the neck. It is composed of the radical "sickness" (*nà*) and the phonetic "infant" (*yīng*), with the tone of "goiter" being *liú*.

"Jū" (疽) and "xiǎn" (癬): the former is pronounced with the initial *q* and final *-yu* (上七余反); the *Shuowen* states that "jū" refers to a long-standing carbuncle (*yòu tōng*), composed of the radical *nà* (疒) and the phonetic *qiě* (且).
The latter, "xiǎn," has the initial *x* and final *-qiǎn* (下仙淺反). "Fánténg" (煩疼) has the final *-dōng* (徒冬反). "Fùzhàng" (腹脹) has the final *-liàng* (張亮反)."
The Sūtra on the Ritual for Reciting the Heart Dhāraṇī of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; from the *Mahāvairocana Sūtra*, the Ancient Sound within the Five-pronged Vajra.

The first character, tiáo (蹢), has the phonetic *tiáo* (條). The *Cangjie pian* states it means "leaping" (*tiaoyong*). The *Shuowen jiezi* defines it as "a leap" (*yue*), formed with the radical for feet and the phonetic *zhao* (兆). The second character, chi (蹢), has the phonetic *chi* (池) and the classifier *ji* (戟). Gu Yewang states it means "lifting the foot. The *Shuowen jiezi* also notes it is formed with the radical for feet and the phonetic *shang* (啇), and is also written as *zhi* (躑). In this scripture, it is written with the hand radical as *zhi* (擲); this is a vulgar usage and incorrect.
"Chánjiào" (噉嚼): the first character is pronounced as *tán-lǎn* (反) and the second as *qiáng-yào* (反).

Regarding the "Guānzìzài Rúyìlún Púsà Niànsonyìguī Jīng" (觀自在如意輪菩薩念誦儀軌經), translated by Bukong: the character "jiǎo" (繳) at the end of the right-hand column is explained in the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) as meaning "entanglement" (*jiǎochán*). The *Yùnyuān* (韻詮) states that it is written with the radical "cloth" (*jīn*) and has the same meaning as "kǎo" (憿).

The term *pán* (蟠) in *chělù* (車輅) is pronounced *bàn* (伴) with the *fǎn* (反) tone. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Líjì* states that *pán* means "to coil" (*wěi*). Gu Yewáng says it means "to wind and turn. According to the *Guījīnyǎ*, it means "curved. In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, it is written with the radical for insect (*chóng*) and the phonetic element *fān* (*番*).

The *Avalokiteśvara-bodhisattva-svacitta-mantra-sūtra*, also known as the *Tārā-citta-amogha*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master [Amoghavajra]. [Note: "Three-pronged grass" (sān léng cǎo) refers to *darbha* grass; "lè dēng fǎn" is a phonetic transcription of the Sanskrit *darbha*.]
"Ūn" (搵蘇): pronounced with the initial *wēn* and the final *kùn* reversed.

"Chù" (捇): pronounced *chǒu* and *gé* reversed; the commentary on the sounds says it means "to open a forest," and it is also written as 𠜂; the version in the sutra uses 坼, which is a vulgar character.
"Héng" (棓): pronounced *páng* and *jiǎng* reversed; the vulgar form is 棒; the version in the sutra uses 捧 from the radical for hand, which is incorrect.
*Wǎnwán*: A type of pea; the *Guǎyá* states it is "liú-dòu" (a bean). In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, it is composed of the radical 豆 (dòu) with the phonetic 宛 (wǎn).
*Gǔzhuāzǐ*: [A type of plant]; the middle character is pronounced *zhǐguā*.
*Jīntíng*: A copper or iron ingot; the *Shuōwén* states it is a "copper-iron block. It is composed of the radical 金 (jīn) with the phonetic 廷 (tíng).

*Jué* (角) [with the radical *shàng* (上) and the phonetic *jiāo* (嶠) reversed; the sound is *jué*; it means to compete or to test]. It is incorrect for the scripture to write this with the hand radical as *zhuó* (捔). Below, *xià* (下) [with the phonetic *zhèng* (証) reversed].

In the *Eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*, "eleven-faced" refers to Avalokiteśvara. Xuanying’s commentary states that *huàn* (換) [with the phonetic *hú* (胡) and *guàn* (灌) reversed] means to exchange; according to the *Shuowen*, it means to change or replace. The scriptural text writes it as *huàn* (逭); however, in the *Erya*, *huàn* means to flee or to go. This [character *huàn*] is not the correct orthography.

*Mo* (𥫱): The pronunciation is *tu* with the *sun* (損) radical; it should be written as *wen* (搵, *wu men*). According to the *Zilin* (字林), "to smear" (*wen*) means to submerge. *Mo* is merely a vernacular term; the scriptural text also uses the character for "to smear" (*tu*).

*Ba* (八): The pronunciation is *kou* with the *huo* (火) radical; it refers to a number. It is also written simply as *guo* (果). The scriptural text uses the character *ke* (堁, *yu wo*), which means "dust. One source says it is a place name, but that is not the meaning here.

The Eleven-Faced Dharani Heart Sutra. Compiled by Hui-lin. Regarding "pustule" (pào): the upper character is pronounced *pú* (with the *jiào* rhyme). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it refers to gas arising on the face. The sutra uses the character with the radical *nà* (疒), which is a vulgar form of the word.

"Yáng-xiǎn": the upper character "yáng" (養) means "a head sore" according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, composed of the radical "疒" (illness) and the phonetic "易" (yì). The lower character "xiǎn" (仙) has the reading qiǎn; the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "xiǎn" means "dry sores," composed of the radical "疒" and the phonetic "鮮" (xiān).

The character *hán* (憨) is pronounced with the initial *lám* (藍) and the final *kǎo* (考); its sound indicates "foolishness. In both ancient and modern times, the correct orthography is from the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "gǎn" (敢). The version in the sutras written as *jiǎn* (𤺍) is incorrect.
A *kundī* (軍持) is a ritual water vessel used for bathing.
*Yun-lu*: The first character is pronounced *yun*; the second is the *dai-lai* rhyme.

*Ekādaśamukha-avalokiteśvara-hṛdaya-mantra-vidhi-sūtra*, Volume One (of two). Compiled by Huilin. *Chen-po*: The first character is pronounced *zhu-lian*; the second is *pu-bei*. This is a Sanskrit word for "flower. That country has it, but this country does not.
*Jù huài* (沮壞): the first character is pronounced *cí yǔ fǎn* (上慈與反) and the second is *huài guài fǎn* (下壞恠反).

It means "to submerge" (*néi*, pronounced *níng fǎn*). The sound is deep and heavy. The *Shuowen Jiezi* correctly writes it as *mù* (沐), stating that it means "to sink into water," composed of the radical for "water" and the character for "person."
*Yàn-dǎo* (厭禱): The first character is pronounced *wū-yán* (烏琰反) and the second is *dāo-lǎo* (刀老反).

It means to pray for blessings. Regarding *luò-li* (瘰癧): the first character is *lì-chuí* (力捶反) and the second is *líng* (零反). The *Wénzì Jílüè* (文字集略) states that "luò" refers to uneven flesh; the *Lìjīn Jié* (歷筋結) and *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) state it is a concretion of skin and flesh. All standard characters from ancient to modern times follow the radical *zhǎi* (疒), with *lèi* (累) and *lì* (歷) serving as phonetic components.

*Yíngluò* (瓔珞): The first character is pronounced with the initial *yì* or *yíng*; the second has the phonetic *luò*. The *Kǎośēng* states it is a neck ornament for women. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of two characters for "shell" (*bèi*). The scriptural text uses *yīngluò* (瓔絡), which is commonly used interchangeably with the former in vernacular usage.

*Fī lǚ*: The upper character is read as *fěi* (with the fanqie *fēi wēi*) and is defined in the *Zìshū* as "to stretch out [a cord] in a crimson color. The lower character is read as *lǚ* (with the fanqie *lì jǔ*). Gu Yewáng states that "lǚ" refers to thread. According to the *Shuowén*, both characters are composed of the radical *mì* (silk/thread), with *piān* and *lóu* serving as their phonetic components respectively.

1. On the right is *cuō* (pronounced with the *cāng* and *hé* rhymes). The "Correct Characters of Antiquity and Today" states that it means to rub or feel with the hands; it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "chā. Its appearance as *jiē* in the scriptures is an error. 2.

In the middle volume, the *Heart Mantra of the Eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva*, middle fascicle: *qiáo* (pronounced with the *dà* and *zhǐ* rhymes). The *Guǎngyá* states that it means to lift or raise. The "Correct Characters of Antiquity and Today" indicates it is composed of the radical "feather" (*yǔ*) and the phonetic "yáo."

"Shi" (to wipe): the upper character is read as *shū* (舒) and the lower as *lún* (倫). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "the tip of the lips," composed of the radical "moon" (月) with the phonetic "chén" (辰).
"Xīn" (heart/navel): the reading is *qíng* (情) and *xī* (奚).

It is slightly curved; the *Kaosheng* states it refers to a bend in water. The standard characters of the present day follow "water" (水) as the radical and "wān" (彎) as the phonetic. The original text of the scripture uses "wān" (彎), which means "to draw a bow," but this does not accord with the intended meaning of the scripture.

*Yǎngchì* (鷹翄): *chì* is pronounced as *shì* (豉) according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*; it means "wing" (*yì*), composed of the radical "feather" (*yǔ*) with *zhī* as the phonetic component; alternatively written as *fàn* (𦐊), the meaning is the same. *Jué* (嚼):
the upper character is *qiáng* (牆) with the phonetic *yào* (藥); this is a vulgar form. The correct forms are *jiǎo* (齧) or *jiǎo* (齧), both meaning "tooth."

Volume Three, Part Two: The Ritual Manual for the Heart Mantra of the Eleven-Faced Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Establishing the Maṇḍala. Volume Three. Translated by the Indian Scholar Viṇyavana (毘紐梵). *Yanyan* (依言) is pronounced with the second tone on the final syllable.
*Chělù* (車輅): *lù* is pronounced as *lù*.

The character 數 (shù) is pronounced yǎng (upper radical: 角, jiao; lower phonetic: 憶, yi; radical: 心, xīn; phonetic: 陵, líng).

The character 踴 (yǒng) is pronounced róng (upper radical: 容, róng; lower phonetic: 隴, lǒng) and yáng (lower phonetic: 羊, yáng). Duan Yucai’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that it means "to leap and jump. Both the standard characters of the ancient and modern periods follow the radical 足 (zú) and the phonetic 甬 (yǒng); the text here uses 踊 (yǒng), which is used interchangeably.
In the *Qing Guanyin Jing* (Avalokiteśvara Sūtra), *qiejin* (舌噤)—where *qie* is pronounced as *qu* with the *yin* tone—means being unable to speak.

Chánpó (蟾婆) is pronounced yánfǎn;

*The Scripture of the Secret Dhāraṇī and Mudrā of Thousand-Eyed and Thousand-Armed Avalokiteśvara*, Volume One, compiled by Huilin. "Xī" (析): The *Shangshu* (Book of Documents) commentary by Kong [Yuan] states that "xī" means to divide. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mu*) and the phonetic "jin" (*jin*). The text here uses "xī," which is an error.

*Táomèi* (檮昧): The upper character is read as *dāo* (刀) with the alternative reading *fǎn* (反). In the *Mencius*, *táo* (檮) denotes the appearance of being ignorant. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mu*) and the phonetic "longevity" (*shòu*). The lower character is read as *méi* (梅) with the alternative reading *bèi* (貝). The *Guoya* states that *mèi* (昧) means "darkness. The *Zuo Zhuan* says: "Not distinguishing the patterns of the five colors is called *mèi* (昧). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "sun" (*ri*) and the phonetic "not yet" (*wèi*).

*Jī* (upper radical *ji*, lower *xi*; pinyin: *jì*)—the *Shuowen* defines it as "to carry objects"; it is composed of the radical *bei* (貝) with the phonetic *qi* (齊) in abbreviated form. It is also written as *jī* (賷). *Gǎo* (lower radical *gāo*, upper *dào*; pinyin: *gǎo*)—the *Shiji* states that Qu Yuan was commissioned to draft legal codes (*xiànlìng*). *Shǔcǎo gǎo* means the draft has not yet been finalized. Gu Yewang’s commentary notes that *gǎo* is synonymous with "draft" (*cǎo*). The *Shuowen* defines it as being composed of the radical *huó* (禾) with the phonetic *gāo* (高); it is also written as *hāo* (蒿).
Jiaye (若耶): the first character is read as shàng (上) and the second as zě (者), with a reversed sound.

Boluo (鉢喇): the first character is read as láng (郎) and the second as gé (葛), with a reversed sound. Jieluonán (羯囉𧹞): the first character is read as jié (羯) and the second as luó (囉); the third character is read as nín (儜) and jiǎn (簡), with a reversed sound.
