The character *zhù* (柱) is a vulgar variant for *zhū* (縷), which in turn is a vulgar variant for *jīng* (經).
The character *fǎng* (跟) follows the character *zhèng* (正); its lower radical is pronounced as *gēn* (根).

Volume 2, Part 2, "The Thousand-Eyed and Thousand-Armed [Avalokiteśvara]": *sà pó hē* (馺皤訶)—the upper character *sù* (蘇) is pronounced as *hé* (合), and the middle character *zhōng* (中) is pronounced as *pó* (婆); these are Sanskrit terms, plain and unrefined.

*Bài* (pronounced *páimài* in the *Huá* [dictionary]; Duan Yucai’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states that *bài* grass resembles grain). Examining its phonetic component, it is derived from *huò* (rice that fails to ripen), with the radical *huò* (grain). *Tīáo* (water; pronounced *jiūyóu*). According to the text, a *tīáo* is a dragon pool (*lóngchí*).

It may be located in deep valleys where mountains are breached to dam water and form a dragon pool, or it may be found in plains and marshes. Wherever there is a dragon pool, it is designated as a *tīáo*, where one may approach to offer prayers. According to the *Shuowén*, it means "narrow" (*àì*) below; it is formed with the radical *shuǐ* (water) and the phonetic *qiū*.

*Po* (pronounced *shāng* with the *zhǎo* tone). *Hūṃ* (*pàn* with the upper *fàn* tone; the Sanskrit character has no tone; it is like the bellowing of an ox; alternatively written as *hūṅ*). *Phan* (lower tone, *pān-mò*).

From the *Qianshou Qianyan Guanshiyin Pusa Muluotani Shenjing*: Regarding the character *dùbié* (慧琳’s reading: upper tone *dú-gù*, lower tone *bì-liè*; the *Fāngyán* says *bié* means "vile"; Kuo Pu’s commentary says it refers to those of a quick-tempered nature; the standard orthography of past and present follows *xīn* [heart] and *biè* [ruin] as its phonetic).
*Shè* (pronounced *zhì jià*) means to tremble; *zhàn* (pronounced *tiáo yào*). *Jī* (upper radical: 居依反, *jū yī fǎn*) and *mèi* (lower radical:

眠結反, *mián jié fǎn*)—Pao Xian’s commentary on the *Lunyu* states that *jī* means to seek out faults (*jiāo*). The *Mao Shih Zhuan* states that *mèi* means to treat lightly. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to treat with ease or contempt"; it is composed of the radical 忄 (xīn, the heart radical) and the phonetic 蔑 (*miè*). The sound of the radical 忄 is *xīn*.
The character 𣸈 (shòu) is pronounced with the "you" (有) and "fan" (反) finals.

Regarding 眩 (xuàn), the *Xuánbiàn* (玄遍) [recension] states that the *Cāngjié piān* says: "It is the lack of clarity in observation. The *Shuowén* says: "The eyes have no constant master. It is composed of the radical 目 (eye) and the phonetic 玄 (xuán).

"Bai" (上祊) is pronounced with the rhyme "mai" (麥). The *Zi shu* (Dictionary of Characters) states that it means to split an object with the hand; the *Shuowen jiezi* (Explaining Simple and Analyzing Compound Characters) says it is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "pi" (辟).
"Rao-ja" (囉惹) is pronounced with the rhymes "ci" (辝) and "he" (何); it is a name for a king in the Sanskrit language.
*Kāśmīra* (上居例反; *shàng jū lì fǎn*).

This is the same as *dǎng* (當浪反; *dāng làng fǎn*). The *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲) states that it means "to state the inner truth" (*zhōng zhōng*), referring to speech that accords with principle; it can also be written as *dǎng*. *Zhā* (磔) is read as *zhé* (竹格反; *zhú gé fǎn*).
The *Guǎngyá* (廣雅) states that *zhā* means "to stretch" or "to spread. In the standard characters of the present and past, it is composed of the radical *shí* (石) and the phonetic *jié* (桀).

*Chao* (上楚巧反; *shàng chǔ qiǎo fǎn*)—the *Fānyán* says it means to dry by fire. The *Shuowén* writes it as *zhù* (鬻), defining it as "to fry" (*zhāo*), composed of the radical *chú* (󲶧) with the phonetic *chū* (芻); it is also written as *chǎo*, *diàn* (㷅), or *dì* (𤌽). *Nǐ* (𩰲) has the pronunciation *lì* (鬲).

The character for *yì* (epidemic) has the upper radical *yì* (phonetic: lì) and the lower radical *lì* (phonetic: zhì, reversed). Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "Lì refers to the disease caused by the disharmony of epidemic vapors. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "malignant illness. Both characters take the "sick" radical (*zhāi*) and the phonetic components *shū* and *wàn*.

The *Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Unobstructed Great Compassionate Heart of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara with a Thousand Hands and a Thousand Eyes*. Compiled by Huilin. "Potalaka Mountain" is a term in the Sanskrit language.

Regarding the character *tīng* (聽) in the phrase "to listen to and permit" (*tīngxǔ*) from the *Jīngfǎn* commentary on the *Lǐjì*, Zheng Xuan’s annotation states: "*Tīng* means 'to attend' (*shì*). According to the *Shuowén*, it means "to hear" (*líng*). It is composed of the radical *shǒu* (𢛳) and the phonetic *ěr* (耳), with *rén* (壬) as the phonetic component. The character *shǒu* (𢛳) has the pronunciation *dé* (德); it is the archaic form of the character *dé*. The character *wáng* (王) has the pronunciation *tíngyǐng* (汀郢).
*Yǒngyuè*: The first character is pronounced *róngzhòng* (with the final *fǎn* tone);
the second is pronounced *yào*. *Cūizhé*: The first character is pronounced *cúwēi*; the *Kǎo Shēng* states it means "to sever," "to damage," or "to ruin.

Both characters are written with the radical "hand" (*shǒu*). *Lúánxiè*: The first character is pronounced *wǔguān*; the second is pronounced *xuānyè*. The *Jíxùn* identifies them as insects that sting. The standard orthography of the past and present uses the radical "insect" (*chóng*) and the phonetic "xiē. The original text’s version using "xié" with the pronunciation *hé* is incorrect.

"Fénpiāo" (焚漂): Floating upwards after being burned; Yěwáng says it means "to burn. The *Shuowen* says it means "to burn a field," written with the radical 火 and the phonetic 林 (also pronounced lín). The second character, Pǐyáo (匹遙), is read as piāo. The *Shuowen* says it means "to drift," written with the radical 水 and the phonetic 票, which has the same pronunciation as above.
*Ucchuṣma* is a Sanskrit term (the initial *u* is pronounced as in "wu" with the first tone).
*Aṅkuśī* is a Sanskrit term (the initial *aṅ* is pronounced as in "yāng" with the fourth tone, followed by *jū* with the first tone). *Śaṅkara* is a Sanskrit term.
*Mahi* (the final syllable is pronounced with the *xi* rhyme) is a Sanskrit term.
*Vosava vosava* (the sounds are pronounced with the *suhe* rhyme) is a Sanskrit term.
*Kūlaṇa* is a Sanskrit term.

Regarding "feng zhí" (逢值): Yě Wáng says it is the "zhí" of "dāng zhí" (當值). In the standard orthography of ancient and modern times, it is written with the radical "ren" (人) and the phonetic "zhí" (直).

Regarding "yuán biè" (黿鼈): the upper character is pronounced "yuán" (元) and the lower is "biàn miè" (編滅). According to the *Shuowen*, both characters share the radical "mǐn" (黽), with "yuán" (元) and "bì" (敝) serving as their respective phonetics. The version in the sutra uses "biè" (鱉), which is a common vulgar character used interchangeably.

"Cuffs, shackles, stocks, and fetters": the first character (杻) is pronounced *chǒu* (as in "cow"), the second (*械*) is pronounced *xié* (with the *jiè* rhyme), and the third (*枷*) is pronounced *jiā*.

The fourth character (*鎖*) is pronounced *suǒ* (as in "suo"). Regarding "ulcers" (*yōngchuāng*): the first character (*yōng*) is pronounced *yōng*. Sima Biao states that "floating heat" (*piāorè*) results in "obstruction" (*biāotōng*), which is an ulcer (*tōn*). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "swelling" (*zhǒng*) and is composed of the radical *nà* with the phonetic *yōng*. Its appearance in the sutra as *wéi* (維) instead of *tōn* (㿈) is an error.

"Nong-xue" (pus and blood): The top radical is "shang" (upper), and the phonetic is "gong" (public). The *Gu jin zheng zi* (Correct Characters of Antiquity and Today) states it refers to the pus and blood from a ruptured carbuncle or abscess; it is composed of the radical "meat" (flesh) with "nong" as the phonetic.

"San-tuo" (spitting thrice): The pronunciation is "tuo" (lying down) with the tone "fan" (reversed). The *Shuowen jiezi* states it refers to saliva; it is composed of the radical "mouth" with "chui" as the phonetic.
The character for *sè* (color/thread) is pronounced with the rhyme *xiàn* (仙) or *jiàn* (箭), and is also written as *xiàn* (線);

the version in the *Jīng* (經) using *yán* (綖) is incorrect. It means "rope" (*suǒ*, pronounced *sāngluò* [桑洛]). Gu Yewáng states: "Twisting cords together makes a rope. The *Chuci* (楚辭) says: "Twisting silk to make a rope. It is composed of the radical *miào* (󲨽) and the phonetic *mì* (糸). The sound of *miào* is *zīwèi* (𦘺味); the sound of *niù* (紐) is *nílín* (尼隣).
"Xiàng" (項) is pronounced as "xiè" (詣) in the upper character and "jiǎng" (講) in the lower character. "Jiē" (階) has the phonetic value of "jiē" (皆). "Lòu" (漏) and "fèi" (沸):

the upper character is pronounced as "róngzhǒng" (容腫) and the lower character as "fēiwèi" (非味). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Yǒng" (涌) means water surging upward; it is composed of the radical "water" (水) with "yǒng" (甬) as the phonetic component. The pronunciation of "yǒng" (甬) is the same as above."
"Chángshēng lèyī luò. [The character] 畫 (huà) is pronounced with the initial *héng* and the final *mǎn*. [The character] 擲 (zhì) is pronounced with the initial *chéng* and the final *jí*;

the *Shuowen* states that "to throw" (*zhì*) means "to cast," written with the radical 手 (hand), with the phonetic component 鄭 (Zhèng) and the final *zhāng* and *lüè*. "Chángshēng lèyī luò. [The character] 畫 (huà) is pronounced with the initial *héng* and the final *mǎn*. [The character] 擲 (zhì) is pronounced with the initial *chéng* and the final *jí*; the *Shuowen* states that "to throw" (*zhì*) means "to cast," written with the radical 手 (hand), with the phonetic component 鄭 (Zhèng) and the final *zhāng* and *lüè*.

"Pulling out its upper part" (*bá qí shàng biàn*): The *Shuowen* states that "to pull out" (*bá zhuó*) means to draw it forth from the surface; it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "ba" (*bà*). "Twisting the rope" (*niǎn suǒ*):
The upper character is read as *shàng niǎn diǎn*. "Pushing aside" (*páng pài*):
The upper character is read as *pú táng*, and the lower as *bài mái*. The *Kaosheng* states that "pái" means a shield; the version in the sutra written as "bǎng bǐ" is incorrect.
The character for *yuèfǔ* (battle-axe) is written as *yuè* with the radical *zhēn* (袁) above;

it is actually *yuè*. The character for *bǎobié* (jewel casket) is pronounced *qián* (謙) with the radical *jiá* (頰). The character for *bǎoluó* (jewel conch) is *lú* (盧) with the radical *gē* (戈); the canonical text originally had *luó* (螺), which is a vulgar form.
*Dúlóu* (skull): the first character is pronounced *dú* (as in *dújiān*), the second is pronounced *lóu*.

*Bǎoduò* (jeweled bell): the second character is pronounced with the *táng* and *luò* finals (i.e., *duò*). According to the *Zhou Lǐ*, a *duò* is a large bell used to regulate the *gǔ* drum; according to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic element *zhì*.

*Yīng* (縈): On the body; pronounced *yíng* (with the initial *y* reversed). The *Kǎośēng* says it means "to entwine. The *Shuōwén* says it means "to gather" (*shòu*). It is composed of the radical *mì* (糸) and the phonetic *yīng* (縈) in abbreviated form.

*Kē yè* (柯葉): On the branches and leaves; pronounced *gē* (with the initial *g* reversed as *hē*). The *Shuōwén* says it means "the branches of a tree. It is composed of the radical *mù* (木) and the phonetic *kě* (可).
*Śīzhù*: the first character is pronounced *shī*, the second *zhù*. *Huíchóng*:
the first character is pronounced *huí*. *Yǎoxīn*:
the character for *yǎo* is pronounced *jiǎo*; it may also be written as *yǎo* with the mouth radical.

*Li* (綟): The upper character is read as *lián* (憐) with the phonetic component *jié* (結). Regarding the *Vajraśekhara-yoga-guhyasamādhi-japa-vidhi*: the various visualizations (*dhyāna*) of the deities each have their distinct differences. *Huìlín* states that *túshī* (塗拭)—the lower character being read as *shū* (舒) with the phonetic component *lì* (力)—is "to wipe. *Zhèng*’s commentary on the *Yílǐ* says, "Wiping is for purification. *Guō Pǔ* says, "Wiping is that by which one achieves cleanliness. In both ancient and modern *Zhèngzì* (Correct Characters), it follows the radical for "hand" (*shǒu*) and takes *shì* (式) as its phonetic; it is also written as *shì* (飾).
*Āṅka*: the first syllable is pronounced with the *ge* rhyme (as in "安葛"), also written as *yè*; it refers to a vessel for holding water.
*Hrīḥ*: the first syllable is pronounced with the *hen* rhyme (an aspirated nasal) and the second syllable is *li* with a retroflex pronunciation.

"Top-wearing" (dìngdài) should be read as *zǎi* (with the tone of *fǎn*). Jia Ji’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states: "Dài means to carry upon one's head. Lexicons state that when written with the radical for the head (*tǒng*), it is called *dài*. Liu Xin says: "It is that which people look up to and honor. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the elements "strange" (*yì*) and "to gather" (*cào*) as its phonetic component; the *Zhouwen* form is written as *dài*, where *cào* is pronounced *zǎilái* (with the tones of *zǎi* and *lái*).
"Unobstructed" (*wú ài*) is also written as "obstructed" (*ài*), with the same pronunciation (the *wǔdài* rhyme group); the Classics use the character 㝵, which is a vulgar form of the word.

*Xia* (blemish) has the upper radical *shàngxià* (the phonetic component for "above and below") and the lower part *zhèng xuān* says it refers to a flaw in jade; it is a small red spot. It is formed from the radical "jade" (*yù*) and the phonetic "duàn" (pronounced *dìngdiǎn*). *Zītǒng* states that *diàn* means a deficiency or flaw, formed from the radical "jade" and the phonetic "zhàn."

"Liǎngjiān (兩肩): Jíyān (吉煙). *Shuōwén* states it means 'shoulders' (*jiānbó*). It is formed from the radical for 'flesh' (*ròu*) and is a pictograph. The version in the sutras written as 'hù' (戶) to form 'jiān' is a vulgar character.

"Lǐǎngchǒu (兩䯗): Pímǐ (鼙米). *Kǎoshēng* states it means 'thighs' (*gǔ*). *Shuōwén* writes it as 'bǐ' (髀), formed from the radical for 'bone' (*gǔ*) and the phonetic 'bēi' (卑). The original version in the sutras written as 'bì' (陛) is incorrect."

The Recitation Method for the Bodhisattva Ārya-Tārā Avalokiteśvara, also titled *The Essential Method* (Śūyao), compiled by Hui-lin. [The character] "Shu" (樞) is pronounced with the first tone (Chū) in the upper part and the second tone (Ě) in the lower part.
*Jìng* (𠜂定): upper tone, pronounced *jiàn* (姦反). *Niù* (紐): upper tone, pronounced *ní* (尼久反). *Xiū* (修): *qīn* (侵) and *lì* (立) rhymes. Zheng’s commentary on the *Shijing* says:

"To *jī* (緝) means to continue (*xù*). The *Erya* says: "It is *yǎo* (𭴄). The *Gōngjīn Zhèngzì* says: "It means to continue (*xù*). It follows the radical *mì* (糸); *qī* (咠) provides the phonetic component. The pronunciation of *qī* is the same as above.

*Tan* (greed) and *ei* (anger). [The character for] *ei* is pronounced with the first tone and the rhyme *ji* (according to the *Cangjie pian*, it means "wrath"; according to the *Shuowen jiezi*, it means "resentment," composed of the radical "heart" and the phonetic "gui").

*Yongmeng* (valiant and fierce): the upper character is pronounced with the second tone and the rhyme *long*. Gu Yewang says: "Valiant, heroic, daring, and resolute. The *Tianxuan jing* says: "To decide and sever. According to the *Shi fa* (Canon of Posthumous Titles), one who knows death yet does not avoid it is called "valiant. According to the *Shuowen jiezi*, it is "qi" (vital breath/energy); it is composed of the radical "force" and the phonetic "yong. The archaic form is written as *yong* or, with the radical "spear," as *yong*. The pronunciation of *qi* is the same as "qi" (breath), and the pronunciation of *yong* is the same as above.
Dig deep; do not [dig] upward.

Reaching the character *xīn* (pronounced with the first tone, the same as the character for "knee"): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *xī* (pronounced *qǐ*) refers to the joint at the top of the shin, composed of the radical *jié* (卩) and the phonetic *qī* (桼), or alternatively written with the radical *ròu* (肉) as *xī* (膝).

*Kāng-bǐ* (糠秕): the first character is pronounced *kāng*; the second is pronounced *bǐ* (with the radical *bi*). *Dūn-jù* (蹲踞): the first character is pronounced *dūn*; the second is pronounced *jù* (with the radicals *jū* and *yù*). *Jú wù* (匊物):

the first character is pronounced *jiū* (with the radicals *liù* and *máo*). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that filling the hands is called *jú*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states that *jú* means "in the hands. The *Shi Jing* says that being in the hands is called *jú*. It follows the phonetic *bāo* (勹) and the radical *mǐ* (米), and it also follows the hand radical to form *jū* (掬).

Its *sāi* (pronounced with the initial *lái* and the final *kǎo*) refers to the flesh within the cheeks of a fish; the *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *cù*, stating it means "the bone within the horn," formed from the radical *jiǎo* and the phonetic *sī*. The *Fǎběn* edition writes it as *sāi*; however, upon examining dictionaries, this character does not exist, so it is likely an error.

*Tánzhǐ* (撣指): The character for *tán* in the canonical text is written with the radical 弓 (bow), which is incorrect; it should be 彈 (*tán*). *Huànjiǎ* (擐甲): The upper character is pronounced *huàn*. *Táodié* (跳躑):

The upper character is pronounced *túliáo*. The *Cāngjié piān* states it means "to leap. The *Guǎngyǎ* states it means "to jump up. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "to leap" (*tiào*), with the radical 足 and the phonetic 兆. The version in the canonical text uses 卓 to form 踔, which is incorrect. The lower character is pronounced *chéngjí*. Gu Yewáng states that *zhízhú* refers to "stamping one's feet repeatedly without moving forward. The *Shuōwén* writes it as 蹢 with the same meaning, with the radical 足 and the phonetic 啇.

*Yīnmò* (湮沒): The first character, *yīn*, is pronounced with the initial *jian* (見) and the final *sheng* (聲). The commentary states it means "to sink into water. The version in the *Jīng* (經) uses *yètūn* (咽吞), which does not carry the meaning of *yīnmò*; it is therefore not adopted here. *Xuǎnzú* (跣足):

The first character, *xuǎn*, is pronounced with the initial *xian* (先) and the final *dian* (典). The *Shuowén* (說文) states it means "to touch the ground directly with one's feet. It is composed of the radical *zú* (足) and the phonetic *xian* (先).
One *hūṃ* (pronounced with the *gǒu* rhyme; also written as *jiù* or *hǒu*). *Xìyàn* (the first character pronounced with the *xīng-yì* rhyme):

the *Shuowen Jiezi* commentary states that *xì* means "a crimson appearance. In ancient and modern standard characters, it is composed of the radical for "red" (*chì*) and the phonetic *sè*; the second character, *yàn*, is pronounced with the *yán-zhàn* rhyme, and while the canonical texts use this form, it is a vulgar character.
*Makara* (摩竭魚) is the name of a large fish; it is written with the radical for "standing" (立), and to write it with the radical for "wood" (木) as *jié* (楬) is incorrect.

*Ratnakaṇṭhaka* (寶瑣)—*suǒ* (瑣) is pronounced *guǒ* (果); the *Guǎngyǎ* states that *suǒ* means "linked," while dictionaries define it as a "linked ring. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the "jade" radical (*yù*) and the phonetic *lǚ* (𧴲); it is also written as *suǒ* (璅), which is incorrect. The pronunciation of *lǚ* (𧴲) is the same as above.

Regarding the term *huánpèi* (ring-bells): the *Erya* states that when the thickness of the metal and the diameter of the hole are equal, it is called a *huán*. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* says that *huán* means "to revolve. Zheng Xuan further explains that *huán* means "to encircle. He Xiu’s commentary on the *Gongyang zhuan* says it means "to surround. According to the *Shuowen jiezi*, the character is composed of the radical "jade" (*yù*) with the phonetic element "quǎn" (*huán*). It is incorrect for the scriptural text to use the character *zǔ* (䋿) instead of *huán*; the pronunciation of *quǎn* is *qióng*.

*Tíng* (澄渟): The upper character is pronounced *zhí* (直) with the *líng* (陵) rhyme group; the lower character is pronounced *jīng* (定) with the *jīng* (經) rhyme group. The *Pīcāng* dictionary states that *tíng* means "water ceases to flow. Lexicons say it means "water stagnates. In both ancient and modern standard characters, the radical is *shuǐ* (水); both *dēng* (登) and *tíng* (亭) serve as phonetic components.

The character for "anvil" (砧) is pronounced *zhǐ jīn*; when recited with the Sanskrit phonetics, its meaning accords with that of the *Yogācāra* system. The current edition of the sutra uses *zhǐ jīn*, which is incorrect.
The character for "above the navel" (臍上) is pronounced *shàng qí xī*.
*Tu-lu-ōṃ*: *ōṃ* is pronounced with the middle tone of *shàng-dù-mù*; it is recited in the Sanskrit sound as *lu*, whereas the scriptural text writes it as *lǒng*, which loses the correct meaning.
*Dùn-gēn*: *dùn* is pronounced with the *shàng-dù-kùn* tone.

Yanmo (上閻贍反): the first character is pronounced as *yán* (閻) and the second as *zhàn* (贍). Lìwàn (綟腕): the first character is pronounced as *lián* (憐) and the second as *niè* (涅), with a secondary reading of *huàn* (𠛠換).

*Ariduōluó tuóluóní* (阿唎多羅陀羅尼): *Ariduōluó tuóluóní* (阿魯力品). Regarding *Ariduōluó tuóluóní*: *A-lǔ-lì-pǐn*. Huìlín’s compilation states that *léng* (棱) is read as *lēng* (勒登反); the *Shuowén* says it means "the tip of a branch" (*mù luò yě*), following the radical for wood and the phonetic *líng* (夌). It is also written as *léng* (楞). The canonical text uses *léng* (稜), which is an error. The pronunciation of *líng* (夌) is *líng* (音陵), and the pronunciation of *luò* (枛) is *gǔ hú* (音古胡反).

The character 僕 (pú): the first radical is pronounced as péng-mù-fǎn and the second as lí-jì-fǎn. The *Zishu* states that it means "a servant. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to attach," composed of the radical 隶 (lì) with the phonetic element 尨 (máng). In the seal script it is written as 𭭳. The pronunciation of 隶 is dì. The text here uses 僕, which is a vulgar form.

*Mìuwàng* (謬忘): The upper character is pronounced *méi yòu* (眉宥). Gu Yewang states that *mìu* means "deviant" (*pì*). According to the *Fāngyán*, it also means "deceitful" (*zhà*). Zheng’s commentary says it means "erroneous" (*wù*). The *Shuowén* explains it as "the forgetfulness of one who is insane. It is composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) with the phonetic element *liáo* (*lìu*).

*Tian* (甜): Pronounced *dié* with the rhyme of *jiān* (兼) and *fǎn* (反). The *Guǎngyǎ* states it means "sweet. The *Shuōwén* says it means "beautiful," composed of the radicals for "sweet" (*gān*) and "tongue" (*shé*), as the tongue is that which perceives sweetness.

*Jiǎo* (角): Pronounced *shèng* with the rhymes of *shàng* (上), *jiāng* (江), and *yuè* (岳). The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* states that "to *jiǎo*" is like "to test" (*shì*). Gù Yěwáng says it means "to exert strength. It refers to contending for victory or defeat. The *Shuōwén* states that the character is a pictograph of animal horns; its appearance in the body of a sūtra as *jué* (桷) is incorrect. *Xia* (下): Pronounced *shēng* with the rhyme of *zhèng* (證).

The character *jié* (割𢧵) has the upper radical pronounced as *gé* and the lower phonetic as *qiánjié*. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states: "Jié means to process. The *Zheng Jie* states: "Jié means to arrange and align. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Jié means to cut; it is composed of the radical *gē* with the phonetic *què*. The text here uses *cào* (𢦏) instead, which is an error for *jié* (截).

*Yixieyi*: "Yi" (衣) is pronounced as *ji* (記); "xie" (纈) is pronounced as *xian* (賢) with the final consonant *jie* (結). The *Kaosheng* states it means "to bind" (*xi*, 繫), referring to binding silk and dyeing it to form patterns. The following "yi" (衣) is read according to its standard character.
*Tushi mo*: "Tu" (鍮) is pronounced as *tanghou* (湯侯); the *Picao* states that *tushi* resembles gold. It is composed of the radical "metal" (*jin*, 金).

*Niè* (捏): This character was formed in the previous year [of the reign] based on the phonetic *fǎn* (反) and the radical *shǒu* (手). It is the correct orthography for both ancient and modern usage, with the phonetic *niè* (捻). The pronunciation of *niè* is as stated above; alternatively, it may be written as *dǎo* (㘿) with the radical *tǔ* (土).

Regarding "pea" (wēi-dòu): the *Guǎngyá* states that "wēi-dòu" is "liú-dòu. In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, it is composed of the radical "bean" (dòu) with the phonetic "yuǎn. "Liú" (䝀) is pronounced liú. Regarding "bone-beating" (gǔ-zhuā):
"zhūā" is pronounced zhé-guā.
*Nāga-yu* (the "yu" rhyme is reversed).

Regarding the *Avalokiteśvara-dhāraṇī for Seeking Unforgetting Retention*, and the *Sādhanā-sūtra of the Vajrakumāra Ākāśagarbha*: composed by Hui Lin. As for the character *bō* (縛撲): the upper part is *fáng* (房) with the *jué* (玃) rhyme, and the lower part is *páng-bó* (龐駮). The *Zītǒng* (字統) states that it means "hand-to-hand combat. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that it means "to throw to the ground. In the standard characters of past and present, it follows the radical for "hand" (*shǒu*) and takes *bù* (菐) as its phonetic.

The character *jiàn* (鍵) is the reverse of *jiǎn* (蹇). Zheng Zhong’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: “*Jiàn* refers to the *yào* (flute-like wind instrument) of the music office. The *Fāngyán* states: “From the region east of the Guanzhong pass, in the areas of Chen and Chu, the *yào* is called *jiàn*. According to the *Shuowen*, it means a lifting hook (*xuàn*), formed with the radical for metal and the phonetic *jiàn*; it is also written as *jiàn* (揵). In the received text, it is written as *tá* (闥) with the radical for gates; this was an ancient form of the character.

Regarding "nude" (lù): the *Huáguǎ* [Dictionary] reads it as *luó*, while the *Shuowén* writes it as *léi*, explaining it as "the ancestor. The *Shēnglèi* writes it as *luǒ* or *nuǒ*. This sutra uses the character *luǒ*; all dictionaries give the traditional pronunciation as *lìguǒ*.
*Shuòdǐ* (爍底): "Shuò" is pronounced as *shāngzhé* (商灼) or sometimes written as *shuò* (鑠). It is a Sanskrit term for a short spear. *Kǒngsǒng* (恐悚): "Kǒng" is pronounced as *qūgǒng* (驅拱).

According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to be terrified. It is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "gǒng" (*gǒng*). It is also written as *kǒng* (𢖶). "Sǒng" is pronounced as *sùyǒng* (粟勇). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states it means "to be fearful. The *Shuowen* also records this character as *cǐ* (愯), which likewise means "to be afraid," composed of the radical "heart" and the phonetic "shuāngshěng" (雙省). Lexicons also write it as *bèi* (𢥠). "Gǒng" has the pronunciation *gǒng* (拱).

"Contracting the eyebrows": *shu* (疏陸反, *shū lù fǎn*). The *Mānsì Zhuàn* (Mānsì Tradition) states that it means "to gather together" (*jìn*). Lexicons define it as "to contract" (*cù*). The *Shuowén Jiězì* defines it as "disorder," formed from the radical "silk thread" (*mì*) with the phonetic "xiù.
It is also written as *chōu*. With the pronunciation *dá*, this refers to the "Lion’s Claw Seal," which is used to stamp upon the ground.

"Bìbó" (臂髆): "Bó" (髆) is read as *bǔ* (補) and *gè* (各). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Bó refers to the shoulder blade; it is composed of the radical 'bone' (骨) with 'zhuó' (尃) as the phonetic. The version in the sutra reads "bó" (膊), which is incorrect. "Yōngtíng" (傭停): "Yōng" (傭) is read as *chǒng* (寵) and *lóng* (龍).

The *Kaosheng* states: "It means that the upper and lower parts are equal. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "It means straight and even; it is composed of the radical 'person' (人) with 'yōng' (庸) as the phonetic. The version in the sutra reads "zhōng" (𦟛), which is incorrect.

*Chì* (𡍩): Pronounced *chí gè fǎn*. The *Guǎngyá* states it means "to split apart. The *Kǎoshēng* states it means "a crack in the earth. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical 土 (*tǔ*) and the phonetic 㡿 (*lè*). The character 㡿 is pronounced *chǐ*. It may also be written with the hand radical as 𠬿 (*shǒu*).

The character *huá* (和) is pronounced with the rhyme *chàng* (唱) and the final consonant *diào* (遶). The *Pīcāng* states that it means "fried wheat" (*mài*). The *Wenzi Dianshuō* says it means "dry, fried flour made from wheat," derived from the radical for wheat (*麥*) and the phonetic *qiū* (酋). The versions of the sutra use *shǎo* (少) instead, which is a vulgar usage. Both *huá* (𩱈) and *chāo* (煼) are pronounced *chǔ jiǎo* (楚狡).

Regarding the term *huàn* (擐) in the sense of "donning" armor on the body: the *Chunqiu Zhuan* (Annals of Spring and Autumn) states, "donning armor and grasping weapons. Du Yu’s commentary explains that *huàn* means "to thread through" (*guàn*). Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* (Discourses of the States) explains it as "wearing armor. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines *guàn* as "the urgency of threading," written with the radical "hand" and the phonetic "quáng" (睘).
*Wu*: (The character is pronounced *wu*; the commentary says it is pronounced *wu*). It refers to the appearance of a short, stunted tree stump.
*Men-kun*: (The gate-threshold; *kun* is pronounced *kun* with the tone *wen*.

It is also written as *kun*). *Pin-cu*: (The upper character is *pin*, which is the correct form; the version in the sutra as *pin* is an error. The lower character is pronounced *zi* with the tone *liu*).
"Twisted" (撚) is pronounced *niǎn* (upper radical *shàn*, classifier *diǎn*).

The *Kǎo Shēng* says it means weaving silk like a rope; the *Shuowén* says it means braiding silk, with the phonetic *yōu*. The original text uses "tāo" (縚), which refers to a bow-case and is not the intended meaning here.
*Khaṭa* (the first character pronounced with the *qiāngjiā* rhyme and the second with the *zhūnjiā* rhyme):
"to bite" (*niè*); this is the term used in the scriptures, whereas the common character is written as "chew" (*jiān*). *Gau* (the first character pronounced with the *gōuhòu* rhyme):
according to the *Kǎoshēng* (Investigation of Sounds), it means to take the milk of oxen or sheep; the version of the scripture that uses the character "gòu" (to build) is incorrect.

Regarding "guā" (melon/vine): the *Guǎngyá* states that the "ancient flowers" (*gǔhuā*) include the dragon’s hoof, tiger’s paw, sheep’s shank, hare’s head, cassia staff, and wildcat’s head—all belonging to the melon family. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "guā, a type of gourd," describing its form; the character used in the scripture as "gū" is incorrect. The lower tone is pronounced "wàn."
*Pīlì* (霹靂): the first character is pronounced *pǐ* (also read as *yì*) and the second is pronounced *lì*; the original text reads *bìlè*, which is a vulgar form. *Qūbì* (驅𢷤):
the first character is pronounced *qū* (also read as *yú*) and the second is pronounced *bìn* (also read as *yìn*). *Ráonǎo* (嬈惱):
the first character is pronounced *nǎo* (also read as *liǎo*).

The Vajrakumāra Recitation Ritual Sūtra; in the title "Vajrakumāra Recitation Ritual Sūtra," Hui-lin [explains] that *quan* (拳) is pronounced with the *juàn* (倦) rhyme, and *yù* (圜) is pronounced with the *yuáng* (墻) rhyme.
*Luó-bēi* (螺盃): The first character is pronounced with the *lú* rhyme and the *gē* final;

the second character is pronounced with the *bō* rhyme and the *méi* final. *Zhíshù* (直豎): Pronounced with the *shū* rhyme and the *rǔ* final. Gu Yewang states that it means "standing upright and straight. The *Shuowen* explains it as "to stand. It is composed of the radical *xián* (臤) and the phonetic *dòu* (豆). In the *Zhuowén*, it is written as *zhù* (豎); the common vulgar form is *shù* (竪). *Chōng* (樅): Pronounced with the *zú* rhyme and the *róng* final. *Xīán* (臤): Pronounced with the *kǒu* rhyme and the *qiān* final.
"Jiǎo" (繳) means to pour upon; the *Fǎnkǎo* says it means "to entangle. The *Shuowén* says it is composed of the radical "silk thread" (糸) with the phonetic "jiǎo" (敫).

Next, "fèng" (捧)—the phonetic transcription is *fú yǒng* (孚勇); Kuo Pu says it means "to hold with both hands. According to the *Gōngjīn Zhèngzì*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (手) with the phonetic "fèng" (奉).

*Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī of the Holy and Majestic Vajrakumāra*. Regarding the characters *jué* (钯) and *zhuó* (斵): The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *jué* means "a large hoe. It is composed of the radical *jīn* (金, metal) with the phonetic *jué* (矍). The lower part is pronounced *zhé* (陟, with the *ǎi* [ㄞ] tone). The commentary on the *Book of Documents* (*Shangshu*) by Kong Yingda states that *zhuó* means "to plane or shave. The *Shuowen Jiezi* classifies it as belonging to the category of *zhāo* (斫, to hack). It is composed of the radical *jīn* (斤, axe) with the phonetic *dòu* (豆). *Jué* is pronounced *xǔ fù* (許縛); *dòu* is pronounced *dòu* (豆). *Jì* (籰) is pronounced *wáng jué* (王钁). *Note: This passage provides a philological analysis of the characters used in the title of the scripture.*
*Jue* (掘): To dig up; the ancient commentary on the sounds says it means "to pierce. It is composed of the radical 手 (hand) and also the radical 土 (earth);

one may also write it as *jué*. *Bìfāng* (畟方): The initial sound is *chūsè*; it is the correct character for both ancient and modern usage. It denotes the appearance of arranging vessels and objects in a neat and orderly fashion. It is composed of the radicals 田 (field) and 人 (person), with 夂 (zhǒu) as the phonetic component; *zhǒu* is pronounced *suī*.
Chā (pronounced chǔlíngfǎn). Fókuò (pronounced kūnbùgǎnfǎn). Sàsà (pronounced sūhéfǎn);
Guō Pǔ says that "sàsà" means the appearance of rapid movement; according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "horse" (馬) and the phonetic "jí" (及).

*Xiǎotà* (小榻): Pronounced *xiǎo lā* (臘) according to the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲); it refers to a small wooden bed. The version in the *Jīngběn* (經本) reads *tǎ* (㯓), which is incorrect. *Zhuóshí* (啄食): The first character is pronounced *zhú jué* (竹角). *Xuànlǚ* (綫縷): The first character is pronounced *xiān jiàn* (仙箭).

The *Kǎoshēng* states it means "thread" (*lǚ*). The second character is pronounced *lì jǔ* (力矩). According to the *Shuōwén* (說文), it means "silk thread" (*xuàn*). Both characters take the radical *mì* (糸) and the phonetic *zán* (戔); *lóu* (婁) serves as the phonetic component for both.

"Smoke, warmth, and light" (*dhūma-uṣman-āloka*)—the character for "warmth" (*uṣman*) is pronounced *nuǎn* (with the *guǎn* rhyme); it is sometimes written as 𭊴 and vulgarly as 暖. These three types constitute the signs of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

"Malignant *zhù*" (*pāpa-niśrita*): the pronunciation is *zhù*. "Hernia" (*xiānpò*): the upper character is pronounced *xián* and is a vulgar form; originally there is no standard character for it, while the lower character is pronounced *pì*.
"Hǐ" (痔) [pronounced with the initial *chí*]: The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is a disease of the anus; it is composed of the radical "illness" (*zhé*) and the phonetic "sì.

"Fēi xiàn" (緋綫): The upper character is pronounced "fēi. The *Zishū* states that "fēi" refers to crimson. In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, it is composed of the radical "silk thread" (*mì*) and the phonetic "fēi."
The title is compiled as *Mián-fǎn* (upper part). Regarding *Mañjuśrī-Yamāntaka-Mahāvidyārāja-Siddhi-sūtra*:

*Mañjuśrī-Yamāntaka-Mahāvidyārāja-Siddhi-sūtra*. Regarding *fèn-xùn* (奮迅): Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states that "fèn" means to stir or move. The *Guǎngyá* states it means to shake or to expand. The *Shuowén* states it is "huī" (翬); "huī" is like flying. It is composed of "suī" (奞) with the phonetic "suī" (雖), located above "tián" (田). The lower part is "xún" (閏); the *Ěryá* states it means rapidity. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of "chuò" (辵) with "xìn" (卂) as the phonetic; "xìn" has the sound of "xìn" (信).

*Mankā* (縵髁): The first character is pronounced *pán* (滿) with a reversed tone, and the second is *kuà* (誇) with a *huà* (化) reversed tone. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "kǎ" (髁) refers to the thigh; it is composed of the radical "bone" (骨) and the phonetic "guǒ" (果). The pronunciation of "bǐ" (髀) is *pí-mǐ* (鼙米) with a reversed tone. The version in the Canon reads *kuà* (胯), which is a vulgar character.
On top of the spear seal (śakti-mudrā), there are two horns, pronounced *fan* (as in "reverse").
They form a topknot (*jaṭā*), pronounced *yin ji* (as in "sound-count").
On top of the conch horn, it is pronounced *lu go fan*; this is a vulgar character; the correct form is *luo*, which is also *li*.

The Sūtra on the Method for the Accomplishment of Great Miraculous Efficacy through Recitation of the Holy King Yamāntaka the Wrathful. Regarding the character *cái* (纔) in the phrase "as soon as one recites" (*cái sòng*) [in the title]: Yuè Wáng’s *Guǐyě* states that *cái* means "merely able. In the standard characters of past and present, it is composed of the radical "silk" (糸) and the phonetic "zǎo" (蚤).
Regarding "鑄" (zhù): the *Shuowen* states it means to cast or melt metal; it is composed of the radical "金" (metal) and the phonetic "壽" (shòu).
Regarding "矟印" (shàoyìn): the reading is "雙捉反" (shuāngzhuōfǎn); the text of the scripture writes it as "鎙" (cóng), which is incorrect.

*Liǎng bì* (two thighs): pronounced *pí mǐ* (鼙米). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "the exterior of the thigh," composed of the radical "bone" (*gǔ*) and the phonetic "bēi" (*bēi*), also written as *yù* (䯗).

In the sutras, it is written with the radical "flesh" (*ròu*) as *bì* (䏶), which is a vulgar character. From the *Mañjuśrī-bodhisattva-Yamāntaka-krodha-mantra-vidhi-sūtra*, [the term] *huì lín* (慧琳) is pronounced *shāo shuó shū zhuó* (燒爍舒灼).

*Yueyan* (月黶): *Yan* is pronounced as *yi* (伊) or *yian* (琰). The *Shuowen* states that it means "darkness in the center" (*zhonghei*); it is composed of the radical *he* (黑) with *li* (𭼩) as the phonetic. *Chiqiao* (嗤誚):

*Chi* is pronounced as *chi* (齒) and *qiao* as *xiao* (樵) or *yao* (曜). Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states it means "to reproach" (*zhuo-rang*). The *Cangjie pian* says it means "to scold. The *Shuowen* says it means "to harass" (*rao*); it is composed of the radical *yan* (言) with *xiao* (肖) as the phonetic, or it may be written as *zhao* (譙).

"Ān-shì (盥飾)": "Ān" is read as huǎn (緩) by Guǎn Yuè-wáng; he says that all objects used for washing are called ān. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Zǎo (澡), to wash the hands; it is composed of 'jiù' (臼) and 'shuǐ' (水) with 'míng' (皿) below. 'Jiù' is pronounced jū (匊); the character below is pronounced shī-lì (詩力)."

*Munchi* (捫持): The upper character is pronounced *mén*. *Ziqi* (漬其) [the second character] is pronounced *zì* (fourth tone). Ziyewang says that *zi* (漬) means "to soak" (*jìn*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "fermentation" (*òu*), written with the radical for water and the phonetic *zé*. The lower character [of the following term] is pronounced *dié*. The *Pīcāng* states that *ruò* (㲲) refers to a cloth made of wool; in character dictionaries it is written as *shè* (󲳴). The version in the scripture uses *xiè* (緤), pronounced *xiānjié*, but this does not accord with the meaning of the scripture.
"Huìdàn" (暉澹): The *Kǎoshēng* (Examination of Sounds) states that "dàn" means adornment. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical for water with "zhān" as the phonetic;
"yán" (簷) has the sound "zhān. "Mùhuàn" (木槵): The sound is "huàn. The *Kǎoshēng* states that "mùhuàn" is the name of a tree.
The character 骨 (gǔ) has the phonetic value *mò*.

The character 霈 (pài) is pronounced with the upper radical *huài* (pèi) and the lower radical *bèi* (bèi); the *Kǎoshēng* states it describes the appearance of heavy rain. All dictionaries write this as 沛 (*pèi*), meaning "overflowing" or "copious. The lower part is pronounced *zhūshù*; it consists of the water radical with the character *zhù* (from the *Jīngwén*) below, written with two [strokes]. This is the non-standard, vulgar form.

Regarding "lèngmèi" (凌懱): the first character, *lèng*, is pronounced with the initial *lì* and the final *chéng*. Gu Yewang states that it means "to violate," "to press upon," or "to hang down. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to overstep," composed of the radicals *zhuì* (夂) and *gǔliù* (󱿒). The text of the sutra writes it as "líng" (凌), which is incorrect. Regarding the second character, "mián" (眠), it is pronounced with the initial *mí* and the final *lú*. It means "to slight" or "to despise. This was already explained in the previous fascicle; the text of the sutra writes it as "miè" (蔑), which is incorrect.
*Ta mo*: upper character pronounced *taná*, a vulgar form; it is correctly written as *tà*. Lower character pronounced *méngbó*. *Nuǒ tǐ*:
upper character pronounced *huāguǎ*; also written as *luǒ* or *lě*. *Qū làn*:
upper character pronounced *qièyú*.
*Zhashi* (唼食): the first character is pronounced *zi* with the *la* rhyme;
the second is *shi*. *Tielou* (葧蔞): the first character is pronounced *pu* with the *gu* rhyme; the middle is *lu* with the *gou* rhyme; the last is *te* with the *deng* rhyme. *Chashu* (𧎮蝨):

the first character is pronounced *zao* with the *lao* rhyme; the second is *shen* with the *zi* rhyme. The *Shuowen* says they are jumping insects that bite people. Both follow the radical *guan* (虫). *Cha* and *xin* are the phonetic components; *xin* is pronounced *xin*, and *cha* is pronounced *zhua*.
*Yǎnshí* (掩襲): The first character is read as *yān* (淹) with the fanqie *yǎn-fǎn*; the second is read as *xún* (尋) with the fanqie *lì-fǎn*.

According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "cùn" (寸) and the phonetic "fǔ" (甫); the text reads it as "yǎn" (𢾭), which is a common variant form.
*Huāmán* (花鬘): the pronunciation is *mán*; it is also written as "màn" (鬘).

*Jīn qiè*: (The character *qiè* is pronounced with the initial *xian* [in the *Xiányèfǎn*]; the *Shuōwén* writes it as *qián*, meaning a casket, formed from the radical *fāng* [a box] and the phonetic *jiá*. That which is formed from the radical *zhú* [bamboo] is an alternative form. *Jiàn* is pronounced *xián*; *fāng* is pronounced *fāng*. *Jùzhī* is pronounced *zhī*.)

The *Amṛtakuṇḍalī-bodhisattva-pūjā-japa-siddhi-vidhi-sūtra*. Regarding the term "mǐn" (愍) in the title: the *Gōngyáng zhù* states that "mǐn" means "to feel pain for [others]" (*kùntòng*). The *Guǎngyá* defines it as "to think of" (*niàn*). The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) with the phonetic "yù" (*yù*, pronounced as above). The original text of this scripture uses "mǐn," which is also acceptable.

Regarding "jiǎo huàn" (deceitful): the upper character is pronounced with the *jiāo* rhyme-group (small). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "To 'jiǎo' means to employ falsehood and artifice. Gu Yewang says: "To falsely claim is called 'jiǎo'. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to usurp," derived from the hand radical and the phonetic *qiáo*. The original text of the scripture uses "jiǎo" (straightening), which does not carry the meaning of "jiǎo huàn."

*Lín* (upper radical: water, phonetic: *jīn*): The *Guǎngyá* states it means "to soak"; the *Shuōwén* defines it as "to drench with water. Some say it refers to the dripping of water from mountains. It is composed of the radical "water" and the phonetic "lín," with the final rhyme being *zhī*. The *Běicāng* states it means "water seeping into the ground. According to the *Gūjīn zhèngzì*, it is composed of the radical "water" and the phonetic "lí".

*Tiào* (跳): In the *Guǎngyá*, it is said that "tiào" means to ascend; according to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "foot" (足) and the phonetic "zhào" (兆). *Diàn* (鈿): In the upper part, read as *tián-liàn* (田練);

the *Kǎoshēng* says it refers to decorating with precious jewels; the *Wenzì Jílüè* says it refers to gold flowers. It is composed of the radical "metal" (金) and the phonetic "tián" (田). In the lower part, read as *shèng-lì* (昇力); this has already been explained in detail and repeatedly above.
*Hǎoxì*: The first character is pronounced *xǐ* (with its opposite meaning); the second character is pronounced *xī* (as recorded in the dictionary).

*Fóshuō Cízhǐ Púsà Tuóluóní Qiú Shàngshēng Jīng* (The Sūtra on the Dhāraṇī Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva for Seeking Rebirth Above). *Wúzì Kěyīn Dàfāngguǎng Wénshùshīlì Jīng Guānzìzài Púsà Shòujì Pǐn* (The Chapter on the Prophecy of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva from the Great Vaipulya Mañjuśrī Sūtra). *Mèilichè*: The first character is pronounced *mián* (with the *jié* radical); the middle character is pronounced *lián* (with the *jié* radical); the last character is pronounced *chǐ* (with the *shē* radical). This is a transliteration of a Sanskrit term for the name of a *brahman*.
"Pi" (its upper radical is *bo* [bǎiméng]) refers to the wrathful Vajra named *Yueyan* (its phonetic component is *yi* [yīyán]).
"Nuó" (its phonetic component is *nuo* [núhuó]) means to rub together with the palms.
*Shāhù* (紗縠): the first character is pronounced *shā* (as in "sand"), and the second is the rhyme of *hóngwū* (紅屋). This has already been explained in the preceding fascicle. *Lánhàn* (欄檻):
the first character is pronounced *láng'ān* (郎安), and the second is the rhyme of *xián'àn* (銜黯).
*Bìshǔn* (陛楯): the first character is pronounced *pímǐ* (毗米), and the second is the rhyme of *shíyǔn* (時允).

Regarding "纖利" (xiānlì): the upper character is pronounced as *xī* (with the radical *xián*). Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states that "纖" means "fine. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical *mì* (silk) and the phonetic *xiān*. However, considering that the nails in the scripture are "纖利," it would be more appropriate to write it with the radical *jīn* (metal), as *xiān* (銛).

"Right shoulder" (*yòu bō*): The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "bō" refers to the shoulder blade; it is composed of the radical "bone" (*gǔ*) and the phonetic "zhuān. The text of the sutra uses "yuè" (moon) instead of "bō," which is incorrect.

The pronunciation is *pǔ mò*. In the *Guanshiyin Pusa Shouji Jing*, compiled by Huilin: "Fanlan" (*fānlán*): The upper character "fān" is pronounced *bānmán*. The *Yunying* states that "fanlan" refers to variegated patterns. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it with the character "biàn" (from the radical "辡"), meaning variegated patterns. The *Gujin Zhengzi* states it is "wén lín" (斑瞵). It is also written as "biàn" (斑), meaning the appearance of patterns, composed of the radical "wén" and the phonetic "piān. The lower character "lán" is pronounced *lì xián*. The interpretation of its meaning is the same [as above]. The *Gujin Zhengzi* sometimes writes it as "lán" (㷠), which is pronounced *lì chén*. "Piān" is pronounced *biān* (邊), and "㷠" is pronounced *lì jìn* (力燼), where "jìn" is pronounced *xī yìn* (夕胤). [Note: This passage provides a philological commentary on specific characters found in the *Guanshiyin Pusa Shouji Jing*, citing various lexicographical sources such as the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *Yunying*, and *Gujin Zhengzi* to clarify their forms, pronunciations, and meanings.]

*Wěi* (煒): The upper character is pronounced *wéi* (韋) with the *guǐ* (鬼) radical. The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (Mao Commentary on the Classic of Poetry) states that *wěi* is the appearance of a crimson color. The *Shuōwén Jiězì* (Explaining Simple and Analyzing Compound Characters) defines it as "intense red," formed from the radical *huǒ* (fire) and the phonetic *wéi*. The lower character is pronounced *yán* (炎). The *Shuōwén* also states that *lè* (㷖) is likewise "intense. It is formed from the radical *huǒ* (fire) and the phonetic *lè* (㷤). The *Shī* (Classic of Poetry) says, "*Lè lè* [is] lightning. In the scripture, this is written as *huá* (華), which is the character for *yè* (曄). The character *lè* (㷤) has the same pronunciation as above.
*Fēnfù* (芬馥): The lower character *fù* is pronounced as *fú* (馮福反). The *Kǎośēng* states it describes the appearance of fragrance;

it is composed of the radical *xiāng* (香) with the phonetic *fù* (復). *Guānzìzài Púsà Shuō Pǔxián Tuóluóní Jīng* (觀自在菩薩說普賢陀羅尼經): *Guānzìzài Púsà Shuō Pǔxián Tuóluóní Jīng*. *Wúzìyīnxùn* (無字音訓): *Shīzǐ Zhuāngyán Wáng Púsà Qǐwèn Jīng* (師子莊嚴王菩薩請問經), *Shīzǐ Zhuāngyán Wáng Púsà Qǐwèn Jīng*. *Bēnló* (駢羅): The upper character *biàn* (辮) is pronounced as *mián* (眠反). Gù Yěwáng states that *bēnló* means "arrayed in rows. The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radical *mǎ* (馬) with the phonetic *bìng* (并); *biàn* is pronounced as *biàn miàn* (便麵反).

"Pèi" (沛) is pronounced *pǔ bèi* (上普貝反). In his commentary on the *Gōngyáng Zhuan*, Hé Xiū states that "Pèirán" (沛然) describes an appearance of abundance and overflowing excellence. The *Mèngzi* says, "The benevolent teachings flow forth abundantly (*pèirán*) and overflow across the four seas. Gù Yěwáng defines it as the pouring down of rain in vast, copious torrents. The *Guǎngyá* defines it as "great. According to the *Shuowén Jiězì*, the character is composed of the radical "water" (水) with the phonetic element "shì" (市); alternatively, it may be written as "pài" (霈), where the phonetic element remains "shì" (市), and the initial sound is *hū wài* (呼外反) for "huì" (濊) and *zhī shù* (之戍反) for "zhù" (澍). *Pèi*: Pronounced *pǔ bèi*. *Hé Xiū*: In his commentary on the *Gōngyáng Zhuan*, he says "Pèirán" is the appearance of having a surplus and being overflowing. *Mèngzi*: "The abundant (*pèirán*) virtue and teaching overflow across the four seas. *Gù Yěwáng*: He defines it as the pouring down of rain in vast, copious torrents (*hù hóng zhù*). *Guǎngyá*: It means "great. *Shuowén*: From the radical "water" (水) with the phonetic "shì" (市). Or written as "pài" (霈), where the phonetic is "shì" (市). *Huì*: Pronounced *hū wài*. *Zhù*: Pronounced *zhī shù*.

To press upon the body is *wū jiǎ* (烏甲), with the auxiliary sound *fǎn kǎo* (反考); it is called "suppressing" (*zhèn*). In both ancient and modern standard characters, it is written with the radical for earth (*tǔ*) and the phonetic *yàn* (厭).
To tear open the body is *shēng* (磔), with the phonetic *jié* (革); this has already been explained previously. The version in the sutra that writes it as *xiè* (榤) is incorrect.

The upper character, 蟲 (chóng), is pronounced huǐ in the *Zhōngyīng* edition; it is used in common parlance today. The lower character, 蟻 (yǐ), is pronounced yǐ. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "蟻" refers to the *bīmáoyóu* (ant); it is composed of the radical 虫 with the phonetic component 豈.
In the *Mahā-aṣṭabodhisattva-maṇḍala-sūtra*, the character for "kua" (髁) is the correct orthography; the version of the sūtra that uses "kuà" (胯) is a vulgar form.

Regarding "Xīyí" (熈怡): the former [character] expresses joy; the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "xī" means brightness and is composed of the radical for fire with "xī" as its phonetic component, pronounced "yí" (音移) and "zhī" (之) in the final rhyme. The latter has already been explained above.

The Mantra of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Born from the Ūrṇā-kośa of All Tathāgatas. This mantra is also known as the Dharma of the Rākṣasī of Blazing Lightning and Terrifying Form. Regarding the character *puk* (匐): in the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is stated that "puk" means to prostrate; it is formed with the radical *baō* (勹) and the phonetic *fu* (畐).

*Xi* (upper character): *xīn yì* (歆邑) in reverse. Zheng’s commentary on the *Shijing* states: "To *xi* is like to draw. The *Guǎngyá* says it means to drink. The *Shuowén* defines it as internal respiration; it is composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic "ji" (*jí*). It is also written as *xī* (歙). The text of the scripture uses *yì* (噏), which is incorrect. *Ha* (lower character): *hū há* (呼蛤) in reverse. The *Shuowén* states: "*Hā* means to gulp down (*chùè*). It is composed of the radical "deficiency" (*qiàn*) and the phonetic "hé" (*hé*). The text of the scripture uses *hā* (哈), which is a vulgar character.
"Qiūbìn (驅擯): *bīn* (牝) is reversed; according to the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲), it means 'to abandon. The text reads *bìn* (儐), which is an error. Mòlìzhītiānnǚjīng (摩利支天女經):

According to the *Kǎoshēng*, *jiǎo* (繳) on the head means 'to wind around' (*jiǎoliǎo*). The *Shuōwén* (說文) takes *mì* (糸) as the radical and *jiǎo* (敫) as the phonetic. The *Yùnxuān* (韻詮) also accepts *jīn* (巾) as the radical, writing it as *jiǎo* (𢅎); this is likewise acceptable."

The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the One Hundred and Eight Names of the Twelve Mudrās of the Great Auspicious Goddess, the Immaculate. [Regarding the term] *yì* (詣): Wang Yè of the Ni-jì-fǎn glossary states that *yì* means "to arrive. The *Cāngjié piān* states it means "to reach. The *Shuōwén* states it means "to wait for arrival," composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic "zhǐ" (*zhī*).

*Mārīcī-devī Sūtra*: No Chinese characters provided for transliteration. *Mahāmaṅgalā-devī-dvādaśanāman Sūtra*: No Chinese characters provided for transliteration. *Dhāraṇī-sūtra for Saving the Face-Burning Hungry Ghosts*: Regarding the character *léi* (羸): - The commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states it means "weak. - Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states it means "ill. - Xu Shuchong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states it means "inferior. - The *Guoya* states it means "extreme. - The *Zishu* states it means "exhausted. - The *Shuowen* defines it as "emaciated" (*chǎn*), composed of the radical "sickness" (*zhǎng*) and the phonetic "ní. - The *Gujin Zhengzi* states that *léi* means "emaciated" (*qú*), composed of the radical "sickness" (*zhǎng*) and the phonetic "yǔ"; *qú* is pronounced *jù yú*, and *yǔ* is pronounced *sù kǒu*.

Regarding "birds and beasts" (*qínshòu*): according to the *Baihûtong*, "birds" is a general term for both birds and beasts.

The term *qín* (禽) refers to those captured and controlled by humans. The *Erya* states: "Those with two feet and feathers are called *qín*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains that *qín* is a general name for beasts;

its head is a pictograph, composed of the radical *nǒu* (禸) and the phonetic *jīn* (今). The head of *qín* resembles that of the *lí* (离) and the *xí* (兕). The lower part [of the character] is pronounced *jiù* (救);
the *Erya* states: "Those with four feet and fur are called beasts (*shòu*). The *Cangjie Pian* also says it is a beast. The explanation is as follows:

The character 文 (wén) signifies "to guard" (shǒu). It is composed of the radical 犬 (quǎn, dog) and the phonetic 嘼 (xiù). The original text of the scripture uses 狩 (shòu), which means "a great hunt," but this does not accord with the meaning of the scripture.
The pronunciation of 禸 (nóu) is rǒu (with the second tone); the pronunciation of 嘼 (xiù) is xiū (or yòu).

*Lì* (轢): To crush to pieces. The *Cāngjié piān* states that *lì* means to tread upon. The *Shànglín fù* says it is that which is trodden over by chariots and infantry. The *Shuowén* defines it as what a carriage treads upon, composed of the radical "carriage" (*chē*) with the phonetic "delight" (*lè*). *Háo* (𨋁) is pronounced *ní zhǎn* (尼展反); *lín* (轔) is pronounced *lì zhēn* (栗珍反), and the final [radical] is pronounced *sū huì* (蘇會反).
*The Sūtra of the Divine Incantation Praising the Merits of the Tathāgata*. "Svā" (騷鞞) [the first character is pronounced with the *su* and *zào* finals reversed];
this is an error for the Sanskrit mantra-syllable "kṣi," which should be written as "kṣi" (乞澀二合). The following "kṣī" (敧箄) is the same as this.

*Bīpí* (the *pí* is pronounced as in *mí*). Twelve Buddha Names Divine Mantra: A Sūtra on the Comparative Merit of Removing Obstacles and Extinguishing Sins. Regarding the term *lǐyūn* (the upper character *fèn* is pronounced as in *wén*; the lower character *yù* is pronounced as in *yún*), the *Kǎoshēng* (Investigation of Sounds) states it is a description of the appearance of fragrant smoke; its meaning has already been fully explained in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-uttamarāja-sūtra*.

Preface to the *Mahāyāna-nyāya-ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra* The Imperial Preface to the *Mahāyāna-nyāya-ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra*. Regarding the character "pǔ" (朴): it is written as "pǔ," with the radical "wood" (木) and the phonetic "bó" (菐), which is pronounced like "bǔ.

It signifies great simplicity (*dà pǔ*). It is contrary to the vulgar usage. Wang Bi stated: "Pǔ is the True (*zhēn*). "True" refers to the state when the primal qi has not yet differentiated. The *Shēnglèi* states: "Generally, when an object has not yet been carved or engraved, it is called pǔ. The *Shuowén* states: "Pǔ is the raw state of wood; it takes 'wood' as its radical and 'bó' as its phonetic. The sound of "bó" is like that of "bǔ."

The character *qiān* (牽) [with the phonetic *qì jiān*] means "to pull" or "to drag," according to the *Guǎngyá*. It also means "to connect. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means "to lead forward"; it is composed of the radical "ox" (*niú*) and the phonetic "xuán" (*xián*), with *mìng* (冖) pronounced as *guǐ yíng*. This [radical] represents the tethering rope of an ox. The common usage of the hand radical (*shǒu*) instead to form *qiān* is incorrect.

Regarding the character *sāng* (喪), Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "To lose or perish is called *sāng*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to be absent" (*wáng*), composed of the radical for weeping with the phonetic *wáng*. The vulgar forms written as *mí* (𠔏) or *sāng* (𦒿) are both incorrect. As for the character below it, *hū* (乎), the *Shuowen Jiezi* says it is "the residual sound of speech," composed of the radical *ǐ* (𠔃) with the phonetic *jié* (󱫛); the pronunciation of *jié* is *piànmiè* (片蔑).

"Ài (愛)" and "è (惡)": the former is pronounced *āi* with the *dài* (代) rhyme; it is a variant form of a vulgar character. Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that "àiyǎn" (愛親) means "to love one's kin. The *Gujin Zhengzi* (古今正字) says it means "to pity and think of. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radicals "wú" (旡, pronounced *jì*) and "xīn" (心). Now it is commonly written as "ài" (愛). "Wú" (旡) has the pronunciation *jì*; Gu Yewang states that "è" (惡) means "to hate," and it is a borrowed character (*jiǎjiè*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of "xīn" (心) and the phonetic "yà" (亞). It is an error for the vulgar form to include the radical "xī" (西).

*Jíliáo* (寂寥): The upper character is pronounced *qíng* with the *lì* rhyme; it is a vulgar form. The *Shuowen* correctly writes it as *𡧯*, meaning "a place where there are no people. It is composed of the radical *mián* (宀) and the phonetic *qī* (戚) in abbreviated form. Alternatively, it is written as *𧧌* with the radical *yán* (言), where the lower part is pronounced *lì* with the *diāo* rhyme. The *Shuowen* omits this entry. The characters for *jìliáo* (寂寥) mean "profound and distant, a place where there are no people. It is composed of the radical *mián* (宀) and the phonetic *liáo* (翏). *Liáo* (翏) is composed of the radical *liǎo* (蓼) in abbreviated form. *Mián* (宀) is pronounced *mián*; *shū* (尗) is pronounced *shū* and is composed of the abbreviated *qī* (戚). *Jìliáo* (寂寥): The upper character is pronounced *qíng* with the *lì* rhyme; it is a vulgar form. The *Shuowen* correctly writes it as *𡧯*, meaning "a place where there are no people. It is composed of the radical *mián* (宀) and the phonetic *qī* (戚) in abbreviated form. Alternatively, it is written as *𧧌* with the radical *yán* (言), where the lower part is pronounced *lì* with the *diāo* rhyme. The *Shuowen* omits this entry. The characters for *jìliáo* (寂寥) mean "profound and distant, a place where there are no people. It is composed of the radical *mián* (宀) and the phonetic *liáo* (翏). *Liáo* (翏) is composed of the radical *liǎo* (蓼) in abbreviated form. *Mián* (宀) is pronounced *mián*; *shū* (尗) is pronounced *shū* and is composed of the abbreviated *qī* (戚).

*Shì* (俟): The pronunciation is *zǐ* with the third tone; this is a vulgar character used in common parlance. The correct form is written as *lì* (竢). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is written as *cóng-lái* (從來) and *zuò-sì* (作𥏳). The *Yunquan* says: "To wait. The *Kaosheng* says: "To await someone's arrival. The vulgar form written as *rén* (人) [i.e., 候] is also acceptable.

"Fen-lun" (紛綸): The first character, "fen," is read as fāng or wǎn; according to the *Guǎngyá*, it signifies "abundant" or "chaotic. The second character, "lún," is read as lǜ or chún; the *Yījīng* states that "lún" means "to manage and order. Song Zhōng’s commentary on the *Tàixuānjīng* says it means "to interlace. Both are phono-semantic compounds (*xiángxīng zì*).

Regarding the character for "flowing upward" (liúyè): according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of "water" (shuǐ) and "lù" (㐬), where "lù" is pronounced *tùn* (with the tone mark reversed). The common practice of omitting the dot is incorrect. Regarding "yè" (liquid): according to the *Shuowen*, "yè" means "moisture" (*jīn*); it is composed of "water" (shuǐ) and "yè" (夜) as a phonetic component. Its pronunciation is *yì*.

*Qiǎnshēn* (千演反): This character is explained in the *Shuowen* as "not leaking" (*bú lòu*). It is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic element "zēn" (*zé*). The pronunciation of "zēn" is *chàxiàn* (察限反). The lower part, "shāngrèn" (傷任反), is the phonetic for "kǎo" (考). *Lòu* means to leak. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of "water" and "mí" (罙); the pronunciation of "mí" is the same as above. Nowadays, it is traditionally transmitted that "mí" is pronounced *shānlín* (山林反). The *Shuowen* states that "lòu" also means "mí," and "mí" is also said to mean a stove hearth (*zào zhǒng*). *Shēn* (深): Deep. *Qiān* (千): Thousand. *Yǎn* (演): To unfold or elaborate. *Fǎn* (反): A suffix indicating a reversed or alternative reading. *Shuōwén* (說文): The *Shuowen Jiezi*, the earliest surviving dictionary of the Chinese language. *Bú* (不): Negative particle, "not. *Lòu* (𣸧): To leak or drip. *Cóng* (從): Radical or component. *Shuǐ* (水): The water radical. *Zēn* (戔): Phonetic element; a rare character meaning "to cut" or "to slice. *Shēng* (聲): Phonetic element. *Chàxiàn* (察限): A specific ancient pronunciation notation. *Xià* (下): The lower part of a character. *Shāngrèn* (傷任): Another ancient pronunciation notation. *Kǎo* (考): To investigate or examine; here used as a phonetic. *Lòu* (𨗉): To leak or flow out. *Yì* (亦): Also. *Tōng* (通): To be applicable or interchangeable. *Mí* (罙): A character meaning "to enter deeply" or "a pit. *Shānlín* (山林): A specific ancient pronunciation notation. *Zào zhǒng* (竈󱹿): A stove or hearth. *Yě* (亦): Also. *Yún* (云): To say or claim. *Qī* (竈): Stove. *Zhǒng* (󱹿): A variant or specific type of hearth.

Regarding "xù" (旭): Xuang Yu’s *Fǎnkǎo* states that it means "bright. The *Shuowén* says it is the appearance of the sun rising at dawn, composed of the radical "sun" (日) and the character "nine" (九), with the latter pronounced as *zhì* (質). The *Shuowén* further notes that it is a pictographic character representing the essence of the great sun.

The upper radical *chuǎn* (舛) is pronounced with the initial *shēng* (識) and the final rhyme *líng* (陵); the *Mao Shī* (毛詩) writes it as *shēng* (昇), and the *Shēnglèi* (聲類) writes it as *shēng* (󲭜). It signifies the rising of the sun. The lower radical *zhòu* (晝) is pronounced with the initial *zhú* (竹) and the final rhyme *jiù* (救). According to the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲), it means daytime brightness. The *Shuōwén* (說文) states: "It is the boundary between the sun’s emergence and entry and the night. It is a compound character formed from 'dawn' (*dàn*) and 'swiftly' (*yù*). It is a word that conveys its meaning through the combination of its components.
The character *yì* (至) is used as a borrowed character (*jiàjiè*) for *zhì* (致); *zhì* also means "to arrive. Furthermore, regarding *zhēng* (蒸): the reading is *yújié* (魚偈).

Kǒng [Yǎng]’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states that *yì* (乂) means "to govern" (*zhì*). Examining its phonetic component, *yì* means "to rest. The *Shuowén* says it means "to clear away weeds"; it is composed of *yāo* (󱫛) and *fǎn* (乀) intersecting, which is called *yì*. *Yāo* (󱫛) is pronounced *yāo* (音夭); the *Shuowén* says it means "to turn left. *Fǎn* (乀) is pronounced *pímì* (音皮密反); the *Shuowén* says it means "to turn right. The lower part, *zhí* (軄), is pronounced *réng* (仍反). In the *Erya* and the *Xiaoya*, *zhēng* (蒸) means "ruler" (*jūn*); in the *Hànshī*, it means "many" (*zhòng*) and "good" (*shàn*). The *Bóyá* says *zhēngzhēng* (蒸蒸) means "filial piety. The *Shuowén* says it is composed of "grass" (艹) and "fire" (灬) with *chéng* (承) as the phonetic; *bìyáo* (必遙) is the pronunciation of *biāo* (灬).

*Kāpiśī* (the "ji" in *jūyì* is pronounced as an upper tone; it is a name for a country in the West according to the Sanskrit language). It is also called *Kāśmīra* or *Kaśmīra*, both of which are erroneous abbreviations of ancient translations. The correct Sanskrit pronunciation is *Kaśmīra*, located within the borders of North India.

The character for *ling* (領) is pronounced with the initial *lì* (郢) and the final *fǎn* (反). The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (毛詩傳) states: "It is the nape of the neck. The *Zhuāngzǐ* (莊子) uses it in the sense of "to collect" (*lù*). Zheng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* (禮記) says it means "to organize" (*lǐ*). The *Liùtǎo* (六韜) calls it the "collar of a garment" (*yīlǐng*). The standard orthography of ancient and modern times is *jiēn* (袊), though today it is commonly written as *lǐng*. It is composed of the radical *xié* (頁, sound *xián jié fǎn*) and the phonetic *líng* (令, sound *qiú léi fǎn*); the latter is a vulgar form. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) says it refers to the edge of a sleeve (*yīmèiduān*). The *Shuōwén* (說文) agrees with this, stating it is composed of the radical *yī* (衣) and the abbreviated phonetic *xiù* (岫). Ancient and modern texts also write it as *zhèn* (襢) from the radicals *ní* (𥝩) and *yī* (衣), and it is also written as *xiū* (褎).

*Yì* (翼): Pronounced *yùn* (軄) in the upper character; Kong’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* says it means "to assist" (*fǔ*). Máo’s *Shīchuán* says it means "reverence. Zhèng’s *Shījì* says it means "to aid. Dú’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* says it means "to assist. The *Eryā* says it means "respect. The *Shuowén* says it means "wings"; the upper part consists of the radical *yǔ* (羽), with *yì* (異) as the phonetic. The lower part is pronounced *róng huì* (穢). Yù’s *Bìzhù* on the *Yìjīng* says it means "to protect. The *Eryā* says it refers to "frontiers. Guō Pǔ says: "To station guards for defense in the outer periphery. The *Shuowén* says it means "to stand guard"; it is composed of the radicals *wéi* (韋), *zà* (帀), and *xíng* (行)—meaning a surrounding formation is called "guarding"—but here it is written in its abbreviated form as *wèi* (衛).

*Dí* (滌) in *Dílù tíng* (滌慮亭): *lì* (歷) is the phonetic component; the commentary on the *Shūjìng* (尚書) by Kǒng [Yǎng] states it means "to cleanse" (*díchú*). The *Shuōwén* states it means "to sprinkle" (*sǎ*). *Sǎ* is pronounced *xī* with the second tone. *Jí* (汲) in *Jǐyǐn* (汲引):

*jīn* (金) and *lì* (立) are the phonetic components; the *Shuōwén* states it means "to draw up water. It is composed of the radical *shuǐ* (water) and the phonetic *jí* (及), which is pronounced *yǐ* with the third tone. The commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* by Dù [Yù] says it means "to guide. The *Shuōwén* states it means "to draw a bow," composed of the radicals *gōng* (bow) and *yè* (曳). In ancient script, it is written with the hand radical as *zhuó* (㧈), or alternatively as *hóng* (弘).

"I hope to rely upon" (shù píng): *píng* is pronounced with the *biéng* rhyme. The *Jìxùn* states that it means "to entrust oneself to. It is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "fēng.

The *Shuōwén* writes it as 󲦌, and it is also read in the fourth tone (*qù shēng*), meaning "to lean against" (*yī ér*). "True fishing trap" (zhēn quán): *quán* is pronounced with the *yuán* rhyme. The *Zhuāngzǐ* says, "The trap (*quán*) is that by which one catches fish; once the fish is caught, one forgets the trap. Gù Yěwáng says it is a bamboo basket for catching fish. *Gǒu* is the pronunciation of *gǒu*.

The character *liáo* (𥲿) is pronounced *diāo* (反). According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means "to be negligent" (*jiǎnqǐ*). According to the *Shuowén*, it means "ringing in the ears," composed of the radical "ear" and the phonetic "yǒu. It is sometimes written as *lèi* (𦗖); however, the current vulgar practice of writing it with the "mǎo" (卯) radical is a traditional error and is incorrect. *Yǒu* (丣) is pronounced *yǒu* (酉), and *diāo* (𥲿) is pronounced *liǎo* (了).

*Gěnggài* (梗槩): The upper character *gěng* (梗) is pronounced with the *xiàng* (杏) rhyme; according to the *Erya*, it means "upright growth. The *Guǎngyá* states it means "rough outline" (*lüèzhēn*). It is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "gèng" (*gèng*). The lower character *gài* (槩) is pronounced with the *ài* (礙) rhyme. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* says it refers to leveling measures such as the *dǒu* and *hú*. Zong [Yi]’s commentary on the *Dōngjīng fù* says that "rough outlines" (*gěnggài*) means not being fine or detailed. The *Shuowen* agrees with Zheng Xuan. It may also be written with the phonetic "jì" (*jì*). Alternatively, it is written as *gài* (概). *Zhēn* (箴) is pronounced like a needle (*zhēn*); *xiān* (纖) is pronounced with the *xījiān* (息尖) rhyme.

Scroll One, Part One: The Mahāyāna-praṇidhāna-ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra, Scroll One. *Kalandaka-kūṭa* (the first character *kā* is pronounced as *jiāng* [qiāng] with the *qǔ* [kě] tone; the older translations render this as *Jiālántuóyī* or *Jiélánduōjiā*, both of which are erroneous). This is the name of the Great Bamboo Grove (*Mahāveṇuvana*), located beside the city of Rājagṛha on the northern side of the Southern Mountains. It was there that this sūtra was preached.

*Dai* (dài; in the *Zheng Jie* commentary on the *Mao Shi*, it means "to reach" or "to arrive"; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical *chuò* with the phonetic *lì*; *lì* is pronounced *duì*). *Asaṃkhyeya* (ā-sēng-qí-yè;

the first character is read as *qīng* [qǐng] and the second as *yǐ* [zhē]; this is a numerical term from the Sanskrit language). According to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, which cites the *Vimukti-sūtra*, among the sixty numbers, *asaṃkhyeya* is the fifty-second number, with each subsequent number increasing tenfold; all details are as explained in that treatise.
*Hu* (in the *Erya*, "to rely upon" or "to depend on"; according to the *Shuowen*, it takes the radical for "heart" and the phonetic *gu*).

*Chen* (upper character *chi* and *lin*; in the *Mao Shi*, "to sink" or "to submerge"; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "thirst," taking the radical for "yin" [pronounced *yin*] and the phonetic *ning* [pronounced *li*]). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of "person" and "water," representing a person submerged in water; it takes the radical for "water" and the phonetic *ruo*.
Regarding "Nánjiě" (難解): the reading with the tone of xià (夏) is incorrect. Regarding "Zhěnglǐ" (整理):

the *Shuowén* states it means "to align" (*qí*) and is composed of the radical "chì" (敕) and the phonetic "zhèng" (正); the common usage with "zhǐ" (止) is incorrect. The pronunciation of "chì" (敕) is chǒu-lì (丑力). The *Shuowén* states that the character "chì" (敕) is composed of "shù" (束) and "pū" (攴), where "pū" (攴) is pronounced pǔ-bǔ (普卜); the common usage with "lái" (來) and "zuò" (作) to form "lì" (力) as "chì" (勅) is merely a vulgar character.
The character 𤡜 (pronounced *yán*) is explained in the *Shuowen* as meaning "satiated," "joyful," or "contented. It is composed of 犬 (dog), 甘 (sweetness), and 肉 (flesh).
The two feet above are pronounced *shuō chuāng*. The *Shuowen* states they are composed of two 隹 (pheasants) and 又 (hand); it is incorrect for the common usage to employ the reversed form.

Regarding the character for "reverence" (gōng): the upper part is explained in the *Shuowen* as "to follow" and "to be solemn. The lower part is the archaic form of the character for "mind" (xīn), with the phonetic component "gòng" (gong). It is incorrect for the common version to use "ěr" (er) instead. Regarding the character for "respect" (jìng): it is said that its phonetic component is "kǎo" (kao), meaning "cautious and careful. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of "pō" (po) and "gǒu" (gou); the pronunciation of "gǒu" is jǐlì (ji-li).

*Ji* (upper radical *ji*, pinyin *yì*): Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that it is a leather halter for the horse's head. The *Shiming* calls it a *jian* (check), so named because it serves to check and restrain [the horse]. According to the *Shuowen*, it takes the radical *wang* (net) and the phonetic *zhu*. *Zhu* has the same pronunciation as above; it is also written as *ji*. *Suo* (lower radical *su*, pinyin *guǒ*): the *Kaosheng* says it means "to record. The *Guangya* says it is a linked ring. It takes the radical *jin* (metal) and the phonetic *luo*. *Luo* has the same pronunciation as above.

Regarding the character for *mingxing* (the morning star): according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical for "moon" and the phonetic element "gui" (pronounced *yǐng*). The "gui" represents a window. As for the "star," it refers to the stars of the Five Elements. To speak of the "morning star" (*mingxing*) does not mean that such a star exists every day; rather, it refers to the planets of gold, wood, fire, earth, and water when they occasionally approach the sun and appear at dawn. Those who practice divination should know that because the sun will soon rise, there is no such thing as a permanent "morning star. Thus, when various sutras occasionally mention the term "morning star," the Buddha uses the planet approaching the sun as a metaphor to say that Bodhisattva Maitreya is adjacent to the stage of Buddhahood. The old interpretation—which claims that those observing the night in the West watch three morning stars, first observing a white star, then a blue star, and finally a red star—is a grave deviation from the intent of the sutras and is a false teaching.

The character for *fàn* (帆) is pronounced with the initial *fán* (凡). The commentary on sounds states that it refers to the sail used on ships to catch the wind; *fànzhǔ* (帆主) refers to the navigator of the sea. It is composed of the radical *jīn* (巾) and the phonetic *fán* (凡). The character for *huíhù* (洄澓) has the initial *huí* (回) for the upper part.

Although the received text uses the archaic character *shù* (󲶳), this is a correct form though not commonly used today. According to the *Erya*, "to go upstream against the current is called *sùhuí*. Guo Pu stated that it refers to a swirling eddy. The lower part is pronounced *fù* (復); it is sometimes written as *fú* (洑), which also denotes the whirling of water. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical *shui* (水) and the phonetic *fù* (復).

*Qin* (侵): To encroach upon; to violate. The *Cangjie pian* states it means "to encroach. The *Shuowen jiezi* states it means "gradual" (*jian*). It is composed of the radicals for "person" (*ren*), "broom" (*zhou*), and "hand" (*you*)—the "hand" signifying that one holds a broom; thus, to advance as if sweeping is called "encroachment. Now it is abbreviated as *qin*. The lower radical is pronounced *he* (何) with the tone *da* (大). The *Cangjie pian* states it means "harmful injury" (*haizai*). The *Shuowen jiezi* states it means "wounding" (*shang*). It is composed of "roof" (*mian*) and "mouth" (*kou*), implying that speech arises from within the home. The phonetic component is the abbreviated form of *feng* (*feng sheng*). The text uses *hai* (害), which is a vulgar character. *Feng* (丰) is pronounced *hai* (害) and is the ancient character.

*Kāruḷa* (迦嚕羅) is the Sanskrit name for the great bird that feeds on dragons. In ancient times it was called *Kālūla* (迦婁羅), also known as the Golden-Winged Bird (*Jinshibiao*), or *Garuda* (揭路茶). In the present text, the two characters for *kāruḷa* do not accurately reflect the phonetic values. The correct Sanskrit is *garuḍa*; *ḍa* is pronounced with the *ning-jia* (儜加) rhyme, and *ru* is pronounced with a retroflex articulation. It is also named *Lóngyùn* (龍惌).

*Tūn* (吞) [with the phonetic *tú* and *lán* reversed]: according to the *Shuowen*, it means "to eat," composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic "xiàn" (*xì*). The forms *càn* (噉) and *dàn* (啖) found in the scriptures are both vulgar characters.

*Lǚ* (僂): [with the phonetic *lì* and *zhǔ* reversed]. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that it refers to one who is hunchbacked. *Lǚ* implies a curvature of the back; the *Guoyaya* defines it as "the body being bent. The *Shuowen* defines it as "weakness" (*wāng*), composed of the radical "person" (*rén*) and the phonetic "lǒu" (abbreviated). Some say that "hunchback" (*bèi lǚ*) and this term share the same meaning.

The character for "naked" (luǒ) is pronounced *lǎng guǒ* (with the final syllable reversed to avoid vulgar taboos). In the *Zuǒzhuan*, it appears as "guān qí luò yù" (observing his naked bathing). Gu Yèwáng states that "luǒ" means to remove one's clothes and expose the shoulders. The *Shuowen Jiezi* uses the character with the "clothing" radical (*yī*) to form "luǒ. The *Zishu* uses the "body" radical (*shēn*) to form "nǔ," while the *Yupian* uses the "human" radical (*rén*) to form "luǒ. These three forms are all interchangeable.

*Dui* (堆): The upper radical is *du* (都), with the phonetic component *lei* (雷). The *Kaosheng* says it is the appearance of high ground. The *Picao* says it is a mound of earth. The *Shuowen* says it is a small hill, formed from the radical *tu* (土) with the phonetic component *zhui* (隹). The version in the scriptures written as *zhun* (準) with the ten-stroke radical is incorrect. It is also written as *yan* (雁) using an ancient character; the form *dai* (塠) is a vulgar character. The lower part, *fu* (扶), has the tone *you* (有); this is the pronunciation in the Wu and Chu regions. The *Yunying* says the tone is *fu* (扶) with the rhyme *wu* (武); the *Shuowen* says it is a vast plain. A hill without rocks is called a *fu*. The archaic form is written as *zuo* (𨸏), a pictographic character.

*Dǐ* (掌/𦛒履反): Duan’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that it means "to level. The *Cangjie pian* states it is a stone for grinding and sharpening. The *Shuowen jiezi* writes it as *dǐ*, meaning a soft stone; it is composed of the radical *hàn* (厂, pronounced *hǎn*) with the phonetic *dǐ*. *Chǐ* (𦛒履反): [The character is] composed of the radical *hàn* (厂) with the phonetic *chǐ*. The radical *hàn* is pronounced *hǎn*. *Zhǐ* (掌/𦛒履反): [The character is] composed of the radical *hàn* (厂) with the phonetic *zhǐ*. The radical *hàn* is pronounced *hǎn*. *Jì* (𦛒履反): [The character is] composed of the radical *hàn* (厂) with the phonetic *jì*. The radical *hàn* is pronounced *hǎn*. *Yǔ* (𦛒履反): [The character is] composed of the radical *hàn* (厂) with the phonetic *yǔ*.
