Regarding *karpūra* (camphor) as described in the *Xiyu ji*: it is the resin of the *karpūra* tree, which has a trunk like a pine but differs in its leaves, flowers, and fruit. When first harvested, the wood is still moist and lacks fragrance; however, after the wood has dried and is subsequently processed and split open, a fragrant substance is found within it, resembling mica in appearance and ice or snow in color. This is what is called *karpūra*.

The character for "shrunken tongue" (shuō) is written as "cóng" (摍) in dictionaries; they are identical. *Shi-chuan* (食篅): "Chuan" (篅) is pronounced with the *shen* (緣) and *fan* (反) finals; according to the *Shuowen*, it refers to a circular bamboo vessel used for holding grain.

"Chuan" (󲳄) is pronounced with the *tu* (徒) and *sun* (損) finals. *Nan-ya* (南庌): "Ya" (庌) is pronounced with the *yan* (顏) and *jia* (假) finals. According to the *Guangya*, "ya" means a house; it refers to a corridor building. The *Shuowen* states that the surrounding buildings around a hall are called "wu" (廡). The *Shiming* says that a large house is called "wu"; people of the You and Ji regions call it "ya. The text reads "ya" (牙), which is not the correct form.
Regarding "lán-quàn" (闌圈): it means to keep livestock in an enclosure. "Xián" (閑) is synonymous with "lán" (闌). Regarding "huàn" (宦):

it is pronounced with the *hú* and *chuàn* finals. In the *Zuǒzhuan*, it says: "He then served as the heir of a high minister," with the commentary stating, "To serve is called 'huàn'. It further states, "Huàn also means to study."
Li-ta (with the "zhù" and "jià" tones);
Jié-chú (with the "zhí" and "jù" tones);
Lín-lóu (with the "lì" and "hòu" tones).

*Wěn* (an ancient form of *mǐn*, pronounced *fěn*) means to wipe.

Khaṃ-pa-ti-bu-te-kha-kaṅ (khaṅ) hu-mo-hu-gōng.

Lè (read as *lè*) hē (read as *hē*), lì (read as *lì*) duì (read as *duì*, with the second character pronounced as *zhuī*); yǎn (read as *yǎn*) zéng (read as *zéng*) lǐng (read as *líng*) cǎo (read as *cǎo*, with the fifth character pronounced as *xī*);

*Qi*: dǐng (with the *lǐ* rhyme). *Xù*:

zhī (with the *sū* and *dùn* rhymes); according to the *Pīcāng*, *sàn* means to spray; according to the *Tōngsūwén*, to hold water in the mouth and spit it out is called *sàn*; the scriptural text writes this as 𠹀, which is a vulgar character.
"Bái huǎn" (白睆): "huán" (還) is read as "zhàn" (棧); Xu Shen’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states that "tú huǎn" (濁睆) refers to a disease characterized by white opacities within the eyes.

The text's reading as "wán" (完) is incorrect. "Cuó guǐ" (痤鬼): "cuó" (痤) is read as "gē" (戈); the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines "cuó" as swelling, referring to carbuncles or boils (*tōng cuó*). The text's reading as "fù" (侳) is incorrect.

The "ma" (痲) ghost [is so called because] its power is the opposite of the *Shuowen* definition of "diseases of the large and small intestines"; according to the *Shenglei*, it refers to frequent urination. The text of the sutra uses the character "lin" (淋), meaning "to leak," which is not the correct form.

The "reed tube" (*wei-tǒng*) used for waiting for the Duke’s return is the same as the "tube" (*tǒng*) in the *Sāncāng*. Guo Pu says it is a bamboo pipe; the *Shuowen* says a "tube" (*tóng*) is a section of cut bamboo. Nowadays, all versions write it with the "wood" radical as *tǒng*. The "wooden *kǎn*" refers to a wooden vessel; *kǎn* is pronounced *tālǎng*. It is a lacquer-receiving vessel that can be used to hold food, but it is not the implement intended here.

*Lín* (pronounced *lì jīn*): The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines this as "to pour water. The *Guangya* states it means "clear. The scriptural text writes it as *líng* (pronounced *lì jīn*): the *Guangya* says it means "drizzling rain," while the *Shuowen Jiezi* identifies it as the name of a valley.

"Liu-xiang" (摎項) is also written as "liu-suo" (𢷶), with the same pronunciation as "li-zhou" (力周) and "ju-mao" (居茅). In the *Cangjie pian*, it means "to bind"; in the *Shuowen jiezi*, it means "to bind and kill. "Liu" (摎) is synonymous with "chi" (糎), a term for binding.
*Chài* (the first character is pronounced *tá*, the second *lè*)—according to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means *zhī* (ant eggs) or *jié* (exhaustion).
*Wèng* (pronounced *nòng*)—according to the *Běicāng*, it is a nasal disease; the *Tōngsùwén* states that "nasal congestion" (*qiú bí*) is called *wèng*; *qiú* is pronounced *qiú*.

The character 蠱 (gǔ) is pronounced gù according to the *Zìlín* (Forest of Characters). The *Spring and Autumn Annals* (Chūnqiū chuán) states, "The illness was like that of *gǔ*. Thus, *gǔ* may refer to a disease; it is neither a ghost nor food. Alternatively, it may mean "to confuse" or "to bewilder. Du Yù (Dù Yù) states that *gǔ* refers to a disease. The text of the scripture uses the characters 厭 (yàn) and 蠱 (gǔ), which are not the correct forms.
*Chāpō* (扠波): First, "jiā" (家) means "to marry for the first time.

Second, "fǎn" (反) refers to the phonetic component. Third, "wěi" (餧)—according to the *Sāncāng*, it means "to feed"; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means "the fodder for oxen"; according to the *Guǎngyá*, it is "wēizhì" (萎𩚅).

Jinmó (金鏝) is the name of a ghost;
Jiānbì (癎病) is pronounced héjiān (核間);

The analogy for the *zhùguǐ* (stinging ghost) is reversed.

Regarding *hòuguǐ* (seizing ghost): "hán" is pronounced with the rhyme *pì* (pì-bì fǎn); according to the *Shēnglèi* (Classification of Sounds), *pì* refers to chronic indigestion. The scriptural text uses the character for "person" (*rén*) to form [the character for] *pì* (pì-chǐ fǎn), meaning crookedness or deviation; however, that [character for] *pì* is not used here.
*Gǔ* (祥公戶反): A type of insect that harms people; "xiáng" (下徐揚反) means auspiciousness according to the *Zílín*. The text of the scripture reads *bì* (辟), which is incorrect.

Cchundi (pronounced *cchun-ti*, with the initial *cch* as in "church" and the final *-i* as in "machine"), Jāṅgulī (pronounced *jāṅ-gu-li*, with the initial *jāṅ* as in "jaw" and the final *-ī* as in "machine"),

2. Second Fascicle. Regarding the term *shùqì* (抒氣): according to the *Guǎngyǎ*, *shù* means "to scoop out" (*yǎo*) or "to drain" (*xiè*). According to the *Shuōwén*, *shù* means "to ladle" (*yì*). To "ladle" (*yì*) implies measuring or pouring. The pronunciation of *yì* is *yú rén*; the pronunciation of *yǎo* is *yú zhǎo*.

3–7: Fascicles Three through Seven (Fascicles III–VII). Items 3 through 7 have no phonetic glosses. 8: Fascicle Eight. "Xingxing" (猩猩): according to the *Jing* (京) [dictionary], this is a beast capable of speech; its form resembles that of a macaque (*míhóu*), and its face is like that of a woman. It is found in Fēngxī (封溪), Jiāozhǐ (交阯); its voice is like the crying of a small child. The *Qūlǐ* (曲禮) states: "The xingxing can speak. This refers to it.

9. Volume Nine. "Xianbu" (先不): The character *bu* (不) is pronounced as *yin* (音). 10. Volume Ten. "Jiangui" (姧詭): The character *gui* (詭) is pronounced as *ju* (居) with the final rhyme *hui* (毀); it means "unreal. According to the *Guangya*, "jiaogui" (姧詭) refers to being wicked and sycophantic, as well as being deceitful and fraudulent.
*Ti-li* (蟄󲴵): A name for a large fish; *ti-li-gala* (蟄󲴵伽羅) should be rendered as *miṅ-ji-lo* (󱶂民祇羅), translated as "fish-swallower," because it swallows large fish and small ones alike.
Volume Eleven, Number Eleven. *Hun* (圂): Also written as *hun* (溷); both read with the *hu* and *kun* rhymes. It refers to a latrine or privy; it signifies being turbid, filthy, and foul.

The ancient character for *bàng* (栽) is written with the radical for "tree" and the phonetic *mǎo* (𣡌). It does not have three forms; today it is written as *niè* (蘖), with the same pronunciation as *wù* (五) and *gē* (割). According to the *Erya*, *bàng* means "remnant" (*yú*) and "to carry" (*zài*). This refers to the fact that the remnants of a tree grow out again as shoots (*bàng*). Thus, *zāi* (栽) means to plant.
*Miǎn* (also written as *mǐng*, same pronunciation) is the reverse of *pǐrěn*; it means to force oneself to do something with effort.

12. Volume Twelve. [The character for] *biè* (to collapse/fall); the ancient forms are *biè* and *yí*, both of which are now written as *biè*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To collapse" (*biè*) means to fall prostrate; to fall prostrate is to stumble.

Ku-jùn (with 私 *si* and 俊 *jùn* as the phonetic components); Duō-zhǐ (with 多 *duō* and 止 *zhǐ* as the phonetic components).
Kū-xīn (with 刳 *kū* and 心 *xīn* as the phonetic components); Xǐ-hè (with 枲 *xǐ* and 荷 *hè* as the phonetic components).
Yù-chǎ-dài-wǒ (with 鬱 *yù*, 哆 *chǎ*, 殆 *dài*, and 我 *wǒ* as the phonetic components); Tí-luó-tā-xī (with 梯 *tí*, 羅 *luó*, 他 *tā*, and 奚 *xī* as the phonetic components).
Xún tuó (xún with the *shùn* rhyme) xī hǒu (hǒu with the *jī* rhyme).

"The Names of Three Thousand Buddhas of the Three Kalpas" (in three volumes, upper, middle, and lower; Volume One, Part One, by Huìlín). Regarding the character *diàn* (電): *Dēng* (鐙) with the *téng* rhyme. Guō Pǔ’s commentary on the *Erya* states that *dēng* is the same as *zhùdēng* (鐙); the *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic component "tóng" (*dēng*).

Regarding "hui-dang" (慧幢), the final syllable is pronounced as *jiang* (濁江) according to Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Fangyan*, which states: "A *dang* is that with which a dancer shields themselves. The *Guoyan* says a *dang* is called a *zhuang*. The standard character for it from ancient times consists of the radical "cloth" (*jin*) and the phonetic "tong" (*tóng*).

"Huǐ" (剖) is pronounced *pǔ* with the *hòu* rhyme; Yuè Wáng of Pǔhuò says it means "to split. Dù’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states it means "to divide in the middle. The *Cāngjiépiān* defines it as "analysis," and the *Shuōwén* defines it as "to separate," written with the radical 刀 (knife) and the phonetic 咅 (*pǔ*), with the final rhyme being *huàguā*.

Regarding "yú" (娛) in the phrase "encountering [them] in entertainment": Duan Yucai’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "yú" also means "pleasure. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "woman" (女) and the phonetic "wú" (吳), with the lower character pronounced as "luò" (洛).

Regarding "qìng" (磬): Gù Yewáng says it is a musical stone instrument. The *Shiben* states that Mǔgōu created the qìng. The *Gujīn zhèngzì* (Orthodox Characters of Antiquity and Today) records it as composed of the radical "stone" (石) and the phonetic "kēng" (殸), where "kēng" is pronounced as "kǔtǐng" (苦挺).

*Ji* (𣗥): Upper radical *jing* (兢), reversed *yi* (億). Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "The *dianji* (顛𣗥) has fine leaves and thorns. The *Shuowen* says: "It resembles the *ji* (𣗥) growing in clusters; it follows [the radical] *bing* (竝) with two bundles. Lower radical *xi* (䧳), reversed *si* (四). Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "The *ji* (莿) is the needle of the *ji* (棘) tree. The *Fangyan* states: "Generally, when the thorns of grasses and trees prick a person, they are called *ji*. The *Shuowen* says: "A wood insect; it follows [the radical] *cao* (艹) and takes *ci* (刺) as its phonetic. The version in the *Jing* (經) is written as *cha* (㓨), which is an error.

*Tian* (恬) is read as *die* (牒) with the secondary rhyme *jian* (兼); Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that it means "peaceful security" (*an*), while the *Fangyan* says it means "stillness. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xin*) and the phonetic "she" (舌) in abbreviated form. *Tan* (淡) is read as *lan* (濫); Gu Yawang says it means "tranquil stillness," and the *Shuowen* states it is composed of the radical "heart" and the phonetic "zhan" (詹).

*Hui wú yá*: "yá" is pronounced *jia* (with the second tone) and *zhui* (with the first tone). Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states that "yá" refers to the edge of water. The *Shuowen* says it is composed of the radical "shan" (厂) and the phonetic "gui" (圭);

it is also written as "ya" (涯). *Shēn xiù*: "xiù" is pronounced *xiu* (with the fourth tone) and *you* (with the fourth tone). The *Shuowen* says it means to bring the nose toward an odor; it is composed of the radical "bi" (鼻) and the phonetic "chou" (臭). The version in the sutra uses the character "xiu" (嗅) with the mouth radical, which is a vulgar form.
The character 𣀩 (meaning "to destroy") is pronounced *shàng* (with the *guāi* and *mài* finals). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "It means to ruin; it is composed of the radical 攴 with the phonetic 褱.

The version in the sutra is written as 󲯳, which is incorrect. In the middle fascicle: the character 濡 (*rú*, with the *zhū* final) means "moist" according to the *Mao Shi Zhuan*. Liu Xi’s commentary on the *Mengzi* states that "濡" also carries the sense of being "stagnant" or "hesitant. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it is composed of the radical 水 with the phonetic 需. The sutra uses the character 濡, which is a vulgar form. The pronunciation of 需 is *xū*.
"Guṇamati" (德鬘): "Mati" is the Sanskrit term; the version in the sutra uses "lián" (𩬞), which does not form a valid character. "Kavaca" (堅鎧):

"kai" is pronounced with the *kai* rhyme; the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "kavaca" refers to armor (*jiǎi*), formed from the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic "qǐ" (*qì*), with the pronunciation of "qǐ" being the same as above.

*Mie* (to extinguish hatred): *yī jì* rhyme. The *Cāngjié piān* states that "hatred" (*è*) means anger; the *Shuōwén* states it means resentment, composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "guī.

*Wú rǎo* (without vexation): *níng liǎo* rhyme. The *Shuōwén* states that "rǎo" means to tease or toy with; one gloss says it means to mock or playfully provoke. It is composed of the radical "woman" (*nǚ*) and the phonetic "yáo," and is also written as *niǎo*.

Volume 3, Part 2 (No phonetic gloss available). *The Scripture of the Names of Five Thousand Five Hundred Buddhas*, Volume One. Xuanying: The ancient form for "pregnant" (*yun*) is written as [𣎜], with the same pronunciation as *yì* and *zhèng*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "pregnant" means to wrap the child within; to contain a treasure is called being pregnant.

The Sūtra on the Ocean-like Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha, Scroll One. Xuanying. Scroll One. *Ratnasaṃbhava* (閱頭檀), also transcribed as *Yueyi* (悅以) [the latter character being pronounced with the initial *yǐ*], translated as King Śuddhodana, or alternatively called King Śuddhānana.

*Kànglì* (伉儷): *kǔ* (苦) and *làng* (浪) with the final tone reversed; below it is also written as *lí* (㒧), which is the same character. It is pronounced *lǐ* (履) with the fourth tone. *Kàng* means "to match" (*kàng*) and *lì* means "to pair" (*lì*). According to the *Guǎngyá*, *lì* means "companion" (*lǚ*); the *Bīcāng* states that *lì* means "partner" (*bàn*).
"Han" (憾) [homophone of 胡感反]: According to the *Guǎngyá*, "han" means to move; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means to shake.
"Ní-dǒu" (𧎗斗) [homophone of 苦禾反]: According to the *Zìshū*, "ní-dǒu" is an aquatic insect; according to the *Ěryá*, "ní-dǒu" is the offspring of a frog.

"Pán-lóng" (coiled dragon): "Báo-hán" (slight cold) reverses the *Lǐjì* [which reads "pán"], meaning to coil upon the ground. Zhèng Xuán says: "Pán" means to fold or rest. The *Guǎngyá* says: "Pán" means to bend or curve.

"Zhǒngxiāng" (heels following one another) is also written as "chóngxiāng"; both have the phonetic "zhī yǒng" (之勇). The *Shuōwén* says: "Xiāng" means footprints; it also means to pursue, and it describes the manner of coming and going.

Regarding "sì gū" (四柧): the character "gū" is pronounced as in "gǔ hú". According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "gū" means a ridge or edge; however, the character used in the scripture refers to a type of vessel, and "gū" is not its intended meaning here.

Regarding "guàn jiàn" (關鍵), it is also written as "tā jiàn" (闥楗); both forms are pronounced as in "qí jiǎn". "Jiàn" refers to the male bolt (the pin). According to the *Fangyan*, what is called "jiàn" in the region east of the Pass is called "yǎn" (鑰) in the region west of the Pass.

*Kai* (pronounced with the *hu* and *la* finals reversed) means "to close"; as the *Shuowen Jiezi* states, it refers to shutting a door. The *Yi Jing* says, "Closing the gates is called Kun," which is this meaning.
*Yongyong* (now written as *yung*) is pronounced with the *yu* and *xiong* finals; the *Shijing* says, "Yongyong and angang," and the commentary states it is an appearance of warmth and reverence.

2. Second Fascicle, Part Two. *Qióng* (穹): The character is pronounced with the "qū" (去) and "gōng" (弓) radicals reversed; it means "vaulted" (*qiónglóng*). *Qióng* also means "exhausted" (*qióng*). *Zhāng* (󲳶):

The *Shuowen Jiezi* records this as *zhòu* (譸), both pronounced with the "zhú" (竹) and "liú" (流) radicals reversed. According to the *Erya*, *zhāng* means "to deceive. It also means "to delude and mislead. The scriptural text writes this as *zhōu* (輈), meaning the shaft of a carriage; however, *zhōu* is not the correct orthography for this term.
*Hou* (喉): *long* (龍) and *gongfan* (公反). According to the *Erya*, it refers to the throat of a bird. Guo Pu says: "Long is also the throat. The *Cangjie pian* states it is the throat. *Lungyu* (肺腴):

also written as *qiyu* (胇腴), both with the phonetic *fuhui fan* (敷穢反). The *Shuowen jiezi* states: "Lung is the fire-vessel (*huozang*). The lower character, *yu* (庾), has the phonetic *ju fan* (俱反). The *Shuowen jiezi* states: "Yu is the fat beneath the abdomen; it is the belly. The *Cangjie pian* states it is the pharynx.

"Liver-diaphragm" (*gan ge*)—the character *ge* (頟) is a variant of *ge* (膈), meaning a partition or barrier. In the scriptures, it is sometimes written as *ruo* (肉); these two characters are used interchangeably.

"Worms" (*huai chong*) is also written as *hui* (蛔), both pronounced with the same phonetic *hu kuai*. The *Cangjie Xun Gu* states that *huai* refers to worms within the abdomen. The scriptural forms *hou* (蚘) and *you* (尤) are incorrect.
*Tuan-luan* (盧端反): "Tuan" means round and complete; it refers to being circular and encompassing.
*Bai-ji* (今作勣, 同子歷反): According to the *Shenglei*, "ji" means merit or achievement. *Chu-ran* (初六反):
"Ran" means upright and straight, or alternatively, the lush growth of grasses and trees.

*Ni-yuan* (霓冤): *Ni* is pronounced as in *yuan-fan*; *yuan* means "to be oppressed" (*ju*). A female rainbow is called *ni-yuan*. *Hong-tuo-xuan-che* (虹柁軒車) refers to its function. The text reads *ji* (倇), which is not the correct form.
*Fa-miao* (髮杪): *Miao* is pronounced as in *mi-liao-fan*; the *Tong-su-wen* states that the tip of a tree is called *miao*. Here we take the meaning to refer to the tips of the hair.
"Both corners" (*shuang ji*): according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "corner" (*ji*) refers to the edge of the eye;
it means the boundary of the eyes. Volume Three, Part Three. "Both lips" (*liang wen*): according to the *Cangjie pian*, this refers to the two sides of the lips; it means the edges of the mouth.
*Hè* (pronounced with the *jī* and *fǎn* finals): According to the *Erya*, *hè* refers to *yǎo*. Guo Pu says it is a weed resembling *bài* that grows spreading over the ground.
*Kānshì* (pronounced with the *kǔ* and *dàn* finals): According to the *Fāngyán*, *kān* means to receive or contain things; according to the *Guǎngyá*, *kān* means to hold or contain.
*Xi*: (pronounced *hu ji* [hú jī]; according to the *Shuowen*, a small mouse that is poisonous; it is also called the "sweet-mouthed mouse"). *Huang*: (also written as *huang*;

the ancient form is the same as *huang*; pronounced *hu guang* [hú guǎng]; below it is also written as *yu* [yù], pronounced *you ju* [yóu jǔ]; according to the *Shuowen*, *huang* means brightness; *yu* means to shine, to be bright, or to be flourishing). *Yu*: (to shine; to be bright; to flourish).

The characters *jiezhi* (竭支) or those written as *sengqi* (僧祇) are all corruptions. One should say *saṃghāṭī*, which is translated as "covering the armpits. If one wears a *guśūra*, one does not wear a *saṃghāṭī*. *Guśūra* means "diagram"; it is named after the shape of its garment.
4. Fourth Fascicle. "Cui" (摧) means to break or snap; "ru" (茹) means weak.

"Xiao-chi" (小螭)—the "chi" (螭) is pronounced *chī* according to the *Guǎngyá*, which states that those without horns are called *chī* while those with horns are called *qiú*; the *Shuowén* says a *chī* is like a dragon but yellow.

The characters for *shùgǎi* (樹稭) both mean straw or stalks; the fact that they are composed of the radicals for "grain" (*禾*) and "all" (*皆*) is not clearly understood as being based on any specific linguistic derivation.

Regarding *tēngbì* (疼痹): it is also written with the two forms *tōng* (痋) and *yǐ* (𦙭), both pronounced *tú dōng*. The *Guǎngyá* states it means "aching pain"; the *Shuowén* defines it as a "dampness-induced illness," while *bì* refers to a condition where one is unable to walk. *Bì* is pronounced *bìng lì*.
5. Fascicle Five. *Qin* (pronounced with the initial *mù* reversed) means to rub or scrub. *Chao* (pronounced with the final *zhōng* reversed) refers to scooping up;
according to the *Tōngsúwén*, floating and taking is called *chāo*, while sinking and taking is called *láo*. The *Guǎngyá* states that *chāo* means to take.

*Pì* (pronounced *pǔ dí*): According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means to split; according to the *Guangya*, it means to crack open. The text reads *pī* (pronounced *pí yì*), but *pī* is not used here.

*Tiezhèn* (iron anvil) is also written as *zhēn* or *zěn*; these two forms are identical and pronounced *zhū jīn*. It refers to a *fūzhèn* (beheading block/anvil). The text reads *zhèn* or *chā*, but these two forms are not the correct characters.

*Lì* (轢): The force of the body; *lì* and *lì* are homophones. According to the *Cāngjiépiān*, *lì* means "to roll over. According to the *Shuowén*, it refers to a carriage treading upon something. *Yǐng* (癭) and *zhòng* (瘇):

The glossary states that the character is now written as *zhǒng* (𰃏), with the pronunciation *yǒng* (同音勇反). The *Tōngsùwén* states that a swelling of the feet is called *zhòng*; it is a disease of the feet. It is incorrect for the scriptural text to write this with the radical for "feet" (*zǒng* [踵]).

The character *shēng* (生) is classified as being phonetically similar to *xián* (燂) and graphically similar to *zhǎo* (詔). The glosses state that it is written as *zhǎo* today, which is identical to *xiánglián* (詳廉) in pronunciation.

The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "hot broth for blanching meat. The character *tiě* (鐵) is pronounced *qígǔ* (奇古); the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "an iron clamp. The *Cangjie Pian* states that "grabbing" (*gǔchí*) refers to taking hold of an object. The text of the sutra uses the character *qián* (鉗), meaning "iron tongs for binding people," which is not the standard form used today.

"Biāo-jū" (瘭疽) is read as *biáo* (必遙反) and *qián yú fǎn* (下千余反). According to the *Guǎngyá* (廣雅), "tōu chéng wéi biāo jiān" (㿈成為瘭㾇) refers to the name of a type of ulcerous sore. The text here uses the character "piāo" (螵), which is identical to "pí" (蜱); it is pronounced with the two rhymes *fǔ zhī pí yáo* (輔支毘遙二反). It refers to the offspring of the cicada (*tángláng*). The character "piāo" is not used in this sense [as a medical term].
The various characters for "comb" (*jiǎ*) are also written as *qú* (with the phonetic component *jì*). They are used to connect and record hairpins.
*Chán* (pronounced with the phonetic component *shì*) refers to a sharp-pointed instrument used to prick objects; according to the *Shuowen*, *chán* means "sharp."
*Nièyǔ* (寱語) [the "niè" being pronounced *yán shì fǎn*]: The *Tōngsùwén* states that dreaming speech is called *niè*; the *Shēnglèi* says it refers to speaking delusions while unconscious.

*Zhé kǒu* (磔口) [the "zhé" being pronounced *zhé gé fǎn*]: The *Guǎngyá* states that *zhé* means to stretch or to open. The text of the scripture writes this as *tuō* (拕), for which no source has yet been found.

6 (The sixth fascicle is missing) 7 Seventh Fascicle. "Niáng" (攘) is pronounced with the rhyme of *yáng* (羊). It means to remove; specifically, it refers to removing the sleeves (*mèi*) and exposing the arms. *Mèi* is pronounced with the rhyme of *mí-shì* (彌世).

*Tadṛṅ* (the first character is pronounced with the *tāng* rhyme and the second with the *dé-héng* rhyme). The *Shìmíng* (Explanations of Names) states: "It is placed before a large bed on a small stool; it is used as a means for ascending to the bed, and is named accordingly."
*Fù* (榑噬): "Bǔ" is the phonetic component; the second character, *shì*, is pronounced as *zhì*. It means to seize or grasp, to bite, and to devour.
8. Fascicle Eight. *Gòu* (󲮴): Also written as *gòu* (姤). The *Erya* states that *gòu* means to encounter or meet.
*Mín* (泯): *mǐn*, with the alternative reading *mín* (彌). According to the *Erya*, *mín* means "to exhaust" (*jìn*) or "to vanish" (*mián*). *Wěitúo* (委佗):

*wēi* (危) with the alternative reading *yí* (迤), and *tuó* (多) with the alternative form *túō* (他). According to the *Guǎngyá*, *wěitúo* means "sloping and crooked" (*wū xié*). Examining the character *wěi*, it is also written as *wēi* (逶) or *yī* (蟡). The *Shijing* says: "Sloping and winding" (*wēiwēi yíyí*) describes the beauty of virtue. The commentary states: "Wěitúo" refers to a gait that can be winding and meandering; it is also a description of one who is self-possessed. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines *wěitúo* as "the manner of walking away."
*Śaila*, pronounced *zhí'ěr* (two syllables), then *chì zhǐ* (two syllables), then *chì yù*.

*Sanghāṭasūtra*, Volume One. By Huìlín. Volume One. Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa (*qíshòu* [two syllables]). This is the name of a sacred mountain in Central India, located within the kingdom of Magadha. There is a vulture there that resembles a hawk but is smaller in form; it flies in flocks and constantly feeds on corpses—it is a strange bird. Because it dwells upon this mountain, it is named Gṛdhrakūṭa. The old translation "Qishajue" is a corruption of the Sanskrit term. Its pronunciation is *wŭgē* [two syllables].
*Āthuna* (the middle character pronounced *zhòu* as a reversal; a name for a son of heaven in the Sanskrit language).
*Sūṣaka* (the middle character pronounced *shē*; the name of a dragon king).
*Hūhū* (the character pronounced *hòu*).

"Zhòngzhí" (植殖): the lower character is pronounced *chí* (職反). Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states it means "to plant trees. Guo’s commentary on the *Fangyan* states it means "to establish. It is the standard orthography of ancient and modern times, composed of the radical "wood" (*mu*) and the phonetic "zhí" (*zhí*). The form used in the scripture, "zhí" (殖), is a vulgar variant.
*Ni-ghaṇṭu* (尼揵子) is a transliteration of the Sanskrit term for the naked ascetics (*nirgrantha*). "Nuo" (裸) is pronounced with the initial *wa* (瓦反).

"Piao-mo" (漂沒) has the upper character pronounced with the initial *pi-yao* (匹遙反); Ku Ye-wang states it means "to flow," while the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to float," composed of the radical "water" and the phonetic "piao" (票). The form used in the sutra, *shao* (㵱), is a vernacular character.
The character 撮 (cuō) is pronounced with the initial *cang* and the final *lǚan*. The *Zìtǒng* states that it means "to take up an object with the hand.

According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical 手 (hand) and the phonetic 最 (zuì). The character 𧿟 (huó), meaning "to kneel," has the initial *hú* and the final *wù*; it is a vulgar character, though it is also written as 胡 and used according to its borrowed pronunciation. The original text of the scripture uses 呀 (yā), which is incorrect. The character 跪 (guì), meaning "to kneel," has the initial *qí* and the final *wèi*. The *Shuowén* states that it means "to bow" and is composed of the radical 足 (foot) and the phonetic 危 (wēi).

2. Fascicle Two. [The character] 過 (guò): Upper radical 土 (earth), lower phonetic 灰 (huī). Liu Huan says it means "to repent and reform. In ancient and modern standard characters, it is written with the radical 心 (heart) and the phonetic 亥 (hài).
[The character] 殑 (qíng): Upper radical 歹 (death), lower phonetic 可 (kě); it is also written as 殑. This is the same as the Sanskrit term.

*Yǒngshēn* (躍身上): *yǒng* is pronounced as *gǒng* (拱) in reverse. He Xiū’s commentary on the *Gōngyáng Zhuàn* states: "To leap upward with the body. The *Shuowén* defines it as "to jump," written with the radical for feet (*zú*) and the phonetic *yǒng* (甬).
*Ròutuán* (肉團): *tuán* is pronounced as *luán* (巒). The original text of the Classics reads *chuǎn* (椯), which is incorrect.
Uttarakuru is one of the four continents, corresponding to Jambudvīpa; it is the Sanskrit term for "execution. Regarding the character *lù* (戮), Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states:

"Lù means to humiliate; having already executed them by beheading, one further humiliates them. Jia Yi’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states: "It means to kill. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical *go* (戈) with the phonetic *liáo* (翏); the pronunciation of *liáo* is *lìjiù*.

3. Third Fascicle. The character 數 (shù) is pronounced with the "dou" and "jiao" finals combined; according to the *Kaosheng*, it means rapid, frequent, or close/urgent. The character 擔 (dān), with the "dàn" and "gān" finals, is also written as 儋 (*dàn*).

The *Guoyaya* states that it means to lift or carry; according to the *Kaosheng*, it means to bear on the back. In the standard characters of antiquity and today, it is composed of the radical 手 (hand) and the phonetic 詹 (*zhān*).

"Wan-chi" (頑癡): the first character is pronounced *shàng* with the *zài* rhyme. The *Guǎngyǎ* states it means "obstinate and dull. Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* says that when the mind cannot fathom the sound of virtue and righteousness, it is called "obstinate" (*wán*). The *Kǎoshēng* says it means "foolish. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical *xié* (head) and the phonetic *yuán*. It was written as *wèn* in antiquity.
"Perhaps" (pō): according to the *Pǔguǎng yǎ*, "perhaps" means "a little. "Golden beak" (jīn zǐ):

according to the *Kǎoshēng*, it refers to the beak of a bird; the *Shuowén* states that this [character] is derived from the phonetic "shù," whereas the current version of the scripture erroneously uses "shù"; the character used in the following passage has the same meaning as "zǐ" (beak).
"Tiáo huǒ shàng tiān" (Picking fire toward heaven). "Tiáo" is pronounced as *tiáo* (with the retroflex *r* sound). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "to poke.

It is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "zhào" (兆). The versions of the scripture that write it with the "wood" radical (木) as "táo" (桃) are erroneous. [Section] 4, Volume Four. "Jīn mài" (Sinews and vessels). "Jīn" (筋) is pronounced as *jǐn yīn*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is "the strength of the flesh. It is composed of the radical "flesh" (肉), the phonetic "zhú" (竹), and the "force" radical (力). Things with many sinews are indicated by the "force" radical; the character for "force" (力) itself is an image of a sinew. The versions of the scripture that write it with the "grass" (艹) or "horn" (角) radicals as "jīn" (𮏴) are incorrect. "Mài" (Vessels). Pronounced as *mèng bó*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as "mài" (衇) and defines it as "the divisions of the blood-channels that travel obliquely through the body. It is composed of the radicals "meat" (𠂢) and "blood" (血); it is also written as "mài" (脈). The versions of the scripture that write it as "mò" (脉) use a vulgar character.

Regarding "yān" (胭) at the neck: the *Yanyán Fǎn Shēnglèi* states that "yān" refers to the throat; the *Gōngjīn Zhèngzì* states it is "yàn" (咽). It is composed of the radical "flesh" (肉) with "yīn" (因) as the phonetic component, the latter being pronounced *jīng yǐng*. The *Shuōwén* states: "The stem of the head; composed of the radical 'head' (頁) with 'xīng' (巠) as the phonetic component."

*Chángtā* (床榻): The character *tā* is pronounced with the initial *t* and final *-a* (貪盇反). The commentary on sounds states it refers to a small wooden board bed. The text of the sutra uses the character *kǎn* (㯓), which is incorrect. *Mùxiāng* (麝香):

The character *mù* is pronounced with the initial *shé* (虵蔗反) or alternatively *shíyì* (時亦反). The *Shān-hǎi jīng* (山海經) states that Mount Cuì has many musk deer (*mù*). The *Shuōwén* explains it as being like a small deer; its abdomen contains a pouch (*pán*) from which the musk is derived. It is written with the "deer" radical and the phonetic *shè* (射). It is also written as *zhì* (󲰩). The version of the sutra using the character *shè* (射) is an error.
*Le-zhu* (樂著): the first character is pronounced *wǎo* (校反) and the second *cháng* (腸略反). *Fa-lu* (法螺): the second character is pronounced *lì* (力戈反). *Xi-fēi* (𡱁浘):

the first character is pronounced *shī'ěr* (失爾反) and the second *nǎidiào* (乃弔反); it refers to human urine. It is written with the "tail" radical (*wei*) and the "water" radical (*shui*), and is also written as *xi* (𡲘) or *niao* (尿).

*Jiǎnrěn* (𥿳䎡): The first character is pronounced *zhèng xì* (正細); the second is pronounced *rú* (儒), with the phonetic component *yǎn* (兖) as its rhyme. The canonical edition has *jiǎo* (𣽈), which is incorrect.

*Bēntuō* (鞭󲯡): The first character is pronounced *bì mián* (必綿); the second is pronounced *tā è* (他遏). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that *tuō* (󲯡) is also a synonym for "whip" (*biān*). The canonical edition has *dá* (靼), which is incorrect.

The term *juā* (撾) refers to striking or beating; the *Yùnlèi* (韻類) states it means to strike or to beat. In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, it is written with the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "guò" (*guòshēng*), and it is also written with the radical "bamboo" (*zhú*) as *nǔ* (𥬸), with the same meaning.
*Li xia* (履屣): The character *xia* is pronounced as *shi* (師) with the *zhi* (滓) rhyme;

it is also written as *shui* (躧) with the radical for "foot. *Li zhuang yan san mei jing* (力莊嚴三昧經), Scroll One: According to Xuanying, the character *lin yun* (𣱦氳) should be written as *fen yun* (葐蒀). The upper character is pronounced as *fu yun* (扶云) and the lower character is written as *yu* (󲭵) with the same pronunciation as *yu* (於云). *Fen yun* (葐蒀) describes a state of profusion and is also used to denote fragrance.

*Hǎidǎo* (Sea Island); *wén* and *dū* are homophones, with the latter pronounced *dōulǎo fǎn*. A mountain in the sea is called an island (*dǎo*); it means "to arrive," as it is where people arrive and congregate.
*Fānlánmiàn jīng* (Sutra of the Lotus Face), Scroll Lower. Compiled by Xuanying. *Mó* is pronounced *sìshì jǐ fǎn*; *jìlì* is pronounced *qíyǐ fǎn*.

*The Scripture of the Great Vaipulya Perfect Enlightenment: The Definitive Meaning*. Regarding the characters for "zu" (consult) and "xun" (inquire): the commentary by Du [Yuan] on the *Zhuo Zhuan* states that "zu" means to inquire about the path of goodness; in both ancient and modern standard orthography, this character is composed of the radical "yan" (speech) with the phonetic "zi" (pronounced as in "zi"). The commentary by Du on the *Zhuo Zhuan* states that "xun" refers to deliberating with one's relatives; in both ancient and modern standard orthography, this character is composed of the radical "yan" with the phonetic "xun."

"Yi" (exchange) means to interchange. Wang Yanwang says that "yi" refers to exchange. Jia Dui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states: "Yi is synonymous with 'different' or 'change. The *Guangya* says it means "to turn. The *Shuowen* states that "Yi" is a pictographic character; according to the Secretariat, "Yi" consists of the sun and moon. One version says it is composed of "wu" (a prohibitive sign) below "chang" (prosperity), which is reversed. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* says: "Chu" (abiding) means to dwell or to stop. The *Shuowen* writes it as "chu," stating: "Chu means to stop; it is composed of 'jiu' (long duration) and 'ji' (a stool), stopping upon the stool. The text here uses "chu," which is a vulgar form.
"Recognize" (認): the first character is pronounced *shàng wáng fǎn* (upper radical *wáng*, reversed), and the second is pronounced *rén zhèn fǎn* (lower radical *zhèn*, reversed);
the scripture reads "recognize" (*rèng*). "At" (於): pronounced *xīng xīng fǎn*. "Gold ore" (金鑛): pronounced *gōng měng fǎn*. "Compassionate estimation" (惻度):
pronounced *cè duò tāng luò fǎn*. "Able to manifest" (能著): pronounced *néng zhù péng lüè fǎn*; the original scripture text reads *bì*, which is incorrect.

*Qì* (詰): Upper radical *qīng* (輕), first tone; the *Shūjìng* commentary on the *Shūjīng* states that *qì* means "to govern. The *Shuowén* says it means "to inquire," composed of the radical *yán* (言) and the phonetic *jí* (吉).

*Mìu* (謬): Upper radical *gē wò* (戈臥), fourth tone; lower radical *méi yòu* (眉幼), fourth tone; Gù Yěwáng states that *mìu* means "deviant. According to the *Fāngyán*, it means "fraudulent. The *Shuowén* says it refers to the deluded words of a madman, composed of the radical *yán* (言) and the phonetic *liáo* (翏).
As for "biao" (標), it necessarily means "to point toward from afar. Conversely, the *Shengyun* (聲韻) states it means "to raise up," or that one uses the hand to point toward something.

In the first fascicle of the *Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* (大方𠊳報恩經), Xuanying’s commentary notes: "The first fascicle [mentions] 'huīyàn' (暉豓). It is also written as 'yàn' (艷), which has the same pronunciation as 'shàn' (贍). In the local dialects of Qin and Jin, it refers to beautiful color; they call a beautiful complexion 'yàn' (𧰚)."
*Chíhú* (池湖): The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means a large embankment; there are five such lakes in the region of Yangzhou. *Zhānshū* (旃叔):
Some say *Zhēnshūjiā* (甄叔迦), others say *Jǐnshūjiā* (緊叔迦); it is the name of a tree whose flowers are red in color. This treasure resembles them, and thus it is named accordingly.
*Āi-zè* (the first character pronounced as *jìn* with the second as *zǐ-yè*): according to the *Shēnglèi*, it means a loud shout; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means a great sound.

*Wēifú* (the second character pronounced as *fēi* with the second as *wú*): according to the *Ēryā*, it means being hidden in obscurity or concealed. The commentary states this refers to fleeing and hiding, and it also implies stopping. It is composed of the radical *chì*.

The character for "to inhale" (呼歙) has two ancient forms, *xī* and *xī*, which today are written as *xī* (吸), both pronounced *xi* (同𦏁及反). According to the *Guǎngyá*, *xī* means "to drink" and "to draw in," referring to the entry of breath.

The character for "to poke at the eyes" (*tiāo mù*) is pronounced *tāo* (他堯反). The *Lèishēng* states that it means "to pick out"; "to pick" (*jué*) is pronounced *wū jué* (烏決反). This refers to picking something out of the eyes.
*Chéng* (里程): "Chéng" is pronounced *chūjīngfǎn*. It means a limit or boundary. As the *Lǐjì* says, it refers to measurement;

as the *Shījīng* says, it refers to a standard or rule. *Guò* (掝眥): "Guò" is pronounced *hùmàifǎn*. "Guò" means to tear apart. The second character, *jìng*, is pronounced *jì*. The term refers to the corners of the eyes. As the *Huáihuánzǐ* states: "To glare with wide-open eyes and split corners. The text here uses the character *guó* (馘) from the beginning; however, *guó* (古獲反) refers to capturing someone alive and cutting off their ears, which is not the meaning intended here.
"Pao" (pronounced with the *pu* and *jiao* finals) is defined in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as "roaring" (*páoquáng*) and also as "great anger.

King Śuddhodana—this is a corruption; the correct term is *Śūddhādana*. This is translated as "Pure Rice" (*Jìngfàn*), though it is not "White Rice" (*Báifàn*). It is incorrect [to call him White Rice].
2. Second Fascicle. *Pán-lán-chūn-lún*: "Chūn" (chì lún fǎn) refers to shape and form. *Qiàn-liàn*:
"Liàn" (yù jiàn fǎn) refers to the appearance of brilliant and flourishing colors.

*Xiàn* (眩): *Hú juān hú biàn* (胡蠲胡遍). The *Cāngjié piān* states that it means "vision is unclear. In the *Guóyǔ*, regarding "beauty bewilders," Jia Dui says: "It means to cause confusion. *Bò qiè* (迫愶): *Bǔ gé fǎn* (補格反). It means "urgency" or "pressure.

The lower character, *xū yè fǎn* (虛業反), is explained in the *Fāngyán* as *qiè* (愶) or *xī* (䦧), meaning "to terrify. This refers to using force or power to instill fear in one another. *Xī* (䦧) is pronounced *hū gé fǎn* (呼隔反). Today, both characters are written as *xié* (脅). It is also said to mean *kǒng hè* (恐赫) or *kǒng qù* (恐󲲦); these are all of the same meaning.
*Ē*: reversed from *wū hē*. In the *Cāngjié piān*, *ē* means to block; in the *Eryǎ*, *ē* means to stop. Guō Pǔ says: "Nowadays, to stop someone by opposing them is called *ē*. *Cái huì*:

the ancient text uses the same character as *huī*, pronounced *hū zuì*. It means wealth and goods. The *Tōngsú wén* states: "Wealth consisting of silk and cloth is called *huì*. In the *Zhōu lǐ*, it says: "The Superintendent of Trade circulates goods and *huì*. Zhèng Xuán comments: "Gold and jade are called *huò*; silks and fabrics are termed *huì*."

*Dou-mei* (兜鍪) [the first character pronounced with the *mo-hòu* fanqie]: The *Guǎngyá* calls it a *zhòu* (helmet); the scriptural text writes it as *chōu* (鉾), which is not the correct character form.
*Qián-sài* (乾曬): [The second character] is pronounced *suǒ-jì* (所寄) with two tones; it refers to drying things.
*Pāna-bhakṣa* (or *tarpaṇa*) is translated as "flour"; *phāsuka-bhakṣa* is translated as "that which may be eaten"; *khādaniya-bhakṣa* is translated as "that which may be chewed."
*Kǎn* (pronounced *ōngǎn* according to the *Zìlín*; it means "to eat" or "to swallow") refers to bringing food toward the mouth; to present food with the palms of the hands is called *kǎn*.
*Qīn* (pronounced *kǔxián* or *qīn*) is defined in the *Guǎngyá* as "lofty peaks"; the *Gōngyáng Zhuàn* states that *qīnyín* refers to the topographical features of mountain ridges.

"羸惙" (léi chuò): "劣" (lüè) is a reversed reading; "聲類" (shēng lèi) states that "惙" (chuò) denotes the appearance of shortness of breath. "惙" (chuò) is also synonymous with "憂" (yōu, sorrow). "唼食" (shā shí): "子盇" (zǐ hé) is the phonetic component;
the *Zílín* (Dictionary of Characters) states that it refers to insects sucking blood. The text of the scripture writes this as "啑" (chì), which is incorrect.

*Rú* (with the phonetic *rǎng-jǔ-fǎn*): to eat; it is also "to consume. The *Erya* states, "to sip and consume. Guo Pu says: "To 'pick up and consume' means to gather up food to eat. *Dānjié* (with the phonetic *qí-yè-fǎn*, same as *jié*):

to carry on one's back. The *Shuowen Jiezi* uses the character *jié*. The *Zuo Zhuan* states, "He lifted a stone to throw at the man," with the commentary explaining that *jié* means "to carry on the shoulder."
*Bin* (髕): The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is the kneecap; it is also written as *shuo* (膞) with the same pronunciation. *Qing* (胇): *Yanhan* (炎旱)—the character *yan* (炎) means "intense heat";
according to the *Erya*, *yanxun* (炎熏) refers to the parching heat of a drought that scorches people. Guo Pu says it refers to the scorching heat of a drought affecting people.
"Věi" (猥) is pronounced with the first tone, followed by "duō" (多); it means "abundant. According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, "věi" also means "multitudinous.

"Ōu-yē" (噢噎) is pronounced with the first tone for "ōu" and the fourth tone for "yē"; the *Bīcāng* states that "ōu-ī" refers to internal grief, meaning the sound of pained lamentation. "Yē" (噎) means "obstruction. Although the scriptural text sometimes reads "yù" (郁), this is not the standard form.

"Jiǎo" (爪) [is pronounced *jū* with the *fù* tone; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to claw"; in the *Cangjie Pian*, it means "to seize and strike"; the *Huainanzi* states that when beasts are cornered they claw, and when birds are cornered they peck—this is what is meant]. The pronunciation of "jiǎo" (𠿒) is *jū* with the *nì* tone.

*Shàn* (單) and *jié* (孑): "gǔ" (古) and "xī" (析) are the phonetic components. According to the *Ziyou*, they mean "orphaned and solitary. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "When one has no right arm, it is called *jié*. This refers to the passage in the *Guoyu*: "How can there be such a solitary figure? *Hàn* (喊) and *hǒu* (㖑):

"hū" (呼) and "jiàn" (檻) are the phonetic components; the latter is also written as *yuè* (䛥) or *kuǎn* (欵). They share the pronunciation "huì" (呼) and "jiè" (戒). The *Fangyan* states: "*Hàn* is a sound; *hǒu* is a shout," referring to the sound of indignation and anger. In the scriptural texts, these may be written as *kàn* (闞), with the pronunciation "hū" and "jiàn"; these two forms are used interchangeably.
*Tà* (with the phonetic *zhāng* and *táng* [read *hé*]) means to tread upon the ground and stare with wide eyes; the scriptural text uses *xī* (from the radical for mouth), which is incorrect.
*Bá* (with the phonetic *lì* and *dé*) refers to the ribs according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*; the scriptural text uses *lè* (the same as the *lè* in *bìlè*), which is not the correct character form.
*Jiǎo* (曒) is an archaic character; *tūn* and *jiǎo* (暾皎) are two forms of it, now written as *jiǎo* (皎), with the phonetic reading *gōng niǎo*.

The *Pīcāng* states: "It means clarity and purity. 3. Third Fascicle. Third Fascicle. *Dí* (嫡): read as *dīng dí*. Lexicons state that *dí* means "legitimate" or "correct. The *Gōngyáng Zhuan* says: "In establishing the legitimate heir, one takes the eldest. Why? Because *dí* implies being peerless (*dí*), meaning the son of the principal consort has no equal in dignity.
*Yèwéi* (耶維), sometimes called *shāpí* (闍毘) or *shāwéi* (闍維), are all corruptions. The correct term is *shábìduō* (闍鼻多); its meaning is "to cremate.

*Diānjié* (蹎蹶)—also written as two characters, 𠑘—is pronounced *dīngxián* for the first character and *jūyuè* for the second; *diānjié* means to fall prostrate or tumble over. The text of the sutra uses *diānjué* (顛厥), which is not the standard form. *Pù* (仆) is pronounced *púběi*.

The characters 㽃瓳 (also written as 墦) share the same pronunciation as 普安 (pǔ ān); the second character has the phonetic value of 戶吾 (hù wú). According to the *Tōngsùwén* (Explanations of Common Usage), a large square brick is called 㽃瓳; this refers to the large square bricks used today.

*Kaì* (pronounced with the mouth reversed): *Kaì-tàn* means a great sigh. According to the *Shuowen*, *wàn-kài* refers to the state of indignation and resentment when a man of valor does not achieve his ambitions.
*Yì* (pronounced *yú* with a rapid tone): According to the *Zilin*, *yì* means unease; according to the *Cangjie pian*, it describes an appearance of being ill at ease.

Fán-yuān (煩冤): *yuān* also means "to vex" or "to be oppressed. The character is composed of *mìng* (冖) and *tù* (兔). Because the rabbit, when covered by a net (*mìng*), does not run away, it takes this radical. The forms appearing in the scriptures as *wǎn* (宛) or *wǎn* (惋) are not the correct forms.

"Wāng" (汪) is pronounced with the "wū" and "huáng" finals; the *Tōngsùwén* states that stagnant water is called wāng, and the *Ēryá* says wāng refers to a pond. The reading in the scripture as "guāng" (洸) with the phonetic value of "guāng" is incorrect.
"Mahallaka" is translated here as "ignorant," or alternatively, as "old."

4. Fourth Fascicle. Regarding "Dàodù" (都道) and "Dùgào" (都誥): the latter is pronounced with the second tone for "dù" and the third tone for "gào. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "dǎo" (告) means to announce matters; "dǎo" (禱) means to pray for blessings; "dǎo" (禱) also means to entreat; and "sì" (祀) refers to sacrifices offered to spirits and deities.
"Spasmodic movement" (瞤動): "Chún" is the phonetic inversion; according to the *Shuowen*, it means the movement of the eyes.

The text reads "shùn" (𥌎), which is not the correct form. "To multiply" (蕃息): "Fú" is pronounced with the *yuán* tone; it means to grow or increase, referring to becoming abundant. The text reads "fán" (繁); while this means flourishing, it also implies abundance.
*Weizhang* (帷帳): According to the *Zuilin*, that which is at the sides is called a *wei*; it refers to spreading a curtain to screen the sides. *Wei* means to encircle.
*Tuanlang* (湍浪): Pronounced *shu-huan*. It is rapid water. The *Shuowen* says it is a rapid torrent (*lai*). When water flows over sand, it is called a *lai*; a *lai* is shallow water.
*Mōng* (pronounced *mó gōng*) refers to having pupils (*móu zǐ*) but being unable to see; it is called *mōng*. Having no pupils at all is called *yǎn*.

*Jǔ fán* (raising the sail) is also written as two characters, *fán* and *fān* (both pronounced *fú yán* and *fú zhuó*). The *Shìmíng* states: "That which is spread out according to the wind is called a sail (*fán*)."

*Zhèn* (zhī-rěn-fǎn): According to the *Xiǎo Ěr Yǎ*, it means "to rescue" or "to provide. The *Shuōwén Jiězì* states it means "to lift up. The text of the classics uses *zhèn* (zhī-rěn-fǎn), meaning "to provide for the poor" (*yǐn zhèn*) or "to enrich the wealthy."

"Cǎo-cài" (pronounced *chā*) refers to withered grass; it also appears as "fēn" in the scripture, but that is incorrect. "Cài" is pronounced *qiān-gǔ* (the *gǔ* rhyme); it means withered grass. Today, those west of Shaanxi call it "cǎo-cài," while those in Jiangnan and Shandong call it "cǎo-cài. In Shandong, "cài" is pronounced *qī-gù*.

*Xiào-hǒu* (also written as *hǔ* with the same pronunciation; the first character is pronounced *jiāo*, the second *jià*). According to the *Tōngsùwén*, the roar of a tiger is called *xiào-hǒu*. 5. Fascicle Five. Fascicle Five. *Báihóng* (White Rainbow).

Anciently written as *gòng* (pronounced *húgōng*). According to the *Shuōwén*, it is the *dìcǒng* or *hóng*. In common parlance it is called the "Beauty"; in Jiangdong it is called the *yú*. According to the *Shìmíng*, *hóng* means "to attack" (*gōng*); it is pure yang attacking the yin qi.

*Ni* (劓) and *ri* (刵) are also written as *li* (㓷), with the same pronunciation as *yu qi* (魚器) for the former and *rang ji* (讓記) for the latter. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *ni* means "to cut off the nose.
According to the *Guoyu*, *ri* means "to cut off the ears. The ancient characters for *yue* (刖) and *ming* (明) share the same form as *yu jue wu gua* (魚厥五刮). *Yue* means "to cut."
*Mō* (摸): The phonetic component is *tā* (他) with the rhyme *hán* (含). According to the *Shuowen*, "to reach out from afar is called *tàn*;

to move the hand is *mō*. *Kù* (酷): The ancient forms are *pò* (俈), *zǎo* (󲯰), and *kū* (焅); all three characters share the same pronunciation, *kǒu dǔ* (口篤). According to the *Shuowen*, "intense" (*kù*) means urgent; it refers to extreme severity, and also denotes cruelty and oppression. The *Baihutong* states that "cruelty" (*kù*) means reaching the ultimate limit; it refers to the extreme strictness of commands and decrees.

*Pou-fa* (掊發): The *Shuowen Jiezi* records this as two characters, *bōu* (枹) and *fú* (桴), both pronounced with the same initial and final (*pǒu*). *Fú* means to pull out or extract. The *Tongsu Wén* records it as *póu*, meaning to grasp with the hand;

it is also called *àn*. 6. Volume Six, Part Six. *Niu-chi* (牛呞): The correct characters are *chí* (齝) and *shì* (𪘍), both pronounced with the same initial and final (*chī*). According to the *Erya*, "oxen *chí*" refers to the act of regurgitating food after it has been eaten.

*Tíng* (pronounced *pí bīng fǎn*): According to the *Běicāng*, it means a bed-platform; specifically, it refers to a single wooden bench for sitting alone. The *Shìmíng* states: "It is called *tíng* because it is level (*píng*); it is made of boards, and its body is flat and upright."
*Sudā* (or *Xiūtuó*) is the food of this deity; it is translated as "white. The *Suixiang lun* states that *sudā* means "good *dā*," which signifies "sincere and substantial."

7. Fascicle Seven. Regarding the character 󱽲 (pronounced *jù* with the *xiàng* tone): dictionaries state that it refers to spreading out a net (*lǎn*) on a path; the scriptural text writes it as 摾, which is a vulgar character.

"Childhood" (*tóngchèn*)—the ancient reading for *chèn* is *chānjìn*. "Dentition" (*chǐ*) means the eruption of teeth; according to the *Shuowen*, males produce teeth at eight months and undergo dentition at eight years, while females produce teeth at seven months and undergo dentition at seven years. The character is composed of the radical "tooth" (*chǐ*) and the phonetic element "seven" (*qī*). The *Shiming* states: "Chèn means 'washing. It refers to the washing away of old teeth so that new ones may grow."

The fifty-three scriptures totaling eighty-two fascicles listed to the right share the same phonetic glosses as this fascicle.

*Pusa benxing jing* (Sutra on the Original Deeds of the Bodhisattva), upper fascicle, compiled by Xuanying. Fascicle One: *Junchi*; the correct term is *kuṇḍikā*, which refers to a double-mouthed water vessel, or translated as a "flask."
The characters 𤈓, 穀, 又, 作, 炒, 㷅, and 󲶟 are all homophonous with the initial *chao* (初狡反). According to the *Fāngyán*, 㷅 means to dry by fire. 牂 (*zāng*, 祖郎反) refers to a three-year-old ewe;

"牂" describes a state of being full and flourishing. The character below, 丁 (*dīng*, 丁奚反), refers to 𦍝, which denotes a hornless ram or a castrated sheep. The text reads 𤘳 (*dīng*, 丁禮反), meaning to butt or gore; however, 𤘳 is not the character used in the scripture.
"Lai yè" (來抴) is also written as "lái yì" (來曳), with the same pronunciation as "yú shì fǎn" (余世反). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "yè" means to pull; it refers to dragging or leading.
"Jié rě" (羯羠) has the pronunciation "jīn jǐ fǎn" (因几反). The *Shenglei* states that "jié rě" refers to a castrated sheep. Xu Guang says that both "jié" and "rě" refer to gelded rams.
"Enraged" (*yùn*) means to respond with anger when questioned; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "anger," and according to the *Cangjie Pian*, it means "resentment.
"Jishāni" (*jīshànní*; the first character is pronounced *jūyī* and the second is pronounced *shìzhàn*) is the name of a dragon prince.

"Cutting off its fish" (*jue*) means five; "bones" (*gu*) means two. "Cutting off" (*fan jue*) is synonymous with "severing" (*ge*). The canonical text reads *wan* (five, with the phonetic *huan*), meaning "to pare smooth.

"Upward-turning" (*xuan*) is pronounced *si yuan fan*, meaning "to rotate. The canonical text reads *ju* (with the phonetic *ju yu fan*), meaning "a square"; a square is a rule, but "rule" is not the intended meaning here.
*Śejun* (邪旬), sometimes called *sháwéi* (闍維) or *shábī* (闍毗), all have the same meaning. The correct pronunciation is *shābìduō* (闍鼻多); its meaning is "to cremate. Section 2, Middle Volume.

Regarding *zāihuò* (災禍), it is also written as *zāizāi* (烖灾) or *zāiyí* (𣏹). These three forms are identical; the character *cái* (才) serves as the phonetic component. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "a fire that destroys life is called *zāi* (災)."

*Xi-lì* (the first character pronounced *si*, the second pronounced *yi-shí*): This refers to the lizard (*xi-lì*) found in the grass; the text’s reading as *yí* is incorrect. *Fú* (pronounced *fū-wù*):
According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means to sweep away, referring to the removal of dust and soil; it means to wipe. The text’s reading with the radical *jīn* (cloth) as *fú* or as *fèn* is incorrect.
3. The final fascicle. "Sāo" (騷) [is pronounced *sāo* with the *sū* and *láo* rhymes]; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "to disturb," that is, to agitate.
"Wànqí" (萬歧) is also written as two characters, *chā* (𨙸) and *jù* (𪨵), both pronounced *jù* with the *yí* rhyme; this refers to the fact that the Way has branches and divisions.

*Huǎng* (晃) is also written as *huài* (晄); the ancient form is the same as *huáng* (熿), with the phonetic *hú guǎng*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "brightness. The *Guangya* states it means "radiant splendor. Below, it is also written as *yù* (煜), with the same phonetic *yóu jū*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "brilliant glare," while the *Bicang* describes it as "the appearance of flourishing intensity."
*Chuāngbān* (瘡瘢): [The character *bān*] is pronounced *púlán fǎn*. The *Cāngjié piān* states it means "scar" (*hén*). [The character *hén*] is pronounced *húgēn fǎn*.

*Fǎjí jīng* (法集經), Volume One, compiled by Huìlín. Volume One: *Lí* (羸). Pronounced *suǒ lì zhuī fǎn*. Dù’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* says it means "weak. Jia’s commentary on the *Guóyuè* says it means "sickly. The *Shuōwén* says it means "emaciated. It is composed of the radical "sheep" (*yáng*) with the phonetic "ní" (*ní*), which is pronounced *luò wò yě* (the sound of a mule lying down).

*Yì* (曀) [top radical]: *ĭ* (繄), reading as *jì* (計). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (毛詩傳) states: "In the *Zhōngfēng* (終風) [poem], it says 'at dawn there was *yì*, and the sun did not appear. The *Erya* (爾雅) states: "Cloudy with wind is called *yì*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文), it is composed of the radical for "sun" (*ri*) and the phonetic *yī* (壹). [Bottom radical]: *ràng* (讓), reading as *shēng* (聲). The *Kaosheng* (考聲) states it means "to obstruct and screen. The *Shuowen* states it means "to block and separate," composed of the radical *zhào* (𨸏) and the phonetic *zhāng* (章).

2. Second Fascicle. "Jùn" (駿) is pronounced *zūn* (峻) according to the Guo commentary on the *Mu Tianzi Zhuan*, which states that it is an elegant appellation for a fine horse. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "the excellence of a horse," composed of the radical 馬 (horse) with the phonetic component 夋 (*qīxún*). The character 夋 is pronounced *qīxún*.

The character *fū* (膚) has the upper radical *fǔ* (甫) with a reversed *mǔ* (無). The *Mao Shi* states that "fū" means beauty; the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "fū" means skin (*pí*), composed of the radical *ròu* (肉) and the phonetic element *lú* (盧) abbreviated. The lower part is *yán* (閻) with *mǔ* (𭼩) as the phonetic. The *Mao Shi* says "beautiful complexion is called *yàn* (𧰚)," and the *Zuo Zhuan* says "beautiful and *yàn*," which is correct. The *Shuowen Jiezi* [also] derives it from *fēng* (豊), *dà* (大), and *xiě* (血); the form using *sè* (色) to compose it as *yàn* (艷) is a vulgar character.

"Hóngqǐ" (虹起) is read as *hú dōng fǎn*. The *Erya* states: "The *dìdòng* is the rainbow. This refers to what is recorded in the *Liji*: "In the month of the last spring, the rainbow first appears. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "insect" (*chóng*) with the phonetic "gong" (*gōng*). *Dì* is pronounced *dì*; *dòng* is pronounced *dòng*.

*Kangliáng* (秔糧): The first character is pronounced as *gé* (革) with the *shēng* (𢖍) radical; it refers to *xiān* rice (秈稻). According to the *Shēnglèi* (聲類), it is a non-sticky rice. The *Shuōwén* (說文) also classifies it as a type of rice, written with the *huò* (禾) radical and the phonetic *kàng* (亢). *Kàng* is pronounced as *kāng* (康) with the *làng* (浪) radical. In the classics, it is written with the *mǐ* (米) radical as *jīng* (粳); *xiān* (秈) is pronounced as *xiān* (仙). This is a vulgar character.

Regarding "flies and ants" (*yíng yǐ*): Zheng’s commentary on the *Mao Shī* states, "As for the insect called the fly (*yíng*), it makes black appear white and white appear black. Guo’s commentary on the *Eryā* says, "Flies are fond of fluttering their wings. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "an insect with a large abdomen; it is written with the radical 'insect' and the phonetic 'mǐng' (pronounced *měng*); the lower part [the phonetic] is pronounced *yǐ* (with the tone *yǐ*). This is the vulgar form; the correct character is *yǐ* (ant). The *Eryā* states, "The *bífú* is the ant; the large ones are called *bífú*, the small ones are called *yǐ*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* further notes, "The ant (*yǐ*) is also the *bífú*; it is written with the radical 'insect' and the phonetic 'qǐ'."

3. Third Fascicle. Regarding the term "máo-shào" (spear/lance): the first character is pronounced as *mò* (with the *móu* rhyme), and the second is pronounced as *shuāng* (with the *chì* rhyme). This was already explained in the third volume of the *Xián-yì* (Explanations of Pronunciations and Meanings) within the *Zhèng-qì-dà-chéng-jīng* (Sūtra on the Realization of the Mahāyāna).

Regarding the character *yuè* (戉) for "battle-axe": Gu Yewang states that the "tongue" [of the character] refers to the use of the axe to decapitate people. The *Sīmǎ Fǎ* (Rituals of the House of Sīmǎ) states: "The Xia dynasty held the dark-colored *yuè*, while the Yin dynasty held the white *qī*. The *Zhōu Shū* (Book of Zhou) states: "The King leaned on the yellow *huáng yuè* in his left hand. Kǒng Āngguó explains it as "an axe decorated with an axe," composed of the radical *gē* (戈) and the phonetic *jiǎn* (𦐚). The phonetic *jiǎn* has the sound *jué*. Alternatively, it may be written with the metal radical as *yuè* (鉞), which is also used interchangeably.

4. Fascicle Four. *Gēn* (跟): "gēn" with the phonetic root *shàng* (上) and the rhyme *huā wǎ* (華瓦). *Ān* (踝): "huǎi" with the phonetic root *xià* (下). *Zhuǎn* (腨): "zhuǎn" with the phonetic root *shàng* (上) as *shí ruǎn* (時䎡) and the phonetic root *xià* (下) as *xíng dìng* (形定). *Tíng* (脛): "jìng" with the phonetic root *xià* (下). *Běi* (髀):

"bǐ" with the phonetic root *shàng* (上) as *pú mǐ* (蒲米) and the phonetic root *xià* (下) as *xīn qī* (薪七). *Xióng* (胸): "xiōng" with the phonetic root *shàng* (上) as *yīn xióng* (音凶) and the phonetic root *xià* (下) as *jiè yè* (𪏽業). *Xī* (脇): "xié" with the phonetic root *xià* (下).

Abdomen and ribs: the first character is pronounced *fēng* (with the initial *wū* reversed) and the second has the phonetic *lè*. Elbows and wrists: the first character is pronounced *zhāng* (with the initial *liù* reversed) and the second is pronounced *wàn* (with the initial *guàn* reversed).

Shoulders and arms: the first character is pronounced *jiān* and the second is pronounced *bèi* (with the initial *mèi* reversed). Head and cheeks: the first character is pronounced *jiān* (with the initial *yè* reversed).

"Jǐngxiàng" (neck): the first character is read as jīng (郢) with the fanqie "jīng yǐng"; the second character is read as gǒng (巩) with the fanqie "gǒng xiáng". "Dúlóu" (skull): the first character is pronounced dú (音獨); the second character is pronounced lóu (音婁). "Kuòzhái" (cave-dwelling):

the first character is read as kūn (坤) with the fanqie "kūn wǎ". "Zhuǎchǐ" (claws and teeth): the first character is read as zhuāng (莊) with the fanqie "zhuāng xiá"; the second character is read as chī (鴟) with the fanqie "chī zhǐ".
Intestines and stomach: the upper tone is *cháng* (長), the lower tone is *wèi* (胃). Spleen and kidneys: the upper tone is *pí* (脾), the lower tone is *shèn* (腎). Heart:
*xiān* (脨) is pronounced with the *fēi* (妃) and *fèi* (吠) finals. Fat and grease: the upper tone is *fāng* (方), the lower tone is *gāo* (膏).

The membrane above the brain: the first character is read as *dǎo* (倒) and the second as *fǎn* (反); the third character is pronounced *xià* (下) with the phonetic *mò* (莫). Nasal mucus and saliva: the first character is read as *tiān* (天) with the phonetic *lì* (利), and the second as *tǔ* (吐) with the phonetic *wò* (臥).
Marrow and brain: the second character is read as *suī* (髓) with the phonetic *suǐ* (雖) and *zǐ* (觜). Tendons and bones: the first character is pronounced *jīn* (筋).
*Chíyìn* (齒齗): The first character is pronounced *yín*. *Hédān* (荷擔): The first character is pronounced *hé*; the second is pronounced *duōgān* (多甘) with the radical 手 (hand).

*Chóulín* (稠林): The first character is pronounced *chángliú* (長流). According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means "dense" (*chóujì*). The above characters from the fourth fascicle mostly concern the thirty-two marks of a Tathāgata. Since these were already fully explained and annotated in the *Pinyin Yì* (Phonetics and Meanings) of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, I have provided only the pronunciations here and not the definitions for the characters.

Volume Five, Part Five. *Jian* (疾): Pronounced *qián* (上) with the *yè* (叶) rhyme; according to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means "vigorous" (*jiàn*). In the dialects of Song and Chu, as recorded in the *Fānyǔ*, wisdom (*huì*) is called *jiàn*. Guo Pu’s commentary states that "wisdom" refers to clear understanding (*liǎohuì*), while "vigorous" refers to being nimble (*biàn*). Gu Yewang says it refers to the appearance of speech and tongue moving swiftly and sharply. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as composed of the radicals for "cloth" (*jīn*), "hand" (*yòu*), and "stop" (*zhǐ*), forming the character *jí* (疾). The *Wenzi Dian* states it is composed of "person" (*rén*) and the phonetic *dié* (疌), and that adding "hand" (*shǒu*) is incorrect.

The upper character, *xiāng*, is pronounced *kān* (as in *kāng*); the *Shēnglèi* states it means "leather. The lower character, *zào*, is pronounced *zāng láo*; the *Shuōwén* defines it as "the dregs of wine. Both characters are composed of the radical for "grain" (*mǐ*), with *kāng* and *cáo* serving as their phonetic components respectively.

*Cháng-lù* (麞鹿): The first character is pronounced *zhāng* (上音章) and the second is *lù* (下音祿). The *Zìshū* (字書) states that the *cháng* (麞) is a species of small deer; those with antlers are called *lù* (鹿), while those without antlers are called *cháng* (麞).

Volume Six, Part Six (Note: This volume lacks a title character). *Ōngchá zhūfǎ xíng jīng* (觀察諸法行經), Scroll One, compiled by Huìlín. *Shègài* (捨㧖): Pronounced *wù gé fǎn* (烏革反). Páo Xián’s commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* states: "A horizontal wooden beam used for binding is what is meant by *gài* (㧖). According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic element "è" (戹); its correct form is *gài* (㧖). The form appearing in the sutra is *è* (扼), which is a vulgar character.

Those wishing to cross [the water] use a *bō* (pronounced fán-fǎn; the character is pronounced *kǎo*; it refers to binding bamboo and wood together to float upon the water). The *Shuowen Jiezi* also states that it is a large boat on the sea, composed of the radical "wood" (*mu*) and the phonetic "fa" (*fā*). Alternatively, it is written as *fá* with the radical "boat" (*zhōu*), or as *fà* with the radical "bamboo" (*zhú*); these are vulgar characters.
"Zhuāng" (撞) means to strike; the *Guǎngyá* says it means to pierce (*cì*), and the *Shuōwén* says it means to pound (*dǎo*). It is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "tóng" (童).
2. Fascicle Two. Second Fascicle. "Ā" (阿) is pronounced with the third tone; "bō" (波) is also pronounced with the third tone.
*Chā* (pronounced with a retroflex *ṛ* vowel) and *nāṃ* (pronounced with a retroflex *ṇ* vowel); the scriptural text uses the non-aspirated nasal (*ṃ*) rather than the anusvāra (*m*).
*Dha* is pronounced in the third tone; *ka* is pronounced as *jiāngqū* (with a retroflex *ṛ* vowel), or again in the third tone.
*Cuō* (with the *zàng* and *hè* finals reversed), *chà* (with the *chè* and *jiǎ* finals reversed). *Lì* (with the *zhái* and *xià* finals reversed). The above are all echoes of Sanskrit sounds;

they do not conform to the interpretation of the characters. 3. Third Fascicle. *Gài*: *gāi* (with *kē* and *hài* finals reversed). Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "A *gài* is that which levels out pecks and bushels. It is also said to mean "measure. The *Shuowen* writes it as *𣏙*; it means leveling pecks and bushels. It is composed of the radical *木* and the phonetic *既*. In current vernacular pronunciation, it is read as *gǔwài*. The character *𣏙* is pronounced *gǔ*. According to the *Shuowen*, *𣏙* means "leveling," composed of the radical *木* and the phonetic *气*.

*Diàn* (雷電): According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, lightning is the radiance produced by the mutual friction of yin and yang; it is composed of the radical "rain" (雨) with the phonetic element "yù" (󱲸), pronounced *xiàpò máo*. *Kǎo* (泡沫): According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, this refers to bubbles floating upon water; it is composed of the radical "water" (水) with the phonetic element "bāo" (包).

4. Scroll Four, Part Four: *Xiāoqīng* (鵁鶄). The upper character is pronounced *jiāo* (交) and the lower is pronounced *jīng* (精). Guō’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "It resembles a *shéng* (𠒎) with high legs and a feathered crest; people in the Jiangdong region keep it, saying it wards off fire disasters. According to the *Shanhaijing*, on Mount Manlian there is a bird named *xiāoqīng* that flies in flocks, its tail resembling that of a hen, and it calls out its own name when it cries. Eating it cures wind ailments. The *Shuowen Jiezi* identifies it as the *xiāoqīng*. Both characters are composed of the radical "bird" (*niǎo*) with *jiāo* and *qīng* serving as phonetic components.

*Jie-kai* (嗟慨): The upper character *jie* (嗟) is pronounced with the *xie* (邪) rhyme. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (毛詩傳) states: "Jie expresses praise. The *Erya* (爾雅) says: "Zi-jie" (咨嗟). The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文解字) explains that *jie* is composed of the radical 口 (mouth) and the phonetic 差 (cha). The lower character *kai* (慨) is pronounced with the *ai* (愛) rhyme. Zheng’s commentary on the *Mao Shi* states: "Kai refers to sighing. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains that *wan-kai* (忨慨)—meaning a man of spirit who does not achieve his ambitions—is composed of the radical 心 (heart) and the phonetic 既 (ji). Alternatively, it may be written as *kai* (愾) with the phonetic 氣 (qi), or as *kai* (嘅) with the phonetic 口 (mouth); these are vulgar forms.

Regarding "tiáo" (調): it is pronounced *tiáo* (弔) with a retroflex final; the *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (Mao Commentary on the Classic of Poetry) states it means "to mock" (*tiáo-cháo*). The lower character is pronounced *xī* (希) with the *yì* (義) final. Guō Pǐng’s commentary on the *Eryā* states: "Xì (戲) refers to mutual joking. According to the *Shuowén Jiězì*, "tiáo" is composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic "zhōu" (*zhōu-shēng*); "jīng" (經) is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and signifies "swaying" (*diào-diào*), which is not the meaning here. The *Shuowén* entry for the character "xì" (戲) is composed of the radical "spear" (*gē*) and the phonetic "qiàn" (*qiàn-shēng*); "qiàn" has the pronunciation *xūyī* (許衣). The "jīng" (戱) found in the classics is a vulgar form of the character.

*Qū* (pronounced *qiū yīn fǎn*): He Xiū’s commentary on the *Gōngyáng Zhuan* states that to strike with the foot against something is called *qū* (pronounced *xià tán hé fǎn*). *Pīcāng* states that *tà* means the foot touches the ground; the *Shuowén* states that *tà* means to tread. Both characters are formed with the radical "foot" (*zú*) and the phonetic component *jiù* (*jìu*), with *tá* (*tā*) as the phonetic. The sound of *jiù* is *tǎ*.

*Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb Sūtra*, Scroll One. Xuanying. Scroll One: *Śrāvastī* (the first character is pronounced with the *shì* rhyme, the second with the *liú* rhyme). According to the *Póshā Shì* (*Vyākhyāyukti*), Śrāvastī is a city in India; it is translated as "dwelling place" (*póshā*). *Śrāvastī* means "the dwelling place of the Able One" (*Śakya*). In the sūtras, it is sometimes called "Śākya City of Emaciation," sometimes "Śrāvastī City," sometimes "Kapilavastu City," or "Kapila City. These are all variations of the Sanskrit name due to differences in the weight of syllables and the corruption of the sound of "Śākya."
*Bi* (pronounced *bei* with a retroflex initial) means to fold or pleat; according to the *Guǎngyá*, *biqū* (folding) and *dié* (the character for *dié*) share this meaning.

*Xùnshēn* (to press against the body): in lexicographical works it is sometimes written as *qín*; they are identical characters. It is pronounced *chǔ* (with a retroflex initial) or *chājìn*. It means to reach or to approach.

*Sa* (唼) and *sou* (嗽)—the former with the particle *zi* (子) and the latter with the particle *he* (盇), both followed by the same character *sou* (欶)—are pronounced as *suǒjiǎo* (所角). According to the *Tōngsùwén* (通俗文), "to inhale and exhale" is called *sou*.

In various scriptures concerning the heavens, this is written as *hètiān* (廅天); this translation renders it as "the Heaven of Radiant Longevity" (*yǒuguāngshòu tiān*). The pronunciation of *hè* (廅) is *wūhé* (烏合).
The Ābhāsvara-devas (sometimes written as Āpāmāśvara or Āpamāśvara), which is translated as "Infinite Light Heaven.
The Apramāṇaśubha-devas (sometimes written as Āpāṅkṣu or Āpāhē).
The characters 相𭣙, 摚㲂, and 掁 are three forms of the same text, pronounced *zhèng* (with the phonetic component *yǒu* and the radical *wén*). They mean "to touch" or "to strike against.

摚 means "to hang" or "to suspend. 哊, pronounced *yù* (with the phonetic component *xián*), according to the *Guǎngyǎ*, means "to spit" or "the throat. The reading in the scripture as 陏 (*duò*) is an error.

*Chich* (also written as *jue*, both pronounced with the initial *bu* and final *ge*; the second character has the initial *zi* and final *li*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *chich* refers to the appearance of flavors entering the mouth.

2. Second Fascicle. Second [Section]. *Bi yan* (pronounced *yu* and *yan*). The *Tongsu Wen* states that slack lips are called *yan*. *Xing xing* (pronounced *chang* and *ruo*) refers to the current phenomenon. The scriptural text reads *yan* (pronounced *yu* and *chan*), which is *yan* (pronounced *yan*). The character *yan* does not convey the intended meaning.

Regarding the character *chuan* (pronounced *shì* with the *yán* tone): the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as a round bamboo vessel used for storing grain; the *Cangjie Pian* states that a *chuan* is a round granary. The text of the sutra uses the character *dan* (pronounced *dān*), which is the name of a different type of bamboo vessel; *dan* does not carry this meaning.

*Gūhuǎo* (the first character pronounced with the ancient sound *gǔ*, the second *hú*) refers to the mole cricket (*lùgū*). The second character, *húguāng*, refers to the *huángbīng*, a type of armored insect as large as a tiger-bean (*hùdòu*) and green in color.

*Bīng* is pronounced *púdīng*. 3. Fascicle Three. [The character] *quàn* (pronounced *sīlǜ*) means to entice; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to lead astray. The version of the scripture that uses *xù* is incorrect.
*Yi* (bowing) and *rang* (yielding) refer to entering [a gate] and moving forward with palms joined; it is also a slight raising of the hands. According to the *Guangya*, *yi* means "to advance.

*Tao* (pronounced *tu gao fan*) and *ye* (pronounced *yi zhe fan*): *táo* refers to making earthenware vessels, while *yě* refers to smelting in a furnace. *Táo* signifies transformation; *yě* signifies melting.
*Saṃnāha* is translated here as "armor" (*kaijia*). It refers to donning and adorning oneself with great armor.

Regarding the *guī* (tortoise) and *tuó* (crocodile)—the latter being pronounced *dú duō fǎn*—the *Sāncāng* states they resemble *jiāo* (a type of eel) but are large. The *Shanhai jing* says that crocodiles (*tuó*) abound in the Yangtze River; Guo Pu states they resemble *xīyì* (lizards), with the larger ones reaching one *wén* (approx. 10 feet) in length, possessing scaly patterns that can be used to make drums. The text of the sutra writes this character with the "fish" radical (*yú*) as *𩵔*, which is incorrect.
*Liǔ*: The ancient form is 㭰, which in modern usage is written as 𠲿; both are pronounced *zǐlèi*. Lexicons state that 㭰 refers to a bird pecking.
*Lúan*: Pronounced *kūjuàn*. The *Tōngsùwén* states that "to scoop up" is called *lúan*; the *Shuowén* defines it as "to draw out [liquid] from a leak."

4. Fourth Fascicle. "Chong-huang" (蟲蝗) [the second character, *huang*, is pronounced with the second tone of *hu* and the fourth tone of *meng*] refers to the locust; it means the migratory locust. The small variety is called *zhong* (蝩), and the large variety is called *huang* (蝗). It is said to be transformed from fish eggs. The pronunciation of *zhong* is *zhong* (鍾). In the scriptural text, it is written as *huang* (蟥), which is not the correct form.
The constellation Jǐn (軫) is pronounced rěn (忍).
The constellation Kàng (亢) is pronounced kè làng (恪浪).
Liáo zhì (撩擲)—also written as liáo qiāo (摷)—is pronounced lǐ diāo (力彫); it means to toss or throw at one another, where "zhì" (擲) means to cast or hurl.
"Zhi" (杖) is pronounced *zhì* (知栗反). According to the *Guǎngyá*, "zhìcì" (桎刺) means to prick with a finger.

Regarding "dàpì" (大辟), there are two archaic forms, *biàn* (𠮃) and *bì* (󰑴), both pronounced *chìfǎn* (尺反). "Pì" (辟) means to fear or to eliminate. The text's reading as "pì" (僻), meaning "hidden or secluded," is incorrect.

"Shan" (pronounced with the "yan" rhyme of "shai") means to mow grass; the *Shijing Zhuan* says, "Shan means to clear away weeds. The text here uses "shan" (pronounced with the "jian" rhyme of "jian"), which refers to a large sickle; however, that [large] sickle is not used for this purpose.

5. Fifth Fascicle. Regarding the character *qiāng* (槍): according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "a pike" (*jù*). According to the *Tongsu Wén*, piercing wood to injure thieves is called *qiāng*; wooden and iron pikes are both written with this character. In the text of this scripture, it is written as *qiāng* (鏘), meaning the sound of jade; it is also written as *qiāng* (鎗), which is incorrect.

The eight treasuries (*kośa*)—the first being the *garbhāvakrānti* (womb-birth) treasury; the second, the *antarābhava* (intermediate state) treasury; the third, the *mahāyāna vaipulya* treasury; the fourth, the *vinaya* treasury; the fifth, the *bodhisattvabhūmi* treasury; the sixth, the *saṃyukta* (miscellaneous) treasury; the seventh, the *vajra* treasury; and the eighth, the *buddha* treasury. In the Sanskrit original, these are called *piṭaka*, where *piṭaka* is used as a substitute for *kośa*.

*The Scripture on the Samādhi of the Broad Manifestation of the Propagation of the Way*, Scroll One (First Volume). "Xian" (先) is not explained [here]. Scroll Two (Second Volume). "Wei" (蔚): pronounced *yù*. It refers to the appearance of literary composition. The *Guangya* states that "wei" means numerous; the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means a profusion of colorful patterns.
Jingfeng (Scorching Wind) occupies the position opposite the shadow among the eight winds; that of the south is called Jingfeng. When this wind moves, insects are born.

Volume Three, Part Three: *Xian* was not explained previously. Volume Four, Part Four: *Lìbèi* (Ancient forms: 奰, 𢘍, 𡘉; three characters; now written as 㔗, all pronounced *pí jì*). According to the *Shuowen*, *bèi* means "mighty and large," referring to exerting strength with a look of wrath. The *Shijing* says: "To be angry without being drunk is called *bèi*."
*Qīngqiū*: In the *Zhuǎnwén*, the pronunciation is *dú* (with the tone of *dá*), and also *fēngyōu*. According to the *Guǎngyá*, "qīngqiū" means to run.

*Shīdēnggōngdéjīng* (*Sūtra on the Merit of Offering Lamps*): Compiled by Xuanying. *Léiwěi*: In ancient texts, there are three forms: *lín*, *wěi*, and *zhí*. They share the same pronunciation *cái yì*. It means emaciated and thin.
