The character *táng* (唐突) is written with two forms, *táng* (搪) and *pù* (揬), both pronounced with the same initial *dú* (徒) and finals *láng* (郎) and *gǔ* (骨). According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to strike," "to encounter," "to push," or "to collide. According to the *Zìshū*, *pù* (揬) means "to rub" or "to scrape."

*Qùtà* (pronounced *qiānliùfǎn* for the first character and *túhéfǎn* for the second): this refers to kicking with the foot; it is called *qù* (to kick). The *Shuowen* states that *tà* means to tread upon;
the *Guangya* states that *tà* means to step on. *Shìshēng* (pronounced *shīchìfǎn*): the *Guangya* says it means "only" (*zhī*) or "just" (*shì*), meaning to approach or to begin.
*Buzhang* (不彰): Also written as *bùzhān* (暲), with the same pronunciation as *zhuó* (灼) [the character for "blazing"]. The *Guǎngyá* states: "To manifest clearly; to be evident;

also to be displayed. 2. Volume Two. *Bùyǐ* (不倚): Pronounced *yǐ* (蟻) with the tone of *yīn* (因). The *Guǎngyá* states: "To rely upon. This means to rely on or depend upon things. It is also pronounced *qú yǐ* (渠蟻); this means to lean against or stand upon.

"Wu-gou" (無咎) [the second character] is pronounced as "qu" or "jiu. The *Shijing* says, "Some are sorrowful, fearing misfortune," where "guo" (咎) refers to fault or transgression. According to the *Guangya*, "guo" means evil; according to the *Shuowen*, "guo" means calamity. As for the character form, it consists of "ren" (人) and "ge" (各): when individuals act in opposition to one another, they create guilt and transgression. Furthermore, when two people are of one mind, their sharpness can cut through metal; when two people are in opposition, their misfortune becomes a disaster. In archaic script, this was used as the character "gao" (皐) in the name Gao Yao.

"You all" (rǔcáo) is also written as 𣍘 (tóng, with the phonetic component *zì* and radical *láo*). In the *Shiji*, it appears as "ten-odd *cáo*" (*shíyú cáo*). Ruochun says that *cáo* refers to a group or cohort. The *Shijing* states, "Then they were auspicious in their *cáo*," and its commentary explains that *cáo* means a multitude.

The characters for *shī* (師), *bǎo* (保), *gǔ* (古), *wén* (文), *jì* (賲), *yǎn* (󲝷), and *yǎn* (𠍂) share the same pronunciation as *bǔ* (補) and *dào* (道). In the *Lǐjì*, it is said: "When going out there is a *bǎo*; when entering there is a *shī*. A *bǎo* is so called because he secures (*ān*) others through the Way; he is a protector (*bǎoshǒu*). The *Shuōwén* defines it as "nurturing and preserving."
*Guǐmíng* (詭名) both mean "to ruin" and are the opposite of "deceitful" (*biànzhà*). *Kǔqí* (苦齊) is said to mean "guǐ" (詭), as is the case in Guānxī.
*Ōudé* (偶得) is the opposite of "arbitrary" (*gǒu*); it means "encountering by chance. Guō Pǔ says: "To encounter each other by chance."

"Chèdiàn" (掣電) is pronounced *chì diàn* (with the second tone on *diàn*). It refers to the intense brilliance of the interaction between yin and yang. The *Shìmíng* (釋名) states: "Diàn is 'dǎn' (猝然); it means that upon being suddenly seen, it immediately darts away and vanishes. The *Shízhōu jì* (十州記) says: "The two eyes of a fierce beast are like the light of *qín-diàn* (䃱磹). Today, in the Wu region, lightning is called *qín-diàn* (pronounced *xī niàn* [first tone] and *dà niàn* [fourth tone]); in the Three Commanderies (*Sānfǔ*), it is called *lèi-diàn* (類電).

"Huóyǔ" (hail and rain)—*huó* is pronounced *pújiǎo* (蒲角). The *Báihùtōng* (White Tiger Compendium) states: "The word *huó* means 'to combine' (*hé*); the concentrated essence of the Yin energy condenses and combines to form hail. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lìjì* says: "Yang initiates the Yin; when it coagulates into ice, it becomes hail. The *Shìmíng* (Explanations of Names) states: "Hail is *páo*; whatever objects it strikes are all crushed and broken, as if trampled by a person. *Páo* is pronounced *fùxué* (父學).

"Suddenly falling" (*zòu duò*) means to fall suddenly; "serving to save" (*shì jiù*) means returning to the state. Regarding "suddenly saving" (*zòu jiù*) from ruin and peril at the proper time, Jia Du says: "Suddenly" (*zòu*) means rapid.
"Wailing" (*háo tāo*)—the characters are *tú* and *láo* reversed—refers to loud weeping. As the *I Ching* says: "First there is wailing, and afterwards there is laughter. This is it.

*Pǒu-lì* (剖裂): *pǒu* is pronounced with the *tǔ-hòu* rhyme; "to split" (*pǒu*) means to break, specifically to divide down the middle. In the *Cāngjié* (蒼頡), it refers to *chǒu* (𡍩); *chǒu* is pronounced with the *chǔ-bǎi* rhyme, meaning to tear apart.
*Suìxīng* (彗星): *suì* is pronounced with the *sū-sū* and *qiú-ruì* rhymes; it is a "broom-star. This means that the light of the star resembles a broom.

"Oyi" (噢咿): the character "yi" (乙) is read with the *qí* (祁) tone; "bei cāng" (卑蒼) means "to grieve," referring to the sound of piteous lamentation. The form "zì yù" (喐郁) found in the *Lunwen* (論文) is not the correct orthography.

*Kǐgǔ* (谿谷): According to the *Ěryá*, water that flows into a stream is called a *kǐ* (谿). Lǐ Xún says: "Water that emerges from a mountain and enters a stream is called a *kǐ*. The *Shuowén* states: "A conduit for a spring that flows into a stream is called a *gǔ* (谷)."

*Ghaṇṭī* refers to striking a wooden block; in the Sanskrit language it is called *ghanṭī*, for which there is no direct translation [into Chinese]. According to older translated versions of the scriptures, it is often rendered as *jiàndí*; this too is merely a phonetic corruption of the Sanskrit term.
"Selecting" (xuǎn) means to choose or cull; it appears as "xiān" and "jiàn" in the *Xiānyùn* and *Xiānjiàn*.

"Folding" (dié) means to layer or accumulate; it appears as "tuó" and "jié" in the *Cāngjié piān*. Furthermore, the *Lùnwén* writes it as "zhé," which has the same pronunciation as "dié. According to the *Shuōwén*, it refers to layered clothing. There is also the county of Diéjiāng in the south; these two forms are used interchangeably.
"Hun" (渾) and "zhuo" (濁) [refer to] later generations being confused and disordered; "hun" is also explained in the *Shuowen* as turbid mud and the sound of flowing water.

"Niu chai" (牛䶗)—also written as "niu chi" (牛齝) and in the *Sancang* as "niu zhi" (牛𪗺), while the *Shichuan* writes it as "niu shi" (牛呞)—is pronounced with the same final as "chou" (丑) [chǐ]. The *Yunjiji* gives the pronunciation "shí" (式). According to the *Erya*, "niu ri chai" (牛日䶗); Guo Pu says: "Having finished eating, one brings it back out and chews it again."

*Kuò* (pronounced *kǒu guō fǎn*): According to the *Guǎngyá*, *kuò* means "empty. According to the *Fānyán*, to enlarge something small is called *kuò*. According to the *Ěryá*, *kuò* means "large. Sūn Yán says: "*Kuò* is the enlargement of what is spread out."

*Kiān* (敲) is also written as *k'iao* (毃) in the *Cangjie pian*; it is also written as *k'iao* (󲮶), with the same pronunciation as *ku-chiao*. It means to strike downward; according to the *Shuowen*, it refers to striking across or striking the head.
*Kun-le* (蜫勒) has the ancient pronunciation *ku-kuai*; this is translated here as "a box for storing things."

3. Third Fascicle. Third Fascicle. *Shè* (to suck) is also written as *sòu* (same pronunciation, with the radical for "mountain" and "corner"). The *Tōngsùwén* states that to inhale and suck is called *sòu*. The *Sāncāng* says *shè* means to suck. The *Shìmíng* says *shè* means "hastening," as it involves using force with urgency. The scriptural text uses the character *cǎo* (𡂡), which is a vulgar form of the character.

*Vīcī*: The first character is pronounced *bì* (with the *xí* radical) and the second is pronounced *chāng-shì*. In the Qin language, it means "bright conduct" (*míngxíng*). Following the characters, *vī* refers to a small drum, and *cī* means "extravagance" or "excess.

*Gāḍha*: Also written as two forms, *gāḍhā* and *gāṭhā*, both pronounced *pújiè*. In the *Ajātaśatru-rāja-sūtra*, it is translated as "understanding the world" (*shìjiānjiě*). Following the characters, it means "fatigue and weakness. According to the *Tōngsùwén*, extreme exhaustion is called *gāḍhā*.

The standard form of "Shé" (舍) is written as "Nián" (諵), pronounced with the second tone of the rhyme "nǚ-hán. It is translated as "person. According to the *Běicāng* (埤蒼), "nián" refers to the sound of speech.

"Hēiyǎn" (黑黶) is pronounced with the second tone of "diàn"; it refers to a black mole on the face. In the *Shuōwén*, it refers to a freckle. In the treatise (*Lùn*), it is written as "Àn" (黯), with the second tones of "gǎn" or "zhǎn. In the *Shuōwén*, "àn" means deep black. "Àn" is not the intended meaning here.

"Circular" (*xúnhuán*) appears to mean "revolving" (*jūn*), yet it refers to winding around and coming and going. The *Erya* states: "To follow, to comply with, to rate, and to circulate are synonyms. Guo Pu says: "It also means to move about in succession. 'Circulate' (*xún*) is also 'to patrol' (*xún*) and 'to pervade' (*biàn*)."

"Fánxī" (蕃息): "Fú" (輔) and "biǎo" (表) are reversed [in the rhyme]. In the *Shàngshū*, regarding "the myriad plants were fánwú" (庶草蕃蕪), Kǒng Àngguó says: "Fán means 'to flourish,' meaning to grow profusely. In the *Zhōu Lǐ*, regarding "using [methods] to fán [birds and beasts]," Zhèng Xuàn says: "Fán means 'to breed' (*fánxī*). The *Shìmíng* says: "Xī (breed/grow) means 'to fill' (*sè*); it refers to things flourishing and filling to capacity. Today, in the Central Kingdom, "fánxī" (breeding/proliferation) is called "máoxī" (茂息). "Máo" (茂) has the phonetic value of "wànwàn" (亡万反). The *Chéngnán Zì* states: "Máoxī" is written as "máoxī" (嬔息). "Tóng" (同) and "shí" (時) form the single character "máo" (嬔), which is also written with this same character.

*Shuā* (also written as *shuā*, same pronunciation, retroflex *suo-lüe*): According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to wipe. According to the *Guoye*, it means "to sweep. According to the *Erya*, it means "to cleanse. Guo Pu states: "A broom and a brush are the means by which one achieves cleanliness."

*Qìng*: The ancient character is written as *𠜜*, pronounced *kě dìng fǎn*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "the interior of a vessel being empty. The *Erya* says, "To exhaust completely. Sun Yan commented: "It refers to the total exhaustion of one's strength.

4. Fourth Fascicle. *Búshí* (Evening): Pronounced *bǔ hú fǎn*. The *Huainanzi* states that when the sun travels to Bei Valley, it is called the evening hour (*búshí*), which corresponds to the addition of the Shen hour.
*Kòu* (扣): To strike or tap. The *Guǎyá* states that *kòu* means to lift up. The *Lúnyǔ* says, "He struck his shins with a staff," and Kǒng Àngguó explains that *kòu* means to strike.

*Zhí* (植): To plant trees; it is also written as *shù* (樹). The pronunciation is *tí* (同) or *shí* (時), with the tone *zhí* (軄). The *Zhōulǐ* states, "Plants should be planted early," and Zhèng Xuán comments: "To 'plant' (*zhí*) refers to things that take root and grow; it also means to plant trees. According to the *Fāngyán*, to plant trees means to establish them upright.

Regarding *yóu* (猶豫) and *yì* (又弋): according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, in Longxi they call a young dog *yóu*. Because the nature of the *yóu* is to be frequently forward-looking and ahead of others, all those who are indecisive are called *yóuyù*. Furthermore, the *Erya* states: "*Yóu* is like a *jǐ* (麂), skilled at climbing trees. Guo Pu says: "It is adept at ascending trees. Another master says: "It climbs trees like a bird."
*Laorǎo* (勞擾): "Like a pond. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "to vex"; the *Guangya* states it means "to disturb. 5. Fascicle Five. *Shū* (抒): *Dàchú* (大除).

Pronounced with the second tone for the characters *lǚ* (呂) and *shí* (時), and the second tone for *rǔ* (汝). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "to draw out" (*yì*) or "to ladle" (*zhé*). The *Guangya* states it means "to drain" (*xiè*). The *Tongsu Wén* states that drawing water out is called *shū*.

The character *lè* (勒) is pronounced with the *kuì* rhyme; in the *Zìshū*, it is said to mean "a horse-tether. It is that by which carriage horses are restrained and gathered in. The *Shìmíng* states: "It is *lè*; it leads and pulls, restraining the horse by its *lè* [reins]. The form of the character consists of the radical *sī* (silk) and the phonetic *lì* (𨊥). The *lè* on the horse's head is the bit (*xián*). The *Shìmíng* states: "The *lè* is *luò*; it is wrapped around its head and pulled."

*Chúnshú* (淳淑): *chún* is pronounced as *shí-jūn-fǎn*; *shú* is pronounced as *shí-liù-fǎn*. In the *Shàngshū*, regarding the phrase "The administration of government lies solely in purity" (*zhèngshì wéi chún*), Kǒng Ānguó says it means "purity" (*chuíyì*), referring to being single-minded and unified. In the *Ěryá*, *chún* means "great. In the *Fānyán*, *chún* means "excellent. Regarding *shú*, the *Shīchuán* says it means "beautiful" (*měi*) or "good" (*shàn*). It is sometimes written as *shú*, which in the *Fānyán* means "cooked" (*xiánshú*).
*Gǔ* (股): Also written as *tòu* (骰), with the same pronunciation as *gōng hù* (公戶). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "The thigh. *Nèi qì* (內慼):

Also written as *hàn* (憾), with the same pronunciation as *qiě* (且). The *Guangya* states: "To draw near. The *Shijing* says: "Miserable are we, brothers," and the commentary explains: "To be close to one another."

The *Bǎnchēng* (Board-Weighing) also writes it as *pānhuà* (climbing-transformation), with two forms: *pǔjiān* and *bùjiān* (both pronounced with the second tone). According to the *Zìlín*, "board" means to lead; according to the *Guǎngyǎ*, "board" means to assist. The *Shìmíng* states: "To *pān* is to turn over; it refers to the act of turning over in succession."

Regarding "five blisters" (wǔ pào): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "pào" refers to a swelling on the face caused by qi. The *Huainanzi* says, "To burst small blisters and bring forth carbuncles. In the *Lunwen*, it appears as two forms, "lǚ" and "pào"; neither source for these characters has yet been identified.

"Yan-ji" (eye-lashes) is also written as "jie" (睫); the *Shiming* (Explanations of Names) writes it as "zhun" (迍), both pronounced with the initial *zi* and the final *ye*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to the hairs at the sides of the eyes; this is what is meant in the *Shiji* when it says, "the eyes have fine hairs (*mao*) but do not see the lashes (*ji*)."

The ancient text for "weizhang" (curtains) reads *wei* (with the phonetic *tong* and *zhui*). According to the *Zilin*, that which is at the side is called *wei*; it refers to hanging silk to screen off the sides. The *Shiming* states: "Wei means 'to surround' (*wei*), referring to surrounding [an area] with cloth. Today, this character is generally written as *wei*.
*Wò* (pronounced *yǐ jiǎo*) refers to a large tent; the *Xiǎo Ěr Yǎ* states that a "covering tent" is called a *wò*, which is a canopy.

*Tiào* (also written as *chào*, pronounced *tā diào*) means to leap or skip; the *Yùn jí* says it means to jump over or to leap while suspended. The version of the *Lùn* (Treatise) uses *chuò* (pronounced *chì gé* or *chì jiǎo*), meaning the shuffling gait of one who is lame; however, this reading does not accord with the intent of the *Lùn*.

The term *gū* (賈) is pronounced *kǔ* when it refers to sitting and selling; according to the *Zhouli*, *gū* is defined as "the seller. Zheng Xuan’s commentary states that "moving about is called *yíng* (行), while staying in one place is called *gū* (賈). The *Baihūtong* says: "The word *gū* signifies 'firmness' (*gù*). It means to stabilize goods and wait for the people to come so as to seek profit from them."

6. The sixth fascicle. Regarding "Hèlóu" (呵膢): the ancient text reads "Lóu" (樓). According to the *Sāncāng* (三蒼), it is the name of a sacrifice performed in the eighth month; the scriptural text sometimes uses the character "Lóu."
*Zhì* (pronounced *shì* according to the character; the *Shīchuán* states that *zhì* means "to harm," while the *Shuōwén* states that *zhì* means "resentment").
*Gài* (pronounced *lài* according to the song; the *Shuōwén* states that *gài* means "to irrigate and pour").

"Nü" (訥) is also written as "Na" (吶), with the phonetic component "nu" (奴) and the radical "gu" (骨). In the *Analects*, it says: "The gentleman desires to be slow in speech. Bao Xian commented: "Nü means sluggish and dull. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as: "Nü means difficulty."

Regarding "enmity" (*yóu*) and "rival" (*chóu*): the *Shīchuán* (Commentary on the Odes) states that a resentful match is called a "rival" (*chóu*). The *Ěryá* says, "Rival" (*chóu*) and "enemy" (*chóu*) are a matched pair. Lǐ Xún says, "Rival" (*chóu*) and "enemy" (*chóu*) are a matched pair of those who harbor resentment.

Regarding "gài": it is the same as the ancient character "kě" (*gōng nèi* according to the *Zílín*). It refers to one who levels out measures such as bushels and pecks. The *Guǎngyá* states, "Gài" means measure; it means to level.

7. The seventh fascicle. *Piǎo* (pronounced with the "pì" and "diào" tones) refers to the azure of heaven; it is like the bluish-white color of silk. The *Shìmíng* (Explanations of Names) states: "*Piǎo* is like *piāo* (to float); it is a light blue that floats. There are azure-green *piǎo*, crimson *piǎo*, and green *piǎo*, each named according to the color it represents.

*Yīn-yì* (陰曀) is an archaic term identical to *yū* (㙪), pronounced *jì* (於計反). The *Shijing* (Book of Poetry) states: "The wind blows constantly and it is *yì*. The commentary says: "When it is cloudy and windy, it is called *yì*. The *Shiming* (Explanation of Names) says: "*Yì* means *yì* (obscuration). This refers to how the vapors of clouds darken and obscure the sunlight, causing it to lose its brightness.
*Yin* (齦): pronounced *niú-jīn* (牛斤) according to the *Cāngjié piān*; it refers to the gums. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means the flesh at the base of the teeth.
*Huǒlè* (火㷮): pronounced *zǐ-láo* (子勞) according to the *Shuōwén*; it means to scorch. According to the *Cāngjié piān*, it refers to the remains of burnt wood.

"Hand-mén" (捫): *mo* and *kun*, with the second character pronounced as *mo* and *ben* (二反). According to the *Shēnglèi* (聲類), "mén" means to touch; the *Zílín* (字林) says it means to grasp or hold. Examining this, "mén" refers to seizing or clutching an object. "Dào-dáoxú" (蹈𨈁):

*tú* and *dào*, with the second character also pronounced as *zì* (自亦反). The *Guǎngyǎ* (廣雅) states that "dào" means to walk; the *Zishū* (字書) says "xú" means to tread upon. The *Shìmíng* (釋名) says: "Dào-dǎodào" (蹈道道); one treads upon it with the feet as if it were a path. "Xú" means a register (*jí*); it resembles a register for the feet. In the *Lùnwén* (論文), it is written as "jí"; however, "jí" is not the correct character form.

8. Volume Eight, Part Eight. "Elder" (*bó*) and "younger" (*zhòng*) refer to brothers. The *Erya* states: "Elder means senior. The *Sharen* says: "The elder is the senior of their station. The *Han Shi* says: "Younger means middle," meaning his station is in the middle. The *Liji* states that children have names, which are replaced by *zi* (courtesy names) upon capping; at age fifty, they are designated as "elder" (*bó*) or "younger" (*zhòng*). The *Shiming* of the Zhou tradition says: "Elder (*bó*) means 'to grasp' (*bǎ'); he grasps and maintains the household administration."

*Ki-na* (罽那)—the "ji" is pronounced with the *ju-li* (居例) tone; in the Qin language, it means "Jewel Accumulation" (*Ratnakūṭa*). An earlier version of the text wrote it as *Ci-na* (刺那), where the "li" is pronounced with the *li-qi* (力逵) tone;

here we follow the latter. Volume Nine, Chapter Nine: "Dragon Coiled" (*Long Pan*)—the "pan" is pronounced with the *pu-han* (蒲寒) tone. In the *Book of Rites* (*Li Ji*), it says "coiling upon the ground," and Zheng Xuan commented that "pan" means "to fold and spread. According to the *Guang Ya*, "pan" means "to bend or curve."

The ancient forms for "mad" (kuáng) were written as 獧 and 㹾 (two characters), both pronounced with the same phonetic *jùmiàn* (俱面反). One who is "mad" (*kuáng*) advances toward the Way of Goodness; one who "observes" (*ǎn*) maintains the principles of non-action (*wúwéi*).

In the *Cangjie pian*, "pāndiàn" (潘澱) is written with the same character as "pān" (潘). It is pronounced *shù* (數) and *xiǎo* (󲛹), meaning "rice-water. The *Shuowen jiezi* states that "fán" (番) refers to the water used for rinsing rice; "xī" (淅) is pronounced *sūlì* (蘇曆). In the north of the Yangtze River it is called "gān" (泔), while in the south of the Yangtze River it is called "pān" (潘). "Diàn" (澱) is an archaic form written with the same character as "dàn" (󲩫), pronounced *dújiàn* (徒見). The *Erya* states: "Diàn is called zhuó (󲱇). Guo Pu commented: "Diàn refers to dregs and sediment; in Jiangdong they call it zhuó. In the *Lunwen* (Discourse on Literature), it is written as "diàn" (淀). Although the "Xinyang" (新陽) [lake] is like a deep pool yet shallow, it is also called "diàn"; however, this "diàn" does not carry the same meaning as the term under discussion. "Zhuó" (󲱇) is pronounced *yújìn* (魚靳), and "diàn" (淀) is pronounced *diàn* (殿).

*Chángjǔ* (long-kneeling) is an archaic term synonymous with *qí*. It is pronounced *qí* and *jǐ*, with the two tones reversed. The *Shuōwén* states that *jǔ* means "to kneel for a long time. The *Shìmíng* says: "*Jǔ* means 'to hold in awe' (*jì*); when one encounters that which is revered or feared, one does not dare to remain at ease."

10. The Tenth Fascicle, the Tenth [Section]. The lunar mansion *Dī* (氐). Pronounced *dǐ*; in the *Erya*, it is called *Tiēngēn* (天根, "Celestial Root"). Regarding the phonetic and semantic interpretation: it is called the Celestial Root because it serves as the root for all the myriad things under heaven; thus it is termed the Celestial Root. Sūn Yán states: "The *Jiǎo* and *Kāng* mansions are attached below to the *Dī*, just as a tree has roots."

The constellation *Kui* (奎) is pronounced *kǒu xié fǎn*; according to the *Erya*, it is "Descending Lou" (*jiànglóu*), meaning *Kui* and *Lóu*. Li Xun says: "Descending Lou is a lunar station of the White Tiger. The constellation *Zi* (觜) is pronounced *zī yí fǎn*;

according to the *Erya*, it is "the mouth of *Jūzī*" (*jūzī zhī kǒu*), referring to the eastern wall of *Yíngshì*. Sūn Yán says: "The exclamation 'Jūzī' refers to the mouth opening; the four stars of the eastern wall of *Yíngshì* are square, and because they form a mouth-like shape, they are named accordingly."
*Duólóu* (skull): The ancient forms are *sù* and *lèi*, both pronounced *dú mù lì hòu*. It refers to the bone of the head. *Lánlǚ* (tattered rags):

The ancient forms are *lán* and also *pí*. Both are pronounced *lí gān*. "Tattered rags" refers to ruined clothing. When the garments and coverlets of ordinary people are ugly and worn out, they are also called *lánlǚ*. The version in the *Lùn-pǐn* (Treatise on Debates) writes it as "indigo-dyed grass"; however, "indigo" is not the intended meaning here.

The ancient forms for "elephant stable" (xiàngjiù) are both written as 凰 and 廄, pronounced *yòu* (homophonous with 宥). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as a "horse shed. The *Shiming* states that "jiù" (stable) means "to gather," as it is where oxen and horses are gathered. According to the *Zhouli*, two hundred and fourteen horses constitute a *jiù*, and each *jiù* has a *púfú* (attendant groom). This is what is meant.

*Yì* (逸): In ancient texts, this is the same as *yì* (軼), with the phonetic transcription *yú zé* (余筫). According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to gallop away," "to run wild," "to be unrestrained," or "to traverse a path.

*Tuí* (搥): Also written as *duī* (磓), with the phonetic transcription *dīng huí* (丁迴). It refers to throwing something down. According to the *Guǎngyá*, *tuī* (搥) means "to strike" (*zhì* [擿]). *Yā* (壓), with the phonetic transcription *yú jiǎ* (於甲), means "to press from above onto below. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "to crush and destroy. In the *Lùnwén*, the character is frequently written as *chū* (󲉃). Regarding the common usage of the character *wù* (物), when things are about to be destroyed, it is called *chū* (虘). This *chū* (虘) is not the same meaning as the one under discussion; its phonetic transcription is *shì jiā* (仕加).

Examining ancient texts, the two characters *liáo* (考掠) and *lì* (剠䝶) share the same pronunciation (*shàngfǎn*). According to the *Cāngjié piān*, *liáo* means "to interrogate," specifically referring to the flogging and beating of persons.

*Hùpái* (戶排) is pronounced *pújīfǎn*; it refers to a wooden bolt used to open a door, similar to a door-hook. Furthermore, all such door-bolts are termed *pài*. It is recorded that after his meal, the Buddha would inspect the *pài* and tour the quarters of the various bhikṣus.
*Kiṇḍi* (pronounced *jiǎndì*, with the second character pronounced as *zhí* and *jīdōulí* [二反]) is translated as "continuity" (*xù*).

Regarding "kinsmen" (*qīnqīn* [親親], with the second *qīn* pronounced as *qiānqīn* [且隣反]): in the *Lǐjì*, it says, "In the rites of kinship, one proceeds from three to five, and from five to nine. The *Cāngxièpiān* states it means "affection" (*qīn'ài*) and "proximity" (*jìn*). The *Shuōwén* defines it as "to reach" (*zhì*). The *Shìmíng* explains: "Kinsmen (*qīn*) are those who embrace (*lí*) one another; they are those who mutually shelter and protect (*yǐnlí*)."
*Tán* (倓): In the *Cāngjié piān*, it means "serene" (*tián*); in the *Shuōwén*, it means "peaceful"; in the *Guǎngyá*, it means "tranquil. It refers to being serene and non-active. *Chù* (黜):

Now written as *chù* (絀), they are identical. Pronounced *chìlù*. In the *Zuǒzhuan*: "He caused them not to be *chù* or arrogant. Dú Yù says: "*Chù* means to banish. In the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to remove. In the *Shàngshū*: "After three examinations, there is promotion or *chù*. Fàn Níng’s *Jíjiě* says: "*Chù* means to dismiss."

Regarding "sù" (肅), which has six variations [in its pronunciation], the *Shàngshū* states: "None fail to revere and be solemn (*sù*). Kǒng Àngguó says: "Sù means 'solemnity' (*yán*)," referring to words of strict gravity; it also means "caution" (*jiè*) and "exhortation" (*jì*).

The character for "to ward off cold" (禦) is a graphic variant of "yu" (敔), with the phonetic component read as *yǔ* (魚舉反). According to the *Guǎngyá*, "yù" means "to stop. The *Shī* says, "the defender of a hundred men," and the *Chuán* states, "yù means 'to meet' or 'to face. The *Ěryá* defines it as "yù, yǔ, jìn" (to ward off, to guard, to prohibit). Shèrén explains: "Yù and yǔ refer to preventing something before it has occurred. In the *Lùn-wén*, it is sometimes written as "yù"; the *Máo-shī* likewise uses "yù" for winter, and the *Chuán* states, "yù means 'to ward off. These two forms are used interchangeably according to regional custom (*suí-yòng*).

*Caòjiè* (草芥): The rhyme is *mài*. It means "grass. In the *Zuǒzhuan*, it says, "regard the people as soil and grass" (*shìmín rú tǔjiè*); in the *Hànshū*, it says, "bending down to the ground to pick up grass" (*fǔdì shíjiè*).

Both refer to this. Volume Eleven, Number Eleven. *Yíngcóng* (營從): This is the same as the archaic form *yìng*. The rhyme is *qióng*. According to the *Cāngjiépiān*, it means "to guard" (*yìngwèi*). *Yíng* also means a "division" (*bù*).

Regarding the "Audience" (zhāo) and "Veneration" (zōng) in the *Zhou Lǐ*: "The audience held in spring is called zhāo; that held in summer is called zōng. Zheng Xuan commented: "These are the protocols for the feudal lords' audiences with the Son of Heaven. 'Zhāo' is like 'morning' (zhāo), expressing the desire for them to come early; 'zōng' is like 'veneration' (zūn), expressing the desire for them to show honor."

The character *pí* (補革反) means "to split" according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*; it also means "to tear. According to the *Guangya*, it means "to divide. The version in the *Lunwen* uses *bì* (補赤反), which means "lame"; it is also written as *pī* (匹尺反), meaning "crooked" or "deviant. Neither of these two forms is appropriate for this context.
12. Volume Twelve. "Zengyi" (贈遺). According to the *Guoyá*, "yi" (遺) means to give. To present someone with articles for amusement or enjoyment is called "zengyi."

In the *Gouyuan* (Distant and Long) section of the *Guoyu*, it says: "The roads are distant. Jia Kui stated: "‘You’ means long. The *Erya* states: "‘You’ means remote. Shen Ren stated: "'You' refers to the distance of one's journey."
Regarding "jūchuáng" (疽瘡): furthermore, the *Shuowen* states that "jū" means a long-standing carbuncle (*yōng*).
Regarding "jìnglì" (勁利): the *Shuowen* states that "jìng" means strong; its character form is composed of the radical "force" (*lì*) and the phonetic "xīng" (*jīng*).

13. The thirteenth fascicle. "Jili" (姞利)—the character for "li" is pronounced with the *qiu* and *fan* tones; it is the name of a dragon. According to the characters, it was the surname of the Southern Yan dynasty.

"Hao-shuang" (豪爽)—the character for "shuang" is pronounced with the *suo* and *yang* tones; according to the *Fangyan*, it means fierce and bold; according to the *Guangya*, it means bright and clear. The character is composed of two "da" (大) radicals; because a great person must possess illumination, it includes the "da" radical.
*Huanqu* (𦇞綣): "Qu" is pronounced as *qū* (with the tone of *ruǎn*). It means to be entangled and lingering, not parting or dispersing. *Mùrán* (憮然): "Mù" is pronounced as *wǔ*.

According to the *Sāncāng*, it is an expression for being disheartened; it is a term used for astonishment and alarm. In the *Lúnyǔ*, regarding the passage "The Master was *mùrán*," Hé Yàn said: "It was because [the interlocutor] did not understand his meaning and thus criticized him. In the *Hànshū*, regarding the term "*mùrán*," Wéi Zhāo said: "It refers to a state where one has the thought but has not yet spoken it."
*Tiè* (鐵鍱): The rhyme is *yú* (餘). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that in the Qi state, *zhèn* (鎭) was called *tiè*. *Cǎo* (鏶) has the pronunciation *jí* (集). *Mǎnfǎn* (僶俛):
The rhymes are *wǎng* (亡) and *rěn* (忍) with the *pàn* (辨) rhyme. This refers to giving away one's own wife; it is as in the *Lunyu*: "He gave his daughter in marriage to him" (*yǐ qí zǐ qī zhī*).

The characters *máo* (毫) and *lì* (𣯛)—the latter being an archaic form of *liàn* (練)—are now written as *máo* (𣮉), both pronounced with the rhyme *li* (力). The "Chronicle of Music and Calendar" (*Lǜlìzhì*) in the *Hànshū* states: "not missing even a hair’s breadth" (*bù shī háo lì*). Mèng Kāng’s commentary notes: "A hair is rabbit hair; ten hairs are called a *lì*. The *Sāncuāng* dictionary defines *lì* as "hair. The character is also written as *lí* (釐), pronounced *xī* (僖). Wéi Zhāo’s *Hànshū Yìnyì* states: "The remains of the meat after the sacrifice to ghosts and spirits is called *lí*. The *Shuōwén Jiězì* defines *lí* as "domestic fortune. These ancient characters are also used interchangeably.
"Shi" (適) is pronounced with the *du* and *li* rhymes; it refers to the primary consort (*zhushì*). "Shanfu" (善府):

according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "fu" means a storehouse; according to the *Sancang*, "fu" means a place where documents, wealth, and goods are stored; according to the *Fengsu Tong*, "fu" means a collection—a place where official documents and valuables are gathered and guarded in a public district.
"Lin-sǒu" (林藪) refers to a marsh; that which has no water is called a "sǒu," which is also a large marsh where water is scarce.

"Xī-xiǎng" (翕響)—the characters are pronounced as hū and jí respectively—refers to the city of Shǔ. In the commentary on "xī-xiǎng huī-huò" (翕響揮霍), it says this means "in the space of a sudden moment."

"To exterminate" (*yímiè*) means "to destroy" (*guǎngyǎ*). According to the *Shìjì*, it refers to the "extermination of three clans" (*yísānzú*). In the *Guóyuè*, regarding the phrase "exterminating the hearth and filling the well," Jia Dui states that "exterminate" (*yí*) means "to demolish" (*huǐ*).

*Wei* (委) means to set aside; *yu* (紆) means to be circuitous or complex. This corresponds to the *Zhou Li*, where it is said that what is small is called *wei* and what is large is called *ji* (積); thus, it refers to accumulation.
*Qing yi* (輕泆) is now written as *yi* (溢), with the same pronunciation. It refers to water being overflowed or surging forth.

The characters *háo* (豪) and *jié* (傑) share the same phonetic component *wǔ*. The first character is pronounced with the rhyme *hú gāo* (胡高), and the second with *qí zhé* (奇哲). The *Huáinán Zǐ* states: "One whose wisdom exceeds that of a hundred men is called a *háo*; one who exceeds a thousand is called a *jié*. Thus, *háo* is synonymous with *jùn* (俊, eminent). The *Dà Dài Lǐ* says: "*Háo* means a master; *jié* means to stand out uniquely, like an *yīngjié* (heroic talent); it also refers to ability and talent. In the *Lùnwén*, the character is written as *jié* (桀). When a rooster perches on a wooden peg, it is called *jié* (桀), but this is not the meaning intended here.

The ancient texts write *guàn* (串) with two forms, *guǎn* (摜) and *jiǎn* (遦), and it is also written as *guàn* (慣) with the same pronunciation as *gǔhuàn* (古患). According to the *Erya*, it means "habitual practice"; She Ren says, "It is the habituation of the mind."

14. Volume Fourteen, Chapter Fourteen. *Mo* (募): Pronounced as *wu* and *ju* (two rhymes) in the ancient style; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to seek extensively. According to the *Cangjie Pian*, it means "to seek within."
Regarding the line "I lodge my complaint with the Great State" (*kòng yú dàbāng*), the *Zhuàn* says: "To lodge (*kòng*) means to lead forth. The *Mānshī* says: "To lodge (*kòng*) means to go toward.

Regarding "to provide relief" (*jiū jiù*, now written as *zhōu*, same pronunciation as *yóu*), it means to give goods and wealth to others; this is called "providing relief" (*zhōu*). The *Rituals of Zhou* states: "Five *dǎng* form a *zhōu*, so that they may provide for one another. Zheng Xuan says: "'Providing' (*zhōu*) refers to when ritual items are incomplete, providing them so they are sufficient. The *Shī* says: "There is no one whom he does not provide for" (*mǐ bù rén zhōu*). The *Zhuàn* says: "'Providing' (*zhōu*) means to rescue. The *Jiàn* says: "He rescues their urgent needs."

*Tǐng* (the boat): "tú" (with the initial *dǐng*) according to the *Fānyán*. In the region of Nanchǔ along the rivers and lakes, small boats are called *tǐng*. Guō Pǔ says: "*Tǐng* is synonymous with *zhǒng*. The *Shìmíng* states: "Those of two hundred *hú* or more are called *tǐng*. *Zhǒng* is pronounced *sī* (with the final *-lù*) and *liù* (with the final *-fǎn*); *zhǒng* is pronounced *diāo*.

"Cuò" (措) is pronounced *gu* (反) [in the *Zìlín*]. It means "to implement" (*cùzhì*). In the *Lǐjì*, it says: "The gentleman is clear regarding ritual and music; he simply lifts them up and implements them (*cuò*). Zheng Xuan said: "Cuò means 'to apply' (*shī*). In the discourse on the *Lùn* [the *Lùn-yǔ*], it is written as "cù" (厝), pronounced *rì* (各) [in the *Shuōwén*]. The *Shuōwén* states: "Cù is a whetstone; it means to grind. As the *Shījīng* says: "The stones of other mountains can be used as cù. This "cù" is not the same character as the "cuò" in the *Lùn*.

*Mo* (pronounced with the *le* rhyme): According to the *Shuowen*, it means to advance suddenly. In the *Guoyu*, regarding the phrase "the Rong and Di *mo* [and] *mei*" (戎狄冒沒), Jia Ji stated that "*mo mei*" is equivalent to "to lightly provoke. The character's form consists of the radicals "mouth" (*yue*) and "see" (*jian*). "Mouth" is pronounced *mang bao*. Nowadays, all versions write it as *mao*. According to this, *mao* is pronounced *wang bao*; it means to cover or to obscure. It also means to covet.
*Tì* (pronounced with the *tí* and *lì* finals reversed): In the *Erya*, *tì* means "to abandon" (*fèi*). Li Xun says: "To set aside and abandon.

*Gāngbì* (pronounced with the *fú* and *bī* finals reversed): In the *Zuozhuan*, *bìjiàn wéibǔ*. Du Yu’s commentary states: "*Bì* means perverse (*lì*). It is further said: "Stubborn and unkind; *bì* means obstinate (*hèn*)."

15. Fifteenth Fascicle. Fifteenth Fascicle. *Mianli* (勉勵) is also written as *jué* (勱), with the same pronunciation. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to exert oneself. The second character, *lǜ* (呂), has the phonetic value *zhì* (制); it refers to encouraging and stimulating oneself.

Regarding "yángtóng" (沸騰): though it is cool to the touch, when boiled it becomes soft and dissolves, appearing vast and overflowing (*yángyáng*). The *Sāncāng* states that "yáng" is the appearance of a great body of water; the *Éryǎ* says it means "overflowing. Guo Pu comments: "Overflowing" means being numerous and abundant.

"Bi" (避) is pronounced *p'jwei* (with the rhyme *pjwei*). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to avoid" (*hui*). According to the *Cangjie pian*, it means "to depart from. It refers to keeping a distance. "Wei" (隈) is pronounced *wu hui* (with the rhyme *wu hui*) and, according to the *Shuowen*, is pronounced *yi you*. It refers to a curved recess of water; that is, a place of concealment. In the treatise, it is written as "wei" (偎), pronounced *wu hui*, meaning "to love. However, "wei" does not carry this meaning here.
"Ji shi" (幾失) is pronounced "qu yi fan" (渠衣反); it means "near. This refers to being close to losing something yet not actually losing it.

"Kun chong" (蜫蟲)—the ancient text uses "gun" (䖵), which is pronounced "gu hun fan" (古魂反)—is explained in the *Liji* as "kun-chong have not yet entered hibernation. Zheng Xuan explains that "kun" means "clear" (*ming*); "clear insects" are those born of yang and hidden away by yin. The *Xiaoxing* states: "Kun are small insects; 'kun' is 'hun. They are called 'hun-hun' because these small insects move about."

*Chuán yù* (穿窬): *zhū* (朱) and *fǎn* (反) are the readings; the *Sāncāng* (三蒼) states that *yù* refers to a small aperture by the side of a gate. The *Shuōwén* (說文) says it is a hole for draining water by the side of a gate, as in the case of Dongfang Shuo’s “piercing and burrowing without following the path. It is also pronounced *tú gòu fǎn* (徒構反); in the *Lǐjì* (禮記), regarding "the *bìmén* (蓽門) and *guīyù* (圭窬)," Zheng Xuan says: "*Yù* is an aperture by the side of a gate; one pierces through the wall to make it, and its shape is like a *guī* (圭). In the *Lùn Wén* (論文), it is written as *yú* (踰), meaning to overstep or to cross; however, *yú* is not the correct character form.
"Yin-yi" (淫佚) is the opposite of restraint; according to the *Guǎyá*, it means "leisurely pleasure," while the *Cāngjiépiān* states it means "licentiousness.

"Bu-mù" (不睦)—also written as "Mù" (穆)—is pronounced with the two rhymes *máng* and *zhú*, and *mò* and *lù*. In the *Shàngshū*, regarding the passage "The nine clans were already in harmony" (*jiǔzú jì mù*), Kǒng Àngguó says that "mù" means "harmony. Furthermore, regarding the passage "I shall act with harmony" (*wǒ qí rú mù*), Kǒng Àngguó says that "mù" means "reverence."

*Pi* (匹尺反): The *Shijing* states, "The people have many *pi*. The *Zhu* commentary says, "*Pi* means depravity. Examining this, *pi* refers to conducting affairs in a crooked and perverse manner that does not accord with principle.
*Kao* (作余昭反): The *Shuowen* defines it as a kiln for firing tiles. The *Tongsu Wen* states that a kiln for pottery is called a *kao*.
*Huǎng* (怳) and *hū* (忽) are two ancient forms of the same character, both pronounced with the *huàng* rhyme.

*Hū* means to forget. *Zōng* (宗): the character is pronounced with the *tóng* rhyme; it refers to what one inherits. According to the *Zílín*, *zōng* means "honored" (*zūn*) and also "master" (*zhǔ*). The *Guǎngyá* states that *zōng* means "root" (*běn*). In the *Chǔcí*, those of the same surname are called *zōng*. *Zú* (族): pronounced with the *cóng* rhyme, it means "kindred. According to the *Zhōulǐ*, four *lǚ* (neighborhoods) constitute a *zú*; Zhèng Xuán says this refers to one hundred households.

16. Volume Sixteen, Part Sixteen. *Feiwěi* (斐亹): *fú wěi*, with the variant reading *wáng fěi*. It means "as if there were. As the *Shijing* says, "There is a magnificent (*fěi*) gentleman," and the *Zhuan* explains that *fěi* is the appearance of patterned ornamentation. Regarding the *Zhouyi*’s phrase "accomplishing the world’s *měnměi*," Liu Huán states that *měn* is like "subtle" (*wēiwēi*).

"Kneeling long" (chángguì) is a phonetic loan for "kneeling with the knees pressed to the ground" (guìjù). The *Shìmíng* states: "Kneeling means 'perilous' (wéi); both knees rest upon the ground while the body remains in a precarious, upright position. The character 𨺙 (yù) is pronounced with the initial *wǔ* and the final *jié*.

In various texts, "ruǎn" (軟) is written identically as "ruán" (耎), with the phonetic gloss "yùn fǎn" (兖反). In the *Hànshū* (Book of Han), the term "ruǎnrúo bù shèngrén" (軟弱不勝任) is written as "ruǎn" (軟).

Regarding "zú" (卒): it is pronounced "zǐ lǜ fǎn" (子律反). According to the *Ěryá* (Classic of Etymology), "zú" means "end. Shèrén says: "Zú refers to the end of illness. Lǐ Xún says: "Zú refers to the completion of an affair."
*Tián-dàn* (恬澹): *dàn* is pronounced with the rhyme of *tú-làn*. According to the *Fāng-yán*, it means "serene stillness. According to the *Guǎng-yǎ*, *dàn* means "tranquil.

*Qiē-tí* (呿提) is also written as *jiē* (㰦), both pronounced with the rhyme of *qiū-shù*; in the language of Qin, it means "empty space. According to the character in the *Běi-cāng*, it means "to open the mouth."

The character 踣 (póu) is sometimes written as 蹷 (jué). Both are pronounced with the two initials *jù* and *yue* (as in *jū* and *yuè*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "踣" means to fall prostrate; it refers to being cast down and lying flat. The *Guangya* states that "踣" means to collapse. The version of the *Lunwen* uses "蹷. The archaic form is 躗, both pronounced with the two initials *jù* and *yue* (as in *jū* and *yuè*). According to the *Erya*, "蹷" means to move suddenly. Upon examination, "蹷" carries the sense of being startled, alarmed, or acting with sudden urgency; it does not mean this [prostration].
*Kànguān* (間關) refers to the appearance of reaching one's destination after traversing rugged and arduous terrain; it also means to establish or arrange. *Guò* (惈) [pronounced *gǔ* or *huò*]:

according to the *Guǎngyá*, *guò* means "courageous"; the *Cāngjiépiān* states that *guò* means "bold" (*hán*). To slay the enemy is called *guò*. According to the *Ěryá*, *guò* means "victory. Sūn Yán said: "*Guò* is the victory of decisive resolve. It is also written as *guǒ* (果). *Hán* (憨) [pronounced *hú* or *lán*].

17. Volume Seventeen. "Qiuhuo" (Autumn Harvest). [The character] *huo* is pronounced as *guò* (in the sense of the *Shuowen*). The *Shuowen* states that *huo* means to reap grain. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chu Ci* says: "For grass it is called *yi* (reaping); for grain it is called *huo* (harvesting)."

"Yingying" (嫇嫇): according to the *Zilin*, it is pronounced "yi-jing" (乙莖) or "mang-jing" (茫莖); it refers to a state of mind, and also means to look closely. The *Lunwen* (Treatise) writes this as "tai" (𥌽), for which no source has yet been found.

"Huangni" (黃髯): the character "lian" (廉) is pronounced "ru" (如); "nian" (髯) refers to the hair on the cheeks. The *Shiming* states: "The area beside the ears on the cheeks is called 'nian'; it moves back and forth with the mouth, appearing 'nian-nian' (fluttering). The *Lunwen* sometimes uses the character "fa" (髮, hair) instead.

*Chì* (pronounced *chì*, with the radical for "teeth" and the phonetic *yì*): according to the *Cāngjié piān*, it means to scold or reprimand. This is as stated in the *Lǐjì*: "In the presence of a guest of honor, one does not scold the dog.
*Dǒu xún* (pronounced *qiě xún*): according to the *Ěryǎ*, *dǒu* means to retreat. Guō Pǔ says: "To *dǒu xún* is to withdraw and step back."

*Yù* (pronounced *yóu tāo* with the second character pronounced *yì zháo*) is explained in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as "brilliant light" (*yù guāng yào yě*). *Yào* is "the light of fire" (*huǒ guāng yě*). According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "blazing" (*chì*); according to the *Bīcāng*, it is an appearance of "abundance" (*shèng*). The *Lùn Wén* uses the character *yù* (昱), saying it means "bright. *Shuò* (pronounced *shì zháo*) is the same character as *shuò* (鑠), meaning "to melt away" (*xiāo shuò*), but this is not the meaning here.

Regarding "shackles" (zhìgù): "gù" is the opposite of "fǎn" (to release) in the *Zhou Lǐ* (Rites of Zhou), where the Master of Prisoners is charged with all captives; for those whose crimes are of middling severity, they are shackled. Zheng Xuan states: "Those on the hands are called zhì;

those on the feet are called gù. Regarding "huímiàn" (a sidelong glance): it is explained as "oblique vision" in the *Shuowen Jiezi*. According to the *Fangyan*, in the region west of the Guanzhong area, specifically among the Qin and Jin peoples, this is called miàn.
*Tián* (古文 *tián*, same as *tújiān*): to fill; according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means to block or stuff. *Yàn* (即 *yàn*, pinyin *īyǎn*):

according to the *Zìyuǎn*, it refers to an inauspicious omen within a bedchamber; according to the *Cāngjiépiān*, that which accords with the human heart is called *yàn*; in the Shandong dialect, it is pronounced *īqiè*; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means to join or press together, and the character is composed of the radical *hǎn* (pronounced *hēqiě*).

The ancient characters for *bǔ* (𤑏) and *zhǔ* (煑) share the same pronunciation as *fúbī* (扶逼). According to the *Fāngyán* (Dialectal Dictionary), *bǔ* means to dry with fire; those from Guānxī, Lǒng, and Jì refer to this process as *bǔ*. The *Shuōwén* states that drying meat with fire is called *bǔ*.

18. Volume Eighteen. The character *hùn* (pronounced with the second tone for *hu* and the fourth tone for *dùn*) is defined in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as a latrine (*cè*). In the *Cangjie Pian*, it is said to be the dwelling place of pigs; the character is composed of the mouth radical with a pig inside, which is its semantic meaning. In the *Lunwen*, it is written as *hùn*; here *hùn* means turbid or chaotic. *Hùn* is not the standard orthography.
"Ji-liu" (稽留)—the "liu" is pronounced as in the *Zilin* dictionary; it means to linger or to stop.

"Xian-sheng" (懸繩)—in the *Lunwen*, this is often written as "xuan" (鉉), which is pronounced as in "hu-da"; this refers to the handle for lifting a cauldron. This [character] is not used here; as for the term "sheng" (繩, rope), its source has not yet been identified.
*Néng jué* (能決): "To resolve" or "to decide. *Guī yuè* (閨恱): According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, this means "to flow downward," or alternatively, "to pierce and break.

*Fǎn shuōwén xià liú yě* (反說文下流也). Furthermore, *chuān jué* (穿決) refers to the same. *Luò luó gè fǎn* (烙羅各反): This refers to burning and boiling things and placing them [therein]. The *Lunwen* (論文) writes it as *sháo* (爍), with the phonetic transcription *shì zhuó fǎn* (式灼反), meaning "to melt. *Sháo* (爍) is not the correct character for the intended meaning.

*Jīmù* (the reading *mò* is a variant). The *Erya* states: "The *shūfú* is the *mù*. Guo Pu’s commentary says: "This is the duck (*yā*). Li Xun says: the wild variety is called *fú*, while the domestic variety is called *mù*; it is also known as the *shūfú*. According to Mr. So-and-so: when in the wild, its wings spread wide for long-distance flight, and it is then called *jīn*."

The character *jù* (距) is the same as *juǐ* (𠲿), pronounced with the *zǐ-lèi* rhyme group. According to the *Guǎngyá*, "距" means "mouth"; according to lexicographical works, it refers to a bird's beak, or is written as *zuǐ* (觜). In the *Lùn-wén*, it is written as *zhì* (𭉨). Upon examining various scriptures and histories, no such character exists; only in Fu Yi’s *Qījī* (*Seven Stimuli*) it says, "The *zhì* (𭉨) drinks from the spring," using this character with the pronunciation *xú-ruǎn*. However, *zhì* does not convey the intended meaning. The archaic forms of *jù* are *jù* (詎) and *jù* (岠), both pronounced with the *jū-lǚ* and *qú-lǚ* rhyme groups. According to the *Shuōwén*, it refers to the spur on a rooster's foot.

*Qi* (蚑) [the character for "crab" is pronounced *jù* (巨) according to the *Tōngsúwén*; the vulgar term for "seeking" is called *qí* (蚑); in the region west of the Pass, *qiū* (溲) is called *qí* (蚑), with the pronunciation *qiú* (求); the *Shēnglèi* states that it is a many-legged insect]. *Sǒu* (溲) [is pronounced *sōu* (誅) according to the rhyme]. It refers to a multi-legged creature.

*Hú-mù* (the screech owl): according to the *Erya*, it is the "strange *chī*" (*guài-chī*). She Ren states that it has one name, "strange bird" (*guài-āo*), and another, "*hú-liú*"; in Nanyang it is called *gōu-xī*. The *Zilin* identifies it as the *chī-hú*.

The character for *jué* (猨狖) is written as 𤠙 or 猳, both sharing the same pronunciation. Adding the radical below, it is read as *jūfó* or *jūbì*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "A large female monkey; she is skilled at looking around and gazing, and the *jué* seizes and holds people. The *Erya* says: "*Juéfù* is skilled at looking around. Guo Pu comments: "The *jué* is like a macaque but larger, with a dark blue-black color; it is skilled at grasping and holding people, and delights in looking around and gazing. The *Gujin Zhu* states: "A monkey transforms into a *jué* after five hundred years. The *Fupuzi* states: "A macaque transforms into a *jué* after eight hundred years; its lifespan is one thousand years. This is correct.

*Tāotuò* (饕餮) is an archaic term written with two characters, *tāo* (䬢/叨) and *tuò* (餮), both pronounced with the same initial *th-*, *gao* (高), and *fan* (反) finals as *tāo* (他). Its correct form is written as *yìn* (飻), also pronounced with the *th-* initial, *jie* (結), and *fan* final. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "greed. In the *Zuo Zhuan*, it is said: "The descendant of the Lord of Jingyun was an unworthy man; he was greedy for food and drink and rapacious for wealth and bribes; he amassed and accumulated treasures without knowing any limit. The people of the world called him Tāotuò. Du Yu commented: "To be greedy for wealth is called *tāo*; to be greedy for food is called *tuò*."

"Sunken eyes" (*yanxian*): In the *Chuci*, "sunken" (*xian*) means to be stuck and unable to advance; Wang Yi says it means "to sink. Examining this, "sunken" (*xian*) is like falling into a person's [misfortune]. The discussion of the treatise uses "sunken eyes" (*xianmu*), which should be close to this meaning.

"Dǎngdí (盪滌): the first character is read as *tóng* with the tone of *tú* (徒), and the second as *lì* (歷). 'Dǎngdí' refers to rinsing vessels; in the *Shàngshū*, regarding 'the nine rivers having their sources dredged' (*jiǔchuān díyuán*), Kǒng Ānguó states that 'dí' means 'to clear away' (*chú*).”

The character for *tièshǎn* (iron skewer) is pronounced *chūyǎn* (初眼) in the *Zìyuàn* (Dictionary Garden); it refers to the iron skewers used today for roasting meat. The *Zílüè* (Brief Dictionary of Characters) states that it means "to pierce meat with a sharp point" (*yīxiān guànròu qí yě*). The treatise uses the character *chǎn*, while the current version uses *chǎn* (剗), which means "to shave" or "to pare."

I have torn apart and examined various dictionaries, but no such character exists. According to the meaning of the characters, it should be written as "jué" (攫). In the *Bǐjiǔ* (碧九), it is read with the two tones *fú* (縛) and *èr* (二). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "to grasp with the claws. The *Liji* says, "The *juéchóng* (攫蟲) grasps [its prey] with its claws."
Regarding the characters *pin* (拼) and *du* (度) in the archaic script, *bi* (鞞) has two forms, both pronounced with the *bu* and *geng* rhyme.

*Pin* means to stretch out the plumb line and the carpenter’s square. *Tuan* (摶) is pronounced with the *tu* and *guan* rhyme; according to the *Tongsu wen*, "to clench with the hand" is called *tuan*; the *Shuowen jiezi* states that *tuan* means "round"; the *Shenglei* says it means "to grasp"; and the *Zilin* uses *tuan* for "clenching," pronouncing it with the *du* and *wan* rhyme. In the *Lunwen*, it is written as *chuai* (揣), with the two rhymes *chu*, *wei*, *duo*, and *guo*, meaning "to measure" or "to estimate. *Chuai* is not the correct meaning here.

The *Ěryā* states that the *bó* (pronounced bù jiǎo) is like a horse with protruding tusks and eats tigers and leopards. Shèrén says the *bó* is a beast of great strength. The *Shānhǎijīng* says that on Mount Qū there is a beast shaped like a horse, with a white body and black mane, a single horn, tiger claws, and a voice like a drum; its name is *bó*, it eats tigers and leopards, and it can ward off weapons. The *Shī* says, "In the marshes are six *bó*. In the third year of the Huángchū era of the Wèi dynasty, six *bó* were seen again in the wilds.
*Yǎo niè* (齩齧) is also written as *chuí* (䶧), sharing the same pronunciation as *wǔ jiǎo* (五狡). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "to bite bone. According to the *Guangya*, it means "to gnaw.

*Jiè chè* (齧掣) is also written as *jiè* (𪘨), sharing the same pronunciation as *zhú jiē* (竹皆). According to the *Tongshu Wen*, "to pull while biting is called *jiè*. According to the *Guangya*, it means "to gnaw and pull."
*Lì* (轢): Pronounced *lè* (variously read as *li* and *liè*). According to the *Cāngjié piān*, it means "to roll over" (*zhǎn*). According to the *Shuōwén*, it refers to what a vehicle treads upon.
It is like *zé* (笮), pronounced *zè* (variously read as *cè* and *gé*). Examining *zé*, it means "to press. Today, it refers to pressing out juice using a trough or press.
*Róu* (蹂) means ancient texts; *ǒu* (厹), *tóng* (同), *rén* (仁), and *qiú rén* (求仁)—the latter two rhyming with *liù* (柳). According to the *Tōngsúwén* (通俗文), to tread upon grain is called *róu*;

the *Cāngjiépiān* (蒼頡篇) states it means to tread. *Zhě* (赭) refers to a field of reddish-brown soil; according to the *Sāncāng* (三蒼), *zhě* is red earth. The *Fānyán* (方言) states that in the regions between Nanchǔ and Dōnghǎi, it is sometimes called *yì* (亦) or *zhě* (赭); Guō Pǔ (郭璞) similarly explains it as clothing that is red.

"Peng" (烹) means "to boil" (羹), specifically to cook by boiling; according to the *Fangyan*, it means "to mature by boiling. South of Mount Song, in the regions of Chen and Ying, they say "peng. In the *Yili*, all that is boiled in a cauldron (*huo*) is called "peng," while that which is boiled in a tripod (*ding*) is called "wai" (外).

The character *xián* (燂) is phonetically similar to *shēng* (聲). It has two variant forms: *xiàn* (燂) and *yù* (鬻). In ancient texts, it was written as *xiàn* (𤏖) and *yù* (鬻). Today, it is written as *xín* (燅), with the same pronunciation as *xiáng-lián* (詳廉) [i.e., *xián*]. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "to *xián*" means to blanch meat in hot water. The *Tongsu Wén* states that removing the hair with boiling water is called *yù*. In the *Lunwen*, it is written as *xián* (爓). According to the *Shuowen*, various commentaries on the *Shudu Fu* give the pronunciation as *yú-zhàn* (余贍) or *yáng-zhàn* (羊占). The *Shuowen* defines *xián* (爓) as "flaming fire" (*huǒ xián-xián*). This [usage of] *xián* is not the meaning used today.

*Zhé* (磔) is the same as the ancient character *ní* (尼), pronounced with the *gé* (格) rhyme. According to the *Guǎngyá*, *zhé* means "to stretch" (*zhāng*) and "to open" (*kāi*). The *Shuōwén* defines it as "the act of execution" (*gū*). The *Ěryá* states, "The sacrifice to the Wind is called *zhé*," and Sūn Yán explains: "Having performed the sacrifice, one tears open [the victim] to disperse its nature through the wind. The version in the *Lùnwén* uses *zhó* (挓), for which no source has yet been found.

Regarding "fierce and resolute" (*mèngyì*), the *Shàngshū* states that one is still "resolute" (*yòu gǎoyì*) because of one's courage and determination. Kǒng Àngguó says: "To kill the enemy is 'courage' (*guǒ*); to bring about that courage is 'resoluteness' (*yì*). The *Shuowén* defines it as "reckless anger," or alternatively, "having a decisive resolve."

"Tièyí" (鐵杙)—the "yí" is pronounced as "yú zhí fǎn. In the *Erya*, it says: "A wooden stake is called yí. Guo Pu states: "Yí refers to a wedge or a pin. In the *Lunwen* (Discourse on Literature), there is a reading "tièsuō" (iron shuttle), which is an error in transcription. "Tú" (樴) is pronounced as "tú dé fǎn."

*Tui* (踼突) is now written identically to *ti* (逷), with the phonetic component *ji* (即). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to snatch" (*qiang*). The *Cangjie pian* describes it as the appearance of galloping; it also means to lose one's tracks. Regarding the sound, it is associated with *tu* (跗). Examining the characters, they should properly be written as *tang* (搪) and *pu* (揬), which are two distinct forms.

"Copper stake" (tóng guì): the character "guì" is pronounced as jù yuè (according to the *Shuowen*). It means a wooden peg or stake (*yí*). The *Lunwen* (Treatise) writes it as "zhān" (鐝). The *Beicang* states it is a "mò zhān. The *Sutongwen* says that when things are leveled, they are called "zhān zhān. This is not the meaning intended here.

*Che* (發撤): Pronounced *chê* with the *liè* (列) and *fǎn* (反) tones. According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means to demolish; it also means to remove. In the *Yílǐ* (Rituals), regarding the passage "one then removes [the vessels]," Zheng Xuan states:

"To remove (*chè*) means to clear away. *Jìnzhàn* (噤戰): The archaic form is the same as *qín* (唫). Pronounced *qú yǐn fǎn*. In the *Chǔcí* (Elegies of Chu), regarding the phrase "mumbling and remaining silent," Wang Yi states: "To close the mouth so that it does not open is called *jìn*."
*Jiexie*: In the *Zilin*, the lower character is read as *jiǎ* (甲). "Jiexie" refers to ice pieces adhering to one another. The version in the *Lunwen* uses *jiǎ* (甲), which is not the correct form.

*Băngzhòu*: The upper character is read as *bóhéng* (薄衡); the lower character is also written as *chī* (笞), with the same pronunciation *chǒuzhī* (丑之). According to the *Zishū*, it means "to flog"; according to the *Guǎngyá*, "bāngchī" (榜笞) means "to strike."

*Ji* (忌): Pronounced *qú jì fǎn*. According to the *Guǎyá*, it means "fear. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means "to detest or loathe. *Dàn* (憚): Pronounced *tú qiě fǎn*. It means "to find difficult or daunting.
*Zǔ* (俎): Pronounced *zé zhuāng lǚ fǎn*. According to the *Fānyán*, it is a "small table" (*jǐ*). According to the *Zìshū*, it is a "meat-stand" (*ròu jǐ*).

"Wèi" (蔚) is pronounced with the rhyme "mào" (茂) and the reverse of "cāngjié" (蒼頡); it describes the flourishing appearance of plants and trees in the *Cāngjié piān*. In the *Lùnwén* (論語), it is sometimes written as "yù" (鬱), pronounced with the rhyme "qū" (屈). The *Shuōwén* states that when trees grow in dense clusters, they are called "yù.
"Pù" (曝) is pronounced with the rhyme "fú" (扶) and "bǔ" (卜). The *Shuōwén* states that "pù" means to expose to the sun to dry; the character is composed of "yuè" (曰), "chū" (出), and "mi" (米).
19. Volume Nineteen. "Xún" (古文同許朝反) means clamor; it refers to noisy and boisterous chatter, as in the *Zuozhuan*: "The water overflowed and the dust was clamorous. This is what is meant.

"Without assistance" (*wúyuán*): "assistance" (*yuán*) refers to the words for relying upon and providing protection. "Pregnant" (*huáiyùn*): the ancient text uses the same character as *yíng* (pronounced *zhèng*).

To contain the fruit within is called "pregnant"; according to the *Sāncāng*, it means "to harbor a child. According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, "pregnancy" (*yùn*) is the same as *huái*. The character is composed of "child" (*zǐ*) and the phonetic "nǎi. In the *Lùnwén*, it is written as "to harbor and conceive" (*huáirèn*); "conceive" (*rèn*) is synonymous with "pregnancy" (*yùn*).

The character *tǐ* (體) is a phonetic reversal of *zhèn* (振). In the *Erya*, "yìn" (胤) means succession; Sharen says, "yìn refers to the succession of generations. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states, "Yin means that sons and grandsons inherit and continue one another; it is a term for successive procreation."

*Ōu* (古遐反, gǔ xiá fǎn): A female deer; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it sheds its antlers at the summer solstice, whereas the *mí* (elk) sheds its antlers at the winter solstice. *Ōu* is an archaic form identical to *yú* (於牛反, yú niú fǎn). According to the *Erya*, "the female deer is called *ōu*; the female cow is called *zì*."

"Shēn" (pronounced shū lín) refers to being pregnant, meaning to carry a fetus in the womb; within these texts, the character "shēn" is also written as "shēn," and both forms are used interchangeably.

*Kuṇḍikā* is the correct transliteration for what is translated here as "bottle"; it refers to a double-mouthed ritual vessel for washing. The form "kùlǐ" found in the treatises has no source and is merely a vulgar variation.

The ancient characters for *qí* (branching path) are two forms, *qí* (𪨵) and *yí* (󲭗), both pronounced with the rhyme *qú-yí*. This refers to the differentiation of skills and meanings. The *Erya* states: "A path with two branches is called *qí*. Guo Pu says: "*Qí* refers to a path that goes straight out. The *Shiming* says: "When things are divided into two, they are called *qí*; that which is on the left side is called *páng* (side); a path is so called because it runs alongside [another]."

*Bo* (in *bolu*, pronounced with the *bu* and *ge* finals reversed) means to strike or clasp; it is like the act of patting or striking. It is also said that [the Duke of Jin] dreamed of wrestling with the Lord of Chu; Du Yu stated this refers to hand-to-hand wrestling (*shoubó*). In the *Konggongji*, it means to strike or beat; furthermore, it means to seize or capture.

20. The twentieth fascicle. The character *pēng* (also written as *pīn*, with the phonetic equivalent *pǔ gēng*) is explained in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as "to strike" (*pēng tán*). It refers, for example, to "striking wool" (*pēng máo*) or "striking a bow" (*pēng gōng*), and so forth.

*Chichuo* (尺蠖) is the same as *wuguo* (烏郭), which is the same as *sangchong* (桑蟲). According to the *Shuowen*, it is a worm that contracts and extends. The *Erya* states: "The *chichuo* is the *chichuo*. Guo Pu says it is the *jizhi* (蝍𧑙), pronounced *zili* (子力) and *zi-liu* (子六); it is also called *bugu* (步屈). She Ren says that in the state of Song it is called *sun* (尋) or *sang* (桑).
21. Fascicle Twenty-one. Regarding the term *yī* (衣): according to the commentary, it means to cover with clothing or bedding; thus, *yīyī* (衣衣) refers to the act of putting on or wearing clothing.
"Shi" (食) is also written as "Si" (飤), with the phonetic gloss *qiu zhi* (囚志). To provide food and drink as an offering to another person is called "shi-shi" (食食);

"shi" (食) here also refers to rice or grain. "Chi" (眵) has the phonetic gloss *chong shi* (充尸); according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means the turbid discharge from the eyes (*meng*, with the gloss *mo jie*). The version in the *Lunwen* (論文) writes it as "yao" (𥄏), which is unclear as to its source.
*Jiéxiāng* (結聹): The "xiāng" is pronounced as the *fǎn* (rhyme) of *lěng* (冷); the *Pīcāng* states that *xiāng* refers to the wax of the ears.
*Yúduō* (俞多): The "yú" is pronounced as the *fǎn* of *yízhū* (弋朱); the *Guǎngyá* states that *yú* means "to increase," and the *Xiǎoyǎ* states that *yú* here means "to strengthen and increase."
*Shǎn* (蝡) means to move; it is read as *rú yǔn* (如允). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *shǎn* also means movement; this refers to the "crawling insects" (*fūchóng*) mentioned in the *Huainanzi*.
*Kù* (崫) is read as *yú quē* (魚屈); the *Pīcāng* states it means to stand upright. This refers to the expressions in the *Shiji*: "standing alone like a *kù*" and "sitting alone like a clod."

22. Fascicle Twenty-two. The character for "bone-trunk" (gǔgàn) is written as 䯎 (pinyin: gē; same as the phonetic component of 歌), with the auxiliary 且 (qiè). It means "to assist," and it also refers to the physical frame or skeletal remains.

"Shi-zhan" (viewing and divining) is a reversal of the *fāng-yán* (dialectal gloss); "zhan" means to view. "Zhan" also means to observe; all acts of mutual observation are called "zhan," for "zhan" implies looking up at or regarding.

(Volume 23 is missing). Volume 24. "Cí-jué" (parting words): "jué" is pronounced as in "gǔ-xué. According to the *Tōng-sú-wén*, the departure of the deceased is called "jué"; the abbreviated character "jué" signifies severance.

"Qi" (pronounced *qí* with the second tone; according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to pray for"; according to the *Ěryá*, it means "to invoke"). Guo Pu says: "Those who perform the sacrifice of *qí* call out loudly while requesting that their affairs be granted. Sun Yan says: "*Qí* is to pray for blessings on behalf of the people; it is a cry of invocation."

The ancient forms of 捍 (hàn), 格 (gé), 古文 (gǔwén), and 𢧀 (chán) have four variations; today they are written as 扞 (hàn, with the phonetic *hú* and *dàn*) meaning "to resist" (*hàn yù*), 格 (gé, with the phonetic *gǔ* and *huí*, or *gǔ* and *fǎn*) meaning "to block" (*gé zhì*) or "to exclude" (*gé jù*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it also means "to strike."

The character *jiàn* (鑒) is written as *jiàn* (鑑) in ancient texts, with the phonetic *chán* (儳). According to the *Guǎngyá*, "to *jiàn*" means to illuminate; it refers to a mirror, by which one examines forms. *Kū* (刳): the mouth radical is *gū* (孤).

According to the *Cāngxiépiān*, "to *kū*" means to slaughter. According to the *Fāngyán*, "to *kū*" means to transmit. According to the *Shuōwén*, "to *kū*" means to split apart. In the *Zhouyì*, it says, "carve wood to make a boat. In this context, "to *kū*" means to hollow out its belly.
*Huixìn* (灰燼): "Temple" (*sì*) follows the Qin pronunciation *jìn*. The *Shuowen* states it refers to the remaining wood from a fire;

this is correct. *Xiānzhǐ* (孅指): This is the archaic form of the character *shēn* (攕). In the written text it is written as *xiān* (纖), with the same pronunciation as *sīlián* (思廉). The *Shuowen* says it describes the appearance of well-proportioned hands. *Xiān* (孅) means fine and sharp. According to the *Fangyan*, it means small or minute. In the regions of Liang and Yi, anything small is called *xiān*.

*Qiān* (pronounced *qiān*, with the radical for "force" and the phonetic *fǎn*) is defined in the *Bīcāng* as fear. The *Tōngsùwén* states that a slight terror is called *qiān*; this is what is meant in the *Gōngyáng Zhuan*: "They were startled *qiānrán*. The version in the *Lùnwén* uses the character *qiáng* (wall), which is merely a near-homophone. It is also written as *sè* (to plow) or *shè* (rough); however, *sè* does not carry this meaning.

*Jianzhi* (閒跱) is an archaic term synonymous with *zhì* (峙), pronounced *chú lǐ* (除理). It means to stand alone. According to the *Guǎngyá*, *zhì* means "to stop. According to the *Shuōwén*, *zhì* is synonymous with *chù* (躇); it refers to halting or standing still without moving forward. The pronunciation of *chù* is *zhí rú* (直如).

*Qíng* (晴): An archaic form of *qíng*. The two characters *qíng* and *jiàn* share the same pronunciation, which is *yíng* (盈) with the second tone. In the *Hànshū*, it says: "When the sky is clear (*tiān qíng*), the Jingxing star appears. Mèng Kāng comments: "Clear (*qíng*) means brilliant and pure (*jīng míng*).

25. Fascicle Twenty-Five. *Fēng* (豐): Pronounced *wū xué* (烏學) with the second tone. The *Shījīng* says: "Gradually like a thick application of cinnabar (*shāo rú wò zhě*). The commentary states: "Thick (*wò*) means abundant (*hòu*)."
*Lǚ* (步力反): The *Tōngsùwén* states that a curved spine is called *yǔlǚ*. The *Guǎngyá* says *lǚ* means "curved.
26. Volume Twenty-six. *Niàng* (女恨反): The *Sāncāng* states that what is produced from rice and yeast is called *niàng*. The *Shuōwén* says that brewing wine is called *niàng*.
*Tāo* (徒刀反): According to the *An*, *tāo* means "to sift" (*tài*). The *Lunwen* writes it as *tài* (徒蓋反). The *Tōngsùwén* states that sifting rice is called *tāoshā*. *Lúguǎn* (力居反):

The *Xiǎo'ěr'ă* says, "A *lú* is a lodging," meaning a place where one stays temporarily; it is also a separate dwelling. It is said that the Yellow Emperor built *lú*s to avoid the cold and heat, leaving them during the spring and autumn and residing in them during winter and summer; hence they are called "temporary lodgings. The *Shìmíng* says, "A *jìzhílú* (lodging for temporary residence) is so called because it provides shelter and consideration (*lù*)"; it takes its name from providing rest and protection. *Guǎn* (古玩反): A guest house. According to the *Zhōuwǔ*, every fifty *lǐ* there was a *guǎn* and a storehouse of provisions (*wěizī*) to await guests arriving on diplomatic missions (*cháo-pìn*). The character is formed with the radical "food" (*shí*) and the phonetic "guàn" (*guànshēng*).
*Tiáo* (pronounced *tú diào*): According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means to deceive, to sell off, or to mock (*zhāotiáo*).

*Líng* (pronounced *lí shēng*): According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means to oppress, to violate, or to insult. In the *Cāngjiépiān*, it means to invade. *Lì* is also written as *lèi* (pronounced *yǐ shì*); in the *Cāngjiépiān*, it means to be arrogant, referring to being complacent. The *Shuōwén* says *lì* means lightness; today it is also written as *yì*.

27 (Volume Twenty-Seven is missing) 28 Volume Twenty-Eight: *Xi-feng* (吸風). The ancient forms were *xi* (歙) and *xi* (噏); the modern form is *xi* (吸), all sharing the same meaning. According to the *Guǎngyá*, "to *xi*" means to drink. According to the *Shuōwén*, it refers to internal respiration; that is, the inhalation of breath, and it also implies drawing in.

"Bing" (兵) refers to military force; "wu" (伍) refers to the five-edged weapons that constitute the army. To revert to the Zhou Li, five men form a *wu*. Zheng Xuan says: "*Wu* means a multitude. In the *Lunwen*, it is written as *wu* (仵), which is pronounced with the same final as *wo* (吾) and means "to oppose" or "to resist. However, *wu* (仵) is not the correct character for this meaning.

The ancient characters for *jiǎn* (stammering) were written as 𧪤 and 謇; today they are written as 吃. The *Shēnglèi* (Classification of Sounds) also writes it as 󲝎, and another form is 󲣴, both pronounced with the rhyme *wǎn* (as in "Wǔzhǎn"). According to the *Fānyán* (Topical Dictionary), *jiǎn* refers to stammering; it is a term used by the people of Chu. In the *Zhōuyī* (Book of Changes), "the stammerer" signifies difficulty. In the *Lùnwén* (Discourse on Literature), it is written as 蹇, meaning a lame person. However, "lame" is not the intended meaning here. The ancient character for *qì* (stammering) was written as 󲂀; both share the pronunciation *qǐ* (as in "Jūqǐ"). It refers to speech that is heavy or labored. The *Tōngsúwényán* (Common Language of Popular Usage) states that when speech is not fluent, it is called 󲣴 or *qì*.
The ancient characters for "deep" (shēn) and "firm" (jiān) have two forms each; the modern characters are written as 浚 and 堅, both pronounced with the same initial as 私 (sī) and the final as 𨳝 (fǎn).
"Deep" means profound; "firm" means solid and adherent, meaning to be closely attached.

29. Fascicle Twenty-Nine. "Bi" (襞) [pronounced *pi* with the initial *b-*, according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*] means the pleating of garments; according to the *Guangya*, it means to fold or crease. "Kuan" (韏) [pronounced *qian* with the initial *k-*, according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*].

"Liángpíng" (梁枰) refers to what is called a "mōliáng" (摸梁); "píng" (枰) is pronounced *píng* (皮兵反). According to the *Pīcāng* (埤蒼), it means a "tà" (榻), which refers to a single-person wooden bench. The *Shìmíng* (釋名) states: "It is called 'píng' because it is level; it is made of boards, and its body is flat and upright."

30. Fascicle Thirty. Regarding the character *bi* (辟) in the ancient script: it has two forms, both identical to the character for "spleen" (*pi*, pronounced with the *pi* rhyme). According to the *Zilin* (Forest of Characters), *bi* means "law" (*fa*). In the *Han Shi* (Poems of Han), it is used in the sense of "to clear away" (*pi chu*) in expressions such as "clearing away [obstacles] in the four directions. This character is composed of the radical *shi* (尸), the component *kou* (口), and the phonetic *xin* (辛), signifying that one restrains transgressions through the mouth by applying the law. The version of the treatise that uses the character *xie pi* (邪僻, "deviant") is incorrect.

"Hù" (祜) is pronounced with the initial *hu* and the final *gu*. The *Shi* (Classic of Poetry) says, "Receiving the blessings (*hù*) of Heaven. The *Jian* (Commentary) states: "Hù means blessing (*fú*). According to the *Erya*, "Hù means abundant (*hòu*).
"Gū" (觚) is pronounced with the initial *zhi* and the final *gu*. Examining "gū," it is like a branch-base; it is not yet clear what language this refers to.

*Leiting* (thunderbolt): *dá* and *dǐng* are both pronounced with a second tone. In the *Zhouyi*, it says, "It stirs them with thunderbolts. Liu Huan stated: "The character *tíng* refers to lightning. In the *Zhèn* hexagram, *léi* (thunder) is assigned, while in the *Lí* hexagram, *diàn* (lightning) is assigned. The *Erya* states: "A swift thunder is called *tíngní*. Guo Pu commented: "It refers to the sudden and violent intensity of thunder. According to the *Cangjie pian*, *tíng* is the same as *pīlì* (a clap of thunder). This is evidenced by the *Gongyang zhuan*, which records: "There was a thunderbolt that struck the temple of Yibo."

31. Volume Thirty-one. Regarding "紹胄" (shàozhòu): in the *Zílín* (Forest of Characters), "胄" (zhòu) is a variant of "胤" (yìn). "胤" means lineage or succession; it refers to continuing the ancestral line of previous generations.

32. Volume Thirty-Two. "San" (參): In the *Guǎngyá*, "san" means three; in the *Fāngyán*, it means a third part. Qí Rù states that Gù Pǔ says it refers to dividing. "Bèi" (倍): In the *Guǎngyá*, "bèi" means half. It is said that one producing two is called "bèi."

*Chenji* (Prophecy Records) refers to the *Buchi Yin* (The Prophecy of the Chu Shadow); it is a secret book originating from the records of the Yellow River and Luo River that provides verified prophecies, meaning that the divinations prove effective later on.

"Bai-ling" (百齡)—the "ling" is pronounced *ding* (反). In the *Liji*, it is said: "In antiquity, 'nian' (years) and 'chi' (teeth) were both called 'ling'; all refer to longevity. The standard character for ancient and modern usage follows the radical for "teeth" (*chi*) and the phonetic element "ling" (*ling*); it may also be written as "mo" (*mei*).

The *Lǐjì* says, "Confucius was moved to tears (*xuǎnrán liú tì*). The *Shuōwén* also defines it as "flowing," composed of the water radical and the phonetic component 玄 (xuán).

The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it means "to connect in succession"; the *Shuōwén* says "to lead forward. The lower character is pronounced *wǎn* (亾) with the *yuǎn* (遠) *fǎn* (反). *Tí* (梯): Pronounced *dèng* (鄧) in the lower register; its phonetic component is *kǎo* (考). It refers to a ladder or a flight of steps, as well as a small slope. The version in the *Lun* (論) uses "qián" (鉗), which is an error. "Wòcù" (惡䓶): The lower character is read as cì (此漬反).

Guō's commentary on the *Erya* states that "cī" (莿) and "cì" (茦) mean needles or thorns, as well as the woodworm (*mùfēi*).
