According to the *Shuōwén*, it is written as *wú* (兀), meaning "high and level above"; it is also used when [the radical] *rén* (人) is placed above.

In the *Wúliàngshòu lùn* (Treatise on Immeasurable Life) compiled by Huìlín, the character "dǒn" (顛) is used in place of "dǎo" (倒). In the *Shāngshū zhù* (Commentary on the Book of Documents), it is noted that "dǒn" means to overturn a coffin; furthermore, "dǒn" means to turn upside down or to fall prostrate. The current form is written as "dǎo" (𠑘); the *Shuōwén* (Explaining Simple and Analyzing Compound Characters) writes it as "diān" (蹎), derived from the radical "rén" (人). The form "diān" (巔) used in this treatise is an error.

The character for "tortoise" (龜) is pronounced as *kui* with the *shangping* tone. The *Baïhù tōng* states: "Tortoise" (*gui*) signifies "long-lasting" (*jiǔ*). The *Màoshī chuán* states: "A great tortoise (*yuán guī*) measures one chi and two cun. The *Shuōwén* says: "It has a shell on the outside and flesh on the inside; it follows the radical 'it' (*tuó*), and the head of the tortoise is depicted in its form. Some say it is also a phonetic component.
In the character 㧋 (in the term *jiànshàngbiàn*), "bá" (拔) is an error for "biàn" (辨).

In the character 蛭 (zhì), the lower radical is pronounced as *zhēn* (真) or *yuè* (曰); according to the *Erya*, it is "zhìqī" (蛭蟣); according to the *Cangjie pian*, it is an aquatic insect; and according to the *Shenglei*, it is also "zhìróu" (蛭蝚) or "zhìzhǎng" (蛭掌). The *Kaosheng* states that "zhìróu" and "zhìzé" (蛭蛒) are both "zhì" (𧖊) or "zhì" (󲠸). The *Shuowen jiezi* uses the "insect" radical (虫); to use the "stone" radical (石) to form "zhì" is an error.
*Huò zhì* (火擿): The lower character is pronounced *zhēng* (隻) with a *kǎo* (考) tone; it means to pluck or select. The *Shuowen* states it means "to throw," written with the radical 手 (hand).

To write it with the radical 火 (fire) as *huò zhì* is an error. *Sānjùzú jīng yōubótíshè* (三具足經憂波提舍): One fascicle. Huilin’s Pronunciations: *Yèchéng* (鄴城)—the upper character is pronounced *yán* (嚴) with a *jié* (劫) tone. The *Hanshu* records that there was Ye County in Wei Commandery, located east of Taiyuan Mountain. The *Shuowen* states it is composed of the radical 邑 (city) with the phonetic 業 (ye).

Tiāo (挑): In the *Shēnglèi* it is read as tiáo; it means to pick up (*tiǎo*). According to the *Zìshū*, it means to pluck (*liáo*). The *Shuōwén* states that it is composed of the radical "hand" (手部) and the phonetic "zhào" (兆).

Xuěduī (雪堆): The lower character is read as duì (對) with the variant léi (雷). Wang’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that *kuíduī* (魁堆) means high. Guō’s commentary on the *Shànglín Fù* states that *duīshā* (堆沙) means a mound. Regarding the phonetics, it refers to the appearance of a high mound of earth. It is also written as *tuī* (塠). This is the correct form according to ancient and modern standards, composed of the radical "earth" (土) and the phonetic "zhuī" (隹). The version in the scriptures written as *bù* (埠) is incorrect.
*Nīlana* (尼羅拏): A proper name in the Sanskrit language; the "na" is pronounced with the *jiǎo* (搦) and *jiā* (加) finals reversed. Regarding the stomach (*wei* 胃):

according to the *Baihutong* (白虎通), it is the "palace" (*fu* 府) of the spleen; the *Shuowen* (說文) defines it as the "palace of grain" (*guofu* 穀府), a pictographic character; its appearance in the scriptures as *𦝩* is an error. Regarding the gallbladder (*dan* 膽): according to the *Baihutong*, it is the "palace" of the liver; the *Wenzidian* (文字典) explains that it is composed of the radical "flesh" (*rou* 肉) and the phonetic "zhan" (詹). Regarding the spleen (*pi* 脾): according to the *Baihutong*, it is the "discriminating organ" (*bian* 辯) and the "repository of earth" (*tuzang* 土藏); the *Guoyaya* (廣雅) states that "spleen" means "humble" (*bi* 卑); the *Wenzidian* explains that the character is composed of the radical "flesh" and the phonetic "bi" (卑).

The character for "ship" (péng, with the *mò* radical) is pronounced like the sound of a boat; it refers to a *kūnlún* vessel and is also written as *jiè*. Sima Biao’s commentary on the *Zhuangzi* states it is the name for a large ship. The *Guǎngyá* calls it a sea-going vessel, and the *Běicāng* calls it a great ship. According to the *Gōngjīn zhèngzì*, it is composed of the "boat" (*zhōu*) radical and the phonetic element "white" (*bái*).

*Mǎngshé* (蟒蛇): "Mǎng" is pronounced with the *mò* and *bǎng* finals. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* states that it is the largest kind of snake. In the *Guījīn zhèngzì*, it is written with the "insect" radical (*虫*) and the phonetic "mǎng. *Xióngpí* (熊羆): "Xióng" is pronounced with the *xū* and *gōng* finals.

According to the *Shuowen*, the bear is a beast resembling a boar that dwells in the mountains; it is written with the "ability" radical (*能*) and the abbreviated "flame" (*炎*) as its phonetic. "Pí" is pronounced with the *bǐ* and *pí* finals. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* states that the brown bear resembles a bear but has a higher head and legs with great strength for uprooting trees; those in Guānxī call it a "bear. According to the *Shuowen*, it is written with the "bear" radical (*熊*) and the abbreviated "brown bear" (*羆*) as its phonetic.

Regarding the character *yè* (孽): the commentary states that the *Kǎo Shēng* says "yuán" (媛) means disaster. When insects and beasts act as monsters, it is called *yè*; when clothing, plants, or trees act as monsters, it is called *zào* (妖). Nowadays, some write it with the "woman" radical (*nǚ*) as *ài* (㜸), or with the "insect" radical (*chóng*) as *lì* (𧕏); the scriptural text uses the "grain" radical (*mǐ*) as *yè*, which does not accord with the meaning of the scripture.

*Zhuanfalun jing youbotishe* (Exegesis on the Sūtra of Turning the Wheel of Dharma), one fascicle; *Wuyinzi* (Phonetics of Unrecorded Characters); *Yijiao lun* (Treatise on the Bequeathed Teaching), one fascicle. Regarding the character *xiá* (瘕): In the *Huilin yinyi*, it is read as *jiā* (夏加反). The *Mao shi jian* states that *xiá* refers to a chronic ailment (*bìng*). Guo’s commentary to the *Shanhai jing* says it is a disease of worms. The *Cangjie pian* says it is a disease within the abdomen. The *Shuowen jiezi* defines it as a disease. Regarding the character *cī* (疵) below, it is read as *zī* (漬茲反). Kong’s commentary to the *Shangshu* states that *cī* is also a disease. In the *Zhouyi*, "defect" (*cī*) is synonymous with "chronic decay" (*xiábài*). The *Shuowen jiezi* explains that this character is composed of *nà* (疒, the radical for illness) and *duàn* (叚), both of which are phonetic components.

The character 𡢬 (shàn) is pronounced with the initial *s* and the final *lie* (according to the Kangxi Dictionary). Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shūjìng* states that "𡢬 also means arrogance. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* identifies it as "familiarity and insolence" (*xié-è*). The *Fāngyán* states that "𡢬 means intimacy" (*xiá*). According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical 女 and the phonetic 󰪑.

*Kiṅ* (坑) [the radical *shàng* and the phonetic *kēng*]: Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states it refers to a pit, a moat, a pond, or a mound; the *Cangjie pian* says it is a ravine and also a depression. It is sometimes written as *kǎng* (阬). Regarding the correct characters of ancient and modern times: it is composed of the radical *tǔ* (earth) and the phonetic *háng* (亢). *Xià* (下) [the radical *xián* and the phonetic *jiàn*]: Gu Yewang says it means to fall or drop into. The commentary on the *Chuci* says it means to sink. The *Guangya* says it means to collapse. The *Shuowen* says it means to descend from a height; one interpretation says it means to fall. It is composed of the radical *fù* (mountain/embankment) and the phonetic *hán* (函).

"Qingzao" (輕躁) means to be fickle and agitated; it refers to being restless. Jia [Yan]’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states it means "to disturb. Zheng’s commentary on the *Lunyu* states it means "not being at peace. Examining its phonetic nature, it signifies impetuosity. In the *Shuowen*, this is written as the character "Zao" (趮), composed of the radical "foot" (足) and the phonetic "Sao" (喿). It is incorrect to derive it from "Can" (叅) as "Jie" (𨅶).

*Téng* (騰): "To leap upward. (The character is pronounced *xià yáng xuó fǎn*). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states it means "to soar"; the *Erya* states it means "swift"; the *Guangya* states it means "to jump" or "to ascend," or "to advance. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *zu* (foot) and the phonetic *zhì*.
*Chào* (踔): To urinate while standing. *Dí* (躑):

*Dí* (石) with the radical *zhǐ* (呈). Yě Wáng says: "To lift one's feet and not move forward. The *Shuowen* defines it as "to stop the feet" or "to stand on tiptoe," also written as *zhí* (蹢). In the *Gujin Zhengzi*, this character follows the radical *zú* (足) and is pronounced according to the *Zhèng* (鄭) school.

Regarding the *hēiwán* (black viper), the character for "wán" is pronounced as *guān* with a retroflex final. The *Baopuzi* states: "There are many species of snakes, but among them, the *wán* snake is the most lethal when it bites a person. One may use a knife to excise the flesh at the site of the bite and cast it upon the ground; the flesh will boil up of its own accord like being roasted by fire until it is completely charred. The person will then survive. If one does not excise it, death is certain. The *Xuánzhōng jì* states: "The *wán* snake is three or four feet long and has four legs. Its shape resembles that of a *shǒuguān* (a type of lizard). Along its spine are needles sharper than knives; it is extremely venomous. Once it bites a person, they will die within half a day. The *Shānhǎi jīng* says: "Its skin can be used to decorate knives and swords. It resembles the skin of the *jiāoyú* (shark), differing only in that its scales are finer."

The character 𠬿 (yì): From the "One Edge" section above, it is annotated in the *Chuci* as "to oppose the king. The *Cangjie pian* states it means "to be filled with indignation. The *Shenglei* describes it as having the appearance of "sorrowful anxiety. The *Shuowen jiezi* says it means "wrath," formed from the radical "heart" (心) and the phonetic "䏍" (yì).

*Sanjuzhilun* (Treatise on the Three Endowments), compiled by Xuanying. "Bo" (舶) refers to a large ship; it is found in the *Shipin* (Rhymes of Ships) and the *Bai Zilin* (White Character Forest). Today, in Jiangnan, all ships that sail upon the sea are called *bo*. Both the Kunlun and the Goryeo peoples ride in them; the largest can hold ten thousand *hu* (a measure of capacity).

*Luoshu* (邏戍)—the character *shu* is pronounced with the *li* (力) and *he* (荷) finals; it refers to a subordinate unit, meaning mobile troops deployed to guard against bandits, as well as those who patrol to prevent violations.

"Fearing incitement" (*kōngchī*) means fearing mutual provocation. In the *Fāngyán* (方言), it is written as *kōngxī* (恐䦧), with the pronunciation *hégé* (呼隔反); it is also called *kōnghè* (恐赫) or *kōngshè* (恐猲), all of which share the same meaning. The character *shè* (猲) is pronounced *xūgē* (虛割反).

*Jiangshi* (pronounced *jiāngshí*) is shaped like ginger. According to the *Tōngsùwén*, ground with many small stones is called *jiangliè*; the character is composed of the "stone" radical (*shí*). To write it with the "earth" radical (*tǔ*) as *jiāng* is not the correct form.
The preceding section is the *Śāstravyākhyāna* (Exegesis of the Sūtras and Śāstras), and the following is the *Arthasaṃgraha* (Compendium of Meaning).

*Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, Fascicle One, composed by Xuanying. Fascicle One: *Kai-li* (Prostration). The ancient character for *li* is the same as *lǐ*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the radical below *kai* means "to bow the head. The *Baihutong* states: "The reason for *kai-li* is to reach [the ground]. *Li* means the chin reaches the ground. This is the first of the nine types of prostration distinguished in the *Zhouli* (Rites of Zhou) by the Grand Master of Prayer: first is *kai-li*, second is *dun-li*. This is it.

"Shao" (紹) is the same as "guwen" (古文). [The character] is pronounced *qi* (綤), with the phonetic component *dai* (逵). According to the *Erya*, "shao" means "to succeed" (*ji*, 繼), referring to continuing the lineage of one's ancestors. The *Shifa* (謚法) states: "To succeed to the position from a distant line is called 'shao'."

"To interweave" (*cuòzōng*) means to arrange the texts and synthesize their meanings. The *Guǎngyǎ* states that "interweaving" (*cuò*) means to intersperse; it refers to alternating [elements] with one another. "Synthesizing" (*zōng*) means to encompass; it refers to summarizing the textual meanings. "Kǎi" (鍇) means to examine; it refers to investigating the principles. The *Shuowén* defines "synthesizing" (*zōng*) as the shuttle of a loom; it refers to holding the threads so that they cross, bending the cord to control the warp, causing it to open and close. It also means to record or to organize. "Jì" (紀) refers to the head of the thread, distinguishing the various strands.
*Shi* (pronounced *shǐ*, with the radical *shan* reversed): According to the *Cangjie pian*, "shi" means rapid; the character is derived from the radical *shi*.

*Shanyu* (pronounced *shànyù*, with the radical *ge* reversed): According to the *Shuowen jiezi*, "yu" refers to the yoke of a carriage; it is that which presses against the neck of the ox at the end of the shaft.

*Ce* (惻) and *cang* (愴) are archaic characters identical to *ze* (𢝔); the former is pronounced with the *chu* and *li* rhymes, and the latter with the *chu* and *liang* rhymes. According to the *Shuowen*, *ce* means "pain";

according to the *Guangya*, *ce* means "sorrow" and *cang* means "wound. *Kātyāyana* is a Brahmin clan name; using the clan name as a personal name, it was formerly called *Jiāzhānyán*, which is a corruption.
"Guǐ" (詭) means to dwell in deception or to act perversely; it refers to artifice, fraud, and unreality. According to the *Guǎngyá*, "guǐ" means to deceive or to cheat. "Jìdàn" (忌憚):

the first character is pronounced with the initial *qú* and the final *jì*; the second character is pronounced with the initial *tú* and the final *qiè*. "Jì" means to fear or to dread; "dàn" means to find difficult, to be startled, or to hesitate.

*Gān* (pronounced *gǔlán*): According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means "to find pleasure in" or "to have a fond desire for. It signifies a fondness that knows no satiety. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means "sweetness. *Mǎnlì* (pronounced *mǐbiàn* and *lìzhì*):

It means "to exhort" or "to encourage," as well as "to exert oneself. This refers to encouraging oneself; *lì* means to mutually encourage one another. It also refers to exerting one's strength. [The character *qiáng* is pronounced *jùliǎng*].
*Chàng* (悵): Pronounced *chì* (勑) and *liàng* (亮) with the second tone; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "to look longingly with regret" and "the mind being dissatisfied.

*Tūn* (吞): Pronounced *tā* (他) and *hén* (痕) with the second tone; "to swallow" here refers to not chewing. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to swallow down"; the *Guoyaya* says it means "to annihilate."

"Creek" (*xī*) and "marsh" (*zhǎo*)—the former is also written as *xī* (with the phonetic gloss *kǔ xī* reversed; the latter is *zhī rào* reversed). According to the *Erya*, "a stream flowing into a river is called a creek.

According to the *Shuowen*, "a marsh is a small pond. "Great" (*jù*)—the phonetic gloss is *qí lǚ* reversed; it means "large. The latter [term] is pronounced *hū gè*. According to the *Erya*, "when flowing water is deep, it forms a *chǐ*; a *chǐ* is also a ditch or pond."

*Yan* (pronounced *lián* in the first instance, and *lì* in the second; the latter also means "to burn") refers to blazing fire. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *yan* is the flame rising upward from a fire. *Liao* refers to setting fire to fields, which is called *liao*.
*Yan* (pronounced *wán* with the *yuàn* and *yú* finals) means that threads are drawn out continuously without interruption.
"Embers" (huìxìn): also written as 燼 (same pronunciation, *jìn*). According to the *Shuowen*, "embers" refers to the remnants of wood left after a fire.
"Plucking the strings" (*kòuxián*): "plucking" (*kòu*) means to strike; "strings" (*xián*) refers to the lute and similar instruments.
*Fu* (拊): The phonetic component is *fang* (芳) and the radical is *zhu* (主). "To *fu*" means to strike; the lower part is read as *gu* (古) and *he* (核).

It refers to the drumskin. *Nian* (黏): The phonetic component is *yong* (勇) and the radical is *lian* (廉). The *Cangjie pian* states that it means "to adhere. The *Shuowen jiezi* says that to stick together is called *nian*. The lower part is read as *yu* (瑜) and *zhong* (種); it refers to being heroic, martial, and resolute. The *Shifa* (Canon of Posthumous Titles) states: "To know death yet not avoid it is called *yong* (bravery); to command benevolence is called *yong*."

*Jìnglǜ* (靜慮): According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "jìng" means to examine with care and "xī" means to find rest; "lǜ" means to contemplate and to think. The old term is *dìng* (定); in Sanskrit it is called *dhyāna*. *Lòukù* (漏匱):

*Lòu* is pronounced with the *qú* and *kuì* finals. To lack wealth is called *kù*. In the *Liji*, regarding the passage "wealth is not *kù*," Zheng Xuan states that *kù* means "lack. The *Shijing* says, "Examine your sons so they are not *kù*," and the commentary states that *kù* means "exhaustion."

2. Second Fascicle. *Upādhyāya* is a Sanskrit term; the first character (*up*) is pronounced as *wu gu* (with the final *gu* reversed), and the second character (*dhyāya*) is pronounced as *tu wo* (with the final *wo* reversed). This is translated as "Preceptor" (*qīnjiào*). It is also called *upādhyāya*, or "One Who Recites Closely" (*jìn sòng*), because when a disciple is young, they do not leave the teacher but constantly follow and stay near them, receiving the scriptures without yet reciting them. Formerly, it was called *héshàng* or *héshé*; these are corruptions of the languages of various countries such as Khotan. In terms of its meaning, one who knows what is an offense and what is not an offense is called an *upādhyāya*.

*Asaṃkhyeya* (in Sanskrit, pronounced with the *chui* rhyme of *qiu*; here translated as "limitless" [wúyāngshù]; the old term *asaṃkhyī* is a corruption and abbreviation). *Wēnxí* (in the *wu-kun* rhyme):

In the *Lúnyǔ*, it says, "By rehearsing what is old, one knows what is new. He Yan said, "To 'wēn' means to seek out. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states, "To practice it at a later time is called 'wēn'; 'wēn' implies warmth. This meaning is adopted here.
3. Third Fascicle. *Mṛdu* (the character is pronounced with the *chuan* [zhuan] tone; in Sanskrit, *mṛdu*; this means "soft" or "pliant," as soft things are called *mṛdu*).
*Āśaya* (this is translated as "intentional inclination"; the tone of *le* is five-toned, i.e., *lè*; it is also called "seed").

The term *srotāpanna* (in Chinese, *yùliú*, with the second character pronounced *shù* following the *fàn* [Sanskrit] pronunciation) means "stream-enterer. One noble path is called a "stream" (*srotas*) because it flows continuously toward *nirvāṇa*. Because one has first realized the fruit of sainthood and for the first time entered the ranks of the victorious ones, it is called "entering the stream" (*srotāpanna*); "entering" (*can yù*) refers to joining. The older translation "Sudāyu" (須陀洹) is an error. It is also called "counter-flow" (*pratisrota*), "human flow" (*manuṣya-srota*), or "reaching the flow" (*srota-āgata*); these all refer to the same thing.

"Ekāvakṣika" (pronounced *yìjiān* in Chinese; in Sanskrit, *ekāvaśeṣa*; *eka* meaning "one" and *avaśeṣa* meaning "remainder") refers to a single interval. Specifically, it denotes a hole in a wall; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "interval" (*jiàn*) means a crack or fissure. This implies that there remains one final interval [of existence] before one can attain parinirvāṇa. The older term "one-seeded" (*yīzhǒngzǐ*) is derived from the Sanskrit *eka-bījika*. This is likely due to either a poor command of Sanskrit by the translator or a scribe failing to consult the original text, resulting in this error.

*Khaḍga* (in the vernacular pronunciation *qūyè*) means "rhinoceros"; *viṣāṇa* means "horn," referring to the single horn of a rhinoceros, where "one" (*eka*) also signifies "solitary. This is a metaphor for the Pratyekabuddha, indicating that each dwells alone in the mountains and forests. The *Vibhāṣā* renders it as *khaga*, while the *Candragarbha-sūtra* renders it as *khaga*; both are corruptions.

Volumes 4–5: Volumes Four and Five were both previously unpronounced. Volume Six: "Shiwu" (什物) is pronounced with the initial *shí* and the final rhyme *wù*. It means a collection or a miscellaneous assortment; it refers to articles for daily life. When people today speak of household goods and utensils, they still say "shiwu," which refers precisely to these implements. In the Jiangnan region, they call them "shiwu"; here [in this text], they are termed "the five categories of implements. The *Shiji* states that Shun made "shiqu" (什器) at Shouchiu; the *Hanshu* mentions that impoverished people were granted fields, houses, and "shiqu"—both of these refer to the same thing.

*Mātṛkā* (in Sanskrit, pronounced with the retroflex *ṭa*, formerly translated as *mòdéjiā* or *móyí*; here translated as "mother of practice" or "root mother"; it is called the "sphere of practice" because it is the basis upon which practice arises and that which can generate practice).
The *Gongzhu zhigao* (The Ritual Master’s Announcement) states that one who excels at their task is called a "craftsman" (*gōng*).

The *Shēnù zìlín* (Dictionary of the Word "Anger") also mentions the *Shēnbō* tree; the *Zīlín* (Forest of Characters) alternatively writes it as *Shēnshù*. This refers to the name of a tree, which this translation renders as "the fruit-bearing wood. It serves as a metaphor for the abundance or scarcity of old leaves in the sutra.
*Suqí* (所祈): "Ju" (巨) is pronounced as *guǎ* (廣); according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to pray for.
Volume Seven, Part Seven: *Shùmiǎo* (樹杪): "Miǎo" (杪) is pronounced as *míráo* (彌遶). According to the *Tōngsùwén*, the tip of a tree is called *miǎo*; *miǎo* refers to something minute and fine.
"Bureaucrat" (liáo) is also written as "liaoyu" (同力雕反). According to the *Erya*, "liaoyu" means "officials"; those who hold office together are called "liaoyu.
Alternatively, it is written as "qiao" (翹, 祇遙反). According to the *Guangya*, "qiao" means "to lift up."
*Guāchóng* (蝸蟲): In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is glossed as "a snail.

Volume Eight, Part Eight: *Jūchì* (俱𦙁). This is a transliteration of the Sanskrit term *krośa*. The *Buddhacarita* (佛本行經) renders it as *jūzhì* (拘致), stating that one hundred times one hundred thousand is called one *krośa*; this numerical value corresponds to one million.
*Sūtra* (素怛纜): This is translated as "thread" (綫); formerly it was called *sūtra*. *Vaiśya* (吠舍):

In the Sanskrit language, this is pronounced *vaiśya* (扶癈反); formerly it was called *vessa*. This means "one who sits and trades. According to the customs of the Indian country, they highly value precious goods; these people seek out wealth and accumulate vast fortunes, sitting [at their stalls] to manage their income and expenditures; hence the name.

*Śūdra* is a Sanskrit term (transliterated as *shou-ju-fan*); the old translation was *shǒuduo*. This refers to those who serve as field officials; scholars say these are the great clans of the kingdom. Volume Nine, Part Nine:
*Īṣādhāra* is a Sanskrit word for the name of a mountain. It is used as a metaphor because this [person] is as lofty and haughty as that [mountain].

10. Fascicle Ten. "Shāng" (merchant) is pronounced *shāng* (initially *shāng*, final *fǎn*) and "Jiǎ" (peddler) is pronounced *gōng hù fǎn*. One who travels about selling is called a *shāng*; one who sits and sells is called a *jiǎ*. The *Báihùtōng* says: "The word 'shāng' means to deliberate (*shāngduó*) upon the distances near and far, circulating the goods of the four quarters to gather them together. 'Jiǎ' means to be fixed; it refers to fixing goods to await the people's coming to seek their profit. *Jiǎ* is also a common term for this.
*Néi* (能): "to sacrifice. According to the *Erya*, *sì* (祀) means "to offer sacrifices"; it is also a sacrifice to the earth. *Fāngyù* (方域): "territory.
According to the *Shuowen*, *yù* (域) refers to a state or domain.
*Jí* (詰): "to interrogate. According to the *Guangya*, *jí* (詰) means "to reprimand"; according to the *Shuowen*, *jí* (詰) means "to question."
"Yù" (pronounced *wù* with a retroflex final) refers to trees growing in dense clusters.
"Sà" (pronounced *sān* with a level tone) refers to the sound of wind blowing leaves from trees.
"Tángjuān" (pronounced *tú* and *zhuān* respectively): "táng" means "to waste," and "tú" means "empty. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it signifies "to diminish."

"Bóshí" (薄蝕): "Bó" is pronounced bù (補) and "shí" is pronounced zhí (職). According to the *Xiǎo Ěr Yǎ*, "bó" means "near. The *Hàn Shū* states: "The moon undergoes 'bóshí. Wei Zhao says that when solar vapor approaches and presses upon it, it is called 'bó'; when it is damaged, it is called 'shí,' like insects eating plants and trees until they wither and fall."

"Rōba" (羅婆) is the Sanskrit term; it is also called "Bilva" (頻螺) fruit, or sometimes "Pīla" (避羅) fruit, though these are all corruptions. The fruit is golden in color and about the size of a tangerine. In the western lands, this wood is frequently used to make banners for temples to adorn and offer in worship to the deities.

Śaṅkha (餉佉): In Sanskrit, this is pronounced *śi* with the *shang* (商) tone; it is translated here as "Moon-Seeing" (*Candradarśana*). Some say it means "Conch" (*Śaṅkha*). Formerly it was written as 儴佉 or 傷佉.

Volume Eleven, Chapter Eleven: *Shàng* (尚). Pronounced *shì* with the *ràng* (讓) tone. According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, *shàng* means "high. According to the *Shuōwén*, *shàng* means "formerly" (*céng*) or "also" (*yì shàng*).
"Chang-nü" (倡女) [the character *chang* pronounced *yáng-fǎn*] refers to a courtesan; according to the *Shuowen*, "chang" means a musician.

"Yuzhong" (雨衆) [the character *yu* pronounced *zhòng-yú-jǔ-fǎn*] is the Sanskrit term *vāri*, also transcribed as *bàlì* (跋利) or *zhòng* (衆). It refers to a group such as a teacher and his disciples, hence it is called "Yuzhong."

*Quánliàng* (銓量) is also written as *quán* (佺), with the same pronunciation as *qīchuán* (七泉反). It means a scale or balance (*chēnghéng*). The *Guǎngyá* states that it is called *quán* because it is used to weigh objects and determine their lightness or heaviness.
*Kāndìng* (刊定) has the pronunciation *gānqiān* (口干反). The *Guǎngyá* states that *kān* means to pare away or cut down; it also means to fix or determine, and to eliminate.

*Língwǔ* (凌侮) is also written as *líng* (夌), with the same pronunciation as *lì* (力𠿒反). In the *Sāncāng*, *líng* means "to encroach upon. In the *Guǎngyá*, *língfàn* (淩犯) has the pronunciation *xià wángfǔ* (下亡府反). In the *Guǎngyá*, *wǔ* (侮) means "to slight"; it refers to speaking lightly or with contempt. *Líng* (淩) is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic "líng" (*líng*).
*Di-hù*: "Di" is the same as "dì" (the ancient character). In the *Fāngyán*, it means "to alternate," that is, to take turns with another.
*Mù xuàn*: "Xuàn" is pronounced *hú juān* (two rhymes). In the *Zílín*, it means "confusion"; in the *Sāncāng*, it means "vision is unclear."
*Cái* (纔): According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "temporary" (*zàn*), "inferior" (*liè*), or "not long.

*Wèiyǔ* (未愈): The ancient form is written as *yù* (瘉), which is the same character. According to the *Fāngyán*, *yǔ* (愈) means "to recover. According to the *Shuōwén*, *yǔ* (瘉) means "the recovery from illness" (*chōu*).

*Kāmalā* (the Sanskrit term formerly translated as *jiāmóluó bìng*): this means "jaundice" (*huángbìng*) or "evil impurity" (*ègòu*). It refers to having an evil impurity within the abdomen, which is said to be incurable.
*Jiǎodōngfēi* (角犎妃): *fēng* (封) with a retroflex *r* sound, also pronounced *fēng*; this refers to the ox-shaped creature that has a small hump (*dōng*) upon its shoulders.
Its form is *nǎn* (愞); according to the *Sāncāng*, *nǎn* means weak.
The sound "si" is also written as "xī" (same as *sū-xī* in the fanqie; according to the *Shuowen*, "xī" means a sound of grief; according to the *Fangyan*, it means to choke with emotion or pain).

The characters "xiao-hǒng" are archaic forms of "xiāo" (same as *hū-jiāo* in the fanqie; according to the *Shuowen*, it is the roar of a tiger; it is also the sound of great rage). The lower character is an archaic form of "xù" (written in two ways, now appearing as "xù" or "hǒu," same as *hū-gǒu* in the fanqie); "hǒng" means to cry out.
*Páo* (咆): The *Huōng* (吽) with the *bù* (蒲) radical and *jiāo* (交) as the phonetic component. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means "to roar.

According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to cry out. *Míngmù* (瞑目): Also written as *mián* (眠), with the same pronunciation. According to the *Shuōwén*, *míng* (瞑) means "the eyes closing," while *mián* (眠) means "to sleep" or "to lie down."

"Dun" (敦) and "sun" (肅) refer to ancient texts; "dun" is pronounced as *dōu* or *zhuō*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "dun" means "thick and generous. "Xià" (下) is pronounced as *sī* or *liù*. "Sù" (肅) means "reverence" and "severity"; it refers to an appearance of solemn orderliness, and also implies "caution" and "self-respect."

*Bǐlǚ* (補美反; *bǔměi fǎn*; the second character is also written as 𨛋 with the same pronunciation): "vulgar and lowly. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, five *zǎn* (酇) form a *bǐ* (鄙); *bǐ* means *lǚ* (𨛋). The *Cangjie Pian* states that the subordinate towns of a state are called *lǚ*. In the *Hanshu*, it says, "Substantial yet not vulgar" (*zhì ér bù lǚ*). Rùchún explains: "Though substantial, it is still not like the vulgar speech of the common villages. *Zǎn* (酇) is pronounced *zǔqiě fǎn*. It refers to the hundred families.
*Gǔ* (麁獷): The second character, *gǔ*, means "fierce" or "stubborn"; it is composed of the radical "dog" (*quán*). *Kuò* (過隙):
The second character, *kuò*, refers to a "hole in a wall" according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*; it is composed of the character "white" (*bái*) with small characters above and below.

The ancient forms for *jiǎn* (stammering) were written as 謇 and 歰; today they are both written as 蹇, with the phonetic *zhǎn*. According to the *Fāngyán*, it refers to stammering (*jiǎn-é*), a term used by the people of Chu. It also means "difficulty" (*jiǎn-nàn*). The lower radical is *suǒ-lì*. The *Shuōwén* states that *sè* (roughness) means not being smooth. The character is composed of four *zhǐ* (stops); the meaning of the character is that when there are four stops, one cannot pass through.
The ancient forms for *sǒng* (to raise) are 竦 and 𢥠; the modern form is 聳, all pronounced *xū fèng* or *suǒ xiàng*. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to rise" or "to leap.
The ancient forms for *kù* (cruelty) are 嚳, 焅, and 悎; the modern form is 酷, all pronounced *kǒu mù*. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means "urgent," "extreme," or "violent and empty."
12. The Twelfth Fascicle. *Dārami*: This is a Sanskrit term (the "mi" is pronounced as in *mīl*) referring to a mantra; it has no direct Chinese equivalent and is retained here in its original form.
*Fu* (傅) is pronounced with the *shen-yu* (脣聿) rhyme; *shu* (述) means to explain its meaning.

In the *Erya*, *shu* (述) is glossed as "to cultivate" (*xiu*). *Moligaluozi* (沒力伽羅子) is a Sanskrit term; it is also called *Wugajialuo* (物伽伽羅伽), which translates here as "hemp-bean" (*hudou*). This refers to the *yuanse-dou* (緣色豆). *Luo* (羅) here means "to take. In the local vernacular, one should say "taking hemp-beans" (*qu yuandou*). This is his clan name. An ancient immortal was named *Mujialuo* (勿伽羅); because he did not eat any other substances but ate only hemp-beans, he was called "Taking Hemp-Beans. Since this [monk] belongs to that lineage of immortals, it became his clan name. The old rendering "Mujianlian" (目揵連) is a corruption and abbreviation.
*Upadeśa* (鄔波第鑠): In Sanskrit, *u-pa-de-śa*; the old [Chinese] term is *yòubōtíshè*, which is translated as "discourse" (*lùnyì*). *Shēnsuì* (㴱邃):
In ancient texts, it is written with the character *èi* (㥞), both pronounced *sīzuì*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "profound and remote."

13. The Thirteenth Fascicle. "Jingken" (精懇): The archaic text uses the character 󲢖, which is the same as 口很 (pronounced kǒu hèn). It is a synonym for 佫 (tóng). To be "jingken" means to be profoundly sincere; it also implies being firm and patient.
Upavāsa is a Sanskrit term also called *upavāsa*, which translates as "near-dwelling. This refers to one who observes the eight precepts dwelling in proximity to virtuous persons such as the Arhats.

*Duṭo* is a Sanskrit term also called *dhūta*; this is translated as "sifting" (*shàitài*), also as "cultivating and purifying" (*xiūzhì*), or as "shaking off" (*dòushǒu*), or as "tossing and vibrating" (*yáozhèn*), or as "removing" (*chú). These are all one meaning, referring to the removal of the three types of desire and greed regarding clothing, food and drink, and dwelling. The old rendering "tóuduō" is an error. In the sutras it is also said that one performs the "twelve vows of practice. The pronunciation of *du* is *dù* (with the initial *d-* and the final *-u*), and that of *tà* is *tài*.

14. Volume Fourteen. Viṣṇu Deva. In Sanskrit he is also called Viṣṇu Deva; this corresponds to the meaning of "delusive illusion. This deity possesses great majestic power and travels upon a golden-winged bird. As he journeys, a wheel serves as his vanguard; wherever he wishes to break through, he breaks through it, and none can withstand him.

*Śreṇika* is a term in the Sanskrit language; *ni* (pronounced with the *lv* reversal) means "possessing," and it is the name of a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*). The older transcription "Xian ni" (先尼) is a corruption.

*Gautama* is a term in the Sanskrit language which has three meanings: first, it refers to a clan (*gotra*); second, it means "born from cow-dung"; and third, it means "born from soil. This is because the name *Gau* signifies nine different meanings. The older term "Jiu" (瞿) is explained in detail according to the scriptural accounts.

*Quánjú* (the first character pronounced *qú* with the *yúan* rhyme, the second pronounced *qú* with the *yù* rhyme; according to the *Pīcāng*, "quánjú" means not being able to stretch out). The *Shuowen* writes it as *zhuán*, meaning to walk with cramped steps. According to this, *juǎn* also means "curved. *Lù* is pronounced *lù*.

"Rao-luan" (嬈亂) is a compound meaning "to vex" or "to disturb. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "rao" means "to playfully disturb. The *Sancang* states that "rao" means "to disturb. Guo Pu says it means "to toy with. The *Guoye* states that it means "to tease, provoke, or harass."

*Li* (pronounced *li* with the initial *lǐ* and the final *fǎn*; the second character is pronounced *hù* with the final *qiě*) means a neighborhood; five neighboring households constitute one *li*, referring to twenty-five families. It denotes a residential area. According to the *Fāngyán*, it refers to the interior of a single *li*. *Hàn* refers to a gate, meaning the gate of an alleyway.

Qián (乾): Ancient pronunciation *gǔ* (古), with a secondary form written as *qì* (㬤) and pronounced *qū jí* (丘及). The *Tōngsùwén* (通俗文) states: "To wish for dryness is called *qián* (㬤). Fifteen–Sixteen: Scroll Fifteen and Scroll Sixteen;

both the fifteenth and sixteenth scrolls have no phonetic notes provided previously. Seventeen: Scroll Seventeen; this scroll is lost (*yì*). In archaic script, it is the same as *yì* (佚), pronounced *yǔ yī fǎn* (與一反). The *Cāngjiépiān* (蒼頡篇) states: "*Yì* means *tì* (惕); *yì* means joy (*lè*). *Tì* (惕) is pronounced *dàng* (蕩).
*Surā* liquor is here translated as "rice wine.
*Maireya* liquor refers to various mixed liquors made from roots, stalks, flowers, fruits, and so forth.
*Madhu* liquor refers to grape wine.
Volume 18, Part 18. No phonetic glosses provided for the preceding section. Volume 19, Part 19. *Valakāri*: In the language of India (*Sanskrit*), this means "striving with strength" (*yùlì* 鬪力).
The *yan* (pronounced with the retroflex *r* sound) is a type of parrot; it is also called a *cāng-yan*. The *Zuǎnwén* states that in the Guanzhong region, the *yan* is known as the *yànlànduī*.

A *cháng-lǒng* (the first character pronounced with the initial *shī-yáng*) refers to a field ridge; according to the *Fānyán*, *dīfēng* means a field ridge, which is a boundary or embankment on the furrows of a plowed field.
20. The Twentieth Fascicle. "Kānàn" (艱難): In ancient pronunciation, it was read as *kian-nan*; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to soil that is difficult to cultivate.
"Pòuxī" (剖析): "Pòu" (剖) is pronounced *pǔ-hòu*; it means to split, as in dividing the soil. "Xī" (析) is pronounced *sī-dí* in the lower character; it means to divide or analyze.

*Pārājika*—in the language of the Brahmans, this is translated as "defeat" (*tasheng*), meaning that one is defeated by precept-breaking afflictions regarding wholesome dharmas. The old translation was *póluóyī*, which means "without remainder. This is because once this precept has been transgressed, one can never again be restored to the pure assembly; hence it is called "without remainder."

From the *Xianyang shengjiao lun song* (Verses of the Manifestation of the Holy Teachings), by Hui Lin: Regarding the term "yúqié" (瑜伽) [Yoga], the upper character is pronounced with the radical for "mouth" (口) and the phonetic "xū" (須) with the final rhyme "gēng" (庚).

It is a transliteration of the Sanskrit word. As for "zōng" (綜): the *Shuowen jiezi* explains it as "the mechanism for weaving; when threads cross and hold one another, it is called 'zōng'. It takes the radical "silk" (糸) and the phonetic "zōng" (宗).

"Jiǎo" (撟) is pronounced as *juāo* or *zhǎo*. The commentary on the *Huainanzi* states that "jiǎo" means to seize or take by force. Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* explains that to call the correct laws of the former kings "jiǎo" [perversion] and to execute the innocent is called "wú" (false accusation). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "qiáo" (喬); the version in the canon has "xì" (燆), which belongs to the "arrow" (矢) section.

*Lí* (羸): The phonetic component is *zhuī* (追) reversed; Duan Yucai’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states it means "weak. Jia Gongyan’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states it means "sickly. Xu Renzhong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states it means "inferior. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "emaciated," composed of the radical "sheep" (*yáng*) with the phonetic *níng* (𣎆).

"Kuànxi" (串習) means "habitual practice. The *Erya* states: "Huàn means 'practice' (*xí*). Examining the phonology, it is formed with the radical "heart" (*xīn*) as "guàn," which also means "practice"; or it is formed with the radical "walking" (*chuò*) as "lián," and their meanings are identical.

In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-vyākhyā* (Commentary on the Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra), compiled by Huìlín, the character "bō" (撥) is explained as follows: the *Mao Shī Zhuan* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry) states that "bō" means "to sever. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* (Songs of Chu) states that "bō" means "to brush away. The *Guǎngyá* (Extended Lexicon) states it means "to remove. According to the *Shuowén Jiezi* (Explaining Simple and Analyzing Compound Characters), the character is formed with the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "fa" (發).

"Biè" (僻) means "partial" and is also the opposite of "straight. The *Mao Shi* states, "The person has many biè," and its commentary explains it as "deviant. Gu Yewang says that "biè" refers to being deviant and crooked, not conforming to principle. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to avoid," composed of the radical "person" (人) and the phonetic "bì" (辟).
*Uddāna*: [The first character] *wu* (烏) and [the second] *ke* (骨) are pronounced with the *fanqie* (反切) *wu* (烏) and *he* (訶) respectively;

in Sanskrit this is called *pada*, which in Chinese means "footprint. *Samāhita* (三摩呬多): the *xin* (馨) is pronounced with the *fanqie* *xi* (馨); it is a term from the Sanskrit language. In the Tang language, it is called "equipoise" (*samāhita*). This refers to the stage of superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*), so called because it is free from dullness and agitation, and possesses the power to equally draw forth all virtuous qualities. Thus it is termed "equipoise."

The *Kǎo Shēng* (Investigation of Sounds) glosses "biāo" (pronounced with the *ráo* rhyme) as "to set forth. Gù Yěwáng states that "biāo" means to mark out on the surface for the purpose of identification. The *Shuōwén Jiězì* (Explaining Simple and Analyzing Compound Characters) derives it from the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic component "piào" (pronounced *bì xiāo*).

*The Treatise on the Correct Principles of Royal Law*, compiled by Xuanying. Regarding the term *xīlài* (錫賚)—the "xī" is pronounced as *xīng* (星) with a retroflex *-r* final—it is defined in the *Erya* as "bestowal" (*cìyǔ*). It refers to the terminology used when a superior bestows gifts upon another.
*Ào èi* (懊恚) means resentment and regret; it is the opposite of retribution (*bào*). *Qìng jié* (罄竭):
the ancient form is the same as *㼸*; the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "the emptiness of a vessel," while the *Erya* states it means "exhausted."

"Yingjie" (英傑): "Yu" (於) is pronounced with the fanqie "jingfan" (京反); "fan" (反) is pronounced with the fanqie "xieli" (下奇列反). The *Huainanzi* states: "One whose wisdom exceeds ten thousand men is called an 'ying' (英); one whose wisdom exceeds a thousand men is called a 'jie' (傑). A "jie" is also one who stands out uniquely; it refers to possessing talent and ability.

*Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccaya-śāstra*, Fascicle One, compiled by Hui-lin. 1. First Fascicle: *Huí* (迥). Pronounced *xiǎng* (󲟤, with the *xiǎng* radical). The *Erya* states that it means "to turn back" (*huí yuǎn*) or "distant" (*huí xiá*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* also defines it as "far," derived from the radical *chuò* (辵) and the phonetic *huí* (冋). *Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccaya-śāstra*, Fascicle One, compiled by Hui-lin. [End of] First Fascicle. *Huí* (迥). Pronounced *xiǎng* (󲟤, with the *xiǎng* radical). The *Erya* states that it means "to turn back" (*huí yuǎn*) or "distant" (*huí xiá*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* also defines it as "far," derived from the radical *chuò* (辵) and the phonetic *huí* (冋).

The character *yóu* (猶) [in the term] *yóuyù* (猶豫, "hesitation") is, according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, a member of the genus of macaques (*jù*). One source states that in Longxi, the puppy is called *yóu*. Gu Yewang says that *yóuyù* means "uncertainty. The *Liji* states: "Divination by tortoise-shell and stalks is used to resolve doubts and determine hesitations. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical for dog (*quán*) with the phonetic element *qiū*.

The character *chuan* (纏) [with the phonetic *che* and *lian* as variants] is explained in the *Shuowen* as "to wind" (*yao*). It is composed of the radical "silk thread" (*mi*) with the phonetic "li. In the sutra, it is written as *cha* (𫮈) with the radical "earth" (*tu*), which differs from the meaning of the original text and is therefore an error.

2. Fascicle Two. "Jiye" (技業)—the character *ji* is pronounced as *qi* with the *yan* rhyme; the *Ziji* (字集) abbreviates it, explaining it as "skillful technique. Gu Yewang states it is synonymous with "art" (*yi*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shou*) and the phonetic "zhi"; its occurrence here as "zhi" is an error.

3. Third Fascicle. Regarding the character 更 (gēng): the *Kǎo Shēng* states it means "alternating," "substituting," or "changing. According to the *Shuōwén*, its correct form is written with the radical 支 (zhī) and the phonetic 丙 (bǐng); the common vulgar form is 更. Below this is the character 胡故反 (hú gù fǎn). Gu Yewáng stated that 互更 (hù gēng) means "to alternate" or "to exchange."

"Layer" (*céng*) means ascending; Guo’s commentary states that "layer" implies repetition. Wang’s commentary on the *Chuci* explains it as "repeated accumulation. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as a multi-storied building, composed of the radical "corpse" (*shī*) with the phonetic element "increasing" (*zēng*).

4. Fourth Fascicle. *Zhū'ù* (株杌): [The character] *zhū* is pronounced with the *chū* rhyme-group (according to Gu Yewang, it refers to the root of a tree trunk; according to the *Kǎoshēng*, it refers to the remains of a felled tree; according to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "wood" and the phonetic "zhū").
*Śaṇḍha* (transliterated as *xiànchāi*, with *chāi* pronounced as *bànzéjiā* [the latter being a variant reading]) is a Sanskrit term.

Regarding the character *guǐ* (軌), the *Guīyǐ* (儀軌) and the *Guǐkǎo* (歸考) state that its sound is *wěi*; the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) says it means "wheel tracks" or "path. Jia’s commentary on the *Guóyuè* (國語) states that *guǐ* refers to the law (*fǎ*). Zheng’s commentary on the *Kǎogōngjì* (考工記) states that *guǐ* refers to the width of the ruts (*zhéguǎng*). The *Shuowén* (說文) explains it as being composed of the radical for "chariot" (*chē*) and the phonetic element *jiǔ*.

Volume Five. Volume Five has no characters for which phonetic glosses can be provided. Volume Six. Regarding the character *yì* (叡): the rhyme dictionary reads it as *yuè* (悅) with the final consonant *sì* (歲). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that *yì* means "enlightened" (*míng*) or "profound" (*jiǎo*). The *Guǎngyǎ* states that *yì* means "wisdom" (*zhì*). The *Shàngshū* states that among the five matters, the mind of reflection is called *yì*. Kǒng Àngguó says: "*Yì* must penetrate the arts. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of *zān* (󲘫) and a simplified form of *gǔ* (谷). The sound of *zān* is *cán* (殘). Volume Six. Volume Six has no characters for which phonetic glosses can be provided.

The *Gongyang Zhuan* states that the qilin (pronounced *liǔ*, with the radical for "tooth" and the phonetic *lǐn*) is a benevolent beast that appears when there is a true king; it is used here to address you. The *Erya* describes it as having the body of an ox, a cow’s tail, and a single horn. Guo Pu’s commentary notes that there is flesh at the tip of its horn. Guo Yuwang says that the *qi* is the female of the *lin*. The *Mao Shi* refers to it as "the hoof of the qilin. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is derived from the character for "deer" (*lù*) with the phonetic *lǐn*.

"Cái" (纔) means "just" or "as soon as. It is explained as being diligent and capable; according to the *Kǎoshēng* (Examination of Sounds), it also means "temporary. The *Shuōwén* states that it is formed from the radical "silk" (糸) with "zhàn" (蹚) as its phonetic component; "zhàn" is pronounced *shì xián* (士咸反).

Volume Seven. Volume Seven contains no characters to be vocalized. *Abhidharma-śāstra*. Compiled by Xuanying, Volume One. 1. Volume One. *Yuan* (pronounced *yu* with the *yuan* rhyme). According to the *Erya*, "yuan" means "at" (*yu*) or "thereupon" (*yu*). Both are particles. "Yuan" also means "to lead" (*yin*). In the *Han Shi*, "yuan" describes the appearance of following a track; it also means "to lead."
"Comprehensive integration" (cānzōng): the first character is pronounced *sān* (with the *niǎn* rhyme) and the second is *zǒng* (with the *sòng* rhyme).

This means to integrate its textual patterns (*wén*) and to comprehend its meanings (*yì*). Regarding "sentient beings" (*yǒuqíng*): the Sanskrit term is *sattva*. *Sat* here means "existence" (*yǒu*), and *tva* means "sentiment" (*qíng*); thus it is called "sentient being. As for the term "living beings" (*zhòngshēng*), according to the Sanskrit original it is *prajñāna*, which is translated as "living beings. These are merely different names for the same thing; therefore, the translation follows the original source.
"Shu" (庶) means "to hope" or "to expect. "Bian yun" (辯蘊): *vyañjana* in Sanskrit; this is translated as "yun" (蘊).

It is called "yun" based on the meaning of "accumulation. The *Zilin* (字林) states that "yun" means "to accumulate. The *Guangya* (廣雅) states that "yun" means "to gather. "Ju" (聚) is pronounced *cai ju* (才句). In the *Zuo Zhuan*, it says "yun zao" (蘊藻); Du Yu stated that "yun" also means "to gather. Because various forms (*rūpa*) are stored therein, they are called the "form aggregate" (*rūpaskandha*). The meanings of the other four—feeling, perception, and so forth—are likewise. In older sūtras and śāstras, they are sometimes called the "five groups" (*pañcagaṇa*) or the "five accumulations" (*pañcapiṇḍa*), which are somewhat close to the correct term, yet they still do not provide a comprehensive name. The old translation of *sat* (薩) has long been lost.

Vipāka (maturation) refers to the maturation of all unwholesome and contaminated phenomena as causes that can induce neutral results. Because the cause and effect differ in kind, and because the cause matures spontaneously in response to its own conditions, it is called a "matured fruit" (*vipāka-phala*). Furthermore, at the time the cause induces the fruit, its power reaches maturity, becoming distinct from its prior state; thus it is called *vipāka*. It is traditionally translated as "fruit-retribution" (*guobao*).
"Jianjing" (堅勁) means "vigorous and strong"; the character is composed of the radical "force" (力).

"Zhantan" (旃檀)—the Sanskrit term pronounced with the second tone on "tu" (徒且反)—is also written as "Zhantanana" (旃檀那). This is a fragrant wood from foreign lands, of which there are various species such as red, white, and purple.

*Satkāyadṛṣṭi* is a term from the Sanskrit language. *Kāya* means "body," while *sat* is indeterminate; it may be said to mean "falsehood," or "impermanence," or "conditioned. Because the interpretations of the various masters of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions are not uniform—since it contains multiple meanings—it is therefore left in its original name.

*Ci* (sacrifice) is read as *si* (similar to this); *si* (offering) is read as *xu* (with the final *li* rhyme). According to the *Erya*, *ci* is the sacrifice to Heaven; *si* is the sacrifice to Earth.
*Xue* (suddenly) is read as *yu* (with the final *wu*) in the *Cangjie Pian*; *xue* means to rise abruptly, and it is also synonymous with "sudden" (*hu*).

*Zhizhang* (執仗): "Zhi" is pronounced as *zhì* (治) and "zhang" as *liàng* (亮). Five-edged blades constitute weapons; that which is grasped and held by people is called a *zhang*. A *zhang* is also a general term for weaponry. *Fenfa* (憤發):
"Fen" is pronounced as *fú* (扶) and *fěn* (粉). In the *Fāngyán* (方言), it means "overflowing with indignation," referring to the fullness of angry qi, as well as emotional delusion.
“Xin” (心): The phonetic component is *li* (戾), which according to the *Zilin* (字林) means “crooked” or “contrary.

The “mind-palace” (*xinfu*, 心府): The phonetic component is *fu* (趺). According to the *Guangya* (廣雅), “palace” (*fu*) means “a collection. The *Baihutong* (白虎通) states: “A person has six palaces, namely the large intestine, small intestine, bladder, stomach, triple burner, and gallbladder.”

"Jian" (慳) is an archaic term synonymous with "lin" (吝). It refers to being excessively attached and stingy; according to local dialects, in the regions between the Jing, Ru, Jiang, and Hu rivers, those who are greedy yet not parsimonious are called "jian."

"Jiao" (撟) [pronounced jiao, with the radical 夭 reversed]: "Jiao" refers to hypocrisy and deception; it means to deceive. To arrogantly claim the commands of the sovereign is called *jiao*; to speak words that are not the legal pronouncements of the former kings is called *jiao*. This character follows the radical for the hand (手); what is written today as "jiao" (矯) is not its original form.

"Yueyu" (悅豫): "Yi" (翼) is pronounced *shù* (庶) with a retroflex *-r* ending; according to the *Erya*, "yu" means joy and happiness, and it also signifies tranquility. "Congrui" (聰叡): the ancient form is "cong-rui" (聰睿);

there are two characters, "he" (壑) and "rui" (睿), which share the same pronunciation, *ruì* (苪). According to the *Guangya*, "rui" means wisdom; according to the *Shuowen*, it means profound clarity. The character is composed of "eye" (目), "valley" (谷 in abbreviated form), and "kan" (𠮧, a variant of 艮). It takes its meaning from the sense of piercing penetration: the valley represents the inexhaustible resonance of sound, while the eye represents clear discernment—a compound character formed by combining these meanings. The phonetic component "kan" (𠮧) has the pronunciation *cán* (殘).

2. Second Fascicle. Second [Section]: *Vyañjana-kāya*. The Sanskrit term is *vyañjana*; this means "that which makes manifest. Because it is through the *vyañjana* (syllable/phoneme) that meaning can be made manifest, it is used here as a substitute. The old translations call it the *rasa-kāya* (taste-body) or the *akṣara-kāya* (letter-body); these are one and the same. *Vyañjana*: the initial *vy-* is pronounced *pū-mien* (蒲眠反). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, when Cang Jie first created writing, he modeled it on categories and imitated forms; therefore, it was called *wen* (pattern/graph). Subsequently, form and sound supplemented one another, and these were called *zi* (character/syllable). A *zi* is so named because it "proliferates" (*zisheng*); it refers to the process of increasing and multiplying.
The term for "the state of being an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*) is *bāla-viśliṣṭa-jana* in the Sanskrit language.
*Bāla* here means "foolish," and *viśliṣṭa* here means "separate."
"Pṛthagjana" here means "born as a separate [being].
One should understand this as referring to a foolish worldling;
that is, one who is shrouded in the darkness of delusion and lacks wisdom.
It is simply because they give rise to the view of self and do not produce the outflow-free (anāsrava) state.

It is also said that "infants arise separately" because their delusion is like that of infants and differs from the arising of the noble ones; thus, in the treatise, they are identified as "infant-like ordinary persons" (pṛthagjana).
They are also called "infant-like ordinary beings" (*ing-ch'i fan-fu*) or "infant ordinary beings.
"Ordinary being" (*fan-fu*) is a semantic translation.
The *Guangya* states: "Fán means light; it is a designation for that which is slight and minute."
In the old translations, it is sometimes called "hair-path ordinary beings" (mào dào fánfū) or sometimes "hair-tip ordinary beings" (mào tóu fánfū).
According to the Sanskrit original, the word for "hair" is *vāla*.
"Foolish" is named *bala*.
This error must have resulted from the phonetic proximity between the sounds *va* and *ba*, which is the fault of the translator.
The character 󲜶 has the pronunciation *yu* with the *qǐ* (departing tone) final.
The sound *va* is pronounced with a retroflex *ka* (like *vakra*).

The characters *ṅa*, *ña*, *ṇa*, *na*, and *ma*—in the Sanskrit language, the former [group] is pronounced with a *u* (like *ukāra*) and the latter [group] with an *i* (like *ikāra*), followed by an *u* (like *ugra*)—these various syllables depend upon auxiliary sounds and dialectal variations to become complete; because they have no distinct meaning of their own, they are collectively termed "meaningless phonemes" (*nirarthaka-vyañjana*).
*Andaja* (egg-born) is also written as *ke* (with the same pronunciation as *koujue* [口角], or *ku* [哭] in the Wu and Kuai regions), referring to the hard outer shell of the egg.

When it is still within the egg, it is called *anda*. *Kalala* is a Sanskrit term; the old translation was *geluo*, which means "congealed mucus. It is formed from the union of the impurities of the father and mother, like honey mixed with curdled milk (*yogurt*). Within the seven days after conception, this congealed mucus is like the cream on top of curdled milk; it gradually solidifies and possesses a slight degree of cohesion.

*Arbuda* is also called *arbuda-tan* or *arbaṭa* in Sanskrit; these are merely variations in the weight of the Sanskrit syllables. This is translated as "blister-knot" (*pao-jie*) or "water-bubble. It refers to the second seven-day period, when a blister-knot forms within the state of "doubt-curd" (*yi-luo*), resembling a grain of millet placed in thick white broth.

The *peśī* is also called *bhiśi*; this is translated as "flesh-mass. By the twenty-first day, it has coagulated and formed a mass of flesh. If it is male, it is broad at the top and narrow at the bottom; if female, it is narrow at the top and broad at the bottom. Although it has formed a lump, it is still soft and has not yet reached the state of painful hardness.
"Zāi" (財) refers to that which people treasure in times of calamity; "huò" (貨) refers specifically to gold. "Zāi" means the means of livelihood, as well as wealth and grain.

"Cái" (材), pronounced with the *zhǎn* (𢧂) tone, refers to materials for use, as well as natural substance or quality. Generally, any wood that has been felled and is ready for the work of a craftsman is called "cái."
Furthermore, "hé" (荷) is an archaic character; it is the same as "hú kě" (胡可) and "hú gē" (胡歌)—the two pronunciations being reversed.

According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "hé" means to lift up or carry on one's shoulders. 3–4: Volumes Three and Four. Volumes Three and Four do not have initial phonetic transcriptions. 5: Volume Five. "Yìn" (胤) is pronounced "yì rèn" (翼刃); "yìn" means succession, referring to the continuous transmission from father to son.
*Māṇava* is a term from the Sanskrit language; it may also be called *māva*, which means "youth" or "one of pure conduct," and is also referred to as "scholar-child" (*routong*) or simply "person.
*Jambudvīpa*—the "Dvipa" pronounced as *shiyen* (時焰)—is named after a tree; the older transliteration is *Yanfou* (剡浮), while some say *Yanfu* (閻浮), both referring to the same thing.

*Acchandika*—in the Sanskrit language, this is translated as "desireless" (*an-iccha*)—refers to one who has never taken pleasure in *parinirvāṇa*. It is also called *icchantika*, which means "having much greed," so named because they crave the pleasures of birth and death and do not seek liberation. They lack faith in and delight in the True Dharma. The old translation was *achanditi*, rendered as "following one's own will."
*Atyantika*: In the Sanskrit language, this is translated as "ultimately without a virtuous mind.

Volume Six, Part Six. *Pūrvavideha*: In the Sanskrit language, it is called *Pūrvavideha*, or alternatively *Pūrvakṣetra*; these are all corruptions of the original Sanskrit sounds. This is translated as "the East."

The name for Aparagoyānī in Sanskrit is sometimes called Kuyāni or Gogāni; "go" means "ox" and "yānī" means "taking and giving," because in that land there are many oxen used for bartering with cattle, just as money and silk are used here in this world.

The northern continent of Uttarakuru is called *Uttarakuru* in Sanskrit, or alternatively *Uttara-mantrin*. This is translated as "Superior" (*gāo shàng zuò*), meaning it is superior to other regions; it is also referred to as the "Victorious Continent" (*shèng zhōu*).

Tuṣita is a term in the Sanskrit language; it is also called Doushiduo or Dousheta, all of which are phonetic corruptions of the Sanskrit sound. This is translated as "The Heaven of Wondrous Feet" (Miaozu Tian) and also as "The Heaven of Contentment" (Zhizu Tian).

The Heaven of Delighting in Transformations (Nirmāṇarati-deva) [is pronounced "Wǔ Kǎo Fǎn"]. Although this heaven possesses actual women, those who undergo transformations are mostly attached to them; the same applies to the men. It is for this reason that it is so named. The old transcription as "Huàlètiān" (Heaven of Delighting in Transformations), with the tone on "Luò," has been erroneous for a long time.

Sumeru Mountain is called *Sumeru* in Sanskrit; it is translated here as "Wondrous High Mountain" (*Miaogao Shan*) and also as "Fine Light Mountain" (*Haoguang Shan*). The older term "Xumi" is a corruption and abbreviation.

"Layer" (*céng*) is pronounced *dēng* (with the final syllable reversed) and "below" (*xià*) is pronounced *jù* (with the final syllable reversed). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "layer" means to pile up; "grade" (*jí*) means a step or succession.

As for the Cakravāḍa Mountains, the Sanskrit term is *Cakravāḍa*, which is translated here as "Wheel Mountain. The old translation was "Iron Enclosure" (*Tiéwéi*). The character "enclosure" (*wéi*) carries the meaning of "wheel" (*lún*); the name "iron" did not originally exist and was merely added by the translators based on the meaning.

*Qíngmíng* is also written as *qíngzé*, both characters being pronounced with the same initial *zìyíng* (自盈) and meaning "the cessation of rain" according to the *Shēnglèi* (Classification of Sounds).

*Gāndharva* is a Sanskrit term; *gàn* is pronounced with the initial *jùjiàn* (渠建). This is translated here as "smelling fragrance" (*xiùxiāng*) or "eating fragrance" (*shíxiāng*). One account states that in the *Lèxīnjīng* (Sūtra on the Joyful Senses), they are called "fragrance deities" (*xiāngshén*). The old transcription *qiándánpó* is entirely erroneous.

"Dying prematurely" (*zhōngyāo*)—the character *wén* (文) is used interchangeably with *yāo* (夭), pronounced *tiáo* (同於矯反). The *Shìmíng* (釋名) states: "To die while still in the prime of youth is called *yāo*. The *Guǎngyá* (廣雅) states: "*Yāozhé* (夭折)," meaning to break off like an object being snapped in the middle. The sense of *yāo* is that one does not complete their natural lifespan.
*Kan-na* (pronounced with a retroflex *n*, also transcribed as *ga-ha-na*) means "solidity"; at the fourth seven-day period, the mass of flesh finally becomes firm and solid.

*Pralaśaka* (in Sanskrit also *parāśaka*) means "limb by limb"; at the fifth seven-day period, distinct features appear. Upon reaching the sixth seven-day period, ears, nose, hands, and feet further emerge from five locations; thus, it is called "repeated limbs. Furthermore, the winds that produce the eyes, ears, and other apertures arise, and great suffering is produced.

7. Fascicle Seven. *Kauṇḍinya* (憒𠆴): The first character is pronounced with the *gōng* and *nèi* finals; the second is pronounced with the *nú* and *xiào* finals. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "confusion" (*kuìluàn*). According to the *Yunjí*, it means "vulgar" (*lìwěi*). *Samāhita* (三摩呬多): The *mó* is pronounced with the *xū* and *lì* finals. This is translated as "equipoise" (*děngyǐn*).

It refers to the stage of superior concentration (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), which is free from sinking and agitation, being able to draw forth (*yǐn*) equality, or that which draws forth equality. That is to say, it draws forth various merits; or, it is that which is drawn forth by equality—that is, because it is like the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) prior to concentration, it is called "that which can draw forth" (*néngyǐn*).
In the *Erya*, "yi" (怡) and "ye" (悅) are glossed as "joyful delight. In the *Zhongyong*, "yi" and "xi" (懌) are glossed as "joyful pleasure.
In the *Guangya*, "yong" (庸) is defined as "harmony"; in the *Xiaoyerya*, "yong" is defined as "goodness," referring to a person who is harmonious and good.
*Ḍāsa* (in Sanskrit, pronounced with the *tu-è* reversal) is translated here as "slave" (*nú*).
*Lǔtǔ* (in Chinese, pronounced with the *lì-gǔ* reversal) refers to hard, barren soil; that which is naturally formed is called *lǔ*, while that produced by humans is called *jiàn*.
*Ūna* (熏坌): In the *Tōngsùwén*, it is written as *chūntǔ*; in the *Shuōwén*, it is explained as the character for "dust" (*chèn*).
*Guṇa* (德): Pronounced *duōlèfǎn*. "Virtue" (*dé*) refers to the virtue of merit; "loss" (*shī*) refers to the loss of transgression. This character signifies the attainment of meaning.

*Jià-sè*: the first character is pronounced *jiā* (with the *xiá* rhyme) and the second is *sè* (with the *suō-lì* rhyme). According to the *Zìlín*, "planting is called *jià* and harvesting is called *sè*. The *Shuōwén* states that the ears and grains of rice are called *jià*; another interpretation says that what is in the fields is called *jià*.

*Kāṅ-què* (pronounced *kǎo* for the first character and *kǔ-jué* for the second): according to the *Tōngsùwén*, "hard and solid" is called *kāṅ-què*; it refers to barren, poor soil. 8. Volume Eight. *Qín-cè-nán*:

*cè* is pronounced *chū-gé*. It means to drive or urge; it signifies diligent labor. The Sanskrit term is *śrāmaṇera*, which is translated here as "the minor one who labors. It is also said to mean "one who rests from cruelty and practices kindness"—this is the literal meaning of the translation. The older term *shāmí* (śrāmaṇa) is a corruption and abbreviation.

*Upāsaka* (in Sanskrit, pronounced with the *u* as in "woo-gu" or also called *upavāsa*) refers to one who has received the three refuges and abides by the five precepts. *Upāha* means "male" (*puruṣa*), or alternatively "lay follower" (*upāsaka*). It is also said to mean "one who dwells near," referring to dwelling near the Three Jewels. Furthermore, it is called "one who dwells well" (*suvāsaka*) or "pure believer" (*śraddhāviśuddha*); these are all interpretive translations. The older term *upāsaka* is a corruption.

The term *upāsikā* is also called *upāsīkā* in the Sanskrit language; *upa* means "to receive" (*śīka*) and *sīkā* means "woman. The remaining meanings are the same as before. The older term *upāsī* is a corruption.

*Śaṇḍha* and *paṇḍaka* are Sanskrit terms; the sound *śaṇḍha* is pronounced with the initial *ch* reversed (i.e., *cha*), while in older sūtras and śāstras it is sometimes written as *baṇḍaka*, which is merely a difference in the weight of the Sanskrit vowels. In Chinese, these are called *huángmén* (eunuchs). There are five types: first, the *paṇḍaka* known as *īrṣyā* (envy), so named because desire arises immediately upon seeing another engage in sexual activity, but not when they do not; they possess male organs yet cannot procreate. Third, the *śaṇḍha-paṇḍaka*, meaning those whose male organs were incomplete from birth and who likewise cannot procreate. Fourth, the *pākṣika-paṇḍaka* (or *lūna-paṇḍaka*), where *lūna* means "cut," referring to those who have been castrated by punishment.
*Jiā* (罝) refers to the rabbit-net; the *Shìmíng* (釋名) states that *jiā* means "to block," as it blocks and captures rabbits. *Ōu* (毆) is pronounced *wū hòu*;
according to the *Shuōwén*, *ǒu* means "to strike with a cudgel," the character being derived from the radical *shū* (殳).

The term *saṃgītika* (literally "house-entertainer") refers to those who perform music and engage in theatrical performances. It is also said that they are "incense-seekers. Such people possess no property or livelihood; they subsist solely by begging. Whenever they see a place where food and drink are available, they go there to provide musical entertainment in order to solicit wealth and sustenance.

Caṇḍāla (the Sanskrit term pronounced with a retroflex *ṭ* and *l*, here translated as "one who seizes the violent and evil," or "evil slayer") is the general name for those whose occupation is butchery and slaughter. When such a person travels, they carry a bell to mark themselves, or a staff made of split bamboo; otherwise, they are known as "old sinners"—this is a corruption of the term Caṇḍāla.
*Kaṭhina* (in Sanskrit *kaṭhin*, pronounced with the *jué* rhyme) refers to those who cook dogs.
*Língmiè* (pronounced *líng* with the *rèn* rhyme and *mòjié* for the second character) means to encroach upon (*líng*) and to insult or wound (*miè*).
*Xiān* (pronounced *xián* with the level tone): According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means "sharp" or "pointed. It refers to the blade of a knife or sword. *Maṇi* (Sanskrit;
pronounced *máng* with the falling tone, also called *mó ní*): This is translated as "precious jewel," which is the general term for pearls and gems.
*Tiao* (苕) is pronounced *tu* (徒) and *diao* (彫); it means "far-reaching.

*Zhou* (洲) is pronounced *tai* (胎) and *zhi* (脂) and *yu* (與); according to the *Erya*, that which can be inhabited within the water is called a *zhou* (island), and a small *zhou* is called a *zhu* (islet).

Volume Nine, Scroll Nine. "Xianbu" (先不) is pronounced as *yin* (音). Volume Ten, Scroll Ten. "Zuzi" (踧踖): the first character is read with the *zi* (子) rhyme group followed by the sixth tone (*fu* [反]), and the second character is also read with the *zi* (子) rhyme group followed by the sixth tone (*fu* [反]). According to the *Guangya*, "zuzi" means "awe and reverence. According to the *Zilin*, "zuzi" means "hesitating and not advancing."

11. Scroll Eleven. "Fěng" (諷) is pronounced as *fèng* (不鳳反). "Fěng" refers to chanting; "sòng" (誦) refers to reciting from memory. The commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "To double the text is called 'sòng'; to regulate it with the voice is called 'fěng'. "Bèi" (倍) is pronounced as *pèi* (音佩).
*Zhuì* (with the *zhāng wèi* rhyme for the first character and *qī lì* for the second) means to continue or to join; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means to join together so that things adhere.
*Lòchā* is a Sanskrit term, also called *lòshā*, which here corresponds to one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*); one hundred *lòshā* constitute one *kūṭhāna*.
*Sarvajña*: In the Sanskrit language this is translated as "All-Knowing" (*yīqièzhì*); the old term *sàpóruò* is a corruption. 12. Volume Twelve. *Gaṅgā*:

In the Sanskrit language, pronounced *jùxīng* (with the second tone on the first character), it is the name of a river. It flows from the Elephant Mouth on the eastern side of Lake Anavatapta and enters the Eastern Ocean. Vārāṇasī is the name of a country; in the language of the Brahmans it is pronounced *vārāṇasī* (with the final syllable rhyming with *nü* and *huá*). Formerly it was called Póluónàiyè, translated as "The Realm Encircled by Rivers. It is said that in this country, colors such as blue, yellow, and others are blended together, hence it is called "the realm of blended colors" (*saṃyukta-rūpa*).
The color of the *umakā* flower and others is called "co-nascent color" (*sahaja-rūpa*) in Sanskrit.
The star *uṣas*—which in Chinese is translated as the "Great White Star"—is taken for its white color.

A *jun* is one who is exceptionally superior to ordinary people."

*Madhyamaka-śāstra*: Preface by Huìlín. Regarding the phonetics of "Gěngjià" (耿价): The *Zhèngjiàn Máoshī* states that "gěnggěng" means "caution" (*jǐng*). *Chǎng* (with the phonetic *xiān-chāng-pǎn*). The *Cāngjié Piān* states that it describes a lofty and prominent appearance; it refers to leveling high ground so that one may look out from afar. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical *pī* (meaning "to strike") and the phonetic *shàng*. The sound of *pī* is *pǔ-bǔ-pǎn*.

"Hou" (喉) [is pronounced with the initial *h* and rhyme *gou*]. The *Cangjie pian* states it means "the throat and pharynx. 3. Treatise, Volume Three. As for the term *quàn* (券): the *Yuèyùn* (韻英) states it means a contract or agreement (*yuē*). The *Shuōwén* (說文) states: "It is a *qì*; it is composed of the radical 'force' (*lì*) and the phonetic component 'shǔ' (*shǔ*)."
*Tū* (pronounced with the *tāi* rhyme): The *Pīcāng* states that *tūshí* resembles gold; the *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic "yú.

*Bèn* (pronounced with the *púmén* rhyme): The *Fāngyán* states that a *bèn* is a ceramic vessel; the *Zhou Lǐ Kǎogōng Jì* states that the potter makes a *bèn*, which holds two *fǔ* and has a thickness of half an inch. The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radical "vessel" (*míng*) and the phonetic "fēn. In the *Lùn Wén*, it is written as *wèng* with the radical "tile" (*wǎ*), which is a vulgar character. *Wēng* (pronounced with the *wēnggòng* rhyme): The *Shuowén* states it means a large jar; it is composed of the radical "tile" (*wǎ*) and the phonetic "gōng. *Fǔ* is pronounced like *fù*.

Regarding "máo" (毫) at the top: according to the *Hugao* (胡高), it is the sound of "kǎo" (考), meaning the length of hair; the *Shuowen* states it is composed of "máo" (毛) and the abbreviated form of "háo" (豪) as the phonetic. Regarding "lí" (𣯛) at the bottom: according to the *Lizhi* (里之), it is the sound of "kǎo" (考); the *Shuowen* states that ten "máo" (毫) constitute one "lí" (𣯛), and it is composed of "máo" (毛) and the abbreviated form of "lī" (釐) as the phonetic.

According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "water" and the phonetic "gàn"; the character in the *Lunwen* (論文), which combines "water" and "wán," is a vulgar form.

*Gai* (pronounced *yú* according to the *Yùfǔ*; the *Běicāng* states that *gai* means to reap). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* says: "For grass it is called *gai*; for grain it is called *huò*. *Ni* (mud): Gu Yewang says that *ni* means "to smear. The *Shuowen* [explains it] as being composed of the radical "water" (*shui*) and the phonetic "ni" (*ni*, read with the *jing* tone as *ji*). The *Shuowen* [explains *ge*] as being composed of the radical "earth" (*tu*) and the phonetic "ji" (abbreviated from *ji*) (*ji*, read with the *jing* tone as *ji*). *Bi* (tiles): the pronunciation is *pu bi*.

*Kian* (pronounced *kian*, with the second character having the *li* and *chan* finals): The *Guoyu* states it is a tool for reaping and harvesting; the *Wenzi Dian* says it is a sickle. The *Shuowen* states that *shian* refers to saliva from the mouth, or alternatively, longing and desire. It is composed of the radical "water" (*shui*) and the phonetic "qian. In the *Shuowen*, the character is written as *yan* (from the mouth) with the phonetic *xi*; in the *Jiaxuan*, it is written as *xian* (from *xuan*), and *yao* (from *xian*) has the same meaning. In the treatise (*lunwen*), it is written as *yan* (from *yan*); this is a vulgar form of the character.

*Liáng* (梁): The upper character is pronounced *lì* with the rhyme *yáng*. The *Erya* states: "The *méi* is called *liáng*. Guo's commentary says it is the main beam of a house. *Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra*, Fascicle One, composed by Xuanying. Fascicle One: Regarding *miè* (篾), the *Bēicāng* dictionary states it refers to splitting the bamboo bark. The *Shēnglèi* states it is *mí* (𥵨). Nowadays, both in the land of Shu and in Guanzhong, bamboo strips are called *mí*. The pronunciation of *mí* is mi; the pronunciation of *xī* (析) is sī-lì. The character is formed from the radical *jīn* (斤) with *mù* (木) below, meaning to split wood; thus it is *xī*. Currently, the common vulgar form is written as *xī*, also using the radical *jīn*.
*Xiémù* (the character *xié* is pronounced with the *xián* and *jié* tones) refers to binding silk with thread and dyeing it; when the thread is removed, a pattern is formed, which is called *xié*.

*Tánzhá* (the character *zhá* is pronounced with the *zhuān* and *xiá* tones) is the *sìzhá* mentioned in the *Sāncāng*; today in Jiangnan, thin slices of wood that have been split and pared are called *sì*, while in Guanzhong they are called *zhá*, or alternatively *sìzhá*. The pronunciation of *sì* is *fūfèi*.

Regarding the characters for *qìng* (甑), the *Shēnglèi* (聲類) states they are also written as *zēng* (𩱭) or *zhì* (󲢤), and in the *Zhòuwén* (籀文) as *qìng* (𩱭); these are all pronounced *zǐ yùn* (子孕). Below that, the *Zhòuwén* form is *zēng* (𩰿), pronounced *cái xīn* (才心). According to the *Zílín* (字林), *qìng* (甑) is a vessel for steaming grain; *zēng* (𩰿) is a large cauldron. One explanation says it is a tripod (*dǐng*) with a wide top and narrow bottom, resembling a *qìng*.

*Utkarṣa* (the first character pronounced with the *wu* and *ke* tones, the second with the *ju* and *ye* tones).

*Xián* (pronounced lián in reverse): According to the *Guǎngyá*, *xián* means "sharp" (*qiān*). It refers to the tip of a blade being called *xián*.

Volume Five, Part Five. *Lóng*: (Pronounced lǐ dōng in reverse). According to the *Shuōwén*, it means "a railing. According to the *Sāncāng*, a *lóng* is a cage used for holding birds and beasts, serving as a railing or enclosure.

Regarding the *gaur* (犎牛), the *Han shu* "Account of the Western Regions" mentions the *miao-niu* (犛牛). Deng Zhan says: "On its back there is a fleshy hump like that of a dromedary; the character for 'difficult' (難) is written as *feng* (犎), pronounced *fei feng*. This refers to the ox found today that is small in stature and has a hump on its shoulder. This is it.

The character *chuíhú* (垂胡) is also written as *huáizhāo* (𩑶啁); both have the same pronunciation, *hùgū* (戶孤反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *hú* refers to the pendulous dewlap hanging from the chin of an ox. The version in the *Lunwen* (論文) uses the character *lǎn* (󲠌), which is not the correct form.

Volume 10: Volume ten. *Shēngguǎn* (莞): the character for *guǎn* is pronounced *gōngduān* (工端) and also has the pronunciation *huán* (桓). This plant resembles an onion on the outside and a rush (*pú*) on the inside, yet it is round. The *Guǎngyá* calls it *cōngpú* (䓗蒲); it can be used to make mats. It grows in water and is also called *guǎnzǐ* (莞子) today.

*Jian* (箭): The pronunciation is *gān* (旱反). According to the *Zilin* (字林), it refers to the shaft of an arrow; the version in the *Lunwen* (論文) uses the character *gan* (竿), which is not the correct character.

*Linjian* (甐堅): Also written as *lin* (粦), with two pronunciations, *lizhen* (力鎭) and *lizhen* (力珍). According to the *Erya* (爾雅), "the *linjian* is the core [of bamboo]. Guo Pu states: "The *lin* is a name for bamboo; its core is hard and can be used to make *xi* (廗, a type of vehicle)."

11. The eleventh fascicle. Furthermore, "fan" (帆) is also written as two characters, 𩗋 and 𩖺, both pronounced with the same initial *fu* and rhyme *yan*. According to the *Tongsu wen* (通俗文), it is said that raising a sail against the wind is called a "fan. The *Shiming* (釋名) explains it as "a sail is a curtain spread according to the wind. Today, it is made either of cloth, reeds, or mats; this is what is meant.

12. The Twelfth Fascicle, Part Two: The *Xianchu* (Toad). [The character for *xian*] is pronounced as *chan* (with the *fanqie* *zhi* and *fan*). According to the *Erya*, it is the *xianqu*. Guo Pu says it resembles a frog and lives on land; the people of Huainan call it *qufu*, and those of Shandong call it *quwen* (*wen* is pronounced as *fangke*). In the common parlance of Jiangnan, the *xianchu* is pronounced as *shiyu*.
13. Volume Thirteen. "Kāpu" (迦逋)—the "pu" is pronounced with the *hu* rhyme—this refers to the "White Pigeon Ground" (Śuklāyasa).

14–15. Volumes Fourteen and Fifteen. Both the fourteenth and fifteenth [volumes] were previously unpronounced.
