Regarding the "army of instruments of action" (*karmakaraṇasena*) among the eight grammatical cases (*vibhakti*): the case of the object (*karman*) is the second, and the case of the instrument (*karaṇa*) is the third. Now, the way of discourse involves establishing and refuting, which is similar to an army; thus, it is given the name "army. The second case expresses the object of the action, and the third case expresses the instrument of the action. The term "army of instruments of action" refers to these two. As for the "eight grammatical cases," they are: (1) substance (*svabhāva*), (2) object (*karman*), (3) instrument (*karaṇa*), (4) recipient (*sampradāna*), (5) point of departure (*apādāna*), (6) relation (*sambandha*), (7) locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and (8) vocative (*āmantraṇa*). This is according to the *Śabdavidyā* (Science of Grammar). Of these, the seven cases are commonly used, while the vocative case is rarely employed.

"Capable of explicating" (néng quán) refers to the capacity to clarify and manifest meaning; "text" (wén) refers to the medium that possesses this capacity. According to the definition, that which fully explains phenomena and principles is called "explication" (quán). The *Huainanzi* states: "Explicating speech means using analogies to explain and illustrate human affairs."

The "Heavenly Māra" (tiānmó) refers to Māra; in this translation, it is called "Obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*), as he can create obstacles for the practice of the Path. He is also called the "Slayer," because the treatises explain that he severs the life-force of wisdom (*prajñājīvitendriya*) and is thus named Māra. He is also called Māra because he constantly practices negligence and thereby harms his own person. Māra is a title or rank, namely the Lord of the Sixth Heaven, whose name is Pāpīyān; this means "Evil Lust," which is the name of the Māra-king at the time when Śākyamuni Buddha appeared in the world. The Māras of each Buddha’s appearance differ; for instance, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, the Māra was named Duḥśīla, which translates as "Evil Anger," and so forth.
"Chǎn" (闡) means to open up and develop; it means to clarify and illuminate.
"Jué" (覺) is pronounced with the first tone; "jué" also means to awaken. According to the *Cāngxièpiān*, to have words after awakening is called "wù" (寤); it refers to awakening after sleep.
*Śūraṅgama* in Sanskrit is translated here as "Valiant Progress" (*jiànxíng*) or "Valiant Aspect" (*jiànxiàng*); it was formerly called *Shòulèngyán*.

*Lucha* (with the second character pronounced like *zhái jiā*) is a suffix that can manifest the meaning of the action performed; wherever there is *lucha*, it necessarily carries the sense of the object of the action. It is not the case that every existing thing must be established by being given multiple names.

The Sautrāntika school emerged from the Sarvāstivāda during the four hundred years following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. This school established only one piṭaka, asserting that there is only the Sūtra-piṭaka. The reason for this designation is that they maintain the Sūtras are the root; since both the Vinaya and the Abhidharma are merely explanations of the meaning of the Sūtras and do not exist apart from them, they establish only the single Sūtra-piṭaka.

"Colors" (cǎi) is pronounced as *qī* (in the "fǎn" [rhyme] category) and "huà" (in the "guà" [rhyme] category). That which is formed by the five colors is called "colors" (*cǎi*); that which depicts their forms and images is called "picturing" (*huà*).
The character for "obstruction" (*guài*) is abbreviated as "huà" (same as the "guà" rhyme), meaning "to hinder" or "to block."

The Vaiśeṣika—its Sanskrit name being *Vaiśeṣika* (the "扶廢反" [fú fèi fǎn] transcription is also rendered as *Vaiśeṣika*, both of which are corruptions)—is so called because its doctrines are superior (*viśeṣa*) to others and because it excels in refuting and destroying the arguments of others. Its system takes six categories (*padārtha*) as its fundamental tenets, though some speak of six truths (*satya*).

"Teacher" refers to the master; "disciple" refers to the student. "Disciple" (zi) also means to utilize or to take up. A good person is the teacher of the not-good person, while the not-good person is the resource for the good person—just as one utilizes material wealth.

*Gāthā* is a term from the Sanskrit language; in this land [of China], it is commonly referred to as "verse" (*sung*) or "summary statement" (*she yan*). Whatever has been composed by the various sages—regardless of whether it is a *geya* (repeated verse) or the number of characters—is termed a *gāthā* provided it consists of four lines per verse. According to the method of counting verses in the Western Regions, thirty-two characters constitute one *gāthā*. The term *gāthā* is sometimes corruptedly pronounced as *gāta*. The old term "ge" (偈) is likewise a corruption of *gāthā*.

*Naraka* is a term from the Sanskrit language; it is also called *Naluo* (那羅柯) and *Niluoye* (泥羅夜). The older transcription *Niluoyeshe* (泥羅耶斯) is merely a variation in dialect within the Sanskrit itself. This translation carries four meanings: first, "unpleasant"; second, "incurable" or "without rescue"; third, "darkness"; and fourth, "hell. When the sutras speak of "hells," this refers to one specific meaning. For these reasons, the original term is retained; alternatively, it is called "non-practice" (*fei xing*), meaning a place where non-dharma practice occurs.

*Āgama* is a Sanskrit term; its pronunciation is *ā-ga-ma*. It is also called *āgamana*, which means "the teaching" (*dharma-deśanā*). Alternatively, it is said to mean "transmission," referring to that which has been handed down successively through successive generations as instruction on the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). The older transliteration *āhan* is a corruption and abbreviation.

"Shi-chan" (市廛) is pronounced zhí-lián; its Sanskrit equivalent is *āpaṇa*, which is translated here as "market stall. The *Liji* (Book of Rites) states, "In the market stalls (*shichan*), no tax is levied," and Zheng Xuan comments that "chan" refers to the shops where goods are displayed—these are the stalls within the marketplace today. The old [translation] "desire to act" (*yùxíng*) is incorrect. According to the Sanskrit manuscript, it is *saṃskāra*, which means "action" (*xíng*). Since "action" was not appropriate for the original context, it was established as "stall" (*chán*).
Regarding "epilepsy" (jiǎn hé): the *Yīnyì* (Classified Pronunciations) states it refers to infantile epilepsy. Volume Two. This is the second volume. "Mahīśāsaka" is a Sanskrit term.

It emerged from the Sarvāstivāda during the third century [after the Buddha’s passing]. The Sanskrit is *Mahīśāsaka*, also called *Mihisāsaka*. This is translated as "Transforming the Land" (*huàdì*), also "Teaching the Land" (*jiàodì*), or "Correct Land. It is the name of a person; however, because this Arhat was a ruler of a kingdom in secular life and transformed the territory, he is called "Transforming the Land. Now that he has entered the Buddha-dharma, he likewise transforms it like the earth, and thus it is named accordingly. The old name "Mi-sha-se" is a corruption.
"Shù (樹)"—the tone is *zhì* (時注反). The *Guǎngyá* states: "To plant, to establish. Generally, all acts of placing or erecting are called "shù";
"shù" also means to sow. "Zhào" (照)—the tone is *yù* (曯之欲反). "Zhù" (曯) also means brightness.
*Guàn* (貫) means to penetrate; it signifies thoroughness. According to the *Cāngjiépiān*, *guàn* refers to piercing through. To thread an object with a cord is called *guàn*.
*Juànsuǒ* (羂索) is also written as *juàn* (󱺍), both pronounced *gǔxuàn* (古泫反). According to the *Shēnglèi* (聲類), *juàn* (𦚋) refers to capturing; to catch a beast with a cord is called *juàn*.
"Untried" (*cháng*) means "never before experienced. According to the *Guǎngyá*, "cháng" means "temporary" or "to test. In the *Ěrshū*, it is read as *lǜ* (律) or *lǜ* (尒);

in the *Ěrpǐ*, it is glossed as "following from oneself," meaning to speak first according to one's own intention. In the *Lúnyǔ*, when Zilu "responded rashly" (*lǜ'ěr*), Hé Yàn explained that this meant he responded before the other three disciples. This is correct.
*Jùshèng* (巨勝): The character *jù* (巨) means "large. The *Bencao* (本草) states that among sesame seeds (*húmá*), those with large grains and black color are called *jùshèng*.

Regarding *zhòngxiè* (眾纈)—the character *xiè* (纈) is pronounced *xiánjié* (賢結)—it refers to binding silk with thread and dyeing it; when the thread is removed, patterns are formed, which is called *xiè*. It is said that in the Western Regions, one uses a liquid extract to dot the fabric to create such patterns, similar to the wax-resist dyeing (*làdiǎnxiè*) practiced here in this land.

*Kṛtva* (訖埵) is a transliteration of the Sanskrit term; it is pronounced *jùguǒ* (都果反). It carries the meaning of "already completed" (*kṛta*). For example, as in the expressions "having finished bathing and eating," or "having crossed the mountain and crossed the river.

Regarding *huòrǒu* (和糅), there are two archaic forms, *niǔ* (鈕) and *jiǎn* (󲜛), both pronounced *nǚjiù* (女救反). According to the *Guǎngyá*, *rǒu* means "to mix. Today, we say that the gathering together of objects of different colors is called *rǒu*.
"Bending the bow" (*wān gōng*) means to draw back the bow; according to the *Xiǎo ěr pǐ*, "bending" (*wān*) and "controlling" (*kòng*) mean to pull or draw.

"Flower garland" (*huá màn*): the Sanskrit term is *mālā*, which is translated here as "garland" (*màn*; pronounced *mán*). It is observed that in the Western Regions, garland-makers mostly string *sumana* flowers in rows to form them; regardless of social rank—whether noble or humble—all use this for adornment and personal decoration.

*Tí* (with the phonetic *lí* in the second tone; the following character is *pú* with the phonetic *xiè*) refers to *tí*, which resembles *bài*; it is a weed that spreads across the ground. *Bǎi* is a grass that resembles grain.
*Mò* (with the phonetic *ná* with the phonetic *mó* in the second tone) is translated here as "mind" (*manas*).
"Hun" (渾) [pronounced with the second tone on the final character *hú*] means turbid; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means chaotic.
"Xian" (鮮) [pronounced *xiān*] means beautiful or excellent according to the *Guoyaya*.

3. Third Fascicle. Third Fascicle. *Fén* (焚): To burn; it is also used in the sense of "to consume. The character is composed of the radical for fire (*huǒ*) and the phonetic *lín*, conveying the meaning of burning a forest.

*Qīn* (𠍴): To offend or transgress; it is also written as *qiān* (愆) or *qiēn* (諐), all sharing the same pronunciation (*qù lián*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *qiān* means "error," "loss," or "crime"; it also implies "offending" or "invading."

*Língyǔ* (囹圄) [the first character pronounced *lìng* with the tone *dīng*; the second character pronounced *yǔ* with the tone *lí*] is the name for a prison. According to the *Zhou Lǐ*, prisons first appeared during the Three Kings. The *Guǎng Yá* states that in the Xia dynasty it was called Xiàtái, in the Yin dynasty Yǒulǐ, and in the Zhou dynasty Língyǔ; these are all specific names for prisons. The *Shìmíng* explains: "Líng" means to lead (*lǐng*), and "yǔ" means to ward off (*yù*); it refers to leading and recording prisoners and warding them off.
*Hui* (穢): *qi* (且) and *li* (歷) are the phonetic components; it refers to an accumulation of stones, called a *qì* (磧). According to the *Guǎngyá*, a *qì* is a rapid current.

Volume Four, Part Four. *Tí* (瞖): *yù* (於) and *jì* (計) are the phonetic components; the *Yùnjí* states it is a disease that obstructs the eyes. *Xuàn* (眩): *xuán* (玄) and *juàn* (絹) are the phonetic components; according to the *Zílín*, it means dizziness or confusion.
"Mengjue" (夢覺) [the first character pronounced *ju* with the *jiao* rhyme;

it means awakening]. "Dànpò" (憺怕) [the first character pronounced *tú* with the *lán* rhyme; the second character pronounced *pǔ* with the *bái* rhyme]. According to the *Guǎngyá*, "dànpò" means silent and desolate (*jìmò*), and also denotes tranquility (*tiánjìng*). It describes a state of stillness and solitude where no people are present.
"Shen mei" (身寐): "mei" is pronounced as "min bi" (民庇). "Mei" refers to being in deep sleep; the *Gongye* says, "The Duke lay down but did not sleep. "Qin" (寢) means to lie down. "Xiong li" (𢤱戾):
"lu gong lu kong" (祿公祿孔) are the two pronunciations. It refers to being perverse, stubborn, and fierce.

*Tuan* (湍) is pronounced *tu* (with the second tone) and *hui* (迴) in the following [character]. "Turbulent water" refers to rushing water; "eddying water" refers to swirling water. "Rushing" means swift and impetuous. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *tuan* is a rapid torrent; it is shallow water flowing over sand.

*Daozhang* (刀仗): *dao* (刀) is pronounced with the *zhì* (直) and *liàng* (亮) finals; it refers to what people grasp and hold as a weapon (*zhàng*). *Zhàng* (仗) is also a general term for bows, spears, pestles, and clubs.

*Chàngyàn* (倡豔): *chàng* (倡) is pronounced with the *chǐ* (齒) and *yáng* (揚) finals; below it is also written as *yàn* (艷), which is the same. *Chàng* means entertainment; *yàn* means beauty. A beautiful countenance is called *yàn*.

The term "者" (zhě) [is pronounced *zhě* or *yě* according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*; it is a word used to establish a matter and also clarifies the emergence of a phrase]. Because it is the fundamental explanation, the word "者" is repeated.

As for "如如" (*rú rú*), since the phenomena traversed are not one, it is called "如如. "如如" refers to the *tathatā* (suchness). "如是" (*rú shì*) likewise refers to the *tathatā*. "如是" is an indication of that very suchness.

Vitarka (尋) and vicāra (伺)—*vitarka* is translated as "seeking" (*xún*) and *vicāra* as "examining" (*sì*). *Vitarka* refers to seeking; *vicāra* refers to close examination. Alternatively, they are [states of] either thought (*cetanā*) or wisdom (*prajñā*) that investigate an object. The coarse state of these two is called *vitarka*, while the subtle state of these same two that scrutinizes the object is called *vicāra*. Therefore, they are termed "vitarka and vicāra. As for the older translation "applied thought and sustained thought" (*jué guān*), according to the Sanskrit originals, *bodha* means "individual awareness" and *vipaśyanā* means "insight" (*guān*). The translators failed to consult the original terminology, resulting in this discrepancy.
*Pánqū* (蟠曲): According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "coiled," "to turn back," or "to bend. *Zǐzhōu* (𦳃子洲): Also written as *zǐ* (𦳃). Pronounced *yīzhē*.

This is an island located several thousand *lǐ* south of the sea from the Kingdom of Siṃhala (Sri Lanka). The people there are short and small, standing only three feet tall; they have human bodies with bird-like beaks and eat only *zǐ* (𦳃) seeds. Since they have no cultivated grains, they do not recognize oxen.

*Kapila* is a Sanskrit term; here it means "red-colored," referring to the Red-Colored Sage (*Kapila Muni*), who composed the *Sāṃkhya-śāstra* and expounded the doctrine of the twenty-five principles (*tattva*).
*Saugata* (pronounced *sāojīduō* in Chinese) is the name of a disciple of the Sugata; the Sugata is one of the ten epithets of the Buddha, meaning "Well-Gone" (*Sugata*).
"Disturbance" (rǎodòng): "Zhao" means to disturb; according to the *Shuowen*, it means to vex; according to the *Guangya*, it means to confuse.
5. Fascicle Five. *Nigantuka* (Ni jiàn chá shū): This is a Sanskrit term translated here as "various names for a collection," such as when a single object has many names.

"Yù (御)" [yù, with the phonetic component 魚 reversed] means to drive or control; according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means to employ. "To drive within" means to do good; it refers to casting aside the banner to direct the horses.
"Bùdài (不逮)" [bù, with the phonetic component 徒 reversed] means "not reaching"; according to the *Ěryá*, "dài" means "to reach."

*Qú* (劬勞): In the *Mao Shi*, it is glossed as "toiling"; in the *Han Shi*, *qú* means "frequent. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that *qú láo* means "sickness. *Shù* (數) has the phonetic reading *suǒ jué*. *Ālánruò* (阿練若): This is a Sanskrit term.

*Ā* here means "without" (*wu*). *Lánruò* has two meanings: first, "sound," meaning there are no human voices nor sounds of clamor and uproar; second, "cutting," meaning there is no cutting or felling [of trees]. Although it is said that a place one *krośa* (one *jùlúshè*) away from a village constitutes an *āraṇyaka* site, one must also remain far removed from places where cutting and felling occur. *Zào* (譟) has the phonetic reading *sāng dào*.
*Krośa* is a Sanskrit term meaning "the sound of a great bull. Its sound can be heard for five *li*; the old translation was "one *krośa*," which here is rendered as "five *li*.

Sixth Fascicle, Part Six: *Rāhula*. In Sanskrit he is also called *Rāhula*. The old translation was "Lohuluo" (羅睺羅); this means "obscuring the moon. He was named because he was born at the time when the Asura Rāhula used his hand to obscure the moon. He remained in his mother’s womb for seven years due to two causes: first, from past karma; second, from present conditions.
"Zhu" (誅) means to pursue and punish for crimes; according to the *Guangya*, it means to kill; according to the *Shuowen*, it means to punish or to reprimand.

"Na yu duo" (那庾多) is a Sanskrit term pronounced with the second tone on "yi" (翼) and the fourth tone on "zhu" (主); the old translation is "nayuta," which corresponds to a number of one thousand billion.
*Jiān* (pronounced *gu-xuán-fǎn*): In the dialects of the South and Chu, "jiān" refers to recovery from illness; it also means to eliminate.

*Zhēn* (pronounced *shì-jīn-fǎn*, with the second character pronounced *qié-xìng-fǎn*): According to the *Guǎngyá*, a dense growth of trees is called *zhēn*. The *Zílín* states that the mountain elm (*shān yú*) is also called *gěng*; it has thorns and can produce *wútí* (the catkins of the elm). *Gěng* means stubborn or strong.
*Agada* (Sanskrit) is also called *agata* or *agatha*; these are phonetic corruptions of the Sanskrit term. It refers to "pills" (*wan-yao*).

*Qie-dan* (also written as *qi*)—the first character pronounced with the *qu* and *ye* finals (*qūyè*)—means to fear greatly; the second character, pronounced with the *xi* and *dan* finals (*xǐdàn*), means to be startled or apprehensive.

7. Volume Seven. "Kuì" (潰) means to disintegrate or dissolve; it is the same as "huàn" (殨). It is pronounced with the rhyme of "hù" (胡對反). According to the *Cāngjiépiān* (Cangjie Pian), "kuì" means to break open from the side; according to the *Shuōwén* (Shuowen), "kuì" means to leak.

To view as an enemy (*yuan-chou*) is the opposite of [viewing as] a friend; according to the *Sancang*, "enmity" (*yuan-ou*) is called "rival" (*chou*), and the *Erya* states that "rival" means "match. *Uddāna* (transliterated as *wu-tuo-nan*;

the first character is pronounced *wu-gu* and the second *tu-wo*, with the final syllable having the sound *nan*) is a Sanskrit term. This is translated as "gathering the scattered," also called "collective bestowal," or "compiling the total of the scattered. The old translation "Yutana" is a corruption.
"Yu-wan" (遊玩): the "Zi-lin" (字林) dictionary defines it as "to dally with"; the "Guang-ya" (廣雅) defines it as "objects of pleasure.
"Ghoṣa-sūtra" (瞿沙經): "Ghoṣa" is translated here as "Wondrous Sound" (妙音); it is a person's name, and the sūtra is named after that person.
8. Fascicle Eight. "Cōngmǐn" (聰敏): "Cōng" (聰) means to hear subtly; it refers to prior knowledge. "Mǐn" (敏) means clear comprehension; it refers to agility and swiftness. 9. Fascicle Nine.

"Jíshì" (即士), also called "yīshì" (依士). "Shì" (士) refers to a master. Because a name is established based on its primary referent, it is called "dependent on the master," as in the case of "eye-consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*) and so forth.

The *karmadhāraya* compound [is explained as follows]: "function" (*karman*) refers to activity. The specific meaning invoked by the establishment of a name is called "function. When two names are established for a single entity, it clarifies that the essence of that entity can maintain two functions—just as when one says, "the eye is itself a *dhātu*," and so forth.

"Shu-er zhi yu fan guo" (The desire to turn the ears toward the state) means fearing that the people of the state will direct their ears and eyes toward oneself. Wei Zhao says: "Shu means 'to pour into' (zhu). The *Yinyi* of the *Hanshu* says: "Shu means 'near' (jin). This is as in the *Shijing*: "The ear is directed toward the wall. (Shu-er zhi yu fan guo).

"Guaranteeing and fulfilling" (*baoren*) is a reversal of the meaning of the characters; "guaranteeing" (*bao*) means to hold fast, and "fulfilling" (*ren*) means to preserve. It signifies that which can be relied upon with confidence.

"Muyi" (Mother Village) is the Sanskrit term *mātṛpura*; this is translated as *mukhara*. *Ma* here means "village. Since "village" (*yi*) is used here to replace "village" (*cun*), it is called "Mother Village. It is so named because it refers to the class of women.

The term *nāga* in the language of the Brahmans has three meanings: first, "dragon"; second, "elephant"; and third, "one who does not come. In the *Kongque jing* (Hamsa Sūtra), the Buddha is called a *nāga* because he will no longer return to the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

Pūraṇa (the first character pronounced with the *bǔ* and *hòu* rhymes, and the second with the *luó* and *gē* rhymes) is the name of one among the six heterodox teachers; the old [translation] calls him Pūraṇa Kāśyapa. "Kāśyapa" is his clan name (*gotra*), while "Pūraṇa" is his personal name. He was a follower of the heterodox path who adhered to the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

10. Volume Ten. "Yu-zhuang" (愚戇): *zhuang* is pronounced as *jue* (絳) with a reversed tone. According to the *Sancang*, it means to be ignorant and lacking knowledge; it is also a synonym for *yu* (戆). The *Guangya* states that *zhuang* means stubborn and dull-witted. The *Shuowen* defines it as being foolish (*chi*). *Zhuang* is also synonymous with *yu*.

"Wan" (頑) and "yin" (嚚): the first is pronounced *huán* (with the tone reversed), and the second is pronounced *yújīn* (魚巾反). According to the *Guǎngyá*, "wan-yin" means "foolish" (*yú*) and "dull-witted" (*duì*). The *Cāngjiépiān* states that "yin" means "wicked. This corresponds to the *Zuǒzhuan*: "When the mind does not fathom the constant path of virtue and righteousness, it is called 'wan'; when the mouth does not speak words of loyalty and good faith, it is called 'yin'. This is what is meant.
Vairocana-rāja is the Sanskrit term; what was formerly called King Vairūḍhaka is one and the same.

It is *vaidūrya*, which is transliterated as *liuli* (lapis lazuli). It is also called *vaidūrya-kṣa*, or *vaidūrya*; it is named after a mountain, namely the Distant Mountain (*Dūra-parvata*), which is Mount Sumeru. This gem is blue in color and cannot be destroyed by any other jewels. Furthermore, it cannot be melted or cast by smoke or flame; only spirits possessing supernatural powers can break it. Regarding its substance, some say it is the shell of a garuḍa egg, which spirits break open to sell this gem to the human world.
*Musāragalva* is a Sanskrit term, also called *masāra*, which is a gemstone of deep blue color.
*Aśmagarbha* is a Sanskrit term, also called *aśmagarbha-va*, which is a gemstone of red color.

The "Indranīla" mentioned here refers to the precious gem of Śakra; it is also blue in color, and because it is the most excellent, it is called "Śakra-blue. Alternatively, it is explained that the ground beneath the Pārijātaka tree where Śakra dwells is made of this gem, hence it is named "Śakra-blue. *Nīla* means "blue," and *mukta* means "pearl"; thus, this gem is used as a pearl.
Mahānīla (Great Blue) is the Sanskrit term; in this [language], it is translated as "Great Blue. It is also a jewel used by Śakra. Kañcanaka-ratna:

in the Sanskrit language, the seventh [character] is *luṣi* (pronounced with the initial *l* and the rhyme *xūyǐ*); *huànkē* (眩柯) means *mukta* (pearl), and *tí* (㕧) is pronounced with the initial *xū* and the rhyme *yǐ*.
The character *zhěng* (拯) in "Zhēngbá" (拯拔) is an upper tone (*shǎngshēng*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "to *zhěng*" means to lift up from below;

it signifies to rescue or assist. *Asaṅga* is a Sanskrit term; here it is called *Ā*. It is pronounced with a short vowel when called thus, but if called with a long vowel, it is rendered as *Zhòng*. The old translation "Sengqie" (僧佉) is a corruption.

*Foxing lun* (Treatise on Buddha-nature), Fascicle One. Xuanying [states]: "The first fascicle, 'nǎi' (臍). The *Kǎoshēng* says it is 'hépí' (膍臍). The *Shuowén* says it is composed of the radical 'flesh' (肉) with 'qí' (齊) as the phonetic. It is also written as 'qián' (䐡); the *Kǎoshēng* says it is 'xiōngyīng' (胷膺). The *Shuowén* agrees; it is also written as 'xiōng' (匈), composed of 'flesh' below and 'xiōng' (凶) above."

*Pǒu*: The rhyme is *gōu*. The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry) says that *pǒu* means "to gather. The *Shuowén* (Explanations of Words and Texts) states it means "to take up," composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic component "fú" (*fú*).

*Kài*: The upper character's rhyme is *lì*; the lower character's rhyme is *huàn*. The *Zhuāngzǐ* says: "The flooding waters irrigate the fields. The *Kǎoshēng* (Investigation of Sounds) says it means "clear. Gù Yěwáng says: "To *guàn* is like to pour down and moisten. The *Shuowén* says it is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic component *jì* (*jì*). The character *guàn* is composed of the radical "water" and the phonetic component *huán* (*huán*); the sound of *huán* is *huán*.

2. Second Fascicle. "Nizhi" (mud/sediment). [The character] "zī" (緇) is pronounced with the final "shǐ" (史) reversed. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "It is dregs and sediment. The *Shuowen Jiezi* also states that "zǎi" (滓) is "diàn" (澱); it takes the radical "water" (水) and the phonetic "zǎi" (宰).

*Chéngtíng* (澄渟): The *Dìngjīng* (定經) reads it as *fǎn* (反). The *Pīcāng* (埤蒼) states it is where water collects; lexicographical works state it is where water stagnates. The *Guǎngyá* (廣雅) also defines it as "stagnant" (*tíngzhǐ*). According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical for water with *tíng* (亭) as the phonetic component.

*Nuoh* (濡滑): The first character is pronounced with the *shang* tone and the phonetic *ru* (汝). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (毛詩傳) states that it means "to soak" (*ni*) or "moisture. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "water" and the phonetic "xu" (需), which is pronounced like *xu*.

*Shuangguan* (䨥觀): The first character is pronounced with the *huo* tone and the phonetic *guo* (郭). Lexicons state that it describes the appearance of heavy rain; ancient and modern classical commentaries also refer to it as *shuangguan*. It is composed of the radical "rain" and the phonetic "zhi" (隻), which is pronounced like *yi*. *Shuangguan*: The first character is pronounced like *yi*.

The character for "spider" (zhū) has the phonetic *qí* (奇) in the upper part and *jù* (俱) in the lower part; it is also written as "zhēngzhū" (鼅鼄) in the *Shuowen Jiezi*. It is also the same as "máo" (蝥). The form used in the scriptures is "zhūzhū" (𧍒𧍒), which is a character used interchangeably with the former.

The character *gǔ* (轂) is pronounced as *shàng gōng mù fǎn*. The *Gōngkǒng Jì* (Record of the Craftsman) states: "The hub (*gǔ*) is for the sake of facilitating rotation. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "It is the point where the spokes converge; it is composed of the radical *chē* (車) with the phonetic *mù* (木). The character *wǔ* (武) is pronounced as *fǎng fǎn*. According to Wang’s commentary on the *Chuci* (Songs of Chu), it refers to the wooden components of the wheel's branches. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "It is composed of the radical *chē* (車) with the phonetic *yáng* (𠕀)."

*Fù* (輻): Pronounced *shàng fǔ mù fǎn*. Yě Wáng’s *Zòuyù* states it refers to the hub (*gǔ*) and the rim (*zhāo*). The *Shuowén* says it is composed of the radical "chariot" (*chē*) with the phonetic element *fú*. Below, it is pronounced *chōng liù fǎn*. In the *Yílǐ*, the axle (*zhóu*) is shaped like a rolling wheel, with both ends carved into sockets (*zhǐ*). The *rǒng* (coffin carriage) is shaped like a long wooden frame; holes are bored through the front and back, and metal pins are inserted to secure the axle. The *Shuowén* says it is composed of the radical "chariot" with the phonetic element *yóu*.

3. Third Fascicle. This third fascicle explains and defines names; it refers back to Ye Wang’s *Yiwen Leiju*, which provides the name as "ming" (with the departing tone). The character for "jing" (sutra) is formed from the radical "yan" (speech), yet the character for "ming" (name) does not exist in the *Zishu* (Dictionary of Characters).

*Zhanran* (湛然): In the *Zhāi xiàn fǎn* (宅陷反), it means "serene peace" (*zhān'ān*). In the *Cāngjié piān* (蒼頡篇), it describes the appearance of water that does not flow. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic "shèn" (*shēn*).

*Jìngyuē* (靖約): The upper character is pronounced *jǐngfǎn*. Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* states: "Jìng means peace. The *Máo shī chuán* (毛詩傳) states: "Jìng also means good. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means "peaceful," composed of the radical "standing" (*lì*) and the phonetic "qīng" (*qīng*). The lower character is pronounced *yāngjiǎofǎn*.

"Piao-sè" (縹色): "pǐ" is pronounced with the retroflex *r* (遶反). Wang’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that it refers to garments shining with a verdant green. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as a white-and-blue silk; it is composed of the radical "silk thread" (糸) and the phonetic "piao" (票). The sound of "silk thread" (糸) is "mi" (覔), and the sound of "piao" (票) is "bi-yáo" (必遙反).

"Duǎn" (short/brief). Pronounced with the final rhyme of duān (端) and the initial of nuǎn (煖). In the *Cangjie pian*, it means "short. According to the *Shuowen jiezi*, when there is a matter of long and short, one uses the character for "arrow" (*shì*) as the standard for what is not long; it is composed of "arrow" (*shì*) and the phonetic element "dòu" (*dòu*). The version in the [present] scripture that uses "dòu" and "cùn" (寸) to form "duàn" (𭔰) is incorrect.

4. Fourth Fascicle. Regarding "pó" (破): *Tángtú* (塘徒) [is the pronunciation]. The *Pīcāng* states that in Changsha Commandery, a dike is called a *dàng* (䧜). To form *dàng* (䧜), according to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "阜" (阜) and the phonetic element "táng" (唐).

*Zhùjīn* (casting gold) is *zhùshù* (red tree); *fǎngù* (looking back) refers to *yěwáng* (Wild Wang), meaning to cast copper into vessels. According to the *Shuowen*, it means to melt gold, composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic "shòu.

*Xiāngkāi* (rubbing against each other) is pronounced *kǒujiē* (mouth-jiē). According to the *Guoyaya*, it means to rub and polish. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "jiē."

*Deciding Treasury Treatise* (*Nirṇayasaṃgrahaśāstra*), three fascicles; compiled by Huilin with phonetic glosses. Fascicle One, Upper Part. "Qingyu" (青淤): the lower character is pronounced *yù* (at the end of a phrase). According to the *Kǎoshēng* (Examination of Sounds), *yū* refers to congealed mud in water. Gu Yewang states that what is now called "mud-grass" in water is *yū*. The *Shuowén* (Explaining Characters and Analyzing Words) defines it as "sediment"; it is composed of the radical "water" and the phonetic "yú."

"Yi (猗) is pronounced as *yǐ* (with the *yì* rhyme). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states: 'Yi is an exclamation; it denotes praise, addition, and selection. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical 犬 (*quān*) with the phonetic 奇 (*qí*); it is also used interchangeably with 依 (*yī*), which is composed of the radical 人 (*rén*)."

2. Middle Volume. "Xī" (睎) is pronounced as *xīn* (欣) with the final rhyme *wàng* (望). Zhuangzi says that the meaning of "xī" refers to speaking with sycophancy (*chǎn*). The *Shuowen* defines it as "to gaze. The *Lunyu* uses the character "xì" (憘), which is formed with the "heart" radical; this is a vulgar variant, and its meaning is the same as [the preceding].

*Qūzhú* (pronounced *shàngqū jùfǎngù*). Yuè Yěwáng says it means to drive away and chase off. The *Guǎngyá* says it means to run. The *Cāngjiépiān* says that to drive repeatedly day after day is also to gallop. The *Shuōwén* says it means to race; it is composed of the radical "horse" with the phonetic "qū."

*Kuángxiāo* (狂痟): The second character, *xiāo*, is pronounced with the *jiǎo* rhyme group (small *jiāo*). In his commentary on the *Zhouli*, Zheng Xuan states that *xiāo* refers to the ailment of "sourness and emaciation" (*suānxiào*) affecting the head. The *Pīcāng* lexicon states that *xiāo* also means thirst and illness. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical *nà* (sickness) and the phonetic *xiào*; *nà* is pronounced *nǚ'è* (female-impediment), and *xiào* is pronounced *xiāodiào* (dissolve-suspend).

3. Scroll 3, Part 2. *Guǐ* (upper character pronounced with the *xià* rhyme group; *shān-hǎi-jīng*: "The waters of Dūnzhēng abound in red *guǐ* fish"; *Zhì* also considers this the same as the *guǐ* in *hán-guǐ*). *Lù* (upper character pronounced *shū-luó*; its *guǐ-liáng* [provisions] refers to this). In the *Gǔjīn zhèngzì*, it follows the radical for fish (*yú*) and takes *guī* as the phonetic component; the lower part is pronounced *sū-gāo*. In the *Shānhǎijīng*, on Mount Niǎoshǔtóngxué, there are many *guǐ* fish, resembling sturgeon (*chán-yú*); when they move, there will be great military conflict. In the *Gǔjīn zhèngzì*, it is said that it follows the radical for fish and takes *mǎn* as the phonetic component. *Zǎo* is pronounced *zǎo*.
*Tuánshí* (搏食): The first character is pronounced with the *duàn* and *luó* rhymes. According to the *Bóyǎ*, "to *tuán*" means to grasp an object with the hand so that it adheres together.

The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "zhuān" (*shēng*). *Jìshù* (𣔳色): The first character is pronounced with the *tāng* and *luò* rhymes. Guō’s commentary on the *Ěryǎ* states: "In the Jiangdong region today, they call the act of cutting an object *jìshù*. Nowadays, some take this to mean striking what one guards; however, the pronunciation is *tuō*. In the *Kǎoshēngjiě*, it is said that wood is split; this refers to the grain being straight. The correct modern orthography is *pàn*. It is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "hè" (pronounced *chǐ*). To derive it from the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and form it as *zhé* is an error.

"Zào" (燥): The character is read as *sān* (竈) and *fǎn* (反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Zào means 'dry' (*qián*). It is composed of the radical 'fire' (*huǒ*) and the phonetic 'sào' (*zào*). "Fāngbiàn xīnlùn" (方便心論): *Fāngbiàn xīnlùn*, one fascicle, compiled by Huìlín.

The pronunciation is *tí* (稊) and *pài* (稗). For the upper character *tí*, it is read as *dì* (弟) and *ní* (泥). The *Jixùn* states: "Tí is the name of a weed; it resembles *pài* but is finer and smaller. It is also called *yīng* (英). The *Shuowen* writes it as *dì* (第), which is used here by extension. For the lower character *pài*, it is read as *mài* (賣). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* says: "*Bǐ pài* refers to weeds that resemble grain. The *Shuowen* states: "It is a specific name for rice. It is composed of the radical 'grain' (*huó*) and the phonetic 'yǎo' (*ǎi*)."

Regarding "zǒng" (摠): the upper radical is "zōng" (宗), pronounced with the *kǎng* (孔) tone. Yuè Yěwáng says it means "to lead," "to unite," "to bind," or "to constrain. According to the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲), it means "all" (*dū*). In the standard characters of antiquity and modern times, it is sometimes written as "zǒng" (総). It takes the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "hūn" (怱), with the lower part pronounced with the *dìng* (丁) and *dì* (弟) tones. Regarding "dì" (諦): according to the *Fāngyán* (方言), it means "to examine closely"; according to the *Shuōwén* (說文), it takes the radical "speech" (言) and the phonetic "dì" (帝).
*Shali* (沙礫): The *Shuowen Jiezi* states this means small pebbles; it is composed of the radical "stone" (*shí*) and the phonetic "le" (*lè*).

*Zuan* (鑽): [The character] *zuàn* has the upper part "zǔ" pronounced as *guān* (官). Gu Yewang says that "zuàn" is synonymous with "juān" (鐫, to engrave) and "záo" (鑿, to bore). Wang Chong’s *Lunheng* states: "The Confucians all say that there is a three-legged crow within the sun; the sun is the essence of Yang and is fire."
Within the moon there is a white hare and a toad; the moon is the essence of Yin and water.
How could a crow dwelling in fire not be scorched, yet a hare residing in water not be drowned?
This appears contradictory, yet the principle is not so.
Li Chūnfēng, in his commentary on the *Jīshèngfù*, quotes the *Bǎopŭzǐ*:

"Those who have now attained the Way and those who possess marvelous arts can likewise enter fire without being burned and enter water without being soaked; yet they both belong to the human race, and their differences are such."

How can this king, who was born in peace, know that the crow in the sun and the toad-rabbit in the moon are not like the human practitioners of arts who can enter water and fire, being different from ordinary crows and common rabbits?

Furthermore, it is said that the retribution of karma resides above the stellar heavens and within the sun and moon; although its form is similar to theirs, it must belong to the category of spiritual beings and cannot be measured by the standards of human logic or ordinary sentiments.

In the *Lùn* (Treatise), it is written as *jiàn* (pronounced with the *zān* rhyme; the *Gǎndì* rhyme is used), which differs in meaning from the former.

Regarding the character *hù* (互): it is explained in reverse by examining its phonetic component as "mutual intersection. The *Zhouli* states that it refers to the alternating succession of affairs; thus, *di* (遞) is also synonymous with *hù*. This is precisely the character *hù*.

As for the *Weishi ershi lun* (Vimśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi), Huilin’s phonetics give *xuàn yì* (眩翳). For the first character, *xuàn*, the *Cangjie pian* states: "Eye-vertigo; seeing unclearly. Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* defines it as "delusive confusion. The *Shuowen jiezi* states: "The eye having no constant master. It is formed from the radical 'eye' and the phonetic 'xuán'."
*Naraka* (the "na" in *naraka* is pronounced with a retroflex *ṇ*, as indicated by the character 反; it is the general Sanskrit name for hell). Regarding the term *dīrgha* (here transcribed as 羝羊):

the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is composed of the radical "sheep" (*yang*) and the phonetic element "di" (*dī*). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* says: "A *dīrgha* sheep is a male ram. The *Guangya* says: "A *dīrgha* is a stallion sheep. Regarding the male sheep, one three years old is called a *dīrgha*. The version in the *Lunyu* (Analects) as "dī" is an erroneous transcription.

*Lí* (羸): The phonetic transcription is *lěi* (累) with a retroflex *-r* suffix (*zhuī fǎn*). Duan Yucai’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states it means "weak"; Jia Gui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states it means "illness. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "emaciated," formed from the radical "sheep" (*yáng*) with the phonetic element "*lí*" (*líng*).
*Laṇḍa* (the first character pronounced with the *lan-da* rhyme and the second with the *nue-ka* rhyme) is a name for a king in the Sanskrit language; the sound *da* is pronounced as *dan-la*.
*Tali* (pronounced *dan-la*) is also a name for a king in the Sanskrit language.
Upāli (the *u* and *gu* reversed) is a name for a householder (*gṛhapati*) in the Sanskrit language.

Regarding the "Postscript to the Treatise" (*Lun hou xu*): "Zhì" (pronounced *zhè*, with the rhyme of *miào* and *zhàn*) means "bright. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that "zhì zhì" means "luminous. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says "zhào zhì" also means "bright. It is sometimes written as "zhé," and both characters are composed of the "sun" radical.
Regarding "hequè" (鶴): some argue it should be read as "gào" (告) and written as "gù" (鵠), but this is incorrect.

Regarding "chěng" (騁) in "chěng yù" (騁馹): the upper character is pronounced *chǒng* (丑領反). The *Guǎngyǎ* states that "chěng" means "to gallop"; the *Shuowén* defines it as "to charge straight on," composed of the radical "horse" (馬) and the phonetic "píng" (甹). The sound of "píng" is *pǐ dīng* (匹丁反); the lower character is pronounced *rén zhì* (人質反). Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states that "yù" (馹) refers to a relay carriage; Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states that "yù" is the general name for a relay carriage or a postal horse. The definition in the *Shuowén* is the same [as the *Guǎngyǎ*], composed of the radical "horse" (馬) and the phonetic "rì" (日).

*Wù* (upper radical 馬, phonetic 付): Wang Yu says it means "wild and rapid galloping. The *Chuci* states, "Suddenly they gallop and pursue," which is this term. The *Guangya* says, "To gallop is to rush. *Xiáng* (lower radical 羊, phonetic 襄): The commentary on the *Mao Shi* says, "To *xiáng* is to yoke. The commentary on the *Xijing Fu* says, "To *xiáng* is to gallop. In the *Shuowen*, both characters follow the radical 馬; *wù* and *xiáng* are their respective phonetics.

"Chenyi (沈曀)"—the character *yi* (曀) is read as *ji fan* (計反). The *Erya* states: "When it is cloudy and windy, it is called *yi*. The *Mao Shi* says: "The constant wind and the *yi*. It does not say "there is *yi*"; according to the *Shuowen*, [the character] follows the radical for "sun" (*ri*) and takes the phonetic *yi* (*yi sheng*). The pronunciation of *yi* is *ai xi fan* (噎兮反).

"Hun-mai" (昏霾) [pinyin: hūnmái]. The *Erya* states: "Wind accompanied by rain and dust is called *mái*. The *Shichuan* (Commentary on the Odes) says: "*Mái* is rain and dust. According to the *Shuowen*, the correct form is written with the radical 豸 (*chí*); the form written with the radical 犬 is a vulgar variant. The sound of 豸 is *chí'ěr*.

Regarding "Xiānglù" (襄麓) and "Lónggǔ" (聾谷), the *Fànshīchuán* (反詩傳) states that "lù" means the foot of a mountain. The *Shuōwén* (說文) explains that "lù" is formed from "lín" (forest) with "lù" as the phonetic component, following the commentary of Lìáng (𭮹梁) which says:

"A forest attached to a mountain is called lù. Regarding "dào yì" (道軼): the *Chǔcí* (楚辭) uses it in the line "yì xùnfēng yú qīngliáng" (軼迅風於清涼), meaning to surpass or overtake. Hé Gǎn’s (何𠇲) commentary on the *Gōngyángchuán* (公羊傳) glosses it as "to pass by," while Dū Yǒu’s (杜預) commentary on the *Zuǒchuán* (左傳) glosses it as "to surge forward. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "cars passing one another," formed from "chē" (carriage) with "shī" (省) as the phonetic component.

The character for *móu* (侔) is pronounced as *mòu* (莫侯反). Zheng’s commentary on the *Kaogongji* states: "Móu means equal (*děng*) and uniform (*jūn*). In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is written in the Xiaozhuan style as *móu* (侔), or with the radical for "force" (*lì*) as *zé* (劺), both meaning "equal. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "person" (*rén*) and the phonetic element "móu" (*móu*).

*Jiàn* (pronounced *jiàn*, with the *qiǎn* rhyme): According to the *Zhouli* (Rites of Zhou), the Director of the Gates (*Sīmén*) was charged with "bestowing official *jiàn*" to open and close the national gates. Zheng’s commentary states that *jiàn* refers to the tube or key (*guǎnyuè*). The *Fāngyán* (Dialects) notes that in the regions of Chen and Chu, the *yuè* (lock-pin) is called *jiàn*. The *Shuowén* (Explanations of Words and Characters) defines it as being composed of the radical for metal (*jīn*) and the phonetic element *jiàn*.

*Jiūshū* (樞). [The character] *chù* (觸) is pronounced as *zhú* (朱). Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "It refers to the pivot of a door or gate leaf. Gu Yewang, citing the *Zhuangzi*, notes: "A thatched door (*péng hù*) was incomplete, so mulberry wood was used for the pivot"—this is correct. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) with the phonetic element "qū" (*qū shēng*).

*Yi* (方宜反, yī; also pronounced yí). As Zhù Chūn notes in his commentary on the *Shìjì*, people of the south say that "mooring" a boat toward the shore is called *yì*. Mèng Kāng’s commentary states it means "to attach"; it refers to a boat being moored against the bank. It is also written as *yǐ*. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical for wood (*mù*) and the phonetic element *yì*.

*Kīn* (克) is pronounced *yīn* (一寅反). Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that *kīn* means "to descend. The *Erya* says it means "to fall away" (*luò*). The *Shuowen* defines it as "to sink," following the phonetic component *yīn*. *Lìng* (臮) is pronounced *qí yì* (其懿反).

The *Kaosengzhuan* states it is a term used for what is encompassed by a multitude. The *Shuowen* says it is a particle used when many things arise together. The preface to the *Yueling* uses it in the phrase "extending to the first day of the month" (*èr yì*). It follows the phonetic component *zì* (自), with the sound *yín* (吟). The *Lunheng* writes it as *jì* (洎). Xu Guang’s commentary on the *Shiji* states that *jì* refers to meat broth. This contradicts the intent of the treatise and is incorrect.

The character *yǒu* (莠) is pronounced *yóu* (由) and *jiǔ* (酒). The *Zhuàn* (傳) says: "The *yǒu* resembles the sprout of grain. The *Shàngshū* (尚書) says: "It is like weeds among the sprouts. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* (文字典說) says: "An evil weed resembling *jì* (稷) that lacks grain. The *Shuowén* (說文) states: "When the stalks of millet (*hé*) produce ears (*xiàng*), it is called *yǒu*; it is composed of the radical 'grass' (*cǎo*) and the phonetic 'xiù' (*xiù*)."

*Pí* (紕): The upper character is read as *pǐ* (毘). The *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲) states it means "principle" (*lǐ*) or "ornamentation" (*shì*). It refers to coarse and thin silk. The *Diǎn Shuō* (典說) states that *pí miù* (紕繆) means "error. It is composed of the radical *mì* (糸) with the phonetic *bǐ* (比); the sound is *miù* (繆), pronounced *méi yōu* (眉憂) in the second instance, and *qī quán* (七泉) in the third. Wáng Yì’s commentary on the *Chǔcí* states that *quán* (荃) is the name for a fine cloth. The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radical *cǎo* (艹) with the phonetic *quán* (全); it is also written as *chuān* (絟).

"Yùn" (蘊) is pronounced *wǔn* (上氳粉反). Ma's commentary on the *Lunyu* states that it means "to store. Du's commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that it means "to gather," and also says it means "to accumulate. Guo's commentary on the *Fangyan* states that it means "luxuriant and flourishing. "Wú" (蕪) is pronounced *fǔ* (下武撫反). Jia's commentary on the *Guoyu* states that it means "weeds and filth. Both the *Shuowen* and other sources derive [the characters] from the radical for grass (*艹*), with *wú* (無) as the phonetic component. The pronunciation of *yùn* (縕) is *wǔn* (氳運反), and *yùn* (蘊) is also read with the departing tone.

*Wèn* (紊): Pronounced *wén fèn* (反). The Commentary on the Book of Documents (*Shūjìng zhù*) by Kǒng [Yáng] states: "It is like a net within a net; there are its lines, yet it is not disordered. The *Shuowén* says: "To disorder. It takes *mì* (糸) as the radical and *wén* (文) as the phonetic.

*Cì* (翳): Pronounced *yī jì* (反). Dú’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* says: "That which provides shade when mounted upon. The *Fāngyán* says: "It is *yì* (翳) and *ài* (薆). Furthermore, *ài* (薆) means "to obscure. The *Shuowén* says: "From the feather (*yǔ*) and the phonetic *yī* (殹); the sound of *yī* is as above. *Ē* (兮): Pronounced *yē* (噎) with a reversed tone. *Wǎi* (外): Pronounced *wū wài* (反). The *Guǎngyá* says: "It is *huì* (薈) and *yì* (翳). The *Shuowén* says: "The appearance of many weeds. It takes *cǎo* (艸) as the radical and *huì* (會) as the phonetic."

*Shan-yi* (芟夷): The commentary states that it means to weed; the *Shuowen Jiezi* says it means to reap grass, composed of the radical "grass" (*艹*) and the phonetic "shu" (*殳*), with the pronunciation *shū* (殊霎). *Xia* (霎): The pronunciation is *shān* (杉夾反). *Chuan-sha-li* (穿沙礫): The pronunciation of *chuan* (穿) is *chuai* (專反);

the *Shuowen Jiezi* says it means to pierce through, composed of the radical "tooth" (*牙*) inside the radical "cave" (*穴*), with the lower part pronounced *ling-di* (零滴反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* says [the character for] small pebbles is composed of the radical "stone" (*石*) and the phonetic "le" (*樂*), with the pronunciation of *chuai* (歠) being *chuǎn-zhuó* (喘拙反).

Regarding "Śāriputra" (鶖鷺): the first character is pronounced *qiū* (with the initial *q-*) and the second is pronounced *lù* (with the initial *l-*). Now, the "śālika" bird is the "double-tongued" bird (*pratika-jihva*). Because Śāriputra’s mother’s eyes resembled this bird, he was named after it; thus he is called the "Son of the Śālika. Both the *Shuowen Jiezi* and other sources derive the characters from the radical for "bird" (*niǎo*), with *qiū* and *lù* as their phonetic components.

The character *zōng* (琮) is pronounced *cú zōng* (徂宗反). The *Baihutong* states: "The word *zōng* means 'to gather' (*jù*), as it symbolizes the gathering together of the myriad things. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "jade" (*yù*) with the phonetic element "zōng" (*zōng shēng*).

The character *chōng* (沖) is pronounced *zhú lóng* (逐隆反). The *Laozi* says: "The greatly full is like the empty (*chōng*). Gu Yewang states: "Empty (*chōng*) is synonymous with void (*xū*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) with the phonetic element "zhōng" (*zhōng shēng*). The character *xùn* (濬) is pronounced *xún jùn* (詢俊反). Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states: "Deep" (*shēn*). It is sometimes written as *xùn* (濬); according to the *Wenzidian*, it is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) with the phonetic element "ruì" (*ruì shēng*), where the sound of *ruì* is *ruì* (*ruì yīn ruì yě*).

*Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*. Compiled by Huilin. Regarding the character *jí* (嫉): the upper radical is *qín* (秦), which is pronounced with the *fǎn* (反) tone; Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that "to harm the worthy is called *jí*. In the *Jīngǔ zhènzì* (Classical and Modern Standard Characters), it follows the *nǚ* (女) radical and takes *jí* (疾) as its phonetic component, with the lower part pronounced *xián* (閑). The *Guǎngyá* states that *jí* means "firm," and the *Běicāng* also states it means "firm. In the *Jīngǔ zhènzì*, it follows the *gé* (革) radical and takes *xiān* (臤) as its phonetic component; *xiān* is pronounced like "firm" (*jiān*). This is a vulgar usage of the character.

Regarding "hài jiāo" (害憍), the *Zhengjian* commentary on the *Mao Shi* states that "jiāo" means dissipation (*yì*). Gu Yewang says that "jiāo" refers to self-conceit, indulgence, and arrogance. In the *Jin Gu Wenzi*, it is written with the "heart" radical and the phonetic "qiáo"; the term "jiāo" is used interchangeably as a common vulgar form.

*Styāna* (昏沈): "Hun" with the *shang* tone, followed by "hu" with the *kun* tone. The *Guoyaya* states it means confusion or delusion (*moha*). The *Shuowen* defines it as "stupefaction," written with the radical for "heart" and the phonetic "hun";

the sound of "niao" is pronounced as *nu jiao*. "Xun" (尋) and "si" (伺)—the latter being pronounced as *si zi fan*. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that "si" means to observe and examine. Gu Yewang says it means to wait upon or watch. The *Gujin Zhengzi* states that "kui," "chan," and "si" all mean to spy or look; it is written with the radical for "person" and the phonetic "si."

*Tāo* (pronounced *dào láo*): The *Huáinán Zǐ* states that it refers to the surging of seawater. The *Wénzìdiǎn* explains that it means a great wave; the tide of the sea is called *tāo*. It is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic "shòu. *Xià bó mó*: Pronounced *xià bó mó*. The *Shuōwén* explains that *bō* means water flowing out; it is composed of the radical "water" and the phonetic "pí."

*Cheng weishi baosheng lun* (The Commentary on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only as a Jewel-Born), Scroll One; also titled *Ershi weishi shunshi lun* (A Concordant Explanation of the Twenty Verses on Consciousness-Only). Compiled by Huilin. Scroll One. *Xuān*: Upper radical *xiōng* (元), phonetic *fǎn* (反). The *Shēnglèi* (Classification of Sounds) states that it means clamor. The *Shuowén* (Explanations of Words and Characters) states it means a startled cry. It is formed with the radical *yán* (言) and the phonetic *xuān* (宣); alternatively, it is written with the radical *kǒu* (口) as *xuān*, which is the common usage. *Huá*: Pronounced *huā*. *Cheng weishi baosheng lun* (The Commentary on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only as a Jewel-Born), Scroll One; also titled *Ershi weishi shunshi lun* (A Concordant Explanation of the Twenty Verses on Consciousness-Only). Compiled by Huilin. Scroll One. *Xuān*: Upper radical *xiōng* (元), phonetic *fǎn* (反). The *Shēnglèi* (Classification of Sounds) states that it means clamor. The *Shuowén* (Explanations of Words and Characters) states it means a startled cry. It is formed with the radical *yán* (言) and the phonetic *xuān* (宣); alternatively, it is written with the radical *kǒu* (口) as *xuān*, which is the common usage. *Huá*: Pronounced *huā*.

"Dāna" (dān-jiǎ-mó): The upper character "dān" (dān, with the *nan* rhyme; colloquially pronounced as "kǎo") means to indulge in or to dote upon. It is written with the "ear" radical (*ér*). "Ghaṣma" (jiǎn-yè-mó): This is a Sanskrit term.
The upper character "jiǎn" (jiǎn, with the *jiǎn* and *yān* rhymes) has the sound of "jiǎn" (jiǎn, with the *jiǎn* and *yān* rhymes); the lower character "yè" (yè) means karma.

*Bǐng* (兵, pīng; fanqie: bing-míng-fǎn). The *Guǎngyá* states that *bǐng* means "bright. In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, it is composed of the radical "sun" (日) with "bǐng" (丙) as the phonetic component. It is sometimes written as *bǐng* (昺), but the character *lǎn* (󲂣) used in the *Lùn* (論) is a scribal error.

*Sūtra* (蘇呾囉): the first character is pronounced *dān* (丹, dān; fanqie: dan-da-fǎn) and the second character, *luó* (羅), is in the third tone (*shēngshǐng*) with a retroflex pronunciation; these are transcriptions of the Sanskrit language.
*Maṇḍala* (the *la* is pronounced with a retroflex *ṛ*, and the *na* is pronounced with a palatal *c*; these are Sanskrit terms).
*Prāṇa* (the *pra* is pronounced with a retroflex *ṛ*, and the *na* is pronounced with a labio-dental *v*; these are also Sanskrit terms).

The character for "sweet" (tián) is read as *niè* (with the initial *n-*) and *dié* (with the final *-e*) according to the *Guǎngyǎ*, which states that "tián" means "sweet. The *Jiāyǔ* says, "Cutting it up to eat it, it was as sweet as honey. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "beautiful," composed of the radical "sweetness" (*gān*) and the phonetic component "tongue" (*shé*). In the *Lùn* (Discourse), it is written as "tián" (sweet), used interchangeably with the pronunciation *niàn* or *tiān*.

*Xuàn* (pronounced *xuán*, with the *jiǎn* radical reversed): The *Cāngjié piān* states that it means "blurred vision. Jia’s commentary on the *Guóyǔ* says it means "to be deluded. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical *mù* (eye) and the phonetic *xuán*.
*Xuànyì* (pronounced *yì*, with the *jì* radical reversed): The *Yùnlüè* states that it means "a film or cataract obstructing the eye. *Ē* (pronounced *yì*, with the *xī* radical reversed).

"Sūmó" (疏膜): "Máng" is pronounced with the *bó* (博) rhyme. According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to the membrane between the flesh, formed from the radical "flesh" (肉) and the phonetic "mò" (莫). In the *Lun* (論), it is written as "mò" (瞙) using the radical "eye" (目) and the phonetic "kǎo" (考); this is said to mean "to look intently. This differs from the intended meaning in the text of the *Lun*, and is an error made by the scribe.

*Śalaka* (鑠羯羅): The first character is pronounced *shāng* (商) with the *yào* (約) rhyme; the second is pronounced *jiàn* (建) with the *yè* (謁) rhyme. This is a Western (Indic) term for "bow. *Tiṃilika* (羝蜜梨迦): The first character is pronounced *dǐ* (底). *Pratibheda* (排擯):

The first character is pronounced *bá* (拔) with the *méi* (埋) rhyme; the second is pronounced *bìn* (賓) with the *lìn* (吝) rhyme. Gu Yewang states that *pái* (排) is synonymous with *dì* (柢). The *Guǎngyǎ* states that *pái* means "to push" (*tuī*). Sima [Qian’s] commentary on the *Zhuāngzǐ* states it means "to discard" (*sǔnqì*). The *Shījì* states "they mutually *páibìn* [each other]," which is correct. In ancient times this character was written with the "hand" radical (*shǒu*); both forms include the "hand" radical and are not pronounced *bìn*.

Volume 2, Part 2: *Ratnākara-śāstra*, Volume Two. Regarding the term "chēng" (稱): the *Yǐnyá* states that "chēng" refers to an instrument for weighing lightness and heaviness; the *Guǎngyǎ* states it means "to measure. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Kǎogōngjì* says, "Chēng is equivalent to 'equal' (děng). The correct character for the sound is "chēng" (稱); the *Shuōwén* records it as "chéng" (秤), following the radical for grain (禾) and the phonetic "chèn" (爯). This latter is a vulgar form.

"Jiáo-yàn" (嚼咽): "Jué" (爵) is read as *jiào* (反). Gu Yewang says that "jiáo" (嚼) is synonymous with "jiào" (噍). The *Zishu* says it is "zu" (咀). "Xià" (下) is read as *yān-jian* (烟見). Gu Yewang says that "yàn" (咽) is synonymous with "tūn" (吞). The *Shuowen* states that [the character] is composed of "kǒu" (口) and "jué" (爵), with "yin" (因) providing the phonetic component. "Jiào" (噍) is pronounced *qiáo-xiào* (樵笑). "Zǔ" (咀) is pronounced *cái-yǔ* (才與). [Note: The provided text consists of a glossary entry for the compound "jiáoyàn" (嚼咽), citing various lexicographers including Gu Yewang and the *Shuowen Jiezi* to explain the meanings and pronunciations of its constituent characters.]

The character *qì* (詰) is pronounced with the initial *qǐ* and the final *jí*. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states that "gào" (誥) means to inquire about matters. The *Kaoseng* (考聲) says that "qì" (詰) means to interrogate to the limit. The *Shuowen Jiezi* also defines it as "to inquire," being composed of the radical "speech" (言) with the phonetic element "jí" (吉).

*Qingxiàn* (青茜): Pronounced *qiān jiàn* (千見). Yě Wáng says that the *xiàn* plant can be used to dye crimson. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *cǎo* (草) with *xī* (西) as its phonetic. The character *qiàn* (蒨) used in the *Lunheng* is also acceptable. *Màn* (蔓): Pronounced *wù fàn* (武販).

The commentary on the *Mao Shi* states that "màn" means "to extend. The *Guoyaya* says "màn" means "long. According to the *Shuowen*, "màn" belongs to the category of *gé* (葛, kudzu/vine), composed of the radical *cǎo* (草) with *màn* (蔓) as its phonetic.

Regarding "lofty walls surging forth," the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "walls" (*yōng*) refers to ramparts; according to the *Erya*, "rampart" is termed *yōng*. In the *Shuowen*, it is written with the radical for earth and the phonetic *yōng*; the pronunciation of *yǒng* (surging) is *yōng* with the second tone.

Regarding "flying eaves" (*fēiméng*): the *Zuozhuan* commentary states that "eaves" (*méng*) refers to the ridgepole of a roof. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "tile" (*wǎ*) with "mèng" (abbreviated) as the phonetic.

Regarding "hòumǐ": the upper character is read as *suīpó* (or *suīdǒu*) and the lower as *yīnměi*. The *Kaosheng* says "hòumǐ" describes the appearance of grasses bowing down. In the *Chuci*, it refers to the "hòumǐ" of duckweed (*píncǎo*). Wang Yi’s commentary states it means "spreading open following the wind. In the *Lunwen*, both characters are written as "cǎo" (grass), forming "cǎohuìmǐ"; this is a vulgar form. If one pronounces it as "huò," it is incorrect.

*Cuìcàn* (皠粲): The first character, *cuì*, has the phonetic gloss *wěi* (猥). The *Pīcāng* states that it describes a fresh and beautiful appearance; the *Kǎoshēng* states that it describes the white appearance of frost and snow. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical "white" (*bái*) with the phonetic element "cuì. It is also written as *cuī* (漼). The second character, *wěi*, has the phonetic gloss *wěi* (猥) with the tone *měi* (每), while the third character, *sàn* (散), has the phonetic gloss *cāng* (倉).

*Bèng* (灒): Pronounced *zāng-sàn* (臧散). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *zàn* refers to splashing and soiling one another; one version says it means water splashing onto a person. It is composed of the radical *shui* (water) and the phonetic *zàn*;

the pronunciation of *zàn* is as stated above. *Xiù* (齅): Pronounced *xiǔ-yòu* (朽又). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that to bring the nose toward an odor is called *xiù*. It is composed of the radicals *bi* (nose) and *chòu* (odor), with *chòu* also serving as the phonetic. The version in the *Lunyu* (Analects) uses *xiù* (嗅), which is incorrect.

Regarding the character *jiàn* (索): the *Juéxuǎn* (決泫) glosses it as "to bind and capture. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that *jiàn* means "to catch birds with a rope. It is also written as *juàn* (羂). The *Wenzìdiǎn* (文字典) explains that the correct form for all periods, ancient and modern, is written with the radical *zī* (𠔿) and the phonetic *yuān* (肙); *yuān* is pronounced *yīchuán* (一椽), which is the departing tone of *yuān* (淵). It is composed of the components "mouth" (口) and "flesh" (肉).

*Zhe* (pronounced *zhan-lie-fan*): *Boya* states that it means "to sting" (*cheshi*). It is also written as *qu*. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "insect" with the phonetic element "dan.
*Naluo-jia* (pronounced *shang-nan-da-fan*): This is a transliteration of the Sanskrit term for the great hells (*mahānaraka*).

"Hen-hai" (墋害): The first character is pronounced *chū* (with the initial *jǐn* [反切]). In Lu Ji’s "Eulogy on the Meritorious Ministers of the Han Founder," it reads: "Vast and boundless is the universe; above it is cruel (*hen*), below it is turbid (*du*)."* Regarding the standard orthography of this character: it is composed of the radical "earth" (土) and the phonetic component "san" (參).

*Chui* (捶) is pronounced *zhui* (隹󲜔反). The *Guoyu* (國語) states: "To whip and beat so as to make them speak. The *Shuowen* (說文) defines it as: "To strike with a staff; it is composed of the radical 'hand' (手) and the phonetic 'chui' (垂), with the lower part pronounced as *kao* (考).
*Man* (鬘) is pronounced as *man* (蠻). In the Western Regions, seasonal flowers are strung together with thread to serve as an ornament for the body; this is called a *huaman* (花鬘, flower-garland).

Volume Three, Part Three: *Ratnasambhava-śāstra*, Volume Three. Regarding the character "tiē" (鐵): the *Kǎoshēng* states it may also be written as "shuān" (丳). The *Bóyá* says it is an iron instrument for roasting meat. The *Shuōwén* states that "qiān" (籤) is called "chǎn" (鏟); it is composed of the radical "jīn" (金) and the phonetic "chǎn" (產). The pronunciation of "qiān" is qièyán (妾鹽反).

"An alarming gale must blow from afar. Zheng’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "A *biao* wind is one that rises upward from below; the *Shizi* says it is a violent, tumbling gale. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "wind" (*feng*) and the phonetic "yan"; it is also written as "biao," with "yan" having the same pronunciation.

The character for *luò* (駱) is pronounced with the first tone *tāng* (湯) and the final rhyme *luò* (鐸). The *Shān-hǎi-jīng* (*Classic of Mountains and Seas*) states: "The *yǔtuó* (𩧐駝) has a fleshy saddle-pad and can carry a thousand *qīn* (斤) [of weight]; it knows the location of springs. The *Zhōu Shū* (*Book of Zhou*), in the section on the "Assembly of Tribute" (*Wáng Huì Zhèng*), records that the *yǔtuó* was presented as tribute; it is capable of bearing heavy loads and traveling great distances, and it abounds in the north. Both characters follow the phonetic element *mǎ* (馬) and the phonetic *tuó* (橐); *tuó* is pronounced *tuō* (託), and *tā* (它) is pronounced as above. The *Lùn* (論) [in the *Shuōwén*] writes it as *luò* (洛), which refers to the color of the horse; it is also the same character as *luòtuó* (駱駝).

Regarding the characters for "scorpion" (xié) and "sting" (zhé): the first character is pronounced with the *qian* (軒) and *ye* (謁) rhymes; the second is pronounced with the *zhan* (展) and *lie* (列) rhymes. The *Guangya* states that the scorpion is a venomous insect. The *Picao* states that "zhé" (sting) is also synonymous with "hé" (to sting). According to the *Shuowen*, both characters are composed of the radical "insect" (虫); "xie" (歇) and "zhe" (折) serve as phonetic components. "Zhe" is sometimes written as "ju" (蛆), composed of "insect" (虫) and the abbreviated form of "da" (怛) as its phonetic component. The version in the *Lunheng* uses the character "ku" (𧈸), which is an error.

*Dian-jué* (顛蹶): *jué* is pronounced as *quàn-yuè* (眷月). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states that *jué* is the appearance of hurried walking. Gu Yewang states that *jué* conveys the sense of being startled, alarmed, or moving with great haste. Jia Gongyan’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that *jué* means to run. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as consisting of the radical "foot" (*zú*) and the phonetic component "jue" (*jué*).
*Pāpā* (the second *pā* is pronounced as *pō*, a Sanskrit term).

Regarding *niok* (the first character is pronounced *kāng* or *jiǎo*; according to Han’s commentary on the *Zhouyi*, it means "firm"; the *Shuowen Jiezi* also defines it as "firm," derived from the radical for stone with *huò* as the phonetic).

*Cuò* (矬): The upper radical is *zuò* (坐) and the lower is *yīngjiě* (櫻解). The *Guǎngyǎ* states that *cuò* means "short. It is also written as *ǎi* (矮). Furthermore, *cuò* is also *cuò*; it is also written as *ǎi*. According to the *Gōngjīn zhèngzì*, *cuò* also means "short. *Cuò* is formed from the radical *shǐ* (矢) with *zuò* (坐) as the phonetic. *Cuò* is formed from the radical *nà* (疒) with *qí* (奇) as the phonetic. Examining the correct forms for *ǎi*, both characters in the *Lùnwén* (論文) follow the radical *rén* (人), *zuò* (坐), and *suì* (歲); the two characters *zòn* (侳) and *zhuó* (𠚏) are incorrect. *Suǒ* (莎): The phonetic is *luòhé* (鏁和).

Regarding the character *chì* (熾), Zhi Guanyu and Ye Wang state that it means "necessarily pure" (*bì jié*), and it is also said to mean "fierce fire. The *Chuán* says it means "flourishing" (*chì shèng*). The *Kǎoshēng* states it is a red color. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical *huǒ* (fire) with the phonetic *zhí* (戠); the pronunciation of *zhí* is *chéngshí* (承識).
*Phoṭī* (頗胝) is a Sanskrit name for a type of gem. Regarding *śrūna* (濕耎):

Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Kaogongji* states that it should be read as *róu* (柔), meaning "pliant. The *Boyá* (博雅) lexicon defines it as "weakness" (*ruò*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical *cong* (從) with the phonetic *huǒ* (火).

Volume Four, Part Four: *Ratnasambhava-śāstra*, Volume Four. "Analysis" (*xi*)—the commentary on the *Shangshu* by Kong [Yuan] states that it means "to divide. The *Shenglèi* states it means "to split. The *Shuowén* defines it as "breaking wood," composed of the radical for "wood" and the character for "axe" (*jin*).

"Huòtuō" (豁脫) is interpreted generally as "emptiness" (kōng). According to Huan Kuògù Yěwáng, "huò" means "vast and great capacity for measurement. The *Guǎngyǎ* states it means "empty" (*kōng*). The *Shuōwén* defines it as "a valley that connects," composed of the radical "valley" (*gǔ*) with the phonetic "hài"; it is also written as "shà" or "làn," but these are incorrect.

*Śuò* (爴烈): *jū* (居) with the reverse *bì* (碧); *yá* (芽): *yǎ* (雅) with the reverse *jiā* (加). The *Guǎngyǎ* states: "A sprout (*yá*) is the beginning. The *Shuowen* states: "A sprout (*yá*) is the same as *méngyá*; it is composed of the radical 'grass' (*cǎo*) and the phonetic 'tooth' (*yá*).

*Wèn xù* (問緒): *xú* (徐) with the reverse *yǔ* (與). Guō Pǔ’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "The term 'thread-end' (*xù*) refers to a beginning or a clue. It also says: "It means the affairs [of a matter]. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states: "It means the work or undertaking. Wáng Yì’s commentary on the *Chuci* states: "It means the remnants. The *Shuowen* states: "The term 'thread-end' (*xù*) is the tip; it is composed of the radical 'silk' (*mì*) and the phonetic 'zhě' (者)."

*Xi* (睎): The *Xǐyī Fǎn* (喜衣反) states that the *Guǎngyá* says *xi* means "to look. The *Shuowén* says *xi* means "to gaze," composed of the radical "eye" (*mù*) and the phonetic "xī. The *Lùn* (論) writes it as *xī* (悕), which is also used interchangeably.

*Yòng* (用): Pronounced *tāngluò* (湯洛反). The *Yìjīng* (易經) says: "Double gates and striking the *tóng* (𣟄) to ward off violent guests. The *Chūnqiū Zuàn* (春秋傳) says: "The state of Lǔ struck the *tóng*, and the sound was heard in Zhū. The *Shuowén* says it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic *tuó* (橐). The *Lùn* writes it as *tuò* (拓), which refers to the appearance of a *shuālò* (柘) tree losing its joints. These meanings differ; [the latter] is an erroneous usage.

Fifth Scroll, *Ratnākara-śāstra*, Fifth Scroll. Regarding the character *hu* (互): it is a reversal of the sound of *kǎo* (考). The commentary states that *hu* means "interchange" (*jiāo*). The *Zhou Li* says that the successive alternation of duties is also termed *hu*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that the form of the character resembles hands with fingers interlaced and grasping one another; this is the intended meaning of the character.

"Sleeping and hanging down" (*shuì xiàchuí*): according to the *Cāngjiépiān*, "sleeping" (*shuì*) means lying down; according to the *Shuōwén*, it is "to sleep," composed of the radical "eye" (*mù*) and the phonetic "chuí. The version in the *Lùn* (Discourse) as "yáo" (lustful) is an error.

"Twistedly entangled" (*chóng chán*): pronounced *chè lián* (or *tián*). The *Huáihuánzǐ* says, "entangled with vermilion thread"; according to the *Shuōwén*, "chán" means to bind, composed of the radical "silk" (*mì*) and the phonetic "lí. It is also written as "chán" (*diàn*).

"Bhikṣu" (苾蒭): the first character is pronounced with the "pin" and "mi" finals reversed (bì), and the second is pronounced with the "cè" and "jū" finals reversed (chù). In ancient Sanskrit translation, it is called *bhikṣu*.

Regarding "tu" (屠) and "kuài" (膾)—the latter is pronounced with the "guāi" and "huì" finals reversed—the *Guǎngyá* states that "kuài" means to cut; the *Shuowén* defines it as finely slicing meat, composed of the radical "flesh" (肉) and the phonetic "huì" (會).

*Weishi lun* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), one fascicle, titled *Pocesin* (Refuting Form and Mind), compiled by Hui Lin. *Die* (迭): Pronounced *tie* (with the initial *t* and final *-ie*). It means to alternate or succeed one another. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states it means "to change. The *Fangyan* states it means "to alternate. The *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of the radical "brother" (*xiong*) and the phonetic element "abbreviated *die*" (*die*). The pronunciation of *xie* is *xianjie* (with the initial *x* and final *-ie*); the pronunciation of *di* is *di*; the pronunciation of *die* is the same as above.
*Ni-ka* (拏迦) is a transcription of a Western Indic word. It refers to the jujube tree (*jī*).

The *Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry* states: "The jujube is sour and prickly. The *Guǎngyǎ* states: "Jujube means thorn. The *Erya* lists ox-jujube, *diān*-jujube, *shāng*-jujube, horse-jujube, and dog-jujube. According to the *Fānyǔ*, wherever grasses or trees have bristling thorns that prick people, those in the region between the Yangtze and Huai rivers call them "jujube" (*jí*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "Jujube resembles the date tree and grows in clusters. It is written with two 'thorns' (*cì*) side by side; the sound of *cì* is *cǐ-zì*. To write it as *lù* (from two 'thorns') is incorrect.

"Biàn niè" (遍躡): "Niè" is pronounced as *zhé* in the *Fāngyán*; it means to step upon. From the Guān region westward, in the areas of Qín and Jìn, they call "ascending" (*dēng*) "niè. According to the *Guǎngyá*, "niè" means to tread; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means to step upon. It is composed of the radical "foot" (*zú*) and the phonetic "niè," with the pronunciation *ní zhān*.
*Kātyāyana* (迦旃延) is a transliteration of the Sanskrit term *Arhat*. Regarding *tà* (蹋): according to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means "to tread upon";

according to the *Shuōwén*, it means "to step on," composed of the radical for "foot" (*zú*) and the phonetic *tá* (其音塔). *Zhàn* (戰): the tone is reversed [from the standard reading]. *Yè* (夜): the tone is reversed [from the standard reading]. *Tàndá* (蹋談答): the tones are reversed. *Guǎngyǎ*: "Tà" (蹋) means "shoes. *Shuōwén*: "To step on. It is composed of the radical for "foot" (*zú*) and the phonetic *tǎ* (󱫕), where the sound of *tǎ* is *tā*.

The first character, *xiā*, is pronounced as *xiá* (the upper tone) and the second, *má*, as *má* (the lower tone). The *Cangjie pian* states that a *xiāmá* is a frog, an aquatic creature. The *Shuowen jiezi* records it as *xiāmá*; it is also known as Tiānfù (Father of the Fields), Chánqú (Toad-Grass), Qīngwā (Green Frog), and Huánghuái (Yellow Embracer).

*Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only), Fascicle One, compiled by Hui Lin. Fascicle One: *Tuo-yue*. (The first character, *tuo*, is pronounced *tāngluò*; the second, *yue*, is pronounced *yángzhuó*). Laozi said: "The space between heaven and earth is like a bellows (*tuōyùè*): empty yet inexhaustible; it moves and ever more produces. The Imperial Commentary states: "A *tuō* is a bellows; a *yùè* is a Qiang flute. It refers to the bellows fanning the wind and the flute directing the breath. Gu Yewang says: "A *tuōyùè* is what a metalworker uses to blow fire so that it blazes intensely. The *Cangjie pian* says: "A bag without a bottom is called a *tuō*. The *Mao Shi zhuan* says: "*Tuō tuō* refers to the exertion of effort. The ancient script is written with the mouth radical as *nèi*. The *Shuowen jiezi* defines it as "a leather bag," composed of the stone radical and a simplified form of *tuō*. *Guǎn* is pronounced *húběn*; *kǒu* is *wéi*; *nèi* is pronounced *bàiyě*; *yě* is pronounced *yě*. *Cheng weishi lun*, Fascicle One, compiled by Hui Lin. Fascicle One: *Tuo-yue*. (The first character, *tuo*, is pronounced *tāngluò*; the second, *yue*, is pronounced *yángzhuó*). Laozi said: "The space between heaven and earth is like a bellows (*tuōyùè*): empty yet inexhaustible; it moves and ever more produces. The Imperial Commentary states: "A *tuō* is a bellows; a *yùè* is a Qiang flute. It refers to the bellows fanning the wind and the flute directing the breath. Gu Yewang says: "A *tuōyùè* is what a metalworker uses to blow fire so that it blazes intensely. The *Cangjie pian* says: "A bag without a bottom is called a *tuō*. The *Mao Shi zhuan* says: "*Tuō tuō* refers to the exertion of effort. The ancient script is written with the mouth radical as *nèi*. The *Shuowen jiezi* defines it as "a leather bag," composed of the stone radical and a simplified form of *tuō*. *Guǎn* is pronounced *húběn*; *kǒu* is *wéi*; *nèi* is pronounced *bàiyě*; *yě* is pronounced *yě*.

"Molten copper surges upward" (鎔銅上涌). "Zhōng" (鍾) is a homophone for "róng" (容); the *Jíxùn* states it refers to the method of casting vessels. Ying Shao’s commentary on the *Hànshū* says it is the shape of iron. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "metal" (金) with the phonetic "róng" (容).

Regarding the character for *píng* (vessel) and *ōu* (bowl): the latter is pronounced with the "Ōu" rhyme-group (as in *hóu*). The *Kǎo Shēng* states that a *ōu* is a small earthenware basin. According to the text, both earthenware bowls and porcelain bowls are called *ōu*. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhou Lǐ* says: "A *ōu* is a small *biān* (shallow bowl). The *Fāng Yán* says: "The smallest of basins is called a *ōu*. The *Shuō Wén* defines it as a small basin, formed from the radical "earthenware" (*wǎ*) and the phonetic component "qū" (abbreviated) with a level tone.

*Dī* (bottom tone, with the phonetic *kǎo*): a dyke, a defense, a limit, and a beam. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* says it is a bridge; the *Shuowen* says it is a pond (*táng*). It may also be written as *dī* with the radical *fù*. *Dàng* (bottom tone, with the phonetic *láng*): to pile up earth to form a path. A *táng* is also a *dī*. It may also be written as *yān* with the radical *fù*.

2. Fascicle Two, *Cheng weishi lun*, Fascicle Two: "Jiao" (焦). The *Kaoseng* states: "The extreme of dryness; it refers to being scorched by fire. The *Yunquan* states: "Black and putrid. The *Shuowen* states: "That which is burned by fire. In ancient scripts, this was written as 𤓪, composed of three "birds" (隹) and "fire" (火); in the current script, it is abbreviated to 焦. The text of the treatise uses 燋 with the radical "fire," which is incorrect. Its pronunciation is *jiàoyào*. It refers to scorching a tortoise shell with fire. The second character, "zhù" (炷), is pronounced *zhúrú*. The *Kaoseng* states: "The wick of a lamp. This character appeared recently; it is not found in the *Yupian*, the *Shuowen*, or any of the standard characters of the past or present.

"Śihai (尸骸, corpse remains): 'Hài' is pronounced with the rhyme *xiàjiè*. Yěwáng says that the bones of the body collectively are called *hài*. Kǎoshēng says it refers to the skeletal frame of the physical form. Yùpǔ says that bone (*gǔ*) is also *hài*. Shuōwén says it refers to the shinbone, composed of the radical for bone and the phonetic *hài*."

3. Third Fascicle, *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only), Fascicle Three. *Méngmèi* (Obscure/Confused). [The character] *méng*: Upper radical 艹 (grass), phonetic 墨崩反 (mo-bēng-fǎn). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Book of Odes) states: "It means confusion. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan* says: "It means vexation. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "It means the eyes are not clear. It is composed of 苜 or 䀏, written as 𥊄 or 䀏. *䀏* means the eyes are flickering. *苜* is pronounced *wǔ fú* (muǒ fú); *䀏* is pronounced *xuán*.

*Shìliú* (駛流). According to the *Cāngjiépiān*, "shì" means rapid; according to the *Kǎoshēng*, it refers to the swift pace of a horse's gallop, meaning speed.
