Dīrgha Āgama, Volume 1. First Volume of the Dīrgha Āgama. *Xianbu* (先不): No phonetic transcription provided. Second Volume. Second Volume. *Fangyu* (防禦): "Yu" is pronounced with the *yu* rhyme (魚舉反). It means to prevent (*fang*) and to restrain (*yu*). According to the *Erya*, "yu" means to prohibit. It refers to the act of checking and resisting. "Han" is pronounced with the *hu dan* rhyme (胡旦反). Both characters for "jin" (禁) and "yu" (禦) are written with the "radical of the divine" (示).

"Chengfu" (乘桴) is also written as "Fang" (艀), with the same pronunciation as "fúliú" (扶流). It refers to a raft made by lashing together pieces of wood; a small raft is called a "fú," pronounced "fǔ. "Mingzhé" (明喆) is an archaic form of "zhé" (哲);

it exists in two forms, "què" (喆) and "zhé" (哲), which are identical today. "Zhé" (哲) is pronounced "zhīliè" (知列). According to the *Erya*, "zhé" means wisdom (*zhì*) and also implies clarity or understanding.

*Tàn* (嘆) and *tà* (咤) are two ancient forms with the same pronunciation, both read as *tā* (with the initial *th* and final *-a*). They mean to sigh or lament. *Tà* (吒) is also written as *zhù* (喥), both read as *zhà* (with the initial *ch* and final *-a*). According to the *Tōngsùwén*, to express pain or regret is called *tà*.
"Tián-sè" (to fill up) is also written as "tián" with the same pronunciation, *dújiān* (反). According to the *Guǎngyá*, "tián-sè" also means "tián-mǎn" (to fill completely).

It is also the name of a person, traditionally pronounced "bǎo," though its origin is unknown. Examining ancient texts, there were two forms, "lù" (󲌊) and "yàn" (饜); today it is written as "bǎo. "Bǎo" still means "full. This should be the character "yàn" (饜), which has been erroneously written as [the current form]; "yàn" is pronounced *yúyàn* (反).

3. Third Fascicle. The character 殞 (yǔn) is written as 隕 (yǔn) in other dictionaries; its pronunciation is the same as that of 于愍 (yú mǐn). According to the *Shēnglèi* (Classification of Sounds), it means "to perish" and also "to fall.

The character 轟 (hōng) is now written as 𨊷; in the *Zìshū* (Dictionary of Characters) it is written as 𨋮, both having the same pronunciation as 呼棚 (hū péng). The *Shuowén* states that 轟 refers to the sound of a multitude of chariots.
*Pángyáng* (both pronounced *fáng yáng*): According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means to lean against or to loiter; it also means to wander about.
*Shēngguō* (the second character pronounced *gōng huó*): It means clamor. According to the *Cāngjiépiān*, it refers to the ears being disturbed and to noisy speech.
*Tuo-hun* (濁渾): "Hun" is pronounced with the *hu-kun* rhyme; it means turbid confusion, and it also refers to the sound of flowing water.
*Tian-dan* (恬淡): "Tian" is pronounced with the *tu-jian* or *tu-lan* rhymes; it signifies tranquility and stillness. According to the *Guangya*, "dan" means peace and composure.

4. Fourth Fascicle. *Xūxī* (歔欷). The ancient text reads *xī* (唏) for the upper character; the lower character is *xīn* (欣), which is reversed to *jù* (居). According to the *Cāngjié piān*, it refers to the lingering sound of weeping, and also denotes sorrow.
*Chù* (final tone, reversed): "to settle," also "to place" or "to bestow.
*Lúnyì* (lún with second tone, reversed): "to sink" and "to obscure"; it means to sink into obscurity and darkness.

"Hu" (in the *lǔhù* [虜扈] compound, "hu" is pronounced with the *gǔ* rhyme) means to move in a zigzag or sprawling manner; it also implies self-indulgence and license, as well as the appearance of being brave and robust. The *Yìnyì* (Phonetic Commentary) to the *Hànshū* states: "Hu" is *bǎohù* (boastful); it signifies arrogance.

The archaic form of "xià" (瑕隙) is the same as "qū" (𡭽), pronounced with the *qiū* and *nì* finals; it means a fissure and also signifies separation. It refers to the cracks and pores at the edges of a wall. The form appearing in the canonical text as "qì" (郄) is not the correct character. The character "xì" (隙) is composed of "xia" (下) and "xiao" (小) above, and "bái" (白) below.

The characters *qì* (企) and *wén* (文) are ancient forms of *yán* (研). They share the same radical and pronunciation as *xū* (墟), which is read as *shì* (豉) in the *Tōngsù wén* (通俗文). The *Tōngsù wén* states that "to raise the heel" is called *lì* (𨀣); this character is composed of the radicals for "person" (*rén*) and "stop" (*zhǐ*).

(Scroll Five–Six Missing) Seven: Scroll Seven. The characters *duì* (隊) and *duì* (隊) are ancient forms of *mèi* (䃍). They share the same pronunciation as *tú duì* (徒對). This refers to groups or troops following one another in succession.

The character "qi" (𥵨) is a variant of "zhi" (支); according to the *Zi Lin*, it refers to bamboo strips (*zhumie*). While some versions of the scripture write it as "mie" (篾), the meaning is the same. Nowadays, scholars in Shu and the Guanzhong region both refer to bamboo strips as "qi. Thus, the reading of the scripture as "qian" (籤) is an error.
*Xiè* (pronounced *sī-liè-fǎn*) means to emit, to overflow, and also to leak.

*Wěn* (the ancient form is the same as *máng-fěn-fǎn*): according to the *Gōngyáng Zhuàn*, "The Duke then cut his own throat and died. Hé Xiū says: *wěn* means to cut; *dòu* (pronounced *dòu*) refers to the neck.

*Kiǎoquè* (the first character pronounced *kiǎo* with the tone of *kǔ*, the second *què* with the tone of *jué*): In common parlance, when referring to soil that is hard and rigid, it is called *kiǎoquè*. Mengzi explained to the disciples: "*Kiǎoquè* refers to land that is poor and infertile."

8. Eighth Fascicle. "Wèi" (pronounced yū fèi in reverse) means not clean and pure; it also means defiled and evil. There are instances in the script where it is written with the radical for grain (禾) or with the radical for wine (酉), forming the two characters 穢 and 𡱁; these are incorrect.

Volumes Nine and Ten. Volume Nine. Volume Ten. [Note: The character *xian* (先) does not have a phonetic reading here. Volume Eleven. Regarding the character *paiji* (排擠): it is pronounced with the rhyme of *zi* (脂) and *zhi* (𢫨); it means to push aside or exclude. According to the *Guangya*, *ji* (擠) and *pai* (排) mean the same. The text of the scripture uses *ji* (濟), which is an error. The pronunciation of *𢫨* is *ér yǒng* (而勇).
To be familiar with one another in an intimate or informal manner is called *xié* (pronounced *xiè*). It is also written as *xié* and *lù*.
The threshold of a gate is also written as *kǔn*, both pronounced *kǔn* (as in *kǔběn*); the *Sāncāng* states that it refers to the door-sill of a gateway.

12. In the twelfth fascicle, within the *Dīrgha Āgama*, in the *Sūtra on the Examination of Cloth* (*Tatpava Sūtra*), there is a passage concerning the characters *tuo* (譒) and *po* (婆), which are used as substitutes for *jian* (絹). This extends through the section on the mutual yielding [of robes] twice over.
In the *Vibhāṣā* (Bi-di-pu-mi-fan), there is an error where the character is formed by adding a "wood" radical below the "bi" radical;
it should be [the correct character]. In various scriptural texts, it is written as "ji" (Qū-jì-fan).
"Yuán-tóu" (猿頭) is sometimes written as "yí" (󲱥), which is the same as "Yù-fán" (禹煩); according to the standard character, it is "yuè" (籰), pronounced "yú-bó-fan."
*Pīnàfúmípúmiè* (the second character is pronounced as *miè* according to the *Guǎngyǎ* dictionary; *pī* means "to strike"). Volume 13, Chapter 13: *Qiāo*.
The *Ěrpǐ* has it as *qiāo*, and the *Cāngjiépiān* has it as *xiāo* (both pronounced as *sìqiào*). It is that which holds a knife; according to the *Fāngyán*, it refers to the sheath of a sword.
*Lài* (pronounced *sì lì gài fǎn*) is based on the *Zílín* (Lexicon of Character Origins), which states it means "water flowing over sand.

*Chí* (pronounced *chí jū nì fǎn*) refers to a *zhuó* (a type of spear); the *Shìmíng* (Explanations of Names) says a *jí* (halberd) has a pronged *zhuó*. It is incorrect for the scriptural text to write this with the character *zhú* (from the radical for metal).
*Juědǎo* (蹶倒): *Jùyuè* (巨月) and *jūyuè* (居月)—the latter being the second reading—according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *juě* means to fall prostrate;

the *Guangya* states it means to collapse and lie down. Volume 14, Number 14: *Xiān* (先) has no phonetic notation. Volume 15, Number 15: *Zhìgùzhīshí* (桎梏之實): *Gǔlù* (古祿)—the second reading—is the pronunciation. According to the *Zhouli*, that which is on the hands is called *zhì* and that which is on the feet is called *gù*; these refer to cangues and fetters.
"Āyù (Aid)" refers to relying on and supporting; as in the *Zuǒzhuan*: "The son has no great aid. Volumes 16–17:

Volumes 16 and 17 both have no phonetic glosses provided previously. Volume 18: "Jīn guāng (Golden Beam)" is also written as "dòu"; they share the same pronunciation "guāng," referring to the cross-beams of a carriage or a ladder.
"Middle rank" (*zhōngjí*) refers to ascending one or two levels within the hierarchy; "rank" (*jí*) means a stage or level.

"Flanking the road" (*jiá dào*)—the ancient pronunciation was *qiè*—means being on both sides; it also implies supporting or holding fast. According to the *Sāncāng*, it means to provide auxiliary support.
*Khāśu* (古文 *qiū* [譸] and *xiǔ* [󲡸])—these two forms are identical; it is pronounced as *zhóu* (由) and *jiū* (鳩). It is the name of a thicket or forest.
*Fàn* (古文 same as *fàn*)—pronounced as *fú jiàn* (孚劒); according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means the appearance of floating, and also refers to flooding.
*Tíng* (pronounced *dí jīng*): According to the *Pīcāng*, water that has ceased to flow is called *tíng*.
*Ní* (pronounced *nú xiào*): The *Cāngjiépiān* states it means *ní* (mud); it also means to be submerged and to be damp.

19. Nineteenth Fascicle. Nineteenth Fascicle. *Chui* (搥) and *qiao* (𥑐) are archaic forms; *dui* (磓) is the same, with the phonetic component *dui* (都迴反). It means to throw down. *Xia* (下) is pronounced *yà* (於甲反); it means to place something from above onto something below. The text of the sutra uses *tui* (推) and *ya* (押), which are not the correct forms.
From the throat, one also forms the character *yǎn* (pronounced with the same initial as *xián*), which refers to the throat; the scriptural text writes it as *yàn*, but its source has not been seen.
*Péngbó* (pronounced *púgōng púmò*): according to the *Guǎngyá*, "fú" (*bó*) signifies the appearance of flourishing abundance.

*Bēn* (古文 *bēn*, 今作 *bēn*, same as 補門反; meaning "to run swiftly"). According to the *Shìmíng*, it means "transformation"; when there is an urgent change, one rushes toward it. *Chāchě* (also written as *kē*, same as 側家反;
according to the *Guǎngyá*, *kē* means "to take" or "to seize"). Below, it is also written as *chì* (same as 昌制反), meaning "to pull" or "to drag."

*Tuoyè* (拕拽): The first character is pronounced *hé* (何) with a retroflex final, while the second is also written as *yè* (曳), pronounced *yúshì* (余世). It means to drag, pull, or haul. *Dōngzhú* (涷瘃):
The ancient form is *zhú* (瘃), pronounced *zhīlù* (知錄). It refers to the development of sores on the hands due to exposure to the cold.

Regarding the archaic term *pīn* (拼), it is synonymous with *bēng* (抨); the phonetic transcription is *bǔgēng* (補耕). It refers to stretching a line or cord as a guide, as in the phrase "to *pīn* the plumb lines and measuring cords. In the *Jīngzhōng* (經中), this is written as the character *bēng* (絣); however, the *Zìlín* (字林) contains no such entry. Furthermore, the character *bēng* (絣) is not used in this sense here.

"Hao-hu" (哮呼) is also written as "Hao" (唬), with the same pronunciation as "hu-jiao" (呼交反). According to the *Tongshu wen* (通俗文), the roar of a tiger is called "hao-xia" (唬嚇); "xia" (嚇) has the pronunciation "hu-jia" (呼嫁反).
"Zhen-shen" (󱸘身) is also written as "Li-diao" (󲏝), with the pronunciations "li-diao" (力鳥) and "li-zhao" (力照) (二反). The *Zilin* (字林) states that "zhen" (󱸘) means "to roast."
*Qiāngpú*: "Qiāng" (qīyáng fǎn) means to move; "pú" (now written as *fù*, pŭběi fǎn) means to fall prostrate. There is a *chuán* (shìzhuān fǎn);

according to the *Zílín*, it is made of split bamboo and used for storing grain. The *Cāngjiépiān* writes it as *chuí* (shíyuán fǎn), meaning a round granary. The text reads *diàn* (yīndàn), which is the name of a vessel; it is a basket (*sì*) and also a container for food. *Sì* (also read *xī*) is likewise a vessel for holding food.

"Yǎ" (瘂) is also "yīn" (瘖), meaning mute; the text reads "ā" (痾), which is pronounced "yú hé" (於何) and means illness—this is not the intended meaning here. It is also written as "yà" (啞), pronounced "yǐ bái" (乙白), meaning the sound of laughter; neither of these is the correct character for this sense.

*Gēng* (古恒反; *gǔ héng*): According to the *Tōngsùwén*, a large rope is called *gēng*; *gēng* is also a cord. The text of the scripture uses *héng* (絙), which is incorrect. *Héng* is pronounced *hú guān* (胡官反).

20. Fascicle Twenty. *Tuí* (石𨹃; *shí tuǒ*; *tuǒ* is read as *dú guǒ* [徒果反]): According to the *Tōngsùwén*, piling up earth is called *tuǒ*. The text of the scripture uses *duò* (墮), which is incorrect.
*Pianwu* (拚舞) is also written as *bianwu* (抃舞), with the phonetic *pi* (皮) and *bian* (變). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *bian* (抃) means to clap one's hands.
*Daowei* (󲢜嵬), with the phonetic *wu* (五) and *hui* (迴), is the name of various sons of the gods (*devaputra*) in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
21. Fascicle Twenty-one. "Jiānhuì" (涓澮): "jiān" (涓) means a tiny stream; "huì" (澮) refers to a mountain waterway or drainage ditch, two *xún* wide and two *rèn* deep.
"Śechi" (蛇池) is the name of a pond; its character "she" (蛇) is an error for "zhe" (遮).

"Xuequan" (穴泉)—the ancient form is written as "duan" (洤), both pronounced with the *jue* (絕) and *yuan* (緣) finals—refers to a spring where water emerges spontaneously; the forms "qian" (󲫰) or "kun" (湶) found in the sutras are not the correct characters.
*Hu-ha*: The ancient characters for *hu* (呼) and *hai* (欱) are two forms of the same character, pronounced with the rhyme *he* (合).

The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *hai* means "to sip. 22. Volume Twenty-two. *Zi* (梓) and *bo* (柏) are also written as *zhi* (榟), all sharing the pronunciation *zi-li* (資里). These are names of trees; they can be used to make *qin* and *se* lutes. *Zi* is also the *qiu* (楸) tree.

"Yì" (異) is an archaic form of "xì" (繫). The two characters share the same ancient pronunciation, *gèi* (古藝反). "Xì" means to bind, to succeed, and to continue. "Fǔ" (拊) has the pronunciation *kǎi* (麩主反);
it refers to patting or striking, as in the *Shàngshū*: "Striking the stone and patting the stone."

The Madhyama Āgama, Volume One, compiled by Xuanying. First Volume. *Kaku* (Bird-beak): according to the *Shuowen*, "beak" refers to the mouth; the character is composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic element "tuàn" (*tā luàn fǎn*). The sound of *tuàn* is *tā luàn fǎn*.

When the general Yu (勇) returned from his campaign against the cow-herders, the Grand Scribe [Shangshu] said: "To kill the enemy is the fruit; to bring about that fruit is the resolve (*xin*). Resolve also implies decisiveness. *E* (堊): Pronounced *wò* (烏各反).

The *Cangjie pian* states it is white earth. The *Erya* says a wall is called *e*; Guo Pu notes it is to decorate a wall with white earth. The *Shiming* explains: "*E* means 'to coat' (*ai*); it is the next step after plastering, where one decorates it with lime."

"Niandou" (黏豆): "Nian" (霑) is pronounced as *zhān* (霑反); it is the name of a bean. "Zhetang" (蔗餹)—also written as "zhetang" (糖)—is pronounced as *tú láng* (徒郎反); it refers to molasses made from sugarcane; this is what is known today as "sugar" (*táng*). Volume Two, Part Two:

"Xianbu" (先不) has no phonetic notation. Volume Three: "Wei-ka" (尾髂)—the ancient form is "wei-qi" (𩩱), now written as "weijia" (䯊)—is pronounced as *kǒu yà* (口亞反). According to the *Pīcāng*, it refers to the bones of the waist. The scriptural text writes it as "ge'e" (骼頟), pronounced as *gē é* (歌頟反); however, "ge'e" refers to withered bones and does not carry this meaning.

4. Fourth Fascicle. *Lìyǎn* (麗𢮓) is also written as *chè* (掣); its Sanskrit equivalent is *pratyandaka*. This is translated as "fine and smooth" (*sūkṣma-spraṣṭavya*). *Kuǐ* (魁) is pronounced with the initial *kǔ* and the final *huí* (反).
The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *kuǐ* refers to the broth of a soup. The forms *huái* (槐) and *mài* (𣛣) found in certain sutra texts are not the correct characters.

*Mài* (pronounced with the *yè* rhyme): According to the *Cāngjié Piān*, it is a large variety of millet; it is also said to resemble millet but not be glutinous. In the region west of the Pass, it is called *mí*. This is correct.

*Zá kǎn* (the *kǎn* pronounced with the *gǔ mǎng* rhyme): The *Shuōwén* defines it as a type of grain. In the scriptures, it is written as *mài* (with the radical for "grain"), which is merely a modern variant character.

"Jian" (箭) refers to the arrow; in the region west of the Pass it is called "jiānjīn" (箭金), while in the region east of the Pass it is called "jiànzú" (箭足). Some say "dí" (鏑) is a term used to distinguish its specific name.
"Jiǎn" (撿) is pronounced with the *nu* and *jiào* rhymes; it means to press or clamp. "Náo" (撓) means to bend or curve. Together, they refer to the process of straightening and refining an arrow.

Regarding the character *zú* (卒): it is pronounced *mò* (沒) in the ancient dialect. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that those who serve as commoners are called *zú*. In antiquity, they dyed their garments and used them to mark and distinguish their status. According to the *Fangyan*, in the regions between Nan Chu and Dong Hai, some call *zú* "zhe" (赭). Guo Pu commented: "This refers to the redness of their clothing; therefore, the character is composed of the radical for 'clothing' (*yī*)."
*Chuàn* (剬): The phonetic category is the same as *zhuān* (剸), with the pronunciation *zhùì*. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to sever the head" and also "to cut.

Volume 5, Chapter 5 (no character present). Volume 6: *Jì* (祭) and *Zú* (餟). The archaic form is *㝹*. The phonetic category is the same as *zhuì* (醊), with the pronunciation *zhūruì*. According to the *Shuowen*, *zhù* (酻)—the phonetic being *lìwài*—is defined in the *Zilin* as "sacrificing wine upon the ground. In the *Fangyan*, *zhù* (餟) is synonymous with *zhù* (𫗙).
"Carrying and hauling" (*fù yǎn*): In the *Huainanzi*, it says "hauling grain to [the destination]. Xu Shu Zhong stated that "yǎn" means "to carry on a shoulder pole.

Today, this is written as "nuǎn" (a sedan chair). [Volume Six is missing. Volume Seven: "Coarse and fine" (*cū xì*) is also written as "chén" (𡄇). It is the same as "cuò" (錯). "Chén" means large; "xì" means small. The text of the scripture uses "chén" (塵), which is an error for "xì" (細).
"Naogēn" (腦根)—the "nao" is pronounced with a retroflex *lao* (老) tone; it refers to the *yùzhěn* (玉枕) at the back of the head.

"Quánchāi" (拳搋)—also written as "quǎn" (捲), both pronounced with the *qúyuán* (渠圓) tone; the second character is also written as "chái" (𭠎), both pronounced with the *chìjiā* (勅佳) tone—this refers to the clenching of the hands.
"Jie" (齶) is pronounced *wu ge fan*; it refers to the palate (*yan*). The forms "jing" (𦞐) and "e" (腭) found in the canonical texts are not the correct characters.

"Ke" (欬) and "sai" (瘶): "ke" is pronounced *kou dai su dou fan*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "ke" refers to the upward movement of qi; it is also "sai. The forms "ke" (咳) and "sou" (欶) found in the canonical texts are not the correct characters.

*He*: (pronounced *tǔ yǐ jiè fǎn*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "thirst. According to the *Cangjie Pian*, it means "to discard" or "also to transcribe. *Bì*: (pronounced *bì lì fǎn*). "Closed" (*bi*) means "obstructed. The scriptural text writes it as *bì*. It refers to a cold-damp disease.

Medical prescriptions often refer to it as a disease of the throat. *He*: (pronounced *tǔ yǐ jiè fǎn*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "thirst. According to the *Cangjie Pian*, it means "to discard" or "also to transcribe. *Bì*: (pronounced *bì lì fǎn*). "Closed" (*bi*) means "obstructed. The scriptural text writes it as *bì*. It refers to a cold-damp disease. Medical prescriptions often refer to it as a disease of the throat.

*Hì* (痔) [pronounced *zhǐ*]: This refers to the ailment of hemorrhoids (*hòubìng*), specifically the moist type where worms consume the anal region. The character used in the scripture is not the standard form.
*Dìàn* (店肆): Now written as *diàn* (坫), both pronounced *duàn*. "Sì" (*shì*) means to display; it refers to places where goods are displayed for sale and purchase.
8. Scroll Eight. Regarding "Huangchi" (潢池): Hu Guang rebelled at Huangchi. "Huang" refers to accumulated water; that which is small is called *wu* (洿), and that which is large is called *huang* (潢).
Regarding "Bi Yu" (碧玉): according to the *Guangya*, it is green jade; according to the *Shuowen*, it is the beauty of stone. Today, Biyu is produced from the mountains east of Yue-zhi.

"Daimei" (玳瑁) is now written with the two characters 蝳蜎; in ancient script, it was written with the two characters 𣫹󲥧. They share the same pronunciation as "dàimèi. The *Yìwùzhì* states: "It resembles a tortoise and is found in the South Sea. The large ones are as big as a *pútú* gourd. On its back there are scales; when one wishes to boil it, its skin becomes supple and can be fashioned into whatever one desires."

Regarding "Chìshí" (赤石), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is the color of the south, composed of the radicals "dà" (大) and "huǒ" (火); its archaic form is written as 𤊨. Regarding "shí" (石), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is mountain rock; it is situated beneath the radical "yǎn" (厂), and the character "kǒu" (口) is used to represent its shape.

The character for *xuánzhū* (revolving pearl) should be written as *miǎo* (𭊕), pronounced with the *cí* and *yuán* finals. The *Mùtiānzǐ zhuan* states: "Among the treasures of Mount Chūnshān, there is the *miǎo* pearl. Guō Pǔ comments: "It is a type of jade.

*Dìqí* (imperial fawn) is sometimes written as *mí* (𭊕); they share the same pronunciation. In the scriptures, it is sometimes written as *dīmí* or *chīmí*; these are merely variations (*zhuǎn*) of the Sanskrit term.

9–10 (Volumes Nine through Ten are missing) 11. Volume Eleven. *Mao* (髦): pronounced *mo* with a high tone; it refers to the color of a dark blue-black horse, its head like that of a crow. This is the Horse-Jewel (*aśvaratna*). It is named after its hair-ornamentation; thus it is called *mao*. In the script of the sutra, it is written as *pao* (䭷), which is not the correct character form. *Pao* is pronounced *li* with a second tone (*lì shè*).
*Jiǎo* (皎) and *jié* (潔): These two forms were both anciently written as *jiǎo* (皦) and *zhì* (𭊕); the modern form is *jiào* (晈), all pronounced with the phonetic *gōng niǎo* (公鳥).

The *Bīcāng* states that *jiǎo* means bright and pure. 12. Volume Twelve. *Huá* (鏵) and *qiāo* (鍬): Also written as *jué* (鐰), all pronounced with the phonetic *qiě xiāo* (且消). According to the *Fāngyán*, in the regions of Zhào and Wèi, the term *zǒng* (𠚏) is called *qiāo* (鍫).
"Shu-shāng" (鼠傷) is read as "shǐ-yáng" (始羊) in the *Pīcāng*; it refers to a molehill (*shǔdiè*). According to the *Fānyán*, "shǔ-diè-fēng-shāng" (鼠垤封傷) means a mound or a wound.
"Wǎn-dòu" (豌豆) is read as "yī-wán" (一丸); it is the name of a type of bean. The text of the scripture writes it as "wǎn" (宛) or "zhǒu" (󲪏), but neither is the correct form.
*Bìdòu* (豍豆): "Bù" is pronounced as in *bùmí* (布迷). According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, *bìdòu* is the same as *dàodòu* (䝀豆). The text reads *pípóu* (蜱), which is not the correct form.
*Luó* (籮): the pronunciation is *luó*. According to the *Zílín*, it is a bamboo vessel; according to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it is a winnowing basket (*jī*).
*Huò* (火) and *gǔwén* (古文) are the same character as *dǎo* (𤑔), pronounced *yuè* (悅). According to the *Tōngsùwén* (通俗文), "to kindle fire" is called *huǒ* (𤋲);

it also means to burn. *Lǎn* (擥) is also written as *lǎn* (攬) or *jiàn* (檻); these two forms are identical, pronounced *lì gǎn* (力敢). The *Guǎngyá* (廣雅) states that "to *lǎn*" means to take; the *Shuōwén* (說文) defines it as to grasp or hold.

13. The Thirteenth Fascicle. *Zēnmǎng* (榛莽): *zēn* is pronounced with the initial *chū* and the final *fǎn*; according to the *Shuōwén*, "a cluster of trees is called *zēn*, and a multitude of weeds is called *mǎng*.
*Pìchù* (僻處): *pì* is pronounced with the initial *pǐ* and the final *chì*; it means "crooked and deviant," and also "secluded and remote. According to the *Shuōwén*, "to be biased is *pì*."

The character *xīng* (猩猩) is pronounced *jīng* (反). According to the *Zílín*, it is a bird capable of speech that knows human names. Its form is like that of a pig, and its head resembles a yellow chicken. It is currently found in Fēngxī of Jiǎozhǐ, where its vocalization sounds like the crying of a small child. The character is composed of the radical "dog" (*quán*) and the phonetic element "star" (*xīng*).
*Jùnshí* (捃拾): The ancient character is *jù* (󲛻), pronounced with the initial *yùn* (同 居 運 反). According to the *Fānyǔ* (方言), it means "to gather" (*jùnqǔ*).

14. Volume Fourteen. [Character]: *Shǒufǔ* (手拊). Pronounced with the initial *fūzhǔ* (夫 主 反). *Fǔ* is equivalent to "to strike" (*pāi*). This is as in the *Shàngshū*: "Striking the stone and clapping the stone" (*jīshí fǔshí*).
*Yù yuò*: *yù* (from the *Shuowen*, "brilliant radiance") and *yuò* (flame-light). The scriptural text writes this as *shàò*, which is not the correct form. *Lú bì*:

*lú* (from the *Shuowen*, "the capital atop a pillar," referring to the square wooden block at the top of a pillar). Regarding *lú-dǒu*, the *Shiming* says: "It is called *lú* because it is 'completely' (*dūlú*) bearing up the roof. The scriptural text writes this with the metal radical as *lú*, which is not the correct form. Below, it should be written as *sǎng* (from the *Shuowen*, "the stone beneath a pillar," i.e., the pillar base). The scriptural text writes this with the metal radical as *bì*, which is an error. *Chǔ* (pillar base) is pronounced *chǔ*.

15. Fascicle Fifteen. Regarding the *Sheng Hong Jingzhou Ji* (Record of the Flourishing Administration of Jingzhou), it states that Xianglan (Fragrant Orchid) is the name of a small mountain in Duliang County. On this mountain, orchids grow everywhere; the common people call the orchid "Duliang," which is derived from the name of the county.
The *Wenji* (Collection of Writings) briefly states: "To hold up an object in front of someone is called *zhēng* (pronounced *gǔ láng*).

As for the monetary fine, it refers to currency; from the dynasties of Tang, Yu, Xia, and Yin, there has always been money. The script in the Classics uses the character *chù* (pronounced *zhū luò*), which refers to the iron tip of a staff and is not used in this sense.
"Buchi" (不啻) [pronounced shì] means "more than" or "abundant," according to the *Cangjie pian*.
Volume 16, Chapter 16: "Pisī" (蜱肆)—the phonetic transcription is "bùmí" (布迷); this is translated as "sending a messenger."
*Li* (pronounced *shi* with the *jian* tone) refers to having a blade for carving and chiseling. *Zhi* (pronounced *zhu* with the *jue* tone) means to pare the flesh;

it is also written as *ti*. They share the same pronunciation (*ta* with the *li* tone). *Ku* and *ti* are synonymous. The *Tongsu* (Popular Explanations) states that removing the bone is called *ti*.

"Zhuo heng" (著蘅): "Heng" is pronounced with the initial *hu* and the final *geng*. It refers to the fragrant herb *du-heng*. This means that he used grass to make a wreath (*man*), which expresses his depravity.

"Liang ju" (兩𨌪) is also written as "liao chui" (輟), both pronounced with the initial *zi* and the final *kong*. According to the *Fangyan*, in the region west of the Pass, a wheel is called "ju. The *Shiming* explains that "ju" signifies entering deeply into the grain.
"Sen-sen" (森森) [the first character pronounced as *so* with a retroflex *r*]: the written characters mean "abundant trees" and describe a state of great length;

here we take only their underlying meaning. "Kuā" (誇): [pronounced *kǔ* with a *huá* rhyme]; according to the *Tōngsùwén* (通俗文), "to boast" is called *kuā*; according to the *Shìfǎ* (謚法), "to speak flowery words without substance" is called *kuā*.

17. Volume Seventeen. Regarding the characters *lǔ* (鹵) and *lǚ* (櫓), they form two distinct forms with the same pronunciation: *lǔ* (鹵) has the radical *li* (力) and the phonetic *gǔ* (古); *lǚ* (櫓) has the radical *bù* (簿) and the phonetic *gǔ* (古). *Lǚ* refers to a large shield. As stated in Cai Yong’s *Duduan*: "When the Son of Heaven departs in his Grand Procession (*dàjià*), he arrays the *lǔbù*. This is precisely what that means.
*Jiàn* (擲羂): Also written as *jiàn* (罥), with the phonetic *gǔ* (古) and *quǎn* (犬) as the rhyme.

The *Shēnglèi* (聲類) states it means "to bind and capture. Volume 18, Chapter 18. *Jiàn* (椷簏): With the phonetic *hú* (胡) and *chán* (讒). The *Shuōwén* (說文) defines it as a "box" (*qiè*). Lexicons define it as a "wooden box. The scriptural text uses the character *jiān* (緘) from the radical for silk (*mì*), which is not the correct form. Below, it is also written as *zhuàn* (篆), with the phonetic *lì* (力) and *mù* (木); this refers to a bamboo vessel.

19. The nineteenth [chapter]. (The preceding does not have a phonetic gloss. 20. The twentieth fascicle. Fascicle Twenty. "Sōng" (菘): the *fāngyán* (dictionary of regional dialects) states that *wēiráo* (蕘) and *wújīng* (蕪菁) refer to the same plant. Guo Pu’s commentary provides the old pronunciation as *fēng* (蜂), but in the Jiangdong region today it is pronounced *sōng* (嵩), and the character is written as 菘. Between Chen and Chu it is called *fēng* (豊), with the pronunciation *fēng*. Between Lu and Qi it is called *ráo* (蕘); in the regions east and west of the Pass it is called *wújīng* (蕪菁). The pronunciation of *ráo* (蕘) is *ráo* (饒).
The character *qīng* (輕) in "闡" should be read as *tuán* (團), with the phonetic components *tú* and *wán*. According to the *Zìlín* (字林), it means "round. Volumes 21–23:

Volumes twenty-one, twenty-two, and twenty-three above have all previously lacked phonetic glosses. Volume 24: Regarding the character *yùn* (蘊) in "蘊" [in the phrase "如蘊"], it should be pronounced *yū wén* (紆文). This refers to gathering bundles of grass to ignite them; it is like the expression in the *Hànshū* (漢書): "Dong yùn qǐ huǒ" (東蘊乞火). The text of the sutra uses the character *yēn* (蒀), which is incorrect. *Péng yēn* (葐蒀) describes the appearance of flourishing smoke, and is not what is intended here. The old pronunciation given as *guǐ* (軌) is entirely incorrect.

*Ményǔ* (門閾): The ancient form is *mén yù* (䦗); both are pronounced *hū yù* (呼域反). According to the *Erya*, what is called *chì* (抶) is the *yǔ* (閾). Guo Pu states it is the threshold of a door. *Chì* (抶) is pronounced *tián jié* (田結反) according to the *Erya*, and *chǒu lì* (丑栗反) according to the *Shuowen*.

23. Fascicle Twenty-Three. [Note on the character] "Huan" (胡緘反): This refers to a wooden vessel used for holding things. The text reads "xian" (臽), which means a pit or hole; the pronunciation of "yao" (舀) does not carry this meaning.
Grass and firewood that can be broken are called *xīn* (薪); the scriptural text reads *xiángsū* (蘘蘇), which is a type of grass-cloth.
*Dàn* (澹) is pronounced *tú làn* (徒濫) for the first character and *tú gǎn* (徒敢) for the second; according to the *Guǎngyá*, both *dàn* and *dàn* mean "peaceful" (*ān*).

The character for *niào* (溺) is written as *wěi* (尾); according to the *Shuowen*, it means "urination" and is composed of the radicals for water (*shui*) and tail (*wei*). The text uses *niào*, which is merely an ancient instance of phonetic borrowing. Volume 24, Part 24.

The archaic forms of *zhàn* (顫) and *qī* (𩑌) are also written as *yù* (䡀), all sharing the same pronunciation as *zhān* (之繕反). The archaic forms *dì* (䤞), *huī* (𤴨), and *qī* (𩑌) appear in three variants; the current form is *wòu* (疣), pronounced *yóu* (尤救反). According to the *Tongshu Wen*, the trembling of the four limbs due to cold is called *zhàn qī*; the *Cangjie Pian* states it refers to the head being crooked. The text’s reading of *qián* (𣏞) is incorrect.

The character for "zàn" (to pile up) is an archaic form identical to "zǔ" (祖), with the phonetic reading *zuǎn* (祖丸反). According to the *Cāngjié piān*, it means "to accumulate" (*cùnjù*), and its radical is the wood radical (*mù*).

The term "cǎozhù" (草貯) has the phonetic reading *zhǔ* (張呂反); "zhù" means to store or accumulate, referring to the act of keeping things stored. The version of the scripture uses the character "zhūn" (𣛰), with the phonetic reading *zhīlüè* (知略反), meaning "to strike. However, "zhūn" does not carry this meaning here.

Regarding the character *yā* (押): according to the *Erya*, it means "to support" (*fǔ*). This refers to "pressing together," "binding," "obstructing," and so forth; all such instances are written as *yā*. Volume Twenty-five.

[The character] *qí* (耆) has the phonetic value *wù* (五) and the rhyme *gài* (葢). In the *Liji*, it says: "At sixty days one is called *qí*; at fifty days one is called *ài*. The *Shiming* states: "*Qí* means 'to point' (*zhǐ*); *ài* also means 'to treat' (*zhì*) or 'to manage. 'To point' (*zhǐ*) means to direct affairs and employ others, rather than performing the labor oneself."
*Jūlì* (pronounced with the *qù* tone; sometimes written as *lóu* in the scriptures) is merely a corruption of the Sanskrit term.

*Niǎnzhí* (the ancient character is the same as *niè*, pronounced *nǎi jié*) means to grasp with the fingers; it refers to pressing with the hand. The second character is pronounced *zhū lì*. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means a fetter (*zhì*).

26. Volume Twenty-Six. Chapter Twenty-Six: The Banner (Donghui). "Hui" is pronounced as in "hu-pi" (呼皮反); it refers to a signal flag used to direct and command the multitude, and the chapter is named accordingly. According to the *Zhou Li* (Rites of Zhou), the great banner (*dahui*) was established for military expeditions; it was the type of banner erected by the Xia dynasty.

A gold ingot is merely a raw bar; "ting" (頂) is pronounced *ding* (topping), while "ting" (鋌) is pronounced *ting* (bar). The raw ore of copper and iron has not yet been fashioned into a functional vessel.

Volume Twenty-seven. [The character for] "xian" (先) is not pronounced as in the modern reading. Volume Twenty-eight. "Yan jie" (眼睫) is also written as "zhan" (聗); they share the same pronunciation, *zi ye* (子葉). They refer to the eyelashes. In the scriptural texts, there are two variant forms, "jing" (𣰍) and "li" (𣯮), but these are not the standard forms.
Regarding *tè* (pronounced with the initial *zhà* and the final *yè*; alternatively written as *gānzhè* or *yúzhè*), since these are words from a Western country, their forms are not fixed.
*Tì* (pronounced with the initial *tì* and the final *huò*; according to the *Erya*, *tì* means "to abandon" or "to cease") refers to extinction; it signifies total annihilation.
Láo (勞): The radical is 力 (lì) with the phonetic component 尞 (liáo). It means "to toil" or "exertion," referring to the exhaustion of one's strength.

The forms 󲤼 and 毖 found in the canonical text are errors. Volumes 29–30: Volumes twenty-nine and thirty were not previously provided with phonetic transcriptions. Volume 31: Regarding the character 暴 (bào), it is also written as 凶 (xiōng) with the same pronunciation, xǔ yóng fǎn. According to the *Erya*, "xiōng" means "calamity. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "xiōng" means "evil. The lower part is pronounced pú bào fǎn. According to the *Guoyu*, "bào" means "sudden" or "impetuous. The character is composed of 廾 (two hands joined) and 日 (sun); from "sun" comes "daybreak," and from "hand" comes "hand" (pronounced tǔ gāo).

The character *qín* (捦) is also written as two other forms, *dǎn* (鈘) and *qín* (㯲), all with the phonetic reading *jūlín*. According to the *Sāncāng*, "to *qín*" means to grasp an object with the hand; according to the *Běicāng*, it means to seize. Nowadays, all are written as *qín* (擒).

*Cuò* (捽): Pronounced *cún-mò* (存沒) as a variant; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to seize by the hair. In the scripture, it is sometimes written as *cuō* (撮), pronounced *zǔ-huó* (祖活), meaning "to grasp" or "to clutch.

*Huò* (豁): An archaic form with two variants, *huò* (奯) and *huò* (𪾤), both pronounced *huó* (呼活). According to the *Guangya*, it means "empty" or "open. In the scripture, it is written with the "heart" radical (*xīn*) as *huò* (𭟙); its source has not yet been identified.
Volume Thirty-Two, Part Three. "Jiang" (漿) is a scribal error for "Daziyangfan" (大紫羊反), which is a transliteration of the name of a *pratyekabuddha*.

"Zhan" (鱣) is written as "Yan" (𩼼) in ancient texts; it is pronounced "zhilián" (知連反). It is a large yellow fish with its mouth located beneath the jaw; the largest specimens reach a length of two or three *zhang* (丈).

The character *xiāo* (梟) is pronounced as *gǎo* (堯) with a retroflex initial; according to the *Shuowen*, it refers to one who is "fierce" (*liè*), meaning one whose head is severed and hung upside down from the top of a wooden pole to exhibit their crime. It is also written as *xiāo* (梟), which the *Shuowen* defines as the "unfilial bird. On the winter solstice, one captures the *xiāo* and dismembers it. This is represented by the form consisting of a bird with its head atop a tree; both forms are used interchangeably.

*Yáng* (揚) is a personal name; its phonetic transcription is *lái* (來) or, alternatively, written as *duān* (端) with the same pronunciation. This is merely a difference in the weight of the Sanskrit syllables.
Regarding the archaic forms *yǎng* (敭) and *yáng* (颺), they share the same phonetic transcription *yúzhāng* (余章). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *yáng* means "to fly up" or "to lift."

33. Fascicle Thirty-Three. Regarding the character *pào* (皰): it is also written as *páo* (𦡕), with the same pronunciation as *pú xiào* (蒲孝反). It refers to a slight sensation of heat. The forms *pào* (疱), *lǔ* (䶌), and *fú* (𦡕) appearing in the sutra texts are not the correct characters.
"Golden door-leaf" (*jīnfēi*): "Fēi" is not the character for "explanation" (*shuōwén*). A door panel is called a *fēi*; the text’s reading as *huì* (𨵈) is an error. "To respond" (*chóudá*):
in ancient texts, this is the same as *chóu*, pronounced *shóuyǎn*. It means to repay the host; *chóu* is also synonymous with "response."

34. The Thirty-fourth Fascicle. Regarding "yáo" (窯): in the *Tōngsùwén* (通俗文), a kiln for firing pottery is called a *yáo*; the *Cāngjié xùnzhu* (蒼頡訓詁) states that a *yáo* is a kiln for burning tiles.

*Tian* (甜) is also written as *mian* (餂), both pronounced *tu jian*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to taste for sweetness"; according to the *Guoyu*, it means "sweetness. It is incorrect for the scriptural text to write this as *wei* (䣶).
*Ya qi* (牙跂) is also written as *ji* (屐), both pronounced *qu ni*. There are wooden, silken, and grass versions of the *ji*; they are not of a single kind.
The characters *jǐngwù* (警寤) and *jìnjǐng* (憼儆) share the same pronunciation (*jǐng*) and both mean "to be on guard" or "to be cautious. The reading *jǐng* (景) in the canonical text is incorrect.

The character *gòuniǔ* (搆牛), pronounced *gǒu*, is an alternative form of *gòu* (搉); it means to milk by squeezing and stroking. The reading *cū* (觕)—which is actually the character for "to touch" (*chù*)—in the canonical text is an error.

35. Fascicle Thirty-Five. Regarding the character "款" (kuǎn): the old edition sometimes writes it as "款" with the same pronunciation; according to the *Guǎngyá*, "款" means affection; according to the *Cāngjié piān*, "款" means sincerity and gravity.
*Jiào* (pronounced *gǔ xiào fǎn*): According to the *Tōngsù Wén*, grain and wheat are stored in a *jiào*. The *Cāngjié Piān* states that a *jiào* is a storage city.

*È* (also written as *yē* in ancient texts, same as *yè*; pronounced *yú hé fǎn*): According to the *Ěr Yá*, *è* means to stop; it refers to stopping one another by way of opposition. *È* also means to block.
36. Fascicle Thirty-Six. Regarding the character *zhuō* (自摑): it should be read as *jué* (俱縛反). It means to seize or to grasp. Regarding the five fingers (*wǔ zhǐ*):

*nà* (乃遏反) refers to pressing with the five fingers of the hand. In the sutras, it is written as *chāo* (𢲉, 千計反); according to the *Běicāng*, this means to pick up or pluck, but it is not used in this sense here.

Compared to the ancient texts, "jiao" (較) is the same as "jiǎo" (㰌), which according to the *Gu xue* (古學) and the *Guang ya* (廣雅) means "clear" or "to see"; it refers to being "obvious and easy to perceive. Within the scriptures, there are instances where it is written as "jiaobi" (挍比) or "jiaojiao" (挍較).
*Bi*: Also pronounced *bei* (in the *Shuowen*, it means "the seams of a garment"; according to the *Guangya*, it means "to fold"). *Kuan*: Pronounced *qiu yuan*. Volume 37:
No phonetic transcription provided for the preceding character. Volume 38: *Zhi*: Pronounced *zhu li*. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to store away," and also "to gather" or "to collect."

39. Fascicle Thirty-nine. "To wait" (*sì*)—the ancient form is *sì*, and the variant forms are *wèi* and *dǐ*. All three forms share the same meaning; according to the *Erya*, "to wait" means "to await."

The "yuán-hóu" (猿猴) is here written as "yuán" (蝯), with the phonetic transcription "yú fán" (禹煩). It resembles a macaque but is larger, with long arms; its color may be black or yellow, and its cry is extremely plaintive. The text reads it as "biān" (𤝌), which is not the correct form.
*Pi* (pronounced *bǔ*, with the rhyme of *gē*) means "to split open"; according to the *Guǎngyá*, it refers to dividing or tearing apart.

*Xù* (also written as *xù*, both pronounced *xūlì*) means "to worry about" or "to provide for"; according to the *Eryā*, it means "sorrow," and it also implies "to collect" or "to gather. To give wealth and goods to others is called "relieving and providing for" (*zhǐn xù*). Its appearance as *jì* in the scriptures is not yet clearly established.

Volumes 40–45: Volumes Forty through Forty-five—Volumes 40, 41, 42, 43, 44, and 45. The above all lack prior phonetic glosses. Volume 46: Volume Forty-six. "Chuang-yi" (瘡痍): *chuang* rhymes with *yu* (𭥲); according to the *Tongsu-wen*, a body wound is called *yi* (痍), and a head wound is called *yang* (瘍). *Yang* is pronounced *yang*.

The characters for *qì* (qi) and *xi* (xu) are the same in ancient script; "xu" is pronounced as in *jù* (墟). It refers to the breath (*qì*). The character below is an ancient form of *luō* (捋), pronounced as in *lì zhuó* (力拙). "Lüè" (劣) means weak; it is an error for the character in the received text to be written as "lüè."

47. Fascicle Forty-Seven. Regarding the term "wei" (謂): when read as *chí* (積) and *xí* (習), it means to accumulate and practice repeatedly. When the scriptural text reads it as *chǒu* (丑) and *jiá* (俠), it means not to cease. This is not the primary meaning of the character.

*Yìdiàn* (曳電) is also written as *yè* (曳), with the same pronunciation as *yúshì* (余世). It means to drag or pull; "diàn" (電) here means to perish suddenly, signifying that what is briefly dragged forth is immediately extinguished.

*Nóngxuè* (膿血) appears in ancient texts in two forms, *nǎng* (𤵷) and *nóng* (膿); the modern form is *nòng* (癑), with the same pronunciation as *núgōng* (奴公), meaning purulent blood. The version in the sutra text as *fǎ* (䐦) is incorrect.
*Chúnjiǔ* (淳酒) is the same as *bùjiāojiǔ* (不澆酒); it is also the wine of the "ten-month" (*shíxún*) vintage.
*Xiàojǔ* (㕮咀) [pronounced with the finals *fǔ* and *cèlǚ*] means to pound and crush.
*Láizhèn* (來鎭) [pronounced with the final *zhǐchén*]; according to the *Shuowen*, *zhèn* means to suppress. The text reads *tián* (填) [pronounced *túdān*], meaning to fill.

48. Volume Forty-Eight. Mṛdvī (or pronounced with the "tie" tone, *dù* according to the rhyme dictionary; the scriptural text writes it as *tǔ*, which is a transliteration; the character *tǔ* is an error for *tú*, which is the correct form). (Note: The character *tǔ* [𣧅] is a phonetic transcription. It is an error for *tú* [蓫], which is the correct orthography.)
*Śīru*: This is the name of a tree; "shu" (樹) is pronounced with the *chou-lian* (丑連) tone. *Tāci* (他支):
In the Qin language, this means "wealth-banner" (*caidāng*); the text reads *tōqī* (咃吱), which is derived from the mouth and involves a retroflex articulation.

It serves as a *ci* (幟). The archaic form is the same as *zhì* (󲋪), pronounced *chǐzhì*. It refers to a banner or mark. The *Sōngsúwén* (通俗文) states: "A *ci* refers to five types of objects such as sword-covers and the like; a *biāo* (幖) is a record or sign."
*Qīchóng* (祗崇): "Qī" means respectful; "chóng" means weighty. *Zhèn* (振) has two ancient forms, *jǐn* (𢈫) and *jù* (拒).

It is pronounced *zhū yìn* (諸胤). According to the *Shuowen*, it means to lift up; in the *Xiaoya*, it means to rescue, and it also means to stimulate or issue forth. The scriptural text writes it as *zhěng* (賑), pronounced *zhū rěn* (諸忍). According to the *Erya*, *zhěng* means wealthy; this refers to secretly providing for those who possess wealth. Thus, *zhèn* (振) and *zhěng* (賑) both apply in two ways.

"Gōn" (鰥) is pronounced as in "gu-wan" (古頑). The *Shiming* (釋名) states: "One without a wife is called gōn; one without children is called dú. It explains that the term "gōn" refers to a man who is sorrowful and depressed, unable to sleep, and whose eyes are constantly wide open and staring like the eyes of a fish, which do not close; thus, the character is derived from the radical for "fish" (魚).

The ancient characters for *suān* (酸), *kù* (酷), *gǔ* (古), *kù* (嚳), *kū* (焅), and *jì* (俈) share the same form and are pronounced with the rhyme *kǔ-mù*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *kù* means "urgent" or "extreme," referring to cruelty and tyranny.

In the compilation of ancient texts, the character *zǎn* (纂) is identical to *zǐ-mǎo* (子卯); the character is sometimes written as *zuàn* (纘). According to the *Erya*, *zuàn* means to continue the labors of former scholars.

49. Fascicle Forty-nine. Fascicle Forty-nine. "Praying" (dǎo) refers to seeking blessings; it means to entreat the spirits and deities. "Thanking" (xiè) refers to expressions of gratitude. It is a term for offering thanks.

"Bào" (蒲報反) is also written as "bào" (菢). According to the *Fānyǔ*, in the regions between Yān and Cháoxiān, the hen sitting on her eggs is called "bào. In the Jiangdōng region, it is called "yù. The character in the received text is "qì" (㲒), the origin of which is unknown.

*Jiàoxìng* (僥倖) is also written as *jiǎo* (儌) with the same pronunciation; the first character is read as *gǔyáo* (古堯) and the second as *xìng* (幸). In common parlance, *xìng* (幸) is called *jiàoxìng*, meaning to be favored by its virtuous grace. It also refers to the hope of encountering such favor. In the *Chuci* (楚辭), the phrase "I wish to rely on *jiàoxìng* while waiting for the right time" refers to obtaining that which one ought not to obtain—this is what is termed *jiàoxìng*.
As for "lao" (烙), it is pronounced with the initial *l* and final *-li* (each reversed); it means to burn an object and cause it to adhere, hence "to cauterize.

As for "ju" (掬) and "bao" (抱), they are also written as "ju" (鞠) and share the same pronunciation, *jū* (with the initial *j* and final *-u* together); according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "ju" means to gather or scoop up, while "bao" means to embrace or hold.

Fascicle Fifty (The character "xiān" [先] does not have the phonetic value "yīn"). Fascicle Fifty-one. Regarding the term "qiyǔ" (綺語): "xū" is pronounced with the rhyme of "yì" (蟻); it means "improper. The text of the sūtra writes it as "yǐ" (倚), which is not the correct form.
*Ráng* (pronounced *yáng* in reverse) means to remove or ward off; it refers to lying down (*xià*) in a state of stupor (*àn*) that does not awaken.

*Sòu* (also written as *sòu*, same pronunciation as *shān jiǎo*) means to suckle; the *Tōng sú wén* states that inhaling and sucking is called *sòu*. The scriptural text uses the character *chū*, which is a vulgar form of this word.
*Kuì* (饋) is the same as *kuì* (餽) in ancient texts; the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to provide food. *Yí* (遺) means "to give.
*Bǐn* (稟) is pronounced *bǔ jǐn*; the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "a bestowed gift," while the *Guangya* defines it as "to grant."

*Yáng* (聾) is pronounced *yú zhāng* (餘章); the *Tōngsùwén* (通俗文) writes it as *xiáng* (詳), meaning empty words. The *Hànshū* (漢書) writes it as *yáng* (陽), meaning not true. The scriptural text writes it as *yáng* (佯), pronounced *sì yáng* (似羊); it means feigning weakness. "Yáng" (陽) does not have this meaning here.

Regarding the locust (*huángchóng*), the *Mao Shi* and the *Chongyu Shu* (Explanations of Insects and Fish) state that the *fùzhōng* is the locust; people today call the young of the locust "locust-children" (*zhōngzi*), and it is also called "silk-worm" (*cán*). Zhang Fei’s commentary on the *Jin Lü* states: "The small ones are called *zhōng*, the large ones are called locusts. *Zhōng* is pronounced as *wénxiōng* or *zhīróng*.

Saṃyukta Āgama, Volume One. Saṃyukta Āgama, Part One. Compiled by Xuanying. Volume Two. [The character] *huò* (獲) [in the phrase] *huò xiú* (獲泅) is correctly written as *xiū* (汓), which is a homophone for *sì yóu* (似由). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "floating on the surface of the water."

*Dàn* (not *dàn*): According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, *dàn* means "to be startled. The *Shījīng* says, "I have no *dàn* [fear] of the heat," and the commentary states that *dào* (sorrow) and *wèi* (fear) are also *jì* (aversion).

Volume 3, Part 3. First, the pronunciation is not provided for this character. Volume 4, Part 4. *Kǒngdá* (恐怛): *Dá* is pronounced *dūdá*. *Dá* means "to fear. The *Guǎngyǎ* says *dá* means "grief"; the *Fāngyán* says *dá* means "pain. Nowadays, it is sometimes written as the characters *jīngdàn* (驚憚).

If one encounters the archaic characters for *huá* (鏵), there are two forms: *mù huá* (㭉鏵). Today these are written as *dǐng* (釫) or *xián* (鋘), both pronounced with the rhyme *hú guā*. These refer to the blade of a plow; it is incorrect for the scriptural text to write this as *chàn* (鑱).
*Jiūjiū* (啾啾) is pronounced with the rhymes *zǐ* and *yóu*; according to the *Cāngjié piān*, it refers to a collective sound, while the *Shuōwén* says it is the sound of small children.

“Lüè-dǐ” (掠詆) is also written as “chì” (呧); in ancient texts, it is the same as “dǐ” (詆), with the phonetic reading *dū-lǐ*. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means to deceive or to scold and stop someone.

5. Fifth Fascicle. “Bá-bài” (拔茇): the first character is read as *bǔ-dá*. According to the *Shuōwén*, it refers to the root of a plant. According to the *Fānyá*, “bài” (茇) refers to the root of a tree; in the region of Dongqí, it is called “bài” or “dù” (杜). This is the character for the word.

*Luó* (𡬽): The *Fángmiào* (芳妙) [recension] of the *Guǎngyǎ* (廣雅) states that *luó* means "to pare" (*xiāo*). The *Cāngjiépiān* (蒼頡篇) says *luó* means "to cut" (*bì*). The *Shuōwén* (說文) says *luó* means "to peel" (*bō*). "To peel" refers to stripping away the skin; it also means to flake off or fall away.

Volume Six, Part Six: The character previously not transcribed with a phonetic. Volume Seven, Part Seven: The character 剬 (also written as 剸, same pronunciation *zhǎn*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "剬" means to cut or to sever. It is not the character 鉛 (lead) found in some editions of the sutra; that is incorrect.

*Wāng-zhài* (尪瘵) is also written as *wāng* (尫) in ancient texts; both share the pronunciation *wū huáng* (烏皇反). The character below has the pronunciation *zè jiè* (側界反). To be short and small is called *wāng*; *wāng* signifies weakness. *Zhài* means illness; in the region of Dongqi, it is called *mò* (瘼).

*Hūn-cuì* (the first character is pronounced *hūn*, with the *kūn* radical; the second is an ancient form of *cuì*; both forms are now written as *cuì* and are identical to *cí*). Pronounced *cí-rǎn*. It means confusion and disorder, as well as stupidity. *Cuì* means injury, sorrow, and illness.

*Piánxiān* (古文同 *piánxiān*)—the first character is pronounced as *púmian*, the second as *sūmian*. According to the *Guǎngyá*, *piánxiān* means to walk with a staggering gait or to move in a circling manner; it also refers to walking around. The reading in the canonical text as *xiānxiǎo* is not the correct form.

"Hóngxóng" (匈匈): "hóng" is pronounced as *xǔgōng* (許恭). It refers to the sound of a tumultuous clamor. In the *Hànshū*, it says, "the tumultuous sound of several thousand people," which is correct. The text of the scripture uses the radical for water (*shuǐ*) to write "xǒng" (洶), which is incorrect.

*Zǐ-xīn* (梓薪) is also written as *zǐ* (梓), with the phonetic transcription *tóng-zī-lǐ*. According to the *Zílín*, it refers to the *zǐqiū* (梓楸) tree; the reading "huà" (樺) in the canonical text is not the correct form.
*Zhāng-xīn* (樟薪)—the phonetic transcription being *yáng* (羊)—refers to the *yùzhāng* (豫樟) tree. It can be identified when seven years old and is an extremely large tree.
*Nán* (pinyin: nán; *ér yǎ*: *méi nán*; Guō Pǔ says it resembles the apricot but its fruit is sour, and its leaves resemble those of the *lèi*).
*Jīn zhí* (also written as *zhì*; pinyin: zhì; *ér yǎ*: *zhí wèi zhī chuán*; Guō Pǔ says it refers to the door-bolt that holds the lock).

"Dùnqiāng" (頓槍)—the "qiāng" is pronounced as "yáng" in reverse; "dùn" means to strike down or arrive, referring to the head striking the ground. In the scriptural text, it is written with the character "qiāng" (蹌) from the "zú" radical; however, according to the *Erya*, "qiāngqiāng" means to move. This [character] "qiāng" does not accord with the intended meaning of the scripture.

*Āo* (pronounced *āo* with the *gāo* rhyme): The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "the clamor of many mouths. The *Shijing* says, "The wailing cry is *āo-āo*," and the commentary states, "Not yet having found peace and settlement, they are in a state of *āo-āo* clamor.

*Diaoyan* is also written as *yanyan* or *yan*. These three characters share the same meaning. It is pronounced *yì* (rhyme of *jiàn*). Regarding the term *míng* (wailing), the *Shijing* says, "Wailing for the living is called *yàn*"; it also refers to wailing for one who has lost their kingdom.

In the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the character "wo" (沃) is transcribed as "wu guo fan" (烏梏反). The *Zilin* (字林) states that it refers to irrigation; "wo" means to water [the fields]. The *Guangya* (廣雅) states it means dampness, and also beauty.
*Han* (pronounced *hu* with the tone of *gan*): According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means resentment and hatred;

according to the *Zílín*, it means a state of unease. *Lù* (pronounced *lì* with the tone of *gù*): According to the *Máoshī Zhuàn*, it means gifts or offerings; that is, using objects to solicit or pay visits to one another.

"Tiǎn" (腆) is an elegant archaic term, written identically as "zhāo" (󲴚), with the phonetic component *tā* (他). According to the *Fāngyán* (方言), it means "respectful" (*chóng*). In the region of Dōngqí, it is called "tiǎn. The *Guǎngyá* states that "tiǎn" means "extreme," "beautiful," "generous," or "excellent."

*Xuántàn* (玄黮): "Xuán" is pronounced as *chìgǎn* (勅感反); it refers to a dark red-black color. According to the *Shēnglèi* (聲類), *tàn* (黮) means deep black; according to the *Shuōwén* (說文), it refers to the blackness of the mulberry fruit (*sāngrèn*). *Yàntàn* (黤黮) means lacking clarity and brightness.
*Jǐng wù*: "Wù" is pronounced *bù jué* (布覺); it is a personal name. This character does not exist in the received texts and must be an error;

it is likely a variant of the character *yàn* (饜). *Xū*: "Xū" is pronounced *mǎn biàn* (許玉反下靡辯反). According to the *Fāng yán*, in the states of Qí and Lǔ, "xū lì" (勗勵) is called "miǎn" (勉). "Miǎn" means to exhort or encourage. The *Xiǎo ěr yǎ* says: "To diligently apply effort to one's tasks."
*Buśèn* (補繕) means to repair; according to the *Guǎyá*, it means to trim and treat. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "to patch. *Bùchì* (不啻) is pronounced *shī* (豉);
it means "more than" or "in addition to. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "to explain. The reading in the canonical text as *chì* (翅), meaning "feather," is incorrect.

In the *Renben yusheng jing* (Sūtra on the Origin of Human Desire), Xuanying compiled [the following]: the character 躡 is written with the radical 㯢; its correct form is 󲫕, which is pronounced the same as 輒 (*zhé*). According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to the footstep beneath a mechanical device (*jī*). The lower part is pronounced *juàn* (*quán*); 㯢 means "to gather."

*Śīkṣānanda-ṣaḍ-abhimukha-praṇāma-sūtra* (The Sūtra on Śīkṣānanda’s Sixfold Prostrations), one fascicle; no characters have phonetic glosses. *Brahmacārin-Ava-bhāṣita-sūtra*, compiled by Xuanying. "Páng huáng" (彷徨): "páng" is pronounced as *pú guāng* (蒲光) and the following character as *hú guāng* (胡光); it means to wander aimlessly. *Běicāng* (埤蒼) states that it is synonymous with "bàng huáng" (傍徨) and "fǎng yáng" (彷徉).

The character "gui" (圭) is pronounced with the ancient rhyme *xie* (攜), and the following character "zhu" (銖) is pronounced with the rhyme *zhu* (珠). Sixty-four grains of millet constitute one *gui*; four *gui* are called one *cuo* (撮); twelve grains of millet weigh one *fen* (分); and twelve *fen* weigh one *zhu* (銖).

*Xiù* (酗) and *yíng* (醟), also written as *hùn* (𨠮), share the same pronunciation: the first character is pronounced *xǔ* (許具反) and the second is *yù* (禹命反). To treat wine as a source of calamity is called *xiù*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *xiù* means *yíng*. The *Tongshu Wén* states: "To be addicted to wine is called *xiù*; to be habitually intemperate with wine is called *yíng*."
*Gūlù* (孤寠): In the *Erya*, *lù* means "poverty"; according to the *Zishu*, *lù* means "emptiness," implying a state of poverty and emptiness lacking propriety.
*Jǐshī* (櫛梳) is also written as *jǐ* (楖), both pronounced *zètiè* (側怢反). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *jǐshī* is the general term for combing; it refers to the act of combing the hair.

*Wān* (彎): The radical is *hù* (戶). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as a bow. The *Zhouyi* states that the Yellow Emperor fashioned strings from wood to make bows and sharpened wood to make arrows, so as to awe the world.
*Féi huáng* (匪惶): Also written as *huáng* (遑), with the same pronunciation (*hù guāng*). It means leisure. According to the *Guangya*, it also means haste; that is, to be in a state of urgency.
*Ūyí* (謣夷) is a personal name; according to the characters, it is also written as *Ūhào* (󲠧號) or *Ūlǚ* (󲝌).

*Kūndì* (昆弟) is also written as *Tí* (罤), both pronounced with the rhyme *gúhún* (孤魂). According to the *Shuowen*, the people of Zhou called an elder brother *kūn*; the *Erya* states that *kūn* means "elder brother."

according to the *Erya*, this refers to the *shūfú* or *jīmù*. Guo Pu states that these are simply ducks (*yā*).

The archaic form of *yì* (stale) is written as *páo*, with the same pronunciation as *yú lì*. In the *Lúnyǔ*, regarding the passage "eating *yì* and [food] that has turned sour," Kǒng Ānguó states: "*Yì* and *è* refer to changes in smell and flavor. *È* is pronounced *wū jiè*.
*Jīchì* (羇縶) is also written as *jīchì* (𮩸), with the same pronunciation as *zhūlì* (猪立). According to the *Mao Shi Zhuan* (毛詩傳), it means "a tether" and also "to restrain.

It is composed of the radical *xiāo* (削) and is also written as *qiào* (鞘) or *shuò* (韒), both with the same pronunciation as *sīqiào* (私誚). The *Fāngyán* (方言) states that in Guānxī, a sword-sheath is called *bǐ* (鞞); it is used to store the blade of a knife or sword. The pronunciation of *bǐ* is *bǔmí* (補迷).

According to the *Guǎngyá*, "chēng" means to stop.

*The Scripture on the Original Nature of All Dharmas Being Without Sound*, one fascicle. Regarding "without sound" (*wúyīn*) in the right-hand column: thirty scriptures totaling fifty-five fascicles share the same phonetic readings as this fascicle.

In the first fascicle of the *Qishi jing* (Scripture on the Arising of the World): Regarding "lěi" (壘) in the first fascicle of the *Qishi jing*: Xuanying states that it is also written as "léi" (垒), with the same pronunciation as "lì" (力癸反). It refers to a military rampart; "lěi" also means "repeated" or "layered. The character below is also written as "dié" (堞), with the same pronunciation as "tújié" (徒頰反). According to dictionaries, it refers to a parapet (*nǚqiáng*).

Jambudvīpa is sometimes called Yamfou Zhou (剡浮洲), sometimes Yanfou Zhou (譫浮洲), and sometimes Zhanbu Zhou (贍部洲). "Yamfou" is named after the tree; "ti" (提) is an abbreviation. One should say "Tibipuo" (提鞞波), which translates as "continent" (zhou). "Yan" (譫) has the phonetic value of zhi-han-fan; the *Pīcāng* dictionary frequently uses this character to mean "much."

Uttarakuru is also called Uttara-kuru, or Uttara-kaurava; the correct term is Uttara-kauṛu. This is translated as "Superior Action" (Gāoshàngzuò), meaning that it is superior to other regions. It is also called "Victorious Kuru" (Shèngjiūlóu); "Kuru" means "action" and is also used to denote a "clan" (gotra).

Pūrvavideha is sometimes called Pūyudai, sometimes Pūrvavideha, and sometimes Purvaviheka; "Purvavi" translates as "front," while "viheka" translates as "separated from the body. Alternatively, it is said that "Pu" is combined with "Videha," or that "Videha" is a corruption [of the original term].

Gōdānīya is also called Kuyāni, Goyāni, or Gōyani; these are all phonetic corruptions. "Gō" (瞿) is translated as "ox" (牛); "dānīya" (陀尼) means "taking and giving" (取與), because there are many oxen there and they use oxen for trade, just as people here use money, silk, and so forth. Alternatively, it is said that there are stone oxen there.
"Róuqí (薔薇)" refers to the double-petaled flower [of the rose].
"Lín (淋)," with the phonetic "líng" (力今反), is the same as the archaic form "lín" (古文臨). According to the *Sāncāng*, it means the dripping of water.

*Jiāng* (礓石): Pronounced *jiāng* (居良反). Its shape resembles ginger (*jiāng*). The character is composed of the "stone" radical; in the *Jīngwén*, it is written as *jiāng* (壃) with the "earth" radical, but this is not the correct form.
*Pānlǎn* (攀擥): Also written as *pānlǎn* (㩜攬); these two forms are identical. Pronounced *lǎngǎn* (力敢反). The *Shuōwén* states: "To grasp and hold; to take hold of."
*Ñok*: To seize; it is also written as *nǚ* (same pronunciation). "To seize" (*ñok*) means to grasp or to take. According to the *Shuowen*, *ñok* means to press down.
2. Second Fascicle. Second [Section]. The name of a horse is *Balahā*; this is translated as "Long-haired."

*Xié'áo* (蟹螯): The character *xié* has the phonetic reading *gāo* (five tones reversed). A crab has two claws (*áo*) and eight legs; the character is derived from the radical "insect" (*chóng*). In the canonical text, it is written as *áó* (鼇), which refers to a giant tortoise.
*Stūpa*: This is translated as "Great Accumulation. The older term "tǎ" (塔) is a corruption and abbreviation.

3. Third Fascicle. "Sēngsǒng" (森竦): "Sēn" (森) is the appearance of many tall trees; the lower character is the same as the ancient form of "xīng" (慫), pronounced *xiānyǒng* (先勇反); "sǒng" (竦) means to stand upright.

The character *yǎn* (黫), also written as *yǎn* (𤚕) with the same phonetic *jiān* (間), refers to a black sheep according to dictionaries; it is incorrect for the scriptural text to use the character *mù* (𤚕) derived from "ox" (*niú*).

The characters *mào* (󰨭) and *mò* (󱨪) have the phonetic *mò* (莫勒反); according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *mào* (󰨭) means "to precede," similar to how *qīng* (輕) and *zhí* (直) mean to advance directly; nowadays these are all written as *mào* (冒).

*Jiè* (the first character is pronounced with the *wǔ* and *jiā* finals; the second is pronounced with the *zhù* and *jiā* finals) means for a dog to bare its teeth. The text of the scripture writes it as *yà*, meaning to glare with wide-open eyes.

*Tiěfū* (the first character is pronounced with the *fāng* and *yú* finals): according to the *Shuowen*, *fū* refers to a tool for chopping fodder; *fū* is also a wooden block for sharpening tools, and it is also a horizontal axe.
Pāng (滂): The phonetic transcription is *pǔ bàng* (普傍). According to the *Sāncāng*, it means "pángtuó" (滂沱), which describes the appearance of water flowing in great abundance.
Dì (顫): Also written as *zhàn* (𫏱) with the same pronunciation. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "stubborn and trembling. According to the *Sāncāng*, it means "the head is not upright."
