10. Fascicle Ten. *Kāgā* (the "gā" is pronounced as *fǎng-ěr*; this is the name for *huòxiāng*, with *huò* pronounced as *hū-guō*).

*Qishi yinben jing*, Fascicle One. Compiled by Huìlín. Fascicle One. *Bèi* (the "bèi" is pronounced as *pó-mèi*); it refers to categories in Fángyóng’s *Tàixuán jīng*. The *Bīcāng* states it means "comparison. The *Shuowén* says that one hundred chariots constitute one *bèi*, composed of the radical "chariot" (*chē*) and the phonetic "Péi" abbreviated. The scriptural text uses "běi" to form "bèi," which is a vulgar character and not the correct form.
*Tíng* (挺): Pronounced *tíng* (庭). The *Shuowen* states it means "to stand upright. It is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "tíng" (廷), where *tíng* is pronounced *tíng* (亭).

*Jí* (級): Pronounced *jí* (岌). Gu Yewang’s *Yupian* states that "jì" (級) refers to the gradations of a flight of stairs. The *Shuowen* states it means "succession. It is composed of the radical "silk" (系) and the phonetic "mì" (覓).

The term *lánshǔn* (欄楯) is composed of "lán" (upper radical: 艸, lower phonetic: 順), which according to the *Shuowen Jiezi* means a railing (*lán*). A vertical bar is called a *lán*, while a horizontal bar is called a *shǔn*. The spaces between the bars are called *língzǐ* (櫺子); in common parlance, these are known as *gōulán* (鈎欄). Both characters for *lánshǔn* are phono-semantic compounds with the radical 木. The character *shǔn* (盾) consists of the radical 厂, the element 十, and the element 目.

*Lěi* (垒): On the top of the ramparts; "lì" (力) and "guǐ" (鬼) are the phonetic components. Zheng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states: "Lěi means layered walls; it refers to a military fortification. The *Guǎngyá* says it means "repeated. The *Shuowén* defines it as "a moat," formed from the radical "earth" (*tǔ*) and the phonetic "lěi" (*lěi*), being a pictographic character. Below, *tián* (恬) and *xié* (協) are the phonetics. Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states: "Dìe refers to the small parapets on top of a city wall, called 'dié'. The *Shuowén* defines it as "the small defensive walls on top of a city," formed from the radical "earth" (*tǔ*) and the phonetic "yè" (*yè*), where "yè" is pronounced as "yánjiē" (塩接).

In the characters *lóu* (樓) and *lǔ* (櫓): *lóu* is pronounced with the final *-ǎn* (as in *lu-hou*), and *lǔ* with the final *-dǔ* (as in *lu-du*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "a *lóu* is a multi-storied building; a *lǔ* is a large shield. The *Kaosheng* states that both are used for defensive combat atop city walls. Both characters are compounds of form and sound (*xing-sheng*) radicals. The character *lù* (魯) is composed of the radicals "fish" (*yú*) and "white" (*bái*); the common variant using "sun" (*yuè*) is incorrect.

Regarding the classification of the terraces on Mount Sumeru, the text states that there are three tiers—broad at the bottom and narrow at the top—and its description of the *yojana* measurements differs from the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*. A verse in the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Extending outward by sixteen thousand, eight thousand, four thousand, and two thousand [yojanas] respectively; from bottom to top, these decrease by half. This sūtra, however, says the lower terrace is sixty, the middle forty, and the upper twenty *yojanas*. Master Lin’s opinion was that he suspected this sūtra was describing the dimensions of the city walls rather than the extent of the ground itself.

The character for *garuḍa* (金翅鳥) is formed with "drum" (*gu*) as a radical and "branch" (*zhi*) as a phonetic component; it is also written as "wing" (*yu*) with "zhì" as a phonetic, or as *jī* with "shì" as a phonetic, which is likewise correct. The sutras state that the *garuḍa* is sometimes called the "Great Gullet Bird" (*dà shù niǎo*). In Sanskrit, it is named *garuḍa*, or *garuḍa*, or designated as the "Dragon-Enemy" (*nāga-dveṣin*); these names are established based on its form and its activities. Among the eight classes of spirits and deities, it constitutes one such class. It possesses great supernormal power and constantly feeds upon various dragons. Dragons possess the four modes of birth—egg, womb, moisture, and transformation—and this bird is likewise so. Within these categories, there are differences in strength, as fully described in the sutra texts. Here, I shall merely synthesize its various names, phonetic transcriptions, and characters.

*Kuṭaśalmali* (the first syllable pronounced as *ku-śa*, or alternatively as *kuṭa-śalmali*) is the name of a great tree; it is the dwelling place of these garuḍas, who take up their residence here to seize and eat nāgas. They dwell upon the four sides of this tree according to their respective species.
*Saughandhika* (上桑到反, pronounced *sāngdào*)—the Sanskrit name for a celestial flower; this flower is utterly non-existent in the human realm.
*Āmrapātaka* (上暗含反, pronounced *ànhán*)—also the name of a celestial fruit; it exists in Western countries but is not found in this land.

Vibhītaka (the first character pronounced with the *bi-mí* rhyme and the second with the *xīng-xí* rhyme) is the name of a fruit; some say it is *vīraka*, which belongs to the same category as *harītakī*. All of these originate from foreign lands.
Ubulin is the same as Ubulin; it is a fruit of a tree that resembles a wood-apple (*kapittha*) but is much larger and extremely fragrant. This very country also possesses it.
Regarding "Nailin" (柰林)—the character "nai" (柰) being pronounced *nu* with a retroflex *-d*—it is incorrect for the text to further add the "wood" radical (*mu*) to make it "Nailin" (㮏).

Qiānwéi (薔薇): the first character is pronounced jiàngyáng (匠陽) and the second wèiféi (味肥). It refers to flowers and trees of five colors; it exists among humans wherever they dwell. The text of the scripture writes it as qiāng (薔), which does not form a valid character.

*Qīnglíng* (清泠): The second character is pronounced *dīng* (with the retroflex *r* initial). The *Cāngjié piān* states that *líng* denotes the appearance of water being clear and transparent; it is a compound character formed from a semantic and a phonetic element.

*Tíngān* (甘甜): The second character is pronounced *yán* (with the palatal *t* initial). The *Bóyá* states that *tián* is also *gān* (sweet); it is sometimes written as *diàn*, which is a vulgar character.

The term "zhuān" (brick) refers to the crude material formed by piling up earth and firing it; it is a variant of the ancient term for "fire-baked earthenware. The *Pīcāng* states that "lǔ-zhuān" means a brick. Regarding the orthography: the standard form consists of the radical "wǎ" (tile) with the phonetic "zhuān"; "lǔ" is an archaic character. The form "zhuān" found in the scriptures, which uses the radical "tǔ" (earth), is a vulgar character.
"Jīnxié" (金脇): the "xié" is pronounced *xiè* (as in *xiè*). It is composed of "flesh" (肉) and "hé" (劦), where "hé" is pronounced *xiè* and consists of "three powers" (三力).

"Jīntián" (金窴): the lower character "tián" is pronounced *tián*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "tián" means "to block" (塞); it is composed of "cave" (穴) and "zhēn" (眞), with "zhēn" also serving as the phonetic component. In the scriptural text, it is written with "earth" (土) as "tián" (填), pronounced *zhēn*; although this is commonly used, it is an error.

*Jiāngshí* (礓石): "Jiāng" is pronounced *liáng* (良) with a reversed final. The *Cāngjié* states that *jiānglì* refers to gravelly stones; it takes the character *jiāng* (畺) as its phonetic. The version in the sutra written as *jiāng* (薑) is incorrect.

*Písuài* (皮𥢶): Below, "suài" is pronounced *kǔ wài* (苦外). The *Cāngjiépiān* states that *suài* refers to chaff (*kāng*). The *Shuōwén* takes the character *huì* (會) as its phonetic. The textual version in the sutra written as *kǎo* (糩) with the radical for rice is incorrect.

The character 捋 (luǒ) [is read as] gōu (gōu) with the *qiú* (候) tone. The commentary on the character states: "捋 means to take the milk from oxen or sheep; it is composed of 手 (hand) and is phoneticized by a simplified form of 彀 (gòu). Gòu has the same pronunciation as above. Alternatively, some write it as 搋 (from 羊) or 𤛓 (from 牛), but these are all errors and not correct. Using 手 (hand) is the standard form. The text of the Classics uses 搆 (gòu), which is not the original character. Below [the entry for 捋], luán (luán) with the guā (kuò) tone is given. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry) says: "捋 means to take [milk]. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that 捋 is pronounced lù (lù) with the hé (hé) tone; it is composed of 手 (hand) and is phoneticized by 寽 (lüè). It is pronounced hū (hū).”

Regarding the character for *zì* (牸): the *Shìyào* (釋要) states that any female ox or cow is called *zì*. The *Shuowén* omits this character, but the *Zìjìng* (字鏡) states it means "a female ox" (*pǐn niú*) and is a compound character formed from both semantic and phonetic components.

*Zī* (upper radical *zǐ*, private [radical] *sī*; according to the *Zìshū*, it means "moisture" or "abundance"; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "to increase," formed with the phonetic *zī* and the radical *shuǐ*). Lower radical: *nǚ* (lóng) *fǎn*. The *Cāngjiépiān* says it means "thick and rich. According to the *Kǎoshēng*, it refers to the thickness of liquid. The *Shuowen* says it means "abundant dew," formed with the phonetic *nóng* and the radical *shuǐ*; alternatively, it is written with the radical *yù*, pronounced *zhèn*, with the same meaning.
*Luàn* (pronounced *luò gǎn*): The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means to grasp or seize; it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shou*) and the phonetic element "lǎn" (abbreviated).

It may also be written with the radical "hand" as *lǎn*, which is likewise correct. *Nièqǔ* (top character pronounced *nǚ è*): The *Shenglei* states it means to seize; the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as pressing down, composed of the radical "hand" and the phonetic element "ruò. The previous commentary on the *Yinyi* gives the pronunciation *nǚ gé*, which is likely merely a local dialectal pronunciation and not the standard reading.

Scroll Two, Part Two: The Sūtra on the Causes and Origins of the World, Scroll Two. Uttarakuru (the Chinese transcription *yù duō luó jiū zhēn*—*zhēn* being pronounced with the initial *wēi* and the final *lǜ* according to the Sanskrit; it is the name for the Northern Continent). Alternatively, it is called Northern Uttarakuru. It lies within the great ocean to the north of Mount Sumeru, and its shape is square. Among the four oceans, this is one of them.

*Shí*: upper radical *dīng*, retroflex *lì* (反); the *Kǎo Shēng* states that *shí* refers to "reality" (*shí*) or "the principal" (*zhǔ*). In vulgar usage, it is sometimes written as *zuò*. Lower radical *mó*, retroflex *bó*; the *Yùn Yīng* states it means "the sun is setting. The *Shuōwén* also says: "The character *yuè* (日) plus *míng* (冥). *Yuè* is [the character] inside *mǎng* (茻), which is a repetition of *cǎo* (草). *Jǐng* (井) is also a phonetic; *jǐng* is pronounced *mǎng*. *Zhì*: upper radical *dīng*, retroflex *lì*; the *Kǎo Shēng* states that *zhì* refers to "the real" (*shí*) or "the master" (*zhǔ*). In vulgar usage, it is sometimes written as *zuò*. Lower radical *mó*, retroflex *bó*; the *Yùn Yīng* states it means "the sun is dark" (*rì míng*). The *Shuōwén* also says: "The character *yuè* (曰) plus *míng* (冥). *Yuè* is [the character] within *mǎng* (茻), which is a duplication of *cǎo* (草), forming *mǎng*. *Jǐng* (井) is also a phonetic; *jǐng* is pronounced *mǎng*.

*Kāṅ-suǒ* (穅𥢶): the upper character is read as *kě gāng* (可岡); according to the *Erya*, it refers to the husk of rice. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radicals for "grain" (*huo*) and "prosperity" (*kāng*), with the lower part being *kǔ wài* (苦外). This has already been explained previously in the first fascicle of this scripture.

Regarding the term *gēng* (羹臛): the first character is pronounced with the initial *gé* (革) and the final *xíng* (行) [as in *gēng*]; the *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲) glosses it as *yuè* (越). It refers to meat or vegetables seasoned with the five flavors, which is called *gēng*. The commentary of Kǒng (孔安國) on the *Shàngshū* states: "Soup (*gēng*) requires salt and vinegar to harmonize it. The commentary of Wáng (王逸) on the *Chǔcí* states: "That which contains vegetables is called *gēng*, and it may be thick; it is made by finely slicing either meat or bamboo shoots. The character is composed of the radical "meat" (肉) and the phonetic element "huò" (霍) abbreviated; the pronunciation of "huò" is *huāngguō* (荒郭). The received text, which writes it with "rain" (雨) above and "zhuī" (隹) below as *hào* (臛), is incorrect.

*Po-sha-tuo* (Upoṣadha) is a transliteration of the Sanskrit; in the scriptures it is called *zhāi* (fasting), and in the Tang language it is called *chángjìng* (prolonged purification). This refers to assembling the community to confess the offenses committed, thereby increasing the white dharmas and purifying one's karma; hence it is named "prolonged purification."

The character *yí* (嶷) is pronounced with the initial *lì* (力) and the final *fǎn* (反). The commentary on the character states that "yí" refers to the appearance of a mountain being lofty and prominent. The phonetic component *lì* (力) has the sound *zhù* (助) and the final *fǎn* (反); it is composed of the radical *shān* (山) and the phonetic *zhuī* (𣅳). The character *zhuī* (𣅳) has the sound *zé* (側) and the final *zhuī* (𣅳); it is composed of the radical *yuè* (曰) and the six strokes [of the number six], its pronunciation being the same as above.
"Do not pound white cotton cloth" (*bó* [páo]—the first character is pronounced *páo*, the second is pronounced *zōng*;

the script in the sutra text is written as *bō*, which is incorrect; this is the correct orthography). Regarding *pī* (髬) and *zōng* (𩮀): the first is pronounced *pī*; the *Běicāng* states that *pī* refers to the appearance of one running with disheveled hair. The second is pronounced *zōng*; the sutra follows the *cōng* (忩) radical, which is a vulgar form. The *Kǎoshēng* states it means "a horse's mane. Both characters for *pī* and *zōng* in the sutra follow the *biāo* (髟) radical, which is pronounced *bìyáo*.

*Shūyán* (姝妍): The upper character *shū* (姝) is pronounced with the initial *chāng* and the final *zhū*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Mao Shi* states that *shū* refers to beautiful countenance. The *Fāngyán* says that in the regions of Zhao and Wei, the term for "beautiful" is *shū*. The *Shuowén* defines it as "beautiful," composed of the radical *nǚ* (woman) and the phonetic *zhū*; it is pronounced with the final *jiān*. *Yán* (妍): According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "lovely. The *Shuowén* defines it as "cunning" (*zhì*), composed of the radical *nǚ* and the phonetic *jiān*; the sound *jiān* is pronounced like *qiān*, being formed by two *gān* (stems) placed side by side.

The character for *báng* (旁) is pronounced with the *xié* rhyme group (諧芥反). The *Shuowen* states: "The crab has two *jī* (𩪋); *jī* refers to its 'hands. It moves sideways on eight legs; it finds no shelter except in the burrows of snakes (*shé*) and *shàn*. It is formed from the radical 'insect' (*chóng*) and the phonetic component 'jiě' (*jiě*). The pronunciation of *jī* is *áo*, and the pronunciation of *shàn* is *shàn*; it refers to a snake.

*Cuō* (pronounced *cuō*, with the *cāng* and *lè* finals reversed): The *Zìlín* states that it means "to grasp. It refers to what Confucius said in the *Lǐjì*: "Now the great earth is but a handful (*yī cuō tǔ*) of soil. It is also pronounced *zōng* or *luō*, and is interchangeable. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is a term for four *guī* (sacrificial jade tablets). It is written with the radical 手 (hand) and the phonetic 最; the pronunciation of 最 is *zǐ nèi*. It refers to grasping with three fingers.

*Yù* (御): Pronounced *yú jù* (魚據). Gu Yewang says it refers to one who directs and commands the horse. The *Shuowen* states it is composed of the radical "horse" (*mǎ*) and the phonetic "you" (*yòu*).

*Chí* (持): Pronounced *pí mèi* (悲媚) in the lower part. The *Mao Shi* says, "Holding the reins as if they were silk cords. The *Shuowen* further states that *shèng* (軎) refers to the iron at the head of the chariot axle; it is a pictographic character. The scriptural text uses *wáng* (亡) instead of *shèng* (軎), which is a vulgar usage and not the correct form. *Zǔ* (組): Pronounced *zǔ* (祖). The *Mao Shi* says, "Holding the reins as if they were silk cords. Gu Yewang says it is the means by which one restrains the horses in the center of the shafts. The *Shuowen* says it is the iron at the head of the chariot axle; it is a pictographic character. The scriptural text uses *wáng* (亡) instead of *shèng* (軎), which is a vulgar usage and not the correct form. *Zǔ* (組) is pronounced *zǔ* (祖).

Regarding *guanzhu* (觀矚): the phonetic analysis (*kaosheng*) states that it means "to gaze intently. That which is the convergence of many eyes is called *zhu*. the *Fengsu Tong* states that *zhu* means "void" (*xu*) and refers to the phonetic analysis of abandoned cities and towns. According to the *Zhouli*, four villages constitute a *qiu*, or what is also called a *zhu*. The *Guangya* states that *zhu* means "dwelling. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* says it is land that has been destroyed and left without descendants. The *Yupian* identifies it as the name for a large mound; *zhu* is the base of a mountain, composed of the radical "earth" (*tu*) and the phonetic "xu" (*xu*).

The character for *cè* (廁) is pronounced with the initial *chǐ* (䇭, *chū shī*) and the final *zì* (胾, *zì*). Its phonetic component is *kǎo* (考). *Cè* refers to a latrine (*cìng*) or a side area; it also implies "mixed" or "collected. The *Jíxùn* (集訓) states that *cìng* is a place where excrement is kept. The character for *hùn* (渾) below is pronounced with the initial *kùn* (困). *Hùn* is also a latrine; the *Jíxùn* states it is where pigs dwell. It is a pictographic character (*xiàngxíng zì*). In the scriptures, it is written as *pèn* (溷) with the water radical; this is incorrect. The pronunciation of *chǐ* (䇭) is *chū shī*, and the pronunciation of *zì* (胾) is *diàn shǐ*.

*Lián-méng* (陌彭反). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states that *méng* refers to the ridgepole of a roof. The *Shuowen Jiezi* provides an interpretation identical to that of the *Zuǒzhuan*: it is composed of the radical 瓦 (*wǎ*) and the phonetic component 夢省 (*mèng*).

"Milk-moment" (nǔqǐng): "xià" is pronounced as *yǐng* (with a retroflex final). The Classics state, "one stroke of cow's milk," meaning the extreme brevity of time; it refers to the interval of a single breath. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "head" (頁) with "bi" (匕) as the phonetic.

*Ūi* (壤): Upper character, *niǎo gù* in reverse; the *Shuowen* defines it as "irrigating," following the water radical with the phonetic *yǎo*. *Yǎo* has the pronunciation *yāng jiāo*. The text reads *yāo*, which is a vulgar character. Lower character, *rǎng*: *shuōwén* gives *róu zhǎng*; Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* says that soil without clods is called *huài*. The *Shuowen* defines it as "soft earth," following the earth radical with the phonetic *xiāng*.

*Kṣauma* (㲲衣): The character *zhì* (庭叶反) refers to a cloth made from the grass-like flowers of Western countries; the text also uses *dié* (疊), which is equally acceptable. *Ning* (釘之): The character *dīng* (丁逕反). *Stūpa* (蘇偷婆):

A Sanskrit term for which the ancient translation was crude and not excellent; the correct Sanskrit pronunciation is *sūtra-pa* (窣覩波), translated as "square mound" (方墳). In the Tang period, it was called a "brick pagoda" (塼塔); this is the reliquary stupa for the remains of a deceased Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*).

"Zàn" (暫) means for a short time; the *Xunyun* states it means "not long. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of "rì" (日) and "zhǎn" (斬) as phonetic components, or sometimes written with "zú" (足) as the radical.

"Zhuān" (甎) is pronounced "chuǎn" (川) with a retroflex initial; according to the *Shuowen*, it means a brick (*āozhuān*), composed of "wǎ" (瓦) and "zhuān" (專) as phonetic components. The form "zhuān" (塼) found in the sutra texts uses the earth radical and is a vulgar character, not the correct one.

*Avīci* is a Sanskrit term; in the Tang language it is translated as "Without Respite" (*wú xiūxí*). It is also called the *Avīci Hell*, which refers to the Great Avīci Hell (*mòdì dìyù*). Because it is situated beneath the great ocean and the great earth, it is named a "hell" (*dìyù*).

Regarding the character 疊 (dié): the *Kǎoshēng* states that "dié" means "repeated" (*chóng*). According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of three [日] and is pronounced "dié"; it has been newly revised to have three [田] below, with [冝] as a semantic component and [吾] as a phonetic component, read as *wú huì fǎn*. Regarding the character 磑 (ài): the *Shuowén* defines it as a millstone, composed of [石] with [豈] as a phonetic component. In antiquity, Lú Bān was the first to create the millstone; "䃺" is pronounced *mò gè fǎn*. The *Kǎoshēng* states that it is a tool for grinding wheat.
*Dāo* (刀) and *tiè* (鍱)—the latter being pronounced *jié* (閻接反)—refer to iron plates (*tiè*). This is a word formed by combining a semantic component (*xíng*) and a phonetic component (*shēng*).

*Tiè* (鐵)—pronounced *zhǎo yāo niè* (爪夭涅反)—is defined in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as "black metal" (*hēijīn*). It is composed of the radical *jīn* (金) with the phonetic *jié* (截), which is pronounced *dú jié* (徒結反). This is the correct orthography (*zhèngtǐzì*). The *tiè* (鐵) appearing in the current sutra text, derived from *jié* (截), is a vulgar character (*súzì*). The character below, *zhuāng* (莊)—pronounced *jiào* (挍反)—is a pictographic character (*xiàngxíngzì*).

"Xiān-cháng" (纖長) [the first character is pronounced with the "yán" rhyme]. The *Guǎngyá* states that "xiān" means minute. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* says it means fine. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* explains that the character is composed of "xì" (系) and "xiān" (韱) as its phonetic component; the character "qiān" (籤) is derived from "xuàn" (䇝), which is pronounced "jiān" (尖). The lower part, "zhí-liáng" (直良), is explained in the *Shuowén* as meaning long-lasting. It is composed of "wù" (兀), "huà" (化), and "dào-wáng" (倒亡). "Wù" means high and remote; because things change through long duration, it includes "huà. *Fēngmáng*: The upper character is pronounced *fēng* (as in "peak") and the lower is pronounced *wángdāo*. It resembles a blade with a grass-like tip; therefore, it is so named. *Nǎopò*:

The upper character is pronounced *zhuāngguō* (as found in dictionaries). It means to split or break apart. The old pronunciation was *jūbì* or *jiǔfù*; however, as these were likely incorrect, they have been revised to this current pronunciation. *Cāo*: Pronounced *zhuāngjiāo*.

"Bì" (to split apart): pronounced *bèng* (as in *mài*, "barley"). In the *Zìshū*, it means to split an object with the hand. The *Kǎoshēng* says it means to tear with the hand. The *Shuōwén* writes it as *pī* (擗), derived from the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "abbreviated *bó*" (*bǐng*).

*Zuàn* (pronounced *guān fǎn kǎo shēng*): "To bore. The *Jíxùn* states it means an iron tool for piercing objects; it is a compound character consisting of a semantic and a phonetic component. *Zhī suǐ* (fat and marrow):

the upper character is pronounced *zhī*, the lower is pronounced *suī* (*suì*). The *Jíxùn* states it refers to the fat within the bones; it is formed from the radical "bone" (*gǔ*) with the phonetic "follow" (*suí*).

Regarding "Five Forks" (Wǔchā): the upper character is *zhé* (pronounced *cè* with the *jiā* tone), meaning an iron fork; the lower character is *cháo* (pronounced *gé*), and according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means to split open or to stretch apart. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means to punish (*gū*), composed of the radical "axe" (*jié*) and the phonetic "stone" (*shí*). The character *jié* is pronounced *jié*. The scripture states that "Five Forks" is the name of a hell; because sinners' bodies are divided and torn apart by these iron forks, it is called the Hell of Five Forks.

The character 㯷 (zhù) is pronounced with an initial *páng* (反) and a final *kǎo* (考). The *Shēngyùn* states that it means to strike with the hand and throw something to the ground. The *Yùnquán* states it means to scoop up with the hands. It may also be pronounced with an initial *pǔ* (普) and a final *lù* (祿), which is likewise acceptable; this is the common usage today. It may be abbreviated as 僕 (pú). The character 著 (zháo) has an initial *cháng* (長) and a final *lüè* (略). Those who follow the grass radical below it are following a vulgar form; it is not correct to write it with two dots.

"Tièqián" (iron vice). "Xiàn" (儉) is pronounced as "yán" (嚴) in reverse. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "an iron vice" (*jiànxù*). It is composed of the radical "metal" (金) with the phonetic "zhàn" (占). The character "qián" (鉗) found in the classics, written with "gān" (甘), is not its correct form; this [present form] is the correct shape according to both ancient and modern standards.

The character 腭 (yè) is pronounced with the initial *go* (five, reversed) and the final *kao* (sound). It refers to the palate and gums. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical 肉 (flesh/meat) and the phonetic 咢 (é). The character 咢 is composed of 吅 (xuān) and 屰 (nì). 吅 is pronounced xuān; 齗 (yín) is pronounced yín. [This is the character.]

Scroll Three, Volume III, *Qishi yinben jing* (Sūtra on the Causes and Origins of the World). Scroll Three. "Ju" (掬) [pronounced with the initial *gong* and the final *fan*]: to scoop up; to grasp with the hand turned downward. The *Shuowen jiezi* states: "In the hand, it is called *ju*. It is composed of *bao* (the phonetic, pronounced *pao*) and *mi* (rice), forming a compound character. It is correctly written as *ju* alone; the form *ju* (with the radical for "hand") found in this scripture is a vulgar character, though it is used interchangeably.

"Pea" (wèi-dòu) refers to a type of bean; in the *Shuowen jiezi*, it is written as 𧯡, an ancient character composed of "bean" (dòu) as the radical and "yuǎn" as the phonetic. "Chàn" (zhān-cì): the first character is pronounced zhì-xián (仕銜反).

The *Shuowen* states that "chàn" means to cut off or to prick with a needle; one interpretation also says it means to plunder or to strike. It is composed of "knife" (dāo) as the radical and "zhuān" (毚) as the phonetic; the second character is pronounced qīng-yì (清亦反). The *Shuowen* states that "cì" means to wound by piercing. It is composed of "knife" (dāo) as the radical and "shù" (束) as the phonetic. "Piāo" (剽) is pronounced pǐ-miào (匹妙反). "Zhāo" (釗) is pronounced zhī-yáo (之遙反).

*Lián-lián* (臠臠). [The character] *lián* is pronounced with the *qièyùn* "luán" (攣) as its phonetic. Ye Wang states that it refers to small pieces of sliced meat. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "meat" (*ròu*) and the phonetic "luán" (䜌); the pronunciation of "luán" is *lìfǔ* (力尃反). This is the correct orthography.

*Xiǎo* (齩): the upper character is pronounced *jiǎo* (絞). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "to gnaw bone," composed of the radical for "teeth" (*chí*) and the phonetic *jiāo*. It is also written as *xiǎo* (󲵊) or *chuí* (䶧). *Niè* (齧): the pronunciation is *yán* (研) and *jié* (結); this is the correct form.

*Jièchǐ* (齜): The first character is pronounced *yá* (崖) and the second is pronounced *xiè* (邂). The *Kǎoshēng* states it means "opening the mouth and gnashing the teeth. The *Běicāng* states it is the sound of dogs fighting. The *Shuōwén* states it is the clashing of teeth. One interpretation says it means "opening the mouth to show the teeth. Both characters are composed of the radical 齒 (teeth) and the phonetic 崖 (yá). The phonetic for 邂 (xiè) is pronounced *xiàjiè* (下介).

Regarding "𠯗嗽" (zà sòu): the upper character is pronounced *zǐ* (with the *là* rhyme); the *Yùnlüè* states that "𠯗" means entering the mouth. The *Shuowén* writes it as "𠾱," while the vernacular form is "唼. The lower character is pronounced *sè* (with the *zhuō* rhyme); the *Yùnlüè* states that "嗽" means the mouth opening and closing. It is correctly written as "嗽"; the version in the sutra as "𠲿" is incorrect.

*Zhǔjīn* (斲斤): The first character, *zhǔ*, is pronounced *zhéjiǎo* (陟角反). The *Shuowen* states it means "to hew" (*qiáo* [斫]), composed of the radical *jīn* (斤) and the phonetic *chē* (𠁁). The version in the sutra uses *chèn* (𣃆), which is a vulgar character.
*Zhèngjué* (󱯾󲟐): The upper character is the correct form of *jué* (脚); the lower character is pronounced *tulà* (徒臘反). The original version of the sutra uses *tà* (蹹), which is a vulgar character.

The character above is pronounced *bó* (with the radical *méng* as a phonetic); the *Kǎo Shēng* states it means "to stroke" (*tán*). According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) with "pīn" as the phonetic; the character below is pronounced *tángluò*. The pronunciation of *tán* is *dá dān*.

The character for "iron jar" (*tiěhú*) has the phonetic *jiǎng*; the *Shuōwén* states that a *húng* is like a *dài* (a large jar) with a long neck, holding ten *shēng*, and is composed of the radical "tile" (*wǎ*) with "gōng" as the phonetic.
Tiè-ào (Iron Griddle): *áo* is pronounced as *gào-fǎn*.
Volume 4, Part 4. *xiāng-jī* (Mutually Stirring): pronounced as *jīng-lì-fǎn*. The *Shuowen* says it means "to hasten," following the radical for water (*shui*) and the phonetic *jiǎo*.

*ér-zhù* (But to Fall): pronounced as *péng-běi-fǎn*. Guō’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "To fall forward is to lie face down. Zhèng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "To fall" (*pó*) also refers to a prostrate corpse. The *Shuowen* [lists] the character from the radical for feet (*zu*) with the phonetic *pò*; *pò* is pronounced as *tǔ-kǒu-fǎn*.

The characters for *póng-pò* (摓𡋯) have the phonetic components *pú* (僕) and *méng* (蒙) in the upper radicals and *pén* (盆) and *mù* (沒) in the lower radicals respectively. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that they describe the appearance of rising wind and dust. They are also written as *cōng-bó* (漨浡), which describes the appearance of misty vapors over water. The versions of the scripture that write them as *fēn-pǒ* (熢㶿) with the radical for fire are vulgar forms.

*Qiùtà* (蹴蹋): The first character is pronounced *qiū* with the second tone, and the second is *tán* with the fourth tone; the *Jīng* (經) reads it as *tà* (蹹), which is a vernacular usage. *Jiānhuá* (姦猾):

The first character is pronounced *jiǎn* with the first tone, and the second is *huán* with the fourth tone; the *Zìshū* (字書) states that "huá" means "clever and sly," while the *Shuowén* (說文) explains it as being composed of the radical "dog" (*quán*) and the phonetic "gǔ" (*gǔshēng*).

Regarding "pào-mò" (泡沫): "pào" (泡) is pronounced with the upper radical as "bāo" (包) and the lower phonetic as "mò" (末). The *Kǎośēng* (考聲) states that "pào" refers to bubbles floating on water, while "mò" refers to foam floating on water. In the standard characters of both ancient and modern times, both characters take "water" (水) as their radical; "bāo" (包) and "mò" (末) are both the correct phonetic components.
*Mài yì* (麥䴬): The *Wenzí jílüè* (Textual Compendium) states this refers to the husk of wheat (*mài pí*). The *Shuowén* says it is composed of the radical "wheat" (*mài*) with "yì" as the phonetic.

*Nǎn zhòu* (赧皺): The upper character is pronounced *níng jiǎn* (儜簡). The *Shuowén* says: "To blush with shame on the face. It is composed of the radical "red" (*chì*) with "zhēn" (㞋) as the phonetic. The scriptural version uses "pí" (皮) instead of "zhēn," which is a vulgar form. *Zhēn* (㞋) is pronounced *ruì* (䎡); the lower part is pronounced *zhuāng shòu* (莊瘦). The *Yùnlüè* (Rhyme Compendium) says it means the skin of the face gathers together. The *Shuowén* says it is composed of the radical "skin" (*pí*) with "chū" (芻) as the phonetic. The scriptural version uses "fú" (󲦶), which is a vulgar form.
*Yǎnzi*: The upper character is pronounced *yǎn* (with the *yì* radical). The *Kǎośēng* states it means "a black mole on the face. The *Shuōwén* says it takes the phonetic *yàn*. *Wǔlǚ*:

The upper character is pronounced *jū* (with the *jué* radical) and the lower is pronounced *lǚ* (with the *zhǔ* radical). The *Bóyá* states it refers to the appearance of a hunched back. The *Shuōwén* says both take the radical *rén*, with *qū* and *lóu* as their respective phonetics.

*Pǒqì* (跛跂): The upper character *pǒ* (跛) is pronounced with the initial *bō* (波) and the final *kě* (可). The *Zhouyi* states: "Lame, yet able to walk; insufficient for traveling. The *Shuowen* says: "Walking improperly. One interpretation holds it means the foot pushes against [the ground]. It is composed of the radical *zú* (足) and the phonetic *pí* (皮); it is also written as *bì* (󲕥). The lower character *qì* (跂) is pronounced with the initial *qì* (詰) and the final *yǐ* (以). Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Shanhaijing* states: "It refers to a person walking whose heels do not touch the ground. The *Shuowen* says: "Having many toes. It is composed of the radical *zú* (足) and the phonetic *zhī* (支).
*Kwang* (尫): The upper radical is pronounced with the *li* and *zhui* finals; the lower character is *shou* (瘦), pronounced with the *shu* and *jiu* finals. *Kuangruo* (尫弱) means weak and frail.

The *Shuowen Jiezi* records it as *kuang* (𡯂), stating that it refers to being lame with crooked legs, taking the large "elephant" radical (*xiang*) to represent the shape of a distorted limb. The archaic form is written with the "life" radical (*sheng*) as *kang* (󲞔). The version in the sutra text as *kwang* (尫) is incorrect.
The meaning of "bèn" (坌) [pronounced with the *mèn* rhyme] has already been fully explained in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-uttamarāja-sūtra*.

Volume Five, Part Five. "Bō" (搏): The upper character is pronounced *bǔ* (補) and *luò* (洛). The *Shēnglèi* states that it means "to capture. Duan Yucai’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* says it means "to take. The *Shuowén* says it means "to search and seize," written with the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "fú" (尃).

Regarding the character for *chī* (owl): the upper part of the character is the reverse of *zhǐ* (tooth). Zheng’s commentary on the *Mao Shi* states: "The *chī* is a bird that utters evil cries. *Mó* (pronounced *máng bó* in the dialects; the *Fāngyán* states it means "to grasp" or "to hold"). Regarding the standard characters for ancient and modern usage: [the character] follows the radical 手 (hand) and the phonetic 草 (cǎo), resembling a wooden peg (*jué*). Regarding *jī* (pronounced *jū yí*): The *Shìběn* states that Shàokāng invented the *jī*.

*Jiu* (臼): [The character] *you* (有) is an error for *tian* (田) in the original edition.

Volume Six, Part Six. *Qí* (pronounced with the *jì* rhyme). The *Erlǚ* says: "A path that branches off in two directions is called a *qípáng*. Guo's commentary states: "A *qí* road is one that branches out from the side. From ancient times to the present, the standard character is written with the radical *shān* (mountain) and the phonetic *zhī*.
"Piao-ling" (飄零): the first character is pronounced *pǐ* (with the rhyme *yáo*) and the second is pronounced *líng* (with the rhyme *lì-chéng*). "Fēn-yūn" (氛氳):

the first character is pronounced *fēn* (with the rhyme *shàng-fén*) and the second is pronounced *yūn* (with the rhyme *xià-yù-yún*). The *Wenzi Jilüe* (字集略) states that "fēn-yūn" describes the appearance of abundant fragrance. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文解字) derives it from the radical "qi" (氣) and the phonetic "fēn" (分). The meaning is already fully explained within the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-uttamarāja-sūtra*.
Lǎo (牢): Upper radical *lǎo*, reversed; pronounced with the *dāo* rhyme.

Chéng (層): Upper radical *zàng*, reversed; pronounced with the *léng* rhyme. Guo’s commentary on the *Shanhai jing* states: "Layered" (*chéngróng*). The *Shuowen jiezi* defines it as a "multi-storied building" (*zhòngwū*), composed of the radical *shī* and the phonetic *zēng*.

The desire to gaze [upon it] is reversed. *Nāḍī* (那墀尼)—the "zhí" (直) is pronounced with a retroflex; this is a Sanskrit term for a pond (*puṣkariṇī*). Regarding *liǎnyù* (輦輿): the upper character is pronounced with the *lì* and *zhǎn* (力展) finals.

Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "A person who pulls a carriage is called a *liǎn*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "*Liǎn* is a carriage; it is composed of *zàn* (㚘) and *chē* (車), meaning that which is led before the carriage. The lower character is the correct form; its pronunciation is *yú*. The *Wenzi Jielüo* says: "*Yù* means to carry. The *Shuowen* says: "*Yù* is a carriage; it is composed of *chē* (車) and the phonetic *dǔ* (󰦄). The original text here represents the correct forms of both ancient and modern usage; writing it as *yù* (轝) is incorrect. *Zàn* (㚘) is pronounced *bàn*; *dǔ* (󰦄) is pronounced *yú*.

"Piao-yang" (飄颺): The *Shuowen* states it means "that which is carried aloft by the wind. It is composed of the radical "wind" (風) and the phonetic "yi" (易); the pronunciation of "yi" is yang (陽). "Xi-xue" (戲謔):
The upper character is pronounced xi (希) with the initial *i*; the lower character is pronounced xiang-yue (香約).
Scroll Seven, Part Seven. *Yīn* (the upper character of *yīn-hūn*) is pronounced as the sound *yin*.

*Tì* (the upper character of *tì-tuò*) is pronounced with the initial *zhī*; the *Shuowen* states it means "nasal mucus" (*ēi*), written with the radical for water and the phonetic *yí*. *Tǔ* (the lower character of *tì-tuò*) is pronounced with the final *wò*; the *Shuowen* states it means "saliva," written with the radical for mouth and the phonetic *chuí*.
*Shùn* (不瞬): *shuǐ rùn fǎn*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To blink; it is composed of 'eye' (目) and the phonetic 'shùn'. In the scriptures, it is written as *xiù* (眴), which is a vulgar character.

*Tāo* (夭): *yǎo jiǎo fǎn*. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "A premature death is called *tāo*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "To bend; it takes the large elephant (大) as its pictographic form. *Shāng* (殤): *shǎng yáng fǎn*. The *Liji* states: "Those among men and women who die before capping or binding their hair are called *shāng*. Those aged nineteen to sixteen are called *cháng-shāng*; those aged fifteen to twelve are called *zhōng-shāng*; those aged eleven to eight are called *xià-shāng*; and those under eight years of age are *wúfú zhī shāng* (those for whom no mourning dress is prescribed). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "It is composed of 'dài' (歹) and the abbreviated form of 'shāng' (傷) as its phonetic. The sound of the character *dài* is *gēn* (矝).
The character above is pronounced *chāng* (with the *zhǎo* radical) and is the classical form;

the common variant is written as *sǎn*. For the character *kāi* (揩), the upper radical is *kè* (客) and the phonetic is *jiē* (皆). The *Bóyá* states that it means "to rub" (*kāimó*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) with the phonetic "jiē. Below, the phonetic is *shū* (舒) and *lì* (力). Guō Pǐng’s commentary on the *Erlǐ* states: "Wiping is the means by which one achieves cleanliness. Zhèng Xù’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states: "It means 'to cleanse' (*jìng*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) with the phonetic "shī" (拭).

"Fish and turtles" (yúbiē): the lower character is read as mièfǎn. The *Kǎogōngjì* states that the turtle has its bones within its shell (*néigǔ*). The *Shuowén* says it is a "shelled insect" (*jièchóng*), composed of the radical *mǐn* with the phonetic *bì*;

*mǐn* is pronounced *měng*. "Turtles and crocodiles" (yuántuó): the upper character is read as yuǎnyuánfǎn. The *Kǎoshēng* says they resemble turtles but have large bellies and spotted heads; the *Shuowén* also identifies them as large turtles, composed of the radical *mǐn* with the phonetic *yuán*. The lower character is read as tánghéfǎn. They resemble lizards but are larger, reaching one *zhàng* in length, and are considered dragons; they dwell in holes along the water's edge. Guo Pu notes their skin can be used to make drums. The *Shuowén* says they are composed of the radical *mǐn* with the phonetic *dān*, and the sound is *ná*.

*Qiúchī* (虬螭): *qiú* is pronounced as *qí yōu* (祁幽反); the *Guǎngyǐ* states that a dragon with a horn is called *qiú*. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "insect" (*chóng*) and the phonetic *yǐn* (乚). *Chī* (螭) is pronounced as *chǐ zhī* (恥知反); the *Guǎngyǐ* states that a dragon without horns is called *chī*. According to the *Shuowen*, it is like a dragon but yellow; in the north it is called *dìlū* (地螻), composed of the radical "insect" (*chóng*) and the phonetic *lí* (离). The character *yǐn* (乚) has the sound *yǐ yóu* (音巳由反), and *lū* (螻) has the sound *lóu* (音慺也).

*Śé* (蛇): Upper radical *shí* (食), read as *zhē* (遮) with a reversed tone. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "It originates from the 'insect' radical; its form represents that which is long, coiled like a grievance, and has a hanging tail. Because people of ancient times lived in nests and suffered from snakes, they asked one another if there were any "other" (*tā*) [troubles]. Thus, *tā* (他) is the present-day character for snake. Lower radical *tā* (他), read as *dá* (達). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "A beast resembling a small dog that dwells in water and catches fish. It takes the 'dog' radical and uses *là* (賴) as its phonetic."

*Ē* (鵝): Upper radical *gē* (何), lower radical *yàn* (諫). *Yàn* (雁): Upper radical *yàn* (何), lower radical *yàn* (諫). *Qú* (鸜): Upper radical *jù* (具), lower radical *yú* (虞). *Yù* (鵒): Upper radical *róng* (容), lower radical *lǜ* (綠).

*Yàn* (燕): Upper radical *yān* (煙), lower radical *jiàn* (見). Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states that people of Qi call the swallow *zhì* (𩾐). The *Liji*, "Monthly Ordinances," also calls it the "Dark Bird" (*xuán niǎo*). The *Shuowen* says it is the Dark Bird; its mouth is narrow, its wings are spread, and its tail is long, forming a pictograph. *Zhì* (𩾐) is pronounced *yǐ*; *niè* (籋) is pronounced *nǚ shè*, meaning "to tread. The lower character is *jiāng yào*. Gu Yewang says it is a small bird that relies upon humans. The *Shuowen* says it is formed from the radical *shǎo* and the phonetic *juī*. *Qiáo* (雀): Lower radical *jiāng yào*. Gu Yewang says it is a small bird that relies upon humans. The *Shuowen* says it is formed from the radical *shǎo* and the phonetic *juī*.

*Bi* (䯗) refers to the upper part of the thigh; *zheng* (正) is an error for *bi* (髀), and *jing* (經) is an error for *bi* (䏶); these are vulgar characters. *Canran* (慘然): the first character is pronounced as *cānggǎn* (倉感).

Volume 8, Part 8. Regarding *chéng huáng* (城隍): *huáng* (皇) is pronounced as *huáng*. The *Ervu* (爾疋) states that *huáng* means "void" (*xū*). The *Shuowen* states that *huáng* refers to moats surrounding a city; where there is water it is called a *chí* (池), and where there is no water it is called a *huáng* (隍). The *Yijing* says: "The city returns to its moat. It is formed with the radical *e* (阝) and the phonetic *huáng* (皇).

*Wǔ* (pronounced with the *wū* rhyme and the *hù* final): The *Shuowen* states it means "a small enclosure," formed from the radical *jié* (卩) and the phonetic *wū*. The text uses *wù*, which is a vulgar character. *Lín hè* (pronounced with the *hú* and *gè* rhymes):

Gu Yewang states that *hè* means "ravine" (*chēng*) or "void" (*xū*). The *Shuowen* states it means "a ditch," formed from the radical *tǔ* (土) and the phonetic *huì* (㕡). The correct form is *xià* (󲆺), though the text uses *lè* (𭐋), which is a vulgar character form.

"Shàn-diàn" (閃電): the upper character is pronounced *shān* (苫) and the lower is *diàn* (𮉼). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Lightning is the radiance produced by the mutual friction of yin and yang; it is written with the radical 'rain' (*yù*) and the phonetic 'diàn' (*diàn*, *shēn*). "Qì" (磧):

the upper part is "qīng" (青) and the lower part is "zhèng" (正), which is the same as the character "qì" (磧). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "A *qì* is a stony shoal in a river; it is written with the radical 'stone' (*shí*) and the phonetic 'zé' (*zé*). In the sutra, it is written as "qì," which is a common vulgar form of the character.

*Ti* (upper character): pronounced *zhèng* (戟) with a retroflex final; the *Shuowen* states that *ti* means "to throw. *Luò* (lower character): pronounced *zhāng* (張) with a lateral final. *Dān* (upper character): pronounced *dá* (荅) with a nasal final.

The Master Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* says: "Excessive pleasure is called *dān*. The *Mao Shi* commentary says: "The excess of pleasure. The *Shuowen* uses the character *tái* (媅), stating it means "pleasure," composed of the radical for "woman" and the phonetic *shèn* (甚); it is also written as *tán* (妉). *Luò* (lower character): the sound is *luò*. The original text of the scripture uses *dān*, which is a vulgar form of the character.

"Yú" (愚騃): The *Cāngjié piān* states that "yú" means to be ignorant. The *Shuowén* says it refers to the appearance of walking with effort; it is composed of the radical "horse" (馬) and the phonetic "yi" (矣). This is the correct orthography. "Yuán" (轅): The upper character is pronounced as "yuán" (袁).

The *Shuowén* says "yuán" refers to the shaft of a carriage; it is composed of the radical "carriage" (車) and the phonetic "yuán" (袁). The lower character is pronounced as "chōngliù" (沖六). The *Shuowén* says "zhóu" (軸) refers to that which supports the wheels; it is composed of the radical "carriage" (車) and the phonetic "you" (由).

*Qiān* (鞭): The upper radical is *mián* (綿) and the phonetic is *fǎn* (反). The *Shēnglèi* (聲類) states that it means "to strike" (*chuí*). The correct character for ancient and modern usage has the radical *mù* (木) and the phonetic *guò* (過). *Qī* (七): The reading is *tà* (榻) with the phonetic *tǔ* (吐) and *là* (臘).

The *Shìmíng* (釋名) states: "A bed that is narrow and long is called a *tà*. The *Shuōwén* (說文) gives the radical *mù* (木) and the phonetic *yú* (󱫕). The character used in the scripture is *tǎ* (㯓), which is a vulgar form; the phonetic *yú* (󱫕) has the same pronunciation as above.
*Yǒng* (耳環璫): *dāng* and *láng* rhyme;

when pronounced it rhymes with *yǒng* (涌), which is read as *róng* and *lǒng*. Gu Yewang says that "surging" (*yǒng*) refers to water waves rising and surging. According to the *Shuowen*, this character is formed from the radical "water" (*shui*) and the phonetic component "yǒng" (*yǒng*). The pronunciation of "yǒng" is the same as above.

*Āidài* (靉靆): The first character is pronounced *āi* (哀代反) and the second is *tái* (臺賴反). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that it means "the sun and moon are obscured and without light.
