Scroll Nine, Part One. *Gǔyù* (羖羊). The first character is pronounced with the initial *gū* (孤鄔反) and the final is the character for "sheep" (羊字). Zheng’s Commentary on the *Shijing* states: "Among sheep, the female is the ewe (*pín*); when it is a black ewe, it is called *gǔ*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it is composed of the radical "sheep" (*yáng*) and the phonetic element "staff" (*shū*).

The character 𣯟 (páo) is pronounced with the *bó* and *mǎng* finals; the *Pīcāng* states that in the local dialects (*fānyán*) it means "cloth" (*yì*). The *Kǎoshēng* says it refers to "hair-cloth" (*máobù*). The *Wénzìdiǎn* explains that it takes the radical 毛 and the phonetic 𣯟; it is also written as 𣮧 or 𣯅, with the pronunciation *jìlì*.

*Bì* (pronounced *bái* with the *mài* tone). Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states: "A weed resembling grain. It follows the radical for grain (*huó*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "A variety of grain; it takes the radical for grain and the phonetic *bēi*."

Regarding "zhūlù" (誅戮): Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that "lù" (戮) means "to humiliate"; Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states it means "to kill. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of "go" (戈) and the phonetic "liáo" (翏); the pronunciation of "liáo" is *lìyòu*.

*Liè* (獵): The upper radical is *lián* (廉). Zheng’s commentary on the *Shijing* states: "Hunting in the open fields is called *liè*. Jia Kui says it means "to take by hunting. The *Shuowen* defines it as "imitating the hunt to pursue game," written with the dog radical and the phonetic *lìe* (巤). The text here uses *xiè* (󲛤), which is a vulgar character; for subsequent characters that have such forms but no provided pronunciation, follow this principle. *Shǔ* (鼠): As stated above.

"Jing" (neck) is pronounced *jǐng* (with the initial *jǐng* as in "郢"). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it refers to the nape of the neck, formed from the radical "head" (*yè*) with the phonetic "jing" (*jīng*). The character below is also pronounced *yíng* (with the initial *yíng* as in "盈"). The *Shuowen Jiezi* says "ying" (*jìng*) refers to a neck ornament; in ancient script, it is written with two "pearls" (*bèi*). "Yè" is pronounced *xián* (as in "賢") with the final *jié* (as in "結"), and "jing" is pronounced *jīng*. "Bèi" is pronounced *bēi* (as in "杯") with the final *mèi* (as in "妹").

The characters for *bìchuàn* (armlets) are pronounced *bēi* (upper radical) and *miàn* (lower radical). Their meaning has already been fully explained in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*. Regarding *chāijiǎo* (hairpins): - The upper character *chāi* is pronounced *cèjiē* (upper radical).

The *Wénzì jílüè* (Compendium of Character Simplifications) states that it refers to "forked hairpins for the topknot. The *Wénzì diǎn* (Dictionary of Characters) says it is a head ornament for women, sometimes made of gold or jade, following the metal radical with the phonetic *chā*. - The lower character *jiǎo* is pronounced *nüè* (lower radical). The *Shìmíng* (Explanations of Names) says: "It is *shè* (to grasp); it means to pull out hair. The *Shuōwén* (Explaining Words and Characters) calls it *zhǎn* (tongs), following the metal radical with the phonetic *qǔ*. In character dictionaries it is written as *niè*, which is the same as the version in this sutra. The pronunciation of *qǔ* is as above; the middle character *zhǎn* is pronounced *qílián*. [Note: The text provided contains a mix of phonetic transcriptions and glosses for specific Chinese characters related to jewelry and hair ornaments.]

The character 鹹 (xián): the first syllable is pronounced xián; the second syllable is pronounced xīng yì fǎn. The *Erya* states that "lǔ" means bitter. In the *Zhouli*, it is written as 瀉 (xià); the meaning of the characters has remained consistent from antiquity to the present. It is composed of the radical 水 (water) with the phonetic 舃 (xī).
*Jiǎo* (澆) and *yì* (𣿙): the former is pronounced *jiāo* (rhyme with *yáo*), the latter is pronounced *zī* (rhyme with *cì*). These are the correct radical forms of the characters. *Xǐdàng* (洗盪):

the former is pronounced *xī* (rhyme with *lǐ*), the latter is pronounced *táng* (rhyme with *lǎng*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Dàng means to wash and cleanse vessels; it is composed of the radical *míng* (皿) and the phonetic *tāng* (湯). The pronunciation of *dí* (滌) is *tíng* (亭) and *lì* (歷)."*
"Mèi" (寐) is a transliteration of a Sanskrit word for a type of fish; its pronunciation in the sutra is "mí-sī" (迷私), and the second character is also explained in this way.
"Bùmò" (簿漠): the first character is pronounced "báng-é" (傍榑) and the second is pronounced "mò" (莫).

Regarding "cuán" (攢) in "cuán-luò" (攢酪): the upper radical is *cú* (徂), pronounced with the *luán* (巒) rhyme; the *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲) states it means "to accumulate," and the meaning in the *Shuōwén* is the same. It takes the phonetic *zàn* (贊). The lower part is pronounced *luò* (洛). The *Shìmíng* (釋名) states that "lào" (酪) is produced from milk. The correct character for this term throughout antiquity and the present takes the radical *yǒu* (酉) with the phonetic *gè* (各).

"Sǔn" (吮): The upper radical is "xuán" (兖, with the retroflex *r* sound). The *Shuowen* states it means "to suckle" (*zhòusò*). It is composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic element "yǔn" (*yǔn*, pronounced *shuò*). It is also written as "sòu" (嗽). "Tǐ" (軀): The upper radical is "qū" (曲, with the retroflex *r* sound).

The *Shangshu Dàfù* states that "qū" refers to the body (*shēn*). The *Shuowen* defines it as "the body" (*tǐ*). It is composed of the radical "body" (*shēn*) and the phonetic element "qū" (*qū*, pronounced *qū*).

Volume Ten, Part Ten. Regarding "yíng" (瑩): Sānyǎng Yěwáng states that *yíng* refers to polishing jade to make it radiant. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as the color of jade; one source says it is a stone secondary to jade. It is composed of the radical "jade" (玉) and the phonetic "yíng" (熒) with its "fire" (火) component omitted. According to this, the character for "polishing" (*yíng*) should be written with the "metal" (金) radical as "yìng" (鎣); those written with the "jade" (玉) radical are erroneous.

The character 牀 (chuáng) consists of the upper radical 正 (zhèng) and the lower component 尃 (fǔ, with the phonetic *wú* as a variant). The commentary on the *Shūjìng* by Kǒng [Yǎng] states that "尃" means "to spread" (*bù*). The meaning is the same in the *Shuōwén*. It is composed of the element "inch" (寸) and the phonetic "fǔ"; it is also written as 敷 (fū) using the character 文. The version in the canonical scriptures uses 敷, which is the vulgar form.

The character 𧘝 (upper radical 衣, phonetic 里) is pronounced *jiǎo*. Dictionaries state it means "to coat" or "to apply a surface layer. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "the upper garment. In antiquity, one wore furs, so the fur served as the outer surface (*biao*). It is composed of the radicals for "hair" and "garment"; the *Jing* (Classics) uses the character 表 (*biao*), which is the common usage. The lower part is pronounced *li*.

*Pei* (偝): The first character is pronounced *pe* with the tone of *mei*; the commentary states it means to turn one's face outward. According to the *Bóyǎ*, it also means "behind" and is written as *bèi* (背). *Yì* (翳): The first character is pronounced *ī* with the tone of *jì*;
the second is pronounced *fù* with the tone of *hóng*. It means to cover or conceal.
Among the five types of seeds, "yong" (勇) is used as a variant.
The five kinds—root-seeds, stem-seeds, joint-seeds, combined-seeds, and seed-seeds—each have the character "zi" (子) added to them.

Regarding "pi-sai" (皮𥢶), "huai" (恢) is the phonetic component; the *Cangjie pian* states that "sai" (穅) means chaff. The *Shuowen jiezi* records it with the radical for "grain" (禾) and the phonetic "hui" (會), which is the correct orthography. The version in the sutra text uses "mi" (米) and forms it as "kai" (糩), which is an error.
*Tuòkuì* (also written as *tuòkuài*): *kuì* has the phonetic value of *kuǎi*. *Fēnjiāng*:

*jiāng* has the phonetic value of *jūliáng*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that *jiāng* means "boundary. The *Shuowen Jiezi* correctly writes it as *jiāng*, derived from *jiāng* (meaning "three boundary lines"). It is also written as *pèi* or *qiáng*; *jiāng* has the same pronunciation as above.

*Zhé* (punishment/reproach): Upper radical *zhé* (pronounced with the *gē* rhyme). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that "to *zhé*" means to reproach one another. The *Shuowen* defines it as "punishment," formed from the radical *yán* (speech) with the phonetic *shāng*. The text also uses *zì* (to pick out), which is likewise acceptable. *Fán* (minor punishment): Lower radical *fàn* (pronounced with the *rén* rhyme). The *Shuowen* states: "The minor form of *zhǎn* (to strike). It refers to cases where one does not yet employ physical force, but merely brandishes a blade and utters insults; such a person should be punished. It is formed from the radical *lì* (force) with the phonetic *lì*. There are those who write it with the radical *cùn*, but this is incorrect.

"Qiānpái" (牽排): The first character is read as xián (賢) with the fanqie "qiān"; the second character is read as bèi (敗) with the fanqie "mái". The *Bōyǐ* states that "pái" means to push; according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "fēi" (非).
"Jiànglùn" (降惌): The first character is read as juǎn (卷) with the fanqie "gōng"; the second character is read as yuán (袁) with the fanqie "yú."
*Kebila* City is a corruption of the Sanskrit term; its correct orthography is *Kapilā*, also known as *Kapiḷa*.
*Maitila* City is already phonetically transcribed in the sūtra text, which is itself a corruption of the Sanskrit city name; alternatively, it is said to be the country of *Necchilā*.
The first character, *huì* (洪屋反), is a king’s name.

The second character, *zǐ* (上撝委反), the *Kǎośēng* states means "to slander," "to defame," "to revile," or "to abuse. The scriptural text writes it as *huǐ*; it is commonly used in vernacular usage. The lower part, *zī* (茲此反), according to Zheng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì*, means "to defame a person with words. This is the correct orthography from ancient times to the present, following the radical for speech (*yán*) and this phonetic (*cǐ*).
*Yá* (崖): *kǎn*, *gān* (反). *Rídǎng* (稻稈): *gān*, *gàn* (反). *Āgama Sūtra* (*Lóutàn jīng*), Scroll One. Compiled by Xuanying. **Scroll One** *Jiàohuàn* (噭嚾):

Also written as *jiào* (󲡺) and *hàn* (譥); both forms share the same pronunciation: *gǔdiào* (古弔反). *Jiào* means to cry out; it means to call. The following character is *huān* (歡), *guān* (觀) (反). It means to call or to invoke. It is also written as *huàn* (喚); *xiāo* (虈) and *huàn* (喚) are two forms with the same pronunciation.

2. Second Fascicle. *Huái* (䲷): Pronounced *zhé* (古堯反). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the *huái* is an unfilial bird. On the winter solstice day, one catches the *huái* and *zhé*-s it. *Zhé* (磔): Pronounced *zhé* (竹格反); it means to spread out and tear apart. The text reads *zhào* (棹), which is likely an error.

The character "lú" (盧) should be written as "lú" (顱), with the same pronunciation as "lìhú" (力胡反). It refers to a horse's forehead; one carves gold into it, which is what is called "lòuxī" (鏤錫). The commentary on the *Shijing* states: "The area above the eyebrows is called 'yáng' (陽); it was decorated by carving gold into it. What is now called 'dānglú' (當盧) is this very thing."

*Mò* (pronounced *mò*, with the initial *gè* reversed) is a term from the local dialects of the South and Chu regions, as well as the Yangtze and Xiang River areas, meaning "a head-wrap" (*luòtóu*). In dictionaries, it is written as *xià* or *jīn* (headcloth/turban), with the radical *巾* (cloth). The form in the scripture using the character *mò* (陌) is not the correct orthography.

*Ba-gui* (the "gui" is pronounced as *hu*): According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *baigui* means a tower; according to the *Tongsu Wen*, wood with four sides is called *leng*, and wood with eight *leng* is called *baigui*. This refers to the fact that the word for "pearl" (*zhu*) has eight facets.

"Shu" (署) means to depart and return to one's position. "Shu" refers to an office. An office is the outward sign of a position. A government building for administrative affairs is called a "shu"; "shu" is synonymous with "to station.
[Volume Three is missing. Volume Four: "Sha" (麮) [pronounced *qū*]. According to character dictionaries, it is a sweet porridge made from wheat; the *Cangjie pian* states it is boiled wheat.

5. Fascicle Five. *Qíngyín* (嶔崟): "Qíng" (嶔) is pronounced *qǐ* (綺) with the second tone; "yín" (崟) is pronounced *yí* (宜) with the second tone. This refers to the high and low, leaning and slanting forms of mountain ridges. The *Chuci* (*Lisao*) states: "The peaks and ridges are jagged and towering" (*líng yín qí é*). The commentary notes that these refer to the slopes and recesses of mountain ridges. [Regarding the reading] *é* (峨) as having the sound *'é*' (俄), that is incorrect. [In the cited passage] *zōu* (陬) has the sound *zé liú* (則流).

*The Dīrgha Āgama: The Sūtra on the Ten Retributions*, Volume One, compiled by Huìlín. Volume One: Section on "Forming a Ball of Rice" (*tuánfàn*). The *Bóyǎ* states: "To hold it in one's hand so that it adheres together. Regarding the term *shēng*: "It means to hold fast. According to the *Shuōwén*: "It means round (*yuán*). It is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic component "zhuān" (*shēng*). The pronunciation of *yuán* is *yuán*. *Note: This entry provides a philological commentary on the term "tuánfàn" (forming a ball of rice) and its associated characters and definitions as found in classical lexicographical works.*

The character *zhāng* (蛘) [is pronounced with the "yang" rhyme of the *shǎng* category]. It is derived from *yǎng* (養) and written as *yǎng* (𧓲), which is a vulgar form. The *Zìshū* (Dictionary of Characters) states: "It refers to the crawling of maggots within a sore. Alternatively, it may be written with the radical for hand (*shǒu*) as *zhuó* (攁), meaning to move or stir. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means "to scratch"; it is formed with the radical for insects (*chóng*) and the phonetic *yáng* (羊). There are those who write it as *yǎng* (痒), but that does not constitute a valid character.

If one reads *mǒ* (as in *yǔ jù fǎn*), this refers to the bowl (*pǎnmǒ*) used as a vessel by high-ranking monastics (*gāodào qǐshì*). It is incorrect for the scriptural text to write it with the "wood" radical (*mù*) as *wū*.

In the second fascicle, [the character] *mò* (read *méng bēng fǎn*): The *Wénzì Shìxùn* states that "mùng mùng" means the eyes are unclear; the *Ěryǎ* says it means "chaotic"; and the *Kǎoshēng* says it means "dull. The *Shuōwén* explains it as composed of "head" (*shǒu*) and "yǎo" (*yǎo* being pronounced *xuán*; *mù* being pronounced *rì*).

"Shí" (適) is pronounced *ding* (丁) with a retroflex initial; the *Kǎoshēng* states that "shí" means to point to or indicate reality. The *Jìxùn* explains it as "spontaneous" (*shírán*). The reading in the scripture as "dì" (帝) resulting in "chì" (啻) is incorrect. "Yùqí" (郁耆):

the first character is pronounced *jiá* (夾) with a labial initial, and the second is pronounced *zhī* (祇). This is a name for a flower in the Western regions according to the Sanskrit language. The form "yù" (郁) in the scripture is a scribal error in its orthography.

The character for "猗" (yī) is pronounced as the upper tone *yī*. This is an archaic usage by ancient scholars; its original meaning is that of the character "依" (*yī*), so it should be corrected to follow "依.

It is used for the sound "瞑" (*míng*). Examining the phonetics, "閉" (*bi*) means to close the eyes. The *Zuozhuan* states: "He was posthumously titled Ling because he did not become angry; he was posthumously titled Cheng because he then closed his eyes (*míng*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to close the eyes," composed of "目" (*mù*) and the phonetic "冥" (*míng*). The pronunciation of "翕" (*xī*) is *xīn* with the second tone.

*Madhyamāgama-vastu-sūtra*, Volume One, compiled by Xuanying. Volume One: *Kuṇḍin*. This is translated as "Ajñāta" (Known). *Kuṇḍin* is his clan name. It refers to the first five persons who were converted; their names are: first, Kuṇḍin; second, Bhadraka; third, Vāṣpa; fourth, Daśabala-Kāśyapa; and fifth, Mānava-Kauṣṭhila.

“*Bùjì* (trembling with fear); in ancient texts it is written as *kūi*, with the same pronunciation as *qí jì* (its season). According to the *Zílín*, it means the heart is stirred; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means the breath is unsettled. In the *Fāngyán*, it is called *kuǐ*; the commentary states this refers to being startled and trembling. The character for *kuǐ* is pronounced like *kuí zhī*.”

*Ping-ying* (with *bei-ying* as an alternate reading) means to be terrified or agitated. According to the *Guangya*, *ping-ying* is synonymous with *zheng-shou*. The text of the scripture reads *bing* (with *fu-zheng* as the phonetic reading), which the *Shuowen* defines as "to combine. However, "combining" is not the intended meaning here.

"Jù zhì" (俱躓) and "gǔ wén qiè zhì" (古文䠟躓) are two ancient forms; the modern form is written as "duì" (疐), with the phonetic gloss *zhū lì* (猪吏反). According to the *Tōng sú wén* (通俗文), when an undertaking is not successful, it is called "zhì" (躓);

when a limit is reached, it is called "ài" (礙). In the second fascicle, under "yāo yǎ" (妖冶): the character below is pronounced *yú zhě* (余者反). Lǐu Yuǎn states that in the *Zhou Yī* (周易), "zhì róng huì yóu" (治容誨媱) refers to "yǎo yǎ" (妖冶). This means an air of arrogant self-satisfaction, characterized by an appearance of bright and elaborate adornment.
*Kuáng-hǎn* (狂憨): *Hǎn* is pronounced with the *lán* rhyme; in character dictionaries, it means "foolish. Guo Pu says: "The *duō* bird is called *hǎn-jí* (foolishly frantic), meaning hollow courage.

*Líng-jìu* (靈柩): *Jìu* is pronounced with the *jiù* rhyme. In the *Xiaoya*, a corpse is called a *jìu*; an empty coffin is called a *cèn*. According to the *Liji*: "That which is in the coffin is called a *jìu*. Zheng Xuan states: "The word *jìu* signifies 'exhaustion' (*jiù*). The *Baihūtong* states: "The word *jìu* signifies 'long-lasting' (*jiǔ*); it refers to that which will not change for a long time."

*Hūn-huáng* (焜煌): The first character is pronounced with the *hú* rhyme-group (the second is pronounced *huāng*). According to the *Fānyán* (方言), *hūn* means "to flourish. Guo Pu states: "*Hūn-huáng* is the appearance of flourishing; *huáng* means 'bright'. In the *Cāngjiépiān* (蒼頡篇), *huáng* means "light. The text here uses the character *huī* (煇), which is not the same as *huī* (暉).

*Xunxun* (恂恂): *si* and *xun* rhyme; in the *Analects*, it appears as "he was *xunxun*. Wang Su says it is the appearance of being warm and respectful. The *Guangya* says it is "like *xunxun*. The *Erya* states that *xunxun* means trembling with awe.

"Bān" (斑) is also written as "biàn" (辨), with the phonetic *bǎi yán* (百顏). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "biàn" means variegated. The *Cangjie Pian* states that it refers to the appearance of variegated patterns; various colors combined constitute "bān. The text of the scripture uses "fān" (斒), with the phonetic *fāng jiàn* (方間); "fān" means mottled. The pronunciation of "làn" (爛) is *lì jiàn* (力間).

*Qīzhī jīng* (Sūtra on the Seven Knowledges), one fascicle; no phonetic glosses. *Xiǎnshuǐ yù jīng* (Sūtra of the Simile of Saline Water), one fascicle. “Xiǎn” (鹹): *qián* (恰緘反). According to the *Erya*, it means “bitter-salty. Guo Pu stated that “bitter” refers to intense salinity. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: “Xiǎn” (咸) is also pronounced *xián*; it is the flavor of the north. It is composed of the radical *lù* (鹵) with the phonetic *xián*. *Note: The character for "salt" (鹹) is formed from the radical "brine/salt-pan" (鹵) and the phonetic "to include/universal" (咸).*

*The Scripture on the Cause for the Gathering and Guarding of All Outflows*, spoken by the Buddha. Compiled by Hui Lin. [Note on the character] *Biēwāng* (弊尫): The upper radical is *pímiè* (毘袂) and the lower is *wūguāng* (烏光). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *wāng* (尫) means "a person with crooked legs. The character is composed of the "elephant" radical (*xiàng*) to signify a distorted form, and the phonetic element *yōu* (尤, pronounced *wāng*) with the "king" radical (*wáng*).

The *Catuḥsatya-sūtra*. Regarding the "Eighteen Mysterious Responses" (*aṣṭādaśa-gambhīra-pratibhāsa*): "Transformation" (*bianhua*) means to change; it means to alter. The *Baihutong* asks: "What is a 'calamity-transformation' (*zai bian*)? It is a transformation that is not the norm. The text of the scripture uses the character 𭵴, which is an error; this character does not exist in the dictionaries.

*Yǒu* (咽瘤): The pronunciation is *liú* (周反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means a swelling; the *Guangya* states it is a disease characterized by growths. The character in the canonical text is written with the radical for the mouth (*kǒu*) as *yǒu* (𠺕), which is not the correct character. *Héngshui jīng* (恒水經): The *Foshuo Hengshui Jing* (Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Ganges) in one fascicle, compiled by Huilin.

*Qīng* (圊) and *hùn* (圂): The upper character *qīng* has the phonetic *jīng* (七精反). Lexicons state that *qīng* is also *hùn*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines *hùn* as a latrine, written with the radical for the mouth (*kǒu*) and the phonetic *wěi qīng* (韋青). The lower character *hùn* has the phonetic *hù kùn* (胡困反). According to the *Shuowen*, it is also written with the radical for the mouth and the character for pig (*zhǐ*). The version in the canonical text is written with the radical for water (*shuǐ*) as *hùn*; this is a vulgar form.

"Wu" (洿) is pronounced with the "gu" (孤) and "fan" (反) finals; according to the *Guangya*, it means "deep. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan* states that it refers to turbid water that does not flow. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radicals "kua" (夸) and "shui" (水); "kua" is pronounced "qu" (區), serving as the phonetic component.

*Benxiang yizhi jing* (The Scripture on the Basis of Fundamental Characteristics), one fascicle, compiled by Xuanying. [The character] *yi* (依) is pronounced with the rhyme *yao* (猗). The *Mao Shi zhuan* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry) states: "To rely upon. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Fangyan* (Dialects) states: "To lean upon. The *Guoyu* (Broad Lexicon) states: "To rely upon and depend on. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (Explanations of Characters and Words) explains it as consisting of the radical for "person" (*ren*) and the character for "clothing" (*yi*). However, the text of this scripture uses the character *yi* (猗) with the radical for "dog" (*quan*). This *yi* is an expletive of admiration and does not accord with the meaning of the scripture.

*Yuanbenzhi jing* (Sūtra on the Fundamental Causes), spoken by the Buddha; one fascicle. Compiled by Huilin. Regarding "ai" (訒): *Ren* (仁) is pronounced with the *qieyun* rhyme *zhen* (振). Kong Qiu’s commentary on the *Lunyu* states: "His speech was *ren*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "speech" (*yan*) and the phonetic "reng" (*ren*).

Xuànyào (眩曜): "Xuàn" is pronounced as *xuán* (玄絹反). Jia [Yuan]’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that it means "to delude. Gu Yewang says that "xuàn" also refers to illusions (*huàn*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "eye" (目) and the phonetic "xuán" (玄); the latter is pronounced as *yáo* (遙) or *xiào* (笑). *Boya* states that "yào" means "bright"; *Buya* states it means "to illuminate. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "mouth" (曰) with "zhì" (翟) as the phonetic; it may also be written as "yào" (燿), which is identical in meaning.

The "xian-jùn" (賢儁) in the *Huainanzi* is pronounced as "jùn-fǎn" (峻反). It states: "One whose talent exceeds that of a thousand people is called a jùn. Nowadays, the common usage is written as "jùn" (俊), but according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the lower radical is "gōng" (弓). The phonetic component is "wéi" (惟), with the pronunciation "xǔ-wéi-fǎn" (許惟反), which is the sound of "juàn" (雋). The character "zhuì" (㺹) found in the canonical text is a vulgar variant.

*The Sūtra on the Story of King Mūrdhaja Spoken by the Buddha*, one fascicle, compiled by Huilin. “Nang” (曩) [pronounced *nǎng* with the initial *nǎng* as in *nǎng-lǎng*]: according to the *Erya*, "nang" means "long ago. Examining its phonology, it is said to mean "of old. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is composed of the radical "sun" (*ri*) with "xiang" (*xiāng*) as its phonetic component. "Xi" (昔) [pronounced *xià xīng lì*]: the version in the *Sūtra* uses this as a vulgar character for "of old."

Fánchóu (繁稠): The upper character is read as *fàn* (䊟) with the phonetic *mǐ* (覓). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (毛詩傳) states: "Fánchóu means 'abundant'. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* (禮記) interprets it as "flourishing. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *xi* (糸). Chóujì (稠穊): The *Guoyaya* (廣雅) defines it as "dense. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states: "Chóu means 'compact'. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "much," composed of the radical *huo* (禾) with the phonetic *zhou* (周). Chōuwǎn (䊟晚): The phonetic is *bān* (班). The pronunciation is *bān*.

*Pò* (揚簸): The lower radical is *bō* (波), read as *wǒ* (我) in reverse. The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (Mao Commentary on the Classic of Poetry) states: "To sift chaff. The *Shuowén Jiězì* (Explaining Simple and Analyzing Compound Characters) states: "To sift grain and remove the husks; it is composed of the radicals *jī* (箕, winnowing basket) and *pí* (皮, skin).

*Bìxì* (睥睨): The upper character is *pì* (紕), read as *jì* (計); the lower character is *xì* (倪), read as *jì* (計). The *Guǎngyá* (Extended Lexicon) says: "A side-long glance. Dictionaries state: "An oblique look. The *Huáinánzǐ* (Huainanzi) says: "Glancing left with the *pì* and glancing right with the *xì*. The *Shuowén* states that both are composed of the radical *mù* (eye), with *bēi* (卑) and *ér* (兒) serving as their phonetic components.

"Miàn" (eye-blinking): the "xuán" (玄) is pronounced with the *jiàn* (絹) rhyme. Wang’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that it means "the manner of looking"; the *Shuowen* says it means "the eyes moving," composed of the radical "eye" (*mù*) and the phonetic "xún" (*xún*). The pronunciation of "xún" is the same.

*The Scripture on King Mandhātṛ*, spoken by the Buddha; one fascicle. Compiled by Huilin. Regarding *láo-xīn* (勞𧶘): the first character, *láo*, is pronounced with the initial *d* reversed (i.e., *l-*) and the final *dài* reversed (i.e., *-o*). The *Erya* states that *xīn* means "to bestow. The commentary on the *Shangshu* by Kong Yingda states that *xīn* means "to give. The *Kaoseng* says that *láo-xīn* refers to mutual consolation and inquiry. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains that *láo* is composed of the radical *li* (力) and the abbreviated form of *yíng* (熒), while *xīn* is composed of the radical *lái* (來) and *bèi* (貝); it is a word formed through both shape and sound.

The reading for "xùn" (問訊) is pronounced as "xīn" with the tone reversed (i.e., the departing tone). The *Cangjie pian* states that "xùn" is also "to inquire. The commentary on the *Mao Shi* says "xùn" refers to speech. According to the *Shuowen jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "speech" (言) and the phonetic "xùn" (卂), where "xùn" also serves as the phonetic component. The pronunciation of "xùn" is "xùn" (迅). The form "qìn" (訙) found in the scriptural text is a vulgar character and not the correct orthography.

*The Sūtra on the Iron City Hell Spoken by the Buddha*. One fascicle. Compiled by Huilin; transcribed by Bi Min (pinyin: bǐ mín). "Bi" is also written as You (yōu); "Di" (dì) is pronounced with the *xi* (奚) tone. This is a term from the Sanskrit language; it does not seek the literal meaning of the characters.

*Yùpào* (雨泡): The first character is pronounced *yǔ* (宇); the second is pronounced *pò* (魄) with the rhyme *máo*. The *Kǎośēng* states it refers to bubbles floating on water. The *Shuōwén* explains it as composed of the radical *shuǐ* (water) and the phonetic *bāo* (包).

*Huì* (喙): The upper part is pronounced *xìng* (兄) and *huì* (穢); the lower part is pronounced *jí* (即) and *suǐ* (髓). The *Kǎośēng* states it refers to the beak of a bird. It is also written as *yì* (𠲿), *xiàn* (󲜘), or *zhì* (󲦚). According to the *Gūjīn Zhèngzì*, "bird-beak" (*niǎohuì*) is composed of the radical *kǒu* (mouth) and the phonetic *shù* (束). The pronunciation of *shù* is *cì*; it is a character formed from its shape.

*Jie* (𢧵): The former character is pronounced *shàngjié* (上節) with a retroflex tone; according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to cut. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means "to sever," composed of the radicals 戈 (*guó*) and 雀 (*què*). The version in the Classics uses 截 (*jié*), which is a vulgar form. The latter character is pronounced *bàijiǎo* (拜角) with a retroflex tone; according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to strip off the skin. The commentary on the *Máoshī* states that it means "to pare. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means "to slice," composed of the radicals 刀 (*dāo*) and 彔 (*lù*; the phonetic *lù* is pronounced *lù*).
*Panshiwu* (槃簁務) is the name of a hell. *Chi* (持) [is pronounced with the second tone on the radical *mu* (母)].

According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the *chi* (𨥨) is two zhang long and was erected upon war chariots; its primary form is pictographic and written as *mao* (矛). It is sometimes written as *hou* (鉾), which is a vulgar character; the archaic form is *fen* (𢦵), both being identical.

*Zhāi* (磔): The phonetic transcription is *kè fǎn*. The *Guǎngyá* states that *zhāi* means "to stretch" (*zhāng*). The *Kǎoshēng* states it means "to open. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical "stone" (*shí*) with the phonetic component "jié" (*jié shēng*).

The version in the scripture written as *dì* (柁) is incorrect. *Kūláishìshījīng* (古來世時經): One fascicle, compiled by Xuanying. The phonetic transcription for *chuī* (炊) is *chū wéi fǎn*. The *Shuōwén* explains *chuī* as *chī* (󲶜), with the phonetic transcription *qī luàn fǎn*, composed of the radical "fire" (*huǒ*) and the phonetic component "qiàn" (*qiàn shēng*).

"Bhikṣu" (比丘) is a transliteration from the Sanskrit language; "du" (都) and "gu" (骨) are reversed [in transcription]. In the *Aniruddha-aṣṭānusmṛti-sūtra* (阿那律八念經), there is one fascicle compiled by Huilin.

Regarding the character "jiǎn" (簏): "huán" (胡) and "jiān" (緘) are reversed. The *Guǎngyá* states that a "qiè" (篋) is called a "jiǎn" (簏). The *Zìshū* (字書) says it is a wooden box (*mùqiè*). The *Shuōwén* also says it is a "qiè" (篋); it follows the radical "wood" (木) and takes "xián" (咸) as its phonetic component, with the reading "lónggǔ" (聾谷) for the lower part. Wang’s commentary on the *Chuci* (楚辭) says it is a bamboo vessel. The *Shuōwén* says it is a tall bamboo box; it follows the radical "bamboo" (竹) and takes "lù" (鹿) as its phonetic component—this is the correct orthography.

*Chai-die* (差跌): "To stumble while going to the toilet. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is formed with the phonetic *shi* (失) and the radical *zu* (足); the pronunciation of *ti* (踢) is *tang*. *Kao-sheng* (考聲): "It does not coincide. The *Yunquan* (韻詮) states that *can-chen* (參差) means uneven. *Xia-tian-jie-fan* (下田結反): The *Guoyaya* (廣雅) states that *die* (跌) is also *cha* (差). The *Kao-sheng* (考聲) states that it refers to the feet stumbling. *Fangyan* (方言): "To trip. *Shuowen* (說文): "The foot kicking. One version says it also means "to leap over" (*yue*). It is composed of the radical *zu* (足) and the phonetic *shi* (失). The pronunciation of *ti* (踢) is *tang*.

"Jin" (筋): The upper character is pronounced *jin* (謹, *jin*, with the *yin* rhyme). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Jin is the strength of the flesh. It is written with the "bamboo" (*zhu*) radical because bamboo is a substance that has much sinew; the *Jing* (經) version writes it as *jing* (䈥), which is a vulgar form. The lower character is pronounced *huan* (胡管, *huan*, with the *guan* rhyme). Zheng’s commentary on the *Kaogong Ji* states: "Huan means 'broad' (*kuan*). The *Erya* says: "It means 'relaxed' (*shu*'). Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* says: "It means 'slow' (*chi*'). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the "silk thread" (*mi*) radical, with the phonetic component *mi* (覓); the initial sound is *yuan* (袁).

*Chòu* (皺): The phonetic transcription is *zè jiù* (側救). Lexicons state that it refers to the gathering of wrinkled skin; the dictionary explains it as the skin becoming loose and gathered. It is composed of the radical *pí* (皮) with the phonetic *chū* (芻);

the pronunciation of *chū* is *chǔ jù* (楚俱). *Xian* (癎): The phonetic transcription is *xiàn jiān* (限間). The *Shēnglèi* (聲類) states it is an epilepsy-like illness in children. The *Shuowén* (說文) takes the radical *nà* (疒) with the phonetic *jiān* (間); the lower part is pronounced *diǎn nián* (典年). The *Guǎyá* (廣雅) calls it "epilepsy" (*diānkáng*). The *Shēnglèi* says it is a wind-illness. The *Shuowén* takes the radical *nà* (疒) with the phonetic *è* (厄) and the sound of *diān* (顛).

The Sūtra of the Five Divine Messengers of King Yama (Yánluówáng Wǔtiānshìzhě Jīng), one fascicle. King Yama is also named Yanmoluó; he should be called Yamaloka, which translates as "the World of Pairs. It is my humble opinion that because suffering and pleasure are experienced together, it is designated as "Pairs" (Shuāng).

*Wánkè* (刓刻) is also written as *Yuán* (园), with the phonetic component *huán* (桓). It means to whet or pare down (*wánxiāo*). According to the *Guǎngyá*, it also means to sever (*duàn*) or to carve and engrave (*lòu*).

*Guǒyùn* (裹蘊) is pronounced with the phonetic component *yún* (云); it refers to gathering grass and weeds and binding them together to burn as fire. This is what is meant in the *Hànshū*: "Binding a bundle of brushwood and begging for fire" (*shù yùn qǐ huǒ*). The pronunciation of *ráo* (蕘) is *ér xiāo*.
The character for *huǒ* (fire) is also written as *㶴* (same as *tóng*, pronounced with the *liáo* and *zhào* finals). According to the *Shuowen*, its correct form is derived from the character *zhì*.

In the *Lishui jing* (Sūtra on Leaving Sleep), one fascicle, compiled by Huilin, the characters are transcribed as follows: *pángyáng* (upper part *bóguāng* final, lower part *yúzhāng* final). Gu Yewang states that *pángyáng* is synonymous with *páihuái* (to loiter or wander). Regarding the correct orthography of these characters: the upper character [of *páng*] is composed of *chù* (the walking radical) and *fāng*; the lower character [of *yáng*] is composed of *chù* and *yáng*.

"Right side" (yòu xiè): "xiè" means the abdomen and both flanks. It is composed of three "li" (force) radicals to form "xié," and from the "meat" radical with the phonetic "jīng. In the scriptures, it is written as "xiē," which is incorrect. "Seeking desires" (qiú yù): In the *Qiúyù jīng* (*Sūtra on Seeking Desires*), one fascicle, spoken by the Buddha and compiled by Huìlín.

"Wash and wipe" (xǐ shì): The upper character "xǐ" (西禮反) means to wash the feet according to the *Shuōwén*. It is now also used for the word "washing" (*zhuànxi*). It is composed of the "water" radical with "xiān" as the phonetic; it is also written as "sǎ. The lower character "shì" (尸翼反): Zhèng’s commentary on the *Yí Lǐ* states that "shì" means to cleanse. Guō’s commentary on the *Ěr Yá* states that "shì" also means to clean and purify. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the "hand" radical with "shì" as the phonetic.
*Tuán* (搏食): The first character is read as *duàn* (段) with the phonetic *luán* (欒). It was already explained in the *Shí bào jīng* (Tenfold Retribution Sūtra) of the *Xián āhán* (前阿含).

The *Shuōwén* states it means "round" (*yuán*), composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "zhuān" (*zhuān*). *Fó shuō shì fǎ fēi fǎ jīng* (The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on What is Dharma and What is Non-Dharma): One fascicle; no characters for pronunciation or glosses. *Fó shuō shòu suì jīng* (The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Observing the Rainy Season Retreat): One fascicle, compiled by Huìlín. *Lì* (戾): Read as *lì* (𥠖) with the phonetic *jì* (計). The *Máo shī jiàn* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Book of Odes) says: "Lì means not good. The *Guǎng yǎ* says: "Lì also means headstrong (*hèn*). The *Shì fǎ* (Canon of Posthumous Titles) says: "Not repenting of past errors is called lì. The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radicals "door" (*hù*) and "dog" (*quǎn*).

*The Brahmāṇa’s Discourse on the Calculation of Purity through Water*, spoken by the Buddha; one fascicle, compiled by Huilin. *Lu*: Pronounced with the *gu* rhyme (as in "ancient"). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: *Jue* (确) has the sound *chengjiao*. It refers to hard, barren ground. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Western salt land; derived from the archaic form of the character *xi* (西), simplified, depicting the shape of salt. *Xi* (西) is pronounced as in "west."

*The Scripture on the Aggregate of Suffering Sounds Spoken by the Buddha*, one fascicle; compiled by Huilin. Regarding the character *zǐ* (in *zǐměi*): it is pronounced as *cī* (the *cǐ* in *cǐshēng*). In the *Liji* (Book of Rites), Zheng’s commentary states that *zǐ* means "to destroy. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "to scold," formed from the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) with the phonetic "this" (*cǐ*), and is also written as *zī*. Regarding the character *mián* (in *miǎnjié*): it is pronounced as *jié* (the *jié* in *jiǎyù*). Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* (Discourses of the States) says that *měi* is equivalent to "extinguish. The sub-commentary (*jiān*) states that *měi* also means "to slight. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radicals "heart" (*xīn*) and "neglect" (*miè*), with a pronunciation identical to the former. It is an error for the scripture text to use the single character *miè* alone.

The character for *yíng* (fly) is read with the initial *lǐng* (反) and the radical *máo* (毛). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states: "The fly is an insect that defiles itself; it makes black appear white. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radicals *chóng* (虫) and *měng* (黽), the latter being pronounced *dāo-lǎo*. It refers to a creature that bites people and leaps away. In the *Shuowen*, it is composed of *chóng* (虫) and *zhuǎo* (𠿒); the character *zhuǎo* is pronounced *zhuǎo*. The form in the current scripture is a corrupted abbreviation of this.

The character *qū* (所蛆知列反) means "to sting" (*biǎo yǎ*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "insect" (*chóng*) and the phonetic element *máo* (*𭥐*). The reading in the canonical text as *dì* (咥) is incorrect; *hè* (螫) is pronounced *shì*.

Regarding the character *qiǎo* (鏚, 七績反), the *Zi shu* states that *qiǎo* refers to an axe. The *Wenzi dian* explains that *qiǎo* is also a battle-axe (*yuè fǔ*), composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic element *qī* (*戚*).

*Chuǎn* (pronounced *chuán*, with the radical for "foot" and the phonetic *zhuān*): the muscles of the calf; the *Wenzidian* states it is derived from the "foot" radical and the phonetic *zhuān*, though it is also written as *zhùn*.

*Bǐ* (pronounced *píngmǐ*): according to the *Shuowen*, this refers to the bone on the outer side of the thigh; its correct form is *dì*, though the scriptural text sometimes uses *bì*, which is incorrect.

The *Kuyin yishi jing* (Sūtra on the Causes of the Aggregate of Suffering), spoken by the Buddha; one fascicle, compiled by Huilin. Regarding the term "shí" (釋) in "Shì Jīdǐjì" (釋羇底寄)—the Sanskrit word is *niḥśreṇī*; the text of the sūtra uses the character "jì" (䩭), which does not form a valid word.
The term *ni-grodha* (transliterated as *ni-ju-lou*) is a transliteration of the Sanskrit word for "banyan tree"; it is also the name of the grove known as Lumbinī.

Regarding the term *páng-yáng* (wandering), the first character is pronounced *páng* and the second *yáng*. This has already been fully explained in the preceding section on the *Śrāmaṇyaphala-sūtra* (Sūtra on the Fruits of the Ascetic Life).

The character *mù* (摸布反) is explained as "to seek" (*qiú*). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to seek extensively"; it is composed of the radical "force" (*lì*) and the phonetic element "admire" (*mù*) abbreviated.

The character *shǒu* (首) with the variant *yáo* (䁶堯反) is explained in the *Shuowen* as a word for "inverted head. It refers to having one's head severed and hanging upside down; the version in the scripture using the character *huī* (䲷) is incorrect.

The character *chāo* (常) is pronounced with the initial *chī* and the final *fǎn* (反); as for the sound *chāo*, it refers to bowing and prostrating. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "foot" (*zú*) and the phonetic "ji" (*jì*).

The *Shemoman Benjing* (釋摩男本經), one fascicle, was compiled by Huilin. Regarding the character *zhé* (磔): in the ancient Wu dialect it is pronounced *gǔ*; Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that *zhé* means "to punish" (*zuì*); Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states that *zhé* means "withered" (*kū*), referring to the act of flaying. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "punishment" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "gǔ. The version of the scripture using the character *zhé* (𦍬) with the "sheep" radical is incorrect. The lower part [of the character] is pronounced *zhé* (陟格反); this has already been explained above in the *Tiéchéng Nílí Jīng*.

Its character for "forehead" (é) is pronounced wùgé; according to the *Fāngyán*, it means "the forehead. The *Shuōwén* states that it is composed of the radical 頁 (yè) with the phonetic element 頡 (jié); the scriptural text uses 客 (kè) instead, which is a vulgar form of the character. "Pài" is pronounced pǔjù;

Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that "pài" means "the manner of moving. The *Guǎngyá* states that "pài" means "great. It also means "to flow. The *Shuōwén* states that it is composed of the radical 水 (shuǐ) with the phonetic element 市 (shì).

*Ānanda-āśī-viṣaya-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Perception of Pleasure), one fascicle; no phonetic glosses. *Buddhabhāṣita-āsrava-vibhaṅga-sūtra* (The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Classification of Outflows), one fascicle. Composed by Hui-lin of the Lesser Vehicle. Regarding "āsrava" (lòu): Gu Ye-wang states that "lòu" means "to leak. The commentary on the *Huainanzi* says it means "to lose" (*shī*). It is also said to mean "to pierce. According to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it says: "All outflows are exhausted; there are no further afflictions. The *Shuowen Jiezi* [explains] it as being composed of the "water" radical and the "lòu" radical; the pronunciation is the same as above.

When the pain was so intense that he raised his halberd and looked back, [the text] says "jù" (劇), meaning it was even more severe than before. In both ancient and modern standard characters, this is written with the radical "knife" (刀) and the phonetic "qū" (豦), pronounced "jù. It is incorrect for the scripture to use the character "jì" (劇).
