The seventy-six sūtras on the right, totaling seventy-eight fascicles, share the same phonetic glosses as this fascicle.

*Gautamī-vaipulya-phala-sūtra*. Compiled by Hui Lin. Regarding the character for *ji* (羇) in *Jidi*: it is pronounced with the initial *yǎn* (冝) and the radical *gang* (冈). In the sūtra text, it is written with the radical *gang*; however, if one removes *gang* and uses *ge* (革) with *qi* (奇), it does not form a valid character. The character *di* (底) at the bottom is erroneously written as *yu* (瘐); this is incorrect. *Jidi* is a Sanskrit term (*jāti*) that is an alternative name for a specific lineage.

The character *teng* (𧄼) has the phonetic *teng* as its upper radical and *meng* (墨) with the *beng* (崩) reversal as its lower component. The *Cangjie pian* states that "teng-meng" (*𧄼瞢*) refers to the appearance of one who has just risen from sleep. "Meng" (*悶*) refers to a state of mental distress; the *Mao Shi zhuan* says "meng-meng" (*瞢瞢*) refers to a state of confusion. Both characters are formed by combining the abbreviated form of "meng" (*夢*) with a semantic and a phonetic component respectively.

*Pu* (乳哺): "Pu" is pronounced with the *mu* rhyme (蒲慕反). Yingyun states that "pu" means to suckle; food held in the mouth is called *bu*. The character used in the sutras as *bū* (餔) is not the original form.

*Ji* (譏): pronounced with the *ji* rhyme (紀冝反). The Guangya defines it as admonishing. Zheng’s commentary on the Liji says it means examining right and wrong. The Shuowen defines it as slander, composed of the radical "speech" (言) and the phonetic "ji" (幾).

The character *zhǒngzhǒng* (種種) is pronounced with the initial *nà* (囊諾郎反). It refers to a bag; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radicals *mí* (󲆍) and a simplified form of *gǔn* (㯻), with *mí* also serving as a phonetic component. The pronunciation of *mí* is *níng* (儜), and the pronunciation of *gǔn* is *hùn* (混).

*The Sūtra on the Bhikṣu of Campā*; *The Sūtra on the Bhikṣu of Campā* (no characters can be transcribed); *The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Subduing Lust*; *The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Subduing Lust*. Compiled by Huilin: The entry for "bié" (pronounced *è*, with the *guō* commentary on the *Fāngyán* stating that "bié" refers to a malicious nature; the *Shuowén* states it is composed of the radical "heart" and the phonetic "bì"; the pronunciation of "bié" is *bì*).

*Móráoluàn jīng* (The Scripture on the Demon’s Disturbance and Confusion), compiled by Xuanying. *Xiāo*: the phonetic component is *jiāo*. According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to the *xiāoqīng* (the moorhen). They fly in flocks with tails resembling those of a hen; they call out to one another as they cry, and eating them cures wind ailments.

*The Scripture on Māra’s Trial of Maudgalyāyana*, compiled by Huilin. Regarding the character *yàn* (黤): Wang’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that it denotes an appearance that is dark and obscure; the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as a bluish-black color, formed from the radical "black" (*hēi*) with the phonetic element *yǎn*.
*Chuan-xi*: "chuan" is pronounced as in *chuān-yǎn*.
*Luǒ-xíng*: "luǒ" is pronounced as in *huā-wǎ*.

Regarding "four *jiào*": "*jiào*" is pronounced as in *jiào-dào*; the *Hànshū* states that it refers to border barriers (*jiàosè*) beyond the frontiers. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical *chì* (pronounced *chǔ chì*) with the phonetic *jiào*. *Chì* is pronounced as in *chǔ chì*.

*Si*: (The character) *si* is pronounced with the *si* rhyme-group (the *si* of *sì*). Yuè Yěwáng states that a *si* is a bamboo vessel for storing clothes; the *Shuowén* says it is composed of the radical "bamboo" (*zhú*) and the phonetic "master" (*sī*).

*Rì dí*: (The character) *dí* is pronounced with the *niè* rhyme-group (the *niè* of *niè*). *Làitáhuólú jīng*: In the *Làitáhuólú jīng*, Xuānyìng compiled [the following]: In the country of Kaurava, the ancient script uses two forms, *jiǔ* and *biàn*, both pronounced with the *tā kǒu* and *tǔ kǒu* rhymes (the *kǒu* of *tǔ kǒu*). *Kuō*: the sound is that of *ū gōu*.
*Jue* (訣) means to part or bid farewell; the *Tongsu wen* (通俗文) states that "a parting due to death is called a *jue*.

In the *Shanshengzi jing* (善生子經), the Buddha speaks to Śreṇika, compiled by Hui Lin: *xi* (晞) is pronounced with the initial *xī* and the final *yī*. The *Mao Shi zhuan* (毛詩傳) says, "Xī is the first rising of the light," and it also says, "Xī means to dry. The *Shuowen jiezi* (說文解字) defines it as "to dry," derived from the character for "sun" (*ri*) and the phonetic component *xi*.

*Dàng* (the "shì" radical with the "táng" phonetic, pronounced lǎng). The commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* states that *dàng* denotes an appearance of vastness and distance. Gu Yewáng says that *dàng* also means to release or let loose. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the "vessel" (*míng*) radical and the "soup" (*tāng*) phonetic; it may also be written as *dàng* or, with the "mind" (*xīn*) radical, as *xiàng*.

The character 狎 (xiá) has the lower radical 犬 (dog) and the phonetic component 甲 (jiǎ). Duan Yucai’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that it means "to become accustomed to" or "to associate with. Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shangshu* defines it as "to draw near. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the dog radical and the phonetic 甲. The version in the [received] Classics written as 狹 (xiá) is incorrect.

*Gòu* (遘): The commentary on the *Mao Shih* states that *gòu* means "to encounter. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* also says it refers to meeting one another. In the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *chuò* (辵) and the phonetic *gòu* (冓). *Chuò* is pronounced *chǔlüè* (丑略反), and *gòu* is pronounced *gǔhòu* (古候反).

*Lì* (莅) at the top [of the character] is pronounced *lì* (力至反). Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states that it means "to preside over" (*lín*). It is also written as *lì* (涖). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) and the phonetic "position" (*wèi*).

*Duǎn* (短) is pronounced *duǎn* (短端管反). The *Cangjie pian* says it means "to shorten"; the *Shuowen* says it means "not long," composed of the radicals "arrow" (*shī*) and "bean" (*dòu*). In the classics, it is written with the hand radical as *bō* (𢭃), which is a vulgar form.

*Mǐ* (弭): [The pronunciation is] *mí bǐ fǎn*. The *Commentary on the Mao Shih* states that *mǐ* means "to stop" or "to cease. The *Han Shih* says it means "to extinguish. Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* defines it as "to forget. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "bow" (*gōng*) and the phonetic "ear" (*ěr*).

*Hui* (𨵵): Pronounced *han-la-fan*. According to the *Erya*, the door-leaf is called a *huì* (扉). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *hui* means "to close"; it is composed of the radical "door" (*mén*) with the phonetic component *hé* (盇), which is pronounced *hé*.

*Ao* (敖): Pronounced *yì-wǔ-gāo-fan*. The *Wenzi Jilüe* states it means "to roam. The *Guangya* says it means "to play. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of "out" (*chū*), "let loose" (*fàng*), and the radical for movement (*chuò*), which is pronounced *chū-lüè-fan*.

Regarding the character *chǔ* (儲): the upper radical is *zhù* (豬), pronounced with the *zhù* (佇) rhyme; the *kǎo* (考) commentary states it means "to accumulate. The *Shuowen* defines it as "to store" (*zǔ*) or "to amass" (*xù*), formed from the person radical with *zhū* (諸) as the phonetic. Regarding the lower part, *chí* (持), pronounced with the *lǐ* (里) rhyme: the *kǎo* commentary states it means "to prepare for" (*dài*), "that which is expected," or "to store. The *Shuowen* defines it as "complete" (*jù*), formed from the person radical with *dài* (待) as the phonetic. In the scripture, it is written with the foot radical as *dí* (𨂄); this is incorrect.

Regarding the term *jībān* (羇絆) in the *Shujing* (數經), Xuanying compiled it as follows: the lower character is pronounced with the *bu* and *pan* rhymes (*bàn*). According to the *Kaozheng Shengyun*, "bàn" refers to the tethering of both feet. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is the bit of a horse, where *mi* (糸) is the phonetic component. The text of the sutra uses the characters *jī* (䩭) and *bàn* (靽), but these do not form valid characters; this is incorrect. The pronunciation of *zú* (馽) is *zhī* and *lì* (*zhílì*), and the pronunciation of *mi* (糸) is *mì*.

The *Brahmacārin Pārayana-pṛcchā-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Brahmin Pārayana Questioning the Honored One of the Lineage). Compiled by Xuanying. "Gǔxū" (qú xū, with the second character pronounced as jū): This refers to an animal resembling a mule, being the offspring of a young ox and a horse.

*Ākhyā* (pronounced *xū bǐ*): A personal name; according to the character, it refers to a waterway through which a river flows. *Śrī-guṇa-maitrī-citta-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Merit of the Three Refuges, Five Precepts, and a Compassionate Mind).

There are no characters in this title requiring phonetic or semantic glossing. *Buddha-preached-to-the-Old-Brahmin-of-Yellow-Bamboo-Garden-Sūtra-on-Learning*. *Huìlín*: Rarely (*xiǎn*). The *Kǎoshēng* (Investigation of Sounds) states it means "few. The *Erya* states that *xiǎn* means "scarcity. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states that *xiǎn* means "empty" (*kōng*). It is sometimes written as *shèn*; the *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of the radicals "woman" and "very little," with the phonetic element *shèn*. It is also commonly written as *xiǎn* (rare/fresh).

The *Brahmāyusūtra*, compiled by Xuanying. "Dǐ" (砥) is also written as "dǐ" (底); the pronunciation is the same as the reversed sound of "zhī" (之). "Dǐ" means level and straight. In the *Shangshu* (Book of Documents), regarding the phrase "grinding on whetstones of *nù*-stone," Kong Anguo stated: "Dǐ is finer than lì; both are stones for grinding. The pronunciation of *nù* (砮) is the reversed sound of "nǎi hū" (乃乎).

"披纚" (pī sǎi) is now read as *zòng* (with the same phonetic as *shān qǐ*). According to the sources, *sēn sǎi* means "a beautiful appearance," while *sà sǎi* means "the appearance of long sleeves. *Sǎi* means "to hang down"; *sà* has the pronunciation *yè dá*.
"Chou" (瘳) [pronounced with the initial *chi* and final *-liu*] means to recover from illness; it signifies recovery or healing.

Regarding the *Sudatta Sūtra*, it was compiled by Hui Lin. "Za" (雜) means mixed; "kuan" (穬) [with the initial *gu* and final *-meng*] refers to unhusked grain. The thirty-fifth volume, the *Adbhuta-dharma-paryāya*, has already been explained.

*Zunshang jing* (The Sūtra of the Most Honorable); *Foshuo zunshang jing* (The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Most Honorable). There are no characters for which there are phonetic glosses. *Yingwu jing* (The Sūtra of the Parrot). Compiled by Xuanying. "Yin'uo" (intonation/recitation) is also written as "Yinzhi" (pronounced with the second tone on *niú* and the fifth tone on *jīn*). In Jiangnan, what is called "feng" (reciting) is termed "yin'uo. The *Cangjie pian* states that it means "sighing and praising."

*Menxu* (門閾): In ancient script it is written as *qian* (䦗), with the same pronunciation as *xuyi* (吁域). The *Erya* states: "The *ju* (㭈) is called *menxu*. Guo Pu says: "It is the threshold of a door. *Fu* (扶) is pronounced *qianjie* (千結). *Doutiao* (兜調):

In the *Foshuodoutiaojing* (佛說兜調經), compiled by Hui Lin, it appears under the section on *Jinsuo* (金𤨏). *Su* (蘇) is pronounced *guo* (果). The *Guangya* states: "*Suo* (𤨏) means 'linked' (*lian*). Lexicons also define it as "interlocking rings. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical for "jade" (*yu*) and the phonetic *ji* (𧴪); *ji* has the same pronunciation as above. The text of the sutra writes it as *suo* (璅), which is incorrect.

Regarding the character *qúlǔ* (氍氀): the first radical is *jù* (具) with the phonetic *qū* (具), and the second is *sè* (色) with the phonetic *yú* (于). The *Pīcāng* (埤蒼) states that *qúlǔ* refers to *tādēng* (毾㲪). The *Shēnglèi* (聲類) states it is also a woolen mat. The *Guǎngyǎ* (廣雅) states that *qúlǔ* is the same as *yī* (𦋺). According to the *Shuōwén* (說文), both characters are formed from the radical "hair" (*máo*) as a combination of semantic and phonetic components.

*Tàdǐng* (毾㲪): the first character is pronounced *tǔ* (with the *hè* [入] tone) and the second is *dé* (with the *néng* [能] tone). The *Bīcāng* states that *tàdǐng* refers to a woolen rug (*máo xí*). Both the *Shuōwén* and other sources derive these characters from the radical "hair" (*máo*) as both semantic and phonetic components. The version of the scripture using the character *kǎidēng* (闟登) is incorrect.

*Fei*: (pinyin: fèi; *Shuowen* glosses it as "to bark," written with the radical for mouth [口] and the character for dog [犬]. The version in the *Sūtra* uses the character *hōng*, which is incorrect).
It means to howl. *Páo*: (pinyin: bào; *Guoyaya* glosses it as "to howl," while *Shuowen* glosses it as "to snort," written with the radical for mouth [口] and the phonetic element *bāo* [包]).
*Jiǎng* (床楚夾反): According to the *Shuowen*, this character is composed of the radicals "man" (于) and "mortar" (臼), representing its form.
It is pronounced *báimá* (白麻反). In the *Kaozheng*, it is written as *bǎ* (把).

Its meaning is explained in the *Yijing* (Classic of Changes) by Foshuo and compiled by Huilin. In the *Mao Shi Zhuan* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Book of Poetry), *jié* (捷) means "victory. According to the *Fangyan* (Dialects), *jié* also means "robust. The *Shuowen* states that it is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic *zhì* (疌); the pronunciation of *zhì* is the same as above. The version in the *Jing* (經) as *jié* (捷) is incorrect.

Regarding the *Yingfa jing* (Scripture on Responding to the Dharma): there are no characters in this *Yingfa jing* that require phonetic glosses. Regarding the *Nili jing* (Scripture on Hell): Xuanying compiled [the following]: the character "zhubei" (竹錍) should be written as "zhubi" (篦). It is pronounced *bōxī* (補奚反). A "bi" (*bi*) is made of bamboo; it refers to one who strikes and beats with a bamboo comb-like instrument.
"Bianzou" (鞭掫) is a vulgar term pronounced *dinglei* (丁類反); it means to strike or lash. The canonical text reads "bō" (䩞), pronounced *táfan* (他煩反), which refers to a leather harness;

however, "bō" does not carry this meaning here. "Fuzhi" (鈇㩫) is pronounced *fangyu* (方于反). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means to chop or hack (*cao*), with "cao" pronounced *canguo* (倉臥反). The *Gongyang Zhuan* states: "I could not bear to subject him to the *fuzhi* [punishment]. He Xiu comments: "It is the crime of having one's waist severed. The *Cangjie Pian* identifies it as a wooden block for execution (*zhin*) and also as a horizontal axe. According to the commentary, a horizontal axe is like a chopping block; the *Piciang* calls it a *zhin*. The canonical text’s reading of "zhen" (鎮) is incorrect.
Regarding the characters *chóng* (蟲) and *zhài* (豸): according to the *Erya*, those with feet are called *chóng* and those without feet are called *zhài*.

In the *Jīngfóshuō zhāijīng* (Sūtra on the Buddha’s Teaching of Fasting), compiled by Huìlín, there is the term *huàn yī* (澣衣). Lùfǔ Liú provided a commentary on the *Gōngyáng chuán* stating that "to remove old stains is called *huàn*. According to the *Shuowén*, this character is composed of the radical *shuǐ* (water) and the phonetic *gàn*; it is also written as *huàn* (浣).

*Fǎpǔyì Jīng* (Sūtra on the Meaning of the Universal Dharma). Compiled and critiqued by Huìlín. [The character] 󲠛 (píng): An examination of sounds; a critique and discussion. It is the correct orthography for "to criticize" (*hē*) throughout antiquity and modern times. According to the *Wénzìdiǎn*, it refers to the title of an official at the Court of Judicial Review (*Dàlǐ Sīguān*). Derived from the radical "speech" (*yán*), pronounced with the level tone (*píngshēng*). [The character] 󲈅 (zhǔn): Pronounced with the departing tone (*chúnrǎn*). An examination of sounds; it denotes a formal notification or admonition. The commentary of Zhèng on the *Lǐjì* states it is an expression of sincerity and earnestness. It signifies "to reach" or "to arrive. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means "to inform and enlighten. Derived from the radical "speech" (*yán*), with 󲈅 as the phonetic component.

Regarding "yì" (抑): it refers to suppressing force and, conversely, examining sound; it means to restrain, to reason, or to press down. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is derived from the character "fǎn yìn" (反印). In modern clerical script (*lìshū*), it has been conventionally adopted as "yì" (抑) with the radical "hand" (手).

From the *Vipula-artha-dharmaparyāya-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Dharma-gate of Vast Meaning) spoken by the Buddha, compiled by Hui Lin: "Kòng" (控). In the *Mao Commentary* on the *Book of Poetry*, it is said that "kòng" means to restrain a horse; it is also said to mean to pull or lead. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the term for the Xiongnu drawing their bows is also called "kòngxián" (控弦), derived from the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "kōng" (空).

*Jièdéxiāng jīng* (Sūtra on the Fragrance of Admonished Virtue); *Jièdéxiāng jīng* [No Phonetic Gloss]. *Xiàjiàn jīng* (Sūtra on False Views); *Xiàjiàn jīng* [No Phonetic Gloss]. *Yōupóyí duòshèjiā jīng* (Sūtra on the Upāsikā Duòshèjiā); *Yōupóyí duòshèjiā jīng*, compiled by Huìlín. [Note]: "Duò" (󲴧) is pronounced as "nú gǎi fǎn" (奴改反). The *Erya* states that "duò" is the character "nǎi" (乃). The *Shēnglèi* says it means "to arrive. The *Shuowén* explains it as composed of "xī" (西) and "yǐn" (乚), with the phonetic value "yǐn" (隱).

Regarding the character *yuè* (閱) in "Reading the Lament" (*Yè'āishàngyuánjué*), the *Mao Shī Zhuàn* states: "Yuè means 'appearance' (*róng*). According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical for "gate" (*mén*) with the phonetic element *duì*.

Regarding *zhū* (珠) and *jī* (璣): *jǐ* is pronounced *xī* (希). Gù Yěwáng states that these are pearls produced by the *yì* (𧉻) fish in the South Sea; when the moon is full, the pearls are abundant, and when the moon wanes, they diminish. Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* notes that *jī* is also a type of pearl. The *Shuōwén* defines *jī* as a pearl that is not perfectly round. Both characters are composed of the radical for "jade" (*wáng*) and the phonetic element *jī* (幾), with *zhū* (朱) serving as the phonetic for both.
*Guliù* (upper character pronounced *jiū*, lower character pronounced *liú*;
a Sanskrit term). *Tíyú* (lower character pronounced *yǔ* or *zhū*;
a Sanskrit term). *Sùmó* (pronounced *sūlù*; a Sanskrit term).

*Vimānasūtra*. Spoken by the Buddha, the *Vimānasūtra*. Compiled and authored by Huilin. Regarding the character *fǎu* (麩) [in the term *pi-fǎu*]: it is read with the *fǔ* (撫) rhyme and the *wú* (無) final consonant. According to the *Cāngjié piān*, it refers to the husk of wheat (*mài*). According to the *Shuōwén*, it refers to the husk of small wheat (*xiǎo mài*), formed from the radical for wheat (*麥*) and the phonetic element *fū* (夫); alternatively, it is written as *fū* (䴸) using the phonetic element *fú* (孚), which is a vulgar form of the character.

The *Bāramōnzǐ mìngzhōng àiniàn bùlí jīng* (Sūtra on the Death of a Brahmin Son and the Inseparable Affection), spoken by the Buddha, was compiled by Huìlín. Regarding the term "nǔxíng" (naked): Guō Yěwáng states it means to strip off clothes and expose one's body. In the *Gōngjīn zhèngzì* (Orthographic Standard of Antiquity and Today), it is sometimes written as "luǒ" or "nuò"; it follows the radical for "person" and the phonetic "guǒ."

In the *Daśāṅga-gṛhapati-aṣṭanagaraka-sūtra* (The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Householder Daśāṅga of the Eight Cities), "zhùàn" (饌) is transcribed as "shì juàn fǎn" (士眷反). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Yili* states: "Zhùàn means to arrange. Ma Rong’s commentary on the *Lunyu* states: "Zhùàn refers to food and drink. The *Guangya* states: "To present; to provide complete food. It is formed from the radical "food" (食) with the phonetic component "xùn" (巽).

In the *Sūtra of the Simile of the Arrow* (*Śalyasūtra*) as spoken by the Buddha, compiled by Hui Lin, it says: "Cang-he" (鶬鶴). The upper character is read as *cuó* (錯) with the *rǎn* (反) suffix; according to the *Erya*, "Cang is the *mí-guā*" (麋鴰), and Guo Pu states, "Cang is *guā*" (鴰). According to the *Shuowen*, "Eǒu is *guā*" (鶥鴰), written with the radical 鳥 and the phonetic 倉; the lower character is read as *hé-gè* (何各). The *Huainanzi* states: "The rooster knows that dawn is near; the crane knows midnight. According to the *Shuowen*, it is a "transcendent bird" (仙鳥), written with the radical 鳥 and the phonetic 鶴; the pronunciation of 鶴 is the same as above. It is composed of the characters 冖 and 隹; the pronunciation of 冖 is *guì-yíng* (癸營).

The *Sūtra on King Prasenajit’s Queen Mother Passing Away and Her Body Being Covered in Dust*, compiled by Xuanying: "Qiyi" (期頤) is reversed [in the text]. According to the *Liji* (Book of Rites), "At one hundred years of age, it is called qiyi. Zheng Xuan explains: "Qi" means "to require" or "to demand," referring to the act of nurturing. It means that the filial son must fulfill the way of providing nourishment to the utmost.

*The Sutra on the Appearance of Four Persons in the World*, spoken by the Buddha. Compiled by Hui Lin. Regarding the characters for *kuíhuì* (魁膾): - The upper character, *kuí* (魁), is pronounced with the initial *kǔ* (苦) and the final *huí* (迴). In the *Liji* (Book of Rites), Zheng Xuan’s commentary states that *kuí* means "head" (*shǒu*). The *Guǎngyá* (Guǎngyá Lexicon) says *huì* means "to mince" (*zhì*). According to the *Shuowén* (Explanations of Simple and Compound Characters), it is composed of the radical *dòu* (斗) and the phonetic *guǐ* (鬼). - The lower character, *huì* (膾), is composed of the radical *ròu* (肉) and the phonetic *huì* (會).

*The Sūtra of the Girl Sumati*, spoken by the Buddha. Compiled by Hui Lin. *Geng* (亘): In the ancient dialects of Yunshang, it is pronounced *qian* (󲟔). In the local dialects, it means "to finish. The *Commentary on the Mao Shi* states that *geng* (亘) means "pervasive. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is composed of "sun" (曰) and "two" (二). It is incorrect for the text of the sūtra to use the character *gen* (絙), which is composed of "silk" (糸); the pronunciation of "silk" (糸) is *mi* (覓).

“Chilín” (赤隣) is an indistinct transcription of a Sanskrit term; it is a clumsy and erroneous translation by the scribe of the scriptures. This is also a name for a treasure, or perhaps it was written incorrectly.

“Líu-li qín” (琉璃琴)—the second character being pronounced as *qín* with the tone *yín*—is a musical instrument made from the precious material *vaiḍūrya*. The lute (*qín*) is also a musical implement of the heavens.

*Shǎn* (睒): "Lightning. It is a variant of *diàn* (電). The *Cāngjié piān* (Cangjie’s Lexicon) states that *qì* (晱) means "a brief appearance"; the *Shuōwén* (Explanations of Words and Texts) states it means "a fleeting glance," composed of the radical *mù* (eye) with the phonetic *yán*.

*Báluómén bìsǐ jīng* (Sūtra on the Brāhmaṇa Avoiding Death): Spoken by the Buddha. There are no characters in this title for which phonetic glosses can be provided. *Bóshuō shíshī huò wǔfú bào jīng* (Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Fivefold Meritorious Rewards for Bestowing Food): Compiled by Huìlín. *Hóngkuò* (弘廓): Pronounced *kǔ guō fǎn*. According to the *Ěryǎ*, *kuò* means "great. The *Guǎngyǎ* states it means "empty. Regarding the correct orthography of ancient and modern times: to enlarge what is small is called *kuò*. It is composed of the radical *guǎng* (厂) with the phonetic *guō*.

*Wei* (暐): The upper radical is *wei* (韋), pronounced with the *gui* (鬼) rhyme; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "vivid brightness. It is correctly written with the radical *huo* (火). The lower part is *yan* (炎), pronounced with the *jie* (劫) rhyme; the *Shuowen* states that *ye* (曅) is a description of the appearance of radiant light. It may also be written as *yue* (曅), which likewise takes the radical *huo* (火) to form *ye* (燁).

"Hao-jian" (耗減): "Hao" is pronounced with the first tone as *ào* (according to the *Beicang*); it means "to diminish" (*xiao*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical for "grain" (*huo*) and the phonetic *mao*. "Xian-zhan" (咸斬) is the second tone; in the *Han Shi* (Mao Commentary on the Book of Odes), it means "to decrease. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan* states: "It is 'hāo' (to waste away); it is 'sun' (to diminish). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical for "water" (*shui*) and the phonetic *xian*.

*Zhì'ài* (躓礙): The first character, *zhì*, is pronounced with the initial *chī* (知利) and the final *shēng* (聲). It means to stumble and fail to advance. The correct form is *duì* (疐). The second character, *ài*, is pronounced with the initial *wǔ* (五) and the final *shēng* (聲); it is said to mean obstruction or separation. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to stop," composed of the radicals for stone (*shí*) and doubt (*yí*). The *Boyá* writes it as *hài* (閡), the *Yunlüe* as *wài* (硋), and the *Wenzí Jílüè* as *ài* (㝵); these are all vulgar characters.

*The Sūtra on King Bimbisāra Visiting the Buddha to Make Offerings*, compiled by Huilin. Regarding the term *jinsi* (金屣): the phoneticist *Kao* states that it refers to footwear that does not have laces (*shè*). Lexicons identify it as *luò* (䩡) or *lǚ* (𩌦), which is the leather shoe worn today. It was customary in the Western Regions to wear this. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *lǚ* (𩌦), a type of *di* (鞮) footwear, derived from the radical "leather" (*gé*) with the phonetic "xi" (*xǐ*). It is also written as *lǚ* (󲱸), both having the same pronunciation. The character *luò* (䩡) is pronounced *gōng tì* (公冾反), and *di* (鞮) is pronounced *dīng xī* (丁奚反).

Regarding the phrase "the handle of the pearl-whisk" (*zhūbǐng fùzhōng*): *bǐng* (handle) refers to the part of an object where it is held. To say "pearl-handle" means the handle of a whisk (*fù*) that is inlaid and decorated with pearls, jade, and the like. Lexicons explain that *bǐng* is the same as *gē* (stem); it is the place where an object is grasped. It is composed of the radical for wood (*mù*) and the phonetic *bǐng*. It is also written as *bǐng* (𥟱), the lower part of which is pronounced *fēn* (物反).

The Scripture on the Six Times a Householder’s Son Leaves Home. Compiled by Huilin. *Méngyá* (萌芽): "Méng" is pronounced as *mài* (麥) with a reversed *fǎn* (反). The *Yùpiān* (玉篇) states that *méng* is also *yá* (芽); the *Shuōwén* (說文) also says it is a sprout of grass, written with the radical for grass (*艸*) and the phonetic *péng* (朋), where *cǎo* (草) is the sound.

In the *Aṅgulimāla-sūtra*, as expounded by the Buddha, the commentary compiled by Huilin states: "To 'comprehensively master' (zōng) the lower schools [of thought]—the character *zōng* is pronounced with the final *rǎn* (as in *sòng*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *zōng* refers to the device for holding the threads when weaving; it is derived from the radical *mì* (silk/thread) and the phonetic component *zōng*. The pronunciation of *mì* is *mò*."

*Bǐng* (upper character: 上, pinyin: shàng; lower character: 彼, pinyin: bǐ; reversed: 錦, pinyin: jǐn). Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shūjìng* states that *bǐng* refers to what a person receives and inherits.

According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of 㐭 and 禾; 㐭 is pronounced *lì jǐn*. *Zī* (upper character: 姊, pinyin: zǐ; private reading: sī; lower character: 諏, pinyin: zōu). The *Kǎoshēng* says that *zī* means to inquire of the virtuous. The *Guǎngyá* says it means "white. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of 言 and the phonetic 咨. The lower character, 諏, has the pinyin *zú xū*. Dù’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* says that *zōu* means to inquire about correct matters. The *Eryā* says it means "to plan. According to the *Shuowén*, it means to gather counsel; it is composed of 言 and the phonetic 取. The text of the scripture uses 󲠵, which is an erroneous transcription.

The character *fàn* (範) is pronounced with the third tone (as indicated by the radical *àn*). According to the *Erya*, *fàn* means "constant" (*cháng*); according to the *Yunying*, it means "standard" (*zé*); and according to the *Kaosheng*, it means "to model" (*mó*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "law" (*fǎ*). In antiquity, laws were shaped like bamboo; they were written upon bamboo slips, which is why it is called "law. It is composed of the radical for bamboo (*zhú*), the character for carriage (*chē*), and the abbreviated phonetic *lěi*. The text of the scripture reads *líng* (鈴, "bell"), which is incorrect; such a meaning is utterly unreasonable.

*Wei* (猥): According to the *Wūcāngjiépiān*, it means "to stoop. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "multitude. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical *quǎn* (dog) with the phonetic *wèi*. The pronunciation of *huì* (猥) is *huī* (灰) with the second tone. *yǎn* (偃): Pronounced *xiàn* (獻). Kǒng’s commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* states it means "to fall prostrate.

Jiǎ’s commentary on the *Guóyǔ* states it means "to rest. The *Guǎngyá* states it means "to stretch out. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical *rén* (person) with the phonetic *yàn*. The pronunciation of *yàn* is the same as above. It is an error in this scripture to write it as *gēng* (𮈧) with the radical *mì* (silk); the pronunciation of *mì* is *mì* (覓).

Regarding "bǎo" (裹): Yu Boyang’s *Guǐyī* states that "bǎo" means to praise or beautify. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Líjì* states that "bāo" (褒) means to advance or promote. The *Shuowén Jiězì* also defines it as a wide hem (*bóqū*), written with the radical "clothing" and the phonetic "bǎo" (󲝷), which is pronounced *bǎo*. The vulgar form is "bāo" (褒); its appearance in the received text as "bāo" is an erroneous transcription.

*Niǎo* (嬲): The upper radical is *nù* (奴) with the bird radical (*niǎo*) reversed; the sound is that of *kǎo*. It means to provoke or to mock and toy with someone; it is also written as *ráo* (嬈). *Zèn* (譖): Pronounced *zé jìn* (側禁).

According to the *Bóyǎ*, it means to slander or defame. He Xi’s commentary on the *Gōngyáng Zhuàn* states: "To say something when there is no basis for it is called *wú* (誣); to report it exactly as it happened is called *zèn* (譖). The *Shuōwén* defines it as "to accuse," formed with the radical *yán* (言) and the phonetic *tì* (替).

Regarding "qiānchè" (牽掣): the second character is pronounced with the *chǎn* rhyme (列反). The *Kǎośēng* (考聲) states that "chè" means to pull or drag suddenly. Gu Yǒuwáng says that "chè" is synonymous with "qiān" (to pull). The *Shuōwén* defines it as "to draw out and release," composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "zhì" (制).

**Cui-zuo (摧捽):** The first character is pronounced *zàng* with the *léi* rhyme; the second is pronounced *cún-mù*. Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that "cuì-zuó" means to seize and drag down. The *Shuowen* says it means to grasp the hair, composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "zuò" (*zú*). **Qì (契):** Pronounced *xī-jì*. The *Kaoseng* says that "qì" is like a contract (*quàn*). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* calls it the language of a formal agreement.

The *Shuowen* defines it as a general term, composed of the radical "kua" (*gǔ-bā*) and the phonetic "dà". It is incorrect to write this as "yún" (*yì*). **Cuò (錯):** A mistake found in the *Shujing*. [The correct character is] "cuò" (錯), meaning to intermingle or err. It is composed of the radical "knife" (*bō*) and the phonetic "cuò" (*cuò*). It is not the same as the character for "cloud" (*yún*). *(Note: The text provided contains a mix of characters and glosses. The above translation reflects the philological analysis of these specific entries as they appear in the source material.)*

*Yao* (邀): Pronounced *yǎo* (with the rhyme of *dào*). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "to invite" (*yāo*) means "to intercept. Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* says it means "to seek. The *Shuowen* defines it as "to block" or "to intercept," written with the radical *chuò* (辵) and the phonetic *jiào* (噭) abbreviated; the pronunciation of *jiào* is *jiào*. Below is *fén* (墳), pronounced *fěn* (粉). Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that "to be indignant" (*fèn*) means "to be abundant. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* says it refers to "the breath of anger being full. The *Fangyan* also uses this term. The *Shuowen* defines it as "to be vexed" (*màn*), written with the radical *xīn* (心) and the phonetic *bēn* (賁).

*Pēn-tà*: The first character is pronounced as *pǔ* (with the *mèn* rhyme) and the second as *zhì* (with the *jià* rhyme). In the *Cāngjié piān*, it is stated that *pēn* is also *tà*. According to the *Shuōwén*, *pēn* means "to snort through the nose. Both characters are composed of the radical 口 (*kǒu*) and the phonetic elements 賁 (*bēn*) and 乇 (*zé*). The sound of 乇 is *zhú-è* (with the *è* rhyme).

The character 牧 (mù) is pronounced with the *chū* and *jù* rhymes; it means to mow wild grass, according to Ye Wang. The *Shuowen* also states it means to mow grass, representing the form of a bundle of grass tied together; the lower radical is read as *mónglù*. The *Guangya* says it means to pasture or raise livestock. In the *Hanshu*, "pasture" (*mù*) is a general term for raising animals. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "ox" (*niú*) and the phonetic component "pǔ" (*pǔ*), which is pronounced *pǔbǔ*.

*Lángjí* (狼藉): "Luò" (洛) should be read as *dāng* (當), and "xiàqíng" (下情) as *yì* (弈). Liu’s commentary on the *Mencius* states that it refers to grass being abundant and disheveled. The *Yùpiān* says it means grass spread out in all directions. The *Shuowén* explains that the upper part consists of the radical for "dog" (*quán*) and the phonetic "liáng" (*liáng*), while the lower part consists of the radical for "grass" (*cǎo*) with the phonetic "jì" (*jì*). The pronunciation of *jì* is the same as above.

*Xiǎng* (饟): The character is pronounced with the *xi* rhyme. Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states it refers to provisions carried for travel. Gu Yewang says it means "to carry. The *Guǎngyá* says it means "to send. The *Shuowén* says it means "to carry as a gift," composed of the radical "貝" (bèi) and the phonetic "齋" (zhāi). The version in the scripture uses "賷" (jī), which is a vulgar form. The lower part is pronounced with the *shì* and *zhǎng* rhymes. The *Erya* says it means "to provide food. The *Fānyán* states that in the state of Zhou, one calls providing food *kuì* (饋). It is composed of the radical "食" (shí) and the phonetic "襄" (xiāng). The version in the scripture uses "餉" (xiǎng), which is likewise a vulgar form. *Kuì* (饋) is pronounced *kuì*.

"Bi" (必) is pronounced as "jiao" (焦) with a small *fanqie* (反); Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* explains it as "moving and cutting," meaning to utterly exterminate. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radicals "force" (力) and "nest" (巢), where "chao" (巢) is pronounced as "chai-jiao" (柴交).

"Tou" (投) is pronounced as "bi-xia" (捭下) with a *bu-ja* (補賈) rhyme; according to the *Guangya*, "bi" (捭) means "to open. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to strike with both hands," composed of the radical "hand" (手) with "bei" (卑) as its phonetic component; it is also written as "pai" (擺).

*Kai qi* (開䦱): The second character is read as *wei* (為) with the alternative reading *pi* (彼). The commentary on the *Guoyu* states that *qi* means "to open"; the *Cangjie pian* says it means "to open"; and the *Shuowen jiezi* defines it as "to open a gate," taking *men* (門) as the radical and *wei* (為) as the phonetic.

*Piejian* (瞥見): The first character is read as *pian mie* (片蔑). The *Kaosheng* says it means "merely seeing. The *Shuowen jiezi* explains it as being composed of *mu* (目) as the radical and *bie* (敝) as the phonetic. The version in the scripture written as *qin* (𣣫) is incorrect.

In the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra*, as spoken by the Buddha, the character "攜" (xié) is annotated by Huìlín as "攜手" (xiéshǒu). Wèi Guī and Huányǎo state that it means "to hold. Hé’s commentary on the *Gōngyáng Zhuàn* says it means "to lead. Mèng’s commentary on the *Hàn Shū* says it means "to connect. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of "手" (hand) and the phonetic "嶲" (suǐ); the pronunciation of "嶲" is the same as above.

"Piāonì" (漂溺): "Piāo" (漂) is pronounced *pǐ yáo* (匹遙反). Yě Wáng says it means "drifting" (*piāoliú*); the *Shuowén* says it means "floating" (*piāofú*). The *Wenzidian* states that it takes the radical "water" and the phonetic "piào" (票), with "piào" pronounced *bì yáo* (必遙反). The version in the Classics written as "niào" (㵱) is an error.

*Jiān* (韁): The initial rhyme is *liáng*. The *Jíxùn* states: "The *jiān* is the halter for a horse; the *xiè* is the tethering rope for a horse. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical *gēng* (metal) with *jiāng* as its phonetic.

*Lìlì yishān jīng* (力士移山經): Transcribed by Xuányìng. *Lǜlì* (勠力): The initial rhyme is *jù*. The *Guóyǔ* says: "To *lǜlì* means to unify one's heart. Jia Dui states: "*Lǜ* means to combine one's strength. The *Shàngshū* says: "He united his strength with them" (*yǔ zhī lǜlì*). Kǒng Àngguó states: "It means to exert one's strength."

"Ming" (míng) is pronounced as "mo" (mò) and "tíng" (tíng). It refers to the engraving of metal and stone to record meritorious deeds. "Ming" means "name"; it signifies that for those who have performed meritorious service, their achievements are inscribed upon the Grand Standard (tàicháng).

*Jué* (pronounced *jū yuè*) means to lift up suddenly; it refers to tossing something upward. In the *Erya*, it is defined as "movement. Guo Pu states: "It is the appearance of shaking, and also the appearance of being startled, alarmed, or acting with extreme haste. It also means to startle awake. *Jué* signifies rising up.

*Mie* (蔑): *xue* (屑) with the initial *wu* (無) and the final *jie* (結); the following character has the initial *xian* (先) and the final *jie* (結). The *Beicang* states that *xie* (󲢇) means to wipe away or extinguish.
*Wei* (餧): *e* (餓) with the initial *nu* (奴) and the final *zui* (罪). In the *Lunyu*, it says, "In plowing, hunger lies within it. Zheng Xuan notes that *wei* (餧) also means hunger (*e*).

"Lín yǔ" (drenching rain): the character "lín" is pronounced as *jīn* with a retroflex initial. According to the *Zuò zhuan*, rain lasting for three days or more is called "lín. The *Erya* states that prolonged rain is called "yín," and "yín" is also called "lín," likewise referring to rain lasting for three days or more.

The *Sūtra of the Four Unprecedented Events* (Catvāry-āścaryādbhuta-sūtra), spoken by the Buddha; there are no characters here that can be phonetically transcribed or glossed. The *Sūtra of the Names and Surnames of the Parents of the Seven Buddhas*, compiled by Xuanying; "pánbiǎo" (盤裱) is pronounced as "fángmiào" (方廟); it refers to the head-wrap (*lingjin*) according to the characters.
*Duojiàntuó* (多鞬陀; pronounced with the *yán* tone). *Fàngniú jīng* (放牛經; Cowherd Sūtra).

Spoken by the Buddha. Compiled by Huìlín. *Móshuā* (摩刷): The second character, *shuā*, is pronounced with the *suǒ* and *guā* tones. Guō Pǔ’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "To brush and sweep; a brush is used for cooling. Gù Yěwáng states: "Shuā also means to clip or shave. The *Shuowén* states: "Shuā means to scrape. It is composed of the radical *dāo* (knife) and the phonetic *lǐ* with the abbreviated form *shěng*. *Guā* is pronounced with the *guān* and *bā* tones.

*Yuanqi jing* (Sūtra on Dependent Origination). Compiled by Huilin. *Yu*: upper radical *yǔ* with the phonetic *yǔ*. According to the *Guǎngyá*, "to be bent" (*yǔ*) is also "to be curved. The *Kǎo shēng* says it means "to bend. The *Shuōwén* says it means "hunchbacked," composed of the radical "person" and the phonetic *qū*.

*Heiyǎn* (黑黶): The first character is pronounced *yǎn* (伊琰反). It refers to a pale black complexion; it also means a black mole. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "black flesh," composed of the radical *hei* (黑) with the phonetic *yàn* (厭).

*Sěnuǎn* (捨㬉): The second character is pronounced *nuǎn* (奴管反). Alternatively, it may be written as *shěnuǎn* (捨煗) using the radical *huǒ* (火). It means warmth. It is composed of the radical *huǒ* (火) with the phonetic *ruǎn* (耎). It also refers to the element of fire (*huǒdà*). It is composed of the radical *yuè* (曰) with the phonetic *ruǎn* (耎).

*The Scripture on the Eleven Contemplations for Recollecting the Tathāgata*, spoken by the Buddha; *The Scripture on the Eleven Contemplations for Recollecting the Tathāgata*, spoken by the Buddha (there are no characters here that can be transcribed or glossed); *The Scripture on the Four Nirayas*, spoken by the Buddha; *The Scripture on the Four Nirayas*, spoken by the Buddha; compiled by Huilin. "Dīpamkara" is a term from the Sanskrit language, which is the name Devadatta.
*Khalila* (the first character pronounced with the *qiāng* and *gā* tones and the second with the *zhī* tone) is a Sanskrit term.

In the *Anāthapiṇḍada-parivartita-sapta-putra-sūtra*, compiled by Huilin, both *Śaṅkha* (the first character pronounced with the *rǔ* and *chāng* tones and the second with the *qiáng* and *gā* tones) are Sanskrit terms. In this sutra, the character for "insect" (*chóng*) is used; however, the pronunciation *niǚ liǎng* is incorrect.

*Mahāprajāpatīparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. Regarding the term *zhūnán* (諄𨚗): Xuanying states that the ancient form is *zhùn* (訰), which is pronounced with the *zhǐ* (之) and *rén* (𨳝) finals combined. This is translated as "crushed" (*suì*) or "unrefined," and does not refer to a personal name. The text of the sutra uses the character *bó* (𣮢), which is an error.

*Fù* (阜) is pronounced *fú* (扶武反). In the *Guoyu*, regarding the phrase "to *fù* wealth and resources," Jia Dui states: "*Fù* means 'thick' (*hòu*); *fù* also means 'abundant' (*shèng*) and 'great' (*dà*). The *Cangjie pian* states: "It is a mountain that is low-lying yet vast."

*The Sūtra on the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha-Mother*, compiled by Huilin. Regarding the character "hōng" (薨): it is pronounced with the lower radical *hu* and *gēng* (肱) as the phonetic. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states that "hōng" means death. The *Guangya* says it means "to perish. According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to the death of dukes and marquises; it is composed of the radical "death" (*sǐ*) and the abbreviated form of "dream" (*mèng*) as the phonetic.

*Zhāng nán zǐ*: "Shàng" (上) is pronounced *zhǎng* (掌), with the rhyme *rǎng* (穰). Yuè Yěwáng says it is a large tree; according to the *Kǎoshēng*, it is the name of a type of wood. "Zhōng" (中) is pronounced *tán* (潭). Guō Pǐng’s commentary on the *Erya* also states it is a large tree. The vulgar form is written as *nán* (楠), and its appearance in the Classics as *péng* (棚) is an error. "Xià" (下) is pronounced *zī* (茲), with the rhyme *sǐ* (死). The *Gōngkōng Jì* says, "Among the master craftsmen of wood, the *zǐ* (梓) makes vessels. According to the *Kǎoshēng*, it is also the name of a type of wood. The *Shūjīng* says, "Pián, zǐ, yù, and zhāng [are trees]. This refers to it.

*Xūxī* (上許居反): Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states that it is the sound of sobbing. Gu Yewang says that "xu" refers to the breath exhaled from the mouth; the *Shuowen Jiezi* also defines it as exhaled breath, composed of the radical "mouth" with "xū" as the phonetic component. *Xǐ* (下喜衣反): this means to sigh in pain. It denotes sorrow without weeping. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is composed of the radical "mouth" with "xī" as the phonetic component.

*The Scripture on King Prasenajit’s Ten Dreams Spoken by the Buddha*, compiled by Huilin. Regarding the character *kǎo* (尻): the *Shēngyùn* states that it refers to the hidden part [of the body]. The *Yílǐ* states, "The two thighs are attached to the *kǎo*. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical *shī* (尸) and the phonetic *jiǔ* (九).

*Ānanda-tongxué-jīng* (The Sūtra on Ānanda’s Fellow Students), spoken by the Buddha and compiled by Huìlín. *Nǐ* (親昵): In the *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Book of Poetry), it says: “*Nǐ* means near. Guō Pǐng’s commentary on the *Eryā* also states that it means “intimate and near. Dù Yǒu’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* likewise states that *nǐ* means “intimate. According to the *Shuōwén Jiězì*, it is composed of the radical 日 (sun) with the phonetic 尼; alternatively, it is written as 暱 with the phonetic 匿.

In the *Pañcaskandha-śūnyatā-sūtra* (Five Aggregates Are All Empty Sutra) as spoken by the Buddha, there are no characters for which phonetic glosses can be provided. Regarding the *Saptasthāna-trivipaśyanā-sūtra* (Sutra on the Seven Stations and Three Contemplations), Xuanying’s commentary states that the character "zhù" (拄) is pronounced with the initial *chǐ* and the final *-lǚ* (亦陟縷反); it means to prop or support. In the sutra text, the character is written with the radical "foot" (足) as "zhù" (跓), which is a vulgar character.

The character 𩕳 (dǐng) is pronounced with the "tǐng" rhyme. The *Cangjie pian* states that it means "the crown of the head" (*diān*). The *Guangya* says it means "the top," and the *Ziyuan* says it means "the top of the head. Nowadays, in common parlance, the crown of the head is called *dǐng-ling*.

The *Ārya-dharmamudrā-sūtra*, spoken by the Buddha. Compiled by Huilin. *Wei*: (pinyin: wéi; *zhōngyùn*: wéi, reversed from *gui*). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "Wei denotes reverence; no denotes assent. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic "zhuī" (*zhuī*). Below is "náng" (pinyin: luò) with an alternative pronunciation of "érzhě" (*érzhě*). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states: "No is a word used for responding. He Xiu’s commentary on the *Gongyang Zhuan* states: "A word used when receiving speech. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic "ruò" (*ruò*).

The *Wuyin piyu jing* (Sūtra of Similes on the Five Aggregates), compiled by Huilin. Regarding the character "pī" (劈): according to the *Guoyu*, it means to split or cleave; the *Bicang* also states it means to divide; and the *Shuowen* defines it as to break, formed from the radical "knife" (刀) with the phonetic "bì" (辟).

Regarding the *Fo shuo shuimao suo diao jing* (The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on Being Washed Away by Water Froth), compiled by Hui Lin: "Ju mo" (聚沫) [is read with] the second character as *man bo* (滿鉢) in reverse; Gu Yewang states that "mo" (沫) refers to the froth floating upon water. Wang’s commentary on the *Chu ci* (Songs of Chu) states that "mo" (沫) refers to tiny droplets of foam. In the standard characters of antiquity and today, it is written with the radical "water" (水) and the phonetic "ma" (末).
Regarding "yīhù" (依怙): according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means to rely upon or depend on; it is composed of the radical "heart" (心) with "gǔ" (古) as its phonetic.

Regarding "yùnyì" (雲曀): according to the *Mao Shi Zhuan*, when it is cloudy and windy, it is called "yì"; according to the *Wenzi Dian*, it is composed of the radical "sun" (日) with "yī" (壹) as its phonetic.

The *Buzishouyi jing* (Sūtra on Not Guarding One’s Intent) and the *Zhuanfalun jing* (Sūtra on Turning the Wheel of Dharma). Regarding these two sūtras above, there are no characters for which phonetic glosses can be provided.

The Sūtra on the Three Turnings of the Wheel of Dharma, spoken by the Buddha; compiled by Huilin. The *Bārāṇasī-ṛṣi-sūtra*. "Nǐ" (the first character) is pronounced *nǎn* (with the second tone) and *xiá* (with the fourth tone); it is a transliteration of a Sanskrit word.

*The Scripture on the Eightfold Noble Path*, *The Scripture on the Explanation of Nandi*, *The Scripture on the Eightfold Noble Path with Phonetic Transcriptions*, and *The Scripture on the Explanation of Nandi*. Compiled by Huilin. "Zuàn" (纂): Pronounced *zuǎn* (with the second tone). The *Guoyu* states that it means "to bore through"; Gu Yewang says it means "to engrave. The collective definition is "to pierce"; it is an iron tool for penetrating objects. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to pierce," composed of the radical "metal" (*金*) and the phonetic "zàn" (*贊*).

The *Sūtra on the Three Characteristics of Horses* (*Bā-yeou san-siang king*). The *Sūtra on the Three Characteristics of Horses* contains no phonetic glosses. The *Sūtra on the Eight Manners of Horses Compared to Humans* (*Bā-yeou pa-t'ai pi-jen king*). Transcribed by Xuanying: *chēlíng* (also written as 󲢙), with the same pronunciation as *lìtíng* (力庭反). According to the *Shuowen*, it is the transverse wood between the poles of a carriage; it is the *chēlíngzǐ* (車軨子).

*Mamo* (the "sha" in *sanghe* is pronounced as such): according to the *Shenglü*, *mamo* means to touch or stroke; it also means to wipe or smear (*mo*). The pronunciation of *mo* is *mogai*; *san* is *soga*.
*Xi* (pronounced *shi*) and *shi* (pronounced *she*): according to the *Guangya*, *xi* means to drink; *shi* means to bite or to eat.
*Pǐ* (pronounced *pǔmǐ*): The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "a head [tilted]"; the *Cangjie pian* defines it as "not upright"; the *Guangya* defines it as "crooked.
Regarding the *Xiangying xiangke jing*, the *Egui baoying jing*, and the *Guiwen mulian jing*: these three aforementioned scriptures all lack phonetic transcriptions or glosses for this character.
From the *Zàzàng jīng* (Saṃyukta-piṭaka-sūtra), compiled by Xuanying: *Yùn* (pronounced yùn, with the rhyme of *yùn*) means to ferment. In the *Cāngjié piān*, it refers to the mother-yeast for wine;

according to the *Guǎngyá*, "to *yùn*" means to pour in [ingredients]. *Zīshū* (pronounced zī, with the rhyme of *lí*)—the *Guǎngyá* states it means wealth; the *Cāngjié piān* states it means property. According to the *Shuōwén*, it refers to redeeming oneself from a minor punishment with wealth. Under the Han laws, there was the "no corvée labor" based on *zī*, and the practice of appointing men as *láng* (officials) based on their *zī*—all refer to this. The scriptural text uses the character *zī* (from the radical for speech), which means to measure or estimate; however, that sense does not apply here.

In the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, according to the compilation by Xuanying, the ancient characters are written as 𨽁 and 中; the archaic forms are 𨞮 and 󲜤, both of which are now written as 聚 (pronounced *jù*). According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to dwell," referring to a place where people gather and reside.

*Tianjia* (田家) is read as *tú nián* (徒年) according to the *Erya*, where *tian* (田) means "land. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "to plant rice and grain is called *tian*. The text here reads *tiàn* (佃), which is read as *tú jiàn* (徒見) or *tú nián* (徒年). The *Shuowen* defines *tiàn* as "the middle. The *Spring and Autumn Annals* commentary says, "riding in the middle *tiàn*" refers to a single-axle chariot; however, *tiàn* does not carry this meaning here.

Regarding "Jutan" (具譚), it is pronounced *tu* with the second tone (*nán fǎn*). In the scriptures, this is frequently written as *Gautama*; its correct pronunciation is *Qiáodámó* (喬荅摩). This is a clan name derived from the name of a seer (*ṛṣi*).
Furthermore, regarding "Chasheng" (叉勝), it is pronounced *tu* with the fourth tone (*dèng fǎn*), meaning "to penetrate" (*tōng*). The scriptural text writes it as *Tóudèng* (投鄧), which is incorrect.
The character 󲬶𫕈 is missing its ancient pronunciation.
First, 挈 (kù jié): the phonetic reversal is kǔ jié; "to lift" (*ti*) is its meaning. The *Shuowen* states that "to lift" means to hold up by suspending; it also means to strike. Next, 憂懣 (yōu mǎn):

the ancient text uses 懣 interchangeably; the phonetic reversal is mò běn. The *Shuowen* states that "懣" means vexation (*fán*). The *Cangjie pian* states that "懣" means distress (*mèn*) and also indignation (*fèn*).

*Nǎo* (憂惱): According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to have resentment or pain. Today, when people of Runan have something they resent, they say "daonao" (大惱), and nowadays this is all written as *nǎo*.

*Shìniào* (矢溺): It is also written as *bèi*. The *Shuowen* writes it as *fèn* (𦳊), both with the same pronunciation *shǐzhǐ* (式旨反). It means feces and urine. The lower character's standard form is *wēiniào* (浘尿), both forms having the same pronunciation *nàidiào* (乃吊反). The form used in the scriptures as *niào* (溺) is merely a phonetic loan.
*Shǔ* (屬) should be read as *yú* (盂), with the same pronunciation as *Yǔ* (禹).

*Yú* refers to a vessel. *Duì* (兊) is pronounced *tú wài*. It means "joy" (*yuè*) or "to appear. Furthermore, the shape of *duì* is called "a face of display" (*tuòmiàn*), being broad at one end and narrow at the other. *Tuò* is pronounced *tāng guǒ*.

"Za za" (pronounced with the "xu" and "yuan" finals) refers to the state where the family way has not yet been established; the following instances are identical. "Zhuang bai" (pronounced with the "zhuang" and "bai" finals) refers to the sound of "za za.
The four scrolls below follow the ancient phonetic glosses of Xuanying; although this scripture is not included in the Kaiyuan Catalogue, it is preserved here without omission.
*The Secret Essentials for Healing the Illnesses of Dhyāna*, Volume One, compiled by Xuanying. Volume One: The character *shù* (樹) is first read as *kǎi* (揩) without a specific phonetic;

*yuǎnquǎn* (縈綣) is pronounced with the upper radical *yuǎn* (遠) and the lower *quǎn* (袪, *wǎn* rhyme). *Quǎnquǎn* (綣綣) is synonymous with *quǎn* (綣); "to be *xiànquǎn*" (繾綣) means not to be separated from one another.
*Yóuyán* (also written as *yóu*, with the same pronunciation as *yúzhōu*)—according to the *Fāngyán*, it is also called *rù'ěr* ("entering the ear"). 2.
Second Fascicle. *Cán mó* (the character for *mó* has the phonetic *gè*)—the *Shuowén* defines it as "the membrane between the flesh. The text of the sutra uses *mò*, which is an error.

*Tòu* (pronounced *tòu* with the second tone, according to the *Dìānshì*): In the local dialects of Song, Wèi, and South Chǔ, this means to startle; the *Guǎngyá* states that *tòu* means to burn. *Biāo* (pronounced *biāo* with the second tone, according to the *Běiyáo*):
The *Guǎngyá* states it refers to the formation of an abscess; the *Bǐcāng* states it is a carbuncle (*biāojū*); the *Shuōwén* states that a carbuncle is a long-standing abscess.
3. Third Fascicle. *Gāi* (古來反): The *Shuowen* states this refers to the root of a plant. The *Fangyan* notes that in the region of Dongqi, the root of a plant is called *gāi*.

*Cà* (子臘反): The *Shuowen* states this means to hold in the mouth. The *Pīcāng* states it means to bite the lips; its meaning is identical to *zhà* (to sip). It means to sip blood. The *Tōngsùwén* writes it as "the master entering the mouth. In the *Zhuangzi*, it appears as *qì*; "mosquitoes and gadflies *qì* the skin" is an example of this.
"Hóng" (pronounced hóng, with the first tone) means "deep and vast" according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*; the *Guangya* states that "hóng" means "deep.
"Pén" (written as 排 or 𣞙, pronounced pújiè) refers to a bellows used by blacksmiths for fanning the fire. These two characters share the same radical and pronunciation.
*Kánggǔ* (the cervical vertebrae) is also written as *wán*; both share the same pronunciation as *táng* (dipper). According to the *Cāngjiépiān*, it refers to the throat;
according to the *Shuōwén*, it refers to the neck. *Dǒupó* is sometimes called *tōupó* or *tápó*; the correct term is *sūdǔpō*, which translates to "temple" (*miào*).

The Secret Essential Dharma for Treating the Illnesses of Meditation, compiled by Xuanying. *Chīxiū* (Owl): according to the *Erya*, it is a "strange owl" (*guǐchī*). Shen Ren says its other names are "strange bird" (*guǐniǎo*) and *xiūliú*. In Nanyang it is called *gōuyē*. The *Zilin* states it is the *chīxiū*.
Āji (the "ji" rhymes with *wū* and *gài*; the Sanskrit term is *ājīka*, which here refers to the *vetāla*, or "corpse-raising ghost").

Regarding the character *xiāo* (the "xiāo" rhymes with *jí* and *yáo*): the *Mao Shi Cao Mu Shu* states that it is the *liúlí* bird; from the Guanzhong region westward, the *xiāo* is called *liúlí*. When its young grow large, they return to eat their mother. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* identifies it as the *tǔxiāo* (earth-owl). The text's reading of it as *jiāo* is incorrect.

The character for *chù* (處) is pronounced *bìlì* (𤹝, with the fanqie 畢利); according to the *Shuowen*, it means "the breath does not reach the feet. The text of the sutra uses the character *bǐ* (肶), which shares the same pronunciation as *bǐ* (鼻尸反). *Bì* (䏶) is not used here. In the *Lunyu*, regarding the passage "Even Yao and Shun found it difficult [to do this]," Kong Yingda’s commentary states: "‘Bìng’ (病) means difficulty."

The four volumes mentioned above are not included in the *Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu*. Regarding the *Zhichanbing Biyao Fa Jing* (The Secret Essential Dharma for Treating the Illnesses of Meditation): it was compiled by Huilin.

The term "pīlì" (霹靂)—the first character pronounced as *pǐ* (with the radical *mi* reversed) and the second as *líng*—is described in the *Shiji* as "the movement of yang energy. Gu Yewang states it is "a great thunderclap," and Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* defines it as "the sudden strike of thunder. All standard characters from antiquity to the present use the "rain" radical (*雨*) and are pronounced with the same phonetic (*pìlì*). The version of this scripture that uses the "foot" radical (*足*) to form *bèi* (躃) or *lì* (躋) is incorrect.

Regarding the character *ru* (乳): the *Yǔjiā* states that it means "to give birth. The *Shuowén* says: "To give birth to offspring, whether human or bird, is called *ru*; for beasts, it is called *chǎn* (產). It is composed of *fú* (孚) and *yǐ* (乙); *yǐ* refers to the *xuánniǎo* (玄鳥, swallow), with the phonetic *dīnglì* (丁歷). [The *Shuowén* further states: "Water falling and adhering to objects is called *ru*. It is composed of *shuǐ* (水) and the phonetic *chì* (啻)."

"Mi-zhì" (密緻): The upper character is pronounced *mín* (旻) with a *bǐ* (筆) final. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that "mi" means "examination" (*shěn*). The *Guǎngyá* says it means "tranquility. The *Shuowén* writes it as *fú* (宓), meaning "serene and still," composed of *mián* (宀) and the phonetic *bì* (必). It is also written as "mi" (密). The lower character is pronounced *chí-lì* (馳利) with a *shēng* (聲) final. The *Kǎoshēng* states that "mi-zhì" refers to the density of silk fabrics; the correct orthography for both ancient and modern times uses the radical *mì* (糸) with the phonetic *zhì* (致).

*Qíng* (to lift/hold up). The rhyme is *jìng* (as in *jìng*). The *Guǎngyá* states that *qíng* means "to raise. Lexicons show it written with the radical *gǒng* (the hands joined) and the phonetic *gǒng*, forming *qíng*; it is also written as *nǐ* or *ní*, both of which are archaic forms. The *Wénzìdiǎn* explains that it takes the radical *shǒu* (hand) and the phonetic *jìng*. To write it with the radical *mǎ* (horse) as *jīng* is incorrect. Below is *zhù* (rhyme *yòng*). Guō’s commentary on the *Mùchóng Tiānzǐ Zhuan* states that *tuìng* means "breast milk. People in Jiangnan today also call breast milk *tuìng*. The correct character for ancient and modern usage takes the radical *shuǐ* (water) and the phonetic *chóng*.

The character for *zhēn* (needle) is pronounced with the initial *rèn* (任). The *Guǎngyá* states that "a needle is a piercing instrument. Gù Yěwáng says it is "that which fastens clothing. The *Kǎoshēng* says, "A needle is that by which one sews clothing; it is the thread. The *Shuōwén* says, "It means to sew; it follows the radical for metal (*jīn*) and takes *xián* as its phonetic component. The character for *zhuì* (to attach/fasten) is pronounced *duīruì* (追銳); the second character [of the following entry] is pronounced *zǔguān* (祖官). The *Mèngzi* says, "To *zuàn* (drill) is to pierce through. The *Shuōwén* says, "That by which objects are pierced; it follows the radical for metal (*jīn*) and takes *zàn* as its phonetic component. It is also written with the radical for knife (*dāo*) as *càn* (劗), with the same pronunciation.

The character for "sucking" (欶) is pronounced *xìng* in the first tone and *shuāng-chuò* in the second tone. The *Cāngjié piān* states that "sucking" (*chù*) is synonymous with "inhaling" (*hà*). The *Wénzì jílüè* says it means to draw [liquid] into the mouth with the lips. The *Shuōwén* says "sucking" (*chù*) means to suckle; it is composed of the radical *qiàn* and the phonetic *shù*. The version in the sutra written as *cǎo* (𡂡) is incorrect.

*Dōngrán* (烔然) is pronounced *dú dōng* in the upper [radical] entry; the *Pīcāng* states that "dōng-dōng" describes the appearance of heat. The *Hánshī* says "dōng-dōng" describes the appearance of drought. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* explains that it follows the radical for fire and shares the same phonetic element as *tóng*.
