The *Buddhacarita-saṃyukta-sūtra*, sixty volumes, Volume One, compiled by Xuanying. Volume One of the *Buddhacarita-saṃyukta-sūtra*, Volume One, compiled by Xuanying. *Kalandaka*: Sometimes called *Kelantuo*, sometimes written as *Jialantuojiā*, or *Jielantuojiā*. These are all variations in the weight of the Sanskrit pronunciation. This is translated as "the bird of beautiful voice. According to foreign records, its shape resembles that of a magpie; however, this bird gathers in flocks and mostly dwells in bamboo groves. Formerly, there was a king who was sleeping in a grove when a snake came intending to bite him. The bird cried out and woke him. The king, grateful for its kindness, scattered food to nourish the bird. The master of the grove, a layman, subsequently took this as its name, calling it *Kalandaka*. Originally, non-Buddhist practitioners resided there, but later they came to revere the Tathāgata.
*Jina* (also transcribed as *Shina* or *Shina*), translated here as "Victorious" (*sheng*), signifies the most supreme.

*Chuangpu* (the second character pronounced with the *pu* rhyme of *hu*) means, according to the *Guangyi*, to spread out or lay out; it also means to distribute or to extend. An example is found in the *Liji*: "He spreads out the stools and mats."

*Vyākaraṇa* (ji-bie; the "bie" is pronounced like *pie*, meaning "to distinguish" or "to analyze"). In older translations, this term is often written as "yin-zhu," and the text is sometimes written with the "cao" radical instead of "bie"—this is incorrect.

*Vairocana* is also called *Veḷuñcana* or *Vilozana*. This is translated as "Pervasive Illumination" (*Biànzhào*). The character "lu" is absent in some manuscripts; the meaning is established by adding the mouth radical. The pronunciation of "lu" should be *lù* (with the second tone).

Śuddhāvāsa—alternatively called Śuddhavāsa or Sthitāvāsa; *śuddha* means "pure" (*jing*) and *vāsa* means "palace" (*gong*), "abode" (*she*), or "dwelling" (*chu*). This refers to the Five Pure Abodes (*pañca śuddhāvāsakāyikā devāḥ*).

2. Second Fascicle. The *Shi* (Classic of Poetry) says: "He was born at the fullness of the months. The *Zhuan* (Commentary) states: "‘Dàn’ means ‘great. The *Jian* (Sub-commentary) explains: "It is great that Houji, having completed the course of human gestation, was born after ten months."

*Chénggézi* (層閣子): the character *chéng* is pronounced as *héng* with a second tone; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to a multi-storied building. The *Shanhaijing* speaks of "cloud-canopies" (*yúngài*) in three layers; Guo Pu states that "layer" (*chéng*) means "repeated" (*chóng*) and also "accumulated" (*lèi*).

"Suddenly" (*kàrán*)—the mouth [of the character] is reversed; in the *Chuci* (Songs of the South), "I would rather die suddenly and let my life flow away," Wang Yi says that "suddenly" (*kà*) means "abruptly" (*yǎn*).

In the *Guǎngpǐ*, "suddenly" (*kà*) means "to rely upon. Regarding "bìlì": the *Cuànwén* states that "bìlì" is the name of a musical instrument of the Qiang and Hu peoples; the scriptural text writes it as "bìlù" (篳篥).

The ancient forms for "to lick" are 舓 and 𦧇; the modern form is 刮, and it is also written as 舐, both pronounced *shí* (with the phonetic component *shí* and radical *mouth*). It means to take food with the tongue. Below, it is also written as 嗽, pronounced *sòu* (with the phonetic component *sòu* and radical *mouth*), as well as in the *Tōngsùwén*, where "inhaling and sucking" is called *chù*. In the *Sāncāng*, *chù* means to suckle; the pronunciation of *yǔn* (suckle) is *sìyuǎn* (with the phonetic component *sì* and radical *mouth*).

3. Third Fascicle. The "Lord of the Eight Edges" (bāshān zhǔ) refers to the master of the eight edges of the world. The *Yìnyì* (Explanations of Pronunciations and Meanings) to the *Hànshū* states: "The eight edges are the eight boundaries of the earth."

*Shù* (巷術): The character *shù* is pronounced with the lips reversed [i.e., *shù*]. In the *Cāngjié piān*, it is stated that "the roads within a city are called *shù*; they are thoroughfares. *Yè* (抴我夷世反又作曳廣疋曳引也說文曳申也牽也):

The character *yè* is pronounced with the lips reversed as *yí* or *shì*, and is also written as *yè*. In the *Guǎngyǐ*, it says "to drag" (*yè yǐn yě*). In the *Shuōwén*, it says "to extend" (*yè shēn yě*) and "to pull" (*qiān yě*).

Volume Four, Part Four. No phonetic glosses provided for the preceding section. Volume Five, Part Five. *Xiāoqīng* (鵁鶄): A name for a bird; its sound is *jiāoqīng*. It is also called the *xiāolúcí* (鵁鸕鶿) bird. On Mount Mánlián, they fly in flocks like hens and resemble the *shéngǎozú* (𠒎高足). They are kept in the regions between the Yangtze and Huai Rivers to ward off fire.

The *guīáo* (龜鼇)—the character for *guī* being pronounced as *gāo*—is the great turtle in the ocean of the "Forest of Seas" (*Zǐlín Hǎi*), whose strength bears Mount Píngyíng and Mount Hú; it is this very mountain.

The *báilù* (白鷺)—in lexicographical texts written as *lú* (鸕), pronounced as *láisu*—is a white bird with long feathers on its head, wings, and back; in Jiangdong, these are taken to make false eyelashes, called the "white heron’s collar" (*báilù cí*)—the character for *cí* being pronounced as *sūléi*.

Lúyù (the character for "lú" is pronounced with the *lang* and *dou* finals; the character below is also written as 鵜 and is identical; the character for "yù" is pronounced *cái* and *zī*; according to the *Zílín*, the lúyù resembles a *wǜ* bird but is black; it is an aquatic bird whose beak is curved like a hook, and it feeds on fish; this bird gives birth from within its womb, disgorging the young from inside its mouth; one brood produces eight or nine; in China, it is sometimes called the "water crow"; *wǜ* is pronounced *wǔ* and *lì*).
6. Fascicle Six. *Jiǎo-yu*: According to the *Zìlín*, that which has a fence is called a *yuàn* (enclosure), while that which lacks a fence is called a *yòu* (park).

A *yòu* is also a restricted enclosure (*jìn-yuàn*). *Shùjǐ*: In the *Yǐyá*, "shùjǐ" means "to hope for" (*shàng*) or "to take one's chance" (*xìng*). Guō Pǔ says: "Shùjǐ" means to seek fortune (*jiāoxìng*). "Shù" is to hope; "jǐ" is to take one's chance. To hope for the path of goodness is "shù. "Jǐ" also means "subtle" (*wēi*).

7. Fascicle Seven. *Wéi* (the first character is pronounced with the initial *niú* and final *huí*; the second is pronounced with the initial *lǜ* and final *wěi*). According to the *Shuōwén*, it means "high and level. *Zuǐ* (the mountain-like appearance). *Shì* (pronounced with the initial *shí* and final *chuò*).

According to the *Shuōwén*, it means "to sip and taste. In the *Ěrǔpǐ*, it says "to sip and chew. Guo Pu said: "To sip" means to pick up food. The *Tōngsùwén* writes it as *yè*. Today, we generally refer to fine foods as *chùe*.

*Qianmo* (阡陌): *Jianfan Fengsu Tong* states that those running north-south are called *qian* and those running east-west are called *mo*. The *Guangyi* defines *mo* as a road. The *Shiji* records that Duke Mu of Qin destroyed the well-drains and mortars and opened up the *qian* and *mo*.

Examining the character dictionaries, "jiàn" (鑑) is pronounced the same as "gǎn" (鑱). The *Guǎngyǐ* states: "Jiàn means to illuminate; jiàn refers to a mirror. The *Shijing* says: "My heart is not like a mirror," and its commentary states: "A mirror is that by which one examines one's form."

*Yùn* (pregnant): In archaic texts, it is written as *yí*. According to the *Sāncāng*, it means to carry a child in the womb. The *Guǎngyǐ* states that *yùn* means *huái* (to harbor). The character is composed of the radical "child" (*zǐ*) and the phonetic "nǎi.

*Lánpí*: Pronounced *lìhán* (or alternatively *liúpíní* or *línméiní*; the correct pronunciation is *lánfànní*). This translates to "salt. It was originally the name of a gardener (*zhǒuyuán*) in antiquity, and the garden was named after him. *Fànánà* (Pāṇa) translates to "forest" (*lín*) in Chinese; it is also translated as "place of liberation," "extinction," or "severance. *Fàn* is pronounced *fǔwǎn*.

"Sān-děng" (鞍隥): "deng" is pronounced as in *dèng* (鄧). It refers to the stirrup (*mǎ-děng*), which is what one steps upon when mounting a horse; the text reads it as "dēng" (鐙), an ancient form of the character for "lamp" (*dēng*). *Kēng-qiang* (鏗鏘) is also written as *xuān* (銵), both pronounced as in *kǔ-gēng* (苦耕);

the second character is also written as *qiāng* (瑲), both pronounced as in *qiě-yáng* (且羊). According to the *Guǎngpǐ*, *xuān* and *qiāng* denote metallic sounds. In the *Lǐjì*, it is said that Zixia listened to their *kēng-qiang*. Furthermore, the *Zìlín* states that [the first character] is pronounced as in *héng* (衡), while the *Bīcāng* states that *qiāng* is a metallic sound.

Jìngyǒng (勁勇): "Ju" (居) is pronounced gùdìngfǎn; "fǎn" (反) is pronounced fǎn. In the *Zílín* (字林), "jìng" (勁) means strong and powerful; the character is composed of the radical "force" (力) with "xīng" (巠) as the phonetic component.

Xīng is pronounced gǔdìngfǎn. Sèhóng (色虹): "Hú" (胡) is pronounced gōngfǎn. Guō Pǔ’s *Ěrpǐ Yīnyì* (爾疋音義) states: "The double appearance of rainbows—those that are brilliant and intense are called 'māle' (雄); the 'māle' is called hóng (虹). Those that are dim are called 'female' (雌); the 'female' is called nǐ (蜺). Nǐ may also be written as ní (霓). Ní is pronounced wǔxífǎn; the vulgar pronunciation is gǔxiàngfǎn. It is a blue-green rainbow."

8. The Eighth Fascicle. Although [the character] *pǔ* (蒲卜反) is used here, it means "to dry" (*qīn xī*). The character is composed of the radical for "sun" (*yù*), "to emerge" (*chū*), and "to hold with both hands" (*kùn*) along with "grain" (*mǐ*). The meaning of the character is thus [to dry grain]. *Kùn* may also be written as *bài* (拜), which is the same; it is pronounced *jù xiōng fǎn* and means "to hold together."

*Āndha* (黤黮) is also written as *ān-ta* (黭黮), both pronounced with the first character having the phonetic *wu-gǎn* and the second having *tā-gǎn*; it means "not bright. The *Zuǎnwén* states that *āndhāndha* refers to a deep black.

*Kalmāṣapāda* (迦𨍟) is pronounced with the first character having the phonetic *zè-jī*; it is the name of a king. Kalmāṣapāda was born from the arm of a man, like King Mūrdhaja (*Dǐngshēngwáng*) and others.
*Xiǎokūhū* (熇拘呼) [the characters *kū* and *lǎo* have two readings each]: This is the Ikṣvāku lineage of the royal clan. *Jiāngshí* (礓石):

[The character *jiāng* is pronounced *jū* with the *liáng* tone; its shape is like ginger. According to the *Tōngsúwén*, ground containing many small stones is called *jiānglì* (礓礫); the character is written with the "stone" radical (*shí*), whereas the form in the canonical texts (*jīngwén*) using the "earth" radical (*tǔ*) is incorrect.

*Jiě* (屩) [pronounced *jūè*]: In the *Shǐjì*, it says "to wear *jiě* and carry a *dēng*. The *Guǎngyǐ* states: "*Jiě* refers to straw sandals (*cǎofèi*). *Féi* (扉) [pronounced *fúwèi*]: It means sandals; it is also called *fù* (屨) or *lǚ* (履). *Dēng* (簦) [pronounced *dūhéng*]: It refers to a large bamboo hat (*lì*) that has a handle.

*Quanti* (or *qiāntí*) means "that which can be moved," as it refers to being lifted and carried; alternatively, it is written as *xuāntí*, meaning it is made from *xuān* grass. It is not a product of this region, but originates from Mount Kunlun.

9. Ninth Fascicle. Regarding the character for *yìng* (媵), the *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *yǎn* (𠊶), which is identical [in meaning]. Other evidence: it is pronounced either *zhèng* (證) or *èr* (二). In the *Ervu*, *yìng* means "to escort"; that is, to escort a woman [to her husband's house] is called *yìng*. The *Gongyang Zhuan* states: "As for *yìng*, what is it? When several feudal lords gather from one state, two states go to escort her, accompanied by her younger sisters (*zhí* and *cí*). The *Shiming* explains: "*Yìng* means 'to receive' (*chéng*); it refers to receiving service for the primary wife and attending to her."
*Kan-ta* (in the *Six Perfections Collection*, it is written as *Guan-de*; the correct pronunciation is *Jian-tuo-ga*, which translates as "to receive" or "to take").
*Kan* (pronounced with the first tone) means "uneven" according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*; *ji* also means "to destroy."

*Ōu* (齵): Pronounced *gōu* (牛) and *jù* (俱), with the second character reversed; according to the *Shuowen*, it means teeth are not straight. According to the *Cangjie pian*, it means teeth have grown back. It refers to teeth that are uneven and not level. *Rì* (毦): Pronounced *rén* (人) and *zhì* (志);
according to the *Guangyi*, it is a type of coarse wool (*táng*). To weave hair or wool is called *jī*; *táng* is the pronunciation for *rì*.

*Zhízhú* (躑躅) is also written as *zhì* (󲟑), with the same pronunciation [chén] for both characters; the second character is also written as *wénzú* (󲱹), with the same pronunciation [wénzú]. According to the *Zílín*, it means "to halt one's steps and not move forward. The *Guǎngpǐ* states: "Zhí, zhù, chí, and rú [are synonyms]."
"不覿" (bù dí): "覿" is pronounced tìng-lì-fǎn. In the *Erlǚ* and *Xiǎnzǎo*, "覿" means "to see.
"黑皯" (hēi gǎn): "皯" is pronounced gǔ-hàn-fǎn. According to the *Tōngsúwén*, it refers to dark spots or freckles on the face. The text of the sutra uses the character "䵟," which is incorrect.

"Gōngbà" (弓把): "bà" is pronounced as in "baiyǎ" (百雅) when used alone; it means "to grasp. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "bà" means "to hold. The character used in the sutra is "bà" (弝), which is a vulgarized form of this word.
"Chòuzhé" (皺襵): "zhé" is pronounced as in "zhīshè" (之涉); it means "not extended. "Zhē" (摺), "qūn" (欇), and "zhé" (襵)—all are written with this character. It refers to being wrinkled or folded.

The character *li* (理) is an archaic form identical to *yu* (𥬰), pronounced with the rhyme *chū-zé*. It refers to bamboo slips (*jiǎn*). Those that are long are two chi, while those that are short are half that length; the next grade consists of one long and one short slip, which again imitates the natural form.
The two characters *liǎng* (兩) and *jūn* (𢫪) are also written as *wǎn* (椀), with the same pronunciation as *wū huàn* (烏喚).

This refers to the joint at the back of the hand. Volume Ten, Chapter Ten. The characters *tú* (顱) and *sàng* (顙) are also written as *wù* (髗), with the same pronunciation as *lù hú* (鹿胡) and *chǐ xià* (尺下). According to the *Shuowen*, *lú* (䫳) means "the skull. According to the *Zishu*, it means "the lid of the brain. The *Guangyi* states that *dùn lú* (頓顱) is called *lù* (䫫) or *lú* (䫳). The *Fangyan* says that *sàng* (顙) and *yǎn* (𬱃) are synonyms. *Dùn* (頓) is pronounced *tú gè* (徒各).

*Shānrán* (澘然): The character *bān* (斑) and *bǎn* (板) are both read with two tones; according to the *Zìlín*, it describes the appearance of tears flowing down. It is as stated in the *Shī*: "With a sorrowful sigh (*shānrán*), tears flowed forth.
*Shēncuì* (身祟): *Sī* and *zuì* are read with two tones; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means a divine calamity. This refers to ghosts and spirits bringing about disasters and misfortunes.
*Jiǎojiǎn* (pronounced *jiǎn* with the rhyme of *yǎn*): the abbreviated form of the character is "eye. It refers to the skin covering the exterior of the eye.
*Bēiwǎn* (pronounced *wǎn* with the rhyme of *huàn*): the abbreviated form of the character is "wǎn-huàn.

It means to be startled or amazed. *Bèi* (pronounced *pú-lài*): according to the *Guǎngpǐ*, it means "north," "behind," or "to oppose. It signifies abandoning, turning away from, or being contrary to. In the scriptural texts, this character is frequently written as *bèi* (from the radical for "man").

"Yú" (愉) [with the phonetic "yì" reversed to "zhū"; the *Zuǎnwén* writes it as "fúyú," meaning beautiful complexion]. The *Fāngyán* writes it as "fú," meaning joy. "Fúyú" refers to a countenance that is harmonious and joyful. The pronunciation of "fú" is "fāngjù" reversed.

"Bì" (pronounced *pǔ dí* according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, meaning "to split"; *Guoyaya*, "to crack open"; *Beicang*, "to cleave") has the phonetic *yǐn pī pí* (according to the dialects of Jiangnan). In the *Puxing jing* (Sutra on Universal Practice), it is read only as *pǔ dí*.
*Jiàn*: (Ancient pronunciation: hú; *Shuowen*: the sound of a child crying; *Guangya*: *jiàn jiàn* is wailing; this refers to the passage in the *Shangshu*: "Qi [Yu] wailed *jiàn jiàn* and wept.
*Fēn*: (Pronounced fū yún; *Shuowen*: *fēn* is an auspicious vapor. According to the text, "auspicious" (*xiáng*) refers to that which is first seen as a sign of good fortune.)
11. The eleventh fascicle. *Pū* (pronounced with the *hu* rhyme).
*Śin* (pronounced with the *shi* rhyme).
*Duo* (pronounced with the *du* rhyme).
The character 󱶐 (zhì) is pronounced with the rhyme of rén (人);
the character 吒 (zhà) is pronounced with the rhyme of zhé jiā (陟家);
the character 侘 (chà) is pronounced with the rhyme of chì jiā (勅家).
The character 𠻬 (zhì) is pronounced with the rhyme *jiā*.
The character 拏 (ná) is pronounced with the rhyme *jiā*. The character 󲠚 (nǎi) is pronounced with the rhyme *kě*.
The character 麼 (mò) is pronounced with the rhyme *kě*.

The character *jiǎo* (勦) is explained in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as being identical to *jiǎo* (𢯇), with the phonetic transcription *zhù jiāo* (助交反). It means "swift and agile," referring to being vigorous, rapid, and robust. In the Middle Kingdom, the term *qiān* (勬) is frequently used; its pronunciation is *jiāng quán* (姜權反).

The character 𠞈 (pronounced *dǐng*, with the rhyme of *hé* in the *Zìshū*) means "to attach" (*zhù*). The characters 𠞈、鉤、𠞈、索、𠞈, etc., are all written with this [radical]. The text of this sutra uses 搭, which is incorrect.

Furthermore, 指撝 (also written as 麾, both pronounced *huī* with the rhyme of *xǔ pí*) refers to what the hand points toward; it is called *huī* because one commands by pointing with a banner or standard, hence the name.
"Dìwěn" (地穩)—the "wěn" is pronounced as in "wǔběn" (烏本)—means peaceful and secure.
"Jìngù" (靳固)—the "jìn" is pronounced as in "jūjìn" (居近)—means stingy or parsimonious.

"Jíqiè" (𩤪䶢)—the first character is pronounced as in "shìjiá" (仕洽) and the second as in "yújiá" (魚洽)—refers to a person who performs acrobatics or plays for amusement. The text of the scripture uses "jiéxī" (唊噏); "jié" is pronounced as in "gǔxié" (古協) and "xī" as in "xǔjí" (許及), but this is not the usage intended here.
The character *biǎo* (騗) is pronounced with the initial *pī* (匹面反); its abbreviated form is *biǎo* (𪏭), meaning "the horse above.

The characters *pī* (批) and *wǎn* (椀) are also written as *bō* (𢱧), both with the pronunciation *pújié* (蒲結反). According to the *Guǎngyá*, *bō* means "to turn over" (*zhuǎn*). In the *Zuǒzhuan*, it says, "He *bō*ed him and killed him," to which Du Yu commented: "He struck him with his hand. The received text reads *bō* (㧙), with the pronunciation *púbì* (蒲必反); however, *bō* means "to push" (*tuī*), and is not used in this context.

*Zhùchài* (築搋): "zhù" is pronounced *zhēng* (徵) with a retroflex final, and "chài" (搋) is pronounced *chì* (勅) with a *jué* (隹) final. According to the *Guǎngyá*, "zhù" means to prick; according to the *Shuōwén*, "zhù" means to pound. "Chài" refers to poking with the fist or hand; thus it is called "chài.
*Ào zhì* (拗胵), also written as *āo* (󲞌), share the same pronunciation *wǔmǎo* (烏夘). "Ào" means to twist; "lì" (捩) is pronounced *lìjié* (力結).

12. The twelfth fascicle. The character *nè* (嫩) is also written as *niǎn* (抐), with the same pronunciation as *nǎi kùn* (乃困). It refers to that which is soft and tender. According to the *Tōngsùwén*, *niǎn* means "regrowth. It is also a near-homophone for *nèn* (嫰).

The term *li-ge* (犁槅)—*ge* being pronounced *ze* (責) and *ge* (*yè*) meaning the yoke—is that by which the ox’s neck is bound. The text of the Classics writes it as *gé* (格), which is not the correct form. *Yè* is pronounced *wū-gé* (烏革). *Tǔ-fu* (土墢) is also written as *fú* (󲒋);

both are pronounced *fú-fā* (扶發). The *Kǎo Gōng Jì* (考工記) states: "The *zhēn* (耟) is five *cùn* wide; two *zhēn* make one *ǒu* (耦). The width of the furrow for one *ǒu* is one foot, and its depth is one foot. Zhong Rong, Zǐ Xuán, says: "Two men work together to open it; the ridge between them is called *kuàn* (甽). The *fu* (墢) on top of the *kuàn*—the word *fu* means 'to bring forth' (*fā*). The *Shuowén Jiězì* states: "One throw of the hoe is called *fú* (󲒋). *Zhēn* is pronounced *cí-yǐ* (辭以), and *kuàn* is pronounced *gǔ-xuàn* (古泫).
"Chóng-zhì" (蟲豸): *zhí* and *ěr* are interchangeable. According to the *Erlǚ*, those with feet are called *chóng* (insects/creatures), while those without feet are called *zhì* (beasts).

"Huǒ-jìn" (火燼): *sì* and *jìn* are interchangeable. The *Shuōwén* states that the remains of burned wood are called *jìn*. In the *Erlǚ*, *jìn* means "remnant. The *Shuōwén* writes this character as 㶳 (*yín*).
"Dead warts" (死疣) is written in the *Zhuowen* script as 𭢝 (*yóu*, same as *jīū*). The *Tongsufǔwén* states that the term for "warts" (*tǐmù*) is *yóu*; the *Guǎpǐ* says a wart is a small swelling.

"Chirping" (*jiūjì*, *zǐxiū* rhyme) refers to the sound of many insects; it means the sound of small crickets. The final character is pronounced *zīlì*. The *Tongsufǔwén* states that the sound of a rat is called *jījì*; this is also a type of chirping sound.

*Jī* (芥) and *jiàng* (醬) are also written as *jì* (齏), with the same pronunciation as *jié-xí* (孑奚). It belongs to the category of sauces. According to the *Tōngsùwén* (通俗文): "To soak scallions is called *jì*; when mixed with minced meat, vinegar, and sauce, they are finely sliced and made into *jì*, which serves as a condiment (*zhū*). In the regions south of the Yangtze River, these are all called *zhū*; in the Central Kingdom (*Zhōngguó*), they are all called *jī*."

*Zadíng* (雜飣): The "dìng" (丁) rhymes with *dìng* (定); in the Jiangnan region, prepared foods are called *dìngshí* (飣食). The scriptural text writes it as *diàn* (奠), which rhymes with *tu* (徒) and means to set down or to present. *Lǎn* (䬦) has the pronunciation *dòu* (豆).

"Jinxiu" (珍羞): The *Zhouli* (Rites of Zhou) speaks of the "Eight Jin. It is precious; in ancient texts, it is written as "Xiu" (𦟤), with the phonetic reading *siyou*. According to the *Fangyan* (Discussions on Words), "xiu" means "cooked. Guo Pu states: "Xiu refers to cooked food. In the *Zhouli*, the Official of Provisions (*Shanfu*) presides over the King’s provisions and *xiu*. Zheng Xuan says: "*Xiu* refers to those things that provide flavor; various flavors are made into *xiu*."
"Dust" (*chén*) and "mud" (*'ū*): "to return dust as mud" means that dust is also mud; when dust flies up and scatters, it is called "mud.

To "send a spy" (*shǐ chàn*, *chàn* pronounced *lián* in the rhyming dictionary) means to look; "spy" is also synonymous with "to watch. This is as stated in the *Zuozhuan*: "He sent a spy to observe them."
The character *chèn* (趁) is pronounced *chǒu* and *rèn*, and it means "to pursue. The *Zuǎnwén* states that in the region west of the Pass, "to pursue things" is called *chèn*.

The *Shuǒwén* says that *chǔ* (儲) is pronounced *zhí* and *yú*; it means "to stockpile" (*zhù*) and "to wait for" (*dài*). Cáo Yōng’s *Quàn xué* states that *chǔ* refers to the "heir apparent" (*fù jūn*).
Regarding *shèng* (勝): according to the *Zuǎnwén* (纂文), the people of Wu used it to refer to a mound of piled earth; *shèng* means "to accumulate. Regarding *jù* (聚):
the reading is *cái jù* (才句). 13. Volume Thirteen. Regarding *láo jìn* (牢靳): the reading is *jū jìn* (居近); it refers to being firm and tight. The reading for *rèn* (肕) is *ér zhèn* (而振).

"Shan" (芟) is read as "shān" (所巖反). The *Shichuan* (詩傳) states that it means to weed or to hack. The text of the scripture uses "shan" (釤), which is read as "shàn" (所鑑反); this refers to a large sickle, and it is not used in this context.
"Jindǒu" (筋陡) is also written as "jīn" (䈥); both characters are pronounced *jū* (居殷反) for the first and *dǒu* (都口反) for the second.
It means being agile and robust. "Xiāngcháo" (相嘲) is also written as "xiāngzhāo" (相啁); according to Cāngjié, it is pronounced *zhāo* (竹交反). It refers to mutual joking and playful teasing.

The character *bi* (pronounced *bǔ dān* according to the *Zīlín*; it belongs to the *bi* radical) also means "category" (*bi lèi*). In the scriptural text, it is written as *bān*, which is a phonetic loan.

It is called *yú mí yíng* (pronounced *yú mí yíng*); it is that by which one summons the essence, meaning a name or title. In the scriptural text, it is written with the "speech" radical as *míng*, a more recent form of the character. The character is briefly explained as "mutually naming," referring to the eyes.
"Fei" (不) is not recorded in the *Beicang* [dictionary]; it is written as "wei" (偉), with the same pronunciation as "yongui" (于鬼反).

According to the *Shuowen*, "wei" means "extraordinary. Volume 14, Chapter 14. "Danzhe" (膽讋): "zhiye" (脂葉反). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "losing one's breath"; it also means "to be terrified. Alternatively, it means "speech that does not cease."

The character *qí* (篪) is also written as *tǎn* (䶵) or *bā* (笆); they share the same pronunciation, *chúlí* (除離). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is a flute with seven holes, as the *Shijing* says:

"The lady of the Zhòng clan blew the *qí*. The term *biànjuān* (㛹娟) is pronounced *yúxuán* (於玄); regarding the phrase "biànjuān" in the *Chuci*, Wang Yi stated that "biànjuān" refers to a beautiful appearance.

"Wòruò" (沃弱) is also written as "㮿" (󲠇), both meaning "bound" (縛). It is pronounced with the second tone on *wū* and the third tone on *jié*. The *Shijing* says, "Its leaves are like *ruò*," and the commentary states that "*ruò* is like being bound. Regarding the line "In the marshy mulberry grove there is *wò*," the commentary says: "*Wò* means supple; it also means beautiful."

"Shanlu" (山麓) is an ancient term; "lu" (麓) is pronounced as *li* with the tone of *gu* (同力穀反). The *Shijing* (*Classic of Poetry*) says, "Behold that dry mountain foot" (*zhān bǐ hàn lù*), and its commentary states, "It is the base of a mountain. This refers to a forest belonging to a mountain being called a "foot" (*lù*).

"Men" (門) is pronounced as *hu* with the tone of *la* (胡臘反); according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "men" means to close. The *Yi Jing* (*Book of Changes*) says, "Closing the gates is called Kun. This is so.
*Yu* (in *yùbèi*) is pronounced with the rhyme *lǚ*. The *Shī* says, "A hundred men guard [it]," and the *Chuán* states that "guarding" (*yù*) means "to be appropriate.

The character is written with the radical *shì*. *Gōngwéi* (palace gate): *yú* is pronounced with the rhyme *guī*. In the *Ěrpǐ*, it is said that the gates within the palace are called *wéi*. Guo Pu says this refers to small connecting doors; they are the lane-gates within the palace.

Regarding the term *jiāofáng* (pepper chamber), Ying Shao’s *Hàngōngyí* (Ceremonial Rites of the Han Palace) states: "The Empress is called the 'Pepper Chamber. A poem says, 'The fruit of the pepper plant spreads and flourishes in abundance. In foreign customs, they admire its prolific growth; they smear the rooms with pepper to take advantage of its warm smoke to eliminate noxious vapors. This is similar to how vermilion is used to plaster the palace floor, which is called the *danchí* (vermilion steps).
"Assisting the son and returning to the *Zhou Li* to assist in what is insufficient. Zheng Xuan says: "To assist (*zàn*) means to aid; it is also a way of conducting oneself.
"Lǎn" (欖) and "píng" (庰)—the former pronounced as *gǔ mǎo*, the latter as *pú dìng*—refer to stirring or agitating. The *Guǎngyǐ* states: "Píng refers to a latrine, a privy, or a cesspool."

*Tou jing* (投穽): The ancient forms are *jing* (阱) and *zeng* (󲜓); both share the same meaning. The character *ci* (茨) has the phonetic *xing* (性). The *Shuowen* states: "A *jing* is a great pit. The *Guangyi* states: "A *jing* is a deep hollow.

Volume Fifteen, Part One. *Jing ji* (驚悸): The ancient form is *qi* (󲝁); they are identical. The phonetic is *ji* (季). The *Zilin* states: "The heart is stirred. The *Shuowen* states: "The vital breath is unsettled."

The characters for *yuān* (to claim grievance) and *yuàn* (resentment) both appear in ancient texts; today they are written as *yùn*, with the same pronunciation as *yuán* (original). It means to be frantic, crooked, or oppressed, and also to be unjustly treated.

*Dí* (dìng zhòu fǎn): refers to the primary heir. Lexicons state that *dí* means "correct" or "authentic. The *Guǎngyá* says *dí* means "sovereign. The *Gōngyáng Zhuan* states: "In establishing the heir, one takes the eldest. What is meant by "heir" (*dí*)? It is because the honor of the principal wife has no equal. *Zhòu* (dìng zhòu fǎn): means continuous succession, or also a lineage.

"Yōng" (墉) refers to a city wall; it is also written as "yǒu" (䧡) or "yòu" (牖), with the same pronunciation as the character for "remaining" (餘) and the rhyme "zhōng" (鍾). According to the *Erya*, a wall is called "yōng," and a city is also called "yōng. As the *Shijing* says: "To attack the high walls of Chóng. The character below has the pronunciation "tujié" (徒頰). "Dié" (堞) refers to a parapet.

*Shao-hong* (the first character pronounced *shao*, the second *hong* with the phonetic *qian-luan*): according to the *Beicang*, a *shao* is one zhang eight chi long; the *Yi-pi* states that what is called *hong* is a *chan* (a small spear). The pronunciation of *chan* is *shi-yian*.

16. The sixteenth fascicle. *Wei-tuo* (逶迤) is also written as *wei-tuo* (蟡). The first character is pronounced with the rhyme *wei* (於危反); the second is also written as *ta* (佗) and is pronounced with the rhyme *luo* (達羅反). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "wei-tuo" refers to a gait that is winding and meandering; it describes the appearance of one who moves with natural ease.

The character for *shēn* (pregnant) is written with the radical for "woman" and the phonetic "lín" (pronounced *zhèn*, second tone). A poem says, "Great *rèn* [is] *shēn*," and the *Zhuàn* says, "*Shēn* means movement. *Shēn* refers to one who is carrying a fetus in the womb. According to the *Guǎngpǐ*, it is also called *wěi*. Today, both are written as "body" (*shēn*), as the two characters "rain" (*yù*) and "through" (*tōng*) are interchangeable.

*Pāngpèi*: "Pāng" is pronounced with the *bǎng* rhyme (lower tone), and "pèi" is pronounced with the *lài* rhyme. According to the *Sāncāng*, it means "overflowing" (*pāngtuó*). "Pèi" refers to the surging flow of water waves;

it also signifies "greatness. *Xīnchōng*: Also written as *zhòng* (same pronunciation). It is pronounced with the *zhīróng* rhyme. According to the *Fānyán*, it means "anxious haste" (*zhēngzhòng huángjù*). Throughout the regions between the Yangtze and the Huai rivers, any state of being distressed, sudden, or terrified is termed "anxious haste" (*zhēngzhòng*).

*Máng* (茫) and *bù* (怖) are also written as *mò* (󲃺), with the same pronunciation as *mò* (莫荒反). *Máng* means "vague" or "dazed," while *bù* refers to people who, day and night, act as if there were no days and no months; because they constantly desire clarity (*míng*), the character follows *míng*. Alternatively, it is said that *bù* refers to people who long for the dawn of heaven, hence the character follows *míng*. It is also written as *huáng* (惶) and *bù* (怖), with the same pronunciation as *pǔ* (普故反), meaning "apprehension and fear. In the sutra text, it is written as *pà* (怕), with the pronunciation *pǐ* (疋白反); this is the colloquial pronunciation *pǐ* (疋嫁反), meaning "timid apprehension" (*dàn pà*).

*Tóng* (瞳) [pronounced *tú gōng fǎn*]: The *Pīcāng* states it is a *zhūzǐ* (a type of pearl). The second character, *xiá*, is pronounced *xiǎn fǎn*. The *Cāngjiépiān* says it is the appearance of eyes protruding;

*xiǎn* is pronounced *wǔ bǎn fǎn*. *Chuí zhì* (垂䫂) [the second character, *dīng kě fǎn*]: The *Guǎngyǐ* states that *zhì* is an ugly appearance. The received text reads *zhì* [pronounced *chǐ zhǐ fǎn*]. The *Eryǐ* states that *zhì* means "to rely" (*shì tiè*). Guo Pu says: "In the Jiangdong region, 'mother' (*mǔ*) is called *zhì*; this is not the original meaning of the character."

The ancient character for *kàbǐ* (髂髀) is the same as *púmǐ* (󲱲). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the outer part of the thigh is called *bǐ*. In the Jiangnan dialect, it is pronounced *bǐ'ěr*; the reading in the received texts as *yì* (䏶) is incorrect.

"Hàn" (鼾) [pronounced with the initial *xà* and final *-dàn*]: according to the *Shuowen*, this refers to the sound of breathing; the character is pronounced "hūyú" (呼于), which is the pronunciation used in the Jiangnan region.
"Dā" (𠞈): [pronounced *dīng-hé*]; according to character dictionaries, it means "to attach. The reading "tā" (搭) in the canonical text is incorrect.
The character *zhǎo* (䶧) is written as *yǎo* (齩) in the *Shuowen Jiezi*, both with the phonetic transcription *wǔ jiǎo fǎn*. It means "to bite" (*yǎo nì*).
*Jiájiá* (戞戞), with the phonetic transcription *gǔ xià fǎn*, refers to the sound of teeth.
*Chèn yǔ* (讇語), with the phonetic transcription *shì yán fǎn* and also pronounced *chǎn*, is merely a colloquial expression heard in the world.

17. Volume Seventeen. Regarding "zhújí" (oar/rowlock), the *Tōngsùwén* (Explanations of Common Terms) states it is written as "jí" with the same pronunciation as "zīliè" (tsi-liat). The *Shījīng* (Book of Poetry) says, "Cypress oars and pine boat. The *Chuán* (Commentary) states, "The oar is that by which one rows the boat. This refers to the passage in the *Zhòuyī* (Book of Changes): "The Yellow Emperor carved wood to make oars. The character for "huì" (cypress) is pronounced "kuò."

*Dà qì* (大磧): "qì" is pronounced *jiè* (反). According to the *Shuowen*, a *qì* is a sandbar (*shǔzhǔ*) in water where there are rocks; according to the *Guǎngyá*, it refers to a rapid (*làì*), the appearance of shallow water where rocks are visible.

Volume 18, Number 18. *Ān diàn* (覢電) is also written as *shǎn* (睒), both pronounced *shì rǎn* (反). According to the *Shuowen*, it means to see momentarily; it also implies uncertainty. In the sutra text, it is written as *shǎnshǎn* (閃閃), meaning to peek one's head out.
The character *sǎn* (如丳字) is pronounced *wǎn* (菀初眼反); it refers to the spit used for roasting meat today. The form appearing in the sutra text as *chǎn* (剗削之剗) is not its correct form.

It is derived from *xiāo* (削). It is also written as *qiào* (鞘), pronounced *sì miào* (私妙反); according to the *Fāngyán*, what is called a *xiāo* (削) in the region east of the Pass is called a *bǐ* (鞞) in the region west of the Pass; it is that which stores the blades of swords and sabers. The pronunciation of *bǐ* is *bù mí* (捕迷反).
"Sū" (乃穌, with the initial sound *hu* reversed) is explained in the *Shenglei* as "reborn" (*gēngshēng*). "Sū" also means "rest"; it refers to resting again.
"Diāo" (凋悴, with the rhyme *dīngyáo*) is defined in the *Shuowen* as "half-injured"; "diāo" also means "worn out. The character is composed of the radical "ice" (*bīng*).
*Póu* (蒲交反): According to the *Tōngsùwén*, to grasp with the hand is called *póu*; according to the *Shuōwén*, *póu* is sometimes written as *bào*, meaning to pull or take up.
Volume 19, Number 19. *Bǎimù* (又作椑, 補買反): According to the *Shuōwén*, it means to strike or shake with both hands.
*Mian* (緜): the rhyme is *zhue* (竹劣反); according to the *Zilin*, it means sorrow, as well as mental instability. *Dizhun* (躓頓):
there are two ancient forms, *zhan* (䠟) and *shu* (󲱶), while the current form is *di* (󲊌); the rhyme is the same as *zhi* (陟利反), meaning to be humiliated or frustrated.

The character for *huángguī* (imperial quarters) has the phonetic *shé* with the radical *xié* reversed. In the *Erya*, the gates within the palace are called *wéi*; those that are smaller are called *guī*.

According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to a gate standing alone. The archaic forms for *qióng* (solitary) are *qióng* and *dǐng*, both pronounced *qúyíng*. In the *Shangshu*: "There were no more solitary orphans. Kong Anguo says: "*Qióng* means 'single,' meaning having no one to rely upon; *dú* means 'alone,' meaning having no son."

20. Volume Twenty. "Ti" (荑): In the *Tongshu Wen* (Explanations of Common Terms), it is said that grasses growing on land are called *ti*. The *Shijing* (Book of Poetry) says, "From the wilds, the *ti* [sprout]"; its commentary states that *ti* refers to the initial growth of *mao* (moss-grass).
*Maò* (pronounced *mǎng*) refers to hair-cloth (*maò-bù*). According to the *Tōngsúwén*, the term *maò* denotes a diagonal pattern; the *Zìlín* states it refers to a square-patterned woolen cloth.

*Yìdiè* (pronounced *tújié*) means an anthill. The *Fāngyán* states that an anthill is a mound of earth. In the regions south of Chu and Zheng, the soil of an anthill is called a *diè*; a *diè* is also characterized by being high in its center.

*Zi* (beard): the character is pronounced *zi* (移反) and also written as *zī* (󱺅), with the same pronunciation; in the Jiangnan region it is pronounced *gan* (甘反), while in the Guanzhong region it is pronounced *lian* (廉反). According to the *Shuowen*, the mustache on both sides of the mouth is called *zi*; the *Shuowen* further defines it as the hair on the cheeks. The form used in the scriptures is *zi*, which is a more recent orthography.
*Qi* (喫) [with the phonetic *ji*]: also written as *qi* (噉), meaning to eat. *Sai* (灑): also written as *pen* (噴), same pronunciation (*pǔ sūn*).

The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it means to blow air; the *Guangyi* says it means to spit out or to spray. This refers to holding something in the mouth and spraying it out. It is also written as *pen* (噴), same pronunciation (*pǔ xùn*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it means to snort through the nose; the *Guangya* says it means to sneeze; the *Cangjie Pian* says it means to scold.
"Xiǎng" (享) means to enjoy; it also means to receive. It means to be appropriate.

According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "xiǎng" also means play (*xì*). Volumes 21–22: Volumes 21 and 22 above have no phonetic transcriptions provided previously. Volume 23: "Qì" (憩) means to rest. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes this as "kè" (愒), with the same pronunciation (*què lì*). The *Ervu* states that "qì" refers to the rest of lying down.

The ancient characters for *kai* (開) and *tuō* (拓) were two distinct forms; the current form is written as *zǐ* (梓), with the phonetic *tā* (他各反). According to the *Guǎngyǐ*, *zhà* (柘) means "large" and also "to open. The character in the scripture is written as *tuò* (拓), which is identical to *zhì* (摭), with the phonetic *zhī* (之石反). *Zhì* (摭) means "to gather," whereas *tuò* (拓) does not possess this semantic meaning.

24. Fascicle Twenty-four. [The character] *yǎn* (偃) is pronounced with the *yà* rhyme; in dictionaries, *yǎn* means "to lean" (*yī*) and is written with the radical for "man. *Yǎnxī* (偃息) refers to resting.

Du [Yuan] states that the *Shuowen Jiezi* uses *shù* (庶) instead, with the same pronunciation as *tú gǔ* (徒古). In the *Guoyu*, regarding "closing one's gate and not going out," Jia Kui says: "Du means to block; it means to close off. In the *Fangyan*, "Du means coarse. Zhao [Zhi] says: "Du is a common colloquial term of the present day. Guo Pu says: "It is like being coarse; because the *Duzi* (杜子) was coarse, he was named after it."

Volume Twenty-five, Part Two: "Not Pronounced as 'Yin'. Volume Twenty-six: "Not *jué* (巨月, 居月, with the second tone). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *jué* means to fall prostrate; according to the *Guoyu*, it means to collapse and lie face down.

*Qiāng* (恇怯): The first character is pronounced *qiū fāng* (恇) and means "to be terrified. The second character is also written as *yī* (㹤), which is the same. *Qiè* (怯) means "timid," "fearful," or "weak";

it refers to having much fear. *Guài wù* (怪迕): Also written as *wù* (啎) or *wǔ* (仵); these two forms are identical. Pronounced *wú gù* (吾故). According to the *Shēnglèi* (聲類), it means "to oppose" or "to encounter adversity. The version in the scripture that reads *wù* (悞) is incorrect.

*Jian* (pronounced *ju-zhan* in the vernacular; it refers to speech that is not fluent in common parlance) is called "stammering. In the *Book of Changes*, *jian* means "difficulty. According to the *Fangyan*, stammering is a term from the Chu dialect. Guo Pu states that it is also a common term used in the north.
"Bái-ǒu" (白鷗)—the "ǒu" is pronounced as in *hóu* (侯) according to the *Zílín*; it is a water osprey (*shuǐ è*). "Quǎn-rú-jīū" (犬如鳩)—the "jīū" is pronounced as in *jiāo* (驕).

"Guō-liè" (摑裂)—this should be written as "jué" (攫); according to the *Shuōwén*, "jué" means to seize; the *Cāngjiépiān* states that "jué" means to pounce. This refers to how when a beast becomes enraged, it immediately pounces.
"Ling" (翎) [pronounced li with the *ding* (丁) tone] refers to bird feathers; in the sutra text it is written as "ling" (零) or as "luo" (󲥖/𮋔), both of which are near-homophonous characters.
"Luo" (󲞨) [pronounced tuo with the *wo* (臥) tone] means "shedding hair" according to dictionaries; in the sutra text it is written as "luo" (󲯙), and both forms are acceptable.

The character *shòu* (瘦) is written as *zǒng* (㾪) in the *Zi Yuàn* (字苑), with the same pronunciation as *suǒjǐng* (所景反). It means emaciation and illness. According to the *Shì míng* (釋名), *zhěng* (眚) is the same as *zǒng* (㾪); it refers to the emaciation of a sick person. The reading *shěng* (省) found in the scriptural text is not the correct form.

*Ōu-tuó* (the first character pronounced with the *wū* and *xiá* finals; the second with the *tú* and *jié* finals). The *Cāngjiépiān* writes this as *fēi-lǐ*. The *Bàopǔzǐ* states: "To be sunken and to be protruding.
*Piǎn-tuó* (the first character pronounced with the *bǔ* and *xiǎn* finals; the second with the *tā* and *xī* finals). The *Cuǎnwén* states: "To be flat and thin; not round."

*Jing* (鯨) and *yi* (鷁) are also written as *qiong* (䲔), with the same pronunciation as *qu-jing*. Xu Shuchong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states that the *jingyu* is the king of fish. The *Yiwuzhi* says that *jingyu* can be several li long; those who catch them all lack eyes, for it is popularly said their eyes have transformed into bright moon pearls (*mingyue zhu*). *Ni* (鯢) is the female of the *jing*. In the *Zuo Zhuan*, the *jingni* are called great fish. The *Shuowen* writes this as *yi* (鶂); Sima Xiangru writes it as *li* (𪁌), or as *yao* (鶝); the *Picao* writes it as *wang* (艗), and the *Zishu* writes it as *yi* (鷁), with the same pronunciation as *wu-li*. It is a water bird that excels at flying high.

*Qinmo* (禽貘), also written as *Momo* (莫貊) with the same pronunciation (*mángbái*), according to the *Zilin* (字林), resembles a bear and is yellowish-black; it originates from Shu. Another name for it is *Bai bao* (白豹). Volume 27, Number 27:

*Xiuliu* (鵂鶹), pronounced *xū niú* (許牛反) for the first character and *lì zhōu* (力周反) for the second. According to the *Guangyi* (廣疋), *xiuliu* refers to the *qili* (樢䲻) bird. In the region west of the Pass, it is called *Hou* (侯), while in the region east of the Mountains, it is called *Hunhu* (訓狐). The *Zuanwen* (纂文) states that at night, it picks up human fingernails.

*Gou-e* (the first character pronounced *gǔ hóu*, the second *jiāng gēng*). According to the *Erya*, it is the *guàihu* (怪䲻); Sharen says it is the *xiūliú* (鵂鶹). In Nanyang it is called *gou'e*; it is also named *jīqī*. It crouches by day and travels at night; its cry is considered a portent.

The *xiāo* (梟) [is pronounced as in "gāo" (堯) and "fǎn" (反)]. It is the *tǔxiāo* (土梟). It is not written as *jiāo* (驕). According to the *Zílín* (字林), it is the *xiūfú* (鵂鳺). Its shape resembles that of a dove (*jiū*) and it is green; it emerges from white mounds on mountains and is a bird of ill omen. The people of Chu call it the *péngniǎo* (鵬鳥); it is also a species of *yù* (䲻). In the region east of the mountains, it is called the *qīngfú* (鸋鳺), with the common name "Clever Woman" (*qiǎofù*). The first character is pronounced as in "nú" (奴) and "dìng" (定); the second is pronounced as in "gōng" (公) and "xué" (穴).
*Chang* (可摚) is also written as *zhuang* (󲠂), with the same pronunciation as *zhái-héng*. It means to touch one another; it refers to the mutual jostling of pillars. *Quèrán* (確然):

the first character is pronounced *kǒu-jué*. In the *Book of Changes* (*Zhouyī*), it says: "Now, the firmness (*quèrán*) shows people the ease [of the Way]. Han Kangbo said: "Firmness is the appearance of solidity."

"Língcēng" (陵𡺿) is a term for the rugged appearance of mountains and hills; in the script, it is written with the "mountain" radical (*shān*) as *wù* (𡺿), which is a variant character. "Wǎn" (阮) is pronounced *wǔhuài* (五壞), and "wěi" (隗) is pronounced *wǔzuì* (五罪).

28. Fascicle Twenty-Eight. Regarding "Ji" (脊): it is now read as "Lü" (呂), with the phonetic component "li" (力) and the radical "ju" (舉). "Pei" (膐) is also a synonym for "ji" (脊). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to the backbone. Taiyue was a minister of Yu; because his heart and backbone were aligned (*wei ru xin lu*), he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Lü.

*Jià* (𦝫髂): The ancient form is 𩩱, now written as 䯊; both are pronounced *kǒu yà*. The *Pīcāng* states that it refers to the bones of the pelvis. The scriptural text writes it with the radical for "flesh" (*ròu*) as 𦝣, which is incorrect.
*Kāo* (尻臀): Pronounced *kǔ láo* (upper) and *dú kūn* (lower). The *Shēnglèi* states that it refers to the buttocks.

The characters for *ǎ* (𣘨) and *nà* (橠) are ancient forms; the two characters *ǎ* (𧙃) and *ǎ* (𣘨) are now written as *ā* (阿), both pronounced *ǎ* (烏可反). The lower character, *nà* (󲢔), is an ancient form; the two characters *nà* (栘) and *nà* (𧙃) are now written as *nà* (郍), both pronounced *nǎ* (乃可反). According to dictionaries, *ǎ* (𧙃) and *yí* (栘) denote a state of weakness and suppleness, and also the flourishing of plants and trees.

*Liào* (盧報反): The *Shuowen* explains it as "clinging" (*liàohù*). According to the *Shenglèi*, it means "to cherish and begrudge [something], unable to let it go. The *Guǎngyá* states that *liào* is synonymous with "as if" (*rú*). *Hù* is pronounced *hú gù fǎn*.

The character *tuó* (麾) is pronounced with the initial *d-*, as in *tú-dào*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "The *tuó* is the *cáo* (翿), which is the *yì* (翳). The *Zhuangzi* commentary says: "The dancer holds it in the left hand; it is used for dancing with feathers. According to the *Fangyan*, in the state of Chu, the *yì* (screen) was called the *tuó*. The pronunciation of *tuó* is *tú-dào*.

*Jing* (旌): *qíng* (資盈反) for the first character; *jù yī* (巨衣反) for the second. Your *Yi* (爾疋) commentary states that Mao [Zixun] says a field-head is called a *jing*. Guo Pu says: "One places a *mao* (ox-tail plume) at the top of the pole. The *Zhouli* says: "Feathered shafts are made into *jing*. Zheng Xuan says: "The feathers are split into five colors and tied to the top of the *jing*. The *Erya* says: "That which has a bell is called a *qi* (旂). Guo Pu says: "Bells are suspended from the top of the pole, and dragons are painted upon the *qi*. This refers to the *Zhouli* statement: "Dragons are used for the *qi*."

Fēnfēi (雰霏): Pronounced fūxià (敷下), though sometimes written as fēn (䬠) with the same pronunciation. It describes the appearance of heavy snow and rain. Fūyùe (鈇鉞): Pronounced fāngyú fāngwū (方于方巫). In the *Lìjì* (Book of Rites), it says:

"The *fū* and *yuè* were what the former kings used to manifest their righteous indignation. According to the *Shuōwén*, *fū* means to chop or hack; it is also a wooden block for sharpening axes. *Yuè* (鉞): Pronounced yúmù (于目), meaning a large axe.

*Xiàn* (霰) is also written as *xīn* (䨘), both pronounced with the initial *xiān* (先) and the final *jiàn* (見). The *Shijing* says, "First gathering, it is but *xiàn*," and the commentary states that it refers to heavy, blizzard-like snow.

*Ōng* (兕) and *xī* (犀) are pronounced *sì* (似) or *xú sǐ* (徐姉). According to the *Erya*, the *ōng-niu* (兕牛) has a single horn, is azure-colored, and weighs a thousand *qīn*. The *Nánzhōu Yìwù Zhì* (Record of Strange Things from the Southern Continent) maintains that its horn is over two *chí* long and shaped like the handle of a horse-whip; its hide is so hard it can be made into armor. The *Guǎngzhì* (Extensive Record) notes that its horn is mottled like a *tuǒ* (埵) and it has ten claws on its feet.

Furthermore, *qiè* (with the phonetic *kǒu jié fǎn*): according to the *Shuowen*, *qiè* means to hold up by suspending; it is like to lift, and also means to tie. *Ěr qiào* (with the phonetic *dīng kě fǎn*):

according to the *Guangyi*, *qiào* refers to a hideous appearance. The scriptural text reads *zhì* (with the phonetic *shí zhǐ fǎn*); *zhì* means to rely upon. It is also written as *zhì* (with the phonetic *nǎi kě fǎn*), which is the name of a vessel.

29. Volume Twenty-nine. "Lie" (鬣巤) is written with two characters; it is pronounced the same as "lüe" (驢涉反). According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to bristling hair, or long hair. The *Tongsu Wen* states that the bristles of a pig are called "lie."

The *Shijing* (Book of Poetry) states: "Fǎn yú lái hè" (He comes back to frighten me). The *Shu* (Commentary) says: "To ward off another is called 'hè'; 'hè' also denotes great anger. "Zì pú" (to fall over oneself);
the modern form is "pù," with the same pronunciation as "púběi. "Pú" means to overturn forward.
*Tuan-luan* (盧端反): "Tuan" means round; it signifies being circular or encompassed.
*Xin-xin* (又作引同尸忍反): "Xin" means to laugh. *Mai-ke* (公玄反): According to the *Shuowen*, this refers to the stalks of wheat;
according to the *Guangya*, it refers to accumulated straw. The form appearing in the scripture as *ke* is not the correct character.
*Shā* (pronounced *jiǎ*): A feather ornament; the feathers hang down. It is composed of the radical *cóng* (垂) and the phonetic *qiè*.

According to the *Shìběn*, King Wǔ created the *shā*. 30. Volume Thirty. *Yúshàn* (also written as *yúshàn* or *yúshàn*; both forms share the same pronunciation *shàn*): The *Huìxùnwén* states that this refers to a snake-fish.
*Zǔn* (pronounced *cái fǔ*, with the second character also written as *fǔ*; according to the *Zìlín*, the *zǔn* is a fish with red eyes) and *fáng* (a fish with a red tail).

*Tí* (pronounced *dá lì*, with the second character pronounced *lǐ*; according to the *Zìlín*, the *tí* is the *nián* [mudfish], while the *lǐ* is the *huá*). According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, the *shī* and *tí* are both the *nián*. In Qingzhou, the *nián* is called *tí*. (*Huá* is pronounced *hú wǎ*; *shī* is pronounced *tú xī*).

Regarding "hibernating" (zhímián): the *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as "concealing. When insects reach the winter solstice, they enter hibernation and do not emerge. Among beasts, those with short fur also hibernate, such as the bear (*xiong*) and the brown bear (*bei*).
31. Scroll Thirty-one. One: *dí* (also written as *shì*, same pronunciation; *tú* and *lì* are the phonetic components). *Ěr* (synonym for *jiān jiā*). Guo Pu says: "This is *yǎo*."

*Shu* (抒): Pronounced *lǚ* and *shí* (the latter being a variant). According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means "to drain" (*xiè*). According to the *Shuōwén*, it means "to ladle out" (*yì*). According to the *Cāngjiépiān*, it means "to take up" (*qǔ*) or "to remove" (*chú*).
*Sàotó* (臊陁): Pronounced *sū láo*. This is a Sanskrit term for the name of a bird, the myna.

The ancient forms for "dark" (àn), "grain" (sàn), "to mix" (sàn), and "to blend" (sàn) are four distinct shapes; today they are written as 糝, with the pronunciation *sāng gǎn*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "mixing rice with soup," or alternatively, "a grain.

*Dajiu* (大虯) is pronounced *qú liú*. According to the *Guangyi*, a dragon with horns is called a *jiǔlóng* (虯龍). Xiong Shì’s *Ruìyingtu* states that the *jiǔlóng* has a black body and lacks scales or armor.

32. Fascicle Thirty-two. Regarding the character *yǎng* (鞅) in *yǎng-rèn* (鞅靭): it is also written as *xián* (󲢘), both with the same pronunciation as *húquǎn* (胡犬). This refers to the leather thong (*yǎng*) of a carriage; all such items are written with this character. In the scriptural text, it is written as *yì* (䩙), pronounced *huǒjiàn* (火見); this character is identical to *xiè* (韅), and *yì* (䩙) is not used here.
33. Fascicle Thirty-three. *Zhi* (脂) and *yu* (腴): according to the *Shuowen*, *zhi* refers to the pubic region below the abdomen;

*yu* refers to the abdomen. 34. Fascicle Thirty-four. *Wang* (輞) and *gong* (釭), also written as *gang* (𨊧), same pronunciation as *gu* (古) and *hong* (紅). According to the *Shuowen*, it is the iron rim at the mouth of a wheel hub (*gu*). According to the *Fangyan*, in the region west of Kai, it is called *gong*; between Yan, Qi, Hai, and Dai, it is called *duo* (鐹), pronounced *gu* and *he* (古和).

The term *zhùjiǎn* (軸鐧) is read as *liàn* (鍊) in the local dialects, with the same pronunciation as *gē* (歌) and *yàn* (鴈). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it refers to iron on a carriage axle. The *Guoya* says that *jiǎn* (鐧) is synonymous with *tàn* (錔), where *tàn* is pronounced *tāhé* (他合).
*Hēilú* (黑纑) has the pronunciation *húlè* (胡勒); the *Zilin* defines it as woven thread.
*Shāo* (燒) is now written as *shè* (𤋲), pronounced *yuè* (悅). According to the *Tōngsùwén* (通俗文), to kindle fire is called *shè*; *shè* also means to burn.
*Bào* (報) is pronounced *zài* (再). According to the text, *sài* (賽) refers to mutual recompense and retribution.

35. Scroll Thirty-Five. "Chi" (杴) and "Chu" (鉏)—the latter pronounced *shì* with the *fǎn* of *fǎn*—refer to agricultural implements. In the *Cāngjié piān*, it says: "With the *chú*, one weeds the seedlings. This is what is meant in the *Hànshū*: "He carried his books while weeding (*chú*)."

*Cuò* (剉): Pronounced with the initial *qian* (千) and the final *wo* (臥). According to the *Shuowen*, it means to hack or wound; "cuò" is synonymous with "zhao" (斫), meaning to cut or to sharpen. *Chūn* (村): Pronounced with the initial *chun* (村) and the final *yun* (殞). *Sòu* (嗽):

Also written as *zà* (齚) or *sòu* (欶), all pronounced with the initial *suǒ* (所) and the final *jué* (角). The *Tongsu Wen* states that to suck or inhale is called *sòu*. The scriptural text writes it as *wèi* (𠲿), pronounced with the initial *zi* (子) and the final *lei* (累). In character dictionaries, it is sometimes written as *ji* (𭪿), or with *zé* (齰) below, both pronounced with the initial *shi* (仕) and the final *bai* (白). *Zá* (齚) means to bite. The scriptural text also uses *za* (咋), which is a variant of *mo* (陌); furthermore, *za za* (咋咋) is an onomatopoeia. *Zháo* (咟) is pronounced with the initial *hu* (胡) and the final *mai* (麥).

The character 󰜥 (also written as 𪙍) is pronounced with the first radical *jiǎ* (㭪) and the second radical *zì* (子). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it denotes the sound of chewing. In the scriptural text, it is sometimes written as 博 (*bó*) or, alternatively, as 峽 (*xiá*), which means to forget one's speech; or it is written as 唼 (*zé*), meaning to sip or slurp. Neither of these two forms corresponds to the original meaning of the word.
36. Fascicle Thirty-Six. Regarding "sòu" (嗽吮): according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "sòu" means to suckle; according to the *Yunjí*, the pronunciation of "sòu" is yìxuǎn.
37. Volume Thirty-Seven. One matter with ten names: *Nirukti* (Etymological Exposition), *Vāda* (Discourse), *Pada* (Phrases), and *Akṣara* (Syllables). This is the *Niruktipravacana*.

The character 欵 (also written as 款) is pronounced with the same initial and final as 口緩 (kǎn). It means "to arrive at" (*cāngjiépiān*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "the intention of having a desire. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "affection."

Volume Thirty-Eight (No. 38). [The character for "previous" (先) does not have a phonetic transcription here. Volume Thirty-Nine (No. 39). The character *hū* (呴) is also written as *hūṃ* (吽) or *kṣau* (𤘽); these two forms are pronounced identically with the rhyme *gǒu*. According to the *Guǎngyǐ*, *hū* means "to cry out. In the *Guóyuè*, it says: "The three armies clamored and *hū*-ed. Jia Dui states: "*Hū* means to snort. This applies to the following instances as well.

*Chán* (慚) and *nǜ* (恧) [are pronounced with six variations]. In the local dialects, *tí* (𢤱) and *nǜ* (恧) mean shame. In the regions of Yang, Qing, and Xu, one says *tí*; in the regions of Liang, Yi, Qin, and Jin, one says *chán*. From the mountains east and west, to feel self-reproach is called *nǜ*. According to the *Sāncāng*, *nǜ* means shame. The *Guǎngyá* states that to be unrighteous or lose one's integrity is called *chán*; it is synonymous with shame (*chánkùi*). The *Xiǎo'ěryá* states that shame felt in the heart is called *nǜ*. *Tí* is pronounced *tuǎndiǎn*.

*Pai-ch'ieh* (白㲲): The ancient text uses *tu-t'ieh* (毾), which is pronounced with the second tone on *t'u* and the fourth tone on *chieh*; it refers to a woolen cloth. The scriptural text writes it as *chih* (縶), pronounced with the first tone on *chih* and the fourth tone on *li*;

however, "to tether" (*chih-p'an*) is not the intended meaning of the character here. 40. Volume Forty. [The character for] *ting* (艇) is pronounced with the fourth tone on *tu* and the third tone on *ting*. The *Shiming* (釋名) states: "Anything below two hundred *hu* in capacity is called a *ting*. The *Fangyan* (方言) says: "In the Jiang and Hu regions of Nan-Chu, a small boat is called a *ting*. Guo Pu says: "It is the same as *qi* (𦨴). [The character for] *zuo* (䑿) is pronounced with the fourth tone on *si* and the sixth tone on *liu*; *qi* (𦨴) has the same pronunciation.
*Bi* (pronounced *bei* with the tone of *yi*) means to fold or pleat an object; *zhé* (pronounced *tu* with the tone of *jié*).
*Tóng*—in ancient texts, it has two forms, *yí* and *zì*—is pronounced *tú* with the tone of *zōng*. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "unadorned"; according to the *Guangya*, it means "scarlet."

41. Fascicle Forty-one. [The character for "first" (先) lacks a phonetic gloss. 42. Fascicle Forty-two. *Han-jin* (寒噤): pronounced as *jǔ* (渠) and *yǐn* (飲) in combination; it is a word meaning to refrain from speaking. Wang Yi says: "To close the mouth is *jin*; *jin* means to be closed."

"Ji-jì" (唧唧)—the "jì" is pronounced with the retroflex *l* (浴栗反); according to the *Tōngsùwén* (通俗文), this is the sound of a rat. Here, we take its meaning; the reading "ti" (呹) in the scriptural text is incorrect.

"Yánliú" (㳂流)—the "yì" is pronounced with the retroflex *q* (翼泉反); according to the *Zílín* (字林), "yán" means to descend following water, that is, to go with the current. "Yán" also means to follow along.

The character *qiàn* (㱇) [is pronounced] with the forceful reverse tone; the *Tōngsúwén* states that a slight fear is called *qiàn*, while the *Pīcāng* says it means "terror. The *Shuōwén* says it means "a state of grief"; the character is composed of *zhèi* (𠬵) and *qiàn* (欠). In the scriptural texts, it is written as *chēn* (懎) with the "heart" radical (*xīn*), yet both [the *qiàn* and *chēn* forms] are not the original body of the character.

Regarding "snake-shedding decoction" (*shé tuì tāng*): *wài* (外) is pronounced *yè* (悅) with a second tone; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to the exuviae shed by cicadas and snakes. According to the *Guoyu*, it refers to the molting of the *fù* (蝮) and *huài* (蜟); *fù* is pronounced *fú liù* (扶六), and *huài* is pronounced *yú liù* (餘六).

*Suǒ* (㴑) is an archaic form of *suǒ* (𣹫), both pronounced with the same rhyme as *sāng* (桑). According to the *Sāncāng*, to flow upstream against the current is called *suǒ*; it means to face toward [the source] and also implies movement.

*Mán* (忛) is also written as *fáng* (渢) and has an archaic form of *fáng* (𩗋), both pronounced with the same rhyme as *fúyán* (扶嚴). According to the *Shēnglèi*, it refers to the sail spread upon a boat. The *Shèmíng* states that the boat follows the wind as the sail (*màn*) is unfurled; the white sail is called *mán*, and because it causes the wind to move swiftly, it is said to be *mán-mán* and *fàn-fàn*.
*Tàn* (pronounced *tú dān* in reverse). Guo Pu says: "In the Jiangdong region today, sand mounds in the water are called *tàn*; *tàn* refers to land in the middle of a river."

I have therefore reversed the characters; the *Zilin* erroneously calls it "誤," but the text of the sutra uses "忤," which is correct. "誤" means to deceive; "忤" means to oppose or go against.
