The character 跌 (dié) consists of "foot" (足) above and "tián jié" (田結) below. Xu Shu-chong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states that "跌" means "to arise. Guo’s commentary says it means "to lie prostrate on the ground. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says "跌" means "to leap over," formed with "foot" (足) as the semantic component and "shī" (失) as the phonetic.

*Zǎoguàn* (澡罐): The first character is pronounced *zǎo* (上音早) and the second *guàn* (下官喚). The *Wenzí jílüè* (文字集略) states it is a vessel for drawing water. It is formed with the radical *shān* (󳹇) and the phonetic *huán* (雚);
the pronunciation of *huán* is as stated above. *Jiǎodāo* (鉸刀): The first character is pronounced *jiǎo* (上交巧反). The *Yùnyīng* (韻英) states it is a pair of scissors; that is, the modern-day scissors.

Regarding the character *hé* (核), the rhyme is *xià* (下). Examining its phonetics, it is said that *hé* means "to exhaust" (*qióng*) or "reality" (*shí*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *kǎo* (考) means "to verify facts. It is composed of the radical *xī* (西) with *jiǎo* (敫) as the phonetic. Alternatively, it may be written as *bì* (𩅢) with the radical *yǔ* (雨). The pronunciation of *xī* is *hū xià* (呼下), and the pronunciation of *jiǎo* is *jīng yì* (經亦).

7. Seventh Fascicle, Part One: *Xiūnǎn* (Shame/Embarrassment). *Kǒng* (Confucius), in his commentary on the *Shūjìng* (Book of Documents), states that it means "shame. In the *Zuǒzhuan*, the character is written as *jù xiū*; *Dù* (Du) comments that it means "shame. The *Shuowén* says: "To present an offering (*xiū*). It is composed of *yáng* (sheep), for that which is presented by sheep; and *chǒu* (the radical for time), which also provides the phonetic. The lower part is pronounced *níngjiǎn*. The *Fānyán* says it means "embarrassment. The *Kǎoshēng* says it means "to feel shame and have one's face turn red. The *Shuowén* further defines "face turning red from shame" as being composed of *chì* (red) with *niǎn* as the phonetic. The *Lǜběn* (Regulations for Texts) uses *pí* (skin) instead to form *niǎn*; this is a vulgar character. *Niǎn* is pronounced *nízhǎn*.

The character for "knock" (扣) has the phonetic component "mouth" (口) at the top. The *Lunyu* states, "He struck his calf with a staff," and Kong Yingda’s commentary explains that "knock" means to strike. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of "hand" (手) and "mouth" (口), with the mouth also serving as the phonetic element.

*Tiao* (絛) is pronounced *tǎo* (上討刀反). Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "Its *fan* (fences) and *ying* (ornamental tassels) were decorated with *tiao-si* (corded silk). Lexicons state that it means "to weave silk into ropes. The *Gujin Zhengzi* (Orthodox Characters of Antiquity and Today) states that it belongs to the category of "weaving" (*bian*). It is composed of the radical *mi* (糸, silk) and the phonetic component *you* (攸) in abbreviated form.

The character for *jiù* (句) has the upper radical *gǒu* (苟) with the phonetic *hóu* (侯). According to the *Kǎoshēng*, it means "to linger," "to pull," or "to bend. The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radicals *bāo* (勹) and *kǒu* (口), and is also written as *gōu* (鉤) with the radical *jīn* (金); its appearance in the *Lǜwén* as *qiū* (怐) is incorrect. The lower part, *niǔ* (紐), has the phonetic *jiǔ* (九). According to the *Kǎoshēng*, it means "a knot that can be untied. The *Shuōwén* states it refers to thread, composed of the radical *xì* (系) with the phonetic *chǒu* (丑).

*Yingwu*: the first character is pronounced *yì* (with the rhyme *yíng*) and the second is pronounced *yōu* (with the rhyme *liù*). The *Kǎo Shēng* says it resembles a grape but has small black berries. The *Shuōwén* says: "The character for *yīng* (the first part) is written with the radical 艸 and the phonetic 奧."

The character 𤌢 (nuǎn) is pronounced with the "water" radical and the "slave" (nú) and "bamboo tube" (guǎn) radicals reversed. The *Shuowen* states that it means "warmth" (*wēn*). It is composed of the "fire" radical and the phonetic "ruǎn," which is pronounced with the "ér" and "yuǎn" radicals reversed.

The character 屆 (jiè) has the "grass" radical above and the "xiè" radical below. Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that it means "to arrive. According to the *Wenzi Dian*, it is composed of the "corpse" (尸) radical and the "follow" (由) radical; it is a semantic compound character meaning "to arrive by following what one has proceeded through."

*Tāo* (逃): Upper radical *táng* (唐), level tone (*láo fǎn*). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "to flee away. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states: "to hide. The *Guǎngyá* states: "to avoid. The *Zishū* states: "to conceal. The *Shuowén* states: "to perish; it follows the radical *chuò* (辵) and takes *zhào* (兆) as its phonetic. *Chuò* is pronounced *chǐu lüè fǎn*. The version in the *Lǜ* (律) is written as *tāo* (逃), which is incorrect. The lower radical is *bó* (伯), level tone (*mèng fǎn*). The *Kǎoshēng* states: "*Tāng* (𡗱) means to scatter and conceal; it is also written as *fú* (𧻓). The *Wenzidian* explains that it follows the radical *tāng* (𡗱) with *píng* (屏) as its phonetic. The version in the *Lǜwén* (律文) follows the radical *chuò* (辵) and is written as *bèng* (迸), which is a vulgar character.

The character 𠛠 (wǎn) is a regular form for "bowl. An examination of its phonetics states that 𠛠 means "to carve or etch. The *Pīcāng* states that 𠛠 is the same as 󲱛. The *Zītǒng* states that 𠛠 is the same as 斗 󲱛. In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, it is composed of the radical 刀 (knife) with 夗 (yuǎn) as the phonetic component; the vulgar form 剜 is also acceptable. The pronunciation of 󲱛 is fúxuán-fǎn.

Volume Eight, Part Eight. *Wen* (紊): Lower tone, pronounced as *wen*. The commentary on the *Shangshu* states that it means "disorder. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical *mi* (silk) with *wen* as the phonetic component. *Kǐng* (謦): Upper tone, pronounced as *qīngyǐng*. The *Cangjie pian* states that it means "sound.

The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "coughing," composed of the radical *yan* (speech) with *kìng* (pronounced *qìng*) as the phonetic component. *Kài* (咳): Lower tone, pronounced as *kāi'ài*. Gu Yewang states that it means "to cough. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "upward-moving qi," composed of the radical *qian* (to yawn) with *hai* as the phonetic component. *Sou* (嗽), pronounced as *sānghòu*, is used here.

The first tone of *di* in *dìpèn* (sneezing) means "to blow the nose," according to the *Cāngjiépiān*. The *Shuōwén* states: "Dì means the release of qi upon awakening; it is composed of the radical 口 (mouth) and the phonetic 疐 (pronounced as above, with the second tone). In the *Zhànguó Cè*, it says: "A steed lowers its head and *pèn*, then raises its head and neighs. The *Shuōwén* states: "*Pèn* means to hiss (*zhà*); it is composed of the radical 口 and the phonetic 賁 (pronounced as above, with the fourth tone). The pronunciation of *hūnpèn* is *pǔmén*."

"Looking around" (顧眄): "顧" (gù) is read as *gu* with the *shangping* tone; Zheng’s commentary on the *Mao Shi* states that "to turn one's head" is called "顧" (*huí shǒu*). The *Guǎng yá* says "顧" means "眷" (*juàn*, to look back). The *Shuōwén* defines "顧" as "to turn the head and look"; it is composed of "頁" (*xié*) and the phonetic "雇" (*gù*), where "頁" is pronounced *xiánjié*. "眄" (*miǎn*) is read as *biàn* with the *xiàping* tone. The *Kǎoshēng* says "眄" means "to look askance. The *Shuōwén* says "眄" means "the eyes are partially closed"; it is composed of "目" (*mù*) and the phonetic "丐" (*gài*), where "丐" is pronounced as above and "衺" (*xié*) is pronounced *yé*.

The upper character 蘿 (luó) is pronounced as "luó," and the lower character 蔔 (bó) is pronounced as "péng" with a retroflex *b* (北反). The *Kǎo Shēng* states that it is the name of a vegetable; the *Shuōwén* calls it 蘆菔 (lúbo), which resembles the 蕪菁 (wūjīng) [mustard]. Both characters are written with the radical 廾 (sǒng) and take 羅 (luó) and 蔔 (bó) as their phonetic components.

The character *duàn* (斷) at the top of the phrase [refers to] the enemy; it is a character that reverses the common form. The *Shūjìng Kǒngzhù* (孔注尚書) states: "To sever. The *Shuowén* (說文) states: "To cut. It is composed of the radical *jīn* (斤) and the phonetic *jié* (㡭); *jié* is pronounced as *jué* (絕). The version in the *Lǜ* (律) reads *jù* (拒), which is incorrect. Regarding the character below, the *Dùzhù Zuǒzhuàn* (杜注左傳) states: "'Dí' (敵) means 'to face' or 'to correspond. The *Fāngyán* (方言) states: 'Those who exert equal force are called *dí*'. The *Shuowén* states: "'Dí' means 'foe. It is composed of the radical *pū* (攴) and the phonetic *shāng* (啇)."

Regarding "dǎ pò" (打撲): Yuè Bùgù (野王) states that "pò" (撲) is synonymous with "dǎ chuí" (打捶), meaning to strike. The *Guǎngyǎ* states it means "to strike. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "bù" (菐), where "bù" has the pronunciation "bǔ".

"Xi" (襲) means to launch a surprise attack. The commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that it refers to "attacking while the enemy is unprepared. The *Zhouli* states that "xi" refers to a sudden raid or ambush. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the character is composed of the radical "clothing" (衣) and the phonetic "long" (龍).

*Xié* (挾): Upper radical *yíng* (盈), reversed *chì* (赤); *Běicāng* (埤蒼) states that *xié* refers to the armpit, the area behind the elbow. In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, it is composed of the radical "flesh" (*ròu*) and the phonetic "ye" (*yè*). *Gé* (胳) has the pronunciation *gè* (各). Lower radical *xián* (嫌), reversed *jiá* (頰). Hé Xiū’s commentary on the *Gōngyáng Zhuan* states: "To *xié* means to harbor. The *Erya* states: "*Xié* means to store away. The *Shuowen* states it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "jiā" (*jiā*). Dǔ’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states: "It removes the sacrifice to the fontanelle (*xìng*). The *Shuowen* states: "It is a sacrifice for removing evils; it is composed of the radical 'altar' (*shì*) and the phonetic 'bá' (*bà*). *Bá* has the pronunciation *pánbō* (盤鉢).

Volume Nine, Part Nine: *Xiàqì* (Gaps/Defects). The upper character, *xià*, is pronounced with the *xià* rhyme (as in "summer"). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "A *xià* is like a transgression. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "A *xià* is a flaw in jade. The *Guǎngyá* states: "It means to split. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical for "jade" (*yù*) and the phonetic element *duàn*; the lower character is pronounced with the *qīng* and *nì* rhymes.

*Xiāo* (嚻): The first character is pronounced with the *qiao* rhyme (許嬌反). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "It means clamor. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states: "It means sound. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "It refers to the breath and sound emerging from the head; it is composed of the radical *ji* (㗊) and the character *ye* (頁), which means the head. The pronunciation of *ji* is *zhuānglì* (莊立反)."

Guō (Dìshàngguān huó fǎn). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "Guō means clamor. The *Cangjie pian* states: "Guō means to disturb the ears. The *Shuowen jiezi* states: "It is clamorous speech; it is formed with the radical 'ear' and the phonetic 'tongue' (*she*)."
The lower radical of 鐵 (tiě) is pronounced fú; it is a vulgar character. Regarding 𧧳 (zàn):

the upper part is read as kuà huā (the "huā" in "kuàhuā"). The Commentary on the Book of Documents by Kǒng [Yǎng] states: "To be arrogant and overbearing (*jiāo zàn*) is to exceed proper limits and thereby bring about one's own premature death. The *Shìfǎ* (Canon of Posthumous Titles) says: "To speak with flowery words that lack substance is called *zàn*. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "boastful exaggeration" (*kuādàn*). It is composed of the radical 言 (speech) and the phonetic element 𡗢; the pronunciation of 𡗢 is the same as above.

Regarding "kūn" (蜫), when combined with "yì" (蟻) it forms "kūnyì" (蜫蟻). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "Kūn insects are those that are born in the yang [season] and hide away in the yin [season]. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes this character as "gūn" (䖵), defining it as a general term for insects.
"Chīxiāo" (鴟梟): the first character is read as zhì (脂) with the fanqie "shàng chì" (上叱), and the second is read as jiǎo (皎) with the fanqie "yáo" (堯).

Zheng’s commentary states they are birds that cry out unpleasantly. Volume Ten, Number Ten: "Hénggān" (桁竿). The first character is read as hè (鶴) with the fanqie "làng" (浪), and the second is pronounced gān (干). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that a *héng* is a clothes rack; in the original text of the *Lǜ* (律), it is written as *háng* (笐) from the "bamboo" radical, which is a musical instrument (pronounced hèláng [鶴郎]), and is not the word for "clothes rack."

The character *zui* (卒髓反) is explained in the *Guǎyá* as "the opening of the mouth" (*jǐkǒu*). Dictionaries state it means "beak" (*huì*). According to the *Shuowén*, this character is formed with the phonetic component *shù* (束); it is also written as *zuǐ* (觜) or *wèi* (𠲿). The pronunciation of *shù* is *cī* (雌四反), and the pronunciation of *huì* is *huī* (暉衛反).

The character *sǎo* (in *sǎosì*) has the phonetic *shāo* (lǎo fǎn) for its upper radical and *suí* (*ruì* fǎn) for its lower radical. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *huì*, defining it as "a broom made of bamboo," composed of the radical *yòu* (hand) holding the character *sè* (pronounced *shèng* [shēng] and *zhēn*). Its ancient form is written as *cáo*.

The character *zhēng* (棖) is pronounced with the initial *zhé* (擇) and the final *gēng* (庚); it refers to the sound produced by striking, as in "to strike" (*zhuàng*). The *Yùpiān* writes it as *chōu* (󳉴), meaning "to prick. It is also written as *qiāo* (敲), meaning "to strike. The *Wénzìdiǎn* explains that it follows the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "long" (長). The version in the *Lǜběn* (律本) is incorrect.

*Niǔdiàn* (鈕扂): the first character is pronounced *ní* (with the *liǔ* rhyme) and was already fully explained in the seventh fascicle; the second character is pronounced *tián* (with the *diàn* rhyme) and was already explained in the third fascicle.
*Zhuānduò* (甎垛): the first character is pronounced *zhuān* and the second is pronounced *duǒ*; both were already explained in the third fascicle.

*Tán* (啗) with the radical *kǒu* (mouth) and the phonetic *xiàn* (臽); *xiàn* is pronounced as *xiàn*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "tán" means to eat. The version in the Vinaya is written as *càn* (噉), which is a vulgar character. The second character, *qiáng yào* (牆藥), is pronounced as *yào*; it was already explained in the first fascicle above.

"Shan-shu" (扇樞): "Shu" is pronounced with the *chu* rhyme (朱反). Han Kangbo’s commentary on the *Zhouyi* states: "The pivot (*shu*) is the master that initiates motion. The *Guangya* states: "The pivot is the root. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as: "The pivot of a door; it is composed of the radical 'wood' (*mu*) and the phonetic 'qu' (*qu*). The pronunciation of "qu" is *quyu* (曲于反).

The character 鎗 (qiāng) is pronounced with the initials *cēng* and *kǎng* and the final *-fǎn*. The *Kǎo Shēng* states it belongs to the category of tripods (*dǐng*). It is also written as 鐺 (chéng), which is a vulgar character.

The character 鍤 (qiāo) is pronounced with the initials *chì* and *jiǎ* and the final *-fǎn*. The *Fāng Yán* states that in the regions between Song and Wei, a shovel is called a *qiāo*; in the regions between Jiang-Huai and Nan-Chu, it is called a *chì*. According to the *Shuōwén*, this character is composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic "chì. The pronunciation of 臿 is the same as above; the pronunciation of 鍬 is *qī* and *jiāo*.

*Zhuōjīn* (斲斤): "Zhù" (斲) is pronounced with the initial *zhú* and final *-jiǎo*. Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjìng* states that it means "to plane or pare. The *Shuowén* says it means "to hew," composed of the radical *jīn* (axe) and the phonetic *chāo*;

*chāo* is pronounced *dòu*. *Tàihuǐ* (󳍅毀): "Tài" (󳍅) is pronounced with the initial *dù* and final *-léi*. The *Guǎngyá* states it means "to collapse or ruin. The *Shuowén* says it is composed of the radical *fù* (hill/mound) and the phonetic *guì*; *fù* is pronounced *fù*.

11. The Eleventh Fascicle, Part Eleven. Regarding the term "汝捥𠛠" (*rǔ wàn jī*), it is corrected to "󳃪" (*wàn*). Its meaning has already been fully explained in the seventh fascicle of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*. In the original Vinaya text, it is written as "肉" (*ròu*); "腕" (*wàn*) is a vernacular character.
*Xiàqún* (下裙): *qún* is pronounced as *jùn* and *yún*. This was already explained in the first fascicle above; the ancient script is correctly written as *qún*.

*Qiánbá* (鉆拔): *qián* is pronounced as *qiáng* and *yán*. The *Shuowen* says: "A metal tool for gripping objects; it consists of the radical 'metal' (*jīn*) and the phonetic 'zhàn'. The *Lüben* (律本) writes this as *qián* (鉗), which refers to an iron collar used to bind the neck, and does not carry the meaning of "gripping and pulling. *Biàn* (辨) is pronounced as *bān* and *bā*. The *Shangshu* (尚書) says: "The great trees were pulled out" (*dàmù bǐbá*). Gu Yewang says: "To pull out is like drawing something forth. The *Guoyaya* (廣雅) says: "To pull out. The *Shuowen* [entry for *bá*] uses the radical 'hand' (*shǒu*) and the phonetic 'bó' (犮); *bó* is pronounced as *pán* and *bō*.
*Lie* (捩): The upper radical is *lián* (憐) with the reversed *niè* (涅); it has already been fully explained and annotated in the fifth fascicle above.

*Jue* (抉): The upper radical is *huì* (恚) with the reversed *yuè* (悅). The *Zuǒzhuan* says, "He used a halberd to gouge out his intestines. The *Zhuāngzǐ* says, "Zǐxū had his eyes gouged out. The *Shuōwén* states that *jue* means "to pick" (*tiāo*) and is composed of the radical *shǒu* (hand) with the phonetic *guài* (夬).

Regarding the character *jù* (saw), it is pronounced as *jū* (御) with a retroflex final. The *Guoyu* states: "In ancient and medieval times, punishments used knives and saws," referring to the penalty of execution (*dàpì*). The *Huainanzi* says: "A skilled craftsman does not rely on knives and saws; he cannot fashion wood [without them], yet the saw is that which can cut objects. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines *jù* as "a *qiāngtáng* (a type of saw); it is composed of the radical *jīn* (metal) and the phonetic *jū*."

*Gǎi* (㓟): The upper radical is pronounced *pí*. According to the commentary, *gǎi* carries the meaning of "stripping off the skin"; it is a vulgar character. The lower part is pronounced *mǎi*. *Máo hóng* (矛𥎞): The upper radical is pronounced *mǔ hóu*.

The *Shuowen* states that it is a *qiú máo* (a type of spear) and is a pictographic character. In ancient script, it is written as *fén* (𢦵) or *hè* (𨥨). The lower part is pronounced *cāng suàn*. The *Guǎngyá* states that *jiǎn* (䂎) is called *tǐng* (鋌); it is a short spear. According to the *Wenzi Dianshuo*, it takes the radical *máo* with *zàn* as its phonetic component.

*Chàn* (on the body): *shēng* and *xí* both read as *shǎi*. The *Huáinán Zǐ* states: "To scar the skin and flesh, to incise the leather; the wound flows with blood. It also refers to needle-pricking. The *Shuōwén* says: "A sharp instrument for carving; it takes the radical 金 (metal) and the phonetic 剡. It is also written as 劖 or 剡; the pronunciation is the same as above.

*Shao* (pronounced *shuāo* with the "dual" [double] tone): The *Guǎngyá* states that a *shào* is a spear (*máo*). The *Běicāng* states it is what is now called a *chūnshào*. The *Wénzìdiǎn* explains that it is formed from the radical "spear" (*máo*) and the phonetic "xiào," with the final tone being *qīng* (*qìng*). Gù Yěwáng says it refers to a sharp point that pierces into human flesh. The *Shuōwén* defines "sting" (*cì*) as straight injury; it is formed from the radical "knife" (*dāo*) and the phonetic "shù."

*Méng* (as in *méngtóng*, "molten copper")—the first character is pronounced *yǒng* with a retroflex *-n* ending (*zhōng* reversed)—the *Hànshū* states: "It is like gold in a crucible, cast only according to what the smith molds. It is also said to mean "molten" or "flowing. *Tóngxiè wéi méng* ("copper filings constitute *méng*"): according to the *Shuowén*, it refers to the method of smelting vessels; it is composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic component "youthful" (*róng*).

*Wù* (pronounced *wú* with a retroflex initial): The *Yùnlüè* states it refers to a tree trunk without branches; the *Zìtǒng* says it is a felled log, or alternatively, a withered tree. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic element "wu" (*wù*).
The meaning of *tanyin* (痰癊)—with the first character pronounced as *tán* and the second as *yǐn* (with the radical *jìn*)—has already been fully explained in the Vinaya of the Sarvāstivāda school.

As for *xiè* (榍)—pronounced *xiān* (with the radical *jié*)—the *Shuowen Jiezi* calls it a *qiē* (楔), which is a wedge; *qiē* is pronounced *zǐlián*. This has already been explained in the thirteenth fascicle.
*Arbuda*: "An" (頞) is pronounced with the *shang* tone (an) and "bu" (部); "da" (陀) is pronounced with the *shang* tone (dà).

This is a transliteration of the Sanskrit term for a fetal stage (*arbuda*). *Ghana* (稠酪): "Chou" (稠) is pronounced with the *shang* tone (zhòu) and "lao" (酪) is pronounced with the *liu* tone (là). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (毛詩傳) states it means "dense"; the *Guang Ya* (廣雅) states it means "thick. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文解字) explains that "chou" (稠) is composed of the radical for "grain" (禾) and the phonetic "zhou" (周), while "ji" (穊) has the pronunciation *ji*; "lao" (酪) has the pronunciation *luo*.
The term *chā* (㰆) is pronounced with the initial *pá* and final *mài*. Its meaning has already been fully explained in the preceding commentary.

Regarding *chā* (插), the *Shēnglèi* states that it means "to prick and enter. The *Shuowén* says it means "to thrust inward. It is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "zhā" (臿). The pronunciation of *zhā* is as stated above; the pronunciation of *càn* (磣) is *chū-jǐn*.

*Hei* (黑): The upper radical is *li* (履, reversed); the phonetic gloss says it means blackish-yellow. In ancient and modern standard characters, it is composed of the radical *hei* (黑) and the abbreviated phonetic *li* (黎).

*Lian* (臠): The upper radical is *lüe* (劣, with *yuan* [兖] as a variant); Gu Yawang says it refers to small pieces of sliced meat. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* (Textual Dictionary of Characters) states it is composed of the radical *rou* (肉) and the abbreviated phonetic *lian* (戀). The pronunciation of *zhi* (胾) is *zi* (緇) and *shi* (史), while the lower part is pronounced *gan* (干) and *he* (曷).

12. The Twelfth Fascicle. Regarding "zha" (唼) in "zhashi" (唼食): according to the *Kaosheng* (考聲), it means "to suck" (*zasu*). The *Zitong* (字統) states that it specifically refers to sucking blood. The correct character is "ya" (𠯗). The *Tongsuowen* (通俗文) says that when flavor enters the mouth, it is called "ya. The *Wenzidian* (文字典) explains that it is composed of the radical "mouth" (口) and the phonetic element "qie" (妾). The pronunciation of "jiu" (咎) is *zafan* (帀感反); the following character is correctly "shi" (食).

Regarding "bāngbǎo" (襁褓), the reading for "bǎo" is *jiāng* (姜) with the *yǎng* (仰) rhyme. In his commentary on the *Lunyu*, Bāo Xián states: "That which is carried by means of a vessel is called a *bāng*. The *Bówùzhì* says: "It is woven from thread, eight inches wide and twelve feet long, used to fasten an infant to one's back. The *Shuowén* defines it as "clothing for carrying a child," composed of the radical "clothing" (*yī*) and the phonetic "qiáng" (*qiángshēng*), with the lower character pronounced *bǎo*. A full explanation has already been provided in the thirteenth fascicle of the *Vinaya* of the Mūlasarvāstivāda school.

*Gài* (上): Pronounced *gēng* (猛反). The *Erya* says, "Straight. The *Guoyu* says, "Briefly. The *Shuowen* says, "From the radical 木, with the phonetic 更. *Gāi* (下): Pronounced *ài* (愛反). Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* says, "That by which one can level bushels and measures. The *Shuowen* says, "*Gai* is to level bushels and measures; from the radical 木, with the phonetic 既. *Kǎi* (杚): Pronounced *kūnwù* (昆兀反). *Gài*: The upper character is pronounced *gēng*. The *Erya* states that it means "straight. The *Guoyu* states it means "briefly. The *Shuowen* states it is composed of the radical 木 and the phonetic 更. The lower character is pronounced *ài*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states that it is "that by which one may level bushels and measures. The *Shuowen* states: "*Gai* is to level bushels and measures; it is composed of the radical 木 and the phonetic 既. *Kǎi* (杚) has the pronunciation *kūnwù*.

*Jin-mai* (筋脈): "Jin" (筋) is pronounced as *jin* with the *yin* tone *gan* (謹). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "the power of muscle and sinew. It is composed of the radical "flesh" (*rou*) and the character "bamboo" (*zhu*), as bamboo is among things that possess many sinews; it is further joined with the radical "strength" (*li*), which symbolizes the sinew itself. The lower part is pronounced *xu* (󳎕), the correct orthography. The *Shuowen* also records it as *mai* (󲲄), stating it refers to the channels of blood that circulate throughout the body. It is composed of the radical "blood" (*xue*) and the phonetic element *li* (𠂢); *li* is pronounced *pu-mai* (普賣). The form used in the *Vinaya* (律本) is a vulgar variant.

*Xián* (㳄唾): The upper character is pronounced *xiáng yán*. The *Shuowen* states that "㳄" refers to saliva; it is composed of the radicals "quàn" (欠) and "shui" (水). The form used in the Vinaya texts (*lüwén*) is "xián," which is a vulgar character. The lower character is pronounced *tǔ wò*. *Fèn guō* (糞鍋):

The upper character is pronounced *fēn wèn*. The *Shuowen* states that "󱯬" means to remove; it is composed of "gǒng" (拱) and "tuī" (推). "Huá" (華) refers to removing excrement. It is composed of "mi" (米), which is the ancient form of the character for "shi" (糞, excrement); it resembles "mi" but is not identical. "Sì" (似) is pronounced *bān*; it belongs to the category of winnowing baskets (*jī*). It is composed of "kǒng" (廾), pronounced *gǒng*, meaning both hands. The form in the Vinaya texts—composed of "mi" and "yì" (異)—is a vulgar character. The lower character is pronounced *gǔ hé*; this too is a vulgar character. The correct form is "󲴄. It refers to a small iron shovel without legs, such as those used for cauldrons (*qiāng fù*). To speak of "fecal 󲴄" is because the heat and steam within the womb are impure and foul, like food boiling in a 󲴄.

*Du* (毒): The *Yùkǎo* (爾雅·釋詁) states that it refers to clotted blood within the skin and flesh; the *Wénzìdiǎn* (文字典) explains it as an accumulation of blood. It is composed of the radical *nà* (疒) and the phonetic *yú* (于). *Tán* (鱓): The upper character is pronounced *chán-chǎn* (蟬闡) with the third tone.

Guō’s commentary on the *Shānhǎijīng* (山海經) states that the *tán* fish resembles a snake. The *Shuowén* (說文) says its skin can be used to make drums; it is composed of the radical *yú* (魚) and the phonetic *dān* (單). The lower character is pronounced *zhēn-chì* (真叱). The *Cāngjiépian* (蒼頡篇) states it is an aquatic creature capable of sucking human blood. The *Shuowén* further notes it is composed of the radical *chóng* (虫) and the phonetic *zhì* (至); *chóng* is pronounced like *huǐ* (虺).

"Bànghé" (蚌蛤): "Bàng" is pronounced with the *páng* rhyme (as in *páng*). Kuo Pu’s commentary states that it refers to the clam (*bàng*). The *Zhouyi* says it is that which has pearls in its belly. The *Chunqiu Guoshi* states: "When the moon is at its fullness, the clams and oysters are full; when the moon is at its end, the clams and oysters are empty. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as a clam (*lì*) and gives the phonetic component *fēng*. The lower radical is *gāndá*. The *Liji* states: "In the ninth month of autumn, the sparrows enter the great waters, the sea. It also says: "A sparrow that lives for a thousand years becomes a *jià*. The *Shuowen* says there are three kinds of *hã*, all of which are produced in the sea. A clam (*lì*) that lives for a thousand years is what a *jā* (a type of gull) transforms into; the state of Qin called this a "strong clam" (*zhuànglì*). The sea clam (*hǎihã*) is what a hundred-year-old swallow transforms into. The *kuái-hã* (a large clam), also known as the *púluó*, is what a bat (*fúyì*) transforms into. The phonetic component is *hé*.
The character for *shànyè* (善軶) is correctly written as *yì* (厄); the version in the *Jīng* (經) as *è* (軛) is a vulgar form.
The character for *ròubào* (肉疱) is pronounced *péngmào fǎn*; according to the *Shuōwén*, it refers to sores arising from facial vapors, though it is sometimes written as *pào* (皰).

The character 頷 (han) [with the phonetic 敢 (gan) as a rhyme]: Yingyun states it means "chin" (yí). Shìmíng states it is "fǔchē" (the jawbones). It is also written as 頥 (yí); in the Nan-Chu region, the chin is called "hàn. It is composed of the radical 頁 (head) with the phonetic 含 (han).

"Palatal bone" (*yàkǔ*)—the character *wò* (我) is a vulgar form. Examining its phonetic component, "palate" refers to the upper palate of the mouth. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "The 'upper arched part of the mouth' (*kǒushàng ā*). It is composed of the radical 'mouth' (*kǒu*) with the phonetic 'gǔ' (谷), pronounced *qiánglüè*. From the radical 'mouth' and 'quàn' (欠), it represents the texture and patterns [of the palate]. What was formerly called 'gè' (各) is now called 'é' (咢); this is a shift in sound."

*Wei* (胃): The upper character is pronounced *xū* (同勗, *gōngfǎn*); the *Shuowen* states it means "the chest. The lower character is pronounced *yì* (音憶, *yì*). It refers to the clavicle (*jī*). In archaic script it is written as *wèi* (󳈰). *Nǎi* (𦙄):

The upper character is pronounced *qīng* (清) and *suì* (歲); the *Guangya* states it means "fragile" (*cuìruò*). The *Zitong* says it means "flesh that is soft and easily broken. The *Wenzidian* says it means "easily shattered. The *Shuowen* says it means "slightly soft and easily broken. It is composed of the radical *ròu* (肉) and the phonetic *jué* (絕) in abbreviated form. The lower character is pronounced *kuí* (逵). The *Wenzidian* says it means "to be fearful while on high. It signifies a person atop a precipice (*chǎn*) who adorns themselves to stop [falling]. The *Shuowen* states it is composed of the radical *jié* (卩) and the phonetic *wěi* (厃). The pronunciation of *wěi* is *wēi* (危) with the final *fǎn* (反). It is composed of the radical *rén* (人) and the radical *chǎn* (厂).

The *cāng* (granary) and the *chuán* (round basket) both have their rims hanging down. Xu Shu’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states: "The *chuán* is a vessel for grain. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* explains: "It is woven from bamboo or wood into a circular shape that can hold grains such as rice and wheat; it takes the radical 'bamboo' (*zhú*) and the phonetic 'duān' (*duàn*); the pronunciation of *chuán* is *dùn*."

Regarding "fáng-gāo" (fat and grease): the upper character is pronounced *fāng*; the *Shuowen* states that "fáng" means "fat," composed of the radical "meat" (*ròu*) with the phonetic "fāng. The lower character is pronounced *gāo*; the *Shiming* says that "gāo" refers to congealed fat, while the *Shuowen* states it means "fat," composed of the radical "moon" (*yuè*) with the phonetic "gāo."
Fēnglè (豐樂): The upper character is 丰 (fēng), and the lower is pronounced lánggè.

Yìcóng (翊從): The upper character is pronounced yíngjí. Gu Yewáng states that "yì" means "to assist. According to the Shuowen Jiezi, it is a compound ideograph composed of 羽 (feather) and 立 (standing). The lower character is pronounced cáiyòng.

"Sen" (森) means "towering. The *Shuowen* states: "Sen refers to the appearance of many tall trees; it is composed of the radical 'tree' (林) and the phonetic 'mu' (木), pronounced like the 'shang' (上) of Shangdang Renshen (上黨人參). The character 'can' (參) has the pronunciation 'suo lin' (所林); the character 'li' (栗) has the pronunciation 'yong' (勇). The *Guoyaya* states: "Sen means 'upward' (上). Gu Yewang states: "It means 'high' (高). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of 'li' (立) and 'shu' (束); 'shu' is derived from 'ziyou shu' (自由束) and also serves as the phonetic component.
The meaning of "jiè" (屆) [with the initial *xiè*] has already been fully explained in the seventh fascicle.

Regarding "shīhái" (屍骸): the *Lǐjì* states, "One who is deceased on their bed is called a *shī*"; Zheng’s commentary explains that *shī* means "to lay out," signifying that the physical form remains. The *Shuowén* states, "*Shī* means death; it is composed of the radicals *shī* and *sǐ*. Lù Yěwáng’s commentary on the *Gōngyáng Zhuan* states that *hài* refers to bones. The *Shuowén* further defines *tǐ* (體) as the general name for the body and bones, while the *Shuowén* also specifies that *tǐ* refers to the leg bone, with *hài* as its phonetic component.

13. Volume Thirteen. *Kūṭa* (氍毹). The first character is pronounced *ju* (具) with the *qu* (于) rhyme; the second is pronounced *shu* (數) with the *e* (󲵥) rhyme. This is a term from the language of the Hu (胡). It refers to a woven-fur cloth made by weaving animal hair into fabric, similar to hemp, used for spreading over beds and mats. It originates from the country of Kapiśa (𦋺賓國). The *Shenglei* (聲類) states it is a "hair mat" (*maoxi*). Both characters are written with the "hair" (*mao*) radical. The phonetic components are *yu* (俞) and *yu* (俞) respectively. It is also written as *zhu* (󱮣) or *lu* (氀).

Regarding the character *kàn* (矸): when pronounced with the initial *hán* (寒) and the final *gàn* (幹), it is explained as the sound of a cold, dry stone. It denotes the white appearance of jade and stone, and is also written as *kàn* (矸). Furthermore, it is also pronounced with the initial *qiān* (千) and the final *hàn* (旱). It is incorrect for the *Lü* (律) texts to write this with the radical for grain (*禾*) as *gǎn* (秆).

The character 帒 (dài) is pronounced with the radical 巾 (cloth) and the phonetic 代 (dài). Guo Pu states that it refers to the skin of muntjac or deer; the *Kaosheng* says it is a "sack" (*náng*). The *Wenzidian* explains that it is formed from the radical 巾 with 代 as the phonetic component. The upper part is pronounced *kè* (with the *gāng* rhyme), while the lower part is pronounced *tái* (with the *lài* rhyme).

Regarding "héng" (pronounced with the *làng* and *fǎn* tones), the phonetic gloss says: "Héng" refers to a clothes rack; the version in the Vinaya (*Lǜběn*) uses "háng," which is incorrect. Regarding "lǐng" (with the *shàng* tone *zhuó* and *jiāng*):

the *Shuowén* says it is a window in a wall (*yǒu*) or a skylight in a roof (*dài*), a pictographic character, or written as "líng" with the radical "cave" (*xué*). The Vinaya text uses "chuāng" with the radical "piàn," which is a vulgar form. Regarding "lì" (with the *dīng* tone): the *Shuowén* says it is the hand between the crossbars of a railing (*shǔn*); it takes the "wood" (*mù*) radical and the phonetic "líng," where the sound of "líng" is the same as above.

*Keng* (骾) [pronounced *geng* with the initial *x-*, as in *xing* (杏)] refers to something stuck in the throat that does not go down. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "bone" (*gu*) and the phonetic "more" (*geng*). In the *Lüwen* (律文), it is written as *jing* (鯁) with the radical "fish," but this does not carry the same meaning. The lower character is pronounced *hou*.

The *jiǎshé bì* (tongue-scraper): "bì" is pronounced as *huá* (in the rhyme of *guān*) and has already been explained in the first volume of the *Shìlù*. According to the *Kǎoshēng*, it refers to the *mí bì* (deer-scraper) and similar tools;

it is also written as *bī*. It should be split (*pī*; *pīng* is pronounced *pǐ* and *bìng*); according to the *Guǎngyǎ*, "pī" means to tear apart; according to the *Běicāng*, it means to cleave; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means to break, composed of the radical "knife" (*dāo*) with the phonetic element "bì."

Regarding the character *qiān* (籤): it is pronounced with the *jié* (閻) rhyme. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *qiān* means "sharp" or "to pierce," written with the radical for bamboo (*zhú*) and the phonetic *qiān*. The pronunciation of *qiān* is *sīlián* (思廉), while the final syllable here is *cǐsì* (此四). The *Vinaya* text uses the form *qiāncì* (籤刺), which is a vulgar variant.

"Suì" (遂) means to grasp; the *Guǎngyǎ* states that "suì" means to hold, and the *Shuōwén* states it means to seize, composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "qīng" (󲷸), also written as "shè" (攝).

"Dòu" (斗) and "jiān" (枅)—the latter pronounced qiān—refers to the wooden beam above a pillar; the *Cāngjiépiān* calls it the "beam above the pillar," and Xu Shūzhòng states it is the "jílú" (櫨). The *Shuōwén* explains it is composed of the radical "wood" (木) and the phonetic "qiān" (幵), where "qiān" is pronounced qiān.

*Bò* (𥿳): Pronounced *bèng* (with the *mài* [麥] radical). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states that *bò* means "to split or tear. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as consisting of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic component "pì" (*pì*).
14. Volume Fourteen. *Chí* (持): Pronounced *suì* (with the *zuì* [醉] radical). This term has already been fully explained and annotated in the preceding Volume Ten.

Regarding "蚤" (yǎo) and "蝨" (shī): The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "蚤" is a biting, jumping insect; it is composed of the radical "䖵" (wén) with the phonetic "卂" (xìn), where "卂" is pronounced *zè qiǎo*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "蝨" is an insect that bites humans; it is composed of the radical "䖵" (wén) with the phonetic "卂" (xìn), where "卂" is pronounced *xìn* and "䖵" is pronounced *kūn*.

*Tāotiè* (饕餮): the first character is pronounced *dǎo* (with the *dǎo* rhyme), the second is *tiān niè* (with the *niè* rhyme). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "To covet wealth is *tāo*; to covet food is *tiè*. *Xùtǒng* (畜筩):

the first character is pronounced *xiū yù* (with the *yù* rhyme), the second has the same pronunciation. The *Fānyán* states: "A *tǒng* is a salt-tube; it is also a tube for chopsticks. The *Shuowen* states: "It is a section of split bamboo; it is formed with the radical 'bamboo' (*zhú*) and the phonetic 'yǒng' (*yǒng*)."

*Pàn-tì* (上盤漫反, 下隄麗反): A term from the Sanskrit language; in the Tang [translation], it means "to pay homage" (*vandana*). *Yǎng* (𭼦癢): - *Sāng-dāo* (桑刀) with the departing tone as an alternative reading.

- The *Zītǒng* states it means "scabies" (*sào-jie*). - The *Guǎngyá* states it means "sores" (*chuāng*). - The *Wénzìdiǎn* explains that it is formed with the radical *nà* (疒, *nǚ è*) and the phonetic *zão* (蚤). - The lower character *yáng* (羊) signifies "not daring to scratch. - The *Shuowén* records it as *xiàng* (蛘), stating it means "to scratch," formed with the radical *chóng* (虫) and the phonetic *yáng* (羊); it is also written as *yǎng*.
*Kang-shi* (礓石): The upper character is pronounced *jiang* (畺), meaning hard soil. Because its shape resembles that of [the character for] *jiang*, it is named accordingly.
*Sai* (摋): Pronounced *da* (打) with the tone *suo-jie-fan* (所誡反);
this is a vulgar character. 15. Volume Fifteen. "Crouching on the ground" (*dun-di-shang* 蹲地上): Pronounced *cu-hun-fan* (徂魂反). This was already explained in the fourth volume above.
The meaning of *pǔ* (醭) [pronounced with the initial *pǔ* and the final *mù*] has already been fully explained in the twenty-seventh fascicle of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*. Regarding *bānbó* (斑駮):

the first character is pronounced *bān* (八蠻反) and the second *bāngmiǎo* (邦邈反). The *Hànshū* states that the mixture of white and black is called *bó*; the *Shuowén* writes it as *bó* and explains it as "a color that is not pure," derived from the radical "horse" (*mǎ*) and the phonetic "jiāo" (*jiāo*).

Having thus explained [the term], it appears in the twenty-second fascicle of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*. Regarding the character for "water" (水), when combined with "nuò" (捼)—pronounced *nèi* (內) and *huí* (𢌞)—it forms [the term for] "scolding.

The *Guǎngyǎ* states that "nuò" (*𠿒*) refers to the sound of anger; the *Cāngjié piān* states it means "to scold" (*hē*). In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, this is composed of the radical "mouth" (口) and the phonetic "xiē" (歇).
"Grasping the calf" (*zhuan*; the character is pronounced *chuan* with the second tone): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "the calf" (*zhuan*) refers to the muscle of the lower leg.
"The buckle" (*gui*; upper radical *kou*, second tone; lower radical *niu*, third tone): this was already fully explained in the seventh fascicle above.

*Wúgěng*: "Gěng" has the phonetic *xìng* (with the *fǎnqiè* *gēng*). Duan Yucai’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "Cíng" (綆) refers to a rope for drawing water. Examining its sound, it is synonymous with *suò* (rope). The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "Jíng" (汲) is the same as *gěng*. *Jí* (汲):
*guàn* (with the *fǎnqiè* *huàn*). It means to draw water into a bucket."

*Qiāng* (牆): The first character is pronounced *jiàng* (匠) with the final *rǎn* (反), and the second is *qiāng* (鎗) with the final *gé* (格). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To weave upright wooden planks together to form a wall; it takes the radical *mu* (木) and the phonetic *zhé* (𠕋). Volume 16, Chapter 16. *Ān qiàn* (安塹):

*Qiàn* (塹) is pronounced *qiān yàn* (僉艷). Gu Yewang states: "What is now called a moat surrounding a city or fortress is termed *qiàn*. Lexicons state it refers to the *chéng huáng* (城隍, moat or ditch surrounding a city). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "A pit; it takes the radical *tu* (土) and the phonetic *zhǎn* (斬)."

"Chí-chěng" (galloping) refers to commanding and leading [troops] while turning back; "chí-chěng" means to display oneself ostentatiously before the multitude. This corresponds to the meaning of the first line of the Jǐ卦 (Guā) in the *Yì* (Book of Changes): "He adorns his feet and abandons his carriage for the road. It is composed of the radical "mǎ" (horse) with the phonetic "pīng"; "pīng" is pronounced pǐ dīng.

*Sengqieqi* (僧󱯾㩻): The character *qi* (㩻) is pronounced *qi* with the second tone (jī). This term is a transliteration of a Sanskrit word; in the Tang language, it means "armpit-covering robe" (*saṃkakṣikā*). Fearing that sweat might soil the three robes (*tricīvara*), one first uses this robe to cover the armpits before donning the three robes.

"Left hip" (*zǒu bì*): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "bì" refers to the outer part of the thigh, formed from the radical "bone" (*gǔ*) with the phonetic "bēi"; it is also written as "yī. It is incorrect for the *Lü* (Vinaya) texts to write it as "yì," which is formed from the radical "flesh" (*ròu*).
"Ignorance" (*wú míng*): the *Kaoseng Zhuan* states that "míng" means the empty skin of the testicles.

*Chūpīng* (麁絣): The lower character is pronounced with the *bǎi gēng* rhyme. The *Kǎo Shēng* states it means "to string" (*pīngluò*). In the original Vinaya text, it is written as *pīn* (拼) with the hand radical, which is also acceptable.

*Chìxǐ* (𡍩洗): The upper character is pronounced with the *chǒu gé* rhyme. The *Kǎo Shēng* states that with the hand radical it becomes *chì* (󱳪), meaning "to remove. The *Shuōwén* states that *chì* (󲲊) means "to tear," with the phonetic component *lè*. The lower character is pronounced with the *xī lǐ* rhyme. Lexicons state it means "to wash. The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the water radical and the phonetic component *xiān*; *lè* is pronounced as *chǐ*.

Regarding "kòu" (扣) at the beginning of the line: the character is pronounced with the initial *k* and the final *ou*. The commentary on the *Shūjìng* (*Shāngshū zhù*) states that "kòu" means to strike.
The character 䝉 (mēng) is read in the third tone; the *Kǎoshēng* states that it means "not intelligent. The original form in the *Lǜ* (律) text is 𭞾, which is a vulgar variant.

Regarding "yòu" (詃誘): the *Wénzìdiǎn* (Dictionary of Characters) states that "yòu" (詃) also means "to entice" (*yòu*). It is formed with the radical "speech" (言) and the phonetic "xuán" (玄). The character below, "yòu" (誘), is read as *yóu* (由) with the phonetic "jiǔ" (夂); the *Kǎoshēng* (Examination of Sounds) states it means "to guide," "to instruct," or "to exhort and move others."
The character *qiè* (搉) is pronounced with the *qiāng* and *jiǎo* finals followed by the *kǎo* tone; it means to strike with the hands.

The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry) states that *qì* (憩) means to rest. The *Shuōwén Jiězì* (Explaining Simple and Analyzing Compound Characters) writes this as *xiē* (蝎), with the same pronunciation.

*Tiao-di* (跳躑): The upper character is read as *shang* with the phonetic *di* (遙反). The *Cangjie pian* states it means "leaping"; the *Shuowen jiezi* states it means "bounding. The lower character is read as *cheng* with the phonetic *ji* (戟反).

17. Volume Seventeen. *Gen-shao* (根梢): The lower character is read as *jiao* (稍交反). The *Kaosheng* states that "shao" refers to the tip of a tree; the *Shuowen jiezi* states it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mu*) and the phonetic "xiao" (*xiao*). In the Vinaya texts, it is erroneously written as "quan" (蕱) with the radical "grass" (*cao*).

The character *wú* (汙) is pronounced with the initial *wū* (烏) and the final *gù* (故). The *Kǎo Shēng* states it means "to defile. Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* says it means "impure. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "mud," composed of the radical *shuǐ* (水) and the phonetic *yú* (于).

Regarding "bǐng" (餅): the upper radical is *fán* (煩) with the late reading *wǎn* (晩). The *Lìjì* (禮記) states: "When eating millet (*shǔ*) with rice, one does not use chopsticks. The *Yùnquán* (韻詮) says: "Cooked rice that is dry is called *fàn* (飯); that which is moist is called *sūn* (飧). The *Shuōwén* (說文) uses the character *fàn* (飯), defining it as "eating," with the lower part read as *chāngshǎo* (昌少). Furthermore, the *Zìdiǎn* (字典) explains: "*Qí* (𪍑) refers to parching dry flour made from wheat; it takes the character *mài* (麥) as the semantic component and *qiú* (酋) as the phonetic component. The literary form is *sǎo* (󰉓), while *qī* (𪍑) is a vulgar character. The pronunciation of *chāo* (煼) is *chāojiǎo* (抄絞).
*Gēxǐ* (革屣): The first character is *gē* (革); the second is pronounced *sī* (師) with the *zǎi* (滓) tone. It refers to leather footwear from Western countries. *Bāosàtuó* (褒灑陀):

The first character is pronounced *bǎo* (保) with the *máo* (毛) tone; the middle character is *shā* (沙) with the *fú* (󲻝) tone. This is a transliteration of a Sanskrit term, which in Chinese means "Prolonged Purity" (*zhǎngjìng*). Formerly it was called *Bùsà* (布薩), which is an abbreviation.

*Kuǎn* (𦝫髁): Pronounced *huà* (化) with a *fǎn* (反) tone. The *Cāngjié piān* (蒼頡篇) states that it refers to the bone of the buttocks (*tún*). The *Shuōwén* (說文) states that it refers to the thigh (*pǐ*). It is composed of the radical "bone" (*gǔ*) and the phonetic element "guǒ" (*guǒ*). *Pǐ* (髀) is pronounced *pǔmǐ* (蒲米); *tún* (臀) is pronounced *túhún* (徒魂).

*Qù*: Pronounced *dào* (with the final *fǎn* reversed). The *Shuowen* says: "The remains of weaving; it takes *mì* as its radical and *kuì* as its phonetic. *Lěi*: Pronounced *lǜ* (with the final *guǐ* reversed).

The *Guǎyá* says: "Layering; it means to pile up. The *Shuowen* says: "A military camp is called *lěi*; the ancient form is written as *léi*, which depicts its shape. The character below is pronounced *jīng* (with the final *yì* reversed); it refers to unbaked bricks made of earth.

*Tào* (to flee) and *cuàn* (to run away in disorder). Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "Cuàn also means to flee. The *Guangya* states: "It means to throw oneself [into hiding]. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "concealment," with the radical of a rat inside a hole.

*Juanji* (pronounced *shàng jué yuán fǎn*): The *Bicang* states that it means to be cramped and unable to stretch out. The *Wenzi Dian* and *Shuowen Jiezi* state that it refers to the curvature of the back while walking, composed of the radical for "foot" and the phonetic element "juan."
*Luǒ* (縷): The upper radical is *lì* (力) and the phonetic is *jù* (矩). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Thread; it follows the radical *mì* (糸) and takes *lóu* (婁) as its phonetic.

18. Volume Eighteen, Chapter Eighteen. *Bìn* (殯): The phonetic is *bīn* (賔). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "Encoffining is the lowering of the coffin into the grave. He Xiu’s commentary on the *Gongyangzhuan* states: "Moving the coffin [to the burial site] is called encoffining. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Encoffining refers to when the deceased is in the coffin and about to be moved for burial; the corpse and the coffin are encountered by the guests. The Xia dynasty encoffined at the eastern steps (*zuòjiē*), the Yin people encoffined between the two central pillars (*liǎngyíng*), and the Zhou people encoffined at the guest steps (*bīnjiē*). It follows the radical *è* (歺) and takes *bīn* (賔) as its phonetic. The sound of *è* is *yín* (矝).
*Caoshù* (pronounced *zhǔn rùn*): *Běicāng* states it means "to entwine"; dictionaries state it means "a bundle of straw," written with the *huò* radical.

*Púlàná* (pronounced *bǔ mù* for the first character, *lán dá* for the middle, and *yè jiā* for the last): this is a Sanskrit term; it is the name for a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*) who is seen undergoing suffering in hell without it having ended.
*Gengkěn* (耕墾): The first character is pronounced *gēng* (上革鸎反) and the second is *kěn* (下肻狠反).

Regarding "to kick" (*cù*, 足右指蹴, pronounced *qiū* [六反]), He Xiu’s commentary on the *Gōngyáng Zhuan* states: "To tread upon with the foot in a contrary direction is called *cù*. The *Cāngjié Piān* says: "*Cù* means to tread upon. The *Shuowén Jiězì* defines it as "treading in a contrary direction," composed of the radical "foot" (*zú*) and the phonetic element *zhǐ* (󱫕).

The character *jǐn* (僅) has an upper radical resembling the *jiǎ* (賈) in Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guóyǔ*, where he states: “*Jǐn* means ‘barely able’ (*cái néng*). He Xiu’s commentary on the *Gōngyáng* states: “*Jǐn* means ‘inferior’ (*liè*). The *Guǎngyǎ* states: “*Jǐn* means ‘few’ (*shǎo*). The *Shuōwén* likewise states: “It means ‘barely able. It is formed from the radical ‘man’ (*rén*) with the phonetic ‘jǐn’ (*jǐn*); the sound of *jǐn* is that of *jǐn* [as in *jǐnshèn*].”

*Kǎn* (坎): The first character is pronounced *kǎn* (with the radical *kān* reversed), and the second is *kūn* (with the radical *gǔ* reversed). Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states that a "kū" is an underground chamber. The *Wenzidian* explains it as being composed of the radical *xué* (cave) and the phonetic *qū*.

*Zhī sǒng* (枝竦): *sǒng* is pronounced *yǒng* (with the radical *yù*). The *Guǎngyá* states that "sǒng" means "upward. Gu Yewang says "sǒng" means "high. The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radicals *lì* (standing) and *shù* (bundle), with *shù* also serving as the phonetic. In literary texts, it is written as *sǒng* (聳) with the radical *ěr* (ear); this is a borrowed usage, yet it is also acceptable.

"Cǎnhài" (慘害): "chǔ" (楚) and "jǐn" (錦) reversed. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "cǎn" (慘) means "poisonous cruelty" (慘毒); it is composed of the radical "heart" (心) with "cān" (參) as the phonetic. In poetic compositions, the character "càn" (磣) made from the radical "stone" (石) is used; this refers to the grit of sand and soil and does not carry this meaning.

The character 𧶜 (shàng, with the phonetic component *zhāng* reversed) is glossed by Zheng Xuan in his commentary on the *Gōngkǒngjì* as "travelling to sell. The *Jixùn* states that it means "to reside as a merchant" (*jiǎ*). Du Yū’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* explains it as "sitting to trade. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* says that 𧶜 refers to assessing the high or low value of goods. Regarding the characters for "sitting" and "selling": the correct form is 坐 (zuò), which is a collective term. It follows the radical 貝 (bèi) and takes 史 (shǐ) as its phonetic. According to ancient explanations, 史 (shǐ) is composed of 人 (rén) plus 自 (zì); the left and right sides represent the shape of a screen or shield. The reading in the classics as 估 (gù) is incorrect.

Regarding the term for "ship" (*chuan*): according to the *Yuanfan*, it is a regional dialect from west of the Guanzhong region where a boat is called a *chuan*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "boat," written with the radical *zhou* (boat) and the phonetic *zhao* (abbreviated) with the pronunciation *bai*. The *Guangya* calls it a "large ship. The *Picao* calls it a "large ship. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* explains it as a large ship on the sea, written with the radical *zhou* and the phonetic *bai*.

19. Volume Nineteen. Mosquito Net (*móuchóu*). The first character is pronounced *bǐ* (inverted) and the second *zhòu* (liú). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhou Li* states: "The mosquito net (*chóu*) is a covering. The *Erya* says: "The mosquito net is called *chàng*. Guo Pu’s commentary notes: "People in Jiangdong today also call *chàng* a *chóu*. The *Shi Jing* says: "I embrace my quilt and cover myself with the mosquito net (*chóu*); the mosquito net is a single-layered *chàng*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* also says it is a single-layered *chàng*, formed from the radical "cloth" (*jīn*) and the phonetic "shòu"; it is also written as *sǒu*.
Three strokes, one radical, five radicals above. *Jiang* (巷) is the phonetic.

The *Shiji* says it refers to fermented fish sauce (*zhaijiang*). The *Cangjie pian* says it is a type of jar (*ping*). The *Shuowen jiezi* says it resembles a *zhi* (𡄣) with a long neck, holding ten sheng; it is written with the radical for earthenware (*wa*) and the phonetic *tu*. It is also written as *gang* (缸) using the radical *zhi* (𡄣).
"不捩" (bù luò): the former character is read as *lián* with the *niè* rhyme; it has already been fully explained in the fifth fascicle. "濾漉" (lǜ lù):

the upper character is read as *lú* with the *zhù* rhyme, and the lower character as *lóng* with the *wū* rhyme. Gu Yewang states that "lù" is synonymous with "lì" (to drip). Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Fāngyán* says: "Lù means the water has completely percolated through. The *Shuowén* defines it as "deep" (*jùn*). One source says it describes the appearance of water flowing downward. It is composed of the "water" radical and the phonetic "lù"; it is also written as "盜" (*dào*) in some character dictionaries. "滲" (*sèn*): the pronunciation is *cān* with the *fǎn* rhyme.

The character 𩋸 (zhèn) is composed of 額 (é) above and 更 (gèng) and 正 (zhèng) below; it is also written as 鞕 (biàn). The lower part is read as 縶 (zhí). Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "The solid block used for hewing wood. The *Cangjie pian* states: "An iron block. The *Kaoseng sheng* states: "A type of stand. The standard form from ancient times to the present is 𩋸, with the radical 木 and the phonetic 甚; it is also written as 枯 (kū) or 𩋸 (zhì), with the same meaning.
*Tiao* (絛): Pronounced *tāo* (with the initial *d* reversed). The *Kao sheng* states: "To weave silk like a rope is called *tiao*.

A *dai* (帶) is a halter (*jiang*). The *Hanshu* says: "It pierces the halter of fame and binds the reins of renown. The *Cangjie pian* says it is the tethering of a horse. The *Shuowen jiezi* writes it with the radical *mi* (糸) as *jiang* (繮), also called *xie* (緤). The pronunciation of *xie* is *xì*.

*Dǔ* (都古反, dǔ gǔ fǎn). The *Pīcāng* states: "To stake. The *Wénzìdiǎn* says: "A gambling game; to bet goods. It is composed of the radical 貝 (péi) and the phonetic component 堵 (dǔ) in abbreviated form. The lower character 䞈 (huò) has the pronunciation *huò*; it is an archaic form of the character 貨 (huò). The *Guǎngyá* states: '䞈' is also 'dǔ'. According to the *Shuōwén*, it takes 貝 as its radical and 為 (wéi) as its phonetic, or it may be written as 󳊱."

*Mí* (deer): pronounced *měi* and *pī* in combination. The *Zhou Lǐ* states that in summer the *shòu rén* (wilderness hunters) present the *mí*. The *Báihù Tōng* says that those who shoot at the *mí* target do so because it also confuses and deludes people; the word *mí* signifies "to be deluded. The *Shuowén* says it belongs to the class of deer; its antlers are shed at the winter solstice, and it takes the radical for "deer" with the phonetic element *mǐ*.

To "jiǎo" (繳) means to wrap around; it is also a synonym for "teng" (縢). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "silk" (糸) with the phonetic "jiao" (敫); it is also written as "jiao" (憿) or "jiao" (敫), both pronounced as above. "Teng" (縢) is pronounced with the initial *t* and the final *deng* (*tédēng*).

20. The twentieth fascicle. Regarding "pi-xian" (leather-thread): Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that "xian" means thread. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "silk" (糸) with the phonetic component "zan" (戔), which is pronounced "can" (殘). In ancient usage it was written as "xian. The *Lüwen* (Legal Texts) uses the character "yan" (延) for it, pronouncing it "yan" (延); this does not accord with the meaning of the classics.

*Liǔ*: The upper character is pronounced *lǐ*; according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of "boat" (*zhōu*) and "following" (*zhòu*). The lower character is pronounced *jù*, meaning a type of shoe; it is also written as *lù*. *Tán*: The upper character is pronounced *tán*;

the *Shengyun* states it means to remove the upper garment so that the flesh of the shoulders is exposed. The *Zitong* states it means "flesh-shoulder. According to the *Shuowen*, it means the seams of a garment have come undone; it is composed of "garment" (*yī*) and "qie" (*qiě*) as the phonetic component. It is also written as *tàn* or *dǎn*, all of which are interchangeable.

*Chánduójiā* (闡鐸迦): The first character is pronounced *chǎn* (昌演反) and the second *tuó* (唐洛反); it is a term from the Sanskrit language, meaning "the servant of the Tathāgata. In ancient times, it was called *Chénì* (車匿). Regarding *jiù* (廐): the pronunciation is *mǎ jiù yòu* (馬鳩宥反).

The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that a "stable" (*jiù*) is where horses and oxen are gathered. The *Shuowén* (說文) defines it as "a house for horses. The character *jiù* consists of the radical *guǎng* (广) and the phonetic *jí* (𣪘); its pronunciation is the same as above. It is incorrect to write this as *jiù* (廐) based on the *Lǜwén* (律文).

*Shuangmou* (雙眸): *Mou* is pronounced as *hou* with a retroflex final. The *Guangya* states that the pupils of the eyes are called *mou*. The *Wenzidian* explains that *mouzi* (眸子) refers to the pupil; it is composed of the radical "eye" (*mu*) and the phonetic element "mu" (*mou*).
*Zhunxi* (瞚息): The first character, *shi*, is pronounced as *run* with a level tone.

"Zongxi" (綜習): "Zong" means to record or organize. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Zong refers to the shuttle-thread that holds the interlacing threads; it takes 'mi' (silk thread) as its radical and 'zong' as its phonetic. Song Zhong’s commentary on the *Taixuan jing* says: "Zong is that by which things are recorded."

*Yíngxiū* (縈󳍳): The upper character *yíng* (縈) is pronounced with the *ying* rhyme-group (反). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (毛詩傳) states that it means "to coil" (*xuán*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文) states it means "to contract and curl. It is composed of the radical *mi* (糸, silk) and the phonetic component *yíng* (熒) abbreviated.

Regarding *xiūliú* (鵂鶹), the upper character is pronounced *xiū* (休) and the lower is pronounced *liú* (流); its meaning has already been fully explained in the thirtieth fascicle of the *Vinaya of the Mūlasarvāstivāda*.

*Tuán* (上段, shàngduàn; 巒, luán; 反, fǎn). The *Kǎo Shēng* says: "To grasp. The *Zì Tǒng* says: "Round. The *Guǎng Yǎ* says: "Good. Gù Yěwáng says: "To press together so that things adhere to one another. The *Shuō Wén* states it is composed of the radical 手 (hand) and the phonetic 專 (zhuān).

The character for *xié* (scorpion) is pronounced with the "xüè" rhyme. The *Guǎngyá* states that *xié* means to sting (*chì*). Dú Bó says it refers to the *chàichǐ* or *xié*. The *Bīcāng* states it means *chù* (to bite). In the *Jīngǔzhèngzì*, the character is composed of the radical "insect" (*chóng*) and the phonetic "qiē" (*xiē*). The pronunciation of *chù* is *huǒgè*; the pronunciation of *chì* is *shìyì*; the pronunciation of *chǐ* is *yǔ*; and the pronunciation of *chài* is *chòujiè*.

21. Fascicle Twenty-one. *Yīluó* (㗨羅)—the first character is pronounced with the initial *yǐ* and the final *láo*. This is the name of a Dragon King in the Sanskrit language. *Nào* (撓)—the second character is pronounced with the initial *shàng* and the final *gāo*.

The *Shēnglèi* (Sound Classifications) states that it means "to grasp" (*lǎn*). The *Shuowén* (Explanations of Words and Characters) states it means "to disturb. It is composed of the radical *shǒu* (hand) and the phonetic *yáo*. The final character is pronounced with the initial *ráo* and the final *shǎo*. Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* (Book of Documents) states it means "confusion" (*luàn*). The *Shuowén* states it means "distress" (*fán*). It is composed of the radical *shǒu* (hand) and the phonetic *náo*; the sound of *náo* is pronounced with the initial *nǎo* and the final *dāo*.

*Yì* (噫): Pronounced *shàng é* (上戹) with the *guǎi* (介) radical; the *Shuōwén* states that *yì* refers to exhaling after being full, composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic "intention" (*yì*).

*Kè* (㓣): Pronounced *qí shàng kǒu jiǎ* (其上口甲); the *Yùnyīng* states that *kè* means "to enter. According to the Vinaya texts, one hides medicine under the fingernails and *kè* (inserts) half a grain into it so that the medicine enters within; thus, one uses the fingernail to *kè* (pierce) an *āmala* fruit and places the poisonous medicine inside.

*Bǐngzhù* (炳著): The first character, *bǐng*, is pronounced with the "bīng" rhyme group (as in *bǐng*). The *Zhouyi* says, "The great man undergoes a tiger-like transformation; his patterns are *bǐng*" (*qí wén bǐng yě*). This explains the brilliance of the pattern. It is composed of the radical "fire" (*huǒ*) and the phonetic "bǐng. It is also written as *ruì* or *yǎng*.
The meaning of *pīliè* (劈裂)—the first character pronounced with the *pǐ* rhyme (*mì*) and the second with the *lián* and *zhé* rhymes—is already fully explained in the thirteenth fascicle.
Regarding *shǐliú* (駛流): the *Cāngjié piān* states that *shǐ* means "swift"; the *Wénzìdiǎn* explains it as being derived from the radical for "horse" (*mǎ*) and the phonetic *shǐ*.
The characters for *xiàngjiù* (elephant stable) and *jiūyòu* (pigeon release) have their meanings already fully explained in the twentieth fascicle.

Regarding *chīxián* (to deride and disdain): the rhyme is *shǐ* (詩). The *Zìshū* (Dictionary of Characters) states that *chī* denotes the manner of playful laughter. The *Wénzìdiǎn* (Dictionary of Written Characters) says it is the sound *chī*; it is composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) with the phonetic "chī. The pronunciation of *chī* is the same as *xià* (下), rhyming with *yán* (閻). The *Shuōwén* (Explaining Simple and Analyzing Compound Characters) states that *xián* means "discontent in the heart"; one interpretation says it means "doubt," composed of the radical "woman" (*nǚ*) with the phonetic "jiān" (*jiān*).

*Kòngyù* (控御): *Kòng* is pronounced with the *gōng* and *fǎn* finals; it means to control or to hold. The *Shuowen* says it means "to lead," composed of the radical *shǒu* (hand) and the phonetic *kōng*.

**Volume 22, Fascicle 22** *Xuánjīng* (旋旍): *Jīng* is pronounced with the *jǐng* and *yíng* finals. The *Zhouli* states: "Of the nine banners, those split from feathers are called *jīng*. Zheng’s commentary says: "Split feathers of five colors are tied to the top of the *jīng*. Kings used them for hunting and for the countryside to symbolize civil virtue. The *Erya* says: "The *máo* and *pú* are called *jīng*. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* says: "*Jīng* refers to insignia. Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* says: "It is a marker. The *Shuowen* uses the character *jīng*, stating: "A banner carried on a traveling chariot; it is a feathered standard (*qí*) with a *máo* and *pú* attached. It is used to encourage the soldiers. It is derived from the sound of *yǎn*. (*Yǎn* is pronounced *yǎn*.)

*Sòu* (驟): The upper radical is *chóu* (愁) with the phonetic *yǒu* (瘐). Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states: "Sòu means rapid. The *Guoyá* states: "Sòu means to gallop. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "The swift pace of a horse; it is composed of the radical for 'horse' (*mǎ*) and the phonetic *jù* (聚)."
*Tànrǔ*: The first character is pronounced *tān dá* (with the initial *tān* and final *dá*); the second character is pronounced *yín gé* (with the initial *yín* and final *gé*).

Regarding "kuì nù" (shame and embarrassment): the *Fānyán* (Explanations of Words) states that "nù" means "cánn" (embarrassment). Guō's commentary on the *Ěryá* says: "To feel shame in one's heart is called *nù*. Whether ancient or modern, the correct orthography uses the radical for "heart" (*xīn*) and this as the phonetic component.
"Zhuhui" (竹篦)—the "bi" (閉) is pronounced with the *fanqie* "mi-fan" (迷反); it is commonly written as "bi" (篦). This has already been fully explained in the fourteenth fascicle of the preceding text.
Regarding "guaqu" (刮去)—the "guan" (關) is pronounced with the *fanqie* "hua-fan" (滑反)—its meaning and gloss have already been fully provided in the first fascicle.

"Xiǎo jù" (小毱) and "qióu" (窮) [sixth tone], as well as "qiú" (毬), are all vulgar characters. Those who now pronounce it according to common usage find that the character "qiú" does not exist in any standard dictionaries; the correct form is "jù" (鞠). Regarding its phonetics, it is said that a bag filled with chaff is used for trampling, which is called "cuò jù" (蹴鞠). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "tà jù" (蹋鞠, kicking a ball), composed of the radical "革" (leather) and the phonetic "匊" (jū). It is also written as "𥷥" or "󲾨," with the pronunciation "jù" (sixth tone).

Regarding "gēngyún" (耕耘) in the sense of "to reap" as it appears in the *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (Mao Commentary on the Classic of Poetry), which states that "yún" means to weed; the *Shuowén Jiězì* (Explaining Characters and Analyzing Words) writes this as 󲴣, defining it as "weeding between the rows of seedlings," with the phonetic component "yuán" (員). It is also written as 𦓷. The character "lèi" (耒) has the pronunciation léi duìfǎn (雷對反).

"Kūn" (髡) has the phonetic component *kūn* (坤). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is named after the state of Jing; "kūn" means to shave the hair. The *Shuowen* states: "𩮜 (tóng) means to shave the hair. It is composed of the radical 髟 (biāo, pronounced bǐ yáo fǎn) with the phonetic element 兀 (wù, pronounced tā yì fǎn)."

The upper character, *shēn* (上室), is pronounced with the true tone (*zhēn fǎn*). Zheng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states: "Shēn is also yín. The lower character, *jí* (下芨), is pronounced with the level tone (*jīn fǎn*). The *Cāngjié piān* states: "Yín means to sigh. According to the *Shuōwén*, both characters are written with the radical 口 and the component 申; today they are all pronounced [as such], and are also written as 軟 or 訡.

Regarding *chóu-sài* (repaying and sacrificing): The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *chóu* means "to present" (*xiàn-chóu*), composed with the radical for "wine" (*yǒu*) and the phonetic *shòu*; the lower character is read as *sì-dài*. The *Wenzi Jílüè* states that *sài-chóu* refers to sacrificing to the spirits to repay their blessings. The *Mao Shī Chuán* says *chóu* means "to recompense. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Yílǐ* says it refers to encouraging guests to drink during meals. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* says it means "mutual repayment and response. *Chóu-sài shàngshòu* (recompensing and offering long life) is derived from this. The *Mao Shī Chuán* says *chóu* means "to report back. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Yílǐ* says it refers to encouraging wine when entertaining guests. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* says it means "mutually repaying and responding. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "presenting and reciprocating," composed with the radical for "wine" and the phonetic *shòu*, with the lower character read as *sì-dài*. The *Wenzi Jílüè* says *sài-chóu* refers to sacrificing to the gods to repay their blessings.

*Dàn* (誕): The upper radical is *kuà* (跨) with the phonetic *huá* (華). Its meaning has already been fully explained in the ninth fascicle. *Tán* (檀): The lower radical is *lán* (爛). Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shūjìng* states: "Dàn means to deceive; it also means great. The *Shuowén Jìzì* states: "It means to be deceptive (*guǐ*). It is composed of the radical 'speech' (*yán*) and the phonetic *yán* (延)."

23. Fascicle Twenty-Three. **Guǐkuàng (詭誑)**: The first character, *guǐ* (詭), is pronounced with the initial *guī* (歸) and the final *wěi* (委). Xu Shuchong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states that it means "arrogance" (*guǐmàn*). Zheng’s sub-commentary on the *Mao Shi* states that it refers to being unwilling to perform what is good and instead following others in doing evil. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "reproach" (*zé*), composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic "huí" (*wēi*). The second character, *kuàng* (誑), is pronounced with the initial *jù* (俱) and the final *kuàng* (況). Jia Dui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that "to *kuàng*" is equivalent to "to delude" (*huò*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "deception" (*qī*), composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic "kuáng" (*kuáng*).

The upper phonetic of 𭻁 (tián) is yán; the *Shàngshū* states that "tián" means "at the outskirts of Luò," and the commentary on the *Shàngshū* by Kǒng Anghuǒ explains it as "hunting. Gù Yěwáng says it refers to pursuing game. Hé Xiū’s commentary on the *Gōngyáng* states that "tián" and "shòu" are general terms for hunting. In ancient times, people consumed meat and wore garments made from the skins of hunted animals; therefore, hunting was called "tián" (field). The *Shuōwén* writes it as 田, stating: "To hunt and capture birds and beasts is 'tián,' because it clears away pests from the fields. It is depicted with four mouths and the character for ten (十), representing the system of *qiānmò* (roads and furrows). It is also written as 𤝗, following the radical for dog.

*Hukou* (餬口): *shàng* is *hù*, reversed; Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* says it means "porridge" (*mí*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it means "to live by borrowing food," composed of the radical for "food" and the phonetic *hú*;

*mí* is pronounced *měi*, reversed. *Youzhì* (幽縶): *xià* is *zhēn*, reversed; the *Mao Shi Zhuan* says it means "fetters. Du’s commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan* says it means "a tether. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* says it is composed of the radical for "silk" and the phonetic *zhí*.

The lower phonetic of *chéngyīn* (城闉) is *yīn*. The *Mao Shī Chuán* (毛詩傳) states that "yīn" means "curved. The *Shuōwén* (說文) states that it refers to a curved city wall or a double gate; it is composed of the radical "gate" (*mén*) with the phonetic "yīn," where the pronunciation of "yīn" is as stated above.

*Jiōngyě* (坰野): The upper character is pronounced *guì yíng* (癸營). The *Mao Shī Chuán* states that "jǐng" (垧) means "distant. The *Shuōwén* uses the character *jiǒng* (冂), stating that what is outside a settlement is called the "suburb" (*jiāo*), what is outside the suburb is called the "wilderness" (*yě*), what is outside the wilderness is called the "forest" (*lín*), and what is outside the forest is called *jiǒng*, representing a distant boundary. It is also written with the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) as *jiǒng* (冋), meaning a multitude of states and settlements. The vulgar form uses the radical "earth" (*tǔ*) to write it as *jiǒng* (垌).

The character *diān* (瘨) is pronounced with the initial *tiǎn* and the final *lián* (according to the Zheng commentary on the *Shijing*, it means "sickness"; according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "madness"; according to the *Shēnglèi*, it means "a wind-related illness"; according to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical *nià* [sickness] and the phonetic *zhēn*).

*Kuīyú* (窺覦): The upper character *kuī* (窺) is pronounced with the initial *kǔ* and the final *guī*. The *Kǎoshēng* states it means "to peek"; the *Shuōwén* states it means "to look at something small," formed with the radical *xué* (穴) and the phonetic *guī* (規). The lower character *yú* (覦) is pronounced *zhū*. Gù Yěwáng states it means "to covet. The *Zuǒzhuàn* says, "The people have no covetous hearts. The *Shuōwén* states it means "desire," formed with the radical *jiàn* (見) and the phonetic *yú* (俞). *Qù* (覻) is pronounced *qīchài*.

*Zhìdùn* (躓頓): The first character is pronounced *zhīlì* (知利). The *Guǎngyá* states that it means "to stumble" (*zhuòtà*). The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical "foot" (*zú*) and the phonetic "zhì" (*zhìshēng*), with the pronunciation of *tà* being *tánlà* (談臘).

*Cāiyí* (猜疑): The first character is pronounced *cǎilái* (採來). The *Guǎngyá* states that it means "to fear. The *Shuōwén* states that it means "resentment" (*hèn*). It is composed of the radical "dog" (*quǎn*) and the phonetic "qīng" (*qīngshēng*).

"Piānfán" (翩翻): The upper character is read as *pǐ mián* (匹綿); the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that "piānpiān" describes the manner of coming and going. The lower character is read as *fú yuán* (孚園); Gù Yěwáng (顧野王) states that "piānfán" describes the manner of turning and circling with light agility. The *Shuowén* (說文) states it means "swift flight. Both characters are composed of the radical "feather" (*yǔ*) with "piān" (*biǎn*) and "fán" (*fān*) serving as their phonetic components.
"Diao" (鵰) is pronounced *jiǎo* (上: jiaoshang; 下: qiúxiù). "Zhènshè" (震懾): the second character is pronounced *zhānshè*.

Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that it means "to subdue. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states that "shè" (懾) means "to be terrified. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "qiè" (懾) refers to "breath," formed with the radical for "heart" and the phonetic "niè."

24. Fascicle Twenty-four. *Jílíng* (鶺鴒). The first character is pronounced *jīng* (精) with the initial *yǎn* (亦) and the final *fǎn* (反); the second is *lì* (歷) with the initial *dīng* (丁) and the final *fǎn* (反). The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (毛詩傳) states: "The *jílíng* is the *yōngqú* (雍渠). When it flies, it cries; when it walks, it wags its tail. The *Wénzì Diǎnshuō* (文字典說) says it resembles a green magpie (*qīngquè*). Both characters are written with the radical for "bird" (*niǎo*) and take *jǐ* (脊) and *lìng* (令) as their phonetic components respectively.

Regarding *zhè* (蜇): the commentary on the sounds states that it refers to the sting of a venomous insect. The dictionary of characters explains that it is composed of the radical "insect" (*chóng*) and the phonetic "zhé" (*zhé*), and is also written with "qiè" (*qiè*) as *jū* (蛆).
Regarding *kūn* (蜫) and *yǐ* (蟻)—the former pronounced *gǔhuán* and the latter *yíjǐ*—these have already been explained in detail in the ninth fascicle.

*Zǐ* (beak): the first character is pronounced *zūn* (with the *suǐ* rhyme) and the second is pronounced *zhé* (with the *jiǎo* rhyme). The *Guǎngyá* states that "to *zuó*" means to bite. The *Chǔcí* says, "it pecks at and harms those below. The *Huáinánzǐ* says, "when a bird is cornered, it pecks. The *Shuowén* says, "it is the eating by a bird; it is composed of the radical 'mouth' with *chù* as the phonetic component. The sound of *chù* is *chǒulù*.

*Chānghén* (瘡痕): The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "hen" (痕) refers to a scar; it is composed of the radical *nà* (疒) and the phonetic *gèn* (艮). It is the character for *Chāngzhèngliáng*. *Jiāoliáo* (鷦鷯):

The upper character is pronounced *jiāo* and the lower is pronounced *liáo*. According to the *Guangya*, the *jiāoliáo* feeds on cicada larvae (*táochóng*). In the *Shuowen*, it is written as *jiāoliáo* (鷦𪃐); this is a corruption of the pronunciation and a shift in the phonetic. Commonly called the "artful female bird" (*qiǎofùniǎo*), it is able to fashion a pouch from chrysanthemum flowers to build its nest, hence it is named the artful female bird. The character *liáo* (𪃐) is pronounced *míxiāo*. It nests in reed branches and eats insects within the *wěi* grass.

*Yan-shu*: The first character is pronounced *yǎn* (with the rhyme *yán*) and the second is pronounced *shù*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Yan" is the same as "shu"; they are eunuchs who guard and close the gates within the palace. The officials of today are the *huángmén*. This is a compound character formed from shape and sound. Regarding the second character, "shu," the *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of "dòu" and "lǜ" with "lì" as its phonetic; this is a vulgarized form. *Hūn* is pronounced *hūn*.

"Zi" (beard/moustache): the first character is pronounced *zi* (with the *si* rhyme) and the second is pronounced *bin* (with the *pin* rhyme). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Zi refers to the hair above the mouth; it is composed of the radical 'xu' (hair) with the phonetic 'ci. The following character 'bin' (side-hair): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it refers to the hair at the sides of the cheeks; it is composed of the radical 'biao' (hair) with the phonetic 'bin. The sound of 'biao' is *biyao*."

The character *jì* (𦊩) is pronounced with the upper radical *jié* (濟). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that it means "to obstruct" (*zhē*). Guo Pu says that *jì* is synonymous with "obstructing. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "a mountain pass," formed from the radical *gāng* (岡) with the phonetic *qiě* (且).

25. The Twenty-fifth Fascicle. *Dhakkā* (transliterated as *Duōqīnà*): the upper character is pronounced as *luò* (with the *táng* tone); the middle character is pronounced as *qí* (with the *yí* tone); the lower character is pronounced as *jiā* (with the *nuò* tone). This is a term from the Sanskrit language.

Regarding the character *zuǎn* (攥): the *Huánfǎnkǎo* states that it means "to grasp" (*qiānchí*). The *Zílín* says it means "to hold. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* explains that it means "to take an object with the hand," following the radical for "hand" and the phonetic element *zuǎn*. The pronunciation of *zuǎn* is *zǐguǎn*; it is also written as *cuō* (撮).

"Quán" (upper radical *jiǎn*, pinyin *juàn*): Hé Xiū’s commentary on the *Gōngyáng Zhuan* states that "quán" refers to clenching the fingers. The *Shuowén Jiězì* takes the radical *shǒu* (hand) and uses *juǎn* as a phonetic component, abbreviated; it is also written as *quǎn*. "Ōu" (lower radical *hǒu*, pinyin *hǒu*): The *Kǎoshēng* states that it means to strike. The *Shuowén Jiězì* uses the radical *shū* (club) to form "Ōu," stating it means to beat with a staff.
