"Zuàn" (足踹): The lower part of the foot; the *Kǎo shēng* says it refers to the calf muscle (*fēicháng*). The *Shuōwén* writes it as "zuàn," with the radical "moon" (*yuè*) and the phonetic "duān.
"Tuī" (推摩): The upper character is read as "tuìléi"; to push something forward from behind is called "tuī."

*Tuī* (推): The upper character is read as *mù* (木) with the suffix *zhuī* (追). The *Shuowen* states that it means "to strike"; it is composed of the radical *mù* (木) and the phonetic *zhuī* (隹), and is also written as *chuí* (搥). *yōngzuò* (癰痤):

The upper character is read as *yǒng* (擁) with the suffix *gōng* (恭), and the lower character is read as *zuò* (坐) with the suffix *hé* (禾). The *Shuowen* states that *zuò* refers to a small swelling; both are composed of the radical *nà* (疒), with *yōng* (雝) and *zuò* (坐) serving as their respective phonetics.
26. Volume Twenty-Six, Part Two. Regarding "捔" (jué), it is written as "角" (jiǎo) above;

regarding "網鞔" (wǎngmán), "網" (wǎng) is pronounced with the *wang* radical and the *fang* rhyme, while "鞔" (mán) is pronounced with the *wei* radical and the *an* rhyme. The meaning has already been fully explained in the thirty-second fascicle of the Sarvāstivāda Vinaya.
*Bīnbīn* (繽紛): the first character is pronounced *pǐ* with the *mín* rhyme; the second is pronounced *fēn*. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that *bīnbīn* describes a state of profusion.
*Yìyào* (熠燿): the first character is pronounced *lì* with the *zhì* rhyme; the second is pronounced *yáo* with the *zhào* rhyme. This refers to *chénhuǒ* (螢火, glowworm fire).

*Tiǎn* (靦): On the face; *tiān* (典) reversed. The *Mao Shi* says, "With a countenance *tiǎn*. The commentary states, "*Tiǎn* means to look at. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says, "*Tiǎn* means to see; it is composed of the radical 'face' (*miàn*) and the phonetic 'jiàn' (*xiàn*). Volume Twenty-seven, Part Two. *Fēngrěn* (豐稔):

Upper character is *fēng* (丰), lower character is *rěn* (任) with the phonetic *shěn* (審). Jia Dui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* says, "*Rěn* means ripeness. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says, "*Rěn* means the ripening of grain; it is composed of the radical 'grain' (*huó*) and the phonetic *niàn* (念)."

Regarding "gǎi qiào" (改醮), Jiao Xiao’s *Fàn Gù* (反顧) states that it refers to the second marriage of a woman according to wedding rites. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it is a sacrifice performed at the rite of capping and marriage; it is derived from "jiǔ" (酉) and "jiāo" (焦). "Jiāo" is also written as "qiáo" (樵).
*Gāi-lǜ* (猜慮): The reading for *gāi* is *cǎi-āi-fǎn*. This has already been fully explained and annotated within the twenty-third fascicle.

*Kuǐ-wěi* (傀偉): The reading for *kuǐ* is *huì-huí-fǎn*. Sīmǎ Biāo’s commentary on the *Zhuāngzǐ* states: "Kuǐ means beautiful. The *Fāngyán* states: "Kuǐ means abundant. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "kuǐ-wěi," composed of the radical "person" (*rén*) and the phonetic "guǐ" (*guǐ*). It is also written as *kuǐ* or *kuǐ*. According to the original scriptural source, it is written with the "jade" (*yù*) radical as *guī*, meaning jade. The reading for *wěi* is *wéi-guǐ-fǎn*. The *Shuōwén* states: "Wěi means extraordinary; it is composed of the radical 'person' (*rén*) and the phonetic 'wéi' (*wéi*)."

*Tiáo* (pronounced *xiào yáo*) refers to the hair of a child. The *Cangjie pian* states it means "hair of a youth," while the *Wenzi jilüe* says it is "the hair of a small child. The *Wenzi dianshuo* explains that it is composed of the radical *biāo* (hair) and the phonetic *zhào*; the form *cháo* (composed of the radical *chí*) is a vulgar character.

*Jue* (抉): The mouth; pronounced *xi* (with the initial *yī* and final *xuè*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To pick or pry open; composed of the radical 手 [hand] and the phonetic component 決 (abbreviated).
*Liú xián* (流涎): Pronounced *xiàn yán*. The correct form is 㳄. This was already fully explained in the fourteenth fascicle above.

It serves as a pit for wild beasts; the *Zhouli* commentary by Zheng Xuan states that one digs the earth to create a deep trench for the purpose of warding off violent predators, so that if they attempt to leap over it, they fall into it; the world calls this a "trap-pit" (*jingdang*). Gu Yewang says a pit is used to capture fierce beasts. The *Guoya* calls it a "yuan. The *Shuowen* also defines it as a "xian" (to sink), written with the radical "阝" and the phonetic "井"; the archaic form is "汬," while the legal texts use "穽" with the radical "穴," which is the vulgar character.

*Tuó* (in *tuóshéng*, "to twist rope"): the first character is read as *nú hé fǎn*; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means to intertwine with the hands, composed of the radical 手 (hand) and the phonetic 妥. The pronunciation of 妥 is *tuò* (in *tuò yīn tuì fǎn*). *Zè lòu* (in *zèlòu*, "mean and lowly"): the upper character is read as *zǔ sè fǎn* and the lower as *lóu dòu fǎn*.

The *Shuōwén* states that *zè* means to lean or tilt, composed of the radical 人 (person) under 厂 (the slope), with 在 as the phonetic. The pronunciation of 厂 is *hǎn*. The character 陋 means narrow or cramped, composed of the radical 阜 (hill/mound) and the phonetic 尨 (which here functions as 婄). The pronunciation of 厂 is *hǎn* and the pronunciation of 婄 is the same as above.

"Jùn (儁)" is pronounced *shuǐn* (陖) when following the sound of "kǎo" (考). It means one whose talent surpasses the masses; it also implies possessing power and majesty. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as "Jùn" (俊), composed of "rén" (人) with "jùn" (夋) as the phonetic component. "Jùn" (夋) is pronounced *qīngxún* (清旬).

*Chōng-dǎo* (舂擣): The first character, *chōng*, is pronounced with the initial *shù* and the final *yōng*. Gu Yewang states that it means "to pound grain into rice. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it refers to pounding millet (*sù*). It is composed of the radical *kǒng* (廾), meaning "to hold," and the pestle (*chǔ*), which serves as the phonetic component; the latter is written in abbreviated form. The second character, *dǎo*, is pronounced with the initial *dāo* and the final *lǎo*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "to push" or "to strike"; another interpretation says it means "to build up. It is composed of the radical *shǒu* (手) and the phonetic component *shòu*. In other character dictionaries, it is written as *chōng* (舂) or *tào* (燾).
*Jian* (撚): Pronounced *nian* (典反). *Qun* (裠):
Pronounced *fu* (上郡) and *yun* (雲); alternatively written as *qun* (帬); already explained in Scroll Eleven. *Fu* (孚): Pronounced *wu* (務反). *Jiang* (繮): Pronounced *yang* (羊反);

already explained in Scroll Nineteen. *Ban* (絆): Pronounced *man* (漫反). The *Kaosheng* states: "The *ban* (絆) binds both feet. The *Shuowen* states: "'Ban' (󲽍) is a tether; it takes 'mi' (糸) as its radical and 'ban' (半) as its phonetic component. The character *zhi* (縶) is [the same].

*Xiàn pàn* (邪盼): The first character, *xiè*, is pronounced with the *jiē* rhyme; it has already been explained in detail in the fourth fascicle. The second character, *pàn*, is pronounced with the *màn* rhyme. The dictionary states that *pàn* refers to the appearance of moving the eyes. The *Shī jīng* says, "Beautiful eyes are *pàn*. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "eye" (*mù*) and the phonetic component "fen" (*fēn*).
28. Fascicle Twenty-Eight, Part Two. *Yílún* (彝倫): "yí" is pronounced as in "yǐzhīfǎn" (以之反). *Chìsuì* (赤穟): "suì" is pronounced as in "suílèifǎn" (隨類反).

The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (毛詩傳) states that "suì" refers to the ears of grain. The *Cāngjié Piān* (蒼頡篇) states that it refers to the ears of rice and wheat. The *Shuōwén* (說文) defines it as the appearance of the ears of grain; it is composed of the radical "grain" (*hé*) with the phonetic "suì. It is also written as 穟 or 穗.
The comprehensive treatment of the essential points has already been fully explained and annotated in the twentieth fascicle above. *Chóuchú* (躊躇):
the first character is pronounced with the *zhòu* rhyme and the *lǐ* final; the second character is pronounced *zhílú*.
Regarding *chuān* (篅) or *chuí* (圌), the pronunciation of the first character is *zhuàn* or *zhuān*; its meaning has already been fully explained in the twelfth fascicle.

Regarding the four *jue* (樁): according to the *Guangya*, a *jue* is a wooden stake (*mayi*). The *Wenzi Dianshuo* explains that it takes the radical "wood" (*mu*) and uses "jue" as its phonetic component.
As for the stake (*yi*), its meaning has already been fully explained in the third fascicle [of this work]. (Note: *yí* is pronounced with the initial *zhí*.)

The character *què* (確) is pronounced with the initial *xìe* (先) and the final *jié* (節) reversed [i.e., *què*]. Han Kangbo’s commentary on the *Zhouyi* states: “*Què* is the appearance of firmness. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* explains that it is composed of the radical *shí* (石, stone) and the phonetic *hào* (寉). The pronunciation of *hào* is that of *hè* (鶴, crane).
The character 鵾 (also written as 鶤) is explained in detail in the nineteenth fascicle. Regarding 騫 (qiān): the upper radical is pronounced xiē (歇焉反).

Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that "qiān" refers to the appearance of raising one's head; the *Guǎngyá* says it means to fly or to lift up; the *Shuowén* describes it as the appearance of flying, composed of the bird radical and the phonetic element hàn (in its abbreviated form). The lower part is pronounced zhū (諸茹反). The *Fāngyán* states that "zhù" means to lift up; in the state of Chu, they called flying "zhù. The *Shuowén* defines it as flying upward, composed of the feather radical and the phonetic element zhě.

"Liánpiān" (聯翩) means "upon the carriage"; however, its phonetic component is "fǎn" (反). It is a type of *liánmián* (聯綿) word, meaning "uninterrupted" or "continuous. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of "ér" (耳, ear) joined to "jiá" (頰, cheek), with the phonetic "pǐmián fǎn" (匹綿反). This has already been explained in the twenty-third fascicle.

The character *niǔ* (儜) is pronounced with the initial *shòu* and the final *yóu*, and is a variant of the character *fǎn*. Examining its phonetics, it is said that *niǔ* means "to seek. The *Wenzi Dianshuō* states that it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic element "old" (*sǒu*).

The meaning has already been fully explained in the thirty-third fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*. As for *niǎo* (儜), the initial is *què* and the final is *yīng*; it is also written as *nián* (嬣). The meaning is already complete in the aforementioned section of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.

To burn on fire (𤑔): the phonetic reading is *zhú* (儒拙反). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "to burn" (*shāo*) is the meaning; the *Cangjie pian* states it means "to kindle" (*rán*). The *Shuowen jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "fire" (*huǒ*) and the phonetic element "yì" (*yì shēng*). It is also written as 𤋲 or 炳.

The character *xian* (燖)—the common form; the correct form is *shao* (󳆵). The *Kao Sheng* (Examination of Sounds) states it means "to boil" or "to cook until done. It refers to pouring hot water over fur to cause it to shed. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to sear meat in boiling water," composed of the radical *zhi* (炙) and the abbreviated phonetic *zhi* (執). It is also written as *shao* (𤏝), *xian* (燂), or *shao* (󳌟); the pronunciation of *yao* (爚) is *yao*.
*Feiyáng* (飛颺): *yǎng* is the phonetic component; the *Shuowen* states it means "that which is flown by the wind," composed of the radical *fēng* (wind) with the phonetic *yì*.

*Bóxiāo* (摶霄): *shàng* is pronounced *duó* (奪); the *Kaosheng* states it means "to attach. The *Zhuangzi* says, "He grasps the *fúyáo* wind and ascends ninety thousand *lǐ*. The *Shuowen* takes the radical *shǒu* (hand) with the phonetic *zhuān*.

The character for *sī* (絲) is pronounced with the *zhōu* rhyme (陸反). The *Shiji* states that Gao Jianli struck the *qin* (琴) at the marketplace of Yan. The *Cangjie pian* says it is a musical instrument. The *Shuowen jiezi* writes it as *qín* (琴), stating that it is used to strike to form melodies. The five-stringed music follows the radical *qin* (琴); the component *chi* (持) indicates holding it, and the component *zhu* (竹) provides the phonetic element. The pronunciation of *qin* (琴) is *jù lǒng* (俱隴反).

*Qièdàn* (怯憚): The upper character is read as *qī xié* (欺脅). Yuè Wǎng states that it means "timid fear" or "inferiority. The *Fāngyán* says it means "to avoid with difficulty. The *Shuōwén* writes it as *ài* (㹤), stating it means "much fear," composed of the radical *quǎn* (犬) and the phonetic *qù* (去). The lower character is read as *tán làn* (檀爛). Zhèng Jiǎn’s *Shī* says it means "difficulty" or "strangeness. The *Guǎngyá* says it means "alarm. The *Shuōwén* [also] says *tán* (撣) means "to dread or loathe," composed of the radical *xīn* (心) and the phonetic *dān* (單).

Regarding "sounding the *pí* drum": it is struck downward and then reversed. Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "When performing the *man* music, the *pí* drum is struck to harmonize with it. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "*Pí* is a type of small drum (*gǔ*); it is composed of the radical 'drum' (*gǔ*) and the phonetic 'bēi'."

Regarding the term *mùfāng* (木枋), dictionaries state it is the name of a type of wood. Examining the legal texts (*lüwén*) now, they speak of "shackling the feet with a single wooden *fāng*"; this refers to the small square pieces of wood with holes bored through them that are passed through the feet to restrain a criminal. That which is used for the hands is called *niǔ* (杻), and that for the feet is called *xiè* (械); these together are also termed *zhígù* (桎梏).
*Bìn-jié* (擯㡿): The first character is pronounced *bì-rèn*; the second has the sound *chǐ*. Their meanings have already been fully explained in the second fascicle.

29. Fascicle Twenty-nine. *Niè-lí-lí* (躡瑠璃): The first character is pronounced *nián-duī*. Guō’s commentary on the *Fāng-yán* states that *niè* means "to step upon" (*dēng*). The *Guǎng-yǎ* states it means "to tread" (*lǚ*), derived from the foot.

*Língpíng* (上歷丁反, 下劈冥反): The *Kǎoshēng* states it describes a state of being solitary and weak, or walking without strength. According to the *Shuōwén*, both characters are composed of the radical "person" (人) with "líng" (令) and "píng" (甹) as their phonetic components; the pronunciation of "píng" is the same as above.

*Qiáo* (樵): On the wood, it is pronounced *shàng qiáo yáo fǎn*. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "It means firewood. He Xiu’s commentary on the *Gongyangzhuan* states: "Because one burns it with firewood (*qiāoxīn*), it is therefore called *qiáo*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "wood," following the radical for wood and the phonetic *jiāo*.

"Bié" (上枚賣反) is pronounced with the *kao* radical; it means "to explain" (*jiěxiǎo*). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to divide," a compound character formed from the "knife" radical and the image of dividing ox horns. The lower part is pronounced *bo*; this is a vernacular term. It should be written as "tán" (撣), pronounced *dá dān* (達丹反); "tán" refers to the *konghóu* lute. The *kao* radical states that "tán" means "to join" or "to touch," like plucking a zither. The Vinaya texts state that "plucking the *konghóu*" is a colloquial term used among commoners in the streets and alleys. It is written with the "hand" radical and the "dān" phonetic.

*Chóumì* (綢密): The upper character *zhòu* is pronounced with the *liú* rhyme. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that "chóumián" (縈綿) means entangled and dense. *Hǎidǎo* (海島): The lower character *dǎo* is pronounced with the *lǎo* rhyme.

According to the *Shuowen*, an island (*dǎo*) refers to mountains scattered throughout the sea that can be relied upon for shelter. The *Shiming* says it means "to arrive," as people flee to them; it is also pronounced *niǎo*, referring to distant mountains in the sea that appear like birds when viewed from afar across the water.

"Boat" (chuán): The phonetic component is "fán" (韈反) and the pronunciation is "bó. It refers to a structure made by binding bamboo and wood that floats upon the water; the larger type is called a "bó," while the smaller type is called a "fú. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "wood" (木) with "fa" (發) as the phonetic. The forms "fá" (筏) and "fá" (栰) found in the scriptures are both incorrect.

*Fan* (upper character: fāng, fan; rhyme: yīng) means to float; it is also written as *fàn*. *Fàn* (lower character: zhāng, liǎng; rhyme: quán) refers to water that is vast and great. *Chībō* (upper character: chì, zhī; rhyme: ěr yǎ):
the *Erya* states this is the *yuán* bird. (Lower character: bān, mèi; rhyme: chī bō) refers to lightly snapping or brushing against objects as one passes by.

30. Volume Thirty. Volume Thirty. On Sacrificial Death (*xùn*). [The character] *xún* is pronounced as *jùn* (with a reversed initial). To follow someone in death is called "sacrificial death" (*xùn*). In ancient times, all practiced burial with human sacrifices; nowadays, people use clay, wood, lacquer, and plain images to represent them instead, calling these "vow-vessels" (*méngqì*).

*Chī* (pronounced *qíxún*): The *Pīcāng* states that it means "cracked" (*chīlì*). It is also said to mean "frozen and cracked. According to the *Jīngǔzhèngzì*, both characters *chī* and *ěr* share the radical "skin" (*pí*) and are phono-semantic compounds. *Lì* is pronounced *qīyào*.
*Fumò* (膜): The membrane beneath; it refers to the membrane within the internal organs. *Zhūqiān* (籤):
"Qiān" is pronounced with the *qiè* and *yán* finals reversed. It means to carve bamboo into a needle-like point and insert it into a child's throat;

thus it is called a "signet" (*qiān*). *Fǔpāi* (撫拍): The first character, *fǔ*, has the *fú* and *wǔ* finals reversed; the second, *pāi*, has the *pēng* and *mài* finals reversed. According to the *Guǎngyá*, "to strike" (*fǔjī*); according to the *Shuōwén*, "a wooden clapper" (*bǎifǔ*). Both are compounds formed from the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) combined with phonetic components.

31. Fascicle Thirty-one. *Kuǎ* (髁): Upper radical *kuā*, *huà* rhyme. The *Cāngjié piān* states that it refers to the outer part of the two thighs. The *Shuōwén* states that *kuǎ* means the hip/thigh (*bǐ*). It is composed of the radical "bone" (*gǔ*) and the phonetic "guǒ. The *Lǜwén* writes it as *kuà* (跨), which is a vulgar character.

**Zàn (灒):** Pronounced *zǎn* (with the radical *mǔ* [子] and the phonetic *fǎn* [󳇭]). The *Shuowen* states: "To splash and soil; another says, to sprinkle water upon a person. It is composed of the radical *shui* (水) and the phonetic *zan* (贊).

**Kù (嚳):** Pronounced *xū shàng kōng gù fǎn*. Gu Yewang states: "Kù means cruelty (*niè*). The *Baihūtong* states: "Kù means 'the ultimate' (*jí*); it refers to the fact that his administration reached its extreme limit. The *Shuowen* states: "The utmost intensity of suffering. It is composed of the abbreviated form of *xué* (學) as the phonetic. In the *Lüwen*, it is written with *yǒu* (酉) as *kù*; this refers to the thick flavor and extreme excellence of wine, which is not the intended meaning here. Alternatively, it is written with the radical *rén* (人) as *jù* (俈).

Regarding "creeping on one's elbows" (*zhǒuxíng*) while ascending the carriage pole (*chōu*): there is a contrary explanation in the *Shuowen Jiezi*, which states that "elbow" (*zhǒu*) refers to the joint of the arm, composed of the radical for "moon" (*yuè*) and the character for "inch" (*cùn*), where "inch" refers to the inch-mark on the wrist. To "creep on one's elbows" means to move by bending the elbows and knees and crawling along the ground; people of the time called this "crawling" (*púfú*).

The character 來 (lái) is pronounced with a reversed *shū* (殊) and *yù* (欲). The *Kǎo Shēng* states it means "to redeem value with wealth. The *Shuō Wén* defines it as "exchange" (*mào*), composed of two characters for "treasure" (*bèi*) and the character 󳍒 (zhàn), which consists of six strokes; 󳍒 is said to mean "to nourish" (*yù*).

32. Fascicle Thirty-two. The character "xiàn" (衒) [in the term xiànsè] is a vulgar form; its correct form is "huán" (𧗳), as stated in the *Shuowen Jiezi*, meaning "to walk while selling. It is composed of the radical for "walking" (彳) and the radical for "speech" (言), or alternatively written with the radical for "utensils" (具) as "nòng" (䝮).
The entry for "xuē" (抉) [meaning to extract] appears in the second volume of the *Yuanxue* (淵血), where it is fully explained.

Regarding "nìhǎo" (昵好): the upper character "nì" is pronounced with the initial *ni* and the final *li*. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (毛詩傳) states that "nì" means "near. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan* (左傳) states it means "intimate. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文解字) uses the character "niè" (暱) and explains it as "the sun being near," formed from the radical "sun" (日) and the phonetic "ní" (匿).

"Mò (驀)" is pronounced with the initial *máng* and the final rhyme *bái* (as in *kǎo*). It means "to cross over. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "horse" (*mǎ*) with the phonetic component "mò" (*mò*).

"Duōniàng (多釀)" is pronounced with the initial *niáng* and the final rhyme *liàng*. The *Huainanzi* states that it refers to being "brewed and fermented" (*yùn niàng*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to obtain wine through brewing"; it is composed of the radical "wine" (*yǒu*) with the phonetic component "xiāng" (*xiāng*).

33. Fascicle Thirty-Three. Regarding "duǎn bàn" (short loops): *bàn* is pronounced with the initial *pà* and the final *màn*. A *bàn* refers to the internal straps of a garment. Generally, all women's skirts (*qún*) and trousers (*kù*) have such loops to be fastened over both shoulders. The *Wénzì jílüè* (Compendium of Characters) calls them "skirt-ties. The *Kǎoshēng* (Investigation of Sounds) calls them "garment loops. The standard orthography for the characters used since antiquity for "fastening the garment over the shoulders" is written as *bàn*, following the radical *yī* (clothing) and the phonetic *pān*. It is also written as *pān*.

*Gēng* (羹) and *fú* (𦞦)—the latter is pronounced with the initial *hó* (訶). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states: "That which contains vegetables is called *gēng*; that which lacks vegetables is called *fú*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "*Gēng* refers to meat soup; it is composed of the radical 'meat' (*ròu*) and the phonetic component 'huò' (*huò*), where *huò* is pronounced *huāng* (荒)."

34. Fascicle Thirty-Four. Regarding "hē zhōu" (欱粥): the upper character *hē* (欱) is pronounced with the initial *hā* and the final *gé*. The *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲) states it means "to gulp down a large amount"; it is sometimes written as *hā* (哈), which is a vulgar character. The lower character *zhōu* (粥) is pronounced with the final *yù*. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means "gruel made from wild millet. The archaic and standard forms are written with the radicals *qū* (󳁱) and *lì* (鬲), forming *yù* (鬻). The pronunciation of *qū* is *yù*, and that of *lì* is *lì*.

Regarding the character *lè* (pronounced with the *lán* and *dá* finals): the general glossaries state that *lè-lè* is the sound of breaking [something] or the sound of eating dry flatcakes (*húbìng*).

Regarding *jīng-è* (the second character pronounced with the *áng* and *gē* finals), the *Jíxùn* states that *è* also means "startled. The *Wénzìdiǎn* explains that it is derived from the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "ài" (*ài*), and is also written as *sù*. The *Lǜwén* (Vinaya texts) uses *è*, which is a vulgar character.

The character 貁 (huáng yòu)—the radical is 由 (you) with the phonetic 就 (jiù)—is described in the *Cāngjié piān* as being like a *sàolǎo* that is skilled at pouncing on mice. The *Wénzì diǎn* states it is formed from the radical 豸 (zhì) and the phonetic 穴 (xué), or alternatively written as 貒 (from the radical 犬). The legal texts (Lǜwén) write it as 㹨, which is a vulgar character.

Regarding *zhà* (赭): the upper character is pronounced with the *zhā* (遮) rhyme-group and the lower character is the standard *bān* (般). Zheng’s commentary on the *Shanhai jing* states: "Zhà is red earth; it also refers to clothing that is red. Examining its phonetic component, it is a red color. According to the *Shuowen jiezi*, it takes the radical for "red" (*chì*) as its phonetic.

"Each 'qì' (葺) means to invade or enter; the commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that 'qì' means to repair or to manage. The *Kaoseng* says it refers to covering a roof with grass. The *Shuowen* defines it as 'cí' (茨), composed of the radical '廾' and the phonetic '咠'."

35. Fascicle Thirty-Five. Regarding the term "dǒusǒu" (抖擻): the upper character is pronounced *dǒu* (with the mouth closed) and the lower is pronounced *sù* (with the lips compressed). The Vinaya text uses the character *shù* (捒), which has the phonetic value of *shù*; this refers to the character for a "packaging basket" (*zhuāngshù*) and is not the character for "to shake off" (*dǒusǒu*). The meaning has already been explained in the second fascicle of the Sarvāstivāda Vinaya.

*Bié* (upper radical *bié*, pinyin *bié*; *Guǎngyǎ* states: "to fold and bend"). Zheng’s commentary on the *Yīlǐ* says: "To *biéjī* means to fold and compress the garments. The *Shuōwén* says: "A type of garment; it takes *bié* as its phonetic. The lower character, *tián-yè* (pinyin *tián-yè*), according to the *Zìshū*, means "to pile up. Examining the phonetics, it is *bié*. The *Shuōwén* defines *dié* as "a layered garment" (*chóngyī*); it takes *zhí* as its phonetic. The *Lǜwén* writes it as *dié*, which deviates from this meaning. *Kuǎn*: sound *juǎn*. *Qū*: sound *qū*.

36. Fascicle Thirty-Six. Regarding "yù" (馭): according to Yuè Yěwáng, "yù" refers to directing and commanding the horse with one's hand. "Qīngshàngyú" (青上魚) is pronounced *jù* (據). According to Yuè Yěwáng, "yù" means to point and command the horse.
37. Fascicle Thirty-Seven. The meaning of "duànshī" (smith) [with the first character pronounced as "duān" with an *lùan* rhyme] has already been fully explained in the third fascicle.

Regarding "qiāokuò" (stony/barren soil): the first character is pronounced "qiǎo" with a *jiāo* rhyme, and the second is "qiāng" with a *jué* rhyme. Gu Yewang states that "qiāo" means firm; when the ground is firm, it is "lean" and unsuitable for the five grains. Mencius says, "There are fertile and stony lands. The *Shēnglèi* (Classification of Sounds) states that "qiāokuò" means thin and poor soil. The *Shuowén* (Explanation of Characters) states that both characters are composed of "stone" (石) and take "yáo" (堯) and "jué" (角) as their phonetic components. The pronunciation of "lì" (礊) is "kǒu è" (口厄).

*Kīngǒu* (枅栱): *Kī* is pronounced as *xí* (奚) with a retroflex *-r* final; the *Cāngjiépiān* states it refers to the wooden beam above a pillar. The *Huáihuánzǐ* says, "When leveling the *duō* (平椓), one does not [use] *jì* (𣂪); when carving the *chǔ* (𡍩), one does not [use] *chǔ* (󳃴). Xǔ Shūzhòng’s commentary identifies *chǔ* as the *lú* (櫨). The *Běicāng* identifies it as the *mù* (󳍠). Below is *gōng* (龔), pronounced as *gōng* (龔) with a retroflex *-r* final. The *Ěryǎ* states, "The *zhí* (樴) is called *yì* (杙); that which is large among the timbers is called *gǒng* (拱). Guō’s commentary notes this distinguishes the various locations and lengths of the *yì*. Both characters are composed of the radical "wood" (*muò*) and the phonetic "qián" (*qián*), which is pronounced as *qiè* (挈) with a hard *jiān* (堅) final.
Lù (lú gù fǎn). 38.
The meaning of the third volume, number thirty-eight, regarding "chì" (chī zhī fǎn), has already been fully explained in the twenty-first volume.

*Fúzhào* (the rhyme of *táo* with the tone of *kǎo*; the *Shēnglèi* says it means "to leap," and the *Shuōwén* says it means "the gait of a magpie," composed of the radical *zhāo* with the phonetic *zhào*).
In the Vinaya texts, it is written as *shuò*, which is the name of a tree and is incorrect; the meaning has already been fully explained in the eleventh fascicle.

Regarding "youzào" (憂懆), which denotes agitation and restlessness, the *Fǎnkǎo* states that "zào" means "insecure" or "burdened. The *Máoshī Zhuàn* says it means "grieving and not joyful. The *Shuowén* explains: "Chóu" (愁) is a state of mind where the heart is unsettled; it is composed of the radical "heart" (心) with "sào" (喿) as its phonetic component. The pronunciation of "sào" is the same as above.
*Guǒtǐ* (裹體): The first character is pronounced *gō* with the tone *huǒ*; the second is *shàng*. Yě Wáng says that *guǒ* is synonymous with *bāo* (to envelop).

The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To wrap; it takes the radical 衣 (clothing) and the phonetic 果. 39. Volume Thirty-nine. *Jiànduī* (健椎): The first character is pronounced *jiàn* with the tone *lián*, and the second is *mù* with the tone *zhuī*. It is a Sanskrit term, equivalent to what is now called *jìngtuī* (a ritual mallet used for striking).

40. Fascicle Forty. Fascicle Forty. *Zuǎnjí* (纂集): "Zuǎn" (纂) is pronounced with the initial *zuǎn* (上鑽管反). According to the *Kǎośēng* (考聲), "zuǎn" also means to collect. Mahākāśyapa collected the holy teachings spoken by the Tathāgata and compiled them into the Three Piṭakas; this is called the *Zuǎnjí*. The *Shuōwén* says: "Zuǎn resembles a woven cord (*zǔ*) and is reddish-black. It is composed of the radical *mì* (糸) and the phonetic *chǎn* (󲆃); the pronunciation of *chǎn* is [as noted above].

*Tuíhuài* (隤壞): The upper character is read as *duì* (𢌞) in the *Guǎngyá*, which glosses it as "to collapse" (*túihuài*). The *Lǐjì* states, "Will Mount Tai collapse? (*tài shān qí tūi hū*). The *Shuowén* defines it as "a collapse," written with the radical *èr* (阝) and the phonetic *guì*; it is also written as *tuī* (頹). The lower character, *bìn* (擯), is read as *huái* (恠). The *Shuowén* defines it as "ruinous destruction," written with the radical *tǔ* (土) and the phonetic *huái*. Its *zhuìwén* (籀文) form is *cōu* (𣀩), and its *gǔwén* (古文) form is *shù* (󲾿). *Huái* (褱) is synonymous with *huái* (懷).

*Khūn* (欻然): "Up" (*yǔn*) with the reverse tone; it means "sudden. The *Shuowen* states that it refers to something being blown up, composed of the radical "mouth" (*qiàn*) and the phonetic "fire" (*yán*).
*Sātāhata* (奢侘摘加): A Sanskrit term; in the Tang [language], it means "deceitful. It is the name of an Arhat.

*Khāng* (坑): The *Shàngtiān yàofǎn yùnjí* states it means "to leap across. The *Shuowén* states it means "the movement of a sparrow," written with the radical *jǐ* (𧺆) and the phonetic *zhào*; it is also written as *tiào* (跳), where the lower part is read as *gēng* (庚). The *Ěryá* states it means "a pit or ruins. The *Cāngjiépiān* states it means "a ravine" or "a depression. The *Wenzìdiǎnshuō* states it means "a moat," written with the radical *tǔ* (土) and the phonetic *kàng* (亢); the pronunciation of *kàng* is *gāng* (岡).

*Tà* (pronounced *tán hé fǎn*): The *Guǎngyǎ* states that it means "to tread upon" (*lì*). The *Cāngjié piān* states it means "to kick" (*tí*). The *Shuōwén* defines it as "to step upon" (*jiàn*), composed of the radical for "foot" (*zú*) and the phonetic component *tán*. The pronunciation of *tí* is *dī*; the pronunciation of *tán* is *tān dá fǎn*.

Regarding "niè" (躡): the *Guǎyá* states that "niè" refers to what the feet tread upon; the *Fāngyán* says it means "to ascend"; the *Cāngjiépiān* says it means "to step repeatedly"; and the *Shuōwén* defines it as "to tread," formed with the radical for "foot" and the phonetic "niè. The pronunciation of "niè" is the same as above, while the pronunciation of "dié" (蹀) is "dié."

*Ning* (nail) is pronounced *ding* (upper radical) with the tone *ding* (reverse), and *quan* (lower radical) with the tone *yue* (reverse). This was already fully explained in the forty-first fascicle of the *Bhikṣu-vinaya*.

*Qiang* (wall) is pronounced *jiang* (upper radical) with the tone *yang* (reverse), and *cheng* (lower radical) with the tone *ge* (reverse). This was already fully explained in the third fascicle of the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*.

The character *wèidàn* (畏憚) is read with the second tone (*dàn*). Zheng’s commentary on the *Mao Shih* states that *dàn* means "difficulty" and also "fear. The *Han Shi Waizhuan* says it means "aversion," while the *Guang Ya* says it means "alarm" or "anger. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to dread"; it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "dān" (*dānshēng*).

"Baiqian" (百釬): The second character is pronounced with the initial *han* (寒) and the final *dan* (旦), and is read as the same as "han" (旱). The *Kaosheng* states that "qian" (釬) means to cause metal and iron to adhere to one another. The *Fangyan* states that what is called a "zui" (鐏) is called "qian" (釬). The *Shuowen* states it is an arm-guard (*bikai*); it is composed of the radical "metal" (金) and the phonetic "qian" (千). "Zui" (鐏) is pronounced *cun* (存) with the final *kun* (困); "kai" (鎧) is pronounced *kai* (開) with the final *dai* (待).

"Věi-nào" (猥鬧): the first character, *wěi*, is pronounced with the *shang* tone (*wei*). The *Cangjie pian* states that it means "to press down"; the *Guangya* states it means "multitude"; the *Kaosheng* states it means "crooked yet warm"; and the *Shuowen* states it is the sound of a dog barking; thus it follows the radical for "dog" and the phonetic *wei*. The second character, *nà* (拏), is pronounced with the *ping* tone (*na*); it is a vulgar character. This has already been fully explained in the forty-fourth fascicle of the preceding section on the Vinaya.

2. Second Fascicle. Regarding "jīshī" (nits and lice): the upper character "jī" (蟣) is pronounced with the *qǐ* rhyme group (飢顗反). According to the *Kǎośēng* (Examination of Sounds), "jī" refers to the eggs of lice. The *Shuōwén* says: "Jī is the offspring of lice; it is composed of the radical 'insect' (虫) and the phonetic 'jī' (幾). The lower character "shī" (蝨) is pronounced with the *zhān* rhyme group (山櫛反). The *Shuōwén* says: "Shī is an insect that bites humans; it is composed of the radical 'insect' (䖵) and the phonetic 'xùn' (卂). In the Vinaya texts, the character is written as "shí" (𧈲) with the radical "insect" (虫); this is a vulgar form and incorrect. The pronunciation of "䖵" is *kūn*, and the pronunciation of "卂" is *xìn*.

The character for "itch" (痒) is pronounced *sāozào* (上搔躁反). The *Cangjie pian* states that it refers to scabies; the *Guoyu* states it refers to sores. Regarding the correct orthography of ancient and modern times, it is composed of the radical *nà* (疒) and the phonetic *zǎo* (蚤, pronounced *zǎo*). The lower part, *yángjiǎng* (羊蔣), is a phonetic loan from the *Kao sheng* dictionary, which explains it as "an itch-like sore; a slight form of pain. The *Shi jing zhuan* (Commentary on the Book of Poetry) states it means "illness. The *Shuowen jiezi* calls it a "wound" (*yáng*) and gives the phonetic *yáng* (羊). In legal texts, it is written as *yǎng* (癢), which is a vulgar usage. The pronunciation of *yáng* (瘍) is *yáng*; the pronunciation of the radical *nà* (疒) is *nuò* (搦).
The term *yì* (exchange) is pronounced with the first radical as *móu* (矛) and the tone-marker as *hòu* (候); it has already been explained in the ninth fascicle of the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*.
The term *yī* (robe) is pronounced with the first radical as *qù* (逵) and the tone-marker as *wèi* (位); it has already been explained in the ninth fascicle of the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*.

Regarding "móu" (蚊幬): do not pronounce it with the sound of "fēn-kǎo. It refers to the mosquito, a flying insect. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as "méng" (蟁), stating: "A biting flying insect that emerges at dusk and hides at dawn; it follows the radical 'fūn' (䖵) and takes 'mín' (民) as its phonetic component; the pronunciation of 'niè' (齧) is yán-jie, and the pronunciation of 'fūn' (䖵) is kūn. [The character for] "zhòu" (宙) below is pronounced liú. Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "Móu means to cover. The *Erya* says: "Móu is called a *zhàng* (curtain). The *Han Shi Waizhuan* says: "Embracing the quilt and the móu"; here, "móu" refers to a single-layered curtain (*chān zhàng*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* also defines it as a single-layered curtain, following the radical "jīn" (巾) and taking "shòu" (壽) as its phonetic component.
Regarding "is qun" (是帬), the character *qun* is pronounced with the *yun* (雲) and *jun* (郡) finals; this was already fully explained in the forty-eighth fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.
Regarding "jian si" (繭絲), the character *jian* is pronounced with the *jian* (堅) and *xian* (顯) initials; this was already fully glossed in the twentieth fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.
*Jian* (衦) is pronounced *shàng gān hàn fǎn* (上 干 旱 反); it has already been explained in the twentieth fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.
Alternatively, *bi* (擘) is pronounced *xià bó mài fǎn* (下 博 麥 反); this has also been fully explained in the twentieth fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.
The character *máng* (尨) is pronounced with the upper radical *miǎo* (邈) and the phonetic *bāng* (邦). The preceding *Fó lù* (部律), fascicle twenty-one, has already provided a complete explanation.

Regarding *mài* (麥): the upper character is pronounced with the radical *měng* (猛). The *Kǎo shēng* (考聲) states that *mài* refers to the "six grains. The *Wénzì diǎn* (文字典) explains that *mài* is written as *mài*; it takes the radical *mài* (麥) and the phonetic *guǎng* (廣).

Regarding the characters for *cūla* (麁糲): the first character is pronounced with the initial *ts’-u* (醋租反) and the final *t’an* (貪敢反). This was already fully explained in the seventh fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*. Regarding the character for *pailan* (偽濫): the first character is pronounced with the initial *wei* (危䞈反).

The *Guǎngyá* states it means "to deceive. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* says it means "to borrow" (*jiǎ*). The *Shuōwén* says it means "to cheat" (*zhà*), composed of the radical "man" (人) and the phonetic "wei" (為). The second character, *lan* (䞈), is pronounced with the rhyme *kuì* (匱). The *Kǎoshēng* says it means "borrowed" (*jiǎ*) or "excessive" (*làn*). The *Máoshī* says, "Neither excessive nor excessive" (*bù jiǎn bù làn*). Gù Yěwáng says it means "overflowing throughout the world. The *Shuōwén* says it means "to soak," composed of the radical "water" (水) and the phonetic "jian" (監). *Note: The term *cūla* (麁糲) refers to coarse food; *pailan* (偽濫) refers to falsehood and excess.*

3. Third Fascicle, Part Three. Title: *Shàngzhǎng* (上𭪿). According to the *Fānyán* (方言), "shàng" is called "cài" (鏨). The *Bóyá* (博雅) states that "shàng" means "záo" (鑿) or "zhuó" (琢). The *Shuōwén* (說文) says "zhuó" refers to carving metal or stone. The *Wenzídiǎnshuō* (文字典說) says it refers to splitting wood; it is the act of chiseling stone, composed of the radical "metal" (金) with the phonetic "juàn" (雋). "Cài" is pronounced *cái'ān* (才甘反); "juàn" is pronounced *quányuǎn* (泉兖反).
To form the character for "loop" (襻), one uses the radical "clothing" (衣) with the phonetic "pan" (攀, pronounced as in *màn*). The *Wenzi jílüè* states: "The loop is the fastening of a skirt.

To form the character for "snip" (鉸), one uses the radical "wood" (交, pronounced as in *jiào*) with the phonetic "xiāo" (効). The *Yùnlüè* states: "A snipping knife. The *Zishū* states: "A snipping knife is the same as the scissors of today."
Regarding "cracked" (*xùn*), the upper radical is *fèn* (奮) and the lower is *fǎn* (反). The preceding section contains a detailed explanation in the seventh fascicle of the *Bùlǜ* (部律).

Regarding "holeless" (*wú xué*): the lower radical is *xuán* (玄) and *jué* (決). The *Guìyuàn zhūcóng* (桂苑珠叢) states that "hole" (*xué*) is a term for a cavity. The *Shuōwén* (說文) states: "A hole (*xué*) is an earthen chamber; it is composed of the radical *mián* (宀, pronounced *mián*) and the phonetic *bā* (八). The sound of *mián* is *mián*.

Regarding the term *xiàn* (line/thread): the *Shuǎngdiǎn* and other dialects state it means "to continue. Gu Yewang says it refers to "mutually connecting and continuing. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as being composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "rán" (*rán*, pronounced *xiānjiàn*). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that it is "thread and fiber. The *Liji* says: "On the right, one wears the needle-case and thread. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* explains that *xiàn* (needle-thread) is composed of the radical "silk" (*mì*) and the phonetic "zán" (*zán*, pronounced *cán*). The character *lǜ* (law/standard) is written with the phonetic "quán"; the form "xiàn" is a vulgar variant.
*Ākṣipta* (㒓額): the first character is pronounced *nà* (儺刺反) and the second is pronounced *gè* (硬格反); this was already explained in the twenty-second fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.
*Saṃhata* (密緻): the second character is pronounced *lì* (直利反); this was already explained in the twenty-third fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.

The characters for "shoes" (*xié*) and "sandals" (*jù*) are all reversed forms of common usage; their correct orthography uses *xī* as the radical to form *xié*. The *Shìmíng* states: "Xié means 'to loosen' (*jiě*). The *Wénzìdiǎn* says: "It is leather (*gé*) used to make *dī*; it refers to today's hemp shoes. It takes *gé* as the radical and *guī* as the phonetic component. *Dī* is pronounced *dīngxī* (with the final syllable having the *yù* tone). The *Cāngjiépian* states: "Jù is the same as *lǚ*. According to the *Shuowén*, it is *dī*; it takes a simplified form of *lǚ* as its radical and *lóu* (pronounced *lǒu*) as the phonetic component. *Lóu* is pronounced *lǒu*.
Volume Four, Part Four. *Cāo* (爮): the first character is pronounced as *bào* (鮑) and the second as *guī* (歸). This has already been explained in Volume One of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*.
*Nàluàn* (𠆴亂): the first character is pronounced as *ná* (拏). This has already been explained in Volume Forty-four of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*.
*Mānatta* (the "ma" is pronounced with a *pi* rhyme; it is a Sanskrit term. In ancient times it was called *mānastha*, a name for reprimand and punishment within the Saṃgha).
Volume Five, Part Five. [The term] *pūti* (the "pu" is pronounced with a *mu* rhyme) has already been fully explained in the twenty-seventh fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.
*Bānbó* (斑駁): The second character, *bāng*, is pronounced *měi* (邈). The preceding section, *Bùlǜ* (部律), Volume Twelve, has already provided a complete explanation.

Regarding *suǐnuó* (水捼): the second character, *nèi*, is pronounced *léi* (雷). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that *nuó* refers to rubbing or kneading; the *Shuōwén* (說文) states it means to crush, and further explains it as the friction and rubbing of two hands against each other, composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic element *wěi* (*yī*).

*Zhānghuáng* (慞惶): The upper character is pronounced *zhǎng* (with the *shāng* rhyme) and the lower is pronounced *huáng*. The *Kǎoshēng* says that *zhānghuáng* describes the appearance of being terrified. Lexicons state it means "anxious fear," while the *Shuowén* calls it "panic and fear. Both characters include the "heart" radical (*xīn*) and take *zhāng* and *huáng* as their phonetic components.

Regarding "tiáo biān" (corded weaving), the former character is pronounced *dǎo* (as in *dāo fǎn*) and was already explained in the fifth fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*. Regarding "xià biǎn" (lower narrow cloth), the former character is pronounced *mián* (as in *mián fǎn*) and was already fully explained in the preface to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.

"Kòng (控)"—the "gōng" rhyme in the *Shīchuán* (Explanations of the Odes) states that it means "to pull" (*yǐn*). It is also said that "to stop a horse" is called *kòng*. The *Kǎoshēng* (Investigation of Sounds) says it means "to hold" (*chí*) or "to receive" (*jiē*). The *Shuōwén* says: "The Huns pull their bows, which is called *kòng*; it is composed of the radical 'hand' (*shǒu*) and the phonetic 'kōng' (*kōng*)."

The character 𠿒 (hé): below it is the phonetic 訶 (hé). The *Cāngjié piān* states that it means "to scold"; the *Guǎngyá* states it means "anger"; the *Wénzì diǎnshuō* also says it means "to scold. It is composed of the radical 口 with 歇 (xiē) as the phonetic.

*Zhuǎn* (腨): The second character is read as *chuán* (遄, with the *rén* [soft] tone). This was already explained previously in the fourth fascicle of the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*. *Tuí* (椎): The first character is read as *mù* (木) with the *zhuī* (追) tone.

This was already explained in the sixth fascicle of the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*. The second character is read as *xù* (勗) with the *yōng* (邕) tone. The *Wenzi Dictionnaire* states that it means "the chest" (*tí* or *yīng*). It is composed of the radical *ròu* (肉) and the phonetic *zhē* (膈); however, the text of the Vinaya uses the character *bāo* (勹), which is a vulgar variant for "chest."

Regarding "hook-and-fastener" (gōuniù): the first character is pronounced *gǒu* (with the *shàngshēng* tone) and the second is *nǚjiǔ* (with the *shàngshēng* tone). This was already explained previously in the eighth fascicle of the *Sifenlü*.
Regarding "rope" (wúgěng): the second character is pronounced *gēngxìng* (with the *shàngshēng* tone). This was already explained previously in the forty-sixth fascicle of the *Sifenlü*.
Regarding the "gān" (罐), the preceding section on the third-fourth fascicle of the *Vinaya* has already provided a full explanation.

As for the "qiánzǐ" (鉆子)—the first character pronounced *qiáng* (強) or *yán* (炎)—the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that a "qián" (鉆) is an iron clamp (*tièxiáo*) and also means "to hold. It is composed of the radical "metal" (金) with the phonetic "zhàn" (占). In the Vinaya texts, it is written as "qián" (鉗) with the "sweetness" (甘) radical; this refers to a neck-shackle, and the character "qián" (鉗) is not the same as the character for "qiánzǐ" (鉆子).

Regarding "phlegm" (*tán-yìn*): the first character is pronounced *dàn* (with the *lán* rhyme) and the second is pronounced *yīn* (with the *jìn* rhyme). This was already explained in the ninth fascicle of the preceding *Vinaya*. Regarding "scraping the tongue": the first character is pronounced *guān* (with the *bā* rhyme);

the *Shuǎngshēng* states that "to scrape" means to apply a blade crosswise, or to shave. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "knife" (*dāo*) and the phonetic "tongue" (*shé*); the pronunciation of "tongue" is *shí-liè* (with the *fǎn* rhyme).
The term "should split" (*pī*)—read as *mí* (覔) with the *fǎn* (反) of *qián* (前)—has already been fully explained in the thirty-sixth fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.

Regarding "stake" (*qiàn*): the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that *qiàn* refers to a small slip of bamboo, a piercing tool, or a pin. The *Guǎngyá* (廣雅) states that *qiàn* is called *chǎn* (鏟). The *Shuōwén* (說文) states it means sharpness; it is composed of the radical "bamboo" (*zhú*) and the phonetic component *xiàn* (韱), with the pronunciation *chǎn* (察限反). The pronunciation of *qiàn* is *xī lián* (息廉反), and the lower character is also read as *qīng yì* (青亦反). Gu Yěwáng states it is a sharp instrument that enters the flesh. The *Shuōwén* defines it as piercing; it is composed of the radical "knife" (*dāo*) and the phonetic component *cì* (朿), with the pronunciation *cì* (次).

The character *shè* (軾) refers to the transverse wood at the front of a carriage. The *Guǎngyá* states that the *zhù* (󱔎) is called *shè*. The *Shuōwén* says it is the wood at the front of a carriage, composed of the radical "carriage" (*chē*) with the phonetic element *shì* (式); the pronunciation of *xiàn* (獻) is *píbì* (皮祕).

Regarding "bōyáng" (揚簸): the character below is pronounced with the *pó* rhyme (i.e., *bō*). The *Kǎoshēng* says it means "to sift and scatter. The *Shūyīn* says, "To sift and scatter it; the chaff and husks remain in front. The *Shījī* says, "To sift away the chaff. The *Shuowén* says, "Yáng means to remove the husk from rice; it follows the radical 'jǐ' (basket) and uses 'pí' as a phonetic component. The pronunciation of "jǐ" is *jī*.

6–7: Fascicle Six and Fascicle Seven. In both the sixth and seventh fascicles, there are no difficult characters requiring phonetic glosses. 8: Fascicle Eight. Regarding the character "zà" (雜) in "záróu" (雜糅), it is pronounced with the lower radical *nǚ* (女) and the counter *jiù* (救). This was already explained previously in the twenty-fourth fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.

Regarding the character *liàn* (楝) in the phrase "leaves upon the *liàn*": the reading is *diàn* (奠), with a sound like *kǎo* (考). It is said that this is the name of a type of wood. The *Shuowen Jiezi* also identifies it as a wooden name, formed from the radical "wood" (*mu*) and the phonetic component "jian" (*jiǎn*). The pronunciation of "jian" is the same as above. In the *Lüwen* (律文), it is erroneously written as "shù" (捒) using the component "shù" (束).

*Pī-pi* (髀𨢘): *zhǐ* (枳) in the first character is pronounced *xì* (上, *xì*); *jī* (雞) in the second character is pronounced *xīng* (馨, *xīng*). This is a medicinal name in the Sanskrit language. *Rè-fēn* (熱饙):

*fēn* (饙) in the second character is pronounced *wén* (粉, *wén*). The *Shīchuán* (詩傳) states it refers to *fēn-liù* (饙餾). The *Ěryá* (爾雅) states it refers to *niǎn* (捻). Lexicons state it means steamed rice. The *Shuowén* (說文) states: "It is *liùfàn* (𩝶飯). It is formed from the radical for food (*shí*) with the phonetic *bèn*. *Liù* (餾) is pronounced *liú* (流, *jiù*) and *jiù* (救, *jiù*). *Liù* (𩝶) is pronounced *xiù* (秀, *yóu*). *Bèn* (賁) is pronounced *fén* (墳, *fén*).

Regarding the character 葷 (hūn): the upper radical is 艹 (grass) and the phonetic is 訓 (xùn), with the tone reversed [to the departing tone]. The *Shēnglèi* states: "Hūn refers to wild garlic. Zheng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* says: "Hūn and xīn (pungent vegetables) are used to ward off demons and evil influences. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* states it is a stinking vegetable; it is composed of the radical 艹 and the phonetic 軍 (jūn). It is incorrect for the *Lǜwén* to write it as 薰 (xūn). The pronunciation of 蒜 (suàn) is that of 筭 (suàn).

"Carved ornamentation" (diāoshì): the "shàng" in "shàng" is pronounced as the *liáo* rhyme-group. Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* says it means "carved and painted. Gu Yewáng says it means "engraved. The *Guǎngyǎ* says it means "incised. The *Shuowén* says it means "carved patterns," composed of the radical "hairy strokes" (*shān*) and the phonetic "zhōu"; the character for "ornamented patterns" (*lùwén*) uses "zhuī" as its phonetic. To use "diāo" (bird) is not this meaning. The sound of "shān" is *shān*; the lower part, "shēngzhí," is pronounced *fǎn*. The *Ěryǎ* says it means "to adorn and purify. Examining the sounds, it is "to polish," "to carve," and "to refine. The *Shuowén* says "adornment and brushing," composed of the radical "cloth" (*jīn*) and the phonetic "sì"; the sound of "sì" is *sì*.

*Tíng-lù* (瀓漉): The first character, *tíng*, is pronounced with the initial *zhí* and the final *líng*. The *Kǎo Shēng* states that *tíng* refers to clear water; the *Shuōwén* defines it as "clear," composed of the radical *shuǐ* (water) and the phonetic *zhēng* in abbreviated form. In the *Lǜwén* (Canon of Phonology), it is written with *dēng* instead, which is a vulgar usage. The second character, *lù* (漉), is pronounced with the initial *lóng* and the final *wū*. Gù Yěwáng states that *lù* means "to drip. The *Guǎngyá* states it means "exhausted"; the *Fāngyán* states it means "extreme"; the *Ěryǎ* states it means "to dry up. The *Wénzìdiǎn* explains it as "to parch," composed of the radical *shuǐ* and the phonetic *lù*; the pronunciation of *lù* is the same as above.

*Kǎn* (癵跛): The upper character is pronounced *liàn-yuán* (反); it was already explained previously in the forty-sixth fascicle of the *Sifenlü* (四分律). The lower character is pronounced *pō-mā* (反). Gu Yewang says it means "lame" (*jiǎn*). The *Zhouyi* says, "The lame can walk," yet they are insufficient for traveling. The *Wenzi Dadian* states that it is composed of the radical "foot" (*zú*) and the abbreviated form of "skin" (*pí*) as the phonetic element. *Mó* (麼) has the pronunciation *mò-kě* (反).

*Khujja* (侏儒): the first character is pronounced *shang* with the fanqie *ru* (儒) and *fan* (反); the second character is pronounced *xia* with the fanqie *ru* (乳) and *zhu* (朱). This was already explained in the twenty-fifth fascicle of the *Abhidharmavibhāṣā-śāstra*.
*Caṇḍāla* (扇侘): the second character is pronounced *cha* with the fanqie *jia* (𭏖) and *jia* (家). In the Sanskrit language, this refers to a eunuch (*paṇḍaka*).

The character for "stammering" (吃) is pronounced *qin-yi* (with the second tone). The *Hanshu* states that Sima Xiangru was a stammerer (*kou-chi*). The *Shenglei* says it refers to the repetition of words. Yang Xiong could not engage in spirited discourse; it is said that his speech was difficult. It is composed of the radical "mouth" (口) and the phonetic "qi" (乞).

*Yuchōng* (愚憃): The upper character is pronounced *jù* (遇俱反). The *Shuowen* states it means "stupidity" (*zhàng*). It is composed of the radical 心 with the phonetic 禺; *zhàng* is pronounced as below. The lower character is pronounced *huáng* (卓降反). Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "The *chōngyú* (憃愚) are those who are born dull-witted and ignorant, like children. Regarding the sound [of the lower character], it refers to the stupidity of a child. The *Shuowen* also defines it as "stupidity," composed of the radical 心 with the phonetic 舂; *chōng* is pronounced *wǔjiè* (五解反).

9. Ninth Fascicle. Regarding "xuānhuá" (clamor): the first character, "xiōng" (兄), is pronounced with the *yuán* rhyme. It has already been fully explained in the twenty-sixth fascicle of the *Sifenlü* (Dharmaguptaka-vinaya).

Regarding "jūgōng" (鞠躬): the first character, "gōng" (弓), is pronounced with the *qū* rhyme. The *Kǎośēng* (Examination of Sounds) states it means "cautious respect. The *Lúnyǔ* says, "Upon entering the gate of the Duke, one bows deeply (*jūgōng*)"; Kǒng [Yǎng]’s commentary states, "Jù means to contract one’s demeanor. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* (Dictionary of Characters and Explanations) states that it is formed from the radical "metal" (*gè*) and the phonetic "pǔ" (*jú*).

"Diānkuáng" (癲狂): "diān" is pronounced as *tiǎn* (上典年反). The *Shēnglèi* (聲類) states that "diān" refers to a wind-disease (*fēngbìng*). The *Guǎngyá* (廣雅) also states that "diān" means "insane" (*kuáng*). According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "zhé" (疒, pronounced *nǚ'ài*) and the phonetic "zhēn" (眞). The sound of "zhé" is *nǚ'ài*.

The character *qīngtí* (青稊) is pronounced with the second tone for the final syllable, following the rhyme *ní*. It has already been fully explained in the twelfth fascicle of the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*. Regarding *niǎolà* (拗拉):

the former character (*niǎo*) is pronounced with the first tone for the initial syllable and the third tone for the final syllable. The *Wenzì jílüè* (文字集略) states that "to *niǎo*" means to crush an object with the hand to break it; it is formed from the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "yòu. The latter character (*là*) is pronounced with the fourth tone for the final syllable. He Xiū’s commentary on the *Gōngyáng zhuàn* states that "to *là*" means to break. According to the standard characters of the present day, it is written as *cuī* (摧), formed from the radical "hand" and the phonetic "lì," and is also written as *zhé* (折) or *zhé* (摺).

*Jiūn* (皴朽): The first character is pronounced with the *qī* and *xún* rhymes. This was already explained in the twenty-seventh fascicle of the *Sifenlü* (四分律). Regarding the second character, *xiū* (朽), Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states: "It means decayed and rotten. The *Lunyu* says: "A rotten root cannot be carved. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* explains that it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mu*) and the phonetic "kǎo" (*kǎo*). The sound of "kǎo" is like that of "kǎo" (考).

*Tàn* (毈壞): The first character is pronounced as *tuán* (團) with the *lù* (呂) rhyme. The *Lǔshì Chūnqiū* states that when a chicken egg has been kept for too long, it becomes *tàn*. The *Kǎoshēng* says *tàn* means the egg is ruined. The *Shuōwén* says *tàn* means the egg does not hatch; it is composed of the radical "egg" (*luǎn*) and the phonetic "duàn" (*duàn*). It is incorrect to write it as *xié* (󳆸) using the "evening" (*xī*) radical instead.

*Guǐkuàng* (deceitful/cheating): The first character is pronounced *guī* (with the *wěi* rhyme) as in the preceding section; it was already explained in the twelfth fascicle on *bhikṣus*. The second character is pronounced *kuàng* (with the *kuāng* rhyme). Jia Dui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states: "To *kuàng* is to delude. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Chunqiu* states: "It means to deceive. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* explains that the character is derived from the radical for speech (*yan*) and the phonetic *kuáng*.

Regarding "xuǎn" (鏇): on the foot [of the character], one reads it as *xuàn* (絢) with a *kǎo* (考) tone; it is said that "xuǎn" means to rotate an axle or to turn a vessel. The *Erya* states: "The ring is called *xuǎn*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "A round brazier; it takes 'jin' (金) as its radical and 'xuàn' (旋) as its phonetic component. The pronunciation of "lú" (鑪) is *lìhú* (力胡).

The character *fù* (拂) is pronounced *fēn* (勿) with a retroflex final; in the *Shijing*, it means "to sweep away," and it is also said to mean "to rectify. The *Guangya* states it means "to remove. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Yili* glosses it as "to wipe," while his commentary on the *Liji* glosses it as "to clear away dust. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to strike," formed from the hand radical with the phonetic *fú* (弗), and read with a final *zhōu* (周) and *shǒu* (守). This was already explained in the twenty-third fascicle of the preceding *Biyulu*.

Regarding the *kūrca* (rug/mat): the first character is pronounced as *jù* (具) with the level tone, and the second is pronounced as *shù* (數) with the rising tone. This has already been explained in the twenty-sixth fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*. Regarding the wooden stool (*kaṭhalla*):
the second character is pronounced as *zhī* (知) with the level tone and *lín* (林) with the rising tone. This has already been fully explained in the second fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.

"Yèjiāng" (曳韁): The first character, yè, is pronounced with the *zhì* rhyme-group. This was already explained in the seventh fascicle of the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*. Regarding the second character, jiāng (襁), the *Kǎoshēng* states that it refers to a horse's bridle. The *Hànshū* says it is the "bridle and shackles of fame. The *Wénzìdiǎn* explains it as a horse's halter (*mǎxiè*). It is composed of the radical 革 (leather) and the phonetic 畺; *xiè* is pronounced with the *xiānjié* rhyme-group.

10. The tenth fascicle. Regarding the character *ji* (逆): the *Xianjie Fanyun* explains that it is used for "stopping" or "blocking. It refers to carving wood to a point and using it to stop or block things. Regarding the character *shu* (櫼): it means a wooden beam or support. It is composed of the radical "wood" (*mu*) and the phonetic component "gan" (*gan*). The pronunciation of *shu* is *jian*.

The term "shao-dao-shang-shuang" (矛刀上霜) [pronounced with the second tone for the first character and the fourth tone for the last] has already been fully explained in the seventh fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.

The term "fang-chuan-xia-zhuàn" (方篅下腨) [pronounced with the fourth tone for the first character and the third tone for the last] has already been fully explained in the third fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.

*Suǒliú* (逆流而上): The *Shīchuán* (詩傳) states that to go upstream against the current is called *suǒ*. It also says *suǒ* means "to head toward. Kong’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* states that to travel up the Yangtze River is called *suǒ*. The *Shuowén* says: "Water wishing to flow downward but being forced upward; it is composed of the radical 'water' and the phonetic element 'sǒu' in abbreviated form."
*Kīlapaṭṭi*: "Kīla" is a transliteration from the Sanskrit (pronounced with the *i* and *li* reversed).

*Nāva-kaṭṭha*: according to the *Shiming*, the stern of a ship is called *nāva-kaṭṭha*; it means the rear of the vessel so that it does not veer off course. The *Wenzidian* explains it as the wooden post at the stern of a ship; it is composed of the radical for wood (*mu*) and the phonetic element *ta*. The sound of *ta* is *tuó*. In the Vinaya texts, it is written as *duó* (舵), which is the character for a carriage's rudder and not the character for a ship's rudder. The final character is pronounced *shàn-rè*.

"Lóng-ài" (聾騃): "Lóng" is pronounced with the *lù* and *dōng* rhymes. The *Cāngjié piān* states that "lóng" refers to being unable to hear with the ears. Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* identifies it as the chest. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "without hearing," composed of the radical "dragon" (*lóng*) and the phonetic "ear" (*ěr*). The second character, "ài" (崖), is pronounced with the *jiě* rhyme. This has already been explained in detail in the nineteenth fascicle of the preceding *Bùlǜ*.

11. The Eleventh Fascicle, Part Eleven. *Chuai* (歠): The upper character is pronounced *chuàn* (川𤑔反). The *Cangjie pian* states that *chui-chai* (𠻜) means to drink. The *Liji* says, "Do not slurp or gulp" (*wú liú chuài*). The *Shuowen jiezi* defines it as *shuo* (󳅙), formed from a simplified *yin* (㱃) with the phonetic *zhua* (叕); *chai* (𠻜) is pronounced *shān-tào* (山𤑔反), and *yin* (㱃) is pronounced *ān-jǐn* (菴錦反). The lower character is pronounced *hàn-hé* (憨合反). The *Taixuan jing* says, "Gulping below, gulping above. Song Zhong’s commentary states that *hai* (欱) means to close together. The *Xijing fu* says, "Gulping down the Li River, spitting out the Hao. The *Shuowen jiezi* also states that *hai* (欱) is synonymous with *chui* (歠), formed from *qian* (欠) with the phonetic *he* (合); *hao* (鄗) is pronounced *háo*.

Regarding the term *luófú* (蘿菔): the first character is pronounced as *luó* (羅), and the second as *péngbǐ* (朋比). The *Erya* states that it is the *tú* (葖) or *lúbó* (蘆菔). Guo Pu’s commentary notes that it belongs to the category of plants lacking *jīng* (菁), having purple flowers and large roots. Lexicons state that *luófú* is simply another name for the vegetable; it is indeed *lúbó*.

*Qiānghuò* (upper character *qiāng*, lower character *huò*). The *Jiùshì* (Old Matters) of the Eastern Palace states that *qiāng* is the name for an iron vessel; the lower character is pronounced *huángguō*. The *Zhōulǐ* states that *dǐnghuò* is a vessel for boiling things. The *Shuōwén* says it means "to engrave" or "a cauldron," written with the radical 金 (*jīn*) and the phonetic 蒦 (*huò*); *zhuān* (engrave) is pronounced *huìguī*, and *huò* is pronounced *wángjué*.

*Yǒng* (涌): Upper radical *róng* (容), reversed; *zhòng* (腫) is the phonetic. Gu Yewang says: "To surge" means the waves of water leaping upward. The *Shuowen* says: "Surge" means to leap up (*téng*); it is composed of the radical *shui* (water) with *yǒng* (甬) as the phonetic. The pronunciation of *yǒng* is as stated above. In the *Lüwen* (律文), it is written with the radical *li* (力) to form *yǒng* (勇); this is a vulgar usage of the character. Lower radical: *fēi* (非), reversed. Gu Yewang says: "To boil" (*fèi*) refers to the surging of waves, like the boiling of broth. The *Shichuan* (詩傳) says: "Boiling" means bubbling out. The *Shuowen* says it is composed of the radical *shui* (water) with *fú* (弗) as the phonetic.

*Niǎo* (撓): To stir up; to disturb. The *Guǎngyá* says it means "to confuse. The *Shuōwén* says it means "to stir," formed with the radical 手 (hand) and the phonetic 堯 (yáo), pronounced *xià jiāo qiǎo*. The *Shīchuán* says it means "to churn milk. Lexicons say it means "to bend" or "to disturb. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is formed with the radical 手 and the phonetic 覺 (jué).

Regarding the character *jiàn* (mirror): it appears in the *Shijing* (*Mao Shi*) as "my heart is not a mirror," and its commentary states that a mirror is used for observing forms. The *Zuozhuan* says, "a mirror is called a *jìng*. Du Yu’s annotation explains it as "caution" or "examination. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *jiàn* refers to that from which the "bright water" is drawn from the moon; it is composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic element "lín" (*língshēng*).

Regarding the characters for *lù* (樚轤): the upper character is pronounced with the *lóng* rhyme (valued as *gǔ*) and, according to the scriptural texts, is written with the radical "carriage" (*chē*). This is incorrect. The lower character is pronounced *dū*. The *Kǎoshēng* states that *lù* refers to a circular rotating device. Gù Yěwáng says it is a water-lifting lever (*jígēng*). The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* explains that *lù* (樚) takes the "wood" (*mù*) radical and the phonetic "deer" (*lù*), while *lú* (轤) takes the "carriage" (*chē*) radical and the phonetic "ox" (*lú*). These are the correct characters from antiquity to the present.

*Yin* (齦): Upper radical *yu* with the phonetic *jin*. The *Cangjie pian* states that *yin* refers to the roots of the teeth. The *Shuowen jiezi* states it is the flesh of the teeth, formed from the radical *chi* with *jin* as the phonetic.

*Dì* (覿): Upper radical *ting* with the phonetic *li*. The *Zuo zhuan* states: "He sent the great officers and the wives of the clan to *dì* [meet] using ceremonial gifts. The *Erya* states that *dì* means "to see. The *Wenzi dianshuo* states it is formed from the radical *jian* with *mai* as the phonetic.

The character 定 (dìng) in 草莛 (cǎo tíng) has the phonetic component 靈 (líng). This was already explained in the thirty-seventh fascicle of the *Sifenlü* (Four-Part Vinaya). The character 慴 (zhé) in 慴怖 (zhé bù) has the phonetic component 葉 (yè);

the *Erya* states that it means "to be cowed with fear," though it is sometimes written as the character 懾 (zhé). The *Dongdu Fu* (Rhapsody on the Eastern Capital) says, "The eight spirits were struck with trembling fear. It is a compound character formed from both semantic and phonetic components.

*Xiè* (戲): The upper radical is *xi* (希) with the reversed *yì* (意). The *Erya* states: "To *xiè-làng-xiào-ào* is to engage in playful banter. The *Shijing Zhuan* states: "To *xiè* is to be dissolute and at ease. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* explains that it takes *go* (戈) as its radical and *qiàn* (䖒) as its phonetic; *qiàn* is pronounced *xī*. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* defines it as mutual derisive banter. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *xiè* is synonymous with *xi* (戲), taking *yan* (言) as its radical and *qiàn* (䖒) as its phonetic.

The term *kang* (糠) has the first tone for its initial and the *ying-zhi* rhyme for its final. This was already explained in the thirty-eighth fascicle of the *Sifenlü* (四分律). Regarding *lang-wu* (廊廡): the character *lang* (廊) has the *lang-tang* rhyme;

Xu Shuchong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states that it refers to the lower part of a corridor building. The *Wenzidian* explains it as *wu* (廡); it is composed of the radical *yǎn* (广) with the phonetic *láng*. *Yǎn* is pronounced *yǎn*, and the final of *wú* (無) is *fǔ*. The *Shiming* states that a large house is called a *wǔ*; the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as the side chambers surrounding a hall, composed of the radical *yǎn* with the phonetic *wú*.

"An iron spade" (tiè-chāi): the "chāi" is pronounced with the *dié* and *fǎn* finals. This has already been fully explained in the twenty-third fascicle of the *Sifenlü* (Dharmaguptaka-vinaya). The *Erya* states: "A *qiāo* is called a *chāi*. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* says: "The characters *qiāo* and *chāi* are synonymous; they are formed with the radical 'metal' (金) and the phonetic 'zhā' (臿). The character 'zhā' (臿) is composed of 'gān' (干) and 'jiù' (臼), where the pronunciation of 'jiù' is *jiù*."

12. The Twelfth Fascicle, Part Two. *Chenyan* (諂言). "Chen" (讇) is pronounced as *chǒu* (𮉼) with the *shang* (上) tone; it is also written as *chian* (諂). He Xiu’s commentary on the *Gongyang Zhuan* states: "Chen is synonymous with *ning* (侫, flattery). The *Zhuangzi* says: "To feign one's intentions and speak according to the Way is called *chen*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "speech" (言) and the phonetic "yan" (閻).

The character 擐 (huàn) has the upper radical phonetic *huàn* (as in *huàn*). Jia Ji’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that it means "to don armor. The *Shuowen Jiezi* further gives it the pronunciation *gū-huàn*, explaining it as being composed of the radical 手 (hand) and the phonetic 環 (huán) with its final element abbreviated.

*Jian* (arrow): The upper character is pronounced *zuǒ* (with the *gǎn* rhyme). *Yùnyīng* states it refers to the bowstring; it is composed of the radical "bow" (*gōng*) with the phonetic element "can" (*cǎn*).
It has a nock (*zú*). The lower character is pronounced *zōng* (with the *sù* rhyme); it was already explained previously in the twenty-third fascicle of the *Fǔlǜ*.

Regarding "scab" (*chuàngyǎn*), it was already explained in the twelfth fascicle of the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*; regarding "eruption" (*xiànyàn*), it was already fully explained in the twenty-sixth fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.

13. The Thirteenth Fascicle. Regarding "pǒbì" (跛躄): the first character is pronounced *bō* (波) with the *mǎ* (麼) tone; the second character is pronounced *bìng* (并) with the *tán* (貪) tone. This has already been fully explained in the nineteenth fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.
Regarding the character *di* (sneezing): the upper radical is *dī* (counter 17). This has already been explained in the thirty-second fascicle of the *Fuyou* (部律).

Regarding *zhǔ* (to carve/dig): the upper radical is *zhú* (counter 24). The commentary on the *Shūshū* states that it means "to pare" (*zhǎo xiāo*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *zhǔ* means "to hew" (*zhé*) and is composed of the radical *jīn* (axe) with the phonetic *chē*; *chē* is pronounced *dòu*. The lower part is *qún* (counter 36). The *Guǎngyá* states that *jué* (digging) means "to bore through. The *Wenzi Dianshuō* explains that it is composed of the radical *shǒu* (hand) with the phonetic *qū*. *Qū* is pronounced *wù*.
"Kǐngkài" (謦咳): the first character is pronounced *qīng* (with the *ding* rhyme) and the second is pronounced *kāi* (with the *dǎi* rhyme).

This has already been explained in the thirtieth fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*. 14. "Yìdìng" (杙釘): the first character is pronounced *yíng* (with the *jí* rhyme) and the second is pronounced *dìng* (with the *dìng* rhyme). This has already been fully explained in the forty-first fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.
The first character, *zhǒu* (󰜐), with the upper radical *yī* and the lower radical *fǎn*, has already been fully explained in the fiftieth fascicle of the *Sifenlü* (*Jiǔbù lǜ*).
The second character, *zé* (㧾), with the lower radical *zhàn* and *shè* (*fǎn*), has already been fully glossed in the tenth fascicle of the *Biqiūní lǜ*.

*Tāotiē* (饕餮): the first character is pronounced *dǎo* (with the *fǎn* [classifier] reversed) and the second is *tiānjié* (with the *fǎn* [classifier] reversed). This has already been explained in the fiftieth fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*. *Chōuzì* (󰜥㗱):

the first character is originally pronounced *mò* (with the *fǎn* [classifier] reversed) and the second is *zànlì* (with the *fǎn* [classifier] reversed). This has already been explained in the fiftieth fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.

*Zàn-yì* (灒溢): The upper character is read as *sàn* (散). This was already explained in the twentieth fascicle of the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*. The lower character is read as *yǐn* (寅). Yù Wáng (*Yǎng Yù*) states that it means "overflowing" (*yíng*). Jiā Duī’s commentary on the *Guóyuè* states it means "remainder. The *Shuōwén Jiězì* defines it as "a vessel being full," composed of the radical water with the phonetic *yì* (益), and is also written as *sù* (㳑) with the radical *mǐng* (皿).

The Hundred and One Karmas of the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Volume One. "Ābhyaṅga" (奧箄迦) is a transliteration of the Sanskrit term; the word itself explains its meaning within the scriptural text. [Note: *Ābhyaṅga* is pronounced with the first syllable as *ā-va-gao* (反) and the second as *bi-mi* (反)].

*Pào-miàn* (疱面): The *Shēngyùn* states that this refers to blisters or sores on the face. The *Shuowén* writes it as *páo-miàn*, explaining it as "vital energy arising on the face," composed of the radical 皮 (*pí*) and the phonetic 包 (*bāo*).

*Tān-huàn* (痶瘓): The upper character is read as *tiǎn* (天典反) and the lower as *tuān* (湍卵反). According to the commentary, *tān-huàn* is a vernacular term for the condition where hair falls out due to heat-toxin wind (*rè-dú-fēng*). This word does not exist in standard character dictionaries. Both characters take the radical 疒 (*zhé*) and are pronounced with the phonetics 典 (*diǎn*) and 奐 (*huàn*), the latter having the sound *huàn* (喚).

*Yè* (噎): The upper radical is *yān* (煙) with the classifier *jié* (結). The *Mao Shi* says, "The heart is as if choked" (*zhōngxīn rú yè*). The *Chuán* (傳) says, "Choked, unable to breathe. Regarding the correct orthography of ancient and modern times: it means the food is obstructed in the throat; it also means grief. It is composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic "one" (*yī*). The lower part is pronounced *yuàn yuè*. The *Lǐjì* says, "One does not dare to *yè* or *yī*. The *Wénzì Diǎnshuō* says, "*Yè* is the gasping of breath; it is composed of the radical 'mouth' and the phonetic 'suì'. *Yī* (噫) is pronounced *yú jiè*.

The character for *zhǐ* (hemorrhoids) is pronounced with the second tone and the initial *chí* (reversed). The *Wenzì jílüè* (Compendium of Character Etymologies) states: "Hemorrhoids are insects that consume the lower parts and drain the blood. The *Wenzi diǎn* (Dictionary of Characters) explains it as a disease of the posterior region, formed from the radical *nà* (sickness) and the phonetic *sì*.

*Ōng* (痈): The character is pronounced *gōng* (上於恭反). The *Wenzi jilüè* (文字集略) states that it refers to a large carbuncle (*tuō*). The *Shuowen jiezi* defines it as a swelling, formed from the radical *nà* (疒) with the phonetic *yōng* (雝), which has the same pronunciation as the preceding and following characters, *zuò* (坐) and *hé* (和). Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Shanhaijing* identifies it as a carbuncle (*zuó*). The *Wenzi jilüè* further notes that *zuó* (痤) refers to a small swelling. Lexicons define it as a carbuncle (*jié*). The *Wenzidian shuō* (文字典說) explains that it is formed from the radical *nà* (疒) with the phonetic *zuò* (坐).

Regarding the character *cǎo* (草) with the phonetic *jiǔ* (󳇡): the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that it means "to bind grass together to form a sheaf. The *Pīcāng* (埤蒼) says, "*Jiǔ* is green. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* (文字典說) says it refers to rice straw (*hégǎn*). It is composed of the radical for grain (*禾*) and the phonetic *jiǔ* (󳂉). The pronunciation of *jiǔ* is *chún*, and the pronunciation of *gǎn* (稈) is *gǔhàn*.

Regarding "cǎo tiǎn" (grass-thatch): the phonetic component is *zhàn* (in the *shè* register). The *Kǎośēng* states that it means "thatch" (*tiǎn-gài*), made by weaving grass. Guō’s commentary on the *Ěryá* says, "White *máo* grass is used for thatch. The *Wénzìdiǎn* explains that *gài* (cover) is written as *tiǎn*, derived from the radical "grass" and the phonetic component "zhàn."
1. *Jībàn* (羈絆): The first character is pronounced as *jì yí* (with the final syllable reversed), and the second is pronounced as *bàn*.

These have already been fully explained and annotated within the preceding introduction to the Vinaya rules. 2. Second Fascicle: There are no characters in this fascicle that require phonetic transcription or annotation. 3. Third Fascicle: For the character *shù* (豎) in *shù shí* (豎石), the reading is *zhū zhǔ* (with the initial syllable reversed). This was previously explained in the thirty-sixth fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.

*Tiao-di* (跳躑): The upper radical is read as *tu* (徒) with the reversed *liao* (聊). The *Cangjie pian* states it means "leaping" (*tiaoyong*); the *Guangya* states it means "ascending"; the *Kaosheng* states it means "bounding" (*yue*); and the *Shuowen* states it means "stumbling" (*jue*), formed with the foot radical and the phonetic *zhao* (兆). It is incorrect to write it as *chuo* (踔) using the phonetic *zhuo* (卓), as it appears in the *Lüzhong*. The lower character is read as *cheng* (呈) with the reversed *yi* (亦). This was already explained in the first fascicle of the "Fuyou" (前有部) section of the *Lü* (律).

The character 𠪟 (kēng): the upper radical is 挑 (tiāo) with the reversed sound; the lower radical is 客 (kè) with the reversed sound *gēng*. The "Correct Characters of Antiquity and Today" states that it means "a pit or a mound" (坑墟).

It is composed of the radical 土 (earth). The character 躡 (niè): the *Fāngyán* states it means "to step upon"; the *Guǎngyá* states it means "to tread upon"; the *Cāngjié piān* states it means "to trample"; the *Shuōwén* states it means "to tread. It is composed of the radical 足 (foot) and the phonetic 聶 (niè). The pronunciation of 聶 is as stated above; the pronunciation of 躡 is *dié*.
