Regarding "kicking" (chùtà), the first character is pronounced *qiū* with the *yù* rhyme, as already explained in the sixth fascicle of the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*; the second character is pronounced *tán* with the *là* rhyme, as already fully explained in the first fascicle of the *Vinaya-saṃgraha*.
*Nia* (陿): Upper radical *xian* (咸), reversed *jia* (甲). This has already been fully explained in the eighteenth fascicle of the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*.

*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha-gāthā*, Fascicle One. *Pou* (剖): Upper radical *pu* (普), reversed *hou* (后). The commentary on the *Shangshu* states that it means "to divide in the middle. It also says it means "to cleave open. The *Zuozhuan* says, "I shall divide [it] with you and eat it. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it means "to split," composed of the radical *dao* (刀) and the phonetic *pou* (咅); the pronunciation of *pou* is *tou-hou* (偷厚). Lower radical *xing* (星), reversed *ji* (积). The *Kaosheng* says it refers to splitting wood; it also means "to divide. The *Shichuan* says it means "to analyze by dividing. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* says it means "to break wood," composed of the radical *mu* (木) and the phonetic *jin* (斤).
*Xiànchà* (扇侘) is a term from the language of Chu;

the first character is pronounced *qíjià* (圻嫁) and the second is pronounced *bōmǎ* (波麼), with *mǎ* having the sound of *mó* (磨) or *bō* (跛). This has already been fully explained in the nineteenth fascicle of the *Sifenlü* (四分律).

Regarding the characters for "piàn" (匾) and "xī" (㔸): the upper part of "piàn" is "biàn" (辮), pronounced with the final *dǐ* (梯) and *kǎo* (考) sounds; it is said that "piàn xī" (匾㔸) means "thin and broad. Both [characters] take "pián" (扁) as their radical and "xī" (虒) as their phonetic. The initial sound of "pián" (扁) is *fāng* (方), and the sound of "xī" (虒) is *tiān-yī* (天伊) reversed (*tiān* being the first syllable and *yī* the second).
"Protruding teeth" (yòu chǐ): the first character is read as gǒu with the *qiú* rhyme. This was already explained in the second fascicle of the *Sifenlü* (Dharmaguptaka-vinaya).

"Staring eyes" (xiàn yǎn): the first character is pronounced xián. The *Yùnyīng* states that it refers to eyes with much white. The *Fāngyán* states it means to look askance (*xiàn miǎn*). The *Cāngjiépiān* states it is an eye ailment. The *Shuōwén* states it means to have bulging eyes (*dài mù*), composed of the radical "day" (*jiān*) and the phonetic "sound" (*shēng*).
The term "㧈行" (yǎnxíng) is read with the initial tone as yǐn; it has already been explained in the twenty-fifth fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.
The term "壞弶" (huàqiáng) is read with the final tone as qiǎngxiàng; it has already been fully explained in the third fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.

The character *gē* (割) is pronounced with the initial *kūn* (昆) and the final rhyme *shàng* (上). The *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲) states that it is a name for the state of *Jīng* (荊), referring to the removal of one's hair. The *Zhèng Zhù Wèn Lǐ* (鄭注問禮) says it means shaving the hair. The *Shuōwén* (說文) defines it as "shaving the hair," composed of the radical *biāo* (髟) and the phonetic *háng* (亢); *biāo* is pronounced *bì yáo* (必遙), and *tì* (鬀) is pronounced *dì jì* (俤計). The lower part [of the character] is pronounced *gān hé* (竿曷). The *Kǒng Zhù Shàngshū* (孔注尚書) says it means "to harm" (*hài*). The *Guǎngyá* (廣雅) says it means "to cut off" (*duàn*) or "to trim" (*cái*). The *Wénzì Diǎnshuō* (文字典說) says it means "to flay" (*bō*), composed of the radical *dāo* (刀) and the phonetic *hài* (害).
2. Second Fascicle. Regarding *yati* (the first character pronounced as *jiāng*): this was already explained in the ninth fascicle of the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*.
It is a Sanskrit term; in the Tang language it means "guardian. The text of the Vinaya also writes it as *yati*, which is the same.

*Zhēn* (pronounced *zēn*, with the second tone). The *Huainanzi* states that it refers to clusters of *zhēn* trees. Examining its phonetics, it signifies the dense growth of plants and trees. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* explains that it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic element "qín. The lower character is pronounced *cú hóng*. Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* says it means "to cluster together. The *Shūjīng* itself states that the gathering of all things is called a *cóng*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "That which is formed by grasses gathering together is called *cóng*; it takes 'xīn' as its phonetic. *Xīn* is pronounced *tǔ jiǎo*. The version in the Vinaya texts writes it as *cóng*, which does not form a valid character; this is incorrect.
*Jiānpó* (詀婆): The first character is pronounced *diǎn nián* (點黏) as a variant;

it is a transliteration of a Sanskrit term. *Hóngqiàn* (紅茜): The second character is pronounced *qiàn xiàn* (霰). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Qiàn (*xiàn*) is *máshōu* (茅蒐), which can be used to dye the color crimson. It is produced from human blood; it belongs to the "grass" radical and takes *xī* (西) as its phonetic component.
*Vandana* (襵婆): "Zhe" is pronounced with the initial *shè* (上古涉反); it is a Sanskrit term. *Vandana* (畔𬀹):
the first character is pronounced *bàn* (上音伴) and the second is pronounced *tí lì* (下提戾反); it is a Sanskrit term. In the language of the Tang, it means "to pay homage. *Dai-mao* (帶𦶇):

the second character is pronounced with the initial *rǔ zhǒng* (下辱種反). The *Guǎngyá* states that *máo* (𦶇) is *máo* (󲽠); it also says *máo* is *jī* (𦋺). The *Wénzìdiǎn* explains it as *máo* (𦇧), derived from the radical "hair" (*máo*) and the phonetic "róng" (*róng*). *Róng* (茸) is the same as above; the pronunciation of *máo* (󲽠) is *sī lù* (思錄反).

*Māng* (尨): The upper radical is *miǎo* (邈). According to this, *māng* refers to the coarse hair of Western countries; the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is the hair of a dog, and further explains that a variegated color not being pure is called *māng*. It is composed of the radical for "dog" (*quán*) and the phonetic *shān* (彡).

Regarding *pātra-śukti* (鉢𤪭): the second character is pronounced with the rhyme of *wen* (聞) and *fen* (奮), and its reading is identical to that of *wen* (問). This was already explained in the forty-second fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (*Qianyou bulü*). Regarding *kīla-lauha* (釬鍱):
the first character is pronounced with the rhyme of *han* (寒) and *gan* (幹), and the second has the sound *ye* (葉). This was already explained in the second fascicle of the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*.

*Shuāxiào* (刷削): "shuā" is pronounced with the tone of *suān* (拴), and "xiào" is pronounced with the tone of *fǎn-suān* (刮反拴). This was already explained in the twentieth fascicle of the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*. Regarding the character *xiàng* (下) [in the compound], it is pronounced with the tone of *què* (鵲). The *Guǎngyá* states that it means "to cut down" (*xuējiàn*). The *Shīchuán* (Poetry Commentary) states that it means "to erode and diminish" (*qīnxiào*).

3. Third Fascicle. Regarding "máo shào" (spear and lance), the first character is pronounced as *xiāng* (with the *zhǎo* rhyme) and the second as *chù* (with the *fǎn* tone); this has already been fully explained in the fourth fascicle of the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*.

Regarding "zhūrú" (dwarf), the first character is pronounced as *zhǔ* (with the *rú* rhyme) and the second as *lǔ zhū* (with the *fǎn* tone); this has already been fully explained in the twenty-fifth fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.
*Khakkhaṭa* (口吃): the second character is pronounced *jǐn yǐ* (斤乙); this has already been explained in the eighth fascicle of the *Vinaya-saṃgraha*.
*Śuṣka-tṛṇa* (𥿳稊): the second character is pronounced *dì ní* (弟泥); this has already been fully explained in the twelfth fascicle of the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*.

Regarding *shǔwǔ* (薯蕷): the upper character is read as *zhǔ* (渚, pronounced like the reversed *zhù*) or *wáng* (王). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that *shǔ* refers to sugarcane (*gānzhè*). Gu Yewang states that the name for *shǔyù* is *shàngshǔ*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* also states it is sugarcane, with the radical "grass" and the phonetic "zhū," pronounced *wǔgǒu*. The *Kaosheng* states that *wǔ* refers to the root of the lotus. The *Erya* states: "The *fúqú* (lotus) has a root called *wǔ*. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* states it is the root of the *fúqú*, with the radicals "grass" and "water" and the phonetic "yú"; the pronunciation of *yú* is the same as above. In the monastic codes (*lüwen*), it is written as *ǒu* (藕), which is also acceptable.

Regarding "liánshāo" (lotus tip): the character *shāo* is pronounced with the *cháo* rhyme group; the *Kǎoshēng* states it means "the end. The *Wénzìdiǎn* explains it as "the tip," following the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic component "xiào" (*xiào*).
Regarding "báiwù" (white mold): the character *wù* is pronounced with the *pǔ* rhyme group; this was already explained previously in the thirteenth fascicle of the *Bìchūnì Lǜ* (Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya).

*Chì* (緻): Upper radical *shǐ* (尸), reversed; already explained in the thirtieth fascicle of the *Sifenlü* (四分律). *Sǎ* (洒): Upper radical *xī* (西), reversed; Hàn Kāngbó’s commentary on the *Zhōuyī* states:

"To wash and cleanse the heart. The *Shuowén* says: "To rinse and purify; it takes *xī* as its phonetic. Lower radical *lú* (盧), reversed. The *Shījìngchuán* (詩經傳) says: "To smear and adhere. The *Guǎngyá* says: "To soil. The *Wenzìdiǎnshuō* says: "Mud; it takes *tú* (涂) as its phonetic. The pronunciation of *tú* is the same as above. *Tú* (涂): Lower radical *dù* (杜), *lú* (盧), reversed. The *Shījìngchuán* says: "To smear and adhere. The *Guǎngyá* says: "To soil. The *Wenzìdiǎnshuō* says: "Mud; it takes *tú* (涂) as its phonetic. The pronunciation of *tú* is the same as above.

4. Fourth Fascicle. Regarding "suan" (醦): the upper radical is *shan* (衫) with the reverse *zhan* (斬), or alternatively *chu* (初) and *jin* (錦). The *Guangya* states that "suan" means "sour" (*cuo*). The *Picao* states that it means "extremely sour. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* explains that it follows the radical for liquor (*you*) and takes "san" (參) as its phonetic component; "san" is pronounced *si* (澀) with the reverse *zan* (簪).

"A startling gale descends upon the distant banner and returns to the city walls. Guo's commentary on the *Erya* states: "A violent wind blowing up and down is called a *biao* (gale). The *Shizi* says: "A violent wind is a collapsing *biao*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "'Fuyao' is a whirlwind; it is composed of the radical 'wind' (*feng*) and the phonetic 'biao. The pronunciation of *biao* is the same as above."
*Niè* (儜惡): The first character is pronounced *nuò* (搦耕反). This has already been explained in the thirtieth fascicle of the *Fóbiàolù* (佛部律).

*Quǎn* (踡): Pronounced *jù* (懼員反). Yěwáng (顧野王) states that it means "to crouch and not stretch out. The *Shuowén* (說文) defines *quǎn* as "the manner of walking; it is composed of the radical 足 and the phonetic 卷."
Regarding "not blowing" (bù chǔ): the character above is pronounced *hē* with the *gè* rhyme; this has already been fully explained in the eleventh fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.

Regarding "chewing" (chǔ zì): the character above is pronounced *bǎng* with the *mò* rhyme, and the character below is pronounced *jìn*; this has already been fully explained in the fiftieth fascicle of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*.

*Zhàng* (脹): The upper radical is *zhāng* (張, pronounced with the *liàng* tone). Duan Yucai’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "it means the abdomen is distended. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* says it refers to abdominal pain from overeating; it is formed with the radical *ròu* (flesh) and the phonetic *cháng* (長). The lower character is *zāi* (哉, pronounced with the *sè* tone). The *Kaosheng* states that *zhàng* (󳊒) refers to the bone within the cheeks of a fish. The *Guiyuan Zhucóng* says it refers to the internal contents filling the cheeks of a fish; it is formed with the radical *yú* (fish) and the phonetic *cōng* (悤).

Regarding the term *qiànjié* (欠㰦): the lower character is pronounced *qù*. The *Tōngsūwén* (通俗文) states that opening the mouth to draw in breath is called *qiànjié*. Gu Yewáng says that *qiànjié* refers to drawing in breath and opening the mouth. The *Wenzídiǎn* (文字典) explains that it is derived from the radical *qiàn* (欠) with the fourth tone (*qù*).

5. Fifth Fascicle. Regarding the *táo-gǔ* (small hand-drum): the first character, *dào*, is pronounced with the *láo* rhyme. This has already been fully explained in the thirty-ninth fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*. As for *yīng-luó* (the drum's frame): the first character, *yīng*, is pronounced with the *yíng* rhyme.

The *Shi zhuan* (Commentary on the Book of Odes) states that it means "to wind" or "to encircle. The *Shuowen jiezi* states it means "to gather the leather [of the drumhead]. It is composed of the radical *mì* (silk/thread) and the phonetic component *yíng* in abbreviated form; the pronunciation of *luó* is *juàn*.

Regarding "gōuniù" (鉤紐): the upper character is read as *gǒu* (苟) and the lower as *niǔ* (久). The script in the *Vinaya* text reads "jū" (拘), which is incorrect; this was already explained in the fifth fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.

Regarding "huàkuà" (𡱼胯): the lower character is read as *huà* (化). This is a vernacular form; the correct character is "kuò" (髁), with the phonetic component "kǎo" (考), meaning the bone above the thigh. The *Cāngjié piān* states that "kuà" (胯) refers to the outer part of the two thighs. The archaic form is written as "yú" (𡱼) or "wū" (𡱗); the script in the *Vinaya* text reads "kuà" (跨), which is incorrect.

*Taishang* (打生): The first character is pronounced with the *qǐng* radical and the *fǎn* (反) suffix; it means to strike with all one's might. This has already been fully explained in the twenty-second fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.

*Kǐngkài* (謦欬): The first character is pronounced with the *qīng* radical and the *dǐng* (頂) suffix; the second character is pronounced with the *kāi* radical and the *ài* (靉) suffix. This has already been fully explained in the thirty-third fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.

*Tānkuè* (灘濄): "Tān" is pronounced *tǎn* with the *lán* rhyme; it was already fully explained above in the thirty-third fascicle of the *Fǔlù* (部律). Below, "kǎo" (考) is pronounced *wō* with the *huó* rhyme. The *Shēngyuán* (聲韻) states that *kuè* (濄) means water swirling in a circular flow; it is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic "guò" (*guò*).

*Qīngcì* (Toilet): The first character is pronounced *qīng*; the second is pronounced *chǔ* (with the radical *shì*). *Yùnyīng* states that a toilet (*cì*) is a privy; it is a pit for discarding filth and excrement.

*Mózhìlǐjiā* (Sanskrit): The final character is pronounced *lì*. This is a Sanskrit term translated into Chinese as "Pitaka" (Basket/Collection). Alternatively, it is called *móduòkějiā*, meaning "the discrimination between the heterodox and the orthodox."

*Vinayakṣudrakavastu-saṃgraha-gāthā*, one fascicle. Regarding the term "comb" (*shū*) at the beginning: the *Shēngyùn* states that "comb" refers to a hairbrush; the *Jīngǔ zhèngzì* says it is for arranging the hair. It is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "sū" (abbreviated from *shū*). The second fascicle of the preceding *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* has already explained the character "shuān" (pronounced *kuà*).
*Kṛkī* (栗㚲毘): This is the Sanskrit term for a royal lineage (*rājavaṃśa*). *Kuddāla* (木杴):
The second character is pronounced *xiǎn* (險) or alternatively written as *jiǎn* (撿).
*Kūṭhāra* (氍毹): The first character is pronounced *jù* (具) and the second *shù* (數). These have already been explained previously in the twenty-sixth fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.

Regarding "矸石" (gànshí): the "gàn" is pronounced with the *han* (寒) and *gan* (幹) finals. According to the textual passages of the Sarvāstivāda Vinaya, "矸石" refers to a medicinal grinding stone (*moyào móshí*). It is incorrect for the Vinaya text to write it as "衦" (from the radical 衣).

Regarding "襯體" (chùntǐ): the "chūn" is pronounced with the *jìn* (覲) final. The *Kǎoshēng* states that "襯" means a cushion or mat; it refers to a garment worn directly against the body, formed from the radical 衣 and the phonetic 親.
"Bānbó" (variegated) is pronounced *xiàbāng miǎo* (下邦邈); it was already explained in the twelfth fascicle of the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*.
"Yílābō" (瑿羅鉢) is pronounced *yìxī* (翳奚) in the upper tone; it is a Sanskrit term.

*Vinayavastu-uddāna-gāthā-saṃgraha*, one fascicle. Regarding the "tub-cloak" (*kuṇḍika-cīvara*): the character *kuṇḍi* (pronounced *chuán*) refers to a tub. A "tub-cloak" is a garment whose seams are joined together all around like a tub; it is called a tub-cloak because its appearance is like that of a tub. This is precisely what women wear today as a skirt (*qún*).

*Chéngzú* (承足) is pronounced *zhīlín* (知林); it refers to a small wooden block (*mùzhèn*). The *Yùnyīng* states that it means "to chop the raw material. It may also be written with the radical for stone as *zhèn* (碪), or with the radical for *pǔ* (攴) as *niàn* (𢷏). It is incorrect for the *Lǜběn* (律本) to use the radical for hand (*shǒu*) to form *niān* (拈).

Purgatives are administered overnight; these purgative medicines are used to eliminate accumulated heat in the five viscera, the intestines, and the stomach, as well as undigested food remaining from previous meals. Thus, the medicine washes away and removes their dregs and impurities, so that the bodily qi may immediately become unobstructed and flow freely—examples include *dahuang* (rhubarb), *puxiao* (natron), *badou* (pungent seeds), *xijiao* (rhinoceros horn), and others.

The character *diǎn* (染衣倀摘更反) is also written as *chǎn* (𢿵). The phonetic gloss states that *chǎn* means "to unfold" (*zhǎn*), composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "chǎng. In the phonological system, it is composed of the radicals "hand" (*shǒu*) and "zhēn" (*zhēn*); to write it as *tiàn* (揁) is incorrect.
*Rèn* (zhèn fǎn, yùn qián) means to recognize; it is derived from the sound of the character for "endure" (*rěn*), though it is sometimes written as *nìn*.
*Cǎo zhuàn* (yīn zhǔn, also zhī rùn fǎn) refers to binding bundles of straw together.

Regarding the term *qúlù*: the first character is pronounced as *qú*, and the second is pronounced as *shù* (with the *jù* rhyme). The *Jixùn* states that it refers to a woolen rug; it originates from the various barbarian kingdoms of the Western Rong, such as Tibet. Another explanation says it is a patterned woolen cloth.

The Fundamental Mūlasarvāstivāda Bhikṣu-śīla-sūtra, one fascicle. *Poṣadha* (the first character pronounced as "bǎo" with the rhyme of "sǎo," and the second as "shā" with the rhyme of "jiǎ") is a Sanskrit term; in the Tang language, it means "nurturing."

The character *léi* (羸) is pronounced with the initial *l-*, followed by the final *ǒu*. Zuǒ Zhuan’s commentary states it means "weak. Jia Dui’s commentary on the Guoyu states it means "ill. Xu Shuchong’s commentary on the Huainanzi states it means "inferior. The *Zishu* states it means "exhausted. The *Shuowen* states it means "emaciated," composed of the radical "sheep" (*yang*) and the phonetic "nǚ" (𣎆). The pronunciation of "nǚ" is *lìguǒ* (力果).
*Manāṭa* (the second character pronounced with the *bi* and *ye* finals; a Sanskrit term translated here as "punishment").

*Huanran* (the first character pronounced with the *huan* and *guan* finals): Liu Zhao’s commentary on the *Gongyang Zhuan* states that "to remove old grime is called *xuan*" (*xiàn*). Zheng’s sub-commentary on the *Shijing* states that "*xuan* means to wash and cleanse. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "*Xuan* means to wash away the grime of clothing; it takes the radical *shui* (water) and the phonetic *gan*. In the ritual texts it is written as *huàn*; this is a vulgar character. The second character (*ran*) is pronounced with the *ru* and *yan* finals. The *Guangya* states: "To stain or defile. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To dye silk with colors; it takes the radical *shui* and the phonetic *za*."
The character 󳎔 (piāo) in the first syllable is pronounced *mò* (with the *hòu* tone). This has already been fully explained in the ninth fascicle of the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*.

Regarding the character 漂 (*piāo*) in the first syllable of 漂衣: Yuè Wáng says that "piāo" means "to flow"; the *Guǎngyǎ* says it means "to impel"; the *Shuōwén* says it means "to float," being composed of the radical 水 with the phonetic 票; the pronunciation of 票 is *piáo* (with the *miào* tone).

Regarding the force on the thread, it has already been explained in the twentieth fascicle of the *Pratimokṣasūtra* (Fǎnběnqiánbù lǜ); as for the subsequent [explanation], it has already been fully annotated in the fourth fascicle of the *Nidānasūtra* (Xiānzǎi fǎnběn qínítuōnà lǜ).

*Péng* (棚): Upper radical *shàng*, pronunciation *bái* (白) with the final consonant *gēng* (耕). The *Guǎngyá* says it is a gate; the *Shènglèi* says it is a pavilion (*xiè*); the *Shuōwén* says it is a wooden platform (*zhàn*), composed of the radical *mù* (木) and the phonetic *péng* (朋).

*Fàn* (󱇅): Upper radical *chǐ* (尺) with the final consonant *zhǎo* (沼). The *Kǎoshēng* says it is parched rice or wheat; the *Bīcāng* says it is parched wheat. The *Wenzìdiǎnshuō* says it is dried wheat flour or meal, composed of the radical *mài* (麥) and the phonetic *qiū* (酋). Its ancient form is *fàn* (󲽗). The pronunciation of *qiū* (酋) is *jiū* (由) with the final consonant *fǎn* (反).
*Dì* (覿) and *yóu* (遊): the former is pronounced *shàng* (上) and the latter *lì* (曆). This has already been explained in the eleventh fascicle of the *Lìshè* (律攝).

*Fēn* (紛): the first character is pronounced *fú wén* (拂文). The *Guǎngyǎ* (廣雅) states it means "multitude. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* (楚辭) describes it as having the appearance of "abundant fragrance. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* (文字典說) states that *fēnyún* (紛紜) means "chaos. It is composed of the radical *mì* (糸) with *fēn* (分) as its phonetic component; the latter is pronounced *ráo zhǎo* (饒沼). Kǒng (孔) in his commentary on the *Shàngshū* (尚書) states it means "disturbance and chaos. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* further states it means "frivolity. It is composed of the radical *shǒu* (手) with *wǎn* (󳃗) as its phonetic component.

*Tiao* (跳): Pronounced *tu diāo* (徒彫反). The *Cangjie pian* states it means "leaping. The *Guangya* states it means "ascending. The *Shuowen jiezi* states it means "to leap" or "to bound," composed of the radical for "foot" (*zu*) and the phonetic element *zhao* (*zhao sheng*).

Below the inner ankle (the character *huǎ* with the radical *wǎn* reversed; Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "The *huǎn* is the heel of the foot"; the *Cangjie pian* states: "The *huǎn* is at the side of the foot"; the *Shenglei* states: "It is the auxiliary bone on the outside of the foot"; the *Shuowen jiezi* states: "The *zuǒhuǎn* [ankle]; it is composed of the radical *zuǒ* and the phonetic *guǒ*).
The character 󱽍 (mèi) [is read as] *niú shàng mǎo bāo fǎn* (the radical is "ox" with the phonetic *mǎo* and *bāo*).

This has already been fully explained in the fiftieth fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā*. Regarding the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-bhikṣuṇī-pratimokṣa-sūtra*, one fascicle: the character 媒 (*mèi*)—[read as] *měi bēi fǎn*—the *Shuowén* states: "To act as a matchmaker means to devise a plan to unite two surnames for marriage. It is formed from the radical "woman" (*nǚ*) and the phonetic "something" (*mǒu*).

The character for "chewing" (噉) has the phonetic component "dan" (敢) with the upper tone; the *Yunquan* states it means "to eat" or "to consume," formed from the mouth radical with "dan" as the phonetic, or alternatively written as "dan" (啖). The lower character for "onion" (蒜) has the phonetic component "luan" (亂); according to the *Shuowen*, it refers to pungent vegetables, formed from the grass radical with "luan" as the phonetic, where "luan" has the same pronunciation as the upper [radical].

Regarding "shujiao" (樹膠)—the character *jiao* is pronounced as *jǎo* (according to the *Jiǎoyào* [切韻]): "tree resin" refers to the hardened sap of trees, such as the resins of peach and plum trees, which resemble animal glue (*píjiāo*) or pine pitch (*sōngzhī*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "resin" (*yì*); it is formed with the radical for "bark" (*pí*), followed by "flesh" (*ròu*), and the phonetic element *liáo*.

Regarding the character for "pregnant" (shēn): its lower radical is the phonetic *shēn*. The *Mao Commentary* on the *Shijing* states: "Shēn means 'to vibrate' (*zhèn*); it refers to being stirred within. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as 㑗, following the radical for "human" (*rén*). The *Shenji Xun* explains it as "a woman carrying a fetus in her womb. Some dictionaries write it as 𡝌, which is an ancient form of the character.

*Xi-qún*: The first character is pronounced *xiān* (with the radical *liǎn*) and the second is *jùn* (with the radical *yún*). It is also written as *qún*, derived from the radical *yī* and *jīn*. *Niǎn-lǚ*:
The first character is pronounced *shàn* (with the radical *nián*) and the second is *lǚ* (with the radical *lì yǔ*). It refers to thread.
"撫" (fǔ) in "拊肩" (fǔ jiān) means to stroke with the hand following [the shoulder].
"蹲行" (dūn xíng) means to walk while crouching.
"庂足行" (zé zú xíng)—the first character is pronounced "zé" and is an archaic form—means to walk on the side of one's feet.
"Small ball" (*xiǎo tuán*, with *tuán* pronounced as *luán-fǎn*): the received text follows the character for "hand" (手) and writes it as "to clench" (摶), which is incorrect.

"Wearing clogs" (*zhuó jī*, with *jī* pronounced as *qíng jí-fǎn*): the *Yùpiān* states this refers to the modern "toothed straw sandals" (*lù*). The *Shuowén* defines it as "a sandal" (*jiè*), written with the radical "hand" (攴) and a simplified form of "sandals" (履).

The *Mahāsāṃghika-śīla-mūla* (The Root Precepts of the Mahāsāṃghika), one fascicle, compiled by the Śramaṇa Xuányìng. [Regarding the character] "nǐ" (擬): it is pronounced with the rhyme of *yú* (魚) and *lǐ* (理). In a dictionary, it means "to direct toward"; according to the *Shuowén*, it means "to measure" and "to compare."
"Jiǎo" (嫽) [pronounced with the initial *l* and final *-diāo*] means to dally or flirt; it means to provoke or to toy with.

"Jiǎo" (攪) is the same as the archaic form "Guò" (捁) [pronounced with the initial *g-*, final *-kǎo*, and tone *shàng*]. According to character dictionaries, "jiǎo" means to stir up or disturb, and also implies disorder.

*Chou* (吮) the finger is also written as *sou* (嗽), both pronounced with the *suo-jue* rhyme. The *Tongsu-wen* states that "to suck in" is called *chou*; it is written as *ca* (𡂡) in the *Jie-wen*, which is a vulgar character.
*Xue* (㗘) and *ze* (㗱) are pronounced with the *bu-mo-zi-li* rhyme; the *Shuowen* defines *xue-ze* as the sound of chewing.

The Mahāsāṃghika Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa Sūtra, compiled by the Śramaṇa Xuanying. Regarding the character *jì* (轡): it is pronounced *bǐ kuì fǎn*. According to the *Zìshū*, it refers to the halter for a horse; it is that which is used to control and restrain chariots and horses. The character *lè* (勒) refers to the bit of a horse; the character is written with the radical *sī* (糸). As for *wèi* (軎), it is the axle-end of a carriage.

The character 遞 (di) is written as 递 (di) in the text; in the *Xiǎo Ěryǎ*, it is glossed as "turning" (tú lǐ fǎn). The *Ěryǎ* states: "Dié means 'to alternate'. Guō Pǔ says: "This refers to taking turns or changing places."
The name *kārṣāpaṇa* is correctly pronounced *kāliśapaṇa*. According to this, eighty cowrie shells constitute one *paṇa*, and sixteen *paṇas* constitute one *kārṣāpaṇa*.
"Disturbance" (*rǎoluàn*) means like a pond; according to the *Shuowen*, "disturbance" (*rǎo*) means vexation. The *Guoyá* states that "rǎorǎo" means disorderly.

"To go to another" (*shītā*)—the character *shi* is pronounced *chì*—according to the *Erya*, "to go" (*shì*) means to proceed. To proceed to serve another is called "going to another. According to the *Fāngyán*, in the regions of Song and Lu, "to go" is called "shì," and "shì" also means to return.
*Khāṭu-khāṭura*: translated here as "small long bed. *Kacchā* (pronounced *zhūjiā*): refers to the pleats of a lower garment (*nivasana*).
It is also pronounced *zhīshè*; the *Tōngsùwén* states that "pleating" (*zhé*) refers to sewing it together.
*Piān kū* (偏刳): "Kū" is pronounced *kǔ* (孤反). It means to hollow out the interior. According to the *Fāngyán*, it means to split open. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means to divide.

*Kāo jiǎo* (󳅄脚): "Jiǎo" is pronounced *qiào* (丘召反). According to the *Shuōwén*, it refers to the manner of walking lightly. One interpretation says it means to lift the feet playfully, or to raise the feet high. The text of the precepts writes this as *qiáo* (蹺), which is incorrect.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-bhikṣu-prātimokṣa-sūtra*, compiled by the Śramaṇa Xuanying. Regarding the character "jīn" (斤): according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "jīn" means to hew wood; it also refers to a mattock. In the *Prātimokṣa* text, it is written as "jìn" (釿), with the phonetic value *niǔ yǐn* (牛引反). According to the *Shuowen*, "jìn" means a chisel (*jì*); "jì" has the phonetic value *zǐ suí* (子隨反) and refers to scissors. However, "jì" does not carry this meaning here.
*Bin* (𣦢): Pronounced *fang* (方) and *chi* (尺) in reverse; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "to be lame and unable to walk.

The character consists of the radicals *pi* (辟) and *zhi* (止). In the *Ten Recitations Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa Sūtra*, compiled by the Śramaṇa Xuanying: *Mian* (闑): Also written as *nie* (臬), both pronounced *yu lie* (魚列); this refers to the threshold of a door. It is also called *kun* (閫), pronounced *ku ben* (苦本).

"Yin-yi" (喑噫): "Yin" (喑) means to sob; "yi" (噫) means to sigh in lamentation, and it also refers to a loud sound. In the text, "jie" (戒) is written as "ai" (嗌), which is pronounced "yì". "Ai" (嗌) means the throat or gullet; however, "ai" is not the intended meaning of the character here.
According to the sequence of the catalogue of the Tripiṭaka, there should be the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-bhikṣu- and bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa-sūtra* in two fascicles;
these have already been included within the sixty-first fascicle of the preceding *Yinyi* (Explanations of Sounds and Meanings).
In order to unify all the various schools of the Sarvāstivāda, this work is included in the preceding volume.

Regarding the *Mīśāsè Jièběn* (The Mūlasarvāstivāda Prātimokṣa Sūtra): it was compiled by the śramaṇa Xuányìng. The term *qíxíng* (企行) is pronounced with the second tone for *qǐ* and the fourth tone for *xíng*. According to the *Shuōwén*, *qǐ* means "to lift the heels"; it also means "to look up expectantly. This is as stated in the *Shuōwén*: "I stand on tiptoe (*qǐ*) looking out for him."

The *Pañcavargika Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa Sūtra*, compiled by the Śramaṇa Huilin. Regarding the term *pèi* (轡): Bei Mi (悲媚) [in his dictionary] states that it is that which controls the horses within a chariot. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it is the horse-rein (*mǎpèi*). It is composed of the radical "silk" (糸) with the phonetic component "yì" (𨊥). *Yì* (𨊥) is the same as *lián* (連). The *Shijing* says: "The six reins are like silk. The pronunciation of *yì* (𨊥) is *wèi*.

*Máo* (pronounced *mǎo bāo fǎn*, with the phonetic component *kǎo*) is the name for a wild ox. The *Shānhǎijīng* states: "On Mount Pánhóu there is a beast shaped like an ox, with hair growing on its four limbs; it is called the *liáoniu*. Guō Pǐng’s commentary says: "The ox's back, knees, and dewlap all have long hair. The *Shuowén* defines it as "the long-haired ox of the southwestern tribes. This refers precisely to the tail of the *liáoniu*. It may be written with the radical *máo* (hair) and the phonetic *yíng* (abbreviated); or it may be written with *yú* as the phonetic, forming the character *máo*.

"Biàn" (pronounced bì rén fǎn) means to cast out; Sima Biao’s commentary on the *Zhuangzi* states that "biàn" means to discard. Gu Yewang says it means to exclude or reject one another. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* explains that the character is formed with the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "bin" (賓).

Regarding the method of "mediation" (méi) for each cup, Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "The word 'méi' means 'to deliberate' (móu); it refers to one who brings together those of different surnames to achieve harmony and completion. The *Shuowen Jiezi* also says it refers to joining two surnames, composed of the radical "woman" (女) and the phonetic "mǔ" (某). The pronunciation of "mǔ" is "mǔ"; [the character] is composed of "mu" (木) and the phonetic "gān" (甘). The *Erya* uses the character "mǔ," which is an error.

*Lí* (羸): The pronunciation is *lǜ* (律) with the final *wéi* (危) reversed. Jia [Yan]’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states it means "sickly. Xu Shuchong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* says it means "inferior. The *Shuowen* says it means "emaciated," composed of the radical for "sheep" (*yang*) and the phonetic *nǚ* (𣎆), which also serves as the phonetic; it is also written as *lí* (羸).
*Kāṣāya* (迦郗那; *kāṣāya*): This is a transliteration of the Sanskrit term for "robe" (*cīvara*) or specifically the "merit-robe" (*guṇa-cīvara*). *Pāpita* (漂衣; *pāpita*):

The character *piāo* (匹遙反) means "to drift," referring to a robe that has been lost by being carried away by water or wind. Gu Yewang states that "drifting" (*piāo*) is synonymous with "flowing. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "water" (*shui*) and the phonetic component "piao" (*piāo*), where the pronunciation of *piao* is *bìxiào* (必肖反).

"Qilu" (乞縷) refers to the sound of hiring weavers; it denotes silk thread. The *Wenzi jilüe* (Collected Abridgments of Characters) states it means "combined threads. The *Shuowen jiezi* likewise defines it as "thread," phonetically derived from "lou" (婁), with the pronunciation of "xian" (綫) being *si-jian* (思箭反). It is also written as "xian" (線).

"Ván (to sell): the pronunciation is *fàn* (as in *wàn*). Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that those who buy in the morning and sell in the evening are called *vàn*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as buying low and selling high; it is composed of the radical *bèi* (treasure) and the phonetic *fàn*."

"Ji" (擊) in "jilishang jing" (櫪上經) also has the alternative reading "li" (歷). "Jilishi" (擊櫪者) refers to a game played by interlacing the fingers to prick one another; "hu" (互) here is the character "xue" (㸦). "Douluo" (兜羅) is pronounced with the initial "gou" (鈎);
"douluo" is a Sanskrit term for the downy fibers of plants and flowers or cotton (*tūla*). "Zhu" (貯) is pronounced with the initial "zhu" (豬). "Lu" (呂) is the rhyme category.

*Zhe-shou* (磔手): *zhe* is pronounced with a *kao* (考) tone; it means to open wide. One *zhe-shou* refers to the span reached by the five fingers of an outstretched hand, measured from the thumb to the middle finger.

*Ge-xi* (革屣): *xi* is pronounced with a *zi* (滓) tone; the *Kao* commentary states it is a sandal that does not secure the heel. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says *lü* (躧) is also a type of sandal. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* explains that it is composed of the radical *shi* (尸) and the phonetic *tu* (徒); alternatively, it is written as *lü* (躧), *zong* (蹤), *jie* (䩥), or *lao* (𩌦), all of which are archaic characters.

*Chù* (畜): "Bèi" (髲) is pronounced *mèi* (媚); it refers to hair-extensions for the head. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (毛詩傳) states it is a head ornament. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "hairstyle" (*biāo*) and the phonetic "pí.

*Biāo* is pronounced *bìyáo*. *Nì* (績): The first tone is *jī* (積). Gu Yewang says it means to spin hemp or ramie to make cloth. According to the *Shuowen*, "nì" means to sew or spin; it is composed of the radical "silk thread" (*mì*) and the phonetic "zé."
*Fan* (𥿳襵): pronounced with the *zhi* and *lie* finals; it refers to small pleats between the layers of cloth, like the fine pleats on a woman’s skirt.

*Fan-chao* (反抄): pronounced with the *chu* and *jiao* finals; it means to gather or collect. To take up the *kāṣāya* over the shoulder is called *fan-chao*. This is the correct character for "modern" (*jin*) and "ancient" (*gu*), written with the radical for "hand" (*shou*) and the phonetic element *shao*.

In the *Xie shou* (Hand-in-Hand), Huìguī cites Yěwáng, who says that *xié* means "to hold. Hé Xiū’s commentary on the *Gōngyáng Zhuàn* states it is equivalent to "to lift and hold. According to the *Shuōwén*, the character is composed of the radical 手 (hand) and the phonetic 嶲; the pronunciation of 嶲 is as stated above. It is composed of 隹 (bird) and 屮 (grass); its lower part is 冏, whose pronunciation is *nǚ huá*. The common vulgar form, which uses 隹 and 乃, is an error for *xié*. The pronunciation of 屮 is *chǒu liè*.

"不挑調" (bù tiāo diào) refers to the sound of "反考" (fǎn kǎo), which means to wave the hands in a circular motion. Regarding the characters: in both ancient and modern times, the correct character is written with the radical 手 (hand) and the phonetic 兆 (zhào);

"擺" (bǎi) is pronounced *bǔ mǎi*. As for "戲笑" (xì xiào): "戲" (xì) is pronounced *xī* (with the tone of *xī*). The *Erya* states that it means "to joke" (*xié*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains that it is composed of the radical 戈 (spear) and the phonetic 䖒 (xī), where "䖒" is pronounced *xī*. It is incorrect for the vulgar version to write it with the character 虛 (xū).

*Yi* (in *yibō*, "overflowing bowl"): the first character is pronounced as *yin* (one tone). According to the *Erya*, *yi* means "full. Gu Yewang states that *yi* refers to being so full that it overflows. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "the vessel being full," composed of the radical *shui* (water) with *yi* as the phonetic; it is correctly written as *sui*.

"不刳" (bù kū): Kanggū Fǎn and Yě Wáng state that "kū" means to empty its belly. The *Shuowen* says it is composed of the radical "knife" (刀) with "kuā" as the phonetic; "kuā" is pronounced *qiūyú* (丘于反). "不摶飯" (bù tuán fàn):

The *Shēnglèi* states that "tuán" means to grasp or clench. The *Lǐjì* also says there is no "clenching of rice. The *Shuowen* says it is composed of the radical "hand" (手) with "zhuān" as the phonetic. The version in the [present] scripture uses "duān" (耑) instead of "chuǎi" (揣); "chuǎi" is pronounced *chūléi* (初累反), which is not the meaning intended by the scripture.

The *Sifen sengjieben* (Four-Part Monastic Code of Precepts), compiled by the śramaṇa Xuanying. Regarding the character "wuyá" (無崖): it is also written as "yá" (厓), with the same pronunciation as "wǔjiā" (五佳反). According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to the high edge of a riverbank. In other texts, it is written as "yá" (涯), with the pronunciation "yíjiā" (宜佳反); this refers to the shore or bank (*yànsì*). It also means "without limit" (*wúyájì*).

*Shīxià* (失轄): The ancient forms are *qiān* (牽) and *xià* (鎋), both pronounced with the same rhyme as *hú-xiè* (胡瞎). It refers to the iron pin at the end of an axle. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *xià* means a bolt or pin. *Zhéshǒu* (磔手):

The ancient form is *kě* (㡯), pronounced with the same rhyme as *zhī-gé* (知格). According to the *Guangya*, *zhé* means to stretch out; *zhé* means to open wide. As stated in the *Tongshu Wén*: "To stretch and extend is called *zhé*. This is correct.

"Dividing the *máng* (ma bāng fǎn). In the *Gōnggōng Jì* (*Record of the Craftsman*), regarding the *gōng guī* (public jade scepter), it says: 'Use a *máng* [ox]. The commentary states that *máng* refers to an ox; the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as 'an ox with a mixture of white and black hair. The character for *jiè* (precept) is written as *lóng* (dān máo yě), meaning a dog with much hair, as in the *Shijing*: 'Do not let the *lóng* bark.'"

*Fù* (苫) is pronounced *shū yán* (舒鹽); according to the *Erya*, "white cover" is called *shàn* (苫). Li Xun says: "Weaving *jiān* (菅, sacrificial grass) to cover a house is called *shàn*. It is also pronounced *shū yàn* (舒燄); *shàn* likewise means to cover.
*Diao-bi* (dropping the arm): The *Guǎngyá* states that *diao* means to move or shake.
*Xi-fàn* (inhaling while eating): The ancient forms were *xī* and *xi*, now written as *xī*; they share the pronunciation *xūjí*. The *Guǎngyá* states that *xī* and *xī* refer to the entry of breath.

The character *máo* (犛牛)—pronounced with the *jiāo* rhyme—according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, refers to the long-haired ox of the southwestern tribes; this ox is found today in Longxi. The character for "cat" in the *Jieziwen* appears in two forms, *māo* and *māo*; it is the animal kept by people today for catching mice. The term *māo* does not carry the meaning [of the long-haired ox].

The *Sifen Biquni Jieben* (The Four-Part Code of Precepts for Bhikṣuṇīs), compiled by the śramaṇa Xuanying. Regarding the term *menkun* (門閫): it is also written as *menkun* (門梱) with the same pronunciation (*kǔběn*). In the *Liji* (Book of Rites), it states: "External words do not enter within the *kun*. The commentary notes that this refers to the threshold of a door.
*Kē* (the mouth sound is *huà*): According to the *Sāncāng*, it refers to the bone of the buttocks; according to the *Zílín*, it refers to the pelvic bone.
According to the catalog of the Tripitaka, there are two fascicles of the *Four-Part Vinaya Precept Manual with Commentary* (*Hánzhù Sífèn Jièběn*), which have not yet been phonetically annotated.

*The Monastic Code of the Dharmaguptaka School*, one fascicle; also known as the *Dharmaguptaka Prātimokṣa Sūtra*, translated by Buddhayaśas (an incomplete version). *The Prātimokṣa Sūtra*, compiled by the śramaṇa Xuanying. Regarding the character 抪 (pronounced pǔ, with the initial *pú*): in the *Zìshū*, it is written as 抪𢾭; this means to spread out or extend. According to the *Shuowén*, 抪 means "to distribute. Today, both characters are written as 鋪, meaning "to lay out" or "to display."

"Entering the *bie* (蒲米反; *pú mí fǎn*)": according to the *Shuowen*, this refers to ascending a high flight of steps; it is synonymous with *chuáng-bie* (bed-step) or *jié-bie* (stair-step). In the ritual texts, it is written as *bì* (補奚反; *bǔ xī fǎn*), which is a term for a prison and is not used here.
*Qi* (敧) is also written as *qi* (崎), with the phonetic *qiu* and *zhi* reversed; it means to lean or tilt and not be upright.

*Qiao* (蹻), with the phonetic *qiu* and *xiao* reversed, according to the *Shuowen*, means to lift the feet while walking high. The *Hanshu* uses the term *qiaozu* (蹻足); Wen Ying says that *qiao* is synonymous with *qiao* (翹). The *Sancang Jieguo* states that *qiao* means to lift the feet. The *Shiji* writes it as *qiao* (翹), and the *Wen* (文) version writes it as *jiao* (𮠃), with the phonetic *kou* and *diao* reversed; this is a name for a type of grass, and *jiao* does not carry the meaning in this context.
*Nie* (pronounced *niè*, with the radical for "earth" and the phonetic *cāng*) means to knead or press; it is also written as *nie* (*nà*).

*Yùzhì* means to prepare or treat. *Làfó* refers to the sitting of the summer retreat (*là*), and *làbǐng* refers to the ritual cakes offered at the conclusion of the summer retreat on the fifteenth day of the seventh month.

The Ten Precepts for Śrāmaṇeras and Their Deportment, compiled by the Śramaṇa Huilin. Regarding the term *xiǎnfēi* (翾飛): according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "fluttering flight. The *Shuōwén* defines it as the appearance of a small flight, composed of the radical for "feather" (*yǔ*) with the phonetic component *huí* (睘); the pronunciation of *huí* is *kuīyíng*. The classics also write this as *yuán* (蝝) using the radical for "insect"; Guo’s commentary on the *Ěryá* states that it is a red insect found in wells. Because this contradicts the meaning in the present scripture, it is not adopted here.

The character *ruǎn* (蝡) is pronounced with the initial *yǐn* (𨳝尹反). The *Kǎo Shēng* states that "ruǎn-ruǎn" describes the manner of insect movement; this is as stated in the *Huánhuái Zǐ*: "Insects and worms move ruǎn-ruǎn. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "insect" (*chóng*) and the phonetic "ruǎn" (耎), where the pronunciation of "ruǎn" is *rúyuǎn* (如兖反). It is incorrect for the classics to use the character *ruǎn* (蠕) with the radical "grass" (*fǔ*).

*Qíxíng* (蚑行): The upper character is pronounced *qí* (as in *qíwén*) and the lower is pronounced *zhī*. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "the crawling of insects," composed of the radical *chóng* (insect) with the phonetic *zhī*.

*Zhānpàn* (瞻盼): The upper character is pronounced *zhè lián* (懾廉). The *Commentary on the Mao Shi* states that it means "to look. This is the standard orthography for ancient and modern times; it is composed of the radical *mù* (eye) with the phonetic *zhān*. The lower character is pronounced *pǔ huàn*. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lunyu* states that *pàn* refers to the appearance of moving the eyes. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to look askance," composed of the radical *mù* with the phonetic *fēn*. It is incorrect to write this as *chǐ* (𠔃) or *chǐ* (󳇜) in the scriptures.

The character *yàn* (隁) is pronounced with the initial *yāng* (央) and the final *jiàn* (建) reversed; its phonetic component is *tǔ* (土). It refers to a dam (*yàn*) constructed by piling wood and earth to block water. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is written with the phonetic *xì* (系) and the radical *bǐ* (匕), meaning "that which collects water. The *Wenzi Dian* explains it as a dike (*dī*) or an embankment (*pí yàn*). In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, it is written with the radical *fù* (阜) and the phonetic *yàn*; it is also written as *yàn* (堰) with the radical *tǔ* (土) in the scriptures, and these forms are used interchangeably.

"Piàodú" (派瀆): "Piào" is pronounced as in "pǔ-mài-fǎn. The *Guǎngyǎ* states: "When water branches out from itself, it is called a piào. The *Shuōwén* states: "It refers to a lateral or separate flow of water; it is composed of the radical 'water' (氵) and the phonetic 'lǐ' (𠂢). 'Lǐ' is the character for 'eternity' (永); its pronunciation is the same as 'shàng' (上). (Note: The character 𠂢 is a rare variant of 永). The sound of 𠂢 is identical to that of 上.

*Chūpú* (攄蒲): The upper character is pronounced as *chì* (勑) with the phonetic *zhū* (猪). According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, "to spread" (*chū*) means to extend. Regarding the *Lǎozǐ zhì chūpú* (老子制攄蒲), the *Chūpú* is a gambling game involving stakes; it is similar to games such as tossing coins, *qí*, and *lù*. The *Jīngǔ zhèngzì* states that "chū" means "to relax" (*shū*); it is written with the radical for "hand" and the phonetic "lù. Its appearance in the scriptures as *chū* (樗) is a vulgar form.

*Pianwu* (拚舞): "Pi" (皮) is pronounced with the *bian* (變) rhyme. Emperor Ku first caused people to perform *pianwu*. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that joining the hands is called *pian*; the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as clapping the hands (*fushou*), composed of the radical "hand" and the phonetic "bian. The version in the Classics which uses the character for "grasping" (*zhuo*) is incorrect.

*Kěn* (upper radical): *kǎng hěn* (reversed). According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to cultivate" (*chū*). The *Fāngyán* states that in the local dialects, *kěn* refers to the exertion of labor. Regarding the correct orthography of ancient and modern times, it is derived from *kěn* with *shēng* as the phonetic component; the version in the scriptures using *quǎn* (dog) to form *qīn* is incorrect. *Jué* (lower radical): *qún qū* (reversed). The *Kǎoshēng* says it means "to dig through" or "to pierce. Gù Yěwáng says it means "to expose the earth by scraping. The *Shuōwén* states that the character *jué* is composed of the hand radical with *qū* as the phonetic.

Regarding the character 𧶝 (found above the word for *bō*): it is pronounced with the first tone and the rhyme *mòu* (as in *mòuhòu*). Yě Wáng states that 󳎇 means "to trade. According to the *Erya*, 󳎇 means "to sell" or "market. Guō Pǐng’s commentary notes that it is a name for extensive exchange. In the standard characters of past and present, 𧶝 follows the radical 貝 (radical 157) and the phonetic 𡖅. The character 卯 is an ancient form of 丣 (yǒu). It is incorrect for the scripture to use the character 𧴵 instead.

*Guñjī*: The first character is pronounced *jun* (君) and the second is pronounced *chi* (池). It is a Sanskrit term for a water jar. In the sutra, it is written as 鍕𨨲, which is incorrect and does not form a valid character.

*Tiebei* (褺被): The first character, *tie* (褺), has the phonetic *tianjie* (恬頰). The *Wenzi Jilüe* (文字集略) states that *tie* refers to clothes that have been folded or rolled up. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文解字) defines it as "layered clothing" (*chongyi*), formed with the radical for "clothing" (*yi*). The phonetic for *bi* (襞) is *bi* (壁) and for *juan* (捲) is *jué* (厥) with the final *fan* (反). In the sutra, it is written as 襞被, which is incorrect.

Regarding the character *wū* (汚) [in *wū-zàn* (汚濺)]: it is pronounced with the initial *wū* (烏臥反). Gu Yewang states that *wū* means "to mutually defile. The *Guǎngyá* states it means "turbidity. It is also written as *yuān* (宛) or *zào* (𣅍), and these forms are interchangeable. The *Wénzìdiǎn* explains that it is composed of the radical *shuǐ* (water) and the phonetic *yú* (亐), with the final rhyme being *jiān* (見反). The *Kǎoshēng* states it refers to impurity. The *Wénzìdiǎn* further explains that *zàn* (灒) means "splashing"; it is composed of the radical *shuǐ* (water) and the phonetic *jiàn* (賤), with the pronunciation of *zàn* being *zàn*.

"Dǒusù" (抖擻): the first character is pronounced gǒu (苟) and the second sǒu (蘇走). The *Kǎośēng* states that "dǒu" means to raise up; it is composed of the radical "hand" (手) with "dòu" (斗) as the phonetic. "Sù" (擻) is found in the *Guǎngyùn*. The form "jiān" (拺) used in the scriptures is incorrect.

Regarding "tiáo yě" (調譺): the upper character is pronounced *tíng zhào* (庭照) as a compound; Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that "tiáo" means "to harmonize or join together. It is a standard character from ancient times, composed of the radical "speech" (言) and the phonetic "zhōu" (周). The lower character is pronounced *yú jiè* (魚誡); the *Kǎośēng* (考聲) states that "yě" means "deceitful or erroneous speech. The *Shuowén* (說文) records it as being composed of the radical "speech" (言) and the phonetic "yí" (疑).

*Pén* (盆): The first character is pronounced with the *pú* (蒲) radical and the *mén* (門) phonetic. The *Zhouli* states that "the potter makes *pén*; it holds two *fǔ*" (*fǔ* is pronounced with the *fāng* radical and *jǔ* [方矩] phonetic). According to the *Fānyán*, to the west of the Guān region, it is sometimes called *pén*. In ancient and modern standard characters, it follows the *míng* (皿) radical with *fēn* (分) as the phonetic; the second character is pronounced with the *wū* (烏) radical and the *lǎng* (朗) phonetic. Guō’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "The *àng* (盎) is also a *pén*. The *Shuowen* follows the *míng* (皿) radical with *yāng* (央) as the phonetic. In the classics, it is written as *pén* (盆) with the *wǎ* (瓦) radical; *à* (㼜) is likewise a vernacular character.

The character *pān* (潘) is pronounced *yuánfǎn*. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that *pān* refers to rice-water, which can be used for washing the head; dictionaries explain it as the water from rinsing rice, composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic element "bàn" (*fān*), with the latter having the same pronunciation.

*Nòng* (pronounced with the initial *lù* and final *-dòng*) is the sound of *kǎo*; it means to play with or dally with. The Du Commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "to *nòng* someone is to deceive and mock them," which also refers to playful sport. In ancient and modern standard characters, this is written with the radical *廾* (the hands joined) and the phonetic *王*. The pronunciation of *廾* is *xǒng*. Alternatively, it may be written as *梇* with the radical *木*, but this is incorrect. It is an error to follow the hand radical (*手*) and write it as *持* (to hold).

The character 㷮 (top: 畫, early reading *zǎo*; phonetic: 刀) is explained as burning the remaining firewood. In the "Guījīn" (Correct Characters of the Present Age), it is written with 火 (fire) above and 曹 (cáo) as the phonetic below.

The character 甌 (bottom: 於, reading *yú*; phonetic: 鈎) is explained as a small earthenware basin; the meaning is the same as in the *Shuowen Jiezi*, which takes 瓦 (pottery) as the radical and 區 (qū) as the phonetic (the pronunciation of 區 is the same).

*Mào* (upper radical *máo*, *bào* as the phonetic; the *Kǎo Shēng* says *mào* means to pluck). The *Mao Shī* says it means to select. The *Shuōwén* says: "The character *mào* for selecting consists of the radical *cǎo* with *máo* as the phonetic. The [text] uses *fú* from the wood radical (*mù*) to form *fú*, meaning winter vegetables; this is incorrect. Below, *fū* (phonetic *wěn*; the *Guǎngyǎ* says *fàn* means to move). The *Shēnglèi* says it means to strike. The *Wénzìdiǎn* says: "The character *fàn* consists of the radical *shǒu* with *fēn* as the phonetic. The [text] uses *fēn* to form *fèn*; this is also incorrect.

*Die* (上: *chǔ*, 宜 *yí*): The *Guǎngyá* states it means "uneven" (*chāiyuán*). Gu Yewáng says it refers to being "irregular and unequal. The *Shuowén* states that *èichā* (貳差) means "not corresponding," following the radical 辶 (left) and the phonetic 傘 (*sǎn*, pronounced *chuí* [downward] and *tiéjié* [field-section]). Xu Shuchong says *die* means "to fall prostrate. In the seal script it is written as 󳈛; it is interchangeable with 跌.

Regarding the character *dào* (道), when used as a verb it is pronounced *táo* (陶) and *lǎo* (老). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that *dào* means "to explain" (*shuō*); his commentary on the *Liji* states it means "speech" (*yán*). The *Wenzi Dianshuo* states that it takes the radical *shǒu* (首) and the phonetic *chuò* (辵); however, the version of the scripture that uses *rì* (日) to form *tào* (噵) is incorrect.

*Śrāmaṇera-īryāpatha-sūtra*, compiled by the Śramaṇa Xuanying. "Pài" (派) is pronounced *pǔ mài fǎn* (普賣反). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "pài" refers to the divergent flow of water; according to the *Guangya*, it means water branching out from itself.
*Khàn-zàn* (the *zàn* is pronounced as in the dialects of Shandong; in Jiangnan it is pronounced *zàn*, with the second character read as *zǐ-qiè* or *zǐ-chān*):
to wash by hand. *Tiáo-zèi* (the *zèi* is pronounced *wǔ-jìe*): according to the *Tōngsù Wén*, "great *tiáo*" is called *zèi*; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means to deceive or mock.

In the *Cangjie pian*, "pan" (潘) is written as "fan" (藩), both pronounced with the same *fū*/*yuán* rhyme. It means "rice gruel. According to the *Shuowen jiezi*, "pan" refers to the water used for rinsing rice; it is called "gan" (泔) in the north of the Yangtze River and "pan" (潘) in the south of the Yangtze River.
*Jiè* (𡊅): Pronounced with the *fú* and *fén* finals. According to the *Shuowen*, "to sweep away, discard, or remove. The *Guangya* states, "*Jiè* means to remove.

*Jiào*: To sprinkle; also written as *zàn*. Pronounced with the *zǐ* and *dàn* finals. According to the *Shuowen*, "to sprinkle sweat. In the Jiangnan region it is called *jiào*, while in Shandong it is called *zhàn* (󳇵), pronounced with the *zǐ* and *jiàn* finals.

*Śrāmaṇerī-lí-jì* (The Śrāmaṇerī Precepts on Abstinence). Compiled by the Śramaṇa Xuanying. Regarding the term *zhǔ* (蓫): it is a homophone for *fǎn* (反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is a seven-holed reed flute; the Qiang flute has three holes. The text of the precepts writes it as *jiàn* (𮆀), which is incorrect.

The Śrāmaṇerī-śīla-sūtra, compiled by the Śramaṇa Huilin. Regarding the character *shāo* (捎) in *shāofù* (捎拂): In the *Zìshū* (字書), it says: "The wind brushes against the tips of the trees. In the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲), it says: "It means to take up or grasp from above. In the *Fāngyán* (方言), it states: "To the west of the Guān region, taking an object from above is called *qiáo shāo* (橋梢). In the *Guǎngyá* (廣雅), it says: "*Fú* (拂) means to sweep away or remove. In the *Jìxùn* (集訓), it says: "It means to wipe. In the *Shuōwén* (說文), it says: "It means to strike past [something]. It is composed of the radical 'hand' (*shǒu*) and the phonetic 'fú' (*fù*). *Śrāmaṇerī-śīla-sūtra* (沙彌尼戒經). *Śrāmaṇerī-śīla-sūtra*. Compiled by the Śramaṇa Huilin. [Note on the character *shāo* (捎): The *Zìshū* states: "The wind brushes the tree-tips. The *Kǎoshēng* states: "It means to take up from above. The *Fāngyán* states: "West of the Guān pass, taking an object from above is called *qiáo shāo*. The *Guǎngyá* states: "*Fú* means to sweep away. The *Jìxùn* states: "It means to wipe. The *Shuōwén* states: "It means to strike past. It is composed of the radical 'hand' and the phonetic 'fú'."

Lung (fèi): "fēi" is the reversed reading; it is the treasury of metal. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "flesh" (肉) and the phonetic "shi" (市), where "shi" is pronounced like "fèi. The scriptural text uses "fǔ" (脯) instead of "shi," which is incorrect. The character below (liver, gān) is pronounced "gān"; according to the *Shuowen*, it is the treasury of wood.

*Hùn* (圂): On top, the phonetic is *hún* (魂). The *Cāngjié piān* says it is where pigs dwell. The *Shuōwén* says it is a *cè* (廁); it is composed of the radical *kǒu* (口) with the phonetic *yīn* (音), and the character *wéi* (韋) is used as a pictograph; it is also a compound ideograph. Below, the phonetic is *chū* (初) with the tone *zì* (胾). The *Shìmíng* says that *cè* is also *hùn*. The *Shuōwén* says it is a *qīng cè* (圊廁); the phonetic is *zāi* (甾) with the tone *fǎn* (反). It is composed of the radicals *ròu* (肉) and *zào* (𢦏); the phonetic for *zào* is *zāi* (災).

The character *huái* (懷) depicts a state of mind; the radical below is *tái* (台), and the phonetic component is *fǎn* (反). It is pronounced *kǎo* (考). Its meaning is that the intentions change and are not constant. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "constant" (*cháng*) means to maintain one's intentions without alteration. It is composed of the radical *xīn* (心) and the phonetic *néng* (能); the pronunciation of *néng* is *nài* (柰).

The *Kāśyapa-śīla-sūtra*, compiled by the śramaṇa Huilin. **Pòtāng (Cauldron Soup):** "Pò" (鑊) is pronounced with the initial *huáng* and the final *guō*. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it refers to a cauldron (*dǐng*). Examining its phonology, one with legs is called a *dǐng*, while one without legs is called a *pò*. The *Shuowén* defines it as a *xuēi* (鑴), following the radical for metal and the phonetic *wò* (蒦). *Wò* is pronounced *wū yù* (烏䝞反); *xuēi* is pronounced *yíng guī* (熒圭反). *Xuēi* is also a type of cauldron.

Regarding "moustache" (xū): the character above is pronounced *yú* (reversed), and the *Kǎo Shēng* states it means "moustache. The *Shuōwén* correctly writes it as 須 (*xū*), meaning "facial hair," composed of 頁 (*xié*, meaning "head") and 彡 (*shān*, representing the appearance of hair). The current scriptural text uses 䰅 from 髟 (*biāo*), which is also acceptable; it is a character commonly used in vernacular practice. Regarding "hair" (fà) below: the pronunciation is *fán* (reversed as *wè*). The *Shuōwén* defines it as "hair on the crown of the head," composed of 髟 (*biāo*) and the phonetic 犮 (*bài*). It may also be written as 󳊦 from 首 or as 㛲; both are archaic characters. 髟 is pronounced *bì yáo*; 犮 is pronounced *pú wèi*. The character 犮 is composed of 犬 (*quǎn*, "dog") with a mark of 󱫛 (*piān miè*) added to it. The *Kǎo Shēng* states: "The character 須 is pronounced *xū*. It is a word for 'moustache. The *Shuōwén* says: 'It is facial hair. It is composed of 頁, meaning 'head,' and 彡, representing the appearance of hair. The current scriptural text uses 䰅 from 髟, which is also correct. It is a character commonly used in vernacular practice. The character 髮 is pronounced *fán*. It is hair on the top of the head. It is composed of 髟 and the phonetic 犮.
