*Zāohán* is also written as *túhán*; both forms share the same pronunciation, *húnán*. According to the *Fāngyán*, *hán* means "to sink. The character is also written as *zhǔn*, meaning "a boat has sunk.
*Zhuìshā* is also written as *chuí*; they share the same pronunciation, *zhíwèi*. This refers to suspending a heavy object, which is what the *Tōngsūwén* calls "suspending a weight" (*zhuì*).

*Pīngshí gǔwén*: The two characters *pīng* (󳆦) and *shí* (𩊖) share the same pronunciation, which is *bǔgēng* (補耕). They refer to the act of stretching a line or using a compass; that is, to align and measure. *Lěishà* (壘柵):
The first character is pronounced *lìkuǐ* (力癸) and the second *chābái* (叉白). A military fortification is called a *lěi* (壘), while a palisade made of upright wooden stakes is called a *shà* (柵).
At that time, *zè* (pronounced with the *zé* rhyme-group)—where *zè* means to press; it is now called "pressing out juice.
*Chǎn* (also written as *chǎn*, both pronounced *chū yǎn*)—the *Guǎngyá* states it means to shave or pare away; the *Shēnglèi* states it means to level.
12. The Twelfth Fascicle. "Jiā" (夾) [pronounced gǔ qià in the footnotes]: to grasp; according to the *Sāncāng*, it means to assist from both sides.
"Niǎnzhì" (捻置): [pronounced nú jié]; according to the *Tōngsùwén*, to hold with the fingers is called "niǎn"; "niǎn" is also a measure of length.

13. The Thirteenth Fascicle. Regarding "wūliù" (屋霤): it is also written as "liú" (瘤), with the phonetic component read as *jiù* (同力救反). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to water flowing down from a roof. Generally, all instances of water flowing downward are called *liù*. In the Vinaya texts, it is written as "liú" (留), which is not the correct form.
*Channa* (孱那) is the name of a *bhikṣu*; it is pronounced with the second tone on the character *shì* (士).
*Rú* (儒) [is pronounced] *ruì* (䎡) and *jù* (俱); according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "rú" means "gentle" (*róu*), a designation for a scholar of the arts; "ruì" means "weak."

14. Volume Fourteen, Chapter Fourteen. *Yòu* (誘): The ancient forms are *yǒu*, *yǒu*, and *yǒu*; these three characters share the same pronunciation as *yú shǒu* (餘手). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To lead; to draw forth; to instruct; also to exhort. *Yǎo* (󰮔): Pronounced *sī lù* (私律). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To entice. The *Guangya* states: "To talk. The text of the *Lüwen* (律文) writes it as *màn* (唀), which is incorrect. The character written below as *xī* (恤) is not the correct form.
The character *bi* (裨) is also written as *bi* (埤) or *ji* (朇); they share the same pronunciation as *pi-yi* (毗移) or the sound *xi* (𤰞). It means to supplement, to assist, to increase, or to augment.
The character *jiu* (殕) is pronounced *fu-jiu* (敷九); according to the *Guangya*, it means "ruined" (*jue-bai*), and according to the *Picao*, it means "rotten" (*jiu-fu*).

The character for *wēng* (翁) is pronounced with the initial *qīn* (親) and the final rhyme *ān* (安). The feathers atop a bird's head are called *wēng*; because the body’s highest point and the most honored ancestor of a household are both designated as *wēng*, the term is used to convey the sense of being supreme and venerable.
*Xi* (細) and *zhi* (𮉙) are written interchangeably with *zhì* (緻), the latter being pronounced with the *chí* (遲) and *zhì* (致) finals.

It refers to density or compactness. Volume 15, Chapter 15. *Fènglù* (俸祿): *fèng* (俸) is pronounced with the *fú* (扶) and *yòng* (用) finals. According to the commentary, *fèng* means "to bestow. Both grain and money granted as rewards are termed *fèng*. *Lù* (祿) means "blessing" (*fú*). According to the commentary, in ancient times when there was no cultivation or sowing, people ate wild deer. Those who held office were deficient in hunting, so the government bestowed goods upon them in place of the deer they would have caught. Later generations followed this practice and called it "eating deer," which was transformed into *lù* (祿). This was done to capture the sense of divine blessing (*shénfú*).
"Wò" (pronounced with the second tone, as in *wù*) refers to being moistened or soaked; "wò" also means thick or abundant.
"Guīshān" (tortoise-fish) is also written as "guīshàn" or "guīshuān," sharing the same pronunciation. The *Xuànxuǎnzhuàn* states it is a snake-fish.
"Xiāngfǔ" (香莩)—the first character pronounced as *fǔ* with the fanqie *jūfǔ*; the Sanskrit term is *uśīra*, which translates here as "bark" or also "flower.

"Bìndǎng" (摒擋)—the first character pronounced as *zhèng* with the fanqie *fāngzhèng*, and the second as *duō* with the fanqie *làng*; according to the *Tōngsúwén*, to remove objects is called "bìndǎng," meaning to clear away or put in order.
The character for *mùtuó* (木摶) should be written as *tuān* (剸), with the phonetic reading *tú-duān*. "Stuān" means to cut or slice. Regarding *shuǐgū* (水觚), it is read as *gǔhú*;

in the *Lúnyǔ*, regarding the term *gū*, Mǎ Róng stated: "The *gū* is a ritual vessel; one *shēng* is called a *jué*, and two *shēng* is called a *gū*. This is correct. The version in the legal statutes (*lǜwén*) uses the character *gū*, which is incorrect.

"Jian" (謇) [with the radical for "mouth" and the phonetic "ju" (居), reversed; the second character "chi" (吃) has the phonetic "ju" (居), reversed]. In common vernacular speech, that which is not fluent is called "jian-chi" (謇吃). The legal texts employ two forms, "jian" (謇) and "jian" (蹇), but these are incorrect.

16. Volume Sixteen. Regarding "ji-mi" (穄米): according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "ji" (穄) resembles *shu* (黍) millet but is not sticky; those in the region west of the Pass call it "mi" (糜). This is what is meant here.
*Wù nǎo*: "Nǎo" is pronounced with the *gāo* rhyme; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means "to disturb. It refers to stirring up or agitating.
*Líáo*: Pronounced with the *lì tiáo* rhyme; it means "to toss" or "to throw. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means "to arrange" or "to manage.
*Fù luó*: Sometimes written as *fú luó* or said to be *fù luó*; the correct pronunciation is *bù luó*. This is translated as "short-calf boots."

Regarding the term *cáng* (傖): the *Jin yangqiu* (晉陽秋) states that the people of Wu who served the Central Kingdom were called *cáng*. Furthermore, according to common custom, those from between the Yangtze and Huai rivers who were mixed with people of Chu were also collectively termed *cáng*.
*Juan die* (the character *die* is pronounced with the *tu* and *jie* finals): it means to fold or pleat; according to the *Zilin*, it refers to double-layered clothing.

*Liu* (the character is pronounced with the *li* and *zhou* finals): the *Shuowen* defines it as a swelling; the *Shenglei* defines it as a fleshy protuberance (*xirou*), referring to a mass that has swollen and knotted but does not suppurate or disperse.
"Tièluò" (鐵烙), with the second character pronounced as *lì* (力各反), refers to burning iron and applying it to an object; the version in the Vinaya texts written as "cuò" (錯) is incorrect.

17. Volume Seventeen, Part Two: "Dìng" (矴), with the second character pronounced as *dìng* (都定反), refers to the stone placed under a pillar; the version in the Sūtra texts written as "dì" (磸) is merely a phonetic approximation.
"Nà-sōu" (pronounced with the "fǎn" [classifier] for foreign medicinal names).

"Zǐ" (now written as "ruó," pronounced with the "rǔ-shuí" rhyme) refers to a medicinal herb; its seed-kernel can treat the eyes. The character is composed of "shēng" (two hands) above and "shǐ" (pig) as the phonetic component.
*Ping*: (píng, bīng, fǎn; *Erya*: "The small is *ping*, the large is *ping*"; the commentary says it is floating duckweed in the water).
Volume 18, Chapter 18. *Xiang*: (xiāng, qiè, sī, yáng, fǎn; below: kǔ, xié, fǎn). A *xiang* refers to a container for clothing.
*Zhǐzhí* (指挃): Pronounced *mǎo lì fǎn*. According to the *Guǎngyǐ*, *zhǐ* means to prick or poke; it refers to touching another person with one's fingers.

*Buddhābhidharma-śāstra* (*Fó āpítán lùn*), Volume One, compiled by Xuanying. *Shēng'è* (生萼): Also written as *léng* (楞), pronounced *tóng wǔ gè fǎn*. That which supports a flower is called a calyx (*è*).

2. Lower Fascicle. "Eunuch" (yán): pronounced as in *jiǎn* (儉). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, a eunuch (*yán*) is one who blocks the gates within the palace; it refers to one whose vital essence (*jīngqì*) is closed and concealed. The *Zhouli* states there were ten eunuchs; Zheng Xuan commented that a eunuch is one whose vital essence is sealed away, now called a *shāngrén* (阉人). Because they are in charge of closing doors and gates, they are called "gatekeepers" (*guān*).

*Œi*: *bù* (not), *nú* (slave), *huí* (return); *nú* and *hé* (harmony) are the two reversed [readings]. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To *Œi* means to crush; it refers to the rubbing of both hands together. *Mén*: *shēn* (body), *wú* (without), *fēn* (division);

it means that when silk has patterns, it is called *mén*. *Wén* (pattern) is written as *wén*; the ancient form is written as *zǎo*. When blue and red combine, they form a pattern. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "It is a variegated drawing."
The character 㾨 (pronounced jiě) is defined in the *Guǎngyá* as "dwarfed" (*cuó*).

The term 氣𠲿 should be read as 欬瘶 (*kài sòu*). *Kài* is pronounced *kù dài*; this pronunciation is current in Jiangnan, while in Shandong it is pronounced *qiū jì*. The lower character, 瘶, is pronounced *sòu* (*sū dòu*). According to the *Shuōwén*, "瘶 is upward-moving qi; it is a disease of the upper breath. The *Cāngjiépiān* states that in the Qi region, 瘶 is called 欬. The version in the *Lùnwén* writes it as 氣, which is incorrect.
*Ku-jian* (枯癎): The character *jian* (癎) refers to a reverse sound; it is what is currently called "childish epilepsy" (*dian*). *Xue-tong* (血痛):

This should be written as *lou* (瘻), with the phonetic value of *lou* (漏); it belongs to the category of abscesses (*yong*). The various types of worms within the body are found everywhere, including the armpits and hidden areas. Alternatively, it may be written as *lou-xue* (漏血), meaning blood leaking like water.
*Yīn-tuí* (陰頹): "Túi" is pronounced as *tú léi fǎn*. According to the *Shìmíng* (釋名), swelling of the limbs is called *tuí*; the *Zílín* (字林) writes this as *ài* (㾽), meaning a severe illness.

*Zhǒng* (尰): also written as *zhòng* (瘇), pronounced as *zhǐ lǒng fǎn*. The *Erya* states that swelling of the feet is called *zhǒng*. This disease is extremely prevalent today in Bāshǔ; those who have it in their arms and hands are also called *zhǒng*.
"Liu" (瘤) [with the initial *li* and final *-pi* reversed]: according to the *Shuowen*, it means a tumor or swelling; according to the *Shenglei*, it refers to a fleshy protuberance (*xīròu*).
"Yue" (噦) [pronounced *yūè*]: according to the *Tongsu Wen*, the upward reversal of qi is called *yue*; according to the *Shuowen*, *yue* is the belching of qi.

*Maoróng* (毛冗): The character *rǒng* is pronounced as *yǒng* (勇) with a reversed tone; it means "scattered. It should be written as *máoróng* (𦶇), pronounced *ér* (而) with a reversed tone, referring to the hanging fleece of *gǔbèi* (古貝, cotton). *Chuì* (毳) refers to a decorative fur trim. *Vinaya-vibhaṅga*, Volume 1–2.

Regarding the first and second volumes of the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga*, the initial characters were not previously transcribed with phonetic annotations. Volume 3. *Chuòzhù* (銼󲼙): The upper character is pronounced *cái gē* (才戈) and the lower character *cái lù* (才鹿) with a reversed tone, followed by *lì gē* (力戈). According to the *Shēnglèi* (聲類), this refers to a small cauldron, or a clay cauldron. It is also called *wǔyù* (鎢錥), pronounced *wū yù* (烏育).

The character *xiàngbá* (相跋) is written as *biàn* (󱄉) in the *Shuowen Jiezi*, with the same pronunciation as *bǔmò* (補末). It means to step upon; *lì* (躐) means to tread upon, pronounced *lìshè* (力涉). *Póhàn* (掊汗) is pronounced *pújiāo* (蒲交);

the *Tōngsùwén* states that holding something with the hand is called *póu* (掊), and the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines *póu* as grasping. In the Vinaya texts it is written as *páo* (刨), which is a modernized form of the character.
The three characters *sì* (俟), *jì* (竢), and *dài* (𥏳) share the same meaning; according to the *Erya*, *sì* means "to wait.

*Zhé* (讁), pronounced with the initial *k* and final *-i* (阿知革反), is defined in the *Fangyan* as "anger"; Guo Pu states it refers to mutual reproach and anger. *Zhé* also means "reproach," "reprimand" (*qiàn*), "rebuke" (*hē*), and "accusation."

4. Fourth Fascicle. "Zhe" (哲) is also written as "Zhe" (悊) or "Zhi" (喆); these two characters are identical in meaning and pronounced with the *qie* (反切) *zhì liè*. According to the *Erya*, "zhe" means wisdom (*zhì*). According to the *Fangyan*, in the region between Qi and Song, wisdom is called "zhe," meaning clarity and lucidity.
Regarding "fu" (傅): its meaning is primarily to apply or adhere; it refers to coating or attaching. This is as seen in the *Hànshū*, where it says "all applied rouge and powder. Regarding "huò" (鐴):
according to the *Běicāng*, it is pronounced with the initial *chì* (赤) and final *fǎn* (反); it refers to the large ears of a plow.
*Chui* (䘢) is also written as *chu* (褚), with the same pronunciation as *zhi* (知) and *shao* (󱲢). According to the *Tongsu Wen* (通俗文), "to dress" is called *chui*.

*Lu* (漉) or *lu* (淥)—with the same pronunciation as *li* (力) and *shui* (水)—is a term for the appearance of water; it means to strain or filter. In the Vinaya texts (*Lüwen*), it is written as *lü* (濾), which is a modernized character.

*Fēn* (思流反; also written as *fēn*, 府云反): According to dictionaries, this refers to steaming rice. The *Guǎngyá* states that *fēn* is called *fēn*; the *Éryá* says *fēn* means *rěn* (to ripen) and is also *liù* (to boil thoroughly).

5. Fascicle Five. "Ke" (刻) and "Lou" (鏤): Ke is pronounced ken (肯) with a reversed final; according to the *Erya*, it refers to water. The commentary states it is a term for treating raw jade. According to the *Guangya*, it means to engrave. Lou is pronounced li (力) with a final dou (鬪); according to the *Erya*, it refers to metal. Lou is carving.

*Tongkui* (銅魁)—the character *teng* (苫) is pronounced with the *hui* (迴) tone; according to the *Shuowen*, it means a ladle for soup. The forms *zhu* (󳄻) and *xuan* (鐦) found in the Vinaya texts are both incorrect.

*Zhushu* (燭樹)—the character *shu* (樹) is pronounced with the *zhi* (時) tone; "tree" here means "to stand. The variant *ju* (竪)—pronounced with the *shu* (殊) and *sou* (廋) tones—is also correct; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "to stand upright. Both readings are acceptable.

*Gǎn* (with the ancient pronunciation *gǔdǎn*): according to the *Sāncāng*, it means "to act with certainty" or "to do something without fear. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "courageous," "to dare to offend," and also "to advance," referring to mutual competition.
*Qi* (䞈): In ancient script it was written as *ji* (𧵥), with the same pronunciation as *ji* (几). According to the *Guǎngyá*, *qi* means "to gamble"; to wager an object is called *qi*. *Zhi* (𢐙):

In Sanskrit it is called *iṣu*, which in this [Chinese] language means "arrow. It is now written as *zhi* (𢐙), with the ancient pronunciation *hòu*. According to the *Shuōwén*, it refers to drawing a crossbow.
*Kuì* (饋): An archaic form of *kuì* (餽); according to the *Shuōwén*, it means "to provide food. To present items to one's superior is also called *kuì*; it is also the name of a sacrificial rite.
Volume Six, Part Six. *Línshuǐ* (淋水): An archaic form of *lì* (瀶); according to the *Zílín*, it means to drench with water or to pour water over.
The master further notes that "fàn" (範) shares the same pronunciation as "fàn" (范). According to the *Erya*, "fàn" means "law" (*fǎ*) and "constancy" (*cháng*).

The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "sāo" (搔) means to scrape; it also means to scratch. The character below is pronounced *mó* (亡各反). According to the *Fangyan*, "mó" means to stroke or caress; it is the same as "mōbǎi" (摸𢱢). In legal texts, it is written as "lāo" (撈), pronounced *lì gāo* (力高反); according to the *Fangyan*, this means to hook and take up. However, "lāo" does not carry this meaning here.

"Xi" (欱) is pronounced as *huó* (合反). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "xi" means to sip or to gulp down; it also means to draw together. In the *Wenzi*, it is written as "ha" (哈), pronounced as *tǔ* (土) and *hé* (合) combined; "ha" refers to suddenly losing one's composure. Lexicons state this character is identical to "dan" (啗), pronounced as *tú* (徒) and *lán* (濫) combined, but neither of these meanings applies here.
*Qī* (欹) is also written as *qí* (𢻪), *qí* (崎), or *zhì* (㩻); these three forms share the same pronunciation, *qiūzhī* (丘知). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states:

"Qīyū" (欹䧢) means uneven and unstable. 7. The seventh fascicle. The character *pǐ* (柿) is pronounced *fù* (敷) with the *fèi* (癈) rhyme. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Xiāopǔ" (削朴) means to plane or shave; *pǔ* (朴) refers to slips of wood, meaning to shave off the bark of wood.
8. Volume Eight. *Tǐzhū* (also written as *tízhè*) is pronounced with the same radical and the phonetic *zhīlù* (知錄). It refers to the formation of sores on the hands or feet due to cold.

*Lí* (籬) is also written as *luó* (攡) or *tuō* (拖), sharing the same radical and the phonetic *tǐlìzhī* (體力支). The *Tōngsúwén* states that a fence made of brushwood is called a *lí*; the *Shìmíng* says it is so named because it is constructed from brushwood, appearing sparse and separated (*shūlílí*).

*Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, Volumes 1–2 (Volumes One and Two). First and Second [Volumes]. Regarding the character *xiàn* (先): it is not pronounced as *yīn* (音). Third Volume. Compiled by Xuanying. The character *fā* (發) is pronounced with the *fǔ* and *yuè* finals; it means "to trigger" (*jīfā*). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to discharge an arrow. According to the *Guoyá*, it means "to raise up. In the Vinaya texts, it is written as *bō* (撥), pronounced with the *bǔ* and *mò* finals; it means "to sweep away" (*bōchú*) or "to remove" (*bōqù*). In this context, it does not carry the meaning of "to refute" (*bōfēi*).

"Piao" (pronounced yao-fan) means the appearance of flying upward; "piao" is like blowing, meaning light and fluttering. In the ritual texts it is written as "piao" (pronounced fang-zhao-fan), which refers to the color of a horse; this [character] "piao" is not used here.
*Pāyana* is the Sanskrit term; it is translated here as "surrounding corridor" or "courtyard.
*Tsi* (pronounced with the *du* and *ge* finals reversed) is from the *Cangjie pian*, meaning "to take. Volume Four, Part Four:

"Gradually staining" (*jianran*)—sometimes written as *jia* with the same pronunciation as *zi* and *lian*—is defined in the *Guangya* as "soaking," "moistening," or "mutually staining and defiling. This is like the account in the *Book of the Later Han* regarding Mozi weeping over white silk, noting that its nature is easily stained by gradual soaking. The scriptural text uses the character *mao* (𮉼), but this character is not used in this context.
*Xū* (also written as *chù*, same pronunciation; *chǐ* with the sixth tone) means "to store" or "to accumulate," according to the *Cāngjié piān*.
*Jiǎ zhòu* (ancient form: *zòu*; same pronunciation; *chú jiù* with the fourth tone) refers to armor or a helmet, according to the *Zílín*. Its appearance in the Vinaya texts as *yōu* is incorrect.
*Dàbàng* (大棒) is also written as *bàng* (棓), with the phonetic *pú* and *jiǎng* (蒲講反). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, a *bàng* is a large staff.
*Yīguǎn* (一丳) has the initial *chū* and the eye-rhyme *yǎn* (初眼反); it refers to the "meat skewers" (*guǎn*) commonly seen today.
"Camel-hair" (tuómáo): "Dàhé" (大河) is a reversal of the character for "camel" (tuó). The Vinaya texts write it with the character for "horse" (mǎ), which is not the correct form.
"Black ram" (gūyáng): "Gōnghù" (公戶) is the phonetic reading; it is also called a "castrated ram" (jiéyáng). According to the *Sāncāng*, it is the "gūlù" (羖䍽).

*Ghaṇṭī* (the "qianzhi" in the current text; the old translations mostly render it as *qianchi*). The Sanskrit term is *bherī-ghaṇṭā*. *Bherī* here means "to strike. The wooden block struck is made either of sandalwood or paulownia wood. There is no direct equivalent for this term because [in India] there were no bells or chimes (*zhongqing*). The frequent rendering of it as *qianzhui* in current sutras and vinayas is an error.

Volume Five. [Note on "Xianbu" (先不): This is not the correct pronunciation. Volume Six. Regarding "Luolai" (羅艻): "Lai" is pronounced with the initial *l* and the final *-ang* (as in the rhyme for "lang"). It refers to coriander (*cuminum cyminum*). In common parlance, it was renamed "Luoxiang" (羅香) to avoid the taboo name of Shi Le (石勒). The version in the Vinaya texts written as "Le" (勒) is not the standard form.

"Húsu" is also written as "suī," and the *Yuanyuan* (Garden of Characters) writes it as "qí," all with the same pronunciation as "sīguī. The *Yunlüe* (Brief on Rhymes) states that "húsuí" is fragrant coriander (*cuminum cyminum*). The *Bowuzhi* (Treatise on the Wonders of Nature) says that Zhang Qian obtained "húsuí" while on an embassy to the Western Regions; today in Jiangnan it is called "húqí," and it is also written as "húlí," pronounced "húxī," though in local dialects it is pronounced "huogū."

7. Seventh Fascicle. *Tittibha* (transcribed as *tuo-chun*, with *chun* pronounced like *zhua* and *gua*). According to the *Erya*: "The *tittibha* is a type of pheasant. Guo Pu says: "It is as large as a pigeon and resembles a female pheasant; it has webbed feet and a forked tail. As a bird, it is dull-witted and flighty, flying in flocks from the northern desert regions. It is commonly called the 'Turkic sparrow' (*tu-jue-que*). The character for 'dull-witted' (*han*) is pronounced like *hu-lan*."
"Chāngkuáng" (猖狂) means to act recklessly; it is also used to mean "madness. *Zhuangzi* says, "To act with reckless abandon is like the behavior of a concubine.

This is correct. Volume Eight, Part Eight. "Yáqí" (牙旗): "Qú" is pronounced as "jī" (渠基反). A "bear-and-tiger banner" (*xiónghù qí*) is so named because its teeth are carved as ornaments upon the flag. The *Lunwen* (論文) reads it as "wèi" (衛), with the phonetic gloss "niú xū" (牛墟反). It describes a manner of movement. It is also written as "wèi yú," "jiā yú," or "jǔ" (魚家魚舉二反). It is also the name of a commandery (*fényì xiàn*) in the region of Fényì. All eight of these characters are used here.

9. The Ninth Fascicle. "Ant-hill" (yì fēng): *fēng* is pronounced *fú* with a retroflex final; it refers to the piling up of earth to increase height. It also implies thickness, as in the term for boundaries (*jīng jiè*).
"Not eating" (bù chī) refers to the opposite of eating;
it is also called "chewing" (chī dàn). To "chew" (jiào) is glossed as "to consume" (jué rú) in the *Guǎngyá*, and as "to masticate" (zǔ) in the *Zìshū*;

it is also synonymous with "gnawing" (jiào jiào). According to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* (Míngliǎo lùn), Xuànyìng’s commentary states that "both" (biàn qǐ) is also written as "together" (bìng tóng); in the *Ěrshì yǐpǐ*, "both" (bìng) is glossed as "combined" (bèng), with the pronunciation being *pú míng*.

*Poṣadha*, or alternatively *puṣadha*, is translated here as "increase" (*zēngzhǎng*). This refers to the fortnightly *kṣamaṇā* (confession), which increases the roots of one's precepts. *Kṣamaṇā* is translated as "patience" (*rěn*), meaning to tolerate and forgive my transgressions. The old name, "chàn" (repentance), is a corruption and abbreviation.

The characters *chuiqiang* (攡牆) are also written as *litiuo* (籬拖); they share the same pronunciation, which is *li* with the second tone (*zhī*). According to the *Tōngsúwén*, a fence made of brushwood is called a *zì*. The *Shìmíng* states that it is constructed from brushwood, appearing sparse and separated.
*Yiqiejing yinyi*, Scroll Sixty-five and Scroll Sixty-six.
*Xiaocheng lun yin*: Compiled by the Śramaṇa Huilin, who translated the scriptures.
*Abhidharma-aṣṭagranthaka-śāstra*, thirty fascicles—Yin; *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, twenty fascicles—Xuan; *Dharmaskandha-pāda-śāstra*, twelve fascicles—Lin;

*Saṃgītiparyāya-pāda-śāstra*, twenty fascicles (upper volume, ten fascicles—Lin; lower volume, first fascicle—Yin); the subsequent fascicles are by Yin. These four treatises, totaling eighty-two fascicles, share the same phonetic attribution as this present volume.

*Abhidharma-aṣṭagranthaka-śāstra*, Fascicle One, compiled by the Śramaṇa Xuanying. 1. First Fascicle. *Khandha* (also transliterated as *varga*) is translated here as "section" (*bu*); it is also another name for a "chapter" (*pin*).
*Śloka* is also called *ślokaka* or *ślokaka*; in Indian numerical treatises, thirty-two syllables constitute one *ślokaka*, which is also termed a *gāthā*, that is, a single verse.

2. Second Fascicle, Part Two (the character "xian" [先] is not pronounced). 3. Third Fascicle, Part Three: *tántiè* (貪餮), also written as *tiān* (飻), with the same pronunciation as *tā jié* (他結反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *cān* (餐) means to greedily eat. In the treatise (*Lun*), it is sometimes written as *tāo* (饕), pronounced *tā láo* (他勞反). Du’s commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan* says: "To covet wealth is called *tāo*; to covet food is called *tiè*."

Volumes 4–16: Volumes four through sixteen—volumes four, five, six, up to sixteen—are all previously unpronounced [in this recension]. Volume 17: Volume seventeen. The characters *hù* (戶) and *fǎn* (𨷲) are archaic forms of *yào* (鑰). They share the same pronunciation as *yúzuó* (余酌). According to local dialects, those in the region east of the Pass call it *jiàn* (鍵), while those west of the Pass call it *fǎn* (𨷲).

The ancient texts write "zhēn" (箴) for both "needle" (針) and "admonition" (箴). Today it is written as "zhēn" (鍼), with the phonetic transcription *zhī-chén* (支諶反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "that which is used for sewing clothes.

Regarding the character "yí" (羠): its pronunciation is *yí* (夷). The *Shenglèi* states that it refers to a castrated ram (*shéng yáng*). Xù Guǎng says that "jié-yí" (羯羠) refers to a fierce and robust ram. The pronunciation of "shéng" (騬) is *shí-líng* (食陵反).
*Mao-niu* (犛牛): The character *mao* is pronounced as *bao* (包) with a reversed [radical]. It refers to the long-haired ox of the southwestern tribes.

The version in the *Lunwen* (論文) writes it as *miao* (猫), which is incorrect. Volumes 18 through 27: From the eighteenth volume down to the twenty-seventh, totaling ten volumes, all previously lacked phonetic glosses. Volume 28: Regarding the character *ti* (替) in Volume 28, it is pronounced as *ji* (計) with a reversed [radical]. According to the *Erya*, "ti" means "to abandon" (*fei*) or "to extinguish" (*mie*). It refers to the act of extinction. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *pu* (暜), stating that when two [strokes] stand side-by-side and one is removed from below, it is called "ti."

29. Fascicle Twenty-nine. *Lè-dǎng* (樂戇): "Dǎng" is pronounced with the second tone, *gōng* (二反); according to the *Zìlín* (字林), it means "foolish. It refers to being greedy for and craving flavors, becoming attached to them without satiety—like a camel eating honey while in the midst of suffering. In the new translations of the sutras and treatises, this is translated as *dānshì* (躭嗜), which is precisely this meaning.

30. Fascicle Thirty. [The character for] *bùrěng* (barren): the ancient script is the same as the remainder; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "to carry a child. According to the *Guangya*, it means "to conceive. To contain a fruit within is called *yùn* (conception).
*Tūyuán* (pronounced *yuán*): According to the *Sāncāng*, a red horse with a white belly is called a *yuán*.
*Sānlǚ*: Also written as *fù* or *shū*, both pronounced *wǔkǒu*; it is the name for a spring. According to the character, it refers to the root of the *fúróng* (lotus).

Regarding the term "Wujiao" (無焦): Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Jiangfu* states that the Great Abyss (*Dahu*) lies beyond the eastern sea, and Wujiao is the place where the waters of its source discharge. Here, it is taken to signify the inexhaustible and the infinite.

*Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, Fascicle 1. Fascicle One of the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*. Compiled by the Śramaṇa Huilin. Regarding "uṣmagata" (煖): according to the *Guǎngyǎ*, "uṣman" means warmth; according to the *Éryǎ*, it means heat. The *Shuōwén* writes it as 煖 (*nuǎn*), derived from the radical for fire and the phonetic *yuán*. It is also written as 㬉; nowadays, "nuǎn" is used universally. The version in this treatise uses 𤏙 with the pronunciation *rénzhū* (而珠反), which is incorrect.

Regarding the character for *yān* (smoke/flame): in the *Zìshū* (Dictionary of Characters), it is correctly written with the radical *yīn* (垔). In the *Lùn-wén* (Treatise on Literature), it is written with the radical *yīn* (因), which is a vulgar usage. The *Cāngjié piān* states: "Smoke is *yūn* (熅). The *Guǎngyá* states: "It is odor. The *Guóyǔ* states: "The smoke of the burning reaches upward. The *Shuōwén* states: "It is the vapor of fire; it takes the radical *huǒ* (fire) and the phonetic *yīn* (垔); the pronunciation of *yūn* is *mù yún* (慍雲反), and the pronunciation of *yīn* is *yī rén* (一人反), while the following [character] is *yán qiàn* (閻塹反). Examining the *Zìshū*, it is correctly written with the radical *yán* (炎) as *yàn* (燄). In the *Lùn-wén*, it is written as *yàn* (焰), which is a vulgar usage. Kong’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* states: "It is like fire burning; *yànyàn* (焰焰) refers to when it is still slight and what it reaches. The *Zìshū* states: "*Yàn* is the flame of fire. The *Shuōwén* states: "It is the subtle flame of fire moving; it takes the radical *yán* (炎) and the phonetic *xiàn* (臽); the pronunciation of *xiàn* is *biǎo* (𨺂)."

*Kalala* (the first term is pronounced with the initial *jian* [jiǎn] and the final *lan* [lán]; it is a Sanskrit term) refers to the name for the initial reception of the vital essence (*śukra-śoṇita*) at conception.
*Arbuda* (the initial syllable is pronounced *an* [ān] and *ge* [gě]; it is also a Sanskrit term) refers to the gradual transformation of that aforementioned embryonic mass.
*Piśācakaṇṭhana*: *kaṇṭha* is pronounced with the *qian* rhyme (its *yan* radical) and is also a Sanskrit term.
*Araṇa*: the second character, *nuo*, has the *jia* rhyme; in Sanskrit it is the name of a dragon king (*nāgarāja*).

**Volume Two** *Qingjie* (Light and Agile): the second character, *qian*, has the *ye* rhyme. The *Kaozheng* states that "agile" means robust and swift. The *Shichuan* says "agile" means to conquer. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* says it means to overcome, and elsewhere says it means to accomplish. The *Shuowen* says it means to seize; it refers to capturing in battle. It is composed of the radical "hand" and the phonetic "die. *Lan* is pronounced with the *zha* rhyme, and *die* has the same pronunciation as above.

*Jiè* (to split/saw): The upper character is pronounced *jū* (with the *yù* rhyme). The *Huáinánzǐ* states: "A skilled craftsman cannot [split] wood that can be cut with a saw. The *Guóyuè* states: "Punishments employ knives and saws. The *Shuōwén* states: "It means *qiāngtáng* (to split open); it is composed of the radical 金 (*jīn*) and the phonetic 居 (*jū*). The lower character is pronounced *xiè*. Jia Dui’s commentary on the *Guóyuè* says: "To split and pare. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Fāngyán* says: "To shed/peel off. The *Guǎngyá* says: "To disperse. The *Shuōwén* says: "To divide; it is composed of the radical 刀 (*dāo*) and depicts cutting apart the horns of an ox."

"Qingzào" (輕躁): "Zào" is pronounced as *sāo* (喿) and *dào* (到). Gu Yewang states that *zào* means "to move. Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* says it means "to disturb. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lunyu* says it means "not being at peace. This is the correct character for ancient and modern times; it is composed of the radical "foot" (*zú*) and the phonetic "quack" (*sāo*).

*Jiāozhē* (焦灼): The upper character is pronounced *jiǎo* (遙反). The *Guǎngyǎ* states that it means "blackened by fire. Zheng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* says it refers to smoke within the fire; it also says it is the "odor of fire. The *Shuōwén* says it is "that which is burned by fire. In ancient script it was written as *jiū* (𤓪), now abbreviated to *jiāo*. Its use in the *Lùn* (論) as *jiāo* (燋) is incorrect. Regarding the lower character *zhē* (灼), the *Kǎoshēng* says it means "to burn. The *Fāngyán* says it means "to startle. The *Cāngjiépiān* says it means "to crackle. The *Wenzídiǎnshuō* says it means "to roast" or "to heat a tortoise shell for divination. It is composed of the radical "fire" and the phonetic "shuó" (勺); *zhào* (爆) is pronounced *bāo* (皃反).

The character *mèng* (𧄼瞢) is pronounced with the upper radical *téng* (隥, *dèng*) and the lower radical *mò* (墨, *méng*), both in the departing tone. The *Zìkǎo* states that *lèngmèng* (𧀧𧄼) describes the appearance of one who has just risen from sleep; *lèng* is pronounced *léng* (稜, *léng*). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* says *lèngmèng* means "stupefaction. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* says *lèngmèng* means "dimness of vision. Both characters are formed by combining the abbreviated form of *mèng* (夢) with *dēng* (登) and *mù* (目), which serve as their phonetic components.

*Tāotiè* (饕餮): the first character is pronounced *tǎo* (with the radical *dǎo*) and the second is *tiē* (with the radical *tiān-dié*). The preceding section, *Fǔlù* (部律), Volume 50, has already been explained. *Tángchuò* (甞啜): the first character is pronounced *shàng zhāng* (尚章). In the *Zìshū* (字書), it is correctly written with the radical *zhǐ* (旨) as *táng* (甞).

The treatise states that writing it with the radical *kǒu* (口) as *chì* (𭋌) is incorrect. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) says: "To taste for delicacy. Gù Yěwáng says: "To taste the flavors within the mouth. The *Báihūtōng* (白虎通) says: "It refers to tasting new grain. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* (文字典說) says: "A name for the autumn sacrifice; it takes *zhǐ* (旨) as the semantic component and *shàng* (尚) as the phonetic component. The second character, *chuò* (啜), is pronounced *xià chuān yào* (下川𤑔). In the *Zìshū*, it is correctly written with the radical *qiàn* (欠) as *chuò* (歠), which is its standard form. The treatise states that writing it with the radical *kǒu* (口) as *chuò* (啜) is a vulgar usage. The *Guǎngyǎ* (廣雅) says: "To eat by sipping. The *Ěryǎ* (爾雅) says: "To chew. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* says: "To taste food; it takes *kǒu* (口) as the semantic component and *zhuó* (叕) as the phonetic component. The pronunciation of *zhuó* is *shāoluè* (𠳤劣)."

3. Third Fascicle, Part Three. Regarding "yè" (軶): it is pronounced with the initial *ying* (鶯) and the final *gé* (格). The *Lunwen* (論文) records it as "yè," which is a vernacular character. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Kaogongji* states: "It refers to the wooden block at the front of the axle that presses down upon the neck of the ox. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "'Yè' is the wooden part at the front of a carriage's axle; it is composed of the radical 'che' (車) and the phonetic 'é' (戹), the pronunciation of which is the same as above."

4. Fourth Fascicle. Regarding "pùliú" (torrential flow): according to the *Cāngjié piān*, it means "to soak. The *Wénzì diǎn* states it refers to the rapid swelling of river waters. The *Shuōwén* says it means "heavy rain," composed of the radical "water" and the phonetic "pù"; the pronunciation of "pù" is as stated above.

Volume Five, Part Five: *Diaoju* (掉舉). [The character] is pronounced with the upper radical *diao* (弔) and the lower radical *ju* (舉). Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states: "To diao is to shake. The *Guoya* states: "To vibrate. The *Chunqiu Zhuan* states: "A tail that is too large cannot be shaken (*bu diao*). The *Wenzi Dianshuo* states: "To vibrate and signal. It is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "zhuo" (卓); the sound of *xun* (訊) is like *xin* (信). The lower part of the character *ju* (舉) consists of the radical "hand" (手).

6. Sixth Fascicle. Regarding "stupefaction" (昏沈): "Hun" is pronounced with the initial *kūn* (反) in the upper tone. Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states: "It means confusion. Zheng’s sub-commentary on the *Shijing* states: "'Childish stupefaction' refers to having no knowledge. The *Guoyaya* states: "It means folly. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "It means lack of clarity or discernment (*liao*). It is composed of the radical 'heart' (*xin*) and the phonetic 'hun. *Liao* is pronounced like *liao* (了); *hun* has the same pronunciation as above. For "deep" (沈), the pronunciation is *zhí-lín* (反) in the lower tone.

7. Seventh Fascicle. [No characters to be transcribed. 8. Eighth Fascicle. *Chen-yì* (塵瞖): The lower radical is *ī* (伊) with the tone *jì* (計). The *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲) states it is a disease of the eyes. The *Zìshū* (字書) states it is a cataract (*zhàngmù*) of the eyes. The *Zílín* (字林) also identifies it as a disease of the eyes. According to the character *yì* (瞖), it refers to an obstruction of the eye that prevents one from seeing. It is composed of the radical "eye" (*mù*) and the phonetic component *ē* (殹); the pronunciation of *ē* is the same as above.

9–10. Fascicle Nine through Fascicle Ten. Fascicle Nine and Fascicle Ten contain no characters that require phonetic transcription. 11. Fascicle Eleven. *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, Fascicle Eleven. *Hui* (穢): The upper radical is *wei* (萎, pronounced *wei*). The *Zishu* states: "Hui means overgrown weeds. Gu Yewang says: "Hui refers to that which is not clean or pure; it is evil. The *Wenzidian* explains: "Hui refers to weedy grass. It is composed of the radical for grain (*禾*) and the phonetic *sui* (歲). It is also written as *yong* (薉). The lower character is *zhuang* (撞) and *xue* (學). The *Cangjie pian* states: "Zhuo (淖) means muddy sludge. Gu Yewang says: "Zhuo is a designation for that which is not clean or pure. The *Wenzidian* explains: "It carries both clarity and turbidity. It is composed of the radical for water (*水*) and the phonetic *shu* (蜀). The pronunciation of *nao* (淖) is *niao* (撓).

The character 𡧯 (ji) is the correct orthography for the upper radical *qíng* (静). In the *Lùn-wén* (論文), it is written as 寂; in common usage, the local dialect calls it 𡧯, meaning "tranquil and still. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is a soundless character (*wúrénshēng*) composed of 宀 (mián) as the phonetic and 尗 (shū) as the semantic component. The lower part, 𡧯, has the pronunciation *běi*. In formal dictionaries, the correct orthography is 𡧯; in the *Lùn-wén*, it is written as 嘿 using 黑; this is the vulgar form. The *Kǎoshēng* states that 嘿 means "not speaking. The *Hànshū* says, "hēhē" (嘿嘿) refers to being dissatisfied with oneself. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* states that 嘿 means "silence," composed of 口 (mouth) as the semantic component and 墨 (mò) as the phonetic.

Regarding the character 卵 (luǎn): the upper radical is pronounced *luán* (short vowel) and the lower part is pronounced *kǔjiǎo*. This has already been fully explained in the nineteenth fascicle of the preceding section of the Vinaya.

Fascicle Twelve, Part Two: Regarding the character 覆 (fù), the lower part is pronounced *fújiù*. Jia Qi’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states: "覆 (fù) means 'to cover' (*gài*). The *Liji* says: 'Heaven has no partiality in its covering. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "It means 'to overturn' (*bǎng*). It is composed of the radical 西 with the phonetic 復; the pronunciation of 覂 (bǎng) is *fēngfèng*."

*Xi* (渴): Lower radical *kan*, reversed *e*. Gu Yewang says: "Ke" means one who desires to drink. The *Cangjie pian* says: "It means to dry up. The *Mao shi* says: "It is not thirst. The *Shuowen jiezi* says: "It means exhaustion; it takes the water radical and the phonetic *he*. *He* is pronounced *hu ge*.

13. Volume Thirteen, Part One. Regarding the character *xīn* (薪): the phonetic gloss states it is the sound of *kǎo* (考). It refers to split wood. Zheng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* says, "Xīn means firewood. His commentary on the *Zhōu lǐ* also says, "Wood is called xīn. The *Wénzì diǎnshuō* likewise says it is "chái" (柴). It is formed with the radical *cǎo* (草) and the phonetic *xīn* (新); the lower part is pronounced *zīsì* (資賜). The *Zhōu lǐ* states that the *Yí rén* (遺人) oversees the *wěijī* (委積). Zheng’s commentary says, "A small amount is called *wěi* (委), and a large amount is called *jī* (積). The *Shuowén* defines it as "a collection," formed with the radical *huò* (禾) and the phonetic *sài* (賽). To write it with the radical *cǎo* (草) as *zhǐ* (𧂐) is incorrect.

*Bo* (搏) [pronounced as above, with the phonetic *luán* reversed; the sound of the commentary says it means "to cause to touch"]. *Bóyǎ* (博雅) states: "*Bo* is like 'to grasp' (*wò*) or 'to hold close' (*fùchí*). Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states: "*Bo* refers to grasping with the hand," and also "to take. The *Zìshū* (字書) states: "To press down upon a circle. The *Shuōwén* (說文) states: "It is a circle (*yuán*); it takes the radical 手 and the phonetic 專."

"Róngxiāo (融銷)": The *Shǎokǎo* (尞考) states that it means "to melt away. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "the steam rising from cooking," composed of the radical 鬲 (lì, dīng xiǎojiāo fǎn) and the phonetic 蟲 (chóng). The *Zheng* commentary on the *Liji* says it means "to disperse. The *Shuowen* also defines it as "to smelt metal," composed of the radical 金 (jīn) and the phonetic 肖 (xiào); its pronunciation is shāngzhé fǎn.

14. Volume Fourteen, Chapter Fourteen. *Tài* (媅): The phonetic gloss states that *tài* means both "to crave" (*shì*) and "to dally with" (*wán*). The *Mao Shī* says, "The dallying of women. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines *tài* as "pleasure," a compound character formed from the radicals for "woman" and "excessive" (*shèn*). In the *Lunwen*, it is written as *dān* (躭) with the body radical; this is a vulgar form. The lower character is pronounced *shí* (至反). The phonetic gloss states it means "greed" (*tān*), "desire" (*yù*), and "love" (*ài*). Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshū* says, "To relish and crave without satiety. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* says, "It means 'lustful joy' (*yùxǐ*), and also 'greed' (*tān*). The *Wenzi Dianshuo* explains it as being composed of "mouth" and the phonetic element "old" (*qí*).

15. Volume Fifteen. "Dull-witted" (*chí*): pronounced with the *chǐ* rhyme; the *Pīcāng* states that it means "foolish and stupid. The *Huáinánzǐ* says, "not escaping from madness and folly. The *Shuowén* says, "lack of wisdom; it takes the radical *nà* (sickness) and the phonetic *yí*. The pronunciation of *ài* is *wǔjiè*; the pronunciation of *nà* is *nǚ'è*.

Volume 16, Chapter 16. [No characters to be transcribed]. Volume 17, Chapter 17. *Jìnglǜ* (靜慮): The *Qíngxìng Fǎn'ěr Yǎ* (爾雅) states that it means "quiet deliberation" (*jìngmóu*). Gù Yěwáng says it means "tranquil," "to govern," "to rest," "harmony," and "thought. The *Shuowén* says it means "to examine" (*shěn*), composed of the radical *míng* (𤯝) with the phonetic *zhēng* (爭); the latter is pronounced *lǚjù* (呂據). Zhèng’s commentary on the *Shī* says it means "deliberation" (*móu*). The *Yǐnyǎ* says it means "thought" (*sī*). The *Guǎngyǎ* says it means "awareness" (*shí*) and "extensive" (*guǎng*). According to the *Wénzì Diǎnshuō*, it is composed of the radical *sī* (思) with the phonetic *hū* (虍); *hū* is pronounced *hū*.

18. Volume Eighteen, Part One. Regarding "tāi" (胎): The *Huainanzi* states that a woman’s pregnancy reaches the stage of *tāi* at four months. The *Cangjie pian* states that *tāi* refers to that which has not yet been born. The *Guangya* states that three months constitute the stage of *tāi*. The *Shuowen jiezi* also states that a woman’s pregnancy lasts for three months; it is composed of the radical "flesh" (*ròu*) with "tái" as the phonetic component. The lower character is pronounced "duǎn" (短) with the initial "luán" (鸞). The *Kaosheng* states that it refers to the young of a crow before their features have differentiated. The *Shuowen* further states: "Generally, those whose destiny is without milk are born from eggs (*luǎn*). This is a pictographic character (*xiàngxíng zì*).

The character 質 (zhì) is phonetically "shùn" and "lún," and its opposite is also written as 󳅿 or 󳇱; the *Lùn* (Treatise) uses it in the sense of "pure" (*chún*), which is a common vulgar usage. According to the analysis of the character 質, it properly consists of the radical 酉 (yǒu) and the phonetic 𨣶 (wēn). The *Hànshū* states: "When a single color forms a body, it is called 𨣶," meaning it is not mixed. Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* says: "It means *cuì* (purity). He further says: "To act with a singular, pure conduct. Jia Kui says: "It means exclusive. The *Guǎngyá* says: "It means profound. The *Shuōwén* states that it takes 酉 as the radical and 𦎫 (kěn) as the phonetic—where 𦎫 has the same pronunciation as above—and it is also written as 純 (*chún*).

19. Volume Nineteen, Part One. *Xiào* (哮): "Xiào" is pronounced with the initial *xiào* (孝) and the final *jiāo* (交). The *Pīcāng* states that it means a great roar of rage. The *Gōngjīn zhèngzì* states it is the sound of a pig in alarm; it is composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic "xiào" (*xiào*). *Hè* (嚇): pronounced *hè* (赫), with the final *gòu* (狗) reversed. Dictionaries correctly write this as *hūn* (吽) or *páo* (咆). The *Lùn* (論) uses "hǒu" (吼); this is a vulgar usage. The *Kǎoshēng* states that the bellowing of oxen and tigers is called *hǒu*. The *Gōngjīn zhèngzì* states it is the crying of the cubs of bears and *pí* (熊羆); it is also said to be the general sound of beasts. It is composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic "kǒng" (孔). *Héng* (噑): pronounced *háo* (豪). *Gòu* (詬): pronounced *hēi gòu* (黑搆). Volume Nineteen, Part One. *Xiào*: "Xiào" is pronounced with the initial *xiào* (孝) and the final *jiāo* (交). The *Pīcāng* says it means a great roar of rage. The *Gōngjīn zhèngzì* says it is the sound of a pig in alarm; it takes the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and "xiào" (*xiào*) as its phonetic. *Hè* (*hè*): the final is *gòu* (*gòu*) reversed. Lexicons correctly write this as *hūn* (*hūn*) or *páo* (*páo*). The *Lùn* (*Lùn*) uses "hǒu" (*hǒu*); this is a vulgar character. The *Kǎoshēng* says the bellowing of oxen and tigers is called *hǒu*. The *Gōngjīn zhèngzì* says it is the crying of the cubs of bears and *pí*; it is also called the sound of beasts, the "míng" (鳴), or the "héng" (噑). It takes the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and "kǒng" (*kǒng*) as its phonetic. *Héng* (*héng*): pronounced *háo* (*háo*). *Gòu* (*gòu*): pronounced *hēi gòu* (*hēi gòu*).
*Hun-chin* (昏沈): The first character is pronounced *hu* with the *shang* tone (忽昆反) and the second is *zhen* with the *lin* tone (下朕淋反).

This has already been explained previously in the sixth fascicle. 20. Fascicle Twenty: *Jue-da* (撾打): The character for *jue* (撾) is pronounced *zhua* (竹瓜反). The *Shengyun* (聲韻) states that it means "to strike" (*kao-sheng yun jue-ji ye*) or "a horse whip. The *Shengllei* (聲類) states it means "to beat" (*jue-chui ye*). The *Wei zhi* (魏志) states, "He struck and broke his leg" (*jue-zhe qi jiao ye*). The *Wenzi dian* (文字典) explains it as "to hit," formed from the radical "wood" (*mu*) and the phonetic "guo" (*guo-sheng ye*).

The term "Miaochi" (妙翅) refers to the sound of its wings; it is named according to its physical form. Its back and both wings are all golden in color, hence it is also called the Golden-Winged Bird (*garuḍa*), which is the Sanskrit name for the *Kāla-rāja* (King of the Garuḍas).
Regarding "dust" (chén), it is pronounced *pén* in the lower character; this has already been explained in the fortieth fascicle of the *Sifen lü* (Dharmaguptaka-vinaya).

Regarding "owl" (*xiūyā*): the upper character is pronounced *xiù yóu*, and the lower is pronounced *liú*. According to the *Kǎo Shēng* (Investigation of Sounds), it is a strange bird. The *Jí Xùn* (Collection of Explanations) states that the owl (*xiūyā*) is the same as the *qīhú*, a wicked bird. The *Erya* says: "The *è* and the *jìxī*. Guō Pǐn’s commentary notes: "In the Jiangdong region today, the *xiūzhòu* is called the *jìxī*, and is also termed the *gùè*. According to this, the bird hides by day and flies by night, nesting in cliff-side caves. Both the *xiūzhòu* and the *qīhú* are named after the sound they emit. It is about the size of a horned eagle (*jiǎo yīng*), with a dark brownish-black variegated plumage, and feeds on various small birds, snakes, mice, and the like.

*Xiān* (凶險): The lower radical is *xiān* (杴), read as *yǎn* (奄) according to Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan*, where he states that "dangerous" (*xiǎn*) means "evil. Jia Kui says it means "perilous. The *Guǎngyá* says it means "difficult. The *Fāngyán* says it means "high edges. The *Shuowén* says it means "obstructed difficulty. It is composed of the radical *jié* (卩) and the phonetic *qiān* (僉). The version in the *Lunwén* (論文) uses *jiǎn* (撿), which is incorrect.

Regarding "duàn" (ditch/trench) in *duàn qiàn* (crossing the ditch): it is pronounced *xiān* (韱, with the radical *yàn*) according to Gu Yewang, who states that what is now called a city moat is termed a *qiàn*. Lexicons state it refers to a city's defensive moat (*chéng huáng*). The *Book of Zhou* states: "There were no canals or ditches, yet they occupied the center. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "*Qiàn* means a pit; it is composed of the radical *tǔ* (earth) and the phonetic *zhǎn*."

Regarding "falsehood" (*mṛṣā-vāda*): the character for "false" (*huàng*) is pronounced with the radical for "speech" and the phonetic *jū* (with the *kùang* tone). The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as "to deceive with words. Jia Qi’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states: "To deceive is equivalent to to delude. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "It means to cheat. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* also says it means "delusion. "Indulgence" (tán) [with the first character pronounced as dǎn and the second as qián; it was already explained in the fourteenth fascicle of the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*;
the correct form is *méi*]. "Exertion" (cèlì) [the first character pronounced as chéngsuǒ and the second as lìzhì; it was already explained in the sixth fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*].

Regarding "罝弶" (*jiāng*): the *Guōzhù* (Commentary by Guō) on the *Ěryǎ* states that "𦊨" (*yì*) is synonymous with "shutting off" (*zhē*). The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* (Dictionary of Characters and Explanations) states that a net for catching hares is called "罝" (*jiā*); it is composed of the radical "net" (*wǎng*) and the phonetic "且" (*qiě*). The sound of "网" (*wǎng*) is as written; the lower character "強" (*qiáng*) has the tone *yǎng*. The correct form is "弶" (*qiáng*); the version in the *Lùn-wén* (Treatise on Literature) using "摾" (*luán*) is incorrect. This was already fully explained in the third fascicle of the preceding section of the Vinaya.
*Kuṇḍa* (捃多): The first character is pronounced *jun* (君) with the second tone, and the second character is pronounced *yun* (惲) with the fourth tone, rhyming with *yun* (縕).

This is a Sanskrit term. *Yan* (隁塞): The first character is pronounced *yan* (蔫) with the fourth tone; it is also written as *yan* (堰) today, but this is not correct according to the *Lunwen* (論文). Gu Yewang says that *yan* (隁) is used for the purpose of retaining and storing water. The *Kao sheng* (考聲) says it means "to block. The *Wenzi dian* (文字典) states that it takes the radical *jie* (卩) and *yan* (匽) as its phonetic component; *yan* is pronounced *shangxia sengze fan* (同上下僧則反), which is a vulgar character. The *Shuowen* (說文) correctly uses the character *zhan* (󳍤) as the phonetic component, writing it as *zhan* (󳍤); the *Kao sheng* says it means "obstructed," "full," or "appropriate. Zheng’s commentary on the *Lunyu* says "blocking" (*se*) is like "concealing" (*bi*). The *Shuowen* says it means "to partition" (*ge*); it takes the radical *tu* (土) and *zhan* (󳍤) as its phonetic component. *Zhan* (󳊯) is pronounced the same as above; *zhan* (󳍱) is pronounced *zhan* (展).

Regarding the character *chāo* (抄) [with the initial *chū* and the final *jiào*]: the *Zìshū* (Dictionary of Characters) states that *chāo* is also *liè* (plunder). The *Jīngǔ zhèngzì* (Orthodox Characters of Antiquity and Today) explains it as the forcible seizure of property; it is formed with the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "shǎo" (*shēng*). The final character *lì* (力) [with the final *zuó*] has already been explained in the tenth fascicle of the preceding section on the Vinaya.

The character 媵 (yèng): the first radical is 女 (nǚ), the phonetic component is 承 (chéng) with the tone zhèng. "Mèng" refers to accompanying a bride on her wedding. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "To escort a woman is called mèng. The *Fāngyán* says: "Mèng means 'to entrust' (*jì*)"; it also says: "It means 'to deposit' (*tuò*). The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* states: "One escorts [her] with her younger sisters (*zhí* and *dì*) to follow the bride; the phonetic component is 勝 (shèng) with the tone shěng."

Regarding the character *qu* (麴): the upper radical is *qióng* (穹) and the phonetic is *jù* (鞠). The *Shàngshū* states: "In making sweet wine (*jiǔtǐ*), there are only malt and yeast. The *Zuǒzhìchuán* says: "Is there barley malt? The *Fānyán* states that in the regions of Song, Wèi, Chén, and Chǔ, malt is called *qiǎo* (󲟌). The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* explains that it is composed of the radical for grain (*mài*) and the phonetic *jǔ* (匊); *qiǎo* is pronounced as *qū* (曲), and *jǔ* is pronounced as *gōngliùfǎn* (弓六反) with the lower part pronounced as *lièfǎn* (列反). The *Kǎoshēng* states that *yè* (糵, yeast) refers to the sprouts of millet or wheat. The *Shuowén* says: "Yá (芽, sprout) refers to rice; it is composed of the radical for grain (*mǐ*) and the phonetic *zào* (𦵮)."

2. Second Fascicle. *Dànpò* (憺怕): The first character is pronounced as in *tán* (談) with the *qièyùn* rhyme *làn* (濫), and the second is pronounced as in *bēng* (伻) with the rhyme *mài* (麥); *bēng* is also pronounced as *pāi* (拍) or *méng* (萌). The treatise [of the *Yīnwénzhì*] writes the first character as *yán* (炎), which is incorrect. Gu Yewáng states that *dànpò* means "tranquil stillness. Wáng Yì’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that *dàn* (憺) means "peaceful" or "sufficient. Lexicons state that *pà* (怕) means "non-action" (*wúwéi*). The *Zǐxū Fù* says: "Tranquil (*pà*) and non-active, calm (*dàn*) and self-sustained. The *Shuowén Jìzì* states: "*Dàn* is peace; *pà* is non-action. Both characters are composed of the radical *xīn* (心) and the phonetic *zhān* (詹) with the tone marker *bái* (白).

Lín (the character for "rain") is pronounced with the radical *zhēn* (上立砧反). *Lín* is the correct orthography; the discussion of the text states that it follows the "rain" (*yù*) radical, while *lín* is a vulgar variant. Regarding its phonetic analysis, it is said that rain lasting three days or more is called *lín*. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "Unceasing long rain is called *lín*. The *Shichuan* (Commentary on the Odes) states: "*Lín* is heavy rain. Jia Dui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states: "Stagnant rain. It follows the "rain" radical and takes "lin" as its phonetic component.

*Kxi* (溪): *jiàn* (澗). The *Shi zhuan* (詩傳) states: "When mountains flank water, it is called a *jiàn*. The meaning in the *Shuowen jiezi* is the same as in the *Shi zhuan*. It is composed of the radical *shui* (水) and the phonetic *jiān* (間). *Ruí* (󱠰): *guì* (叡).

The *Lunwen* (論文) uses the character *rú* (󱠰), which is a vulgar form. The *Shangshu* (尚書) says: "To listen is called *rú*. The *Mao Shi zhuan* (毛詩傳) says: "*Rú* means to hear. The *Han Shi waizhuan* (韓詩外傳) says: "It means clarity. The *Shuowen* says: "It means to observe. It is composed of the radical *er* (耳) and the phonetic *hu* (忽); the pronunciation of *hu* is the same as above [in the *Shuowen*]. The *Shangshu* writes *ruì* (叡) as *shèng* (聖). Kong’s commentary (*Kong zhu*) says: "It means wisdom. Jia Dui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* says: "It means clarity. The *Shuowen* says: "It means profound clarity. It is composed of the radicals *can* (󲘫), *mu* (目), and the abbreviated form of *gu* (谷) as the phonetic; the pronunciation of *can* is *zān* (殘).
*Saṃghāṭī*: The lower tone for *zhī* is a transliteration of the Sanskrit term; in the Tang language, it means "the Great Robe" (*dàyī*) or the nine-panel robe.

Regarding *bùyū* (不迃): the character *yū* is pronounced with the *yuǎn* rhyme (禹反). Bāo Xián’s commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* states: "Yū means 'distant' (*yuǎn*). Zhèng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states: "It means 'broad' (*guǎng*) or 'great' (*dà*). Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* states: "It means 'to avoid' (*bì*). The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* explains that *huíqū* (迥曲) is the meaning: it is composed of the radical *chuò* (辵, pronounced *chùlüè*) and the phonetic *yú* (亐, pronounced *yīyú*). The pronunciation of *chuò* is *chùlüè*, and the pronunciation of *yū* is *yìyú*.

3. Third Fascicle. The character *sì* (駛) [is used here]. In the *Lùn-wén* (論文), it is written with the phonetic *shǐ*; this is certainly not the correct meaning. Examining the *Shēng-lèi* (聲類) and the *Cāngjié piān* (蒼頡篇), both state that it means "the swift gallop of a horse. The *Jīngǔ zhèngzì* (古今正字) also states it means "rapid. It is composed of the radical "horse" (*mǎ*) and the phonetic *yù* (*㕜*).

*Àotàn* (懊歎): The first character, *ào*, is pronounced with the *gǎo* rhyme. It refers to the sound of lamentation; it denotes the feeling of distress and regret. According to the standard orthography of ancient and modern times, it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "àu" (*ào*), where *ào* is pronounced with the *āgào* rhyme.

Volume Four, Part Four: *Ōng* (癰): The second character, *yǒng*, is pronounced with the *gōng* rhyme. 6. Fascicle Six. Regarding the character for "wrinkles" (*zhòu*) below [the entry for] "face": it is written as *zhòu* in the standard treatise (*lùnwén*), though in common usage it is written as *zhuó*. This is due to the abbreviation of cursive script (*cǎoshū*). The *Kǎoshēng* states: "Wrinkles refer to the gathering of the skin. The *Wénzìdiǎn* explains: "The skin is wide and gathered. It is composed of the radical "skin" (*pí*) and the phonetic component "cǎo" (*cū*). The pronunciation of "cǎo" is *cèyú* (first tone).

The character for "𦠍" (páng) is pronounced with the initial *ǎng* (as in *āng*). The *Kǎo shēng* (Explanations of Sounds) states that "𦠍" means "to sever," composed of "flesh" (*ròu*) and the phonetic component "㖾" (*ǎi*, same pronunciation as above). This character does not appear in the *Shuōwén*. The correct form is "谷" (*gǔ*), where "上" (*shàng*) means "mouth" (*ā*) and is a pictographic character. "谷" is pronounced *qiánglüè*. It is also written as "𠶸" or "臄," both of which appear in the *Shuōwén*. Nowadays, the common usage of "腭" (*è*) or "齶" (*yà*) is incorrect.

The character for *sòu* (disease): the upper radical is *sāng* (桑) with the *zòu* (奏) phonetic; it is the correct form according to ancient and modern standards. It is formed from the radical *nà* (疒) and means a cold disease, a cough. The *Lùn-wén* (論文) states it is formed from the radical *kǒu* (口) as *sòu*, which is incorrect. The *Kǎo-shēng* (考聲) says it is a disease where qi strikes the throat. The *Běicāng* (埤蒼) says it is a disease caused by alternating cold and heat. The *Zìshū* (字書) says it is a disorder within the chest and diaphragm (*dǐ*). The *Wén-zì-diǎn-shuō* (文字典說) states it is formed from the radical *nà* (疒) with the phonetic *chù* (欶); the pronunciation of *chù* is the same as above.

"Yī" (噫) [the radical is 口, the phonetic is 界]. The *Kǎo Shēng* states that it refers to the sound of belching after eating a full meal. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states that "huì-yī" refers to a disorder within the throat and chest. The *Wénzì Diǎnshuō* states it is a word of resentment or the sound of painful injury; it is formed from the radical 口 and the phonetic 意.

Regarding the character for *lái* (癩) [pronounced with the initial *dài*]: the *Wenzí jílüè* (Collection of Simplified Characters) states that *lái* refers to a wind-disease of the five viscera; the *Yǎ* (Elegant Explanations) states that *lái* is the great wind-disease (*mahā-vātavyādhi*). In both ancient and modern standard characters, it is composed of the radical *nà* (疒, "sickness") and the phonetic *làì* (賴).

The character *lí* (痳) is pronounced with the initial *zhēn* (砧) and the final rhyme of *shēnglèi* (聲類). It states that *lí* refers to frequent urination accompanied by difficulty in voiding. The *Wénzìdiǎn* (文字典) explains it as a type of *shàn* (疝) ailment, and further describes it as a condition characterized by aching or obstruction during urination. It is formed with the radical *nà* (疒) and the phonetic component *lín* (林).

*Diǎn* (癲). The upper radical is *diǎn* (典, with the phonetic *nián*); according to the *Wenzi jílüè*, it is formed from *nà* (疒). It refers to the disease of madness caused by "thieving winds" (*zé fēng*) entering the five viscera. The *Guǎngyá* states: "Madness. The *Shēnglèi* states: "A wind-disease. The *Wenzí diǎnshuō* also states: "A malignant wind-disease. It is formed from *nà* (疒) and has *diān* (顛) as its phonetic.

The character *ǒu* (嘔) is pronounced with the initial *ǒu* and the final *kǎo*. The *Kǎoshēng* states that "to *ǒu*" means wishing to vomit. Lexicons state it is a disease of the stomach. The *Shuōwén* states: "*ǒu* means to vomit; it is formed from the radical *qiàn* (欠) and the phonetic *qū* (區)."

*Zhòngyǐng* (重癭): The upper character is pronounced *zhǎng* (長) with the *lèi* (類) rhyme. The *Zuǒzhuan* states there is the disease of "sinking, drowning, and heavy *zhòngyǐng*. Du’s commentary says *zhòngyǐng* means swelling. It refers to wind entering the small intestine. The *Guǎngyá* says *zhòngyǐng* is the disease of swelling of the genitals. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* says it is *zhòngyǐng*. It is composed of the radical *nà* (疒) and the phonetic *zhuī* (追). The lower character is pronounced *yīng* (嬰) with the *yǐng* (郢) rhyme. According to the *Shānhǎijīng*, on Mount Gānzǎo there is a beast named Bái Nèng; eating it cures *yǐng*. In ancient texts, this is written as the character *fú* (𦢆). The *Shuōwén* says it is the disease of swelling of the neck, composed of the radical *nà* (疒) and the phonetic *yīng* (嬰).

The upper phonetic of "di-xià" (㿃下) is *dài*. The *Cangjie pian* states that "di-xià" refers to a disease of women. The *Shiming* states that when diarrhea is most severe, with both red and white discharge, it is called "di. The *Guangya* states it is an ulcer within the abdomen. The *Wenzi dian shuo* states it is the disease of dysentery; it is composed of the radical "nà" (疒, pronounced *nǚ è*) and the phonetic "dài. The pronunciation of "nà" is *nǚ è* (female-impediment).

*Leu-xie* (漏泄): On the upper character, *lóu* (樓) is pronounced with the *dòu* (豆) rhyme; the sound is said to mean "to leak" (*lòu-luò*). Gu Yewang states that *leu* (漏) also means "to leak. Xu Shuchong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* says it means "a hole," "an aperture," or "loss. The *Cangjie pian* says it means "to gradually depart. The *Wenzi dianshuo* says it is formed from the radical "water" (*shui*) and the phonetic "lòu" (*lòu* having the same pronunciation as above); the lower character, *xiān-liè* (先列), has the rhyme *xiān-liè*. The *Shichuan* (Poetry Commentary) says it means "to leak away. Zheng’s *Jian* (Sub-commentary) says it means "to emerge" or "to issue forth. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* says it means "to diminish. The *Fangyan* says it means "to cease. The *Guangya* says it means "to flow out. The *Wenzi dianshuo* says it is an appearance of "relaxed dispersal"; it is formed from the radical "water" and the phonetic "shì" (*shì*).

Regarding the character for *xián* (痃) in *xián-pì* (痃癖): the radical above is "sickness" (疒). The character below is written with "string" (絃) minus its final stroke as a phonetic; it is read as *pié* (匹亦反).
