The character *màn* (慢): the upper radical is *gōng* (公) with the phonetic *máo* (毛); the *Mao Shi* commentary states it means "to hear clearly. The *Han Shi* states it means "clarity," and the *Shuowen* explains it as "clear discernment. It is composed of the radical *ěr* (耳) with the phonetic *hūn* (怱) [simplified form]. The lower part is *mán* (蠻) with the phonetic *biàn* (辦). Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that *màn* means "to treat the sacred teachings lightly. The *Shuowen* states that *màn* means "laziness"; it is composed of the radical *xīn* (心) with the phonetic *màn* (曼).

34. Fascicle Thirty-Four. Regarding the character *shàn* (苫): the first tone is pronounced as *pī* (披), and the second tone is a compound of *zhān* (詹) and *jiǎo* (攷). It refers to thatched grass. The *Erya* states: "The white canopy is called *shàn*. Guo’s commentary notes: "The *shàn* is made of white *máo* grass; it is currently called *gài* (蓋) in Jiangdong. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical for grass (*cǎo*) with the phonetic *zhān*.

The character *jiù* (炷) has the radical *shù* (朱) in the upper part and the phonetic *yáo* (遙) in the lower part; its pronunciation is *jiāo*. It means "to burn until dry and extreme," as in being scorched by fire. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "blackened by fire. In his commentary on the *Lìjì*, Zhèng Xiǎozhōng states that smoke arises from within the fire. The *Shuōwén Jiězì* correctly writes this character as *jiào* (𤓪), explaining it as "that which is burned by fire," composed of the radical *huǒ* (火) with the phonetic *zá* (雥); the pronunciation of *zá* is *zá*. The version in the *Lùn* (Discourse) written as *jiāo* (燋) is incorrect.

*Xiāo* (虛): The upper radical is *xiāng* (香) with the variant *jiāo* (驕). Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that it means "clamorous noise" (*xiāohuán*). The *Zuo Zhuan* says "narrow, cramped, and clamorous with dust" (*jiǎo'ài xiāochén*), which refers to this. According to the *Shuowen*, it denotes the sound of breath emerging from the head; it is composed of *jí* (㗊) and *yè* (頁). *Yè* means "head," though it may also be written as *mǎi* (買). *Jí* is pronounced *zhuànglì* (壯立); *yè* is pronounced *xié* (纈).

Volume Thirty-Five, Volume Thirty-Five, No Characters for Pronunciation Guide. Volume Thirty-Six, Volume Thirty-Six: *Gài* (Irrigation). The upper character, 溉 (*gài*), is pronounced as *jī* (base radical) with the phonetic *guò*. Gu Yewang states it means "to pour. The *Shuowen Jiezi* also states it means "to irrigate. The lower character, 灌 (*guàn*), is pronounced as *guàn* (base radical) with the phonetic *huàn*. Gu Yewang states it means "to drench" or "to pour down. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that both characters take the water radical (*shui*) and the phonetic *ji* (or *guàn*). Volume Thirty-Six, Volume Thirty-Six: *Guàn* (Irrigation). The upper character, 溉 (*gài*), is pronounced as *jī* (base radical) with the phonetic *guò*. Gu Yewang states it means "to pour. The *Shuowen Jiezi* also states it means "to irrigate. The lower character, 灌 (*guàn*), is pronounced as *guàn* (base radical) with the phonetic *huàn*. Gu Yewang states it means "to drench" or "to pour down. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that both characters take the water radical (*shui*) and the phonetic *ji* (or *guàn*).

*Pāng* (upper radical *pu*, *máng* reversed; according to the *Shuowen*, "a flood"; also written as *pōng*) and *yì* (lower radical *yǐn*, *fǎn*; according to the *Guǎngyá*, "abundance" or "overflowing"; according to the *Shuowen*, "the filling of a vessel"). Both characters take the water radical on the left and the phonetic *yì* on the right. The version in the *Lun* [Treatise] uses *yì*, which is a vulgar character.

37. Fascicle Thirty-Seven. Regarding "Saw" (jù): according to the *Cangjie pian*, it is a tool for cutting objects; according to the *Shuowen jiezi*, it means "to hack. It is composed of the radical "metal" (金) with the phonetic "ju" (居). The lower character is pronounced with the *qieyun* rhyme "xie" (蟹) in the third tone. According to the *Kaoseng zhuan shengzhi* (or *Kaosheng*), it means "to open"; according to the *Wenzi dian shuo*, it means "to divide. It is composed of the radical "knife" (刀) and the character "pan" (判), signifying the dividing of ox horns.

"Cānchui (慘顇) means 'to dare to oppose'. The *Mao Shichuan* states: "Cān (慘) is equivalent to 'sorrowful' (*qi*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: 'Cān means sorrow; it is an expression of resentment. It is composed of the radical 心 (heart/mind) with 參 (can) as the phonetic, pronounced *cizu* (慈醉). The *Cangjie Pian* states: 'Chui (顇) means sorrow. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: 'Jiaochui (憔顇) means haggard and worn. It is composed of the radical 頁 (head) with 卒 (zhu) as the phonetic."
The character *kuān* (寬) has the phonetic *xián jiǎ fǎn* (咸甲反). This was already explained in the nineteenth fascicle above.

Regarding *zhōng* (𧄼): the upper part is read as *dēng dèng fǎn* (登鄧反); according to the *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲), *zhōng* refers to the appearance of one just beginning to wake from sleep. The lower part is read as *mò dèng fǎn* (墨鄧反). Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒ Zhuan* states it means "stupefaction" (*méng mèn*). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (毛詩傳) says it means "confusion. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文) says it means "lack of clarity. It is composed of the radicals *mù* (苜) and *shuò* (䀏); *shuò* refers to the eyes flickering repeatedly.

"Jue" (撾) means to strike; it refers to the sound produced when striking bamboo. The *Shenglei* (聲類) states that "jue" means to beat (*chui*). The *Wenzidian* (文字典) explains that it is composed of the radical "water" (氵) and the phonetic "guo" (過), with the latter pronounced as *ding-leng* (丁冷反). The *Kaosheng* (考聲) states that it means to strike; its correct form is "zhi" (󲿰).

Regarding the character *pi* (俳優): the upper radical is *bai* (敗) with the phonetic *mai* (埋) reversed, and the lower radical is *yu* (郁) with the phonetic *niu* (牛). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that *piyou* refers to those who engage in jesting and merriment. Gu Yewang says that *piyou* are performers whose role is to provide comic entertainment for their own amusement. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "theatrical performance" (*pai*) and "a jester" (*you*). Both characters are composed of the "person" radical (*ren*), and neither has *you* (憂) as its phonetic component.

*Qícáo*: the first character is pronounced *jī* (with the *jié* rhyme) and the second is *cáo* (with the *zāo* rhyme). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *qícáo* refers to the wood-boring insect known as the *xié*. Both characters are written with the radical for insects (*虫*), and *zhī* and *cáo* serve as their phonetic components.

38. Fascicle Thirty-Eight. "Cao" (皺) is pronounced with the initial *zou* and the final *shou*. It refers to the wrinkling and gathering of the skin. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* (Dictionary of Characters and Explanations) states: "It means the skin is wide and gathered; it takes the phonetic element 'pi' (皮) and the sound 'chu' (芻). The pronunciation of 'chu' is *ce-jū*."

"Bèi lǚ" (背僂)—the rhyme is *jù* (矩); according to the *Guǎngyá*, "lǚ" means "curved. The *Shuōwén* states it means "humpbacked. [The character] "bèi" (背) follows the radical for "person" (人) and uses "lóu" (婁) as its phonetic; the "lùn" (論) [in the *Shuōwén*] is written with the radical for "flesh" (肉) as "lǚ" (膢), which is incorrect.

Yǎn (黶): Pronounced with the *yān* rhyme (鴨減反). Wang Sù’s commentary on the *Jiayu* states that *àn* is also black. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines *yǎn* as a deep black appearance; it is also written as *àn*. Volume 39, No. 39: This volume contains no phonetic glosses.

Volume 40, No. 40: Wǎn (󳆔): Pronounced with the *kuǎn* rhyme (款丸反). According to the *Kaosheng*, it refers to the hip bone (*wān*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as the thigh (*bǐ*), formed from the radical "bone" (*gǔ*) and the phonetic "kuǎn. In the *Lunyu*, it is written with the "flesh" radical (*ròu*) as *wān*; this is also acceptable.

The character for *hàn* (頷) [is pronounced] *gǎn* (感) with a retroflex *r*. The *Shuowen* says: "The jaw; it is formed from *xié* (頁) and *hàn* (含) as phonetic components. In antiquity it was written as *yǔ* (󲽕). The character *lùn* (論) is formed from *ròu* (肉); *yǔ* (𦛜) is a vulgar form. Regarding *gān* (肝) and *fèi* (肺): the former is pronounced *gàn* (幹) with a level tone, and the *Shuowen* says:

"The liver; the water-organ (*shuǐ-zàng*). The latter is pronounced *fú* (孚) with a falling tone. The *Baihūtong* says: "'Fèi' means 'noble' (*guì*); it is the essence of metal; its color is white. The *Shuowen* says: "The metal-organ (*jīn-zàng*). Both are formed from *ròu* (肉) with *yú* (于) and *shì* (市) as phonetic components; *shì* is pronounced *bèi* (軰). The character *lùn* (論) is used as *fèi* (肺), which is a vulgar usage.

*Spleen* (pí): the second character is pronounced *mí*. The *Baihūtong* states: "The meaning of 'spleen' (*pí*) is 'to manage' (*biàn*). It is that which accumulates essence and receives qi; it is the quintessence of Earth. Its color is yellow. The *Shuowen* defines it as "the organ of Wood" (pronounced *shírèn*). The *Baihūtong* states: "'Kidney' (*shèn*) means 'guest' (*bīn*). It is that which receives and discharges the essence of Water. Its color is black; because it is Yin and weak, it is doubled. The two characters in the *Shuowen* both follow the radical for "flesh" (*ròu*) with the phonetic component *xiān* (pronounced *jiān*).

The character 𦞅 (dǎn) is pronounced as the opposite of guì (貴). The *Baihùtōng* states: "The gallbladder (*dǎn*) is the *fǔ* (organ) of the spleen; it governs the reception of qi. The stomach (*wèi*) is the repository of grain. The *Shuowén* says: "It is the *fǔ* of grain; it follows the radical 肉 (flesh) and uses 𠮧 (zhān) as a pictographic representation. The lower part is pronounced dānlǎn (擔覽). The *Baihùtōng* says: "The gallbladder is the *fǔ* connected to the liver. As for benevolence (*rén*), if one is not patient, one must use the gallbladder to sever [the impulse]; therefore, the benevolent person must possess courage. The *Shuowén* says it follows the radical 肉 with the phonetic 詹. The version in the *Lùn* (Treatise) is written as 𦝩, which is a vulgar form.

The character for *shǐ* (excrement) is composed of *shì* (the opposite of *shī*) above and *zhuāng* below; the *Zhuāngzǐ* states that it was used to mean "to carry excrement in a basket. The *Wénzìdiǎn* explains that *shǐ* means "feces," and its original form is written as *fèn*. It is also an archaic character (*gǔzì*) written as *fēn*, and another variant is *fēi*. The *Lùn-wén* uses the character *shǐ*, which is a vulgar form (*súzì*). Below this is *niào* (urine), with the phonetic component *diào*. Gù Yěwáng states that *shǐ* is synonymous with *niào*. Regarding *niào*, the *Shuōwén* defines it as "urination," composed of the radicals for "tail" (*wěi*) and "water" (*shuǐ*).

Fifth Bundle, Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fifth Bundle, Fascicle Forty-one. [The term] *jiàsè* (稼穡)—the first character pronounced as *jiā* (家) with the second tone, and the second as *suò* (所) with the fourth tone—has already been fully explained in the twenty-first fascicle above.

*Fēng* (豐) means abundance. The *Zhouyi* says it signifies "greatness. Zheng Xuan says it means "abundant and great. Jia Kui says it means "flourishing. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* says it means "luxuriant. The *Shuowen* says it refers to the fullness of a vessel; it follows the character for "bean" (*dòu*) and takes its form from that. The lower part, *rén*, is pronounced *shèn*. Jia Kui says it means "ripening. Gu Yewang says it means "to reach maturity. The *Shuowen* says it means "the ripening of grain"; it follows the character for "grain" (*huó*) and uses *niàn* as a phonetic.

42. Fascicle Forty-two. Regarding "tāo tiè" (饕餮): the first character is pronounced *tǎo* (with the initial *dǎo*) and the second is pronounced *tiè* (with the initial *tiē*). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "To covet wealth is called *tāo*; to covet food is called *tiè*. The forms used in secular texts as *tāotiè* are vulgar characters.

The upper character, *jù* (疾), means "to chew" (*cǔjiào*), following the *Cāngjiépiān*; its pronunciation is *cízhào*. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "chewing flavors. The lower character, *jiào* (匠略反), Gù Yěwáng states, is also "to chew. The *Guǎngyá* calls it "to eat" (*rú*). According to the *Shuōwén*, both characters are composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) with the phonetic component *qiè* (*jué*).

*Chùe* (upper tone, pronounced *cháng*). The *Lunyu* says: "When the ruler grants food, one must straighten one's seat and taste it first. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that it means "to try" (*chàng shì*). The *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of the radical *zhǐ* with the phonetic *shàng*; however, the character *lùn* is not written as *𭋌*. The lower part is read as *chuān* (jìng) or *jiǎo*. The *Shuowen* also states that *chùe* also means "to taste," being composed of the radical *kǒu* with the phonetic *zhuó*, which is pronounced *zhí luò*.

The term *qiào* (誚) means to reproach or censure; this is the commentary of Kong [Yuan] on the *Shūjìng*. According to the *Shuowén*, *qiào* means to harass or annoy, composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic "xiào" (*xiào*). It is also written as *jiāo* (譙), with the pronunciation *niǎo* (niǎo).

The upper phonetic of "guī" (tortoise) is *guī*; the *Guǎngyá* states that the tortoise is a creature with a shell. The lower phonetic of "jiè" (crab) is *mǎi*. Hàn Kāngbó’s commentary on the *Zhòuyī* says that the crab has its shell on the outside. The *Shuōwén* contains two characters for "guī": one is "bǐng" (𧑃), meaning a creature with eight legs that moves sideways; it is composed of the radical "insect" (*chóng*) and the phonetic "jiě" (*jiě*, pronounced *áo*). The character "bǐng" is pronounced *áo*.

"Jinkuang" (gold ore) refers to the raw material of iron, copper, and other metals; the *Guoyang* states that "tiefuáng" (iron sulfide/ore) is the unworked stone (*pú*). What is called *pú* is termed *fuáng*; according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "stone" and the phonetic "huáng. The *Lunheng* uses the character "kuàng," which is also acceptable.

Cù (鏃): The character for the body [of an arrowhead]. In the *Shuowen*, it is defined as "a barb" (*cì*). It is composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic "zú" (*zú shēng*), or alternatively written with the radical "bamboo" (*zhú*) as "cù" (*cù*).

It is incorrect to derive it from the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) as "lún" (*lún*). Volume 43, No. 43: This volume contains no phonetic glosses. Volume 44, No. 44: Diān jué (蹎蹶). The upper character is pronounced *diǎn lián* (典蓮反); the lower character is pronounced *juàn yuè* (卷月反). These were already explained previously in Volume 14.

*Mǐ* (in *rúlí*, "milk gruel"): The upper radical is *róu* (反) and the lower is *měi* (悲反). The *Wénzì jílüè* (Collection of Abridged Characters) states that *mǐ* refers to thick porridge. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical *mǐ* with *má* as the phonetic.

*Fēi* (in *fēidì*, "consort" and "sister-in-law"): The upper radical is *fěi* (微反). Gù Yěwáng says that a *fēi* is like a *hòu* (empress). The *Lǐjì* states that the consort of the Son of Heaven is called a *hòu*. The lower radical is *tí* (麗反). The *Ěryá* states that among women who marry at the same time, the one born first is called *shì* and the one born later is called *dì*. Guo’s commentary notes that this means they both marry and serve the same husband. The *Wenzì diǎnshuō* (Dictionary of Characters) states that both characters are composed of the radical *nǚ* (woman), with *yǐ* and *dì* respectively as their phonetics.

*Ulu-piluo* (隖盧頻螺): The first character is pronounced with the *wu* rhyme group and the *gu* final; the second is pronounced with the *lu* rhyme group and the *he* final. This is the Sanskrit name for an Arhat (*arhan*). *Suìdèng* (隧隥):

The first character is pronounced with the *sui* rhyme group and the *zui* final. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* identifies it as a "tunnel" (*daotong*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is composed of the radical *dao* (𨸏) and the phonetic *sui*; it is incorrect to write it as *yǒu* (𡑞) with the radical *tu*. The second character is pronounced with the *deng* rhyme group and the *deng* final. This was already explained previously in the twenty-ninth fascicle.

45. Fascicle Forty-Five. No phonetic glosses for characters in Fascicle Forty-Five. 46. Fascicle Forty-Six. *Gai* (in the phrase *gai qu*) is pronounced as *qu* with the tone of *fan*. According to the *Guangya*, it means "to grasp" or "to hold. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *ge*, stating it means "to seize," composed of the radical "hand" and the phonetic "li. Its usage in the *Lun* [Treatise] is also correct.

The *yin* (harness strap) is tied above; according to the *Mao Shi Zhuan*, the *yin* is that by which one leads. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* states: "That which is at the chest is called the *yin*; it follows the radical 'metal' (*革*) and takes 'yin' as its phonetic component; the lower character is pronounced *ji*."

*Tí* (梯): The first character is pronounced *tǐ* (with the radical *lǐ*). Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that it means "steps. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "a wooden staircase," formed with the radical *mu* (wood) and the phonetic *dì*. The second character, *dēng* (登), is pronounced *dèng* (with the radical *dēng*); it means "to ascend" or "successive paths."

Volume Forty-Seven, Part Four. *Tánmiǎn* (耽湎): The upper character is pronounced with the initial *dàn* and the final *hán*; it was already fully explained in Volume Two. The lower character is pronounced with the initial *mián* and the final *biǎn*. Master Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states that "mǎn" refers to the broad extent of excessive indulgence in wine. The *Shuowén Jiězì* states: "To be addicted to wine. It is composed of the radical *shuǐ* (water) and the phonetic *gài*.

48. Volume Forty-Eight. "Piao-ji" (漂激): The upper character "piao" (漂) is pronounced with the *shang* tone, following the *pi* rhyme; Ku Yewang states that "piao" means "to flow. The *Shuowen* defines it as "to float. The lower character "ji" (激) is pronounced with the *xià* tone; Sima Biao’s commentary on the *Zhuangzi* states that "rapid currents are called ji. The *Shuowen* defines "ji" as "congealed, crooked, and swift waves. Both characters are composed of the "water" radical (*shui*), with "piao" and "jiao" serving as their phonetic components respectively.

*Chuí* (隹水反): The glossary *Kǎo* states it means "to strike"; the *Zìtǒng* states it means "to strike with a staff. It is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "chuí" (垂). *Yuán* (遠元反): The *Kǎogōngjì* states: "In making a shaft (*yuán*), its length is three times the height of the wheel;

divide that length into two parts, with two in the front and one in the back. The *Shuowén* defines *yuán* as "the pole (*zhòu*). [The character is] *yīng* (嚶革反). Zhèng Xuān’s commentary on the *Kǎogōngjì* states: "The *yè* (軶) is the wooden yoke at the end of the shaft that rests upon the ox's neck. Both characters in the *Shuowén* are composed of the radical "cart" (車) and the phonetics "yuán" (袁) and "è" (戹) respectively. The *Lùn* (論) uses the character *è* (軛); this is a vulgar form. *Zhòu* (音肘留反): [The character is] *zhòu*. The sound is *zhǒu liú* (肘留反). This refers to the pole.

Qiū (upper character: 七由反, qī yóu fǎn; sound: 考 kǎo) refers to the leather thong of a carriage, also written as qiū or qiū. Yāng (lower character: 央仰反, yāng yǎng fǎn): The *Wenzi Jilüe* states that an *yāng* is a head-harness for oxen and horses. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it is the leather on the neck, formed from the radical "leather" (革) with the phonetic "yāng. It is also written as zhí or dǎ. Dǎ (phonetic: 之列反, zhī liè fǎn).

49. Fascicle Forty-Nine. *Zhān* (pronounced *zhǎn-lián*). Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "The *zhān* is a large fish; its mouth is located beneath its jaw, its body is without scales, and its flesh is yellow. The largest measure three or two *zhang*. In Jiangdong, it is called the 'yellow fish' (*huángyú*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical for "fish" with the phonetic element *shèn*.
Fifty: Volume Fifty. *xingqu* (興瞿)—the Sanskrit name for a medicinal substance; in the Tang language, it is called *āyuē* (阿魏).
*xīnlà* (辛辢)—in ancient and modern standard characters, *lǎ* (辢) also means "pungent"; it is composed of the radical *xīn* (辛) and the phonetic *shù* (束).

"Mánggǔ" (blind): the upper character "máng" (陌耕反) is defined in the *Shuowen* as "having no pupils in the eyes"; the lower character "gǔ" (姑五反) is defined in the *Shuowen* as "one who has no eyes. Both are composed of the "eye" radical with "wáng" and "gǔ" as their phonetic components.
*Āṭa* (the first character is pronounced with the *shàng* tone as *ài*, the second with the *sì* tone as *sī*;
this is a transliteration of the Sanskrit term). *Khara* (the first character is pronounced with the *shàng* tone as *wǔ*, the second as *gǔ*;

this was already fully explained in the eighth fascicle above). *Pratigraha*: - The first character, *fáng* (pronounced *fáng*), according to Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji*, means "to prepare for defense"; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "an embankment," composed of the radical *fù* (阜) and the phonetic *fāng* (方). - The second character, *hàn* (pronounced *hán*): the *Kaoshi* states it means "to ward off"; the *Wenzi Dianshuo* states it means "to guard," composed of the radical *shǒu* (手) and the phonetic *gān* (干), also written as *gǎn*.

"Zhì" (縶) [pronounced zhì]: The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (Mao Commentary on the Classic of Poetry) states that it means "to bind. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuǒ Zhuan* defines it as "restraint. The *Wénzìdiǎn* (Dictionary of Characters) explains that it takes "mì" (糸) as the radical and "zhí" (執) as the phonetic.

6. The sixth bundle (*zhì*) of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Volume 51, Part 51. Regarding the character "chǐwò" (尺蠖), the pronunciation is "zhù" (郭反). It was already explained in detail in the previous Volume 24; the character should be written as "chán" (蚇) from "chóng" (虫), and not otherwise.

*Lìjiǎn* (利鐮): The first character is pronounced *yán* (𣫍炎反); according to the *Fāngyán* (方言), it refers to a sickle used for reaping. The *Wénzìdiǎn* (文字典) explains that it is composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic "fish" (*yú*), though it is also written as *jiǎn* (鐮𠛎), with the pronunciation *gǒusì* (苟俟反).

*Guāngtī* (桄梯): The upper character is pronounced *guāng* (上音光). According to the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲), it is written as *héng* (橫), meaning "to place across," and it also refers to the crossbar of a bed. The lower character is pronounced *xī* (奚反). The *Shuōwén* (說文) defines it as a wooden step or ladder. This has already been explained in the forty-third fascicle [of this work].

*Huàn jiǎ* (to don armor). "Guān" is pronounced with the *huàn* tone; the commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that *huàn* means "to pierce through. Jia Dui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that it refers to "putting on armor. According to the *Shuowen*, the character is composed of the radical "hand" (*shou*) and the phonetic element "simplified *huán*" (*huán*).

*Kwāng* (尫) [pronounced *yāo huáng*]: The *Shuowen Jiezi* correctly writes this as *kwāng*, meaning "to have a lame and crooked leg. It is derived from the character for "elephant" (*xiàng*) with a radical indicating a distorted shape. The *Lunwen* (論) treats *kwāng* as an archaic form of the character. *Chū* (󲸈) is pronounced *zào*.

Fifty-second Fascicle. [The character] *gǔ* (轂): In the *Shuowen*, it is defined as "the point where the spokes converge. It is composed of the radical *chē* (車) and the phonetic *hè* (殼). The pronunciation of *hè* is *kǔjué*.

Regarding *què* (pronounced *juàn* in the *Zhuāngzǐ*): the *Zhuāngzǐ* states, "In front there are the ornaments of the bit and the *què*. Examining its phonetics, *què* refers to a short, pointed piece of wood. The *Wenzìdiǎn* explains it as a wooden stake (*yì*), with the phonetic component *jué*. The version in the *Lùn* [the *Huáyán jīng lùn*] writes it as *shuān*, which is a vulgar character and incorrect.

*Kàng* (in the phrase *kàng dí*, "to oppose an enemy"): the upper radical is *kāng* (pronounced *làng* in reverse). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that *kàng* also means "to match. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it is composed of the radical *ren* (人) with the phonetic *kàng* (亢). The lower part is *tíng* (亭) in reverse. Gu Yewang says it means "a pair" (*ǒu*) or "to resist" (*xiāng jù*). The *Shuowen* says it is composed of the radical *zhī* (攴) with the phonetic *chì* (啻). The character is written as *kàng* in the *Lunyu*; it is a vulgar form. *Chì* is pronounced *dí*.

Volume Fifty-Three, Part Five. Regarding "frost and hail" (*shuangbo*): according to the *Baihutong*, "hail is formed when yin qi gathers and coagulates. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states, "Yang manifests as rain; when yin qi oppresses it, it congeals and becomes hail. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says, "Hail is rain-water; it takes the radical 'rain' and the phonetic 'bao'; in ancient script it was written as 𤿓."

*Menkǔn* (門閫): *kǔn* is pronounced as *kun* with the *zhǎng* tone. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states that "the *kǔn* is the threshold of a door. The *Zītǒng* states it is composed of the radical "door" (*mén*) and the phonetic "enclosure" (*kùn*), though some versions write it with the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) as *kǔn*.

Volume Fifty-four: Volume fifty-four contains no characters with phonetic transcriptions. Volume Fifty-five: *Yīhù* (依怙): *hù* is pronounced as *hú* with the *gǔ* tone. The *Erya* states that "it means to rely upon or depend on. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "ancient" (*gǔ*).

The character *nǎo* (煩) is pronounced with the "nu" and "lǎo" finals; its phonetic component is said to signify "sorrowful vexation. Women often experience much vexation and resentment; thus, the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is formed from the radical "woman" (*nǚ*) and the phonetic component "a simplified form of *lǎo*" (*lǎo*). The character used in the *Lunyu* (Analects), *nǎo*, is also interchangeable.

Fifty-sixth Fascicle. Vairambha Wind (the *v* in *Vairambha* is pronounced as in "fū" [扶], and the *l* in *Lambha* is pronounced as in "lán" [覽]; in Sanskrit, this wind is named the Great Fierce Wind).

Volume Fifty-seven, Volume Fifty-seven. No phonetic glosses for characters. Volume Fifty-eight, Volume Fifty-eight. "Guǎngxiá" (廣陿): both characters are pronounced *jiǎ* (甲). This was already explained in the seventeenth volume above; the term "xiá" (狹) is derived from "quǎn" (犬) [dog] and is a vulgar character.

Volume Fifty-nine, Part Five. "Pivot" (*shū*). The upper character *chù* (觸) is pronounced *zhú* (朱). Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "The pivot of a door leaf. He further notes: "The pivot is that which holds the door, serving as its support for stability. Han Kangbo’s commentary on the *Zhouyi* states: "The pivot is the master of motion. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "qu" (*qū*). The lower character, the standard form for "fan" (*shàn*), is pronounced *xiānzhàn* (羶戰).

60. Fascicle Sixty. Regarding the character 滴 (dì): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "the pouring of water. It is composed of the radical 水 (water) with the phonetic 啻 (chì). It is also written as 適 (shì); the version in the *Lun* (Treatise) uses 渧 (tì), which is a vulgar character.

Volume Seven of the Seventh Bundle of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Volume Sixty-one. Regarding the character for "māo" (貓): according to Gu Yewang, it resembles a tiger but is smaller; those kept by common households are used for catching rats. The *Zitong* states that it is composed of "zhài" (豸) as the radical and "miao" (苗) as the phonetic. The treatise (*lun*) writes it as "mao" (猫). Regarding the character for "li" (貍): according to Gu Yewang, it is also a species of cat that is fond of stealing chickens from people's homes. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as a crouching beast, composed of "zhài" (豸) as the radical and "li" (里) as the phonetic. The treatise writes it with the "dog" radical as "li" (狸), which is a vulgar form. The pronunciation of "zhài" (豸) is "chi" (雉).

62. Fascicle Sixty-two. Regarding the character *shuang* (雙), Jiang Fanggu said that *shuang* means "two. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* states that it consists of two *jui* (隹) held by two hands, following the *chou* (雔) radical; to derive it from two [characters] to form *wang* (䨥) is incorrect.

63. Fascicle Sixty-three. "Ling-lie" (羸劣): *Du*’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that it means "weak"; the *Shuowen* says it means "emaciated," composed of the radical "sheep" (*yang*) with the phonetic "ling" (*ling*), pronounced as *luo-wo* (騾臥反).

64. Fascicle Sixty-Four. *Zhémiè* (擇滅). [Note on characters: "Zhé" (擇) is pronounced *zhènggé* (棖格). It means to examine or select; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is formed with the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "yào" (睪), which is pronounced *yì* (亦). The reading "cōng" (捀) found in the *Lùn* (論) is an error.

65. Fascicle Sixty-Five. "Ogha" (pùliú): [The character] *bào* (pronounced *fǎo*) is explained in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as "swift rain," composed of the radical for water (*shui*) and the phonetic element *bào*. It is also pronounced *bào*.
The term *yè* (轅) is pronounced *guìfǎn* (革反); its detailed explanation is completed in the forty-eighth fascicle of the preceding volume.

66. Fascicle Sixty-six. Regarding *qílǒng* (畦壟): the upper character *qí* (畦) is pronounced *huìguīfǎn* (惠圭反). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states: "A *qí* is like a *qū* (區, a plot). The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it is composed of the radical *tián* (田) with *guī* (圭) as the phonetic. The lower character *lǒng* (壟) is pronounced *lóngzhǒngfǎn* (龍腫反). Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* states that a *jièlüè* (界埒, a boundary embankment) resembles a plowed ridge (*gēnglǒng*), and thus it takes this as its name. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as a "mound" (*qiūlǒng*) composed of the radical *tǔ* (土) with *lóng* (龍) as the phonetic.

*Yun* (耘) and *nou* (耨): The former is pronounced with the initial *yun-jun* (上運君反). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that "yun" means to clear away weeds among the seedlings. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as consisting of the radical *lei* (耒) and the phonetic *yun* (云); the version using the radical *mu* (木) to form *yong* (枟) is an error. The latter, *nou*, is pronounced with the initial *nu-hou* (奴候反). According to the *Kaoseng Zhuan*, it is a farming tool for removing weeds; it is also written as *nou* (耨).
The term *gula* (劬勞)—with the first character pronounced as *ju* (具) and the second as *fu* (俱)—has already been fully explained in the fourteenth fascicle above.

*Śaṅkha* (餉佉)—the first character pronounced as *shāng* (商) with the radical *huài* (壞) and the second as *qiāng* (羌) with the radical *jiā* (迦)—is a name for a rishi (seer) from the Western land of India.

67. Volume Sixty-seven. "Mao" (貿): The initial radical is *mao* (矛, with the *hou* [候] tone). Gu Yewang states that "mao" means "to exchange. The *Erya* says, "Mao is market trade," and it also means "to sell. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the "shell" (*bei*) radical and the phonetic "yuan" (夗); it is also written as "mo" (󲯻). The version in the *Lunyu* (Analects) uses "fu" (𧴵), which is a vulgar character.

Volume Sixty-Eight. Regarding "Warmth" (*uṣman*): In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "warmth" (*uṣman*) means "to warm. It is composed of the radical "fire" (*huo*) and the phonetic "ruan" (*nu duan fan*). It is also written as *yuan* or *nan*.

Volume Sixty-nine. "Shūhōng" (倏怱): The *Chuci* states that "shūhōng" describes a state of haste. The *Wenzi Dian* explains it as being composed of the radical "fire" (火) and the phonetic "you" (攸); the character "shu" (儵) is also used interchangeably.

70. Fascicle Seventy. Regarding "xīnxiǎng" (歆饗): the upper character "xīn" (歆) is pronounced with the initial *x* and final *-iǎn* (according to the Duan [Zhu] commentary on the *Zuozhuan*, it means "to enjoy"; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "the spirit consuming qi," composed of the radical "quàn" [欠] and the phonetic "xiāng"). The lower character "xiǎng" (饗) is pronounced with the initial *x* and final *-zhǎng*. Hé Xiū’s commentary on the *Gongyang Zhuan* states: "To drink fine broth is called xiǎng. Zhèng’s commentary states: "The spirits and deities xīnxiǎng [enjoy]. According to the *Wenzi Dianshuo*, it is composed of the radical "shí" (食) and the phonetic "xiāng" (鄉).

*Mi-shùn* (不瞬): *shùn* is pronounced with the water radical and the *rùn* rhyme. The *Shuowen* states: "To open and close the eyes repeatedly; it is written with the radical 'eye' and the phonetic 'shùn. It is also written as *zhùn*.

Volume 8, Eighth Bundle, *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Volume 71, Bundle 8. *Jīng-zhé* (驚慴): *zhé* is pronounced with the *zhān-yè* rhyme. The *Erya* states: "To be terrified. The *Shuowen* states: "It is written with the radical 'heart' and the phonetic 'xí. It is also written as *zhè*."

72. Volume Seventy-two. "Zuan" (pronounced *cuàn*) is a homophone for "luán. It is a name for fire; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "metal" (*jin*) with the phonetic element "zan" (*zàn*).
"Shuo" (pronounced *shuò*) is a homophone for "shāng"; "jiéluó" (pronounced *jiéluó*; first tone) is a homophone for "cìjiàn" (pronounced *cìjiàn*; fourth tone). This is the Sanskrit name for Śakra.

73. Volume Seventy-Three. Regarding "yìshì" (polishing/wiping): the upper character is pronounced *yīng* (with the tone reversed) as in the first volume previously explained; the lower character is pronounced *shī* (with the tone reversed). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means to wipe clean or to purify; it is formed from the radical "hand" (*shou*) with the phonetic component "shì" (*shi*).

*Chuán* (篅) is pronounced *shù yuán fǎn* (述緣反). Xu Shuchong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states: "A *chuán* is a deep pit. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "A *chuán* is a circular bamboo vessel for holding grain; it is composed of the radical 'bamboo' (*zhú*) and the phonetic 'duān' (*duān*). It may also be written as *chuí* (圌); *tún* (窀) is pronounced *dú hù fǎn* (徒䘱反)."
*Tāo* (pronounced *dào láo fǎn*): The *Wenzi Didian* states that *tāo* means a great wave; the tide of the sea is called *tāo*. It is composed of the radical "water" (*shui*) and the phonetic "shòu.

*Biāo zhì* (pronounced *bì yáo fǎn*): Gu Yewang says that *biāo* refers to erecting a marker to identify something. The *Wenzi Didian* states it is composed of the radical "water" (*shui*) and the phonetic "piào"—this is an error for "hand" (*shou*) as the radical when forming *biāo*. The lower character is pronounced *chī chì fǎn*. The *Guǎngyá* states it means "to flutter" (*chì lián*). The *Wenzi Didian* states it is composed of the radical "cloth" (*jin*) and the phonetic "zhí"; *zhí* is pronounced *zhí*.

Volume Seventy-four. Volume Seventy-four contains no phonetic glosses. 75. Volume Seventy-five. Regarding "piàn" (派): according to the *Guǎyá*, it means water branching out in separate streams; the *Shuōwén* defines it as water flowing obliquely and separately, being a pictograph. In the *Lùn* (Discourse), it is written with the "water" radical (*shuǐ*), and its meaning is the same.

*Xièhà* (上袄典反): The *Wenzí jílüè* says it is an aquatic-shelled insect; it resembles a clam but is smaller. It is also written as *xiǎn*, meaning a small slug, and is also called *yìnǚ*. (下甘臘反): According to the *Kǎoshēng*, it is a species of clam or oyster. The *Shuōwén* states that there are three kinds of *líng* all produced from the sea: the *hálì* is transformed from a thousand-year-old sparrow; the *hǎi gù* is transformed from a hundred-year-old swallow; and the *kuáihé*—also called *fùlěi*—is transformed from a *fùyì*. [The character is] composed of "insect" (*chóng*) and the phonetic "hé."

The character for *dàn* (gallbladder) has the phonetic "xiàn-yán" as its upper radical and "kǎo" as its sound. *Xián* (saliva) refers to the moisture in the mouth; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "liquid from the mouth," composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) with "qiàn" as its phonetic, or alternatively written as *sǎn*, *yīn*, or *tián*. In the *Lunheng*, it is written as *xián*. This is a vulgar form. The lower part has the phonetic "dān-lǎn. The *Baihutong* states: "The gallbladder (*dàn*) is the *fǔ* (organ) of the liver (*gān*). According to the *Shuowen*, [the character for *gān*] is composed of the radical "flesh" (*ròu*) with "zhān" as its phonetic.

*Kāo* (窑): Pronounced *zhāo*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "A kiln for firing tiles; it is formed with the radical 'cave' (*xué*) and the phonetic 'lamb' (*lǎo*). The *Lunheng* uses the character *táo* (陶), meaning to form clay; it refers to the master potter. According to the *Shiben*, Kunwu invented pottery (*táo*); he was a minister of Jie of the Xia dynasty. This does not carry the meaning of "kiln. *Dào* (竈): Pronounced *zāo*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "The hearth for cooking; it is formed with the radical 'cave' (*xué*) and the abbreviated phonetic 'qū' (*qǔ*). The sound of *qū* is *cáilù*. Alternatively, the character may not be abbreviated.

*Chen-feng* (鍼風): *chen* is pronounced as *zhí* (熎) and *fǎn* (反). According to the *Guǎyá*, it means "to prick" (*cì*). The *Shuōwén* states that it is composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) with the phonetic component "xián" (*xiánshēng*).

There is the wind called *pójǔlāmó* (婆咀窶拉摩); *zuǒ* (咀) is pronounced as *cáiyǔ* (才與) and *fǎn* (反), *jǔ* (窶) as *qúrǔ* (劬乳) and *fǎn* (反), and *là* (拉) as *lánhé* (嵐合) and *fǎn* (反). These are Sanskrit terms; *lán* (嵐) is pronounced as *lúhán* (盧含) and *fǎn* (反).
The character for "throat" (喉) is pronounced with the initial *k'ao* and the final *shin*.

It refers to the palate (*yin*). 76. Volume Seventy-Six. The character for "owl" (鵂鶹) has the initial *hsiu* (朽憂反) and the final *chou* (󳌞周反). According to the commentary, the owl belongs to the class of strange birds; its species are indeed numerous.

Volume Seventy-seven, Volume Seventy-seven, No Phonetic Explanations. Volume Seventy-eight, Volume Seventy-eight. *Jiāo* (膠): Upper tone, pronounced like *jiāo* (交) or *kǎo* (考). It means "to solidify. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "glue" (*jiāochí*). It is made from animal hide; it follows the radical for "flesh" (*pí*) and takes *liáo* (翏) as its phonetic component. Below, *nièlián* (聶廉) is the reading. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to adhere" or "to paste"; it follows the radical for "grain" (*mǐ*) and takes *zhàn* (占) as its phonetic component. The correct form is *nián* (黏).
Volume Seventy-nine. *Cini* (pronounced *yi-ni*, first tone;
*mi-ni* pronounced *mi-bi*, second tone);
*tàn* (pronounced *tán*, fourth tone)—these are Sanskrit terms.
*Dàfǎng* (達𮒅): The *fǎnqie* (phonetic analysis) is *pó-zàn-xiá*. This is the name for the Four Heavenly Kings in the Sanskrit language. [80] Volume Eighty. [The character] *kǎo* (穬):

The *fǎnqie* is *mǎng-fǎn*. It is the sound of *kǎo*. *Kǎo* refers to large wheat (*dàmài*). Dictionaries of characters state that it is derived from the radical "grain" (*huò*) and the phonetic "broad" (*guǎng*), or sometimes written as *jù* (󰎣). To claim it is derived from "rice" (*mǐ*) and written as *chōu* (䊯) is incorrect.

9. The Ninth Bundle of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, from Volume Eighty-one to Volume Two Hundred.
Volume Eighty-one. Regarding "pú-hú" (瓠壺):

Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states that "pú" means a gourd-pitcher (*hú*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "gourd" (*guā*) with the phonetic component "kuā" (詡, pronounced *xǔ yú* or in the upper tone). Furthermore, the term for "discourse" (*lùn*) is written with the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) as "lún" (󲾰), which is a vulgar character.

82. Volume Eighty-two, Part Two. *Cūn* (皴). [The character is pronounced with the initial *qūn* (七荀反). *Pīcāng* states: "It refers to *cūn* (皴皵). The *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of the radical *pí* (皮) and the phonetic *jùn* (夋); *jùn* has the same pronunciation as above, while *qiè* (皵) is pronounced with the initial *qī* (七略反). Guo's commentary on the *Shanhaijing* states: "*Qiè* is also called skin *cūn*."

83. Volume Eighty-three. [The character] 𥎞 (móu): the upper radical is 莫 (mò) with the phonetic value *hóu*. The *Shuowen* states it is a *qiú-móu* (a long spear), two zhang in length, mounted on a war chariot; it is a pictograph. In ancient and modern usage, it is written as 𢦵. The lower part is 催 (cuī) with the phonetic value *suàn*. According to the *Kao*, *hóng* refers to a short spear. The *Guangya* states that *hóng* is called *chán*. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* explains that it takes 矛 (*móu*) as the radical and 贊 (*zàn*) as the phonetic component; *chán* is pronounced *kǒu-yán*.

Śāri (鶖鷺): the first character is pronounced *qiū* (autumn) and the second is pronounced with the *lù* (ancient: *gù*) rhyme; it is both the name of a pond in Western countries and the name of a bird. Śarabha (蚇蠖):
the first character is pronounced *niǎo* (bird) and the second with the *shēng* (ancient: *kǎo*) rhyme; it is the name of an insect commonly known as the "stepping-bend" (*bùqū*) insect.

Regarding the characters 塳 and 𡋯: the former is pronounced *pú* (with the radical 僕) and the latter is pronounced *mén* (with the radical 盆沒). In the *Lunwen* (Treatise), "塳𡋯" refers to the appearance of smoke and vapors; the character is now written as 𤑫 or 烰, yet neither of these forms exists in the standard dictionaries.
*Vasiṣṭhā*: "Chai" (坼) is pronounced according to the *ke* (坼) rhyme; it is a term from the Sanskrit language (*Brahmī*) referring to the name of a wife of a *brahmin*.

Regarding the character "gua" (刮), Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "Gua means to scrape away using a blade. The *Wenzi Dian* (Dictionary of Characters) explains: "It is formed with 'dao' (刀, blade) as the radical and 'she' (舌, tongue) as the phonetic component; the pronunciation of 'she' is 'hua' (滑)."

Regarding the character *jīng* (矜), it is pronounced as *huā* (花) in the reverse [rhyme]. Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shūjìng* states: "Jīng is like *jiāozì* (憍恣); it means to be excessively self-important. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical *yán* (言) and the phonetic *wù* (𡗢). It is composed of *dà* (大) and *pǔ* (󱸰), with the latter pronounced as *kūhuà* (枯化). Those who claim it is composed of *kuā* (夸) are incorrect.

Volume Eighty-Four. [The character] 脹 (zhàng): the upper radical is 犭 (pú, pronounced with the *jiǎng* rhyme); according to the *Pīcāng*, it also means "corpulent" or "bloated. The lower part is 張 (zhāng, pronounced with the *liàng* rhyme). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that it refers to the abdomen being full and bloated. In both ancient and modern standard characters, it follows the meat radical (月) and the phonetic 丰 (fēng) with the sound *cháng*; alternatively, it may be written as 庠 (xiáng) with the illness radical (疒), meaning "to swell" or "to be bloated."

Volume Eighty-Five. [The character] *wǎn* (pronounced with the initial *yuǎn*): according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to turn" (*zhuǎn*). It is composed of the radical "night" (*xī*) and the phonetic "ba" (*pā*). The pronunciation of "ba" may be abbreviated, or it may also be written as *wǎn*, which is likewise acceptable.

*Bào nòng* (抱弄): The first character is pronounced *shàng páo lǒng dōng fǎn* (上袍籠東反) and the second is pronounced *dù zhù zuǒ zhuàn yún nòng xì yě* (杜注左傳云弄戲也). The *Erya* (爾雅) states it means "to play with" (*wán yě*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文) explains it as composed of the radical *kǒng* (廾) and the phonetic *yù* (玉). The reading *cǎo* (艸) with the pronunciation *gǒng* (拱) found in the *Lun* (論) is incorrect. It should be *jié* (挊).

86. Volume Eighty-Six. *Diaoju* (掉舉). [The character] "diao" (掉) is pronounced with the tone of *diao* (弔); the *Guoyu* commentary states that it means "to sway. The *Guoyi* (廣雅) defines it as "to shake. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文解字) explains it as being composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "zhuo" (卓).

87. Volume Eighty-Seven. Regarding "si" (伺), Yě Wáng states that "si" means "to wait" (候). Zhèng Xuàn’s commentary on the *Zōu Lǐ* states that "si" means "to observe" (察). According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "person" (人) with "si" (司) as its phonetic.

Volume Eighty-Eight, Volume Eighty-Eight: No Explanatory Glosses. Volume Eighty-Nine, Volume Eighty-Nine: *Jí* (嫉). The upper radical is *qín* (秦), which is pronounced with the *xī* (悉) rhyme. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that "to harm the worthy is called *jí*. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *nǚ* (女) and the phonetic *jí* (疾), with the lower part pronounced with the *kè* (客) rhyme. It means "to be stingy" (*lìn*). The *Gōngjīn zhèngzì* (Ancient and Modern Standard Characters) states that it is composed of the radical *gé* (革) and the phonetic *xiān* (臤); the character *qiān* (慳) used in the *Lùn* (論) is a vulgar form.

90. Fascicle Ninety: Fascicle Ninety. *Kalala* and *Arbuda*. (The term *arbuda* is pronounced according to the Sanskrit; it refers to the first and second weeks after conception, when the union of semen and blood has been received but has not yet taken form.)
*Xiù* (to smell): *xiū* (with the final syllable reversed). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to bring the nose toward an odor.

It is composed of the radical for "nose" and the character for "odor," with the latter also serving as the phonetic component. Volume 10, the tenth fascicle of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicles 91–96. Fascicle 91, Fascicle 92, Fascicle 93, Fascicle 94, Fascicle 95, Fascicle 96. The above six fascicles have easily legible text and are not provided with phonetic glosses. Fascicle 97. Fascicle 97: *Āgama*. *Āgama*: *jīn* (with the final syllable reversed).

Volume Ninety-Eight, Scroll Ninety-Eight. *Qíng* (勍): The upper radical is *qù* (巨), pronounced with the *yíng* (迎) rhyme. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "martial"; according to the *Běicāng*, it means "vigorous. The *Zuǒzhuan* states, "a person of *qíng* strength," which refers to this. The *Shuowén* defines it as "strong" (*qiáng*), composed of the radical *lì* (力) and the phonetic *jīng* (京). The lower character is *tíng* (亭), pronounced with the *lì* (歷) rhyme.

Volume Ninety-nine, Scroll Ninety-nine. *Piao* (飄): Upper radical *piāo* (匹霄反). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states: "Piao is like blowing. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as a whirling wind, composed of the radical *feng* (wind) with the phonetic *piao*. *Piao* is the same [as the following character]. Lower radical *shān gàn* (珊幹反). Gu Yewang says: "San" means to disperse, flowing apart and flying away without gathering. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as flying and scattering, composed of the radical *zhi* (支) with the phonetic *xi* (昔); alternatively, it is written as *bō* (󲿂) with the radical *huán* (雚). The version in the *Lunyu* uses "san" (散), which is a vulgar character.
*Mihou* (獼猴): The first character is pronounced *mi* (with the rhyme *miǎn*), and the second is pronounced *hòu* (with the rhyme *gōu*).

This is the name of a region in the Western Countries. 100. Volume One Hundred. *Hebin* (訶擯): The first character is pronounced *he* (with the rhyme *bì*), and the second is pronounced *bìn*. Sīmà Biāo’s commentary on the *Zhuāngzǐ* states that *bìn* means "to cast away. The *Shījì* says, "They mutually excluded and cast one another out. The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "bīn" (*bīn shēng*). The version written as *pìn* (擯) is a vulgar character.

Volume Eleven of the Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Volumes 101–102. Volumes 101 and 102 contain no word-by-word commentary or glosses. Volume 103. Regarding the character 𦞦 (fù) in the title of Volume 103: according to the *Cangjie pian*, it means "to overturn. Lexicons state that it is pronounced with the initial *xī* and the final *fù*. According to Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci*, when there are vegetables it is called *gēng* (soup), and when there are no vegetables it is called *fù*. The *Shuowen jiezi* states it is composed of the radical 肉 (meat) and the phonetic 𦞦, and its pronunciation is *huò* (呼郭反).

Regarding the character for *luàn* (羂): the upper radical is *jiān* (㳙, pronounced with the *qiǎn* and *yǎn* finals). The *Guìyuàn Zhūcóng* states that to encircle and bind an object with a rope is called a *luàn*. The *Zītǒng* writes it as *jù* (󱺍), stating it means "to lay a rope upon a path. It is composed of the phonetic *yuán* (肙) with the lower radical *sāng* (桑, pronounced with the *gè* final). Gu Yewáng says that to twist ropes together is called a *suǒ* (索). The *Shuōwén* states: "Herbs and trees that have stems and leaves can be used to make ropes and cords; it is composed of the radical *mì* (糸) and the phonetic *shì* (市)."

*Shao* (pronounced with the initial *mo* and the final *si*, reversed; a sound like *kao*; a type of *ge*). It was already explained previously in the eighty-third fascicle. Sometimes it is written as *mao*. According to the *Guangya*, *shao* is a weapon, and it is also a *mao*. The *Picao* states that the *shao* is one zhang eight chi in length. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* says it follows the radical for *mao* and takes *xiao* as its phonetic component; the *Lun* [text] writes it as *nan*, which is incorrect.
