According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical for "food" (*shí*) and the phonetic *ěr*. **Èr (Bait)**: Pronounced with the initial *ěr*. It refers to food. The *Daida li* says it is the bait obtained by hawks, falcons, fish, and turtles. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical for "food" (*shí*) and the phonetic *ěr*.

Regarding "bian" (鞭) and "ta" (撻): Bian refers to using leather to strike those who have committed offenses. The *Yiwen leiju* states that bian uses leather to punish criminals. The *Shuowen jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "metal" (革) with the phonetic "bian" (便), and the character below is pronounced "tada" (他怛反). Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that ta means "chastisement" (笞). Zheng Xuan interprets it as "to support" (扶). The standard orthography of the present day is composed of the radical "hand" (手) with the phonetic "da" (達). The archaic form is written as "ta" (撻). To compose it from the radical "grass" (艹) as "zha" (靼)—pronounced "zhe" (折)—is incorrect in meaning.
*Yātana* (transliterated as 󰁨邏吒): the first character is pronounced *pí* (with the *jì* tone), the middle *luó* (with the *hè* tone), and the last *chá* (with the *xiá* tone).

This is a Sanskrit term. Regarding "imprisonment" (*qiú zhì*): *zhì* is pronounced with the *zhèn* (with the *lì*) tone. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that *zhì* means to restrain, bind, and fetter. This was already explained in the fiftieth fascicle [of this work].

"Cuàn" (pronounced with the *qī* and *luàn* tones; Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states that "cuàn" means "to hide"; Gu Yewang says "cuàn" is synonymous with "to flee"). This character for "correct orthography" from ancient to modern times consists of the "cave" (*xué*) radical and the "mouse" (*shǔ*) component, forming a semantic compound.
126. Fascicle One Hundred and Twenty-Six. *Vāśiṣṭha* (the character *se* is pronounced *xi*; the character *ji* is pronounced *li*).
This term has already been fully explained in the seventh fascicle of this treatise.

*Tiánjì* (恬寂): The upper radical is *dàn* (簟, read as *jiān fǎn*). The Master Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states that *tián* means "peaceful" (*ān*) and according to the *Fāngyán*, it means "tranquil" (*jìng*). It is formed from the semantic element *xīn* (心) and the phonetic element *shé* (舌); it is also a word formed through a combination of meaning and sound. 127. Fascicle One Hundred and Twenty-Seven. *Xiàohǒu* (哮吼):

The upper character is *xiào* (孝, read as *jiāo fǎn*). The *Bīcāng* states that *xiào hè* refers to a great rage. The *Gōngjīn Zhèngzì* states that *xiào* is the sound of a startled pig; it is formed from the semantic element *kǒu* (口) and the phonetic element *xiào* (孝). The lower character is *hǒu* (吼, read as *xū gǒu fǎn*). The *Kǎoshēng* states that this refers to a loud cry. For oxen and tigers, it is called *hǒu*. The *Gōngjīn Zhèngzì* writes it as *hūn* (吽), referring to the sound of beasts; it is formed from the semantic element *niú* (牛) and the phonetic element *kǒu* (口). It is also written as *jū* (拘) or *fǔ* (呴).

128. Fascicle One Hundred and Twenty-Eight. *Maśaka-makṣikā* (Mosquitoes and Gnats). The first character, *wu*, is pronounced as in *wufen* (勿分); the second, *mian*, is pronounced as in *mianjie* (眠結). This has already been fully explained in Fascicle One Hundred and Twenty.

129. Fascicle One Hundred and Twenty-nine. No Phonetic Explanations for Characters. 130. Fascicle One Hundred and Thirty. *Yìn* (飲): *xuàn* (吮) is pronounced with the *xiàn* (兖) rhyme. The *Jìxùn* states that *yǔn* (嗍) refers to sucking at the mouth. The *Shuōwén* defines *yǔn* as sucking (*chù*) and explains it as being composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic component "yǔn" (*yǔnshēng*). The version in the *Lùn* (論) written as *𠵷* is incorrect; it is sometimes written as *yuān* (冤).

*Meng* (melted bronze): Upper radical *yǒng* (zhōng fǎn). The *Hànshū* states: "It is like gold in the crucible, depending solely on what the smith casts. The *Shuowén* says: "A method for forging vessels; it takes the metal radical and the phonetic *róng*."

The character 舌 (tongue) is pronounced with the radical 口 (mouth) and the phonetic 昂 (áng); the sound 考 (kǎo) refers to the gums. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as 㖾; the version following the mouth radical as 舌 is incorrect.

The character 沙 (sand) is pronounced with the radical 水 (water) and the phonetic 單 (dān). The *Erya* states that "潬" (tàn) means sand emerging [from the water]; the sound 孝 (xiào) indicates that it is sand emerging from within the water. The *Shuowen Jiezi* takes the water radical and the phonetic 單.

*Jiewan* (嗟惋): The upper character is pronounced *jie* (邪反). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that "jue" (嗟) is an exclamation. The *Gujin Zhengzi* states it is an expression of sorrowful lamentation, composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic "cha" (*chā*). The lower character is pronounced *wàn* (烏喚反). The *Kaosheng* states it is a sigh of regret; the *Wenzi Jilüe* states it means astonishment or wonder, composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "wǎn" (*wǎn*).

The character 𨥨 (hóng) is pronounced with the upper radical 莫 (mò) and the phonetic 侯 (hóu). It was previously explained in the 103rd fascicle. The ancient form was 矛 (máo). The lower part, 倉 (cāng), has the pronunciation 喚 (huàn). The *Kǎoshēng* states that 𨥨 is a short spear; the people of Nan Yue call it 𥍟. The *Guǎngyá* states that 𨥨 is called 鋋 (chán). Regarding the standard characters for "ancient" and "modern," they follow the radical 矛 (máo) and the phonetic 贊 (zàn). The archaic form is 󳌅; the version in the current *Lùn-wén* (Treatise on Characters) as 攢 (cuán) is incorrect.

14. The Fourteenth Bundle: Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Volume 131 (Fourteenth Bundle). 131. Volume One Hundred and Thirty-One. *Dengnie* (登躡): In the *Fangyan*, it means "to step upon. In the *Guoyaya*, it means "to tread. In the *Shuowen*, it means "to tread. It is composed of the radical for "foot" (*zu*) and the phonetic element *nie*.

The term *zhǔnduō* (準陀)—where *zhǔn* is pronounced with the initial *zhū* and rhyme *yǔn* according to the *Fàn yǔ* (Sanskrit)—is translated as "to mix. In the *Zhèng zhù* (Commentary by Zheng) on the *Lǐjì*, it states that *róu* means "to intermingle.

The *Wénzì diǎnshuō* (Dictionary of Characters and Explanations) explains that the character is composed of the radical *mǐ* (grain) and the phonetic *róu*; its correct form is *jiē* (粈). *Zhǔnduō* (準陀): *Zhǔn* is pronounced with the initial *zhū* and rhyme *yǔn* according to the *Fàn yǔ*. 132. Volume One Hundred and Thirty-Two. Volume One Hundred and Thirty-Two. *Xiāng* (相): pronounced with the final *jiù* (糅). In the *Zhèng zhù* on the *Lǐjì*, it says *róu* means "to mix. The *Wénzì diǎnshuō* states it is composed of the radical *mǐ* and the phonetic *róu*; the correct form is *jiē*.
133. Fascicle One Hundred and Thirty-Three. *Panta-pata* (the sound of *panta-pata* is pronounced with the *tu-ye* rhyme). This is the Sanskrit term for the "Great Calamity Wind."

*Fán* (翻): The upper radical is *fú* (孚) with the phonetic *yuán* (袁). The *Guǎngyǎ* states it means "to fly. Gù Yěwáng says it means "to soar upward. The *Shuōwén* explains it as composed of the radical *fēi* (飛) and the phonetic *fān* (番); it is also written as *fān* (翻). The lower character is *dèng* (登) with the phonetic *dēng* (登). The *Mānhàn Shī* states it means "to ascend" (*téng*). There is nothing that one does not ascend; it is deep. The *Guǎngyǎ* states it means "to gallop. The *Shuōwén* states it means "to race. It is composed of the radical *mǎ* (馬) and the abbreviated phonetic *téng* (騰). That which is composed of the radicals *zhōu* (舟) and *yuè* (月) is incorrect. *Shèng* (勝): [The character] is composed of the radical *zhōu* (舟) and the radical *yuè* (月); this is incorrect. [It should be composed of the radical *shǒu* (手) and the phonetic *shèng* (勝)]. (Note: The final sentence regarding *shèng* appears to be a philological correction appended to the entry for *fán*, pointing out an error in the composition of the character *shèng*.)

Regarding "plowing" (耕): it is pronounced *jù* (according to the rhyme dictionary). Regarding "driving" (馭), the character dictionary explains that it means to drive or harness horses; it is composed of the radical for "horse" (馬) and the hand (又), and is identical to "to guide" (御).
Regarding "striking" (𭢗), it is pronounced *cú huán* (according to the rhyme dictionary); this was already explained previously in the one hundred fifteenth fascicle.

134. Fascicle One Hundred and Thirty-Four. *Yīngchán* (縈纏). The upper character, *yīng* (縈), is pronounced with the initial *yī* (伊) and the final *yíng* (營). The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (毛詩傳) states that it means "to wind and turn. The *Shuōwén* (說文) defines it as "to gather and fold," composed of the radical *mì* (糸) and the phonetic *yíng* (熒) in abbreviated form. The lower character, *chán* (纏), is pronounced with the initial *chè* (徹) and the final *lián* (連). The *Shuōwén* defines it as "to bind and constrain," composed of the radical *mì* (糸) and the phonetic *chán* (廛).

135. Fascicle One Hundred and Thirty-Five. **Bǎi (擺):** Upper radical *bāi* (八), read with the *shàng* tone; the *guǎng yǎ* states that it means "to open" (*pī kāi*). Regarding its phonetic value, it refers to waving the hands. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "striking with both hands," composed of the radical *shǒu* (hand) and the phonetic *bà* (罷). It is also written as *yā* (押); the version in the *Lùn* (論) using *bǎi* is an error. Lower radical: *tú* (訥), read with the *dù* tone. The *Guǎng yǎ* states that it means "to guard" (*wèi*). Lexicons state it means "to rub" (*kuài*). The *Shuōwén* defines it as being composed of the radical *shǒu* (hand) and the phonetic *tū* (突). *Tū* (突) is composed of *xué* (穴, cave) and *quǎn* (犬, dog); the version in the *Lùn* using *shān* (山, mountain) for *tū* is incorrect. **Tù (捽):** Lower radical: *tú* (訥), read with the *dù* tone. The *Guǎng yǎ* states that it means "to guard" (*wèi*). Lexicons state it means "to rub" (*kuài*). The *Shuōwén* defines it as being composed of the radical *shǒu* (hand) and the phonetic *tū* (突). *Tū* (突) is composed of *xué* (穴, cave) and *quǎn* (犬, dog); the version in the *Lùn* using *shān* (山, mountain) for *tū* is incorrect.

136. Fascicle One Hundred and Thirty-Six. *Ji* (upper character pronounced *qin* and *ru*, lower character pronounced *jing* and *xi*). The *Mao Shi Jian* states that *ji* means "to continue. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* says it means "to succeed" or "to follow. The *Shuowen* also uses this character. Both characters are written with the radical for silk (*mi*) and take *ze* and *ju* as their phonetic components.

*Chui* (毳): The character is pronounced *shuan* (巛) with the *rui* (苪) rhyme; Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states that it refers to the finest of animal hairs. Zheng Zhong says it is a garment made of *chui* wool. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of three [strokes representing] hair.

Regarding *dou sou* (抖擻): the first character is pronounced *dou kou* (兜口) and the second *sou hou* (涑厚). The *Kaosheng* states that *dousou* means to shake or toss. The pronunciation of *sou* is *sou si* (叜俟).

Volume 137, Scroll 137; No Phonetic Explanations. Volume 138, Scroll 138. Regarding "須" (xū): In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical 彡 (sān) and the phonetic 頁 (yè). Gu Yewang states that it refers to the necessity or waiting for something. It is written with 彡 as the radical. [Note: There is also a character written with 水 (shui), pronounced huì. Although this common usage has long been established, we shall follow it here. Regarding "斂" (liǎn): Pronounced yán according to the *Kaozheng*. Regarding "鎌" (lián): It is an implement for reaping. In the *Fangyan*, it is called "刈𠚸" (yì zhì). In the *Shuowen*, it means "to cut" (kè). It is composed of the radical 金 (jīn) and the phonetic 兼 (jiān). It may also be written as 鐮, which is likewise correct. "𠚸" is pronounced gōu.

*Chā* (pronounced with a retroflex *ch*, as in *chū*) is a term from the *Shēnglèi* (Classifications of Sounds). It means to pierce an object so that it enters. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "zhǎo" (*zhǎo*).

The character "zhǎo" is composed of "thousand" (*qiān*) and "mortar" (*jiù*). Volume 139–140. Volumes 139 and 140 contain no phonetic glosses. Fascicle 15 of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*. Fascicle 15. Volume 141. Volume 141. *Jiāonìng* (upper: *jiǎoyáo*; lower: *níngdìng*). The commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* by Du Yu states that *nìng* means mud. Regarding the sound, it refers to muddy mire. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic "níng. The pronunciation of *nào* is *nǚjiào*.

The character *jú* (局) is pronounced with the initial *kai* and the final *fan*. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that it means "crooked" (*qū*) and "curled" (*juǎn*). The *Guang Ya* defines it as "near" (*jìn*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "*Jú* means 'constricted' (*cù*); it is composed of the radical *kǒu* (mouth) beneath the character *chǐ* (foot), and is further joined by the element *gù* (hook). It is a pictograph."

142. Fascicle One Hundred Forty-Two. *Púfú* (匍匐): The first character is pronounced *pú* (with the phonetic component *bǔ*) and the second is pronounced *fú* (with the phonetic component *běi*). The *Mao Shī Jiàn* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry) states: "‘Púfú’ means to exert one’s utmost strength. Gu Yewáng says: "It refers to crawling on hands. The *Shuōwén* (Explanations of Simple and Compound Characters) states: "‘Pú’ is crawling on hands; ‘fú’ is prostrating on the ground. Both characters are written with the radical *bāo* (勹). *Fǔ*, *fù*, and *bāo* are all homophonous sounds derived from *bāo*.

*Tān* (灘): Pronounced *tā-dān-fǎn*. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "a shallow place where water has receded and dried up. It is composed of the radical *shui* (water) with the phonetic *tān*. The lower character is pronounced *qīng-lì-fǎn*. The *Guangya* states that *cè* (磧) refers to a rapid or a shoal; it is a place where the water is shallow and stones are visible. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *shi* (stone) with the phonetic *zī* (𧵕).

Regarding "xué" (穴): the *Fǎnmao Shījì* states that digging into the earth is called a "xué"; the *Shuowén Jiězì* defines it as an earthen chamber, written with the radical "mián" (宀) and the phonetic "bā" (八).

Its occurrence here as "xué" is an error. 143. Volume One Hundred Forty-Three. Regarding "píng" (缾): both [readings] are pronounced "míng" (冥). Gù Yěwáng states that a "píng" is a vessel for drawing water. The *Wenzí Diǎnshuō* explains that it takes the character "gǔn" (𦅂) as its radical and "bìng" (并) as its phonetic.

*Cuòmiù* (錯謬): The first character, *cuò*, is pronounced with the initial *cāng* and the final *luò*. It means error or mistake. Gu Yewang states that it uses the "mistaken" (*cuò*) sense of intermingling and confusing; it follows the radical *chuò* (辵) and takes *xī* (㫺) as its phonetic component, reading *méi yòu*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* explains it as "delusion and error. The second character, *miù*, according to the *Shuōwén*, refers to the speech of a madman; it follows the radical *yán* (言) and takes *liáo* (翏) as its phonetic component.

144. Fascicle One Hundred Forty-Four. Fascicle One Hundred Forty-Four. No Phonetic Explanations. 145. Fascicle One Hundred Forty-Five. Fascicle One Hundred Forty-Five. *Mamanda* (the character *da* is pronounced like the second tone of *yu*); this is a Sanskrit term. 146. Fascicle One Hundred Forty-Six. Fascicle One Hundred Forty-Six. No Phonetic Explanations. 147. Fascicle One Hundred Forty-Seven. Fascicle One Hundred Forty-Seven. *Dun zuò* (the character *dun* is pronounced like *cu hún*; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to squat," composed of the radical for "foot" and the phonetic *zūn*; the character *jù* is pronounced like *jū yù*).

148. Fascicle 148. Regarding "埏埴" (yán zhí): the upper character is read as shè (set) with the fanqie "氈反" (zhān fǎn). The *Huainanzi* states that it means to knead and press earth to form vessels. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "延" (yán); those who write it with the radical "earth" (土) are incorrect. The lower character is read as zhí (shí) with the fanqie "軄反" (zhí fǎn). Master Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that when soil is sticky, it is called "埴" (zhí). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "earth" (土) and the phonetic "直" (zhí).
*Kon-nao* (Confusion/Chaos): The first character is pronounced *huí* (with the *wài* radical) and the second is pronounced *ná* (with the *xiào* radical).

This was already explained in detail in the twenty-sixth fascicle above. 149. Fascicle One Hundred and Forty-nine. *Mò-xīn* (Powdered Fuel): The first character is pronounced *mángbō* (with the *fǎn* radical) and the second is pronounced *xījīn*. This is a medicinal name from the Western Regions; in this country, it refers to things used for producing fire with mugwort (*ài*). *Hā*: Pronounced *gǎnhé* (with the *fǎn* radical).
"Nián" (拈): Pronounced tiān-fǎn; according to the *Guǎngyá*, "nián" means to hold with the fingers. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "zhàn" (占);

the *Lùn* (論) writes it as "niè" (捻), which is a vulgar character. "Xuàn" (眩): Pronounced xuán-zhuàn-fǎn; Jia’s commentary on the *Guóyuǎ* states that "xuàn" means either "confusion" or "to be dazed. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "the eyes having no constant object," composed of the radical "eye" (目) and the phonetic "xuán" (玄).
Volume One Hundred and Fifty. *Khaṭikā-hūka* (the first character pronounced as *qiān* with the *rǎn* tone, the second as *gǒu* with the *hóu* tone). A term from the Sanskrit language.

*Tiāo* (to pick out): In the *Shangchao Liaofan Shenglü*, it says that *tiāo* is synonymous with *jué* (to extract). The *Shuowen* states it is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "zhào" (兆), with the pronunciation *yī jué*.

*Nè* (to press down): In Duan Yucai’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan*, he notes that *nè* is also *zé* (to squeeze). It refers to what is called "pressing down" (*zhèn zé*) in the *Liji*. The *Shuowen* states it is composed of the radical "earth" (土) and the phonetic "yàn" (厭), with the pronunciation *xiàng gé*. The *Shenglü* says it means "oppressive" (*bò*). The *Kǎoshēng* says it means "narrow. The *Wenzi Dian* explains it is composed of the radical "walk" (辶) and the phonetic "zhà" (乍), and is also written as *zhǎi* (窄).

Regarding the term *jintāo* (金絛), it refers to the labor involved in its manufacture; Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that its *fán* (樊) and *yīng* (纓) were adorned with *tāo* (絛) silk. Examining the phonology, *tāo* is a woven fabric resembling a cord. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "woven" (*zhì*), taking *móu* (糸) as the radical and *tiáo* (條) in abbreviated form as the phonetic. It is incorrect to derive it from *wéi* (韋) to form *tāo* (韜) or to write it as *tāo* (縚).

*Niǎo* (撓) means to disturb; *jiǎo* (攪) means to stir up. The *Guǎngyá* states that it means "to confuse. The *Shuōwén* explains it as "to stir," formed with the radical 手 and the phonetic 堯; it is also written as 薅. The version in the *Lùn* (Treatise) uses 㧌, which is incorrect. The lower character is pronounced *qiǎo* (巧). The commentary on the *Máoshī* states it means "to confuse. Lexicons define it as *niǎo*. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical 手 and the phonetic 覺.

Volume 151, the One Hundred and Fifty-first Volume of the Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, the Sixteenth Bundle (Part 16). [The term] *qíchóu* (蠐螬)—the first character pronounced with the *zǎi* (薺) rhyme and the *zhāo* (遭) tone, and the second character pronounced with the *zāo* (遭) tone—has already been fully explained in the previous twenty-seventh volume.

The character for *biāo* (飈) is pronounced with the *tiáo* (褾) rhyme. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "Biāo is a violent wind blowing from below upward. The *Shizi* says: "A violent wind is called *biāo*. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* explains that it is composed of the radical "wind" (*fēng*) and the phonetic component "biāo" (*bīng*).

152. Fascicle One Hundred and Fifty-two. No phonetic glosses for characters. 153. Fascicle One Hundred and Fifty-three. Regarding the term *gāndī*: the first character is read as *jian* (焉反) and the second as *chi* (馳致反). It is a Sanskrit word. 154. Fascicle One Hundred and Fifty-four. Regarding the character *shi* (翅) in *shihè* (翮): the upper part is read as *shi* (施至反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* records it as *chi* (翄), meaning "wing. It is composed of the radical *yu* (羽) and the phonetic *zhi* (支); it is also written as *chi* (翨). Regarding the lower part *xing* (行): it is read as *ge* (革反). Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "The *he* (翮) is the root of a bird's feather. The *Shuowen* states: "It is the stem of a feather. It is composed of the radical *yu* (羽) and the phonetic *li* (鬲)."

"Pān-lǎn" (攀攬): "Shàng-pàn" (上盼) is pronounced *mán* (蠻). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that it means "to pull up" (*yǐn*). The *Guǎngyá* states it means "to long for" (*liàn*). The *Shuowén* gives the character as 艸 (*cǎo*), stating it means "to draw forth" (*yǐn*) and is composed of the radical 艸 with the phonetic 反; it is now written as 攀, composed of the radical 手 with the phonetic 樊 (pronounced *lán-dǎn*). The *Guǎngyá* states that "lǎn" (攬) means "to grasp. The *Shuowén* states it means "to seize" (*cuō chí*) and is composed of the radical 手 with the phonetic 覽; it is also written as 擥.

"Jealousy and stinginess" (*jīmān*): the first character is pronounced *qín* (with the initial *xī*) and the second is pronounced *kèjiān* (with the initial *fǎn*). This has already been fully explained in the eightieth-ninth fascicle above.

Fascicle 155. Fascicle 155 contains no phonetic glosses. Fascicle 156. Fascicle 156: The character "撥" (*bō*) is pronounced with the final *bàn* and *mò*. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that "撥" means "to regulate. Wang Yi states it means "to discard. The *Guangya* states it means "to remove. It is also like "to sever. The *Shuowen Jiezi* also states it means "to regulate," composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "發" (*fā*).
The term "不夗" (bùyuǎn) is a transcription of the sound *pūrvan* (with the initial *p-*) and was already explained in the eighteenth-fifth scroll [of this work].

157. Regarding the one hundred and fifty-seventh scroll: the character "拳" (*quán*)—with the phonetic component "倦" (*juàn*)—is glossed in the *Shengyun* as "the fist. According to the *Lunwen*, "joining the five fingers to form a fist" refers to clenching the palm. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "the hand," stating it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shou*) with "卷" (*juǎn*) abbreviated as its phonetic. The version in the *Lunwen* adds "力" (*lì*) to read "捲力" (*juǎnlì*), meaning "to exert force," which is not its correct meaning.

158–160: Fascicles 158 through 160. Fascicle 158, Fascicle 159, and Fascicle 160: none of these contain phonetic glosses. Volume 17: *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Volume 17. Fascicle 161: Fascicle 161 contains no phonetic explanations. Fascicle 162: Fascicle 162. Regarding the character "憚" (dàn): the *Mao-shi-zhuan* states that "憚" means difficulty or fear. Lexicons explain that it is composed of the radical "心" (heart) and the phonetic "單" (dān).

*Luile* (羸劣): The upper character is read as *lei* (累) with a reversed tone; the lower character is read as *lian* (戀) with a reversed tone. This was already explained in the sixty-third fascicle above. *Youyu* (猶豫): Read as *yuru* (余茹).

Wang Yewang states that "hesitation" (*youyu*) refers to being undecided. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *yu* is the name of a beast; it is composed of the radical for "elephant" and the phonetic element *mao*.

163. Volume One Hundred and Sixty-Three. No Phonetic Explanations for Characters. 164. Volume One Hundred and Sixty-Four. *Xiū* (朽): *fǎi* (反) is the phonetic reversal; according to the *Cāngjié piān*, it means decayed and rotten. The *Shuōwén* writes it as 󳍊, with the same meaning, composed of 歺 (skeleton) and 丂 (sound). It is also written as 朽 when composed of 木 (wood/tree). It is an alternative character.

Volume 165. Volume 165 contains no phonetic glosses. Volume 166. Regarding the character for *fá* (栰) in the title: it is pronounced with the fanqie *fán-fā*. Master Ma’s commentary on the *Analects* states that the large is called a *fá* and the small is called a *fú*. Examining the sounds, a *fá* is constructed by binding bamboo and wood to float upon the water. The *Shuowen Jiezi* correctly writes it as *bǎi* (橃), defining it as "a large boat on the sea," taking *mù* (木) as the radical and *fā* (發) as the phonetic; it is also written as *jū* (𦪑) or *fá* (筏).

*Ū*: Pronounced *yù* (with the radical *yù*). The *Guǎngyǎ* states that *ū* refers to illness; the *Shuōwén* defines it as accumulated blood, composed of the radical *nà* (sickness) and the phonetic *yù*.
*Pēngzhàng* (swelling): the upper character is pronounced *pójiāng* and the lower is *zhāngliàng*. This was already explained in the eightieth-fourth fascicle above.

Regarding *gūsuǒ* (the *suǒ* being pronounced as the *fǎn* of *guǒ*), the *Hànshū* states that "it is linked by means of rings. The *Kǎoshēng* says it refers to connected rings. The *Wénzìdiǎn* explains it as being composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic "yǎo" (*yǎo*); however, the version in the *Lùn* [i.e., the *Shuōwén]* as *xuǒ* is incorrect.

*Pī* (pronounced with the *bì* and *mǐ* finals reversed) refers to the *kǎo* (thigh); it is the outer part of the thigh. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "bone" (*gǔ*) and the phonetic "bēi. The character *yì* (from the "flesh" radical) used here is a vulgar variant.
Regarding the *hàn lún* (jaw-circle), this has already been fully explained in the eighth fascicle of this treatise.

Regarding "zǎo" (澡) and "shòu" (漱): the former is pronounced *zāo* (上遭草反). Gu Yewang states that "zǎo" means to wash clean; the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as washing the hands, composed of the radical "water" (水) and the phonetic "sào" (喿). It is an error to write it with the radical "grass" (艹). The latter is pronounced *shòu* (搜󳈮反). Gu Yewang states that "shòu" means to rinse and cleanse; the correct character for all time is composed of the radical "water" (水) and the phonetic "sòu" (欶).
The character *sǒng* (𦝫) [pronounced *tiáo* with the *dāo* tone] has already been explained in the one hundred and fiftieth fascicle.

The *Guǎngyǎ* states that *sǒng* means "to rise up"; Gu Yěwáng says *sǒng* means "high. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical *lì* (立) and the phonetic *cì* (朿). Its appearance in the *Lùn* (論) as *nǒng* (聳) is an error.

The character *qu* (曲) is pronounced with the rhyme *liú* (蔞, main tone) and the auxiliary *kǎo* (考); the *Yùnyùn* (韻) states that *yǒu lǚ* (傴僂) means to bend the body forward. The *Guǎngyá* (廣雅) states that *lǚ* (僂) refers to a hunched back; *lǚ* is also "curved. The *Shuowén* (說文) defines *lǚ* (僂) as "hunchbacked" (*wāng*), composed of the radical "person" and the phonetic *lóu* (婁).

167. Fascicle One Hundred and Sixty-Seven. *Chóngqū* (蟲蛆): the sound of the second character is similar to *qū* (七余反). According to the *Shēnglèi* (聲類), it refers to maggots or fly larvae. The *Shuōwén* (說文) states that it means "worms within flesh," written with the radical *chóng* (虫) and the phonetic *qiě* (且); alternatively, it may be written as *tán* (䏣) using the radical *ròu* (肉).

Volumes 168–170: Volume 168, Volume 169, and Volume 170. The above contain no phonetic glosses. The Eighteenth Section: Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Section Eighteen. Volume 171. Regarding Volume 171: [the term] *jì* (see) is pronounced *jù* (five tones, *gǔ* rhyme); it has already been fully explained in the eighth volume mentioned previously.
The fourteenth volume, [entry] 148, *jūluàn* (𠆴亂), pronounced with the initial *ná* and the rhyme *xiào*, has been fully explained.
Volume 172, [entry] 172, *chūrán* (欻然), pronounced with the initial *xūn* and the rhyme *yù*, has been fully explained in the fifteenth volume of this treatise.

*Hào-gēi*: The upper character *hào* is pronounced with the initial *hú* and rhyme *gāo* (as in the *Chuci*, "The tigers and leopards roar"). According to the *Shuowen*, *hào* means "to howl" (*páo*), composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic "gāo. The lower character *gēi* is pronounced with the initial *jiāo* and rhyme *qiào*. Gu Yewang states that *gēi* means "to call out. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "a loud voice," correctly written as *jiào*, composed of the radical "many mouths" (*jí*) and the phonetic "líu. Its ancient forms are *zōu*, *xū*, and *jiǎo*. The form *gēi* is a vulgar character. *Jí* is pronounced *zé lì*; *líu* is pronounced *jí liú*.

*Tángwēi* (煻煨): "On top" (*shàng*) means *dàng*, which is the sound of *fǎnkǎo* (a type of cauldron). It refers to hot ashes mixed with a fine fire. "Below" (*xià*) is pronounced *huǐ* (with the *huí* rhyme). The *Guǎngyǎ* states that *wēi* means *yùn* (warmth); the *Shuōwén* defines it as fire within a basin. Both characters are composed of the radical "fire" (*huǒ*). The phonetic for *táng* is *wèi*; the phonetic for *wēi* is *yùn* (pronounced *wén fǎn*).

*Xiān* (pronounced *lián* with a retroflex *-r* in the Han Shu Yinyi) means "sharp. According to the Cangjie pian, *xiān* refers to iron; it is derived from the phonetic *tiáo* in the sense of sharpness for knives and swords. The Shuowen jiezi states that it is composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic *shé*; the character *tiáo* is pronounced *jiē* with a retroflex *-r*.

Regarding the character *tiě* (鐵) in the compound *tiějǐ* (鐵𭪿), where *jǐ* is the reverse of the character for "intoxication" (*zuì*), dictionaries state that *jǐ* means "a bird's beak. The *Wenzi Dadian* explains that it is composed of the radicals "from" (*cóng*) and "thorny" (*cì*), and is also written as *zǐ* (觜). The *Lun* (論) writes it as *yì* (𭉨); this is a vulgar form, while the correct character is *tiě* (鐵).

*Chèhùn*: the first character is pronounced *zé* (with the initial *ts-*) and the second is *huń* (with the initial *h-*). This has already been fully explained in the twelfth fascicle of the preceding [text]. *Jǔlàpó*:
the first character is pronounced *jù* (with the initial *k-*) and the second is *lán* (with the initial *l-*) and *tà*; these are Sanskrit terms.

Volume One Hundred and Seventy-Three. Volume One Hundred and Seventy-Three. Aṅgulimāla (the first character pronounced as *yang* with the *jiang* tone, and the second as *qun* with the *wu* tone; this is a transliteration of the Sanskrit term).

*Màn* (上): Pronounced *áo* (誥反) according to Duan Yucai’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan*, which states that *màn* means "lack of reverence. The *Guǎngyá* also notes that *ào* (arrogance) is synonymous with *màn*. Lexicons define it as *jù* (haughtiness). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as being composed of the radical "man" (人) and the phonetic element "gù" (𢾕), stating that this is incorrect; it should instead be written as *ào* (慠) from the radical "heart" (心). *Màn* (下): Pronounced *yàn* (晏反). Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that *màn* refers to "neglecting and slighting the sacred teachings. Gu Yewang says that *màn* is equivalent to "slighting and insulting. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "laziness," composed of the radical "heart" (心) and the phonetic element "màn" (曼).

The Zheng commentary on the *Liji* states that "bèng" (󳍧) means "to scatter and disperse. Lexicons state it also means "to run away in dispersal. The *Wenzidian* explains that it is composed of the radical "辵" (chuò) and the phonetic "并" (bìng), and is also written as "跰" (pén).

Volume One Hundred and Seventy-Six, Part Two. Regarding the "māṅ" (蟒) [in the phrase] "māṅshēn" (蟒身): according to Guo’s commentary on the *Erya*, the "māṅ" is the largest among snakes. This was already explained in Volume One Hundred and Seventy-Seven above.

*Tuán* (一摶): *duàn* (叚) and *luán* (巒) in reverse; the *Guǎngyá* states that "to *tuán*" means to grasp with the hand so that things adhere to one another. The *Shuōwén* [explains it] as being composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "zhuān" (*zhuān*).
*Qízhōng* (畦中): *huì* (惠) and *guī* (圭) in reverse; this was already fully explained previously in the sixtieth-sixth fascicle of this treatise.

*Chou-ch'ü* (躊躇): The first character is pronounced *shang* with the *chou* and *liu* finals; the second is pronounced *chu* with the *lu* final. The *Guangya* states that "chou-ch'ü" means hesitation (*yu-yu*). Gu Yewang says it refers to lingering and hesitating. According to the *Shuowen*, both characters are written with the "foot" radical (*zú*), and "shou" (*壽*) serves as the phonetic component for both.

177. Fascicle One Hundred and Seventy-Seven. *An* (not): pronounced as *a* with the *jia* rhyme; it means to embrace or hold. It is said that "an" refers to being sunken or depressed; it is a phonetic character meaning "middle-low. It is a pictographic character.

The character for *tū* (凸) is pronounced *jiàn* (結反); the *Yùnlüè* (韻略) states that it means "a high protrusion" and is a pictographic character (*xiàngxíng zì*). The character for *gēn* (跟) is pronounced *lín* (艮痕反).

The *Shìmíng* (釋名) states that the rear of the foot is called the *gēn*. The *Shuōwén* (說文) defines it as the heel of the foot (*zúzhǒng*), composed of the radical for "foot" (*zú*) and the phonetic component *lín* (*艮*).

*Zòu huǎn* (皺緩): the upper character is pronounced *jùn* with the *shòu* rhyme group; this has been fully explained in the thirty-eighth fascicle of this treatise. The lower character is pronounced *huán* with the *guǎn* rhyme group. According to the *Erya*, "huǎn" means relaxed (*shū*). Gu Yewang says that "huǎn" is synonymous with spacious (*kuān*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is composed of the radical *mì* (silk) and the phonetic *yuán*.

The character *luán* (攣) is pronounced like the "fǎn" (反) in *kǎo* (考). It means to be cramped or constrained. Gu Yewang states that *jié* (癵) refers to being bent or crooked. According to the *Shuowen*, it is a derivative of *sūn* (孫); it takes the radical "hand" (手) with the phonetic *luán* (䜌), or alternatively, it is written as *jié* (癵) with the radical "sickness" (疒). The form *liàn* (戀) used in the *Lunheng* (論衡) is an error.
The character *ēnì* (繄) is pronounced with the *xī* (奚) and *fǎn* (反) finals. It is a transliteration of a Sanskrit term.

Regarding the character *qī* (欹), Gu Yewáng states that it means "to lean" or "to be unbalanced. It is composed of the radical *zhī* (攴) and the phonetic *qí* (奇). The character *qí* (奇) is correctly written with the *jiè* (介) radical; *zhī* (攴) is formed from half a *zhú* (竹) radical.
The character 幖 (biǎo) is pronounced yáo in the first instance and chì in the second; this was already explained previously in the seventy-third fascicle.
The term 哳 (zhá) [is pronounced zhǎn liè in the commentary] is a Sanskrit term for numerical methods.
*Balāśa* (跋邏攙): The upper character *bá* is pronounced with the *pán* rhyme; the middle character *luó* is pronounced with the *hè* rhyme; the lower character *xiàn* is pronounced as *shǎn*.

This is a Sanskrit term. 178. Volume One Hundred and Seventy-Eight. *Gēyì* (割劓): The upper character *gē* is pronounced with the *yù* rhyme. The commentary on the *Shūjīng* by Kǒng [Yáng] states that it means "to harm. The *Guǎngyǎ* states it means "to cut off. The lower character *yì* is pronounced as *yí qì*. Zhèng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states: "To *yì* is to cut off the nose. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "the nose," both following the radical for "knife" (*dāo*). It is sometimes written as *lún*.

*Bu shù* (the rhyme is *shùn*; the *Zhuāngzǐ* says: "one gazes all day without blinking"; the *Lǚshì chūnqiū* says: "ten thousand generations are but a single blink"). The *Shuowén* defines it as the opening and closing of the eyes; it is also written as *shùn*.

Volume 179, Number 179. *Jiāocuì* (憔悴): The first character, *jiāo*, is pronounced as *qíáo* (遙); the second character, *cuì*, is pronounced as *cízuì* (慈醉). In the *Chuci* (Bitter-Plum Lyrics), it refers to the appearance of one who is distressed and sorrowful. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is sometimes written as *jiāo* (憔) or *jù* (󳈆); the character *cuì* may also be written with the "head" radical (*xié*) as *cuì* (顇). Both forms are interchangeable.

Xiūn (羞𧹞): The first character is pronounced *xiù* (秀) with a reversed *yóu* (由), and the second is *ná* (拏) with a reversed *jiǎn* (蕳). According to the *Fāngyán*, *xiūn* means shame (*kuì*). According to the *Shuōwén*, it refers to the face turning red from embarrassment;

it is composed of the radical "skin" (*pí*) and the phonetic "red" (*chì*). 180. Volume One Hundred and Eighty. Ruǐ (䎡): Pronounced *ruǐ* (兖) with a reversed *jiǎn* (反). According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "fire" (*huǒ*) and the phonetic "ěr" (而).

Volume Nineteen of the Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Volume One Hundred and Eighty-one. *Qiāo* (蹻): Pronounced *jiǎo* (反文). In his commentary on the *Hànshū*, Wén Yǐng states that *qiāo* is synonymous with *qiáo* (翹). The *Shuōwén* defines it as the appearance of lifting one’s feet high; it is composed of the radical for "foot" (*zú*) and the phonetic *qiáo*. It is also written as *qiāo* (趫).

"Rough whip" (麁鞭): the first character is pronounced *shù* (醋胡反) and the second is pronounced *gèng* (額更反). It is the "correct character" (*zhèngzì*) for "firm" (*láo*). It is a phonetic compound of "to examine" (*kǎo*) and "solid" (*jiān*). The standard form is "hard" (*biàn*), which is also written as "rigid" (*yìng*); these are vulgar characters.

*Sūtra-vinaya*: *sūtra* (pronounced with the initial *tán* and final *luó-dàn*) is the Sanskrit term translated into Chinese as "Scriptures" (*jīng*) and "Discipline" (*lǜ*), referring to the Pitakas of Sūtra and Vinaya.

Volumes 182–185: Volumes One Hundred and Eighty-two through One Hundred and Eighty-five. For the volumes above, there are no characters for which phonetic pronunciations can be provided. Volume 186: Volume One Hundred and Eighty-six. *Chìxiào* (嗤誚): The character *chì* (嗤) is the opposite of *chǐ* (齒). According to the *Zìshū*, it denotes the appearance of mocking laughter. The *Wénzìdiǎn* explains that it is composed of the radical "mouth" (口) and the phonetic element "zhì" (𠮧); alternatively, it may be written as *pī* (㰩) or *qì* (㰤), which are composed of the archaic form of "it" (之) and the radical "insect" (虫). The lower part is pronounced *qiáo* (樵) or *xiào* (笑). In his commentary on the *Shàngshū*, Kǒng [Yǎng] states that it means "to reproach" (*qiào* [譙]). Alternatively, it may be written as *qiào* (譙).

187. Fascicle One Hundred and Eighty-Seven. *Danpo* (憺怕): "Dan" (憺) is pronounced with the *tan* and *lan* rhymes; Gu Yewang states that "dan" means tranquility (*tianjing*). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* says "dan" is equivalent to being at ease (*an*). The lower character, "pa" (怕), is pronounced with the *pu* and *bai* rhymes. The *Zixu Fu* says: "Pa [he is] without action; dan [he is] self-sustaining. The *Guoya* states that "pa" means stillness (*jing*), and the *Shuowen* defines it as non-action (*wuwei*). Both characters follow the radical for the heart (*xin*) and take *zhan* and *bai* as their phonetic components. To write it with the water radical as *dantuo* (澹泊) is not this term.
*Kài* (溉): The base character is *qī* (基). Wang Yewang says it means "to pour" (*guàn*). The *Shuowen* says it means "to pour," written with the radical *shui* (水) and the phonetic *jì* (既).

188. Volume 188. *Tiě* (鐵): The reading is *mǎng* (猛). The *Erya* states that the raw ore of iron is called *huáng* (磺). The *Shuowen* says it is the raw ore of copper and iron, written with the radical *shí* (石) and the phonetic *huáng* (黃). The *Lunyu* uses *guà* (丱), which is used interchangeably; it is also sometimes written as *kuàng* (礦).

*Lǔ* (pronounced with the initial *l* reversed as *tou*) refers to the watchtowers on city walls used for defense; the lower character is pronounced *lu-gu*. According to the *Shiming*, a *lǔ* is a structure on top that is exposed and lacks a covering roof. The *Shuowen Jiezi* also derives it from the radical "wood" (*mu*).

*Píè* (埤堄): The first character is pronounced *pǔ* with the *bì* rhyme; the second is *ní* with the *jì* rhyme. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it refers to the parapet on top of a city wall. This has already been fully explained in the one hundred and fifth fascicle.

*Luǒxíng* (裸形): The character for *luǒ* is pronounced *huā* with the *wǎ* rhyme. Gu Yewáng states that "nude" (*luǒ*) means to remove clothes and expose the body. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is written with the radical for clothing (*yī*), though it is also written as *nuǒ* or *lě*.

189. Volume One Hundred and Eighty-Nine. "Fǔ" (腐): [The character] is pronounced *fǔ* (with the *wǔ* rhyme). According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means putrid and decayed; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means rotten. It is composed of the radical "meat" (*ròu*).

190. Volume One Hundred and Ninety. *Tanqi* (耽嗜): The first character, *tan*, is pronounced as in *dān* (荅含反); according to the *Erya*, it means to indulge excessively in pleasure. The second character, *qi*, is pronounced as in *shí* (時至反). Master Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that "to have a craving (*shì*) for something means one is never satisfied. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains that "human beings crave desires and take pleasure in them. It is also written as *zhe* (啫), *yú* (𩝙), or *mǎn* (𨢍).
*Jiè hàn* (to harbor resentment): *hàn* means "resentment. According to the *Wenzi Dianshuō*, it is composed of the radical *xīn* (heart) and the phonetic *gǎn*.

Volume 20, the twentieth bundle of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Volume 191. *Jīng qiè* (to be terrified): *qiè* is pronounced with the *zhān* and *shè* finals. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states that it means "fear and trepidation. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines *qiè* as "to be frightened"; it is composed of the radical *xīn* (heart), or alternatively written as *zhè*.
"Startled and terrified" refers to being struck with fear in the world of shoes. Volume 192 (No phonetic glosses) Volume 193 *Liṅyǔ* (囹圄):

The upper character *lì* is pronounced as *lì-dīng-fǎn*; the lower character *yǔ* is pronounced as *yú-jǔ-wén*. In the *Líjì* (Book of Rites), Master Zheng’s commentary states: "Liṅyǔ is that by which those to be restrained and imprisoned are kept; it is like the separate prisons of today. The *Shuowén* (Explanations of Words and Texts) defines it as "to guard. Both characters are composed of the radical *wéi* (囗, pronounced *wéi*).

Volume 194, Scroll 194. No Phonetic Explanations. Volume 195, Scroll 195. *Jìsì* (繼嗣), Upper Part. *Kī* (雞) is pronounced *yì* (藝). Wáng Bǐ, in his commentary on the *Zhou Yī*, states: "Succession (*jì*) means not to sever. Jiǎ Duī, in his commentary on the *Guóyuè*, states: "Succession (*jì*) means the remainder. The *Ēryá* states: "Succession (*jì*) means to continue. The *Shuōwén* states: "To continue (*xù*). It is composed of the radical *mì* (糸) and the character *jǐ* (㡭); *jǐ* also provides the phonetic. Alternatively written as *jǐ* (㡭); *jǐ* is pronounced *jué* (絕). Below [the entry for] *cí* (詞), it is pronounced *zì* (恣). Kǒng [Yǎng], in his commentary on the *Shàngshū*, states: "Succession (*sì*) is also succession (*jì*). The *Máo Shī Jiān* states: "Succession (*sì*) means to continue (*xù*). The *Shuōwén* states: "A ruler who succeeds to a state (*hòusì guó*). It is composed of the radical *kǒu* (口) and the character *cè* (冊); *sī* (司) provides the phonetic. Alternatively written as *sì* (孠), which is an archaic form. *Cè* is pronounced *lǎn* (󳌫)."* *Note: The phonetic transcriptions provided here follow the conventions of the source text's era.*

Volume 196, Scroll 196. No Phonetic Explanations. Volume 197, Scroll 197. *Tuǎi* (隤): Upper radical *Duì* (隊), level tone; *léi* (雷) rhyme. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to collapse. According to the *Shuowén*, it means "to fall down," composed of the radical *fù* (阜). It is also written as *tuǎi* (頽). *Xià* (下): *rǎng* (穰), palatalized tone. In the commentary on the *Shàngshū* by Kǒng [Yáng], it is said that ground without clods is called *huài* (壞). Lìu Zhào’s commentary on the *Gǔliáng Zhuàn* states: "To dig into the earth and bring forth soil is called *rǎng* (壤). According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical *tǔ* (土) and the phonetic *xiāng* (襄).

*Chuángwòu* (瘡疣): The *Guǎngyá* states it refers to swellings or warts; the *Cāngjiépiān* says it is a wart disease. The *Shuōwén* explains that it is composed of the radical *nà* (疒), or alternatively written as *yóu* (疣) with the radical *ròu* (肉), and also written as *huì* (𤴨).
Volume 198. The entry for *Qiánchí* (pronounced with the *qiān* of *qiánfǎn*) has already been explained previously in Volume 126.

*Shǒu'ài* (守阸): "Āi" is pronounced as *yīng* with a retroflex *r* (賣反). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "āi" refers to a dangerous terrain. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that "āi" means precarious or perilous. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to block," written with the radical for mountains (*fù*). It may also be written as *ài* or *ài*; these are vulgar forms.
*Jiā* (撾): To strike or beat. The *Fǎnyì yǔlèi* states it means to chastise or flog. Volume 199, No. 199. Phonetic Explanations for Characters Without Radicals. Volume 200, No. 200. *Xīngyí* (𧋍蜴):

The first character is pronounced as *xīng* (亦反), and the second as *yíng* (隻反). The *Erya* states: "The *xīngyuán*, *xīngyí*, *wànyán*, and *shǒugōng* are synonyms. Guo Pu’s commentary notes that these are four different names for the same creature. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "The *wànyán* is called *xīngyí* when on the grass. [The characters are composed as follows: *xīng* (蠑) has the phonetic *róng* (音榮); *yuán* (螈) has the phonetic *yuán* (音原); *wàn* (蝘) has the phonetic *yǎn* (音偃); *yán* (蜒) has the phonetic *tián-diǎn* (音田典反). *Wànyán* (蝘蜒): The *wànyán* is called *xīngyí* when on the grass. [The characters are composed as follows: *xīng* (蠑) has the phonetic *róng* (音榮); *yuán* (螈) has the phonetic *yuán* (音原); *wàn* (蝘) has the phonetic *yǎn* (音偃); *yán* (蜒) has the phonetic *tián-diǎn* (音田典反).
The Phonetic Explanations of All Scriptures,
Volume Sixty-nine and Volume Seventy,
compiled by the Scripture-translating Śramaṇa Huilin.
The *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* translated by Paramārtha in twenty-two fascicles and the *Abhidharmakośakārikā* in one fascicle;
the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* translated later in thirty fascicles and fifty-three fascicles share the same phonetic transcriptions as this fascicle.

*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Fascicle One, compiled by Xuanying. Fascicle One: *Kośa*. This translation [of *kośa*] means "treasury," which is a general term for a storehouse; its substance is that of a silkworm cocoon, used here as a metaphor.

"Zhū míng mò tíng mò dìng" (諸冥莫庭莫定). This is read twice. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "míng" (冥) means "obscure," "darkness," or "night. It refers to the night when nothing can be seen. The character is composed of "sun" (日) and "six" (六); after sixteen days, the moon begins to wane, which is "míng. The phonetic component is "mìng" (冖), pronounced "míng bì" (銘壁). *Note: The term "zhū míng mò tíng mò dìng" appears to be a transcription or gloss related to the phonology or etymology of the character "míng" (冥), likely from a commentary on the *Shuowen Jiezi*. The instruction to "read it twice" (二反) refers to the method of recitation.*

*He*: "Fu" (負) and "ke" (可) [are pronounced with] the second tone; it means "small. *Er-pi* (爾疋): *He* (何) means "to carry" (*dan* 擔); according to the *Guang-yi* (廣疋), *he* means "to bear" (*ren* 任). Nowadays, all are written as *he* (荷). *Kiao* (竅):
"Kou-diao" (口弔) [is its pronunciation]; *kiao* means "aperture" (*kong* 孔). According to the *Shuo-wen*, *kiao* means "hollow" (*kong* 空) and *xue* (穴) means "an earthen chamber" (*tu-shi* 土室).

The *Guī* (tortoise) and *Táo* (crocodile) are listed in the *Sāncāng*; they resemble *jiāo* (dragon-eels), though the former is large. According to the *Shānhǎijīng*, the *Jiāngshuǐ* (Yangtze River) abounds in *táo*. Guō Pǔ said: "They resemble *xīyì* (lizards); the larger ones reach one *zhàng* in length and have scaly patterns that can be used to make drums. The poem says, "The *táogǔ* (crocodile drums) thump loudly," referring to this very thing. The character is composed of the radical *mǐn* (黽) and the phonetic *nà* (𠹈). The pronunciation of *nà* is *nà*, and the pronunciation of *mǐn* is *mògěng* (莫耿反).

*Gōuè* (鉤鵅): *gǔ* (古) and *hóu* (侯); the second character is read with the *jiā* (加) and *é* (額) rhymes. Your dictionary (*Erlǚ*) reads it as *jīqī* (忌欺). Guo Pu says: "In the Jiangdong region today, the *xiūliú* (鵂鶹, owl) is called *gōuè* (鉤鵅), pronounced *gé* (格). The *Guǎngyǐ* (廣疋) states: "*Jiǎoliú* (䳡鶹), *zhì* (𪁟), and *chī* (鵄)"—these are also strange birds; they are blind by day and see at night. In the Guanxi region they are called *xùnhóu* (訓侯), while in Shandong they are called *xùnhú* (訓狐). In the *Lùnwén* (論文), the character *gù* (鴝) is used, which shares the same pronunciation as *jùyú* (具榆)—that is, the *gù* (鴝) of the *gùyù* (鴝鵒, starling) bird. However, that *gù* (鴝) does not carry this meaning.

2. Fascicle Two. Regarding the character *xiāng* (相): it is pronounced with the rhyme of *chī* (󳇕抶) and the tone of *wèi* (味). People of the south refer to the character *xiāng* (相) as *xiāng* (相); this is a vulgar corruption (*pǔ*) of the character *xiāng* (㩌). Regarding *xiāng kē* (相磕):

*kē* (磕) is pronounced with the rhymes of *kǔ* (苦) and *hé* (盍). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *kē* refers to the sound of stones striking one another. Nowadays in Jiangnan, whenever one speaks of smashing an object to pieces, one says "to *kē* it" (*kē pò*); this also implies a loud sound.
The ancient character for *kì* (隙) is the same as *qù* (去, pronounced *nì*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "A gap is a hole at the edge of a wall. The *Guangya* states: "A gap means to separate.

Regarding *gǔ* (鼓), it is pronounced *sāng lǎng*. The *Pīcāng* states: "It is a type of drum. Lexicons state it refers to the material for making drums. The *Lunwen* (Discourse on the Text) uses the character *sàng* (顙). According to the *Fāngyán*, *sàng* means the forehead; in the region of Dongqí, it is called *sàng*, but that is not the meaning here.

"Zhù" (駐) is an archaic character; "zhù" (住), "tǎo" (討), "yì" (𨔦), and "yì" (𠊪) share the same four radical forms as "zhì" (雉). "Jù" (具) is pronounced with the two tones *zhèng* and *èr*. It is the name for receiving punishment in hell. According to the *Cāngjié piān*, it means "to stop"; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means "to halt a horse."
*Yan-lan* (pronounced *jiǎn*): the character is abbreviated as "eye"; it refers to the skin outside the eye. *Nǎn-gēn* (pronounced *nú wò*):
according to the *Sāncāng*, it means weak or soft. *Zhōu* (pronounced *yóu*):

according to the *Erpǐ*, that which can be inhabited within water is called a *zhōu*. Sūn Yán says: "It is a level ground within water where one may dwell. The *Shìmíng* says: "*Zhōu* means a gathering place; it is a location where humans, birds, and beasts gather to rest."

3. Third Fascicle. 4. Fourth Fascicle. Regarding the character *yù* (預): in ancient texts it was written as *yù* (預) or *yù* (忬), and in modern times as *yù* (豫). They are identical. According to the *Cāngjié piān*, "to anticipate" (*yù*) means to be at peace; it also means to prepare in advance. Because one prepares for something beforehand, it is called "anticipation. In the *Zhou Yī*, it says "anticipation and indolence. Hàn Kāngbó said: "Anticipation means to relax and unwind."

The character 𩑶 (also written as 胡𦙶) shares the same pronunciation as 戶孤 (húgū), referring to the pendulous dewlap of an ox. As the *Shijing* says, "The wolf treads upon its dewlap" (*láng bá qí hú*). In the *Lunyu*, it is written as 壺; however, according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, 壺 refers to a round vessel and is not used in this sense.

"Dì" (遞) is an archaic term; "dì" (迭) is a variant reading with the phonetic gloss "tú lǐ" (徒禮反). It means "to alternate" (*ěr pǐ*). Guo Pu states: "Dì means to change or alternate. In the *Lunwen* (論文), it is written as "dié" (迭) with the phonetic gloss "tú jié" (徒結反); according to the *Fāngyán* (方言), "dié" also means to alternate. These two characters are used interchangeably, and one should read them according to their respective characters.

5. Fascicle Five. Regarding "rice chaff" (dào ráng): according to the *Guǎngyǐ*, rice chaff is called *gàn*. Furthermore, "ráng" also means "disorderly. The treatise text writes it as *xiāng*; *xiāng* is the name of a bitter herb (*kē cǎi*), which is not the intended meaning here.

6. The Sixth Fascicle. Regarding "Jambū," it is pronounced with a gradual reversal [of sounds]; it is also called *Yánfú* (閻浮) or written as *Zhānfú* (譫浮), both of which are corruptions. The correct term is *Zhànbù* (贍部). It is named after a tree; the old translations call it the "Realm of the Foul Tree" (*Hèshùyù*). *Zhàn* (譫) is pronounced *zhī-hán-fǎn*, and *zhàn* (贍) is pronounced *shí-yàn-fǎn*.
*Ēr-dāng* (ear-ornament): *dōu-táng* (all-hall) is reversed; according to the *Shìmíng* (Explanation of Names), "to pierce the ear and apply a bead" is called *dāng*.

It originally originated from the Western Rong. Regarding *jiǎo* (the suburban area): *wài-gǔ* (outside-ancient) is pronounced *bāo*; according to the *Sīmǎfǎ* (Method of Sīmǎ), in a royal state, one hundred *lǐ* is the *jiǎo*, fifty *lǐ* is the near *jiǎo*, and one hundred *lǐ* is the distant *jiǎo*. The *Báihūtōng* (General Discourse on the White Tiger) asks: Why must kings and feudal lords have a *jiǎo*? Above, the *jiǎo* connects with the heavenly deities; below, the *jiǎo* connects with the feudal lords; for feudal lords, the *jiǎo* connects with neighboring states.
"Duo" (butuo, with the second tone) means to remove or to discard; it is also written as "ye.

"Chengce" (chengce, with the third tone)—the ancient forms being 𠕋, 𥬰, and 󳌷—are identical in meaning; they refer to the whip used for striking a horse, by which one lashes the horse to drive it forward.

The boatman (chuan): according to the *Shiben*, Gonggu and Huodí were the ones who fashioned boats. Song Zhong says they were subjects of the Yellow Emperor. In the *Fangyan*, it is stated that from the Guanzhong region westward, a boat is called a *chuan*. The *Shiming* explains that "boat" (*chuan*) means "to follow," referring to following along the water. The version in the *Lunwen* uses the character *huāng* (pinyin: huāng), which does not carry this meaning.

In the *Guǎngyǐ*, "qíngdiān" (蜻蜓) is written as such with the pronunciation qīngtíng; in the *Zhuāngzǐ*, it is written as "qīnglíng" (蜻蛉) with the pronunciation líng being lǐliǎo-fǎn. "Cái" (纔) is read as zāi-fǎn in the *Guǎngyǐ*, meaning "temporary" (*cànzàn*).

In the *Hànshū*, it is written as "cái" (纔) meaning "merely" (*jìnyě*), "inferior," or "not long. Zhèng Xuán’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* writes it as "cài" (裁); the *Dōngguān Hànjì* and various other histories write it as "cái" (財), and Jiǎ Duī’s commentary on the *Guóyuè* also writes it as "cái" (財). Thus, its form varies according to the context.

The ancient forms for "decline" (shuāi) and "senility" (mào) were written as 𠅸 and 耄; today they are written as 耗, both pronounced mào (with the tone mark 4). According to the *Liji* (Book of Rites), at eighty years of age one reaches senility (*mào*). Zheng Xuan commented: "Senility (*mào*) refers to mental confusion and disordered faculties."

It further relies on the three ancient characters *rén*, *zhèng*, and *dàn*, which share the same pronunciation as *líng*. According to the *Erlǐ* (Classic of Rites), "still" (*réng*) means "therefore" (*nǎi*) or "consequently" (*yīn*). Guo Pu states that it refers to "causal conditions" (*yīnyuán*).
*Fèi nǎo* (沸撓): "Nǎo" is pronounced as *fǎn guǎng pǐ*. It means to disturb; according to the *Shuowen*, it means to agitate; according to the *Shenglei*, it means to disturb.
7. Volume Seven. *Bǐ shī* (俾尸): Pronounced as *bǐ ěr fǎn*. Translated as "a mass" or "formed into a ball. According to the characters, *bǐ* means "to cause."
*Lie* (烈): The force that breaks and overturns. According to the *Shuowen*, "fierce fire" means intense heat; according to the *Guangyi*, "intense heat.
Regarding the character *han* (含), its form is written as *han* (唅) with the phonetic *hu gan* (胡紺反); it means to provide for others so that they may give rise [to virtue].

Next is *yí* (飴), which is also written as two characters, *yín* (𩞫) and *lù* (䬮); in the *Zhuowén* it is written as *gǎn* (弇), all sharing the same pronunciation as *yì* (弋). The *Shuōwén* states that it is "rice (*mǐ*) fried in oil (*shān*). The *Shìmíng* says: "It is smaller and weaker than *xī* (錫) in its form; it is *yí-yí* (怡怡) [in appearance]. The pronunciation of *xī* is *sìyíng* (似盈).

"Yào-shù" (要術): "Shù" is pronounced with the *shu* rhyme of *chún* (唇). "Shù" means method; furthermore, a road within a city is called "shù," as it signifies thoroughness—there is nothing it does not penetrate.
"Bō-tā" (波扡): "Tā" is pronounced with the *hé* rhyme of *tài* (太); according to the character, "tā" means to drag (*yè*).

8. Volume Eight. "To swallow" (tūn): the character is pronounced as *tān* when referring to another's field. According to the *Shuowen*, it means to swallow. The *Guangyi* states that swallowing is to extinguish. "Recovery" (*yù*):
the ancient form is the same as *yǔ* (pronounced *zhǔ*). According to the *Fangyan*, the dialectal term for recovery is *yù*. The *Shuowen* defines *yù* as the healing of illness.
"Hanging" (guà): when used in the sense of forming hexagrams, it is pronounced guà (same as in "ancient" [gǔ]). In the *Guǎngyǐ*, "guì" means to suspend.

"Dàbó" (大浡) is now written as "dàbó" (󳁛), pronounced pú-mù (same as in "submerge" [mù]). In the *Shànglín Fù*, it refers to a dense marsh; the *Hànshū Yìnyì* states that this describes the appearance of water contracting, wrinkling, and gathering in coils.

*Wei* (萎) and *zào* (燥) are also written as *yí* (𣨙), with the same pronunciation as *wēi* (危). According to the *Shēnglèi* (聲類), *wěicǎo* (萎草) refers to large withered grass; in Guānxī (關西) they say *yūn* (菸), while in Shāndōng (山東) they say *niān* (蔫), and in Jiāngnán (江南) they also say *yí* (𣨙)—these are regional dialects. The character below [of *zào*] is pronounced *dàochéng* (道乘); *zào* means dry.

"不噎" (bù yē): "噎" is glossed in the *Shuowen* as "the choking of rice"; the pronunciation of "窒" is *zhīlì*. It means "to obstruct. In the treatise (*Lun*), it is frequently written as "咽" (*yàn*, with two pronunciations: *yújiàn* and *yúxián*). "咽" means "to swallow" or "the throat. However, "咽" is not the correct radical form [of the character].
*Ché* (畟): The phonetic reading is *chǔ lì fǎn*;
it refers to a square shape. *Mántuó* (瞞陀): The phonetic reading is *jì ān fǎn*. According to the *Shuowen*, this character means "to look level.

*Tieqian* (鐵鉆): The phonetic reading is *qí zhān fǎn*. According to the *Shuowen*, this character means "an iron clamp. In the *Cangjie pian*, *qian* (鉆) is glossed as "to hold"; *qian* (銸) is also written as *qian* (鉆).

"Another term for 'returning' is *fú* (同扶福反; same as *fú* with the fanqie *fu-fu*). In the *Hanshu*, it says 'the streams were blocked and the *xi* were *fú*' (*chuān sè xī fú*). Sū Lín said: 'As for *fú*, it means to submerge deeply. It would be appropriate for the *Dìjì* to read it as *huí* (澓), meaning water that turns back."

The term *miǎo* (pronounced with the retroflex -r) refers to the fine twigs at the very end [of a branch]; it is called *chāo* in the *Tōngsúwén*. In the *Fāngyán*, *miǎo* means "small. Guo Pu states: "As for *chāo*, it refers to what is slender, minute, and scant."

9. Fascicle Nine. "Huàn jiǎ" (Donning Armor). The character "huàn" is pronounced as *hú* or *màn*; in the *Zuǒzhuan*, it appears as "huàn jiǎ zhí bīng" (donning armor and grasping weapons), to which Du Yu comments: "Huàn means to thread or pass through. In the *Guóyuè*, it says "fú bīng huàn jiǎ" (wearing weapons and donning armor), to which Jia Kui comments: "It means to clothe oneself in armor."

"Chǔ" (儲) means "to store for future use. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to wait" or "to provide. One interpretation states it refers to the accumulation of wealth. The archaic form of the character below is "Xù" (稸), which is interchangeable; it means "to accumulate" and "to gather. It is pronounced with the rhyme group of "chǐ" (恥). "Xù" (蓄) also means to accumulate and to gather.
"Xiāng-yào" (相要) means to summon from afar; "yào" (要) also means *jiāo* (徼), which means to seek. *Jiāo* is pronounced *gǔyáo*.
"Cháng-qǔ" (長取) is pronounced *chúliàng*; it means to be full and overflowing, or to have a surplus.

*Liánzǐ* (奩子) is now written as *lián* (籢), with the phonetic transcription *tóng lì zhàn fǎn*. According to the *Shuōwén*, it refers to a mirror case (*jìng lián*), specifically one with a square bottom; what exists today in Jiangnan, such as the *qí lián* (chess box), is of this type.

*Kāi* (開) is written as *zhòu* (𡍩) in the *Běicāng*, with the phonetic transcription *tóng chǐ gé fǎn*. According to the *Shuōwén*, *zhòu* means to tear apart; according to the *Guǎngpǐ*, it means to divide.

*Zhùcào* (the character *cào* is pronounced as *dá* according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*; the *Shuowen* states that *cào* refers to a *zhēng* [a type of musical instrument], and its sound is like that of bamboo shoots; it is the name for the inner bark of bamboo). Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Fangyan* states: "In the region east of the Yangtze River, they call a coarse, plain-woven mat with straight stripes *cào*, while one with diagonal stripes is called *fèi*. It is also known as *hángtán*. Between the regions of Song and Wei, they call a small round mat (*dān*) that is woven from reeds *qúchú*. The *Shuowen* defines *qúchú* as a coarse bamboo mat made by weaving reeds.

*Kubē* (古貝) [the "gài" rhyme] refers to cotton cloth (*karpāsa*) of five colors; it is the name of a tree, and the cloth is made from its flowers. 10. Volume Ten. *Ē* (厭惡) [the "lù" rhyme]: *Ē* means "to loathe.

In the *Lǐjì*, we have "How could I use my emotions? (*wú è yòng wú qíng*); in the *Lúnyǔ*, we have "I loathe the purple that defiles the vermilion" (*è zǐ zhī rǎn zhū*). This refers to the human mind’s capacity for rejection and acceptance, or preference and aversion. Both pronunciations—*hào-è* (好惡)—are in the departing tone (*qùshēng*).

Regarding the character *zhōng* (隒): it should be explained as a reversal of the character for *dī* (堤). The *Pīcāng* states that in Changsha, a dike is called *zhōng*; this is correct. It means a dike (*dīfáng*), which is that which prevents water; it also means a barrier. It refers to piling up earth to form a mound that serves as a limit and barrier to obstruct water.

*Guó* (郭): Ancient pronunciation *huò*. According to the *Cāngjié piān*, "guó" refers to city walls. The *Gōngyáng zhuan* asks: "What is a *guó*? It is a vast enclosure. The *Shìmíng* states: "A *guó* is a broad perimeter situated outside the city. Regarding *yì* (邑), the *Zhōu lǐ* states: "Four *jǐng* (wells/squares) constitute a *yì*. Zhèng Xuán says: "It is two *lǐ* square. The *Zuǒ zhuan* states: "Any settlement that has ancestral temples and the spirit-tablets of former lords is called a *dū*; one that lacks these is called a *yì*. *Huò* (鑊): Pronounced *hú guò*.
11. Volume Eleven. Verse: "From the pasture, I bring back the young shoots" (*tí*; *dí* and *xí* are reversed). The Commentary says: "The young shoots are the newly sprouted tips of the *máo* grass."
*Jí* (瘠): The ancient forms are 𤹠, 𤶬, and 膌; they share the same pronunciation as *cái* (才赤反). It means "barren" and also "emaciated. *Jiā* (嘉): The ancient form is 恕;
it shares the same pronunciation as *jiǎ* (賈遐反). It means "excellent"; according to the *Erlǚ*, it means "beautiful."

12. Volume Twelve. Pit (Keng). In archaic texts, it is written as *jing* (阱). The two forms are identical; according to the *Cisheng*, it is pronounced *zheng* (反). The *Shuowen* states that a pit (*jing*) is a great depression. The *Guangyi* states that a pit (*jing*) is a trench (*keng*). The *Sancang* states that a pit refers to digging the ground into a depression for the purpose of trapping birds and beasts.

The ancient character for *chuǎi* (揣) is the same as *wěi* (委), with the initial rhyme *chū wěi*. It means to gauge or measure another person. In the south of the River, this pronunciation is used; it is also pronounced *dōu guǒ*, meaning to estimate or to test. In the north, this pronunciation is used. According to the intent of the treatise, the character should be written as *jiān* (㨊), with the initial rhyme *chū wěi*. *Jiān* means to feel or grope. This is correct according to the *Tōngsùwén*: "To grope with the hand is called *jiān*."

*Páo-chú* (庖廚): *páo* is pronounced as *pú jiāo*. "Páo" means "to enclose. To wrap meat is called *bāo*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *páo* refers to a kitchen; a *chú* is a kitchen building. The *Cangjie Pian* defines it as one who prepares food.

"An island in a stream" (*shuǐ zhǔ*) refers to its counterpart, the small islet; a "zhǔ" is called a small islet. Li Xun says: "Because it is surrounded by water on all four sides and is uniquely high enough to be inhabited, it is called a zhǔ. The *Shìmíng* states: "Zhǔ means 'to block' (*zhē*); because its body is high, it can block the water, causing it to flow around it."
*Chuan*: Pronounced *jiào* (with the ancient reading *xiào*). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "earth store" (*dìcáng*).
*Zú*: Pronounced *zǐ yù* (with the reading *zǐ*). "Zú" is equivalent to "accomplish" (*chéng*);

it means to be mutually sufficient for accomplishment. *Chǎn*: Pronounced *chǒu nìng* (with the lower reading *nú dìng*). To seek another's favor and speak according to their words is called *chǎn*. According to the *Shuowen*, one who is skillfully sycophantic and possesses high talent is called *zhì*; furthermore, to perform good deeds is also called *zhì*.

In the vernacular it is pronounced *huà*, written as 譮 in ancient script and 󲈫䛡 in another form; these two characters share the same pronunciation, which is *húyàng*. According to the *Guǎngpǐ*, "huà" means "to jest," referring to playful banter. According to the *Shēnglèi*, "huà" refers to "corrupt speech."
13. Volume Thirteen. *He* (和) and *mu* (穆) are also written as *mù* (睦). [The characters] *máng* (亡) and *lù* (鹿), and *máng* (亡) and *zhú* (竹) are pronounced with the second tone (*fǎn*).

*Mu* means harmony and reverence. *Xīn* (薟) is an archaic form; today it is written as *lián* (蘞). It is pronounced with the third tone (*fǎn*) following the principle of *tǐng* (理) and *jiǎn* (儉), or *zhān* (沾). According to the *Shuowen*, *xīn* is white and gray; it is a trailing plant that grows in the wild.
*La-na*: Following the character *la*, it means "contrary" (*la*). The radical of the character consists of "bundle" (*shù*) and "knife" (*dāo*).
Volume 14, Volume 14. *Āi-chén*: Pronounced as *niǎo-lái*. According to the *Tōngsú Wén*, "ash-dust" is called *ài*; thus, *ài* is also dust.
"Zhíxiàzhīshí" (石下之石): The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains "zhí" as the sole of the foot; it is also written as "zhí" (蹠) or "niè" (躡). It refers to water that does not cling [to the feet]. Volume Fifteen:

The preceding character is not phonetically indicated. Volume Sixteen: "Xuéyóu" (學泅): The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes this as "wū" (汙), or with "qiú" (囚) as the radical to form "yóu" (泅). The pronunciation is *sìliú* (似流反); it means floating on the surface of the water. In the region south of the Yangtze River, they say "pàifú" (拍浮).

The ancient character for *zhé* (磔) is the same as *ǒu* (㡯), with the phonetic component *zhú* (竹) and the radical *gé* (格). According to the *Guǎngyǐ*, *zhé* means "to stretch" (*zhāng*) and "to open" (*kāi*). The *Tōngsùwén* states that "stretching and extending" (*zhāngshēn*) is called *zhé*. This term appears as *zhé* in the *Lùnwén*, though its source has not yet been identified.

One *xun* (尋) is an ancient measure; it is sometimes written as 尋 or 同, with the phonetic reading similar to that of *lin*. It refers to the two arms of a person. The *Huainanzi* states: "A person is eight feet tall; a *xun* is double that, therefore eight feet is called a *xun*."

17. Volume Seventeen. Regarding the character *zhèn* (鎮) as used in the phrase "to suppress" (*zhènzhì* 鎮制): it means to subdue and also to bring peace. According to the *Cāngjié piān* (蒼頡篇), *zhèn* means to press down upon.

The characters *guàn* (串) and *xiū* (脩) form the compound "habitual cultivation" (*guànxiū*). The two forms are identical; in the *Lùn-wén* (Discourse on the Text), it is written as *guàn*, with the same pronunciation as *gǔhuàn* (古患). According to the *Ěrpǐ* (Dictionary of Correspondences), it means "habitual practice. Sharen (舍人) states: "It is the habituation of the mind."
*Pi* (僻): pronounced *pǐ* (匹赤反). "Bi" (僻) means deviant; it refers to conducting affairs with crookedness and injustice.

Volume 18, Chapter 18. Although *dié* (跌): pronounced *tuó* (徒結反). "Guǎng pǐ" (廣疋) states that *dié* means to stumble. The *Zìshū* (字書) says it is a corruption of *zhí* (跖). The *Fānyán* (方言) says *dié* means to trip and fall. Guo Pu says: "To lie prostrate on the ground."
"Not stumbling" (*bì*): *bì* also means "oblique. (19) Volume Nineteen.
"Deciding and measuring" (*jué dù*): *dù* is pronounced *tuó* in the Tang dialect; it means "to measure. "Discerning and measuring" (*bō dù*): it means "to weigh and measure."

*Chí* (馳) and *dòng* (動) are understood as the opposite of "direct" (*zhí*). According to the *Guǎnpǐ*, it means "to gallop"; the *Shuōwén* says it means "a great drive. To run swiftly is called *zǒu*.

*Yì* (弋), *lùn* (論), and also written as *yì* (杙), share the same pronunciation, *yúzhí* (余軄). The *Ěrpǐ* states: "The *tè* (𢴠) is called *yì* (杙). The commentary notes: "A *yì* is a wooden pin. The character *tè* (𢴠) is pronounced *túdé* (徒得). This is the term used in the Guanzhong region; in Jiangnan, they say *zhù yì* (樁杙).

*Kōn* (古弄反) means *gòng* (貢), which is the same as *zhì* (廌). According to the *Guǎngyǐ*, it means "superior" (*shàng*). *Xià* (下) is pronounced *xūjiàn* (虛建反). *Xiàn* (獻) means "to present. In antiquity, the term used for presenting objects to one's superior was called *xiàn*.

20. Volume Twenty: The preceding [term] is not pronounced [as such]. 21. Volume Twenty-one: "Shì" (適) has the phonetic component "shī" (尸). It is a broad synonym for "good" (*śubha*). This means being virtuous and excellent, such that it accords with the hearts of people.

"Hao-li" (毫氂) is also written as "hao" (毫) with the phonetic gloss "hu gao fan" (胡高反); the second character is an archaic form of "li" (氂), which in modern usage is written as "hao" (耗) with the phonetic gloss "li zhi fan" (力之反). The *Han shu*, *Lü li zhi* (律曆志), states: "not missing even a hair's breadth" (*bu shi hao li*). Meng Kang explains that "hao" refers to rabbit fur; ten hairs are called one "li. According to the *Sancang* (三蒼), "li" means hair; today it generally refers to fine texture or pattern. These ancient characters were used interchangeably.

Regarding "village" (*jù*): in the *Hànshū*, the school in the district is called *xù* (序) and that in the village is called *xiāng* (庠). Zhang Yan states: "These are names for settlements. Wei Zhao’s commentary on the *Xiǎopǐ* says: "A village is where people gather; 'luò' (落) means a dwelling, where people reside. This refers to the passage in the *Hànshū*: "He did not burn down the villages. *Note: The character 𡦗 in the source text is a variant or error for 落 (luò).*

*Abhidharmakośa-kārikā*, one fascicle. (Huilin’s Pronunciations: *Tang* is the upper tone for *tángwēi* (Hot Ashes); *wěi* is pronounced with the lower tone *huǐ* (as in *wěihuí*). This is the name of a hot hell. "Hot Ashes" refers to hot embers and fire; it also includes the Hell of the River of Ashes. All these are manifested according to the evil karma of the beings themselves. The sinners perceive them as their own experience—doing the deeds themselves and receiving the retribution themselves. All such matters of suffering are exactly like experiencing pleasure and pain within a dream.

The Karoṭapāṇis, the Mālādharas, and the Apsarases—namely, the Karoṭapāṇi devas, the Mālādhara devas, and the Apsarā devas—all reside upon the terraces of Mount Sumeru; they are all earth-dwelling devas who are subordinate states of the Four Great Kings and serve as the generals of the Lord Śakra.
*Śaṇḍha* (pronounced with the final syllable reversed) is a term from the Sanskrit language; it is a specific name for a eunuch (*pandaka*), as has already been fully explained in the preceding text.

*Pūrvavimāna* (the first and last being *pūpa*, pronounced *bāo* [with the initial *p* changed to *b*] and *dāng* [with the final *g* changed to *m*])—this refers to the *pārijātaka* tree atop the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, which in the language of Tang is called the "Perfectly Born Tree" (*yuánshēng shù*). When its flower buds emerge, their fragrance is perceived from afar, and all the devas rejoice.

The character 𡱈 (jiè) is pronounced with the initial *qióng* (the opposite of *yù*) and the final *kǎo*. It means realm (*jiè*), division (*fēn*), curvature (*qū*), or class (*cáo*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means urgency (*cù*) or proximity (*jìn*), composed of the radicals for "foot" (*chī*) and "mouth" (*kǒu*). The pronunciation of 卭 (*qióng*) is *gòng yóng*.

*Chōur-yé* (󲙼流軶): The first character is pronounced *páo* (袍) with the *qièyùn* rhyme *jǐ*, and the second has the sound *ài* (厄). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "The water that flows over the ox's neck at the tip of the carriage pole (*chē yuán*) is called *chōur*. This *yé* (軶) is also like this. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) says: "*Chōu* (󲙼) refers to water flowing suddenly during rain. It serves as a metaphor for the great river of birth and death, where karma acts as the water that sweeps away sentient beings. Bound by the *chōur-yé* (the flood and the yoke), they are driven through transmigration, emerging and sinking, born and dying, without any autonomy. *Niǎo* (㲻) is pronounced *nǚlì* (女力).

*Gūsuǒ* (骨鎖): *Suo* is pronounced with a retroflex *k* (如考). "Suo" means a chain; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to a linked ring. It is composed of the radical "metal" (金) and the phonetic "ruo" (𧴪), where "ruo" has the same pronunciation as above. It is composed of the small radical (小) and "bei" (貝); there are those who write it with "lao" (𧴲), which is incorrect. In the treatise, it is written with the "jade" (玉) radical as *suǒ* (瑣), but the sound of "yu" (玉) is not used here.

*Kṛkī* (pronounced *lì* with the *ǎn* tone) is the name of an auspicious beast, resembling a rhinoceros horn; because it has a single horn upon its head, this single horn is used as a metaphor for Pratyekabuddhas, who are also called "the solitary-horned.
*Aratni* (pronounced *fú* with the *děng* tone) means "like a wheel-spoke," as in the spokes of a chariot wheel.

The character 貶 (biǎn) is pronounced with the upper radical *biàn* and the phonetic *ān*. The *Kǎo Shēng* states that "biǎn" means to diminish or deplete wealth. Sīmà Xiāngrú used the archaic form 㝵; the *Shuōwén* defines it as "to diminish," composed of the radical 貝 with the phonetic 乏. The character 量 (liàng) is composed of 曰 as its radical and 童 as its correct body.

*Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, thirty fascicles. Fascicle One. [The phonetic glossary] by the Śramaṇa Xuanying. Regarding "Kośa" (俱舍): this is translated as "Treasury" (藏). It is a general term for a granary, a cocoon, or a sheath; it is so named because the meaning of "containing" (含藏) is identical. The character for "cocoon" (繭) is pronounced *jingyǎn* (經演); the character for "sheath" (韒) is pronounced *sīmào* (私妙), referring to a sword-sheath. "Treasury" has many names, and this is one of its designations.

*Zhūmíng* (諸冥): Pronounced *jiǎn* (覓) with a retroflex initial and *dìng* (定) with a labiodental final. The *Cāngxié piān* states that "zhū" (諸) means "not one. The *Shēnglèi* says it is a general term for words. The *Erlǚ* says "míng" (冥) means "darkness" or "obscure. The *Shuowén* says "míng" (冥) means "deeply hidden" and also "night. The character is composed of *mìng* (冖, pronounced *míng* with a *bì* [壁] final) and *yuè* (曰). "Yuè" (曰) is the number sixteen; when the moon begins to wane, it is called "míng" (冥), which conveys the meaning of the character.

*Lún* (淪): The pronunciation is *jūn* (均) with a reversed final. According to the *Guǎngyǐ*, *lún* means to sink; it also means to drown. Furthermore, *lún* means deep; it also means to fall or descend. *Jiè* (誡):

The pronunciation is *juài* (薤) with a reversed final; the character below is pronounced *xūyù* (虛玉). To warn or admonish is called *jiè*; to exert oneself for self-improvement is called *xù*. Furthermore, *jiè* also means to caution or advise; *xù* refers to striving with diligence.
Kātyāyanīputra—formerly translated as Jiāzhānyánzǐ—is named after his clan; some say that "Kātyāyana" is a phonetic variation of the same name.

*Udāna* (the first character pronounced like *wu gu*, the second like *tu wo*): this is translated as "Spontaneous Declaration," meaning that which is spoken of one's own accord without waiting for a question. The old translation, *Ūdana*, refers to the *Anupṛṣṭa-svayaṃbhāṣita-sūtra* (Sūtra of Unquestioned Self-Declarations).

Regarding *Vibhāṣā*, some say it is derived from the term *nirvibhāṣā*; when expressed according to its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it becomes *vibhāṣā*. This is translated as "Extensive Explanation" (*guǎngjiě*). Others say it means "Extensive Exposition," or "Various Explanations," or "Segmented Explanations"—all of which convey the same meaning.
*Tiè* (等謝): *tiè* is pronounced with a final *-xiǎn* (似夜反). According to the *Guǎngyǐ*, *tiè* means "to go" or "to depart.

*Sūn* (所吞): *sūn* is pronounced with a final *-huán* (他痕他賢二反). According to the *Guǎngyǐ*, *sūn* means "to swallow up" or "to extinguish"; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means "to swallow. *Tìè* (吞謝): *tìè* means "not chewing.
