According to the *Guǎngyǐ*, it means "to swallow up and destroy"; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means "to swallow."

"Contest" (zheng) is also written as "strife" (zheng). According to the *Cangjie pian*, it means "to dispute" (*zhengsong*) or "to lead" (*yin*). The *Shuowen jiezi* defines it as "when two parties compete to pull an object toward themselves."
*Qì téng* (氣騰): *téng* is pronounced as *dēng* (徒登反). According to the *Guǎngyǐ*, it means to ascend; it also means to gallop. *Kuào xì* (竅隙): *kuào* is pronounced as *kǎo* (口弔反);

below it is also written as *qī* (𡭽), which is the same. According to the *Guǎngyǐ*, *kuào* means a hole, and *xì* means a crack. The *Shuōwén* states that *kuào* means an empty space, and *xì* refers to a hole at the junction of a wall. The character is composed of *kuài* (𨸏) and *bái* (白); "small" (*xiǎo*) refers to the top and bottom parts [of the character].

*Āgāga* is translated here as "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*). The prefix *ā-* has two meanings: it may mean "non-" (*na*) or it may mean "extreme" (*ati*); since it thus contains both interpretations, the original name was established accordingly.

2. The second fascicle concludes. *Piśāca*: In older translations this is called *Vijñā*. It is also known as the *Bìshèzhà* ghost; it is the name for a type of spirit, specifically one that is superior among the hungry ghosts (*preta*).

The *śiśumāra* is shaped like an elephant; in older sūtras and vinayas it is sometimes written as *shīshu móluo* or *shīshǒu móluo*, which are merely variations in the Sanskrit pronunciation. It is translated as "the child-killer fish. The *Sudarsana-vinaya* calls it the crocodile (*krokodila*). It is over two zhang in length, has four legs resembling those of a *táo* (a large lizard), and its teeth are extremely sharp; if it bites birds, deer, humans, or water animals, they are severed instantly. It is native to Guangzhou, where it is found in the local waters.

The bat sleeps facing downward and has eyes on its back. *Cui Bao’s Ancient and Modern Notes* states: "The bat is also called the 'Immortal Mouse' (*xiānshǔ*) and the 'Flying Mouse' (*fēishǔ*). At five hundred years of age, its color becomes white and its brain grows heavy; when it alights upon objects, its head hangs down, hence it is called the 'Inverted-Bat' (*dàoguà fīfáng*). Eating it leads to immortality."

*Húliú* (鵂鶹) [the first character pronounced *xǔ* with the *niú* tone; the second character pronounced *lì* with the *zhōu* tone]. According to the *Erya*, it is called *gēi*. Guo Pu says: "In the Jiangdong region today, the *húliú* is called the *gōugēi*; *gēi* is pronounced *gé*. The *Guangya* states that the *húliú*, *jiāo*, and *shù* are synonyms; *jiāo* is pronounced *miǎo* with the *fǎn* tone. It is also said to be a strange bird that is blind by day but can see at night, and its cry is considered ominous. In the region west of the Pass it is called *hòuhóu*, while in the region east of the mountains it is called *hòuhú*. The *Zuǎnwén* says that at night it picks up human fingernails."

*Śṛgāla* (Sanskrit) refers to a creature with a body color that is blueish-yellow like a dog; it travels in packs and howls at night with a voice like a wolf. The character is also written as *shègān*. The *Anshi xu fu* (Rhapsody on the Capital) states: "Tengyuan and Shègān [roam]. Sima Biao, Guo Pu, and others in their commentaries all state that the Shègān resembles a fox but is smaller and can climb trees (*shè* pronounced as *yè*). The *Guǎngzhì* says it nests on perilous cliffs and tall trees. This is the same creature mentioned in the *Chan jing* (Dhyāna Sūtra), which speaks of seeing a wild fox and then a *shègān*.

"Those who serve as jackals and wolves all turn against [their masters]. The *Huángdì Cāngjié Xuànhù* explains: "The jackal resembles a dog; it is white in color, possesses claws and fangs, is swift and agile, and is skilled at seizing and biting. In the *Ēryà*, it says: "The jackal has the feet of a dog. The pronunciation of "shì" (seizing/biting) is *shízhì* (時制).

*Māo* (cat) is the same as *māo* (cat); it is read as *wú* (without) in the first instance and *bāo* (to wrap) with the second tone in the latter. It refers to that which catches mice. According to the *Guǎngyǐ*, it is the *lí* (wild cat), and it is also called the wild *lí*.
Kumāralāta is translated here as "Child-Head" (Tóngshǒu), meaning he was the foremost among all children.
Regarding *pāo* (pronounced *bō máo*), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it refers to the inner membrane of a child at birth.

*Ti* (洟) and *tuo* (唾) are ancient characters; *ti* is pronounced as in *ta-jì*. According to the *Sāncāng*, *ti* is the liquid from the nose. In the *Zhouyi*, it says "to weep and flow with tears and *ti*"; that which comes from the eyes is called *ti*, and that which comes from the nose is called *ti*.
"Defense and assistance" (*fángyuán*)—the "fǎn" in *yǔfǎn* means "to guard, watch over, and protect. "Yuán" is also a character for "to take," derived from the radical for "hand.

*Sphaṭika* (pronounced *zhěshī* as a reconstruction)—also called *sāpòjiā*—is the name of a treasure from the Western Regions; the old translation "phōlí" is an abbreviated corruption. This is translated here as "water-jade" or "white pearl. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that this treasure comes from within mountain caves and is formed when ice that has existed for a thousand years transforms into *sphaṭika* pearls; such things may indeed exist. However, the Western Regions abound in this substance, yet they have no ice there—by what could it possibly be transformed? It is merely a type of stone.

"Zhā" (樝) is also written as "zhē" (抯), both with the phonetic *zèjiā* (側加); the second character is also written as "mó" (摩), with the phonetic *chōngshì* (充世). "Shì" (釋) means each [finger] individually. "Zhā" (樝) refers to the five fingers all going together to grasp and take hold. "Chè" (掣) means to restrain; it means to constrain and suppress them so that they become compliant with oneself. "Chè" (掣) also means to pull.
*Mǎishí* (礠石): Pronounced *cú zī* (徂茲反). According to the *Běicāng*, "magnet stone" refers to that which attracts iron.
*Fǔshǒu* (拊手): Pronounced *fāng zhǔ* (芳主反). "Fǔ" is like "pāi" (to clap). According to the *Guǎngyǐ*, "fǔ" means to strike; furthermore, "fǔ" is also "fǔ" (to stroke/caress).

*Miǒu* (糅) is an archaic character; it has two forms, both pronounced *nǚ jiù* (女救反). In the *Guǎngyǐng* (廣詠), it means "mixed" (*zà*) or "intermingled. Today, when objects of different colors are combined together, it is called *miǒu*.
*Xiàng* (向) is pronounced *xǔ liàng* (許亮反); according to the *Sāncāng* (三蒼), it refers to a window facing north. *Xiàng* is also synonymous with *chuāng* (牕).

The character for *xiāngsuǐ* (coriander) is also written as *suǐ*; the *Yuán* (Garden) states it is the same as *qí*, with the phonetic *sī* and *zhuī*. The *Yùnlüè* (Rhyme Summary) says it is the "barbarian *suǐ*" or "fragrant herb. The *Bówùzhì* (Treatise on the Wonders of Nature) states that Zhang Qian obtained the "barbarian *qí*" during his mission to the Western Regions; this is it. Today in Jiangnan, the barbarian *qí* is also called *húsù* (pronounced *húxī*), though this was recently changed to *xiāngsuǐ*.
*Huá pí* (桦皮): A name for a type of tree; its bark can be used to ornament bows. *Guān* (冠) means to wear; it is a synonym for "adornment.

The term below is the Sanskrit *mālā*, which in this translation is rendered as "garland" (*huán*). [The character] is pronounced *mò bān*. According to the Western regions, garland-makers mostly use *sumana* flowers, stringing them in rows to form strands. Regardless of whether they are male or female, noble or humble, all use these to adorn themselves—either on their heads or their bodies—as a mark of beauty. Thus, in various sutras, there are references to flower garlands, celestial garlands, and jewel garlands, all of which are similar to this. The character is written with the radical *biāo* (pronounced *suó xián*) and the phonetic *miǎn* (pronounced *mí rán*).

*Gū* (桑朗反; *sāng lǎng fǎn*) is defined in the *Pīcāng* as the frame of a drum (*gū shǔ*). Lexicons state it refers to the material of the drum; today in Jiangnan, the rim of the drum is called *gū kuāng*, while *shǔ* is pronounced *wǔ guǎ* (*wǔ guǎ fǎn*).

*Zhǐ gǒng* (now written as 㧺) is pronounced *dú dá* (*dú dá fǎn*). The *Shuowen* defines it as a leather strap for a finger-guard (*zhǐ gǒng wéi gǒng*), which is the same as the leather guard used by archers today.

*Naraka* (pronounced *nu-ge* with a retroflex *ṇ*) is a place where suffering is experienced; alternatively, it refers to those who undergo punishment (*nāraka*). This is translated as "that which is not to be enjoyed" (*a-sukha*), or "not a [proper] course of action," meaning a place of unrighteous conduct. It may be located among mountains or on the shores of the great ocean, not merely beneath the earth; thus, "earth-hell" (*di-yu*) is one sense in which it is translated.

3. Third Fascicle. Regarding the *śaṇḍha-paṇḍaka* (the third type of *paṇḍaka*): in the older sūtras and śāstras, it is sometimes called *baṇḍa* or *baṇḍaka*; these are regional variations in pronunciation, with differences in weight between the northern and southern dialects. *Paṇḍaka* is translated here as "eunuch" (*huángmén*) and serves as the general name for this category. There are five types of such individuals; the third among them, the *śaṇḍha-paṇḍaka*, refers to one who from birth lacks the male organ and is also incapable of procreating offspring.
*Yan* (pronounced *jian* with the radical *ju* and the phonetic *yan*; the character is abbreviated as *wei*) refers to the outer skin of the eyes. Volume Four, Section Four.

*Jing* (in ancient texts written as *jing*, both forms share the pronunciation *ying*): to be on guard, to exercise caution, to admonish, to instruct, and also to arouse. According to the *Guangpi*, "to be on guard" means to be uneasy and to be prepared.

*Yìn* (pronounced with the *yī* and *zhèn* finals) means a seal of authorization (*yìn-xìn*). It refers to a written record that is trusted and put into practice wherever it is applied. The character is composed of the radicals for "melon" (*guā*) and "seal" (*jié*, pronounced *jiē*).

*Yǒng* (pronounced with the *huán* final; the second character has the *hú* and *qiě* finals): "Courageous" (*yǒng*) refers to being valiant, martial, and resolute. The *Shìfǎ* (Canon of Posthumous Titles) states: "To know death yet not avoid it is called courage; to risk one's life for benevolence is called courage. The *Shuōwén* says: "Fierce and courageous, possessing strength. The *Sāncāng* says: "Fierce and outstanding. "Outstanding" (*jié*) means one whose wisdom surpasses a thousand men.

"Not conversant with the forms of characters" (不閑字體) refers to the character 𢡿, which is pronounced *hé* (same as the rhyme of 艱). "Conversant" (*xián*) is a term for being practiced and proficient; to be habituated and skilled is called "conversant.
Its pronunciation is *zhǐ* (same as the rhyme of 脂). The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as 恉, meaning intention or will.
"Untried" (*wèicháng*) is pronounced with the rhyme of *guǎng-pǐ*; it means "to test," "for a moment," or "light. "Never tried before" (*wèicháng*) means "never yet.

"Flattery" (*chǎn*) is pronounced with the rhyme of *chǒu-kuì*; it means to seek out another's intentions and repeat their words—this is called flattery, meaning to bend one's body to show subservience. Flattery is also a form of deception. "Deception" (*kuàng*) means to delude or to cheat.

"Jiǎolàn" (撟亂) [pronounced *jiǎo* with the tone *yāo*] means to feign, deceive, and delude others. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "jiǎo" (撟) means to usurp authority; to arrogantly claim the sovereign's commands is called "jiǎo. The character is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "qiáo" (喬); nowadays, it is all written as "jiǎo" (矯).

*Lie* (烈): "Li" and "zhe" are reversed; "guang" and "pi" mean extensive. *Lie* means flourishing. According to the *Shuowen*, "liehuo" means fierce fire. *Ju* (舉) and *shi* (恃) are archaic forms of *bu* (怖);
"shi" is pronounced with the initial "ti" and final "zhong. It means to rely upon. In the *Han Shi*, "What does one rely on without a mother? means to depend on. *Fu* (負) means to carry.

* Língmèi (凌懱): *líng* is pronounced with the fanqie *lìshēng* (反下) and is also written as *lǐng* (󱢾), both having the same pronunciation (*mòjié* 反). According to the *Cāngjiépiān*, "líng" means to invade or encroach upon; according to the *Shuōwén*, "mèi" means to treat one another with contempt. * Àoyì (傲逸): *ào* is pronounced with the fanqie *wǔdào* (反).
According to the *Guǎngyǐ*, it means arrogance and haughtiness, or a lack of reverence. It refers to being disdainful toward others; "yì" (逸) refers to license or unrestrained indulgence.

*Fénshāo* (焚燒) and *fènsǐ* (炃燌)—the two forms are identical, pronounced *fúyún* (扶雲反). According to the *Shuowen*, "burning fields" (*fénshāo tiányě*); the character is composed of "fire" (*huǒ*) and "forest" (*lín*), signifying the meaning of burning a forest.
*Tángjuān* (唐捐)—pronounced *zhuānyuán* (專反). *Táng* means "idle" (*tú*) or "vain" (*kōng*). According to the *Shuowen*, "to discard" (*juànqì*).
5. Fifth Fascicle, Part One. *Cīrṣa* (pronounced with a retroflex *ṣ*, formerly transcribed as *nāsa*): the fruit is shaped like a winter claw and its flavor is extremely sweet. *Kuru*:

here it is called "Superior" (*xiangsheng*) or "Born of Excellence" (*shengsheng*). In older translations it appears as *Uttarakuru*, or *Uttaravatsa*, or *Uttarakaulu*; these are all variations in the weight of the Sanskrit pronunciation.

*Śreṇī* (pronounced *zhì lián* in Chinese; in Sanskrit, *āpaṭa-ratha*, here translated as "market district" or "commercial quarter"). In the *Liji* (Book of Rites), it says: "There were well-districts and market-districts, but no taxation. Zheng Xuan commented: "Market-districts (*chán*) refers to shop-houses for selling goods. *Chán* means dwelling; it is where people reside. The *Fangyan* (Dialect Dictionary) states that in the region between the Eastern Qi, the sea, and Mount Dai, they call a residence a *chán*. The old explanation [of *śreṇī*] as "desiring to travel" is likely an error. According to the Sanskrit name, "traveling" is *saṃskāra*.

*Kuǐfàn* (軌範) is also written as *fàn* (笵), which is homophonous with *fàn* (范). It means "standard" (*guǐzé*) and "model" (*fànfǎ*). That is to say, it refers to that which may serve as a standard, as well as the method for instructing others. The Sanskrit term is *ācārya*; the older transliteration *āshílí* (阿闍梨) is a corruption.
*Jiāng* (居良反; the same as the archaic *pǔ*) means to lie face upward; *fù* (蒲北反) means to lie face downward. It refers to lying prostrate or prone.
*Fèn* (扶粉反) means fullness according to the *Fān yán*; the *Shuōwén* says it means "fullness. It refers to the swelling and overflowing of one's indignant energy.
"殞沒" (yǔnmì) is also written as "隕" (yǔn), with the phonetic reading *mǐnrén* (as in *mǐnrén*). The *Shēnglèi* states it means "to perish" (*biémò*) and also "to fall.
"Dàlmíluó" (達弭羅) is read as *mǐ'ěr* (as in *mǐ'ěr*); this is translated here as "the teaching that inspires awe."

*Uttara* (the first syllable pronounced with a retroflex *u*, here translated as "superior reception") and *Gaṅgila* (the second syllable pronounced as *ji*, here translated as "reception of the Ganges") are both personal names.

The "egret" (*bài lù*)—so called because it is a water bird with long feathers on its head, wings, and back—is used in the Jiangdong region to make false eyelashes; the *Li sao* says, "The egret has *sūléi* (pronounced *sū léi*) feathers."

The character *sì* (嗣) is pronounced *cí tóng yí fǎn* (辝同辝利反). According to the *Erya*, "to succeed" (*sì*) means to continue; it refers to continuous succession. The character *fēng* (犎) is pronounced *hú fēi fēng fǎn* (胡妃封反), with another reading as *fēng* (封);

below it is also written as *xié* (頡) or *yàn* (咽), both forms being interchangeable. It refers to a hump-backed ox whose back has a fleshy pad like that of a camel; this is the "fēng. Now there is an ox of this shape, small in stature, with a *fēng* upon its shoulders. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "A hump-backed ox with a dewlap hanging from the chin. The *Shiming* explains: "A 'hú' is that which hangs down from the throat."

"Still" (仍) is pronounced *niù* (initial *n*, final *iu*) and has the same radical as "to exceed" (*líng*). According to the *Guǎngyǐ*, "still" means "repeatedly"; according to the *Ěryǐ*, "still" means "thereby" (*yīn*) or "then" (*nǎi*).

The middle character is pronounced *mí* (initial *m*, final *éng*) and is called a "signifier" (*biāozhì*), which is also what constitutes its essential nature and its self-designation. The *Zuǒzhuan* states, "Names are used to establish righteousness. According to the *Guǎngyǐ*, "name" (*míng*) means "to accomplish. The character is composed of "mouth" (*kǒu*) and "evening" (*xī*); "evening" implies not seeing one another, and thus the mouth is required to name them—this is the meaning of the character.

Regarding the term "wénzì" (text/characters), according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, Cang Jie invented writing by modeling forms after categories and images; thus it was called "wén" (pattern). Subsequently, as forms and sounds supplemented one another, they were called "zì" (characters). "Zì" means "to produce"; like the procreation of offspring, they gradually increased in number.
The syllable *a-u* may be called a meaningless phoneme (*akṣara*).
The term *uṇ-ādi* (with *uṇ* pronounced with a retroflex *ṛ*) refers to the *dhātu* (verbal roots); this signifies the collection of meanings and bases, namely the alphabet.

6. The Sixth Fascicle. *Kalala* (the *lú* in *lu-ge* is pronounced as such, or it is written as *jié-ló-lán*, or spoken of as *gē-luó-luó*; all refer to the same thing). This is translated here as "doubt-slippery" (*yí-huá*) or "conjunction" (*hé-hé*). It refers to the impurities of the father and mother, which, like honey mixed with curd, merge into one. During the first seven days of conception, this "doubt-slippery" stage is like the cream on top of curd.
"Rùn wò" (moistening and nourishing) is an archaic term synonymous with "wù" (pronounced with the "niǎo mù" rhyme). "Wù" means to irrigate, to water, or to soak.

"Nuoqutuo" (諾瞿陀) is an old transliteration for the *nyagrodha* tree; it is also written as *nijulutuo*, *nijulituo*, or *nijuluduo*, all of which refer to the same thing. Former translations rendered it as "the knotless tree" (*wujie shu*) or "the tree that spreads from its base" (*congguang shu*).

"Zhongyao" (premature death) is also written as "yao" with the same pronunciation (*jiao* fanqie). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "yao" means to bend or contract; according to the *Guangya*, it means to break off prematurely. The character for "zhong" (middle) takes the form of a large animal that is not fully extended. Furthermore, the meaning of the character is to die before completing one's natural lifespan, which is called "yao."
*Yazú* (pronounced *yàjia*): It is said that because the grass resembles a crow’s foot, it is named accordingly.

*Nóngfū* (farmer): In ancient texts, there were two forms, *㭕* and *莀*, both pronounced *núdōng*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* correctly records it as *nóng*, meaning "to plow"; the current form *nóng* is a vulgar character.

7. Fascicle Seven. *Sǒnggàn* (聳幹). The ancient texts present two forms: *sǒng* (聳) and *sù* (竦), which are identical in meaning. One must hold [the head] high; "yǒng" (勇) is read with the second tone. According to the *Guǎngyǐ*, it means "to rise up. The character below is read as *gōngdàn* (公旦). "Gàn" (幹) refers to the stem or root, as well as the branches and trunk.

"Xizhao" (先兆) is read as *chāo* (矯). Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states: "A 'zhao' (兆) refers to a manifested form; it is also a 'jizhao' (機兆, omen-sign). That which is perceived beforehand regarding an event is called a 'zhao'. Regarding "zhanxiang" (占相), "zhan" is read as *yan* (塩).
The *Fangyan* states: "To 'zhan' means to look at; it is also to observe. Generally, to observe and wait for [signs] is called 'zhan'; 'zhan' is also synonymous with 'zhan' (瞻, to gaze)."
"Duō" (咄): In the *Zílín*, it is pronounced with the rhyme of *dū* (都) and *yù* (杌). It means "to address. In lexicographical works, it is also used as "to scold.

Its phonetic value is *chì* (叱), with the rhyme of *chǐ* (齒) and *yì* (逸). (8) Volume Eight, Part Eight. "Fànzhì" (反質): Rhymes with *yì* (逸). In the *Guǎngpǐ*, it means "to question" and also "to correct."

"Eggshell" (luǎnquè) is also written as "luǎnkuò," with the same pronunciation as "kǒujué" (the corner of the mouth). The character for "kuò" (殼) has the phonetic component "hùi" (會) and the radical "mouth" (口), pronounced "kù" (哭). It refers to the hard exterior of an egg; when it is still within the egg, it is called a "ké" (殼).
Furthermore, "xu" (欻)—pronounced "yùwù" (吁物)—the *Cāngjié piān* states that it means to arise suddenly; it also means "abruptly."

"Cái" (纔): "Cái" means "just," "merely," "inferior," or "not long. According to the *Guǎngpǐ*, "cái" means "temporary. According to the *Sāncāng*, "cái" means "slight. "Gù" (固): Only in ancient texts is it written as "hú" (怘).
"Gù" is pronounced with the initial *hù* (古護反). "Gù" means "certainly" or "necessarily. According to the *Xiǎo'ěrpǐ*, "gù" also means "therefore" or "thus."

"Zha" (pronounced *zhā* with the retroflex *zh* as in *zhǎng*) refers to what is currently called in the Jiangnan region "shì" (a wooden slice cut and planed), while in Guanzhong it is called "zhā" or "shìzhā. "Shì" is pronounced *fūfèi*.
*Xiṅbèng* (星迸): "Ancient text reads *pénpén* (跰) or *bān* (𧻓), both pronounced *bān* (孟反). *Bèng* means to scatter and run away. *Wǔtuónán* (嗢柁南):

Pronounced *wǔmò* (鳥沒反) for the first character and *tú'ě* (徒我反) for the second. *Wǔ* here means "to gather" (*jí*); *tuónán* here means "to bestow" (*shī*), meaning that having gathered [the offerings], one bestows them upon people. The character is written with the "wood" radical.

Yama (pronounced with the *yan* rhyme, sometimes written as Yamarāja, or simply Yama, or also as Yamaloka)—these are all variations of the Sanskrit sound corrupted through regional dialects. This is translated as "Binding" (*bó*) or "The Twin World" (*shuāng shì*). I personally believe it is so named because suffering and pleasure are experienced together. Furthermore, it is called "Bound Yama" (*fù yán mó*), which means "Twin King" (*shuāng luó shè*). This refers to the fact that both the elder brother and the younger sister serve as kings of hell; the elder brother governs the affairs of men, while the younger sister governs the affairs of women, hence they are called the "Twin Kings."

9. The Ninth Fascicle. *Koṭi* (pronounced *zhìchí* with the second tone; alternatively read as *jùzhì*, which corresponds to the Chinese term *yì*, meaning ten million). Alternatively, one hundred thousand is called *yì*, or ten thousand times ten thousand is called *yì*. In Western countries, a *koṭi* may refer to ten million, one billion, or ten billion; because these definitions vary greatly, the original Sanskrit name has been retained here.
*Kṛkī* (pronounced with the *jǔ* rhyme and the *zhǐ* final) is the name of the father-king of Kāśyapa Buddha.

*Fěngsòng* (the first character pronounced with the *fèng* rhyme and the second with the *cí yòng* rhyme): *fěng* refers to chanting and reciting; furthermore, because it is modulated by tone, it is called *fěngsòng*, meaning laudatory chanting.
Regarding the characters for *xiong* (bear), *ma* (horse), and *hu* (wild boar) in the *Shuowen Jiezi*: "The bear is like a pig that dwells in the mountains and hibernates in winter;

its paw resembles a human hand and is called *fán* (pinyin: fán). Regarding *bēi* (brown bear): "It is like a bear, yellowish-white. Guo Pu says it resembles a bear but has a long neck, is like a horse in its build, has high legs, is fierce and powerful, and can uproot trees; it is called *jiāhǎn* (pinyin: jiāhàn) in Guānxī. *Hǎn* is pronounced *hūlàn*; *jiā* is pronounced *jiā*.
*Kaṭhina* is another name for this [robe].

A *lu* (廬)—pronounced with the initial *l* and the final *ju* reversed—is a place where one dwells; it refers to a separate shed. The Yellow Emperor established these *lu* in order to avoid the cold and heat; the *Spring and Autumn Annals* states that one dwells in them during winter and summer.

*Kiṇāhu* (the initial *ki* is pronounced with a retroflex *n*; the old transcription was *gahana*, which means "hard and thick"). This refers to the fact that by the fourth week, the mass of flesh finally becomes firm and thick. *Bhiṣa* (the initial *bhi* is pronounced with a retroflex *ṣ*;

the *Shijing* says, "I think, yet it does not open," and its commentary states that *bhi* means "to close" or "not to follow"). The character below is written as *se* (pronounced *suo-li*), meaning "not slippery. The character is composed of four "stop" radicals (*zhǐ*); two are inverted and two are upright, which immediately conveys the meaning of "obstruction."

A physician (*yi*) is one who is skilled in treating illness through the reversal of symptoms; thus it is a "craftsman" (*gong*). The nature of the physician requires wine to administer medicine, for without wine the medicine does not disperse; therefore, the character is composed of *you* (wine) and *e*. *E* is the phonetic component, pronounced *yixi* (or *yī*), and is sometimes written as *yi*; both forms are vulgar characters.

"Infant" (yīng'ér) is read as yíngfǎn in the *Sāncāng*. The *Shìmíng* states: "A girl is called yīng and a boy is called ér. When a person is first born, they are called an 'infant' (yīng'ér). That which is before the chest is called 'yīng'; because one holds [the child] in front of the 'yīng' and nourishes them in a disordered manner, they are therefore called 'ér'."
*Xiǎn*: *wèilí* (the second character is pronounced with the *shì* and *rǎn* finals). It is a slippery grass used for washing the hands; it makes them very smooth and lustrous. *Kuìlàn*:
The ancient text uses *huàn* (same as above) interchangeably. In the *Cāngjié piān*, "kuì" refers to breaking open at the sides; according to the *Shuōwén*, "kuì" means to leak.

"Po" (叵) is pronounced "pǔ" with a retroflex initial. The *Sāncāng* states: "Po means 'not possible'. The character "po" is formed by reversing "shòu" (受); "fǎn" (反) means to reverse; "kě" (可) becomes "po" when reversed—these are all based on the semantic principles of the characters.

Regarding "shù" (述), it is pronounced "chún yù" (脣聿). Confucius said: "Shù means 'to cultivate' (修). Examining the gloss for "shù," its meaning is "principle" (理). In the *Erlǚ* (爾疋), it says: "Shù means 'cultivation' (修) and 'practice' (行)."

"Tì" (涕) and "lèi" (淚) [are pronounced with the *zhǎng* and *rén* tones respectively]. The *Shijing* says, "Tìsì pāngtuó" (涕泗滂沱), meaning weeping; that which flows from the nose is called *tì*, and that which flows from the eyes is called *lèi*.

According to the *Guǎngpǐ*, *tì*, *qì*, and *lèi* are synonymous. *Líxì* (離繫) is also called *bùxì* (不繫); the Sanskrit term is *nirgrantha*, also *nijianlian* (泥揵連). These non-Buddhists (*tīdào*) pluck out their hair, expose their bodies, possess no stored goods, beg for food with their hands, and eat whatever they obtain immediately.

Pāśupata (also written as Pāsu; this refers to the non-Buddhist practitioners who smear ashes over their bodies). They smear ashes all over their bodies, and as for their hair, they may either shave it or leave it unshaven. Their clothing merely covers the body, provided it is not red—this is the distinction. They serve the deity Maheśvara.

Pāṇḍarabhikṣu (also called Pāṇḍaravāsaka) means "one who wears white garments. Nārāyaṇa leaves a small tuft of hair on his crown and shaves the rest entirely; he wears an undergarment that merely covers his body, which is ugly in appearance and dyed a color resembling red earth.

10. The Tenth Fascicle. "Zhèn" (鎮): Zhēn (知) and Zhèn (陣) are homophones; it is also pronounced Zhēn (珎). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means to suppress or to bring peace. The *Guangya* states that it means heavy or weighty.
Since the term *bhūta* already carries multiple meanings, its original name is retained.

Regarding "famine" (*jīn*), the ancient texts write it as 飢 or 饉, both pronounced with the same phonetic component as 几 (jiǎ). The *Erlǐ* states: "When grain does not ripen, it is called famine (*jī*); when vegetables do not ripen, it is called scarcity (*jìn*). Generally speaking, all edible plants and trees are collectively termed "vegetables" (*sūcài*).

"Yángtóng" (洋銅) is read as "zhāngfǎn"; it refers to copper that has been boiled until it dissolves and becomes fluid (*yāngyāngrán*). According to the *Sāncāng*, "yāng" describes the appearance of a vast body of water; the character is also written simply as "yàng," which explains metal.
"Zhànbù" (贍部) is read as "shíyàn fǎn"; it is the name of a tree. In older translations of the scriptures, it is sometimes written as "Shányóu" (剡浮) or "Yánfú" (閻浮), both of which are corruptions.
*Yán* (pronounced *lián* in the *Liǎn* rhyme) appears in the *Shī*: "Hè hè yán yán" (Blazing, blazing). The commentary states it means "intense heat.

Regarding the three calamities (*sānzāi*), in the *Zhuówén* script they are written as 災 or 烖; these two forms are identical. *Zāi* (pronounced *zǎi*, rhyming with *zāi*) means "to injure. According to this, anything that harms or injures people is called a *zāi*. Furthermore, when Heaven acts contrary to the seasons, it is called a *zāi*; thus, *zāi* also refers to illness.
"Bathing" (mù yù): according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "washing the hair is called bathing (mù), and sprinkling the body is called bathing (yù).
"Dust" (ái): according to the *Cangjie Pian*, "dust refers to the wind blowing up fine particles."
*Xiāo* (性嚻) means clamor; it refers to the appearance of noisy and restless commotion. Volume Eleven, Part One. *Yojana* (踰繕那):

this is pronounced *shì zhàn* and translated here as "conjunction" (*hé*) or "correspondence" (*yīng*). It refers to a calculated distance that should be joined together; it is equivalent to a *lǐ* (li) in this land [of China]. Since ancient times, the sage-kings have referred to it as a "journey" (*xíng*). According to the Western regions, there are both large and small *yojanas*; some are thirty *lǐ*, while traditionally forty *lǐ* has been taken as the standard. In the older sūtras and śāstras, it is sometimes written as *yúshéna* (踰闍那), sometimes as *yóuyán* (由延), and also as *yóuxún* (由旬); it is also called *yòujù* (俞句), all of which are corruptions or abbreviations.
*Nokhena* (諾健那) is the name of a powerful deity who appears naked.

It is the same as *chuan* (篅), which according to the *Cangjie pian* (蒼頡篇) is pronounced with the rhyme *shi-yuan* (市緣反); it refers to a circular granary. The *Shuowen jiezi* (說文) defines it as a split bamboo vessel, round in shape, used for storing grain. This pronunciation (*shi-yuan*) is used in the Jiangnan region, while in the Central Plains (China proper), it is pronounced with the rhyme *shang-xian* (上仙反).
*Tuán* (with the tone of *tú huán fǎn*): to join; it means round or thick. According to the *Hǔpǐ*, *tuán* means to adhere; to press them together so that they stick to one another. *Sumeru*:
this is translated as "Wondrous High Mountain" (*Miaoshāoshān*) or "Fine Light Mountain" (*Hǎoguāngshān*). The old translations "Xūmí" or "Xūmílóu" are all corruptions.

The term *gandharva*—an older transliteration of which is *yòuqiāntuóluó shān* (由乾陀羅山)—is translated here as "Mount Yugaṃdhara" (Mount Holding the Pair). It is so named because the mountain peaks have two ridges or paths, hence the name.

*Īṣādhara*, formerly called *Īṣādhāra*, means "Holder of Sovereignty" (*īśvara-dhara*). It is also said to mean "Holder of the Axle" (*īṣā-dhara*), because this mountain has many peaks shaped like the axles of chariots, and is thus named accordingly.

Kailāsa (pronounced *kai-di-lo-jiā*, with the final syllable reversed); this is translated as "Mountain-Bearing Tree. It is said that because the precious trees on this mountain are shaped like the tree that bears its load, it was named accordingly.
Sudarśana; this is translated as "Good to Behold. It is said that because this mountain is so majestic and exquisitely beautiful that one praises it as "good" upon seeing it, it was named thus.
Aśvakarṇa (pronounced with a retroflex *k*): this means "Horse Ear. It is named for the fact that the shape of its mountain peaks resembles a horse's ear.

Vinataka (pronounced with a retroflex *ṭ*): this means "The Obstructing Deity. There is a spirit in human form whose head always creates obstructions whenever it sees the affairs of others; because this mountain peak resembles the head of that deity, it is so named.

*Nimindhara*—formerly called *Nimindara*—is translated as "Earth-Supporting Mountain" (*dichi shan*). It is also the name of a fish; because the peaks of this mountain resemble the head of that fish named *Mindhara* found in the ocean, it is also known by that name.

*Vaiḍūrya* (the "fu" in *fèi* is pronounced as *fèi*; the old transcription is *vīriya*, also called *vitūriya*; some say *vaidūrya*, and it is also written as *veḍūrya*—these are all variations in the pronunciation of the Sanskrit term). It is named after a mountain, *Vitūriya*. This mountain produces this gem; it is called the "Gem of the Distant Mountain," and the Distant Mountain is none other than Mount Sumeru. This gem is blue in color, and no other gems can destroy it, nor can it be melted by smoke or flame; only spirits and deities possessing supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) can break it into objects. Some say it is the shell of the golden-winged bird’s (*garuḍa*) egg, which is made of this very gem; the spirits and deities break it to sell to those who trade in treasures.
Śāṭha (pronounced with the initial *chā* as in *jiā*, and the final *th* as in *fǎn*). Koḷa-pa (the first syllable pronounced with the initial *kǔ* as in *yǔ*, and the final *pa* as in *luó-dá*).

Rākṣasa, or alternatively called A-rākṣasa; this is a general name for evil spirits. It is also said that *rākṣasa* means "protector" (*hùzhě*); if female, they are called *rākṣasī*. The old transliteration *luóchà* is an abbreviated corruption.

"From broad to narrow" means "small. In the *Erlü* (爾疋), "from" (*cóng*) signifies length. As the *Han Shi Zhuan* states: "The south-north direction is called 'from' (*cóng*), and the east-west direction is called 'crosswise' (*héng*). This is correct. The Ganges River (殑伽河; qióngjiā hé) is transcribed as *héng* (恒).

In various sutras and treatises, it is sometimes written as *Héng Hé* (恒河), or referred to as *Héngjiā Hé* (恒迦河), or written as *Qiángjiā Hé* (彊伽河); all of these are corruptions. This river flows from the East toward the Elephant's Mouth (*Gajamukha*) of the Anavatapta Lake (無熱惱池) and flows into the Eastern Sea. The old translations say it "comes from the heavenly palace" (*tiāntáng lái*). According to non-Buddhist texts, it originally emerged from the top of Mount Meru, flowing from the ear of a deity onto the earth. Because this deity manifested a transformation body atop the Snowy Mountains (*Himavat*), such a statement was made; seeing that it comes from a high place, it is said to "come from the heavenly palace."
The Sindhu River—formerly called the Xintou (辛頭) River, which here means the "River of Verification"—flows from the silver ox’s mouth on the southern side of the lake and enters the Southern Ocean.

The Sītā River (pronounced with a retroflex *r* as *sīr*, or alternatively as *Sīta* or *Sitā*; these are all variations of the Sanskrit pronunciation)—which here means the "Cold River"—flows from the lapis lazuli horse’s mouth on the western side of the Anavatapta Lake and enters the Western Ocean. This is the source of the great river of this country; the small streams that branch off from it are its tributaries.

The Bāhuka River—formerly called Bocha, or alternatively Bacha, and also known as the Pocha River—is one and the same. This means "Blue River. It flows from the northern face of the lake through the mouth of a crystal lion. It is the same as the river that flows into the Northern Sea; it is also this very Yellow River.
*Ṭhaṅ-khāi* (the first character pronounced *tú láng fǎn*, the second *wū huí fǎn*; the *Tōngsù wén* states that hot ashes are called *ṭhaṅ-khāi*).

*Avīci* (pronounced *ā bí zhǐ* [zhǐ pronounced *zhǐ*] or *ā pí zhì*; also called *Āpídìyù* or *Ābídìyù*—these are synonymous). This means "Without Interval" (*Anantara*). There are two types of "without interval": first, the body is without interval; second, the suffering is without interval.

The *nigoda* (also pronounced *jùtá* with the second character read as *liáng* and *yǔ* respectively; here translated as "excrement and urine worm") has a mouthpart like a needle and is also called the "needle-mouthed worm" (*sūcīmukha-kṛmi*); it pierces bone and consumes marrow.
*Zǐ* (pronounced with the *li* and *lei* finals): According to the *Guǎngyǐ*, it means "mouth. In the *Fāngyán*, it refers to the beak of a bird.

*Wǎ* (to eat) is an archaic form of *zì* (pronounced with the *zì* and *lì* finals), also written as *zhà* (pronounced with the *zì* and *hé* finals). The *Tōngsùwén* states that eating by the human mouth is called *wǎ*, while insects eating is called *zhà*.
*Xiān* (pronounced *xiān*, with the rhyme of *sīliánfǎnguǎngzhèng*): *Xiān* means sharp. It refers to the keen edge of a blade; thus, a sharp knife is called *xiān*.
*Tàn* (pronounced *tàn*, with the rhyme of *tuóhántǎnhuìtáohánfǎn*): According to the *Shuowen*, "to reach out and take with the hand is called *tàn*; *tàn* means to feel about."
The "iron staff" (*tièzhàng*) used for subduing rebellions is called a "staff" (*zhàng*), which is the general term for weapons; this includes items such as swords, spears, pestles, and clubs.

Regarding the "sword" (*dāo*) and the "spear" (*qiāng*): Cāngjié Jiěgǔ states that a wooden object with sharp points at both ends is called a spear. The *Shuowén* defines a spear as "a weapon for striking."

*Yu* (禦) is an archaic form identical to *yu* (敔), with the phonetic reading *yú jǔ*. In the *Xiǎo Ěrǎ* (小爾雅), it is said that *yù* means "to resist" (*kàng*) or "to oppose" (*dāng*). In the *Ěrǎ*, it is also said that *yù* means "to prohibit" (*jìn*), which refers to preparing in advance for what has not yet occurred. The character is composed of the radical "divinity" (*shì*) with "hand" (*yòu*) below; it is also written as *hàn* (扞), with the phonetic reading *hú qiě*. According to the *Shuōwén Jiězì*, *hàn* means "to stop," "to ward off," and also "to protect."
"適" (shì) is written as "這" (zhè) in the *Sāncāng* (Three Cang); its pronunciation is also "chì" or "shī". It means "near," "beginning," or "a jade tablet.
"Nièluò" (尼剌洛)—the second character pronounced "gē" (割)—is translated here as "to split," meaning that the blisters on the body burst open.
*Atata* (the first character is pronounced with the *wu* and *he* finals; the second is pronounced with the *zhi* and *xue* finals): these names are derived from sounds.
*Hahava* (the first character is pronounced with the *hu* and *ming* finals): these are all names derived from the sounds of suffering.

"Branch" (zhī) is pronounced *pǔ* with a retroflex final; "division" (*fèn*) refers to the branching of water, as the *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "A division of water. According to the *Erlü*, a stream originating from the Fen River is called a "branch" (*pài*).

*Krośa* appears in various sūtras as *gōulushè*, *jūlóushā*, or *jūlùshè*; these are all variations in the weight of the Sanskrit pronunciation. It refers to the sound of a large bull's bellow heard at a distance of five *li*. It is also said that five hundred *bāng* (bows) constitute one *krośa*, which is one *yojana*, equivalent to forty *li*. In ancient times, it was also called the "range of a sage-king's travel."

"Jià-sè" (稼穡): "jià" is pronounced with the *jiā* rhyme-group and the *xiá* final; "sè" is pronounced with the *suǒ* rhyme-group and the *lì* final. According to the *Zílín*, planting is called *jià* and harvesting is called *sè*. According to the *Shuōwén*, the ears and grains of the rice plant are called *jià*; alternatively, it is said that what is in the fields is called *jià*.

*Chéng* (層): The character is always pronounced as *fǎn xià* (恒反下) or *jū jí fǎn* (居及反). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means a multi-storied building or a superimposed structure; *jí* (級) refers to the successive steps of a staircase. *Fēng* (封): Pronounced as *fǔ féng fǎn* (甫逢反).

It refers to the act of raising earth to establish boundaries, signifying a noble title or fief. According to the *Zhouli*, four *jǐng* (wells/squares) constitute a *yì* (邑), which is two *lǐ* square. Generally, a *yì* that possesses ancestral temples and the spirit-tablets of former lords is called a *dū* (都); one without these is called a *shè* (社).
*Gouluomian* (兜羅綿; the old term for *tūlā-piṇḍa*). "Jue" (角) is the same as the ancient character *zhao* (斠);

it means to compare or measure (*gǔzhuó*). In the *Liji*, it says: "Practice archery and charioteering, and compete in strength. In the *Guǎngyǐ*, it says: "Jue means to measure. It also means to test. According to the *Shuowen*, "jue" refers to leveling measures such as *dǒu* and *hú*. These characters are all written simply as *jue*, or sometimes as *zhuo* (捔). This is the ancient form of the character *cū* (粗), pronounced *gǔ*. *Tǒng* (桶) means roughly or approximately.

"Fēn" (芬) [the first character] is pronounced *yún* (雲) in reverse; "fú" (馥) [the second character] is pronounced *fú* (福). According to the *Fānyán* (方言), "fēn" means harmony (*hé*), referring to the harmonious blending of fragrant scents.

The *Zílín* (字林) defines "fú" as fragrance. "Yōng" (擁) is pronounced *è* (遏) in reverse; according to the *Cāngjiépiān* (蒼頡篇), "è" means to block or obstruct. In the *Ěrǔpǐ* (爾疋), "è" means to stop. What we call "obstructing" today refers to stopping one another in opposition.

The character for "to smile" (*xiào*) is pronounced *sī* with the *miào* rhyme. According to the *Zílín*, "smiling" means joy; the character is composed of "bamboo" (*zhú*) and "dog" (*quǎn*), as bamboo was used to make musical instruments, and the gentleman smiles only after he has rejoiced. It is also written as *xiào*, which is a vulgar form.

Regarding "India" (Yindu): the first character is pronounced as *zhèn* (with the tone of *fǎn*) and the second as *tú* (with the tone of *gù*). It is sometimes called Tiānzhú (Heavenly India), sometimes Shēndú (Poisonous Body), and sometimes Xiándòu (Worthy Bean); these are all corruptions. The correct term is Yindu. "India" means "Moon. The moon has a thousand names, and this is one such appellation. This is because the sages and worthies of that land have succeeded one another in awakening the multitude of living beings, just as the moon shines upon them; thus it was named accordingly. One tradition states that the original name was Indraprastha, which translates here as "The Abode of the Lord. "Lord" refers to the Heavenly Emperor (Indra). It should be understood that because the Heavenly Emperor protects [the land], it has been so called for a long time.
*Bāha* refers to *ma*; *bāha* here means a *duōn* (or *chuán*) measure for hemp—namely, sesame (*hú-má*). The pronunciation of *duōn* is *tú-sǔn*.
*Qiélí* here means one *hú*, which refers to ten *dǒu*.

12. Volume Twelve. Regarding "zhōu" (洲) and "zhǔ" (渚): they are opposites. That which can be inhabited within the water is called a *zhōu*; a small *zhōu* is called a *zhǔ*. A *zhōu* refers to a level piece of land amidst the water that can be inhabited. The *Shìmíng* (Explanations of Names) states: "Zhōu means 'gathering' (*jù*); it is a place where people, birds, and beasts gather and rest."

"Fen" (焚) and "liao" (燎) share the same radical and are pronounced with the *liáo* rhyme (*tóng-lì-zhào-fǎn*). "Liao" refers to setting fire [to fields]; burning fields for hunting is called *liao*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Liao means burning fields.

"Huī-jìn" (灰燼)—also written as "shì" (󲍎)—shares the same pronunciation (*sì-jìn-fǎn*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "The remaining wood of a fire is called *jìn*. The *Xia'erjing* states: "*Jìn* refers to what remains."
*Saṃkhyeya* (the *qū* and *shì* rhymes are pronounced as in "qū" and "shì") means "innumerable"; it is a corruption of the old term *asaṃkhyeya*.

*Utsaṅga* (the *wù* and *cēng* rhymes are pronounced as in "wù" and "cēng," with the latter followed by the *qī* and *dèng* rhymes) [is followed by] *vaha* (the *hū* and *gé* rhymes are pronounced as in "hū" and "gé").
Jiǎn (pronounced with the initial *x* and final *-u*, rhyming with *xī*); nián (pronounced with the initial *n* and final *-e*, rhyming with *jiān*);
luó (pronounced with the initial *l* and final *-ān*, rhyming with *chā*).

The logic regarding the *qilin* (unicorn) is that it is the opposite of a benevolent beast. According to the *Erya*, the *qilin* has the body of a deer and the tail of an ox, with a single horn; as for the mention of its "horn," the tip of its horn is covered in flesh.
"Chenliao" (ministerial officials) is also written as "liáo" (同力彫反); according to the *Erya*, it refers to "guanliao" (officials), meaning those who share the same office are "liáo."

Gautama is his clan name; "Jiao" (喬) is a phonetic transcription for "Qu" (瞿), with the initial sound reversed. This has three meanings: first, the Solar Clan (*Sūryavaṃśa*); second, the Cow-Dung Clan (*Go-maya-vaṃśa*); and third, the Earth-Coating Clan (*Mṛttikā-vaṃśa*). The traditional rendering "Qiutan" (瞿曇) is an abbreviation.

"Yùfú" (鬱馥): the first character is read as *wù* (勿) with the second as *fú* (福). According to the *Erlǚ*, "yù" refers to vapor; it means that the fragrant aroma rises up in abundance. "Chāngkuáng" (猖狂):

the first character is read as *chí* (齒) with the second as *yáng* (陽). This refers to the transformation of one's emotional nature; it also denotes madness or delusion. As in the *Zhuāngzǐ*: "He wanders about wildly and acts recklessly."

"Quánliàng" (詮量) is also written as "quán" (󲹐), with the phonetic component pronounced as *ch'üan* (七泉反). In the *Guǎngyǐ* (廣疋), it is called "quán" (銓), meaning to weigh and determine lightness and heaviness. In the *Hànshū*, Ying Shào states: "Quán" refers to the balance scale (*língchēnghéng*), while "liàng" refers to the measures of capacity such as the *shēng* and *hú*.
"Poor" (*pin*) means destitute; "destitute" (*qi*) refers to having no wealth, while "poverty-stricken" (*fan*) means lacking resources; it also implies exhaustion.
"Cease" (*chuo*)—the character is pronounced *ding* with the second tone—means to stop; according to the *Erya*, "cease" also means to end.

Harītakī—formerly called *hālílè*—is translated as "brought by the Lord of Heaven. This fruit is suitable for medicinal use and possesses extremely many therapeutic functions, much like the addition of *dùshí* (stachyurus) and other ingredients used by people here in this land.
"Yin" (殷) is pronounced *jīn* (反). The *Shijing* says, "It is yin and full," and the commentary states: "Yin means numerous; yin means great. "Lin" (霖) is pronounced *lì jīn* (反).
According to the *Zuozhuan*, rain lasting three days or more is called *lin*. The *Erya* states that long-lasting rain is called *lin*, and *lin* is also called *lin*.

*Yì* (翳): Pronounced *yì* (one tone). The *Yùnjí* (韻集) states it is a disease that obstructs the eyes. The *Shuōwén* (說文) records it as *yì* (瞖), meaning a film or clouding arises in the eye. Volume 13, Number 13: *Ūrkana* (鬱金).

This is the name of a tree originating from the kingdom of Kapiśa (*Jíbīn*). Its flowers are yellow; one takes the flowers, places them in a single location, and waits for them to rot. One then presses them to extract the juice, which is mixed with other substances to make incense. Even the dregs of the flowers still possess fragrance and are likewise used as incense.

*Huò* (㷮): The character is pronounced *zǔ láo*. According to the *Zílín*, it means "to burn wood until it is charred. The *Shuōwén* states that *huò* means "charred. *Mèi* (寐): The first character is pronounced *bì*.
It means "deep sleep"; this is as in the *Guóyǔ*: "Duke Xiàn slept but did not sleep" (*qiǎn ér bù mèi*). It also means "lying down."

*Dī* (隄) and *táng* (塘) are archaic characters; *dǒu* (陡) is pronounced *dū xī* (with the final syllable reversed), and the following character *jí* (即) is pronounced *tú jí* (with the initial syllable reversed). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *dī* means "an embankment" (*yāng*). The *Erlia* states that an embankment is called a *liáng* (梁). Li Xun says it means "a dike" (*fáng*) or "a barrier" (*zhàng*). In the *Hanshu*, regarding the phrase "without dikes," Wei Zhao says it refers to "accumulated earth used as a boundary or limit."
"栽" (zāi) means to plant; nowadays, planting in grass or water is called "栽.
"痼疾" (gùjí)—also written as "󳀋" (gù)—is pronounced with the initial *k* and the finals *hù* (gǔ); it means a chronic illness. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as a long-standing malady.
14. Volume Fourteen. Regarding the term *śikṣamāṇā* (正學), in the Sanskrit language it refers to one who studies the precepts for two years.

It is also written as 𧻜 (pronounced with the *qiú* and *lèi* finals). Nowadays in Jiangnan, kneeling while standing is called 𨄰󳋏. The people of the Central Kingdom say "hújì" (胡跽), where "hú" is pronounced *qízhǐ* and "jì" is pronounced *hù*; "𨄰" is pronounced *wényáng*. In the *Lǐjì*, it says, "When receiving [an object] while standing, one does not 𨄰," which uses the character "kneel" (*guì*) as a borrowed character.

The term *caitya* was formerly called *zhiti*, *zhidi*, or *futu*; these are all corruptions. It should be translated as "place worthy of offerings. All sites where the Buddha attained parinirvāṇa, where he was born, and where he preached the Dharma are called *caityas*, and all must be honored and venerated.
"Taking a wife" (*qǔ qī*)—the seven characters are reversed as "taking" (*qǔ*). The *Shijing* says, "How does one take a wife? and the *Zhuan* states, "To marry is to take a woman.
Regarding "to treat illness," the *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *liao* (same pronunciation as *liáo*, lǐ zhào fǎn); the *Sancang* states that *liao* means to cure disease.
*Surā*, *maireya*, and *madhu*: *surā* refers to grain liquor; *maireya* refers to liquor made from various ingredients such as roots, stalks, flowers, and fruits; *madhu* refers to grape wine.

15. Volume Fifteen. Section Fifteen. *Tu* (屠): According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means to slaughter and cut. According to the *Guangyi*, it means to destroy. Upon examination, *tu* refers to the carving and slicing of sacrificial meat.

*Quái huì*: "quái" (the first character) is pronounced with the *kǔ* rhyme-group followed by the *huí* rhyme-group; the second character is pronounced *gǔ wài*. It refers to a chief executioner (*huì*) who cuts meat—that is, one whose primary duty is to kill people. Some write it as *huì* (儈), which has the same pronunciation as *huì* (膾); however, according to the *Shēnglèi* (Classification of Sounds), *huì* (儈) refers to a broker who brings together people at the market, and this meaning does not apply here.

*Jiāng* (罝弶) has two archaic forms: *jī* (𦋽) and *jiàng* (󳄫). The first character is pronounced *zǐ xié* (子邪反), and the second is *jù liàng* (渠亮反). According to the *Erlǚ* (爾疋): "The net for catching hares is called *jiāng*. Guo Pu states: "*Jiāng* means to block; it refers to blocking and capturing hares. The *Yùn jí* (韻集) says: "To set a snare on a path is called *jiāng*. Today, hunters use *jiāng* to capture birds and beasts; its shape resembles a bow.

"Dian" (典) means to preside over; it is also written as "dian" (󳈡), with the same pronunciation as "dingjian" (丁繭). In the *Guangya*, it is defined as the presiding official. The second character, "xing" (刑), has the phonetic "hu-jing" (胡經). It refers to inflicting punishments for crimes. The *Yi* says, "The hexagram *Da* is law. *Jing* is taken as the law. The *Chunqiu Yuanming Bao* states: "The character *da* (刑) is composed of 'knife' (刀) and 'well' (井). The well provides drink for people; when people enter the well, they contend for the water and fall into the spring. To guard them, one uses a knife to sever their carnal desires, so that people have awe and caution to preserve their bodies and lives. Therefore, the character is composed of 'knife' and 'well'."

*Xiōngbò* (凶勃) is also written as *xiōng* (兇), with the same pronunciation as *xǔgōng* (許恭反). The following characters—*bèi* (誖), *kuàng* (愂)—share two forms and have the same pronunciation as *pómù* (蒲沒) and *bǔguì* (補憒). They also mean *xiànyǎo* (𠒋惡, perverse/evil), *bèiluàn* (悖亂, rebellious chaos), and *yì* (逆, contrary/rebellious).

*Qi* (pronounced *gài* in the *Cangjie pian*). The character is composed of "person" (*ren*) and "above" (*shàng*), signifying that when a person lacks wealth or goods, they go forth to beg and request them.
Vihāra is also called vihāra, which is translated here as "wandering," referring to the places where the Saṃgha travels; in this land [of China], it is represented by the term "temple" (si).
Cuṇḍa—pronounced with the second tone on the final syllable—is translated here as "wondrous meaning" (miàoyì); the old rendering "Chúntuó" is a corruption.

*Nanyǔ* (難愈) is an archaic term; *yǔ* (㢏) is the same character as *yú* (臾), with the phonetic *rǔ*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *yù* (瘉) means the recovery from illness. In the *Fāngyán*, *chāyǔ* (差愈) and *chōu* (瘳) are used; the pronunciation of *chōu* is *chǒuyóu*.

The potters also write it as *táo* (匋), with the same phonetic as *dà láo* (大勞). Alternatively, the character *yáo* (遙) is borrowed for its sound; the *Shiji* states that *táo* refers to earthenware vessels. The *Cāngjiépiān* defines *táo* as a house for making tiles. It is said that Shun first practiced pottery by the banks of the River. According to records, the lands of the Western Regions are mostly low-lying and damp, so one cannot dig kilns (*yáo*); instead, they merely stack ceramic vessels and fire them in the open air. The pronunciation of *yáo* is *yáo* (姚).

"Hán-lǔ" (鹹鹵): "Hú" is pronounced as in *hú* (胡) and "lǔ" as in *lì-gǔ* (力古). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "lǔ" refers to the salty lands of the West; it refers to hard, thin soil. That which is produced by Heaven is called *lǔ*; that which is produced by humans is called *yán* (salt). Salt is found in the East, while *lǔ* is found in the West. The *Shiming* states: "When the land does not produce [vegetation], it is called *lǔ*. Thus the character is composed of the 'West' radical (*xīng*) below, with the shape of salt depicted beneath."

*King* (坑) and *jing* (穽)—the ancient forms of which are *jing* (阱) and *zeng* (𣚃), both sharing the same phonetic component *cai* (才) and *xing* (性)—are explained in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as "a large pit. The *Cangjie Pian* states that a *jing* refers to a hole dug in the ground to trap birds and beasts.

16. Volume Sixteen. *Chuan* (initially pronounced *chui*, with variants *chuǎi* and *duō*). To feel with the hand; in common usage, it is also said that to stroke or touch is *chuan*. There is also the form *chuai* (initially pronounced *chui*, with variants *chuí* and *duǒ*). *Guǎng chuǎi* (extensive feeling); to test, to measure, and to estimate.

The character *sì* (飤) is pronounced *cí zì* (恣反). According to the *Guǎngyǐ*, it means "to wither" (*wēi*). In the *Cāngjié piān*, it means "to satiate. It refers to providing food and drink to others as an offering; thus, the character includes the radical for "person" (*rén*). *Wēi* is pronounced *yú wèi* (於偽反); it is sometimes written as *xiāng* (餉), which is a vulgar form.
"Qi (祈)"—according to the *Guangyi*, it means "to entreat"; according to the *Erya*, it means "to announce.
"Cai (猜)"—the ancient forms are both written as 𦞁 and 猜; the modern form is 𢘺, all pronounced *cāi* (same as 󱍮). It means "to suspect"; according to the *Guangyi*, it means "to fear."

"Bālāsī" (pronounced with a reversed *lan* and *ge*) is also called Bārs; it is said that "Bārs" is the name of a country situated near the Western Sea, which abounds in rare treasures. People from various nations who come to sell their goods all have their wealth taken by this [country]. Because of its dragon-like majesty and extraordinary power, it was esteemed by the ancients.
*Nirjarā* (尼延底) is a term meaning "deep" or "profound," another name for *tṛṣṇā* (craving). It is so named because it exhausts [the self] without satiety.

*Posadha* (布灑他)—the latter character being pronounced with the *he* tone—is here translated as "increase," meaning that during the half-monthly *poṣadha*, the roots of the precepts are increased. *Poṣadha* (叉磨) is translated as "patience," meaning the forbearance of one's transgressions. The old term "confession" (*chàn*) is an error. Some call it *puṣpa-pi* (逋沙比), while others say *poṣadha* (布薩); both are corrupted abbreviations.

"Ńìng (佞)"—the "nú" in "nú-dìng-fǎn" (奴定反) refers to flattery and sycophancy. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, one who is artful, fawning, and possesses superior talent is called a *nìng*; furthermore, one who feigns goodness is also called a *nìng*. This character is composed of "woman" (女) and "benevolence" (仁). In the *Lunyu*, it says, "I detest the *nìng*," which follows the meaning of the "woman" radical. In the *Zuo Zhuan*, it says, "I, your humble servant, am not *nìng* [incapable]," meaning I cannot serve my father and elder brothers; this follows the meaning of the "benevolence" radical.

The characters *huǐ* (毀) and *cī* (呰) share the same radical and phonetic; *cī* is pronounced as *zǐ* (子) with the tone *ěr* (爾). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *cī* means "to revile. In the *Liji* (Book of Rites), it states: "As for *cī*, there is none who does not know it; it is that from which ritual (*li*) arises. Zheng Xuan commented: "To revile with the mouth is called *cī*."

*Chàngjì* (倡伎): *chàng* is pronounced with the initial *fǎn* of *yáng* (楊) and the final *qǐ* (綺); according to the *Shuowen*, it means "musician" (*lè*). According to the *Sāncāng*, it refers to "performers" (*páiyì*). *Jì* (伎) refers to "artistic skills" (*yínéng*). *Cí* (祠): pronounced with the initial *sì* (似) and the final *zī* (茲);

the second character is pronounced with the initial *xú* (徐) and the final *lǐ* (理). According to the *Erya*, it is the sacrifice to the *tóng* (桐). Furthermore, sacrifices to Heaven are called *cí*, while sacrifices to Earth are called *sì*.

17. Volume Seventeen. *Ti* (替): pronounced with the *jiàn* (計) and *fǎn* (反) tones; it is synonymous with *pì* (疋). It means to replace, to abolish, to cease, or to extinguish; it refers to coarse silk (*shī*).
Pūraṇa (the *lò* in *luò* is pronounced as *gé*; alternatively written as *bǔ* in *bǔ-là-ná*, which is translated here as Pǔ; the older term is Fúlánánā).

Khaṇḍika (in the sūtras, it is sometimes written as *lóng*, with the same pronunciation as *lí-dǒng*; in the *Sāncāng*, it is written as *lì*, with the same pronunciation as *lí-jì*; it means "obstinate" (*hěn-lì*), referring to being stubborn and headstrong.
*Guīmù* (乖穆) is also written as *mù* (睦), with the phonetic transcription *mò gǔ*. *Mù* means harmony. According to the *Erlǚ*, *mù* means reverence and thickness [of relations].

*Kāoquè* (磽确): the first character is pronounced *kǔ jiāo*; the second has two pronunciations, *hú jué* and *kǔ jué*. Mencius said that *kāoquè* refers to thin and barren soil. The *Tōngsùwén* states that when objects are hard and rigid, they are called *kāoquè*; when the earth is hard, it is unsuitable for the five grains.

Regarding the character *lè* (辢): the *Zi yuan* (Dictionary of Characters) states it is the same as *qiū* (萩), with the phonetic *lú gè* (盧葛). The *Tōng sú wén* (Popular Texts) says that what is called *lè* in Jiangnan is called *xīn* (辛, pungent) in the Central Kingdom.
Regarding the character *tián* (填): the later form is the ancient *tí* (窴), with the phonetic *tú jiān* (徒堅). The *Guǎng pǐ* (Extended Glossary) says it means to fill or block up.

18. Volume Eighteen, Part Two. "Pao" (皰) is also written as "piao" (靤). It is pronounced *bù xiào* (捕孝反). It refers to a small swelling. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "pao" means the rising of a vapor on the face.

"Recite with warmth (*wēn*). The character *wēn* is pronounced as *ū-kūn* (with the second tone). Regarding "reciting the old to know the new," He Yan stated that *wēn* means "to seek out. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* says: "To practice it at a later time is called *wēn*; *wēn* also means 'warmth,' and this meaning is adopted here. In all such cases, the term refers to "recitation" (*sòng*).
The third punishment, for minor offenses, is called *śulka* (pronounced *fu-fa* with the retroflex *ṛ*); it also signifies subduing or suppressing.

It is the name of a great *sāla* tree and carries the meaning of a family of great wealth and nobility. According to records from the Western Regions, the sons and younger brothers of high-ranking officials and the very wealthy were addressed as *sāla*.

The character 荷 (hé) has two forms: 拘 (jū) and 何 (hé). They are pronounced as *hú-gē* and *hú-kě* respectively. It means "small" or "slight," and is synonymous with 爾 (ěr) and 苟 (gǒu). 揭 (jié) means to carry or bear; 荷 (hé) means to take responsibility for.

The character 析 (xī) is pronounced as *ēn-lì*. It means to divide or split. The character is composed of 斤 (jīn) and 分 (fēn); "斤" refers to a wood-cutting tool. In modern vernacular usage, it is written as 析, which is composed of two 片 (piàn) radicals.
*Tiṣya* (pronounced *dǐ shā*; the old transcription was *fúshā*, which means "bright").

*Hèyì* (pronounced *hè gē* for the first character and *yú shí* for the second) means "brilliant"; the *Xiǎo Ěrpǐ* states that *hècāo* means "bright," while the *Guǎngpǐ* states that *hèyì* means "magnificent brightness. The character is composed of the radical "great" (*dà*) and the phonetic *cāo* (pronounced *yì*).
The *madhuka* fruit (formerly transcribed as *mó tóu*; this means "excellent fruit"). The *nimba* fruit (the second character pronounced *zhèn*, rhyming with *nǚ*;
its shape is like that of the *kǔ liàn* tree here in this land; the third character *liàn* is pronounced *fāng jiàn*).
*Dhātu* (pronounced with the *tu* and *è* tones) means "solid" or "substantial"; it is merely another name for the bodily relics (*śarīra*) of the Tathāgata.

Volume Nineteen, Chapter Nineteen: *Airāvata* (the first character pronounced with the *wǔ* and *zhì* tones; formerly named *Elabhadra*, also called *Pīrabhadra*). *Airā* here translates as "fragrance," and *vata* translates as "elephant. Thus, it means a "fragrant elephant. It is the name of a fragrant elephant.

20. Volume Twenty. Regarding the term *jì* (姬): the first character is pronounced as in *jū-yí* (居疑反), and the second as in *yú-zhèng* (餘證反). According to Rùchún’s commentary on the *Hànshū*, "Lady Bó" (*Bó Jī*), the mother of Emperor Wén, [he states]: "Jī is the general name for the many concubines; it is also a female official title. As for the rank of *zhàibǐ èrqiānshí* (祑比二千石), its position is below that of *jiéhǎo* (婕妤). In the *Zuǒchuán*, regarding the sending of a *yèng* (媵) to Duke Mù of Lèi, Dù Yǔ says: "To send a woman with a bride is called *yèng*; *yèng* means to escort or to provide. The *Gōngyángchuán* asks: "What is a *yèng*? When a feudal lord has only one state, two other states send a *yèng* to accompany her with their own sisters-in-law (*zhí*) and younger sisters (*dì*). The *Shìmíng* says: 'The sisters-in-law and younger sisters are called *yèng*; *yèng* means to support, as they support and serve the primary wife. Thus, it is correct that those of the third rank are called *jī* and those of the fifth rank are called *yèng*."

The characters 纏 (chán) and 壓 (yā) combine to form the difficult character 䆘 (zhá), which means to press or squeeze; it is pronounced the same as 甲 (jiǎ). The *Cāngjié piān* states that it means to suppress or to weigh down. The character 拶 (zà) is pronounced *zǔ hé*.
*Yǒngfàn* (涌泛) is now written as *fàn* (氾), with the same pronunciation as *fūjiàn* (敷釰). In the *Guǎngyǐ* (廣疋), *fàn* means the appearance of floating; it also means rapid movement. *Piāojì* (漂激):

the first character is pronounced *yáo* (遙) and the second *gǔdí* (古狄). Floating and blowing is called "drifting" (*piāoliú*); moving rapidly is called "surging" (*jī*). "Drifting" (*piāo*) also implies swaying and tossing.
21. Fascicle Twenty-one. "You" (尤) means especially heavy; it is a reversal [of expectation], meaning exceedingly so, or much, or different, or excessive.

"Fángluò" (防邏): *lù* is pronounced with the rhyme of *liè* (力賀反). The *Shùshǔ yùnlüè* (戍屬韻略) states: "Lù" refers to patrolling to prevent violations; it refers to mobile troops used to guard against bandits.
*Yǒngmèng* (𧄼瞢): The first character is read as *tú* (徒登反) and the second as *máng* (亡登反). The *Yùnjí* (韻集) states: "To be *yǒngmèng* means to be utterly exhausted from lying down.

22. Fascicle Twenty-two. Fascicle Twenty-two. *Yè* (睫): The *Shuōwén* (說文) writes this as *jié* (䀹); the *Shìmíng* (釋名) writes it as *zhāo* (𣮌). Both are pronounced *zǐyè* (子葉反), meaning the hair at the side of the eye. In the villages and fields of Shandong, it is pronounced *zǐjí* (子及反).

"Xù" (序) is a term from ancient texts; it is pronounced "tóng" with the initial "xú" and the final "fǎn. It means "sequential order. The *Baihūtong* states: "Xù refers to arranging the elderly and the young.
"Bìdòu" (蓽豆)—the first character is pronounced "fū" with the final "mì"—is also cultivated by people at home for consumption; it is excellent for making cleansing soap (*zǎodòu*).
*Shǐ* (pronounced with the *sì* and *li* finals): According to the *Cāngjié piān*, "shǐ" means rapid. *Chàngwàng* (pronounced *chì liàng*):
According to the *Shuōwén*, "chàngwàng" means resentment or longing regret.
*Chóng qian* (pronounced *qián yú*): According to the *Tōngsú wén*, worms within the flesh are called *dǎn*. The *Sāncāng* states that maggots produced by flies within the flesh are called *qian*.

"Huānbǐ" (髖髀) is also written as "huān" (臗), with the two phonetic transcriptions being *kǔ huán* and *kǔ kūn*. The *Pīcāng* states that "huān" refers to the buttocks (*kāo*). The *Guǎngyǐ* states that "huān" refers to the thigh (*tún*). The character below is an archaic form of "pǐ" (䠋), with the phonetic transcription *pú mǐ*. According to the *Shuōwén*, it refers to the outer part of the thigh. Northerners use this pronunciation, while in Jiangnan, the pronunciation *fāng ěr* is used; it is sometimes written as "bì" (䏶), which is a vulgar character.

*Zhe* (one span) is an archaic character; it is the same as *zhà* (pronounced with the initial *t* and ending in *-gé*). According to the *Tōngsúwén*, "to stretch" (*zhāng*) means to extend or to open. *Vaiḷamba* (pronounced *lìhán*):

according to the old sūtras and śāstras, it is sometimes written as *Pilánpó*, sometimes as *Xuánlánpó*, and also as *Bǐlánpó* or *Suílánpó*; these are merely different dialectal variations of the Sanskrit. This is translated as "the Swift and Fierce Wind."

23. Fascicle Twenty-three. "Anusmṛti-kāya" (Recollection of the Body). "Xun" (循) is an archaic term; it is similar to "zun" (遵), and according to the *Erya*, it means "to follow" or "to observe. Guo Pu’s commentary states that it also means "to traverse. "Xun" (循) also implies "universality" and "circumambulation."

*Qin* (欽): Pronounced *qù jīn fǎn* (去金反). It means to revere. The *Shìfǎ* (Mnemonic Rules for Posthumous Titles) states: "To have one's dignified demeanor fully perfected is called *qin*. *Pī* (披): Pronounced *yǐn shuō fǎn* (飲說反). It means to open and examine.

The *Xiǎopǐ* (Small Lexicon) says: "*Jù* (具) means to possess; to possess [the items] within the gate is *jù*. *Jiǎn* (簡): A slip of bamboo or wood used for writing. *Jù* (具): To provide or prepare. To provide the necessary items within the gate is *jù*.

The name of the Kāśyapīya school is *Kāśyapa* in Sanskrit. *Kāśyapa* is translated here as "Light-Wave" (*Guangbo*). In the local language, it is called "Drinking Light" (*Yin Guang*). There are two meanings for "Drinking Light": first, Kāśyapa was an ancient rishi whose body possessed such radiance that he could "drink up" other lights so they no longer appeared; this arhat is of his lineage, and thus he is named after him. Second, the body of this arhat is golden in color and constantly emits light; when compared with a statue made of Jambūnada gold, the light from the human figure outshines the light of the golden statue so that it no longer appears, and for this reason he is called "Drinking Light."

*Tái* (臺) and *guàn* (觀) are pronounced with the tones *dú* (徒) and *fǎn* (反) respectively. According to the *Erya*, "That which is square and high is called a *tái*. The text says: "A *guàn* is called a *tái*. Sun Yan states: "The twin towers at the palace gates are called *guàn*. The *Shiming* says: "As for *guàn*, it is so called because one observes and looks out from atop it."

24. Fascicle Twenty-four. *Dàn* (憺): Pronounced *tú* (with the tone of *lán*) in the first instance; pronounced *pǐ* (with the tone of *bái*) in the second. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *dàn* means "peaceful," referring to a state of serene and joyful ease. *Dàn* also implies placid stillness. *Pà* (怕) refers to tranquility and non-action (*wuwei*). The *Zilu Fu* (賦 by Zilu) states: "Placid and non-active, serene and self-sustained. *Fascicle Twenty-four* (卷第二十四): [This is a repetition in the source text. *Fascicle Twenty-four* (卷第二十四): [This is a repetition in the source text. *憺怕* (Dàn-pà): [The phonetic analysis and definitions provided above. *Zilu Fu* (子盧賦): "Placid and non-active, serene and self-sustained. [This is a quotation from the *Zilu Fu*. [End of Fascicle Twenty-four]

Kauṇḍinya (formerly transcribed as *Jiāochénrú*, which is an error) means "Fire-Weapon" by nature; his name is also called "First Wisdom," because he was the first to realize non-existence and thereby attained the wisdom of his original vow.
"Only" (*wéi*) means merely; "item" (*mù*)—the character *mù* is pronounced with the *mo* and *lù* tones—refers to a record or a catalogued heading.

Volume Twenty-Five. Volume Twenty-Five. "Kaiding" (楷定)—the character *kǎi* is pronounced with the *kǒu* and *hài* tones—is the same as "guǎngpǐ" (廣疋); it refers to a model, a standard, or a formal pattern. "Fa" (法) means law or method.
Although "jué" (蹷) is also written as "jūn" (𨇮), both share the phonetic "juè" (巨月) with two readings. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Jué means to fall prostrate;
it is to lie on one's back. Volume 26, Fascicle 26. "Jīnkuǎng" (金礦) is an archaic form of "jiānmǎng" (硾猛). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Kuǎng refers to the unrefined ore of copper."

"Ascending the throne" (*dengzu*) refers to returning to the position of sovereignty. The *Guoyu* states, "That which Heaven and Earth bestow as their blessing" (*zuo*); Jia Gui explains that "blessing" (*zuo*) means "emolument" (*lu*). Volume 27, Number 27: Nārāyaṇa.

*Nara* here is translated as "man" (*wei ren*), and *āyaṇa* is translated as "birth-source" (*shengben*). This means that the birth-source of humanity is none other than Mahābrahmā. The non-Buddhists (*waidao*) claim that all people are born from Brahmā; therefore, he is called the "birth-source of man."

"Coiled and entwined" (*pánjié*): in the *Lǐjì*, it says "coiling upon the ground. Zheng Xuan states that "pán" means "to coil" (*wěi*). The *Guǎngyǐ* states that "pán" means "to bend" (*qū*) or "to turn back" (*huí*). According to the *Fānyǔ*, a dragon that has not yet ascended to heaven is called a "coiled dragon" (*pánlóng*). This is what is meant here.

*Kaṇḍalī* is the name of a female mantra-holder; she is named after her country, and this woman is addressed with a feminine pronunciation, whereas *Kaṇṭhala* is the masculine form of the country's name.
*Iṣṭāni* (pronounced with the retroflex *ṣ*: *iṣṭāni*) means "divination" or "observation through signs."
Mandhātṛ (the *maṇḍa* is pronounced with a retroflex *-ḍ-*; here it means "I nourish") is the name of King Māndhātṛ.

28. Volume Twenty-Eight. Āgama (*āgama* is pronounced with a retroflex *-g-*; here it means "teaching") refers to the transmission of words and teachings, meaning the successive instruction passed down from the Deer Park.

29. Fascicle Twenty-nine. "To view as an enemy" (*yuánchóu*) means to increase one's malice and resentment in opposition; thus it is called an "enemy" (*chóu*). It is a counterpart. In the *Shīyǐ* (Erya), it says: "An enemy is a match. This is what is meant by the term "enemy" when referring to those with whom one has a grudge, as in the *Chunqiu*.
*Qing-yū* (靑瘀): "Yū" is pronounced *yù* (反). According to the *Shuowen*, it means accumulated blood; according to the *Guangyi*, it refers to a disease.
*Bǐ* (鄙) is pronounced *bēi* (悲) with a final *mǐ* (美) tone. It means vile or evil; according to the *Guangya*, it means shame, humiliation, or bashfulness.
*Ē-hù*: "Ē" is pronounced with a reversed *hù*; it means to rely upon or depend on. According to the *Han Shi*, "one who has no father is called *hé-hù*";
*hù* means to rely upon. *Ē-yàn*: "Yàn" is pronounced with a reversed *yú zhān*; this refers to that which is known. The old transcription was *Ē-yán*, which is the same.
"Què" (確) is explained as "cái" (埤), "cāng" (蒼), "gǎo" (槁), and also "duò" (碢), all pronounced with the *kǔ* rhyme-group.
The *Guǎngyǐ* states that "què" means hard, rigid, and firm. "Rútóng" (儒童): "rú" (儒) is "róu" (柔), meaning soft; "tóng" (童) is "yòu" (幼), meaning young. In Sanskrit, this is called *māṇavaka*.

Bimbisāra—also called Bimbasāra or Piṅśa—is one and the same person. This name means "one of upright countenance," or "one of exquisite physical form. Furthermore, *bimba* refers to an image made by carving wood or painting; the Bhikṣu [the Buddha] was named after this.
*Pāṭali* (the "tu" and "wo" in the phonetic transcription are reversed; it is the name of a small jujube fruit common in the Western Regions, and this *bhikṣu* was named after it).
[30] Volume Thirty. [30] *Phalguna* (the "pu" and "he" in the phonetic transcription are reversed); this is the name of a lunar mansion of the twelfth month, and this person was named after it.
*Va-ts'o* (pronounced *pó-luó* in the old [translation] tradition) refers to the Brahmin caste.

"P'in" (pronounced *pǐn*)—the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as the mother of livestock; the female is called *p'in*. As the *Shijing* says, "The pheasant cries out seeking its mate," this term applies not only to livestock.
Uttara (the *u* and *di* are pronounced with a retroflex; the following is a borrowed sound; *ding-li* is the phonetic transcription) is a personal name.
Caitra (the *cai* and *da* are pronounced with a retroflex) is also a personal name; it is the name of a lunar mansion in the first month, which the Westerners call Taurus (*Taurus*).
*Puṣaha*: "Pu" is the sound of a universal mantra; "Saha" means "well-spoken. *Kucīra*: [The first character is pronounced] *jū* (with the second tone) and the [second] *yǎn* (with the fourth tone).

The *Guǎngpǐ* states that it resembles a tangerine but is larger, about the size of a grain of rice; it can be used for washing and soaking hemp. It is currently produced south of Fanyu; it is cut into strips, soaked in honey, and made into *zòng* (sticky rice cakes) to be eaten. *Zhuī* is pronounced *pān*; *zōng* is pronounced *sāng* (with the third tone).

*Jikuang* (pronounced *gǔměng*) refers to the juice of the *pāṭala* tree; its color is extremely red and is used to dye leather and cotton cloth. This tree is called *cīnaka*, and it is so large that a single flower is as big as a peck-measure (*dǒu*), intensely red, and exceedingly hard and tough, such that people sew it together to make bags. (The character *lèn* is pronounced *rèn*).
At that time, *niàng* (pronounced *ruǎng*, with the second tone; it refers to the internal segments of a gourd) is like the internal segments within a gourd.
The character for *bàn* (segment) is pronounced *pú xiàn*.
*Yīqièjīng yīnyì*, Scroll 70 and Scroll 71.
Compiled by the Sramana Xuan Ying, who translated the scriptures:
*Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (The Treatise on the Correct Theory in Accordance with Abhidharma), Volume 80, Part 1. **Volume One** *Jiashui* (嘉瑞): "Jia" is pronounced as in *jia-xia* (賈遐);

"shui" is pronounced as in *shi-zhui* (時惴). The *E-pi* (爾疋) states: "Jia" means good or beautiful. The *Cangjie pian* (蒼頡篇) states: "Shui" means response or omen. This signifies that when one possesses virtuous and beautiful qualities, a corresponding sign of trustworthiness arises; this is a trustworthy omen (*xin-shui*). ... [The remainder of the text continues with phonetic glosses and definitions related to the title and introductory commentary] ... [End of Volume One]
Aśita (pronounced Āshìduō; here translated as "Unconquerable" [Wúshèng]; formerly called Āqíduō or Āyíduō, both of which are corruptions) is Maitreya’s name in his present life.
"Sàn" (slander) and "bàng" (calumny). According to the *Cāngjiépiān*, "sàn" means to slander; according to the *Guǎngyǐ*, "sàn" and "bàng" mean to defame.
"Lòu" (leakage/disclosure). Pronounced with the final *-xiè* (as in *xīliè*). According to the *Guǎngyǐ*, "lòu" means to overflow, to divulge, and also to leak.

Aṅgulimāla (the "Finger Garland")—*aṅguli* meaning finger and *māla* meaning garland—is also called Aṅgulimālya. "Aṅguli" is translated as "finger," and "māla" as "garland. Because he tied together severed fingers to form a garland and wore it upon his head, he received this name.

Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa—translated here as "Under the Wood-apple Grove"—was so named because he practiced the Way beneath a wood-apple grove. Kāśyapa is his clan name; the older transliteration was *Yǒulúpíluó*. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "At that time, the three brothers of the Kāśyapa clan resided there; the eldest brother was this one."

*Táng* (攪): the ancient pronunciation is *gǔmǎo*; *táng* means "mere" (*tú*) or "empty" (*kōng*). According to dictionaries, *jiǎo* means "to disturb" (*náo*), with the phonetic reading *hūdāo*; *náo* means "to agitate. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to confuse. *Tàcèjiā* (怛策迦):
the first character is pronounced *dūdá*, and the second is *chūgé*; these are names of dragons.
*Kòu* (扣) and *jī* (擊) are written as *kǔ* (𢼒) in the *Shuowen Jiezi*, with the same pronunciation as *kǔhòu* (苦厚反).

*Kòu* also means to strike. *Nuǎn* (愞) and *ruǎn* (耎) have the pronunciation *nùkè* (奴課反); the lower character [of *ruǎn*] is pronounced *rǎnyuǎn* (而兗反). According to the *Sāncāng*, *nuǎn* means weak; according to the *Guǎngyǐ*, *ruǎn* means supple.
