The *Kao sheng* says that *chuan* is a bamboo granary. The *Shuowen jiezi* states: "A *chuan* is a circular vessel made of bamboo for storing grain; it takes the radical 'bamboo' (*zhu*) and the phonetic 'duan' (*duan*). It is also written as *chuan* (圌) and used interchangeably. The phonetic *duan* (耑) is pronounced as *duan* (端).
*Kakudaka* (the first character pronounced with the *xian* and *ge* finals; this is the name of one of the seven golden mountains in the Sanskrit language).
*Kuru-pā* (the second character pronounced with the *ju* and *yu* finals, followed by *lan* and *da* finals; this is also a Sanskrit term) refers to the continent of Kuru.

Regarding "tángwēi" (煻煨): the first character is pronounced *dǎng* (with the radical *láng* reversed) and the second is pronounced *ū* (with the radical *huí* reversed). The *Kǎo Shēng* states that "táng" refers to ash combined with fine embers; the *Wénzì Diǎn* explains it as the remaining ashes and cinders from a fire. Both characters include the "fire" radical (*huǒ*), while "táng" and "wēi" are both phonetic components.

Regarding the character *sō* (拼): when combined with the radical for "hand" (*shǒu*), it means to look back, as Yuè Wáng’s *Yǎo Wǎng* states: "To bind with cord is called *sō*. The *Chǔcí* says: "Twisting fine threads together to form a cord. Wén Dài says: "Ten *xún* [of length] is called a *sō*. According to the *Gǔjīn Zhèngzì*, this character follows the radical "thread" (*mì*) and takes *fǔwù* as its phonetic component; the latter, *bǔgēng*, is the pronunciation. Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* states: "*Sō* means to employ. The *Kǎoshēng* says: "*Sō* means to pull or stretch. The *Yùnquán* defines it as "stretching a cord and leveling a line. The *Yǎryǎ* states: "*Sō* means to follow. According to the *Gǔjīn Zhèngzì*, this character follows the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and takes *bìng* as its phonetic component.

*Chá*: Upper radical *shā* (反切: *shā-fǎn*; pronounced like *kǎo*). The glossary states that *chá* refers to a log floating in midstream. In the standard characters of antiquity and today, it is written with the radical *mù* (wood) and the phonetic *chā*. The text of the scripture uses the character *jiǎn* (󱨋), which is identical in meaning. Lower radical *dài* (反切: *dài-fǎn*). Wáng Yì’s commentary on the *Chuci* states: "Lài" also means a rapid torrent. The *Hànshū* says that in the regions of Wú and Chǔ, such places are called *lài*. The standard characters of antiquity and today state: *lài* refers to water flowing over sand; it takes the radical *shuǐ* (water) and the phonetic *lài*.

"Chou-se" (臭澀): the upper character is *chou* (醜), with the phonetic *shou* (狩). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, a dog is that which knows the tracks of fleeing birds by smelling them; thus it is composed of "dog" (*quan*) and "nose" (*zi*). This is a compound character based on meaning. The lower character is *sen* (森), with the phonetic *ji* (戢); this was already fully explained in the fourth fascicle above.

The character *zǐ* (㭰) is pronounced with the rhyme *sù* (髓) as a reversed reading; the *Wenzidian* explains that *zǐ* refers to a bird’s beak, formed from the radical *cì* (朿) and the phonetic *cǐ* (此). In the treatise (*Lùn*), it is written as *zǐ* (觜), which is used interchangeably with it. The sound of *cì* (朿) is *qī sì* (七四反).

*Yā* (𠯗): In the *Shangzǎn Dǎfǎn Zìtǒng*, it says that what enters the mouth is called *yā*. The *Kǎoshēng* states that *yā* means to suck; it is also written as *zhà* (唼) or *zhā* (𠾱). According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) with the phonetic component *zà* (帀), where the pronunciation of *zà* is the same as above.

*Xiānlì* (銛利): The upper character is pronounced with the *xī* and *yán* rhymes. The *Yìnyì* (音義) of the *Hànshū* states that *xiān* also means "sharp. The *Cāngjiépiān* (蒼頡篇) says *xiān* means *qié* (鑯); *qié* is pronounced with the *zǐ* and *lián* rhymes. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) says *xiān* refers to the blade of a knife or sword. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* (文字典說) says it means "keen and sharp," composed of the radical for metal (*jīn*) and the phonetic *shé* (舌).
The character *wù* (烏) in *bó* (駮)—pronounced *bān* (邦) according to the *Wénzìdiǎn*—is explained as meaning "spotted. It is composed of the radical "horse" (*mǎ*) and the phonetic *jiāo* (交).

Regarding *niè* (齧): the *Lǐjì* states, "Do not bite the bones. The *Shuōwén* explains it as "to gnaw" (*shì*). It is composed of the radical "teeth" (*chǐ*) and the phonetic *bié* (㓞), which is pronounced *yǐ xià* (乙黠).

*Xiǎo* (to bite): On the head of the character *zú* (foot), it is pronounced *lè jiǎo* (樂狡). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Xiǎo is also the same as *qiè* (to gnaw); it is composed of the radical *zhī* (teeth) with *jiāo* (cross) as the phonetic.

*Niè* (to gnaw): On the head of the character *jǐng* (neck), it is pronounced *kè yá* (客牙). The *Guǎyá* states: "Niè means to gnaw. The *Pīcāng* states: "It means to gnaw greatly. The *Wenzì Diǎnshuō* states: "Niè is the same as *yǎo* (to bite); it is composed of the radical *zhī* (teeth) with *kě* (can) as the phonetic."

"Bai" (擘): Upper radical *pi* (拼), read as *ge* (革) with the reversed *gu* (顧). Wang Yewang says it means "to split with the hand. The *Guangya* says it means "to divide. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* says it means "to tear open. It is formed from the radical *shou* (手) and the phonetic *bi* (辟). The lower character, *yu* (庾), is read as *zhu* (朱). Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* says "fatty parts" (*yu*). The *Shuowen* says: "Fatty parts refers to the fat beneath the abdomen. It is formed from the radical *rou* (肉) and the phonetic *yu* (臾). The pronunciation of *yu* is the same as above.

The character *kuǎi* (爴) [in the phrase] "tearing open the abdomen" (*kuǎifù*) is followed by the phonetic gloss *shàngguī bìfǎn*. Upon examining the classics, histories, and various dictionaries, this character *kuǎi* does not exist. Now, interpreting the meaning of "tearing open the abdomen" (*kuǎifù*) as discussed in the treatise, it means to destroy and rip open the abdomen with one's hands.

"Grasping at the heart" (搯心): "tāo" is pronounced as *dǎo* with a reversed tone (i.e., *tǎo*). The *Book of Zhou* says, "To draw out weapons and grasp blades. The *Kǎoshēng* says, "Grasping means to take hold of. The *Shuowén* says: "Tāo (*tǎo*); the phonetic component is *yǎo* (pronounced *yáo* with a small tone). It is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "yǎo" (舀). The pronunciation of "yǎo" is *yáo* with a small tone.

*Chā* (upper character pronounced *zhǎ*, with the phonetic element *shā*): The commentary states that it means "to seize. It is also written as *chāo* or *chāi*, and likewise as *chī*; these are identical. The *Guījīn zhèngzì* (Correct Characters of the Present Age) states that it means "to grasp with the claws," following the radical for "hand" (*shǒu*) and taking *chū* as the phonetic element; *chū* is pronounced *zuò hé* (modern *zuò hē*). The lower character, *chèn*: The commentary states that it means "to pull or drag. The *Wénzìdiǎn* (Dictionary of Words and Characters) explains that it follows the radical for "hand" and takes *zhì* as the phonetic element. It is also written as *zhì* or *zhōu*, all of which are identical.

*Chàn* (鑱): *Shàng* (上) and *shì* (仕) with the *shān* (衫) radical; Gù Yěwáng says that *chàn* refers to the blade of a needle used for piercing. The *Cāngjié piān* says it means to chisel or bore. The *Guǎngyǎ* says *chàn* is called *pī* (鈹), pronounced *pǔ pí* (普皮). The *Wénzì diǎnshuō* says *chàn* is a pointed knife for piercing; it is composed of the radical *jīn* (金) and the phonetic *chán* (毚), which has the same pronunciation as above, while the lower part is *qīng* (青) and *jì* (迹) with the *fǎn* (反) radical. Gù Yěwáng says "piercing" (*cì*) refers to a sharp instrument entering the flesh. The *Kǎoshēng* says "piercing" (*cì*) means striking with a blade; the *Wénzì diǎnshuō* says "piercing" (*cì*) is synonymous with killing; it is composed of the radical *dāo* (刀) and the phonetic *cì* (朿), which is pronounced *bǐ sì* (匕四).

*Tàn* (探): The upper radical is *tǎ* (塔), with the phonetic *nán* (南). The *Erya* says: "To *tàn* is to seize by means of a decoy. The *Shenglèi* says: "To *tàn* is to take from deep within. The *Shuowén* says: "It means to take from afar; it is composed of the radical *shǒu* (hand) and the phonetic *mí* (罙). *Mí* is pronounced *dàgǎn* (大感). The lower character is *zhú* (竹), with the phonetic *jué* (角). The *Shī* says: "Do not peck at my millet. The *Guǎngyá* says: "'To *zuò* (啄)' is to bite. The *Shuowén* says: "'To *zuò*' is the feeding of birds; it is composed of the radical *kǒu* (mouth) and the phonetic *chù* (豖). *Chù* is pronounced *chōulù* (丑錄)."*

Regarding "under the sword and spear" (*dāoqiāng*), the *Guoyu* says, "he brandishes his spear. The *Cangjie pian* states, "A *qiāng* is a wooden object with sharp points at both ends. The *Shuowen jiezi* defines it as, "A *qiāng* is a sharp prong; it is composed of the radical 'wood' (*mù*) and the phonetic 'cāng' (*cāngshēng*). The character *jié* (in *xiéqīāng*) is pronounced according to its rhyme.

"Yùhàn" (禦捍): "xià" (下) is pronounced as "dàn" (旦). Duan's commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "hàn" (捍) means "to guard and protect. "Hàn" is also synonymous with "yù" (禦). The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "Hàn" refers to a cloak; it is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "hàn" (旱)."
*Arbuda* (𦞦婆): This is a transliteration from the Sanskrit; in the Tang language, it refers to one of the names for the Eight Cold Hells (*aṣṭau śītanarakāḥ*).

*Pao* (疱) is pronounced with the initial *pao* (皃) and the final *liè* (烈); Xu Shuchong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states that it refers to "gas-filled sores on the face. The *Shuowen Jiezi* records it as *pao* (皰), which is the same character, composed of the radical "skin" (皮) and the phonetic "bao" (包).

"Analysis" (*pǒuxī*): "Pǒu" is pronounced as *kǒng* (with the mouth open). The commentary on the *Shàngshū* states that "pǒu" means "to divide. The commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* by Du Yu states that "pǒu" refers to dividing something down the middle. The *Cāngjiépiān* states that "pǒu" also means "to split. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* states it means "to separate," written with the radical "knife" (*dāo*) and the phonetic "tǒu" (pronounced *tā kǒu*). The second volume [of this work] has already provided a full explanation of the latter character, "xī" (pronounced *xīng jí*).

The character *guī* (乖) is followed by *é* (訛), which is pronounced with the "five" tone (*gō*) according to the rhyme scheme. Zheng’s commentary on the *Shijing* states that *é* means "falsehood. Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that *é* refers to "deceptive speech. It is formed from the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic "huà" (*huà*), and it is also written as *tuó* (譌) with the same meaning.

*Jian* (踐): To tread upon. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states it means "to step upon. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lunyu* says it means "to trample. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* says it means "to kick. It is composed of the radical 足 with the phonetic 戔; the pronunciation of 戔 is *can*. The character below is 黏, pronounced *zhe*. The *Fangyan* says *jian* means "to ascend. The *Cangjie pian* says it means "to dance" (*die*; pronunciation *die*). The *Guangya* says *jian* means "to wear shoes. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* says it means "to tread. It is composed of the radical 足 with the phonetic 聶; the pronunciation of 聶 is the same as that of "up" (*shang*).

*Ché* (畟): Upper radical *chū* (初), phonetic *sè* (色). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: “*Ché* means ‘to lean’ (*zé*). Gu Yewang states: “It means ‘square. In ancient and modern standard characters, it is composed of the radical *tián* (田) and the phonetic *rén* (人), with *fǎn* (反) as the sound component.

Regarding "jue" (捔): the upper radical is *shang* (上) and the phonetic is *jiang* (江) with the retroflex *e* (岳) final. The commentary on the sounds states that "jue" means to monopolize, to abridge, and also to measure. Lexicons also write it as "kue" (搉). The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "Jue also means to strike; it is composed of the radical 'hand' (手) and the phonetic 'jiao' (角)."

17. Volume Seventeen. Regarding the term *jīshí* (nits and lice): the character for *jī* (蟣) is pronounced with the initial *jū* (居) and the final *chē* (󳅅). According to the *Kǎo Shēng* (Examination of Sounds), *jī* refers to the eggs of lice. The *Shuōwén* (Explaining Graphs and Analyzing Characters) states that *shí* (蝨) is a biting insect; it is composed of the radical *guǐn* (䖵) and the phonetic *xìn* (卂). The radical *guǐn* is pronounced *kūn* (昆), and the phonetic *xìn* is pronounced *xìn* (信). In the *Lùn* (Treatise), it is written as *shī* (虱), which is a common vernacular form.

Regarding the character for *kǎn* (穬): in the *Guóměng* (虢猛), it is pronounced as *gǒu*. The *Cāngjiépiān* states that *kǎn* refers to *sù* (粟, millet). The *Guǎngwùzhì* states that among varieties of *gāng* (秔, non-glutinous rice), there is "wū-gāng" (烏秔), which is black in color; the pronunciation of *gāng* is *gǔhéng*. The *Shuōwén* states that *kǎn* refers to awned millet (*máng-sù*), composed of the radical "grain" (*huó*) and the phonetic component "guǎng."

*Xuānzhèng* (喧諍): The upper character, *xuān*, is pronounced as *huǐ yuán fǎn*. The *Shēnglèi* states it means "clamor"; Gu Yewáng also says it means "clamor. The *Wénzìdiǎn* explains that it follows the radical "speech" (*yán*) and takes *xuān* as its phonetic. The lower character, *zhèng*, is pronounced as *gèng fǎn*. Gu Yewáng says that "to *zhèng*" is now considered "to contend" (*zhēng*). The *Zìshū* says "to contend" (*zhēng*) is to offer remonstrance. The *Kǎoshēng* says "to *zhèng*" is like contentious speech. The *Shuōwén* says "to *zhèng*" is to stop; it follows the radical "speech" (*yán*) and takes *zhēng* as its phonetic.
Regarding "qíljiǎo" (麟角), the character for "lì" (栗) has the phonetic *zhēn* (珍) as its rhyme; this has already been fully explained in the preceding "Phonetics and Meanings of the Ratnakūṭa" (寶積音義).

Volumes 18 and 19—Volumes Eighteen and Nineteen—contain no characters requiring phonetic glosses. Volume 20—Volume Twenty—regarding "yǎyáng" (瘂羊): the character for "yǎ" (瘂) has the phonetic *ā yǎ* (鴉雅); the *Pīcāng* states that "yǎ" means "dumb. The *Kǎoshēng* states that "yǎ" refers to being unable to speak; it is also written as 𤺘. The *Shuowén* [explains it] as being composed of the radical "sickness" (疒, with the phonetic *nǚ è* [女厄]). Volume 20—Volume Twenty—regarding "yǎyáng" (瘂羊): the character for "yǎ" (瘂) has the phonetic *ā yǎ* (鴉雅); the *Pīcāng* states that "yǎ" means "dumb. The *Kǎoshēng* states that "yǎ" refers to being unable to speak; it is also written as 𤺘. The *Shuowén* [explains it] as being composed of the radical "sickness" (疒, with the phonetic *nǚ è* [女厄]).

Regarding "jiāng" (罝弶): the first character is pronounced with the *zhé* rhyme (邪反). The *Shī* (詩) says, "Sù sù tǔ jiān" (肅肅兔罝), and its commentary states, "Jiān means a net for catching hares. Guō's commentary on the *Ěryá* says, "Jiān is like 'obstructing' (*zhē*). The *Wénzì Diǎnshuō* says that "jiān" is pronounced with the *qiè* sound (*qiě*). The second character is pronounced with the *qiáng xiàng* rhyme. The *Wénzì Diǎnshuō* says, "'Jiāng' refers to setting a snare (*mí*) on a path; it takes the radical 'bow' (*gōng*) and the phonetic 'jīng' (*jīng*)."

*Jī* (上) is pronounced *chí* (希) with a retroflex *r* (反). Hé Xiū’s commentary on the *Gōngyáng Zhuàn* states: "To criticize (*jī*) is equivalent to to reprimand (*qiàn*). Zhèng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states: "It means to scold and examine. The *Guǎngpǐ* states: "It means to admonish (*jiàn*), to inquire (*wèn*), and also to pierce (*cì*). The *Wénzì Diǎnshuō* explains that it is composed of the radical "speech" (言) and the phonetic element "qí" (幾). *Xià* (下) is pronounced *cī* (雌) with a *s* (四) retroflex. The *Máo Shī Zhuàn* states: "To criticize (*cì*) is to reproach (*zé*). The *Kǎoshēng* states: "To criticize (*cì*) is also to censure (*jī*) and to slander (*fěi*). The *Shuōwén* explains that it is composed of the radical "knife" (刀) and the phonetic element "cì" (朿), where the sound of *cì* is the same as above. The character used in the *Lùn* (論) is *lì* (刾), which is a vulgar form.

*Xiōngbó* (兇勃): The upper character is pronounced *xù* (with the radical 几 and the phonetic 凶). The version in the *Lùn-wén* (論文) as *xiāo* (󰉾) is an error. The lower character is pronounced *mén* (with the radical 皿 and the phonetic 沒). It means violent anger. The *Erya* says, "Bó means to act. Gu Yewang says, "Bó means sudden and intense. Zheng Zhong’s *Liji* says, "It means to oppose. The *Fāngyán* says, "It means disorder. The *Shuowén* says, "It means to push aside; it takes the radical 力 and the phonetic 孛 (pronounced as above). The version in the *Lùn-wén* that takes 孚 as the phonetic to form *fú* (㔜) is incorrect.

21. Fascicle Twenty-one. **Śaṇḍha** (扇搋): The lower character, *chāi*, is pronounced with the *chè* (坼) and *jiā* (加) finals. It is a term from the Sanskrit language referring to one who lacks the male organ. **Khaṭa** (坑阱): The upper character, *kēng* (坑), is pronounced with the *kè* (客) and *gēng* (耕) finals.

The *Cāngjiépiān* (蒼頡篇) states it means a pit or chasm. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it means a depression or hollow. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* (文字典說) states it means a moat, formed with the radical for earth and the phonetic *háng* (亢). *Háng* is pronounced *gāng* (剛). The lower character, *jǐng* (阱), is pronounced with the *qíng* (情) and *yǐng* (郢) finals. The *Guǎngpǐ* (廣疋) states that *jìng* (阱) is also a pit. The *Kǎoshēng* states it means digging into the ground to trap animals. The *Shuowén* (說文) states it is formed with the radical for *xié* (𨸏) and the phonetic *jǐng* (井). In the *Lùn* (論) [the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya*], it is written as *jìng* (穽), which is a vulgar usage of the character; alternatively, it is written as *biè* (弊) or *xīn* (汬), which are ancient characters.

Regarding "wrinkled face" (miàn zhòu): the second character is pronounced with the *jiù* rhyme. The *Kǎo Shēng* states that it means the skin is gathered; the *Wénzì Diǎn* says it means the skin is wide. It is formed from the radical "skin" (pí) with the phonetic "chū"; the pronunciation of "chū" is *cè jū*.

22. Fascicle Twenty-Two. **SHE (蛇)**: The *Kao* dictionary states that this refers to venomous insects. It is also pronounced *ta*. In ancient times, when people lived in nests and caves, they would ask one another, "Have there been any snakes (*she*) coming? The *Wenzi Dianshuo* explains it as being composed of the radical for "insect" (*chong*) and the phonetic *ta* (pronounced *tuó*). The *Lunwen* writes it as *she*, and the current vernacular character is also acceptable. **XIE (蝎)**: Pronounced *xuan-ye*. Jia Qi’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that this refers to the venom of the scorpion. The *Guangya* says, "The scorpion (*xie*) is a stinging insect. The *Buya* says, "A stinging insect that inflicts poison. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* states that *chai* and *xie* are different names for the same creature. It is composed of the radical for "insect" and the phonetic *xie* (pronounced as above). *Chai* is pronounced *chui-jie*; *qu* is pronounced *qi-yu*; and *shi* is pronounced *shi-yi*.
*Qiṅlì* (𢤱戾): The first character is pronounced with the *lǒng* rhyme; the second is pronounced with the *lí-dì* rhyme. Regarding the meaning of the passage:

it describes a state of being stubborn and violent. 23. Fascicle Twenty-three. *Jiàsè* (稼穡): The first character is pronounced with the *jiǎ* rhyme. Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "Planting the five grains is called *jià*. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* says: "The flowering of the grain is *jià*"; it is composed of the radical *禾* (grain) and the phonetic *家*. The second character is pronounced with the *zè* rhyme. Zheng’s sub-commentary on the *Shijing* states: "Gathering the taxes [of grain] is called *sè*. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* says: "It refers to the harvest of Hou Ji. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "Grain that may be harvested is called *sè*; it is composed of the radical *禾* and the phonetic *嗇*."

*Kiǎoquè* (磽确): The first character is pronounced *qiǎo* (反) and the second *jiǎo* (反). Gu Yewang states that "kiǎo" means firm and hard; this refers to what Mencius says regarding "the land having the saline and the *kiǎo*" (*dì yǒu yán kiǎo*). The *Huáinánzǐ* says, "They struggle over the *kiǎoquè* [barren] places. The *Shēnglèi* says, "*Kiǎoquè* means stony and thin soil. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* says, "*Quò* means the land is emaciated and poor. The *Shuowén* states that *kiǎoquè* is also *liè* (礊), both following the radical "stone" (*shí*) with "yáo" and "jiǎo" as their phonetic components. *Liè* (礊) is pronounced *kǒ è* (反).

Regarding the character *lǎ* (in the phrase *guǒ lǎ*, where *lǎ* is pronounced with the lower radical *lán* and the suffix *dǎn*): the *Guìyuàn Zhūcóng* states that *lǎ* means "pungent"; the *Kǎoshēng* states that *lǎ* means "extremely pungent. According to the standard orthography of past and present, it is composed of the radical *xīn* (radical 159) and the phonetic element *cì*.

To this day, as the *Shijing* says, "down to the present" (*yǐ qǐ yú jīn*). The *Erya* states that *qì* means "to arrive at. The *Wenzi Dian* explains that it is formed with the radical *chuò* (meaning "to walk") and the phonetic *qǐ*; the sound of *chuò* is *chūlüè*.
*Bāo* (皰): The upper character is pronounced *pào* (炮) with the *mǎo* (貌) rhyme; this was already fully explained in the sixteenth fascicle above.

24. Second Fascicle, Part Two: *Gaṅgā*. In the Sanskrit language, the upper character is pronounced *jīng* (鯨) with the *zhěng* (拯) rhyme, and the lower character is pronounced *jīng* (鯨) with the *qiē* (佉) rhyme.

Regarding the character *jí* (緝): the upper radical is *qīn* (侵) with the final rhyme *jì* (入). Zheng’s commentary on the *Shijing* states that *jí* means "to continue. A passage from the *Shijing* says: "Profound was King Wen; he continued and brightened his reverent stillness. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* states that *jí* means "to weave" (*jì*). It is composed of the radical *mì* (糸) and the phonetic *qí* (咠); the sound of *qí* is *qīn* with the final rhyme *xí* (習).

25. Fascicle Twenty-Five. Regarding the term *pūga* (translated as "torrential flow" [pùliú], with the first character pronounced *bào*): the *Wenzidian* states it refers to the rapid swelling of river waters; the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means heavy rain, composed of the radical for water (*shui*) and the phonetic component *bào*, with the pronunciation of *bào* being as stated above.
Āḷāra (the first character is pronounced *āi* [ai-] and the second *nǎo* [nao-]): In Sanskrit, this is the name of a Dragon King (*nāgarāja*). Volume 26, No. 26:

There are no characters in this volume requiring phonetic glosses or explanations. Volume 27, No. 27: Regarding the character *liúyè* (流軶): the second character, *yè*, is pronounced *yīnggé* [ying-ke]. The *Lǎojì* (老子) states that for a carriage-maker, the shaft (*yè*) is six feet long. Guō Pǔ says it is the wooden piece at the end of the axle that rests upon the ox’s neck. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* (文字典說) says it is the curved wood atop the ox’s neck. It is composed of the radical for "carriage" (*chē*) and the phonetic component *è* (戹); the pronunciation of *è* is as noted above. The *Shànglùn* (上論) uses the character *è* (軛), which is a vulgar form.

Regarding "zào" (躁) in "zàolì" (躁利): it is pronounced as *zāo* (譟). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lunyu* states that "zào" means not being at peace and stillness. The *Kǎoshēng* says that "zào" refers to an impatient temperament; it also means movement. The *Shìfǎ* states that one who delights in changing and disturbing others is called "zào. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* explains that the character is composed of "zú" (足) and the phonetic "sào" (喿); "sào" is pronounced as *sāo* (竈).

"Unable to endure" (bù nài): "nài" is pronounced *dài* in the *Zuozhuan*, where it says "not enduring one another. Gu Yewang states that "nài" means "to be able. The *Kaosheng* says it means "to endure. The *Wenzidian* explains that all matters concerning laws and regulations derive from the character "cùn" (inch); they are measured by the inch so that the law does not exceed its bounds. It follows the radical "radical 54" (the hand) and the element "cùn."

Regarding "not being conversant" (bù'ān): it contains a hidden pun. The *Dongguan Hanji* states that [the Emperor] was conversant with the number of trees growing as sprouts upon the imperial mausoleums. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* defines "ān" (諳) as "to know thoroughly"; it is derived from the radical for speech and relates to sound.

*Ani* (pronounced *nǐ*, with the *qì* radical): The *Zhou Li* states that it means "to conceal" (*àn*) in the context of military matters. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Chunqiu* states that *ānì* also means "to hide. The *Guǎngyá* defines *ānì* as "to conceal. The *Shuowén* defines *ānì* as "to disappear" (*wáng*). It is composed of the radicals *jiǎn* (𠃊) and *yī* (一), with the phonetic component *fù* (覆). The sound is that of *yǐn* (音隱).

28. Fascicle Twenty-Eight. Regarding the term *teng-mo-beng* (𧄼瞢): the first character is pronounced as *teng*, and the second is pronounced as *mo-beng*. This has already been fully explained and annotated in the preceding seventh fascicle.

"Dùn (遲鈍): Tún is also chī (slow). The *Shiji* states that those who are wán (stubborn) and dùn are such; the *Shuowen Jiezi* says dùn is also wán, meaning the mind is not sharp. It is composed of the radical 金 (metal) and the phonetic 屯."

29. Fascicle Twenty-nine. Regarding "yù" (瘀) in "miè yù" (𤯝瘀): the phonetic gloss states it refers to suspected blood within the skin and flesh. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "Yù also means accumulated blood. It is composed of the radical 'nà' (疒) and the phonetic 'yú' (於). The sound of 'nà' is nǚgè (女革)."

*Pāng* (胮): Upper radical *pó* (璞), with the phonetic *bāng* (邦). The *Pīcāng* (埤蒼) dictionary states that *pāng* also means "swollen. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* (文字典說) explains it as being composed of the radical "flesh" (*ròu*) and the phonetic *xiōng* (夅), pronounced *hù dōng* (戶冬). The version in the *Lùn-wén* (論文) uses *féng* (逄) instead of *mào* (𮌨), which is a vulgar character. Lower radical *zhāng* (張), with the phonetic *liàng* (亮). Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states: "Zhāng" refers to the abdomen being full. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* explains it as being composed of the radical "flesh" (*ròu*) and the phonetic *cháng* (長).

"Qi-bin" (驅擯): the second character is read as *bì rèn* (必仞). Sima Biao’s commentary on the *Zhuangzi* states that it means "to cast out and abandon. The *Shiji* (Records of the Grand Historian) states that it refers to "mutually pushing aside and excluding. The *Wenzi Dian* (Dictionary of Characters) explains that the radical is "hand" (手) and the phonetic component is "bin" (賓).

*Fēnáng* (𩍁囊): The first character, *fēn* (𩍁), is pronounced with the initial *pí* (脾) and the final *bài* (拜). Gu Yewang states that a *fēn* is a bag used for blowing on smelting fires to make them blaze. The *Pīcāng* dictionary writes it as *fēng* (𩏕) following the radical *wéi* (韋). The *Wenzidian* explains that a *fēn* is a leather bag for blowing fire; it follows the radical *wéi* (韋) and takes *pí* (󲊰) as its phonetic component. The pronunciation of *pí* (󲊰) is *pí* (祕) with the final *fǎn* (反). The version in the *Lùn-wén* (論文) writes it as *pò* (㰆), but this is not found in the standard characters of either the ancient or modern traditions.

*Kuān* (髖): Pronounced *guān* (with the initial *k* reversed). The *Pīcāng* states it refers to the buttocks (*wǎn*). The *Kǎoshēng* states it refers to the bone of the thigh (*tí*). The *Shuōwén* states: "The hip is above the thigh; it is composed of the radical 'bone' and the phonetic 'kuān. It may also be written as 'wǎn,' which is identical [in meaning], with the pronunciation *kǎo gāo fǎn*. The character for *bì* (䏶) has the pronunciation *bià xià píng mǐ fǎn*. The *Yùnjiàn* states that the *bì* is the same as the *gǔ* (thigh); the inner part is called *gǔ*, while the outer part is called *bì*. The *Lǐjì* states: 'Do not grow weary of the *bì*. The *Shuōwén* states: 'The *bì* is on the outside of the *gǔ*; it is composed of the radical 'bone' and the phonetic 'bēi. It is also written as 'pǐ,' which is the ancient form. The vulgar form is 'bì'."*

Regarding the form of the *jing* (shin) above the ankle: the commentary on the *Lunyu* states that *jing* refers to the shin of the leg. Gu Yewang says it is the bone in front of the calf (*fei*). The *Wenzi Dianshuo* says *jing* is the bone of the leg (*jiao-jing*). It is composed of the radical "flesh" (*rou*) and the phonetic "xing" (*xing*, pronounced *jing*); *fei* (calf) is pronounced *fu-fei*; *jing* (bone) is pronounced *xing* (or written as *xiong*), with the same meaning. Below, [the character] is pronounced *hua-wa*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* says the ankle is the heel. The *Cangjie Pian* says the ankle is at the side of the foot. The *Shenglei* says it is the inner and outer bones above the instep (*fu*). The *Shuowen* [explains it] as being composed of the radical "foot" (*zu*) and the phonetic "guo. The discussion in the *Lunwen* that it is composed of "flesh" to form *fan* (腂) is incorrect. *Fu* (instep) is pronounced *fang-yu*.

*Ti-hu*: the first character is pronounced *diàn* (with the second tone) and the second is *hùgū* (with the fourth tone). *Ti-hu* is the most refined essence extracted from clarified butter (*sū*), which does not congeal. Lexicons and dictionaries both derive it from the radical for "wine" (*yǒu*) and the abbreviated form of "is" (*shì*), as well as from the sound *hú*.

*Qí* (as in *qídào*, "rice fields") is pronounced with the *hú* and *guī* rhymes. Mencius says, "Is he ill from working on the summer *qí*? Liu Xi states that in current vernacular usage, twenty-five *mǔ* constitute a small *qí* and fifty *mǔ* constitute a large *qí*. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that *qí* is synonymous with *qū* (a plot). The *Shuowen Jiezi* also states that fifty *mǔ* make a *qí*; it is formed from the radical *tián* (field) and the phonetic *guī*.

Volumes 30–34: Volumes Thirty, Thirty-one, Thirty-two, Thirty-three, and Thirty-four. The five volumes listed above contain no characters requiring phonetic glosses. Volume 35: Volume Thirty-five. Regarding the character *zǐ* (孳) in *zǐshǎn* (孳產): the *Wénzìdiǎn* (Dictionary of Characters) states it means "the sprouting of all things" or "germination. The *Shuowén* (Explanations of Graphs) states: "To breed and give birth, reproducing and gradually increasing. It is composed of the radical *zǐ* (子) with the phonetic *zī* (茲).

36. Fascicle Thirty-Six. "Xiàojiàn" (驍健): The first character, xiào (驍), is pronounced with the initial *yáo* (堯) according to the *Yǔjiāo* (許叔重). The commentary on the *Huáinánzǐ* states that *xiào* means "brave. The *Guǎngyá* states that *xiào* also means "vigorous. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "horse" (*mǎ*) and the phonetic "yáo" (*yáo*).

37. Fascicle Thirty-Seven. Regarding "guǐ" (軌): it is pronounced with the initial *guī* (歸) and the final *wěi* (委). The *Guānglù Shì* (穀梁傳) states that "guǐ" means law or principle (*fǎzé*). The *Shuōwén* (說文) defines it as the ruts of a carriage, formed from the radical "carriage" (車) and the phonetic "jiǔ" (九). In archaic script it is written as 󰹓, and also as 𧗝; the version in the *Lùn-wén* (論文) writes it as 軓, which is a vulgar character.

Fàn'ěr (泛爾): Upper radical *shǔ* (阜), phonetic *fú* (孚) with the variant *fàn* (梵). The *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲) states it means "not specifically designated. The *Shuōwén* (說文) takes *shuǐ* (水) as the radical and *fá* (乏) as the phonetic; those who take *fán* (凡) as the phonetic are incorrect.
38. Volume Thirty-Eight. Jūyuè (拘𢷻): Upper radical *jù* (俱), lower phonetic *yuán* (緣). This is the name of a fruit from the Western Regions.

*Niǎo-luàn* (嬈亂): The first character, *niǎo*, is pronounced with the *niū* rhyme reversed (i.e., *niǎo*). The *Kǎośēng* (考聲) states that it means "to disturb" or "to toy with. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical *nǚ* (woman) and the phonetic *yáo*.

It is also written as *niǎo* (嬲), which is interchangeable. 39. Volume Thirty-nine. Volume thirty-nine has no characters requiring phonetic or explanatory notes. 40. Volume Forty. Volume forty: *Rú póluónǐsī* (如婆羅痆斯). *Nǐ* (儜) is pronounced with the *níng* rhyme reversed (i.e., *nǐ*). This is a Sanskrit term; the old translation was *Póluónà* (波羅奈). *Yǎ* (軋) is pronounced with the *yàn* and *zhá* rhymes reversed (i.e., *yǎ*).

The above is from Xuanying’s Pronunciations. *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, Volumes 1–3 (First, Second, and Third Volumes). The above were previously not provided with pronunciations. **Fourth Volume** *Tusita* (pronounced *dǒu shī duō*, with *dài* reversed; in the sūtras it is sometimes written as *Tusida* or *Tusiduo*; these are all corruptions. The correct term is *Dṛṣṭasatya*. This is the Heaven of Contentment, also called the Heaven of Wondrous Contentment.)

Brahmapurohita is the second heaven of the first dhyāna. This is translated as "Brahma’s Foremost Benefactors" (*Sanskrit: Brahmā-purohita*). It is so named because these deities constantly contemplate the benefit of the Brahma Heaven while preceding it. Formerly they were called the "Brahma-foregoing" (*Brahmapūrva-gata*) or the "Brahma-assistants" (*Brahmapārṣadya*); "foregoing" means preceding the Brahma King, and "assistants" means assisting the Brahma King.

*Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* by Dharmottara, Volume One. Volume One of the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* by Dharmottara. First, regarding the character "bù" (不): [This entry is missing from the source]. Volume Two. Compiled by Xuanying. Regarding the character "biàn" (辮): the *Sāncāng* and the *Biànzì* both read it with the phonetic "púdiǎn" (蒲典). The *Shuowén* states: "Biàn means to weave patterns."

The characters *xì* (係), *jì* (繼), and *xì* (繫) are homophonous, read as *gù dì* (古帝反). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *xì* means "to tie up" (*jiéshù*) and "to succeed one another" (*xiāng jìsì*).
Volume Three, Section Three: *guàn* (慣), *chuàn* (串), *guàn* (遦)—these three forms are homophonous, read as *gǔ huàn* (古患反). According to the *Erya*, *chuàn* also means "habituation" (*xí*).

*Huáiyùn* (懷孕): The *Sāncāng* states that this is the archaic form of the character *huái* (懷). The lower part is the archaic form of *zhēn* (娠), with the phonetic component *yú* (余) and the radical *fǎng* (反). The *Shuōwén* defines it as "to carry a child. The *Guǎngyǐ* states that *yùn* (孕) means *shēn* (娠), which refers to being pregnant with a child. To "contain" (*hán*) the fruit [of conception] is called *yùn*; it is composed of the radical *zǐ* (子) and the phonetic *nǎi* (乃).

Volumes 4–5: Volumes Four and Five both lack the phonetic glosses provided previously. Volume Six: Regarding the character for *akṣi* (eye-secretion), the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as *chī*. Currently, in Jiangnan, it is called *chīdōu*. The character is pronounced with the initial *mò* and the final *jié*. The version in the *Lunwen* (Treatise) uses the character *zhī*, which is incorrect.

*Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, Fascicle One. Compiled by Xuanying. In the *Munigāthā*, it is sometimes written as *Vani*; the old translation says "Ren" (Benevolent). It should be called *Mani*, which here means "Rishi" (*Ṛṣi*). This term applies to both Buddhists and non-Buddhists, referring to those who have long cultivated their minds and studied the Way in mountain forests.
*Śūra* is also translated as *śūlin*, which in this context means "real forest" (*śat-sen*), referring to that which is steadfast and real. Regarding *mṛdu*:

while the standard form is written with the character for "soft" (*ruǎn*), it is pronounced *ruán* (same radical, different tone). The Sanskrit original says *mṛdudu*, which is translated here as "soft" or "weak."

"Roughness" (*sè*) is also written as "obstruction" (*sè*), with the same pronunciation as *suòlì*. It means that which is not smooth. The character is composed of "four stops" (*sì zhǐ*); "four stops" signifies the meaning of being obstructed. In the *Lun* (Treatise), it appears in two forms, "𭱖" and "澁," but these are not the correct characters.

"Tianzhu" (India) is sometimes called "Shendu" or "Xiandou," both of which are corruptions. The correct name is *Indu*; "Indu" is one of the thousand names for the moon. It is named thus because the sages and worthies of that land have succeeded one another in awakening sentient beings, illuminating them like the moon. One tradition states that "Xiandou" is originally *Indravatana*, which means "Abode of the Lord," referring to the Heavenly Emperor (*Indra*). It is likely that it has been called by this name for a long time because it was protected by the Heavenly Emperor.

*Mili-che* (彌離車) or *Mili-che* (彌戾車) are both corruptions; the correct pronunciation is *Mleccha*. This refers to those from the borderlands who possess no knowledge. Regarding the term for a military host (*junzhòng* 軍衆): in the *Zilin* (字林), "army" (*jun* 軍) means to surround.

Four thousand men constitute an army (*jun*), and three thousand five hundred men constitute a division (*shi* 師). The character is composed of the radical *baō* (勹)—pronounced *bǔjiāo*—which signifies encircling a chariot to form an army, and the element *zào* (𠂤), which signifies a surrounding wall to form a division; these are the meanings inherent in the characters.

*Qie* (詰): Pronounced *qù zhì fǎn*. According to the *Guǎyá*, it means "to reprimand"; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means "to interrogate. *Huā* (華) and *mǎn* (󳍹) are also written as *huā* (花), all pronounced *hū guā fǎn*.

The character below, the Sanskrit term *mālā*, is here transcribed as *mǎn* (󳌃), with the phonetic *mán*. It is recorded that in the Western Regions, *mālā*-makers (*mālākāra*) mostly use *sumana* flowers; they string them in rows to form garlands. Whether male or female, noble or humble, all use these for adornment—either on the head or the body—as ornaments. In various sutras, terms such as "celestial garland" (*divyamālā*), "jewel garland" (*ratnamālā*), and "flower garland" (*puṣpamālā*) refer to these same *mālākāra* artisans. In the *Śāstra*, this is also written as *lín* (𩬞), but this is not the correct orthography.

*Tuán* (徒官反): The *Tōngsùwén* states that what the hands roll into a ball is called *tuán*; the *Sāncāng* says it refers to a lump of rice. The *Lùn-wén* writes it as *chuǎi* (初委反), which the predecessors of the North measured as *chuǎi*. In the Jiangnan region, this pronunciation is used, as well as *dūguǒ* (都果反). The *Shuōwén* explains it as "to measure," hence *chuǎi*. This pronunciation is used in the Guanzhong region, but neither is the correct meaning here.
Gài’s residence has not yet returned. According to the *Shuowen*, "gài" means to irrigate or to pour down.

As for "qíng," it is also written as "xīng" or "yì"; these two forms share the same pronunciation, zìyíng, meaning that it does not rain. In the *Shenglèi*, "qíng" is defined as the ceasing of rain. The version in the *Lunwen* uses the character "fú," which is incorrect.

"Hu-chu" (戶樞) [the character "chu" is pronounced as *zhǒu*]: this refers to the pivot-hole of a door. According to the *Erya*, the pivot is called *wéi*. Guo Pu states: "It is the socket for the pivot of a door. The *Guoye* says: "The pivot is the root. The pivot mechanism is that which governs movement and rotation. *Wéi* is pronounced as *wǎi* (五迴反).

2. Second Fascicle. *Yi* (猗) [pronounced qi in the rhyme dictionary]; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "to lean" (*yi*). According to the *Guangya*, it means "to rely upon" (*yin*). It refers to lying down while leaning against something. The character is composed of the "person" radical (*ren*). In the *Lunyu*, it is written as *yi* (猗), pronounced *qi* (one-ji). It means "beauty."

"Zào-dòng" (躁動) is also written as "zào-tóng" (趮同), with the latter character pronounced as *zì-dào* (子到反). "Zào" means movement; it signifies agitation and restlessness. The *Lunyu* states: "To speak of what one has not yet reached is called 'zào'. Zheng Xuan commented: "This means not being at peace and still. The *Shiming* explains: "Zào" is "zào" (燥); it means that when an object is dry, it moves and flies upward.

"Diao" (掉) [the radical is "tu" (徒) and the tone is "diao" (弔); according to the *Zilin*, it means "to sway"; according to the *Guangyi*, it means "to vibrate"]. The version in the *Lunwen* (Treatise on the Treatises) writes it as "tiao" (恌), which is incorrect.
"Ji" (忌) [the radical is "liang" (梁) and the tone is "ji" (記); it means "to find difficulty in" and also "to fear"; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "to loathe and detest"].

"Jí" (envy) is written with two ancient characters, 𧪠 and 㑵, both sharing the phonetic "lì" (qīngtóng fǎn). In the *Chuci*, it says: "Therefore, he gives rise to envy and jealousy in his heart. Wang Yi comments: "To harm the worthy is called jí; to harm the beautiful is called dòu."

"Xièdài" (懈怠): "Xiè" is pronounced with the initial *g* (古) and the final *-mai* (賣) reversed; "dài" (怠) has the initial *dú* (徒) and the final *-gai* (改). In the *Ervu* (爾疋), it is glossed as "lethargy. The *Jizhu* (集注) states: "Xiè" means "extreme," while "dài" means "indolence. The *Shiming* (釋名) says: "Xiè" means "to loosen"; it refers to the bones and joints becoming loose and slack."

"Zhendan" (振旦) is sometimes written as "Zhen dan" (震旦), and "Zhendan" (真丹)—all are one and the same. The old translations called it the "Han Kingdom" (漢國); it is also rendered as "Zhina" (脂那) in the scriptures, while today it is written as "Zhina" (支那). This has no direct translation; it is simply the name of the land of Shenzhou (神州).

*You* (yóu): the first character is pronounced with the *yì* rhyme (as in *yì-zhōu*), while the second is the same as the archaic form of *yǔ*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, in Longxi they call a puppy *yóu*; because the nature of the *yóu* is to be full of hesitation (*yù*) when among people, all those who are indecisive are called *yóu-yù*. Furthermore, the *Erlü* states: "The *yóu* is like a *jǐ* (a kind of deer) that is skilled at climbing water. Guo Pu says: "It is adept at climbing trees."
"Mí" (麋) is pronounced *wang pi* (亡皮); it means to rot and decay, to disintegrate and fall apart.

"Hùxiàng" (戶向) is pronounced *xǔ liàng* (許亮); according to the *Shuowen*, it refers to a north-facing window. According to the *Guangya*, it is a small window. The character's structure consists of the radical 艸 (grass), the mouth radical 口, and the roof radical 宀 (pronounced *wang xian*).
*Kvala* (穬麥): In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is glossed as "wild millet" (*yun su*); today, large barley is called *kualmai*.

*Krośa* (拘屢), also written as *juluo* or *julu she*, is sometimes called *klūsa*; this is translated as "five hundred *dhanus*. One should say *krośa*; the sound of *lu* is pronounced like *luo* (犖). This refers to the bellowing of a great ox, whose sound can be heard for five *li*. Eight *krośas* constitute one *yojana* (踰繕那), which is forty *li*. This was the distance traveled by the sage-kings of old in a single day.

"Dying prematurely" (yāo): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "yāo" means to bend; the *Guangya* says it means to break off prematurely. The *Shiming* explains that to die while still in one's youth or prime is called "yāo," like taking an object and breaking it in the middle. The character consists of the "human" radical (*xiàng*) as its form, signifying being unable to stretch out fully. One who does not complete their allotted lifespan is termed "yāo."

3. Third Fascicle. Regarding "tu" (屠): according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means to eviscerate (*ku*). According to the *Guoyaya*, it means to destroy. Upon examination, "tu" refers to the carving and slicing of sacrificial meat.

*Siè* (司): *Guǎngyǎ* states it means "to preside over" (*zhǔ*). *Shuōwén* states that when a minister (*chén*) presides over affairs outside [the palace], he is called a *sī*. The character *sī* is formed by reversing the character *hòu* (后). Regarding the meaning of the term:

according to the *Zhou Lǐ*, one hears out lawsuits (*tíng sòng*) to seek the truth through five types of observation: first, listening to physical form; second, listening to facial expression; third, listening to the breath; fourth, listening with the ears; and fifth, listening with the eyes. "Listening" (*tíng*) refers to examining right and wrong. *Shuōwén* defines "lawsuit" (*sòng*) as "contention" (*zhēng*).

In ancient texts, "zhāijì" (齋戒) was written as "jiè" (誡), with the phonetic reading "xiè" (薤). The *Yì* (易) states, "By means of this, one observes zhāijì. Hàn Kāngbó said: "To cleanse the mind is called zhāi; to guard against misfortune is called jì. According to the *Zílín*, zhāijì means "purity"; zhāi is also synonymous with "qí" (齊). The *Guǎngyá* defines jì as "preparation. The character is composed of "廾" (two hands joined) holding a "gē" (戈, halberd) to guard against unforeseen calamities; "廾" is pronounced "gǒng" (拱). It is also written as "bài" (拜).

"Brahman" is a corrupt and abbreviated term; it should properly be called "Brahmaṇa. This means "one who inherits and practices the Great Dharma. As for their lineage, they themselves claim to have been born from the mouth of Brahmā; because they are the most excellent among the four castes, they alone take the name "Brahmā. This exists only in the five regions of India and is absent in other countries; even the "Brahmacārin" mentioned in the sūtras is this very same term. Its correct pronunciation is "Jìngyìn" (Pure Lineage), meaning that they are the descendants of Brahmā.
*Kṣatriya* should be translated as *Kṣatradhara*; this is rendered in Chinese as "Lord of the Land," referring to the noble lineage of the royal clan.

*Vaiśya* (the retrograde form of *Viś*) is correctly pronounced *Veśya*; this means "sitter," referring to those who sit [in their shops] as merchants. According to the customs of India, artisans and commoners highly value precious goods; because they seek out and accumulate wealth in the hundreds of millions, sitting [at their stalls] to handle income and expenditure, they are so named.
*Śūdra* should be called *śūdraka*, meaning those who cultivate fields, serve as officials, or study; these four castes constitute the great clans of the kingdom.
*Zī* (pronounced with the initial *shì* and final *fǎn*) means "to provide," "to utilize," "to take," or "to accomplish," according to the *Guǎngyǎ*.

Uttarakuru is sometimes called *Udantavā*, sometimes *Uttarakuru*, and sometimes *Dutara-kulu*. The correct term is *Udantara-kulū*, which is translated as "High and Superior" (*Gāoshàngzuò*), meaning it is higher and superior than other regions. It is also called "Victorious Continent" (*Shèngzhōu*). *Kulu* means "maker" (*zuò*) or "clan" (*xìng*), though the specific significance of its name remains uncertain.

Jambudvīpa is sometimes called Yanfouzhou, sometimes Shanyouzhou, and sometimes Zhanyuzhou. "Yanfu" is named after the tree; "ti" is an abbreviation. It should properly be called "Tibipuo," which means "continent" (dvīpa). "Zhan" is pronounced with the *zhēn* rhyme (the second tone).
Pūrvavideha is also called Pūrvadeśa, or Xìn Fúví Tíhē (信弗毘提訶), or Tōnglì Bōbítíhē (通利婆鼻提訶); *Bōlípó* (逋利婆) means "front" (*pūrva*), and *Tíhē* (提訶) means "leaving the body" (*videha*).

Gōdānīya is sometimes written as Kuyeni, Goyeni, or Gōyani; these are all corruptions. "Gō" here means "ox," and "dānīya" means "giving and taking. Because there are many oxen there, they use oxen for barter, just as people in this region use money and silk. Some say it is so called because there are stone oxen there.
"Cíjí zìzī fǎn ěr pǐ": *Cí* is another name for *jílí*. Guo Pu says: "It spreads along the ground as a creeping vine with fine leaves; its seeds are triangular and prickly, piercing people."

“*Kṣi-ròu*” (瘜肉) is transcribed in the *Fāngyán* as “*sī-lì*” (𦞜); the *Shuōwén* defines it as “extraordinary flesh” (*qí-ròu*), while the *Sāncāng* calls it “vile flesh” (*è-ròu*). According to the *Lùn-wén*, it is pronounced “*xī*” (息), meaning it is not part of the [body’s] proper substance.
“*Mó*” (模) is also written as “*mó*” (摹), both pronounced “*mò-nú*” (莫奴); it means “scale and model” (*guīmó*) or “pattern” (*fǎ*). It refers to capturing and reproducing an image.

4. Fourth Fascicle. Regarding the term *zhé* (㧗): according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means to pinch or grab. The pronunciation of *ji* (撠) is *jū* with the *yì* (逆) tone, meaning to grasp or seize. According to the *Tongsu Wen*, to pull or drag is called *zhé*.

The *Luying* (Nursing Infant) refers to the fact that the master [Xu Shen] further explains that when humans and birds give birth to offspring, they are called "nurse" (*ru*). The *Sancang* states: "To nurse an infant" (*ruzi*); "infant" (*zi*) means to nourish. The phonetic of "infant" (*ying*) is *yú yíng*. The *Sancang* also says: "A girl is called *ying*; a boy is called *ér*. The *Shiming* says: "When a person is first born, they are called an 'infant' (*yīng'ér*). That which is before the chest is called 'the infant' (*yīng*). Because one throws them before the infant [of the mother] and nurses them, they are therefore called an 'infant' (*yīng'ér*)."
*Yǎn* (also written as *gēng*, same pronunciation as *yān* and *gé*): that by which the neck of an ox is bound; it is also a crossbar.
*Xì* (pronounced *sī-liè*): according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means overflowing, as well as emitting and leaking.

The claim that this word is a corruption of "xìngqú" (興蕖) is erroneous; it should be stated as "xìngyú" (興虞). The character "xìng" (興) should be pronounced with the borrowed sound of "yānyíng" (嫣蠅). It originates from the country of Wūchápótánà (烏茶婆他那) beyond the passes, where the people of that land commonly eat it. The local tradition here identifies it as "yúntái" (蕓薹), but that is incorrect. The pronunciation of "yān" (嫣) is "xūyán" (虛延).

The "wuan" (蚖) snake is written as the character "yuan" (螈) in ancient texts, with the phonetic reading *wu-guan*. According to Cui Bao’s *Gujin Zhu* (Notes on Ancient and Modern), the *yingxuan* (蠑螈) is also called the "snake-healer" (*sheyi*); when large, it reaches three feet in length, its color is dark purple (*xuan*), and it is skilled at bewitching people; it is also known as the "dark *yuan*" (*xuan-yuan*). The *Hanshu* (Book of Han) mentions the "dark *wuan*" (*xuan-wuan*), which Wei Zhao explains as a black *wuan*, a type of lizard (*shixi*). The "black *wuan*" mentioned in the scriptures likely refers to this creature, though it is not stated whether it harms people through poison; this remains undetermined. Various scriptures also refer to the *hui* (虺), with the phonetic reading *xu-gui*; it is a venomous insect with two mouths on one body, where the head and tail resemble each other.
5. Fifth Fascicle. "Piao-bo" (飄薄): *bo* is pronounced as in *pu-mo*. It means "to press closely. When the wind presses closely upon something, it is called *bo*.

"Yù-huài" (瘀壞): *yù* is pronounced as in *yu-lü*. According to the *Shuowen*, *yù* refers to accumulated blood; according to the *Guangya*, *yù* refers to illness. In the *Lunwen* (Treatise), it is written as "ni-yi" (泥滓), meaning "mud and dregs."

Regarding the character for "stung" (shè): it is also explained in reverse as "a worm that moves poison" according to the *Shuowen*. In the region west of the Pass, this is pronounced *chā* with the second tone; in the region east of the Mountains, it is pronounced *zhé* with the fourth tone; these are the common dialects of the East and West.
*Fángluò* (防邏) is a term for a subordinate unit of military garrisoning; it refers to roaming troops used to ward off bandits, as well as those who patrol to investigate violations of the law.

*Xiǎobèng* (小迸)—also written as *péng* (跰) or *bìng* (𧼲)—has three forms with the same pronunciation *bǔzhèng* (補諍); it means to scatter or to flee. In the region south of the Yangtze River, they say *zàn* (𧻓𨘧), where *zàn* is pronounced *zàn* (讚).
The zhělóuchóng (folding-crawling insect) is also called xúnsāng (seeking-silkwood), yì named cánwò (moulting-moth), or sometimes sānghé (silkwood-shutter), or bùqū (step-bend).
Regarding *sūxī* (reviving-resting)—*sū* being pronounced with the initial *hù* in reverse—the *Shēnglèi* says that *sū* also means "resting," which refers to taking further rest.

"Ascending the throne" (*dēng zuò*) refers to departing from one's former state and returning to the position of sovereignty. In the *Guoyu*, regarding the phrase "that which Heaven and Earth bestow" (*tiāndì zhī suǒ zù*), Jia Gui states: "Zù means 'emolument' (*lù*)."

6. Sixth Fascicle, No Sound. 7. Seventh Fascicle, *Veda* (sometimes called *Veda*, both being corruptions; it should be called *Vedā*, which means "division" or "knowledge"). There are four names: first, *Āyurveda*, meaning "life," referring to medical arts and related matters; second, *Yajurveda*, meaning "sacrifice"; third, *Sāmaveda*, meaning "equal," referring to state etiquette, divination, physiognomy, music, and the art of war; fourth, *Atharvaveda*, meaning "incantations. These four were spoken by Brahmā. If one is born of the Brahmin caste, at seven years of age they shall approach a teacher to study them; once their studies are complete, they become a National Preceptor (*Rājaguru*) and are honored by the ruler of men. Furthermore, the Rishi Vyāsa, a grandson of Brahmā, composed eight *Vedas*.
*Duò* (pronounced *táng* with the second tone) means to measure; according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means to gauge or to assess. *Zhītí* is also called *zhīdì*;

*fútú* is translated here as "accumulation of marks" (*jùxiàng*), referring to structures such as piled-up stones that serve as markers. Some say they are square mounds, while others call them shrines; these are all explanations based on their respective meanings.

8. Fascicle Eight. The shin bone (*jinggu*) is also written as *xing* (same pronunciation, with the final rhyme being *ding*; according to the *Shuowen*, it refers to the lower part of the leg). The character *hang* (pronounced *xia meng* in fanqie) is what is called the *hang* in Jiangnan today; in Shandong it is called *hang*. The character *zang* (pronounced *zhang meng* in fanqie) is also used for the shin. Both *jing* and *hang* are names for the two bones below the knee. According to the *Shiming*, "shin" (*jing*) means "stem" (*jing*); it is straight and downward-pointing like the stem of an object.

The *kuàng* bone (髖骨) is also written as *wān* (臗), with the phonetic component *kǒu huán fǎn*. The *Pīcāng* states that *wān* refers to the buttocks (*kāo*). The *Shuōwén* states that *wān* is above the thigh (*bǐ*). The version in the *Lùn-wén* writes it as *kuān* (寬), which is not the correct form.

The *liáo* bone (髎骨) has the phonetic component *lì yáo fǎn*. The *Zílín* identifies this as the eight *liáo* bones. The *Tōngsùwén* states that the bones of the buttocks are called the eight *liáo*. The version in the *Lùn-wén* writes it as *liáo* (膫), referring to fat and grease; *liáo* is not used in this sense here.

Regarding the five grains, according to the *Monthly Ordinances* (*Yueling*) of the *Book of Rites*, the Son of Heaven eats wheat in spring. Zheng Xuan says: "Wheat has a husk and shell, which belongs to Wood. In summer, he eats beans; "beans have a firm and complete husk and shell, which belongs to Water. In late summer, he eats millet, the chief of the five grains; "it belongs to Earth, as Earth is in the center. In autumn, he eats hemp; "its fruit has veins and patterns, which belongs to Metal. In winter, he eats broomcorn millet; "its awns spread out and disperse, which belongs to Fire. He eats these in accordance with the seasons to bring peace to his nature.
9. Fascicle Nine. "Jí bǐ" (極鄙): "bǐ" (鄙) means base or evil. According to the *Guǎngyǐ*, "bǐ" means shame or humiliation. "Suǒ bǐn" (所稟): "bǐn" (稟) is read as *bǔ jǐn* (補錦).
According to the *Shuōwén*, "bǐn" means a bestowed gift; according to the *Guǎngyǐ*, "bǐn" means to grant or bestow.

*Dī* (隄) is an archaic form identical to *dū* (䧑), pronounced *dú xī* (with the second character read as *tú láng*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "a dike" (*dīyáng*). The *Erya* states, "A dike is called a *liáng* (bridge)," and Li Xun explains it as "a flood control embankment" or "a barrier. In the Han pronunciation, there was no distinction between *dī* and *wéi*. Wei Zhao explained it as "an enclosure formed by piling up earth."

Volume Ten, Chapter Ten: The *Kulinda Aviddhakṣa-kalpa-sūtra* (also titled the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*). "Kulinda" is a corruption of the Sanskrit term; some versions render it as "Julun," "Julun," or "Julin. This is translated as "The First to Understand the Dharma at the Original Limit (*mūlānta*). In this sūtra, the Venerable Aviddhakṣa is this very person. The *Lalitavistara-sūtra* states that "Kulinda" means "one who understands the original limit. "Aviddha" means "already known"; in correct terminology, it means "thoroughly understood. "Kulinda" is also a clan name; it is a corruption of "Kauṇḍinya. The *Madhyamāgama-bhūta-utpatti-sūtra* states that among the first five [disciples], the first was named Kulinda, the second Pūrṇa, the third Vatsīputra, the fourth Daśabalakāśyapa, and the fifth Mānamkula.

"Yángtóng" (洋銅) is pronounced with the "liáng" (良) rhyme; it refers to boiling until it melts and dissolves, flowing and surging (*yángyáng*). According to the *Sāncuāng*, "yáng" means great water; according to the *Ěrǐchí*, it means "overflowing" (*yángyì*). It takes its meaning from this sense of overflowing and abundance.

The *ju* (拒) [a type of tripod stand] is the opposite of this; it is an externalist vessel, round like a gourd, with three legs joined together to lift the vessel. In various sutras, it is sometimes called the "three-pronged upright *ju*" or the "trident upright *ju*"; both refer to the same thing.

11. Volume Eleven. "Jin" (Famine). The ancient character is the same as 𩚮 (fǎn). The first character is read as *fán* (凡), and the second as *qí zhèn* (奇鎭). According to the *Erlü* (爾疋): "When grain does not ripen, it is called *jī* (famine); when vegetables do not ripen, it is called *jìn* (scarcity). Li Xun’s commentary states: "All edible greens that fail to ripen are called *jìn*. Furthermore, the *Guliang Zhuan* of the *Chunqiu* says: "When two grains do not reach a full harvest, it is called *jī*; when three grains do not reach a full harvest, it is called *jìn*; when five grains do not reach a full harvest, it is called *dà jī* (great famine). "Shēng" (升) means to ascend; it refers to the [grain] reaching maturity.

Harītakī is called "Heavenly Holder" (Tianzhu) here; this fruit serves as medicine with extremely versatile efficacy, penetrating all ailments just as ginseng,石斛 (dùshí), and other such herbs do in this land.

In the *Zuǎnjí Sāncāng*, it is written that "zuǎn" (撰) has the phonetic component *tóng* with the auxiliary rhyme *miǎn*. In the *Guǎngyá*, it states that "zuǎn" means "to determine" (*dìng*) or "to narrate" (*shù*). The pronunciation of "shēn" (申) is *shì* with the auxiliary rhyme *yì*. "Shù" (述) refers to explaining its meanings and principles. In the *Ěrǔpǐ*, it says "shù" means "to cultivate" (*xiū*) or "to follow in practice" (*xúnxíng*).

Lin: The eighteen treatises on the right, totaling one hundred and thirteen fascicles, share the same phonetic notes as this fascicle.

*Amṛtarasa-abhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle 1, Upper Volume. Compiled by Xuanying. "Lǔ" (魯) is an ancient character for "huān" (歡); its pronunciation is read as "guān" (官). This should instead be written as "là" (臘), pronounced with the "hé" (盍) rhyme.

The character *qiao* (𡨥) is pronounced with the *pian* rhyme-group and the *hou* final. The *Shangshu* commentary on "Robbers, Thieves, and Villains" (*Jieze Jiangui*) by Fan Ning’s *Jijie* states that it refers to those who attack and plunder in groups; here we adopt its meaning. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "sudden violence," while the *Guangya* defines it as "plundering. The character is composed of the radicals *wan* (complete) and *zhi* (branch). The pronunciation of *piao* (剽) is with the *pi* rhyme-group and the *miao* final.
*Zhì* (忮) is pronounced with the *shǒu*, *yǔ*, *shì*, *jǐ*, and *zhì* (two tones) finals;

according to the character, it means "to harm. Volume 2, Part 2. Regarding the *Suixiang lun* (Treatise on Characteristics and Sub-characteristics): "Characteristics" (*xiāng*) and "sub-characteristics" (*suixiāng*) refer to the production of *zhā* (樝). It is pronounced with the *zè* and *jiā* (two tones) finals. It is a type of *míngmíng* (榠𣛼), resembling an *ūbó* (烏勃) in shape and about the size of a bowl; its taste is astringent and sour, so it should not be eaten in excess. The text of the treatise writes this as *chá* (査), which is incorrect.
*Xiù* (漱糗): The first character is pronounced *chǒu* (搜皺反) and the second *jiǔ* (丘久反). Nowadays in Jiangnan, when pine nuts (*línqīn*) ripen and shatter into pieces, they are called *xiù*. *Ān* (三辢):

The *Zìyuàn* (Character Garden) writes this as *qiū* (萩), with the same pronunciation as *lúgě* (蘆葛反). The *Tōngsùwén* (Tong-su-wen) states that "extreme pungency" is called *ān*. In Jiangnan it is called *ān*, while in the Central Kingdom it is called *xīn* (辛). The *Lùnwén* (Discourse on Writing) calls it *cì* (刺), meaning "contrary and perverse. However, *cì* is not the correct orthography for this term.

The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (The Treatise Compiled by the Venerable Vasumitra), Fascicle One. Fascicle One of the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, compiled by Xuanying. "Vasumitra" (*Moyu*—the *yu* is pronounced with the *zhu* rhyme) is a personal name. Etymologically, it is derived from the transformation of the character *yu*.
"Chéng" (敕行反) means "to stare straight ahead," according to the *Cāngjiépiān*. "Yì" (於冀反) means "excellent and beautiful," according to the *Ěrpǐ*;
this character is composed of "yī" (壹) as the semantic component and "zì" (恣) as the phonetic component. The version in the *Lùnwén* is written as "shǎi" (󳃭), which has been a long-standing error.
*Bá* (pronounced *chéng* with the rhyme *wén* and *méng* reversed) refers to the nock of an arrow.

*Guǎ* (pronounced *gǔ* and *huó* reversed) is explained in the *Shìmíng* as "advancing" (*jiàn-jìn*). Its base is called the *zú* (foot), its shaft is called the *gàn* (body/stem), and its tip is called the *huà* (meeting point); it is so named because it meets with the bowstring. On either side of the *huà* is the *chā* (fork), which is shaped like a fork.
*Wu* (with the first tone, reversed by *hu*) refers to a large body of water called *huáng* and a small one called *wū*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *wū* means turbid water that does not flow.

Regarding *ménkùn* (also written as *guǎn*), it is the same character with the phonetic *kǔběn*. In the *Liji* (Book of Rites), "External words do not enter the *kùn*," where the commentary states: "*Kùn* refers to the threshold of the door."

*Yá-pào* (the "páo" being pronounced as *xiàng*): according to the *Shuowen*, this refers to a hot vapor arising on the face; here we adopt that meaning. The version in the *Lunwen* (Treatise) uses the character for *báo* (hail), which is incorrect.

*Shé-huì*: in ancient texts, these appear as two forms, *chóng* and *huì*, both pronounced as *guǐ*. It is a venomous insect. The *Hanfeizi* states: "There is an insect called *huǐ*; it has one body with two mouths, and they compete for food, biting and chasing one another until they kill each other."

*Dāna* (檀) is also called *dakṣiṇā* (達嚫, pronounced with the second tone on the final syllable), which here means the dharma of giving material wealth and giving in return; it is named *dakṣiṇā*. Furthermore, according to the *Xiyu ji* (Record of the Western Regions), the correct term is *dakṣiṇā*, or sometimes *dakṣiṇī*; it is so called because one receives what others give with the right hand, thereby generating merit, and thus establishes oneself through it.

2. Second Fascicle. 3. Third Fascicle. Regarding the archaic form of *menxu* (門閾), it is written as *qi* (𨵨) with the phonetic *xū* (吁) and *yù* (域) as the radical; it is also pronounced *yù*. According to the *Erlü* (爾疋), *qí* (柣) is called *yǔ* (閾). Guo Pu states that it refers to the threshold of a door. *Qí* (柣) is pronounced *qiánjié* (千結).

"Quèrán" (確然) is also written as "quèháo" (碻塙); both forms are pronounced with the mouth-corner [initial] and the *fǎn* (反) [final]. In the *Book of Changes* (*Zhouyī*), it says: "Now, Qian is quèrán and yì. Han Kangbo said: "Quèrán is the appearance of firmness. In the *Discourse on Literature*, it is written as "kuò" (搉), which is not the correct form.
In the past, "nu" (曩) and "lang" (朗) are phonetic transcriptions of the Sanskrit word *nā*, meaning "long ago" (*nā-pūrvam*). It refers to times long past, ancient and remote antiquity.

Regarding "zao" (澡), it is pronounced as *gong* with the *huǎn* rhyme; the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "washing the hands. However, in the context of all things related to wine, the term "guàn" (盥) is used; this does not refer merely to the hand.

2. Lower Fascicle, Treatise, Fascicle Lower. *Ā* (𧙃), *I* (贀), *U* (隖). [The first character] *ā* has the phonetic value of *ā-kě*; the next, *ī*, has the phonetic value of *yǐ-yǐ*; and the last, *ū*, has the phonetic value of *wū-gǔ*. These three characters are all transcriptions of Sanskrit sounds. In the text of the treatise, the characters *āi* (哀) and *yi* (壹) are scribal errors; furthermore, one character *ū* has been omitted. The intent of the treatise is to explain the three bodies (*trikāya*), the body of names (*nāmakāya*), the body of phrases (*padakāya*), and the body of syllables (*vyañjanakāya*). These three are distinct, just as the three characters *ā*, *ī*, and *ū* are distinct. For example, the Heavenly King Maheśvara has three eyes on his face; the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also clarifies this meaning in full. Although their essence is one, their functions are different; if even one is missing, they cannot together constitute a single meaning, and thus they are called the "three aggregates of the body" (*triskandhakāya*).

"Jie" (𢛡) is a phonetic transcription representing the appearance of being distressed; it refers to a physical state resembling that of death, and thus serves as its name.

The *Guǒzhào* establishes that the characters *fū* (枹) and *fú* (桴) are homophonous, both pronounced *fújīu*. They share the same radical and refer to the mallet used for a drum; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *fū* (枹) is the handle for striking a drum.

6. Fascicle Six. "Shichu" (桎梏): The first character is pronounced with the *yi* rhyme; the second is pronounced as *gulu*. That which is on the hand is called *zhì* (桎), and that which is on the foot is called *gù* (梏); these refer to the wooden cangue and fetters.

7. The seventh fascicle. Regarding the *jīvañjīvaka* (the "living-together" bird; the character *zhú* [bamboo] is pronounced *guā* [scratch] as a gloss): the commentary states that it is now like a pigeon in size, or some say it is like a quail (*quán*) and resembles a female pheasant. It has mouse-like feet, lacks a hind claw, and has a forked tail. It is a bird of a fierce and urgent nature that flies in flocks. It originates from the desert lands of the north. Its flesh is delicious, and it is commonly called the "Tujue (*tújué*) sparrow. It is born among the *hǎo* (mugwort) and vegetables. The pronunciation of *hǎn* (fierce/urgent) is *hū làn*.

8. Fascicle Eight. [The character for "xiān" (先) is not pronounced here. 9. Fascicle Nine. *Shèlú* (舍廬): *Lú* is pronounced with the initial *lì* and the final *jū*. It refers to a separate dwelling or a place where one stays temporarily. During the time of the Yellow Emperor, dwellings (*lú*) were constructed to avoid the cold and heat; these were abandoned during the spring and autumn, and inhabited during the winter and summer.

"Ruzhi" (入支) [pronounced with the "yi" rhyme of "ji"] refers to the water-pitcher of these non-Buddhist outsiders. It is round like a gourd and lacks feet; three staffs are crossed to support and lift the pitcher. In various sutras, it is sometimes called a "triple-pronged stand" (*sanqi lilu*) or a "triple-forked stand" (*sancha lilu*); both refer to this. The treatise text writes it as "duan" (鈘), which is incorrect.

"Golden Spear" (Jinqiang) refers to a thousand sheep; the *Commentary on the Cangjiepian* explains it as follows: "A wooden object with both ends sharpened is called a spear (*qiang*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines "spear" (*qiang*) as "to thrust. The version in the *Lunwen* (Discourse on Literature) uses "jingling" (*qiang*), which is not the correct form.

*Xiǎo* (狗齩) is also written as *xiǎo* (䶧), with the same phonetic transcription *wǔ jiǎo*. This is the pronunciation used in the Guānzhōng region. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "a swirling abyss. Below, it is also written as *fù* (復) or *xī* (垘); these three forms share the same phonetic transcription *fú fú*. *Xī* means "deep," and it also refers to "whirling water."

The character *zāi* (栽) is pronounced *cái* (才反). It is an ancient variant of *mù* (木). There are three forms: *mù*, *fǎi* (㮆), and *zāi* (栽); the modern form is *zhí* (植), which is the same as *wù* (五) and *gē* (割) combined. According to the *Erya*, *fǎi* means "remnant" (*yú*) and "to carry" (*zài*). This refers to the fact that the remnants of a tree grow back as new shoots or saplings.
11. Fascicle Eleven. Regarding *hūnxīn* (葷辛): according to the *Cāngjié piān*, *hūnxīn* refers to pungent vegetables; generally, any substance that has a pungent odor is called *hūn*.

12. Fascicle Twelve. The ancient texts use the characters *qú* (孤) and *xīn* (煢) as two forms with the same meaning, both pronounced *qú* (with the rhyme *yíng*). One who has no father is called *gū* (孤); one who has no son is called *dú* (獨); one who has no brothers is called *xīn* (煢), which means "single" (*shàn*). To be *xīnxīn* (煢煢) means to have no one to rely upon. The character is composed of *xùn* (卂) and a simplified form of *yíng* (營) as its phonetic component; *xùn* is pronounced *suīrùn* (with the rhyme *ruì*). *Note: The character 卂 (xùn) is a rare variant of 迅 (xùn), meaning "swift," and is here used as a phonetic element.*

The character for "dying from heat-stroke" (暍) is also written as 㷉 or 㷊; these two forms share the same pronunciation as *xie* (歇). According to the *Zilin*, it means being injured by heat; that is, being distressed and confused by the heat to the point of wishing for death. Furthermore, when red or purple [complexions] lose their luster due to wind, this is called *huise* (失色), and it is from this that the term for dying from heat-stroke (*yehuo*) is derived.

The character *guāng* (桄) has two ancient forms, one horizontal and one vertical; today it is written as *guāng* (同), with the phonetic reading *gǔ huáng* (古黃反). "Hibernating insects" (*zhíchóng*): "chí" means to stand up; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "zhí" means to hide away. Animals with short fur, such as bears and brown bears, also hibernate.
Volume Seventeen, Part One. "Kǎojiǎn" (Examination/Investigation): "kǎo" is pronounced like *kǔlǎo* (old); it refers to a thorough inquiry or an interrogation.

"To dry" (*xī*)—also written as *xī* with the same pronunciation (*xūyī*)—is defined in the *Zílín* as "to become dry. According to the *Fāngyán*, it means "to expose to the sun. In the regions between Beiyān and Hǎidài, they call exposing [something] to the sun "drying" (*xī*).

The character 剗 (also written as 鏟) shares the same pronunciation as 初眼反 (*chū yǎn fǎn*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to flat iron. The *Tongsu Wen* states that "to scrape a board" is called 剗; it is a square-edged tool provided with a handle.

Regarding the character for "hatching eggs" (抱卵), its forms are written as 菢 or 包, both sharing the pronunciation 蒲󰂛反 (*pú bì fǎn*). The *Tongsu Wen* notes that when a hen incubates her eggs, the people of Beiyān call this 菖 (*bào*), while those of Jiangdong call it 蓲 (*yāngfù fǎn*). In these terms, 伏 is pronounced as 輔又反 (*fǔ yòu fǎn*).

*Ṭ*: This character is also written as *kǔ* (same pronunciation as "mouth-corner" [kǔ], with the Wu and Kuaiji dialectal pronunciation *kù*). It refers to the hard shell outside an egg; when it is still within the egg, it is called *ṭ*.
