*Daodi jing* (Stages of the Path Sutra), one fascicle, compiled by the śramaṇa Huilin. Regarding the character "zé" (笮) in the title *Zegganlu shang* (Pressing the Ambrosia Above): the character used in the text is erroneously written; it is suspected to be an archaic form of the character "tiān" (天). I request that those who are wise examine this carefully. The reading "zé" (to press/squeeze) makes no sense here.

The character *piào* (in the phrase *piàolè*) is pronounced with the initial *pǐ* and the final *miào*. The *Fāngyán* states that *piào* means "light. In the regions of Jing and Chu, what is light is called *piào*. The text erroneously writes this as the character *biāo* (from the radical for "person" and "music"). The archaic form of *piào* is written as *shèn* (from "person," "brain," and "fire"). Failing to recognize this, scribes instead wrote it with the radical *piào*, which is a grave error. The *Shuowén* defines *piào* as "light," composed of "person" and the phonetic "piào. In modern vernacular usage, the "fire" radical has been changed to "small."

"Kǎo (不可擭): The phonetic gloss for 'wù' is 'guō'. The commentary states that it means to grasp or seize with the hand; it is composed of the radical 'hand' (手) and the phonetic 'luò'. It is also acceptable for the scriptural text to use 'luò' alone. 'Huán' (雈) has the phonetic value of 'huán'; it is composed of the radical 'you' (又), which is the archaic form of the character for 'hand'."
*Zuòmù* (啄木): The upper character is pronounced *zhuó*. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "a bird that eats"; it is formed from the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) with the phonetic element "pig" (*zhī*).

The pronunciation of "pig" (*zhī*) is *chǒulù* (反). *Měihuái* (枚䭷): The upper character is pronounced *měibēi*. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that *mèi* refers to a horse-whip. The lower character is pronounced *máo*. The *Kaosheng* says *huái* means "the long, fine hair of a horse. The *Shuowen* notes it is a word formed by both shape and sound. The pronunciation of *jùn* (駿) is *jìndōng* (反).

*Chí* (籌) in *chí-chóu* (持籌) means "to calculate"; according to the *Shuowen*, it is written with the radical 竹 and the phonetic 壽. In the sutra text, it is written as 𥯽 with the radical 奇; this is a scribal error. *Zhěn* (枕) has the pronunciation *rèn* (荏);
according to the *Shuowen*, it means "a pillow for the head while lying down"; it is written with the radical 木 and the phonetic 冘 (*yín*). It consists of the enclosure 冂 and the person 人.
Dān (pronounced like the *gān* of *gān-kǎo*): meaning to carry on one's back; it is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "zhān" (詹).

Chúhùn (pronounced *huó-kùn*): according to the *Shuowen*, this means a latrine; it is composed of the radical "mouth" (囗, the sound of which is *wéi*) and the element "pig" (豕), signifying that the pig is within it.

*Māozi* (蟇子): The *bā* (巴) is pronounced as *fǎn* (反). This refers to the water-insect known as the frog (*xiāmā*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "insect" (*chóng*) with the phonetic *mò* (莫); it is also written as *má* (蟆). *Tǎnnǜ* (袒裸):

*Tǎn* (袒) is pronounced as *shàngtáng-lǎn-fǎn* (上堂懶反), and *kǎo* (考) states it refers to the garment on the shoulders. In the *Zuozhuan*, it means "exposing the flesh. In the *Liji*, regarding "laboring without exposure," Zheng Xuan says: "On the left, one removes the garment. The *Shuowen* is composed of "dan" (*dàn*) and "flesh" (*ròu*), forming *shàn* (膻), which is also defined as being exposed. For now, we follow the *Tongsuowen*, which uses the "clothing" radical (*yī*) with the lower part pronounced *lángguǒ-fǎn* (郎果反). The *Wenzidian* explains that it is composed of "ren" (*rén*) to form *luǒ* (倮), meaning to strip off clothes and expose the body. The vulgar pronunciation is *huǎwǎ-fǎn* (華瓦反), or it may be composed of "shēn" (*shēn*) to form *nuǒ* (躶); the pronunciations are identical. These are examples of "form-phonetic" characters (*xíngshēng zì*). In the scriptures, both characters are composed of "yue" (*yuè*) and "dan" (*dàn*) to form *dǎn* (膽) and *biàn* (腂), which are not valid characters. When copying the Tripitaka, they should be corrected to the forms previously described.

"Chángzhuǎo" (長抓) [the "zhǎo" is pronounced *chuǎo*] is also written as 爪 (claw), which is a pictograph representing its form. In the scriptural text, it is written with the hand radical as 扴; this is incorrect. The pronunciation of 扴 is *jiá*, which does not accord with the meaning of the scripture.

"Xiāo" (狧) refers to the hair on the temples. The pronunciation of 狧 is *shí* with the *ěr* rhyme. It is an archaic form of the character 舐 (to lick). Next is the character 鬢 (bìn); its pronunciation is *bì* with the *chǒu* rhyme. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is the hair between the cheek and the ear; it takes the radical 髟 and the phonetic 賓. In the scripture, it is written as 䰅 with the head radical; this is an error. Below is 蕃 (fán); according to the *Wenzi Jilüe*, it means the hair of the head. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* says it is the hair upon the head; it takes the radical 髟 and the phonetic 犮. The pronunciation of 犮 is *pán* with the *mò* rhyme.

Regarding the phonetic transcription "jiān" (奸) for *guǎn* (菅): it is said that *guǎn* grass is a type of sedge; its leaves are like blades. It is composed of the radical "grass" (艸) and the phonetic "guān" (官). There is no character "luò" (蓏); the character "luò" is pronounced *lángguǒ* (郎果).

The *Zìshū* (字書) states it is "grass fruit. The *Shuowén* (說文) states: "That which grows on trees is called 'guǒ' (果), while that which grows on the ground is called 'luò' (蓏). It is composed of the radical "grass" (艸) and two melons side-by-side, with the pronunciation *yǔ* (庾).

"Fen" (芬) [pronounced *fǎn*] refers to the *máo* (茅) plant; the *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that "the *tǎn* (菼) is the *yù* (蘆) reed," and further says, "The *cuì yī* (毳衣) is like the *tǎn*. It is composed of the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) and the phonetic "fire" (*yán*), making it a compound character formed by both shape and sound. According to the *Erya*, the *tǎn* grass is greenish-white in color.

*Zhan* (咸反, xian fan): In the *Mao Shi*, it describes the appearance of mountain rocks that are steep and lofty; it is also written as *chan* (巉) or *can* (磛), all three being vulgar characters used interchangeably. Below: *ya* (銜反, xian fan). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states: "Yanyan" describes the appearance of accumulated rocks. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan* defines it as "precipitous. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "a cliff," formed from the radical "mountain" (*shan*) with the phonetic "yan" (*yan*). It may also be written with the radical "stone" (*shi*) as *ran* (礹), which is a vulgar character. In archaic script, it is written as *yan* (嵒) with the radical "three" (*pin*), used interchangeably.

The character 𢬁 (tuán) has the same meaning as 奪 (duó). Examining its phonetic component, it is derived from 支; 𢪛 (zhì) means to take by force. The correct form is 𢪛, with 兌 (duì) as its phonetic. Some commentaries state that 𢪛 means to release or to escape. In the subsequent scripture, the characters 鳥蹹挩 (niǎo tà tuō) follow this pronunciation; "tà" is pronounced tán hé fǎn.
"Entering the cage" (*jù lán*): the *Xián'ǎn* commentary on sounds states that this means "a great storehouse" or "a prison," following the radical for wood with the phonetic *jiàn*.
"Four surges" (*sì jī*) is pronounced *jiào*; according to the *Zìshū*, it refers to a rapid current of water.

Regarding the two phrases "reversed day" (*fǎn zhī*) and the subsequent scriptural text mentioning "taboo days involving blood" (*xiě jì*), "leakage" (*lòu*), "piercing" (*cì*), and so forth—these are all names for inauspicious days within the system of Yin-Yang numerology. The translators of the scriptures cited these explanations as metaphors to reveal the profound meaning of the sutra.

"Guā" (刮): In the *Tōngsùwén* (通俗文), a horizontal blade is called a *guā*. In character dictionaries, it is said that *shuà* (刷) is also a *guā*. It is composed of the radical "knife" (刀) and the phonetic component "zhì" (㕞) in abbreviated form; the pronunciation of "huò" (佸) is wánhuá (頑滑) and the pronunciation of "shuān" (栓) is shūyù (踈𤼙). [The latter] is composed of the "wood" (木) radical and "quán" (全); [it means] complete.

Regarding the character *ōu* (甌): according to the *Fāngyán*, a small basin is called an *ōu*; it is a word formed from both its shape and sound. The current scriptural text, as traditionally transmitted, uses *guó* (國) to form *yuànwèi* (爴), which must be a scribal error that has persisted for a long time. It is utterly meaningless [to use *guó* here] and should instead follow *ōu*.

*Pai-jing*: The upper character *pai* (䟊) has the phonetic reading *qú yù*; the *Kǎo Shēng* states that to run while holding something is called *pai*. The *Yùn Quán* says it means "sudden"; the *Zìshū* says it means "fearful. It refers to a courier horse or carriage.

The characters for *zhì* (䵴) and *gàn* (䵟) have the phonetic components *shèng* (亘) and *yú lǎn* (于嬾) respectively. Some say they should be written as *gàn zhì* (䵟䵴), or with the radical *pí* (皮) as *gǎn* (皯), or with the component *céng* (曾) as *zēng* (󲽳). The *Wénzì jílüè* (Textual Compendium) states that these refer to the disease of black spots on the face. The transcription *tà gàn* (咤幹) found in ancient translations of the scriptures is utterly devoid of meaning; it is likely either a scribal error by those who transcribed the texts or a result of the translator using unconventional characters. For now, I have revised them to *zhì gàn* (䵴䵟); let the wise examine this further.
"Huan" (pronounced with the "xiong" and "yuan" finals) is also suspected to be an erroneous character; moreover, it does not accord with the textual context.
"Jie" (pronounced with the "wei" and "mei" finals) refers to lying down facing outward; it is also written as "bei" (back), which has the same meaning.

"Pus and blood" (nóng xuè): the "dōng" in "nú dōng" is pronounced as in "shēng lèi," which states it refers to the blood from the bursting of carbuncles or abscesses. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "swollen blood," composed of the radical "blood" (xuè) and the phonetic "shǒng" (a simplified form of 䢉). The text here uses "guàn" (盥), which is an archaic character for this term.

*Zǎo* (上我蓋反; shàng wǒ gài fǎn). The dictionary of characters explains that it means "to stop" (*yǐ*). It is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic element "doubt" (*yí*). In current vernacular usage, it is sometimes written with the radical "stone" (*shí*) as *ài* (礙), or with the radical "mind" (*xīn*) as *qì* (𢣕); these are also acceptable. The lower character is pronounced *zāo lǎo fǎn* (遭老反). The *Commentary on the Mao Shih* (*Mao Shi Zhuan*) states: "A plant that grows by trailing in the water. Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* says: "A kind of aquatic plant with patterns. The *Han Shih* states: "Those floating are called *zǎo*; those submerged are called *pín*. Both are plants with patterns within the water, where fish and turtles hide. The *Shuowen Jiezi* omits this and does not explain it.

*Kāngkài* (忼愾): The first character is pronounced *kāng* (康朗反) and the second is *kāng* (康蓋反). The *Jixùn* (集訓) states: "Kāngkài refers to a valiant man who does not achieve his ambitions. Zheng’s commentary on the *Mao Shī* says it means "sighing deeply" (*tàixī*). The *Guǎngyá* says it means "frustration" (*màn*). It is also written as the character *kāngkǎi* (慷慨). According to the *Shuōwén*, it is a compound character formed from the semantic radical "heart" (*xīn*) with both components serving as phonetic indicators.

Regarding "si" (涎) and "ti" (洟): for the former, the *Ji xun* states it is pronounced "xiángyán" (祥延) and defines it as "the liquid of the mouth," composed of the radicals "water" (水) and "to pant" (欠). Its appearance in the scriptures as "xiàn" (羡), composed of "sheep" (羊), is incorrect. For the latter, the pronunciation is "yí" (夷); according to the *Shuowen*, it is pronounced "tiānjì" (天計), but I suspect this is not correct based on the phonetic evidence.

*Biēfēng* (䟊風): The character *biē* is pronounced with the *qú* and *yù* rhymes (as in *qǔ*). This was already explained previously; Jia Gongyan’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that it means "speed" or "quickness.

The *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of the radical "to run" (*zǒu*) and the phonetic *jù*. The text here uses the radical "grass" (*cǎo*), which is incorrect. *Nēnfēng* (鍼風): The upper character *nēn* is pronounced with the *rèn* rhyme. In vulgar usage, it is written with the radical "ten" (*shí*) as *zhēn*, or with the radical "bamboo" (*zhú*) as *zhēn*. The *Shuowen* defines it as "an implement for attaching clothing. All three forms are *xing-sheng* (phonetic-semantic) characters. According to the *Shenglèi*, it refers to "pricking with a needle. The text says "needle-wind" (*nēnfēng*); when a person is about to die, a transformation occurs and a wind arises that courses through the body like the prick of a needle, causing the person to experience various sufferings.

The character for *miè* (marrow) is read as *shāi* (柴) in the upper part and *tiān* (天) in the lower part. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it refers to the fat within the bones, composed of the radical "bone" (*gǔ*) and the abbreviated form of "follow" (*suí*) as its phonetic. Regarding the lower part, the *Yunquan* states that *miè* is the yellow fluid between the bones; it is said that when a person approaches death, the marrow transforms into this yellow fluid and flows out. This is thus a compound character formed from both semantic and phonetic components.

In the character 膝 (xī), the upper radical is 辛 (xīn) and the lower is 胘 (xiàn). In the preceding *Yinyì* (Explanations of Pronunciation and Meaning), the various glosses and interpretations are all examples of *xíngshēng* (phonetic-semantic) characters.

In 澀 (sè), the reading is *cānzhī* (參戢). According to the *Shuowén*, it means "not slippery. It is composed of the radicals 水 (water) and 四 (four). The two "stop" (止) radicals in the upper part are written inverted, while the two "stop" radicals in the lower part are written upright; this is the intended meaning of the character 澀. It is a *huìyì* (compound/associative) character. The text of the scripture uses the radical 人 (person) with three "stops," which is incorrect and does not form a valid character; it is an error in the transcription of the character 人.
The "skeleton" (gè) is transcribed as *kǒng* (with the phonetic *lín jiǔ* for *kǒng*). "To shake" (*chèzhèn*) is pronounced with the initial *chēn rě*. It is like a lamp being extinguished;

the upper character is *dēng*, or it may be written with the radical for fire as *dēng* (a vulgar form commonly used in transmission). According to the *Shuowen*, this refers to a lamp-stand (*dìng*). A *dìng* is simply a lamp; one without legs is called a *dēng*, while one with legs is called a *dìng*. Alternatively, it may be written as *dǎng* with the radical for hands (*gǒng*), or as *bàng* with the radical for tiles (*wǎ*); these are all archaic characters.

The character for "swelling" (shǒng) [is read as] zhōng with the *yǒng* rhyme; it is incorrect that the canonical text uses the character with the "bone" radical (*ㄑ*). The intended meaning of the scripture does not form a coherent semantic unit with that character;

the correct character should be "swelling" (*shǒng*), and it is likely a scribal error. For example, regarding "cooked *wūqǔ*" [read as] qū with the *jǔ* rhyme: the *Cāngjié piān* states that "to boil barley porridge is called *qǔ*"; it takes the "barley" radical (*麥*) with the departing tone. The character "barley" (*麥*) is composed of "coming" (*來*) below and "夂" (*zhǒu*, sound *suī*) above.

The five *tuǒ* (埵)—the character for "tuǒ" being pronounced as *guǒ* (果) in this context—refer to the five locations where the semen within the womb spontaneously coalesces; these are called *tuǒ*, or alternatively, "five blisters" (*wǔ bào*). The scriptural text’s use of the character for "flesh" (*ròu*) instead of "pustule" (*tuī*) is incorrect. It is properly derived from the sound of "soil-hanging-down" (*tǔ chuí*). Variants such as *duǒ* (朵) or *duò* (垛) are both archaic forms; all are correct characters, though they are not commonly used today.

The character 臏 (bǐn) [pinyin: bǐn; *pingmin* fanqie]: The *Kaozheng* says it refers to the knee bone. It is composed of the radical "flesh" (肉) with the phonetic "bin" (賓). It is also interchangeable with 𩪯 (composed of "bone" [骨]), which is likewise correct.

Regarding 著 (zhù) at the throat: the upper tone is *chánglüè* fanqie. The *Shuowen* states it is composed of "grass" (艹) and "zhe" (者); the text here uses two dots below, which is a cursive (草書) and vulgar form. The following text follows this principle; "throat" (喉) has the sound of "hóu," meaning the pharynx.
*Jing* (脛): Pronounced *ding* (定) with a retroflex final; according to the *Shuowen*, it means the shinbone (*jiaoheng*).

It is composed of the radical "flesh" (*rou*) and the phonetic "xing" (*jing*). *Wei-lei* (碨𥗬): The upper character is pronounced *wu hui* (烏賄) with a third tone; the lower character is pronounced *lei wei* (雷猥). The *Kaosheng* states that *wei-lei* refers to the appearance of a mass of bones. The character *wei* in the canonical text is written with the "ghost" (*gui*) radical, which is an error. It is also written as *lei* (礧) or *li* (𤳳); these are all archaic characters.
"Shòu fèi" (受痱): According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, this refers to a wind-related illness. The radical "nà" (疒) has the phonetic value of "nǚ è" (女戹); it is not a sound itself. "Páichè" (俳掣):
The first character is pronounced "bài mái" (敗埋) and the second is pronounced "chāng rè" (昌熱). It refers to the manifestation of a wind-related illness.

The character 䁾 (lì) is pronounced with the upper radical *mián* (苾) and the reverse rhyme *fǎn* (呂氏春秋 states it means "to be distorted" or "blind"; the *Shuowen* says it refers to eye discharge). It is a phono-semantic compound. The lower part is pronounced *lián* (結); according to the *Shuowen*, it is a semantic compound formed from 戶 (hù) and 犬 (quǎn). The text of the scripture uses 睙 (from 目), which is incorrect.

Some write this character as [a variant], yet none of the various character dictionaries contains it; judging by its meaning, it should be the character *wān* (烏桓反), meaning "to gouge out," though its derivation from the "body" radical (*shēn*) remains unclear. Others write it as *tuí* (徒雷反);

this is an error by the translators of the scriptures, for it is derived from "ghost" (*guǐ*) and "bird" (*zhuī*), which is the name of a beast and certainly not the intended meaning of the scripture. It should correctly be written with the "head" radical (*yè*) as *fán* (䫋). *Fán* refers to a disease of the lower abdomen, also called the "boiling entrails" (*yù cháng bìng*) or the "sinking downward" (*xià zhuì bìng*) ailment.
Regarding "shǐ" (尻): Xuān’s commentary states that it refers to the inner part of the buttocks (*tún*).

Regarding "chí" (𩲓): Gùopǔ’s commentary on the *Shānhǎijīng* states that "shén chǐ" (神𩲓) refers to a *chìmèi* (𩲓魅). The common pronunciation of "mèi" (魅) is *chǒulì* (丑栗), which is a phonetic corruption. The *Shuōwén* defines it as a "fierce ghost" (*lìguǐ*). In the scriptural texts, it is sometimes written as "lí" (𩲶) or "zhì" (𩲠); these are used interchangeably.

Regarding the characters *qū* (𮫫) and *yí* (󳈨): the upper phonetic of *qū* is "Shǔ" and the lower is "Qí," with an alternative pronunciation of "Qú-jì. The *Jīngyìjì* states: "The *qūyí* are a class of short, dwarfed minor ghosts and cruel, malevolent spirits."

*Meichu* (鬽魖): The first character is pronounced *mei* (with the radical *mièi*) or, according to some, from the root *mèi*. It refers to a class of ghosts; their types are numerous, including foxes, wildcats, or various other species, as well as spirits or deities, all of whom can bewitch people. The second character, *xū* (虚), has the phonetic *xū*. It refers to the *xūhào* ghost. The *Yìyuàn* states: "Wherever the *xūhào* ghost goes, it causes people to lose their wealth and property until their storehouses are emptied; thus it is called a 'depleting ghost' (*hào-guǐ*). Its form is not uniform; it is a monstrous creature."

The "upper palate" (shàng yǎ) in the mouth refers to the gums and palate. The *Shuowen Jiezi* omits this character; some books write it as 齶 with the radical "teeth. The *Jixun* states: "The 'gums and palate' (yín yǎ) is the upper part of the mouth. It is correctly written with the radical "flesh" (肉) and the phonetic component 㖾 (which has the same pronunciation as above). The character 㖾 is composed of 叩 (kòu) and 屰 (nì, meaning "contrary"). Nowadays, the vulgar form uses 子 (zǐ) to make 咢. The scriptural text uses 嚯 (huò, pronounced hū guō), which deviates from the intended meaning of the scripture; therefore, I have revised it here and do not accept the former reading.

The character *zǔ* (足) [refers to] the calf; according to the *Shuowen*, it means the lower leg (*feichang*). It is sometimes written with the radical "foot" as *chuàn* (踹) or as *chōu* (󰈷); the pronunciation is identical for all, though they differ in form. These variations arose because ancient scholars could no longer recall the correct radicals and thus composed them arbitrarily—sometimes using the "flesh" radical and sometimes the "foot" radical. Subsequent generations imitated these forms and transmitted their usage, so there is no definitive standard. Here, both versions are presented.

The character "lì" (舐) [pronounced with the second tone] is an erroneous usage. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "to take things with the tongue. It is correctly written as "shì" (舓), or alternatively as "tè" (𦧇); both are the correct radical forms. Some character dictionaries write it as "chī" (󳍗), "tā" (狧), or "huài" (咶); these are either vulgar characters or archaic characters.

*Shìtián* (嗜甜): "Shì" (嗜) is pronounced with the *shí* (時) and *lì* (利) rhymes. The Master Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states: "To find sweetness delightful without satiety. Zhèng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states: "To delight in and covet. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "desire," composed of the radical 口 (mouth) and the phonetic 耆 (*qí*). "Tián" (甜) is pronounced with the *dié* (牒) and *jiān* (兼) rhymes. The *Guǎngyá* states: "Tián means sweet. The *Shuōwén* further defines it as "beauty," composed of the radicals 甘 (sweetness) and 舌 (tongue), a compound character based on meaning. It is also written as 𩚵, both being used interchangeably.

*Jiàn* (踐): The upper radical is *qián* (錢) and the phonetic is *yǎn* (演). Zheng’s commentary on the *Mao Shi* states it is the appearance of a carriage in motion; it also means to tread upon. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *zu* (足) and the phonetic *jiān* (戔), where *jiān* is pronounced *cán* (殘). The lower part is read as *tán* (談) and *hé* (盍). Gu Yewang says it means to trample or kick. The *Guoya* says it means to tread. The *Shuowen* also defines it as treading, composed of the radical *zu* (足) and the phonetic *tā* (󱫕), where *tā* is pronounced *tà* (塔). The reading in the current scripture as *tà* (蹹) is incorrect.

"Holding a sickle" (chí lián): the lower character is pronounced jiǎn (with the variant zhàn). The *Fānyǔ* states that west of the Guān region, the tool used for cutting things is called a *lián*. The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radical "metal" (金) with "jiān" (兼) as its phonetic. The form used in the scriptures is "lái" (鐮), which is a vulgar character.

*Du*lóu (top character pronounced with the *tóng* and *lù* finals; bottom character pronounced with the *lēi* and *hóu* finals). The *Pīcāng* states it is the skull; the *Shuōwén* states it is the cranial bone. Both are compounds of the "bone" radical (*gǔ*) with a phonetic component. The scriptural text uses the character *yè* (head) as *suì* or *lèi*, which are vernacular forms; these are also acceptable in common usage, though they are not the standard orthography.

Regarding "èlù" (惡露): Wu Gùfǎn (顧野王) states that "è" (惡) means "to loathe. The *Yùpiān* (玉篇) states that "èlù" refers to leaking and being exposed without covering. This is a phono-semantic compound character; the form with the radical "person" (亻), written as "qìlù" (僫露), is a vulgar variant and not the correct orthography.

Regarding the character "yi" (依) in the phrase "yi xu shang" (依洫上): the reading in the sutra text as "single-layered robe" (單衣) is incorrect. According to the underlying meaning, it should follow the person [in the preceding context] and be read as "yi" with the phonetic "xu yu" (吁域反). The *Zhouli* states: "The *xu* (洫) is that by which water is conducted to the rivers. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Ten *li* constitute a *di* (地); a trench eight feet wide and eight feet deep is called a *xu*. It follows the radical for water and takes 'xue' (血) as its phonetic; a *xu* is also a drainage ditch (*gou*)."

The character *bìng* (病) is pronounced *chǔ jǐn fǎn*. Gù Jī’s "Eulogy on the Merits and Achievements of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn" states: "Vast and boundless is the universe; above it is chaotic and below it is turbid. According to the *Shuowen*, this character follows the radical *shì* (士) with the phonetic *cān* (參); the canonical text follows the radical *shí* (石), which is also commonly used.

*Xiūxíng Dàozhì Jīng*, Scroll One. This scroll is the same scripture as the subsequent *Xiūxíng Dàozhì*. Xuānyìng [comments]: "Scroll One" (*dìyī juǎn*). *Jiào* (較) is an archaic term; its pronunciation is the same as *gǔ xué fǎn* (古學反). It means roughly or approximately. According to the *Guǎngyá*, *jiào* means "clear" (*míng*) and also "to compare. *Xiūxíng Dàozhì Jīng*, Scroll One. This scroll is the same scripture as the subsequent *Xiūxíng Dàozhì*. Xuānyìng [comments]: "Scroll One" (*dìyī juǎn*). *Jiào* (較) is an archaic term; its pronunciation is the same as *gǔ xué fǎn* (古學反). It means roughly or approximately. According to the *Guǎngyá*, *jiào* means "clear" (*míng*) and also "to compare."
"Zàizǐ" (栽子) refers to planting or transplanting; nowadays, the term "zài" (栽) is used for planting trees, grasses, and shrubs, meaning that which can be planted as a sapling.

Biǎnquè (扁鵲), pronounced with the initial *pú* (蒲) and the final *xiǎn* (顯), was an eminent physician of antiquity whose surname was Zhèng. According to the *Hànshū*, Wei Zhao states that he was a man from Dàshān Xiǎolú, named Yuèrén, and served as a physician during the time of Marquis Huán of Wèi.

Regarding the term *cāngtóu* (蒼頭) in the *Hànshū*, Ying Shào states: "In the Qin dynasty, the common people were called *qiánqī* (黔𩠐); *qián* means black, and *qī* means head. A slave was called a *cāngtóu* (蒼頭), not because he was purely black, but to distinguish him from the common people."

*Yù* (pronounced *yù*, with the *wù* rhyme): In the *Erya*, it means "vapor" (*qì*) and also "sorrowful reflection" (*āisī*). The character below is an archaic form; both *mào* and *mào* are used today interchangeably. *Mào* (pronounced *mò xiào*): countenance; it also means "to see. It is also written as *fèng* (pronounced *mò bào*), meaning "blinded by wealth" (*xuàn fèng*). In the canonical text, it is written as *mào*, a phonetic loan for "to cover" (*fù*). The character *pǐ* is a variant.

"Zàng" (pronounced *cái* with the second tone, meaning "to accumulate," like a storehouse) refers to the five internal organs of a person: the liver, lungs, spleen, heart, and kidneys. The character used in the scriptural text is "zǎng" (*sǎng*), which is not the correct form.

*Chai* (𧮂): Pronounced *zé* with the tone of *jin*. According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, *chai* means to destroy; it also means slander. Another explanation states that to enter from the side is called *chai*. *Zhu* (𧌲):

Written in ancient forms as *zhēn* (鼅) or *zhū* (鼄), these two characters share the same pronunciation, which is *zhī* or *zhū*. This refers to the "grass spider" (*cǎo zhū*) and the "earth spider" (*tǔ zhū*). The text in the [relevant] scripture uses the character *qù* (𧑱), which is incorrect.

"Sòuhóu" (嗽喉) is also written as "suòhóu" (欶), both pronounced with the same *suǒ* and *zhòu* finals; it refers to sucking or suction. The character "shù" (數) used in the canonical text is a vulgar form.

"Dòngxiàn" (湩現) has two pronunciations: *zhùyòng* (竹用) and *dūdòng* (都洞); according to the *Tōngsúwén* (通俗文), milk is called "dòng. People in Jiangnan today also call breast milk "dòng. The character "nài" (𡣢) with the *núzuì* (奴罪) pronunciation found in the canonical text is incorrect.
In the text of the *Yinchai jing* (Silver Ash Scripture), the character for "silver" (*yin*) is erroneously written as two forms:

*yin* and *chi*. 2. Second Fascicle. "Benzou" (奔走): The ancient form was *bin* (𩦥); the modern form is *ben* (奔), both pronounced with the *bǔmén* (補門) rhyme. According to the *Erya*, it means "to run" (*bēn-zǒu*), and it also means "to hasten."
*Pánjié* (蟠結): "Thin cold" (*bóhán*). According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to coil" (*pánqū*) and also "to bend down" (*wěi*).

*Jìnxiè* (噤齘): *qǔjǐn* for the first character, *hùjiè* for the second. The *Shuōwén* states that *xiè* refers to the teeth grinding against one another. The *Fānyǔ* states that *xiè* means "anger. Guo Pu says: "It refers to the sound of *jìnxiè* (chattering the teeth)."

*Huán* (雚) is the same as *wěi* (葦); the "Mao Commentary on the Plants and Trees" (*Mao Shi Cao Mu Shu*) states that *jiā* (葭) and *tǎn* (菼) are called *wàn* (薍), and when they mature in autumn, they are called *huán*. The "Xi Xia" [section] of the *Xiaoya* says: "When the *wěi* has not yet flowered, it is then called *huán*. The pronunciation of *wàn* is *wǔ huàn* (五患).
"Fei-āo" (飛鳥): "Fū" (甫) is pronounced as "wei-fan" (韋反). It means that birds fly upward. The character in the canonical text written with the dog radical (𪇔) is an error.

3. Third Fascicle, Part Three. "Zōng" (綜): Pronounced as "zǐ-sòng-fan" (子送反). It means to practice thoroughly or to organize. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "zōng" refers to the shuttle-thread on a loom; it denotes the thread held by the mechanism that interlaces with the warp.

The *yuán* (pronounced with the "yuan" rhyme) resembles a turtle but is large; the *tuó* (pronounced with the "tuhe" rhyme) resembles a lizard and is one zhang long and scaly. The characters *wàn* and *gù* found in the canonical text are two forms that do not represent the correct characters.
"Miàn" (麵) should not be read as "biàn" (遍); it refers to something being crushed or broken, not like flour. The reading "miè" (蔑) in the scripture is an error regarding the sound.
"Pīn" (拼) is pronounced "zhíbǔgēng" (直補耕); it means to snap a string or marking-line, hence "pīn. The reading "bó" (帛) [meaning silk] in the scripture is incorrect and does not convey this meaning.

Regarding "tiěgǎng" (iron casing): in non-standard texts (*sōngsúwén*), the silk-reeling wheel is called *gǎng*. *Gǎng* means a reel; the pronunciation of *cuó* is *sāngláo* (桑勞), and the pronunciation of *chù* is *hù* (護).
Regarding *fán*: it is also written as *dàn*, both pronounced *fúyuán* (扶袁); adding the radical for fire makes it *dàn*. *Fán* also means to burn and to dry.
*Tièshǎn* (Iron Skewer): In the *Zìyuàn*, the initial rhyme is *yǎn* (眼). This refers to piercing meat with a skewer and roasting it. The pronunciation of *qiān* (籤) is *qiělián* (且廉).

4. Fourth Fascicle. *Cháo* (Mockery): To speak of ancient texts in a derisive manner; "cháo" is also written as "zhōu" (啁), which are identical. It is pronounced *zhǐjiāo* (陟交). Furthermore, according to the *Cāngjié piān*, "zhōu" (周) refers to mutual joking and teasing.

*Xiāngchēng* (相樘) is also written as *xiāngchēng* (𢾊棖) or *xiāngchēng* (󲍅); these three forms share the same pronunciation, *zhànggēng* (丈庚). It means to touch one another, and it also refers to striking a pillar.

*Bùzī* (不訾) is also written as *bùzī* (𢋀), sharing the same pronunciation, *zǐsī* (紫斯). It means to estimate or measure. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *zī* (訾) means "to think. The form used in the sutra text as *zī* (貲)—meaning wealth—is incorrect.
*Gài* (槩) is an archaic term synonymous with *gài* (杚), pronounced *gù-ài-fǎn*. According to the *Guǎngyá*, "to *gài*" means to rub or level; it refers to leveling a bushel or a measure.

*Jiǔsháo* (九韶) is an archaic term synonymous with *shìzhāo* (󲐂), pronounced *shì-zhāo-fǎn*. It is the name of the music of Shùn; "Sháo" means to continue or succeed, signifying that Shùn was able to carry on the virtue of Yao. This refers to the passage in the *Shàngshū*: "The *Xiāosháo* [music] was performed nine times."

5. Fascicle Five. "Nǔ" (擭) [the character is pronounced with the *guō* rhyme]. The *Guǎngyǎ* states it means "to hold. The *Xījīng fù* says, "nǔ zāihu hú," and the *Zǒngshì* explains that this refers to grasping or seizing. "Zāi" (獑) is pronounced "chán" (讒).

*Cheng-chui* (秤錘): *zhí* (直) and *wéi* (危) are the tones; according to the *Guǎngyá*, *chuí* (錘) is called *quán* (權), which is precisely a scale-weight. According to the *Fāngyán*, *chuí* means "heavy"; in the states of Song and Lù, it is called *chuí*. *Chī-zhū* (鴟豬):

*chī* (鴟) is pronounced *zhī* (尺脂) and the following character is *zhú* (豬) with the tone *zhì* (陟於); *chī* means to spread out or expand. This refers to a person who spreads out like an owl (*chī*) and is as large as a pig (*zhū*).

The *Bōyǎn Zuǎnwén* states: "Bó" refers to the game of Six Bós, which uses six markers and six pieces; this is called "Six Bós. "Yǎnpū" refers to the game of leaping coins, commonly known as "Shèshù" (Shooting Numbers) or, according to some, "Shèyì" (Shooting Intent).

*Lìshèng* (櫪㯕): The first character is pronounced with the *lì* radical and the *lì* rhyme (the second character is pronounced with the *sāng* radical and the *xī* rhyme). The *Tōngsùwén* states that the tools used for interrogating prisoners are called *lìshèng*. The *Zílín* says it is used to press down the fingers. *Luǎnluǎn* (臠臠):

The first character is pronounced with the *lì* radical and the *zhuǎn* rhyme; it refers to cutting meat. Large pieces are called *zì* (胾), while small pieces are called *ròuluǎn* (肉臠). The scriptural text reads *fúfú* (𦟪𦟪), which is incorrect. *Zì* (胾) is pronounced *cèshǐ*.

Regarding the "Bu-yao" (step-shaker) head ornament, its definition states that it is so called because the beads hanging from it sway as one walks. The text’s use of the character "yáo" (from the term *qióngyáo*) is incorrect.

As for "jié cǎo" (straw), the ancient pronunciation is *bā* (as in *gǔ bā fǎn*). In the *Shàngshū*, regarding the passage "Three hundred li submit straw and labor," Kǒng Àngguó says: "Jié means *gǎo* (husks/stalks); 'submitting straw and labor' means performing labor with husks."

*Hu-kou* (餬口) is also written as *hu-kou* (𩚩), both pronounced with the *hu-gu* rhyme. According to the *Fangyan*, it means "to live on handouts" (*ji-shi*). In the region between the Yangtze and Huai rivers, eating while staying in another's home is called *hu*. The *Erya* states: "*Hu* is *zhi*. Guo Pu says: "This is simply *mi* (porridge). *Zhi* is pronounced *zhi-ran*.

*Sūtra on the Stages of Cultivating the Path*, Scroll One. Revised and not abbreviated; identical to the previous edition of this same scripture. Re-edited by Huilin. 1. Scroll One: *Zhào wù* (照寤). [The character] *wù* (寤) is pronounced with the "five" (*gù*) tone. The *Mao Shi* states that *wù* means "to awaken. The text uses *wù* (寤), which is an error.

"Blind" (máng): the upper radical is "eye" (目) with the phonetic "mo" (莫, pronounced *gǐng* according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, meaning "to have no pupils"); the lower radical is "ding" (丁, pronounced *mò*). The *Mao Shi* states that "míng" (冥) means "night. The scripture uses "míng," which is a vulgar character.
*Dàjiào* (大較): "Jiāng" and "Yuè" are reversed; the *Bóyǎ* states it means "to compare. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "chariot" (*chē*) with "jiāo" as its phonetic.

*Jī* (機): "Wēi" is read as *xī* (希); the Commentary on the *Shūjīng* by Kǒng [Yáng] states that "jī" is also "wēi. Modern character dictionaries mostly do not include the "wood" radical and simply write it as *jǐ*. *Wěi* (尾): "Fēi" is read as *fēi* (非). The received text writes it as "wēi," which is incorrect; it should correctly be written as *jiàn* (㪜), and does not derive from the "person" radical.

"Qiè" (輒) is pronounced zhì yè (陟葉反). The *Hànshū* states that "qiè" means "exclusive" or "solely. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "chariot" (車) with "qie" (耴) as the phonetic component; the reading in the current text as "qiè" is incorrect. "Qie" (耴) is pronounced zhì yè (陟葉反).
"Jiāomàn" (憍慢) is pronounced jiāo qiáo (矯橋反), with the second character pronounced màn bàn (蠻瓣反). The text's writing as "jiāo" (憍) is incorrect; it is also written as "jiāo" (驕).

*Qú* (pronounced *jù*): The *Erya* states that *qú* refers to a road with access from four directions. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "walking" (*xíng*) and the phonetic element "gǔ" (*qú*).

Regarding the bird *diāo*: the *Kǎoshēng* states that the *diāo* resembles the *è* (osprey). The *Mu Tianzi Zhuan* describes it as a bird of prey; it is also written as *diāo*. The lower character is pronounced *jiù*. The *Shanhaijing* states that it is the name of a bird, also called *diāo*, though the correct form is *zhào*.

The character for *mǎo* (䭷) is pronounced "máo" when referring to a horse; it does not exist in standard dictionaries or scriptural texts, nor is it mentioned in the *Zuǎnfén*. This horse is actually the Horse-Treasure (*aśvaratna*) of a Cakravartin King. It is a deep blue-black color with long hair resembling that of a beast; its head is like that of an elephant, and because its hair is so long, it is named the "Hairy Horse" (*Mǎomǎ*).

*Chúhùn* (除溷): *Hún* is pronounced as in *huìnkùn*. The *Bóyǎ* states that it means turbid. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "huì" (*huì*). The pronunciation of *huì* is the same as above. *Zhǐbǐ* (指髀): *Pǐ* is pronounced as in *pīmǐ*.
The *Shuōwén* states it refers to the outer part of the thigh. It is also written as *bì*, composed of the radical "bone" (*gǔ*) and the phonetic "bēi" (*bēi*).

*Nǔ* (upper radical *hu*, *wǎ* rhyme; Mencius says it means "to expose the body"; also written as *luò* or *léi*). Lower character: *xiān* (rhyme *diǎn*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To have bare feet touching the ground. It is composed of the radical *zú* (foot) with *xiān* as the phonetic.

"Zhuo" (捉) and "yè" (拽)—the latter pronounced with the rhyme *yan* and *zuo* reversed—refers to the sound of dragging; the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "from the hand," with the pronunciation *yi* (勢) reversed for *yè*, and *tuō* (拕) pronounced *tuōhé* (託何) reversed.
*Shù* (𢿘) is read as *shuāngchì* (雙捉) reversed; in the scriptures it is written as *shù* (數), which is a vulgar character.

*Tuó*: pronounced *luán fǎn*. *Niè*: pronounced *ní zhé fǎn*. The *Shuowen* states that "yào" (to leap) is also "dǎo" (to tread); it is composed of the radical "foot" (*zú*) and the phonetic "niè. The text uses "niè," which is a vulgar character; its pronunciation is as above. *Táo*: pronounced *dào fǎn*. The *Shuowen* states that "dǎo" (to tread upon) means to step on; it is composed of the radical "foot" and the phonetic "yǎo," and the same applies to the following characters.

Regarding "tà" (in the rhyme *tán* and *là*), the editions of the Classics write it as "tà" (蹹), which is incorrect. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "tà" means to tread upon; it is composed of the radical "foot" (足) and the phonetic "dàn" (󱫕), where the sound of "dàn" is *tān* and *hé* (合).
Regarding "bō chè" (撥掣), the upper character is pronounced *bó* (博) and the lower character *chì* (叱); the text of the Classics writes it as "shè" (𢮓), which is incorrect.

The character for *jiǎn* (eyelashes) is pronounced with the radical for "hand" and the phonetic *qiè* (僭), reversed. The character for *tāo* (to scoop out) is pronounced with the radical for "hand" and the phonetic *dǎo* (刀), reversed; the commentary on the sounds says it means "to take deeply," or it is written as *tāo*. According to the *Shuowen*, it takes the radical for "hand" and the phonetic *yǎo* (舀); the sound of *kòu* (叩) is *kǒu* (口).

*Duó máo*: "Máo" is pronounced with the *yán* rhyme. The *Shuowen* states that it refers to the beard on the cheeks; it is formed from the radical "mustache" (*xū*) and the phonetic "máo. The form "rán" used in the sutra is also acceptable. *Gǔ*: The upper tone is *gǔ*.
Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* identifies it as "poisonous bewitchment" (*gǔ dú*). The *Shuowen* states it is composed of the radicals "insect" (*chóng*) and "vessel" (*míng*).

The character for *pí* (to skin) is pronounced with the radical *péi* (反考) and the phonetic *yún*; it means to skin as well. The scriptural text uses the character *kēng* (㓟), which is a vulgar form derived from the radical *dāo* (knife). The lower part is pronounced *bāng* (角). The *Xià xiǎopǐ* states that it means to pare or shave. The *Shuōwén* defines it as carving; it takes the radical *dāo* and the phonetic *lù*.

"Chen" (梴) is read as *zhí-lián* (直連). The *Mao Shi* states that "chen" means long wood. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "wood" (*mu*) with "yan" (*yán*) as its phonetic.

"Zhan" (顫) is read as *zhī-shàn* (之善) for the upper character and *yòu* (又) for the lower sound. The *Cangjie Pian* states that "zhan" refers to the head not being upright. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "Yan-zhan" (𤴨顫) is the ailment of shaking the head; it is composed of the radical "illness" (*nà*) with "you" (*yòu*) as its phonetic."

*Jiā*: On the *Zhuōguā* (Classified Sounds), it is said to mean "to strike with a staff"; according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "guò" (*guòshēng*). *Xiàbó*: Pronounced *jiǎngfǎn*; according to the *Kǎoshēng*, it means "to strike with a staff"; it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "fèng" (*fèngshēng*).

*Wǎo* (皰): pronounced *báo* (雹) with a *fǎn* (反) tone; the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it refers to a heat-induced blister or sore on the body. It is also written as *pào* (疱), composed of the radical "skin" (*pí*) and the phonetic "bao" (*bāo*).

*Huān* (髖): pronounced *kuò* (闊) with a *wán* (丸) tone; according to the *Guangya*, it refers to the buttocks (*kǎo*). *Tún* (臀) is pronounced *dú* (徒) with a *kūn* (昆) tone; *kǎo* (尻) is pronounced *kǎo* (考) with a *gāo* (高) tone; it is also written as *wān* (臗).

*Chuǎn* (腨): The character is pronounced with the initial *shuō* (耎) and the final *fǎn* (反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "The calf muscle (*chuǎn*) is the *bìcháng* (腓腸); it is composed of the radical 'flesh' (*ròu*) and the phonetic 'duān' (*duān*)"; it is also written as *fēi* (󰈷). The phonetic *fēi* (符非反) has a long vowel, while the sound of *cháng* (腸) is short; *duān* (耑) has the final *fǎn* (反).

"Shi-ur" (屎尿). The *Shizi* (字書) states that "shi" (屎) means excrement; its correct form is "lü" (蓾), though the sutras use "shi," which is a vulgar character. The second character, "nu-diao" (奴弔), the *Shuowen* explains as urine; it is also written as "xian" (𡲘), while the vulgar form "niao" (尿) is incorrect.

*Zhen* (pronounced *ju*, with the rhyme of *lin*): The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "a needle is for sewing and piercing; it is composed of the radical 'metal' (*jin*) and the phonetic 'xian' (*xian*). It is also written as *zhen* (with the rhyme of *sui*). The *Zishu* states that it refers to the "beak of a bird"; it is also written as *zui*. The form used in the sutra, *zhong*, is a vulgar character.

*Tuì* (spittle/saliva). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Spittle is the liquid of the mouth; it is composed of the radical 口 and the phonetic 垂. It is also written as *tuò*. The character below is *xiàn* (pronounced with the second tone). The *Kaosheng* states: "*Sì* is the moisture in the mouth. The *Shuowen* states it is composed of the radical 水 and the phonetic 欠. The form used in the scriptures is *xián*, which is a vulgar character.

2. Second Fascicle. *Pīlì* (霹靂): the first character is pronounced with the initial *pǐ* and the final *mò* (反); the second character is pronounced with the initial *líng* and the final *dī* (反). The *Erya* states that *pīlì* refers to the roar of thunder. The version in the Sutra uses *pílè* (礕礰), which is a vulgar character.
*Huàjiù* (化捄): *Jǔyú Fǎnyǎn* (矩愚反) states that *jiù* means "method" (*fǎ*). According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "qiú" (*qiú shēng*).
*Pánjié* (蟠結): *Bóyǎ* (博雅) states that *pán* means "to coil" (*qū*). According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "insect" (*chóng*) and the phonetic "fān" (*fān shēng*).

*Chòu* (pronounced with the *zōu* rhyme and the *kǎo* tone): the *Shuowén* states it means "wrinkled skin gathered together. It is composed of the radical "skin" (*pí*) and the phonetic "chū. The text uses *zhì* (𩑠), which is a vulgar character.
*Jìn* (pronounced with the *jì* rhyme and the *xì* tone): the *Chu cí* states it means "closing the mouth. The *Shuowén* states it is composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic "jìn."

"Go" (鵝) and "wu" (鶩). [The character for] "go" has the phonetic component *wo* (我) and the radical *mu* (木). Wang Yewang states that the form of the goose resembles that of a wild goose (*yan*) and is what is raised by people. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the bird radical with the phonetic *wo*. [The character for] "wu" has the phonetic component *wu* (敄). The *Erya* states that "wu" is another name for the duck (*ya*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the bird radical with the phonetic *wu*.

"Guān" (雚) and "wěi" (葦): "hú" (胡) is pronounced *luán* (鸞). Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that guān is also wěi. In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is written with the radical for grass (*cǎo*) and the phonetic *guān*; its pronunciation is the same as above. [The version in] the Classics uses "guān," which is incorrect. "Wěi" (葦): "wéi" (韋) is pronounced *guǐ* (鬼). In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "lú" (蘆); it takes the radical for grass and the phonetic *wéi*.
3. Third Fascicle. "Wēiyí" (逶迤): the first character is read as *wěi* (委) with the fanqie *wěi* (為); the second is read as *tuóhé* (徒河). "Bēnzǒu" (犇走):
the first character is read as *běn* (本) with the fanqie *běn* (門). The *Erya* states: "Bēn (犇) is also 'to run'. It is also written as "bēn" (奔). The *Hanshu* uses the character "bēn" (犇).
"Lu-biao" (鹿猋)—the second character is pronounced *bei* (卑) with the tone *yáo* (遙). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "biao" (*biāo*) means the appearance of a pack of dogs running together.
"Mao jue" (貌絕)—the first character is pronounced *mào* (皃); it refers to the appearance of one whose mental faculties have ceased, meaning they are dazed and unconscious, having no awareness.

*Zuànchuān* (鑽穿): The *Zhuanzi* reverses [the order] of this; *Mencius* says "to drill through" (*zuàn*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical 金 (metal) with the phonetic 贊 (zàn); the lower character is pronounced as *chuān*. *Lüēbǎng* (撾搒):

The upper character is pronounced as *zhuóguā*; according to the *Shuowen*, "to strike with a staff. It is also written as 𥬲. The lower character is pronounced as *báigēng*; according to the *Shuowen*, "to flog or whip," composed of the radical 手 (hand) with the phonetic 旁 (páng).

*Guǎn* (官): *wǎn* (椀) as a variant, or *gǔ huàn* (古奐) as another reading. Gu Yewang states: "In general, any object used for washing is called *guǎn*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "*Guǎn* means to wash one's hands; it is composed of the radicals for vessel (*míng*), mortar (*jiù*), and water (*shuǐ*). The version in the *Classic of Waterways* (*Shuijing*) uses *guàn* (灌), which is incorrect.

Regarding *pīngshēn* (拼身): the commentary on the phonetics states that *pīng* means "to stretch" (*pīngtàn*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "hand" and the phonetic "yǎo. The form used in the sutras is a vulgar character. As for *zuò* (笮):
according to the *Yunquán*, *zuò* belongs to the category of "pressing" (*zè*). It is composed of the radical "bamboo" and the phonetic "zhà"; *zè* is pronounced as *chōuzhōu*.

*Pìní* (睥睨): The first character is pronounced *pǐ* (匹計反) and the second is *ní* (倪計反). The *Shuowen* states that *pìní* means the appearance of looking askance; both characters follow the radical "eye" (*mù*) with the phonetic component *bǐ* (*ér*).

*Zhé* (磔): Pronounced *zhé* (陟格反). The *Kaosheng* states that *zhé* means to stretch out. The *Boyaya* states that to kill and then flay the corpse is called *zhé*. The *Shuowen* writes it with the radical "stone" (*shí*) and the phonetic component *jié* (*jiē*). The version in the sutra uses the character *jié* (桀), which is a vulgar form; its pronunciation is *jié* (竭).

"Zhēn" (鍼) is pronounced *zhǐ* (之林反), though it is sometimes written as "zhēn" (針); the character below is pronounced *suǐ* (髓反), and is also written as "zǐ" (觜). The version in the *Jīng* (經) is written as "yì" (𭉨), which is not the correct character.

"Tiěchǎn" (鐵鏟) is pronounced *tiānjié* (天結反) for the first character and *chàyǎn* (察眼反) for the second; the *Bóyǎ* (博雅) states that "chǎn" means to shave or pare, and it is also written as "chǎn" (剗). According to the *Shuōwén* (說文), it is composed of the radical "metal" (金) with the phonetic "chǎn" (產).
Regarding "chāo" (鈔), according to the *Chuōfān* (楚交反) glossary, it means to take property by force;

it is also written as "chāo" (抄). Volume Four, Part Four: Regarding "cuò" (剉), the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that it means to chop finely. The *Shuōwén* (說文) indicates it is composed of the radical "knife" (刀) with the phonetic "zuò" (坐). The text's reading of "cuì" (󳎗) is incorrect. Regarding "zhǎn" (斬), the *Kǎoshēng* states it means to hack or chop. The *Shuōwén* states it means to cut through, composed of the radical "axe" (斤) with the phonetic "chē" (車).

*Qíguī*: The upper character, *qí*, is pronounced with the initial *jù* and the final *yí*. The *Běicāng* states: "Qí refers to rare and beautiful treasures; it is also *wěi* (extraordinary). The *Shuōwén* indicates that it is composed of the radical *wáng* (jade) with *qí* as its phonetic. The lower character, *guī*, is pronounced with the initial *gǔ* and the final *huí*. Dictionaries state: "Guī refers to stone that ranks below jade. The *Běicāng* says: "It is a rare treasure. The *Shuōwén* says: "Qí refers to that which is round and fine," composed of the radical *yù* (jade) with *guì* as its phonetic. The text here uses *guī*, which is a vulgar form; it is also written as *guī* or *guāi*.

*Yú'ài* (愚騃): The first character is pronounced with the *yǔ* rhyme-group (jù fǎn) and the second with the *yái* rhyme-group (kuāi fǎn). According to the *Cāngjié piān*, it means "extremely foolish. The *Jíxùn* states it means "dull-witted.

*Kàngyù* (抗禦): "Yù" is pronounced *yǔ* with a retroflex initial; it means to ward off. The *Shijing* says, "I say there is one who wards off insults," and the *Zhuan* states that martial ministers who break the enemy's momentum are said to "ward off insults.

*Guǐ* (軌): There are two ancient forms, *gǔi* and *qí*. It is pronounced *jūměi*. According to the *Guǎyá*, it means tracks; according to the *Shuowén*, it means the ruts of a carriage wheel; according to the *Guoyu*, it means law or standard.

2. Second Fascicle. *Zhìwǎn* (also written as *kè*, with the same pronunciation as *zé*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *kè* means "to grasp. To hold it so that it fills the hands is called *zhì*. The *Guoya* states that *zhì* means "to hold."
*Shùn* (pronounced *lún*) means "to twitch"; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to the eyes flickering. The reading *xùn* found in the scriptural text is not the correct form.

"Fúyù" (怫鬱) is pronounced as *fù wù* (父勿). "Fúyù" means the mind is unsettled; it also refers to the spirit being unable to relax or find ease.

It refers to digging into the earth to create a chamber for storing the five grains. *Mahāyāna-caryā-bodhisattva-mukha-sarva-sūtra-arthasaṃgraha* (大乘修行菩薩行門諸經要集), three fascicles. 5. Fifth Fascicle. *Makṣikā* (the character is pronounced with the *jué* rhyme, meaning "fly").

6. The sixth fascicle. "Pure" (*chui*) is also written as "sui" (same pronunciation as *si lei*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "pure" means not mixed; it also means fine. The *Yi* says, "pure" refers to refined essence. It is also said that being uniform and harmonious is called "pure."

The *Erya* states that the large are called *bífú* (蚍蜉) and the small are called *yǐ* (蟻); sometimes written as *yì* (螘) or *qí* (𧕶). "Zhoumei" (frowning): "Shangce" (upper side) is pronounced *shòu* (反) with the rhyme *quán* (詮); it refers to the gathering of facial skin. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of "pi" (皮) and "chu" (芻); "chu" is pronounced *chǔ jū* (楚拘反), having the sound of "chu" (芻). "Xià" (下) is pronounced *měi bēi* (美悲反); according to the *Shuowen*, it refers to the hair above the eyes, composed of "mu" (目) and the shape of "mei" (眉), with the upper part representing the lines of the forehead.

*Mianlài* (眄睞): The first character, *miè*, has the variant reading *biàn*. According to the *Fāngyán*, in the regions west of Guān, specifically between Qín and Jìn, this is called *mǎi*. The *Shuōwén* states it means "to look askance," or alternatively, "the eyes are partially closed. It is composed of the radical 目 with the phonetic 丐 (*gài*; the pronunciation is the same as above, *lǎidài*). The *Guǎngyá* states it means "to gaze. The *Shuōwén* further states it refers to a child's gaze being not upright; it is composed of the radical 目 with the phonetic 來 (*lái*).

*Gouli* (垢圿): The lower character is read as *jian* (姦) with the *bao* (拜) radical. The *Kaosheng* states that *li* (圿) also means "dirt"; in both ancient and modern times, the meaning is the same. It is composed of the "earth" (*tu*) radical and the phonetic *jie* (介).

*Cū* (蹴): The upper character is read as *qiu* (秋) and *yu* (育). The *Cangjie pian* states that *cū* means "to tread upon. He’s commentary on the *Gongyang zhuan* says: "To kick upward with the foot is called *cū*. The definition in the *Shuowen jiezi* is the same. It is composed of the "foot" (*zu*) radical and the phonetic *jiu* (就). *Zhe* (陟): The lower character is read as *ju* (俱). The *Shuowen jiezi* states it refers to the root of a tree. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means "to drive or gallop," composed of the radical "gè" (革) with the phonetic "biàn" (便), the latter having the pronunciation "chǒuzhī" (丑之). Regarding "tái" (笞) in the *Hànshū Yìnyì* (漢書音義): "tái" means "to strike. According to the *Shuōwén*, it also means "to strike," composed of the radical "zhú" (竹) with the phonetic "tái" (台).

The preceding character [in the title] is pronounced as *lónggù* (籠穀).

"Yan-jie" (眼䀹): The *Kao* dictionary states this refers to the eyelashes on the upper eyelid (*jǐn*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* derives it from "eye" (*mù*) and the phonetic "jia" (*jiá*). It is also written as "jie" (睫). The form "mo" (𥇒), derived from "qie" (妾), is a vulgar character.

*Kèlì* (剋勵): "Lǜ" is pronounced with the *zhì* (制) rhyme. Yù Yěwáng states that *lì* (勵) means "to exert" (*miǎn*). Dù's commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states that *lì* also means "to encourage. *Shìliú* (駛流): In the *Cāngjiépiān*, "shì" means "swift. According to the analysis of sounds (*kǎoshēng*), it also refers to the swift gallop of a horse, and by extension, speed. The meaning of the character has remained consistent across ancient and modern times. It is composed of "horse" (馬) as the radical and "shǐ" (史) as the phonetic component.

*Jùn-zú* (駿足): Pronounced *zūn-xùn* (遵迅) according to the *Erya*, where *jùn* means "swift. Guo’s commentary states: "Jùn" is like "rapid. "Qi-yan" (choking): "xian-jie" (smoke-knots) refers to the hair on the back of the neck standing up. The *Shi-jing* Commentary states that "yan" means one cannot breathe. "Shen-lou" (hunchbacked): Pronounced "li-ju-fan. He’s commentary on the *Gongyang Zhuan* says "lou" means sickness. The *Guoya* says it means "qu" (crooked). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "kwang" (weak/crippled), composed of the radical "ren" (person) and the phonetic "lou."

*Zhì'ài* (躓礙): "Zhì" is pronounced *zhì* (知膩反) according to Gu Yewang; it means to stumble or fall. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "zhì" means to tumble. The *Shuowen* says it is composed of the radical "foot" (*zú*) and the phonetic "zhì" (*zhì*).

*Shīwēi* (失韋): "Wēi" is pronounced *páimài* (排賣反). The *Cangjie* says it is a leather bag. The *Kaosheng* says it is a tool for blowing fire. The character in the scripture is written as this *pēn* (㰆), which is an archaic form.

*Foyi jing* (Sūtra of the Buddha-Physician), one fascicle. *Xuan Ying*: *Bu zī* (not *zī*) is also written as *zhǐ*; they are homophonous, with the pronunciation *zī yí*. It means to measure; according to the *Shuowen*, it means to think of or weigh according to one’s intent.

The character for *chì gǒu* (fierce dog) is written as *chì* or *zhǐ*—these two forms—and is also written as *jì*, all being identical. The pronunciation is *chāng zhì* or *jū shì*. It refers to a mad dog.

The *Zan jing* (Miscellaneous Difficulties Scripture), one fascicle, compiled by Huilin. Regarding the character for "receiving" (*shòu*), it is pronounced with the initial *biàn* (劣反) and the final *kǎo* (考); according to the *Shēng yùn*, it is also written with the radical "bamboo" (*zhú*) as *bì* (䇷). *Tang* (樘): Pronounced *zhái* (宅) with the final *jǐng* (莖) reversed. According to the *Guǎyá*, *táng-jù* (樘拒) means "to resist. According to the *Shuōwén*, *táng* (樘) means "a pillar," formed from the radical *mù* (木) and the phonetic *táng* (堂).

Regarding "nài" (耐) in the phrase "nàitòng" (耐痛): Nǎi Dài and Gu Yǎwáng state that "nài" means "to be able. Dù Lín’s commentary on the *Hànshū* notes that all characters representing laws and regulations are followed by the radical "cùn" (寸); according to the *Shuōwén*, this is because "cùn" provides the phonetic component.

"Shang (上)" means to pull from above; "xia qie (下挈)" means to firmly look back. According to Wang Yan's *Yanying Yinyi*, "qian (牽)" also means to lead forward. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is composed of "xuan (玄)" and "mi (冖)," meaning an ox.

"Yi zhen (意這)" is pronounced "sheng yan jian fan (生言件反). The *Cangjie pian* states that "zhen (這)" means to welcome. *Zi* (戢) is pronounced *zhāng* (莊) and *lì* (立). According to the *Shīchuán* (詩傳), it means "to gather" (*jù*). The *Zhǔjiàn* (註箋) states that *zizhí* (戢莊) means "to collect. The *Shuōwén* (說文) defines it as "concealing weapons," composed of the radical *guō* (戈) and the phonetic *qí* (咠).
*Qián* (揵) has the upper tone and the pronunciation *zhé* (陟); it is a Sanskrit term. It is the name of the white horse ridden by Prince Siddhārtha.

Regarding "lì" (to lick): when it comes to the character for "licking," the *Shuowen* explains it as taking food with the tongue; it is composed of "shé" (tongue) and "shì" (phonetic), with "shì" having the same pronunciation as above.

Regarding "zhěn" (pillow): it is pronounced "zhēn" or "rèn. Gu Yewang says it is that which one uses for the head while lying down; the meaning in the *Shuowen* is the same. It is composed of "mù" (wood) and "yín" (phonetic). This refers to the line in the *Mao Shi*: "Turning over and over, prostrate upon the pillow."

Regarding "huǐ" (虺), Yu Guǐfàn and Jīng Zhuāng both take it to be the character for *fù-huǐ* (蝮虺). The *Shuowen* states: "It is *fù-huǐ*; it follows the radical 'insect' (*chóng*) and takes *wù* as its phonetic.
Regarding *huò-sù-mì*, the *Zhōngshēng* says it is pronounced *sòu-zòu* and is a term from the Sanskrit language.

*The Scripture on Kāśyapa’s Visit to the Buddha*, one fascicle, compiled by Huilin. **Xiá (狎):** - In the *Commentary on the Analects* by Kong [Qiu], it means "to draw near. - In the *Commentary on the Zuo Zhuan* by Du [Yu], it means "to practice" or "to become familiar with. - According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of "da" (大) and the phonetic "jia" (甲). - In Guo Pu's *Commentary on the Erya*, it refers to a species of leopard, originating from the state of Mo. - In the *Shangshu* (Book of Documents), regarding the phrase "like tigers, like *pi*," Kong [Yingda]'s commentary states that it is also a species of tiger. - In the *Fanyi* (Explanations) of the *Mao Shi*, it is also a fierce beast. - According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of "zhi" (豸) and the phonetic "yu" (𤠞). The sound of "zhi" is that of "zhì" (雉). The character in the scripture is written as "jié" (𤜻), which is a vulgar form.

*Bo* (搏): Upper radical bù (補), lower radical luò (洛). Gù Yěwáng states that *bo* is synonymous with *fǔ* (拊, to pat or strike). Dù’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states it means "to take. The *Cāngjiépiān* also states that *bo* means "to arrive. The *Shuōwén* defines it as consisting of the radical for "hand" (手) and the phonetic element *fú* (尃); the pronunciation of *fú* is *fú*.

The *Bodhisattva-ha-se-yu-jing* (Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Censure of Desire for Form), one fascicle, compiled by Xuanying. Regarding the term *fuzhi* (鈇質): *fu* is pronounced as *fang* with the *fu* rhyme; in written texts, *fu* may also be read as *fu*, referring to a horizontal axe. In antiquity, executioners used axes for killing. The lower character is the standard form, while *zhi* (之) is a variant. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *fu* means "to chop" (*cuozuo*). The *Picao* states that *zhi* refers to the wooden block for execution. The *Gongyang Zhuan* says: "He could not bear to apply the *fuzhi* to him. He Xiu comments: "This refers to the crime of decapitation."
*Zǔ* (side note: *jǐ*; in character dictionaries, *zǔ* means "to place meat on a stand"; *zǔ* is also a small four-legged tray).

Regarding the "Four Categories of Learning Methods" (*Sìpǐn Xuéfǎ*) in one fascicle, compiled by Huìlín: *Jù* (side note: *ài*; according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "obstructing"; the *Kǎoshēng* says it means "embracing"; the *Shuōwén* says it means "to stop," composed of the radical for "hand" with *jù* as the phonetic).

*The Scripture on the Vajrapāṇi’s Lamentation*, compiled by Huìlín. "Zhēn" (榛) [is pronounced with the initial *shǐ* and final *zhēn*; according to the *Huáinánzǐ*, a grove of trees is called *zhēn*; the *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "qín"].

*Míngxuàn* (瞑眩): The upper character *míng* is pronounced as *mián* (眠) with the *biàn* (遍) rhyme; the *Shàngshū* states, "If medicine does not cause *míngxuàn*, the grievous illness will not be healed. The *Shuowén* defines it as "the closing of the eyes," written with the radical 目 and the phonetic 冥 (*míng*). The lower character *xuàn* is pronounced as *xuán* (懸) with the *juàn* (絹) rhyme. Jia [Yan]’s commentary on the *Guóyǔ* identifies it as "delusion. The *Cāngjié piān* defines it as "vision that is unclear. The *Shuowén* also notes it is written with the radical 目 and the phonetic 玄 (*xuán*); the version in the scriptures using 𥈅 (from 面) is incorrect. This is a vulgar usage.

*Sī* (the first character is pronounced with the *xī* radical reversed): The *Cāngyún* states that "sī" means the sound of scattering; the *Fāngyán* states it is the sound of sobbing. The *Shuōwén* says it is a sound of grief, formed from the mouth with the phonetic *sī*, though it is also written as *sì*.

The *Kātyāyanīputra-dharmaparyāya-nirodha-gāthā-sūtra*. [Note on the character "汲" (*ji*): 1. Xuán Yìng says: "In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, 'jí jí' (汲汲) means 'to walk hurriedly. The *Guangya* states that 'jí jí' means 'sudden haste. Nowadays, all texts write this as 'jǐ' (汲), following the radical for water. *Kātyāyanīputra-dharmaparyāya-nirodha-gāthā-sūtra*, Chapter One.

The character for *quàn* (券) is read as *wàn* (万) with the variant *fǎn* (反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "A *quàn* is a contract (*bié*). A contract is a document; it is called *bié* because its side is incised with a knife. The *Shiming* states: "It is written in large characters on top and split down the middle to distinguish it."

*Zhishen jing* (Sutra on Governing the Body), spoken by the Buddha; one fascicle, compiled by Huilin. "Yi-hua" (已黠)—the phonetic transcription of "hua" is *jia*; the *Shengyun* dictionary states it means "sharpness," while the *Fangyan* states it means "wisdom. In the regions of Zhao and Wei, wisdom was called "hua. Thus, "yi-hua" refers to wisdom. The language of the ancients was质朴 (*zhuti*, plain and substantial).

*Fó zhìyì jīng* (Sūtra on the Buddha’s Governing of the Mind), one fascicle. Huìlín. Early in life he encountered the Elder [Dharmakṣema] and, upon returning, reflected: "The *Zá nán jīng* (Sūtra of Miscellaneous Difficulties) has already been explained. As for the *Wǔmén chánjīng yàoyòngfǎ* (Essential Methods of the Five-Gate Dhyāna Sūtra), one fascicle," Huìlín said.

He applied his mindfulness [to it]. "Jì" (pronounced *xī*) in *jìniàn* (to apply mindfulness): according to the *Ěryǎ*, "jì" means to continue; according to the *Shuowén*, "jì" means to bind together. It is also written as *xì*. "Xì" also means to connect or string together. It is composed of the radical "person" (*rén*) and the phonetic "xì. The pronunciation of "xì" is *xí* (as in *xíyì*). *Fó zhìyì jīng*, one fascicle. Huìlín. Early in life he encountered the Elder [Dharmakṣema] and, upon returning, reflected: "The *Zá nán jīng* has already been explained. As for the *Wǔmén chánjīng yàoyòngfǎ*, one fascicle," Huìlín said. He applied his mindfulness [to it]. "Jì" (pronounced *xī*) in *jìniàn*: according to the *Ěryǎ*, "jì" means to continue; according to the *Shuowén*, "jì" means to bind together. It is also written as *xì*. "Xì" also means to connect or string together. It is composed of the radical "person" and the phonetic "xì. The pronunciation of "xì" is *xí* (as in *xíyì*).

*Ying* (盈) is pronounced *yì* (益); according to the *Cāngjié piān*, it refers to the area behind the elbow. The *Shuowén* states that it is composed of the radical "flesh" (*ròu*) with the phonetic component *yè* (*yèshēng*).

*Ruoxiàn* (如綫) is pronounced *xiānjiàn* (仙箭). In the *Zhouli*, the section on the *Féngren* (Master of Sewing) states: "He presides over the sewing and thread for the royal palace. Zheng Zhong says that "thread" (*xiàn*) is also "fibers" (*lǚ*). The meaning in the *Shuowén* is the same; it is composed of the radical "silk" (*xì*) with the phonetic component *zān* (*zānshēng*), where *zān* is pronounced *cán*. The text here uses *xiàn* (綖), pronounced *yán*; this refers to the covering on top of a cap and is not the character for "thread. Sometimes it is written as *xiàn* (線), which is also a vulgar form.

*Duān* (煗): The upper radical is *tán* (曇贍反); in Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci*, it means "tranquil" (*dàn*). Gu Yewang states it means "serene and still. The *Shuowen* says it is composed of the heart radical and the phonetic *zhān* (詹), pronounced *zhān* (占). The lower character is *yù* (庾), pronounced *xū* (須).

In Zeng’s commentary on the *Lunyu*, it means "a harmonious facial expression"; the *Erya* says it means "joy. The *Shuowen* says it is composed of the heart radical and the phonetic *yú* (俞). *Yóu* (愉): The upper radical is *tán* (曇贍反); in Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci*, it means "tranquil" (*dàn*). Gu Yewang states it means "serene and still. The *Shuowen* says it is composed of the heart radical and the phonetic *zhān* (詹), pronounced *zhān* (占). The lower character is *yù* (庾), pronounced *xū* (須). In Zeng’s commentary on the *Lunyu*, it means "a harmonious facial expression"; the *Erya* says it means "joy. The *Shuowen* says it is composed of the heart radical and the phonetic *yú* (俞). (Note: The text repeats the definition for *duān* and *yóu*. The intended meaning is that *duān* refers to a state of calmness or tranquility, while *yóu* refers to a pleasant or joyful countenance.)

*Qī* (惻): The upper radical is *kāng* (康) with the variant *hèn* (佷). Zheng’s commentary on the *Kaogongji* states it means "the appearance of hardness. In the *Liji*, it says, "*qī hū qí zhì yě*" (惻乎其至也). The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains that *qī* is composed of *xīn* (心) and *kàn* (豤), and its pronunciation is the same as above; it is composed of *zhǐ* (豕) and *gèn* (艮). In the classics, it is sometimes written with *zhì* (豸) instead of *kàn* (豤), which is an error.

The upper character *mèn* (捫) is pronounced with the initial *mo* and the final *bēn*; the lower character *mó* (摸) is pronounced with the initial *máng* and the final *bó*. The *Shēnglèi* states that *mèn* is also *mó*, and the *Cāngjiépiān* states that *mó* is also *mèn*. According to the *Shuōwén*, both characters are composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic element "mén" (門), with "mò" (莫) and "jù" (俱) serving as their respective phonetics.

*Tí-děng* (梯隥): The first character is pronounced *tǐ* with the *ní* rhyme; the second is pronounced *dēng* with the *dèng* rhyme. Guo Pu says: "Děng means a slope (*bǎn*). The sound of *bǎn* is *fǎn*. The *Kǎoshēng* says it means 'to tread upon. The *Shuowén* also states that *děng* means 'to look up,' being composed of the radical *dìu* (𠂤) with the phonetic *dēng*. It is incorrect for the scripture to write this as *chéng* (橙) with the radical *mù* (wood).

The character *yún* (蝖) [is pronounced] with the initial *hū* and the final *yuán*; the *Kǎo Shēng* states that *yún* and *zhì* [are synonyms]. The *Fān Yǔ* says that east of the Guān region, it is called *yún-zhì*. According to the *Shuō Wén*, it is composed of the radical "insect" (*chóng*) and the phonetic "xuān" (*shuān*). The lower part [of the character *fèi*] is *fù* and *wèi*. Guō’s commentary on the *Ěr Yǎ* identifies it as the stinking insect *jī fù chàn*. The *Zuǒ Zhuan* states that although there were *fèi* insects, they did not cause calamity. The standard characters for "ancient" and "modern" forms are written as *fèi*, composed of the radical "insect swarm" (*gūn*) and *chā*; it is also written with the radical "insect" (*chóng*) as *fèi*.

*The Dhamatrāta-dhyāna-sūtra*, Volume One (Upper). Xuanying: "Zhèn" (軫) means the tracks [of a carriage], it means to turn, and it means to unfold. In the *Gonggong Ji* (Record of the Artisan), regarding the note "the zhèn of a chariot is four chi," it states that this refers to the horizontal beam at the rear of the carriage body; today we call it the "starting point" of the carriage's turning.

"Fen-qui" (分逵) is also written as "qi-qui" (馗), both meaning the same. Furthermore, according to the *Erya*, a "nine-way intersection" is called a "qui. Guo Pu states: "It is where four roads cross and further have lateral branches."
*Chán* (pronounced *jiàn* with a retroflex) refers to the appearance of benevolence and prudence; it also denotes being weak and yielding. According to the *Guǎngyá*, *chán* means "wicked.

In the *Jiāngjì Shēnglèi*, the archaic form is the same as *niè* (pronounced *qí qì* with a retroflex). In the *Zuǒzhuan*, regarding the phrase "fearing that one will not *jì* [reach]," the commentary states: "*Jì* means 'to arrive. In the *Érpǐ*, "*jì*" means "not to reach" or "to bestow."
One *kuì* (逵位反; *kui*, with the phonetic *wei*) is a basket for earth; it is also written as *kuì* with the radical "bamboo," while the *Jīng* (Canon) writes it as *kuì*, which is an error.
*Hé* (眾胡臘反; *huà*, with the phonetic *lā*) means a gate; according to the *Shuōwén*, it refers to a city gate.

*Shan-shuo* (閃鑠; *shǎn shuò*; "flashing and shimmering," with the second character pronounced *shū-zhuó*): This refers to appearing momentarily and being indeterminate. The text in the sutra is written as *shǎo* (󳊳), which is incorrect.
*Er-yan* (尒炎): This is a Sanskrit term (*jñeya*). In this translation, it is rendered as "that which is known" (*suǒzhī*) or also "that which should be known" (*yīngzhī*).
*Tī* (with the second tone for *tā*, and the fourth tone for *chì xì*) is explained in the scriptures as the dwelling place of the mind.
*Juānliú* (with the first tone for *gǔ xuán*) refers to a small stream; according to the *Zílín*, it describes water flowing in a gentle, continuous trickle.
*Jian* (pronounced *zi yan* in the *Tongsu Wen*) means to soak or immerse; the *Zilin* states that *jian* means to drench. *Pin ju* (pronounced *qiu yu*): according to the *Erya*, *ju* means poverty.

Guo Pu says it refers to being base and ugly; the *Zishu* says it means empty. The commentary on the *Mao Shi*’s line "Finally poor and destitute" (*zhong ju qie pin*) states: "Ju" means lacking ritual propriety.

2. Lower Fascicle, Part Two. *Chen mei* (塵塺). *Wu gai* (武該) and *wu he* (武賀)—the latter being pronounced with the second tone—are terms from the *Tongsu wen* (通俗文). To be "matured" (*shu*) is called *mei*; *mei* is also dust.

*Nan ju* (難沮)—*ju* is pronounced with the *cai-yu* (才與) rhyme—refers to what the *Shijing* (詩經) calls "how can this be *ju*? The commentary states that *ju* means "to ruin. According to the *Sancang* (三蒼), *ju* means "gradually" (*jian*) or "to decay and ruin" (*bai huai*).

*Fáng*: (The character for *fáng* has the phonetic *fǔ* with the rhyme *fáng*; according to the *Shuowen*, *fáng* means "fat. (The character for *qiāng* has the phonetic *qiān* with the rhyme *yáng*; according to the *Shuowen*, *qiāng* means "to thrust. According to the *Cangjie pian*, a wooden object with sharp points at both ends is called a *qiāng*. The text reads *qiāng* [as in] "the tinkling sound of jade pendants"; however, *qiāng* is not the primary meaning of the word.)

*Fùjī* (伏鷄) is also written as *fù* (勽), with the same pronunciation as *chì* (抶, qù fǎn), meaning that a hen crouches over her eggs. The *Huainanzi* states, "crouching over the eggs before they have hatched," which refers to this very thing.

*Bǐgǔ* (󳋓骨) is now written as *bǐ* (髀), with the same pronunciation as *pú mǐ* (蒱米 fǎn); the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that the outer part of the thigh is called *bǐ*. In the dialects of Jiangnan, it is pronounced *bǐ'ěr* (必尒 fǎn).

"Qí-lù" (歧路) is also written as two characters, 󳇽 and 󳆾, both pronounced with the same initial *jù* and final *-yí*. It refers to a branch of a road. According to the *Erlǚ* (爾疋), "the three ways that reach through are called qípáng (歧旁). Guō Pǔ says: "Qípáng refers to a road that branches out from the side."

2. Lower Fascicle. Regarding the term *kǎn kē* (輱軻) in the *Jiù zá pì yù jīng* (Old Miscellaneous Parable Sutra): it should be written as *kàn kē* (埳軻). The upper character is pronounced with the same initial and the rhyme *gǎn* (感); the lower character is pronounced with the initial *kǒu* and the rhyme *zuǒ* (佐). In the *Chǔ cí* (Elegies of Chu), it says: "Thus he was *kàn kē* and remained stranded. Wang Yi (*Wáng Yì*) states: "*Kàn kē* means not meeting with fortune."

The character *zōu* (鄹) is an ancient form; it has two variants, *zōu* (鄹) and *jù* (𨛿), which today are written as *jù* (聚). It is pronounced *cái jù* (才句). According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "a cluster" (*jūjù*), referring to a place where people congregate. The reading *chāo* (󳇤) in the canonical text is an error.

The character *jì* (跡) is pronounced with the initial *shī* and the final *rèn* (尸任反), meaning "depth" as in "deep and shallow. The scriptural text reads *zōng* (淙, with the tone *zōng* [宗反]). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *zōng* refers to the sound of water; according to the *Guangya*, it means "soaking. Neither of these meanings accords with the sense of the scripture.

*Bǎo* (棓) is also written as *pěng* (捧); both share the pronunciation *báo* (雹, *báo*). It refers to a large staff. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *bǎo* means "to strike" (*chāo* [󳄑]), and the character is composed of the radical for wood and *chāo* (徒活反, *túhuó fǎn*).

*Xùn xíng* (徇行) is also written as *xùnxíng* (𢓈同); both share the pronunciation *cíjùn* (辭俊, *cíjùn fǎn*). *Xùn* (徇) is synonymous with "to patrol" (*xún*). According to the *Erya*, *xùn* means "to pervade" (*biàn*), which signifies to go around completely; it also means to issue a proclamation.

*Gāṇḍī* is correctly pronounced *gānzhì*; it refers to the wooden block that is struck. It is sometimes written as *zhui*, which is an error. The character in the sutra text is *gān* (dú lǐ fǎn), which is incorrect.

*Chéng wǔ* (城隖): *wǔ* (ā gǔ fǎn); according to the *Zílín*, it means a small city. According to the *Tōngsùwén*, a fortified residence is called an *wǔ*; the character is composed of the radical *duǐ*.

"Xi (襲) means to inherit and maintain; 'gu' (古文) and 'ji' (㦻) have the same meaning. 'Li' (立) is pronounced fan (反). Xi means to receive; according to the *Guangya*, it also means to reach or to continue—as in 'the descendants inherit the emoluments. In the *Zuo Zhuan*, regarding military expeditions, those that are light are called xi; the commentary states: 'to strike while the enemy is unprepared.
