*Zì* (知利反): Wang Yewang states that *zì* means "to stop" (*dùn*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "foot" (*zú*) and the phonetic "zhì.

*Duan* (澣之桓椀反): Zheng’s commentary on the *Mao Shi* states that *duan* means "to wash. Liu Zhao’s commentary on the *Gongyang Zhuan* says that removing old grime is called *duan*. The *Shuowen* defines it as "washing away the dirt of clothing," composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic "gàn"; it is also written as *huàn*. The version in the *Pǔ* (Genealogy) uses *huàn*, which is a vulgar character.
"Píngshā" (蓱沙): "Píng" is read as *míng* (冥) in the upper character; it is the name of a king of the Western Regions.

The *Pǔ* (譜) records it as "Píng," which is an error. "Sāo" (騷): "Sāo" is read as *sāng láo* (桑勞). Guō’s commentary on the *Erya* states that "sāo" means to shake or move. The correct orthography from ancient times to the present uses the radical "horse" (*mǎ*) and the phonetic "zào" (*zǎo*). The *Pǔ* records it as "Sāo" (搔), which refers to scratching or stroking and deviates from the meaning of movement. "Ér" (而): "Zhǎo" (沼) is the correct reading for the lower character; it is the standard form of the character.

*Bin* (殯) and *lian* (斂): the upper radical is *pin* (牝, pǐn); the lower radical is *lian* (廉, lián). He Xiu’s commentary on the *Gongyang Zhuan* states: "To place [the body] into the coffin after the great dressing is called *bin*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means that when the deceased is in the coffin and about to be moved for burial, the guests encounter them; it is composed of *e* (歺, meaning bones) and *bin* (賓, bīn) as the phonetic. The version in the *Puyi* (譜) is written as *bin* (儐), which is an error.
*Ji* (羝羊): The first character is pronounced *zhǐ* (with the initial *lǐ* as a variant). It refers to a ram; the *Pǔ* (dictionary) records it as *hú*, which is a vulgar form.
*Xia* (下): Pronounced *niè* (with the initials *nǚ* and *shè*). *Chéngjiè* (懲誡): The first character is pronounced *zhí* (with the initial *líng*). It means to warn or admonish.

*Mó* (摹): pronounced with the initial *mù* and the final rhyme *hú*. The *Pīcāng* states that it means "to take up an image. The *Shuowen* says it means "a compass" (*guī*), composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "mò" (*mò*).
*Wù* (霧): pronounced with the initial *ài* and the final rhyme *gǎi*; already explained previously in the sixth fascicle of the *Pǔ*.

Regarding the character *xún* (循): its upper radical is pronounced *xún*. The *Guǎngyá* states that *xún* means "to follow. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "walking," formed from the radical *chì* (彳) with the phonetic *dùn* (盾).
*Shā* (沙) is pronounced *chāorào* (昌遶反); it is a vulgar form; the correct character is *qín* (𪍑), formed from the radical *qiū* (酋).

*Gě lěi* (葛藟). [The character for *lěi*] is pronounced *lüì* (律) according to Guo’s commentary on the *Erya*, which states: "Lěi is a climbing vine (*téng*). The *Wenzi Dianshuo* says it is a herb; it is also a creeping vine of the *gě* plant. It is composed of the radical *ǒng* (廾) with the phonetic *lěi* (畾); the pronunciation of *lěi* is *léi* (雷).

*Shijia fangzhi*, Scroll One (Upper). Regarding the character *shu* (輸) [in the name *Shujin*]: the dictionary states that *jin* (賝) means "precious jade. According to the *Gujin zhengzi*, it is composed of the radical "shell" (貝) with the phonetic element "mi" (罙). *Shijia fangzhi*, Scroll One (Upper). Regarding the character *jin* (賝): the dictionary states that *jin* means "jade. According to the *Gujin zhengzi*, it is composed of the radical "shell" (貝) with the phonetic element "mi" (罙).

Regarding the character for *zhì* (贄) in the phrase "the second of the ritual offerings presented" (*fèng zhì zhī èr*), the *Gǔjīn zhèngzì* states it means "ritual gifts" (*zhìbì*). It is composed of the radical *bèi* (貝) and the phonetic *zhí* (執).

Regarding *yán mào* (延袤), it is pronounced with the final *mòu* (莫候) reversed; the *Shēnglèi* states that *mào* means "length. The *Shuowén* explains that north-south is called *mào*, composed of the radical *yī* (衣) and the phonetic *móu* (矛).
Líntāo (臨洮): A commandery name in Lǒngyòu (隴右) situated near the Tāoshuǐ River. Kōngtóng (崆峒): A mountain name;
the first character is pronounced *kōng* and the second *tóng*. Rìdī (日磾): The second character is pronounced *xī*;
it refers to black stone that can be used to dye silk. It is also the name of a person, Jin Rìdī (金日磾), mentioned in the *Hànshū* (Book of Han).
The term *xiǎngjiǎn* (緗簡) is explained in detail within the eighteenth fascicle of the *Yìyì* (釋音義).

Regarding *yóuxuān* (輶軒): the upper character is pronounced *yóu* (音猶), and the lower character is pronounced *xièyán* (歇言反). The *Màoshī Zhuàn* (毛詩傳) states: "A *yóu* is a light carriage. According to the preface to the *Fānyǔ* (方言): "The *yóuxuān* envoys were those who traveled through the myriad states to collect and examine diverse dialects; during the late Zhou and Qin periods, this profession fell into ruin and was abandoned—it is like the modern-day *cǎifǎng shǐ* (採訪使)."

In the *Zhenguan* [edition], its meaning is explained as "to reach" (*fǎn*). Dugu Yanshou’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that it means "to arrive. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of "yi" (依) and the phonetic "zi" (自); nowadays, it is also frequently written with "dan" (旦). The character "ji" (𠂢), pronounced "yin" (吟), is composed of three "ren" (人) radicals.

Regarding "Xun-yun" (獯狁): the upper character is pronounced *xùn* (with the tone reversed) and the lower is pronounced *yǔn*. According to the *Kaosheng*, it is an alternative name for the Hún-nú. What was called Xūn-yù in the Tang dynasty, Xiàn-yǔn in the Zhou dynasty, and Hún-nú in the Han dynasty is now called Tujue; all are northern barbarians.

*Qī* (西敧): Pronounced *yí fǎn* (宜反). Gu Yewáng says that *qī* means "not upright. It is also written as *chē* (𢼨). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *zhī* (支) with *qí* (奇) as the phonetic.

*Múwěi* (蕪薉): The upper character is pronounced *wú* (音無); the lower is *yū wèi fǎn* (紆衛反). Gu Yewáng says that *wěi* refers to being unclean. In both ancient and modern standard characters, it is composed of the radical *cǎo* (草) with *wú* (無) and *suì* (歲) as the phonetics.
Wuqian (烏𨭝) is pronounced with the "jie" (戒) rhyme.
Shanshan (鄯善): the first character is pronounced as "shan" (善).

Dunhuang (燉煌): the first character is pronounced as "tu-kun" (徒昆). The *Hanshu* states that it is the name of a commandery established by Emperor Wu in the first year after the Later Yuan era, having been separated from Jiuquan. Du Lin maintained that it was the ancient Guazhou, which is the present-day Shazhou.
Tuyuhun (Zhongyin) is the name of a tribe of the Yufan.

Daidu (the "du" is pronounced with a retroflex *r* [ṛ]) has already been explained in the eighth fascicle of the preceding genealogy; the character is correctly written as 𠂤 (*zhì*), while the form 塠 is also acceptable.

*Hui-zhu*: The first character is pronounced *jiǎ* (as in "armor"), and the second is pronounced *chú-lù* (as in "remove worry"). According to local gazetteers, the original meaning of *hui-zhu* is that it is made from lacquered cloth with a pattern resembling a *tuōkōng* (a type of insect).

*Wèi* (the character for *wèi*) is pronounced *wèi* (as in "squirrel"); according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, its form and bristles resemble those of a wild boar (*háo zhū*), though it is smaller, and it takes the phonetic element *wèi*. It belongs to the "insect" radical.
On Mount Gokhara (Gūṅqiéshān), the characters are arranged in reverse order;
"biàn" (匾) is pronounced with the initial *piàn* and the final *tǐng*; "zhì" (志) is written with the radical *chuò* (辵); "biàn" (遍) is correctly written with the radical *fāng* (匚).

*Pai-ye* (白䃜) [the characters *bai* and *ye* have the phonetic component *xi* (奚) as their rhyme]. The *Wenzi Jilüe* (文字集略) states it is a treasure from Black Mountain (*Heishan*). Regarding the correct orthography throughout antiquity and the present, it is written with the radical "stone" (*shí*) and the phonetic "yi" (*yī*); the character "yi" (*yì*) used by Zhì is also acceptable.
*Mòngjiàn* (瞢健) [the upper character *mòng* has the phonetic component *dí* (𡶤) as its rhyme].
*Khara*: The first character is pronounced as *miao* (苗) with the initial *he* (呬); the second character is pronounced as *xi* (醯) with the initial *yi* (異). *Dāruṇa*:
The first character is pronounced as *lu* (鹿) with the initial *dong* (董), and the second character is pronounced as *li* (力) with the initial *ji* (計);
it means "stiff and stubborn. *Vimala*: Also written as *ying* (瑩); the pronunciation is *ying* (縈) with the initial *ming* (暝).

Fù (覆) is pronounced *fú* (with the radical 田 and the phonetic 目). Bān (盋) is pronounced *bàn* (with the radical 木 and the phonetic 未). Hū (忽) is pronounced *hú* (with the radical 心 and the phonetic 林).

Lǐng (懍) is pronounced *líng* (with the radical 心 and the phonetic 靈). Ruò (弱) is pronounced *ruò* (with the radical 力 and the phonetic 口). Líng (齡) is pronounced *líng* (with the radical 齒 and the phonetic 令).

*Chen-chi* (齔齒): The first character is read as *chū* with the initial *jin*; it refers to the loss of baby teeth. *Wei-ge* (為笴): The second character is read as *yú* with the initial *dàn*. *Uṭṭara* (嗢呾):
The first character is read as *wēn* with the initial *gǔ*, and the second as *dān* with the final *là*; these are Sanskrit terms.
*Cheng* (縆): *geng* (with the radical *heng* [恒] as the phonetic). The *Shuowen* states: "A rope; it takes the radical *mi* [糸] and has *heng* as its phonetic.
*Xiao* (銷): *yi* (with the phonetic *ying* [蠅]).
A wooden stake or wedge. *Boluoxi* (婆羅屖): *la* (with the phonetic *xi* [奚]). A great mountain ridge.
*Shidi* (飤虎): The upper character is explained in the *Shuowen* as "a person with the sound *shi*.
*Banunuo* (半笯蹉): The national pronunciation is *nu*, and the sound of *ca* is the reverse of *canghe*.
*Zhejia* (磔迦): The upper character is pronounced *zhuai*.
*Suyǐng* (俗癭): "Yǐng" is pronounced with the rhyme of *ying*. The *Shuowen* says it is a goiter on the neck, composed of the radical *nà* (疒) and the phonetic *ying*.

Furthermore, *qūlǚ* (且󳁬): "Lǚ" is pronounced with the rhyme of *long*. The *Erya* says that swelling of the feet is called *lǚ*; the *Shuowen* writes this as *dù* (𤺄), stating it is swelling of the lower leg due to qi, composed of the radical *nà* (疒) and the phonetic *tóng*. The *Zhizhiwen* (志文) uses *wù* (兀) to form *dù* (󲷕); this is the character for *e* (𥰣). *Wù* is pronounced *kuāng*.
Sulūk-jì-nà (Sūmò-fǎn) Ē-hài-chè-dà-luó Guó (Ūluò-fǎn, next Xīngjī-fǎn; Chè yīn Chāngzhì-fǎn; Jǔ yīn Dānkuí-fǎn).

*Pingkǎi* (平塏): *kǎi* is pronounced as *kāi* (開改反). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that *kǎi* means "dry"; the *Shuowen* defines it as a high and prominent place, derived from the radical for earth (*tǔ*) with the phonetic component *qǐ*.
*Vīśoka* (鞞索迦國): *shàngbìyí* (上婢移反) and *cìshēngchǎi* (次生㧡反); these are Sanskrit terms.
The character for *Aṅguli* (鴦窶利) is pronounced as *jǔ* (其矩反).

The character for *chù* (處) is pronounced as *jiǎo* (上江缶反), though it is also written as *zhé* (斠); the character *tǒng* (桶) found in the *Zhì* (志) [commentary] is incorrect. The meaning has already been fully explained above in the eighth fascicle of the *Shijia pu* (釋迦譜), under the entry for the character *chù* (正處).
*Shāo* (髾) [the radical is *biāo* (髟), the phonetic is *xiào* (肖)]; the *Pīcāng* dictionary states it refers to hanging topknots. This is the standard orthography for both ancient and modern times.
*Hù* (笏) is pronounced *hū* (忽).
*Lìtiēpó* (栗呫婆) [the phonetic for *tiē* is *tā* (他) and *chē* (󲾽)]; this is a Sanskrit term.

Regarding "xià" (廈), Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "Xià refers to the present-day door-porches (*ménwǔ*); their form is wide at the sides and low. Whether ancient or modern, the correct character is composed of the radical "yǎn" (广) with "xià" as the phonetic component.
*Āci-pa-li* (the *li* is pronounced with a retroflex; it is a Sanskrit term).

*Sā shǎng* (the *shǎng* is pronounced with a palatal affricate; the *Yìnyì* of the *Hànshū* states that "sǎ" means to disperse; the *Shuōwén* states it means to sprinkle water, composed of the radical for water and the phonetic *lì*; the *Fāngzhì* writes it as *sǎ*, with the *xī* and *lǐ* pronunciations, which is incorrect; *fàn* is pronounced *xìn*).
"Xuìnjìn" (徐進) is a variant of "yǐngtóng" (𦎟). "Jiàfǔ" (架釜):
the upper character is pronounced jià (嫁), the lower is pronounced fù (父).

Volume 2, Part 2, "Fangzhì" (方志), Volume Lower, is an error. The upper character [of "zhì"] is the phonetic *wúgē* (吾戈); the *Zhèngjiān* commentary on the *Máoshī* states that "yué" (譌) means "false" (*wèi*). The *Shuōwén* defines "wèi" (偽) as "deceptive speech," written with the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic "wéi" (*wéi*). "Zhì" (志) is written as "é" (訛), which is a vulgar character; it is also written as "huó" (吪).
*Nāga-araṇa* (the *ra* sound is pronounced like *lan* and the *ge* sound is pronounced like *ka*; this is a Sanskrit term).

According to the *Guǎyá*, "araṇa" means "to seize" (*zhí*), referring to the seizing and subduing of various birds; it denotes those among birds that are courageous and fierce. According to the *Shuowén*, it means "to strike and kill a bird"; it is composed of the radical "bird" (*niǎo*) with the phonetic component "seize" (*zhí*).
The term "shēngpào" (生皰)—the character *pào* being pronounced with the *bǔ* rhyme—is already fully explained in the commentary on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*.

Regarding "shài" (曬): the local dialect (*fāngyán*) says it means "to expose to the sun" (*xiàobào*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "sun" (*rì*) and the phonetic "lì" (*li*).

*Kǎnqīng* (紺青): The upper character is read with the *gān* rhyme (with the retroflex *hàn* as a variant). The *Shuowen* states: "Dyed silk that is deep blue yet reflects a reddish hue; it takes the radical *mì* (silk) and the phonetic *gān*. *Qiàojué* (陗絕):

The upper character is read with the *jiè* rhyme (with the retroflex *qiào* as a variant). Xu Shuchong states: "A steep mountain ridge. The *Shuowen* states: "High; it takes the radical *yù* (mountain) and the phonetic *xiào*."

"Pánshí" (磐石): "Pán" is pronounced as *pān* (反) and *bān* (般). Wang Bi’s commentary on the *Zhouyi* states: "Pán refers to the stability of mountain rocks. Gu Yewang says: "Pán means to have a foundation or basis. The *Shenglèi* says it is a large rock. The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radical "stone" (*shí*) with "bān" as its phonetic component.
Gṛdhrakūṭa (𮓌株): the first character is pronounced with the shàngshǎng tone (also written as 󳉳);

Gṛdhrakūṭa-parvata (姞栗陀羅矩吒山): the first character is pronounced with the qì tone and the second with the zhāi tone. In the Sanskrit language, this is called Gṛdhrakūṭa; in the language of Táng, it is translated as "Vulture Peak Mountain."
*Jùnzhì* (峻峙): Pronounced *zhì*, like the sound of a pheasant (*chì*).

*Nùjí* (搙績): Pronounced *jì* with the *qīngxī* (精息) tone; the *Erya* states that it means "task" (*shì*) or "occupation" (*yè*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "silk" (*mì*) and the phonetic "zé" (*zē*).
*Īlán nà* (伊爛拏): Pronounced *nuò* with the *jiā* tone; this is a Sanskrit term.
*Kuñjika* (捃稚迦): The first character is pronounced *jun* (君) with the *yun* (殞) rhyme; the middle character is pronounced *chi* (馳) with the *ni* (膩) rhyme;

it is a Sanskrit term. *Mánlǎo* (蠻獠): The first character is pronounced *mó* (莫) with the *bān* (班) rhyme. The *Guǎngyá* states that "mán" means "arrogant" (*màn*). The *Shuowén* says that the Southern Mán people are of the "serpent race," written with the radical for "insect" (*chóng*) and the phonetic *luán* (䜌). The lower character is pronounced *lǎo* (老). The *Zìshū* states that there are the Lǎo-yí (獠夷) in Zāngkē. The *Yìwù míng* states that the Lǎo-yí are a species of beast; they lack moderation in their desires and use humans as food. When they commit an offense, they kill secretly while moving through the water, using spears to catch fish and turtles. When dead, they bury them upright in coffins rather than laying them down. [Note on "wù" (誤): The *Shuowén* says it is written with the radical for "dog" (*quán*) and the phonetic *liáo* (尞). The pronunciation of *luán* (䜌) is *lì-zhuān* (力專).
*Karṇikā* (the first character pronounced with the *lì* rhyme and the *chéng* final;

the second character, *liáo*, is pronounced with the *lì* rhyme and the *diāo* final). The *Cāngjié piān* states that *liáo* means "a small opening. The *Shuowén* defines it as "a hole," formed from the radical for "cave" (*xué*) and the phonetic *liáo*.

*Xiàlǔ* (潟鹵): The first character, *xiè*, is pronounced with the *xing* and *yi* rhymes. The *Erya* states: "Xiè means bitter. Guo Pu says: "It refers to bitter soil. Regarding the characters of the past and present, the correct form follows the radical "water" (*shui*) and the phonetic "xi" (*zhi*). The original text’s *xì* (舄) is an error. The second character, *lǔ*, is pronounced with the *lu* and *gu* rhymes. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "Lǔquè refers to land that is parched and thin. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "It is a salty land in the west. It is formed by the abbreviated radical 'hal' (*lu*), resembling the shape of salt. In the east it is called *kē* (㡿), and in the west it is called *lǔ* (鹵)."
*Niú* (椰子) is the name of a tree; *yě* (嗟反) is its phonetic component. *Lèjiā* (䮚迦) is the name of a mountain; *lè* (勒恒反) is its phonetic component. *Hóngchǎng* (宏敞):

the upper character *hóng* (宏) has the pronunciation *héng*; the commentary on the *Shūjìng* states it means "vast and great," while the *Shuowén* defines it as "the deep interior of a house," composed of *mián* (宀) and the phonetic *gōng* (厷), with the lower character *chǎng* (敞) having the pronunciation *chāngliǎng*. The *Cāngjiépiān* states that *chǎng* means "high and prominent," while the *Shuowén* defines it as "leveling high ground so that it can be seen from afar," composed of *wén* (攵) and the phonetic *shàng* (尚).
Pōtí (Skt. sphāṭika) means "crystal.
Lín (pronounced with the second tone on 臨) is the country of Lǐn.
Fànchú (the first character pronounced with the fourth tone on 飯) is the country of Fànchú.
Pao-xi (上鮑交反, 下喜冝反): This was the title of the Three Augusts of antiquity. Gao-jie (上工老反, 下音皆):
The meaning is already fully explained in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*); the local gazetteers (*fangzhi*) write it as "Wei," which is incorrect.
"Dùwǔ" (黷武): The first character is pronounced "dú.
"Huòlù" (貨賂): Pronounced "lù. "Fànzhàng" (泛漲):
Pronounced "zhāng" with the second tone; the original text's "zhì" (志) as "xiàn" (涱) is incorrect.
Huá-lóu (upper character *hu* with the radical *mǎ*, lower character *lóu* with the radical *lì*). Tàizǎi Ē (upper character *tài* with the radical *zǎi*, lower character *ē* with the radical *pī*).

Jùrán (upper character *jù* with the radical *qú*, lower character *rán* with the radical *yù*). Dū’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states that *jù* means "fearful"; the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "distressed," formed from the radical *chuò* and the phonetic *jù*. Fāng Zhì writes it as *cù* with the radical *xīn*; this is a vulgar variant.

*Jiān shì yù*: "jiān" (蠲) is pronounced *jué xuán fǎn* (上決玄反); "shì" (嗜) is pronounced *shí zhì fǎn* (下時至反). *Kàn Zé* (闞澤): "kàn" (闞) is pronounced *kān làn fǎn* (上堪濫反); he was the Director of the Imperial Secretariat (*Zhōngshū lìng*) of Wú.

*Hù dú kǒu*: "hù" (滬) is pronounced *hú gǔ fǎn* (上胡古反). The *Shānhǎi jīng* (山海經) states: "Mount Yángxū borders the waters of Xuánhù. Guō Pǔ says: "Cángjié [instructed] the Emperor that at Lín-hù Water, a numinous tortoise carried forth a book. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) with the phonetic "hù" (*hù shēng*). The following character, "dú" (瀆), is pronounced *lù fǎn* (下鹿反).
Xī Huī’s superiors were ashamed that they knew he was rebelling, while his subordinates suffered from his attempts to turn people back [from rebellion]. This is a person's name.

*Bēi* (pronounced with the *pī* and *bì* finals) is glossed in the *Pīcāng* as "the sound of treading upon the ground. In the standard characters of antiquity and today, it is written with the radical 足 (foot) and the phonetic 畐; the pronunciation of 畐 is the same as above.

*Kui* (巋然): The upper radical is *shan* (山); the phonetic component is *gui* (軌). The *Shengyun* states it means "a mountain standing alone. In both ancient and modern standard characters, the form follows *shan* as the radical and *gui* as the phonetic.
*Gao li* (高悝): The character *li* (悝) has the pronunciation *ku hui*. It is a personal name.

The upper character of *yōn-liǎng* (轀輬) is pronounced *wēn* and the lower is pronounced *liáng*. Mèng Kāng says: "It is like a carriage for clothing; it has windows and shutters, so that when closed it is warm and when opened it is cool. Rú Chūn says: "Its form is broad and large, and it is equipped with ceremonial insignia (*yù-yí*). Since the Hàn dynasty, it has been used exclusively for carrying coffins. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is a reclining carriage. Both characters follow the radical for "carriage" (*chē*), and *wūn* (昷) and *jīng* (京) serve as their phonetic components.

Regarding *zhéng* (pronounced *xìnggēng*): the *Dàdài Lǐ* states that the upper part of the jade belt (*pèiyù*) consists of two *héng*, while the lower part consists of two *huáng*. The *Shuōwén* defines *héng* as "the uppermost part of the jade belt; it is used to regulate movement and stopping. It is composed of the radical "jade" (*yù*) and the phonetic "xing" (*xíng*).

Regarding the character *chǔ* (礎), Xu Shuzhong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states that in the state of Chu, the pillar-base was called *chǔ*. The *Gujin zhengzi* explains: "When mountain clouds rise and moisten the pillar-base, it is called *chǔ*; it is composed of the radical 'stone' and the phonetic 'chǔ'; the pronunciation of *chǔ* (𥖽) is *xī*."

Regarding the character for "to feed" (sì): the *Shangcí zìfǎn* states it is composed of "person" (人) and "upward food" (仰食). The *Shuowén* writes it as 飤 (shì), composed of "person" (人) and the phonetic "food" (食). Fāngzhìbó’s 飼 is a vulgarized form.

According to the *Catalogue of the Tripitaka*, the *Śākyamuni-pūrvapraśasti* (Shìjiā pǔ), the *Abridged Pūrvapraśasti* (Lüèpǔ), the *Local Gazetteers* (Fāngzhì), and others, there should be twenty fascicles of the *Essentials of Various Sutras* (*Zhūjīng yāoji*). There are fifty fascicles of the *Differences between Sutras and Vinaya* (*Jīnglù yìxiàng*), for which the phonetic glosses have already been completed; these two fascicles of its own *Phonetic Explanations* (*Yìnyì*) are not included in the count. There are twenty-two fascicles of the *Sui Dynasty Catalogue of Scriptures* (*Suí cháo jīngmù*), including its various sections, for which the phonetic glosses have not yet been completed. There are twenty fascicles of the *Sui Dynasty Catalogue of Scriptures*, for which the phonetic glosses have not yet been completed. In total, these amount to sixty-two fascicles for which the glosses are missing. Since these are merely excerpts from the canon or ancient catalogues that have long been redundant and their commentaries have fallen into disuse, they are now all left unglossed. Those who read them must skip over them. Therefore, following the sequence of the *Tripitaka Catalogue*, subsequent fascicles with identical phonetic glosses have been taken to complete the total of one hundred fascicles.

*Shìmén xìlù* (Genealogy of the Śākya School): Regarding "bìn" (banishment/punishment), it is pronounced *jùn* (反). Sīmǎ Biāo’s commentary on the *Zhuāngzǐ* states that "bìn" means to cast away (*qì*). The *Shījì* says, "They mutually criticized and bìn-ed [him]," which is correct. In the standard characters of past and present, this is written with the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "bīn" (賓). The lower character, "fán" (煩), is pronounced *fā* (發). The *Shuōwén* states that "fá" (punishment) refers to minor offenses for transgressions; it means that although one has not yet used a blade to issue a warning, merely holding a blade while reviling others merits punishment. This is a compound character formed by the semantic element "blade" (刀) and the phonetic "lì" (詈). *Bāo* (襃): Upper radical *bǎo* (保). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "Bāo means to promote. Gu Yewang states: "Bāo means to extol beauty. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical for "clothing" (*yī*) and the phonetic component *pó* (󲝷); the pronunciation of *pó* is *bǎo*.

*Yu* (㝢). Upper radical: *yú* (愚, yú); reversed: *dù*. The commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states that it means "to lodge" (*yù*) or "to entrust. Lower radical: *huàn* (患, huàn). The *Wenzi Dadian* explains it as "the territory within a state's borders," and also "the interior of the borderlands. It is composed of the *mián* (宀) radical with *huán* (睘) as its phonetic.
"Sì" (in "sìmǎ") is pronounced as the first tone, sì.
"Xián" (in "xiánbò") is pronounced with the initial *x* and the final *jiàn*.

"Yì" (in "yìhuà") is pronounced with the initial *yú* and the final *lì*; the *Shàngshū* commentary by Kǒng [Yáng] states that "yì" means "to assist," and the *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical "feather" (*yǔ*) and the phonetic "stand" (*lì*).

*Jiangxun* (將詢). Pronounced *zunfan*. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states it means "to inquire. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan* states it refers to "consulting the opinions of relatives. The *Gujin Zhengzi* states it means "to deliberate. It is composed of the radical "speech" (言) with "xun" (旬) as its phonetic.

Regarding "jì dà wěi" (稽大偽): the *Shàngshū zhù* (Commentary on the Book of Documents) states that "jì" means to examine; the *Guǎngyá* states it means to inquire; and the *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical "grain" (*huó*) and the phonetic "jiǔ-zhǐ. The pronunciation of "huó" is gōng-mí-fǎn, and that of "xià-wéi" is wēi-wèi-fǎn.

Regarding "qīyí" (reaching one hundred years): the *Book of Rites* (*Lǐjì*) states, "At one hundred years of age, one is said to be qīyí. Wang Bi’s commentary on the *Book of Changes* (*Zhouyī*) explains that "yí" means nourishment. According to the *Shuowén*, it is a pictograph composed of the radical 𦙃; when written with the head radical 頁, it becomes "yí. Its seal script form is 頤, and its clerical script form is 󳉪.

*Kèqín* (恪勤): "Kè" is pronounced with the initial *kǎng* and final *-yì* (反). The commentary on the *Shūjīng* by Kǒng [Yǔ] states that *kè* means reverence (*jìng*). The *Shuōwén* records the correct form as *kè*, which shares the same meaning; it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "guest" (*kè*).
*Sēngqiè* (僧䂮): the pronunciation is *lüè*. *Sēng* is a name.

The first character of 戡難 (kānnàn) is pronounced as the "kǎn" in kǎnlán (坎藍); the second character is pronounced as "nàn.
The first character of 幖幟 (biāozhì) is pronounced as the "biāo" in bìyáo (必遙); the version written as 摽 (biāo) is an error; the second character is pronounced as "zhì."

In "播植" (bō zhí), the first character is pronounced *pō hè* (rhyme *hè*), and the second is pronounced *shí lì* (rhyme *lì*).

Liu Huan’s commentary on the *Zhouyi* states: "Ji (賾) is the ultimate designation for that which is profound and deep. In the standard orthography of ancient and modern times, this character is written with the radical *zhēn* (𠚫) and the phonetic *zé* (責).
*Yù* (駕馭, to guide or drive) is pronounced *shàng yú jù fǎn* and is also written as 御 (*yù*).

According to the *Guǎngyá*, *huì* (彙) is pronounced *wéi guì fǎn*; it means "category" or "kind," referring to leading one another according to their kind. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical *sǔ* (󳐗) with *wèi* (胃) as a phonetic component; *sǔ* is pronounced *tí jì fǎn*.
*Kṣānti* (羼提): The first character is pronounced *chà* (察) and *xiàn* (莧);

*Chóujiào* (讎挍): The first character is pronounced with the *shǒu* rhyme (*liú fǎn*), and the second with the *jiāo* rhyme (*xiào fǎn*). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "chóu" means "to face" (*duì*); the *Erya* says it means "a match" (*pǐ*). Liu Xiang’s *Bièlù* states that "collating the classics" (*chóujiào jīng zhōng*) refers to examining and comparing them. The *Fengsùtong* says that two people facing each other in comparison constitute "chóujiào. The *Jixùn* further states that when two people compare texts against their original versions, it is called "chóu. The *Shuowen* defines "chóu" as "an answer" (*yìng*), written with the radical for speech (*yán*) and the phonetic *cháo*. The version of the classic using the characters "zhōu" and "yán" to form "chóu" is incorrect. The pronunciation of *cháo* is the same as above.

"Ju-mèi" (寤寐): "Ju" (寤) is pronounced wù gù fǎn; the *Shuowen* states that when one awakens from sleep and speaks, it is called "ju. Both characters are simplified forms of "meng" (㝱), with "wu" (吾) and "wei" (未) serving as their phonetic components respectively.

*Chūsè* (麤歰): The second character is read with the *shēn* and *jí* rhymes. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "rough and not smooth. It is composed of four *zhǐ* (止) radicals, two upright and two inverted; the common vulgar form written as *shì* (澁) is incorrect. *Chégǔ* (車轂):

The second character is read with the *gōng* and *wū* rhymes. According to the *Shuowen*, it is the point where the spokes converge. It is a compound character consisting of a semantic and a phonetic element.
*Jian* (減): To diminish; to reduce; to subtract; to exclude. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *shui* (water) and the phonetic *xian*.

*Bujing* (不眴): *Xuan* is pronounced as *xuán* (as in *xuánjuàn*). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that it refers to the manner of gazing. Gu Yewang says it is the way people today move their eyes when whispering warnings to one another. According to the *Shuowen*, it means the eyes flickering; it is composed of the radical *mu* (eye) and the phonetic *chuo*. The pronunciation of *chuo* is the same as above.
*Utrāna* (the "na" sound is pronounced *tan* with the *nan* rhyme-reversal; it is a name for non-Buddhist outsiders in Sanskrit, or alternatively called *Udraka*).

*Xīn* (the first character is pronounced *xiǎn* with the *tiān* rhyme-reversal): according to the *Cāngjié piān*, *xīn* means to scold (*hē*); according to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means anger; according to the *Shuōwén*, *xīn-xīn* refers to contentious speech. It is formed from the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic "jiān" (pronounced *qiān*). The version of the scripture that writes it as *gàn* is incorrect; this character does not exist in standard dictionaries.

*Ti* (蕛稗): Upper radical *ti*, lower *ni* (反). Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "Tí is like *bài*; it grows spreading over the ground, a noxious weed. It is sometimes written as *tí*; the *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *di*. This is the correct form for both ancient and modern usage; it belongs to the grass radical and uses *tí* as its phonetic component. (Pái-mài) *bài*: Lower radical *du*. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "The *bài* weed resembles grain. It is sometimes written as *bài*; this is the correct form for both ancient and modern usage, meaning a distinct variety of rice. It belongs to the grain radical and uses *bei* as its phonetic component.

The character *lǐn* (林) with the phonetic *qín* (寢) reversed [is found in] the *Běicāng*. It denotes the appearance of lamenting with a mournful cry. The Commentary on the Book of Documents by Confucius states it is the appearance of being in peril and apprehension. The *Fāngyán* also says it means "respectful. The *Wénzìdiǎn* explains that it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "lǐn" (*lǐn*). The pronunciation of *lǐn* is the same as above. The text of the scripture uses *lí* (󳊼), which is an error.

"Mǐgǔ" (grain) is pronounced gōng wū fǎn. Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that the "nine grains" refer to varieties such as rice. The *Erya* says "grain is fortune," while the *Shuowen Jiezi* says it means "continuity. It is the collective name for the hundred grains. It is composed of the radical "禾" (rice) and the phonetic "𣪊" (pronounced kōng jiǎo fǎn).

*Bi* (粃): The upper character is pronounced *bi* (畢) with the secondary tone (*mi* [弭]). Gu Yewang states that it refers to grain that has not reached full maturity; it is also written as *pi* (秕). In the standard orthography of the past and present, it is composed of the radical *mi* (米) and the phonetic *bi* (比). The lower character is pronounced *gang* (剛) with the secondary tone. The *Shenglei* (聲類) states that it refers to the husk of grain; it is also written as *chao* (󳄮) or *chao* (󳃝). In the standard orthography of the past and present, it is composed of the radical *mi* (米) and the phonetic *chao* (󳃝).

*Kū* (upper tone, pronounced *kū*) means "to carve out" according to the *Fāngyán*. It is explained as being synonymous with *zhī*; phonetically it is derived from *tú*, meaning "to butcher," and refers to cutting open and removing the internal contents. The *Shuowén* defines it as "to split," following the radical for "knife" (*dāo*) and the phonetic *kuā*. The lower character, *tīng* (also pronounced *tìng*), is defined in the *Yùnyīng* as "to disarticulate bones. Phonetically it is derived from *bō*; the *Shàngshū* uses the archaic form *zhī*. Both characters share the "knife" radical and are examples of *xíngshēng* (phonetic-semantic) compounds.

*Jiāoráo* (㑴嬈): The first character, *jiā*, is pronounced with the *qie* rhyme *jī-rén*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "gradual progress," written with the radical "person" (*rén*) and holding a broom (*zhǒu*), as if sweeping forward. The second character, *ráo*, is pronounced with the *qie* rhyme *níng-niǎo*. According to the *Bowuya*, it means "to dally and jest. The archaic form is written as *shè* (𤲶). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to toy and mock," written with the radical "woman" (*nǚ*) and the phonetic element *yáo*.
*Jiā* (上卓瓜反): The *Shuowen* states it means a horse-whip; it also means to strike. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* says it means to flog or beat; it follows the radical "hand" (手). *Sì* (河師事反):
The *Yunying* says it means rapid or swift; it follows the radical "historian" (史).

The character 󲙸 (upper part: 苞, *bāo*; lower part: 皃, *mào*) is from the *Wenzi Jilüe*. It is the character for fire (*huǒ*). "Fire" (*fù*) refers to burning firewood and bamboo; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "to scorch.

The characters 峛崺 (*lǐyǐ*)—also written as 邐迤—are pronounced with the same sounds as above: the upper part is *lǐ* and the lower part is *yǐ*. The *Kaosheng* states that they describe the appearance of a sand dune (*shāqiū*), meaning "low yet long" and "windingly connected. According to the standard orthography of the past and present, 峛崺 refers to the continuous ridges of a mountain. Both characters are phono-semantic compounds (形聲字) derived from the radical for "mountain" (*shān*).

The character 𥔐 (in "碎𥔐") is pronounced with the initial *kan* and final *ge* (i.e., *kǎn*). It refers to the sound of stones striking one another; both characters are regular forms derived from the radical "stone" (*shí*) and are transitive characters. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "It is the sound of stone; it takes 'stone' as its radical and 'hé' as its phonetic component. The pronunciation of 盇 is *hán* and *là*.

"Zhuǎn zào" (to become restless) is followed by "zāo" (uproar). Wáng Yěfǎn’s *Guǐyì* states that "zào" means agitation. Zhèng’s commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* says it means lack of tranquility. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is sometimes written as the character "jiào" (趮), composed of the radical "foot" (足) and the phonetic "sào" (喿); the pronunciation of "sào" is "dào" (到) with the *rùshēng* (entering tone).

The character 穬 (pronounced with the lower radical *guō* and the radical *měng*) refers to large barley according to the dictionaries; it may also refer to "coarse grain," which is the weakest variety of rice. It is characterized by having many husks and little grain, and is also called "wild barley" (*kuàngmài*), as it likewise has many husks and little flour.

*Chánkuì* (慚愧): The first character is pronounced with the *shàng* tone and the *jiān* rhyme (as in *jiān*). The *Shàngshū* states: "Only the virtue of shame" (*wéi chán dé yě*). According to the *Shuōwén*, both *chán* and *kuì* are written with the radical for "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic *zhǎn*.

The text here uses *cán* (慚), which is identical in meaning. *Pílì* (霹靂): The first character is pronounced with the *piān* tone and the *mí* rhyme; the second is pronounced with the *líng* rhyme. The *Yùpiān* states it refers to the great roar of thunder. Both characters take the radical for "rain" (*yǔ*).

"Ān-lǎng" (攬掠): The lower character is pronounced "lüè," meaning to seize or take by force; it is sometimes written as "lùè" or "lìng," with the latter pronounced "yǐng," meaning to strike, but this is likely incorrect.

Volume Two, Part Two: "Qiē-cuō" (切磋): The lower character is pronounced "cāng hé" (倉何). According to the *Erya*, it refers to a craftsman working on ivory. However, in this context, "qiēcuō" means to engage in debate and exhaustively investigate the principles of a doctrine.
The *Chenji* (Prophecy Records) states that Chu forbade [the practice], yet auspicious books appeared in the regions of the Yellow and Luo Rivers;

this is a matter of verification. Regarding "borrowing troops" (*jiebing*), the upper radical is *jing* (also read as *fan*). The *Cangjie pian* states: "Jie" means to borrow from another; it is a correct character of ancient times. It is composed of the radical "man" (人) and the phonetic "xi" (昔). The text here uses "zhai" (債), which is the character for debt or obligation, and is not the character for borrowing; this is an error resulting from scribal transmission.

*Chiai* (癡騃): The lower character is pronounced *kai* with a rising tone (*shǎngshēng*). It means to be foolish, small-minded, and lacking wisdom; it denotes ignorance. *Huàiqì* (坏器): The lower character is pronounced *méi*.
An unfired earthenware vessel is called *huài*; it refers to a clay vessel that has not yet been fired.
*Vīri* (the first character pronounced as *vī* with the second as *lǐ*, following the *miàn* [rhyme] of *fàn*;
it is a Sanskrit name for a king). *Bùqù* (pronounced *jù*; means "to be terrified" or "to fear"; this character does not exist in any standard lexicons).
*Bēnzǒu* (pronounced *bēn*; means "to run away").

*Jiè* (疥): The upper character is pronounced *jiè*, meaning "wind-sores" (*fēngchuāng*). The lower character is pronounced *dāo chōng*. It refers to a disease where wind causes the skin to thicken and rise up. The *Yùpiān* states it means "exhausted illness" (*píbìng*) or "chronic old ailment" (*lǎogùbìng*). The *Shuōwén* defines it as "illness from exhaustion" (*bàibìng*). It is a phono-semantic compound character.

*Pā* (pronounced *pǔ*, with the initial *bǎi* as a phonetic component) means to strike, to pat, or to beat; it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic component "white" (*bái*). *Bì* (pronounced *pí*, with the initial *mǐ* as a phonetic component) refers to the outer part of the thigh; the version in the sutra uses *bǐ*, which is a vulgar character.
3. Third Fascicle. "Xuēliú" (Blood-flow) is an archaic form of the character for "flow.
"Jù" (Reject) is an archaic form of the character for "short"; it is now written as "duǎn" (short).
"Jūshǎnmí" (Kauśāmbī)—the first syllable is pronounced *jù* and the second is the phonetic *shǐrǎn*—is a name for a Western country according to the Sanskrit language.

"Tuō" (拖): the upper character is "yin" (音) and the lower is "tā" (他), with an alternative pronunciation of "yì" (以勢). It means to drag or pull; both characters are formed from the hand radical as the semantic component and the phonetic component.
"Jiǎo" (角): the upper character is "jiāng" (江) and the lower is "yuè" (岳); it is also written as "jiào" (較) and was formerly written as "jué" (斠); both forms are interchangeable.

*Bìliè* (擘裂): The first character is pronounced *bān-mài* (反). It means to tear with the hands; the *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *pì* (擗). The second character is pronounced *lián-zhé* (連哲). *Tòu* (捊):

Pronounced *dì-zì-máo* (地自茅), or alternatively written as *bào* (抱) or *póu* (掊)—these two are identical. It means to scoop with the fingers. The version in the sutra uses the character *pǎo* (跑) from the "feet" radical, which is incorrect; its pronunciation is *báo* (雹).

"Ben-tu" (奔突) means to rush upward; it is a homophone for "shǒu" (走), meaning to run. It is also written as "bēn" (犇); in ancient script it is written as "fén" (𩦥) or "yún" (𩣺). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "quán" (犬, dog) and the phonetic "bēn" (賁) in abbreviated form, pronounced "dùn-nù" (鈍訥). It refers to a dog suddenly bursting out. It is also written as "táng-tu" (搪揬), meaning to charge or collide. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "quán" (犬) and "xué" (穴, hole), signifying a dog emerging from within a hole.
*Cǎn* (慘): Upper radical *cāng* (倉), gan (敢) and fǎn (反) as phonetic components; it signifies sorrow or distress (*qì*). *Lǚ* (僂): Upper radical *lì* (力), zhǔ (主) and fǎn (反) as phonetic components;

according to the *Zuǒ Zhuàn*, it means hunchbacked (*yǔ*); according to the *Guǎng Yǎ*, it means crooked. It is composed of the radical *rén* (人) with *lǚ* (縷) abbreviated as the phonetic component. The lower part has the pronunciation *shēn* (申). According to the *Zhou Yī*, it means to bend in order to seek extension; according to the *Shuō Wén*, it means to bend and extend. It is composed of the radical *rén* (人) with *shēn* (申) as the phonetic component.

The character for *chún-àn* (quail) is composed of "bird" (*niǎo*) and "to offer" (*xiǎng*) as its phonetic, with the lower radical pronounced *yàn*. The *Huáinán Zǐ* states that shrimp transform into *yòuchún* quails. The commentary on the *Guóyǔ* explains that *àn* refers to the *fú* bird, which cries out at the commencement of spring and departs at the commencement of autumn; it is a character formed from both shape and sound.

*Suò-ài* (所閡): The second character is pronounced *wǒ-gài* (我蓋) as a reversed reading, or it may be written as *ài* (礙). It means "to obstruct" or "to stop. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is derived from *hài* (亥).

Volume Four, Part Four. *Těng-cháng* (膞腸): Pronounced *chuán-rǎn* (船耎). The *Kaosheng* states it refers to the calf muscle. It may also be written as *zhùn* (腨) or *zhuǎn* (󰈷). The second character has the phonetic *cháng* (長). The *Kaosheng* states it means "to flow through" or "to be unobstructed," referring to the free passage of qi.
*Chao* (𢷏) means to strike down; *shang* (上) is pronounced *páng* (龐) with the fanqie *páng-fǎn*; it means to throw to the ground. *Xià* (下) is pronounced *lǐ* (禮) with the fanqie *lǐ-fǎn*;
it means to execute, to behead, or to sever life. *Lǚbù* (僂步) is pronounced *lìzhǔ* (力主); *lǚ* (僂) means to be bent, and it refers to walking with a stooped back.

Regarding "舐" (lì) [in the phrase "licking the Bodhisattva’s feet"]: the *Erya* (爾雅) states it means "to take food with the tongue. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文解字) explains it as being composed of the radical "tongue" (舌) and the phonetic "氏" (shì);

its archaic form is written as "舓" (shí). Regarding "xūxī" (歔欷): the upper character is pronounced xū and the lower is pronounced xī. Gu Yewang states that it refers to the sound of sighing or lamentation produced from the mouth, a sobbing sound, or the retention of breath. The *Cangjie pian* (蒼頡篇) describes it as the lingering sound remaining after weeping. Alternatively, it may be written with the radical "mouth" (口) as "xūxī" (噓唏).

*Bǐng* (昺): Upper radical *bīng* (兵), phonetic *mǐn* (皿). According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "bright" (*míng*). It may also be written with the fire radical as *bǐng* (炳). The Classics use *bǐng* (昞), which is the same character. This is the correct form according to ancient and modern standards. It is composed of the sun radical (*rì*) and the phonetic *bǐng* (丙). The sound of *mǐn* (皿) is *míng* (明); the sound of *bǐng* (丙) is the same as above.

*Yǒng*: (homophone for *yōng*; the *Mao Shi* says it is the appearance of respectful gravity; the *Shuowen* says it is the appearance of a large head, formed with *xìe* [head] and *wú* as the phonetic component;

*wú* has the same pronunciation as above). *Nǎi*: (Qianshanggouhou; the *Kaosheng* says it means taking the milk of oxen and sheep; alternatively written with *yáng* [sheep]; the *Gujin Zhengzi* uses *shǒu* [hand] and *jié* as the phonetic component).

*Yǎnbì* (掩蔽): The first character is pronounced *yǎn* (音奄); the second is *bìmèi* (卑袂反). It means to obstruct, to conceal, or to restrain. It is also written as *yǎnfù* (掩覆), meaning "to cover" or "to have a surplus. These are transposed characters (*zhuǎnzhù*). *Níngníng* (嫈嫇): The first character is *èjīng* (厄莖反) and the second is *màipéng* (麥彭反).

The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states this refers to the appearance of a common village woman, or the manner of a new bride. Both characters are composed of the radical 女 (woman/wife) with the phonetic element 螢 (firefly) abbreviated. The character *níng* (嫇) is sometimes written as *pín* (嬪) in the scriptures, which is an error in transcription.

*Táo* (upper radical: *hào*, reversed; lower radical: *táng*, *láo*): The *Yùpiān* states that "to wail and *táo*" means to weep loudly. In the *Zhouyì*, it appears as "first wailing and *táo*. The *Jìxùn* explains it as the sound of pain. The *Wénzìdiǎn* says it is formed from *xī* and has *hào* as its phonetic.
"Many twitches" (shuǎn): the first character is pronounced *chuō* (as in *chuāng-chuō*) and the second is pronounced *lún* (as in *rùn-lún*);

it refers to the eyes moving without cause. 5. Fascicle Five. "Iron wedge" (*tiě gē*): the character for *gē* is pronounced like *yíng* (as in *fēng-yíng*); it refers to a wooden stake or wedge used for marking sounds, also written as *yì*.

*Kūn* (髠): The upper radical is *wù* (兀). The *Shuowen* states it means "shaved hair," formed with the radical *biāo* (髟) and the phonetic *wù*. *Biāo* is pronounced *bìyáo* or *shān*; *tīng* (聽) is also pronounced *yìfǎn*. *Yì* (杙):

Pronounced *yì* (upper radical *yùn*, *jífǎn*). The *Kaosheng* states it means "a wooden peg. The *Shuowen* says it is formed with the radical *mù* (木) and the phonetic *yì*. The text here uses *yì* (釴) with the radical *jīn* (金), which refers to a handle on a cauldron and does not carry this meaning.

The king suddenly (*xū*) one day gave rise to a wholesome mind that permeated all things. "Suddenly" (*xū*) means to arise abruptly; it is a compound character formed from the semantic components of *yán* (flame) and *qiàn* (deficiency). "One handful" (*yī cuō*;

*cuō* pronounced *cāng kuò* according to the *Zuǒzhuan* commentary by Du Yu, meaning to gather together); if it were read with a different tone, it would not accord with the intent of the scripture. The *Jíhuì* states that it refers to gathering with both hands, or sometimes gathering with a vessel. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "zuì" (*zuì*).

*Qigē* (乞𠣏): According to the *Cāngjié piān*, it means to beg for alms or to seek. The *Shuōwén* states that it is composed of the radicals "death" (亡) and "person" (人); if a person's wealth and goods are lost, they then beg and plead (*qígài*). The pronunciation of *gē* is *gǎi-hái* (改孩), and the pronunciation of *kài* is *wǒ-gài* (我蓋).

*Tian-dan* (恬憺): The first character, *tian*, is pronounced with the combined finals *die* and *jian*. In the *Shangshu*, it means "peaceful ease"; in the *Fangyan*, it means "stillness. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xin*) and the phonetic element "suan" (*tian*) in abbreviated form. The second character, *dan*, is pronounced with the finals *tan* and *lan*. Gu Yewang states that it refers to a state where the mind and will are peaceful and settled, being *dandan* (恬然) and leisurely tranquil.
*Pò* (pronounced with the initial *p* and final *-o*, reversed): according to the *Shuowen*, this is the character for "impossible.

*Tìjì* (the radical *tì* pronounced *kuí-wěi*): according to the commentary, this means the heart is agitated; it means to be startled. It is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) with the phonetic component "season" (*jì*).
*Shì'ěr* (䑛耳): Pronounced *shí'ěr*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as taking food with the tongue; the version in the sutra as *chī* (蝭) is incorrect. *Zhēn* (榛木): Pronounced *zhì* (上仕臻反).
The *Guoyaya* defines it as trees growing in thickets. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mu*) and the phonetic element "qín" (*qín shēng*).
"Elephant-treading" (xiàngtà): "tà" is pronounced with the *tan* and *he* finals;

it means to trample with the feet. "Food-sticking" (shíyē): "yē" is pronounced with the *yan* and *jie* finals; according to the *Shuowen*, it means food being obstructed. It refers to food remaining in the chest and not descending. "Zhì" is pronounced with the *zhen* and *li* finals.
Regarding "che-lì" (轢): the phonetic transcription is *líng* (零). The commentary states it means "to crush with a wheel.

6. Volume Six, Part Six. Regarding "fó-zī" (佛頿): the phonetic transcription is *zǐ* (紫). *Yùnyīng* (韻英) states it refers to the beard (*zī-xū*). It is also written as "zī" (髭); the *Shuōwén* (說文) defines it as facial hair, specifically the hair around the mouth of the Tathāgata. The version in the sutra uses "yǎn" (𣯃), which does not form a valid character.

It is also called *chǐ* (with the rhyme *líng*). The *Yùnyīng* says it means "measure" (*chéng*); the *Kǎoshēng* says it means "to determine its lightness or heaviness. The *Shuōwén* explains it as "to weigh," written with the radical for grain (*禾*) and the phonetic *chèn*. The pronunciation of *chèn* is the same as above. The text in the Classics uses *píng*, which is incorrect.

*Huan* (pronounced *shàng xuán* with the *fǎn* [rhyme] of *xuán*). The *Liji* states: "Confucius shed tears and wept. The *Yunquān* says: "*Huàn* refers to the luster of dew. Regarding King Wuyou shedding tears: according to the *Jīngǔ zhèngzì*, this character is composed of the radical *shuǐ* (water) and the phonetic *xuán*.

*Pó* (剝): Pronounced *miào* (妙) with a retroflex *r* (󲦂) in reverse; according to the *Shuowen*, it refers to the awn of grain and the tip of a banner-pole, composed of the radical "grain" (*禾*) and the phonetic "shǎo" (*少*).

*Páitáng* (排搪): The first character is pronounced *bài mái* (敗埋) and the second has the sound *tāng* (湯). When King Aśoka wished to destroy stupas and monasteries, various benevolent deities, for the sake of protecting the Dharma, pushed and struck great mountains within the seas, pressing them down upon the king and his fourfold army, killing them all at once so that the destruction of the stupas and monasteries was averted.

"Pushing and squeezing" (tuīzè) is read as *tuí* with the tone of *huí*, and *xià* with the tone of *zhēnggé*. This refers to the aforementioned pushing and shoving of great mountains to come and press down upon the king's fourfold army.
"Mahinda" (*móshěnduó*; *shǐrěn* is read as *shǐrèn*) is the Sanskrit name for an Arhat.

The "deficient-basin bone" (quèpén gǔ) refers to the transverse bone above the clavicle on the right side of the Tathāgata’s body, located below the neck and upon the chest; it is the *śarīra*. Regarding the character for "thorn" (*jìcì*):

the upper part is pronounced *jìng* (as in *jìnglì*) and the lower part is pronounced *cì*; this is the correct orthography. The scriptural text that uses the character *cǎo* (grass) to form *jì* (thorn) is incorrect.
*Āmra* (pronounced *ā-mú-ló* with the second syllable following the *hòu* rhyme) is the name of the queen of the King of Siṃhala in the language of India.

*Cūḍikābandha* (pronounced *chōu-chā-shàng* with the first syllable following the *chū-liú* rhyme and the second following the *chā* rhyme) refers to the appearance of roots growing from the branches of the Bodhi tree.
"Ābhāṣa" (the *r* and *yao* are reversed; it is a name from the Sanskrit language).
"Jī" and "jiē" are both erroneous transcriptions in the scriptural text for the sound [of the original term].
"Hé" (pronounced with the *he* of *xìng* and *gé*) refers to the stone of the Bodhi tree fruit.
*Zhù* (pronounced *chú* with the initial *zhù* and final *-fǎn*) refers to several trees; it is formed from the radical *mù* (tree) and the phonetic *zhū*.

*Luán gǒng* (*lǔ huán fǎn* for the first character, *gōng lǒng fǎn* for the second) is explained as having the phonetic *kǎo*; it refers to curved *jī* (beam-heads), which are sloping, curved wooden supports.

Regarding "bì" (敝) in "bìfān" (弊幡): the *Zhuo* commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "bì" means "ruined" or "decayed. The lower character, pronounced "fán," is composed of "jīn" (巾, a cloth) and "bì" (敝). The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as "wéi" (㡀), composed of "bā" (八) and "jīn" (巾), depicting a garment that has been torn apart.
*Zhuàn* (zhǎn, with the first tone for the radical and the fourth tone for the suffix):

To float upon the water without a fixed destination; a vulgar character, its correct form is *fàn*. The *Shuowen* defines it as "overflowing," composed of the radical "water" and the phonetic "jiǎ. *Fàn* (yáng, with the fourth tone for the radical and the third tone for the suffix): A boat upon the waves. The *Shuowen* defines it as composed of the radical "water" and the phonetic "yàng"; the pronunciation of "yàng" is the same as above.

7. The seventh fascicle. *Kuī* (闚): The first character is pronounced as *quān* (犬) and *guī* (規); the second is pronounced as *gēng* (庚) and *zhū* (朱). The *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲) states it means "to peek. *Qù* (覷) is pronounced as *qīng* (青) and *yù* (豫). *Kuī* is also "to peek. The *Jí Xùn* (集訓) defines it as "stealthily looking. According to the *Shuōwén*, both characters are formed with the radical "gate" (*mén*) and are phonetic-semantic compounds.

*Zì* (自) is pronounced *páng* (龐) with a retroflex final; it means to seize and toss upward, lifting something high and throwing it to the ground. It is formed from the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) with the phonetic component *pú* (*pú*). *Dān* (檐) is pronounced *dá nán* (荅南);
it means to lift up, to carry on one's back, or to bear on the shoulders as a palanquin. The lower character, *guān* (官), refers to the outer coffin (*guò*).
*Nǔxù* (nǔ-mù): To suckle; it refers to food in the mouth that one chews while nursing an infant.
*Huòrán* (huāng-guō): Suddenly awakened or enlightened.
*Cūguǎng* (cū-měng): A coarse and fierce nature.
*Ruanchui* (耎脆): the first character is read as *shàng* with the phonetic *yuǎn*, and the second character is read as *xià* with the phonetic *chuán suì*.
It refers to being soft and fragile. *Ganjī* (感激): the *jī* is read as *jīng yì*.

It means the flowing of water. *Xiamíhóu* (瞎獼猴): the first character is read as *xiào bā*. The *Kǎoshēng* states that it means the eyes cannot see objects; it is composed of the radical "eye" (*mù*) and the phonetic "harm" (*hài*).

The character "ji" (集), meaning "to gather," is pronounced with the radical "mi" (米) and the phonetic "mao-hou" (矛候). The *Jixun* states that it means "to collect things"; the *Shuowen Jiezi* says it means "to exchange goods. It is composed of "yuan" (夗) and "bei" (貝), a character formed from both shape and sound.
"Xiè" (螫): the lower character is pronounced with the *shēng* (initial) *yì* (亦) and the *fǎn* (rhyme) *xié* (邪). The *Shuowén* says it means "a worm that moves by secreting poison. "Jiūsù" (拘鎖):
the upper character is pronounced *jù* (俱) and the lower is *sāngguǒ* (桑果). It is a term from the Sanskrit language (*vaṃśa*). "Bìjué" (躃絕):

the upper character is pronounced with the *pí* (毘) and *yì* (亦) rhymes. It means "to fall prostrate and break one's body. It is a *zhuǎnzhù* (transferred-notation) character derived from the radical "foot" (*zú*) and the phonetic "bì" (*bì*).

"Xūmó" (須摸) is the name of the celestial being Kiṃnara in the Sanskrit language; those who transcribed and orally transmitted the sutras have rendered it quite inaccurately by interpreting it according to their own whims. It is likely that "xū" has the upper tone (level tone), while "mó" has the lower tone (departing tone), with the latter pronounced as *mo* with the *hu* rhyme.
"Śuǎn-dòng" (蠕動): "śuǎn" is pronounced as *yǐn* (𨳝尹反); it refers to the movement of insects. (8) Eighth Fascicle, Part 8. "Shòu" (售):

The lower radical is pronounced as *shòu*. The *Yùnyīng* states: "To sell goods so that they are taken away. It means to transact. The *Yùnquán* states: "To sell goods in abundance. According to the *Gōnjīn Zhèngzì*, this character is composed of the radical "bird" (*zhuī*) and the phonetic "mouth" (*kǒu*), and is also a semantic compound.

*Chandi* (羼提): The first character is pronounced *shā* (上察簡反) and the second is pronounced *dì* (下音弟兮反). This is a transliteration of the Sanskrit term *kṣānti-pāramitā*, referring to the name of a rishi.

*Tóngzhēn* (同臻): The first character is pronounced *chī* (櫛詵反) and the second is pronounced *zhēn* (至也聚也). In ancient texts, it was written as *èr zhì* (從二至作臸). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of *zhì* (至) and the phonetic element *qín* (秦). *Zhǐ* (櫛): The pronunciation is *zhuāngsè* (莊瑟反). *Shēn* (詵): The pronunciation is *sè zhēn* (瑟臻反).

Regarding the character *xiàn* (眴), the *Xuankuan Fan* (玄絹反) and the *Kaosheng* (考聲) state that it means "the movement of the eyes," and it is also written as *shù* (䀏). Both characters are composed with the "eye" radical (*mù*). Although many classical texts use *shù* (䀏), the pronunciation given for *xiàn* (眴) as *shùn* (舜) is incorrect because its etymological source is not understood; other instances should be treated similarly.

*Zhí* (戢): Pronounced *zī* (澀反). In the *Mao Shi*, it means "to gather. Zheng’s commentary (*Zhengjian*) states it means "parsimony. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "concealing weapons," composed of the radical *go* (戈) with the phonetic *qī* (咠); *qī* is pronounced *qīn xí* (侵習反). *Zān* (簪): Pronounced *zhuāng yīn* (莊音反). The *Mao Shi* states that *zhí* means "to gather. Zheng’s commentary says it means "parsimony. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as "concealing weapons," using the character *qī* (咠) as its phonetic component; *qī* is pronounced *qīn xí* (侵習反). *Zān* (簪) is pronounced *zhuāng yīn* (莊音反).

Huìhuì (潰潰): The phonetic transcription is *huì* (會). The commentary states it means "cavernous" (*xué*) or "dispersed" (*sàn*). It is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic element "guì" (*guì*).

Fǎngfú (髣髴): The upper character is pronounced *fǎng* (芳罔反) and the lower is *fèi* (妃未反). The commentary states it is a sound indicating that something is seen but not clearly discerned. The *Yùnyīng* says it means "chaotic. The *Yùnyuán* says it is an expression used when a time is about to arrive.
*Āvila* (ā-yú): According to the *Zìshū*, it refers to foul, stagnant mud in a pool where water does not flow; long-settled mud is called *āyú*.
*Yīnzhài* (yīn-zhài): It refers to the severity of a disease.
"Zhǐzhuǎ" (指爪) [the "zhǎo" is pronounced with the retroflex *jia*]: this is a pictograph representing the fingernail. The character used in the classics, "zuò" (作), means to scratch;

it is a vulgar form. "Zìjué" (自攫) [the "jué" is pronounced with the *yue* rhyme]: to seize or claw at one's own body with one's own hands and nails, tearing the skin and flesh until blood flows. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "tǐ" (扟) means to scratch; it is composed of "shǒu" (手) and "qú" (瞿). Its pronunciation is the same as above. "Yuè" (籰) has the pronunciation "wángyuē" (王約).
"Quǎnquē (捲屈)" means curled up and not extended; it is pronounced with the "yuán" (圓) and "fǎn" (反) finals.
"Yànguāng" (燄光) is pronounced with the "yàn" (閻) and "jiàn" (漸) finals, meaning "flame-light"; the version of the Sūtra that uses "liàn" (僉作㷿) is incorrect.

"Guǎnyī" (葌衣) is pronounced with the "jiǎn" (音簡) and "yán" (顏) finals. According to the *Yùpiān*, it is a fragrant herb; the *Shuōwén* says it grows on Mount Wúlín and is a soft grass suitable for weaving into a grass garment, also called a "two-layered robe" (*liǎng yī*).
*Hǎn-yì* (欣懌) means also "joyful. *Jī-yì* (羈伇): the first character is pronounced with the initial *yí* (宜) and the final *fǎn* (反); it means a tether, a bond, or a succession. *Tiǎo* (挑):

the body of the character is pronounced *yáo* (姚); it means to probe or extract. One probes and extracts using awls, knives, and the like; it follows the radical for "hand" (*shǒu*) and takes *zhào* (兆) as its phonetic component. *Jué* (抉): the pronunciation is *yuān-yuè* (淵悅).
*Zìyán*: the first character is pronounced *dān* (with the tone of *gān*).
It means to carry on one's shoulders. *Lǎomào*: the second character is pronounced *máo bào*. It means senility and forgetfulness;
it is a vulgar character. *Lìchóng*: the pronunciation is *lài*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it is like a *jī* (a type of shellfish), a carapaced insect found in rivers and seas.

*Bēn* (上本門反, *shàng běn mén fǎn*): The sound is like that of *kǎo*. It means to run. Today it is written as *bēn*. According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to a herd of oxen running. It is a compound character (*huìyì*) formed from three "ox" radicals.
*Yáodǔ* (都古反, *dū gǔ fǎn*): It means to see.

Volume Nine, Chapter Nine. "Yìgè" (衣裓): The lower radical is *gēn* (剋, reversed); it is a phonetic transcription of the sound *gè*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is composed of the radical for "clothing" (*yī*) and the phonetic *jiè* (戒).

"Tòngyǎng" (痛痒): The lower radical is *yáng* (音羊, reversed); it refers to wind [affecting] the skin and flesh. It is composed of the radical for "sickness" (*niè*, 疒) and the phonetic *ní'è* (尼戹, reversed).
"Pào" (pronounced with the *pó* and *máo* finals): The dictionary explains this as a bubble floating on water; it is composed of the radical "water" and the phonetic "bāo.
"Ōuhēshā" (the first syllable pronounced with the *ā* and *hóu* finals): This is a transliteration of a Sanskrit term (*audārika*) referring to various Buddha-lands. It is not a literal Chinese word.
*Zihuǐ* (訿毀): The upper character *zī* is the opposite of *cī* (資); it refers to malicious abuse, defamation, and humiliation. *Bènmiàn* (坌面):

The upper character *bèn* is pronounced with the *mén* rhyme; according to the *Shuowen*, it means dust or dirt, or to smear with filth. It may also be written as *fèn*, taking *tǔ* (土) as the radical and *fēn* (分) as the phonetic.

"Dī" (dǐng lì fǎn): The *Shuowen* states this means a drop of water. It is composed of the radical "water" (shui) with the phonetic element "shāng" (shāng shēng). The pronunciation of "shāng" is as stated above. Its occurrence in the sutra as "tì" (tì) is incorrect.

"Zhǐzhuó" (zhǐ zhuó cháng zhuó fǎn): The *Kao* states this means to select or discern. It is composed of the radical "hand" (shou) with the phonetic element "dí" (dí shēng). The pronunciation of "dí" is "zhái" (zhái), derived from the "feather" (yu) radical.
"𢶏" (sǎo) means to scoop up; its lower phonetic component is pronounced "gōu. "㪻" (juàn) means to draw water;

according to the *Guǎngyá*, "㪻" means to ladle out (*shū*); according to the *Shuowén*, "㪻" means a measure, composed of the radical "斗" with the phonetic "䜌," where "䜌" is pronounced "lì zhuān. The text's reading as "卷" (*juǎn*) is incorrect.

*Piāo* (漂): Upper radical *zhōu* (舟), upper phonetic *pǐ* (匹) with a retroflex *yáo* (遙) reversal. The *Yùpiān* says it means "drifting" (*piāoliú*); the *Shuōwén* says it means "to float" (*fú*). It is composed of the water radical and the phonetic *piào* (票).

The version of the scripture using the character *cùn* (寸) is incorrect. Section 10, Volume 10. *Bōtáo* (播鼗): Lower radical *dào* (道) with a lateral *páng* (旁) reversal. Zheng’s commentary agrees. According to the *Lǐjì*, the *tàogǔ* (鼗鼓) is a small hand-drum with a handle held by a person; as they shake it, the leather ears hanging on the sides strike against each other to produce sound. This is a word formed from both its shape and its sound.

*Shì* (upper tone, pronounced *sì*) means to give food to birds and beasts; according to the *Shuowen*, it means provisions (*liáng*). It is a compound character formed by combining the radical *shí* (food) with the semantic component *rén* (person).

The *Jīng* (Scripture) writes it as *yí*; this is incorrect. *Juémiànkuàngyuè* (also read as *yuè*, with the phonetic *yù* and *yuē* combined): *kǎo shēng* states that *tuó* means to seize. *Yì* refers to grasping with the hand; thus, it means to clutch and seize someone’s face. This is a character formed by combining the semantic component *xíng* (form) with the phonetic component *shēng*.

"Vánmài" (販賣) means to buy low and sell high. The lower part, "bàifèi" (敗), is the radical; it is composed of "chū" (出) and "mǎi" (買). The common usage today, which employs "tǔ" (土), is a corruption and abbreviation.

Regarding the characters for *guǒluò* (fruit and melons): the upper character, *guǒ*, is a vulgar form. The lower character, *luò*, is pronounced with the initial *lú*. That which grows on trees is called *guǒ*; that which grows on the ground is called *luò*. It is composed of the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) and two melon shapes, forming a character based on both form and sound.

The character *yǒng* (鷹) is pronounced with the initial *shàng máo hòu* (上矛候) and is used in the common parlance for trade (*huòyì*). It is formed with *mǎo* (卯) below; it signifies possessing knowledge of things. The lower part is pronounced with the initial *yì shēng* (億矝). It refers to a bird of prey capable of seizing rabbits. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "bird" (*niǎo*) and the phonetic element "wild goose" (*yàn*).

Pāngpèi (滂沛): The first character is pronounced pǔ (with the *máng* rhyme), and the second has the sound pèi; it means a great flow of water overflowing. It is a phono-semantic compound character (*xíngshēng*). Jīròu (肌肉):
The first character has the sound jī, and the second has the sound ròu (with the *róngliù* rhyme); it is a radical-based character (*zhèngtǐ*). The vulgar form is not the same as liù (六).
*Chuāngyí*: "Chuāng" (上) is pronounced *chuāng* with the rhyme *chuāng*; it means flesh being torn away. "Yí" (下) is pronounced *yí*;
it is a variant name for a sore (*chuāng*). *Mílù*: "Mí" (上) is pronounced *měibēi*;
it is a species of deer. *Xióngpī*: "Xióng" (上) is pronounced *xióng*; "Pī" (下) is pronounced *bēi*; it is larger than a bear.

"Diao" (上音雕): A large bird capable of eating deer, wild boar, foxes, and rabbits; "jiu" (下音就) is its phonetic component. "Zong" (󱹄猥, 上宗董反): According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to bind" or "a multitude.

According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to gather and collect"; it is formed with the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "hu" (忽). The character used in the sutra is "zong" (捴), which is a vulgar form. "Wui" (下烏悔反): It means "irregular" or "excessive"; it is formed with the radical "dog" (犬) and the phonetic "wei" (畏).

*Shòu cī*: The upper character is pronounced *shū zòu* (with the radical *shù*). It is a vulgar form; its correct orthography is *𤸃*, which has long since fallen out of use. The lower character is pronounced *cí* and means a sore. When black hair grows on the flesh, it is called a *cī*.
*Qiāng*: (two tones, also level tone) means the head strikes the ground. *Nùrán*: (upper radical *nǚ*, sixth tone;
according to the *Fāngyán*, *nù* means shame; it denotes a flushed face, a feeling of inner guilt, and disgrace. It is composed of the "heart" radical with *ér* as the phonetic.)

*Zhòng* (𠊲眾) is pronounced with the upper radical *dùn* (鈍) and the suffix *nè* (訥). It means to strike or collide. *Kuì* (爴) was formerly pronounced with the upper radical *guǐ* (鬼) and the suffix *bì* (碧).

According to the intent of the sutra, this refers to the punishment of *zhé* (磔), pronounced with the upper radical *zhāng* (張) and the suffix *gé* (革). One is to be moved to a crossroads where the multitude may point at, hack, and humiliate them; anciently it was said that "punishment by *zhé*" refers to such a crime.

"Kāi-huò": "huò" is pronounced *guǎng* (反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means clouds dispersing; its correct radical form is *yǔ* (rain) with *zhuī* (隹), written as *huò*. The *Shuowen* defines *zhuī* as a bird flying in the rain, making a *huò-huò* sound. The text here uses *huò* with the radical *huǒ* (fire), which is incorrect; it is a scribal error.

"Gōu-gǎng" (溝港): "gōu" is pronounced as in "gǒu-dài" (苟待), and "gǎng" is pronounced as in "xiāng-xiàng" (巷巷); these are both alternative names for water channels, both following the radical "water" (氵) for their semantic component and the phonetic components.
"Zhāng-zǐ" (樟梓): "zhāng" has the pronunciation of "zhāng" (章), and "zǐ" has the pronunciation of "sī-sǐ" (死死); these are both names for large trees found in the south.

The character 氈 (zhān) has "zhāng" as its first radical and "rán" as its second; the lower part is "jīng" with the tone "lì. The received text writes it as 旃, which is incorrect. The *Jixùn* states that it refers to a woolen cloth; the lower part is sometimes written as 󱻟, meaning a mat woven from wool.
The character for "hun" (溷) is pronounced with the first tone (an upper tone). It means turbid; it is not clear. 11. The eleventh fascicle.

Regarding the character "ji" (屐), it is pronounced *jü* (with the *ju* and *ni* tones reversed); this refers to the modern-day toothed sandal. The *Zishu* states that "ji" belongs to the category of footwear (*li*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "Footwear with wooden soles; it is a contraction of 'li' with the phonetic element 'zhi'. The text uses "li" (履), which is a vulgar form of the character.

*Chīxiào* (嗤笑) refers to the upward-turning hair on the upper teeth; it denotes the manner of playful laughter. The *Mao Shi* states it is the manner of a mind and will that is harmonious and joyful. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* explains that it is composed of the radical "mouth" (口) with the phonetic "chī" (蚩); the pronunciation of *chī* is as stated above.

*Jue* (掘): The *Qun xu* (群欻) glossary reads "jue" as *chua* (欻). The *Yupian* (玉篇) states that "jue" means to thrust a spade into the ground to excavate it; the *Guangya* (廣雅) defines it as "chuan" (穿, to pierce). The *Wenzi dian* (文字典) explains that the character is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "qu" (屈). Below it, "kanghen" (康很) is the reading for the phonetic. According to the *Kao sheng* (考聲), "ken" (墾) means to plow. Guo's commentary on the *Fangyan* (方言) states that "geng ken" (耕墾) involves exerting effort while simultaneously using a mattock. In the standard characters of antiquity and today, the character is composed of the radical "earth" (土) and the phonetic "kan" (豤).
*Jiè* (pronounced *zhài*, with the tone of *kǎo*) means to bite; the *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *zé*.
It is also pronounced *chēngzé* (with the tone of *pó*, *mó*). This was already explained previously in the fifth fascicle.
The character for *mārga* (monkey) is pronounced with the initial *mòu* and the final *qián*; it was already explained in the seventh fascicle.

Regarding the character for *kāṅ* (snare), the abbreviated collection of characters reads *kāṅ*, which refers to setting a trap on a road. Examining its phonetic component, it uses the radical for "bow" (*gōng*) because one uses a bow to snare birds and beasts. In the standard orthography of both ancient and modern times, it follows the radical for "bow" and takes *jīng* as its phonetic.

Regarding the character *mǎnǎo* (top: *má*, bottom: *nǎo*): the phonetic gloss states that *mǎnǎo* resembles jade and has black patterns; it is also called "spotted jade" (*bānyù*). Lexicons state that *mǎnǎo* is a stone second only to jade. The *Wenzi Dianshuō* explains that both characters are written with the "stone" radical (*shí*) and the phonetic component *mǎ* (or *máo*), with the same pronunciation as above; alternatively, it may be written with the "jade" radical (*yù*) as *mǎnǎo*.

12. The Twelfth Fascicle. "Yuji" (雨霽): the second character is read as *ji* (齊) with the retroflex *qì*. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states that "the cessation of rain is called *ji*. Examining the phonology, it means clear and bright. The *Shuowen Jiezi* also defines it as the cessation of rain, composed of the radical "rain" (*yù*) and the phonetic component "ji" (*qì*).

"Jiānhuì (奸穢): the first character is pronounced yàn (澗) and the second is pronounced fèi (廢). In dictionaries, it means 'unclean. According to the standard characters of ancient and modern times, it means 'filth' (穢惡). It is composed of the radical 禾 (grain) with the phonetic 歲; it may also be written as 薉, which is likewise correct."

*Wú-héng* (誣撗): The upper character (*wú*) is pronounced *móu*; Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that *wú* means "to deceive. Examining its phonetic component, it also carries the meanings of "to slander" and "to be crooked. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states that *wú* is equivalent to "arbitrary" (*wàng*) or "to ensnare" (*wǎng*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to add words," taking the character *wū* (巫) as its phonetic; *wū* has the same pronunciation as above, namely *huánghuáng-mèng-fǎn*. The *Yunlüe* defines it as "that which comes from what is not right. The *Shiji* uses it in the sense of "licentiousness. Examining the sound, it is said to mean "not following principle. Regarding the standard characters of past and present: it follows the hand radical (*shǒu*) with the phonetic *huáng*. In the received texts, it is sometimes written with the wood radical (*mù*) as *héng* (橫), which is also acceptable for dual use.

In the lower section of the character *bó* (蜜搏), *luán* is the phonetic component; according to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means "to dig with the hands" or "to join together. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical *shǒu* (hand) and the phonetic *zhuān*.
The characters for *pú sà* (溥𩠐)—the former pronounced *pǔ*—are names for a Bodhisattva and are composed of the character *fú* (*fēn*).

"Perilous and fragile" (危脆): the second character is pronounced *chuan* with the *rui* rhyme. According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means "brittle. According to the *Shuowen*, "fragile" (*cui*) refers to flesh that is soft and easily broken; it is composed of the radical "flesh" (*rou*) and the phonetic element "abbreviated *jue*" (*jue-sǒng*), while "soft" (*ruǎn*) is pronounced *ér-yuǎn*.

*Jin* (筋): The upper radical is *jin* (斤). In the *Zhouli*, the Physician is tasked with "nurturing the sinews" (*yang jin*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "the strength of muscle and sinew. That which follows the bamboo radical (*zhu*) refers to things that possess abundant sinews; the character following the strength radical (*li*) represents the form of the sinew itself. The version in the [standard] Canon text that uses the grass radical (*cao*) to form *qiu* (荕) is incorrect.

Xī-má (蝦蟆): the first character is pronounced with the "jiā" rhyme and the second with the "bā" rhyme of the "mǎ" rhyme group. According to the *Cāngjié piān*, the shrimp-ma is an aquatic insect; it is also called the *chánqú* (蟾蠩). The *Shuōwén jiězì* writes it as "xiā-má" (蝦蟇), both characters being composed of the "insect" radical (*chóng*).
*Yíngluò* (瓔珞): The first character is pronounced with the initial *yì* (益) and the final *yíng* (盈); the second character is pronounced *láng* (郎) and *gè* (各).

It is a compound character consisting of the semantic radical "jade" (玉) and the phonetic component. 13. Volume Thirteen. *Yùbēi* (鬱鞞): The second character is pronounced *bì* (陛) and *mí* (迷). It is a term from the Sanskrit language.

*Chouhuì* (愁憒): The second character is pronounced with the *gǔ* and *duì* rhymes. It is a homophone for *kǎo*. It means to be distressed or troubled; according to the *Cāngjié piān*, it refers to mental confusion.

It is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "guì" (*guì*). *Jīngjué* (驚覺): The second character is pronounced with the *jiāo* and *xiào* rhymes, or as the character itself. It is a homophone for *jue*. It means to awaken from sleep. Gu Yewáng states it refers to sleeping; the *Shuōwén* defines it as waking up. It is composed of the radicals "to see" (*jiàn*) and a simplified form of "to learn" (*xué*) as the phonetic. This is a character used by extension (*jièyīn*).

*Yù niè* (欲齧): "niè" is pronounced with the *jiàn* (研) and *jié* (結) finals. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "niè" means "to bite" (*chìshì*) and is composed of the radical "teeth" (*chǐ*) with the phonetic "kuài" (*kuài*). The pronunciation of "kuài" is *qiān* (慳) with the *bā* (八) final. In the classics, it is written as "niè" with the "mouth" radical (*kǒu*), which is a vulgar character and not the correct form.

The character for *zhì* (緻) has the radical *móu* (矛) and the phonetic *hòu* (候). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to trade" or "to sell," composed of the radical *bèi* (貝) and the phonetic *yí* (彖), which is an ancient form of the character *mǎo* (夘). The lower part [of the second character] has the radical *chí* (持) and the phonetic *lì* (利). In the commentary on the *Liji*, Zheng [Xuan] states that *zhì* means "dense" or "compact. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *mì* (糸) and the phonetic *zhì* (致); it is a character formed by combining shape and sound.

"Under the rock cave (kū)," with the hair shaved off; "reversed bone. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that a "cave" (*kū*) is an underground chamber. According to the *Shenglèi*, it is where a rabbit lies hidden. The *Gōngjīn zhèngzì* says it is written with the radical for "cave" (穴) and the phonetic "quǎn" (屈), or it may be written as "jué" (堀).

*Dàng* (盪): Upper radical *dǎng* (黨), reversed; Du [Yan]’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "To shake and sway. It also means "to move. The *Shuowen* says: "To wash a vessel. It is composed of the radical *míng* (皿) with the phonetic *tāng* (湯).

*Chù* (黜): Lower radical *chūn* (椿), reversed; Fan Ning’s *Jijie* states: "To dismiss and retreat. Kong [Yingda]’s commentary on the *Shangshu* says: "To offend. Du [Yan]’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* says: "To diminish" or "to banish. The *Shuowen* says: "To degrade. It is composed of the radical *hēi* (黑) with the phonetic *chū* (出). *Xia* (下): Lower radical *chāngzhī* (昌隻), reversed; the *Guliang Zhuan* says: "To point at. The *Boyaya* says: "To push.
