Regarding "Lin-yi" (臨沂) in the case of the "Fish Machine" (魚機) rebellion: Lin-yi refers to the Lin-yi Commandery of Yi-zhou in Dong-hai. The *Lu* (錄) states that it is the place name from which the clan origin of Xiao Daocheng, the Emperor Gao of the Qi dynasty, derives. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the character for "Yi" (沂) is composed of the radical "water" and the phonetic "jin" (斤), meaning the Yi River originates from the southern side of Mount Tai in the east and flows into the Si River.

"Extensively search for the eminent and talented. Regarding "shàngsè" (上色), Zōu Fǎn [reads it as such]; Dù’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states that "sǒu" (󱨯) means "to examine" (*jiǎn*). *Shēnglèi* says it means "to take up"; *Kǎoshēng* says it means "to seek" (*suǒ*). The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radical "hand" (手) with "sǒu" (叜) as the phonetic component; "sǒu" is pronounced *sūgǒu*. The following instances of "sǒuchǎi" (󱨯採) and so forth are all the same; recording it as "sōu" (搜) is the vulgar form. Next is "máo" (毛): the *Mao Shī Zhuàn* says "máo" (髦) means "the eminent" (*juàn*). Guō’s commentary on the *Eryā* says: "The talent among scholars is like the fine hair (*háo*) among the fur (*máo*). The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radical "hair" (髟) with "máo" (毛) as the phonetic component. "Jùn" (儁) is pronounced *jùn*; "biāo" (髟) is pronounced *piāo*.
Yu Xie (庾頡): "Xie" is pronounced as *xián* (結反); this is the name of a Palace Attendant (*shìzhōng*) of the Qi dynasty.

Liu Qiu (劉虬): The character "Liu" follows the *Shuowen Jiezi*, being composed of "mao" (夘) and "zhao" (釗) above, and "qi" (耆) with the "you" (由) pronunciation below; this is the name of a recluse from Jingzhou of the Qi dynasty.
Zhīlín was Liu Zhīlín of the Liáng dynasty, who rose in rebellion at Lìzhèn. *Zǔ* (祖): Pronounced *shàng zū* (古反). The *Erya* states:

"The ancestor (*zǔ*) is the beginning. Gù Yěwáng says: "The father who is the origin is the ancestor. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Ancestor (*zǔ*) is the ancestral temple; it is composed of the radical 'deity' (示) with the phonetic 'qù' (且). The character below is pronounced *ní* (泥禮反); this is a vulgar form. The correct form is written as *ní* (禰). Zhèng Zhòng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "The *ní* is the temple of the father. Whether ancient or modern, the correct character is composed of the radical 'deity' (示) with the phonetic 'ní' (爾).

The character *luǒ* (覶) in *luǒlǚ* (覶縷): the upper radical is read as *lùgē* (魯戈). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *luǒ* means "to look with care. In the standard characters of the present day, it is composed of the "treasure" (*bèi*) radical and the phonetic *làn* (𤔔). The pronunciation of *làn* (𤔔) is *luàn*. In ancient scripts, *làn* (𤔔) was written with the "hand" (*yòu*) radical; Li Si later changed it to the "inch" (*cùn*) radical to form *làn* (𤔔), both being identical in meaning. The lower character [of *lǚ*] is read as *lúnzhǔ* (倫主).

The father is *Tóng* (肜), pronounced *yù* (育) with the reversed [radical]. *Tiě* (鐵) is pronounced *lòu* (鏤) with the reversed *shàngtiān* (上天) [phonetic]; in standard orthography it is the character *tiě*. The *Shuowen* states: "Black metal; composed of the radical *jīn* (金) and the phonetic *jié* (結), pronounced *tiánjié* (田結); the lower part is *lóuhòu* (樓候). The *Shuowen* further states: "*Lòu* (鏤) refers to hard iron that can be engraved; composed of the radical *jīn* (金) and the phonetic *lóu* (婁)."

*Chǐ*: Pronounced *zhī* (with the *ěr* tone). In the *Cāngjié piān*, it is written with the radical for "stone" (*shí*) as 砥; it refers to a whetstone for sharpening. The record also contains 厎, which is identical. *Dì*:

Pronounced *jù* (with the *dīng* and *lì* tones). *Mò*: Pronounced *chóu* (upper part *méng* and *běi*; the record [states] it follows the radical for "speech," which is incorrect). The lower part is pronounced *zhōu*; the record writes it as 詶, which is incorrect.

"Ti-qie" (提挈): the second character is read as *qié* (結反). He Xiu’s commentary on the *Gongyang zhuan* states: "Ti-qie means 'to lift' (*ti*). The *Shuowen jiezi* defines it as "suspended holding," composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "kua" (*kuān-bā-fǎn*). The pronunciation of "kua" is *kuān-bā-fǎn*.

"Yán-hé" (研覈): The first character is pronounced with the *ni* rhyme (霓) and the second with the *héng-gé* rhyme (衡革). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Hé" (覈) means to examine and verify actual facts. The *Hanshu* says: "The duty of careful examination and verification follows the ancient laws. The *Shenglèi* states: "It means to review. The correct form for both ancient and modern usage is written with "Xi" (覀) as the radical and "Jiao" (敫) as the phonetic. "Xi" (覀) is pronounced *ya-jia* (呀賈), and "Jiao" (敫) is pronounced *jing-li* (經歷).”
Correction: Regarding the character 訂 (dìng), the *Shuowen jiezi* states that "訂" means to deliberate and discuss; it is composed of the radical 言 (speech) with the phonetic element 丁 (dīng).

Regarding 炳 (bǐng), the *Guoyu* states that "炳" means great brilliance; the *Zhouyi* says, "The Great Man undergoes a transformation like a tiger, his patterns brilliant and radiant. The *Shuowen jiezi* states it is composed of the radical 火 (fire) with the phonetic element 丙 (bǐng), or it may be written as 昺.
The character *suí* (隨) is pronounced with the *péng* rhyme group (陌反). Regarding *tǎngdí* (蕩滌):

the upper character *tǎng* (蕩) is pronounced with the *tángdǎng* rhyme group (唐黨反). The Commentary on the Book of Documents (*Shūjì*) by Kǒng [Yù] states: "As for *tǎng*, it refers to water rushing forward and surging so as to wash away and clear out [impurities]. Dú Yǔ’s Commentary on the Zuǒ Zhuan states: "As for *tǎng*, it means to shake or move. According to the Shuowén Jiězì, it is composed of the radical *shuǐ* (water) and the phonetic *tāng* (𦳝), where the sound of *tāng* is *tālǎng* (他朗反).

*Tì-sì* (tears and snot). "Up" is pronounced *tiān* (天); "down" is pronounced *xià* (下) with the rhymes *fǎn* (反) and *sī* (恣). The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry) states: "That which issues from the eyes is called *tì*; that which issues as liquid from the mouth is called *sì*. Gu Yewáng states: "*Sì* is simply *tí* (nasal mucus). According to the *Shuowén*, both characters for *tì* and *sì* are written with the radical "water" (*shuǐ*); *dì* (弟) and *sì* (四) serve as their phonetic components.

*Pāngtuó* (the first character pronounced *pǔ máng* and the second *táng hé*): The *Guǎngyá* states that "pāngpāng" describes the appearance of flowing water. According to the *Shuowén*, both characters "pāng" and "tuó" are written with the "water" radical (*shuǐ*) on the left and the phonetic element "bié" (*bié*) on the right.

Regarding "guǎn" (莞) in the phrase "guǎn xí" (莞席), Huánguān Fǎngù and Yě Wáng state that the guǎn is similar to the pú (蒲) reed but is round. According to the *Gōngjīn Zhèngzì* (Correct Characters of Antiquity and Today), the guǎn grass can be used to make mats. It is composed of the radical "廾" (meaning "to hold") and the phonetic "完" (huán); "廾" is pronounced "cǎo."

The character for *yù* (芋) [is composed of] "grass" (*cǎo*) above and "yú" (于) with the phonetic "gòu" (句) above it; according to the standard characters of ancient and modern times, it refers to a plant with large leaves whose tuberous roots are startlingly large, hence it is called *yù*, taking "grass" as the radical and "yú" as the phonetic. The character for *ráng* (穰) [is composed of] "grass" above and "zhuó" (酌) with the phonetic "jiǎn" (冉) below; it is also a root vegetable.

In "yìjiǎn" (翼鞬), the character jiǎn (鞬) is pronounced with the *gē* (羯) rhyme-group (the *yán* [言] final). Dú Yù’s commentary on the *Zuò Zhuàn* states: "A *jiǎn* is that by which one stores bows and arrows. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical "metal" (*qié*) and the phonetic "jiàn" (建).

In "zèpī" (櫛批), the upper character *zè* (櫛) is pronounced with the *cè* (側) rhyme-group and the *sè* (瑟) final, while the lower character *pī* (批) is pronounced with the *pín* (頻) rhyme-group and the *mì* (蜜) final; together they describe the appearance of being closely joined and continuous.

"Yan" (掩). [The character is pronounced with the initial *yān* and the final *jiǎn*. The *Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry* states: "Yan refers to the appearance of overcast clouds. The *Guǎngyá* states: "The Great Yin (the dark clouds). The *Shuowén* [explains it as] composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic "yǎn" (*shēng*). The *Guǎngcāng* writes it with the radical "rain" (*yù*) as 𠯗; the *Yùpiān* writes it with the radical "two hands" (*kòng*) as 弇. Their pronunciations and meanings are identical. [In this record, I follow the form with the radical "water," which is the common usage.]

*Pài* (with the second tone): The *Guǎngyǎ* states that when water flows out, it is called a *pài*. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "the oblique flow or branch of water; it is composed of the radical for water and the character 𠂢. The pronunciation and meaning of 𠂢 are identical to those of 派.

The character 鍒 (rú) is read as 如州反 (rú zhōu fǎn). The *Pīcāng* states that 鍒 means "to soften" (róu). It follows the radical 金 (metal) and takes 柔 (róu) as its phonetic component. To follow [the variant] 糅 (ròu), which is composed of 米 (grain), is incorrect; 糅 means "mixed rice," which is not its original meaning. *Ná* is read as 拏救反 (ná jiù fǎn); 糅 refers to mixed rice, which is not the primary sense [of the term].

"Grasping the willow branch with a grass-knife. The *Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry* states: "Grasping (*cāo*) is equivalent to picking up (*lǎn*). The *Cāngjié piān* states: "Grasping means holding fast. The *Guǎngyá* states: "It means to seize. In the standard characters of antiquity and today, it is written with the radical for "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic element "sāo" (pronounced *liú*, *yǒu*, or *fǎn*). In character dictionaries, it is correctly written as "willow" (*liǔ*), which is the name of a river. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical for "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic element "yǒu. The form used here [in the text] is "lù," which is a vulgar character.

The character for *bō* (盋) is pronounced with the first tone and the rhyme *wei* (未); in standard orthography, it is written as *bǎn* (𥁊). Fu Qian’s *Tōngsùwén* states: "The *bǎn* is the monastic vessel. The text of the *Lù* (Record) uses *bō* (鉢), which is a vulgar character. The second character, *wǎn* (盌), is pronounced with the third tone and the rhyme *kuǎn* (款). The *Fāngyán* states that in the regions between Song and Chu, what is called *hé* (盍) is termed *wǎn*. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of *míng* (皿, vessel) and the phonetic component *yuǎn* (夗); the pronunciation of *yuǎn* is *wàn* (菀).

Furthermore, regarding "cu" (殂), with the phonetic component *zú* (祚) and the radical *ěr* (爾): the *Erya* states that "cualuo" (殂落) means death. In the *Shuowen*, it is formed from the radical *dài* (歹, pronounced *gēn*) and the phonetic *qiě* (且).

Regarding "guǐ" (詭), with the phonetic component *guī* (歸) and the radical *wěi* (委): the *Huainanzi* states that "Sū Qín achieved one instance of sincerity through a hundred guǐ. The *Guoyá* states that "guǐsuí" (詭隨) means wickedness. In the *Shuowen*, it is defined as "to blame," formed from the radical *yán* (言) and the phonetic *wēi* (危).

Regarding "Duyè" (都鄴), the character for "yè" (鄴) is read as *jié* (劫) in the *Hànshū*. The *Hànshū* states that there is a county of Yè in Weijun; the *Shījì* records that Ximen Bao served as the Magistrate of Yè. As for "Duyè" (都鄴), this refers to the capital where the Wei Emperor resided. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "city" (邑) with "yè" (業) as its phonetic component.

The surname Mòqí (萬俟) is pronounced "wàn" with the tone of *mò* (墨), and "qí" (期) for the second character. According to the *Zhou Shu*, Mòqí is a Xianbei clan name. Mòqí Tiānyì was skilled in Sanskrit and was a translator of Buddhist scriptures.

5. Fifth Fascicle. *Gèng* (更): On the upper character, *gē* (革) and *héng* (衡) follow. Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states: "Gèng means 'to replace' (*dài*). Zhèng’s commentary on the *Lìjì* states: 'To change' (*yì*). The *Shuōwén* states: 'To alter' (*gǎi*). It is also said that the phonetic component is *xià* (下) and *mà* (罵). The *Wenziàn* explains: "*Bǐn* (󰊉) is like 'to grasp' (*bǎ*). The *Zuǒzhuan* says: 'Duke Wén first *bǐn*'—meaning he coerced the feudal lords and took hold of their affairs. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical *yuè* (月) with the phonetic *pǔ* (浦) and *mò* (莫). *Pǔ* is pronounced *pǔ mò* (浦莫), *xié* (脅) is pronounced *méi jié* (枚劫).

The character 󳋕 (fú) under the radical 雨 (rain) is read as *sù* (inverted). In the *Zìshū* (Dictionary of Characters), it is correctly written with 毓 (*yù*) as its phonetic component, forming 𩱱, which means "to sell. According to the *Shuowen*, it takes 𩰲 (*lì*) as its radical and 毓 (*yù*) as its phonetic; 𩰲 is pronounced *lì* and 毓 is pronounced *yù*.
The character 斌 (*bīn*) under the radical 文 (*wén*) is read as *bǐmín* (inverted); it is a personal name.
*Sengmeng* (僧勐): *Meng* (勐) is pronounced like *mǎng*. It is the name of a high monk; it is derived from *li* (力) and *méng* (孟). Regarding *zhixian* (智僊):

*xian* (僊) is pronounced with the *qian* (煎) rhyme. The *Guoyaya* states that *xian* means "transformation" (*hua*). The *Shiming* states that one who is old yet does not die is called a *xian*. The *Shuowen* defines it as a person who attains longevity, composed of the radical "man" (人) and the phonetic "qian" (䙴); the pronunciation of *qian* (䙴) is *qian* (遷), though the correct reading is *qian* (淺).

Regarding the character *chè* (轍): it is read as *liè* (列) with the retroflex initial. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "The ancient and modern correct orthography is from the radical *chē* (車) and the phonetic *chè* (徹) in abbreviated form. To write it with the radical *zú* (足) as *jiàn* (𨅊) is incorrect.

"An iron *qian* (鉆) for pulling up. [The *Shanhai jing*] says, "Mount Tiankui has much iron. The *Shuowen jiezi* states: "Iron (*tie*) is black metal; it is composed of the radical 'metal' (*jin*) and the phonetic 'zhi' (*zhi*), pronounced *tian-jie* (田結). It is read as *ci-jian-yang* (次儉嚴). The *Cangjie pian* states: "'Qian' (*qian*, 鉆) means to grip or hold together. The *Shuowen* further states: "It is an iron clamp (*tie-qian*, 銸); it is composed of the radical 'metal' and the phonetic 'zhan' (*zhan*), pronounced *nian-zhe* (黏輒). 'Qian' (*qian*, 鉗) is pronounced *ju-yan* (巨嚴), and the second character is read as *bai-ba* (白八). The *Shuowen* states: "'Ba' (*ba*, 拔) means to pull out; it is composed of the radicals 'hand' (*shou*) and 'ba' (*ba*), pronounced *pu-mo* (蒲末)."

*Luó* (the character for "deaf") is pronounced with the lower radical *jù* (qū fǎn). It is a term for the Sangha; according to dictionaries and phonetic studies, its sound is categorized under the "hair mat" (*máo xí*) group.

*Lóngwén* (the character for "deafness") is pronounced with the upper radical *lù* (dōng fǎn). The *Zuǒzhuan* states: "When the ears do not hear the harmony of the five notes, it is called deafness. Du Yu’s commentary notes: "Deafness implies darkness. The *Cāngjiépiān* states: "The ears have no hearing. The *Shuowén* explains that it is composed of the radical "ear" (*ěr*) and the phonetic component "dragon" (*lóng*).

"Gǔ" (in "gǔshì," where the first character is pronounced gūwǔ) refers to one who cannot distinguish between good and evil; the *Shangshu* commentary by Kong [Yuan] states that one whose eyes cannot discern what is beautiful or ugly is called "gǔ. Bao Xian’s commentary on the *Lunyu* states that "gǔ" means blind. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "eye" with "gu" as its phonetic.

"Bìxíng" (躄行) is pronounced with the *bì* (伇) rhyme. The *Lǐjì* states: "The mute, the deaf, the lame, and the *bì*. Gù Yěwáng says: "*Bì* refers to having withered and shriveled feet such that one cannot walk. In the *Gōngjīn zhèngzì*, it is written with the "foot" radical (*zú*) and the phonetic "bì" (*pì*). "Bō" (跛) is pronounced with the *bōmǎ* (波麼) rhyme.

*Fǐ* (匪): *qiú* (𡱈), with the phonetic transcription *xià qú lù fǎn*. The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (Mao Commentary on the Classic of Poetry) states: "Qiú is like 'curved' (*qū*). Zheng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states: "Qiú refers to 'divisions' (*fēn*, pronounced *qùshēng*). The *Dà Dài Lǐ* states: "The feudal lords each occupy their *qiú*," meaning they take their respective positions. The *Erya* states: "*Qiú* means division. The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of "mouth" (*kǒu*) below "one foot" (*chǐ*), with a "hook" (*gù*) above; it is also a pictographic character representing the movement of chess pieces on a board. *Gù* (句) has the phonetic transcription *gǔ hóu fǎn*.

*Yùchì* (鬱歭): The first character, *yù*, is pronounced with the *mùn* and *xū* rhymes. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Kaogongji* states that "it means not expanding or dispersing. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* says it is the appearance of vapors rising up. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it refers to trees growing in dense clusters; it is composed of the radicals for *jiù* (臼), *mì* (冖), and *fǒu* (缶), with *zhì* (𦙶) as its ornamentation. This describes how the flowers of the hundred grasses appear lush and flourishing from afar. The second character, *chí* (歭), is pronounced with the *ěr* rhyme. Gu Yewang states that "it means to stand still or hesitate, unable to move forward. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says "it means to linger or pause," composed of the radical for *zhǐ* (止) with *sì* (寺) as its phonetic component. *Chù* (躇) is pronounced with the *zhù* and *zhū* rhymes.
*Zhixuan* (pronounced *xuán*, with the rhyme of *jiàn*) is a monastic name.

*Qì* (pronounced *què*, with the rhyme of *lì*)—the *Mao Shī Zhuàn* states that *qì* means "to rest. *Cì* (pronounced *zhé*, with the rhyme of *yáng*)—the *Hànshū* states it is the name of the Qīngzhāng River, which originates in Shangdǎng Commandery. *Bīn* (pronounced *bì*, with the rhyme of *mín*)—Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* states that *bīn* refers to the edge of a riverbank.

*Jiàn* (Key). The upper character is pronounced *qián* with the *yǎn* rhyme. According to the *Zhouli* (Rites of Zhou), the Director of Gates (*Simen*) "holds the *jiàn*" for the purpose of opening and closing. Zheng’s commentary states: "*Jiàn* is synonymous with *zhuàng* (a bolt). The *Fangyan* says that east of the Guanzhong region it is called *jiàn*, while west of the Guanzhong region it is called *yào*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as being composed of the radical *jin* (metal) and the phonetic *jiàn*. The lower character is pronounced *yáo* with the *zhuó* rhyme. The *Yupian* states that the character composed of *jin* and *zuò* is *yào*, which is identical to *jiàn*. Lexicons also write it as *hè* with the radical *mén* (gate), which is likewise like a *guānjiàn* (door-bolt). The *Shuowen* further defines *hè* as "the bolt inserted beneath the gate," composed of the radical *mén* and the phonetic *yuè*. It shares the same meaning as *yào*. The recorded text uses *yào*, but the initial consonant of *zhuàng* is *mǔ*, and the rhyme of *yuè* is the same as above.

"Yin" (湮) is pronounced with the initials *yī* and the final *chén* (反). The *Erya* states that "yin" is equivalent to "luò" (to fall). The *Kaosheng* states it means "mò" (to sink). It is the name of a temple. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "water" (水) and the phonetic component "yin" (垔); the pronunciation of "yin" (垔) is *yīn*.

The character for *yù* (carriage/palanquin): In the *Shuowen*, it is explained as "crossing a barrier by lifting both ends together. The phonetic component *shēng* also means "to lift. According to the standard orthography of ancient and modern times, it is composed of the radical *shǒu* (hand) and the phonetic *shēng*. The lower part is pronounced *yù lǜ* (余慮). The *Shuowen* also writes it as *yú*; *yú* is also a type of vehicle, composed of the radical *chē* (chariot) and the phonetic *jì* (󲈪). The form written as *yù* (轝) is a vulgar character. The sound of *jì* (󲈪) is *yú* (余).

"Hóngbó" (泓博): "Hóng" is pronounced with the initial *wū* and the final *hóng*. The *Guǎngyá* states that "hóng" means "profound. The *Shuowén* says it refers to being deep and vast below; it is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic "hóng," with the final sound being "bǔmò. Zhèng’s commentary on the *Kǎogōngjì* states that "bó" is equivalent to "guǎng" (broad). The *Kǎoshēng* says it means "thick. The *Shuowén* says it means "great penetration"; it is composed of the radical "ten" (*shí*) and the phonetic "fú," where "fú" is pronounced "pǔ."

*Chuǎi* (in the second character of *wén chuǎi*): The initial is *chū* with the retroflex *wěi*. Guō’s commentary on the *Fāngyán* states that it means "to estimate. The *Shuōwén* states it means "to measure. It is a compound character formed from the radical *shǒu* (hand) and the semantic component *duān*. *Cǎizhì* (in the second character of *cǎizhì*): The initial is *zhēng* with the final *shì*.

The *Fāngyán* states that *zhì* is synonymous with "to take. The *Shuōwén* states it means "to pick up. It is formed from the radical *shǒu* (hand) and the phonetic *shù*; the sound is also derived from *kǎo*. The character may also be written as *zhà*, and both the pronunciation and meaning are identical.

*Jīmó* (upper radical *jǐ*, *yí* as an alternative reading). Duan Yucai’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states it refers to a horse’s halter (*mǎjī*). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that a leather network over the horse’s head is called a *jī*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as composed of the radicals *gé* (metal) and a simplified form of *lǐng* (which itself contains *xié*); there are also versions with *qiú* (prison), which are incorrect. The lower character is read as *méi* or *bēi*. The *Guoyaya* states that *mó* is synonymous with "to bind" (*xì*). The *Shiji* says "to bind and entice so they are not enrolled [among the subjects]. The *Shuowen* explains it as composed of the radicals *mí* (silk) and the phonetic *má*.

"Bīn" (豳) is pronounced *qí shàng bǐ mín fǎn*. Zheng Xuan’s *Shǐpǔ* states that Bīn is the name of a territory belonging to the Róng-dì (the Rong tribes). The *Jīngǔ zhèngzì* says that Bīn was the fiefdom where Gōnglú was enfeoffed; it is composed of the radical "mountain" (*shān*) and the phonetic "huán" (*huán*), with the same pronunciation as above. The *Zìshū* states that "huán" refers to two pigs born together.

Regarding the character *jiàn* (荐) in the phrase "the barbarians repeatedly [occupied] the land" (*bīng jiàn qián jiàn fǎn*), the *Zuǒzhuan* states: "The Róng and Dí repeatedly settled there. Du Yu’s commentary explains that "repeatedly" (*jiàn*) means "successively" (*réng*) or "thickly clustered" (*cóng*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical *kǒng* (廾) with the phonetic *cún*.

Regarding "Xian-yun" (玁狁): the first character is pronounced *xian* (上杴, with the rhyme *yan*) and the second is *yün* (下聿笋, with the rhyme *sun*). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that Xianyun is the name for the northern Di tribes. The *Zheng Jian* states they are the present-day Xiongnu. The *Han Shu* states that even during the era of Yao and Shun, there were already the Di and Yu tribes, with the Xianyun dwelling on the northern frontiers. According to the standard characters of antiquity and modern times, both characters for Xianyun follow the radical "dog" (犬). In the case of Yan (嚴), it is also a phonetic component. In lexicographical works examining sounds, some write it as "Lian" (獫, pronounced *lian* [贍]), but this is not the original character and is therefore not accepted.

Regarding "míng" (top character pronounced píng): the *Mao Shī Zhuàn* states that the locusts that eat the heart of the grain are called *míng*. The *Shuōwén* further states that those which eat the leaves of the grain follow the radical "insect" (*chóng*) and are phonetically indicated by "míng" (bottom character pronounced lé). The *Erya* states: "Insects that eat leaves are called *gǔ*. The *Shijing* says: "Remove its *míng* and *gǔ*. When officials beg for loans, *gǔ* are immediately produced; the *Shuōwén* follows the radical "insect" and is phonetically indicated by "tè" (pronounced tā lé). The recorded text writes it as *qín* (𧑞), which is the same as in the *Yueling* (Monthly Ordinances). According to lexicographical works, *qín* is pronounced téng. The *Erya* states: "*Qín* is a snake; it belongs to the class of dragons. This does not have the meaning of *míng* and *gǔ*.

"Ri-gàn" (日旰) means the sun has descended to the banks of the Jūn River. Duan Yucai’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states: "Gàn" is synonymous with "rì-yàn," meaning late in the day; the meaning in the *Shuōwén* is the same. It is composed of "rì" (sun) as the semantic component and "gān" (竿) as the phonetic component. Examining the sound, it is written as "gàn" (𣈨), and its pronunciation is the same as above.
Xuánwǎn (玄琬) is a monastic name; "xuán" (玄) is pronounced with the rhyme of yuānyuǎn (冤遠).

Xuányùn (玄惲) is a name for a śramaṇa; according to the *Fāngyán* (方言), "yùn" (惲) means "to plan"; Guō's commentary states it means "to deliberate. The *Shuōwén* (說文) explains that it is composed of the radical "heart" (心) with the phonetic "jūn" (軍).

*Jī* (齎): The character *xi* (奚) follows with the rhyme *fàn* (反). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "To *jī* means to provide resources while traveling, and also to present offerings. The *Guǎngyá* states: "To *jī* means to scatter. The *Shuowén* states: "To hold and bestow; it takes the radical *bèi* (貝) and uses *qí* (齊) as its phonetic. The version recorded here as *jī* (賷) is a vulgar form.

Regarding the character 璟 (Jing) in the Tang Records (*Tang lu*) as being pronounced with the *guǐ yǒng* rhyme: the *Shūyù piān* states that the character 璟 is pronounced *yǐng*, and there is no pronunciation of *guǐ yǒng* for it; furthermore, 璟 means "bright" (*míng*), whereas the pronunciation *guǐ yǒng* [corresponds to the character] 瑩.
*Huize* (慧賾): The second character, *ze*, is pronounced with the *zheng* rhyme. It is a title for a *śramaṇa*. *Bimi* (紕紊): The first character, *bi*, is pronounced with the *mi* rhyme.

In the *Liji* commentary by Zheng Xuan, it is stated that "bi" means "to err" (*cuo*), referring to coarse and thin silk. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "silk" (*mi*) and the phonetic "bi" (pronounced with the *fen* rhyme in the following text). In the *Shangshu* commentary by Kong Yingda, it is stated that "wen" means "disorder. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "silk" (*mi*) and the phonetic "wen."

"Shan-hui" (訕毀): The *Commentary on the Analects* by Kong [Qiu] states that "shan-bang" (訕謗) means "yan" (䛼). [In the text,] the character below "hui-ghost" (暉鬼) is correctly written as "yan" (䛼). "Zong-xia" (宗轄):

Below "xian-jia" (閑戞), the character is correctly written as "qian" (牽) in the *Zishu*. It refers to the pin at the head of a carriage axle. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of "chuan" (舛)—meaning two things facing away from each other—and a simplified form of "xie" (卨). Gu Yewang says that "qian" (牽) is the same as the carriage pin (*che-ha*), and it is also interchangeable with the character written with the "metal" radical as "xia" (鎋). This is also correct.

*Liṅlì* (凌轢) is the reverse of *líng* (零). The *Cāngjiépiān* states that "lì" (轢) is synonymous with "chāo" (𨋁). The *Lǚshìchūnqiū* says it refers to "trampling upon the feudal lords. The *Shuowén* explains that "lì" means what a carriage treads upon; it is composed of the radical "carriage" (車) and the phonetic "yuè" (樂).

Qīngwǎng (輕惘): "Wǎng" is pronounced *fǎn* (反). Volume Six, Part Six: **Quán (筌):** Pronounced *qiān* (上七宣反). The *Zhouyi Xici* and the *Zhuangzi* both state: "The *quán* is that by which one catches fish; once the fish is caught, one forgets the *quán*. Gu Yewang says: "The *quán* is a fish-trap (*gǒu*). In the standard characters of past and present, it is written with the radical 'bamboo' (竹) and the phonetic 'quán' (全); *gǒu* is pronounced *gǒu* (音苟). The character below [in the *Zhuangzi*] is *xí* (奚), pronounced *xí* (下第奚反). The *Zhuangzi* and the *Zhouyi* both state: "The *tí* is that by which one obtains freedom; once freedom is obtained, one forgets the *tí*. The *Shuowen* states: "It is written with the radical 'foot' (足) and the phonetic 'dí' (虒); *dí* is pronounced *zhì* (音雉). The text here uses *dì* (帝) as *tí*; this is a vulgarly interchangeable character. **Tí (蹄):** Pronounced *tí* (下第奚反). The *Zhuangzi* and the *Zhouyi* both state: "The *tí* is that by which one obtains freedom; once freedom is obtained, one forgets the *tí*. The *Shuowen* states: "It is written with the radical 'foot' (足) and the phonetic 'dí' (虒); *dí* is pronounced *zhì* (音雉). The text here uses *dì* (帝) as *tí*; this is a vulgarly interchangeable character.

*Gěnggài* (梗槩): The upper character *gěng* (梗) is pronounced *gēng* (羹, with the *ǎi* rhyme). The *Erya* states that "gěng" means "straight. The *Guangya* states that "gěng" refers to a "general outline" (*dàlüè*). In the *Zhèngzì* (Correct Characters) of ancient and modern times, it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "gēng" (*gēng*). The lower character *gài* (槩) is pronounced *gāi* (陔, with the *ài* rhyme). Ban Gu’s *Dōngdū Fù* says, "I have roughly provided my guest with the general outline (*gěnggài*) of it. The commentary to the *Zuǒzhuan* states, "It is not fine or detailed. This character is likewise composed of the radical "wood" and the phonetic "jì" (*jì*).

7. Seventh Fascicle. *Bian'ai* (褊隘): The upper character *bian* (褊) is pronounced *bian* (with the initial *b* and final *-an*). The *Guangya* states that "broad" (*bian*) is synonymous with "narrow" (*xia*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical for "clothing" and the phonetic *pian* (扁), where *pian* is pronounced *bian*. The lower character *ai* (隘) is pronounced *yi* (with the initial *y* and final *-ai*). The preface to the *Mao Shi* states: "The territory of Wei was narrow and constricted; its people were ingenious and pursued profit. Guo's commentary on the *Liji* says it means "narrow and mean. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical for "to increase" (*yi*) and the phonetic *zeng* (𨸏). The lower part consists of *xiang* (󳐙) and *gou* (冓); *xiang* is pronounced *xiang*, and *gou* is the character for "ancient benefit" (*gu-yi*).
*Kēng* (the initial *kēng* with the final *gēng* reversed).

*Dùn* (the initial *pén* with the final *mèn* reversed). The *Guìyuàn Zhūcóng*, the *Zílín*, and the *Zītǒng* all state that *dùn* refers to dust. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "earth" (*tǔ*) and the phonetic "fēn" (*fēnshēng*).

Volume Eight, Fascicle Upper. *Chí* (pronounced with the initial *lì* in the *Cāngjié piān*): it means "to wrap. The *Kǎoshēng* says it means "to envelop. The *Wénzì diǎnshuō* says it is "a case for books. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "clothing" (*yī*) and the phonetic "shī" (pronounced with the final *chōng* and *liù*). The *Fāngyán* says: "Zhùzhóu" means "axle. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "chariot" (*chē*) and the abbreviated phonetic "zhòu."

Regarding the term *qiǎn* (籤) [in *qiǎnbǎng* (籤牓)], the *Qièyùn* reads it as *jié* (妾); the *Shuowén* states that *qiǎn* refers to a person who is examined. The *Kǎoshēng* says that *qiǎn* is a small bamboo slip. In antiquity, titles were inscribed on slips to report matters, which were called *qiǎn*. The standard character for this in both ancient and modern times is written with the radical "bamboo" (*zhú*) and the phonetic "xiàn" (韱), where *xiàn* is pronounced *xiān* (暹) with the second tone, followed by *bó* (博) and *mǎng* (莾). Now, a *qiǎnbǎng* consists of each title of a scripture being inscribed, thereby distinguishing its systematic organization and marking the meaning of its fascicles and volumes.
9. Ninth Fascicle. *Shě* (捨): *bō* (襪) is pronounced *fán* (襪); *táo yòu* (陶誘) — *táo* (陶) is pronounced *tú láo* (徒勞) and *yòu* (誘) is pronounced *yóu shǒu* (由首).

Hé Yàn’s commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* states that "to induce" (*yòu*) means to advance; it refers to the Master advancing and exhorting people by means of the Right Way. *Zílín* (字林) states that "to induce" (*yòu*) is synonymous with "to entice" (*lù*) and is also "to lead. The *Shuowén* (說文) defines it as "to guide" (*dǎo*), composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic "xiù" (*xiù*). It may also be written as *zhǒng* (䛻) using the radical "shield" (*dùn*), or as *yǒu* (羑); the pronunciation and meaning are identical. *Lù* (󳈙) is pronounced *xiān jiǔ* (先九).

10. The Tenth Scroll. *Wěiwěi* (斖斖). [The character] *wěi* is pronounced *fěi* (匪) according to Guo’s commentary on the *Erya*, which states: “*Wěiwěi* means to strive diligently (*mǎnfǔ*). Liu Huán’s commentary on the *Zhouyi* states: “It means subtle (*wēi*). Regarding the standard orthography of ancient and modern times, it consists of the radicals *qiě* (且) and *wén* (文), forming a compound ideograph (*huìyì zì*). The pronunciation of *mǎn* (僶) is *mǐn* (泯).

*Yù* (毓) is pronounced *shàng róng zhù fǎn*. It is written as *yù* (育) in the *Yùpiān*. Guō’s commentary on the *Ěrshī* states: "Yù means to nourish. The *Máo Shī Zhuàn* says it means "the young. The *Shuowén* says: "Yù means to nourish; it causes one to follow what is good. It is composed of the radical *huì* (㐬) and the phonetic *měi* (每). The sound of *huì* is *tuó hū fǎn*; the lower part [of the phonetic] is *mài péng fǎn*.
The character 㴉 (pronounced jié with a fine retroflex *r* [jiě] in the ancient pronunciation) is the same as the character 濟; it has been erroneously recorded as 㴉 through tradition.
"Liu Qiu" (劉璆): the character 璆 is pronounced qíyōu (with the second tone on *qí* and the first tone on *yōu*); this is the name of Liu Qiu, a military official of the Liang dynasty.

Regarding "Sēngkūn" (僧琨): the second character, *kūn*, is pronounced with the initial *h* (魂) and final *n* (反); it is a monastic name (*sēngmíng*). Kǒng [Yáng]’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* states that *kūn* refers to beautiful jade. Regarding "Shāróu" (沙揉):

the second character, *róu*, is pronounced with the initial *r* (仍) and final *w* (周) [in the *fǎnqie* system]. Examining the phonology, *róu* is synonymous with *nuò* (捼). According to the *Lùwén* (錄文), "rubbing gold with sand" (*shānuò jīn*) refers to the act of *nuòhuàn* (捼扞). *Nuò* is pronounced with the initial *n* (內) and final *huì* (迥); *huàn* is pronounced with the initial *g* (干) and final *hǎn* (罕).

*Guǎiwù* (詿誤): The upper character *guǎi* is pronounced as *huà* (畫) according to the *Hànshū*, which states that those "misled by the amnesty decree" (*shèshū wèi suǒ guǎiwù zhě*) shall all be pardoned and exempted. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) with the phonetic "jade" (*guī*). The lower character is pronounced *wù* (悟).
Regarding the character for "tiger" (hǔ), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "crouching" (*dūn*) means "squatting" (*jù*), composed of the radical "foot" with "zūn" as the phonetic.

Regarding the character for "ghost" (guǐ) in the term *daoguǐ* (道鬼), it is pronounced *yǒng*. The *Cangjie pian* states that *guǐ* means "fire-light," while the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it refers to the light shining through the openings between windows and shutters; it is a pictographic character.

The character *zhuàn* (鐫) has the phonetic component *yuán* (緣) as its radical and is reversed [in meaning]. The *Fāngyán* states that *zhuàn* is synonymous with *tuó* (琢, to carve). The *Guǎngyá* states that *zhuàn* is also *záo* (鑿, to bore). The *Shuōwén* states: "To split wood is *zhuàn*; it is composed of the radical 'metal' (*jīn*) and the phonetic 'juàn' (*juàn*), pronounced *quán-yuǎn*."

"Then he drove [him] down (*nǎi qū xià*, *qū* pronounced as in *ōu* [as defined in the *Shuowen Jiezi*]: 'To drive' (*ōu*) means to strike or beat; it is composed of the radical *zhī* with the phonetic *qū*;

the sound of *qū* is like that of *qū* [to drive away]). This continues the *Dàtáng nèidiǎnlù*. Compiled by Huìlín, the volume number is indicated by the character *chí* (pronounced as in *chén lì*). The eighth fascicle of the previous *Nèidiǎnlù* has already explained this.

Regarding *quán* (筌) and *tí* (蹏): the former is pronounced *yuán* (緣) and the latter *xī* (奚). The *Book of Changes* (*Zhouyī*) states: "The *quán* is used to catch fish; the *tí* is used to catch rabbits. These have already been explained previously. Now, regarding *yú* (爰) and *jì* (暨): the latter is pronounced *qí* (其) with the intent [of the following character].

The *Erya* states: "Ji means 'to reach' (*jí*). Kong's commentary on the *Book of Documents* (*Shàngshū*) states: "It means 'with' (*yǔ*). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "It means 'to arrive at' (*zhì*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of *dàn* (旦) and the phonetic *jì* (既); the version in the *Lù* (錄) which writes it as *jì* (洎) is incorrect.
*Jiāochún* (澆淳): The first character, *jiāo*, has the phonetic *yáo*; the second character, *chuí*, has the phonetic *lún*. *Fánná* (煩挐):

The second character, *ná*, has the phonetic *nǚ zhū*. The *Huáinánzǐ* states: "To resolve and disentangle (*jué ná*) is to govern the complex. Xù Quánzhòng says: "*Ná* means disorder. The *Chu cí* states: "The branches are complex and intertwined (*fánná*). According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) with the phonetic "rú" (*rú shēng*).

The character *yùn* (蘊) [is pronounced *yun* with the departing tone; the Zheng commentary on the *Mao Shi* states it means "to accumulate," while the Du commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan* states it means "to gather algae," and the Zheng commentary on the *Zhou Li* states it means "a mat"]. In the standard characters of antiquity and today, it is composed of the radical "grass" (*cao*) and the phonetic "yun" (*yun*, same pronunciation as above). The character *jiè* (藉) [is pronounced *jie* with the departing tone].

Regarding "wěnshì" (抆飾): "wěn" (抆) is pronounced as *pén-mù* (上聞粉反). The *Guǎngyá* states that "wěn" is synonymous with "shì" (to wipe). In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, it is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "wén" (文); the version in the *Lùwén* (錄文) as "𣼶" is an error. Regarding "bèi" (孛):
it is originally pronounced as *pén-mù* (上盆沒反), which is the archaic form of the character "bèi" (孛) found in the classics.

*Dousha* (兜沙) [the first character pronounced with the *dou* rhyme and the second with the *tou* rhyme] is the name of a scripture; it is a term from the Sanskrit language. In the first volume of the *Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu* (compiled by Huilin), the first entry concerning the character *pian* (胼): The *Guoyu* states that *jue* (贅) [the first character pronounced with the *bian* and *mian* rhymes] means "to add" (*jin*). Regarding the correct orthography of ancient and modern times, this character is composed of the radical *bei* (貝) and the phonetic *bing* (并). However, the text of the present record uses the character *pian* (駢) [composed of the radical *ma* (馬) and the phonetic *pian* (扁)], which refers to yoking two horses together; since the meaning diverges, it is not accepted here. Regarding the "Record of the Temple on Gōngtíng Lake," the character used for the place name is written as "䢼" (yù), which was produced by the local district office; however, this character does not exist in the standard lexicons and is therefore an error. The character for *jīng* (驚) is pronounced with the lower radical *áng* (昂) and the reversed radical *gǎo* (各). In character dictionaries it is written as 󳊲, which means "to startle. It is a name for a monk (*seng*). *Xuán* (懸) means to hang; *gēn* (縆) is pronounced with the radical *guàn* (亘) or *héng* (恒) as a level tone. "Ji" (亟) means to go directly; "shang-jing-yi-fan" (上兢憶反) is its phonetic transcription, though some write it as "qian" (䩯). The *Mao Shi* commentary states that "ji" (亟) means urgent. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "Ji" means to be self-urgently admonished; it is composed of "jian" (芉) in abbreviated form and "bao" (勹), where "kou" (口) signifies being cautious in speech. The recorded text writes it as "han" (凾), which is a vulgar character and incorrect. The following "jing-ding-fan" (定反) means road; the recording of it as "jing" (經) is an error.

The character *wǎnkǎi* (惋慨): the upper radical is *huàn* (󰦥換) reversed; the *Wénzì jílüè* (文字集略) states it means "to be startled, amazed, or to sigh in resentment. Regarding *wēijìn* (煨燼): the upper character is pronounced *wěihuí* (猥𢌞); the *Guǎngyǎ* states that it means "smoldering heat" (*wēiyùn*). The lower character is pronounced *cíjìn* (辭進); Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states it refers to fire in a basin. *Jìn* (燼) is correctly written as *jìn* (󱽃); it refers to wood that has not been completely consumed by fire, composed of the radical "fire" and the abbreviated phonetic "jìn. Both refer to the remnants after things have been burned away.

*Qíng* (upper radical *shǎo*, *jīng* as phonetic; *Guǎngyá* says it means "martial"; *Shuōwén* says it means "strong," formed with the radical *lì* and the phonetic *jīng*; *Bīcāng* says it means "vigorous").
