The character *lěi* (忍) [with the phonetic *xì*] is listed in the *Zītǒng* under the radical for "filiality" (*xiào*) with the same pronunciation; both state that *lěi* means "cold. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* states: "*Lěi* refers to shivering from cold; it takes *jìn* as its phonetic and *bīng* [radical] as its semantic component. The reading *jìn* (噤) found in the records is incorrect.

As for "choking" (é): it refers to the obstruction of breath; according to the *Fāngyán* (Dialectal Dictionary), it means the cessation of respiration. The *Shuōwén Jiězì* states: "It is when food remains in the throat and does not descend; it is also called 'food being blocked. It is composed of the radical 口 (mouth) with the phonetic element 壹."
"Huang Fa-ji" (黃法𡅏) is a personal name; "ji" (𡅏) is pronounced with the *qu* (俱) rhyme.
As for "gandi" (揵搥), the first character is pronounced *gan* (乾) and the second *zhui* (墜); it refers to the wooden instrument used to alert the assembly, which is placed in the dining hall.
*Naiśī* (痆斯) is the name of a country in the Western Regions;

*Zhixuan* (知鉉) is the name of a monk; *Yanzong* (彥琮) is the name of a monk. (The characters are pronounced as follows: *Naiśī*: *ni* [with the second tone] and *si*; *Zhixuan*: *zhi* and *xuán* [with the fourth tone]; *Yanzong*: *yàn* and *zōng* [with the first tone]).

The character *jiǒng* (窘) is pronounced with the lower radical *jūn* (君). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that "to be *jiǒng*" means to be distressed (*kùn*). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chu Ci* defines it as "urgency" (*jí*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as "to be pressed" (*pò*), consisting of the radical *xué* (穴) with the phonetic component *jūn* (君).

*Guīqí* (瑰奇): The upper character *guī* is pronounced with the *huì* rhyme (回). The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (毛詩傳) states: "Guī is a stone that ranks just below jade. Du Yù’s commentary on the *Zuǒ Zhuan* states: "Guī is a pearl. The *Běicāng* states: "Guīwěi means rare and extraordinary. The *Shuowén* states: "To take *zhēnguī* as *kuǐ* [怪]"; this is also found in the *Rén* (人) radical section. The current form uses the *yù* (玉) radical and the phonetic *guǐ* (鬼). The version recorded with the *yī* (衣) radical is an archaic form; it is a vulgar character. Lexicons also write it as *kuǐ* (傀), where the lower part is *jù* (巨) and *jī* (基) rhymes, and the radical is *dà* (大) and the phonetic is *qí* (奇). The version recorded as *qí* (奇) is a vulgar character.
*Seng* (僧) in *Sēngkūn* (僧琨): the first character means "bone" (*gǔ*) and the second "soul" (*hún*), thus forming a name for a monk (*sēng*).

*Jīmí* (羈縻): the first character is pronounced *jìyí* (几冝反) and the second *měibēi* (美悲反). According to the commentary, *jīmí* refers to the bit and bridle of a horse—those things that bind, tie, and connect [the animal].

Ōu (甌) and Mín (閩): the former is pronounced *hóu* (侯) with an initial *r*-reversion; Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* states that Dongōu (東甌) is located in the midst of the sea. He further comments on the *Shanhaijing* that Minyue (閩越) is the same as Xiōu (西甌), which is present-day Jian’an. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Ōu-Mín refers to the southeastern Yue; it is written with the radical 瓦 (wa) and the phonetic 區 (qū); the latter is pronounced *wǔjīn* (武巾)."
*Kiṇa* (上音建反，下音搦加反): This is a name for a city in the Western Regions according to the Sanskrit language; it has already been fully explained above. *Chí-chú* (上音遲，下音住踰反):

The *Han Shi* states that *chí-chú* is synonymous with *zhí-zhú*. The *Guang Ya* states that it is the appearance of being hesitant and lingering. *Zhí* is pronounced *zhì*; *zhú* is pronounced *chú-lù*.

8. Volume Eight. "Xuanzang" (玄奘) is a monastic name. According to the *Erya*, "zang" (奘) means "qiang" (駔); "qiang" is pronounced with the initial *zuo* and the final *lang*. Guo Pu states it means "great. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains that it is composed of the radical "da" (大) and the phonetic "zhuang" (壯).
Xuanyi (玄嶷) is a monastic name; "yi" (嶷) is pronounced with the *qi* (疑) and *ji* (棘) finals.

Jí (勣) is pronounced with the *jing* (精) and *xi* (昔) initials; the *Shēnglèi* (聲類) states that jí is synonymous with gōng (功). Examining its phonology, it refers to merit and efficacy. In the standard orthography of both ancient and modern times, it is composed of the radical "force" (力) and the phonetic "zé" (責).

*Huishè* (慧賾): The second character, *shè*, is pronounced with the *zhēng* and *zé* rhymes. It is a Buddhist term. The character is written with the "mountain" radical (*fù*) as *shè* (𮥜), which is a vulgar form.

Wang Bi’s commentary on the *Zhouyi* states that *shè* means "profound. *Zhuólùò* (卓犖): The second character, *lùò*, is pronounced with the *lì* and *jué* rhymes. Ban Gu’s *Xi du fu* says, "卓犖諸夏" (*zhuólùò zhūxià*), meaning "surpassing all under heaven. The *Kǎoshēng* states that *zhuólùò* signifies a lofty appearance; the *Shuowén* gives the same meaning. It is composed of "ox" (*niú*) and the abbreviated form of "labor" (*láo*) as the phonetic.

*Chuǎnzhěn* (輟軫): *zhǎn* is pronounced with the *shàng* tone and the *lüè* rhyme. Zheng’s commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* states: "Chuǎn" means to stop. The *Ěryǎ* states: "Yǐ" (already). "Yǐ" is pronounced as *yǐ*. The *Gǔjīn zhèngzì* says: "The sound of the carriage is slightly deficient. It is composed of the radical *chē* (carriage) and the phonetic *chuò*, which share the same pronunciation. Below, *zhēn* is pronounced with the *rěn* rhyme. Xu Shuchong said: "Zhěn" means heavy. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Kǎogōng jì* says: "Zhěn" is the horizontal wood at the rear of the carriage. The *Tàixūn jīng* says: "Zhěn turns upon its way. Song Zhong said: "It is like unfolding. The *Shuowén* [states it] is composed of the radical *chē* and the phonetic *zhǐn*; *zhǐn* has the same pronunciation as above. The text in the *Lù* reads *zhěn*, which is a vulgar character.

*Tāo* (韜) means "to conceal" (*dǎo*, 討, lǎo, 勞). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that *tāo* is equivalent to "to store away. The *Guangya* states it means "broad. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is the sheath for a sword, composed of the radical *wei* (韋) and the phonetic *yao* (舀); the pronunciation of *yao* is *yǎo* (窅).

*Gěnggài* (梗槩): The upper character *gěng* (梗) is read as *jìng* (更) or *fǎn* (反). The *Erya* states: "Gěng means straight. Sima Biao’s commentary on the *Zhuangzi* says: "Gěng means a straightforward person. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mu*) and the phonetic "geng" (*gēng*). The lower character *gài* (槩) is read as *dài* (代). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* says: "Gài means level. Ban Gu’s *Dongdu Fu* states: "I have roughly provided my guest with its *gěnggài*. The *Zuǒzhuan Yinyi* says this refers to that which is not fine or detailed. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mu*) and the phonetic "ji* (既). *Note: The original text contains a typographical error regarding the phonetic for the lower character; it should be "ji* (既)" rather than "ji* (既). The translation reflects the correct form.*

*Zhēn* (箴). Upper radical: *zhí* (執), read as *shēn* (深) according to the commentary on the *Shūjìng* by Kǒng [Yáng]. The *Shūjìng* states: "Zhēn is like *guī* (規, a compass). Jia [Yì]’s commentary on the *Guóyǔ* states: "Zhēn means instruction. Dú [Yù]’s commentary on the *Zuǒchuán* states: "It means admonition. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is a compound character formed from the phonetic *xián* (咸) with the semantic component of bamboo (*zhú*).

The *Shangshu Dazhuan* states that "chun" (蠢) is pronounced with the *yin* rhyme and means "to emerge. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* states that "chun" refers to the appearance of movement and agitation. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines "chong" (虫) as "movement," composed of the radical "gung" (䖵) with "chun" (春) as its phonetic component; "gung" is pronounced "kun" (昆).

Regarding the character for *qiào* (誚) in the title of the *Jù*: the correct form is written with the radical 言 (speech), pronounced the same as *qiáo* (樵). The commentary on the *Shūjìng* by Kǒng [Yáng] states: "Qiào means to reprimand. The *Cāngjié piān* states: "It means to scold. The *Shuōwén* records it as being composed of 言 and the phonetic 肖 (xiào), with the pronunciation qǐng-nì-fǎn. Gù Yěwáng states: "Jù means 'extreme' or 'excessive'. The *Cāngjié piān* also states: "It means 'intense' or 'earnest'. In the standard characters of antiquity and today, it is written with the radical 刀 (knife), with 豦 (qǔ) as its phonetic.
*Xiūnyóu* (薰蕕): The first character, *xiūn*, is pronounced with the *yun* rhyme; it refers to fragrant grasses. The second character, *yóu*, is pronounced with the *zhōu* rhyme;

it refers to foul-smelling grasses. This has already been explained previously. *Kǎojiē* (槀街): The first character, *gǎo*, is pronounced with the *gǎo-lǎo* rhyme. Gu Yewang states that *kǎo* is synonymous with "grass. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "grain" (*禾*) and the phonetic "high" (*高*). The second character, *jiē*, is pronounced with the *jiā-hài* rhyme. The *Shangshu* states that *Kǎojiē* refers to the location of the guest houses for the Man and Yi peoples. The *Shuowen* defines a "street" (*jiē*) as a thoroughfare where four roads meet, composed of the radical "walk" (*行*) and the phonetic "jade" (*圭*).

Regarding "扼捥" (è wàn): the upper character is read as *yǐng* (with the phonetic *gǒng*). The *Guǎngyá* states that "扼" means to grasp. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Shuōwén Fùzhuan* says: "That which fills the hands is called 㧖. The *Shuōwén* defines 㧖 as "like holding; it takes the radical 手 and the phonetic 戹. The pronunciation of 戹 is *è*. The correct form is 󳎶, which is also written as 󲵽; their pronunciations and meanings are identical. [The text] records it as "扼," which is a vulgar character. Regarding the lower character "剜": it is read as *huàn*. Yang Xiong says it means "to grasp" (*wàn*). The *Shuōwén* states it takes the radical 手 and the phonetic 宛.

"Then he bound [him] and placed him upon the block. (The character *zhì* [砧] is pronounced *zhǎn* when standing alone; Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuǒ Zhuan* states that *zhì* means "to seize"; Fan Ning’s commentary on the *Guliang Zhuan* says it means "to bind"; the *Gōngjīn Zhèngzì* states that binding and tethering is equivalent to "binding. It follows the radical for "silk" (*xì*) and the component for "seize" (*zhí*). This is the correct form of the character *zhì*. It is sometimes written as *dí* (馽), which has the same pronunciation.

Regarding "ní" (祖禰): the lower character is pronounced with the *nì* rhyme (as in *ní*). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "Ní is the ancestral temple of one's father. This is the correct orthography for both ancient and modern times; it follows the radical "shì" (示) and the phonetic "ěr" (爾). Having completed the explanation of these characters: Regarding "zhì" (桎) and "gù" (梏):

the upper character is pronounced with the *zhēn* (*zhēn*) rhyme, and the lower is pronounced with the *gōng wò* (*gù*) rhyme. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "Those applied to the hands are called zhì, and those applied to the feet are called gù; they are the implements used for punishing criminals. Zheng Zhong further states: "Zhì and gù refer to constraining both hands with a single piece of wood. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, both characters follow the radical "mù" (木), and "zhì" also uses "gào" (告) as its phonetic.

The radical for *zōng* (宗) is *xián* (閑, with the phonetic *jiá* [戞]) and the sound component is *kǎo* (考), both of which are correct. The character *cóng* (從) consists of two parts, both of which are abbreviated forms of *yǒu* (有). The character *jiàn* (轂) has the phonetic *chuān* (川) and *yǎn* (兗); it is now commonly written as *xiá* (轄), and may also be written with the metal radical as *xiá* (鎋). Gu Yewang states that it refers to the iron at the end of a carriage axle. This was already explained in the fifth fascicle of the *Qián nèidiǎn lù* (前內典錄).

*Tiáo* (調): In the *Guǎngyá*, "tiáo" is equivalent to "cháo" (to ridicule); it is also explained as "deceit. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) with the phonetic "zhōu. In the *Lùwén*, it is erroneously written with the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) as "diào" (掉). Below, *xī* (希) is pronounced with the reverse [tone]. The *Màoshī Zhuàn* states: "Xì (戲) means 'leisure' (*yìyù*). Guō's commentary on the *Ěryǎ* says: "Xì means 'ridicule' (*cháo*). The *Guǎngyá* says it means 'deviance' (*xié*). According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "spear" (*gē*) with the phonetic "qiān" (䖒); the pronunciation of "qiān" is *xī*.

Regarding the character *jiè* (解) in *jièchèn* (解讖): the upper radical is pronounced *jiè* (玠), and the lower part is pronounced with the rhyme of *chā* (插) and *jiàn* (鑒). According to the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲), *chèn* (讖) refers to one’s own confession of transgressions before the Buddha. The vulgar form *xiān* (韱) and the form *chèn* (韯) found in recorded texts are incorrect.

*Ni-se* (痆斯) is a transliteration of the Sanskrit term [Vārāṇasī]; *yú-dùn* (于遁) is also the name of a country. *Tián-yē* (窴噎): *tián* is pronounced as *diàn jiān*; the *Erya* states it means "the appearance of being full," and Guo Pu’s commentary says it is the sound of a crowd moving together.

The *Cangjie pian* writes it as *zhì* (寘), meaning "to block" (*sè*), with the same meaning as the character *tián*. The "Western Metropolis Rhapsody" (*Xidufu*) says "it blocks the city and overflows the suburbs. The *Shuowen* also defines it as "blocking," written with the radical for "cave" (*xué*) and the phonetic *zhēn* (真, *zhēn zhī rén*); the lower part is *yān jié* (煙結). Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Fangyan* says *yē* (噎) means "choked" (*yàn sè*). The *Mao Shi* and *Zuozhuan* say "choked so as to be unable to breathe. The *Shuowen* says *yē* means "food stuck in the throat," written with the radical for "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic *yī* (壹). The record [in the source] using *tián* (闐) is incorrect. *Zhì* (窒) is pronounced *zhēn lì*. *Note: This text provides a philological commentary on the characters used to transcribe foreign place names and explain related Chinese terminology.*

*Xuānhuá* (喧譁): The first character, *xuān*, is pronounced with the *huàn* rhyme. The *Shēnglèi* states that *xuān* is identical to *huá*. Ji Kang’s *Sìfù* says, "Not *xuānhuá* yet flowing and spreading. The *Shuōwén* correctly uses *huán* (from the radical *huán*) to form this character; it shares the same meaning as *xuān*. The *Hànshū* says, "Before arriving, there was no *huānhuá*," which is correct. The record here uses *xuān*, which is the same as what is used in the *Shū* and its commentaries. The second character, *huá*, is pronounced with the *guā* rhyme. Kong’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* says, "Huá is the sound of *huān*. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical *yán* (speech) and the phonetic *huá*.

*Níngyìng* (上音挺反，下音縈定反). The *Kǎoshēng* says: "Níngyìng" refers to small bodies of water. According to the *Gānquán Fù*, it is written as *róngróng* (弱水之濎瀅); the correct characters for both ancient and modern usage are also written as *róng*, with the same meaning. [The character] follows the radical for water and takes *yìng* as its phonetic. The record writes it as *tīngyìng*; *tīng* has the sound *tīng*. Wáng Yì’s commentary on the *Chuci* states: "It is the levelness of a *tīngzhōu* (island). Because this differs from the original meaning, it is not accepted here. [The character] *yìng* (因逈反).

*Míngbó* (溟渤): The upper character is read as *píng* (萍) with the *shēngmǔ* (initial radical) *fǎn* (反); the lower character is read as *pén* (盆) with the *shēngmǔ* *fǎn*. According to the *Zhuāngzǐ*: "In the Northern Míng there is a fish called Kūn (鯤). When the sea circulates, it is about to head for the Southern Míng; both *Míng* and *Bó* are names for the northern and southern seas. Regarding the correct characters of past and present: [the character for Míng] is composed of the radical *mù* (木) and the phonetic *míng* (冥). Regarding *Bó*, according to the *Yìnyì* (音義) of the *Hànshū*, it is an alternative name for the Bohai Sea (*Bóxiè*). The *Wénxuǎn* states: "Digging a pond resembles the Míng and Bó. Regarding the correct characters of past and present: *Bó* is also a sea; it is composed of the radical *shuǐ* (水) and the phonetic *bó* (勃).

Fú (扶袁反): Dúyù’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states that Fúchuān is the name of a district (*xiāng*) in Jīngzhào; alternatively, it is said that Yángfú City is also the name of a district in Dúlíng. According to the *Shuowén*, this character is composed of the radical "city" (*yì*) with the phonetic component "fán" (*fán shēng*).

Regarding the term *qúchú* (𥴧篨): the upper character is pronounced *qú* and the lower is pronounced *chú*. Xu Shuchong stated that *qúchú* refers to a mat made of grass. Guo’s commentary on the *Fānyǔ* states it is also called *fùfèi* (𥳊). According to the *Shuowén*, both characters for *qúchú* are written with the radical "bamboo" (*zhú*), where *qú* is pronounced *qúchú* and also functions as a phonetic component.

The following day: *yì* (翌). Xu Yingzhi’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states that *yì* means "bright" (*míng*). The *Ēryá* also defines it as "bright. In the standard orthography of ancient and modern times, the character is composed of the radical *yǔ* (羽) and the phonetic *lì* (立), with the pronunciation *dì*.

*Tì* (嚏): *zhì* (󲺵), pronounced *tì*. The *Kǎoshēng* states that it is the rushing of qi through the nose resulting in a sneeze. The *Cāngjiépiān* says that *tì* is the same as *pèn* (to spit/sneeze). The *Shuōwén* says: "*Tì* refers to the awakening of the breath and its release. It is composed of the radicals *kǒu* (口) and *zhì* (疐), with the pronunciation *dì*.

The character *fà* (斂) is pronounced with the lower radical *lián* (廉) and the phonetic *jiǎn* (撿). The *Zìtǒng* states that "to *lián*" means to collect or gather. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Yílǐ* explains it as "to store away. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical *qiān* (僉) and the phonetic *pǔmù* (攴); the text of the *Lùwén* records it as *liàn* (殮), which is a vulgar form of the character.

Regarding the character *chéngyī* (澄漪), its meaning should be understood as "fine ripples. The *Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry* states: "Yī refers to the wavy patterns of water; its sound also refers to fine ripples. In both ancient and modern standard characters, it is composed of the radical for "water" (*shuǐ*) with "yī" (*yī*) as the phonetic component.

*Jiànshí* (to gather): The upper character is pronounced *jūn* with the *yun* rhyme. Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that it means "gathering ears of grain. The *Fangyan* states it means "to take. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical 手 (*shǒu*) and the phonetic 䴢 (*jùn*); the version written with the radical 君 (*jūn*) is a vulgar form.

9. Volume Nine. *Qíqū* (崎嶇): The upper character is pronounced *qǐ* (with the radical *jiǎn*) and the lower is pronounced *qū*. The *Erya* states that *qíqū* means "sloping and tilted. The *Pīcāng* states that *qíqū* means "unstable. The *Kǎoshēng* states it is the appearance of a mountain precipice. In the *Gōngjīn Zhèngzì*, both characters for *qíqū* follow the "mountain" radical (*shān*), with *qí* and *qū* serving as their respective phonetic components.

Regarding "嗜欲" (shìyù): when it appears as "時至反" (shízhìfǎn) in the *Liji*, Zheng Xuan’s commentary states that "嗜" (shì) means "greed. Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that "嗜" (shì) means "to have no satiety. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "耆欲" (qíyù) means "to take pleasure in"; it is composed of "口" (mouth) and the phonetic "耆" (qí); those who take "目" (eye) as the phonetic are incorrect."

The character for Bīn (豳) State is pronounced *shàng* (上) with the rhyme *bǐ* (筆) and *mín* (岷); dictionaries also write it with the radical for "city" (*yì*, 邑), as in *Bīn* (邠), which was the fief of Gōngliú. It is identical to the character *Bīn*. The *Máo Shī* contains the "Book of Bīn. Regarding the standard orthography of ancient and modern times, it is written with the radicals for "mountain" (*shān*, 山) and *huán* (豩), pronounced *bīn* (斌). The two characters for "hog" (*chǔ*, 豖) also signify a gait.

Yanzong submitted a memorial stating: "The character for 'yan' (彥) is pronounced *fan* (反); the *Erya* says that a man of excellence is called a 'yan. The character for 'cong' (悰) is pronounced *zong* (宗); the *Shuowen* says that 'cong' means joy (*le*), composed of the radical 'heart' and the phonetic 'zong'; it is a name for a śramaṇa. Previously, there was a character written with the jade radical as 'cong' (琮), the details of which I have not yet ascertained."

Regarding "xié" (脅) in "xiélèi" (脅壘): the *Zuǒzhuan* says, "I heard that he had joined ribs" (*píxié*). The *Kǎoshēng* states that "xié" refers to the ribs. The *Shuōwén* says, "Xié refers to the two flanks; it is composed of the radical 'flesh' (肉) and the phonetic 'hé' (劦, hújie). The character *xié* (脇) is recorded as being composed of three "force" (力) radicals; it is a vulgar form.

*Tiáo-èr* (髫齔): The first character is pronounced *tiáo* (苕); the second is pronounced *chū-jǐn* (初謹反). Regarding *tiáo*, the *Cāngjié piān* states that *tiáo* means "hanging down" (*chuí*). The *Bīcāng* states that *tiáo* refers to the *máo* (topknot hair). The *Kǎoshēng* states that *tiáo* refers to a child's shaved hair with two side-strands left. In the *Gōngjīn zhèngzì*, it is written with the radical *biāo* (髟) and the phonetic *zhào* (召); *biāo* is pronounced *biāo*. The second character, *èr*, is pronounced *chū-jǐn* (初謹反). Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhōu lǐ* states that *èr* refers to the "destruction of teeth" (*huǐchǐ*). At age eight for boys and seven for girls, this is called *èr*. In the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical *chǐ* (齒) and the phonetic *qī* (七).

*Jiǎngzhǐ* (降祉): The lower character is pronounced *chīlǐ* (絺里). The *Mao Shi* states that "zhǐ" (祉) is synonymous with "fú" (福, blessing). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "zhǐ" is also synonymous with "lù" (祿, emolument). The meaning is the same as in the *Shuowen*. It is composed of the radical "示" (shì) and the phonetic "止" (zhǐ). The text records it as "zhǐ," which is a vulgar form of the character.

Regarding "lǜ" (to filter): the upper radical is *lú* (翥, zhù; rhyme: *quán*). The *Yùnquán* states that "lǜ" is synonymous with "xǐ" (to wash). According to this, "lǜ" refers to the practice of śramaṇas protecting living beings by using silk as a sieve to strain out insects and filth from water in order to maintain purity. This character "lǜ" is not recorded in various dictionaries. The lower part is read as *lónggǔ* (聾穀). The *Kōnggōng Jì* says: "Strain and clarify its water. Wányáng states: "Lù (漉) is synonymous with lì (瀝), to drip. The *Zílín* says it describes the appearance of water flowing downward. In the *Gōngjīn Zhèngzì*, it is written with the "water" radical and the phonetic "lù" (鹿).

*Dí* (滌) [in *dísè*] has the upper radical *ting* (亭) and the phonetic *lì* (歷); Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states that "dí" means "to remove. Zheng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* says it means "to shake off. The *Shuowén* says it means "to sprinkle," composed of the water radical and the phonetic *tiáo* (條).

The character 䞈 (pronounced *guǐ*) is the opposite of *gōng* (honest). The *Guǎngyǎ* states that "䞈" means "to gamble. The *Jīngǔ zhèngzì* states that it is also written as 貨 (*huò*). The *Yùpiān* lists it as an alternative form of 𧵥, with the same meaning. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical 貝 (shell/wealth) and the phonetic 為; it is also pronounced *guì* or *wǎ*.

The upper character *jiān* (涓) is pronounced with the radical *jué* and the phonetic *yuán*. The *Shuōyuàn* states: "If a tiny stream (*jiānjiān*) is not dammed, it will eventually become a river. Gu Yewáng says that *jiān* refers to a small current. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical *shuǐ* and the phonetic *yùan* (pronounced *mèi* and *xiàn*). The [text] records it as *jiān*, which is a vulgar form. The lower character *lì* (瀝) is pronounced *dīng*. In lexicographical works, it correctly uses *chì* (啻) as its phonetic component, appearing also as *lí* (𣾪) or *dí* (󳁡). Gu Yewáng says that *lí* means to drip or leak. According to the *Shuowén*, it means the pouring of water; it is composed of the radical *shuǐ* and the phonetic *shāng*. *Chì* has the same pronunciation. The [text] records it as *tì* (渧), which is an error resulting from the omission of the character *kǒu* (口) during transcription.

10. Volume Ten. Regarding "Qiānluǒ" (牽裸): The upper character "qiān" (牽) is pronounced with the initial *yán* (延); Gu Yewáng states that "qiān" means "to lead. This has already been explained previously. The character is written as "qiān" (牽), which is a vernacular form. The lower character "luǒ" (裸) is pronounced with the final *guǒ* (果). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Luǒ" (裸) is equivalent to "zǔ" (祖). It is composed of the radical "clothing" (衣) and the phonetic "guǒ" (果). This has already been explained previously. End of entry.

"Yuan" (㳂) is pronounced as "shang" (上) with the reversed "yue" (悅) and "juan" (涓). Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states: "To go downstream following the current is called yuan. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "following water," with "yan" (󱯀) as the phonetic component; "yan" (󱯀) is pronounced as "yuanxuan" (緣選). It is incorrect for Lu to have written "gong" (公) instead of "yuan" (㳂).

“Lěi” (儡) is pronounced with the same initial as *lú* and *duī* (a retroflex). The *Qūlǐ* (曲禮) states: “The mother’s *lěi* [is the same]. There is no record of its phonetic value; the *Shēngyùn* (聲韻) states that *lěi* is the same as *wú*, meaning “no distinction. According to the *Shuowén* (說文), it is composed of the radicals for “person” (人) and “enclosure” (畾), with the phonetic component *léi* (雷).
11. The eleventh fascicle. *Nurou* (濡𩠐): the former character is pronounced with the initial *ru* and the final *zhu*; it means "to pass before the eyes. *Achu* (阿閦):
the latter character is pronounced with the initial *chu* and the final *suo*; it is the name of a scripture.

*Shòuhuàn* (授幻): The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains this as "bestowing" (*dàoyǔ*). The scripture uses the character *huàn*, which is a vulgar form. This is the title of the scripture. *Bùxiùn* (不眴): The second character is pronounced *xuèjiàn*.

Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that "míngxiùn" (眴) refers to the manner of looking. Gu Yewang says that "míngxiùn" means to cause one's eyes to move. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it means "the eyes flicker," written with the radical for "eye" (*mù*) and the phonetic *xún* (旬; same pronunciation).
*Lengqie* (楞伽): The first character is pronounced *lé* (with the *dēng* rhyme) and the second is pronounced *qié*;
it is a Sanskrit term. Volume 12: The twelfth volume; *xiàngyàxià* (象腋下): The second character is pronounced *yì* (with the *yí* rhyme); it is the name of the scripture.
*Śyāma-putra* (the character *shǎn* is pronounced with the *shī* and *fàn* finals; this is the name of a sūtra).
*Pāśa* (the first character is pronounced with the *juān* and *yuǎn* finals, and the second with the *sāng* and *luò* finals;
this is the name of a sūtra). *Koṭi* (the second character is pronounced with the *zhì* and *chī* finals; the sūtra text uses the vulgar character *yí*).
*Luòdǎn* (羅亶) [the second character pronounced *zhǎnlián*]: this is the name of a scripture. *Āntí* (菴提) [the first character pronounced *yánhán*]:

this is the name of a scripture. *Zhì* (摭): the first character is read as *zhēngshí*. Kǒng Ānguó’s *Preface to the Book of Documents* (*Shūxù*) states: "I have gathered and selected (*cǎizhì*) the words of various masters to establish commentaries and transmissions. According to the *Fāngyán*, *zhì* means to gather or pick up; it refers to taking an object with the hand. The *Kǎoshēng* states that *zhì* is also synonymous with *shí* (to gather). The *Zìshū Guìyuànzhūcóng* also writes it with the radical "stone" (*shí*), and its pronunciation and meaning are identical. The *Shuowén* explains it as a compound character formed from the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic element "shù" (*shù*).

"Without bending" (wú róu): "róu" is pronounced as *rǒu* (with the radical *yǒu*). The *Zhouyi* says, "Bending wood to make a gate. The *Kaosheng* says it means to burn wood and twist it so that what was straight becomes curved. In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, it follows the "wood" radical with the phonetic "róu"; alternatively, it is also written with the "fire" radical as *róu*, which is likewise acceptable; the same applies to the following text.

"Yecheng" (鄴城): The first character is read as *yǎn* and the second as *jié* (with the radical reversed). The *Weishu* states that Yecheng was the capital of the Wei dynasty; it refers to the county of Yecheng mentioned in the *Hanshu*. "Jiejuan" (解捲):
The first character is read as *juǎn* and the second as *yuán* (with the radical reversed). This is the title of a scripture, as previously explained.

13. Volume Thirteen. Regarding "tuōxī" (脫躧): the second character is pronounced as *shī* (師) with the *zǐ* (滓) rhyme. Mencius says: "He regards the abandonment of the world as the casting off of worn-out sandals (*bìxī*). Thus, "abandoning righteousness" (*qì yì*) is identical to "casting off sandals. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that *xī* (躧) belongs to the category of footwear. The *Shuowén* (說文) writes it as *lín* (𩌦), taking *jié* (革) as the radical and *shī* (師) as the phonetic. The *Shēnglèi* (聲類) records it as such; the modern standard character is written as *xī* (屣), formed by the abbreviated form of *lǚ* (履). It is interchangeable with *xī* (屣).
*Ārāḍa* (the first character pronounced with the *zhǐ* and *ān* tones) is a name for a person in the Sanskrit language;
*Datta* (the second character pronounced with the *duō* and *tuó* tones) is the title of a scripture;
*Aṅgulimālya* (the first character pronounced *yāng* and the second *qún* and *lǜ*) is the title of a scripture.
"Yutian" (于闐)—the lower tone is "diàn"—is the name of a kingdom in the Western Regions; it is recorded as "Yan" (釬) or "Zhen" (鎭), which is incorrect, as has already been explained previously.
14. Volume Fourteen, Scroll Fourteen: "Aśoka" (阿闍貰)—the lower character is "she-zhi" (設制), which should be corrected to "zheng" (正); the record uses "shei" (貰), which is an error.
*Dūnhuáng*: the first character is pronounced *tú* (with the tone *huán*) and the second has the sound *huáng*. The *Púsà hào lù* (Record of Bodhisattva Names) writes it as *cǎo*, which is incorrect.
*Mùqié*: the second character is pronounced *qiāngjiā*. It is the name of a scripture. *Ōuhé*:
the first character is pronounced *qūhóu* and the second has the sound *hé*. It is the name of a scripture.
The name of the treatise is *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (the "Yoga" is pronounced with the initial *yǔ* and the final *xū* reversed).
Volume Fifteen. The title of the scripture is *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (the "Bi" in *Bìsù* is pronounced with the initial *bì* and the final *miè* reversed). Volume Fifteen.
*Hūla* (the first character pronounced with the *hu* tone and reversed as *gù*) is a name for a scripture.
*Heqie* (the first character is correctly the word *bō*; those who follow the original text have erred; the second character is pronounced *qū yù*) is also a name for a scripture.

Regarding *Jinbi*, the old commentary states that it is sometimes written as *fù*. The text of the record uses the character *niǚ* (woman) to form the character *chán*, but this character does not exist in the dictionaries.

*Xiéwáng* (蠍王): The first character is pronounced *xiān* (歇) with a reversed *xīn* (軒) tone; it is a name from a scripture. The entry in the *Lù* (錄) uses *hè* (曷), which has the pronunciation *hé* (褐); this deviates from the original meaning and is therefore not adopted. *Jiàoxìng* (僥倖):
The first character is pronounced *jiǎo* (皎) with a *yáo* (堯) tone, and the second is pronounced *héng* (衡) with a *gěng* (耿) tone; it is a name from a scripture.

*Seng-she-tuo-lü* (僧歰多律) is the Chinese transcription of the Sanskrit name for a scripture; it is written with the character *she* (歰), which follows the radical for fire—this is incorrect. *Shen-xie* (繕寫) [is pronounced with the first tone on *chan-zhan*]:

Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that *shen* means "to repair"; its phonetic analysis indicates it means "to create. The *Shuowen* also says it means "to supplement," following the radical for silk (*mi*) with the phonetic *shan*. The second character, *xie* (寫), is pronounced with the third tone on *xi-ye*; the *Guangya* states it means "to copy" (*xicheng*). The phonetic analysis says "copying" is synonymous with "writing. To write it with the character *xiao* (寫) following the radical for knives is a vulgar form. The character *jing* (冖) is pronounced *mi*. *Note: This passage provides philological commentary on the transcription and orthography of Buddhist technical terms.*

16. Volume Sixteen, Part Sixteen. The character *jiǔ* (究) [is composed as follows]: According to the *Shuowen*, it is written with the radical *wǎng* (網). It is pronounced *hē-tǎn* (訶坦). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that *jiǔ* is synonymous with *xī* (希). Gu Yewang says it means "sparse" (*xīsū*). The record uses *hǎn* (罕), which is an error. The lower part is pronounced *jiū* (鳩). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that *jiù* (究) is equivalent to *qióng* (窮). Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* explains it as meaning "to investigate exhaustively" (*hèjìn*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *xué* (穴) and the phonetic *jiǔ* (九).

Regarding "覽" (lǎn): below it is the character "𠂢," which is explained in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as "the oblique flow of water. It is formed from the reversed form of "永" (yǒng); the form written with "錄" (lù) is a vulgar character. Regarding "謦欬" (qǐngkài):

the first character is read as "輕" (qīng) with the phonetic "󲯑" (qiè), and the second is read as "開愛" (kā'ài). These are names for sounds in the classics; they were already explained previously. The form written with "口" (mouth) following [the radical] is a vulgar character for "謦."
*Pǔbù*: the first character is pronounced as *pǔ* (with the *pu* rhyme) and the second is the character *bù*. This is the title of a sutra. *Chàntí*:
the first character is pronounced as *chǎn* (with the *chàn* rhyme) and the second has the sound *tí*. This is also the title of a sutra. *Ráoluàn*:
the first character is pronounced as *rǎo* (with the *niǎo* rhyme). These are titles of sutras.

Regarding "chóng" (insect) and "hú" (fox): the former is pronounced yě; according to the *Zìshū* (Dictionary of Characters), it should be written with the radical 皿 as 蟲, yet in the current records it is erroneously written with three 虫.

Regarding "wū" (crow): it is sometimes written as "niǎo" (bird). Regarding "yǒng" (brave) and "cí" (eloquent) in the term "Fànzhì" (Brahmin): the upper character is pronounced yǒng (sǒng); the *Zìshū* correctly writes it as 勇, meaning courageous, fierce, and robust. The ancient form is now written as 甬 to form 𭟵; in the recorded texts, 𭟵 is a coarse transcription of the name of a scripture.
*Yezhǒng* (曳踵): the first character is pronounced *yán* with the *jì* tone; the second character is pronounced *zhōng* with the *lǒng* tone.
This is a name from a scripture. *Lúhǔ* (羅怙): the second character is pronounced *hú* with the *gǔ* tone.

This is a name from a scripture. *Bìchū* (苾芻): the first character is pronounced *pín* with the *mì* tone; the second character is pronounced *chǔ* with the *yóu* tone. This is a name from a scripture. The character *chū* (芻) used in the catalog is a vulgar form.
*Śaila-patthaka*: This is the name of a scripture; in the catalog, it is erroneously written as *yī* (from the mouth radical).
*Ghoṣita*: This is the name of a scripture; in the text of the catalog, it is written as *shòu*, which is a vulgar character.
"Qiáo" (二僑) [the second character pronounced with the *qiáo* and *yǎo* rhymes] is a name from the scriptures.
"Bèi" (唄) [the second character pronounced with the *bái* and *mài* rhymes] is a name from the scriptures.
"Qùláng" (𧏙蜋) [the first character pronounced with the *què* and *xiāng* rhymes; the second character pronounced with the *lì* and *zhāng* rhymes] is a name from the scriptures.

17. Volume Seventeen, Part One. The character *fan* (繁) is pronounced with the initial *fu* (伐) and the final *zheng* (證). According to the *Zishu*, it is correctly written with the radical *zhou* (舟). The *Shuowen* states that *fan* means "to resemble" (*ru*) when objects are presented to one another as gifts. The *Guoyu* says it means "a model" (*shi*), and the *Kaosheng* says it means "a surplus" (*yu*). In both ancient and modern times, the meaning of the correct character is the same. It is composed of the radicals *bei* (貝) and a simplified form of *yi* (𠢧). To write it with the radical *yue* (月) as *sheng* (賸) is a vulgar character.

*Udāna*: "U" (鄔) and "da" (陁) are pronounced as *wǔ* (烏) and *gǔ* (古) respectively; this is the name of a sutra in the Sanskrit language. *Kṣepa* (𠜂削): "Kṣe" (𠜂) is pronounced as *chǎn* (產) and *jiān* (姦);

the *Shēnglèi* (聲類) states that *kṣe* is equivalent to "fixed" (*dìng*). The *Jiāyǔ* (家語) says, "The Master fixed the Odes and the Books. The *Shuowén* (說文) defines it as "to cut" (*chuò*, 剟). It is pronounced as *zhú* (竹) and *liè* (劣); "cutting and shaving" (*chuòxiào*). It is composed of the radical "knife" (刀) and the phonetic "lán" (𠕋), which is pronounced *cè* (策); "lán" refers to bamboo tablets (*jiǎn*). This is a compound character. *Xià* (下): pronounced as *xiāng* (廂) and *què* (雀); the *Guǎngyǎ* (廣雅) states it means "to reduce" (*xuējiàn*). The *Shuowén* states it is composed of the radical "knife" (刀) and the phonetic "shàng" (尚).

*Wúdiàn* (無玷): The second character is pronounced *dīngyǎn* (丁黶). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (毛詩傳) states that *diàn* (玷) is synonymous with *quē* (缺, deficiency). It is a standard character from ancient times to the present, composed of the radical "jade" (*yù*) and the phonetic "zhān" (*zhàn*).
*Líohì* (療痔): The first character is pronounced *lízhào* (離照) and the second is *chílǐ* (持里). This is the name of a medical treatise.

*Bì* (裨): Pronounced *bì mí* (with the final syllable reversed). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Yīlǐ* states: "The word *bì* means *bǐ* (to augment). The *Shuowén* says it means "to add," composed of the radical *yī* (clothing) and the phonetic *bēi*.

Volume 18, Fascicle 18. *Dōngchǎn* (東闡): Pronounced *dōng chǎn xià shàn fǎn*. The *Cāngjiépiān* states: "The word *chǎn* is equivalent to 'opening'. Hàn Kāngbó’s commentary on the *Zhōuwǔ* states: "It means 'clarifying'. The *Shuowén* says it is composed of the radical *mén* (gate) and the phonetic *dān*.

To "seek and examine" (xún yuè): the upper radical is *xī* (pronounced *xiǎn* with the *fǎn* [rhyme] *jiǎ*). Jia Ji’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states: "Seeking" (*xún*) means "to employ. The *Fāngyán* states: "It means 'long'. Guo Pu’s commentary states: "'Seeking' refers to length; it is the breadth of laws and measures. The *Shuowen* states: "'Seeking and examining' (*xúnyì*) means to investigate principles. It is composed of *gōng*, *kǒu*, and *chà*. *Gōng* and *kǒu* signify disorder; *chà* and *cùn* signify the meeting point where principles are divided. It is a word formed through associative meaning (*huìyì*). The lower character is *yuán* (pronounced *xuě*). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "'Examining' (*yuè*) means 'to select' (*jiǎn*). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "'To examine' means 'to enumerate' (*shù*). The standard character for all periods consists of the radical *mén* and the phonetic *duì*.

The character 放 (fàng) is pronounced with the *shang* and *wang* finals (*fang*). Liu Zhao’s commentary on the *Gongyang Zhuan* states: "Fàng means to compare. Kong’s commentary on the *Lunyu* states: "It means to rely upon. The *Guangya* also defines it as "to follow. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical 攵 (pǔ) and the phonetic 方 (fāng). To add the radical 亻 (rén) to form 倣 (fǎng) is incorrect; the latter is simply the character for "practice" (xí).

Regarding "wěigō" (訛舛): Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states that "wěi" means transformation (*huà*). The *Kǎoshēng* says it means error (*miù*). According to the standard characters of the past and present, this is a compound character formed from "speech" (*yán*) and "transformation" (*huà*), conveying the meaning through their combined sense. Lexicons correctly write it with "speech" (*yán*) above; "tuó" (譌) is merely a phonetic transcription with the same meaning. Regarding "chuānyuǎn" (舛): Gù Yěwáng states that "chuǎn" means discrepancy or unevenness. The *Shuowén* says "chuǎn" means to lie facing opposite directions. It is composed of "night" (*xī*, pronounced suī) and "kuàihuà" (󱸰, pronounced kuàihuà), signifying things turning their backs upon one another.

"Qīngguā" (青呱): "Guā" is pronounced as "yǐ" and "zhǎo. According to the *Qīngguā*, it is the common name for a toad; this character does not exist in standard dictionaries, but it is the title of a scripture.

"Wúmǎn" (蕪穬): The upper character "wú" has the phonetic value "mù. The *Zītǒng* states that "wú" means wasteland or overgrown weeds. Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* also defines it as "wèi" (weeds). The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "grass" (艸) with "wú" as its phonetic. The lower character "mǎn" is pronounced as "gǔmǎng" (虢猛). The *Cangjie pian* states that "mǎn" is simply "sù" (grain). The *Zilin* says it refers to grain that has awns. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines "mǎng" as "sù," composed of the radical "grain" (禾) with "guǎng" as its phonetic.

The character *biè* (莂) is pronounced as *liè* (列) with the final consonant *fǎn* (反). It refers to the act of distinguishing or classifying. The *Pīcāng* states: "To *biè* means to divide and transplant seeds where they are dense. This character does not appear in standard dictionaries; however, according to the *Kǎoshēng*, it may be read as *guǎng* (廣), while the *Guǎngyùn* derives it from the radicals for "grass" (*cǎo*) and "separate" (*bié*). *Jì* (穊) is pronounced *jì* (既), and *shì* (蒔) is pronounced *shì* (是).

The character for *bìn* (擯) is pronounced *shàng bì rěn fǎn*. Sima Biao’s commentary on the *Zhuangzi* states: “*Bìn* means to discard. The *Shiji* says: “They cast each other out (*pái bìn*); this is what it refers to. In the standard characters of antiquity and today, it is written with the radical *shǒu* (hand) and the phonetic *bìn*. The lower character is pronounced *chí*.

*Liè* (𩠐): Pronounced *liáo* (良灼反). The *Monthly Ordinances* (*Yueling*) states, "There shall be no fourfold *liè*. *Liè* refers to robbery and plunder; it is the same as *lù* (錄) and *luò* (錄). According to the character dictionaries, all treat this as the character *lüè* (略). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* says, "*Lüè* means to take. The *Fangyan* says it means "permanence" (*yǒng*). The *Shenglèi* says it is the *lüè* of glancing over. The *Shuowen* says, "*Jīnglüè* (經略) means territory; it is composed of 田 (field) and 各 (gè) as the phonetic component. The pronunciation of *liè* as *liàng* (亮) is a significant error in meaning and is not accepted.

*Shè* (pronounced with the *tǎmòhòu* rhyme) is the name of a place in Kuàijī. There is the Aśoka Stūpa in Mò County; according to the *Shuōwén*, the character for Mò is composed of the radical "city" (*yì*) and the phonetic element "shèn" (*shēng*).

*Shàn* (pronounced with the *yánrǎn* rhyme): according to the *Ěryá*, "shàn" means sharp; according to the *Pīcāng*, it means to pare. The *Yìjīng* says, "carve wood to make an oar. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means to make something pointed and sharp; it is a compound character formed from both its shape and its sound.

Regarding "guǎngmào" (廣袤): the second character is pronounced with the *móu* rhyme. The *Yùnyuán* states that *mào* means "extending. The *Shēnglèi* says that *mào* is synonymous with "long. The *Shuowén* explains: "That which is east-west is called *guǎng*; that which is north-south is called *mào*. It is formed from the radical 'clothing' (*yī*) and the phonetic 'móu'."
"Platter full of eels": *man* (鰻) is a name for the eel; it is composed of the radical "fish" (魚) with the phonetic *man* (曼), which is pronounced like *wan*.

"Wu" (誣): The upper character is read as *wu-fu* (武夫反). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan* states that "Wu" means to deceive. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* says "Wu" means to slander. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says "Wu" is to add false words; it is composed of the radical "speech" (言) with the phonetic *wu* (巫). The lower character is read as *zi-ci* (資此反). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* says "Zi" (訾) is to defame a person with speech. The *Shuowen Jiezi* [states it] is composed of the radical "speech" (言) with the phonetic *ci* (此).

*Huān* (歡): The upper radical is *huò* (豁), with the phonetic component *guān* (官). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "joyful delight," though it is also written as *huān* (歡). *Cǎn* (慘): The lower radical is *gǎn* (感). According to the *Erya*, it means "sorrow. Guo Pu says it refers to the appearance of a worthy person in a state of grief and resentment. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "poisonous" or "cruel," and it is also written as *cǎn* (憯) meaning "pain. It is a word formed by combining a semantic and a phonetic component.

*Bashang* (灞上): "Ba" is pronounced as *ba* with the *ma* tone; it is the name of a river in Qin, located east of the city of Chang'an. According to the *Shuowen*, it is a transitive character composed of the radicals for "rain," "metal," and "moon.

*Juezhuo* (鸑鷟): "Jue" is pronounced as *wu* with the *jiao* tone; "Zhuo" is pronounced as *shi* with the *jiao* tone. The *Guoyu* states: "When the Zhou dynasty rose, the *juezhuo* bird sang on Mount Qi. Jia Dui’s commentary notes that it is a divine bird and another name for the *feng* (phoenix).

"Cūla" (麁穬): the first character is pronounced *cāng zú* (正體 from three "deer" [鹿] to form 麤); the second character is pronounced *měng* (󳌴). This was already explained in the previous *Nèidiǎnlù* (內典錄).
"Zhāngyè" (張掖) is also the name of a commandery (*jùn*).

*Dàduī* (大堆): In the *Chuci* commentary by Wang Yi, it is stated that *kuíduī* means "high. The *Wenzidian* says that *duī* refers to a small mound; it is composed of the radical *tǔ* (earth) and the phonetic *zhuī*, and is recorded as *duī* in its vulgar form. The second character, *tān* (貪), has the pronunciation *dá* (荅). The *Wenzidian* says it refers to a pagoda or temple.

*Jiǎokǎi*: The first character (*jiǎo*) is pronounced as *shuāng* (two tones), and the second character (*kǎi*) is pronounced as *kāigǎi* (two tones). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *jiǎo* means "bright," and *kǎi* refers to "high and dry ground. To say it is *jiǎokǎi* means that the steps are already high and large, and furthermore are situated upon a ridge; being high, prominent, and commanding a clear view, it is named *jiǎokǎi*.

*Xiǎnyǔn*: The first character is pronounced *xián* (with the variant *jiǎn*) or sometimes written as *xiàn*; the second is pronounced *yǔn*. The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* states: "Xiǎnyǔn is an alternative name for the northern Di tribes.

*Yù* (jade): The character is pronounced *yì* (with the variant *xī*). The *Wénzì Jílüè* states: "Yù is black jade. The recorded texts also write it with the "jade" radical as *yī*, which is likewise acceptable.

The character for *lú* (櫨) is pronounced "lú" (upper radical) and "dānggǒu" (lower radical). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "The *lú* is the *jī* (枅) atop a pillar; the *zhǒu* (枓) is the square wooden block at the head of the pillar, shaped like a *dǒu* (斗). The character for *jī* (枅) is pronounced "qìjiàn" (upper radical) and "fǎn" (lower radical); both are phono-semantic compounds.

"Piāoliè (剽掠): The upper character is pronounced *pǐ yào* (匹曜反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that 'piāo' refers to the plundering of people's wealth and goods. The text here follows the form with the radical *shān* (彡), which is incorrect. The lower character is pronounced *lì zhuó* (力灼反). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states that 'liè' means 'jié liè' (劫掠, to plunder by force). Dictionaries give the pronunciation *liàng* (亮), but this meaning is erroneous; it is not accepted here."

*Nào* (pronounced with the *níng* and *xiào* finals): The *Guǎngyá* states that *nào* is synonymous with *ní* (mud) and also means "multitude. Zheng’s commentary on the *Yílǐ* states it means "universal" (*pǔ*) or "harmonious" (*hé*). The *Huáihuánzǐ* states that water is so called because it is *nào*, meaning it is capable of drowning and is moist and slippery. The *Shēnglèi* states that *nào* is synonymous with *nì* (to drown). According to the standard characters of ancient and modern times, this character is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic "tuó" (*zhuó*).
"Gai" (上音渙反, 下音機未反): The *Shuowen* states it means "to irrigate. It refers to moistening the roots and stems of plants currently being cultivated with water.
"Wa" (倭國, 烏和反) is the name of a small country in the Eastern Sea; it borders Silla (新羅). [The character] is written with the radical 𨸏 (from 錄); to write it otherwise is incorrect.
Dǎo (倒) and gǔ (𤝔): the upper tone is as written, the lower tone is *chái* (柴).

Gé (葛) and lěi (藟): the lower tone of *lěi* is pronounced *luí* (倫委反). Guō Pú’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "Lěi is a type of climbing vine. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* says it is the creeping stem of the *gé* plant. The character *lù* (錄) is written as *tè* (󳎴), which is incorrect.
*Wèi* (upper character pronounced *huǐn*, lower character pronounced *yíng*) means "to hang oneself.

The *Zuozhuan* states: "The Marquis Mo hanged himself at Guānhuáng Valley. The *Kǎoshēng* says: "To 'hang' (*yì*) is to die by one's own hand. The *Gōngyáng Zhuan* states: "King Lìng hanged himself and died. Hé Xiū’s commentary notes: "This refers to dying by hanging oneself (*jīng*)."

Regarding "祇速" (zhī sù): the character for "祇" (zhǐ) has the phonetic component "日" (rì) with the radical "攵" (pén). The commentary states that "祇" means "just as" (jiù shì) and also "peaceful" (ān). Regarding "鐵碪" (tiě zhèn):

the character for "碪" (zhèn) has the phonetic component "縶" (zhí) with the radical "石" (shí); it is also written as "砧" (zhēn), but in the *Lù* (Record/Dictionary), the version with the radical "木" (mù) and the character "杭" (háng) is incorrect; it is also written as "椹" (zhēn).

"Huǎngyù": the upper character is pronounced *huángguǎng*;

the *Shuowen* states that "huǎng" means brightness. The lower character is pronounced *yǔlù*; the *Shuowen* states that "yù" means radiance or brilliance, and also implies intensity. Regarding "yá-lán" (牙匳): the phonetic component is "kǎo" (考), which follows the radical "fāng" (匚) to form "lán" (匳); this is the correct orthography. It resembles a box with raised edges and joints, used for containing objects. In the *Guìyuàn Zhūcóng* (桂苑珠叢), it is written as "lián" (籢) with the "zhú" (竹) radical, referring specifically to a case for holding a mirror. According to usage, there are incense boxes (*xiāng-lán*) and ivory mirror cases (*xiàngjìng-lán*). The "ivory case" (*yá-lán*) mentioned here refers to a small casket made of ivory.
*Pai-ch'ieh* (white cotton cloth): the second character is pronounced *t'ien-hsieh*.

*P'ou-chi* (to split and strike): the first character is pronounced *pu-kou*. Master Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states: "To *p'ou* is equivalent to to break. Master Kuei’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "To divide in the middle is called *p'ou*. The *Cangjie pian* states: "It means to analyze. The *Shuowen jiezi* states: "It means to separate; it is composed of the radical 'knife' (*dao*) and the phonetic component 'tou' (*tou*), which is pronounced *tu-kou*."

The character *tǐng* (珽) consists of "zhèng" (正) on top and "tíng" (汀) with the radical "jǐng" (井) below; it is pronounced with the final *-ing*. The *Shuowén* says: "The *tǐng* is a large *guī* (jade scepter). It is three chi long; the 'chi' used in antiquity was eight *cùn*, which is equivalent to two chi and four *cùn* by present-day measure. It is composed of the radical 'yù' (jade) and the phonetic 'tíng' (廷)."

The character 𧷽 (yú) is pronounced as "zhèng-fǎn. The *Zìshū* states that 𧷽 means "remainder. It is the correct orthography from ancient times to the present, composed of 貝 (bèi) and a simplified form of 𠢧 (yí).

To record it as 𧷽 is a vulgar character. The character 溳 (yún) is pronounced as "yú-qún-fǎn. The *Shuōwén* states: "The river Yún originates in Kuíyáng County of Nányáng Commandery; flowing eastward, it enters Xiàkǒu. It is composed of 水 (shuǐ) with 員 (yuán) as the phonetic component. The pronunciation of 員 is yún.

According to the *Guoyu*, "quán" (銓) means "to provide fully" (*jù*). The *Erya* states that "quán" is "law" (*lǜ*) or "to weigh" (*quán*). Xinli (莘里): Zhēn (臻) is the phonetic inversion; the *Mao Shi* commentary states that Xin is the name of a state and also the name of a village.

it is a personal name. Xūxī (歔欷): The first character is pronounced xǔyú (許魚) and the second is xǔyī (許衣). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that "xūxī" refers to the appearance of weeping with sobs. He Xiu’s commentary on the *Gongyang Zhuan* states it means "sorrow. The *Cangjie Pian* states it is the lingering sound of weeping. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "xūxī" is the emission of breath. Both characters include the radical 欠 (quàn), while xū and xī are their respective phonetic components.

Regarding "mó" (pronounced with the initial *mo* and the final rhyme *hu*): the *Guǎngyá* states that "mó" means to copy a form; the *Shēnglèi* says it refers to a model or method; and the *Shuōwén* defines it as "a plan or pattern," written with the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "mo. It is also written as "mō."

"Mínyuè (閩越): míng (閔) is pronounced as bīn (彬), and yuè (越) is pronounced as xiàyuányuè (下爰月). Guō’s commentary on the *Shānhǎijīng* states that Mínyuè refers to Xī’ōu (西甌), which is the present-day Jiàn'ān Commandery. The *Shuōwén* says it is a region of the southeastern Yùe people; it is also a type of snake. It is composed of the radical 虫 (insect/creature) and the character 門 (gate) with 省 (shěng) as its phonetic."

"Qiān" (牽) is pronounced with the rhyme *shàng* and *yán*. The *Guǎngyǎ* states that "qiān" is synonymous with "wǎn" (to pull). Zhèng Xuān’s commentary on the *Zhōu Lǐ* says that when an ox stands at the front of a carriage, it is called a "qiān. The *Shuōwén* says: "To lead forward; it is composed of 'jiǒng' (冂) and 'yǐn' (引). 'Jiǒng' represents the halter of the ox, and 'xuán' (玄) is the phonetic component. The character below is pronounced with the rhyme *bǎn* (𠕀坂); alternatively, it may be written as "wǎn" (輓) with the "chē" (車) radical, while the version written as "mǎn" (𢱍) in the records is an error.

"Ji" (揊): The upper radical is "丕" (pī, bī). The commentary on the sounds states that it is the sound of heavy binding; according to the *Guǎngyá*, it is the sound of striking. The entry in the *Lù* (錄) uses "tǔ" (土) to form "fú" (堛), where "fú" is like a clod of earth. This is not the original meaning, so it is not adopted here.

"Doulu Baop" (豆盧褒): "Baop" is the second character of the surname Lou; it is pronounced with the final *pao* (保) and *mao* (毛) rhymes. It is a personal name. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states that "baop" means to promote or to extol beauty. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "clothing" (*yi*) and the phonetic "bao" (*pao*).

The character *jùn* (畯): the upper radical is read as *tè néng fǎn*. Dictionaries state it is derived from "water" (*shuǐ*) and the abbreviated form of "to restrain" (*yí*). The lower part is read as *zūn jùn fǎn*. This was *Jùn* (畯), the Governor of Jiangling during the Jin dynasty. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that the character *jùn* refers to one who previously cultivated the fields and instructs the *sèfú* (village overseers). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is composed of "field" (*tián*) and "to be swift" (*jùn*) as its phonetic.

The character for "tiè" (締) is pronounced with the initial *xi* and the final *fǎn*; the *Shuowen* states that it means "to bind and not untie," and it also implies "firmness. It is composed of the radical "silk thread" (*xì*) and the phonetic "dì. The character below, "gǔ" (古), is pronounced with the final *hòu*. According to the *Yupian*, the correct form is "gòu" (冓), which is identical to "gòu" (構). "Gòu" means "to join together" or "to complete. The *Shuowen* states that it means "to accumulate timber. It is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "gòu."

The second tone of *shà* (汰) is *tài*. King Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that *tài* means "surging waves. The *Guǎngyá* says it means "to wash. The *Kǎoshēng* says that *tài* refers to the appearance of surging waves and bleaching (*làn*). The *Shuowén* defines *tài* as "surging waves; to select," taking *shuǐ* (water) as the radical and *tài* as the phonetic component. *Làn* (湅) is pronounced *liàn*.

*Dōngrán* (烔然): The *Dongfanhàn Shī* states that "yùnlóng" (薀隆) means *dōngdōng* (烔烔); the *Pīcāng* says it is an appearance of being *dōngdōng*. In both ancient and modern standard characters, it is composed of the radical "fire" (火) and shares the same phonetic element.

"𭫲桁" (shuāng-háng): "率" is pronounced as *shuài* (following the commentary on the *Erya*, which states that *chuī* is the same as *chuán*, meaning rafters); "下" is pronounced as *xìng* (gēng), and the *Kǎoshēng* says it refers to the ridge-beam of a roof. "武彠" (wǔ-yuè): "央" is pronounced as *yāng* (jiǎo), which was the taboo name for Empress Wu;

the *Kǎoshēng* says *yuè* means to measure, specifically to measure according to a standard (*guī*). *Note: The transcription provided contains several non-standard characters. The translation above interprets them based on the phonetic and semantic glosses provided in the source text.*

Zhou Ji rebelled, deceiving [the authorities]. "Lǎomǔ" (old woman) is read as *cìmó* (補反). The *Jiāngbiǎo zhuàn* (Biographies of the South of the Yangtze) states that "mǔ" refers to an elderly woman; it is also written with the "horse" radical as "mā," with the same pronunciation. The *Shuowén* explains *jī* (齎) as "carrying objects while traveling on a road"; it is composed of the "treasure" radical (*bèi*) and the phonetic "qí" (*zhì*). *Xià jì xī fǎn* (下祭奚反): [The character] is pronounced *xià* (祭) and *xī* (奚). *Shuōwén yún* (說文云): The *Shuowén* says... *Cái xí chí wù yú dào xíng yě* (携持物於道行也): Carrying objects while walking along a path. *Cóng bèi zhī shēng* (從貝齊聲): It takes the "treasure" radical and "qí" as its phonetic.
"Qiao" (譙) is pronounced *jiāo* (齊焦反). The *Hanshu* states that the ancient state of Qiao was the present-day Pei Commandery. "Zhi" (蹠) is pronounced *zhī* (章亦反);
the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "zhi" means the sole of the foot, composed of the radical "foot" (足) with the phonetic component "shu" (庶).
*Yè* (三謐, pinyin: yè; note: *mín bì fǎn*):

The *Hànshū zhù* states that the *yèmén* is a small side gate adjacent to the main gate within the palace. The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) with the phonetic component "night" (*yè*).

To "raise the *yu* banner" means to go among the people below; the *Zhou Li* states that a bird with a hawk (*yǔnsǔn*) serves as the *yu*. The *Cishi* (Inspector of the State) raises the *yu* banner within the commanderies and districts. Zheng Xuan’s commentary says this symbolizes their courage. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* states that the *yu* consists of the skin and feathers of a bird placed atop a pole. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "flag" (*yàn*) and the phonetic "yǔ."

"Sure and immovable" (què bù yí): "què" is pronounced with the upper tone of the *qiāng* rhyme group and the reversed tone of the *qiāng* rhyme group (alternatively, the *kǔ* and *jiāng* rhymes). In the *Commentary on the Words* (*Wényán*) of the *Book of Changes* (*Zhouyì*), it says: "It is surely so, such that it cannot be pulled out. Furthermore, the *Appended Phrases* (*Xící*) states: "Now, Qian is surely resolute, showing people its ease" (*yì*; *yì* is pronounced with the level tone of the *zhì* rhyme group). Han Kangbo’s commentary says: "Sure" (*què*) describes the appearance of firmness and solidity. The *Kǎoshēng* says: "Sure" (*què*) refers to being solid and firm.

The character for *chuan* (輲) is pronounced *chuán*, with a reading identical to that of *chuán* (船). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "A wheelless carriage is called a *chuan*; it means to roll along by attaching to the ground. Sima Biao’s commentary on the *Zhuangzi* states: "*Chuan* is equivalent to 'rolling' (*zhuan*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "*Chuan* refers to a low-wheeled enclosed carriage (*fanche*). The correct form is the character *shuān* (輇), which shares the same pronunciation and meaning.

*Jin* (僅): Pronounced *qín*. The *Guǎngyá* states that "jin" means "few" or "scarcely able. Whether ancient or modern, the standard character is composed of the radical "person" (亻) and the phonetic "jin" (堇).

The pronunciation of "jin" is *jǐn*. *Xuēi-jìn* (煨燼): The upper character, *xuēi*, is pronounced *wū huái*. The *Guǎngyá* states that "xuēi" means "smoldering heat. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "fire in a pan," composed of the radical "fire" (火) and the abbreviated phonetic "wèi" (畏). The lower character, *jìn*, is pronounced *xī jìn*. Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states that "jìn" refers to the remaining wood from a fire. The *Yùpiān* records the correct form as *chén* (𣂉), with the same pronunciation and meaning as above.

"Mián" (綿) is pronounced *shàngmiǎn* (上沔篇). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that "mián" means "to entwine. The *Fenmen* (Mao Shi Zhuan) says: "Miánmián describes a state of being long and uninterrupted. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "silk" (*xì*) and the phonetic "bó" (*bó*). The lower character is pronounced *gǔdèng* (古鄧). The *Fenmen* says: "Gèn" (亘) means "pervasive" (*biàn*) or, according to the *Fangyan*, "ultimate" (*jìng*). Regarding the character with the "wood" (*mù*) radical and the phonetic "guò" (*guò*), written as *jié* (󲼊), it refers to something being extremely distant.

"Jingxuan" (驚眩): "Xian" (眩) is pronounced as *xuàn* (with the radical *liàn* reversed). The *Cangjie pian* states that it means "vision is unclear. Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* explains it as "to be affected. According to the *Shuowen jiezi*, it is composed of the radical *mu* (eye) with the phonetic *xuan*.

Regarding the character *zhù* (矚) in the phrase "jìn zhǔ" (近矚): the *Xiàzhōng Rǎnyùn Lèi* states that it means "to gaze," "extreme," or "that which all eyes turn toward. The *Yùpiān* writes it with the radical *shī* (尸), as in *shǔ* (屬), meaning "to connect" or "to link. In the *Hànshū*, it is used in the sense of "near. In dictionaries, the character *shǔ* (屬) does not include the radical *mù* (目).

*Jì* (戰悸): The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (Mao Commentary on the Classic of Poetry) states that "jì-jì" means having a rhythmic beat. The *Shuowén* says: "Jì" is the appearance of the heart moving; it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "jì.

*Zhù* (種紵): The lower character is pronounced *chú lǚ*. The *Zhou Lǐ Dǎn Xǐ* (Rites of Zhou, Director of Fibers) states: "Zhù is a plant of the hemp family. Zhèng Xuán’s commentary notes: "A cord of fifteen *zhǎn*; when the cloth is spun fine and white, it is called zhù. The *Shuowén* says: "It belongs to the *qīng* (hemp) family and is of a fine variety; it is composed of the radical 'silk thread' (*xì*) and the phonetic 'níng. The pronunciation of *níng* is as above."
Regarding "di" (墌) in "tiandi" (田墌): the phonetic gloss states that "di" is the same as "ji" (基, foundation).

Regarding "chi" (褫) in "chituō" (褫脫): the *Cangjie pian* states that "chi" means to remove or take off clothes; "che" (撤) is pronounced "chilie" (勅列). The *Shuowen jiezi* states that "tuo" (脫) means to strip off clothes, composed of the radical "yi" (衣) with the phonetic "xi" (虒); "xi" is pronounced "zhilü" (雉錄). It is incorrect to write it with the "tu" (土) radical as "dian" (󳋻).

In "Liu Yun" (劉韞), the upper character is "zheng" (正) and the lower is "fu-fen" (紆粉) in tone; it is a given name. In "Liu Quan" (劉悛), "quan" (悛) is pronounced "yuan" (緣); it is a personal name. Regarding "yong-zhong" (勇鍾) in "rong-zhuo" (鎔斲):

the *Hanshu* states that it refers to what is cast in a smelting furnace (*yongye*). The *Shuowen* states that "rong" (鎔) refers to copper filings; it is a term for the method of smelting and forging vessels, composed of the radical "metal" (金) with the phonetic "rong" (容). The lower character "zhuo" (斲) has the pronunciation "zhuo-kong" (卓孔). The commentary on the *Shangshu* defines it as "chopping and carving. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "zhi-zhuo" (執斲) refers to a master carpenter. The *Shuowen* defines it as "to hack" (斫), composed of the radicals "axe" (斤) and "dou" (𠁁), where "dou" (𠁁) is pronounced "dou" (豆). Alternatively, it may be written as "ji" (斵) with the radical "ji" (𠁬), where "ji" (𠁬) is pronounced "ji" (戟). The version in the record uses "zhuo" (斲), which is an error resulting from transcription.

"Yòngshū" (用紓): "Shū" is pronounced zhùfǎn. In the *Zuozhuan*, it appears in the phrase "to alleviate the difficulties of the state of Chu. Du Yu’s commentary states: "Shū means 'to delay' (*huǎn*). The *Fāngyán* says it means 'to resolve' (*jiě*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "silk thread" (*mì*) and the phonetic "yú"; the version here that uses "zà" (*bā*) to form "shū" is an error.

"Guà" (絓) is pronounced as *hú* (胡卦反). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that it means "to hang" (*xuán*). The *Fāngyán* says it means "to hold. The *Zuǒzhuan* records: "The side horse was snagged (*guà*) on a tree and came to a halt. Gu Yewang says it means "obstructed. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "silk" (*xì*) with "guī" (*guī*) as its phonetic component.

*Shao* (pronounced with the "shuang" and "jiao" finals reversed): The *Guangya* states that a *shao* is a long spear; the *Bicang* states that a *shao* is a spear, and further states that a *shao* is an eighteen-foot spear. It is formed from the radical "spear" (*mao*) and the phonetic element "xiao."

*Chàn-zàn* (剗鏨): The upper character is pronounced *chū-chǎn* (初產反). *Bóyǎ* (博雅) states that "to *chǎn*" is synonymous with "to pare" (*xiāo*). In the *Shēnglèi* (聲類), it is written as *chǎn* (鏟), and both the pronunciation and meaning are identical. The lower character is pronounced *cán-dàn* (慚淡反). *Guǎngyǎ* (廣雅) states that "to engrave" (*zhuān*) is called "to *càn*" (*zàn*). The *Shuōwén* (說文) states: "*Càn* (鏨) is [the same as] *zhuān* (鐫); it is composed of the radical 'metal' (*jīn*) and the phonetic component 'zhǎn' (*zhǎnshēng*). *Zhuān* (鐫) is pronounced *zǐ-quán* (子全反).
Zi-qian (子蒨) is a personal name; the first character is pronounced qiàn (見反), and the second is rén (人). *Wōnliáng* (轀輬):

the upper character is pronounced wū kūn (烏昆反) and the lower is lüè cháng (略常反). The *Shìjì* states that the *wōnliáng* was a bed-chariot; because the First Emperor of Qin died without the funeral rites being formally proclaimed, it subsequently became the vehicle for carrying the coffin. Mèng Kāng’s commentary says: "The *wōnliáng* was originally a carriage for transporting clothing; it had windows and casements—when closed it was warm, and when opened it was cool. The *Kǎoshēng* says it refers to a light carriage. In the *Shuowén*, both characters *wōn* and *liáng* are written with the radical 車 (chariot); *wēn* (京) is also the phonetic component. The pronunciation of *wēn* is the same [as *yīng*].
Regarding "Du Kan" (杜龕): the character *kan* (龕) is a personal name; it is recorded as being used in conjunction with "he" (合) to form the common character *kan* (龕).

Regarding "shēn yín" (呻吟): the upper radical "shēn" (呻) is pronounced *shīzhēn* (詩眞); Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states that "shēn" is also "yín" (吟). The *Cangjie pian* states that "shēn yín" refers to sighing. According to the *Shuowen jiezi*, both characters are composed of the radical "mouth" (口).

The character for "fester" (膿) is pronounced *nóng* (with the initial *dōng* and final *-fǎn*). In standard dictionaries, it is correctly written with the radical for blood (*xiě*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Fester (*nǒng*) refers to swelling blood; it takes the radical for blood and uses *róng* (abbreviated) as its phonetic. The *Kaosheng* says: "The 'fester' of blood is *nǒng*. Wei Hong also wrote it as *nóng*, and it is also written as *sǒng*; these are used interchangeably. To record it as *nóng* is the vulgar form.
"Yānzhàng" (煙漲): The first character is read as *zhāng* (下張). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) says: "Zhàng" means "full. It also uses the character "zhāng" with the departing tone;

the meaning is the same. "Chírán" (歭然): The first character is read as *chí lǐ* (上池里). The *Kǎoshēng* says: "Chí" means "standing. The *Shuowén* states it is composed of "zhǐ" (止) and "sì" (寺) as phonetic components, or written as "zhì" (跱) with "zú" (足) as the radical. To record it here, it is written as "zhì" (峙) with "shān" (山) as the radical; this refers to mountains standing tall.

"Tièkǒng" (iron ore): "shàngtiān" (upper heaven) is read as *jié fǎn zhèng* (the phonetic component of jié and the radical zhèng); "xiàgǔměng" (lower ancient fierce) is read as *fǎn* (a suffix). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Líjì* states: "Kǒng refers to the raw ore of gold, jade, copper, iron, and so forth. It is also written as 丱 (*guàn*) or 𨥥, and also as 磺; the pronunciation and meaning are identical.

"Ji (猜忌): The upper radical is 采 (cǎi), with the phonetic 哉 (zāi). Duan’s commentary on the *Shuowen* states that in the *Zhuangzi*, it means 'to have lingering doubts. The *Fangyan* says it means 'resentment. The *Shuowen* explains: 'Ji refers to resentment and malice; it is composed of the radical 犬 (dog) and the phonetic 青 (qīng).'"

Regarding the characters 碌 (upper radical *lóng*, reversed; lower radical *cōng*, reversed): the *Cāngjié piān* states that "lù-ài" refers to the white appearance of sand and stones. The *Kǎoshēng* states it describes the uneven surface of a stony ground. The reading "lù" in the text is an error for "lù. Regarding 䃙 and 𮀼, these are erroneous variants.

Regarding the character *niǔ* (拗): the upper radical is pronounced as *wū jiǎo* (烏絞反). The *Wenzi Jilüe* (文字集略) states that "to *niǔ* the hand" means to break or snap it. Regarding the character *jǔ* (舉): the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that "to *jǔ*" means to recommend or to carry on a litter (*yù*). The *Shuowén* (說文) states that it means to lift up together; it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic component "yǔ" (*yǔ*).

Regarding "lǐng" (櫺) and "chū" (䆫): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that what is on a wall is called a *yǒu* (牖), while what is on a door is called a *lǐng* (䆫); it is also written as *lǔ* (鹵), all of which are pictographic characters. The text of the *Lù* (the commentary) writes it as *chuāng* (窓), which is a vulgar character. The pronunciation of *chū* is *cèjū* (測駒反), and the following [character] is *lìdīng* (歷丁反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *líng* (櫺) and *lǐng* (䆫) refer to the lattice-work of a window; it may also be written as *jīng* (㯪). The text of the *Lù* writes it as *líng* (櫺), which is incorrect.

*Ba leng*: the "leng" is pronounced with a retroflex *deng* (反). The *Shuowen* states that "leng" means having corners or prongs; it is correctly written as *ji*. *Ji* is pronounced *gu*. *Yingzhong*: the "ying" is pronounced with a retroflex *ding* (反).

Lu Yanjiji’s commentary on the *Ganquan fu* states that "ning-ying" refers to the appearance of small streams. Its meaning is identical to "zhen. As previously explained and recorded, the character was taken from *ying* to form *liang*, which is an error.

The character *hu* (門罅) is pronounced as *jià* (嫁) with a retroflex final; it refers to the sound of a crack. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "The character *hà* (鏬𰊋) means a fissure; it is composed of the radical *fǒu* (缶) with the phonetic *hū* (虖), and is also written as *hù* (嘑) or *hú* (㙤). To record it as *hàn* (𨬆) is incorrect."

In general, it means "to replace" or "to substitute. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "Gai (概) is equivalent to 'level' (ping). The *Hanshu* says that those who possess "principles and integrity" (*jie-gai*) are also said to have a capacity for leveling. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the character is composed of the radical "wood" (*mu*) and the phonetic "ji" (*ji*).

*Kēng* (上客, *shàngkè*; 耕反, *gēngfǎn*). The *Líjì* states: "Zi Xia [described] the *zhōng* and *gǔ* as *kēngqiāng*. The commentary on the sounds says these are the sounds of metal and stone. In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, it is composed of the radical 金 (*jīn*, metal) and the phonetic 堅 (*jiān*, firm).

"Dǐng" (澧) is pronounced *péng* (逢) with a retroflex final. The *Hànshū* states that the Dǐng River originates from Mount Luónán (洛南), located east of Hù County, and flows northward into the Wèi River. In ancient and modern times, the correct character is written with the "water" radical (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic element "fēng" (豐). The pronunciation of "fēng" is the same. In the transcribed text, it is written as "Fēng" (鄷) with the "city" radical (*yì*), which refers to a place name.
*Guǒ* (pronounced *wō* in the *fǎn* system): Li Shàn’s commentary on the *Jiāng fù* states that the Guǒ River winds and swirls (*huí rào xuān guǒ*).
*Qìn* (pronounced *qī jìn* in the *fǎn* system): This is the name of a prefecture. *É* (pronounced *wǔ gè* in the *fǎn* system):

The *Kǎo shēng* says it is correctly written as *yè*, meaning the initial sprouts of a tree; the commentary on the *Shàngshū* by Kǒng [Yáng] states that *é* refers to the regrowth of wood stumps (*yú shēng yù zāi*). *É* is used interchangeably with *yè*.

*Liáng* (悢悢): *Líáng* with the *yǎng* rhyme. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that it signifies a sense of regret and inability [to attain one's goal]. The *Guǎngyá* states it means "regretful longing. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical *xīn* (heart) and the phonetic *líáng*. 3. *Quán* (詮): *shàng* with the *qī* rhyme.

The *Huainanzi* states that "one who *quán*-s [interprets] words does so to set forth the principles of order and chaos. The *Shuowén* defines *quán* as "to provide" (*jù*), composed of the radical *yán* (speech) and the phonetic *quán*. The preface to the [Tripitaka] Catalogue uses the bamboo radical to write *quán* (as in *quán*, a fish-trap), but this is a net for catching fish and does not carry the meaning of "discerning" or "explaining"; therefore, it is not adopted here.

*Cuò* (upper radical *shǒu*, phonetic *guǎng*): The *Guǎnyǎ* states that it means "to grasp" or "to hold. It also refers to picking up with the hand. The standard character for ancient and modern usage follows the radical *shǒu* and the phonetic *zuì*.

*Jiē* (upper radical *xī*, phonetic *jié*): The *Shuōwén* states that it means "to carry on the shoulder. It is like lifting something high. The standard character for ancient and modern usage follows the radical *shǒu* and the phonetic *hé*.

"Zhoukan" (周瞰): "Kan" (瞰) is pronounced with the *gan* (紺) rhyme. The *Cangjie pian* states that "kan" is synonymous with "shì" (視, to look). "Qiú" (求) is written as "mén" (門), and "zuò" (作) is "kàn" (闞); "kàn" (闞) means "wàng" (望, to gaze). According to this, "zhoukan" carries the meaning of looking out and surveying all four directions.

*Yán* (pronounced *jiē* [jiān] in the upper tone; the *Cāngjié piān* states that it refers to the high edge of a mountain; pronounced with the lower tone *jiǎn*, its reading is identical to *yǎn*). Guō Pǔ’s commentary on the *Eryā* states: "A *yǎn* is a mountain formation resembling a stack of *zèng* (steamer baskets). The *Guǎngyá* states: "A *yǎn* is precisely a *qiàn-fù* (overhanging belly) cliff. The *Shuōwén* states: "*Yǎn* means a precipice; it is formed from the radical *huì* (𨸏) with *jiān* as the phonetic component."

The character for *qìng* (stone chime) is pronounced qīng (輕) with the radical *fǎn* (反). In the standard dictionaries, it correctly uses the stone radical (*shí*) to form *qìng*. Gu Yewáng states that it refers to musical stone chimes; the *Shàngshū* mentions "floating *qìng* from the banks of the Sī River," while the *Shìběn* attributes its creation to Mùgù. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "musical stone," shaped like a suspended *yú* vessel, struck with a mallet (*shū*). It is composed of the stone radical and the phonetic *kèng*. The archaic form of *qìng* is written as 設, with the same pronunciation.
*Bai-chàng* (upper radical *wù*, lower radical *fàn*; pronounced *bǎo*): the sound of chanting; it refers to the sound of reciting Sanskrit hymns (*brahman-stotra*).

*Wǎn-hèn* (upper radical *wū*, lower radical *huàn*; pronounced *wǎn*): according to the *Wénzì jílüè*, it means to be startled, distressed, and to sigh in resentment. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the "heart" radical with the phonetic element *wǎn*.

Regarding the characters for *fàn* (sail) and *tuó* (rudder): the character for *fàn* takes the radical for "offense" (*fàn*) with the second tone. The *Shìmíng* states: "The sail (*fàn*) refers to the awning of a boat. It is also written as *fán* or *lín*; the form *dīn* in the *Lùwén* is a vulgar character. The character below is pronounced *tuó-hè*. According to the dictionaries, it correctly follows the phonetic *tuó* and the radical *kǎo*. *Qì* (stern) refers to the rear of a boat. The *Shìmíng* states: "It is used to straighten the stern; it is a vessel-fitting. The form in the *Lù* following the radical *shì* to make *tuó* is a vulgar character.

The character *fēng* (風) [is pronounced] with the rhyme of *liú* (流). The *Guǎngyǎ* states: "Fēng is the sound of wind. The standard orthography of the past and present follows the radical of wind and uses *sǒu* (叜) as the phonetic component; *sǒu* is the archaic form of the character *sǒu* (叟). It is incorrect to write it as *fēng* (󲽀) following the *Lùwén* (錄文).

Regarding the characters 槽 (cáo) and 櫪 (lì): the *Kaosheng* states that "槽" refers to a horse stall. The *Gujin Zhengzi* states that it is a vessel for feeding beasts and livestock.
