*Tisi* (提撕): "Xi" and "fan" are the phonetic components; *tisi* means to analyze each point individually and explain it well.

It is also written with the hand radical. *Buyi* (逋逸): "Bu" and "hu" are the phonetic components. The *Guangya* states that it means "to flee in hiding. The *Cangjie pian* states it means "not arriving. Kong's commentary on the *Shangshu* states it means "to run away."

*Jū* (拘) and *zhì* (縶)—the latter pronounced with the initial *lì* (立) and final *fǎn* (反). The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (毛詩傳) states: "Ji (*zhì*) means a tether. It is composed of the radical *mì* (糸) and the phonetic *zhí* (執). According to this, *zhì* also means to bind.

*Jī* (羇) and *lǚ* (旅)—*lǚ* is pronounced with the initial *yí* (宜) and final *fǎn* (反). The *Guǎng Yǎ* (廣雅) states: "Ji (*jī*) means to lodge as a guest. It is composed of the radical *zī* (𠔿) and the phonetic *qī* (䩭); the pronunciation of *qī* is the same as above. In the *Lí Jì* (禮記), the character is written with the radical *mǎ* (馬), but that is not the usage here. The lower part, *lǐ* (力), is pronounced with the final *fǎn* (反). Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒ Zhuan* says: "Ji-lǚ means a lodging guest. The *Shuō Wén* (說文) states it is composed of *yǎn* (㫃) and *cóng* (从). *Cóng* is the ancient form of *cóng* (從); both signify two people following one another.
The character for *xún* (巡) is pronounced *gài*; it is composed of "person" (人) and "perish" (亡). *Gài* means to beg.
The first character of *tōushí* (媮食) is pronounced *tōu*. The *Yuǎnshuō* states that it means to act with negligence or expediency.

Regarding *chúnlí* (醇醨): the first character is pronounced *shùn lún* (順倫反). The *Guǎngyá* states it means rich or thick; the *Shuowén* defines it as wine that is not diluted. In the *Liji*, it appears as *chún*, which uses a vulgar character. It is correctly written with the radical "grain" (𦎫) and the phonetic *lí* (離) below. The *Shuowén* defines it as thin wine. Both are phono-semantic compounds.

Regarding the upper character *shàng* (商): the *Guǎyùn* commentary states it means "to tie silk. Regarding *shāngjué* (商榷): the upper character is pronounced with the *shǎng-yáng* rhyme; Wang Bi’s commentary on the *Zhouyī* says it means "to deliberate. The *Shìfǎ* states:

"When benevolence is seen both within and without, it is called *shāng*. The *Shuowén* explains that it means "to know the interior from the exterior"; it is composed of *jiǒng* (冏)—pronounced *nǚhuá*—and the abbreviated form of *zhāng* as its phonetic. Regarding the lower character *jué* (榷): the pronunciation is *jiǎo*. Xǔ Shūchóng’s commentary on the *Huáinánzǐ* states: "*Yángjué* (揚榷) means to treat roughly or briefly. The *Shuowén* explains it is composed of *mù* (木) and the phonetic *hè* (鶴), whose pronunciation is the same as above. The *Shuowén* further explains it is composed of *zhuī* (隹) and *mì* (冖)—pronounced *guǐyíng*; those who claim the upper part is *yù* (欲) emerging from *mì* and thus take *mián* (宀) instead are incorrect.

Regarding the character *zhǎ* (赭): the upper radical is *zhě* (者), which according to the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) means "red" and also "to feel shame. To feel shame necessarily causes the face to turn red. The lower part has the phonetic value of *è ā gè fǎn* (惡阿各反). Guō’s commentary on the *Shānhǎijīng* (山海經) states that *à* (堊) resembles earth and is white in color; according to the *Kǎoshēng*, it means "to plaster. It is composed of the radicals *yà* (亞) and *tǔ* (土).

"Shu" (淑) and "te" (慝) form the first pair of opposites. The *Mao Shi* commentary states that "shu" means "good. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "clear and limpid," stating it is composed of the radical "water" and the phonetic "shu"; however, its use as "shen" (󱮫) is incorrect. The second character, "te" (慝), is pronounced with the initial *th* and the final *le*. Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that "te" means "evil. The *Mao Shi* commentary defines it as "depravity," while Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* defines it as "concealing filth. According to the standard characters of antiquity and today, "ni" (匿) means "to feel shame"; it is composed of the radical "heart" and the phonetic "ni."

*Líjiù* (罹咎): "Lí" is pronounced with the *zhǐ* rhyme group (liǎo). According to the *Erya*, it means "to suffer poison. Examining its phonetic component (*shēng*), it means "to encounter" or "to be beset by. In dictionaries, it is defined as "mental anxiety," formed from the radical *xīn* (心) and the phonetic *wéi* (惟). In the *Zòngshū*, the character for "crime" (*zuì*) is also written with this [radical]. Below, "qiúyǒu" (qíú yǒu) is the pronunciation. In the Commentary on the *Shàngshū*, Kǒng [Yǎng] states that "jiù" means "evil. The *Yùnquán* says "jiù" means "fault. The *Shuōwén* says it means "calamity," formed from the radicals *rén* (人) and *gè* (各). "Rén gè rén gè" (each person separately) implies "contradiction"; it is a compound character based on meaning. Alternatively, it is further written with *rén* as *qiū* (倃), which the *Shuōwén* defines as "destruction"; this is also interchangeable.

Regarding the character *cāo* (操), when it appears as the reversed rhyme *fǎn* (反), Yuàn Qiūn says it means "to hold fast to one's will with refined integrity. Gù Yěwáng says it means "to maintain one's will with steadfast firmness. This refers to a gentleman who, even when encountering calamity or harm, does not lose his integrity. It may also appear as the character *chī* (𣀉) in the *Wén bù* (文部).

*Zàiqiào* (re-marriage) is pronounced *jiāo xiào fǎn*. Yùquán states that it refers to performing sacrificial rites while drinking wine alone, without the ritual of mutual response. In the *Lǐjì*, it says, "The father performs the *qiào* rite for his son and commands him to go meet [the bride]," which refers to the *qiào* rite performed when taking a wife. It is a word formed from both semantic and phonetic components (*xíngshēng zì*).

Regarding "usurpation" (*chuàn*) and "regicide" (*shì*): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that to seize by force in opposition is called "usurpation" (*chuàn*); it is composed of the radical *sī* (meaning "selfishness") and the phonetic *chuàn*, with the pronunciation *shìzhìfǎn*. The *Baihutong* states that "regicide" (*shì*) is synonymous with "to kill. It refers to a minister or son killing his sovereign or father; the *Shuowen* also states it means "a minister kills his ruler," composed of a simplified form of *shā* (to kill) and the phonetic *shì*.
*Jià* (駕) [pronounced *yú jù fǎn*]. *Xié* (挾) [pronounced *xián jiá fǎn*]:

The *Mao Shi* says, "I draw my bow and take up my arrows" (*zhāng wǒ gōng xié wǒ shǐ*); the *Gōngyáng Zhuan* says, "He took up his bow and removed his arrows" (*xié gōng ér qù shǐ*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines *xié* as "to hold."

The character *lǔ* (pronounced with the initial *l-*, rhyme *kǎo*) refers to a large shield; it is also written as *lǔ* or *gǔ*, all of which are interchangeable and equally valid. Regarding "spear and shield" (*máo shùn*):
the first character is read as *mò hóu* (rhyme *hóu*), and the second as *xù yǐn* (rhyme *yǐn*). A shield is a large defensive screen; this is stated in the *Zìshū* (Lexicon of Characters).

*Jiànjí* (狷急): The upper character is pronounced *jiàn*, with the phonetic component *kǎo*. It means to be narrow-minded yet to maintain one's integrity. It is sometimes written as *xuàn* (獧) or in archaic script as *zhé* (󳌚). To maintain one's principles and remain non-active. *Yì* (劓): Pronounced *ní qí* (疑器).

Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states it means "to cut off the nose. Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states it means "to excise. It is also sometimes written with the radical *niè* (臬) as *yù* (㓷).

"Hangye" (荒裔) refers to the "barbarians" (夷). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "ye" means "distant. The *Fangyan* says it is a name for the tribes of the four frontiers, the Yi and Di. According to the *Shuowen*, the character is composed of "yi" (衣) and "jiong" (冏); "jiong" has the phonetic value of "nühuá" (女滑).
*Nuǎnruò* (愞弱): The first character is pronounced *nú* with the *luàn* rhyme.
The *Cāngjié piān* states that *mó* (摩) refers to the heel; it may also be written as *zhǒng* (踵) with the radical for feet, which is likewise acceptable.
*Jìluó guǒ* (葪羅果): The first character is pronounced *jì*.
*Pānasa* (the *pānasa* fruit; this is the name for the fruit in Sanskrit; do not seek the meaning of the characters).
*Bíshì* (the upper character is pronounced *bī*, the lower is pronounced *shì*).
*Kěntián* (the *kěn* is pronounced with the *kǔ* and *hèn* finals).
The *huṇḍa* vegetable is the *guǎndá* (mugwort) found among humans. Regarding *jiāo* (醪), pronounced with the "dāo" rhyme of "lǎo":

the *Zhànguó Cè* states that Yí Dì, the daughter of the Emperor, presented wine to Yu; Yu tasted it and said, "In future generations there will be those who cause the loss of the world through wine," whereupon he whipped her and sent her away. This is also a type of fermented, heated wine. The *Shuōwén* says it is "wine consisting of dregs and liquid"; it is a word formed by combining semantic and phonetic components.

*Kuò* (釜鑊): the character *kuò* is pronounced with the *hú* and *guō* rhymes. Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states it is a vessel for boiling meat. The *Shuowen* says it is a *xuī* (鑴), pronounced with the *hú* and *guī* rhymes;
it also belongs to the category of *huò*. *Qīqiào* (欺誚): *qiào* is pronounced with the *zhì* and *yào* rhymes. The *Kaosheng* states it means to reproach or to mock.
*Pǐ* (皮鄙反): A word of *kǎo-shēng* (a derivative sound) meaning to destroy or to break down; the *Yùnquán* states it means the collapse of a cliff.

It is a *xíngshēng* (phonetic-semantic) character. *Pù* (布蓬木反): The *Yùnquán* states it refers to water falling from a precipice; the *Kǎoshēng* states that water flowing in a cascade is called a *pùbù* (waterfall).

*Fǎngfú* (髣髴): The upper character *fǎng* (髣) is pronounced *fāng* (芳) with the *wǎng* (罔) rhyme, and the lower character *fú* (髴) is pronounced *fèn* (忿) with the *wù* (勿) rhyme; it is also pronounced *fāngwèi* (芳味). In the *Hànshū* (Book of Han), it means "resembling" or "vague impressions from what has been heard or seen. Lexicons define it as "not clearly perceived. The character *fǎng* (髣) may also be written as *fǎng* (仿) with the radical for "man" (亻); its pronunciation and meaning are identical. The character *fú* (髴) may also be written as *fó* (彿) with the radical for "man," or as *fén* (𢘍) with the radical for "heart" (心); their meanings are the same.

*Qiàn* (譴): To reprimand. The *Guǎngyá* states that *qiàn* is also "to blame. The *Cāngjiépiān* says it means "to scold. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "to interrogate for punishment" (*zhéwèn*), composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic "qiàn.

*Zhuóhuàn* (濯澣): The upper character is pronounced *zhuó*. The *Máoshī zhuàn* says "to wash and cleanse. As the *Máoshī* states: "Wear clothes that have been washed and cleansed. The *Guǎngyá* says "to wash," and the *Shuōwén* says "to launder. It is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic *zhái*, pronounced *zhái*. The lower character is *huán*, with the tone *guǎn*. The *Máoshī* says: "Thinly launder my clothes. The *Jiàn* (Commentary) says this refers to "laundering and washing. Lǚ Zhào’s commentary on the *Gōngyáng zhuan* says: "To wash raw silk is called *sù* (涑), pronounced *sānghòu*; to wash away old stains is called *huàn* (澣). The *Shuōwén* defines *huàn* as "the dirt of clothing," composed of the radical "water" and the phonetic *gàn*. In the scriptures it is written as *huàn* (浣), which is a vulgar form. *Dí* (滌) is pronounced *tínglì*.

Regarding "for the shaft" (*gǎo*, with the *shàn* and *hàn* finals; according to the *Shàngshū Dàzhuàn*, it refers to the shaft and notch of an arrow; Zheng Xuan says: "The ancient and modern correct character is written with the radical 'bamboo' [竹] and the phonetic 'ke' [可]").

Regarding "a full ten-day period" (*jiāchén*, with the *zǐ* and *yè* finals; Zheng Zhong’s commentary on the *Zhōu Lǐ* states: "As for *jiā*, from *jiǎ* to *guǐ* is called *jiā*; it means to reach through completely").
*Qiānqiè* (恇怯): The upper character is pronounced *kuāng*; the lower is the phonetic *qiàn* with the radical *yè*.

The *Kǎoshēng* states it means "weak" (*ruò*) and "timid" (*wèi*). *Tuípǐ* (隤圮): The upper character is pronounced *duì* with the radical *léi*. The *Kǎoshēng* states it means "to destroy. The *Guǎngyá* states it means "to ruin. The *Lǐjì* says, "Will Mount Tai not crumble? (*tái hū*). The *Shuōwén* defines it as "to descend" (*duì xià*). Lexicons state it is written with the radical *xié* and the phonetic *guì*. The version in the *Zìjì* uses *tuí*, which is incorrect.
"Niè" (齧) is pronounced with the *jié* (結) rhyme; it means "to bite back. The lower radical is the "mouth" radical, and the phonetic component is pronounced with the *shēng* (聲) tone.

"Mí cuò" (靡措): "cuò" (措) is pronounced with the *cāng sù* (倉素) rhyme. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that "cuò" means "to settle" (*ān*) or, according to the *Fāngyán*, "to store" (*cáng*).

*Zé* (pronounced *zhài*, with the rhyme category *nǎi*): The *Shiji* states, "Internally ashamed, he shut his door, bit his tongue, and committed suicide. The *Shuowen* defines *zé* as "to bite" (*yì*). It is also written as *zé*; it is a character composed of the radical on the left and the phonetic on the right.
*Sù-hàn* (宿憾) means to harbor resentment; it is a term for harboring malice. *Yù-zhì* (鬻𧷓) is a vulgar character pronounced with the initial *róng* and the final *sù*.

In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the correct form is written as *zhì* (𧷓), meaning to sell or to advertise. It is composed of the radical *bèi* (貝, "shell/wealth") and the phonetic *lǔ* (󳋿). *Lǔ* is an archaic form of the character *lù* (陸, "land"). The character *shú* (贖, "to redeem") is composed of *mài* (賣, "to sell") and *bèi* (貝). The version using *mài* is a vulgar form. The lower part [of the character *mài*] is pronounced *jiè* (懈); the versions composed of *chū* (出, "to emerge"), *mǎi* (買, "to buy"), or *tǔ* (土, "earth") are vulgar forms.

*Tán* (覃) is pronounced *dàn* (淡). The *Mao Shih Zhuan* states that *tán* means "long" (*cháng*). It also says it means "extended," and that its sound reaches [far]. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "a long flavor," composed of the radicals *hòu* (󳐆) and a simplified form of *xián* (鹹). According to the *Yupian*, the lower part is not *bēi* (卑) but *hòu* (󳐆), where *hòu* is pronounced *hòu* (候) and its upper part is *xī* (西).

"Jùnzhì" (捃摭): The upper character "jùn" (捃) is pronounced with the *yun* rhyme of the *jun* (君) and *yun* (運) finals; it is the correct orthography for "to gather. It may also be written as "shí" (拾), or with the radical "deer" (鹿) and the radical "wood" (木), forming "shè" (󱻝). The lower character "zhì" (摭) is pronounced with the *yi* (亦) rhyme; it is the correct orthography for "to pick up. It may also be written as "shí" (拾), or with the radical "stone" (石), forming "tuó" (拓).

*Shěn* (哂): Pronounced with the initials *shēn* and the final *-rn* (according to the *Sùyǔ*). This is a vernacular character; in ancient texts it was written as *xín* (弞). The *Kǎo Shēng* states: "A smile that does not break the countenance is called *xín*; its meaning is the same as *shěn*, denoting the manner of a slight smile. In the *Lǜyì Jì* (Record of Ritual Meanings), it is written as *lǚ* (󳌳); its pronunciation and glossary are not yet fully established.

3. Volume Three, *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions), Volume Three: Eight Kingdoms. **Ōngyù (蓊鬱):** Sī Mǎ Xiāngrú stated that this refers to the appearance of luxuriant vegetation. It is composed of the radical *cǎo* (grass) with the phonetic *wēng*. The lower character is pronounced *yùn*. According to the *Shuowen jiezi*, it means "dense growth of grasses and trees. It is composed of the radical *lín* (forest) in its ancient form; [it may also be written] with *jiù*, *nán*, *miào*, or *chàng* (pronounced *chì liàng*). It is also written with the three strokes (*sān*) below. In modern usage, it is often incorrectly written with *gèn* and *cùn*. [Note: This entry provides a philological analysis of the term *ōngyù* (蓊鬱), citing the authority of Sī Mǎ Xiāngrú and the definitions in the *Shuowen jiezi*, while also noting common orthographic errors.]

*Qiènuǒ* (怯愞): The first character is pronounced *qiāng yè* (羌業) with a reversed final, and the second is *nú luàn* (奴亂) with a reversed final; both have been fully explained previously. *Juéguǐ* (譎詭):

The first character is pronounced *huán xué* (詃穴) with a final sound like *jué* (決), and the second is *guī wěi* (歸委) with a reversed final; both have been extensively explained in the preceding text.
*Mong-kie-li* (瞢揭釐) is a Sanskrit term; it is the name of a city and its meaning is not sought [here].
*Āpālā* (阿波邏羅)—the latter syllable pronounced as *lè-hè*—is a Sanskrit name for a nāga king.

*Xù* (pronounced *chǒu* with the sixth tone; in the *Yùpiān*, it means "to accumulate" or "to gather," or written with the radical for "grass" as *chù*; a phono-semantic compound). *Kuì* (upper part pronounced *dá* with the second tone;

in the *Yílǐ*, it refers to presenting cooked food; in the *Shuōwén*, it means "to provide provisions"; a phono-semantic compound). Lower part pronounced *wéi* with the fourth tone (*èi*). According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to give"; Gù Yěwáng says it means "to present. It is a character used by extension (*jiǎjiè*).
*Zhuóyī* (濯衣): The character *zhuó* is pronounced with the rhyme of *zhào* (卓) and is glossed as "washing" (*zhuóhuàn*). It is a phonetic loan character; it means to wash clothes. *Tà* (榻):

Pronounced with the rhyme of *tān* (貪) and *dá* (荅). According to the *Guǎngyá*, "a *tà* is flat. The *Shìmíng* states: "A wooden bed that is narrow and long is called a *tà*; it is derived from the radical for wood with the phonetic *mí* (󱫕). The pronunciation of *mí* is the same as above.

*Jinili* (the *li* rhymes with *fan*): Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that *ni* means "smooth. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "fat," derived from the radical for "flesh" (*rou*) with the phonetic component *er*.
*Sapākaḍi* (the *di* rhymes with *bao* and *mao*): a term in the Sanskrit language.

"Zuò" (啄) in the first character is pronounced *zuì* (醉) and *suǐ* (髓) in combination; it means "to peck. The second character is pronounced *zhuó* (卓). It refers to how the Holy Peacock King used his beak to peck at a stone cliff until a spring flowed forth, which exists today as a Heavenly Pond (*tiān chí*).
*Dianfu* (蹎仆): the first character is read as *dingjian* (丁堅) and the second as *pobei* (蒲北); both have been explained in detail previously.
*Zhibi* (自斃): the second character is read as *mi* (袂). The *Shengyun* (聲韻) states it means to collapse or fall prostrate; the correct vulgar form is written as *zha* (𡚁).

To *sì* (pronounced *cí zì fǎn*). Yě Wáng says it means to provide food for someone. The *Shuowén* defines it as "provisions"; it is a compound character (*huìyì zì*). It is also written as *sì*, which is a vulgar form.

*Jiedi* (枳底): the upper character is pronounced *jǐ* with the departing tone, and the lower character is pronounced *dǐ* with the entering tone; this is the Sanskrit name for the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. *Gēngsuò* (縆索): the upper character is pronounced *gēng* with the level tone;

the *Cāngjié piān* (蒼頡篇) states that *gēng* means "a large rope," while the *Yùnquán* (韻詮) states that *gēng* means "tense. It is a word formed by combining semantic and phonetic components (*xíngshēng zì*).

The character 棧 (zhàn) is pronounced with the "chāi-hàn-fǎn" (the final -n of chāihàn) and has the phonetic component 戔 (zēn). It refers to a wooden structure built on dangerous terrain as a road, known as a *gé-dào* (gated passage). It is composed of the radical 木 (wood) and the phonetic 戔; it is a common variant for "a gallery-like bridge supported by beams."

*Chuán* (椽): The rhyme is *yuán* (攣), and the *Yùnqiān* (韻詮) states that it is so called because it refers to the rafters of a house; it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "tuàn" (*tún*), with the lower part pronounced *yì*. According to the *Erya*, *yì* (杙) means "a stake" (*liú*) or "a peg" (*zhǎi*). Guo Pu’s commentary states it is a "stake" (*jué*), composed of the radical "wood" and the phonetic "yì."

*Huángyù*: "Fú" and "lián" are the two rhymes. The *Guǎngyǎ* states it means "blazing"; the *Bīcāng* describes it as a state of abundance; the *Shuōwén* defines it as "brilliant radiance," formed with the radical 火 and the phonetic 昱;

the sound of 昱 is the same as above. *Xiéyǐn*: "Huì" and "guī" are the two rhymes. The *Yùnquán* states it means "to carry or lead"; it is formed with the radical 手 and the phonetic 巂; the sound is the same as above.
*Jue* (抉) means "to pick out" (*yuan-yue*, with *yuan* pronounced as *ui-yuan*). The *Tongsu-wen* states that *jue* means "to pluck" (*tiao*;

*tiao* is pronounced as *tian-diao*). Regarding *qi-te* (乞貣): *te* is pronounced as *ta-le*. Zheng Zhong’s commentary on the *Zhouli* says: "To borrow from others is called *ji*. Now, *te* also means "to borrow."

The character *gēng* (耿) signifies sorrow and anxiety; it denotes the mind being unsettled. It is composed of the radical *ěr* (ear), according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, because the state of *gēnggèngrán* (a state of anxious vigilance) is associated with the ear; it is further combined with the phonetic element *huǐng* (炯) in abbreviated form.

The character *pìmiù* (紕繆) has the phonetic component *bǐ* for the upper part and *méi yòu* for the lower part. The *Lǐjì* states: "If even a single object is *pìmiù*, then the people will not obtain their natural death. Zheng Xuan commented: "*Pì* means 'to err' or 'to confuse. Both characters consist of a semantic radical on the left and a phonetic element on the right."

*Qián yǒng* (潛泳): The first character is pronounced *jiàn* with the radical *yán* reversed; the second character has the phonetic *yǒng*. The *Yùpiān* states: "Qian" means to sink; "yǒng" means to float. *Tàn zhī* (啗之):
The character is pronounced *tán* with the radical *lán* reversed. The *Shuōwén* states: "Tan" means to eat; it is also written as *dàn*.

*Shíkān* (石龕): The *Guǎngyá* states that *kàn* (龕) means "to contain" or "to hold. According to this, a stone niche (*shíkān*) refers to a shallow, small stone cave within a mountain cliff. The *Shuowén* explains that [the character for] "dragon" (*lóng*) has the appearance of a dragon, being composed of the radical "dragon" and the phonetic element "kàn" (含) in abbreviated form.

The character *yíng* (塋) is pronounced with the first tone for the initial radical (*yíng*) and the second tone for the phonetic component (*wéi*, *bì*). According to the *Guǎngyá*, it refers to a burial site; according to the *Shuōwén*, a cemetery is called a *yù* (域).

Both characters are composed of the "earth" radical (*tǔ*) and the abbreviated form of "yíng" as the phonetic. The character *yuán* (援) is pronounced with the second tone. Examining its components, "yuán" refers to factions protecting one another and taking turns acting as intermediaries or supporters. As the *Zuǒzhuan* states: "You have no great support," and "He sought to establish a great alliance"—this is what is meant. It is a character formed with the left side as the semantic indicator and the right side as the phonetic.

"Què" (確) does not follow the command; "shàng" (上) is pronounced *kǔ* with the *jiǎo* (角) rhyme. It is a variant of "yì" (易) in the *Xià cí* (繫辭). "Què" means firm (*jiān*). According to the *Běicāng*, it is composed of "shì" (士) and written as "huò" (塙); the *Wénzìdiǎn* explains it as being composed of "shí" (石) and the abbreviated form of "kuò" (搉) as its phonetic component. "Kuò" (搉) has the pronunciation *jiǎo*.

*Yúmiǎo* (逾邈): *yú* is pronounced with the *zhū* and *zhù* finals; the *Guǎngyǎ* states that it means "distant. Kong’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* says it means "to surpass. The *Shuōwén* says *yuè* means "to advance," composed of the radical *chuò* (辶) and the phonetic *yú*. *Miǎo* is pronounced with the *máng* and *bō* finals; Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chǔcí* says it means "far. The *Fānyán* says it means "gradual" or "vast. Guo’s commentary describes it as having the appearance of being expansive and remote. According to the *Jīngǔ zhèngzì*, it is composed of the radical *chuò* and the phonetic *mào*; *máng* is pronounced *mǔbāng* and *mào* is pronounced *mào*.

*Tiè* (鍱): According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means a bar of metal; according to the *Zìshū*, it refers to a nail or a plate; the *Běicāng* states that a soft, thin bar is called *tiè*. This is a character where the left part is the radical and the right part provides the phonetic.

*Lüè* (㡿): The upper part is pronounced *zhú* (逐) and the lower part *chǐ* (齒). Gu Yewáng says that *lüè* means "sparse" or "distant. The *Yìnyì* commentary on the *Hànshū* says *lüè* means "not used. The *Guǎngyá* says *lüè* means "to push away. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "a recessed roof," composed of the radical *guǎn* (广) with the phonetic *nì* (屰). It is incorrect for the vulgar form to use the radical *hàn* (厂) with the phonetic *gān* (干); *nì* is pronounced like *nì* (逆).

"Each [soldier] carries a sharp blade in his sleeve. "Próu" (囚) is a phonetic loan character; its correct form in the ancient script is written with the radical for "clothing" (衣) and the character "bǎn" (釆), forming the section "bāo" (褒). According to the *Fāngyán* (方言): "A *rú* (襦) has sleeves; it is a garment for the arms. The commentary on the *Máoshī* (毛詩) states: "The *xiù* (袖) is the *qū* (袪); the *qū* is the *mèi* (袂). Now, regarding the term "sleeve-blade" (*xiùrèn*): it refers to a hand-sword used for sudden, hidden attacks. The scabbard is bound beneath the arm, and one draws it out secretly to stab. Thus it is called a "sleeve-blade. The pronunciation of "chōu" (抽) is *chǐliú* (丑留).
*Qīmào*: "Qī" (pronounced with the *máo* and *bào* finals) means a cap; according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "cloth" (*jīn*) and the phonetic "píng" (*máo*). *Jīngzhè*:

"Zhè" (pronounced with the *jiē* and *yè* finals) means to be startled or terrified; according to the *Shuowen*, it means to be afraid, composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "niè," though it is also written as *zhè*.
"Zhōngzhuàn" (中饌): The commentary on the *Lunyu* states that "zhuàn" refers to food and drink; here it represents the serving of food to the monks.
"Shìhé" (駛河): Pinyin *shī*, with the tone-marker *sè*; it means a rapid flowing stream. "Wěidà" (偉大):
Pinyin *wěi*, with the tone-marker *guǐ*; "wěi" also means great.
"Nei jiu" (Inner Stable) refers to the stables and stalls for elephants and horses.
"Ban nu cuo" (Half-Nu-Cuo) is a transliteration of a foreign name; "nu" is pronounced as in "nǔ.

"Bixie" (鄙褻): the first character is pronounced *bi* with the rhyme *bei*, and the second is *xian* with the rhyme *xie*; these have already been explained previously. "Yan yu zhong xie" (言語重褻) means that the speech is redundant and indistinct. Alternatively, the character is pronounced *zao*; the *Kaoseng Zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks) states it means "arrogance. "Xia jin nü ren" (狎近女人) means to become intimate with women; it is read with the single tone (*du*). It is also written as "ya" (󲷹).

*Jíyí* (孑遺): The upper character is pronounced *jié jí*; its gloss states that *jí* means "solitary. The *Yùnyīng* says it means "without remainder" or "short. The *Shuōwén* says it refers to one who lacks a right arm; it is a pictographic character. *Qīs cuàn* (捿竄):
The upper character is pronounced *xī*, and the lower is pronounced *cāng luàn*.

*Ē*: (phonetic gloss: *ài*, rhyme: *yì*) Yingyun states it means "obstructed ground. It is also written as *ài*; the upper character means "narrow," and the lower character (*xiǎn*) has the phonetic gloss *jiǎn*, meaning "dangerous obstacles.
*Jín*: (phonetic gloss: *qín*, *chú*, *yín*) means "to seize" or "to capture."
*Fóuqióu* (俘囚): the first character is pronounced *fú* (upper tone), and the second is pronounced *siyóu* (with the final *r* reversed).

*Huīfèi* (隳廢): the first character is pronounced *xīngguī* (upper tone); the *Yùnyīng* states it means "to destroy. It is composed of the radical *ěr* (爾) and the abbreviated form of *suí* (隋) as its phonetic.
*Li-xie* (縲紲): The first character is pronounced *li* (力追反) and the second is pronounced *xie* (音𦵮). Kong’s commentary on the *Lunyu* states that these are used to restrain and bind criminals;

*xie* means a tether or fetter. *Ying-shǒng* (癭尰): The first character is pronounced *ying* (嬰郢反) and the second is pronounced *shǒng* (時冗反). The *Wenzi Jilüe* says that *ying* refers to a swelling of the neck caused by the accumulation of wind and water vapors as a disease; *zhǒng* (種) also refers to a swelling of the head. It may also be written as *zhǒng* (種), with "nine" (*jiǔ*) and "sound" (*shēng*) as its phonetic components. *Rǒng* (冗) is pronounced *rú* (辱反).

*Molǒulá* (秣兔羅): the first character is pronounced with the upper tone *mó* (摩) and the second with the third tone *tù* (兔). *Piānlá* (駢羅): the first character is pronounced with the second tone *biàn* (便) and the second with the second tone *luó* (羅).

*Yīnmìe* (湮滅): the first character is pronounced with the first tone *yīn* (寅). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it means "to submerge" (*yīnmò*) or "to extinguish" (*miè*). The *Guìyuàn Zhūcóng* (桂苑珠叢) states it means "to fall. According to the *Wénzì Jílüè* (文字集略), it refers to sinking underground; sometimes it is written as *yīn* (垔), and in dictionaries it is written with the earth radical as *yīn* (堙), which is a vulgar form.

*Liánméng* (連甍): "méng" is pronounced as *xià* (下) or *gēng* (耕), with the phonetic component *shēng* (聲); it refers to the ridgepole of a roof. *Jiànzhì* (間峙): "zhì" is pronounced as *chí* (池) or *lǐ* (里), or alternatively written as *zhù* (𥩳). *Guìwù* (詿誤): "guì" is pronounced as *guǎ* (寡) with one stroke;

Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states that when something is obtained by others, it is called a "note" (*zhù*). It is written with the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the abbreviated phonetic "guǎ" (*guǎ*). *Note: The term "省聲" (abbreviated phonetic) indicates that the character is formed with a simplified version of the original phonetic element.*
Regarding "jíliú" (激流): the upper character is pronounced *jī* or *jiào*. The *Guìyuàn zhūcóng* states that it refers to water rushing and shooting forth with turbulent waves.

Regarding "lǎosǒu" (老叟): "sǒu" is a vulgar character for the phonetic *shòu*. The *Kǎoshēng* states it is a term for an old man. There have been many variant forms throughout antiquity and modern times that share the same pronunciation; some are written as *lǐ*, others as *lǎo*, and still others as *mín*, all of which are ancient characters. Today, the vulgar form is commonly used as "sǒu."

"Věi" (猥) is pronounced with the upper radical *ǝu* (烏) and the rhyme *huǎi* (賄), meaning "base" or "unrefined. The lower part is pronounced with the radical *lǐng* (陵) and the phonetic *kǎo* (考); the *Shōngyùn* (聲韻) states it means "to receive" (*chéng*) or "to succeed to. The *Máoshī chuán* (毛詩傳) says it means "to continue" or "to follow in succession. The *Shuowén* (說文) writes it as *Chéng* (承), stating it is "one body" [with the preceding character]. The *Shuowén* defines it as "to receive," composed of the radicals for "hand" (*shǒu*), "seal" (*jié*), and "joining together" (*kùn*).

Regarding the character *fǔ* (撫), the *Fùjí xùn* (集訓) states: "To stroke with the hand; it means to comfort. It is composed of the radical *shǒu* (手) and the phonetic *wú* (無). The *Shuōwén* (說文) writes it as *fù* (拊), which is also used interchangeably, though it is not the original form.
*Mayūra* (the Sanskrit term; in the Tang language, it means "peacock").
*Ahi-cchatrāḥ* (the *chā* is pronounced as *xīng*; the *cchat* is pronounced as *chāng-rè*).

Qīpǐ (傾圮): the first character is pronounced qīng (上音) and the second is pronounced pí (下音, with the fanqie "fǎn xià pí měi fǎn"). This has already been explained at the beginning of this fascicle. Jǐjué (剞劂):
the upper character is pronounced qí (音奇) and the lower is pronounced jué (音厥). This has also already been explained at the beginning of this fascicle.
Volume Five. *Xiyuji*, Volume Five. Six Countries. *Wei-she* (威懾): "She" (懾) means to be terrified or cowed. *Hong-yi* (弘毅): "Yi" (毅) is read as *qi* (氣);

the *Yunying* states it means resolute and courageous (*guoyi*), while the *Kaosheng* states it means majestic and inviolable. It is sometimes written with the radical "shu" (殳) and the phonetic "gui" (豙), where "gui" has the same pronunciation as above.

The character 應 (yìng) in "should betroth" (應娉): the first character is pronounced with the departing tone (qùshēng), and the second is pronounced as pǐng (pǐng, with the initial *p* and final *-ing*). This is an inquiry regarding the sound. To take a wife with wealth is called "betrothal" (娉). It is composed of the radical 女 (woman) and the phonetic 甹 (pīng, pronounced pǐng, with the initial *p* and final *-ing*). In the *Jì* (Records/Classic), it is written as 娉; this is a vulgar form and not correct.

*Beiyǒu* (背傴): *yǒu* is pronounced with the rhyme of *yù*. The *Yùnchuán* states: "Wǒlǚ" means a curved back; it is composed of the radical "person" (人) and the phonetic "qū" (*qū* is pronounced with the rhyme of *qiāng yú*). One interpretation says it refers to a curved spine.
*Qínkěn* (勤懇): *kěn* is pronounced with the rhyme of *kāng hèn*. The *Yùnyīng* states: "Kěn" means utmost sincerity; the phonetic component "kǎo" (考) signifies trustworthiness.

"Lì" (勠力) is pronounced *lóng* (with the rhyme of *zhú*). Yùnyīng says it means "to combine one's strength. In the standard characters of antiquity and today, it is composed of "force" (力) and the abbreviated form of "liáo" (翏) as the phonetic.

"Xié" (攜手) is pronounced *huì* (with the rhyme of *guī*). The *Shuowen* says it means "to lift or carry by the hand," composed of "hand" (手) and "xuěi" (巂) as the phonetic; the sound of "xuěi" is the same as above. In the *Jìwén*, it is written with "nǎi" (乃), and there are vulgar forms written as "xié" (擕).

Jìng (靜): The phonetic component is mì (蜜); the ancient pronunciation was *min* (民) with a reversed tone. The commentary on sounds states that it signifies "the absence of sound. Yùn (韻): This character explains "tranquility" (*jìng*). Yùn (韻): This character explains "caution" (*shèn*). It is composed of the semantic component "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic component qí (𥁑). The pronunciation of qí is the same as above.
*Máo-jùn* (髦俊): The upper character *máo* is pronounced as in "hair" (*mao*). The *Jíxùn* states that it means "to select. *Xūn-mù* (曛暮):
The upper character is pronounced as *yún-fǎn*. The *Yùnyīng* states that the time when the sun sets is called "dusk" (*xūnhuáng*).
*Pūmiè* (撲滅): Pronounced *pǔ-bǔ-fǎn*. The *Shuōwén* states that it means "to strike. It is a compound character formed by *shēngxīng* (phonetic determinative).

*Fén*: "To burn to ashes"; *xiáng* (祥) is pronounced *jìn* (盡); it refers to wood remaining after being burned by fire. The text of the *Jì* (Record) uses the character *cèn* (燼), which is a vulgar form of the word.

*Jǐn*: "Distressed and urgent"; *qún* (群) is pronounced *yǔn* (殞); it means to be in a state of urgency. *Róng*: "To melt and cast"; the upper character is pronounced *yóng* (音容), and the lower character is pronounced *zhù* (音注).

The character *juàn* (鐫) is pronounced with the initial *zuì* (醉) and the final *yuán* (緣) reversed; the *Kǎośēng* (考聲) states it means "to engrave. The *Jíxùn* (集訓) states it means "to carve stone. According to the *Gōngjīn Zhèngzì* (古今正字), it takes the radical *jīn* (金) and the phonetic *juàn* (雋); the pronunciation of *juàn* is *cú yuǎn* (徂兗).

6. Volume Six, *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions), Volume Six: Four Countries. *Kui* (巋): Pronounced *qiū* (軌) with a final rhyme of *guǐ*. The *Yingyun* states it describes a lofty and precipitous appearance. It is composed of the radical "mountain" (*shān*) and the phonetic "shēng" (*shēng*).

*Nièyǎn* (齧齗): The upper character is pronounced *jié* (結) with a final rhyme of *jié*. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to bite" or "to devour. It is composed of the radical "teeth" (*chǐ*) and the abbreviated phonetic "qiè" (*qiè*).
*Kǐng* (坑) [the second character pronounced *jìng*]: a pit for trapping animals. *Biāo* (飈):

the first character is read as *fǔyáo*. According to the *Kǎoshēng*, a swift wind blowing from below upward is called *biāo*; alternatively, it may be written with three dogs (*biāo*), which has the same pronunciation, though some also write it as *biāo*.
*Tui* (穨圮): The upper radical is *dui* (兌) with the reversed sound; it means to fall. The lower part is *pi* (皮) with the reversed sound *mei*;

this was already explained previously. *Pi qi sang* (批其顙): The upper character is *pi* (匹) with the reversed sound *bi*; the *Zishu* (字書) states that *pi* is synonymous with *kuai* (摑). *Kuai* (摑) has the phonetic *guo* (󳍶). The lower part is *sang* (桑) with the reversed sound *lang*. The *Yunying* (韻英) states that *sang* (顙) refers to the forehead (*liang* [𬱃]); it is a compound character formed by both shape and sound.

"Kick its breast" (qū): the character for "breast" (yì) is read as qiū yù fǎn; the *Jixùn* says that to tread upon with the foot against the grain is called "kick" (qū). The character for "breast" (yì) is read as xià yìng lì fǎn; the *Kǎoshēng* says it refers to the chest. In ancient script, it was written as 󳋸.

Regarding the character for "collecting" (shōu) in the term *shōkai* (收骸): the upper part follows the character 文 (*wén*) and 殳 (*shū*) as its phonetic component. The pronunciation of 殳 is *jūyóu* (居由反), and that of 解 (*kai*) is *jiè* (皆反). The *Yùnyīng* states: "The collective name for all parts of the body is *hái* (骸)."

*Yì* (瘞): Upper radical *yīng* (英), counter *jì* (計). The *Kǎo Shēng* says it means "to bury. The rhyme dictionary *Yīng* says it means "to conceal in darkness. The archaic form is written as *fú* (𨻊) or *yà* (圠). The *Shuōwén* states that it follows the radical *guǎn* (广) and takes the archaic form of *fú* (*fú* being a simplified form) as its phonetic. The *Lí Jì* uses *yì* (瘞), which is interchangeable.

The character for *qiè* (憩) is pronounced with the radical *qiān* (騫). The *Shēngyùn* states that it means "to rest" (*xiè*). In archaic script, it is written as *qì* (𡳅), meaning "to cease and rest. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is formed from the radical *xīn* (心) with *jié* (偈) abbreviated as its phonetic component; *qì* (愒) also means "to rest," being formed from *xīn* (心) with *jié* (偈) abbreviated as its phonetic.

*Shān* (芟): The upper radical is *shuāng* (霜) with the variant *xián* (銜). Zheng’s commentary on the *Shijing* states it means "to weed. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to reap," a compound character formed from *kǒng* (廾) and *shū* (殳).

*Jí* (亟): Pronounced *jiān* (矜) with the variant *yī* (憶); this is a vulgar form. The correct orthography is *gǒu* (苟). *Gǒu* means "extreme" (*jí*). It may also be written as *jì* (󲼻) with the radical *gé* (革), which is a transitive character.
*Dà* (大) is a radical for the sound *chǐ*. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "extravagance" (*shē*) and is composed of "person" (*rén*) and a simplified form of *chā*.
*Xián* (銛) is pronounced *xīlián*; the *Yunchuan* states it means "sharpness" and is composed of "metal" (*jīn*).
*Lèi* (槲) is pronounced *hóngmù*; it is the name of a mountain tree resembling the *qīnglíng* but with larger leaves and blackish, rough bark that grows on low mountains.
*Xūxī* (上音虛, 下音希): The *Jìxùn* (集訓) states that *xūxī* refers to exhaling while weeping in sorrow; it also denotes grief, longing, and despondency.
*Chènshēn* (襯身): Pronounced *chūnjìn* (初近反); it refers to the white cotton cloth (*pāṭa*) closest to the body.

*Zòu* (驟): To be suddenly submerged; the sound is reversed from *jiù* (救). The commentary on the phonetics states that *zòu* means "numerous. It is composed of the radical "horse" (*mǎ*) and the phonetic element "jù" (聚) in abbreviated form.
*Lóngméi* (龐眉): Pronounced *miǎo bāng* (邈邦). Long eyebrows that are also thick and abundant.
"Ci" (嚌) is pronounced with the *qí* rhyme group and the *xì* final; the commentary on the sounds states it means "to reach the teeth" or "to bite.

7. Volume Seven, *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions), Volume Seven. "Huòmǐ" (靃靡): The upper character is pronounced *suǐ*; according to the *Yùnyīng*, "huòmǐ" refers to the appearance of weak grasses bending as they follow the wind.
*Zhuìjì* (椎髻): the first character is pronounced *chuí* (with the final rhyme of *zhuī* reversed), and the second has the phonetic value *jì*.
*Tóushí* (鍮石): the first character is pronounced *tōu* (the metal inferior to gold, a pale white metal).
*Lǐnlǐn* (懍懍): the first character is pronounced *lǐn* (with the final rhyme of *lì* reversed); it means perilous fear.
*Shāo* (髾): The upper radical is *jiāo* (交); the *Pīcāng* dictionary states that it refers to the hair tied in a topknot with loose strands hanging down.
*Suì* (遂): Pronounced *liè* (涅) in this context;
it means to twist or contort. *Zòngliáo* (縱撩): Pronounced *lìdiāo* (力彫); in the *Hànshū*, it means to take hold of, to hunt, or to plunder. It is written with the "hand" radical.
*Chāngjué* (猖厥): The first character is pronounced *chāng* (same as in *chāngkuáng*, "wild and frantic"); it refers to being crazed and deranged. *Jiélú* (結廬):
The second character is pronounced *lǚ* (with the *zhù* tone); this has already been explained in detail in the preceding preface. *Lú* (廬) here means a tent or screen. *Xiǎnlǐ* (鮮鯉):
The first character is pronounced *xiān* (same as in *xiānshēn*, "immortal") and the second is pronounced *lǐ* (same as in *lǐyù*, "carp").
The woodcutters' sentiments are far-reaching as they return with their firewood.
"Yi" (嶷然) is pronounced *níng* (凝); the *Yùnyīng* (韻英) states that *zéyì* (崱嶷) describes the appearance of towering, precipitous mountains.
"Kūgǎo" (枯槁), the latter character is pronounced *kǎo* (考).
Huàn (歡灌反): Yingyun states that "huàn" means literary brilliance or clarity. Chóng (󱻘祟): The upper character is read as yāo (夭驕反) or dì (地反) according to the *Zuozhuan*.

The lower character is read as suì (雖醉反). The *Shuowen* defines it as "a spirit that causes calamity. It is composed of "out" (出) and "to manifest" (示). In the *Shuowen*, the character is written with "zōng" (宗), which is incorrect.
*Tuò* (拓): The upper radical is *shàng* (上) and the phonetic is *tāngluò* (湯洛). The commentary on the sounds states: "To expand; it is also 'great.

It is a transitive character. *Huīfēi* (翬飛): The upper radical is *huì* (諱) and the phonetic is *wéi* (韋). The *Yùnyīng* (韻英) states: "The five colors are fully present. Guō's commentary on the *Erya* says: "When all five colors are complete and form a pattern, it is called *huī*."
"Hui-du" (毀讟) means to slander and revile those with whom one dwells together.
"Mao-niu" (𤛆牛), pronounced *mǎo bāo*, refers to the long-haired ox of the southwestern Rong and Yi tribes; this has already been explained previously.

"Xian-bei" (險詖), pronounced *bi jì*, the *Cangjie pian* states that "bei" means sycophantic flattery; the *Guangya* states "bei" means cleverness; the *Shuowen jiezi* defines it as "to argue or persuade," following the radical for speech with the phonetic *pi*.

8. Volume Eight, *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions), Volume Eight: The Kingdom of Magadha. Regarding the character 墊 (*diàn*): the *Kǎo shēng* (Investigation of Sounds) states it means "to drown" or "to store. The *Yùnyīng* (Rhyme Mirror) states it means "low-lying. The *Xiàshī* (Lower Shi) reads it as *rù* (entering tone). The *Shuōwén* (Explanations of Characters and Terms) defines it as "gloomy dampness."
"Jiyou" (羇遊) means "to travel as a sojourner"; it refers to being bound by fetters. "Xuanshuai" (袨服):

according to the *Kaoseng*, the character means "beautiful clothing. The lower part is the radical "fu" (服), which is the correct form of the character; it is composed of the "zhou" (舟) radical with "ren" (㞋) as its phonetic component. The pronunciation of "ren" is the same as that of "shang" (上).
*Kēchōu* (苛󳋜): the first character is pronounced *hé*; the second is pronounced with the initial *páo* and the final *chāng*.

*Lánhàn* (欄檻): the first character is pronounced *lángdān*; the second is pronounced *xiánǎn*. It refers to the balustrades of a palace; it has already been explained previously. *Diàn* (殿): it refers to the hook-balustrades. This was already fully explained above.
*Liányī*: "Lián" (upper tone) and "yī" (lower tone, *yī*). According to the *Kǎoshēng*, "lián" refers to small waves, while "yī" refers to fine ripples;

both are distinct names for water. *Xìyú*: "xì" (pronounced *jìqì*) and "yú" (pronounced *yǔzhū*). According to the *Yùnyīng*, "xìyú" means the mind harboring hopes. According to the *Kǎoshēng*, it means "to covet. "Jì" (the initial sound of *jìqì*) is also pronounced as *qì* or *kè*.
"Rěn-gòu" (忍詬): "Gòu" means to revile; it is also pronounced "hǒu," following the radical for speech (言) with "hòu" as the phonetic component. "Qī-yǔ" (葺宇):
"Qī" is read as "qìn" (侵) or "rù" (入); the *Kǎoshēng* says it refers to covering a roof with leather.
The character *xī* (翕) is used in the sense of "gathering together. According to the *Kǎoshēng*, it means "the vapor rising when an object is heated by fire.

Regarding *jiào* (較), its upper radical is pronounced *jiǎo*; the *Kǎoshēng* says it means "to weigh" or "to measure," while the *Yùnyīng* says it means "to compare" or "to clarify. The *Yùnquán* says it means "to compete. It is also written as *chuò* (輟), and the meanings employed for both are identical.

"Hai" (駭): The first character is pronounced with the "xie" (諧) and "ke" (楷) rhymes, in the third tone. According to the *Guǎngyá*, "hai" means to startle or be alarmed. "Máo yàn" (髦彥): The first character is pronounced as "máo" (毛).

The *Shīchuán* (Commentary on the Book of Poetry) states that "máo" refers to the eminent and talented. Guō Pǐng’s commentary on the *Ěryǎ* says: "Among scholars, those who are eminent are like the fine hairs among the fur. The *Guǎngyá* defines it as "to select. The *Shuowén Jiězì* defines it as "hair," written with the radical "biāo" (髟) and the phonetic "máo" (毛). The second character is pronounced with the "shàn" (扇) rhyme. The *Kǎoshēng* states it refers to a "beautiful scholar"; since a scholar must possess patterns or refinement, it is composed of the radicals "wén" (文) and "sān" (彡).

*Uán*: "The wall. (The character is pronounced *guò* in the first instance, and also *lù* in the second; Fu Qian says it refers to the outer enclosure wall of the palace. The lower character is pronounced *yuán*. The *Mao Shih Zhuan* says it means 'enclosure wall'. Another interpretation says it is a small outer wall or the outer perimeter wall.)
*Zhì* (摯) is pronounced *zhì* in the upper tone; the *Tōngsùwén* (通俗文) states that it refers to species such as eagles and vultures, or those belonging to the class of hawks and falcons.
*Modàpó* (摩沓婆) is also called *Mónàpó* (摩納婆), which means "Youth" (*maṇava*); he was one who was intelligent and brilliant from childhood, possessing broad knowledge and eloquence.

*Cuòruì* (挫銳): The first character, *cuò*, has the phonetic *zǔ guò* (祖過) as its rhyme; the *Yùnyīng* states that "to crush" (*cuò*) means to destroy. The second character, *ruì*, has the phonetic *yuè huì* (悅惠) as its rhyme; it means sharpness or keenness. *Ōuxuè* (歐血): The first character, *ōu*, has the phonetic *kǒu* (口) as its rhyme;
the *Yùnyīng* states that "to vomit" (*ōu*) means to spit out. The common vulgar form uses the mouth radical to write *òu*. The pronunciation of *ōu* is *ā hóu* (阿候).

*Xiù* (褎): Pronounced as *bǎo* with the *máo* rhyme. It means "to praise," taking the radical for "clothing" (*yī*) and the phonetic *xiū*. This *xiū* is the archaic form of the character *bǎo*. *Lún*: The first tone, pronounced as *lún*.

The *Yùnquán* states that it means "to sink. *Xī*: Pronounced as *lǚ*. The *Guǎngyá* states it means "to slip/sink" or "sparse. *Xǔ*: Pronounced as *xǔ*. The *Guǎngyá* states it means "to sink" or "sparse. (Note: The text combines *lún xǔ* as a single entry; the commentary provides separate glosses for each character).
"Jue-liè" (攫裂): the first character is pronounced with the *qū* and *yuè* finals; it is homophonous with "jué" (钁). The second character is pronounced with the *yùè* final. "Yě-róng" (冶容):
the first character is pronounced with the initial *yě*. "Xū-liè" (鬚鬣): the first character is pronounced with the *xiāng* and *yú* initials; the second character is pronounced with the *liè* final.
Fǎnghuáng (the first character pronounced bàng, the second huáng);
Yífàn (the first character pronounced yí, the second fàn).

Volume Nine, *Xīyùjì* (Record of the Western Regions), Volume Nine; Magadha Country, Part Two; Mount Kukkuṭapāda (the "pāda" pronounced jùn and lù in Chinese; in Sanskrit, it means "cock," which in the Tang language is translated as "chicken").
*Qiào* (pronounced *qiāo* with the second tone) means steep and precipitous; it signifies being rugged and dangerous.
*Xīkǒupōu*: the first character (*xī*) is pronounced as *xī*, the second (*kǒu*) as *kǒu*, and the third (*pōu*) as *pǔkǒu*.
*Yǎn'è* (the first character *yǎn* is pronounced *jiǎn*, and the second *è* as *wǔgè*): this refers to the appearance of mountain cliffs that are perilous and obstructed.
*Yinlin* (pronounced *yǐn lín*, with *lín* being a variant of *zhěn*): "Yinlin" refers to the appearance of mountain ridges connecting and gradually receding into the distance.
*Chānán* (pronounced *chāi nán*, with *chāi* being a borrowed phonetic character):

*Kǎoshēng* states that this refers to the remaining stumps of trees after they have been cut down; the *Shuowén* writes it as *è*, meaning the regrowth of a stump. This is not the usage here. The *Shuowén* entry for *fù* (伐木餘) correctly uses *mǎo*; its ancient form is *tú*. The *Shàngshū* says: "It is like an uprooted tree having a *yóumǎo* [regrowth]."
"Shanlu" (山麓) means the forest at the foot of a mountain; it is called "linlu" (林麓).
"Shai" (曬)—pronounced *shā* with the second tone according to the *Yunying*—means to dry in the sun; the *Yunying* glosses it as "to expose to the sun.

"Jinghai" (驚駭)—pronounced *jīng* with the second tone according to the *Xiehui*—the *Yunchuan* glosses it as "the startled form of a horse"; it is a word formed from both semantic and phonetic components.
"Yǎngyǎng" (怏怏) means the emotions are not relaxed or at ease. "Jùnzhì" (峻峙):
the lower character is pronounced zhì. "Chúncuì" (淳粹):
the upper character is pronounced shílún; it is a vulgar form [of the character], while the lower character is pronounced suǐzuì.

"Ji (殪)"—the phonetic component is *yi* (翳). Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states: "Ji means to kill. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "Ji means to exhaust. The *Erya* states: "Ji means death. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *dai* (歹) with the phonetic *yi* (壹); the character *e* (歺) has the pronunciation *can*.

*Qīnǚ* (妻孥): The pronunciation of *nǚ* is *nú*. The *Xiàndá Yìyùn* states that it is a general term for wife and children; the *Yùnyīng* states that *nǔ* means children. In archaic script it is written as *zǎ* (㚢), and its meaning is the same as above.
10. Volume Ten. *Xīyùjì*, Volume Ten: Seventeen Kingdoms. *Jìzhǒng*: pronounced *zhù yǒng* (燭勇).
*Chánggēng* (長縆): "Gēng" is pronounced as *hén* (古恒反) in the ancient reading;
it refers to a large rope. *Qín-yín* (嶜崟): The first character is pronounced *zǐxīn* (子心反) and the second is pronounced *yín* (音吟);
this describes the appearance of a mountain. *Jūnzhìjiā* (君稚迦): This is a Sanskrit term, which refers to the *kundika*, the copper water-pot used by monks.
"Guyü (孤嶼)" is a compound where "yù" (嶼) is pronounced with the third tone; Yìngchūn says it refers to mountains within the sea, while Kǎoshēng says it refers to mountains on an island.

"Bānnuósàguǒ" (般橠娑果): "bān" (般) is pronounced as "bàn" (半) with the second tone, and "nuó" (橠) as "tuó" (多); these are names for fruits from Western countries. These fruits are as large as winter melons; when ripe, they are yellowish-red, and their flavor is sweet and delicious. The character "nuó" (橠) is a phono-semantic compound consisting of the radical "wood" (木), the phonetic "yi" (衣), and the determinative "duō" (多).

"Mán-lǎo" (蠻獠): the upper radical is "bān" (斑) with the reversed form, and the lower phonetic is "lǎo" (老), though it may also be pronounced "cháo" (嘲); the character for "jiǎo" (狡) has the reversed form, and its radical is "jiǎo" (𮙥), forming "mèi" (䝤), or with the radical "cháo" (巢), forming "yí" (󲾧). These are the barbarians and indigenous peoples of the southern coastal regions; all those south of Min and Yue belong to this category. Originally of serpent lineage, they thus take "jiǎo" (𮙥) as their radical. This class of people lacks benevolence and righteousness, delights in practicing secret cruelty, and habitually uses force to deceive the weak; they prey upon one another through eating and killing as their primary occupation.

*Li-tan* (黧黮): The upper character is pronounced *li* (犁) and the lower *cha* (叉), which is a vernacular form; it is also written as *li* (釐). The lower part is pronounced *tan* (貪) with the tone *gan* (感). It refers to a dark, unclear color, black in appearance like the hue of a mulberry fruit (*sangshen*).
"Kǎo" (笴) is pronounced as in "gān" (旱); this character for an arrow-shaft has already been explained in the second fascicle above.
"Císhí" (礠石) is pronounced as "cí" (慈); it is the name for a medicinal stone. "Juànkuǎng" (狷獷):

the upper character is pronounced as in "juàn" (絹). The *Kaosheng* says it refers to one who is narrow-minded yet adheres to their proper limits. The *Lunyu* asks, "Is he a 'mad' or a 'restrained' person? Bao Xian’s commentary states: "The 'mad' person strives to advance toward the path of goodness; the 'restrained' person maintains their integrity and does nothing improper. This has already been explained in the second fascicle above. "Xià" (下) is pronounced as in "tóng" (󳌴) or "měng" (猛); it refers to the vicious nature of a dog.
"Méngsú" (氓俗): "Méng" (氓) is pronounced as "míng" (萌) [in the upper tone]; it refers to the common people. "Tǎngcáng" (帑藏):
"Tǎng" (帑) is pronounced as "tālǎng" (他朗) [in the upper tone]; it refers to a repository for gold and silk. "Pǒjué" (剖劂):
"Pǒ" (剖) is pronounced as "qí" (奇) [in the upper tone] and "Jué" (劂) is pronounced as "jué" (厥) [in the lower tone]; this was previously explained as referring to extreme skill.
*Yuán* (pronounced *yuán* in the first tone and *yóu jiù* in the second) refers to the *yuán-hóu* (monkeys), *hú-sūn* (apes), and their kind.

*Jiān-guǐ* (pronounced *jiān* in the first tone and *guǐ* in the fourth): the *Yùn yīng* states that this means a thief within. It is composed of *mián* (pronounced *mián*) as the radical *mián*, and the character *jiǔ*.

The first character, 潟 (xì), is pronounced *xī* (as in "ancient"). It refers to land that is both saline-alkaline (*jiǎn-lǔ*) and low-lying and damp. In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is written simply as 舃 (*xī*), with the same meaning; this is the character for "sandals" (*xī-lǚ*) and is not used here. The second character, 鹵 (*lǔ*), is pronounced *lǔ*. According to its phonetic analysis, it means "saline land. In the Western regions, such land is called *lǔ*; it is a pictographic character.

11. Volume Eleven of the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions), Volume Eleven: Twenty-three Kingdoms. Regarding the character "zì" (倳) [in the term *zìrèn* (倳刃)], the *Yùn yīng* states that "zì" means "to thrust" (*chā*).
"Square-jawed" (*fāng yí*) means the upper character is pronounced *yí* and the lower is *sāng lǎng*.
"Fur" (*máo liè*)—the latter character is pronounced *lián zhé*—refers to fine body hair.
"Frozen and starved" (*dòng èi*)—the latter character is pronounced *nǔ lěi*—means hunger.
*Nārikela* (Nai-zi): "Night-covering" is a transliteration; it is the name of a mountain fruit.
*Uṣṭra* (Tuó-tuó): The upper tone is *tuò*; it refers to the animal, the camel. *Avandhya* (Ā-fàn-chá):
This is a Sanskrit term meaning "not seeking. Its literal meaning is as follows: [text continues].

12. The Twelfth Volume of the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions), Volume Twelve: Twenty-two Kingdoms. *Āluṇāo*: This is the Sanskrit term. It refers to a steep, precarious path (*wéidòng*). The character *qīng* (𢼨) is pronounced with the initials *q* and *d* (qíng).

The lower radical *qǐ* (起) is pronounced with the finals *y* and *f* (qǐ). According to the phonetic analysis, it signifies "not level" or "uneven. It is sometimes written as *qíqì* (崎𢻪); the common form is *qù* (𢽽), which is also correct. The *Shuowen jiezi* states that it is composed of the radical *wéi* (危) and the phonetic *bō* (攴).
*Peǒu* (the first character pronounced *pú hòu fǎn*, the second *lóu hòu fǎn*): The *Tōngsùwén* states that this refers to the mounds of earth built by ants.
*Lǐyǐ* (the first character with the phonetic *lǐ*, the second with *yǐ*): This describes the appearance of mountain ridges rising and falling in continuous succession.

*Jiāochī* (鮫螭): the first character is pronounced *jiāo* (交), the second is pronounced *chǐzhī* (恥知) with a reversed tone; both are species of dragon-fish. *Sùbǎo* (鷫鴇): the first character is pronounced *sù* (肅), referring to the *sùbǎo* bird. Mǎ Róng said:

"The *sùbǎo* resembles a wild goose, its feathers are green, it has a high head and a long neck; because the horse resembles it, the *Zuǒzhuan* states that Dōng Chénggōng possessed two *sùbǎo* horses. The *Shuowén* says: "The *sùbǎo* is a divine bird of the West. The second character is pronounced *bǎo* (保). The *Máoshī* says: "The feathers of the *sùbǎo* gather in clusters. *Xǔxǔ* (栩栩): pronounced *yūyǔ* (吁禹) with a reversed tone. In the *Shuowén*, it is written as *pǔ* (鳵) with the radical *xùn* (卂), which is also acceptable. The correct form uses the radical *cǎo* (𠤏); *cǎo* is pronounced *bǎo* (保). It is also written as *qù* (鴝), which is the same.
*Qiānqiǎo* (乾𣈏): the pronunciation of *qiǎo* is *xī*;
it refers to dried meat. *Wūshā guó* (烏鎩國): the pronunciation of *shā* is *shā*;

it is a foreign term. *Lóngzōng* (巃嵸): the initial sound of *lóng* is *lóng* and the final sound of *zōng* is *zǒng*. *Lóngzōng* describes the appearance of a mountain that is high, steep, and perilous.

"Yayan (崖隒) [yán]: the second character is pronounced qiè (篋), with the rhyme-terminus yǎn (琰). It refers to a mountain cliff with a concave belly. Chéngzhā (崢查): the first character is pronounced héng (衡). Xuēmù (抉目) [jué mù]:
the first character is pronounced yuān (淵), with the rhyme-terminus yuè (悅). It means to gouge out the eyes."
"Drinking and sucking" (yǐnchún): the first character is pronounced as *quán* (with the rhyme *yǎn*);
it means to suckle milk. "Śiṃśapā Mountain" (*shìshēngqié shān*): the second character is pronounced as *zhèng* (with the rhyme *lì*); it is a foreign word, also pronounced as *zhěng*.
"Finger-nail cords" (*jiǎlián*): the second character is pronounced as *lián*; these are cords made from fingernails.
Yìn jiàn (飲餞): the pronunciation of jiàn is zàn.
Pí mí (󰁨摩): this is a foreign [Sanskrit] word; the pronunciation of pí is pǐ. Hú kǒu (餬口):
the pronunciation of hú is hú.
"Qiūrán" (巋然)—the "qiū" is pronounced *guǐ* (鬼) in reverse—describes the appearance of being lofty, steep, and standing alone; this was already explained previously in the sixth [section].

"Chī" (摛)—the "chī" is pronounced *chǒu* (丑) in reverse—the *Yùnyīng* (韻英) states that "chī" means to unfold or spread. In the *Jì* (記), it is written as "qín" (擒) when following the character for "bird" (*qīn* [禽]), which is interchangeable.
"Unrevealed" (未攄): according to the *Yùnyīng*, "to unfold" (攄) means "to extend" (舒). "Secluded" (閟):

the Master Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shūjìng* states it means "cautious" (慎); the *Yùnyīng* states it means "closed" (閉), composed of the radical "gate" (門) and the phonetic "bì" (毖) in abbreviated form.
Guī of Yuī is the name of a river and also a place name;
*qì* (pronounced with the final *-ing* and *-qin*) means to repair or manage;
*Huí* (pronounced with the initial *gǔ* and *-wài*) refers to Kuìjī.
"Suddenly shifting" (*zòuyí*) refers to the reversal of one's anxieties;
"shénzhōng" (the character for *zhōng* is recorded as 󳁿, which does not form a valid character) means "in the heart.
"Jīngxǐ" (the character for *xǐ* is pronounced with the *sì* rhyme) refers to a type of chest or box used for storing scriptures.
*Tiáo* (眺): Pronounced *tiáo* (with the initial *t* and final *-ao*), meaning "to gaze from afar. *Xūxū* (瞴瞴):

The phonetic transcription is *wú* (無); the *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲) states it means "the beauty of a field," while in the level tone (*píngshēng*) it is read as *xū* (from the *mù* rhyme), with the *Yīngyùn* (英韻) stating it means "eyes slightly closed."
Jìnshèn (搢紳): the first character is pronounced jìn (晉) and the second shēn (申).
Dǎnglùn (讜論): pronounced tǎng (湯) and lǎng (朗), or alternatively dāng (當) and làng (浪).
Yuánfāng (圜方): pronounced wǔ (五) and guān (官); it refers to a circle. Níè (訛): the corner [of the character].
*Zhǎodiāo*: "Zhào" is pronounced as in "zhuó" (卓); "diāo" is pronounced as in "dīngyāo" (丁幺). It means to carve or chisel. *Biǎn néng*:
"Biǎn" is pronounced as in "biānqián" (邊󱒓); it means narrow or small. *Gěnggài*:
"Gěng" is pronounced as in "gèngxìng" (更幸).
The "twentieth year of Huangji" refers to the twentieth year of the Zhenguan era; "Huangji" signifies that the Emperor had been on the throne for twenty years.

"Kuafu" is a vulgar character meaning "to suffer," "hua" means "to return," and "fan" means "to examine. "Sheng" (sound) removes extravagance; it is foolishness, it is greatness. It refers to the vulgar character [depicting] one who chased the sun, running until he died of thirst in the wilderness.

*Waiyòu* (外囿) [the character *yòu* pronounced as *jiù*] refers to a forbidden garden (*jinyuàn*). A *yòu* is a park for raising deer; it is a park for raising wild beasts. The Son of Heaven has a hunting park of one hundred *lǐ*, while feudal lords have thirty *lǐ*.
*Yǒu* (󱹶) [the character read as *gǔ* and *huǒ*] means distant.
The character "燾" (tào, with the departing tone; composed of "壽" and "灬") means to cover universally.
The character below, "敷" (fū, with the going tone), means to spread.
*Yiqie jing yinyi*, Scroll 82. *Yiqie jing yinyi*, Scroll 83.

Compiled by the Sramana Huilin, *The Pronunciations for the Biography of the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of Ci’en Monastery in the Great Tang*. Regarding the preface to the *Biography of the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of Ci’en Monastery in the Great Tang*:

as for the character "ji" (暨), its phonetic transcription is "shàng qí qì fǎn" (上其器反). The *Erya* states that "ji" means "and" (*yù*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "dàn" (旦) with "jì" (既) as the phonetic component.

"Jiū" (逗) [the first character is pronounced *hòu*]; according to the *Zìshū*, it means "to linger. The *Shuowén* states that "jiū" also means "to stop," being composed of the radical "辵" (*chuò*) with the phonetic "豆" (*dòu*), the latter being pronounced *jì xī*. The *Kǎoshēng* says "jī" means "clarity. Kǒng's commentary on the *Shàngshū* says it means "subtle. The *Shuowén* also says it means "to initiate," being composed of the radical "木" (*mù*) with the phonetic "幾" (*jī*). The transmission of the text erroneously uses "手" (*shǒu*) as the radical for "jī."

Regarding "pōu" (剖), Yuè Wǎng’s *Pǔguǐ* states that "pōu" means "to break. Dù Yù’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* says "dividing in the middle is called pōu. The *Shuowén* [explains it] as consisting of the radical "knife" (刀) and the phonetic "pòu" (咅, xianli fǎn). Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* says it means "to analyze and divide. The *Shuowén* also defines "pò" (破) as "breaking wood," consisting of the radical "wood" (木) and the phonetic "jīn" (斤). The character "chuan" (傳) is written as "piàn" (片) and "jié" (㭊); these vulgar characters are used interchangeably.

*Yì* (譯): Pronounced *yíng-yì-fǎn*. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to translate the languages of the four barbarian tribes. It is composed of the radical *yán* (言) and the phonetic *gào* (睪); its pronunciation is the same as *shàng-xià-suī-zuì-fǎn* (上下雖醉反). Wang’s commentary on the *Chuci* states it means "essence" (*cuì*). According to the *Shuowen*, *cuì* means "not mixed. It is composed of the radical *mǐ* (米) and the phonetic *zú* (卒).

*Zhìzé* (至賾): The second character is pronounced with the *shì* and *zé* rhymes. The *Zhouyi* states that "zé" refers to the ultimate depth and mystery. The correct orthography for ancient and modern times follows the radical *zhēn* (𠙥) and the phonetic *zé*.

The character *zhēn* (𠙥) has the pronunciation *yí*. *Jìngzhěn* (竸軫): The second character is pronounced with the *zhī* and *rěn* rhymes. In Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Kaogongji*, "zhěn" refers to the horizontal wooden bar at the rear of the carriage body (*yú*). In the *Taixuanjing*, it means "to turn its path. The meaning in the *Shuowen jiezi* is the same. It follows the radical *chē* (車) and the phonetic *zhǐn* (㐱), which has the same pronunciation as above, in the third tone.

The *Mao Shi* (*Rongche lunbiao*) states that "lunbiao" refers to the horse's bit; the *Wenzi jilüe* also identifies it as a horse bridle. The *Shuowen jiezi* defines it as "the horse's bit," written with the radical for metal (金) and the phonetic element "piao" (麃). "Yong" (輶) is pronounced *you*, and "piao" (麃) is pronounced *bojiao*.

*Xián mǐ* (玄弭): The second character is pronounced *mǐ* (with the *mí* rhyme). According to the *Erya*, a bow without a rim is called a *mi*. The *Shuowen* states it is composed of "bow" (*gōng*) and the phonetic element "ear" (*ěr*).

*Bèi xuī* (佩觿): The first character is pronounced *pú mèi* (蒲昧反). Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "To wear objects upon the body is called *pei*. The *Shuowen* defines it as "the *pei* [sash] of a large belt," composed of "person" (*rén*) and the phonetic element "*chǎn*" (*chǎn*). It must have a cloth cover; "cloth" (*jīn*) refers to its ornamentation. The second character is pronounced *xǔ guī* (許規反). The *Mao Shi* commentary states: "A *xuī* is used for untying knots; it is the custom of one who has become an adult. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "Its shape is like a chisel, made from ivory. The *Shuowen* defines it as composed of "horn" (*jiǎo*) and the phonetic element "*xuǐ*" (*xuǐ*). The version in the [Mao] *Zhuan* as *guī* is a vulgar character and incorrect. *Xuǐ* is pronounced *huì guī* (惠圭反).
"Every time I lament that the opening of compassion has instead resulted in the examination of sounds, 'kai' (慨) means to sigh with emotion.

According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical 'heart' (心) and the phonetic 'ji' (既). 'Dü' (蠧), pronounced *dùgù*, refers to the book-eating insect. The *Biographies of King Mu* states that 'dù' is the worm that devours books; the *Shuowen* also identifies it as a worm within wood, composed of the radical 'insect' (䖵) and the abbreviated phonetic 'tuó' (橐). 'Gūn' (䖵) is pronounced *kūn*, and 'tuó' (橐) is pronounced *tuò*."

*Kǎo fú* (the *fú* is pronounced according to the rhyme of *yún* in the *Yìnyì* commentary on the *Hànshū*; *fú* is the war chariot of the Xiongnu; the *Shēnglèi* also states it is a chariot for attacking and fighting; the *Shuōwén* defines it as being composed of the radical "chariot" with the phonetic element "bèn," where *bèn* is pronounced like *bēn*).

Regarding the character *jù* (巨): the phonetic gloss states it means "great" (*dà*). The commentary’s rendering as the character *chén* (臣) is incorrect. Regarding the character below, *chī* (䲭): the phonetic gloss states it refers to a "banner-mark. It is made of silk five feet long and half a span wide, attached to the top of the flag. The correct form throughout antiquity and today follows the radical *jīn* (巾) with the phonetic *zhì* (戠). The commentary’s rendering as *chì* (𢡠), following the radical *xīn* (心), is erroneous. The pronunciation of *zhì* is *shí* (識).

Regarding "yòu" (郵): above, it means "to seek"; Zheng’s commentary on the *Erya* states it means "passing along a road. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states it means "a boundary marker. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "a lodging for couriers traveling between borders," composed of the radical "city" (邑) and the phonetic "chuí" (垂). The *Chuanshuo* writes it as "xiè" (卸), with the pronunciation xīngyè; however, this is the character for "unbuckling a horse's saddle" and deviates from the original meaning. Below, the reading is zūnjùn (遵峻). Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* says it is a term of praise for a horse. "Jùn" (駿) also means "swift. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "the excellence of a horse," composed of the radical "horse" (馬) and the phonetic "jùn" (夋).
*Yà* (迓): Upper radical 5, phonetic *jià*. The *Erya* states: "Yà means to welcome. The standard character for ancient and modern usage takes the radical 辵 (*chuò*) with the phonetic *yá*.

*Tán* (闐): Radical 109, phonetic *nián*. The *Erya* states: "Tán-tán is the appearance of abundance. Guo's commentary says: "It is the sound of a multitude moving together. The *Shuowen* takes the radical 門 (*mén*) with the phonetic *zhēn*.

*Qiang qiang* (the final *qiang* pronounced as *jiang*): The *Mao Shi* Commentary states that "qiang qiang" refers to the dignified bearing of scholar-officials. The *Zhuan* states that "qiang qiang" also means "assembling. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines "qiang qiang" as a state of magnificence, derived from the radical "foot" (*zu*) and the phonetic "jiang" (*jiang*). The *Zhuan* further notes that it is sometimes written with the "metal" radical (*jin*) as "qiang qiang," referring to the sound of musical instruments.

"Bīng" (豳國) is pronounced *shàng bǐ mín* (上筆旻反). Zheng Xuan’s *Shīpǔ* (譜) states that Bīng is the name of a territory bordering the Róng-Dì (戎狄), the fiefdom established by Gōngliú. In ancient and modern standard characters, it is written with "shān" (山) as the radical and "huán" (豩) as the phonetic; "huán" is pronounced *bīn* (斌).

Zhù (矚): Pronounced zhōng (with the tone reversed). It means to examine sounds; it is that toward which many eyes turn. It is composed of the radical 目 (eye) and the phonetic 屬 (zhǔ); it is a vulgar character for what was originally written as 囑.

Zuàn (鑽): Pronounced zuǎn (guān reversed). Gù Yěwáng states that zuàn refers to engraving and carving. The *Shuowen* says it is that by which one pierces. It is composed of the radical 金 (metal) and the phonetic 贊 (zàn).

*Xiāo gǎo* (削槀): The first character, *xiāo*, has the phonetic *xiàng* (略反). According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means "to eliminate. The *Shuōwén* states it is formed from the radical "knife" (*dāo*) with the phonetic "xiào" (*xiào shēng*). The second character, *gǎo*, has the phonetic *gǎo* (高老反). In the *Shìjì*, it is said that Qu Yuan was "drafting" (*shǔ gǎo*), meaning the draft had not yet been finalized. Gu Yewáng states that *gǎo* is synonymous with "grass" (*cǎo*). The *Shuōwén* defines it as "straw" (*gǎn*) formed from the radical "grain" (*huó*) with the phonetic "gāo" (*gāo shēng*). The form "lǎo" (藁) found in the commentary is a vulgar variant.

The character 購 (gòu): the upper radical is 周 (zhōu), pronounced with a reversed tone; Duan Yucai’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states it means "to seek" (*qiú*). The *Zishu* also says it means "to seek. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of 手 (shǒu) and the phonetic 叜 (sǒu). In the transmitted texts, it is written as 搜 (sōu) from 叟 (sǒu), which is a vulgar form. The lower part is read as gōu-lòu. The *Shuowen* defines it as "to seek by means of wealth," composed of 貝 (bèi) and the phonetic 冓 (gòu); the pronunciation of 冓 is the same.

The character 翰 (hàn) is pronounced with the initial *láo* (勞) and the final *fǎn* (反). According to the *Shuowen*, "to grasp" (*cāo*) means to embrace or hold; it is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "sào" (喿), with the final *fǎn* being *hán* (寒) and *gàn* (幹). The character 羽 (yǔ) refers to bird feathers; according to the *Shuowen*, it also refers to the feathers of the celestial rooster (*tiānjī*), composed of the radical "feathers" (羽) and the phonetic "gàn" (倝), with the final *fǎn* being *gàn* (倝). The character 傳 (chuán) is written as 翕 (xī) when forming 翰; this is a vulgar form. The pronunciation of 喿 is *sāngdào* (桑到), and the pronunciation of 倝 is *yù'àn* (于岸).

*Húanlán* (汍瀾): The first character is pronounced with the *hú* rhyme group and the *guān* final. It describes the appearance of flowing water; it is also written as *huán*. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mu*) and the phonetic "wán. The second character is pronounced with the *xià* rhyme group and the *gān* final. According to the *Erya*, large waves are called *lán*; according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "water" (*shui*) and the phonetic "lán."

*Fuyi* (腷臆): The first character is pronounced *pī* (逼) as a fanqie, and the second is *yìng* (應) and *jí* (極) as a fanqie. Guo Yuangui states that *fuyi* means "full" (*yíngmǎn*). In the *Fānyǔ*, Guo’s commentary notes that *fuyi* also refers to being full of breath. The *Yùpiān* records a variant written with the "heart" radical (*cì*) as *bì*. The *Shuowén* records an archaic form written with the "ethereal" radical (*yì*) as *jì*. The current form with the "moon" radical (*yì*) is the common vulgarized version.

"Miù wǎ shí" (糅瓦石): "nǚ yòu fǎn" (女又反). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Yīlǐ* states that "miù" means "mixed. Lexicons also record it as "zǎo" (󲜛), with the same pronunciation. The standard character for ancient and modern usage is composed of the radical "grain" (米) and the phonetic "róu" (柔).

*Línqiú* (琳璆): The first character, *lín*, is pronounced with the final *-fǎn* (入聲); Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shūjìng* states that *lín* is a name for jade. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical "jade" (*yù*) and the phonetic "yù" (玉). The second character, *qiú*, has the pronunciation *jiū*; Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shūjìng* also states that *qiú* is jade. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical "jade" (*yù*) and the phonetic "liáo" (翏).

"Cuo-zōng" (錯綜): "cuò" (錯) is pronounced gǎo-fǎn (各反); Kǒng's commentary on the *Shūjīng* (尚書) states it means "intermingled. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "metal" (金) with "xī" (昔) as its phonetic component. "Zōng" (綜) is pronounced zōng-sòng-fǎn (宗送反). According to the *Shuowén*, it means "to hold threads together in a weaving loom," composed of the radical "silk" (糸) with "zōng" (宗) as its phonetic component.

Scroll One, Volume One: A Biographical Account of the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. Scroll One. Guoshi (緱氏): Pronounced *gǒu* (the "gǒu" in *Gǒuhòu* [苟候] being pronounced with a retroflex *-ou*). The *Hànshū* states that there is a Guoshi County in Henan. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical for "silk" (*miè*) and the phonetic component *hòu*.

"Jie" (屆) is pronounced as "jiè" (上皆薤反); Master Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjìng* states that "jie" means "to arrive. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "shī" (尸) with the phonetic "yóu" (由).

"Xuánzàng" (玄奘): "xuán" (玄) is pronounced as "lǎng" (下藏朗反); according to the *Fānyǔ*, "xuán" means "great. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "dà" (大) with the phonetic "zhuàng" (壯).

The character for *sī* (司) is pronounced *lì*. The *Chunqiu Zhuan* states: "The *sījiǎo* (司𨽻) oversees the laws of the five *jiǎo* (𨽻). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* notes that this was a low-ranking official. The correct orthography of the character from ancient times to the present follows the radical for grain (*米*) and takes *rù* (入) as its phonetic component.

*Guīzhāng*: The upper character is *guī* (pronounced *kǎi* with the *fǎn* [rhyme] *xié*). Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that the *guī* held by the King is one chi and two cun in length. According to the *Báihùtōng*, "the word *guī* signifies purity (*jié*). The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radical "jade" (*yù*) and the phonetic "guī. The lower character is *zháo* (pronounced *yáng* with the *fǎn* [rhyme] *rǎng*). Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that half of a *guī* is called a *zhāng*. According to the *Báihùtōng*, "the word *zhāng* signifies clarity (*míng*). The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radical "jade" (*yù*) and the phonetic "zhāng."

*Huánhuài* (闤闠): The first character, *huán*, is pronounced with the initial *shuāi* and final *guān*. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "the road. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical 門 (*mén*) and the phonetic 睘 (*huán*). The second character, *huài*, is pronounced with the initial *hú* and final *duì*. According to the *Shuōwén*, it refers to the outer gate of a marketplace, composed of the radical 門 (*mén*) and the phonetic 貴 (*guì*).

*Caó* (the first character is pronounced *zào* [sào-láo] and the second is *cái-hé*): according to the *Guǎngyá*, "caó" means sound; according to the *Jīngǔzhèngzì*, it refers to the sound of a drum. Both follow the mouth radical and the *cáo* phonetic. The character *zàn* is used as a phonetic component, resulting in *zá*, which is a vulgar form.

"Xiángzhù" (翔翥): the first character is pronounced with the *shàng* tone as *xiàng*, and the second as *zhū lǜ*. According to the *Fānyán* (方言), *zhù* means "to lift up"; the *Chǔcí* (楚辭) says it means "to fly and soar. The *Shuōwén* (說文) also states it means "to fly and lift up," being composed of the radical "feather" (*yǔ*) and the phonetic element "zhě" (*zhě*).
*Fuying* (伏膺): *yìng* is pronounced with the initial *y* and the final *líng*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *yìng* means "chest," composed of the radical "flesh" (*ròu*) and the phonetic "gàn.
*Jiezhi* (桀跖): The first character, *jié*, is pronounced with the initial *qián* and the final *jì*;

the second, *zhí*, is pronounced with the initial *zhēng* and the final *yì*. *Kukuo* (刳斮): *kū* is pronounced with the initial *kǔ* and the final *gū*. According to the *Cangjie pian*, *kū* means "to butcher"; according to the *Fangyan*, it means "to cut out [the internal organs]. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "knife" (*dāo*) and the phonetic "kuā. *Zhuó* is pronounced with the initial *zè* and the final *lüè*. According to the *Guangya*, *zhuó* means "to sever. Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that *zhuó* means "to behead.
