According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "axe" (*jīn*) and the phonetic "xī."

In the *Mao Shi*, "shānyí" (芟夷) means to cut down weeds; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of "cǎo" (艹) as the radical and "shū" (殳) as the phonetic, with the pronunciation "zhī-fǎn" (之反). The *Erya* states that "yí" (夷) means level or to extinguish; in the *Zhou Li*, it refers to using water to eradicate weeds and cut them down. According to the *Wenzi Dian*, because the people of the "yídí" (夷狄) were fond of large bows, the character is composed of "dà" (大) and "gōng" (弓).
*Yáng* (煬) is the posthumous title of the Sui Emperor; according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "fire" (火) with the phonetic *yáng*.

*Zǎn* (酇) is the name of a commandery in the state of Pèi during the Han dynasty, the fief bestowed upon Xiāo Hé; it now belongs to Qiáo Jùn. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "city" (邑) with the phonetic *zàn*.

"Eight Horizons" (*bāhóng*) appears in the *Huáinánzǐ* (The Master Who Embraces Simplicity), where it says: "He knows the forms of the eight horizons and nine fields. Xu’s commentary states: "Horizon (*hóng*) means a binding cord. The *Shuowén Jiězì* explains it as being composed of the radical for "silk" (*mì*) and the phonetic element *húng*; *húng* has the same pronunciation as *hóng*. In the aforementioned text, it is written with the radical for "roof" (*mián*), forming *hóng*, meaning "vast" (*hóngdà*).

*Tuí* (隤) in *túigāng* (隤綱). The upper radical is *duì* (隊), pronounced with the *rǎi* (雷) rhyme. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to collapse"; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means "to fall downward," composed of the radical *huì* (𨸏) and the phonetic *guì* (貴). It is traditionally written as *tuí* (頹), which is a vulgar character; it is also sometimes written as *tuí* (頹).

*Bāo* (pronounced *bǔ máo fǎn*): According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to wrap. It refers to being wrapped up. In the commentary, it is written as *bāo* with the radical for grass (*艸*) and the phonetic *zuò*; this is also interchangeable. Below, *zū* (pronounced *zū wò fǎn*): According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to break" or "to frustrate. It is formed from the radical for hand (*手*) with the phonetic *zuò*.
"Yán" (問上恤遵反; qǐwèn shàng xù zūn fǎn) means to follow along a river upstream (江上悅㳙反;

jiāng shàng yuè juān fǎn). The *Commentary on the Book of Documents* by Kǒng [Yáng] states: "To go downstream with the current is called *yán*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "water" (水) and the phonetic component "yǔn" (𠂇).

*Kiṃśā* (嚫施): The first character is pronounced with the initial *jìn* (靳) and the final *fǎn* (反). This is a collection of abbreviated characters for *kiṃśā*. The commentary states that it is written as *juàn* (䞋) based on the *Jùshì* (具釋), though *qiān* (䞋) is also acceptable.

*Wúyǐng* (無𣖀): The second character is pronounced with the initial *gēng* (庚) and the final *gěng* (哽). It means illness, fierceness, straightforwardness, and strength. Gu Jia’s commentary on the *Guóyuè* (國語) states that *gěng* (梗) is like "harm. According to the *Shuōwén* (說文), it is composed of the radical *mù* (木) with the phonetic *gēng* (㪅).

"Hóngtāo" (洪濤) means "great waves. In the *Shàngshū* commentary by Kǒng [Yǎng], "Hóng" (洪) means "great. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is water; it is composed of the radical "water" (水) and the phonetic "gòng" (共), with the pronunciation "xià táng háo fǎn" (下唐豪反). Cāngjié says it refers to great billows. According to the *Shuōwén*, "Tāo" (濤) refers to the surging of tidal waters; it is composed of the radical "water" (水) and the phonetic "shòu" (壽), with the pronunciation "shòu" (壽).

*Xiōngyǒng* (洶湧): "Xiōng" (洶) is the same as *yǒng* (涌). It refers to the appearance of water surging and billowing; it is composed of the radical "water" (水) with the phonetic "hūn" (匈), pronounced *xià róng zhǒng* (下容種). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "yǒng" (涌) also means to surge; it is composed of the radical "water" (水) with the phonetic "yǒng" (勇), and is also written as *yǒng* (湧).

The character for "boat" (fǎn) is pronounced with the rhyme *fan* (韈). According to the *Cangjie pian*, it means "to attach. The *Shuowen jiezi* states that it refers to a large ship on the sea, composed of the radical "wood" (*mu*) and the phonetic "fa" (*fa*). The version in the *Chuanshuo* which uses the radical "wood" (*mu*) to form the character *shu* (󳋪) is a vulgar variant and is incorrect.

*Jùnqiào* (峻峭): The first character is pronounced *jùn* (反) with the initial *jun*; the second is pronounced *qiào* (反) with the initial *qiao*. According to the *Shēnglèi*, *qiào* also means a steep mountain. The *Shuōwén* states that it may also be written as *shào* (陗), using the radical *shuǎo* (𨸏).

*Bóbiāo* (摶飇): The first character is pronounced *duànluán* (反) with the initials *duan-luan*. According to the *Shēnglèi*, *bó* (摶) means to seize or grasp. The *Shuōwén* indicates it is composed of the radical *shǒu* (手) and the phonetic *zhuān* (專). The second character is pronounced *píyáo* (反) with the initials *pi-yao*. According to the *Éryá*, "fúyáo" (扶搖) is called "biāo" (颷). Guō’s commentary states it refers to a violent wind that blows upward and downward. It is composed of the radical *fēng* (風) and the phonetic *biāo* (猋).

"Sā" (pronounced with the "san" and "he" finals reversed) means to look back; Wang Ye says it refers to the sound of wind blowing tree leaves. The *Shuowen* defines it as a soaring wind, composed of the radical "wind" (fēng) and the phonetic "li" (lì). "Jiě" (稽) and "sǎng" (顙) [together form] "jiěsǎng" (稽顙), pronounced with the "sang" and "lang" finals reversed.
This refers to bowing the head to the ground so that the forehead touches the hands.

The Moheyan Qish (pronounced *qīng* and *lì*) lies one thousand *li* west of Guzang; it is a desolate region where human habitation ceases, lacking both water and grass, consisting solely of sand, hence it is called a "qish" (a desert), the character being pronounced with the sound of "ze" from the radical for stone.

*Chouhuì* (愁憒): *gōng* and *duì* are the phonetic components; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "confusion. It is composed of the radical *xin* (heart) and the phonetic *guì*. *Ōuyǎng* (憂󳇳): the pronunciation is *wú*.

Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states that *wú* implies a state of being "without consciousness. The *Shuowen* depicts this as a pictograph (*xiàngxíng*). The character *chuí* (傳) is written with the radical *xin* as *yǎng* (󳈁), which is a vulgar form used interchangeably with the standard character.
Dūn-huáng (the first character is pronounced with the *dùn* rhyme, while the second has the sound *huáng*): a commandery name in the region of Lǒngyòu; it is present-day Shāzhōu.

Jī-píng-guǒ (the first character is pronounced with the *shàng* tone *jì*, and the phonetic component is correctly written as *zī*; the transmitted text uses *jī*, which is a vulgar form; it is composed of the radical *bèi* [貝] and the phonetic *qí* [齊]).

*Ji* (𧵍): The character for "clothing and provisions. The upper radical is *mao* (矛, *máo*). In the *Erya*, it means "to sell" (*jià*) or "the market" (*shì*). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to exchange goods. It is composed of the radical *bèi* (貝) and the phonetic *cì* (次). *Bù yì* (不懌): The character for "displeasure.

The reading is *yíng* (盈, *yíng*) with the final consonant *yì* (益, *yì*). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to be pleased" (*yuè yì*). It is composed of the radical *xīn* (心) and the phonetic *gāo* (睾, *gāo*).
The character for *guǐmèi* (鬼魅) is composed of "ghost" (鬼) and "frown" (眉), with the latter pronounced as *bì* (祕).

Regarding *guànshòu* (盥漱): according to Gu Yewang, all acts of washing or rinsing objects are termed *guàn*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as water from a mortar (*jiù*) poured onto a vessel (*míng*). The lower radical is pronounced as *sòu* (所救反). When written with the "mouth" radical (*kǒu*) as *shòu*, this is the character for *shòu* (漱); when written with the "mouth" radical as *sou*, this is the character for *kaisuò* (咳嗽).
"Què (pronounced jué according to Hàn Kāngbó) means 'firm' or 'solid. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical 'stone' (石) and the phonetic 'què' (寉).

Jíerán (上音 jié; *shàngyīn* jié): in the *Fānyán*, jíe means 'single' or 'alone'; in the *Guǎngyá*, jíe means 'short. According to the *Shuowen*, it is a pictographic character representing a person without a left arm."

*Qiú hè*: the first character is pronounced *qiú*; the second is pronounced with the initial *hán* and the final *gé*. *Tuó*: pronounced *tú hé*, it refers to a camel (*luòtuó*). *Shào*: pronounced *shuāng zhuō*;

according to the *Kǎośēng*, it is written as *shào* and refers to a large spear. *Bù*: written with the radical for wood (*mù*) as *shuò*, which is the name of a river (as in the following instance). According to Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhōulǐ*, *dào* is a banner topped with a tuft of feathers. Cáo Yōng’s *Dúduàn* states that a *dào* is made from the tail-hair of a *máo* ox. The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radical *xuán* with the phonetic *dú*.

*Yù* (𤑔): The rhyme is *yuè* (儒悅反). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that *yù* means "to burn. The *Cangjie pian* says it means "blazing. The *Shuowen jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) and the phonetic "rè" (*rè*).
*Sāngzǐ* (桑梓): The lower character is pronounced *zǐ*. It is the name of a tree.

*Xiàn* (跣): Pronounced *xiān* (as in *xiāndiǎn*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means to tread directly upon the ground with the feet because they lack shoes or sandals; it is composed of the radical "foot" (*zú*) and the phonetic "xiān. *Kèhàn* (可汗): Pronounced *kě hán*.
This is a borrowed word for the title of the kings of the Northern Di tribes. It corresponds to the sound *khaghan*.

The character *pí* (疲) [is pronounced with the initial *yì* (怡) and the final *zhì* (制)]. According to the *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (Mao Commentary on the Classic of Poetry), it means "exertion" (*yì*). The *Guǎng Yǎ* (Extended Lexicon) states it means "suffering. The *Shuōwén Jiězì* (Explaining Simple and Analyzing Compound Characters) also states it means "toil. It is composed of the radical "force" (*lì*) and the phonetic "shè" (*shài*). Alternatively, it may be written as *yì* (𠡫) with the radical "slave" (*lì*). The version in the *Zhuàn* (Commentary) that uses "shè" (*shài*) to form *yì* (勩) is incorrect.

The character for *yán* (閹) is pronounced *yān* (掩炎反). Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "A *yán* is one whose vital essence (*jīngqì*) is closed and concealed. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as: "A *yánshù* is one who guards the palace gates; a *yán* is one who closes the gate in a state of dullness. It is composed of the radical 'gate' (*mén*) with the phonetic component 'yān' (*yǎn*)."

Regarding "Fenjin" (汾晉): "Shangfo" (上佛) is pronounced as *wen* (聞). Regarding "Shanhaijing" (山海經): "Fenshui" (汾水) originates at Shangyu (上窳); it flows from north to south and enters the Yellow River. "Xiajin" (下津) is pronounced as *jin* (燼). "Rangmei" (攘袂):

"Rang" (攘) is pronounced as *ruo* (若) with the *yang* (若) rhyme. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that it means to brush away or repel (*rangque*). Gu Yewang says it means to remove the sleeves of one's garment and extend the arms. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "hand" (*shou*) and the phonetic "xiang" (*xiang*).

*Jian-chue* (漸惙): *zhé* (陟) and *lüe* (劣) are the reversed [readings]. The *Shenglèi* (聲類) states that "chue" is the appearance of shortness of breath. The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (毛詩傳) states that "chue" is also anxiety. The *Shuowén* (說文) says it is composed of the radical "heart" (心) with "zhue" (叕) as the phonetic.

It is read as *dēng* (蹬, 登, 鄧). The *Guǎyá* (廣雅) states that "deng" (蹬) means footwear. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) writes it as *dèng* (隥), which also means footwear and "to look up. The *Shuowén* says it is composed of the radical "foot" (𨸏) with "deng" (登) as the phonetic. The text of the *Zhuàn* (傳) writes it as *cèng-dèng* (蹭隥), meaning the manner of walking where one loses one's footing; this is not the meaning here.

*Zhòu* (舟): The tip of a boat; the phonetic component is *jiǎn* (檝). The commentary states it refers to the type of oar used for propelling a vessel; it is composed of the radical *mù* (木) and the phonetic *jí* (戢). The character *chuán* (傳) is written with the radical *zhōu* (舟) as *shì* (艥), which is a vulgar form.
*Càn* (讖): The upper part is pronounced *chǔ yìn* (楚蔭); according to the *Shuowen*, "a prophecy" (*càn yàn*). It is composed of the radical *yán* (言) and the phonetic *xiān* (韯).
*Chou-chü*: The first character is pronounced *shàng zhòu liú fǎn*; the second is pronounced *xià zhù lǚ fǎn*. *Chā-chì*: The first character is pronounced *shàng tiān jiā fǎn*;

the second is pronounced *xià chì lì fǎn*. Wang’s commentary on the *Chuci* states: "The appearance of one whose will is lost and who stands dejected. The *Gōngjīn Zhèngzì* (Orthodox Characters of Antiquity and Today) also records that "standing dejectedly with lost will" is written as *chā*, both following the radical for "man" (*rén*) and having *zhái* and *jì* as their phonetic components.

Regarding "small snail" (xiǎo luó): the *Kǎoshēng* states that "luó" refers to the snail (*guāniú*). The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radical "insect" (虫) with the phonetic "yōu" (𣎆), and it is also written as "chóng" (蟸). The common form "luó" (螺) and the transmitted form "lù" (𧋠) are errors.
*Rénrǎn* (荏苒): "Rén" is pronounced with the *jin* rhyme-group and the *fan* (final) of *jiǎn* (錦);

"rǎn" is pronounced with the *xià* rhyme-group and the *fan* (final) of *yàn* (琰). *Qióngdú* (煢獨): "Qióng" is pronounced with the *kuí* rhyme-group and the *ying* (營) rhyme; in the *Shàngshū* commentary by Kǒng [Yáng], it means "solitary. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical *xùn* (卂, pronounced *xìn*) and the phonetic element *ying* (營) abbreviated. *Xùn* is pronounced *xìn*.

Volume Two, Part Two. The Original Biography of the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. Volume Two. *Zhuan* (甎): Upper tone, pronounced *zhuan*. The *Beicang* states it refers to a brick (*luozhuan*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical for "tile" (*wa*) with the phonetic component *zhuan*; the pronunciation of *luo* is [lu].

*Yinkuang* (銀礦): The character *keng* (礦) is pronounced with the initial *mǎng* (猛) and the final *-ǎn* (反). The *Shuowen* states it refers to the unrefined ore (*pó*) of copper, iron, gold, and so forth. It is also written as *huáng* (磺) or *hóng* (鑛), following the radical "stone" (*shí*) and the phonetic "guǎng" (*guǎng*).

*Chuānyá* (川崖): *Chuān* (川) is pronounced with the final *-é* (頟). The *Kaosheng* states that *yá* (崖) refers to a steep, dangerous bank at the edge of a mountain torrent. The *Shuowen* defines it as a high edge, following the radical "mountain" (*shān*) and the phonetic *yá*. The pronunciation of *yá* is the same as above.

*Níng-hù* (凝冱): The second character is pronounced with the *hú* rhyme group (*gù*). Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states that *hù* means "to close" or "to seal. Wang’s commentary on the *Chuci* says that *hù* also means "cold. In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, it is written with the radical *shuǐ* (water) and the phonetic *hù*.

*Āi* (pronounced with the *xī* rhyme): The *Shuowen* states this is the appearance of frost and snow; it is composed of the radical "white" (*bái*) and the phonetic "qǐ". *Xījìng* (upper character pronounced with the *xì jī* rhyme):

In the *Liji*, Zheng’s commentary states that "xījìng" means a path. In the *Zhuozhuan*, Du’s commentary also states that "xī" is a path. The *Shuowen* states it is composed of the radical "foot" (*zú*) and the phonetic "xī".

Qixū (崎嶇): The first character is pronounced qi (綺羈反) and the second is pronounced qū (音區). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "qixū" means narrow and constricted; it also means uneven. Both characters are composed of the radical "mountain" (山), with "qi" (奇) and "qū" (區) as their phonetic components. Some traditions write the second character as chù (岴) using the radical "hill" (丘), but this is a vulgar variant.
*Fù* (in *fùlǚ*, "double-layered shoes"): the upper character is read as *fú* (伏). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "A double-walled garment; it takes the radical 衣 (*yī*) and the phonetic 复 (*fù*).
*Chuī* (in *érchuī*, "and cooking"): the lower character is read as *chì* (齒). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To cook or heat; it takes the radical 火 (*huǒ*) and the phonetic 欠 (*qiàn*)."

The upper character 𣨙 (wěi) is pronounced with the *wěi* rhyme; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "sickness" and takes *wěi* as its phonetic component. The lower character 凍 (dòng) is pronounced with the *dòng* rhyme; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "ice" and takes *bīng* (the character for ice) as its radical and *dòng* as its phonetic component.
*Tián* (畋): In the *Shuowen*, this means "level field" (*píngtián*). It is composed of the radical *tián* (田) with the phonetic *zhī* (攴).

*Lì* (裏): In the *Shuowen*, this refers to the "forehead" (*é*). It is composed of the radical *xiè* (頁) with the phonetic *gè* (各). The character *fú* (傳) [in some texts] is written as *é* (額); this is an erroneous vulgar form.

*Chui-mao* (毳毛): *shu* and *rui* rhyme; Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that "chui-mao" refers to the fine, downy hair of a beast. Zheng Zhong says it is a garment made of coarse wool. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as the fine tail-hair of a beast, written with three "hair" radicals.

*Chóngyīn* (重茵): "Yīn" is pronounced with the *lín* rhyme. Zheng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states that "yīn" refers to a mattress (*bèi*). According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) and the phonetic "yīn.

*Fūrù* (敷蓐): "Rù" is pronounced with the *róng* and *zhú* rhymes. It is a word for grass and signifies thickness or abundance. It is composed of the radical "grass" and the phonetic "rú. The *Chuán* (Commentary) writes this as "wù" with the radical "silk" (*mì*), which is a vulgar form and incorrect.
*Suhun* (上蘇沒反, 下胡昆反): According to the original biography, this is an implement of the barbarians. *Gengzhu* (僸𠇱; 上音禁, 下音末):
The *Yunchuan* states that "geng" means the appearance of looking upward; the *Kaosheng* identifies it as the name of a music of the Yi people.

*Kēngqiāng* (铿锵): The upper character is pronounced *xíng* (with the "fǎn" [rhyme] *quèliáng*); the *Yùpiān* states that both *kēng* and *qiāng* denote the sounds of objects, and the *Shuōwén* indicates they are both composed of the radical for metal (*jīn*).

*Pēngxiān* (烹鲜): The upper character is pronounced *pāimáng*; the *Wenzì jílüè* defines it as boiling water to cook food. The lower character is pronounced *xiányán*; the *Shuōwén* correctly uses three fish (*yú*) radicals, while the transmitted texts write it as *xiān*, which is a vulgar character used interchangeably.
“Lao” (羔) has the upper tone *gāo*; “du” (犢) has the lower tone *dú*.

One set (*yī xí*)—*xí* is pronounced with the initial *xún* and the final *lì* (according to Guō’s commentary on the *Erya*, *xí* means “double”). In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical “clothing” (*yī*) and the phonetic component “tá” (龖) abbreviated; the pronunciation of “tá” is *dà zà*.
The country of Zheshi (the first character pronounced with an initial *shā* and final *-ye*, reversed; the name of the country; in the language of Tang, "Stone Country").
The country of Sàwèijiàn (the first character pronounced as a triphthong *sān-hé*; the second character pronounced as *wǎn-fā*; the name of the country; in the language of Tang, "Kang Country").
The kingdom of Hehan (喝捍國)—the first character pronounced with the *hu* and *ge* rhymes, the middle sound being *han*; in the language of Tang, it is called Dong'an (東安國).

Its gates have door-leaves (*ménfēi*)—the second character pronounced with the *wēi* rhyme; according to the *Shuowen*, *tiè* (鍱)—the first character pronounced with the *yú* and *jié* rhymes—is what the state of Qi called *cāorù* (鏶), meaning a thin plate of metal, formed from the radical *jīn* (金) and the phonetic *yè* (枼).
"為鈴" (wéi líng): "歷" (lì) is pronounced with the *ding* (丁) rhyme;

"篡立" (chuàn lì) means to usurp the throne, where "篡" (chuàn) is pronounced with the initial *guàn* (慣). "考聲" (kǎo shēng) means to kill [the predecessor] and seize his position; it is also a term for taking [power]. The upper radical is "竹" (zhú). "顯敞" (xiǎn chǎng):

"敞" (chǎng) is pronounced with the *huài* (壞) rhyme. According to the *Cāngjié piān*, it means lofty and prominent; according to the *Shuōwén*, it refers to high ground that can be seen from afar, composed of the radical "攵" (pǔ) and the phonetic "尙" (shàng).

*Yú-rùn* (腴潤): The upper character is pronounced *yú* (as in the *Zhèng* commentary on the *Lǐjì*, where it notes that "fatty" [refers to] the winter qi being present). According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of "flesh" (*ròu*) with "yú" as its phonetic. The lower character is pronounced *rún* (with the *yun* rhyme).
*Zǎo-guàn* (澡罐): The upper character is pronounced *zǎo*; the lower character is pronounced *guàn-luàn*. It is a vessel made of fired clay (*kǎoshēng wǎqì*). It is also written as *sōng*.

"Guāngshuì (光瑞)" is read as xiàchuí wèifǎn (下垂偽反). It is a term for auspicious response (*ruìyìng*) from the *Cāngjié piān*. In his commentary on the *Líjì*, Zhèng states that "auspiciousness" (*ruì*) also means "trustworthy evidence" (*xìn*). According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "jade" (*yù*) and the phonetic "duān" (*耑*); the sound of "duān" is the same as "duān" (端).

The handle of the broom (zhǒu) [is pronounced] *zhōu* (with the radical *yǒu* and the phonetic *gù*). According to Yu Yewang, a broom is that by which filth and impurities are swept away. In the *Shuowen*, it is written with the radical *yòu* (hand) and the phonetic *chí* (to hold), meaning one who sweeps the right side of the gate. The lower part is pronounced *bīng* (with the radical *mìng*) and means "to grasp" or "to hold. In other character dictionaries, it is written with the radical *mù* (wood) and the phonetic *bǐng*. *Zhǒu*: Radical *yǒu*, phonetic *gù*. A broom is used for sweeping away filth and impurities. In the *Shuowen*, it is composed of *yòu* (hand) holding *chí* (a cloth) to sweep the right side of the gate; the lower part is pronounced *bīng* (with the radical *mìng*), meaning "to grasp," "to hold," or "to take. In the *Shuowen*, it is composed of *mù* (wood) and the phonetic *bǐng*.

Regarding the initial character *jī* (基): Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states it means "footprints"; Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* also says it means "feet. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical *zu* (足) and the phonetic *zhǐ* (止).

Regarding *mi* (蜜): the sound is *chāng rǎo*. The *Kaoseng Zhuan* states that *shào* (熬) refers to parching rice or wheat; the *Chuan* (傳) uses *shǎo* (少) as a variant for *sǎn* (󰉓), which is a vulgar form. Regarding *xià* (下): the sound is *bì* (必).
*Zhèjiā* (磔迦) is the name of a country; *zhè* (上) is pronounced with the *zhé* (陟) and *gé* (革) finals.
*Yǒngyóu* (游泳) is explained in the *Ěryá* as "swimming" (*yóuyóu*); according to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) with "yǒng" (*yǒng*) as its phonetic.
*Tan* (暫): *ji* (霽) with the reversed phonetic *xia* (下) and *zi* (子). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "the ceasing of rain," composed of the radical "rain" (*yu*) and the phonetic *qi* (齊).
*Tou* (鍮): *lou* (樓) with the reversed phonetic *tou* (透). The *Kaosheng* states that *toushi* (鍮石) is a metal resembling gold, composed of the radical "metal" (*jin*) and the phonetic *yu* (俞).

*Jiàng* (pronounced with the first tone, as in *jiāngxiàng*): The character *jiàng* denotes the color red. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "Jiàng also means red; it is composed of the radical *mì* (silk) and the phonetic *hóng*.
*Zhèn yǔ* (pronounced *zhēnlìn*): This commentary [reads] *zhuàn* from *zhǎn*; it is incorrect to write it as *qiǎn*.
"Shǒu" (少): Pronounced *zī* (簪歰反). The commentary on the sounds states that it means "to gather" (*jiàn*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical 戈 with the phonetic 咠.

"Qiè" (愜): Pronounced *qián xié* (謙協反). The *Guoyá* states that it means "acceptable. It is also glossed as "submission" (*fú*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical 心 with the phonetic 匧; the pronunciation of 匧 is the same as above. It may also be written as 㥦.
*Mleccha*: the first character is pronounced with the upper radical *miè* (pie) and the lower *lì* (li); in the Tang language, it means "frontier lands. *Huìjìn* (灰燼):

the lower character is pronounced with the radical *cí* (ci) and the phonetic *jìn* (jin). The *Mao Shi Jian* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry) states: "The remains of fire are called *jìn*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes this as 󱽃, composed of the radical *huǒ* (fire) and the phonetic *yù* (聿).

Suddenly [shù]: The *Guǎngyá* states it means "flame"; the *Chuci* uses it to describe a state of extreme rapidity; the *Shuowen* defines it as "a dog running," formed with the radical 犬 and the phonetic 攸. It is an error to write it as 倐 from the radical 火.

*Xi-rong* (熈融): The *Mao Shi* commentary (*Shu*) states that *xi* means "bright. In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is written with the radical for fire and the phonetic *yi*; the pronunciation of *yi* is [yí]. *Meng-ji-li-cheng* (瞢揭釐城):
The first character is pronounced *meng-peng* (墨朋) and the second is pronounced *li-zhi* (里知). This is a city name in the Western regions according to the Sanskrit language.

*Feifei* (霏霏): The commentary on the *Mao Shi* states that "feifei" describes the appearance of snow. The *Gujin Zhengzi* records that it is composed of the radical "rain" (雨) and the phonetic "fei" (非).

Regarding *shen* (身), the *Shenglei* glosses it as "feeding" (*shi*) or "nourishing" (*bu*). In the *Liji*, Confucius says, "The young Mr. Shi said, 'He feeds me according to the rites. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radicals "food" (食) and "person" (人).

*Gēngsuǒ* (縆鎖): The upper character *gēng* (縆) is pronounced as *huán* (亘). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "rope" (*suǒ*) and is composed of the radical *mì* (糸) with the phonetic *húan* (亘). The commentary [of the *Fanyi Mingyi Ji*] writes it as *héng* (絙), pronounced *húguān* (胡官); this is not the meaning of the commentary's text. The lower character *suǒ* (鎖) is pronounced as *guǒ* (果). Dictionaries state it means "linked rings. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is composed of the radical *jīn* (金) with the phonetic *jiǎo* (𧴪). The commentary writes it as *luò* (鏁) using the character *cháo* (巢); this is a vulgar form.

*Jian* (踐) and *nie* (躡): the former is pronounced *yan* (演) with a retroflex final, and the latter is pronounced *zhian* (輒) with a retroflex final. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states that *jian* means "to tread upon," while the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *nie* means "to trample. Both characters are composed of the radical "foot" (*zu*) and the phonetic components *can* (戔) and *nie* (聶) respectively.
*Kè* (木肯勒反): The *Shuowen* states it means "carving"; it is composed of the radical 刀 with the phonetic 亥.
*Pòlà pózhōng lánzǔ fǎn*: This is a Sanskrit term; in the language of Tang, it means "Moonlight. *Yānhuà shàng yànxián fǎn*:
The commentary reads it as the sound *yān*, but this is incorrect, as it would then carry the meaning of "smoke" (*yānyūn*).

*Xūhéng* (盱衡): The upper character is pronounced *xū*. The *Cāngjiépiān* states it means "to open wide one's eyes. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "eye" (*mù*) with the phonetic "yú" (*yúshēng*).
*Ūbōdìshuòlùn* (鄔波第鑠論): The upper character is pronounced *shāngzháo*. The old reading as *Yōubōtíshè* (優波提舍) is an error.
Luó màn (the first character pronounced láo, the second wàn):

"tòuchū" (the first character is read as tōu, the second lù; this is the correct orthography for ancient and modern times) means "to startle," derived from the radical 辵 (chuò) with the phonetic component 秀 (xiù).

Jǐn ér (the first character qín, the second yìng): according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "scarcely"; according to the *Shuōwén*, it is derived from the radical 人 (rén) with the phonetic component 堇 (jǐn), where jǐn is pronounced jǐn.
"Riverside" (Hébīn) is the sound *Bin*.
"Kanyakubja" (*Jiērujūshé*) is the sound *Jú*; it is a word from the Sanskrit language.

Regarding "ministers" (*liáo*): the commentary on the *Shūking* by Kǒng [Yáng] states that "liáo" refers to officials; according to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "man" (*rén*) with the phonetic element "lào" (*láo*).

*Xiùjié* (秀傑): *Mao Shi* states that "jié" means to stand out prominently. The *Huainanzi* says that one whose wisdom exceeds that of a thousand people is called a "jié. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "ren" (人) with the phonetic "jé" (桀). *Láolóng* (牢籠): The upper character, "lǎo," is pronounced with the final *-dāo*. In the *Zhouli*, Zheng’s commentary glosses it as "to confine.

The *Shuowen* defines it as a pen for raising oxen and horses, composed of the abbreviated form of "dōng" (冬) and the phonetic "fàn" (凡), which signifies being surrounded on all four sides. The lower character, "lóng," is pronounced with the final *-dōng*. The *Zhuangzi* passage "the pigeon in its cage" (*jī zhī zài lóng*) is an example of this. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "zhú" (竹) with the phonetic "lóng" (龍).

Volume Three. The Original Biography of the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. Volume Three. *Hài* (大駭): the second character is pronounced with the *xié* and *ě* rhymes. According to the *Cāngjié piān*, *hài* means "to be startled. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "horse" (*mǎ*) and the phonetic component "hài" (*hài*).

"Shàn" (墠) is pronounced as "shàng" (上) with the final consonant "chǎn" (闡) according to the *Mānsì* (韓詩). The *Mānsì* states that "shàn" means "tàn" (坦坦, level and open). The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文) defines "shàn" as "wilderness" (野), formed from the radical "earth" (土) and the phonetic "dān" (單). According to the original biography, it refers to land that is level and uniform.

*Kan* (甎龕): The first character is pronounced *kàn* (勘) with the *han* (含) radical; the second is *kān* (龕). According to the *Guǎngyá*, "kān" means "to contain. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means "the appearance of a dragon," composed of the "dragon" radical and the phonetic element "shěng" (省) from "hán" (含). The tradition that it follows "hé" (合) is incorrect. *Céngjì* (層級): The upper character is pronounced *zèng* (贈) with the *céng* (曾) radical;
the lower character is pronounced *jì* (今) with the *lì* (立) radical.

*Duì* (堆): In the capital city, it means "to pile up" (*huí fǎn*). Wang’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that it means "high. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *tǔ* (earth) and the phonetic *zhuī*. The reading below is *dài jiá fǎn*. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that *dié* refers to "female walls" (*nǚqiáng*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *tǔ* and the phonetic *yè*.

"Yuan lei" (垣壘): "xuān" (喧) is a reversed reading; according to the *Shuowen*, "yuan" (垣) means wall. "Ling gui" (羸鬼) is a reversed reading; the *Guangya* states that "lei" (壘) means layered or multiple.

"Qing ze" (傾𣅳): "zhuāng" (莊) is a reversed reading; the *Shuowen* says it refers to the sun being slanted in the west, composed of "shi" (時) as the radical and "ze" (仄) as the phonetic, or written as "ze" (昃), both being identical.

I contemplate deeply that "mian" (緬) is pronounced as *miǎn* (with the radical 糸 and phonetic 面; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "an appearance of deep reflection," and may also be written as 󳌔).
"Wuye" (嗚噎) is pronounced as *wū* (鄔) for the first character and *yānjié* (煙結) for the second.
*Bīngláng* (檳榔): the upper character is pronounced *bīn*, the lower *láng*.
*Dòukuò* (荳蔲): pronounced *hūgòu*. *Qiú* (虯) in *Qiúdòng* (虯棟):

the upper character is pronounced *qíyóu*, the lower *dōnglòng*. It is written as *qiú*; according to the *Guǎngyá*, it refers to the ridgepole (*yǐndòng*) or the roof peak (*wūjí*), composed of the radical *mù* (wood) with the phonetic *dōng*.

*Xiù* (繡): *lú* (櫨). The character *lú* is pronounced with the initial *dū* (都) reversed; it refers to the wooden block at the top of a pillar, taking *mù* (木) as its radical and *lú* (盧) as its phonetic.

*Wén* (文): *pí* (󳋒), pronounced *bī* (卑); according to the *Cāngjiépiān* (蒼頡篇), it means the eaves (*yán* [檐]); according to the *Shēnglèi* (聲類), it means the continuous rafters of a house; according to the *Shuowén* (說文), it is the *wǔ lǚ* (屋梠) [the overhanging eaves], taking *mù* (木) as its radical and *lí* (󳌘) as its phonetic. The tradition of deriving it from the hand to form *jì* (𭪣) is incorrect.

"Méng" (甍) is pronounced as "mèng" (萠). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "méng" refers to the ridgepole of a house; the *Shuowen Jiezi* also defines it as the ridgepole of a house, composed of the radical "tile" (瓦) with "mèng" (夢) as a phonetic component abbreviated.

"Chuī" (榱) is pronounced as "lián shì zhuī" (連世追). The *Erya* states that the "jue" (角, rafters) are called "chuī"; Guo’s commentary identifies them as the eaves-rafters (*chuān*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as composed of the radical "wood" (木) with "shuāi" (衰) as a phonetic component.
*Kang-mi* (秔米): "Keng" is pronounced with the *geng* and *heng* finals. According to the *Shuowen*, it is a species of rice, composed of the radical "grain" (*禾*) and the phonetic "kang" (*亢*).
*Jili-tuolujuzha* (姞栗陀羅矩吒): "Qi" is pronounced with the *ji* final.

This is a term from the Sanskrit language. *Hugai* (戶隙): "Qing" is pronounced with the *ji* final. Gu Yewang states that "xi" (隙) refers to a hole or breach. According to the *Shuowen*, "xi" refers to the edge of a wall, composed of the radical "crack" (*𨸏*) and the phonetic "yu" (*𡭽*); the pronunciation of "yu" is the same as above.
Kuhaka (窶訶) Mountain—*Gū* (瞿) being pronounced with a reversed *jù* (矩)—is the name of a mountain in the Western Regions.

*Śahē* (鎩翮)—*shā* (鎩) being pronounced with a reversed *bā* (八)—refers to the maiming of a bird’s wings. In the *Huainanzi*, it says: “Flying birds have their wings maimed (*śāhē*), and running beasts have their feet paralyzed. Examining the phonology, *śā* refers to the injury of a bird’s feathers. In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is written as *shè* (從金殺聲), while in the *Chuán* (傳) it is written as *chù* (錣); the latter is an error.

"Yanxian" (巖巘): The lower character is pronounced *jian* (蹇). Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "A *yan* is a mountain formation resembling stacked rain-stoves (*zeng*). The *Shuowen* says it is composed of the radical "mountain" (*shan*) with the phonetic "xian" (*xian*).

"Goulan" (鈎闌): The upper character is pronounced *gouhou* (苟侯). Liu Huan’s commentary on the *Zhouyi* says: "To hook and pull it. The *Shuowen* defines it as "curved," composed of the radical "metal" (*jin*) with the phonetic "gou" (*gou*). The lower character is pronounced *dandan* (單). It is explained that a *lan* is a wooden screen used to block a gate; the transmitted text uses "lan" (欄) with the radical "wood" (*mu*), which is the name of a type of wood and not the original meaning.

*Juṇṭika*: The first character is pronounced *jun* (with the tone of *jun*) and the second is pronounced *chi* (with the tone of *ji*). This is explained within the transmission of the Sanskrit language itself. Volume 4, Part 4:

*Dàtáng Sānzàng Xuánzàng Fǎshī Běnzhuàn* (The Biography of the Tripitaka Master Xuánzàng of the Great Táng). Volume 4. *Kè*: Pronounced *kuò*, with the tone of *kuān*. According to the *Kǎoshēng* (Investigation of Sounds), it means "the gate is wide. It is composed of the radical *mén* (gate) and the phonetic *huó*. The character *fù* (transmission) is written with the radical *shé* (tongue); this is incorrect.

*Chái* (top tone, pronounced *chái*): According to the *Shuowen*, it belongs to the category of wolves, written with the radical *zhì* (beast) and the phonetic *cái*. (Bottom tone, pronounced *sì*): The *Shanhaijing* states that the *xī* lives east of the tomb of Shun, south of the Xiang River; it is shaped like an ox, dark blue-black in color. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* notes: "It has one horn, is azure-colored, and weighs a thousand *qīn*. The *Shuowen* says it is like a wild ox but green, representing its form; its head is identical to that of the *qín* and *yǎng*."

Regarding "black leopard" (hēibão): the commentary on the phonetics states that "leopard" is the name of a beast; it is composed of the radical "zhài" (豸) and the phonetic "sháo" (勺), with the suffix "quàn" (犬). To write it as "bǎo" (豹) is a vulgar character and incorrect. The pronunciation of "zhài" (豸) is "zhì" (雉). Regarding "jue-wan" (掘挽):
the first character is pronounced "qún-yù" (群欝) and the second is pronounced "wǎn" (晚).

*Chuí* (錘): Pronounced *zhì* (追) with a retroflex final. The commentary on sounds states it refers to an iron hammer. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* explains that it is composed of the radical for "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic *zhì* (追);

the lower part is pronounced *zì luàn* (子亂). *Dǔoqǔ* (斲取): The upper character is pronounced *zhú jué* (竹角). Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* glosses it as "carving and planing. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *dǔo* is also synonymous with *zhāo* (斫); it is composed of the radical for "axe" (*jīn*) and the phonetic *chē* (𠁁).

Regarding the character 鐫 (zuī): the upper radical is 子 (zǐ), and the phonetic component is 旋 (xuán) with the tone reversed; it is glossed as "to engrave" or "to carve stone. The lower part, read as gè (with the tone reversed), is transmitted in some texts as 𩀟 (zhào); this is a vulgar form resulting from a scribal error in transcription.
*Kajū-ukilā* (羯朱嗢祇羅) is the transliteration of the Sanskrit word *kañcukilā*. "Fen-xing" (芬馨) is the reading;

the *Shangshu* (Book of Documents) states, "The bright virtue alone is fragrant. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "fragrance" (*xiang*) refers to a scent that is perceived from afar. It is composed of the radical "fragrance" (*xiang*) and the phonetic element "ding" (*keng*), which is pronounced like *keng*.
*Taṃmalipti*: the first character is pronounced with the *shang* tone (dá hán fǎn), the middle with the *zhōng* tone (lín zhì fǎn), and the last with the *xià* tone (dīng lǐ fǎn);

*Pū* (upper radical *pu*, reversed *lù*). According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means "to strike. The *Cāngjié piān* states it refers to "striking the head. The *Shuōwén* defines it as being composed of the radical *shǒu* (hand) with the phonetic *pú*. The lower character is *jiān* (reversed *jiàn*). Duan Yucai’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states that *jiǎn* means "to exhaust" or "to annihilate. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lìjì* states that *jiǎn* is synonymous with "to kill. The *Shuōwén* further defines it as being composed of the radical *yǔ* (feather) with the phonetic *qián*. It may also be written as *jiàn*. To write it with the radical *dāo* (knife) as *jiǎn* is an error.

*Jingni* (鯨鯢): the first character is pronounced *shang* with the *qin* rhyme, and the second is pronounced *xi* with the *ji* rhyme. In the *Zuozhuan*, it says "he took its *jingni*"; Du Yu’s commentary states these are large fish. Xu Shen’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* says, "The *jing* is the king of fish. Both the *Shuowen Jiezi* and [the *Erya*] derive them from the radical for "fish" (*yu*) and take *jing* and *er* as their phonetic components.

Regarding the characters *zhàng* (staff) and *yuè* (battle-axe): according to the *Sīmǎfǎ* (The Art of War by Sīmǎ), in the Zhou dynasty, the left hand held a yellow *xū* (halberd) and the right hand grasped a white *máo* (banner). The *Shuōwén* explains that *yùe* is a large battle-axe; its correct form is *yùe*, though it is often written as *yuè* with the "metal" radical (*jīn*) and used interchangeably.

the character is read as *mào bào* (毛報);

Regarding "xi" (吸): on the water, it is pronounced as *xīn* (歆) with a reversed radical; the *Mao Shi Jian* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Book of Poetry) states that "xi" means "to draw in. Zaogujuzha (漕矩吒) State; Mèngjiàn (瞢健) State—the latter being a name for a Western country; Xīmótuóluó (呬摩怛羅) State—the latter being a name for a country. (Note: "Zào" [漕] is pronounced with the upper tone;
"Mèng" [瞢] is pronounced as an inverted rhyme of "mò" [墨] and "bēng" [崩]; "Xīn" [馨] is an inverted rhyme of "xīn" [馨] and "yì" [異].)

*Mǎng* (pronounced *mǎng*, with the *bǎng* rhyme of the *Chuci*): In the *Chuci*, "the plants and trees are *mǎng-mǎng*" (*cǎomù mǎngmǎng*). Wang Yi’s commentary states that *mǎng-mǎng* means "flourishing. The *Guǎngyá* says *mǎng-mǎng* means "luxuriant. The *Shuowén* explains it as the name for the large, excellent grass used for chasing rabbits in Nanchang; it depicts the grass within the character and uses *mǎng* (茻) as a phonetic adjunct. The transmission of this character as *xīn* (𣾘), written with the water radical, signifying the appearance of distant waters, is incorrect.

*Jiāo*: The phonetic component is *guó* (官活反); the *Shuowen* defines it as "clamorous speech," formed with the radical for the ear and the phonetic *qí* (𠯑). It is transmitted as *kuò* (聒), which is a vulgar character. *Jù*: The phonetic component is *táo* (󱽏坑岳反).

Gù Yěwáng states that the skin of all things is called *táo*. In character books, it is written as *fú* (孚) or *fēn* (𣪊). The *Shuowen* records it as *fēn* (𣪊), formed with the radical for the egg (*luǎn*) and the phonetic *fēn* (𣪊).
*Kie-pan-t'o* (朅盤陀) is the name of a country;
*wu-zhui* (烏餟) is the Indic term for a mountain peak (*śṛṅga*).
The character *yā* (𭥦) is pronounced *gǎo* (各) and refers to a precipitous cliff. In Zuo Si’s "Wei Du Fu" (魏都賦), it describes the shape of a mountain; the pronunciation of *yā* (𭥦) is *wǔ-gǎn* (五敢).

*Shān* (pronounced with the *sà* and *gān* finals): This refers to the appearance of long, hanging hair. The commentary (*chuán*) writes it as *sān* (from the radical *cǎo*), which is a vulgar character and incorrect; it is also sometimes written as *shàn*. *Dí*: Pronounced with the *cè* and *gé* finals.

In the commentary on the *Mao Shi*, *dí* means "accumulation. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states that *dí* refers to a bed. The *Shuowen* writes it with the radical *zuò* and the phonetic *zé*; the commentary writes it with the radical *zhú* as *dì*, which is an error. It is also sometimes written as *dàn*.

The character *duàn* (斷) in "the fasting group’s chaotic reversal of the case" (*duànshí tuánluàn fǎn'àn*) means to sever or cut off; it is pronounced *duàn*. The variant *duàn* (叚) is a person's surname; its original meaning is entirely different [from the sense of severing]. Regarding *còulǐ* (腠理): the upper character is pronounced *còu* (湊);

Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Yílǐ* states that *còu* refers to the skin and its texture (*fūlǐ*). Whether ancient or modern, the correct orthography and meaning are the same: it is composed of the radical *ròu* (肉) with the phonetic *zòu* (奏).

Regarding the striking of the *gandi*: although the sound produced by its repeated striking is phonetically correct, the character itself is properly written as 擊 (jī). To strike means to beat. The traditional transmission of this character using the radical for "silk" (*糸*) to form 繫 (xì) is incorrect; that is fundamentally the character for "binding. Thus, the original meaning is distorted.

"Qiǎorán" (愀然)—the character "qiǎo" is pronounced with a sevenfold retroflex turn according to the dictionary; it means "to be displeased," consisting of the radical "heart" (心) and the phonetic "qiū" (秋).
"Zhàn" (𥿳)—the character "zhàn" is pronounced with a *yan* (延) retroflex turn; the transmitted text writes this as "zhàn" (氈), which is a vulgar character.
*Jiǎ* (pronounced *jiān* with the *kǎo* and *shēng* initials): This is black jade; it is correctly written as *jiǎ*, following the "jade" radical (*yù*). *Yī* is a vulgar character and is incorrect.
*Bójiāyí* City: *pén* with the *mò* initial.

*Shàn* (鄯) at Jù and Mò: The first character is pronounced *shàn*, the middle is pronounced *qīlù* (反), and the last is pronounced *mànbō* (反). These are Sanskrit terms.

Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states that *chā* means "to block. Examining its phonetic, it refers to clearing the road ahead for a carriage. The *Shuowen Jiezi* also defines it as "to block," composed of the radical *chuò* (辵) with the phonetic *liè* (列).
*Qiùbù* (a single step): "To look up from a single step. According to the *Fānyán*, one half-step is called a *qiù*. In the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical 足 with the phonetic 圭.

the lower character is pronounced *huì*. *Tídèng* (ladders and steps): Pronounced *dēng*. According to the text, *tídèng* should properly be written with the character 𨸏 as 隥; the current transmission using 足 as 蹬 is a vulgar form.

The pronunciation of "shàn" (繕) is "shàn" (上音善). In the Du Commentary on the *Zuozhuan*, it means "to repair"; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "shàn" means "to patch," being composed of the radical "silk" (糸) with the phonetic "shàn" (善).

The *luányú* (imperial carriage) is so called because its bells are at the tips [of the poles]; according to the ritual protocols of the *Zhou Lǐ*, the movement of the carriage is regulated by the *luán* and *huó* bells. Zheng’s commentary states that these are all made of metal as bells; the *Shuowén* explains that the character is formed with "metal" (*jīn*) and "lán" (*làn*) as the phonetic component.
*Pán-mù* (蟠木) means "coiled tree"; it refers to the *pán-pí* (蟠枇) and *qiè* (󲵑) trees of the Eastern Sea.

*Hǔ* (楛) [pronounced with the initial *hú* and the final rhyme *gǔ*]—the commentary on the *Shàngshū* by Kǒng [Zhǐguǐ] states that the wood of the *hǔ* is suitable for arrow shafts; according to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "bitter" (*kǔ*).

*Ku* (pronounced *kǒu*, with the initial *gū*): In the *Book of Zhou*, it says "carving wood to make a boat. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *ku* means "to split," written with the radical 刀 and the phonetic 夸.

*Yin* (pronounced *fāng yú shàng zhēn*): In the commentary on the *Book of Shangshu* by Confucius, it means "to block up"; Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan* also identifies it as an earthen mound. Regarding the correct orthography for this character across ancient and modern times, it is written with the radical 土 and the phonetic 垔; it is also sometimes written as this [variant], with the same pronunciation *shàng tóng*.
Lè-yòu (the sound of "yòu" is as in yòu).
Měng-sì (the first character is pronounced měng; the second is pronounced sì).

Wěi-jìn (the character jìn has the phonetic value of qín-rèn); according to the *Cāngjiépiān*, "jìn" refers to wealth and goods; according to the *Shuowén*, it means "to present gifts," written with the radical 貝 (bèi) and the phonetic 賝 (pronounced the same as above).

"Jìngmì (靜謐)": "Mì" is pronounced *bì* according to the *Yǐnyá*; the *Shuōwén* explains "mì" as "tranquil. It is composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic "qí" (pronounced the same as above).

"Qiūzhōng (秋螽)": "Zhōng" is pronounced *zhòu* or *róng*. The *Kǎoshēng* states that "zhōng" refers to the name of an insect, also written as "zhù. The *Shuōwén* also identifies it as a locust, composed of the radical "cáo" (pronounced *kūn*) and the phonetic "dōng."

*Nǎng* (曩): In the *Erya*, "nǎng" means "long ago. Regarding its phonetic analysis, it is derived from the radical "sun" (日) with the phonetic element "xiāng" (襄). *Xuěxiù* (雪岫): Pronounced *xiù*. *Bōtuó* (坡陀): The first character, *pō*, is pronounced with the initial *pò*.

According to its phonetic analysis, it refers to a "sloping path" (*bǎn*). It is also written as *bēi*, *ě*, *ě*, or *jì*; it describes a slanted or uneven appearance. In the *Erya*, it is said that what is "pō" is a "bǎn. In the *Shuowen*, it is derived from the radical "earth" (土) with the phonetic element "pí" (皮). The second character, *tuó* (馱), is pronounced *hé*.
*Maòu* (pronounced *mòu*): According to the *Shiji*, it means "length. The *Shuowen* states that the term for north-south is *maòu* and the term for east-west is *guǎng*.

It is formed from the radical *yī* (clothing) with the phonetic *móu*. *Kuáfù* (pronounced *kuá fú*): According to the *Liezi*, Kuafu was skilled at running and could race against the sun; the place where he died transformed into the Deng Forest (*Dènglín*).

*Wei*: (Pronounced *shàng wēi*, with *huí* as the reversed component; in the *Cāngjié piān*, it means "to stop. In the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical 犬 [dog] and the phonetic 畏. *Chénjuàn*: (The upper character *chén* is pronounced *shì rén*;

according to the *Wénzìdiǎn*, *chén* refers to the "ultimate realm" (*zhì yǔ*). The Purple Palace (*Zǐchén*) was the residence of the Son of Heaven; it is composed of the radical 宀 [roof, sound *mián*] and the phonetic 辰. *Juàn*: (In the *Shàngshū*, "The August Heaven bestowed its mandate," Kǒng's commentary states that *juàn* means "to look upon. In the *Shuōwén*, it means "to look back. It is composed of the radical 目 [eye] and the phonetic 睠, which is pronounced *juàn*. The version in the *Chuán* [Commentary] that uses 睠 is an error.)

*Shēngxuǎn* (升鉉): *húquǎn* (胡犬). In the *Zhou Lǐ*, *xuǎn* refers to the handle of a cauldron; the *Shuowén* states that the handle of a cauldron is called *xuǎn*, following the phonetic *xuán* (玄) with the radical for metal (*金*).
*Huàitíng* (槐庭): *shàng huàiguī* (上壞乖). A name for a type of tree.

Regarding "yōngxī" (癰熈): the first character, "yōng" (癰), is pronounced with the *gōng* rhyme; according to the commentary, it was originally written as "yōng" (噰) from the mouth radical, but the character "xī" (熈) is an error. It correctly uses the "yǎn" (广) radical and is also written as "yōng" (雍).

Regarding "jiāofēng" (澆風): the first character is pronounced with the *jiǎo yáo* rhymes; the *Wenzi Dianshuō* (文字典說) states that "jiāo" (澆) means frivolous and insubstantial, consisting of the water radical and the phonetic "yáo" (堯).

"Huìfú" (卉服): The first character, "huì," is pronounced as guì (貴) with the *shàng* (上) tone. Confucius’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states that "huìfú" means "grass clothing. The *Shuowén Jiězì* defines it as the general name for grasses, composed of three "cǎo" (屮) radicals.

"Jīsǎng" (稽顙): The second character, "sǎng," is pronounced as lǎng (朗) with the *xián* (咸) tone. The *Fānyǔ* states that "sǎng" refers to the forehead; the *Shuowén Jiězì* explains it as being composed of the "yè" (頁) radical with "sāng" (桑) as its phonetic component.

*Yí* (邸): Pronounced *dǐ* (仾禮反). According to the *Cāngjié piān*, it means "dwelling"; according to the *Shuōwén*, it is the residence of subordinate states, composed of the radical *yì* (邑) with the phonetic *dǐ* (氐).

*Xiǎnyǔn* (玁狁): The upper character is pronounced *xiǎn* (音險) and the lower *yǔn* (音允). The *Máoshī chuán* identifies them as Northern Di tribes. According to the *Kǎoshēng* and *Chèyùn*, the correct form is *xiǎnyǔn* (玁狁); the *chuán* uses *xiànyǔn* (獫) with the radical *quǎn* (犬), which is a vulgar variation used interchangeably.
Fēnghào: the first character is pronounced fēng (as in 豐) and the second hào (as in 浩). Míngdí:
the second character is pronounced dīnglì (as in 丁歷). Gāolì:
the second character is pronounced lí (as in 黎).
*Ban die* (the first character pronounced *die*, the second *lang* with the initial *l-*, the final *dang* reversed, followed by *bei* with the final *gai* reversed).

*Zhubi* (the first character pronounced *bin* with the final *mi* reversed; Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that *bi* means to stop those passing to clear the road; according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "foot" and the phonetic "bi").

Regarding "kai" (凱) in *shàngkāi*: it is the opposite of "fǎn" (反). It signifies the joy of returning from a military expedition; it is a correct character from ancient times to the present. "Kǎi" means great; it is composed of "jǐ" (几) as the radical and "qǐ" (豈) as the phonetic, or it is written as this "qǐ".

Regarding "fú" (俘) in *fúwú*: Duan’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "fú" refers to prisoners taken in war. The *Shuowen* says it is composed of "rén" (人) as the radical and "fú" (孚) as the phonetic. Regarding "huī" (䤋) in *huīhuò*: Duan’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "huī" is used for cutting off the ears [of captives]. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* maintains that the correct form is "niè" (聝), composed of "ěr" (耳); the form "huī" (䤋) found in the *Zhuan* (commentaries) with "qiū" (酋) as its component is a vulgar character.

Yingjue (熒爝): "Zi" (子) is pronounced as "yue" (躍). Lü Buwei said: "Tang obtained Yi Yin at the 'jue' (爝) [of his body]. "Zhi" (之) is pronounced as "yi" (亦). "Da-xia" (大廈): "Xia" (廈) is pronounced as "xia" (下).

Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states that the gate called "xia" has no distinct shape; it is wide on the sides and low. The dictionary *Wenzi Dianshuo* explains that the character is composed of the radical "guǎng" (广) with "xià" (夏) as its phonetic.

*Tíng* (upper tone *tīng*, level tone; lower tone *róng*, with the *huí* rhyme) and *yìng* (with the *kǎo* rhyme) both describe the appearance of small waters. In Yang Xiong’s *Gān'è Fù*, it appears as *yìng*; the commentary uses the two characters *tíng* and *xíng*, which are errors.

Regarding the characters for Yǎn (兖), Xiāng (相), Jīng (荊), and Yáng (楊): the character for Yǎn State (兖州) does not take the "water" radical (氵); the version currently transmitted with this radical is incorrect.

Regarding the character for Zuò (作) in the phrase "upper storehouse" (上藏): it is transmitted as "from speech" (從曰), but the reading *zuò* (昨) is correct; the transmission of it as *záo* (鑿) is an error in transcription.

"Broken tiles and debris" (wálì língdī): the first character is pronounced fǎn. Volume Seven. The Seventh Scroll: A Biography of the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. "Track" (guǐzhú): the first character is pronounced jū (with the rhyme of wěi), and the second is pronounced chónglù (with the rhyme of zhòng). According to the *Shēngyùn*, the correct form is *zhú*; the version in the *Biography* (chuán) as *chù* is a vulgar character.
*Liǎnrèn* (斂衽): The pronunciation is *rèn*. The dictionary explains that in the *Qūlǐ* (曲禮), "holding the hem" (*zhí rèn*) refers to the lower garment;

it follows the radical *yī* (衣) and has the phonetic *rén* (壬). *Jīnkuì* (金匱): Pronounced *qiú guì* (求貴). Wáng’s commentary on the *Chūsī* (楚辭) states that *kuì* means a casket. The *Shuōwén* (說文) takes *fāng* (方) as its phonetic and *guì* (貴) as the sound component.

The upper tone of "diàn" (甸) is pronounced *diàn*. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that "diàn" means "to cultivate" (*zhì*). Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhou Li* says that "diàn" is synonymous with "tián" (field). Kong’s commentary on the *Shang Shu* states that "diàn" refers to the area five hundred *li* from each side of the royal city. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "tián" (田) and the phonetic component "bāo" (勹), where "bāo" is pronounced *máo* (茅). The sound [of the character] is derived from "máo."

The first character, *tiáo* (髫), is pronounced with the initial *tiáo* and the final *kǎo*. It refers to the practice of shaving a young child’s head while leaving two tufts on either side. The *Wenzi Dianshuō* (*Wenzi Dictionary*) states that *tiáo* means the hair of a small child, composed of the radical *biāo* (髟) with the phonetic *zhào* (召). The second character, *chén* (齔), has the pronunciation *chū jìn* (初靳反). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that at age eight for boys and seven for girls, they undergo *huǐchǐ* (the cutting of teeth). The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical *chǐ* (齒) with the phonetic *qī* (七).

*Chāo* (敫): Pronounced *zhī fǎn*. It means to spread out (*chén bù*). In his commentary on the *Tàixuánjīng*, Sòng Zhōng states it means "to extend. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "yǎo" (*yǎo shēng*). *Jiá* (浹): Pronounced *jiān yè fǎn*.

In his commentary on the *Zhōulǐ*, Zhèng states that the period from the day *jiǎ* to the day *guǐ* is called *jiá*. In the *Hànshī*, it is said to mean "to penetrate. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic "jiā" (*jiā shēng*).

*Beishi* (Stone Inscription): The *Shiming* (Explanation of Names) states that it is written to commemorate the merits of one’s lord and father, recording them upon the stone. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "stone" (*shí*) and the phonetic "humble" (*bēi*). *Jiùqiàn* (Reproach/Blame):

The upper character is pronounced *jiù* (as in "old"), and the lower is pronounced *qiānzhàn* (the *qiān* rhymes with "battle"). The *Guoya* (Broad Lexicon) defines it as "reproaching. The *Shuowen* says it means "to censure," composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic "send" (*qiǎn*).

"Zhe qi (陟屺)"—the pronunciation of *qi* is as in "qi. In the *Mao Shi* (Classic of Poetry), regarding the line "Ascending that qi," the *Zhuan* (Commentary) states: "A mountain with trees and grass is called *qi*; according to the *Shuowen*, one without trees or grass is called *qi*, formed from the radical 'mountain' and the phonetic 'yi'."

*Yìjiù* (益疚): "Jiù" is pronounced with the lower radical *jūn* (君) and the suffix *lìu* (霤). According to the *Erya*, it means illness (*jízhèng*). In the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *nà* (疒) and the phonetic *zhòu* (夂). *Dāolì* (忉利): The upper character is pronounced *dāo* (音刀).

According to the *Chunqiu Zhuan*, *Bān* (班) refers to Gongshu Ban, a master craftsman during the reign of Duke Ai of Lu. The lower character is pronounced *suì* (睡規). Zheng’s commentary on the *Shanhaijing* states that *Chuí* (倕) was the skilled artisan of Yao. In the *Gujin Zhengzi*, this character is written with the radical *rén* (人) and the phonetic *chuí* (垂).
*Zǐguì* (梓桂): the first character is pronounced *zīlǐ* (茲里) and the second is *guīruì* (圭銳). According to the commentary, both are names of trees. *Yùzhāng* (豫章):

the first character is pronounced *yújù* (余據) and the second is *zháoliáng* (灼良). According to the commentary, this is the name of a commandery (*yùzhāng jùn*). In current transmissions, all versions write it with the radical for wood as *yuànzhāng* (櫲樟).
*Zhè* (the upper radical is *zhǎo*, the lower radical is *lǘ*; both are names of trees). *Zhìzé* (*zé* pronounced as *chái* or *zǎi*);

Liu Huán says that *zé* is a term for the ultimate depth and obscurity. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical *hén* with the phonetic *zé*; the pronunciation of *hén* is *yí*.
*Jingcuì* (Essential Purity): Although its phonetic component is similar to that of *shuōwén*, "cuì" means not being mixed. It is composed of the radical "grain" (*mǐ*) with "zú" as the phonetic.

*Niǎozhuàn* (Bird Script): Pronounced *chuányuǎn*. The *Shuōwén* cites it as a script of the Zhou dynasty; the Grand Scribe Shǔfù of King Xuān of Zhou produced fifteen chapters of *Dàzhuàn* (Great Seal Script). It is composed of the radicals "bamboo" (*zhú*) and "tuan."

"Bā-shān" (八埏) [the character "shān" is pronounced zhān according to the *Yìyì* of the *Hànshū*; it refers to the boundaries of the earth; according to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "tǔ" with "yán" as its phonetic].

"Níng-liú" (凝旒) [the character "liú" is pronounced zhōu; the *Màoshī Jiàn* states it refers to the hanging tassels of a banner; the standard characters for ancient and modern times are 旒 and 垂; the jade *liú* is composed of the radical "yǎn" with "lù" as its phonetic; "lù" is pronounced tā-gǔ].
*Tán* (覃): In the *Mao Shī Zhuàn*, it means "extended" (*yán*) and also "long. The *Shuōwén* writes it as *sǎn* (󳌓), while the ancient form was *sǎn* (󳋯). *Mí* (覓) is pronounced *píng* (瓶). *Lí* (蠡):
Pronounced *luò* (魯) with the *guò* (過) tone; the preceding section has already explained this.

Regarding the character 暨 (qí jì), the Du Zhu commentary on the *Zhuàn* states that it means "to arrive at" (*zhì*). The *Erya* also defines it as "also" (*yì*) or "reaching" (*jí*). The *Zhuàn* writes it with the radical for water (*shuǐ*), as 洎 (jì). Xu Guang notes that this refers to meat broth (*ròuzhī*), which deviates from its original meaning.

The character *mào* (貌) is pronounced with the upper radical *yì* (詣) and the phonetic *jī* (雞). The *Pīcāng* states that it refers to the *zūn* (捘) of the *ní* (猊). Gu Yewáng identifies this as the lion (*shīzi*). In the *Gōngjīn zhèngzì*, it is written with the radical *zhài* (豸) and the phonetic *ér* (兒); alternatively, it is written as *ní* (猊) with the radical *quǎn* (犬).

*Xiān*: Pronounced *xiě yuán* (with the final *fǎn* reversed). In the *Erya*, it means "fluttering flight"; the *Shuowen Jiezi* also defines it as "small flight," composed of the radical 羽 (*yǔ*) with the phonetic 睘 (*huán*).

*Kuàijiàn* (lower character): Pronounced *qǐ jiǎn*. In the *Fangyan*, between the region east of the Guanzhong pass, in Chen and Chu, the word for a lock is called *jiàn*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as composed of the radical 金 (*jīn*) with the phonetic 建 (*jiàn*).

The term *tíháng* (梯航) is pronounced with the initial *dǐ* (低) and the final *gāng* (崗) reversed. Regarding the dialectal usage east of the Guanzhong region, a boat is called a *háng*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "boat" (*zhōu*) and the phonetic "kàng" (*kàng*).

*Kuàxuán* (跨懸) is pronounced with the initial *kuā* (誇) and the final *huà* (化). Gu Yewang states that it refers to lifting one's feet. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* says that "to *kuà*" means to pass over something. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *kuà* means to cross; it is composed of the radical "foot" (*zú*) and the phonetic "kuā" (*kuā*), where *kuā* is pronounced *kǔhuā*.

*Shūchén* (pronounced *chǐ lín fǎn*). According to the *Zìshū*, *chén* means "treasure. The *Erya* states that precious jade is called *chén*. It is also written as *jēn*. In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, it is composed of the radical "jade" (*yù*) and the phonetic "deep" (*shēn*), with "shěng" serving as the phonetic component.

Regarding "zhēnxiàn" (needle and thread): the first character is pronounced as *lín* (林) with the *fǎn* (反) [rhyme category] of *shān* (山), and the second is pronounced as *xiān* (仙) with the *liàn* (練) [rhyme category]. According to the *Kǎośēng* (考聲) and *Yuèyùn* (切韻), it is correctly written as *xiàn* (綫);

the form following the radical *mì* (糸) as *xiàn* (線) is a vulgar character. Regarding "dàoxí" (rice field): the second character is pronounced as *huìguī* (惠圭). Wang’s commentary on the *Chǔcí* (楚辭) states that *xí* (畦) is equivalent to *qū* (區, a plot). The *Shuōwén* (說文) defines it as fifty *mǔ* (畝) of a field; it is composed of the radical *tián* (田) with the phonetic *guī* (圭).

The character *jiàn* (荐), with the phonetic *qián* (前) and the radical *cǎo* (艹), is explained in the *Wenzi Dianshuō* as "repeated" (*chóng*). The lower part, *zè* (側) and *jīn* (巾), has the phonetic *cè* (側).

The character *dāo* (刀), with the phonetic *jù* (居) and the radical *jīn* (金), is defined in the *Cāngjiépiān* as the saw used for cutting objects; the *Shuowén* states it takes *jū* (居) as its phonetic.
*Chán* (慚) and *nǜ* (恧): "Nǜ" is a variant reading for "chán"; according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xin*) and the phonetic "er.

*Fǔlǚ* (俯僂): the upper character *fǔ* has the pronunciation *fǔ*; Gu Yewang states that *fǔ* refers to the head. According to the *Gōngjīn zhèngzì*, *fǔ* means "bent"; it is composed of the radical "person" (*rén*) and the phonetic *fǔ*. The lower character *lǚ* has the pronunciation *lǐ jǔ*; according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "crooked. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "person" and the phonetic *lóu*.

*Jùjí* (跼蹐): The upper character is pronounced *qú* (with the *yù* rhyme). Gu Yewang states that "to be cramped" (*jù*) means not being able to stretch out, which is also to be bent. In the *Gōngjīn zhèngzì*, this character follows the radical for feet (*zú*) with *jú* as its phonetic component. The lower character is pronounced *zī* (with the *yì* rhyme). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "a small step," following the radical for feet (*zú*) with *jī* (pronounced *jī*) as its phonetic component.

*Chen* (塵) and *du* (黷) share the same pronunciation as *lu* (祿). In the *Cangjie pian*, they mean "dirt" (*gou*). According to the *Shuowen jiezi*, "du" refers to the dirt from grasping and holding things; it is composed of the radical "black" (*hei*) with the phonetic "mai" (*mai*).

*Cuan* (纂) is pronounced as *zuan* (鑽) or *mao* (卯). Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that "cuan" means "to collect. It is composed of the phonetic "kao" (*kao*), which also implies "to collect. According to the *Shuowen jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "silk" (*mi*) with the phonetic "xiuguan" (*xi guan*); alternatively, it may be written with the radical "grass" (*cao*).

*Jìmù* (櫛沐): The first character, *jì*, is pronounced *zǔsè* (阻瑟) according to the *Líjì*. It refers to the hair being dried using an ivory comb (*xiàngjì*). "Comb" (*shū*) and "grooming brush" (*bǐ*) are general names for such tools;

they follow the radical for wood and the phonetic *jié*. *Kàn* (󲸚): Pronounced *kǎnhán* (坎含). In the commentary on the *Shàngshū*, Kǒng [Yǔ] states that *kàn* also means "to overcome. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "also meaning to overcome," following the radical for the weapon *guō* and the phonetic *jīn*. The *Zhuān* (傳) writes it with the character *kěn* (戡), which is pronounced *zhúshèn* (竹甚); this deviates from its original meaning.

Regarding "lúnhuàn" (輪奐): the second character is pronounced with the *huān* rhyme (as in *guàn*). It denotes the appearance of brilliant colors and patterns; according to the *Cāngjié piān*, it also denotes the appearance of literary compositions. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means "a dog" on one day; it is composed of "two" (*shuāng*) as the radical and "gǒng" and "xiòng" (abbreviated) as the phonetic components.

The character 礎 (chǔ) is pronounced with the initial *qiú* (葵營反) in the upper part and *lǚ* (初呂反) in the lower part; it refers to the stone base of a pillar in the *Chu Ci* (Songs of Chu). In the "Zhǔxì" (柱舄) chapter, it is called a *chǔ*. The "Guījīn" (古今正字) states that it is composed of the radical "stone" (石) and the phonetic "chu" (楚).
The character 銅 (tóng) is pronounced with the rhyme *tán-hé* (談合反); the transmission of this as "this yǎo" (此杳) is incorrect.

"Below the *xuán* (軒) are the *jiàn* (檻). The character *jiàn* is pronounced with the "xian" rhyme group (咸減反). Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that *jiàn* refers to a railing (*lán*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* also states that *jiàn* is a cage (*lóng*), formed with the radical "wood" and the phonetic "jian" (監). The *Chuan* (commentary) writes it as *yán* (轞) with the "che" (車) radical; however, since *yán* is merely the sound of a carriage, this deviates from the original meaning.

The character *hōng* (訇) is pronounced with the upper radical *hū* (呼) and the phonetic *hóng* (宏); its sound is like that of a great noise. According to the *Shuowen*, it takes the "speech" radical (*yán*) and the phonetic *yún* (勻) in abbreviated form. The lower part, *kàn* (看) and *gē* (割), refers to the sound of stones striking one another. The *Zizhi* states it is a loud sound. In the *Shuowen*, it takes the "stone" radical (*shí*) and the phonetic *hé* (盇). The version in the *Chuanshuo* that uses the "stone" radical with *wù* (𥕤) is incorrect.

In "jiāzhù" (夾紵), the second character is pronounced with the *chú* and *lǜ* rhymes. In the *Zhouli* (周禮), *zhù* refers to a type of hemp plant; Zheng Xuan’s commentary states that when it is white and coarse, it is called *zhù*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *qīng* (檾) has the phonetic value of *qǐng* (頃); it belongs to the category of fibers and is formed with the radical *xì* (糸) and the phonetic element *níng* (宁).

*Yi* (under the eaves): *wú* with the reverse sound *fǔ*. The *Shìmíng* states: "A large roof is called *lǚ*. The *Shuōwén* [explains it] as following the radical *yǎn* (廣) with the phonetic *wú*, which has no sound.

*Bù jiǎo*: *jiāo* with the reverse sound *yáo*. The *Pīcāng* states: "*Jiǎo* means bright. The *Shuōwén* [explains it] as following the radical *rì* (日) with the phonetic *jiǎo* (敫), which has the reverse sound *yáo*.

The characters for *bómò* (浡澥) are pronounced with the initial *pú* (蒲沒反) for the first and *xié mǎi* (諧買反) for the second. The *Wénzìdiǎn* (文字典) explains that *bómò* is the name of a sea; both characters follow the radical for wood (*mù*) and take *bèi* (孛) and *jiè* (解) as their phonetic components.

Regarding *kēnghuāng* (鏗鍧), the second character is pronounced with the rhyme *huā hóng* (花泓反). According to the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲), *kēnghuāng* refers to the sound of bells, and the correct form is indeed this character *huāng*. The traditional texts sometimes write it as *hóng* (宏) or *yíng* (鋐), but these characters are not found in the *Zìshū* (字書).

*Dǐhé* (詆訶): Pronounced *dī lǐ fǎn xǔ fǎn*. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to revile. In the *Fangyan*, *hé* (訶) also means "anger. Both are formed with the radical 言 (speech) and take 氐 (dǐ) as the phonetic component.

*Tǐng* (挺): Pronounced *chōnghé tíng dǐng fǎn*. Derived from the sound of 考 (kǎo). It means "prominent" or "extraordinary. The correct form is this *tǐng*; the version transmitted with the hand radical (手) as 󲊸 is incorrect.

Xūn-xūn (pronounced xún). Jiā-yóu (pronounced jiā in the first tone and yóu in the second): Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* states that *yóu* means "counsel"; according to the *Shuowén*, it may also be written as *yáo*.

Xié-háng (first tone: xiánjié; second tone: hánglàng): The *Màoshī Zhuàn* explains that flying upward is called *xié* and flying downward is called *háng*; according to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical 頁 with 吉 and 亢 as phonetic components.

Scroll Eight. The Original Biography of the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang Dynasty, Scroll Eight. Commentary: "Zhu" (pronounced yù) means "to annotate" according to the *Guǎngyǎ*; it means "to explain" according to the *Běicāng*. In the standard characters of past and present, this character follows the radical for speech (言) and the phonetic element "zhǔ" (主), and is identical in meaning to "zhù" (注).

Regarding "diàn yào" (電燿): in the *Guliang Zhuan*, it is glossed as "diàn tíng" (電霆); in the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is defined as "the violent flash of yin and yang," with the radical "rain" (雨) and the phonetic "shēn" (申), while the second character is "yáo xiào" (遙笑). To write it with the radical "fire" (火) as "yào" (燿) is incorrect; in the *Dazhuan* (大傳), it is written with the radical "foot" (足) as "yuè" (躍), with the pronunciation "yào. These original meanings are fundamentally divergent.
*Bān* (頒): Upper tone, *bǎn* (反) and *kǎo* (考) as the phonetic components; it means "to distribute. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of "head" (*yè*) and "part" (*fēn*) as the phonetic.

*Gǎo* (稾): Upper tone, *gāo* (高) and *lǎo* (老) as the phonetics. According to the *Yupian*, the correct character is *gǎo* (槀), which does not take "grass" (*cǎo*) as its radical. The transmission [of the text] uses "grass" (*cǎo*) to form *gǎo* (藁), which is a vulgar form; it is not accepted here.

*Jùjiàng* (pronounced *jù yǔ* in reverse). According to the *Yìnyì* (Explanations of Pronunciation and Meaning) section of the *Hànshū* (Book of Han), regarding the consumption of *tángxiàng jùjiàng* by the people of Nányuè: "The tree resembles the *gǔshù* (valuable tree); its fruit is like the fruit of the mulberry. When made into sauce, it is sour and delicious; the people of Shǔ consume it. Some write it with the radical for wood (*mù*) as *gǒu*, while others follow the character for wine (*yǒu*) as *qiú*; these are incorrect.

*Zhāozhè* (昭晣): The second character is read as *zhé* (下折列反). It refers to sound; *zhè* means luminous brilliance. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Zhāozhè" also means clarity; it is composed of the radical "sun" (*rì*) and the phonetic element "zhé.

*Hánzhàng* (函杖): The first character is read as *hé* (合甘反). The commentary on the *Mao Shi* states: "*Hán*" means to contain or accommodate. This is as in the *Liji*: "Between the mats, one places the staff (*xiánzhàng*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* describes it as a pictograph; its archaic form is written with the "bow" (*gōng*) radical. The phonetic value of "gōng" is *hàn*, which also serves as the phonetic for this character.
Upon reading this, one finds it pleasing to the ear. Regarding "From Huai, Guanghui returned": Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that Huai was located northeast of Mì County in Róng County.

Regarding "píwèn" (confusion/disorder): Zhong Zeng’s commentary on the *Liji* says "pí" means "to err. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains "pí" as meaning "erroneous," with the radical "silk" (糸) and the phonetic "bǐ. The lower character "wén" (聞) has the pronunciation "mùn" (慍). Kǒng Anghui’s commentary on the *Shangshu* identifies it as "luanwěn" (disorder). The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it with the radical "silk" (糸) and the phonetic "wén" (文); the version in the [Zuozhuan] that uses "nài" (柰) from the "wood" (木) radical is not the original meaning.
*Yuánqióng* (Round Vault): *qiū* (hill) and *gōng* (bow) are reversed; according to the *Erya*, *qióngcāng* (round azure) refers to the Great Heaven (*tiān*) or the "Great" (*dà*).

The *Shuowen* states it is composed of the radical *xué* (cave) and the phonetic *gōng*. *Hànhàn* (Vast and Expansive): *hào* (upper) is pronounced *háo gào*; *hàn* (lower) is pronounced *hán gàn*. Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* says: "Vast and expansive means grand and flourishing. The *Shuowen* states both are composed of the radical *shuǐ* (water) with *gào* and *gàn* as their respective phonetics.
*Yīngchán* (縈纏): the first character is pronounced *ēi* (恚) with the *yíng* rhyme; the second is pronounced *zhí-lián* (直連). *Xíshǔ* (鼷鼠):
the first character is pronounced *xì* (系) with the *jī* rhyme; this has already been explained in the preceding text.

*Kūnláng* (崑閬): the second character is pronounced *jí-dàng* (即蕩). According to the *Guǎngyá*, Mount Kūnlún has three peaks named Lángfēng (閬風), Bǎnxuānpǔ (阪懸圃), and Xuánpǔ (懸圃). According to the *Shuōwén*, it means a high gate, formed from the radical "gate" (*mén*) with the phonetic element "liáng" (*liáng shēng*).

*Zhūmóu*: the first character is pronounced *zhū* (with the *qū* rhyme) and the second is pronounced *mòhòu*. According to the *Erya*, the spider is the *zhūmóu*. In the *Fangyan*, it is noted that in the regions between Qin and Jin, the spider is called *móu*; this is the same as *móu*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that both characters are composed of the "insect" radical (*chóng*).

Wāng (烏黃反, wū huáng fǎn). Mō (摸) and kāi (揩): the former is read as 莫蒲反 (mò pú fǎn), the latter as 口騃反 (kǒu ái fǎn). Jìnshèn (搢紳): the former is read as 津燼反 (jīn jìng fǎn). This refers to the passage in the *Líjì* (Book of Rites):

"The *duānbì* [square-cut cap] and the *shèn* [sash], with the *hù* [tablet] inserted. Zhèng’s commentary states that *jìn* means "to insert. The *Shuōwén* explains it as composed of the radical 手 (hand) and the phonetic 晉 (jìn). The latter character, shèn (紳): the reading is 失真反 (zhī shēn fǎn). Kǒng’s commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* states that the *shèn* is the large sash (*dà dài*). The *Guǎngyá* states that the *shèn* is a binding. The *Shuōwén* explains it as composed of the radical 糸 (silk) and the phonetic 申 (shēn).
Regarding the character *xi* (檄): its name is explained as "to incite" (*jī*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mu*) and the phonetic "jiao" (*jiāo*, read as *yáo*).

The character *lù* (𥅟, read as *mǎo*)—according to Gu Yewang—is the appearance of upright and straightforward speech; in the *Gujin Zhengzi*, it is also "to warn. It may also be written as *è* (㖾) or as *miè* (㦍), which consists of the radical "speech" (*yan*) and the phonetic "è."

*Kunkun* (悃悃): The character *kun* is pronounced *kuan* (with the rhyme of *yuan*). Wang’s commentary on the *Chuci* states: "Kunkun means a will that is pure and singular. The *Guangya* states: "Kun also means ultimate sincerity. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical *xin* (heart) with *kun* as its phonetic.

*Feifei* (婓婓): The character *fei* is pronounced *fu*. The *Wenzi Dian* explains: "Feifei describes the appearance of coming and going. It is composed of the radical *nü* (woman) with *fei* as its phonetic.

Regarding *liánbiāo* (連鑣): the lower character is pronounced *máobiǎn* (表苗反). The phonetic examination shows it should correctly be written as *cìfēi* (此鏕). The commentary follows the character *mǎ* (馬) and writes it as *yōu* (䮽), which is an incorrect vulgar form. Regarding *quántí* (筌蹏): the upper character is pronounced *qīyuán* (七緣反). Gu Yewang states that it is a bamboo fish-trap.

The *Shuowen* takes *zhú* (竹) as the radical and *quán* (全) as the phonetic. The commentary follows the character *cǎo* (草) and writes it as *tuán* (荃), which is a vulgar form. The lower character is pronounced *dìlí* (弟黎反). Gu Yewang states that it is the tool used for catching rabbits. The *Shuowen* takes *zú* (足) as the radical and *tí* (虒, with the pronunciation *tí*) as the phonetic. The commentary writes it as *tí* (蹄), which is a vulgar form.

*Hùn* (壺): The character *hùn* is pronounced *kūn-gǔn-fǎn*. In the *Erya*, it refers to the alleys within a palace; Zheng’s commentary states that an alley (*xiàng*) is a path between dwellings, and the *Shuowen Jiezi* also defines it as a path within a palace. *Yà* (亞) represents the image of the corridors and pathways of an official compound; the upper part is the shape of the walls, and the lower part is pronounced *shǒu-ào-fǎn*. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states it is the hidden and secluded place within a room. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical *miào* (冂); the phonetic component *lǐ* (𠬪) is pronounced *jū-liù-fǎn*, and the sound of *xiàng* (巷) is the same as *xiàng* (巷).

The character *fei* (悱) is pronounced *fei* (妃尾反).
