According to the *Gujin zhengzi*, this character follows the radical for "eye" (*mù*) and takes *yú* as its phonetic.

Emperor Yang (the character is pronounced *liàng* with the radical for "sheep" [羊] and the phonetic for "opposite" [反]; the *Fùdì Shìfǎ* states: "To defy Heaven and oppress the people is called *Yáng*; to be fond of internal pleasures and neglect government is called *Yáng*").
The character *biāo* (pronounced *yáo* with the radical for "man" [正] and the phonetic for "far" [遙]) refers to the first star at the tip of the handle of the Big Dipper (*Beidǒu*).

The character 鼇 (pǎo) [with the phonetic *gāo* reversed] is explained in the *Shēngyuán* as a large tortoise. The version in the *Lùn* uses the character 鰲, which is a vulgar form and should not be used.
Regarding the character 刊 (kān), the commentary by Du on the *Zuǒzhuan* states it means "to remove"; the *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical 刀 with the phonetic *gān*.

*Chǎn* (剗): On the sea. [Pronunciation: *chá jiǎn* (察簡). The *Guǎnyá* states that it means "to shave" or "to pare. In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, it is composed of the radical *dāo* (刀) and the phonetic *jiǎn* (戔).

*Màn* (縵): On the eyelid. [Pronunciation: *mán pān* (蠻攀). The *Kǎoshēng* states that it means "slack" or "relaxed. It is sometimes written as *màn* (嫚), but this is incorrect; it should be composed of the radical *mù* (目) and the character *màn* (慢). *Xià* (下): [Pronunciation: *jiàn yǎn* (劍奄).

*Báobó* (咆勃): The upper character *báo* is pronounced with the *máo* rhyme-group (a retroflex *-p*). The *Guǎngyǎ* states that it means "to roar. The *Shuowén* defines it as "to howl," composed of the radical *kǒu* (mouth) and the phonetic *bāo*. The lower character *bó* is pronounced with the *méi* rhyme-group. Gù Yěwáng states that it means "intense and flourishing. The *Cāngjiépiān* states it means "sudden and intense. In the *Jīngūnzhèngzì*, it is composed of the radical *lì* (strength) and the phonetic *bèi*.
*Dānmiǎn* (耽湎): the first character is pronounced *dǎn* (with the initial *chǎn* as a variant), and the second is pronounced *miǎn* (with the initial *biǎn* as a variant).

*Jíqū* (蝍蛆): the first character is pronounced *zǐlì* (子力) and the second is pronounced *zǐyú* (子餘). The *Fāngyán* states that it is the *mǎxián* (earthworm). In the standard characters of both ancient and modern times, both characters follow the radical for insects (*虫*) and take *jí* (即) as their phonetic component.

*Chongzheng lu*, Volume One. Regarding the character *weiǒu* (韋㡚): "ǒu" is pronounced like *gǒu* (狗). The *Shiming* (*Explanation of Names*) states: "ǒu refers to a single-layered garment that lacks a collar (*hú*). Lexicons define it as the upper part of a garment. Examining the term *weiǒu*, it is the leather clothing of the barbarians. In ancient and modern standard characters, it follows the radical for cloth (*jīn*) with the phonetic *gòu* (冓); it is also written as *guǒu* (褠) with the same phonetic *gòu*. The pronunciation of *gòu* is the same as *shàng* (上).

*Chuì-mù* (upper character pronounced *chāng* with the *ruì* rhyme; lower character pronounced *mù*). According to the commentary, *chuì-mù* refers to the felt tents of the frontier tribes, such as hair canopies and the like. *Bì-láo* (upper character pronounced *bìng* with the *xí* rhyme).

Wang Su’s commentary on the *Jiayu* states that *bì-láo* means prison. The *Jixùn* states it is a wooden enclosure outside the gate. Examining the phonetics, it follows the radical for wood (*muō*) and is not from the radical for earth (*tuō*); it is written as *bì*, a name for a prison. The common vulgar usage of the radical for person (*biàn*) to write it as *bèi* is an error. The *Shuowen* defines it as "a place for confining animals. It does not follow the abbreviated form of *bì* (stairs) as its phonetic component. In the *Lunyu*, it uses the radical for dog (*quǎn*) to write it as *bèi*; this is incorrect.

*Pú-jiè* (酺醵): The first character, *pú*, is pronounced with the initial *bù-hú* (meaning *bù*). The *Shiji* states that in the twenty-fifth year of the First Emperor, there was a great *pú* for five days throughout the realm. According to the Han laws, those who drink in groups of three or more without cause were fined four *liǎng* of gold; this present grant allows them to assemble and drink for five days. The second character, *jiè*, is pronounced with the initial *qú-nüè*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* says it means "pooling money to drink wine. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines *pú* as "the virtue of the King spread abroad; a great drinking of wine," following the radical for *yǒu* (wine) and the phonetic *fǔ*. *Jiè* means "to assemble for food and drink," following the radical for *yǒu* and the phonetic *qū*; it may also be written as *zuò*.

*Yù* (󱈜). Pronounced *xuán yuán fǎn*. Guo Pu states that *yù* is the name of a jade. The *Mu Tianzi Zhuan* says that among the treasures of Mount Chun there are *yù* pearls. Gu Yewang states that this refers to the pearl contained within the *yì* (𧉻) [a type of fish]. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "a beautiful woman," taking the radical *yù* and the phonetic *ruì*. The *Zhòuwén* form is written as *hè* (壑), and the ancient script (*gǔwén*) is written as *shēng* (󳂲). The lower character is pronounced *gāo fǎn*.

*Tianzhòu* (天授): the second character is pronounced *chóuyòu* (雔宥); the original text uses the character *wèi* (偽), which is a character from the Tianzào (天朝) [imperial] style and is unfit for practical use; it is therefore not adopted here. *Yù* (馭):
in the sense of governing a region, it is pronounced *yǔjù* (上魚據反); it is identical to this character *yù* (御).

"Tuīyī" (推揖): "Ān" (揞) is pronounced as "xí" (習) and "zhāngjiàn" (張戩). Yī means to raise one's hands in a formal gesture of respect to show mutual reverence; it is also written as "yì" (󳂻). The Lù edition reads "yì" (挹), which shares the same pronunciation but has a different meaning; here it refers to "weighing and adjusting" (斟酌).
"Not bright" (*bù jiǎo*) means the opposite of clarity.
2. Second fascicle. "Wisdom" (*zhì*) is pronounced *liàn* (with the *lián* and *shàn* finals).
"Vexation and redundancy" (*fán rǒng*): according to the *Shēnglèi*, "redundancy" (*rǒng*) refers to being scattered and miscellaneous; those who have no food are all called "redundant."

*Yōngxiǎo* (庸謏): "Xiǎo" is glossed by Zheng Xuan in his commentary on the *Liji* as meaning "small" (*xiǎo*). The *Gōngjīn zhèngzì* (古今正字) states that it is composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic "sǒu. *Jiǎowěi* (撟僞): The upper character, "jiǎo," is pronounced with the final *-xiǎo*.

Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* explains: "To employ deception and fraud for the sake of gain is 'jiǎo'. Gu Yewang says: "To falsely claim something is 'jiǎo'. Jia Dui says: "That which is not the law of the former kings is called 'jiǎo'. The *Chuci* says: "To employ this seductive charm to dwell broadly [is 'jiǎo']. The *Shuowen* defines it as "to usurp" (*shàn*), composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "qiáo. The editions recording it as "jiǎo" (from the radical "arrow" [*shì*]) have the same pronunciation but deviate from the original meaning.
"Guǐwàng" (詭妄) is read as *guī* (上) and *wěi* (歸委) in reverse;

it means "to fabricate. The character *zhòng* (重) is pronounced *jiān* (堅顯); the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that the skin rises up in a hollow like a tuft of grass (*cán*). The standard characters for this in ancient and modern times are *kē* (𩋨), *jī* (枅), or *tí* (䄯). The current edition records it as *niàn* (躎), which is an error.

"Jiū" (推鞠) is pronounced *jiǔ* (鳩) with the second tone; Zhang Jian’s commentary on sounds states that "ju" (*jù*) means to exhaustively investigate a criminal. It is correctly written as 󳁖, composed of the radicals for person (亻), bamboo (竹), and speech (言); it is also written as 諊 or 󳂧.

"Yú" (愚) and "guǎng" (獷)—the latter pronounced *gōng* (觥) with the third tone—the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "guǎng" means one who cannot be associated with. It is composed of the radical for dog (犬) and the phonetic element "guǎng" (廣).
*Qi* (齊): Pronounced *mèng* (麥) with a reversed *péng* (彭).
*Shèn* (昚): Pronounced *shàn* (上) and *chén* (臣) with a reversed *rèn* (刃); this is an ancient script form, now written as *shèn* (慎). *Lǐ* (𨡴):

Pronounced *shǐ* (使) with *yǒu* (酉) and *zhōu* (周) as finals; the *Mao Shi* says "the *lǐ* chariot has *luán* bells on its bit-ornaments," and the *Zhuàn* says "the *yǒu* is a light chariot," referring to a messenger in a single-wheeled carriage.
In the kingdom of Khotan (Yutian), the character for "field" (tian) is pronounced with the *lian* rhyme.

The pronunciation of "farewell" (jie) is like that of "decide" (jue). Regarding the character for "ghost" (gui), the *Zhouli* commentary by Zheng Xuan states: "The *mi* (so-called from its following people and things) refers to those who follow [the dead] as both persons and objects. It is said that the sacrifices to Heaven and Earth are called *baiwu* (hundred things), while the spirits of these things are called *mi*. The *Shanhaijing* states: "As for the nature of the *mi*, it has a human body with a black head. The *Shuowen Jiezi* correctly writes it as *mi* (pronounced *mei*), stating: "The essence of an aged object; it follows 'ghost' (*gui*) and has 'hair' (*mao*) and 'strokes' (*san*). Today it is also written as *mei* or *miao*."

Yú Huàn (魚豢): "huán" is pronounced with a retroflex *mǎn* (慢反). *Zènzèng* (噂𠴲): the first character is pronounced with a level tone *zūn* (尊) and the fourth tone *sǔn* (損); the second character is pronounced with a departing tone *tán* (談) and the entering tone *hé* (合). The commentary on the *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (毛詩傳) states: "*Zènzèng*, *zènzèng*: to speak to one another. The *Shuōwén* (說文) says it means "to converse in a group," both characters being composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) with *zūn* and *tà* as phonetic components. It is also written as *zēn* (僔), but the current recording [of the character] with the "foot" radical (*zú*) as "dūn" (蹲) or "tà" (踏) is incorrect.

3. Third Fascicle. [This fascicle is missing from the original manuscript; no phonetic glosses provided. 4. Fourth Fascicle. *Wěi* (煒). The upper character is pronounced as *wéi* (韋), and the lower character as *zhé* (輒). This is the archaic and standard form of the character. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Book of Poetry) states that it signifies a crimson appearance. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (Explaining Graphs and Analyzing Characters) states that it signifies a brilliant and flourishing appearance, composed of the radical "fire" (*huo*) with the phonetic element "wei" (*wéi*). The *Guinyan* (Broad Lexicon) states that it signifies the appearance of radiant light. The standard form of the character in both ancient and modern texts is composed of the radical "fire" with the phonetic element "xù" (󲘶). The pronunciation of *xù* is the same as above. The version recorded as *bì* (熚) is an error.

*Kūmìng* (刳命): The first character, *kū*, is pronounced with the initial *gū* and the final *fǎn*. Yě Wáng says it means "to hollow out its belly. The *Shuōwén* says it means "to split," composed of the radical *dāo* (knife) and the phonetic *kuā*. *Mǎngshé* (蟒蛇):
The first character, *mǎng*, is pronounced with the initial *huǎng* and the final *fǎn*.

*Luǎn*: Upper radical *lǚ*, lower radical *jiū* (read as *zhān* and *niàn*). The *Pīcāng* states: "It refers to a horse lying down in the dust. Zhāng Jiàn says: "It means a horse rolling about. In the *Gōnjīn zhèngzì*, it is composed of the "horse" radical with "zhǎn" as the phonetic.

Regarding the two characters for *chān* (襜), the *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that the garment which covers the front is called *chān*. The *Fang Yan* says that *chān* is called *ye* (掖); Guo Pu explains this as the area under the armpits of a garment. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "a garment covering the front," composed of the radical 衣 and the phonetic 詹. The version in the [commentary] uses 祲 (from the radical 示) with the pronunciation *jīn* (子㾗反), which lacks semantic meaning.

*Liǎobiǎo*: *bēiliǎo* (反). The *Guǎngyǎ* states that *biǎo* refers to the *mèi* (sleeve); the *Bīcāng* states it is the sleeve of a garment. In the "Correct Characters" of ancient and modern times, it is written with the radical 衣 (*yī*) and the phonetic 票 (*piào*).

Volume Twelve. Regarding the term *tōuǎi* (投󱨈): the character *ǎi* is pronounced with the *guī* (歸) and *wěi* (鮪) finals.
The Master Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shūjìng* states that it refers to a *kǔi* (匭), which is a casket. Such items are currently in existence, distinguished by their four directions.
Regarding "lā" (拉), Huan Xiu’s commentary on the *Gongyang zhuan* states that it means "to break. The *Shuowen jiezi* says it means "to snap," written with the radical 手 and the phonetic 立;

it is also written as 摺. Regarding "láng wǔ" (廊廡): the upper character is pronounced lánɡ and the lower is pronounced wú fǔ. The *Shiming* states that a large building is called a *wǔ*; the *Shuowen* defines it as the corridor surrounding a hall, written with the radical 广 and the phonetic 無.
*Kǔn* (悃): The first character is pronounced *shèn* (慎) with the true initial;

the second character is pronounced *yī* (衣) with the *qǐ* (蟣) rhyme. Regarding the term *kǔnkǎn* (悃款), Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that it is synonymous with "sincere intent" (*zhì dùn*). The *Guǎngyá* defines it as "intent. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic element "trouble" (*kùn*).

The character *pǐn* (品) is pronounced with the *guì* rhyme; the *Guǎngyá* states that *huì* (彙) means "categories" (*lèi*), as it refers to categories being drawn together. According to the *Wénzìdiǎnshuō*, it is composed of the radical *xiāo* (󳊘) and the phonetic *wèi* (胃) in abbreviated form; the sound of *xiāo* is pronounced with the *xī* rhyme.
"Dan" (慊) is pronounced with the initial *qian* (謙) and the final rhyme *dian* (簟); the *Kao Sheng* (考聲) states that "dan" means "to feel satisfied" (*qingqie*) and "to be sufficient.
"Sui" (眭) is pronounced with the initial *sui* (髓) and the final rhyme *ji* (寂); it is a surname.

Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* identifies it as a slip of bamboo or wood.
Gu Yewang states that it is what is used to transcribe records and document events.
The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as a document or tablet.
The character "shēng" (聲) in "zhújiān shēnglùn" (竹間聲論) is an error for "jiǎn" (蕳). The character below [the radical] is pronounced with the *qiāng* (鎗) and *zé* (責) finals.
The *Zhouli* states: "For feudal lords of the ninth rank, the mandate is inscribed upon a tablet."
Zheng Xuan says that this refers to writing the King’s commands on bamboo slips (*jian*).
Cai Yong’s *Duduan* states that *zhi* means bamboo slips;
if the text does not reach one hundred characters, it is not written on bamboo slips.
Their dimensions were two chi in length, with the shorter ones being half that size.

The next grade consisted of one long and one short tablet, both bound together at the top and bottom with characters inscribed in seal script (zhuànshū) recording the date; all appointments of feudal lords and dukes, as well as deaths or dismissals due to offense, were recorded entirely in large-character script (zhìshū).
The *Shuowen* explains that it is a "symbolic mandate" (*fuming*).
When the feudal lords advanced to receive it from the King, it was modeled after a bamboo slip, one long and one short, with two binding cords in between.
In archaic script, it is written as 𥬰, derived from the radical for "bamboo."

"Pì" (紕) is pronounced with the initial *p* and rhyme *i* (upper radical *pí*, lower *yòu*). The *Kǎoshēng* says it refers to coarse and thin silk. "Mí" (謬) is pronounced with the initial *m* and rhyme *yòu*; it means falsehood, deception, or error.

"Jū" (籧) is pronounced with the initial *jù* and rhyme *yú*. Zhāng Jiàn says it refers to the *jūhú* (a type of insincere flatterer who cannot look down). "Lú" (廬) is pronounced with the initial *lǚ* and rhyme *zhū*. The *Kǎoshēng* says it is a type of thatched hut; it means a temporary shelter or lodging.

The character *yì* (誼) is pronounced with the rhyme *ji* (冝). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states: “*Yì* refers to the appropriateness (*yí*) in regulating affairs. Wang Bi’s commentary on the *Zhouyi* states: “*Yì* is equivalent to principle (*lǐ*). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states: “It means goodness (*shàn*) and appropriateness (*yí*). "Dào-gāi" (道該): Jia Kui states that "gāi" means "to be fully equipped. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "speech" (言) with "hai" as its phonetic.
"Sī-jian" (斯鑑): The *Kao* states it means "clarity" or "illumination"; it is also written as "jian" (鑒).

"I venture to trace back to the original meaning. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "Sù (遡) means 'to face toward' (*xiàng*). The meanings of the correct characters for 'ancient' and 'modern' are the same. It follows the radical *chuò* (辵) and uses *shuò* (朔) as its phonetic; it may also be written with the radical *rén* (人) as *sù* (傃)."
"Jiǎndú" (簡牘) is pronounced *jiǎn dú* (鹿反). "Jùrán" (瞿然): the first character is read as *jù* (具遇反).

Gu Yewáng says it is the appearance of being startled and fearful; the *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (毛詩傳) says it is the appearance of having no constancy. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of "zhuī" (隹) and the phonetic "zhù" (䀠), where "zhù" is written with two eyes (*mù*) and means looking left and right. The current version of the commentary [reading it as] "jù" (懼) is an error.

*Dǒng* (pronounced with the *mèng* rhyme): The commentary on the sounds states it means "shame" or "despair. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *lěng*, stating it means "lack of clarity," composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "mèng.

*Zhài*: Pronounced *jié yǎn*. This character does not appear in any dictionaries or in the classics and histories; when inquiring among Daoists, it is traditionally said to be pronounced *jiǎn*, though its meaning remains unknown.

Regarding "yángquè" (楊榷): Xu Shuchong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states that "yángquè" means "roughly summarized. In the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radicals for "wood" (木) and "crane" (鶴), with the pronunciation being the same as above.
Regarding "jiānxiāng" (縑緗): the upper character is pronounced jiáxián, and the lower character is pronounced xiǎngyáng.

Dìkù (帝嚳) [the character *kù* is pronounced with the initial *k-*, retroflex *u*, and final *-r*]: the father of Yao. Huángfǔ Mí (皇甫謐) [the character *mí* is pronounced with the initial *m-* and final *-r*]: a high-minded gentleman of the Jin dynasty. The character 󲔢 (jiāo): 1. The upper radical is 垂 (*chuí*, pronounced with the final *-l*);

the Master Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* says it means "pure" (*cuì*). The *Guǎngyá* says it means "thick" (*hòu*). The *Shuowén* says it means "not diluted" (*bù jiāo*), following the phonetic component 󲈅 (*ēn*), which has the same pronunciation as above. The *Lúntǐng* uses the character 純 (*chún*), which has the same pronunciation but a different meaning; this is incorrect. 2. The lower part is 晈 (*jiǎo*, pronounced with the final *-r*); the *Kǎoshēng* says it means "thin and diluted" (*jiāo bó*).

*Xián* (贙): The upper radical is *xuán* (玄), pronounced with the *qiǎn* (犬) rhyme. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "It originates from the Western Sea; those in the kingdom of Da Qin (大秦) raise it. It resembles a dog and possesses great strength. The *Shuowen* distinguishes it as being composed of *yán* (虤)—meaning mutual contention—and *bèi* (貝). *Yán* is pronounced with the *wǔ xián* (五閑) rhyme. The version in the *Lunheng* (論) uses *gū* (𧷠), which is an error. The lower radical is *cí* (辭), pronounced with the *sì* (姊) rhyme. The *Shanhaijing* states: "The *xi* (兕) is located to the south of the Ming Water at the eastern site of Shun’s burial. Its appearance is like an ox, dark blue-black in color. Guo Pu says: "It has one horn and is azure-colored; its weight is several *jin* (斤). The *Shuowen* says: "It is like a wild ox but green; it is a pictographic character. Its head is identical to that of the bird *lí* (离). The original text of the *Lunheng* uses the character *xiān* (先).
The character for "guǐ" (鬼) is pronounced with the initial *chì* (勅知反) and the final rhyme *kǎo* (考); it refers to *chīmèi* (魑魅), mountain spirits.

The character for "pài" (派) has the initial *pā* (葩瓦反); the *Shuowen* states that "pài" means the branching of water, composed of the radical "water" (水) and the phonetic element "lǚ" (𠂢), where "lǚ" is pronounced *pǔmài* (普賣反). The *Lun* (論) uses "pái" (沠), which is a vulgar and erroneous character.
Fuxi (pronounced xiāo jiǎo fǎn) was an ancient sovereign; he is also called "Nest-Dweller" (*Cháo-jū*).
Suìrén (pronounced suì rén) was also an ancient sovereign; he first produced fire through friction to transform raw food into cooked food.

*Tāo* (韜): The upper character is pronounced *dǎo* (刀) with the variant *fǎn* (反). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that *tāo* means "to store away. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of *wéi* (韋) and has *yǎo* (舀) as its phonetic.

*Zài* (再): Pronounced *tóng* (同) with the variant *lù* (鹿). Jia Kui says it means "repeatedly" (*dúguò* 媾). Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* says it refers to doing something repeatedly without propriety. According to the *Shuowen*, *dú* (黷) means "to grasp and hold"; it is composed of *hēi* (黑) and *mài* (賣), or alternatively written as *nuò* (嬻).

Zhíshí (摭實): The upper character, zhì, is pronounced zhèng and shí; the *Fānyán* states that it means "to gather. The *Shuōwén* writes it as tuò and defines it as "to abandon," formed with the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "stone" (石).

Pōxī (剖析): The upper character, pō, is pronounced pǔ and hòu; the lower character, xī, is pronounced xīng and yì. The *Shuōwén* defines "xī" as "to split wood" or "to divide," formed with the radical "wood" (木) and the phonetic "axe" (斤). The version in the *Lùn* (Treatise) written as 㭊 is incorrect.

"Chuang" (創): The first character is pronounced with the initial *chū* and the final *xiàng*. Jia Dui says it means "to begin. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "establishing laws and founding enterprises," composed of the radical "two blades" (*bing*) and the phonetic "ren" (*ren*). In the *Lunyu*, it is written as "chuang" (創), though the common usage is the character with the phonetic "ren," which is pronounced *chǔ liáng* (楚良).

The character 章 (zhāng) is pronounced with the *jiāo* (焦) and *xiào* (肖) finals; its meaning has already been explained. It is also written as 彰 (zhāng) in the *Biànzhènglùn* (Discourse on the Rectification of Truth).

The character 考 (kǎo) is pronounced with the *gē* (戹) final; the *Shuowén* states that it means "to examine facts. The character 覈 (hé) is pronounced with the *fū* (敷) and *zhē* (遮) finals; it refers to obtaining the reality of one's words, which is "verification" (*hé*).
*Zhī chàn* (之槧): *chàn* is pronounced with the *gǎn* rhyme. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Chàn" refers to a writing tablet (*dú*) or a block;

it is derived from the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "zhǎn. *Zhī gū* (之觚): *gū* is pronounced with the *hú* rhyme. Ma Rong’s commentary on the *Lunyu* states: "The *gū* is a ritual vessel (*lìqì*) with a capacity of two *shēng*. Examining the meaning of the text, it refers to the category of writing implements—specifically those for handling the tablet and applying the brush—as in the expression "to handle the *gū* and dip the pen. It is also written as *zō* (㧓).

Regarding the title of the divination slip (qián): it is read as *yán* (the opposite of *yán*) and *zhāng* (as in *zhānjiàn*). It refers to a small note (*xiǎojiǎn*). In antiquity, writing on a bamboo slip to report a matter was called a *qián*; today, the official title *diǎnshàng* (Director of Memorials) derives from this practice of reporting matters. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "to verify a person" is written with the radical for bamboo and the phonetic *xiàn*. The pronunciation of *xiàn* is *jiān*.

The character *jǐ* (𥷴) is pronounced with the upper radical *shàng* and the phonetic *liù*; its sound indicates "exhaustion. The character used in the *Lùn* (Treatise) is *jù* (鞫), which is a vulgar form.
The character *shuò* (鑠) is pronounced with the upper radical *shāng* and the phonetic *ruò*; the character used in the *Lùn* is *sháo* (爍), which loses the original meaning.

"On the tip of a snail's horn" (guǎhuā fǎn). *Zhuangzi* says: "There was a state on the left horn of a snail belonging to the Chushi clan, and a state on the right horn of a snail belonging to the Man clan; they frequently contended with one another for territory and fought, leaving tens of thousands of corpses, pursuing the defeated for fifteen days before returning. Gu Yewang states that this is the same as the *chíyú* (the slow-worm/snail). The *Shuowen* defines it as "a weak creature," written with the radical 虫 and the phonetic 咼.

*Mōngyì* (蒙翳): The first character is pronounced with the "mù péng" rhyme group; the second is pronounced with the "yī dǎo" rhyme group. This is a name for Heaven according to the Daoist school. *Liàng* (諒):

The first character is pronounced with the "liáng shàng" rhyme group. The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (Mao Poem Commentary) states that *liàng* means "trustworthy. It is called *liàng* because it is trusted by the multitude. According to the *Wénzì Diǎnshuō* (Dictionary of Characters and Explanations), it is composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic "jīng" (*jīng shēng*).
"Bian" (辯) is pronounced *you* with the *jiu* rhyme;

"ci" (詞) is pronounced *po* with the *pu* rhyme. The *Shuowen* states: "Poa" (*pa*) means flower; it is composed of the radical for grass and the phonetic *pang*. "Zhi" (之) is pronounced *xu* with the *ju* rhyme.

The *Guangya* states: "Xu" means cultivation and warmth. The *Shuowen* says it means to grow; one version says it is the appearance of a crimson color, and another says it means warm and lustrous; it is composed of the radical for fire and the phonetic *xu*.

"Autumnal gales must blow from afar. *Dàquè* (大噱) means "to laugh loudly"; the *Shuowen* states that it is written with the radical for the mouth and the phonetic *jù* (豦). *Jūgōng* (狙公) refers to one of the species of macaques;

according to the *Zhuangzi*, the Monkey Lord said to the monkeys, "How about three in the morning and four in the evening? The monkeys were all angry. He then said, "How about four in the morning and three in the evening? The monkeys were all pleased. The *Shuowen* writes this character with the radical for the dog and the phonetic *qiě* (且). The *Lunheng* also uses the character *jū*.

*Shi* (󳏠): The ancient pronunciation is *huái*. The *Guǎngyá* states that it means "to turn one's back" (*bèi*) or "oblique" (*xié*). The *Shuōwén* says it means "crooked" (*lì*). It is composed of *ér* and *běi*; the archaic form is *bié*. The phonetic component *shí* (𦫳) is pronounced *guàn*; the radical *chuān* (川) and *yǎn* (兗) follow. Gù Yěwáng states that *shí* means "uneven" (*chāpòu bùqí*). Mèng Kāng states it means "interlaced" (*jiāo*). The *Shuōwén* says it means "lying face-to-face" (*duìwò*). It is composed of *xī* and *dì* facing each other in opposition. *Xī* is pronounced *suī*; *dì* is pronounced *kuà*. Yang Xióng writes it as *cuī* (蹖).

Volume Two, *Zhengzhilun* (Treatise on Discerning the Correct), Middle Volume. [The character] *ji* (玑) has the upper radical *xi* (夕) and the lower radical *xi* (希). The *Book of Yu* (*Yushu*) states: "Using the *ji* and jade balance to align the seven celestial offices."

*Zhùjǐng* (駐景): *zhù* is pronounced as *jù fǎn* (具反). The *Cāngjié piān* states that *zhù* means "to stop. The *Shuōwén* says it means "to halt a horse," composed of the radical "horse" (*mǎ*) and the phonetic element "master" (*zhǔ*).
*Liǎn'ǎi* (斂靄): *ài* is pronounced as *āi gài fǎn* (哀蓋反).

Regarding "què" (firmness): Han Kangbo’s commentary on the *Zhouyi* states that "què" means firm. The correct orthography from ancient times to the present uses the radical "stone" (石) with the phonetic "hào" (寉). To write it as "lùn" (論) is an error.

*Wò* (upper radical *wān*, reversed *huó*): Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that it means "to turn. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it is composed of the radical *dǒu* with the phonetic *wò*. *Yīn* (upper radical *yú*, reversed *jīn*):

The *Fangyan* states that in the regions between Qi and Song, a cry so intense that no sound remains is called *yīn*; colloquially, this refers to being mute from sobbing. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it is composed of the radical *kǒu* with the phonetic *yīn*.

*Fāxiè* (發洩): *Guǎngyá* states that it means "to leak. The commentary on the *Máoshī* states it means "to emit. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical *shuǐ* (water) with the phonetic *yè*.

It is also written as *xiè*. *Lí* (醨): Pronounced *lǐ* in the vulgar dialect. *Guǎngyá* states that it means "thin wine. According to the *Shuowén*, it means "sour [wine]," composed of the radical *yǒu* (wine) with the phonetic *lí*.

Regarding "juzha" (狙詐): the initial radical is "ju" (七余反). The *Guoyu* states that "ju" refers to the macaque. The *Hanshu* speaks of deploying "the military arts of ju-zha. Gu Yewang says that "ju" means "to face toward," which refers to waiting in ambush. In the *Hanshu*, it takes the radical "dog" (犬) and is pronounced with the sound of "qie" (且).

Regarding "yuè-chuì" (月竁): Duan Zichun’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that "chuì" refers to the excavation made for a burial pit. Today in Nanyang, digging the ground is called "chuì. This is the correct character from ancient times; it is composed of the radical "cave" (穴) and the phonetic "cuì" (毳).

The character for "peduncle" (dì) is pronounced as dī (with the initial *d-*) according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*. It is explained as meaning "to hold" (*dāng*), composed of the radical "grass" (艹) with the phonetic component "buckle" (帶). Its middle tone is *fú* (扶), while the character for "lotus" (荷) has the lower tone *jù* (巨魚). Thus, "lián hé" refers to the lotus.

"Unfurled" (chū): according to the *Fǎnyǎ*, "chū" means to spread or to extend. In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, it is composed of the radical "hand" (shǒu) and the phonetic "lù. "Hé" (in *Hélánzhū*):
the first character is pronounced with the initial *hàn* and final *liè*; the second is pronounced with the initial *lǚ* and final *jū*.
*Jǐ* (賷): Pronounced *shàng jì* (上濟), meaning "to carry" (*chí*). In the *Gōngzuò* (工作) it is written as *zāi*. *Tíngléi* (雷霆):

Pronounced *shàng lú duī* (盧堆) and *zhèng* (正); below, pronounced *dìng* (定). The *Ěryǎ* states: "A swift thunder is called *tíng*. Guo Pu says: "It refers to the sudden and violent [aspect] of thunder. The *Cāngjiépiān* calls it *pīlì* (霹靂). The *Shuowén* says: "It is the lingering resonance of thunder; its 'líng líng' sound is that by which all things are brought forth. It is composed of the radical for rain (*yù*) with *tíng* as the phonetic.
The character *zhì* (之玷) is pronounced *diǎn*.
Regarding *līzhū* (驪珠), the first character is read with the *qùshēng* (departing tone) *zhī*; it refers to what is called the pearl of the black dragon (*lílóng zhū*).

*Cānròu* (參糅): the second character is read with the *jiù* rhyme; Zheng’s commentary on the *Yí Lǐ* states that *róu* means "mixed. The correct form is *chāo* (󲜛); the *Shuōwén* says it is composed of the radical *mǐ* (grain) and the phonetic *chǒu*.

*Kou* (摳): The initial sound is *kou* (溝). The *Liji* (Book of Rites) states: "With both hands, one gathers up the hem of the robe, keeping it one chi above the ground. Gu Yewang says: "This refers to lifting the front of the garment with the hand. The *Guypu* (廣疋) glosses it as "to raise. Regarding the character's form: the *Gujin Zhengzi* (古今正字) maintains that it follows the radical for "hand" (*shou*) with the phonetic element *qu* (區); it is incorrect to follow the *Lunheng* (論衡) and write it with the radical for "wood" (*mu*) as *chu* (樞).

*Chèrèn* (撤軔): The first character is read as *chánliè* (上緾列反); the *Bóyǎ* states that "chè" means "to set in motion. The second character is read as *nízhèn* (下尼震反). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that "rèn" means "to turn" or "a wheel," referring to a wheel turning upon the ground. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "that which obstructs a carriage," composed of the radical "carriage" (*chē*) with the phonetic "rèn" (*rén*).
"Wen-zu" (踠足): "Wen" is pronounced with the upper tone *yuan* (阮) and the lower tone *jian* (戩). Zhang Jian says it means the feet have not yet had their run;

it signifies being broken or thwarted. "Shen-huang" (沈艎): "Huang" is pronounced with the light tone *guang* (光). The *Pīcāng* states it is the same as "Yi-huang" (艅艎), the name of a Rong vessel. It refers to the boat in which the Rong prince Xian rode when he halted his advance against the Chu army. "Yi" (艅) is pronounced *yu* (餘).
The meaning of "regarding the myriad species as superior" (*wànhuì wéi guì*) has already been explained in the *Chóngzhèng lù* (Record of Honoring the Correct) under the opposite sense.

Regarding "arrogance toward things" (*àowù*), the *Kǒng zhù* (Commentary of Kǒng [Yáng]) on the *Shūjīng* (Book of Documents) states that it means "haughtiness. The character *mào* (from the radical for "heart") has the same meaning as *ào*.
Fuxi, also written as Xuji and alternatively called Paoxi, is so named because he discussed the preparation of food; the character for "preparation" (作) is likewise the same.

Regarding the term *zhánhui* (邅迴), the upper radical is read as *zhǎnlián*; Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that it means "to turn back. In the standard orthography of past and present, this character follows the radical "walk" (辵) and takes *dàn* (亶) as its phonetic.
Ji Shuye (稽叔夜)—the "shang" and "xi" in "Shuye" are pronounced as "jì" and "jī" respectively—was a person of the Jin dynasty and one of the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove.
"Lao" (㡿) refers to the spirit; its upper radical is pronounced "chǐ," and it is the correct orthographic form, though some treatises use the vulgar character "láo" (󲆛).
*Āng zāi*: "Ōng" (upper radical) and "zǎng" (lower radical). According to the *Kǎo shēng*, it means "to stop" or "to remove. The lower radical "zǎi" is the correct form;

the character "zāi" is a vulgar variant. *Mén cǎi*: "Wěn fèn" (phonetic reading). According to the *Kǎo shēng*, in the regions of Wu and Yue, small-patterned silk was called "wén. The lower radical "cāi" (reading "zǎi") refers to colored silks and fabrics.

Volume 3, Part 2: *Zhēnzhènglùn* (Treatise on the Rectification of Falsehoods), Volume 2. **En** (恩): The *Shuowén* states that "en" refers to the corners of the mouth (*kǒnbian*). It is composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) with the phonetic "wù" (*wùshēng*).
**Jué** (爝): Pronounced *jiāngyào*. The *Zìshū* states that "jué" refers to a torch (*jùhuǒ*). The *Shuowén* states it is composed of the radical "fire" (*huǒ*) with the phonetic "jué" (*juéshēng*).
*Chéng yào* (層曜): The first character, *chén*, has the phonetic *zèi* and *dēng*.
Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Shānhǎijīng* states that *chéng* means "repeatedly" (*chóng*). The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* explains it as being composed of the radical *shī* with the phonetic *zēng*.
*Xi*: (upper character read as *xīn*, reversed; from the *Shuowen*: "to inhale breath," composed of the radical 口 and the phonetic 及; the *Lunheng* uses the vulgar form 喰). *Gū*:
(an ancient form of 𧪖, which is the same as 昚, an archaic form of 慎).

*Bǐng*: (upper character read as *bīng*, with 皿 as the phonetic; the *Lushu* says: "bǐng means brightness"; according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical 火 and the phonetic 丙, or alternatively written as 昺).
*Wǔzù* (祚臧, with *zè* as the phonetic gloss; Zheng’s commentary on the *Shijing* states that *zù* means *luò*, the name of a palace of Emperor Wu of the Han).

*Yúnhè* (雲褐, with *hàn* and *è* as the phonetic glosses): according to the *Fāngyán*, people of Chu call a *páo* robe a *hè*. This refers to the fact that those of the Daoist school often paint patterns of clouds and mists upon their garments.

*Níshāng* (霓裳): *xì* (鷁) is pronounced as in *xìfǎn* (奚反). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states: "Ní is a cloud with colors resembling a dragon. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "Ní is the female *hóng* (rainbow). It is also depicted on the robes with various colors interspersed, sometimes blue and sometimes red. A solar halo resembles the *hóng* and *ní*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as: "The curved *hóng* is a yin qi; it follows from *yù* (rain), with *ér* (兒) as its phonetic component."
"Each gallops away" (mù): according to Yuè Wáng’s *Yìshū*, "mù" means to gallop swiftly; the *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radical "horse" (mǎ) with the phonetic "wù.

"Pausing" (dòu): the upper character is read as tóu lù; according to Yuè Wáng, "dòu" also means to stop. The *Hànshū Yīnyì* states that "dòu" refers to moving in a curve to avoid the enemy; the *Shuōwén* defines it as "to stop," composed of the radical "walking" (chuò) with the phonetic "dòu."

"Jian and Ji" (涓棘): "Jian" is pronounced with the initial *xue* (玄) and the final *fan* (反); "Ji" is pronounced with the initial *sheng* (矝) and the final *li* (力). These are the names of two individuals, namely Shi Jian and Chengzi. "Di" (締):
pronounced with the initial *ti* (提) and the final *li* (戾), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "di" means "to bind," composed of the radical for "silk" (糸) and the phonetic "di" (帝).

Regarding the term *tán-zuǎn* (壇纂): *tán* is pronounced with the initial *dān* (丹) and the final *fǎn* (反); according to Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lǐjì*, a *tán* is a mound of earth (*fēng-tǔ*) used as a sacrificial site, and the word *tán* signifies *dá* (怛), meaning "to clarify the imperial majesty. *Zuǎn* is pronounced with the initial *zuàn* (鑽) and the final *fǎn* (󲆃), where *fǎn* has the sounds *suān* (酸) and *zuǎn* (纂). Now, regarding the ritual form of the *tán-zuǎn*: at every time of *qiào-jì* (consecration sacrifices), one erects wooden stakes around the four sides of the altar and carves or paints upon the soil or the hair [of the animals]. This is like the people of Chu today who, whenever they offer prayers, bind *máo* grass into bundles, cut them short, thread them onto poles, and plant them upright in the ground; they set out incense and wine to pray, and only depart once the sacrifice is finished. This, however, is not the meaning of "compiling" (*zuǎn*).

The character *gāohuáng* (膏肓) has the upper radical *gāo* (膏) and the lower radical *huáng* (荒). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states that it means "to obstruct. Gu Yewang says it is the obstruction of the chest above the heart. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as "obstructing from above the heart"; it is composed of the radical *xīn* (心, heart) with *yuè* (月) and *wáng* (亾) as phonetic components.

*Shen-gù* (沈痼): The first character is pronounced *zhèn* (朕) with the *lín* (林) rhyme; the second is pronounced *gū-hù* (孤互). The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *jiǔ* (㽽), meaning "sickness," composed of the radical *nà* (疒) and the phonetic *gǔ* (古).

*yī-gài* (一槩): Pronounced *gāi-ài* (該愛). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states that a *gài-liàng* (槩量) is a leveling tool for bushels and pecks; the *Shuowen Jiezi* takes the radical *mù* (木) and the phonetic *jì* (既).

*Jiǎn* (上居輦反): The *Zhouyi* states that "jiǎn" means difficulty; according to the *Fāngyán*, it refers to stammering. The correct character from ancient times to the present is composed of the radical "speech" (言) and the phonetic "hán" (寒) in abbreviated form. *Nù* (下奴兀反): Bāo Xián’s commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* states that "nù" means slow and dull; the *Shuōwén* says it means difficult, composed of the radical "speech" (言) and the phonetic "nèi" (內). The version in the *Lúnyǔ* as "jiàn" (蹇) is an error.

"Bóyáo" (搏搖): the first character is pronounced luán (鸞) and the second yáo (遙). The *Zhuangzi* states: "In the Northern Ocean there is a fish whose name is Kūn; it transforms into a bird whose name is Péng. About to head for the Southern Ocean, its wings stir up waters three thousand li. It soars upon the *fúyáo* wind for ninety thousand li, like a cloud hanging from the sky—this is its marvel."
"Coughing and spitting" (*kaishuō*): the first character is read as *kāigài* (開蓋) in reverse;

the second is read as *tǔwò* (吐臥) in reverse. "Shaving the straw" (*xiāogǎo*): the first character is read as *xiāngyào* (相藥) in reverse; the second is read as *gāolǎo* (高老) in reverse. This refers to those who write down the origins and endings of plants and trees, or who trim and shave them; today we still see the term "shaved grass" (*gǎocǎo*) used in speech.

"Sōu" (蒐) and "shòu" (狩): the former is pronounced liú (流) and the latter shòu (收) with the yòu (宥) tone. Guo's commentary on the *Erya* states that hunting in spring is called "sōu" and hunting in winter is called "shòu"; these are the names for hunting during those two seasons.

*Guǒ* (𢧵馘): The phonetic transcription is *qiánjié* (前節). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To sever. It is composed of the radical *go* (戈) with the phonetic *què* (雀), and the lower part is read as *huò* (獲). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states: "To capture by cutting off [the ear] is called *guǒ*. Those who do not die in battle are killed and their ears are presented; this is called *guǒ*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* says: "To capture someone alive and cut off their ear. The *Shuowen* further defines it as: "In military combat, to sever the ear. It is composed of the radical *shǒu* (首) with the phonetic *huò* (或); the correct form uses the character *ěr* (耳) and is written as *niè* (聝).

*Zǎi* (宰) is pronounced *xī* (喜) with the *jī* (羈) rhyme. *Fúxǐ* (符璽) is pronounced *sī* (斯) with the *shì* (氏) rhyme. Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that *xǐ* (璽) means "seal" (*yìn*); it is also written as *xǐ* (璽), but the version in the *Lun* (論) is incorrect.

*Xìmiǎn* (餼芉): the first character is pronounced *xī* (希) with the *jì* (既) rhyme. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that living sacrificial animals are called *xì*; the *Pīcāng* states that *xì* means "to provide food. In both ancient and modern standard characters, this is written with the radical for "food" (*shí*) and the phonetic component "breath" (*qì*).

Regarding "Duyou" (杜郵): Zheng Zhu’s commentary on the *Liji* states that a *you* (郵) is a boundary marker or a place where the field overseer (*tianjun*) supervises and regulates the common people within the well-field system (*jing*). Gu Yewang says it is a postal station for traveling messengers located along the borders. Guo Pu says it is a place passed through on the road; it is also written as "xie" (卸).
*Fēnbāo* (分鑣): "Piao" is the phonetic component; the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it refers to a horse's bit (*máxián*), composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) with "piao" as the phonetic.

The upper character, *wǔ*, has the pronunciation *xiān*. The *Zhuangzi* says: "Weary of the world, one ascends to transcendence (*xiān*), riding upon white clouds to reach the Imperial Palace. The *Guǎngyá* states it means "transformation" (*huà*). According to the *Shuowen*, "longevity and transcendence" (*chángshēng xiānqù*) is composed of the radical "person" (*rén*) with "qiān" (abbreviated) as the phonetic.

*Laijin* (來賵): "Jin" is pronounced *feng* (諷) according to Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan*, which states that *jin* refers to items provided to assist with funeral rites. Regarding the character for "carriage and horses" (*che ma*), the *Gujin Zhengzi* (古今正字) notes that it is composed of the radical "貝" (bai) and the phonetic "䍃" (*yao*).

*Chaojue* (勦絕): The upper character is pronounced *jiao xiao* (焦小). The *Kaosheng* (考聲) states that "chao" means to sever or to cut. It is an error to derive it from the radical "力" (li) as "chao. *Luoncong* (論從): Derived from the radical "力" (li), this is an error. It should be read as "chao. (Note: This appears to be a correction regarding the etymological derivation of the preceding term).

The *zhāo jùn* (morning mushroom) dies in a single day; the commentary on the sounds explains that *jùn* refers to a fungus growing from the ground. The *Zhuangzi* states: "The morning mushroom does not know the difference between the end of the dark period and the beginning of the bright period.
The *dà chūn* (great chun tree) has the phonetic reading *chùnlún*; the *Zhuangzi* states: "The great chun tree lives eight thousand years for a spring and eight thousand years for an autumn."

*Yán* (妍): The upper radical is *qiè* (齧) with the pinyin *jiān*. The *Guǎngyǎ* states that it means "lovely. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "obstinate" (*zhì*) or "intelligent" (*huì*), composed of the radical *nǚ* (woman) and the phonetic *jiān* (幵), where *jiān* is pronounced *jiān*. The version in the *Lùn* (論) uses *yán* (妍), which is the vulgar form.
*Xiǎo* (蓼) is the name of a vegetable; its pronunciation is *liáo* (聊), with the bird radical and the radical for "to turn.

*Tuīguāng* (隤光): *tuī* (隤) is pronounced *dùilei* (上隊雷反); the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) says that *tuī* means objects falling downward. The *Shuowén* (說文) defines it as "falling down," composed of the radical for "to fall" (*huì*) and the phonetic *guì* (貴). The version in the *Lùn* (論) using *tuí* (穨) is incorrect.

"Rei" (禮) is pronounced "rei" (反). *Tenmon Benwaku Ron*, Volume Upper, Part One: "
*Shèn*: Upper radical *shǐn*, with the phonetic *jīn* (read as *xìn*). *Luó hù*: *hù* is read as *hóng wù*. *Nǎi juàn*:

The upper character is pronounced *nǎi* (as in the *Zhèngzhù* commentary on the *Yílǐ*, which states: "Nǎi" is equivalent to "ér" [then]; Gu Yěwáng says it means "to go"; the *Shuōwén* takes *xī* and *yǐn* as its phonetics; *yǐn* is the archaic form of the character *nǎi*; the *Lùn* [Treatise] writes it as *juàn* with the radical *chuò*, but this is a vulgar usage and incorrect). The lower part is read as *juàn* (qūyuàn). Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* states: "Juàn means 'to look'. The *Máo Shī Zhuàn* and the explanations of Gu Yěwáng and the *Shuōwén* share the same meaning. It takes the radical *mù* and *juǎn* (abbreviated) as its phonetics. The *Lùn* writes it as *juàn*, which is a vulgar character.

"Shěn (矧): The upper radical is 'shēn' (申) with the phonetic 'rěn' (忍). Guō's commentary on the *Erya* states: 'Shěn means "moreover" (*kuàng*). The *Shuowen* says it means "moreover" and is a particle. It is composed of the radical 'zhì' (矢) and the phonetic 'yǐn' (引) abbreviated; the character in the *Lùn* (論) is written as 'shěn' (矧), which is a vulgar form."

*Weijin* (煨燼): the first character is pronounced *wei* (猥, *huí*) with a level tone, and the second is *cí* (詞) with an even tone. The *Guǎngyá* states that it means "smoldering heat" (*wēnyūn*). Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* explains that it refers to the remaining wood of a fire. It is correctly written as the character *zǎi* (󱽃).

*Huān* (喧): *huī yuán* rhyme. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states it means "clamorous noise. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it is from the radical "speech" (*yan*) with the phonetic component "guàn" (*guàn* pronounced as *guān*).
*Hài jī* (醯雞): *xīn jī* rhyme. The middle character is the "insect" (*chóng*) radical; it is another name for the *mièměng* (gnat).
The meaning of "daqu" (大噱), which implies forceful cruelty and contrariety, has already been fully explained in the first fascicle of the *Zhengzhilun* (甄正論).

Regarding "juepi" (絕膐): the lower character is pronounced as lù (盧貯反). Jia Kui stated that "li" (膂) refers to the spine; the *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "flesh" (肉) with the phonetic component "lü" (旅). The version in the *Lun* (論) using "lü" (膂) is incorrect.
*Jiāo* (徼): "Mysterious and subtle. From the *Shànggǔ* (Ancient Texts), with the phonetic *diào*.

According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical *chì* (walking) and the phonetic *jiào*. *Sìyíng* (四瀛): "The four oceans. From the *Kǎoshēng* (Investigation of Sounds), it is said that *yíng* refers to the sea, meaning the four seas.

*Lúnhuàn* (輪奐): "Circular and magnificent. From the *Máoshī Zhuàn* (Commentary on the Mao Odes), it describes a state of brilliant splendor. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means "great," composed of the radical *qǒng* (joined hands) and the phonetic *xiòng* (abbreviated form).

*Mi-sù* (pronounced *sù*). The *Zhouyi* says: "The tripod's legs break, overturning the lord’s *sù*. Gu Yewang says it refers to the contents of a tripod. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* states that it is formed with the radical for food (*shí*) and the phonetic *shù*.

*Huì-hùn* (upper character pronounced *yūfèi*, also written as *yě*; lower character pronounced *húnkùn*). The *Cangjie Pian* says: "A *hùn* is where pigs dwell. The *Shuowen* says it is a latrine, formed with the radical for the mouth (*kǒu*) and the pig (*zhū*) inside it.

The character *zhǐ* (𧂟) is pronounced with the *qí* rhyme (位反). Zhang Jian states that it is a grass vessel used for transporting earth. The *Lunyu* says, "In building a mountain, when it is nine *ren* high, the work may be deficient by one *zhǐ*. The meaning in the *Shuowen* is the same: it is composed of the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) and the phonetic element "guì" (*guì shēng*).

Although the character *chōu* (䔏) is read as *shòu*, the Du Commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "chōu" means "to supplement" (*fù*). The *Kaosheng* says it means "to intermingle" (*cè*). The correct form of this character throughout antiquity and modern times follows the radical for grass (*cǎo*) with the phonetic *zào*. It is an error to follow the bamboo radical (*zhú*) and write it as *chòu* (簉).
*Yǎn* (伯𦆖; also written as 󲍛). *Yǎn* (有渰;

*yān*)—the *Mao Shī Zhuan* states that "yǎn" refers to the appearance of dark clouds. In the standard characters of antiquity and today, it is composed of the radical "water" (氵) and the phonetic "yǎn" (弇); "yǎn" is also written as 󱜋.
*Shuji*: The first character is pronounced *chāng* (with the *shang* tone) and the second is pronounced *xī* (with the *xi* tone).
Regarding *biǎn*: Hé Gu Yewáng states that it means "narrow. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "clothing" (*yī*) with the phonetic element "piān" (*biǎn*).

The upper radical 𠛠 (ying) and the lower radical 革 (ge) are corrected to form 搹; the *Lun* (Treatise) calls it 扼, which is a vulgar character. The lower part 𢍅 is the correct radical form, also written as 捥; writing it as 腕 is incorrect.

*Jiàoxìng* (僥倖): The upper character is pronounced *jiǎo* (with the radical *yáo*); according to the phonetic analysis, it means to seek what is beyond one's lot. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is composed of the radical "man" (*人*) with the phonetic "yáo. The lower character is pronounced *gěng* (with the radical *jīng*); according to the phonetic analysis, it means to border upon or to covet (*jiāo*). It refers to being favored and loved by those of high status. According to the *Gujin Zhengzi*, this character is composed of "man" (*人*) and the phonetic "zàn" (*㚔*), and is written as *jiào* (*󲷶*) in other character dictionaries.

Volume 2, Part 2: *Ten Gates for Discerning Delusions*. Regarding "chuāngxiāo" (瘡痟): "xiāo" (痟) is pronounced with a small *yáo* (遙) rhyme. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that "xiāo" means "sourness and emaciation. It refers to a head ailment, specifically a headache. The *Bicang* identifies it as a disease of thirst; the *Shuowen Jiezi* agrees in meaning. It is formed from the radical "nà" (疒) and the phonetic "xiào" (肖).

Regarding the character *cí* (茨): the upper part, *zì* (自), is pronounced as *fǎn* (反) and *kǎo* (考); the sound indicates it means "brambles" (*jílí*) or "to gather. The lower part, *jīn* (矜), is pronounced as *yì* (憶) and is the radical component. The *Biànhuòlùn* (辯惑論) uses the character *jí* (棘) instead, which is incorrect.
*Lu-mǎng* (鹵莽): The first character is pronounced with the initial *lú* and the final *dǔ*;

the second is pronounced with the initial *mó* and the final *bǔ*. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry) states it means "to weed. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical *lei* (耒) and the phonetic *yuan* (員); it is also written as *yun* (𦓷). The *Lunyu* (Analects) uses this term; it is commonly used in the vernacular.

*Bǎng* (pronounced *lǎng*, with the rhyme of *háng*); the *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that *bǎng* refers to *tóng-lǎng*. Guo Pu says it is a type of awn. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains that when rice or millet sprouts but does not mature, it is called *tóng-lǎng*; the correct form is written as *liáng*, composed of the radical *gòng* (two hands) and the phonetic *láng*.
*Dī* (pronounced *zhì*, with the *rǎn* tone): The *Shuowen* states that a *dī* is a small islet; it is composed of the radical "earth" (*tǔ*) and the phonetic "dī.
*Bìlì* (upper character pronounced *pí*, with the *jì* tone; lower character pronounced *lí*, with the *dì* tone): A fragrant herb according to the *Kaosheng*.

*Jian* (芙蓉上朅焉反): In the *Fāngyán*, the dialect of South Chu refers to "taking" as *jian*. The *Cāngjié piān* states it means "to pull out and take. It is also written as *yī* (㩙), and the version in the *Lùn* (Discourse) uses *qiǎn* (搴), which is likewise a vernacular character.

*He* (禾) and *shu* (菽) are pronounced with the "six" (*liù*) rhyme; the *Sushuzikao* (俗字考) states that *shu* refers to beans (*dòu*). The correct form is this: *cǔ* (尗). Regarding *móu* (麰) and *lái* (󳃣): the first character is pronounced *mòhóu* (墨侯) and the second is *làigāi* (賴該).

Liu Xi’s commentary on the *Mencius* says: "Móu-mài (麰麥) is wheat that has two furrows. Nowadays, it is especially abundant in the north of Qi and the Yellow River region; sown in spring, it ripens in summer. The *Guoyá* (廣雅) states: "Móu is large wheat; lái is small wheat. The *Shuowen* (說文) defines *móu* as being composed of the radical for "wheat" (*麥*) and the phonetic *móu* (牟). The *Gujin Zhengzi* (古今正字) states that *lái* is composed of the radical for "wheat" (*麥*) and the phonetic *lái* (來), or it may be written as *lái* (󳈩). In the *Zishu* (字書), it is written as *zhōng* (䅘), which is the same as in the *Lùn* (論).

Now, the character for "lazy" (duò) is written as 憜 in the *Shuowen Jiezi*, which states it means "disrespectful," composed of the radical 心 and the phonetic 隋; alternatively, the radical 𨸏 may be omitted to form 惰, which is synonymous with 論; its archaic form is 媠.

*Kǐn* (噤): Following the *Qín* (琴). Wáng Yì’s commentary on the *Chǔcí* states that *kǐn* means "to close the mouth. The *Shuōwén* states it is written as *yín* (唫), following the radical for the mouth and taking *jīn* (金) as its phonetic.

*Bǐ* (比): Following *Yuán* (元). The *Kǎogōngjì* states: "When the carriage-maker constructs a carriage, for every axle (*yúan*), he makes it three times the length of the wheel. He divides its total length into three parts: two in the front and one in the rear. The *Shuōwén* defines it as the shaft (*zhōu*) of a carriage, following the radical for the chariot and taking *yuán* (袁) as its phonetic.

*Chí* (馳) is pronounced *chǒu* (丑) with the retroflex final (*lǐng-fǎn*). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that it means "to gallop" (*qǐng*); the *Guǎngyǐ* says it means "to run. The meaning of the character has remained consistent from antiquity to the present. It is composed of the radical "horse" (*mǎ*) and the phonetic element "píng" (*pīng*), which is pronounced *pǐ-dīng-fǎn*.

Regarding the term *shì* (弑), its intent is to commit rebellion; the *Baihutong* says: "What is *shì*? It is synonymous with 'to kill' (*shā*). It refers to a minister or son who kills his sovereign or father, waiting for an opportunity to strike when he can gradually test the moment. According to the *Shuowen*, it is derived from a simplified form of *shā*, with *shì* as its phonetic component.

*Lànshāng* (the first character pronounced with the *shàngshēng* tone as *dàn*, meaning "to moisten"; the second character pronounced with the *shǎngshēng* tone as *shāng*). The *Shuōwén* states that *shāng* refers to a cup; when full it is called *shāng*, and when empty it is called *zhì*. It is composed of the radical *jiǎo* (horn) and the phonetic *lèi*; the ancient script is written as *máng*. *Zhì* is pronounced *zhì*. The original text of the *Lùn* (Treatise) uses the character *zhì* (𨢩), which is an error.

*Niǎo* (not-niǎo): *qiǎo* reversed. The commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that it means "to disturb"; the *Shuowen* says it means "to agitate," following the radical for the hand (*shǒu*) and the phonetic *yáo*.

*Zhònglài* (zhòng-lài): *dài* reversed. Examining this, this *lài* is not the *xiāo* flute; rather, it refers to deep, secluded rock valleys where bamboo and trees grow densely. When a light breeze stirs them, the myriad sounds are cool and clear—this is what is called the "myriad *lài*s. The *Shuowen* follows the radical for the bamboo (*zhú*) and the phonetic *lài*.
"Xián" (咸) means "to manifest" (*chī*, with the *shàn* rhyme); Han Kangbo’s commentary on the *Zhouyi* states it means "to raise. The *Cangjie pian* states it means "to open.
"Minrán" (泯然) [the first character] is read as *shàngmín* (上民) and the second as *yǎn* (引).
"Bān Chuí" (班倕)—the first character is read as *bǎnmán* (板蠻) and the second as *chuí* (垂)—are the names of two individuals.

"Zhuiji" (舟檝): The phonetic component is "jian" (尖) with the tone "fan" (反); the *Kao* states it refers to the equipment for rowing a boat, such as oars. The interpretation that the character "lun" (論) is written as "lei" (艥) is incorrect.
"Hua yi" (畫鷁): The phonetic component is "dian" (電) with the tone "li" (歷); it refers to a water bird.
"Fāng náo" (芳橈) means to row; "náo" is pronounced with the *zhão* (昭) and *fǎn* (反) finals.
"Bì chuò" (萆輟) is pronounced with the *zhī* (知) and *liè* (劣) finals; the *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲) states that "chuò" means to stop.

"Pǒu" (剖) is pronounced with the *pǔ* (普) and *hòu* (厚) finals; the *Shuōwén* (說文) states that "pǒu" means to split wood, following the radical for "knife" (*dāo*) and the phonetic *pǔ*. To follow the hand-radical and write it as "póu" (掊) is incorrect.
"Huang (恍)"—the "shang" and "huang" rhymes reversed; Zhang Jian says it describes a state of vast emptiness and openness. "Wu (迃)"—the "yue" and "ju" rhymes reversed;

Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* says it means "obscure and deviant," while Zheng Xuan says it means "vast and great. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "chuō" (辵) with the phonetic "yu" (亐).

Regarding the term *dàn* (憺): the commentary on sounds states it means "tranquil" (*jìng*) or "peaceful" (*ān*). The *Lùn* (論) [i.e., the *Shuowen Jiezi*] interprets it as "the appearance of water moving," which is incorrect.

Regarding *zhǐqīng* (沚淸): the *Cāngjié piān* states that *zhǐ* (沚) refers to a small islet. Examining this through the mirror, when [water] is clear and still (*zhǐ*), its form is visible; when it flows, its reflection is disturbed; when it is still, it is settled. Thus, it should be written as *zhǐ* (止). To write it with the radical for water (*shuǐ*) is to lose its original meaning.
Suddenly it expands upward (shū, with the retroflex -r final);

then it becomes tranquil and silent (mì, with the labio-dental -n final). The *Erya* states that "mì" means "tranquility. The correct orthography for this character from ancient times to the present follows the radical "speech" (言) and the phonetic "qí" (𥁑), where the pronunciation of "qí" is the same as above.

"Quèrán" (喟然) is read with the initial *kù* and the final *àn*. In the *Commentary on the Analects* by Hé Yàn, it is said that "què" is a sound of sighing; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "a deep sigh," written with the radical for the mouth and the phonetic *wèi*.
"Jǐngwā" (井哇) is read with the initial *wū* and the final *guā*; it refers to the frog.

*Qī zòu*: the upper character is pronounced *xī*, the lower is pronounced *zōu* (with the *jiù* rhyme). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "A well-rim (*jing-zòu*); it is composed of the radical *wǎ* (tile) with the phonetic *qiū*.

*Zé àn*: the character for *àn* is pronounced *yàn*. Jia Gui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states: "The *àn* is the *hu* bird. Du Yu states: "It is the *cāng-àn*. It chirps at the start of spring and departs at the end of autumn; it is correctly written as *àn*.
The character 嘈 (pinyin: cáo; radical 攵, phonetic 囂) is explained in the *Wenzi Dadian* as meaning "to loathe" (*yàn*).

The upper part is pronounced *cáo* and the lower part *cái-hé*. The *Guǎngpǐ* states it means "sound," while the *Kǎoshēng* describes it as the appearance of clamorous and excessive noise. It is also written as 嚗 or 囐, with the same meaning.

Regarding the character *qióng* (煢): the upper part is read as *kuí* (揆) with the phonetic component *yíng* (營). The Master Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shūjìng* states: "Qióng means 'solitary' (*dān*). Zhèng’s commentary on the *Zhōuwǔlǐ* says: "One who has no brothers is called *qióng*. The *Màoshī Zhuàn* states: "It means having nothing to rely upon. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of *xùn* (卂) and the abbreviated form of *yíng* (熒) as its phonetic; it may also be written as *qióng* (惸), which is identical in meaning to *lùn* (論), or as *juān* (嬛), the latter being read as *lǐ* (理). The *Kǎoshēng* states that *qióng* refers to a widowed woman. The reading *lì* (釐) in the *Lùn* (論) is an error.

"Hun" (昏) is pronounced *ding* with the *nian* (念) final. Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that "hun" means to be submerged and distressed by a flood disaster. According to the *Fangyan*, it means "downward. The standard character of ancient and modern times takes "tu" (土) as its radical and "mi" (𡨥) as its phonetic.

*Yu*: The upper character is pronounced *yù*. *Qiǎn*: The upper part is read as *kuī* (with the radical *yì*). The *Pīcāng* states that *qiǎn* means "stillness. In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, it is composed of the radical *mén* with the phonetic *xī*.

*Kǎn*: The upper part is read as *kǎn* (with the radical *gān*). The Master Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* says, "*Kǎn* means to overcome. The *Dàzhuàn* says it means "to subdue. The *Shuōwén* says it means "to kill. In the current pronunciation, the archaic form was *kàn*. In the *Lùn*, it is written as *kān*. It is a common vulgar character for the following [character]. *Jiān*: Read as *xiān*. It means "to cut off."

*Hù* (扈) is pronounced *shàng hú gǔ fǎn*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Kǎogōngjì* states that *hù* means "relaxed" (*huǎn*). The *Zuǒzhì yǒngjiàn mào* (The Appearance of Valor and Vigor) says it is an appearance of courage and vigor. *Guǎngpǐ* (Broad Lexicon) says it means "to employ. The lower character is pronounced *cáiyòng fǎn*.
Fǎngfú (髣髴): The first character is read as fāng (芳𠕀反) and the second as fū (敷勿反).

Nǎnggòu (曩構): The first character is read as náng (囊朗反); Jia Dui states that "nǎng" means "recently" (曩向), and the *Erlǐ Pǐ* (爾疋) glosses it as "long ago" (夂也); the meaning in the *Shuowen Jiezi* is the same; it is composed of the radical "sun" (日) with the phonetic "xiāng" (襄). The second character is read as hòu (侯候反).
*Āi* (藹): Upper radical *jūn* (君), lower phonetic *ài* (埃). The *Kǎo Shēng* states that *ài* refers to the appearance of one’s deportment; it signifies a minister exhausting his loyalty. *Sù* (邃):

Upper radical *suī* (雖), lower phonetic *cuì* (翠). The *Shuōwén* states that *sù* means "deep" (*shēn*). It is composed of the radical *xué* (穴) with the phonetic *suì* (遂). *Qiàn* (鍵): Lower phonetic *qiān* (偃). According to the *Zhou Lǐ*, the *Sīmén* (Director of Gates) was charged with receiving the *guǎnqiàn* (locks and keys) to open and close the national gates. *Zhèng Zhòng* stated that *qiàn* means "strong. The *Fāngyán* identifies the *yuè* (tongue-lock) as a *qiàn*. The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radical *jīn* (金) with the phonetic *jiàn* (建).
*Tanzé* (探賾): The first character is read as *tàn* (upper radical *cǎn*, pinyin *nán*;

lower radical *shì*, pinyin *gé*). The second character is read as *rèn* (upper radical *rén*, pinyin *zhèn*). The *Lunyu* states: "The benevolent person is reticent in speech. It means that because acting is difficult, can one help but be reticent when speaking? According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to pause" (*dùn*). It is composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) with the phonetic element "knife" (*rèn*).
