*Yin Fǎlín Fǎshī Zhuàn* (Biographies of the Dharma Master Yin Fǎlín), five fascicles; *Jí Shāmén Bùbài Sú Yì* (Collected Discourses on the Non-prostration of Śramaṇas to Laypeople), six fascicles. These two collections comprise eleven fascicles in total, sharing the same title as this volume.

*Shì Fǎlín Zhuàn* (Biography of Śramaṇa Fǎlín) of Longtián Monastery on Zhōngnán Mountain, five fascicles; *Shì Fǎlín Běnzhuàn Xù* (Preface to the Autobiography of Śramaṇa Fǎlín). Regarding the character 洎 (*jì*): the upper part is pronounced *yǐn* (sound) and the lower part is pronounced *nǎi* (乃). Dù Yǔ’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states it means "to reach. The *Yùn yīng* says it means "to arrive at. The *Shuōwén* notes that it is rarely seen [there], being composed of 旦 (*dàn*) with 既 (*jì*) as its phonetic component.

*Jiè* (絕): The *niǔ* rhyme is pronounced as in *jiǔ* (九). According to the *Guǎngyá*, "niǔ" means "east"; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means "silk thread. It refers to that which is knotted and can be untied; it takes the radical *mì* (糸) and the phonetic *chǒu*. *Tuí* (隤):

The upper character is pronounced as in *tú léi* (徒雷); the lower character is the regular form of *gāng* (岡). According to the *Guǎngyá*, "tuí" means "to collapse" (*huài*). In the *Hánshī*, it means "to leave behind" (*yí*). Regarding the sound, it refers to objects falling downward or being destroyed. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means "to fall down"; it takes the radical *duì* (隓) and the phonetic *guì* (貴). Alternatively, it may be written with the radical *tǔ* (土) as *diàn* (墤), with the same meaning. In transmitted texts, it is sometimes written with the radical *xié* (頁) as *tuī* (頹), but this is not used here.
"Already confused" (*yiwèn*): Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states that "wèn" means "to confuse. It is composed of the radical "silk thread" (*mì*) and the phonetic "wén.

"Submerged and extinguished" (*yīniè*): The first character, "yīn," has the pronunciation *shàngyǐn*. Jia Gongyan’s commentary on the *Guóyuè* states it means "to sink down. The *Ěryá* says it means "to fall. The *Shuowén* says it means "to submerge. It is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic "yīn. The character "yīn" shares the same pronunciation as the first [character].

The character *zōng* (悰) is used in the title of the *Songfan Erya*. It signifies "concern" (*lù*) according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, and "joy" (*yuè*) according to the *Shuowen*; it is a compound character formed from a semantic and a phonetic component. It is also the name of the Great Virtuous Dharma Master Yanzong of the Tang Dynasty.

*Jùnzhì* (捃摭): The first character, *jùn*, is pronounced with the *jun* rhyme (君運反). According to the *Fāngyán*, it means "to take. The *Shuōwén* also defines it as "to pick up," formed with the radical for "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic *jun*. The second character, *zhì*, is pronounced with the *zhēng* rhyme (征亦反). According to the *Fāngyán*, *zhì* also means "to take"; the *Shuōwén* likewise glosses it as "to pick up."

Volume One, Part One: The Original Biography of Dharma Master Fali. *Yùdié* (jade tablet): *dāng ān fǎn* (pronounced as such). In the commentary on the *Shūjīng* by Kǒng [Yáng], it means "to exhaust. According to the *Shuowén*, "to exhaust" (*dàn*) is written with the radical *è* and the phonetic *dān*. A "jade tablet" (*yùdié*) refers to Buddhist scriptures and treatises bound in fascicles.

Yǐndùn (隱遁): "Dùn" is pronounced *tún* (with the tone of *túnhún*). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states it means "to hide in concealment. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states it means "to flee. The *Guoyá* states it means "to avoid the world. It is also written as 遁 (*dùn*), following the radical for movement (*辵*) with the phonetic component *tún*. The pronunciation of *tún* is *túnhún*.

*Kēnghuáng* (鏗鍠). When the honored guest performs the ritual, Zixia said, "The sound of the bells is *kēng-kēng*," which refers to this. The *kēng* produced by striking is written as *huán* (鍠); according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of 車 (*chē*) and 眞 (*zhēn*), forming 䡩, or alternatively 銵; these are all phonetic components. The lower character has the pronunciation *hóng*. The *Commentary on the Mao Shijing* states: "The bells and drums are *huáng-huáng*"; the commentary says this means "harmonious joy. The *Erya* also says, "*huáng* is the sound of music. Guo Pu says, "*huáng* is the sound of drums. The *Shuowen* says it is the sound of bells. In dictionaries it is written as 鍠, or sometimes as 喤; these are all one and the same. The form used in the commentaries, 鋐, is a vulgar variant.

"Subduing the carriage" (fù yàn) [the character yàn being pronounced xīn àn] refers to the *jiànchē* (cangue-cart). According to the *Kǎo Shēng* (Investigation of Sounds), it is a cart for transporting prisoners. Master Yù intended to crush the heterodox faction; he first cultivated his standing within other schools and then sought victory. For nine years, he lived in concealment among the Daoist practitioners at Huangzhong, serving as their leader. He thoroughly investigated the fraudulent arts of the Three Zhangs and personally practiced the texts of talismans, *qiǎo*, and memorial petitions (*zhāng zòu*), exhausting every root and source before finally returning to the fundamental to compose his treatise—like a fierce beast crouching within its carriage.

*Chun-chun* (pronounced *chūn-yǔn*): The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that "chun-chun" means insects moving. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *gūn* (insects) with the phonetic *chūn*; *gūn* is pronounced *kūn*. *Dian-zhui* (pronounced *dīng-zhuì*): The *Erya* states that "dian" means the summit. The *Guoyaya* says it means "above.

Examining the phonetics, it also means "end" or "to perish. It is composed of the radical *shan* (mountain) with the phonetic *diān*; the correct form of the character *diān* has *yè* on the right and *zhēn* on the left. The common version with two *zhēn*s on the left is an error. *Xia-zhilei* (pronounced *zhí-lèi*): The *Erya* states that "zhuì" means to fall. The *Shuowen* says it is composed of the radical *gāo* (height) with the phonetic *duò*; it is composed of the radical *luó* with the phonetic *shēn*. The common usage of adding the earth radical (*tǔ*) is also acceptable.
The upper character for *gǔn-lóng* (衮龍) is pronounced *gōng-běn-fǎn*. Its meaning has already been fully explained and refuted in the *Poxie lun* (Treatise on Refuting Deviant Doctrines).

The upper character for *xū-fà* (須髮) is pronounced *sù-yú-fǎn*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that "xū" refers to the beard below the chin; according to the *Shuowen*, it means facial hair and is composed of the radicals "head" (*xié*) and "three strokes" (*shān*). Although the vulgar script also uses "long hair" (*biāo*) to form *bì* (鬢), this is incorrect. The pronunciation of *xié* is *xián-jie-fǎn*, and the pronunciation of *biāo* is *bì-yáo-fǎn*.

*Jí* (戢): Pronounced *zhān* (簪) and *lì* (立) in reverse; the *Zheng-jian* commentary on the *Shi jing* states that *jí* means "to gather" (*liǎn*). The *Shi zhuan* states it means "to assemble" (*jù*). The *Shuowen jiezi* defines it as "concealing weapons," composed of the radical *gē* (戈) with the phonetic *qī* (咠).

*Huì* (憓): The upper tone is pronounced *huì* (惠); the *Mao Shi zhuan* states that *huì* means "loving-kindness" (*ài*). The *Kǎoshēng* states it means "compassion" (*cí*) and "benevolence" (*rén*). The textual meaning in the *Shi jing* is the same. It is composed of the radical *xīn* (心) with the phonetic *huì* (惠). The archaic form is written as *mǐ* (󲾭), composed of the radical *huǐ* (芔) with the phonetic *huì* (惠). The upper tone is pronounced *jí* (緝) in reverse.

"Dùn (塵)" is pronounced *tóng* with the rhyme of *lù* (鹿). Yě Wáng says that "dùn" means "arrogance" (*màn*). Jiǎ Dú says it means "familiarity" (*xié*). The *Cāngjié piān* says it means "filth. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "black" (*hēi*) and the phonetic "mài" (*mài*). "Xié" is pronounced *xīliè*.

*Qiào* (誚): Pronounced *xiāoyào* (曜反). The *Fāngyán* states that in the regions between Qi, Chu, Song, and Wei, "to yield" is called *qiào*. The *Cāngjiépiān* defines it as "reproaching"; it refers to mutual reprimand and yielding. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radicals "speech" (*yán*) and "likeness" (*xiào*).

Regarding the character *chāng* (猖): it is pronounced with the initial *chǎng* (敞) and the final *shāng* (商). The *Zhuangzi* says, "to act wildly and recklessly" (*chāngkuáng wàngxíng*). As for the term *chāngyán* (猖言), it is like the boastful words of a wild and reckless person in a wine shop; such words are not to be trusted. In both ancient and modern standard characters, it is composed of the radical *quán* (犬, dog) and the phonetic *chāng* (昌); the pronunciation of *chǎng* (敞) is *chāngzhǎng* (昌掌).

Regarding the character *zhǔ* (矚): when placed above the radical for "metal" (鍾), it is pronounced with the initial *yù* (欲) and the final *fǎn* (反). Examining its phonetics, it signifies "intense gazing"; it is that which all eyes converge upon. The common (simplified) character is correctly written as *zhǔ* (矚). When read with the lower tone, it is also a personal name.
The character above [the first one] is pronounced *chì*; it is erroneously written as *shǔ* in common usage.
*Zhōuháng* (pronounced *huò láng*) means "boat. *Xūnhuá*:
the first character is read as *yún* and the second as *guā*; these are the names of the two emperors of the Tang and Yú periods. Emperor Yao’s name was Fàngxūn, and Emperor Shùn’s name was Chónghuá.

Zhong Yong’s *Fanjie* states that "zhong" (踵) refers to the heel of the foot; Wang Yi’s *Liujing Zhuan* states it means "to succeed"; the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "to pursue," composed with the radical "stop" (止) and the phonetic "zhong" (重). The version in the *Chuanshuo* is erroneous for using "zhong" (踵).

"Jiàn-léi" (洊雷): the first character is pronounced with the radical *zhàng* and the phonetic *yáng* (jìāng-yáng); the second character is pronounced with the radical *jiè* and the phonetic *qiè* (jiē-qiè). The meaning has already been fully explained and refuted in the *Poxie lun* (Treatise on Refuting Heresies). "Qiāng-qian" (牆塹): the first character is pronounced with the radical *jiàng* and the phonetic *yáng* (jiāng-yáng);

the second character is pronounced with the radical *qiè* and the phonetic *qiè* (jiē-qiè). "Gùn-mǎn" (憒懣): the first character is pronounced with the radical *fén* and the phonetic *wěn* (fén-wěn); the second character is pronounced with the radical *mén* and the phonetic *běn* (mén-běn). The meaning has already been fully explained and refuted in the *Poxie lun*.
*Chendú* (磣黷): The first character is pronounced *chūjǐn* (初錦反) and the second is pronounced *dú* (音獨). Their meaning has already been explained in the *Poxie lun* (破邪論).

*Yuánliáo* (原燎): Pronounced *lìzhào* (力召反). The *Shàngshū* (尚書) states: "Like fire spreading across the wilds (*yuán*)" (*ruò huǒ zhī liáo yú yuán yě*). The *Shuowén* (說文) defines it as setting fire [to the land], composed of the radical 火 with the phonetic 尞.

The character *diǎo* (刁) is pronounced with the upper radical *niǎo* (鳥) and the lower radical *liáo* (聊); the lower part is pronounced *dōu* (兜). Its meaning has already been explained and refuted in the *Poxie lun* (破邪論).

The character *xū* (胥) is pronounced with the upper radical *xī* (息) and the remainder *yú* (余). Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that *xū* means "mutually" (*xiāng*). Zheng’s sub-commentary on the *Shijing* states it means "all. According to the *Shuowen jiezi*, it is composed of the radical for "flesh" (*ròu*) and the phonetic *pǐ* (疋), where *pǐ* is pronounced *shū* (疏).
*Dàizǎi* (太宰): *zǎi* is pronounced *bǐ* (反) [in the Zhuan], though *zài* (再) is commonly used; it is the name of the office. *Zài* (再): pronounced *chāng liǎng* (反);
the *Kǎoshēng* says "to open" and "to clarify"; according to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical *pī* (攴) with the phonetic *shàng* (尨).

"Ē (叵)" is pronounced with the initial *pō* and the final *mǎ*. The "Zhèngzì" (正字) of the ancient and modern eras states that it means "not possible. The "Shuowen" (說文) explains it as the opposite of "kě" (可). In the "Zuǒzhuan" (左傳), the character for "kě" is written [with this variant]. The pronunciation of "mǎ" (麼) is *mó* with the final *fǎn* (反).

The character 倫 (lún) is pronounced with the rhyme *pi* (閉反). Xu Shuchong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states that it means "to pair" (*ǒu*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to match" (*pèi*), composed of the radical 女 (woman) and the phonetic 󳌛; the pronunciation of 󳌛 is *bi* (閉) with the rhyme *mi* (迷) as its final.
"Tóngjìn (同燼) and Qínjìn (秦進)" are used to mean "to rectify" (*fǎngzhèng*); the vulgar pronunciation is similar to *jìn*, but this is incorrect.
"Tuōxǐ (脫屣)" is pronounced *shī'ěr fǎn*; it refers to leather sandals (*gēngxǐ*). "Kǎnlǎn (坎壈)" is pronounced *lán gǎn fǎn*;

the *Kǎoshēng* says it describes the appearance of being separated by a long distance. In both the ancient and modern standard characters, these two words are written with the radical "earth" (*tǔ*) and the phonetic "qiàn" (*qian*). They are pronounced accordingly.

*Qùlǐ* (腠裏): *qù* is pronounced as *cāng zòu* (倉奏) according to Zheng’s commentary on the *Yí Lǐ*; it means the texture of the skin. The *Kǎo Shēng* states it refers to the interior of the skin. In both ancient and modern standard characters, it is composed of the radical "flesh" (*ròu*) with the phonetic element "present" (*zòu*).

*Qīngjiū* (清遒): *Jiù* is pronounced as in the rhyme of "you" (由). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (毛詩傳) states that *jiū* means "to surround" (*zhōu*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文) indicates it is formed from the radical "walking" (*chuò*) with the phonetic element *qiú*.

*Xìntán* (哂談): *Shēn* is pronounced as in the rhyme of "rěn" (忍). Master Ma’s commentary on the *Lunyu* (論語) says *xǐn* means "to laugh. Master Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* (禮記) states that *xǐn* refers to the roots of the teeth; he says a great laugh reveals the teeth. According to the *Jīngǔ Zèngzì* (古今正字), this character is formed from the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) with the phonetic element *xī*; it is also written as *yǐn* (吲) or *mǐn* (𠸄).
The term *qin* (殫) means "exhausted" or "ended," as in the sound *dan*.

Regarding *ke-dou* (𧎗蚪): the upper character is pronounced *ku-huo* (苦禾反) and the lower is *dou-kou* (兜口反). Lexicons state that *ke-dou* is an aquatic creature, the offspring of a toad. In the commentary, the character is written as *qiu* (蚪), which has the same form as *dou* (蚪).
"Qiǎn" (闃然): The upper part is read as *qīng* (覔反). It is a sound derived from "gate" (*mén*). Regarding the character "chòu" (臭), it is composed of "eye" (*mù*) and "dog" (*quǎn*).

"Yán" (鹽): Pronounced *gū hù* (姑戶反). Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Fāngyán* states that "yán" means "sudden urgency. The *Shījīng* says, "The king's business knows no yán. The *Shuowén* states it is formed from a simplified version of "jiàn" (*jiān*) with "gǔ" as its phonetic component.
*Jùn* (捃): On the path; the rhyme is *dào* (道), with a reversed *yùn* (運). The *Fānyán* (方言) states that *jùn* means "to gather" (*qǔ*). It is written with the hand radical. *Sǒngjié* (悚慴):

The upper character *sǒng* (悚) has the rhyme *lì* (栗) and *yǒng* (勇). Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states that *sǒng* means "to be terrified" (*jù*). The *Shuōwén* correctly writes it as *bǐ* (𢥠), composed of the heart radical and the phonetic *shuāng* (雙); in some books it is written as *bǐ* (𢥠), while the transmitted texts use *sǒng*. Today, these characters are used interchangeably in common usage. The lower character *jié* (頰) has the rhyme *jiá* (頰). The *Erya* states that *jié* means "to be fearful" (*jù*). Guo Pu says it means "to be cowed" (*shè*). The *Shuōwén* [correctly] writes it with the heart radical and the phonetic *xí* (習).

*Zhèn nǎn*: "Nǎn" is pronounced with the *jiǎn* rhyme. The *Kǎo Shēng* states it means being ashamed and blushing in the face; the correct form is *nǎn*. *Jì zhǐ*: "Zhǐ" is pronounced with the *zhī* rhyme.
The *Shuōwén* states that "zhǐ" means to settle or stop; it is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic component "zhī" (*shì*).

*Jiūyǒu* (拘羑): The character *yǒu* is pronounced with the rhyme *liǔ* (反). The *Shuowen* states that it is the place where King Wen was imprisoned; *Yǒulǐ* (羑里) is located in Tāngyīn (湯陰), derived from the radical *yáng* (羊) and the phonetic *jiǔ* (久). The tradition [of the *Shuowen*] writes it as *qiāng* (羌), which is incorrect. *Zádá* (雜遝): The character *tán* (潭) is pronounced with the rhyme *hé* (合).

The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that *tà* (遝) means "walking hurriedly" or "ahead. *Zhùdá* (䢔遝) describes the appearance of many people walking together. The *Shuowen* defines it as "to reach," derived from the radical *chuò* (辵) and the phonetic *mí* (󱳭); the phonetic *mí* has the same sound as above, while *zhù* (䢔) is pronounced *hé*. The tradition [of the *Shuowen*] writes it as *pō* (󳋐), which is incorrect.

*Zhèngmù* (爭騖): *Guǎngyá* states that *mù* means "to gallop"; Gù Yěwáng states it means "to rush swiftly. In the *Jīngǔ zhènzì*, this character follows the radical for "horse" (馬) and uses *wù* as its phonetic.

*Zhùjiě* (註解): The upper character, *zhù*, has the pronunciation *zhūjù* (上誅句反). *Guǎngyá* states it means "commentary" (*zhùshū*); *Běicāng* states it means "explanation. In the *Jīngǔ zhènzì*, this character follows the radical for "speech" (言) and uses *zhǔ* as its phonetic. Nowadays, many write it with the pronunciation *zhùyù* (注朱喻反), but this meaning does not apply; the lower character should all have the pronunciation *mǎi* (下皆買反), which is the same as *jiǎ* (音賈), and [the former reading] is incorrect.
Xīn xǔ (辛諝): the second character is pronounced as lǚ (旅) in the *Zhōu Lǐ* commentary by Zheng Xuan; it is a term for one who possesses talent and wisdom.
Cuì cǎn (璀璨): the first character is pronounced as huì (會) and the second as dàn (旦).

The character *biàn* (辯) has the phonetic *yóu* with the *jiù* rhyme. Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that a *yòu* is what is called a *yuàn* (garden/park) today. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains that a *yuàn* is so named because it has a perimeter wall (*huán*), hence it takes *yòu* as its phonetic; *yòu* is pronounced *wéi*.

*Mian* (靦): *tian* with the radical *tian* (天) and the phonetic *dian* (典). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (毛詩傳) states that *mian* means "jealousy" (*dou*). Zheng’s *Shuowen Jiezi* commentary states it means "to have a face and eyes while being jealous. The *Kaoseng* (考聲) says it refers to being shameless. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *mian* (面) and the phonetic *jian* (見).

*Juéhuǒ* (爝火): The first character is pronounced *shàng* (上) and is the character for *jué* (爵). The *Shūshū* (字書) states it refers to a torch. The *Shuowén* (說文) defines it as "using fire to sweep away darkness (*míng* [冥]); it is composed of the radical 'fire' and the phonetic 'jué'.
*Xī Chāo* (郗超): The first character is pronounced *shàngchǐní* (上恥尼反). It is the name of a person. Its appearance in other texts as *Chà* (剎) is an error.

Volume Two, Part Two: Commentary on the Original Biography of Fali. **[Interlinear Notes]** *Wǎng* (上上音罔): The *Kǎoshēng* (Examination of Sounds) states that this means to deceive and mislead with words.

*Kàn hé* (勘劾, 下音恒得反): This means to investigate and indict. Gu Yewang says it refers to the testimony presented in legal proceedings. The *Shuowén* defines it as "a person who has committed a crime. *Gāo* (皐) is the archaic form of the character for "crime" (*zuì*); it is composed of the radical *lì* (力) and the phonetic *hài* (亥), and does not take *rèn* (刃) as its phonetic. The version in the [Biography] using *zhuó* (𠜨) is incorrect.

*Li-xie*: The first character is pronounced *lei* (lèi) with the level tone; the second is pronounced *xián-yuè* (xiān-yuè). Confucius’s commentary on the *Lunyu* states: "Li" refers to black ropes, and "xie" means to bind or constrain; these are used to restrain criminals. In both ancient and modern standard characters, they are written with the radical for "silk" (*mi*). "Lei" and "yue" serve as the phonetic components. The correct form is *xì*, though the vulgar form is *xiè*.
"Zhùlíng" (佇聆): The *Cāngjiépiān* states that "líng" means to listen; according to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "ear" (耳) with the phonetic "lìng" (令).
"Dǎomèi" (擣昧): The upper character is pronounced "dāolǎo" (刀老); the *Kǎoshēng* states it means mental distress, and it is composed of the radical "hand" (手).

The character *tāo* (叨䔏): the upper radical is *dǎo* (討) and the lower radical is *chōu* (搊). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that *tǎo* means "to supplement" (*fù*). The *Kaosheng* says it means "to intermingle" (*cè*) or "to align" (*qí*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* takes *zào* (造) as its phonetic component; however, the version in the [Zuozhuan] commentary uses the bamboo radical to form *chòu* (簉), which is incorrect.
*Pú zāo*: "pú" is pronounced *bǔ* (with the final tone reversed) and "zāo" is pronounced *zāo*.
*Chuài lí*: "chuài" is pronounced *chuán liè* (reversed) and "lí" is pronounced *lí*.

*Mí zhēn*: "mí" is pronounced *mì bēi*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Yīlǐ* states it means "to increase" (*yì*); it is a borrowed character (*jiǎjiè*). The *Shuōwén* correctly writes it as 󳊚, composed of the radical 弓 and the phonetic 󲑦; the common form is written as 彌.

*Hù* (mud): Upper radical *kūn*, upper phonetic *wù*. The *Kǎo Shēng* says it describes the appearance of flowing water; it means to stir until it becomes turbid. *Wéi Zōng*: Upper radical *zú*, upper phonetic *zōng*.

*Zhā lí* (quince/pear): Upper radical *zé*, upper phonetic *jiā*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* says: "The *zhā* and *lí* are those [fruits] that are not of good quality. Guo Pu says: "The branches and trunks are all red, the leaves are yellow, the flowers are white, and the fruit is black. The sweet *zhā* grows on Mount Ji."
*Chèn* (pronounced *shàng kǔ jiǎo fǎn*) means "to state clearly.

*Fùyǐ* (pronounced *fù yī qǐ fǎn*) refers to the screen behind the throne. The *Zhou Lǐ* states: "In all cases of enfeoffing a state or appointing a feudal lord, the position [of the ruler] is established behind a *fǔyǐ* (axe-patterned screen). Zheng’s commentary on the *Yí Lǐ* says: "It is like a screen made of silk or plain cloth, decorated with axe designs, used when facing west from the door. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical *hù* (door) and the phonetic *yī* (clothing).

*Mí* (靡): the first character is pronounced *shàng méi pǐ fǎn* (上眉彼反) and the second is *dìng lì fǎn* (亭歷反). The commentary on the *Gōngyáng Zhuàn* by Hé [Guang] states: "To *dí* (覿) means to see. There is also a version written as *mò* (覿), which has the same meaning and gloss. The correct character for the present day follows the radical for "to see" (*jiàn*) and uses *mài* (賣) as its phonetic component.

Regarding *ān* (pronounced *ān* with the *wū* and *cāng* finals): Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states that *ān* refers to a hut (*lú*). The *Guǎngyá* says it is a grass shed. In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, it is composed of the radical *yǎn* (meaning "broad" or "covering") and the phonetic *yǎn*.
Regarding *zǒu cù*: the upper character is pronounced *wū xué* and the lower is *chuāng jiǎo*. The *Kǎoshēng* states that *zǒu cù* describes a state of being narrow and cramped.
Regarding "Dào Zhí zhēng yì fǎn rén míng" (The name of Dào Zhí, who went on an expedition and returned): according to the *Zhuāngzǐ*, he was the younger brother of Liù Xiàhuì.

The character 逺 (*yuǎn*) is pronounced with the initial *shǎng* and final *pīng*. Lìu Zhào’s commentary on the *Guliáng Zhuàn* states that "逺" also means "to distance oneself. According to the *Shuōwén Jiězì*, it is composed of 𡕥 (pronounced *huǒ luè*) above and 人 (person) inside 穴 (cave). 𡕥 is pronounced *huǒ luè*.

Volume Three, Part Three: An Explanation of the Original Biography of Fali. Volume Three. *Jiao* (徼) is pronounced with the initial *gao* (古弔反). It refers to the borders beyond the frontiers. The *Yunquan* states it means "minor paths" or the "frontier barriers of the Man and Yi peoples. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *jiao* (敫) and the phonetic *chi* (彳); the sound of *chi* is *chouyi* (丑亦反).
Jùlù (鉅鹿) is the name of a commandery; the second character is pronounced as qǔ (渠) with a retroflex *r* (上渠語反).

Yuánjīng (袁旍) is the name of a Daoist practitioner; the second character is pronounced as jìng (井) with a retroflex *r* (井情反). Yèqì (噎氣) means to choke on air; the first character is pronounced as yānjié (煙結) with a retroflex *r* (上煙結反).

Regarding the character *zhōng* (終) in the phrase "at the end of all military campaigns": the *Pīcāng* states that *zhōng* means "to perish" or "death. In the standard orthography of the past and present, it should follow the radical *è* (骨, meaning bone) with the phonetic *dōng* (冬). The current form, which follows the radical *mì* (糸), is used interchangeably [with the former]. The pronunciation of *è* is *chǒu gé*.

*Dàng* (蕩): *jiè* (瘵) is pronounced with the *qi* and *ài* finals. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that *jiè* means "sickness. The *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of the radical *nà* (疒), pronounced *nǚ è*, and the phonetic *jì* (祭).

*Lóngduī* (龍堆): *duī* (堆) is pronounced with the *léi* final. Guo Pu says it is a high mound of piled earth. The standard character for ancient and modern times is composed of the radical *tǔ* (土) and the phonetic *zhuī* (隹); it is also written as *tuī* (塠), with the same meaning.

*Lín* (麟): The upper radical is *lì* (栗), with the phonetic component *zhēn* (珍). The *Gōngyáng Zhuàn* states: "The *lín* is a benevolent beast; when a sage-king appears, it arrives at his outskirts. The *Ēr'á* says: "The *jǐn* (麕) has the body of a deer and the tail of an ox, with a single horn; at the tip of the horn there is flesh. Gu Yěwáng says: "The male is called *qí* (麒), the female is called *lín* (麟). The *Shuowén* [explains] it follows *lù* (鹿) as the radical and *lìn* (粦) as the phonetic; it is also written as *jǐ* (𪊺). The lower character is *guǐ* (軌), with the phonetic component *yún* (筠). The *Gōngyáng Zhuàn* states: "There was a *méi* (麋) with horns. Liú Zhào says: "It is a *cháng* (麞) [a type of deer]. The *Máoshī* says: "In the wilds there is a dead *jǐn* (麕). The *Shuowén* says: "This is the ancient form of the character for *jǐn*; it correctly follows *lù* (鹿) as the radical and *quǐn* (囷) in abbreviated form as the phonetic. The vulgar forms are written as *pí* (󰦶), which are identical in meaning.

Li Tan (the "tan" being pronounced with the *gān* rhyme) is Laozi. The *Guoyu* calls him Zhuxia Shi Boyang; the *Shiji* calls him Li Er. Regarding the character *tāo* (to stir): the *Pīcāng* states that *tāo* means *zhù* (to remove).

*Liú-miǎn*: "miǎn" is pronounced *biǎn*. *Tuī-gāng*: "tuī" is pronounced *duì léi*; the *Kǎo Shēng* says it means objects falling downward, to collapse, to ruin. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical *huì* (𨸏) and the phonetic *jiǎn* (󲆪); the pronunciation of *jiǎn* is as above. This is the correct character for ancient and modern usage; the version in the *Chuán* (Tradition) using *tuí* (穨) is incorrect. "Gāng" (綱): "gāng" is pronounced *háng*. *Note on Pronunciation:* * 綿 (miǎn): biǎn * 隤 (tuī): duì léi * 󲆪: jiǎn (same as above) * 穨 (tuí): gē háng (incorrect variant) * 綱 (gāng): háng (variant reading)

*Nü* (覈): Upper radical *shànghéng* (上衡), reversed; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "to examine and verify actual facts. It is composed of the radical *xī* (西) and the phonetic *jiǎo* (敫). *Xī* (西) has the pronunciation *hējia* (呵嫁);
*jiǎo* (敫) has the pronunciation *yào* (藥). *Chī* (郗): Upper character *chǐlí* (恥離); lower character *yìlǐ* (挹󰯌). This is the name of a person.

*Lún-xǔ*: The first character is pronounced *lǜ* with the *chén* (脣) rhyme group; the second is pronounced *xī-yú*. The *Yùnlüè* states that *xǔ* means "to sink. The *Wenzídiǎn* explains it as being composed of the radical *shuǐ* (water) and the phonetic *xū*; it is traditionally written as *xiāo*, which is a vulgar character.

"Bhuai" (壞) [upper radical *pei*, lower *mei*]: The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it refers to unbaked pottery; it is composed of the radical *tu* (earth) and the phonetic *bu*. "Huan" (還) [lower radical *guan*]: "Guai" (詿) [upper *gu*] and "wu" (誤) [lower *gu*].
The former is pronounced with the ancient sound *mai*; the latter is pronounced with the sound *wu gu*.

*Jian* (𦪝): Pronounced *shang* (with the initial *deng* as a variant). The *Shuowen* states: "To tie up or bind. The *Zhou Shu* contains the term "golden *jian*" (*jinjian*). It is composed of the radical *mi* (糸) and the phonetic *zhen* (朕).
*Kua* (窊): Pronounced *yǐguā* (with the initial *yǐ* as a variant). The *Shuowen* states: "A depression; a low-lying, uneven place. It is composed of the radical *xue* (穴) and the phonetic *guā* (瓜).

"Miǎo" (邈): The first character is pronounced *máng* (剝反) and the second has the phonetic value *ěr* (音爾). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that "miǎomiǎo" means "far away. Regarding the correct orthography of this character across ancient and modern times, it is composed of the radical "辵" (*chuò*) and the phonetic "貌" (*mào*). It is incorrect to write it as the plant name "貌" (*mào*).
*Wěi-wěi*: The *Guǎngyùn* states that the sound is *fǎn*; it means "beautiful" and "exerting oneself. It is correctly written as *wěi*.

*Jí shāmén bùbài sú děng shì jí* (A Collection of Matters on Why Śramaṇas Should Not Bow to Laypeople), Six Volumes, with Preface. Volume One: The Preface to the *Jí shāmén bùbài sú yì* (Discourse on Why Śramaṇas Do Not Bow to Laypeople). *Duānchén*: The *Shènzhēn fǎn* (Shèn-true fan) and Jia’s commentary on the *Guōyǔ* state that *chén* refers to the inner chamber. The *Shuōwén* says it is composed of *míán* (roof) and the phonetic component *chén*.

*Sù yǐ* (肅扆): *yǐ* is pronounced *qǐ fǎn*. According to the *Erya*, that which is between the door and the window is called *yǐ*. Guo Pu says it is the east of the window and west of the door. The *Shuowen* states it is composed of the radical *hu* (door) with *yi* as the phonetic.

*Bān xī* (斑屣): *xī* is pronounced *bān fǎn*. The *Shenglei* says it means variegated; the *Xiaolu* says it means a mixture of patterns; the *Dali* says it means a manifest appearance. The *Shuowen Jixun* uses the character *bān* (composed of the radical *dāo*) with a different meaning. The correct form is *biàn*; the *Shuowen* also writes it as *juān*. *Jué* is pronounced *yǎo jué*. Below, *shī* is pronounced *qǐ fǎn*. The *Shenglei* says it is *di*; the *Shuowen* says it is a slipper; it is also written as *xī* or *xiè*.

The character 儁 (jùn) is pronounced with the *zhǔn* rhyme; Xu Shuchong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states that one whose talent exceeds a thousand others is called 儁. Examining its phonetics, it is said to possess extraordinary power and majesty. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of 󲽾 and 倠; however, in current collections of texts, it is mostly written as 俊, which is a vulgar form. The character 凹 (āo) consists of a horizontal bow-shape.

"Chi-niu" (弛紐): This is a reversal of Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan*, which states that "chi" means to loosen (*jie*). According to the *Guangya*, it means to relax (*huan*). The *Shuowen* defines it as composed of the radicals for "bow" and "she"; the latter character is pronounced with the second tone and the phonetic index *jiu*.

"Xing-xun" (星潯): Pronounced with the second tone and the phonetic index *lin*. Xu Shuchong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states that "xun" means a shore or limit (*ya*). The *Shuowen* defines it as being deep on the sides.

*Ti* (with the phonetic *zhào* and *ěr* as variants; the sound is *kǎo*). *Ti* means "to strip off. The *Shuowen* states it is composed of the radical "clothing" (*yī*) and the phonetic "xi" (*xī*); the *Jiwen* writes it as *ti*, which is incorrect.
*Jibin* (with the phonetic *jū* and *lì* as variants) is the name of the kingdom of Jibin.
*Tong xi* (同嬉): Its opposite is *xi* (戲). According to the *Cangjie pian*, it means "playful sport. The *Shuowen jiezi* also writes it as *xi* (娭). *Ai* (曖): *er ai dai* (而哀岱) rhyme.
The *Kaosheng* states that *ai* refers to the radiance of sunlight. The *Shuowen jiezi* takes the radical *ri* (日) and the phonetic *ai* (愛).

Yīn (茵): *yì* (壹) and *lín* (隣) as reversed; Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states it refers to a mat (*yīnrù*). Xià (下): *āi* (哀) and *gài* (蓋) as reversed. In the *Erya*, *ài* (藹) means "dignified bearing" (*róngzhǐ*) and also "abundance. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) with the phonetic element *yè* (謁).
The character *zōng* (悰) is used here as a substitute for the monastic name *sōng* (聳). Regarding the character *sōng*:

it is pronounced with the initial *kō* (反) and the final *shō* (反). It means "to rise high. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "ear" (耳) and the phonetic "sound" (聲); it is also written as 聳.

*Kua* (姱): The pronunciation is *ku* with the tone *kǔ*. According to the *Zílín*, it means "great. In Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci*, it is glossed as "beautiful. The *Shuowén* states that it is composed of the radical *nǚ* (woman) and the phonetic *kuā*; it is also written as *kuā* or *chū*.

*Qiū luè* (秋䗲): "luè" is pronounced with the initial *xìn* (信). It refers to the sound of the firefly; the *Mao Shi* commentary calls it *yì yào*. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical for "life" (*shēng*) and the phonetic *lín*;

it is also written as *lín* or *lìng*. *Chūn wā* (春蛙): "wā" is pronounced with the initial *guā* (瓜) in its voiced form. It is derived from the character *guāi* (乖) in its voiced form. According to the *Shuowen*, *wā* refers to the frog; it is correctly written as *wā* (鼃).
"Chen Xi" (臣翜): "Shan" (翜) is a person's name; "jia" (甲) is a classifier for people. "Kun" (髠):
pronounced with the *ku* and *kun* rhymes; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "kun" means to shave the head, formed from the radical "biao" (hair) and the phonetic "wu" (兀).
"Wang Mi" (王謐): pronounced with the *mi* and *bi* rhymes; a person's name.

*Juàn* (眷): The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry) states it means "to look back"; Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* (Book of Documents) says it means "to gaze. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical 目 (eye) and the phonetic 卷 (abbreviated). The lower character is pronounced *mò biàn*. According to the *Shuowen*, *miàn* (眄) means "to look askance with the eyes partially closed"; it is composed of the radical 目 and the phonetic 丐 (pronounced *mí yǎn*).
*Mí* (㦎): Pronounced *hu-mài-fǎn*. According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means "wisdom. The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "huà.

*Mí* (彌): Pronounced *níng-mì-yí-fǎn*. Zhèng’s commentary on the *Yílǐ* says it means "increasing. The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radical "bow" (*gōng*) and the phonetic "ěr. It is written as *mí* in the *Jíwén*, which is a vulgar character. *Nóng* (濃): Pronounced *xià-nǚ-lóng-fǎn*. The *Shuōwén* states it describes the appearance of being thick or abundant.
*Yíng* (pronounced *wū dìng fǎn*): According to the *Bóyá*, it means to adorn; it is also written as *yìng*. *Mǐàn* (pronounced *zhì mí yǎn fǎn*):

Jia Gongyan’s commentary on the *Guōyǔ* states it is an expression of deep reflection. Liu Zhao’s commentary on the *Gōngyáng* states it means light and thin. In the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical *mì* (silk) and the phonetic *miàn*; it is also written as *mián*.

Regarding "the trap and the snare" (quán tí), the character for "trap" (quán) should properly be written with the radical for "bamboo" (䇶) and the phonetic "quán" (全). Sima Biao’s commentary on the *Zhuangzi* states that the trap is an implement for catching fish. The *Shuowen Jiezi* records it as having the radical for "grass" (艹) and the phonetic "quán," but this is not its correct meaning.

In the *Zuozhuan*, "zongche" (宗轍) is read as zhí (直) and lè (列), contrary to the Du [Yan] commentary; "che" means "wheel tracks. The *Ji-lüe* (集略) writes it as 𨅊 from the radicals "foot" and "man," which is incorrect.

"Jingji" (敬戢) is read as cè (側) and lì (立). In the *Fanzilin* (字林凡), it is said that all stored objects are called "ji" (戢). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (毛詩傳) states that "ji" means "to gather. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "or" (或) with "ji" (咠) as the phonetic; "ji" has the pronunciation qī rù (七入反).

"Hao" (濠) is listed as "gāo" (高) in the *Fanyunlüe* (反韻略), but it refers to the "Hao Bridge" (濠梁). It was the place where Zhuangzi and his wife strolled. Gu Yewang stated that it is the name of a river; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is formed with the radical "water" (水) and the phonetic "hao" (豪).

Regarding the term *xìyáng* (餼羊), Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "living [meat] is called *xì*, while cooked [meat] is called *yōng*. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Yili* defines *xì* as referring to sacrificial animals; it is synonymous with *lìngjì* (廩給, grain-rationing) and means *kuì* (饋, to present food). According to the *Pīcāng*, it means to provide food, and the *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical for "food" (*shí*) and the phonetic element *qì*.
*Tīfà* (Tearing out the hair): Zheng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states that "tī" means to shave the hair; it is correctly written as *tì* (鬄), and in ancient script as *tí* (逖). Volume Two, Part Two:

*Sānmén bù bàisú yì* (Discourse on Why Śramaṇas Do Not Bow to Laypeople), Volume Two. *Dùnshì* (Retreating from the world): The character is pronounced *dùn*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* explains that "dùn" means to flee. Wáng Yì’s commentary on the *Chūcí* says it means to hide. The *Guǎngyá* says it means to avoid. It also means to depart. It is correctly written as *dùn* (遁); it is the same as [the character for] "to hide," or sometimes written as *dùn* (󳏙).

The key character [guàn] is pronounced *huán* in the first tone and *qián* in the fourth tone in the latter instance. According to the *Zhouli*, the Official of the Gates (*Simen*) was charged with "bestowing the tubes and keys" (*guanjian*) for opening and closing the national gates. The *Fangyan* states that in the region east of the Passes, the word for a lock is called *jian*.
*Ji* (pronounced *jī*, with the rhyme of *qí*): According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to lodge as a guest. The *Shuōwén* explains it as composed of the radicals *yǒng* and *jì*;

the *Jíwén* writes it as *jì*, which is an archaic form (*gǔzì*). *Gǔ*: (pronounced *gǔ*, with the rhyme of *wǔ*): In his commentary on the *Lǐjì*, Zhèng notes that those without eyes are called *gǔ*. The *Shuōwén* explains it as composed of the radical *mù* and the phonetic *gǔ*; the lower part is pronounced *sū*. In his commentary on the *Lǐjì*, Zhèng notes that those who have eyes but lack pupils are called *zhēng*. The *Shuōwén* explains this as composed of the radical *mù* and the phonetic *wěi*; the *Jíwén* writes it as *wěi*, which is incorrect.

*Hòu* (餱) [pronounced *hòu*, with the phonetic *gōu* reversed]: The *Mao Shi Zhuan* says it means "dried food"; the *Shuowen Jiezi* says it means "dry food," written with the radical *shi* (food) and the phonetic *hóu*. The *Jiwen* writes it as *hóu* (糇), which is a vulgar character. *Xià* (下) [pronounced *xià*, with the phonetic *lì* and *zhāng* reversed]: Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shangshū* states that "provisions" (*liáng*) refers to stored grain, providing sufficient food. Gù Yěwáng says that *liáng* is "provisions," and it is also written as *liáng* (糧).

Regarding the character *huán* (鸛), the *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (Mao Commentary on the Classic of Poetry) states: "The *huán* is a water bird that delights in long calls. The *Jiān* (Sub-commentary) adds: "When this water bird is about to face cloudy rain, it cries. The *Mu Tiānzǐ Zhuàn* (Annals of King Mu of the State of Tíān) says: "The *huánjī* flies eight hundred *lǐ* in a single day. Guō Pǔ states: "It belongs to the species of the *juānjī* and the *hù*. According to the *Shuōwén*, the character is composed of the radical 鳥 (bird) and the phonetic 雚; the latter has the pronunciation *wén*.

*Nú* (駑): Pronounced *nú* (with the rhyme of *nǔ* and *hú*). According to the *Bóyá*, it refers to a slow or untrained horse. The *Lìjì* states that at the age of three (*sìnián*), one rides a *nú* horse. Gu Yewáng says it is the lowest of the six types of horses.
*Dí* (逷): Pronounced *tìng-lì* (with the rhyme of *tīng* and *lì*). The *Ěryá* says *dí* means "distant. It is correctly written as *tì* (逖).

Lóng-dí (pronounced with the "fú" and "ěr" finals): according to the *Erya*, a large expanse of land is called a *dí*; according to the *Guangya*, a mound without stones is called a *dí*. This is a pictographic character; the composite form written as *bù* is incorrect.

Jìn-bǎo (pronounced with the "qín" and "xìn" finals): the *Cangjie pian* states that *jìn* refers to wealth and goods; the *Shuowen jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "貝" (bèi) and the phonetic "𭴘" (mí).

*Jiē*: Pronounced *mài* (耕) with the tone *fǎn*. According to the *Bóyǎ*, it means "foolishness. According to the *Shuowén*, it refers to "a peasant" (田民), composed of the radical "field" (*tián*) and the phonetic "wáng" (*wáng shēng*).

*Kèng*: Pronounced *hú* (胡) with the tone *dào* (*fǎn*). In the commentary on the *Shàngshū* by Kǒng [Yǎng], it means "to issue commands. The version in the *Jíwén* writes this as *tí*, which is incorrect.
*Dǎng* (讜): Pronounced *dǎng* (朗反). It refers to excellent or upright speech. Gu Yewang states that *dǎng* means direct speech. In the *Mao Shī Zhuàn*, it is said that *yī* (猗) is an exclamation;

the *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical "beast" (*犭*) with the phonetic element "qi" (*奇*), pronounced *xià yǔ zhū* (下與諸反). In the *Lúnyǔ* commentary by Kǒng, it is noted that *yū* (歟) is a particle. The *Yùnlèi Lèi Jié* writes this character as *zhuó* (㺞).

Volume Three, Part Three: A Treatise on the Śramaṇa’s Non-Prostration to Laypeople. *Jian* (pronounced *ju-zhan*): In the *Zhouyi*, "jian" means difficulty. In the *Fangyan*, "jian" refers to stammering; it is a term from the language of Chu. Guo Pu states that it is also a common term in the north. In the *Shenglei*, it is also written as *jia*. The second character, *wo-ge*: Guo Yewang states that "jian" refers to upright speech. The *Guangya* states that "jian" means speech.

Regarding the term *zhú* (躅): it is recorded again according to the phonetic glosses of the *Hànshū*. *Zhú* means "tracks" (*jì*). In the Three Commanderies (*Sānfǔ*), the hoofprints of oxen are called *zhú*. *Lài* (瀨) is pronounced *lái gài*. Regarding *yóu xuān* (輶軒): according to the *Máoshī chuán*, *yóu* refers to a light carriage.

The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical "carriage" (*chē*) with the phonetic element *qiú*; *qiú* has the same sound as in the following line, which is pronounced *xǔ yán*. According to the *Zuǒchuán*, those who ride in *xuān* are the carriages of Great Officers (*dàfū*). The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical "carriage" with the phonetic element *yú*.

"Liao" (寮) has the phonetic value of "diāo" (彫); according to the *Erya*, "liao" means "official. It is also written as "láo" (潦). "Cai" (寀) has the phonetic value of "cǎi" (改); according to the *Erya*, "cai" means "official"; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "mián" (宀) with the phonetic "cǎn" (釆).

"Qiè shè qī lì fǎn ěr yǎ": *Qì* means "to count" (numerous); its pronunciation is *shuò*, and it is also pronounced *jīng-lì-fǎn*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radicals for two, person, mouth, and hand; the character for "hand" (*yòu*) has the pronunciation *shǒu*. This signifies that among Heaven, Earth, and humanity, the mouth and hands constitute what is called *qì* (urgency/abundance).

*Wūlóng* (窊隆): "Wū" is pronounced with the *wūguā* rhyme; the *Shuowen* states that *yá* (𮃹) means "low," following the radical for "cave" (*xué*) and the phonetic *guā*. "Xià" (下) is pronounced with the *lìzhōng* rhyme.

*Jiǔgāi* (九垓): "Gāi" is pronounced with the *gǎihái* rhyme; Xu Shuchong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* notes that these nine *gāi* refer to the nine heavens, following the radical for "earth" (*tǔ*) and the phonetic *hài*.

*Chán* (慙): The *Záhán* (雜含) reads it as a reversed character; the *Shuowén* states it means shame (*chánkuì*). It is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "zhǎn" (斬), with the lower part pronounced *tiānlì* (天曆). Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* says it means fear (*jù*). The *Màoshī Zhuàn* says it means *táodāo* (忉忉); *dāo* (忉) is pronounced *dāo*. The *Shuowén* states it is composed of the radical "heart" and the phonetic "yì" (易).

*Tí* (稊) and *pài* (稗): *tí* has the phonetic *dì* (弟); according to the *Erya*, *tí* resembles *pài*, also named *yīng* (英). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *huo* (禾) with *dì* as its phonetic; *pài* has the phonetic *pí* (卑). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan* states that *pài* resembles grain but is not grain. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *huo* (禾) with *pí* as its phonetic.

*Diáo* (凋): The phonetic component is *niǎo*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "carving and engraving patterns. Its standard form is *diāo*; the *Erya* uses *diāo*, and the archaic form is *diāo*.

*Qiè* (󳍿): The phonetic component is *qiān* (or *zhuàn*). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* says, "*Qiè* means to steal. The *Shuowen Jiezi* derives it from the radical for "cave" (*xué*) and the character *niàn* (廿), with *mǐ* (米) as the phonetic; the *Jiwen* (集文) derives it from the radical for "board" (*zhuāng*) and forms it as *qiè*, which is incorrect.
The Heavenly regard for his exhaustion has already been explained above. Regarding *kū* (刳), the reading is *ku* (苦) with the final rhyme *gu* (姑);

Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states it means "to carve and strip. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as being composed of the radical "knife" (*dāo*) and the phonetic "kuā" (*kuā*). Regarding *zé* (斮), the reading is *zé* (側) with the final rhyme *lüè* (略); Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states it means "to cut off," while the *Erya* says "to pare," and the *Guangya* says "to sever. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as being composed of the radical "axe" (*jīn*) and the phonetic "xī" (*xī*).
*Fú* (靡靡陂反) means "to waste" (*fèi*). *Bó* (邦角反):

Sīmǎ Biāo’s commentary on the *Zhuāngzǐ* states that "bó" means "disordered and inconsistent. The *Shuōwén* says: "Bó" means "impure"; it is composed of the radical "horse" (*mǎ*) and the phonetic "yáo" (*爻*).

*Zanfu* (簪紱): The *Cangjie pian* states that *zan* means a hairpin (*jī*); men use it to secure their crowns, while women use it as a head ornament. "Yan" (pronounced with the *shàn* final) means "profound" (*bóyǎ*) and "to contemplate maturely. The *Ěryá* says it means "constant. This refers to the passage in the *Shàngshū*: "The constant patterns (*yílún*) were thereby arranged. Zhōng (衷): Pronounced *zhōu* with a retroflex *d* (竹隆反). The *Shuowen* states that it means "sincerity" (*chéng*). It is composed of the radical "clothing" (*yī*) and the phonetic "middle" (*zhōng*).

The entry in the *Jiwen* [which reads] *zhēn* is incorrect. Fù (復): Pronounced *rèn* with a level tone (*rén zhèn fǎn*). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* says: "Fù means the wooden prop used for a carriage. The *Shuowen* states it means "to obstruct a carriage. *Xuān-péng* (翾鵬): "Blood" (*xuán*) is reversed; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "the flight of a small insect," with the phonetic component *huíng*. The lower radical is read as *pú-téng*. The *Zhuangzi* states: "In the Northern Ocean there is a fish named Kūn; Kūn transforms and becomes a bird called Péng."
The *yì* (逸) bird: the *jiǎ* (賈) commentary on the *Guóyuè* states that *yàn* is another name for *yàn* (鴈), or it is written as *àn* (鴳).

*Shān* (芟): the rhyme is *xián* (銜). The *Máoshī* says "to cut down weeds. The *Shuōwén* [gives the character] with the radical *cǎo* (草) and the phonetic *shū* (殳); the lower part is read as *jì* (計). *Tì* (薙): according to Zheng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì*, it means to cut the grass close to the ground and burn it so that the grass does not grow again; when heavy rain falls upon such ground, it becomes fertile and suitable for plowing and sowing. The *Shuōwén* [gives the character] with the radical *cǎo* (草) and the phonetic *zhì* (雉).
*Dì* (with the phonetic *fǎn* [fan]) refers to the category of sounds; *dìguǒ* (蒂果) means the nose. *Xià* (下) with the phonetic *fāngwén* (芳文) means fragrance according to the *Fānyán* (方言).

*Sāoshǒu* (搔首): *sāo* (搔) is pronounced *xiāodāo* (㛮刀); Xu Shuchong’s commentary on the *Huáihánzǐ* states it means "to scratch," while the *Shuōwén* says it means "to scrape," being composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic *zão* (蚤).

"Ménxīn" (捫心) means "to touch with the hand"; it is read as *mòu* and *bēn*. It is explained that it means "to feel with the hands"; according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "mén" (門).

"Huīgān" (隳肝) is read as *xū* and *guī*. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "huī" means "to destroy"; according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radicals "ěr" (爾) and "suí" (隋) as its phonetic.

"Yì" (叡) [is pronounced *yuè* with the *sui* (歲) rhyme]. Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that it means "bright"; the *Guangya* says it means "wisdom"; Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* says it means "sage. The *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of the radicals for "to think" (*chuan*) and "eye," with "valley" (*gu*) abbreviated as the phonetic component. The archaic form is written as 睿, the *Zhouwen* as 󳎳, and the *Jiwen* as 󳐫. It is not the character 𣦻, which has the pronunciation *zài* (在).

In the *Huai-yan*, "yuan" is reversed to "quan"; examining the phonology, it says it means "to extend benefits. The *Shuowen* states: "Yan (lead) is a blue metal; it takes 'jin' as its radical and 'yan' as its phonetic.

In the *Wan-lei*, "lai" is reversed to "dai"; the *Yunchuan* states that "lai" is a type of herb. Gu Yewang’s *Yupian* states it belongs to the genus "hao" (mugwort); "lai-hao" and "zhi-hao" are both types of mugwort. The *Shuowen* [further] states it takes "cao" as its radical and "lai" as its phonetic.

*Tiǎn* (靦): In the *Tiāndiǎn* (天典), it is glossed as "the face feeling ashamed. In the *Yùnyīng* (韻英), it is glossed as "the face feeling abashed. It is also written as 𩉊, 󳆥, or 𡆎. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that when one is humiliated, the face is filled with shame. The *Shuowén* (說文) defines it as "the appearance of seeing," composed of the radical 面 and the phonetic 見.

*Niǎn* (pronounced with the female radical *jiǎn*): The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "the face blushing with shame. It is composed of the radical *chì* (red) and the phonetic *jí*; the pronunciation of *jí* is *zhǎn*.

[The claim that it is composed of the radical] *pí* (skin) is incorrect. Volume 4, Part 4: *Jishashenbaisu yi* (Discourse on the Śramaṇa Not Bowing to the Laity), Volume 4. *Pèi*: The name of a commandery; pronounced with the male radical *fù* and *gài*.

*Chōng* (沖) means profound; *jì* (寂) means quiet and still. According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to a soundless state. In ancient times it was written as 󲚌 or 𡧯; nowadays, the common form is used as 寂. *Jìn* (紉): *nǚ* (女) and *cán* (󰂿) are the phonetic components. Guo Yewang states that *jìn* refers to stringing together threads.

Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Fangyan* notes that it is also written as 線 (*xiàn*), meaning to thread a needle. The *Guoyaya* states that *jìn* means to sew or stitch. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical for silk (*mì*) with the phonetic *rèn* (刃). The lower part, *zǐ* (滓) and *jī* (基), is the phonetic. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* says that *jìn* (帛) is black-colored silk. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical for silk with the phonetic *lè* (󳈌); the sound of *lè* is the same as *jìn*. The *Jiwen* writes it as 緇, which is a vulgar character.

*Kixiang* (稽顙): The first character is pronounced *shang xi li fan* (上溪禮反). The *Kaosheng* (考聲) states that it refers to bowing so that the head reaches the ground and further reaches the hands. It is also written as *zhang* (󲙚), and the *Boya* (博雅) writes it as *zhang* (󲙚). The second character is pronounced *sang lang fan* (桑朗反). According to the *Fangyan* (方言), *xiang* (顙) means the forehead. He Xiu’s commentary on the *Gongyang zhuan* states: "Kixiang refers to knocking one's head upon the ground."

*Gǔ* (drum): Upper radical *gū* (five strokes), meaning "to move. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of *qǐ* and *dǎo* (sound *tǎo*). The *Jiwen* erroneously uses *pí* to form *gǔ*. The lower radical *zhù* (sound *zhūshù*) has the phonetic *zǐyè*. According to the *Mao Shi Zhuan*, *jiá* is a vessel for propelling a boat; it is also a paddle, and is also written as *yī*.

*Háng* (in *zhōuháng*, "boat"): *hú* and *láng* are reversed; *háng* is a name for a boat. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical 舟 (*zhōu*) and the phonetic 元 (*yuán*). The *Jiwen* writes it as 𮎃, which is a vulgar character. *Tàn* (in *tànzé*, "to investigate"): *tā* and *hán* are reversed.

According to the *Shuowen*, *tàn* means to taste or try, taking its meaning from the hand radical and the phonetic 罙 (*mí*; the sound is *shēn*). Below is 仕 (*shì*) and 責 (*zé*). Liu Xian’s commentary on the *Zhouyi* states that *zè* refers to the ultimate depth of the profound. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical 𦣞 (*jiǎo*) and the phonetic 責 (*zé*). The *Jiwen* writes it as 賾, which is a vulgar character.

*Dàng* (the "dù" in *duō* reversed): According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to traverse what one goes toward," and also "to pass beyond. It is composed of the radical *mián* (roof) and the phonetic *shí*. *Yǎo*: According to Guo's commentary on the *Erya*, it means "profound stillness.

According to the *Shuowen*, it means "deep and far-reaching. It is composed of the radical *xué* (cave) and the phonetic *yòu*. *Míng* (lower part *mò píng* reversed): The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states it means "night. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "dark and obscure. It is composed of the radicals *yuè* (sun/moon) and *liù* (six), signifying that after sixteen days the moon begins to wane, with *mìng* as the phonetic. It is composed of the radical *mì* (canopy) and the phonetic *mìng*.
The character *yí* (嶷) [is pronounced with the initial *shǔ* and the final *lì*]. The commentary states: "The upper radical signifies the appearance of a mountain peak;

the lower radical, read as *zhǐ*, signifies clarity. According to the *Kǎo Shēng*, it describes the appearance of water being limpid; according to the *Shuō Wén*, it is composed of the radical *shuǐ* (water) and the phonetic *shèn*."

*Niù* (six repetitions of the character for "gold woman"): Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that *niùní* refers to a blush of shame appearing on the face. The *Guoyá* says it means "sorrowful sighing. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "heart" (*xin*) with the phonetic element "shèn" (*shēn*).

*Chūráo* (蒭蕘): The first character is pronounced *cè jù* (測俱反) and the second is *jiǎo yáo* (皎堯反). The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (毛詩傳) states that *chūráo* refers to grass and firewood. *Zūnzǔ* (樽爼): The first character is pronounced *zǔ kūn* (祖昆反).

Zeng’s commentary on the *Zhōu Lǐ* identifies it as a vessel for holding wine; the *Shuōwén* writes it as *zūn*, also as *zuì*, and also as *zhuǒ*. The second character is pronounced *zé suǒ* (側所反). Kǒng’s commentary on the *Lùn Yǔ* identifies *zǔ* as a ritual vessel; according to the *Fāngyán*, it is a wooden stand for meat. The *Shuōwén* explains it as consisting of half a piece of meat placed upon the character *qiě*.

[The character] 󳉃 (xuán): "To hear" (from the *Cāngjié piān*). [The character] 󳉂 (xuán): "To hang a written notice for something sought" (from the *Shuōwén*). Also, "idle talk" (from the *Shuōwén*). Furthermore, "speech that is not true," formed with the radical 言 and the phonetic 敻. In the *Jí*, it is also written as 󳉂, which does not form a valid character.

*Jiē*: *xī* (頰) reversed; in the *Han Shi*, it means "to moisten thoroughly" (*zhān chè*) and "to pervade. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* says it means "to penetrate" (*dá*). The *Shuowen* states it is composed of "water" (*shui*) and "jiā" (*jiá*). *Xù*: *yōng* (榮) reversed; *xù* is pronounced *xìng* (兄) or *yù* (域). In the *Mengzi*, it means "to dwell within boundaries. The *Shuowen* says it means "to enclose" (*fēng*). It may be written with "earth" (*tǔ*) or with the phonetic "hóng" (*héng*).

"Colorful patterns" (*cǎixiàn*): the term *xiàn* (絢) is glossed in the *Lunyu* as "the appearance of ornamental patterns. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Yili* states that when colorful patterns are formed, it is called *xiàn*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "silk" (*mì*) and the phonetic element "ten" (*xún*).
*Kaniṣka* (the *ni* is pronounced with a retroflex *ṛ*, as in the Sanskrit royal title).

*Qīn yú* (the *yú* is pronounced with a retroflex *u*, as noted in the *Zhuo zhuan*; "qū" means to bend; according to the *Shuowen jiezi*, it means to wind, composed of the radical "silk" [糸] and the phonetic "yú").

*Bi* (之蹕): *bīn mì* (賓蜜). Zheng [Yuzhi] states that in the *Zhouli*, *bi* means to stop passersby to clear the road, similar to the "jing-bi" (police patrol) of the present day. The *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of the radical "foot" (*zu*) with the phonetic "bi.

*Ning* (凝): *yú líng* (魚陵); the following character is *xiě xuán* (血縣). Liu Zhao’s commentary on the *Guliang Zhuan* states that *ning* means "deep and far-reaching. (Měng and Dèng, with the phonetic *fǎn*) Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that it means "stupefaction. It is derived from the sound *kǎo*; it signifies shame. It is also written as *mèng*.

*Xìn* (釁): Pronounced *xǔ* (許) with the final *fǎn* (覲). Duan’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that *xìn* means "guilt. The *Shuowen* says it is composed of *fēn* (分) and *yǒu* (酉); the *Jíwén* (集文) writes it as *xiàn* (𦍑), which is incorrect.

*Tīngzhǔ* (聽矚): Pronounced *zhōng* (鍾) with the final *rú* (辱). The *Yùnlüè* (韻略) states that *zhǔ* means "to look. The *Shuowen* says it is composed of *mù* (目) and has *shǔ* (屬) as its phonetic; the *Jíwén* writes it as *zhǔ* (矚), which is a vulgar character.

*Huánzhōng* (寰中): "Slippery Pass" (*huànguān*). This refers to the commentary by Liu Zhao on the *Guliang Zhuan*. *Huán* means the royal domain within a thousand *li*. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *mián* (roof) with the phonetic *guān*.
*Chǐfǎ* (弛法): "poised" (*shǐzhǐ*); this has already been explained previously.

"Wen" (紊) is pronounced *wen* (with the final *-fan*). Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that it means "to disorder. "Er" (而) is pronounced *yu* (with the final *-bi*).

Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states it means "to flow away. According to the *Fangyan*, it also means "speed. It is composed of the radical "water" (*shui*) with "yue" as its phonetic; the pronunciation of "yue" is *yue*.

*Xún* (pronounced *xún*, with the radical for "to follow" and the phonetic *chuān*). The *Bóyǎ* states: "To tame birds and beasts; to make them docile and familiar. Sīmà Biāo’s commentary on the *Zhuāngzǐ* says: "To follow obediently. The *Shuōwén* explains it as "following," with the character *mǎ* (horse) as the semantic component and *chuān* as the phonetic.

*Chuài* (not *chuǎi*): In the *Zhuozhuan*, it means to estimate; according to the *Shuowen*, it means to measure. It is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic element "shuì" (abbreviated).

*Bì* (pronounced *biàn*, with the rhyme of *miè*): Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that this refers to the painted *bì* pheasant, which is what is called the "huachong" (flowering insect). The *Shanhai jing* says, "Mount Hua has many red *bì*. Guo’s commentary notes it is a species of pheasant with a red crest, a golden back, a green head, and a tail containing bright red feathers. The *Erya* says it resembles a mountain fowl but is smaller. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* says, "The *bì* is a mountain pheasant that arrives at the beginning of autumn and enters the water at the beginning of winter, where it transforms into a clam. The *Shuowen jiezi* takes the radical of bird (*niǎo*) and the phonetic of *biè*; the latter is pronounced *piàn*. The *Shuowen* defines *biàn* as a ceremonial crown.

Regarding "ruòchén" (weak-toothed): the *Lìjì* states, "At twenty, one is called ruòguàn. The character "chén" (齓) is pronounced as *chūjǐn* (初謹反). Zeng Qi’s commentary on the *Zhōuwǔlǐ* says: "For males, the eighth year is called 'huǐchǐ' (teeth falling out), which is termed 'chén'. The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radical "tooth" (齒) with "qī" (七) as its phonetic component; the version in the *Jíwén* (集文) that uses "chén" (齓) is incorrect.

"Qianshou" (黔首) means "the common people"; according to the *Liji* commentary by Zheng Xuan, it refers to the populace. In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "black" (黑) with the phonetic "jin" (今).
"Dànbó" (澹泊) is read as tán (談) pò (濫); the second character is pronounced bàng (傍) bō (博).

"Shen-shen" (莘莘) refers to what is attained; the *Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry* states that "shen-shen" means "in great numbers," and it also means "long. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "grass" (艹) with "xin" (辛) as its phonetic.
"Chang-yi" (長撎) is pronounced "ji-yi" (依計反); according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to bow respectfully" (揖揖), composed of the radical "hand" (手) with "yi" (壹) as its phonetic.

*Xi* (pronounced *si*, with the *zi* rhyme): Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that *xi* means a seal; Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* says it refers to the sealing of documents; Ying Shao’s commentary on the *Hanshu* says it means trust (*xin*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "jade" (*yu*) and the phonetic "er" (*er*), with the final tone being *gao* (*hao*). The *Erya* defines *ge* as "cautious"; in ancient times this was the title of kings, and today it is used for careful instructions.

Furthermore, regarding the character 殫 (dàn): Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjìng* states it means "to exhaust" (*yàn*). The *Shuōwén* states it means "end" or "explanation," being composed of the radical 攴 (zhī) and the phonetic 肅 (sù). The *Jíwén* erroneously writes it as 殫 (dān), using the radical 犬 (quǎn).

*Kuì* (愧) means "to feel shame" (*kuì-cán*) according to the commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan*; it is "shame" (*chǐ*) according to the *Bóyá*. The *Shuōwén* writes it as *kuì* with the radical *cáng* and the phonetic *fǎn*. The *Shuōwén* states that *zuò* (怍) means "to be ashamed" (*cán*) and is composed of the radical *xīn* (心) with the phonetic *zhà* (乍).
"Yí" (猊) refers to the five *xi* (猞), which are lions; it is sometimes written as "jǔ" (麂).
"Shān" (山) with the phonetic "hóng" (紅) is a scribal error for "cōng" (蔥) as found in the *Jíwén* (集文). 6.

*Yú* (諛): The *Shuowen* states that "yú" means flattery; it is composed of the radical "speech" (言) with "yú" as the phonetic. The *Jiwen* writes it as *yù* (諭), which is a vulgar character.

*Mò* (𧶝): Pronounced *zhòng* (眾) and *mò* (莫) and *hòu* (侯). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* says it means to purchase. The *Shuowen* states it is composed of the radical "treasure" (貝) with "mǎo" (卯); the *Jiwen* writes it as *mò* (𧴵), which is a vulgar error.

The character *pǐ* (偶批, pinyin: pǐ) is pronounced with the tone of *kǎo* (考); it means "match" (*pǐ*) or "companion" (*bǐ*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *fēi* (妃) means "consort"; it is composed of the radical *nǚ* (女) and the phonetic *bǐ* (𣬉), where *bǐ* is pronounced *bēijī* (卑雞).

The character *zhàng* (󳐘杖) is pronounced *gān* (甘). The *Yupian* states that it refers to a hollow bamboo; colloquially it is called "full-bamboo" (*mǎnzhōng zhú*), originating from the southern regions and suitable for use as a staff. The correct orthography consists of the radical *zhú* (竹) and the phonetic *hán* (函).
*Chù* (pronounced *chūn lǜ fǎn*): According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means "sewing. The *Shuōwén* states that it is composed of the radical "silk" (*miè*) with the phonetic "chūn.
*Lún xǔ* (pronounced *xiāng yǔ fǎn*): The *Yùnquán* states it means "the appearance of dew," composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*).
"Armor of Patience" (*rěn kǎi*): "Armor" (*kǎi*) means a coat of mail; it is composed of the radical for metal with the phonetic *qǐ*, or it may be pronounced in the third tone (*gài*).

"To don armor" (*guàn kǎi*): this refers to wearing armor; it is also written as *jiāo* or *zhuó*. "Armor of Endurance" (*kùn kǎi*): this refers to wearing armor; it is also written as *jiǎo* or *zhuó*.
*Tiemo* (慴魔): In the *Erya*, "jù" (懼) means to be afraid; it is also written as *zhè* (懾). *Dou-sǒu* (斗藪): The upper character is pronounced "dòu";

the *Kaosheng* states that "dou-sǒu" means to shake and toss, or to brush away one's garments. Alternatively, it is said that *tóutuó* (頭陁) means "dou-sǒu," which refers to afflictions (*kleśa*); it signifies having few desires and being content.
*Zhé* (衣上占葉反): According to the *Bóyǎ*, it means to fold or pleat garments; according to the *Shuōwén*, it is derived from the radical *yī* (clothing) and the phonetic *niè*.
*Zīzī* (孜孜子思反): In the commentary on the *Shàngshū*, Kǒng [Yǔ] states that it means unremitting diligence; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means urgency or haste.

*Yǔ* (𤼙傴): The character is pronounced with the *quán* (拳) rhyme and refers to a disease of the hands and feet. The *Jíwén* (集文) records it as *luán* (攣), which is also interchangeable. The *Bóyá* (博雅) states that *yǔlóu* (傴僂) means a curved spine. *Chǐ yǔ* (齒齲): Pronounced with the *qū* (驅) rhyme;
according to the *Shuōwén* (說文), it refers to the disease of decayed teeth, composed of the radical "tooth" (*chǐ*) and the phonetic "yǔ" (*yǔ*).
Tanzi (郯子) was a man of the Dan (淡) surname from the Nanfan (南反) region who specialized in bird divination (*zhan*).

Regarding the character *xunxun* (恂恂): Wang Su’s commentary on the *Lunyu* states that it denotes an appearance of being "warm and respectful"; the *Guangya* says it means "reverence"; Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* says it means "constantly trembling"; and the *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "heart" (*xin*) with the phonetic element "shun" (*xun*).

The character *gǔ* (蠱) has the upper radical *yīn* (音) as *gǔ*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "Gǔ means poison. In the *Zhouyi*, there is the hexagram Gǔ; the lower character is pronounced *jiāo* (交) with the reverse tone.

It consists of six lines (*biān*). *Tán qiào* (談誚): *qiào* is pronounced *yáo* (曜) with the reverse tone. Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states: "Qiào means to reprimand one another. The *Cangjie pian* states it means to scold (*hē*) and also to harass (*niǎo*). According to the *Fangyan*, in the regions between Qi, Chu, Song, and Wei, they call "reproach" (*ràng*) "qiào"; it is also written as *qiáo* (譙).

*Dù* (都故反): The *Biographies of King Mu of Tianzi* states that it refers to book-eating insects; the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as an insect within the inner bark of wood. *Míng* (覔瓶反) and *té* (下鄧得反):

The commentary on the *Mao Shi* states that those which eat the heart of the grain seedlings are called *míng*, and those which eat the leaves of the seedlings are called *té*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes this with the character 󲻋, while the *Jiwen* writes it as 󳇧; these are errors.

*Bāhóng* (八紘): Pronounced *mèng* (萠) according to Xu [Zhu]. The *Huáinánzǐ* states that the "eight *hóng*" refers to the eight directions. In the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical *mì* (糸) with *hóng* (厷) as the phonetic component.

*Pányù* (盤蔚): Pronounced *yūn* (氳). The *Cāngjiépian* states that *yù* (蔚) means "ornamental patterns" and also "abundance. In the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical *qǒng* (廾) with *wèi* (尉) as the phonetic component.
*Mí* (糜): Pronounced *měi* (悲反) and *biān* (反). The *Shuowen* states it means "millet porridge.

*Yán* (埏): Pronounced *xié* (形) and *lián* (設連反). Xu’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states: "To mold clay (*liùtǔ*) into vessels. The *Shuowen* explains that it is composed of the radical "earth" (*tǔ*) with the phonetic element "tíng" (*tíng*).

*Dùn* (塵): Pronounced *tóng lù fǎn*. The *Cāngjié piān* states it means "dirt" (*gòu*). The *Shuowén* says it means "to hold dirt"; it is composed of the radical *hēi* (black) with the phonetic *mài*. *Yǐ* (扆): Pronounced *yī qǐ fǎn*.

In the *Zhoulǐ*, Zheng’s commentary states: "The *yǐ* is called *fǔ*; it is embroidered silk with black patterns, using crimson and dark purple as its base material. The form of the *yǐ* is like a folding screen. In the *Yílǐ*, Zheng’s commentary states: "It is like a folding screen made of plain silk, featuring axe-patterns (*fǔ*) to manifest majesty. The *Shuowén* says it is composed of the radical *hù* (door) with the phonetic *yī*. *Líu* (旒): Pronounced *xià liǔ yóu fǎn*. The *Máoshī chuán* says it refers to the tassels of the ceremonial cap. Gù Yěwáng states that *líu* is the same as *yóu*. In the *Lǐjì*, it is said: "The Son of Heaven wears the *yùzǎo* (jade-crested cap) with twelve *líu*. The *Shuowén* says it is composed of the radical *yú* with the phonetic *lǜ*. The character *yú* is pronounced *yǎn*, and *lǜ* is pronounced *liú*.

*Fūcòu* (膚腠): *Còu* is pronounced as *cāng hòu* (倉候) according to Zheng’s commentary on the *Yǐlǐ*. He states that *còu* refers to the texture of the skin (*fū lǐ*). According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "flesh" (*ròu*) with the phonetic element "zòu.

*Qídié* (耆耋): *Dié* is pronounced as *tián jié* (田結). The *Erya* defines *dié* as "old. The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* says, "Eighty years of age is called *dié*. Sūn Yánzi states that the facial complexion of an old man becomes like iron. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "old" (*lǎo*).

"Shì biàn" (式抃): Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that "shì biàn" means to clasp one's hands together. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "Biàn" refers to clapping the hands; it is composed of the radical "hand" (手) with the phonetic "biàn" (卞). It is also written as "pèn" (拚).
*Chui* (楚箠): Pronounced *zhui* (隹累反). According to the *Shuowen*, it means to strike with a staff; it is written with the radical for bamboo (*zhu*), or alternatively as *chui*.

*Qing* (罄): Pronounced *jing* (輕逕反). According to the *Erya*, it means "exhausted" or "all gone. According to the *Shuowen*, it is written with the radical for jars (*fan*). Its phonetic is *keng* (音口耕反), and the second character is pronounced *zhiyao* (子藥反). According to the *Zishu*, *jiao* (爝) refers to a torch made of *ju* grass. The *Shuowen* states that it means to sweep away evil spirits with fire; it is written with the radical for fire (*huo*).

*Yuan* (淵): Pronounced *wu* (烏) with the *xuan* (玄) final. The *Shuowen* states that "a deep pool" (*yuan shui shen ye*) is written with the radical for water and the phonetic *yan* (𣶒). When reciting temple names, it is pronounced as *quan* (泉). The *Shanhaijing* calls it a "ravine" (*he xi ye*), and the *Erya* calls it a "void" (*xu ye*). The *Shuowen* further states it is a "ditch" (*gou ye*), written with the radicals for *jian* (󲘫) and *gu* (谷). The *Jiwen* (集文) also records the form written with the radical for earth (*tu*) as *fu* (󳐦), which is likewise acceptable.

The *Wenzi Dianshuo* states that "Cai" (蔡) means "harmony" (*yinhe*), composed of the "heart" radical and the phonetic "sound" (*yīn*). Cai Yin is a personal name.

Regarding "Luoyi" (雒邑), "luo" is pronounced *lánggè*. The *Liu Xiang Dianyue* states that the Han dynasty takes fire as its virtue (*huode*); since water overcomes fire, the "water" radical was removed and the "jui" (*zhuī*) radical was added instead.

*Chuìhèn* (懟恨): The first character, *chuì*, is pronounced with the initial *chuí* (classifying it as a retroflex). The *Erya* states that *chuì* means resentment. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "duì" (*duì*).

*Bùquān* (不悛): The second character, *quān*, is pronounced with the initial *quān*. Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that *quān* means to reform or change. According to the *Shuowen*, it means to improve; it is composed of the radical "heart" and the phonetic "jùn" (*jùn*), which is pronounced with the initial *qīxún*.

Regarding "Gǒnglóng on Yútíng Lake," the *Yùnwén* states that "Yù" is the name of a commandery. The *Biography of Guō Pǔ* in the *Jìn Shū* says that "Yù" is also the name of a pavilion (*tíng*). According to the *Jùn Guó Zhì*, which examines maps and records, there is Yútíng Lake in Yúzhāng Commandery. This has already been explained in the *Shēngyì* commentary on the internal scriptures.

Regarding "praise" (zàn): according to the *Shìmíng* (Explanations of Names), "praise" means to extol the beauty of a person; the *Wénzìdiǎn* (Dictionary of Characters) states that "praise" is synonymous with lauding one's virtuous qualities. It is composed of the radical "speech" (言) and the phonetic "zàn," which shares the same pronunciation as the preceding character. Regarding "chanting" (bài): it refers to the chanting of Sanskrit sounds (*brahman*). It is composed of the radical "mouth" (口) and the phonetic "bèi. *Note: The text contains phonetic transcriptions for the characters 贊 (zàn) and 唄 (bài). "Kneeling for a long time" (*chángjǔ*) refers to the "strange ant" (*qíyǐ*). The *Zhuāngzǐ* states: "Lifting the body, kneeling, and bowing with clasped hands are the rites of a minister. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To kneel for a long time" (*jǔ chángguì*)—it takes the radical 足 and the phonetic 忌; it is also written as 󳎞.
