The *Shuōwén* defines it as a *qiè* (box), formed with the radical for wood and the phonetic "xián. In the transmitted texts it is written as "hán," which is also an ancient character used in common parlance.

Regarding *máo* (spear) and *dùn* (shield): *máo* is pronounced *gǔhóu* (反). Zheng’s commentary on the *Shijing* states it is "my weapon. The *Gongji Ji* says, "The *qiú-máo* (long spear) is four chi long. The *Shuowen* says, "A *máo* is twenty zhang long; it is built upon the war chariot and is a pictographic character. In archaic script, it is written with the *jīn* (metal) radical as 𨥨, or with the *gē* (halberd) radical as 𢦵. In the commentaries, it is written with the *móu* (ox horn) radical as 鉾; its phonetic and semantic glosses are identical, though it is a vulgar character. Regarding *dùn* (shield), it is pronounced *zhǔn* (反). Zheng’s annotation to the *Zhouli* says, "A *dùn* is that which can serve as a protective screen. According to this, the *dùn* is what we call a *pái* (plaque/shield) today. The *Shuowen* says, "A *dùn* is a *fá* (buckler); it is used to protect the body and shield the eyes; it is a pictographic character. *Dǎng* (the second character) is pronounced *dài*.

*Tu* (圖): In the *Shangdu* (上度), it is pronounced as *nu* (奴) with a retroflex (*fan*). In the *Zuozhuan*, it refers to paintings; it also means a plan or model. Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that "tu" refers to the terminology for examining performance. He’s commentary on the *Gongyangzhuan* says it means calculation. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "painting and calculating difficulties," composed of the radical *kou* (口) and the phonetic *tu* (󲅭); the pronunciation of *tu* (󲅭) is *tan* (徒難), meaning difficulty. It is a transitive character. Below, it is pronounced as *chi* (楚譖) with a retroflex. The *Cangjie pian* says "chen" (讖) means verification. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as being composed of the radical *yan* (言) and the phonetic *xian* (韱); the pronunciation of *xian* (韱) is *qian* (僉).

"Hunmo" (惛漠): The first character, "hun" (惛), is pronounced with the *shu* radical and the *hu* and *kun* finals (*hūn*). The Commentary on the Book of Documents (*Shangshu zhuyi*) states it means "confused and disordered. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Hun means not clear-sighted; it is composed of the 'heart' radical and the phonetic 'hun' (*liǎo*, pronounced *xià*). The second character, 'mo' (漠), is pronounced with the *bó* and *pó* finals (*mò*). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Erya* states: 'Mo refers to quiet observation. The *Chuci* says: 'Desiring to be silent and still, one cuts off all traces. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines 'mo' as the dark and remote desert of the north; it is composed of the 'water' radical and the phonetic 'mo'."

*Qiāng*: An excellent strategy; it is a character contested for its meaning. The *Yǔnshū* states that *qiāng qiāng* is the sound of footsteps. The *Shuowén* says it is composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic "cāng. *Zhēn*: Upper part read as *zhí lín*. Guō’s commentary on the *Eryā* states:

"A *zhèn* refers to a block of wood used for hewing. The *Cāngjiépiān* calls it a *fū* (axe). Examining the sound, it refers to a stone for pounding clothes. It is composed of the radical "stone" (*shí*) and the character *zhèn*; it is identical to the character *zhēn*. The *Wenzìdiǎn* says it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "shèn. The *Zìshū* further records it as written with the radical "zhī" (*zhī*), forming *zhèng*, or as *kū*; the pronunciation and glosses are all the same. *Chuì*: Lower part read as *zhuī*. The *Fāngyán* says: "A *chuī* is heavy. Examining the sound, it refers to a *qì chuī* (hammer). The *Wenzìdiǎn* explains it is composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic "zhuī," and is also written with "chuí" (*chuí*), forming *chuí*; the pronunciation is the same. The version in the *Chuánwén* uses *chuí*, which is a vulgar character.

*Kē* (苛) means "tyrannical cruelty. Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states it means "harsh and cruel"; the *Boyá* states it means "wrathful"; the *Guǎngyá* states it means "oppressive vexation. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) with the phonetic "kě" (*kě*). The reading as *hè* (荷) in the transmitted text is incorrect.
Sun Chuo (孫綽), courtesy name Xingong (興公), was a person of the Jin dynasty who served as a Palace Attendant (侍中).

The character *chū* (欻) is pronounced with the initial *xūn* (薰) and the final *lù* (律); according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "sudden" (*hū*) and is composed of the radical "mouth" (*qiàn*) with the phonetic element "fire" (*yán*).

The character for *Dūnhuáng* (燉煌) has the radical *shàng* (上) with the phonetic *dùn* (遁) and the reversed form *hún* (魂), while the lower part is pronounced *huáng* (皇). The *Hànshū* states that Dūnhuáng Commandery is Shāzhōu; it was established in the first year of Emperor Wǔ’s reign by dividing Jìquán Commandery. Dú Lín’s commentary notes that Dūnhuáng is considered the ancient Guāzhōu. According to the standard characters of antiquity and modern times, both characters for "Dūnhuáng" are *xíngshēng* (形聲) characters, with both components following the radical "fire" (*huǒ*).

"Rinse" (shù): the water radical with the phonetic *yòu* (read as *yǒu*). The character dictionaries state that "rinse" means to agitate and cleanse. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "washing and rinsing the mouth. It is composed of the water radical and the phonetic *sòu* (pronounced *shuò*), and it is also a semantic compound (*huìyì zì*). The pronunciation of *sòu* is *shuò*.

Regarding "Qiānyáng County" (汧陽縣): the *Shàngqián* (上遣) is pronounced as *yánfǎn*. Bān Gù’s *Xīdū fù* (西都賦) states, "Qiān surges to its west. The *Zílín* (字林) says, "The water of Qiān originates from Yòufúfēng. The *Zītǒng* (字統) says, "Qiān flows into the Xiáo, Hán, and Wèi rivers to the northwest. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) with "kāi" (*kāi*) as the phonetic; *jiān* (幵) is pronounced *qiān*.

Regarding the character for "resentment" (㥲) used here to mean "to scold," the *Zi shu* states that its correct form is 悳. Gu Yewang says that 悳 refers to anger; it is the standard character from ancient times to the present, composed of the radical "heart" (心) and the phonetic "zhen" (眞).

Lángyá Wáng Mǐn (琅瑘王珉): "Láng" (琅) is pronounced as in "làngdāng" (浪當); the *Hànshū* states that Lángyá Commandery is present-day Yīzhōu (沂州). "Mǐn" (珉) is a personal name; "mǐn" (珉) is pronounced as in "pǐbǐn" (彬), with "bǐn" (彬) sounding like "bǐ" (彼) and "mǐn" (珉).

Jin Midi (金日磾): "Mi" is pronounced with the *yin* rhyme of *ren* (人) and the *di* (邸) rhyme of *ni* (泥); it is the surname and given name of a Han Shizhong (侍中). "Tiao-nian" (髫年): "Tiao" is pronounced with the *tian* rhyme of *yao* (遙);

the *Cangjie pian* states that "tiao-mao" (髫髦) refers to the hair of a child. The *Wenzi jilüe* records it as "zhou" (䯾), meaning the hair of a small child. The *Zitong* states that "tiao" refers to the hair of a small child used as an ornament. The *Wenzi dianlüe* records it as "shao" (召) following the radical for hair (*biao*), and also as "chiao" (齠) following the radical for teeth; "mao" (髦) is pronounced *máo*.

Regarding "fū" (敷) in the upper character [of *fēn-xī* (敷析)], it is pronounced with the initial *fǔ* (撫) and the final *wú* (無). Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* states: "Fū means to bestow (*shī*). The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical *pū* (攴) and the phonetic *jiāo* (󳏋). Regarding "xī" (析) in the lower character, it is pronounced with the initial *xīng* (星) and the final *jī* (積). Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* states: "Xī means to divide (*fēn*). The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* states: "It means to split (*pōu*); it is composed of the radical *mù* (木) and the phonetic *jīn* (斤). In the *chuán* (transmission/commentary), it is written as *jí* (㭊), which is a vulgar form.

2. Second Fascicle. "Tītǎng" (倜儻): the first character is pronounced *tīng* (with the level tone) and the second is pronounced *tāng* (with the rising tone). Sīmà Xiāngrú’s *Fēngshàn Shū* states: "Tītǎng means to exhaustively transform. Gù Yěwáng says: "Tītǎng is like standing out from the crowd. The *Shījì* says: "To admire what is extraordinary and tītǎng. Regarding the correct characters for "tītǎng" throughout antiquity and today, both characters are composed of the radical "person" (亻); "tī" and "dǎng" are both phonetic components.

*Yuanchui* (淵粹): The first character is pronounced *xuán* (上玄反); the second is pronounced *suì* (下雖醉反). Wang Bi’s commentary on the *Zhouyi* states it means "refined purity" (*jingchun*). The *Guangya* states it means "pure. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *chui* means "not mixed," composed of the radical for rice (*mi*) and the phonetic *zú*. It may also be written as *zuì* (睟) with the radical for eyes; the pronunciation and meaning are identical.

*Yan* (研): Upper radical *qiè* (齧) with the reverse *jiān* (堅). *Bóyǎ* (博雅) states: "To investigate means to mature one's deliberations. The *Shuowén* (說文) states: "To grind (*yánmó*)"; it is composed of the radical *shí* (石) and the phonetic *jiān* (幵), where *jiān* is pronounced *qiān* (牽). Alternatively, it may be written as *tián* (揅) or *jié* (𣗥), both of which are archaic characters; their pronunciation and glosses are identical. *Hé* (核): Lower radical *héng* (衡) with the reverse *gé* (革). *Shēnglèi* (聲類) states: "*Hé* means to verify. The *Hànshū* (漢書) states: "The duty of its careful verification was based on ancient laws. The *Shuowén* states: "To examine and substantiate actual matters"; it is composed of the radical *xī* (西) and the phonetic *jiǎo* (敫), where *xī* is pronounced *hùjià* (呼嫁) and *jiǎo* is pronounced *jī* (擊).

*Qíng* (勍): Upper radical *jìng* (竸), reversed; from *pī cāng* (埤蒼), it means "vigorous. From the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means "martial. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means "still strong," composed of the radical *lì* (力) and the phonetic *jīng* (京). Lower radical *tíng lì* (亭曆); Duan Yucai’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states that "enemy" (*dí*) means "to oppose. It also means "to match. The *Erya* says it means "a pair. The *Shuōwén* says "enemy" (*dí*) means "to recount," composed of the radical *pū* (攴) and the phonetic *shāng* (啇). The sound of *shù* (述) is *qiú* (求), and it also means "to be a mate. The sound of *pū* (攴) is *pǔ bǔ* (普卜); the sound of *shāng* (啇) is *dì* (的). The text of the *Zhuàn* (傳) uses the character *pí* (𰚇), which is a vulgar form.

The reading of "lángbèi" (狼狽) is *láng* for the first character and *bèi* for the second. The *Wenzí jílüè* (Collection of Simplified Characters) states that "lángbèi" means disorder and ruin. The *Guìyuàn zhūcóng* (Cluster of Pearls from the Garden of Cinnamomum) states that "lángbèi" means sudden panic. Examining the phonetic component, it indicates "sudden haste. Furthermore, "lì" (戾) is also "láng" (狼). According to the standard characters of antiquity and today, both "láng" and "bèi" take the "dog" radical (*quán*) as their semantic component and the phonetic components. The reading of "cù" (猝) is *zú*.

"Jin" (僅) means "scarcely" or "few," as stated in the *Guangya*. He Xiu’s commentary on the *Gongyang zhuan* says it means "inferior. Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* says it means "barely able. The *Shuowen jiezi* also states it means "barely able"; it is composed of the radical "person" (亻) and the phonetic "jin" (堇), with "jin" pronounced "jin" (謹).

*Wàngjuàn* (忘倦): The upper character (*wàng*) is pronounced as *máng*; Gu Yewang states it means "not to remember. The lower character (*juàn*) is pronounced *quánjiàn*. Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjìng* states that "juàn" means "lassitude. The *Cāngjiépiān* states that "juàn" means "to contract. The *Guǎngyá* states it means "the extreme" and also "to perish. The *Shuowén* states it means "fatigue," composed of the radical "man" and the phonetic "quǎn. According to the *Shēnglèi*, it is composed of the radical "force" (*lì*) and forms "quàn. The *Bópǐ* writes it as "quàn," which is also interchangeable.

*Pìpì* (紕僻): The first character, *pì*, is pronounced with the initial *pǐ* and the final *mí*. The *Lǐjì* states: "If one thing is *pìmìu* (紕繆), the people will not obtain their proper death. Zheng’s commentary says: "*Pì* means error. The *Shuowén* [explains it] as consisting of the radical *mì* (糸) and the phonetic *bǐ* (比); the sound of *mì* is *mò*. The second character, *pì* (僻), is pronounced with the final *bì*. Zheng’s sub-commentary on the *Máoshī* says: "*Pì* refers to being depraved and biased. Gù Yěwáng says: "*Pì* refers to acting in a way that is crooked and does not accord with principle. The *Shuowén* says: "*Pì* means to avoid; it consists of the radical *rén* (人) and the phonetic *pì* (辟)."
*Seng* (僧) is pronounced with the second tone and the final *ruò* (若); it is a name for a monk (*śramaṇa*). According to the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲), *què* (䂮) means to whet a blade.

*Sēngyuì* (僧叡) is pronounced with the second tone and the final *guì* (桂); he was a *śramaṇa*. Kǒng (孔) in his commentary on the *Shàngshū* (尚書) states that *yuì* (叡) means wisdom. The *Shuōwén* (說文) explains it as composed of the radicals for "to harm" (*cán*, 𣦻), "eye" (*mù*), and a simplified form of "valley" (*gǔ*, 谷); the sound of *cán* is *cān* (殘).

*Ōu huì* (歐噦): The first character, *ōu*, is pronounced with the initial *gǒu* (as in "dog"). The *Zuozhuan* states, "He lay prostrate and vomited blood (*fù ōu xuè*)," which refers to this. The *Shuowen* says: "To vomit (*ōu*) is like to spit (*tǔ*); it is composed of the radical *qiàn* (欠) and the phonetic *qū* (區). *Ōu* is pronounced as *tāo* or *qū hóu*. The second character, *huì*, is pronounced with the initial *yuān yuè*. In the *Liji*: "When a son attends upon his father, he does not dare to *huì*, *yī*, *zhì*, or *kài*. The *Shuowen* says: "To *huì* is like the awakening of breath; it is composed of the radical *kǒu* (口) and the phonetic *suì* (歲). *Yī* is pronounced as *è jiè*. *Zhì* is pronounced as *dì*. *Kài* is pronounced as *kāi gài*.

*Jī* (齎) is pronounced *xiànfǎn*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "To *jī* means to expend wealth while traveling. His commentary on the *Liji* further states: "*Jī* is that which is provided for distribution. Gu Yewang says it means "to hold. The *Guǎngyá* says it means "to escort. The *Shuowen* defines it as "to hold and present as a gift"; it takes the radical *bèi* (貝) and is voiced by *qí* (齊). The character used in the *Chuán* (傳) is *jiān* (賷), which is a vulgar form.

The character 棄 (qì) [is used here] as a variant for 諠 (xuān). The *Zìshū* states that it is written with the radical 雚 and forms 讙 (huān). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* says it refers to the sound of clamor. The *Fāngyán* says it means "to yield" (*huānràng*). The *Guǎngyá* says it means "to cry out. In ancient texts, it was written with the radical 雨 and the character 口 to form 吅 (xuān); this is synonymous with "startled. Its meaning is identical to both 諠 and 讙, as has already been seen in previous explanations.

The character *chóu* (酬) is pronounced with the initial *zhōu* (周). The *Erya* states: "Chou means recompense. Guo Pu’s commentary says: "Chou refers to mutual response and repayment. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* says: "The word 'chou' means 'complete' (*zhōu*); it signifies being thorough in loyalty and good faith. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "an offering" (*xiàn*), composed of the radical "wine" (*yǒu*) and the phonetic "state" (*zhōu*). It was also written in antiquity as *chóu* (醻). In the transmitted texts, it is written as *chóu* (詶) with the radical "speech" (*yán*), which is a vulgar form. Below [the character for "recompense"] is the character *duì* (對), pronounced *shìjiǎo* (士角); in the transmitted texts it is written as *duì* (對), which is also a vulgar form.

*Qièyìng* (妾媵): The first character, *qiè*, is pronounced with the upper radical *jiǎn* (叶) reversed [i.e., *jiǎn*]. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "The word *qiè* means 'to receive' (*jiē*). The *Baihūtong* says: "It means to be received for an audience at the proper times. The *Wenzi Dian* explains it as a compound ideograph consisting of the radical *nǚ* (woman) and the element *lì* (standing), signifying the union of these meanings. The second character, *yìng*, is pronounced with the final *zhèng* (证) reversed. The *Erya* states: "*Yìng* means 'to escort' (*sòng*'). He Xiu’s commentary on the *Gongyang Zhuan* says: "*Yìng* refers to the escorting of nieces and younger sisters. Regarding the characters in their current standard forms: they consist of the radical *nǚ* and the phonetic *tí* (䜌). *Tí* is pronounced *dié*; *dì* is pronounced *dì*.

Regarding "jí" (thorn) in the phrase "jí-lín" (thorn forest): the *Zhouli* commentary by Zheng Xuan states that "jí" is taken because it is red and has external thorns. The *Maozhuan* on the *Shijing* says, "Jí is the jujube (*zǎo*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "jí resembles the jujube and grows in thickets"; it is a compound character formed from the phonetic "bìng" and the semantic element "cì."

"Cāo bǐ" (Grasping the brush). "Cāo" means to grasp or hold; it is composed of the radical "hand" (手) with "sào" (喿) as the phonetic component. "Sào" is pronounced "zào. The character below is pronounced "pīmì" (悲密). Guō's commentary on the *Erya* states that people of Shu call a brush "bùlǜ" (不律). The *Shiji* states that Móng Tián invented the brush. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "bamboo" (竹) with "yù" (聿) as the phonetic component. The version in the transmitted texts written with "máo" (毛) as "bǐ" (笔) is incorrect. "Tián" is pronounced "diéjiān" (牒兼).
*Yǔ qìn* (with *qìn* pronounced as *chǔ jìn*): This character is identical to *qìn*, meaning "monetary offerings to monks.

*Tài zǐ hóng* (Prince Hóng; *hóng* pronounced as *è hóng*): A personal name. The *Bóyá* states that *hóng* describes the appearance of deep water. The *Shuowén* defines it as "the depth of water," formed with the radical *shui* (water) and the phonetic *hóng*.

Yutian (于闐): The character "tian" is pronounced with the *lian* (練) tone when following "yu. It is a Hu-language name for a Western country; it is currently located more than two thousand li southwest of Anxi and is administratively attached to Anxi. The sound is transmitted from the word "men" (門), which is rendered as "tian" (填).

*Guǐhuá* (詭滑): The first character, *guǐ*, is pronounced with the initial *g* and the final *wěi* (歸委反). The *Mao Shi* states: "Do not let the *guǐsuí* (詭隨) run wild. Zheng’s Commentary (*Zhèngjiàn*) says: "Do not listen to those who act deceptively and follow others in doing evil. The *Huainanzi* says: "Sū Qín achieved one instance of sincerity through a hundred deceits. Xù Shūzhòng stated: "*Guǐ* is like being negligent. The *Shuowen* defines it as "to reproach," written with the radical for speech and the phonetic *wéi*. The second character, *huá*, is pronounced with the final *huánbāfǎn* (還八反). The *Shuowen* defines it as "smoothness," written with the radical for water and the phonetic *gǔ*.

*Bàngdú* (謗讟): "Bàng" (謗) is pronounced with the initial *bó* and the final *làng*. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "Bàng means to defame. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic "páng" (*xiàngdòngfǎn*). The *Fānyán* states: "Dú means to feel pain. The *Guǎngyá* states: "It means evil. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "It means to slander. The *Shuowen* defines *dú* as "painful resentment," composed of the radical "double speech" (*jìng*) and the phonetic "mài. The text of the [present] *zhuan* uses "hēi" (*dù*) instead; this is incorrect. The pronunciation of *jìng* is *jìng*. *Bàngdú*: "Bàng" (謗) is pronounced with the initial *bó* and the final *làng*. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "Bàng means to defame. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic "páng" (*xiàngdòngfǎn*). The *Fānyán* states: "Dú means to feel pain. The *Guǎngyá* states: "It means evil. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "It means to slander. The *Shuowen* defines *dú* as "painful resentment," composed of the radical "double speech" (*jìng*) and the phonetic "mài. The text of the [present] *zhuan* uses "hēi" (*dù*) instead; this is incorrect. The pronunciation of *jìng* is *jìng*.

The character for *bó* (舶) has the phonetic value of *bái* (白). The *Zhuangzi* states: "If one takes water as a boat, then it is called a 'boat of water' (*shuǐzhōu*). Regarding *tàibái* (太白), Sīmà Biāo’s commentary notes that *tàibái* is also the name of a type of vessel. The *Guǎngyá* says: "A *bó* is a ship. The *Cāngjiépiān* says: "A *bó* is a large ship. In the standard characters of both ancient and modern times, it is composed of the radical *zhōu* (舟) with the phonetic *bái* (白).

*Yōng*: To hire for weaving. (The character *zhōng* is pronounced with the initial *yǒng*. Mencius says that *yōng* means to employ one’s labor. Gu Yewang says that it means to provide labor in exchange for wages. The *Guǎngyá* says it means to be employed as a servant. The *Jīngǔ zhèngzì* defines it as one who provides their labor at a price to others. *Yì*: To serve others. (The character follows *rén*; the phonetic component is *yōng*, pronounced with the final *tān-dá*. The *Bīcāng* says that *tǎdēng* refers to a woolen mat (*máo-xí*). The *Shìmíng* says that *tǎdēng* is what is spread upon a small stool placed before a large bed. The *Kǎoshēng* says that *tǎdēng* is a textile woven from animal hair with patterns, originating from the Western Regions. The *Jīngǔ zhèngzì* states it is composed of the radical "hair" (*máo*) and the phonetic component "to ascend" (*dēng*). The pronunciation of *dēng* is the same as above.

*Chánwù* (慚悟): The upper character is pronounced *zágān* (雜甘) and the *Shuowén* states it means "shame" (*cángkuì*). It is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) with the phonetic element *zhǎn*. The lower character is pronounced *wúgù* (吾故) and the *Shuowén* states it means "awakening" (*wùjué*), which is like being clear and discerning (*míngliǎo*). It is composed of the radical "heart" with the phonetic element *wú*. In transmitted texts, it is written as *cán* (慚), which is an error, though it is also acceptable. The pronunciation of *liǎo* is *liǎo* (了).
Tuoba Tao (the second character is pronounced *pan* with the final tone *dao*; this is the name of the third sovereign of the Wei dynasty).
*Yan* (the first character is pronounced *yu* with the final tone *yan*): according to the *Mao Shi Zhuan*, *yan* means "peace" (*an*); it is also interchangeable with *yan*.

3. Third Fascicle. Regarding the term *tiáo-èrn* (髫齔): the first character, *tiáo*, was explained in the first fascicle. The second character, *èrn* (齔), is pronounced with the initial *qian* (前) and the final *fan* (反) as *jin* (謹). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "The term *èrn* refers to the loss of primary teeth, occurring at eight years of age for boys and seven years of age for girls. The *Zitong* states: "Girls produce their teeth at seven months and lose them at seven years; boys produce their teeth at eight months and lose them at eight years. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the character is composed of the radical *chi* (齒) with the phonetic *qi* (七).

*Chuan* (舛) is pronounced *shuǎn* (上川兗反). Sima Biao’s commentary on the *Zhuangzi* states that it refers to "discordant and contradictory words. Xu Shuchong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states that it means "mutually opposed. Gu Yewang states that it means "discrepancies and unevenness. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "lying face-to-face" (*duìwò*); it is composed of the radicals for "night" (*xī*) and "back-to-back" (*xiāngbèi*), forming a compound character through semantic combination. In the transmitted text, it is written as *chuan* (舛), meaning "to pass through."

*Nie* (in *niè xuán gēng*) means "to ascend"; the *Fāngyán* states that *niè* is synonymous with "to climb. The *Cāngxiè piān* states that *niè* means "to extend. It resembles a bright rainbow, greatly arched and spanning the sky; when one uses a rope to span toward [the goal] and crosses straight across, it is called *gēng*. The transmitted text writes it as *qiū* (from the *lì* radical), which is an error in transcription and not correct. The character below is pronounced *héng*. The *Shuōwén* states: "*Gēng* is a rope; it takes *mì* and *héng* as its phonetic components. It is also written as *lí* (from the *mù* radical), meaning "a state of intense urgency."

*Jin-zhan* (噤戰): The first character, *qín*, is pronounced with the *yǐn* rhyme. The *Chuci* (楚辭) states that "to *jin*" means to close one's mouth and not speak. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* says that closing the mouth constitutes *jin*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic "prohibit" (*jìn*). It is also written as *yín* (唫).

*Quán* (pronounced *jù*, with the radical *qú* and the phonetic *kūn*). The *Huainanzi* states that *quán* is synonymous with *jù*. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* explains it as sitting while gathered together. The *Shuowen Jiezi* also defines it as *jù*, composed of the radical *zú* (foot) and the phonetic *zūn*.

*Shi* (舓): The upper radical is *shi* (時), with the phonetic *er* (耳). The *Shuowen* states: "To lick; to take up things with the tongue. It is written with the radical *she* (舌) and the phonetic *yi* (易), or alternatively with *shi* (氏) as the phonetic.

*You* (幽): The upper radical is *you* (一), with the phonetic *yiu* (由). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* says: "Deep and remote. It also says: "Black in color. The *Erya* says: "A narrow path. The *Shuowen* says: "Hidden and secluded. It is a compound character formed from *xuan* (𢆶) and *shan* (山). *Xuan* (𢆶) has the same pronunciation as *shangxia gengxingfan* (上下耕杏反). The *Zhuangzi* says: "Obstructed and blocked. The *Shuowen* says: "The *shanyu* tree can be made into *wuyi* (a type of vessel); it is also like 'straight. It is written with the radical *mu* (木) and the phonetic *geng* (更).

"Jùn" (儁): The upper radical is "zuǎn" (峻). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that it means "extraordinary and distinct. Examining its phonetic component, it refers to one whose talent exceeds a thousand men. In both ancient and modern standard characters, it is written with the "ren" (人) radical and the phonetic "zhuàn" (雋). It is also written as "jùn" (俊). The pronunciation of "jùn" (雋) is "quán yuǎn" (全兖反).

The *yú* (盂) vessel for holding curdled milk (*tiào*)—the former character pronounced *yú* according to the *Fāngyán* (方言), where it states that a *wǎn* (椀) bowl without legs is called a *yú*. The *Shuōwén* (說文) explains it as being composed of the radical *míng* (皿) with the phonetic *yú*; "shèng" (盛) is pronounced *chéng*. In the *Zhōuwǒ* (周禮), the commentary by Zhèng states that what is contained in a vessel is called "shèng. The *Shuōwén* defines "shèng" as a vessel for millet and sacrificial grain, composed of the radical *míng* with the phonetic *chéng* (the latter character is pronounced *láng*). The *Lǐjì* (禮記) states it is used for sweet wine (*lǐ*) and curdled milk (*tiào*). Zhèng’s commentary on the *Tiāolǐ* (醯醢) section notes that *tiào* is fermented sour milk. The *Shìmíng* (釋名) says that *tiào* is produced from breast milk. Regarding the correct orthography of the characters through antiquity and modern times: [the character for] *lǐ* (醴) is pronounced *lǐ*, and [the character for] *zài* (𧟭) is pronounced *zài*. The character for *tiào* (酪) is composed of the radical *yǒu* (酉) with the phonetic *gè* (各). *Note: The original text contains a complex discussion regarding the etymology, pronunciation, and historical usage of several characters related to vessels and dairy products.*

*Huángjù* (上音黃): The *Cangjie pian* states it means "fearful and anxious"; the *Guangya* states it means "to dread. In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, it follows the radical for movement (*chuò*) with the phonetic element *huáng*. Alternatively, it may follow the radical for the mind (*xīn*) as *huáng*, and its glosses are identical. The second character, *qù* (下渠御反), according to Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan*, means "timid fear. According to Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji*, "jù" (遽) is equivalent to "sudden" (*cù*). The *Kaoseng zhuan* states it means "urgent and rapid. In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, it follows the radical for movement (*chuò*) with the phonetic element *qū*. *Cù* (猝) is pronounced *cānggǔ*; *chuò* (辵) is pronounced *chǐluè*. The text of the *Zhuan* uses *qì* (懅), which is the same character.

*Mǐnfǎn* (the first character pronounced *mián*, with the retroflex *biǎn* as a variant; the second pronounced *miàn*). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states: "Mǐnfǎn means to exert one's strength. The *Guìyuàn Zhūcóng* also states it means "to strive. The *Kǎoshēng* says: "Mǐnfǎn means never tiring. In both the ancient and modern *Zhèngzì*, the characters are composed of the radical *lì* (force/strength) and the phonetic *miàn*. These are both form-phonetic compounds (*xíngshēng zì*). In the transmitted texts, they are also written as *mǐnmǐn* (from the radical *mǐng*), which is interchangeable.

Regarding the term *huījìn* (煨燼): the upper character is read as *wěi* (猥) with the *huí* (回) rhyme; the *Guǎngyá* states that *huī* is synonymous with *yūn* (熅, a lingering glow). The *Shuowén* defines it as "the fire in a pan (*pén*)," composed of the radical *huǒ* (fire) and the phonetic *huī*. The lower character is read as *cí* (辭) with the *jìn* (盡) rhyme; this is a vulgar form. The correct form uses the radical *huǒ* and is written as *chén* (燼), which the *Fānyán* explains as "the remains of fire. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states: "Cinders (*jìn*) are the remaining wood from a fire. Thus, the Imperial Commentary to the Preface of the *Xiàojīng* says: "How much more so when [the teachings] were obliterated in the Qin dynasty—those who obtained them possessed but the dregs of the cinders. The *Shuowén* records this as being composed of the radical *huǒ* and the abbreviated phonetic *jìn*.
*Qì* (upper radical 肉 [flesh], phonetic 㪔; lower radical 欠, phonetic 刈): *qīng yì* (Qing-yi). It means to rest.

*Kè jié* (upper radical 克, meaning "to be able"; according to the *Erya*, it means "to conquer"). The commentary on the text uses the character 剋 (from radical 刀), which has the same meaning. Lower radical 潛, phonetic 葉 (*qián yè*). The commentary on the *Mao Shi* states that *jié* is simply "victory. Du’s commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan* states that *jié* is also *kè*. The *Kaosengshengyun* states that "victory in battle is called *jié*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "*Jié* means to win; it is composed of the radical 手 with the phonetic 疌. The pronunciation of 疌 is the same.
*Kěn* (傔): *qián* (謙) and *niàn* (念) are the rhymes. Yingyun states that *kěn* means "to follow" (*cóng*).

It is composed of the radical "person" (*rén*) with the phonetic element *jiān*. *Kěn* (懇): The upper part is read as *kāng* (康) and *hěn* (很). Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that *kěn* refers to an appearance of firm endurance. The *Liji*, in the "Tangong" chapter, says "earnestly sincere" (*kěn qí zhì*). The *Kaosheng* states that *kěn* means "sincere" (*zhéng*). The *Shuowen* says it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) with the phonetic element *kǔn* (豤); *kǔn* is pronounced *kūn* (坤) and *wěn* (穩). The lower part is read as *chǔ* (楚) and *sè* (色). The *Guoyaya* states that *cè* (惻) means "sorrow"; the *Shuowen* says it means "pain. It is composed of the radical "heart" with the phonetic element *zé* (則).

"Qianshou" (黔首): the first character is read as *shàng* (上) with the phonetic *jiǎn-yán-fǎn* (儉炎反). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "Qianshou refers to the common people. The *Shiji* records that in the twenty-sixth year of the First Emperor, the name for the people was changed to Qianshou. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it: "Qian means black; it is composed of the radical 'black' (*hēi*) and the phonetic 'jīn' (*jīn*)."

*Kunkpi* (悃愊): The first character is pronounced *ku-ben* (上苦本反) and the second is pronounced *ping-bi* (下憑逼反). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states: "The will (*zhi*) is pure. The *Guangya* states: "It means ultimate (*zhi*). Zhang Yan’s commentary on the *Hanshu* states: "Kunkpi is equivalent to utmost sincerity (*zhicheng*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "When indignation reaches the point of utmost sincerity, it is called kunkpi. Both characters are formed with the radical for the heart (*xin*); *kun* and *fu* serve as their phonetic components.

"Sǒngzhǐ" (聳峙): "Sǒng" (聳) is pronounced *shànglì* (上栗) or *yǒngfǎn* (勇反). Guo’s commentary on the *Fāngyán* states that "sǒng" means "high. It is sometimes written as "sǒng" (竦); the *Zhuāngzǐ* says, "standing tall and high. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of "ér" (耳) and "shēng" (聲). The *Kǎoshēng* states that "zhǐ" (峙) means "mountains standing alone. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of "zhǐ" (止) and "sì" (寺) as phonetic components; the *Chuánwén* writes it with "shān" (山), which is the common usage.
*Shàn* (pronounced *shàn*, with the radical for "counties" [邑] and the phonetic *jiǎ*): This is the name of a commandery in the Han dynasty’s Jiaozhi Commandery; it is also a place name.

*Shàn* (pronounced *shàn*, with the radical for "earth" [土] and the phonetic *shàn*): This is the name of a kingdom among the Western Qiang tribes in the western desert. It is the easternmost of the four military garrisons (*sì zhèn*) of Anxi; its capital is Yanqi, located seven hundred li west of Anxi.

"Throwing away the *zān* (簪): the character is read as *sēn* (森) with the *fǎn* (反) radical *ji* (集). The *Xùnzú* (集訓) states: 'The jade hairpin within a head-dress. It refers to the hairpin attached to the head-dress to prevent it from falling. The *Shuowén* (說文) writes it as *lán* (兂), meaning 'the hairpin on the head,' which is a pictograph. The form in the transmitted texts as *zān* (簪) is a vulgar character."

Regarding "huo-gan" (fire-ship): the character *gan* is pronounced as *xian* with the *ai* rhyme. The *Guangya* states that a *gan* is a boat; the *Picao* states that a *gan* is a vessel with a roofed deck; and the *Kaosheng* states that a fire-ship refers to a warship. In the standard orthography of past and present, *gan* refers to a boat with double layers above and below; it is composed of the radical "boat" (*zhou*) and the phonetic "jian" (*jian*).

The character 濟 (jì) in the commentary [of the *Shuowen*] is read as míng (ming) with the rhyme bǐng (bing); it is an error for 令 (lìng) in the transmitted text. The following section reads jì (ji). Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states: "Ji means to cross. The *Shuowen* explains it as consisting of the radical 水 (water) and the phonetic 齊 (qi), with the archaic form written as 㴉; its pronunciation and gloss are identical. The "ji" in the transmitted text is a vulgar character.

"Water-measure" (*shuǐqí*): the second character is pronounced *xìng* (with the *qīn* and *fǎn* finals). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "To regulate by means of a measure is called *qí*. The *Kǎoshēng* says: "The term for a portioned segment (*fēnduàn zhījì*) follows the radical 'knife' (*dāo*); it is a borrowed form based on the transmitted text."

The character *shǐ* (深駛) is read with the tone of *shī* (師事). The *Cāngjié piān* states that *shǐ* means "rapid" or "swift. The *Wénzì diǎnshuō* explains that *shǐ* refers to the swift gallop of a horse. In both ancient and modern standard characters, it is composed of the radical for "horse" (*mǎ*) and the phonetic element "historical record" (*shǐ*).

Regarding "Qiáo" (譙): it is pronounced *cú xiāo* (上徂宵反). According to the *Hànshū*, there was Qiáo County in Pèi Commandery, which was the territory of the fief of the Prince of Qiáo. The *Shuowén* states that the character is composed of the radical "speech" (言) with "jiāo" (焦) as its phonetic. Regarding "ànjìu" (諳究): "àn" is pronounced *àn hán* (上暗含反). The *Guǎngyá* states that "àn" means "to recite" (*fèng*). The *Bīcāng* states it means "to chant" (*sòng*).

The *Dōngguān Hànjì* states that they all "àn" the numerical reckonings. The *Kǎoshēng* states that "àn" means "to record. The correct orthography for "àn" throughout antiquity and modern times is "speech" (言) with the phonetic "yīn shēng" (音聲); it is also written as "lùn" (論), which is pronounced *jiū yòu* (下鳩又反). The *Máoshī Zhuàn* states that "jiù" (究) means "to exhaust" (*qióng*). Guō's commentary on the *Eryǎ* states it means "to the end" (*jìn*). The *Shuowén* states that the character is composed of the radical "cave" (穴) with "jiǔ" (九) as its phonetic.

"Die" (迭) is pronounced *shang* with the *tie* (田) and *jie* (結) finals; Guo’s commentary on the *Fangyan* states that "die" is synonymous with "dai" (代). The *Shuowen Jiezi* also defines it as "moreover" (*geng*); it is composed of the radical "chuō" (辵) and the phonetic "shi" (失), where "chuō" is pronounced *chou-lüe*. The *Shenglü* (Classified Phonology) writes it with the radical "zu" (足) as "fu-die" (趺跌), meaning "to pass by," which is not this intended meaning.

*Shu* (樞) is pronounced *chu* (觸, with the *zhu* rhyme). Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "The pivot of a door leaf. The *Guoyi* states: "The root. Han Kangbo’s commentary on the *Zhouyi* states: "The pivot is the master of initiating motion. The preface to the *Xiaojing* states: "And to grasp its essential pivots. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical for wood (*mu*) and the phonetic element *qu* (*qu*).

The character for *yǎnchàng* (掩唱) is read as *yān* with the *yǎn* rhyme. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry) states that "yǎn" means "to stroke" (*fǔ*). Lexicons record it as written as *ān* (奄), and when following the hand radical as *yǎn* (掩), its meaning is the same. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "Yǎn means to cover and gather; it follows the hand radical and takes *gān* (弇) as its phonetic component. *Gān* has the same pronunciation as *shàng* (上).

4. Fascicle Four. *Zhuoluo* (卓犖): The second character, *luo*, is pronounced with the *longjue* (龍角) rhyme. Ban Gu’s “Rhapsody on the Western Metropolis” (*Xidu Fu*) states: “*Zhuoluo* among the various regions of China. Lü Yanjie’s commentary states: “*Zhuoluo* means transcendent and extraordinary. The *Kaoseng* states: “*Zhuoluo* is the appearance of loftiness. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical *niu* (牛) and the phonetic component *laosheng* (勞省).

Yǔ Qí (庾敱)—the character for "Qí" is pronounced with the *zhài* (𦫿) radical and the *hái* (孩) rhyme; it is the name of a high-minded scholar from Yíngchuān. The *Zuǒzhuan* states that the Gāoyáng clan had eight talented sons, such as Tuī Qí and others. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "Qí" means "to govern"; it is composed of the "wen" (文) radical and the phonetic "qǐ" (豈).

*Hǔxiǎng* (肸響): The first character, *hǔ*, is pronounced with the initial *xìn* and the final *shuō*. In Yang Xiong’s *Gānquán Fù* (Rhapsody on Ganquan), it says, "Resounding and richly pervasive" (*hǔxiǎng fēngróng*). Liu Liang’s commentary states: "Resounding and pervasive means spreading out. The *Mèngzi* says, "The sound resounds and spreads everywhere. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radicals *bā* (eight) and *ròu* (flesh), written as *xiāo* (󲷐). It refers to the blood vessels within the flesh pulsating and moving. Now, *xiǎng* (響) is the echo of a sound. When sound travels toward high cliffs or large buildings and returns in response, it is called an "echo" (*xiǎng*). The commentary explains that this refers to sound spreading far and wide.

The character 麈 (zhǔ) is formed from 正 (zhèng) above and 執 (zhí) below; it is derived from 犭 (the radical for beasts) and 豕 (shǐ), with 豕 also serving as its phonetic component. 犭 is pronounced *jǐ* (as in *jǐ*) and 豕 is pronounced *nǚ shè* (reversed), followed by *zhū yǔ* (reversed). Guo’s commentary on the *Shanhai jing* states that the *chǔ* resembles a deer but is larger. The *Shenglèi* says that the *chǔ* tail can be used as a fan. The *Jin shu* records that Wang Yifu once held a jade-handled *chǔ* tail so firmly that it was indistinguishable from his own hand. The *Shuowén* states that the *chǔ* belongs to the class of deer; it is large and has a single horn, being formed from 鹿 (*lù*) and the phonetic 主 (*zhǔ*). The character below is the standard form of 尾 (*wěi*, tail).

*Shatai* (沙汰): The pronunciation of *tai* is broad; in the *Guangya*, it means "to refine" (*taolian*). To "refine away" (*shatai*) means to eliminate evil things. *Youlie* (遊獵): The second character, *lian*, is pronounced with the *qieyun* rhyme *zhefan*.

Zheng’s commentary on the *Mao Shi* states that hunting at night is called *lie*. Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that *lie* is synonymous with "to take. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *quan* (dog) with the phonetic *lie*; the text of the tradition also writes it as *ge* (獦), which is the same.

Regarding "zuò xué" (鑿穴): the upper character is pronounced *zuò*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radicals for metal (*jīn*), the cluster *zhù* (pronounced *shìjué fǎn*), a mortar (*jiù*), and a mallet (*shū*) (pronounced *xuéjué fǎn*), as has already been explained previously. The lower character is pronounced *xuán*. *Jiè fǎn* (決反) means "to decide" or "to resolve."

Regarding "wearing clogs" (*zhù jī*): the first character is pronounced *zhāng* (with a light retroflex final) and the second *qíng* (with a retroflex final). The *Kǒng Cóngzǐ* states that one wore high-topped square clogs when visiting the Marquis of Píngyuán; this is what is meant here. In the *Zhuāngzǐ*, clogs (*jī*) and sandals (*jiǎo*) are considered types of footwear, referring to the toothed leather shoes of today. According to the *Shuōwén*, a "leather shoe" (*lǚ*) refers to a sandal (*jiǎo*), formed with the radical "foot" (*lǚ*) abbreviated and the phonetic "zhī."
"Shan" (剡) is pronounced as "shàn" (時冉反). According to the present-day geography, it refers to the mountain in Shan County of Yuezhou.

Regarding "chao" (嘲), it is pronounced as "zhào" (之陟交反). The *Cangjie pian* states that "chao" means to tease; Gu Yewang says "chao" refers to mutual jesting and teasing; the *Shuowen jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "mouth" (口) with the phonetic "chao" (朝).

*Fù* (錢): The first character is read as *fú* (扶務反). Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that *fù* refers to providing assistance to a mourning household to supplement what is insufficient. The *Guliang Zhuan* says: "To present gifts for the deceased and to bestow them upon the living is called *fù*. The correct orthography for this character from ancient times to the present consists of the radical *bèi* (貝) and the phonetic *fū* (尃), where *fū* is pronounced as *pǔ* (普) and *fēng* (豐) with the tone *fǒng* (諷反).

Regarding the character *cǎo* (才藻): it is used below [in the compound] *lǎofǎn*. The Commentary on the Book of Documents (*Shūjìng*) states: "Cǎo is an aquatic plant that possesses patterns. The Explanatory Notes on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry (*Máoshī chuán*) states: "Cǎo is an aquatic vegetable. Examining the character *cǎo*: it refers to the talent of a person being like the patterns of the cǎo plant. In ancient and modern times, the standard form is written with the radical *cǎo* (艸) and the phonetic *sào* (喿); *sào* is pronounced *zào* (燥) with the final tone *dào* (到). According to the *Shuowén*, it is also written with the radical *wáng* (王) as *zǎo* (澡), which has the same meaning.

*Jùn* (駿): Upper radical *zūn* (遵), pinyin *jùn*. Guo’s commentary on the *Mùtiānzǐzhuan* states it is an epithet for the excellence of a fine horse. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states that *jùn* means "swift" (*xùnsù*) and also "rapid" (*jí*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it refers to the superior material of a horse; it is composed of the phonetic element *jùn* (夋), which is pronounced *qīxún*.

Regarding "Jie" (桀) and "Zhi" (跖): the phonetic glosses state that Jie was the posthumous title of a sovereign of the Xia dynasty. Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that Jie’s capital was An-yi. The *Shifafa* (Methods of Posthumous Titles) says: "One who harms many people through accumulation [of evil] is called Jie. Liu Xi states: "Because he oppressed the virtuous with wicked rebellion, he was imprisoned; thus 'Jie' became his posthumous title. The *Shuowen* says: "Jie means 'lofty' (*jiejie*). It is composed of 'evening' (*xi*) and 'well' (*jing*); the 'gu' is above the 'mu'. The pronunciation of *xi* is *sui*, and *jing* is *jie*; the latter tone is also *zheng*. The *Zhuangzi* refers to "Dao Zhi" as a person of fierce evil. The *Shuowen* says: "To privately profit from wealth and goods is called 'dào' (thief). The *Yupian* says: "Zhi means the underside of the foot. This character is also used today. Jie was the ruler who lost the kingdom; Zhi refers to the thief Daozhi, a type of fierce man.

"Chí jūn lái shàng chí" (遲君來上池): "Ěr" is the correct form of the character for "chí" according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*. It is composed of "niú" (牛) as the radical and a simplified "wěi" (尾) as the phonetic. The transmitted texts write it as "zhí" (迟), which is a vulgar form. "Bāo jié shàng bì xiāo fǎn":

Sīmǎ Biāo’s commentary on the *Zhuāngzǐ* states that the original text reads "biāo" (摽). The *Zhàngguó Cè* says, "lifting the biāo very high. According to the *Shuowen*, this is composed of "shǒu" (手) as the radical and "piào" (票) as the phonetic; "piào" is pronounced "bì yáo fǎn. The second character, "chù" (處), is pronounced "niè fǎn. Zhèng’s commentary on the *Zhōulǐ* states: "To manifest one's intent is called 'jié' (揭). Gù Yěwáng says: "'Biāo' refers to setting up a banner or marker to identify something. The *Shuowen* states: "'Jié' means to raise high"; it is composed of "shǒu" (手) as the radical and "hé" (曷) as the phonetic.

The character 󱾃 (pronounced *wēi*, with the *fǎn* [classifier] *fěi*) is explained by Liu Xian’s commentary on the *Zhouyi* as being equivalent to "minute" (*wēi*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is a variant of 微. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* explains it as "exertion" (*miǎn*), while the *Han Shi Waizhuan* explains it as "advancement" (*jìn*). The *Chuci* uses it in the sense of "exerting restraint" (*miǎn è zhōng*). According to the standard characters of antiquity and the present day, this character is composed of 酉 (yǒu) and a simplified form of 爨 (cuàn).

"Bǐng" (秉) is pronounced as "zhàng" (兆) with an initial "shàng" (上) and a final "bīng" (兵) [as in *míng*]. The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (Mao Commentary on the Classic of Poetry) states that "bǐng" means "to grasp" (*cāo*) and also "to embrace" (*bào*). Jia Dui’s commentary on the *Guóyuè* states that "bǐng" is equivalent to "to hold" (*zhí*). The *Guǎngyá* states it means "to maintain" (*chí*). The *Shuōwén* states that "bǐng" refers to holding grain; it is a compound character formed from the radical "hand" (*yòu*) holding grain. The text in the *Zhuàn* (Commentary) reads "chéng" (乘), which is an error for "bǐng."

*Linmo* (the second character pronounced *bú*): The *Pīcāng* states that it means to copy the forms of things; the *Guǎngyá* also says it is a "model form. The *Shuōwén* says it means "a standard" (*fǎ*), composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "mò"; the transmitted texts write it with the radical "hand" (*tǐ*) as *mō*, and they are used interchangeably.

"Qi-líng" (齊齡): the character "líng" is pronounced *ding* (with the retroflex -n final). The *Guǎngyǎ* states that "líng" means "year. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* says, "Líng refers to the teeth; it is the measure of a person's lifespan. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "teeth" (*chǐ*) with the phonetic "líng. According to the text of the *Chuán*, "equaling the span of the two polarities" (*qí líng èr yí*) means that one's longevity is equal to that of Heaven and Earth.

*Yáo* (誣): This is a phonetic compound with *shàng* (上) as the semantic component and *jiāo* (嬌) as the phonetic; it is also read as *kǎo* (考) with the sound *yún* (云) and *dì* (地) as variants. It means "earth," "ghostly anomaly," or sometimes written as *xiào* (訞) with the semantic component *yán* (言). According to the *Shuowen*, it takes *shì* (示) as the semantic component and *yǎo* (芺) as the phonetic; *yǎo* has the same pronunciation as above. When written below as *yāo* (妖) with the semantic component *nǚ* (女), it is interchangeable. The lower character is pronounced *wú* (無) and *dù* (杜). The *Zuozhuan* commentary states it means "to deceive" (*wūqī*). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states it means "frivolous," "to slander," or "to defame. According to the *Shuowen*, it takes *yán* (言) as the semantic component and *wū* (巫) as the phonetic; both are compounds of form and sound.

"Qiú (禱) is pronounced dǎo (下刀老反). Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: 'To pray for blessings is called qiú (禱). Bāo’s commentary on the *Lunyu* states: 'To pray means to petition the spirits. The text of the *Jì* says: 'To announce matters and seek blessings. It is composed of the radical 示 (pronounced zhī) and the character 壽 (shòu)."

"Fen" (奮) means "to exert" (分, fèn; 問, wèn). Máng Róng’s commentary on the *Shūjìng* states that it means "to clarify. The *Shuowén Jiězì* says it means "to fly up"; it is a compound character formed by the radical "xuīn" (奞, meaning a spreading tail) above the "field" (田). The phonetic for "xuīn" is suī (雖), and the final rhyme is bèimèi (悲媚). The *Máoshī* says, "Holding the reins as if they were silk threads. Gù Yěwáng states that the reins are used to control the horses within the carriage. Furthermore, "pèi" (轡) refers to the horse's bridle. The *Shuowén Jiězì* defines it as "the horse's bridle"; it is a compound character formed by "silk" (絲) and "huà" (軎). The phonetic for "huà" is wèi (衛).

*Shòu liú* (漱流): The character *shòu* (漱) is pronounced with the initial *shǔ* (上) and the rhyme *yǔ* (󱨯). The *Yùnyīng* (韻英) states it means "to wash and cleanse the mouth. The *Yùnquán* (韻詮) states it means "to hold water in the mouth to scrub between the teeth. Now, when we speak of "washing one's mouth in a stream" (*shòu liú*), it refers to those who study the Way in the mountains, consuming pine and cedar and drinking from long-flowing streams to nourish their natural years, while severing ties with worldly pleasures to cultivate the Way. It is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic "suck" (*chù*).

The character for *yǔn* (縕) is pronounced with the initial *lǎ* and the final *dān*. Confucius’s commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* states that it refers to "hempen stuffing" (*má yùn*). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lìjì* also states that *yùn* refers to "cotton batting" (*mián kuàng*), and further notes that it is "old hempen fibers" (*jiù wèi*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *yùn* (縕), derived from the radical "silk" (*sī*) with the phonetic "wǔn" (*wēn*, sound *wēn*; the final is *lóng nǚ*, sound *nǚ*). The *Shuowen* explains that *yùn* means "silk-like fabric," derived from the radical "silk" (*mì*) with the phonetic "lóu" (*lóu*, sound *lóu*).

*Ji-jí* (踧踖): The first character is pronounced *zǐ-yù* (子育) and the second *jīng-yì* (精亦). The *Kǎo Shēng* states that *jǐ-jí* means "hesitating in one's steps. The *Guǎng Yǎ* says it means "awe and reverence. Mǎ Róng’s commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* describes it as an appearance of respectful gravity. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "walking with ease and composure. Both characters are composed of the radical 足 (*zú*), with *shū* (叔) and *xī* (昔) as their phonetic components. The transmitted text sometimes writes this as *fū* (跗), which is a vulgar variant.

*Pòchú* (破雛): The upper character is *kòng* (控) with the *fǎn* (反) of *fàn* (缶). The *Guìyuàn Zhūcóng* (桂苑珠叢) states that *tuò* (㲉) refers to the outer skin of an egg. In the *Gōngjīn Zhèngzì* (古今正字), it is written with *mǎo* (卯) and *qiào* (殼); *qiào* is the phonetic component, its pronunciation being the same as the *shàng chuán wén* (上傳承文) character *qiào*. The vulgar form is below, pronounced *chú yú* (鋤娛). Guō’s commentary on the *Erya* says: "A *chú* is one that eats by itself after hatching. The *Shuowén* says: "A *chú* is the offspring of a rooster; it follows the radical *zhuī* (隹) and uses *cū* (芻) as the phonetic component. *Cū* is pronounced *chǔ jù* (楚俱). The *zhòuwén* (籀文) form is *chú* (鶵), while the *chuán wén* (傳承文) form is *chú* (雛); both are interchangeable.

Regarding "Wu" (餘姚塢): the character is pronounced as *gu* (烏古反). The *Zitong* (字統) states that "Wu" refers to an old city. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文解字) writes it with the radical *duo* (𨸏) as *wu* (隖), meaning a small barrier; the version in the transmitted texts written with the radical *tu* (土) as "Wu" (塢) is a vulgar form.

*Yicāo* (異操): The lower character is read as *cānggào* (倉誥). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states: "Cāo" (操) is equivalent to "zhì" (志), meaning will or intent. Gu Yewang states: "To maintain one's will with integrity and firmness is called cāo. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Cāo means to embrace and hold; it is composed of the radical 'hand' (手) and the phonetic 'sāo' (喿). The pronunciation of *sāo* is *xiàndào* (先到).

*Yú* (雩) [upper tone]: pronounced *xǔ yú* (詡于). The *Hànshū* states it is the name of the commandery *Yúlóu* (雩婁); the *Kǎoshēng* says it is the name of a town in Wú. The transmitted text writes it as *yǐng* (嶀) with the "mountain" radical (*shān*), yet neither the *Zìshū* nor the *Jùnguózhì* contains this character *yǐng*; it is likely a scribal error in transmission. *Duǒ* (塖): [lower tone] pronounced *shéng* (繩). The *Kǎoshēng* writes it as *duǒ* (埵) with the "earth" radical (*tǔ*), meaning a small mountain. According to the *Jùnguózhì*, Duǒ Tíng (埵亭) is located on Mount Shàn (剡山).

*Wā* (窪) and *lóng* (隆). [Regarding *wā*: ] The *Guǎngyá* states that *wā* means "low. The *Huáinánzǐ* states that the hollows in an ox's hoof do not produce sturgeon or shark; it describes the appearance of small water. The *Shuōwén* takes *xuē* (穴) as the radical and *wā* (洼) as the phonetic component; *wā* has the same pronunciation. [Regarding *lóng*: ] Guō Pǔ’s commentary on the *Eryā* states that *lóng* refers to the center being high. Zhèng Xù’s commentary on the *Lìjì* states that *lóng* means "flourishing. The *Shuōwén* takes *luó* (𨸏) as the radical and *è* (㚅) as the phonetic component. *Lóng* has the pronunciation *shàngxiàliùchōngfǎn*.

Regarding "zǎo mù" (to bathe): the character for "zǎo" is pronounced with the upper radical *lǎo* and the phonetic *guàn*. Yuè Wǎnyáng states that "zǎo" means to wash clean. Regarding "xiǎn néng" (rarely able):

the character for "xiǎn" is pronounced with the upper radical *xiān* and the phonetic *qiǎn*. Jiǎ Dú’s commentary on the *Guóyuè* states that "xiǎn" means few. According to the *Shuōwén*, "néng" means "able"; it is a compound character formed from the phonetic *shǎo* with the radical *shì*.

*Kēngqiāng* (Resonant Clanging). Regarding the phrase "the sound of the bells is *kēngqiāng*" in the *Lǐjì*, Zixia said that it refers to the sound produced by striking the bells. Kong’s commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* states: "*Háng'ěr* is the sound of throwing down the *sè* lute. In the *Máoshī Zhuàn*, it says: "*Qiāngqiāng* is the sound of the horse bits. According to the *Shuowén*, both characters *kēng* and *qiāng* are written with the radical *jīn* (metal) and the phonetic *jiān jiāng*. The pronunciation of *biāo* (horse bit) is *bǐmiáofǎn*.
*Shuhù* (倐忽): upper character pronounced *shū* (from the rhyme category *yǔ* [魚]); lower character pronounced *hù* (from the rhyme category *liù* [六]).

The *Fāngyán* (方言) states that in the regions of Liáng and Sòng, a horse stall is called a *chōu*. Guō’s commentary notes that *chōu* is a vessel for feeding horses. The *Chuán* (傳) uses the character *sàn* (󳈎), which is likely an error; it is not correct. This character also appears in the *Gàntōng lù* (感通錄) with the same meaning, and it is recorded in the biography of Dào'ān (道安).

Regarding the character 󰪐 (mǎdōu): according to the *Guǎngyá*, it refers to a "lódòu" or a horse-saddle bag; the *Shuowén* also states it is a vessel for feeding horses, formed with the radical 竹 (bamboo) and the phonetic component 兜 (dōu). The version in the *Chuánwén* (Tradition Text) uses 兜, which refers to armor (*kǎi*), but this is not its original meaning.

Xi Zuochi’s "Explanation of the Character Zheng" (正): The character is composed of the radical "feather" (羽) and the phonetic "white" (白). Its secondary pronunciation is *zuò* (昨), and its lower component is pronounced *ěr* (耳) with the *qièyùn* rhyme *xià* (下). Xi Zuochi was the name of a high-minded scholar from Xiangyang.

Regarding the character *lóng* (籠): Zhuangzi says, "It is like a dove in a cage"; *lóng* means to cover. In the *Guījīn zhèngzì*, it takes the radical "bamboo" (*zhú*) and the phonetic "lóng" (with the reading *jiào*). The *Zìshū* states that it means to cover or enclose. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* says that a *zhào* is a net for catching fish; the *Shuowen* also defines it as a net for catching fish, taking the radical "mountain" (*gāng*) and the phonetic "zhuó". The version in the *Chuánwén* (傳文) using the character *chǒng* (寵) is incorrect.

Regarding "Langfeng" (閬風): according to the *Guangya*, Kunlun has three peaks, one of which is Langfeng. The *Shuowen* states that "lang" (閬) means a high gate, composed of the radical "gate" (門) with the phonetic element "liang" (良).

*Jiangmei* (江湄): The lower character is read as *mei* (美) with the *bi* (悲) rhyme. The *Shijing* says, "by the water's edge" (*zai shui zhi mei*). The *Erya* states, "where water and grass meet is called *mei*. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *shui* (水) and the phonetic *mei* (眉).

*Qianhu* (千斛): The lower character is read as *honggu* (紅穀). The *Yili* states, "ten *dou* are called one *hu*. The meaning in the *Shuowen* is the same; it is composed of the radical *dou* (斗) and the phonetic *jiao* (角). The version transmitted from [the *Lunheng*] uses *ge* (㪶), which is a vulgar character.

Regarding the character *yù* (龠): according to the *Cāngjié piān*, one *yù* is equivalent to five *cuō*. The *Hànshū* states that the ancient *yù* originated from the *huángzhōng*; one *yù* has a capacity of one thousand two hundred *shǔ* grains and weighs twelve *zhū*. Two *yù* make one *hé*; a *hé* is the measure of a *yù*. The *Shuowén* says that *yù* means "to manage" (*lǐ*) and also refers to a musical pipe; it is a compound character formed from *pǐn* and *lún*. The reading for *liàng* (量) is *liángwénfǎn*. In the transmitted texts, it is sometimes written as *yè* (蘥) with the "grass" radical, which is interchangeable.

Regarding the seal-script inscription above, it is read as *chuán-liàn-fǎn-wáng*. The commentary on the *Zhouyi* states: "Seal-script (*zhuàn*) means 'transmission' (*chuán*). It was created by Shi Zhou, a minister of King Xuan of Zhou, as the "Great Seal" (*dà zhuàn*). Later, Li Si of the Qin dynasty created the "Small Seal" (*xiǎo zhuàn*), which reduced the characters of the Great Seal; it is composed of the radical "bamboo" (*zhú*) and the phonetic element "tuàn."

*Chùbǔ* (輟哺): The first character is read as *zhuǎn liè* (轉劣) according to Zheng’s commentary on the *Lúnyǔ*. *Chù* (輟) means to stop; it is composed of the radical "carriage" (*chē*) and the phonetic "zhùe" (*zhùe*). The second character, *bǔ* (哺), has the reading *púmù* (蒲慕). Regarding the method of teaching a child to eat for the first time, Xu Shuchong said: "It refers to chewing food in one's mouth and giving it to them. The *Shuowén* says: "*Bǔ* means to chew; it is composed of the radical 'mouth' (*kǒu*) and the phonetic 'fǔ' (*fǔ*). The pronunciation of *jǔ* (咀) is *qínyǔ* (秦與).

*Lín* (懍): The character is pronounced *shèn* (甚) with a reversed final; according to the *Fāngyán*, it means "reverence. Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states that it denotes an appearance of perilous apprehension. In both ancient and modern standard characters, it is composed of the radical *xīn* (心) and the phonetic *lǐn* (稟).

*Lóngxiāng* (龍驤): The lower character is pronounced *xiào*yáng* (削陽). The *Jìnshū* records that Wang Jiong served as General Longxiang. Lü Zàn’s commentary on the *Hànshū* states that *xiāng* means "to rise" and also "to gallop. The *Shuowén* defines *xiāng* as "the rising and falling [of a horse]" and is composed of the radical *mǎ* (馬) and the phonetic *xiāng* (襄).

Regarding "xiāngzhěn" (pillow-case): the *Fǎnyǐn* glosses it as "a pillow for resting the head upon. The *Shuōwén* states that it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "yín" (pronounced *yín*).
Regarding "Yáo Cháng": the character below "wén" is pronounced *liáng*. He was the Grand General of Former Qin’s Fú Jiān; he usurped the throne from Fú and became the ruler of Later Qin.

Regarding the character for *xié* (靴), with the phonetic *yú hé* (吁禾) as the radical: the *Zìshū* (字書) states that *xié* refers to sandals (*sà*). The *Shìmíng* (釋名) states it means "to cover" (*mào*), as one covers each of the two feet with a single piece of leather. Upon examination, *xié* was likely a name for clothing among the Hu people, composed of the radical *gé* (革) and the phonetic *huá* (華). As for the character for *mào* (帽), with the phonetic *bào* (報) below: the *Jīngǔ Jìngzì* (古今正字) states that *mào* refers to a cap (*guān*), composed of the radical *jīn* (巾) and the phonetic *wēi* (𭥗).

“Shé” (覈): The upper radical is *xiàng* (象) with the reversed *yáng* (羊); the *Mao Shi* states it means “to examine in detail. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *yán* (言) with *yáng* as the phonetic. The lower part is *héng* (衡) with the reversed *gé* (革); the *Hanshu* states that its purpose is to “examine and verify” according to ancient laws. According to the *Shuowen*, it means “to investigate and substantiate matters,” composed of the radical *yòu* (又) with *jiǎo* (敫) as the phonetic; *jiǎo* is pronounced *jīng* (經) with the reversed *ì* (鷁).

Regarding "Dongguan Xiwan": the term *Xiwan* (下浣) refers to an official post; Dongguan was likely a place name of the Qi state. As for *zhucheng* (麈󲏟) [knocking on the table]: the first character, *zhu* (主), is pronounced as in *zhǔ* (主);

the second character, *cheng* (正), is the same as the character for "tail. *Zhucheng* refers to the fan held before one. It has already been explained and annotated: the pronunciation of *kou* (扣) is *kǒu*; the *Lunyu* commentary states that *kou* means "to strike. The *Guangya* says it means "to hold. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains that *kou* (as in striking) is composed of the radical for "hand" (*shou*) and the character for "mouth" (*kou*); in archaic script, it is sometimes written as *ke* (𧥣) or *kou* (叩). The phonetic and semantic explanations are essentially the same.

Next is *pián* (pronounced *biàn* with the final *-n* reversed), as annotated in the *Zuǒzhuan*: "Pián means the joining of trunks. Gu Yewang says: "Pián refers to being arranged in rows. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical for horse (*mǎ*) and the phonetic element *bìng*.

"One grain" (li): the character *li* is pronounced with the phonetic component *li*. The *Shangshu* states, "Grain food is called *li*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states, "*Li* means *san* (boiled rice); it is composed of the radical for 'grain' (*mi*) and the phonetic *li*; *san* is pronounced with the rhyme *sāngǎn*."

"Dī" (one drop): the character is pronounced with the initial *ding* and the final *li* (dǐng lì). Gu Yewang states that "shāng" (shāng) refers to dripping or trickling. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "Dī means the pouring of water; it takes the radical 'water' and the phonetic 'dī,' with the pronunciation of 'shāng. The reading 'shāng' is the same as above. The transmitted text uses 'tì' (渧), which is a vulgar character."

Zǎoyáng (棗陽): The upper tone is *zǎo*. According to the present-day geography, Zǎoyáng is the name of a county in Suízhōu. The *Shuowén* explains it as a compound ideogram formed from two "bamboo" (*cì*) radicals.

Qiānlǒng (汧隴): The upper tone is *yíxián*. Bān Gù’s “Western Metropolis Rhapsody” (*Xīdū Fù*) states, "Qiān surges to its west. In both ancient and modern standard orthography, Qiān is the name of a river originating in Qīan, Right Fúfēng; it is also the name of a commandery (*xiàn*). It flows northwest into the Wèi River. It is written with the "water" radical and the phonetic *jiān*, which has the same pronunciation as above.

The character *yùn* (允) is pronounced as *jí* (集). The *Erya* states: "Jí means 'to harmonize' (*hé*). Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shangshu* also treats it as the character *jí*. Gu Yewang says it means "to accord and harmonize. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "chariot" (*chē*) and the phonetic "qī" (*qī*), with the pronunciation *jí* (*jī*).

*Máolí* (毫氂): The first character is pronounced *hào* (with the initial *gǎo* reversed) and the second is pronounced *lí* (with the initial *zhī* reversed). The *Hànshū* states, "not missing even a *máolí*. The *Yìnyì* (Phonetic and Semantic Commentary) says that ten *háo* (hairs) are called one *lí*; it may also be written as *máo* (毛) or *cǎi* (綵), with the same phonetic and semantic values. The version in the *Chuán* (Commentary) uses *lǐ* (釐), which is incorrect.

*Yīwèi* (猗蔚): The first character, *yī*, is pronounced with the initial *yǐ* (反切: 倚冝反). The *Guǎngyá* states that *yī* is an exclamation of praise; the commentary on the *Máoshī* also treats it as an exclamatory particle. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical *dà* (大) and the phonetic *qí* (奇). The second character, *wèi*, is pronounced with the initial *yūn* (反切: 氳物反). The *Zhòuyī* says, "The noble man undergoes a leopard-like transformation, his patterns becoming *wèi*. The *Cāngjiépian* states that *wèi* describes the lush appearance of grasses and trees. In the standard characters of the present day, it is written with the radical *cǎo* (艸) and the phonetic *yù* (熨) in abbreviated form (*shěng*). The archaic script is written differently.

*Què* (upper radical *qiān*, *fǎn* *wǎn*): The *Yī Jīng* says, "It stands firm and cannot be pulled out. Regarding the sound, it means "solid and firm. It is a compound character consisting of a semantic and a phonetic element. *Nǐ* (upper radical *qīn*, *fǎn* *rèn*):

The *Shuō Wén* says it means "lying down to sleep," formed with *mián* as the semantic and *yǎn* as the phonetic; the lower part is pronounced *zhài*. Regarding the sound, it means "sickness. It is a compound character consisting of a semantic and a phonetic element.

6. Volume Six, Part Six. *Guizhang* (圭璋): *Gui* (珪) is pronounced as *gui* (上桂畦反). The *Rites of Zhou* states that the *gui* is a jade scepter (*tǐng*); from the Son of Heaven down to the five grades of feudal lords, each held it to preserve their person. The *Baixiūtong* states that the word *gui* signifies purity (*jié*). The *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of "repeated earth" and being an auspicious jade; it is round at the top and square at the bottom. In archaic script, it is written with the "jade" radical (*yù*) and the character *gui*. This is the same as the text of the tradition. *Zhuo* (灼) is pronounced as *zhuó* (陽反). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Rites of Zhou* states that a half-gui is called a *zhang* (璋). The *Baixiūtong* states that the word *zhang* signifies clarity (*míng*). The *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of "jade" and having the phonetic element *zhāng*.

"Comprehensively synthesizing" (*zōng*) and "supreme correctness" (*shàng zhèng*). Regarding the character for "comprehensively synthesizing" (*zōng*), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Broad and pervasive; it is composed of 'ten' (*shí*) and 'extensive' (*fǔ*, pronounced *pǔ*; 'pǔ' is like 'to spread'). The lower radical is *zōng* (pronounced *sòng*). The *Taixuan Jing* says: "Then one synthesizes (*zōng*) names. Song Zhong’s commentary notes: "That by which things are recorded and synthesized. The *Shuowen Jiezi* further states: "A shuttle-thread; that which holds the threads together in weaving; it is composed of 'silk' (*mì*, pronounced *mì*) and the phonetic component 'zōng'. The character for "silk" (*mì*) is pronounced *mì*.

*Nán* (南): The phonetic transcription for *dòu* (逗), with the rhyme *tóu* (頭) and the reversed *hòu* (候). The character dictionaries state it means "to detain" (*zhuīliú*); the *Shuowen* states it means "to stop. It is composed of the radical *chuò* (辵) with the phonetic *dòu*. *Biǎnxiá* (褊陿):

*Biǎn* (褊) has the upper part *biān* (鞭) and the lower part *miǎn* (沔). The *Guǎngyá* states that "broad" (*biǎn*) is synonymous with "narrow" (*xiá*). The *Chuci* says, "shallow wisdom and narrow ability," which refers to this. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *yī* (衣) with the phonetic *biǎn*. *Xiá* (陿) has the lower part *xiánjiǎ* (咸甲). The character dictionaries treat this as the "narrow" of breadth and width; it is composed of the radical *jiǎo* (𨸏) and *qiè* (匧). It means "constricted" (*xiàì*). In the transmitted texts, it is written as *xiá* (狹) with the radical *quǎn* (犬), but that is not its meaning here.

Regarding "pù" (cascade) in *Péngmù*: the *Shuowén* states, "Pù means rapid; it is composed of the radical 'water' (氵) and the phonetic 'pào' (暴). The *Kǎoshēng* says that when water flows down from a height, it is called a pùbù (cascade). According to this, a pùbù refers to a mountain spring flowing over a sheer cliff, resembling the shape of a waterfall curtain. Sūn Chè’s *Tiāntái Shān Fù* (Tiantai Mountain Rhapsody) says, "The cascading water flows forth, dividing the path," which is precisely this. The transmitted text uses "rì" (sun) instead of "pù," or uses "pào" (fierce); both are incorrect.

"Yàn" (豔) is pronounced with the initial *yán* and the final *-jiàn*. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Book of Poetry) states: "Yàn refers to beautiful color. The *Fang Yan* (Dialectal Lexicon) states: "In the regions between Qin and Jin, beautiful color is called yàn. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "It means that which is beautiful and long; it is composed of the radical *fēng* (豐) and the phonetic *hé* (盍). The character *fēng* has the pronunciation *fēng*. The version in the [Mao] *Zhuan* as "yàn" (艶) is a vulgar character.

*Huìzhēng* (彙征): The first character, *huì*, is pronounced *guì* (韋貴反). The *Guǎngyá* states that *huì* means "category" (*lèi*). The *Zhouyī* says, "Pulling up the *máo* grass by its roots, they advance as a category—auspicious. Wang Bì’s commentary explains: "Advancing as a category means being drawn along by one's own kind. 'Zhēng' means 'to go. In the *Shuowén*, it is written with the abbreviated form of *xiǎn* (󳊘) and the radical *guǒ*; it is a transcribed character. The pronunciation of *xiǎn* is *dì*."

"Jì (悸)" is pronounced as xià kuí jì fǎn. The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* says, "jì has a rhythmic quality. The *Shuōwén* says, "jì means the heart moves; it is composed of the radical 'heart' and the phonetic 'jì'.

"Fù jiǎ (父嘏)" is pronounced as xià jiā yǎ fǎn. The *Ēryá* says, "jiǎ means great. The *Shuōwén* says, "jiǎ means distant; it is composed of the radicals 'ancient' and 'duàn' as its phonetic. It is the name of the person Guǎngyuǎn (遠公).

*Zizī* (孜孜): Master Zisi’s commentary on the *Book of Documents* states that *zizī* means "unflagging diligence. The *Guǎngyá* states it means "exertion. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical *pī* (攴) with the phonetic *zǐ* (子).

*Tianlián* (天溓): The *Cāngjiépiān* states that *lián* (溓) means "to soak" (*yān*). Song Zhong’s commentary on the *Tàixuānjīng* says that *liánrán* (溓然) is the appearance of encompassing stillness. Gu Yewang states that when the governance of a king achieves Great Peace (*tàipíng*), there are auspicious omens such as the rivers becoming *lián* (calm) and the seas becoming *yí* (tranquil). The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical *shuǐ* (水) with the phonetic *jiān* (兼).

The character *pǐ* (圮) is pronounced *pí* (皮美反). Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shūjìng* states that *pǐ* means "to destroy. Guō Pǔ’s commentary on the *Ěryǎ* states that it means "to ruin and examine. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "earth" (*tǔ*) and the phonetic component "ji" (*yǐ*), where the pronunciation of *yǐ* is *sì*.

*Tūshí* (鍮石): The upper radical is *tòu* (透). The *Pīcāng* states that *tūshí* resembles gold. The *Kǎoshēng* also says that *tūshí* resembles gold; Western countries manufacture it by combining copper, iron, and medicinal herbs. It is also written as *kě* (鋀), with the same pronunciation as above. The meaning of the character is consistent across ancient and modern *Zhèngzìyì*; it is composed of the "gold" radical (*jīn*) and the abbreviated phonetic element "thief" (*tōu*).

The character for *xiàn* (餉) is pronounced with the lower radical *shāng* (傷) and the suffix *ràng* (讓). The *Guǎngyá* states it means "to send as a gift"; the *Zílín* says it means "to provide food"; the *Shuōwén* also defines it as *rào* (饟), composed of the radical *shí* (食) and the phonetic *xiàng* (向). *Kuì* (饋) is pronounced *kuì* (匱), and *rào* (饟) has the same pronunciation; alternatively, it may be written as *shàng* (尚) or *lǐn* (𩜋), with the same meaning of "providing food."

"Short rope" (duànqǐng): "qǐng" is pronounced as *gēng* (as in *gēngxìng*). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states: "Qǐng is the same as the rope used for drawing water. The *Fānyán* says that in the region between Hàn and Fēng, a cord is called *qǐng*. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical "silk" (*miè*) with the phonetic element "gēng."

"Body emaciated" (*tǐ léi*). "Tǐ" (body) is pronounced *shàng tī* (上梯). Yě Wáng says that "tǐ" refers to form; it is also a general term for the body. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "bone" (*gǔ*) and the phonetic "fēng" (*fēng*). The text here uses "shēn" (body) as the phonetic component, which is a vulgar character.
