This fascicle covers from the first to the fifth [section]. Regarding the term *yí* (彝) in the *Xù gāosēng zhuàn*, Fascicle One:

The commentary by Kǒng [Yáng] on the *Shàngshū* states that *yí* means "constant" (*cháng*). Examining its phonetics, it is a name for a ritual vessel. The *Zhōu lǐ* mentions the "Six *Yí* Vessels. The *Shuowén* says they are permanent vessels of the ancestral temple and are pictographic characters (*xiàngxíng zì*). They are composed of the radicals for "grain" (*mǐ*), "silk" (*mì*), and "twenty" (*èrshí*). The phonetic component is *gǒng*; "to hold the vessel with both hands" implies it is filled with contents. The character *wáng* (王) is the phonetic; *wáng* is pronounced as *jīng* (京) with a reversed tone. In the transmitted text, the character is written as *fēn* (分), which is an error for *yí* (彝) in the *Shū*.

Regarding "jiao" (澆) and "chun" (淳): the former is pronounced as *yáo* (堯) according to the *Huainanzi*, where it means "thin and frivolous"; the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to pour," following the phonetic *yáo* with the radical for water, and the character is read as *chuí xià lún* (垂下倫). The *Gujin Zhengzi* states that "chun" (淳) is synonymous with "lì" (𥂖); it follows the radical for water with the phonetic *xiǎng* (享), and the character *lì* (𥂖) is pronounced *qī* (󱡱).

"Kòu" (扣): In the *Shàngyīn* (上音), it is pronounced *kǒu-hǒu-fǎn* (口吼反). The commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* states it means "to strike. The *Guǎngyá* (廣雅) says "to hold," while the *Shuōwén* (說文) defines it as consisting of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "mouth" (口), with the lower part pronounced *jì-xī-fǎn* (既希反). The *Shuōwén* further defines [the character for] "generation" (生) as "to produce and develop," consisting of the radical "wood" (木) and the phonetic "machine" (機).

The character 煥 (huàn) is pronounced with the initial *huan* (as in "歡貫"). The *Kǎo Shēng* states it means "radiance. According to Cāngjié, it describes the appearance of literary compositions. In the standard characters of antiquity and today, it is composed of the radical 火 (fire) and the phonetic 奐; the pronunciation of 奐 is the same as above, namely *huàn*. It is used in the sense of "to spread" or "to extend."

*Jiàn* (纘) is pronounced *zuàn* (鑽); it means "to continue" (*yì* [繫] in the *Erya*). According to the *Shuowen*, it takes *móu* (糸) as the radical and *zàn* (贊) as the phonetic. Generally, *dàdǐ* (大抵) is pronounced with the lower character as *dīnglǐ* (丁禮);

"generally" (*dàdǐ*) is similar to "approximately" (*dàyuē*) or "broadly speaking" (*dàkuàng*). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to press" (*jǐ* [擠]). It takes *shǒu* (手) as the radical and *dǐ* (氐) as the phonetic. *Jǐ* (擠) is pronounced *jì* (祭), and *dǐ* (氐) is pronounced *dǐ* (氐), both being the same as above.
"Tāi-zú" (駘足) means "awaiting the arrival [of a better mount]"; the *Chuci* says, "I employ a sluggish tāi to take the road. The *Yupian* states that tāi is a slow horse.

"Pǔ" (譜): the upper character is pronounced bù-hù; the *Guoyaya* calls it pǔ-cáo. The *Shiming* explains it as "pǔ" meaning "to spread" (*bù*), as it spreads out and displays events from ancient times to the present. It is a character formed according to its shape and sound.

*Zhu* (divided as *chu-lü*, with the first tone) is a character belonging to the rhyme division *Ying*. Ying states that it means "to stand for a long time. Examining its phonetic component, it means "to wait. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical *li* (立) with the phonetic *ning* (宁). It is also written as *zhu* (佇), where *ning* is the same pronunciation as above.

*Tí* (逖): Pronounced *shàng-tīng-lì-fǎn*. The commentary on the *Shūjìng* by Kǒng [Yáng] states that it means "distant. Zhèng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* says it means "to cleanse" (*dí*) and describes the appearance of rapid coming and going. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical *chuò* (辵) with the phonetic *dí* (狄); it is also written as *tī* (逷), with the same pronunciation and meaning.

"Bianwei" (編韋): "Shangbian" (上褊) is pronounced *shàng biǎn*. Liu Zhao’s commentary on the *Gongyang Zhuan* states: "Bianwei means to arrange and connect the strips of leather. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "the sequence of bamboo slips," written with the radical for "silk" (*mi*) and the phonetic *piǎn*. The lower character "wei" (位) is pronounced *guī*. The *Shuowen* further defines "wei" (韋) as "leather from animal hides that can be used to bind curved objects," written with the radical for "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic *chuānyuǎn*. The "mouth" (*kǒu*) is pronounced *guī*, and "wei" (*yǎn*) is pronounced *bǐyǎn*; it takes the radical for "clothing" (*yī*).

"Jìngdìngshàngshājiān" (𠜂定上殺姧) is a phonetic category. "Jìng" (𠜂) means to settle or determine a matter; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means to cut or excise, composed of the radical "knife" (刀) and the element "zhē" (𠕋). The pronunciation of "zhē" is *chuò* (竹劣反), and the pronunciation of "zhē" (𠕋) is *cè* (策).
"Yide" (懿德): the upper character is pronounced "yi" (meaning "intention").

It has already been distributed among the eight barbarian tribes (*bānmán*). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* identifies it as "Xūbù. It means to proclaim and display; according to the *Fāngyán*, it means to arrange; according to the *Shuowén*, it means to divide. It is composed of the radical "head" (*xié*) and the phonetic "fēn"; the pronunciation of "xié" is like that of "jié."

*Chéngyīn* (城闉): *yín* is pronounced with the first tone. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that *yīn* means "curved. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as the curved section of a city's double gates; it is a compound character formed by a semantic and a phonetic element.
*Xuànzhī* (衒之): *xuàn* is pronounced with the level tone (*xián*). This is a personal name.
Zhìqiào (智璬) is a vulgarized form of the monastic name [Jiǎo] (澆). Yán'ù (炎燠):

the first character is pronounced yīng (英) with the final kù (菊), or alternatively ào (奧); according to the *Shuowen*, it means "warmth" (*xuān* [煗]), referring to heat within, composed of the radical "fire" and the phonetic element "ào" (*ào* [奧]).
*Biè* (江泌) is pronounced *bēi-mèi-fǎn*; it is a person's name. *Bǎi-bō* (擺撥) is pronounced *bǎi-bō-bǎi-fǎn*; this is a vulgar character;

its correct form consists of *bēi* (卑) and *shǒu* (手), with *bǎo* (捭) as the phonetic component, meaning to wave the hand. The lower part is pronounced *bān-mò-fǎn*. Hé’s commentary on the *Gōngyáng Zhuan* states that *bō-lǐ* (撥理) means "to manage disorder. The *Guǎngyá* states it means "to remove. The *Shuōwén* says it consists of *shǒu* (手) and *fā* (發) as the phonetic component; it is a compound character based on both form and sound.

"Mín Yuè" (閩越): the first character is pronounced *mǐn* (with the radical *miǎo* and the phonetic *bīn*), and the second is pronounced *yuè* (with the radical *yuán* and the phonetic *yuè*). Guo’s commentary on the *Shānhǎijīng* states that Mín Yuè is the same as Xī Ēu, which is Jiàn'ān Commandery and borders the sea. The *Shuōwén* says: "Mín is a serpent-like tribe of the Southern Yuè; it is written with the radical 'insect' (*chóng*) and the phonetic 'gate' (*mén*). The second character, "Yuè," is written with the radical "orphan" (*huò*) and the phonetic "axe" (*yuē*), and its pronunciation is the same as the former [character].

"Zhuìbǐ" (綴比) means to pursue and connect the records of the Wei Jia [Annals]. The *Guoyu* commentary states that "zhuì" means to link together; the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to join and attach," composed of the radical "silk thread" (糸) and the phonetic "chuè" (叕), with the lower character pronounced "pín mì" (頻蜜). The *Yunyi* (韻英) states that "bǐ" (比) means to arrange texts in sequence; however, it is incorrect to write this with the character "pī" (紕), which is composed of the radical "silk thread" (糸)—the pronunciation of which is "mì" (覓)—and the phonetic "chuè" (叕)—the pronunciation of which is "zhuǎn liè" (轉劣). *Note: The provided text contains a complex philological discussion regarding the characters for "zhuì" (綴), "bǐ" (比), and "pī" (紕), their radicals, pronunciations, and definitions across various classical lexicons.*

*Lín* (臨): To gaze down. *Nì* (睨): According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means to look askance; it is composed of the radical "eye" (*mù*) and the phonetic "er" (*ér*). One source states it refers to the loopholes in a city wall.

*Líng* (𩜈): To eat to satiety. According to the *Mao Shi Zhuan*, it means to be full. The *Wenzi Dian* explains that it means to be satiated; it is composed of the radical "food" (*shí*). It is pronounced with the initial *yī* and the final *jù*.

The characters for *lángwǔ* (廊廡) have the second tone for *láng* and the fourth tone for *wǔ*; both refer to the buildings on the two sides beneath the hall. The dictionaries state that a large building is called a *lǔ* (廡), while a small building with short eaves is called a *láng* (廊); these are words formed from shape and sound.

The character *hán* (寒) is read with the lower radical *zūn* (遵) reversed; the *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲) states that when one’s talent surpasses those of a thousand men, it is called *hán*, meaning to possess awesome power and extraordinary distinction. The lower part is a compound character (*huìyì zì*) composed of the radicals for "bow" (*gōng*), "sparrow" (*zhuī*), and "person" (*rén*).

The character for *xiǔ* (seal) is pronounced as *shàng* (with the *sī* and *zǐ* finals). The *Yùnyīng* states it refers to the "State-Bestowing Jewel" (*chuánguóbǎo*). Examining its phonetics, the *Kǎoshēng* says it is the jade seal of the Son of Heaven; in ancient script it was written with the radical for earth (*tǔ*), but now it uses the jade radical (*yù*) as a semantic component and the sound component.

*Shíshàng* (拾上): "Guǐ" (鬼) and "yùn" (運) are the phonetic components; *kǎo* (考) is the radical sound. *Shí* (拾) also means to gather. In the standard characters of antiquity and today, it is written with the "hand" radical (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "qūn" (君).

*Qūn* has the pronunciation *jūn*. *Shānzú* (芟足): "Shā" (沙) and "xián" (咸) are the phonetic components. The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (毛詩傳) states: "To cut grass with a knife. The *Shuōwén* (說文) defines it as "to reap grass," composed of the "grass" radical (*cǎo*) and the "pestle" radical (*shū*). The lower part, *jīngyù* (精裕), is the phonetic component. The rhyme dictionary *Yīngtiān* (韻英添) notes that this is a borrowed character (*jiǎjiè zì*).

"Engraved" (juàn): the upper radical is *yǎn* (反) and the phonetic is *jiàn* (反). According to the *Fānyán*, "juàn" means to carve (*zhuó*). The *Shuōwén* states that it is used for engraving metal and stone to record events; it takes *juàn* (雋) as its abbreviated phonetic. "Cavern-niche" (yánkān):

the upper character is *yá* (牙) and *jiān* (監), and the lower is *kàn* (勘) and *gān* (甘). The *Guǎngyǎ* states that "kān" means to contain (*shèng*). The *Shuōwén* states it takes *lóng* (龍) and *hán* (含) as its abbreviated phonetics.

*Jibǐ* (櫛比): The first character, *jī*, is pronounced with the *shè* rhyme (as in *shè*). The *Shuowen* states that "comb" (*jī*) is a general term for combs and brushes. The second character, *bǐ*, is pronounced with the *mì* rhyme (as in *mì*).

The *Guangya* says it means "connected," while the *Shuowen* says it means "dense. *Lìjīn* (鍒金): The first character, *lì*, is pronounced with the *zhōu* rhyme (as in *zhōu*). The *Yupian* says it refers to making metals such as gold and iron supple and soft; it takes the radical "metal" and the phonetic "róu. The commentary on the *Chuanwen* states that using stone to soften metal is a mistaken explanation.

Regarding "yī bō" (robe and bowl): the pronunciation of the lower character is *bō*. Dictionaries state that *bō* is the same as *biǎo*; it is the correct orthography (*zhèngtǐzì*). It is composed of the radical *mǐng* (vessel) with the phonetic component *bó*.

To write it as *bō* is the vulgar form. Regarding "dì xiāng": the pronunciation of the upper character is *dì*. According to the *Kǎoshēng*, *dì* means "alternating" or "successive. It is also written as *di* with the third tone; this character is composed of the phonetic *xí* (pronounced *zhì*) with the radical *chuò* (to walk).

The character 渰 (yǎn) is pronounced yǎn. The *Mao Shi* commentary states that it describes the appearance of overcast clouds. In the "Correcting Characters of Antiquity and Today" (*Jīngǔ zhèngzì*), the character 雲 (yún) is changed to 渰 (yǎn). The character 擢 (zhuó) is pronounced zhuó, meaning "to select" or "to pick"; it describes rain and is composed of the radical 木 with the phonetic 弇 (yǎn), its pronunciation being the same as above.

*Shāng* (商) is pronounced with the initial *shāng*, meaning "to deliberate" (*shāngliáng*). The lower tone is *jiǎo*, meaning "to examine sounds" (*kǎoshēng*) or "to monopolize profit" (*zhuānlì*). The *Shījì* states that it refers to "deliberately weighing the prices of goods in buying and selling. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical *mù* (wood) and the phonetic *hè*. *Hè* is pronounced *hé gè* (何各反). It is formed from *guòng* (冂) and *zhuī* (隹); that which emerges from *guòng* is called *hè*.

SHU (俗字, also written as 斛): The upper character is the surname of the Lou clan; the lower character is the name of a person, also the name of a tree. It is a phono-semantic compound character. (The initial of the upper part is pronounced *shu* [red/valley reversed]; the initial of the lower part is pronounced *chi-lun* [reversed]).
*Zīzī*: (The first character is pronounced *cí*; the second is the sound of *kǎo*). The commentary says it means "unwearied," "earnest love," "to overcome," and "intense.
*Liáo huī*: (The first character is pronounced *shàng diāo*; the second is pronounced *huǐ wéi*). *Yùnyīng* states that *huī* means "to wave the hand"; it is formed with the radical *shǒu*.

The character *guàn* (盥) is pronounced with the initial *shàng* (上) and the final *zhǎn* (椀), both in the third tone; it is a semantic compound (*huìyì zì*). It is composed of *jiù* (臼, phonetic value *jú*) and *shuǐ* (水), and *mǐng* (皿). The character below, *xīng* (星) with the final *lǐ* (禮), or alternatively written as *xǐ* (洗), are both phonetic-semantic compounds (*xíngshēng zì*) formed from the radical *shuǐ*.

*Yú-ào* (隅隩): The upper character is pronounced *yù* (遇俱反); the *Kǎogōngjì* (考工記) states it means "corner" (*yújiǎo*). The *Shuowén* (說文) defines it as *zhōu* (陬). The lower character is pronounced *ào* (音奧); Guō’s commentary on the *Eryā* (爾雅) states that *ào* refers to a hidden or secluded place. The *Cāngjiépian* (蒼頡篇) states that *ào* means "to store away. The *Shuowén* notes that both characters, *yú* and *ào*, are phono-semantic compounds (*xíngshēngzì*) derived from the radical *fù* (阜).

The *chù* (held in the hand) is pronounced *hūn gǔ fǎn*; it is the simple tablet held by the worthy at court. It is made either of ivory or wood. In antiquity, these were used to record matters for fear of forgetfulness. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the character is composed of "bamboo" (*zhú*) with "wù" (*wù*) as its phonetic component.
*Chai* (採): The upper radical is *can* (釆) and the lower is *zhi* with the *ge* (革) rhyme. The *Yunying* states it means "to take with the hand";
it is also written as *ze* (擿). *Zhi* (智): The lower part is *xue* with the *yan* (延) rhyme.

*Seng* (僧): A stone inscription. *An* (諳): The upper part is *an* with the *han* (含) rhyme. The *Kaosheng* states it means "to recite," "to chant," or "to explain. It is a vulgar character; the correct form follows the radicals for *you* (酉) and *yan* (言), written as *gan* (諗). Now it is written in its abbreviated form following the sound.

The character 選 (xuǎn) [is pronounced with the upper radical *shū* and the phonetic *zōu*]. The dictionary explains it as "to seek. Regarding its phonetic classification, it means "to gather" from the *Zìshū* (Dictionary of Characters); it is composed of the radical 手 (hand) and the phonetic 叟 (*sǒu*).
The character 氓 (méng) [is pronounced with the upper radical *mò* and the phonetic *péng*]. It refers generally to the common people; "lí méng" (黎氓) refers to the common folk or the masses.
*Fàn bó* (the lower character pronounced *bái*): A large vessel on the great seas; it enters sixty *chi* into the water and is constructed by piling together wooden beams.

*Yě* (upper character pronounced *róng*; the phonetic gloss says it is the method for casting metal; the *Shuowen* says it is the method for forging vessels; it is a compound character of form and sound; the lower character pronounced *yě*: the *Kaogongji* calls it the artisan who works with metal; the *Shuowen* says it means to cast, composed of the radical *bīng* [ice/water] and the phonetic *tái*).
Gōng ěr (公頠) is a personal name; *wēi* (危) and *guǐ* (鬼) are reversed in order.
*Chí* (󱫕) [water-top, *shàng* tone, *tán* and *hé* rhymes]: to spread lotus leaves upon the water and ride upon them. *Cǐ suǒ* (佌瑣) [top: *cǐ*; bottom: *suǒ*, *sū guǒ* rhyme]:

the appearance of mean people, composed of the radical "person" (*rén*) with the phonetic *cǐ*. In the *Chuánwén* (傳文), it follows the character "king" (*wáng*), which is not its original form. Bottom: *suǒ*. According to the *Ěryā*: "Cǐ cǐ suǒ suǒ" also describes a small appearance.
Huái (懷): chǎng (敞), with the palatal initial *ch-*, according to the *Kǎo Shēng* it means "to open" or "to illuminate"; it is formed from the radical *pī* (攴) with the phonetic *shàng* (尚).
Fǎ (法): nǐ (󱮣), with the labio-dental initial *n-*; this is the personal name of the official Huang Shijun; it belongs to the class of words for fine hair or brocade.

Upper radical *shàng* with the phonetic *gǎi* (read as *hái*). Jia’s commentary on the *Guóyǔ* states that *gāi* means "to prepare" (*bèi*). *Qian* (𨶑): Pronounced *qīng* (with the *yì* and *fǎn* finals). It denotes a state where no one is present. *Jimo* (寂寞): It denotes an empty and desolate expanse. It is composed of the radical *mén* (門) and the phonetic *jù* (具).

*Liang* (涼): Pronounced *liǎng* (with the *zhāng* final). The commentary states that *liang* means cold. It is composed of the radical *shui* (水) and the phonetic *ào* (奧). *Yu* (燠): It means heat. *Zhuì* (綴): The upper radical *zhui* (追) has the phonetic value *wei* (衛) with the reversed tone; it means to connect sounds together. The lower radical *li* (立) has the phonetic value *qing* (清) with the reversed tone. Zheng’s commentary on the *Mao Shih* states that *zhuì* means "to continue.

It is a phono-semantic compound character. *Jiǎo* (敫): The phonetic value is *yáng* (陽) with the reversed tone *zhāo* (斫). The *Yùn Yīng* states that it refers to the flowing of light and shadow. The *Wén Zì Diǎn Shuō* explains it as a semantic compound character formed from *bái* (白) and *fàng* (放).

It is composed of *huáng* (冋) and *jí* (及).'"

"Ān" (諳) refers to being proficient in seal script (zhuàn) and clerical script (lì); it is pronounced fǎn (反) in the *Pīcāng* lexicon and means "to recite" (*ēngróng*, 諷誦). In the *Erya*, it is pronounced fèng (誦). Next, "chuán" (傳) is pronounced miǎn (免). It refers to the *Dàzhuàn* (Great Seal Script) created by Shì Zhòu and the *Xiǎozhuàn* (Small Seal Script) made by Lǐ Sī, the Chancellor of Qin; this is cited in the *Shuowén*. [The character for] "shū" (書) follows the radical "zhú" (竹) and takes "tuàn" (彖) as its phonetic component; "tuàn" is pronounced tuōluàn (脫亂). Below, "lí" (黎) and "dì" (帝) follow. Chéng Miǎo created the Clerical Script (*Lìshū*), which transformed Lǐ Sī’s Small Seal Script into the Clerical style. Sometimes it is written as "lì" (隷), which in the *Shuowén* follows the radical "lì" (󲷫) and takes "lì" (隶) as its phonetic component.

Scroll 3, Volume Three of the Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks (Xu Gaoseng Zhuan), Scroll Number Three. Sixteenth: Hui-Zheng (慧正). "Zheng" (正) is the correct radical character; it is the name of a monk. "Zheng" (正) is pronounced with the second tone (chá xíng fǎn). The character "Zheng" (正) is composed of "Yi" (夷) as the phonetic and "Zhé" (責) as the semantic component. "Yi" (夷) is pronounced yí. "Zhé" (責) is pronounced zé.
*Shùzhuó* (樹卓): *shù* is pronounced as *jīng* (精) with a reversed [final], or alternatively written as *jì* (績), with the phonetic component *lì* (力) and the radical *zé* (責).

*Zhuó* (卓) is pronounced *zhé* (陟) in the first tone and *lì* (力) in the fourth tone. This term has already been fully explained and annotated in the previous section of the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, Volume Four.

*Dàoquè* (道闋): *què* is pronounced as *yuè* (悅) in reverse; according to the *Mao Shī Zhuàn*, it means "to cease. Zheng’s commentary on the *Yí Lǐ* states it means "to finish. The *Shuōwén Jiězì* explains it as "the completion of an affair and the closing of a gate," composed of the radical *mén* with the phonetic *guǐ*.

The character 鑑 (jiàn) has the radical 亾 (wáng) above and the phonetic 監 (jiàn)—read as jiàn or alternatively written as 鑒; these are one and the same, with identical explanations. The *Guǎngyá* states that "鑑" means to reflect; the *Máoshī chuán* says it means to examine forms; the *Shuōwén* defines it as a compound of form and sound.

"Màn" (pronounced with the *shàng* tone, as in *mán*): Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states that "màn" means "to slight. Gu Yewáng says it means "to treat with contempt. The *Shuowén* explains it as composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "màn," where "màn" is pronounced as in *wàn*. Below, [the character] is pronounced as in *xiāng yǒng*. Guo’s commentary on the *Fānyǔ* states it means "to desire. Regarding the sound: "gāo" (high) is composed of the radical "ear" (*ěr*) and the phonetic "shēng. The *Shuowén* explains it as composed of the radical "ear" and the phonetic "shēng."

The character for *hán* (函) has the phonetic *hán* (含) and the radical for "sound" (*shēng*). It means "to contain" or "to hold. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is a pictographic character derived from the radical for "bow" (*gōng*).

It is sometimes written as *hán* (涵). The character for *yíng* (瑩) has the phonetic *yīng* (縈) with the tone *dìng*. In the *Chuánwén*, it is written with the radical for "metal" (*jīn*) as *yìng* (鎣). The *Guǎngyá* states it means "to polish," referring to rubbing and wiping pearls, jade, and the like to cause them to emit radiance. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to the luster of jade; it is composed of the radical for "jade" (*yù*) and the phonetic *yíng* (熒) in abbreviated form.

*Zhili* (砥礪): The first character is pronounced *zhǐ*; the second is pronounced *lì* (with the *yè* rhyme). Guo’s commentary on the *Shanhaijing* states that it means "to sharpen" (*mò*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "a fine-grained whetstone for grinding; it comes from Mount Yuankai."

*Leiting* (雷霆): "Thunder descending upon the courtyard. It refers to a great clap of thunder. According to the *Erya*, a swift clap of thunder is called *ting* (霆), which is the same as *pilili* (霹靂).

In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, both are compound characters formed through phonetic-semantic principles (*xingsheng*). *Tuoshi* (脫屣): The first character is read as *tuóhuò* (吐活) and the second as *suǒqǐ* (所綺). The *Kaosheng* states that it refers to footwear whose heels are not secured; it is sometimes written as *yīn* (𩌦). Both forms are interchangeable.

Regarding the character *miǎn* (靦): the *Shang Tian Dian* (上天使典) states that it is the opposite of *máo* (毛). The *Mao Shi* says, "There is a countenance (*yǒu miǎn miàn mù*). Examining its phonology, *miǎn* means shame (*cán*). In both ancient and modern standard characters, it is written as *miàn* (面). It is a phono-semantic compound character, derived from the radical *miàn* (面) and the phonetic *jiàn* (見).

*Niùní* (忸怩): The upper character is pronounced *ní* (with the second tone), and the lower character is pronounced *ní* (with the fourth tone). The *Guoyu Zhu* (Commentary on the Guo Language) states that *niùní* refers to a face flushed with shame. The *Guangya* (Broad Lexicon) defines it as *cuòjí* (to be abashed). The *Fangyan* (Regional Dialects) calls it *nǎnkuì* (shameful embarrassment). The *Shuowen Jiezi* (Explanation of Graphs and Sounds) defines it as "the blush of the face. It is a word formed by combining a semantic component and a phonetic component.

*Niǎn* (赧然): The upper radical is *nǐng* (儜) with the phonetic *jiǎn* (簡). The *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲) states it means "to feel shame and embarrassment. The *Shuōwén* (說文) says it is composed of *chì* (赤) and the phonetic *jí* (及).

*Lóngzhào* (籠罩): The upper character is *lùdōng* (祿東) and the lower is *cháojiào* (嘲教). Both *lóng* (籠) and *zhào* (罩) refer to containers that cover things. One covers a bamboo basket so that fish and birds cannot fly or walk away. Sometimes written as *lóng* (䍜) or *zhào* (䈇); both are common forms. These are phono-semantic compounds, both containing the radical *yǒng* (𠕀).

*Jie niǔ* (接紐): "Niǔ" is pronounced with the ninth tone (upper tone). It refers to the knot of a garment's fastener. According to the *Guǎngyá*, "niǔ" means to bind. That which is knotted so as to be unloosable is defined in the *Shuōwén* as being composed of the radical "silk" (*mì*) with the phonetic component "chǒu."

The character *chí* (蹖馳) is pronounced with the upper radical *shù* (束) and the phonetic *róng* (容). According to the *Bóyǎ*, "to *chí*" means to leap and bound. The *Kǎo shēng* states that "to *chí*" is the form of leaping and running; in the standard orthography of the present day, it follows the radical for feet (*zú*) and takes *chōng* (舂) as its phonetic. The pronunciation of *chōng* is the same as above. It also follows the radical for mortars (*jiù*), the pronunciation of which is *jiù*.

"Quàn zhǐ tú xià" (眷砥途下): "Zhǐ" (止) refers to a whetstone; it means level. Looking at the level road as if it were a whetstone, he sighed. In ancient and modern times, the correct orthography follows the character "shí" (石) with "dī" (氐) as its phonetic component. The pronunciation of "dī" is dǐng lǐ (丁禮反); it is also written as "dǐ" (底).

*Zhìguǒ* (炙輠): The first character is pronounced *zhēng* (also *chēng*) and the second is pronounced *guǒ*. It refers to the metal linings (*gāng*) at both ends of a chariot hub (*gǔ*). One interpretation says it refers to the grease (*zhī*) in the corners. To "roast" (*zhì*) it means the grease comes out. Emperor Wen of Wei said, "The *gē* is like roasting a *guǒ*," meaning that Huijing’s erudition and talent were likewise so. This derives from the sound of the characters for "chariot" (*chē*) and "corner" (*guǒ*).

"Chuo qi rui" (挫其銳): The first character, *cuò*, has the ancient reading *zǔ guò* (祖過). Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states it means "to break and frustrate. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to destroy," being composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "zuò" (*zuò*). The second character, *yuè*, has the reading *suì* (歲). The *Guangya* states that *ruì* (銳) means "sharpness," being composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic "duì" (*duì*).

In the phrase "shēng mào" (聲懋), the second character is pronounced as mò (莫候反). In his commentary on the *Shūjīng* (尚書), Kǒng [Yǎng] states that "mào" means "to encourage" (勉). In the standard orthography of ancient and modern times, this character is composed of the radical "heart" (心) with the phonetic element "mào" (楙);

the pronunciation of "mào" is the same as above. In the phrase "yǎn yǎ" (掞雅), the first character is pronounced as yàn (艷). Gù Yěwáng states that it means "illuminating radiance. It is composed of the radical "hand" (手) with the phonetic element "yán" (炎).
*Tíáoyáo* (岧嶤): The upper character is pronounced *tiáo* (tone 4) and the lower is pronounced *yáo* (tone 2). It describes the appearance of being as high and steep as a mountain.

*Huáiyán* (懷鉛): The lower character is pronounced *yuán* (tone 2). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "Lead (*yán*) is a blue metal. It is composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic "gōng" (*gōng*), where the pronunciation of "gōng" is the same as above.
*Zhǒng*: The upper character is pronounced *yǒng* (with the fanqie *zhōng yǒng fǎn*), and the lower character has the sound *guǐ*.
*Guàn suì*: The upper character is pronounced *guān huàn fǎn*. The *Zuǎnyùn* states that it refers to the hair between the horns; it is a pictographic character. *Jiǎn*: The sound is *zǒng*.
"Shēnshāo": the first character is pronounced *sè* (with the *sè* radical) and the second is pronounced *suōjiāo*.

"Fārèn": the second character is pronounced *rèn*. Wang Yi’s commentary states that in Sanskrit it refers to the "branch-wheel wood. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as the wood used for a chariot, formed with the "chariot" radical and the phonetic element *rèn*.

*Língjiā* (聆嘉): The upper character is read as *lì* (歷) and *dīng* (丁); according to the *Cāngjiépiān*, it means "to hear" (*tīng*). It is composed of the radical "ear" (*ěr*) and the phonetic element *líng* (*lìng*).
*Wǔnzī* (韞茲): The upper character is read as *wēi* (威) and *fěn* (粉); the lower character is read as *zǐ* (子) and *sī* (思). According to the *Kǎoshēng*, it means "to store up" (*yùncáng*).

*Méngdùn* (矛盾): "Móu" (矛) is pronounced with the *fú* rhyme of the lower tone; according to the *Shuowen*, it means a spear (*qiāng*) or a halberd (*jì*). "Dùn" (盾) means a shield (*pái*). Both are pictographic characters. *Chão* (勦):
pronounced with the *jiāo-liǎo* rhyme.
"Talking-stick" (*tánbǐng*) refers to things such as the *rúyì* (wishing-pearl) and the like.
"Temporarily brandish" (*huī*)—the pronunciation is *huī*; it means to wave the hand.
"Startled and cowed" (*jīngzhè*)—the pronunciation is *zhè* (alternatively written as *jié*); it means to be terrified and afraid. This is the sound [of the word].
*Cuòlā* (挫拉): According to the *Shuowen*, this means to break or snap; it is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "lì" (立), and it also refers to folding or crushing with the hand.
*Mòdùn* (磨鈍): The lower character is read as *tún* (屯) or *hùn* (混); it means not sharp, dull, or blunt, referring to an edge that is not keen.
*Chūi* (吹噓): "Below" is read as *xū* (許居反); it refers to the breath exiting the mouth. *Cóngyíng* (叢楹):
"Above" is read as *zú* (族公反) and "below" is read as *yíng* (音盈). It refers to pillars. "Cóng" means to cluster; it takes the radical *zhù* (丵) and the phonetic *shēng* (聲).

"Dié" (疊) is pronounced with the initial *tián* and the final *-yè* (反考聲); it means "to accumulate" or "to layer. "Qián" (乾) is pronounced with the initial *qián* and the final *-àn* (反); it refers to the wooden planks used for walls today.

"Wēiruí" (葳蕤) has the initial *wēi* and the final *-ér-zhuī* (而隹反); it is the name of a medicinal herb. According to the textual meaning of the commentary, "the spiritual appearance is wēiruí" means that the Buddha possesses a countenance of compassion, like the appearance of a divine herb hanging with its blossoms.

"Hxi-xiang" (肸響): The upper character is pronounced *xin-ya* (欣⺄反); it means the throbbing of the pulse. The lower character is pronounced *xiang-liang* (香兩反); it refers to the unfathomable resonance of majestic spiritual power. "Yong-cui" (擁萃):

The upper character is pronounced *yung-gong* (邕拱反) and the lower character is pronounced *ji-zui* (疾醉反). It is a compound character formed from both semantic and phonetic components, meaning to gather together and wait.
*Suǒxǔ*: The lower character is pronounced *xīnglǚ* (with the upper tone);
it is a person's name. *Dòng*: The upper character is pronounced *rúyǐn*; according to the *Wenzìdiǎn*, *dòngdòng* refers to the movement of insects. *Huòluò*:

The upper character is pronounced *huángguō* and the lower is pronounced *luò*. The *Kǎoshēng* states that *huòluò* describes the vast appearance of water; here it means that the prose of that treatise is expansive and grand.
*Gěnggài*: The first character is pronounced *gēng* with the rising tone (shǎngshēng), and the second is pronounced *gài*. "Gěnggài" refers to its general outline. *Tísī*:
The first character is pronounced *dìxī*, and the second is pronounced *xīngxī*. It means to lift up the net and briefly arrange it.

The "morning mushroom" (chūn-jùn) mentioned above—where "chūn" is pronounced as *chí* and *lún*—is the name for a great divine fungus that does not wither for eight thousand years. The "morning mushroom" mentioned below—where "qún" is pronounced as *yǐn*—refers to a fungus upon manure and soil that is born in the morning and dies in the evening.

*Jiào* (爝火): "jiāo" is pronounced with the *xiàng* and *shuō* finals; it refers to a small torch, like a firefly. *Yán* (妍): Above, *niè* and *jiān*; the radical is *zhèng* and the character is *yán*.

It means beautiful, fine, or wise. Below, it is pronounced with the *chǐ* final. According to the *Shìmíng*, it means "stupidity. The *Shēnglèi* says it means "foolishness. According to the *Kǎoshēng*, it means "vile. The *Shuōwén* states that it is composed of the radical *chóng* (insect) and the phonetic *zhī*. *Zhī* is an ancient character. *Chī* (蚩): [The text continues with the definition of this character].
*Lu-hu*: "Red" (hóng). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "silk" (mí) and the phonetic element "ke" (kè) in abbreviated form.
*Cū-ráo*: The upper character is pronounced *cè-jù*; it means grass. The lower character is pronounced *ěr-zhāo*; it refers to the appearance of grass when it first sprouts.
*Kēng* (鏗然): "Kēng" is pronounced with the initial *g-*, meaning firm or solid. *Chīyàn* (摛掞):
"Chī" (上) is pronounced with the initial *ch-*, and "Yàn" (下) has the phonetic value *yàn*.
*Dùnyù* (頓袪): "Dùn" (頓) is pronounced with the final *-u*; "qū" (袪) means to remove or cast off.
"Each withdraws their shame" (chè) [pronounced chǐ liè fǎn]; "reduces their giving" (jiǎn shī yě).
"Thereupon" (nǎi) [the upper character nǎi is an ancient form]. "Resplendent" (cuì cǎn):
the upper character is pronounced cuī suì fǎn; the lower character is pronounced cāng làn fǎn.
*Fú* (upper tone *fú*, lower tone *hé gè fǎn*): *fú* is a water bird; *hè* is a divine bird.
*Hè yuè* (lower tone *yào*): *yuè* means a spoon. *Duō* (upper tone *zhú liè fǎn*):
[the character] follows the hand radical with the phonetic *zhuó*; the pronunciation of *zhuó* is the same as that of *shàng*.
"Jie" (掲): its phonetic component is *qián* (䖍) and *bǐ* (糵). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "to lift high with a staff," following the radical for "hand.
Regarding "jinghua" (菁華): the first character is pronounced *jīng* (音精) and the second *huà* (下話瓜反). The *Kaosheng* states that "jīnghua" refers to the finest blossoms.
"懦夫" (nuǎnfū) [the first character pronounced with the *shàng* tone and the rhyme *nú*, the second with *qièruò*]:

this refers to a person who is timid and weak. **Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks, Volume 4, Biography of Dharma Master Xuánzàng.** Regarding "Xuánzàng": "Zàng" [pronounced with the *xià* tone and the rhyme *làng*] is the name for a Chinese Tripiṭaka Master. The *Fāngyán* states that "zàng" means "great" (*dà*). The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical "great" (*dà*) and the phonetic "zhuàng. This character has other pronunciations as well, which are not adopted here.
The original name [Hui] (pronounced *huī*, rhyme with *yǐ*): the *Yùnyìng* states it signifies the beauty of form; it is composed of the radical "clothing" (*yī*).
[Jie] (*yīng*, pronounced *yíng*): the neck-ribbon of a cap;

it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*). [Chángjié] (*qián*, pronounced *qián*): the personal monastic name of Xuanzang’s biological elder brother. It is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*).
*Ya* (pronounced *ya* with the second tone) means to sigh in admiration or lament.
*Kua* (upper character pronounced *kuā*, lower character pronounced *cháo*) means to cross over; it refers to a bamboo fish-trap used for catching fish.
*Ye* (pronounced *yè*) is the name of a commandery located in the northern region; it was the capital of Ye.
"Zhǐxià" (指下) means to pick up with the back of the hand.

"Wúyán" (無𣀇): the pronunciation is also *yùn* (韻); *Quān* (詮) says it is "yǎo" (𩞹). It is composed of "pū" (攴, pǔshí fǎn) and the phonetic "gào" (睪). "Yǎo" (𩞹) has the pronunciation *īyàn* (伊焰); "yǎo" (𩞹) means satiated.

Qizi (𣏌梓): the first character is pronounced qǐ (as in qǐ) and the second is pronounced zǐ (as in zǐ). Qǐ refers to the *qǐgǔ* (𣏌枸) tree, while zǐ refers to the *qiū* (楸) tree; both are names for trees that grow near water. Suì (睟):
the radical is "eye" (目) with the phonetic component "zhōu" (周), read as jiān (尖) and yè (葉) in combination. It takes the meaning of "surrounding" or "encircling."
Xiao Yu (the "Yu" being his given name): "Jieqian" (解籤) is pronounced *yán* (閻).
According to the *Kaosheng* (考聲), it means a small slip of paper, a tally, a verification, or a written report; it is a phono-semantic compound character (*xingshengzi*).

*Féngyǐng*: The upper character is pronounced *fēng*; the lower character is pronounced *yíng* (with the *bìng* rhyme). The *Kǎoshēng* says: "Yǐng" means the awn of grain; it follows the radical for grain (*禾*) and takes *qǐng* as its phonetic.

*Yóùrù*: The upper character is pronounced *yóu*. The *Wénzì Jílüè* says: "A lodging on the borders; a guest house for envoys; the modern-day *yì* (post station). It follows the radicals for *chuí* and *yì*. The version in the *Chuánwén* written as *xiè* is incorrect. *Xiè* is pronounced *xīngyè*, and is not used here.
Regarding "huìlù" (賄賂): the upper character is pronounced *huì* and the lower *lù*. The *Yùnquán* states it refers to coarse silk. Regarding "sǎozhǒu" (掃帚):
the upper character is pronounced *sāngdào* and the lower *zhīyǒu*. These are implements for sweeping away filth and excrement; both follow the radical for "hand" (手).

Regarding the character *xiàn* (獻): the *Wenzidian* states that parching wheat and grinding it into flour is called *jiǎo* (𪍑); it is derived from the radical for "wheat" (*麥*) and the phonetic element *qiú* (酋).
The transmitted texts write it as *jiǎo* (󰉓), which is a vulgar form. Regarding the character *gǎo* (笴): the *Yunquan* states that *jiǎo* means "shaft" (*gǎn*); it is also written as *gān* (竿).
The character for *pātra* (盋) has the upper radical *bo* (音鉢); its correct form is *𭽽* or *𥁄*.

The character for *shàn* (睒) is pronounced *fèng* (奉) and *shāng* (商) with the final *rǎn* (冉) reversed; it is the correct ancient and modern character meaning "to glance" (*zànshì*), composed of the radical *yùe* (曰) and the phonetic *yán* (炎).

Regarding *zhǐ* (蹠), the lower part is pronounced *zhēng* (征) with the final *yì* (亦) reversed. According to the *Guǎngyá*, *zhǐ* means "footwear"; according to the *Chuci*, it means "to tread upon. The *Huainanzi* states: "Birds fly through the void by pushing against the air; beasts run over solid ground by treading (*zhǐ*) upon it. This is a compound character formed from shape and sound.
*Zhèjiā* (磔迦) country: *zhè* (上) is pronounced with the *gē* (革) radical and *fǎn* (反) tone; it is a foreign name transcribed from the Sanskrit language.
*Jiélüè* (劫掠): the lower character is pronounced *lüè* (略). Zheng’s commentary on the *Yueling* (*Monthly Ordinances*) states: "to plunder" means to seize by force or to take away by compulsion.
*Zhao* (釗): The upper radical is *yao* (姚) with the fanqie reading *shang zhang yao*. The "Correct Characters of Antiquity and Today" states that *zhao* means "to cut" (*chan*) or "to scrape.

It is a phono-semantic compound formed from the radical "knife" (*dao*). *Tangzang* (帑藏): The upper radical is *tang* with the fanqie reading *tang lang*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "tong" (*tang*) is the name for a treasury where gold and silk are stored. It is a compound character based on combined meaning.
The reading for 周睇 (zhōu dì) is dì; the standard characters for ancient and modern usage state it means "to gaze askance.
The reading for 趾蹠 (zhǐ zhí) is zhǐ for the first character and zhēngyì for the second; it follows the radical 足 (foot), and the version following the radical 土 (earth) is incorrect.

The character 湮 (yīn) has the initial sound *yin*. According to Guo’s commentary on the *Erya*, "to sink" (*yinchen*) means "to perish. It is composed of the radical 垔 (yīn), with the phonetic element 省 (shěng).
The character 捔 (jué) has the initial sound *jué*. It means "to compare the superior and inferior. It is composed of the radical 手 (shǒu).

*Tui-chi* (穨褫): The upper character *tui* (穨) is pronounced with the *dui* rhyme (兊回反). According to the *Cangjie pian*, it means "to fall. The lower character *chi* (褫) is pronounced with the *er* rhyme (池爾反). The *Shuowen jiezi* states that it refers to the falling of one's robes; it is composed of the radical "clothing" (衣) with the phonetic element "ti" (虒), which is pronounced with the *tian-yi* rhyme (天伊反).
*Ni-si* (the first character pronounced with the *nǎn* and *jié* finals): a name for a western country in the language of India (*Sanskrit*).
*Gāṅgā* (the first character pronounced with the *yí* and *děng* finals): a name for a river in a western country in the language of India (*Sanskrit*).
*Zhu-dāng*: the second character is pronounced *dāng*; "dāng" refers to an ear-bead, meaning an ornament for the ear.
"Si" (四): The lower phonetic reading is "di" (弟). It means to tilt the head and glance briefly; this is the correct character for both ancient and modern usage.

It serves as the radical for "ti" (梯), which is read as "ti" (坁) with the fanqie "ti-ti. Ancient and modern sources state that it means a wooden staircase; it takes the radical "mu" (木) and uses "di" (弟) as its phonetic component.

*Hè* (石罅): *Hè* is pronounced as *hè* (with the retroflex initial). The *Boyá* states it means "crack. The *Shuowen* defines it as "to split" or "to break," written with the radical *fǒu* (缶) and the phonetic *hū* (虖); it is a character formed by transposition. *Sìè* (睥睨):

The first character is pronounced as *pī* (批閉反) and the second as *xì* (霓計反). The *Pīcāng* states it means "to look askance. The *Shuowen* records both characters as being composed of the radical *mù* (目) and are examples of characters formed by shape and sound.

Gṛdhrakūṭa Parvata: "Gṛdhra" means vulture; "kūṭa" means peak. In the ancient Indian translation, it was called *Qisheshuqie* (耆闍崛); in the Tang translation, it is called *Jiufeng Shan* (鷲峰山), also known as *Lingjiu Shan* (靈鷲山). This mountain abounds in vultures.
*Dòuhài* (豆䔽): The second character is pronounced with the *hēgòu* (訶遘) rhyme. It is the name of a medicinal herb originating from Jiǎozhǐ Commandery.

*Huǒhài* (火䔽): The second character is pronounced with the *āihài* (哀害) rhyme. The *Wénzìdiǎn* (文字典) explains that *hài* (䔽) means "lid" (*gài*); it is a compound character formed by combining a semantic radical and a phonetic component.

"Yǎn (𣹆)"—the upper radical is "nan" (納) reversed; Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states: "It arrives suddenly and unexpectedly; it is said that 'yǎn' is the sound of water rushing together. "Hé" (盇) is pronounced "hé" (合).
Zàolì (皂利) is the name of a country in the Hu language; the first character is pronounced as "zào" (上音造).

*Guǎngyá* states that "wéiwéi" (嵬嵬) describes a lofty appearance; the second character is pronounced as "áng" (昂各反), and according to the *Kǎoshēng*, it refers to precipitous cliffs (*èyá*). Its correct form consists of "xuán" (吅) and "nì" (屰), written as 㖾; the version in the commentaries, 㟧, is a vulgar character.

*Kunlun-xū* (崑崙虛): The first character is pronounced *kūn* (upper tone), the second *lùn* (level tone), and the third *qú* (departing tone); it is sometimes written as *xū*. It is an alternative name for the Snow Mountains (*Himālaya*).

Regarding "gradually" (*jiàn* [漸]): Dong [Yuan] reads it as *jiān* (entering), while Kong [Yingda], in his commentary on the *Book of Documents*, reads it as *qiáng* (wall) with the same meaning as "upward" (*shàng*).
"Miaoman" (眇漫) means to look far off toward the sublime heights;
"liao" (了) is the reversed reading. "Suoliu" (㴑流) means to go against the current of a river;

the upper character is pronounced "su" (素). "Qingkou" (勍寇) means a powerful enemy; according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "li" (力) with "jing" (京) as the phonetic. The version in the *Chuanshuo* (傳文) which uses "dao" (刀) to form "ling" (剠) is incorrect.
*Yá* (upper character pronounced *yǎ*, lower character pronounced *guǎng*) refers to a double cliff; the *Kǎoshēng* states that a square cliff resembles a double *zèng* (steamer).
*Qièpántuó* (upper character pronounced *qiānbiè*; a foreign name for a country).

"須髮" (xū fā): "上" (shàng) is pronounced as "臾" (yú); it refers to the hair above the mouth. It follows the radical "彡" (shān), which according to the *Shuowen Jiezi* means "to resemble. "汎漲" (fàn zhàng):
"上" (shàng) is pronounced as "孚梵" (fú fàn) or may be written as "泛" (fàn); "下" (xià) is pronounced as "張兩" (zhāng liǎng), and it is also in the departing tone.
*Xiōngguǎng* (凶獷): "Guǎng" is pronounced as *guōměng* (虢猛). *Tántiān* (闐𨶮):
The first character is pronounced *tián* (音田); the second is pronounced *yēyānjié* (音噎煙結). It means "full" and "obstructed. *Xiǎnyǔn* (獫狁):
The first character is pronounced *xiǎn* (音險); the second is pronounced *yǐn* (音尹). This is an alternative name for the Northern Di tribes.
"Chā" (pronounced with the "jiǎn" rhyme) is explained as "applying the mind"; it is also a vernacular term meaning "to be fitting.
"Sōu-zhuó" (the first character pronounced with the "shuāng-zōu" rhyme, the second with the sound "zhuó") means to search for and extract; it refers to the translation of sutras and śāstras.

*Zèlòu* (仄陋): The first character is pronounced *zè*; the second is the phonetic transcription of *lóudòu*. Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states: "To seek out men of talent among those in humble and obscure positions.

*Biǎnnéng* (褊能): The first character is pronounced *biān* (with the radical *biān*). According to the *Erya*, it means "narrow-minded" or "hasty. Examining the phonology and rhyme dictionaries, both Ying and others state it means "narrow" or "small. The *Shuowén Jiězì* explains it as being composed of the radical *yī* (clothing) and the phonetic *piǎn*. The traditional interpretation [of it being derived from] *dà* (great) is incorrect.
*Zhuìjí* (綴緝): the first character is read as *zhuī* (衛反) and the second as *qīn* (侵入反).
It means to join together. *Lianpí* (連紕): the second character is read as *bìn* (嬪蜜反). It refers to arranging in sequence. *Suǒlián* (鎖聯):
the first character is read as *sāngguǒ* (桑果反) and the second as *lián* (音連). It refers to a category of linked or connected things.
"Fanfu" (繁複): The upper character is pronounced *fá* (袁反) and means "redundant"; the lower character is pronounced *mù* (風目反); "chóngchóng" (重重) means "accumulated. "Qiónghé" (窮覈):

The lower character is pronounced *gé* (行革反); the *Yùnchuán* (韻詮) states it means "to investigate and seek out actual facts. It is composed of "xī" (西) and "jiǎo" (呀, pronounced *jiǎ*). "Jiǎo" (敫) has the pronunciation *yào* (音藥).
The Nine Continents (Jiuying) refer to the islands and immortal states within the Eastern Sea; "ying" is pronounced *yǎng* when used as a homophone for "infant.
"Kuà" (跨) means to span across the ages from antiquity to the present; the *Zhèngzì* (Correct Characters) states it is a compound character formed by a semantic radical and a phonetic element.

"Chen" (宸) refers to the imperial gaze; "jue" (厥) means his; "juan" (倦) is sometimes written as "quan" (眷), which share the same phonetic component; "kao" (考) refers to the sound. "Juan" (眷) means to look back upon or to cherish with affection. "Yan ya" (巖涯):
"ya" (涯) is pronounced with the initial *y* and final *-a* (as in "yǎ"); it refers to the edge of a riverbank. "Xiao Yu" (蕭瑀):
the character "Yu" (瑀) is pronounced *yǔ*; this is a personal name.
Xiao Jing (蕭璟): "Jing" is a personal name; "ghost" (鬼) is pronounced as *yǒng* with a retroflex final.
"Chou" (儔) is pronounced as *zhòu* with a retroflex final; it means "companion" or "match.
"Sangzi" (桑梓): the second character is pronounced *zǐ*.

*Suǎn* (旋): To place in the coffin; the *Shuowen* states it is derived from *fǎn* (反) with *bīn* (賓) as the phonetic component. *Mái* (埋): To bury; the character *yì* (󱽹) has the pronunciation *yùjì* (於計).
*Qí* (其): Its enclosure; the pronunciation is *yíng* (營), meaning a tomb. *Chéng* (城): A city wall; the pronunciation is *qièyàn* (妾焰). *Qiàn* (壍): A moat.
"Ti-xiē" (提挾): the first character is pronounced as *dì* (弟) with the *ǎn* (𠔃) radical; the second is pronounced as *xián* (嫌) with the *jiá* (頰) radical. "Qí-qū" (崎嶇):
the first character is pronounced as *qǐ* (起) with the *yí* (宜) radical; the second is pronounced as *qiāng* (羌) with the *yú* (愚) radical. "Shān-zhí" (埏埴):
the first character is pronounced as *shāng* (傷) with the *rán* (然) radical; the second is pronounced as *chéng* (承) with the *lì* (力) radical.
*Huīhuī*: The phonetic component is *kǔ*, with the reversed sound *huí*; the commentary on the phonetics states it means "ambitious" (*zhì dà*).
It is also written as *㮛*. *Gòngjī*: The phonetic component is *jīng*, with the reversed sound *yì*; the commentary on the phonetics states it means "water rushing and shooting forth. *Cūráo*:
The upper character *cū* has the phonetic component *cè* with the reversed sound *chú*; the *Yùnyīng* states it means "grass. The lower character *ráo* has the reversed sound *zhāo*.
Regarding "fǔzǎo" (斧藻): it is encountered in the *Lǎozǐ* (老子). Examining the phonetic glosses, it refers to aquatic plants that possess patterns.
Regarding "zhòngzhòng" (踵踵): the phonetic gloss says it refers to the heel; it is also written as "zhòng" (踵).

Scroll Five, Volume V, Continuation of the Biographies of Eminent Monks (Xu Gaoseng Zhuan), Scroll Five. *Deng* (staring): [The character] is pronounced with the initial *zhì* (as in *zhèng*) and the final *fǎn*. According to the *Pīcāng*, it means "to stare straight ahead. In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, it is composed of the radical *mù* (eye) and the phonetic *chéng* (abbreviated) as its sound component.

*Zǔ'ài* (obstruction/blockage) is the term used in the *Zuǒzhuan*. Du Yu’s commentary states it means "to obstruct. Alternatively, it is written as *qū* with the radical "mountain" (*shān*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to remove," taking the phonetic element *zhuō* (which is pronounced *jīng yú* in the upper tone and *wǎ gài* in the lower tone). The *Guǎngyá* defines it as "to hinder or block. The *Shuowen* also defines it as "to stop," taking the phonetic element *yí*; it is a compound character (*huìyì zì*) based on its semantic components. It is also written as *hài*, which has the same meaning.

*Jiang-fen*: "fen" is pronounced with the *fu-wen* (扶文) rhyme; according to the *Zi-lin*, "fen" refers to the water's edge. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "water" (*shui*) and the phonetic element "ben" (*bin*), pronounced with the *bu-men* (補門) rhyme.

*Yan-xue*: "xue" is pronounced with the *xiang-yue* (香約) rhyme. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states that "xue" means mutual jesting and teasing. According to the *Shuowen*, it means playful speech; it is composed of the radical "speech" (*yan*) and the phonetic element "nüe" (*nuo*).

Líjí (羸瘠): The upper radical is *zhuī* (追) and the lower is *qíng* (情); the phonetic component is *shòu* (瘦). It means emaciated. According to the *Zìshū* (Dictionary of Characters), "emaciation" refers to the ailment of being thin and weak; it is also written as *lì* (膌). It is composed of the radicals for "backbone" (*jì*, 脊) and "sickness" (*nà*, 疒), with *jì* serving as the phonetic.
Ruǎn (阮) is the surname; Táo (韜) is a personal name, pronounced with the initial *d* (as in *dāo*). It is composed of the radical *wéi* (韋) and the phonetic *yǎo* (舀).
Zhōu Yú (周顒), pronounced with the initial *j* (as in *ji*), was the name of a Gentleman of the Central Secretariat (*Zhōngshū Jìláng*) during the Liáng dynasty.
*Kāi* (in *kāizhātāng*, *zhā* pronounced as *zhà*) means "great" according to the *Guǎngyá*; it is also a word formed from the shape of an open hand combined with a phonetic component.
*Quòrán* (pronounced *kǔjué*) means "firm and solid," as stated in the *Kǎoshēng*; this was already explained previously in the seventh fascicle.

*Kṣiṇa-dāna* (䞋施): The first character is pronounced *chǔ jìn* (楚慬反); the *Yùnyīng* states it means "to bestow. It refers to relying on this bestowed merit to invoke superior fruits. *Bùjù* (怖遽): The first character is pronounced *pǔ bù* (普布反) meaning "to fear";

the second is pronounced *qú yù* (渠御反), in the departing tone. Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states it means "to be awestruck. Alternatively, it may be written with the radical for "heart" (*xīn*) as *cù* (懅), which has the same meaning. According to the *Shuōwén*, it takes the radical for "movement" (*chuò*, sound *chǐu lüè* [丑略反]) and the phonetic *qū* (豦, sound *qú*). The lower part of *qū* consists of the character for "pig" (*shǐ*).

Chǎng (敞): On the upper character, read as chāng (昌掌反). The *Cāngjié piān* states that "chǎng" means high and prominent; the *Shuowén* says it refers to a high place from which one looks afar, composed of the radical 攵 with the phonetic 尨. Yánxian (剡縣): On the upper character, the pronunciation is yǎn (音琰).
It is the name of a commandery in the state of Yuè, composed of the radical 刀 with the phonetic 炎.

*Jùn-cǎi*: The first character is pronounced *jūn* (with the *yun* rhyme) and the second is *cài* (with the *gai* rhyme). According to the *Fāngyán*, it means "to gather"; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means "to pick up. In archaic script, it was written as 𢹲 with the radical 麏; now it is written with the abbreviated form and the radical 手, with the phonetic element 君.
Xiao Bingyong’s rebellion.
Hui (pronounced *xū* or *yǔ*) is a name for a monk; it means great, pervasive, and harmonious.
*Chái* (pronounced *shì* or *jiē*) refers to a class or group; it denotes those of equal status or kind.
*Gěng* (梗): Pronounced *gēng* (杏) with the *kǎo* (考) rhyme. It means straight, fierce, and strong. It is composed of the radical *mù* (木) with the phonetic *gèng* (更).

*Qíng* (勍): Pronounced *qiáng* (強) with the *yíng* (迎) rhyme. The commentary states it means great strength, force, and martial prowess. It is composed of the radical *lì* (力) with the phonetic *jīng* (京).
*Chéngmóu*: "Chéng" is pronounced with the initial *shàng* (as in *chánglíng*) and the final *xià* (as in *mùfú*); it refers to the pupils of the eyes. *Zīzī*:
"Zī" is pronounced with the initial *zǐ* (as in *zīcí*); the *Kǎoshēng* says it is *zhī*, now written as *wénlüè*.

The upper phonetic of *lángbèi* (狼狽) is *láng*, and the lower is *bèi*. The *Wenzí jílüè* (Collection of Simplified Characters) states: "Lángbèi" means to be disheveled and rampant; it refers to a state where the mind is in turmoil and order is lost. *Hūn* (昏) is pronounced *bēimèi* (悲媚).

The *Kǎoshēng* (Investigation of Pronunciation) states it means treacherous and mean. It is to be eloquent yet not upright; to be cunning yet possessing wisdom. According to the *Shuōwén* (Explaining Simple and Analyzing Compound Characters), it is composed of the radical for speech (*yán*) and the abbreviated form of *bǐ* (*pǐ*) as its phonetic.
"Ji (亟)" means to exert one's strength deeply; it implies urgency and extremity.
"Juan (睠)"—the commentary on the Book of Documents by Kong [Yingda] states that it means to look upon or to look back.
"Dongxian (東莧)"—the pronunciation is *huàn*; it is the name of a place.
Liu Xie disliked that "Jie" (頰) was a component of a personal name, so he titled his book *The Master Liu* (劉子).
Cai Zun (蔡樽): "Zun" (樽) is pronounced with the retroflex -n ending;

it is a component of a personal name. Luán (欒): "Luán" (欒) is pronounced with the final -n in the first tone. According to the *Guǎngyá*, what is called a "curved beam" (*qǔ tuò*) is termed *luán*; this refers to the modern *gǒng* (architrave). The *dǒu* (斗) is located at both ends of the *luán*. The lower character [of *luán*] is pronounced *lú*. According to the *Shuowén*, *bó luán* (薄櫨) refers to the *jī* (capitals) atop a column; *jī* is pronounced *qì jiàn* (企見).

*Yánliù* (檐霤): "Yán" (檐) refers to the eaves; it is the overhanging portion of the roof outside the pillars. It is composed of the radical "wood" (木) and the phonetic "zhān" (詹); the inclusion of the radical "hand" (手) is incorrect. "Liù" (霤) is pronounced *jiù* (救). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Liu" (霤) refers to the two streams of water flowing down from the roof. It is composed of the radical "rain" (雨) and the phonetic "liú" (留). *Yán* (檐): Pronounced *yán* (閻), it means the eaves. It refers specifically to the hollow eaves extending beyond the columns. It takes the "wood" radical and uses "zhān" as its phonetic component; the addition of the "hand" radical is erroneous. "Liù" (霤): Pronounced *jiù* (救). The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "Liu" (霤) refers to the rainwater flowing down from both sides of the roof. It takes the "rain" radical and uses "liú" as its phonetic component.

The character *guāng* (桯) is composed of "light" (*guāng*) above and "bed" (*chuáng*) below; it refers to the horizontal crossbar in the middle of a bed. Regarding the phonetic component, some texts write it as "horizontal" (*héng*), with the lower part of the character pronounced *dīng*. The *Yùnyuán* states that this is synonymous with "pestle" (*duì*). It also refers to the long planks on both sides of the bed, and is alternatively called the "bed-ribs" (*chuángbì*). The transmitted text writes it with the radical for "food" (*shí*) as *zhǐ* (㯖), which is incorrect; it is likely a scribal error. The one who recorded the text should have used the radical for "wood" (*mù*) to form *zhǐ* (󲹈), yet even this does not constitute a standard character. The phonetic component is written as *yǎo* (󳆲).
Lù Chuí (陸倕) is a person's name; its pronunciation is "chuí. Lú-lián (鑪匳):

the upper character is pronounced "lú" and refers to an incense burner; the lower character is pronounced "lián" and refers to an incense casket—that is, a lid for containing an incense burner. Zhǔ-zhū (麈󲏟):
the upper character is pronounced "zhǔ" and refers to a fan made from the tail of a deer; it is a fly-whisk made from the tail of a *zhǔ* deer.

*Jiē wǎn*: The first character, *jiē*, has the phonetic *yáng jīng yé fǎn*; it means to sigh, lament, or praise. The second character, *wǎn*, has the phonetic *guàn huàn fǎn*. The *Wénzì jílüè* (Compendium of Characters) states that *wǎn* refers to being startled and alarmed, or to sighing with regret; it is a sense of resentment. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "yuǎn" (*yuǎn*). *Niù ní* refers to being startled and distressed.
*Jiáobó* (澆薄): The first character is pronounced *jiāo* (rhyming with *yáo*), and the second is pronounced *bó* (rhyming with *bó*).
It means to look at someone furtively. In the *Yùquán*, it is also written as *qiū*. The pronunciation is *qīngyù*. It means to lower one’s head and see something in secret.

*Mù* (pronounced *mòu*, with the rhyme of *hòu*; in the *Chuci*, it means mental distress or mental confusion; according to the *Shuowen*, it means lowering one’s eyes to look intently, composed of the radical "eye" and the phonetic "wù").
*Huì* (Liu Huì was a person's name; his pronunciation is *huì*).
"Dongguan" (東莞) refers to the place name Huguan (胡官). "Jinhe" (巾褐):

"he" is pronounced with the initial *han* and the final *ge* (寒葛反); the *Mao Shi* commentary states that "he" is coarse woolen cloth (*maobu*). Xu Shuzhong says that the people of Chu called a robe a "duanhe. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "clothing" (*yi*) and the phonetic component "he" (*he*).
*Mokling* (袜陵): "Mok" is pronounced with the *fanqie* "manbo" (滿鉢). It is the name of a place in Wu Commandery, also known as Jinling, which was the capital of the Liang dynasty.

*Jingkai* (𠁊塏): "Jing" is pronounced with the *fanqie* "shuangliang" (霜兩). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "jing" means "bright. The *Shuowen* gives the seal-script form of the character "jing. The *Erya* states "jing is martial prowess"; the *Maoshi* states "jing is ruin"; the *Fangyan* states "jing is fierce. Regarding the correct orthography of the character throughout antiquity and modern times: it is composed of "zhue" (叕)—pronounced "li" (麗)—and "da" (大), with "kai" (開) reversed (改反) beneath it. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "kai" means "dry"; the *Shuowen* defines it as "high and dry."
"Qiangjin" (锵金): "Jin" is pronounced as "que" or "yang" (羊). "Qiangjing" (铿锵) describes the abundance of jade and gold; "keng" (铿) is pronounced as "keng" (坑).
"Houxu" (候旭): "xu" is pronounced as "yu" (󱇈). It refers to the sound of examination; "xu" means dawn and beauty.
*Fen-yun* (𣱦氳): The first character is pronounced *fu-wén* (扶文反) and the second is *wēi-yún* (威云反); it describes the appearance of fragrant vapors. *Pò-xī* (剖析):
The first character is pronounced *pǔ-kǒu* (暜口反) and the second is *xīng-yì* (星亦反); it means to analyze the words and meanings so as to cause others to understand them.

Panyú (番禺): The first character is pronounced *bān* (with the fanqie *pán-bàn*), and the second has the phonetic value *yú*. It is the name of a place; specifically, it is the name of a district within Guǎngzhōu. Hūnxīn (葷辛):
The first character is pronounced *huīyún* (with the fanqie *huī-yún*). It refers to the "five pungent vegetables" (*wǔxīn*), such as scallions, leeks, and the like.

*Chí-chú* (踟蹰): The first character is pronounced *shǔ* (上) with the rhyme *chú* (除) reversed; the second character is pronounced *zhù* (柱) with the rhyme *zhū* (誅) reversed. The *Yùnquán* (韻詮) states that it means "a brief moment" or "hesitation.
*Yī* (衣) and *zhěn* (賑): The latter is pronounced *zhēn* (真) with the rhyme *rěn* (忍) reversed. This was already fully explained in the seventh fascicle above.

However, [the character] *pài* (pronounced *bó* in the *Shuowen*)—the *Shuowen* states that "pài" refers to a secondary or divergent flow of water, formed with the radical for "water" and the phonetic *fǎn*—is used here.

Regarding *zhōnxī* (upper character pronounced *zhuī lún*; lower character pronounced *xī*): the commentary on the *Zuozhuan* by Du Yu states that "zhōn" means "thick" and "xī" means "night," referring to being buried underground in the long night. In the *Shuowen*, both "zhōn" and "xī" are compounds of the radical for "cave" (*xué*) combined with a formative and a phonetic element.
"Da sāo" (大騷) refers to encountering rebellion and disorder; it means being agitated and unsettled. Regarding "fuyi" (負扆):
Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that "yi" (扆) is a soft headrest. The space between the door pillars is called "yi"; it is formed with the radical "men" (門) and the phonetic "yi" (衣).

*Shǔ*: The upper character is pronounced *shí* (as in *shí fàn*) according to the *Yùnyīng*; it means a village or the wilds, and what is outside the suburbs is called *shǔ*. It is also pronounced *yě*, with the same meaning. The lower character is pronounced *mǔ*, referring to an elderly woman in a village. This is a compound character formed by combining the meanings of its components.

From the sixth fascicle to the tenth. Fascicle Six of the Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks (Xu Gaoseng Zhuan), Part Six: Chou Ren (稠人). [Note on the character "稠" (chóu): The Commentary on the Mao Version of the Book of Poetry (Mao Shi Zhuan) states that "chóu" means dense, as straight as hair. The Cangjie Pian states that "chóu" refers to a multitude. The Shuowen Jiezi states that "chóu" means many; it is composed of the radical "grain" (禾) with the phonetic "zhōu" (周).

Regarding "mó" (model) in the upper character: the *Zhengjian* commentary on the *Mao Shi* states that "mó" means method or pattern. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "a compass; it takes the radical 'hand' (手) and the phonetic 'mo' (莫). Regarding "kǎi" (standard) in the lower character: the *Guangya* states that "kǎi" means to wipe or polish. Lexicons define it as "to trace" or "to mold. The *Shuowen Jiezi* further explains it as "taking the radical 'wood' (木) and the phonetic 'jie' (皆)."
Xiè Yuè (謝籥): "Yuè" is pronounced with the radical for sheep (羊) and the phonetic zhé (灼).

It is a personal name. Zhěng Nì (拯溺): The first character is the same as the upper part of the character zhēng (蒸) with the lower part nìng (寧). An explanation has already been provided in full in the seventh fascicle of the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*).
"Suddenly" (倏然): the radical is 上 (shàng). "Injury to the flesh" (傷肉): this has already been fully explained in the sixth fascicle of the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*).

"Mí" (麛) [when used as a verb]: the radical is 上 (shàng); it is pronounced with the phonetic *mí* (鼙), read like *mí*. The commentary on the *Rites of Zhou* (*Zhouli*) states: "Mí refers to the young of a deer. The *Shuowen Jiezi* takes 鹿 (deer) as its semantic component and 弭 (mǐ) as its phonetic component. "Lian" (輒): the radical is 下 (xià); it is pronounced *zhé*. Zheng’s sub-commentary on the *Mao Shi* states: "Hunting at night is called *lie* (hunting). Regarding the "correct characters" (*zhengzi*) for these terms from antiquity to the present: [the character for] hunting takes 犬 (dog) as its semantic component and 鼠 (mouse) as its phonetic component; the sound of 鼠 is the same as above.

The character 御 (yù) is pronounced with the *jǔ* rhyme; it is homophonous with the character 宇 (yǔ). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that "character" (*zì*) means "dwelling. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical 宀 (mián) and the phonetic 禹 (yǔ), or alternatively written as 𢉠 (also pronounced yǔ) with the radical 广 (guǎng). The radical 宀 is pronounced mián.

*Jiān*: "On the upper cheek" (*shàngjiá*, *jiá* pronounced with the *xián* tone). The *Shuowen* says: "Jiān is silk fabric made by combining threads; it takes the radical *mì* (silk) and the phonetic *jiān*. *Jiān* is the correct form of the character. *Kuàng*: "Below" (*xiàkuòhuáng*, *kuàng* pronounced with the *huáng* tone). Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* says: "Kuang is cotton. The *Shuowen* says: "Kuàng is wadding; it takes the radical *mì* and the phonetic *guǎng*."

*Jiǎolù* (剿戮): The "shàng" (上) is pronounced *yú* (魚) with a small *fǎn* (反) [retroflex] tone. Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* (*Shāngshū*) states: "Jiǎo means 'to cut off'. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "force" (*lì*) and the phonetic "cháo" (*cáo*). The "xià" (下) is pronounced *lóng* (隆) with a *shū* (叔) tone. The *Zìshū* states: "Lù means 'to kill'. Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhōulǐ* states: "It means 'to disgrace'. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "spear" (*gē*) and the phonetic "liáo" (*liáo*), pronounced *lì* (力) with a *jiù* (救) tone.

Regarding "lin jue" (臨訣), the *Yùnlüè* (韻略) states: "Jue" means to part; it refers to a final parting with someone at death, specifically the permanent farewell at the moment of passing. Regarding "rú mù" (孺慕): "Rú" is pronounced as the *shù* rhyme.

Dictionaries state that "rú" signifies attachment. The *Shuowén* explains: "Rúzǐ" (孺子) is the same as "zhìzǐ" (稚子), a young child. It is composed of the radical "zi" (子) with "xū" (需) as the phonetic component; "xū" is pronounced as "xū."

"Jie" (秸) is pronounced as "gu" (古) and "ba" (八). Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that "jie" is synonymous with "gao" (稾). The *Yupian* states it refers to the straw of grain crops. "Gao" (槀) is pronounced as "gao" (高) and "lao" (老). The *Shuowen Jiezi* also records it as "jie" (稭), which is the archaic form of the character "jie" (秸).

*Lì* (pronounced with the initial *zhì* and final *fǎn*) means "to attend to" or "to preside over," according to the *Fānyán*. Guō’s commentary on the *Ěryá* states it means "to inspect. The *Shuōwén* explains that it is composed of the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) and the phonetic "wèi" (*wèi*); the character *kǎo* also uses this as its phonetic, and it is further written as *lì* (with the radical "water") with the same pronunciation. It also means "superior" or "above."

*Mǔn* (麕) and *jiā* (麚): *mǔn* is pronounced as *jūn* (桾) with the *yun* rhyme, and *jūn* is pronounced as *jūn* (軍) with the *fǎn* rhyme. Liu Zhao’s commentary on the *Gōngyáng Zhuàn* states that *mǔn* refers to the *cháng* (麞, the Chinese elk). According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "deer" (*lù*) and the phonetic "qūn" (囷), which is pronounced as *jùn* (郡). It is also written as *jūn* (麏) in character dictionaries with the same pronunciation. *Jià* (嫁) and *yá* (牙) are pronounced as *jià* (下) and *yá* (上) respectively. The *Erya* states that *jiā* (麚) is the male deer; the *Shuowén* states that *jiā* is the female deer. On the day of the summer solstice, the deer sheds its antlers. It is composed of the radical "deer" and the phonetic "duàn" (叚), which is pronounced as *jiǎ* (賈). The *Zhuàn* (傳) uses *jiǎ* (䴥), which is a vulgar character.

Regarding "fú-mù" (wild ducks): according to Wu Fang, the *Shuowen* states that "fú" refers to the water duck (*shuǐyā*). This was already explained in the third fascicle above. The character below is pronounced "móng-bǔ" (also read as "wù"). Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states that "mù" is also a type of duck. The *Shuowen* defines "mù" as a "shū-fú" (slow duck), composed of the radical "bird" and the phonetic "wù."

Regarding "hawk" (*yīng*), the *Zhengjian* commentary on the *Mao Shih* states: "The hawk is a bird of prey. In the standard characters of antiquity and today, it is written with the radical for "bird" (*niǎo*) and the phonetic element "yàn" (reading *rán* in the following chapter). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is also written with the phonetic element "dàn. The *Tianzi Zhuan* likewise uses the character "zhān" (hawk).
*Nǎo* (媼): Pronounced *ào* (下奧反). The *Shuowen* states: “*Nǎo* refers to an elderly woman; it is formed with the radical 女 and the phonetic 󲔰 (*ǎo*).

The pronunciation of 󲔰 is *wúhún* (烏魂反). *Tú* (圖): Pronounced *dù* (上杜謨反). The *Guangya* states: “*Tú* is synonymous with *dù* (to measure/calculate). The pronunciation of *dù* is *duó* (鐸). The *Shuowen* states: “*Dié* (牒) is synonymous with *zhá* (strips of bamboo); it is formed with the radical 片 and the phonetic 枼 (*yè*). According to this, *jiǎn*, *zhì*, *tú*, and *dié* may be made of either bamboo or wood. It is incorrect to write *cáo* (牃) using the radical 片, or *dié* (諜) using the radical 言. *Dié* (諜) refers to a spy or a traitor; this is not the original meaning here and is therefore not adopted.

*Tianyu* (恬愉): The upper character is read as *dié* (牒) with the secondary reading *jiān* (兼). The *Fāngyán* (方言) states it means "tranquil" (*tiánjìng*). The *Shuōwén* (說文) also defines it as "peaceful," composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic component "simplified *tián*" (*tián-sǐng*), where *tián* has the same pronunciation as above. The lower character, *yú* (庾), is read as *zhū* (珠) with the secondary reading *fǎn* (反). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* states that "pleasance" (*yú*) refers to a harmonious facial expression. The *Guǎngyá* (廣雅) says it means "joy" (*xǐ*). The *Ěryá* (爾雅) says it means "delight" (*lè*). According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "heart" and the phonetic component "yú" (*yú-shēng*).

*Dìyù* (疾瘉): The lower character is pronounced *yǔ*. Gu Yewáng states that *yù* means the illness has become slight and light. The *Shuowen* states: "Hé (癒) means the illness has recovered; it is composed of the radical *nà* (疒) with the phonetic *yú* (俞).

*Chàn guó* (覘國): The upper character is pronounced *chí zhān* (勅占反). Dù’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that *chàn* means to spy or wait in ambush. The *Shuowen* states: "It means to look; it is composed of the radical *jiàn* (見) with the phonetic *zhān* (占)."

"Zhù" (竚) is pronounced *chú* (呂反). The *Mao Shi* states that "zhù" means standing for a long time. According to character dictionaries, it is written with the radical "standing" (*lì*) as "zhù," and its meaning is identical to the character "zhǔ" (佇). Regarding the correct orthography of ancient and modern times, it is written with the phonetic "níng" (宁); "níng" is pronounced *chú* (除), followed by *lì* (下) and *dīng* (歷丁反). This was already explained previously in the third fascicle.

"Dàn" (啖): the upper radical is "tán" (談) and the phonetic is "gǎn" (敢). This was already explained in the tenth fascicle of the *Gaoseng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks). The text uses the common character "chàn" (噉).
"Lián" (連): the lower part is "qín" (禽) and "jìn" (禁). This was already explained in the third fascicle of the *Gaoseng zhuan*.

Regarding the character *zhèng* (正) in *mángjiè* (芒屩): the upper part is the character *zhèng* (𦬆), and the lower part is pronounced *jiānglüè* (姜略). Xu Shuchong said: "It is the name for a straw sandal. The *Cangjie pian* says: "Jiè, lǚ, and jī are synonyms," and its pronunciation is the same as *jiǎo* (脚). The *Shuowen jiezi* says: "It is a type of footwear (*lǚ*). It is formed from a simplified form of *lǚ* with the phonetic element *qiáo* (喬)."
*Śrīmālā-abhyudgata-saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*. "Abhyudgata" (shèngmán) means "ascending to realize.

"Sàndhí" (fǎnxià yīn mán) is the title of the scripture. "Kǎnlǎn" (kàn lǎn): the second character, "lǎn," has the phonetic value of *gǎn*. Dictionaries state that "kǎnlǎn" refers to uneven ground; the *Kǎoshēng* (Examination of Sounds) describes it as having the appearance of being wide apart or desolate. As the ancient poem says: "Kǎnlǎn, with much bitterness and toil. "Lǎ" (lǎ) has the phonetic value of *là*.

"Xu-heng" (盱衡). Regarding "xu" (酗) in the phrase "xu yu" (酗于), Sima Biao’s commentary states: "Xu means the appearance of looking on with no awareness. The *Cangjie pian* says: "Xu means to open wide the eyes. The *Shuowen jiezi* says: "Xu [as a radical] refers to being afflicted by sorrow; it is composed of 'eye' (目) and the phonetic 'yu' (于). The transmitted text uses "ri" (日) instead, forming "xiu" (𦒿), which is an error. Regarding the character "heng" (衡) below: examine its phonetics. It is composed of "xing" (行) and "jue" (角) with "da" (大) as the phonetic. This means that when an ox gored someone, one would place a horizontal beam across its horns; thus "heng" (衡) means "horizontal" (橫). It is a compound character based on associative meaning (*huiyi*). The *Wenzi dian* explains that "heng" (衡) is formed from "xing" (行) and "jue" (角) as the phonetic. This is the correct form of the character "heng" (衡).

"Xiào'ão" (嘯傲): Zhong Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states that "xiào" refers to curling and contracting the tongue to blow out sound. According to this, "xiào'ão" refers to those who, dwelling in the seclusion of the land, chant and whistle in the vast wilderness. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it with the radical "quàn" (欠) as "xiào"; here it is written as "xiào," which carries the same meaning. The character below is read as "áo gào" (熬誥). The *Bowuya* states that "ào" means dissolute and unrestrained; the *Shuowen* defines it as "arrogant" (*jù*), written with the phonetic "áo" (敖) and the radical "rén" (人). The version in the transmitted text, written with the radical "kǒu" (口) as "áo" (嗷), is incorrect.

The first tone of *xīshuài* (蟋蟀) is *xī*, and the second is *cuī lù* (衰律). The *Monthly Ordinances* (*Yueling*) of the *Book of Rites* states: "In the fifth month, the *xīshuài* dwells in the walls. The *Commentary* (*Zhuan*) on the *Mao Shi* says: "The *xīshuài* is an insect that chirps in autumn. The *Zhengzi* (Correcting Characters) of the past and present says: "It is the *qiūqióng* (秋蛬). Both characters for *xīshuài* are written with the radical for insects; *xī* and *shuài* are both phonetic components. *Qióng* is pronounced *gòng yóng* (共顒).

Regarding "zhān" (饘) and "zhōu" (粥): the upper radical is "zhàn" (戰), with the phonetic "xiān" (羶). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "zhān" is the same as "mí" (麋); the *Shuowen Jiezi* agrees that it is "mí," which is composed of the radical "shí" (食) and the phonetic "dàn" (亶), while "mí" is pronounced "méi" (眉).

"Hukou" (餬口): the upper character is pronounced "hu. The *Erya* states that "hu" means "mí" (麋). Guo Pu’s commentary notes that "hu" is also "mí. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains that "hukou" refers to subsisting by eating the food of others; it is written with the radical for "food" and the phonetic "hu."

"Ào cuì" (奧粹): The second character is read as *xià suǐ fǎn* (下雖反). It refers to the "purity and essence" (*chúnyuànjīng*) of the *Zhouyi*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Cui means not being mixed. It is composed of the radical "grain" (*mi*) with "zuò" (*zú*) as the phonetic.

"Tǐ luí" (體羸): The second character is read as *lèi zhuī fǎn* (累追反). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* says it means "weak. Jia Gui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* says it means "sick. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it means "emaciated. The middle part is "yang" (*yáng*) with "ní" (*lí wò fǎn*) as the phonetic.
Xiè Fǎoxià (謝譓下) and Xié Guìfǎn (携桂反) are personal names. Regarding *zī* (貲) in *zīcái* (貲財):

it is pronounced with the initial *zǐ* and the rhyme *yí*. Gù Yěwáng states that *zī* refers to the assets and productive resources within a household; the *Guǎngyá* says it means wealth (*zhīhuò*). According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "jade" (貝) and the phonetic "this" (此).

*Dunzi* (塵滓): The second character, *zī*, is pronounced with the *shǐ* rhyme (as in *shǐ*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Dregs (*zǐ*) are like sediment (*diàn*). It is composed of the radical *water* and the phonetic *zǎi*; *diàn* is pronounced with the *tián-liàn* rhyme. *Tianzhuo* (湔濯):

The first character, *jiān*, is pronounced with the *xiān* rhyme. The *Wenzi Jilüe* states: "To wash soiled garments. The second character, *zhuó*, is pronounced with the *zhuàng-jué* rhyme. The *Guoyá* states: "To wash. The commentary on the *Mao Shi* states: "To cleanse. Gu Yewang states: "To bathe. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to wash. It is composed of the radical *water* and the phonetic *zhái*; *zhái* is pronounced with the *zhái* rhyme.

The character *jiě* (解) in "jiě-huàn" (解澣) is pronounced *shàng jiē fǎn* (上皆買反); it means to split or divide. It is a compound character (*huìyì zì*) formed from the radical "knife" (*dāo*) and the meaning of splitting a cow's horn. The character *huàn* (澣) below is pronounced *guǎn fǎn* (管反). Zheng’s commentary on the *Mao Shi* states: "Huàn refers to washing. Liu Zhao’s commentary on the *Gongyang Zhuan* states: "To remove dirt is called *huàn*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* uses the character *huàn* (浣), written with the radical "hand" (*gàn*). The pronunciation and meaning are identical.
