it means to lock or shut. *Yānqì* (淹漬): The first character is read as *yǎn* (掩) with the *yan* (炎) rhyme; according to the *Zuǒzhuan*, it means long immersion. The *Shuōwén* states that *qì* (漬) means soaking (*òu*) and also means immersing (*jìn*).

*Da* (打): Pronounced with the initial *tu* and the final *ding* (反) [i.e., *táng*]. Also written as *téng* (楟). The *Shuowen* states it means "to strike" (*dǎzhuàng*). *Zhuàng* (撞) has the pronunciation *zhújiāng*. *Shàn gòu* (繕構): The upper character is pronounced *shàn*.

Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states it means "to repair. The *Shuowen* defines it as "to supplement. The lower character is pronounced *hòu*. The *Yupian* defines it as "a wooden frame for building a house. The *Shuowen* defines it as "a roof-covering. It is a word formed by a combination of semantic and phonetic components (*xíngshēng zì*).

The character *si* (厮) is pronounced with the initial *xian* and the final rhyme *kao*; the commentary states it means "obscured" (*yi*) and "broken sound" (*po*), referring to lowly persons; thus, they are the "slaves and inferiors" (*sixa*).
The character *qing* (情) is pronounced with the initial *gai* and the final rhyme *ai*; the commentary states it means "section" (*jie*), a compound character formed from the radical "wood" (*mu*).
To crack open with a sound is called *bào* (爆). To go barefoot (*túxiǎn*) means to be in direct contact with the ground without wearing sandals;
according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "foot" (*zú*) and the phonetic "xian" (*xiān*).
*Zhì* (upper radical: 止, pinyin: zhǐ; lǐ): According to the *Yùpiān*, it means to stumble or fall; according to the *Kǎoshēng*, it means to fail to advance.
*Bāo* (upper radical: 人, pinyin: bǎo; mào): To praise and extol.

*Kuṇhuáng* (焜煌): The first character is read as *húnwěn* (魂穩) in reverse; the second has the phonetic *huáng* (皇). According to the *Fānyán* (方言), it describes the appearance of brilliant light, meaning "to shine radiantly. The *Shuōwén* (說文) states that *huáng* (煌) means "radiance" (*huī*) and is a compound character formed from a semantic and a phonetic component.

*Kǎn* (嚫): Read as *chūxìn* (初阠); the second character is pronounced *xīn* (莘) or *jìn* (儭). The commentary on the text claims it is written with the radical "貝" (shell/beast), but this is incorrect. The *Yùnyīng* (韻英) states it means "to bestow personally"; it takes "口" (mouth) as the semantic component and "莘" (xīn) as the phonetic component.

The characters 機 (jī), 捷 (jié), 潛 (qián), 葉 (yè), 反 (fǎn), and 考 (kǎo) have the phonetic "shēng" (聲). *Kǎoshēng* says they mean wisdom, swiftness, victory in battle, vigor, and so forth. In the *Shuowén*, [the character 捷] is formed from the radical "hand" (手) with "zhì" (疌) as its phonetic;

the pronunciation of "zhì" is the same as above. The characters 歔 (xū) and 欷 (xī) have the initial phonetic "xū" and the final phonetic "xī. *Kǎoshēng* says they mean sorrowful lamentation—the lingering sound of weeping. Both are compound characters formed from the radical "quàn" (欠) combined with phonetics.

*Lián-éi* (連洏) is a rhyming compound with *ěr* (耳). The *Yùnlüè* (韻略) states that "lián-éi" refers to the appearance of streaming tears; it corresponds to the passage in the *I Ching*: "Weeping blood, lián-éi. It is a word formed by combining a semantic component and a phonetic component. *Zhuó* (擢) has the pronunciation *zhī* (知) with the tone *zhuó* (濁);
it means to discern or select. *Jiǎn-zé* (揀擇) also means to discern or select.
*Kāo-xiè* (the *xiè* pronounced as in *xiān-yè*, with the *kǎo* sound; it is said to be like a wooden clog but thick and without a foot) and *zhī-zhē* (the *zhē* having the same pronunciation;
made of wood for a sole). *Hé-dān* (the *dān* pronounced as in *dá-nán*; the *Yùn-quán* says it is a wooden object used to carry goods on the hand; the *shàng* [radical] is pronounced as *hè*).
Yíngzhōu (瀛洲): The first character is pronounced yíng (with the initial *y* and the rhyme *zhēng*).

Jiàn’ěi (荐餧): The first character is pronounced qián zài (錢廌). The *Kǎoshēng* states that when successive years are not bountiful, it is called jiàn; according to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical 艸 (grass) with the phonetic 存 (cún). The second character is pronounced nú wěi (奴猥). Kǒng’s commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* states that 餧 means "to starve. This is a zhǎnzhu (transferred-phonetic) character, composed of the radical 食 (food) with the phonetic 委 (wěi).
*Bì* (毖) [pinyin: bì; *Yùnyīng* glosses it as "to die"; it is a compound character]. *Mǐnbō* (岷嶓): *mǐn* [pinyin: mì; *Bīn* (彬) has the sound *bǐ* and *mín*];

these are the names of mountains in the region of Shu from which the River Jīng (江) originates. *Bō* (嶓) [lower tone, *bō*]: this is the name of a range of mountains. The source of the River Hán (漢) is located in Hánzhōng (汉中).

"Quē" (喎) means a crooked mouth; the upper character is read as kuài (快) with the fanqie "chuí" (垂), and the lower character is read as piān (篇). It is a compound character formed from shape and sound. "Yào" (隩) means a corner;
the upper character is read as ào (奧) and the lower as yú (愚); both are derived from the radical 阜 (fù).

*Zì* (自): *yì* (縊) is pronounced with the initial *jì* (計) reversed; Duan’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states it means "to die by hanging. The *Shuowen* says it is composed of the radical *mì* (糸) and the phonetic *yì* (益).

*Shāngjiù* (商搉): The lower character is pronounced with the finals *jiǎo* (角) and *shēng* (聲); it means "to monopolize" and "to summarize. The *Shuowen* says it is composed of the radical *shǒu* (手) and the phonetic *què* (鶴).
*Tàn yà* (歎訝): The second character, *yà*, is pronounced with the initial *ya* and the final *jià* (牙稼反).

It is a sound imitative of a cry. *Xù zhì* (秀峙): The second character, *zhì*, is pronounced with the initial *chí* and the final *lǐ* (馳里反). It is a sound imitative of a cry. The commentary states that it means "a mountain standing alone. It is also written as *zhì* (跱); both forms are identical in meaning.
*Qiāngqiāng* (锵锵): The *qù* radical with the *yáng* radical;
it describes a solemn and orderly appearance. *Yíngdì* (迎睇): The *tí* radical with the *lì* radical; this has already been explained in the fourth fascicle above.
*Lángwǔ* (廊廡): The *yīn* radical with the *wǔ* radical; this has already been explained in the first fascicle above.
"Tiègòu" (締構): the first character is pronounced "dí"; the commentary on the *Chuci* states it means "to construct" or "the framework of a hall.
"Huāihuī" (恢恢): the second character is pronounced "huí";
it means "vast. "Xiōngjīn" (胸襟): the first character is pronounced "xiōng"; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "the chest," though "xióng" (匈) may also be used interchangeably.
Zhiju (the "ju" is pronounced as in "ju," a monastic name).
His father was Huiji (the "ji" is pronounced as in "xi" with the "qi" radical; the name of Zhiju’s master). It follows the "yi" radical.

Han Ti (the first character is the "lao" radical with the "dao" radical inverted; it is a compound character following the abbreviated form of "mian" and the "niu" radical; this is the original meaning of the character's construction).

Regarding "hūnxīn" (葷辛): the first character is pronounced *huī* (暉) with the *yun* (雲) rhyme. This has already been fully explained in the twelfth fascicle of the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*).

Regarding "jiùqǎn" (舊垗): the lower character is pronounced *ào* (奧). The *Shuowen jiezi* states it is the archaic form of the character *ào*. The *Wenzi dian* states it means a "burial pit. It also has the two pronunciations *zhào* (趙) and *yáo* (姚); the *Shuowen* identifies it as a kiln, a furnace for firing tiles. The version in the [present] biography that reads "tiāo" (烑) is incorrect.

Regarding the character *qiāo* (鍤): the upper radical is *qiāo* (峭), pronounced with the *xiāo* rhyme; according to the *Yùpiān*, it is written with the radical *zào* (喿) as *yuè* (鐰). The *Fāngyán* states that in the regions of Zhào and Wèi, it is called *qiāo*. Guō’s commentary on the *Ěryǎ* and other texts write it as *qiāo* (鍫), which is also defined as *qiāo*. The *Ěryǎ* also writes it as *tiāo* (庣), which has the same pronunciation; the lower part is *chǔjiǎ* (楚甲). *Qiāo* is also *qiāo* (鍫), or sometimes written as *chū* (󳄼), which is an archaic form. *Chā* (臿) has the same pronunciation as the upper part.

"Yōu-liè" (幽洌): the second character is read as *jiē* (下連哲反). In the *Zhouyi* (Book of Changes), "The well is pure; one drinks from the cold spring. Wang Bi’s commentary states: "Lìe (洌) means pure, cold, and clear.

It is a word formed by combining a semantic and a phonetic component. 13. Scroll Thirteen. *Xu gaoseng zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks), Scroll Thirteen. "Zhì-cuǐ" (智璀): the second character is read as *lěi* (崔磊反); it is a personal name.

*Qin-yi* (䞋遺): The upper character *ce* (測) is pronounced as *jin* (近); it refers to the giving of goods. The lower character *wei* (惟) is pronounced as *bi* (恚); according to the *Kao Sheng* (考聲), it means to bestow or to grant, signifying mutual kindness.
*Xiao Yu* (蕭瑀): Pronounced as *yu* (迂), it shares the same sound as *Yu* (禹); he was the chief official of the Southern Department of the Tang Dynasty.
Wēn Yí (溫彞) reads it with the initial *zhī* and the final *fǎn*; he says it means "constant" (*cháng*) and refers to a personal name.
Xuānhuá (諠譁): the upper character is pronounced *xuān* and the lower *huā*; it means "many people. Sùliú (㴑流): the upper character is pronounced *suǒ*;
it means to flow upstream against the current. As seen in the *Yùnquán* and the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic element *lò*.

"Cāi (猜)" means to suspect or conceal; it is formed because one cannot clarify the opposite meaning. It resembles the character for dog (*quán*) as dogs are naturally suspicious, hence the radical "dog" (*quán*);

"qīng" (*cāi*) is its phonetic. "Jiān" (*jiān*) means to patrol or station troops. Its form is "jiān" (*jiǎn*). It is a compound ideograph: holding two grains of rice in the hand is called "jiān. The lower part, "liè" (*liè*), is its phonetic; it signifies clarity and purity, and implies the act of chilling or refreshing.

"Pei-jian" (瞥見) means to see for a brief moment; it refers to seeing something for only a short duration. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is composed of the radical "eye" (目) and the phonetic "bie" (敝).

"Yin-yu" (愔鬱) means a state of harmonious joy and tranquility. The upper character is pronounced with the initial *yi* and the rhyme *yin*; the lower character has already been explained in the preceding text of the sutra and vinaya.
*Míngbó* (pronounced *míng* in the first syllable and *bó* in the second) is an alternative name for the Eastern Sea.

A *fúbò* (pronounced *bái* in the second syllable) is a large ship on the sea constructed by piling together wooden planks; the boards are so thin that they cannot withstand great waves, so they are bound together with coconut-fiber ropes instead of iron nails, fearing that the friction between them would produce fire. These ships are manned by a thousand men and can reach a length of one hundred *wén*.
"Mian" (緬) is pronounced as "shangmianbianfan" (上綿遍反); it means "to contemplate deeply.

"Rou" (糅), with the phonetic "ni" (尼) and "jiu" (救) as its components, is glossed by Zheng Xuan in his commentary on the *Yili* as "mixed. This is the standard character for ancient and modern usage, composed of the radical "rice" (米) and the phonetic "rou" (柔). It is sometimes written as "zhuo" (󲜛), with the same pronunciation; it is also pronounced as "erjiu" (而救).

*Chuan* (絢): The character is pronounced with the *shangsheng* (rising tone) as *xue* (血). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Yili* states: "Vivid patterns are called *chuan*. The commentary on the *Lunyu* says: "*Chuan* refers to the appearance of patterns. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical *mi* (糸) and the phonetic *xian* (䀏); the pronunciation of *xian* is *xian* (縣), and the pronunciation of *mi* is *mi* (覓).

Regarding "zhì zōng" (warp and woof): the second character is pronounced as *zōng* (with the *qù* tone). In the *Lie nü zhuan* (Biographies of Exemplary Women), it says that the weaver can serve as a metaphor for governance; pushing away and drawing in [the threads] is called "zōng. According to the *Shuowen jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "silk thread" (*miè*) with the phonetic component "zōng" (*zōng shēng*).

"Carrying a *nang* (囊) [the *nang* is pronounced with the retroflex *l* in the sense of *nuo-lang* (諾郎); the *Mao Shi* commentary states: 'That which has a bottom is called a *nang*, and that which has no bottom is called a *tuo* (橐);

the pronunciation of *tuo* is *tuō*']. *Lilè* (𨀗轢): the first character is pronounced *kuā-guǎ*; it was already explained in the fourth fascicle above. The lower character is pronounced *líng*. The *Cangjie pian* says: 'To *li* (轢) means to tread upon. This is as stated in the *Lüshi Chunqiu*: 'He tramples upon all his contemporaries. The *Shuowen* says: 'To *li* (轢) means what a carriage rolls over; it is composed of the radical for 'carriage' and the phonetic element *lè*. The pronunciation of *niǎn* (𨋃) is *ní-zhǎn*."

*Zhi* (頿): The radical is *zi* (子) with the phonetic *si* (斯). The *Zuǒzhuan* states that King Ling was born with a beard (*zhi*). The *Shuowen* says it refers to the mustache above the mouth, composed of the radical *xu* (須) and the phonetic *ci* (此). The text of the *Zuǒzhuan* uses the character *zi* (髭) with the radical *biao* (髟), which has the same meaning. *Ran* (染) below: the phonetic is *zhan* (占). *Ran* (髯): this refers to the mustache on the cheeks. It is composed of the radical *xu* (須) and the phonetic *ran* (冉). Zhuangzi says, "beautiful mustaches and whiskers," where *mao* (𩓿) refers to the hair on the cheeks. The text of the *Zuǒzhuan* uses *ran* (髯), which is also correct; it is a character currently in common use. The pronunciation of *ran* (冉) is the same as that above.

*Kingǎn* (坑坎): The upper character is read as *gēng* (庚) or sometimes written with the radical *fù* (阜) as *kōng* (阬). Gu Yewáng says it refers to a pit or a ravine, and also to a gradual slope leading into a pond. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *keng* (坑) means a ruined site, composed of the radical *tǔ* (土) and the phonetic *kàng* (亢). The lower character is read as *kān* (堪) or *gǎn* (敢). The *Kaosheng* states it refers to a small pit.

*Zu* (祖): Upper radical *zū* (古, gǔ). According to the *Erya*, "zu" means "beginning. Gu Yewang says, "zu" means "ancestor. The *Guoye* says it means "origin" or "distant. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Zu" is the ancestral temple at the beginning; it is composed of the radical *shi* (示) with the phonetic *qù* (且). The lower part is read as *ní* (泥, ní). The archaic form is written as *ní* (禰). In current vernacular usage, it is written with the grass radical (*cao*) and *zhí* (𧋠), forming *nì* (檷). According to the *Zhouli*, it refers to the father's temple. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* states that it is composed of the radical *shi* (示) with the phonetic *ěr* (爾), and is a transcribed character.

*Huǎn* (上還綰反; shàng huán wǎn fǎn). The *Lunyu* states that it is the appearance of a slight smile. The *Mao Shi* describes it as a beautiful appearance. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "eye" (*mù*) and the phonetic component "mào" (*mào*). The pronunciation of *mào* is *zhìguān* (治官反; zhì guān fǎn).
*Śāichén* (灑塵): "Shā" (沙) is pronounced with the *yǎ* (雅) rhyme; it means sprinkling water on the ground. *Cìfú* (刺服):
"Cì" (刺) is pronounced with the *cǐ* (此) and *sì* (四) rhymes; its radical form is *cī* (㓨). *Xìng rèn* (鉎刃):
"Xìng" (鉎) has the phonetic value of "shēng" (生); it refers to a coating produced when fire is applied to soft iron, making the blade hard and sharp.

"Pengjǔ" (鵬舉): The upper character, "péng" (鵬), is pronounced like "péng" (朋) and refers to the name of a great bird; it is a compound character formed from both shape and sound. The lower character, "jǔ" (舉), follows the radical for "hand" (手).

"Línsǒu" (林藪): The lower part of "lín" (林) is pronounced as "sāngzǒu" (桑走). Zhèng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "A marsh without water is called a sǒu. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as a large marsh; it follows the radical for "grass" (草) and takes "sǒu" (藪) as its phonetic component.
*Xiàn-cái* (衒才): "Xiàn" (上玄) is pronounced *xuán* (上玄絹反). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to sell on foot," derived from the radical "to walk" (*xíng*) with "xián" (*xuán*) as the phonetic;

it is also written as *yù* (𧗳). *Zhìgù* (桎梏): The upper character is pronounced *zhì* (音質) and the lower is pronounced *gù* (音谷). It is also called *chǒuxiè* (杻械). That which is on the hand is called *jié* (桔), and that which is on the foot is called *zhì* (桎). In the *Shuowen*, both characters are composed of the "wood" radical (*mù*) as the semantic component and their respective phonetics as the phonetic components.

*Yù* (鬻): Upper radical *dé* (德), read *róng* (融) with the variant *zhòu* (祝). In the *Zhou Lǐ* (周禮), it means "to sell. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical *lì* (鬲) and the phonetic *zhōu* (粥);

*lì* is pronounced *lì* (歷). *Cháo* (嘲): Upper radical *zhāngjiāo* (張交), read *jiāo* (交); alternatively written with the mouth radical as *zhāo* (啁). The *Cangjie Pian* states it means "to mock" (*cháodiào*) or "to jest. Lower radical *xiāngyuē* (香約), read *yuē* (約). Guo's commentary on the *Erya* states: "To use words to tease and joke with one another. This is a *xingsheng* (形聲) character.

*Fěi-wěi*: The upper character is *zhèng* (correct) and the lower is *sú* (vulgar). The preceding text has already fully explained the glosses. *Wāng-huì*: The upper character is read as *huáng* (with the phonetic *wāng*) or *huáng* (with the phonetic *kuàng*). Xuánchá (玄詧) is a person’s name; the pronunciation is chá (察). Regarding *zhùbì* (駐蹕):

the upper character, *zhù* (駐), means to stop or to halt, as stated in the *Cāngjié piān* (蒼頡篇); the lower character, *bì* (蹕), has the pronunciation bì. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zōuli* (周禮) states that when a ruler’s carriage travels, the road is cleared, which refers to the present-day *jǐngbì* (警蹕). It is sometimes written with the radical for "to run" (*zǒu*) as *zhùbì* (䟆), or with the radical for "speech" (*yán*) as *zhùbì* (𧫤); the meaning and explanation are identical. According to the *Shuowén* (說文), it is derived from the radical for "feet."

*Jiǔ bān rù mán*: "To distribute among the barbarians. It is sometimes written as *bān*. In the *Zuǒzhuan*, it means "to distribute" (*bānbù*) or "to arrange in rows" (*liè*). According to the *Shuowen*, the character *fēn* (分) is composed of the radical *bā* (八) and the element *dāo* (刀).

*Bǎi bó*: Pinyin *bǎi* (上聲), *mài* (去聲). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to wave the hand. It is sometimes written as *bī* (𢳂), both forms including the hand radical. The lower part is read as *mò* (末). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to push aside an object with the hand," where the hand radical serves as the phonetic component.
*Guǎn* (pronounced *xián* [with the second tone] and *jiá* [with the first tone]; *jiá* is pronounced *jiàn* [with the fourth tone]) refers to the hard iron at the head of a carriage axle.
*Zhìwéi* (*zhì* with the second tone, meaning "to bind" or "to restrain"; *wéi* with the second tone, meaning "a corner" or "a boundary") refers to the tethering ropes.

"Tìtǎng" (倜儻) is composed of "tiān" (天) as the semantic component and "tāng" (湯, with the radical 日) as the phonetic component. In Sima Xiangru’s *Fengshan* (封禪), it is glossed as "exhausting transformations" (*qióngbiàn*) and "valiant and robust" (*xiãojiàn*). According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "extraordinary and eminent" (*zhuóyì*). Both characters are formed from the human radical (*rén*) with a phonetic component.

The character 𡗢 (fù) is pronounced with the *jiā* rhyme (as in 𨀗瓜). Zhuangzi said, "Yu and Yue ran until they died of thirst in Beidi. In the *Shuowen*, it is composed of 大 (dà) and the phonetic 㐄; the sound of 㐄 is *kǔ fēng*. The version in the *Lunyu* uses 夸, which is a vulgar character.
The character 𦖁 (xiān) has the phonetic *xi* as its lower radical. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "to look up at" (*wàng*). It is also written as 希 (*xī*).
The character 瀅 (*yíng*) has the upper radical *yīng* with the phonetic *dìng*. This was already explained previously in the tenth fascicle. The character 捫 (*mén*) has the upper phonetic *mén*.
The *Shenglei* states that "捫" is synonymous with "摸" (*mō*, to feel/touch); it is formed from the hand radical with the phonetic *mén*.

The character *kuěi* (傀) appears in the "Upper Section on Public Figures" (*Shànggōng huífǎn*). The *Fānyán* states that *kuěi* means "abundant"; Sima Qian’s commentary on the *Zhuāngzǐ* states it means "beautiful. The lower character is read as *guǐ* (韋鬼反). The *Guǎyá* states it means "extraordinary. Both characters are composed of the "person" radical (*rén*).
Fán (樊) is a personal name; Chè (綽) is pronounced with the "chāo" rhyme.

*Zuò* (坐) is pronounced with the "bīn" rhyme. Regarding *bìn* (殯): in the *Lǐjì*, Master Zhèng’s commentary states that when the deceased is in the coffin but not yet buried, and is temporarily placed upon the western steps, it is called *bìn*. The *Shuōwén* explains this character as being composed of *è* (歺, meaning "bones") and the phonetic *bīn* (賓). The version in the *Chuán* (傳) which uses *tǔ* (土) to form *yín* (𡒨) is incorrect; its correct radical is *gài* (丐).
*Línluò* (淋落): The first character is pronounced *lín*, the second *luò*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to the sound of pouring water.
Volume 14, Number 14. *Xu Gaoseng Zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks), Volume 14. *Huīyǒng* (慧頵): The final character is pronounced *lún* (at the end of a rhyme). This is a monastic name.
Huìyú (慧瑜): The second character, yú (瑜), is pronounced with the *shǒu* and *zhū* rhymes reversed [i.e., *yú*].
It is also a monastic name. Fù Míng (父珉): The second character, míng (珉), is pronounced with the *mì* and *bīn* rhymes reversed;

it is the name of Zhīlín’s father. Āngxíng (昂形): The first character, áng (昂), is pronounced with the *wǒ* and *gāng* rhymes reversed. According to the text, Āngxíng is a designation for a "lofty and majestic man" (*ángcáng zhàngfū*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is composed of the radical "sun" (*yuē*) and the phonetic "qióng" (*ēng*). Lexicons write it as 昂 with the radical "seal" (*jié*), while 卭 has the same pronunciation as above.

Regarding the character *jiào* (皭) in the Master’s name: its upper radical is pronounced *jué*. Xú Guǎng’s commentary on the *Shìjì* states that it denotes the appearance of white floating [on water]. The *Shuōwén* explains it as a light blue-white color, composed of the radicals *jué* and *bái*. The version in the transmitted text, which uses *ròu* (肉) instead to form *fēi* (𦣅), is incorrect; *jué* is the correct orthography.

The character for *Pí* (邳) is pronounced *shàng bèi fǎn* (上被悲反). According to the *Zuǒzhuan*, Xí Zhòng was moved to Pí, which is the present-day Xiàpí. The *Shuowén* states it is composed of the radical *yì* (邑) with *pī* (丕) as its phonetic; *pī* is pronounced *pī* (披).

Regarding *fēngdí* (鋒鏑), the upper character is pronounced *fēng* (烽) and the lower is pronounced *dīng lì fǎn* (丁歷反); this has already been fully explained in the first fascicle of the *Chángān Sēngzhuàn*.

"Unburnt" (未爇): Below, "nǜi" is pronounced as *zhuó* (反), and "ruán" is pronounced as *ruǎn* (音耎, 反). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "yào" means "to burn. It is also written as "rǎn" (然) in the *Shuowen Jiezi*, following the radical for fire (火) and the phonetic element "yì" (蓺); alternatively, it may be written as "rè" (𤋲), with the same pronunciation and meaning.

*Jiá* (浹): The rhyme dictionary *Xiánjiǎ* explains it as "to moisten thoroughly. A period of ten days is called a *xún*; it begins with *jiǎ* and ends with *guǐ*. *Lǐn* (凜): The *Shànglín* glossary reads *jǐn* (錦);

the *Kǎoshēng* states that *lǐn* means "reverent awe" or "a clear awareness in the mind. The *Běicāng* calls it *lǐnlè* (懍悷). Regarding the correct orthography for the modern era: it is composed of *bīng* (冰) and the phonetic *lǐn* (稟). *Huái* (懷): In the *Lúnyǔ*, it means "to cherish security. The *Yùnyīng* glossary defines it as "thought. The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of *xīn* (心) and the phonetic *huái* (褱), with the same pronunciation.

*Xi-jìng* (蹊逕): The first character is pronounced with the *jiǎn-diǎn* (上聲) tone as *jī* (鷄), and the second with the *xī* (奚) rhyme as *xì* (糸). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states that *xi* is synonymous with *jìng*. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* defines *xi* as "the path for birds and beasts. Regarding the characters themselves, the "correct orthography" (*zhèngzì*) from ancient times to the present follows the radical *zú* (足) and the phonetic *xī* (奚). The latter, *jìng* (徑), is pronounced with the *jìng* (脛) rhyme. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhōuwǔlǐ* explains it as "a path for vehicles and foot-soldiers to pass through to the capital. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* further explains *jìng* as "a direct crossing. The *Shuowén Jiězì* writes it as *jìng* (徑), defining it as "straight."

The character *yú* (旟) is pronounced with the rhyme of *xià* (下) and *fǎn* (反). The *Yùnyīng* (韻英) states it refers to a "hawk-banner" (*shǔnyú*); hawks and falcons are painted upon it to signify their swiftness. Guō Pǐng’s commentary on the *Eryā* says that bird skins are peeled and placed atop a pole to represent its bravery. The *Yùnquán* (韻詮) states that the banner moves as swiftly as a hawk or falcon. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical *mò* (𭤨) and the phonetic *yǔ* (與).

Regarding the term *qíyì* (歧嶷): the upper character *qí* (歧) is pronounced as *jù* (巨) with a shifting rhyme; *Yīng* (英) says it means "divergent paths. The lower character is pronounced *níngjí* (凝棘) as a fanqie reading, or it is written as *kǒu* (口) to form *hài* (㘈); this describes how the force of its speech is as lofty and grand as Mount Qishan.

*Jìnshèn*: the first character is pronounced *jìn* (as in "Jìn" 晉) and the second is pronounced *shēn* (as in "Shēn" 申). According to the sources, the *jìnshèn* refers to the great sash (*dàidài*). It was made of red and white silk and served as a noble ornament for the robes and caps of antiquity; it was used to record events.

Regarding the character *lǚ* (履) in the term *lǚshì* (履軾): according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radicals *shī* (尸), *chì* (彳), and *jiǔ* (久). A boat is made from hemp; the lower radical *shì* (式) has the phonetic value of *shì*. The *Yingyun* states that it refers to the horizontal wooden bar at the front of a carriage. It signifies reverence. According to the *Guangya*, the *shì* of a carriage is called *shì*; it is made by tying horse tails with colored cords to form the *shì*.
*Yu* (upper tone *yǔ*) refers to within the universe (*yǒuzhòu*).

*Kān* (read as *gé* in the Chu Ci) appears in the *Chuci*: "I would rather die suddenly (*kān*) than wander in exile. Examining the phonology, it means a great flood arrives suddenly; it is also written as *kè*, which is likewise acceptable.

*Gāomiǎo* (High and Lofty). *Xiàpáng* (Lower and Vast): the character *páng* is pronounced with the *bō* rhyme. According to the *Mao Shī Zhuàn*, *miǎo* means "vast. Wang’s commentary on the *Chūcí* states it means "distant," while the *Fāngyán* states it means "broad";

it describes an appearance of vast distance. *Chéngqiàn* (City and Trench). The upper character is *chéng*. Its standard form contains the radical *dīng*. The *Shìběn* states that *líng* was used for *chéng*. The *Huáinánzǐ* says, "The dark *líng* [makes] a city of nine *rèn*. Seven feet is called a *rèn*. The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of *shì* and has *chéng* as its phonetic. The lower character is *qiàn*, pronounced with the *yàn* rhyme. According to the *Zìshū*, a trench is the moat surrounding a city wall; the *Shuōwén* states it is composed of *tǔ* and has *zhǎn* as its phonetic.

*Jie* (皆): Below the character is *chū* (初) and *shòu* (瘦) as the phonetic reversal. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that *jie* means "to match" (*fù*). The *Yunquan* states it means "grass roots. The *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of the radical for grass (*cǎo*) with *zào* (造) as the phonetic.

*Méngshù* (氓庶): The upper character has the pronunciation *míng* (盲). The *Fanyi* of the *Mao Shi* states that *méng* refers to "the people. Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states it means "the multitude" (*yàn*), having the appearance of being ignorant.
*Huàn* (擐): The *Zuozhuan* commentary states that it means "to pierce through. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) with the phonetic element *huáng*.
The pronunciation of *guàn* (貫) is *guān*. *Hé* (闔): The *Erya* states that *hé* refers to the *gù* (雇), meaning "to close. The pronunciation of *há* (蛤) is *gāndá*.

*Wěi-chuì* (萎悴): The upper character, *wěi*, is pronounced with the *wéi* rhyme-group. The *Mao Shih Zhuan* states it means "the death and decay of plants and trees. The lower character, *chuì*, is pronounced with the *suí* rhyme-group. Guo’s commentary on the *Fang Yan* states it means "injury"; the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "sorrow," derived from the radical for the heart (*xīn*).

In the phrase "tán xiè" (談謔), "xiè" is pronounced as yuē (約) with a reversed tone; it is a transcription of the character *hu* (虎), which means to intimidate, though it is a scribal error for *huà* (嚇). This was already explained in the fifth fascicle above.
In "zhǐ lì" (砥礪), the first character is pronounced zhī (之) with an *ěr* (耳) tone and the second is pronounced lì (力) with a *zhì* (制) tone; both characters refer to whetstones.
The *Zhīpài xià pāimài* (Branches and Sub-branches Auction) says: "Water branching" (*shuǐ fēnliú*). The *Shuowén* says it is derived from the reversed form of the character for "eternity" (*yǒng*).

Regarding *zhuó* (to carve): its upper radical is pronounced *zhuó*. Kong’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* states that *zhuó* means "to hew. It is also written as *zhuō* or *zé*. The *Ěryá* says it means "to pare. The *Shuowén* also defines it as "to hew," derived from the radical *jīn* (axe) with the phonetic *chāo*; *chāo* is pronounced *dòu*.

Regarding "kàn" (龕): the rhyme dictionary *Yùnquán* states it refers to a dragon’s lair or an earthen chamber; the *Yùnyīng* says it refers to the appearance of a dragon. According to the *Shuowén*, it denotes the place where a Buddha image is enshrined, composed of the radical "dragon" (龍) and the phonetic element "shǎn" (省) from "hán" (含).

*Qióngbǐ*: The first character is pronounced *gōng* (as in *gōngjìng*, "respectful"); the *Hànshū* states that there was a district of Qióng in Shǔ Commandery. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "city" (*yì*) with "gōng" as the phonetic. The second character is pronounced *péngběi*. The *Shēnglèi* says that *bǐ* is a branch of the Qiang people. According to the *Shuowén*, [the character for] "barbarian" (*mán yí*) is formed from the radical "person" (*rén*) with "jí" as the phonetic; "jí" is pronounced *jīn* (as in *jīnlì*). It is composed of two "cài" (thorns) placed side-by-side, not the character "shù" (bundle). *Jíjié*: This refers to the Man-yi tribes. It is formed from the radical "person" with "jí" as the phonetic. "Jí" is pronounced *jīn* (as in *jīnlì*). It consists of two "cài" (thorns) placed together, not the character "shù."
*Zān* (酇國): The upper character is pronounced *hé* (何) as a reversed reading; according to the *Shuowen*, there is a *Zān* county in Nanyang, and there is also a *Zān* county in Pei Commandery.

*Zàn* (贊): This is the correct form of the character. *Tiānhuáng* (天潢): Pronounced *huǎngguāng* (晃光); Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that *huáng* refers to a pond (*wūchí*), a place where water stagnates, or a reservoir of accumulated water. Another interpretation identifies it as *huánglǎo* (潢潦), referring to floodwaters.

The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "‘Di’ (Emperor) is the title for one who rules over the world; it is derived from the ancient form of the character ‘shang’ (upward) with the phonetic ‘si’. In ancient script it is written as ‘di’ [with the radical ‘xi’ below]. ‘Xi’ is pronounced ‘ji’ (in the sense of ‘to calculate’). The *Shiben* contains the chapter on ‘Di-xi’, meaning that descendants inherit one after another in continuous succession without interruption. The *Shuowen* further states: ‘Xi’ means to bind; it is derived from the radical ‘mi’ (silk thread) with the phonetic ‘yi’. ‘Yi’ is pronounced ‘ye’."

"Bā-yán" (八埏): "yán" is pronounced as *yǎn* according to the *Yìnyì* (Phonetic Commentary) of the *Hànshū*. It refers to the furthest extremities of the earth. In the standard orthography of both ancient and modern times, it is written with the radical "earth" (*tǔ*) and the phonetic "yán. The version in the transmitted text that uses the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) is incorrect.
*Zhìqiào* (智䂮): "Qiào" is pronounced with the *liáng* and *zhuó* rhymes; it is a name for a monk (*saṃgha*) and signifies "excellent talent.
*Wúbèi* (吳濞): "Bèi" is pronounced with the *pī* and *yú* rhymes. This is the name of Liu Bèi, the King of Wu.

According to the *Shānhǎijīng* (Classic of Mountains and Seas), when the Yellow Emperor arrived at the waters of Xuánhù, a numinous tortoise carried forth a map; this refers to these very waters. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* (Dictionary of Characters) states that the character is formed from the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic "hù"; the pronunciation of "hù" is the same as above, while the final rhyme is "dú."

The character *huī* (揮) is pronounced *biāo* (上音暉, 下比宵反); the rhyme *yīng* (英) states it is a name for wind. Guō’s commentary on the *Erya* says: "A wind blowing from above downward is called *biāo*. The pronunciation is the same as above; it is composed of three dogs (*quǎn*) and does not include the radical fire (*huǒ*).

*Kǎn* (upper radical: *mén*, phonetic: *gǎn*; lower radical: *huáng*/*guì*): According to the *Cāngjié piān*, it means "to look. It may also be written with the radical *mù* (eye), forming *kàn*, though this is an error; the meaning is the same. According to the *Shuōwén*, it takes *mén* as its radical and *gǎn* as its phonetic. *Huí* (lower radical: *chuò*, phonetic: *huí*): According to the *Ěryá*, it means "distant. According to the *Shuōwén*, it takes *chuò* as its radical and *huí* as its phonetic.

*Dao* (道): The second character is pronounced with the *xián* rhyme (*jiá*). In the *Erya*, it means "harmony"; in the *Shuowen*, it means "thought. It is a compound character formed by combining a semantic component and a phonetic component.

*Xiao hǒu* (哮吼): The first character is pronounced with the *xiào* rhyme (*jiāo*). The *Pīcāng* states that "xiao hè" refers to a roar of anger. In the *Shuowen*, it is formed from the "mouth" radical with "xiào" as the phonetic. The second character is pronounced with the *hē* rhyme (*gǒu*). In the *Chuci*, "bears and cubs roar and howl" (*xù háo*) refers to the sound of bears and tigers howling.

The character *qiān* (遷) has the upper radical *qiān* (千) and the phonetic *jiǎ* (賈). The *Guoyu* commentary states it means "to change" (*yì*) or "to follow. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states it means "to move" (*yí*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "to ascend" (*dēng*), composed of the radical *chuò* (辵) and the phonetic *shè* (䙴), where *shè* is pronounced *qiān*. The lower part, *máo* (矛), is pronounced *hòu* (侯). The *Yupian* states that *jiān* (𧵍) means "to exchange" (*jiaoyì*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines *yì* (易) as "the exchange of wealth," composed of the radical *bèi* (貝) and the phonetic *mǎo* (夘).

"Ji" (汲) in "Jizhong" (汲冢) has the upper tone *jí* and refers to a place name; there was an ancient tomb of King Anlai (安斄王) in Ji Commandery. During the Jin dynasty, someone illicitly excavated this tomb and obtained several bundles of bamboo slips, all of which were ancient funerary classics. The common people of the time called them the "Jizhong Jishe" (汲冢記說). In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the character for "tomb" (*zhong*) [冢] is composed of "bao" (包) and "chui" (豖); "chui" is pronounced *chùlù* (丑錄反), and it also serves as the phonetic component.

As for *xiá* (陿), Xià Jiǎfǎn and Gu Yěwáng state that it means "not vast. The *Shuowen Jiezi* derives it from the radical "hill" (阜) with the phonetic "qiè" (匧); the pronunciation of "qiè" is qián-yè-fǎn. The version of the text that uses the radical "hand" (手) to form "zhǔ" (󳇚) is incorrect.

Regarding *wei-yi* (帷扆): the upper character *wei* (帷) is pronounced with the *biei* (悲) rhyme; Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that what is at the sides is called *wei*, and the *Guangya* identifies it as a curtain (*weizhang*). The *Shuowen* defines it as composed of the radical *jin* (巾) and the phonetic *zhui* (隹). The lower character *yi* (扆) is pronounced with the *qi* (豈) rhyme; Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states that the screen behind the throne facing west is called *yi*. The *Shuowen* defines it as composed of the radical *hu* (戶) and the phonetic *yi* (衣).

"Ci-jian" (賜縑): "Xià" (下) is pronounced as in "xià-fǎn" (下頰); "guǎng-yǎ" (廣雅) states that "jí" (緝) means "jiān" (縑). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines "jiān" as silk fabric, with the radical "mì" (糸) and the phonetic "jiān" (兼). "Lì-zé" (笠澤):

The upper character "lì" (笠) is pronounced as in "lì-xia" (立下), and the lower character "zé" (澤) is pronounced as in "zhái" (宅). The *Zishu* (字書) states that Lì-zé is the name of a marsh in the region of Wu. This marsh has no trees; because one always travels there holding a sunshade (*gài*) or a hat (*lì*), it was named accordingly. It is composed of the radicals "zhú" (竹) and "lì" (立).

*Mian-liu* (the ceremonial cap and its net). The upper character *mian* is pronounced *miǎn*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "The six robes share the name *mian*; this is an ornament for the head. Furthermore, it says: "*Mian* refers to the covering over the *yan* (the front board of the cap). The *Shiben* states: "The Yellow Emperor invented the *mian*. The *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of the radical *ri* (sun) with the phonetic *mào miǎn*. The lower character *liu* is pronounced *liú*. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states: "The *zhuan* (net) is an ornament for the heads of the honorable; pearls are suspended from it to cover the hair. The *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of the radical *yu* (jade) with the phonetic *liu*; it is a word formed through both shape and sound.

*Fù* (upper tone): The rhyme dictionary *Quán* states that providing wealth and silk to assist a bereaved family in its deficiencies is called *fù*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "貝" (bèi) with the phonetic "尃" (*fū*, pronounced *fèn* or *fēn*). It is also written as *𮚐*. The rhyme dictionary *Yǒng* states that sending carriages and horses to accompany the deceased is called *𮚐*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "貝" with the phonetic "󰂛" (*zhuì*, pronounced *zhèi* or *dèng*). It refers to bestowing wealth upon one another. The *Yupian* states it means to present gifts; the rhyme dictionary *Yǒng* states it means to send things to accompany someone. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "貝" with the phonetic "曾" (*céng*).
The character *di* (遞) is pronounced with the second tone; it was already explained previously in the first section.

*Hui* (慧) is pronounced *xiang* (臧) with the level tone, or alternatively written as *zǒng* (駔); it is a name for a monk. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states it means "a fine horse. Regarding the interpretation of the characters' meanings, *zǒng* (駔) is the same [as the previous character]; one version says it refers to a horse that covers a thousand *li*. It is a compound character (*huìyì*). *Jùn* (駿) is pronounced *jùn* (俊).

*Wanyan*: The first character is pronounced *yuǎn*; the *Yùpiān* states that it refers to a jade *guī*. The second character is pronounced *yán* (with the tone *rǎn*); the *Shuōwén* states that it is a jade *guī* nine inches long, held as a token of authority when going on a punitive expedition against those who act unrighteously.
*Huìquǎn* (慧懁): "Quǎn" is pronounced with the *è* rhyme (emphatic) and conveys a sense of urgency.
*Gǎoshī* (暠師): The first character, *gǎo*, is pronounced *gāo lǎo*; it is a personal name. *Guǎnglì* (獷厲):
The first character is pronounced *guō měng* and the second *lì zhì*; "guǎnglì" refers to a harsh and evil disposition.

Scroll 15, Volume Fifteen, Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks (Xu Gaoseng Zhuan), Scroll Fifteen. "Hui-tiao" (慧眺)—the character for "tiao" is written with the radical for "moon" (月) followed by "zhao" (詔), which is an error; it should be written with the radical for "moon" (月) followed by "pao" (𫋏). This is a monastic name. In the text of the biography, the character is mistakenly written with the radical for "moon" (月) as "mo" (朓).

"Yú" (踰) is pronounced *shàng yǒu* (上庾). The *Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry* (*Mao Shī Zhuàn*) states that it means "to overstep. The *Guǎngyá* states that it means "to cross. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "foot" (*zú*) with "yú" as its phonetic component; the lower character "kūn" (坤) is pronounced *běn fǎn* (本反). Zheng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states that the "gǔn" (閫) is the threshold of a door. According to the *Shuowén*, it is written as "kùn" (梱) with the radical "wood" (*mù*), meaning the wooden pegs at the doorposts.

"Wu-ye" (sobs): the upper radical is *wu* (pronounced *gu* with a retroflex *r*), and the phonetic component is said to be the sound of lamentation; dictionaries also write it with the radical *qian* as *mi*. The lower part is *yan* (pronounced *jie* with a retroflex *r*), and dictionaries state that the phonetic component is also written with *yi* as *e*. The *Shenglei* (Classification of Sounds) says it is the sound of unease, and it also refers to the upward reversal of breath.

"Shēn" (pregnant) [is pronounced] zhēn (zhēn reversed). In character dictionaries, it correctly follows the "person" radical (*rén*) and is written as *wěi*. The *Guǎngyá* states: "*Wěi* is precisely *yùn* (conception); bearing a heavy burden is *shēn*. The pronunciation and meaning of *shēn* and *wěi* are identical. The *Shuōwén* explains it as following the "person" radical with "shēn" as the phonetic component.

Regarding the character for *zhúgǎo* (bamboo shaft): the next character is *gǎo* (pronounced with the initial *kě* and the final *hàn*, as in the *Shàngshū Dàzhuàn*). The *Shàngshū Dàzhuàn* states: "The *gǎo* is like the *gǎo* in the *Shèyí* (Ritual of Archery). Zheng Xuan’s commentary says: "It refers to the shaft of an arrow. The standard orthography of ancient and modern times follows the radical for bamboo (*zhú*) and the phonetic *kě*. The second character is pronounced with the final *shuāngchī* (as in *fǎn*). The *Guǎngyá* says: "A *shuò* is a spear. The *Běicāng* says: "A *shuò* is a spear eight *chǐ* in length. The *Wénzì Diǎnshuō* says: "The present-day *jǐshuò* (halberd/spear) is written with the radical for spear (*máo*) and the phonetic *xiào*; the text in the [Shàngshū] *Zhuàn* uses the water radical to form *shuò*, which is a vulgar character."

"Ruì" (芮) in "Ruìchéng" (芮城) is pronounced with the radical *shǎng* (上) and the phonetic *fèn* (憤). The County of Ruìchéng is currently located in Héduō. "Wènluàn" (紊亂) has the radical *wén* (聞) and the phonetic *fèn* (憤).

Confucius’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* (尚書) states that it means "disorderly"; the *Shuowén* (說文) states that "wèn" also means "chaos," formed from the radical *mì* (糸) and the phonetic *wén* (文), and is the character for "to confuse" or "to disorder. "Lùnzá" (亂字) refers to the character for "chaos."

The character *chí* (𢙼) is pronounced with the initial *zhì* (志) and the final *fǎn* (反). The commentary on the *Shūjīng* by Kǒng [Yǎng] states: "‘Chí’ means ‘already. ‘Already’ is equivalent to ‘retreat. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical *kǒng* (廾, pronounced *gǒng*) and the phonetic *yǐ* (已).

The character *xīn* (咸) is pronounced with the initial *xīn* (𢙼) and the final *fǎn* (反). Wáng Yì’s commentary on the *Chǔcí* states: "‘Xīn’ means resentment. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* also says it means resentment. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical *xīn* (心) and the phonetic *jīng* (巠, pronounced *jīng*).

Regarding "bù zhàn" (補綻): Gù Yěwáng states that "bù" (補) means to block its deficiencies and repair its flaws. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as consisting of the radical "clothing" (衣) with "fǔ" (甫) as the phonetic. Regarding "zhàn" (綻): it is pronounced "chéng xiàn" (棖限). It refers to the tearing of a garment's hem or seam and the subsequent mending with needle and thread. Zhèng’s commentary on the *Liji* states that "zhàng" (椗) means to unravel; the *Wenzi Dianshuo* states that "zhàng" (椗) means to tear, consisting of the radical "clothing" (衣) with "dìng" (定) as the phonetic.

Because of contact (*chù*), it surges upward; when about to be reversed, the transmitted text writes it as *tǎn* (󳐏), which is an ancient form of the character *chù*. The *Guǎngyá* states that *chù* means "to strike" (*tù*). The *Shuōwén* states that it means "delight"; it is composed of the radical "horn" (*jiǎo*) and the phonetic "shǔ."
*Li*: Upper character pronounced *feng* (反); the Li River; the lower character pronounced *hu* (胡) with the *gu* (故) rhyme; a county name already explained previously. *Yan-pu*:

Upper character pronounced *ye* (謁) with the *jian* (蹇) rhyme. Kong’s commentary on the *Lunyu* states: "Yan means to lie stiffly; pu means to fall. The *Guangya* states: "Yan is like 'looking up' (*yang*). The *Shuowen* takes *ren* (人) as the radical and *yan* (匽) as the phonetic. Lower character pronounced *peng* (朋) with the *bei* (北) rhyme. The *Zitong* states: "Pu means to collapse and overturn. The *Kaosheng* states: "To fall forward and overturn. The *Wenzidian* explains it as taking *ren* (人) as the radical and *bu* (卜) as the phonetic.

Regarding "xiyuan" (西院): Xu Shuchong [in the *Shuowen jiezi*] states that a *yuan* is used for observing wind and rain, and it is also a surrounding wall (*zhouhuan*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "阜" (mountain/earth) with "完" as the phonetic component; "完" is pronounced *huán*. The reading in the transmitted text as "𨺙" is an error.

The character *yì* (裔) in "Southern Border" (*nán yì*) has the phonetic *xià yán yì fǎn*. Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states that "border" (*yì*) means "the extremity. Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states it means "distant. The *Guǎngyǎ* states that "border" (*yì*) means "the outer edge. The *Shuowén* defines "border" (*yì*) as "the hem of a skirt," composed of the radical "clothing" (*yī*) and the phonetic "guǎng" (*jiǒng*), with the pronunciation of *jiǒng* being *nǚ huá fǎn*.

Regarding the name Huānzhōu (歡州), the *Jùn Guó Zhì* (郡國志) states that Huānzhōu is now under the jurisdiction of Jiāozhōu Ānnán. As for the character *chuǎi* (揣): the upper radical is pronounced *chū wěi* (初委).

Guō Pǔ’s commentary on the *Fāng Yán* (方言) states that it means "to complete through measurement. The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* says it refers to the measurement of heights and depths. The *Shuō Wén* (說文) defines it as "to measure," composed of the hand radical with *duān* (耑) as the phonetic; *duān* is pronounced *zhī huán* (知桓).

*Ji* (䊪): The upper radical is *lan* (蘭), read as *heng* (恒). The *Huainanzi* states it refers to food made of coarse grain (*lè liáng*). The *Cangjie pian* states that *ji* (䊪) and *nǎo* (󱍮) refer to rice; it is also rice from which the husks have been removed. According to the *Shuowen*, the character is composed of *mi* (米) and the phonetic *wan* (萬). The transmitted text uses *chan* (厂) instead, forming *lè* (糲), which is a vulgar variant.

Yanjiao (琰皭): The first character is pronounced as yán (鹽) with the rǎn (苒) rhyme; the second is pronounced as qiáng (牆) with the lüè (略) rhyme. These two characters, Yanjiao, are the names of eminent monks, which have already been explained previously.
Kantan (坎壇): This has already been fully explained in the sixth fascicle.

"Liánbiāo" (聯鑣) is pronounced lián-chán-fǎn. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "In antiquity, 'lián' was always written as 'lián'; according to the *Shēnglèi*, it means 'continuous and unbroken. The *Shuowén* says: 'Lián means to connect; it is composed of 耳 (ěr) and 𢇇 (sī); it signifies a connection that does not cease. This was already explained previously in the tenth scroll.

"Qiào-jí" (the upper character pronounced qiào) refers to the steepness of mountains and hills. The *Guǎngyá* states that "qiào-jí" means steep. Xu Shùzhòng’s commentary on the *Huáinánzǐ* says it means "steep" (*shuì*) and also "severe and harsh. The *Shuōwén* also defines it as "steep," formed with the radical "阜" (mountain) and the phonetic "肖. The version in the transmitted text is written as "qiào," which is a vulgar character.

Volume 16, Part 16 of the Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks (Xu Gaoseng Zhuan), Volume 16, "Linsou" (Forest and Thicket)—the "sou" (蘇) in "lin-sou" (林藪) is pronounced with the *zǒu* (走) tone. The preceding Volume 13 has already been explained in full.
"Xiāo Yuǎn" (蕭淵) is a personal name; "Yuǎn" is pronounced as *yī* with a retroflex *ēn* (壹玄反).

The character for "jī" (擊) in "dǐ jī" (狄擊) is pronounced as *xíng* with a retroflex *áng* (狄形反); it was already explained previously in the tenth fascicle. The lower character, "zhèng jī" (正擊), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Jī means to strike (*zhī*). It is composed of the radical 'hand' (手) and the phonetic 'qì' (𣪠); the pronunciation of 'qì' is *kě* (喫)."

Regarding "senglin" (僧廩): the character "lin" (林) is pronounced as "jin" (錦). In standard dictionaries, it is correctly written as "lin" (㐭). In the *Zhouli* (周禮), the "Linren" (㐭人) office is charged with the enumeration of the nine grains. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the ritual text states: "In Lu, this is called a 'mi-lin' (米廩, rice granary). The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文解字) explains that "lin" (㐭) refers to where grain is distributed, derived from the radical "grain" (禾); it is written as "lin" (廩). In the transmitted texts, it is written with the "rice" radical (米) as "ling" (󳂳), which is a vulgar form.
"Kuàndiàn" (荒荐): the second character is pronounced qián (錢) with the *xiàn* (羨) rhyme; this was already explained in the eleventh fascicle above. "Tàzhì" (蹋𨁻):

the first character is pronounced tán (談) with the *hé* (合) rhyme, and the second is hú (怙) with the *xié* (叶) rhyme. The transmitted text writes it as "yǎn" (𮜂), which is an error. The second character is pronounced duò (惰) with the *huó* (和) rhyme; according to the *Zìshū* (字書), the correct form uses the stone radical (*shí*, 石) to form "tuó" (碢). The transmitted text uses the metal radical (*jīn*, 金) to form "chén" (䤻), which is a vulgar character.
"Seng" (僧) is the name for a monk; "Chou" (稠) is pronounced with the first tone for "zhou" (宙) and the fourth tone for "liu" (流).

"Yan" (埴) is pronounced with the second tone for "shan" (扇) and the fourth tone for "ran" (然) in the upper character, and the second tone for "cheng" (承) and the fourth tone for "shi" (食) in the lower character. In the *Laozi*, it says, "He kneads the clay to make vessels," and Master He Shanggong’s commentary states: "Yan means to blend; shi means soil."

*Hé sì* (riverbank): *xià* is pronounced as *chú* (with the *shǐ* rhyme) according to the *Shuowén*. It also means the edge of water, composed of the radical *shuǐ* (water) with the phonetic *yǐ*. *Chuán xí* (transmitting a proclamation): *xià* is pronounced as *xíng yì*.

The *Shìjì* states that when Zhang Yi was Chancellor of Qin, he drafted a written proclamation (*wén xí*) against the Chancellor of Chu; this is what is meant. Gu Yewang says: "A *pán shū* is a document used to accuse and reprimand contemporaries, while a *chuán xí* is a document used to inform, persuade, and console the common people. The *Hànshū* states: "It can be transmitted across a thousand *lǐ* to settle matters. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical *mù* (wood) with the phonetic *jiào*.

*Tàidài* (澄汰): "Dài" is pronounced *dá*. The *Guǎngyá* states that *tàì* means "to wash. Guō Pǐng’s commentary on the *Éryā* says it means "to remove soil with water. Xǔ Shūchóng’s commentary on the *Huáinánzǐ* says it means "to reach. The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic "tài" (*shēng*).
"Lead ink" (qián mò): the first character is read as xuē (with the fanqie "shàng yuè xuān fǎn"). This was already fully explained in the third fascicle above. "Liao Gōng" (Liáo gōng):
the second character is read as le (with the fanqie "shàng le xiāo fǎn"); this is a personal name. "Tuo shì" (tuo shì):

the first character is erroneously written as "wén" (culture) instead of "zhù" (wood). According to character dictionaries, it should be written with the "speech" radical (言) as "tuō. The *Fāngyán* states that "tuō" means "to entrust" (*jì*) or "to rely upon" (*yī*).
"Bowl" (bō) is pronounced with the second tone, as in "half" (xià); the same applies below, as explained previously.
"Xingtao" (廮陶): the first character is pronounced yīng or jǐng; the *Hanshu* states that there was a Xingtao County in Zhao Prefecture.

*Xié* (挾) is pronounced *xiá* (上嫌莢反). He Xiu’s commentary on the *Gongyang zhuan* states: “*Xié* means to carry within one’s bosom. The *Shuowen jiezi* states: “*Xié* means to hold; it is composed of the radical 手 (hand) and the phonetic 夾 (jiá), read as *zhōu liǔ* (周柳反) in the lower tone. The *Shiben* states that Shao Kang invented the *ji* (winnowing basket) and *zhòu* (broom). The *Shuowen jiezi* states: “*Zhòu* means to sweep away filth; it is composed of the radical 又 (hand) holding a cloth (*jīn*) to sweep inside the enclosure (*mìng*), a word formed through associative meaning (*huìyì*).”

*Páo xiǎng* (roaring): "Páo" is pronounced with the *jiāo* rhyme of *bão*. The *Chuci* says, "The bears and *pí* roared. The *Guǎngyá* says, "Páo is the sound of crying out. The *Shuowén* says, "Páo is *háo* (howling); it is composed of the radical 'mouth' (*kǒu*) and the phonetic 'color' (*sè*)."

Regarding the character *jiā* (家) [in the context of "Jiāmo"]: in ancient times it was written as *jì* (寂). The *Shuowén* states that it follows the radical for "man" (*rén*), yet the commentary erroneously explains it as such; the correct form in the *Shuowén* is *jì*, which lacks the sound of "man. Regarding *zhéshān* (摺山):

in the *Guǎngyá*, *zhé* (摺) is pronounced with the initial *lán* (藍) and the final *hè* (蛤). It means "to break" (*zhé*). The *Kǎoshēng* says it means "ruined"; the *Shuowén* also says it means "ruined," following the radical for "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic *xí* (習), pronounced with the final *chǐzhī* (恥知). Lexicons correctly write it as *yǎo* (𡼁). Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states: "*Yǎo* is a mountain deity in the shape of a beast. The *Shuowén* says *yǎo* is also a fierce beast, following the radical for "bird/beast" (*qín*) and the head for "beast" (*nóu*), with the phonetic *cǎo* (屮), pronounced with the final *érjiǔ* (而九). The character in the transmitted text is written as *chī* (螭) with the radical for "insect" (*chóng*); this is not its original meaning. *Nóu* is pronounced *érjiǔ*; *chóng* is pronounced *huǐ*.

*Xiāo* (虓) [in *xiāo hǔ*] is pronounced with the upper radical *xiào* (孝) and the phonetic *jiāo* (交). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that when a tiger is enraged, it makes the sound *xiāo*; this refers to the roar of an angry tiger. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines *xiāo* as "the roar of a tiger," composed of the radical *hǔ* (虎) and the phonetic *jiǔ* (九).
*Tuí* (mountain): the character is pronounced *duì* (with the *huí* tone); in standard dictionaries it is correctly written as *tuí*. This was already fully explained in the previous fourth fascicle.

*Chīwěn* (gargoyle/dragon-head ornament): the upper character is pronounced *chǐ* (with the *zhī* tone); in standard dictionaries it is correctly written as *fǎo*. The lower character is pronounced *wén* (with the *fěn* tone). According to this, the *chīwěn* refers to the decorative ornaments at both ends of the ridge-pole on modern halls and palaces.

"Double pupils" (chóngtóng): "Upper-chú lóng-fǎn" (a type of dragon) and "lower-tóng" (a child). The *Shàngshū Dàzhuàn* states that Shun had four pupils. The *Bīcāng* states that "pupil" (tóng) refers to the eyeball. The *Wénzì Diǎnshuō* states it is composed of the radical "eye" (目) and the phonetic "tóng."

Regarding *yǒulǚ* (傴僂): the first character is pronounced *yū* (紆禹反) and the second is pronounced *lù* (錄主反). Gu Yewang states that "yǒulǚ" refers to the body being curved due to excessive reverence. The *Guǎngyá* says it is a curvature of the back. The *Shuowén* says "yǒulǔ" means to be hunchbacked (*wāng*). Both characters follow the radical for "person" (人); *qū* (區) and *lóu* (婁) serve as their phonetic components. *Qū* is pronounced *qū* (駈), and *lóu* is pronounced *lóu* (樓).
"Li Gong": "Gong" is pronounced as *neng* (能) with an initial retroflex; it is the name of a state and also the title of the fief of Xiahou Ying according to the *Hanshu*.
"Li Yishi": The first character is pronounced as *li* (歷) and the second as *ji* (箕); the *Hanshu* states that this is the personal name of a man.
*Sengwei* (僧瑋): "Wei" (韋) is pronounced with the *gui* (鬼) rhyme;

it is a monastic name. *Lun-huan* (輪奐): "Huan" (歡) is pronounced with the *wan* (玩) rhyme. The *Book of Rites* (*Liji*) states: "How magnificent! How grand! Zheng Xuan’s commentary says: "Huan means bright. This has already been explained in the tenth fascicle of the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*).

Regarding "hàn-lào" (drought and flood): the phonetic gloss for "lào" is *fǎn-kǎo*. It is said that "lào" refers to water submerging the seedlings. In the "Monthly Ordinances" (*Yueling*) section of the *Liji*, it is written as "lǎo," stating: "The floods of water ruin their city walls. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "water" with "láo" as the phonetic; "láo" is pronounced *lì-zhào-fǎn*.

*Xiāo* (囂) in the first character is pronounced *xūjiāo* (虛嬌). Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states that *xiāo* means "clamor. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "*Xiāo* refers to breath escaping from the head; it is formed with *jí* (㗊) as the phonetic and *yè* (頁) as the semantic component; *jí* is pronounced *zhí* (戢), and *yè* is pronounced *xié* (纈). *Náo* (撓) in the second character is pronounced *náoyǎo* (拏咬). The *Guangya* states that *náo* means "to disturb"; the *Shenglei* states that *náo* means "to stir up" or "to agitate. It is formed with *shǒu* (手) as the semantic component and *yáo* (堯) as the phonetic.
On Mount Li, there was the rebellion of Li Zhi. The *Shanhai jing* states that this is a mountain name; it has already been explained previously. Regarding "jué" (譎):

the upper radical is "jiān" (涓) with the phonetic "yuè" (悅); Zhong's commentary on the *Lunyu* says "jué" means deceitful. Zhong's sub-commentary on the *Mao Shi* says it means not speaking directly. The *Shuowen jiezi* says "jué" means expedient deception; it is composed of the radical "yán" (言) with the phonetic "yù" (矞), where "yù" is pronounced "jù yù". The following character "zhèng" (正) has already been explained as before.
The entry for *zuàn* (鐫勒) with the upper radical *jué* (蕝) reversed [is] already explained at the beginning of the first fascicle.

Regarding *sàngǎi* (繖蓋): the upper character is pronounced *sāng* (桑) with the *dàn* (亶) rhyme, and the lower is *gài* (該) with the *ài* (愛) rhyme; it is the name of a mountain. The *Dongguan Hanji* (東觀漢書) states: "When it rained from heaven, those on horseback held *sàngǎi* [parasols] while following over a hundred riders. The *Zhuge Liang Ji* (諸葛亮集) says: "One must not carry a *sàngǎi*," which is correct. The *Gujin Zhengzi* (古今正字) states: "*Sàn* (繖) is simply *gài* (蓋). It follows the radical *mì* (糸) and uses *sàn* (散) as its phonetic component; it is traditionally written as *sǎn* (傘), which is a vulgar form.

*Jiē* (揭): The upper character is pronounced *qián* (虔) with the *yù* (蘗) radical; the *Shǐjì* (史記) states that "to *jiē*" means to lift up or raise high. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the "hand" radical and the phonetic *hé* (曷). The lower character is *kǎn* (坎) with the *gān* (甘) radical; the *Fāngyán* (方言) states that a *kǎn* is a ceramic vessel. The correct orthography for both ancient and modern times uses the "earth" radical and the phonetic *gān* (甘).
The Phonology and Semantics of All Scriptures,
Scroll Ninety-three and Scroll Ninety-four,
compiled by the Scripture-translating Śramaṇa Huilin.
From volume seventeen to thirty, totaling fourteen volumes. Volume seventeen:

*Xu gaoseng zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks), Volume Seventeen. The characters "Zhì" (智) and "Jiè" (鍇)—the latter pronounced as in "jiē" (皆)—are both names of monks. According to local dialects, "jiè" means "firm."

The Xiancheng Mountain (仙城山) is also called Xianshan (仙山). [The characters] "pian" (駢), "luo" (羅), "xiao" (瀟), "xiang" (湘), "reng" (仍), "hui" (揮), "yan" (飫), "ya" (押), and "jie" (接) are phonetic transcriptions of the names of insects.

Regarding "gou pi" (構甓): "gou" (構) is pronounced as *gōu* (上鈎候反); this was already explained in the twelfth volume above. "Ping" (萍) is pronounced as *píng* (下萍覓反). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (毛詩傳) states that "di" (躄) refers to a brick (*ān*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文解字) explains it as being composed of the radical for "tile" (*wǎ*) with the phonetic element "bi" (*bì*). "Ān" (㼾) is pronounced as *lù* (音祿), and "zhuān" (甎) is pronounced as *zhuān* (音專).

*Gān*: The *Yinyì* (Phonetic Commentary) to the *Hànshū* states that "gān" means radiant light; according to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) with the phonetic component "yán. *Zhū*: The upper character is pronounced *zhù*, and the lower is pronounced *sī*.

Dú Yù’s commentary on the *Zuǒchuán* states: "The Zhū River is north of the city of Lǔ. The lower character is pronounced *sì*. The *Shānhǎijīng* states: "The Sī Water originates northeast of Wú, passes through Húlíng, and flows into the Eastern Sea. According to the *Shuowén*, both characters for "Zhū" and "Sī" are composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*).

The character above is *yì* (壹) with the variant *yàn* (艷); Kuo Pu’s commentary on the *Fāngyán* states it means "to be satiated. The *Shuowén* states it means "to be full from eating," composed of the radicals for "sweetness" (*gān*), "meat" (*ròu*), and "dog" (*quǎn*). The transmitted text writes it as *yàn* (饜) with the radical for "food" (*shí*), which is a vulgar form. The character below is *jù* (據) with the variant *yū* (於); the commentary on the *Máo Shī* states it means "to be full. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states it means "to be satiated. The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radical for "food" (*shí*) and the phonetic *āo* (芺).
*Jùnzhì* (捃摭): The first character is pronounced *jūn* (君運反) and the second is *zhì* (之亦反). This was already explained in the first fascicle above.

*Kè wà* (係韤): The first character is pronounced *jī yì* (鷄詣反). The *Shuowen* states: "To tie; it means to bind. It is composed of the radical 人 (person) and the phonetic 系 (xi). The pronunciation of 系 is *xì* (奚計反). The second character is pronounced *wǎn fā* (晚發反). The *Shuowen* states: "A garment for the feet; it is composed of the radical 韋 (leather) and the phonetic 蔑 (miè). The transmitted text uses 䌩 with the radical 糸 (silk), which is incorrect.

"Tuō" (咄): The upper radical is *dūn* (敦) with the *fǎn* (反) suffix; the *Zìshū* (字書) states it means "to scold. The *Cāngjiépiān* (蒼頡篇) states it means "to rebuke. The *Shuowén* (說文) states that "tuō" is like addressing one another; it is a sound produced from the mouth.

"Envy and jealousy" (yuànjí): "ji" is pronounced as *qín* (秦) and *yì* (逸) in reverse [i.e., *yì-qín*]. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states: "To harm the worthy is called jealousy. In the standard characters of antiquity and today, it follows the radical for "woman" (女) and takes the sound of "disease" (疾).

"Hen-poison" (zhèndú): "zhèn" is pronounced as *chú-jìn* (除禁). The *Shanhaijing* states: "Mount Nüji has many *hen* birds. Guo Pu’s commentary says: "The *hen* is a purple-hued, long-tailed bird with a red beak; it is a snake-eating bird. It follows the radical for "bird" (鳥) and takes the sound of "yin" (冘). Its "yin-quì" (淫喙) is pronounced as *xū-wèi* (吁衛), and the same applies below. The *Shuowen* states: "A plant that harms people. It follows the radical for "grass" (屮) and takes the sound of "poison" (毒). "Chǐ-liè" (恥列) is the pronunciation of "grass" (屮).
"Gāowù" (high-velocity): the lower character is pronounced *zhēng* with the *chì* tone; this has already been explained in the sixth fascicle of the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*).
"Jīdǐ" (foundation-base): the lower character is pronounced *zhēng* with the *chì* tone; this has already been explained in the tenth fascicle of the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*.

*Jì* (上居例反): The *Shuowen* defines this as *xié*, meaning a rabid dog; it is composed of the radical *quán* (dog) and the phonetic *zhé*. In the *Zuozhuan*, "from making" (*cóng zhì zuò*) refers to *jì*. *Xī zhěn* (上緗妻反):

Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* states that the rhinoceros (*xī*) is shaped like a water buffalo with a pig's head, a large belly, short legs, three hooves, and a black color; it has two horns, one on the crown of its head and one on its snout. A "rhinoceros pillow" (*xī zhěn*) is a pillow made from a rhinoceros horn. The *Shuowen* explains that *xī* is composed of the radical *niú* (ox) and the phonetic *wěi*; the character for "pillow" (*zhěn*) below is correctly written with the radical *mù* (wood) and the phonetic *yín* (pronounced *yín*).
"Qílù": the upper character is *zhèng* (正); the lower character is pronounced *lù* (鹿). "Wǎnyǐ":
the upper character is pronounced *wǎn* (晚); the lower character is the phonetic transcription of *yí* (儀).

It is a monastic name. "Xiánchǎng": the lower character is transcribed as *chāng* (掌). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To level high ground is called *chǎng*. It is composed of the radical *pō* (攴) with the phonetic *shàng* (尚)."

*Chánhuán* (潺湲): The first character is pronounced *shàn* (with the *xián* rhyme), and the second has the sound *yuán*. The *Zītǒng* states that "chánhuán" describes the appearance of flowing water; the *Wénzìdiǎn* explains it as the sound of water making noise. *Míù* (繆): This follows the former [reading] as *měibiāo*;

it also has the two pronunciations *mí* and *yòu*, and is also a surname. According to the *Wǔdiǎn*, those with the surname Míù are scholars and officials. The transmitted text uses the character *zhuó* (䋚) with the radical for "feather" (*yǔ*), which is an error resulting from the omission of the lower part of the character *quán* (全).

Regarding "huā-dìng" (flower-lamp): the *Wénzìdiǎn* (Dictionary of Characters) states that "dìng" means a lamp. The transmitted text says that "thousand-branch flower-lamps" refers to lamps made of a thousand branches. Regarding "jiàn" (eyelid): the upper tone is pronounced as "jiǎn.

The *Zìshū* (Book of Characters) states it refers to the skin above and below the eyes. The *Wénzìdiǎn* states that "jiàn" refers to the eyelids; it is derived from the radical "eye" (目) with "qiān" (僉) as the phonetic component.

Regarding the character *xiè* (嫌) in "xièqiào" (嫌誚): the first character has already been explained above. The second character is pronounced *qiáo* (樵曜反). The Commentary on the Book of Documents by Kong [Yuan] states that it means "to reproach" (*qiào-ràng*). According to the *Cangjie pian*, the standard form of the character is written with the radical for "fire" (*huǒ*) as the phonetic component, meaning "to scold and reprimand. It is also written as *zhāo* (譙).

Qíqū (崎嶇): The first character is pronounced as qǐ (起) with a reversed tone, and the second as qū (曲) with a reversed tone. The *Pīcāng* states that "qíqū" means "unstable"; the *Bóyá* states it means "tilting. It may also be written as shǐyū (陭䧢), which has the same pronunciation; the "shàng" (上) refers to the radical 阜 (mountain).
The character for "miǎn" (慊) is read as *qiè* (篋簟反). This was already explained in the third fascicle of the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*).

Regarding the character for "zhèn" (蕈) below, it is read as *xún-rěn* (尋荏反). Lexicons state that "zhèn" refers to mushrooms (*jùn*) or earth fungi (*dìjùn*). The *Shuowen jiezi* states: "Zhèn is a type of mulberry mushroom (*sāngjùn*); it is formed with the radical 'grass' and the phonetic 'tán'; the pronunciation of zhèn is the same as the character above."

"Dān" (殫) is pronounced with the initial *dàn* and the final rhyme *fǎn*. The commentary on the *Shūjìng* by Kǒng [Yǎng] states that "dān" means "exhausted. The *Shuōwén* says "dān" means "the ultimate limit"; it is composed of the radical *dài* (歹) and the phonetic *dān* (單). The sound of *dài* is *wǔdá fǎn*.

The character 恖 (sī) is pronounced with the upper radical *chí* (知反). Zheng’s preface to the *Erya* states: "‘恖’ is the flower garden of those who possess literary talent (*hàn*); it means to expand. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical 手 (hand) and the phonetic 恖; the sound of 恖 is the same as that of 上下 (shàng xià). The *Zishu* states that it is the formal orthography for the character 思 (sī).
"Yangdi" (煬帝) is the posthumous title of the Sui Emperor; "yang" (煬) is pronounced with the initial *shang* and final *-fan*.

"Jinye" (金鑰) is pronounced with the initial *yang* and final *-zhuo*; according to the *Zishu*, the correct form follows the gate radical (*men*) as "yue" (𨷲), though the *Qianshi jiaolu* has already explained that it is written with the bamboo radical (*zhu*) as "yue" (籥), which is a vulgar character, yet both are used interchangeably.

*Tui-hui* (穨毀): The first character, *tui*, is pronounced as in *duì léi* (隊雷). This was already explained in the fourth fascicle above. The second character, *hui*, is pronounced as in *huī wěi* (揮委). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "to be deficient. It is composed of the radical "earth" (土) and the phonetic "shui" (毀, in its abbreviated form). In archaic script, it is written with "wang" (王) instead.

The character for *mò* (millstone): the upper radical is *shí* (石), pronounced *duì* (對) in reverse; the *Shìběn* (Shìběn) states that Gōngshū [Zhòng] first made the stone mill. The *Shuowén* says: "A *mò* is a *shǒu* (磨). It is composed of the radicals 'stone' (*shí*) and 'qǐ' (*qǐ*); *shǒu* is pronounced *mó* (摩) with the final *pò* (破) tone. The lower part is *nǚ* (女) with the *è* (𩥇) radical, pronounced in the departing tone. The *Zìkǎoshēng* says: "*Shà* (砐) refers to stone; *shà* (砐) refers to ground rice. It is composed of 'stone' (*shí*) and 'jí' (*jí*); it is a phonetic-semantic compound."

Regarding the character *xiǔ* (𣧩): the *Bīcāng* states that it means "to die" (*mò*); the *Guǎngyá* states that it means "extreme" (*jí*). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* says: "One who dies in old age is called *xiǔ*. The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radical *dài* (歹) with the phonetic *dōng* (冬).

The term *xié* (脇) does not refer to an object; it is pronounced *jiān* (上杴劫反). The *Zuǒzhuan* states, "I have heard of his joined ribs" (*wén qí pián xié*). The *Shuowén Jìzì* explains that *xié* refers to the two sides of the abdomen (*dù liǎng bǎng yě*). It is composed of the radical for flesh (*ròu*) and the phonetic element *lí* (from which the sound is derived); *lí* is pronounced *xián* (頰反).

The sound of "bào" (爆) is pronounced with the initial *bao* and the final *mào*. The *Guǎngyá* states that it means "to heat intensely. The *Kǎoshēng* says it is the sound of burning firewood or bamboo. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "to scorch," composed of the radical "fire" and the phonetic "bào" (pronounced *bào* with the tone *wū*). The character is written as 爆.
“Stinging the Thigh” (*cì gǔ*): The first character, *cì*, is pronounced *zhèng* (in the sense of “correct”) and *zì* (in the sense of “to prick”), with the latter sound being *gǔ*.

This was already explained in the thirteenth fascicle above. “Variegated” (*bān bó*): The first character, *bān*, is pronounced *bānmán*. The *Zītǒng* also writes it as *biǎn* or *bān*; its meaning is the same as *bān*, signifying a variegated or mottled pattern. It is also said to mean the appearance of a distinct pattern. The sound is *biàn*. The transmitted text writes it with the radical for “knife” (*dāo*) as *bān*, which is a vulgar form. The second character, *bó*, is pronounced *bāng miǎo*. The *Hànshū* states that the blending of black and white is called *bó*. The *Shuowén* says it refers to a horse of impure color, taking the radical for “horse” (*mǎ*) and the phonetic *xiáo*. The transmitted text writes it with the radical for “cross” (*jiāo*) as *bó*, which is a vulgar form.
"Chunsui" (淳粹): although the character "zui" (醉) here is pronounced as "fan" (反), it has already been explained in the eighth fascicle of the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*).
Fascicle 18, Volume 18: "Huizanzha" (慧瓚): the character "zha" (旱) is pronounced as "fan" (反); this is a monastic name.
The character 權 (quán) is formed with the radical 會 (huì); it is a surname. The transmitted text [of the *Shuowen*] uses the radical 心 (xīn), which is incorrect.

The character 嫗 (yù)—with the phonetic component 紆 (yū)—Gu Yewang states that in modern times women are called "yù. The *Shuowen* says: "Yù is a term for an old mother; it is formed with the radical 女 (nǚ) and the phonetic 區 (qū)."

The character 𩮀 (pronounced *zōng* with the *kǒng* rhyme) is explained in Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* as "the appearance of a woman's high hair-knot. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* states that it means "a comb for binding the hair," derived from the radical 髟 and the phonetic 悤; the transmitted text writes it as 𩮀, which is a vulgar form.
"Suì cuàn" (遂竄): "cuàn" is pronounced as *chùan* (下󱍮筭反); "cuàn" means to flee or to run away; this has already been explained in the seventh fascicle of the *Chuan* (傳).
"Shēn zé" (深賾): "zé" is pronounced as *chéng zé* (下崢責反); this has already been explained in the previous commentary on the *Jiàolù* (教錄).

*Bò* (upper tone, *bǎi*): Gu Yewáng says it means to split with the hands or to break apart. The *Guǎngyǎ* says it means to divide. The *Shuōwén* says it means to part (*huī*), composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "bì" (*pì*).
*Quánfù* (upper tone, *qīxuān*): This has already been explained previously.
"Bènglèi" (迸淚) [the first character pronounced as bǎi, the second as mèngfǎn] appears in the tenth fascicle [of the *Shuowen Jiezi*], where it has already been explained.

Regarding "tá" (榻): the *Guǎngyá* states that "tá" means "píng" (a gaming board); the *Shìmíng* states that "tá" is a narrow, long bed; and the *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* states that "tá" is a "tà" (stepping) bed, formed with the radical "wood" and the phonetic "㚔" (*tà*).

"Fen-yun" (紛紜): "Fen" is pronounced as *fu* with the *wen* rhyme; according to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means "confusion. The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radical "silk thread" (*miè*) and the phonetic "fen. "Yun" has the pronunciation *yin* with the *yun* rhyme; according to the *Kǎośēng*, "fen-yun" describes the appearance of disorder.

"Feng-wěi" (風痿): "Wěi" is pronounced as *wei* with the *wei* rhyme. Zheng’s commentary on the *Lìjì* states that "wěi" refers to a disease. The *Cāngjiépiān* states that "wěi" means the feet are too weak to walk. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "wěi-bì" (paralysis/numbness), composed of the radical "sick person" (*nà*) and the phonetic "ui."
*Lü-lǚ* (the first character pronounced with the *lú-gē* rhyme and the second with the *lóng-yǔ* rhyme) has already been fully explained in the eighth fascicle above.
*Qīrén* (pronounced *qī-jī*) is stated in the *Kǎoshēng* to be the name of a county in Zizhou.

The character 鐓 (dùn) is pronounced *tuò* (with the radical for "foot" and the phonetic for "opposite"). The *Liji* (*Book of Rites*) states: "When advancing with the *yue* and *ji* halberds, one holds the butt forward and the blade behind. The commentary on the *Mao Shi* says: "The *dùn* is the socket of the *ge* spear; 'socket' (*zùn*) is pronounced *cún-xùn*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "'Dùn' refers to the bronze socket at the base of the shaft of a lance or halberd; it is composed of the radical for 'metal' and the phonetic 'dūn. The character 'bi' (pronounced *mì*) refers to the handle of the lance."

Regarding the character for "iron spear" (qiāng): the *Yèyáng* [dictionary] reverses the character, while the standard script correctly takes "wood" (木) as its radical. The *Cāngjié piān* states: "A spear is wood sharpened at both ends. The *Wénzìdiǎn* explains: "A spear is used for warding off; it is a weapon. It takes 'wood' as its radical and 'cāng' as its phonetic. To write it with the "metal" (金) radical as "qiāng" is incorrect.
"Min" (憫然) is pronounced *mǐn* (with the tone of *yǔn*, 殞). This has already been explained in the eighth fascicle of the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*).

Regarding "kan" (刊), *Du Yu’s Commentary on the Zuo Zhuan* states that it means "to remove" or "to determine. *Zheng Xuan’s Commentary on the Liji* states it means "to pare down. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is composed of the radicals for "knife" (刀) and "shield" (干).

Regarding "linluò" (淋落): the upper character is pronounced as the "li" in "lìjīn" (立金). The *Zītǒng* states that "lin" means to drench the ground with water. Regarding "fùèr" (𦨕餌): the upper character is pronounced as "fú";

the *Zìshū* correctly identifies it as "fú," which has already been explained previously. The lower character is pronounced as the "zhì" in "érzhì" (而志). *Cāngjié* says "èr" means food; the *Shuōwén* says "èr" is the same as "bǐng" (a flat cake), formed from the radical "food" (食) with the phonetic "ěr" (耳).
*Shān* (in the *Mao Shī Zhuan*, it is written as 󱺜): the upper character is pronounced *shān* (as in *shānmáo*). It means to clear away weeds. Gù Yěwáng states that *shān* means to reap grass.

*Qì* (隙): the upper character is pronounced *qīng jí*. The *Shuōwén* states it means a hole cleared out in a wall; it is composed of the radical *fù* (阜), with *bái* (白) below, and *xiǎo* (小) at the top.
