The character for *tiān* (天) is pronounced *jué* (厥) with the *fǎn* (反) [classifier]; in standard dictionaries it is correctly written as *quàn* (眷). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (毛詩傳) states: "Quàn means 'to look back' (*gù*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文) also defines it as "to look back," composed of the radical *mù* (目, eye) and the phonetic *juǎn* (卷) abbreviated; the version in the *Zhuan* (傳) is written as *juàn* (睠), which is a vulgar form.

The characters for Xiǎnyǔn (獫狁)—the first pronounced xiǎn and the second yǔn—are correctly written as Xiǎnyǔn (玁狁) in the standard lexicons. This was already explained previously in the twelfth fascicle of the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*). Although the text of that biography uses the character "xiàn" (獫), it is also acceptable.

*Chengkuo* (sincerity and integrity): the first character is pronounced *qiàng* with the *jiǎo* (departing tone) as a reversed reading; this has already been fully explained in the second fascicle [of this work].
*Bai-zàn* (chanting and praise): the first character is pronounced *bài* and the second *zàn*; this has already been fully explained in the first fascicle of the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*.
The character for *qī* (妻) is pronounced with the radical *shéng* (繩) and the phonetic *zhèng* (證). This has already been explained in the second fascicle of the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*.

The character for *xião* (驍) is pronounced with the radical *jiǎo* (晈) and the phonetic *yáo* (堯). Xu Shuchong stated that it means "valiant and urgent. The *Hànshū* says it refers to the General of the Valiant Cavalry (*xiãoqí jiāngjùn*). The *Guǎngyá* says it means "robust. The *Shuowén* says it means "a fine horse," composed of the radical *mǎ* (馬) and the phonetic *yáo* (堯). The lower part is pronounced with the radical *hán* (寒) and the phonetic *dàn* (旦). This has already been explained in the nineteenth fascicle. It is also written as *tán* (忓) with the radical *xīn* (心), having the same meaning.

*Zhuī hè*: the first character is pronounced *chuī* (with the radical *chui* [隹]) and the second is pronounced *héng kè* (with the radical *heng* [恒] and *ke* [尅]). Gu Yewang states that *hè* refers to the written testimony and accusations submitted in legal proceedings; it is also the document used for the interrogation of a case. Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* says it is "the essential summary of the various forms of crimes in litigation. The *Shiji* uses this term, while the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "legal punishment for having committed a crime," stating it is composed of the radical *dao* (刀) with *hai* (亥) as its phonetic. The version using the radical *ren* (刃) is an error.
"Bān gào shàng bāmán fǎnzìshū zhèng zuò bān" (The Announcement to the Eight Mán Barbarians, Reverse Character Dictionary, correctly titled Bān) was already fully explained in the first scroll above.
"Jǐn chú shàng jù yú fǎn xià yīn chú" (Jǐn Chú; the upper character is pronounced jù yú, the lower is pronounced chú) was already explained in the eighth scroll above.

"Tán" (耼) is pronounced with the initial *th* and final *-an* (上他含反); it is the name of Lǎozi. In transmitted texts, it is sometimes written as "tián" (甜) with the radical for the tongue, but this is not its original meaning; this was already explained in the previous "Discourse on Rectifying the Meaning. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the correct character is written with the radical for the ear and the element "two" (冄). Alternatively, it may be written as "shēn" (𨈜) with the radical for the body.

In the "Gu die" (Ancient Edict), the character is pronounced *tián* (with the *tiān* and *qù* finals reversed); according to the *Zìshū* (Dictionary of Characters), it is written with the radical *piàn* as *dié*. When used in the sense of transmitting texts, it is written with the radical *yán* as *dié*.

This was not previously seen; see the explanation given earlier. Regarding "jiù shì" (to rescue the world), the pronunciation is *qiú* (with the *jù* final); this was already explained in the ninth fascicle above.
The character 憓 (héi) is read as xié (桂反). This has been fully explained in the twelfth fascicle of the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*).

The character 槀 (gǎo) is read as dào (高道反). Gu Yewang states that "gǎo" is synonymous with "cǎo" (grass). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of 禾 (grain) as the radical and 高 (gāo) as the phonetic; the lower part, 界 (jiè), is read as hài (諧反). Gu Yewang says that a "jiē" (street) is a thoroughfare for four-way traffic. The *Hanshu* states that Gaojie was the residence for the barbarians. In the standard characters of past and present, it is written with 行 (walking) as the radical and 圭 (guī) as the phonetic.

*Fenjin* (氛祲): The first character is pronounced *fen* (上音紛); the second is pronounced *zi* with the rhyme *zhen* (下子鴆反). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "Jin refers to the qi of Yin and Yang intermingling and gradually forming calamities. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "Jin is the qi of *fu* (auspicious/atmospheric). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Jin means the qi that evokes auspicious signs; it is composed of the radical '示' (shì) and the phonetic component '侵省' (qīn-sǐng)."

“Xūnyóu” (薰蕕): the first character is pronounced as xùn (訓) with the rhyme Yun (雲), and the second is pronounced as yóu (酉) with the rhyme Zhou (周); these were already explained in the *Shìjiào lù* (釋教錄).
“Sùjí” (素嫉): the pronunciation of the second character is jí (疾); this was already seen in the previous explanation.

The character *wǎng* (罔) is formed by adding the radical "speech" (言) to *shàng* (上); it is a corrupted form of the character *gāng* (綱). The *Erya* states: "*Wǎng* means 'none' (*wú*). In the *Lunyu*, [the phrase] "one may be deceived, but one cannot *wǎng*" [is used]. Ma Rong’s commentary glosses it as "to falsely accuse" (*wú*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *gāng* (𠕀), explaining that it represents the appearance of intersecting lines.
Wei Cong (韋悰) is a name; "cong" (悰) is the opposite of "zong" (宗).

Regarding the wife's character: the *Shuowen* explains that "zheng" (正) means "the wife. It is one who is equal to oneself. In the *Shuowen*, [the character for wife] is composed of "nü" (女, woman) and "you" (又, hand), signifying the performance of the duties of a wife; it takes "chuo" (屮) as its phonetic component. "Chuo" (屮) is pronounced "chilie" (勑列反).

*Wen* (縟): upper radical *jin* (錦), pinyin *ru* (燭) with retroflex *fan* (反). Lu Ji’s *Wénfǔ* (文賦) states: "Brilliant as intricate embroidery. The *Shuowén* (說文) states: "Intricate (*wén*) means profuse ornamentation; it takes the radical *mì* (糸) and the phonetic *rú* (辱). *Nǎi* (靄): upper radical *yān* (淹) with *xiǎn* (險) *fan*. The commentary on the *Máoshī* (毛詩) states:

"Nǎi is the appearance of overcast clouds. The *Gōngjīn zhèngzì* (古今正字) states: "The character below [the radical] takes *yǔ* (雨) and the phonetic *yǎn* (奄). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states: "Nǎi is the appearance of mist and clouds; it takes the radical *yǔ* (雨) and the phonetic *yè* (謁). The version in the *Chuánwén* (傳文) uses *cǎo* (草) as the radical, writing it as *ǎi* (藹), which is a semantic error.
*Ku* (the upper tone) is the Sanskrit word *kṣu*; *da* means "blessing" (*puṇya*). *Jiangmi* (the lower tone): *mi* is pronounced as in *mǐ* (as in *mǐbi*).

The *Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry* states that *mi* means "to stop. He Xiu’s commentary on the *Gongyang Commentary* states it means "not yet resting. Jia’s commentary on the *Discourse of the States* states it means "to calm. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *mi* refers to the end of a bow; it is also said to mean "to turn back," being formed from the radical for "bow" with the phonetic element "ear" (*ěr*).

"Jiāngzhà" (將詐): "shàng" (上) is pronounced *qí* (七余反); the *Guǎngyá* states that it refers to the monkey (*jūmíhóu*). The *Cāngjiépiān* states that it means to lie in wait (*sìhòu*). The *Shuōwén* states that it belongs to the class of *jūsī* (𤤿), following the radical for dog (*quán*) with the phonetic component *qiě* (且); the pronunciation of *qiě* is *zǐyú* (子余反), and the second character [of the name] is pronounced *zéjià* (責駕反).

Scroll 25, Volume Twenty-five. [The character] *ruǎn* (蝡): according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to move slightly"; it is composed of the radical "insect" (*chong*) and the phonetic element *ruan*. It has already been explained previously.

Regarding "dù" (賭) as in "dù mǎ" (賭馬), the *Wùzhì* (吳志) states that it refers to competing in games for profit. In ancient and modern times, characters with the phonetic component "bèi" (貝) follow this pronunciation.
As for "sè" (色) in "sè xiàn" (色綫), it is pronounced xiānjiàn (仙箭); the character "xiàn" (綫) has already been explained previously in the glossary.

The character for "eyelash" (䀹) is pronounced *jié* (with the radical *shàng* [上] and the phonetic *càn* [僣]). In standard dictionaries, it is correctly written as *jié*. The *Zhuangzi* states: "The eyelashes (*jímáo*) are the hairs of the eyes. The *Wenzi jílüè* writes it with the radical *máo* (毛) as *mǎo* (𣮌). The *Wenzi diǎnshuō* states: "The eyelashes (*jímáo*) are the hairs at the sides of the eyes; it takes *mù* (目) as the radical and *jiá* (夾) as the phonetic. The pronunciation of *mǎo* (𣮌) is the same as above.

The character 賸 (qian) is pronounced zheng (as in "zhengfan"). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Jia means to present wealth to another; it is composed of the radical 貝 (bai) and the phonetic 朕 (zhen). One interpretation says: "Jia means to increase things. The character 朕 is pronounced zhen. The version in the *Chuanshuowen* writes it as 賸, which is a vulgar form.
The character *jī* (𤼣) is pronounced *juàn* (上戀圓反); its explanation has already been seen previously. Regarding *kùxǐ* (袴褶):

the upper character is pronounced *kù* and the lower is pronounced *zhé*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "The *xǐ* is like the *jiá* (a double-layered garment). The *Shiming* says: "The *kùxǐ* means that the *xǐ* covers [the body]. In both ancient and modern standard orthography, it is written with the radical for "clothing" (*yī*) and the phonetic element *xí* (*shēng*).

*Fūchū* (轒䡴): The upper character *fū* is pronounced with the *fēn* rhyme (扶分反). The *Yìyì* (音義) of the *Hànshū* states that the *fūchū* is a chariot of the Xiongnu. Thus, Yang Xiong’s *Chángyáng Fù* says, "The *fū* was crushed and the *chū* broken," referring to the *qiónglú* (felt tents). The lower character *chū* is pronounced *yūn* (氳). The *Shuōwén* states that in Huaiyang it is called a chariot; *qiónglóng* (穹隆) is composed of the radical *chē* (車) and the phonetic *bèn* (賁), where *bèn* is pronounced *fēn* (濆). The *Dùzhù* (杜注) to the *Zuǒzhuàn* states that the *chū* is a battle-chariot (*zhànchē*). The *Shuōwén* states it is an arrayed chariot (*zhènchē*), composed of the radical *chē* and the phonetic *tóng* (童). It is also pronounced with the *yīng* rhyme (亦聲).

Regarding the character *mò* (袜): the upper radical is *mán* (蠻) with the phonetic *bāo* (八). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that it means "to bind. The *Zìjìng* (字鏡) also writes it as *huì* (𭘕) with the radical *jīn* (巾), and its meaning is the same as *mò*. The *Yùnquán* (韻詮) likewise writes it as *huì* (𭘕) with the radical *jīn*. The transmitted texts write it as *zhì* (袹), pronounced *mài*, which is incorrect; we do not adopt this. The character *gè* (革) with the reading *yìng* (硬) is the correct form for *é* (額). The *chuán* (傳) [texts] write it as *é* (額), which is a vulgar form.

Regarding "holding a pickaxe" (執钁): the character for "upper holding" (上執) has already been explained previously. The lower character is "kuàng" (誑), with the phonetic component "yuè" (籰). According to the *Huainanzi*, it means "to dig. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "jué" (钁) is composed of "jīn" (金, metal) as the semantic element and "jué" (矍) as the phonetic element; the pronunciation of "jué" is the same as above. "Yuè" (籰) is pronounced "yú fù" (于縛).
The characters for *fēng* (峯) and *ào* (㟧)—the former pronounced *zhèng fēng* and the latter *xià áng* respectively—have both already been explained previously.

Regarding *chǎn yán* (巉巖): the upper character is pronounced *shì shān*. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that "chǎn yán" means "precipitous and obstructed. The *Guījīn zhèngzì* states that both characters for "chǎn yán" are composed of the "mountain" radical (*shān*) and are phoneticized by *chán* and *yán*.
The term "shénzhēng" (神鉦) [with the second character pronounced as *zhī* or *yíng*] has already been explained in the tenth fascicle above.

Regarding "wěizòng" (薳縱) [with the first character pronounced as *wéi*], the *Kǎoshēng* states that "wěi" means "words. In both ancient and modern standard characters, it is written with the radical "grass" (艸) and the phonetic "yuǎn" (遠).

Regarding the character *shēng* (聲) in *shēng'ā* (聲嗄): the first character is the standard form for "sound," while the second is pronounced *suǒ zhà* (所詐反). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that *shēng'ā* means "the voice is broken. Neither dictionary nor lexicographical work records this character; however, the *Guǎngcāng* (廣蒼) includes it as *qìn* (欠), written as *yīn* (𣣺), with the same phonetic and semantic glosses.

Regarding the character *jiào* (嚼): the upper radical is *qiáng* (牆) with the phonetic *lüè* (略). Dictionaries state that *jiào* is synonymous with *jǔ* (咀). Gu Yewang says it means *jiào* (噍). The *Wenzi Dianshuo* (文字典說) states it means *jiàorú* (嚼茹). It is composed of the radical *kǒu* (口) and the phonetic *jué* (爵). The lower part is *qiáo* (樵) with the phonetic *xiào* (笑). The *Liji* (禮記) states: "Frequently chewing [with the mouth open] lacks the proper deportment. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* states: "It means to bite (*niè*) and to chew (*jiào*). It is composed of the radical *kǒu* (口) and the phonetic *jiāo* (焦)."

The character 窴 (tián) in 窴噎 (tián'ē) [is pronounced] dìàn (dìān) according to the *Chuánwén*. It is written with the radical 門 (mén) and the phonetic 闐 (tián); it is a vulgar form. The *Bóyá* states that "tián" means to block or fill. The *Shuōwén* states that it means to block; it is composed of the radical 󲈺 (zhèn) and the phonetic 真 (zhēn).

*Cuò* (矬陋): The upper character is pronounced *gē* (戈反); the *Guǎngyá* states that *cuò* means "short. Regarding the correct orthography of ancient and modern times, it is composed of the radical *zhì* (矢) with the phonetic *zuò* (坐). The lower character is pronounced *hòu* (候反); the *Shuōwén* states that *lòu* means "narrow and cramped," composed of the radical *fù* (阜) with the phonetic *lú* (󱾈), the sound of which is identical [to *hòu*].

"Si" (偲) is a monastic name; according to the *Zi Shu* (Dictionary of Characters), the character "Si" (思) is correctly written as "Si" (偲), because it is derived from "Si" (思). "Han" (撼) [is pronounced with the initial *han* and final *-gan*]:
the *Shuowen Jiezi* says it means to shake or sway, derived from "Shan" (手) as the semantic component and "Gan" (感) as the phonetic component.

Regarding "ǎoliè" (拗捩): the first character is pronounced with the *wū* rhyme and the *jiǎo* final; the second character is pronounced with the *lián* rhyme and the *niè* final. According to current usage, "ǎoliè" refers to crushing or breaking an object with one's hands.

Regarding "zhìbāo" (志褒): the second character is pronounced with the *bǎo* rhyme and the *máo* final. This has already been explained previously; the version in the *Xuánzhuàn* (玄傳) text erroneously writes it as "póu" (裒).
Regarding "jìng" (柩): the upper character is pronounced jiù; it has already been explained previously. The text of the *Zhuan* (傳) writes this as "jìu" (柩), which is an error.

Regarding "kài sòu" (欬嗽): the upper character is read as kāi'ài and the lower as sǒudòu; it has already been explained previously. The text of the *Zhuan* writes this as "kài" (嘅), which is a vulgar and erroneous character.

Volume 26, Scroll 26. The name *Tánqiān* (曇瑎)—the second character, *qiān*, is pronounced with the "hài" rhyme (i.e., *qiān*). According to the *Zìshū* (Dictionary of Characters), *qiān* refers to black jade.

*Nìng* (mud/slush). [The character is pronounced with the initial *dǐ* and final *-ě*. Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states: "Mud is ground where springs leak and the soil is damp. Gu Yewang says: "Mud is simply a coating; it is earth that becomes soft and rotten when it meets water. Regarding the standard orthography of past and present: it follows the radical for water (*shuǐ*) and uses *ní* as its phonetic component. The final rhyme is *níng-dìng*. The *Zuǒzhuan* states: "He turned back in the slush and stopped. Du Yù’s commentary says: "Slush is mud. The *Guǎngyá* says: "It is clear. The *Shuōwén* defines it as: "A shallow pool; it follows the radical for water and uses *níng* as its phonetic."
*Nǎng* (齆): Pronounced *wù gòng* (屋貢反). The *Pīcāng* states that *nǎng* refers to the illness of nasal congestion. The meanings of the ancient and modern *zhèngzìyì* (正字義) are the same;

it is formed from the radical "nose" (*bi*) with the phonetic element *yōng*. *Huǒ* (夥): Pronounced *guǒ* (果反) with the third tone. Guo’s commentary on the *Fāngyán* states that the people of Chu called "many" *huǒ*. The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the character "many" (*duō*) with the phonetic element *guǒ*.
*Fǎkǎi* (法楷): The second character is pronounced *hè* (駭) with a level tone;

it is a name for a monk. *Huíkàn* (迴瞰): The second character is pronounced *kàn* (濫) with a level tone. The *Pīcāng* states that *kàn* means "to look down. It may also be written as *kàn* (闞), which has already been explained previously.
The pronunciation of *yíng* in "Yíngzhōu" has already been explained previously.

Regarding *ài dài*: the first character is pronounced *āidài* (反) and the second is *táilài* (反). The *Bīcāng* states that *àidài* refers to the indistinct appearance of clouds; the *Kǎoshēng* states it is the form of clouds.

Regarding the characters for *yín* (吟) and *xiào* (嘯): the character for "to lament" (*xiào*) is correctly written with the radical *qiàn* (欠), as in the *Shuowen*. It means to sing; it refers to making a sound by puckering the mouth and curling the tongue. Thus, the *Shijing* says, "His singing was accompanied by lamentation" (*qí xiào gē yě*). The *Shuowen* defines it as "sighing" (*yín*), composed of the radical *qiàn* and the phonetic *sù*. The form *xiào* (嘯) found in the *Chuanwen* (傳文) is a vulgar character.

Volume 27, Part 27. Regarding "Fuling" (涪陵): the upper character is pronounced "fú. The *Hanshu* states that there was Fuling County in Guanghan; it is the present-day Fuzhou within the Gorges region.

*Hèi* (300; *jiàng* in the rhyme): The *Wenzi Jilüè* states that *hèi* belongs to the Rong tribes. The *Kǎoshēng* says *hèi* is a title of the Rong, formed with the radical "dog" (*quán*) and the phonetic "xiāng. *Páixì* (upper character: *bài mái*; lower character: *xī yì*):

The *Bóyǎ* states that *píyóu* refers to performers of music. The *Kǎoshēng* says *píyóu* means a singer or entertainer. The *Shuowén* says it means "acting out a play," formed with the radical "man" (*rén*) and the phonetic "fēi. The *Máoshī Zhuàn* states that *xì* means "leisurely indulgence. Guō’s commentary on the *Eryǎ* says *xì* means "jesting. The *Shuowén* [gives a different analysis], formed with the radical "spear" (*gē*) and the phonetic "qian" (*xī* in sound). The character *qian* has the pronunciation *xī*.
"Lǐn (懍)"—the upper radical is *shànglín* (上林), the phonetic is *jǐn* (錦). This concludes the explanation of the fifth fascicle of the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gāosēngzhuàn*).

"Bù shùn" (不瞬)—the lower character is read as *shūn* (𨳝). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To blink; the eyes move and shake. It is composed of the radical 'eye' (*mù*) and the phonetic 'shùn' (*shùn*); it may also be written with 'yǐn' (*yǐn*), and the pronunciation is the same."

*Pǔ* (pronounced *pǒu*, with the phonetic components *běn* and *fǎn*). The *Rites of Zhou* states: "In all cases of those who have killed a person, they shall be *pǔ* [overturned] in the marketplace. Zheng Xuan’s commentary notes: "*Pǔ* means to lie prostrate (*jiāng*). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "*Pǔ* means to collapse and die. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "*Pǔ* means to fall forward. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical *zú* (foot) and the phonetic *pòu*; *pòu* is pronounced *tǔ kǒu*. It is also written as *shù* (composed of the radical *zǒu* [to run]) with the same pronunciation. Furthermore, it is also written as *shàng*.

Regarding *chēng* (棖觸): the rhyme dictionary *Yùnlüè* states that *chēng* also means "to touch. In both ancient and modern standard characters, it is written with the radical for wood (*mu*) and the phonetic *zhǎng* (長).

Regarding *bō* (𢗌裹): the *Guǎngyá* states that *bō* means "to wrap. In both ancient and modern standard characters, it is written with the radical for cloth (*jīn*) and the phonetic *bā* (巴); the lower part is pronounced *guǒ* (果), and the reading *guǒ* found in transmitted texts is an error.

Regarding "luò zhà" (湯諾反): the *Kǎo Shēng* states that "luò tuō" means having lost one's joints; it also means to open. Lexicons write this character with the radical "clothing" (衣) as "tuō," which does not accord with the meaning transmitted in the text; therefore, we do not adopt it here.

"Qiao Mountain" (嶠山) is the name of a mountain; its pronunciation is *qiǎo*. Alternatively, it is pronounced with the second tone on the final syllable (*qiáo*). It likely does not refer to the "high" appearance of a mountain.

Regarding the character for *jīng* (麖): the upper part is the correct form of the character *qīng* (靑). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *qīng* is the color of the east; because wood produces fire, it takes the character *dān* (丹) below it. The *Erya* calls it a "large deer," and the *Shuowen Jiezi* explains that this character for *jīng* (麖) is formed from the radical "deer" (*lù*) with *jīng* as the phonetic.

Regarding "ruò lǐng" (箬笭): the *Wénzìdiǎn* (Dictionary of Characters) states that "ruò" refers to bamboo bark; it is composed of the radical "zhú" (bamboo) and the abbreviated form of "ruò," which is an archaic character for "ruò," with "kǎo" as its phonetic. It further states that "ruò" refers to the leaves of the *zhújiàn* (cane bamboo). Regarding "lǐng": the *Guǎngyǎ* states that "lǐng" is the same as "lóng" (a basket); the *Shuōwén* states it is the same as "yíng" (a wicker basket), composed of the radical "zhú" and the phonetic "lìng."

*Wéng* (屋甍): Pronounced *mài pīng fǎn*. According to the *Shuowen*, *wéng* refers to the ridgepole of a roof; it is composed of the radical *wǎ* (tile) and the phonetic *hūn* (abbreviated as *hóng*) in reduced form.

*Tù* (䖶): Pronounced *huí huǐ fǎn*. The *Pīcāng* states that *tù* means "a pig rooting in the ground. The meaning of the character is consistent across ancient and modern *Zhèngzìyì*; it is composed of the radical *shǐ* (pig) and the phonetic *chóng* (insect).

*Mian-lai* (眄睞): The first character, *mian*, is pronounced with the initial *m* and the final *pian* (反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To look askance; it is composed of the radical 'eye' (*mu*) and the phonetic 'gai' (*gai*). The pronunciation of *gai* is *mian*. The *Cangjie Pian* states: "To look with the eyes. The *Shuowen Jiezi* further states: "The pupils are not aligned; it is composed of the radical 'eye' and the phonetic 'lai' (*lai*). It may also be written as *ze* (䚅), with the same pronunciation."
Regarding "xiāo" (虓) in "Tiger-like" (虓虎): the upper radical is *xiào* (孝). It has already been fully explained in the fifteenth fascicle above.

Furthermore, regarding "luò" (烙) in the lower part: the transmitted text reads "lè" (垎), which is a vulgar character; in standard dictionaries, it correctly uses the metal radical (*jīn*) to form "gě" (鉻), meaning "to burn. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it means "to iron or cauterize. The correct character for ancient and modern usage uses the metal radical and the phonetic "gè" (各); the *Shuowén* (說文) also uses the blade radical (*dāo*) to form "gǎo" (㓢). The same applies to all subsequent instances.

*Xià péng* (lower shelf/platform): "Péng" is pronounced *báig máng fǎn*. Bóyǎ states that it means a wooden platform or rack (*zhàn*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "péng.
Regarding *pú jiè* (rush sandals), the pronunciation *jiǎo* has already been explained previously.

The character for "roaring" (páo) is composed of "mouth" (kǒu) and the phonetic "bāo" (with the *bǎo* rhyme). The *Chuci* states: "Tigers and leopards snarl; bears and brown bears roar. The *Guoyá* says: "Páo means to howl. The *Shuowén* says: "Páo also means to cry out (*húng*); it takes 'mouth' as the radical and 'bāo' as the phonetic. The pronunciation of "bēi" (in *bēilí*) is *bēi*; the pronunciation of "húng" (in *húngjiào*) is *hāo*.
The character *páo* (咆) [in *páoxiū*] is pronounced with the second tone, *tíng* (汀) and the third tone, *dǐng* (頂). It is a specific name for one who knows his fate.

The character *xiū* (烋) [in *páoxiū*] is pronounced with the fourth tone, *xiào* (孝) and the first tone, *jiāo* (交). The *Shijing* (Book of Poetry) says: "You roar and bellow (*páoxiū*) in the Middle Kingdom. Zheng’s Commentary (*Zhengjian*) states that this describes the appearance of one who boasts of his own vigorous spirit; its meaning is identical to the character *xiāo* (虓). The *Kaosēng* (Examining Sounds) says it is the appearance of one who is fierce and violent. Its meaning as a correct orthography from ancient times to the present is the same: it is composed of the radical "fire" (*huǒ*) and the phonetic element "rest" (*xiū*).

*Tóulú* (頭顱): The phonetic gloss says *tóulú* means the skull. The *Shuowen* says it is *dònlú*. It is composed of the radical *xié* (頁) with the phonetic *lú*; *dùn* is pronounced *duò*. *Nà* (額): *Yágé* is the reading. The *Fāngyán* says it is the forehead (*yǎngsàng*).

In the Central Plains, the forehead is called *nà*. The *Fāngyán* says it is the chin (*hàn*). The *Shuowen* states that *yǎng* and *hàn* are the same character, both composed of the radical *xié* (頁), with *hàn* serving as the phonetic. The versions in the transmitted texts written as *xī* (𩓘) or *lǐng* (領) are all errors.

*Yíngzhōng* (瀅中): the first character is pronounced *wū* with the *dìng* tone; it is written as *fú* (㼆) in the commentary, which has already been explained in the tenth fascicle above. *Xuánguō* (旋濄):

the first character is pronounced *xuān* with the *huàn* tone, and the second is pronounced *wū* with the *gē* tone. According to the *Kǎoshēng*, "guō" refers to water swirling in its flow. The correct orthography from ancient times to the present uses the radical "water" (水) and the phonetic "guō" (過).
As for the strange character *guài* (怪) from antiquity, its interpretation has already been fully explained in the preceding commentary.

Regarding the character *yuàn* (院)—which is written as *mén-bǎi-xià* (門󳁢下) in vulgar and erroneous texts—this character appears frequently in transmitted manuscripts; thus, it has already been clarified in this writing, and the same applies to all instances before and after.

Regarding "píhěn" (皮鞕): the lower character is read as *gèng* (更). In ancient and modern standard orthography, it is correctly written with the radical 革 (leather) and the phonetic 更 (more). It signifies firmness and solidity. Lexicons and dictionaries explain the meaning in this same way. According to the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲), there is also a variant written with the radical 石 (stone) as 硬 (yìng); this is the character currently in general use. The transmitted text sometimes uses 䩕 (from 卭), pronounced *jī*; the *Zìshū* (字書) states that 䩕 refers to a type of leather footwear (*dīshǔ*), which is not the original meaning and is therefore not adopted here.

*Shēnjìn* (上失人反): Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states it means "groaning" (*shēnyín*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as consisting of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic "shēn. *Qínjìn* (下琴禁反): The *Chuci* says "to clench the mouth and remain silent. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states it means "closing the mouth. Regarding the orthography of these two characters, *shēnjìn* and *qínjìn*, both take the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetics "shēn" and "jìn" respectively.

*Kū* (upper character: *kǔ*, with the *gū* rhyme; from the *Cāngjié piān*: "to castrate"; the *Fānyán* says: "to cut open the abdomen"; the *Shuōwén* says: "to split," composed of the radical *dāo* [knife] and the phonetic *kuā*; Gù Yěwáng says: "to hollow out the belly"; *kuā* is pronounced like *kuā*). The lower character is *tīng* (with the *lì* rhyme). The *Guǎngyá* says: "to carve. In standard dictionaries, it is correctly written as *zī* (pronounced *zhē*), which has the same meaning as *tī*. The character for "to govern" (*zhì*) is composed of the radical *dāo* and the phonetic *yì*. (Note: This entry provides a philological analysis of the characters *kū* (to castrate/hollow out) and *zhì* (to govern/treat), citing various lexicographical sources including the *Cāngjié piān*, *Fānyán*, *Shuōwén*, *Guǎngyá*, and *Zìshū*.)

The character *nùtái* (奴儓) is pronounced with the lower radical *dài* (岱) and the final rhyme *lái* (來). The *Zuǒzhuan* states that *táipú* (儓僕) is a name for a subject; from the *zào* (皂) to the *lì* (𨽻) and down to the *táipú*, there are ten grades. It is said that *tái* means "to match" or "equal. Furthermore, in the southern regions of Chu, the vulgar and lowly were called *tái*. Guō Pǔ’s commentary notes that *tái* refers to one who is dull and slow-witted. In both ancient and modern standard characters, it is composed of the radical *rén* (人) and the phonetic *tái* (臺).

Regarding "shēnhào" (sighing and crying out): the upper character *shēn* has already been explained previously. As for the lower character *hào*, Duan Yucai’s commentary on the *Zuǒ Zhuan* states that it means "wailing. The *Bóyá* says it refers to a loud clamor. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "to call out," composed of the radical *háo* with the phonetic *hǔ*. The text of the *Zhuàn* uses the character *háo*, which refers to the cry of a beast; this is not the original meaning and is therefore not adopted here.

*Ni* (劓) and *ri* (刵): The former is pronounced *yì* (宜器反); Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states that *ni* means "to cut off the nose. The *Shuowén* says: "*Ni* means to cut off the nose; it is composed of the radical 'knife' (*dāo*) and the phonetic 'niè' (*niè*, pronounced *jué* [決] or *yì* [藝]). In dictionaries and the *Shūjīng*, both use the phonetic *niè*. The common usage of *ni* is interchangeable with this, as their pronunciation is identical. The latter, *ri*, is pronounced *èr* (上音餌); Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states that *ri* means "to cut off the ears. The *Shuowén* says: "*Ri* means to sever the ears; it is composed of the radicals 'knife' and 'ear' (*ěr*), with the phonetic 'è'."

Regarding "shēndiàn" (deep pond): the character "diàn" is pronounced "tiánliàn" (田練) in the *Wèidū fù* (Wei Capital Rhapsody) by Zuo Taichong, which states: "The pond where carp are grasped. Lü Yanjie’s commentary notes: "Diàn is also the name of a body of water located west of Yìmù County in Héjiān. A 'diàn' is like a deep pool (*yuān*) but shallow; the character for 'yuān' is pronounced 'wūxuān' (烏玄). The meaning of the characters is the same in both ancient and modern times: it is composed of the radical 'water' (水) and the phonetic 'dìng' (定)."

The character *bēng* (堋) is followed by "while ascending, it collapsed" (*měng*, with the phonetic *měng* and *dèng*). The transmitted text follows the ancient form 𭩀, which is incorrect. The *Zuozhuan* states, "At noon they made the *bēng*," and Du Yu’s commentary explains that *bēng* refers to the ground where the burial takes place. It is formed from the radical for earth and the phonetic *péng*. *Péng* is the correct usage; the character is also written as 𥥝 in character dictionaries, with the same pronunciation.

Regarding "zhuìwǒu" (cyst/tumor): the upper character is pronounced *zhuì* (with the *rù* rhyme). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that "zhuì" means "to accumulate. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "a cyst; it is composed of the radical '貝' (*bèi*) and the phonetic '敖' (*áo*). The lower character is pronounced *xiū*. The *Zishu* states it is "a disease of warts," while the *Kaosheng* explains it as "a wind-concretion on the skin."

*Hàngxiè* (沆瀣): The first character is pronounced *háng* (as in *shàng-háng*) and the second is pronounced *xiè* (as in *xié-jìe*). The *Chuci* (*Songs of Chu*) states: "Ingesting the six qi and drinking *hàngxiè*. Wang Yi’s commentary notes: "In summer one eats *hàngxiè*; *hàngxiè* is the qi of the north at midnight, the hour of *zǐ*. The *Guǎngyá* says it is the "constant qi" (*chángqì*). The *Jīn-gǔ-zhèng-zì* also states: "Ingesting the six qi and drinking *hàngxiè*. Both characters are written with the radical *shuǐ* (water). The phonetic for *háng* is *kàng*, and for *xiè* is *yòu*. The pronunciation is as stated above. In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *yòu* is formed from *jiǔ* (leek) and the abbreviated form of *ruì* as the phonetic; *ruì* is pronounced *gài*.

Volume 28, Scroll 28. Regarding the character "jìngyà" (驚訝): "yà" is pronounced with the initial *j* and the final *a* (牙駕反). The *Kǎośēng* states that "yà" means "to be startled and sigh in admiration. In both ancient and modern standard orthography, this character is composed of the radical "speech" (言) and the phonetic "tooth" (牙).

The character for *biān* (to lance a disease) is verified as being a variant of the character for *bié* (to distinguish). It is correctly written with the radical *jié* (a seal-script form), appearing as *biǎn*. It is also written as *biàn* (to prick). The *Guǎngyá* states: "Biān is called *cì* (to prick). The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* states: "Biān refers to using a stone needle to prick a disease. The *Shuowén* also states: "It means to prick a disease with a stone; it takes the radical *shí* (stone) and the phonetic *fá*."
"Yin" (陻) [pronounced yī or lín; the *Kǒng* commentary on the *Shūjìng* states it means "to block"]. In dictionaries, the character is written as 垔 or 堙 below.
"Lí Róng" (驪戎): the upper radical is "li" (里) [pronounced zhī]; this has already been explained previously.
*Bi-fen* (苾芬): The prefix *bi* (毘必反) refers to a fragrant herb of the Western Regions, as previously explained.

*Chao-lü* (鈔𢴨): The prefix *chao* (上策教反) is defined in the *Fangyan* as "to snatch" (*chao*), meaning to take things by force; the *Shuowen* states it means to take things by right. It is composed of the radical "metal" (*jin*) and the phonetic "shao. One theory says it means "to plunder," or it is written with the character *chao* (抄). The suffix *lü* (下陟革反) has already been explained previously.
"Huiquan" (慧銓): The lower character "quan" (銓) is pronounced as in "shengquan" (詮釋, to explain). It is a name for a monk; in the transmitted text it is written as "ling" (鈴, bell), which is an error.
"Song Gong Yu" (宋公瑀): The lower character "yu" (瑀) is pronounced as in "yuzi" (宇字).

This is the name of a Beiliang (梁) *tejin* (特進, special advancement). Volume 29, Part 29: "Hunmai" (昏霾): The lower character "mai" (霾) is pronounced with the *piai* (牌) rhyme. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (毛詩傳) states: "Mai is rain-soiled earth. The *Erya* (爾雅) states: "Wind accompanied by raining soil is called mai. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文解字) indicates that it is composed of "rain" (雨) and the phonetic "li" (貍). Therefore, the *Shi Jing* (詩經) says: "The constant wind and the mai."

"Carrying [the child] on the back in a *qiāngfù* (襁負). (The character for *qiāng* is pronounced *yǎng* when reversed. Bao Xian’s commentary on the *Lunyu* states: "A *qiāng* is a vessel used for carrying; that which is carried by it is called *qiāng*. The *Huainanzi* states: "King Cheng was in the midst of his *qiāngbǎo* (infant swaddling). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as: "Clothing for carrying a child on the back; it takes the radical 衣 (*yī*) and the phonetic element 強 (*qiáng*)."

Regarding the *tàbiàn* (獺弁): the first character is pronounced as *tān* (攤) with the *qièyùn* (切韻) rhyme *gé* (葛), and the second is *bié* (別) with the rhyme *biàn* (變). According to the commentary, the *lùbiàn* (鹿弁)—the headgear of those who have retired from the world—is made of otter skin for the *guān* (冠) and deer skin for the *biàn* (弁). As for *miǎn* (冕), the *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文解字) states that *biàn* and *miǎn* are identical. The correct form is written as 𡭪, derived from 皃 (mào) and being a pictographic character. The seal-script (篆文) form is written as 弁, derived from 󳎸 (pronounced *gǒng*); today it is commonly written as 弁. This is correct.

The character *yǐ* (陭) is pronounced with the initial *yì* (倚). The commentary states it refers to a slope (*bǎn*) and is identical to the character *yī* (猗). According to the original meaning in the transmitted text, it should be written with the radical "mountain" as *qí* (崎). *Qí* (崎) signifies a steep and precipitous cliff; this is seen in the *Bóyá*. Furthermore, Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that *qí* describes the rugged and uneven appearance of mountain ridges. Because the meaning is considered doubtful, both forms are retained here.

Regarding "iron ore" (鐵磺): the character for "iron" (鐵) has already been explained previously. The character below, pronounced with the *guō* and *měng* finals, is defined in the *Guǎngyǎ* as "iron ore is called *huáng*" (*tiě pò wèi zhī huáng*). The *Shuowén* states it means "copper ore" (*tóng pù*) and is composed of the radical "stone" (石) with the phonetic "huáng" (黃); it is also written as "kuàng" (鑛), which has the same pronunciation.

Regarding the character *zàn* (鏨): the upper radical is *zhān* (雜, Gān-jiǎn rhyme); the *xiǎo-shēng* (考聲) states it means "to chisel. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "A small chisel; it follows the metal radical and takes *zhǎn* (斬) as its phonetic component. The lower part is *zhé* (陟, Zhé-jué rhyme). The *Commentary on the Mao Shi* says: "To treat jade is called *zhuó* (琢). Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* says: "*Zhuó* means to carve jade; it follows the jade radical and takes *shǐ* (豕) as its phonetic component. The sound of *shǐ* is *chǒng* (寵, Chǒng-wǎn rhyme).

In the name *Chī Huī*, the upper character is pronounced with the initial *ǔ* (as in *wǔn*) and the final *huán* (as in *huán*), while the lower character is pronounced with the initial *huí* (as in *huí*) and the final *fǎn*.

It is a personal name. Regarding *yōnliǎng*: the upper character is pronounced with the initial *wěn* (as in *wěn*) and the final *hún* (as in *huán*), while the lower character is pronounced with the initial *lüè* (as in *lè*) and the final *zhāng* (as in *zhāng*). The *Shìjì* states that when the First Emperor of Qin traveled in the *yōnliǎng* carriage, its construction was like that of a chariot with windows; when closed it was warm, and when opened it was cool. Its form was vast and grand, adorned with feathers. Furthermore, when the Han dynasty’s Huò Guāng passed away, his coffin was carried in a *yōnliǎng* carriage, which resembled a *féi* carriage and had four wheels. Since the Han dynasty, these have been used exclusively for carrying the *zǐgōng* (the coffin). The character *liǎng* is also written as *liáng* or *yì*; the *Shuōwén* explains that *yōnliǎng* refers to a bed-chariot. Both characters are composed of the "chariot" radical (*chē*) and the phonetic components *wūn* and *jīng*; the sound of *wūn* is that of *wēn*.

*Héng* (珩) and *pèi* (佩): *héng* is pronounced with the initial *xìng* and the final *gēng* (耕); Zheng Zhong’s commentary on the *Dàdài Lǐ* states that the *héng* is the jade of the girdle used to regulate movement and stopping. Furthermore, regarding the jade of the girdle, there are two *huáng* (璜) above; *pèi* (佩) is pronounced with the final *mèi* (妹). Zheng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states that the *pèi* is the jade worn at the waist. According to the *Shuowén*, both characters for *héng* and *pèi* are written with the radical "jade" (*yù*). In *héng*, *xíng* (行) and *chóng* (𠋫) also serve as phonetic components; in *pèi*, *rén* (人) serves as the semantic component and *fán* (凡) as the phonetic. A *pèi* must have a cloth sash (*jīn*), which is called its ornamentation.

*Yíngshì* (ornamentation/decoration). "Yíng" is pronounced *yǐng* (as in *dìng*). The *Bóyá* states that *yíng* is called *shì* (decoration); the *Cāngjiépiān* states it means "to refine"; the *Shuōwén* states it means "to treat a vessel. It is composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic component "a contraction of *yíng*" (*huīng*).

Yáng-qi (陽𧙍): The second character is pronounced *jī* with the *lì* rhyme. The *Lǐjì* states that when Wǔ defeated Shāng, he descended from his chariot to enfeoff the descendant of the Yellow Emperor at Qi. The *Hànshū* records that the county of Yáng-qi in Yān-guó was the fief bestowed upon Gāo-gōng. In both ancient and modern standard characters, it is written as *qì* (契), and its pronunciation and glosses are identical. The *Yùpiān* also writes it as *qi* (𧙍), and its pronunciation and glosses are likewise the same.

"Poyang" (鄱陽): the first character is pronounced *bó* (波反). The *Hanshu* states that there was Poyang County within Yuzhang Commandery. Regarding the correct orthography throughout antiquity and the present, this character is composed of the radical "city" (邑) and the phonetic "fan" (番), which is pronounced *pān* (潘).

The character *què* (闋) is pronounced as *jié* (決) with a retroflex final. The *Cāngxié piān* states that *què* means "to review" (*yuè*). The *Zìtǒng* states that *què* means "the completion of affairs. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* says: "The music for ascending the hall has ceased (*què*). It is examined as the cessation of sound; it is also written as *què* (闋). Wèi Hóng wrote it as *huán* (𨴊), which has the same pronunciation. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical *mén* (門) and the phonetic *guǐ* (癸).

The character for "lock" (鎖) is pronounced with the first tone on the upper radical and the *guǒ* (果) rhyme on the lower part; the *Chuánwén* (傳文) writes it as "cáo" (鏁), which is a vulgar form. This was already explained previously in the ninth fascicle of the *Gāosēngzhuàn* (高僧傳). Regarding the character for "rose" (薔薇):

the upper part is pronounced with the *jiàng* (匠) rhyme and the *yáng* (陽) tone, while the lower part is pronounced with the *wěi* (尾) rhyme. This was already explained previously in the *Hóngmíngjí* (弘明集); the *Chuánwén* writes it as "qí" (󳈿), which is an error.

*Chuè* (top character: 川, *chuān*; radical: 爇, *ruò*). The pronunciation of *ruò* is *yú-zhuó*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "to sip" (*chuè*) means "to taste. It is also written as *huò* (*chùè*), with the same pronunciation. The upper character in the transmitted text is written as *chuè*, which is a vulgar form. The lower character is pronounced *shí-yù*. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that *shū* (菽) means "beans" (*dòu*). Regarding the phonetics, the correct form is *qū* (尗), while the *Zhuan* writes it as *shū* (叔), which is a vulgar form.
*Tī* (褫) is pronounced with the *shangping* tone as *chí* (耳反). This was already explained in the fourth fascicle above. *Jǐn* (緊) is pronounced with the *yinyun* tone;

according to the *Shuowen*, it means "to tightly wind thread. It is composed of the radical *sī* (絲) and the phonetic *xiān* (臤), where *xiān* is pronounced *qiān*. *Rèn* (韌) is pronounced with the *renzhuan* tone; the *Bicang* states that it means "suppleness. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *wéi* (韋) and the phonetic *rèn* (刃).

Regarding "jié" (接): the character below is pronounced with the *zhōng* and *lǒng* rhymes; the transmitted text writes it as "tóng" (曈), which is an error. The *Kǎo Shēng* states that "jié" means "to tread upon the tracks of another. The *Shuōwén* states it means "to follow one another's tracks," being composed of the radical "man" (彳) and the phonetic "chóng" (重).

*Méi-ěi* (糜餧): The first character is pronounced *méi*; the second is pronounced with the initial *wēi* and the final *wèi*. The *Guǎngyá* states that "ěi" means to feed (*sì*). The character is composed of the radical "food" (*shí*) and the phonetic element "wěi," which also serves as the sound indicator.

*Líng-sī* (淩凘): The first character is pronounced with the initial *lì* and the final *chéng*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhōu Lǐ* states that "líng" refers to the sound [of ice]. The second character is pronounced with the final *sī*. The *Shuōwén* states that "sī" means flowing water. It is composed of the radical "ice" (*bīng*) and the phonetic element "sī."
Regarding "lúchuí" (爐錘): the character for "lú" (爐) is read as *zhèng* (正), while the character for "chuī" (錘) is read as *zhuì* (墜) with the *shuāngshēn* (雙聲) suffix *zhuī* (追).

This has already been explained previously. Regarding "duòyú" (惰寙): the character for "duò" (惰) is read as *tuó* (碢) with the *shuāngshēn* suffix *wò* (臥), which is itself read as *tú* (徒) with the *shuāngshēn* suffix *gē* (戈). The *Commentary on the Book of Documents* (*Shūjì zhù*) by Kǒng [Yáng] states: "Duò means indolent. The *Guǎngyá* states: "It means lazy. The *Shuōwén* states: "Duò means lack of reverence; it is composed of 'heart' (心) and the abbreviated form of 'suí' (隋). It is correctly written with "suí" (隋); "lěi" (憜) has the same pronunciation and meaning. The character for "yú" (寙) is read as *yú* (踰) with the *shuāngshēn* suffix *zhǔ* (主). Lexicons state that it is correctly written with two "melons" (瓜) as "lán" (㼌). Xú Guǎng’s commentary on the *Records of the Grand Historian* (*Shǐjì*) states: "Suí means lazy. The *Shuōwén* says "lán" (㼌) is composed of two "melons" (瓜). The version transmitted with the "roof" radical (宀) as "yú" (寙) is an error.

Regarding "jìlèi" (sacrificial libation): the upper character is "zhèng" (正), and the lower character is "léi" (雷) with the phonetic component "wài" (外). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Lèi means to pour out offerings during a sacrifice; it is composed of 'yǒu' (酉, wine) and takes 'zhuàn' (󲽚) as its phonetic. "Zhuàn" (󲽚) is pronounced "liàn yuè" (戀月), and "dì" (餟) is pronounced "chuò" (輟).

"不揆" (bù kuí): The "季" (jì) in "揆" is pronounced as "反" (fǎn). The *Shàngshū* commentary by Kǒng [Yǎng] states that "揆" means "to measure. The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "癸" (guǐ);

the text of the *zhuan* (commentary) uses "揆," which is an error. Volume 30, Number 30. Regarding "貌裁" (mào cái): The upper character "貌" (mào) is pronounced as "才載反" (cái zài fǎn). According to this, "貌裁" refers to appearance, demeanor, form, and likeness. This corresponds to the common vernacular expression "hú cái" (胡裁). The text of the *zhuan* uses the character "𬿢" (which is composed of the radical "person" [人]), for which the origin is unclear.

"Cāo bǎoshàng cǎo" (曹操抱上草) contains the erroneous character "fǎn" (反). In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "cāo" (操) means "to grasp and hold," written with the radical "shǒu" (手) and the phonetic "sào" (喿), where "sào" is pronounced "xiāndào fǎn" (先到反). In the phrase "chuán sǎnsǎn" (傳摻摻), the character below is erroneously "pǐ móu fǎn" (匹謀反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "bào" (抱) refers to the mallet used for striking a drum, written with the radical "mù" (木) and the phonetic "bāo" (包). The *Kaosheng* (考聲) also states it is written with "mù" and "bāo," meaning a drumstick. It is incorrect for the commentary to write it as "fú" (桴).

The character for *gǔn* (閫) is pronounced as *shàng kùn běn fǎn* (上坤本反). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states that "the *gǔn* is the threshold of a gate. The *Shuowen Jiezi* further records it with the radical for wood (*mù*) as *kùn* (梱); however, the correct form from ancient times uses the radical for gate (*mén*) with *kùn* as its phonetic component.

Regarding "línqín" (林檎): the modern reversed form is correctly written as "qín" (檎). An examination of its phonology states that "línqín" is the name of a fruit; the version in the *Biànwen* (傳文) uses "qín" (擒), which is a vulgar character.
Regarding "Zhuàn Zǎi" (傳縡): the final tone is "zǎi" (宰); it is a personal name, as already explained previously.

*Hàng-yǎng* (上黃反羊掌反): According to the text, *hàng-yǎng* describes the appearance of water; *yǎng* may also be written as *yàng*, with the same pronunciation. *Dài-dì* (上唐各反): In dictionaries, the character is correctly written as *dù* (𢜬), though it is also written as *bèi* (𢖲);

both pronunciations are identical. The *Guǎngcāng* states that *dài* means "to punish. Xu Shuōzhòng says it means "to be weary with grief" (*chuò yōu*) or "to stand on tiptoe" (*qǐ*). The meaning in the *Gōngjīn zhèngzì yì* is the same. It is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "zhái" (*zhái shēng*). The lower part is pronounced *chì-lì* (勅厲反). Gù Yěwáng says *dì* means "the shade of a tree at rest" (*mù yóu xiūyáng*). This is the same as the passage in the *Zīxū fù*: "In his breast, he was not even slightly affected" (*xiōng zhōng céng bù dàijiè*). The *Shuōwén* says it means "extreme" (*jí*) and is composed of the radical "heart" and the phonetic "dài" (*dài shēng*).

Regarding "fánglóng" (房櫳): the character below "lóng" is pronounced as the same as "fǎn" (反); the version in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Gaoseng zhuan) writes it as "chèn" (櫬), which is incorrect, as has already been demonstrated in the *Bianzheng lun* (辯正論).

Regarding "qǐngkài" (謦欬): the first character is pronounced "qīngtǐng" (輕挺) and the second is pronounced with the "kāigài" (開蓋) rhyme; this was already explained in the fourteen volumes of the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*.
The term *kē* (磕)—the first character pronounced with the *pǔ* and *péng* rhymes, and the second with the *kàn* and *gé* rhymes—has already been explained in the nineteenth fascicle.

Regarding *língshàn* (櫺扇): the first character is pronounced with the *lì* and *dīng* rhymes. According to the *Fāngyán*, "lǐng" refers to the eaves of a house. The *Cāngjié piān* states that the horizontal bamboo placed beneath the carriage pole is also called *hàn*. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "the lattice between railings" (*shǔn*), where *shǔn* is pronounced *shùn* and is derived from the radical "wood" (*mù*) with the phonetic component "líng" (pronounced the same). The version in the transmitted text written as *líng* (櫺) is an error.

"Bǐlǐ" (鄙俚): "Běi" (悲) with the "měi" (美) rhyme; Duan Yucai’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states it means "rustic and uncivilized. The *Shiji* states it means "mean. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states it means "small. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as composed of "yì" (邑) and "lí" (㒸) as the phonetic component; "lí" (㒸) has the same pronunciation as "shàngxiàlíěr" (上下梨耳). He Xiu’s commentary on the *Gongyangzhuan* states that "yě" (野, rustic) is synonymous with "bǐ" (鄙, mean). Therefore, the *Hanshu* says, "substantial yet not bǐ," where Ru Chun’s commentary explains this as the speech of the commoners of the neighborhoods. The *Shuowen* [explains it] as composed of "yì" (邑) and "lǐ" (里) as the phonetic component; the text in the [commentary on the] *Zhuan* uses "rén" (人) instead, which is a vulgar usage of the character.

Regarding the character 逞 (chéng): the imperial decree reads *lǐng* (領) with the radical 反 (fǎn). Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that it means "to act with unrestrained speed. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "to penetrate," being composed of the radical 辵 (chuò) and the phonetic 呈 (chéng), with the lower part pronounced *xuán*. The "Correct Character" (*Zhengzi*) from ancient times is composed of the radicals 言 (yán) and 行 (xíng), written as 𧗳, meaning "to walk while selling. The text of the *Chuan* (傳) uses the character 玄 (xuán), which is a vulgar form.

*Yànshì* (豔飾): The upper character is read as *zhàn* (贍) with the *qièyùn* (反切) *shàng* (上). The *Zuǒchuán* (左傳) states that in the speech of a Great Officer, it means "beautiful and elegant" (*měi ér yàn*). The *Shuōwén* says it means "lovely and long. It is composed of *fēng* (豐) and the phonetic *hé* (盍). *Fēng* is the correct form of the character *fēng*, and *hé* is the correct form of the character *hé*. The lower character is read as *shēngyì* (昇弋). The *Shuōwén* says: "The meaning of *shì* (飾) is 'to polish' (*shuā* [刷]). It is composed of *jīn* (巾) and the phonetic *shí* (食). *Shuā* (刷) is pronounced *shūbā* (梳八).
*Yinmai* (湮埋): the first character is pronounced *yīn*, as previously explained. *Yán'ǎi* (琰皧):
the first character is pronounced with the *yán* and *rǎn* rhymes, and the second with the *āi* and *gài* rhymes;
both are names of monks. *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*, Volume 30; *Phonetic Explanations of the Entire Canon*, Volume 94.
The *Yiqiejing yinyi* (Phonetics and Meanings of All Scriptures), Scroll 95, compiled by the Scripture-translating Śramaṇa Huilin.
*Yongming ji* (Collection for the Propagation and Clarification of the Doctrine), fourteen scrolls; *Yongming ji*, fourteen scrolls.

This fascicle is the first of four. **Fascicle One** **Táo (陶):** The upper character is pronounced *dào* (as in *dàodǎo*, "to refine"), and the lower is *zhú* (as in *zhúrù*). Gu Yewang states that *táo* refers to making earthenware vessels. The *Mencius* says, "Shun personally engaged in plowing, sowing, tilling, and fishing. The *Guǎngyá* says, "Táo means transformation. The *Hànshī zhuan* says, "It means change. The *Shuowén* writes it as *páo* (*wāo*), stating it refers to earthenware vessels; it is composed of the radical *fǒu* (a jar) and the phonetic *sè* (abbreviated). It further states that when written with the radical *shī*, it becomes *táo*, which is both a place name and a title for Emperor Yao. This usage has long been common. The *Zuǒzhuan* says, "To cast tripods and image things," meaning to smelt copper to create vessels. The *Kǎoshēng* says, "Yóng means to pour molten metal. The *Shuowén* says, "Xiāo means to liquefy gold"; it is composed of the radical *jīn* (gold) and the phonetic *shòu*. The pronunciation of *róng* is *yóng*. **Zhù (鑄):** The *Kǎoshēng* says, "Yóng means to pour. The *Shuowén* says, "Xiāo means to liquefy gold. It is composed of the radical *jīn* (gold) and the phonetic *shòu*. The pronunciation of *róng* is *yóng*.** (Aligned with the source structure, the final definition of *zhù* follows the provided commentary. **Note:** The text provides a detailed philological analysis of the characters *táo* (tilling/refining), *páo* (earthenware), and *zhù* (casting), citing various classical sources such as the *Mencius*, *Guǎngyá*, *Hànshī zhuan*, *Shuowén*, and *Zuǒzhuan*. It explains their etymologies, variant forms, and historical usage, particularly regarding the titles of ancient figures like Emperor Yao. The final section clarifies the technical process of casting bronze vessels.

*Shian* (挻埴): The first character is pronounced *shàn* (上扇反) and the second is pronounced *chí* (下承力反). Lǎozi says: "One kneads clay (*shian-zhi*) to make vessels; when it is empty, it possesses the utility of the vessel. Sòng Zhōng says: "To knead means to harmonize. Xū Shūzhòng says: "It means to press down. *Shēnglèi* says: "It means supple. *Kǎoshēng* says: "It means to soften. The *Shuowén* states that it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "yán" (*yánshēng*). The *Shàngshū* says: "Its soil was red and *zhí*. Kǒng’s commentary states: "Sticky soil is called *zhí*. *Shèmíng* says: "*Zhí* means greasy, like the grease of fat. The *Shuowén* defines it as sticky soil, composed of the radical "earth" (*tǔ*) and the phonetic "zhí" (*zhíshēng*).

*He* (鶡) is pronounced *dan* with the *han* and *ge* finals; the *Shanhai jing* states that the Mount Xuanzhu is rich in *he*. Guo Pu says they resemble pheasants but are larger, blue-green in color, and possess bristly horns, fighting until death before ceasing. The *Yin yi* commentary to the *Hanshu* states that the *he* bird is also called *su*, and its tail was used for the caps of warriors. The *Shuowen jiezi* says it resembles a pheasant and is formed from the radical "bird" (*niao*) with the phonetic "e" (*he*), read as *dan* with the *han* final. The *Fangyan* states that east of the Guanzhong region it is called *dan*. The *Shuowen* further notes it is formed from "bird" with the phonetic "dan"; the editions that omit the "bird" radical may be erroneous. *Xuan* (煇) is pronounced like *hui*.

The character *shì* (眡) is pronounced with the initial *shí* and the final *fǎn*. The *Shuowén* says it denotes "the appearance of looking"; it is also an ancient form of the character *shì* (視). A dictionary states it means "to gaze," composed of the radical *mù* (eye) and the phonetic *dǐ*; the pronunciation of *dǐ* is *dī*.

*Juān*: Upper radical *jué*, phonetic *xuán*. Wáng Yě says it means "a small stream. The *Shuōyuàn* states: "A tiny trickle (*juānjuān*) that does not cease will eventually form a river. The *Shuowén* also defines it as a small stream, with the water radical and the phonetic *yūan*, pronounced *ài* (in the *sàng* register). In the *Zhuāngzǐ*, it refers to dust and the "wild horses" of the air. The *Cāngjiépiān* says it is "dirt and grime," or "dust raised by the wind. Wáng Yì’s commentary on the *Chuci* identifies it as "dust. The *Gōngjīn Zhèngzǐ* states it takes the earth radical and the phonetic *yǐ*, pronounced *yǎo*.

*Yíngdài* (瀛岱): "Yíng" is pronounced *jīng* (精) with a retroflex final; examining its phonetic component, it refers to the "Yíng Sea. The *Liezi* states: "In the northeast there is a great abyss, within which are five mountains; the third is called Yíngzhōu," referring to this very place. The *Gǔjīn zhèngzì* (古今正字) explains that it is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic "yíng" (*yíng*). "Dài" (岱) is pronounced *lái* (賚) with an affricate final; the *Shàngshū* (Book of Documents) records: "In the second month, he made a tour of inspection to the east, arriving at Dàizōng," which refers to this. Fàn Nìng stated it is Mount Tàishān, the foremost of the Five Peaks. The *Shuowén* (Explanations of Characters) states it is composed of the radical "mountain" (*shān*) and the phonetic "dài" (*dài*).
Mo Di (墨翟) and Ting Li (庭歷) were the names of those who opposed [the Buddha]; the books they authored in the world are what we call the "Mozi," which laments the natural whiteness of silk.
Ze Rong (笮融) was the name of one who contended against [the Buddha] from above; he was the General of the Household for Wu.

"Mò" (pronounced with the *mo* rhyme, following the Zheng commentary on the *Shijing*, which states "mò means to nourish"; the *Jīngǔ zhèngzì* says it means "to feed," written as 秣, with the radical 禾 and the phonetic 末; it is also written as 䬴).

"Lì" (the correct character for "stable" or "tethering post," pronounced with the *líng* rhyme, following the *Kǎoshēng* which states "lì refers to a manger"; the ancient poem says "an old horse longs for its place in the stable"; the *Shuowén* says "lì is a manger, with the radical 木 and the phonetic 歷"; it is also written as 㯕, pronounced *xī*).

*Niang* (攘): The first character is pronounced *shāo* (饒) with the *zhǎo* (沼) rhyme; the second is pronounced *rǎng* (掌) with the *rǎng* (掌) rhyme. Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that *niang-rang* means "to be arrogant" (*zhi*), a description of one who follows their own will and desires. The *Shuowen* says *niang* means "to be vexed" (*fan*) and *rang* means "to push" (*tui*). Both characters are formed with the radical "hand" (*shou*); they are also phonetic complements of *nan* (*yuan*) and *xiang*. *Yuan* is pronounced *naidao* (乃刀), and *xiang* is pronounced *xiang* (相).

The strings of the *qín* shimmer with light. The *Shijing* (Book of Poetry) says, "Sitting side by side, they beat upon the *huáng*. The *Shiben* (Book of Origins) states that Nüwa invented the *huáng*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains that the *huáng* is the reed within the *shēng* (mouth-organ), composed of bamboo with the phonetic element "huáng."

*Xūxī* (歔欷): The first character is pronounced *xǔ* (with the *yù* rhyme) and the second is pronounced *xū* (with the *yī* rhyme). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states: "Xūxī is the appearance of weeping. Another source says it refers to the emission of breath. He Xiu’s commentary on the *Gongyang Zhuan* states: "Xi (*xī*) means sorrow. The *Cangjie Pian* states: "It is the lingering sound of weeping. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, both characters are formed with the radical *qiàn* (欠), and their sounds are *xū* and *xī*.

*Chī* (絺) and *qì* (綌): the former is pronounced with the initial *chǐ* (恥) and the latter with *qīng* (卿) and *nì* (逆). According to the *Shuowen*, both refer to *gé* (葛, ramie). It is said that *chī* is also written as *xī* (悕), and *qì* is written as *qì* (𥿭). *Chī* is composed of the radical *mì* (糸, silk) and the phonetic *xī* (希); *qì* is composed of the radical *mì* (糸) and the phonetic *dà* (𠫤), also written as *lìn* (恡).

*Wánshàn* (蜿蜒): The first character is pronounced *yuān* (冤) and the second *chán* (蟬). The *Shànglín Fù* (上林賦) states: "The elephants and *xiǎo-xiǎn* (虬蟺) roam at will. Gu Yěwáng (顧野王) of the Western Capital examined this and noted that *xiǎo-xiǎn* refers to a beautiful form of winding, twisting, and turning. The *Wénzì Diǎnshuō* (文字典說) explains that it is composed of the radical "insect" (*虫*) with the phonetic component "wǎn" (*宛*). It is also written as *xiǎo-xiǎn* (虬蟺). The *Shuowén Jiězì* (說文解字) states: "*Xiǎn* (蟺) is the same as *xiǎo-xiǎn* (虬蟺)," composed of the radical "insect" with the phonetic component "dǎn" (*亶*). The *Jíběn* (集本) version reads *yán* (蜒), which is incorrect. *Dǎn* (亶) is pronounced *dān* (丹) with the tone marker *fǎn* (反).

The character *máo* (毫) is pronounced with the initial *gāo* (高) and the final *lǐ* (里). The *Zhouyi* states: "To err by a hair's breadth leads to a deviation of a thousand li. Ten hairs are called a *máo*. Dictionaries explain that it is written with the radical *máo* (毛) and the phonetic *gāo* (高). The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "*Máo* refers to coarse, curved hair that can be used to fasten clothing; it is written with the abbreviated form of *liáo* (犛) and the phonetic *lái* (來). The archaic form is *chí* (󳐑), which is an abbreviation of *máo*. The *Jiben* (集本) edition reads *háo* (豪), referring to a beast shaped like a piglet with white hair; it is as large as a hairpin (*jī*) and has black tips, which are called *háo*. *Lí* (釐) is a variant character for this. The pronunciation of *liáo* (犛) is *máo* (茅).
The meaning of "wálì" (瓦礫) has already been explained in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-uttamarāja-sūtra*. Regarding "shānfù" (山阜):

the *Erya* states that "that which is high and level is called *lù* (陸), and a large *lù* is called *fù* (阜). The *Cangjie pian* says it is a mountain that is vast; the *Guangya* says a *qiū* (丘) is a mound without stone; and the *Shuowen jiezi* says *dàlù* (大陸) is a mountain without stone. It is a pictograph. The correct form is 𨸏; the archaic form is 巨, and it is also written as 𨸏. The character in the *Ji* (集) is 阜, which is used interchangeably with the others.

*Bǒ* (pronounced *bō*, with an initial *kě* in retroflexion). Yuè Yěwáng states it means "lame. In the *Zhouyī*, it says: "The lame can walk, yet they are not sufficient for long journeys. The *Shuowén* defines it as "walking not straight," composed of the radical *zú* (foot) and the phonetic *pí*.

The character *qí* (麒) has "jù" (巨) as its upper radical and "lì" (栗) as its lower component; it is pronounced according to the sound of "kǎo" (考). *Qílín* (麒𪊭) refers to an auspicious beast. According to the *Gōngyáng Zhuan*, it is a benevolent beast; the *Erya* describes it as having the body of a *jūn* (麞, a kind of deer), the tail of an ox, the hooves of a deer, and a single horn. Guo Pu stated that there is flesh at the tip of the horn. Ruyang Wang said that the female is called *qí* and the male is called *lín*. When a ruler of sage virtue extends his grace to birds and beasts, this creature appears at his borders. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *qí* (󳎥) and *lín* (󳎤); the explanations are the same as in the *Erya*. Both characters take "lù" (鹿, deer) as their radical, with "qí" (其) and "lí" (離) as their phonetic components. To write it otherwise [as 麟] is incorrect. The collected edition uses *qílín* (騏麟), which is the name of a fine horse.

The *Yǐchū* (fledgling) serves as the opposite of the *èr'ǎ* (the *Ěryǎ* states: "those that are fed by mouth are called *kòu*; those that can feed themselves from birth are called *zhòu*"; Zōu and Guō state they are those capable of feeding themselves from birth). The *Shuowén* says it means a chicken's egg; it is composed of the radical *zhuī* (bird) with the phonetic *cū*; the pronunciation of *cū* is *chǔyóu*.

The *Wénzì Diǎnshuō* explains that these two characters are composed of "horse" (*mǎ*) and "zhé" (*zhē*), with "tā" (*tā*) serving as the phonetic component. *Beilǔ* (背僂): The primary meaning is "to bend backward. The *Guǎngyá* states that *lǔ* means "a curved spine. The *Shuowén* defines it as "humpbacked," composed of the radical 人 with the phonetic 婁;

*Xiǎo* (虓) in *xiǎohǔ* (虓虎): the upper character is pronounced *jiāo* (交). The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (毛詩傳) states that when a tiger is enraged, it roars *xiǎo-rán*. The *Shuōwén* (說文) defines it as the roar of a tiger, composed of the radical "tiger" (*hǔ*) and the phonetic element "nine" (*jiǔ*).

The character for *shèngzhé* (聖喆) is pronounced with the lower radical *zhī* (知) and the phonetic *liè* (烈). The *Erya* states that *zhé* (喆) means wisdom (*zhì*). The archaic form is written as *jìn* (󴻞), composed of three *jí* (吉). It is also written as *zhì* (悊). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as the handle of a drum, composed of the radical *mù* (wood) and the phonetic *bāo*. The *Jíběn* edition uses the character *fú* (桴), which is actually the character for the ridgepole of a roof.

"Zhuài" (詐) means to deceive; He Xiu’s commentary on the *Gongyang zhuan* states that "zhuài" means to doubt, while Liu Zhao says it means to cheat one another. The *Shuowen jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "silk" (糸) with "tái" (台) as its phonetic.

"Yán gōng" (嚴公) is pronounced shàng zhuàng shuāng fǎn; it is a borrowed term for the posthumous title of a Lord of Lù, used by both the *Gongyang* and *Guliang* commentaries to avoid the taboo name of a Han Emperor.

*Tuo* (橐) and *yue* (龠): the first character is read as *tang* (湯) with the *ge* (各) rhyme; Wang Bi states that it refers to a bellows (*pai-tuo*). Gu Yewang says it is a fire-blower used by smelters. The *Cangjie pian* defines it as a bag without a bottom. The *Shuowen jiezi* states it is a *tuo*; it is formed from a simplified form of *tuo* with the phonetic element *shi* (石). The second character, *yue*, is read as *yangzhuo* (羊灼). The *Ervu* states that a large tube is called a *yue*.

*Chen* (讖): Pronounced *chu* (楚) and *nao* (𧮂). The *Cangjie pian* states that the *Chen* books refer to the *He* and *Luo* [River] charts; this is confirmed by the fact that they are recorded in the *Huainan chen shu*. Gu Yewang says they are divinations that later prove effective. The *Shuowen jiezi* defines them as "verification" (*yan*), composed of the radical "speech" (*yan*) with the phonetic "xiian" (*wei*). The *Daidai li* states that east and west are the *wei* (warp); the *Shuowen* defines *wei* as horizontal weaving, composed of the radical "silk" (*mi*) with the phonetic "wei."

*Jing* (旍): Upper radical *zhong* (井), pinyin *yíng* (盈). The *Zhou Li* states: "Feathers are split to make the *jing*. Zheng Xuan comments: "The feathers are split and bound with five colors, attached to the top of the *jing*. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan* says it is a "banner" (*zhang*). Lower radical *qú* (渠), pinyin *yí* (宜). Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhou Li* says: "To summon the multitude, one plants the flag; this is to set a time for those beneath it. Gu Yewang [states] it consists of birds, falcons, tortoises, and snakes. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan* also says it is a "flag-marker" (*qi-biao*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that both characters are derived from *yú* (於) and *líng* (令), with *qíng* (其) as their phonetic component. It is also written as *jīng* (旌) or *qí* (旗); *ǎn* (㫃) has the pronunciation *yǎn* (偃).

Ruǐbīn (蕤賓): "Ruǐ" is pronounced as *ruǐ* (with the radical for "grass" and the phonetic *shuǎi*). It is the name of a musical pitch-pipe (*lü*) in the "Monthly Ordinances" (*Yueling*) section of the *Liji*.

It is also written as *ruí*; the same applies to its usage below. Shāngyāng (商鞅): "Yāng" is pronounced as *yāng* (with the radicals for "bird" and "two"). He was the name of the Chancellor during the time of Duke Xiào of Qin, as recorded in the *Chunqiu Houyu*. His surname was Gōngsūn, and he was enfeoffed at the city of Shāng.

Qú Yuàn (the first character pronounced *jù* with the *gū* tone; the second character pronounced *yuán* with the *juàn* tone) was the personal name of a man who served as a Grand Minister (*dàfū*) of Wèi; his courtesy name was Bóyù, and he was a man of noble character. Yù Jū (the first character pronounced *zǐ* with the *yú* tone;
the second character pronounced *jū*) was the personal name of a man.

"Qiùdiè" (丘垤) [is pronounced] *qiū jié* (田結反). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (毛詩傳) states: "Diè" (垤) refers to an anthill (*yìfáng*). According to the *Fāngyán* (方言), south of the capital of Chu (Chǔyǐng), the mounds of earth made by ants are called *diè*. The *Shuowén* (說文) defines it as "an ant's mound," composed of the radical "earth" (*tǔ*) with the phonetic element "zhì" (*zhìshēng*). The character for "ant" (*yì*) is pronounced *niú yǐ* (牛倚反), meaning *bífú* (蚍蜉). *Note: The term "yìfáng" (螘󱴀) is a rare archaic transcription for "yìfáng" (螘房/蟻房). The character "zhì" (至) is used here as a phonetic indicator for the pronunciation of the character "diè" (垤).*

Although "wēn" (溫) is read as "hún" (渾), Yě Wáng says in his *Guǐyīn* that it means "gradually heating. The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radical "water" (氵) and the phonetic "wūn" (昷). The version in the *Jíběn* reads "yūn" (熅), which is an error; "wūn" (昷) has the same pronunciation as "shàng" (上).

*Dian-xie* (蹀𨇾): The first character is pronounced *tián* (協) and the second is *xiān* (先) with the *jié* (浹) rhyme. The *Kǎo Shēng* states that it describes the manner of small, shuffling steps. The *Huáinán Zǐ* says, "The feet performed the dance of Yáng Ā. The *Shuōwén* writes it as *chà* (䠟), composed of the radical 足 and the phonetic 執. The *Jíběn* version reads *biè* (爕), which is interchangeable.

Regarding the term *piáo-gū* (瓢觚): the upper character *piáo* (瓢) is pronounced with the initial *piao* (驃摽反). The *Kǎo Shēng* states that a *piáo* is half of a gourd (*hù*). Zheng Xuan says it refers to a sweet gourd whose stem is cut off and used as a wine vessel. According to the *Fān Yán*, in the regions between Chen, Chu, Song, and Wei, the *yīn* (𧋠) is sometimes called a *piáo*. The *Shuō Wén* writes it as *shé-lí* (󳏞蠡), meaning a ladle; it is composed of the radical "gourd" (*guā*) and the phonetic "piao" (*piào*). The lower character *gū* (觚) is pronounced with the initial *hú* (古胡反). Mǎ Róng’s commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* states that the *gū* is a ritual vessel: one *shēng* is called a *jué*, and two *shēng* is called a *gū*. The *Shuō Wén* further notes that the drinking vessel for feasts is a *gū*, or alternatively, a *gū* holds three *shēng*. It is composed of the radical "horn" (*jiǎo*) and the phonetic "guā" (*guā*). The pronunciation of *piáo* is *bì-yáo* (必遙反).

*Xiān* (仙): In the *Shuowen*, it says that *xiān* means longevity or to ascend as an immortal; it is composed of the radical "person" (*rén*) and the phonetic element *xiàn*. It is also written as *qiān* (仚). The pronunciation of *xiàn* is *qiān*. *Hùkòu* (虎鞹): Pronounced with the final *-guò* (曠郭反).

The *Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry* states that *kòu* refers to leather. In the *Analects*, regarding the passage "The leather of tigers and leopards is like the leather of dogs and sheep," Kong’s commentary notes that this refers to hides from which the hair has been removed. The *Shuowen* states that it is composed of the radical "metal" (*gēng*) and the phonetic element *guò*.

*Zuìcán* (蕞殘): The upper character is pronounced with the *wài* rhyme; the *Kǎośēng* states it means "small and inferior. The *Cāngjiépiān* says it means "gathered. The *Wénzìdiǎn* explains that it is composed of the radical *kòng* (廾) and the phonetic *zuì* (最); the *Jíběn* (集本) erroneously writes it as *zhuān* (菆).

"Dǎo" (禱) is pronounced *dāo* (考反). Zheng Xuan says it means "to seek blessings. Bao Xian’s commentary on the *Lunyu* states: "Dǎo means to pray; it is to petition the spirits and deities. The *Guǎngyá* defines it as "to thank. The *Shuowén* explains: "To report one's affairs and seek blessings is called dǎo; it is composed of the radical '示' (shì) and the phonetic '夀' (shòu)."

*Zhu* (邾): Upper radical *shang* (上), lower radical *zhi* (陟) with the phonetic *fan* (反); the character for *lu* (魯) below it follows the radical *yue* (曰). According to the *Chunqiu*, both are names of states. *Diao* (盜):

Radical *zheng* (征), phonetic *shi* (石) with the phonetic *fan* (反); the *Kaoseng* (*Kao sheng*) says it means "under the feet. It is also written as *zhí* (蹠) and is a personal name; the *Zhuangzi* says he was the younger brother of Liu Xiaji.

*Zǎi* (宰) and *lì* (𧯻): "Běi" (丕) is the phonetic inversion; it is a personal name. In the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, there was the office title of *Tàizǎi* (太宰). *Zhū* (𦵔) and *hǎi* (醢): "Shǔ" (疏) is the phonetic inversion.

The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *zhū* refers to pickled vegetables preserved in vinegar, written with the radical for grass (艸) and the phonetic *zǔ* (爼). The lower character [for *hǎi*] has the sound *hǎi* (海); the *Erya* says that *hǎi* is meat sauce, written with the radical for liquor (酉) and the phonetic *yù* (𥁓). The collected editions write this with the character *gài* (蓋), which is incorrect. *Yù* (𥁓) is pronounced *yú jiù* (于救).
*Wū* (upper radical *wù*, pinyin *guā*): The *Shuowen* states that *wū* means "sunken, depressed, or low"; it is composed of the radical *kué* (cave) with *guā* as the phonetic.

*Wèi* (upper radical *yǔn*, pinyin *wù*): Zhong You’s commentary on the *Liji* states that *wèi* refers to a small net; the *Shuowen* states it is composed of the radical *ròu* (flesh) with *wèi* as the phonetic.

*Zu* (踧) occurs six times in the preceding text; the *Guǎngyá* states that *zújí* (踧踖) means "timid and reverent. This is exemplified in the *Lìjì*: "The Master, feeling *zúrán* (踧然), withdrew from his seat. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical *zú* (足) with *shū* (叔) as its phonetic. The *Jíběn* (集本) edition uses *zú* (蹐) interchangeably.

*Mǒng* (𥉕): The upper radical is *mù* (目); the phonetic is *péng* (蓬). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states: "To have pupils but no sight is called *mǒng*. The *Shuowen* defines it as "lack of clarity," following the character *zhǒng* (冡) as the phonetic. The lower part is pronounced *gǔ*. The *Lunyu* states: "To speak without having observed the facial expression is called being *gǔ* (blind). The *Shuowen* notes that for the eyes, there is only the character *shì* (眣). It is like the skin of a drum; it follows the radical *mù* with *gǔ* as the phonetic. The *Jiben* (Collected Edition) uses *mǒng* (矇) interchangeably with this character. It has been used thus for a long time.
This is a refutation of false arguments.

"Jùyōu" (聚麀)—the character *yǒu* is pronounced with the *yù* rhyme group (*yǒu*, *yù*)—according to the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲), refers to a female deer. The *Máoshī* (毛詩) states: "The female deer gather in herds (*lù yǒuyǒu*). According to the *Qūlǐ* (曲禮), when human ethics lack propriety, fathers and sons will "gather at the same female deer. The *Shuōwén* (說文) explains that it is derived from "deer" (*lù*) and the abbreviated form of "female" (*pǐn*). The character *yǔ* (麌) is pronounced with the *yú* and *yǔ* rhymes.

"Lan" (婪) is pronounced with the initial *l* and the final *dan* (臘耽反). The *Kaosheng* states it means "greedy and cruel," or "lack of purity. Du Lin of the *Shuowen* says that those who practice divination deceive one another in their examinations, which constitutes "lan"; it is composed of the radical "woman" (*nü*) and the phonetic "lin" (*lin*), and is also written as "lin" (惏) or "nan" (𢛓).

*Xìn* (釁): To rejoice at an audience. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "Xìn means movement, transgression, or a flaw/gap. Jia Gui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states: "Xìn means a portent," meaning there is an omen of calamity. The *Shuowen* defines it as "blood sacrifice"; it depicts the image of a sacrificial hearth (*cuàn*)—abbreviated from *cuàn*—with the character *fēn* as its phonetic component. The original text uses *xì* (舋), which is the vulgar form.

*Āi bì* (the character *bì* is pronounced with the *mí* rhyme). The *Zuǒzhuan* states: "Those guarding the *bì* all wept. Du [Yuan] says: "The *bì* are the *pī'è* (parapets) on top of a city wall. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it: "The *bì* are the walls atop a city; it is composed of the radical *é* (阝) and the phonetic *bēi* (卑); the ancient form is written as 𦎢. The collected editions that write it as *bī* (錍) with the radical *jīn* (金) are incorrect. *Běi* is pronounced as *bì*; *è* is pronounced as *ní* (with the *xí* rhyme), and it is also written as 𨺙, which has the same pronunciation.

*Jìn* (盡): In the *Kě Gēng Fǎn Guì* (客庚反顧), Ye Wang says it means a pitfall (*kēngxiàn*), a ravine (*hè*), or a moat (*qiàn*). The dictionary explains that it takes the radical *tǔ* (earth) and the phonetic *kàng*. *Dūyóu* (杜郵): Below [the character], there is the reading *qiú fǎn* (求反).

The *Wénzì Jílüè* (文字集略) says: "A postal station (*yòu*) is a place passed through by couriers. According to the *Chūnqiū Hòuyǔ* (春秋後語), Dūyóu was ten *lǐ* west of Xiányáng, where Bái Qǐ died. The *Shuōwén* explains it as taking the radical *yì* (city/county) and the phonetic *chuí*. The *Jíběn* (集本) version reads *xiè*, which is an error.

Xuàn (眩): "yú" in the upper character; according to Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu*, it means "to delude. According to the *Cangjie pian*, it means "dimness of vision. According to the *Shuowen jiezi*, it refers to the eyes having no fixed focus; it is composed of the radical "eye" (目) with the phonetic "xuán" (玄).

*Xiáo* (殽): The upper radical is *xiào* (效); the lower radical is the character for "disorder" (*luàn*). Jia Dui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that it means "mixed. The *Guoyá* states it means "disorder. The *Shuowen* defines it as "intermingling," formed with the radical *shū* (殳) and the phonetic *yáo* (肴).
