Guo Pu says its color has light and dark patches that appear mottled; it is what is now called the "linked-coin" (*liánqián*) horse. The *Zìshū* (Dictionary of Characters) states it is a black-lipped horse. The *Jīngǔ zhèngzì* (Correct Characters of Antiquity and Today) takes "horse" (*mǎ*) as the radical and *lín* (粦) as the phonetic, with the lower part read as *wúgāng* (吾剛). The *Chǔcí* (Elegies of Chǔ) says: "The *yǎnyǎn* (驎驎) are like colts of a thousand *lǐ*. The *Běicāng* (Supplement to the Cangjie Dictionary) says it means a horse shaking its head. The *Jīngǔ zhèngzì* says it is the appearance of an angry horse, taking "horse" (*mǎ*) as the radical and *yǎng* (卬) as the phonetic; *yǎng* (卬) has the pronunciation *áng* (昂).
*Nüwa* (寡 *guǎ*) is the title of an ancient sovereign; it is pronounced with the rhyme of *huā* (花).

*Tǔ* (稌) is pronounced with the rhyme of *tù* (兔); the *Erlǚ Pǐ* states that *tǔ* is *dào* (稻, rice), while Zhèng Zhòng says it is *gēng* (秔, non-glutinous rice). According to the *Shuowén*, it means "abundant harvest" (*niǎn*), composed of the radical for grain (*huó*) and the phonetic *yú*.

*Wúyín*: "Yín" is pronounced with the *gǎi* rhyme (as in *gǎi*). The *Kǎośēng* states it means "shore or boundary. The correct character for all periods of antiquity and today is composed of the radical "earth" (*tǔ*) and the phonetic "lìng" (*lìng*). *Gǎi* is pronounced with the *wūshuāi* rhyme (as in *shuāi*). *Bōzhí*: The first character, *bō*, is pronounced with the *bómó* rhyme (as in *mó*);

the second, *zhí*, is pronounced with the *shílì* rhyme (as in *lì*). Zheng’s commentary on the *Máo Shī* states: "Bō is equivalent to planting. The *Shuōwén* also defines it as "planting," though one tradition says it means "to spread. It is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "fān" (*fān*). The version in the *Jíběn* is written as *bò*, which belongs to the category of winnowing baskets and is not the character for "planting."

"Mí" (迷) [is pronounced with the "máo-hòu" rhyme]. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "Mù-mù (瞀瞀) means the eyes are unclear. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "Dī-mù-jǐn (低目謹) means to lower one's gaze with caution; it is composed of 'mù' (目) as the radical and 'wù' (敄) as the phonetic component. The pronunciation of "wù" is "wǔ" (武).
The character for *huì* (𧉨) is read as *yǒng* (𡱈) in the first instance and *qiáng* (強) with the *yú* (魚) radical in the second.

The *Erlü* states: "In the west there is the beast called the *bǐjiān* (shoulder-to-shoulder). It is associated with the *qióngqióng* and *qiónghuì*. When the *qiónghuì* bites sweet grass, if there is danger, the *qióngqióng* and *qiónghuì* carry it away on their backs; each of these is called the *jué*."
The *Lüshi Chunqiu* states that in the north there is a beast named *jué*.

Its forefeet resemble those of a rabbit; when it trots, it halts, and when it runs, it tumbles. Thus, the *qióngqióng* and *jiāoxū* must also follow behind like rabbits; because their front legs are too long, they cannot reach sweet grass, and therefore they require the *jué* to eat for them.
Now, on Mount Xiawu in Guangwu County, Yanmen, there is a beast shaped like a rabbit but larger;
they travel by carrying one another on their backs, and the local custom calls them *ju-shǔ*. The *Shuowen* states: "The *jù* is a beast;

it is composed of the radical 'insect' (*chóng*) and the phonetic 'qióng. The character *jù* is composed of the radical 'insect' (*wūn*) and the phonetic 'jù. The version in the *Ji* (the *Shuowen Jiezi*) reads *jù*, which is like a horse and is not this beast."

This is a grave error. *Jiè* (蟨) has the phonetic value *jū* (居衛反); *qióng* (卭) has the same phonetic value as above; *fùn* (䖵) has the phonetic value *kūn* (昆), and the same applies to the following character.

*Miào tiāo* (廟祧) has the phonetic value *táo* (他彫反). The *Liji* states: "Remote ancestral temples are called *tiāo*. Zheng [Xuan] says: "*Tiāo* means 'to transcend' (*chāo*); it signifies ascending and leaving behind. The spirit-tablets of the transferred temples are stored together with those of the *zhāo* and *mù* generations within the two *tiāo* temples. The standard characters for these terms from ancient times to the present follow the radical *shì* (示) and the phonetic *zhào* (兆).

Regarding "tánshàn" (altar and cleared ground): the first character is pronounced *dān* (with the *fǎn* [rhyme] of *dān*) and the second is pronounced *chán* (with the *fǎn* of *chán*). Confucius’s commentary on the *Shūjìng* states: "To pile up earth is to form an *tán*; to clear the ground is to form a *shàn*. The *Shuowén* says: "*Tán* is a sacrificial enclosure; *shàn* is open wildland. Both characters are composed of the radical "earth" (*tǔ*) with "dàn" and "dān" as their phonetic components; subsequent examples follow this principle.

10. The Tenth Fascicle. *Chuǎng* (瘡): [The character] is pronounced *guǐ* (軌) as a variant; the *Cāngjié piān* states it means "to inflict a wound. The *Shuōwén* says it is *chǔi* (󳁶), composed of the radical *niè* (疒) and the phonetic *yǒu* (有); its rapid pronunciation is *shī* (施).

*Zhì* (滯): Pronounced *zòu* (皺瘦). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to the bricks used for lining a well (*jǐng bì*). It is composed of the radical "tile" (*wǎ*) with the phonetic element "qiū" (*qiū shēng*). *Bì* (甓) is pronounced *pímò* (鼙覓).

The *Kaogong Ji* states that these are what are called "those that croak with their necks. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to a frog (*xiā mó*). It is composed of the radical "mud-bug" (*mǐng*) with the phonetic element "guī" (*guī shēng*). *Mǐng* is pronounced *měng*. It is also written as *wā* (蛙).

Regarding the character *háng* (舟航), the *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that "háng" means to cross over. Gu Yewang says that what is currently called a boat for crossing over is termed a *háng*; thus, the meaning of the correct character has remained the same from antiquity to the present. It is composed of the radical "boat" (*zhōu*) and the phonetic element "kàng. It is also written as *zhāng* (斻) and pronounced *zhǎo*.

"Jiǎ biàn" (嘉抃): The *Kǎo Shēng* states that "biàn" means to clap the hands. The *Shuōwén* writes it as "jiàn" (㭓), stating that it means to pat the hands, composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "biàn" (弁); the pronunciation of "biàn" is the same. The *Jíběn* (集本) uses "jiàn" (抃), which is interchangeable.

The character 𣀇 (yíng) has the phonetic component 迹 (jì) as its radical and 反 (fǎn) as its phonetic. The commentary on the *Shūjīng* by Kǒng [Yǎng] states that it means "a cauldron. The *Shuowén* defines it as "laziness. It is the correct orthography for "end" (*zhōng*) throughout ancient and modern times; it is composed of the radical 支 (zhī) and the phonetic 睪 (yáo). The *Jíběn* also contains the character 歝, which is an error; the same applies to its occurrence below.

*Chǔn* (踳淪): The upper character is pronounced *chūn* (准反). Sima Biao’s commentary on the *Zhuangzi* states that *chǔn* means "variegated and inconsistent. Xu Shuzhong says it means "to go against one another. It is a discrepancy between the ancient and modern standard characters. It is composed of the radical 足 (foot) and the phonetic element 春 (spring); it is also written as 舛 or 偆. The *Huainanzi* writes it as 僢; the pronunciation and meaning are identical.

The character 摑 (with the radical 手 and phonetic 居碧反) does not appear in any of the various character dictionaries; it is considered a vulgar or colloquial form. Regarding 諐 (with the radical 言 and phonetic 朅焉反):

the Commentary on the Book of Documents by Kong Yingda states that it means "transgression or error. Du Yu’s Commentary on the Zuo Zhuan states it means "to fail" or "to lose. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that this is the original form of the character 諐, correctly written as 愆, sharing the same meaning: it takes the radical 心 and the phonetic 衍. It may also be written as 㥶, 𢙣, or 𢙣, all of which are identical in meaning.

*Chánhhuái* (徘徊): The first character is pronounced *zhǎnlián* (展連) and the second has the phonetic *huí*. The *Kǎośēng* says it means "to turn about" (*chántuǎn*) and "to roam about" (*huáishī*). The standard characters for ancient and modern times are written as *zhān* (邅), with the same meaning; it takes *chuò* (辵) as the radical and *dàn* (亶) as the phonetic. *Huái* (徊) takes *chì* (彳) as the radical and *huí* (回) as the phonetic. The *Jíběn* (集本) erroneously writes this as *chánhuí* (儃佪); *chuò* is pronounced *chǐluè* (丑略) and *chì* is pronounced *chì* (勅).

"Ji" (擠): Its upper radical is "qi" (齊), which is pronounced as "xi" (系) when reversed. The *Zi shu* (Dictionary of Characters) states it means "to push down" (*jì zhuì*). The *Fān yǔ* (Dialectal Dictionary) says it means "to extinguish. The *Guǎng pǐ* (Broad Glossary) says it means "to push. The *Shuō wén* (Explanations of Words and Texts) says it means "to shove," composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "qi" (齊).
Xu Gunkun's edition reads it as "fǎn" (反). It is also the name of a person, Liang Huangmen Shilang (梁黃門侍郎).
Wang Jian (pronounced *jiān* with the rhyme *xiàn*): a person's name.
Liu Yun (the upper character is "zhèng" and the lower is *yù* with the rhyme *wěn*; *wěn* is pronounced *wén* or *fěn*):
a person's name. Liu Cheng (pronounced *chéng*): a person's name.

The imperial decree on the *Chiji* (Record of the Mechanisms) states that "fan" (反) refers to the sound of examination. It says: "Chi" (摛) means to unfold or spread out; in Zuo Si’s *Shu du fu* (Rhapsody on the Capital of Shu), it appears as "chi zao yan tian" (摛藻掞天). The *Shuowen Jiezi* (Explanation of Words and Analysis of Characters) defines it as "to extend," composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "li" (离); the pronunciation of "li" is the same as above.

*Tié* (惵惵): The phonetic transcription is *tián yè*. Wang Ye stated that *tié* means "fear. This is as seen in the *Dōngjīng fù* (Tōngdōng Fù), which says, "The common people (*qínnshǒu*) are *tié tié* [in fear]. The meaning of the character is consistent across ancient and modern times. It is formed with the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic element "yè" (*yè*, pronounced like *yè*). The pronunciation of *yè* is *yè*.

Lù (pronounced lú, with the rhyme of *gǔ* reversed): The *Pīcāng* dictionary states that "lùlù" means "abundant sand and stones. The meanings in the *Gǔjīn zhèngzìyì* are identical. It is composed of the radical "stone" (*shí*) and the phonetic "lù" (pronounced lù). Bǐu (pronounced pí, with the rhyme of *biāo*):

The commentary on the *Máo Shī* states that "bǐu" refers to the appearance of flowing water. The *Guǎngyǐpǐ* has the same meaning. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic "biāo" (abbreviated) (pronounced bǐóu, with the rhyme of *bǐóu*).

Regarding "gōu shēn" (hooking the profound): the upper character is read as gǒu (苟) with the fanqie 侯反, and the lower character is read as shěn (審) with the fanqie 株反. The *Commentary on the Appended Phrases* (*Zhouyī xìcí*) states: "Hooking the profound and reaching the distant. The *Kǎoshēng* says: "Gōu means to seek, to take, and to draw. The *Zìshū* says: "Shēn means depth and measurement. The current collected edition reads "jū shèn" (拘𨗉), which deviates from the meaning; I suspect it is an error resulting from transcription. I have revised it to "gōu shēn," which accords with the meaning. Please examine this matter carefully.

*Zhun* (pronounced *chún*, with the tone *fǎn*)—Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states that it refers to an appearance of sincerity and earnestness, meaning to inform someone with diligence. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to instruct until one is thoroughly enlightened. It is composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic element "qín" (*qì chún*). The *Jiben* edition reads *zhūnzhūn* (諄諄), which is a common vulgar form of the character. The sound of *qín* is *jì chún*.
"Zhōngmèng" (終懵): "Mèng" (懵) is pronounced *bēng* (同音崩), meaning "confused. "Lìdù" (蠡度):
The first character is pronounced *lúgē* (盧戈反) and the second is pronounced *tángluò* (堂洛反).
"Hédá" (何炟): Pronounced *dāndá* (丹達反); it is a personal name. The version compiled [in other texts] as "Hézhǔ" (何𢙏) is an error.

"Āi" (僾): The rhyme is *shàng* (上) with the phonetic *ài* (哀). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (毛詩傳) states that "āi" means "to sigh" (*nǎo*). The *Zheng Jian* (鄭箋) states that it causes people to sigh. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文解字) defines it as "vague and indistinct" (*fǎngfú*), composed of the radical "person" (人) and the phonetic "ài" (愛); "nǎo" should be written as "yì" (悒), with the pronunciation *yì*.

Regarding "yù" (嫗) and "xù" (煦): the upper radical of "yù" is *yū* (紆), and the lower radical is *jù* (句). Gu Yewang states that "yù" refers to bowing down to cause [the child] to be warmed. The *Han Shi Zhuan* says "xù" means warmth. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* explains that "xù" refers to the breath while "yù" refers to the physical body. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as "xū" (昫), stating: "The sun emerges and it is warm; it takes 'rì' (日) as the radical and 'jù' (句) as the phonetic. For "yù" (嫗), it takes 'nǚ' (女) as the radical and 'qū' (區) as the phonetic; the pronunciation of 'qū' is *qū*.

Regarding "qíxíng" (creeping), Wang Shàngqì (王上詰) states in his *Yěwáng* (野王) that it refers to animals such as the *jūn* (麞) and deer, which move by lifting their hind legs; it is also written as "bō" (跛), meaning to lift one foot. The *Gōngjīn zhèngzì* (古今正字) states that "qíxíng" (蟲行) is composed of the radical "insect" (虫) with "zhī" (支) as its phonetic component.

*Xuān* (翾): Pronounced *shèng* (上血緣反). The *Kǎo Shēng* states that it means "the appearance of small flight. In the standard characters of past and present, it is composed of the radical *yǔ* (羽) and the phonetic *huíng* (睘) in abbreviated form.
*Xiāo Zhěn* (蕭眕): Pronounced *zhēn rěn* (真忍反); this is a personal name.
*Fú* (伏) is a personal name; *gēng* (絙) is pronounced with the rhyme *dèng* (鄧). *Gēng* is pronounced with the rhyme *gǔ dēng* (古登).

*Zhì xíng* (侄行) is pronounced with the rhyme *zhēn lì* (珍栗); the *Kǎo shēng* (考聲) states that *zhì gǔ* (侄仡) denotes an appearance of not moving forward, and it is also an appearance of stupidity (*chí*). The *Wén zì diǎn* (文字典) explains that it is derived from the radical "person" (*rén*) with the phonetic component *zhì*.

"Yìn huì" (飲憓): the second character is read as *zhuì* (檇, with the radical "mouth" and the phonetic "ruì"). Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "To provide clothing and food is called 'huì' (惠). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "huì" means benevolence (*rén*); it is composed of the "heart" radical and the character "wèi" (叀, pronounced *wèi*). The *Jiben* (集本) edition reads "huì" (憓), which is identical in meaning.

The character *dǒu* (䪴): The upper part is read as *zhēn* (針) with the variant *rěn* (稔). The *Cāngjié piān* states that *dǒu* refers to the appearance of a head hanging down. The *Shēnglèi* says it refers to something resting upon the nape of the neck. According to the *Kǎoshēng*, it is the bone at the back of the brain; what is called today the *yùfán* (玉煩). The *Shuōwén* defines it as "the pillow of the nape," written with the radical *xié* (頁) and the phonetic *yóu* (冘). One should note that the "pillow" used for supporting one's limbs is written with the wood radical (*mù*) as *zhěn* (枕); this is correct. The pronunciation of *yóu* is *yǎo* (󰯌).

"Huo (豁然)"—the first character is pronounced with the *shang* tone and read as "huā" (栝). The *Guǎnpǐ* states: "Huo means empty (*kōng*). Gu Yewáng says: "Huo means a broad and expansive capacity; it also has the appearance of opening. Regarding the correct orthography of ancient and modern times, this character follows the radical "valley" (谷) and the phonetic "harm" (害). The character written as "shè" (󳊝) in the *Jí* is an error.

"Kai" (愾) refers to sighing deeply in aspiration for what has passed; Zheng’s commentary on the *Shijing* states that "kai" means to sigh. The *Guangya* says it means "man" (懣), and the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as a great sigh, composed of the radical "heart" (心) with the phonetic elements "qi" (气) and "sheng" (聲). The pronunciation of "man" (懣) is "men" (悶).

*Chuan* (相舛) is pronounced *chuǎn* (川臠反). The *Guǎngyǐ* states that "chuan" means to be opposed to one another; the *Shuowen* says it means to lie facing each other. It is composed of the radical *xié* (夕) and the phonetic *pí* (󱸰);

*xié* is pronounced *suī*, and *pí* is pronounced *kuà*. *Huìgū* (蟪蛄): the first character is pronounced *huì* (携桂反) and the second *gū* (古吳反). The *Fānyán* states that the *jiéluó* (劫蟧) is called *huìgū*. The *Zhuangzi* says, "The *huìgū* does not know spring or autumn. In all modern and ancient standard characters, this is written with the radical *chóng* (虫). *Hui* (惠) is the ancient phonetic for *guī* (古), and *gū* (虭) is pronounced *dāo*; *láo* (蟧) is pronounced *láo*.

*Chóngfēn* (重雰): Pronounced *fú yún fǎn*. The *Cāngjié piān* states it means "mist. The *Shuōwén* writes it as *fēn*, with the same meaning; it is composed of the radical *qì* (氣) and the phonetic *fēn* (分). *Lǐzú* (躧足): Pronounced *shī zǎi fǎn*.
The *Cāngjié piān* says it describes the manner of walking slowly. The *Gǔjīn zhèngzì* says it is composed of the radical *zú* (足) and the phonetic *lì* (麗); it is also written as *xī* (屣).

Regarding the term *tiān zǎo* (天璪), the early commentary by Zheng Xuan on the *Zhouli* states: "That which has five colors is called *zǎo*; it is a name for variegated patterns. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains: "It is an ornament like water-weeds (*shuǐ zǎo*). It is composed of the radical 'jade' (*yù*) and the phonetic 'sào' (*sāo*)," with the pronunciation of *sào* being *sū dào* (蘇到反).

"Chán" (覘) and "lián" (諂) are opposites. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Chán means to peek or to look; it is composed of the radical 見 (jiàn) with the phonetic 占 (zhān). The pronunciation of "kuī" (闚) is *gōu guī*. "Huán" (還) is pronounced *zhé* (折).
The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states: "Zhi" (晣) means brightness. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Zhaozhi" (昭晣) also means brightness; it is composed of the radical 日 (rì) with the phonetic 折 (zhé)."

*Qi* (齊): Pronounced *jiao* (驕) with a retroflex final. According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to the bit of a horse; it is composed of the radical "metal" (*jin*) and the phonetic "piao" (*biao*). It is also written as *qi* (𧥍). *Piao* (麃) is pronounced *bo jiao* (薄交).

Volume Eleven, Part One. *Di he* (詆呵): *Di* (詆) is pronounced *di li* (低禮). The *Cangjie pian* states it means "to deceive. The *Guangyi* states it means "to destroy. The *Shenglei* states it means "to revile. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to scold"; it is composed of the radical "speech" (*yan*) and the phonetic "di" (*di*), where *di* is pronounced *di*.
"Zhou Yi" (周顗) is a person's name; "Yi" (宜) is pronounced "qi" (豈). "Yin Ji" (殷覬) is a person's name; "Ji" (覬) is pronounced "ji" (冀).

Regarding "jiao tan" (較談), "jiao" (較) is pronounced with the initial "jiang" (江) and the final "yue" (岳) [i.e., *jiǎo*]. The *Kaosheng* states that it means "to simplify" (*juelü*); the *Guangyi* states it means "clear"; the *Hanshu* states it means "obvious and easy to know"; and the *Shuowen* states that it is composed of the radical for "chariot" (*che*) and the phonetic "jiao" (*jiao*).

"Hui" (毀) and "du" (讟)—the latter being pronounced as in the rhyme of "lu" (鹿). Du-zhu (杜注), commenting on the *Zuozhuan*, states: "Du means 'to slander' (*feihui*). The *Guangyi* states: "It means 'evil'. Guo Pu says: "'Du' refers to slandering, defaming, resentment, and grievance. The *Shuowen* defines it as: "'Du' is pain and distress (*tongyan*). It is composed of 'ying' (誩) and takes 'mai' (賣) as its phonetic component. "Ying" is pronounced as in "jing" (競). The original text reads "du" (讀); this is a vulgar character, identical to those appearing later in the tenth fascicle.
Lǐ Miǎo (李淼): A personal name; "Miǎo" is pronounced with the initial *mí* and the final *biǎn*. Shāngqū (蠰佉): The first character is pronounced with the initial *ér* and the final *zhāng*;

the second character is pronounced with the initial *qī* and the final *jiā*. Zōulǔ (鄒魯): The first character is pronounced with the initial *jīng* and the final *sōu*; the second character is the standard form "Lǔ. According to the *Kǎoshēng*, Zōulǔ refers to the ancient state of Zhū, which Lord Mù of Lǔ changed to Zōu. Since the Master’s father was a high official of Zōu, it is said that the original text used the character 𨽁, which is a vulgar variant of "Zōu."
*Línzī* (臨淄): "Zǐ" (滓) is pronounced *sīfǎn* (師反); it is the name of a commandery located in Qí (齊). The *Jíběn* (集本) edition reads *shāo* (󳋁), which is incorrect. *Pièxiǎng* (瞥想):
The first character, *piè* (瞥), is pronounced *piànmìèfǎn* (片蔑反). The *Shuōwén* (說文) states: "Piè means 'to see for a moment'; it is composed of the radical 目 (eye) with the phonetic 敝."

Regarding the character *hé* (絓): the phonetic transcription is *guā* (瓜), with the tone of *guà* (卦). The *Guǎngyǐ* states that it means "to stop. The *Shēnglèi* says it refers to "that which is obstructed. The *Fāngyán* defines it as "to hold. According to the *Shuōwén*, *shǎn* (󳐓) refers to dregs; *hé* (絓) refers to the head of a sack filled with cotton-wool, formed from the radical *mì* (糸) and the phonetic *guī* (圭).

The character *chán* (孱) is formed by placing *zhuàn* (孨, pronounced jiǎn) beneath *shī* (尸). It means to ascend the scaffolding. Conversely, the *Shēngyùn* (韻書) states that *chán yán* (孱顏) describes an uneven appearance; it also means feeble or weak. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means to pierce; another interpretation says it refers to groaning (*shēnyín*). It is composed of *zhuàn* (孨) situated below *shī* (尸). *Zhuàn* (孨) is pronounced *jiǎn*.
The first character, 統 (tǒng), has the upper phonetic "lüè" and refers to the name of a monk.

The second character, 頡 (xié), has the upper radical "xián" with the reversed sound "jié," and the lower radical "hè" with the reversed sound "láng. The *Kǎo Shēng* states that "xié-háng" means rising and falling alternately. The *Shuōwén* defines "xié" as "straightening the neck," composed of the "head" radical (*yì*) and the phonetic "jí. The standard orthography of the present day defines "háng" as "the throat," composed of the "head" radical (*yì*) and the phonetic "kàng."
Hándān (上汗蘭反, 下怛蘭反): The *Hànshū* states it is the name of a commandery belonging to Zhào; Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* identifies it as Guǎngpíng County. Púfú (上步摸反, 下朋北反):

Gù Yěwáng says it means to crawl along with the hands supporting the ground. The *Shuowén* says: "Pú" is walking on one's hands; "Fú" is prostrating. Both characters are composed of the radical 勹 (phonetic *bāo*) and the phonetic 畐 (phonetic *bēi bī*). *Bāo* is pronounced like *bāo*; *bēi* is pronounced like *bēi*, and *bī* is pronounced like *bī*.
*Bào* (暴) [upper radical *páo* (袍), lower *sài* (賽), pinyin *cái*]. *Guān* (鰥): upper *guàn* (慣), lower *huán* (還). Gu Yewang states:

"One who is old and without a wife is called a *guān*. Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states: "When marriages are not performed at the proper time, they are called *guān*. The *Shiming* explains: "It refers to being so distressed and depressed that one cannot sleep, and the eyes are constantly staring blankly (*guānguān*). Therefore, the character is composed of 'fish' (*yú*), as the fish keeps its mouth agape and does not close it. The *Shuowen* states it is composed of 'fish' and the phonetic *huán* (環) with the radical omitted. The *Jiben* (集本) edition uses *zhuó* (䚪), which is an error.

*Mò* (耄): The upper character is pronounced *máo* (反) and the lower is *tián* (結) with a reversed final. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Chunqiu* states that *mào* means "confusion. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states it means "obliviousness. The *Erbai* states that *tié* means "old age. Sun Yan says it refers to an old man whose facial complexion is like iron. The *Shuowen* writes it as *yǎo* (𦽡), meaning ninety years of age; it is composed of "old" (*lǎo*) and the abbreviated form of "mugwort" (*hāo*) for its phonetic. *Tié* (耋) means eighty years of age; it is composed of the abbreviated form of "old" (*lǎo*) for its phonetic, and is also written as *tí* (󲂠).

The characters for *Yanzī* (崦嵫) are pronounced *yīlián* (上猗廉反) for the first and *zīsī* (下子斯反) for the second. The *Shān-hǎi-jīng* (山海經) states that three hundred and sixty *lǐ* southwest of Mount Niǎoshǔ-tóngxué (鳥鼠同穴) is Mount Yanzī. Wáng Yì’s commentary on the *Chūcí* (楚辭) says it is located below Mount Mǒngshuǐ (濛水), where the Yúyuān (虞淵) is situated; this is where [the sun] enters. The meanings of these two characters as standardized in ancient and modern times are identical. Both characters are composed of the "mountain" radical (*shān*) and the phonetic components *yǎn* (弇) and *zī* (茲). They are also written as *Yǎn* (崦).
The characters for *Mōngsì* (濛汜) have the upper phonetic *mēng* and the lower phonetic *sì*. An explanation was already provided in the second fascicle. Regarding *yuèzù* (鸑鷟):

the upper character is pronounced with the *yán* and *jiǎo* rhymes, and the lower character with the *chóng* and *xué* rhymes. The *Guǎngpǐ* states that it belongs to the class of the phoenix (*fèng*) and is a divine bird; the meaning is the same in the *Shuowén*. It further notes that when the Zhou dynasty flourished, this bird cried out on Mount Qí. There is also a bird in the Yangtze River resembling a bird but larger, with red eyes. Both characters are written with the "bird" radical (*niǎo*), and *yù* and *zú* serve as their respective phonetics.

*Huìdú*: The first character is pronounced *huī*; the second is pronounced with the initial *tú* and the final *lù*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "A *dú* is a wooden writing tablet (*shūbǎn*). It is composed of the radical *piàn* (a piece of wood) and the phonetic *mài*.

12. The Twelfth Fascicle. *Làngfēng*: The first character is pronounced *làng*. The *Guǎngyǐ* states: "The ruins of Kunlun have three mountains: Lángfēng, Bǎntóng, and Xuānpǔ. The *Chuci* says: "Gazing upon Lángfēng and Bǎntóng. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is composed of the radical *mén* (gate) and the phonetic *liáng*.

"Qiān" (僉) is pronounced *shàng qiè yán fǎn*. The *Guǎnpǐ* states that "qiān" means "many. Kong's commentary on the *Shūjīng* says it means "all. Guō Pǔ says it means "unanimous. The *Shuowén* also says it means "all," composed of the radicals *jí* (亼), *kòu* (叩), and *cóng* (从). *Léi* (亽) is pronounced *cái rù fǎn*; *kòu* (叩) is pronounced *xuān*; *cóng* (从) is pronounced *cí róng fǎn*.
The fifth fascicle of the *Wànqiào shīdiào fǎnyǐ shì* (The Poetic Lament on the Ten Thousand Apertures:

A Reverse Explanation). Regarding the sound of "nùhǔ" (怒唬): the character "hǔ" (唬) is read as "háo dāo fǎn" (號刀反). The *Kǎoshēng yún* (Examination of Sounds) states that "hǔ" (唬) is derived from "kǔ" (口) and has the phonetic component "hǔ" (虎). It is also written as "hēng" (噑). The original edition of the *Jí* (集) uses the character "yù" (𥃳), which is an error. "Hǔ" (諕) is pronounced "hū gù fǎn" (呼故反).

*Fei-tun*: (The character is pronounced with the *zhūn-nè* rhyme. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "Fat (*tún*) means full or plump. The *Fangyan* says it means abundant. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains: "Fat refers to oxen and sheep; 'fat' (*tún*) refers to pigs. It is composed of the radical for the moon (*yue*) and the phonetic component *dùn*.

*Tianyang* (覜仰): the first character is read as *xiào* (𫋺弔反). The *Huangpi* states it means "to look at"; Guo Pu says it means "to examine. The meaning is the same as in the *Shuowen*. It is composed of the radical *jian* (見) and the phonetic *zhao* (兆); the variant form *tian* (覜) is an error.

The character 轍 (zhé) is read as chǎn-liè; Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that it means "tracks. This is the correct orthography for all periods, composed of the radical 車 with the phonetic 𨅊 (simplified from 𨅊); the form 𨅊 used in the *Jiji* is a vulgar character. The term 宗𨅊 appearing later in the text follows this same principle.

Regarding the character for *yíng* (螢) with the radical "sun" (日) on top: I have consulted various dictionaries and it is not found therein; I suspect it is an error in transcription. The only version that approaches the pronunciation "guāng" (光) is the one with the radical "chariot" (車), written as 𨎩; its meaning may be somewhat close, though perhaps not entirely correct. Furthermore, there is a version with the radical "jade" (圭), written as 黊, pronounced *hú guǎ* (胡寡反); the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines this as "the appearance of brightness," which is slightly closer to the intended meaning. It is uncertain whether this is acceptable.
*Jù zhì*: Pronounced *zhī lì* (知利). Yuè Wáng says it means "to stumble" (*dùn*). The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radical "foot" (*zú*) and the phonetic "zhì" (*zhì shēng*).

*Bù wěi*: Pronounced *wéi guǐ* (違鬼). Dù’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* says *wěi* means "right. The meaning in the *Shuōwén* is the same; it is composed of the character "is" (*shì*) and the phonetic "wéi" (*wéi shēng*).

*Kài* (欬): Pronounced *kǎi* (上開愛反). Gu Yewang says it means "coughing" (*kèsòu*) or "upward-moving qi. It is composed of the radical *qiàn* (欠) with the phonetic *hài* (亥). The *Jíběn* (集本) edition reads *hái* (咳), with the pronunciation *hài* (亥); I fear this may be an error for *āi* (哀). Below, *dīng* (丁) and *jì* (計) are reversed [in the rhyme]. The *Cāngjiépiān* (蒼頡篇) says it means "sneezing" (*shèpèn*). The *Shuōwén* (說文) says it means "the awakening and releasing of breath. It is composed of the radical *kǒu* (口) with the phonetic *zhì* (疐). The pronunciation of *zhì* is *zhúlì* (竹利). *Sì* (嚏): Pronounced *dìng* (丁) and *jì* (計) reversed. The *Cāngjiépiān* says it means "sneezing" (*shèpèn*). The *Shuōwén* says it means "the awakening and releasing of breath. It is composed of the radical *kǒu* (口) with the phonetic *zhì* (疐). The pronunciation of *zhì* is *zhúlì* (竹利).

If it is the character *wěi* (pronounced with the *wěi* rhyme-group and the *kǎi* final), Xu Shuchong states that it means "common" (*fán*); the *Cāngjié piān* says it means "sudden" (*dùn*); the *Guǎngyǐ* says it means "multitude" (*zhòng*); and the *Shuōwén* says it is formed from the radical "dog" (*quǎn*) with the phonetic component "fear" (*wèi*).
Bi Shen (裨諶): the first character is read as bì (with the variant reading bí [上婢彌反]) and the second as shèn (with the variant reading xīn [下甚王反]); he was a Great Officer of Zheng. Mianliu (冕旒):
the first character is pronounced miǎn (variant miàn [音免]) and the second liú (variant liù [音流]); these have already been fully explained in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*).

*Chǔ Shà* (褚翜): "Shà" is a homophone for *fǎn* (反). The *Jíběn* (集本) edition reads *Shè* (翜), which is an error; the same applies to the following passage. *Zhào zhào* (炤炤): "Zhào" is a homophone for *yào* (曜).

The *Cāngjié piān* (蒼頡篇) states that it means "to illuminate" (*zhào chù*). The *Guǎngpǐ* (廣疋) states it means "bright. The correct character of ancient and modern times consists of the radical "fire" (*huǒ*) and the phonetic "zhào" (*shào*); it is also written as *zhào* (照).

*Lóu* (pronounced with the *lòu* rhyme): Dictionaries state that it means an appearance of earnestness and reverence; in the standard characters of past and present, it is composed of the "heart" radical (*xin*) and the phonetic "lóu.
*Zhāng Chǎng* (pronounced with the *chāng liǎng* rhymes) is a personal name.

Regarding the character 𠝶 (hu): the *Chuǎn* (𠁊) radical is pronounced as *chuǎn*. The *Zìshū* (Lexicon of Characters) states that it is the same as 𠝶. The correct form from ancient times to the present follows the "knife" (刀) radical with "𠁊" as the phonetic component. The *Jí* (集) edition writes it as 𠝶, yet upon examining various character lexicons, this character does not exist. Although the character 𠝶 exists, its meaning remains不通 (unresolved/inconsistent); therefore, both forms have been presented here.

Regarding "Háo" (the moat), Gāofǎngù Yěwáng states that it is the name of a river; it is recorded in the *Zhuāngzǐ* that Zhuāngzi and Huìzǐ strolled upon the bridge over this Háo River. In both ancient and modern orthography, the character is composed of the radical "water" (氵) and the phonetic "háo" (豪).

Regarding the character *xì* (餼): Xi Jī reversed it; the "Correct Characters of Antiquity and Today" states that *shēng* (生) is called *xì* and *shú* (熟) is called *yōng* (饔). It follows the radical for food (*shí*) and takes *qì* (氣) as its phonetic component. *Yōng* is pronounced *yú róng*. *Láo* (僚): The upper part is read as *shàng le diāo* (上了彫);

the lower part is the correct character *shǔ* (屬). Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* says: "Láo means officials. Furthermore, the *Zuǒzhuan* says: "Dàfū (high ministers) have *chén* (subordinates) who are *shì* (scholars); *tǔ* (commoners) have *chén* who are *zào* (servants); *zhuó* (charioteers) have *chén* who are *yú* (carriages/crowds); *yú* have *chén* who are *lì* (slaves); *lì* have *chén* who are *láo*. Gù Yěwáng was a person of the ninth rank. The *Shuowén Jiězì* says it follows the radical for man (*rén*) and takes *liáo* (尞) as its phonetic; it is also written as *liáo* (寮).

*Hèidú* (穢黷): The first character is pronounced *yū* (上紆) with the *fèi* (廢) rhyme; the second is pronounced *lù* (鹿). Jia Dui states that *dú* (黷) means "to be familiar or disrespectful" (*xiè*). The *Shēnglèi* says it means "black. The *Guǎngpǐ* says it means "obscure" (*méng*). The *Shuōwén* defines it as "the grime held in the hands," composed of the radical *hēi* (黑) and the phonetic *mài* (賣).
*Liúlián* (流漣): *liè* and *chán* are reversed [in the rhyme]. Yě Wáng says that *liánlián* is the appearance of tears falling.

According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) with the phonetic component "lián" (*liánshēng*). 13. Volume Thirteen. *Chí Jiābīn* (郗嘉賓): *shàng* is pronounced *chǐzhī* (恥知). This is a surname.
"King" (王) is pronounced *gāi* (with the tone *ǎi*); it refers to a person's name. "Crawling" (蝡動):
the first character is pronounced *rǔn* (with the tone *yùn*).
"Sudden" (倏忽): the first character is pronounced *shū* (with the tone *lù*); the *Jíběn* (集本) edition reads *shū* (儵), though the common usage is this character.

The character *qiān* (愆) is pronounced with the initial *qǐ* and the final *yǎn*; its meaning has already been fully explained in the preceding commentary. The character *jí* (集) is written as *zǔ* (󳇮), an archaic form; its lower radical is *zhū* (豬) and its phonetic is *lǜ* (慮).

The character *pàn* (盻) is pronounced *fú* (扶) and *wù* (務). The *Guǎngyǐ* states that "bǔ" (鮒) refers to a fish; this is the same as the "fish shot from the well-mouth" mentioned in the *Zhouyī Jīng* (*Well and Valley shoot at the bǔ-fish*). The *Shuōwén* also identifies it as a fish, formed from the radical "fish" (*yú*) with "fù" (*fù*) as its phonetic.

Regarding the characters *yùn* (韞) and *chú* (韣): the former is pronounced with the initial *yù* and the final *kěn*, while the latter is pronounced *dú*. The *Kǎo Shēng* states that *yùn* means "to wrap and conceal. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* says it means "a case" (*yùnhuì*). The *Cāngjié Piān* says it means "to bind. The meanings of these two characters as correct orthography in both ancient and modern times are identical; both follow the radical *wéi* (韋) and take *wēn* (昷)—pronounced *wēn*—as their phonetic component. *Wēn* is pronounced like *wēn*.

Guòchuí (過棰): the first character is pronounced as duō (鵽) and the second as jī (佳累). The *Gōngjīn zhèngzì* states that "zhūa" (檛) and "chuí" (棰) both mean to strike; both characters are composed with the radical for wood (木), while "guò" (過) and "chuí" (垂) serve as their phonetic components.

Qiǎnquǎn (繾綣): The first character is pronounced qiān (牽) with the *shàn* (善) rhyme group; the second is quǎn (闕) with the *ruǎn* (阮) rhyme group. The *Commentary on the Mao Shi* states that "qiǎnquǎn" means "repeatedly turning back"; Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan* states it means "not being separated or scattered. The meaning of the characters as correct orthography has been consistent throughout antiquity and modern times. Both characters are formed with the radical 糸 (silk/thread) and the phonetic components 遣 (qiǎn) and 卷 (juǎn).

*Zhǐ* (祉): The upper radical is *chōu* (抽) with the reverse *lǐ* (里). The *Mao Shi* states that it means "blessing" (*fú*). The meaning in the *Shuowen* is the same; it is composed of the radical *shì* (示) and the phonetic *zhǐ* (止).

*Zàn* (閘): The upper radical is *wū* (烏) with the reverse *jiǎ* (甲). The *Shuowen* states that it means "a gate for opening and closing. It is composed of the radical *mén* (門) and the phonetic *jiǎ* (甲).

The character *zǎ* (苲) is pronounced with the upper radical *zàng* (藏) and the phonetic *gǎo* (各); the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it is a designation for the people of the southwestern tribes, and it is also written as *zuò* (莋). The lower part, *qióng* (卭), has the phonetic *gǎo* (各); it refers to a flower calyx (*huādū*). The *Jíyì* (集) states it is the enclosure of the calyx (*zhīnè zhī jiàn*), though its meaning remains unclear.

*Jù* (巨) is pronounced *huáng guō* (黃郭). Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that it is a cauldron (*dǐng*) and also a vessel for boiling meat. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is a *xuì* (鑴); it is composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic "huò" (*wò*), with the pronunciation *yū fú* (紆縛) for the former and *hú guī* (胡圭) for the latter.
*Sanli* (三朸): *li* is pronounced with the *zhí* (職) rhyme. The *Shuowen* states that "li" refers to the grain of wood (*mùlǐ*), formed with the radical "wood" and the phonetic "force" (*lì*).

This meaning is also not yet fully understood. *Lidǒu* (利㭰): *dǒu* is pronounced with the *zuìsuǐ* (醉髓) rhyme. The *Kaosheng* states it refers to the beak of a bird. The *Shuowen* derives this from the phonetic "prickly thorn" (*cì*). It is also written as *zǐ* (觜). The *Jiben* (集本) edition uses *zǐ* (呰), which is the character for "to revile" (*huǐzǐ*) and is incorrect. *Zǐ* is pronounced *zǐ* (子); *cì* (朿) is pronounced *qīsì* (七四) rhyme.

*Chānqīng* (攙槍): "shàng" (上) is pronounced *shì* (仕); "xià" (下) is pronounced *què* (鵲). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it means "to thrust upward in opposition. Both ancient and modern standard characters take the radical *mù* (木). *Cháncuī* (毚鶀): "cāng" (倉) is the phonetic; *cuī* (鶀) is pronounced as above.

*Jiǎo* (狡): When used as a prefix in "upper" (*shàngjiāo*), it is pronounced *mǎo*. The *Shānhǎijīng* states: "There is a beast shaped like a dog with leopard-like markings and horns like an ox; it is named *jiǎo*, and its cry is like the barking of a dog. In the lands of the Hu, there is the *jiǎoquán* (狡犬), which has a large mouth and a black body. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* says: "*Jiǎo* means slippery or cunning (*huá*). The *Guǎngyǐ* says: "It means robust or vigorous (*jiàn*). The *Shuōwén* says: "A young dog. It is written with the radical 犬 and the phonetic component 交."
The character *fei* (斐) [is pronounced] with the upper radical *fei* (妃) and the lower radical *wei* (尾). It has already been explained in the sixth fascicle of the *Śāstra*.

The character *bi* (苾): the upper radical is *pin* (頻) and the lower radical is *mi* (蜜); the *Zilin* states that "bi" means "great fragrance. It is derived from the radical *jun* (廾) and the phonetic *bi* (泌), and is also written as the character *bi* (馝).

*Shuò* (爍): "Shuò" is pronounced with the *shāng* and *zhé* finals. Gu Yewang says it means "to melt. The *Jīngǔ zhèngzì* says: "The people are *shuò* and not firm. It takes the radical *huǒ* (fire) and the phonetic *lè*.

*Xí* (遐): "Xí" is pronounced with the *zhǐ* and *yíng* finals. Gu Yewang says it means "distant. The *Shuowén* says it means "to walk. It takes the radical *chùo* and the phonetic *zhèng*. *Chùo* is pronounced with the *chǒu* and *lüè* finals; it is also written as *zhēng* (to set out).

*Chūn* (椿): The upper radical is *zhùn* (屯, retroflex *n*). The *Zhuangzi* says there is a great *chūn* tree that takes eight hundred years for spring and eight hundred years for autumn. Regarding the standard character for "ancient" and "modern," it is composed of the radical *mù* (木) and the phonetic *chūn* (春). The lower part is *quī* (逵, retroflex *n*). Guo Pu says: "A fungus is a mushroom growing from the ground; it resembles a lid. The *Zhuangzi* says: "The morning fungus (*cháo-jùn*) does not know the difference between the end of day and the beginning of night. Sima Biao says: "It is a short-lived *zhī* (芝). It grows on manure when the sky is overcast. The meaning in the *Shuowen Jiezi* is the same as Guo's. It is composed of the radical *sòng* (廾) and the abbreviated phonetic *qūn* (囷). *Qūn* is pronounced *qūlún* (屈倫). *Tàn* (蕈) is pronounced *shēnrěn* (深荏). *Jùn* (菌): The upper radical is *sòng* (廾). The phonetic is the abbreviated form of *qūn* (囷). *Qūn* is pronounced *qūlún* (屈倫). *Tàn* (蕈) is pronounced *shēnrěn* (深荏). At the end of the character *qióng* (駉), it is pronounced *shànggǔ yíngfǎn*. The *Shuowen* states: "Qióng refers to a horse-pasture; it is composed of the radical 'horse' (馬) with 'jiǒng' (冋) as the phonetic component.

The pronunciation of *jiǒng* is the same [as *yíng*]. The character *xiá* (黠) is pronounced *xiánzhà fǎn*. The *Fangyan* states: "To the east of the Guanzhong region, between Zhao and Wei, they call wisdom *xiá*. Guo Pu comments: "It means to be intelligent and discerning. The *Shuowen* defines it as "hard and black," composed of the radical 'black' (黑) with 'jí' (吉) as the phonetic component. The pronunciation of *zhà* is *wúxiá fǎn*.

"Yóngyóng" (喁喁)—in the *Huáinánzǐ*, it says: "Of all living beings, there are none who do not look up at its virtue with yearning. According to the *Shuowén*, it means "a multitude of mouths looking upward"; it is composed of the radical "mouth" (口) and the phonetic "wú" (禺), and is pronounced like "wú."

*Liǎosū*: The upper character *liǎo* (了) is explained in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as "the pungent herb *liǎo*; it is formed with the radical *gòng* (廾) and the phonetic *liù* (翏). The lower character *sū* (蘇) is pronounced *hú* (胡). The *Erya* states, "*Sū* is *guìrěn* (桂荏)"; the meaning is the same as in the *Shuowen*. It is formed with the radical *gòng* (廾) and the phonetic *sū* (穌). The phonetic *liù* (翏) is pronounced *lìjiù* (力救), and the pronunciation of *sū* (蘇) is as stated above.

*Yìyào* (熠燿): The first character is read as *yì* (󰯌挹反) and the second as *yáo* (怡照反). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that *yìyào* refers to *lín* (燐), which is the firefly. The definition in the *Shuowen Jiezi* is identical; both characters are composed of the radical "fire" (*huo*) with the phonetic component "xi" (*xí*). It is also written as *yù yào* (煜燿), with the same pronunciation and meaning. *Lín* (燐) is pronounced *dǎo* (𠫤).
Regarding *gāohuī* (high-flying): it violates the *Shuowen*. The *Shuowen* states: "Huī means to fly high; it is composed of the radical 'feather' (*yǔ*) and the phonetic element 'jūn'.
Regarding *jiàngzhēn* (carpenter’s block): it is pronounced *zhì* with the *qì* rhyme; its explanation is already provided in the *Zaśilü* (Vinaya on Miscellaneous Matters).

*Śǎnshū* (睒倏): The upper character is pronounced *tiān* (苫) with the phonetic element *rǎn* (染); the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it means "the eyes are restless. The standard orthography of the past and present uses the radical *mù* (目) with the phonetic element *yán* (炎). The lower character is pronounced *shū* (舒). This has already been fully explained.
"Pie" (瞥) [the first character is pronounced *pǔ miè* according to the rhyme dictionary]. This has already been fully explained in the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga*.

"Xuān" (眴): the first character is pronounced *xuán juàn*. Wang Yi states that "xuān" means the appearance of looking; Gu Yewang states it refers to the way people today move their eyes to secretly communicate with one another. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "a movement of the eyes," composed of the radical "eye" (*mù*) and the phonetic "chui" (*chōu*).

*Jiǎngdiàn* (炯電): "Jiǎng" is pronounced as *huǐng*. The *Cāngjié piān* states that it means "bright. The *Shuōwén* says it means "light," composed of the radical "fire" (*huǒ*) and the phonetic component "huǐng" (*huǐng*). The pronunciation of "huǐng" is the same as that of "huīng" (*huǐng*). The pronunciations for "jiǎng" and "tóng" (*tóng*) in the following text are identical to this.

Regarding "shíbão" (stone-bão), the *Yǎo Fǎn* commentary on the *Shuōwén* states that "fúyáo" is called "bão. Guō Pǐng says it refers to a violent wind blowing from above to below; the meaning in the *Shuōwén* is the same. It is composed of the radical "wind" (風) with the phonetic "biāo"; the pronunciation of "biāo" is the same as "shàng" (above).

The character 鵬 (péng) has the upper phonetic *péng* and the lower phonetic *kūn*. According to the *Zhuangzi*, the pèng is a transformation of the kùn fish; its back is said to be several thousand li in length, and it soars ninety thousand li upon the whirlwind *fúyáo*. The *Chuci* describes the kùnjī as crying out with a mournful, discordant sound. Gu Yewang states that its appearance is like a crane but much larger. The *Shuowen Jiezi* notes that both characters are composed of the radical "bird" (*niǎo*) and take *kūn* as their phonetic component; it is also written as 鶤.

14. Volume Fourteen, Part One. *Zhuiji* (玑): The upper character is pronounced as *yuan* (緣) and the lower as *ji* (機). The *Shangshu* (Book of Documents) states: "With the *zhuiji* and the jade balance, one aligns the seven celestial offices. Kong Yingda’s commentary notes that these are instruments for regulating astronomy that revolve. The definition in the *Shuowen Jiezi* is identical. Both characters are composed of the "jade" radical (*yu*) and the phonetic element *rui* (睿). The form *tong* (珽) is a vulgar variant.

*Xiáng-áo* (翔翱): "Xiáng" (上) is pronounced *áo* (敖, high tone); "áo" (下) is pronounced *yáng* (羊, level tone). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* says: "Xiáng-áo is like *fǎng-yáng* (仿徉). Zheng [Yun] says it means "xī-yáo" (逍遙, carefree wandering). Guo Pu says it refers to a bird spreading its wings as it flies. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "circling flight. Both characters are composed with the radical "feather" (羽); "gāo" (皐) and "yáng" (羊) serve as their phonetic components. The form written as *jì* (𦒡) is vulgar.

The upper phonetic of "qì" (𭖪) is dú; the lower phonetic is qí jì. The *Kǎo Shēng* states it is that which is produced by yīn and yáng and that which is perceived through the sense of smell. The *Shuōwén* says it is "cloud-vapor," a pictographic character; it is also written as "qì. The original text of the *Jí* uses "qì" (炁); this is an ancient script, and the same applies to the following instances in this text.

The characters for *yuán* (黿) and *tuó* (鼉): the first is pronounced with the *ruǎn* and *yuán* rhymes, and the second with the *dù* and *hé* rhymes. The *Shuōwén* states that *yuán* is a large turtle (*bì*) formed from the radical *mǐng* (黽) and the phonetic *yuán*. The *Shānhǎijīng* says that the Jīng River produces *tuó*; Guō Pǔ notes they resemble lizards, the larger ones being long and having scales and variegated markings; their hides can be used to make drums. The *Shuōwén* identifies them as aquatic creatures; the remaining meanings are the same. Guō [Pǔ] takes *mǐng* (黽) as the radical and *shàn* (單) as the phonetic. The *Jíběn* (集本) reads *huán* (魭) and *hè* (䰿), which are vulgar forms. *Bié* (鼈) is pronounced *bǐ miè*; *mǐng* (黽) is pronounced *méng gěng*.

*Jūjué* (狙玃): The first character, *jū*, has the phonetic value *qíyú* (七餘反); the *Guǎngpǐ* states that *jū* refers to a species of macaque. The *Shuōwén* says it belongs to the category of *jué*. It is formed with the radical "dog" (*quán*) and the phonetic element "qiè" (*qiě*). The second character, *jué*, has the phonetic value *jūyuè* (居籰反). Guō Pǔ’s commentary on the *Ěrshīyā* states that it resembles a macaque but is larger, being dark blue-black in color; it can seize and hold people and is fond of looking back with a startled gaze. The *Shuōwén* says it is a female monkey (*mùhóu*). It is formed with the radical "dog" and the phonetic element "jué" (*jué*). The pronunciation of *jué* is *jùfù* (俱縛反), *yuè* is *wángjué* (王矍反), and *jué* is *xūyuè* (吁籰反).
*Huolizi*: The upper character *huo* (禾) is the Sanskrit term. *Yiran*:

The upper character *yi* (曀) is pronounced with the initial *i* and the final *ji*. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states: "When it is cloudy and windy, the sun is obscured (*yi*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical for "sun" and the phonetic *yi*.

The character *guī* (歸) is pronounced *qiū* (緱) with a reversed tone. The dictionary states that *qiū* means song, joy, or chanting; its meaning has remained consistent from ancient times to the present. It is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic element "district" (*qū*). It is also written as *ōu* (謳) or *ǒu* (嘔), with the same pronunciation and semantic meanings.

Regarding the phrase "the rear division (*duì*) of soldiers turned back," Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "division" (*duì*) means a unit; one hundred men constitute one division. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as 隊, with the phonetic component 遂 (*suì*). The version compiled here as 󳁟 is erroneous and deviates from the correct meaning. It is not right.

*Miè* (蕛稗): The first character is pronounced *tí* (泥反). Guo says it is a weed resembling *bài* grass that spreads and grows rankly. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) with the phonetic "tí" (*shēng*). The second character is pronounced *pài* (懈反). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states it is a weed that resembles grain. The meaning of the characters has remained consistent from ancient times to the present; it is composed of the radical "grain" (*huó*) with the phonetic "bēi" (*shēng*).

*Bahù* (跋扈): The first character is pronounced *pán-mò* (反), and the second is *hú-gǔ* (反). The *Yìnyì* (音義) of the *Hànshū* states that "bàhù" refers to the appearance of acting with unrestrained license. *Zuò Cóng* (𦵮琮) says it refers to the appearance of being brave and robust. The character "bà" has already been explained; according to the *Shuowén*, "hù" (扈) means "to follow," with the phonetic component "hù" (戶).

*Kāoxiáng* (highly arched): The *Shuowen* states that it means the horse’s head is raised. It is composed of the radical "horse" (*mǎ*) and the phonetic "xiāng. The same applies to its usage below. *Cō'é* (towering):

The upper character is pronounced *zuóhé* and the lower is *wǒgē*. The *Guǎngpǐ* states it means "lofty appearance. Wang Yi says it refers to a mountain peak so high and steep it blocks out the sun. All standard characters from ancient times to the present use the radical "mountain" (*shān*). *Chāwǒ* is the phonetic component. *Jīzhē* is a vulgar variant.

*Shànchén* (熯晨): The upper character is *rán*, which is pronounced with the *shàn* rhyme; it also has the pronunciation *hàn*. The *Cāngjiépiān* states that it means "to dry with fire. The *Shuowén* states that it also refers to the appearance of being dried; it is composed of the radical "fire" (*huǒ*) and the phonetic component "hàn" (abbreviated).

*Zǔní* (祖禰): "ní" is pronounced with the *lǐ* rhyme. Zheng Zhong states that *ní* refers to the ancestral temple of the father. The meaning of the correct characters has remained the same from antiquity to the present; it follows the radical "示" (*shì*) and takes "爾" (*ěr*) as its phonetic.
*Duò* (畷󱻗): the first character is pronounced with the *zhīhuì* rhyme.
The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that "zhuè" refers to boundary markers.

Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* explains that it refers to the places between the *jing* plots where the field overseers (*tiánjùn*) supervise and bind the common people; they serve to mark out the rows.
The *Shuowen* states that it is a path between two fields.
It is six feet wide; the character is formed from "tian" (田) with "zhuo" (叕) as its phonetic component.
The final radical is pronounced "cha jia fan" (查駕反).

The *Book of Rites* states: "The Son of Heaven performs the Great Sacrifice (*dàlì*). Lord Yíqí was the first to institute the sacrifice of the plow (*lí*). 'Lí' means to seek; in the twelfth month of the year, one gathers all things together to seek them out and offer them in sacrifice. This sacrifice of the plow primarily honors the First Steward (*xiānsè*) and sacrifices to the Steward (*sīsè*). One sacrifices to the hundred kinds of grain to repay the labor of cultivation. This is the height of benevolence and the perfection of righteousness."
"Those in yellow robes and yellow caps perform the sacrifice to rest the field laborers.

Zheng Xuan says: "The 'sacrifice' refers to the *jisi* (winter solstice) sacrifice to the ancestors and the five sacrificial spirits; at this time, the farmers are rewarded and allowed to rest. There are eight [such occasions]."
First, Xiānsè; second, Sīsè; third, Nóng; fourth, Biǎozhuì; fifth, Māohù; sixth, Fáng; seventh, Shuǐyōng; eighth, Kūnchóng. The *Guǎngyǐ* states: "It means sacrifice.
In the Xia dynasty it was called Qīngsì; in the Yīn, Jiāpíng; in the Zhōu, Dàzhòu; and in the Qín, Là."
In the *Gujin Zhengzi*, the character is written with the radical "clothing" (衣) and the phonetic "xi" (昔); it is also written as "là" (蜡), which is likewise acceptable.

Regarding "jīzhǐ" (基址): the fanqie is "ěr" (耳). The *Shuowen* states: "Zhǐ (址) means foundation (基); it takes 'tǔ' (土) as the radical and 'zhǐ' (止) as the phonetic. The original version in the *Ji* (集) has "yè" (墌), which is likely an error.
*Tan* (耼) is read as *tan* (菼甘反); it refers to the Old Lord (*Laojun*). *Fan* (燔) is read as *fan* (上伐袁反);

the *Shuowen* states that *fan* means "to burn," composed of the radical *huo* (fire) and the phonetic *fan*. *Jin* (燼) is read as *jin* (下似進反); Zheng’s commentary on the *Shijing* states that what remains after burning is called *jin*; the *Shuowen* writes this as *yan* (󱽃), also stating it means "the residue of fire," composed of the radical *huo* and the phonetic *yue* (聿).
