[Regarding the term] "jiāo" (澆): it is pronounced with the rhyme of *zhào* (晈) and the radical *yǔ* (許). Xu Shuchong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states that "jiāo" means "thin" (*bó*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic "yáo" (*yáo*).

The character *qíng* (情) is composed of *hùn* (溷) below and *hún* (魂) as its phonetic component; according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means turbid; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means disorderly, formed with *shuǐ* (水) and the phonetic *hùn* (圂), where *hùn* is pronounced *hún* (魂) with the final *fǎn* (反) of *kùn* (困). The sequence [of strokes] follows *kūn* (昆) to form *hùn* (混); the *Shuōwén* defines this as the appearance of water flowing in abundance, which is not the intended meaning here.

"Xuánzhǒng zhōng yǒng fǎn wáng" (In an instant, Zhongyong rebelled against the King). The commentary on the *Chuci* states that "zhǒng" means succession. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines "zhǒng" as the heel of the foot; here it refers to the "zhǒng" of pursuit. It is composed of the radical "foot" (足) with "chóng" (重) as its phonetic component, or alternatively written as "xún" (歱) with "zhǐ" (止) as the phonetic component. The pronunciation of "gēn" (跟) is *gèn* (艮, with the second tone).

Jiǎ (𠆙): This character is pronounced as the rhyme of *héng* (衡) and *cǎo* (草). According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to investigating matters at a place where words are obstructed and intercepted (*yī-xī-zè*), thereby obtaining the reality and verifying the facts. It takes *xī* (覀) as its radical and *jiǎo* (敫) as its phonetic component. *Xī* is pronounced as *mǎ* (󳍡) with the second tone; *jiǎo* is pronounced as *jī* (擊).

Regarding "蔽" (bì), Du Yu’s commentary states it means "to manifest. The *Guǎngyǐ* says it means "hidden. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "grass" (艹) with "biè" as its phonetic.

Regarding "biàn bó" (辯駁), it is pronounced bāng bó. Gu Yewang states that "bó" refers to being "unharmonized. This is the correct orthography for both ancient and modern times, composed of the radical "horse" (馬) with "jiāo" as its phonetic.

Regarding the character *jiào* (較), Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Shangshu Dazhuan* states: "Jiào means 'to see' (*jiàn*). In the standard characters of the present day, it is composed of the radical *chē* (車) and the phonetic *bó* (駮) in abbreviated form; its correct form is *jiào*.

"Biāo-jǔ" (標舉) is pronounced biāo-jù; "biāo" means to raise up or highlight. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "wood" (木) with "piào" (票) as its phonetic. "Liàng-zī" (諒資) is pronounced liàng-zī; "liàng" means sincerity or trustworthiness.

According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "speech" (言) with "jīng" (京) as its phonetic. In the *Shijing* commentary, it means faithfulness. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "speech" (言) with "jīng" (京) as its phonetic.
*Ōu* (pronounced *sū hǒu*): According to the *Fānyán*, *ōu* means "to examine. The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radical *yòu* with the phonetic *zāi*.
*Xúnyì* (pronounced *xún yí zhī*): According to the *Fānyán*, *yì* means "to analyze. Guo's commentary states that *yìyì* refers to unraveling and explaining, derived from the radical *mì*.

*Nìngxìng* (佞倖): The upper character is read as *níng* (寧) with the *dìng* (定) radical; according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the "woman" (*nǚ*) radical and the phonetic "benevolence" (*rén*). The version compiled [in the *Guangyun*] uses *nìng* (侫), which is a vulgar form. The lower character is read as *héng* (衡) with the *gěng* (耿) radical. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that it means "obstinate and perverse" (*xìnghěn*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the "man" (*rén*) radical and the phonetic "fortune" (*xìng*). It may also be written as *xìnghěn* (婞很). The pronunciation is *hén* (痕) with the *kěn* (懇) rhyme. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "perverse" (*hěn*) means "rebellious and evil" (*lì è*).

*Bá cuì* (蒲八反; *pú bā fǎn*): Wang Yanwang says that *bá* means "to draw forth. The *Shuowen* defines it as "to extend," written with the radical 手 (hand) and the phonetic 犮 (*bó*, pronounced *pán bó fǎn*). The second character, *cuì* (全遂反; *quán suì fǎn*), in the *Zhouyi*, refers to "gathering. The *Shuowen* states it is written with the radical 艸 (grass) and the phonetic 卒 (*zú*).

"Meng" (濛) is the character for "spray" or "mist"; the *Mao Shi* commentary states it describes the appearance of rain, while the *Shuowen Jiezi* says it is composed of the radical "water" with the phonetic "meng.
"Ai" (藹) is pronounced as "ai" (哀); it is a personal name.

*Zhuìpiān* (Tie-pian): "Zhui" is pronounced *shàng zhuī réi fǎn*. Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states it means "to connect. The *Shuowen* says it is composed of the radical *mì* (silk) with *zhuē* as its phonetic.

*Niè* (Nie): "Niè" is pronounced *shàng nián tiě fǎn*. The *Guǎngyá* says it means "mud. Kong’s commentary on the *Lunyu* states that "niè can be used to dye black. The *Shuowen* says it is black earth found in water; "niè" is composed of the radical *rì* (sun) with *niè* as its phonetic. *Xiàzǐ* (Xia-zhi): "Xià" is pronounced *shī fǎn*. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* says "black is the color of *zī*. The *Shuowen* says it is composed of the radical *mì* (silk) with *zāi* as its phonetic. *Xù* (Xu): This is written with the radical *shuǐ* (water) as *Zī*, the name of a river originating from Mount Tai.

Regarding the passage "The *zǎo* mirror encountered old age," the commentary on the *Shūjìng* by Kǒng [Yáng] states: "'*Zǎo*' refers to aquatic plants that have patterns; according to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical 'grass' (*cǎo*) and the phonetic 'bath' (*zǎo'), and this *zǎo* is what Wáng [Guǐzhī] refers to."

*Chuǎi* (義): The initial rhyme is *rěi*. Wang Yewang says that *chuǎi* means to measure and estimate. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To measure height is called *chuǎi*; it takes *duān* as its phonetic component. *Duān* is pronounced like *duān*. 1. Fascicle One, Part One:
Rectifying the Return (*Guīzhèngpiān*). *Tàizǎi Pǐ* (丕): The rhyme is *měi*. This is the name of the Grand Chancellor of Wu. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it takes *xǐ* as its phonetic component.
*Hài* (大駭): *héng* (矮) and *fǎn* (反). In the *Cāngjié piān*, it means "to be startled. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "horse" (*mǎ*) and the phonetic "hài" (*hài shēng*).
*Zhī xū* (之墟): *qù yú* (去魚). A mound or hill; also written as *xū*. *Wēi rén* (偎人): *wū huí* (烏回).

The *Shānhǎi jīng* states that in a corner of the Northern Sea there is a land called *Wēirén*. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "person" (*rén*) and the phonetic "wèi" (*wèi shēng*).

"Chenli" (琛麗): "Lin" is pronounced as *fan*. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that "chen" means treasure (*bao*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical for jade (*yù*) and the phonetic element "shen" (*shěng*) with its "sheng" component omitted.
"Jian" (緘): Pronounced as *jia-xian-fan*. The *Shuowen* defines it as a bound casket (*shuó qiè*). It is composed of the radical for silk (*mì*) and the phonetic element "xian" (*xián*).
Cai Yin (蔡愔): "Yi" (揖) is pronounced with the *shǎn* (󰯌) radical; it is a personal name. *Wei* (煨): The upper character is pronounced with the *wěi* (猥) and *huí* (回) finals.

According to the *Guǎngyá*, "wei" (*wēi*) is synonymous with "wēiyùn" (*煨熅*, smoldering). The lower character is pronounced with the *jìn* (似進) final. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states that "jin" (*jìn*) refers to the remnants of fire. The Imperial Preface to the *Xiaojīng* composed by the Tang Emperor says, "the state of being mere embers (*wēijìn*). The *Shuowén Jiězì* explains that "wei" (*wēi*) is written with the "fire" radical and the phonetic "wèi" (*wēi*). "Jin" (*jìn*) is correctly written as "jìn" (󲍎); the form "cùn" (燼) found in the *Jízi* is a vulgar variant.

Regarding the character *jiéyǔ* (婕妤): the upper radical is *zī* (咨) and the lower is *fǎn* (反), with the phonetic component *zhū* (諸). The *Wenzidian* explains that *jiéyǔ* is an official title for a consort; both characters follow the "woman" (*nǚ*) radical. The phonetic element is *dié* (疌), which is pronounced *qián yè fǎn* (潛葉反).
"Fan" (范) and "Yan" (曅) are names of people from the *Fanjie* (炎劫).
"Jing" (精) and "Cu" (醋) are pronounced with the rhyme *-suo*. It is also a variant of "jiao" (󱍮), using a borrowed phonetic character.

"Ju" (遽) is pronounced *qú jù*; Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "ju" means "timid fear. Examining the phonetics, the correct form is "ju," though the *Ji* (集) version writes it as "cu" (懅); this is a vulgar usage found within the classics.

*Dǐ* (pronounced with the initial *dǐng* and final *-li*): According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to butt" (*lùè*). It is also said to mean "a general outline" (*dà lüè*). The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* states that it is sometimes written as *dǐ*; furthermore, when written with the radical for "ox" (*niú*) as *ní*, or with the radical for "hand" (*shǒu*) as *zhǐ*, these forms deviate from this meaning.

*Dǐngzhì* (鼎峙): The upper character *dǐng* is pronounced with the fanqie *lǐngfǎn*; it is also written as *dǐng*, which is a vulgar form. The lower character *zhì* is pronounced with the fanqie *chílǐfǎn*; its phonetic component is *shèng*. "Zhì" means to stand out prominently. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical *shān* (mountain) and the phonetic *sì*. It is also written as *zhì*.

*Máocí* (茅茨): The upper character *mǎo* (茅) has the phonetic *sǎo* (夘); the lower character *cí* (茨) has the phonetic *fǎn* (反). According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means "to cover"; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means "to cover a house with *máo* grass," formed from the radical *cǎo* (艸) and the phonetic *cì* (次).
*Kànzé* (闞澤): The reading is *kēlánfǎn* (珂濫反); it is the name of a person.
Zhou Yi (the character for "Yi" is pronounced with the *qǐ* tone).
Que Chaoqing (the character for "Chao" is written as the common character *Chǐ* here).
Wang Tan (the character for "Tan" is pronounced with the *hǎn* tone).
Wáng Mì (王謐), pinyin: mí, bǐ, fǎn;
Dài Kuí (戴逵), pinyin: guì, zhuī, fǎn;
Yīn Jì (殷覬), pinyin: jī, yì, fǎn. The above are all personal names.

The entry for *shī* (蓍) first appears as "divining stalks" (*shī cè*) in the *Cāngjié piān*. Gu Yewáng states that these stalks are used for divination; forty-nine pieces are placed on a tray to form the hexagrams. The *Zhōuyī* says: "In determining the good and ill fortune of the world, nothing is more manifest than the *shī* and the tortoise shell. The *Báihùtōng* says: "*Shī* means trustworthiness. The *Shuowén* says it belongs to the genus *háo*; it grows for a thousand years and has three hundred stalks. It is written with the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) and the phonetic "qí" (*shēng*). The pronunciation of *shè* (揲) is *shíshè* (時設). *Shè* means to count. The *Shuowén* also contains the character *dài* (󲰥).
2. Fascicle Two. "Kān" (戡) means to relieve or overcome suffering; it is pronounced with the rhyme *gan* (甘), though sometimes written as 堪 (*kān*) or 勘 (*kàn*).

"Zōng" (綜) means to synthesize or examine thoroughly; the rhyme is *zōng* (宗). Sòng Zhōng’s commentary on the *Xuánjīng* states that "xuán-zōng" means "to sever. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "silk" (糸) and the phonetic element "zōng" (宗).

"Miaoze" (妙賾): "Zé" (賾) is pronounced *zhèng* (革反). Liu Huan’s commentary on the *Zhouyi* states: "Zé is a term for the ultimate depth and obscurity. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical 󱮮 with the phonetic 責; the pronunciation of 󱮮 is *yí* (以之反).

The character 㮵 (top part) is pronounced zhàn (with the *yan* rhyme); it refers to the sound of the *kāśmīra* sandalwood. The character 󱻟 (bottom part) is pronounced jū (with the *li* rhyme). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, 󱻟 refers to the woolen cloth of the Western Hu; it is composed of the radical 糸 with the phonetic 𦋺. The pronunciation of 𦋺 is the same as above. The *Ji* edition uses 𦋺, which is also acceptable.

Regarding the character *huì* (繪) in the phrase "to paint" (*huìshì*), Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states: "Huì means to assemble the five colors. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* states: "It is painting. The *Shuowén Jiězì* takes the radical *mì* (糸, silk thread) and the phonetic *huì*; it records the variant form as *huì* (繢), meaning "the remains of woven silk," which does not carry the sense of "remains" in this context.

*Wǎn* (綰): Pronounced *wǎn* with a retroflex initial; Xu Shuchong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states that "wǎn" is equivalent to "guàn" (to thread through). The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "silk" (*mì*) and the phonetic "guān. *Hǎn* (鯇): Pronounced *huán* with a retroflex final.
*Shìzǔ* (世祖): Pronounced *tuò* with a retroflex final; this is the imperial title. *Dì* (帝): Emperor.
Yáo Hóng (姚泓) and Wū Hóng (烏宏) are proper names. *Xiǎn* (跣): pronounced *xiān* (先);
according to the *Shuowen*, it means "to tread directly upon the ground with one's feet," composed of the radical for foot and the phonetic *xiān*. *Sāo* (騷): upper character pronounced *sào* (掃遭);

the *Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry* says it means "agitated movement. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states it refers to the appearance of shaking. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical for horse and the phonetic *zǎo* (蚤), which is pronounced *zǎo* (早).

The upper character is pronounced *yāo* (as in *tiāo*) and the lower is pronounced *jié*. It is a phonetic derivative of *kǎo*. *Yáo* also refers to calamities and portents. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, anomalies among clothing, songs, and chants, or among plants and trees, are called *yáo*; anomalies among birds, beasts, insects, and locusts are called *jié*. *Yáo* may also be written with the radical for "clothing" (*yǎo*), or *jié* may be written with the radical for "insects" (*niè*), both using *kǎo* as the phonetic component. Alternatively, it may be written with the radical for "woman" (*xiè*); all these forms are interchangeable.

*Kuan-ch'i* (寬弛): "Broad and relaxed. *Ch'i-huan* (弛緩) is glossed by Du Yu in his commentary on the *Zuozhuan* as "ch'i is equivalent to 'to loosen' (*jie*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "bow" (*gong*) with the phonetic element "*li*" (*shi*). It may also be written as *chi* (㢰) or *li* (㐌); the pronunciation of *li* is the same as that of the character *ta* (它).
"Chán (讒) [is pronounced] xián; the *Jíwén* (集文) records it as written with the character 讒, which is a vulgar form. Kǎn (轞) [is pronounced] xiàn;

according to the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲), it refers to a carriage for transporting prisoners. The *Shuōwén* (說文) states that [the character] follows the radical 車 and takes jiàn (監) as its phonetic component. The *Jíwén* writes it with the character 檻 (lán), stating it means 'a cage' (*lóngquān*), which is not the meaning of 'a prisoner's carriage'."

Regarding the character *shǒu* (溲), Yuè Suǒliú (樂所流) and Guī Yěwáng (顧野王) state that "shǎo shǒu" (少溲) refers to the urine of the tail. The *Shuowén* (說文) defines it as consisting of the radical *shuǐ* (水) with the phonetic *sǒu* (叜). The character compiled here is a vulgar form; the pronunciation of *sǒu* (叜) is *sū zǒu* (蘇走反).

The character 𠿼 (pronounced *áo*, with the radical 𠿼 reversed) represents the sound of the *kǎo* rhyme; its correct form is the character 𠿼. The *Mao Shi* states: "The wild geese fly up, crying out *áo-áo*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical 口 and the phonetic 敖; *áo* also serves as the phonetic component. The character 嗷 (*áo*) is a vulgar variant.

The character [縊] is pronounced with the second tone of *yī*. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "to hang oneself" (*jì*) means to die by hanging; the *Shuowen Jiezi* also defines it as "hanging," composed of the radical "silk" (*miè*) and the phonetic "yì. Its correct form is [縊], while the form written as [縊] is a vulgar character.
The *Yijue* (Bequeathed Instructions) states: "Jian" (涓) is pronounced with the rhyme of *xue* (穴) and *fan* (反); "yuan" (韻) is explained as meaning death and parting.

"Jue" (蹷) is pronounced with the rhyme of *juan* (眷) and *yue* (月). Examining its phonetics and form, it refers to the manner of leaping up. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "foot" (足) and the phonetic "jue" (厥), or alternatively, it is written as "jue" (󳌽) with the radical "run" (走).

The character 鐫 (zhuàn) [with the phonetic *xuān* reversed] is explained in the *Guǎngyǎ* as "to engrave" (*zuì*). According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of 金 (*jīn*) and the phonetic 雋 (*juàn*; pronounced *quán-yuǎn* reversed); it refers to the arrowhead (*zhuī*) shot from a bow (*gōng*). It is also written as 鐏; the form with 乃 (*nǎi*) as the phonetic, written as 㑺, is incorrect.

Regarding the character *kàn* (龕): the *Guǎngpǐ* states that it means "to contain" (*chéng*). The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* explains that it is the place where Buddha images are enshrined. It is composed of the radical "dragon" (龍) and the phonetic "jin" (今). To combine these with "hé" (合) to form *kàn* (龕) is incorrect.

The character for *chuī* (榱) is pronounced with the initial *zhui* (追) and the final *fan* (反) in the upper part; the character for *dòng* (棟) is pronounced with the initial *dong* (冬) and the final *nuo* (弄) in the lower part. The *Erya* states: "The *jue* (桷) is called *zhuǎn* (󲵋); the *dòng* (棟) is called *fú* (桴). Guo's commentary says: "*Zhuǎn* refers to the rafters of a house; *fú* refers to the ridgepole. The *Zhouyi* says: "Above the ridgepole and below the eaves, one awaits wind and rain. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "The *dòng* (棟) refers to the apex of the roof. Both [characters] follow the radical for wood (*mu*) and take *shuai* (衰) and *dong* (東) as their phonetic components. The sound of *fú* (桴) is *fu-liu* (扶留); the sound of *wěn* (穩) is *yin-jin* (殷謹). *Wěn* (穩) refers to the *lin* (檁) beam; the sound of *lin* (檁) is *lin-jin* (臨錦).

*Méi* (楣) and *yíng* (楹): *méi* is pronounced as *měi* (美) and *bēi* (悲); the *Erya* states that *méi* is called *liáng* (梁). Guo’s commentary says it is the horizontal beam atop a gate; *xià* (下) is also pronounced as *zhēng* (征). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* says *yíng* means a pillar. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says both characters are composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) with *méi* (眉) and *yíng* (盈) as their phonetic components.

The character *jiǎo* (湫) [is composed of] the radical *shāo* (椒) with the phonetic *xiǎo* (小); it is pronounced *jiǎo*. The character *jiǎo* (㘭) [is composed of] the radical *dì* (地) with the phonetic *mǎn* (滿). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states that *jiǎo* means "low-lying. Gù Yěwáng says that *ài* (隘) means "constricted" (*pòzé*). According to the *Shuowén*, *jiǎo* takes *qiū* (秋) as its phonetic, while *ài* takes *yì* (益) as its phonetic.

Yecheng (鄴城) is the name of a place where the rebellion of Shi Jian (石嚴劫) occurred during the Wei dynasty; according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "city" (邑) with "ye" (業) as the phonetic.
Daoxi (道晞), pronounced with the rhyme of *xuyi* (許衣), and Huigong (慧顒), pronounced with the rhyme of *yugong* (愚恭), are both names of monks.

*Wei* (猥): *làn* (濫), with the phonetic component *wū* (烏) and the determinative *zuì* (罪). It refers to a sound that is incorrect and excessive; according to the *Shuowen*, it takes *quán* (犬) as its radical and *wèi* (畏) as its phonetic.

*Dì Kù* (帝嚳): *kōng gǔ* (空穀) in transcription. It is an ancient title for a sovereign. According to Wang Daogui’s *Diji* (帝紀), Emperor Kù was of the Gaoxin clan; he was the son of Qiaoji and the grandson of Shao Hao. He ruled from Hao. According to the *Shuowen*, it takes *gào* (告) as its radical and *xué* (學) in abbreviated form as its phonetic.
"Zǎn (𠕀)"—pronounced *wǎng* according to Bāo Xián’s commentary on the *Lúnyǔ*, which states: "If one does not contemplate its meaning, one is *zǎn*. It is sometimes written as this character *zǎn*.
*Zhōubǐ*—pronounced *pǔlǐ*—is the ancient treatise on mathematics created by [the sage] Gāngzhǒng.

Regarding "qí" (旗): Qūjī (渠基) [in the *Shuowen*] states that the *Zuozhuan* commentary says it is a "biao" (表, banner/sign). The *Shuowen* defines it as being composed of the radical "yu" (於) with the phonetic "qí" (其), read as chāngzhì (昌志). In the *Shiji*, it refers to a person holding a single "biao-qi" (表幟, banner-sign). The *Guangya* states that "qi" (幟) is a "fan" (幡, pennant). The *Shuowen* further defines it as being composed of the radical "jin" (巾) with the phonetic "zhì" (戠), where "zhì" is pronounced yǎn (偃) and "zhì" is pronounced zhīxí (之習).
Cui Yi used it to form the name of a person.
Qi (祁) is pronounced with the finals *xian* and *xi*, and it is also a personal name.

Zhi (櫛) is pronounced with the initial *ze* and the final *se*; according to the *Wenzi Dianshuo*, "zhi" is the general term for a comb, composed of the radical "wood" (*mu*) and the phonetic "jie" (*jie*).
Jùlù (鉅鹿): The name of a commandery; it is located in Xíngzhōu (邢州). Yújiàn (餘熸): "Jiàn" is pronounced *lián* (子廉反).

Dǔ’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states that in the regions between Wú and Chǔ, the extinguishing of fire is called *jì*. The *Shuowén* explains this character as being composed of "fire" with "cǎn" (*shēng*) as the phonetic component. Tì (替): Pronounced *jiēniàn* (接念反).

3. Fascicle Three. "Míngxìng" (溟涬): *héng* reversed (i.e., *gěng*). The *Pīcāng* states that "míngxìng" describes the appearance of overflowing water. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "water" (*shui*) and the phonetic "xìng" (*xìng*); the common form is written as this character "xìng."

*Nüwa* (寡 *guǎ*, 華 *huá* reversed; ancient pronunciation *kǎo shēng*) was the title of an ancient female sovereign. Gu Yewang stated that Nüwa had a serpent’s body. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "The divine personage and sage woman of antiquity is called *Guā*. She transformed all things. She is written with the radical 'woman' (*nǚ*) and the phonetic 'guā' (*guǎ*). The sound of *guā* is *kǒuhuā* reversed."

*Duōlù* (涿鹿): the character *duō* is pronounced as in *dīngjiǎo* (丁角) according to the *Hànshū*; it is located in *Shànggǔ* (上谷), and today there is a *Duōlù* County (*xiàn*). According to the *Shuōwén*, [the character] is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic "zhū" (*zhū*), where *zhū* is pronounced as in *chǒnglù* (寵綠). *Chī* (蚩) is pronounced as in *chǐzhī* (齒之). This was the site where the ancient Yellow Emperor fought against Chīyóu.

The character 羿 (pronounced *yì*, with the phonetic component 研 and the radical 計) is explained by Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Analects* as follows: "Yi was the ruler of the state of Youqiong and was skilled at archery; he was killed by his own minister, Han Zuo. In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is written with the radical 羽 and the phonetic 幵 (*jiān*). The form 羿 found in the *Jiji* is a vulgar variant.

The *Dizhi* (Topography) states that Wangfu (𡗢父, pronounced kuǎo fù) and Yuzhu (與逐) fled into the wilderness; they became thirsty at Kebi (渴比) and, before reaching the Great Marsh, died of thirst on the way. The *Chongxu jing* (Scripture of Emptiness and Voidness) says that when Wangfu died, his corpse was abandoned there, and the places where his fat and flesh were gnawed grew into the Denglin Forest, spanning thousands of li. Sun Chuo’s *Zi* (Discourse) says that the trees in Denglin have a circumference of thirty thousand *xun*, rise straight up for a thousand *li*, and their shade covers several states.

"Chengdan" (誠亶): the character "dan" (亶) has the phonetic reading zhan-lian-fan. Wang Bi’s commentary on the *Zhouyi* states that "dan" means "difficulty. The *Guiyuan Zhucun* states that "dan" refers to matters of hardship and calamity. Examining its phonology, it means being beset by obstacles such that one's progress is blocked; alternatively, it is written with the radical for "walking" (辵) as "zhan" (邅).

*Rùshǒu* (蓐收): "Rù" is pronounced with the *rú* (儒) and *zhǔ* (燭) finals; it is an onomatopoeic transcription of the sound. *Rùshǒu* is the deity of the Western Quarter. In the *Shuowen*, it is written with the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) and the phonetic "humiliation" (*rú*);

"shǒu" (收) is a vulgar character. *Huànlóng* (豢龍): The pronunciation is *huàn* (患). Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that raising dogs and pigs is called *huàn*. In the *Shuowen*, it is written with the radical "pig" (*shǔ*) and the phonetic "quarrel" (*jiàn*); *jiàn* is pronounced like *juàn* (眷).

"Lintao Dao-fan": *Han shu* records that Lintao was the name of a commandery, located in Longxi Commandery. The dictionary *Shuowen jiezi* explains that it is composed of the radical "water" (氵) and the phonetic "zhao" (兆); the character "tao" (洮) used here is a vulgar variant.

*Zhōng* (鍾) is pronounced with the *qú* and *lǚ* rhymes. The *Erya* states: "The wooden stand for bells is called a *zhōng*. Guo Pu’s commentary says: "It is the wooden stand upon which bells and stone chimes are suspended. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* conveys the same meaning as Guo’s commentary on the *Erya*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains that the tree supporting the bells and drums is adorned with fierce beasts; it follows the radical *hú* (虎), and its lower part is formed by the character *xiàng* (象). *Hú* is pronounced with the *hǔ* rhyme. *Fū* (柎) is pronounced like *fǔ*. The character is composed of *jì* (集) and *qiū* (丘); in ancient script, it was written as *xū* (虛).

Regarding "Wōguó" (倭國): Guo’s commentary on the *Shānhǎijīng* states that Wōguó is located within the great sea to the east of Dàifāng; its custom is to take women as [primary] companions, they have no needle-workers, and they smear their bodies with vermilion (*dānzhū*). The *Shuowén* also identifies it as a country in the central part of the Eastern Sea, derived from the radical for "person" and the phonetic "wěi."

In the *Shulun* (Description of the Banks) it says "xún," and the commentary on the *Mao Shi* states that "xún" means a bank (*yá*). Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* explains that a place where the ground above is level and the water below is deep is called a "xún. The *Shuowen Jiezi* also defines it as a riverbank, taking the character "chún" (lip) as its phonetic component.

*Qizhong* (跂踵): The first character is read as *qìzhǐ* (棄止) and the second as *zhōngyǒng* (鍾勇). According to the *Shānhǎijīng* (Classic of Mountains and Seas), there was a people called the Qizhong people whose two feet were both large. Guo’s commentary states: "When these people walk, their heels do not touch the ground. The *Shuowén* (Explanations of Words and Texts) explains that both characters are composed of the radical "foot" (*zú*) with "branch" (*zhī*) and "heavy" (*chóng*) as phonetic components; the pronunciation of "heel" (*gēn*) is *gēn*.
*Cù* (猝): To suddenly eliminate; it refers to a state of sudden and violent onset. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical 犬 (dog) with the phonetic 卒 (zú).
*Bèi* (偝): To turn away or rebel. Yěwáng says that "bèi" means to turn one's back on or to rebel. According to the *Shuowen*, it may also be written as 背 with the radical 月.

Regarding "xiè" (渫), the *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that it means "to remove. The *Guang Ya* says it means "to overflow. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "water" with "yè" as its phonetic component; the correct character is "xiè" (󳁁), where "yè" is pronounced "dié."

*Cháo-chuó* (the first character pronounced as *zháo* according to the *Yǐnyùn*; the *Erya* states that a well which has water at one time and none at another is called *lì-chuó*; Guo’s commentary on the *Shanhaijing* notes that the *Tianjing* [Heavenly Well] has water in summer and no water in winter; the *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "water" and the phonetic "chuo," with the pronunciation of *jù* being *jù-lì*).

The character *zhīhuǒ* (之夥) is pronounced with the final *hú* (胡) and the initial *guǒ* (果). The *Fānyán* states: "In the regions of Qi and Song, and between Chu and Wey, when things are in great abundance, they are called *huǐ*. The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radical *duō* (多) with *guǒ* (果) as its phonetic; thus, the correct form is indeed *huǐ*.

Regarding the character *guǎn* (筦) in the phrase "the official's shortness of stature binds [him]," Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "*Guǎn* is synonymous with *bāo* (a bundle); it is formed from the radical 'bamboo' (*zhú*) and the phonetic component 'wán' (*huán*). The pronunciation of *wán* is *huán*. Alternatively, some editions of the *Zhongjing* (Classical Collection) write it as *guǎn* with the phonetic component *yì* (*yíng*), but this character does not exist."

"Freezing and starving slaves commit crimes"—the *Guoyu* says, "The ruler bestows kindness upon his ministers so that they do not suffer from cold or hunger. The *Shuowen* defines it as "hunger," derived from the radical "food" (食) with the phonetic "wei" (委).
Zhi, the robber, was a person whose skull was like a stone, contrary to the ancient norm where the fontanelle (*xion*) was open.

Zhuang Qiao’s forceful stratagem was reversed. "Qi" (欺) means to deceive; "gui" (詭) means to ruin or subvert. Regarding the sound of "gui," the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is composed of the radical "yan" (言) with "wei" (危) as its phonetic. The character is also written as "ci" (詆), which is a vulgar form.
"Bu chi" (不啻) has the reading "shi zhi" (尸志). The *Wenzi Dian* explains that "chi" (啻) is a term signifying excess; it is composed of the radical "kou" (口) with "di" (帝) as its phonetic.

"Qianshou" (黔首): The *Shiji* states that in the twenty-sixth year of the First Emperor, the name for the people was changed to "Qianshou. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "black" (黑) and the phonetic "jin" (今).
"Shangkuo" (儴佉): the upper character is pronounced *huai-yang* (壞羊) and the lower is *que-jia* (卻迦); this is a name for a Western country in the Sanskrit language.

*Kang-mi* (秔米): The character *kang* is pronounced with the rhyme *geng* (格𢖍反). Dictionaries state it belongs to the category of rice (*dao*). It is composed of the radical "grain" (*he*) and the phonetic *kang*, which is pronounced *kang-lang* (康浪反).

*Qi-nu* (妻孥): The character *nu* is pronounced with the rhyme *du* (都反), following the sound of *kao*. *Nu* is a general term for wife and children; according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "child" (*zi*) and the phonetic *nu*, or it is also written as *tang* (帑).
*Yú* (with the phonetic *gēng zhū*): The *Erlǚ pǐ* states that *yú* also means "joy. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) with the phonetic "yú.

*Huángjié* (with the phonetic *xián jié*): The *Cāngjié* states that he was the person who first created written characters in antiquity. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "head" (*yè*) with the phonetic "jí."

The character 方 (fāng) is pronounced chùgé in its initial and medial tones; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to receive a mandate. It represents the ritual of feudal lords receiving [investiture] from the King, depicted with one long and one short [line], with two interwoven lines in the center. It is also written as 𥬰, which is an archaic form of the character.

"Zhuì" (綴) in "zhòu" (斿): the upper character is pronounced *zhú* (with the retroflex -r). Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that it means "to connect. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "silk thread" (*mì*) with the phonetic "zhuō" (*zhū luò*). The lower character is pronounced *yóu*.

*Jiè* (𡢔): Pronounced *zhèng* (正) and *yì* (驛), with the final consonant of *kǎo* (考). It is the surname of the Qin of Yíng. "Shǐhuáng" (始皇) is the formal designation of his name. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical *nǚ* (女) and the phonetic *yíng* (贏) in abbreviated form.

*Xié* (挾): Pronounced *xián* (嫌) and *jiá* (頰). In the *Erya*, "xié" means "to store. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical *shǒu* (手) and the phonetic *jiā* (夾). The pronunciation of *jiā* is *jiǎ* (甲).
Ji (上) is pronounced *jū* (居) with the fanqie *lì* (立), and Xīn (歆) is pronounced *xī* (翕) with the fanqie *jīn* (金); both characters are personal names.
Xún (荀) is pronounced *xù* (恤) with the fanqie *xún* (旬), and Xiù (勗) is pronounced *yù* (吁) with the fanqie *yù* (玉); this is a personal name.

"Xiàoluàn" (淆亂): the first character is pronounced with the *jiāo* rhyme-group; it means "mixed" (*kǎoshēng*) or "intermingled. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it also means "disorder. It is sometimes written as "xiáo" (殽). "Xiè Fěi" (謝朏):
the second character is pronounced *fēi*; it is a personal name.

The character 󱨯 (pronounced *jìn*, with the variant *shòu* and *zhǒu*) is explained in the dictionary as "to seek" (*qiú*). It is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic element "old" (*sǒu*), which is pronounced *sōuzǒu*.
The character 𨜈 (pronounced *zèjiū*) is the name of Zu Gěng (pronounced *jūdèng*).
*Xiāng* (in *xiāng-náng*, "yellow silk bag"): the initial sound is *liáng*. Regarding the character *xiāng*, it refers to a light yellow color and is composed of the radical *mì* (silk).

*Jìnshèn* (in *jìn-shèn*, "girdle"): the upper character *jìn* has the initial sound *jīn-xùn*. In the *Zhou Lǐ* (Rites of Zhou), regarding the phrase "inserting the large *guī* (jade tablet) into the *shèn*," Zheng’s commentary states: "It is tucked between the *shèn* and the sash, like the way one gathers the sash today. In the *Shuowen*, this is composed of the radical *shǒu* (hand) and the phonetic *lǎn*; it is the same character as *jìn*. The lower character *shèn* has the phonetic *shēn*. In the *Lùnyǔ* commentary, Kǒng [Yǎng] says: "The *shèn* is the great sash (*dà-dài*). In Zheng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì*, he says: "That by which one binds oneself. In the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *mì* (silk) and the phonetic *shēn*.
Regarding the term *bǎng* (pronounced *bó láng fǎn*), the *Guìyuàn Zhūcóng* states: "It means to inscribe or designate; it is derived from the radical 'wood' (*mu*).

Regarding *fùhǎi* (pronounced *fù hǎi gǎi fǎn*), Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "Hǎi refers to meat sauce. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical 'wine' (*you*) with the phonetic component *lǔ*; *lǔ* has the pronunciation *yòu*.

*Nì* (as in *nì lù chuáng*, "to gaze at the deer-bed")—the character is pronounced with the *ní* and *jì* rhymes. The *Lǐjì* states, "He gazed at it, yet still considered it distant. The *Wénzì Diǎnshuō* says it means "to look with the eyes," composed of the radical "eye" (*mù*) and the phonetic "child" (*ér*).

Regarding "jūn-jia" (麕麚): the first character, "jūn," is pronounced *jū-yún* (居筠反); Liu Zhao’s commentary on the *Gongyang zhuan* states that "jūn" refers to the *zhāng* (麞) deer. The *Shuowen jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "deer" (*lù*) and the phonetic element "qūn" (*quǐn*) abbreviated. The second character, "jia," is pronounced *gé-xiá* (革瑕反). The *Erya* states that "jia" is a male deer; the *Shuowen jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "deer" (*lù*) and the phonetic element "duàn" (*duàn*).

"Cán yù" (驂馭): "Cán" (上忩) is pronounced hán; the *Mao Shi* commentary states that those at the side are called "cán. The *Shuowen* defines it as the horse used for drawing a carriage (pronounced yù jù). Gu Yewang says that "yù" refers to directing and commanding the horses. Both [definitions] in the *Shuowen* derive from the radical "horse" (馬) with "cān" (參) acting as the phonetic component.

*Luji* (騄驥): The upper character is pronounced *long* (龍) and the lower *chu* (燭). The *Biographies of King Mu of Zhou* states that it was the name of the swift horse of King Mu of Zhou, known as *Luer* (騄耳). The lower character, *ji* (驥), is pronounced *yi* (義). The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains that *luji* (󰀪) refers to a horse capable of a thousand li, which was selected by Sun Yang (孫陽). Both characters are formed with the radical for "horse" (馬); *lu* (󰀪) and *ji* (驥) both serve as phonetic components. The pronunciation of *lu* (祿) is *lu*.
"Yán" (妍) is pronounced with the "shén" (神) and "yú" (魚) radicals reversed; it is written as "yán" (妍), a vulgar character.
Póyáng (鄱陽) is a commandery name located in Yùzhāng (豫章); it is pronounced with the "pú" (蒲) and "bō" (波) radicals reversed.

Zhìkuì (致饋): according to the *Shuowen*, "kuì" (饋) means to provide food; it is composed of the "shí" (食) radical and the phonetic "guì" (貴), while "xiǎng" (餉) is pronounced with the "yīn" (音) and "shāngliàng" (傷亮) radicals reversed.

The character *zèng* (贈) [is pronounced with the initial *shàng* and the rhyme *fēng*]. The *Guliang Zhuan* states: "To present gifts for the deceased is called *zèng*. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan* says: "*Zèng* refers to items provided for a funeral. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical *bèi* (貝) and the phonetic *mào* (冒).

4. Fascicle Four. Fascicle Four. *Guǎnxí* (莞席): "Guǎn" is pronounced as *huóguān* (活官). Gu Yěwáng states that *guǎn* resembles *pú* (蒲) but is round. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it is a grass that can be used for mats; it is composed of the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) with the phonetic component "wán" (*huán*). The pronunciation of *wán* is *huán*. It is also written as *fū* (𦯜).

*Caǒjù* (草屨): Both characters read *yù fǎn*. In the *Cāngjié piān*, *jù* is synonymous with *lǚ* (shoes). The *Shuōwén* states it is a simplified form of *lǚ*, with the phonetic *lóu*; the vulgar form *zhū* is an error. *Nà* (𤓡):

Pronounced *huǎng jiāng xiào fǎn*. Lǚ Bùwéi says: "A torch (*jiào*) is made from *guàn* fire. The *Shuōwén* identifies this as a torch made of reeds (*jù huǒ*), composed of the radical *huǒ* and the phonetic *jiè*; the character *jiè* itself is correctly written with *chàng* and *yòu*. The collective edition writes it as *jué*, which is a vulgar character. *Guàn* is pronounced *gū wàn fǎn*.
The character for "saṃghāṭī" (沙門衣) is pronounced *bàn* (half of *mò*).
It is the same as the character for "bowl" (*bō*). The term "my name" (*míng*) is pronounced *píng* (half of *bìng*);

it is a phonetic transcription of a name. Regarding *pijiǎ* (𥷥糱): the first character is pronounced *xiòng* (half of *jūn*) and the second is *jié*. The commentary on the *Shūshū* by Kǒng states: "Wine and sweet spirits require *qū* and *pijiǎ* to be completed. The *Shuowén* says: "*Pijiǎ* refers to the sprouting of rice; it is composed of the radical *mǐ* with the phonetic *xué*. The form written with the radical *mài* as *pínà* (𮮂) is incorrect.

*Zhēn* (箴): The upper radical is *zhì* (汁, pronounced with the *shēn* rhyme). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states it means "to admonish. According to the *Shuowen*, it is formed from the bamboo radical with *xián* as the phonetic component.

*Kuòhū* (確乎): The upper radical is *kǔ* (苦, pronounced with the *jiǎo* rhyme). The *Zhouyi* says, "It stands firm and cannot be uprooted. According to the *Shuowen*, it denotes the appearance of solidity; it is formed from the stone radical with *hè* (寉) as the phonetic component, where *hè* has the same pronunciation as above.

Regarding "zhì" (縶): the *Shijing* says, "I bind him, I fetter him. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to restrain and seize," composed of the radical "silk" (糸) and the phonetic "zhí" (執). The character written as "zhì" (集作縶) is a vulgar form. Regarding "bà" (󳏩):

the upper part is read as "bǎi" (百) and the sound is "mà" (罵). It is used to investigate sounds and seek names; its correct form is "bà" (霸), composed of "biàn" (䨣) and "yue" (月). "Biàn" (䨣) is pronounced "gé" (革). The character written as "bà" (集作󳏩) in the *Jíshì* is a vulgar form.
"㳅" (liú) is the archaic form of the character "流" (liú).

"連鑣" (liánbiāo): biāo is pronounced piao with the *jiao* rhyme; according to the *Shuowen*, "biāo" refers to the horse's bit, written with the radical "金" (metal) and the phonetic "麃" (piao, pronounced bójiāo).
"埳井" (kǎnjǐng): kǎn is pronounced gan with the *gan* rhyme; according to the *Pīcāng*, "kǎn" means a pit, or it may be written as "坎" (kǎn) with the radical "欠" (deficiency).

Regarding "yúfáng" (榆枋): the first character is pronounced *zhū* (庾) and the second *fāng* (昔). This is a metaphorical expression from Zhuangzi; its precise meaning is not detailed [in other sources].

As for "jù" (詎), it is pronounced *qú* (渠). Examining the phonology, "jù" means "not yet. In the standard characters of both ancient and modern times, this character is composed of the radical "speech" (言) with the phonetic element "gǔ" (巨).
*Cuì* (pronounced *cuì*, with the tone reversed): "To gather together. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means to assemble; it is composed of the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) and the phonetic "sù.

*Xuē* (pronounced *xié*, with the initial *xian* and final *lie* reversed): The name of Shun's minister. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, he was the son of Gaosin and the ancestor of the Yin dynasty; it is composed of the radical "person" (*rén*) and the phonetic "qiè."

The characters *quán* (upper tone, pronounced *shuān*) and *tí* (lower tone, with the radical *dì* as a phonetic) are explained in the *Zhuangzi*: "Having obtained the fish, one forgets the trap; having obtained the hare, one forgets the snare. Gu Yewang states that the *quán* is a fish-trap, while the *tí* is an implement for catching hares. According to the *Zhèngzǐ* of ancient and modern times, *quán* is composed of the radical "bamboo" (*zhú*) and the phonetic "all" (*quán*), while *tí* is composed of the radical "foot" (*zú*) and the phonetic "emperor" (*dì*); it is also written as *tí*.

*Cu'é* (the first character is pronounced with the *zi* and *liu* rhymes; the second is pronounced *an* and *ge*). The *Mencius* says: "They raised their heads in distress and knitted their brows (*cu'é*) as they told one another [of their plight]. According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to the bridge of the nose; it may also be written with the "nose" radical as *nǎ* or as *é*.

Regarding "the wilderness of those clad in ochre robes" (*zhǎyī zhī yě*), Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Fānyán* states that "ochre robes" means red; the *Kǎoshēng* also says it is a crimson color. The *Shuowén* defines it as "red earth," taking the phonetic component "zhě" (者).

*Lǐ* (俚): Pronounced *lí* (with the initial *zhǐ* reversed). He Xiu’s commentary on the *Gōngyáng Zhuàn* states: "Lǐ means vulgar. Alternatively, it is written with the radical for city (*yì*) as *yě* (野). *Bèi* (敻): Pronounced *xuè* (with the initial *pīng* reversed).

Liú Zhào’s commentary on the *Gōngyáng Zhuàn* states: "Bèi describes the appearance of being deep and remote. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical for person (*rén*) and *xiūn* (𥄎) within the cave radical (*xué*). *Xiūn* has the phonetic value of *xūn-liè* (with the initial *fǎn* reversed).

"Dun" (惇) means "historical record" (*shǐ*) at the Gate of the Capital; the *Erya* says it means "thick and sincere" (*dūnhòu*). The correct form is this [character] 󳈍; according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) with "󳈍" as the phonetic component. The character 𦎫 has the pronunciation *shíchūn*. The character "Dun" (*dūn*) in the collected editions is a vulgar form; the character "Shi" (*shǐ*) in the collected editions is likewise a vulgar form.

*Qiāngcí* (Wall Hedges): The first character is pronounced *jiàng* (with the final *rǎn*) and the second is *zì* (with the final *fǎn*). According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of "grass" (*cǎo*) and "sequence" (*cì*) as its phonetic. The version in the *Jí* (Collection) is the common vulgar form of this word. *Jiānjiā* (Ivy and Reed):

The first character is pronounced *jiān* (sound *jiān*) and the second is *géxiá* (with the final *fǎn*). According to the *Shuōwén*, "jiān" refers to *dí* (Phragmites) and "jiā" refers to *lú* (Saccharum spontaneum) when they have not yet flowered; "jiān" is called *dí* and "jiā" is called *lú*. Both are composed of "grass" (*cǎo*), with "jiān" using "jiān" and "jiā" using "duàn" as their phonetics.
*Kṣiṇ* (嚫施): The first character is read as *jìn* (蔪, with the initial *chú* and final *jìn*). It is erroneously written as *quán* (䞋). The second character, *jìn* (蔪), has the phonetic *jūn* (居舋反).

Regarding *quán* (銓) in *quánhéng* (銓衡): the upper radical is pronounced *quán*. Guō’s commentary on the *Ěrǎpǐ* states: "The means by which laws and statutes weigh lightness and heaviness. The *Guǎngyá* states: "A standard measure. It is called a *quán* because it is a scale; the *Shuōwén* also defines it as a balance (*héng*), composed of the radical *jīn* (金) and the phonetic *quán* (全).
"Sǒng" (pronounced *sù* with a retroflex *yǒng* rhyme) means "lofty. "Shǒng" (pronounced *shǎo* with a retroflex *shēng* rhyme) means "high.
"Mìè" (the first character pronounced *zǒng* with a retroflex *gōng* rhyme, the second character pronounced *mián* with a retroflex *jié* rhyme) is a personal name from the Spring and Autumn period.

*Pài*: pronounced *pǔ mài* (with the *mò* tone). According to the *Shuowen*, "pài" refers to water dividing into branches; it is formed from the character for "water" (*shuǐ*) with the radical for "water" added below. This is the common usage. *Kuài*:
pronounced *kǔ guài* (with the *guǎi* tone). A personal name.
*Káng* (亢) is pronounced *kàng* (康浪反).

*Qiū* (秋) is pronounced *qiān* (先典反); the *Erya* states that hunting in autumn is called *jiǎo* (獠), and Guo’s commentary notes it is "in accordance with the killing qi. In the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *quán* (犬) and the phonetic *xǐ* (璽), where *xǐ* is pronounced *xǐ* (徙).

The character 襁 (upper part: *jiāng*, two tones; lower part: *bǔdào*) is explained in the *Huáinánzǐ* as referring to King Cheng being young and in his swaddling clothes (*qiāngbǎo*). The *Shuōwén* states that 襁 is a garment for carrying a child on the back; it is also a small child’s coverlet. Both characters are composed of the radical 衣 (clothing) with 強 (qiang) and 保 (bao) as their phonetic components respectively. It is incorrect to compose them from the radical 糸 (silk) as 繈 (qiāng) and 緥 (bǎo).

*Jin* (pronounced *qín jìn fǎn*). Jia Ji’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states: “*Jin* is synonymous with ‘barely able. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical for "person" (*ren*) and the phonetic *jin* (pronounced *jin*, or alternatively *jin*); it is also written as *jin* or *yin*. It means "scarcely" or "only just."

*Bu* (step): *wò* (note: *guō* as a variant). According to the *Shuowen*, *wò* refers to a worm that contracts and extends; it is written with the radical for insects and the phonetic *huò*. The pronunciation of *huò* is *yì guó*. *Yì chāng*: The lower character is pronounced *dāng*.

The version in the *Zhongjing* (Collection of Scriptures) reads *chāng*, which is incorrect. One should examine that *yì chāng* refers to a spider-like insect dwelling within earthen burrows. Because it constantly keeps its burrow entrance closed while residing therein, it is called *yì chāng*. It dwells with its back turned to the light in darkness, serving as a metaphor for ignorance (*avidyā*). Just as the Rākṣasa King of Death devours the life-force of sentient beings, one says: "Upon realizing that the *yì chāng* has attached itself to one's back, and seeing the wild wolf facing one—metaphors for the mind of greed and desire—one knows that the time of peril and ruin is pressing upon them. Thus, the greedy passion is finally extinguished, and one is able to maintain the observance of the precepts."
*Huǎng*: "Alas! To go back and forth. According to the *Shuowen*, it means an appearance of losing one's composure; it is composed of the radical "heart" (心) and the phonetic "xiong" (兄).

Volume Five, Part Five. *Shè* (懾): Pronounced *zhān* (詹) with the *shè* (涉) rhyme. Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that *shè* means "to submit" (*fú*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "heart" (心) and the phonetic "niè" (聶); the pronunciation of *niè* is *ní zhé* (尼輒).

*Lùlù* (碌碌): The *Pīcāng* dictionary states that "lùlù" describes the appearance of sand and stones; the *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "stone" (*shí*) with "lù" as its phonetic.

*Tiáorán* (迢然): The *Kǎoshēng* dictionary states it means "distant"; the *Wenzi Dianshuō* says it is composed of the radical "walk" (*chuò*) with "zhào" as its phonetic. It is incorrect to compose this character from the radical "grass" (*cǎo*).

"Upon the Hao": *Hao* (上) is pronounced *gāo* (晧高反). This refers to when Zhuangzi and Huizi were strolling upon the Hao Bridge (*háo-liáng*). Gu Yewang states that "Hao" is the name of a river; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is formed with the radical "water" and the phonetic "háo," and is located in Zhongli Commandery.

*Xiǎnyǔn* (玁狁): the first character is pronounced *jiǎn* (上䝱撿反) and the second is *yù* (下聿笋反). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that what was called *Xízhōu* (󱻴粥) during the Tang and Yú [dynasties] was called *Xiǎnyǔn* during the Zhōu, and what was called *Hánnú* (匃奴) during the Hàn; all of these were names applied to them based on their malevolence. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* (文字典說) states it is the name for the Northern Di tribes, both characters following the radical "dog" (犬), with *qiān* (僉) and *yǔn* (允) as their phonetic components. *Xiǎn* may also be written as *xián* (嚴); *xiǎn* is pronounced *xūn* (勳) and *zhōu* is pronounced *róng* (融) with the *fǎn* (祝) tone.

"Jian" (殲) is pronounced as *jie* (接) and *lian* (廉). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that "jian" means "to exhaust" (*jin*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical *dai* (歹) and the phonetic *jie* (截); *dai* is pronounced as *wu* (五) and *ge* (割), while *wei* (韱) is pronounced as *xi* (息) and *lian* (廉). The variant forms found in the *Ji* (集) are both vulgar characters.

*Yuàn* (楥榆): The first character is read as *xuān* (暄) with the phonetic *yuàn* (願). According to the *Erya*, "yuan" refers to the *li* (梠), which can be used for drinking; according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mu*) and the phonetic "yuan" (*yuan*).
*Chí* (郗): Read as *chī* (勑) with the phonetic *zhī* (知); it is a personal name.

*Nóu-yuán* (the first character pronounced *náo*, with the initial *gāo* reversed; the second pronounced *yuè*, with the initial *yuán* reversed). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that the *nóu* is also a species of ape (*yuán*). Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* says: "The *yuán* resembles a macaque but is larger; its arms are long, and it is agile and swift. In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, both characters follow the radical for dog (*quǎn*), while *róu* and *yuán* serve as their phonetic components.

Regarding the character *hé* (蛤), it is pronounced with the initial *gān* and the final *hé*. The *Liji* (*Book of Rites*) states: "In the last month of autumn, sparrows enter the great waters and become *hé*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains that there are three kinds of *hé*, all of which are produced in the sea: the *haigé* (sea clam) is what a hundred-year-old swallow transforms into; it is also called *buluo* (蒲螺), and is what an aged *fu-yi* (蟾蜍, a type of toad) transforms into; the *helì* (oyster) is what a thousand-year-old quail transforms into. The *Jiyun* (集韻) states that the claim that a pheasant transforms into a *hé* is an error in the application of the source material.

Regarding the character *shèn* (pronounced *chén* with the *rěn* tone; Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that *shèn* refers to the large clam), the *Dai Li Xia Xiao Zheng* says, "The pheasant enters the Huai River and becomes a *shèn*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical for insects and the phonetic *chén*. The *Ji* (the *Erya*) states, "The swallow enters the sea and becomes a *shèn*," which is an error.

*Mó* (木胡反): This refers to the method of imitation (*mófǎ*). According to the *Bīcāng*, it means to capture the image; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means a compass (*guī*). It is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "mò. It is also written as *mō*. *Zào* (躁, 遭到反):

The *Shìfǎ* states that one who delights in changing and agitating the people is called "restless" (*zào*). According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "foot" (*zú*) and the phonetic "zào" (which has the pronunciation *sāo* and *dào*). The *Jí* edition writes it as *cháo* (󳃆), which is a vulgar character.

*Ki* (愒) means "to be parched" or "to stagnate. The Du Anshu commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that *ki* means "greed. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* states that *ki* refers to "greedy longing. In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is written with the radical for "heart" (*xin*) and the phonetic "he" (*he*). The pronunciation of *he* is *han-ge* (寒葛反), and the pronunciation of *xian* (羨) is *yan-zhan* (延戰反).

*Pián mǔ* (蒲田反, 下莫厚反). The *Zhuāngzǐ* states: "The extra toe. According to the *Wénzìdiǎn*, the character 駢 (*pián*) is composed of 馬 (*mǎ*) as the phonetic and 并 (*bìng*) as the semantic component; the character 拇 (*mǔ*) is composed of 手 (*shǒu*) as the semantic component and 母 (*mǔ*) as the phonetic.

The character *zhòu* (譸) has the phonetic *zhǒuliú* (肘留). The Master Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjìng* states: "To *zhòuzhāng* means to deceive. There is no such thing as mutual deception or illusion (*huàn*). According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) with the phonetic "longevity" (*shòu*). Some versions follow the character "chariot" (*chē*) to form *zhōu* (輈), which refers to the pole of a chariot; this is not its meaning here. The pronunciation of *huàn* (幻) is *huàn* (患).

The term *róng-mò* (戎貊) refers to the hundred [tribes] of the blind; in the *Zhouli*, the Office of the Nine Regions (*zhìfāng*) presides over the people of the nine *mò*. Zheng Zhong’s commentary states that those in the north are called *mò*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "beast" (*zhài*) and the phonetic "hundred" (*bǎi*). Some versions of the phonetic element are written as "this" (*cǐ*), and the collected editions write it as *mó* (狛), with the pronunciation *bì*, which is not correct in meaning.

*Sà* (馺): Pronounced *sū hé* (蘇合). Guo’s commentary on the *Fāngyán* states that *sà-sà* describes a state of rapid movement. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical "horse" (*mǎ*) and the phonetic element "jí" (*jí*).

*Xiāo* (梟) and *zhèn* (鴆): The upper character is pronounced *jiào yáo* (晈堯). The *Shuōwén* defines it as the bird of unfiliality. On the day of the summer solstice, one captures and decapitates the *xiāo*, hanging its head from a tree. *Zhé* (磔) is pronounced *zhú è* (竹厄). It is composed of the radical "bird" (*niǎo*) with "in the tree" (*zài mù shàng*). The lower character [of *zhèn*] is pronounced *shěn jìn* (沈禁). Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒchuán* states that the feathers of the *zhèn* are poisonous; if wine is painted with them and drunk, one dies. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical "bird" (*niǎo*) and the phonetic element "yóu" (*yóu*). *Yóu* is pronounced *yú zhēn* (餘針).

"Dào Huìgōng wài fǎn" (The Duke of Huì was stolen away and returned). Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states that Huì was the ancient state of Huì, located northeast of Mì County in Xíngyáng. In the *Shuowén*, it is written with the radical "city" (邑) and the phonetic "huì" (會).

"Bèi jī" (Striking with a club). Pronounced pāng jiǎng (反). Xu Shùchóng’s commentary on the *Huáinánzǐ* states that a bèi is a large staff. In the *Shuowén*, it is written with the radical "wood" (木) and the phonetic "pò" (咅); the pronunciation of pò is tǔ kǒu (反).

"Guǎikuài" (譎怪) is pronounced jiān-xué-fǎn. Zheng’s commentary on the *Mao Shī* states: "Guǎijiàn" (譎諫) refers to singing and chanting that is indirect and does not speak plainly. The *Shuowén* says it means "erroneous. To deceive Heaven is called guǎi; it is written with the radical for speech and the phonetic "yù" (矞). The pronunciation of "yù" is wéi-jú-fǎn."

"Zuǎiěr" (蕞尒): Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that it means "small in appearance. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says "zuǎiěr" refers to the appearance of a small state; it is composed of the radical "grass" (艸) and the phonetic "zuì" (最), with "zuì" pronounced as *zǐhuì*. The character "cáo" (菆) formed by adding the radical "taking" (取) has the pronunciation *zèliú* and refers to the stem of hemp; this does not accord with the meaning here.

Regarding the term *wòcuò* (偓齪): the first character is pronounced with the initial *yú* and the final *jiǎo* (於角反), while the second is pronounced with the initial *chuāng* and the final *zhuō* (牎捉反). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that it describes an appearance of being cramped and foolish. Examining its phonetic component (*shēng*), it denotes a narrow and small appearance. In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, *wò* follows the radical for "man" (*rén*) and uses *wū* as its phonetic; *cào* (考) is used as the phonetic, or sometimes written as *lián* (䠎). The *Jí* (集) [radical] uses the character for "teeth" (*chǐ*) to form *wò* (齷); this character does not exist in the *Zìshū* (字書). The *Wénzìdiǎn* (文字典) explains that *cuò* (齪) denotes an appearance of haste and urgency; it follows the radical for "teeth" (*chǐ*) and uses *zú* as its phonetic, or is also written as *cuò* (齪).

*Diti* (the "Di" rhymes with *ding* and the "xi" with *xi*)—in the *Liji*, it refers to the people of the five regions whose languages were not mutually intelligible and whose desires differed; to communicate their desires was called *diti*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "metal" (*ge*) and the phonetic element "is" (*shi*).

*Nà zhì* (pronounced *zhī* with a second tone): The character dictionary explains that this means "tribute" (*zhì bì*). It follows the radical "貝" (bèi) and takes "執" (zhí) as its phonetic; the form "贄" found in the *Jí* (Jìshì) is a vulgar variant. *Qiàn fù* (pronounced *qiān* with a level tone):

Zheng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states that it is the appearance of regret and dissatisfaction. The *Shuowén* says it means "not being satiated," following the radical "欠" (qiàn) and taking "兼" (jiān) as its phonetic; the form "嗛" found in the *Jí* (Jìshì) refers to having food held in the mouth, which does not accord with the meaning in the *Jí*.
The "Autumn Hunt" (qiū xiàn) [is discussed here]; the preceding fourth fascicle has already explained this. Regarding "fawn" (mí): the reading is mí;

Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that a fawn is the offspring of a *mí* deer. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as composed of the radical for "deer" with "mǐ" as the phonetic component. "Mǐ" is pronounced mí zhǐ (with the second tone), and "mí" is pronounced měi bēi (with the first tone).

Regarding "liao" (燎), the *Mao Shih Zhuan* states that burning fields for hunting is called *liao*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as setting fire [to the fields], composed of the radical "fire" (火) and the phonetic "liao" (尞). The character "lao" (𤊽), pronounced as above, is what is used in the *Jiji* (集); it is a vulgar form.

"Han-yíng (酣醟): To indulge excessively in wine. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Yíng (䣱) means intoxication; yíng (醟) means being drunk. It is composed of the radical 'jiu' (酉, wine) with 'yíng' (滎) as the phonetic component. The pronunciation of yíng (䣱) is xūgù (吁句反); it may also be written with 'xiōng' (凶)."

*Kuī* (upper character): *quē* (guī fǎn). According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to slaughter. According to the *Shuōwén*, it means "to stab," composed of the radical "knife" (dāo) and the phonetic "guī" (*guī shēng*). *Kū* (lower character): *kǔ* (gū fǎn). The *Cāngjiépiān* states that *kū* also means "to slaughter. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "knife" and the phonetic "kuā" (*kuā shēng*). The pronunciation of *kuā* is *qiūguā* (fǎn).
*Tōng* (通) is pronounced *yù gài fǎn* (與蓋反); it is the same as this character *ài* (礙). Some write it with the radical *hài* (亥), which is incorrect.

6. *Jí* (集), Volume Six. *Jí* (集), Volume Six. *Sī* (廝) is pronounced *tú tú yí fǎn* (徒徒移反). Gu Yewáng says that *sī* refers to lowly laborers. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it takes the radical *guǎn* (广) and is phoneticized by *sī* (斯). Alternatively, it is written as *wēi* (㒋) with the radical *rén* (人). *Guǎn* (广) has the pronunciation *yǎn* (儼).

*Jiè-láng*: The first character is pronounced *tú-xí*. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "A weed resembling *bài* that grows spreading over the ground. The *Shuowen Jiezi* derives it from the radical for grass with the phonetic *tī* (pronounced *tǐ-jī*). Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "A type of *yòu* grass," or alternatively written as *jié*.

Shi Foming’s entry on the fifth character, *qì* (隙), states that the Marquis of Nì reversed his gaze; Yuè Wáng says it means resentment or grievance. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as composed of the radicals *huò* (𨸏) and *yì* (𡭽), with *yì* also serving as the phonetic component. The *Jí* (集) edition records it as *qì* (郄), a commandery of the Jin dynasty, which does not carry the meaning of "gap" (*qì*).
Wáng Kuǐ (王巋) is the name of a Daoist practitioner; "Kuǐ" is pronounced like "guǐ" (鬼).
Wáng Bǎo (王堡) is the name of a person; "Bǎo" is pronounced like "bǔ" (補), though it is sometimes written as "mèi" (媬); it is the name of a place located to the east of the suburban area.
Fú Zhì (伏𨤲) is pronounced with "Zhì" like "zhī" (知).
*Míng* (名) is pronounced *dào* (到) with a retroflex final; it was the name of Emperor Shizu of the Later Wei dynasty.
*Yì* (翼) and *jiān* (鞬) are pronounced *yán* (言) with a retroflex final;

these are also personal names. *Ài* (愛) is pronounced *qiú* (渠) with a retroflex final. In the *Cāngjié piān*, it means "to request again. In the *Shuōwén*, it means "to use wealth to bribe officials and violate the law as a form of apology"; it is composed of the radical *bèi* (貝) and the phonetic *qiú* (求).
*Mí* (靡): *jiān* (監) with the *gū* (孤) and *wǔ* (五) rhymes.

*Hàn* (扞): *chéng* (城) with the *hán* (寒) and *dàn* (旦) rhymes; Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states it means "to resist" (*yù*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "gān" (*gān*), or alternatively written as *gǎn* (桿).

*Fěi* (菲): *fú* (孚) and *wěi* (尾) rhymes; Mǎ Róng’s commentary on the *Lunyu* says it means "meager" (*bó*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) and the phonetic "fēi" (*fēi*).
"Zi-yun" (子贇): "yun" is pronounced as *yún* (委雲反); it was the name of an emperor of the Later Zhou dynasty. "Kū" (刳): "zhuāng" is pronounced as *lüè* (莊略反).

In Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu*, "zhé" (斮) means to execute by cutting; according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means to sever. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "knife" (刀) with "què" (皵) abbreviated as its phonetic.
Yùn (qūn, qī lún fǎn): A personal name. Xūn-yóu:

The first character is read yún (xún fǎn) and the second is read yǒu (yǒu zhōu fǎn). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, xūn is a fragrant herb and yóu is a foul-smelling herb; both are written with the "grass" radical (艹). Xūn also includes the phonetic element "yú" (尢), while [the character for] yóu is correctly written with the "grass sprout" radical (屮) as its phonetic component.

The character *āng* (鞅) is pronounced *yǎng* in the first instance (with the radical *zhǎng* [掌]) and *xiàng* in the subsequent chapter (with the radical *zhuāng* [章]). The *Mao Shī Jiàn* states: "Āng is like bearing; zhǎng is like cradling. The *Shuōwén* follows the radical *jié* (革) with the phonetic *yǎng* (央). Some editions follow the radical *rì* (日), forming *yìng* (映), with the pronunciation *yú lǎng* (於朗); this refers to the appearance of being obscured and unclear, which is not the meaning of *āng*.
Wang Hong (王紘): "Hong" is the sound of his name.

"Gangbi" (剛愎)—*bi* being pronounced as *ping* and *bi* in reverse—Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states it means "obstinate" (*li*) and "headstrong" (*hen*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xin*) with the phonetic "fu" (*fu* being pronounced as *fu*).

"Dǎoyí (刀夷)"—the "dǎo" is pronounced as in "dǎolǎo" (刀老) and the "yí" as in "fǎn" (反). The Commentary on the Book of Documents by Kǒng (孔) states: "The island-dwellers of the South Sea; they are included within the jurisdiction of Yángzhōu. According to the Shuowén Jìzì, it is composed of the radical "mountain" (山) with "niǎo" (鳥) as the phonetic.
"Dī" (磾)—pronounced as in "dīngxī" (丁奚)—is mentioned in the *Hànshū* (Book of Han), which notes that there was a court attendant named Jīn Rìdī (金日磾).

*Kōngdòng* (空峒): The *Dúgōng Fǎn'ěr yǎ* states that the region north of the North Pole is called *Kōngdòng*. In both ancient and modern times, the correct character is written with the "mountain" radical (*shan*) and the phonetic "tóng" (*tong*).

*Biǎn'ài* (褊隘): Pronounced *biānmiǎn* (鞭緬). The *Guǎngyǎ* states it means narrow. In the *Chǔcí*, it refers to shallow wisdom and narrow capability. The *Shuowén* explains it as composed of the "clothing" radical (*yi*) and the phonetic "piān" (*piān*), with "piān" also serving as the phonetic. It is an error to compose this character with the "dog" radical (*quan*) as *biān* (猵).

*Nu* (砮) is pronounced with the initial *nǔ* (怒) and the final *dǐ* (都) reversed, followed by *zhī* (之) and *ěr* (耳). Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states: "Grindstone (*zhǐ*) is finer than whetstone (*lì*). *Nu* is used for arrowheads, such as those of Danzhu. Both the *Wenzi* and the *Dianshuo* follow the character *shí* (石) [as the radical] and *nú* (奴) [as the phonetic]. The sound of *shì* (氏) is *jí* (集); thus, this work uses *zhǐ* (砥), which is a vulgar form of the character.
"Zhízhī" (執志) is "zhēn rù" (針入); it is erroneously written as "zhì" (縶).
"Yúyuàn" (虞愿) is "yuán juàn" (原眷), a personal name.

Regarding "dǐhē" (詆訶): the upper character is "dī lǐ" (低禮). The *Guǎngpǐ* states that "dǐ" means to slander. Guō's commentary on the *Fāngyán* says it means to reprimand one another. The *Shuōwén* states that "dǐ" is also "hē" (to scold), both following the radical "氐" with the phonetic "可"; "氐" has the same pronunciation as above. It is erroneously written as "𧥮" in the *Jí* (集), which is a vulgar character.

7. Fascicle Seven. *Hui*: (盾, *dùn*; *chún*, *zhǔn* reversed) According to the *Shuowen*, it is a pictographic character representing that which protects the body and shields the eyes. *Yi*: (悒, *yī*; *yīn*, *jí* reversed) The *Kaosheng* states it means resentment. The *Cangjie pian* states that *yi* refers to an appearance of being unrelaxed.

The *Shuowen* says it means unease; it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) with the phonetic "city" (*yì*). Below, *yāng* (仰, *yǎng*) is reversed. The *Guangya* states *yàng* means forceful. The *Shuowen* says it means indignation; it is composed of the radical "heart" with the phonetic "center" (*yāng*). *Duì* (懟, *duì*; sound *dà nèi* reversed) means resentment. *Yàng*: (怏, *yàng*; *qiáng*, *qiǎng* reversed) The *Shuowen* says it means indignation; it is composed of the radical "heart" with the phonetic "center" (*yāng*). *Duì* (懟, *duì*; sound *dà nèi* reversed) means resentment.

*Jiànshí* (to eat repeatedly): Qian and Jian’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "jiàn" means "frequently. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "grass" (艹) with the phonetic "cún" (存). *Tíjiá* (the *tí* and *jiá* sacrifices): The upper character "tí" is pronounced as *dì* (帝);

Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states that "tí" refers to a major sacrifice (*dàjì*). The lower character "jiá" is pronounced as *jiǎ* (甲). The *Baihūtong* says: "Once every three years there is a *jiá* sacrifice; once every five years there is a *tí* sacrifice. According to the *Shuowen*, both characters are composed of the radical "clothing" (衣); "hé" (合) and "jiē" (皆) serve as their phonetics.

*Śrāddha* (𧘑): The character is pronounced as *jì yáng* (祭羊). The *Erlü* (爾疋) states: "The summer sacrifice is called *śrāddha*. Zheng’s commentary says: "This refers to fresh vegetables that may be roasted. The *Shuowen Jiezi* takes the radical as "clothing" (*yī*) and the phonetic as "ladle" (*sháo*), while the *Jiyun* (集韻) uses "grain" (*huò*) instead; both are incorrect.

"Qiǎo" (愀) [the "jiāo" and "xiǎo" pronunciations are reversed; according to Zheng's commentary on the *Liji*, "qiǎo" refers to an expression of shifting emotion; the *Wenzi Dianshuō* states that "qiǎo" means being unhappy; it is composed of the radical "heart" and the phonetic "qiū"].

*Yībō*: *bō* (盌) is pronounced as *bō*. *Chái*: The upper character is pronounced *chái*; according to the *Shuowen*, it belongs to the genus of wolves (*láng*). It is composed of the radical *lí* (the head of the "heart" radical) and *cái*. To compose it with the radical *quǎn* (dog) to form *wǔ* (𤝔) is incorrect. The lower character is pronounced *wǔ*; its original form was the character for "tiger," now written as *wǔ* to avoid imperial taboo names.
"Zhang-chi" (張㢮): "Chi" (㢮) means to unstring a bow; it is used with the character for bow (*gong*). "Fan-zhen" (范縝): "Ni" (尼) is pronounced *lin*;
it is a personal name. "Li" (轢): pronounced *di-wang-ling* (帝王零);
according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "li" means to tread upon; it is composed of the radical for chariot (*che*) and the phonetic element *le*.

*Guàfān*: The upper character is pronounced *guā* (with the *huà* radical reversed) or is written with the *mí* radical as *chúnghuàn*; the lower character is pronounced *fúyuán* or is written with the *jīn* radical as *fān*.

*Jíkòu*: Pronounced *tāngluò*. Zheng Zhong’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "A *kòu* is that which is struck by those who provide the night watch. The *Zhouyi* says: "One strikes the *kòu* at the double gates to await violent guests. The *Shuowen* [explains it] as being from the *shuǐ* radical; *tuó* and *tuó* are also its phonetic components. The *Ji* [edition] writes it as *zhāi*, which is also common usage.

*Gǔn*: The first character is pronounced *gǔ* (with the *bó* and *huīn* finals); the second is pronounced *zhí* (with the *zhōng* final). According to the *Shuowen*, "gǔn" is a general term for insects; it is composed of two "insect" characters (*chóng*).

*Jiù*: Pronounced *qú* (with the *rǔ* final). According to the *Erya*, "jiù" means poverty. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *mián* (pronounced *mián*) with the phonetic *lǒu*. The radical *mián* has the sound *mián*.

*Mángjiè* (芒屩): Pronounced *jūlüo*. Xu Shuchong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states that a *jiè* is a sandal (*lǚ*). The *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of the abbreviated form of *lǚ* with the phonetic *qiáo*.

*Dānshēng* (殫生): Pronounced *duōhán*. Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* states that *dān* means "exhausted. The *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of the radical *dài* with the phonetic *dān*; *dài* is pronounced *wǔyuǎn*. The character assembled here as *dān* is a vulgar form.
