The *Shuowen* [as cited above] defines it as the drawing forth of breath from the mouth. It remains uncertain which of these is accurate.

*Pū*: Upper radical *pu*, lower radical *bo* (with the *bo* pronounced as *bǔ*). Gu Yewang says that *pū* means to strike or beat. Lower radical *di*, with the *li* pronounced as *lì*. *Shēnglèi* says *di* means to damage. The *Shuowén* states both follow the hand radical and take *pù* and *dì* as their phonetic components; *pù* has the same pronunciation as above.

Regarding the terms *xìng* (sacrificial victim) and *quán* (complete): *xìng* is pronounced *shàng suǒ gēng fǎn xià jué yuán fǎn*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Mao Shī* states: "Oxen, sheep, and pigs are called *xìng*. Kǒng Ānguó’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* states: "Those of pure color are called *xī* (sacrificial victims); those with complete bodies are called *quán*. Zhèng Zhòng’s commentary on the *Zhōu Lǐ* states: "*Quán* refers to pure color. The *Shuowén Jiězì* explains both characters as being composed of "ox" (*niú*) and "whole" (*shēng quán*), with "jiàn" (*jiē shēng*) as their phonetic component.

*Xiè* (血) [read *diāo* (彫) with the *fǎn* (反) of *liǎo* (了)]; Zheng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states it refers to the fat between the intestines. The *Shuowén* sometimes writes it as *liáo* (膫). *Yuè* (礿) [read *yáng* (羊) with the *fǎn* of *zháo* (灼)];

the *Erya* states: "The summer sacrifice is called *yuè*. Guo’s commentary says this means fresh vegetables that can be roasted (*zháo*). It is sometimes written as *yù* (禴), which follows the radical for bamboo (*zhú*) and forms the character *yuè* (籥), meaning a pipe or flute; this is not the intended meaning here.

*Mian* (賣) is pronounced *shān* (蟬) with the final consonant *chuan* (展) reversed; it is the name of a fish. The *Shanhai jing* (Classic of Mountains and Seas) calls it the *huá* (滑) fish. Guo’s commentary states that the *shān* fish resembles a snake. According to the *Shuowen jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "fish" (*yú*) and the phonetic "dan" (*dān*).
The character *bù* (布) [with the phonetic *pǔ* as a variant] means "to spread" according to the *Zìshū* (字書); Gu Yewáng says it means "to unfold," or it is written as *pū* (鋪).

*Jiā* (罝) [with the phonetic *fú* as a variant]—Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states that *jiā* means "to screen"; examining its sound, *jiā* refers to a snare for catching hares. The *Shuowen* also writes it as *jū* (𢾭) or *jù* (󲯴/󲳵) [with the phonetic *fúliú*]. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* says it is a net for capturing beasts; the *Shuowen* also says it is a snare for catching hares. Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that *jì* (𮊁) is simply a net.

Regarding *jìqū* (蝍蛆): the first character is pronounced *zhàng* (上甑) with the rhyme *lì* (力), and the second is *zǐyú* (子餘). Xu Shuchong, in the *Huainanzi*, states that *jìqū* is also called *wúgōng* (吳公). In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, both characters follow the radical for insects (*虫*) and take *jí* (即) and *qiè* (且) as their phonetic components.

*Kān* (甘) is pronounced *dì* (螮, with the *tài* [太] radical). Regarding the sound *kāo* (考), *dì* refers to a snake; according to the *Táng yùn*, it also means a snake, or sometimes written as *dài* (帶). *Chái* (豺) is pronounced *chuáng* (床, with the *jiē* [皆] radical).

Guō’s commentary on the *Ěryǎ* states that the feet of the *chái* resemble those of a dog. The *Shuōwén* says it belongs to the category of wolves (*láng*), formed from the *zhì* (豸) radical with *cái* (才) as the phonetic component; *zhì* is pronounced *chí'ěr* (池爾). The version in the *Jí* (集) [dictionary] writes it with the *quǎn* (犬) radical as *shǒu* (𤝔); this character does not exist, and thus that version is incorrect.

Regarding *yègān* (野干), Guo Pu states that the *shègān* (射干) is able to climb trees; the *Guǎngzhì* says it gathers fruit from perilous cliffs and tall trees. To compose this character with the "dog" radical (*quán*) as *gàn* (犴) is incorrect.

This character [yíng] (盈) is pronounced with the *zhī* (隻) and *fǎn* (反) finals; its phonetic component is *lì* (歷). It is correctly written as [bìng] (病); it is a vulgar form derived from [jí] (集). This character [lǚ] (癩) is pronounced with the *zhōu* (周) final;

the *Guǎngyá* states that "lǚ" means illness, and Gù Yěwáng states it means a swelling that does not suppurate or disperse. The *Shuowén* defines it as a swelling, composed of the radical [shǒng] (𤕫) and the phonetic component [lǐ] (󳂌); it is written as [lǚ] (癩) in the *Jí* (集), which is a vulgar form.

This is *lòu* (with the rhyme *dòu*; Kuo Pu’s commentary on the *Shānhǎijīng* states it is *lòu-tuō*; the *Shuōwén* defines it as a swelling of the neck, formed with the radical for "neck" and the phonetic *lóu*;

the collected edition writes it as *lóu*, which is a vulgar character). 27. Volume Twenty-seven. *Lóu* (rhyme *li*) and *chí* (upper part rhymes *li*, lower part rhymes *lí*). The *Zhōulǐ* states that for sacrifices, *chí* is provided to the *Shòuhài-rén*. Zheng Zhong’s commentary says: "*Chí* are ant eggs. The *Shuōwén* [defines it] with the radical for "insect" and the phonetic *dǐ*; the sound of *dǐ* is *dī*.
The "Hao-liang" (濠梁) [refers to] Hu Gao; this is the name of a place.

Having finished the explanation, [we turn to] *jī-nì* (飢惄), where *nì* is pronounced as *níng*. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "Nì is like the hunger of one who has fasted. It is also written as *nì*.
The serene countenance contemplates the return of Ji.
Having finished the previous explanation, "Jian" (pronounced *jiān*) is a personal name.

"Xiyou" (pronounced *xī yóu*): in the *Erya*, "you" means "to pass by. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states that it refers to the places passed along a road; the *Guangya* calls it a "relay station" (*yì*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* takes the radical "city" (*yì*) and the phonetic "lǒng" (*lóng*); the version compiled here as "lǎo" (*lǎo*) is incorrect.

Wānghuì (汪濊): the first character is pronounced wūhuáng (烏黃反) and the second wēiwèi (威衛反). Gù Yěwáng states that wānghuì means "pángtuó" (滂沱), describing a state of abundance. The *Guǎngyá* identifies it as water; huì may also be written as shēn (󳍮). Tuó is pronounced dáhé (達何反).

"Xuán" (憮然) means "to be despondent. He Yan’s commentary on the *Analects* states: "Xuán means that one does not understand another's meaning and thus disparages them. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "heart" (心) and the phonetic "wu" (無).

The character 靖 (jìng) is pronounced with the *qǐng* and *jǐng* finals (as in *qǐng* and *jǐng*). Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states it means "tranquil and pure"; the *Shuowen* defines it as "clear adornment. It may also be written with the radical 立 (standing), forming 靖.
The term 袠 (*chí*) is pronounced with the *lì* final; it may also be written as 帙, while its ancient form was 袟. The reading 𧙿 found in the *Ji* edition is incorrect.

"Qiūbù" (跬步): *kuǐ* (with the phonetic *guǐ*). In the *Lǐjì*, it says: "The gentleman does not dare forget [the Way] even for a single step. According to the *Fāngyán*, one half-step is called a *qiū*. Gu Yěwáng states that it means to lift one foot. Two *qiū* make one *bù* (step). The character *kǎo* (考) is written as *xié* (䞨), and *qiū* is used interchangeably with it.

*Lìnlì* (懍厲): the first character is pronounced with the upper radical *lín* (林) and the phonetic *jǐn* (錦); the second character is pronounced with the lower radical *lián* (憐) and the phonetic *jì* (計). The *Bīcāng* states that *lǐn* is also *lèi*; these are mutually explained terms. According to the *Shuowen*, *lǐn* is formed from the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "bǐn" (*bǐn*). *Lì* may also be written as *luò* (捩).

*Yì* (in *yuèyì*) has the phonetic *rú zhì* as its final; the Commentary on the Book of Documents by Kǒng [Yǎng] states that *yì* means "to cut off the ears. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* explains it as being composed of the radical "knife" (*dāo*) and the phonetic "ear" (*ěr*).

*Gù* in *gùjiè*: the upper character should be pronounced *gù*, but the *Jí* edition erroneously writes it as "Zhou. The lower character has the phonetic *jiè hài*. It is said that *jiǎi* means "hardness. The *Shuowén Jiězì* states: "In the Nine Provinces, iron is called *jiǎi*; it is composed of the radical 'metal' (*jīn*) and the phonetic 'all' (*jiē*)."
*Nonghua* (穠華): "Nong" is pronounced with the *kao* (考) radical and *sheng* (聲) phonetic;

it describes the appearance of flowers in full bloom. *Ke* (愒): pronounced with the *ku* (枯) radical and *dai* (帶) phonetic; the *Zuozhuan* states, "to dally with the years and *ke* the days. Du Yu’s commentary says, "*Ke* means greed. He Yan’s commentary on the *Gongyangzhuan* says, "*Ke* means urgency. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the "heart" (*xin*) radical with the "he" (*曷*) phonetic.

The character above is *xī* (希嬌反); Gu Yewang states that *xī* refers to hot vapor. According to the *Shuowen*, it means the appearance of gas escaping. The character below is *kū* (虛厄反); according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of two *chì* (赤) radicals. The compilation [of the canon] as *sù* (䓇) is incorrect.

*Zǒng*: (The character is pronounced with the *sài* and *lái* finals; according to the *Guǎngyá*, "zǒng" means to move. In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, "táizǒng" means to shake and hasten. It is composed of the radical "hand" and the phonetic "sī. Examining the phonetics, the correct form is "zǒng"; the form "jí" used in some texts is a vulgar character.)

The character 󳂯 (ǒu): the first radical is pronounced *bi* (as in *bì*) and the second is pronounced *yóu* (as in *yóu-gǒu*). Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states that it is also called 󳂯; this is a character whose meaning has been shifted through association (*zhuǎnxùn*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, 󳂯 means "consort" (*fēi*); it is composed of the radical 女 (*nǚ*) with the phonetic component 𣬉 (*pú-lí*; the pronunciation of 𣬉 is *pú-lí*), and the pronunciation of 妃 is *pèi*.

*Chuí* (high resentment): The classifier is *lei* (class). The *Shuowen* explains that "resentment" (*chuí*) means enmity; it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xin*) and the phonetic "duì" (*duì*).

Alternatively, it may be written with the radical "speech" (*yan*) as *zì*. *Ní* (thin ice): The classifier is *cí* and *zī*. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that "ní" refers to melting ice. The *Shuowen* says it refers to floating ice; it is composed of the radical "ice" (*bing*) and the phonetic "sī". The *Jishuo* states that it is written with the radical "water" (*shui*) as *sī*, meaning a name for a river located in the Northern Sea.

"Jiàn" (驗) means "to verify. "Lái" (來) means "to come back. Yěwáng (野王) says that "cái" (纔) is equivalent to "jìn" (近), meaning "nearby. Some editions write it as "cái" (裁), while the *Jí* (集) edition writes it as "mǎn" (絻); both are incorrect. Alternatively, it is written as "cái" (纔), which is a vulgar character.

"Xiūhuò" (脩嫭): "hù" (嫭) is pronounced "hùgù" (胡固). According to the *Guǎngyǎ* (廣雅), it describes a beautiful appearance. Some editions write it as "hù" (婟). It is composed with the radical "yú" (雩); writing it as "huò" (嫮) is a vulgar character.

"Ti" (睇): read as *jì* (計) with the final consonant reversed; according to Zheng's commentary on the *Liji*, "ti" means to look askance. The meaning of this character has already been explained previously.
"Qióng" (瓊): read as *yuān* (阮) with the final consonant reversed; this has already been explained previously.
Shan (剡) is a place name in the region of Yue; it is pronounced "she" (𮉼, with the fanqie "shé").

Xu Biao (徐鑣), pronounced "biao" (驕, with the fanqie "jiāo"), states in the *Shuowen* that it refers to a horse's bit, composed of the radical "metal" (金) and the phonetic "piao" (麃, with the fanqie "luó jiāo"); however, the character in the *Ji* (集) is written as "yu" (䮽, with the fanqie "lù yě"), meaning a wild horse, which is not the intended meaning here.

28. Fascicle 28. *Tú-liǎo* (荼蓼). The first character, *tú*, is pronounced with the initial *dú* (the "nu" radical) and the final *nù*. The *Erya* states: "Tú is bitter vegetable. The second character, *liǎo*, is pronounced with the initial *liao* (the "niao" radical) and the final *jiǎo*. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states: "Liǎo is an aquatic plant. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "A pungent vegetable. Both characters are composed of the "grass" (*cǎo*) radical; the phonetic component for *yú* (in *tú*) is *liáo*, which is pronounced *liú* (the "jiù" radical). The phonetic component for *jiù* (in *liǎo*) is *liáo*. 28. Fascicle 28. *Tú-liǎo* (荼蓼). The first character, *tú*, is pronounced with the initial *dú* (the "nu" radical) and the final *nù*. The *Erya* states: "Tú is bitter vegetable. The second character, *liǎo*, is pronounced with the initial *liao* (the "niao" radical) and the final *jiǎo*. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states: "Liǎo is an aquatic plant. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "A pungent vegetable. Both characters are composed of the "grass" (*cǎo*) radical; the phonetic component for *yú* (in *tú*) is *liáo*, which is pronounced *liú* (the "jiù" radical). The phonetic component for *jiù* (in *liǎo*) is *liáo*.

"Qiàn fù" (歉腹) is pronounced qiān diàn fǎn. Liu Zhao’s commentary on the *Guliang Zhuan* states: "Qiàn refers to eating without fullness. It follows the radical for "lack" (欠) with "jiān" (兼) as its phonetic. The character is sometimes written with the radical for "mouth" (口) as "qián" (嗛), meaning that something is being held in the mouth; this is not the same as "qiàn fù" (歉腹).

*Cháng-réng* (食仍反): According to the *Cānjié piān*, it refers to the ridges between fields (*rén-pàn*). The *Bīcāng* states it is equivalent to *luò*. It may also be written with the "field" radical as *zhuàng* or *tòng*.
*Néng-yú* (瑜主反): Gu Yewang says that *yú* means "slight" or "light. The *Shuowén* states that *yù* means "illness. It may also be written as *yù*.

Qingti (靑緹): "Ti" is pronounced with the *xi* rhyme-group (悌奚反). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that *ti* is the color of *quan* (縓); the *Shuowen Jiezi* says it is a reddish-yellow color. It is composed of the radical for "silk" (糸) and the phonetic element "shi" (是), while *quan* (縓) is pronounced with the *xuan* (宣) and *juan* (絹) rhyme-groups.
*Xiǔ* (詡) and *yù* (吁) are reversed forms of personal names.

*Ān* (㤇) and *nǎo* (惱): the former is pronounced *yú zǎo* (於早); the *Wenzi Jílüè* (文字集略) states that it means "the sorrowful heart is knotted within" (*àonáo*). *Ān* may also be written as *ào* (懊), but the version in the collection following the "earth" radical (*tǔ*) as *biāo* (󲷢) is incorrect. *Nǎo* may also be written as *náo* (憹), but the version in the collection following the three "stop" radicals (*zhǐ*) as *shǒu* (󱹟) is incorrect.
*Wú-ài* (魚蓋反): In general, the scriptural text writes this as *ài* or *hài*; it is incorrect to derive it from the radical *hài* (亥) to form *wèi*.
*Cōng* (楚雙反): The *Zǐxū Fù* states that "one strikes the metal drums. The *Pīcāng* states that "cōng" is synonymous with "to strike"; alternatively, it is written with the hand radical as *cōng*.

*Shèn* (pronounced *sēn*, with the initial *jǐn* [jǐn] as a variant). Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "Those who construct *shèn* today pile firewood together in the water; when the fish encounter the cold, they enter inside, whereupon they are captured. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains that it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mu*) and the phonetic "san" (*cān*).

*Xiào zhà*: The character *zhà* is pronounced with the *zé* and *yà* finals (i.e., *zhà*). Wang Yewang states that *zhà* is synonymous with scolding or rebuking. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic element *tè*. The sound of *tè* is pronounced with the *zhú* and *gé* finals (i.e., *tè*).

*Dēng rí*: The second syllable, *rí*, is pronounced with the *ér* final (i.e., *rí*). The *Kaosheng* states that *Rí* is the name of a place in Hedong. Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that *Rí* is located south of the bend in the Yellow River. It is composed of the radical "mountain" (*shān*) or is alternatively written as *ěi*.

Regarding the *Liǎo'é* (Lament for the Mugwort): the *Fǎnshī* (Explanations of the Poems) states, "Tall and luxuriant is the *é*. Guo's commentary on the *Erya* says it is the mugwort known today as *é-hāo*. The *Shuowen* [explains it] as being composed of the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) and the phonetic element "I" (*wǒ*).

Regarding *xùnyè* (the sounding-boards): *xùn* is pronounced *xún yǔn* (with the final *-n* rhyming with *-ǔn*). Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* says: "The *xùn* is that by which bells are suspended; those that are horizontal are called *xùn*, and they are decorated with scales and the like. The *yè* is made of large wooden boards. Some write it as *xiàn* using the "wood" radical (*mù*), while others write it as *zhì*; these are incorrect.
*Shui* (虞倕): *shuì* (隹反). Guo’s commentary on the *Shanhai jing* states that Shui was the skilled artisan of Yao.

*Shu* (󲹛𤐷): upper radical *bào* (鮑), lower *bāo* (苞) rhyme; the *Yunying* says it refers to food cooked by fire, though it is sometimes written as *zhai* (𤇗). Lower radical *ǎo* (襖), *hāo* (蒿) rhyme; the *Jixun* says it refers to roasting or baking things over hot embers. "Nowadays" (*jin*), it is sometimes written as *yu* (燠) or *ao* (爊); the ancient script uses *gǔn* (袞); in the *Zhong*, it is written with the bird radical as *jiao* (𪀀). *Shuang* (鷞) is not yet fully understood.

"Do not be arrogant" (*ào*). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "arrogance" means a lack of reverence. Regarding the phonetic component, the *Erya* writes it as *ào*, and it is also written as *sǎo*; it is incorrect to follow the "heart" radical and write it as *mào*.

The character *jiè* (介) is pronounced as *xiè* (皆械反). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that *jiè* refers to turtles, soft-shelled turtles, and other such creatures that dwell in water. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as composed of the radical for "person" (*rén*) and the character for "person" (*rén*) with the addition of "fish" (*yú*), forming the word *jié* (魪), which is the name of a type of fish; this does not accord with the meaning of *jièpǐn* (介品).
*Zhǒng* (種): *huì* (彙), with the phonetic *guì* (貴) as the radical; it means "categories" (*huìlèi*) in the *Zhouyī*. The preceding explanation of its meaning is complete.

*Càn fū* (噆膚): *càn* (噆), upper radical *zǐ dá* (子荅); the *Zhuāngzǐ* says that mosquitoes (*méng wén*) bite the skin so one cannot sleep all night. The *Pīcāng* says it means "to gnaw. The *Shuōwén* says it means "to suck. Alternatively, the phonetic *kǎo* (考) indicates that the correct form is *yǎn* (𠯗).

The character for "net" (網) is pronounced *bǐ* (逼) as a reversed reading; the *Erya* states that "nine nets" (*jiǔ wǎng*) are "fish traps" (*yú wǎng*). Guo’s commentary notes that this refers to what is now called the "hundred-sack net" (*bǎi náng wǎng*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "net" (*wǎng*) with "or" (*é*) as its phonetic component.
*Zhòng huì*: "Huì" (pronounced with a retroflex *fǎn*) is a term from the *Fāngyán* [Dialectal Lexicon] meaning that things are abundant;

this has already been explained. *Qiàn qiàn*: "Qiàn" (pronounced with a retroflex *fǎn*) is derived from the sound *qiàn*; it expresses a sense of earnestness or sincerity. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic element "jiān" (*jiān*).
*Qiǎng* (閴): *qīng* (傾) and *yì* (伇) in rhyme; the *Běicāng* states it means "tranquil. It is composed of the radical *jù* (具) with the phonetic *jù* (俱) in rhyme.
This has already been explained above. *Yìng* (應): *fù* (敷) and *wù* (務) in rhyme; it is identical to the character *fù* (赴).

29. Fascicle Twenty-nine. [Fascicle Twenty-nine]. *Tú* (屠) is pronounced with the *mǎo* rhyme and *huò* (獲) tone. The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (毛詩傳) states: “*Tú huò* means to capture. Those who do not submit are executed, and their ears are offered; this is called *tú*. It is also written as *mǎn* (𭍷) following the character for ‘state,’ or as *ěr* (聝) following the character for ‘ear. In archaic script, it is also written as *zhí* (聀).”

The phrase "the *chū* and tiger were executed" actually refers, through reversed characters, to the favor shown to the man *Chū*. When the man *Chū* emerged from the *Gōnyū* clan, he was able to manifest as a tiger; the *Ming* on "Extraordinary Creatures" states: "The *chū* emerged from the *Gōnyū* clan, transforming and changing like a deity. When it acted as a tiger, one did not recognize it as a human. In the *Shuowen*, [the character for *chū*] is formed with *zhì* (豸) and the phonetic *qū* (區); the pronunciation of *zhì* is that of *zhì* (雉).

*Zhú* (舳) and *lú* (艫): The first character is pronounced with the sixth tone (zhù). According to the *Fāngyán*, the rear of a boat is called *zhú*; it is that which controls the water. Guo’s commentary states: "In the Jiangdong region today, the *tuō* (拖) is called *zhú*. The *Shuowén* says it is composed of the radical *zhōu* (舟) and the phonetic *xǐng* (省). *Tuō* (拖) is pronounced *tuō* (它可反); the second character, *lú* (艫), is pronounced *dū* (都反). Li Fei’s commentary on the *Hànshū* states: "It is the place at the front of the ship where the oars are pulled. The *Shuowén* says it is the prow of the boat, composed of the radical *zhōu* (舟) and the phonetic *lú* (盧).

*Jian* (入𦪙): the phonetic component is *tan* (貪) and the radical is *he* (合); it refers to the sound of two boats joined together. The *Wenzi Jilüe* (Textual Compendium) states it refers to large boats used by both parties; the *Jí* (集) edition writes it as *qù* (䑽), which is a vulgar character. *Cheng* (成): the phonetic component is *sheng* (生) and the radical is *geng* (梗).

Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* (Book of Documents) states that *cheng* means "transgression" (*guo*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* (Explaining Simple and Analyzing Compound Characters) says it is composed of the radical *mu* (目) and the phonetic *sheng* (生).

*Táo* (pronounced *gāo* in reverse): The *Cangjie pian* states that it means an expression of harmony and joy; the *Shuowen jiezi* says it means "joyful," composed of the radical "heart" (*xin*) and the phonetic component "yǎo" (the pronunciation of which is the same as above).
*Yīn* (pronounced *yīlín*): Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states it means "to block" or "to fill up"; it is also written as *yīn*.

*Bò* (pronounced *pén-mù-fǎn*). According to the *Guǎyá*, "bóbó" means fragrance; according to the *Běicāng*, it means great fragrance. The *Shuōwén* states that it is composed of the radical "xiāng" (fragrance) with "pèi" as the phonetic component. The sound of "pèi" is the same as above. "Pèi" is composed of the radical "fú" (the character for boiling) and the component "zǐ. The sound of "fú" is *fèi*.

The characters for *wǎnwǎn* (婉娩) are pronounced with the first character as *yuānyuǎn* (冤遠) and the second as *wúfǎn* (無返). According to the phonetic examination, *wǎnwǎn* describes the gentle and compliant appearance of a woman. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states that *wǎn* means "coquettish charm" (*mèi*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "compliant. Both follow the radical for "woman" (*nǚ*). In the *Jí* (集) [dictionary], it is written as *wǎnrì* (晼曰), yet the *Rì* (曰) section does not contain this character. *Wǎn* (晚) refers to the evening when the sun sets; its profound meaning remains undetermined.

"Zhí shí zhēng shí fǎn" (Treading on reality and seeking the stone-like). The *Huainanzi* states: "Birds fly through the void, while beasts tread on reality as they run. Xu Shu-zhong’s commentary says: "Zhí means to tread upon; it also means to walk. It is sometimes written as the character 蹠; it is not correct to compose it from the radical 庶 as 蹠.

Língpíng (竛竮): The upper character is pronounced lěngdīng (冷丁) and the lower is pǐbìng (匹并). Lexicons state that "língpíng" means walking unsteadily; both characters follow the radical 立 (standing), and it is incorrect to combine them with the radical 足 (foot) to form 跉 or to use 跰 as a variant.

*Āo*: The upper character is pronounced *nuǒ* (with the initial *n-*) and the lower is pronounced *wǎo* (with the initial *w-*). It refers to a nurse who suckles an infant. According to Wen Ying’s commentary on the *Hanshu*, in Youzhou and Hanzhong, old women are called *āo*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is a term for an aged woman. Both characters follow the radical "woman" (*nǚ*). The phonetic component for the first is *ěr* and for the second is *wēn*; *wēn* is pronounced *wēn*, and *yù* (the second character) is pronounced *jū* (with the initial *j-*) and the final *-ǔ*.
The explanation of the preceding characters *liao* (遼), *huī* (隳), and *huí* (迴) is concluded.

Regarding *jiǎomíng* (蟭螟): the first character is read as *zǐxiāo* (子消) and the second as *mìpíng* (覓瓶). The *Liezi* states: "Yin Tang asked Xia Ji, saying: 'Among things, are there large and small? He replied: 'The *jiǎomíng* is a tiny insect found among the marshes of the Yangtze River; when they fly in swarms and nest upon the tips of mosquito wings, the mosquitoes do not even perceive their coming and going. Both characters follow the radical for insects. *Mó* (麼) is pronounced *mó* (魔) with the tone of *bō* (跛); *mó* means small. *Jié* (革) is pronounced *jīnyì* (矜憶)."

*Kūn* (鯤) and *péng* (鵬): the first character has the phonetic *fǎn* (反) with the sub-reading *pú* (蒲) and *fǔ* (甫). The *Zhuāngzǐ* states: "In the Northern Ocean there is a fish whose name is *kūn*; it transforms into a bird whose name is *péng*. The back of the *péng* is several thousand *qī* (千里) li in length. Sīmǎ Biāo’s commentary notes that *kūn* is a large fish; the *Shuōwén* explains it as consisting of the radical "fish" (*yú*) and the phonetic "gūn" (*kūn*). The collective form *kūn* (蜫) written with the "insect" (*chóng*) radical is incorrect. *Péng* consists of the radical "bird" (*niǎo*) and the phonetic "péng" (*péng*).

"Shêng-hu" (升岵): "Hu" is pronounced as "gǔ. The *Mao Shih Zhuan* states that a mountain without grass is called *hu*. The *Han Shih* states that a mountain with trees but no grass is called *hu*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as consisting of the radical "mountain" (*shan*) and the phonetic component "ancient" (*gu*).

Regarding the term *wéiquè* (魏闕), which denotes high nobility, the *Huáihuánzǐ* states that "the mind dwells at the *wéiquè*," while the *Zhōulǐ* refers to the celestial gates as *xiàngwéi*. *Wéi* is a designation for height and grandeur. It is composed of the radicals *wěi* (委) and *guǐ* (鬼) as its phonetic component; it is also written with the radical *mǎ* (馬) as *kuí* (騩), pronounced *guì*. The *Zìtǒng* explains that this refers to a horse of a light black color, and does not carry the meaning of "palace gate" (*wéiquè*).

*Liè* (pronounced lián zhé in reverse; the *Shēnglèi* states that *liè* means "sharp wind"; according to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "wind" [風] with *liè* as its phonetic). *Gūchú* (pronounced shì yú in reverse):

Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states that a bird which is able to feed itself from birth is called a *chú*. According to the *Shuowén*, it is sometimes written with the radical "bird" [隹] as *chú*; the character used here, *chū*, is a vulgar form.

*Jin* (捦): Pronounced *ji jin fan*. It means "to seize" according to the *Pei Cang*; it means "to grasp the hem of a garment" according to the *Shuowen*. It is also written as *duan* (鈘) with the radical *zhi* (攴), or as *jian* (㩒) with the radical *jin* (禁).
*Kuai* (隗): Pronounced *tong wu wei fan*. It is a personal name. *Wei* (猥) is pronounced *wu zui fan*.

Regarding "chóng niǎo" (虫鸟): the first character is pronounced *lóng* (隆) with the *zhù* (逐) tone, and the second is pronounced *diāo* (彫) with the *liǎo* (了) tone; the meaning is that these are two distinct characters for "insect" and "bird. To combine them into the character "chén" (𦫀) is a profound error on the part of scribes.

Regarding "téng chěng" (𦫀騁): the first character is pronounced *tè dēng* (特登); it means to leap or gallop. Its correct form is "téng" (𦫀), while the character "téng" (腾) found in the *Jí* (集) is a vulgar form. The second character, "chěng" (騁), is pronounced *líng* (领) with the *fǎn* (反) tone; the *Jí* (集) erroneously writes it as "zhōng yāng" (从央). The pronunciation of "chěng" (檉) is *chěng* (逞) with the *zhēn* (贞) tone.

*Píng* (pronounced *píng*, with the rhyme *xuān* and the retroflex *yǎn*): Wang Yanwang says that what is now called a canopy (*bùzhāng*) atop a carriage is the *píng*. The *Shìmíng* states that the *píng* of a carriage is for warding off heat. The *Shuōwén* [gives it] as *màn* (from the radical *jīn* and the phonetic *chē*), but the version compiled here is a scribal error.

The character 𥔐 (pronounced *kǎn*, with the phonetic component *hé*): According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to the sound of stones striking against one another. It is composed of the radical 石 (stone) and the phonetic component 盇 (*hé*). The character 盇 is composed of 大 (great) and 𮕜. In current vernacular usage, it is commonly written as 磕; however, to follow the *Ji* (the *Jiyun* or similar lexicographical collections), writing it as 𥕤 is incorrect.

The character 嶮 (xiǎn) is composed of the radical 山 (mountain) and the phonetic 希 (xī). It refers to rugged and uneven terrain; it describes the appearance of a mountain that is high and perilous. According to the *Gujin Zhengzi* (Orthodox Characters of Antiquity and Today), it takes the phonetic 僉 (qiān, pronounced qiè yán). The character 𨸏 (qióng, pronounced qī yǎn) is the phonetic for the second part; it is pronounced qiāo zào. In the *Shēnglèi* (Classification of Sounds), it is defined as "steep and precipitous. It may also be written with the radical 𨸏 as 陗 (qiào).

*Chán* (巉): Pronounced *chuán-xián-fǎn*. "Chányán" (*巉巖*) means the appearance of rugged mountains; it is also written as *zhǎn* (嶄) or *chèn* (磛). The character in the *Jí* (集) is "chán" (巉), which is a vulgar form. *Wú* (䫻): Pronounced *yún-mì-fǎn*.
According to the *Shuōwén*, it denotes the appearance of a great wind; it is composed of the radical "wind" (風) and the phonetic "rì" (日).

*Zēn* (蓁): Pronounced *zhì* (上櫛巾反). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that "zēnzēn" describes the appearance of flourishing vegetation; the *Guang Ya* says it means "luxuriant. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* explains that it follows the radical for grass (*艹*) and takes *qín* as its phonetic component. Below, *rén* (仍) is pronounced *zhèng* (仍證反); the *Kaosheng* states it means dense grass that has not been trimmed. The *Shuowen Jiezi* also defines it as dense grass, following the radical for grass and taking *rén* as its phonetic, or sometimes with *rén* abbreviated.

*Yūyǔ* (紆𡵒): The upper character *yǔ* (傴) is pronounced with the *yú* rhyme. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that *yū* means "curved. The *Shuowen* defines it as "to bend," composed of the radical *mì* (糸) and the phonetic *yú*. The lower character *jié* (結) is pronounced with the *jié* rhyme. Zhāng Xiàn’s commentary on the *Liùdū fù* states that a mountain bend is called *yǔ*. The *Shuowen* [also] defines it as composed of the radical *shān* (山) and the phonetic *yǐ* (巳), where *yǐ* also serves as the phonetic.

Regarding "捊磬" (*póu qìng*): the character for *póu* is pronounced with the initial *fú* and the final *yóu*. The *Shàngshū* states, "At the banks of the Sī, there floated *póu*. Kǒng’s commentary says, "Stones seen in the water that can be used as grinding stones. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic "fú" (*fú shēng*). Some collect it under the radical "hand" (*shǒu*), pronouncing it *pú gōu*. The *Hànshī* says, "To *póu* means to gather," which does not accord with the meaning of a *qìng* (stone chime).
"Tǔliù" (吐溜): "liù" is pronounced with the *jiù* (救) rhyme; it is written as "liù" in the collected editions, though this is a vulgar character.

"Lianyi" (漣漪): The first character, "lian," is pronounced with the *liechan* (列纏) rhyme. The *Mao Shi* (毛詩) states: "The waters of the River are clear and have *lianyī*. The commentary says: "When the wind blows and the water forms patterns, it is called *lian*. The second character, "yi," is pronounced with the *yí* (倚) rhyme. The *Mao Shi* commentary states that anciently it was read as *zhí* (直); *yī* (猗) refers to overlapping waves. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文解字) defines *lianyī* as ripples on water. Both characters take "water" (水) as their radical; "lian" and "yī" serve as their phonetic components.

*Wúshí* (玞石): *fǔ* (甫) has no radical reversal. Guo’s commentary on the *Shānhǎijīng* states that *wǔwúshí* resembles jade; it is produced today in Línhú County of Chángshā, being blue in ground with white veins, its color lush and verdant, such that it cannot be clearly distinguished [from jade]. Gu Yěwáng says it is the same as *jiànshí* (瑌石) or *yán* (琰). According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical for "jade" (*yù*) and the phonetic *fú* (夫).

"Shen-zhi" (神質) means "truly transcendent. Han Kangbo’s commentary on the *Zhouyi* states: "Zhi" (質) is equivalent to "ti" (體, body/substance). Song Zhong’s commentary on the *Taixuanjing* states: "Zhi" is the "qu" (軀, physical frame). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "貝" (biàn) and the phonetic "斦" (yín); "斦" has the pronunciation yín. It is incorrect to compose it with the radical "竹" (zhú) as "筫" (zhí)."

*Tíáo* (上徒聊反, 下鷁消反): The phonetic component is *kǎo*. It describes the appearance of mountains standing side by side in towering height. Guo’s commentary on the *Fāngyán* states that *yáo* denotes a high and precipitous form. The *Guǎngyá* defines it as "towering and perilous. The phonetic component is *kǎo*, though it is sometimes written as *tíyáo*. *Hì* is pronounced *ní* (激反). *Tiáo yáo*: This refers to the appearance of mountains standing together in lofty prominence. Guo’s commentary on the *Fāngyán* notes that *yáo* signifies a high and steep aspect. The *Guǎngyá* defines *tiáo* as "perilously high. The phonetic element is *kǎo*, though it is occasionally written as *tíyáo*. *Hì* is pronounced with the rhyme *ní* (激反).

The character 𡻱 (wěi) is composed of the phonetic 雷 (léi) and the radical 山 (shān). The *Kǎo Shēng* states that it describes the appearance of a mountain; it is also written as 𡾊 or 𡾊. Among the standard characters of the past and present, 峞 (wěi) takes the radical 山 and the phonetic 危 (wēi); it is also written as 峞.

*Lǒngchóng* (巃嵸): The first character is pronounced *lóng* (with the initial *dǒng* reversed); the second is pronounced *cōng* (with the radical *zhòng*). The *Bīcāng* states that it describes the appearance of high peaks. The semantic analysis has been completed previously. *Chǎnghuǎng* (敞恍):

The first character is pronounced *chāng* (with the initial *zhǎng* reversed). The *Cāngjiépiān* states that "chǎng" means high and prominent. The *Shuowén* defines it as leveling high ground so that one can look out from afar. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical *pī* (攴) with the phonetic *shàng* (尚). The second character is pronounced *huáng* (with the initial *guǎng* reversed). The *Kǎoshēng* states that *huǎng* describes an appearance of vast emptiness; it is the same character as in the *Zhōngzì*. The *Wenzìdiǎn* explains it as looking out from a distance. It is also written as *huāng* (慌).

Regarding the character *yáo* (嶤) in *wú gǔ* (吾骨): the *Fǎnzǐ* (反字) dictionary states that *qù* (屼) denotes the appearance of a bald mountain. In both ancient and modern standard characters, it is written with the radical "mountain" (*shān*) and the phonetic "wù" (*wù shēng*). The form *qū* (𡵆) is also a common variant. Regarding *shì* (市) in *shì qī* (市𮠔): the *Chèlián* (徹連) dictionary reads it as *fǎn* (反);
the *Jí* (集) dictionary claims it is composed of "gate" (*mén*) and "longevity" (*shòu*), but this is incorrect.

*Chéng* (澄渟): The phonetic transcription is *dí dīng*. The *Pīcāng* states it means "water ceasing to flow"; the *Zìshū* says it means "water stagnating. The *Wénzìdiǎn* explains that it is composed of the radical "water" and the phonetic element "tíng.

*Xiāo* (歊暑): The phonetic transcription is *xī jiāo*. Gù Yěwáng says that *xiāo* refers to hot vapors. The *Shuōwén* describes *xiāoxiāo* as the appearance of vapor emerging. The definition of this character has been explained above.

*Hào* (pronounced with the *jiān* and *kǎo* finals) refers to the white pheasant (*bái hán*). "White pheasant" is the name of a bird; it resembles a pheasant but is white in color with fine black markings. Its cheeks are red, and its crown has hair-like blue feathers. Beneath its belly is the *niǎo-sūn*. Sun Miǎn’s *Táng yùn* states that its tail is five or six feet long. The *Wénzì diǎnshuō* explains that [the character] follows the bird radical with the phonetic *xián* (final *hú niǎo*). The *Cāngjié piān* states that *hào* means "bright," following three white strokes.

*Kī* (溪圻): The phonetic transcription is *jì yí fǎn*. The Master Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states that *kī* means "boundary. The *Shuowén* says it is composed of the radical "earth" (*tǔ*) with the phonetic element "chop" (*jīn*).

*Huángfù* (黃𦽌): The phonetic transcription is *bī bǐ fǎn*. It is a name for a type of herb. The *Pīcāng* states that *fù* grows as a creeping vine and its fruit is edible. In the "Correct Characters of Antiquity and Today," it is written with the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) and the phonetic element "zhè" (*zhè*). *Zhè* is also the phonetic component.

The *Hongmo* (Redberry) and its kin are classified by Xu Shu zhong according to the *Huainanzi*, which states that the fruit resembles the mulberry (*sangshen*) and grows along the banks of rivers; the *Cangjie pian* notes that it is edible. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* identifies it as *baomei* (pronounced *piǎo*), stating that its fruit resembles *guípén* but is larger, red, sour-sweet, and edible. The *Shuowen jiezi* calls it *mamei* (Horse-berry), though it is also written as *bō*.

Regarding the character *yīngǔ* (蘡薁): the first radical is pronounced *yīzhēn* (伊貞反) and the second is *yúliù* (於六反). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* (毛詩傳) states that *yīngǔ* is the name of a plant. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) says it resembles the grape (*pútáo*) but has small, black berries. Both the *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文) entries follow the "grass" radical (*cǎo*). The phonetic components are *yīng* (嬰) and *ào* (奧); the pronunciation of *ào* is as stated above.

*Qīnggāi* (青荄): "Gāi" is pronounced *xié* (諧) with a retroflex final. The *Erya* states that "gāi" means "root. The *Fangyan* notes that in the eastern state of Qi, the root is called "gāi. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "the root of grass," formed from the radical for "grass" (*cao*) and the phonetic "hai" (*hài*).

Regarding *chán* (蟬), it is pronounced *cháng rán* (常然) with a retroflex final. The *Jiyun* writes it with the mouth radical as *yǐn* (吲), with the pronunciation *shī rěn* (施忍). The *Liji* states, "Laughter does not reach the *yǐn* [stage]," but this is not the meaning of *chán*.

*Zhāozhà* (啁𠹗): the first character is pronounced *zhé* (with the *jiāo* rhyme) and the second is pronounced *zé* (with the *jiá* rhyme). Gu Yewang states that *zhāozhà* is the cry of a large bird. Examining the phonology, *zhāozhà* describes the sound of a bird. *Zhāo* may be written as *cháo*, and *zhà* may be written as *zhè*; both are used interchangeably.

"Guǎng" (廣) [pinyin: wǔ, with the final radical reversed]: according to the *Shuowen*, it refers to the side galleries surrounding a hall; it is composed of the "guǎng" (广) radical and the phonetic "wú" (無).

"Yán" (嚴): [pinyin: zhōu, with the final radical reversed]. "Liè" (列): [pinyin: tǐng, with the final radical reversed]; Guo's commentary states that "tǐng" describes the manner of walking. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the "chì" (彳) radical and the phonetic "shì" (是); "chì" has the sound "chěng-chǐ" (逞尺).

*Jiàn* (亘): In the *Mao Shī Zhuàn*, it means "pervasive. The character in the *Jí* (集) [dictionary] is written with the radical *mì* (糸), forming *gēng* (絙); this is an ancient form of the character. *Dèng* (瞪): Pronounced *zhì zhèng* (直證).
The *Běicāng* states it means "staring straight ahead. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical *mù* (目) and the phonetic *dēng* (登).

*Chǎi*: Pronounced *kāi-gǎi*. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "chǎi" means clarity; "kǎi" means dryness. The *Shuowen* defines it as having the appearance of being high and dry. The radical components have already been explained previously.

*Chǎn*: Pronounced *tān-chá-jian*. The *Guangya* states that "chǎn" means to pare away; the *Shenglei* states that "chǎn" means to level. The *Shuowen* explains it as derived from the radical "knife" (*dāo*) with the phonetic "zen" (*shēng*), pronounced *cán*.

The character *yào* (爚) is pronounced with the initial *r* (羊灼反). The *Zìzhǐ* (字指) states that it describes the appearance of flickering lightning; the *Shuowén* also defines it as light, formed from the radical *huǒ* (fire) and the phonetic *yuè* (龠), with *yuè* also providing the sound. The *Jí* (集) [i.e., the *Shuowén Jiézi*] writes it as *làn* (㷿) using the radical *qiān* (僉), but this character does not exist; it is a scribal error.
The character 𩇕 (qíng) is pronounced with the *jing* rhyme group; its previous explanation concluded the analysis of its radical components.

As for 環 (huán), it is pronounced with the *chuan* rhyme group. Examining its phonetic component, it refers to a ring made of jade or gold used to pass through the arm. The compilation [of the dictionary] that writes it as 玔 with the "king" (*wang*) radical is incorrect.

*Língpíng* (伶俜): The upper character is pronounced *líng*; the lower character is pronounced *pǐdīng*. It is also written as *língpíng* with the character *lì* (立). This was explained previously. *Qīngruí* (靑緌): The character *ruí* is pronounced *wěi*.

Zheng’s commentary on the *Yīlǐ* states that "ruí" refers to an ornament for a cap. Guō’s commentary on the *Eryā* identifies it as a *yīng* (sash/neck-strap). The *Shuowén* defines it as that which continues the cap-sash; it is purple-blue in color, composed of the radical *mì* (糸) and the phonetic *wěi*.

*Zài* (pronounced *zhāo* according to Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli*). Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that it is the ornament on the forehead of a horse; it is made by engraving metal, which is what is called *lòu zài*. The commentary on the *Mao Shi* states that the term for the top of the head is *zài*, though it is sometimes written as *xī*.

*Shenbie* (神莂) is pronounced *zhuo-fan*; it refers to the sound of examining [the results]. *Bicang* states that *bie* means the emergence of seeds sown densely or transplanted. According to this, it shares the same meaning as "discrimination" (*fenbie*). It is also written as *binbie* (𧧸莂), both forms being acceptable.

*Lǐyí* (峛崺): The first character is pronounced *lí* (with the level tone) and the second is *yí* (with the departing tone). This term refers to a low and long slope. The *Erya* states: "Lǐyí refers to sand dunes. Guo's commentary says: "It means extending and stretching out along the side. Alternatively, it may be written with the radical for "walking" (*chuò*) as *lǐyí*. The pronunciation of *páng* (旁) is *pú máng* (蒲忙反).

*Bǎozhì* (貏豸): The first character is pronounced *pí* (皮) with the *bǐ* (彼) rhyme; the second is pronounced *chí* (池) with the *zhǐ* (紙) rhyme. It is an onomatopoeic word for the appearance of a steep slope (*bǎi bǎn*). It is composed of the radical *zhì* (豸) and the phonetic *pí* (陂), which is pronounced *pō* (叵) with the *bō* (波) rhyme.

*Nòngzēng* (硱磳): The first character is pronounced *huī* (虧) with the *yún* (雲) rhyme; the second is pronounced *zé* (崱) with the *líng* (陵) rhyme. Wang’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that *nòngzēng* refers to "towering and jagged peaks. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *shí* (石) and the phonetics *kùn* (困) and *zēng* (曾). *Cuī* (崔) is pronounced *cú huí* (徂迴); *wéi* (嵬) is pronounced *wú huí* (吾回); *zēng* (𡸨) is pronounced *zǐ yú* (子余); and *yú* (嵎) is pronounced *wáng jū* (王俱).

*Kuǐguǐ* (磈硊): The first character is pronounced *wēi* (威) with the *guǐ* (鬼) rhyme; the second is pronounced *huǐ* (危) with the *guǐ* (鬼) rhyme. The *Pīcāng* states that *qióngsēngkuǐ* (硱磳硊) refers to rugged and winding terrain. The *Shuōwén* explains that both characters are composed of "stone" (*shí*) and "ghost" (*guǐ*), with "danger" (*wēi*) and "peril" (*huǐ*) serving as their phonetic components. *Kuǐ* (𨒅) is pronounced *xiāngnì* (鄉逆); in the *Zhouyì*, it is written with the "speech" radical (*yán*) as *hù* (誳), pronounced *qū* (屈). *Guǐ* (硊) is written with the "speech" radical as *guǐ* (詭), pronounced *guǐ* (鬼), as noted by Xǔ [Shèn] in the *Huáinánzǐ*, where it means "deceit. These [other readings] are not the meanings of *qióngsēngkuǐ* (硱磳硊) or *kuǐguǐ* (磈硊); the profound mysteries of these terms remain unclear.

"Bānzhī" (坂坻): The upper character is pronounced wǎn (晚) with a retroflex final, meaning "precipitous. The lower character is pronounced zhì (雉) with an initial *k*. The *Shijing* says, "Like a mound (*zhī*), like a mountain (*jīng*). According to the *Shuowen*, "bān" (坂) is also "pō" (坡); it may be written with the radical 𨸏 as "bǎn" (阪). "Zhī" (坻) takes the radical 土 and the phonetic 氐; the pronunciation of 氐 is dì-xī (帝奚). The *Jí* (集) uses 犀 to form "chuí" (墀), referring to the vermilion courtyard of the Son of Heaven; this does not carry the meaning of a steep slope (*bǎn*).

Jiē (upper radical *qián*, second tone; lower radical *jié*, second tone): The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* states that "Jiēniè" describes a high and precipitous appearance. According to the *Shuōwén*, the character *jiē* is composed of the mountain radical and the phonetic *yù*; *niè* is alternatively written as *niè* or *shì*, with the latter being composed of the *chǔo* radical.
*Hóngchéng* (pronounced *wū hóng*): The *Guǎngyǎ* states that *hóng* means "deep"; the *Shuowén* also defines it as "deep and vast," taking *shuǐ* (water) as the radical and *hóng* as the phonetic.

*Ruǎnshí* (pronounced *rú yuǎn*): The *Shānhǎijīng* states that Mount Fūzhū abounds in *ruǎnshí*. Guō’s commentary notes: "In the mountains of present-day Yànmén, there is *ruǎnshí*; the white variety is like ice, while half of it has a reddish hue. The *Shuowén* defines it as "a stone resembling jade. It may also be written with the *yù* (jade) radical as *jiàn*.

"Ā-chí (摛): Bái-zhǐ says it means 'to know' and 'to turn back. Xuán-zhàn’s commentary on the *Shǔdū Fù* states that it means 'to unfold' (*ā-fā*). The *Shuowén* says it means 'to extend. The analysis of its radical was completed previously; the character is formed by combining [the radicals], while *ā-chí* is a vulgar form."

Regarding the term *yùndāng* (篔簹): the first character is pronounced as *yùn* (君反) and the second as *dǎng* (黨即反). Zuo Taichong’s *Wúdū Fù* (吳都賦) states: "As for bamboo, there are the *yùndāng* and the *línlú*. Examining their sounds, these are all names of bamboo species. Both the *Wénzì Diǎnshuō* (文字典說) and other sources state that they are written with the radical for "bamboo" (*zhú*). The phonetic component for *yuán* (圓) serves as the initial sound; *lín* (林) is the pronunciation of *líng* (箖), and *yú* (於) is the pronunciation of *yú* (箊).

*Dilì* (the first character pronounced *shàng dīng lì* and the second *xià líng*): According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, this refers to the color of a bright pearl; it is sometimes written with the "jade" radical as *dílì*.

*Chuízōng* (the first character pronounced *chuí* and the second *zǒng dōng*): According to the *Fangyan*, people of Qi, Yǎn, and Jì call small branches *zōng*; it is also sometimes written with the "bamboo" radical as *zōng*.

*Níng* (upper radical *dīng* with retroflex *l*; lower radical *níng* with final *dìng*). Regarding the sound *qīng*: *nìng* describes the appearance of water. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "clear"; according to the *Shuōwén*, it means "a small stream" (*yíng*), formed with the radical *shuǐ* and the phonetic *níng*. It is also written as *hóng* or *dòng*.

Dúgàn (獨𪄻): The first character is pronounced as *lù* (祿) and the second as *shù zhōng* (束鍾). It is a name for a bird. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states it is the "bird of Qiú-dàn. According to the *Fāngyán*, in the regions between Zhou, Wei, Song, and Chu, it is called Dúchōng (獨舂) or Dìngjiǎ (定甲), also known as Zhègàn (䳚鴠). Guo Pu’s commentary notes that it resembles a pheasant, has five colors, lacks feathers in winter, is naked and red, and cries day and night. The characters 𪈌 and 𪆊 found in the *Jí* (集) are vulgar inventions.

The *Nan Yue Zhi* (Record of Nan Yue) states that the *jiang-ou* (river gull) is also called the *hai-ou* (sea gull). The *Cang Jie Pian* (Cang Jie’s Lexicon) says it is as large as a *wei*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (Explaining Graphs and Analyzing Characters) states: "The *ou* is a water-owl (*shui-xiao*). It is also called the *yi*. It belongs to the 'Bird' radical with the phonetic component 'qu'; the sound of *xiao* is pronounced *yi-jiao*."

The character for *pìdǐ* (鸊鵜): the upper radical is *bìng* (并) with the tone *yì* (伇), and the lower part is *tǐ* (體) with the tone *dī* (低). According to the *Fāngyán* (方言), in regions outside the South and Chu, the small wild duck that submerges itself in water is called *pìdǐ*; its larger variety is called *hùtí* (鶻啼). Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states that its fat can be used to polish knives. Both the *Shuowen Jiezi* and other sources derive it from the bird radical with *pì* (辟) and *xī* (虒) as phonetic components; *xī* has the same pronunciation as above. The character *dǐ* (鵜) in the current collection is a vulgar form.

The character 𠮟 (guǎng) is pronounced as the "lǎo" rhyme. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains that 𠮟 refers to the vast, bright expanse of the primordial qi; it is composed of 日 (sun) and 𠮟 (pronounced gōnglǎo), where the latter character consists of 大 (great) and the eight strokes. Those versions composed of 日 and 天 are vulgar forms. In the *Ji*, it is sometimes written as 昊, sometimes as 莫, or sometimes as 𠮟; all of these are incorrect.

Regarding "xínglíng" (荇蔆): the upper character is pronounced *xìng* (杏). Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "Xíng grows in clusters in the water; its leaves are round, and the length of the stalks varies according to the depth of the water. In Jiangdong, it is eaten and called xíng, or sometimes written as xǐng. The lower character is pronounced *lì zhēng* (力蒸反). Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "Líng is the water chestnut (*qū*) of today. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) and the phonetic "líng" (*líng yì shēng*). The pronunciation of *qū* is *qí jì* (其記反).

*Hàn-dǐ*: the first character is pronounced *gǎn* (as in *gǎn-dàn*) and the second is pronounced *gǎn* (as in *tán-gǎn*). The *Erya* states: "The lotus is called *hé*, *jiǎo*, or *qú*; when its flower has already opened, it is called *fúróng*. It is composed of the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) and the phonetic "hán" (*hán-shēng*), or alternatively written as *hěn* or *hán* (pronounced *yā-xiàn*). The character *dǐ* is composed of the radical "grass" and the phonetic "yán" (*yán-shēng*), or alternatively written as *zhǎn* or *kǎn*; these latter forms do not constitute valid characters.

Lùwù (硉矹): The first character is pronounced *lùn wù* (論兀); the second is *wú gǔ* (吾骨). It describes the sound of large rocks; alternatively, it may be written as *lù'ér* (峍屼) with the radical for mountain (*shan*). Tuító (隤陀): The first character is pronounced *tú huí* (徒回). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to fall down.

Alternatively, it may be written as *kuì* (憒) with the radical for heart (*xin*). The second character is *tá hé* (堂何). Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that a collapsed mountain is called *tuó*. According to the *Shuowen*, it is derived from *tuó* (𨸏), where *tuó* also serves as the phonetic component. The form *tá* (陁) is a vulgar character.

*Sanshao*: the first character is read as *xiá* (上翣銜反) and the second as *shūjiā* (下踈加反). According to the *Kaosheng*, *sanshao* describes the appearance of hanging hair; both characters are written with the radical *biāo* (音必遙反). *Yìyào*:
the first character is read as *xúnlì* (上尋立反) and the second as *yáo zhào* (下遙照反). According to the *Shuowen*, *yìyào* means intense light; both characters are written with the radical *huǒ*.

*Tiānhuáng* (天潢): "Shining light. It is the opposite of *zuǒzhuan* (左傳). *Huáng* (潢) refers to water from ditches or runoff; one interpretation says it refers to what is offered to spirits and deities. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *shui* (水) with *huáng* (黃) as the phonetic.

*Tànglǎng* (曭朗): "Bright and clear. Pronounced *tānglǎng*. According to the *Gujīn zhèngzì*, *tàng* (曭) means "obscure and indistinct," composed of the radical *ri* (日) with *dǎng* (黨) as the phonetic.

*Xiāngbì* (香馝): *Bì* is pronounced as *mì* (with the *ping* tone). According to the *Pīcāng*, *bì* means "great fragrance. The *Shuowen* states it is composed of the radical *xiāng* (fragrance) and the phonetic *bì*.

*Jiǎojiǎo* (敫敫): Pronounced as *yángzhuó* (with the *shang* tone). The *Shuowen* states that *jiǎojiǎo* describes the appearance of flowing light; it is composed of the radicals *bái* (white) and *fàng* (release).
Regarding "zhī bā" (之軷): *pán* (槃) has not yet returned. *Fán* (燔) and *zhì* (炙):

*fán* is pronounced with the initial *fá* (伐) and the final rhyme *fán* (蕃). The *Mao Shih Zhuan* states that Mao [Dong] says: *páo* (炰) is pronounced with the initial *pú* (蒲) and the final rhyme *jiāo* (交); adding fire is called *fán*, while roasting over a fire is called *zhì*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it is formed from the radical "fire" (*huǒ*) and the phonetic component "bàn" (*fān*).
*Tīng rán* (聽然): According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, this means "the appearance of laughter. It is composed of the radical 口 (mouth) with the phonetic 斤 (jīn). *Yǒng lòu* (㟝嶁):
The first character is pronounced *pú kǒu* (蒲口) and the second is *lóu zǒu* (婁走); alternatively, they may be written as 培塿 using the radical 土 (earth).

"Carved walls" (*diāo qiáng*): "Birds perch upon them. Kǒng's commentary on the *Shūjīng* states that "diāo" means "carved and painted. The *Shuowén* says it is composed of "shān" (meaning "hairy") and "zhōu" as its phonetic. The *Jí* (the *Shuowén Jíshì*) writes it with "niǎo" (bird) instead, which is incorrect. "Qiáng" (walls): the lower radical is "yáng" (pronounced *rǎng*). The *Jí* writes it with "tǔ" (earth), which is a vulgar character.

Regarding the characters *lùcǎi* (碌䃚): the first character is pronounced with the initial *lóng* (籠) and the final *dù* (䔍), while the second is pronounced with the initial *cōng* (葱) and the final *lù* (祿). According to the *Kǎośēng* (考聲), *lùcǎi* describes the uneven appearance of stone. The *Jí* (集) [dictionary] follows the character for "grass" (*cǎo*) and writes it as *fú* (𦾯); this character does not exist in the *Zìshū* (字書). Some write it as *cù* (蔟), meaning a gathering of old silkworms; however, the etymological principles of this character remain unclear, and I fear it may be an error.

*Qì* (讋): [The character] *zhān* (詹) and *yè* (葉) are reversed; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "to lose one's breath while speaking," following the radical "speech" (言) and the abbreviated form of "dragon" (龍); the phonetic is *tán* (潭), combined with *hé* (合). This has also been explained previously. *Cù* (踧) and *jí* (踖):

*Cù* is pronounced *jiū* (啾) and *liù* (六) in combination; *jí* is pronounced *jīng* (精) and *yì* (亦) in combination. Ma’s commentary on the *Lunyu* states that *cùjí* is the appearance of respectful decorum. The *Guangya* says *cùjí* means awe and respect. *Cù* may also be written as *cù* (踧); the *Shuowen* states that *jí* (踖) follows the radical "foot" (足) and the phonetic *xī* (昔). The *Ji* (集) edition writes it as *cù* (蹙), meaning "to gather," which is not the meaning of *cùjí*.
*Jiangwan* (pronounced *go*) is the name of a place and also the name of a person. *Jiejin* (kun-wu fan):
according to the *Guangya*, "to tie" (*jiejin*) means not to untie; according to the *Shuowen*, *jin* also means to tie, or it may be written with the radical for "heart" (*xin*) as *kuè*.
"Zi (𢡚)": *qi* and *cuo* are reversed; according to the *Shuowen*, "zi" means pain, composed of the radical "heart" (*xin*).
"Tuo" (陀): *tu* and *he* are reversed; according to the *Fangyan*, "tuo" means to revile. It is assembled from the radical "person" (*ren*) to form "ta"; this is not yet fully understood.
*Nèi* (內): *pí* (皮) with the *mǐ* (美) rhyme; the commentary on the *Shàngshū* states that *pǐ* (圮) means "ruined.

It is composed of the radical *tǔ* (土). *Xū* (欻): *fēng* (逢) with the *yù* (吁) and *wù* (勿) rhymes; the commentary on the *Xījīng fù* states that *xū* (欻) means "sudden. The *Shuōwén* says it is composed of the radical *qiàn* (欠) and the phonetic *yán* (炎). The character *jí* (集) uses *yì* (邑) instead, reading as *tán* (郯) with the *tán* (彈) and *gān* (甘) rhymes; this is a place name and does not carry the meaning of "sudden."

*Di* (遰): Pronounced *dì* (with the radical *jì* reversed). Liu Kui’s commentary on the "Rù Dū Fù" states: "To look out at a distance across a precipitous gap. The *Shuowén* says it means "to depart," composed of the radical *chuò* (辵) and the phonetic *dài*.

*Yǔnxī* (殞欷): Pronounced *yǔn xī* (with *xī* having the initial *xìn*). Hé Xiū’s commentary on the *Gōngyáng Zhuàn* states: "Xī means sorrow. The commentary on the *Cāngjié Piān* says it is a residual sound. The *Shuowén* says it is composed of the radical *qiàn* (欠) and the phonetic *xī*.
*Sù* (傃): Pronounced *sū* with the *gù* (故) rhyme. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "Sù means to face toward. It follows the person. *Mò* (覛):

Pronounced *wǎng-méng-bè* (往萌蘗). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Mò refers to a sidelong glance. It is composed of the radical *jiàn* (見) and the phonetic *lì* (𠂢); *lì* is pronounced *pǔ-bài* (普拜). The character *yǐng* (永) is used in the *Jí* (集), but it is a vulgar form of the character *gēi* (𧠧).

*Bǎo* (in the *Hànshū*, it means the hair on a person's head is like the appearance of *péngbǎo* [wild grasses in a thicket]). According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) and the phonetic element "bǎo.
*Hù* (pronounced *gū wù*): according to the *Shuowén*, it refers to a chronic illness; its correct form is written as *guì*.
*Kǎn* (with the *dàn* and *gān* finals): to exhaust; to bring to an end.

*Jù* (with the *rùn* and *chún* finals): according to the *Erya*, a bull seven chi tall is called *rùn*. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that a yellow ox with black lips is called *rùn*; it is also simply called *rùn*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "ox."
*Zuǎi* (蕞): The opposite of *cuī* (摧). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "small" (*xiǎo*) and is composed of the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) with the phonetic element *zuì* (*㝡*).

The inclusion of the "hand" radical (*shǒu*) to form *zuō* (*撮*) is an error. *Jìng* (競): Pronounced *dòng* (冬). Both the *Yunjí* and various character dictionaries state that *jìng* refers to the sound *zhì* (*𠯗*). It is also written as *jìng* (*𠯗*).

The character *chō* (捉) is pronounced *hsié* (頡) with the *jian* (堅) radical; the *Wenzi Jilüe* (文字集略) states that "string" (*xián*) refers to drawing a bow. It is incorrect for the *Jí* (集) to write it as *yuè* (䩙) with the *ge* (革) radical.

The character *wàng* (望) is pronounced *shì* (是) with the *shi* (時) radical; it is an ancient form of the character *shi* (時). It is incorrect for the *Jí* (集) to write it as *shèn* (𣆊) with the *zhōng* (中) radical.

*Song* (駷): pronounced *sù* (with the *yù* radical reversed); He Xi’s commentary on the *Gōngyáng Zhuàn* states it means "to pull at the bit and gallop. The *Shuowén* says it is composed of the radical *mǎ* (馬) and the phonetic *shù* (束).
*Jiǎo* (矯): pronounced *péimèi* (反); the *Jí* (集) edition writes it as *fēn* (𦇷), which does not form a valid character; it is the same as below.
*Qíqū* (pronounced *qǐyí* for the first character and *qū* for the second).

*Jìyù* (pronounced *níjì*). It refers to incoherent speech where one is unaware of what is being said; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "sleep-talking" (*miányǔ*). It is composed of the abbreviated form of *mèng* (dream) with *niè* as the phonetic component. *Niè* is pronounced *yánjié*. The version in the *Jí* (Jiyun) which uses the character *kǒu* (mouth) to form *nì* is incorrect.

"Piercing through" (*jié*)—the *zhèng* commentary on the *Zhouli* states that from the day *jiǎ* to *guǐ*, it is called "piercing through"; the *Mao shi zhuan* says it means "to reach," and the *Erya* says it means "to penetrate. It is written with the radical for water.

*Tàtuo* (涾沱): The first character, *tán*, is pronounced with the *dá* rhyme. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "overflowing" (*tàyì*) and is composed of the radical "water" (*shui*) with *dá* as its phonetic. The *Ji* (Collection) version writes it as *tà*, which is incorrect. The second character, *tuó*, is pronounced with the *hé* rhyme. The *Kaosheng* states it describes the appearance of copious rain or water (*pāngtuó*). The *Ji* version writes it as *tó*, which does not form a valid character.
"Jianxiang" (磵響) is pronounced *jiānyàn*; it is a false name for the title of General (*jiāngjùn*). "Chanjì" (剗跡) is pronounced *chǎnjì*;

according to the *Guǎngyá*, "chan" means to shave or pare away; according to the *Shēnglèi*, it means level or smooth, though some versions write it with the "metal" radical as "chǎn" (鏟), which is incorrect; the *Jí* (集) version writes it as "chǔn" (剷), which is also incorrect.

"Lièzhèn" (列陣): "liè" is read as liánchèfǎn (連徹反). Yuè Wáng says that "liè" means to arrange or deploy in rows and order. The version compiled by Jí reads it as "lì" with the phonetic value lì, which does not carry the meaning of "array.
"Jùn" (駿): "jì" is read as yízhìfǎn (移質反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it refers to a horse with swift feet; it is composed of the radical "horse" (馬) and the phonetic component "shī" (失).

*Tuǒ* (with the phonetic *dú* and *dōu* as counter-phonemes) is the name of a mountain; it is also written as *tú*, which is a false borrowing used for its meaning. The character is formed with the radical *jīn* (metal), forming *tuó*; this character does not exist [in standard dictionaries].

*Yìjié* (with the phonetic *tián* and *jié* as counter-phonemes): according to the *Erya*, *jié* means "old. The commentary on the *Mao Shi* states that eighty years is called *jié*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it is composed of *lǎo* (old) and the phonetic *zhì*.

The character 奰 (pì) is pronounced *bì* (with the *fù* radical). The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* states: "To be angry without being drunk is called *pì*. The *Shuōwén* correctly writes it as 奰, composed of three dogs and three eyes; two eyes constitute the character 尨 (*māng*), and adding one more eye increases its meaning. The pronunciation of 尨 is *quàn*.

*Jiàn* (隙): The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that this character is formed from *jiǎo* (𨸏) and *yì* (𡭽) as its phonetic component; it is also written with *dù* (𠫤). It refers to a place name (*chí*) and does not carry the meaning of "a gap" (*jiàn*).

*Cè* (策): Pronounced *qí* (疑) or *gē* (革). In the *Liji*, it says: "When the ruler's carriage is about to be driven, the charioteer holds the whip and stands before the horses. Gu Yewang stated: "A whip is used to strike horses. It is formed from the bamboo radical.

The character *huá* (姡) is used in the sense of "to snatch" (*huó*) and in the *Fāngyán* as "cunning" (*jiǎo*). According to the *Shuōwén*, *tiǎn* (靦) means "the face"; it is composed of the radical *nǚ* (女) with *fèn* (䏦) abbreviated as the phonetic. The correct form is *huá* (姡), pronounced *hú guā* (胡刮反); *tiǎn* (靦) is pronounced *tiān xiǎn* (天顯反). *Tiǎn* also refers to being shameless.

"Piao-biao" (飄猋)—the second character is pronounced *yáo* according to Guo’s commentary on the *Erya*, which states that it refers to a violent wind rising from below. Some write it as "piao" (飈) with the radical for wind added, or as "yan" (焱) with three fire radicals; the latter is pronounced *yàn* and is not correct in meaning.

The upper character [of 㤹] is pronounced *qí* (with the *zī* and *fǎn* finals). According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "difficult" (*nán*). Gu Yewáng says it refers to a state of mental hesitation and lingering doubt. Regarding the phonetic component, it correctly follows the radical for "running" (*zǒu*) to form [the character], which is also written as [the character]. The *Jí* (Collection) writes it as [the character], but this character does not exist in standard dictionaries. The lower character [of 㤹] is pronounced *yú*. Regarding the phonetic component, it correctly uses [the character]; the *Guǎngyá* uses the radical for "eyes" (*mù*) to form [the character], while the *Yùnjí* (Rhyme Collection) writes it as [the character], which is identical to the character in the *Jí*.

*Péngyǒng* (淜泳): The former character is pronounced *píng* (皮冰反) and the latter *yǒng* (上榮命反). According to the *Erya*, it refers to crossing a river on foot (*túshā*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means to cross a river without a boat or oars; it is also written as the character *píng*. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* says: "To *yǒng* means to travel by submerging oneself at the bottom of the water. The *Shuowen* states that the sound of the character is derived from *yǒng* (水永聲).

*Zǔ* (阻): The glossary *Yǐyá* (爾雅) defines *sì* (涘) as *yá* (厓). Guo’s commentary states it refers to the water’s edge. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains that it is composed of the radical *shui* (水) with the phonetic *yǐ* (矣). *Wéi* (為): Pronounced *fǔ* (撫) or *fū* (膚).

According to the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲), this refers to binding bamboo and wood upon the water; it is called *fū*. The *Wenzi Dianshuō* (文字典說) states that *fū* (泭) is made by weaving bamboo and wood, composed of the radical *shui* (水) with the phonetic *fù* (付). The version in the *Lúnyǔ* (論語) uses *fú* (桴) or *chèn* (𣻜); the version in the *Jí* (集) uses *fù* (附), which is an error.
*Bò* (in the *Shuowen*, "to tread upon," composed of 足 and 貪 with the phonetic 合; in the *Ji*, it is written as 󳃂 with 弇 as the phonetic—this character does not exist in standard dictionaries).
*Xì* (in the *Shuowen*, "to gaze," composed of 目 and 兮 with the phonetic 兮).

The character *zī* (孜) is pronounced with the final *fǎn* (反). Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjìng* states that it means "diligent and unremitting. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical *pī* (攴) and the phonetic *zī* (子); some editions of the *Jízhōng* write it as the character *jìng* (敬), which is incorrect.

*Shēn* (攕): In the *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry), it says that *shēnshēn* is equivalent to *xiānxian* (slender). Kong’s commentary on the *Shàngshū* states that "fine" (*xiān*) means thin; this is the same as the character *xiān*. 30.

Fascicle 30, *Guǎng Hóngmíng jí* (Extended Collection for the Propagation and Clarification of the Light). Fascicle 30. *Zhào* (櫂): Pronounced with the initial *zhái* and final *-jiào*. Wáng Yì’s commentary on the *Chǔcí* (Elegies of Chǔ) states that *zhào* refers to oars. According to the *Fāngyán*, oars are also called *zhào*; alternatively, they are written as *zhào* (棹). *Dá* (柁): Pronounced with the initial *dá* and final *-kě*. The *Shìmíng* (Explanations of Names) states that the stern of a boat is called *dá*; *dá* also implies dragging. Examining the sounds, *yè* (拽) is also explained as *dá*, and they are mutually glossed. The *Shuōwén* writes it as *dá* (柁), while the *Jí* (Collection) writes it as *dà* (柂); the latter is a vulgar form.

*Qiè* (契) means "to clarify" (*míng*) or "to match" (*chóu*). In the *Shuōwén*, it is glossed as "xiān" (疇), with the phonetic component *xī* (溪) and the counter *jì* (計). Yuè Wáng says that all mutual agreements are called *qiè*. Dù’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states: "*Qiè* refers to words of agreement. The *Shuōwén* takes *dà* (大) as the radical and *kuài* (㓞) as the phonetic; *kuài* is pronounced *kǒubā* (口八反). It is an error to take *zuò* (作) as the radical and form *xiē* (楔).
*Ē* (糲): The heart radical with the phonetic *lǎn* (蘭) and the reversed *dǎ* (達); alternatively written as *jiè* (䊪). *Míng* (鳴):
The bird radical with the phonetic *qín* (禽) and the reversed *jīn* (金); the *Jí* (集) edition writes it as *mǐ* (𤢌), which is incorrect. *Xì* (隙):

The "window" radical with the phonetic *qīng* (卿) and the reversed *yù* (逆); the *Jí* (集) edition writes it as *qì* (郄), which is incorrect, as it refers to a place name rather than the meaning of a window crack.
The character *shén* (神) with the radical *pèi* (轡) is a vulgar and erroneous variant; it is incorrect.

*Hài* (咍)—with the phonetic *huǎn* (歡) and the radical *wáng* (王)—Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that *hài* means "to laugh," for the people of Chu called laughter *hài*. It is sometimes written as *chēng* (󳇫).
*Tíáo* (dí diāo fǎn): *Wěiwěi* (wú wěi fǎn).
According to the *Shuowen*, this means "the appearance of height," composed of the radical *guǐ* (𨸏) with the phonetic *guǐ*.

*Piǎobiè* (shàng piāomiǎo fǎn; xià piānmie fǎn): Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that "piǎo" refers to the gaze upon the light of a comet, while "biè" means it flickers. According to the *Shuowen*, "piǎo" means a bluish-white color, composed of the radical *mì* with the phonetic *piào*; "biè" means merely to see, composed of the radical *mù* with the phonetic *bì*. *Piào* is pronounced *pǐxiāo* (fǎn).
"Ran-dun" (染沌) is written with the character "chui-lun" (垂綸), which is also the character "chun" (純).
"Kun-kuang" (崑󲕕): the upper character has the phonetic "kun" (昆) and the lower has "ang" (昂) as its respective finals; the *Ji* (集) version writes it as "e" (崿), which is a vulgar form.

"Yi-ming-pian" (椅明翩): the upper character "yi" (椅) has the phonetic "yi-yi" (倚冝); Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states that "yi" is the same as "qiu" (楸); according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "wood" (木) with "qi" (奇) as its phonetic.

*Wǎnluǎn*: The first character is read as *yùn* (with the radical *shǒu*), and the second as *luán* (with the radical *shǒu*). The *Jí* edition writes it as *liàn*, which is an error. *Kān*: Read as *qiǎn* (with the radical *jiān*).
The *Jí* edition writes it as *kān*, which is a vulgar character. *Céngróng*:

The first character is read as *zhā* (with the radical *zēng*), and the second as *huò* (with the radical *méng*). The *Jí* edition follows the *Yíng* edition in writing it as *yǐng*, which is an error.
*Mó* (摹): the initial rhyme is *tài-mù-hú-fǎn*.

*Chéngtiáo* (承蜩): the final rhyme is *tíng-liáo-fǎn*. The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* states that *tiáo* refers to the cicada (*chán*). According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "insect" (*chóng*) with the phonetic element *zhōu*.
*Lěi* (纍): the final rhyme is *wēi-lěi-wěi-fǎn*; it is also written as *lěi* (絫).
"Biāo" (標) means "to mark" or "to indicate. Yěwáng (野王) says it is a "marker" (*biǎo*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) with the phonetic "piào" (*piào*).
"Juǎn" (捲) is pronounced *jué yuàn* (厥苑); the phonetic "kǎo" (*kǎo*) indicates the meaning of "to roll up," "to gather," or "to collect. It is also written as "quǎn" (卷).
In the character 倅 (cuì), the radical is 人 (rén) and the phonetic is 崔 (cuī).
In the character 驪 (lí), the radical is 馬 (mǎ) and the phonetic is 麗 (lì); the *Shuowen* states it refers to a horse that can travel a thousand li.

In the character 朏 (fěi), the radical is 月 (yuè) and the phonetic is 出 (chū); the commentary on the *Shangshu* by Confucius states that "fěi" means brightness, while the *Shuowen* states it is composed of the radical 月 and the phonetic 出.

The character 間 (jiān) is pronounced as *shì*. Some editions have 集 (jí), while others have 垂 (chuí); however, upon examining various books, this character is not found there. Furthermore, it differs from the original rhyme; its description remains unclear.

The character 󳄹 (guì) is pronounced as *gāng láo zǎo fǎn*. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that it means "rafters" (*chuī*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* says 󳄹 means "purlins" (*chuán*), composed of the radical 木 with the phonetic 𤊽; the sound of 尞 is *liáo*.
*Shí-děng* (石隥): "Děng" is pronounced with the *dèng* rhyme (as in *dèng*). Guo’s commentary on the *Mu Tianzi Zhuan* states that *děng* means a slope or embankment;

it is sometimes written as *dèng* (蹬) with the radical for feet. *Hàn* (󲾷): "Hàn" is pronounced with the *tán* rhyme (as in *tán*). Regarding the term for a flower that has not yet opened, it is called *hàn*. The interpretation of this character's meaning was completed previously in the twenty-ninth fascicle; the variant *hàn* (菡) is also acceptable.

"Qi-dai-tai" (欺紿臺) refers to rebellion against Liu Zhao; the commentary on the *Guliang Zhuan* states that "dai" (紿) means mutual deception. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines "dai" as "to doubt," written with the radical "silk" (糸) and the phonetic "tai" (台), pronounced *shū-zhì-tái-gǎi-fǎn*.
Guo's commentary on the *Erya* states that "zhì" (䈚) refers to the sprouts of the *jiàn* (箭) bamboo; the *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it with the radical "bamboo" (竹) and the phonetic "dài" (怠).

*Bei* (珠琲): "Pei" is pronounced *mei fan gu*. Wang Ye stated that "pei" refers to the name for a string of pearls; one hundred pearls constitute a string (*guan*), and five strings constitute a *pei*. It is also written as *bei*. *Lao* (龍澳): "Ao" is pronounced *yu liu fan*.

The *Commentary on the Mao Shih* states that "ao" means a sheltered recess or bay. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it is composed of the radical "water" (*shui*) with "ao" as its phonetic component; "ao" also serves as its sound.

*Diao-sai* (the character *sai* pronounced as in the sixth tone): According to the *Guǎyá*, it means "to arrive. The *Shuowén* states that it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) with the phonetic element *sai*.
*Tímàn*: the character *màn* is pronounced as in *dì-xī*. The previous commentary has already explained its meaning.
*Huái-xù*: the character *xù* is pronounced as in *xú-yǔ*. According to the *Kǎośēng*, *xù* refers to a riverbank or inlet.

Regarding "cǎi rǐ" (彩毦), its meaning refers to looking back; Wang Yanwang stated that it denotes adorning with feathers. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "hair" (毛) and the phonetic "qu" (取).

Regarding "shèn" (沈󳐀), the rhyme is *wǔ bèi* (侮輩); the *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that "shèn" means illness. The correct form is "shèn" (󳐀), while the version in the *Jiji* (集) as "huì" (痗) is a vulgar character.
The golden scalpel reverses the closed-off delusion.

*Qin* (pronounced with the *can* rhyme): according to the *Shuowen*, this describes the rapid gait of a horse; it is composed of the radical "horse" (*ma*) and the phonetic "sheng" of the abbreviated form of "qin.

*Zao* (pronounced with the *lao* rhyme): Gu Yewang states that *zao* means to wash clean; according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "water" (*shui*) and the phonetic "sao," where *sao* is pronounced *sudao*.

"Shānyīng (Mountain Oriole)" [pronounced *ēng* with the *gēng* rhyme]. The *Mao Shì Zhuàn* says: "It is called *yīng* because it possesses patterns. Examining the phonology, this refers to the appearance of the bird's plumage patterns. "Liúliàng (Clear and Resonant)":

the first character is read as *liù* with the *zhōu* rhyme, and the second as *liáng* with the *zhàng* rhyme. The edition that writes the second character as *tūn* following the radical for water is incorrect.

"Míng bō fú móu fǎn kǎo shēng" (The sound of the drumstick striking the drum, the plan for rebellion is examined). "Bō" refers to the mallet used for striking a drum. The *Jí* (Collection) follows [the reading] "fú" and writes it as "fū. Master Ma’s commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* states that "fū" refers to bamboo and wood woven together; thus, the name is not "bō," which carries the meaning of a drumstick.

*Luo* (upper tone) and *luǎo* (second tone). The *Mao Shi* says, "The *luǎo* and the *nǚluó* spread over the pines and cypresses. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Luǎo is a parasitic plant; it is composed of the radical 'grass' and the phonetic 'niǎo'; the final rhyme is *púkuàng*. The *Shuowen* also states: "Páng means to walk in close attachment; it is composed of the radical 'chěng' and the phonetic 'páng. The *Jí* [dictionary] uses the radical 'grass' to write it as *bàng*, which is incorrect.

*Zǐ* (輜軒): Pronounced *zǐ* (with the initial *jī* as a variant). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "chariot" (*chē*) and the phonetic "zāi" (*zāi* also serves as the phonetic). The version compiled [in the *Jiji*] as *shǐ* does not form a valid character and is incorrect.
*Xian* (下): Pronounced *xiān* (with the initial *qiān* as a variant). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to advance"; it is composed of the radical "walking" (*chuò*) and the phonetic "qiān."
*Ā* (㜪) is pronounced as *si* with the *shèng* (臻) rhyme; it is a name for a state.

*Cìfēi* (佽飛) is pronounced as *cī* with the *lì* (利) rhyme; it is the name of an office for men of physical prowess during the Han dynasty. The semantic interpretation has already been explained previously.
*Jì* (亟) is pronounced as *liú* with the *qí* (欺) rhyme; it is a number. *Shuāng* (雙) is pronounced as *zhuō* (捉); when written as *hán* (凾), it is the character *xián* (咸).
*Bǎi lǎng* (郎, dǎn): The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* states that *lǎng* means "bright. It is also written as *lǎng* or *lǎng*; both are interchangeable. *Yáo dùn* (遯, tún):
According to the *Shuōwén*, *dùn* means "to move away" or "to withdraw. It is sometimes written as *dùn* or *dùn*; the character *mèi* (𦟥) in the *Jí* (集) is an erroneous transcription for *zhú* (逐).
*Fayun* (the first character pronounced with the *yù* and *yún* rhymes) is a monastic name. *Sāsǎ* (the second character pronounced with the *sū* and *hé* rhymes).

*Mín* (the third character pronounced with the *mì* and *bīn* rhymes): the *Shān-hǎi-jīng* states that Mínn is located within the sea, and to its northwest there is a mountain; according to the *Shuōwén*, it refers to the Yuè people of the southeast, derived from the radical "insect" (*chóng*) and the phonetic "mén."

*Bian* (砭): The pronunciation is *lian* (廉) with a reversed tone. The *Cangjie pian* states it means "dead thorns. The *Shuowen jiezi* says it is using stone to prick away illness. It is correctly written as *bian* (󲺃). *Xu* (橚) and *sen* (槮):
