The upper character is pronounced *xiao tiao* (小條) and the lower is *xia lin* (下林). The *Shuowen jiezi* states that *xu sen* describes the appearance of tall trees. Both follow the radical for wood (*mu*). *Su* (肅) and *can* (參) are their phonetic components. It is an error to combine *xiao* (蕭) to form *xu* (橚).
The character "liáo" (寥) is read as "jì" (寂). The entry from the *Shuowen Jiezi* stating that it is formed from "water" and "liáo" (條) is incorrect.

Compiled by the Sramana Hui-lin: *Fayuan zhulin* (Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Dharma), one volume; *Faxian zhuan* (Biography of Faxian), one volume; *Hui-chao zhuan* (Biography of Hui-chao), three volumes;

*Wuxing fashi shu* (Treatise by Dharma Master Wuxing), one volume; *Zhao lun* (Treatise of Zhaolun), two volumes; *Zhi guan men lun* (Treatise on the Gate of Stopping and Contemplation), two volumes; *Anle ji* (Collection on Peace and Bliss), two volumes; *Baofa yi lun* (Treatise on the Meaning of the Precious Dharma), one volume; *Baowang lun* (Treatise on the King of Jewels), three volumes; *Jinbi juemo lun* (Treatise on the Golden Scalpel for Piercing the Veil), one volume; *Biqiuni zhuan* (Biographies of Bhikṣuṇīs), four volumes; *Guansin lun* (Treatise on Contemplating the Mind), one volume; *Qunyi lun* (Treatise Resolving Various Doubts), seven volumes; *Shiyi lun* (Treatise Resolving Ten Doubts), one volume; *Yuxiang fa* (Method for Bathing the Image), one volume; *Zuifu yaohang* (Essential Practices for Sin and Merit), one volume; *Shouyong sanshui* (The Three Waters for Enjoyment), one volume; *Fangsheng yi* (Ritual for Releasing Living Beings), one volume. Excluding those with old pronunciations, forty-one new volumes have been added; none of these have yet been provided with phonetic glosses, as noted above.

The aforementioned seventeen collections, including the *Fǎlùn* (Discourse on the Dharma) and others, comprise thirty-six fascicles; their phonetic readings are identical to those in this present fascicle.

Regarding the term *kǎi* (慨) in the *Fǎxiǎn zhuan* (Biography of Faxian): the *Shī* (Odes) commentary by Zhèng states that *kǎi* means "to sigh. In both ancient and modern standard characters, it is written with the "heart" radical (*xīn*) and the phonetic component "jì" (*jì shēng*).
*Huiwei* (慧嵬) is a monastic name; the character *wei* (嵬) is pronounced with the outer radical *wai* (猥).
*Noutan* (耨檀) is a personal name in the Xianbei language; the first character is pronounced with the upper radical *nong* (農) and the second with *dan* (丹).
*Zhangye* (張掖) is the name of a commandery in the desert region; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the "hand" radical (*shou*) and the phonetic element *ye* (夜).

*Dūnhuáng*: The first character is pronounced *tú* (with the tone of *huán*) and the second has the sound *huáng*. The *Hànshū* states that it is the name of a commandery established by Emperor Wǔ in the first year after the *yòu-yuán* era, having been separated from Jīuquán; Dù Lín considered it to be the ancient Guāzhōu. To write it as *Túnhuáng* is an error.

Regarding the character "qí" (崎嶇): the first radical is pronounced as *yí* (儀) and the second as *qū* (曲). This has already been explained in the first fascicle of the *Chánfǎ zhènghuì zhuàn*. Within this biography, the reading of "qī" (踦) for the character "zuǒ" (作) is incorrect.
*Chū* (upper radical *zhàn*, *rán*): Gu Yewang states that *chū* means "roughly" or "briefly. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *mi* (grain) with the phonetic *qiě*.

In the transmitted texts, it is also written as *zhān*, which is likewise acceptable. *Zhān* (lower radical *hán*, *è*): The commentary on the *Mao Shi* states that *hè* refers to a coarse woolen cloth (*máo bù*). It is made by twisting camel hair and weaving it into a garment. It is composed of the radical *yī* (clothing) with the phonetic *hé*; the pronunciation of *hé* is the same as the upper character.
Regarding the *Yanguo shangye* (The Tribute of the Yanguo State), it was already discussed previously in the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions).

As for *duohu* (埵壺)—the first character is pronounced *tuo* (吐臥反) and the second has the phonetic value *hu*—the *Shuowen jiezi* states: "A *hu* is a round vessel of Kunwu; it is a pictograph formed from the character for 'large' (*da*) with its lid. It is now written as *hu*.
"Carving stone" (záo shí): the first character is pronounced as cáng (cáng-lo) and was already fully explained in the previous fascicle.

"Ladder" (tī): the second character is pronounced as dī (dī-tǐ). The *Kǎo Shēng* states that "tī-děng" means it can be used for climbing. In the standard characters of antiquity and today, this is written with the radical "wood" (木) and the phonetic "di" (弟). The transmitted text writes it with the radical "foot" (足) as "𨁃," which is incorrect.

Regarding the character 縆 (pronounced *gēng*, with the ancient reading *háng*): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that 縆 means "a large rope. It is composed of the radical 糸 (silk/thread) and the phonetic 恒. The transmitted text writes it as 絙 (*huán*), which is incorrect; this is also due to the omission of the "heart" (心) radical in the transcription.
*Shài* (曬): Regarding the phonetic reading, it is pronounced *shà* (上, 色, 懈). The *Kǎośēng* states that it means "to expose to the sun" (*bào*).

The *Shuōwén* says it is composed of the radical *rì* (sun) and the phonetic *lì*. *Niè* (𧵍): Regarding the phonetic reading, it is pronounced *móuhòu* (上, 矛, 候). Gù Yěwáng states that *niè* is synonymous with *jiāoyì* (exchange). The *Erya* says *niè* means "market. The *Shuōwén* says it means "to exchange goods" and is composed of the radical *bèi* (treasure/wealth) and the phonetic *yuàn*. The transmitted text uses *fèn* (𧴵), which is a vulgar character.
The name of the king is *Rājā Śrīṣeṇa* (𦋺膩色迦王). "Śrī" (*śì*) is pronounced with the initial *x* (例反) and the final *ni* (尼利反); this is the Sanskrit term for "king.

"Zhen" (椹) is pronounced with the initial *y* (上音員) and the final *zhī-lín* (下知林反). The *Cāngjié piān* (蒼頡篇) states that "zhen" refers to a wooden block used for axes (*fū-zhèn*). Guō’s commentary on the *Eryǎ* says it is the "substance for hewing wood. In both ancient and modern standard characters, it is written with the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "shèn" (*shēn*). The characters *dàn* (碪), *zhèn* (砧), and *chèn* (磓) are all identical in meaning.

Regarding *qiāo* (敲): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "to strike," composed of the radical *pō* (攴) and the phonetic *gāo* (高). Regarding *bō* (鈸): the *Kaosheng* states it is the name of a musical instrument; its shape is like a small stack of coins with a loop on the back, which is struck with the mouth to harmonize the music. It is pronounced *pán* (盤) and *bō* (鉢) [for the character 鈸]. *Kǎo* (考) is the phonetic for the character *shēng* (聲). *Jin-zhan* (噤戰): The upper character *qín* (琴) is reversed [to *jǐn*] (琴錦反). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that “closing the mouth is called *jin*. The *Shuowen* says it is composed of the radical 口 with the phonetic 禁;

it is also written as *yin* (唫). *Tong-du* (銅𥁄): The lower character is *yǔ* (羽) reversed [to *dù*] (俱反). He Lin’s commentary on the *Gongyang* states that “*du* is a drinking vessel. The *Fangyan* says that a footless bowl is called a *du*. The *Shuowen* says it is a drinking vessel composed of the radical 皿 with the phonetic 亐; the version in the [commentary] is written as *wu* (杅), which is a vulgar character.
"Pīlì" (霹靂): the first character is pronounced with the *pǐ* rhyme and the *mò* radical; the second is pronounced with the *líng* rhyme. It is not correct to write it as "pìlè" (礔礰). "Wèirán" (蔚然):

the first character is pronounced with the *wěi* rhyme. The *Cāngjié piān* states that "wèi" describes the lush appearance of grasses and trees. According to the *Guǎnpǐ*, it means "dense shade. In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, it follows the "grass" radical and uses "wèi" as its phonetic component.

*Caṇḍamānā*: The first character is pronounced *zhān* (with the *rán* tone); the second character is pronounced *yǎo*. This is a Sanskrit name for a female follower of non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*).
*Pīliè* (劈裂): The first character is pronounced *pǐ* (with the *mò* tone);

the second character is pronounced *liè*. *Ráogù* (嬈固): The first character is pronounced *nǎo* (with the *niǎo* tone). The *Shuowen* states that "rào" means "harshness" (*kē*). Another interpretation says it means "to mock and toy with one another. It is composed of the radical "woman" (*nǚ*) and the phonetic "yáo."
*Ra-ba-si-p'o-mi*: the final *ba* is pronounced like *pan*; this is the name for the son of a Brahmin in the Sanskrit language.

*Ch'eng-lu*: the final *lu* is pronounced like *hu*; the *Shuo-wen* states that *lu* refers to the bracket-capital atop a pillar, composed of the radical "wood" (*mu*) with the phonetic "lu," and the final *dou* is pronounced like *dang-gou*.

"Two *pi* (pronounced *bin* with a retroflex *r*). The *Erya* states that "a *pi*" means a pair or a union. The *Huainanzi* says: "The number of the five notes is five; multiplying five by eight intervals yields forty. Therefore, four *zhang* constitute one *pi*. A *pi* is the measure of the two hands of a person of average stature. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "It is four *zhang*. It is composed of the radical *xi* (box) and the character *ba* (eight); *ba* is also the phonetic component. The transmitted form *pu* is a vulgar character."

Cánbǒ (殘跛): The first character is read as cái (才) with the *fǎn* (反) tone; the second is read as bō (波) with the *wǒ* (我) *fǎn* tone. Gù Yěwáng states that it means "lame. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it means "walking unsteadily," composed of the radical 足 (foot) and the phonetic element 皮 (pí).
Bóshān (搏山): Read as bēn (奔) with the *mò* (莫) *fǎn* tone.

Regarding "xiǎn xī" (險巇): the first character is pronounced *yǎn* (儼). Wang Yanwang states that "xiǎn" means "obstruction" (*zǔ*). Jia's commentary on the *Guoyu* says it means "perilous" (*wēi*). The *Fānyán* says it means "high. The *Shuowén* says it means "obstacle and difficulty" (*zhǔ nán*), composed of the radical 山 and the phonetic 僉; the version in the *Chuán* (傳) as "zhǎn" (嶮) is incorrect. The second character is pronounced *qí* (奇). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* says "xiǎn xī" means "overturned and precarious" (*diān wēi*). The correct character for both ancient and modern usage is composed of the radical 山 and the phonetic 戲.

"Rurmi" (乳麋): The second character is pronounced *bei* (美悲反). This refers to rice gruel boiled with cow’s milk, thick like a cake or porridge; it is colloquially called "milk-porridge" (*rurmi*), though this is not the standard terminology. Regarding "tian xian" (天獻): "Tian" is pronounced *xuan* (軒) and "xian" is pronounced *jian* (建).

Zheng’s commentary on the *Shijing* states that "xian" means to offer or to present. Zheng’s annotation to the *Zhouli* says: "In antiquity, when one presented objects to a ruler or elders, it was called 'xian'. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical for "dog" and the phonetic "yan" (鬳), where "yan" is pronounced *yan* (言) and *jian* (建). The version in the *Zhuan* (傳) uses "pou" (捊), which is incorrect and is therefore not adopted here. The subsequent mention of "merchants presenting *qiang*" (賈客獻𪍑) follows this same explanation and will not be repeated.
The character for *jumi* (𪍑蜜) is read as *chāngzhǎo* (昌沼); it is the correct form, though its transmission has often been written as the vulgar character *sǒu* (󰉓).

One *ju* (掬)—pronounced *jiū* (鳩) with the level tone—is defined in the *Guǎngyǐ* as "a handful" (*jù zhù*). The *Shuowén* explains that *jù* (󳇃) means "to grasp with both hands," composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "jù" (󳇃), which is an abbreviated form; the pronunciation of *jù* (󳇃) is the same as above. The *Shànglèi* writes it as *jú* (匊), and the ancient script as *jiù* (臼); their meanings are identical. The pronunciation of *cuō* (撮) is *cāngluō* (倉捋).

*Dui* (碓): The upper radical is *dui* (堆, pinyin: duī) and the lower phonetic is *jiù* (舊, pinyin: jiù). Gu Yewang states that a *dui* is used for pounding grain. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "stone" (*shí*) and the phonetic "zhui" (*zhuī*). A *jiù* (臼) is also for pounding grain. In antiquity, mortars were dug into the ground; later, they were carved from wood or stone. The central dot represents its shape.
*Bǎiyīng* (百甖): "yīng" is pronounced as *è gēng* (厄庚) and is also written as *yíng* (罌).
*Zhēn* (榛): the upper character is pronounced as *shì zhēn* (仕臻); the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it means the luxuriance of grasses and trees. *Jūlín* (拘驎):
the upper character is pronounced *jù* (俱) and the lower is *lì zhēn* (栗珎); this is a transliteration of a Sanskrit term, formerly translated as *jùlún* (俱倫).
*Kauśāmbī* (the first character is pronounced *tiǎn* with the *zhǎn* tone, and the second is *mì* with the *pí* tone; these are Sanskrit terms).
*Pratigraha* (the first character is *zhèngdá*, and the second is *chūjìn*).
*Sopāna* (the first character is *tǐdīng*, as previously explained; the second is *dēngdèng*; it is transcribed as *dèng* in the transmitted texts, though this is a vulgar usage).
The character 挑 (tiāo) [is read as] tiáo, with the radical 手 (shǒu) and the phonetic 兆 (zhào).

It refers to white *tāpasa* cloth (*bái tāpó*). The correct form is 㲲 (xié), though current editions all write it as 縶 (zhì, pinyin zhēn), which is incorrect. Examining its semantic principles, it should be 白㲲 (báiyiè), written with the radical 衣 (yī); even the meaning of the former is lost. Now it should be written as 㲲, which is correct.

"Meng" (蒙) is pronounced with the initial *jī* (積); the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "to accumulate," written with the radical for grain (*禾*) and the phonetic *zé* (責). The commentary writes it as 𧂐 with the radical for grass (*艸*), which is a vulgar form.

"Rēi" (輀) is pronounced with the initial *zhī* (之); the *Shiming* states that the carriage for the coffin is called a *rēi*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as a funeral carriage, written with the radical for chariot (*車*) and the phonetic *ér* (而). The commentary writes it as 轜, which is a vulgar usage and incorrect.
"Jūn-chí-yī-chí" (君墀音馳) is the transliteration of the Sanskrit term for a copper pitcher (*tāmraghaṭa*).

Regarding "lí-huò" (藜藿): the first character is pronounced with the *lǐ* rhyme and the second with the *huáng-guō* rhyme. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "Huò is the leaf of the small bean. The *Kao-shēng* (Examination of Sounds) states: "Huò is the sprout of the bean. The *Gōnjīn Zhèngzì* (Orthographic Standard of Antiquity and Today) states: "It is the younger [stage] of the *shū* (bean); it follows the radical for grass and takes *huò* as its phonetic."
Li Yi’s *Yujin fanren ming* (Names of Rebellious Persons Executed by Fish) [is here].

*Hui Chao’s Record of Travels to the Five Regions of India*, Volume One, Part One. Geming (閣蔑): pronounced as *mian* and *bie*. This is a term from the Kunlun language. It was formerly known as the Kingdom of Lin-yi. Among all the Kunlun kingdoms, this country is the largest, and its people also revere and believe in the Three Jewels.
*Bāṭì* (the first character pronounced *bō*),
*kělǎdū* (a foreign word with the middle character pronounced as the *láng* rhyme of *gé*),
and *píngliú* (the second character pronounced *píng*) refer to sailing on a distant voyage by boat, like duckweed floating upon the water, drifting without fixed direction according to the wind.

"Shaving" (tí): the upper character is pronounced jì (as in 計) and the lower is xiānyú (as in 相臾). The people of the Southern Yi tribes have various ways of adorning themselves: some shave their hair, some trim their beards, some tattoo their bodies, some wear topknots, some pierce their ears, and all go barefoot. Their morning garments, such as the *gēmán* (a type of robe), are all like this. The character may be written with the "ti" radical (弟) as 鬀, or with the "knife" radical (刀) as 剃; however, the current transmitted texts use the "hair" radical (髟) as 鬄, which is correct for the term "shaving" (*xū*).
"Chao lüe" (plunder): the first character is pronounced chū jiào (initial *chū*, final *jiào*) and the second is pronounced yīn lüè;

both are borrowed characters and not their original forms. "Tún è" (siege/distress): the first character is pronounced zhuī lún; the *Yùnchuán* states that "tún" means to block or obstruct, and the *Zhouyi* commentary on the hexagram "Nan" (Difficulty) uses the character "zhūn" (辵 + 屯), which refers to "zhūn chán" (impeded progress). The second character, the standard form "è," is composed of the radical "hù" (門) and the phonetic "yǐ" (乙).
*Huí* (迴): In the *Guǎngyá*, it means "distant. It is composed of the radical *chuò* (辵) and the phonetic *huí* (冋);
*huí* (冋) represents the image of a distant boundary. *Piānpiān* (翩翩): Pronounced *piān*. *Piānpiān* describes the manner of a bird’s flight.
"Yǎoyǎo" (pronounced with the "xiǎo" rhyme): The *Yùnyuán* states that "yǎoyǎo" means empty and distant, as well as deep and secluded.

"Guàxī" (pronounced with the "guǎ" rhyme): The *Yùnyuán* states that "guà" means to hang or suspend. Furthermore, in the Wu dialect, it is pronounced "guài. The explanations in the *Huìshì* are generally consistent; it is also written as "guà."
"Pàn" (盼): "To gaze at. The *Shuowen jiezi* states: "The *Shijing* says, 'Beautiful eyes, pàn-xī. It is composed of the radical 'eye' (目) and the phonetic 'fēn' (分). "Láo luàn" (撩亂):
The upper character is pronounced "liáo" (遼) and the lower is pronounced "luàn" (亂).

Shān-pǎ (the "pǎ" having the phonetic component *bā*): This character denotes the sound of a mountain echo; it also describes the white appearance of flowers. It is composed of the radical "white" (白) with the phonetic "bā" (巴). The transmitted text uses "mountain" (山) instead of [the radical], which is incorrect. Pǎ also refers to a mountain slope.

*Kǒnglìn* (倥侗): The first character is pronounced *kǔ gòng* (苦貢反) and the second is *zǒng gòng* (惣貢反). The *Kǎoshēng* states that *kǒnglìn* describes an appearance lacking joy; alternatively, it is written with the hand radical as *kòng* (控) or *zùn* (捘), meaning the mind is hurried.
*Yánèn* (牙嫩): Pronounced *nú dùn* (奴鈍反). The *Kǎoshēng* states it means small and weak; alternatively, it is written as *nuǎn* (㬉).
*Chāncī* (參差): The upper character is pronounced *chǔ*; the lower is pronounced *cè* (or *zhè*). It may refer to front, back, left, and right.

*Niàoqí* (邀祈): The upper character is pronounced *yín*; the lower is pronounced *qí*. Some say it means "to pray. It refers to seeking blessings and making petitions at the abodes of spirits, deities, worthies, and sages.
It is exactly like the character *jiǎ* (with the radical for "mouth" and the phonetic *xiàng*).

*Gǔn* (with the phonetic *wēn*)—the *Yùnqiān* states it means to turn with the hand so that something falls; alternatively, one may write it as *huì* (from the hand), meaning to turn with the hand, or as *hùn* (with the phonetic *kǎo*), meaning to turn like the hub of a wheel.

"Rugged" (*qíxū*): the first character is pronounced *qǐ* (with the fanqie *yǐ-fǎn*) and the second is pronounced *qū* (with the fanqie *yù-fǎn*). This was already explained previously in Faxian’s *Biography*; both follow the mountain. "Spear" (*qiāngshào*):
the first character is pronounced *qī* (with the fanqie *yáng-fǎn*) and the second is pronounced *chuō* (with the fanqie *shuāng-fǎn*); it refers to a long lance.

The character for *zhānglù* (麞鹿) is pronounced with the first tone on *zhāng*; it refers to an antelope without horns, also called *páolù* (麃鹿), with *páo* as the pronunciation of *páo*, or *jǐlù* (麂鹿), with *jǐ* as the pronunciation of *jǐ*.

These are all varieties of the same species. The character for *dàimào* (玳瑁) is pronounced with the first tone on *dài* (or written as *dài*) and the fourth tone on *mèi*. According to the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲), it is a type of tortoise whose shell has patterns that are polished; some say its color is like gold, radiant and pure, without distinct grain-like markings.

The "guī" (tortoise) and "biè" (turtle): the former is pronounced *guī* (as in *guīyǐng*); they are the most exposed among the armored insects (*jiǎchóng*) and their species are numerous, as described in detail in the *Erya*. The latter, pronounced *miè* (as in *xiàbiān*), refers to the smaller variety of the *yuán* (soft-shelled turtle); its shape is round like that of a tortoise, yet it lacks a shell on its underside.
*Bèng* (bǎi mèng fǎn): The *Yùnyuán* states that it means to scatter and fall. *Ní* (yí jí fǎn):
The appearance of a cliff standing high and precipitous. *Bōxiè* (shàng pén mò fǎn; xià xié mǎi fǎn):
The surging and gushing of the great ocean; alternatively, it is said to be the name of a giant turtle (*dàáo*).
"Peng qióngcāng" (湓穹蒼): "Peng" is pronounced as in "pǔmèn" (普悶); it refers to the surging of great waves. "Qióngcāng" (穹蒼) refers to the void of space, the heavens.
"Chuàn" (𧺆竄): the correct radical form is "zǒu" (走); it is composed of "yāo" (夭) and "zhǐ" (止). Below, "cāngluàn" (倉亂) is the pronunciation; when a rat runs to its burrow, it is called "chuàn" (竄).

The *yuán* (upper tone *yuán*) is a large turtle; after a long time, it becomes possessed of spiritual power, able to harm people and also to bewitch them. The *tuó* (lower tone *tuó*) is an aquatic crustacean; its form resembles that of a *shǒugōng* (gecko), having four legs and a tail, with a body length of five or six feet. Its skin is suitable for making drums and is covered in square scales, patterned like the squares on a chessboard.

The *nārikela* (coconut)—the first syllable pronounced as *nyō* with the *cha*-rhyme—is the name for a fruit tree of the south. Its shape is like that of a plantain; its leaves are suitable for mats, and its bark is suitable for ropes used to bind ships, being water-resistant, non-rotting, and firm. The fruits of large vessels are all made from this; they are as large as cups and bowls, covered in thorns, and their shells are extremely hard, serving as cups and ladles. The inner pulp is white and sweet as honey; it is considered the finest fruit-flavor of the south.

Regarding the character *mùcè* (木柵): the people of the frontier regions dwell in mountains and live in the wilds; they erect wooden posts to form walls, which are called *mùcè*. The character *cè* (柵) is composed of the radical "wood" (*mu*) and the phonetic element "ce" (*cesheng*). The pronunciation of "ce" (*cesheng*) is as stated above; it represents the appearance of a bamboo slip being pierced [to form a register].
*Kālaṇa* (杆欄): the first character is pronounced as *gān* and the second as *lán*. A wooden structure encircling a place to prevent birds, beasts, and the like is called a *kālaṇa*.
*Sūcī-mukha* (錐頭): the first character is pronounced as *jiā*; a large needle is called a *sūcī*.
*Yābó* (the first character pronounced with a level tone, the second with a departing tone) refers to a large ship in the vast ocean.

*Pāodǎng* (the first character pronounced as *pǔ* with a falling tone, the second as *dǎng* with a departing tone) means to cast or throw an object from afar; the rhyme dictionary *Yīngyùn* explains it as "to strike."

Jùn (峻): The upper part is pronounced *sǔn* (笋); it refers to a mountain cliff standing upright. The lower part is pronounced *guā* (刮); it means not being rough. Guō (聒): The upper part is pronounced *guān* (官) and the lower part is pronounced *huó* (活).
It means a sound that clamors in the ears; it is formed with "ear" (耳) as the radical and "tongue" (舌) as the phonetic.

2. Middle Volume. Regarding the Land of the Naked (Nǔxíng Guó): they are called "naked" (lě) because they are bare-bodied and without clothing. It may also be written with the radical for "person" as 倮, or with the radical for "body" as 躶. Now, to avoid vulgar taboos, it is pronounced *huǒ* (with the third tone). Middle Volume. Regarding the Land of the Naked: they are called "naked" because they are bare-bodied and without clothing. It may also be written with the radical for "person" as 倮, or with the radical for "body" as 躶. Now, to avoid vulgar taboos, it is pronounced *huǒ* (with the third tone).
*Ti-ge*: The first character is pronounced *zhāng* with the *gē* rhyme; the second is the Tibetan word *ba*. *Fei-shài*:
The first character is pronounced *suǒ* with the *jiè* rhyme. *Zhàng-bō*:
The character is *bàn* with the *mò* rhyme, followed by the radical for "hand" (*shǒu*).
Reaching as far as [the character] xiāng (with the phonetic notation yǐ fǎn); barefooted [xiǎn zú with the phonetic notation xiān diǎn fǎn];
hú lu (the character lù is pronounced by curling the tongue; with the phonetic notation hū gǔ fǎn).

*Pò* (自撲): *páng* (龐) with the reversed radical; the pronunciation is the same as *báo* (雹). The character *lù* (󲍻) has the phonetic *máng* (痝); it is also pronounced *bō* (剝), and *máng* (痝) is pronounced *mǎ bāng* (馬邦).
*Fén lǒng* (墳壠): The upper character *fén* (墳) is pronounced *fú wén* (扶聞); the lower character *lǒng* (壠) is pronounced *lì jiā* (力家).
"Hand-grasped bow" (shǒujù gōng) is read six times [in the text].
"Vārāṇasī" (bōluóní sī)—the final *sī* is pronounced as *níngxiá*—is a Sanskrit term; in this text, it is written with the character for "sun" (*rì*) followed by *ní*, which is incorrect.
"Aśoka" (āshùgǎo)—the final *gǎo* is pronounced as *gē*—is a Sanskrit term meaning King Without-Sorrow.
Chā tóu (插頭): the radical is "hand" (手), the phonetic is "thousand" (千), and "mortar" (臼) serves as the semantic component; it is a compound character formed by its constituent meanings.

Tuí huǐ (頹毀): the first character is pronounced tú léi (徒雷); it means to crumble or destroy. Miǎo miǎo (淼淼): the first character is pronounced mí biǎo (彌褾); it describes the appearance of vast, surging waters.
One *tàn* (毯) [is so called because] others dare not oppose it.
A *máo hè* (毛褐) [is so called because] it cuts through the cold.
A *tǔ wō* (土堝) [is so called; "wō" is pronounced gǔ hé] refers to an earthen cauldron.
3. The lower fascicle. "Babō" (婆簸) is a transcription of a foreign word;
it refers to a yak (*gaur*), a long-haired ox. The character "māo" (貓, cat) used in some commentaries is incorrect.

"Chewing lice and nits": "jiē" (齧) is pronounced with the upper radical *nián* and the phonetic *jié* (結); "jǐ" (蟣) has the phonetic *jǐ* (几); "shī" (蝨) has the phonetic *sè* (瑟). These are colloquial characters transmitted in the commentaries; they are written as "fēng" (風), but do not form a standard character. "Kāo-kě" (磽磕):

"kāo" (磽) is pronounced with the upper radical *qiǎo* (巧) and the phonetic *jiāo* (交); "kě" (磕) is pronounced with the lower radical *kěn* (堪) and the phonetic *hé* (合). This describes a state where the soil is narrow, the mountain passes are constricted, and there are many stones.

*Qiàn* (pronounced *qiàn*, with the rhyme of *niàn*) is glossed by Yìngyùn as "attendant" (*qiàn cóng*). It refers to one who serves a master and follows them. Regarding *cāo* (pronounced *cāo*, with the rhyme of *cāng hé*):

it may be written with the hand radical as *cuō*, meaning the two hands rubbing against each other. In the commentaries, the character is sometimes written with the foot radical as *cuō*; this is the character for *cuōtuó* (skipping/stumbling) and is not used here.
"Feeding" (餧) means to give food to the five yakṣas; "wěi" (萎) has the same pronunciation as "wèi" (畏).
"Niǎn" (捻) means to grasp the corner of one's robe with the hand.
"Pāo" (拋) means to cast one's body into a pool of water. "Pāi" (拍) means to throw oneself into a pool of water.

*Āi-dài*: the first character is pronounced *āi* (with the *gǎi* tone) and the second is *tái* (with the *nǎi* tone). This refers to clouds that are about to rain, which are dense and thick when they first appear.
*Xiè wù*: *wù* is pronounced *yù*. It is a foreign term; some say it refers to the country of Xièyuè, which belongs to the realm of Tukhāra.
*Xiān* (羶): The upper character is pronounced *shàn* (反); it refers to the stench of sheep. *Zhān* (氈):

The upper character is pronounced *zhān* (章然反) and the lower is pronounced *zhuàng* (音壯); it refers to making a shirt (*shān*) out of felt (*zhān*). *Chí* (匙): The upper character is pronounced *shí* (音時);

it is a spoon for rice. The lower character is pronounced *lǜ* (除慮反). According to the standard characters of antiquity and today, it is composed of "bamboo" (*zhú*) and the abbreviated form of "to place" (*zhù*) as its phonetic. In the *Chuánwén* (傳文), it is written with "zhù" (*zhù*), forming *zhù* (筯), which is not the correct or common character.
Húmìe (胡篾): "miè" is pronounced with the initial *b* and the final *-gě* (波箇反).
This is a place name. Qiàoyì (峭嶷): "qiào" is pronounced with the initial *chān* and the final *-xiào* (千笑反);
"yì" is pronounced with the initial *yí* and the final *-jí* (冝棘反). It refers to a mountain that is high, steep, and precipitous.
"Bìdì" (擘地): the first character is pronounced "bǎi.
"Pùbù" (瀑布): the first character is pronounced "pú"; it refers to suspended flowing water. "Yízhēn" (頤貞):
the first character is pronounced "yí"; it is the name of a person, the Anxi Jiedushi (Governor-General of Anxi).
*Chang mo zhi* (the *zhi* is pronounced with the *dang* and *lang* finals) is a name for a person in the language of Fan (*Fan yu*).
*Jia shi ji li ji* (the *ji* is pronounced with the *qin* and *yi* finals) is a term from the language of the Hu; in the language of Tang, it means the "Onion Ridge Garrison" (*Congling Zhen*).

*Ji nai* (the upper character *ji* is pronounced with the *qi* and *ji* finals; the lower character *nai* is pronounced with the *ni* and *di* finals) is the name of a medicinal herb. It is said that the root of *a-wei* resembles this medicine, yet its odor is like that of garlic; when boiled down, it becomes the medicinal drug *a-wei*.

*Xiōngshā* (囟沙) is a white mineral medicine; its pronunciation is *náo* (撓) and *jiāo* (交). It is used for gilding and is similar to alum (*báifǎn*) but softer. *Kèjié* (剋捷) is pronounced with the second tone on *qián* (潛) and the fourth tone on *yè* (葉).
*Míngyùn* (明惲) is pronounced with the first tone on *wēi* (威) and the third tone on *fěn* (粉); it is a monastic name.
The surname Quǔ (pronounced with the *qióng* rhyme) is a Qiang clan name.
Shào Zimíng (the character for Shào is pronounced *shào*, meaning "succession") is also a personal name.

Regarding the letter from the Dharma Master Wúxíng: it was written by the Śramaṇa Wúxíng of Jingzhou, sent via the Central Kingdom to the various Venerables of the Táng state. The term *shū* (pronounced with the *shàng* rhyme) is explained in the *Kǎoshēng* as "the appearance of sudden radiance and movement. The *Jìxùn* states: "Without realizing it, the passage of time has shifted; it refers to the swift passing of time."
*Qiāo* (翹): The character *yīng* (英) is pronounced *zhāo* (秖) with a retroflex final; the character follows the radical for grass (*cǎo*). *Jiě* (解):

The character is pronounced *làn* (纜) with an initial *shǎi* (騃) and an upper tone; if it is pronounced *jiǎ* (賈), it is incorrect. *Xì* (繫): The lower part is pronounced *lán* (藍) with a level tone; it refers to the rope used to moor a boat, following the "silk" (*mí*) radical as a semantic indicator and the phonetic component.

"Xunming" (殉命): "Xun" (殉) is pronounced with the rhyme of "jun" (旬) and reversed; Yuan Shu explains that to sacrifice one's life for another is called "xun. "Baoshu" (寶嶼): "Shu" (嶼) is pronounced with the initial of "yu" (與) and the final tone of the upper level;

it refers to an island in the sea. "Yu" (與) is pronounced as "yu" (與). "Shangsheng" (上聲) refers to the third tone. "Zi" (字) means a character. "Haizhongzhou" (海中洲) means an island within the ocean. "Yusheng" (與聲) means the sound of "yu" (與).**

*Liǎngchè* (two tracks): *chánliè*, with the rhyme reversed. The *Yùnyīng* states: "The tracks left by the wheels of a carriage. The *Shuōwén* states: "From *chē* (carriage) and the phonetic component *chè* (abbreviated) plus *shēng* (sound).
*Língyǔ* (feathers): *lìdīng*, with the rhyme reversed. The *Yùnyīng* states: "The feathers of a bird. [The character] is from *yǔ* (feather) and the phonetic component *líng* (sound).
*Xuānbīāo* (玄飆): The commentary on sounds states that this refers to a swift wind blowing from below upward; it is formed with the phonetic *bīāo*. *Bīāo* has the same pronunciation as above.
*Cāngmíng* (滄溟): The upper character is pronounced *cāng*; it is a specific name for the Eastern Sea, while *míng* is the name for the Northern Sea. There is also a Southern Sea.
Preface to the *Treatise on the Beginning* (Zhàolùn), composed by Xiǎozhāotí. Hùilín’s Pronunciation Notes: Sēngruì (the character 睿 is pronounced with the second tone, *ruì*;

it is a monastic name). *Shàn* means to examine thoroughly (*xíng*, second tone; as in the *Hànshū*, the term "shèn-hé" refers to the business of careful examination). The *Shuowén* states that it examines actual facts; it is composed of 覀 (pronounced *hǔjiǎ*) and the phonetic element 敫. To compose the character for "discussing the treatise" (*lùn-wén*) using two [identical] characters is incorrect.

*Jing-sou* (精󱨯): "Sou" is pronounced as *zōu* (鄒). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states it means "to scrutinize" (*yue*). Dictionaries define it as "to seek. The *Shenglei* defines it as "to search. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is composed of "hand" and "sou" as the phonetic. The version in the *Lunwen* writes it as "sou" (搜), which is a vulgar character and incorrect.

"Yi" (懿). The rhyme is *qi* (猗). In the *Erya*, "yi" means "beautiful. The *Shifa* (Canon of Posthumous Titles) states: "To be gentle yet radiate light is called 'yi'; to embody harmony and abide in the center is called 'yi'. The commentary on the *Mao Shi* says it means "great. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of "yi" (壹) and the phonetic "zi" (恣). In the *Lunwen* (Discourse on Literature), "zi" (恣) is used for "yi"; this is the archaic form.

"Yuan" (淵) is pronounced *yǎn* (with the "huì" [涓] radical reversed). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that "yuan" means deep water. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "whirling water," formed from the "water" radical with the shape of the water itself depicted between the left and right banks. It was originally written as "kun" (囦), or sometimes the "water" radical is omitted. In the *Lunwen*, it is written as "yuan" (𣶒), which is an error.

*Wěi* (pronounced *wū huǐ*): Xu Shen’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states that it means "to aggregate" or "in general"; the *Cangjie pian* states it means "suddenly"; the *Guangya* states it means "multitude. According to the *Shuowen jiezi*, it refers to the sound of a dog barking; it is composed of the radical "dog" (*quán*) and the phonetic element "fear" (*wèi*).

Regarding the character *yuan* (爰): the Master Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states it means "and" (*yu*); Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states it means "to" (*zhi*); the *Erya* states it means "and" (*ji*); and the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "to appear clearly" (*po jian*). It is composed of the radical *dan* (旦) and the phonetic *ji* (既). Regarding the character *ji* (暨): the Master Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states it means "and" (*yu*); Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states it means "to" (*zhi*); the *Erya* states it means "and" (*ji*); and the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "to appear clearly" (*po jian*). It is composed of the radical *dan* (旦) and the phonetic *ji* (既).

The proverb states, "The word 'yán' (諺) is the reverse of 'biàn' (變). The *Kǎo Shēng* says, "A proverb transmits ancient speech. This is evidenced by the existence of "Zhou yán" (proverbs of Zhou) in the *Zuǒ Zhuan*. The *Shuōwén Jiězì* defines it as: "Yán (諺) is formed from the radical 'yán' (言) with 'yàn' (彥) as its phonetic."

Regarding "guǐ" (詭): it is read as *wěi* (委) in the Mao version of the *Shijing*, which states, "Do not let the guǐsuí (詭隨) run wild. The *Yùnhuì* (韻詮) glosses it as "deceit"; the *Guǎngyá* (廣雅) glosses it as "fraud"; and the *Shuowén* (說文) glosses it as "reproach," stating it is composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) with the phonetic "wēi" (*wēi*). One source also claims it means "the various ends of discourse. It is uncertain which of these two interpretations—*guǐshuō* (詭說) or *guǐsuí* (詭隨)—is correct.
*Shì* (俟): The rhyme is *zǎi*. According to the *Erya*, "shì" means "to wait. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is composed of the radical "person" (*rén*) with the phonetic element "yi" (*yǐ*).

*Kìng* (罄): Rhyme is *qīng* or *jìng*. The *Mao Shi* says, "There is nothing that is not appropriate" (*qìng wú bù yí*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "the interior of a vessel is empty," composed of the radical "jar" (*fǒu*) with the phonetic element "qìng."

Regarding the term *han* (翰) in *dú* (牘): it is pronounced with the initial *hán* and the final *gàn*. The *Mao Shi* states: "Words and calligraphy (*cí-hàn*), literary calligraphy (*wén-hàn*), and ornate calligraphy (*zǎo-hàn*); 'calligraphy and ink' (*hàn-mò*) takes its name from the brilliance of its patterns, like those of a pheasant. The *Zhengjian* commentary says: "It refers to the spreading forth [of talent] like the flying feathers (*hàn*) of a bird; among these, the most eminent and talented take their inspiration from the elegant explanations of great pheasant feathers. It is composed of the radical *yǔ* (羽, 'feather') and the phonetic *gàn* (倝)."

1. Volume One, *Zhao Lun* (Treatises by Sengzhao), Volume One. *Upāya* (the "u" and "hou" rhymes are reversed; it is a Sanskrit term meaning "wisdom"). *Díqiān* (the "dié" rhyme is pronounced as *tiánjié*;

Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that *dí* means "alternation," while the *Fāngyán* dictionary states it means "substitution"; according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "walk" [辶] with the phonetic "shī" [失]).

"Alas! Regarding the 'yi' (噫) in the Master's commentary on the *Analects*, it says: 'Yi is a sound of sighing and resentment. Dictionaries explain it as a sound of pain and sorrow, formed from the radical for the mouth and the phonetic for 'yi'. In the *Cangjie pian*, it is written with the radical for speech and explained as having the same meaning."

"㦍" (è): the upper radical is read as *wǔ* (five) with a reversed stroke; in character dictionaries, it means "startled. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to speak directly"; it is formed from the semantic component "heart" (*xin*) and the phonetic component "㖾" (*ge*). In the *Lunwen* (Treatise on Debates), it is written as "愕" (*è*), which is commonly used as a vernacular variant.

*Líng* (聆): In the *Cāngjié piān*, it means "to listen. The *Wénzì diǎnshuō* explains that the meaning is the same; it is formed with the radical "ear" (*ěr*) and the phonetic "líng" (*lìng*). *Zhīzhū* (蜘蛛): *Zhī* is pronounced *zhī*; *zhū* is pronounced *zhù* (with the second tone).

According to the *Bóyá*, it means "hesitation" (*chízhuó yóuyù*). It is correctly written as *chóuchú*. The *Wénzì diǎnshuō* states it is also *zhízhuó*. Both are formed with the radical "foot" (*zú*), with *zhī* and *zhū* serving as the phonetics. Regarding the character *zhū*, the *Lùn-wén* writes it as *chú*; it is a vulgar form and not authentic.

"Dài" (殆) is likely not read as "gǎi" (改) or "fǎn" (反). The *Mao Shih* commentary by Zheng Xuan states that "dài" means "near" (近). Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states it means "almost" (幾). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "dangerous" (危), formed with "dài" (歹) as the semantic component and "tái" (台) as the phonetic component.

*Dí* (滌): The upper character is read as *tíng* (亭) with the variant *lì* (歷). Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* (尚書) states it means "to cleanse. The *Shuowén* (說文) says it means "to sprinkle," composed of the radical *shuǐ* (水) and the phonetic *tiáo* (條).

*Xūhuò* (虛豁): The upper character is read as *hù* (呼) with the variant *shè* (適). The *Hànshū* (漢書) states, "The will of the Gāozǔ was as open as the void (*yì huò rú yě*). Gu Yewáng says it means "vast and magnanimous. The *Wénzìdiǎn* (文字典) says it refers to a valley pass, composed of the radical *gǔ* (谷) and the phonetic *hài* (害).
*Tāo* (韜): In the *Cangjie pian*, it means "to conceal. In the *Shuowen jiezi*, it means "a sheath for a sword," written with the radical *wei* (韋) and the phonetic *yao* (舀).

*Hun* (渾): Read as *hu* (胡) and *zhuo* (󱠻). Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states that it describes the appearance of water falling. The *Guangya* says it means "great. The *Wenzi dian* explains it as the appearance of non-discrimination. It is written with the radical *shui* (水) and the phonetic *jun* (軍).

*Míng* (明) is pronounced with the *yǒu* and *zhū* finals. The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry) states that it means "to transgress. The *Shuowén* (Explanations of Words and Texts) defines it as "to cross," composed of the radical *zú* (foot) and the phonetic *yú*.

It may also be written as *yú*, with the same meaning. *Bì* (弊) and *zhài* (瘵) have the *zé* and *jiè* finals. The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* states that *zhài* means "illness. The *Wenzìdiǎn* (Dictionary of Characters and Meanings) explains it as being composed of the radical *nà* (sickness) and the phonetic *jì*.

The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "qi" (企) means to stand on tiptoe; it is derived from the radical "person" (人) and the phonetic "zhi" (止), or it may be written as "qizhi" (跂). The *Mao Shichuan* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry) says it is like a person standing on tiptoe. Sima Biao’s commentary on the *Zhuangzi* says it means to look up expectantly. The *Shuowen Jiezi* further explains: "To raise one's heels and look. It is composed of the radical "person" and the phonetic "zhi," or it may be written as "qizhi" (跂).

*Xun* (pronounced *xún*, with the phonetic component *shùn* reversed): Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states that *xun* means "trustworthy" (*xìn*). Wáng Sù’s commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* says it is an appearance of being "warm and respectful. The *Guǎngyá* says it means "reverence. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* says it means "evenness" (*jūn*). It is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "ten" (*xún*), or its pronunciation may be *xún*.

Regarding "qīngjùn" (清儁): *zūn* is pronounced as the opposite of *jùn* (峻). Xu Shuchong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states: "One whose talent surpasses a thousand others is called a *jùn*. In the standard characters of antiquity and today, this is written with the radical for "person" (人). *Jùn* (雋) is pronounced as *xuán* or *yuǎn*. In the *Lunwen*, the character is mistakenly written as *yǒng* (㺯).

*Jiǎn* (pronounced with the initials *shān* and final *-ǎn*): Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* states that "the meaning of *jiǎn* is 'to reap' (*shān*). The *Cangjie pian* says it means "gradually. The *Shuowen jiezi* says it means "to advance slowly"; it is composed of the radical *fēng* (豐) and the phonetic *zhǎn* (斬), or it is written as *jiàn*.

Although "mian" (緬) is pronounced with the retroflex *r* (衍反), Guo Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that it means "the appearance of deep reflection. The *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of the radical "silk" (糸) and the phonetic "mian" (面).

"Wuyang" (无恙) has the pronunciation *yang* (羊) and *liang* (亮) [as a rhyming compound]. In the *Erya*, "yang" means "anxiety"; the *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of the radical "heart" (心) and the phonetic "yang" (羊).

Regarding "zhì kǎi" (致慨), the *Huainanzi* states that "kāng kǎi" (慷慨) means indignation at not having one's will fulfilled; it is a state of agitation and lamentation. The *Wenzi Dadian* explains that "wǎn fèn" (惋憤)—meaning resentment—is composed of the radical "heart" (心) with the phonetic "jì" (既); it is also written as "kǎi" (愾) or "kài" (嘅).

"City moat" (*chéngqiàn*): both characters have the phonetic *yàn*. In the *Zuozhuan*, it says: "They dug a moat (*qiàn*) around the defense gate and guarded it. In the *Zhoushu*, it says: "There were no canals or moats (*qúqiàn*) with which to guard [the city]. One interpretation states that a city moat is a defensive embankment (*yí*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to dig" (*chān*); it is composed of the radical "earth" (*tǔ*) and the phonetic "zhǎn," with the pronunciation *yǔqiàn*.

*Yi* (上亡倣反): According to the *Erya*, it means "none. The *Wenzi jilüe* also states it is synonymous with "false" (*wu*). It is also written as 𠕀; the *Shuowen jiezi* writes it as 𣥙. The character below is pronounced *yu* (汲反). The *Daidai li* says: "To maintain this state of *yi-yi* for one's entire life. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* identifies it as *juan-yi*. The *Shuowen jiezi* defines it as "displeasure," derived from the radical "heart" (*xin*) with "city" (*yi*) as the phonetic component.

Regarding the contrast between tranquility and agitation, the *Shiming* (Explanations of Names) states: "To delight in changing the people is called 'agitation' (*zào*). Jia [Yan] notes that in the *Guoyu*, it means to disturb. The *Lunyu* says: "To speak before one has reached [the audience] is called agitation. The *Wenzidian* explains it as movement; it is composed of the radical for "foot" and the phonetic "sào."

2. Scroll 2, Part 2. *Miǎo* (upper radical: water; phonetic: *miǎo*; pinyin: miǎo). The *Wenzi Dianshuō* (Dictionary of Word Explanations) states it means "vast and expansive. The *Gujin Zhengzi* (Correct Characters of Antiquity and Today) states that *miǎo* refers to a vast appearance, composed of the radical water with *miǎo* as the phonetic, and the lower part *máng* (pinyin: bàng). Wang’s commentary on the *Chuci* (Songs of Chu) says *miǎo* means "level. The *Huainanzi* says: "The misty and vast expanse (*ménghóng miǎo*)—one knows not its gate. Gu Yewang says it is an appearance of being broad and great. The *Wenzi Dianshuō* also says it is *jiāmiǎo* (pervasive and vast), composed of the radical water with *rǔ* as the phonetic.

*Kuòrán* (廓然): "Kuò" (廓) is pronounced with the *shàng* (上) tone and the *kǔ* (苦) rhyme group according to the Zheng commentary on the *Lìjì*. It describes an appearance of profound sorrow and lamentation dwelling within the heart. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "empty. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical *guǎng* (广) and the phonetic component *kuò* (郭).

"Hu-ho" (惚): the upper character is pronounced with the *hu* rhyme and the *guǎng* final; the lower character is pronounced with the *hūn* rhyme and the *gǔ* final. The *Laozi* says: "The Dao, as a thing, is only *huo* and *hu*. Wang’s commentary on the *Chuci* says it is an expression for losing one's composure. The *Wenzi Dianshuo* says it is an expression for being confused and disordered. Both [characters] take "heart" (心) as the semantic component and "huang" (巟) as the phonetic component. "Huo" (怱) is likewise.

*Yǎo* (窈): Upper radical *jiāo* (晈). Guo’s commentary on the *Mao Shi* states: "Yǎo means secluded and still. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it means "profound and distant," composed of the radical for "cave" (*xué*) and the phonetic *yòu*. Its usage in the *Lunwen* as *shào* (󲿵) is an error. Lower radical *mòpíng* (莫瓶). The *Mao Shi* Commentary states: "Míng is also yǎo. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "Those who are young and immature are míng-mèi (obscure). The *Wenzi Dianshuo* says it means "dark. It refers to the moon beginning to wane on the sixteenth day. It is composed of the radical for "sun" (*rì*), the number "six" (*liù*), and the phonetic *mìng* (冂). *Míng* (冥): Lower radical *mòpíng* (莫瓶). The *Mao Shi* Commentary states: "Míng is also yǎo. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "The young and immature are míng-mèi (obscure). The *Wenzi Dianshuo* says it means "dark. It refers to the moon beginning to wane on the sixteenth day. It is composed of the radical for "sun" (*rì*), the number "six" (*liù*), and the phonetic *mìng* (冂).

*Kuàng* (pronounced *yāng-liàng* in reverse order): According to the *Cāngjié Piān*, it means resentment or indignation; this is as seen in the *Shǐjì*: "His mind was *kuàng-kuàng*, dissatisfied. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means forceful or persistent. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is formed with the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "yāng."

"Huà (to scratch or carve): read as huā (mài fǎn). This refers to what Mencius said: 'breaking tiles and scratching walls' (*huì wǎ huà quán*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as scratching with a chisel or knife; it is composed of the radical 刀 (knife) and the phonetic 畫 (huà). The pronunciation of yuán is xuān."

Wèi (蔚) [is pronounced with the initial *w-*, final *-ei*, and tone *yǎn*]. According to the *Cāngjiépiān* (蒼頡篇), "Wèi" means the flourishing of plants and trees; the *Zhòuyī* (周易) states, "Its patterns are wèi. Gù Yěwáng says it refers to the profusion of colors and textures. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* (文字典說) says it means luxuriant growth. It is composed of the radical "grass" (艸) with the phonetic element "wèi" (尉). [The character] *yù* (䫻) is pronounced with the initial *y-*, final *-ūn*, and tone *yù* (欝).
*Qiào* (竅): In the *Liji* commentary by Zheng Xuan, it means "pore" (*kǒng*). In the *Shuowen*, it means "cavity" (*xué*), formed from the radical *xué* with the phonetic *jiǎo*.

*Tí* (提): *Bǎng* (百萠) is the pronunciation. In the *Guangya*, it means "to strike" (*bǎngjī*). This refers to the "hundred lashes" mentioned in the *Hanshu*. In the *Shenglei*, it means "to whip" (*chāi*). In the *Shuowen*, it means "to cover" (*yǎn*), formed from the radical *shǒu* with the phonetic *páng*.

*Qì* (憩): In the seventh fascicle of the *Jiǎo* (覺), with the phonetic *qī* (𦋺) as a reverse component; the *Máo Shī Zhuàn* (毛詩傳) states that it means "to rest. The *Wénzì Diǎnshuō* (文字典說) explains the meaning in the same way. It is formed from the radical *xīn* (心); *kè* (愒) is used interchangeably in its training. *Shénjì* (神驥):

With the phonetic *jī* (飢) as a reverse component. It is not called by its strength but by its virtue. The *Shuowén* (說文) says it is a horse that travels a thousand *lǐ*; it is formed from the radical *mǎ* (馬) with *jì* (冀) as the phonetic.

The *Xuānshū* (Mysterious Pivot) states that the "zhū" (bead/pearl) reverses the *Zhouyī*. The *Yìjì* says: "The pivot and mechanism are what initiate movement from the mouth. Hàn Kāngbó stated: "The pivot and mechanism are the masters of motion. The *Guǎngyá* says it is the "root. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* explains that a "shànshū" (fan-pivot) is composed of the radical "wood" (木) and the phonetic component "qū" (區).

Regarding the characters for *zhì* (桎) and *gù* (梏): the upper radical of *zhì* is read as *fǎn* (反), and the lower radical of *gù* is read as *gōng wū fǎn* (公屋反). Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that those held in the hands are called *zhì* and those held at the feet are called *gù*. The *Wenzi Dian* explains that *zhì* refers to a hand-shackle and *gù* refers to a foot-shackle; both take the radical "wood" (*mu*) and have "to arrive" (*zhì*) and "announce" (*gào*) as their phonetic components.

The character *tāi* (胎) [is pronounced with the *kǔ* and *jiǎo* finals]. According to the *Zìshū*, it refers to the skin of a bird’s egg; the *Shuōwén* states that "it means the egg has already [hatched]," following the radical for "egg" (*luǎn*) and the phonetic "shell" (*kè*).

The character *náo* (撓) [is pronounced with the *niáo* final]. The *Zuǒzhuan* says, "It confuses and disturbs our allied states"; the *Guǎngyá* says it means "to disorder. The *Shēnglèi* says it means "to stir up," and the *Shuōwén* says it means "to disturb," following the radical for "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "Yáo" (*yáo*).

*Gui* (規): "The upper character is *gui* (癸), with the reversed reading *hui* (隳); *gu* (顧) refers to Wild Wang [Yue Wang]. *Gui* means 'round. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of *fu* (夫) and *jian* (見). The lower part, *ju* (俱), has the reversed reading *yu* (禹). In the *Erya*, *ju* (矩) means 'constant' (*chang*). Ma Rong’s commentary on the *Lunyu* states it means 'law' (*fa*). The *Wenzi Dianshuo* says it is 'the compass and square' (*guiju*). It is composed of *shi* (矢) and the phonetic *ju* (巨); it is also written as *ju* (榘)."

"Guǎikuài" (strange and grotesque). Regarding "xué" (cavernous/ancient), Zheng's commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* states it means "guǎzhà" (deceitful). According to the *Fāngyán*, in the regions east of Guān, deceit is called "guǎ. The *Shuowén* states that in Liáng and Yì it is called "miù," and in the world it is called "guǎ"; it is written with the radical for speech and the phonetic "yù," or it may be written as "jiē."

*Gāi* (not appropriate) is pronounced *ài* when reversed; it is glossed as "to prepare" (*bèi*) in the *Guoyu*, "slander" (*zèn*) in the *Guangya*, and "all" (*xián*) in the *Fangyan*. The *Wenzidian* states that it means "all" (*jiē*), taking the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic "hài."

*Fǎngfú* (髣髴): The first character is pronounced *fāng* with the *ǎn* tone; the second is pronounced *fāng* with the *wù* tone. In the *Hànshū*, it is said that "the *mièyīn fǎngfú*" means they resemble one another. The *Xījīng Fù* states, "The resemblance is as if *miè*," which refers to this. The explanations in various dictionaries regarding these characters are not definitive. Both characters follow the radical *biāo* (髮部), with *fāng* and *fú* serving as their phonetic components.

*Tian dan* (恬澹): The first character is read as *jie* (疊) with the variant *jian* (兼). Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that "tian" means peace and security (*an*). The *Wenzi Dianshuo* says it means stillness (*jing*). It is composed of the "heart" radical (*xin*) and the phonetic element "tian" (*xian*) in abbreviated form.

*Mokui* (莫窺): Read as *gui* (䂓) with the variant *fei* (䂓). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "kui" means to look at something from a small opening. It is composed of the "cave" radical (*xue*) and the phonetic element "gui. It may also be written as *kui* (闚), which is identical.

"Jí" (戢): In the *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry), it says "jí means to gather. In general usage, to store away objects is called "jí. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "gē" (戈) with "qī" (咠) as the phonetic.
"Yě" (冶): The pronunciation is "yě. According to the *Shuōwén*, "yě" means to smelt gold and cast it; it is composed of the radical "bīng" (冫) with "tái" (台) as the phonetic.

The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains that "nang" (囊) is derived from "tuo" (橐) and the phonetic component "xiang" (襄). "Tuo" is pronounced *tuò*, and "xiang" is pronounced *xiāng*. The character is formed with "tuo" as the radical and "xiang" as the phonetic. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states: "A large bag is called a nang. Lexicons define it as a bottomless vessel; the *Shuowen* indicates it is composed of "tuo" and the phonetic "xiang. (Note: The term "shang nuo dang fan" [上諾當反] appears to be a scribal or transmission error for a phonetic notation, likely intended to clarify the pronunciation of "nang" as *náng*.)

"Wāng" (汪): *wū guāng* (烏光). Dǔ’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states it refers to a "pool"; Wáng’s commentary on the *Chuci* states it means a vast expanse of great water without limit. The *Hànshū* describes it as "a pond of ten thousand *qīng* [li] of depth and breadth. The *Shuowén* writes it as 󳂥 (*wāng*), meaning deep and broad water; it is composed of the radical 水 with the phonetic 王, the latter having the pronunciation *zāi*. In the *Yùnquán*, it is said to be a particle used for speech; the *Shuowén* states it is used between words, composed of the radical 口 with the phonetic 󲹌, which has the same pronunciation. The common vulgar form is 󶙢.

*Zhi guan* (Cessation and Contemplation), Volume One, Upper. Compiled by the Śramaṇa Huilin. Regarding "Zhìyǐ" (智顗): according to the *Erya*, "zhì" (顗) means "tranquility"; according to the *Shenglèi*, it means "familiarity with practice"; according to the *Zishū*, it means "an appearance of excellence"; and according to the *Shuowén*, it means "an appearance of careful solemnity," being formed from the radical "head" (頁) and the phonetic "qǐ" (豈). This is the name of the Dhyāna Master who composed this treatise.

Regarding the character for *jí* (jealousy) in the "Xiàdū" section of the *Shuowén*: it is said that a wife is jealous of her husband; it arises from [the pursuit of] fame and profit. Following this principle, one should understand that it is a compound character consisting of "woman" (*nǚ*) as the semantic component and "door" (*hù*) as the phonetic component. There are also versions with "lady" (*hòu*) or "stone" (*shí*), but these are all incorrect.
The character *jiè* (藉) is pronounced with the initial *qíng* (夜反) and the radical *cǎo* (草).
It is explained as "that which is easy to practice but difficult [to master]"; "easy" is pronounced *yí* (音移), and "practice" is pronounced *xìng* (音幸) or *gēng* (耕).

Regarding *jiētī* (階梯): the upper character *jié* (階) is pronounced *kǎo* (考). The *Yùnyī* (爾雅) states it refers to the steps for ascending a hall; the *Shuowén* (說文) defines it as "a step. It is composed of the phonetic *dài* (𨸏) and the determinative *jié* (皆). The lower character *tī* (梯) is pronounced *tǐ* (㕆反). Jia [Yuan]’s commentary on the *Guoyu* (國語) states that "ti" means "steps" (*jiētī*). The definition in the *Shuowén* is the same as Jia Kui’s; it is a compound of shape and sound.

"Zhi" (知) [in the context of "touch"] is a vulgar character for "zhong" (中, middle); the same applies to subsequent instances, which should be understood accordingly. "Diao-hui" (掉悔): "diao" (條) is pronounced "yao" (曜) and refers to movement;

according to the *Shuowen*, it means "to shake," being composed of the radical "hand. In the context of "stopping and contemplation" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), the character "dao" (悼) [is used] instead, which is incorrect; this is an error made by the scribe.

*Xiè* (戲) is pronounced with the initial *xī* and the final *yì* (義). *Ěr* (爾) and *pǐ* (疋) mean "to joke. *Xiè* (戲) also means "to jest. *Kǎo* (考) means "to toy with" or "to dally. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *go* (戈) and the phonetic *qiàn* (䖒); *qiàn* is pronounced with the final *xiè* (虐). Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states that it refers to mutual teasing and joking. In the *Shuowen*, *xiè* (謔) is identical to *xiè* (戲), composed of the radical *yan* (言) and the phonetic *xiè* (虐). Regarding the character *nüè* (虐): the upper part is *hū* (虍) and the lower part is *yǎngguā* (仰瓜). The form written with *shān* (山) and *wáng* (亡) is a vernacular variant.

The character for "scouring" (sāo) is pronounced with the radical for "hand" and the phonetic "zǎo" (pronounced zǎo, as in "morning"). It means to brush or sweep; it is also written with the radical for "horse," which conveys the same meaning. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to gather" (guā). The phonetic "zǎo" is pronounced zǎo (as in "morning"); the upper part is written as "bì" (必), which is the ancient form of the character for "claws" (zhǎo). The pronunciation of "guā" is guānhuá (反).

Second, *chuǎn* (pronounced with the *chuān* rhyme and the *ruǎn* final). The *Yili* states that it means "to pant" (*chuǎn-zhuǎn*). The *Hanshu* records that Bing Ji saw an ox panting; this is an example. According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to rapid respiration through the mouth, with *duān* as its phonetic component.

The characters 唌 (pronounced xiáng yán) and 𣵿 are both vulgar forms; the *Shuowen* correctly writes it as 㳄. Because people of later times did not clearly understand this, they confused it with the character 次, and various scholars arbitrarily produced different forms. Shuō Chè used 唌, Jia Yi used 㵪, and the Da Zhuan of Shi Zhòu used 𣶙, which consists of two water radicals. This is the most archaic form, yet it was not employed in common usage at the time. The *Shuowen* original text writes it as 㳄, composed of the radicals 水 and 欠. The *Jixun* states: "唌 refers to the dregs and fluids within the mouth. Here, we follow the *Shuowen*; all other versions are not accepted.

"Fan-zào" (煩躁) is a term used when encountering adversity; Jia Gongyan’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that "zào" means agitation (*rǎo*). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lunyu* states that it means a lack of tranquility. Gu Yewang says it means restless movement. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "to run" (*zǒu*) with "sào" as its phonetic component; "sào" is pronounced *sāngdào*.

*Zuàn* (pronounced *duān* with a retroflex final) means a fire-drill; the *Shìběn* states that the Lord Suí produced fire by drilling wood. The inclusion of the phonetic component *zàn* (from the metal radical) is incorrect; in the context of *zhǐguān* (calm abiding and insight), it refers to the hands performing the act of *cuán* (gathering or rubbing).
The character 儔 (chóu) is pronounced zhòu (with the retroflex *r* sound).

It is derived from 童 (tóng). As for 對 (duì), it is used as a countermeasure; the correct form of the upper radical is 丵 (zhuó), pronounced chuáng xué (with the retroflex *r* sound), composed of 土 (tǔ) and 寸 (cùn). The current vulgar form with 至 (zhì) is incorrect. The lower part is pronounced chí.

Regarding the characters *chéng* (憕) and *méng* (懵): the former is pronounced with the initial *dēng* and the latter with *mò* (both in the departing tone). According to the *Kǎo Shēng*, *méng* means "the spirit is not clear. Both [the characters for *chéng* and *méng*] follow the radical for the mind (*xīn*). As for *zhǐguān* (止觀), it follows the radical for the eye; it is incorrect to write it as *dèng* (瞪) or *móng* (矒). The pronunciation of *bèng* (堋) is *běi méng*.

2. Lower Volume: *Zhiguan* (Cessation and Contemplation), Lower Volume. Regarding the character "shùn" (瞬): in the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is defined as "the movement of the eyes. It is also written as "zhèn" (瞚). In the *Zhiguan*, the character used for "xuán" (䀏) is "xiù" (眴); this is the character for "xuán" (懸). It is also incorrect to use the character for "xún" (旬) [as a variant].

Regarding the character *wěidǎ* (萎嚲): the upper part, *wěi* (委), is pronounced with the *wéi* rhyme; the *Zìjìng* (字鏡) states that it means the withering and fading of grasses and trees. It may also be written as *wěi* (󲱁) with the radical for "bad" (*dài*), which carries the same meaning. The lower part, *duō* (多), is pronounced with the *kě* rhyme; the *Yùnquán* (韻詮) states that it describes the drooping appearance of withered grasses and trees. The reading *wěituó* (委陀) found in the *Zhǐguān* (止觀) is likely incorrect, as it misses the intended meaning of the scripture.

Regarding "jìngmèi" (精魅): the *Kuǎnzhōngshēngyùn* states that it refers to spirits and ghosts manifesting as monsters. The *Shuowén Jiězì* defines it as the essence of aged objects, composed of the radical "hairs" (彡) with "guǐ" (鬼) as the phonetic. It is also written as "mèi" (魅) with the radical "woman" (女), or as "pò" (𩲐) with the radical "wù" (勿); both of these are vulgar forms. The current usage in the *Zhìguān* (止觀) of writing it as "mèi" (媚) with the radical "woman" is incorrect; "mèi" means to please, to be beautiful, or to love, which does not accord with the meaning of the scripture.

*Duī* (堆): Upper radical *tuó* (都回反), lower radical *huǐng* (亦反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that the correct form of the character *duī* is 𠂤 (*dūi*), which is a pictograph. In the context of *zhiguan* (止觀), using the character 垖 (*duì*) with the earth radical is incorrect. The character *tí* (惕) consists of the heart radical and the character *yì* (易); it is the name of an evil ghost. One need not seek the meaning of the word [in this context].

The character *hù* (tiger) is pronounced with the initial *gǔ* and the final *fǎn*. The *Shuowen* explains it as "the lord of mountain beasts. It follows the radical *hú* (the tiger's head); its feet resemble human feet, therefore the lower part follows the radical *rén* (person). The pronunciation of the lower part is *sì*. The *Shuowen* states that it is a beast like a wild ox, blue in color, and is a pictograph. Its head is the same as that of the character *qín* (bird/beast). To write it as *shǒu* (from the radical *quǎn*, dog) is incorrect.

*Tù* (兔): The character *shǔ* (麈) is pronounced with the *gù* (固) rhyme; according to the *Shuowen*, it is the name of a beast. It takes the form of a crouching rabbit head and is identical to the head of the *ruǎn* (㲋) animal, hence it uses a simplified form of *ruǎn*. The subsequent radical *zhǐ* (󱫛) represents its tail. The lower part is pronounced *zhǔ* (主); according to the *Shuowen*, it belongs to the class of deer. It is large and has a single horn, taking the character *zhǔ* (主) as its phonetic component. The entry sound is *miè* (篾) according to the *Pian*. *Jù* (麈): Pronounced with the *zhǔ* (主) rhyme. According to the *Shuowen*, it is a species of deer. It is large and has a single horn, taking the character *zhǔ* (主) as its phonetic component. The entry sound is *miè* (篾) according to the *Pian*.

"Lóng-táo" (龍鼉): "Táng-hé" (唐何) is the phonetic component; according to the *Shuowen*, it is an aquatic creature. Its long body resembles a chameleon (*xīchì*) but is larger. It follows the radical "mǐn" (黽) with the phonetic "dān" (單, pronounced nà). The inclusion of "huán" (吅) and "liú" (里) and the omission of "dān" (單) is an error. In the *Zhiguan* (止觀), the character following "guī" (龜) is incorrect.

*Shé-mǎng* (蛇蟒): "Shé" is pronounced with the initial *zhē* (遮) and the final *fǎn* (反); "mǎng" is pronounced with the initial *mò* (莫) and the final *bǎng* (榜). The largest among snakes is called a *mǎng*. *Hóu jué* (猴玃):

The first character is pronounced *hóu* (侯) and the second *guǐ yuè* (鬼籰). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is a large female monkey that is skilled at looking back and forth (*gù miàn*) and seizing people. A *hóu* is a *yuán-hóu* (猿猴); in common parlance, they are called *húsūn* (胡孫).
"Shoujingmiu" (狩精鬽): "Shou" (狩) is pronounced with the first tone and the reversed sound of "shou" (收). It is also erroneously written as "shoushou" (獸守), which is the correct form. "Pupó" (匍匐):

"Pu" (匍) is pronounced with the second tone and "peng" (朋), and "bei" (匐) is pronounced with the fourth tone and "bei" (北). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to travel on hands and knees. Both characters follow the radical "baou" (勹), which is pronounced "bao" (包); these are words formed through the combination of shape and sound.

Regarding the phrase "the person with leftover food" (*shèngshí qírén*) in the subsequent passage, it further states: "The character *shèng* (剩) is pronounced *chéngzhèng* (承證) in the vernacular; it is also a colloquial term used in the region of Chu and Ying. To say 'leftover' (*shèng*) in this context means 'how could it be that it is already like this? This is the intended meaning. It is likely the local accent of the Great Master’s hometown, a dialect of the Chu region."

*Kují* (枯瘠): The first character is pronounced *kǔ* (孤) with a reversed tone; the second is pronounced *qíng* (情) with a reversed tone. The commentary on the *Gōngyáng Zhuàn* states: "Jí means illness; it is a term from the language of the Qi people. It is a compound character formed from the semantic element *nǚ* (女) and the phonetic element *é* (戹).

*Yē* (噎): "To choke. It is pronounced with the *jié* (結) rhyme. It refers to the sound of gasping as the breath is blocked in the chest and throat; it is also the inability to swallow food. The character for *xià* (下) is pronounced *sēng* (僧). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to obstruct" (*zhì*). It is composed of *gǒng* (拱) as its phonetic component, *mián* (綿) as the radical *mián*, and the components *zhǎn* (展) and *tǔ* (土). The *mián* represents a roof, while *zhǎn* signifies "even" or "level. The pronunciation of *zhǎn* is *zhǎn*.

*Ānleji* (Collection on Peace and Bliss), two fascicles; *Yinyi* (Explanations of Pronunciation and Meaning) compiled by Huilin. Fascicle 1, Upper. The character for the upper fascicle (*shàngjuàn*) is written as 𭤆. The radical is 了 (*liǎo*), with the phonetic component 東 (*dōng*). Examining the sound, it means "to select" (*kǎoshēng*). In the *Tōngsùwén* (Popular Texts), it is written as 撩 (*liáo*); nowadays, this form is most commonly used. According to the *Shuōwén*, 撩 (*liáo*) means "to choose" (*zé*); it takes the hand radical and the phonetic 尞 (*liáo*). Although 撩 is the correct orthographic form, it is difficult to use due to its archaic nature. In this collection, the character is written as 䉼 (with the grain radical and the phonetic 斤), which is incorrect. The character for the lower fascicle (*xiàjuàn*) is written as 姦, with the phonetic component 眼 (*yǎn*). Examining the sound, it means "to select" (*jiǎnzé*). According to the *Shuōwén*, 柬 (*jiǎn*) means "to distinguish" (*fēnbì jiǎnzhī yě*); it takes the radical 柬 and the component 八, where 八 signifies "distinction. In vulgar usage, it is sometimes written as 棟 (with the hand radical and 柬), which is an error. In this collection, it is written as 蕳, which is not semantically appropriate. One should understand that subsequent characters follow this principle.

"Discerning (biàn) the various superiors": "biàn" means to investigate and question until a definitive conclusion is reached; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "biàn" means to rectify, composed of the radical "speech" (言) and the phonetic "biàn" (辨), with the pronunciation "biàn" (變). The version in the *Zhongjing* (Collection of Classics) uses "biàn" (弁), which is not used here."

*Zuàn* (pronounced *zuǎn*): To bore into damp wood. In the *Lúnyǔ*, it says "boring for fire-drills and changing the firewood. In the *Hànshū*, "boring" (*zuàn*) means to engrave or sharpen. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "that by which one pierces; it is composed of the radical 金 and the phonetic 贊. The *Jíběn* version writes it with the radical 木 as 欑, which is incorrect. The character below is pronounced *rù*. Gù Yěwáng states it means "moistened. The *Kǎoshēng* defines it as "to soak. The *Shuōwén* further defines it as "deep moisture; it is composed of 一 and 一, signifying covering. Because water is present beneath the covered earth, it is moist. The *Jíběn* version writes it as 濕, which is a vulgar form and incorrect.

Regarding the character *xī* (析) in the phrase "splitting dry firewood" (*xī qián xīn*), the commentary on the *Shàngshū* by Kǒng [Yù] states that it means "to divide. The *Shēnglèi* writes it as *pī* (劈), and the *Shuōwén* defines it as "breaking wood," composed of the radical for wood (*mù*) and the phonetic *jīn* (斤). The form with the hand radical (*shǒu*) and the element *piàn* (片), written as *zhì* (㭊), is a vulgar character and is incorrect.

"Follow" (fǎng) means to imitate; it is also used in the sense of "relying upon" in the *Gōngyáng zhuan*. According to the *Shuowen jiezi*, it is written with the radical "person" (亻) and the phonetic "fǎng" (放), meaning "to resemble. In the *Zhuowen* script, it is written as 㐻.

*Bǐng* (昞然): Upper radical *shàngbīng*, with the phonetic *míng* (皿). According to the *Guǎngyá*, *bǐng* means "clear" (*míng*). The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radical *rì* (日) and the phonetic *bǐng* (丙);
it is also written as *bǐng* (昺), which is the same meaning. *Yuán* (󱨯原): Upper radical *shòuzōu* (瘦鄒). This has already been fully explained in the preceding *Zhàolùn*.

The character *biàn* (偏) is pronounced as *gòng* (共) with the *yù* (獄) radical reversed. According to the *Guǎngyá* (廣雅), *biàn* means "near" (*jìn*). According to the *Ěryá* (爾雅), *biàn* means "division" (*fèn*). The *Dà dàlǐ* (大戴禮) states: "The feudal lords each took their respective positions according to their *biàn*. The commentary on the *Máoshī* (毛詩) says *biàn* means "crooked" (*qū*). The *Zuǒzhuan* (左傳) speaks of "each presiding over their own *biàn*," and Zheng’s commentary on the *Lìjì* (禮記) identifies it as "sections" (*fùbèn*). The *Shuowén* (說文) defines *biàn* as "to narrow" (*cù*). It is a pictographic character formed from "mouth" (*kǒu*) beneath "corpse" (*shī*), further enclosed by "enveloping" (*bāo*).

The character 貿 (mào) [with the phonetic *hou* reversed] means "to trade. Gu Yewang states that "貿貿" (mào mào) is like "market exchange. In both ancient and modern standard characters, it follows the radical for "treasure" (貝) and takes *you* (夘) as its phonetic component; *you* is pronounced like *mao*. Its inclusion in the "Market" (集) section is an error.

*Shū’ěr* (倏尒): The upper radical is *shū* (舒), with the phonetic *yù* (育). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that "it is like lightning, sudden and fleeting. The *Guǎngpǐ* says it means "light. The *Cāngjiépiān* says it means "sudden. It is a character for the "coming and going" of the ancients and moderns. It is composed of the radical "fire" (*huǒ*) and the phonetic "you" (*yōu*). Alternatively, it may be written with the radical "dog" (*quǎn*), forming *shū* (倏); both are used interchangeably.

The *hen* bird (鴆) is a poisonous bird that emits a deep, resonant cry. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states it is as large as a small eagle (*diau*), purple-green in color, with a long neck and a red beak; it eats snakes and is commonly called the *tan* bird. Du’s commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan* notes its feathers are poisonous. Regarding the character itself: in the "Correct Characters" of ancient and modern times, it is composed of the radical "bird" (鳥) and the phonetic "yin" (冘), with "yin" pronounced *yin*. Editions that write it with the radical "wine" (酉) as *dun* (酖) are incorrect.

The character *sū* (穌) is pronounced with the initial *zú* (租) and the final *fǎn* (反). Regarding its sound, it is said that *sū* means "awakening" (*wù*). Confucius’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* (Book of Documents) states it means "rest" (*xī*). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* (Book of Rites) states that "to rest again" is called *sū*. According to the *Shēnglèi* (Classified Sounds), it means "reborn. The correct orthography from ancient times to the present uses the radical for grain (*huó*, 禾) and the phonetic element *yú* (魚). The form used in the *Jí* (集) [Dictionary] as *suō* (甦) is a spurious character from the Great Zhou dynasty and is incorrect.

*Chí* (馳): "To gallop. *Xīng* (騁): "To race. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to gallop directly. It is a phono-semantic compound character. *Pīng* (甹) has the pronunciation *pǐdīng*. The *Jí* (集) [the *Shuowen Jiezi*] erroneously uses *chóng* (從) and *zēng* (󲒢) to form *chěng* (騁).

*Sòu* (漱): Pronounced *sòu* (叟) with the *zhòu* (皺) rhyme. The *Jí* explains it as "to rinse"; it refers to washing one's palms. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *shui* (水) and the phonetic *sou* (欶), which shares the same pronunciation.

2. *Xiàn* (險), Volume Lower. In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "xiàn" is glossed as "dangerous. Gu Yewang states that "xiàn" means "obstructed. Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* says it means "perilous. The *Fangyan* says it means "high. The correct character for ancient and modern usage is "nán" (難). It is composed of the radical *fù* (阜) and the phonetic *qiān* (僉); *fù* is pronounced *fǔ*. To compose it with the radical *shān* (山) is incorrect. Below, *jīng* (徑) is pronounced *dìng* (定). The *Guangya* says "jīng" means "crooked. It means "to pass through"; it means "a track. To proceed by winding paths rather than following the great road is called a "jīng. Gu Yewang says it is a "small path. The *Shuowen* says it is a "footpath. It is composed of the radical *chè* (彳) and the phonetic *jīng* (巠).

The character for *mài* (millstone) is pronounced with the five-tonal finals *huì* and *fǎn*. Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states that it refers to something hard. The *Kaosheng* says it is a tool for grinding wheat. The *Shiben* records that Gongshu [Zi] first invented the millstone. The *Shuowen* defines it as "grinding," composed of the radical "stone" (*shí*) and the phonetic element "qǐ" (*qǐ*).

The character *shǐ* (駛) [is pronounced with the initial *chāng* and the final *jié* according to the *Cāngjié piān*; it means "swift. The *Wénzìdiǎn* states that it refers to the swift gallop of a horse; it is composed of the radical "horse" (*mǎ*) and the phonetic element "historical record" (*shǐ*).
The character *zhù* (幢) [is pronounced with the final *jiāng*; it is composed of the radical "cloth" (*jīn*), not the radical "heart" (*xīn*).]

To "xiāng" (禳) means to avert calamities; Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that it refers to warding off anomalies. The *Guǎngyá* says it means to apologize for transgressions. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as consisting of the radical "示" (shì) and the phonetic "xiāng" (襄). The version in the *Zhongjing* (Concentrated Collection) uses the radical "手" (shǒu) and the character "rǎng" (攘), which does not convey this meaning. The pronunciation of "示" is qí.
*Rǎng* (餉): In the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to give as a gift. The *Shuōwén* states that it is "rǎo" (饟), composed of the radical "food" (食) with "xiàng" (向) as the phonetic component;

the pronunciation of rǎo is the same as rǎng. *Jí* (棘): Pronounced *jìngyí* (上兢嶷反). The *Guǎngpǐ* states it is "thorn" (針). Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* says "jí is like a halberd" (戟如也). The *Jīngǔzhèngzì* states it is a small jujube growing in clusters, composed of "bìng" (並) and "cì" (朿); the collected edition [of the dictionary] writes it as "jī" (蕀), which is incorrect. *Cī* (刺): Pronounced *cīsì* (下雌四反). The *Guǎngyá* states it is "needle-thrust" (鍼刺). It is composed of the radical "knife" (刀) with "qiú" (求) as the phonetic component; the collected edition writes it as "cì" (莿), which is incorrect.

The character 霹 (pí) has the radical 雨 (rain) on top and the phonetic 立 (lì) below; its pronunciation is *pí* (the opposite of *fǎn*). The preceding section has already explained this. The character 靂 (lì) has the radical 雨 on top and the phonetic 零 (líng) below; its pronunciation is *lì* (the opposite of *fǎn*). This was previously explained. The character 獸 (shòu) has the radical 犬 (dog) on top and the phonetic 爪 (zhǎo) below; its pronunciation is *shòu*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is formed from "dog" and "sound," meaning "to hunt in winter. This is not the meaning intended here. The character 反 (fǎn) has the radical 厂 (yǎn) on top and the phonetic 又 (yòu) below; its pronunciation is *fǎn*. It means "to turn back" or "opposite.
