*Xiáoxiáng* (翱翔): the upper character is pronounced *ào gāo fǎn* (上傲高反) and the lower character is pronounced *xiàng yáng fǎn* (下象羊反). Zheng’s commentary on the *Mao Shi* states that *xiáoxiáng* means "leisurely wandering" (*xiāoyáo*). The *Han Shi* states it means "to roam. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains that both characters follow the radical for "feathers" (*yǔ*) and take *gāo* and *yáng* as their phonetic components.

"Hunmào" (昏耄): The second character is pronounced with the *máo* rhyme (毛報反). The *Liji* states that those in their eighties and nineties are called "mào. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* explains it as "confusion. In the standard characters of ancient and modern times, this character is composed of "lǎo" (老) as the radical and "máo" (毛) as the phonetic.

*Qióng* (葵營反, *kui yíng fǎn*; the sound of *kǎo*) means "solitary" (*āigu*); Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states it means "single," and the *Màoshī Zhuàn* says it means "having no one to rely upon. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of *xùn* (卂) and the abbreviated form of *yíng* (熒) as its phonetic; the character *qíng* (焭) used in the *Jíshì* is a vulgar form.

*Zhōngzhōng* (忪忪): *Bīcāng* states that *zhōngzhōng* means "sudden haste. *Shēnglèi* says it also has the pronunciation *zhōng*. The *Jìxùn* explains that *zhōngzhōng* means "the heart is agitated. In the *Gǔjīn zhèngzì*, *zhēngzhōng* (怔忪) means "hastening and urgency," following the radical for "heart" (*xīn*) and using "gōng" as the phonetic. *Jù* (遽) has the pronunciation *qúyù*; *jù* is synonymous with "urgent."

The *Ratnadharmārtha-śāstra*, composed by the Chan Master Chou; phonetic glosses by Huilin. *Gǔ*: Pronounced as in *gōngwǔ*. Examining the sounds, it means "to be without eyes," which is called *gǔ*. According to the *Shìmíng*, *gǔ* means "blind" (*mián*). It refers to one who is dully and blindly like a blind person; the image of the skin over the eyes is used to name it. The *Shuōwén* says: "The eye having only a bulging [lid] like a drum; from the radical 'eye' and the phonetic 'gǔ' (drum)."

*Shenjing* (深阱): *qíng* (情) with the phonetic *yǐng* (郢). Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "One digs the earth to create a moat (*qian*) for the purpose of capturing wild animals. The *Liji* says: "They are trapped and placed inside a pit (*jiao*). The *Guoyu* says: "A pitfall (*jing*). In archaic script it is written as *zheng* (󲜓). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to sink" (*xian*), composed of the radical *dui* (𨸏) and *jing* (井), with *bing* (并) as the phonetic.

"Qiān" (僉) means "all" or "unanimous. Guo's commentary on the *Fāngyán* states that it means "the same"; the *Guǎngyǐ* states it means "many"; and the *Shuōwén* states it means "all. It is composed of the radicals 亼 (jí, jìn), 吅 (xuān), and 从 (cóng). 亼 is pronounced jí (jìn); 吅 is pronounced xuān; and 从 is pronounced cóng.

"Di" (遞) means "to alternate" (*dì*) according to the *Erya*. It refers to the changing of characters from antiquity to the present; it is composed of the radical "walk" (*chuò*) and the phonetic "xi" (*xī*). It is also written as "di" (递), which is the archaic form. The character "xi" (*xī*) has the pronunciation *xǐ* (徙貲反). In the *Lunwen*, it is written as "zhi" (𤙖), which is a vulgar usage that does not constitute a valid character.

"Nián" (黏): On the outside, it is pronounced with the initial *l* and the final *-ian* (as in *lián*). The *Kǎo Shēng* says it means "to stick. The *Cāngjié Piān* says it means "to join. The *Shuōwén* says it means "to adhere," written with the radical for grain (*shǔ*) and the phonetic *zhàn*. The form "zhān" (粘) used in the *Lùn* [Treatise] is a vulgar character; "nián" is the standard form.

The character *chí* (pronounced with the initial *ch-*, the final *-i*, and the level tone) is explained in the *Guǎngyǐ* as "sticky. According to the standard characters of antiquity and modern times, there is a resinous substance used for catching birds called *chīshù* (sticky tree); it is written with the radical for "grain" (*shǔ*) and the phonetic *lí*. In the *Lùn-wén*, it is written as *yún*; this is a vulgar character resulting from corruption and abbreviation.

"Yǔn" (殞): The phonetic transcription is *jiǒng* (窘) with the tone *fǎn* (反). The *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲) states that "yǔn" means death. The *Wénzì Diǎnshuō* (文字典說) says it means to pass away; it takes the radical *dài* (歹) and the phonetic *yuán* (員). It is also written as *yǔn* (隕). In the *Lùnwén* (論文), it is written as "yǔn," which carries this meaning.

The webbed hands (*jālāvanaddhahastapāda*): between the ten fingers of the Tathāgata’s hands there is a web-like membrane connecting them, like the feet of a king of geese; it possesses patterns and colors like those of a net, and is thus called "webbed."

*The Jewel King Treatise on the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation*, Volume 1 (of 3). Regarding "Hui-lin ming xiù" (慧琳明齅): the character *xiù* (齅) is pronounced with the lower radical *xiū* (宥). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To bring the nose to an odor is called *xiù*; it is composed of the radical 'nose' and the phonetic 'odor' (*chòu*)."
Regarding the term *zhīchú* (錙銖): the first character is pronounced *zǐ* (with the rhyme *shī*), and the second is pronounced *shū*.
According to texts such as the *Sūnzi Jiǔzhāng* (The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art), all measurements designated by "yi" (乙) originate from the *shǔ* (黍) grain.
Ten *xǔ* (bristles) make one *lěi*;
ten *lěi* make one *zhū*;
six *zhū* make one *zī*.
"Zi" (錙) means a division.
Its pronunciation is fen-wen-fan.
Four "fen" constitute one "liang."
Sixteen *liang* make one *jin*;
thirty *jin* make one *jun*;
four *jun* make one *shi*.
This is equivalent to one hundred and twenty *jin*.
I have carefully examined various dictionaries regarding the term *zi*, which has three distinct definitions.
According to the *Fengsu tongyi*, six *zhu* constitute one *zhui*.
Two *chui* constitute one *zi*;
two *zi* constitute one *liang*.
According to this reckoning, half a *liang* is called one *zi*.
One part is called a *chui*.
Twenty-four *zhu* constitute one *liang*.
Only this single text differs from all other scriptures in this regard.
Most dictionaries provide largely the same explanations.

Having carefully consulted the *Zilin*, *Zitong*, *Ziyuan*, *Zijing*, *Yunjí*, *Yunlüe*, *Yunpu*, *Yinwenzi*, *Jielüe*, and the *Wenzidian*—which record ancient and modern characters and establish correct orthography—I have compiled this work.
Furthermore, according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the *Jiuzhang* (Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art), and thirteen other such texts,
they all uniformly define six *zhu* as one *zi*;
thus, four *zi* constitute one *liang*.
Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* defines one *zi* as eight *liang*.

Although the *Jixun yunquan* follows Zheng’s statement that it is eight *liang*, the origin of this meaning remains unclear. I have therefore compiled here the differing views of various scholars regarding what to accept or reject, leaving the final decision to the reader's own judgment.
For now, I have respectfully relied upon the *Jiuzhang suanshu* (Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art) and adopted the most prevalent tradition to establish that six *zhū* constitute one *zí*.
As for the *Fengsu tongyi* and the commentary of Zheng Xuan, they do not clarify the origins of this; thus, the profound intent of the ancients remains unfathomable.

Regarding "the banner of pride" (mānadhvaja): it is pronounced *zhújiāng* (濁江) in reverse. As for the banner of pride, it refers to being deceitful, insulting, and disrespectful; it denotes arrogance, heedlessness, and self-exaltation. It is likened to a banner because its sharpness is comparable to that of a spearhead (*śūla*). Thus it is used as a metaphor.
*Le* (upper character *lè*, lower character *héng* reversed; lower character *zé*, *héng* reversed) is the appearance of being raised high.

*Kāng* (upper character *kàng*, *gāng* reversed): The *Shēnglèi* states that *kāng* is the husk of grain. The standard orthography of the past and present uses *mǐ* (grain) as the radical and *kāng* as the phonetic. *Sù* (lower character *kǒu*, *wài* reversed): Lexicons state that *sù* is *kāng*. The *Shuowén* also identifies it as *kāng*, using *huì* as the phonetic with *huò* (grain) as the radical. The version in the *Lùn* (Treatise) writes it as *gǎo*, which is an erroneous vulgar usage.

"Li (罹)"—pronounced *zhī* (知) in the upper tone according to Guo’s commentary on the *Erya*—means "to suffer grief. Regarding its phonetic derivation, it is said to mean "to be afflicted by" or "to encounter. The *Gujin Zhengzi* states that it signifies "thoughts of bitter distress. It is composed of the radical "net" (*wǎng*) with "wei" (*wéi*) as its phonetic. In the *Lunwen*, it is written with four strokes; this is a vulgar character.
The character "zhī" (之) is pronounced *chāng* (昌) with the *zhèng* (證) rhyme;

the same applies to its occurrence in the following text. Regarding "bì nǚ" (嬖女): the upper character is pronounced *bī* (篦) with the *qí* (䛧) rhyme. The *Guǎngyá* states: "Bì means to be favored, to be intimate, and to be affectionate. Lǐu Xī’s commentary on the *Shìfǎ* states: "To serve a person based on their beauty. The *Shuōwén* states: "'Biànbì' (便嬖) means to be fondly loved. It is composed of the radical "woman" (女) and the phonetic "pì" (辟). The pronunciation of "bī" (篦) is *bì* (閇) with the *mí* (迷) rhyme. The pronunciation of "mí" (謎) is *mí* (迷) with the *fǎn* (反) rhyme.

*Dian* (顛) and *jue* (蹶) are both pronounced with the *yue* rhyme. *Fu* (鈇) and *zhi* (質): *fu* is pronounced as *fu yu*. The *Gongyang Zhuan* says, "I could not bear to subject him to the *fu-zhi* [punishment]," and it also says, "the crime of decapitation. The *Liji* states that feudal lords were granted *fu-yue* (battle-axes). Thus, it follows the meaning of execution. Regarding the "correct characters" (*zhengzi*) of ancient and modern times: *cuo* (莝) means to chop; it takes the radical *jin* (金) and the phonetic *fu* (夫), with *cuo* pronounced as *qi zuo*. *Fu* (鈇) and *zhi* (質): *fu* is pronounced as *fu yu*. *Kūcháng* (刳膓): The first character, *kǔ*, is pronounced with the initial *hú* and the final *fǎn*. Yě Wáng says it means "to hollow out its belly. The *Cāngjié piān* says it means "to slaughter. The *Shuōwén* says it means "to pare" (*tī*). It is composed of the radical "knife" (*dāo*) and the phonetic "kuā"; *kuā* is pronounced with the initial *qiū* and the final *yú*, while *tī* is pronounced with the initial *tīng*.

The *Zǔ* (meat-stand) is what is placed upon the *jī* (carving board); according to the *Fāngyán*, the *zǔ* is also called the *jī*. The *Zìshū* says: "The *zǔ* is for meat. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* says: "It is a vessel for holding things; it is composed of 'half-meat' (*bàn ròu*) atop the character *qiě*."

*Líng* (聆): Upper radical *fú* (佛) and lower *dǐng* (丁) reversed; the *Cāngjié piān* states that *líng* means "to listen. The meaning in the *Shuowén* is the same: it is formed from the radical *ěr* (耳) with the phonetic *lìng* (令). *Yòu* (仇): Lower radical *jiù* (舊) and *yóu* (尤) reversed;
Kǒng’s commentary on the *Shūjīng* states that "enmity" (*qiú*) is also "resentment" (*yuàn*). The *Shuowén* explains *chóu* (讎): it is formed from the radical *rén* (人) with the phonetic *jiǔ* (九).

2. Middle Volume. Regarding the character *qū* (袪) [in the phrase] "to remove outflows" (*qū yǒu lòu*): the *Kǎo Shēng* says *qū* means "to remove. The *Wénzì Diǎn* and the *Shuōwén* explain it as "to cut open its hem" (*pī zhǎn qí qū*). It is composed of the radical "clothing" (*yī*) and the phonetic "remove" (*qù*), with the latter pronounced in the departing tone (*qù shēng*).

"Buxun" (不眴): "Xuán" is pronounced as "jiàn" (反). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that "xun" (眴) denotes the appearance of looking. *Zhǐ*: Pronounced *shī* (upper radical *zhōu*). The *Kǎo Shēng* says it means "to rise" or "to rest. The *Shuōwén* says it means "a mountain," composed of the radical "water" and the phonetic "zhǐ";

it is also written as *chí*. *Cīn*: Pronounced *qīlín*. The *Máo Shī* says, "He gallops on and on, cīn-cīn. The *Shuōwén* says it describes the rapid pace of a horse's movement, composed of the radical "horse" and the phonetic "lí"; the pronunciation of "lí" is the same as above.
*Mùhuàn* (木槵) is the name of a type of wood; "huàn" is pronounced with the *guàn* (慣) and *kǎo* (考) finals.

*Bì* (辟) is pronounced with the *píng* (并) and *pì* (癖) initials; Du’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states it means "to manage" (*lǐ*), while the *Hànshī* says it means "to remove. According to the *Wenzi Dadian*, this is a word formed through semantic compounding (*huìyìzì*), composed of the radicals for door (*hù*), bitter/painful (*xīn*), and mouth (*kǒu*).

The character *tuí* (隤) is pronounced with the upper radical *duì* (隊) and the phonetic *léi* (雷); the *Kǎo Shēng* states that it means "to slant" (*xié*). Although the character *zhuì* (朝) is written with the radical for "grass" (*cǎo*), Mencius says, "The color of his living countenance was *zhuìrán*. The version in the *Lunwen* (Treatise on the Discourses) uses the character *fú*, which does not carry this meaning.

The character *yuàn* (苑) is pronounced with the *jiù* (尤) and *jiù* (救) finals; the *Kǎo Shēng* states that it means a garden (*yuán*). The *Cāngjié piān* (蒼頡篇) states it means "to scold" (*hē*). The *Wénzì diǎnshuō* (文字典說) explains that it is composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) with the phonetic component "xiào" (*xiào*).
*Meng* (懵): Upper radical *mo* (墨), reversed as *beng*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Meng means 'not clear' (*bù míng*). It is composed of the radical *xīn* (心) with *mèng* (瞢) as the phonetic;

the pronunciation of *mèng* is the same as above. *Jinbi juemo lun* (金錍決瞙論): One fascicle, compiled by Huilin. *Tan* (探): Upper radical *tan* (錔), reversed as *nan*. Regarding the character *huǎng* (怳): when searching for its upper radical, it is not found; this must be an error in the character.

The *Kǎo Shēng* (Examination of Sounds) states that *huǎng* means "suddenly startled" (*huǎnghù*). It refers to the loss of one's spiritual composure (*hún shī shǒu*), a state of madness. the glossary states that *mao* refers to the easy exchange of goods. It is correctly written as *sui* (󳅕); the poem says, "embracing cloth and *sui* silk. It is composed of the radical *bei* (貝) and the phonetic *mao* (卯). The *Lun* (論) uses *mao* (𧴵), which is a vulgar form.
"Xiàn" (陷): The upper radical is "water" (咸, pronounced xián); the phonetic component is "kǎo" (考). The gloss states it means "a pit" (穴) or "to collapse" (潰). The standard form is "xiàn" (陷);

the *Lùn* (論) version uses "xiàn" (陷), which is a common usage. "Lí" (罹): The lower radical is "li" (麗, pronounced lì). It causes one to gather and repair what has been degraded, invaded, or corrupted, returning it to its proper state. *Zēn* (矰): *jiǎo* (繳) is pronounced *shàng-zǐ-dēng-fǎn*. In the *Zhou Lǐ*, it states: "The *zēn* arrow is used for shooting with a bow. "Cái" (才): The upper radical is "人" (rén). According to the *Kǎo Shēng* (Examination of Sounds), it means "momentary" or "briefly. Its correct form is "Cái" (才); the form "Cǐ" (此) is a common vernacular usage.

*Wòwèn*: The first character is pronounced *wǔ gē* (five-go) and the second is pronounced *wèn*. "Wò" means error; "wèn" means disorder. It is composed of the radical "silk thread" (*mì*) with the phonetic element "wen. *Yuèzhì*:

The character 󱨯 (qí) is pronounced with the initial *shòu* and the final *zhù* (reversed);

Dōnggài (東槩) is a place name located in the regions of Wú and Yuè.
Regarding the character 槩 (gài): the *Zhìguǎn* (志概) reads it as gài; the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that "gài" means "to regulate" or "strategic planning," and it is composed of the radical 木 (wood).

Regarding 綰 (wǎn): the *Yùnyīng* (韻英) states it means "to tie"; the *Kǎoshēng* states it means "to knot. According to the *Shuōwén* (說文), it is composed of the radical 糸 (silk) with the phonetic 官 (guān). 睆 (huǎn) has the pronunciation guānhuàn with the third tone.

The character *cháo* (nest) in *wū cháo* (crow’s nest) is the same as *biāo* (branch). Niao’uo said: “The form of ‘nest’ (*xiàngxíng*) appears in the commentaries as *qiáo*;

it does not constitute a valid character. The character *qiàn* (to be satisfied) is pronounced *zhì qiān*. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states: “*Qiàn* means to be satiated (*yàn*). 2. Second Fascicle. "Xuánzǎo" (玄藻): The sound is *yùnyīng* (韻英). It means literary elegance (*wénzǎo*). It is derived from the radical "grass" (*cǎo*).
"Huìqióng" (慧瓊): The pronunciation is *kuíyíngfǎn* (葵營反). It refers to a beautiful jade. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it is a red jade; it is derived from the radical "jade" (*yù*).
Regarding "Meng Yǐ" (孟顗): the character *yǐ* (豈) is a phonetic component; it signifies tranquility and reverent respect, derived from the radical "head" (頁) with the phonetic "qǐ" (豈).
Regarding "zhòng" (󳇿): the upper part is pronounced "hé" (合), meaning to close.

Regarding "zhuàn yī" (襈衣): "shì juàn" (仕眷) is the pronunciation; the *Pīcāng* states it means "bordering" or "fringe. The *Shìmíng* states it refers to blue or crimson colors, derived from the radical "clothing" (衣) with the phonetic "xùn" (巽).

The character for *mǎi* (尾) is pronounced with the initial *kǎo* (考) and means "beautiful," "to exert oneself," or "to advance. It is a compound character formed from *wén* (文), *yǒu* (酉), and a simplified form of *cuàn* (爨), and is a transitive character (*zhuǎnzhù*).

The character for *pèi* (憊) has the upper part pronounced *lì* (力) with the final *zhuī* (追) and means "weak"; the lower part is pronounced *bài* (敗) with the initial *kǎo* (考), meaning "severe illness" or "exhaustion of strength. It is composed of *xīn* (心) and the phonetic *bèi* (備); the pronunciation of *bèi* is *bèi* (被).
"Ōuyáng shàng (the first character is pronounced *ǒu*, the second *hóu* with a reversed tone); *lǔ* is the surname of a high-ranking official.
*Xūxī* (the first character is pronounced *xū*, the second *xī*); the *Yùnyīng* states it means weeping in sorrow.
*Xié* (first character *huì*, second *guī* with a reversed tone); it means to lift up or take hold of."
"Hai" (駭) is pronounced with the *jiè* rhyme; it means a horse is startled. The lower radical of the character "fu" (服) is "zhou" (舟).

"Jiēn" (㞋) is pronounced with the same sounds as above. "Guī" (鮭) refers to rice; the upper radical is "hé" (核). It is used in the phrase "lù keng" (陸坈), where it says, "he provided him with guī-láng" (給其鮭粮); this is correct. Alternatively, it may be written as "xié" (膎), meaning dried fish.
*Guān* (not peeping): *guī* (1st tone), *fǎn* (rhyme); the *Jíxùn* states it means to see surreptitiously through a gate.
*Guānsàng* (forehead): *sāng* (1st tone), *lǎng* (rhyme); the *Kǎoshēng* states it means the brow. The *Wénzì jílüè* states it refers to the face; it follows the radical *sāng*.

The character *què* (確) is pronounced with the *qiāng* and *yuè* finals; its phonetic component is said to mean "solid. Neither the ancient nor the modern standard characters derive from the radical "stone" (*shí*). It is composed of the phonetic element "crane" (*hè*) in abbreviated form, with the pronunciation *jué*. Alternatively, it may be written as *kǎo* (碻), derived from the character "high" (*gāo*).
3. Third Fascicle. "Yanxue" (言謔): "Xue" (謔) is pronounced as *xiāo* (香約反). According to the *Erya*, it means "jesting and laughing.
"Dengchu" (燈燭): "Chu" (燭) is pronounced as *zhōng* (鍾辱反). It is composed of the radical "fire" (火) and the phonetic "shu" (屬). In some texts, it is written as "zhu" (󳆅), which is incorrect.

*Pǒháo xīzhì*: "Pǒ" is pronounced as in *pǔkǒu* (upper tone); "xī" is pronounced as in *húgāo* (second tone), though its phonetic transcription is *xīngyì* (upper tone). This is a common character; its correct form is composed of "wood" (*mù*) and "axe" (*jīn*), or sometimes "tablet" (*piàn*).
*Sūlà*: "Sū" is pronounced as in *lán dá* (upper tone). The *Yùnchuán* states it refers to unpolished rice. It is composed of "grain" (*mǐ*) and "fierce" (*lì*) for its sound.
"Tiègòu" (締構): the first character is pronounced *tǐng* (挺) with the *jì* (計) rhyme; the second character is pronounced *hòu* (后) with the *gōu* (鈎) rhyme.
"Niè bù zī" (涅不緇): the first character is pronounced *niè* (年) with the *jié* (結) rhyme;

the second character is pronounced *zǐ* (滓) with the *shī* (師) rhyme. "Mó bù lín" (磨不磷): the first character is pronounced *mó* (摩); it is derived from the character for "stone" (*shí*) with the radical *lì* (力) and the phonetic *zhèn* (陣). Confucius’s commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* states that "lín" means "thin. Because white cannot be dyed black, it is said that "it is not blackened by mud" (*niè bù zī*).

"Hun-ai" (氳靄): the upper character is pronounced *yù* (same as in "cloud") and the lower is pronounced *shuāi* (same as in "canopy"). It describes the appearance of smoke and mist as clouds hang down and spread.
Gaozu's name is Yù (毓), which is pronounced *yù* (same as in "nurture"). The *Yùnquán* states that "Yù" is composed of the radical "child" (*zhì*) with the phonetic element "mǔ" and "lǚ."
4. Fourth Fascicle. Regarding *fendai* (粉黛): Da Yun Ying states that *dai* is a dark blue-green color; it is used by women to paint their eyebrows, or it may be black.
*Hànshuì* (鼾睡): "Hàn" (上) is pronounced *hán* (寒); "àn" (岸) is pronounced *fǎn* (反).
It refers to the sound of sleeping. *Chànshì* (覘視): "Chàn" (覘) is pronounced *chì* (勅) with the tone *yàn* (燄). The *Kǎośēng* (考聲) states it means "to scout. It also means "to look furtively.

This is a compound character (*huìzì*). *Yèzòng* (葉粽): "Yè" (葉) is pronounced *jié* (閻) with the tone *jiē* (接); it means "gourd leaf. "Zòng" (粽) has the phonetic *zǒng* (總). People of Shǔ pronounce it with a departing tone. "Zòngzi" (粽子) is also a vulgar form. The correct orthography is composed of "mǐ" (米, rice) and "zūn" (㚇), forming "zòng" (糉). This is the "zòngzi" (粽子) favored by the people of Chǔ on the fifth day of the fifth month.

*Shen* (𣶒): The upper character is pronounced *huìyuán* (恚緣); the rhyme dictionary (*Yùnyuán*) explains it as "profound. The lower character is pronounced *chāigé* (柴格); the rhyme dictionary (*Yùnyīng*) states it means "deep and difficult to know.
It is composed of the radical *guǐ* (𦣞) and the phonetic *guì* (貴). *Bù xiào* (不斅): Pronounced *xiáojiào* (爻教); the rhyme dictionary (*Yùnyīng*) states that *xiào* means "to learn."

Yusheng (雩塖): The first character is pronounced *yú* and the second *shèng*. Yusheng is the name of a small mountain located in Qiánzhōu; it has already been fully described in the fourth fascicle of the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*. It is also the name of a county. In the aforementioned biography, the characters are written as *Yǎngshèng* (嶀嵊), which are not common vulgar characters.

In the *Guānxīn Lùn* (Treatise on Contemplating the Mind), composed by the Great Master Shenxiu, the term "jiānjiān" (涓涓) is glossed with the phonetic "juéyuán" (決緣). Yuè Wang states that "jiānjiān" refers to a small stream. This is consistent with the *Shuōyuàn*, which says: "If a trickle is not dammed up, it will eventually become a river and a great stream. Both characters are radicals for water.

Regarding "bōtāo" (波濤): according to the *Cangjie pian*, "tāo" means a great wave; Xu Shuzhong’s commentary on the *Huainanzi* states that when tidal waters surge upward and shift, it is called "tāo. It is composed of the radical "water" (水) and the phonetic "shòu" (壽).

*Xiānxīng* (羶腥): The upper character is pronounced *shàng* with the rhyme *rán* (然); the *Yùnyīng* (韻英) states it refers to the odor of sheep and goats. The lower character is pronounced *xīng* (星); the *Jíxùn* (集訓) notes it refers to the foul smell of fish.

It is also written as *shèng* (勝). *Kēngfū* (糠麩): The upper character is pronounced *kě* with the rhyme *láng* (郎); the *Zìshū* (字書) states it is the husk of grain. The lower character is pronounced *fū* (敷); the *Jíxùn* (集訓) explains that grinding wheat into fine powder and removing the small bran is called *fū*; it is the skin of the wheat.
"Zhù" (鑄) is pronounced with the initial *zhū* and the final *fǎn* (反) as *kǎo* (考); it means to melt and cast. Gu Yewang says that to fashion a vessel from molten copper is called "casting.

"Zòu" (驟) has the correct radical of "walk" (走) above; its lower part is pronounced with the initial *chóu* and the final *shòu* (瘦) as *sòu*; it means a collection or number. The *Jixùn* (集訓) states that the rapid pace of a horse is a "light trot," and it takes the radical of "horse" (馬) with the phonetic component of "collect" (聚).

"Hua" (畫) is pronounced with the initial *lù* and the final rhyme *shàng* (華罵反); it is used here by borrowing its pronunciation, though its original pronunciation is *huò*. It is a compound character (*huìyì zì*) composed of "yù" (聿)—meaning a writing brush—and "tián" (田)—meaning a field—with a single stroke ("yī") representing a boundary. The lower part, pronounced *lóng zhú* (龍燭反), means "color"; it is a phonetic-semantic compound (*xíngshēng zì*) derived from the appearance of minerals within stone.

*Qunyi lun* (Treatise on the Multitude of Doubts), seven fascicles; missing from the canon; no phonetic glosses available. *Shiyi lun* (Treatise on the Ten Doubts), one fascicle; composed by Huilin. Regarding the character for "feather" (*yù*) in the title *Yuhé*: the upper part is a pictograph; the lower part is pronounced *héng* with the *gè* radical. According to the *Ěrǎ pǐ*, the root of a feather is called *hè*. The *Shuowén* states that *hè* is the base of a feather, formed with the radical for "feather" and the phonetic *lì*.
*Píng* (膨): the first character is pronounced *pǔ* (朴) with the *bāng* (邦) rhyme;

the second character is pronounced *zhāng* (張) with the *liàng* (亮) rhyme. *Lànhuài* (爛壞): the first character is pronounced *lángdàn* (郎旦). "From fire" (*huìguài* [懷怪]) means to break down from within; that which breaks apart on its own is called "ruined" (*huài*).

A complete record of the ritual for bathing the Buddha image in the Western Regions, compiled by Huìlín, including phonetic annotations: Copper, tin, brass, and bronze: "copper" refers to red copper and white copper; "tin" is pronounced *là* (拉), referring to white tin; "lead" and "solder" (*xiān-xī*); "brass" is pronounced *tōu* (偷); "stone" (*shí* [石]) refers to bell-metal (*chuīyú jīn* [吹於金]), all of which are used to make vessels.

*Qing* (磬): [The character] is read as *lu hé* (魯和) in the upper part; it is a sea-shell (*hải yíng*). It is blown to produce a ritual sound for making offerings. *Qing* (磬): [The character] is read as *qīng jìng* (輕徑); it is a type of bell, made either of bronze or stone, used to capture the sound.
"Ūn" (pronounced with the *wēn* and *kùn* finals) means to submerge one's head in water.
"Qiáo" (pronounced with the *qī* and *yáo* finals) means to raise one's head.

"Tián" (the first character is pronounced with the *dìng* and *yán* finals) means sweet; "cuì" (the second character is pronounced with the *quán* and *suì* finals, with "yue" as the radical and "wei" as the phonetic) means crisp.
"Naked-bodied" (nǜtǐ) means to expose one's body;
"small ladle" (xiǎo sháo) refers to a type of vessel with a handle;
"basin" (yú) and its like (zhōu) refer to similar items.

Regarding the method for confessing transgressions (*āpatti-pratideśanā-vidhi*): "Niè" (齧) means to bite slightly; it is composed of the radical "teeth" (*dantai*) and the phonetic "kuài" (㓞), pronounced *qiān* (慳) with the final tone.
"Qǐngkài" (謦欬) is read as *qīngyǐng* (上) and *kāi'ài* (下); the *Yùnyīng* (韻英) states that it refers to the sound of breath passing through the throat.
In the Sanskrit text, the word *āvartika* explains itself: the sound *varti* is pronounced as *bi*.
*Vaitālika* is pronounced with the sound *qi*.
*Chappatika*—the character *chao* is pronounced as *shi*; *patika* refers to sandals or shoes.
The upper character in "筒槽" (tǒng cáo) has the same pronunciation as the lower character in "曹" (cáo).

The character "塊" (kuài) is pronounced with the pinyin *kuǎi* (with the *guǎi* rhyme). The upper character in "塼板" (zhuān bǎn) has the same pronunciation as the lower character in "專" (zhuān), and the lower character is pronounced with the pinyin *jiǎn* (with the *jiǎn* rhyme).

The Essential Method for Using the Three Kinds of Water. Regarding "filtering" (lǜ): the upper character is pronounced *lù* and the lower is pronounced *lù*. Regarding "cauldron" (*qiāng*): the radical is *chǔ* (read as *gēng*);

the commentary on the sounds states it is a type of tripod, though the vernacular form is written as *dēng*. The lower character is read as *chángyào*; this is a vernacular character. The archaic and correct form is simply *sháo*, which is a pictograph representing its shape.
The character for "burden" (fù) has the first radical *fu* (武) and the second radical *dān-làn* (躭濫). It follows the hand radical.

Regarding the "Dharma for Protecting Life and Releasing Creatures": the character for "insects" (*fùn chóng*) has the first phonetic *kūn* (昆) and the second phonetic *zhú-róng* (逐融); it is written as *kūn* in the scriptures, but this is a vulgar character and incorrect.
The character *tóng* (銅) has the phonetic *niǔ* (鈕) with the radical *zhǒu* (肘) reversed.

*Tái* (擡) has the upper part pronounced as *tái* (臺); it means to lift an object with the hand, while the lower part is pronounced *xì* (奚) or *jì* (計). It can be used for carrying or holding by the hand; it is composed of the radical *mì* (糸) and the element *jiǎo* (󱫛).

The two works encompass ancient teachings and provide phonetic glosses;

they extract and compile passages from Sanskrit scriptures until they are richly expanded. They examine and correct sounds and meanings, and scrutinize the forms of characters, for the most part following the traditional expositions left by the masters of the sūtras during the Han and Wei dynasties.
Furthermore, it draws extensively from various scripts dating back to the Tang dynasty and earlier;
its elegant phrasing unfolds like spreading clouds, and its subtle meanings are threaded together with precision—
resplendent and brilliant!
Truly, there is much here worthy of admiration.
Ling’s work not only synthesizes the phonetic glosses of the four masters Xuan Ying, Hui Yuan, Kui Ji, and Master Yun,
but was also personally authorized by the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra, who verified its Sanskrit transliterations and meanings.
It reaches upward to the regions of Qin and Wei and extends downward to the eras of Sui and Tang;
even the dialects, literature, and geography of the Western lands are recorded therein, neither omitting nor exaggerating anything.
It encompasses all existence, wherein phenomena and principle are mutually unimpeded;
truly, there is nothing beautiful that it does not contain.
